real_life_example.event: The Nabataeans made Petra, in an arid region between the Red Sea and the Dead Sea, the rock-cut capital of their kingdom and a major caravan centre. They built channels, tunnels, diversion dams and a vast network of cisterns and reservoirs that controlled and conserved the seasonal rains. This water system allowed a large population to live in an essentially arid area.
real_life_example.explanation: Petra shows a desert city whose food, drink and very existence depended on catching rain that fell only in one season.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says rain both produces the food people eat and is itself their drink, and Petra's cisterns and channels kept the stored rain serving the city in both ways.

tamil:
விண்இன்று பொய்ப்பின் விரிநீர் வியனுலகத்து
உள்நின்று உடற்றும் பசி.
transliteration:
Vin indru poyppin virineer viyanulagaththu,
Ul nindru udatrum pasi.
meaning: If the sky fails to send rain, hunger will settle inside this wide world circled by the sea and make every living thing suffer.
elementary: Imagine standing right next to a swimming pool while you are terribly thirsty — all that water, and not a drop you can drink. This kural says the world is surrounded by ocean, but if rain stops falling, people will still go hungry, and hunger will hurt from the inside.
university: The verb பொய்ப்பின் (poyppin) literally means "if it lies" — Valluvar personifies the sky as a party that can break faith, which is why English renderings often speak of clouds that "deceive." The phrase விரிநீர் வியனுலகம் (virineer viyanulagam), "the broad world of spreading waters," sets up a deliberate irony: a planet ringed by ocean can still starve, because salt sea is not rain. உடற்றும் (udatrum) is a strong verb of tormenting or harrying, and உள்நின்று (ul nindru, "standing within") places the affliction inside the body rather than outside it. The couplet is frequently cited in modern Tamil discussion of drought and food security precisely because it distinguishes water-in-general from usable fresh water.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Rāmāyaṇa, the kingdom of Anga under King Romapada suffers a devastating drought and famine; on the advice of his counsellors the king brings the young ascetic Rishyasringa into the land, and with his arrival the rains return and the famine ends.
hinduism.explanation: The episode treats a failed monsoon as a national emergency whose remedy is sought through a holy person, and it opens the Rāmāyaṇa's account of Dasharatha's sacrifice.
hinduism.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that when the sky fails, hunger becomes the defining condition of an entire kingdom.

christianity.quote_or_event: "And Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead, said unto Ahab, As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word."
christianity.explanation: Elijah announces a multi-year drought as judgement on Ahab; the narrative that follows describes a severe famine gripping Samaria until the rains return.
christianity.tie_back: It is the same sequence the Kural compresses into two lines: the sky withholds, and hunger takes hold of the land.

islam.quote_or_event: "Say, 'Have you considered: if your water was to become sunken [into the earth], then who could bring you flowing water?'"
islam.explanation: The Qur'an closes Surah al-Mulk with a challenge: human beings have no fallback if the water that sustains them simply disappears.
islam.tie_back: Both verses press the reader to imagine the world's water failing and to recognise that nothing human can substitute for it.

judaism.quote_or_event: "And also I have withholden the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest … So two or three cities wandered unto one city, to drink water; but they were not satisfied: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD."
judaism.explanation: Amos describes a partial drought — rain on one town, none on the next — and the desperate migration of thirsty, hungry populations that followed.
judaism.tie_back: It gives concrete social texture to the Kural's abstract claim that a failed sky means hunger settling into a whole land.

buddhism.quote_or_event: According to the Pali commentarial tradition, the city of Vesālī was struck by drought, which brought famine, then corpses in the streets, then plague; the Buddha was invited, walked the city reciting the Ratana Sutta, and a great rain fell that washed the city clean and ended the crisis.
buddhism.explanation: The story is the traditional origin narrative for one of Theravada Buddhism's most widely chanted protective discourses.
buddhism.tie_back: Its causal order is the Kural's own: rain fails first, and hunger and suffering follow from that failure.
buddhism.source: Ratana Sutta (Sn 2.1 / Khp 6) and its commentarial background narrative on the famine at Vesālī

jainism.quote_or_event: Digambara tradition holds that a twelve-year famine in north India drove the teacher Bhadrabahu to lead an exodus of monks south to Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, joined, the tradition says, by Chandragupta Maurya, the first Mauryan king, who had become a Jain monk.
jainism.explanation: In Digambara memory a famine scattered the whole monastic community and moved Jainism south. Some scholars treat the migration as the start of the Digambara–Svetambara split, and Svetambara accounts instead send Bhadrabahu to Nepal.
jainism.tie_back: It is a Jain memory of just what the Kural warns: when the rains fail, hunger seizes the land and overturns even the life of a religious order.
jainism.source: Bhadrabahu–Chandragupta famine-migration tradition (Digambara), as summarised in Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Bhadrabahu I'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The hunger of the hungry is not appeased, even by piling up loads of worldly goods.”
sikhism.explanation: In the opening stanza of Japji, Guru Nanak says that heaping up material goods never satisfies hunger. The deeper hunger is only met by obeying God's hukam (will).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures a world ringed by oceans that still starves without rain. Japji likewise says that surrounding yourself with plenty does not end hunger.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "Often even a whole city suffers for a bad man who sins and devises presumptuous deeds, and the son of Cronos lays great trouble upon the people, famine and plague together, so that the men perish away, and their women do not bear children, and their houses become few"
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that Zeus punishes collective injustice with collective calamity, and famine heads his list of instruments.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural's picture of hunger afflicting an entire population from within, though Hesiod traces the cause to human wrongdoing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "Famine seems to be the last, the most dreadful resource of nature."
philosophy.explanation: Malthus argues that when milder checks on population fail, hunger is the ultimate and most terrible constraint that reasserts the limits of the earth's productivity.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts treat hunger as the inescapable consequence when the land's capacity to produce food gives out.
philosophy.source: Thomas Robert Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798), Chapter VII

real_life_example.event_title: The North China Famine
real_life_example.place: Shandong, Shanxi, Henan, Zhili and Shaanxi provinces, China
real_life_example.event: A long drought struck large parts of northern China from 1876, spreading from Shandong westward through Shanxi, Henan and beyond. Harvests failed and famine reached its peak in Shanxi and Henan in 1878; official accounts stated that Shanxi lost about half of its population. Estimates of the total death toll range from about nine to thirteen million people.
real_life_example.explanation: It was one of the deadliest famines of the 19th century, and it was triggered by rains that simply did not come.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that if the sky breaks faith and withholds rain, hunger will take up residence in the wide world, and the North China Famine is that warning carried out on a vast scale.

tamil:
ஏரின் உழாஅர் உழவர் புயல்என்னும்
வாரி வளங்குன்றிக் கால்.
transliteration:
Erin uzhaaar uzhavar puyal ennum,
Vaari valam kundrik kaal.
meaning: When rain, the world’s great source of riches, does not fall enough, even farmers will stop ploughing their fields.
elementary: A bicycle is useless if the tyres have no air in them; you can own it, but you cannot ride it. This kural says a farmer's plough is like that. However strong the farmer is, if the rain does not come, the plough just sits there.
university: The economic vocabulary here is deliberate: வாரி (vaari) is a revenue term, the yield or income of a realm, so Valluvar literally calls rain the kingdom's principal income stream — a framing that anticipates the Poruṭpāl's treatment of statecraft and chapter 104 on உழவு (agriculture). உழாஅர் (uzhaaar, "they do not plough") carries an அளபெடை, a metrical elongation that lends the line a note of weary finality. புயல் (puyal) denotes rain in its abundant, gusting monsoon form rather than a drizzle. The couplet's force lies in its choice of the farmer as subject: of all people the ploughman is the most industrious, and if even he downs tools, no amount of human effort can substitute for the sky.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya's Arthaśāstra instructs the state's superintendent of agriculture to measure annual rainfall in droṇas for each type of terrain — dry, wet and marshy country — and to decide which crops may be sown on the basis of how much rain has actually fallen.
hinduism.explanation: The treatise makes rainfall data an explicit input to agricultural planning and revenue forecasting for the realm.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the administrative version of this Kural: below a certain rainfall the ploughing simply does not happen.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book II, Chapter 24 (Shamasastry translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: "Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain."
christianity.explanation: James takes the farmer as the model of patience precisely because the farmer's work is hostage to rain he cannot command.
christianity.tie_back: Both verses make the farmer's dependence on rainfall the definitive example of human effort waiting on the sky.

islam.quote_or_event: "And have you seen that [seed] which you sow? Is it you who makes it grow, or are We the grower?"
islam.explanation: The Qur'an confronts the farmer with the limits of his own agency: he can sow, but the growth is not in his hands.
islam.tie_back: It makes the Kural's point from the other direction — ploughing and sowing are worthless unless a power beyond the farmer supplies the water.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah prescribes an escalating public response when the winter rains fail: after successive rounds of communal fasts pass unanswered, Jews are to cut back on business, on building and planting, on betrothals and weddings, and on greetings between neighbours.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic law treats a failed rainy season as grounds for suspending ordinary economic activity, including planting itself.
judaism.tie_back: It legislates exactly what the Kural observes — when the rain does not come, the planting stops.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "Conviction is my seed, / austerity my rain, / discernment my yoke & plow, / conscience my pole, / mind my yoke-tie, / mindfulness my plowshare & goad."
buddhism.explanation: Challenged by the brahmin farmer Kasi Bharadvaja to justify eating without ploughing, the Buddha answers by mapping each part of the plough team onto a quality of spiritual practice.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha's metaphor concedes the Kural's literal premise — no rain, no ploughing — which is exactly why rain can stand for the indispensable element in any cultivation.
buddhism.source: Kasi Bhāradvāja Sutta, Sutta Nipāta 1.4 (Thanissaro Bhikkhu translation)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The husbandmen throw the corn on high ground and on low ground, hoping (for a return). For the like motive give unto me; I may be the field which may produce merit (as the return for your benevolence).”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk Harikesha, refused alms at a Brahmin sacrifice, appeals to the farmer's hope of a harvest to show that giving to a self-controlled ascetic is a field that yields merit.
jainism.tie_back: It draws on the same farming life the Kural describes, in which ploughing and sowing are acts of hope in a return, though the Jain verse uses farming as a metaphor rather than speaking of drought.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make your mind the farmer, good deeds the farm, modesty the water, and your body the field. Let the Lord’s Name be the seed, contentment the plow, and your humble dress the fence.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak, who spent his last years farming at Kartarpur, uses the farmer's whole round of work as a picture of the spiritual life. Water is one of its essential inputs.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures the ploughman as the most hard-working of people, whose labour stops without rain. Guru Nanak builds a spiritual farm in which water is a necessary part.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "Mark, when you hear the voice of the crane who cries year by year from the clouds above, for she gives the signal for ploughing and shows the season of rainy winter; but she vexes the heart of the man who has no oxen."
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's farming calendar ties the start of ploughing to the arrival of the rainy season, announced by migrating cranes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both poets treat ploughing as an activity that begins only when the rains arrive and is meaningless without them.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "A prayer of the Athenians: Rain, rain, O dear Zeus, down on the ploughed fields of the Athenians and on the plains."
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius cites this old Athenian prayer as his model of how one should pray at all — simply, nobly, and for the one thing the fields actually need.
philosophy.tie_back: It puts the Kural's insight in the mouth of a whole city: the ploughed field is finished work until rain falls on it.

real_life_example.event_title: The Dust Bowl drives farmers off the Great Plains
real_life_example.event: Severe drought struck the southern Great Plains in the 1930s, and crops began failing from 1931. Without deep-rooted prairie grasses to hold the over-ploughed soil, it blew away in great dust storms. With no way to make a living, many farm families abandoned their land, and hundreds of thousands of people left the region.
real_life_example.explanation: The Dust Bowl showed how quickly a farming society collapses when the rain on which its ploughing depends fails.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when rain, the great source of a land's yield, fails, even farmers stop driving the plough, and the Dust Bowl saw farm families abandon their fields entirely.

tamil:
கெடுப்பதூஉம் கெட்டார்க்குச் சார்வாய்மற் றாங்கே
எடுப்பதூஉம் எல்லாம் மழை.
transliteration:
Keduppadhoum kettaarkkuch chaarvaai matraange,
Eduppadhoum ellaam mazhai.
meaning: Rain can hurt people by not falling. And when it falls again, that same rain lifts those people back up. Rain does it all.
elementary: Fire can burn your hand, and fire can also cook your dinner — the same thing can hurt you or help you. This kural says rain is like that: too little or too much can wreck everything, and then the right rain at the right time puts it all back together.
university: The couplet is built on a tight antithesis — கெடுப்பது ("that which destroys") against எடுப்பது ("that which lifts up") — each carrying the அளபெடை elongation -தூஉம் that gives the line its rocking, pendulum rhythm. Commentators divide on the mechanism of ruin: Parimelazhagar reads கெடுப்பது as rain destroying by withholding itself, while modern paraphrasts such as Kalaignar Karunanidhi allow the destructive flood as well, and both readings are defensible from the Tamil. Strikingly, Valluvar assigns the double agency to rain itself rather than to a god who sends it, and the closing எல்லாம் ("all of it") refuses to split the credit. The verse is a favourite of Tamil ecological writing because it treats the same natural force as both hazard and remedy without moralising either face.

hinduism.quote_or_event: "O Arjuna, I control heat, the rain and the drought. I am immortality, and I am also death personified. Both being and nonbeing are in Me."
hinduism.explanation: Krishna claims both the withholding and the sending of rain as his own act, and in the same breath claims both deathlessness and death.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural's double agency exactly — the identical power that destroys by withholding also restores by pouring.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 9.19 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, 1972)

christianity.quote_or_event: "He causeth it to come, whether for correction, or for his land, or for mercy."
christianity.explanation: Elihu, describing the clouds, says the same rain may arrive as chastisement, as ordinary provision for the land, or as sheer mercy.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim that rain both ruins and raises, condensed into a single verse.

islam.quote_or_event: During a drought a man interrupted the Friday sermon to say that livestock were dying and the roads cut off, and asked the Prophet to pray for rain; rain then fell for a week until people returned asking him to pray for it to stop, and he said, in effect, around us and not upon us — whereupon the clouds broke apart over Medina.
islam.explanation: This well-known hadith of the istisqā (rain-seeking prayer) records a community harmed first by too little rain and then by too much within a single week.
islam.tie_back: It is a lived instance of the Kural's paradox: rain ruins and rain restores, and the difference is only measure and timing.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 1013–1014 (Book of Istisqā), narrated by Anas ibn Malik

judaism.quote_or_event: Honi the Circle-Drawer, asked to pray for rain in a drought, drew a circle and refused to leave it until rain fell. Drops came, and he objected that he had asked for more; a violent, destructive downpour followed, and he objected again; only then did rain of goodwill and blessing fall.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah preserves this story as a study in the difference between rain that is too little, rain that is ruinous, and rain that is a blessing.
judaism.tie_back: It stages the Kural's whole couplet as a narrative — the same rain destroying and then lifting up.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "Just as rain seeps into a poorly roofed house, lust seeps into an undeveloped mind. Just as rain doesn't seep into a well roofed house, lust doesn't seep into a well developed mind."
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pairs two verses in which the identical rain either penetrates and damages or is harmlessly shed, depending entirely on the condition of what receives it.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's structure of one rain producing opposite outcomes, though here the rain is harmful in both halves.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Then the clouds will be without water. Clouds of acid and clouds of vinegar, clouds of poison, fire, and lightning will rain what is similar to themselves.”
jainism.explanation: Jain cosmology pictures the worst age ending with destructive rains that ruin fields, forests, and grass, after which the five nourishing clouds of the next age bring the earth back to life.
jainism.tie_back: This two-sided picture of rain that first lays the world waste and then raises it again closely mirrors the Kural's claim that rain both ruins and restores.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book X (Mahaviracharitra), ch. XIII, 'The sixth spoke' (tr. Helen M. Johnson)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Some sing that He fashions the body, and then again reduces it to dust. Some sing that He takes life away, and then again restores it.”
sikhism.explanation: Japji lists the ways people praise God: as the one who both destroys and restores, who takes life away and gives it back.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural gives rain this double power to ruin and to raise up again. Sikh scripture gives the same double power to God working through hukam.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 3, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Angered by human wickedness, Zeus unleashes unending rain and floods the world, drowning the whole race except Deucalion and Pyrrha; when the waters recede the pair are told to throw the bones of their mother behind them, and the stones they cast become a new human race.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's telling makes the same downpour the instrument of annihilation and the prelude to humanity's re-founding.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's couplet in mythic form: rain destroys utterly, and then the destroyed are raised up again.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.253–415 (the flood of Deucalion and Pyrrha)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Philosophy, speaking in the voice of Fortune, tells Boethius that turning her wheel is simply what she is: she delights in raising the lowest to the top and bringing the highest down, and no one who steps onto the wheel may complain when it comes round.
philosophy.explanation: The Consolation uses the wheel to argue that a single impersonal power is responsible for both elevation and ruin, and that expecting only its upward motion is a category error.
philosophy.tie_back: It matches the Kural's insistence that one and the same force is the destroyer and the lifter-up — "all of it."
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose 2 (Fortune's wheel)

real_life_example.event_title: Egypt completes the Aswan High Dam
real_life_example.event: After about eleven years of construction, the Aswan High Dam across the Nile was completed in 1970. Its main purpose was to store enough water in its reservoir, Lake Nasser, to protect Egypt from years when the Nile flood was too high or too low. The dam ended the old cycle of damaging floods and droughts along the Egyptian Nile.
real_life_example.explanation: Egypt built one of the world's largest dams because the same seasonal waters that made its farmland fertile could also ruin it, by flooding or by failing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says rain both ruins people and raises them up again, and the Aswan High Dam was built precisely to manage the waters that had long done both to Egypt.

tamil:
விசும்பின் துளிவீழின் அல்லால்மற் றாங்கே
பசும்புல் தலைகாண்பு அரிது.
transliteration:
Visumbin thulivizhin allaal matraange,
Pasumpul thalaikaanbu aridhu.
meaning: Unless rain falls from the sky, you will hardly see even the tip of a blade of green grass on the earth.
elementary: Put a seed in a pot of soil and give it no water at all. Nothing happens — not even a tiny green shoot. This kural says that is what the whole world would look like without rain: not one blade of grass anywhere.
university: விசும்பு (visumbu) is the open expanse of sky rather than the cloud, so the drop is imagined falling from the whole heavens at once. The argument is a fortiori and depends on Tamil biological classification: பசும்புல் (pasumpul), green grass, is the standard example of an ஓரறிவு உயிர் — a one-sense living being, the humblest grade of life in the Tamil-Jain scheme — so if even that cannot appear, nothing above it can. தலை here means the tip or head of the blade, sharpening the claim from "no grass" to "not even the tip of grass." The verse's spare, almost photographic minimalism has made it one of the most quoted lines of the chapter in Tamil environmental writing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: "Forth burst the winds, down come the lightning-flashes: the plants shoot up, the realm of light is streaming. Food springs abundant for all living creatures, what time Parjanya quickens earth with moisture."
hinduism.explanation: The Rigveda's hymn to Parjanya, god of the rain-cloud, describes plants springing up the moment the storm breaks and moisture reaches the soil.
hinduism.tie_back: It states the positive form of the Kural's negative claim: the sprouting of plants begins exactly when the drops fall.

christianity.quote_or_event: "And every plant of the field before it was in the earth, and every herb of the field before it grew: for the LORD God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was not a man to till the ground."
christianity.explanation: Genesis explains the pre-vegetative state of the newly made world by a single fact: it had not yet rained.
christianity.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural's proposition — no drops from above, therefore no green thing below.

islam.quote_or_event: "And you see the earth barren, but when We send down upon it rain, it quivers and swells and grows [something] of every beautiful kind."
islam.explanation: The Qur'an contrasts the visibly dead, barren ground with the same ground stirring into growth the moment rain reaches it.
islam.tie_back: Both verses make the visible presence or absence of green growth the direct index of whether rain has fallen.

judaism.quote_or_event: "There is not a single blade of grass that does not have a constellation in the firmament that strikes it and says to it: 'Grow.'"
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi's midrash makes the growth of every individual blade of grass depend on a specific influence descending from the heavens.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural it insists that even the humblest blade of grass is entirely dependent on something coming down from the sky.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "cows graze on the lush meadow grass … Right then a vast cloud rained forth, soaking the uplands and valleys."
buddhism.explanation: In the Dhaniya Sutta a wealthy cattleman and the Buddha trade verses each ending "so rain forth, heavens, if you wish," and at the close a great cloud does exactly that, soaking the grazing land the herdsman depends on.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's chain of rain to green pasture, though the sutta's real interest is in what makes a person ready for the rain.
buddhism.source: Dhaniya Sutta, Sutta Nipāta 1.2 (Bhikkhu Sujato translation)

jainism.quote_or_event: “'For in the rainy season living beings, grass, seeds, mildew, and sprouts frequently come forth.'”
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra's rules for the monsoon retreat tell monks to inspect the ground with special care in the rains, because that is when grass and countless small lives spring up everywhere.
jainism.tie_back: It confirms from the Jain side the Kural's observation that grass appears only when rain falls, and for Jains each such blade is itself a living, one-sensed soul to be protected.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis §55 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “First, there is life in the water, by which everything else is made green.”
sikhism.explanation: Arguing against ideas of ritual impurity, Guru Nanak notes that life begins in water and that water is what turns everything green.
sikhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point in one line: without water from the sky, not even a blade of grass turns green.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 472, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "a most dreadful and cruel year for mankind over the all-nourishing earth: the ground would not make the seed sprout, for rich-crowned Demeter kept it hid"
greek_mythology.explanation: Grieving for Persephone, Demeter suspends the earth's fertility entirely, so that sown seed simply does not come up.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's image of an earth on which not even a green shoot can be seen.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter, lines 305–309 (Evelyn-White translation)

philosophy.quote_or_event: "Lo, the rains perish which Ether-father throws / Down to the bosom of Earth-mother; but then / Upsprings the shining grain, and boughs are green / Amid the trees, and trees themselves wax big / And lade themselves with fruits"
philosophy.explanation: Lucretius uses rainfall to demonstrate his atomist thesis that nothing is annihilated: the rain vanishes, but reappears transformed as crops and foliage.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives the Kural's claim a physical mechanism — the green blade is literally the rain in another form.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.250–254 (W. E. Leonard translation, 1916)

real_life_example.event_title: The Sahel drought
real_life_example.place: West African Sahel (including Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso and Chad)
real_life_example.event: From 1968 the rains in the West African Sahel deteriorated, and only in the 1974 rainy season did near-normal conditions return. The long drought led to the near-total failure of crops and the loss of an estimated 50 to 70 percent of cattle, with the pastoral grazing zones of the northern Sahel hit hardest. Large numbers of people died or were displaced by the resulting food shortages.
real_life_example.explanation: When the rains failed, the grasslands that supported herds across the Sahel withered, and a whole pastoral way of life collapsed with them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that without drops from the sky not even the tip of a blade of grass will be seen, and the Sahel's dying pastures showed the humblest green life vanishing first.

tamil:
நெடுங்கடலும் தன்நீர்மை குன்றும் தடிந்தெழிலி
தான்நல்கா தாகி விடின்.
transliteration:
Nedungadalum than neermai kundrum thadinthezhili,
Thaan nalkaadhaagi vidin.
meaning: Even the huge sea will lose its fullness if the clouds, which draw water up from it, stop giving that water back as rain.
elementary: Imagine a piggy bank you keep taking coins out of but never put any coins back into. Sooner or later it is empty. This kural says even the huge ocean is like that piggy bank: the clouds take water from it, and if they never return it as rain, even the sea runs low.
university: எழிலி (ezhili) is the rain-cloud and தடிந்து means "having cut off, drawn up," so the line describes evaporation as an act of extraction from the sea. The phrase தன் நீர்மை (than neermai) is a fine pun: நீர்மை means both "wateriness, fullness of water" and "one's own proper nature or quality," so the sea loses its water and its character at once. What makes the couplet remarkable is that it states a closed evaporation-and-precipitation cycle — cloud takes from ocean, must return to ocean — many centuries before that cycle was formalised in European science. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward also read a social allegory here, developed vigorously by Kalaignar Karunanidhi: those who rise out of a community and do not give back diminish the very source that raised them.

hinduism.quote_or_event: "Uniform, with the passing days, this water mounts and fails again. The tempest-clouds give life to earth, and fires re-animate the heaven."
hinduism.explanation: This riddle-verse from the Rigveda's great cosmological hymn describes water as a single quantity that rises and descends in an unbroken rhythm.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts describe rain as the return leg of a circuit rather than a one-way gift.

christianity.quote_or_event: "For he maketh small the drops of water: they pour down rain according to the vapour thereof: which the clouds do drop and distil upon man abundantly."
christianity.explanation: Elihu describes rain as vapour drawn up and then condensed back into drops — an explicit two-stage account of the water cycle.
christianity.tie_back: It supplies the mechanism the Kural relies on: the cloud must give back what it first drew up.

islam.quote_or_event: "And We have sent down rain from the sky in a measured amount and settled it in the earth. And indeed, We are Able to take it away."
islam.explanation: The verse presents rainfall as a measured quantity deposited in the earth, with the explicit reminder that the same power can withdraw it.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural's accounting sense of water as a finite stock that can be drawn down as well as replenished.

judaism.quote_or_event: "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again."
judaism.explanation: Kohelet observes the circulation of water between sea and river as his opening example of nature's endless, unaccumulating repetition.
judaism.tie_back: It describes the same closed circuit the Kural describes, viewed from the rivers' side rather than the cloud's.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "Mendicants, when the ocean surges it makes the rivers surge. When the rivers surge they make the streams surge. When the streams surge they make the lakes surge … When the ocean recedes it makes the rivers recede."
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the linked rise and fall of ocean, rivers, streams and ponds as an image for how the twelve links of dependent origination swell and subside together.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's picture of ocean and the waters above it as one interdependent system that rises or falls as a whole.
buddhism.source: Upayanti Sutta, Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.69 (Bhikkhu Sujato translation)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The function of the souls (jīva) is to help one another.”
jainism.explanation: Umasvati's sutra, parasparopagraho jivanam, became the motto of Jainism: living beings exist in a web of mutual support and mutual dependence.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's sea that shrinks when the cloud stops giving back illustrates the same principle of reciprocity: what is taken must be returned, or even the greatest reserve declines.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.21 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever he takes, he does not give back. Seeking to earn more and more, he is troubled and uneasy.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the man who prospers by taking without ever giving back. Sikh ethics answers this with vand chhakna, sharing what one has earned.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's cloud diminishes the sea if it takes water and never returns it. Commentators read that as a warning about people who take from their community without giving back, which is exactly the person this salok condemns.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "deep-flowing Ocean, from whom all rivers flow and every sea, and all the springs and deep wells"
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles names Okeanos as the single ultimate reservoir from which every river, sea, spring and well derives its water.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts make the ocean the master account from which all other water is drawn, which is why its depletion would matter.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "When the sun is near, the stream of vapour flows upwards; when it recedes, the stream of water flows down, and the order of sequence, at all events, in this process always remains the same."
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle sets out the first systematic Greek account of the hydrological cycle: solar heat lifts water as vapour, which cools and falls again, endlessly.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the scientific statement of the circuit the Kural assumes when it warns that the cloud must give back what it took.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Meteorologica II.2 / I.9, 346b (E. W. Webster translation)

real_life_example.event_title: Pierre Perrault measures rain and river flow in the Seine basin
real_life_example.event: In his book De l'origine des fontaines, published in 1674, Pierre Perrault made quantitative estimates of rainfall and of river discharge in part of the Seine basin. He showed that rainfall was more than enough to sustain the flow of rivers and springs, refuting older theories that rivers were fed by seawater returning underground. His work, followed by that of Edme Mariotte and Edmond Halley, marked the start of quantitative study of the water cycle.
real_life_example.explanation: Perrault helped establish that the world's waters move in a closed cycle in which rain is the essential link.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes the cloud drawing water from the sea and having to give it back, and Perrault's measurements began the scientific proof that rain is the link that keeps that cycle full.

tamil:
சிறப்பொடு பூசனை செல்லாது வானம்
வறக்குமேல் வானோர்க்கும் ஈண்டு.
transliteration:
Sirappodu poosanai sellaadhu vaanam,
Varakkumel vaanorkkum eendu.
meaning: If the sky dries up, the festivals and the daily worship offered to the gods here on earth will stop.
elementary: You cannot have a birthday party if there is no food, no cake and no candles — the party just does not happen. This kural says the same about temple festivals and daily prayers: if the rain stops, there is nothing left to offer, and the celebrating stops too.
university: பூசனை (poosanai), from Sanskrit पूजा, denotes the regular daily offering, while சிறப்பு (sirappu) here carries its technical sense of the annual festival or special honour, so the couplet covers the whole ritual calendar from daily to yearly. வானோர் (vaanor), "those of the sky," is a neat counterpoint to வானம், the sky itself — the sky-dwellers are made hostage to the sky's own generosity. The adverb ஈண்டு ("here," i.e. in this world) localises the collapse: heaven is not harmed, but heaven's honours on earth cease. The argument is quietly subversive of ritual priority, inverting the ordinary Vedic sequence in which sacrifice causes rain, and it is one of the passages most often cited to show Valluvar's materially grounded, non-sectarian ethics.

hinduism.quote_or_event: "An oblation duly thrown into the fire, reaches the sun; from the sun comes rain, from rain food, therefrom the living creatures (derive their subsistence)."
hinduism.explanation: Manu describes a closed circuit in which ritual offering generates rain, rain generates food, and food generates the creatures who will make the next offering.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural cuts the same circuit at a different point: break the rain link and the offering at the other end becomes impossible.

christianity.quote_or_event: "The meat offering and the drink offering is cut off from the house of the LORD; the priests, the LORD'S ministers, mourn."
christianity.explanation: Joel's account of a devastating agricultural catastrophe notes that the Temple's grain and wine offerings simply stop, because there is no grain and no wine to offer.
christianity.tie_back: It is exactly the Kural's claim: when the land dries up, worship itself cannot proceed.

islam.quote_or_event: "And if only the people of the cities had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied [the messengers], so We seized them for what they were earning."
islam.explanation: The Qur'an links a community's religious state to whether the heavens open over it with blessing.
islam.tie_back: It binds worship and rainfall together as the Kural does, but reverses the direction of dependence — here piety conditions rain rather than rain conditioning piety.

judaism.quote_or_event: "At four times of the year the world is judged: On Passover judgment is passed concerning grain; on Shavuot concerning fruits that grow on a tree … and on the festival of Sukkot they are judged concerning water, i.e., the rainfall of the coming year."
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah organises the entire pilgrimage-festival calendar around agricultural verdicts, with the autumn festival of Sukkot devoted to the coming year's rain — the occasion of the Temple's water-libation ceremony.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts make festivals and rainfall a single interlocked system rather than separate spheres.
judaism.source: Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:2 (Koren–Steinsaltz, William Davidson Edition)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Vinaya establishes the vassa, the three-month rains retreat: monks must settle in one place for the monsoon rather than wander, and the year's central communal observances — including the Kathina robe ceremony that follows it — are timed entirely by the rainy season.
buddhism.explanation: The monastic ritual calendar of Theravada Buddhism is literally built around the arrival and departure of the monsoon rains.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural it treats the rhythm of religious observance as something set by the rain rather than independent of it.
buddhism.source: Vinaya Piṭaka, Mahāvagga III (Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka, the chapter on entering the rains)

jainism.quote_or_event: “In that period, in that age the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra commenced the Paggusan when a month and twenty nights of the rainy season had elapsed.”
jainism.explanation: Paryushana (here Paggusan), the most important annual Jain festival of fasting, confession, and scripture-reading, is fixed by the rainy season, when monks stay in one place and lay people gather around them.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural says, the great festivals and regular worship depend on the rains, and the chief Jain festival is literally timed by the monsoon.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis §1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: At Hardwar, while pilgrims threw water east as offerings to their ancestors, Guru Nanak threw water west. He said he was watering his fields in Punjab, and asked how their water could reach ancestors so much farther away. He then taught that the true sacrifice of the age was giving food to those who remember God's Name.
sikhism.explanation: In Macauliffe's account of Guru Nanak's life, the Guru turns a water-offering ritual into a lesson. Water is for living fields, and real worship is feeding people and remembering the Name, not offerings to gods or the dead.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says worship of the celestials stops when rain fails. Sikhism agrees that water sustains life but rejects such ritual worship and puts feeding the hungry in its place.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter IV, pp. 50-52

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "So she would have destroyed the whole race of men with cruel famine and have robbed them who dwell on Olympus of their glorious right of gifts and sacrifices, had not Zeus perceived and marked this in his heart."
greek_mythology.explanation: Demeter's withdrawal of the earth's fertility threatens not only humanity but the Olympians themselves, who would lose the offerings that only a fed humanity can make.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact argument: when the earth stops yielding, the gods are the ones deprived of their worship.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter, lines 310–313 (Evelyn-White translation)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero's Stoic speaker explains that whenever something brought great benefit to humankind, the ancients took it to come from divine goodness and gave the thing itself the name of a god — so that grain came to be called Ceres and wine Liber.
philosophy.explanation: The argument makes the names and cults of certain gods derivative of the material goods they supply.
philosophy.tie_back: It runs parallel to the Kural's inversion: the honours paid to the celestials depend on the material bounty that makes those honours possible.

real_life_example.event_title: Megadroughts contribute to the decline of Angkor
real_life_example.event: Tree-ring records show that Angkor, the capital of the Khmer Empire and its great temple complex, suffered decades-long droughts in the mid-14th and early 15th centuries, separated by periods of intense monsoon flooding. Researchers conclude that these climate extremes strained the city's water system and, together with other factors, contributed to Angkor's decline as a capital.
real_life_example.explanation: Even one of the greatest temple cities ever built depended on reliable monsoon rain, and its long decline followed the failure of that rain.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that if the sky dries up, the festivals and daily worship of a land cannot go on, and Angkor's temple capital weakened when its monsoon failed.

tamil:
தானம் தவம்இரண்டும் தங்கா வியன்உலகம்
வானம் வழங்கா தெனின்.
transliteration:
Thaanam thavam irandum thangaa viyan ulagam,
Vaanam vazhangaadhenin.
meaning: If the sky stops giving rain, then neither giving to others nor tapas (strict self-discipline) will last anywhere in this wide world.
elementary: You cannot share your lunch with a friend if you have no lunch, and it is not brave to skip a meal if there was never any food to skip. This kural says that giving to others and going without on purpose both need there to be something in the world first — and rain is what puts it there.
university: The two nouns are the twin pillars of Valluvar's ethical architecture: தானம் (thaanam, Sanskrit dāna) is the householder's virtue of giving, treated at length in chapter 23 ஈகை, while தவம் (thavam, Sanskrit tapas) is the renunciant's discipline, treated in chapter 27. By yoking them in a single line and making both contingent on rainfall, Valluvar establishes the material precondition of the entire இல்லறவியல் and துறவறவியல் sections before he has begun to expound either. The verb தங்கா ("will not abide, will not stay") is carefully chosen — it is not that such acts become wrong, but that they can no longer hold their place in the world. The move is characteristic: ethics in the Kural is never floated free of the economy that supports it.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Upanishad, gods, humans and demons each come to Prajapati for instruction and each receives the single syllable "Da," from the voice of the thunder. Each hears it differently: the gods hear damyata, restrain yourselves; humans hear datta, give; demons hear dayadhvam, be compassionate.
hinduism.explanation: The thunder of the rain-cloud is made the teacher of the three great disciplines, with self-restraint and giving at the head of the list.
hinduism.tie_back: The Upanishad has the rain-cloud itself pronouncing the very two virtues — giving and self-restraint — that this Kural makes depend on rain.
hinduism.source: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.2.1–3 (the teaching of the thunder, 'Da Da Da')

christianity.quote_or_event: "Now he that ministereth seed to the sower both minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits of your righteousness;"
christianity.explanation: Paul, urging the Corinthians to a collection for the poor, argues that God's supply of seed and bread is what makes generous giving possible and fruitful.
christianity.tie_back: It makes the same link the Kural makes — material provision from above is the precondition of charitable giving.

islam.quote_or_event: "And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking means to the approval of Allah and assuring [reward for] themselves is like a garden on high ground which is hit by a downpour - so it yields its fruits in double."
islam.explanation: The Qur'an likens sincere charitable spending to a well-sited garden struck by heavy rain, which returns twice the harvest.
islam.tie_back: Charity is figured precisely as a rain-fed yield, matching the Kural's claim that giving depends on what the sky supplies.

judaism.quote_or_event: "Where there is no bread, there is no Torah; where there is no Torah, there is no bread."
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah states the mutual dependence of material sustenance and religious life — study and observance cannot be sustained by a starving community.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's proposition in rabbinic form: spiritual practice cannot abide in the world without the food that underwrites it.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (Mishnah Yomit, Dr. Joshua Kulp translation)

buddhism.quote_or_event: "As water raining on a hill / flows down to the valley, / even so does what is given here / benefit the dead."
buddhism.explanation: This verse on offerings made for departed relatives uses rainwater running downhill as the image of how a gift made here reaches those who can no longer provide for themselves.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts join rain and dāna directly, treating giving as something that flows from an upstream supply.

jainism.quote_or_event: “At that moment the gods caused a rain of perfumed water and flowers, and showered down heavenly treasures; they struck the drums, and in the air they praised the gift.”
jainism.explanation: When the outcaste-born monk Harikesha, after fasting a whole month, finally receives alms, the gods rain down perfumed water and treasure to honour both the gift and the austerity.
jainism.tie_back: The story joins exactly the Kural's pair, dana (the gift) and tapas (the month-long fast), and marks their meeting with a rain from the sky.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.35–36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Pilgrimages, austere discipline, compassion and charity - these, by themselves, bring only an iota of merit.”
sikhism.explanation: Japji names the same pair the Kural does, austerity (tap) and charity (daan), and says that alone they earn only a speck of merit. What matters is cleansing oneself with the Name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says both charity and austerity collapse without rain. Japji puts them in a different order: both are real goods, but both depend on something deeper, the Name.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 21, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Zeus and Hermes travel in Phrygia disguised as poor strangers and are turned away from a thousand homes; only the elderly Baucis and Philemon share their meagre supper. The gods then flood the whole ungenerous district, spare the old couple's cottage, and transform it into a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's tale ties together hospitality, divine water sent in judgement, and the founding of a place of worship.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It brings giving, rain and piety into one story, though it does not make giving depend on rainfall as the Kural does.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "it is impossible, or not easy, to do noble acts without the proper equipment"
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that virtuous activity requires external goods — friends, wealth, political power — as its instruments, so material circumstance conditions how far a life can be excellent.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the general philosophical form of the Kural's specific claim that charity and austerity cannot abide without the rain that supplies them.

real_life_example.event_title: The Ancestral Pueblo people leave Mesa Verde during the Great Drought
real_life_example.event: The last tree-ring date for new construction in the Mesa Verde region is 1281. A drought lasted from 1276 through 1299, probably causing food shortages for a large population, and by about 1300 the Ancestral Pueblo people had left Mesa Verde and the Four Corners region, moving south into present-day New Mexico and Arizona. The National Park Service notes that drought combined with other stresses, such as depleted land and resources.
real_life_example.explanation: A long-settled society with rich communal and ceremonial life could not continue in its homeland once the rain failed for a generation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that without rain neither giving to others nor disciplined religious life can remain in the world, and Mesa Verde's whole community life left with the rains.

tamil:
நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகெனின் யார்யார்க்கும்
வான்இன்று அமையாது ஒழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Neer indru amaiyaadhu ulagenin yaaryaarkkum,
Vaan indru amaiyaadhu ozhukku.
meaning: No one in the world can live without water. In the same way, good behaviour cannot last in the world without rain.
elementary: Think of electricity in a house. The lights, the fridge, the heating — none of it works if the power is cut. This kural says rain is the power supply for the whole world, and even being good to each other gets much harder when it fails.
university: The couplet's force rests on a deliberate pun in its final word, ஒழுக்கு (ozhukku), which means both "a flowing, a stream" and, through its near-twin ஒழுக்கம், "right conduct" — the subject of chapter 14. Valluvar thereby makes one word carry both the hydrological and the moral sense of "keeping to its proper course," closing the chapter by fusing the two. யார்யார்க்கும் ("for anyone whosoever") universalises the claim across rank, region and creed, an emphasis that recurs throughout the Kural's ethics. Placed as the last verse of the chapter, it is the hinge that carries the reader into chapters 3 and 4 on the greatness of the renunciant and the assertion of virtue: the whole moral edifice that follows has just been shown to rest on rainfall.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Gita sets out a turning wheel in which prescribed duty produces sacrifice, sacrifice produces rain, rain produces food, and food produces living beings; Krishna then says that whoever does not help turn this wheel lives in vain.
hinduism.explanation: Rain is a load-bearing link in a single circuit that runs from moral obligation through nature and back to moral obligation again.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes right conduct and rainfall parts of one system rather than separate domains.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.14–16 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, 1972)

christianity.quote_or_event: "For the earth which drinketh in the rain that cometh oft upon it, and bringeth forth herbs meet for them by whom it is dressed, receiveth blessing from God:"
christianity.explanation: Hebrews uses rain-fed ground yielding a useful crop as the image of a human life that responds rightly to what it has received.
christianity.tie_back: It makes the same move as the Kural's pun, letting rain-fed fruitfulness stand simultaneously for agricultural and moral productivity.

islam.quote_or_event: "And said, 'Ask forgiveness of your Lord. Indeed, He is ever a Perpetual Forgiver. He will send [rain from] the sky upon you in [continuing] showers.'"
islam.explanation: Noah tells his people that setting their moral account right with God is what will open the sky over them in abundant rain.
islam.tie_back: Both verses tie rainfall and right conduct into a single proposition, refusing to treat them as unrelated.

judaism.quote_or_event: "That I will give you the rain of your land in his due season, the first rain and the latter rain, that thou mayest gather in thy corn, and thy wine, and thine oil … And then the LORD'S wrath be kindled against you, and he shut up the heaven, that there be no rain"
judaism.explanation: The second paragraph of the Shema, recited twice daily, makes the rainfall of the land the direct consequence of Israel's faithfulness or unfaithfulness.
judaism.tie_back: It is the most systematic statement anywhere of the Kural's thesis that rain and right conduct stand or fall together.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 11:13–17 (KJV, rendering the Hebrew Tanakh; the second paragraph of the Shema)

buddhism.quote_or_event: "Furthermore, humans become unprincipled. This is the fifth obstacle to rain, which the forecasters don't know, and which their vision does not traverse."
buddhism.explanation: Listing five causes of drought that no weather-reader can detect, the Buddha ends with human beings becoming adhammika — unrighteous, not living by Dhamma.
buddhism.tie_back: It makes rainfall and moral conduct two faces of one order, exactly as the Kural's closing pun does.
buddhism.source: Vassa Sutta (Obstacles to Rain), Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.197 (Bhikkhu Sujato translation)

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the morning there will be destruction of right-conduct; at mid-day, of kingly duty; in the afternoon, of fire.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra's account of the coming age of pure sorrow links the collapse of right conduct with a world where 'the clouds will be without water', so moral and natural order fail together.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's pun on ozhukku as both flowing water and right conduct, the Jain picture treats the failure of rain and the failure of conduct as one decline.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book X (Mahaviracharitra), ch. XIII, 'The sixth spoke' (tr. Helen M. Johnson)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Food and wealth are produced in abundance when it rains, if it is the Will of God. Consuming it, the minds of His creatures are satisfied, and they adopt the lifestyle of the way.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das links rain to food, food to a contented mind, and a contented mind to living rightly, the way of life.
sikhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's own conclusion: right conduct, like the world itself, cannot carry on without rain.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1282, Raag Malar, Vaar Malar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "Neither famine nor disaster ever haunt men who do true justice; but light-heartedly they tend the fields which are all their care. The earth bears them victual in plenty, and on the mountains the oak bears acorns upon the top and bees in the midst."
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's just city is rewarded with fertility and plenty, while the unjust city is visited with famine — justice and harvest are one subject for him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's closing line, it refuses to separate the moral order of a community from the productivity of its land.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "It is not the consciousness of men that determines their existence, but their social existence that determines their consciousness."
philosophy.explanation: Marx's 1859 formulation of historical materialism holds that the material conditions of production shape the ideas, morality and institutions a society is able to sustain.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the modern, secular form of the Kural's final claim: the moral life of a people rests on the material base that supports it.
philosophy.source: Karl Marx, Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859)

real_life_example.event_title: The Water Tribunal of Valencia
real_life_example.date: Medieval origins; still meets weekly (UNESCO recognition 2009)
real_life_example.event: The Water Tribunal of the Plain of Valencia, whose roots go back to the al-Andalus period, meets every Thursday at noon at the Apostles' Door of Valencia Cathedral to settle disputes among farmers over irrigation water. Its members are elected representatives of the irrigation districts, its proceedings are oral, and its rulings are not appealed. In 2009 UNESCO inscribed it, with the Council of Wise Men of Murcia, on its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.
real_life_example.explanation: For about a thousand years a community has kept its water flowing fairly by keeping its people's conduct in order, showing how closely right conduct and water are bound together.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural plays on a word that means both flowing water and right conduct, and the Valencia tribunal is a living institution in which the flow of water and the order of conduct are kept together.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கத்து நீத்தார் பெருமை விழுப்பத்து
வேண்டும் பனுவல் துணிவு.
transliteration:
Ozhukkaththu neeththaar perumai vizhuppaththu,
Vendum panuval thunivu.
meaning: All the good books agree that people who live by strict self-control and have given up their desires deserve more praise than anyone else.
elementary: Imagine every good book in the world lined up on one shelf, and you ask them all the same question: “Who is the greatest kind of person?” This kural says they would all give the same answer — the person who keeps to good habits and stops grabbing for things they want.
university: Valluvar grounds the authority of asceticism not in revelation but in textual consensus: “panuval thunivu” means literally “the settled resolution (thunivu) of learned works (panuval).” His renunciant is “neeththaar,” “those who have let go” — a participle from nee- (to leave, to separate) rather than a sectarian title such as sannyāsin or bhikkhu, so the ascetic is defined by an act rather than by membership in an order. Crucially he binds renunciation to “ozhukkam,” disciplined conduct, refusing to let letting-go collapse into licence: greatness belongs only to those who stand “ozhukkaththu,” inside conduct. The word “vizhuppam” (pre-eminence, the choicest thing) makes the claim comparative rather than merely approving — not that renunciation is good, but that it is the highest good the books know. This opening move is characteristic of Tamil didactic poetry, which establishes authority by appeal to accumulated learned opinion, and it lets the chapter exalt renunciants without endorsing any one religion's account of why they matter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A yogī is greater than the ascetic, greater than the empiricist and greater than the fruitive worker. Therefore, O Arjuna, in all circumstances, be a yogī.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna closes the chapter on meditation by ranking the person of disciplined inner practice above the body-mortifying ascetic, above the scholar, and above the ritual performer.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's move: a canonical text explicitly ranking the disciplined renunciant at the top of every other class of person.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.46 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.”
christianity.explanation: The author of Hebrews ends a long roll-call of the faithful by saying that the world did not deserve those who gave up home and comfort to wander destitute in the wilderness.
christianity.tie_back: Scripture here does precisely what the Kural says scripture does — it declares the homeless, self-denying figures to be worth more than the world itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth easily, and when the ignorant address them [harshly], they say [words of] peace, And those who spend [part of] the night to their Lord prostrating and standing [in prayer]”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an's portrait of the ʿibād ar-Raḥmān, the servants of the Merciful, describes people marked by humility, gentleness under provocation, and night-long vigil rather than by worldly appetite.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, revealed scripture singles out the self-disciplined, desire-restraining person for its highest praise.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Such is the way [of a life] of Torah: you shall eat bread with salt, and rationed water shall you drink; you shall sleep on the ground, your life will be one of privation, and in Torah shall you labor.”
judaism.explanation: The closing chapter of Pirkei Avot lays out deliberate material deprivation as the proper setting for a life devoted to Torah, and promises that such a life is blessed in this world and the next.
judaism.tie_back: A revered Jewish text setting austerity and discipline at the top of its scale of value, which is the Kural's exact claim about what books conclude.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 6:4 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though month after month for a hundred years one should offer sacrifices by the thousands, yet if only for a moment one should worship those of perfected minds that honor is indeed better than a century of sacrifice.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada measures a lifetime of ritual offerings against a single instant of reverence for the perfected and finds the ritual wanting.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis in Buddhist form: the settled verdict of the text is that honouring the renounced outranks every other meritorious thing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Obeisance to all the Saints in the world.” … “This five-fold obeisance is destructive of all sins and is the foremost amongst all the auspicious.”
jainism.explanation: The Namokar (Navkar) Mantra, the first formula every Jain learns and the opening of the Saman Suttam anthology, ends its five salutations by bowing to every renunciant in the world, and the verse that follows declares this homage the foremost of all auspicious things.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural says the settled verdict of all worthy books is to praise renunciants above every other excellence, Jainism's own first and most-recited formula makes reverence for the world's renunciants, alongside the Jinas, the highest auspicious act.
jainism.source: Namokar Mantra as Saman Suttam vv. 1-2, Mangalasutra (tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; text via jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The God-conscious being is always unattached, as the lotus in the water remains detached.”
sikhism.explanation: Sukhmani's praise of the brahm giani (God-conscious being) begins with detachment. Unlike the Kural's ascetic, though, the Sikh ideal stays in household life and is detached in the midst of it, like a lotus that sits in water without getting wet.
sikhism.tie_back: Both texts rank highest the person who has let go of desire. Sikhism places that person inside worldly life rather than in renunciation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 272, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 8, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Zeus turns his eyes away from the fighting at Troy to the northern peoples, among them the milk-drinking Hippemolgoi and the Abioi, whom Homer calls the most righteous of men — a people imagined as living without wealth, war or luxury.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek epic occasionally idealises distant peoples whose material simplicity is taken as proof of moral superiority to the acquisitive Greek world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the nearest thing in Greek epic to the Kural's claim that the texts reserve their highest praise for those who own and want least.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus devotes a whole discourse to the Cynic vocation, describing the true Cynic as a man with no house, no property, no wife and nothing but his own body, whom Zeus sends into the world as a messenger and a scout to show other people where good and evil actually lie.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus the propertyless wanderer is not a social failure but the highest human office, because only someone who wants nothing can testify credibly about what is worth wanting.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, a teaching tradition places the disciplined renunciant at the summit of its own scale of human excellence.

real_life_example.event_title: Francis of Assisi renounces his inheritance
real_life_example.event: In early 1206 Francis's father, the wealthy cloth merchant Pietro di Bernardone, brought him before the bishop of Assisi and demanded that he renounce all claims and return his goods. Francis gave up his inheritance and handed back even the clothes he wore, and the bishop covered him with his own cloak. Francis went on to live in poverty and founded the Franciscan order, which has honoured him ever since.
real_life_example.explanation: Francis's public act of letting go of wealth became one of the most celebrated renunciations in European history, and he is still revered across the world eight centuries later.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the settled verdict of all good books is to praise those who have let go of desire, and Francis's renunciation is among the most praised such acts in the Christian tradition.

tamil:
துறந்தார் பெருமை துணைக்கூறின் வையத்து
இறந்தாரை எண்ணிக்கொண் டற்று.
transliteration:
Thurandhaar perumai thunaikkoorin vaiyaththu,
Irandhaarai ennikkon datru.
meaning: Trying to measure the greatness of those who have given up worldly life is like trying to count all the people who have ever died on earth.
elementary: Imagine someone asked you to count every leaf that has ever fallen from every tree in the world. You could start, but you could never finish. This kural says that asking “how great are people who have let go of wanting things?” is that same kind of question — too big to ever finish counting.
university: The force of the verse is in “thunaik-koorin” — “if one were to say the measure (thunai) of it.” Thunai here is quantity, extent, an amount; the couplet is not saying the renunciant's greatness is hard to describe but that it is the wrong sort of thing to put a number on. The chosen comparison is deliberately brutal: “vaiyaththu irandhaarai ennikkondu,” tallying up everyone who has ever died in the world, an arithmetic that is not merely large but principled endless, since the dead accumulate faster than any count. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward read the simile as one of category error rather than mere magnitude. Placed second in the chapter, it functions as a rhetorical guard-rail: having just claimed in Kural 21 that the books rank renunciants highest, Valluvar immediately blocks the reader from imagining that this ranking could be cashed out in any scale or quantity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Taittiriya Upanishad measures out a ladder of bliss, multiplying each rung a hundredfold from human joy up to the bliss of Brahman, and then breaks off its own arithmetic by saying that from that bliss words turn back, together with the mind, unable to reach it.
hinduism.explanation: The text deliberately starts an enumeration in order to demonstrate that enumeration fails: the highest state is reached by abandoning the measuring apparatus, not by extending it.
hinduism.tie_back: The same structure as the Kural — begin to count, then show that counting is the wrong instrument for this object.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets:”
christianity.explanation: The writer of Hebrews abandons his own list of the faithful mid-sentence, conceding that the catalogue of the righteous outruns the time available to recite it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the text stages its own failure to enumerate as the strongest possible tribute to those it is praising.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account [i.e., limit].”
islam.explanation: The closing clause of the verse promises the ṣābirūn — those who endure and hold back — a reward given bi-ghayri ḥisāb, without reckoning, outside the ordinary ledger of deeds and payments.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an makes the same point about the self-restrained that the Kural makes about the renounced: their worth is explicitly taken off the accounting scale.

judaism.quote_or_event: “These are the things that have no definite quantity: The corners [of the field]. First-fruits; [The offerings brought] on appearing [at the Temple on the three pilgrimage festivals]. The performance of righteous deeds; And the study of the torah.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah opens the tractate on gleanings by listing the obligations that Jewish law deliberately leaves without a fixed measure, so that no ceiling can be placed on them.
judaism.tie_back: A legal text formally declaring certain goods to be unquantifiable, which is exactly the move the Kural makes about the greatness of renunciants.
judaism.source: Mishnah Peah 1:1 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who reveres those worthy of reverence, the Buddhas and their disciples, who have transcended all obstacles and passed beyond the reach of sorrow and lamentation — he who reveres such peaceful and fearless ones, his merit none can compute by any measure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that even the by-product of honouring the perfected — the merit accruing to the one who honours them — defeats every attempt at calculation.
buddhism.tie_back: A near-verbatim parallel: the greatness attaching to the renounced is declared, in as many words, incomputable by any measure.

jainism.quote_or_event: “‘All sounds recoil thence, where speculation has no room,’ nor does the mind penetrate there.” … “he perceives, he knows, but there is no analogy (whereby to know the nature of the liberated soul).”
jainism.explanation: At the close of its fifth lecture the Acaranga Sutra describes the state of the one who has left the round of birth and death, and says that words, reasoning and even comparison cannot reach or measure it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that trying to put a measure on the greatness of renunciants is like counting all the dead, a category error rather than a hard sum; the Acaranga likewise says the renouncer's final state has no measure in words or analogy.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.5.6.3-4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The God-conscious being cannot be appraised... Who can describe the limits of the God-conscious being? Only the God-conscious being can know the state of the God-conscious being. The God-conscious being has no end or limitation.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says again and again that the greatness of the God-conscious person cannot be valued, measured or put into words.
sikhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's own point: trying to measure such greatness is like counting all the dead.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 273, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 8, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Odysseus summons the dead at the edge of the world and they come up in such numbers, with such a cry, that he loses his nerve and flees back to his ship rather than face the countless tribes of the perished.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer uses the sheer unmanageable multitude of the dead as an image of something a living person cannot confront or take stock of.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It supplies the Kural's own comparison in narrative form — the dead of the world are the standing Greek image of a number no one can take.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”
philosophy.explanation: The final proposition of the Tractatus marks off a domain — value, ethics, the sense of the world — which Wittgenstein holds can be shown but never stated in propositions that measure facts.
philosophy.tie_back: It formalises the Kural's instinct that some kinds of greatness are not the sort of thing about which a measurement can be pronounced at all.
philosophy.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, Proposition 7 (trans. C.K. Ogden, 1922)

real_life_example.event_title: Mother Teresa receives the Nobel Peace Prize
real_life_example.event: Mother Teresa, who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta (Kolkata), India, in 1950 after taking religious vows, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for 1979. The Norwegian Nobel Committee cited her work for bringing help to suffering humanity. She received the prize in Oslo in December 1979.
real_life_example.explanation: The world's most prominent peace award was given to a nun who owned almost nothing, recognising a kind of greatness that cannot be measured in wealth or power.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says measuring the greatness of renunciants is like counting all the dead, and the Nobel honour for a woman who had given up everything shows the world struggling to put a measure on such greatness.

tamil:
இருமை வகைதெரிந்து ஈண்டுஅறம் பூண்டார்
பெருமை பிறங்கிற்று உலகு.
transliteration:
Irumai vakaitherindhu eendaram poondaar,
Perumai pirangitru ulagu.
meaning: Nothing in this world shines brighter than the greatness of those who have weighed the two kinds of life and chosen to live a life of goodness here.
elementary: Some people look at two roads and can actually tell which one leads somewhere good and which one just looks fun for a little while. This kural says the people who can tell the difference — and then actually start walking the good road today, not someday — are the brightest people in the whole world.
university: “Irumai” — “twoness” — is the pivot, and the commentators do not agree on what the two are. Parimelazhagar takes them as this birth and the next (iham and param); Manakkudavar and several modern readers take them as birth and release from birth, the round of rebirth against liberation; a third reading makes them pleasure and good, the transient and the abiding. Valluvar leaves the ambiguity intact, which is characteristic: what matters is not which pair you name but that you have actually distinguished (“vakai therindhu,” sorted out the kinds) rather than drifted. Against that discernment he sets the sharply temporal “eendu” — here, in this place, in this life — so that the verse refuses to let the insight be postponed to a future existence. “Pirangitru” (from pirangu-, to shine forth, to be conspicuous) makes the resulting greatness visible in the world rather than hidden in it; the renunciant's virtue is not an inward secret but the brightest public fact the world contains.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The good is one thing, the pleasant another; these two, having different objects, chain a man. It is well with him who clings to the good; he who chooses the pleasant, misses his end.”
hinduism.explanation: Death himself teaches Nachiketas that the preyas (the pleasant) and the shreyas (the good) present themselves together, and that everything depends on being able to tell them apart before choosing.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's “irumai vakai therindhu” almost word for word: discerning the two kinds, then binding oneself to the better one.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad 1.2.1-2 (trans. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.”
christianity.explanation: Paul contrasts two orders of reality — the visible and passing against the invisible and lasting — and says the Christian's whole orientation follows from keeping that distinction in view.
christianity.tie_back: Same structure as the Kural: two kinds are distinguished, and greatness lies in ordering one's present life by that distinction.

islam.quote_or_event: “But you prefer the worldly life, While the Hereafter is better and more enduring.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an rebukes the human habit of choosing the immediate over the lasting, and names the two options plainly so that the choice cannot be made in ignorance.
islam.tie_back: The verse presents exactly the two kinds the Kural says the great have discerned, and identifies which one the wise take up.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Jacob said: this world is like a vestibule before the world to come; prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the banqueting-hall.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah's image makes the present world real but preliminary, and makes preparation in the here and now the only access to what follows.
