judaism.tie_back: Both the two-order distinction and the Kural's insistence on “eendu,” acting here rather than later, are present in a single sentence.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:16 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Lead a righteous life; lead not a base life. The righteous live happily both in this world and the next.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's chapter on the world sets the two possible ways of living side by side and reports the outcome across both existences.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the choice of dharma here the thing that determines standing in both orders of existence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who, in the world, comprehends and renounces these causes of sin, is called a reward-knowing sage (muni).”
jainism.explanation: The very first lesson of the Acaranga Sutra sets out the twofold knowledge (parijna): first understanding the causes of sin and rebirth, then renouncing them. Only the person who does both is called a true sage (muni).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's renunciant first discerns the two orders of existence ('vakai therindhu') and then takes up virtue here and now. That is the same two-step the Acaranga sets at the head of the Jain canon, where comprehension has to pass into renunciation in this life.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.1.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, one is happy here and hereafter.”
sikhism.explanation: Sukhmani often pairs this world and the next (halat palat). Spiritual discernment lived out now, in the company of the holy, brings good in both.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises those who have discerned the two orders of existence and live virtuously here and now. This line speaks to the same two worlds and to living them well now.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 272, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 7, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plato closes the Republic with the myth of Er, a soldier who dies, travels to the place where souls are judged and choose their next lives, and returns to tell the living what he saw — the point of the account being that a person who has seen both worlds will choose the just life rather than the merely attractive one.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story is designed to give the reader the vantage point of someone who has surveyed both existences at once, so that the choice between them can be made knowingly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises exactly the Kural's claim that greatness begins with having actually discerned the two orders, not merely heard of them.
greek_mythology.source: Plato, Republic X (the Myth of Er, 614b-621d)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For I deem that the true disciple of philosophy is likely to be misunderstood by other men; they do not perceive that he is ever pursuing death and dying.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues on his last day that philosophy just is the practice of separating oneself from the body's demands, so that the philosopher has been rehearsing for the other order of existence all along.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's renunciant, the philosopher is great precisely because he has taken the measure of both states and arranged his present life around the better one.

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Charles V abdicates and retires to the monastery of Yuste
real_life_example.event: In Brussels on 25 October 1555, Charles V, ruler of the Holy Roman Empire, Spain and the Netherlands, began giving up his realms, handing the Netherlands and Spain to his son Philip and the imperial title to his brother Ferdinand. He sailed to Spain in 1556 and in February 1557 moved to the monastery of Yuste. He lived there in relative seclusion until his death on 21 September 1558.
real_life_example.explanation: The most powerful monarch in Europe chose to lay down his crowns while still alive and end his days beside a monastery, an almost unique act among rulers of his age.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises those who have weighed this world against the other and taken up the path of virtue here and now, and Charles V, having held more of the world than almost anyone, chose to leave it for a life of retreat.

tamil:
உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்
வரனென்னும் வைப்பிற்கோர் வித்து.
transliteration:
Uranennum thottiyaan oraindhum kaappaan,
Varanennum vaippirkor viththu.
meaning: A person who controls the five senses with a strong mind, the way a hook controls an elephant, is a seed for the best world of all, freedom from being born again.
elementary: A person riding a huge elephant carries a small hooked stick, and with that one little stick they can steer an animal far stronger than they are. This kural says your five senses are like five elephants, and a steady mind is the little hook that steers them — and steering them is how something wonderful gets planted.
university: The image is precise and technical: “thotti” is the ankusa, the mahout's hooked goad, and the “oraindhu,” the five, are the sense-faculties imagined as five rutting elephants. Against their bulk Valluvar sets “uran,” mental firmness or resolve — the smallest instrument mastering the largest force, which is the whole argument of the verse in one picture. The payoff clause is theologically loaded: “varan” (from Sanskrit vara, the choicest) names the supreme estate, and “vaippu” is a deposit or treasure-store, so the ascetic becomes “or viththu,” a single seed, for that store. The seed metaphor matters — the sense-controller is not said to have arrived, but to be the germ from which the highest state grows, which keeps the emphasis on practice rather than attainment. The Tamil Shaiva tradition heard this verse as close kin to Tirumular's Tirumandiram, which likewise sets the goad of knowledge against the elephants of the senses.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, and the mind the reins. The senses they call the horses, the objects of the senses their roads.”
hinduism.explanation: The Katha Upanishad's chariot allegory assigns each part of the person a role in a single vehicle, and makes everything depend on whether the driver holds the reins firmly enough to control the animals.
hinduism.tie_back: The same claim with a different draught animal: a small instrument of resolve governing the powerful senses is what carries a person to the highest place.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad 1.3.3-4 (trans. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.”
christianity.explanation: Paul borrows the vocabulary of athletic training to describe a deliberate, forcible mastery of his own appetites, undertaken because he does not consider himself exempt from failing.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats bodily self-restraint not as an optional austerity but as the very condition of reaching the prize.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an sets out a two-step condition — reverent awareness, then active restraint of the soul's appetite — and attaches Paradise directly to it.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's causal chain exactly: restraint of appetite now is what makes the highest estate one's destination.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’ (Proverbs 16:32).”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines strength itself: real power is not what a person can do to the world but what a person can do to the yetzer, the appetitive drive inside.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts locate the decisive strength in the small inner instrument that governs appetite, not in outward force.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Formerly this mind wandered about as it liked, where it wished and according to its pleasure, but now I shall thoroughly master it with wisdom as a mahout controls with his ankus an elephant in rut.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's Elephant chapter pictures the untrained mind as a musth elephant and wisdom as the mahout's hooked goad that brings it under control.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's exact image — goad, rutting elephant, faculty of restraint — appears here in an independent tradition.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard these well-spoken words of the virtuous lady, he returned to the Law like an elephant driven by the hook. Protected in thoughts, words, and acts, subduing his senses and keeping the vows, he practised true Sramanahood throughout life.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Rathanemi, overcome by desire on seeing the nun Rajimati, is brought back by her firm rebuke as a mahout's hook brings back an elephant. He then masters his senses, and the lecture says both of them became omniscient (kevalins) and reached perfection.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's own image almost word for word: the goad (thotti, the ankusa) of firm resolve turns the elephant of the senses back, and the person so controlled becomes the seed of the highest estate, which in this story ends in liberation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.46-48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895); vv. 42-46 recur in Dasavaikalika Sutra 2

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The mind is the elephant, the Guru is the elephant-driver, and knowledge is the whip. Wherever the Guru drives the mind, it goes. O Nanak! Without the whip, the elephant wanders into the wilderness, again and again.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das uses the mahout's picture: the mind is a powerful elephant, steered by the Guru with the goad of knowledge.
sikhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own image: an elephant held in check by a small goad as the way to the highest state.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 516, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe, Odysseus has his crew stop their ears with wax and orders them to lash him upright to the mast and to tighten the ropes if he begs to be freed, so that he can hear the Sirens' song and survive it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus does not try to resist the pull of sensory pleasure by willpower in the moment; he binds his future self in advance, using a deliberate physical restraint as a substitute for restraint of desire.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Greek world's clearest picture of the Kural's claim that a deliberate instrument of restraint applied to the senses is what saves a person.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The human charioteer drives his in a pair; and one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed; and the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him.”
philosophy.explanation: In Plato's allegory the soul is a chariot whose driver, reason, must control an obedient horse and an unruly appetitive one if the soul is to rise toward the truth.
philosophy.tie_back: Same claim as the Kural: the ascent to the highest state depends on a governing faculty keeping the appetitive powers in hand.

real_life_example.event_title: Eric Liddell declines to run on Sunday at the Paris Olympics
real_life_example.event: When the programme for the 1924 Paris Olympics was issued, the Scottish sprinter Eric Liddell learned that the heats of the 100 metres, his strongest event, would be run on a Sunday. As a devout Christian who would not compete on the Sabbath, he withdrew and trained instead for the 200 and 400 metres. He won bronze in the 200 metres and gold in the 400 metres in an Olympic record time of 47.6 seconds.
real_life_example.explanation: Liddell gave up his best chance of glory because of a principle he had settled in advance, and still triumphed in an event that was not his speciality.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the one who controls the five senses with the goad of firm resolve, and Liddell's steady resolve held back the strongest desire an athlete has, the desire to win in his best event.

tamil:
ஐந்தவித்தான் ஆற்றல் அகல்விசும்பு ளார்கோமான்
இந்திரனே சாலுங் கரி.
transliteration:
Aindhaviththaan aatral akalvisumbu ulaarkoman,
Indhirane saalung kari.
meaning: Indra, the king of the gods in heaven, is proof enough of how powerful a person becomes by controlling the desires of the five senses.
elementary: Imagine the strongest king in the world admitting that someone else is stronger than him. That would settle the argument, wouldn't it? This kural says the king of the sky-world himself is the living proof of how powerful a person becomes when they put out the fire of wanting.
university: “Aindhavith-thaan” is built on avi-, to extinguish or quench, so the ascetic has not merely restrained the five but put them out, as one puts out a lamp. Against this Valluvar sets a legal metaphor: Indra, “akal visumbu ulaar koman,” king of those in the wide sky, is the “kari” — the witness, the one whose testimony settles a case. The choice of Indra is doubly pointed. In Puranic narrative Indra's own sovereignty was won by tapas, so his throne is itself an exhibit of what austerity produces; and Indra is famously the god who panics when a human ascetic's penance grows strong enough to threaten his seat, which makes his testimony that of a reluctant expert witness. Some commentators, including Parimelazhagar, also read a darker allusion to the Ahalya episode, in which Indra's own failure to quench desire cost him everything — in which case the god testifies not by his glory but by his fall. Notably, the Kural cites Indra only as evidence, never as an object of worship.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana's account of Vishvamitra, the king-turned-ascetic's austerities grow so formidable that Indra, fearing for his own throne, sends the apsara Menaka to break the sage's concentration — and the heavenly court's alarm becomes the measure of what the ascetic had achieved.
hinduism.explanation: The recurring Puranic pattern is that the gods intervene against human tapas not out of malice but out of well-founded fear: accumulated austerity is a real force that can rival theirs.
hinduism.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural's evidentiary move — Indra's own conduct is what proves the power of the man who has quenched the five.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (the Vishvamitra and Menaka episode, sargas 63-64)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus explains his disciples' failure to cast out a spirit by pointing to a power that only sustained prayer and fasting confer — asceticism is presented as producing real, verifiable capacity.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats ascetic self-denial as the source of a demonstrable power rather than as mere piety.

islam.quote_or_event: “By Him in Whose Hands my soul is, the smell coming out from the mouth of a fasting person is better in the sight of Allah than the smell of musk. (Allah says about the fasting person), ‘He has left his food, drink and desires for My sake. The fast is for Me. So I will reward (the fasting person) for it and the reward of good deeds is multiplied ten times.’”
islam.explanation: In this hadith God Himself speaks about the faster, claiming the fast as His own and declaring that the physical evidence of hunger is more pleasing to Him than perfume.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, it is the highest authority in the heavens who furnishes the testimony about what self-denial is worth.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud reports that a heavenly voice went out each day declaring that the whole world is sustained on account of Hanina ben Dosa — a sage so poor that he lived on a measure of carob pods from one Sabbath eve to the next.
judaism.explanation: The passage deliberately juxtaposes extreme material deprivation with cosmic significance, and puts the assessment in the mouth of a voice from heaven rather than of admiring humans.
judaism.tie_back: A heavenly authority testifying to the power of a man who has renounced appetite is the Kural's exact structure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even the gods hold dear the wise one, whose senses are subdued like horses well trained by a charioteer, whose pride is destroyed and who is free from the cankers.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's chapter on the perfected states plainly that the arahant's standing is recognised by the devas themselves, who occupy a lower rung than the liberated human.
buddhism.tie_back: Same claim, same witnesses: the gods' regard is offered as the proof of what sense-mastery accomplishes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Throwing off the guise of a Brahmana, and making visible his true form, Sakra saluted him respectfully and praised him with these sweet words” … “Here (on earth) you are the highest man, Reverend sir, and hereafter you will be the highest”
jainism.explanation: When King Nami renounces his throne, Sakra (Indra), king of the gods, comes disguised as a Brahmin to test him with arguments for worldly duty. When Nami's resolve holds, Indra shows his true form, praises Nami for having conquered anger, pride, delusion and greed, and circles him in reverence.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural names Indra as the witness to the power of the one who has quenched the five senses. In the Uttaradhyayana Indra literally takes that role, first testing the renouncer and then publicly testifying to his supremacy.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.6-58, esp. 9.55-59 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Ahalyaa was the wife of Gautam the seer. Seeing her, Indra was enticed. When he received a thousand marks of disgrace on his body, then he felt regret in his mind.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak retells the Puranic story of Indra, who failed to master desire and was disgraced for it. He uses it to show that only those who accept God's hukam stay free of such falls.
sikhism.tie_back: Some commentators, Parimelazhagar among them, read the Kural's Indra as a witness through his fall. Guru Nanak calls Indra up in exactly that role, as proof of what unmastered desire costs.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1344, Raag Prabhati, Dakhni, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, after a life of imposed labours and endurance, is burned free of his mortal part on Mount Oeta and taken up to Olympus, where the gods who had set him his trials receive him as one of their own.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth's one clear case of a human ascending to divine rank makes endurance and hardship, rather than birth, the qualification — and the Olympians' acceptance is what certifies it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Indra's testimony in the Kural, the divine court's own recognition is what establishes that a human being's self-conquest has reached superhuman force.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Alexander the Great, at the height of his power, sought out Diogenes the Cynic sunning himself and asked what he could do for him; Diogenes asked him only to stop blocking the sun, and Alexander afterwards told his companions that if he were not Alexander he would wish to be Diogenes.
philosophy.explanation: The most powerful man in the world publicly concedes that the man who owns nothing occupies the more enviable position, and the concession is what gives the anecdote its force.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's evidentiary logic transposed to the human plane: the king himself is the sufficient witness to the ascetic's superior power.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 14; cf. Diogenes Laertius 6.32

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Akbar honours the hermit Salim Chishti at Sikri
real_life_example.event: In 1568-69 the Mughal emperor Akbar visited the Sufi hermit Shaikh Salim Chishti, who lived on the ridge at Sikri, and Chishti foretold that Akbar would have an heir. Akbar's son Salim, the future emperor Jahangir, was born at Sikri in 1569. Akbar then moved his court there and built Fatehpur Sikri, whose Jama Masjid, completed in 1571-72, came to enclose the saint's tomb.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the most powerful emperors in the world built an entire capital beside a hermit's dwelling, a striking public acknowledgement of an ascetic's standing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says Indra, king of the heavens, is witness to the power of one who has quenched the senses, and here an earthly emperor bore that witness by building his capital in honour of a hermit.

tamil:
செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர் சிறியர்
செயற்கரிய செய்கலா தார்.
transliteration:
Seyarkariya seyvaar periyar siriyar,
Seyarkariya seykalaa thaar.
meaning: Great people do things that are hard to do. Small people cannot do what is hard to do.
elementary: Two people stand in front of the same steep hill. One starts climbing even though it hurts; the other says “too hard” and walks away. This kural says that is the whole difference between a big person and a small one — not how they look, just which one starts climbing.
university: The couplet is built as a chiasmus, with “seyarkariya” (things difficult to do) standing at the head of both halves so that the same object divides humanity into two classes. What is striking is the definition's austerity: Valluvar offers no content for greatness at all, no list of virtues, only a functional test. “Periyar” and “siriyar” — the great and the small — are terms he uses throughout the Kural as a moral rather than a social ranking, and here he strips them of every birth-based or wealth-based criterion. In context the difficult things are the ascetic disciplines named in the surrounding verses: quenching the senses, discerning the two worlds, holding anger. Later Tamil tradition, reading the chapter alongside yogic literature, glossed the “hard things” as the eight limbs of yoga from yama through samadhi. The verse's blunt symmetry has made it one of the most-quoted couplets in Tamil, routinely cited well outside any ascetic context.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Rise, awake! having obtained your boons, understand them! The sharp edge of a razor is difficult to pass over; thus the wise say the path (to the Self) is hard.”
hinduism.explanation: The Katha Upanishad refuses to soften the demand: the road to self-knowledge is compared to walking a razor's edge, and the hearer is roused rather than comforted.
hinduism.tie_back: It supplies exactly what the Kural leaves implicit — that the thing which separates the great from the small is a path most people will not attempt because it is hard.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad 1.3.14 (trans. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But Jesus beheld them, and said unto them, With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.”
christianity.explanation: The disciples have just watched a wealthy man refuse the demand to sell everything and follow, and they ask in astonishment who then can be saved; Jesus concedes the difficulty outright before answering it.
christianity.tie_back: The passage stages the Kural's division exactly — one man finds the hard thing undoable and walks away, and the difficulty is named as the whole issue.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Paradise is surrounded by hardships and the Hell-Fire is surrounded by temptations.”
islam.explanation: The hadith pictures the two destinations as walled in by what stands in front of them: to reach Paradise one must push through what is unpleasant, while what is pleasant leads the other way.
islam.tie_back: It gives the Kural's criterion a topography — doing the hard thing is literally the only route, and failing to do it is what defines the lesser path.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Hei Hei's maxim in Pirkei Avot, l'fum tza'ara agra, teaches that the reward is in proportion to the difficulty — the harder the exertion a mitzvah demands, the greater what is earned by it.
judaism.explanation: The rabbinic principle turns difficulty into a measure of value rather than a reason for exemption, so effort itself becomes the unit of account.
judaism.tie_back: Both sayings make the capacity to shoulder what is hard the index of a person's standing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though one may conquer a thousand times a thousand men in battle, yet he indeed is the noblest victor who conquers himself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada sets the hardest available achievement — self-conquest — above the most spectacular external one, and awards greatness accordingly.
buddhism.tie_back: Same verdict as the Kural: the title of 'great' goes to whoever can do the thing that is genuinely difficult to do.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As it is difficult to cross the heavenly Ganges, or to swim against the current, or to swim with one's arms over the sea, so it is difficult to get over the ocean of duties.” … ‘but in this world nothing is difficult for one who is free from desire.’
jainism.explanation: Mrigaputra's parents list at length how hard a monk's life is, from lifelong non-injury to swallowing 'iron grains', to talk him out of it. He answers that for one free of desire nothing is too hard, then takes the vows and reaches perfection.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural defines the great as those who do what is hard to do. The Uttaradhyayana spells out exactly how hard renunciation is, then shows a great soul doing it anyway.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 19.24-44, esp. 19.36 and 19.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. When you place your feet on this Path, give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak calls the spiritual path the hardest commitment there is: one must be ready to give up one's head and ignore what others think.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural separates the great from the small by whether they do what is hard. Guru Nanak's path is open only to those willing to do the hardest thing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles is set twelve labours that no other man could survive — strangling the Nemean lion whose hide no weapon can pierce, fetching Cerberus out of the underworld — and his standing in Greek myth rests entirely on his having completed tasks designed to be impossible.
greek_mythology.explanation: The labours are explicitly chosen for their undoability; the hero's greatness is constituted by the doing of them rather than demonstrated by anything else.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Greek myth's central definition of a great man is the Kural's definition: the one who does what cannot be done.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…it is no easy task to be good. For in everything it is no easy task to find the middle… to do this to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive, and in the right way, that is not for every one, nor is it easy; wherefore goodness is both rare and laudable and noble.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that virtue consists in hitting a mean that is difficult to locate and harder to hit reliably, and concludes that this difficulty is exactly why goodness is rare and admirable.
philosophy.tie_back: He reaches the Kural's conclusion by analysis: it is the difficulty of the thing that makes those who manage it great, and its rarity that makes most people small.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.9, 1109a24-30 (trans. W.D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Hillary and Tenzing make the first ascent of Everest
real_life_example.event: On 29 May 1953 Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa mountaineer, reached the summit of Mount Everest, becoming the first people known to stand on the world's highest mountain. Tenzing had taken part in six earlier attempts on the mountain going back to 1935. The two men spent about fifteen minutes on top before descending.
real_life_example.explanation: After decades of failed attempts, the climb became a worldwide symbol of doing what had seemed impossible.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines the great as those who do what is hard to do, and the first ascent of Everest is one of history's clearest cases of people achieving what others could not.

tamil:
சுவைஒளி ஊறுஓசை நாற்றமென்று ஐந்தின்
வகைதெரிவான் கட்டே உலகு.
transliteration:
Suvaiyoli oorosai naatramendru aindhin,
Vakaitherivaan katte ulagu.
meaning: The whole world is in the hands of the person who fully understands the five senses: taste, sight, touch, hearing and smell.
elementary: Everything you know about the world came in through five doors: what you taste, see, feel, hear and smell. This kural says the person who really understands those five doors — how they work and how they fool you — is the one who has the whole world figured out.
university: Valluvar lists the five not as organs but as their objects — suvai (taste), oli (light or form), ooru (touch), osai (sound), naatram (smell) — which is the classical Indian tanmatra scheme, each sense-object paired with one of the five elements. The operative phrase is “vakai therivaan,” the one who discerns the kinds, and “kattu” means a bond, a grip, or a thing held fast: the world is in his hold. Commentators split productively here. Parimelazhagar reads it epistemically — the one who analyses the sense-modes comprehends the world, since the world is nothing but what arrives through them. Others, including modern commentators like Salomon Pappaiah, read it practically — the one who has severed the desires arising through the five has the world at his command. Both readings depend on the same underlying premise, which is arrestingly close to later phenomenology: the world is not encountered apart from the five channels, so mastery of the channels is mastery of the world.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, the nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons. They arise from sense perception, O scion of Bharata, and one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit phrase Krishna uses, mātrā-sparśāḥ, means literally the contacts of the sense-measures — he is telling Arjuna that pleasure and pain are just the coming and going of sense-contact, and that knowing this is what makes them bearable.
hinduism.tie_back: Both verses hold that understanding the nature of the five sense-channels is what puts a person on top of experience rather than underneath it.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.”
christianity.explanation: John analyses 'the world' into a short taxonomy of appetites, treating it not as a place but as a set of channels through which desire operates on a person.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it identifies the world with what comes in through the senses, and makes knowing that taxonomy the first step to not being ruled by it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an makes the sense-faculties themselves accountable, treating hearing and sight as agents that will be interrogated rather than as neutral instruments.
islam.tie_back: Both verses take the sense-channels as the decisive site of a person's relation to the world, and make knowledge of them the governing requirement.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it shall be unto you for a fringe, that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them; and that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go a whoring:”
judaism.explanation: The Torah's command of the tzitzit works by installing a counter-sign in the visual field itself, on the explicit reasoning that the eyes and the heart lead a person astray by their own momentum.
judaism.tie_back: It rests on the Kural's premise that the senses are the channel through which the world takes hold of a person, so the remedy has to be applied at that channel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the All? Simply the eye & forms, ear & sounds, nose & aromas, tongue & flavors, body & tactile sensations, intellect & ideas. This, monks, is called the All. Anyone who would say, ‘Repudiating this All, I will describe another,’ … would be unable to explain, and furthermore, would be put to grief.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines the totality of what there is exhaustively in terms of the sense-bases and their objects, and rules out in advance any 'world' lying outside them.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim made into doctrine: the world simply is the field of the sense-channels, so the one who has discerned them has the world.
buddhism.source: Sabba Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.23 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The five senses, anger, pride, delusion, and greed--difficult to conquer is one's self; but when that is conquered, everything is conquered.”
jainism.explanation: Answering Indra's challenge to go out and conquer rival kings, the royal sage Nami says that the real enemies are the five senses and the passions, and that whoever masters them has mastered everything.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the world is in the grip of the one who fully understands the five, taste, sight, touch, sound and smell. Nami says the same thing: once the five senses are conquered, everything is conquered.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak recasts the yogi's discipline in inward terms. Whoever masters his own mind has mastered the world, with no need to retreat from it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the world lies in the grip of whoever understands the five senses. Japji says the world is won by whoever wins his own mind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib, Pauri 28, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe turns Odysseus' crew into swine by way of food and drink; Odysseus alone walks into her hall unharmed because Hermes has given him the herb moly and told him the nature of her drugs in advance, so he drinks and is not transformed.
greek_mythology.explanation: The crew are undone by sensory pleasure taken without understanding, while Odysseus meets the same pleasure with prior knowledge of what it is and passes through it intact.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's point that it is knowing the nature of sense-experience, not avoiding it, that leaves a person in command.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus separates the raw sense-impression from the judgement a person adds to it, and locates all disturbance in the second, which is the part within our power.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes analysis of how impressions reach us the lever by which a person stops being at the world's mercy.

real_life_example.event_title: Helen Keller understands the word water
real_life_example.event: Helen Keller, who had lost her sight and hearing in early childhood, began lessons with her teacher Anne Sullivan in March 1887. On 5 April 1887 Sullivan held Helen's hand under a water pump and spelled w-a-t-e-r into her other hand, and Helen suddenly understood that the finger signs named the water. By that evening she had learned some thirty words, and she went on to become a writer and lecturer.
real_life_example.explanation: With two senses closed to her, Keller gained her hold on the whole world by understanding deeply what touch could tell her.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world is in the grasp of one who truly discerns the nature of the senses, and Keller's breakthrough came when she grasped what a single sense could carry.

tamil:
நிறைமொழி மாந்தர் பெருமை நிலத்து
மறைமொழி காட்டி விடும்.
transliteration:
Niraimozhi maandhar perumai nilaththu,
Maraimozhi kaatti vidum.
meaning: The greatness of wise people whose words always come true is shown on earth by the holy sayings they leave behind.
elementary: Some people say things that just stay true, long after they have gone — you can still hear them repeated hundreds of years later. This kural says you do not need to have met such a person to know how great they were; the words they left behind tell you.
university: The couplet turns on a pair of near-rhyming compounds. “Nirai-mozhi” is full speech — words so complete that what they say comes about; “marai-mozhi” is hidden or sacred speech, the mantra, the word set apart. Valluvar's claim is evidential: the greatness of such people is not something we take on trust but something the surviving sayings “kaatti vidum,” show up, display, on the earth (“nilaththu”). The verse encodes an old South Asian doctrine of the efficacious utterance — the satya-vakya or act of truth, in which a perfected person's word alters reality because it proceeds from a life that contains no falsehood. What is distinctly Valluvar's is the inversion: rather than arguing that great people produce powerful words, he argues from the words back to the people, making the surviving text the standing proof. The line has an obvious reflexivity for a reader holding the Kural itself, and Tamil tradition has not missed it.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Vedic tradition holds that the hymns were not composed but seen — each sukta is assigned to a named rishi who is its mantra-drashta, its seer — so that the surviving mantra is the standing evidence of the seer's realisation, and the anukramani indexes preserve those names alongside the verses.
hinduism.explanation: In this framework the sage does not own the mantra and the mantra does not flatter the sage; the relationship is evidential, with the enduring efficacious word testifying to the state of the one who saw it.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact logic — the sacred saying left on earth is what displays the greatness of the person of full speech.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda and the rishi-attribution tradition of the Sarvanukramani

christianity.quote_or_event: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus claims a durability for his sayings greater than that of the physical cosmos, making the words rather than any monument the lasting evidence of who spoke them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats surviving speech as the thing that carries a person's greatness forward into the world.

islam.quote_or_event: “Many a person with disheveled hair and covered with dust is turned away from the doors (whereas he is held in such a high esteem by Allah) that if he were to adjure in the name of Allah (about anything) Allah would fulfil that.”
islam.explanation: The hadith describes a person whose outward appearance invites contempt but whose word, sworn before God, is honoured — his unregarded speech is the exact index of his standing.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's doctrine of full speech: the word of the renunciant is effective, and its effectiveness is what reveals a greatness the world had missed.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 2622 (Book of Virtue, chapter on the virtue of the weak and downtrodden)

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud draws from a verse about one who rules over people justly the astonishing corollary that the righteous rule over the fear of God: God decrees and the tzaddik may annul the decree.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis take the efficacy of a righteous person's word to such a limit that it is said to override heaven's own pronouncement, making speech the visible measure of sanctity.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions read a holy person's greatness directly off the power their words are found to carry.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Sent to help a woman in obstructed labour, the former bandit Angulimala performs an act of truth, declaring that since he was born in the noble birth he has never intentionally taken a life — and on the strength of that true statement the woman and her child are delivered safely.
buddhism.explanation: The saccakiriya works only because the statement is true of the speaker; the power belongs not to the formula but to the life that can say it without falsehood.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's claim — the efficacy of the surviving utterance is what discloses what kind of person stood behind it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “That alone is true Scripture which is the word of a Tirthamkara, which cannot be over-ridden in disputation, nor falsified by perception, reason or testimony, which reveals the nature of things, which is helpful to men, animals and all other kinds of beings, and which is potent enough to destroy all forms of falsehood.”
jainism.explanation: Samantabhadra grounds the authority of Jain scripture in the person who spoke it. A Tirthankara, free of every fault and omniscient, utters words that cannot be refuted and that benefit every living being.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the sacred sayings left on earth by people of perfected speech show their greatness. Jain tradition makes the same tie between the perfected person and the sacred word, though it argues from the speaker to the scripture rather than from the scripture back to the speaker.
jainism.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara v. 9 (tr. Champat Rai Jain, The Householder's Dharma, 1917)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Word, the Bani is Guru, and Guru is the Bani. Within the Bani, the Ambrosial Nectar is contained.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sikhism the Gurus' recorded words are the Guru. That is why Guru Arjan compiled them into the Adi Granth (1604), and why the scripture is honoured today as the living Guru.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the greatness of perfected people is shown by the sacred words they leave behind. Sikhism goes further and treats those words as the Guru's presence itself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 982, Raag Nat, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tiresias, the blind Theban seer, is the one figure in Greek myth whose pronouncements always prove true — Oedipus rages at him and disbelieves him, and every word he has spoken comes about regardless, while he alone among the dead retains his mind and prophesies to Odysseus in the underworld.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tradition marks out the seer precisely by the fact that his speech is not opinion but something that happens, and his standing is established retrospectively by the fulfilment of his words.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the greatness of the man is displayed by the words rather than the words by the man.
greek_mythology.source: Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus 300-462; cf. Homer, Odyssey 11.90-151

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And the Sibyl, with raving lips uttering things mirthless, unbedizened, and unperfumed, reaches over a thousand years with her voice, thanks to the god in her.”
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus contrasts the Sibyl's unadorned, unattractive speech with its reach, arguing that her words outlast a millennium precisely because they carry something other than ornament.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the Kural's point in a single sentence: the plain sacred utterance persists, and its persistence is what testifies to the one who spoke it.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, Fragment DK B92 (trans. John Burnet)

real_life_example.event_title: The Diamond Sutra, the world's earliest dated printed book
real_life_example.event: A Chinese copy of the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist scripture, was printed from carved wooden blocks and dated by its colophon to the equivalent of 11 May 868. It was found in the early 20th century among tens of thousands of scrolls in a sealed cave at the Mogao Buddhist cave site near Dunhuang. It is the earliest dated complete printed book known and is now held by the British Library.
real_life_example.explanation: The words of a teacher of renunciation were thought important enough to become the subject of the first dated printed book, and they have survived more than eleven centuries.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the greatness of those whose words are full of power is shown by the sacred sayings they leave behind, and the Diamond Sutra is a striking case of such sayings being preserved and spread.

tamil:
குணமென்னும் குன்றேறி நின்றார் வெகுளி
கணமேயும் காத்தல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Gunamennum kundreri nindraar veguli,
Kanameyum kaaththal aridhu.
meaning: If people who stand on the high hill of good character ever get angry, the person who angered them can hardly be protected, even for a moment.
elementary: Some people almost never get angry — so if one of them finally does, you know something has gone very wrong. This kural says the anger of a truly good person is like that: rare, and so serious that nobody can protect whoever caused it, not even for a second.
university: The couplet works by compounding two improbabilities. “Gunam-ennum kundru” — the hill called character — puts the sage at an elevation, and “nindraar,” having stood, stresses that he has held the position; such a person's “veguli,” hot anger, is by definition rare. Against that rarity Valluvar sets “kanam,” the blink of an eye, the smallest unit of Tamil time-reckoning, and the verb “kaaththal,” to guard or protect: even for a kanam the offender cannot be guarded. Commentators read the verse in two compatible ways — as a warning about the objective force of an ascetic's curse, a commonplace of Indian narrative, and as a moral observation that the anger of the habitually gentle is uniquely devastating because it can only mean a real wrong has been done. The verse is also a fine example of Valluvar's economy with sound: gunam / kundru and kanam / kaaththal set up internal echoes that make the couplet memorable in recitation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Indra, riding his elephant, treats a garland given to him by the sage Durvasa with contempt and lets it be trampled, the sage curses him on the spot; the gods immediately lose their splendour and their sovereignty, and only the vast labour of churning the ocean for the nectar restores them.
hinduism.explanation: A single moment's disrespect toward an ascetic costs the king of the gods his kingdom, and no power in the three worlds can shield him from the consequence once the word is spoken.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's warning in narrative form: no one, not even Indra, can be protected for an instant from a sage's roused anger.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 8.5-8 (the curse of Durvasa and the churning of the ocean)

christianity.quote_or_event: Ananias and his wife Sapphira sell property, secretly hold back part of the price, and lie about it to the apostles; Peter confronts each of them in turn, and each falls down dead at his words, so that great fear comes on the whole church.
christianity.explanation: The narrative gives no interval for appeal or protection — the apostle's rebuke and the consequence arrive together, and the community's reaction is fear rather than dispute.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the offender against a holy man's integrity cannot be shielded even briefly once the sentence is spoken.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah said, ‘I will declare war against him who shows hostility to a pious worshipper of Mine.’”
islam.explanation: This hadith qudsi opens by putting God Himself on the side of the devoted servant, framing hostility toward such a person not as a private quarrel but as a declaration of war with heaven.
islam.tie_back: It states the Kural's warning at maximum force: whoever provokes a person of realised piety is beyond anyone's protection.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6502 (Book of Ar-Riqaq, chapter on humility)

judaism.quote_or_event: “And [he also said:] warm yourself before the fire of the wise, but beware of being singed by their glowing coals, for their bite is the bite of a fox, and their sting is the sting of a scorpion, and their hiss is the hiss of a serpent, and all their words are like coals of fire.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer urges closeness to the sages and in the same breath warns that the same heat which warms can burn, cataloguing the danger in escalating animal images.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact caution — the roused anger of a person of high character is a thing from which no one can be safely protected.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:10 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One should not strike a holy man, nor should a holy man, when struck, give way to anger. Shame on him who strikes a holy man, and more shame on him who gives way to anger.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada protects the holy man from assault and in the same verse denies him the right to retaliate in anger, holding him to the higher standard precisely because of his attainment.
buddhism.tie_back: It addresses the Kural's situation and deliberately takes the other side: offending the holy is wrong, but the holy person's anger is a fault rather than a force.

jainism.quote_or_event: ‘do not injure him who cannot be injured, lest he consume you all by the fire (of his virtue).’ … ‘for in his wrath he might reduce the world to ashes.’ … “There is not the least hatred in me, neither now, nor before, nor in future.”
jainism.explanation: When Brahmin youths beat the outcaste-born monk Harikesa, the lady Bhadra warns them that such an ascetic's power could burn the world, and his attendant Yakshas strike the attackers down. The monk himself then says he bears no hatred at all.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the story warns that whoever provokes one who stands on the hill of virtue cannot be shielded even for a moment. Jainism, though, takes the anger away from the monk: the danger lies in his power and in his divine protectors, while he himself stays free of wrath.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.19-33, esp. 12.23, 12.28, 12.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Slandering the Saints, one’s life is cut short... One who is cursed by a Saint cannot be saved... But if the Compassionate Saint shows His Kindness, O Nanak! In the Company of the Saints, the slanderer may still be saved.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan warns that wronging a saint brings ruin, and that someone cursed by a saint cannot be saved. He ends by leaving room for the saint's mercy.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that no one can be shielded from the wrath of those who stand on the hill of character. Sukhmani gives the same warning and adds the saint's power to forgive.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 13, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Chryses, priest of Apollo, is insulted and driven off by Agamemnon when he comes to ransom his daughter; he walks along the shore, prays once to his god, and Apollo comes down in anger and shoots a plague into the Greek camp that burns for nine days until the army is forced to submit.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad opens with this episode precisely to show that slighting a holy man is not a social misstep but a catastrophe, and that the whole army cannot be shielded from the consequence of one man's arrogance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's claim, dramatised: the offender and everyone near him are defenceless the moment a holy man's anger is provoked.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues at length in De Ira that anger is not a useful tool that a good person may occasionally deploy but a temporary madness that no one of genuine virtue would consent to entertain even briefly, and that the truly wise man therefore does not become angry at all.
philosophy.explanation: Stoicism treats freedom from anger as constitutive of the sage, so the notion of a virtuous person's wrath carrying moral authority is ruled out from the start.
philosophy.tie_back: It engages the Kural's subject directly and rejects its premise: for Seneca, a person standing on the hill of character does not get angry, so there is nothing to be shielded from.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira (On Anger), esp. I.1 and III.5

real_life_example.event_title: Emile Zola publishes J'accuse
real_life_example.event: The celebrated novelist Emile Zola published an open letter to the President of France, Felix Faure, in the newspaper L'Aurore, defending Captain Alfred Dreyfus and accusing the army of covering up his wrongful conviction for treason. About 200,000 copies were sold that day, and the letter became the turning point of the Dreyfus affair. Zola was convicted of libel, but the case was reopened and Dreyfus was fully cleared in 1906.
real_life_example.explanation: The public anger of a respected figure turned a buried injustice into a national cause that the guilty could no longer hide.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that when those of high character are roused to anger the offender cannot be shielded, and Zola's letter stripped away the protection around those who had wronged Dreyfus.

tamil:
அந்தணர் என்போர் அறவோர்மற் றெவ்வுயிர்க்கும்
செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுக லான்.
transliteration:
Andhanar enbor aravormatru evvuyirkkum,
Sendhanmai poondozhuga laan.
meaning: The people called anthanar (holy, wise people) are the truly good ones, because they treat every living thing with a kindness that never stops.
elementary: People sometimes think you are important because of the family you were born into. This kural says no: the title of the highest kind of person belongs to whoever treats every living creature — people, animals, everything — with real kindness, all the time.
university: The chapter's last couplet is also its most socially radical. “Anthanar,” the honorific ordinarily applied to Brahmins, is here redefined by conduct alone: anthanar are “aravor,” the virtuous, and the reason given is grammatical rather than incidental — the whole second line is a causal clause ending in “ozhuga-laan,” because they conduct themselves so. Traditional Tamil etymology reads anthanar as am (beautiful, gracious) + thanmai (coolness), and Valluvar exploits this by giving them “sen-thanmai,” upright or true coolness, a quality of unheated, unfailing graciousness extended to “ev-uyirkkum,” every living thing without exception — a phrase that takes the claim past human society and into the treatment of animals. Nothing about birth, ritual, thread or learning appears. The verse anchors the ahimsa ethic that Valluvar develops at length in the later chapters on compassion (Arul-udaimai) and abstaining from meat (Pulaal maruththal), and it has been a central text in modern Tamil arguments against caste, including in the work of the twentieth-century reform movements.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The humble sages, by virtue of true knowledge, see with equal vision a learned and gentle brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater [outcaste].”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna's list is constructed to cross every boundary at once — caste, species, and ritual purity — and to say that real knowledge dissolves the distinction between them.
hinduism.tie_back: Both verses redefine the brahmin by a levelling regard for all living beings rather than by birth or rank.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 5.18 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: Francis of Assisi, having given away his property, is remembered in the early lives for preaching to a flock of birds by the roadside, addressing them as his sisters and urging them to praise their creator, and for treating wolf, lamb and leper alike as creatures owed courtesy.
christianity.explanation: The Franciscan tradition made the extension of charity beyond humanity to animals and the whole created order the signature of sanctity rather than an eccentric footnote to it.
christianity.tie_back: It gives the Christian form of the Kural's test: the mark of the genuinely holy is a gracious bearing toward every creature, not a status.
christianity.source: Bonaventure, Legenda Major XII.3 (the sermon to the birds); cf. the Canticle of the Creatures

islam.quote_or_event: “So, he went down the well again and filled his shoe with water and watered it. Allah thanked him for that deed and forgave him. The people said, ‘O Allah's Messenger! Is there a reward for us in serving the animals?’ He replied: ‘Yes, there is a reward for serving any animate (living being).’”
islam.explanation: A man's sins are forgiven for the single act of climbing back into a well to bring water to a thirsty dog, and the Prophet generalises the principle to every creature with a moist liver.
islam.tie_back: The same moral test as the Kural: standing before God turns on gracious conduct toward every living thing, including the least regarded.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs uses treatment of animals as the diagnostic for righteousness, a verse the rabbis took as a scriptural anchor for the principle of tza'ar ba'alei chayim, the prohibition on causing animals distress.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it identifies the truly virtuous person by an attentiveness that reaches past human beings to other living creatures.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth does one become a holy man. But he in whom truth and righteousness exist — he is pure, he is a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's closing chapter systematically strips the word brahmana of every inherited and ritual meaning and reassigns it on the basis of conduct alone.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's operation performed on the same word: anthanar / brahmana belongs to whoever lives rightly, not to whoever was born right.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who thoroughly knows living beings, whether they move or not, and does not injure them in any of the three ways, him we call a Brahmana.” … “By one's actions one becomes a Brahmana, or a Kshattriya, or a Vaisya, or a Sudra.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha tells a sacrificing priest that a true Brahmin is defined not by birth or ritual but by conduct, above all by not harming any living being, moving or unmoving, in thought, word or deed.
jainism.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's redefinition of 'anthanar' by unbroken kindness toward every living thing. The Jain text is even more explicit that the title belongs to non-injury, which reaches to beings that do not move, rather than to birth.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.19-33, esp. 25.23 and 25.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, modesty the knot and truth the twist. This is the sacred thread of the soul; if you have it, then go ahead and put it on me.”
sikhism.explanation: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, the boy Nanak refused the Brahmin's sacred thread (janeu). He asked instead for a thread spun from compassion and truth, which cannot break, get dirty or burn.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's redefinition of anthanar, Guru Nanak redefines the mark of the twice-born as compassion lived out, not birth or ritual.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the last book of the Metamorphoses, Ovid gives Pythagoras a long speech urging humanity to stop slaughtering animals for food, arguing that souls pass between all bodies and that the ox which has worked the fields should not be repaid with the knife.
greek_mythology.explanation: The speech makes kinship with all animate life the ground of a specific ethical discipline, and presents it as the teaching of a sage set apart from ordinary appetite.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the nearest Greek-mythological articulation of the Kural's standard — the truly holy are known by a compassion that covers every living thing.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV.60-478 (the speech of Pythagoras)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In On Abstinence from Animal Food, Porphyry argues against the Stoic position that justice applies only between rational beings, holding instead that animals perceive, suffer and reason after their fashion, and that the philosopher's justice must therefore extend to every ensouled creature.
philosophy.explanation: Porphyry makes the scope of a person's justice the measure of their philosophical attainment, so that abstaining from harm to animals is not sentimentality but the completion of the ascetic life.
philosophy.tie_back: Same conclusion as the Kural: the person who deserves the highest title is the one whose gracious conduct excludes no living thing.

real_life_example.event_title: Albert Schweitzer and Reverence for Life
real_life_example.event: Albert Schweitzer, a theologian, musician and doctor, went in 1913 to Lambarene on the Ogooue River in what is now Gabon, where he and his wife Helene built a hospital. In 1915, while travelling on the river, the phrase Reverence for Life came to him, and it became the centre of his ethics, extending moral concern to every living thing. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for 1952, cited for his altruism, reverence for life and tireless humanitarian work.
real_life_example.explanation: Schweitzer turned a principle of compassion toward all life into decades of practical service, and the world honoured him for it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the truly virtuous are those who wear unbroken compassion toward every living being, and Schweitzer's Reverence for Life is almost a restatement of that standard in modern form.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

tamil:
சிறப்புஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும் அறத்தினூஉங்கு
ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Sirappu eenum selvamum eenum araththinooungu,
Aakkam evano uyirkku.
meaning: Doing what is right brings both respect and riches. So what could be better for any living being than doing right?
elementary: Imagine a tree that gives you both shade and fruit — you would not chop it down looking for something better. Doing the right thing is like that tree: it gives you a good name and it gives you good things in life, so there is nothing better to plant.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a rhetorical question rather than a command, staking out the claim that அறம் (aram, virtue/dharma) is not merely one good among many but the most productive of all. The pairing சிறப்பு (sirappu, 'distinction', glossed by the classical commentator Parimelazhagar as வீடுபேறு, liberation) with செல்வம் (selvam, wealth) collapses the usual opposition between otherworldly merit and worldly gain: virtue delivers both. This anticipates the tripartite scheme of aram–porul–inbam (dharma–artha–kama) that structures the Kural itself, and mirrors the classical Indian doctrine that dharma is the root from which artha and kama grow. The unusual archaic form அறத்தினூஉங்கு, with its alapedai (lengthened vowel), is metrically marked and gives the line its emphatic weight.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “With uplifted arms I am crying aloud but nobody hears me. From Righteousness is Wealth as also Pleasure. Why should not Righteousness, therefore, be courted?”
hinduism.explanation: This is Vyasa's despairing summary of the entire Mahabharata — the so-called Bharata Savitri — insisting that both material gain and enjoyment are downstream consequences of dharma, not rivals to it.
hinduism.tie_back: It makes exactly Valluvar's argument: since virtue is the source of both honour and wealth, nothing else can be a greater good.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata 18.5, Svargarohanika Parva (Bharata Savitri), trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.”
christianity.explanation: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus tells anxious listeners that food, drink and clothing follow on from putting righteousness first, rather than being secured by chasing them directly.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks righteousness above material gain precisely because material gain follows from it.

islam.quote_or_event: “So be mindful of Allah to the best of your ability, hear and obey, and spend in charity—that will be best for you. And whoever is saved from the selfishness of their own souls, it is they who are ˹truly˺ successful.”
islam.explanation: The verse frames God-consciousness and generosity as what is genuinely 'best for you' (khayran li-anfusikum), redefining self-interest around righteous conduct.
islam.tie_back: Both texts argue that righteous conduct is the truly profitable course for a human being, not a sacrifice of profit.
islam.source: Qur'an 64:16, At-Taghabun (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “The following are the things for which a man enjoys the fruits in this world while the principal remains for him in the world to come: Honoring one’s father and mother; The performance of righteous deeds; And the making of peace between a person and his friend; And the study of the torah is equal to them all.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah classifies certain good deeds as paying a 'dividend' that can be enjoyed immediately while the capital is preserved for the world to come.
judaism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's double yield precisely: righteous action produces both present prosperity and ultimate distinction.
judaism.source: Mishnah Peah 1:1 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The doer of good rejoices here and hereafter; he rejoices in both the worlds. He rejoices and exults, recollecting his own pure deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: One of the Dhammapada's 'twin verses', contrasting the evil-doer who grieves in both worlds with the good-doer who rejoices in both.
buddhism.tie_back: Same claim that virtue pays out in this life and the next, leaving no greater good available to a living being.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Religion is supremely auspicious; non-violence, selfcontrol and penance are its essentials. Even the gods bow down before him whose mind is ever preoccupied with religion.”
jainism.explanation: The Dasavaikalika Sutra opens by declaring dharma, made up of non-injury, restraint and austerity, the highest good (mangala), and says even celestial beings honour the person whose mind rests always in it.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's opening question, 'what greater good than virtue?', this text places dharma above every other good and says it wins the highest honour. The Kural adds wealth to the list of virtue's rewards; the Jain verse does not.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 1.1, as Saman Suttam v. 82, Dharmasutra (tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; text via jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
sikhism.explanation: In a Sri Raag ashtapadi Guru Nanak ranks sach aachaar, truthful conduct, above even the knowledge of Truth itself; the same hymn says that the companionship of the Naam brings the most excellent honour.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's rhetorical question, it names right living as the highest good a person can possess, the source of true honour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But they who give straight judgements to strangers and to the men of the land, and go not aside from what is just, their city flourishes, and the people prosper in it… The earth bears them victual in plenty… They flourish continually with good things.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the city of the just as materially blessed by Zeus with peace, fertility and abundance, in direct contrast to the famine and ruin visited on the unjust city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in mythic-agricultural form: righteousness itself is what generates prosperity.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225-237, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue come money and every other good of man, public as well as private.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial Socrates defends his life's work of urging Athenians to care for the soul before possessions, claiming that goods flow from virtue rather than the reverse.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost a direct Greek restatement of Kural 31: virtue is the source of wealth and every other good, so nothing exceeds it.

real_life_example.event_title: The Cadbury brothers move their works to Bournville
real_life_example.event: In 1861 the brothers George and Richard Cadbury took over their father's failing cocoa business, and in 1879 they moved their factory four miles out of industrial Birmingham to a rural site they named Bournville. There they introduced a private social security programme and working conditions far in advance of their time, and from 1893 George Cadbury built a model village of houses with large gardens, which he handed to the Bournville Village Trust in 1900. The firm grew into the highly prosperous Cadbury Brothers company, and Bournville became a model for later garden cities and suburbs.
real_life_example.explanation: The Cadburys showed that a business run on ethical principles could become both rich and widely respected, its decent treatment of workers adding to rather than draining its success.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says virtue yields both honour and prosperity, and the Cadburys' firm gained both the wealth and the lasting good name that their humane practices earned.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

tamil:
அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கமும் இல்லை அதனை
மறத்தலின் ஊங்கில்லை கேடு.
transliteration:
Araththinooungu aakkamum illai adhanai,
Maraththalin oongillai kedu.
meaning: Nothing helps you more than doing what is right, and nothing hurts you more than forgetting to do it.
elementary: Think of brushing your teeth. Doing it is the best thing for your teeth, and forgetting to do it is the worst thing for them. This kural says goodness works the same way — doing it is the best thing possible, and forgetting about it is the worst.
university: The couplet is built on a deliberate chiasmus: ஆக்கம் (aakkam, increase/gain) is set against கேடு (kedu, ruin/loss), and the pivot between them is not 'doing evil' but மறத்தல் (marathal, forgetting). Valluvar's diagnosis of moral failure is therefore cognitive rather than volitional — Parimelazhagar glosses the forgetting as arising from மயக்கம் (delusion), not defiance. This makes the verse subtly different from ordinary two-path moralism: the opposite of virtue is not vice but inattention. The verse also repeats அறத்தினூஉங்கு from Kural 31, a rhetorical device (antadi-like linkage) binding the chapter's opening pair into a single argument.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Justice, being violated, destroys; justice, being preserved, preserves: therefore justice must not be violated, lest violated justice destroy us.”
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit maxim dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ presents dharma as reciprocal: it guards whoever guards it and destroys whoever abandons it.
hinduism.tie_back: It states the Kural's exact two-sidedness — maximum gain from upholding virtue, maximum ruin from letting it go.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 8.15, trans. Georg Bühler (Sacred Books of the East, 1886)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sets total worldly acquisition against the loss of one's own self, arguing that no quantity of gain compensates for that loss.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures gain and ruin on a single scale and concludes that moral loss is the greatest possible ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “Successful indeed is the one who purifies their soul, and doomed is the one who corrupts it!”
islam.explanation: The closing oath-sequence of Surah Ash-Shams distils all human outcomes into a single antithesis between purifying (zakkāhā) and corrupting (dassāhā) the soul.
islam.tie_back: Both couplets reduce human fortune to one binary: maintaining moral integrity is the whole of gain, abandoning it the whole of ruin.
islam.source: Qur'an 91:9-10, Ash-Shams (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day: I have put before you life and death, blessing and curse. Choose life—if you and your offspring would live—”
judaism.explanation: Moses' closing charge presents obedience to the covenant not as one option among many but as the choice between existence and annihilation.
judaism.tie_back: It gives the same stark two-sided accounting the Kural does: righteousness is all gain, its abandonment all ruin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a person commit evil, let him not do it again and again. Let him not find pleasure therein, for painful is the accumulation of evil. Should a person do good, let him do it again and again. Let him find pleasure therein, for blissful is the accumulation of good.”
buddhism.explanation: This paired verse presents merit and demerit as accumulating stocks whose eventual ripening is guaranteed, pleasant in one case and painful in the other.
buddhism.tie_back: Same symmetrical ledger as the Kural: the accumulation of good is the greatest gain, its opposite the greatest loss.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!” … “Thus the soul which suffers for its carelessness, is driven about in the Samsara by its good and bad Karman”
jainism.explanation: In the 'Leaf of the Tree' lecture Mahavira warns his chief disciple Gautama, in a refrain repeated throughout, never to lapse into carelessness (pramada) even for a moment, because heedlessness is what keeps the soul drifting through rebirths.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural places the worst ruin not in active vice but in forgetting virtue. Jainism likewise names inattentive carelessness, pramada, as the root of the soul's undoing.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.1 and 10.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In your mind, you do not remember the One Lord-you fool! You have forgotten the Lord; your virtues shall wither away.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak pictures people sinking in a swamp of attachment and diagnoses their fall not as deliberate wickedness but as forgetting, warning that once God is forgotten, virtue itself withers.
sikhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's striking claim that the deepest ruin comes from forgetting rather than from open defiance.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus' Eumenides the Furies, ancient goddesses of blood-vengeance, argue before the Athenian court that if Orestes goes unpunished every restraint on human wrongdoing will dissolve, and they warn the city that there are times when dread must sit enthroned over the heart, since neither anarchy nor tyranny follows where reverence is kept.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Furies are making a civic argument: the forgetting of retributive justice is not a local error but the collapse of the moral order that holds a society together.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's second line — the forgetting of dharma is itself the supreme catastrophe.
greek_mythology.source: Aeschylus, Eumenides, the Furies' choral ode (ll. 490-565)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Republic Book IV Socrates concludes that justice is the health, beauty and good condition of the soul while injustice is its disease, deformity and weakness — so that asking whether injustice pays is as absurd as asking whether it pays to have a ruined body.
philosophy.explanation: The argument makes moral condition intrinsic rather than instrumental: virtue is what the soul's flourishing consists of, and vice is its destruction.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim rendered as an argument: nothing can outweigh virtue as gain, and nothing can rival its loss as ruin.

real_life_example.event_title: The collapse of Charles Ponzi's scheme
real_life_example.event: In late 1919 Charles Ponzi, an Italian immigrant, opened a business in Boston promising investors a 50 percent return in 45 days from trading international postal reply coupons. In fact he paid earlier investors with money taken from later ones, and he became very rich within months. After journalists at the Boston Post investigated, the scheme collapsed in August 1920; Ponzi was arrested, convicted of mail fraud and imprisoned, several banks failed in the aftermath, and he was later deported to Italy, dying in poverty in Brazil in 1949.
real_life_example.explanation: Ponzi's name became the standard term for this kind of fraud, and his rapid rise and total fall is one of the best-known warnings about wealth built on deceit.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says there is no greater ruin than forgetting virtue, and Ponzi's fortune, built by setting honesty aside, ended in disgrace, prison and poverty.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

tamil:
ஒல்லும் வகையான் அறவினை ஓவாதே
செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாஞ் செயல்.
transliteration:
Ollum vakaiyaan aravinai ovaadhe,
Sellumvaai ellaanj cheyal.
meaning: In every way you can, and without ever stopping, do good wherever good can be done.
elementary: You do not need to be strong to help. If you can carry one book, carry one book. This kural says: do whatever good you can manage, wherever you happen to be, and do not stop.
university: Three qualifiers do the work here. ஒல்லும் வகையான் ('by the means available to you') scales the obligation to individual capacity — Parimelazhagar specifies that the householder gives according to his means and the ascetic according to his bodily strength. ஓவாதே ('without ceasing') removes any notion of virtue as an occasional act. செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம् ('in every place it can reach') is glossed by the commentators as the three instruments of mind, speech and body (மனம், வாக்கு, காயம்), yielding good thought, good word and good deed. The verse thus converts virtue from a discrete achievement into a continuous disposition, and does so without ever specifying a quantity — a characteristically Tamil ethical move that keeps the demand universal and the standard personal.
