hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, without being attached to the fruits of activities, one should act as a matter of duty, for by working without attachment one attains the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna's central instruction in the karma-yoga chapter is that right action is to be performed constantly (satatam) as duty, without calculating its returns.
hinduism.tie_back: Both verses make virtuous action a continuous obligation rather than an occasional or result-driven one.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.19 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges the Galatians to sustained rather than sporadic good-doing, and to take every opportunity as it arises.
christianity.tie_back: It reproduces all three of the Kural's qualifiers — as you are able, without slackening, wherever the chance arises.

islam.quote_or_event: “So be mindful of Allah to the best of your ability, hear and obey, and spend in charity—that will be best for you.”
islam.explanation: The phrase mā istaṭa'tum — 'to the extent you are able' — is the Qur'an's standard scaling of religious obligation to individual capacity.
islam.tie_back: It is the Qur'anic equivalent of ஒல்லும் வகையான்: do the good that lies within your power, whatever that power happens to be.
islam.source: Qur'an 64:16, At-Taghabun (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon's maxim releases a person from the impossible demand of completing the moral task while forbidding them to opt out of it.
judaism.tie_back: It captures the Kural's balance exactly: do what you are capable of, but never stop doing it.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:16 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hasten to do good; restrain your mind from evil. He who is slow in doing good, his mind delights in evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada treats slowness in doing good not as neutral but as actively dangerous, since the unoccupied mind drifts toward harm.
buddhism.tie_back: It sharpens the Kural's ஓவாதே: there is no safe pause in the practice of virtue.

jainism.quote_or_event: Umasvati's Tattvartha Sutra defines yoga as the activity of body, speech and mind, says this activity is the channel through which karma flows into the soul (asrava), and teaches that wholesome activity is the cause of merit (punya) while unwholesome activity is the cause of demerit (papa).
jainism.explanation: In Jain doctrine, every movement of mind, speech and body draws karmic matter to the soul. The layperson is therefore asked to make each of these three channels wholesome, as far as their capacity allows, while the monk aims to restrain them altogether.
jainism.tie_back: Parimelazhagar glosses the Kural's 'every place good can reach' as the three instruments of mind, speech and body. These are exactly Jainism's three yogas, which must be kept wholesome without letting up.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 6.1-3 (Umasvati; cf. tr. Nathmal Tatia, That Which Is, 1994)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak! He knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok that rejects holy men who live by begging, Guru Nanak defines the true path as honest labour and sharing from one's own earnings, the Sikh ideals of kirat karni and vand chhakna.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's 'by whatever means you are able', it measures the duty of doing good by what each person actually has and earns.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang (Sarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, to expiate his crime, is set twelve labours by Eurystheus and must complete every one of them; when two are disallowed on technicalities he is made to perform substitutes, and only after the whole sequence is finished without exception does he earn release and, ultimately, immortality.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes the point that the labours cannot be partially discharged — the reward attaches to the unbroken completion of the whole series, in whatever terrain and by whatever means each demands.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It offers a mythic image of the Kural's 'ceaselessly, by every means, wherever the work can be done'.
greek_mythology.source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5 (the Twelve Labours of Heracles)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the things we have to learn before we can do them, we learn by doing them, e.g. men become builders by building and lyreplayers by playing the lyre; so too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle's doctrine of habituation holds that moral character is not taught but built up through the repeated performance of the corresponding actions.
philosophy.tie_back: It supplies the reason behind the Kural's insistence on unceasing practice: virtue exists only as sustained activity.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (1103a-b), trans. W. D. Ross

real_life_example.event_title: Chiune Sugihara issues transit visas to refugees
real_life_example.event: In the summer of 1940 Chiune Sugihara, Japan's consul in Kaunas, was approached by Jewish refugees from Poland who needed Japanese transit visas to escape Europe. Although many applicants did not meet the conditions his Foreign Ministry required, he kept issuing visas until his consulate closed, stamping some passports himself and enlisting helpers when time ran short, and by the time he left Lithuania he had issued visas to more than 2,000 people. Yad Vashem recognised him as Righteous Among the Nations in 1984.
real_life_example.explanation: Sugihara used the one tool his position gave him, his consular stamp, as fully and as long as he could, and thousands of people escaped because of it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural urges doing good by whatever means one has, without letting up, wherever good can reach, and Sugihara kept writing visas with the means of his office until the very last day it was open.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

tamil:
மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்தறன்
ஆகுல நீர பிற.
transliteration:
Manaththukkan maasilan aadhal anaiththu aran,
Aakula neera pira.
meaning: Keeping your mind free of anything bad is true goodness. Everything else is just noise and show.
elementary: You can wash the outside of a cup and still leave it dirty inside, and nobody would want to drink from it. This kural says goodness is about being clean on the inside; showing off on the outside is just noise.
university: This is one of the Kural's most radical reductions: அனைத்து அறன் — 'that is the whole of virtue' — locates morality entirely in மனத்துக்கண் மாசு, stain in the mind. The dismissive ஆகுல நீர ('of the nature of clamour') is aimed, on Manakkudavar's reading, at conduct performed so that others will notice it; Parimelazhagar extends it to outward religious garb (வேடம்) and pious talk. Coming immediately after a verse commanding ceaseless outward action, Kural 34 prevents that command from collapsing into ritualism, and it prepares the ground for Kural 35's inventory of specifically mental vices. The move parallels — but does not derive from — the Jain and Buddhist emphasis on cetanā (intention) as the locus of karma, and is one reason the Kural has been read as compatible with renunciant and householder ethics alike.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And satisfaction, simplicity, gravity, self-control and purification of one’s existence are the austerities of the mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna distinguishes austerities of body, speech and mind, and defines mental austerity as inner purification rather than any visible act.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats purity of mind as a discipline in its own right, distinct from and more fundamental than outward observance.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.16 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that charitable acts performed for an audience have already received their entire payment in the applause they collect.
christianity.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural's ஆகுல நீர — outward virtue done to be seen is clamour, not virtue.

islam.quote_or_event: “The reward of deeds depends upon the intentions and every person will get the reward according to what he has intended.”
islam.explanation: The opening hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari — innamā al-a'mālu bi'l-niyyāt — makes inward intention the thing that determines the moral value of any outward act.
islam.tie_back: It states the Kural's thesis in legal form: the mind's condition is the whole of the act's worth.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 1, narrated by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab

judaism.quote_or_event: “Pay no attention to his appearance or his stature, for I have rejected him. For [God sees] not as humans see; humans see only what is visible, but God sees into the heart.”
judaism.explanation: God rebukes Samuel for judging Saul's successor by outward impressiveness, and directs him instead to David on the basis of what is inward.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts insist that the real seat of worth is the heart, and that visible impressiveness proves nothing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's opening verse makes mind the origin of all conduct, so that the moral quality of speech and action is entirely derivative of the mind's condition.
buddhism.tie_back: It grounds the Kural's claim: if all action is mind-wrought, then freedom from stain in the mind really is the whole of virtue.

jainism.quote_or_event: Near the end of the Samayasara, Kundakunda says that deluded people take up the many outward marks (linga) of monks or of householders and call them the path to liberation. No outward mark is that path, he says: the Jinas teach that the path is right faith, right knowledge and right conduct within the soul.
jainism.explanation: Kundakunda, the most influential Digambara teacher, insists that a monk's robes or nakedness, a householder's observances and any other outward sign of religion count for nothing in themselves. Only the inner purity of the soul is the way to release.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that a mind free of stain is the whole of virtue and that everything else is mere noise and show, and Parimelazhagar names outward religious garb (vedam) as part of that show. Kundakunda makes the same move, refusing to let outward marks stand in for inner purity.
jainism.source: Samayasara of Kundakunda, gathas on linga, c. 408-411 (numbering per Amritachandra's recension; varies between editions)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Pilgrimages, austere discipline, compassion and charity - these, by themselves, bring only an iota of merit. Listening and believing with love and humility in your mind, cleanse yourself with the Name, at the sacred shrine deep within.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Japji, Guru Nanak gives outward religious acts, even charity, only a sliver of worth, and locates true cleansing at an inner place of pilgrimage within the mind.
sikhism.tie_back: Both texts make purity of mind the substance of religion and treat outward show as secondary noise.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 21, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus tells of Glaucus the Spartan, famed for honesty, who was entrusted with another man's money and later considered keeping it. He asked the Delphic oracle whether he might swear an oath and retain the deposit, and the Pythia replied that merely to have tempted the god with such a question was as fatal as the perjury itself; Glaucus returned the money, but his family line was wiped out regardless.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story makes the intention alone — never acted upon, and immediately renounced — fully sufficient for ruin, because the stain was already in the mind.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that moral reality is located in the mind's condition, not in the outward deed.
greek_mythology.source: Herodotus, Histories 6.86 (the story of Glaucus of Sparta)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will.”
philosophy.explanation: Kant opens the Groundwork by arguing that talents, temperament and even happiness can all be turned to harm, so that the only unconditionally good thing is the will's inner orientation.
philosophy.tie_back: It is Kural 34 as a philosophical thesis: moral worth resides wholly in the inner disposition, and nothing outward qualifies without it.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, opening of Section I, trans. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott

real_life_example.event_title: Wilhelm Röntgen declines to patent X-rays
real_life_example.event: After discovering X-rays at Würzburg in November 1895, the physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen chose not to take out a patent on his discovery, because he felt his work should benefit everyone. He rejected an offered title of nobility and offers from industry to market the rays, and when he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 he donated the prize money to the University of Würzburg.
real_life_example.explanation: Röntgen's quiet refusals let X-ray imaging spread rapidly through medicine while he himself sought neither profit nor rank from it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says virtue lies wholly in a mind free of stain and that the rest is noise and show, and Röntgen turned away both profit and titles, keeping his discovery free of private gain.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

tamil:
அழுக்காறு அவாவெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல் நான்கும்
இழுக்கா இயன்றது அறம்.
transliteration:
Azhukkaaru avaavekuli innaachchol naankum,
Izhukkaa iyandradhu aram.
meaning: True goodness means living while keeping away from four things: jealousy, greed, anger and harsh words.
elementary: Four things spoil a good day: wanting what your friend has, wanting more and more for yourself, losing your temper, and saying something mean. This kural says being good mostly means steering around those four.
university: Valluvar here gives virtue a negative definition — a via negativa built from four named faults, each of which will later receive its own chapter or sub-treatment in the Kural. அழுக்காறு (envy at another's prosperity), அவா (craving running out through the senses), வெகுளி (the anger that erupts when craving is blocked) and இன்னாச்சொல் (the harsh word that anger produces) are arranged by Parimelazhagar as a causal chain rather than a list, so the four are really one process caught at four stages. The verbal form இழுக்கா ('not slipping') is a negative participle drawn from the vocabulary of footing and balance, so the image is of walking a path without stumbling. Note the textual crux: some manuscripts and a persistent popular tradition read ஈயாமை (miserliness) in place of நான்கும், but the reading with நான்கும் is the one carried by the major commentarial tradition and by the standard printed editions used here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names kāma, krodha and lobha as the three entrances to ruin, and makes their abandonment the precondition of any genuine spiritual progress.
hinduism.tie_back: Three of Valluvar's four faults appear here as a named set to be renounced, defining right conduct by exclusion just as the Kural does.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.21 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists the interior dispositions and their verbal outlets together, treating the malice behind the words and the words themselves as one package to be discarded.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the Kural's structure of defining virtue as steady conduct cleared of a short, named list of faults.

islam.quote_or_event: In a hadith recorded by Muslim, the Prophet forbids a cluster of interpersonal faults in a single breath — envying one another, driving up prices against one another, hating one another, turning away from one another, undercutting one another's sales — commands believers to live as brothers, and then strikes his own chest three times saying that piety (taqwa) is here.
islam.explanation: The list works exactly like a definition by exclusion, and the gesture toward the chest relocates piety from the listed outward behaviours to the heart that produces them.
islam.tie_back: It gives virtue the same shape the Kural does: a named set of interpersonal faults avoided, with the real seat of the matter in the heart.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 2564a, narrated by Abu Hurayra

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: A compact rabbinic maxim naming three appetites that destroy a person's standing in this world and the next.
judaism.tie_back: It is the same rhetorical move as the Kural — a short enumerated list of faults whose avoidance constitutes a whole ethic.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:21 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Saleyyaka Sutta the Buddha itemises the ten courses of unwholesome action for the brahmins of Sala, and among them are harsh speech — words that are rough, bitter and abusive to others — covetousness for what belongs to another, and a mind of ill will; conduct in accordance with the Dhamma is then defined simply as the abstention from each of these.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta's whole method is to define right conduct as the negation of an enumerated list of bodily, verbal and mental faults.
buddhism.tie_back: Three of the Kural's four faults appear in that list, and the definitional method — virtue as what remains when the named faults are excluded — is identical.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 41, Saleyyaka Sutta (the ten courses of unwholesome and wholesome action)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.” … “One ought to put an end to anger through calmness, pride by modesty, deceit by straight-forwardness and greed by contentment.”
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics names four passions (kashaya), anger, pride, deceit and greed, as the fundamental stains that bind karma to the soul. The Dasavaikalika says what each one destroys and which virtue overcomes it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural defines virtue as conduct that steadily avoids four named faults. Jainism likewise defines purity through a fixed set of four passions, two of which (anger and greed) are the same as the Kural's.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 8.38-39 (numbering varies by edition), as Saman Suttam vv. 135-136, Samyamasutra (tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; text via jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O anger, you are the root of conflict; compassion never rises up in you.” … “O greed, you cling to even the great, assaulting them with countless waves.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Salok Sehskriti Guru Arjan addresses lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego one by one as personified enemies, the vices Sikh teaching calls the five thieves.
sikhism.tie_back: Two of Valluvar's four faults, anger and greed, appear here as named forces that destroy compassion and right conduct.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sehskriti, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid's Metamorphoses Athena, angered by the jealous Aglauros, sends her to the house of Invidia (Envy) — a black, rotting dwelling where the goddess sits gnawing vipers, never smiling, wasting away at the sight of others' good fortune. Invidia breathes her poison into Aglauros' breast, and the girl is consumed from within until she hardens into black stone on the threshold she had jealously guarded.
greek_mythology.explanation: Envy is portrayed as a self-destroying corrosion that literally petrifies the person who hosts it, rather than as an injury done to its object.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It gives vivid mythic form to the first item in the Kural's list of four, and to the idea that these faults ruin the person who harbours them.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But not every action nor every passion admits of a mean; for some have names that already imply badness, e.g. spite, shamelessness, envy, and in the case of actions adultery, theft, murder… It is not possible, then, ever to be right with regard to them; one must always be wrong.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle carves out an exception to his own doctrine of the mean: certain named passions and acts are bad in themselves, admitting no correct amount or occasion.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's four, these are faults to be excluded outright rather than moderated, and virtue is what proceeds without slipping into them.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (1107a), trans. W. D. Ross

real_life_example.event_title: Nelson Mandela wears the Springbok jersey at the Rugby World Cup final
real_life_example.event: Nelson Mandela, imprisoned from 1962 until his release in 1990 and elected South Africa's president in 1994, attended the 1995 Rugby World Cup final between South Africa and New Zealand. Before the match he walked into the Springbok changing room wearing a Springbok jersey with captain Francois Pienaar's number six, and after South Africa's victory he presented the trophy to Pienaar on the field while wearing it. The Nelson Mandela Foundation describes the moment as an enduring symbol of the democratic government's approach to reconciliation and nation-building.
real_life_example.explanation: Mandela embraced a sporting symbol cherished by many white South Africans, choosing reconciliation over resentment after decades of imprisonment under apartheid.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines virtue as conduct that steadily keeps clear of envy, greed, anger and harsh words, and Mandela's public gesture of goodwill toward former opponents shows anger and bitterness set aside.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

tamil:
அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது அறஞ்செய்க மற்றது
பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை.
transliteration:
Andrarivaam ennaadhu aranjeyka matradhu,
Pondrungaal pondraath thunai.
meaning: Do good now, and do not say, ‘I will do it later.’ When you die, the good you did is the friend that does not die with you.
elementary: If you keep saying you will pack your bag tomorrow, one day the bus leaves without you. This kural says do good things today, because they are the only things that stay with you when everything else is gone.
university: The idiom அன்றறிவாம் — literally 'we shall know on that day' — is the voice of procrastination personified; Parimelazhagar expands it as the young person's reasoning, 'we are young now, we will do it at the hour of death.' Against this Valluvar sets the wordplay that gives the couplet its force: பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை, 'at the time of perishing, the unperishing companion', built on repetition of the root பொன்று- in opposite senses. The image of virtue as துணை (companion, escort) that accompanies the soul past the body's dissolution is shared with Jain and Buddhist merit-doctrine, and Manakkudavar reads it explicitly as support in the next birth; the Dravidian rationalist commentator Kalaignar Karunanidhi instead reads it as imperishable fame. The verse is one of the clearest places where the Kural's deliberate theological reticence allows two very different readings of the same line.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: Son of Pṛthā, a transcendentalist engaged in auspicious activities does not meet with destruction either in this world or in the spiritual world; one who does good, My friend, is never overcome by evil.”
hinduism.explanation: Answering Arjuna's fear that an unfinished spiritual effort is simply wasted, Krishna assures him that accumulated good is never destroyed and carries across the break of death.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural's promise in reverse: because good done is indestructible, there is no reason to defer it and every reason to begin.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.40 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.”
christianity.explanation: The vision declares that a person's deeds accompany them past death — the labours cease but the works travel on with the doer.
christianity.tie_back: 'Their works do follow them' is almost a translation of பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை, the companion that does not perish.

islam.quote_or_event: “When a man dies, his acts come to an end, but three, recurring charity, or knowledge (by which people) benefit, or a pious child, who prays for him (for the deceased).”
islam.explanation: The hadith of ṣadaqa jāriya identifies the specific forms of good whose benefit continues to accrue to a person after the account of their deeds has otherwise closed.
islam.tie_back: It names exactly what the Kural means by the unperishing companion — the good done in life that outlives the doer.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 1631, narrated by Abu Hurayra

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eliezer said: Let the honor of your friend be as dear to you as your own; And be not easily provoked to anger; And repent one day before your death.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud records that Rabbi Eliezer's students objected that no one knows the day of their death, to which he answered: all the more reason, then, to repent today — lest one die tomorrow.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first line almost word for word: do not tell yourself you will attend to it when the time comes.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:10 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria); cf. b. Shabbat 153a

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As kinsmen welcome a dear one on arrival, even so his own good deeds will welcome the doer of good who has gone from this world to the next.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures a person's accumulated merit waiting for them on the far side of death like family gathered to greet a returning traveller.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the Kural's 'companion that does not perish', rendered as a homecoming rather than an escort.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who can call Death his friend, or who can escape him, or who knows that he will not die, might perhaps decide: this shall be done tomorrow.” … ‘Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.’
jainism.explanation: The two young sons of the priest Bhrigu refuse their father's advice to put off renunciation until old age, since no one has a pact with death. Later Queen Kamalavati tells the king that at death dharma alone goes with a person and protects them.
jainism.tie_back: This covers both halves of the Kural. One should not say 'we will see to it later', and the Law is the one companion that does not perish when the body does.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.27 and 14.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! That which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately! Later on, you will not be able to do anything, when death hangs over your head.”
sikhism.explanation: In one of his saloks preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, the bhagat Kabir attacks procrastination, insisting that good be done at once because death leaves no time for it later.
sikhism.tie_back: It is almost exactly Valluvar's rebuke of 'we will see to it when the time comes': do good now, before death arrives.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir 138 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Do not put your work off till to-morrow and the day after; for a sluggish worker does not fill his barn, nor one who puts off his work: industry makes work go well, but a man who puts off work is always at hand-grips with ruin.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's farming advice to his brother Perses treats deferral itself as the decisive cause of poverty and disaster, independent of ability or circumstance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's first line transposed to the farm — the one who says 'later' is already losing.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 410-413, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White

philosophy.quote_or_event: “While we are postponing, life speeds by.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca opens his first letter to Lucilius by urging him to gather and hold his time, since time is the only thing truly ours and the only loss that cannot be made good.
philosophy.tie_back: It supplies the reason the Kural forbids 'we shall know on that day': the day one is reserving for virtue is being spent right now.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 1 (On Saving Time), trans. Richard M. Gummere

real_life_example.event_title: Terry Fox's Marathon of Hope
real_life_example.place: St. John's, Newfoundland, to Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada
real_life_example.event: Terry Fox, who had lost his right leg to cancer at 18, set out from St. John's on 12 April 1980 to run across Canada and raise money for cancer research, covering 5,373 kilometres in 143 days, nearly a marathon a day. He was forced to stop near Thunder Bay on 1 September 1980 when his cancer returned, and he died on 28 June 1981. Before his death his goal of one dollar for every Canadian had been reached, and the annual Terry Fox Run held in his name has since raised hundreds of millions of dollars for cancer research.
real_life_example.explanation: Fox did not wait for a better time to act; he ran while he could, and the good he began has continued long after his death.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns against saying we will do good later and calls virtue the companion that does not perish when we perish, and Fox's run, made in the time he had, lives on in the yearly runs and research funded in his name.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

tamil:
அறத்தாறு இதுவென வேண்டா சிவிகை
பொறுத்தானோடு ஊர்ந்தான் இடை.
transliteration:
Araththaaru ithuvena ventaa sivikai,
Poruththaanotu oorndhaan itai.
meaning: No one needs to explain what doing good brings. Just look at the difference between the man carrying a palanquin (a covered chair carried on poles) and the man riding in it.
elementary: Some things you do not need explained — you just look. Two people are on the same road: one is carrying the chair, one is sitting in it. This kural says the difference between doing good and not doing good shows up like that, plain to see.
university: This is the Kural's most striking piece of epistemology. Parimelazhagar reads the verse in the technical vocabulary of Indian logic: there is no need for ஆகம அளவை (scriptural testimony, verbal authority) because காட்சி அளவை (pratyakṣa, direct perception) settles the matter. Valluvar is arguing that karmic consequence is empirically visible in the unequal fortunes of the palanquin-bearer and the palanquin-rider, an argument for virtue that requires no revelation. The verse has also been the chapter's most contested: modern readers, including Kalaignar Karunanidhi in his widely read commentary, have resisted the implication that social inequality is morally deserved, and reinterpret the pair as contrasting inner ease with inner burden rather than birth-station. Either way the rhetorical claim stands — the strength of virtue is a matter of observation, not argument.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Among them, those who did good work in this world [in their past life] attain a good birth accordingly. They are born as a brāhmin, a kṣatriya, or a vaiśya. But those who did bad work in this world [in their past life] attain a bad birth accordingly, being born as a dog, a pig, or as a casteless person.”
hinduism.explanation: The Chandogya's teaching of the two paths explains the visible inequality of births as the direct ripening of conduct in a previous life.
hinduism.tie_back: It supplies precisely the doctrine that makes the Kural's palanquin image legible — present station reads off past conduct.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles? Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus offers an empirical test for distinguishing true teachers from false: do not weigh their claims, observe what their lives produce.
christianity.tie_back: Same epistemic move as the Kural — do not expound the fruit of virtue in words, point at what is visible.

islam.quote_or_event: “They will each be assigned ranks according to their deeds. And your Lord is not unaware of what they do.”
islam.explanation: The verse establishes that differences of rank (darajāt) among created beings correspond exactly to what each has done.
islam.tie_back: It gives the Kural's contrast its principle: the gap between bearer and rider is a difference of rank proportioned to deeds.
islam.source: Qur'an 6:132, Al-An'am (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “With the measure that a person measures, he is measured with it.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah states the principle of middah k'neged middah, measure for measure, and then reads a series of visible outcomes as exactly proportioned to the conduct that produced them.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts read observable difference in fortune as a legible record of prior conduct.

buddhism.quote_or_event: King Ajatasattu asks the Buddha whether there is any fruit of the contemplative life that can actually be seen here and now, in the way a trainer of elephants or a cook can point to the visible benefit of his craft. The Buddha answers by asking the king what he would do if his own slave were to go forth and live virtuously — would he order him back to servitude? The king admits he would rise and offer him a seat; and the Buddha says: that is a fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now.
buddhism.explanation: The whole sutta is constructed around the demand for sandiṭṭhika — a result that can be pointed at rather than merely asserted — and the Buddha meets it with an everyday social observation.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the Kural's argument staged as a dialogue, complete with a contrast between the man who serves and the man who is served.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta (The Fruits of the Contemplative Life)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Every good deed will bear its fruit to men; there is no escape from the effect of one's actions.” … “You are now a king of great power and prosperity, enjoying the reward of your good actions”
jainism.explanation: The brothers Citta and Sambhuta, once born together as outcaste Svapakas, meet in a later life, one as the universal monarch Brahmadatta and the other as a monk. They explain their very different stations as the visible fruit of past karma.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural points to the gap between the palanquin-bearer and the rider as visible proof of virtue's fruit. The Jain story makes the same point, reading a king's splendour and an outcaste's misery as the open results of past deeds.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.1-20, esp. 13.10 and 13.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “By His Command, some are high and some are low; by His Written Command, pain and pleasure are obtained.”
sikhism.explanation: In the second stanza of the Japji, Guru Nanak traces every difference of high and low, pain and pleasure, to hukam, the divine order, and says that one who understands it no longer speaks in ego.
sikhism.tie_back: Both texts read the visible gap between the fortunate and the burdened as the working of a moral order, though Gurbani assigns it to God's Command rather than to one's own past virtue alone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 2, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as travellers, are turned away from a thousand doors in Phrygia until the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon take them in and share what little they have. The gods lead them up the hillside, and from there the couple watch the whole inhospitable district sink beneath a marsh while their own cottage is transformed into a gleaming temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: The reward and the ruin are made simultaneously visible from one vantage point, so the moral difference between the couple and their neighbours becomes a difference anyone can see in the landscape.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's roadside scene, it asks the observer simply to look at two conditions side by side and read the fruit of virtue off them.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Republic Book IX Socrates sets the just and the tyrannical lives side by side and argues that anyone who could see inside the tyrant would find the least free and most wretched of men, despite his apparent mastery — and he invites Glaucon to judge the ranking of lives by inspection rather than by argument.
philosophy.explanation: The argument turns on the claim that the true condition of a life is discoverable by looking at it whole, and that appearances of mastery and servitude can be exactly inverted.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the same comparative method as the Kural's palanquin, with the added twist that the one who appears to ride may be the one who is carried.

real_life_example.event_title: Charles Booth maps London's wealth and poverty street by street
real_life_example.event: Charles Booth, a successful businessman who doubted a claim that a quarter of Londoners lived in extreme poverty, funded and led a street-by-street inquiry into living conditions from 1886. In 1889 he published the first of his Descriptive Maps of London Poverty, colouring every residential street from yellow for the wealthy to black for the poorest, so that rich and poor streets could be seen side by side. His survey found that about 30.7 percent of Londoners lived in poverty, more than he had expected.
real_life_example.explanation: Booth's maps made the gulf between fortunes in one city visible at a glance, and they became a founding example of social mapping.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says no argument is needed because the difference in fortunes can simply be seen, as between palanquin-bearer and rider, and Booth's coloured streets let anyone see such differences for themselves.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

tamil:
வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை நன்றாற்றின் அஃதொருவன்
வாழ்நாள் வழியடைக்கும் கல்.
transliteration:
Veezhnaal pataaamai nandraatrin aqdhoruvan,
Vaazhnaal vazhiyataikkum kal.
meaning: If you do good every day, without letting a single day go by empty, it becomes a stone that blocks the road to being born again.
elementary: Imagine a gate that keeps swinging open, and every day you do a good thing you push a stone a little closer to it. Do it every single day and eventually the stone sits right in the gateway and the gate cannot open again.
university: The couplet turns on two metaphors that must be held together. வீழ்நாள் — a 'fallen day', a day let slip without good done — is set against கல், a blocking stone. Parimelazhagar reads வாழ்நாள் வழி as the road by which embodied life keeps recurring, so the daily practice of aram literally walls up the passage of rebirth; he glosses the whole verse as the statement that virtue yields வீடு (liberation), and imports the five kleśas of the Sanskrit tradition to explain what keeps the road open. The image of blocking rather than escaping is unusual and concrete — the Kural does not speak of transcending the cycle but of obstructing it, as one blocks a cattle-track with a boulder. Modern rationalist commentators such as Kalaignar Karunanidhi, resisting the rebirth reading, take கல் instead as a paving-stone that smooths the road of one's own life.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “By thus engaging in devotional service to the Lord, great sages or devotees free themselves from the results of work in the material world. In this way they become free from the cycle of birth and death and attain the state beyond all miseries.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes janma-bandha-vinirmukta — release from the bondage of birth — as the outcome of sustained right practice.
hinduism.tie_back: It names exactly what the Kural's stone accomplishes: the closing of the road by which birth recurs.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.51 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges the Ephesians to buy back their days from waste, treating each day as something that can be lost or reclaimed.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the Kural's first line — let no day fall away — though Christianity has no equivalent for blocking rebirth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do good deeds properly, sincerely and moderately and know that your deeds will not make you enter Paradise, and that the most beloved deed to Allah is the most regular and constant even if it were little.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet commends sustained daily practice over intense but intermittent effort, explicitly valuing regularity above magnitude.
islam.tie_back: It is the Kural's 'let no day fall away' stated as a rule of spiritual method: small and daily beats large and occasional.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Tarfon said: the day is short, and the work is plentiful, and the laborers are indolent, and the reward is great, and the master of the house is insistent.”
judaism.explanation: The saying presses the urgency of each day against the size of the moral task, treating any idle day as a real and irrecoverable loss.
judaism.tie_back: It captures the Kural's insistence that a day without good done is a day that has fallen.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:15 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “O house-builder, you are seen! You will not build this house again. For your rafters are broken and your ridgepole shattered. My mind has reached the Unconditioned; I have attained the destruction of craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's verse of victory addresses craving as the builder who has repeatedly constructed the house of embodied existence, and declares that it will never build again.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the Kural's image in construction rather than obstruction: the mechanism of repeated birth is permanently disabled.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse without profit to him who acts contrary to the Law. The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse with much profit to him who acts up to the Law.” … “We will even now adopt the Law, after the adoption of which we shall not be born again.”
jainism.explanation: Bhrigu's sons tell their father that each day spent without dharma is lost for good, while each day spent in it bears fruit, and that by taking up the Law now they will close off future births.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's practice of letting no day fall away empty, which becomes a stone blocking the road of rebirth, appears here in almost the same terms. In Jain terms the blocking is samvara, the stopping of karma's inflow.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.24-25 and 14.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe. Nothing else will work.”
sikhism.explanation: In this hymn from the evening Sodar liturgy, Guru Arjan presents human birth as a rare opportunity, warns that life spent in the love of Maya is squandered, and urges every effort to cross the world-ocean.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's warning against letting a single day fall empty, it treats life's time as the chance to close the road of rebirth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Orphic gold tablets buried with initiates in Southern Italy and Crete give the dead soul explicit instructions for the underworld: avoid the first spring you come to, go instead to the Lake of Memory, declare to the guardians 'I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven,' and drink — so that the soul may pass out of the wheel of grievous, deep-cycling births and be released.
greek_mythology.explanation: These are practical texts for escaping metempsychosis, a doctrine the Orphic and Pythagorean traditions held in common with Indian thought.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They offer the nearest Greek equivalent to the Kural's stone: a way of closing off the road that leads back into birth.
greek_mythology.source: Orphic gold tablets (Thurii and Petelia lamellae, 4th-3rd c. BCE)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Every moment think steadily as a Roman and a man to do what thou hast in hand with perfect and simple dignity, and feeling of affection, and freedom, and justice; and to give thyself relief from all other thoughts.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus prescribes a discipline organised around the present moment and the task actually at hand, refusing to postpone right action to some more suitable occasion.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives the Kural's 'no day allowed to fall' as a practical daily regimen rather than a cosmological promise.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations II.5, trans. George Long

real_life_example.event_title: Florence Nightingale's night rounds at Scutari
real_life_example.event: Florence Nightingale reached the British army's military hospital at Scutari during the Crimean War in late 1854 with a party of nurses. She organised cleaning, food kitchens and laundries, wrote letters home for soldiers and set up reading rooms, and in the evenings she went through the wards carrying a lamp to tend patients; a paper lantern she used on these rounds is now in the National Army Museum. She remained at Scutari until 1856, and she became known as the Lady with the Lamp, a name later fixed in Longfellow's poem Santa Filomena.
real_life_example.explanation: Nightingale's daily and nightly care helped transform nursing into a respected profession and set standards for modern hospital care.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises doing good without letting a single day fall away empty, and Nightingale's work, continued even through the nights, filled every day she spent at Scutari.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

tamil:
அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம் மற்றெல்லாம்
புறத்த புகழும் இல.
transliteration:
Araththaan varuvadhe inpam matrellaam,
Puraththa pukazhum ila.
meaning: Only happiness that comes from doing right is real happiness. Everything else is not happiness at all, and it brings no respect either.
elementary: Winning a game by cheating does not really feel like winning, and nobody claps for it. This kural says the only fun that is truly fun is the kind you got the right way.
university: The key word is புறத்த — 'they are outside', i.e. outside the category of இன்பம் (inbam, pleasure) altogether. Valluvar is not saying illicit pleasure is a lesser pleasure; he is saying it does not belong to the class at all, and Parimelazhagar completes the logic by noting that what lies outside pleasure is துன்பம், pain. The second clause adds a social criterion: such gains are also புகழும் இல, devoid of honour. Reading the verse against the third book of the Kural, the காமத்துப்பால் devoted entirely to erotic love, shows that Valluvar is not renouncing pleasure but defining its legitimate channel; Parimelazhagar accordingly glosses அறத்தான் as இல்லறத்தோடு பொருந்தி, 'in accordance with domestic virtue'. The verse thus quietly integrates the three aims of life rather than ranking them.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That happiness which is derived from contact of the senses with their objects and which appears like nectar at first but poison at the end is said to be of the nature of passion.”
hinduism.explanation: In his taxonomy of the three kinds of happiness Krishna distinguishes rājasic pleasure, sweet at the outset and toxic in its outcome, from sāttvic happiness that begins hard and ends in clarity.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts deny the name of real pleasure to enjoyment that is not grounded in right conduct.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.38 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;”
christianity.explanation: Moses is praised for rejecting Egypt's enjoyments as temporary — 'for a season' — in favour of a harder path with a lasting outcome.
christianity.tie_back: It draws the Kural's line between pleasure that comes through righteousness and pleasure that does not, and denies the latter any standing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds.”
islam.explanation: The promise of ḥayātan ṭayyiba — a good or wholesome life — attaches a present-tense quality of living, not merely a future reward, to righteous action.
islam.tie_back: It affirms the Kural's positive claim that the pleasure worth having is the pleasure that arrives by way of virtue.
islam.source: Qur'an 16:97, An-Nahl (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Her ways are pleasant ways, And all her paths, peaceful.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs personifies Wisdom and claims that the experience of walking her road is itself pleasant and peaceful, not merely instrumentally rewarding.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates genuine pleasantness inside the righteous path rather than as a prize at its end.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells the householder Anathapindika that there are four kinds of bliss available to a layman — the bliss of having wealth, of using it, of being free from debt, and of blamelessness — and concludes with a verse saying that the first three together are not worth one sixteenth of a sixteenth of the bliss of blamelessness, which consists in blameless action of body, speech and mind.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta grants that material enjoyments are real pleasures for a householder, then ranks the pleasure of an unreproachable life incomparably above them.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches both halves of the Kural — virtue-derived pleasure is the real thing, and the criterion involves blame and praise.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta (Debtless), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “All singing is but prattle, all dancing is but mocking, all ornaments are but a burden, all pleasures produce but pains. O king, pleasures which the ignorant like, but which produce pains, do not delight pious monks who care not for pleasure, but are intent on the virtues of right conduct.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citta tells King Brahmadatta that pleasures pursued for their own sake only end in pain, and that the joy of the wise lies in the virtues of right conduct.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that only what comes through virtue is true pleasure, and that everything else falls outside pleasure altogether. Citta likewise reclassifies sense-pleasure as pain and places real delight in right conduct.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.16-17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Baba, the pleasures of other foods are false. Eating them, the body is ruined, and wickedness and corruption enter into the mind.”
sikhism.explanation: In this Sri Raag hymn Guru Nanak sets the 'thirty-six flavours' found in love of the One against the pleasures of food, dress and riding, repeating in a refrain that all such pleasures are false and breed corruption.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, it denies the name of true pleasure to any enjoyment cut off from the right way, treating it as a source of harm.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus' allegory, reported by Xenophon, the young Heracles is met at a crossroads by two women. Vice promises him the shortest and pleasantest road, with every enjoyment taken without effort. Virtue answers that Vice does not even wait for genuine desire before gorging, so that she eats without hunger and drinks without thirst — and that of all things truly good and noble, the gods give nothing to men without toil.
greek_mythology.explanation: Virtue's rebuttal is not that pleasure is bad but that Vice's shortcuts destroy the very conditions under which pleasure can be felt, and earn no honour from gods or men.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It argues the Kural's exact case: pleasure taken outside virtue is not really pleasure, and brings no praise with it.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus, The Choice of Heracles, in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely and well and justly, and it is impossible to live wisely and well and justly without living pleasantly.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus — a hedonist by definition — makes justice and prudence not constraints on pleasure but its necessary conditions, so that the unjust life cannot be a pleasant one.
philosophy.tie_back: This is Kural 39 as a philosophical identity: pleasure and virtue are not two goods to be traded off but one.

real_life_example.event_title: Ben Johnson is stripped of his Olympic gold medal
real_life_example.event: On 24 September 1988 the Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson won the 100 metres at the Seoul Olympics in a world-record 9.79 seconds. Three days later he tested positive for the steroid stanozolol, and the International Olympic Committee stripped him of the gold medal and awarded it to the runner-up, Carl Lewis. Johnson, celebrated as the world's fastest man one day, became a byword for cheating in sport.
real_life_example.explanation: The episode is one of the most famous reversals in sporting history and a lasting lesson that victory gained by breaking the rules brings disgrace rather than glory.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says only what comes by way of virtue is true joy, while everything else is outside joy and brings no honour, and Johnson's triumph, won by forbidden means, was taken away within days and left only dishonour.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

tamil:
செயற்பால தோரும் அறனே ஒருவற்கு
உயற்பால தோரும் பழி.
transliteration:
Seyarpaala thorum arane oruvarku,
Uyarpaala thorum pazhi.
meaning: What a person should do is always what is right. What a person should avoid is always what deserves blame.
elementary: There are only two piles in life: things to do and things to keep away from. This kural puts everything kind and fair in the first pile, and everything you would be ashamed of in the second.
university: The chapter closes by compressing its whole argument into a definition. செயற்பால ('the doable', what belongs to the category of what should be done) is equated with அறன், and உயற்பால ('the avoidable') with பழி — blame, or what is blameworthy. The particles ஓரும் are treated by Parimelazhagar as அசைநிலை, metrical fillers carrying no independent sense, while the emphatic ஏ in அறனே is carried over to the second line by implication, making both halves exclusive. Manakkudavar adds a pointed reason for placing this verse last: Kural 38 had promised that virtue blocks rebirth, and a reader might suppose that good deeds could simply be added on top of bad ones — so Valluvar closes by insisting that the avoidance of blame is as constitutive of the definition as the doing of good. Notably, Valluvar chooses பழி (blame) rather than a word for sin, keeping his ethics answerable to public judgement rather than to divine law.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, that understanding by which one knows what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, what is to be feared and what is not to be feared, what is binding and what is liberating, is in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines sāttvic intelligence by its capacity to sort actions into kārya and akārya — what must be done and what must not.
hinduism.tie_back: It uses the identical binary that closes the Kural's chapter: the whole of practical wisdom is knowing what to do and what to shun.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.30 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul reduces ethical life to a double movement of recoil and attachment, addressed to the disposition rather than to particular rules.
christianity.tie_back: It is the Kural's two-column summary in the same compressed imperative form.

islam.quote_or_event: “Let there be a group among you who call ˹others˺ to goodness, encourage what is good, and forbid what is evil—it is they who will be successful.”
islam.explanation: This is the locus classicus for al-amr bi'l-ma'ruf wa'l-nahy 'an al-munkar, the twin obligation to enjoin the recognised good and forbid the recognised wrong.
islam.tie_back: The Islamic formula and the Kural's couplet share not just content but structure — a paired positive and negative that together exhaust moral duty.
islam.source: Qur'an 3:104, Ali 'Imran (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shun evil and do good, seek amity and pursue it.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm's instruction to the one who wants a good life pairs departure from evil with the doing of good as a single inseparable movement.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's two categories, stated in the same order and with the same finality.
judaism.source: Psalms 34:15 (JPS/Sefaria Tanakh; numbered 34:14 in Christian Bibles)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To avoid all evil, to cultivate good, and to cleanse one's mind — this is the teaching of the Buddhas.”
buddhism.explanation: Known as the Ovāda-pāṭimokkha, this verse is presented as the common teaching of all Buddhas, reducing the whole path to three clauses.
buddhism.tie_back: The first two clauses are Valluvar's two categories exactly, and the third recalls Kural 34's insistence on purity of mind.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One should desist from one thing, and practise another: desist from neglect of self-control, and practise self-control.”
jainism.explanation: The 'Mode of Life' lecture opens by reducing the whole Jain discipline to one twofold rule: turn away from lack of restraint (asamyama) and take up restraint (samyama).
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's closing definition, the Jain rule splits all conduct into what is to be done and what is to be shunned. The Jain criterion is restraint for the soul's sake, where the Kural speaks of public blame (pazhi).
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 31.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Virtue and vice do not come by mere words; actions repeated, over and over again, are engraved on the soul. You shall harvest what you plant.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Japji, Guru Nanak teaches that virtue and sin (punn and paap) are made by repeated deeds, which leave their mark on the self and bear their own fruit.
sikhism.tie_back: Both close on the plain binary of good to be done and wrong to be avoided, judged by deeds rather than talk.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 20, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “To you, foolish Perses, I will speak good sense. Badness can be got easily and in shoals: the road to her is smooth, and she lives very near us. But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first; but when a man has reached the top, then is she easy to reach, though before that she was hard.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's two roads divide all conduct into a smooth descent toward kakotēs and a steep climb toward aretē, with the gods themselves having fixed the difference.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It renders the Kural's two categories as two roads, one to be taken and one to be shunned.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 286-292, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Crito, Socrates gets Crito to agree that one must never do wrong — not even in return for wrong, and not even when wronged first — and treats this as the single fixed premise from which every practical decision, including whether to escape from prison, must follow.
philosophy.explanation: The argument establishes wrongdoing as an absolute category to be shunned without exception, rather than something to be weighed against consequences.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it reduces the whole of practical deliberation to one thing to be done and one thing to be avoided under all circumstances.

real_life_example.event_title: Frances Kelsey refuses to approve thalidomide
real_life_example.event: In 1960, during her first month as a medical officer at the US Food and Drug Administration, Frances Oldham Kelsey was assigned the application to market thalidomide, a sleeping pill already sold in many countries. Despite constant pressure from the company, she refused to approve it until she had scientifically reliable evidence of its safety. About a year later researchers linked the drug to severe birth defects in thousands of babies in other countries; thalidomide was never marketed in the United States, and in 1962 President Kennedy gave Kelsey the President's Award for Distinguished Federal Civilian Service.
real_life_example.explanation: By doing exactly what her duty required and refusing what would have been blameworthy, Kelsey prevented a tragedy in her country and helped bring about stronger drug laws.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says what ought to be done is virtue and what ought to be avoided is what deserves blame, and Kelsey held firmly to the one and refused the other under heavy pressure.

tamil:
இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் இயல்புடைய மூவர்க்கும்
நல்லாற்றின் நின்ற துணை.
transliteration:
Ilvaazhvaan enpaan iyalputaiya moovarkkum,
Nallaatrin nindra thunai.
meaning: A person who truly lives family life is a steady helper on the good path for the three other kinds of people who depend on them.
elementary: Think of a family like a table. The person who runs the household is the tabletop — everyone else rests on it. Parents, partner, children (and in the old way of counting, students, hermits, and wandering monks) all lean on the householder, and a good householder holds them all up and keeps them going the right way.
university: The chapter that opens the இல்லறவியல் (illaraviyal, “the way of domestic virtue”) begins by defining the householder functionally rather than sentimentally: he is a துணை (thunai, “support/companion/prop”) who stands நல்லாற்றின் (nallaatrin, “in the good way”). Commentators split sharply on who the “three” (மூவர்) are. Parimelazhagar and the older Sanskritising tradition read them as the other three ashramas — brahmacharin, vanaprastha and sannyasin — aligning the verse with Manu's grihastha doctrine; Kalaignar Karunanidhi and Salomon Pappaiah read them domestically as parents, spouse and children (or children, parents and kin). Valluvar's deliberate vagueness lets both readings stand, which is characteristic of his non-sectarian method. The crucial word is நின்ற (nindra, “having stood firm”) — not occasional charity but a standing, load-bearing role, and the standing must be *on the right path*, so that support which enables wrongdoing does not count.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As all living creatures subsist by receiving support from air, even so (the members of) all orders subsist by receiving support from the householder.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu argues that the student, forest-hermit and renunciant orders cannot function at all without the householder's food and gifts, which is why he calls the householder's order the most excellent.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the same sentence as the Kural: the householder is the firm support of the other three orders.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 3.77 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes material provision for one's household not an optional kindness but the minimum test of genuine faith.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts define the householder by the duty of being a reliable support to dependents, and treat failure there as a failure of virtue itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “All of you are guardians and responsible for your wards and the things under your care. The Imam (i.e. ruler) is the guardian of his subjects and is responsible for them and a man is the guardian of his family and is responsible for them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet frames every social role as a trust (ra'iyyah) for which one will be held accountable, with the head of a household explicitly named.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the householder's accountable support of dependents the defining content of the role, not an extra.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 893, Book of Friday Prayer

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud enumerates the obligations a father owes a son — to circumcise him, redeem him, teach him Torah, marry him off, and teach him a trade (some add: teach him to swim) — treating the household head as legally bound to equip those in his care for life.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic law turns paternal affection into an enforceable list of duties, so that being a householder is a bundle of specific obligations rather than a status.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions define the householder as one who is obligated to be a practical, ongoing support to those naturally dependent on him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha reinterprets the young householder Sigala's ritual worship of the six directions as the householder's reciprocal duties toward parents (east), teachers (south), wife and children (west), friends (north), workers (below) and ascetics and brahmins (above).
buddhism.explanation: The sutta is the classic Buddhist charter of lay life: the householder is the hub of a web of mutual obligations, including support of the renunciant community.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the householder the structural support of several distinct groups, explicitly including those who have renounced.

jainism.quote_or_event: “It will not behove me, during the life of my parents, to tear out my hair, and leaving the house to enter the state of houselessness.”
jainism.explanation: While still in the womb, Mahāvīra resolves not to renounce the household while his parents live, so that the future Jina himself first fulfils the householder's obligation to those who depend on him.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar defines the true householder as the steady support of those who rely on him, and the Kalpa Sūtra has the greatest Jain renouncer defer his own vocation until that support is no longer needed.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §94 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who have meditated on the Naam, the Name of the Lord, and departed after having worked by the sweat of their brows - O Nanak! Their faces are radiant in the Court of the Lord, and many are saved along with them!”
sikhism.explanation: The closing salok of the Japji joins the two halves of the Sikh householder ideal, remembrance of the Name and honest labour, and says that such a life carries many others along with it.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's householder who is the steady support of those who depend on him, the one who works and remembers God is pictured as someone whom many others are carried by.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib, closing Salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “First of all, get a house, and a woman and an ox for the plough … and make everything ready at home, so that you may not have to ask of another, and he refuses you, and so, because you are in lack, the season pass by and your work come to nothing.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's farmer's almanac treats the establishment of a self-sufficient household as the first move in a virtuous life; the ellipsis omits his harsh qualification that the woman be a hired labourer rather than a wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts put the household first in the moral order, though Hesiod's emphasis is self-sufficiency where the Kural's is supporting others.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Duties are universally measured by relations. Is anyone a father? If so, it is implied that the children should take care of him, submit to him in everything, patiently listen to his reproaches, his correction.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus derives concrete obligations directly from one's place in a web of relationships — father, brother, neighbour, citizen — rather than from abstract rules.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's method: the householder's virtue is defined by the relations he stands in and what those relations require of him.

real_life_example.event_title: Young Anton Chekhov supports his family
real_life_example.event: When Anton Chekhov's father went bankrupt and, facing prison, moved the family to Moscow, the teenage Anton stayed behind in Taganrog from 1876 to 1879, earning his living as a tutor and sending money to his parents. After entering the medical faculty of Moscow University in 1879, where the family lived in poverty, he supported them by writing large numbers of comic stories and sketches for humorous magazines while he studied.
real_life_example.explanation: Before he became one of the world's great writers, Chekhov's early work was driven by the need to keep his parents and siblings afloat.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines the true householder as the steady support of those who depend on him, and the young Chekhov became the mainstay of his parents and siblings through honest work.

tamil:
துறந்தார்க்கும் துவ்வாதவர்க்கும் இறந்தார்க்கும்
இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை.
transliteration:
Thurandhaarkkum thuvvaadhavarkkum irandhaarkkum,
Ilvaazhvaan enpaan thunai.
meaning: A family person supports those who have given up worldly life, those who are poor and hungry, and those who have died.
elementary: Imagine one family in a village that keeps a pot of rice always ready. The travelling monk who owns nothing eats from it. The hungry neighbour eats from it. And a share is set aside in memory of grandparents who have died. That one household quietly feeds three groups who cannot feed themselves.
university: Valluvar names three classes with three neat participial nouns: துறந்தார் (thurandhaar, “those who have let go”), துவ்வாதவர் (thuvvaadhavar, literally “those who do not eat” — the destitute), and இறந்தார் (irandhaar, “those who have passed”). The last is the most striking to a modern reader: the dead are treated as an ongoing claim on the living, through the memorial offerings (தென்புலத்தார் rites) that the next couplet will name explicitly. The verse is a deliberate argumentative move within a Tamil intellectual landscape in which Jain and Buddhist renunciant ideals were culturally prestigious: Valluvar concedes the renunciant's standing and then points out that the renunciant literally eats because a householder cooked. Economic dependency becomes a moral argument for the dignity of domestic life.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Charity given out of duty, without expectation of return, at the proper time and place, and to a worthy person is considered to be in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna classifies charity by motive: sattvic giving is given because it ought to be given, to those who genuinely merit it, with no thought of return.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's householder gives to renunciants, the destitute and the dead — three classes that by definition can never repay him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.”
christianity.explanation: James relocates the essence of religion from ritual to the concrete care of society's most defenceless members.
christianity.tie_back: Both verses define true piety as practical support for those who cannot support themselves, rather than as withdrawal or ceremony.

islam.quote_or_event: “…but [true] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask [for help], and for freeing slaves…”
islam.explanation: The famous 'verse of righteousness' lists the specific categories of dependent people whose support constitutes real piety, against merely outward observance.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures a person's virtue by the list of unrepaying dependants he sustains out of his own household wealth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Charity is given to the living, while acts of kindness are performed both for the living and for the dead.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud ranks gemilut chasadim above tzedakah partly because kindness extends to the dead — burial and mourning rites are called chesed shel emet, 'true kindness', since the recipient can never repay.
judaism.tie_back: This is an unusually exact parallel: the Kural likewise lists the dead alongside the poor as recipients of the householder's support.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 49b (Koren-Steinsaltz / William Davidson Edition)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Householders & the homeless / in mutual dependence / both reach the true Dhamma: / the unsurpassed safety from bondage. / From householders, the homeless / receive requisites: robes, lodgings, / protection from inclemencies.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the lay-monastic relationship as reciprocal: householders supply material requisites, monastics supply the Dhamma, and neither reaches the goal without the other.
buddhism.tie_back: This states the Kural's first clause outright — the renunciant (துறந்தார்) survives because the householder supports him.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Yathavat atithau sadhau dine cha pratipatti-krt : Diligent in succoring the ascetics, the righteous and the needy.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra counts care for ascetics and the destitute among the defining qualities of a good Jain layman, and the lay vow of atithi-saṃvibhāga commits the householder to eat only after feeding mendicants.
jainism.tie_back: Two of the Kural's three dependants, those who have renounced and those who have nothing to eat, are exactly the people Jain lay ethics charges the householder to support.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra 1.47–56 (the thirty-five householder qualities, no. 19), English as given in V. A. Sangave, Ethics of Jainism

sikhism.quote_or_event: Sent by his father with money to start trading, the young Nanak met a band of holy men who had not eaten for days, gave them the money, and bought them food, saying he had spent it to the best advantage.
sikhism.explanation: Macauliffe retells this Janamsakhi episode, remembered by Sikhs as the sacha sauda or true bargain: the first act of the future Guru's working life is to feed renunciants and the hungry from household money.
sikhism.tie_back: It enacts the Kural's claim that the renunciant and the destitute eat because a householder provides, here literally with a householder's trading capital.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter III, pp. 30-31

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles' Antigone, Antigone defies Creon's edict and performs burial rites for her brother Polyneices, insisting that the unwritten laws owed to the dead outrank a ruler's decree, and accepts death rather than leave him unburied.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek religion held that the dead had an enforceable claim on their kin for burial and grave offerings, and that failing them polluted the whole household and city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural's most distinctive element — that the dead (இறந்தார்) remain dependants of the living household.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues in De Officiis that we are not born for ourselves alone — our country, our parents, our friends and our fellow human beings each claim a share of our existence — and that this is why generosity and beneficence are duties of justice rather than optional favours.
philosophy.explanation: Stoic-influenced Roman ethics grounds the obligation to support others in the claim that a person's life is partly owned by the communities that made it possible.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts derive the householder's obligation to support non-reciprocating others from the simple fact of belonging to a community.

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Harsha's five-yearly gift-giving at Prayag
real_life_example.event: Harsha, who ruled much of northern India from 606 to 647, held a great gathering every five years at Prayag, where the Ganges and Yamuna meet. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who travelled in India between 629 and 645, recorded the king's generosity there, describing how he gave gifts and donations to scholars and ascetics. At these ceremonies of giving, most of the wealth gathered over the previous five years was given away in charity.
real_life_example.explanation: Harsha's assemblies became one of the most celebrated examples of royal charity in early Indian history, preserved by an eyewitness from another land.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names the householder as the support of those who have renounced the world and of the destitute, and Harsha's gifts to ascetics and to the needy at Prayag show such support given on a grand scale.

tamil:
தென்புலத்தார் தெய்வம் விருந்தொக்கல் தானென்றாங்கு
ஐம்புலத்தாறு ஓம்பல் தலை.
transliteration:
Thenpulaththaar theyvam virundhokkal thaanendraangu,
Aimpulaththaaru ompal thalai.
