meaning: The main duty of a family person is to take good care of these five: their ancestors who have died, the gods, guests, relatives, and themselves.
elementary: A good household is like a table set with five plates. One is for the grandparents who have passed away, one is for God, one for whoever knocks at the door, one for the family, and one for yourself. Forgetting any plate — including your own — means the table isn't really set.
university: This is the Kural's compressed version of the fivefold domestic obligation. தென்புலத்தார் (thenpulaththaar) literally means “those of the southern region” — the dead, since the south is Yama's quarter — and is the standard Tamil term for the ancestors (pitṛ). The other four are தெய்வம் (theyvam, the gods), விருந்து (virundhu, the guest — a theme Valluvar gives a whole chapter to at 9), ஒக்கல் (okkal, kin), and தான் (thaan, oneself). The inclusion of *oneself* is philosophically important: Valluvar's domestic ethic is not self-erasing asceticism but a balanced distribution, captured by ஓம்பல் (ombal, “to cherish/tend/guard”) and by தலை (thalai, “the head, the foremost thing”). The scheme corresponds closely to the Brahminical pañca-mahāyajña, but Valluvar strips it of ritual technicality and states it as household budgeting of love and resources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But he who does not feed these five, the gods, his guests, those whom he is bound to maintain, the manes, and himself, lives not, though he breathes.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu's formulation of the five great sacrifices makes daily household life itself a continuous ritual obligation toward gods, guests, dependants, ancestors and self.
hinduism.tie_back: The five items and their order are effectively identical to the Kural's ஐம்புலம் — gods, guests, kin, the departed, and oneself.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 3.72 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews grounds Christian hospitality in the Genesis episode of Abraham unknowingly hosting divine messengers, making the guest a potential bearer of the sacred.
christianity.tie_back: It fuses two of the Kural's five claims — the guest (விருந்து) and the divine (தெய்வம்) — into a single duty of the household.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should not harm his neighbor, and anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should entertain his guest generously and anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet lists domestic and neighbourly conduct — not private devotion — as the direct proof of belief in God and the hereafter.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats honouring the guest and one's immediate circle as the householder's headline religious duty.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018, Book of Good Manners (Al-Adab)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hospitality toward guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence.”
judaism.explanation: Rav derives this from Abraham asking God to wait while he attends to three travellers (Genesis 18:3), making hachnasat orchim outrank even direct communion with God.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural lists guests alongside the gods among the five claims; the Talmud goes further and ranks the guest above the divine visitation.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 127a (Koren-Steinsaltz / William Davidson Edition)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “…performs the five oblations: to relatives, guests, the dead, kings, & devas. This is the fourth benefit that can be obtained from wealth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the householder Anathapindika that righteously earned wealth should be used for five purposes, one of which is a set of five customary offerings.
buddhism.tie_back: Four of the Kural's five claims appear verbatim here — relatives, guests, the dead, and the gods — as duties of household wealth.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.41, Adiya Sutta, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “The six daily activities or duties of householders are : worship of God, worship of the preceptor, study of scriptures, practice of self control, practice of austerities, and giving gifts.”
jainism.explanation: A widely cited Sanskrit verse (devapūjā gurūpāstiḥ svādhyāyaḥ saṃyamas tapaḥ / dānaṃ ceti gṛhasthānāṃ ṣaṭ karmāṇi dine dine) gives the Jain householder a fixed list of daily duties.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism has its own list of the householder's daily duties that sits beside Valluvar's fivefold one, though the two lists are not the same.
jainism.source: Ṣaḍ-āvaśyaka verse for householders, as quoted and translated in V. A. Sangave, Ethics of Jainism (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He does not honor his ancestors while they are alive, but he holds feasts in their honor after they have died. Tell me, how can his poor ancestors receive what the crows and the dogs have eaten up?”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose hymns the Gurus included in the scripture, mocks memorial feasts for the dead and offerings to gods made of clay, and asks people to honour their elders while they live and to remember the one Lord who has no ancestors.
sikhism.tie_back: It speaks to two of the Kural's five claims, ancestors and gods, but turns them around: Sikh teaching keeps the duty to kin and guests and drops ritual offerings to the dead and the gods.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 332, Raag Gauri Bairaagan, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how Jupiter and Mercury, travelling disguised, are turned away by a thousand homes until the poor elderly couple Baucis and Philemon welcome them into their one-room cottage, share their scant food, and are spared the flood that destroys their impious neighbours.
greek_mythology.explanation: The tale is the definitive Greco-Roman statement of xenia — the sacred obligation of the household hearth to the stranger, enforced by Zeus Xenios himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises three of the Kural's five claims at once: the guest, the gods, and the household itself, all met at a single hearth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero maps the degrees of human fellowship in concentric circles and holds that the first bond of society is that between husband and wife, then parents and children, then the household — which he calls the foundation of civil government and, as it were, the nursery of the state.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, moral obligation is graded: we owe most to those nearest, and the household is the training ground from which civic duty grows.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts organise the householder's duties as a ranked set of claims radiating outward from the home.

real_life_example.event_title: UNESCO recognises Mexico's Day of the Dead
real_life_example.event: In 2003 UNESCO proclaimed the indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead, as practised in Mexico, a masterpiece of humanity's intangible heritage, and in 2008 inscribed it on its Representative List. At the end of October and start of November, families lay flower petals and candles along the path from the cemetery to their homes, prepare the favourite dishes of departed relatives, and place them with offerings on home altars and graves. The custom blends pre-Hispanic rites with the Catholic feasts of All Saints and All Souls.
real_life_example.explanation: The festival shows a whole society setting aside time each year to honour its ancestors through family gatherings, shared food and religious observance.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural lists the householder's duty to the departed ancestors, the gods, kin and others, and the Day of the Dead joins remembrance of ancestors, worship and family feasting in a single household observance.

tamil:
பழியஞ்சிப் பாத்தூண் உடைத்தாயின் வாழ்க்கை
வழியெஞ்சல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இல்.
transliteration:
Pazhiyanjip paaththoon utaiththaayin vaazhkkai,
Vazhiyenjal egngnaandrum il.
meaning: If a family fears doing anything shameful and shares its food with others, its family line will never die out.
elementary: Suppose a family grows apples honestly and always gives some away to neighbours. Everyone keeps trading with them, everyone helps them in a bad year, and the orchard keeps going for generations. A family that steals its apples and eats them alone soon has neither friends nor orchard.
university: Two conditions are compressed into one line: பழியஞ்சி (pazhi-anji, “fearing blame/reproach”) governs *acquisition*, and பாத்தூண் (paath-ūṇ, from பகுத்து உண்ணல், “eating after apportioning”) governs *consumption*. The reward is stated negatively and absolutely: வழி எஞ்சல் … இல் — “there is never a failing of the line.” வழி (vazhi) means both “way” and “lineage,” so the promise is simultaneously that the household's path and its descendants will not run out. Note that Valluvar's ethical lever here is பழி (pazhi, public blame) rather than sin — an honour-and-reproach vocabulary rooted in Tamil Sangam social ethics rather than in a theology of divine punishment, which is part of why the Kural reads as secular to modern audiences.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The devotees of the Lord are released from all kinds of sins because they eat food which is offered first for sacrifice. Others, who prepare food for personal sense enjoyment, verily eat only sin.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna contrasts food that has first been offered and shared with food cooked purely for one's own gratification, calling the latter itself a form of wrongdoing.
hinduism.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural's பாத்தூண் principle: eating only what has first been apportioned to others is what keeps the household clean.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor: his righteousness remaineth for ever. Now he that ministereth seed to the sower both minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits of your righteousness.”
christianity.explanation: Paul uses an agricultural image: giving away is sowing, and the giver's store is replenished and multiplied rather than depleted.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts promise that the household which shares its food does not diminish but endures and multiplies.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they give food in spite of love for it to the needy, the orphan, and the captive,”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Insan praises the righteous specifically for giving away food they themselves want, and promises them lasting reward.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's second condition exactly — the household's virtue lies in apportioning its own meal outward.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread. He is ever merciful, and lendeth; and his seed is blessed.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist's lifelong observation is that generosity and descendants' security go together — the open-handed man's children do not end up beggars.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact promise: the household that shares its bread finds its line never fails.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada makes generosity the decisive factor in a layperson's future welfare, and hoarding the decisive obstacle.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts tie the household's long-term fortune directly to whether it shares what it has.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Nyayasampannavibhavah : Possessed of honestly earned wealth.” … “Papabhiru : Apprehensive of sin.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra's list of the ideal layman's qualities opens with wealth earned by just means and soon adds fear of wrongdoing, putting ethical acquisition first among the householder's virtues.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's 'fearing blame' in earning is matched almost word for word by Hemacandra's first and third qualities, honest wealth and fear of sin, and the Jain duty of giving supplies the Kural's 'sharing what one eats'.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra 1.47–56 (the thirty-five householder qualities, nos. 1 and 3), English as given in V. A. Sangave, Ethics of Jainism

sikhism.quote_or_event: At Saiyidpur Guru Nanak stayed with Lalo, a poor carpenter, and declined the feast of Malik Bhago, a steward grown rich by bribery and oppression. Holding Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Bhago's rich bread in the other, he squeezed them; milk came from Lalo's and blood from Bhago's.
sikhism.explanation: Macauliffe tells this well-known Janamsakhi story to show the Sikh principle that food earned by honest labour is pure, while food gained by exploiting others is tainted, however lavishly it is shared.
sikhism.tie_back: It is the Sikh image of Valluvar's two conditions: earning without blame and sharing what one eats; Bhago shares but fails the first test, and so his bread is refused.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter IV, pp. 43-44

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Wealth should not be seized: god-given wealth is much better; for it a man take great wealth violently and perforce, or if he steal it through his tongue … the gods soon blot him out and make that man's house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that dishonestly gotten wealth is punished by Zeus not just personally but at the level of the household, which is brought low.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's first condition stated as its negative: the household that does not fear blame in acquiring will see its line fail.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle analyses liberality (eleutheriotes) as a mean concerning wealth: the liberal person gives the right amounts to the right people at the right time, gives from his own resources rather than by taking wrongly, and cares more about giving well than about getting.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the virtue is not generosity alone but the pairing of clean acquisition with well-judged distribution — the two are aspects of a single disposition.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes exactly that pairing: blameless earning and apportioned eating are two halves of one household virtue.

real_life_example.event_title: Mitsui Takatoshi opens the Echigoya shop
real_life_example.event: Mitsui Takatoshi, a merchant from Matsusaka who had earlier returned home to care for his mother, opened a textile shop called Echigoya in Edo in 1673. The shop became known for selling for cash at fixed prices with no mark-ups, as its signboards announced, and it grew into the largest textile store of the Edo period. Echigoya became the forerunner of the Mitsukoshi department store, and the family's money-exchange business led eventually to the modern Mitsui group.
real_life_example.explanation: Mitsui's plain, fair pricing helped build one of the longest-lasting family enterprises in the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural promises that a household that earns without blame will never see its line fail, and the Mitsui name, founded on openly fair dealing, has continued for more than three centuries.

tamil:
அன்பும் அறனும் உடைத்தாயின் இல்வாழ்க்கை
பண்பும் பயனும் அது.
transliteration:
Anpum aranum utaiththaayin ilvaazhkkai,
Panpum payanum adhu.
meaning: If family life has love and goodness, then that is both its true nature and its reward.
elementary: Think of a fruit tree that is both beautiful and gives fruit. You don't grow it for some other prize somewhere else — the tree being what it is *is* the prize. A home with love and goodness in it is the same: it is not a step toward the good life, it already is the good life.
university: The verse turns on a deliberate identity statement: பண்பும் பயனும் அது — “its quality and its fruit are *that*.” Valluvar collapses the usual ethical distinction between a virtue and the reward the virtue earns. அன்பு (anpu, love) and அறன் (aran, virtue/dharma) are not instruments for obtaining household happiness; they *constitute* it. This is a genuinely Aristotelian move — the household, rightly constituted, is an end in itself, not a means — and it is what allows Valluvar in the following verses to argue that the householder need not look elsewhere (46) and outranks the ascetic (48). அன்பு gets a full chapter later (8, அன்புடைமை); here it is paired with அறன் so that affection alone is not enough, nor correctness alone.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In that family, where the husband is pleased with his wife and the wife with her husband, happiness will assuredly be lasting.”
hinduism.explanation: Amid a chapter of ritual prescriptions, Manu states plainly that mutual delight between spouses is the condition of a household's durable well-being.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts locate the household's happiness in the quality of affection inside it rather than in any external result.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 3.60 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.”
christianity.explanation: Writing to a household-based congregation, Paul lists the virtues and then names love as the binding agent that holds them together and completes them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same claim structurally: love plus virtue is not a route to completeness but is the completeness itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought.”
islam.explanation: Marriage is presented as a sign of God, its purpose being sakīnah (tranquillity), with mawaddah (affection) and raḥmah (mercy) placed between the couple.
islam.tie_back: Affection and mercy are named as the constituents of married life exactly as அன்பு and அறன் are in the Kural, and the tranquillity is the state itself, not a later payoff.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs weighs a household's material abundance against its emotional quality and decides unambiguously for love.
judaism.tie_back: Both couplets say that the household's worth lies in the love inside it, not in what the household yields.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If both husband & wife want to see one another not only in the present life but also in the life to come, they should be in tune [with each other] in conviction, in tune in virtue, in tune in generosity, and in tune in discernment.”
buddhism.explanation: Answering the devoted couple Nakulapita and Nakulamata, the Buddha says that a marriage endures on shared moral qualities, not on feeling alone.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it insists on the pairing: affection must be matched by shared virtue for domestic life to be what it should be.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Uvāsagadasāo the wealthy merchant Ānanda of Vāṇijyagrāma takes the twelve lay vows from Mahāvīra, and his wife Śivanandā goes to Mahāvīra and takes the same vows, so that the couple share a single discipline as householders.
jainism.explanation: The first and model story of the Jain lay canon shows a household whose love is joined to shared observance of the vows, with both husband and wife counted as members of the fourfold community.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says love joined with virtue is both the nature and the fruit of household life, and Ānanda and Śivanandā are the Jain canon's model of that union of affection and dharma in one home.
jainism.source: Uvāsagadasāo (Upāsakadaśāḥ) ch. 1, story of Ānanda (tr. A. F. R. Hoernlé, 1890); summary at jainworld.com

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They are not said to be husband and wife, who merely sit together. They alone are called husband and wife, who have one light in two bodies.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das defines marriage not by living under one roof but by an inner unity of love and spirit, a verse often read at Sikh weddings.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, who says love and virtue are both the nature and the fruit of domestic life, the Guru places the whole meaning of the household in the shared inner life of the couple.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “May heaven grant you in all things your heart's desire — husband, house, and a happy, peaceful home; for there is nothing better in this world than that man and wife should be of one mind in a house. It discomfits their enemies, makes the hearts of their friends glad, and they themselves know more about it than any one.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, shipwrecked and naked, blesses Nausicaa with the highest good he can name: homophrosynē, the like-mindedness of husband and wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in Homeric form — that a household of shared mind and heart is simply the best thing there is, not a means to something better.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that the friendship between husband and wife exists by nature, combines the useful and the pleasant, and becomes best of all when the partners are good, so that each delights in the other's virtue; on that basis children too are a bond.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the highest form of philia is between good people who love each other for their virtue, and he explicitly applies this to marriage.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact combination — love and virtue together — as what makes a household both what it ought to be and worth having.

real_life_example.event_title: The von Trapp family leaves Nazi-annexed Austria
real_life_example.place: Salzburg, Austria, to Stowe, Vermont, United States
real_life_example.event: The von Trapps of Salzburg had turned their family love of singing into a professional choir after losing most of their wealth when their bank failed in the early 1930s. After Nazi Germany annexed Austria in 1938, Georg von Trapp refused to fly the Nazi flag on their house, declined a naval command and turned down a request for the family to sing at Hitler's birthday party. Unwilling to compromise their principles, the family left Austria by train for Italy and went on to America, where they toured as the Trapp Family Singers and settled on a farm in Stowe, Vermont.
real_life_example.explanation: The real von Trapps chose to give up home and possessions together rather than serve a regime they abhorred, and they rebuilt their life as a family.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that love and virtue are both the character and the reward of domestic life, and the von Trapps, bound by affection and holding to principle, found their wealth in each other rather than in what they left behind.

tamil:
அறத்தாற்றின் இல்வாழ்க்கை ஆற்றின் புறத்தாற்றில்
போஒய்ப் பெறுவ தெவன்?
transliteration:
Araththaatrin ilvaazhkkai aatrin puraththaatril,
Pooip peruva thevan?
meaning: If a person lives family life in the right way, what more could they gain by leaving it for some other path?
elementary: If the water in your own well is clean and cold, why walk ten miles to another village's well? The answer is: there's no reason to. Living well at home already gives you what you would go looking for elsewhere.
university: The couplet is framed as a rhetorical question — பெறுவது எவன்? (“what is there to obtain?”) — and the expected answer is “nothing.” புறத்தாற்றில் (puraththaatril, “on the outside path”) is the polite euphemism for the ascetic's road, the துறவறம் that Valluvar treats sympathetically in chapters 3 and 35. The argument is not that renunciation is false but that it is redundant *for someone already doing the domestic path properly*, the operative qualifier being அறத்தாற்றின் (“by the way of virtue”). Note the doubled ஆறு/ஆற்று root — path, path, outside-path — which makes the verse a small meditation on the metaphor of the road itself. This is the pivot on which the whole chapter, and arguably the whole of Book I's householder section, turns.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is unattached to the fruits of his work and who works as he is obligated is in the renounced order of life, and he is the true mystic, not he who lights no fire and performs no duty.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna redefines sannyāsa as an inner condition available to anyone doing their duty, explicitly denying that extinguishing the household fire makes one a renunciant.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's argument almost verbatim: the household path rightly followed already contains whatever the outside path was supposed to supply.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils; … Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.”
christianity.explanation: The Pastoral Epistles attack an early ascetic movement that treated marriage and food as impediments to holiness, calling the doctrine demonic.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts push back against the assumption that leaving domestic life is a higher spiritual road.

islam.quote_or_event: “Are you the same people who said so-and-so? By Allah, I am more submissive to Allah and more afraid of Him than you; yet I fast and break my fast, I do sleep and I also marry women. So he who does not follow my tradition in religion, is not from me.”
islam.explanation: Three men had resolved to pray all night, fast perpetually, and never marry; the Prophet rebuked them, making moderate married life the normative religious path.
islam.tie_back: It answers the Kural's rhetorical question with a flat 'nothing' — there is no superior road outside the ordinary married life.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud records Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's view that the nazirite who abstains from wine must bring a sin-offering because he denied himself something permitted, and that anyone who afflicts himself by further such abstentions is called a sinner.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic Judaism is structurally suspicious of voluntary self-denial: creation's permitted pleasures are to be sanctified in ordinary life, not renounced.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions deny that stepping outside ordinary domestic life earns any additional merit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither going about naked, nor matted locks, nor filth, nor fasting, nor lying on the ground, nor smearing oneself with ashes and dust, nor sitting on the heels (in penance) can purify a mortal who has not overcome doubt.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha, who had himself tried extreme austerity, denies that any external ascetic practice purifies anyone by itself.
buddhism.tie_back: It grants the Kural's premise that the outside path holds no automatic advantage, though it does not go on to prefer the householder.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Bark and skin (of a goat), nakedness, twisted hair, baldness--these (outward tokens) will not save a sinful ascetic. … A sinner, though he be a mendicant (friar), will not escape hell; but a pious man, whether monk or householder, ascends to heaven.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana denies that the outward marks of renunciation are worth anything in themselves: a virtuous householder reaches heaven just as a virtuous monk does.
jainism.tie_back: When the Kural asks what a virtuous householder would gain by taking the 'other path', the Jain sūtra answers in part: the ascetic's insignia gain nothing on their own.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.21–22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak! Meeting the True Guru, one comes to know the Perfect Way. While laughing, playing, dressing and eating, he is liberated.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that liberation is not reserved for those who leave the world; it is found in the middle of ordinary life, by one who follows the Guru's way.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar asks what more anyone could gain by leaving a virtuous home for another path; the Guru answers that even liberation is reached within everyday life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 5, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Held for seven years on Ogygia by the goddess Calypso, who offers to make him immortal and ageless if he stays as her husband, Odysseus refuses and weeps on the shore, choosing his mortal wife Penelope and his house on Ithaca over deathlessness.
greek_mythology.explanation: The episode is Greek epic's sharpest statement that domestic life with mortal kin is worth more than a transcendent condition outside it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus answers the Kural's question in narrative form: even godhood on another path is not worth leaving a rightly ordered home.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “he who is unable to live in society, or who has no need because he is sufficient for himself, must be either a beast or a god”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that human flourishing is constitutively social, beginning in the household; the solitary self-sufficient life is not a higher human option but a non-human one.
philosophy.tie_back: Both deny that stepping outside the household and its bonds leads anywhere better for a human being.

real_life_example.event_title: Martin Luther marries Katharina von Bora
real_life_example.event: Martin Luther, a former Augustinian friar, married Katharina von Bora, a former Cistercian nun who had left her convent in 1523, on 13 June 1525. According to Britannica, Luther was convinced that marriage was an honourable order of creation and chose to take a public stand against clerical celibacy. The couple raised six children in the former monastery building in Wittenberg, where Katharina ran the household and its finances, which also came to include her relative, six of Luther's sister's children and student lodgers.
real_life_example.explanation: Luther's marriage made the family home of a former monk a model of married life that many later clergy followed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what more a person could gain by another path if household life is lived in virtue, and Luther left the monastic path to make a household the setting of his religious life.

tamil:
இயல்பினான் இல்வாழ்க்கை வாழ்பவன் என்பான்
முயல்வாருள் எல்லாம் தலை.
transliteration:
Iyalpinaan ilvaazhkkai vaazhpavan enpaan,
Muyalvaarul ellaam thalai.
meaning: A person who lives family life the way it should be lived is the best of all who try to do good.
elementary: In a race, lots of people train in fancy ways. But the one who simply runs correctly, step after step, finishes first. The person who does ordinary family life properly is that runner — ahead of everyone who is trying harder in more dramatic ways.
university: The decisive word is இயல்பினான் (iyalpinaan) — “by [its] nature,” the same root as இயல்புடைய in kural 41. Valluvar is not praising domestic life as such but domestic life lived *according to what it intrinsically is*, which chapters 41-46 have just specified: support of dependants, the fivefold obligation, blameless earning, shared food, love and virtue. Against that, முயல்வாருள் எல்லாம் தலை — “the head of all who exert themselves” — uses முயல் (muyal, to strive/labour), a word that in the religious register covers ascetic exertion and spiritual practice. The claim is competitive and startling for its time: the householder is not merely an acceptable alternative to the striving religious, he outranks them. Parimelazhagar's commentary reads this as Valluvar explicitly ranking இல்லறம் above துறவறம்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And in accordance with the precepts of the Veda and of the Smriti, the housekeeper is declared to be superior to all of them; for he supports the other three.”
hinduism.explanation: Having described the student, hermit and ascetic orders at length, Manu concludes by ranking the householder above all of them on the ground that he sustains them.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact claim — the householder is the head of all who strive — and with the same supporting reason.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 6.89 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)

christianity.quote_or_event: “One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity; (For if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?)”
christianity.explanation: The qualification for the highest office in the early church is not ascetic achievement but demonstrated competence as a householder.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat well-run domestic life as the benchmark against which other forms of religious striving are measured.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best of you is the best to his wives, and I am the best of you to my wives, and when your companion dies, leave him alone.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet locates the measure of a person's excellence squarely in domestic conduct, and names himself as the example.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes 'best of all' a ranking decided inside the home rather than by any extraordinary religious exertion.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that a man without a wife lives without joy, without blessing and without goodness, and in the surrounding discussion treats marriage and the household as the normal setting in which a Jew fulfils his obligations.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic culture made the married scholar, not the celibate ascetic, the ideal type; an unmarried man was considered incomplete for religious as well as social purposes.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions put the householder, not the solitary religious striver, at the top of the scale.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Instructing the layman Dighajanu, who says he cannot live as a renunciant, the Buddha lays out four conditions for welfare in this life — persistent effort, protecting what one earns, good friendship, and balanced livelihood — and four for the life to come, treating lay life as a complete and honourable path.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha gives householders a full curriculum rather than a consolation prize, though the monastic life remains the higher road in the Theravada scheme.
buddhism.tie_back: It affirms the Kural's respect for the striving householder without going as far as ranking him first.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Gautama, Mahāvīra's chief disciple, doubted the lay votary Ānanda's claim to have attained avadhi-jñāna (clairvoyant knowledge), Mahāvīra told him Ānanda was right and that Gautama himself should ask forgiveness, and Gautama went back to the householder and apologised.
jainism.explanation: In the Uvāsagadasāo a disciplined householder reaches a degree of spiritual knowledge that the foremost monk had wrongly doubted, and the Jina publicly confirms the layman's standing.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar places the true householder at the head of all who strive, and the story of Ānanda has Mahāvīra rank a householder's attainment above the senior monk's judgment.
jainism.source: Uvāsagadasāo (Upāsakadaśāḥ) ch. 1, story of Ānanda (tr. A. F. R. Hoernlé, 1890); retold in Jain Story Series, 'Anand Shravak'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Yoga is not the patched coat, Yoga is not the walking stick. Yoga is not smearing the body with ashes... Remaining unblemished in the midst of the filth of the world - this is the way to attain Yoga.”
sikhism.explanation: Answering yogis, Guru Nanak lists the outward marks of the ascetic striver one by one and rejects them all, placing true discipline in staying pure while living in the world.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's householder who stands at the head of all who strive, the person who stays pure in worldly life is here given the very title the ascetics claimed.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 730, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “So Zeus the Father gave her an high honour instead of marriage, and she has her place in the midst of the house and has the richest portion. In all the temples of the gods she has a share of honour, and among all mortal men she is chief of the goddesses.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hestia, goddess of the hearth at the centre of every Greek house, received the first portion of every sacrifice; the household fire was literally the first claim in Greek worship.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Greek cult makes the household hearth the foremost object of honour, as the Kural makes the householder foremost among all who strive.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Remember that you are an actor in a drama, of such a kind as the author pleases to make it. If short, of a short one; if long, of a long one. … For this is your business, to act well the character assigned you; to choose it is another's.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus insists that excellence consists in performing well the role one actually has, not in acquiring a grander role.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's இயல்பினான் says the same: greatness comes from living domestic life according to its own proper nature, not from trading it for a loftier path.

real_life_example.event_title: Guru Nanak settles as a farmer at Kartarpur
real_life_example.event: After about twenty years of travel preaching his message, Guru Nanak settled again with his family in the Punjab, became a farmer and established the village of Kartarpur. Disciples gathered around him in a community of work and worship, and he devoted the last twenty years of his life to shaping the first Sikh community there. Before his death in 1539 he appointed a faithful follower, Guru Angad, as his successor.
real_life_example.explanation: The founder of Sikhism chose to lead his community as a working family man rather than as a wandering ascetic, setting a pattern for the faith that followed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who lives household life as it should be lived stands foremost among all who strive, and Guru Nanak made a farming family life the base from which he guided his followers.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி அறனிழுக்கா இல்வாழ்க்கை
நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Aatrin ozhukki aranizhukkaa ilvaazhkkai,
Norpaarin nonmai utaiththu.
meaning: A family life that helps others stay on the right path, and never turns away from what is right itself, is stronger than the strict self-discipline of people who give up home life.
elementary: One person sits alone on a hill and eats nothing for a week — that's hard. Another person gets up every day, stays honest, feeds the family, and gently keeps everyone else honest too — for fifty years. This kural says the second one is doing the harder, stronger thing.
university: The verse builds a careful two-part condition before making its comparison. ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி (aatrin ozhukki) is causative — “having caused [others] to conduct themselves on the path” — while அறனிழுக்கா (aran-izhukkaa) is negative and reflexive: “not itself slipping from virtue.” Only a household meeting both conditions is then said to possess நோன்மை (nonmai) exceeding that of நோற்பார் (norpaar, those who undertake நோன்பு, austerity/penance). The pun is the point: நோன்மை means both “endurance under penance” and “strength,” so Valluvar claims the householder wins the ascetic's own contest on the ascetic's own metric. This is the chapter's most polemical line and reflects a broader Tamil bhakti-era and post-Sangam argument against Jain and Buddhist monastic prestige.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Whatever action a great man performs, common men follow. And whatever standards he sets by exemplary acts, all the world pursues.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna cites the householder-king Janaka, who attained perfection through action, to argue that a person of standing must keep working precisely in order to guide others by example.
hinduism.tie_back: This supplies the Kural's first condition exactly — the householder's virtue is measured by his capacity to keep others on the path.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus places the moral value of visible, ordinary good conduct in its effect on others, immediately after warning against hiding a lamp under a bushel.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts make guiding others by one's own consistent conduct the measure of a life, rather than private feats of self-denial.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, over which are [appointed] angels, harsh and severe…”
islam.explanation: The verse is traditionally read as commanding the head of a household to instruct and morally safeguard his dependants, not merely himself.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's dual condition precisely: keep yourself from slipping and keep your household on the right path.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.”
judaism.explanation: The Shema makes the ordinary rhythms of household life — sitting, walking, lying down, rising — the setting for transmitting the commandments to the next generation.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி in practice: the household is where others are actually steered onto the right path.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One should first establish oneself in what is proper; then only should one instruct others. Thus the wise man will not be reproached.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's self-chapter insists on the order of operations: self-correction precedes the correction of others, or the teaching is worthless.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural states the same two requirements in the same order — not slipping oneself, and guiding others along the path.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Some householders are superior to some monks in self-control; but the saints are superior to all householders in self-control.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's teaching admits that a disciplined householder can surpass a lax monk in self-restraint, while still ranking the true saints above every layman.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a virtuous household has more strength than the penance of ascetics, and the Uttarādhyayana grants the same point for some householders against some monks.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “How have you put off yogic garb and attired yourself in a household way.” … “You, while distancing and repudiating house hold life, go again to those householders for begging. Except their offerings you don’t get anything.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh scholar and scribe of the Adi Granth, describes the yogi Bhangar Nath at Achal Batala mocking Guru Nanak for living as a householder, and the Guru replying that renunciants who reject household life still live on householders' gifts.
sikhism.tie_back: It is the Sikh form of Valluvar's boldest claim: the householder who keeps to virtue is stronger than the ascetics, who depend on him for their food.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 40 (tr. Dr Jodh Singh)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “To you, foolish Perses, I will speak good sense. Badness can be got easily and in shoals: the road to her is smooth, and she lives very near us. But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Works and Days is framed as a farmer-householder correcting his idle brother, arguing that ordinary honest labour is the long steep road to virtue.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod's householder both walks the hard path himself and works to pull a wayward kinsman onto it — the Kural's two conditions in a single poem.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The Stoic Musonius Rufus argued in his lectures that marriage is no handicap to philosophy, that the philosopher must marry and raise children, and that the shared household is itself the arena in which self-control, justice and endurance are actually practised.
philosophy.explanation: Against the Cynic model of the unencumbered sage, Musonius insisted that the demands of spouse, children and household are harder training in virtue than solitude.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in Roman Stoic form: domestic life possesses more real endurance than the withdrawn ascetic's regimen.
philosophy.source: Musonius Rufus, Lecture XIV, 'Is Marriage a Handicap for the Pursuit of Philosophy?'

real_life_example.event_title: Susanna Wesley's household at Epworth
real_life_example.event: At the rectory in Epworth, Susanna Wesley raised the ten of her nineteen children who survived infancy and taught them herself on a strict daily timetable, with lessons from nine to noon and two to five, girls as well as boys learning to read from the age of five, and prayers at rising and bedtime. During her husband's long absences she also read prayers and sermons to neighbours at the rectory, gatherings that at one time drew around 200 people. Her sons John and Charles Wesley went on to found the Methodist movement, and she is often called the Mother of Methodism.
real_life_example.explanation: Susanna Wesley's ordered, devout household shaped two of the most influential religious leaders of the eighteenth century and reached out to her whole village.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises a household that keeps others on the right path while never slipping itself as stronger than the austerities of ascetics, and Susanna Wesley's home guided her children and neighbours alike.

tamil:
அறனெனப் பட்டதே இல்வாழ்க்கை அஃதும்
பிறன்பழிப்ப தில்லாயின் நன்று.
transliteration:
Aran enap pattadhe ilvaazhkkai aqdhum,
Piranpazhippa thillaayin nandru.
meaning: Family life is what is truly called the good life. The other life, of giving up the world, is also good, as long as no one can find fault with it.
elementary: Imagine someone asks, "What does 'being good' actually mean?" This kural answers: it means running a home well. And it adds, politely, that the other way — going off to be a monk — is fine too, as long as nobody can point at it and say something is wrong.
university: The emphatic particle in அறனெனப் பட்டதே (aran-enap-pattadhē, “the very thing that has been called virtue”) is a definitional claim: domestic life is not *a* form of aram, it is what the word names. The second half is one of the Kural's most gracious sentences — அஃதும் (“that too”) concedes the ascetic path, but hedges it with a condition (பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின், “if there is nothing for another to reproach”) that Valluvar never attaches to the householder. Commentators differ over whether அஃதும் refers to the renunciant life or to a second grade of domestic life; the majority reading, followed by Mu. Varadarajan and Salomon Pappaiah, takes it as the ascetic path. Note the recurrence of பழி (pazhi, blame) from kural 44 — reproachability is Valluvar's working test for ethical failure throughout this chapter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As all rivers, both great and small, find a resting-place in the ocean, even so men of all orders find protection with householders.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu's closing image of the ashrama system makes the householder the ocean into which every other way of life eventually drains for support.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make domestic life the substantive centre of dharma, with the other paths defined in relation to it.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 6.90 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews affirms the moral standing of marriage without qualification, while attaching the reproach to its abuse rather than to the institution.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares married domestic life honourable in itself and locates blame only where conduct is actually faulty.

islam.quote_or_event: “…And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy and monasticism, which they innovated; We did not prescribe it for them except [that they did so] seeking the approval of Allah. But they did not observe it with due observance.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an treats Christian monasticism as a human innovation God never commanded, and notes that those who adopted it largely failed to keep it properly.
islam.tie_back: This is an almost eerie match for the Kural's second clause: the other path is conceded as possibly good, but only if it is actually kept without reproach.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.”
judaism.explanation: The first thing declared 'not good' in the Hebrew Bible is solitude, and the remedy is a partner — establishing companionate household life as the created norm.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's definition of virtue as domestic life has its scriptural counterpart here, where paired household existence is what God calls good.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are these four kinds of bliss that can be attained … by a householder … The bliss of having, the bliss of [making use of] wealth, the bliss of debtlessness, the bliss of blamelessness. … these are not worth one sixteenth-sixteenth of the bliss of blamelessness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that of everything a householder can enjoy, the incomparably greatest is anavajja-sukha, the happiness of being beyond reproach.
buddhism.tie_back: Blamelessness is exactly the test the Kural applies — the standard by which a way of life is judged good.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “The householder, whose interior is illumined with Right Faith, follows the ‘path;’ but the ascetic involved in wrong beliefs is nowhere near it; for this reason the ‘enlightened’ householder is considered superior to an ascetic devoid of true faith.”
jainism.explanation: Samantabhadra holds that inner right faith, not the outward state of life, decides who is on the path to liberation, so an enlightened householder outranks a deluded ascetic.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls household life virtue itself and accepts renunciation only where it is beyond reproach, and Samantabhadra likewise makes the ascetic's worth depend on his being sound within.
jainism.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra v. 33 (gṛhastho mokṣamārgastho…), tr. Champat Rai Jain, 1917, pp. 18–19

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Says Nanak, one who meets the Perfect Guru, is celebrated as a householder as well as a renunciate.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan does not set household life and renunciation against each other; one who lives by the Guru's teaching is both at once, a householder outwardly and inwardly detached.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar calls domestic life virtue itself and grants that the other path is also good if blameless; the Guru keeps the renunciant's virtue but places it inside the householder.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 496, Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad VI, Hector leaves the battlefield to find Andromache and their infant son Astyanax at the Scaean Gate; he removes his terrifying helmet so the baby will not cry, prays for the child's future, and tells his weeping wife that he fights precisely so that this household may stand.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's most tender domestic scene sits deliberately inside a war poem, presenting the household as the good that all the heroism is ultimately for.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It implicitly makes the Kural's claim — that domestic life is the substantive good — though by dramatisation rather than definition.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the family is the association established by nature for the supply of men's everyday wants”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle begins the Politics by deriving every larger association from the household, which he treats as natural and prior rather than as a compromise or a lower stage.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts make the household the primary and defining human association rather than a preliminary to something higher.

real_life_example.event_title: Father Damien serves the Hansen's disease settlement on Molokai
real_life_example.place: Kalawao, Kalaupapa Peninsula, Molokai, Kingdom of Hawaii (now Hawaii, United States)
real_life_example.event: In 1873 Father Damien, a Belgian Catholic priest, went to the isolated settlement at Kalawao on Molokai, where the Hawaiian government sent people with Hansen's disease (leprosy). He helped build about 300 of the settlement's 325 buildings, including homes and churches, constructed water lines and roads, administered medicine, improved food supplies and founded two orphanages. After twelve years he contracted the disease himself, and he died there on 15 April 1889 after sixteen years of voluntary service.
real_life_example.explanation: Damien's life of celibate service among people shunned by society won worldwide admiration even in his own lifetime, and he was later declared a saint.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural concedes that the renunciant path is also good if no one has cause to reproach it, and Damien's selfless life among the outcast is a renunciant life that drew praise rather than reproach.

tamil:
வையத்துள் வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன் வான்உறையும்
தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Vaiyaththul vaazhvaangu vaazhpavan vaanuraiyum,
Theyvaththul vaikkap padum.
meaning: A person who lives on this earth the way people should live will be counted among the gods in heaven.
elementary: You don't have to go anywhere special to become great. If you live rightly here — kindly, honestly, taking care of people — the world will think of you the way it thinks of the shining beings in the sky. Being good on the ground is what puts you up there.
university: The chapter's closing couplet is built on a deliberate spatial contrast: வையத்துள் (vaiyaththul, “within the world/earth”) against வான் உறையும் (vaan uraiyum, “sky-dwelling”). The pivot is the untranslatable வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன் — “one who lives in the manner of living,” i.e. one who lives as living is properly done. The passive வைக்கப்படும் (vaikkap-padum, “will be placed/reckoned”) is carefully non-supernatural: Valluvar does not say such a person *becomes* a god or *goes* to heaven, but that he will be *counted among* them — an evaluative rather than metaphysical claim, which is why the verse has been read comfortably by Saiva, Vaishnava, Jain and secular-humanist commentators alike. It is also the structural answer to kural 1: the book opened by putting God first; it closes this chapter by putting the good householder alongside the gods.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, the sage Kaushika, proud of his ascetic powers, is sent to learn dharma from Dharmavyadha — a butcher in Mithila who supports his aged parents and does his ordinary trade honestly; the householder-butcher then instructs the brahmin ascetic in the highest teaching.
hinduism.explanation: The Vyadha Gita makes an ordinary working householder the spiritual superior of a forest ascetic, precisely because he lives his worldly duties as they ought to be lived.
hinduism.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that living rightly in this world is what places a person among the highest, above those who chase higher states.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Vyadha Gita / the story of Dharmavyadha)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust.”
christianity.explanation: 2 Peter articulates what the Eastern churches call theosis — that human beings living rightly come to share in God's own nature.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's promise in Christian terms: right living on earth results in being counted with the divine.

islam.quote_or_event: “[To the righteous it will be said], 'O reassured soul, Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him], And enter among My [righteous] servants And enter My Paradise.'”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Fajr closes by contrasting the greedy who neglect the orphan and the poor with the soul at peace, who is welcomed into the ranks of God's servants.
islam.tie_back: Both passages describe the reward as being *placed among* an honoured company — the Kural among the sky-dwelling gods, the Qur'an among God's servants.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Jacob said: this world is like a vestibule before the world to come; prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the banqueting-hall.”
judaism.explanation: Pirkei Avot makes present, ordinary life the preparation whose quality determines one's place in the world to come.
judaism.tie_back: Both sayings make how one lives here the sole determinant of the honoured company one joins hereafter.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 4:16 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Living with Brahma are those families where, in the home, mother & father are revered by the children. Living with the first devas are those families where, in the home, mother & father are revered by the children. … 'Brahma' is a designation for mother & father.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that a household which honours its parents is already living in the company of Brahma and the devas — and that the parents themselves *are* what those words name.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim almost exactly: rightly ordered domestic life places ordinary people among the gods.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When under such discipline he lives piously even as a householder, he will, on quitting flesh and bones, share the world of the Yakshas.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana promises a heavenly rebirth among the gods to a householder who keeps the lay rules and the fortnightly fast.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the one who lives as life should be lived will be counted among the sky-dwelling gods, and the Jain sūtra gives the same reward to the pious householder.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak tells his listeners that selfless service done within ordinary worldly life is what wins honour before God.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's householder who lives on earth as one should and is counted among the gods in heaven, the one who serves within the world is given a place of honour in the divine court.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But after earth had covered this generation -- they are called pure spirits dwelling on the earth, and are kindly, delivering from harm, and guardians of mortal men; for they roam everywhere over the earth, clothed in mist and keep watch on judgements and cruel deeds, givers of wealth”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's golden race, who had lived rightly and died gently, were not simply extinguished but promoted to the status of daimones who guard and watch over the living.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that mortals who lived as one ought are afterwards reckoned among the divine order rather than merely remembered.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Wherefore we ought to fly away from earth to heaven as quickly as we can; and to fly away is to become like God, as far as this is possible; and to become like him, is to become holy, just, and wise.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates defines the philosopher's goal as homoiōsis theōi — likeness to God — and immediately glosses it in purely ethical terms: holiness, justice, wisdom.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the same move, defining nearness to the divine as a matter of how one lives rather than where one goes.

real_life_example.event_title: Imhotep, builder of the Step Pyramid, is later worshipped as a god
real_life_example.date: c. 27th century BCE; worshipped in the Late Period
real_life_example.event: Imhotep was a high official of King Djoser of Egypt's Third Dynasty; his name and titles are carved on the base of a statue of the king, and he is credited with designing Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara, Egypt's first monumental structure in stone. His memory lasted for millennia: by the New Kingdom he was listed among the wise men of the past and revered as patron of scribes, and in the Late Period he was worshipped as a god of medicine and son of the god Ptah, later identified by the Greeks with Asklepios.
real_life_example.explanation: Imhotep is one of very few people in Egyptian history known to have been raised to divine status after death, purely through the regard in which his life and wisdom were held.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who lives on earth as one ought will be counted among the gods in the sky, and Imhotep, a human official remembered for wisdom and achievement, was literally later counted among Egypt's gods.

tamil:
மனைத்தக்க மாண்புடையள் ஆகித்தற் கொண்டான்
வளத்தக்காள் வாழ்க்கைத் துணை.
transliteration:
Manaith thakka maanbudaiyaL aagith thaR koNdaan,
vaLath thakkaaL vaazhkkaith thuNai.
meaning: A true wife has the good qualities a home needs and runs the home within what her husband earns.
elementary: Imagine two people rowing one boat. It only moves straight if they pull together with the strength each of them actually has — not with strength they wish they had. This kural says a good partner is the one who runs the home well and spends what the family really earns, not what it pretends to earn.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition rather than a eulogy, and the definition is startlingly practical: the wife's worth is located in maanbu (moral excellence fitted to the household) plus vaLaththakkaaL — living proportionate to income. Parimelazhagar's classical commentary glosses the "good qualities" as hospitality to ascetics and guests and compassion to the poor, and the "good deeds" as knowing what the household needs, competence in the kitchen, and oppuravu (civic generosity) — so domestic thrift is framed not as miserliness but as the material precondition of ethical generosity established in Chapter 5 (Il-vaazhkkai). The chapter's title is also significant: Valluvar does not call it "manaiviyin maanbu" (the greatness of a wife) but vaazhkkaith-thuNai nalam, "the worth of a life-companion," a word choice Tamil commentators have long read as elevating the wife from an object of the household to its co-agent. Modern feminist readings of the Kural note the asymmetry — the chapter addresses the wife's duties to a far greater extent than the husband's — while also observing that Valluvar's criterion is competence and character rather than birth, beauty, or dowry, which was itself a notable move in the ancient Tamil context.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Manusmriti assigns the wife direct charge of the household economy — the gathering and spending of the family's wealth, the keeping of the house, the preparation of food, and the care of the household goods — making her the manager rather than merely a resident of the home.
hinduism.explanation: Manu 9.11 hands the wife operational control of income and expenditure, precisely the competence Valluvar names.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts define the good wife by her stewardship of what the household actually has.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 9.11 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies. The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil. She will do him good and not evil all the days of her life.”
christianity.explanation: The Proverbs 31 portrait opens by defining the excellent wife economically — her husband needs no plunder because her management supplies the house.
christianity.tie_back: Same criterion as the Kural: worth measured by trustworthy provision within the household's own means.

islam.quote_or_event: “The lady is a guardian and is responsible for her husband's house and his offspring; and so all of you are guardians and are responsible for your wards.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet's 'each of you is a shepherd' hadith assigns the wife a defined stewardship over the home and children, for which she is answerable.
islam.tie_back: Both make the wife the responsible steward of the household, not a dependent within it.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 5200 (Book of Wedlock/Marriage), narrated by 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.”
judaism.explanation: The foundational Hebrew account of marriage names the wife an ezer kenegdo — a helper corresponding to, and fitted for, the man.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'vaazhkkaith thuNai' — life-helper — stated as a creation principle.
judaism.source: Genesis 2:18 (King James Version); Hebrew ezer kenegdo

buddhism.quote_or_event: “She's well-organized in her work. She manages the domestic help. She's not unfaithful. She preserves his earnings. She's deft and tireless in all her duties.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Buddha's lay code, these are the five ways a wife reciprocates a husband who honours her — with 'preserves his earnings' as an explicit duty.
buddhism.tie_back: 'Preserving his earnings' is the Pali equivalent of vaLaththakkaaL — living to the measure of what he brings in.
buddhism.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)

jainism.quote_or_event: “If in time of distress, when the meal of the whole family is cooked by the water of a small pot, if a host of relatives sufficient to consume the water of the sea should come all at once, the softly-speaking woman, who shows herself as bounteous as the ocean, is the glory of her house.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain-authored Tamil Nālaṭiyār praises the wife who stretches scant household means into generous hospitality without complaint.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's ideal partner has the household virtues and orders the home to suit her husband's means, and this quatrain shows exactly that: hospitality matched to a meagre pot.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 39 'Chaste Women', st. 2 (= st. 382), English translation in The Indian Antiquary

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Balwand says that Khivi, the Guru’s wife, is a noble woman, who gives soothing, leafy shade to all. She distributes the bounty of the Guru’s Langar; the kheer - the rice pudding and ghee, is like sweet ambrosia.”
sikhism.explanation: The bards Satta and Balwand praise Mata Khivi, wife of Guru Angad, who ran the community kitchen, as a noble woman whose management of the household's food made it a shelter and blessing for everyone.
sikhism.tie_back: She embodies Valluvar's ideal life-partner, whose household skill and good qualities turn the home's means into generosity for others.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar, Pauri 3, Rai Balwand and Satta Doom (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Queen Arete of the Phaeacians is so honoured by her husband Alcinous and by the people that Odysseus is told to appeal to her knees first, because she settles disputes even among men and her goodwill decides whether he reaches home.
greek_mythology.explanation: Arete is the Homeric picture of the wife as functional co-ruler of the household, not an ornament within it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Homer measures a wife's worth by the practical weight she carries in running the house.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Xenophon's Oeconomicus, Ischomachus explains that he and his wife are partners in one estate: he brings in from outside, she guards and distributes within, and their joint prosperity depends on her spending in careful proportion to what comes in.
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon's Socratic dialogue is the classical world's fullest treatment of the wife as household economist and co-manager.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the kural's thesis in Greek dress: the wife who matches expenditure to income is the partnership's foundation.

real_life_example.event_title: Abigail Adams runs the family farm and finances during the Revolution
real_life_example.event: From early in their marriage Abigail Adams proved exceptionally capable of managing the family's finances and household. When John Adams left for the Continental Congress in Philadelphia in 1774, and later served as a diplomat in Europe from 1778, she stayed on the farm at Braintree, managing it and the family's business affairs, paying the bills, coping with wartime shortages and educating their children. She also made investments, including trading in war bonds and a small business importing European goods, that added to the family's prosperity.
real_life_example.explanation: Abigail Adams kept the household not only running but growing through a decade of war and separation, freeing her husband for public service.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines the true life-partner as one who has the qualities household life needs and orders it to suit her husband's means, and Abigail Adams managed the Adams farm and finances wisely through years of scarcity.

tamil:
மனைமாட்சி இல்லாள்கண் இல்லாயின் வாழ்க்கை
எனைமாட்சித் தாயினும் இல்.
transliteration:
Manaimaatchi illaaLkaN illaayin vaazhkkai,
enaimaatchith thaayinum il.
meaning: If a wife does not have the good qualities a home needs, then however grand a man’s life may be, it is worth nothing.
elementary: A house can have the shiniest roof, the biggest garden and the nicest furniture — but if the roof leaks, none of the rest keeps you dry. This kural says the wife's goodness is the roof: if it's missing, everything else stops counting.
university: The rhetorical engine here is the word il, which Valluvar uses twice in different senses — il as 'home/household' and il as 'is not, amounts to nothing' — so the couplet ends on the flat negation that domestic splendour without domestic virtue simply is not. Parimelazhagar notes precisely this, glossing the final il as meaning 'useless', not 'absent'. The Tamil didactic tradition amplified the point: the Naaladiyaar declares that a mansion with jewelled lamps but no worthy mistress is 'a cruel forest', an image the anthologist of this chapter explicitly quotes. Comparative scholars often pair this couplet with the near-universal wisdom-literature topos that a household's moral weather is set by the spouse rather than by its wealth — a topos with strikingly parallel formulations in Hebrew Proverbs, Hesiod, and the Pali canon. It should be noted that Valluvar states the principle asymmetrically here; the Kural does address husbandly failure elsewhere (notably Chapter 91, Penvazhich cheral), but this chapter's frame is the wife's contribution.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Shakuntala reproves King Dushyanta by declaring that the wife is a man's own half and his first friend, the root of dharma, artha and kama and even of liberation, and that the house not occupied by a wife is as desolate as a wilderness however grand it may be.
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala's speech makes the wife the constitutive element of the household, without which the other goods of life have no ground.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say the household's splendour collapses into nothing once wifely worth is subtracted.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva §74 (Shakuntala to Dushyanta; trans. K. M. Ganguli, 1883–96)

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs makes the same trade Valluvar makes: a spacious, splendid house is worth less than a bare corner if the marriage inside it is bad.
christianity.tie_back: Both couplets weigh domestic virtue against domestic magnificence and find the magnificence worthless.

islam.quote_or_event: “The whole world is a provision, and the best object of benefit of the world is the pious woman.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ranks a righteous wife above every other worldly good a person could possess.
islam.tie_back: Where the Kural says other splendours are worth nothing without her, the hadith says she is worth more than all of them.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 1467, Book of Suckling, Chapter: Advice with regard to women (narrated by 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Tanḥum said that Rabbi Ḥanilai said: Any man who does not have a wife is left without joy, without blessing, without goodness.”
judaism.explanation: The Gemara derives from three separate scriptural verses that joy, blessing and goodness all enter a man's life through his wife.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts make the wife the channel through which a household's goods become real goods at all.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 62b (Koren Noé / William Davidson Edition)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When the husband is ethical, bountiful, rid of stinginess, but the wife is unethical, miserly and abusive, she's a zombie living with a god for a husband.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's four types of marriage make the point that one partner's virtue cannot carry a household whose other partner lacks it.
buddhism.tie_back: Even a wholly virtuous husband's life 'amounts to nothing' as a household when the wife's character is absent.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.53, Paṭhamasaṁvāsa Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)

jainism.quote_or_event: “This Revai, the wife of that Mahasayaga, possessed ancestral property consisting of eight kror measures of gold and eight herds, each herd containing ten thousand head of cattle.” Yet in the canon's story Revati, ruled by greed and craving, does away with her co-wives, takes to meat and drink, and tries to pull her husband, a lay disciple of Mahavira, out of his vowed retreat, while he silently 'continued in the meditation of the Law'.
jainism.explanation: The seventh Anga sets a household of enormous wealth and a devout husband beside a wife without virtue. Revati's own riches cannot save her: she dies within seven days and, the text says, is reborn in hell.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that if a wife lacks the excellence of domestic virtue, whatever greatness a household has is nothing, and Mahasataka's house, though one of the richest in Rajagriha, is undone by Revati's conduct.
jainism.source: Uvāsagadasāo, Lecture 8 (Mahāsayaga), §§ 233–257, esp. § 234 and § 247 (tr. A. F. Rudolf Hoernle, Bibliotheca Indica, vol. 2, Calcutta, 1888; scan at archive.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O bride, decorate yourself, after you surrender and accept your Husband Lord. Otherwise, your Husband Lord will not come to your bed, and your ornaments will be useless.”
sikhism.explanation: Using the image of the bride-soul, Guru Amar Das teaches that outward finery counts for nothing unless it comes with inner surrender and love; only then are the ornaments 'acceptable and approved'.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's claim that a household's splendour is worthless without the wife's excellence, the verse says that outer adornment is useless without the inner quality that gives it meaning.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For a man wins nothing better than a good wife, and, again, nothing worse than a bad one, a greedy soul who roasts her man without fire, strong though he may be, and brings him to a raw old age.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's farming poem states the good-wife/bad-wife polarity as a maxim of practical life, not as myth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost the identical proposition: no external strength or wealth survives a bad marriage.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 702–705 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White, Loeb Classical Library, 1914)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Between husband and wife friendship seems to exist by nature, for man is naturally disposed to pairing.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle grounds the household not in property or utility alone but in a natural philia between spouses, from which the rest of the household's goods follow.
philosophy.tie_back: If the marital bond itself fails, then on Aristotle's account the household has lost the very thing that made it a household.

real_life_example.event_title: Queen Victoria withdraws from public life after Prince Albert's death
real_life_example.place: Windsor, Balmoral and Osborne, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Prince Albert died in December 1861 at the age of 42. Queen Victoria, who had relied on him as her husband and principal trusted adviser in affairs of state, wore black for the rest of her reign and for years rarely appeared in public, spending long periods at Balmoral and Osborne. The public, at first sympathetic, grew increasingly impatient with its absent sovereign, and only gradually, from the late 1860s and 1870s, did she resume her public duties.
real_life_example.explanation: Victoria's long seclusion shows how the loss of a life-partner could empty even the grandest position of its meaning for the one left behind.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that without a worthy life-partner a household's splendour amounts to nothing, and Victoria, still ruler of a vast empire, found the throne's splendour hollow once the partner who shared her life was gone.

tamil:
இல்லதென் இல்லவள் மாண்பானால் உள்ளதென்
இல்லவள் மாணாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Illadhen illavaL maaNbaanaal uLLadhen,
illavaL maaNaak kadai.
meaning: If a man’s wife is truly good, what does he lack? If she is not, what does he really have?
elementary: Think of a key. If you have the right key, every locked door in the house opens — so nothing is really shut to you. Lose the key and it doesn't matter how many rooms you own; you can't get into any of them. This kural says a good partner is that key.
university: The couplet is built as a matched pair of rhetorical questions — illadhu en? ('what is lacking?') against uLLadhu en? ('what is there?') — and the symmetry is the argument: presence and absence of wifely maaNbu are made to exhaust the possibilities, with nothing in between. This antithetical-parallelism structure is a signature of Near Eastern and Tamil wisdom poetry alike, and it produces here a deliberately absolute claim that later Tamil moralists softened or literalised in various directions; Avvaiyar's Moodhurai rewrites it as the image of a house turning into a sour thicket.
