jainism.explanation: When their Brahmin father argues that there is no better world for men without sons, the two sons of Bhrigu reply that sons cannot save anyone; only one's own conduct under the Law frees the soul.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism agrees with Valluvar that the seven births matter, but it rejects the idea that a child's goodness can shield a parent's soul: in Jain doctrine each soul bears its own karma, which is the opposite of what this kural claims.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.8 and 14.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those, within whose minds the Lord abides, are robed with honor in the Court of the Lord. They are carried across, along with all their family, and the whole world is saved along with them.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das teaches that one person in whom God dwells brings blessing beyond themselves, carrying their whole family across the world-ocean with them.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's virtuous child whose good character keeps evil away from the family through seven births, the God-filled person here becomes the means of the family's release.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 310, Raag Gauri, Gauri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the oxen were not ready, the brothers Cleobis and Biton yoked themselves to the cart and drew their mother, priestess of Hera, all the way to the temple; the watching Argives praised her for such sons, and she prayed the goddess grant them the best thing a human can receive — whereupon they fell asleep in the temple and never woke.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus tells the story as Solon's example of true human happiness: sons whose conduct honours their mother so visibly that the community credits her for them, and the goddess seals it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, blameless children are what keeps evil from reaching the parent — here the mother's happiness is made secure precisely by her sons' virtue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato argues in the Laws that the human race is by its nature a partner of all time, and that a person attains to immortality not by outliving death but by leaving children, and children's children, so that the line never breaks.
philosophy.explanation: Marriage law in Plato's ideal city is grounded on this: procreation is how a mortal being participates in something that does not end.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts make offspring the mechanism by which a person's fate extends safely across spans of time they will not personally live through.

real_life_example.event_title: Suor Maria Celeste takes on her father Galileo's penance
real_life_example.event: In June 1633 the Roman Inquisition condemned Galileo Galilei over his Dialogue on the two chief world systems and imposed a penance that included the repeated recitation of the penitential psalms. His eldest daughter, Suor Maria Celeste, a Poor Clare nun at the convent of San Matteo in Arcetri, took on that part of his penance herself. Throughout his trial she wrote to him constantly and looked after his household affairs while he was away in Rome.
real_life_example.explanation: A daughter of good character stood in for her father and shouldered the burden laid on him, one of the best-documented acts of filial devotion in the history of science.
real_life_example.tie_back: Parimelalagar reads this kural as saying that a virtuous child's good acts lift the burden from the parent, and Maria Celeste literally performed her father's penance in his place.

tamil:
தம்பொருள் என்பதம் மக்கள் அவர்பொருள்
தம்தம் வினையான் வரும்.
transliteration:
Thamporul Enpadham Makkal Avarporul,
Thamdham Vinaiyaan Varum.
meaning: The wise say children are their parents’ true treasure. And each child’s own worth comes to them through the things they do.
elementary: Grown-ups sometimes call money their "treasure." This kural says the real treasure is your children. And here's the second part: nobody can just hand a child a good life the way you hand over a coin — what each child ends up with comes from the things they themselves do.
university: The couplet turns on a deliberate double use of பொருள் (poruḷ, "wealth, substance, thing of worth"): children are the parents' poruḷ, and the children in turn have a poruḷ of their own, which arrives by வினை (viṉai, "deed, act, karma"). Parimēlaḻakar reads the second line as meaning that the good deeds children perform on their parents' behalf return to the parents as wealth; Maṇakkuṭavar and several moderns read it more directly, that each person's fortune follows from their own acts. Valluvar's compression permits both, and the ambiguity is productive: the family is a genuine economy of worth, yet no share in it is transferable by mere inheritance. The phrase தம்தம் ("each one's own") is the load-bearing word — it individuates moral responsibility inside a verse that has just made the family a single unit of value. That tension between collective wealth and non-transferable desert is what makes this the philosophically sharpest couplet in the chapter, and it anticipates the Kural's later chapter on ஊழ் (Fate).

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Upaniṣad teaches that a person is made of desire — as their desire is, so is their resolve; as their resolve, so the deed they do; and as the deed they do, so is what they come to inherit.
hinduism.explanation: This is one of the earliest formulations of karma as personal moral causation: what accrues to a person follows from what that person has actually done, not from station or lineage.
hinduism.tie_back: It is precisely the Kural's second line — each one's wealth comes by each one's own deeds.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children are their fathers.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb makes the generations each other's ornament: the old are crowned by their descendants, and the young are honoured by their parentage.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the Kural's first line — offspring counted as the substance and glory of a family — but not its second, which insists each person's fortune is self-earned.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives, And that his effort is going to be seen.”
islam.explanation: The verses deny that anyone can be credited or debited with another's account: what a person has is what a person has worked for.
islam.tie_back: This is a direct scriptural statement of the Kural's claim that each child's wealth comes by that child's own deeds.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.”
judaism.explanation: Ezekiel is correcting a popular proverb about children's teeth being set on edge by their parents' sour grapes, and insisting that moral accounts are strictly individual.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's second line stated as law: what belongs to each comes from each one's own doing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Student, beings are owners of kammas, heirs of kammas, they have kammas as their progenitor, kammas as their kin, kammas as their homing-place. It is kammas that differentiate beings according to inferiority and superiority.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha answers a young brahmin who wants to know why people are born into such unequal circumstances: the inheritance that actually matters is not property or birth but one's own accumulated action.
buddhism.tie_back: The Pali even uses the vocabulary of inheritance to say what the Kural says — the real estate anyone comes into is their own deeds.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikāya 135, Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta (trans. Ñāṇamoli Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As long as a tree retains its branches, it is really a tree; when they are lopped off, it is called a trunk. As a bird without its wings, as a king in battle without his followers, as a merchant on a boat without his goods, even so am I without my sons.”
jainism.explanation: The priest Bhrigu, about to follow his renouncing sons into the order, says that a man's sons are his branches, wings, retinue and cargo, and without them he is diminished.
jainism.tie_back: Bhrigu's merchant 'without his goods' makes the same point as the kural's opening line, that one's children are one's true wealth.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.29–30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “His sons did not obey His Word; they turned their backs on Him as Guru... Whatever the Guru said, Lehna did, and so he was installed on the throne.”
sikhism.explanation: The bards Satta and Balwand explain why Guru Nanak passed the Guruship to his disciple Lehna (Guru Angad) and not to his own sons: the inheritance went to the one whose deeds proved him worthy.
sikhism.tie_back: It sharply illustrates the second half of the Kural: whatever wealth the next generation receives comes through each one's own deeds, not by birth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar, Pauri 2, Rai Balwand and Satta Doom (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Thou too, my friend, for I see that thou art comely and tall, be thou valiant, that many an one of men yet to be born may praise thee.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena, disguised as Mentes, tells Telemachus that his father's estate is being eaten away and that he cannot go on relying on Odysseus' name — he must act, and earn a reputation of his own.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The goddess makes the Kural's point to a son's face: the wealth and honour that will be yours must come from your own deeds.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 1.301–302 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1919)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus instructs the student never to say of anything that it has been lost, but that it has been given back — and to apply this to a child as much as to an estate, since both were only ever on loan.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, calling a child "mine" in the possessive sense is a category error that guarantees suffering; what one has is custody, not ownership.
philosophy.tie_back: It qualifies the Kural's opening claim in exactly the way the couplet's own second line does: children may be called one's wealth, but they are not one's property.

real_life_example.event_title: Andrew Carnegie publishes 'Wealth', the Gospel of Wealth
real_life_example.place: United States (published in the North American Review)
real_life_example.event: In June 1889 the industrialist Andrew Carnegie published an essay titled 'Wealth' in the North American Review, setting out what came to be called the Gospel of Wealth. He argued that a person who accumulates great wealth holds it as a trustee and should use the surplus for the improvement of mankind during his own lifetime, and he questioned the practice of passing great fortunes down to heirs. Carnegie went on to give away the great majority of his fortune to libraries, universities and foundations.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the richest men of his age publicly argued that children are not best served by inherited riches, and that each person's standing should come from what they themselves do.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says children are a parent's true wealth while their own wealth must come through their own deeds, which is close to Carnegie's case against handing heirs great fortunes.

tamil:
அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதேதம் மக்கள்
சிறுகை அளாவிய கூழ்.
transliteration:
Amizhdhinum Aatra Inidhedham Makkal,
Sirukai Alaaviya Koozh.
meaning: Plain porridge that your own children have stirred with their small hands tastes far sweeter than amrita (the drink of the gods).
elementary: Imagine the most delicious dessert in the world — the kind a king would eat. Now imagine ordinary rice that your little brother or sister has squished and messed up with their tiny fingers. This kural says the messy rice tastes better. Not because of the rice — because of whose hands were in it.
university: This is perhaps the most quoted couplet in the Kural's domestic chapters, and its power lies in a calculated collision of registers. அமிழ்து (amiḻtu, Sanskrit amṛta) is the immortalising nectar of the gods, the top of the classical scale of sweetness; கூழ் (kūḻ) is at the bottom — a thin boiled gruel or mash, the plainest food in the Tamil larder. Between them Valluvar inserts the word that does all the work: அளாவிய (aḷāviya), "stirred, mixed about, dabbled in" by a சிறுகை, a "small hand." Parimēlaḻakar glosses அளாவல் by quoting a Puṟanāṉūṟu line about a child "dropping and touching and mouthing and churning" the ghee-rice until it is smeared everywhere — that is, he understands the verse to be describing genuine mess, not a decorous gesture. The theological move is quietly radical: the transcendent standard of sweetness is beaten not by a better food but by a relationship, and the sensory language of the next two couplets (touch, hearing) shows Valluvar building a deliberate small phenomenology of parenthood through the bodily senses.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa's Kṛṣṇa cycle dwells on the infant god raiding the butter pots, smearing curds over himself and the household, and being caught with his hands in the food — and on Yaśodā's helpless delight at exactly this, which becomes the devotional mode called vātsalya, love in the manner of a parent for a small child.
hinduism.explanation: An entire branch of Hindu devotion is built on the claim that God is most lovable in the form of a messy toddler with food on his hands.
hinduism.tie_back: Both traditions locate supreme sweetness not in the food but in the small hands that have been in it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?”
christianity.explanation: Andrew points out a boy's plain, inadequate packed lunch — barley was the cheap grain — and that humble food from a child's hands becomes the meal that feeds five thousand.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts take the poorest imaginable food, pass it through a child's hands, and find it has become more than the finest fare.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Allah, shower blessings upon us in our city, and in our fruits, in our mudd and in our sa', blessings upon blessings,” — and he would then give that fruit to the youngest of the children present.
islam.explanation: When the season's first fruit was brought to the Prophet, he would pray over it and then hand the choicest first taste not to an elder or a guest but to the smallest child in the room.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats food as something whose value is completed by a child's hands rather than by its own quality.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 1373b, Book of Pilgrimage (narrated by Abū Hurayrah)

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it shall come to pass, when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service? That ye shall say, It is the sacrifice of the LORD's passover.”
judaism.explanation: The Passover meal is legislated from the outset around the child's question, so that the family's central ritual dinner is structured by and for the children at the table.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions make the presence of children the thing that transforms an ordinary family meal into the sweetest one there is.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Ashokāvadāna a small boy named Jaya, playing in the dirt, sees the Buddha passing on alms round and, having nothing else, drops a handful of dust into his begging bowl as if it were food; the Buddha accepts it, and predicts the child will be reborn as the great emperor Aśoka.
buddhism.explanation: The offering is literally worthless and literally dirty, yet it is received as the most consequential gift in the story because of the hands and heart it came from.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, what a child's small hand has put into the food is worth incomparably more than the food itself.
buddhism.source: Ashokāvadāna, the gift of dust (Divyāvadāna, ch. 26)

jainism.quote_or_event: On the twelfth day after Mahâvîra's birth his parents prepared plenty of food, drink, spices and sweetmeats, invited friends, relatives and the Jñâtrika Kshatriyas, and sat down with them to eat, taste and share the meal before announcing the child's name, Vardhamâna.
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra makes a shared family meal the centre of the celebration of a newborn son.
jainism.tie_back: The scene links food and the joy of a child, but nothing in it matches Valluvar's image of a meal made sweeter than nectar by a small child's hands.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §§104–107 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “As many mistakes as the son commits, his mother does not hold them against him in her mind.” … “If the son, in anger, runs away, even then, his mother does not hold it against him in her mind.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir uses a parent's indulgent love, which overlooks whatever mess or mischief a child makes, as the image for God's forgiveness of the devotee.
sikhism.tie_back: It reflects the same parental tenderness the Kural celebrates, in which food a child has messed with becomes sweeter than nectar instead of spoiled.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 478, Raag Asa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “for by day rich-crowned Demeter would anoint him with ambrosia as if he were the offspring of a god and breathe sweetly upon him as she held him in her bosom”
greek_mythology.explanation: Disguised as a nurse in the house of Celeus, the grieving goddess Demeter secretly feeds the infant Demophoön the food of the immortals, trying to make a mortal child divine.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Greek scene runs the Kural's image in reverse — there a goddess gives ambrosia to a child, while Valluvar says a child's hands make plain gruel beat ambrosia outright.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn 2 (To Demeter), 235–237 (trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, 1914)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And so plain savours bring us a pleasure equal to a luxurious diet, when all the pain due to want is removed; and bread and water produce the highest pleasure, when one who needs them puts them to his lips.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus argues that the pleasure of eating peaks with simple food properly met, and that expensive fare adds nothing to the actual quality of the experience.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts dethrone luxury food, though Valluvar's plain gruel wins by affection where Epicurus's bread wins by the analysis of desire.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus (trans. Cyril Bailey, 1926)

real_life_example.event_title: Victor Hugo publishes The Art of Being a Grandfather
real_life_example.event: After his son Charles died in 1871, Victor Hugo took charge of the upbringing of his two young grandchildren, Georges and Jeanne. In May 1877 he published L'Art d'etre grand-pere (The Art of Being a Grandfather), a collection of poems devoted to the two children and their everyday play. The book was a great success, and Georges and Jeanne became famous through it.
real_life_example.explanation: France's most celebrated poet, near the end of a career spent on epic and political themes, chose small children and their ordinary doings as the subject of one of his last collections.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the plain food a child's little hands have stirred is sweeter than the nectar of the gods, and Hugo set the small daily doings of his grandchildren above the grand themes of his earlier work.

tamil:
மக்கள்மெய் தீண்டல் உடற்கின்பம் மற்றுஅவர்
சொற்கேட்டல் இன்பம் செவிக்கு.
transliteration:
Makkalmey Theendal Udarkinbam Matravar,
Sorkettal Inbam Sevikku.
meaning: Touching your children is a joy to your body, and hearing them talk is a joy to your ears.
elementary: Your body has different ways of being happy. Hugging someone you love makes your whole self feel warm — that's happiness for your skin. Listening to someone you love chatter away makes your ears happy. This kural says children give you both at once.
university: Valluvar constructs the couplet as a strict parallel built on two of the five senses: உடற்கு இன்பம் ("pleasure for the body") paired with செவிக்கு இன்பம் ("pleasure for the ear"), with தீண்டல் (tīṇṭal, touching) answering கேட்டல் (kēṭṭal, hearing). Read against kural 64, which handled taste, the three verses form a deliberate sensory triptych — the chapter argues for the value of children not by doctrine but by cataloguing the specific bodily goods they confer. Parimēlaḻakar makes an interesting interpretive choice here: he notes that Valluvar writes simply சொல் ("speech") rather than the மழலைச்சொல் ("lisping speech") of the following couplet, and concludes that the verse covers not only infant babble but the learned speech of grown children as well, so that the ear's pleasure lasts a lifetime. The grammatical abstract nouns தீண்டல் and கேட்டல் are, in his reading, standing by metonymy for the acts themselves — a small point of Tamil grammatical commentary that shows how closely this tradition read the couplets.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Kṛṣṇa childhood narratives Yaśodā's happiness is rendered almost entirely through the senses — the weight of the child on her hip, the smell of his hair, the sound of his prattle and of the anklet bells as he crawls — and these become the canonical images of vātsalya-bhāva, the devotional mood of parental love.
hinduism.explanation: Hindu devotional poetry treats the physical, sensory experience of handling and hearing a small child as a legitimate and even the highest form of religious feeling.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates the value of children in the concrete pleasures of touch and hearing rather than in abstract benefit.
hinduism.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8 and the vātsalya tradition

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them.”
christianity.explanation: When the disciples try to keep children away from Jesus, he is indignant, and the Gospel records the physical detail — he picks them up and lays hands on them rather than merely speaking a blessing.
christianity.tie_back: Mark records the same instinct the Kural describes: with children, the body wants contact.

islam.quote_or_event: Allah's Messenger kissed Al-Hasan bin 'Ali while Al-Aqra' bin Habis at-Tamim was sitting beside him. Al-Aqra said, “I have ten children and I have never kissed anyone of them.” Allah's Messenger cast a look at him and said, “Whoever is not merciful to others will not be treated mercifully.”
islam.explanation: A chief boasts of never having embraced any of his ten children, and is rebuked — physical tenderness toward children is treated here not as sentimentality but as a moral obligation.
islam.tie_back: The hadith defends precisely the bodily pleasure the Kural celebrates: the touch of one's children is a good, and refusing it is a fault.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 5997, Book of Good Manners (narrated by Abū Hurayrah)

judaism.quote_or_event: “then shall ye suck, ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees. As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you.”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah reaches for the most immediate physical images available — nursing, being carried on the hip, being bounced on the knees — to describe the consolation God intends for Jerusalem.
judaism.tie_back: The prophet assumes exactly the Kural's premise: handling a small child is one of the most intensely good bodily experiences there is.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that every bond of affection — and the commentarial story attached to these verses concerns a man devastated by the death of his son — carries an exactly proportionate load of future sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the honest counter-voice to the Kural: the very sensory delight Valluvar praises is, for early Buddhism, the precise mechanism by which suffering gets in.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Feeling her child quivering, trembling, moving, and stirring, the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ--glad, pleased, and joyful, &c.--spoke thus: ‘No, forsooth, the fruit of my womb has not been taken from me, it has not died, it is not fallen, it is not lost. Formerly it did not move, but now it does move.’”
jainism.explanation: After the unborn Mahâvîra lay still out of compassion for his mother and she feared him dead, he stirred slightly, and her grief turned to joy at the feel of her child moving.
jainism.tie_back: Trisalâ's delight at simply feeling her child is a scriptural instance of what this kural says: the touch of one's child is the body's greatest pleasure.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §§92–94 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The mind of the poor child is so fickle that he even touches snakes and fire. His mother and father hug him close in their embrace, and so he plays in joy and bliss.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan draws on the parent's embrace of a small child as a picture of how God holds and protects the devotee.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's delight in touching one's children, the verse makes the parents' embrace the centre of the image, a moment of shared joy.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1266, Raag Malaar, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Glorious Hector pulled the glittering helmet off and set it on the ground. Then he kissed his dear son and held him in his arms.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector reaches for his baby son on the walls of Troy; the child screams at the bronze and the nodding horsehair crest, so the greatest warrior of Troy takes off his helmet, laughing, in order to hold him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's line dramatised — a man who sets down his armour because the touch of his child is worth more.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 6.472–474 (trans. Ian Johnston, Vancouver Island University)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Thee now no more / The joyful house and best of wives shall welcome, / Nor little sons run up to snatch their kisses / And touch with silent happiness thy heart.”
philosophy.explanation: Lucretius is reporting — in order to refute — the standard human lament about death, and the thing he takes as the most obviously precious loss is small children running up to be kissed.
philosophy.tie_back: The Epicurean poet picks out the identical two goods the Kural does: the child's rush into your arms and the wordless delight it produces.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 3.894–896 (trans. William Ellery Leonard, 1916)

real_life_example.event_title: Kangaroo mother care is developed in Bogota
real_life_example.event: Facing a shortage of incubators and high infection rates among low birth weight babies, the Colombian paediatricians Edgar Rey Sanabria and Hector Martinez-Gomez began in 1978 to have mothers carry their premature infants in continuous skin-to-skin contact on their chests. The method, combined with breastfeeding and early discharge, became known as the Kangaroo Mother Program. It was later studied internationally, and the World Health Organization published guidelines on kangaroo mother care in 2003.
real_life_example.explanation: Doctors found that a parent's touch, not only machines, could keep the most fragile newborns warm and help them thrive, and the practice spread around the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls the touch of one's child the body's delight, and kangaroo care made that very touch, skin to skin, into a recognised form of medicine for both mother and baby.

tamil:
குழல்இனிது யாழ்இனிது என்பதம் மக்கள்
மழலைச்சொல் கேளா தவர்.
transliteration:
Kuzhalinidhu Yaazhinidhu Enpadham Makkal,
Mazhalaichchol Kelaadhavar.
meaning: ‘The flute is sweet, the harp is sweet,’ say only those who have never heard the baby talk of their own children.
elementary: Some people say the most beautiful sound in the world is music. This kural teases them a little: they only think that because they have never sat and listened to a toddler talking nonsense. If they had, they would know which sound really wins.
university: The couplet is the Kural's most famous piece of wit, and its structure is a rhetorical trap. Valluvar never asserts that a child's babble is sweeter than music; he simply reports who it is that ranks music first — namely, those who have not heard மழலைச்சொல் (maḻalai-c-col), the half-formed lisping speech of a small child. Parimēlaḻakar identifies the remainder as a குறிப்பெச்சம், a deliberately unspoken implication that the reader is left to supply, and Maṇakkuṭavar makes it blunt: "those who have heard do not say it." The two instruments named are not decorative: the குழல் (kuḻal, the transverse flute) and the யாழ் (yāḻ, the ancient Tamil harp-lute) were the paired standards of vocal-and-instrumental excellence in the Caṅkam musical system, so Valluvar is measuring the child's voice against the recognised summit of the art. The word maḻalai has since passed into ordinary Tamil as an affectionate term for toddler-speech largely on the strength of this verse.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kṛṣṇa's flute is treated across Vaiṣṇava poetry as the most irresistible sound in creation, drawing cows, rivers and gopīs out of themselves; yet in the same literature Yaśodā's happiness comes not from the flute at all but from her child's broken half-words and the noise of his anklets.
hinduism.explanation: The devotional tradition holds both claims at once — the flute as supreme music, and the child's voice as what a mother actually treasures.
hinduism.tie_back: The two sounds the Kural sets against each other, flute and toddler-speech, are the same two that Hindu devotion places side by side in the Kṛṣṇa cycle.
hinduism.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8–10.21 (the flute of Kṛṣṇa and Yaśodā's vātsalya)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Yea; have ye never read, Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise?”
christianity.explanation: The chief priests are indignant at children shouting in the temple; Jesus answers by citing scripture to the effect that infant voices are the medium through which praise reaches its completed form.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts rank the untrained sound of small children above the accomplished performances of adults.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Jesus] said, 'Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet.'”
islam.explanation: Mary, challenged over her newborn, points to the infant; and the child in the cradle speaks — the Qur'an's most striking instance of a baby's voice silencing a crowd of adults.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural's premise that an infant's speech carries a weight no adult performance can match, though for the Qur'an the weight is miraculous rather than affectionate.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength because of thine enemies, that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm places the voices of the very youngest at the centre of a poem about cosmic majesty, making infant sound a source of strength rather than mere noise.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it deliberately elevates the least trained human voice above everything more impressive.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the Buddha returned to Kapilavatthu, Yasodharā sent their young son Rāhula to him saying that he should ask his father for his inheritance; the boy followed the Buddha through the city repeating the request, and the Buddha's answer was to have him ordained, giving him the Dhamma instead.
buddhism.explanation: The scene is one of very few in the early canon that lingers on a small child's persistent, artless speech to a parent.
buddhism.tie_back: It offers the Kural's situation — a father hearing his small son's voice — but the tradition treats the moment as an occasion for renunciation rather than for delight.
buddhism.source: Vinaya, Mahāvagga I.54 (the ordination of Rāhula)

jainism.quote_or_event: When Trisalâ believed her unborn child had died, ‘in the palace of king Siddhârtha the music of drums and stringed instruments, the clapping of hands, the dramatical performances, and the amusements of the people ceased, and mournful dejection reigned there.’
jainism.explanation: Once the child seemed lost, the royal musicians and players fell silent, because without the child their music had nothing to celebrate.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks a child's prattle above flute and lute, and here music loses all its sweetness when the child seems gone, which places the child above the instruments.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §92 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “As the child places so much faith in his father, I speak as it pleases the Guru to have me speak.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn celebrating the birth of his son, Guru Arjan likens his own speech before the Guru to a small child talking with complete trust to its father.
sikhism.tie_back: Both texts linger on the voice of a child before a loving parent, though only the Kural ranks that voice above the finest music.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 396, Raag Asa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The satyr Marsyas, having taken up the aulos (the reed pipe), challenged Apollo and his lyre to decide which instrument was sweeter; Apollo won and flayed him alive for the presumption.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth stages the question of pipe versus lyre as a literal contest, and treats the answer as so serious that the loser is destroyed for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar names the same two categories of instrument, pipe and stringed lute, and then dismisses the whole contest — neither wins against a toddler talking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius, describing how early humans first softened, writes that it was the coming of children and the winning ways of their affection that broke down the fierce, proud temper of primitive men and made settled life possible.
philosophy.explanation: For the Epicurean poet, the charm of small children is a causal force in human history, not a sentimental aside — it is what taught the species gentleness.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives a naturalistic account of why the Kural's claim is true: children's artless voices and gestures really do disarm adults in a way art cannot.

real_life_example.event_title: Charles Darwin records his infant son's first expressions and sounds
real_life_example.event: From the birth of his first child, William Erasmus, on 27 December 1839, Charles Darwin kept a notebook recording the baby's movements, cries, smiles and responses to sounds, and he continued the observations for several years. The notes later fed into his 1872 book on the expression of emotions. In 1877 he drew on them for the article A biographical sketch of an infant, published in the journal Mind.
real_life_example.explanation: The great naturalist turned the same patient attention he gave to finches and barnacles on his own baby, and the Darwin Correspondence Project notes the obvious pride and joy that shows through the notes.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who rank the flute and lute sweetest have never heard their own child's babble, and Darwin, among the most observant minds of his age, found his infant's first sounds worth recording for decades.

tamil:
தந்தை மகற்காற்றும் நன்றி அவையத்து
முந்தி இருப்பச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Thandhai Makarkaatrum Nandri Avaiyaththu,
Mundhi Iruppach Cheyal.
meaning: The best thing a father can do for his son is to make him good enough to sit in the front row among learned people.
elementary: A dad can give his child lots of things — toys, money, a bike. This kural says the best gift is different: teach your child so well that when clever grown-ups sit down to talk, your child is the one they want sitting at the front.
university: The couplet defines the father's duty with unusual precision. நன்றி (naṉṟi) here means the benefit or good office a father performs, and the content of that benefit is not property but standing: to be able to sit முந்தி (muntī, "foremost, ahead") in the அவை (avai), the learned assembly. The avai was a real institution in the Tamil and broader Indic world — the court or scholarly council where reputation was won by demonstrated learning and skill in speech — and the Kural devotes two later chapters, அவையறிதல் and அவையஞ்சாமை, to how one conducts oneself there. Parimēlaḻakar draws the sharpest possible conclusion from the wording: making a son wealthy, he says, cannot count as நன்றி at all, because wealth brings suffering; only education does. The couplet thus quietly converts the entire chapter's language of "wealth" into a claim about cultural capital, and it is this verse, with 68, that makes Chapter 7 one of the most-cited passages in modern Tamil arguments for universal education.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Uddālaka Āruṇi tells his son Śvetaketu, at twelve years old, to go and live as a student, on the grounds that in their family no one has ever remained unlearned — no one has been a brahmin merely by birth; the boy returns at twenty-four full of learning and conceited with it, whereupon his father begins the teaching that culminates in tat tvam asi.
hinduism.explanation: The father's obligation in this foundational Upaniṣadic scene is specifically educational: he will not permit his son to hold a status he has not earned by study.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural's rule enacted — the father's gift to the son is the learning that lets him stand among the learned in his own right.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.”
christianity.explanation: Paul addresses fathers directly and makes formation — instruction and discipline — the specific content of the paternal role, over against mere authority.
christianity.tie_back: Both verses single out the father and define his duty as the shaping of the child rather than the provision of goods.

islam.quote_or_event: “No father has given a greater gift to his children than good moral training.”
islam.explanation: The hadith ranks the cultivation of a child's character above every material provision a father might make.
islam.tie_back: Both texts define the father's best gift as formation rather than inheritance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A father is obligated with regard to his son to circumcise him, and to redeem him if he is a firstborn son who must be redeemed by payment to a priest, and to teach him Torah, and to marry him to a woman, and to teach him a trade.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud lists the father's legal duties as a closed set, and two of the five are educational — Torah study and a marketable craft.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the father's obligation to his son concrete, enumerable, and centred on equipping him to hold his own place in the community.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigālovāda Sutta the Buddha lists the five ways parents show compassion to their children: they restrain them from evil, encourage them to do good, have them trained in a profession, arrange a suitable marriage, and in due time hand over their inheritance.
buddhism.explanation: This is the fullest statement of lay parental duty in the Pali canon, and professional training sits at its centre.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts define what a parent owes a child as a duty of equipping them for a public role, not simply of loving or feeding them.
buddhism.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (the six directions: parents)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He studied the seventy-two arts, and acquired knowledge of the world; he was in the bloom of youth, and had a fine figure and good looks.”
jainism.explanation: Samudrapâla, son of the Jain layman Pâlita, was raised in his father's house to master the seventy-two arts before he went on to renounce the world and reach liberation.
jainism.tie_back: A devout Jain father seeing his son fully educated in all the recognised arts is close to Valluvar's idea of a father's duty to make his son pre-eminent among the learned.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 21.5–6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Sikh tradition credits Guru Angad, the second Guru, with standardizing the Gurmukhi script and setting up schools to teach the young to read and write in their own Punjabi language rather than in classical Sanskrit.
sikhism.explanation: Britannica reports these traditional attributions, which are central to Sikh memory of Guru Angad, while noting that historical documentation for some of his attributed institutions is limited.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the best thing a father can give his son is learning that wins him a place in the assembly of the wise; Sikh tradition remembers its second Guru as the one who opened learning to the community's children.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guru Angad' (Britannica Editors)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For this reason he sent me to instruct you in all these things, to be both a speaker of words and a doer of deeds.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The old tutor Phoenix reminds Achilles that Peleus sent him along precisely because the boy was untaught in war and in the assemblies where men win distinction — so Phoenix was to make him excellent at both speech and action.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Homeric father's stated aim for his son is the Kural's word for word: to hold the first place in the assembly.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 9.442–443 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1924)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “As soon as one of them grasps what is said to him, the nurse, the mother, the tutor, and the father himself strive hard that the child may excel, and as each act and word occurs they teach and impress upon him that this is just, and that unjust, one thing noble, another base, one holy, another unholy, and that he is to do this, and not do that.”
philosophy.explanation: Protagoras is arguing that virtue is taught, and his evidence is the sheer relentlessness with which Athenian households instruct their children from the first moment they can understand language.
philosophy.tie_back: It supplies the argumentative backing for the Kural's assumption that a child's eventual standing among the learned is something a father actively makes.
philosophy.source: Plato, Protagoras 325c–d (trans. W. R. M. Lamb, Loeb Classical Library)

real_life_example.event_title: Philip II of Macedon engages Aristotle as tutor to Alexander
real_life_example.event: King Philip II of Macedon summoned the philosopher Aristotle to act as tutor to his 13-year-old son Alexander. Aristotle taught the prince for about three years, from roughly age 13 to 16. Ancient tradition, reported by Plutarch, places the lessons at Mieza, where archaeologists have excavated a complex believed to be the school.
real_life_example.explanation: Philip, already a powerful king, judged that the best thing he could give his heir was the finest teacher in the Greek world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines a father's duty as making his son fit to sit in the front rank of the learned, and Philip secured for Alexander the most learned tutor of the age.

tamil:
தம்மின்தம் மக்கள் அறிவுடைமை மாநிலத்து
மன்னுயிர்க் கெல்லாம் இனிது.
transliteration:
Thammindham Makkal Arivudaimai Maanilaththu,
Mannuyirk Kellaam Inidhu.
meaning: When children become wiser than their parents, it brings joy not only to the parents but to everyone on this great earth.
elementary: When you get better at something than your teacher or your parents, nobody minds — everyone is delighted. This kural says that is one of the few kinds of being-beaten that makes the whole world happy.
university: The compressed opening தம்மின்தம் மக்கள் அறிவுடைமை carries an ambiguity the commentators split over. Parimēlaḻakar reads தம்மின் as "more than to themselves" — the children's wisdom is sweeter to all the world's beings than it is even to the parents — and takes மன்னுயிர் ("enduring lives") to stand specifically for the discerning, since only they can appreciate learning. Most moderns, including M. Varadarajan and Karunanidhi, read தம்மின் comparatively of the children instead: that the children surpass the parents in wisdom. Either way, the verse performs a striking widening of scope. Having spent four couplets on the private senses — taste, touch, hearing — Valluvar suddenly extends the circle to மாநிலத்து மன்னுயிர்க்கெல்லாம், every living thing on the great earth. The claim is that a child's intelligence is a non-rival public good: unlike wealth or rank, one family's gain in wisdom costs no one anything and delights everyone. That move, from the household to the biosphere in a single line, is characteristic of the Kural's method throughout the household chapters.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The boy Naciketas, sent in anger to Death by his father Vājaśravasa after questioning the worthlessness of the cows his father was giving away, refuses Yama's offers of wealth, long life and pleasure, and holds out for the knowledge of what lies beyond death — obtaining a teaching that surpasses anything his father possessed.
hinduism.explanation: The Upaniṣad's entire teaching is delivered to a child precisely because the child's discernment outstrips the adult world around him.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the text takes evident pleasure in a son whose wisdom exceeds his father's.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions. And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers.”
christianity.explanation: The only episode the Gospels record from Jesus' childhood is this one: a twelve-year-old sitting among the teachers in the temple, and the reaction is astonishment from everyone present, not just his parents.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's scenario almost exactly — a child's understanding delighting an entire assembly beyond the family.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Allah] said, 'O John, take the Scripture with determination.' And We gave him judgement [while yet] a boy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents Yaḥyā (John) as receiving ḥukm — sound judgement and discernment — while still a child, an explicit divine endorsement of precocious wisdom.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat a child's wisdom outrunning ordinary adult expectation as something good, given, and worth announcing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the child Samuel grew on, and was in favour both with the LORD, and also with men.”
judaism.explanation: Samuel, given over to the sanctuary as a small child, grows into the prophetic authority that his elders — including the priest Eli and Eli's own sons — conspicuously lack.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a child's growing discernment is recorded as a good that reaches beyond his family to everyone around him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The Wise desire a child that is / Superior or just the same, / But not for one inferior, / Who will break up the family”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha classifies children into three kinds — atijāta (born beyond, surpassing the parents), anujāta (born after, equal to them), and avajāta (born below) — and says the wise hope for the first.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact thesis, in a canonical taxonomy: the child who exceeds the parent is the one to be wished for.
buddhism.source: Itivuttaka 74, Puttasutta, vv. 504–505 (trans. Ānandajoti Bhikkhu, Buddhist Wisdom Verses)

jainism.quote_or_event: “In this way all (these) professors of the Law gradually obtained enlightenment … The king and the queen, the Brahmanical Purôhita, his wife, and his sons, they all reached perfection.”
jainism.explanation: Bhrigu's two sons, wiser than their Vedic father, first convert him and their mother, and through that example the king and queen of Ishukâra are converted too, so all six reach liberation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says children wiser than their parents delight the whole world. In this Jain story the sons' greater wisdom spreads beyond the family to the king and queen and frees them all.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.6–7 and 14.51–53 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that knowledge truly reflected upon does not stay private; it turns its owner into someone who does good for others.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's claim that a child's wisdom delights every living being on earth, the Guru treats knowledge as a good that spreads outward to benefit others.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Asa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the day he is born, the infant Hermes climbs out of his cradle, invents the lyre from a tortoise shell, steals Apollo's cattle and covers his tracks by making them walk backwards, then argues his own case before Zeus so cleverly that Zeus laughs aloud with delight and the gods settle the quarrel in friendship.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Homeric Hymn is essentially a comedy about a newborn whose intelligence outmatches an established Olympian's, and whose father's reaction is open delight.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the child's surpassing wit is pleasing to everyone who witnesses it, not only to the parent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates takes an untaught slave boy from Meno's household, asks him a series of questions about doubling the area of a square, and draws a correct geometrical demonstration out of him — to the visible astonishment of Meno, who had assumed the boy knew nothing.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the scene to argue that understanding is latent in every person, so that a child of no standing can be shown to possess what the educated master does not expect.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts stage the pleasure and surprise of finding wisdom in someone from whom no one expected it.

real_life_example.event_title: Leopold Mozart sets aside his own career to train Wolfgang
real_life_example.place: Salzburg, Austria, and courts across Europe
real_life_example.event: Leopold Mozart was a court musician in Salzburg and the author of a 1756 violin method that became a standard text and was widely translated. In the years after his son Wolfgang was born in 1756, he largely, though not entirely, gave up composing in order to teach his two gifted children, Nannerl and Wolfgang, and took them on long concert tours across Europe. Wolfgang went on to surpass his father completely as a composer.
real_life_example.explanation: A respected musician deliberately made room for a child whose gifts exceeded his own, and the son's music became a lasting pleasure for listeners all over the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that a child wiser than the parent delights not only the parents but every living being on earth, and Wolfgang's surpassing of Leopold produced music the whole world still enjoys.

tamil:
ஈன்ற பொழுதின் பெரிதுவக்கும் தன்மகனைச்
சான்றோன் எனக்கேட்ட தாய்.
transliteration:
Eendra Pozhudhin Peridhuvakkum Thanmakanaich,
Chaandron Enakketta Thaai.
meaning: A mother who hears people call her son a good and wise man feels more joy than she did on the day he was born.
elementary: The day a baby is born is one of the happiest days a mother ever has. But this kural says there is a day that beats it: the day she overhears other people saying her child has grown up to be a genuinely good person.
university: The couplet's force comes from the word சான்றோன் (cāṉṟōṉ), from the root சால் — "filled up, complete, sufficient." A cāṉṟōṉ is not merely a clever or successful man but one who is full in character, and the term carries enormous weight in Tamil ethical vocabulary; the Kural devotes a whole later chapter, சான்றாண்மை, to the quality. The second load-bearing word is கேட்ட (kēṭṭa, "having heard"): the mother's supreme joy arrives not from seeing but from hearing others say it. Parimēlaḻakar reads this carefully, arguing that the ordinary joy of birth is the joy of what is seen with the eyes on one's lap, while this is the distinct and greater joy of hearing one's child pronounced complete by those qualified to judge. He also notes that the couplet names the mother specifically because her joy admits of no measure, which is why Valluvar separates it from the father's case in 67. Read alongside 70, the chapter closes with a matched pair — the mother's joy, then the father's requital — with public reputation as the currency of both.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kausalyā's happiness in the Rāmāyaṇa is repeatedly portrayed not as pride in having borne a prince but as joy at the universal testimony of Ayodhyā's people to Rāma's righteousness — and her deepest grief, at his exile, is grief at being separated from a son whom everyone calls good.
hinduism.explanation: The epic consistently locates a mother's happiness in what the community says about her son's character rather than in his rank or her own act of bearing him.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make the mother's great joy depend on hearing her son publicly reckoned a man of worth.
hinduism.source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa (Kausalyā and Rāma)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.”
christianity.explanation: The elder writing to Gaius reports that travelling brethren have brought back news of Gaius's conduct, and says that receiving such a report is the height of his happiness.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact structure — the joy is in hearing the report of a child's moral worth, and it is named as the greatest joy there is.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when she delivered her, she said, 'My Lord, I have delivered a female.' And Allah was most knowing of what she delivered... Every time Zechariah entered upon her in the prayer chamber, he found with her provision. He said, 'O Mary, from where is this [coming] to you?'”
islam.explanation: The wife of ʿImrān dedicates her child before birth and is initially disappointed at the outcome; the narrative then vindicates the daughter through Zechariah's repeated astonishment at Mary's standing with God.
islam.tie_back: It touches the Kural's theme — a mother's estimate of her child transformed by what is later witnessed of that child's worth — but only obliquely.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The father of the righteous shall greatly rejoice: and he that begetteth a wise child shall have joy of him. Thy father and thy mother shall be glad, and she that bare thee shall rejoice.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb moves from the general case to a direct address, and singles out the woman who gave birth as the one who will rejoice.
judaism.tie_back: The phrase "she that bare thee shall rejoice" is almost a translation of the Kural's ஈன்ற... தாய் — the one who bore you, rejoicing at your wisdom.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Rūpasārī, the brahmin mother of Sāriputta, had long resented her son's renunciation; on the night of his death in the room where he was born, she saw the great deities of the heavens come in succession to attend him, realised what her son actually was, and only then rejoiced in him — after which he taught her and she attained stream-entry.
buddhism.explanation: The commentarial tradition preserves this as the story of a mother who came late and overwhelmingly to the knowledge of her son's true stature.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the mother's supreme joy arrive not at birth but at the moment her son is recognised for what he has become.
buddhism.source: Pali commentarial tradition on Sāriputta's death (Dhammapada Commentary; see also SN 47.13)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Then the eye-disease was washed away like mud by Lady Marudevī’s copious tears of joy, when she heard this. She saw her son’s Tirthakṛt-splendor accompanied by the supernatural powers, and from joy at the sight of that, her absorption-in-that took place.”
jainism.explanation: Marudevî had wept herself nearly blind with grief for her son Rishabha, the first Tîrthankara, who had become a wandering ascetic; when Bharata told her of her son's glory, her tears of joy healed her eyes and she attained omniscience and liberation then and there.
jainism.tie_back: A mother whose joy on hearing her son praised exceeds anything she felt before is exactly this kural's picture, and the Jain account makes that joy powerful enough to liberate her.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book I (Âdîshvaracharitra), ch. III, part 12, 'Marudevî's omniscience and death' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS, 1931)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O son, this is your mother’s hope and prayer, that you may never forget the Lord, Har, Har, even for an instant. May you ever vibrate upon the Lord of the Universe.”
sikhism.explanation: In this hymn, known among Sikhs as 'Poota Mata Ki Asees' (a mother's blessing to her son), Guru Arjan puts into a mother's mouth her deepest wish: not wealth or rank for her son, but a life of constant remembrance of God.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's mother, whose greatest joy is to hear her son called a person of true worth, this mother's highest hope is fixed on her son's character, not on his birth or fortune.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 496, Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “She then, seized with wonder, went back to her chamber, for she laid to heart the wise saying of her son.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope has come down to ask the bard to stop his song; Telemachus, for the first time in the poem, answers her as a grown man and sends her back upstairs — and Homer records that what she takes away is not offence but amazement at his wisdom.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's moment precisely: a mother's wonder at hearing her son reveal himself as a man of sense.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 1.360 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1919)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that mothers who have given their children away to be raised elsewhere go on loving them and rejoice when they recognise them prospering, without ever seeking to be loved in return — because loving, rather than being loved, is what the affection of a parent consists in.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle a mother's characteristic pleasure is in the child's good as such, not in any benefit she receives from it.
philosophy.tie_back: It explains philosophically why the Kural's mother rejoices at a report she gains nothing from — it is the good of the child, heard about, that constitutes the joy.

real_life_example.event_title: Einstein sends his ailing mother news that his theory has been confirmed
real_life_example.event: In September 1919 Albert Einstein learned by telegram from the physicist H. A. Lorentz that British eclipse expeditions had confirmed the bending of starlight by the Sun predicted by his general theory of relativity. He at once sent a postcard with the good news to his mother, Pauline, who was seriously ill, and in the same card wished he could keep her company. Einstein became world-famous after the results were announced in November 1919, and his mother, whom he brought to his Berlin home at the end of that year, died there in February 1920.
real_life_example.explanation: In the last months of her life, a mother heard that her son had been proved right before the whole scientific world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a mother's joy on hearing her son called a person of true worth exceeds her joy at his birth, and Pauline Einstein lived just long enough to hear her son acclaimed.

tamil:
மகன்தந்தைக்கு ஆற்றும் உதவி இவன்தந்தை
என்நோற்றான் கொல்எனும் சொல்.
transliteration:
Makandhandhaikku Aatrum Udhavi Ivandhandhai,
Ennotraan Kol Enum Sol.
meaning: The best thing a son can do for his father is to live so well that people ask, ‘What great good did his father do to have such a son?’
elementary: How does a child pay a parent back? Not with money. This kural says you pay them back by being so good that when people meet you they think, "Wow — whoever raised this person must have done something really special."
university: The chapter closes by completing the reciprocal pair begun in 67: there the father's duty was to place the son foremost in the assembly; here the son's உதவி (utavi, "help, requital") is to generate a particular sentence in other people's mouths. The verb நோல் / நோற்றல் (nōṟṟal) means to undertake tapas — ascetic austerity, penance — so என்நோற்றான் கொல் literally asks "what penance can he have performed?" The idiom presumes the karmic economy in which a son of high quality is earned by merit, and Valluvar's wit is to make the son's whole filial duty consist in causing that inference to be drawn. Parimēlaḻakar underlines the point that the requital is owed specifically to the father who made him learned — i.e. it answers couplet 67 directly — and he glosses சொல் as standing, by metonymy, for the conduct that produces the saying. Note what the couplet conspicuously does not say: nothing about supporting parents in old age, obedience, or ritual duty. The entire obligation is discharged through character as publicly perceived, which is a strikingly reputational, non-transactional construal of filial piety.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Daśaratha, childless and aging, performs the putrakāmeṣṭi sacrifice under Ṛṣyaśṛṅga to obtain sons, and receives Rāma and his brothers; thereafter the people of Ayodhyā speak of Rāma's virtues in terms that reflect glory back onto the father who obtained him by austerity.
hinduism.explanation: The epic supplies the literal background the Kural's idiom assumes — a father who performed rites and austerities in order to deserve a son, and a son whose excellence publicly vindicates them.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's imagined bystander asking what penance the father performed is asking exactly the question Daśaratha's story answers.
hinduism.source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla Kāṇḍa (the putrakāmeṣṭi of Daśaratha)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
christianity.explanation: At the Jordan, the father's satisfaction in the son is declared publicly, before the crowd, at the moment the son begins his work.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts make the son's worth into a public utterance that redounds to the father, though here the father speaks rather than the onlookers.

islam.quote_or_event: “And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, 'My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up [when I was] small.'”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an prescribes the son's requital to his parents in old age as humility and intercessory prayer, framed as repayment for the upbringing he received.
islam.tie_back: Both texts define what a grown child owes a parent, though the Qur'an makes it prayer and deference while the Kural makes it reputation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb states the return on parenting in the simplest possible form: the child's character is what the parent receives.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts make the son's standing, rather than any material support, the thing the parent actually gets back.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says that even if one carried one's mother on one shoulder and one's father on the other for a hundred years, tending them the whole time, one would still not have repaid them; but whoever establishes parents who lack faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom in those four things has repaid them and more.
buddhism.explanation: Physical service is declared structurally insufficient as repayment; only raising the parents' own moral and spiritual condition counts.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it rejects material or bodily support as the true filial return and substitutes something the son achieves in the realm of character.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.34 (Book of the Twos, on repaying one's parents)

jainism.quote_or_event: Mahâvîra stayed in his parents' house until they died, then fulfilled his promise and renounced the world, and the Laukântika gods hailed him: ‘Victory, victory to thee, gladdener of the world! … Establish the religion of the law which benefits all living beings in the whole universe!’
jainism.explanation: The son kept his vow not to leave home during his parents' lifetime, and his later life drew the praise of gods and men.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says a son repays his father by living so that others marvel at the father who produced him; Mahâvîra's dutiful wait and the praise that followed match this only loosely.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §§110–111 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Blessed, blessed is the father; blessed, blessed is the family; blessed, blessed is the mother, who gave birth to the Guru.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das praises the True Guru by calling his father, family and mother blessed for having produced him; the child's greatness reflects back on the parents.
sikhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the response Valluvar says a worthy son should draw from people: seeing him, they call his father blessed.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 310, Raag Gauri, Gauri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Zeus, all you other gods, grant that this child, my son, may become, like me, pre-eminent among the Trojans, as strong and brave as me. Grant that he may rule Troy with strength. May people someday say, as he returns from war, 'This man is far better than his father.'”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector, holding his infant son on the walls of Troy, prays not that the boy honour him but that strangers one day judge the son superior to the father — and counts that as the outcome he most wants.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's mechanism exactly: the son discharges his debt by causing a particular sentence to be said about him in public, which redounds to the father.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 6.476–481 (trans. Ian Johnston, Vancouver Island University)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Would anyone have heard of Aristo and Gryllus except through Xenophon and Plato, their sons? Socrates keeps alive the memory of Sophroniscus.”
philosophy.explanation: Arguing that a son can repay and even surpass what his father gave him, Seneca points out that many fathers are remembered only because of what their sons became, citing Agrippa’s obscure father alongside the fathers of Plato, Xenophon and Socrates.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s idea of a son’s service exactly: the child’s worth becomes the way the world comes to honour the parent.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Benefits (De Beneficiis), Book III, ch. 32 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: Dorabji Tata completes his father Jamsetji's steel works
real_life_example.event: Jamsetji Tata began planning India's first large-scale iron and steel works in the early 1900s but died in Germany in May 1904. His elder son Dorabji carried the project forward, and the Tata Iron and Steel Company was incorporated in 1907, with a plant and township built at the village of Sakchi. In 1919 the township was renamed Jamshedpur in Jamsetji's honour.
real_life_example.explanation: The son's work kept his father's name at the centre of the achievement, so that a whole city came to be named after the father.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a son repays his father by living so that people ask what the father did to deserve such a son, and Dorabji's work made Jamsetji's name permanent in the city of Jamshedpur.

tamil:
அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ் ஆர்வலர்
புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்.
transliteration:
Anbirkum undo adaikkundhaazh aarvalar,
Punkaneer poosal tharum.
meaning: Is there any lock that can keep love hidden? When someone dear is suffering, the tears of sorrow of those who love them will give it away.
elementary: Imagine trying to keep a puppy shut inside a box — it will still wiggle and whine and everyone will know it's there. Love is like that. Even if you never say "I love you," the moment someone you care about gets hurt, your eyes fill up and everybody can see exactly how you feel.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter on அன்பு (anbu, love) with an argument from evidence rather than exhortation. தாழ் (thaazh) is the wooden bolt or latch of a door, and the rhetorical question அடைக்குந்தாழ் உண்டோ — "is there a latch that shuts it in?" — treats love as a physical presence that leaks past every attempt at concealment. The proof offered is deliberately small: புன்கணீர் (punkaneer), literally "mean" or "slight" eye-water, a single involuntary tear shed for an ஆர்வலர் (aarvalar, one who is loved/desired). The commentator Parimelalhagar notes that love may not be available to காட்சி அளவை (perception) directly, yet it is established by அனுமான அளவை (inference) — a striking use of the technical vocabulary of Indian epistemology to argue that inner states are publicly readable through their effects. பூசல் (poosal) means a public outcry or uproar, so the couplet's paradox is that the quietest possible sign makes the loudest possible announcement.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A devotee whose speech is sometimes choked up, whose heart melts, who cries continually and sometimes laughs, who feels ashamed and cries out loudly and then dances — a devotee thus fixed in loving service to Me purifies the entire universe.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Uddhava that genuine love for God cannot stay inside a person; it breaks out involuntarily as a choked voice, uncontrollable weeping, and even dancing.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's point: love overflows the body's locks, and tears are the first thing to escape.
hinduism.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam) 11.14.24, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus wept. Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!”
christianity.explanation: At the tomb of his friend Lazarus, Jesus breaks down in tears, and the bystanders immediately read those tears as evidence of how deeply he had loved the dead man.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's mechanism acted out literally: the tear is what tells the crowd about the love.
christianity.source: Gospel of John 11:35–36, King James Version

islam.quote_or_event: “The eyes are shedding tears and the heart is grieved, and we will not say except what pleases our Lord, O Ibrahim!”
islam.explanation: When his infant son Ibrahim died, the Prophet Muhammad wept; challenged by Ibn ʿAwf for weeping, he answered that this was mercy (raḥma), then spoke these words.
islam.tie_back: The Prophet does not try to latch his love away — he names the tears as the visible overflow of an inward bond.
islam.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1303 (Book of Funerals), narrated by Anas ibn Mālik

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him… And he wept aloud: and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph has spent the whole scene disguised and composed before his brothers; the love he has been suppressing finally bursts out as weeping so loud that the Egyptian court hears it.
judaism.tie_back: A textbook case of the Kural's claim — the bolt fails, and the tears become a public announcement (பூசல்).

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the account of the Buddha's final days, the attendant Ānanda withdraws to a doorpost and weeps at the news that his teacher will soon pass away; the Buddha sends for him and gently acknowledges his long devotion before teaching him about impermanence.
buddhism.explanation: Ānanda tries to go off alone precisely so no one will see him cry, but his grief is discovered and read by the community as the measure of his attachment and love.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the attempt to shut love away behind a door fails, and tears betray it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “O great king, my loving and faithful wife moistened my breast with the tears of her eyes. The poor lady did not eat, nor drink, nor bathe, nor use perfumes, wreaths, and anointment, with my knowledge or without it.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anâthin tells King Srenika how, when he lay gravely ill, his wife's love showed itself in tears and in her refusal of food and adornment, though her love could not cure him.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says love cannot be locked away and shows itself in tears at a loved one's pain; this wife's tears on her sick husband's breast are exactly that.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.28–29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I cannot survive without seeing my Beloved. My eyes are welling up with tears.”
sikhism.explanation: In a Maajh hymn of longing, Guru Ram Das describes love for the Beloved Lord that cannot be held in silence: separation shows itself at once in tears.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's single tear, the welling eyes are the outward proof that betrays a love the heart could not lock inside.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 94, Raag Maajh, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Odysseus concealed the tears he shed from all the rest, but Alcinous alone marked him and took heed, for he sat by him, and heard him groaning heavily.”
greek_mythology.explanation: At the Phaeacian feast, Odysseus pulls his cloak over his head to hide his weeping as the bard sings of Troy, but the king sitting beside him notices anyway.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's image exactly — a man bolts his feelings behind a cloak, and the tears still give him away.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 8.93–95, trans. A. T. Murray (Loeb, 1919)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature, which interest him in the fortune of others, and render their happiness necessary to him, though he derives nothing from it except the pleasure of seeing it.”
philosophy.explanation: Adam Smith opens his moral philosophy by arguing that fellow-feeling is not chosen or calculated but built into human nature and triggered automatically by the sight of another's condition.
philosophy.tie_back: Smith gives the Kural's claim a philosophical form: the response to another's suffering is involuntary, which is precisely why it cannot be bolted in.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), Part I, Section I, Chapter I

real_life_example.event_title: Jim Redmond helps his injured son Derek finish the Olympic 400 metres
real_life_example.event: In the 400 metres semi-final at the Barcelona Olympics, the British runner Derek Redmond tore his hamstring on the back straight and began hobbling towards the finish alone. His father, Jim Redmond, came down from the stands, got past the stewards, put his arm around his son and helped him along the track. Just before the line his father let go, and Derek finished the race as a crowd of about 65,000 stood to applaud.
real_life_example.explanation: The father's love could not be held back by rules, officials or the setting of an Olympic stadium; it showed itself openly and at once when his son was suffering.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks whether any bolt can lock love in, and a father pushing past security to hold his weeping son shows love breaking out the moment a loved one is in pain.

tamil:
அன்பிலார் எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர் அன்புடையார்
என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Anbilaar ellaam thamakkuriyar anbudaiyaar,
Enbum uriyar pirarkku.
meaning: People without love keep everything for themselves. People with love feel that even their own bones belong to others.
elementary: Think about two kids with a bag of sweets. One says, "These are mine, nobody touch them." The other hands them around until the bag is empty, and is happier for it. This kural says a loving person gives so completely that they would give away their very bones if it helped someone else.
university: The couplet is built on a sharp antithesis of possession: எல்லாம் தமக்கு உரியர் ("all things belong to them") versus என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு ("even bones belong to others"). The word உரிமை/உரியர் is a legal term of ownership, so Valluvar is deliberately using the vocabulary of property law to describe self-giving. என்பு (enbu, bone) is the harshest, least giveable part of the body — the opposite of the money or grain one might expect a charity verse to mention — and its choice pushes generosity past the limit of comfort. Note also the chapter's internal sound-play: அன்பு (love) and என்பு (bone) are near-rhymes that Valluvar will exploit again in Kurals 73, 77 and 80, binding the ethical argument to the anatomy of the body. Many commentators, including Manakkudavar and Parimelalhagar, read the second line as covering not only the corpse but the whole living self placed at the disposal of others.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The sage Dadhīci, asked by the gods for a weapon that could destroy the demon Vṛtra, voluntarily gives up his own body so that his spine can be forged into the thunderbolt (vajra) that saves the worlds.
hinduism.explanation: Dadhīci's asceticism had made his bones uniquely hard, and rather than refuse, he yields his skeleton to the common good and abandons the body by yogic will.
hinduism.tie_back: This is Kural 72's second line taken absolutely literally: a loving man whose very bones belonged to others.
hinduism.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam) 6.10 — the story of Dadhīci

christianity.quote_or_event: “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus names self-surrender to the point of death as the definitive measure of love, spoken on the night before his own execution.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural's scale: love is measured not by what one gives away but by whether one's own body is still one's own.
christianity.source: Gospel of John 15:13, King James Version

islam.quote_or_event: “They give ˹the emigrants˺ preference over themselves even though they may be in need. And whoever is saved from the selfishness of their own souls, it is they who are ˹truly˺ successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qurʾān praises the Anṣār of Medina, who housed and fed the refugees from Mecca while themselves in poverty — the virtue called īthār, preferring others over oneself.
islam.tie_back: The verse draws the same line Valluvar draws: the loveless hoard for themselves, the loving treat what is theirs as belonging to others.
islam.source: Qurʾān 59:9 (Sūrat al-Ḥashr), The Clear Quran, trans. Dr. Mustafa Khattab
