judaism.quote_or_event: “If I am not for myself, who is for me? But if I am for my own self only, what am I? And if not now, when?”
judaism.explanation: Hillel the Elder's three-part aphorism refuses both self-neglect and self-enclosure, insisting that a life lived only for oneself forfeits its claim to be a human life at all.
judaism.tie_back: Hillel's middle clause is Valluvar's first line: the person who is only for himself has become something less than a person.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sasa Jātaka, the Bodhisatta born as a hare has nothing to offer a hungry traveller, so he shakes the insects from his fur and throws himself into the fire so that his own body may serve as the guest's meal.
buddhism.explanation: The tale is the canonical Buddhist illustration of dāna-pāramī, the perfection of giving, where the gift is the giver's own flesh because nothing else is available.
buddhism.tie_back: The hare's body is not his own to keep — precisely the Kural's claim that the loving hold even their bones on behalf of others.
buddhism.source: Sasa Jātaka (Jātaka no. 316), Pāli Jātaka collection

jainism.quote_or_event: “I will give you my own flesh, weighing it with the dove. Be satisfied. Do not die.”
jainism.explanation: When a hawk demanded a dove that had fled to his lap, King Megharatha (an earlier birth of the Tîrthankara Shântinâtha) cut off his own flesh to balance the dove on the scales and finally climbed onto the scales himself.
jainism.tie_back: Megharatha treats his own body as belonging to others, which is precisely Valluvar's picture of the loving, who count even their bones as others' property.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book V (Shântinâthacaritra), ch. IV, part 7, 'Story of the dove and hawk' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Why do you say, "Mine, mine"? Look to God, who has given it to you.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan diagnoses the possessive cry of mine, mine as a symptom of moh (attachment), one of the five thieves, and reminds the listener that everything held was given and is not truly owned.
sikhism.tie_back: It answers the first half of the Kural exactly: the loveless claim everything as their own, and Gurbani names that claim as the false root to be uprooted.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 50, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Fates allow Admetus to escape death if someone will die in his place, his parents refuse, and only his wife Alcestis consents; she dies for him and is later brought back from the underworld by Heracles.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides' play turns on the fact that everyone in Admetus' household regards their own life as their own — except Alcestis, whose love makes hers transferable.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The play stages the Kural's two lines as two characters: the loveless keeping what is theirs, the loving surrendering even the body.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is true of the good man too that he does many acts for the sake of his friends and his country, and if necessary dies for them; for he will throw away both wealth and honours and in general the goods that are objects of competition.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that proper self-love is not hoarding but spending — the good person secures what is truly noble by giving away the goods everyone else competes for.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle inverts ownership the way Valluvar does: the loving person's goods, and finally his life, are held on others' account.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, 1169a, trans. W. D. Ross

real_life_example.event_title: Maximilian Kolbe offers his life for a fellow prisoner at Auschwitz
real_life_example.event: After a prisoner escaped from Auschwitz in July 1941, ten men were selected to be starved to death in reprisal. When one of them, Franciszek Gajowniczek, pleaded for his wife and children, the Polish Franciscan priest Maximilian Kolbe stepped forward and asked to take his place, and the SS accepted. Kolbe died in the cellar of Block 11 on 14 August 1941; Gajowniczek survived the war, and Kolbe was canonised in 1982.
real_life_example.explanation: Kolbe gave up his own body and life for a stranger, the furthest extent to which a person can give themselves to another.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the loving regard even their own bones as belonging to others, and Kolbe literally gave his body in exchange for another man's life.

tamil:
அன்போடு இயைந்த வழக்கென்ப ஆருயிர்க்கு
என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Anbodu iyaindha vazhakkenba aaruyirkku,
Enbodu iyaindha thodarbu.
meaning: The wise say our precious life is joined to a body of bone and flesh for one reason: so it can live a life of love.
elementary: Why do you have a body at all — arms, hands, a voice? This kural says: so that you can love people with them. A hug needs arms. Helping needs hands. The body is the tool love uses, and that is what it is for.
university: This is the philosophical hinge of the chapter. The couplet pairs two uses of இயைந்த (iyaindha, "joined with"): the soul's joining with என்பு (bone/body) and the life's joining with அன்பு (love), and asserts that the first exists as the வழக்கு — the settled practice, warrant, or rationale — of the second. ஆருயிர் (aaruyir, "rare/precious life") marks the soul as something hard-won, which sharpens the question of what it is embodied for. Parimelalhagar and later commentators read the verse causally, with some giving it a karmic gloss (embodiment as the fruit of love practised in a former birth) and others, including modern readers like M. Varadarajan, reading it teleologically: bodily existence is *for* loving. Either way Valluvar refuses a view in which the body is a mere prison for the soul — a pointed position in a South Asian intellectual landscape crowded with world-renouncing ascetic schools — and instead makes embodied relationship the point of having been born.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Teaching his wife Maitreyī before renouncing the world, Yājñavalkya explains that a husband is not dear for the husband's sake, nor a wife for the wife's sake, nor wealth or children for their own sakes — all are dear for the sake of the Self.
hinduism.explanation: The Upaniṣad grounds every particular love in a single underlying reality, making love rather than possession the thread that runs through all relationships.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats love as the reason our embodied attachments exist at all rather than as an accidental feature of them.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.”
christianity.explanation: James argues that an inward commitment which never becomes embodied action is not a live thing at all, using the body-and-spirit pair as his analogy.
christianity.tie_back: James uses exactly Valluvar's structure — the soul/body bond as the model for a virtue that must be joined to lived conduct.
christianity.source: Epistle of James 2:26, King James Version

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of the believers in their affection, mercy, and compassion for each other is that of a body: when any limb aches, the whole body reacts with sleeplessness and fever.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the community of believers as a single organism in which love is the connective tissue that makes one person's pain register in everyone else.
islam.tie_back: Both texts use the bone-and-body image to say that love is what makes a collection of parts into one living thing.
islam.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6011 (also Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2586), narrated by al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr

judaism.quote_or_event: Commenting on “love your neighbour as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18), Rabbi Akiva declares: “This is a great principle of the Torah.”
judaism.explanation: Akiva singles out one commandment as the organising principle from which the entire body of Jewish law takes its sense.
judaism.tie_back: Both make love the rationale that the rest of a life — or a legal system — is arranged around, not one item within it.
judaism.source: Sifra, Kedoshim 4:12; cf. Jerusalem Talmud, Nedarim 9:4

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even as a mother protects with her life her child, her only child, so with a boundless heart should one cherish all living beings.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha takes the most embodied, most instinctive human love — a mother's — and prescribes it as the model for an unrestricted attitude toward every creature.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats embodied love as the standard and purpose of a living being's existence, not as a private sentiment.
buddhism.source: Karaṇīya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipāta 1.8 / Khuddakapāṭha 9, trans. Amaravati Sangha

jainism.quote_or_event: “As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to kill. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to tyrannise over. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to torment.”
jainism.explanation: The Âcârânga teaches that the righteous person sees every other living being's suffering as their own, and for that reason neither kills nor causes others to kill.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the soul is embodied for the sake of love; the Jain sutra grounds kindness in the soul's recognition of itself in every other embodied being.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.5.5.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn recited daily in the Sikh evening prayer, Guru Arjan teaches that human birth is a rare gift whose whole purpose is loving union with God.
sikhism.tie_back: Both texts give embodiment a reason: the precious life takes a body in order to live out love.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa (So Purakh section of Rehras), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, an aged couple who unknowingly host the disguised Zeus and Hermes, ask as their reward only that neither should outlive the other; at the end of their lives they are transformed into an oak and a linden growing from one spot, their branches intertwined.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid gives the pair a single fate because their lives had already become a single life; even their transformed bodies remain joined.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is Valluvar's image of a life and a body inseparably joined by love, rendered as a pair of trees that cannot be separated.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Empedocles taught that the four roots of all things are moved by two opposing cosmic powers, Love (Philotēs) and Strife (Neikos): Love draws the elements together into living, articulated bodies, while Strife pulls them apart again.
philosophy.explanation: In his physics, love is not a feeling added onto matter but the literal binding force that assembles scattered elements into a living creature.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in cosmological form — the joining of life to flesh and bone is itself the work of love.
philosophy.source: Empedocles of Acragas, On Nature, fragments DK B17, B35 (5th century BCE)

real_life_example.event_title: Viktor Frankl writes Man's Search for Meaning
real_life_example.event: The Viennese psychiatrist Viktor Frankl was held in four Nazi camps, including Auschwitz, between 1942 and 1945, while his wife, parents and brother died. After liberation he dictated, within nine days, the book later published in English as Man's Search for Meaning. In it he describes a winter march during which he held on to the image of his wife and concluded that love reaches far beyond the physical person of the beloved and finds its deepest meaning in the beloved's inner self.
real_life_example.explanation: Frankl's account, written from the extremity of the camps, argues that the meaning of a human life is found in love, even when the body is reduced to bare survival.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural claims that the soul's union with the body exists for the sake of love, and Frankl found that, stripped of everything else, love was what gave his embodied life its point.

tamil:
அன்புஈனும் ஆர்வம் உடைமை அதுஈனும்
நண்பு என்னும் நாடாச் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Anbu eenum aarvam udaimai adhu eenum,
Nanbu ennum naadaach chirappu.
meaning: Love makes us eager to be close to others. That eagerness brings friendship, a great treasure that comes to us without our looking for it.
elementary: Love works like a seed that grows into a plant that makes more seeds. First you care about somebody. Then you want to be around them and do things for them. Then, before you notice, you have a friend — and friendship is one of the best things anyone can have.
university: The couplet is constructed as a genealogy, with ஈனும் (eenum, "begets, gives birth to") repeated to stage a two-step generation: அன்பு → ஆர்வம் → நண்பு. ஆர்வம் (aarvam) is warm eagerness or attentive desire toward another — the same root that gave ஆர்வலர் in Kural 71 — and Valluvar places it as the middle term that converts a disposition into a relationship. The closing phrase நாடாச் சிறப்பு is the verse's most striking move: நாடா means "unsought" or "not to be searched out," so friendship is an excellence that cannot be acquired by pursuit and arrives only as the by-product of love already given. This anticipates the entire நட்பியல் (the book of friendship, chapters 79–87) in the Poruṭpāl, and it separates Valluvar from purely transactional accounts of alliance: friendship here is emergent, not negotiated.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That very ancient science of the relationship with the Supreme is today told by Me to you because you are My devotee as well as My friend.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that the highest teaching is being entrusted to him not because of rank or learning but because of the affectionate friendship (sakhya) between them.
hinduism.tie_back: Devotional love is what produces the friendship, and the friendship is what makes the greatest good available — the Kural's sequence exactly.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gītā 4.3, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus reclassifies his disciples from servants to friends, and the reclassification follows directly on his command that they love one another.
christianity.tie_back: Friendship is presented, as in the Kural, as the crowning outcome of love rather than as a separate arrangement.
christianity.source: Gospel of John 15:15, King James Version

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes an outward-turning desire for another's good — not merely refraining from harm — a condition of faith itself.
islam.tie_back: This is precisely Valluvar's middle term ஆர்வம்: love turned into active eagerness for another's welfare, which is what makes people friends.
islam.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 13 (Book of Belief), narrated by Anas ibn Mālik

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.”
judaism.explanation: The text describes friendship arising spontaneously and involuntarily out of love — Jonathan does not decide to befriend David; the bond simply forms.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's நாடாச் சிறப்பு, the unsought excellence: friendship that is not gone looking for but is begotten by love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie is actually the whole of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: Correcting Ānanda's guess that good friendship is half the spiritual life, the Buddha says it is the entirety of it, since the whole path unfolds from it.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts rank friendship at the very top of the scale of goods — Valluvar's "excellence beyond seeking" and the Buddha's "whole of the holy life."
buddhism.source: Upaḍḍha Sutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.2, trans. Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “Benevolence (maitrī) towards all living-beings (sattva), joy (pramoda) at the sight of the virtuous (guṇādhika), compassion and sympathy (kāruṇya) for the afflicted (kliśyamāna), and tolerance (mādhyasthya) towards the insolent and ill-behaved (avineya) are the other observances.”
jainism.explanation: Umâsvâti lists four attitudes to cultivate, starting with maitrî (friendliness toward all beings), and Pûjyapâda's commentary defines pramoda as 'fervent affection' toward the virtuous.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's sequence of love, then warmth toward others, then friendship has a Jain counterpart in maitrî and pramoda, which the sutra presents as cultivated dispositions supporting the vows.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.11 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the change that comes from the company of the holy (sadh sangat): once love has replaced jealousy, everyone becomes a friend and no one remains an outsider.
sikhism.tie_back: As in the Kural's chain from love to warm eagerness to friendship, friendship here is not pursued but arrives as the by-product of a heart already changed by love.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pythias, condemned to death by the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse, is allowed to go home to settle his affairs only because Damon offers to stand as hostage and die in his place; Pythias returns just in time, and the astonished tyrant releases them both and asks to be admitted to their friendship.
greek_mythology.explanation: The legend's whole point is that a bond of affection produced a degree of mutual trust the tyrant had assumed impossible between human beings.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The tyrant's request to join them dramatises Valluvar's நாடாச் சிறப்பு — friendship as an excellence that cannot be obtained by asking for it.
greek_mythology.source: The legend of Damon and Pythias, recounted in Cicero, De Officiis III.45 and Valerius Maximus, Memorable Doings and Sayings IV.7

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle opens his two books on friendship by ranking philia above every other external good, arguing it is both a virtue and the condition of a liveable life.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle's valuation matches the Kural's: friendship is not one good among many but the excellence that makes the rest worth having.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1, 1155a, trans. W. D. Ross

real_life_example.event_title: Jesse Owens and Luz Long become friends at the Berlin Olympics
real_life_example.event: At the 1936 Berlin Olympics the American Jesse Owens won the long jump gold medal and the German Luz Long took silver. Owens later wrote that what he remembered most was the friendship he struck up with Long, and the two corresponded by letter until the war broke out in 1939. Long was killed in the Second World War in 1943, and after the war Owens kept up the friendship through correspondence with Long's son.
real_life_example.explanation: A warm regard between two rivals, formed in the most politically charged Games of the century, grew into a friendship that outlasted a war and a death.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural traces a lineage from love to warm eagerness to friendship, an unsought excellence, and the Owens and Long friendship arose unlooked-for out of goodwill between competitors.

tamil:
அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கென்ப வையகத்து
இன்புற்றார் எய்தும் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Anbutru amarndha vazhakkenba vaiyagaththu,
Inbutraar eydhum sirappu.
meaning: The wise say that the happiness and success people enjoy in this world come from living a life of love.
elementary: Have you ever noticed that the happiest people you know are usually the ones with the most love around them — not the ones with the most stuff? This kural says that is not a coincidence. The good life people admire grows out of loving.
university: Kural 75 reuses the frame of Kural 73 — வழக்கென்ப, "the wise call it the natural practice/consequence of" — but shifts the payoff from metaphysics to lived happiness. The key verb is அமர்ந்த (amarndha), "settled, seated, at rest in": love here is not a passing rush of feeling but a stable condition one dwells in. சிறப்பு (sirappu) denotes honour, distinction, the visible excellence others recognise in a life. Crucially Valluvar locates this reward வையகத்து, "in this world," not in a heaven — a consistent feature of his ethics, which repeatedly argues that virtue pays here and now in the ordinary domestic register of the இல்லறவியல் (the book of household life). The couplet therefore functions as a rebuttal of the assumption that the loving must sacrifice their own happiness: for Valluvar, love is not the price of a good life but its mechanism.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress… such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna's portrait of the devotee he holds dearest is built almost entirely from relational qualities — friendliness, compassion, absence of envy — rather than ritual or ascetic achievement.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes a loving disposition the source of a person's highest standing rather than a separate obligation.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gītā 12.13–14, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him.”
christianity.explanation: The letter identifies love not as a commandment issued by God but as the very medium in which God is present, so that to inhabit love is to inhabit God.
christianity.tie_back: The verb 'dwelleth' matches Valluvar's அமர்ந்த — love as a settled dwelling-place from which the highest good follows.

islam.quote_or_event: “The merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful on the earth, and you will be shown mercy from Who is above the heavens.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ties the mercy a person receives directly to the mercy they extend to others, making compassion the mechanism of one's own well-being.
islam.tie_back: Both texts claim the good life returns to the loving person as a consequence of the loving, not as an unrelated reward.
islam.source: Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 1924, narrated by ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb sets the cheapest possible meal eaten among people who love one another against a feast of fattened beef eaten in hatred, and declares the first better.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis in a single domestic image: the happiness people envy in a household comes from love in it, not from what is on the table.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One sleeps easily, wakes easily, dreams no evil dreams. One is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists eleven concrete, largely present-life benefits that follow from cultivating mettā — beginning with sleeping well and being beloved by those around one.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural's claim: the ordinary, visible good fortune of a happy life is the fruit of love.
buddhism.source: Mettānisaṁsa Sutta, Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.16, trans. Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “Compassion (anukampā) towards the living-beings (bhūta) in general and the devout (vratī) in particular, charity (dāna), restraint-with-attachment (sarāgasaṃyama), etc., contemplation on the aforementioned, equanimity (kṣānti), and purity (śauca)–freedom-from-greed–lead to the influx (āsrava) of karmas that cause pleasant-feeling (sātā vedanīya).”
jainism.explanation: In Jain karma theory, compassion and giving draw in the specific karmic matter that later ripens as pleasant experience.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says the happiness of the fortunate is the fruit of a life settled in love; Umâsvâti says the same in karmic terms, with compassion as the cause of pleasant experience.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 6.12 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Sing, and listen, and let your mind be filled with love. Your pain shall be sent far away, and peace shall come to your home.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Japji, the opening hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak promises that a mind settled in love brings peace into the home here and now.
sikhism.tie_back: It mirrors Valluvar's claim that the happiness of those who live well in this world is simply the fruit of a life settled in love.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib, Pauri 5, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For nothing is greater or better than this, when man and wife dwell in a home in one accord, a great grief to their foes and a joy to their friends.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, shipwrecked and in rags, blesses the princess Nausicaa with what he considers the supreme human good: a household held together by likemindedness (homophrosynē).
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus names the same prize Valluvar does — the distinction of a happy life on earth — and grounds it in loving concord at home.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.182–185, trans. A. T. Murray (Loeb, 1919)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Of all the things which wisdom acquires to produce the blessedness of the complete life, far the greatest is the possession of friendship.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus, whose entire ethics is organised around a settled, untroubled happiness, ranks friendship first among everything wisdom can supply toward it.
philosophy.tie_back: Epicurus and Valluvar agree that loving bonds are not a cost to one's own happiness but the single largest contributor to it.

real_life_example.event_title: Elizabeth Barrett and Robert Browning marry and settle in Florence
real_life_example.event: The poets Elizabeth Barrett and Robert Browning, whose courtship began with letters in 1845, married secretly at St Marylebone Parish Church in London in September 1846 and a week later left for Italy, because her father would not allow any of his children to marry. They made their home at Casa Guidi in Florence for fourteen years, where her health improved markedly and their son Pen was born in 1849. Both continued to write and became among the most celebrated poets of their age until her death in 1861.
real_life_example.explanation: The Brownings' marriage is one of the best-documented examples of a life built around love that also brought health, creativity and lasting public distinction.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the distinction of those who live happily in this world is the fruit of a life settled in love, and the Brownings' settled married life in Florence was the setting for their happiest and most admired years.

tamil:
அறத்திற்கே அன்புசார் பென்ப அறியார்
மறத்திற்கும் அஃதே துணை.
transliteration:
Araththirke anbusaar benba ariyaar,
Maraththirkum aqdhe thunai.
meaning: Only people who do not understand say that love helps only in doing good. Love also gives strength for brave action against wrong.
elementary: People think being loving means being soft. But think of a mother bird when something comes near her nest — she will fight anything. The same love that makes you gentle is what makes you brave when someone you love is in danger.
university: This is the most counter-intuitive couplet in the chapter and the one most argued over by commentators. The pair அறம் / மறம் (aram / maram) is a classical Tamil opposition: aram is righteousness and dharma, while maram is martial valour, ferocity, the warrior's fighting spirit (the word also shades toward "wrath" or "cruelty"). Valluvar's claim is that அன்பு is the துணை — the support, companion, aid — of both. Parimelalhagar reads maram narrowly, as the legitimate severity with which a ruler punishes wrongdoing; modern commentators such as Karunanidhi read it broadly as வீரம், heroism. Either way the verse blocks a sentimental reading of the whole chapter: love in the Kural is not synonymous with mildness, and Valluvar will later devote whole chapters to armies, kingship and punishment without contradiction. The underlying logic is that ferocity in defence of what one loves is itself a form of love, not its abandonment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Hanumān, searching for the captive Sītā out of devotion to Rāma, allows himself to be captured in Laṅkā and, when the demons set his tail alight, turns the humiliation into an assault that burns the city — an act of extraordinary destructive force arising wholly from love for his lord.
hinduism.explanation: The Sundara Kāṇḍa presents Hanumān's ferocity as inseparable from his bhakti; he is gentle to Sītā in the same episode in which he devastates Rāvaṇa's capital.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly Valluvar's point — the same anbu that supports virtue also supplies the nerve for maram.
hinduism.source: Vālmīki, Rāmāyaṇa, Sundara Kāṇḍa (the burning of Laṅkā)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables.”
christianity.explanation: The Gospels' gentlest figure acts with deliberate physical force against those exploiting worshippers; John's narrator glosses it as consuming zeal for God's house.
christianity.tie_back: The episode is the Christian counter-example to 'love is only ever mild' — the same love underwrites the whip.
christianity.source: Gospel of John 2:15, King James Version

islam.quote_or_event: “And what is [the matter] with you that you fight not in the cause of Allah and [for] the oppressed among men, women, and children who say, 'Our Lord, take us out of this city of oppressive people…'”
islam.explanation: The verse rebukes believers for inaction and grounds the obligation to fight explicitly in compassion for the defenceless who are being oppressed.
islam.tie_back: Here the Qurʾān makes love and pity the motive for maram, which is precisely the Kural's contention.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Abram hears that his nephew Lot has been carried off by a coalition of kings, he arms three hundred and eighteen trained men of his own household, pursues the raiders as far as Dan, defeats them by night and brings Lot and all the captives back.
judaism.explanation: Abram, elsewhere a peaceable herdsman who avoids quarrels, mounts a night raid purely because a kinsman he loves has been taken.
judaism.tie_back: Love of kin is what converts a peaceable man into a warrior — the Kural's claim in narrative form.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahāyāna tale of the sea-captain "Great Compassion," the Bodhisattva learns that a bandit aboard his ship plans to murder five hundred merchants; out of compassion both for the merchants and for the bandit, who would otherwise incur unimaginable karmic ruin, he kills the bandit himself and accepts the karmic consequence.
buddhism.explanation: The story is the classic Buddhist test case for whether compassion can ever require a violent act, and it answers yes — provided the motive is wholly love and the actor accepts the cost.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the nearest Buddhist analogue to the Kural's claim that love underwrites maram as well as aram.
buddhism.source: Upāyakauśalya Sūtra (Skill-in-Means Sūtra), the tale of the sea-captain

jainism.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, … making Zeal his bow, its string Carefulness in walking, … piercing with the arrow, Penance, (the foe's) mail, Karman--(in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Samsâra.”
jainism.explanation: When Indra urges King Nami to build fortifications like a true Kshatriya, Nami turns every military image into a spiritual one: the only war worth fighting is against karma.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says love supports martial valour (maṟam) as much as virtue; Jainism keeps the warrior's courage but points it inward and rejects outward violence.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.18–22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. … give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak makes love of God a path that demands total self-offering; Sikh tradition sees this ideal enacted when Guru Gobind Singh, founding the Khalsa in 1699, asked for volunteers ready to give their heads, joining devotion to the courage to defend others.
sikhism.tie_back: It supports Valluvar's counter-intuitive point that love is the companion not only of virtue but of fearless, even martial, valour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek (salok 20), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles has withdrawn from the Trojan war and no appeal to honour or plunder can move him; only the death of Patroclus, whom he loved, sends him back to the field, where he fights with a ferocity that terrifies gods and men alike.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad makes love, not martial ambition, the hinge of its plot: grief for a beloved companion produces the poem's most devastating violence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Iliad is a four-hundred-page demonstration of the Kural's line that love is the ally of maram.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad, Books XVIII–XXII (the wrath of Achilles after Patroclus' death)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Love, and do what thou wilt.”
philosophy.explanation: Augustine's maxim, preached on 1 John, argues that once charity is genuinely the root of an act, the same charity may express itself as severity, rebuke or punishment just as readily as as indulgence — the outward form varies, the root does not.
philosophy.tie_back: Augustine supplies the principle behind Valluvar's couplet: love licenses sternness as well as gentleness, because both can be its instruments.
philosophy.source: Augustine of Hippo, Homilies on the First Epistle of John, Tractate VII.8 (c. 407 CE)

real_life_example.event_title: Desmond Doss rescues wounded comrades on Okinawa
real_life_example.event: Desmond Doss, a Seventh-day Adventist and conscientious objector, served as an unarmed US Army medic with the 77th Infantry Division because he refused to carry a rifle. During the Battle of Okinawa he went repeatedly into exposed ground under fire and is credited with bringing about 75 wounded men to safety, and he was himself wounded several times. On 12 October 1945 President Truman presented him with the Medal of Honor, the first awarded to a conscientious objector.
real_life_example.explanation: Doss's extraordinary battlefield courage came not from hostility but from devotion to the men around him, showing that love can drive the hardest physical bravery.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural rebukes those who think love supports only gentle virtue, and Doss showed love powering valour in the midst of war.

tamil:
என்பி லதனை வெயில்போலக் காயுமே
அன்பி லதனை அறம்.
transliteration:
Enbi ladhanai veyilpolak kaayume,
Anbi ladhanai aram.
meaning: Just as the hot sun burns a worm, which has no bones, goodness itself burns a life that has no love in it.
elementary: Have you ever seen a worm caught on hot pavement in the sun? It has no shell and no bones, so it shrivels fast. This kural says a person with no love in them is just as unprotected — goodness itself will feel unbearable to them.
university: The couplet works by a tight phonetic parallel: என்பு இலதனை ("the boneless one") and அன்பு இலதனை ("the loveless one") differ by a single vowel, so the analogy is carried in the sound before the sense arrives. The traditional referent of என்பிலது is the earthworm or grub, a creature with no skeleton, which the Tamil commentators from Manakkudavar onward identify explicitly (புழு, worm). The force of the verse lies in its reversal of expectation: அறம் (aram, righteousness/dharma) is normally the protector, but here it is the destroyer — not because it attacks, but because the loveless creature has no internal structure with which to withstand it. Valluvar is claiming that love is to moral life what bone is to a body: the load-bearing frame. Without it, exposure to the moral order is simply lethal. This also sets up Kurals 79 and 80, which make the anatomical metaphor explicit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Justice, being violated, destroys; justice, being preserved, preserves: therefore justice must not be violated, lest violated justice destroy us.”
hinduism.explanation: The classic formulation of dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ: dharma is not a passive rule but an active power that protects those who uphold it and turns destructive toward those who do not.
hinduism.tie_back: Identical logic to the Kural — righteousness itself, not an external punisher, consumes the one who fails it.
hinduism.source: Manusmṛti (Laws of Manu) 8.15, trans. Georg Bühler (Sacred Books of the East, 1886)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then shall he answer them, saying, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me.”
christianity.explanation: In the judgement scene, those condemned are not accused of any crime — only of failing to feed, clothe and visit — and their sentence is to everlasting fire.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the absence of love is itself the fatal condition, and the moral order burns those who lack it.
christianity.source: Matthew 25:45 (in context of 25:41–46), King James Version

islam.quote_or_event: “So woe to those who pray — [but] who are heedless of their prayer — those who make show [of their deeds] — and withhold [simple] assistance.”
islam.explanation: Sūrat al-Māʿūn condemns not unbelievers but scrupulous worshippers whose religion has no kindness in it; withholding even the smallest neighbourly help is what draws the woe.
islam.tie_back: Religious observance without love does not shelter a person from judgement — it exposes them, which is the Kural's point exactly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven… But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings.”
judaism.explanation: Malachi's closing oracle uses one image for two opposite effects: the same burning day that reduces the wicked to stubble rises as a healing sun over the faithful.
judaism.tie_back: Malachi supplies the Kural's exact figure — righteousness as a sun that heals some and scorches others depending on what is inside them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts, suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's opening verse makes suffering the automatic consequence of an unwholesome inner state, following as mechanically as a cart-wheel follows the ox.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts describe an impersonal moral order in which the defective inner condition generates its own torment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the poison Kâlakûta kills him who drinks it; as a weapon cuts him who awkwardly handles it; as a Vêtâla kills him who does not lay him; so the Law harms him who mixes it up with sensuality.” … “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
jainism.explanation: Speaking of false monks, the sage warns that the Law itself turns against anyone who misuses it, and that the pitiless person is undone by their own nature.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's image of dharma scorching the loveless life as the sun scorches a boneless worm matches this teaching that the Law harms those who abuse it and leaves the man without pity to remorse.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.44 and 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without love, there is no devotional worship. Without the Shabad, no one finds acceptance.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that religious practice emptied of love has no standing before God; the loveless soul is simply not accepted in the divine order.
sikhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's verdict that, without love, a life cannot stand up to the moral order meant to sustain it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 67, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus' Eumenides the Erinyes hound Orestes across the world for the murder of his mother — not as agents of any court, but as the personified reaction of violated blood-kinship itself, which will not let the offender rest.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Furies represent a pre-legal moral order in which the breach of the bond of natural love automatically generates its own relentless pursuer.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like aram in the Kural, the moral order here does not merely disapprove of the loveless act — it actively torments the one who committed it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book IX of the Republic Socrates argues that the tyrannical man — the person whose soul is ruled entirely by appetite and who is therefore incapable of genuine friendship — is of all human beings the most wretched, and is most wretched precisely in proportion to his power.
philosophy.explanation: Plato's claim is that injustice is not chiefly harmful because of external punishment but because it disorders the soul, leaving it permanently unsatisfied and friendless.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar agree that the loveless person's punishment is not administered from outside but arises from the moral structure of the life itself.

real_life_example.event_title: Belgium takes the Congo Free State from King Leopold II
real_life_example.place: Congo Free State (now Democratic Republic of the Congo) and Brussels, Belgium
real_life_example.event: From 1885 King Leopold II ruled the Congo Free State as his personal possession, forcing its people to gather rubber and ivory for export by brutal methods. Reports such as Roger Casement's investigation for the British government and campaigns by E. D. Morel, missionaries and writers including Mark Twain produced an international outcry. In 1908 the Belgian parliament annexed the territory, ending the king's personal rule over it.
real_life_example.explanation: A regime run purely for profit, with no regard for the people it ruled, was brought down by the moral outrage it provoked across the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says righteousness scorches the loveless as the sun scorches a boneless worm, and Leopold's pitiless rule could not withstand the moral exposure turned on it.

tamil:
அன்பகத் தில்லா உயிர்வாழ்க்கை வன்பாற்கண்
வற்றல் மரந்தளிர்த் தற்று.
transliteration:
Anbagath thillaa uyirvaazhkkai vanbaarkan,
Vatral marandhalirth thatru.
meaning: A life without love in the heart is like a dead, dried-up tree in a desert trying to grow green leaves.
elementary: Picture a dry stick standing in hot sand suddenly growing green leaves. It could not really happen, and if it looked like it did, something would be wrong. This kural says a life with no love in it is like that: it might look like it is going fine, but it is not really alive.
university: The comparison is doubly impossible and that is the point. வற்றல் மரம் is a tree already dried dead, and வன்பாற்கண் is the வன்புலம் or hard, waterless tract — the பாலை landscape of classical Tamil poetics, the desert region associated in akam convention with separation and deprivation. A dead tree sprouting in the desert is not merely unlikely; the couplet's force is that it is a contradiction dressed as a phenomenon. Valluvar is not saying the loveless life is unhappy — he is saying it is not life (உயிர்வாழ்க்கை) at all, only its outward semblance. The use of the tiṇai landscape vocabulary quietly imports the whole emotional register of பாலை (barrenness, loss, the unwatered heart) into an ethical argument, a characteristic Valluvar move of compressing a poetic tradition into seven words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Teaching his son Śvetaketu, Uddālaka points to a great tree: if the living essence leaves one branch, that branch withers; if it leaves a second and a third, they wither too; but when it leaves the whole tree, the whole tree withers and dies.
hinduism.explanation: The Upaniṣad uses the withering tree to show that what looks like a living structure is only alive so long as an invisible animating essence remains in it.
hinduism.tie_back: Same image, same argument: the outward form of a life persists for a while after the thing that made it alive has gone.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned.”
christianity.explanation: In the vine discourse — which culminates in the command to love one another — Jesus says a branch severed from its source does not slowly decline but simply becomes dead wood.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's withered tree and John's withered branch make the identical point: separation from the source of love leaves only the shape of life.
christianity.source: Gospel of John 15:6, King James Version

islam.quote_or_event: “…a good word is like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches [high] in the sky… And the example of a bad word is like a bad tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, not having any stability.”
islam.explanation: The Qurʾān contrasts two trees — one deeply rooted and perpetually fruiting, one torn loose and unable to stand — as images of speech and the inner state behind it.
islam.tie_back: Both texts test a life by whether its tree is genuinely rooted and watered or only standing there without any source of life.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah contrasts the person who trusts in mere human strength — a shrub in a salt desert — with one rooted by water, whose leaf stays green even in drought.
judaism.tie_back: Jeremiah's desert shrub and Valluvar's dry tree in the வன்பால் are very nearly the same image used to make the same judgement.
judaism.source: Jeremiah 17:6 (in context of 17:5–8), King James Version

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of colour but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practise them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada judges a display that has everything except the one quality that would make it real — colour without scent, speech without practice.
buddhism.tie_back: Both verses describe an outward flourishing that is hollow because the inward animating quality is missing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He is empty like a clenched fist, (of no value) like an uncoined false Kârshâpana or like a piece of glass resembling turquoise, he is held lightly by men of discernment.”
jainism.explanation: An ascetic who keeps the outward forms but neglects vows, penance and self-control is like a hollow fist, a counterfeit coin, or glass passed off as a gem.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's dead tree sprouting in a desert is another picture of apparent life with nothing real behind it, which is what this verse describes.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.41–42 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My body is like the simmal tree; seeing me, other people are fooled.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak compares a life lacking true virtue to the tall, imposing simmal (silk-cotton) tree, whose appearance promises fruit that never satisfies.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's dead tree putting out shoots in the desert, it pictures a life with the look of flourishing but nothing real inside.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Narcissus, who has rejected every lover including the nymph Echo, falls in love with his own reflection in a pool; unable to love anything outside himself, he refuses food and drink, wastes away beside the water, and is found only as a flower.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid gives the incapacity for outward love a literal physiological result: a beautiful young man dies of thirst beside a spring.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Narcissus is the Kural's withered tree in the barren place — abundant water and beauty all around, and no life in him at all.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But he who is unable to live in society, or who has no need because he is sufficient for himself, must be either a beast or a god: he is no part of a state.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that human beings are constitutively political and relational, so a person genuinely needing no one has stepped outside the human category altogether.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, denies the self-enclosed person the status of a real human life rather than merely criticising it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics I.2, 1253a, trans. Benjamin Jowett

real_life_example.event_title: The world learns of Romania's state orphanages
real_life_example.event: After the fall of the Ceausescu government at the end of 1989, the outside world learned of large state institutions in which abandoned children were raised with severe psychosocial deprivation; one Bucharest institution held about 850 children under three in 1989. From 2000 the Bucharest Early Intervention Project compared institutionalised children with those placed in foster families. It found that children who stayed in institutions scored far below the others in development, and that foster care, especially when begun early, improved cognitive and emotional outcomes.
real_life_example.explanation: The Romanian findings showed that bodily care without love and attention produces only the outward form of a growing child, not a flourishing one.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares a loveless life to a dead tree putting out shoots in the desert, an appearance of life with nothing behind it, and the orphanage children's stunted development proved how much love is needed for real growth.

tamil:
புறத்துறுப் பெல்லாம் எவன்செய்யும் யாக்கை
அகத்துறுப்பு அன்பி லவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Puraththurup pellaam evanseyyum yaakkai,
Agaththuruppu anbi lavarkku.
meaning: What use are all the outer parts of the body to people who lack love, the body’s most important inner part?
elementary: A guitar can have perfect strings, shiny wood and beautiful tuning pegs — but if there's no hollow space inside it, it makes no music. This kural says love is the inside part of a person. Without it, all the outside parts don't accomplish anything.
university: Valluvar builds the couplet on a precise anatomical contrast: புறத்து உறுப்பு (external organ/limb) against அகத்து உறுப்பு (internal organ), and then makes the startling classificatory claim that அன்பு is itself an உறுப்பு — a bodily organ, not a sentiment. யாக்கை (yaakkai) is the physical frame or corporeal body. The rhetorical question எவன் செய்யும் ("what will they accomplish?") is not asking whether the limbs are pleasant but whether they can function at all, on the analogy of a body whose vital inner organ has failed. Commentators split on the referent: Parimelalhagar and Solomon Pappaiah extend it to the "external organs" of a household — its wealth, servants and property — arguing that a home without love is equally inoperative, while Varadarajan and Karunanidhi keep it to the individual body. Both readings converge on the same deflationary verdict about outward equipment, and the verse reads as a direct ancestor of the argument in Kural 80.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who restrains the senses of action but whose mind dwells on sense objects certainly deludes himself and is called a pretender.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna distinguishes genuine discipline from its imitation: outwardly immobilised organs of action mean nothing if what is inside is unchanged.
hinduism.tie_back: Both verses judge the body's outward apparatus worthless when the inner condition is absent.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gītā 3.6, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul concedes every impressive outward performance — eloquence, prophecy, total almsgiving, martyrdom — and declares each one to be worth exactly nothing without love.
christianity.tie_back: This is Valluvar's எவன் செய்யும் answered in full: the external apparatus, however complete, accomplishes nothing without the inner organ.
christianity.source: 1 Corinthians 13:3 (in context of 13:1–3), King James Version

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your bodies nor to your faces but He looks to your hearts.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet, pointing to his chest as he spoke, denies that outward form or status carries any weight in divine assessment, which attends only to the inward state.
islam.tie_back: Precisely the Kural's hierarchy: the outward parts count for nothing beside the inner organ.
islam.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2564c, narrated by Abū Hurayra

judaism.quote_or_event: “…for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
judaism.explanation: Samuel is about to anoint Jesse's tallest and most impressive son when he is stopped and told that stature and countenance are not what is being assessed.
judaism.tie_back: The verse states the Kural's principle as a rule of judgement: outward endowments are simply not the relevant organ.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by a shaven head does an undisciplined man who utters lies become a monk. How can he who is full of desire and greed be a monk? He who wholly subdues evil deeds, both small and great, is called a monk, because he has overcome all evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada refuses to let the visible markers of the monastic life — the shaved head, the robe — count for anything without the inward transformation they are supposed to signify.
buddhism.tie_back: Same verdict as the Kural: the outward apparatus, however correct, accomplishes nothing without the inner quality.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One does not become a Sramana by the tonsure, nor a Brâhmana by the sacred syllable ôm, nor a Muni by living in the woods, nor a Tâpasa by wearing (clothes of) Kusa-grass and bark. One becomes a Sramana by equanimity, a Brâhmana by chastity, a Muni by knowledge, and a Tâpasa by penance.”
jainism.explanation: Jayaghosha tells the priest that outward marks make no one holy; only the inner qualities behind them do.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks what use the outer limbs are without love, the inner organ; this sutra likewise rejects outward marks that lack the inner quality.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.31–32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without her Husband, the soul-bride's youth and ornaments are useless and wretched.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the bride-soul image: without the inner bond of love with the Husband Lord, all outward beauty and adornment serve no purpose.
sikhism.tie_back: As the Kural asks what good the outer limbs are without love as the inner organ, Gurbani declares outer endowments useless without the inner relationship.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 58, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pygmalion carves an ivory woman more beautiful than any living one, dresses her, lays her on a couch and speaks to her — but she remains cold ivory until Venus, moved by his prayer, grants her life and her flesh grows warm under his hand.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid dwells on the statue's flawless external form precisely to make the point that flawless form is not the same as a living body; something has to be given from within.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The statue is Valluvar's body with every outward organ and no inner one — perfectly equipped and entirely inert.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods … for what is the use of such prosperity without the opportunity of beneficence, which is exercised chiefly and in its most laudable form towards friends?”
philosophy.explanation: Opening his treatment of friendship (philia), Aristotle argues that wealth, office and power are worthless to someone with no bond of affection through which to use them.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural’s question of what use the outer limbs are without love, Aristotle asks what use the outer goods are without friendship, and the answer in both is: none.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII, ch. 1 (1155a) (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Harry Harlow presents The Nature of Love
real_life_example.event: In his 1958 presidential address to the American Psychological Association, titled The Nature of Love, the psychologist Harry Harlow reported experiments in which infant rhesus monkeys were given a bare wire surrogate mother and a cloth-covered one. The infants went to the wire figure only to feed, if it held the bottle, and spent their time clinging to the soft cloth figure, especially when frightened. The work showed that comfort and contact, not feeding alone, were the basis of attachment.
real_life_example.explanation: Harlow's experiments demonstrated that meeting a creature's bodily needs is not enough; an inner bond of comfort is what makes development possible.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use the outer limbs are without love, the body's inner organ, and Harlow showed that the food-giving apparatus was nearly worthless to the infants without the comfort of contact.

tamil:
அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை அஃதிலார்க்கு
என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு.
transliteration:
Anbin vazhiyadhu uyirnilai aqdhilaarkku,
Enbudhol porththa udambu.
meaning: A body that lives with love is truly alive. For people without love, the body is just bones covered with skin.
elementary: A house with people laughing and cooking inside is a home. The same house with nobody in it is just walls. This kural says a person without love is like that empty house — everything is still standing, but nobody is living there.
university: The chapter closes by pushing its anatomical argument to its conclusion. உயிர்நிலை (uyir-nilai) means the "state" or "seat" of life — the condition in which a body actually counts as living — and Valluvar makes that condition dependent on அன்பின் வழி, the path or way of love. The second line's என்பு தோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு is deliberately clinical: bone with skin stretched over it, the description of a cadaver or a scarecrow, and it completes the அன்பு/என்பு wordplay that has run through Kurals 72, 73 and 77. The couplet is frequently cited as the single most quoted line of the chapter and has become proverbial in Tamil. Philosophically it takes a definite position in a live ancient debate about what individuates a living being: Valluvar's answer is neither breath nor consciousness but relationship. A body that does not move along love's path may be biologically intact and is nonetheless, by his definition, not the seat of a life.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Certainly that heart is steel-framed which, in spite of one's chanting the holy name of the Lord with concentration, does not change when ecstasy takes place, tears fill the eyes and the hairs stand on end.”
hinduism.explanation: The Bhāgavata diagnoses a devotee who performs every practice correctly yet feels nothing as having a heart made of metal rather than flesh.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts identify an unloving interior as a kind of non-living material — steel in one case, dry bone and skin in the other.
hinduism.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam) 2.3.24, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that loveth not his brother abideth in death.”
christianity.explanation: The letter asserts that love is not evidence of spiritual life but its actual criterion — those who do not love are described as still residing in death, present tense.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's definition in five words: without love, what looks like a living person is a body in the condition of death.

islam.quote_or_event: “Beware! There is a piece of flesh in the body; if it becomes good (reformed) the whole body becomes good, but if it gets spoilt the whole body gets spoilt, and that is the heart.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes the condition of one internal organ determinative of the condition of the entire body, using the same part-whole anatomy the Kural uses.
islam.tie_back: Both take the inner organ, not the frame, as the thing that decides whether the whole body amounts to anything.
islam.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 52 (Book of Belief), narrated by al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr

judaism.quote_or_event: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.”
judaism.explanation: Ezekiel's promise of restoration is described as an organ transplant: the defining change is the replacement of a heart of stone with a heart capable of feeling.
judaism.tie_back: Ezekiel and Valluvar both treat the unloving person as physically miscomposed — stone where flesh should be, bone and skin where a life should be.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ere long, alas! this body will lie upon the earth, unheeded and lifeless, like a useless log.”
buddhism.explanation: Spoken over a monk whose diseased body had been abandoned by his fellows, the verse strips the body of every claim to significance once life has left it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Dhammapada's useless log and the Kural's bone wrapped in skin are the same reduction of a body without what animates it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “This body is not permanent, it is impure and of impure origin; it is but a transitory residence (of the soul) and a miserable vessel of suffering. I take no delight in this transitory body which one must leave sooner or later, and which is like foam or a bubble.”
jainism.explanation: Prince Mrigâputra tells his parents why he will renounce the world: the body is only an impure, temporary lodging of the soul.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that without love the body is just bones wrapped in skin; the Jain prince shares the view of the bare body as a mere vessel, but finds the remedy in renunciation rather than love.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 19.12–13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, that body, within which love of the Lord does not well up - look upon that body as a cremation ground.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sufi saint Sheikh Farid declares that a body in which love does not arise is not truly alive but a place of the dead.
sikhism.tie_back: It is almost exactly the Kural's verdict: without love, the body is mere bone wrapped in skin, a corpse rather than the seat of life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 36) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld Odysseus meets the dead as bodiless shades — 'strengthless heads' that flit and gibber, that he must feed with sacrificial blood before they can even speak, and that his arms pass straight through when he tries to embrace his own mother.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's shades retain their shape and their memories but have lost everything that made them able to hold or be held by anyone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They are the Kural's loveless body from the other direction: a human form that can no longer participate in any bond, and so is not really alive.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Suppose that the eye were an animal — sight would have been its soul… when seeing is removed the eye is no longer an eye, except in name — it is no more a real eye than the eye of a statue or of a painted figure.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that the soul is the actuality or functional form of a body, so an organ that cannot perform its function is an organ in name only, however intact its matter.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle supplies the exact metaphysics of Valluvar's closing line: a body that cannot do what a body is for is bone and skin bearing the name of a person.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, De Anima II.1, 412b, trans. J. A. Smith

real_life_example.event_title: Baba Amte founds Anandwan for people with leprosy
real_life_example.event: Murlidhar Devidas Amte, known as Baba Amte, gave up a prosperous legal career to serve people with leprosy, who were widely shunned. In 1951, with his family, six leprosy patients and a lame cow, he settled on a stretch of stony wasteland in Chandrapur district and built Anandwan, the Forest of Joy, a self-supporting community run by and for people with the disease. He received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 1985 and shared the Templeton Prize in 1990.
real_life_example.explanation: Amte's whole life was organised around love for people others rejected, and it turned barren land into a living community.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a body that moves along the path of love is truly alive, and Amte's life, spent in the service of the shunned, is a vivid example of that path.

tamil:
இருந்தோம்பி இல்வாழ்வ தெல்லாம் விருந்தோம்பி
வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு.
transliteration:
Irundhombi ilvaazhva thellaam virundhombi,
Velaanmai seydhar poruttu.
meaning: People live a family life and save what they have for one main reason: to welcome guests and help others.
elementary: Why does a family have a house, a kitchen and food in the cupboard? This kural says it isn't just so the family can eat. It's so that when someone knocks on the door — a traveller, a neighbour, someone hungry — there is something ready to share. The house is like a well: it holds water so that whoever is thirsty can drink.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter on hospitality with a startling inversion of economic logic: the entire apparatus of the household — இருத்தல் (settling/dwelling), ஓம்புதல் (guarding, tending, husbanding resources) — is declared instrumental to விருந்தோம்பல், the cherishing of guests. The key term வேளாண்மை (vēḷāṇmai) is untranslatable in one word: it carries the sense of 'husbandry' and of unrepayable benevolence rendered without expectation, and Valluvar reuses it at Kural 212 for the purpose of earned wealth generally. Parimelalagar's classical commentary sharpens the point by contrasting the householder with the forest renunciant: one stays in the house precisely in order to have something to give, so that if no benevolence is done, the toil of acquisition has no fruit at all. This makes hospitality not a courtesy appended to domestic life but its justifying cause — a claim structurally parallel to the Sanskrit doctrine that the household exists to sustain the other three āśramas, yet arrived at here without any appeal to caste, ritual, or scripture.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “अतिथिदेवो भव” — “Be one to whom a guest is a god.”
hinduism.explanation: In the Taittiriya Upanishad's convocation address, a graduating student is charged with a series of reverences — mother, father, teacher, and guest — each named as divine.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly as in the Kural, the arriving guest is not an interruption of household life but the sacred point of it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.”
christianity.explanation: The letter to the Hebrews closes with practical instructions to a Christian household, and makes hospitality to unknown travellers a standing obligation, alluding to Abraham's visitors in Genesis 18.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat the ordinary household as the site where hospitality must be permanently ready, not occasionally offered.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, should serve his guest generously. The guest's reward is: To provide him with a superior type of food for a night and a day and a guest is to be entertained with food for three days, and whatever is offered beyond that, is regarded as something given in charity.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes hospitality a test of faith itself and then legislates its minimum content, fixing a concrete household obligation rather than leaving it to sentiment.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats the householder's provisions as existing partly in trust for whoever arrives.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6135, Book of Good Manners (Al-Adab)

judaism.quote_or_event: Yose ben Yochanan of Jerusalem taught that one should let one's house be wide open and let the poor be members of the household — the rabbinic charter for hachnasat orchim, the mitzvah of welcoming guests.
judaism.explanation: The saying, preserved among the earliest teachings in Pirkei Avot, defines the ideal Jewish home architecturally: doors open on every side, with the needy counted as household members rather than outsiders.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions define the good house by its openness to those outside it, making guests constitutive of the household rather than incidental.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Ādiya Sutta the Buddha tells the householder Anāthapiṇḍika the five proper uses of wealth rightly earned: to make oneself happy, to make family and workers happy, to make friends happy, to guard against calamity, and to make the customary offerings — among them the offering to guests.
buddhism.explanation: The discourse answers the question of what accumulated wealth is actually for, and answers it by listing obligations rather than pleasures.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the same move the Kural makes — property is justified by what it lets you give, and guests are named explicitly among the claimants.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.41, Ādiya Sutta (Benefits to be Obtained from Wealth)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Charity and worship are the primary doties [sic] in religion of a house-holder; without them, one cannot be sravaka (house-holder). Meditation and study of scriptures are the primary duties of a virtuous monk; there can be no monk without them.”
jainism.explanation: Jainism splits religious life between the renouncing monk and the lay householder. Here giving (dāna) is not an extra for the householder but part of what makes him a lay follower at all.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the whole household exists in order to cherish guests, and the Jain verse likewise says that without giving one is not a true householder.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 297 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Every gurdwara keeps a langar, a communal kitchen where all who come are fed sitting together in a line, a practice that grew up as a protest against caste; the Gurus also praised the life of the ordinary householder over withdrawal from the world.
sikhism.explanation: Sikhism rejects renunciation and locates the religious life in the household, and its central institution of hospitality, the langar, turns every congregation into a host that feeds anyone who arrives.
sikhism.tie_back: As Valluvar says the whole point of keeping a home is to cherish guests, the Sikh householder and the gurdwara exist in large part to feed the stranger.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, articles on langar and Sikh practice, and on Guru Amar Das (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “for from Zeus are all strangers and beggars, and a gift, though small, is welcome from such as we.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Eumaeus the swineherd, the poorest host in the Odyssey, says this while feeding a ragged stranger who is in fact his disguised master; Zeus Xenios was the god who personally guaranteed the guest-bond.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both passages make hospitality a non-negotiable duty of the household rather than a function of the host's means.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 14.57–58 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Third Definitive Article of Toward Perpetual Peace, Kant argues that cosmopolitan right must be limited to the conditions of universal hospitality — meaning the right of a stranger not to be treated with hostility simply for having arrived on someone else's ground.
philosophy.explanation: Kant is careful to say he is speaking of right and not of philanthropy: hospitality here is a minimal legal entitlement of the visitor, owed by every polity.
philosophy.tie_back: It converts the Kural's household ethic into a political one — the settled community, like the settled house, owes the arriving stranger a claim.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Toward Perpetual Peace (1795), Third Definitive Article

real_life_example.event_title: The Rule of Saint Benedict orders that guests be received as Christ
real_life_example.event: Benedict of Nursia wrote his Rule for monks around 530, and it became the foundational rule of Western monasticism. Its chapter 53 directs that all guests who arrive be received as Christ himself, citing the gospel words about welcoming the stranger. It sets out how the abbot and community are to meet guests, wash their hands and feet, give special care to the poor and pilgrims, and keep a separate guest house and kitchen so that visitors can always be served.
real_life_example.explanation: Benedict built hospitality into the very structure of the monastic household, making the reception of guests one of the purposes the community existed to serve.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the whole business of keeping a home exists in order to cherish guests, and the Rule organised an entire household, with its own guest house and kitchen, around that duty.

tamil:
விருந்து புறத்ததாத் தானுண்டல் சாவா
மருந்தெனினும் வேண்டற்பாற் றன்று.
transliteration:
Virundhu puraththadhaath thaanundal saavaa,
Marundhu eninum vendarpaatru andru.
meaning: Eating alone while a guest waits outside is not right, even if the food were a medicine that stops death.
elementary: Imagine you were handed a magic sweet that would let you live forever. But your friend is waiting outside the door, hungry, and you shut the door and eat it alone. This kural says: then the magic sweet isn't worth having. What you eat matters far less than who you eat it with.
university: Valluvar builds the verse on a deliberately extreme hypothetical: சாவா மருந்து, the 'deathless medicine' (the amṛta of pan-Indian myth, the elixir gods themselves fight over). The rhetorical structure is a fortiori — if even immortality is not worth eating alone, then plainly nothing else is. புறத்ததா ('being outside') is doing precise ethical work: the fault is not refusing the guest outright but the far commoner domestic evasion of simply not noticing that someone is out there. Manakkudavar's tenth-century gloss defines the whole chapter as the rule that 'when strangers arrive at mealtime, one must divide and eat,' locating hospitality at the specific moment of consumption. The verse belongs to a widespread ancient horror of solitary eating, found equally in the Vedic yajña-remnant doctrine and in Greek sympotic ethics, but Valluvar states it with unusual economy: the guest's presence, not the food's value, determines whether a meal is worth taking.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The foolish man in whose house a Brahmana guest remains without food, all his hopes and expectations, all the merit gained by his association with the holy, by his good words and deeds, all his sons and cattle, are destroyed.”
hinduism.explanation: The Katha Upanishad opens with the boy Nachiketa left standing three nights at Death's door unfed; Death is warned that an unfed guest burns away everything a household has accumulated.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say that the guest left outside while the host eats annihilates the value of the household's goods.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells of a rich man who feasted sumptuously every day while a starving beggar, Lazarus, lay at his gate covered in sores, longing for the crumbs from the table; after death their positions are reversed and the gulf between them is fixed.
christianity.explanation: The parable's whole moral weight rests not on any cruelty the rich man commits but on the gate — he ate well while someone hungry was just outside it.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact scenario: the fault is eating one's fill while another waits outside the door.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they give food in spite of love for it to the needy, the orphan, and the captive,”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Insān praises the righteous precisely for handing over food they themselves want — the merit lies in the fact that they were hungry for it too.
islam.tie_back: Both verses locate virtue at the moment of the meal, when what one wants to eat is what one gives away.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let all who are hungry come and eat.”
judaism.explanation: The Ha Lachma Anya declaration, recited in Aramaic near the very start of the Passover seder, has the household throw its door open before anyone eats a bite of the festival meal.
judaism.tie_back: Ritually enacts the Kural's rule — the meal may not begin while someone hungry is still outside.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If beings knew, as I know, the results of giving and sharing, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of selfishness overcome their minds. Even if it were their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat without having shared, if there were someone to receive their gift.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes what ordinary people would do if they could actually see the karmic consequences of generosity — they would find solitary eating unthinkable.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a restatement of the Kural: nothing on the plate, not even one's last mouthful, is worth eating alone while someone is there to receive.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a householder be not called greedy who does not offer food etc. to an ascetic, who is full of virtues and accepts gift (food) like a honeybee without causing harm to others, when he (the ascetic) visits his home?”
