jainism.explanation: Amṛtacandra counts failing to feed a visiting ascetic as plain greed, and so as a form of himsa (harm). The next verse says that feeding him from the family's own meal loosens greed.
jainism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, who says no food is worth eating alone while a guest stands outside, Amṛtacandra condemns the householder who keeps his meal while a worthy visitor is at the door.
jainism.source: Amṛtacandra, Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya v. 173 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2012), as quoted in the explanatory note to Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 113 on wisdomlib.org

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Amar Das made it a rule that anyone who wished to see him had first to eat in the langar, sitting alongside everyone else; tradition holds that even the Mughal emperor Akbar ate in the casteless langar before meeting him.
sikhism.explanation: The third Guru made shared eating the precondition of every meeting, so that no one, however powerful, could be received while others went unfed or were kept apart.
sikhism.tie_back: It enacts the Kural's refusal to eat alone while a guest waits outside: at the Guru's court no one dined privately while others were left out.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guru Amar Das' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus and his men enter the Cyclops' cave and claim the guest-right of Zeus; Polyphemus answers that the Cyclopes care nothing for Zeus, and proceeds to eat his guests instead of feeding them, gorging himself on milk and raw flesh while his visitors cower.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer makes Polyphemus the definitional anti-host of Greek literature — solitary, herding alone, consuming everything himself and sharing with no one.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Polyphemus is the Kural's warning made monstrous: the man who eats while the guest stands unfed before him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca relays Epicurus's advice that one should consider very carefully with whom one eats and drinks before considering what one eats and drinks, since a meal of meat without a friend present is the life of a lion or a wolf.
philosophy.explanation: For the Epicureans, the value of a meal was set by the company; solitary feasting was regarded as a bestial, not a luxurious, condition.
philosophy.tie_back: Both hold that the presence of another at the table, not the quality of the food, is what makes a meal worth taking.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 19.10, quoting Epicurus

real_life_example.event_title: The villagers of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon shelter refugees
real_life_example.event: Led by Pastor Andre Trocme, his wife Magda and Pastor Edouard Theis, the people of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon and the surrounding plateau sheltered an estimated 5,000 people between 1940 and 1944, about 3,000 to 3,500 of them Jews. Refugees who arrived at the door were housed in private homes, farms, hotels and schools, and residents forged identity and ration cards for them; Pastor Trocme and Pastor Theis were arrested and held for 28 days in 1943. In 1990 Israel recognised the inhabitants collectively as Righteous Among the Nations.
real_life_example.explanation: In a time of scarcity and danger, an entire community refused to keep its food and shelter to itself while strangers were left outside.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says eating alone while a guest stands outside is not worth wanting even if the food were the elixir of life, and Le Chambon chose to share even its rations rather than turn strangers away.

tamil:
வருவிருந்து வைகலும் ஓம்புவான் வாழ்க்கை
பருவந்து பாழ்படுதல் இன்று.
transliteration:
Varuvirundhu vaigalum ombuvaan vaazhkkai,
Paruvandhu paazhpadudhal indru.
meaning: A family that welcomes guests every single day will never be ruined by doing it.
elementary: People sometimes worry: if I keep giving food away to visitors, won't I run out? This kural says no — like a well that keeps filling back up the more you draw from it, a home that keeps feeding guests doesn't dry up. Giving every day doesn't empty the house.
university: Having established the duty, Valluvar now answers the obvious objection: won't constant hospitality bankrupt you? The reply hinges on two compact words — பருவந்து (suffering hardship, being worn down) and பாழ்படுதல் (falling into waste, ruin). வைகலும் ('every day') is essential: the claim is specifically about habitual, repeated hospitality, not a single grand feast. Mu. Varadarajan's modern commentary reads the verse as a promise that such a life will never be ruined 'on account of that' — the causal clause matters, since Valluvar is not promising immunity from all misfortune but denying that hospitality is the cause of any. This is characteristic of the Kural's ethical naturalism: rather than invoking divine reward, it states a claim about how generous households actually fare, one echoed in the near-universal folk motif of the vessel that never empties.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The riches of the liberal never waste away, while he who will not give finds none to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: Rig Veda 10.117, the hymn 'Liberality,' is an unusually direct piece of Vedic social ethics, opening with the declaration that the gods did not ordain hunger as a form of death and that generosity is self-sustaining.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact claim — the giver's substance is not depleted by giving.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.1 (trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For thus saith the LORD God of Israel, The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth.”
christianity.explanation: A starving widow at Zarephath gives Elijah the last of her flour and oil during a famine; her jar and cruse then supply her household continuously for the duration of the drought.
christianity.tie_back: The story is the Kural's promise dramatised: a household that feeds the arriving guest is not emptied by it.

islam.quote_or_event: “The food for two persons is sufficient for three, and the food of three persons is sufficient for four persons.”
islam.explanation: A practical maxim of the Prophet used to remove the standard excuse for turning someone away — that there simply isn't enough — by insisting that a household's portion always stretches.
islam.tie_back: Answers exactly the anxiety the Kural addresses: feeding one more arrival will not impoverish the house.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 5392, Book of Food and Meals

judaism.quote_or_event: Abraham, sitting at his tent door in the heat of the day, sees three strangers, runs to meet them, bows, fetches water for their feet, hurries Sarah to bake fresh cakes and has a calf dressed for them — and in return receives the promise that Sarah will bear a son.
judaism.explanation: Genesis 18 became the founding text of hachnasat orchim; the rabbis noted that Abraham, aged and recovering from circumcision, still ran, and that the visit brought his household its future rather than costing it anything.
judaism.tie_back: The household that lavishes itself on arriving guests is not diminished but established — precisely the Kural's claim.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sīha Sutta the Buddha lists the results of generosity visible in this present life: the generous giver is dear and agreeable to many, good people keep company with him, a good reputation spreads about him, he enters any assembly confidently — and only fifth does he mention rebirth in a heavenly world.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta was preached to a general who wanted to know whether giving pays off now rather than only after death; the Buddha answers that four of the five fruits are immediate and worldly.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it insists that habitual giving strengthens rather than erodes the giver's actual position in this life.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.34, Sīha Sutta (To General Sīha)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Not saying they have very little, not saying they have not anything, let them ever exercise fruitful charity to all. Like the pitcher of the mendicant who enters the house-door for alms, it will, in due course, gradually become full.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain-authored Tamil Nālaṭiyār answers the fear that giving drains a household. Regular giving fills up over time, like a mendicant's alms-pitcher filled a little at each door.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar promises that daily hospitality never wears a household into ruin, and the Nālaṭiyār makes the same promise with the image of a pitcher that only fills.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 10 'Liberality', st. 9 (= st. 99), English translation in The Indian Antiquary vol. II (1873)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Siblings of Destiny meet together, and eat and spend, but these resources do not diminish; they continue to increase.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes a treasure that grows the more it is shared and spent together; the hymn's treasure is the divine Name, though the image draws on the experience of shared food and wealth.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's assurance that daily hospitality never ruins a household, Gurbani holds that what is shared is not exhausted but increases.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 186, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as travellers, are turned away from a thousand doors before the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon take them in; during the meal the wine bowl keeps refilling itself, and afterwards their cottage becomes a temple while the inhospitable neighbourhood is drowned.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's most famous theoxeny takes pains to show that the couple's poverty was never an obstacle — they had almost nothing, gave all of it, and ended with more than they began.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The self-refilling bowl is a mythic image of the Kural's exact promise: the hospitable household is never worn down by its hospitality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that the virtues are acquired by repetition: we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, and generous by doing generous acts — habituation is what makes a disposition stable rather than exhausting.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, repeated generous action does not drain the agent but settles generosity into character, so that giving becomes easier and more natural rather than harder.
philosophy.tie_back: Supplies a philosophical mechanism for the Kural's 'day after day': habitual hospitality strengthens the host rather than wearing him out.

real_life_example.event_title: Guru Amar Das makes the free kitchen central to Sikh life
real_life_example.event: The Sikh langar, a free communal kitchen introduced by Guru Nanak, was strengthened by the third Guru, Amar Das, who made it a rule that anyone wishing to see him had first to eat in the langar, where all sit in rows as equals. The Mughal emperor Akbar is recorded as having eaten in the langar. The Guru ka Langar at the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in Amritsar serves cooked food to visitors of any religion or background, day and night, with its costs met from temple funds.
real_life_example.explanation: The langar shows that feeding all comers every day can be sustained across centuries without exhausting those who provide it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the household that tends arriving guests day after day will never be worn down into ruin, and the langar has fed guests daily for generations without collapsing.

tamil:
அகனமர்ந்து செய்யாள் உறையும் முகனமர்ந்து
நல்விருந்து ஓம்புவான் இல்.
transliteration:
Aganamarndhu seyyaal uraiyum muganamarndhu,
Nalvirundhu ombuvaan il.
meaning: Lakshmi, the goddess of good fortune, gladly makes her home in the house of someone who welcomes good guests with a smiling face.
elementary: Good luck is pictured here as a guest too — and she only stays where she feels welcome. If you greet visitors with a warm, happy face, Fortune decides she likes it in your house and moves in. A frown at the door sends her away again.
university: The verse turns on a deliberate mirroring: அகன் அமர்ந்து ('settling gladly within') describes the goddess, while முகன் அமர்ந்து ('gladdening the face') describes the host — the same verb அமர் binds the host's countenance to the deity's contentment. செய்யாள், 'the red one,' is the Tamil epithet for Lakshmi/Śrī, the goddess of prosperity, invoked here not as an object of worship but as a personified consequence. Crucially, Valluvar specifies நல்விருந்து, the *good* guest, introducing discrimination into hospitality that the chapter elsewhere leaves open. The verse also quietly introduces the chapter's second great theme, which will dominate Kural 90: that the host's face, not the host's larder, is the operative instrument of hospitality. It is one of the few places in the Aṟattuppāl where Valluvar permits himself a mythological figure, and even here Śrī functions less as a deity than as a way of saying that wealth behaves like a guest and stays where it is well received.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him not eat any (dainty) food which he does not offer to his guest; the hospitable reception of guests procures wealth, fame, long life, and heavenly bliss.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu's householder chapter states the reward of hospitality in strictly worldly terms first — wealth and reputation — before mentioning heaven at all.
hinduism.tie_back: The same promise as the Kural: prosperity takes up residence with the householder who receives guests well.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 3.106 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, collecting for the Jerusalem church, insists that the disposition of the giver, not the size of the gift, is what is acceptable — and promises that God will make all grace abound toward such a giver.
christianity.tie_back: Both verses make the giver's gladness the decisive quality and attach blessing specifically to it.

islam.quote_or_event: “Then he went to his family and came with a fat [roasted] calf. And placed it near them; he said, ‘Will you not eat?’”
islam.explanation: Abraham, meeting unannounced strangers, does not merely permit them to stay but hurries off to his household and returns with the best animal he has, pressing it on them — and the visit ends with the good tidings of a learned son.
islam.tie_back: The eager, warm host of the Qur'anic account is exactly the Kural's smiling-faced householder, and his house is blessed in consequence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hospitality toward guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav derives this from Genesis 18:3, where Abraham, in the middle of an encounter with God, asks God to wait while he attends to three approaching strangers.
judaism.tie_back: Where the Kural says the goddess of fortune settles in the welcoming house, the Talmud says the Divine Presence itself is what the guest displaces — and outranks.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Anāthapiṇḍika, the Sāvatthī merchant whose very name means 'feeder of the destitute,' bought Prince Jeta's grove by covering it with gold coins and kept his house perpetually open to the Sangha and the poor; the canon names him the foremost of lay donors, and he remained one of the wealthiest men in the city.
buddhism.explanation: The Pali tradition consistently presents his fortune and his hospitality as companions rather than competitors, and portrays him as a serene and delighted rather than grudging giver.
buddhism.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural's picture of a glad host in whose house prosperity settles and stays.
buddhism.source: Anāthapiṇḍika narratives, Pali Canon (Vinaya Cullavagga VI; Aṅguttara Nikāya)

jainism.quote_or_event: “At that moment the gods caused a rain of perfumed water and flowers, and showered down heavenly treasures; they struck the drums, and in the air they praised the gift.”
jainism.explanation: After the Brahmin household finally feeds the outcaste-born monk Harikeśa with respect, gods shower treasure on the place of the gift. Jain tradition tells of this kind of shower at worthy almsgiving.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar pictures Fortune gladly settling in the house of a cheerful host, and the Jain story has wealth literally rain down where a guest is honoured.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Balwand says that Khivi, the Guru's wife, is a noble woman, who gives soothing, leafy shade to all. She distributes the bounty of the Guru's Langar; the kheer - the rice pudding and ghee, is like sweet ambrosia.”
sikhism.explanation: The minstrels Satta and Balwand, in a ballad included in the Guru Granth Sahib, praise Mata Khivi, wife of Guru Angad, for the warmth with which she ran the langar and the abundance it gave everyone.
sikhism.tie_back: As the Kural says Fortune dwells in the house of one who welcomes guests gladly, the scripture pictures plenty flowing from a household mistress whose welcome was shade to all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar), Satta and Balwand (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hestia, goddess of the hearth, was honoured with the first and the last portion of every household libation and was believed to dwell permanently at the centre of the house; the Homeric Hymn calls on her to come into the house and dwell there, bestowing grace on the dwelling.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek domestic religion placed a goddess literally inside the home, at the fire where guests were received, making her presence identical with the house being a proper household at all.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Supplies the same image the Kural uses — a goddess taking up residence in the well-kept, welcoming house.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Hospitality also is a theme of Theophrastus's praise, and rightly so. For, as it seems to me at least, it is most proper that the homes of distinguished men should be open to distinguished guests.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero commends hospitality as a fitting use of wealth and adds that, for those seeking honourable influence, generous entertainment of guests brings popularity and standing at home and abroad; he cites Cimon’s open-handedness as an example.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts treat the open, welcoming home as a source of good fortune for the host, though Valluvar stresses the glad face and casts the reward as Fortune herself taking up residence.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book II, §64 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))

real_life_example.event_title: Gander takes in the passengers of 38 diverted airliners
real_life_example.event: When North American airspace was closed after the attacks of 11 September 2001, 38 airliners landed at Gander, bringing nearly 7,000 passengers and crew to a town of about 10,000 people. Residents housed the travellers in schools, halls and their own homes for several days, volunteers fed them, local businesses donated supplies and pharmacists filled prescriptions at no charge. The town was later honoured in Washington, and Lufthansa named one of its aircraft Gander-Halifax in recognition of the care given to passengers.
real_life_example.explanation: Gander's cheerful, open-handed welcome to thousands of strangers earned it lasting gratitude, honour and goodwill around the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says fortune comes to dwell gladly with the one who welcomes guests with a glad face, and Gander's warm welcome brought the town honour and lasting friendship.

tamil:
வித்தும் இடல்வேண்டும் கொல்லோ விருந்தோம்பி
மிச்சில் மிசைவான் புலம்.
transliteration:
Viththum idal vendum kollo virundhombi,
Michchil misaivaan pulam.
meaning: Does a person who feeds guests first and eats only what is left even need to sow seeds in their field?
elementary: Think of someone who always lets visitors eat first and takes the leftovers for himself. This kural asks, with a smile: does his field even need seeds? It's saying his land will be so full of grain that it seems to grow all by itself. Sharing plants a crop you never had to sow.
university: The verse is a rhetorical question — கொல்லோ is a Tamil particle of wondering interrogation — and its force is hyperbolic rather than agronomic. மிச்சில் ('the remainder, the leftover') is the pivot: the householder who eats the remnant after his guests have eaten is participating in a pan-Indian sacrificial logic in which the leftover of an offering, far from being inferior, is the sanctified portion. Valluvar's innovation is to transpose that logic from the ritual fire to the ordinary dinner and from the priest to the guest. Manakkudavar and later commentators read the question as asserting that such a person's field yields without sowing; modern readers often take it as saying that his generosity is itself the sowing. The agricultural metaphor for giving — seed, field, harvest — is one of the most widely distributed in world religious literature, appearing independently in Vedic, Buddhist, Qur'anic and Pauline texts, and the Kural's compressed version is among the most elegant.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The devotees of the Lord are released from all kinds of sins because they eat food which is offered first for sacrifice. Others, who prepare food for personal sense enjoyment, verily eat only sin.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna sets out a strict binary: food consumed as the remnant of an offering purifies, while food cooked and eaten for oneself alone is itself a transgression.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's householder who eats only the மிச்சில், the leftover after the guests, is precisely the Gita's eater of the sacrificial remnant.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.13 (A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully.”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes the farming metaphor explicit in a passage about a charitable collection, treating gifts to others as literal seed whose yield is proportional to what was scattered.
christianity.tie_back: Same metaphor, same claim: generosity is a form of sowing, and the harvest answers to it.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a seed [of grain] which grows seven spikes; in each spike is a hundred grains. And Allah multiplies [His reward] for whom He wills.”
islam.explanation: The parable puts a precise multiplier on generosity — seven hundredfold — using the same grain imagery as the Kural to say the return vastly exceeds the outlay.
islam.tie_back: Both texts convert the act of giving food into an image of a field yielding far beyond what was put into it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days.”
judaism.explanation: Qohelet's famously enigmatic counsel is read in most Jewish commentary as advocating generosity that appears wasteful at the moment of giving but returns to the giver in time.
judaism.tie_back: Both verses claim that food given away is not lost but constitutes an investment whose return is unaccountably large.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Khetta Sutta the Buddha compares giving to planting: seed sown in a field endowed with good qualities yields abundantly, and in just the same way a gift given to recipients endowed with good qualities yields great fruit.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta is built entirely on agricultural imagery, treating the worthy recipient as the fertile soil into which the donor's seed is cast.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural's exact figure of speech — hospitality as an act of sowing whose harvest returns to the household.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The husbandmen throw the corn on high ground and on low ground, hoping (for a return). For the like motive give unto me; I may be the field which may produce merit (as the return for your benevolence).”
jainism.explanation: Speaking for the begging monk Harikeśa, the yaksha describes giving to a worthy guest as sowing seed in a field that yields merit. A few verses earlier he asks that the mendicant receive what is left over.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks whether a man who feeds his guests first even needs to sow his field, and the Jain verse uses the same farming image: the guest is the field and the gift is the seed.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make good deeds the soil, and let the Word of the Shabad be the seed; irrigate it continually with the water of Truth.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak turns farming into a picture of the moral life, in which good conduct is the field that yields the true harvest.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's field that needs no sowing for the man who feeds guests first, it treats right action itself as the sowing that brings the crop.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 24, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Demeter, disguised as an old woman and grieving for Persephone, is taken in and cared for by the household of King Celeus at Eleusis; in return the goddess of grain teaches Celeus's son Triptolemus the art of agriculture and her sacred rites, and through him the growing of crops spreads to the rest of Greece.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Homeric Hymn makes the gift of cultivated grain itself the repayment for one household's kindness to a stranger at the well.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Nowhere else is the Kural's linkage of hospitality with the fertility of fields so literal: a family fed a guest, and received the knowledge of how to sow.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca's treatise on benefits argues that a benefit is not a transaction to be balanced in a ledger; the giver should give as the earth gives and count the good already done as the whole of the return, expecting nothing and yet finding that benefits circulate back.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca is deliberately attacking the accountant's view of generosity, insisting that the person who gives with an eye on the repayment has not really given.
philosophy.tie_back: Touches the Kural's theme of generosity that yields without being sown, but from the opposite direction — denying rather than promising a harvest.

real_life_example.event_title: The Choctaw Nation sends famine relief to Ireland
real_life_example.place: Choctaw Nation, Indian Territory (now Oklahoma), United States
real_life_example.event: In 1847, less than two decades after their forced removal from their homelands on the Trail of Tears, Choctaw people gathered and raised 170 dollars for the relief of the Irish famine. The money was sent through relief committees in the United States to help buy food for the starving in Ireland. The gift is still commemorated in both nations, including by the Kindred Spirits sculpture in County Cork and a Choctaw-Ireland scholarship.
real_life_example.explanation: A people who had themselves suffered dispossession gave from their own scarcity to strangers an ocean away, and the gift is still remembered as a bond between the two nations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the one who feeds others first and lives on what remains, and the Choctaw gave to the hungry before attending to their own hardships.

tamil:
செல்விருந்து ஓம்பி வருவிருந்து பார்த்திருப்பான்
நல்வருந்து வானத் தவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Selvirundhu ombi varuvirundhu paarththiruppaan,
Nalvarundhu vaanath thavarkku.
meaning: A person who cares for the guest who is leaving and watches the road for the next guest will be a welcome guest of the gods in heaven.
elementary: Some people are glad when the visitors finally leave. This kural describes the opposite kind of person: he waves one guest off and then sits by the door looking down the road, hoping someone else will come. That person, it says, is exactly the kind of visitor heaven would love to have.
university: The verse is built on a triple play with விருந்து: செல்விருந்து (the departing guest), வருவிருந்து (the arriving guest), and நல்விருந்து (the good guest) — the host, by attending to the first two, becomes the third. Parimelalagar glosses the final phrase as meaning that the man is reborn a deva and becomes a welcome guest among those in heaven, while Manakkudavar adds the sharper practical note that 'watching for the arrival' means not eating at all until a guest is present. The verse thus introduces the chapter's only explicitly eschatological claim, and it does so by an elegant reversal: the perfect host is rewarded not with wealth or honour but by being transformed into the perfect guest. Note that the Tamil here reads நல்வருந்து rather than the expected நல்விருந்து; this is the received reading, attested across the manuscript tradition and reproduced by Parimelalagar, who nonetheless glosses it as நல்விருந்து.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Rantideva, after forty-eight days of famine and fasting, is about to break his fast when a brahmin arrives; he gives him his food. Then a śūdra comes, then an outcaste with dogs, then finally a thirsty man — and Rantideva surrenders even his last cup of water, saying he wants nothing but to relieve the suffering of beings. The gods then reveal themselves before him.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana's most celebrated hospitality narrative has guest after guest arrive in sequence, each one received more eagerly than the last.
hinduism.tie_back: Rantideva is the Kural's host who, having served one guest, is already waiting for the next — and is met by the heavenly ones as a result.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:”
christianity.explanation: In the judgement scene, the King welcomes the righteous into the kingdom on the sole ground of how they treated hungry and strange arrivals, whom he identifies with himself.
christianity.tie_back: Both passages make the earthly host into the honoured guest of heaven on the strength of how he received those who came to his door.

islam.quote_or_event: “Gardens of perpetual residence; they will enter them with whoever were righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their descendants. And the angels will enter upon them from every gate,”
islam.explanation: The passage pictures the reward of the faithful as a dwelling into which angels enter from every side to greet them with peace — the believer received as an honoured resident of heaven.
islam.tie_back: Supplies the same final image as the Kural: the righteous householder ends as the one being welcomed by heaven's inhabitants.
islam.source: Qur'an 13:23 (Sahih International); the angels' greeting follows at 13:24

judaism.quote_or_event: On each night of Sukkot, Jewish households invite the ushpizin — seven exalted guests, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Aaron and David — into the temporary booth, and tradition holds that these heavenly visitors will not enter a sukkah unless the poor have also been welcomed there.
judaism.explanation: The custom, rooted in the Zohar, makes an ordinary family's booth simultaneously a place where earthly guests are fed and where celestial guests are received.
judaism.tie_back: Enacts the Kural's double movement — the host who keeps receiving guests becomes a host to, and a guest of, heaven.
judaism.source: Ushpizin custom of Sukkot (Zohar, Emor 103b; widespread liturgical practice)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As kinsmen welcome a dear one on arrival, even so his own good deeds will welcome the doer of good who has gone from this world to the next.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the image of a traveller returning home to relatives who run out to greet him, and applies it to the merit that awaits a person after death.
buddhism.tie_back: Both verses picture the good householder arriving in the next world and being received there as a welcome guest.

jainism.quote_or_event: “To those men the gates of heaven shall never be closed, who with tender hearts and with a mind in accordance with their alms, greatly rejoicing, give even in poverty according to their ability, even as they did in the day of prosperity.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār promises a heavenly birth to the steady, glad giver who keeps giving even when poor. In Jain terms this reward comes from merit (puṇya), not as a god's gift.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's host, who tends the departing guest and watches for the next, becomes a welcome guest in heaven, and the Nālaṭiyār likewise opens heaven's gates to the habitual, glad-hearted giver.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 10 'Liberality', st. 1 (= st. 91), English translation in The Indian Antiquary vol. II (1873)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that selfless service (seva) done in ordinary worldly life earns a seat of honour in God's presence.
sikhism.tie_back: As the Kural's perfect host becomes a welcome guest of the gods, the one who serves here is given a seat in the divine court.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Aye, and the gods in the guise of strangers from afar put on all manner of shapes, and visit the cities, beholding the violence and the righteousness of men.”
greek_mythology.explanation: A suitor rebukes Antinous for striking a beggar, warning that any unknown arrival might be a god in disguise testing how a household behaves.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Grounds the Kural's logic: because the next arrival at the door may be a heavenly being, the host who keeps watching the road is watching for heaven.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 17.485–487 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Derrida distinguishes conditional hospitality — extended to a guest whose name, status and arrival time are known — from unconditional or absolute hospitality, which means holding the house open to whoever may come, without demanding in advance that the arrival announce or identify himself.
philosophy.explanation: For Derrida the ethical charge of hospitality lies entirely in this readiness for the unexpected arrival, since a guest who has been fully vetted is no longer truly a stranger.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the posture of the Kural's host — having finished with the guest he knows, he sits watching for the one who has not yet come.

real_life_example.event_title: The hospice of the Great St Bernard Pass is founded
real_life_example.event: Around 1050 Bernard of Montjoux, archdeacon of Aosta, founded a hospice at the summit of the Great St Bernard Pass to shelter and protect travellers crossing the Alps. Canons have lived there ever since, welcoming every traveller, and from the seventeenth century the monks kept dogs that helped them find travellers lost or buried in the snow. Bernard was later venerated as a saint and the pass and the dog breed bear his name.
real_life_example.explanation: The hospice community did not merely receive those who reached its door; it went out watching and searching for the travellers still on the road.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural honours the host who cares for the departing guest while watching for the one still to come, and the St Bernard monks spent centuries tending travellers and looking out for the next.

tamil:
இனைத்துணைத் தென்பதொன் றில்லை விருந்தின்
துணைத்துணை வேள்விப் பயன்.
transliteration:
Inaiththunaith thenbadhondru illai virundhin,
Thunaiththunai velvip payan.
meaning: The good that comes from the holy offering of caring for guests has no fixed size. It is as great as the worth of the guest you serve.
elementary: If you plant a seed, you can roughly guess how much will grow. But this kural says you can't do that with kindness to guests. How much good comes back depends on who walked through your door — and you can never know that in advance, so you should treat everyone well.
university: Valluvar here names hospitality வேள்வி — sacrifice, the Tamil equivalent of yajña — making explicit what the chapter has implied: feeding a guest is a liturgical act, one of the five great daily sacrifices of the householder, with the guest standing where the fire normally stands. The verse's rhetoric is built on repetition and negation: இனைத்துணைத்து ('of just this much extent') is flatly denied, and replaced by துணைத்துணை ('measure by measure'), a reduplication meaning proportionality without a stated quantity. Parimelalagar defends the claim by quoting Nālaṭiyār 38 — a small gift in worthy hands covers the sky — and concludes that this verse explains why hospitality yields fruit in both this world and the next. The doctrine that merit scales with the recipient's worth is one of the most cross-culturally robust ideas in religious ethics, appearing in nearly identical form in the Pali Abhidhamma, in Jesus's saying about receiving a prophet, and in the Mishnah's list of deeds without measure.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Teaching (and studying) is the sacrifice (offered) to Brahman, the (offerings of water and food called) Tarpana the sacrifice to the manes, the burnt oblation the sacrifice offered to the gods, the Bali offering that offered to the Bhutas, and the hospitable reception of guests the offering to men.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu's enumeration of the pañca-mahāyajña, the five great daily sacrifices of the householder, formally classifies receiving guests as a sacrifice in its own right — the nṛ-yajña or offering to human beings.
hinduism.tie_back: Supplies precisely the category the Kural invokes when it calls hospitality a வேள்வி and speaks of its 'yield.'
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 3.70 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East)

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that receiveth a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet's reward; and he that receiveth a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man's reward.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus, sending out the twelve, tells them that whoever hosts them will be rewarded according to the standing of the person hosted, down to a cup of cold water given to a little one.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's rule stated almost identically: the host's reward is measured by the measure of the guest.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever provides the food for a fasting person to break his fast with, then for him is the same reward as his (the fasting person's), without anything being diminished from the reward of the fasting person.”
islam.explanation: The host's return is not a fixed sum but is set by whatever spiritual state the guest happens to be in — the host inherits the guest's own merit.
islam.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's principle: the measure of the guest is the measure of the benefit.
islam.source: Jami` at-Tirmidhi 807 (graded Sahih), Book on Fasting

judaism.quote_or_event: “These are the things that have no measure: The Peah [corner of the field that must be given to the poor], the Bikurim [first-fruits], the appearance-sacrifice, acts of kindness, and the study of the Torah.”
judaism.explanation: The very first mishnah of Tractate Peah opens the rabbinic law of charity by declaring that certain obligations, hospitality and loving-kindness among them, have no fixed minimum or maximum quantity.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's opening clause — 'there is nothing of which one can say it is just this much' — is almost a translation of this mishnah.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta the Buddha enumerates fourteen kinds of personal offering ranked by recipient and states their relative yield: a gift to an animal may be expected to repay a hundredfold, to an immoral ordinary person a thousandfold, to a virtuous ordinary person a hundred-thousandfold, and so on up through stream-enterers, once-returners, arahants and finally a fully enlightened Buddha, whose worth is incalculable.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta is the canonical Buddhist treatment of exactly this question — how the merit of a gift is determined — and answers it entirely in terms of the recipient's spiritual attainment.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the Kural's proposition worked out in systematic detail: the measure of the gift's fruit is the measure of the one who receives it.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikāya 142, Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta (The Exposition of Offerings)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The effect of giving of the gift–dāna–has distinctions based on the specific manner in which it is given–vidhiviśeṣa, the specific thing given–dravyaviśeṣa, the specific nature of the giver–dātṛviśeṣa, and the specific nature of the recipient–pātraviśeṣa.”
jainism.explanation: Umāsvāti's sutra says the merit of a gift varies, depending partly on the worth of the person who receives it. Pūjyapāda's commentary compares this to good soil making a seed yield a rich harvest.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the fruit of the 'sacrifice' of hospitality cannot be fixed in advance but depends on the worth of the guest, which is exactly the Jain teaching of pātraviśeṣa.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Recognize the Lord's Light within all, and do not consider social class or status; there are no classes or castes in the world hereafter.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that every person carries the divine Light, so worth is never to be judged by caste or social rank, a principle the langar puts into practice by serving all alike.
sikhism.tie_back: Where the Kural says the merit of hospitality is measured by the guest's worth, Gurbani locates every guest's worth in the same divine Light.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 349, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon entertain two unremarkable travellers with the last of their food; only when the wine bowl refills itself do they realise they are hosting Jupiter and Mercury, whereupon their reward — their cottage transfigured into a marble temple, their lives extended, their death granted as a single shared moment — is scaled to the rank of the guests they had unknowingly received.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's theoxeny turns on the gap between what the hosts thought they were doing and who their guests actually were.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural's claim from the inside: the reward could not have been named in advance, because it was set by the measure of the guest.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle's account of distributive justice holds that what is just in distribution is a proportion, and that the proportion must be fixed by axia — worth or merit — so that equals receive equally and unequals unequally according to their desert.
philosophy.explanation: The point of the doctrine is that no absolute quantity can be specified in advance; justice consists in the ratio between what is given and the worth of the recipient.
philosophy.tie_back: Provides the formal structure of the Kural's claim: not a fixed amount, but a measure indexed to the worth of the person involved.

real_life_example.event_title: Lorenzo de' Medici takes the young Michelangelo into his household
real_life_example.event: Lorenzo de' Medici, ruler of Florence, opened a school of sculpture in his garden of San Marco, where the teenage Michelangelo attracted his attention. Lorenzo invited the boy to live in the Medici palace, where he was brought up like a member of the family, studied the Medici collection of ancient sculpture under Bertoldo di Giovanni and mixed with Lorenzo's circle of scholars. Michelangelo's early works such as the Battle of the Centaurs date from this stay, which ended with Lorenzo's death in 1492.
real_life_example.explanation: Lorenzo's hospitality to a gifted boy yielded a return far beyond anything he could have measured, through Michelangelo's later art.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the fruit of hospitality cannot be fixed in advance but matches the worth of the guest, and the Medici household's guest turned out to be one of the greatest artists in history.

tamil:
பரிந்தோம்பிப் பற்றற்றேம் என்பர் விருந்தோம்பி
வேள்வி தலைப்படா தார்.
transliteration:
Parindhombip patratrem enbar virundhombi,
Velvi thalaippadaa thaar.
meaning: Those who never cared for guests will one day cry, ‘We worked hard and saved, but now we have nothing to hold on to.’
elementary: Picture someone who spends their whole life putting food in a locked cupboard and never once shares it. One day they open the cupboard and it's empty, or they're too old to eat it — and they say, sadly, “What was all that for?” This kural says that's what happens when you save everything and give nothing.
university: The verse is structured as a reported lament: பற்றற்றேம், 'we have become without support/without anything to grasp,' is put directly in the mouths of the failed householders, a rhetorical device Valluvar uses sparingly and to great effect. பரிந்து ('with pain, with anxious care') and ஓம்பி ('guarding') together characterise hoarding as an exhausting labour, quietly contrasting with the same verb ஓம்பி used throughout the chapter for tending guests: the same effort, spent on goods rather than people, ends in destitution. The word வேள்வி again marks hospitality as sacrifice, and தலைப்படாதார் means those who never even embarked on it. The pathos of the verse lies in its temporality — it describes a realisation that arrives too late — placing it in the long tradition of wisdom literature about the rich fool, from Qohelet through the Gospels to the Stoic epistles.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But he who does not feed these five, the gods, his guests, those whom he is bound to maintain, the manes, and himself, lives not, though he breathes.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu's verdict on the householder who omits the five daily offerings is not that he is punished later but that he is already, in the present tense, not alive in any meaningful sense.
hinduism.tie_back: The same judgement as the Kural: a life of accumulation without the sacrifice of hospitality amounts to having nothing at all.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 3.72 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?”
christianity.explanation: The rich man in the parable has just resolved to pull down his barns and build bigger ones so he can store everything and take his ease; God interrupts the plan with the question of who will actually get the goods.
christianity.tie_back: The parable stages the exact lament of the Kural — a lifetime's careful hoarding ending in the recognition that it secured nothing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who collects wealth and [continuously] counts it. He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal.”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Humazah opens with a curse on the scorner and mocker, and identifies his defining behaviour as the compulsive tallying of a fortune he believes will secure him permanently.
islam.tie_back: Names the same futile labour the Kural describes — anxious guarding of goods that in the end supports nothing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt.”
judaism.explanation: Qohelet observes that hoarded wealth does not merely fail to benefit its owner but actively harms him, and goes on to describe such riches perishing through bad venture and leaving nothing for his son.
judaism.tie_back: Identical diagnosis to the Kural: wealth guarded rather than shared turns into the source of the owner's own destitution.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The verse was spoken, according to the commentary, in connection with a famously unrivalled act of almsgiving, and contrasts two ministers — one who rejoiced at the giving and one who could only see the waste.
buddhism.tie_back: Draws the same line the Kural draws: the one who never gave ends up with nothing on the far side of his own effort.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who in this life has done no good actions and has not practised the Law, repents of it in the next world when he has become a prey to Death.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra warns his rich former brother, King Brahmadatta, that wealth and kin are left behind at death and only karma goes with a person. Whoever neglects good deeds will regret it too late.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar has hoarders who never took up hospitality lament too late that they have nothing to hold on to, and the Jain sage gives the same warning of a regret that comes only after death.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.21 (cf. 13.24) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “For the sake of this wealth, so many were ruined; because of this wealth, so many have been disgraced. It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
sikhism.explanation: In an Aasaa hymn, Guru Nanak reflects on hoarded wealth that brings its owners ruin and cannot be carried beyond death.
sikhism.tie_back: It echoes the late lament of the Kural's hoarders, who toiled to guard their goods and are left with nothing to hold.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Midas, granted his wish that everything he touched turn to gold, finds that his bread hardens in his hands and his wine solidifies in his throat; surrounded by unimaginable riches he is starving, and begs the god to take the gift back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's telling makes the point with almost mathematical cruelty — the more perfectly wealth is accumulated, the less it can be used or shared.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Midas starving amid his gold is the visual form of the Kural's lament: everything hoarded, nothing to hold on to.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus instructs the student never to say of anything that he has lost it, but rather that he has given it back — since nothing we hold, including property and the people in our household, was ever ours to begin with.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic point is that the language of loss presupposes a false claim of ownership, and that the pain of the lament is generated by that false claim rather than by the event.
philosophy.tie_back: Diagnoses the very cry the Kural puts in the hoarder's mouth — 'we have nothing left to hold' — as the predictable end of a life spent gripping.

real_life_example.event_title: The fall of Heshen, the Qianlong emperor's favourite
real_life_example.event: Heshen rose from imperial bodyguard to the highest offices of the Qing state under the Qianlong emperor and amassed an enormous private fortune through corruption. When Qianlong died in February 1799, his son the Jiaqing emperor had Heshen arrested, stripped of all his posts and condemned to death, and his vast estate was confiscated. Official inventories of the seized wealth, possibly exaggerated by his enemies, listed huge quantities of silver, pawnshops, furs and gold.
real_life_example.explanation: A lifetime spent gathering and guarding wealth for himself ended with Heshen losing all of it at a single stroke.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who never took up the sacrifice of hospitality will one day lament that they toiled and saved and have nothing to hold on to, and Heshen's hoard was taken from him entirely.

tamil:
உடைமையுள் இன்மை விருந்தோம்பல் ஓம்பா
மடமை மடவார்கண் உண்டு.
transliteration:
Udaimaiyul inmai virundhombal ombaa,
Madamai madavaarkan undu.
meaning: Being poor while having plenty is what happens when you refuse to welcome guests. Such foolishness is found only in fools.
elementary: Someone can have a full fridge, a big house and lots of money, and still be poor — if they never share any of it. This kural calls that a kind of silliness: having everything and enjoying none of it, because you're too closed-up to let anyone in.
university: The verse is built on two paradoxes stacked on each other. The first, உடைமையுள் இன்மை ('destitution inside possession'), is a genuine oxymoron and the phrase for which the couplet is best known. The second is the near-tautology of the closing line: மடமை மடவார்கண் உண்டு, 'that folly exists in fools' — a construction that looks empty but functions as a sharp dismissal, refusing to dignify such conduct with any explanation beyond stupidity. மடமை denotes not mere ignorance but a wilful dullness of perception, the inability to see what is obvious. Valluvar thus classifies the inhospitable rich not as wicked but as stupid, a rhetorically devastating move that resurfaces in the Hebrew Bible's treatment of Nabal (whose name is literally 'fool') and in Jesus's address to the rich man as ἄφρων. The couplet completes the chapter's argument: having established hospitality as purpose (81), habit (83), sacrifice (87) and lost opportunity (88), it now names its absence as a form of self-inflicted poverty.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The man with food in store who, when the needy comes in miserable case begging for bread to eat, hardens his heart against him — even when of old he did him service — finds not one to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Rig Veda's hymn on liberality moves from praising the generous to a direct portrait of the man who has plenty and withholds it, and pronounces him friendless.
hinduism.tie_back: Same figure as the Kural's: the man whose stores are full and whose life is nonetheless empty.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.2–6 (trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:”
christianity.explanation: The letter to Laodicea diagnoses a community whose self-assessment as prosperous is precisely what conceals its actual destitution from it.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's paradox stated in identical terms — poverty existing inside, and hidden by, possession.

islam.quote_or_event: “Every day two angels come down from Heaven and one of them says, ‘O Allah! Compensate every person who spends in Your Cause,’ and the other (angel) says, ‘O Allah! Destroy every miser.’”
islam.explanation: The hadith is placed by Bukhari under the Qur'anic verses contrasting the one who gives with the one who is stingy and thinks himself self-sufficient, and pictures the two fates being petitioned for daily.
islam.tie_back: States the Kural's claim as a standing cosmic arrangement: withholding turns possession into ruin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him”
judaism.explanation: Nabal, a man of vast flocks in Carmel, refuses food and drink to David's men who had protected his shepherds; his wife Abigail intercepts the reprisal with this assessment of her husband, and he dies within ten days.
judaism.tie_back: The Bible's paradigm case of exactly what the Kural describes — enormous wealth, refused hospitality, and folly named as the cause.
judaism.source: 1 Samuel 25:25 (King James Version); narrative at 1 Samuel 25:2–38

buddhism.quote_or_event: King Pasenadi tells the Buddha of a Sāvatthī financier who died heirless leaving many millions, and who in life had eaten only broken rice and sour gruel, worn coarse hemp, and travelled in a dilapidated cart. The Buddha replies that when an unworthy person acquires great wealth and neither makes himself happy with it nor shares it with ascetics and brahmins, it goes to waste, unused — like a pool of cool clear water in a demon-haunted place that no one drinks from.
buddhism.explanation: The simile of the undrunk pool is the Buddha's image for wealth that exists but nourishes nobody, not even its owner.
buddhism.tie_back: An almost exact narrative rendering of உடைமையுள் இன்மை — a millionaire living in destitution because nothing he owns is ever shared.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who employs not his time in enjoying his property, or gives not of it to ascetics, but lays it up (like a miser)--at him, the foolish one, about to perish, his hoarded wealth shall mock, and the favour of the world shall mock.”
jainism.explanation: In its chapter on illiberality, the Nālaṭiyār calls the rich man who neither uses nor gives his wealth a fool. His hoard ends up mocking him.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls poverty in the midst of plenty a folly found only in fools, and the Nālaṭiyār likewise names the wealthy man who will not give 'the foolish one'.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 28 'Illiberality', st. 3 (= st. 273), English translation in The Indian Antiquary vol. II (1873)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, those houses in which neither the Holy nor the Lord are served - those houses are like cremation grounds; demons dwell within them.”
sikhism.explanation: In one of his saloks in the Guru Granth Sahib, Kabir says a household that does not serve holy visitors is spiritually dead, whatever it possesses.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's poverty in the midst of plenty, a house that fails to serve those who come to it is counted as empty and lifeless.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Kabir (salok 192) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon, who scorned the gods and felled the sacred grove of Ceres, is punished with a hunger no food can satisfy; he consumes his whole fortune, then sells his own daughter repeatedly to buy more, and finally, with nothing left, begins to devour his own limbs.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's most grotesque cautionary tale makes appetite without reverence into a self-consuming engine that converts abundance into absolute want.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The extreme literalisation of the Kural's paradox — a rich man made destitute by an inability to direct any of it outward.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca, quoting Epicurus and saying he crosses into the enemy's camp as a scout rather than a deserter, argues that contented poverty is not poverty at all, and by the same logic that discontented wealth is.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's உடைமையுள் இன்மை, poverty inside possession, as a philosophical proposition.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 2.6 (trans. Richard M. Gummere), quoting Epicurus

real_life_example.event_title: The voyage of the St. Louis
real_life_example.place: Havana, Cuba, and the Atlantic coast of the Americas
real_life_example.event: In May 1939 the liner St. Louis sailed from Hamburg carrying 937 passengers, almost all Jewish refugees from Nazi Germany. Cuba admitted only 28 of them and ordered the ship to leave, and the passengers' appeals to the United States and Canada were turned down. The ship returned to Europe, where Britain, the Netherlands, Belgium and France agreed to take the passengers; 254 of them were later killed in the Holocaust.
real_life_example.explanation: Wealthy nations with room to spare turned away desperate guests at their very shores, a refusal now widely remembered as a moral failure.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls the failure to keep up hospitality poverty in the midst of plenty and a folly found only in fools, and the St. Louis was refused by countries that had ample means to receive it.

tamil:
மோப்பக் குழையும் அனிச்சம் முகந்திரிந்து
நோக்கக் குழையும் விருந்து.
transliteration:
Moppak kuzhaiyum anichcham mugandhirindhu,
Nokkak kuzhaiyum virundhu.
meaning: The anicham flower (a very delicate flower) wilts when you just smell it. A guest wilts just as fast when you look at them with a cold, turned-away face.
elementary: There's a flower so delicate that it droops the moment you sniff it — you don't even have to touch it. This kural says guests are even more delicate than that. You don't have to say anything unkind; if your face just goes cold when you see them, they wilt.
university: The chapter closes on its most celebrated image. The அனிச்சம் (anicham) was proverbial in Sangam-era Tamil for extreme delicacy — Valluvar returns to it at Kural 1111 and 1120 in the love poems — and the point of the comparison is a fortiori: the flower at least requires contact with the nostrils, whereas the guest is wilted by nothing more than a look. Parimelalagar's commentary makes the structural argument explicit, listing the three indispensable things a host owes a guest in order: a welcoming face when the guest is still at a distance, kind words as he draws near, and material aid once he is received. Since the face operates first and at a distance, its failure destroys the encounter before hospitality can even begin — which is why Valluvar ends the chapter here rather than with any point about provisions. The couplet is thus the culmination of an argument that has been narrowing steadily from the household's economy (81) to its resources (85) to its liturgy (87) to, finally, a single expression. Note that the received manuscript tradition transmits the second line's verb in a corrupted form in several digital editions; the correct reading, confirmed by Parimelalagar's own gloss, is குழையும், repeating the verb from the first line.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Grass, room (for resting), water, and fourthly a kind word; these (things) never fail in the houses of good men.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists the irreducible minimum of hospitality that even the poorest household can always supply, and makes a kind word one of the four — placed alongside physical necessities as equally indispensable.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts insist that the immaterial part of hospitality — the word, the face — is not an optional refinement but part of the minimum.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 3.101 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Use hospitality one to another without grudging.”
christianity.explanation: Peter's terse instruction to scattered Christian households addresses not whether to host but how — the Greek aneu gongusmou means literally 'without muttering,' targeting the grudging manner rather than the act.
christianity.tie_back: Identifies exactly what the Kural identifies: hospitality can be technically performed and still be destroyed by the host's demeanour.

islam.quote_or_event: “Don't consider anything insignificant out of good things even if it is that you meet your brother with a cheerful countenance.”
islam.explanation: Abu Dharr reports the Prophet elevating a facial expression to the status of a genuine good deed, on the grounds that its effect on the other person is real.
islam.tie_back: Both sayings insist that the host's countenance is not a trivial accompaniment to hospitality but an act in its own right.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 2626, Book of Virtue and Good Manners

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shammai says, ‘Make your Torah [study] fixed, say little and do much, and receive every person with a pleasant countenance.’”
judaism.explanation: The maxim is preserved in Pirkei Avot under the name of Shammai, whose own temperament was proverbially severe — which the tradition notes made the instruction all the more pointed.
judaism.tie_back: Nearly identical instruction to the Kural's: the reception is made or broken by the face that meets the arriving person.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot (Mishnah, Tractate Avot) 1:15 (Sefaria Community Translation)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sappurisadāna Sutta the Buddha describes the five gifts of a person of integrity: he gives with conviction, gives attentively and with respect, gives at the proper time, gives with a sympathetic heart, and gives without injuring himself or others — the manner of the giving being specified in every case alongside the gift.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta goes on to say that the results of a gift correspond to the way it was given, so that a gift given respectfully produces a very different fruit from the same object given carelessly.
buddhism.tie_back: Makes the Kural's point systematically: the object handed over is not what determines the act, the manner of handing it over is.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.148, Sappurisadāna Sutta (A Person of Integrity's Gifts)

jainism.quote_or_event: “And the right manner for giving of gift consists in: respectful welcome, a high seat, washing the feet, worshipping, bowing, purity of mind, speech and body, and purity of food.”
jainism.explanation: Jain rules for hosting a visiting monk put the manner of welcome first: respectful greeting, a seat, and purity of mind and speech, before the food itself. The Sarvarthasiddhi likewise ranks a gift by whether the guest is received 'with reverence or without reverence'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says a guest wilts at a face that turns aside even before the meal begins, and Jainism likewise makes the respectful welcome the first and essential part of the gift.
jainism.source: Amṛtacandra, Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya v. 168 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2012), as quoted in the explanatory note to Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 113 on wisdomlib.org; cf. Sarvārthasiddhi on Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all. Do not break anyone's heart; these are all priceless jewels.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid teaches that every heart is a priceless jewel in which God dwells, so even one harsh word or slight can shatter it.
sikhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's sense of how fragile the guest is: like the anicham flower, a heart can be wounded by a cold word or look alone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 129) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Telemachus, seeing a stranger standing at the gate while the suitors feast, is ashamed that a guest should be kept waiting at the door; he goes straight to Athena in her disguise as Mentes, takes her right hand, relieves her of her spear and greets her before asking a single question about who she is.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer devotes several lines to the immediacy of the greeting, and the poem's whole moral architecture depends on the contrast between this instant welcome and the suitors' indifference.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Dramatises the Kural's principle that the guest is won or lost in the first look, before any food appears.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Levinas argues that ethics begins not in reasoning but in the face-to-face encounter: the face of the other person makes a claim on me before I have decided anything, and he describes the fundamental ethical relation as a welcome extended to the other — subjectivity itself, he writes, is structured as hospitality.
philosophy.explanation: For Levinas the face is not a physical surface to be read but the point at which another person's claim becomes unavoidable, which is why his entire ethics is framed in terms of reception and welcome.
philosophy.tie_back: Supplies the philosophical case for the Kural's final image: the face is the exact site where hospitality succeeds or fails.
philosophy.source: Emmanuel Levinas, Totality and Infinity (1961), Section I and Section III

real_life_example.event_title: Marian Anderson is refused Constitution Hall and sings at the Lincoln Memorial
real_life_example.event: In 1939 the Daughters of the American Revolution, owners of Constitution Hall in Washington, refused to let the celebrated contralto Marian Anderson perform there because she was Black. First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from the organisation in protest, and with the help of Interior Secretary Harold Ickes an open-air concert was arranged on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. On Easter Sunday, 9 April 1939, Anderson sang there to an integrated crowd of about 75,000, with millions more listening on the radio.
real_life_example.explanation: A great artist was turned away by the very hosts who should have welcomed her, and the snub became a landmark of the civil rights movement.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a guest withers at a host's averted face, and the hall's cold refusal of Marian Anderson shows how wounding an unwelcoming reception is.

tamil:
இன்சொலால் ஈரம் அளைஇப் படிறுஇலவாம்
செம்பொருள் கண்டார்வாய்ச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Insolaal eeram alaiip padiru ilavaam,
Semporul kandaarvaaich chol.
meaning: Truly sweet words come from people who have understood the truth. They are full of warm love and have no trickery in them.
elementary: Kind words are like real honey, not sugar water that only looks sweet. Some people say nice things but are secretly trying to trick you. This kural says real sweet talk has two ingredients: it has to be warm and loving, and it has to be honest. If either one is missing, it isn't the real thing.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter by defining his terms, a move typical of his method. The Tamil packs three conditions into a single couplet: ஈரம் (eeram, literally 'moistness' — the warmth or tenderness of a heart that is not dry), படிறு இல (padiru ila, 'without guile or fraud'), and செம்பொருள் கண்டார் (semporul kandaar, 'those who have seen the straight/true substance'). Sweet speech is therefore not a rhetorical technique but a moral by-product: it issues from a particular kind of person. This explicitly rules out flattery, the counterfeit that classical ethical traditions across Eurasia were equally anxious to distinguish from genuine kindness — the Tamil padiru occupies almost exactly the space that Greek kolakeia (flattery) and Sanskrit anrta (falsehood in speech) occupy in their respective systems. Placing this definition first also protects the whole remaining chapter from being read as advice on charm or social technique.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him say what is true, let him say what is pleasing, let him utter no disagreeable truth, and let him utter no agreeable falsehood; that is the eternal law.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu prescribes a fourfold rule for speech: it must be both true and pleasant, and neither quality may be purchased at the cost of the other.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact double requirement — words mixed with affection (pleasing) and free of guile (true) — stated as a single legal maxim.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 4.138 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East, vol. 25)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Ephesians that Christian maturity requires holding truth and love together rather than trading one off against the other.
christianity.tie_back: Same fusion the Kural demands: the word must carry affection (eeram) and must be true (free of padiru).

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'anic phrase qawlan sadidan denotes speech that is straight, sound and upright — the opposite of crooked or self-serving talk.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's insistence that sweet speech must proceed from someone aligned with what is genuinely right (semporul).

judaism.quote_or_event: “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes betrayal by a close companion whose speech was deliberately soothing while his intent was hostile.
judaism.tie_back: It is the exact negative image of the Kural: the outward sweetness is present, but the eeram is absent and padiru fills the gap.
judaism.source: Psalms 55:21 (Hebrew Bible; King James Version rendering)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It is spoken at the right time. It is spoken in truth. It is spoken affectionately. It is spoken beneficially. It is spoken with a mind of good-will.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the five marks of a statement that is 'well-spoken' and therefore blameless in the eyes of the wise.
buddhism.tie_back: Truth and affection appear side by side in the Buddhist list exactly as they do in the Kural's definition of insol.
buddhism.source: Vācā Sutta, Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.198 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk who avoids all speech that is likely to hurt others and speaks only what is good to himself and to others observes the fourth virtue of truthfulness.”
jainism.explanation: In the list of ten virtues, Jain truthfulness (satya) is defined by its effect, not just by factual accuracy. True speech is speech that hurts no one and does good to both the speaker and the hearer.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar defines sweet words as the guileless, kindly words of those who see what is right, and the Jain verse likewise defines true speech as words that do no harm and do good.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 92 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Her speech is sweet, and her way of life is humble. She enjoys the Bed of her Husband Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the soul-bride who has found her Husband Lord through the Guru: her inner union shows outwardly as sweet speech and humble conduct.
sikhism.tie_back: As Valluvar says truly sweet words come from those who have grasped what is right, Gurbani treats sweet speech as the fruit of a soul that has found the Truth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 31, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Then among them arose Nestor, sweet of speech, the clear-voiced orator of the Pylians, from whose tongue flowed speech sweeter than honey.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer introduces Nestor at the height of the Achaean quarrel; his authority rests not on force but on speech that is at once honeyed and trustworthy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Nestor personifies the Kural's claim that genuinely sweet words belong to those who have perceived what is right.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 1.247–249 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb / Perseus)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Ninth, consider that a good disposition is invincible, if it be genuine, and not an affected smile and acting a part … And thou must do this neither with any double meaning nor in the way of reproach, but affectionately and without any rancour in thy soul.”
philosophy.explanation: Among his rules for dealing with people who give offence, Marcus Aurelius says kindness only has power when it is real: speech must come from genuine affection and carry no hidden meaning or concealed ill-will.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s sweet words are likewise defined by being steeped in affection and free of deceit, not by being pleasant on the surface.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book XI, §18 (ninth rule) (tr. George Long)

real_life_example.event_title: Vaclav Havel's first New Year's address as president
real_life_example.event: Days after becoming president at the end of the Velvet Revolution, the playwright and former dissident Vaclav Havel gave a New Year's address that broke with the upbeat official messages of his communist predecessors. He told citizens plainly that their country was not flourishing and that the worst problem was a contaminated moral environment, in which people had grown used to saying something different from what they thought. He added that all had helped to sustain the old system, and lamented that values such as love, compassion and forgiveness had lost their depth in everyday life.
real_life_example.explanation: Havel's speech was valued precisely because it was honest and free of the comforting deceptions citizens had heard for forty years, yet it was spoken with warmth and shared responsibility rather than blame.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines truly sweet words as those of people who have seen what is right, steeped in affection and free of deceit, and Havel's address joined truthfulness to goodwill in exactly that way.

tamil:
அகன்அமர்ந்து ஈதலின் நன்றே முகனமர்ந்து
இன்சொலன் ஆகப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Aganamarndhu eedhalin nandre muganamarndhu,
Insolan aagap perin.
meaning: A smiling face and kind words are even better than giving gifts with a happy heart.
elementary: Imagine two people give you a birthday present. One hands it over without looking up. The other is grinning, says your name, and tells you they hoped you'd like it. The second present feels bigger — even if it cost less. This kural says the warm face and the kind words are worth more than the gift itself.
university: The couplet sets up a deliberate comparison between two goods that the previous chapters have already praised: ஈதல் (eedhal, giving) and இன்சொல் (insol, sweet speech). Valluvar does not dismiss generosity; he ranks a cheerful countenance and kind word above even generosity offered with an expanded heart (அகன் அமர்ந்து, agan amarndhu — 'the inner self settled in gladness'). The wordplay is structural: அகன் அமர்ந்து (inner gladness) is answered by முகன் அமர்ந்து (mugan amarndhu, 'face settled in gladness'), so the verse argues that the outward, relational expression completes what the inward disposition begins. This ordering — manner above material — is one of the most widely paralleled ideas in world ethical literature, appearing almost verbatim in Ben Sira and in the rabbinic calculus of blessings attached to charity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In its closing charge to departing students, the Taittiriya Upanishad rules that a gift must be given with faith, never without faith, given in abundance, given with modesty, given with a kind of awe, and given with fellow-feeling — the manner of giving being legislated as carefully as the giving itself.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad's convocation address treats dāna not as a transfer of goods but as a relational act whose inner and outward bearing determine its worth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates the value of a gift in the warmth and bearing that accompany it rather than in the object handed over.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Shall not the dew asswage the heat? so is a word better than a gift. Lo, is not a word better than a gift? but both are with a gracious man.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira compares a kind word to dew cooling the heat of the day and states outright that it surpasses a material present, while noting the generous person offers both.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis almost word for word: the kind word ranks above the gift.

islam.quote_or_event: “Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ranks a gentle word above almsgiving that is spoiled by reproach or humiliation of the recipient.
islam.tie_back: Identical ordering to the Kural: the sweet word outweighs the material gift.
