judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Yitzhak teaches that one who gives a coin to a poor person receives six blessings, but one who consoles him with words receives eleven — the count drawn from successive verses of Isaiah 58.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud quantifies the difference, using scriptural proof-texts to show that comforting speech outranks the coin nearly two to one.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's claim rendered as an arithmetic: the kind word is worth more than the gift.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Among the four saṅgahavatthu — the 'bases of sympathy' by which a person binds a community together — the Buddha places dāna (giving) and peyyavajja (kindly speech) side by side, followed by beneficial conduct and impartiality.
buddhism.explanation: Kindly speech is listed as a full social virtue in its own right, not as an accessory to generosity.
buddhism.tie_back: It puts the kind word on the same footing as the gift, though without the Kural's explicit ranking of one above the other.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As giving safety is the best of gifts, as the best of true speeches is that which causes no distress, as chastity is the highest of austerities, so is the Śramaṇa Jñātṛputra the highest of men.”
jainism.explanation: In its hymn to Mahāvīra, the Sūtrakṛtāṅga ranks the gift of safety, a gift of how one treats others rather than of goods, above all other gifts. It ranks harmless speech highest among truthful speech.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks a cheerful face and kind word above a material gift, and the Jain hymn similarly sets a harmless manner toward others (safety, non-distressing words) at the top of its scale of gifts and speech.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.6.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He speaks sweetly, moves humbly and giving away something by his hands for the well being of others feels happy.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh exegete, lists sweet speech, humble conduct and giving with one's own hands as the marks of the Guru's Sikh.
sikhism.tie_back: It sets kind speech beside generous giving, the very two goods the Kural compares, though without ranking one above the other.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 28, Pauri 15 (English translation as given on BaniDB / searchgurbani.com)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, an aged and desperately poor couple, are the only people in their district to welcome Zeus and Hermes travelling in disguise; they have almost nothing to offer but receive the strangers with delighted faces, bustling warmth and constant talk, and are rewarded while their wealthy neighbours are destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's point turns entirely on manner: the gods are honoured by the couple's gladness, not by the value of the meal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's ranking — the beaming face and warm words outweigh what is materially given.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues throughout On Benefits that the benefit is never the coin or the object but the goodwill behind it, and that a favour delivered grudgingly — with frowning brows and muttered words — is like a stone thrown at a hungry man instead of bread.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca the gift is merely the visible trace of a benevolent intention; a harsh manner cancels it entirely.
philosophy.tie_back: It supports the Kural's ranking: what is actually received by the other person is the manner, not the material.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Beneficiis (On Benefits), Books I–II

real_life_example.event_title: Princess Diana shakes hands with an AIDS patient
real_life_example.event: In April 1987 Diana, Princess of Wales, opened the first hospital ward in the United Kingdom dedicated to patients with HIV and AIDS, at London's Middlesex Hospital. At a time when many people wrongly believed the virus could be spread by touch, she shook hands with a patient without wearing gloves. The photographed gesture was widely credited with helping to change public attitudes towards people with the disease.
real_life_example.explanation: A warm, open manner did more to help people with AIDS than any material gift could have, because it challenged fear and stigma directly.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks a glad face and a kind manner above even generous giving, and a single ungloved handshake changed more than donations alone could have.

tamil:
முகத்தான் அமர்ந்துஇனிது நோக்கி அகத்தானாம்
இன்சொ லினதே அறம்.
transliteration:
Mugatthaan amarndhu inidhu nokki agatthaanaam,
Inso linadhe aram.
meaning: A welcoming face, a kind look, and sweet words that come from the heart: that is true goodness.
elementary: When someone talks to you while looking at their phone, even nice words feel cold. But when a person turns to you, smiles, actually looks at you, and means what they say — that feels completely different. This kural says that whole package isn't just being polite. It IS being good.
university: The couplet is structured as an ascending sequence of three organs of kindness: முகத்தான் (mugatthaan, by the face), நோக்கி (nokki, by the look), and அகத்தான் (agatthaan, from within). The claim in the final word is unusually strong — Valluvar does not say such conduct leads to அறம் (aram, virtue/dharma) or is a part of it, but that it is aram, full stop. Given that aram is the governing category of the entire first book of the Kural, encompassing householder duty, ascetic restraint and social justice, identifying it with a warm face and a heartfelt word is a striking democratisation of virtue: it makes the moral life available in every ordinary encounter, requiring neither wealth nor renunciation. The insistence that the word must arise அகத்தான் — from the interior — also forecloses the reading that this is mere etiquette.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna classifies pleasant, non-agitating speech as a form of tapas — spiritual discipline — placing it on the same plane as bodily and mental austerity.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats gentle speech not as social lubricant but as a religious practice in its own right.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs traces the visible face directly back to the inner state, treating the countenance as an honest readout of the heart.
christianity.tie_back: It underwrites the Kural's chain from within (agatthaan) to the face (mugatthaan).

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not belittle any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ranks a welcoming expression as a genuine act of ma'ruf (good), not a trivial courtesy.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim exactly: the welcoming face is itself moral action, not a preliminary to it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Make your Torah fixed, say little and do much, and receive every person with a cheerful countenance.”
judaism.explanation: Shammai, famously the stricter of the two great first-century sages, nonetheless makes a welcoming face one of his three foundational rules of conduct.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's mugatthaan amarndhu — the settled, glad face turned toward the other — is precisely Shammai's sever panim yafot.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind is the forerunner of all states... If with a pure mind a person speaks or acts, happiness follows him like his never-departing shadow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's opening pair establishes that speech and action take their entire moral quality from the mental state that generates them.
buddhism.tie_back: It grounds the Kural's insistence that the sweet word must come agatthaan — from within — to count as virtue.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who does not think crookedly, does not act crookedly, does not speak crookedly and does not hide his own weaknesses, observes the virtue of straightforwardness.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain virtue of straightforwardness (ārjava) requires thought, action and speech to line up, with nothing hidden behind the words.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar counts a welcoming face and gaze, with sweet words that come from within, as virtue itself, and the Jain verse likewise makes inner and outer straightness of thought, deed and word a virtue (dharma) in its own right.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 91 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My Dear Lord and Master, my Friend, speaks so sweetly. I have grown weary of testing Him, but still, He never speaks harshly to me.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes God himself as a Friend whose speech is unfailingly sweet, making gentle speech an attribute of the divine.
sikhism.tie_back: If sweetness of word is the Lord's own character, then, as the Kural says, a kind word from the heart is itself virtue rather than a mere means to it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 784, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod names the three Charites — Aglaia, Euphrosyne and Thalia — daughters of Zeus and Eurynome, from whose glancing eyes a melting sweetness flows; they are the goddesses who make gracious social exchange possible, and Greek thought derived the whole vocabulary of charis (grace, favour, gratitude) from them.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Graces divinise exactly the cluster the Kural lists: the warm look, the pleasing manner, the reciprocity of goodwill.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They mythologise the gaze and countenance the Kural names as the outward face of virtue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Such as a man's character is, he immediately shows it in his eyes, just as he who is beloved forthwith reads everything in the eyes of lovers … The good and simple and benevolent show all these things in the eyes, and there is no mistaking.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius mocks the man who announces that he means to deal fairly, saying real goodness needs no announcement because it shows itself at once in a person’s eyes and bearing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise locates virtue in the welcoming face and kindly gaze, and treats these as outward signs of what is inside rather than as decoration.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book XI, §15 (tr. George Long)

real_life_example.event_title: Pope John XXIII's Moonlight Speech
real_life_example.event: On the evening of the opening day of the Second Vatican Council, Pope John XXIII came unexpectedly to his window to greet a large crowd holding candles in St Peter's Square. Speaking without a prepared text, he remarked that even the moon seemed to have hurried out to watch, called himself a brother speaking to them, and asked them to go home and give their children a caress from the Pope, to dry any tears and to say a good word. The improvised greeting became one of the best-remembered moments of his papacy.
real_life_example.explanation: The speech is remembered not for doctrine but for its warmth, simplicity and evident sincerity, which reached people far beyond the square.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a welcoming face, a kindly gaze and sweet words that come from within are themselves virtue, and John XXIII's unscripted greeting was exactly such heartfelt kindness.

tamil:
துன்புறூஉம் துவ்வாமை இல்லாகும் யார்மாட்டும்
இன்புறூஉம் இன்சொ லவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Thunburooum thuvvaamai illaagum yaarmaattum,
Inburooum inso lavarkku.
meaning: People who speak words that make everyone happy will never suffer the pain of poverty.
elementary: Think of someone at school everybody likes because they're kind to everyone — not just their own friends. When that person needs help, ten people offer. Being warm to everybody builds up a kind of invisible savings account. This kural says people like that don't end up with nothing.
university: The key word is யார்மாட்டும் (yaarmaattum, 'toward anyone at all'), which universalises the obligation and rules out selective charm directed at the useful. துவ்வாமை (thuvvaamai) is a striking choice: it derives from துவ்வு (to eat/enjoy) and so denotes destitution specifically as the inability to consume or enjoy — want at the level of the body. Valluvar claims that the person who gives everyone the enjoyment (இன்புறூஉம், inburooum) of a kind word will not suffer the want of enjoyment. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward have read this both prudentially (goodwill converts into material support) and karmically (the merit of universal kindness bears fruit). The verse also uses the elongated alapedai forms துன்புறூஉம் / இன்புறூஉம் to set the two states of misery and delight in exact metrical opposition.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A widely transmitted Sanskrit maxim states that all creatures are gratified by the giving of pleasing words, and therefore one should speak only in that way — asking, pointedly, 'where is the poverty in words?'
hinduism.explanation: The verse notes that kind speech is the one currency that never runs out, so there can be no economic excuse for withholding it.
hinduism.tie_back: It joins kind speech directly to the vocabulary of poverty (daridratā), exactly as the Kural joins insol to thuvvaamai.
hinduism.source: Subhāṣita, attributed to Chāṇakya Nīti 16.13 (also collected in the Subhāṣita Ratna Bhāṇḍāgāra)

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that loveth pureness of heart, for the grace of his lips the king shall be his friend.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs links a pure heart and gracious speech to concrete advancement — securing the favour of the most powerful patron available.
christianity.tie_back: It makes the Kural's prudential claim that gracious speech protects a person from destitution.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that every good word is itself an act of charity (sadaqah), placing speech within the same economy of giving and reward as almsgiving.
islam.explanation: The hadith reclassifies speech as a transferable good, so the person with nothing to give materially is never actually empty-handed.
islam.tie_back: It supports the Kural's link between kind speech and freedom from want by making the kind word a form of wealth.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 2989 (Book of Jihad, chapter on charity)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Sweet language will multiply friends: and a fairspeaking tongue will increase kind greetings.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira presents pleasant speech as an investment that compounds: it generates a widening circle of allies and reciprocal goodwill.
judaism.tie_back: This is the practical mechanism behind the Kural's promise that the kind speaker will not fall into destitution.
judaism.source: Ben Sira / Ecclesiasticus 6:5 (King James Version, Apocrypha)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Maṅgala Sutta, the Buddha's catalogue of the highest blessings (maṅgala) available in a human life, lists well-spoken speech alongside vast learning, mastered discipline and skilled craft as among the things that make a life auspicious and secure.
buddhism.explanation: Pleasant, well-formed speech is counted as an actual component of worldly good fortune, not merely of moral character.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's claim that kind speech produces the good fortune that keeps misery-bringing want at bay.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I forgive all living beings and may all living beings forgive me; I cherish feelings of friendship towards all and I harbour enmity towards none.”
jainism.explanation: This well-known Jain formula of mutual forgiveness and friendship toward all beings is recited at the close of Paryuṣaṇa. It extends goodwill to every creature without exception.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's speaker gladdens everyone he meets, whoever they are, and the Jain vow of friendship toward all beings expresses the same universal goodwill.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 86 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “A mild spoken, humble and giver through his hands moves in equipoise and remains happy.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas holds that the person who speaks gently, walks humbly and gives freely lives in calm contentment.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's promise that those who speak gladdening words to all will escape misery, it ties mild speech to a life free of distress.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 12, Pauri 16 (English translation as given on BaniDB / searchgurbani.com)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...they pour sweet dew upon his tongue, and from his lips flow gracious words.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the Muses' gift to a king they favour at birth: his gracious speech settles disputes, and in consequence the whole people look to him and he is conspicuous in the assembly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It ties honeyed speech directly to standing and security, the same causal link the Kural draws.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Acquire the Reputation of Courtesy; for it is enough to make you liked. Politeness is the main ingredient of culture,—a kind of witchery that wins the regard of all as surely as discourtesy gains their disfavour and opposition...”
philosophy.explanation: Gracián, writing a manual of worldly survival for the seventeenth-century court, treats courtesy as the cheapest and most reliable instrument of advantage available to anyone.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the Kural's prudential argument stated frankly: kind speech is what keeps a person from being left with nothing.
philosophy.source: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom, §118 (trans. Joseph Jacobs, 1892)

real_life_example.event_title: Fred Rogers testifies to the US Senate for public television
real_life_example.event: When President Nixon proposed cutting the planned 20 million dollar budget of the new Corporation for Public Broadcasting by half, the children's television host Fred Rogers testified before the Senate Communications Subcommittee. In a calm, gentle statement he described how his programme dealt with the inner drama of childhood and recited the words of one of his songs. The subcommittee chairman, Senator John Pastore, said the testimony had given him goosebumps and that Rogers appeared to have earned the 20 million dollars.
real_life_example.explanation: Rogers won over a sceptical senator through gentle, sincere speech rather than argument or pressure, helping to protect the funding his work depended on.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural promises that those who speak words that gladden everyone will not be overtaken by want, and Rogers's kindly words helped secure the support public broadcasting needed.

tamil:
பணிவுடையன் இன்சொலன் ஆதல் ஒருவற்கு
அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற.
transliteration:
Panivudaiyan insolan aadhal oruvarku,
Aniyalla matrup pira.
meaning: Being humble and speaking kindly are a person’s true jewels. Nothing else deserves to be called a jewel.
elementary: You can put on the nicest shoes and the coolest jacket and still have nobody want to sit with you. But if you're kind and you don't act like you're better than everyone, people want to be near you. This kural says humility and kind words are the jewellery that actually works.
university: அணி (ani) in Tamil poetic usage covers both physical ornament and rhetorical figure, so Valluvar's metaphor carries a faint irony: the true 'figure of speech' is not an embellishment of language but a quality of the speaker. The pairing of பணிவு (panivu, humility/bending) with இன்சொல் is deliberate — sweet speech without humility collapses into condescension, while humility without kind speech remains invisible. The closing அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற ('other things are not ornaments') is an absolute exclusion, and Tamil commentators note it as a rejection of the courtly display culture in which jewellery signified rank. The trope of speech-as-the-only-true-ornament is remarkably widespread: Bhartrihari's Sanskrit formulation is so close that some comparatists have argued for shared circulation of the image across the Deccan in the early centuries CE, though no dependency can be demonstrated.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrihari writes that armlets do not adorn a person, nor necklaces bright as the moon, nor bathing, nor perfumes, nor flowers, nor dressed hair — one thing alone adorns a person, and that is cultivated speech; all other ornaments perish, but the ornament of speech is the enduring ornament.
hinduism.explanation: The verse works through a catalogue of conventional finery and dismisses each in turn before naming refined speech as the sole real adornment.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural's claim in almost identical terms, including the explicit denial that anything else counts as an ornament.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.”
christianity.explanation: 1 Peter contrasts visible finery with an inward disposition of meekness, and names the latter the genuinely valuable ornament.
christianity.tie_back: Same metaphor, same exclusion, and the same pairing of humility with the true ornament.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth easily, and when the ignorant address them [harshly], they say [words of] peace,”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an's portrait of the ideal believer fuses humility of bearing with gentleness of speech, even under provocation.
islam.tie_back: It names the Kural's exact pair — humility plus kind speech — as the defining marks of the highest human type.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Yishmael taught that one should be yielding to a superior, pleasant and easy toward the young, and should receive every person with gladness.
judaism.explanation: The maxim binds deference upward, gentleness downward and warmth in all directions into a single rule of bearing.
judaism.tie_back: It couples humility with pleasant speech exactly as the Kural does, as the whole of a person's proper adornment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada repeatedly dismisses outward religious markers — matted hair, animal-skin robes, ritual bathing — as worthless while the interior remains impure, insisting that the only real distinction is an inward one.
buddhism.explanation: The verses attack the assumption that visible tokens can stand in for the cultivated qualities they are supposed to signify.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's logic that external adornments are not ornaments at all; only inner quality is.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He alone is really worthy of proud who is careful not to insult other people. A person who merely boasts, has no virtues, cannot command respect.”
jainism.explanation: In the Jain virtue of humility (mārdava), real standing comes from never belittling others, not from display or boasting about one's family, beauty or learning (the preceding verse).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says humility and kind speech are a person's only true ornament, and the Jain verse likewise grants honour only to the one who neither boasts nor insults.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 89 (cf. v. 88) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Asa di Vaar, after describing the showy but fruitless simmal tree, Guru Nanak names sweetness and humility as the very core of all good qualities.
sikhism.tie_back: It is nearly the Kural's own verdict: humility and sweet speech are a person's true ornament, and nothing else deserves the name.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For one man is inferior in comeliness, but the god sets a crown of beauty upon his words, and men look upon him with delight, and he speaks on unfalteringly with sweet modesty, and is conspicuous among the gathered people, and as he goes through the city men gaze upon him as upon a god.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Stung by a young Phaeacian's mockery of his unimpressive appearance, Odysseus replies that the gods distribute gifts unevenly and that gracious, modest speech outshines physical beauty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis dramatised: speech joined to modesty is the adornment that actually makes a person admired.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 8.169–175 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb / Perseus)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Politeness is to human nature what warmth is to wax.”
philosophy.explanation: Schopenhauer's point is that courtesy softens people who are otherwise rigid and hostile, making them workable — a small expenditure with disproportionate effect.
philosophy.tie_back: It backs the Kural's claim that humble, kind speech is the one quality that genuinely does the work other displays only pretend to.
philosophy.source: Arthur Schopenhauer, Counsels and Maxims, ch. III 'Our Relation to Others', §36

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi attends the royal reception at Buckingham Palace in his dhoti
real_life_example.event: While in London for the Second Round Table Conference on India's future, Mahatma Gandhi attended King George V's reception for the conference delegates at Buckingham Palace. He went in his customary dhoti, the garment the press called a loincloth, and slippers rather than formal court dress. Queen Mary recorded that he caused great excitement in what she called his odd get-up.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi treated humility and simplicity, not costly dress, as the proper adornment even at the most formal court in the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says humility and kind speech are a person's only real ornament, and Gandhi appeared before a king wearing nothing grander than his everyday dhoti.

tamil:
அல்லவை தேய அறம்பெருகும் நல்லவை
நாடி இனிய சொலின்.
transliteration:
Allavai theya arampperugum nallavai,
Naadi iniya solin.
meaning: If a person thinks about what is truly good and then says it kindly, wrongs will fade away and goodness will grow.
elementary: It's like weeding a garden. Every time you plant something good — a kind, helpful word — there's a little less room for weeds. Do it often enough and the weeds shrink while the flowers spread. This kural says kind, useful words work on the world like that.
university: The verb நாடி (naadi, 'having sought out, investigated') is the hinge of the couplet and is easy to miss. Valluvar is not recommending spontaneous niceness but a deliberate search for what will actually benefit the hearer, delivered pleasantly. The two clauses form a causal pair with a striking agricultural logic: அல்லவை தேய ('evils wearing thin, eroding') and அறம் பெருகும் ('virtue swelling, increasing') — a single practice simultaneously depletes one and augments the other. This is one of the few places where Valluvar assigns speech a world-altering rather than merely personal effect, anticipating the argument of chapters 19 (on not slandering) and 20 (on avoiding useless words). The claim that gentle words can actually reduce the quantity of evil in the world finds its most dramatic mythic expression in Aeschylus and its clearest scriptural statement in Qur'an 41:34.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Patanjali prescribes that by deliberately cultivating friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, gladness toward the virtuous and equanimity toward the wicked, the mind becomes clear and undisturbed.
hinduism.explanation: The sutra treats chosen benevolent attitudes as a technique: adopting them dissolves the mental afflictions that generate harmful action.
hinduism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's mechanism — deliberately sought-out goodwill erodes what is bad and increases what is good.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks for speech selected specifically for its capacity to build up the hearer — the negative rule and the positive purpose stated together.
christianity.tie_back: 'Good to the use of edifying' is the Kural's நல்லவை நாடி — seeking out what is genuinely good to say.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad deed. Repel [evil] by that which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an prescribes a better response as the active means of dissolving hostility, converting an enemy rather than defeating him.
islam.tie_back: It is the Kural's claim that evil wears away and good grows precisely through the better, gentler word.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud describes the person who studies Torah, is honest in business and speaks pleasantly with people: of such a one others say, 'happy is the father who taught him Torah — see how fine his ways are.' The one whose dealings and speech are unpleasant produces the opposite response, and thereby desecrates the divine Name.
judaism.explanation: Pleasant speech is treated as having public theological consequence: it makes holiness attractive, while harshness discredits it.
judaism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's claim that pleasant, well-chosen speech visibly increases virtue in the world around the speaker.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He speaks words that are soothing to the ear, that are affectionate, that go to the heart, that are polite, appealing and pleasing to people at large.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's positive definition of right speech to Cunda the silversmith, given as the direct replacement for abusive speech rather than merely its absence.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the Kural's programme exactly: abandoning harsh speech in favour of deliberately pleasing speech is what causes evil to decline and good to grow.
buddhism.source: Cunda Kammāraputta Sutta, Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.176 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Every beneficial advice given by a group-fellow though unpalatable to the mind at first, proves wholesome in the end, like a medicine which is better in taste becomes agreeable in effect.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching on truthful speech puts benefit (pathya) to the hearer first, and accepts that benefit sometimes comes in words that are hard to hear.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks the speaker to seek out what is genuinely beneficial before speaking pleasantly, and the Jain verse shares that stress on benefit, though it tolerates bitterness where the Kural insists on sweetness.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 94 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger. Your body shall not suffer from any disease, and you shall obtain everything.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid counsels returning good for evil without harbouring anger, promising wholeness and every good thing as the result.
sikhism.tie_back: As the Kural says good words sought out and kindly spoken make evil wane and virtue grow, Farid holds that answering evil with good overcomes it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381-1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 78) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I love the eyes of Persuasion, who guided my tongue and mouth against the fierce refusal of these deities.”
greek_mythology.explanation: At the close of the Oresteia, Athena wins over the vengeful Erinyes not by force but by Peitho (Persuasion); they are transformed into the Eumenides, the Kindly Ones, and the cycle of blood-vengeance ends.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's claim enacted on a civic scale: gentle words literally cause evil to wear away and blessing to increase.
greek_mythology.source: Aeschylus, Eumenides 970 (cf. 885) (trans. H. W. Smyth, rev. Bannon and Nagy)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates distinguishes the mere knack of flattery from a genuine art of rhetoric, which he defines as psychagōgia — a leading of souls — and argues that it is legitimate only when the speaker knows the truth and knows what will genuinely benefit the particular soul in front of him.
philosophy.explanation: Plato makes the ethical worth of persuasive speech depend entirely on whether the speaker has sought out what is actually good for the hearer.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's நல்லவை நாடி — the prior search for what is genuinely good — made the precondition of legitimate speech.

real_life_example.event_title: Nelson Mandela appeals for calm after the killing of Chris Hani
real_life_example.event: On 10 April 1993 the South African Communist Party leader Chris Hani was assassinated, and the country, then in the middle of negotiations to end apartheid, faced the risk of widespread violence. Nelson Mandela, president of the African National Congress, went on national television that night and again on 13 April, appealing for discipline and calm, asking people to honour Hani through peaceful memorial services and urging that a date be fixed for democratic elections. Negotiations continued, and within weeks the date of the first democratic election, 27 April 1994, was agreed.
real_life_example.explanation: Carefully chosen, steadying words from a trusted leader helped hold a country back from violence at one of its most dangerous moments.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when a person seeks out what is good to say and says it well, evil wears away and virtue grows, and Mandela's addresses turned a moment of fury toward peaceful action.

tamil:
நயன்ஈன்று நன்றி பயக்கும் பயன்ஈன்று
பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியாச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Nayan eendru nandri payakkum payan eendru,
Panbin thalaippiriyaach chol.
meaning: Words that truly help the listener and never go against good manners bring the speaker both goodwill and good results.
elementary: There's a difference between a friend who tells you what you want to hear and a friend who tells you something helpful, kindly. The second kind of talking does two jobs at once: it helps the other person, and it makes you a better person too. This kural is about that double win.
university: The couplet is built on a careful distinction between two returns: நயன் (nayan, goodwill, favour, social benefit accruing to the speaker) and நன்றி (nandri, here in its older sense of moral good or merit rather than gratitude). The condition for both is that the speech must be பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியா — literally 'not parting from the head of good character' — a striking idiom implying that speech remains tethered to the speaker's cultivated disposition rather than floating free as mere technique. This anticipates by some centuries the point Aristotle makes about ethos, that the most potent mode of persuasion is the character the speech itself displays. The doubled ஈன்று (eendru, 'having borne/given birth to') repeated in both lines gives the verse a generative, almost obstetric image: beneficial speech reproduces itself as both goodwill and merit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita's four conditions — truthful, pleasing, beneficial, non-agitating — must all hold simultaneously; satisfying only some of them does not qualify.
hinduism.tie_back: 'Beneficial' (hita) and 'pleasing' (priya) held together is exactly the Kural's demand that speech yield real benefit without departing from good character.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks for speech that is simultaneously gracious and substantive — salt being the ancient image for what preserves and gives savour, i.e. usefulness.
christianity.tie_back: Grace plus substance is the Kural's pairing of pleasantness with real benefit.

islam.quote_or_event: “And tell My servants to say that which is best. Indeed, Satan induces [dissension] among them.”
islam.explanation: The instruction is comparative — not merely to say what is acceptable but to select what is best — and is immediately justified by the social damage that lesser speech causes.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's standard that speech must actively benefit rather than merely avoid offence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs gives kind words a double effect: immediate sweetness to the spirit and actual restorative benefit to the body.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's twin yields — pleasantness and real benefit — are the honeycomb's sweetness and health.
judaism.source: Proverbs 16:24 (Hebrew Bible; King James Version rendering)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathāgata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, and endearing and agreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha sets out a six-part grid of speech and will utter only what is both true and beneficial, adding pleasantness and timing as further filters — he will never say what is untrue or unbeneficial, however agreeable it might be.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the Kural's exact requirement: benefit and pleasantness together, never at the expense of good character.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A person who speaks the truth becomes trustworthy like a mother, venerable like a preceptor to his people and dear to all others as their relatives.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching holds that truthful, harmless speech wins trust, reverence and affection among people, alongside its spiritual value; the next verse calls truthfulness the source of all other virtues.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says beneficial speech that stays true to good character brings the speaker both goodwill (nayan) and merit, and the Jain verse likewise promises the truthful speaker trust and affection from all.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 95 (cf. v. 96) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “By speaking sweetly, behaving humbly and bestowing charities with one's own hands, even the fallen ones have become pure.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas teaches that sweet speech joined to humble conduct and giving is so powerful that it can redeem even those who had fallen.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speech that never strays from good character and so brings both goodwill and merit, Bhai Gurdas ties sweet words to conduct and credits them with moral transformation.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 29, Pauri 4 (English translation as given on BaniDB / searchgurbani.com)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Muses greet Hesiod on Helicon with the taunt that they know how to speak many false things as though they were true, but also know, when they will, to utter true things — then breathe into him a divine voice and send him out to sing.
greek_mythology.explanation: The scene explicitly separates two capacities that sound identical from outside: persuasive falsehood and persuasive truth, with the poet's gift lying in the second.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's condition that pleasing speech must never part company with integrity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Persuasion is achieved by the speaker's personal character when the speech is so spoken as to make us think him credible... We believe good men more fully and more readily than others.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle makes ethos one of the three proofs, insisting that the persuasive force resides in the character displayed by the speech itself, not in a reputation held independently of it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியாச் சொல் — speech that never departs from the speaker's good character — analysed as a technical principle.

real_life_example.event_title: Ashoka's Rock Edict XII on restraint in speech
real_life_example.event: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka had a series of edicts carved on rocks across his empire setting out his idea of dhamma. Rock Edict XII teaches that the root of growth in essentials for all religious groups is restraint in speech: people should not praise their own sect or condemn others without cause, and any criticism should be mild. It states that honouring other sects benefits both one's own and theirs, while disparaging them harms both.
real_life_example.explanation: Ashoka made gracious, restrained speech a matter of public policy, arguing that it served the speaker's own community as well as others.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says useful words that never depart from good character bring the speaker both goodwill and merit, and Ashoka's edict taught that courteous speech towards others enriches both speaker and hearer.

tamil:
சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய இன்சொல் மறுமையும்
இம்மையும் இன்பம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Sirumaiyul neengiya insol marumaiyum,
Immaiyum inbam tharum.
meaning: Kind words with no meanness in them bring joy both in this life and in the next.
elementary: Some people say something nice but slip a little insult inside it, like a stone hidden in a cake. This kural says the kind words that count are the ones with nothing mean tucked inside — and those are the ones that make you happy now and keep on paying you back later.
university: சிறுமை (sirumai) means smallness, and by extension pettiness, meanness or baseness; the phrase சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய ('having departed from smallness') therefore screens out the backhanded compliment, the sweetly delivered slight, the kindness offered as a display of superiority. Valluvar then makes his only eschatological claim in the chapter, invoking the standard Tamil pairing இம்மை / மறுமை (immai / marumai, this birth and the next). The pairing is significant for the Kural's interpretive history: it has been read by Jain scholars as evidence of a rebirth framework, by Saiva commentators as reference to heaven, and by twentieth-century secular readers as a rhetorical intensifier meaning simply 'always'. The formula 'in this world and the next' is one of the most durable rhetorical structures in world ethics, recurring near-verbatim in the Dhammapada, the Gita and the Mishnah.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Son of Pṛthā, a transcendentalist engaged in auspicious activities does not meet with destruction either in this world or in the spiritual world; one who does good, My friend, is never overcome by evil.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reassures Arjuna that the effort spent on good conduct is never wasted, in either of the two arenas of existence.
hinduism.tie_back: It uses the Kural's exact two-world structure to guarantee the durability of good action.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.40 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment. For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus makes speech itself the basis of eschatological verdict, treating words as fully weighted moral acts rather than as incidental noise.
christianity.tie_back: It carries the Kural's speech into the next world as decisively as into this one.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes good speech a direct corollary of belief in the hereafter, placing every utterance inside the horizon of final accounting.
islam.tie_back: It links kind speech to the world to come precisely as the Kural does with marumai.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah lists certain acts — honouring parents, deeds of loving-kindness, and making peace between people — as those whose fruits a person consumes in this world while the capital remains intact for the world to come.
judaism.explanation: The financial metaphor is precise: these acts pay a dividend immediately without depleting the principal reserved for the hereafter.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's double payoff — happiness in this life and the next — expressed as an accounting relationship.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Here he rejoices, hereafter he rejoices. In both worlds the doer of good rejoices. He rejoices, he is exceedingly glad, seeing the purity of his own deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's twin verses set the wrongdoer and the doer of good in exact parallel, each receiving his result in both worlds.
buddhism.tie_back: Structurally and substantively the same promise the Kural makes for speech free of meanness.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not tell anything sinful or meaningless or hurtful, neither for his own sake nor for anybody else's, nor without such a motive.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana's rules of discipline forbid hurtful or empty speech for any motive. The same lecture promises that one who masters himself 'will be happy in this world and in the next' (1.15).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar promises joy in this birth and the next for kind words free of meanness, and the Jain text joins a ban on hurtful speech to the same promise of happiness in both worlds.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.25 (cf. 1.15) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, speaking insipid words, the body and mind become insipid. He is called the most insipid of the insipid; the most insipid of the insipid is his reputation. The insipid person is discarded in the Court of the Lord, and the insipid one's face is spat upon.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak warns that harsh, graceless speech sours the speaker inwardly, ruins his name among people and leaves him rejected in God's court.
sikhism.tie_back: It states the Kural's promise in reverse: kind words free of meanness bring joy in this life and the next, while their opposite brings disgrace in both.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod records that the righteous race of heroes was not extinguished but settled by Zeus at the ends of the earth on the Isles of the Blest beside deep-swirling Ocean, where the grain-giving earth bears honey-sweet fruit three times a year.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth does contain a picture of continued blessedness after death, but it is awarded for heroic worth and divine favour rather than for everyday moral conduct.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It offers the nearest Greek analogue to the Kural's marumai — happiness continuing past this life — without linking it to speech.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates closes the Gorgias with a myth of judgment in which souls are stripped of body and reputation and judged naked, and argues from it that rhetoric is worth having only if it is used to serve justice, since the orator's own soul is what is finally at stake.
philosophy.explanation: Plato subordinates the entire question of persuasive speech to the speaker's condition in a post-mortem reckoning.
philosophy.tie_back: It reproduces the Kural's move of evaluating speech by its consequences in both this life and the next.

real_life_example.event_title: Abraham Lincoln's Second Inaugural Address
real_life_example.event: As the Civil War neared its end, Abraham Lincoln took the oath of office for a second time and delivered a short address at the Capitol. He named slavery as the cause of the war but avoided triumph over the defeated South, closing with the words with malice toward none, with charity for all, and calling on the nation to bind up its wounds. The address is inscribed on the wall of the Lincoln Memorial.
real_life_example.explanation: At the moment of victory Lincoln chose words free of pettiness or revenge, and the speech remains one of the most admired in American history.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises kind words with no trace of meanness, and Lincoln's address spoke to a defeated enemy without spite at the very moment he could have gloated.

tamil:
இன்சொல் இனிதீன்றல் காண்பான் எவன்கொலோ
வன்சொல் வழங்கு வது.
transliteration:
Insol inidheendral kaanbaan evankolo,
Vansol vazhangu vadhu.
meaning: Why would someone who has seen the joy kind words bring use harsh words instead?
elementary: You already know how good it feels when someone is nice to you. So why would you ever be mean to someone else? You've already felt both sides. This kural is basically asking, with a raised eyebrow: what are you even doing?
university: This is the chapter's only rhetorical question, and Valluvar uses it for maximum force. எவன்கொலோ (evankolo) is an idiom of genuine puzzlement — 'whatever for?' — rather than condemnation, which makes the couplet feel less like a prohibition than an expression of bafflement. The argument's structure is a pure appeal to first-person evidence: the person addressed is a காண்பான், one who has himself seen and experienced the pleasure that kind words produce. Harsh speech is therefore presented not primarily as wicked but as irrational, a failure to reason from one's own experience to another's. This is precisely the logic of the Golden Rule in its negative form, and the verse's structure makes it the Kural's closest approach to that formula. The contrast pair இன்சொல் / வன்சொல் (sweet word / hard word) also sets up the culminating fruit-image of Kural 100.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Arrogance, pride, anger, conceit, harshness and ignorance — these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists pāruṣya (harshness, especially harshness of speech) among the defining marks of the āsurī or demoniac disposition, in direct contrast to the divine qualities catalogued just before.
hinduism.tie_back: It names harsh speech itself as the disorder the Kural finds so inexplicable in someone who knows better.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.4 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs states the practical asymmetry: the gentle reply defuses a situation while the harsh one escalates it, so harshness is self-defeating.
christianity.tie_back: It supplies the answer to the Kural's question — there is no good reason for harsh words, since they only make matters worse.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allah, [O Muhammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: Revealed after the reverse at Uhud, the verse tells the Prophet that his community held together because of his gentleness, and would have scattered had he been harsh.
islam.tie_back: It makes the Kural's point concretely: harsh speech destroys what gentle speech has built, so there is nothing to be gained by it.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Yohanan taught in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai that the transgression of verbal mistreatment (ona'at devarim) is graver than that of monetary exploitation, because the one touches a person's very body while the other touches only his money — and the verse on verbal wronging alone concludes 'and you shall fear your God'.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis rank wounding words above financial fraud, on the reasoning that money is recoverable and dignity is not.
judaism.tie_back: It gives full weight to the harm the Kural's harsh speaker is inflicting without apparent reason.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak not harshly to anyone, for those thus spoken to might retort. Indeed, angry speech hurts, and retaliation may overtake you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada argues against harsh speech on grounds of reciprocity: the words you send out come back, and the cycle is unprofitable for everyone.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's puzzlement given an answer — harsh speech is simply a bad calculation by someone who already knows how words feel.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Disobedient, rough speaking, ill-behaved pupils will exasperate even a gentle teacher; but those will soon win even a hot-tempered teacher who humour him and are polite.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana appeals to plain experience: rough words sour even a kind listener, while polite words win over even a harsh one.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks why anyone who has felt the pleasure of kind words would speak harshly, and the Jain verse points to the same everyday evidence of what rough and polite speech do.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor. Harsh words bring only grief. Listen, O foolish and ignorant mind!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak contrasts words that bring honour with harsh words that bring only grief, and calls the mind that still chooses harshness foolish.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's puzzled question, it treats harsh speech as plain folly in one who knows how much good kind words do.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Thersites, the only common soldier in the Iliad given a speaking part, is described as the ugliest man at Troy and an unmeasured, abusive railer who reviles the kings out of habit; Odysseus strikes him with the royal staff and the whole army laughs at him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer draws Thersites as a man whose speech is harsh for no strategic reason at all, and the episode ends with his humiliation rather than any gain.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the walking answer to the Kural's question: the habitual harsh speaker achieves nothing but his own diminishment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Consider how much more pain is brought on us by the anger and vexation caused by such acts than by the acts themselves, at which we are angry and vexed.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius, in his list of remedies against anger, points out that the reaction consistently costs more than the provocation did.
philosophy.tie_back: It supplies the missing calculation behind the Kural's question: dealing out harsh words costs the speaker more than it could ever return.

real_life_example.event_title: The Seventeen-Article Constitution warns against anger
real_life_example.event: The Seventeen-Article Constitution, traditionally attributed to Prince Shotoku and dated to 604, set out moral principles for officials of the Japanese court, beginning with the rule that harmony should be valued and quarrels avoided. Its tenth article tells officials to restrain their anger when others disagree with them, reasoning that everyone has a heart and inclinations of their own, that none is wholly wise or wholly foolish, and that all are ordinary people. Some scholars think it was composed after Shotoku's death in his honour.
real_life_example.explanation: The constitution argued against angry words by appealing to shared human nature, asking officials to reason from their own fallibility to tolerance of others.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks why anyone who knows the pleasure of kind words would deal out harsh ones, and Shotoku's tenth article makes the same appeal to self-knowledge against anger.

tamil:
இனிய உளவாக இன்னாத கூறல்
கனிஇருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Iniya ulavaaga innaadha kooral,
Kani iruppak kaaikavarn dhatru.
meaning: Speaking hurtful words when kind words are ready to use is like picking unripe fruit when ripe fruit hangs right there.
elementary: Picture a tree with sweet ripe mangoes hanging low and hard green ones next to them. Nobody would reach past the sweet ones to bite a sour green one. But that's exactly what people do when they say something harsh when a kind thing would have worked just as well.
university: The chapter closes on its most famous image, and the comparison is chosen with care: கனி (kani, ripe fruit) and காய் (kaai, unripe fruit) come from the same tree at the same moment, so the choice costs nothing and requires no extra effort — which is exactly the point. உளவாக (ulavaaga, 'there being available') carries the weight: the pleasant words are already present and to hand. The verse thus completes the chapter's argument by removing the last excuse, since harsh speech can no longer be defended as necessary, cheaper, or more efficient. The kani/kaai contrast belongs to a wider Tamil poetic register of fruit imagery, and the comparative particle அற்று (atru, 'is like that') is the classical Tamil marker of simile. Strikingly, three other traditions independently reach for fruit or tree imagery at exactly this point — James on the fig and the vine, the Qur'an on the good and evil tree, Proverbs on apples of gold — suggesting how naturally the ethics of speech attracts the metaphor of cultivation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him not, even though in pain, (speak words) cutting (others) to the quick; let him not injure others in thought or deed; let him not utter speeches which make (others) afraid of him, since that will prevent him from gaining heaven.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu rules out cutting speech even under the one circumstance that might seem to excuse it — the speaker's own suffering — and attaches an eschatological penalty.
hinduism.tie_back: It removes the excuse for harsh words just as the Kural does, on the ground that nothing is gained by them.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 2.161 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East, vol. 25)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter? Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries? either a vine, figs? so can no fountain both yield salt water and fresh.”
christianity.explanation: James's discourse on the tongue uses agricultural and hydrological images to argue that sweet and bitter speech cannot legitimately issue from the same source.
christianity.tie_back: It reaches for exactly the Kural's register — fruit, sweetness, bitterness — to make the same point about the incoherence of choosing the bitter.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you not considered how Allah presents an example, [making] a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches [high] in the sky? It produces its fruit all the time, by permission of its Lord... And the example of a bad word is like a bad tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, not having any stability.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an sets the good word and the bad word side by side as two trees, one endlessly fruitful and rooted, the other torn up and worthless.
islam.tie_back: It is the Kural's ripe-fruit / unripe-fruit choice extended into a full arboreal parable.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs values the well-chosen word by comparing it to precious fruit set in a worked silver frame — something both beautiful and deliberately fashioned.
judaism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's fruit-metaphor for the well-chosen word, treating the good option as the obviously superior one.
judaism.source: Proverbs 25:11 (Hebrew Bible; King James Version rendering)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha sorts people into three kinds by their speech: those whose speech is like dung, those whose speech is like flowers, and those whose speech is like honey — the last being the person whose words are gentle, pleasing to the ear and spoken with affection.
buddhism.explanation: The image deliberately ranges from the repulsive to the delicious, making the choice between them look as obvious as a choice between foods.
buddhism.tie_back: It uses the same sensory-appetite logic as the Kural's ripe-versus-unripe fruit: nobody deliberately chooses the worse thing to consume.

jainism.quote_or_event: “What is not laudable? That which causes pain and suffering to the living beings is not commendable. It does not matter whether it refers to the actual fact or not.”
jainism.explanation: Pūjyapāda's commentary on the Tattvārtha Sūtra's definition of falsehood counts hurtful words as a breach of the vow of truth (satya) even when they are factually true, because the vows exist to guard non-violence.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says choosing harsh words when kind ones are at hand is like picking unripe fruit beside ripe, and Jain ethics makes that choice a fault, since needlessly hurtful speech counts as falsehood.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.14 with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He thinks that the ripe coconut hangs on the barren simmal tree; what a stupid, idiotic fool he is!”
sikhism.explanation: In a Raamkalee hymn Kabir mocks the deluded person who mistakes worthless fruit for good and turns from what would truly nourish him.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's man who grabs unripe fruit while the ripe hangs beside it, Kabir's fool chooses the barren over the good through sheer perversity.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 972, Raag Raamkalee, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The best treasure a man can have is a sparing tongue, and the greatest pleasure, one that moves orderly; for if you speak evil, you yourself will soon be worse spoken of.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod, in the practical wisdom that closes Works and Days, ranks a measured tongue as a man's chief asset and notes that abuse simply returns amplified.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It reaches the Kural's conclusion by the same practical route: the harsh option is plainly the worse buy.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 719–721 (trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The man who is pleasant in the right way is friendly and the mean is friendliness, while the man who exceeds is an obsequious person if he has no end in view, a flatterer if he is aiming at his own advantage, and the man who falls short and is unpleasant in all circumstances is a quarrelsome and surly sort of person.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle constructs a virtue of everyday social pleasantness, positioned between the flatterer who gives pleasure dishonestly and the churl who gives pain for no reason at all.
philosophy.tie_back: His 'quarrelsome and surly' person is precisely the Kural's fruit-picker who reaches past the ripe for the green.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.6, 1126b (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Bismarck edits the Ems Dispatch
real_life_example.event: On 13 July 1870 a telegram from Bad Ems reported to Otto von Bismarck a meeting between King William I of Prussia and the French ambassador, Vincent Benedetti, over the Spanish throne. Before releasing it to the press, Bismarck shortened it so that the king's courteous exchange read as a curt and final rebuff to France. The published version inflamed opinion in both countries, and France declared war on Prussia on 19 July 1870.
real_life_example.explanation: Bismarck deliberately turned a measured, civil message into a wounding one, and the result was a war.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural likens harsh words chosen when pleasant ones are at hand to picking unripe fruit beside the ripe, and Bismarck had the courteous text in his hands and chose to publish the harsh one.

tamil:
செய்யாமல் செய்த உதவிக்கு வையகமும்
வானகமும் ஆற்றல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Seyyaamal seydha udhavikku vaiyagamum
Vaanagamum aatral aridhu.
meaning: Help given to you when you had done nothing for the helper is so great that even earth and heaven together could not repay it.
elementary: Imagine a kid you barely know shares their lunch with you on a day you forgot yours, even though you never did anything for them. This kural says a kindness like that is so big that even if you gave them the whole world and the sky too, it still would not be enough to pay it back.
university: The chapter opens with its most extreme claim. Parimelazhagar reads செய்யாமல் செய்த உதவி as help rendered to someone who had done no prior service to the giver: a benefit that is not itself a repayment and therefore springs from pure goodwill. The predicate வையகமும் வானகமும் ஆற்றல் அரிது (earth and heaven can hardly equal it) deliberately places the debt beyond any possible exchange; if the terrestrial and celestial worlds together are inadequate, gratitude cannot be discharged by payment and must become a permanent disposition instead. This anticipates a problem that Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics 8.14) and Seneca (De Beneficiis) would both recognise: a class of benefits, above all those from parents and gods, that no return can equal. Placing the chapter in the இல்லறவியல் (householder's section), immediately after Pleasant Speech, frames gratitude as a social virtue that sustains the web of reciprocity on which household and community life depend.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That trouble (and pain) which the parents undergo on the birth of (their) children, cannot be compensated even in a hundred years.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu say that what parents go through to bring a child into the world is a debt so large that a whole century of repayment would not settle it.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names a kindness that no amount of return can ever balance out.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 2.227 (G. Bühler trans., Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says God's love is shown by the fact that Christ died for people before they had done anything to deserve it, while they were still in the wrong.
christianity.tie_back: This is the ultimate 'help given when nothing was done to earn it', the exact kind of help the Kural calls beyond repayment.

islam.quote_or_event: “He who does not thank the people is not thankful to Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that a person who fails to thank the humans who help them has not truly thanked God either.
islam.tie_back: It raises gratitude to a human helper to the level of a religious duty, echoing the Kural's claim that such help outweighs heaven and earth.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4811 (graded sahih by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then she fell on her face, and bowed herself to the ground, and said unto him, Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I am a stranger?”
judaism.explanation: Ruth, a poor foreigner gleaning in Boaz's field, bows to the ground in astonishment that a stranger with no obligation to her would show her such kindness.
judaism.tie_back: Ruth's response models the Kural's attitude: overwhelming gratitude for kindness she had not earned from the giver.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If you were to establish your mother & father in absolute sovereignty over this great earth, abounding in the seven treasures, you would not in that way pay or repay your parents.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that even making your parents rulers of the whole earth and all its treasures would not repay what they did for you.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost the same image as the Kural: the entire earth is not enough to repay a great kindness.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.32 (Kataññu Sutta, Thanissaro Bhikkhu trans.)

jainism.quote_or_event: Asked who should receive the rain of treasure that fell when she fed Mahāvīra, the former slave-girl Candanā answered: “Sheth Dhanāvaha, truly my father because of his protection of me.”
jainism.explanation: In Hemacandra's life of Mahāvīra, the merchant Dhanāvaha buys the captive princess Vasumatī off the street purely out of compassion, though she was a stranger who owed him nothing; when the gods later shower treasure on her, she gives the whole of it to him.
jainism.tie_back: Dhanāvaha's help came to a girl who had never done anything for him, and Candanā's answer treats that unearned rescue as worth more than a divine treasure, which is the measure Valluvar sets for help given without prior cause.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. IV, part 7 'The story of Candanā' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You bless me with everything, showering me with Mercy; And I am such an ungrateful wretch!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan contrasts God's unearned, unceasing generosity with the human failure to acknowledge it; in Gurbani every blessing is grace, given before any merit of ours.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's help given to one who had done nothing to deserve it, the Lord's gifts here are wholly unearned, and the only fitting response is a gratitude that can never repay them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 809, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, the swineherd Eumaeus welcomes a ragged stranger (Odysseus in disguise) who has never done anything for him, feeds him from his own scanty stock, and says strangers and beggars come from Zeus; Odysseus prays that Zeus grant his host his heart's desire in return.
greek_mythology.explanation: A poor servant freely feeds a beggar he owes nothing to, and the beggar, moved, asks the gods to repay what he himself cannot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows unprompted kindness whose worth is so great that only the gods can balance it, close to the Kural's heaven-and-earth image.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for no one could ever return to them the equivalent of what he gets, but the man who serves them to the utmost of his power is thought to be a good man.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that with gods and parents we can never pay back an equal amount, so a good person simply does as much as they possibly can.
philosophy.tie_back: Same insight as the Kural: some benefits are too large to repay, so gratitude becomes a lifelong attitude rather than a settled account.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.14, 1163b (W. D. Ross trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: Raoul Wallenberg protects the Jews of Budapest
real_life_example.event: Swedish businessman Raoul Wallenberg, recruited by the US War Refugee Board and given diplomatic status by the Swedish legation, arrived in Budapest on 9 July 1944 and began distributing Swedish certificates of protection to Hungarian Jews. Using Swedish and War Refugee Board funds he set up hospitals, nurseries, a soup kitchen and more than 30 protected houses, and he repeatedly intervened in person to have holders of protective papers released from deportation columns. He was last seen with Soviet officials on 17 January 1945 and disappeared in Soviet custody.
real_life_example.explanation: Wallenberg had no prior tie to the people he protected and nothing to gain from them; many of those he helped never had the chance even to thank him, and his fate has never been fully explained.
real_life_example.tie_back: Help given to strangers who had done nothing to earn it, at the risk of the giver's own life, is exactly the kind of benefit the kural says earth and heaven together could not repay.

tamil:
காலத்தி னாற்செய்த நன்றி சிறிதெனினும்
ஞாலத்தின் மாணப் பெரிது.
transliteration:
Kaalaththinaal seydha nandri siridheninum
Gnaalaththin maanap peridhu.
meaning: Help given at the right time, when it is truly needed, may be small, but it is worth more than the whole world.
elementary: If you are thirsty in the middle of a race and someone hands you one small cup of water, that cup feels more valuable than a whole shop full of drinks later. Help that comes right when you need it is the biggest kind of help, even if it is tiny.
university: The operative word is காலத்தினால், 'by reason of the time', that is, timeliness. Valluvar shifts the measure of a benefit from its quantity (சிறிதெனினும், 'though small') to its moment, and then inflates it past ஞாலம், the whole earth, with the intensifier மாண ('exceedingly'). Kurals 102 to 104 form a graded triad of hyperbolic comparisons (world, sea, palmyra palm), each isolating a different factor that magnifies a benefit: timing, disinterestedness, and the recipient's discernment. The underlying intuition is almost economic: the value of help peaks at the point of greatest need, which is why Solomon Pappaiah glosses the phrase as help given in our time of crisis. Aristotle records the same argument from the benefactor's side, noting that givers insist their help came 'in times of danger or similar need' (Nicomachean Ethics 8.13).

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Ravana carries Sita off, the aged vulture-king Jatayu flies at him and fights until he is mortally wounded. Dying, he tells Rama what happened; Rama grieves for him as for his own father and performs his funeral rites with his own hands.
hinduism.explanation: An old bird who could not really win still threw himself into the fight at the exact moment Sita needed help, and Rama honoured that help as if Jatayu were family.
hinduism.tie_back: Jatayu's help was small in outcome but came at the critical hour, and Rama treated it as immeasurably great, just as the Kural says.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 49-51 and 67-68 (sarga numbering varies by edition)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus's parable of the judgment, the King counts simple acts like a meal, a drink, or a bed given to someone in need as done to him, with eternal consequences.
christianity.tie_back: Small, timely help given in someone's moment of need is valued far beyond its size, which is the Kural's point.

islam.quote_or_event: “So he (went down the well), filled his shoe with water, caught hold of it with his teeth and climbed up and watered the dog. Allah thanked him for his (good) deed and forgave him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet told of a man who saw a dog dying of thirst, climbed down a well to fill his shoe with water for it, and was forgiven by God for that one small act.
islam.tie_back: A tiny act done at the exact moment of need is treated as enormous, even by God, just as the Kural says timely help outweighs the world.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rashi, following the Midrash, explains that Aaron rather than Moses struck the Nile to begin the plagues, because the river had sheltered Moses when he was placed in it as an infant; Moses would not strike what had once protected him.
judaism.explanation: Even a river that once kept baby Moses safe in his moment of danger was owed gratitude, so Moses would not hit it.
judaism.tie_back: Help given at the critical moment, even by water, earns lasting gratitude, far out of proportion to the 'size' of the act.
judaism.source: Rashi on Exodus 7:19 (drawing on Midrash Tanchuma)

buddhism.quote_or_event: According to the Pali commentarial biography, in the second week after his awakening the Buddha stood gazing without blinking at the Bodhi tree that had sheltered him during his final struggle; the spot is honoured at Bodh Gaya as the Animisa (Animeshlochana) Cetiya, and later tradition reads the act as gratitude to the tree.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha spent a whole week simply looking at the tree that had given him shade while he struggled for enlightenment.
buddhism.tie_back: Shade is a small gift, but given at the decisive moment it was honoured as something immense, like the Kural's timely favour.
buddhism.source: Jataka Nidanakatha (commentarial biography); Mahabodhi Temple Complex, Bodh Gaya

jainism.quote_or_event: “Master, even if this food is not suitable, nevertheless, accept it, you who delight only in benefits to others. Favor me.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra had vowed to accept alms only under very exacting conditions, and kings, ministers and wealthy households failed to feed him for months; the chained Candanā finally offered him a little kulmāṣa (boiled pulse) from the corner of a winnowing basket, and the gods marked the moment with a rain of treasure.
jainism.tie_back: The humblest possible gift, given at the one moment it was needed, ended a fast of almost six months that all the riches of Kauśāmbī could not, which illustrates Valluvar's point that timeliness makes a small help outweigh the world.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X, ch. IV, parts 6-7 'Vīra's special vow' and 'The story of Candanā' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Where there is no mother, father, children, friends or siblings - O my mind, there, only the Naam, the Name of the Lord, shall be with you as your help and support.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan praises the Naam as the help that arrives at the hour when every human support has fallen away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural prizes help given at the moment of real need above the whole world; Gurbani likewise exalts the support that comes precisely when no one else can help.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 264, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Aesopic fable of the Ant and the Dove, an ant falls into a stream and is drowning when a dove drops a leaf or twig beside it, letting it climb to safety; later the ant stings a bird-catcher's foot just as he is about to snare the dove.
greek_mythology.explanation: A leaf is almost nothing, but dropped at the exact moment the ant was drowning it saved its life, and the ant never forgot it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A tiny, timely favour is repaid as if it were enormous, which is the Kural's lesson.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, The Ant and the Dove (Perry Index 235; G. F. Townsend trans.)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues that a benefit given promptly, before it has to be asked for, is received with far greater gratitude, while one that is delayed or extracted by long pleading loses much of its value; hesitation, he says, is close to refusal.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman Stoic says the same gift is worth more when it comes quickly, right when needed, than when it arrives late.
philosophy.tie_back: Timing multiplies the worth of a favour, exactly the variable the Kural isolates.

real_life_example.event_title: The little ships help evacuate Dunkirk
real_life_example.place: Dunkirk, France, and the English Channel
real_life_example.event: With British, French and Belgian troops trapped around the French port of Dunkirk, the Royal Navy organised Operation Dynamo to bring them back across the Channel.
