Because large warships could not approach the shallow beaches, the British Admiralty appealed to the owners of small boats, and these little ships, many of them requisitioned and mostly crewed by naval personnel, ferried men from the beaches to the larger vessels offshore. More than 338,000 British and French soldiers were rescued, far more than the government had first expected.
real_life_example.explanation: Many of the vessels were small pleasure craft and launches, yet arriving at the one moment when the army's survival hung in the balance made them part of a rescue that kept Britain's trained army intact.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a favour done at the moment of need, however small, outweighs the world; the little ships mattered because of when they came, not because of their size.

tamil:
பயன்தூக்கார் செய்த உதவி நயன்தூக்கின்
நன்மை கடலின் பெரிது.
transliteration:
Payandhookkaar seydha udhavi nayandhookkin
Nanmai kadalin peridhu.
meaning: When someone helps you without thinking about what they will get back, the goodness of that help, if you weigh it, is bigger than the sea.
elementary: Some people help you because they want something later, like a sticker trade. Others help just because they care. This kural says the second kind of help is bigger than the whole sea.
university: The couplet hinges on a pun on தூக்கு, 'to weigh': the benefactor is பயன்தூக்கார், one who does not weigh the return, while the recipient is invited to weigh (நயன்தூக்கின்) the help's goodness or love (நயன், from நயம்). Gratitude is thus framed as an act of moral appraisal that the giver refused to perform on his own behalf; the asymmetry is the point. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah gloss நயன் as the love (அன்பு) behind the act, so the 'sea' measures not the material help but the disinterested affection it expresses. This parallels the Bhagavad Gita's category of sattvic giving (17.20), made 'without expectation of return', and Aristotle's remark (Nicomachean Ethics 8.13) that it is noble to benefit another without a view to repayment even though most people prefer to receive. The kural quietly criticises transactional benevolence while insisting that recipients never take pure generosity lightly.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Charity given out of duty, without expectation of return, at the proper time and place, and to a worthy person is considered to be in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the highest, purest kind of giving is giving that expects nothing back.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita praises exactly the kind of help the Kural says is 'vaster than the sea': help given without weighing the return.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers to do good and lend without hoping to get anything back, because that is how God himself behaves.
christianity.tie_back: 'Hoping for nothing again' is the Kural's பயன்தூக்கார், the one who does not weigh the return.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Saying], “We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We wish not from you reward or gratitude.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the righteous feeding the poor, the orphan and the captive while telling them they want neither payment nor even thanks, only God's pleasure.
islam.tie_back: This is the purest form of help 'that does not weigh the return', whose worth the Kural calls greater than the sea.

judaism.quote_or_event: Commenting on Jacob's request that Joseph bury him in Canaan, Rashi explains that kindness done for the dead is called chesed shel emet, 'true kindness', because the one who does it expects no repayment.
judaism.explanation: Jewish tradition says the truest kindness is the kind you do for someone who can never pay you back, like caring for the dead.
judaism.tie_back: Judaism, like the Kural, ranks help that cannot be repaid or calculated as the highest and most precious form.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Diamond Sutra teaches that a bodhisattva should practise giving without being supported by any notion (of self, recipient, gift, or reward), and that the merit of such giving is as immeasurable as space in every direction.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching says the best giving is done without thinking 'I am giving' or 'what will I get', and that such giving is too vast to measure.
buddhism.tie_back: Its 'immeasurable as space' matches the Kural's 'greater than the sea' for help given without calculation.

jainism.quote_or_event: “They say that in the time of drought the well of spring-water will preserve the inhabitants, though by drawing its water they subsist. So the duty of liberality is found with the great, even when in declining circumstances; with others, even when they are rich, it is rare.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain-authored Nālaḍiyār pictures true generosity as a spring-fed well that keeps giving in drought without asking anything back.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's benefactor gives without weighing the return, and the Nālaḍiyār's well that sustains the village in drought is the same unreckoning goodness that the recipient should judge greater than the sea.
jainism.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 19 'Greatness', st. 4 (= st. 184), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who performs selfless service, without thought of reward, shall attain his Lord and Master.”
sikhism.explanation: Seva done nihkam, without desire for any return, is one of the central Sikh ideals; Sukhmani Sahib makes such service the path to God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's benefactor who helps without weighing the return is exactly the Sikh nihkam sevadar, though the Sikh verse praises the giver where the Kural asks the receiver to weigh the gift.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid's tale, the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon welcome two unknown travellers (Jupiter and Mercury in disguise) whom richer households had turned away, and share their meagre food with no hope of return; the gods reward them by turning their hut into a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: A very poor couple shared everything they had with strangers without expecting anything back, and the gods counted that kindness as enormous.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hospitality given without weighing any return is judged immensely great, as the Kural says.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.618-724 (Roman retelling of a Phrygian legend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “now it is noble to do well by another without a view to repayment, but it is the receiving of benefits that is advantageous.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle observes that helping without expecting repayment is the noble thing, even though most people would rather be on the receiving end.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle names the same 'not weighing the return' that the Kural says makes help vaster than the sea.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.13, 1162b (W. D. Ross trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: CERN puts the World Wide Web in the public domain
real_life_example.event: British scientist Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN, the European particle physics laboratory, to help scientists share information. On 30 April 1993 CERN published a statement putting the World Wide Web software in the public domain, making it available royalty-free to anyone; a later release was issued under an open licence. CERN states that these actions allowed the web to flourish.
real_life_example.explanation: By declining to charge for the technology, CERN let anyone add a server, create pages or build a browser, and the web spread around the world within a few years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises help given by those who do not weigh what they will get back; releasing the web free of royalties is a gift whose value to the world is hard to measure.

tamil:
தினைத்துணை நன்றி செயினும் பனைத்துணையாக்
கொள்வர் பயன்தெரி வார்.
transliteration:
Thinaiththunai nandri seyinum panaiththunaiyaak
Kolvar payantheri vaar.
meaning: People who know the value of help see even a tiny favour, as small as a millet seed, as big as a palm tree.
elementary: A millet seed is tiny, smaller than a grain of rice. A palm tree is huge. A grateful person takes even a tiny kindness, like someone lending a pencil, and treats it like something huge.
university: தினை (foxtail millet, among the smallest grains in the Tamil diet) and பனை (the palmyra, the tallest and most useful tree of the Tamil landscape) form one of the Kural's most memorable scale contrasts; the same pair recurs in Kural 433, where those who fear disgrace treat a fault the size of millet as if it were the size of a palm. The subject பயன்தெரிவார், 'those who discern the fruit or benefit', makes gratitude a cognitive virtue: the grateful person perceives consequences that the literal size of the gift conceals. Kalaignar's gloss exploits the palmyra's many uses (fruit, leaf, timber, sap) to suggest that a small help ramifies into manifold benefit. The same inversion of scale appears in the Gospel's widow's mite, in the Talmud's 'good guest' of Berakhot 58a, and in Seneca's argument that a benefit lies in the intention rather than in the object given.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If one offers Me with love and devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, I will accept it.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says he gladly accepts even a single leaf or a little water when it is offered with love, treating the tiny gift as precious.
hinduism.tie_back: The One who needs nothing treats the smallest offering as great, the same 'millet seen as palm' attitude the Kural praises (compare Krishna's welcome of Sudama's handful of rice in the Bhagavata Purana).

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury:”
christianity.explanation: Jesus watches a poor widow drop two tiny coins into the temple box and says she gave more than all the rich donors.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus sees a millet-sized gift as palm-sized because he looks at what it really means, just like the discerning people in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it,”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says that even the tiniest good deed, the weight of an atom, is noticed and counts on the Day of Judgment.
islam.tie_back: No good deed is too small to matter; the Kural asks the grateful person to see small kindnesses with that same attention.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good guest, what does he say? How much effort did the host expend on my behalf, how much meat did the host bring before me.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud contrasts a good guest, who counts up everything the host did for him, with a bad guest, who says he only ate one piece of bread and the host did it all for his own family anyway.
judaism.tie_back: The good guest is exactly the Kural's பயன்தெரிவார்: someone who sees a modest meal as a great kindness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada commentary tells of Radha, a poor old brahmin whom no monk would ordain. The Buddha asked whether anyone remembered a kindness from him; Sariputta recalled that Radha had once given him a single ladleful of rice, and out of gratitude he ordained and trained Radha, who became an arahant. The Buddha praised Sariputta's gratitude.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's chief disciple remembered that a poor man had once given him one spoonful of rice, and repaid it by becoming his teacher.
buddhism.tie_back: One ladle of rice treated as a debt worth years of teaching is a perfect 'millet seen as a palm tree'.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 76 (Radha Thera story)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who are at the bottom in (the scale of) friendship are like the areca-tree; those others who are in the middle are like the cocoanut-tree. The friendship of those who have experience of the past is like the palmyra-tree, (whose uses are) difficult to reckon.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaḍiyār grades friends by trees, placing at the top those who remember the past, whose benefits are as uncountable as the palmyra's.
jainism.tie_back: Both texts use the palmyra as the image of immeasurable worth, but the Kural's point is that the grateful magnify a millet-sized favour into a palm, while the Nālaḍiyār only ranks friendships by the palm, so the parallel is mainly in the imagery.
jainism.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 22 'The choice of friends', st. 6 (= st. 216), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Countless sins are erased, by even a tiny particle of the Lord's Name.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das uses a scale contrast: a mere particle of the Naam outweighs countless sins.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's millet seed seen as a palm tree is a similar contrast of tiny and vast; Gurbani applies it to the immense worth of the smallest gift of grace.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1283, Raag Malaar, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Aesopic fable of the Lion and the Mouse, a lion scoffs at a mouse's promise to repay him for sparing its life, but when the lion is later caught in a hunter's net the mouse gnaws through the ropes and frees him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The lion thought a mouse could never help him, but the little creature's small help ended up saving the king of beasts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It teaches, like the Kural, that small help can be enormous in value to those wise enough to see it.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, The Lion and the Mouse (Perry Index 150; G. F. Townsend trans.)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues that a benefit does not consist in the thing given (money, a meal, an office) but in the goodwill of the giver, so a small gift given with a good heart can be a greater benefit than a lavish one.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic says what makes a favour great is the kind intention behind it, not how much it costs.
philosophy.tie_back: Those who 'know the value' in the Kural look past the millet seed's size to the goodwill it carries.

real_life_example.event_title: Gail Halvorsen, the Candy Bomber of Berlin
real_life_example.event: During the Berlin Airlift, US Air Force pilot Gail Halvorsen met children at the fence of Tempelhof airfield and shared two sticks of gum with them, then began dropping chocolate and gum tied to small handkerchief parachutes from his transport plane, at first without permission. The airlift commander, Lt. Gen. William H. Tunner, approved and expanded the drops as Operation Little Vittles, and an estimated 46,000 pounds of candy was dropped on more than 250,000 parachutes. Halvorsen later commanded the American air base at Tempelhof from 1970 to 1974, and in 1974 the West German government awarded him its Order of Merit.
real_life_example.explanation: Sweets dropped to hungry children were tiny compared with the food and coal of the airlift, yet Berliners and the wider world remembered the Candy Bomber for the rest of his life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who understand kindness treat a millet-seed favour as if it were a palm tree; a few sweets on handkerchief parachutes were honoured by a whole nation decades later.

tamil:
உதவி வரைத்தன்று உதவி உதவி
செயப்பட்டார் சால்பின் வரைத்து.
transliteration:
Udhavi varaiththandru udhavi udhavi
Seyappattaar saalbin varaiththu.
meaning: The worth of help is not measured by the help itself. It is measured by the goodness of the person who receives it.
elementary: If a friend gives you a small gift, how much you give back is not just about the size of their gift. It is about what kind of person you are. A really good-hearted person gives back even more than they got.
university: Built on a fourfold repetition of உதவி (help), the couplet admits two readings. Parimelazhagar, followed by Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah, takes the first உதவி as the return-favour: requital is not bounded by the size of the original help but by the சால்பு (nobility, fullness of character) of the one who was helped, so a noble recipient repays abundantly. Kalaignar reads it evaluatively: the value of a help is assessed according to the recipient's worth. Both readings converge on the claim that gratitude measures the recipient rather than balancing a ledger, linking this chapter to the later chapter on சான்றாண்மை (perfect character). Aristotle frames the same dispute, whether to measure a service by its utility to the receiver or by the benevolence of the giver (Nicomachean Ethics 8.13), and Cicero, citing Hesiod, urges us to imitate fertile fields that return more than they receive (De Officiis 1.48).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna's poor boyhood friend Sudama visits him bringing only a handful of flattened rice. Krishna eats it with delight, and Sudama returns home to find his hut transformed into a palace; the return is measured by Krishna's greatness, not by the rice.
hinduism.explanation: A poor friend gave Krishna a tiny gift, and Krishna repaid it with far more than it was 'worth' because of who Krishna is.
hinduism.tie_back: The repayment matched the giver-back's own greatness, not the size of the help, which is the Kural's point about சால்பு.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises that generosity returns in overflowing measure, pressed down and running over.
christianity.tie_back: The return is not limited to the original amount but overflows, much as the Kural says a noble recipient's requital is not bounded by the original help.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet [in return] with one better than it or [at least] return it [in a like manner]. Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, an Accountant.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells believers to answer a greeting with a better one, or at least an equal one.
islam.tie_back: A good person's response is set by their own goodness and aims higher than what they received, the Kural's standard for repaying help.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And he said unto his daughters, And where is he? why is it that ye have left the man? call him, that he may eat bread.”
judaism.explanation: When the fugitive Moses drove off shepherds who were bullying Jethro's daughters at a well, Jethro scolded them for not bringing the stranger home; he took Moses in and later gave him his daughter in marriage.
judaism.tie_back: One act of help at a well was repaid with a home and a family, a return set by Jethro's generosity rather than by the size of the favour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A person of integrity is grateful & thankful. This gratitude, this thankfulness, is advocated by civil people. It is entirely on the level of people of integrity.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that gratitude is what marks a person of integrity, while ingratitude marks a person without it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the way we respond to help a measure of our own character.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.31 (Kataññu Sutta, Thanissaro Bhikkhu trans.)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Krtajna : Grateful.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra's list of thirty-five qualities of the ideal Jain householder includes kṛtajña, literally 'one who knows what has been done (for him)', alongside being ready to serve others and supporting dependents.
jainism.tie_back: Jain householder ethics treats gratitude as part of a person's settled character, which matches Valluvar's claim that the worth of a requital depends on the nobility of the one who received the help.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of 35 qualities of the ideal śrāvaka, no. 28, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Sikh tradition remembers that Amar Das, already an old man, became a disciple of Guru Angad and served him with extraordinary devotion for over a decade, fetching water before dawn and serving in the community kitchen; his humble service led Guru Angad to name him the third Guru in 1552.
sikhism.explanation: The episode shows a disciple whose response to the grace he received was measured not by any calculation but by the depth of his own devotion.
sikhism.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural's claim that the return for a benefit is bounded by the nobility of the one who received it rather than by the size of the benefit.
sikhism.source: Wikipedia, 'Guru Amar Das' (paraphrase of traditional accounts)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod advises taking fair measure from a neighbour and paying it back fairly with the same measure, or better if you are able, so that you may find him reliable when you are in need again.
greek_mythology.explanation: The old Greek poet tells farmers to repay what a neighbour lent them with at least as much, and more if they can.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Repaying 'better if you can' makes the requital depend on the character and ability of the recipient, as in the Kural.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 349-351 (H. G. Evelyn-White trans.)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But if, as Hesiod bids, one is to repay with interest, if possible, what one has borrowed in time of need, what, pray, ought we to do when challenged by an unsought kindness? Shall we not imitate the fruitful fields, which return more than they receive?”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero says that if we repay loans with interest, we should repay an unasked-for kindness even more generously, like good soil that gives back more than was sown.
philosophy.tie_back: A good person's requital overflows the original favour, just as the Kural says it is measured by the recipient's nobility.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis 1.48 (Walter Miller trans., Loeb 1913)

real_life_example.event_title: Andrew Carnegie repays Colonel Anderson's library
real_life_example.place: Allegheny (now part of Pittsburgh), Pennsylvania, United States
real_life_example.event: As a poor working boy in Allegheny, Andrew Carnegie borrowed books from Colonel James Anderson, a retired businessman who opened his personal library of about 400 volumes to working boys every Saturday. Carnegie later became one of the richest men in the world, and starting in 1881 he and later his foundation gave some $56 million to build 2,509 public libraries. In 1904 a monument by the sculptor Daniel Chester French honouring Anderson's generosity was placed near the Carnegie library in Allegheny.
real_life_example.explanation: A modest weekly loan of books was repaid on a vast scale by a recipient who never forgot it and who said he resolved to lend books to others if he ever had surplus wealth.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the worth of a favour is set by the character of the one who receives it; Anderson's small library became thousands of libraries because of the man who received the kindness.

tamil:
மறவற்க மாசற்றார் கேண்மை துறவற்க
துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Maravarka maasatraar kenmai thuravarka
Thunbaththul thuppaayaar natpu.
meaning: Never forget the friendship of good, pure-hearted people. Never leave the friendship of those who stood by you in hard times.
elementary: Some friends are simply good people, so don't forget them. And some friends helped you when you were sad or in trouble, so never walk away from them, even after things get better for you.
university: The couplet is built as two parallel prohibitions, மறவற்க ('do not forget') and துறவற்க ('do not forsake'), each governing a class of relationship: the கேண்மை (bond) of the மாசற்றார் (the stainless) and the நட்பு (friendship) of those who became துப்பு (strength, support) in துன்பம் (distress). Commentators take the first half to concern those free of fault in knowledge and conduct and the second those who helped in adversity; the chapter thereby widens gratitude from discrete favours to durable relationships. The verb துறத்தல், the same root used for renunciation, suggests that abandoning a former helper is a kind of moral apostasy. The theme anticipates the Kural's later friendship chapters (79-83), where adversity is repeatedly named as the true test of a friend.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, when Krishna reveals to Karna that he is Kunti's eldest son and offers him the throne if he joins the Pandavas, Karna refuses: Duryodhana had honoured and befriended him when others scorned his low birth, and he will not abandon that friend on the eve of war.
hinduism.explanation: Karna turns down a kingdom because he will not desert the friend who stood by him when everyone else looked down on him.
hinduism.tie_back: Karna lives out the Kural's command: never forsake the friendship of one who was your support in your time of humiliation.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Karna's reply to Krishna; K. M. Ganguli trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: “The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain:”
christianity.explanation: From prison, Paul blesses the family of Onesiphorus, who kept visiting and comforting him and was not ashamed to be seen with a prisoner.
christianity.tie_back: Paul refuses to forget the friend who stood by him 'in his chains', the exact friend the Kural says never to forsake.

islam.quote_or_event: Aisha reported that, years after Khadijah's death, the Prophet mentioned her very often and, whenever he slaughtered a sheep, sent portions to Khadijah's women friends; when Aisha objected, he would reply by recalling what Khadijah had been to him.
islam.explanation: The Prophet kept honouring his first wife Khadijah, who had supported him from the very beginning, long after she died, even sending gifts to her friends.
islam.tie_back: He never forgot or let go of the bond with the one who had been his strength in the hardest early years, as the Kural commands.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thine own friend, and thy father’s friend, forsake not; neither go into thy brother’s house in the day of thy calamity: for better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs tells us never to abandon an old friend, or a friend of the family, and says a friend close by in trouble is worth more than a distant relative.
judaism.tie_back: 'Forsake not' is the Kural's துறவற்க, applied to the friend who is near in calamity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “in misfortune he does not forsake one,”
buddhism.explanation: In advice to the layman Sigala, the Buddha lists the marks of a true friend, including that he does not abandon you when misfortune strikes.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha defines a real friend by the same test the Kural uses: staying with you in hard times.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (Narada Thera trans.)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men cleave not to those to whom their hearts cleave not, within a short space of time; but will the friendship which cherishes the memory of those who are intertwined with one's heart be abandoned, though they are absent from us for a long time?”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaḍiyār holds that a bond woven into the heart is not given up, however long the separation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar forbids both forgetting the friendship of the stainless and forsaking those who stood by us in distress, and this quatrain likewise insists that a true bond is neither forgotten nor abandoned.
jainism.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 22 'The choice of friends', st. 4 (= st. 214), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone are my friends, who travel along with me; and in that place, where the accounts are called for, they appear standing with me.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak defines the true friend as the one who stays beside you at the moment of reckoning, when everyone else falls away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's friend who was your strength in distress and must never be forsaken is the same kind of friend Guru Nanak names: one who stands by you when it counts.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides' Heracles, after the hero has killed his own wife and children in a god-sent madness, Theseus arrives, recalls that Heracles once rescued him from the underworld, refuses to shun him as polluted, and offers him a home and honours in Athens.
greek_mythology.explanation: When everyone else would run from Heracles after his terrible disaster, Theseus stands by him because Heracles had once saved him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Theseus refuses to abandon the friend who had been his rescuer, embodying both halves of the Kural.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Heracles (c. 416 BCE), the Theseus episode

philosophy.quote_or_event: In On Friendship, Cicero quotes Ennius's line that a sure friend is discerned in an unsure situation, and argues that people who desert friends in adversity, or who grow proud in prosperity, show themselves unfit for true friendship.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero says you only really find out who your friends are when things go wrong, and that leaving a friend in trouble shows weak character.
philosophy.tie_back: He makes adversity the test of friendship, the same test behind the Kural's 'do not forsake'.

real_life_example.event_title: The Netherlands' yearly gift of tulips to Canada
real_life_example.event: After Germany invaded the Netherlands in 1940, Princess Juliana and her daughters took refuge in Ottawa, where her third daughter Margriet was born in 1943; Canadian troops also played a significant role in liberating the Netherlands in 1945. After returning home, Princess Juliana presented 100,000 tulip bulbs to Canada in gratitude and kept sending bulbs after she became queen. The gift became a lasting tradition, and every year the Dutch royal family and the people of the Netherlands each send 10,000 bulbs to Ottawa.
real_life_example.explanation: The gift began as thanks for shelter and liberation in wartime and has been renewed every year for decades, long after the danger passed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says never to forsake the friendship of those who stood by you in hard times; the Dutch have kept that friendship alive with tulips every spring since 1945.

tamil:
எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும் உள்ளுவர் தங்கண்
விழுமந் துடைத்தவர் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Ezhumai ezhupirappum ulluvar thangan
Vizhuman thudaiththavar natpu.
meaning: Good people remember, through all seven births (all their lives to come), the friendship of those who wiped away their sorrow.
elementary: If someone wiped away your tears when you were really hurting, you should remember them for a very, very long time. The kural says: for seven whole lifetimes!
university: விழுமம் denotes grave affliction, and துடைத்தல், 'to wipe away', evokes the wiping of tears, an image that G. U. Pope's verse translation foregrounds. எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும் is variously parsed: traditional commentary reads it within the South Asian doctrine of rebirth as 'through sevenfold births', while modern commentators such as Kalaignar treat it as hyperbole meaning 'without any limit of time'. Either way, the couplet turns gratitude from a transaction into a form of memory (உள்ளுவர், 'they will keep in mind') whose duration exceeds a single life. The motif of long-lived or even inherited gratitude, such as David's kindness to Jonathan's son, Rama's avowed debt to Hanuman, and the Buddha's thought of the five companions after his awakening, shows how widely traditions have treated rescuers as creditors whose claim outlives the moment of rescue.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Uttara Kanda, as Hanuman takes leave, Rama tells him that he would give his life for each single service Hanuman has done and still remain in his debt, and that he wishes these favours to stay unrepaid within him, since a return is needed only when a benefactor falls into misfortune.
hinduism.explanation: Rama tells Hanuman he can never finish repaying him, and even hopes he never gets the chance, because that would mean Hanuman was in trouble.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama's gratitude to the one who wiped away his sorrow is lifelong and open-ended, just like the Kural's 'seven births'.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (Rama's farewell to Hanuman; chapter numbering varies by edition, commonly 7.40)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I thank my God upon every remembrance of you,”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the church at Philippi, which had supported him from the start, that every time he remembers them he thanks God.
christianity.tie_back: Gratitude that returns with every memory is the Kural's 'they will keep in mind', applied to those who helped in hardship.

islam.quote_or_event: “And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, “My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up [when I was] small.””
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells believers to be humble to their aged parents and to pray for them, remembering how they cared for them as little children.
islam.tie_back: Gratitude here reaches back across a whole lifetime to care received long ago, like the Kural's unending remembrance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And David said, Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
judaism.explanation: After his friend Jonathan died, King David searched for any surviving relative so he could repay Jonathan's friendship, and found and cared for Jonathan's disabled son Mephibosheth.
judaism.tie_back: David's gratitude to the friend who protected him outlived the friend himself, the kind of remembrance the Kural stretches across 'seven births'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After his awakening, when the Buddha considered whom to teach first, he thought of his former teachers Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta (both had died), and then of the group of five monks who had attended him during his years of striving, recalling that they had been very helpful to him.
buddhism.explanation: The first people the newly enlightened Buddha wanted to share his discovery with were those who had helped him through his hardest years.
buddhism.tie_back: Even at the moment of enlightenment, the Buddha's mind turned first to those who had eased his hardships, as the Kural says the good always do.

jainism.quote_or_event: Prince Pārśva pulled a log from the ascetic Kaṭha's fire and saved the serpent burning inside it; reborn as Dharaṇa, king of the Nāgas, the serpent came when Pārśva was later assailed in meditation, raised him on a lotus, sheltered him with seven hoods, and told the attacker, “I am the servant of the Compassionate.”
jainism.explanation: In Hemacandra's life of Pārśvanātha, a benefit received in one birth is remembered and repaid in the next, when the rescued serpent, now a Nāga king, shields his rescuer from Meghamālin's flood.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the good remember, through seven births, those who wiped away their distress, and Jain narrative gives exactly that: gratitude that survives death and rebirth.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book IX (Pārśvanāthacaritra), ch. III, part 9 'Attacks by Meghamālin' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “A hundred times a day, I am a sacrifice to my Guru; He made angels out of men, without delay.”
sikhism.explanation: Opening the Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak expresses unending gratitude to the Guru who transforms ordinary people; the disciple's thankfulness is renewed again and again.
sikhism.tie_back: As the Kural's good remember through seven births the one who wiped away their sorrow, the Sikh offers ceaseless gratitude to the Guru who lifted him out of his lowly state.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 462, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Odysseus leaves Phaeacia, the princess Nausicaa, who found him naked and shipwrecked on the shore and brought him to safety, asks him to remember her, since he owes her his life; Odysseus answers that if he reaches home he will pray to her as to a goddess all his days.
greek_mythology.explanation: The young princess who rescued Odysseus from his worst moment asks him not to forget her, and he promises to honour her for the rest of his life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Lifelong remembrance of the one who ended your affliction is exactly the Kural's teaching.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius opens his Meditations with an entire book listing, person by person, what he owes to his grandfather, mother, teachers, friends, his adoptive father Antoninus, and the gods, naming the specific good each gave him.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman emperor began his private notebook by writing down everyone who had helped him become who he was, and exactly how.
philosophy.tie_back: Book 1 is a written act of the long remembrance the Kural prescribes: keeping benefactors in mind across a whole life.

real_life_example.event_title: Turkey repays Japan for the Ertugrul rescue
real_life_example.event: In September 1890 the Ottoman frigate Ertugrul, returning from a goodwill visit to Japan, broke up in a typhoon off the island of Kii Oshima near Kushimoto, and islanders worked through the night to rescue 69 survivors; local physicians later declined Turkey's offer to pay for their care. In March 1985, during the Iran-Iraq War, more than 200 Japanese were stranded in Tehran after Iraq warned it would target aircraft over Iran, and at Japan's request Turkey sent airliners that carried 215 Japanese nationals to safety. When Japan expressed its thanks, Turkish officials cited their nation's debt of gratitude from the Ertugrul rescue 95 years earlier.
real_life_example.explanation: A rescue by poor villagers was taught to generations of Turks and repaid almost a century later, when the original rescuers' countrymen were themselves in danger.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the good remember through all their births those who wiped away their sorrow; Turkey remembered Kushimoto's kindness across nearly a hundred years and repaid it.

tamil:
நன்றி மறப்பது நன்றன்று நன்றல்லது
அன்றே மறப்பது நன்று.
transliteration:
Nandri marappadhu nandrandru nandralladhu
Andre marappadhu nandru.
meaning: It is not good to forget a kindness done to you. But it is good to forget a wrong done to you that very same day.
elementary: Keep the good things people do for you in your memory box forever. But if someone is mean to you, try to let it go before you go to bed that night.
university: The couplet is a celebrated piece of Valluvar's wordplay, circling the root நன்று (good) through நன்றி (a benefit), நன்றன்று (not good) and நன்றல்லது (what is not good, i.e. an injury), and pivoting on அன்றே, 'that very day'. It proposes an asymmetric economy of memory: benefits are to be retained indefinitely, injuries released at once. Ethically, this protects gratitude from being eroded by later grievances, a theme the next couplet (109) develops; psychologically, it anticipates modern research that treats gratitude and forgiveness as complementary dispositions. The instruction to let go of a wrong 'that very day' closely parallels Ephesians 4:26 ('let not the sun go down upon your wrath'), while the Psalmist's 'forget not all his benefits' supplies the other half of the Kural's pairing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Ravana's defeat, Hanuman offers to punish the demon women who had tormented Sita during her captivity, but Sita forbids it, saying they only acted under orders, that a noble person shows compassion even to wrongdoers, and that there is no one who never errs.
hinduism.explanation: Sita refuses revenge on the guards who frightened and bullied her for months and lets the wrong go as soon as she is free.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita forgets the injury immediately, the second half of the Kural's teaching.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Hanuman's report to Sita; commonly sarga 113-116 depending on edition)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:”
christianity.explanation: Paul says anger itself may happen, but you should not let it last past sunset.
christianity.tie_back: 'Not letting the sun go down' is almost exactly the Kural's 'forget it that very day' (அன்றே).

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those of virtue among you and wealth swear not to give [aid] to their relatives and the needy and the emigrants for the cause of Allah, and let them pardon and overlook. Would you not like that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: Revealed, according to the commentators, when Abu Bakr vowed to stop supporting a relative who had joined in slandering his daughter Aisha, the verse told him to pardon, overlook, and keep giving.
islam.tie_back: It tells the believer to drop the injury rather than let it cancel the relationship of kindness, the Kural's balance of forgetting wrongs and keeping goodness alive.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist tells his own soul to praise God and never forget any of the good things God has done.
judaism.tie_back: 'Forget not all his benefits' is the Kural's first half, நன்றி மறப்பது நன்றன்று; Leviticus 19:18's ban on bearing a grudge supplies the second.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who do not harbor such thoughts still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that people who stop replaying the wrongs done to them are the ones whose hatred fades.
buddhism.tie_back: Not harbouring the memory of injury is the Kural's 'forget the wrong'.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
jainism.explanation: Among the twenty-two hardships a Jain monk must endure, Mahāvīra lists abuse, which is to be let go of at once rather than nursed as a grievance.
jainism.tie_back: This matches the second half of the Kural, letting go of a wrong that very day, though the Jain verse does not pair it with the duty to remember a kindness.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir places God's presence wherever there is forgiveness, khima, one of the virtues Gurbani asks of the Sikh.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks us to forget a wrong the same day it is done; Kabir's verse treats such forgiveness as the very place where God dwells.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir 155 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Achilles ends his long wrath against Agamemnon, telling the assembled Achaeans that they should let what is past be past, painful as it was, and master the anger in their hearts.
greek_mythology.explanation: After nursing his grudge for most of the war, Achilles finally decides to let it go.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the release of an injury that the Kural recommends, though Achilles gets there far too late.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca writes that of all the ungrateful, the most ungrateful is the one who has forgotten a benefit, since someone who has let it slip from memory has clearly never thought about repaying it.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic says that forgetting a kindness is the worst kind of ingratitude, because it shows you never even tried to pay it back.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's first half, 'forgetting a benefit is not good', stated as philosophy.

real_life_example.event_title: Pope John Paul II forgives the man who shot him
real_life_example.place: Rome, Italy (Gemelli Hospital and a Rome prison)
real_life_example.event: On 13 May 1981 Pope John Paul II was shot and seriously wounded in St Peter's Square by Mehmet Ali Agca. Four days later, in a message recorded at the Gemelli hospital and broadcast in St Peter's Square, he said that he was praying for the brother who had shot him, whom he had sincerely forgiven. In 1983 he met Agca in prison and offered him forgiveness in person.
real_life_example.explanation: The Pope declared his forgiveness within days, while still recovering from his wounds, rather than waiting for the trial or for time to soften the injury.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says it is good to let go of a wrong on the very day it is done; John Paul II released the gravest of injuries almost at once.

tamil:
கொன்றன்ன இன்னா செயினும் அவர்செய்த
ஒன்றுநன்று உள்ளக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kondranna innaa seyinum avarseydha
Ondrunandru ullak kedum.
meaning: Even if someone who once helped you later hurts you terribly, like a killing blow, the pain goes away when you remember the one good thing they did.
elementary: Suppose a friend who once caught you when you were falling later does something that really hurts you. If you remember the time they caught you, the hurt shrinks. One good memory can melt a big hurt.
university: கொன்றன்ன இன்னா, 'an injury like killing', is the strongest possible provocation, and the verb கெடும் ('will perish') leaves its subject implicit: commentators take it to be the injury, or the pain and resentment it causes, that is destroyed merely by recalling (உள்ள) one (ஒன்று) earlier good (நன்று). The kural thus makes gratitude an active remedy rather than merely a debt: memory of a past benefit is prescribed as the means of dissolving present grievance. Valmiki's portrait of Rama in Ayodhya Kanda 2.1.11, gladdened by a single good deed and forgetting a hundred wrongs, is close enough to suggest a shared South Asian ethical ideal. A concrete legal-historical parallel is the Prophet Muhammad's pardon of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a, whose betrayal was weighed against his earlier service at Badr.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That Rama, because of his good bent of mind, feels glad even by whatever way a good thing is done to him. He does not remember any number of bad things done to him.”
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki describes Rama as someone who is made happy by even one good thing done for him and simply does not keep count of the wrongs done to him.
hinduism.tie_back: One remembered good cancelling many injuries is the very mechanism of this Kural.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 2.1.11 (K. M. K. Murthy trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: After Peter had three times denied knowing Jesus on the night of his arrest, the risen Jesus meets him by the Sea of Galilee, asks him three times whether he loves him, and restores him with the charge to feed his sheep.
christianity.explanation: Instead of punishing Peter for his betrayal, Jesus remembers Peter's love and loyalty and gives him back his place.
christianity.tie_back: A painful betrayal is overcome by recalling the good bond that came before it, close to the Kural's remedy.

islam.quote_or_event: When Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a was caught sending a secret letter warning the Meccans of the Prophet's plans, Umar asked permission to execute him as a traitor; the Prophet refused, saying that Hatib had fought at Badr and that God may have looked upon the people of Badr and forgiven them.
islam.explanation: A companion committed a serious betrayal that could have cost lives, but the Prophet pardoned him because of the great service he had once given at the Battle of Badr.
islam.tie_back: One remembered good (Badr) outweighed an injury as grave as treason, exactly the Kural's teaching.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother: thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian; because thou wast a stranger in his land.”
judaism.explanation: Even though Egypt later enslaved and oppressed the Israelites, the Torah forbids hating Egyptians, because Egypt once gave Jacob's family refuge in a famine.
judaism.tie_back: The earlier good (shelter) outweighs even the later near-deadly harm (slavery), precisely the Kural's teaching.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that you can never end hatred by hating back; only letting go of hatred ends it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it seeks to dissolve the pain of injury inwardly rather than answer it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Even though they do what is disagreeable, one should preserve as gold those who ought not to be forsaken. Daily do men seek for fire and keep it in their house, though it has consumed both their good house and gold.”
jainism.explanation: In its chapter on bearing with the faults of others, the Nālaḍiyār teaches that those bound to us by past good are kept, like the household fire, even after they have done us grave harm.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says even a near-mortal injury from a former benefactor fades when one recalls their one good deed, and the Nālaḍiyār likewise lets past worth outweigh present harm.
jainism.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', st. 5 (= st. 225), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He obtains ten things, and puts them behind him; for the sake of one thing withheld, he forfeits his faith. But what if that one thing were not given, and the ten were taken away? Then, what could the fool say or do?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the ungrateful person who forgets ten gifts because of one thing he did not receive.
sikhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's moral calculus turned inside out: where the grateful let one remembered kindness erase a deadly injury, the ingrate lets one grievance erase ten kindnesses.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 268, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: During the slaughter of the suitors, Telemachus begs Odysseus to spare the herald Medon, who had served in the suitors' company but had cared for Telemachus when he was a child; Odysseus spares him, along with the bard Phemius.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the middle of his revenge, Odysseus lets one of the suitors' servants live because that man had once looked after his son.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An old kindness saves a man even when he stands on the side of those who did deadly harm, echoing the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that a person who lives by the guidance of reason tries, as far as possible, to repay another's hatred, anger, or contempt with love or nobleness, because hatred answered with hatred only increases.
philosophy.explanation: The philosopher says a reasonable person answers hurt with kindness instead of revenge, since revenge just makes hatred grow.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts aim to neutralise injury rather than retaliate, though the Kural's method is remembering a past kindness.

real_life_example.event_title: Akbar pardons his former regent Bairam Khan
real_life_example.event: Bairam Khan, a general and friend of Emperor Humayun, guided the young Akbar as regent after he inherited the throne at the age of 13 in 1556. In 1560 Akbar took the government into his own hands, and Bairam rebelled for a time before submitting; Akbar forgave him and offered him the choice of a high place in the army or an escort for a pilgrimage to Mecca, and Bairam chose the pilgrimage. Bairam was killed by Afghans on the way in 1561, and Akbar took his four-year-old son Abd ur-Rahim into his household; the boy grew up to reach the highest rank in the Mughal hierarchy.
real_life_example.explanation: Akbar treated a rebel who had once secured his throne with mercy and later raised the rebel's orphaned son, rather than letting the rebellion cancel the earlier service.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says even a grievous injury from a former benefactor fades when one remembers the good he once did; Akbar's pardon of Bairam Khan shows past service outweighing present offence.

tamil:
எந்நன்றி கொன்றார்க்கும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்வில்லை
செய்ந்நன்றி கொன்ற மகற்கு.
transliteration:
Ennandri kondraarkkum uyvundaam uyvillai
Seynnandri kondra magarku.
meaning: People who destroy any other kind of goodness may still be saved. But there is no saving the person who is ungrateful for help they were given.
elementary: People can make lots of mistakes and still fix them. But this kural says the one thing that is almost impossible to fix is being ungrateful to someone who helped you, so that is the one mistake you should never make.
university: The chapter closes with its severest verdict. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah, following the traditional commentary, read the first நன்றி as அறம் in general ('whoever has killed any virtue'), against which செய்ந்நன்றி கொன்ற மகன், the man who has 'killed' a benefit by forgetting it or returning harm for it, stands uniquely without உய்வு (escape, deliverance). The idea has deep roots in Tamil and Sanskrit tradition: the Sangam anthology Puranānūru (poem 34) is commonly cited alongside this kural for declaring that there is no escape for those who destroy a benefit, and Valmiki's Kishkindha Kanda (4.34.12) says atonement is ordained for cow-slayers, drinkers, thieves and vow-breakers but not for the kṛtaghna, the ingrate. Outside South Asia, Cicero held that no duty is more imperative than proving one's gratitude (De Officiis 1.47), and Hume chose ingratitude as the most horrid and unnatural of crimes (Treatise 3.1.1). This agreement suggests that ingratitude was treated not as one vice among many but as the destruction of the reciprocity on which moral community rests.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The savants have ordained atonement for slayers of cows, for drinkers of liquors, thus for thieves and infringers of solemnity, but no atonement is available to a treacherous person.”
hinduism.explanation: Lakshmana, rebuking Sugriva for forgetting his promise to Rama, quotes an old verse: even killers, drunkards and thieves can atone, but there is no atonement for someone who is ungrateful (kṛtaghna, rendered 'treacherous' by this translator).
hinduism.tie_back: Almost word-for-word the Kural's claim: every other sinner has a way out, but the ingrate has none.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 4.34.12 (Desiraju Hanumanta Rao trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Jesus answering said, Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine? There are not found that returned to give glory to God, save this stranger.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus heals ten lepers, but only one, a Samaritan foreigner, comes back to thank him, and Jesus asks sadly where the other nine are.
christianity.tie_back: The story singles out ingratitude after a life-changing kindness as something that grieves even Jesus.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed, 'If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favor]; but if you deny, indeed, My punishment is severe.'”
islam.explanation: God promises more blessings to the grateful and warns of severe punishment for those who deny His favours.
islam.tie_back: Ingratitude (kufr of blessings) carries grave consequences, echoing the Kural's warning that it has no escape.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that anyone who repays good with evil will never be free of trouble in their household.
judaism.tie_back: 'Evil shall not depart' is a close match for the Kural's 'there is no escape' for the one who kills a kindness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Silavanaga Jataka, the Bodhisatta, born as a noble elephant, rescues a lost forester and carries him to safety. The man returns three times to saw off the elephant's tusks, which are freely given; on his way home the third time the earth splits open and swallows him.
buddhism.explanation: A man keeps taking the tusks of the elephant that saved his life, and after his third betrayal the ground itself opens and swallows him.
buddhism.tie_back: The ingrate who repays rescue with injury meets a doom from which there is no escape, the Kural's verdict told as a story.
buddhism.source: Jataka No. 72, Silavanaga Jataka (E. B. Cowell ed., vol. 1)

jainism.quote_or_event: “What crime against you was committed by the Lord, when he showed the snake being burned inside the log, if you were prevented from sin at that time? Good advice then led to your hostility, villain, like rain-water on saline soil.”
jainism.explanation: Kaṭha, reborn as the demon Meghamālin, repays Pārśva's kindly correction with lifelong hostility. Confronted by Dharaṇa, he is terrified: “I can not remain in the three worlds because of the crime against him … Where shall I go for a refuge?”
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar holds that whoever kills a benefit has no escape, and Hemacandra's ingrate himself finds no refuge anywhere in the three worlds for returning good with harm.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book IX, ch. III, part 9 'Attacks by Meghamālin' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one can save such an ungrateful person; he is thrown into the most horrible hell.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan names the akirtghan, the one who forgets what has been done for him, as a person whom nothing can save.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says any other sin may find expiation but not the killing of gratitude; Gurbani likewise singles out ingratitude as leaving one beyond rescue.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1086, Raag Maaroo, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar tells how Ixion, whom Zeus had purified and received as a guest among the gods, tried to seduce Hera; bound forever to a winged, turning wheel, he proclaims to mortals that they must repay a benefactor with kind returns.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ixion was forgiven and welcomed by Zeus, then betrayed him, and was punished for all eternity as a warning to everyone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ixion is Greek myth's model ingrate, and his punishment is endless, the Kural's 'no escape'.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Of all crimes that human creatures are capable of committing, the most horrid and unnatural is ingratitude, especially when it is committed against parents, and appears in the more flagrant instances of wounds and death.”
philosophy.explanation: The Scottish philosopher David Hume uses ingratitude as his example of the crime everyone agrees is the worst, especially ingratitude toward parents.
philosophy.tie_back: Hume ranks ingratitude at the very top of human crimes, matching the Kural's claim that it alone has no escape.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 3.1.1.24

real_life_example.event_title: Brutus joins the conspiracy against Julius Caesar
real_life_example.event: Marcus Junius Brutus fought on Pompey's side against Julius Caesar, but after Pompey's defeat at Pharsalus in 48 BCE Caesar pardoned him, made him a highly honoured companion, and later put him in charge of Cisalpine Gaul and gave him high civic office. In 44 BCE Brutus joined Cassius and other conspirators in assassinating Caesar in Rome. In the Inferno, written in the early fourteenth century, Dante placed Brutus and Cassius, as betrayers of their benefactor, beside Judas in the lowest region of Hell.
real_life_example.explanation: For centuries Brutus's name became shorthand for betrayal of a benefactor, and Dante gave him the harshest place in his entire vision of punishment.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says there is no escape for one who destroys gratitude for a kindness received; Dante's verdict on Brutus expresses the same judgment in literary form.

tamil:
தகுதி எனவொன்று நன்றே பகுதியால்
பாற்பட்டு ஒழுகப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Thakudhi enavondru nandre pakudhiyaal
Paarpattu ozhukap perin.
meaning: Being fair is truly good when a person treats everyone rightly, whether they are enemies, strangers or friends.
elementary: Imagine a referee who calls the game the same way whether the player is his best friend, a stranger, or someone he doesn’t like. That fairness to everyone is what this kural calls a truly good quality.
university: The chapter opens by naming impartiality with the word தகுதி (thakudhi, “fitness, propriety, worthiness”), implying that fairness is not one virtue among many but the very measure of whether a person is fit to be trusted. The key phrase பகுதியால் பாற்பட்டு (“keeping to what is due in each division”) was read by the medieval commentator Parimelazhagar, and after him by modern commentators such as Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi, as the threefold division of people into enemies, strangers (neutrals) and friends; the test of justice is that the same standard applies across all three. Placing this chapter in the Illaraviyal (the householder’s section) signals that Valluvar sees impartiality as an everyday domestic and civic duty, not only a king’s or judge’s duty (royal justice is treated separately in chapter 55, செங்கோன்மை). The idea parallels the classical definition of justice as rendering to each their due, and Aristotle’s observation that justice, unlike the other virtues, is directed essentially toward others.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person is considered still further advanced when he regards honest well-wishers, affectionate benefactors, the neutral, mediators, the envious, friends and enemies, the pious and the sinners all with an equal mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists every kind of person, from friends to enemies to neutral bystanders, and says the advanced person treats them all with the same even mind (sama-buddhi).
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the same list the Kural’s commentators give (friends, strangers, enemies), with the same demand: one equal standard for all of them.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors.”
christianity.explanation: James warns churches against giving rich visitors the good seats and poor visitors the floor. Favouritism, “respect of persons,” is called outright sin.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat favouring one group over another as a moral failure, and even-handed treatment as the real virtue.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an commands believers to stay just even toward people they hate. Hostility is no excuse for bending fairness.
islam.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s point that fairness must hold even toward enemies, the hardest of the three “divisions.”

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids tilting a judgment either way, whether out of pity for the poor or deference to the powerful.
judaism.tie_back: Same principle as the Kural: every category of person gets the same straight standard.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by passing arbitrary judgments does a man become just; a wise man is he who investigates both right and wrong. He who does not judge others arbitrarily, but passes judgment impartially according to the truth, that sagacious man is a guardian of law and is called just.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada’s chapter “The Just” says a person earns the title “just” only by judging impartially and according to truth, not by hasty or biased verdicts.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural and the Dhammapada both define the just person by impartiality, not by status.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Impartiality towards all beings in the world, whether friends or enemies, and abstention from injury to living beings throughout the whole life: this is a difficult duty.”
jainism.explanation: When the prince Mṛgāputra seeks to renounce, his parents warn him that the monk's path demands an even-handed attitude toward friend and foe alike, together with lifelong non-injury.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar defines the virtue of fitness as acting rightly toward every group, whether enemies, strangers or friends, and Jain scripture names this same impartiality as one of the hardest duties.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 19.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: During the fighting at Anandpur, Bhai Kanhaiya, a Sikh of Guru Gobind Singh, carried water to the wounded of both armies, Sikh and Mughal alike. When Sikhs complained that he was helping the enemy, he answered that he saw no enemy, only the Guru in every face, and the Guru approved and gave him ointment to dress the wounds of all.
sikhism.explanation: The story is the classic Sikh image of service that makes no distinction between friend and foe; it inspired later Sikh humanitarian seva.
sikhism.tie_back: It is a lived version of the Kural's fitness: dealing rightly and equally with enemies, strangers and friends.
sikhism.source: SikhNet, 'The Story of Bhai Kanhaiya Singh' (paraphrase of the Sikh tradition)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But they who give straight judgements to strangers and to the men of the land, and go not aside from what is just, their city flourishes, and the people prosper in it”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his brother that Zeus blesses cities whose judges treat foreigners and citizens with the same straight justice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s “strangers and men of the land” lines up with the Kural’s strangers and one’s own people, both judged the same way.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For this same reason justice, alone of the virtues, is thought to be ‘another’s good’, because it is related to our neighbour; for it does what is advantageous to another, either a ruler or a copartner.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle notes that justice is the one virtue that looks outward to others, so it is tested in how we treat people other than ourselves.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats justice as a relational virtue proved by how fairly we deal with every other person.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Henry Dunant and the women of Castiglione after Solferino
real_life_example.place: Solferino and Castiglione delle Stiviere, Lombardy, Italy
real_life_example.event: Swiss businessman Henry Dunant arrived near the northern Italian town of Solferino in time to witness the aftermath of the battle of 24 June 1859 between the French and Piedmontese-Sardinian armies and the Austrian army. In nearby Castiglione delle Stiviere he joined local people caring for the wounded in the town's main church, which sheltered more than 500 men, and the town's women tended French, Italian and Austrian soldiers without distinction. Dunant's book A Memory of Solferino (1862) led to the founding of the Red Cross movement and to the first Geneva Convention, signed in 1864.
real_life_example.explanation: Care given equally to allies and enemies on a battlefield became the founding principle of impartial humanitarian aid.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls it true fitness to deal rightly with enemies, strangers and friends alike; Dunant and the women of Castiglione treated soldiers of every army the same.

tamil:
செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கஞ் சிதைவின்றி
எச்சத்திற் கேமாப்பு உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Seppam udaiyavan aakkanj sidhaivindri
Echchaththirku emaappu udaiththu.
meaning: The riches of a fair-minded person do not fall apart. They last and support even their children and grandchildren.
elementary: Think of a house built on strong, straight foundations. It doesn’t fall down; the grandchildren can still live in it. Wealth earned fairly is like that house, and it keeps protecting the family.
university: செப்பம் (seppam, “straightness, rectitude”) is used here as a synonym for naduvu nilaimai, and the couplet makes a claim about consequences: the ஆக்கம் (aakkam, “increase, prosperity”) of the just person is சிதைவின்றி (“without disintegration”) and furnishes ஏமாப்பு (emaappu, “security, protection”) to the எச்சம் (echcham, “what remains after one”), which the commentators read as descendants or posterity. The point is intergenerational: unjust gain may be large but brittle, while justly earned wealth is durable. The idea that righteousness is an inheritance for children’s children is widespread, found in Proverbs, the Psalms, the Qur’anic story of the orphans’ buried treasure, and Hesiod’s claim that the truthful man’s “generation” prospers. The word echcham reappears in Kural 114, where its meaning (offspring or legacy) becomes a matter of commentarial debate.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: Son of Pṛthā, a transcendentalist engaged in auspicious activities does not meet with destruction either in this world or in the spiritual world; one who does good, My friend, is never overcome by evil.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reassures Arjuna that a person who does good is never destroyed, in this life or the next.
hinduism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s promise that right conduct leads to lasting security rather than ruin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children’s children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.”
christianity.explanation: This proverb, part of the Christian Old Testament, says a good person’s legacy reaches even grandchildren, while the wicked person’s wealth ends up with others.
christianity.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s exact claim: the upright person’s wealth lasts and benefits their descendants.

islam.quote_or_event: “And as for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and there was beneath it a treasure for them, and their father had been righteous. So your Lord intended that they reach maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord.”
islam.explanation: In the story of Moses and al-Khidr, a wall is repaired so that two orphans’ hidden treasure stays safe, explicitly because their father had been righteous.
islam.tie_back: The righteous father’s goodness protects his children’s wealth after him, which is the Kural’s “security to posterity.”

judaism.quote_or_event: “His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed. Wealth and riches shall be in his house: and his righteousness endureth for ever.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm describes the upright person: their descendants are blessed, their house has wealth, and their righteousness lasts forever.
judaism.tie_back: Same three elements as the Kural: uprightness, lasting prosperity, and blessing to descendants.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who acquires his wealth in harmless ways like to a bee that honey gathers, riches mount up for him like ant hill’s rapid growth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the householder Sigala that wealth gathered without harming anyone grows steadily, the way an anthill rises.
buddhism.tie_back: Both say that wealth gained righteously grows and endures.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Nyayasampannavibhavah : Possessed of honestly earned wealth.”
jainism.explanation: The first of Hemacandra's thirty-five qualities of the ideal Jain householder is wealth acquired by just means (nyāya).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar promises that the prosperity of the upright endures, and Jain householder ethics likewise puts justly earned wealth first, though it makes no explicit promise about its lasting for descendants.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of 35 qualities of the ideal śrāvaka, no. 1, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “It does not run short, and it does not run out.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the wealth of the Lord's Name as a treasure that never diminishes however much it is used.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural promises that the upright person's prosperity does not crumble; Gurbani makes the same claim, but for the spiritual wealth of the righteous rather than material gain.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 375, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For whoever knows the right and is ready to speak it, far-seeing Zeus gives him prosperity; but whoever deliberately lies in his witness and forswears himself, and so hurts Justice and sins beyond repair, that man’s generation is left obscure thereafter. But the generation of the man who swears truly is better thenceforward.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says Zeus gives prosperity to the one who speaks what is right, and that this person’s descendants fare better, while the perjurer’s line fades into obscurity.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An exact counterpart: justice brings prosperity that carries over to one’s descendants (echcham).

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then this must be our notion of the just man, that even when he is in poverty or sickness, or any other seeming misfortune, all things will in the end work together for good to him in life and death”
philosophy.explanation: At the end of the Republic, Socrates concludes that the just person is ultimately secure: whatever happens, things work out for his good.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s conviction that justice yields lasting security rather than eventual collapse.

real_life_example.event_title: Ernst Abbe creates the Carl Zeiss Foundation
real_life_example.event: Physicist Ernst Abbe, who became head of the Zeiss optical works after Carl Zeiss's death in 1888, was concerned that future owners might enrich themselves at the expense of the companies and their employees. In 1889 he set up and endowed the Carl Zeiss Foundation, which became sole owner of the Zeiss works in 1891, and his 1896 foundation statute gave employees rights such as profit-sharing, paid holidays, sick pay and pensions, with an eight-hour day introduced at Zeiss in 1900. The ZEISS company credits Abbe with a decisive role in the continued existence of ZEISS and SCHOTT, both of which still operate today.
real_life_example.explanation: Abbe chose to build fairness to workers into the ownership of the firm itself, so that it could not easily be undone by later owners.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the prosperity of the just does not crumble but supports those who come after; Abbe's fairly organised enterprise has outlasted him by more than a century.

tamil:
நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கத்தை
அன்றே யொழிய விடல்.
transliteration:
Nandre tharinum naduvikandhaam aakkaththai
Andre yozhiya vidal.
meaning: Even if it seems to bring only good, give up any gain that comes from being unfair, that very same day.
elementary: Suppose you find out you won a prize only because the judge was your uncle and cheated for you. Even though the prize is nice, the right thing is to give it back right away.
university: The couplet anticipates the objection that injustice might sometimes pay: நன்றே தரினும் (“even if it yields only good”). Valluvar’s answer is categorical. Gain acquired by நடு இகந்து (“transgressing the middle/the just mean”) must be relinquished அன்றே (“that very day”), with no waiting to see whether it turns out well. The emphasis on immediacy suggests a psychological insight: ill-gotten advantage becomes harder to renounce the longer one holds it. The ethic parallels Socrates’ insistence in the Apology that wealth pursued at the cost of the soul is shameful, the Qur’anic ban on consuming others’ property unjustly, and Hesiod’s warning that seized wealth stays only “for a little time.” Philosophically it is a deontological stance: the injustice of the means cannot be redeemed by the goodness of the outcome.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Bound by a network of hundreds of thousands of desires and absorbed in lust and anger, they secure money by illegal means for sense gratification.”
hinduism.explanation: In describing the “demoniac” nature, Krishna names gathering wealth by unjust means (anyāyena, literally “by non-justice”) as a defining mark.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita condemns exactly what the Kural tells us to drop: wealth gathered by departing from justice.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus asks what any gain is worth if it costs a person their soul.
christianity.tie_back: Both say that no gain, however great or “good,” is worth the moral loss involved in getting it wrongly.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly or send it [in bribery] to the rulers in order that [they might aid] you [to] consume a portion of the wealth of the people in sin, while you know [it is unlawful].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids taking others’ wealth unjustly, including bribing judges to rule in one’s favour.
islam.tie_back: Gain won by corrupting fair judgment is exactly the “gain beyond the middle” the Kural says to reject.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says a small income gained justly is worth more than a large one gained unjustly.
judaism.tie_back: Same trade-off as the Kural: prefer less with justice over more without it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is indeed virtuous, wise, and righteous who neither for his own sake nor for the sake of another (does any wrong), who does not crave for sons, wealth, or kingdom, and does not desire success by unjust means.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada defines the righteous person as one who does not seek success by unjust means, whether for himself or for others.
buddhism.tie_back: Both refuse success that comes through injustice, however attractive it looks.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The consequences of violence, falsehood, stealing, unchastity and attachment are calamity and reproach in this world and in the next birth.”
jainism.explanation: Umāsvāti teaches that whatever is gained by breaching the vows, including taking what is not rightly one's own, brings disaster and disgrace both now and hereafter.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says gain won by abandoning fairness must be given up that very day even if it seems to bring only good, and the Tattvārtha Sūtra explains why: such gain carries calamity in this life and the next.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.9 (English rendering on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
