sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak makes taking another's due, haq paraia, as abhorrent as the strongest taboo of each community.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to give up at once any gain won by abandoning fairness, however good it looks; Guru Nanak treats such gain as utterly forbidden food.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Wealth should not be seized: god-given wealth is much better; for if a man take great wealth violently and perforce, or if he steal it through his tongue, as often happens when gain deceives men’s sense and dishonour tramples down honour, the gods soon blot him out and make that man’s house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that wrongly seized wealth, “when gain deceives men’s sense,” is soon destroyed by the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The phrase “gain deceives men’s sense” matches the Kural’s “even if it seems to give good”: the benefit is an illusion that will not last.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “are you not ashamed of heaping up the greatest amount of money and honour and reputation, and caring so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul, which you never regard or heed at all?”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial Socrates says his mission is to shame Athenians who pile up money and reputation while neglecting their souls.
philosophy.tie_back: Both put the integrity of the self above material gain.

real_life_example.event_title: Eugenio Monti lends his bolt to his rivals
real_life_example.place: Igls, near Innsbruck, Austria (Winter Olympic Games)
real_life_example.event: During the two-man bobsleigh competition at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Olympics, a bolt on the sled of British rivals Tony Nash and Robin Dixon broke, threatening to put them out of the event. Italy's Eugenio Monti, one of the world's leading drivers, gave them a replacement bolt from his own equipment, and Nash and Dixon went on to win the Olympic title. Monti also had his team help repair the sled of the Canadian four-man crew, who won that event, and the International Olympic Committee later honoured him with its first Pierre de Coubertin fair-play award.
real_life_example.explanation: Monti could have gained a medal simply by staying silent, but he refused to profit from a rival's misfortune.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says any gain that comes from abandoning fairness should be given up at once; Monti gave up a likely advantage on the spot rather than win by his rivals' accident.

tamil:
தக்கார் தகவிலர் என்பது அவரவர்
எச்சத்தாற் காணப்ப படும்.
transliteration:
Thakkaar thakavilar enbadhu avaravar
Echchaththaar kaanappa padum.
meaning: Whether a person was fair or unfair will be shown by what they leave behind after they die, such as their good or bad name.
elementary: You can tell what kind of gardener someone was by what is still growing in the garden after they leave. People are like that too: what remains after them shows whether they were fair.
university: The couplet turns on எச்சம் (echcham, “that which remains”). Parimelazhagar reads it as offspring: the worth of the just is visible in good descendants, a reading reflected in G. U. Pope’s translation (“By each one’s offspring shall the truth be clear”). Mu. Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi instead read it as the reputation, praise or blame, that remains after death, while Solomon Pappaiah combines wealth, fame and the conduct of one’s children. Either way the claim is that a verdict on a life’s justice can only be given in retrospect, from its durable effects. This echoes Solon’s advice to Croesus (in Herodotus) to call no one happy until their end is seen, Jesus’ “by their fruits ye shall know them,” and the hadith that a righteous child is among the deeds that continue after death. Note on the text: all three consulted editions (thirukkural.net, ytamizh.com, Project Madurai) print காணப்ப படும்; many printed editions give காணப் படும். The meaning is unaffected.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that people’s lasting verdict on his conduct will outlive him, and that a dishonoured name is worse than death.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat the reputation that survives a person as the real verdict on their character.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that true character shows itself in results, the way a tree is known by its fruit.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the just and unjust are known by what they produce and leave behind.

islam.quote_or_event: “When a man dies, his acts come to an end, but three, recurring charity, or knowledge (by which people) benefit, or a pious child, who prays for him (for the deceased).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that after death only three things keep adding to a person’s account, one of which is a righteous child.
islam.tie_back: Fits both readings of echcham: the good that remains after a person, and especially good offspring.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb contrasts the lasting, blessed memory of the just with the decaying name of the wicked.
judaism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Varadarasanar reading: praise or blame after death shows who was just.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not the sweet smell of flowers, not even the fragrance of sandal, tagara, or jasmine blows against the wind. But the fragrance of the virtuous blows against the wind. Truly the virtuous man pervades all directions with the fragrance of his virtue.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the reputation of virtue spreads everywhere and lasts in a way no perfume can.
buddhism.tie_back: Both see virtue as leaving a lasting, perceptible trace by which the person is known.

jainism.quote_or_event: “My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anāthin tells King Śreṇika that each person's condition is the result of their own good or bad conduct, with no outside protector.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says a person's justice or injustice shows in what they leave behind, and Jain karma doctrine likewise holds that what follows a person is simply the fruit of acting well or badly.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Celebrated and approved is the coming into the world of such a person, who saves all his generations as well.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das says a life is approved when its good extends to the whole family line.
sikhism.tie_back: Read with Parimelazhagar's gloss of echcham as offspring, the Kural says the worth of the just is shown in what they leave behind; Gurbani likewise judges a life by its benefit to the generations.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1094, Raag Maaroo, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The fame, therefore, of her virtue shall never die, and the immortals shall compose a song that shall be welcome to all mankind in honour of the constancy of Penelope.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the underworld, Agamemnon’s ghost contrasts Penelope’s undying good name with the hateful song that will follow his murderous wife Clytemnestra.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the Kural’s contrast in mythic form: the worthy and the unworthy are told apart by the fame or infamy that outlives them.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Call him, however, until he die, not happy but fortunate.” … “But in every matter it behoves us to mark well the end”
philosophy.explanation: Solon tells King Croesus that no life can be judged until its end is seen.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that a person’s true worth is visible only from what the whole life finally amounts to.

real_life_example.event_title: Justice Harlan's lone dissent in Plessy v. Ferguson
real_life_example.place: Supreme Court of the United States, Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: In Plessy v. Ferguson the US Supreme Court, by a vote of 7 to 1, upheld a state law providing for racial segregation and established the separate but equal doctrine. Justice John Marshall Harlan was the lone dissenter, arguing that the Constitution recognised no superior or ruling class among citizens and warning that the decision would plant the seeds of race hatred in state law. In 1954, in Brown v. Board of Education and related cases, the Court repudiated the separate but equal doctrine, and Britannica notes that in the twentieth century the Court vindicated many of the positions Harlan had taken in dissent.
real_life_example.explanation: Harlan was outvoted in his lifetime, but the judgment that survived him was his, while the majority's ruling is now remembered as a grave injustice.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says whether a person was just or unjust is revealed by what remains after them; history's verdict on Plessy showed who had judged fairly.

tamil:
கேடும் பெருக்கமும் இல்லல்ல நெஞ்சத்துக்
கோடாமை சான்றோர்க் கணி.
transliteration:
Kedum perukkamum illalla nenjaththuk
Kodaamai saandrork kani.
meaning: Loss and gain come in every life. The jewel of good people is a mind that stays fair in both.
elementary: Some days you win, some days you lose; that happens to everyone. A good person plays fair on both kinds of days, and that fairness is their best jewel.
university: The first line states a plain fact: கேடும் பெருக்கமும் இல்லல்ல (“ruin and increase are not things that do not exist”), that is, they are inevitable. Parimelazhagar attributes them to past deeds (ūḻ), which is reflected in Pope’s “not mere accident” and Solomon Pappaiah’s “already ordained.” Given that fortune is outside our control, the only thing that distinguishes the சான்றோர் (saandror, “the accomplished/noble”) is நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை, “not bending in the heart.” The verb கோடு (“to bend, to be crooked”) is the key image of the chapter and returns in Kurals 118 and 119. The ethic is close to Stoic doctrine, which separates externals from the governing faculty, and to the Gita’s samatva (evenness in gain and loss). The refrain கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி is repeated word for word in Kural 118.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do thou fight for the sake of fighting, without considering happiness or distress, loss or gain, victory or defeat – and by so doing you shall never incur sin.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna to treat gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal and keep doing his duty.
hinduism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s lābha-alābha (gain and loss) theme: stay steady in right action whatever fortune brings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound”
christianity.explanation: Paul writes from prison that he has learned to stay the same person in poverty and plenty.
christianity.tie_back: Both portray inner steadiness through ups and downs as the mark of a mature person.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an explains that knowing all events are decreed should keep believers from both despair at loss and arrogance at gain.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural (as Parimelazhagar reads it), it accepts loss and gain as ordained and asks for an unshaken heart in both.

judaism.quote_or_event: “till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me. My righteousness I hold fast, and will not let it go: my heart shall not reproach me so long as I live.”
judaism.explanation: Job, having lost wealth, children and health, refuses to give up his integrity.
judaism.tie_back: Job is the model of a heart that does not bend when ruin comes, the Kural’s kōdāmai.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares the wise to a rock that storms cannot move. The next verse adds that they show no elation or depression in happiness or sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: The same picture of the noble person’s steady heart amid the “worldly winds” of gain and loss.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He was indifferent to success or failure (in begging), to happiness and misery, to life and death, to blame and praise, to honour and insult.”
jainism.explanation: Mṛgāputra, once a monk, holds the same even mind whether things go well or badly.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar grants that loss and gain will come and calls the unbent heart the ornament of the noble, and this verse shows the Jain ideal of a mind that stays level through both.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 19.90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That man, who in the midst of pain, does not feel pain, who is not affected by pleasure, affection or fear, and who looks alike upon gold and dust;”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person who stays even and unshaken through loss and gain, pain and pleasure.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says loss and gain will surely come and the noble person's ornament is a heart that does not bend in either; Guru Tegh Bahadur paints the same steadiness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus, back in his own house disguised as a beggar and seeing the suitors’ outrages, restrains his rising heart by reminding it that it has endured worse before, and keeps to his course rather than acting rashly.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus is the Greek model of a man who stays steady through twenty years of loss and reversal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the ideal of a heart that does not swerve under changing fortune, though Odysseus’ steadiness is about endurance, not fairness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Don’t demand that things happen as you wish, but wish that they happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that outcomes are not in our control, and that serenity comes from accepting them while governing our own choices.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s structure is the same: fortune is not ours to command; the uprightness of the heart is.

real_life_example.event_title: Justice H. R. Khanna's dissent in ADM Jabalpur
real_life_example.place: Supreme Court of India, New Delhi, India
real_life_example.event: During the national Emergency of 1975-77, the Supreme Court of India ruled 4 to 1 in ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla that detained citizens could not approach the courts to enforce their right to life and liberty while the Emergency lasted. Justice H. R. Khanna, next in line by seniority to become Chief Justice, was the lone dissenter, holding that life and liberty could not be at the mercy of the executive; he later wrote that before the judgment he had told his sister it would cost him the Chief Justiceship. In January 1977 a junior judge, M. H. Beg, was appointed Chief Justice instead, and Khanna resigned the same day; in 2017 a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court overruled the majority judgment.
real_life_example.explanation: Khanna knowingly gave up the highest judicial office in India rather than bend his reading of the law to the pressure of the moment.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says loss and gain will come, and the ornament of the noble is a heart that does not bend in either; Khanna accepted the loss and did not bend.

tamil:
கெடுவல்யான் என்பது அறிகதன் நெஞ்சம்
நடுவொரீஇ அல்ல செயின்.
transliteration:
Keduval yaan enbadhu arika than nenjam
Naduvoreei alla seyin.
meaning: If your heart leaves fairness and turns to doing wrong, take it as a sure sign: ‘I am going to be ruined.’
elementary: When a car starts drifting out of its lane, a warning beeps. This kural says that when your heart starts wanting to be unfair, that is your warning beep: trouble is coming if you don’t steer back.
university: The couplet is written as an internal monologue: கெடுவல் யான் (“I shall perish”) is what one should say to oneself the moment the heart நடு ஒரீஇ (“having abandoned the middle”) turns toward அல்ல (“what is not [right]”). Commentators differ on emphasis. Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi stress the intention itself as the omen (“if the heart even thinks of it”), while Pope renders it “let man impending ruin’s sign discern.” Either way, injustice is presented as self-destructive, not merely harmful to others. This matches the Manusmriti’s maxim that violated justice destroys the violator, the Qur’anic warning to David that following desire in judgment leads astray, and Plato’s argument that injustice is a disease of the soul.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Justice, being violated, destroys; justice, being preserved, preserves: therefore justice must not be violated, lest violated justice destroy us.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu state the principle dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ: dharma (justice) destroys whoever violates it and protects whoever protects it.
hinduism.tie_back: An almost exact counterpart: whoever abandons justice should know it will destroy them.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 8.15 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that a person inevitably reaps the consequences of what they sow.
christianity.tie_back: Both warn that wrongdoing carries its own ruin back to the doer.

islam.quote_or_event: “O David, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow [your own] desire, as it will lead you astray from the way of Allah.”
islam.explanation: God tells King David to judge by truth and not by personal inclination, warning that following desire leads astray and to punishment.
islam.tie_back: The same inner movement as the Kural: when the heart leaves fairness for desire, ruin follows.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity: and the rod of his anger shall fail.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says whoever sows injustice will harvest emptiness, and his power will fail.
judaism.tie_back: Injustice leads to the doer’s own ruin, the self-warning of the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever through desire, hate or fear, Or ignorance should transgress the Dhamma, All his glory fades away Like the moon during the waning half.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names the four biases (agati: desire, hatred, fear, delusion) that lead people to act wrongly, and says whoever is swayed by them declines like the waning moon.
buddhism.tie_back: The agati are exactly the forces that pull a heart away from the “middle.” The Kural and the Sutta both predict decline.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
jainism.explanation: The sermon to King Śreṇika warns that a person's own inner corruption ruins them more surely than any outside foe.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks one whose heart turns from fairness to recognise it as the sign of their own ruin, and the Uttarādhyayana likewise names the perverted heart as the real destroyer.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not harbor evil intentions against others in your mind, and you shall not be troubled, O Siblings of Destiny, O friends.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan ties freedom from suffering to keeping ill will toward others out of one's heart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the person whose heart turns to wrong to read it as a sign of coming ruin; Gurbani teaches the converse: keep the heart free of ill intent and trouble will not come.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And there is virgin Justice, the daughter of Zeus, who is honoured and reverenced among the gods who dwell on Olympus, and whenever anyone hurts her with lying slander, she sits beside her father, Zeus the son of Cronos, and tells him of men’s wicked heart, until the people pay for the mad folly …”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod portrays Dike (Justice) as a goddess who reports every injury done to her to Zeus, who then punishes the wrongdoers.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both warn that turning away from justice brings certain ruin, and Hesiod even locates the problem in the “wicked heart.”

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then virtue is the health and beauty and well-being of the soul, and vice the disease and weakness and deformity of the same?”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that injustice is to the soul what disease is to the body: it harms the unjust person first.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats departure from justice as self-destruction.

real_life_example.event_title: Former Prime Minister Tanaka and the Lockheed bribery scandal
real_life_example.event: Tanaka Kakuei, prime minister of Japan from 1972 to 1974, was accused of having accepted, while in office, the equivalent of about 2 million US dollars from the American aircraft maker Lockheed to influence All Nippon Airways to buy Lockheed airliners. He was arrested on 27 July 1976, and in 1983 the Tokyo District Court found him guilty and sentenced him to four years in prison and a fine of 500 million yen. He remained free while appealing, suffered a serious stroke in 1985 after which his power and influence waned, and died in 1993 before the appeal was decided.
real_life_example.explanation: A leader at the height of power who turned public office toward private gain saw his reputation and influence destroyed, and the case became a lasting symbol of political corruption in Japan.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that when the heart turns from fairness to wrongdoing, ruin is near; Tanaka's fall followed from a decision to sell the influence of his office.

tamil:
கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம் நடுவாக
நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் தாழ்வு.
transliteration:
Keduvaaga vaiyaadhu ulagam naduvaaga
Nandrikkan thangiyaan thaazhvu.
meaning: When a fair person who does what is right becomes poor, the world does not see it as a fall.
elementary: If a shopkeeper loses money because she refused to cheat anyone, people don’t think of her as a failure. They respect her even more.
university: Kural 117 answers an objection that Kural 112 might invite: what if the just person does not prosper? Valluvar grants that the one who நடுவாக நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் (“abides in goodness, keeping to the middle”) may suffer தாழ்வு (“lowness, decline, poverty”), but insists the உலகம் will not regard it as கேடு (“ruin”). Here “the world” means the wise or discerning, as Pope (“wise man’s sight”) and Pappaiah (“the great”) make explicit. Social esteem is separated from material fortune: honour tracks justice, not wealth. The theme recurs across traditions: Proverbs’ “better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness,” the Beatitude for those persecuted for righteousness, Socrates’ poverty for the sake of his mission, and the Hindu legend of Harishchandra, who lost everything rather than break his word.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, to honour a promise made to the sage Vishvamitra, gives up his kingdom and wealth and is reduced to selling his wife and son and working at a cremation ground. He never abandons truth, and the gods finally restore and exalt him.
hinduism.explanation: Harishchandra is the classic Indian example of a righteous man whose poverty is a mark of honour rather than disgrace.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s point in story form: the poverty of one who stays righteous is not counted as ruin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus declares that those who suffer because of their righteousness are blessed, not defeated.
christianity.tie_back: Both reframe hardship caused by righteousness as honour rather than failure.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says true nobility is measured by righteousness, not by tribe or wealth.
islam.tie_back: Both put a person’s standing in their righteousness, not their material state.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness, than he that is perverse in his ways, though he be rich.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb ranks an upright poor person above a crooked rich one.
judaism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural: poverty with uprightness is not degradation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth does one become a holy man. But he in whom truth and righteousness exist — he is pure, he is a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says true worth comes from truth and righteousness, not from outward status.
buddhism.tie_back: Both separate real standing from external circumstances.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The good, though they be poor and emaciated, will not guiltily ascend and rise over the bounds (of duty); binding their courage, as much as in them lies, with the cords of a mind free from anxiety, they will do the things that ought to be done.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaḍiyār describes the good as keeping within the bounds of right conduct even in poverty, unashamed and steady.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the world does not count the poverty of one who holds to fairness as a downfall, and the Nālaḍiyār shows such a person poor in means yet unbroken in duty.
jainism.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 16 'The Good', st. 3 (= st. 153), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You are the wealth of the poor, the Guru of the guru-less, the honor of the dishonored.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak praises God as the honour of those the world holds in no esteem.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the world will not count the poverty of the upright as a fall; Gurbani goes further, saying the poor and dishonoured have God as their wealth and honour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 992, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor old couple in Phrygia, are the only household to welcome the disguised gods Jupiter and Mercury. The gods spare them when the region is flooded, turn their hut into a temple, and grant their wish to serve it and to die together.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth honours a poor but righteous couple above their wealthier, inhospitable neighbours.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their poverty is no mark of lowness in the gods’ eyes; their goodness is what counts.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “my occupation quite absorbs me, and I have no time to give either to any public matter of interest or to any concern of my own, but I am in utter poverty by reason of my devotion to the god.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells the jury that his poverty is the direct result of his commitment to his philosophical mission.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates is a model of poverty that comes from integrity, and history has honoured rather than despised it.

real_life_example.event_title: Sir Walter Scott chooses to repay his creditors
real_life_example.place: Edinburgh and Abbotsford, Scotland, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: In January 1826 the collapse of Scott's publisher, Archibald Constable and Co., brought down the Ballantyne printing firm in which Scott was a partner, leaving him liable for debts of about 121,000 pounds. Rather than take trade bankruptcy, which would have let him pay creditors only a fraction of what they were owed, he placed his entire literary income in a trust for his creditors, sold his Edinburgh house and wrote intensively for the rest of his life. The creditors accepted, partly from reluctance to ruin a man regarded as a national treasure whose misfortune had aroused great public sympathy, and the debt was finally cleared after his death through the sale of his copyrights.
real_life_example.explanation: Scott chose poverty and years of overwork over an easier legal escape that would have shortchanged the people he owed, and his public standing survived the financial collapse.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world does not count it a downfall when one who holds to fairness becomes poor; Scott's ruin brought him sympathy rather than disgrace.

tamil:
சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல் அமைந்தொருபால்
கோடாமை சான்றோர்க் கணி.
transliteration:
Saman seydhu seerthookkung kolpol amaindhorupaal
Kodaamai saandrork kani.
meaning: Like a scale that is first set level and then weighs things exactly, a good person stays steady and does not lean to either side. This is their jewel.
elementary: A good weighing scale sits perfectly flat before you put anything on it, then shows the true weight, no matter whose apples they are. A fair person is like that scale: steady and not tipping toward anyone.
university: This is the chapter’s central image. The துலாக்கோல் (tulaakkol, balance-beam) first சமன்செய்து (“makes itself even”), then சீர்தூக்கும் (“weighs rightly”), and does not ஒருபால் கோடாமை (“incline to one side”). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah stress the two-stage sequence: the judge must first be internally level, free of prior bias, and only then evaluate. That is a sharp account of impartiality as a disposition as well as a procedure. The scale is a near-universal emblem of justice: Zeus’s golden scales in Homer, the Qur’anic mīzān, the “just balances” of Leviticus, and the Dhammapada’s sage who weighs good and evil “as if holding a balance-scale.” Aristotle’s description of the judge as “animate justice” and “intermediate” states the same idea philosophically. The second line repeats the refrain of Kural 115, linking inner steadiness under fortune to outer impartiality in judgment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Shibi, when a hawk demands a dove that has taken refuge with him, refuses to wrong either bird. He offers his own flesh equal in weight to the dove, placing it on a scale, and finally climbs onto the scale himself, after which the gods (Indra and Agni in disguise) reveal themselves and praise him.
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata, Shibi will not favour the dove at the hawk’s expense or the hawk at the dove’s, and a literal pair of scales settles the matter.
hinduism.tie_back: An Indian story in which the scale itself is the emblem of refusing to lean toward either party.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Shibi and the dove)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his critics to judge by what is truly right, not by surface impressions.
christianity.tie_back: Like the level scale, righteous judgment weighs the real substance and not appearances or bias.

islam.quote_or_event: “That you not transgress within the balance. And establish weight in justice and do not make deficient the balance.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says God set up the cosmic balance (al-mīzān) and commands people not to violate it but to weigh with justice.
islam.tie_back: The same image of the balance as the model of justice, which must not be tipped.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure. Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have”
judaism.explanation: The Torah puts judgment and weights and measures in the same command: both must be exact and fair.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s scale-and-judgment pairing appears here in one sentence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by observing silence does one become a sage, if he be foolish and ignorant. But that man is wise who, as if holding a balance-scale accepts only the good.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada uses a balance-scale image: the true sage weighs things carefully, taking the good and rejecting the evil.
buddhism.tie_back: A direct balance-scale metaphor for the discerning person, as in the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He, in whom attachment and aversion do not create any disturbance, (is said to have) steadfast equanimity, according to the preaching of the omniscient.”
jainism.explanation: Kundakunda defines true equanimity (sāmāyika) as a mind that neither attachment nor aversion can tip.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's balance-beam first sets itself level and leans to neither side, and Kundakunda's sage, unmoved by attachment or aversion, is that balance in Jain terms.
jainism.source: Kundakunda, Niyamasāra 9.128 'Supreme Equanimity' (English rendering on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Mind is the scale, consciousness the weights, and the performance of Your service is the appraiser.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the merchant's balance as an image for the inner discipline by which a person weighs rightly.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's balance-beam first sets itself level and then weighs without leaning; Guru Nanak likewise makes the mind itself the scale that must be true.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 731, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the father of all balanced his golden scales and placed a doom in each of them, one for Achilles and the other for Hector. As he held the scales by the middle, the doom of Hector fell down deep into the house of Hades”
greek_mythology.explanation: Even Zeus, who pities Hector, does not decide by favour; he weighs the two fates on his golden scales, holding them “by the middle,” and accepts the result.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The balance held level at the centre, deciding without favour, is the Kural’s image.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “to go to the judge is to go to justice; for the nature of the judge is to be a sort of animate justice; and they seek the judge as an intermediate”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle describes the judge as justice in living form: a mean point that restores equality between two parties.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s judge-as-intermediate is the philosophical version of the Kural’s level balance-beam.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.4 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Athens chooses jurors by allotment machine
real_life_example.date: 4th century BCE (procedure described); surviving machines mid-2nd century BCE
real_life_example.event: Classical Athens chose many officials and jurors by lot rather than by election. The Aristotelian Constitution of the Athenians gives a detailed account of how jurors for the courts were allotted, and stone allotment machines called kleroteria, found in and around the Athenian Agora, confirm that picture: citizens' bronze tickets were inserted into rows of slots, and an attached mechanical device made the selection by chance. The surviving inscribed machines date to the mid-second century BCE.
real_life_example.explanation: The Athenians built the removal of favouritism into the procedure itself, so that the panel was settled by chance before any case was weighed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the just to a balance that first sets itself level and then weighs; the allotment machine levelled the scale before judgment began.

tamil:
சொற்கோட்டம் இல்லது செப்பம் ஒருதலையா
உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை பெறின்.
transliteration:
Sorkottam illadhu seppam orudhalaiyaa
Utkottam inmai perin.
meaning: Fair words are truly fair only when the heart is also firmly fair and does not secretly take one side.
elementary: A shiny apple can still be rotten inside. Saying fair-sounding words isn’t enough; your heart has to be fair on the inside too, and then your words will be truly straight.
university: The couplet pairs சொற்கோட்டம் (“crookedness of word”) with உட்கோட்டம் (“inner crookedness”) and makes the first depend on the second: straight speech is செப்பம் (rectitude) only if one ஒருதலையா (“definitely, without fail”) has an unbent inner state. The target is the sophisticated partiality of someone who says the right things while privately favouring one side. That concern fits a chapter aimed at those who arbitrate, give testimony or advise. Commentators read it both ways. Varadarasanar treats inner straightness as the condition, while Pappaiah and Karunanidhi treat straight speech as its natural result. The same principle, that honest speech flows from an honest heart, appears in Jesus’ “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh,” Achilles’ contempt for the man “who says one thing while he hides another in his heart,” and Plato’s distinction between the lie in words and the “true lie” in the soul.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita treats right speech as a discipline (tapas) grouped with discipline of mind and body in the neighbouring verses.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat truthful, straight speech as a moral discipline linked to inner purity.

christianity.quote_or_event: “for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that words reveal and flow from what fills the heart.
christianity.tie_back: The same dependence the Kural states: straight words need a straight heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “So follow not [personal] inclination, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allah is ever, with what you do, Acquainted.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an links inner inclination (hawā) with distorted testimony, and warns that God sees both.
islam.tie_back: Inner bias and twisted words are named together, the Kural’s utkottam and sorkottam.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm describes the person fit to dwell with God as one whose truthfulness goes all the way into the heart.
judaism.tie_back: “Speaketh the truth in his heart” is close to the Kural’s requirement that straightness be internal as well as spoken.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with a pure mind a person speaks or acts happiness follows him like his never-departing shadow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada opens by teaching that the mind comes first and speech and action follow from it.
buddhism.tie_back: Both locate the source of straight speech in the state of the mind.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Crooked and deceptive actions of mind, speach and body, and criticising the right actions and prompting for wrong actions cause the influx of inauspicious physique-making karmas.” The next sutra adds: “The opposites of these (namely straightforward activity and honestry or candour) cause the influx of auspicious physique-making karmas.”
jainism.explanation: Umāsvāti names crookedness (yoga-vakratā) as a single fault running through mind, speech and body together, and its cure as straightforwardness (ārjava) in all three.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says straight speech is true rectitude only if the heart is also unbent, and the Tattvārtha Sūtra likewise treats crookedness of mind and of speech as one fault to be removed together.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.22-23 (English rendering on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone are true, whose love for God is deep and heart-felt. Those who have one thing in their heart, and something else in their mouth, are judged to be false.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose verses are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, condemns the gap between heart and mouth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says straight speech counts as fairness only when the heart itself is free of crookedness; Farid says the same split between inner and outer marks a person as false.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Him do I hate even as the gates of hell who says one thing while he hides another in his heart; therefore I will say what I mean.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles rejects Agamemnon’s envoys, declaring that he despises anyone whose words differ from their heart.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The gap between heart and speech that the Kural condemns, named in Homer.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the true lie, if such an expression may be allowed, is hated of gods and men” … “the lie in words is only a kind of imitation and shadowy image of a previous affection of the soul”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates distinguishes the lie in words from the “true lie” in the soul, and says spoken falsehood is only a shadow of a prior distortion inside.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural has the same two layers: crookedness in word depends on crookedness within.

real_life_example.event_title: The secret file at Alfred Dreyfus's court-martial
real_life_example.event: In autumn 1894 French intelligence found that a secret military document had been sent to the German military attache in Paris, and Captain Alfred Dreyfus, the only Jewish officer on the army General Staff, was arrested on the basis of handwriting analysis. At his court-martial the war ministry placed before the judges a file of secret, and in some cases forged, documents that his lawyer was not allowed to see, and he was convicted of treason. Evidence later pointed to another officer, Ferdinand Walsin-Esterhazy, and in July 1906 the verdict against Dreyfus was set aside and he was exonerated.
real_life_example.explanation: The trial had the outward form of military justice, but the outcome was driven by hidden evidence and, according to the US Holocaust Memorial Museum, by anti-Jewish prejudice.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says fair words count as fairness only when the heart is free of bias; the Dreyfus court-martial shows a correct-looking procedure corrupted by crooked intent within.

tamil:
வாணிகம் செய்வார்க்கு வாணிகம் பேணிப்
பிறவும் தமபோல் செயின்.
transliteration:
Vaanigam seyvaarkku vaanigam penip
Piravum thamapol seyin.
meaning: For traders, the right way to trade is to protect other people’s goods and interests as carefully as their own.
elementary: A good shopkeeper weighs your rice as carefully as if it were for her own family, and charges you the same fair price she’d want to pay herself. That’s what honest business means.
university: The chapter closes by applying impartiality to commerce, the everyday setting where people most often weigh and measure for one another. பிறவும் தமபோல் (“others’ [goods] as their own”) is the principle: the merchant must take no more and give no less than they would accept if the roles were reversed. Parimelazhagar notes the scale imagery carried over from Kural 118, since trade literally involves weighing. The doubled வாணிகம் (“trade … trade”) is emphatic: only this is real trade, and anything else is disguised theft. Parallels include the Qur’anic curse on those who give short measure, the Talmudic tradition that the first question at the heavenly judgment is “Did you conduct business faithfully?”, Hesiod’s counsel to give fair measure “or better,” and Kant’s honest shopkeeper who charges a child the same as anyone else. Kant adds that honesty practised only because it pays is not yet fully moral, which fits the Kural’s demand for inner straightness in Kural 119.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He is a perfect yogī who, by comparison to his own self, sees the true equality of all beings, in both their happiness and their distress, O Arjuna!”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna praises the person who judges others’ joys and sufferings by comparison with their own (ātmaupamya).
hinduism.tie_back: The same “as one’s own” standard the Kural applies to a merchant’s dealings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus gives the Golden Rule as the summary of the whole law.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural applies the Golden Rule to buying and selling.

islam.quote_or_event: “Woe to those who give less [than due], Who, when they take a measure from people, take in full. But if they give by measure or by weight to them, they cause loss.”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Mutaffifin (“The Defrauders”) condemns traders who demand full measure for themselves but short others.
islam.tie_back: The exact opposite of the Kural’s ideal: these traders use a double standard, one for themselves and another for others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “when a person is brought to judgment for the life he lived in this world, they say to him in the order of that verse: Did you conduct business faithfully?”
judaism.explanation: Rava teaches that the very first question asked at the heavenly judgment is whether one did business honestly (nasata ve-natata be-emunah).
judaism.tie_back: Both make honest trade a central religious and moral test.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; life is dear to all. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada grounds ethics in putting oneself in another’s place.
buddhism.tie_back: The same self-other comparison underlies the Kural’s rule of treating others’ goods as one’s own.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Prompting others to steal, receiving stolen goods, underbuying in a disordered state, using false weights and measures, and deceiving others with artificial or imitation goods are the five transgressions of non-stealing.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain layperson's vow of non-stealing explicitly forbids false weights and measures and adulterated goods, which binds merchants to honest dealing.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the true way of trade is to guard others' interests as one's own, and the Jain householder vow writes this into commerce by forbidding cheating in weights, measures and goods.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.27 (English rendering on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Macauliffe records that Nanak, as storekeeper for Governor Daulat Khan at Sultanpur, carried out his duties to everyone's satisfaction, giving most of his own allowance to the poor; when weighing out provisions and reaching thirteen, tera, he would repeat the word, which also means 'Thine'. When complaints of extravagance were investigated, the store was found full and his accounts correct, with money owed to him.
sikhism.explanation: The story presents Guru Nanak's honest handling of another's goods as an act of devotion.
sikhism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's rule for traders: guard other people's goods as carefully as one's own.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, ch. III, pp. 33, 42-43 (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Take fair measure from your neighbour and pay him back fairly with the same measure, or better, if you can; so that if you are in need afterwards, you may find him sure.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod advises his brother to deal with neighbours using an honest measure, returning as much or more.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same measure for self and other is the Kural’s formula for honest trade.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is always a matter of duty that a dealer should not over charge an inexperienced purchaser; and wherever there is much commerce the prudent tradesman does not overcharge, but keeps a fixed price for everyone, so that a child buys of him as well as any other.”
philosophy.explanation: Kant’s famous shopkeeper charges everyone, even a child, the same fair price. Kant adds that doing so only out of self-interest would not yet show true moral worth.
philosophy.tie_back: The honest merchant who treats every buyer alike is the Kural’s ideal. Kant’s caveat about motive echoes Kural 119’s demand for an unbent heart.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section (trans. T. K. Abbott)

real_life_example.event_title: The first Fairtrade label, Max Havelaar
real_life_example.place: Netherlands, with coffee from Oaxaca, Mexico
real_life_example.event: Indigenous coffee farmers of the UCIRI cooperative in Oaxaca, Mexico, asked the Dutch development organisation Solidaridad for access to European markets on equitable terms. Rather than start its own coffee brand, Solidaridad created the Max Havelaar label, launched on 15 November 1988, which could be placed on coffee of any brand whose buyers paid the farmers a price above the market rate plus a premium. The first labelled coffee came from UCIRI and was sold through world shops and mainstream retailers across the Netherlands, and similar labels spread across Europe, leading in 1997 to the umbrella organisation Fairtrade International.
real_life_example.explanation: The scheme asked traders and shoppers to treat the farmers' interests as part of the bargain instead of simply paying the lowest possible price.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says true trade means guarding others' interests as one's own; Max Havelaar turned that principle into a working label for ordinary commerce.

tamil:
அடக்கம் அமரருள் உய்க்கும் அடங்காமை
ஆரிருள் உய்த்து விடும்.
transliteration:
Adakkam amararul uykkum adangaamai
Aarirul uyththu vidum.
meaning: Self-control lifts a person up to live among the gods. A lack of it pushes them into a deep darkness they cannot escape.
elementary: Picture two staircases. One climbs up to a bright room full of wise, kind people; the other goes down into a dark basement with no lights. Every time you hold yourself back from doing something wrong, you climb one step up. Every time you just do whatever you feel like, you slip one step down.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter by setting the stakes in the starkest possible terms: amarar (the immortals, the devas) versus aar-irul (a darkness that is ‘hard to bear’ or ‘dense’), which the medieval commentator Parimelazhagar glosses as a particular hell. Parimelazhagar defines adakkam as the condition in which body, speech and mind (mey, mozhi, manam) do not stray into wrong paths, and explains that the chapter follows ‘Impartiality’ because one who sees his own faults as clearly as others’ will naturally restrain himself. Modern commentators such as Karunanidhi read the couplet in this-worldly terms — restraint earns undying renown, indiscipline darkens life itself — showing how the couplet supports both a religious and a secular reading. Its two-path structure, one road upward and one downward, is among the most widespread forms in world ethical literature, from the Dhammapada’s ‘path to the Deathless’ to Paul’s sowing to the flesh or the Spirit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names the unrestrained passions as the literal doorways into hell and tells Arjuna that a sensible person closes them.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita makes unrestraint the road into darkness, so restraint is what keeps a person out of it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes two harvests: indulging the flesh yields decay, while living by the Spirit yields eternal life.
christianity.tie_back: Same two destinations as the Kural: giving in to impulse leads down, disciplined living leads up to everlasting life.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an promises Paradise to the one who restrains his soul from its unlawful desires out of awe of God.
islam.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s first line: holding back the self is what brings a person to the heavenly realm.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A man’s pride shall bring him low; but he that is of a lowly spirit shall attain to honour.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that pride drags a person down while humility lifts him to honour.
judaism.tie_back: The same up-or-down outcome as the Kural, with humility (a core sense of adakkam) as the thing that raises a person.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless. Heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful die not. The heedless are as if dead already.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha presents watchful self-guarding as the road to the Deathless (Nibbana) and careless living as the road to death.
buddhism.tie_back: Same two-road teaching: guarding oneself leads to the highest state, letting oneself go leads to ruin and darkness.

jainism.quote_or_event: “My own Self is the river Vaitaraṇî, my own Self the Śâlmalî tree; my own Self is the miraculous cow Kâmaduh, my own Self the park Nandana. My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anāthi tells King Śreṇika that the soul itself becomes the hell-river and thorn-tree of the damned or the wish-cow and paradise-garden of the gods, depending on how it governs its own conduct.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes self-command the only thing that decides whether a person rises to the realm of the gods or sinks into the darkness of hell.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.36–37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They conquer the five thieves, and enshrine the True Lord in the heart.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that subduing the five thieves (lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego) opens the heart to God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says self-restraint lifts a person to the company of the immortals; in Sikh terms, conquering the five thieves leads to union with God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 223, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus warns his son Icarus to fly a middle course on their wax-and-feather wings. Icarus, thrilled by flight, soars too near the sun; the wax melts and he plunges into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows the fate of a youth who could not hold himself back from excess even when warned.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Icarus shows the Kural’s second line: lack of restraint doesn’t just fail, it sends a person plunging down.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates pictures the soul as a charioteer driving a noble horse and an unruly one. Souls whose charioteer masters the unruly horse follow the gods up to the heavens and see true reality; those dragged about by it lose their wings and sink to earth.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, the soul’s rise or fall depends on whether reason can govern appetite.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s myth has the same two directions as the Kural: self-mastery carries the soul up among the gods, unruliness drags it down.

real_life_example.event_title: Stanislav Petrov judges a missile alert to be false
real_life_example.place: Early-warning command bunker near Moscow, Soviet Union (now Russia)
real_life_example.event: Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov was on duty at a Soviet early-warning bunker outside Moscow when the satellite system reported that the United States had launched five intercontinental ballistic missiles at the Soviet Union. Reasoning that a real American first strike would use far more than five missiles, and with ground radars not confirming the launches, he reported the alert as a false alarm rather than treating it as an attack; the satellites had mistaken sunlight reflecting off clouds for missile launches. He was reprimanded over paperwork rather than rewarded, the incident stayed secret until after the Soviet Union collapsed, and he later received international honours including the 2013 Dresden Peace Prize, although Russia's UN mission argued that no single officer could have started or prevented a nuclear war.
real_life_example.explanation: In a period of high tension, one officer's refusal to act on alarm rather than evidence is widely credited with avoiding a possible catastrophe.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural sets restraint, which raises a person among the immortals, against its absence, which leads into thick darkness; Petrov's restraint is remembered worldwide, while the alternative could have meant darkness for millions.

tamil:
காக்க பொருளா அடக்கத்தை ஆக்கம்
அதனினூஉங் கில்லை உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Kaakka porulaa adakkaththai aakkam
Adhaninoovung killai uyirkku.
meaning: Guard self-control like a treasure, because no living being has anything that does more good than this.
elementary: People lock their money in a safe so nobody can take it. This kural says self-control is worth even more than money, so you should protect it just as carefully. You can lose toys or money, but if you hold on to your self-control, it keeps you good.
university: The key word is porulaa, ‘as wealth’ or ‘as a thing of real value’; Parimelazhagar glosses it as uruthip porul, an ultimate or assured good. The couplet turns ordinary economics upside down: restraint is not a sacrifice that costs us something but an asset (aakkam, ‘growth, prosperity’) that must be actively guarded (kaakka). That implies it can be lost or stolen, presumably by the passions. Parimelazhagar notes that uyir (‘living being’) here means human life in particular, since only humans can understand restraint and benefit from it. The idea that inner self-command is the truest possession has close relatives in the Stoic distinction between what is ‘up to us’ and what is not, and in the Mishnah’s redefinition of the mighty and the rich.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One must deliver himself with the help of his mind, and not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that a disciplined mind lifts a person up while an undisciplined one drags him down, so one’s own mind is either best friend or worst enemy.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat mastery over oneself as the greatest resource a person has, something to be protected and used for one’s own uplift.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sets the soul above the entire world’s wealth: nothing could be worth trading it for.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Jesus reorders what counts as ‘profit’: the inner life outweighs any outward gain.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth is not in having many possessions, but rather (true) wealth is feeling sufficiency in the soul.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet defines real wealth as an inner state of contentment rather than an accumulation of things.
islam.tie_back: Both sayings move ‘wealth’ from outside to inside: a governed, satisfied soul is the true treasure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines might as self-conquest, and in the same teaching defines the rich man as ‘he who rejoices in his lot.’
judaism.tie_back: Just as Valluvar calls restraint the highest wealth, the Mishnah calls self-mastery true strength and contentment true riches.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Wonderful, indeed, it is to subdue the mind, so difficult to subdue, ever swift, and seizing whatever it desires. A tamed mind brings happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises the taming of the restless, grasping mind as the source of happiness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts name disciplining oneself as the single greatest good a person can obtain.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Subdue your Self, for the Self is difficult to subdue; if your Self is subdued, you will be happy in this world and in the next.”
jainism.explanation: The first lecture of the Uttarādhyayana presents self-subjugation as the hardest task and the surest source of well-being in both lives.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to guard restraint as our treasure since no greater good exists for a living being; Mahāvīra's verse likewise makes the subdued self the source of happiness here and hereafter.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Let self-control be the furnace, and patience the goldsmith.”
sikhism.explanation: In the closing pauri of Japji Guru Nanak lists self-control (jat) as the first part of the mint where the true coin of the Shabad is struck.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks us to guard restraint like a treasure; Japji makes self-control the furnace in which life's real gold is made.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib, Pauri 38, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads, the young Heracles meets two women, Vice and Virtue. Vice offers an easy life of pleasure; Virtue tells him the gods grant nothing truly good without toil and discipline. Heracles chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable presents disciplined virtue as the path to real and lasting goods, and easy pleasure as a false bargain.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles treats disciplined virtue as the treasure worth choosing above all, just as the Kural urges.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus’ ‘Choice of Heracles,’ in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21–34 (paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Temperance, I replied, is the ordering or controlling of certain pleasures and desires; this is curiously enough implied in the saying of ‘a man being his own master’”
philosophy.explanation: Plato defines temperance (sophrosyne), one of the four cardinal virtues, as the well-ordered rule of the self over its desires.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato ranks self-mastery among the soul’s most precious possessions, much as Valluvar ranks restraint above all wealth.

real_life_example.event_title: Father Theobald Mathew's temperance pledge
real_life_example.event: On 10 April 1838 the Capuchin priest Theobald Mathew presided at the first meeting of the Cork Total Abstinence Society in his own schoolhouse and took the pledge of total abstinence himself. Between 1838 and 1842 he travelled throughout Ireland, where whole crowds took the pledge, and by 1841 the number of abstainers in Ireland was estimated at 4,647,000. Britannica records that within three years consumption of spirits fell by about half, much of the decrease being attributed to his efforts.
real_life_example.explanation: Millions treated a vow of self-restraint as something worth guarding, and contemporaries credited the movement with improvements in public order, though historians note that its gains were weakened by the Great Famine.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says to guard self-restraint like a treasure, since no living being has a greater good; the pledge movement asked ordinary people to do exactly that.

tamil:
செறிவறிந்து சீர்மை பயக்கும் அறிவறிந்து
ஆற்றின் அடங்கப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Serivarindhu seermai payakkum arivarindhu
Aatrin adangap perin.
meaning: If a person learns what is worth knowing and controls themselves in the right way, good people will notice, and it will bring them respect.
elementary: Think of a kid who quietly does the right thing in class without showing off. At first nobody seems to notice, but the teacher does, and soon everyone respects that kid. Quiet goodness gets noticed in the end.
university: The couplet turns on two uses of arindhu (‘having known’). In arivarindhu, the person first understands what true knowledge is; Parimelazhagar reads this as grasping that restraint itself is our wisdom. In serivarindhu, that restraint comes to be known and recognized, by the wise, in Parimelazhagar’s reading. The result is seermai, excellence or eminence. The qualifier aatrin (‘in the proper way’) rules out showy or grudging restraint. Manakkudavar adds a sensory reading: one must know the five sense-objects (taste, sight, touch, sound, smell) and restrain the five organs that seek them. Joining knowledge to restraint echoes the Delphic ‘Know thyself,’ which Greek thought tied to sophrosyne, and Aristotle’s view that the temperate person desires ‘as reason directs.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who restrains his senses, keeping them under full control, and fixes his consciousness upon Me, is known as a man of steady intelligence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that sense-restraint is the mark by which a person of steady wisdom is known.
hinduism.tie_back: Both link restraint to wisdom and say it is what makes a person recognized as wise.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:”
christianity.explanation: Peter promises that those who humble themselves will be lifted up at the proper time.
christianity.tie_back: Same arc as the Kural: restraint and humility practised now bring honour and distinction later.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth easily, and when the ignorant address them [harshly], they say [words of] peace,”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an identifies the true servants of God by their gentle bearing and restrained response to provocation.
islam.tie_back: Restrained conduct is what distinguishes these people and earns them their honoured title, much as the Kural says restraint brings distinction.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men that were upon the face of the earth.”
judaism.explanation: When Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses, the Torah records his exceptional humility, and God then publicly vindicates him.
judaism.tie_back: Moses’ restraint is noticed and honoured from on high, the same recognition the Kural promises to the restrained.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even the gods hold dear the wise one, whose senses are subdued like horses well trained by a charioteer, whose pride is destroyed and who is free from the cankers.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the wise one with tamed senses and no pride is cherished even by the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts join wisdom with sense-restraint and humility and say such a person wins high regard.

jainism.quote_or_event: “An intelligent man who has learned (the sacred texts) takes his duties upon himself, and he becomes renowned in the world; as the earth is the dwelling of all beings, so he will be a dwelling of all duties.”
jainism.explanation: In the lecture on discipline, the pupil who joins learning to disciplined, willing conduct gains renown and becomes a support for every duty.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural promises distinction, recognized by the good, to one who knows what true knowledge is and is restrained in the right way; this verse likewise pairs learning with disciplined conduct and promises renown.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.45 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, he is a brave warrior, who conquers and subdues his vicious inner ego.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das redefines heroism as the conquest of one's own haumai.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says restraint, understood as wisdom, wins recognition from the good; Gurbani gives the person who masters himself the honoured title of true hero.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 86, Siree Raag, Siree Raag ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The maxims ‘Know thyself’ and ‘Nothing in excess’ were inscribed at Apollo’s temple at Delphi. In Plato’s Charmides, Critias argues that this self-knowledge is the very heart of sophrosyne (temperance).
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek religious tradition joined knowing oneself to keeping within limits.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘knowing that restraint is wisdom’ matches the Delphic joining of self-knowledge and self-limitation.
greek_mythology.source: Delphic maxims, discussed in Plato, Charmides 164d–165a (paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the temperate man craves for the things he ought, as he ought, and when he ought; and this is what rational principle directs”
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, temperance is desire rightly ordered by reason, neither suppressed blindly nor indulged.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s ‘as he ought’ matches Valluvar’s aatrin, restraint practised in the proper way and guided by understanding.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.12, 1119b (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Albert Luthuli receives the Nobel Peace Prize
real_life_example.place: Groutville, South Africa, and Oslo, Norway
real_life_example.event: Albert Luthuli, a teacher and chief who was elected president-general of the African National Congress in December 1952, became the spokesman of a campaign of nonviolent civil disobedience against South Africa's racial segregation laws, inspired by Gandhi's philosophy. He was dismissed as chief, repeatedly banned and confined to his rural district, and arrested in the treason arrests of 1956, yet he continued to appeal for nonviolence and a shared society. The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded him the 1960 Nobel Peace Prize for his non-violent struggle against apartheid, making him Africa's first Peace Prize laureate; he received it the following year.
real_life_example.explanation: Luthuli's disciplined refusal to meet persecution with violence was recognised by the wider world even while his own government silenced him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that restraint understood as wisdom and practised rightly will be recognised by the good and bring distinction; Luthuli's restraint earned the world's highest honour for peace.

tamil:
நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான் தோற்றம்
மலையினும் மாணப் பெரிது.
transliteration:
Nilaiyin thiriyaadhu adangiyaan thotram
Malaiyinum maanap peridhu.
meaning: A person who controls themselves and never leaves their proper path in life stands taller than a mountain.
elementary: A mountain stays put no matter how hard the wind blows. A person who stays calm and humble and keeps doing the right thing, without bragging, looks even ‘taller’ to others than a mountain.
university: Parimelazhagar reads nilai (‘station’) as the householder’s way of life, which fits the couplet’s place in the Illaraviyal (the section on domestic virtue). He takes ‘restraint without swerving’ to mean self-governance while still legitimately using the senses: disciplined participation in ordinary life, not ascetic withdrawal. Manakkudavar instead glosses nilai as one’s varnashrama duty. Thotram, ‘appearance’ or ‘stature,’ is read by Solomon Pappaiah as the impression such a person leaves in others’ minds, and the paradox is deliberate: the one who lowers himself appears the loftiest. The mountain works as an image of both height and immovability, which invites comparison with the Stoic promontory and the Buddhist unshaken rock.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who is not disturbed by the incessant flow of desires – that enter like rivers into the ocean, which is ever being filled but is always still – can alone achieve peace, and not the man who strives to satisfy such desires.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna likens the steady sage to the ocean, which rivers keep pouring into without ever disturbing it.
hinduism.tie_back: Where Valluvar uses a mountain, the Gita uses the ocean: both picture the unswerving, restrained person as vast and unmoved.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that self-exaltation leads to humiliation and humility to being raised up.
christianity.tie_back: The same paradox as the Kural: the one who holds himself low ends up standing highest.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear the earth [apart], and you will never reach the mountains in height.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an mocks arrogance: however proudly a person struts, he will never be as tall as the mountains.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an says arrogance can never reach a mountain’s height; the Kural says restraint rises above it. Both use the mountain to show that true greatness comes from humility.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; And he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs ranks the self-controlled person above the warrior and the conqueror.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say self-rule gives a greatness beyond the world’s most impressive achievements, a conqueror’s in one case and a mountain’s height in the other.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures the wise person as a solid rock that storms cannot move.
buddhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s mountain, the rock stands for someone who stays steady and does not swerve from his course.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By possession of conduct he obtains a stability like that of the king of mountains (viz. Mêru), whereby a houseless monk destroys the four remnants of Karman which even a Kêvalin possesses.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's catalogue of spiritual exertions teaches that steady conduct gives the soul the immovability of Mount Meru, the axis of the Jain cosmos, and carries it to liberation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the stature of one who stays restrained without swerving is greater than a mountain; the Jain text uses the greatest mountain of all, Meru, as the image for the person firm in conduct.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.61 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Through the Word of the Guru's Shabad, they conquer the five thieves.” … “Even as householders, they lovingly attune themselves to the True Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes Gurmukhs who master the passions while living the ordinary householder's life.
sikhism.tie_back: Parimelazhagar reads the Kural as praising restraint that never leaves the householder's station; Sikhism likewise sets self-mastery within family life, not in renunciation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 230, Raag Gauree, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Back home in disguise as a beggar, Odysseus is mocked by the suitors and the disloyal maids. Though his heart ‘growls’ within him, he tells it to endure, recalling that it once endured worse in the Cyclops’ cave, and holds himself back until the right moment.
greek_mythology.explanation: The hero of the Odyssey shows restraint by refusing to strike prematurely, staying true to his purpose despite provocation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus stays restrained without swerving from his goal, and that restraint is exactly what makes his eventual victory so great.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius tells himself to stand like a rocky headland that waves keep hitting without moving it.
philosophy.tie_back: Marcus’ unmoved promontory and Valluvar’s mountain are the same image: a steady, self-governed person standing tall above life’s turmoil.

real_life_example.event_title: George Washington resigns his commission
real_life_example.place: Maryland State House, Annapolis, Maryland, United States
real_life_example.event: After British troops evacuated New York at the end of the American Revolutionary War, General George Washington, commander-in-chief of the Continental Army, bade farewell to his officers and travelled to Annapolis, where the Continental Congress was meeting. On 23 December 1783, in the Senate chamber of the Maryland State House, he resigned his commission before Congress in an emotional ceremony. He left Annapolis at dawn the next day and reached his home at Mount Vernon on Christmas Eve, a private citizen for the first time in almost nine years.
real_life_example.explanation: At the height of his power and popularity, Washington handed military authority back to the civilian government and returned to private life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the stature of one who stays restrained and does not swerve from his proper path rises higher than a mountain; Washington's voluntary return to private life is still commemorated in the room where it happened.

tamil:
எல்லார்க்கும் நன்றாம் பணிதல் அவருள்ளும்
செல்வர்க்கே செல்வம் தகைத்து.
transliteration:
Ellaarkkum nandraam panidhal avarullum
Selvarkke selvam thakaiththu.
meaning: Being humble is good for everyone. But in rich people, humility shines like a second kind of riches.
elementary: Imagine a kid with the coolest new bike who still lets others ride it and never brags. Everyone likes that kid even more. Being humble when you have a lot is like having a bonus treasure on top of everything else.
university: Panidhal (‘bowing, humility’) makes explicit the social side of adakkam. Parimelazhagar explains why the rich are singled out: learning and noble birth already tend to restrain a person, so humility in the learned or well-born does not stand out, but wealth naturally breeds pride (perumitham). Humility in the rich is therefore especially striking, a ‘wealth added to wealth’ (selvam thakaiththu). He also points out that couplets 121–125 treat restraint in general, while 126 turns to bodily restraint, 127–129 to restraint of speech, and 130 to restraint of mind. The couplet reflects a view found in many traditions that prosperity, more than hardship, is the real test of character.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He, who is the master of riches but not of his senses, certainly loseth his riches in consequence of his want of mastery over his senses.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura warns King Dhritarashtra that wealth without self-mastery destroys itself.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura puts from the negative side what Valluvar puts positively: for the wealthy, restraint is what keeps and crowns their wealth.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 34 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to warn the wealthy in particular against pride.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Paul singles out the rich as the people for whom humility matters most.
