islam.quote_or_event: “Charity does not decrease wealth, no one forgives another except that Allah increases his honor, and no one humbles himself for the sake of Allah except that Allah raises his status.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that giving doesn’t diminish wealth and that humility raises a person’s standing.
islam.tie_back: Both sayings treat humility as an enrichment, something that adds to a person’s worth rather than taking away from it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “and when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, and thy silver and thy gold is multiplied, and all that thou hast is multiplied; then thy heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God”
judaism.explanation: Moses warns Israel that prosperity is exactly when pride and forgetfulness of God set in.
judaism.tie_back: Same insight as the Kural: wealth is the moment humility is most needed and most tested.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To be respectful, humble, contented and grateful; and to listen to the Dhamma on due occasions — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: In his list of life’s highest blessings, the Buddha includes humility.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha counts humility among life’s greatest blessings, close to Valluvar calling it a further wealth.
buddhism.source: Maha-mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: King Śreṇika, ruler of Magadha and owner of horses, elephants, a city and a harem, first mocks a young monk and offers him pleasures, then is so taught by him that he begs forgiveness: “When the lion of kings had thus, with the greatest devotion, praised the lion of houseless monks, he, together with his wives, servants, and relations, became a staunch believer in the Law, with a pure mind.”
jainism.explanation: The richest king of the age bows his head before a monk with no possessions, and the canon presents this humility as his true gain.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says humility suits everyone but shines as a second wealth in the wealthy; Śreṇika's bow before the penniless sage is a canonical picture of exactly that.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.2, 20.14–15 and 20.54–59, quoting 20.58 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who has the Guru on his side - how could he be proud of his wealth?”
sikhism.explanation: Bhatt Nal, a court poet whose Savaiye are in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that one guided by the Guru does not grow proud of riches.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says humility in the wealthy shines like a second wealth; the Bhatt's verse names that same freedom from the pride wealth breeds.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1399, Savaiye (Bhatt Nal) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The fabulously rich King Croesus of Lydia asks the Athenian sage Solon who is the happiest of men, expecting to be named. Solon refuses to call any man happy before his end. Later, defeated and on the pyre, Croesus remembers Solon’s words and calls out his name.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tradition used Croesus as the classic case of a rich man whose pride is humbled by fortune.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus learns too late what the Kural teaches: in the rich, humility is the crowning quality and pride the fatal flaw.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “These reasonings are unconnected: ‘I am richer than you, therefore I am better’; ‘I am more eloquent than you, therefore I am better.’ … But you, after all, are neither property nor style.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus points out the logical error in letting wealth inflate one’s sense of personal worth.
philosophy.tie_back: Epictetus shows why a rich person has no grounds for pride, which is why humility in the wealthy is the fitting response the Kural praises.

real_life_example.event_title: Princess Elizabeth trains as an army mechanic
real_life_example.place: Auxiliary Territorial Service training centre, southern England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Princess Elizabeth, heir to the British throne, turned 18 in April 1944, and in February 1945 she enlisted in the Auxiliary Territorial Service, the women's branch of the British Army, as Second Subaltern Elizabeth Alexandra Mary Windsor. On a driving and vehicle maintenance course she learned to service, maintain and drive heavy army vehicles, and the Imperial War Museums notes that she was treated the same as the rest of her company. She became the first woman in the Royal Family to be a full-time member of the armed services and qualified as a driver before the war ended.
real_life_example.explanation: The press nicknamed her Princess Auto Mechanic, and her willingness to do ordinary work alongside other young women was widely admired.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says humility is good in everyone but shines like a second wealth in the wealthy; a future queen in overalls changing tyres displayed exactly that kind of humility.

tamil:
ஒருமையுள் ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல் ஆற்றின்
எழுமையும் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Orumaiyul aamaipol aindhadakkal aatrin
Ezhumaiyum emaap pudaiththu.
meaning: If, in one life, a person can pull in their five senses the way a tortoise pulls in its legs, that power will protect them for seven births (all their lives to come).
elementary: A turtle pulls its head and four legs into its shell when danger comes. We have five senses: eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin. If we can ‘pull them in’ when they want something harmful, we are protected just like the turtle in its shell.
university: The tortoise image (aamai) also appears in Bhagavad Gita 2.58 and in the Pali Kumma Sutta, which points to a shared South Asian stock of contemplative imagery rather than direct borrowing. Parimelazhagar explains the simile exactly: the tortoise withdraws its five members (four legs and head) so that harm cannot get in, and a person should restrain the five senses so that sin cannot get in. He classes this couplet as teaching bodily restraint (meyyadakkam). The contrast of orumai (‘one birth’) and ezhumai (‘seven births’) draws on karma doctrine: effort in one life gives a safeguard (emaappu, ‘protection, fortress’) across many lives, though Karunanidhi secularizes it as ‘for all time.’ The tortoise does not destroy its limbs; it withdraws and extends them at will, so the ideal is mastery of the senses, not mutilation of them.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is able to withdraw his senses from sense objects, as the tortoise draws its limbs within the shell, is firmly fixed in perfect consciousness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna uses the very same tortoise image for the sage who can pull his senses back from their objects.
hinduism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: the same animal, the same withdrawal of the senses, the same idea of protection through self-mastery.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes disciplining his body like an athlete so that he is not himself disqualified.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat mastering the body as a safeguard that protects a person’s ultimate destiny.

islam.quote_or_event: “Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an commands believers to guard their eyes and bodies as a means of purity.
islam.tie_back: Guarding the senses, like the tortoise guarding its limbs, keeps a person pure and protected.

judaism.quote_or_event: “that ye go not about after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go astray;”
judaism.explanation: The commandment of the tzitzit (fringes) is given so that Israel will not be led astray by roaming heart and eyes.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see the unrestrained senses as what lead a person astray, and reining them in as what protects.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a tortoise with its limbs withdrawn in its shell, so the monk, the thoughts of the heart.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Kumma Sutta, a tortoise keeps its four legs and neck withdrawn until a hungry jackal gives up; likewise Mara finds no opening in a monk whose sense-doors are guarded.
buddhism.tie_back: The same tortoise and the same five withdrawn members (four legs and neck) as in the Kural, with the same lesson: guard the senses and harm finds no way in.
buddhism.source: Kumma Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.199 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a tortoise withdraws his limbs within his own body, even so does the valiant withdraw his mind within himself from all sins. He also withdraws his hands, legs, mind, sense-organs, sinful moods, evil words, pride, and deceitfulness. This indeed is the valor of the valiant.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga uses the tortoise drawing in its limbs as the model for the heroic ascetic who withdraws the senses, speech and passions from sin.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's own image: drawing in the five senses like a tortoise its limbs, which in Jain terms stops the inflow (āsrava) of karma that would bind the soul over many births.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.8.16–18, English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I have brought the ten sensory organs under my control, and erased every trace of the five thieves.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Namdev describes bringing all the senses under control and wiping out the passions that ride on them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's tortoise drawing in its limbs is the image of the senses withdrawn and guarded; Namdev's verse states the same mastery of the senses directly.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 693, Raag Dhanaasree, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: To pass the Sirens, whose song lures sailors to their death, Odysseus stops his crew’s ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast so he cannot act on what he hears.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus survives by deliberately shutting off, or binding, his senses’ power to pull him toward destruction.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the tortoise, Odysseus protects himself by pulling his senses back from a deadly attraction.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Philosophy, Socrates says, frees the soul by “persuading her to retire from them, and abstain from all but the necessary use of them, and be gathered up and collected into herself”
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedo, the philosopher draws the soul back from the deceptive senses into itself.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s soul ‘gathered into herself’ is almost the tortoise drawing into its shell: withdrawal from the senses as the path to safety and truth.

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi's three vows before sailing to England
real_life_example.event: When the 18-year-old Mohandas Gandhi prepared to leave Rajkot to study law in England in 1888, his mother feared that young men there took to meat and liquor and hesitated to let him go. Becharji Swami, a Jain monk and family adviser, administered a solemn oath in which Gandhi vowed to abstain from wine, women and meat, and only then did his mother give her permission. Gandhi recounted the episode in his autobiography, The Story of My Experiments with Truth.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi later treated keeping these vows as an early discipline of his life, and self-restraint of the senses became central to his ideas.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises drawing in the five senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs; Gandhi's three vows were a deliberate withdrawal from the pleasures his mother feared would capture him abroad.

tamil:
யாகாவா ராயினும் நாகாக்க காவாக்கால்
சோகாப்பர் சொல்லிழுக்குப் பட்டு.
transliteration:
Yaakaavaa raayinum naakaakka kaavaakkaal
Sokaappar sollizhukkup pattu.
meaning: Whatever else you fail to guard, guard your tongue. If you do not, you will suffer because of the mistakes in your own words.
elementary: If you can only remember one rule, remember this: watch what you say. A friend who blurts out a secret or says something mean in anger can lose friends in a second. Even if you mess up other things, keeping your words kind protects you.
university: The couplet performs its own lesson in sound: the syllable kaa (‘guard’) recurs in yaa-kaavaar, naa-kaakka, kaavaak-kaal and so-kaappar, which makes the verse itself an exercise in controlled, measured speech. Parimelazhagar treats sokaappar (‘they will grieve’) as a single verb, like allaappar, and reads yaa (‘whatever’) as meaning ‘all things without exception.’ This couplet opens the three-verse unit on restraint of speech (mozhi adakkam, 127–129). Its claim that the tongue ranks above every other thing needing guard is a striking priority that other traditions also make: the Hadith pairs the tongue with chastity as the key to Paradise, and the Epistle of James calls the untamed tongue a fire.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita counts disciplined speech as one of the three forms of austerity (tapas), alongside those of body and mind.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat control of the tongue as a spiritual discipline in its own right, not a mere nicety.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man’s religion is vain.”
christianity.explanation: James says that all outward religion is empty if a person does not bridle his tongue.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, James makes guarding the tongue the one indispensable restraint, the test of all the rest.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever can guarantee (the chastity of) what is between his two jaw-bones and what is between his two legs (i.e. his tongue and his private parts), I guarantee Paradise for him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet singles out guarding the tongue (with chastity) as the key to Paradise.
islam.tie_back: Both texts pick out the tongue as the one thing a person above all must guard.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoso keepeth his mouth and his tongue keepeth his soul from troubles.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that guarding one’s speech protects one from trouble.
judaism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s point: guard the tongue, or suffer the troubles that loose speech brings.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let a man guard himself against irritability in speech; let him be controlled in speech. Abandoning verbal misconduct, let him practice good conduct in speech.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers to guard and control their speech and give up verbal misconduct.
buddhism.tie_back: Both use the language of ‘guarding’ speech and warn against faults of the tongue.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By watchfulness of speech he keeps free from prevarication; thereby he enables his mind to act properly.”
jainism.explanation: Vāg-gupti, the guarding of speech, is one of the three Jain guptis (guards of mind, speech and body); the Uttarādhyayana says that guarding the tongue keeps one from falsehood and steadies the mind.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks the tongue above every other thing a person must guard; Jain discipline likewise makes guarding speech one of the three basic protections of the soul.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.54 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “and who speaks insipid words with his tongue, is ruined, again and again.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das warns that the person whose tongue speaks harsh, insipid words brings ruin on himself over and over.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to guard the tongue above all, since those who do not come to grief through their own words; Gurbani says the unguarded tongue leads to repeated ruin.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 594, Raag Vadhans, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The best treasure a man can have is a sparing tongue, and the greatest pleasure, one that moves orderly; for if you speak evil, you yourself will soon be worse spoken of.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod, the poet of the Theogony, advises that a sparing, orderly tongue is a person’s greatest treasure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod, like Valluvar, ranks the guarded tongue above other goods and warns that careless speech comes back on the speaker.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 719–721 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And let silence be the general rule, or let only what is necessary be said, and in few words.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus makes restraint of speech a basic rule of the Stoic life.
philosophy.tie_back: Both philosophers see a guarded tongue as the base of a disciplined life.

real_life_example.event_title: Kaiser Wilhelm II and the Daily Telegraph interview
real_life_example.place: London, United Kingdom, and Berlin, Germany
real_life_example.event: On 28 October 1908 the London Daily Telegraph published an account of conversations in which Kaiser Wilhelm II spoke with what the paper called impulsive and unusual frankness, telling the English they were mad as March hares and saying that much of his own people was unfriendly to England. The remarks angered the British public, were seen in France and Russia as a diplomatic blunder, and set off a political crisis in Germany: in the Reichstag debate of 10 and 11 November all parties criticised the Kaiser, who considered abdicating, and Chancellor Bernhard von Bulow demanded that he change his behaviour. German History in Documents notes that the affair discredited him in the eyes of many Germans and ultimately weakened his position.
real_life_example.explanation: An emperor's unguarded talk, meant to improve relations, instead offended three foreign nations and his own parliament at once.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that whatever else you fail to guard, guard your tongue, for those who do not will grieve; the Kaiser's careless words brought him exactly that grief.

tamil:
ஒன்றானுந் தீச்சொல் பொருட்பயன் உண்டாயின்
நன்றாகா தாகி விடும்.
transliteration:
Ondraanum theechchol porutpayan undaayin
Nandraakaa thaaki vidum.
meaning: If even one word you speak hurts someone through its meaning, all the good you have done becomes useless.
elementary: Imagine a big glass of milk with just one drop of poison in it. You can’t drink any of it now. In the same way, one really mean word can spoil lots of kind things you have said and done.
university: Parimelazhagar identifies ‘evil words’ (theechchol) as falsehood, slander (kuralai) and harsh speech, and reads the couplet to mean that if even one harm reaches another person through such words, the good earned by all one’s other virtues is turned to evil. Manakkudavar offers a subtler alternative: even a single word that sounds sweet but carries a harmful meaning (porutpayan) makes the speech bad. Karunanidhi’s image of a drop of poison in a pot of milk captures the moral asymmetry: harm is not simply offset by good but contaminates it. That puts the Kural at odds with purely additive ‘merit ledgers’ and aligns it with Ecclesiastes’ dead flies in the perfumer’s ointment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Pride, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance – these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita lists harshness of speech (parushyam) among the marks of a demonic nature.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat harsh speech as something that corrupts a person’s whole character, not a minor slip.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be. Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?”
christianity.explanation: James says a mouth that both blesses and curses is as unnatural as a spring giving sweet and bitter water.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say that bad words poison the good that comes from the same mouth.

islam.quote_or_event: “A slave (of Allah) may utter a word which pleases Allah without giving it much importance, and because of that Allah will raise him to degrees (of reward): a slave (of Allah) may utter a word (carelessly) which displeases Allah without thinking of its gravity and because of that he will be thrown into the Hell-Fire.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that a single careless word can outweigh a person’s standing and cast him into the Fire.
islam.tie_back: Same asymmetry as the Kural: one evil word can overturn the good of a lifetime.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Dead flies make the ointment of the perfumer fetid and putrid; so doth a little folly outweigh wisdom and honour.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes teaches that a small amount of folly can spoil a great store of wisdom and honour, just as dead flies ruin fine perfume.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the same image as Karunanidhi’s poison in milk: a small corruption spoils a large good.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Surely, when a person is born, an axe is born in his mouth, with which he cuts himself— the fool saying a bad statement.”
buddhism.explanation: The monk Kokalika slanders the Buddha’s chief disciples Sariputta and Moggallana despite three warnings; though a monk, he falls into hell, and the Buddha speaks this verse.
buddhism.tie_back: Kokalika’s religious life counted for nothing once he spoke evil, which is exactly the Kural’s warning that one harmful word undoes all good.
buddhism.source: Kokalika Sutta, Sutta Nipata 3.10 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “One may have a tuft or matted hair on the head or a shaven head, remain naked or wear a rag. But if he tells a lie, all this is futile or fruitless.”
jainism.explanation: The Digambara text Bhagavatī Ārādhanā teaches that a single untruth empties every outward austerity of its worth.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says one harmful word turns all a person's good to no good; this verse makes the same asymmetric claim, that one false word cancels all accumulated religious effort.
jainism.source: Bhagavatī Ārādhanā 843 (Śivārya), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are in the Guru Granth Sahib, forbids even one harsh word because the Lord lives in every person addressed.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a single harmful word can turn all one's good to no good; Farid's 'not even a single harsh word' carries the same weight on one utterance.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, a mortal so favoured that he dined at the table of the gods, is cast into eternal punishment. In Euripides’ Orestes, Electra says the cause was his ‘unbridled tongue,’ which she calls a most shameful disease.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this telling, a man who had every divine honour lost all of it through unrestrained speech.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tantalus shows the Kural’s asymmetry: a lifetime of divine favour undone by a failure of the tongue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “out of words light as air, in very deed the greatest enmities and hatreds spring up.”
philosophy.explanation: In the Laws, Plato forbids abusive speech because light words grow into the greatest enmities.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar both see that small, harmful words produce harm out of all proportion to their size.

real_life_example.event_title: Gerald Ratner's speech destroys his company's reputation
real_life_example.place: Institute of Directors convention, London, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Gerald Ratner had built Ratners Group into Britain's biggest jewellery chain by selling inexpensive jewellery to a mass market. Speaking at the Institute of Directors' convention in London in April 1991, he joked that one of his firm's products was so cheap because it was rubbish, using a crude word, and that a pair of its earrings would probably not last as long as a prawn sandwich. The remarks were widely reported, the value of the group fell by around 500 million pounds, nearly causing its collapse, and Ratner was removed as chief executive the following year.
real_life_example.explanation: Years of commercial success were undone in a few seconds, and doing a Ratner became a British phrase for a self-inflicted business blunder.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that if even a single harmful word does its damage, all the good a person has done turns to no good; Ratner's few words wiped out the reputation he had spent years building.

tamil:
தீயினாற் சுட்டபுண் உள்ளாறும் ஆறாதே
நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு.
transliteration:
Theeyinaar suttapun ullaarum aaraadhe
Naavinaar sutta vadu.
meaning: A burn from fire heals inside, but a wound made by the tongue never heals.
elementary: If you touch a hot stove, it hurts a lot, but in a week or two it heals. If someone says something really hurtful to you, you might remember it for years. Words can burn deeper than fire.
university: Parimelazhagar notes Valluvar’s careful word choice: the fire-burn is called pun (a wound, which heals), while the tongue-burn is called vadu (a scar, which stays). He classifies the couplet as vetrumai alankaram, a figure of contrast: fire and harsh words share the act of burning, but because harsh words never heal they are shown to be worse than fire. The phrase ul aarum (‘heals within’) concedes that a fire-burn may leave an outward mark while the inner hurt fades; with verbal wounds the reverse holds. This is among the most widely quoted of all kurals, and its near-twin in the Mahabharata’s counsel of Vidura shows how old and widespread the insight is. Modern research on the lasting psychological effects of verbal abuse gives it contemporary resonance.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A forest pierced by arrows, or cut down by hatchets may again grow, but one’s heart wounded and censured by ill-spoken words never recovereth.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells Dhritarashtra that physical damage recovers but hearts wounded by harsh words never do.
hinduism.tie_back: The same structure as the Kural: physical harm heals, word-wounds do not.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 34 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity: so is the tongue among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell.”
christianity.explanation: James calls the tongue a fire that sets a person’s whole life ablaze.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts compare the tongue to fire, and both say its burning is worse than ordinary fire.

islam.quote_or_event: “Woe to every scorner and mocker … It is the fire of Allah, [eternally] fueled, Which mounts directed at the hearts.”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Humazah condemns the backbiter and mocker to a fire that reaches right into the heart.
islam.tie_back: The link is fire and hearts: in the Kural wounding words burn the victim’s heart, and in the Qur’an the mocker is repaid with a fire that reaches his own.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword; but the tongue of the wise is health.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares careless speech to sword-thrusts; the Talmud (Bava Metzia 58b) goes further, likening public humiliation to shedding blood.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts treat words as weapons that can wound as deeply as physical violence, or more.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak not harshly to anyone, for those thus spoken to might retort. Indeed, angry speech hurts, and retaliation may overtake you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that harsh speech wounds and brings painful consequences back on the speaker.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts insist that harsh words really wound, so they must be held back.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One can bear all kinds of unbearable pain caused by spikes in expectation of wealth etc. But he alone who tolerates, without any motive of worldly gain, harsh words spoken to him is venerable.”
jainism.explanation: The Daśavaikālika sets harsh words beside iron spikes and treats bearing harsh words as the harder test; the next verse in the same lesson (9.3.7) goes on to contrast iron thorns, which are pulled out, with thorns of speech that stay and breed enmity.
jainism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's fire-burn that heals and tongue-burn that never does, the Jain text ranks the wound of harsh words above physical injury.
jainism.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra 9.3.6, English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Sweetness of honey cannot match the sweetness of sweetly spoken words. No poison is as discomforting as bitter words.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas compares bitter words to poison and sweet words to honey; the next line of the same Kabit sets the coolness of sweet words against the burning heat (tapat) of harsh ones.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the scar of a burning tongue never heals; Bhai Gurdas likewise ranks the injury of harsh words above any physical poison.
sikhism.source: Kabit Savaiye Bhai Gurdas, Kabit 256 (English translation as given in the BaniDB database used by searchgurbani.com)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon publicly insults Achilles and takes his prize, Briseis. The dishonour sparks Achilles’ wrath, which lasts through most of the war and costs countless Achaean lives before he is finally reconciled.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad’s whole plot turns on a wound of words and dishonour that proves harder to heal than any battle wound.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ lasting wrath shows the Kural’s point: a verbal and public wound can outlast and outweigh physical injury.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Anger may be defined as an impulse, accompanied by pain, to a conspicuous revenge for a conspicuous slight directed without justification towards what concerns oneself or towards what concerns one’s friends.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle analyses how an unjust slight, often delivered in words, causes real pain and lasting resentment.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle explains the psychology behind the Kural: slights wound self-worth, which is why their pain lingers.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric II.2, 1378a (trans. W. Rhys Roberts)

real_life_example.event_title: Lincoln's unsent letter to General Meade
real_life_example.place: Executive Mansion (White House), Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: After the Union victory at Gettysburg, Confederate General Robert E. Lee's army escaped back across the Potomac River, and General George Meade, stung by word of the president's disappointment, asked to be relieved of his command. On 14 July 1863 Abraham Lincoln wrote Meade a letter thanking him for Gettysburg but sharply criticising him for letting Lee escape, calling the lost chance a misfortune that would prolong the war. Lincoln never sent it; he placed the letter in an envelope on which he wrote that it was to Gen. Meade, never sent, or signed.
real_life_example.explanation: Lincoln put his anger into words on paper but kept those words from wounding a general he still needed, a habit the American Battlefield Trust describes as one of his favourite coping mechanisms.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a burn from fire heals but a wound from the tongue never does; by holding back a cutting letter, Lincoln avoided inflicting a wound that could not be undone.

tamil:
கதங்காத்துக் கற்றடங்கல் ஆற்றுவான் செவ்வி
அறம்பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து.
transliteration:
Kadhangaaththuk katradangal aatruvaan sevvi
Arampaarkkum aatrin nuzhaindhu.
meaning: Goodness itself waits on the path, looking for the right time to meet the person who controls anger, has learned much, and stays self-controlled.
elementary: Usually we have to go looking for good things. But if you learn a lot, stay calm when you’re angry, and stay humble, goodness comes looking for you, like a friend waiting at your door.
university: The closing couplet personifies Aram (Virtue; Parimelazhagar calls it ‘the deity of Dharma’) as a suitor who enters a person’s path and waits for his sevvi, the opportune moment when his mind, speech and face are gracious enough to be approached. This reverses the usual quest: instead of the seeker pursuing virtue, virtue pursues the restrained person. The condition has three parts: katham kaaththu (guarding against anger), katru (having learned) and adangal aatruvaan (being capable of restraint). Manakkudavar adds that the learned must also restrain the pride their learning can breed. Parimelazhagar classes this couplet as restraint of mind (manavadakkam), which completes the body–speech–mind triad around which the chapter’s second half is built. The pairing of anger control with learning parallels the Talmudic teaching that anger drives wisdom out of the sage.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Before giving up this present body, if one is able to tolerate the urges of the material senses and check the force of desire and anger, he is well situated and is happy in this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the one who checks the force of desire and anger is truly established and happy.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts promise that the one who masters anger will find the good (happiness, or virtue itself) coming to him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.”
christianity.explanation: James teaches that restraint in speech and anger opens the way to God’s righteousness, which human wrath cannot produce.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts link anger-restraint and readiness to learn (‘swift to hear’) with the arrival of righteousness.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allah] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who restrain their anger and forgive, and says God loves them. A famous hadith (Bukhari 6114) adds that the strong man is the one who controls himself when angry.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the one who restrains anger becomes the object of the good’s love and favour, rather than having to chase it.

judaism.quote_or_event: Reish Lakish teaches that whoever becomes angry, if he is a sage, his wisdom departs from him, and if he is a prophet, his prophecy departs from him, and he proves it from Moses, who forgot a law after becoming angry.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud warns that anger drives learning and prophecy out of even the greatest.
judaism.tie_back: The same pairing as the Kural: learning stays with the person who guards against anger and leaves the one who doesn’t.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who checks rising anger as a charioteer checks a rolling chariot, him I call a true charioteer. Others only hold the reins.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says true mastery is checking anger the moment it rises.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts make guarding against anger the defining mark of real self-mastery.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By conquering anger he obtains patience; he acquires no Karman productive of anger, and destroys the Karman he had acquired before.”
jainism.explanation: In the same lecture, acquiring sacred knowledge 'destroys ignorance' (29.24), and conquering anger, pride, deceit and greed (29.67–70) leads the soul step by step toward liberation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's three conditions, guarding against anger, learning and being restrained, map onto these Jain steps, and the good that 'waits' for such a person corresponds to the karmic release they bring.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.67 (with 29.24) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To practice forgiveness is the true fast, good conduct and contentment.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak lists forgiveness, good conduct and contentment as the true discipline of the person in whom God dwells.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's person who guards against anger and stays restrained is the one Virtue seeks out; Gurbani makes forgiveness (the opposite of anger) and good conduct the real religious practice.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 223, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Achilles begins to draw his sword against Agamemnon, the goddess Athena comes down from heaven, seizes him by the hair and urges him to hold back. He obeys and sheathes the sword, and she promises him gifts three times as great later.
greek_mythology.explanation: A goddess personally comes to meet the hero at the very moment he restrains his anger.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A striking echo of the Kural: when a man checks his anger, the divine comes to meet him on his path.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The man who is angry at the right things and with the right people, and, further, as he ought, when he ought, and as long as he ought, is praised.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle praises the good-tempered person (praotes), whose anger is governed by reason.
philosophy.tie_back: Both see governed anger as a mark of virtue; Aristotle allows fitting anger, while Valluvar urges guarding against it altogether.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.5, 1125b (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Abdul Ghaffar Khan and the nonviolent Servants of God
real_life_example.place: North-West Frontier Province, British India (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
real_life_example.event: Abdul Ghaffar Khan, a Pashtun reformer from near Peshawar who founded schools to spread education, established the Khudai Khidmatgar (Servants of God) movement, dated by The Tribune to 1929, an unarmed volunteer force of tens of thousands that resisted British rule through civil disobedience. On joining, members swore to forgive anyone who oppressed or mistreated them, to lead a simple life and to perform social service for at least two hours a day. Repeatedly imprisoned by both British and Pakistani governments, he was honoured by India in 1987 as the first non-Indian recipient of its highest civilian award, the Bharat Ratna.
real_life_example.explanation: Khan asked people from a region with strong traditions of armed revenge to master their anger, and his steadfast restraint brought him honour in several countries in his own lifetime.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says virtue itself waits on the path of one who guards against anger, is learned and is capable of restraint; recognition sought out Abdul Ghaffar Khan rather than the other way round.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கம் விழுப்பந் தரலான் ஒழுக்கம்
உயிரினும் ஓம்பப் படும்.
transliteration:
Ozhukkam vizhuppam tharalaan ozhukkam
Uyirinum oampap padum.
meaning: Good behaviour is what makes a person truly great. So guard it even more carefully than your own life.
elementary: Think of your good behavior as the most precious treasure you own, even more precious than your own body. It is what makes people trust and respect you, so you protect it more than anything else.
university: The chapter opens with a deliberately extreme ranking: ozhukkam (conduct, from ozhuku, ‘to proceed along a course’) is to be guarded (ompa) above uyir, life itself. The reason clause, vizhuppam tharalaan (‘because it confers eminence’), grounds the claim in what conduct produces rather than in divine command; bare life, as Pope's rendering notes, is something ‘all men share’, while conduct is what distinguishes. The word ozhukkam frames the first line at both ends, so the verse itself performs the act of guarding. Parimelazhagar reads ozhukkam as the conduct proper to one's station, whereas modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Karunanidhi) make it universal. The idea that some values outrank survival recurs widely, from Socrates' refusal to weigh life against right action to the rabbinic rule that certain sins must be refused even on pain of death.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The rule of conduct is transcendent law, whether it be taught in the revealed texts or in the sacred tradition; hence a twice-born man who possesses regard for himself, should be always careful to (follow) it.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu calls ācāra, the rule of conduct, the highest law, and tells anyone with self-respect to follow it with constant care.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it puts conduct at the top of all values and asks that it be guarded vigilantly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.”
christianity.explanation: The risen Christ tells the church at Smyrna to stay faithful even if it costs them their lives, and promises a crown in return.
christianity.tie_back: Both place faithful conduct above survival and attach a reward of eminence (a ‘crown’ in one, vizhuppam in the other) to it.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet is reported to have said that he was sent to perfect (complete) good character.
islam.explanation: In this saying, the Prophet describes the whole purpose of his mission as bringing good character to completion.
islam.tie_back: Both treat conduct and character as the central human good, though the hadith does not rank it above life.

judaism.quote_or_event: The rabbis ruled that for three transgressions (idolatry, forbidden sexual relations and murder) a person must accept death rather than commit them: yehareg ve'al ya'avor, ‘let him be killed and not transgress.’
judaism.explanation: Jewish law normally lets almost any commandment be set aside to save life, but for these three core wrongs it requires a person to give up life instead.
judaism.tie_back: This puts into law the Kural's claim that some conduct must be guarded even above life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better it is to live one day virtuous and meditative than to live a hundred years immoral and uncontrolled.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha measures a life by its virtue, not its length. One good day is worth more than a century of bad conduct.
buddhism.tie_back: Both value conduct over the mere continuation of life.

jainism.quote_or_event: Rājīmatī to the monk Rathanemi, who tried to seduce her: “Fie upon you, famous knight, who want to quaff the vomited drink for the sake of this life; it would be better for you to die.”
jainism.explanation: Rājīmatī, true to her vows, tells a lapsing monk that death is preferable to breaking his conduct, and her words turn him back to the Law; the verse also recurs in the Daśavaikālika (2.7).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says conduct must be guarded above life itself, and Rājīmatī states that rule in its starkest form: better to die than fall from one's vows.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 22.40–46, quoting 22.42 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: In 1675 the ninth Guru, Tegh Bahadur, was executed in Delhi by the Mughal authorities. He is remembered as the second Sikh martyr and for his stand for religious freedom; Sikh tradition holds that he accepted death rather than yield.
sikhism.explanation: Sikh memory treats Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom as the model of a principle held more dearly than one's own life.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks right conduct above life itself; the Guru's martyrdom is Sikhism's defining example of exactly that ranking.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guru Tegh Bahadur' (Tamanna Nangia, fact-checked by Britannica Editors)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Antigone buries her brother Polyneices against King Creon's decree, knowing the penalty is death, because she holds the unwritten laws of the gods above her own survival.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antigone would rather die doing what is right than live by breaking a sacred duty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She guards right conduct above her life, just as the Kural asks.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “a man who is good for anything ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial, Socrates says a good person does not weigh survival at all. The only question is whether an action is right.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's ranking: right conduct first, life second.

real_life_example.event_title: Jan Hus refuses to recant at the Council of Constance
real_life_example.event: The Czech priest and reformer Jan Hus travelled to the Council of Constance in 1414 expecting to explain his views, but he was imprisoned soon after he arrived. At his hearings in June 1415 he was presented with a list of teachings attributed to him and urged to recant in order to save his life; he refused, and maintained that he did not hold all of the teachings as charged. On 6 July 1415 the council condemned him as a heretic and handed him over to the secular authorities, who executed him by burning that same day.
real_life_example.explanation: Hus chose death over disowning what he believed, and his execution made him a lasting national and religious symbol in Bohemia and an inspiration to later reformers such as Martin Luther.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks right conduct above life itself, and Hus, offered his life in exchange for a recantation he considered false, guarded his integrity at the cost of his life.

tamil:
பரிந்தோம்பிக் காக்க ஒழுக்கம் தெரிந்தோம்பித்
தேரினும் அஃதே துணை.
transliteration:
Parindhoambik kaakka ozhukkam therindhoambith
Therinum aqdhe thunai.
meaning: Work hard to guard your good behaviour. Think about everything else, and you will find that good behaviour is the only friend that truly stays with you.
elementary: Imagine testing every toy, game and friend to find the one that will stay with you forever. Valluvar says that after checking everything, the one thing that never leaves you is being good, so take good care of it.
university: Two phrases of care frame the couplet: parindhu ompi kaakka (‘guard it, cherishing it even through pain’) and therindhu ompi therinum (‘even after examining and weighing all’). The second line sounds almost empirical. After surveying the alternatives (wealth, learning, kin, other virtues), one finds that conduct is the only thunai, companion or support. Parimelazhagar and Pappaiah gloss thunai as the aid that goes with a person into this life and the next, which ties the couplet to a widespread image: good conduct is the one thing that ‘goes with’ a person at death. Karunanidhi stresses bearing hardship to keep it. Aristotle offers a close philosophical parallel when he calls virtuous activity more lasting than even scientific knowledge.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For in the next world neither father, nor mother, nor wife, nor sons, nor relations stay to be his companions; spiritual merit alone remains (with him).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu says every human tie falls away at death, and only the merit a person has built by right living goes on with them.
hinduism.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's ‘it alone is the companion’: after every alternative is weighed, conduct is what remains.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take fast hold of instruction; let her not go: keep her; for she is thy life.”
christianity.explanation: The father in Proverbs tells his son to hold on to moral instruction and never let it go, because it is life itself.
christianity.tie_back: It shares the Kural's language of guarding and holding fast to the discipline of right living.

islam.quote_or_event: “When carried to his grave, a dead person is followed by three, two of which return (after his burial) and one remains with him: his relative, his property, and his deeds follow him; relatives and his property go back while his deeds remain with him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says that of everything that follows a person to the grave, only their deeds stay with them.
islam.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that conduct is the one true companion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “when a man passes away there accompany him neither gold nor silver, nor precious stones nor pearls, but Torah and good deeds alone”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yose ben Kisma turns down a fortune because only Torah and good deeds go with a person when they die.
judaism.tie_back: Both identify right conduct as the companion that outlasts every other possession.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Good is virtue until life's end, good is faith that is steadfast, good is the acquisition of wisdom, and good is the avoidance of evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises virtue (sīla) that is kept all the way to the end of life.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats virtue as something to be guarded for a whole lifetime.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Neither his kinsmen, nor his friends, nor his sons, nor his relations will share his suffering, he alone has to bear it; for the Karman follows the doer. Leaving behind bipeds and quadrupeds, his fields, his house, his wealth, his corn, and everything; against his will, and accompanied only by his Karman, he enters a new existence, either a good or a bad one.”
jainism.explanation: The sage Citra tells King Brahmadatta that at death everything is left behind and only one's karma, the fruit of one's conduct, goes along.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar finds after weighing everything that conduct alone is the companion that stays; Citra's sermon makes karma, the fruit of conduct, the only thing that goes with a person into the next life.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.23–24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, as many as are the sins one commits, so many are the chains around his neck. If he possesses virtues, then the chains are cut away; these virtues are his brothers, his true brothers.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says faults bind a person like chains, while virtues free him and stand by him like real kin.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural finds conduct to be the one true companion after weighing every alternative; Guru Nanak calls virtues a person's only true brothers.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus' fable of the Choice of Heracles, Virtue offers the young hero a hard road but calls herself a faithful helper and ally in labor, in peace and in war, while Vice offers only easy pleasures.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles is shown that Virtue is a companion who stays with you through every hardship.
greek_mythology.tie_back: After comparing the alternatives, the chooser finds virtue to be the one reliable companion, as in the Kural's second line.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “no function of man has so much permanence as virtuous activities (these are thought to be more durable even than knowledge of the sciences)”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that virtuous activity is the most stable and lasting thing a human being can have, more lasting even than knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: Both conclude, after comparison, that conduct is the most dependable human possession.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1.10, 1100b (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Boethius writes the Consolation of Philosophy in prison
real_life_example.event: Boethius, a Roman senator who had become Master of Offices, one of the most senior officials at the court of the Ostrogothic king Theoderic, fell out with others at court, was accused of treason and of practising magic, and was imprisoned and later executed. While awaiting death he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy, an imagined dialogue in prose and verse between the prisoner and a lady who personifies Philosophy. In it Philosophy distinguishes the goods of fortune, such as riches, status and power, from the true goods of virtue and wisdom, and argues that his fall had not taken from him the things of real worth.
real_life_example.explanation: Written by a man who had lost wealth, office and freedom, the book became one of the most widely read works of the Middle Ages and a classic statement that virtue is the one possession fortune cannot remove.
real_life_example.tie_back: Like the kural, Boethius weighed wealth, rank and power one by one and concluded that virtue alone remained a true companion when everything else was gone.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை இழுக்கம்
இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்.
transliteration:
Ozhukkam udaimai kudimai izhukkam
Izhindha pirappaai vidum.
meaning: Having good behaviour is what makes a person’s family noble. Losing it turns their birth into a low one.
elementary: Coming from a ‘good family’ is not about your last name. If you act kindly and honestly, you are from a good family. If you behave badly, it is as if you did not come from a good family at all.
university: Kudimai (lineage, the dignity of one's house) is redefined here in terms of behaviour. Possessing ozhukkam is itself nobility of birth, while izhukkam (lapse, slipping) ‘becomes’ (aai vidum) a base birth. The verb matters: a lapse does not just disgrace one's family, it converts one's birth into a low one after the fact. Commentators differ on scope. Parimelazhagar and Pappaiah tie conduct to the duties of one's station, a view that fits a varna framework, while Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi read the couplet as a universal critique of status by birth. Either way, it belongs to a long Indian debate, also voiced by the Buddha in the Vasala Sutta and by Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata, over whether birth or behaviour makes a person noble.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the boy Satyakama Jabala admits that his mother does not know who his father was, the sage Gautama accepts him as a Brahmin student. He reasons that only a true Brahmin would speak such an unflattering truth.
hinduism.explanation: Satyakama's honesty, not his known lineage, proves his worth and earns him entry to Vedic study.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, conduct (here truthfulness) is what establishes noble standing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.”
christianity.explanation: John the Baptist warns the religious elite that descent from Abraham means nothing without repentance and good fruit.
christianity.tie_back: Both reject lineage as a substitute for conduct.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allāh is the most righteous of you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says tribes and lineages exist so that people may know one another, but true nobility is measured by righteousness.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's redefinition of nobility almost word for word.

judaism.quote_or_event: “a mamzer who is a Torah scholar precedes a High Priest who is an ignoramus”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah sets out an order of precedence by birth, then overturns it: a person of the most stigmatized birth who is a scholar outranks the highest-born priest who is ignorant.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, personal attainment overrides the rank one is born into.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by birth is one an outcast; not by birth is one a brahman. By deed one becomes an outcast, by deed one becomes a brahman.”
buddhism.explanation: Called an outcast by a Brahmin, the Buddha answers that high and low status are made by one's actions, not by birth.
buddhism.tie_back: This states both halves of the Kural: good conduct makes one noble, misconduct makes one low.
buddhism.source: Vasala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.7, v. 21 (tr. Piyadassi Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The value of penance has become visible, birth appears of no value! Look at the holy Harikêśa, the son of a Śvapâka, whose power is so great.”
jainism.explanation: Harikeśa-Bala, born among the Śvapākas (outcastes) and mocked by priests 'stuck up by pride of birth', is honoured by gods for his discipline, and the scene ends with this verdict.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says conduct is what makes birth noble and its lack makes it low; the Jain canon dramatizes the same reversal, with an outcaste's conduct outranking the priests' high birth.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.1, 12.5 and 12.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “God does not ask about social class or birth; you must find your true home. That is your social class and that is your status - the karma of what you have done.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak rejects birth as the measure of a person and says one's real class and standing are the deeds one has done.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says right conduct is itself noble birth and a lapse makes one's birth low; Guru Nanak likewise makes deeds, not lineage, one's true jaat and pat.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1330, Raag Prabhati, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nobly born suitors of Ithaca eat up Odysseus' household with insolence and abuse the disguised king, while the slave swineherd Eumaeus shows him true hospitality. The suitors end in death and disgrace.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Odyssey, the aristocrats behave basely and the lowly servant behaves nobly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Conduct, not birth, shows who is truly noble, as the Kural claims.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues that philosophy does not look at pedigree, and that a hall full of ancestral busts does not make a nobleman. Only the soul (animus) makes a person noble, and it can rise above any condition of birth.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, virtue is open to slave and aristocrat alike, and nobility belongs to the character, not the family tree.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the same relocation of nobility from lineage to conduct.

real_life_example.event_title: Narayana Guru consecrates a Shiva lingam at Aruvippuram
real_life_example.event: Narayana Guru, a sage and social reformer whose family belonged to the Ezhava community, then ranked low in the Hindu caste order, consecrated a stone taken from the Neyyar river as a Shiva lingam at Aruvippuram in 1888. At the time only Brahmin priests were allowed to install temple deities, so the act broke orthodox practice and was challenged by upper-caste critics who questioned his right to perform it. The shrine became the Aruvippuram Shiva temple, and Narayana Guru went on to found temples in southern India and Ceylon that welcomed people of all castes.
real_life_example.explanation: The consecration is regarded as a turning point in Kerala's social reform movement, because it asserted that spiritual authority comes from a person's life and learning rather than from the caste into which they are born.
real_life_example.tie_back: On the reading of modern commentators who take the kural as a critique of status by birth, Narayana Guru's act embodies its claim that conduct, not birth, is what makes a person noble.

tamil:
மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும் பார்ப்பான்
பிறப்பொழுக்கங் குன்றக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Marappinum oththuk kolalaagum paarppaan
Pirappozhukkam kundrak kedum.
meaning: A Brahmin (a member of the priestly class) who forgets the Vedas (holy texts) can learn them again. But if he loses the good behaviour of his birth, his birth itself is ruined.
elementary: If you forget your spelling words, you can study them again. But if you become a bully, no amount of studying fixes that. You lose something that is much harder to get back.
university: This couplet is the chapter's sharpest test case. The paarppaan (Brahmin) is the figure whose status depends most on birth and learning. Valluvar concedes that forgotten Vedic learning (oththu) can be recovered, but if pirappozhukkam, the conduct attached to that birth, declines (kundra), the birth itself is ruined (kedum). The logic is asymmetric: knowledge is a stock that can be replenished, while character is a foundation whose collapse brings down everything built on it. Commentators split between reading the couplet as upholding Brahmin duty (Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah) and as ranking birth below conduct (Karunanidhi). It closely echoes Manu 1.109, where a Brahmin who departs from the rule of conduct ‘does not reap the fruit of the Veda’, and Yudhishthira's answer to the Yaksha in the Mahabharata.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is neither birth, nor study, nor learning, that is the cause of Brahmanahood, without doubt, it is behaviour that constitutes it. One's behaviour should always be well-guarded, especially by a Brahmana.”
hinduism.explanation: Asked by the Yaksha what makes a Brahmin, Yudhishthira rules out birth and study and names conduct alone. He adds that a Brahmin in particular must guard it.
hinduism.tie_back: This is nearly the same argument as the Kural: study is secondary, and conduct is what preserves Brahmin standing.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 311 (Yaksha Prashna), tr. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that even perfect knowledge counts for nothing without love.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks sacred knowledge below the quality of one's conduct.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that the person whose deeds hold him back will not be carried forward by his lineage.
islam.explanation: Noble descent cannot make up for a lack of good deeds.
islam.tie_back: This fits the Kural's claim that a high birth is ruined when conduct fails.

judaism.quote_or_event: “anyone whose deeds exceed his wisdom, his wisdom is enduring, but anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, his wisdom is not enduring.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa teaches that learning only lasts when it rests on deeds.
judaism.tie_back: Both rank conduct above learning and warn that learning without conduct collapses.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are brahmans born in the family of preceptors, kinsmen of (veda) hymns. They are often seen committing evil deeds. In this life itself they are despised, in the next they are born in an evil state of existence. High birth does not prevent them from falling into a woeful state, or from censure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha points to Brahmins of Vedic families who do evil, and says their birth cannot save them from contempt.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the same case as the Kural, a Vedic Brahmin undone by misconduct despite his birth.
buddhism.source: Vasala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.7, vv. 25–26 (tr. Piyadassi Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who are full of anger and pride, who kill, lie, steal, and own property, are Brâhmaṇas without pure birth and knowledge; they are very bad fields. You are only the bearer of words as it were, you do not understand their meaning, though you have learned the Vêdas.”
jainism.explanation: Answering Brahmin priests who claim to be the best recipients by pure birth and learning, the Jain monk says that their misconduct has already destroyed both their birth and their knowledge.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says a Brahmin who forgets the Vedas can learn them again, but one who falls from conduct ruins his birth; this passage likewise says that conduct, not Vedic learning, decides whether a Brahmin's birth counts as pure.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.13–15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is a Brahmin, who knows God. He chants and meditates, and practices austerity and good deeds. He keeps to the Dharma, with faith, humility and contentment.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak redefines the Brahmin by inner knowledge and conduct, not by descent or ritual learning.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a Brahmin's conduct, not his Vedic recitation, is what keeps his birth from ruin; Guru Nanak goes further and makes conduct the whole of what a Brahmin is.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1411, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles, son of a goddess and pupil of the wise centaur Chiron, drags Hector's corpse day after day. Apollo protests to the gods that Achilles has destroyed pity and has no shame, and the gods intervene against him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Neither divine birth nor the finest education protects Achilles from the gods' anger once his conduct becomes shameful.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This echoes the Kural: high birth and learning are undone by a lapse in conduct.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Boethius, through Lady Philosophy, argues that nobility is only praise earned by one's ancestors' merits. If it has any good at all, it lies in obliging the nobly born not to fall short of their ancestors' virtue.
philosophy.explanation: Noble birth carries no worth of its own; it only puts the heir under an obligation of conduct.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural: birth keeps its value only while the matching conduct is kept up.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy III, prose 6

real_life_example.event_title: Francis Bacon falls from office for taking gifts from litigants
real_life_example.event: Francis Bacon, the philosopher and essayist who had been Lord Chancellor of England since 1618, was charged in Parliament in 1621 with accepting gifts from people whose cases were before him. He pleaded guilty, was heavily fined and sentenced to imprisonment in the Tower of London; the fine was later waived and he spent only a few days in the Tower, but he was never again allowed to sit in Parliament or hold political office. Bacon maintained that the gifts had not affected his judgments, and he devoted his remaining years to writing and philosophy.
real_life_example.explanation: The episode shows that even one of the most learned men of his age could not recover his public standing once his conduct in office was found wanting, while his intellectual work continued and grew.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says lost learning can be regained but a lapse in conduct ruins one's standing; Bacon's learning stayed with him and kept producing books, but his lapse ended his public career for good.

tamil:
அழுக்கா றுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம்போன்று இல்லை
ஒழுக்க மிலான்கண் உயர்வு.
transliteration:
Azhukkaaru udaiyaan-kan aakkampoandru illai
Ozhukkam ilaan-kan uyarvu.
meaning: Just as riches never stay with jealous people, greatness never comes to people without good behaviour.
elementary: A jealous kid spends so much time being upset about what others have that he never enjoys his own things. In the same way, someone who behaves badly never really rises high, no matter what.
university: The couplet works by analogy (ponru, ‘just as’). Azhukkaaru, envy, is so incompatible with aakkam (increase, prosperity) that its absence is proverbial, and uyarvu (elevation, rank) is just as surely absent from a person without ozhukkam. Envy gets a whole later chapter (17). Pappaiah reads uyarvu as ‘high lineage’, keeping the chapter's theme of birth, while Varadarasanar reads it as elevation in life generally. The pairing of envy with misconduct is deliberate: Tamil ethics treats envy as the model inner corruption that eats away at outward fortune, which a later couplet (Kural 168) develops. The claim is about incompatibility more than reward: certain dispositions cannot coexist with certain goods.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Seeing the splendour of the Pandavas' palace and the wealth brought to Yudhishthira's Rajasuya sacrifice, Duryodhana is consumed by envy. That envy drives him to the rigged dice game, which ends in the destruction of his whole line.
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata, envy of another's prosperity sets off Duryodhana's moral collapse and his eventual ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: Duryodhana has birth and wealth, yet envy and misconduct keep true eminence from him, as the Kural predicts.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta Parva), tr. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that envy breeds disorder and every kind of wrongdoing.
christianity.tie_back: Both treat envy as corrosive and incompatible with anything good growing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Avoid envy, for envy devours good deeds just as fire devours fuel or (he said) ‘grass.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares envy to fire that burns up whatever good a person has stored.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes envy the thing that consumes a person's gains.

judaism.quote_or_event: “envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar names envy first among the traits that destroy a person.
judaism.tie_back: Both see envy as ruining one's place in the world.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by mere eloquence nor by beauty of form does a man become accomplished, if he is jealous, selfish and deceitful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says jealousy and deceit cancel out every outward advantage.
buddhism.tie_back: This echoes the Kural's point that the envious and ill-conducted cannot reach true eminence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana teaches that prosperity won through wrong conduct does not last, because the passions that produced it also undo it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that, as prosperity never settles on the envious, so eminence never comes to one without conduct; this verse makes the related point that gains without right conduct do not endure.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One whose heart is filled with jealousy of others, never comes to any good.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das warns that a person who harbours envy of others will never prosper.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural builds on the proverb that envy and prosperity never meet; Gurbani states that same incompatibility outright.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 308, Raag Gauri, Gauri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Minerva sends Invidia (Envy) to poison Aglauros, who is consumed by jealousy of her sister's good fortune with Mercury. When she tries to block the god's way, she is turned to stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Envy eats Aglauros from the inside and leaves her with nothing, frozen and ruined.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This vividly shows the Kural's premise that envy and prosperity cannot coexist.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines envy as a form of hatred that makes a person pained at another's good fortune and glad at their misfortune. For him, every such sad passion lessens a person's power of acting.
philosophy.explanation: Envy is not only unpleasant but actually weakens the one who feels it.
philosophy.tie_back: This helps explain why the Kural says the envious cannot prosper.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Definitions of the Emotions 23

real_life_example.event_title: Boris Onishchenko is disqualified for a rigged epee at the Montreal Olympics
real_life_example.event: During the fencing event of the modern pentathlon at the 1976 Olympic Games, the epee of the Soviet pentathlete Boris Onishchenko registered hits on opponents it did not appear to have touched. The British team asked for the weapon to be inspected, and it was found to have been modified so that it could register a hit even when none had been made. Onishchenko was disqualified, the Soviet team was eliminated, and Great Britain went on to win the team gold medal.
real_life_example.explanation: The case remains one of the most notorious acts of cheating in Olympic history, and it showed that a rise won by deceit can collapse in an instant once the means are exposed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural holds that true eminence never comes to a person without right conduct, just as prosperity never settles on the envious; Onishchenko's rigged weapon brought him not honour but lasting disgrace.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கத்தின் ஒல்கார் உரவோர் இழுக்கத்தின்
ஏதம் படுபாக் கறிந்து.
transliteration:
Ozhukkaththin olgaar uravoar izhukkaththin
Edham padupaak karindhu.
meaning: Strong-minded people never slip in their behaviour, because they know the trouble a slip brings.
elementary: A smart bike rider always wears a helmet, not because they are scared, but because they know how badly a fall can hurt. Strong people keep behaving well for the same reason: they know what happens when you don't.
university: Uravor, ‘the strong’, refers to strength of mind rather than of body (uram means firmness or resolve). Their steadiness is not naive. It rests on knowing (arindhu) the edham (fault, harm, calamity) that falls on those who lapse. That makes the couplet an argument about moral knowledge: firmness comes from seeing consequences clearly. Olkaar (‘they do not bend or slacken’) suggests constant, everyday vigilance rather than heroic resistance to one temptation. Pappaiah adds that they hold on ‘even when it is hard’ and reads the harm as loss of standing. Many traditions picture true strength as self-mastery: Ben Zoma's ‘Who is mighty?’, the Buddhist rock unshaken by the storm, and Odysseus binding himself because he knows what the Sirens do.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Yama teaches Nachiketas that the good (śreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both come to a person. The wise one examines them and chooses the good, while the fool, out of greed, chooses the pleasant and falls short of the goal.
hinduism.explanation: Wisdom lies in seeing where each path leads and holding firmly to the good one.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's uravor, the wise stay steady because they understand the cost of the other path.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he disciplines himself constantly because he knows he could fall and be disqualified.
christianity.tie_back: This is the same logic as the Kural: steady discipline driven by awareness of the danger of lapsing.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that the strong person is not the one who overpowers others in wrestling, but the one who controls himself when angry.
islam.explanation: Real strength is inner mastery, not physical force.
islam.tie_back: This fits the Kural's word uravor: strength means holding firm in one's conduct.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma defines the mighty person as the one who masters their own impulses.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same redefinition of the ‘strong’ that the Kural's uravor implies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a storm cannot prevail against a rocky mountain, so Mara can never overpower the man who lives meditating on the impurities, who is controlled in his senses, moderate in eating, and filled with faith and earnest effort.”
buddhism.explanation: The disciplined person is compared to a mountain that no storm can move.
buddhism.tie_back: Both picture the firm person who never gives way.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though others sleep, be thou awake! Like a wise man, trust nobody, but be always on the alert; for dangerous is the time and weak the body. Be always watchful like a Bhâruṇḍa bird!”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra urges constant vigilance (apramāda), because the monk knows how dangerous time is and how easily one falls.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's strong-minded never slacken in conduct because they know the harm a lapse brings; the Jain call to unsleeping watchfulness rests on the same clear sight of danger.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who remain awake and aware are saved, while those who sleep are plundered.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that only constant alertness against the vices keeps one's inner wealth from being stolen.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's strong-minded never slacken because they know the harm a lapse brings; Gurbani likewise prizes unbroken vigilance and warns that the careless are robbed.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 34, Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe that the Sirens' song lures sailors to their death, Odysseus has his crew plug their ears and has himself bound to the mast so that he cannot give in.
greek_mythology.explanation: Knowing the danger in advance, Odysseus arranges things so that he cannot slip.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural: firmness grounded in knowing exactly what harm a lapse would bring.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's image of the soul as a charioteer with two horses, the charioteer must keep a firm grip on the unruly dark horse, which always pulls toward what is shameful, if the soul is not to be dragged down.
philosophy.explanation: Reason must hold desire steady at every moment, or the whole soul falls.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's uravor are like the firm charioteer who never loosens the reins.

real_life_example.event_title: Jackie Robinson promises Branch Rickey he will not retaliate
real_life_example.event: At a meeting in 1945, Brooklyn Dodgers executive Branch Rickey spent hours acting out the racial hostility Jackie Robinson would face as the first Black player in modern major league baseball, and told him he wanted a player with the courage not to fight back. Robinson, who by his own later account had believed in retaliation since childhood, promised that there would be no incident. When he joined the Dodgers in 1947 he endured abuse without striking back, and he went on to become one of the game's stars.
real_life_example.explanation: Robinson's self-control was a deliberate strategy: both men understood that a single angry incident could be used to halt the integration of the sport.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes the strong-minded who never slacken because they know the harm a lapse would bring; Robinson held firm precisely because he understood what one lapse would cost.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கத்தின் எய்துவர் மேன்மை இழுக்கத்தின்
எய்துவர் எய்தாப் பழி.
transliteration:
Ozhukkaththin eydhuvar menmai izhukkaththin
Eydhuvar eydhaap pazhi.
meaning: Through good behaviour people become great. Through bad behaviour they earn a shame they never needed to suffer.
elementary: When you are kind and honest, people look up to you. When you cheat or lie, you get a bad name, and it is a bad name you could easily have avoided.
university: The couplet is built as a strict parallel: ozhukkaththin eydhuvar menmai / izhukkaththin eydhuvar eydhaap pazhi, ‘by conduct they attain eminence; by lapse they attain unattainable blame’. The paradoxical phrase eydhaap pazhi (‘blame that should not be attained’) is read in different ways: as undeserved, as unbearable, or as blame one had no need to incur.
