Pope's ‘censures undeserved’ takes the first reading, and most modern commentators take the last. Either way, the couplet makes the social stakes of conduct explicit, because menmai (eminence) and pazhi (blame) are verdicts passed by others. Here the chapter moves from inner firmness (136) to public consequence. The same pairing appears in Sanskrit dharmashastra, in the rabbinic ‘crown of a good name’, and in Hesiod's steep path to excellence.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For a man of bad conduct is blamed among people, constantly suffers misfortunes, is afflicted with diseases, and short-lived.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists the results of bad conduct, and public blame comes first.
hinduism.tie_back: This spells out the second half of the Kural: a lapse brings disgrace among people.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs sets the lasting honour of the righteous against the rotting reputation of the wicked.
christianity.tie_back: Its two-part structure (honour through goodness, disgrace through wickedness) matches the Kural's parallel lines.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nothing is heavier on the believer's Scale on the Day of Judgment than good character. For indeed Allah, Most High, is angered by the shameless obscene person.”
islam.explanation: Good character carries the greatest weight, while shameless conduct draws God's displeasure.
islam.tie_back: Both set honour through good conduct against disgrace through bad conduct.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are three crowns: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of royalty, but the crown of a good name supersedes them all.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shimon ranks a good name, earned by conduct, above learning, priesthood and kingship.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes eminence (menmai) the fruit of conduct.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “But the fragrance of the virtuous blows against the wind. Truly the virtuous man pervades all directions with the fragrance of his virtue.”
buddhism.explanation: The good name of a virtuous person spreads everywhere, even against the wind, which no flower's scent can do.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first half: conduct brings a widely recognised eminence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a bitch with sore ears is driven away everywhere, thus a bad, insubordinate, and talkative (pupil) is turned out. … Hearing a man thus compared to a dog and a pig, he who desires his own welfare, should adhere to good conduct.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline contrasts the disgrace of the ill-behaved, who are driven out everywhere, with the honour of those who follow the conduct of the wise and 'will not incur blame' (1.42).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural pairs greatness gained by conduct with needless disgrace earned by lapse; the Uttarādhyayana draws the same contrast in social terms of expulsion versus honour.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.4–6 (with 1.42) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “As are the deeds done, so is the reputation one acquires.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says the name a person earns follows directly from the deeds he does.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says conduct brings eminence and a lapse brings blame; Guru Nanak ties reputation to deeds in the same direct way.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Badness can be got easily and in shoals: the road to her is smooth, and she lives very near us. But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his brother that vice is easy to reach, while excellence has to be climbed to by effort.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both contrast the high standing won by virtue with the low road of vice.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 287–291 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: At the close of the Republic, Socrates argues that in the long run the just are honoured by gods and men. The unjust are like runners who start fast and fail at the finish, ending in contempt and disgrace.
philosophy.explanation: Over time, justice brings honour and injustice brings public disgrace.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors both halves of the Kural's parallel.

real_life_example.event_title: South African cricket captain Hansie Cronje admits taking bookmakers' money
real_life_example.event: Hansie Cronje, captain of South Africa's national cricket team and one of the country's most admired sportsmen, was charged by Delhi police in April 2000 with fixing one-day matches played in India, which he at first denied. He was sacked as captain, and in testimony before the King Commission of inquiry in June 2000 he admitted taking money from bookmakers and offering teammates money to underperform. In October 2000 the United Cricket Board of South Africa banned him from cricket for life.
real_life_example.explanation: Cronje's fall was so striking because his reputation for leadership had been built on years of disciplined play, and it was undone by choices he had no need to make.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural contrasts the eminence gained through conduct with the needless disgrace a lapse brings; Cronje rose through the first and fell through the second.

tamil:
நன்றிக்கு வித்தாகும் நல்லொழுக்கம் தீயொழுக்கம்
என்றும் இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Nandrikku viththaagum nallozhukkam theeyozhukkam
Endrum idumbai tharum.
meaning: Good behaviour is the seed of good things. Bad behaviour always brings trouble.
elementary: Plant an apple seed and you get an apple tree. Plant weeds and you get weeds. Being good is like planting a good seed, because nice things grow from it. Being mean only grows trouble.
university: The farming metaphor vittu (seed) makes nallozhukkam generative. Good conduct is not the good itself but the cause from which good (nandri, here ‘benefit’ or ‘virtue’ rather than ‘gratitude’, though one modern commentator reads it that way) grows over time. Its opposite, theeyozhukkam, gives idumbai (distress) endrum, ‘always’, which suggests a continuous harvest rather than a single punishment. Pappaiah extends the fruit to this life and the next (immai, marumai), which aligns the couplet with karmic causation, while Karunanidhi keeps it within this life. The seed image is nearly universal, from Paul's ‘whatsoever a man soweth’ to the Upanishadic ‘as he acts, so he becomes’ and Aristotle's view that character arises from like activities.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “according as he acts and according as he behaves, so will he be:--a man of good acts will become good, a man of bad acts, bad. He becomes pure by pure deeds, bad by bad deeds.”
hinduism.explanation: Yajnavalkya teaches that what a person does shapes what they become.
hinduism.tie_back: Both say conduct is the seed of what follows: good grows from good, and evil brings its own results.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.5 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.”
christianity.explanation: Paul uses sowing and reaping to show that the kind of life a person plants decides what they harvest.
christianity.tie_back: It shares the Kural's seed metaphor and its two-sided outcome.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you not considered how Allāh presents an example, [making] a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches [high] in the sky?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an compares a good word to a deep-rooted tree that keeps bearing fruit.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural's image of goodness as something that grows from a seed or root.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For one commandment leads to another commandment, and transgression leads to another transgression; For the reward for performing a commandment is another commandment and the reward for committing a transgression is a transgression.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Azzai teaches that good and bad deeds each multiply their own kind.
judaism.tie_back: Both describe conduct as self-propagating, with good bearing good and bad bearing bad.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: Actions done with a corrupt mind bring suffering that follows as surely as a cart wheel follows the ox.
buddhism.tie_back: This echoes the Kural's second half: bad conduct always brings sorrow. The next verse (Dhp 2) gives the good half.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain doctrine of karma holds that deeds bind subtle matter to the soul and ripen into their own results in this life and later ones.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls good conduct the seed of good and bad conduct a constant source of sorrow; the burglar crushed by his own tunnel is the Jain image of misconduct bearing its own painful fruit.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “As she has planted, so does she harvest; such is the field of karma.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Baarah Maahaa, Guru Arjan calls the body a field of deeds in which each person reaps what she has sown.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls good conduct a seed and bad conduct a lasting source of sorrow; Gurbani uses the same sowing-and-reaping image for deeds.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 134, Raag Maajh, Baarah Maahaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He does mischief to himself who does mischief to another, and evil planned harms the plotter most.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that wrongdoing comes back on the one who does it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that bad conduct brings sorrow to its doer.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 265–266 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Thus, in one word, states of character arise out of like activities.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that repeated acts build up into a settled character of the same kind.
philosophy.tie_back: Conduct is the seed of character, as the Kural's vittu suggests.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.1, 1103b (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Nicholas Winton's rescue of children from Czechoslovakia comes to light
real_life_example.place: Prague, Czechoslovakia, and London, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Nicholas Winton, a London stockbroker, went to Prague at the end of 1938 and, working with colleagues including Trevor Chadwick and Doreen Warriner, organised transports that brought 669 children, most of them Jewish, from Czechoslovakia to Britain in 1939. He said little about it for nearly fifty years, until his wife found his 1939 scrapbook of the children's names and photographs. In 1988 he appeared on the BBC programme That's Life!, where he was surprised to meet some of the people he had rescued, now adults.
real_life_example.explanation: A single season of good work in 1939 grew, unseen, into hundreds of lives and the families that followed them, and was recognised only decades later.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls good conduct a seed from which good things grow; Winton's actions bore fruit long after they were done, in people he had not seen for half a century.

tamil:
ஒழுக்க முடையவர்க்கு ஒல்லாவே தீய
வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்.
transliteration:
Ozhukkam udaiyavarkku ollaave theeya
Vazhukkiyum vaayaal solal.
meaning: People with good behaviour cannot speak bad words, not even by mistake.
elementary: Some people are so used to being kind that even when they are angry or surprised, mean words just don't come out. Being good becomes so natural that it even protects your mouth.
university: The key word is vazhukkiyum, ‘even when slipping’ or ‘even by inadvertence’. Valluvar does not say the disciplined hold back evil speech by effort. He says it is ollaa for them, impossible or unfitting: conduct has become so much second nature that even an unguarded moment is safe. This is a strong claim about habituation, close to Aristotle's view that the virtuous person does the right thing with pleasure and without inner struggle. Tamil ethics gives speech special attention, with chapters on sweet speech (10) and on avoiding useless speech (20). Parallel traditions do too: the Gita counts truthful, non-distressing speech as an austerity, rabbinic ethics condemns lashon hara, and Buddhism places right speech on the Eightfold Path.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Words that do not cause distress, are truthful, inoffensive, and beneficial, as well as regular recitation of the Vedic scriptures—these are declared as austerity of speech.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names speech that never wounds as a form of spiritual discipline.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat freedom from harmful speech as a mark of disciplined character.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers that no corrupt word should come from their mouths at all.
christianity.tie_back: Both require that no evil speech escape a person of good conduct.

islam.quote_or_event: “anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes good speech, or silence, a sign of real faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes clean speech a direct expression of inner character.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist names guarding the tongue as the path to a good life, a verse central to the later Jewish laws against lashon hara (evil speech).
judaism.tie_back: Both make freedom from evil speech a core part of right conduct.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who utters gentle, instructive and truthful words, who imprecates none — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha includes gentle, truthful speech that curses no one among the marks of a holy person.
buddhism.tie_back: Both treat blameless speech as the sign of perfected conduct.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk should avoid untruth, nor should he speak positively (about future things, his plans, &c.); he should avoid sinful speech, and always keep free from deceit. He should not tell anything sinful or meaningless or hurtful, neither for his own sake nor for anybody else's, nor without such a motive.”
jainism.explanation: The disciplined monk avoids harmful speech whatever the circumstances, even when he has no motive at all.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says people of right conduct cannot utter evil words even by a slip; the Jain rule likewise rules out hurtful speech 'without such a motive', that is, even when it would be idle or unintended.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.24–25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So speak the Truth, in righteousness, and do not speak falsehood.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid's hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib tells the seeker to speak only truth and righteousness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the disciplined cannot utter evil words even by a slip; Farid gives the positive rule of speech such people live by.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Asa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Queen Niobe boasts that her fourteen children make her greater than the goddess Leto, who has only two. Apollo and Artemis kill her children, and Niobe, frozen in grief, is turned to stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: One arrogant speech brings total ruin on Niobe.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the reverse image of the Kural: the harm that evil words bring.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises being silent for the most part, or saying only what is necessary in few words, and avoiding talk that is vulgar or that speaks ill of others.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic sage controls speech as part of a disciplined character.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's picture of the well-conducted person whose tongue does not slip into evil.

real_life_example.event_title: The Chofetz Chaim publishes his code on the laws of harmful speech
real_life_example.event: In 1873 Rabbi Yisrael Meir Kagan, then about thirty-five and living in Radun, published a book that systematically set out the Jewish laws forbidding lashon hara, harmful speech about others, and gossip. The work, titled Chafetz Chaim, became the authoritative text on the ethics of speech, and its author became known everywhere by its name. He also wrote a companion ethical treatise on guarding the tongue, Shemirat HaLashon.
real_life_example.explanation: Kagan treated careful speech not as occasional politeness but as a discipline to be trained until it becomes habit, and his book still shapes Jewish teaching on speech.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says people of right conduct cannot speak evil even by a slip of the tongue; Kagan devoted his first book to building exactly that habituated guard over speech.

tamil:
உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் பலகற்றும்
கல்லார் அறிவிலா தார்.
transliteration:
Ulagaththoadu otta ozhugal pala-katrum
Kallaar arivilaa thaar.
meaning: People who have not learned to live in step with the world are still unlearned and foolish, no matter how much they have studied.
elementary: Someone could read every book in the library, but if they cannot get along with people, share, or be polite, they have not really learned the most important lesson.
university: The chapter closes on a paradox: pala-katrum kallaar, ‘having learned much, they have not learned’. What they lack is ulagaththoadu otta ozhugal, conduct that ‘sticks to’ or fits with the world. Commentators differ on what ‘the world’ means. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar take it as the worthy (uyarndhor). Pappaiah boldly reads it as adapting the old ethical texts to present circumstances and dropping what no longer fits, which turns the couplet into almost a charter for moral reasoning over rote rule-following. On any reading, social wisdom is the test of learning. This echoes the rabbinic principle that derech eretz (right conduct) comes before Torah, and Aristotle's scorn for people who ‘take refuge in theory’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Professors and pupils, in fact, all who study the scriptures, if addicted to wicked habits, are to be regarded as illiterate wretches. He only is learned who performeth his religious duties.”
hinduism.explanation: Yudhishthira tells the Yaksha that scholars without good conduct are really unlearned, and that only right action makes a person learned.
hinduism.tie_back: This is nearly identical to the Kural's ‘having learned much, they have not learned’.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 311 (Yaksha Prashna), tr. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes people who keep studying but never reach real understanding.
christianity.tie_back: It captures the Kural's paradox of much learning without true knowledge.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an compares those who carry scripture without living by it to a donkey loaded with books.
islam.tie_back: This is the same point as the Kural: knowledge carried but not lived counts as no knowledge at all.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Where there is no Torah, there is no right conduct; where there is no right conduct, there is no Torah.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah makes learning and derech eretz (proper conduct in the world) depend on each other.
judaism.tie_back: Both hold that learning without right conduct in the world is empty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the learned person who does not practice to a herdsman counting cattle he does not own.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's paradox exactly: much learning, no real gain.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Acknowledging the truth about bondage and liberation, but talking only, not acting (in accordance with these tenets), they seek comfort for themselves in mighty words. Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it? Fools, though sinking lower and lower through their sins, believe themselves to be wise men.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra condemns those who know the doctrine but do not live it, calling them fools who think themselves wise.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who have learned much but cannot live in harmony with the world are ignorant; the Jain verse likewise judges learning without matching conduct to be no wisdom at all.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.8–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If an educated person is a sinner, then the illiterate holy man is not to be punished.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that learning counts for nothing at the reckoning; a learned wrongdoer is judged by his deeds, while an unlettered good person is safe.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the much-read who do not live well with the world remain ignorant; Guru Nanak likewise refuses to let book-learning stand in for right living.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod names Eunomia (Good Order), with her sisters Dike (Justice) and Eirene (Peace), as a daughter of Zeus and Themis. She personifies the lawful harmony that holds human communities together.
greek_mythology.explanation: For the Greeks, living in well-ordered harmony with the community was itself a divine gift.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This loosely matches the Kural's ideal of conduct in harmony with the world.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But most people do not do these, but take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers and will become good in this way, behaving somewhat like patients who listen attentively to their doctors, but do none of the things they are ordered to do.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle mocks people who think that studying ethics makes them good without practising it.
philosophy.tie_back: Both hold that learning without conduct is not real knowledge.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.4, 1105b (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Ignaz Semmelweis fails to win over his colleagues
real_life_example.event: In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis, a doctor at the maternity clinic of the Vienna General Hospital, required staff to wash their hands in a chlorinated lime solution before examining patients, and deaths from childbed fever fell sharply. Many colleagues rejected his explanation, partly because it implied that doctors themselves were carrying the disease to their patients. He set out his findings in a full book only in 1861, and after unfavourable reviews he answered his critics with harshly worded open letters; his doctrine was generally accepted only later.
real_life_example.explanation: Semmelweis was right on the science, yet his discovery saved far fewer lives in his own time than it might have, in part because he could not bring the medical world along with him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who cannot live in harmony with the world remain ignorant however much they have learned; Semmelweis's case shows how knowledge without the skill of persuading others can fail to do its good.

tamil:
பிறன்பொருளாள் பெட்டொழுகும் பேதைமை ஞாலத்து
அறம்பொருள் கண்டார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Piranporulaal pettozhugum pedhaimai gnaalaththu,
Aramporul kandaarkan il.
meaning: People in this world who truly understand goodness and wealth are never so foolish as to desire another man’s wife.
elementary: Imagine someone who has studied all the rules of a game very carefully. That person would never try to grab another player's pieces, because they understand how the game works and why the rules matter. This kural says people who really understand what is right and good would never want someone else's husband or wife.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter by framing adultery first as a failure of intelligence (பேதைமை, 'folly') rather than simply as a sin. The phrase அறம்பொருள் கண்டார் — 'those who have seen aram and porul' — deliberately invokes the first two aims of life that structure the Kural itself (virtue and worldly prosperity), implying that a person who grasps either domain properly would recognise such desire as self-defeating. The word பொருளாள் ('she who is another's porul') reflects the social vocabulary of its age, in which a wife was spoken of as belonging within another's household; modern readers often recast it as a violation of another's committed bond. The kural thus locates the root of the wrong in ignorance, a move that parallels Socratic and Buddhist views that wrongdoing flows from failed understanding.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him not show particular attention to an enemy, to the friend of an enemy, to a wicked man, to a thief, or to the wife of another man.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu, a classical Hindu code of dharma, lists another man's wife among the people a householder should not seek out or single out for attention.
hinduism.tie_back: Those who have studied dharma (aram) are taught this rule explicitly; the Kural says those who truly understand it never fall into the folly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication: That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour; Not in the lust of concupiscence, even as the Gentiles which know not God.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers that sexual self-control is part of knowing God, and contrasts it with the behaviour of those who do not know God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts tie sexual restraint to knowledge: those who 'know' (God, or aram) do not act on such lust.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [also prohibited to you are all] married women except those your right hands possess. [This is] the decree of Allah upon you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an lists married women among those whom a man is forbidden to seek, calling this a decree of God.
islam.tie_back: Anyone who knows the divine law knows a married woman is off-limits, just as the Kural says those who know aram never pursue another's wife.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.”
judaism.explanation: The tenth commandment forbids even desiring a neighbour's wife, listing her among the things that belong within the neighbour's household.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Torah forbids the desire itself (not only the act), and frames the wife as part of another's household.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Knowing well these causes of downfall in the world, the noble sage endowed with insight shares a happy realm.”
buddhism.explanation: At the end of a list of the causes of a person's downfall (which includes going to the wives of others), the Buddha says the wise person who understands them avoids ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: The same logic as the Kural: true understanding of what ruins a life keeps the wise from this folly.
buddhism.source: Parabhava Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.6 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Being infatuated, he is unable to discriminate between the good and the evil. And he is not able to do anything right or proper.”
jainism.explanation: In explaining why the vows must be guarded, Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi says that unchastity first destroys a person's judgment, and from that come all the other harms.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls coveting another's wife a folly (பேதைமை) that people who know dharma never fall into, and the Jain commentary likewise calls it a loss of the very power to tell good from evil.
jainism.source: Tattvārthasūtra 7.9, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi on unchastity (abrahma) (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You have abandoned your own wife, but now you sneak glances at other women. God is not found by wearing religious robes; you are utterly miserable!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan exposes the man who makes a show of religion while his eye strays to other men's wives, and says such a life brings only misery.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who have truly grasped virtue never fall into this folly; Guru Arjan shows that outward religiosity without that understanding does not prevent it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1348, Raag Prabhati, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Paris, a Trojan prince, was welcomed as a guest by King Menelaus of Sparta and then carried off Menelaus's wife Helen. In the Iliad (Book 3) his own brother Hector rebukes him as a disgrace, and his act brings war and ruin on all of Troy.
greek_mythology.explanation: Paris had every advantage of rank and upbringing, yet his desire for another man's wife showed a complete lack of good judgement.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris is the classic example of the 'folly' the Kural names: a failure to see what virtue and plain self-interest both demand.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But most people do not do these, but take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers and will become good in this way.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle warns that knowing moral theory is not enough; people become good only by actually practising good acts.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar's 'those who have seen aram' are people whose understanding shows in conduct; Aristotle agrees that real ethical knowledge is proven by action.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.4 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Edward VIII abdicates to marry Wallis Simpson
real_life_example.event: King Edward VIII wished to marry Wallis Simpson, an American who was still married to her second husband, Ernest Simpson, when the king's attachment to her became a matter of state; she obtained a preliminary divorce decree only in October 1936. As head of the Church of England, the king faced firm opposition from Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin's government and the Church to his marrying a divorced woman whose former husbands were living, and Baldwin rejected a proposed morganatic marriage. Edward abdicated in December 1936, telling the nation by radio that he could not carry out his duties without the help and support of the woman he loved, and his brother became King George VI.
real_life_example.explanation: Edward had been raised from birth to understand the duties and public role of the crown, yet he gave up the throne rather than give up a woman who had been another man's wife.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the folly of desiring another man's wife is not found in those who truly understand virtue and worldly affairs; Edward's choice cost him the very position his whole training had prepared him to fill.

tamil:
அறன்கடை நின்றாருள் எல்லாம் பிறன்கடை
நின்றாரின் பேதையார் இல்.
transliteration:
Arankadai nindraarul ellaam pirankadai,
Nindraarin pedhaiyaar il.
meaning: Of all people who do wrong, no one is a bigger fool than the man who stands at another man’s door, wanting his wife.
elementary: Think of all the silly, wrong things people can do. This kural says that out of all of them, the silliest is waiting outside a neighbour's house because you want the person who belongs to that family. It is the worst kind of wrong choice.
university: The couplet turns on a pun with the word கடை, which can mean both 'the outermost/lowest point' and 'a gate or doorway': அறன்கடை ('beyond the edge of virtue') is set against பிறன்கடை ('at another's gate'). Valluvar thus ranks wrongdoers and places the would-be adulterer, loitering at a neighbour's door, at the very bottom for sheer foolishness. The image of standing at the gate stresses both the humiliation of the act and its risk: the man is exposed, waiting, and dependent on another's household. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read this as a claim that even among sinners this particular vice is uniquely irrational, because it brings danger without any lasting gain.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Ravana, a learned and powerful king, disguises himself as a wandering holy man and comes to the door of the forest hut where Sita, Rama's wife, is alone. He uses the disguise to deceive her and carry her away, which leads to his own destruction.
hinduism.explanation: Ravana literally stands at another man's door, hiding his desire for that man's wife behind a false appearance.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's image of the fool standing at another's gate, and the epic presents it as the folly that ruined one of the greatest kings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Men do not despise a thief, if he steal to satisfy his soul when he is hungry; ... But whoso committeth adultery with a woman lacketh understanding: he that doeth it destroyeth his own soul.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs compares the thief, who at least has an understandable motive, with the adulterer, whom it calls lacking in understanding and self-destructive.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts rank wrongdoers and put the man who pursues another's wife below the others for foolishness.
christianity.source: Proverbs 6:30-32 (KJV), part of the Christian Old Testament

islam.quote_or_event: “I asked the Prophet, ‘What is the greatest sin in the Sight of Allah?’ ... I asked, ‘What is next?’ He said, ‘To commit illegal sexual intercourse with the wife of your neighbor.’”
islam.explanation: Asked to rank the greatest sins, the Prophet listed adultery with a neighbour's wife among the three gravest.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, this ranks the pursuit of a neighbour's wife near the very worst of all wrongs.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If mine heart have been deceived by a woman, or if I have laid wait at my neighbour's door; Then let my wife grind unto another ... For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges.”
judaism.explanation: Job swears he has never waited at his neighbour's door out of desire, calling such conduct a heinous crime.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the same picture as the Kural: the man lurking at a neighbour's door, judged the worst of offenders.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not to be contented with one's own wife, and to be seen with harlots and the wives of others — this is a cause of one's downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists pursuing the wives of others among the chief causes that bring a person to ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts rank this conduct among the most self-destructive choices a person can make.
buddhism.source: Parabhava Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.6 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The enjoyment of the man of unstable heart, who under the influence of infatuation approaches his neighbour's wife and sets his affections upon her, while neighbours spread abroad his guilt, and kinsmen dread and mourn, is like (that of the person who takes pleasure in) licking a serpent's head.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain-authored Nālaṭiyār has a whole chapter on not desiring other men's wives, and this quatrain mocks the man who chases another's wife as a fool tasting pleasure from a serpent's head.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that of all who stand outside virtue, none is a greater fool than the man who waits at another's door, and the Nālaṭiyār gives that folly its picture: licking a cobra for sweetness.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār 87 (ch. 9, 'The Not Desiring Other Men's Wives'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You gaze upon the wives of others, O my soul; you steal and commit evil deeds.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak rebukes the wayward soul for eyeing other men's wives and joining that to theft and other wrongs.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks the man who lingers at a neighbour's door for his wife as the greatest fool among wrongdoers; Guru Nanak names the same longing gaze among the soul's chief failings.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 155, Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, over a hundred suitors spend years in the house of the absent Odysseus, feasting at his expense and pressing his wife Penelope to marry one of them. When Odysseus returns, he and his son kill them all.
greek_mythology.explanation: The suitors linger at another man's hearth, wanting his wife and wasting his goods, until the owner comes home.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They are the Kural's 'those who stand at another's gate' on a grand scale, and the epic judges them the greatest fools of all.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But not every action nor every passion admits of a mean; for some have names that already imply badness, e.g. spite, shamelessness, envy, and in the case of actions adultery, theft, murder.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says adultery is not a matter of 'too much or too little'; like theft and murder it is simply bad, always.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle places adultery among the plainly wrong acts; Valluvar goes a step further and calls it the most foolish of them.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Publius Clodius is caught in Caesar's house during the Bona Dea rites
real_life_example.place: Rome, in the official residence of Julius Caesar as pontifex maximus
real_life_example.event: The rites of the Bona Dea, a festival from which all men were excluded, were held that year in the house of Julius Caesar, and the young aristocrat Publius Clodius Pulcher entered disguised as a woman musician. According to Plutarch he was seeking Caesar's wife Pompeia; he was recognised by his voice, the rites were halted by Caesar's mother Aurelia, and he was found and driven out. Clodius was tried for sacrilege and escaped conviction, reportedly through bribery, while Caesar divorced Pompeia.
real_life_example.explanation: The scandal became one of the most notorious in Roman history, exposing Clodius to prosecution and public ridicule and creating lasting enmities, notably with Cicero, who gave evidence against him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls the man who lingers at another's door for his wife the most foolish of all wrongdoers; Clodius was literally caught inside another man's house, disguised and exposed.

tamil:
விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர் மன்ற தெளிந்தாரில்
தீமை புரிந்துதொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Vilindhaarin verallar mandra thelindhaaril,
Theemai purindhozhugu vaar.
meaning: People who do wrong with the wife of someone who trusts them completely are surely no better than dead.
elementary: Suppose a friend trusts you so much that they let you into their home anytime. If you used that trust to try to take what is most precious to their family, you would be like a broken, empty person inside, with nothing good left alive in you. That is what this kural says.
university: The key word தெளிந்தார் means 'those who are clear' or 'those who trust without suspicion': the victims here are friends who have let the man into their home precisely because they do not doubt him. Valluvar's verdict, விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர் ('not different from the dead'), is a moral rather than literal death: the betrayer has extinguished what makes a person trustworthy and therefore socially alive. Commentators note the intensifier மன்ற ('certainly'), which removes any softening. The couplet thus adds betrayal of trust to the chapter's charge of folly, anticipating the ancient idea, shared by Stoics and scriptural traditions, that faithlessness destroys the essence of a human being.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For in this world there is nothing so detrimental to long life as criminal conversation with another man's wife.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu say nothing shortens a man's life more than an affair with another man's wife.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts link this wrong with death: Manu speaks of shortened life, Valluvar of a man who is already as good as dead.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James describes how desire grows into sin and how sin, once fully grown, produces death.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's 'no different from the dead' matches James's picture of lust ending in death.

islam.quote_or_event: “And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him. She closed the doors and said, ‘Come, you.’ He said, ‘[I seek] the refuge of Allah. Indeed, he is my master, who has made good my residence. Indeed, wrongdoers will not succeed.’”
islam.explanation: When his master's wife tries to seduce him, the prophet Joseph (Yusuf) refuses, pointing to the kindness and trust his master has shown him.
islam.tie_back: Yusuf refuses to do exactly what the Kural condemns, betraying the household of someone who trusted him, and says such wrongdoers cannot succeed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, my master wotteth not what is with me in the house, and he hath committed all that he hath to my hand; There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
judaism.explanation: Joseph tells Potiphar's wife that his master has trusted him with everything, and that betraying that trust with her would be a great wickedness.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact situation: the one who is fully trusted in a household refuses to wrong that household.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as rust arising from iron eats away the base from which it arises, even so, their own deeds lead transgressors to states of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares wrongdoing to rust that eats away the very iron it grows on.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says the betrayer is hollowed out and lifeless; the Dhammapada says wrong deeds consume the doer from within.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the assembly he pronounces holy (words), yet secretly he commits sins; but the wise know him to be a deceiver and great rogue.”
jainism.explanation: In the lecture on 'Knowledge of Women', the Sūtrakṛtāṅga condemns the man who keeps a respectable face in public while secretly sinning with women, and says the wise see through him.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar condemns the man who plots against the home of friends who trust him without suspicion, and the Sūtrakṛtāṅga likewise condemns the hidden betrayal of a man who looks trustworthy, though it does not share the Kural's verdict that such a man is 'no different from the dead'.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.4.1.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: In the Charitropakhyan of the Dasam Granth, the narrator recalls being taught never, even by mistake or in a dream, to go to another's wife's bed, and warns that such love is like a sharp dagger and an invitation to death.
sikhism.explanation: The passage presents adultery as something that kills the one who commits it, not only the one wronged.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who plot against the home of a trusting friend are no different from the dead; this text likewise treats such desire as death already working in the body.
sikhism.source: Dasam Granth, Charitropakhyan (Charitar 21), verses 51-53 as numbered on BaniDB (attributed to Guru Gobind Singh; authorship contested)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Look at Aegisthus; he must needs make love to Agamemnon's wife unrighteously and then kill Agamemnon, though he knew it would be the death of him; for I sent Mercury to warn him not to do either of these things.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Zeus (Jove) explains that Aegisthus seduced King Agamemnon's wife while the king was away at war, and was warned that it would cost him his life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Aegisthus wronged the household of an absent king and was, in the Kural's words, already a dead man.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “How shall I consider you, man? As a neighbour, as a friend? What kind of one? As a citizen? Wherein shall I trust you? So if you were an utensil so worthless that a man could not use you, you would be pitched out on the dung heaps.”
philosophy.explanation: Speaking to a man caught in adultery, Epictetus says the adulterer has made himself impossible to trust, and so useless as a neighbour, friend, or citizen.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar says the betrayer of trust is 'no different from the dead'; Epictetus says he is a useless thing to be thrown away, for the same reason.

real_life_example.event_title: Richard Wagner and Cosima von Bulow
real_life_example.place: Munich, Bavaria, and Tribschen near Lucerne, Switzerland
real_life_example.event: Cosima von Bulow, a daughter of Franz Liszt, was married to the conductor Hans von Bulow, one of Richard Wagner's foremost champions, who conducted the premiere of Wagner's Tristan und Isolde in Munich in 1865. Cosima's relationship with Wagner began while she was still married to Bulow, and she had children with Wagner during the marriage; in 1868 she left her husband and went to live with Wagner at Tribschen in Switzerland. Bulow granted her a divorce in 1870, and she married Wagner later that year.
real_life_example.explanation: The affair is one of the best-known episodes in musical history, remembered partly because the man betrayed was a friend who had devoted his talents to Wagner's work.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural condemns those who plot against the household of people who trust them; Bulow had welcomed Wagner into his professional and domestic life and was deceived within it.

tamil:
எனைத்துணையர் ஆயினும் என்னாம் தினைத்துணையும்
தேரான் பிறனில் புகல்.
transliteration:
Enaiththunaiyar aayinum ennaam thinaiththunaiyum,
Theraan piranil pugal.
meaning: However great a man may be, what is his greatness worth if he goes after another man’s wife without thinking even a little about how wrong it is?
elementary: Imagine the best player on a team, who is famous and loved by everyone. If that player cheated in a very unfair way without stopping to think, all their fame would be worth nothing. This kural says the same about a person who goes after someone else's husband or wife: being important cannot save them.
university: The couplet plays two measures against each other: எனைத்துணை ('however great a measure') and தினைத்துணை ('a millet grain's measure'), the smallest unit in Tamil idiom. A man may possess vast greatness, yet if he does not reflect (தேரான்) for even a millet grain's worth before entering another's home, that greatness is worthless. The rhetorical question என்னாம் ('what does it become?') leaves the answer, nothing, to the listener. The emphasis on failing to reflect links to the chapter's theme of folly: the danger lies in the thoughtless moment in which rank and reputation are thrown away, a pattern visible in stories of kings and heroes across many cultures.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Kichaka, the powerful commander of King Virata's army, becomes infatuated with Draupadi, the wife of the Pandavas, who is living disguised as a maid at the court. Ignoring her refusals and warnings, he pursues her and is killed at night by Bhima.
hinduism.explanation: Kichaka's power and position did him no good once he recklessly pursued another man's wife.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: however great one is, entering another's home for his wife without a moment's thought ends in ruin.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (narrative summary; trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus asks what worldly success is worth if a person loses their soul in the process.
christianity.tie_back: Same rhetorical move as the Kural: 'however great he may be, what is it worth?' if he destroys himself through wrongdoing.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse. Indeed, it is ever an immorality and is evil as a way.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an forbids not only the act but even approaching it, calling it an evil path.
islam.tie_back: The Kural blames the man who steps into another's home without a moment's reflection; the Qur'an tells believers to stop well before the first step.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul; ... thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword, and hast taken his wife to be thy wife.”
judaism.explanation: The prophet Nathan confronts King David: God had given him a kingdom, yet he took another man's wife and arranged her husband's death.
judaism.tie_back: David is the Kural's 'however great' man: a king whose greatness could not cover his taking of another's wife.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who plays with dice and drinks intoxicants, goes to women who are dear unto others as their own lives, associates with the mean and not with elders — he declines just as the moon during the waning half.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that a man who goes to women cherished by others loses his standing, fading away like the waning moon.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say whatever brightness a man has, he loses it by going after another's cherished wife.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Some men of great intelligence who perform their duties as supporters of women, get into their power … (The adulterers’) hands and feet are cut off, their skin and flesh are torn off, they are roasted alive, and acid is poured into their wounds.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga warns that even men of great intelligence are brought down by illicit passion and then suffer the brutal punishments of the day, and yet, it adds, they 'will not promise not to do the same again'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks what a man's greatness is worth if he enters another's home without weighing the wrong even a millet-grain's worth, and the Sūtrakṛtāṅga shows great intelligence counting for nothing once a man is in passion's power.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.4.1.20–21 (cf. 22) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Ahalyaa was the wife of Gautam the seer. Seeing her, Indra was enticed. When he received a thousand marks of disgrace on his body, then he felt regret in his mind.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak retells how Indra, king of the gods, lusted after a sage's wife and was marked with disgrace, regretting it only afterwards.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what greatness is worth if a man enters another's home without a moment's thought; Indra's story shows the highest rank undone by exactly that thoughtlessness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1344, Raag Prabhati, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Ill deeds do not prosper, and the weak confound the strong. See how limping Vulcan, lame as he is, has caught Mars who is the fleetest god in heaven.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Ares (Mars) is caught with Hephaestus's (Vulcan's) wife Aphrodite in a hidden net, the other gods laugh that even the swiftest, strongest god was trapped.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Just as the Kural says, great strength and rank were worth nothing to a god who went after another's wife without thinking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now in everything the pleasant or pleasure is most to be guarded against; for we do not judge it impartially. We ought, then, to feel towards pleasure as the elders of the people felt towards Helen.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle warns that pleasure clouds our judgement, and says we should treat it as the wise Trojan elders treated Helen: admiring her beauty, yet wishing her sent away to avoid ruin.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural blames the man who does not reflect for even a moment; Aristotle says pleasure is exactly what stops us reflecting, so it must be kept at a distance.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.9 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The O'Shea divorce case ends Parnell's leadership
real_life_example.event: Charles Stewart Parnell, leader of the Irish Parliamentary Party, was at the height of his popularity and often called Ireland's uncrowned king when Captain William O'Shea filed for divorce from his wife Katharine at the end of 1889, naming Parnell as co-respondent. The case was not defended and the divorce was granted in November 1890. When Parnell refused to step down, Gladstone made clear that the Liberal alliance would end, the Catholic hierarchy declared against him, and in December 1890 most of his party withdrew from his leadership; he died in October 1891 still fighting to regain it.
real_life_example.explanation: The split divided Irish nationalism and damaged the cause of Home Rule for years, showing how one private choice could undo a great public career.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what a man's greatness is worth if he enters another's home for his wife; Parnell's immense standing proved worthless once the affair became public.

tamil:
எளிதென இல்லிறப்பான் எய்துமெஞ் ஞான்றும்
விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி.
transliteration:
Elidhena illirappaan eydhum enjnjaandrum,
Viliyaadhu nirkum pazhi.
meaning: A man who goes after another man’s wife, thinking it is easy, earns a shame that never dies and stays with him forever.
elementary: Some mistakes are like writing on sand: they wash away. Others are like carving into stone: they stay forever. This kural says that going after someone else's husband or wife might seem easy at the time, but the shame is carved in stone and never goes away.
university: Valluvar contrasts the ease of the act (எளிது, 'easy') with the permanence of its consequence (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி, 'blame that stands undying'). The verb இல்லிறப்பான் combines இல் ('home') and இறப்பு ('crossing over, transgressing'), so the offender is literally 'one who oversteps a home'. The couplet reflects a culture where reputation (புகழ்) was treated as the only thing that outlives a person, a theme developed in the Kural's later chapter on fame; adultery produces the exact opposite, a lasting infamy. The asymmetry between a moment's ease and an eternity of blame is a common moral argument, found in scriptural warnings about reproach that 'shall not be wiped away'.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Indra, king of the gods, disguises himself as the sage Gautama to approach Gautama's wife Ahalya. The sage discovers him and curses him, and the episode is remembered ever after as a lasting stain on Indra's name.
hinduism.explanation: Even the king of the gods, who thought the deception would be easy, could not escape a disgrace that followed him permanently.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'undying blame': an act taken lightly leaves a mark that never fades.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
christianity.explanation: The letter to the Hebrews says marriage must be kept pure, and that God himself will judge adulterers.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say what seems easy and hidden will not simply pass: the Kural speaks of lasting blame, Hebrews of divine judgement.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity or kill the soul which Allah has forbidden [to be killed], except by right, and do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse. And whoever should do that will meet a penalty. Multiplied for him is the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein humiliated.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says whoever commits these grave sins, including unlawful intercourse, will face a multiplied penalty and remain in humiliation.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an's 'abide therein humiliated' echoes the Kural's disgrace that 'never dies'.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone who descends to Gehenna ultimately ascends, except for three who descend and do not ascend, and these are they: One who engages in intercourse with a married woman ...; and one who humiliates another in public; and one who calls another a derogatory name.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud teaches that most sinners are eventually released from punishment, but someone who commits adultery with a married woman is among the few who never come back out.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts stress permanence: the Kural's blame 'never dies', and in the Talmud the adulterer 'does not ascend'.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz translation)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “An evil deed is better left undone, for such a deed torments one afterwards. But a good deed is better done, doing which one repents not later.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says evil deeds keep tormenting the doer long after they are done.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say that a wrong that seems small at the moment leaves a lasting burden behind.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If any one see, disgrace lights on the house; if any hand should seize, leg's maimed; in the doing of the shameful deed is dread; it yields as fruit vast hell's affliction: tell me, O profligate, what measure of delight is thine?”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār sets the adulterer's small pleasure against a lasting price: disgrace on the family, bodily punishment, constant dread, and the long suffering of hell as karmic fruit.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the man who thinks it easy to cross into another's home earns a disgrace that never dies, and the Nālaṭiyār weighs that 'easy' pleasure against disgrace and suffering that follow him into the next life.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār 84 (ch. 9, 'The Not Desiring Other Men's Wives'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those men who go out to enjoy other men's women shall suffer in shame.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says plainly that men who pursue other men's wives will be put to shame.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that the man who thinks it easy to cross into another's home earns a disgrace that never dies; Guru Arjan names the same shame as the certain outcome.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1362, Phunhay Mahala 5, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ixion, a king who was a guest at Zeus's own table, tried to seduce Hera, Zeus's wife. As punishment he was bound to a fiery wheel that turns forever, and the poet Pindar says his fate is a lasting warning to all mortals.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ixion thought he could wrong his host's wife and get away with it; instead his punishment became eternal and his name a byword.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ixion embodies the Kural's 'blame that stands undying': a moment's reckless desire, an eternity of consequence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “When you have been overcome in sexual intercourse with a person, do not reckon this single defeat only, but reckon that you have also nurtured, increased your incontinence.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus warns that giving in once is never a single event: it strengthens the bad habit and leaves a lasting mark on the character.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the 'easy' act leaves a permanent stain on one's name; Epictetus says it leaves a lasting mark on one's soul.

real_life_example.event_title: Georges d'Anthes and the duel that killed Pushkin
real_life_example.event: Georges d'Anthes, a French officer serving in Russia, openly courted Natalya Pushkina, the wife of the poet Alexander Pushkin, and in 1836 anonymous letters mocking Pushkin over his wife circulated in St Petersburg. D'Anthes married Natalya's sister Ekaterina in January 1837, but the gossip continued, and later that month the two men fought a duel in which Pushkin was mortally wounded; he died two days later. The tsar stripped d'Anthes of his military rank and expelled him from Russia.
real_life_example.explanation: Russia lost its greatest poet, and in Russian memory d'Anthes has been remembered ever since chiefly as the man who killed Pushkin.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that the man who thinks it easy to cross into another's household earns a disgrace that never dies; d'Anthes' pursuit of Pushkin's wife left his name permanently tied to that loss.

tamil:
பகைபாவம் அச்சம் பழியென நான்கும்
இகவாவாம் இல்லிறப்பான் கண்.
transliteration:
Pagaipaavam achcham pazhiyena naangum,
Igavaavaam illirappaan kan.
meaning: Enemies, sin, fear and shame: these four never leave a man who wrongs another man’s home.
elementary: Picture someone who takes a thing that belongs to another family. Now four shadows follow them everywhere: people are angry at them, they know they did wrong, they are always scared of being caught, and others think badly of them. This kural says those four shadows never go away.
university: This couplet is a compact catalogue: பகை (enmity from the wronged husband and his kin), பாவம் (sin, the moral or karmic stain), அச்சம் (constant fear of discovery and revenge), and பழி (public blame). The verb இகவா ('they do not depart') makes all four permanent companions. The list covers the social, spiritual, psychological, and reputational costs of the act, a strikingly complete analysis for two lines. Its closest parallel is Dhammapada 309, which also names exactly four misfortunes for the man who goes to another's wife, a resemblance that scholars have noted when discussing shared ethical currents in early South Asian literature.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to the hell of self-destruction for the soul—lust, anger, and greed. Therefore, one should abandon all three.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names lust first among the three gateways that lead a person to self-destruction.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural lists four evils that follow lust for another's wife; the Gita names lust itself as a gate to ruin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter: because that the Lord is the avenger of all such, as we also have forewarned you and testified.”
christianity.explanation: In a passage about sexual purity, Paul warns that anyone who wrongs his brother in this way will face God as avenger.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say the wrongdoer cannot escape consequences; Paul's 'avenger' corresponds to the Kural's enmity and fear.

islam.quote_or_event: “When an adulterer commits illegal sexual intercourse, then he is not a believer at the time, he is doing it”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that at the moment of committing adultery, the person's faith leaves him.
islam.tie_back: The Kural lists sin among the four things that cling to the adulterer; this hadith shows that sin as the loss of faith itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wound and dishonour shall he get; and his reproach shall not be wiped away. For jealousy is the rage of a man: therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance. He will not regard any ransom; neither will he rest content, though thou givest many gifts.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs describes what follows adultery: injury, dishonour, lasting reproach, and a husband's jealous fury that no payment can calm.
judaism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural's list: enmity (the husband's rage), fear (no ransom will help), and disgrace (dishonour and reproach).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Four misfortunes befall the reckless man who consorts with another's wife: acquisition of demerit, disturbed sleep, ill-repute, and (rebirth in) states of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists four misfortunes for the man who goes to another man's wife: bad karma, sleepless nights, a bad name, and a painful rebirth.
buddhism.tie_back: An almost exact match: four evils that cling to the man, including sin (demerit), fear (disturbed sleep), and disgrace (ill-repute).

jainism.quote_or_event: “Virtue, praise, friendship, greatness, all these four draw not anigh the men who covet their neighbour's wife. Hatred, disgrace and guilt, with fear, these four possessions abide with men who covet their neighbour's wife.”
jainism.explanation: In its chapter on not desiring other men's wives, the Nālaṭiyār lists the four things the adulterer gains: hatred, disgrace, guilt and fear.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar names enmity, sin, fear and disgrace as the four things that never leave the man who wrongs another's home, and the Nālaṭiyār names the same four (பகை, பழி, பாவம், அச்சம்) in almost the same Tamil words.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār 82 (ch. 9, 'The Not Desiring Other Men's Wives'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Caught in slander and attachment to the wealth and women of others, they eat poison and suffer in pain.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes those drawn to others' wealth, others' women and slander as eating poison and living in pain.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural lists enmity, sin, fear and disgrace as companions that never leave the adulterer; Guru Nanak likewise says this desire brings lasting suffering.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1255, Raag Malar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Alike with him who does wrong to a suppliant or a guest, or who goes up to his brother's bed and commits unnatural sin in lying with his wife, ... truly Zeus himself is angry, and at the last lays on him a heavy requittal for his evil doing.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that a man who lies with his brother's wife earns the anger of Zeus and a heavy punishment in the end.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod names the enmity of the gods and the sin and punishment that follow; the Kural adds fear and public disgrace to the list.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, ll. 327-334 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is just as if the wasps complained because no man cares for them, but all fly from them, and if a man can, he strikes them and knocks them down. You have such a sting that you throw into trouble and pain any man that you wound with it.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the adulterer that he is like a wasp: everyone avoids him, and anyone who can will strike him down.
philosophy.tie_back: This captures the Kural's enmity, fear, and disgrace: the adulterer is shunned, hated, and always in danger.

real_life_example.event_title: Alexander Hamilton publishes the Reynolds Pamphlet
real_life_example.event: In 1791, while serving as the first US Secretary of the Treasury, Alexander Hamilton began an affair with Maria Reynolds, a married woman. Her husband, James Reynolds, then demanded money to keep quiet, and Hamilton paid him, including $1,000 in two instalments by January 1792. When a journalist accused him in 1797 of illegal speculation with Reynolds, Hamilton published a pamphlet confessing the affair and the blackmail in order to clear himself of financial wrongdoing; the revelation humiliated his family and ended any hope he had of becoming president.
real_life_example.explanation: Hamilton cleared his name of corruption only by publicly confessing a private wrong, and the affair shadowed the rest of his career.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names enmity, sin, fear and disgrace as the four companions of the man who transgresses against another's home; Hamilton met all four, from the husband's hostility and years of fear of exposure to lasting public disgrace.

tamil:
அறனியலான் இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் பிறனியலாள்
பெண்மை நயவா தவன்.
transliteration:
Araniyalaan ilvaazhvaan enbaan piraniyalaal,
Penmai nayavaa thavan.
meaning: A man who does not desire a woman who belongs to another is the one called a true family man, living the right way.
elementary: What makes someone a good member of a family? This kural gives a simple test: a good family person is happy with their own family and never wishes for someone else's husband or wife. Being loyal is part of being good at home.
university: Here Valluvar turns from warning to definition: the true இல்வாழ்வான் (householder), the central figure of the whole இல்லறவியல் section, is identified by a negative mark, not desiring பிறனியலாள் ('she who moves within another's sphere'). The word இயல் appears twice, linking அறன்இயலான் ('one whose conduct is shaped by virtue') to பிறன்இயலாள் ('one whose life is joined to another'), so the couplet balances two kinds of belonging. By defining domestic virtue through fidelity, the Kural treats chastity as a duty of husbands as much as of wives, which some modern commentators highlight as notably even-handed for its era. The idea that the good household is built on the spouse's exclusive devotion appears in many traditions' ideals of marriage.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Rama is honoured as ekapatnivrata, a man vowed to one wife. Even when he performs a great royal sacrifice after Sita is gone, he does not remarry but uses a golden image of Sita in her place.
hinduism.explanation: Rama is held up as the ideal householder precisely because his devotion belongs to his wife alone.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural defines the virtuous householder by his fidelity; Rama is the Hindu tradition's model of exactly that.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For this, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet; and if there be any other commandment, it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. Love worketh no ill to his neighbour.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says all the commandments, starting with the ban on adultery, are summed up in loving one's neighbour.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's good householder shows his virtue by not wanting his neighbour's wife; Paul says this is simply what love for one's neighbour looks like.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they who guard their private parts ... But whoever seeks beyond that, then those are the transgressors.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the successful believers as those who guard their chastity except within marriage, and calls anyone who goes beyond this a transgressor.
islam.tie_back: Both texts define the good person by keeping desire within one's own marriage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well. ... Let them be only thine own, and not strangers' with thee. Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs uses the image of drinking from one's own well to urge a man to find joy only with his own wife.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's ideal householder desires only his own; Proverbs pictures that same faithful household as a blessed fountain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In five ways, young householder, should a wife as the West be ministered to by a husband: (i) by being courteous to her, (ii) by not despising her, (iii) by being faithful to her, (iv) by handing over authority to her, (v) by providing her with adornments.”
buddhism.explanation: In his code for lay householders, the Buddha lists faithfulness among a husband's duties to his wife.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts make fidelity a defining duty of the good householder.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain ethics makes 'contentment with one's own wife' (svadārasantoṣa) the fourth of the five minor vows (aṇuvrata) taken by every lay householder. The Tattvārthasūtra lists 'intercourse with an unchaste married woman' among the transgressions that break it.
jainism.explanation: Jainism asks only monks for total celibacy. For the householder, chastity means being faithful to his own spouse, and this vow is one of the marks of a proper lay follower (śrāvaka).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar defines the true householder as the man who does not desire another's wife, and Jainism builds that same restraint into the vows that define its lay householder.
jainism.source: Tattvārthasūtra 7.28, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Sikh ought to treat beautiful women of others as his mothers, sisters, and daughters.”
sikhism.explanation: In a pauri on what a Sikh ought to do, Bhai Gurdas makes regarding other men's women as mother, sister or daughter a mark of the true disciple.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines the true householder by his not desiring another's wife; Bhai Gurdas defines the true Sikh, himself a householder, by the same restraint.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 29, Pauri 11 (English translation as published on BaniDB and searchgurbani.com)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus finally returns home in the Odyssey, Penelope tests him by asking for their bed to be moved. Odysseus reveals that he built the bed himself around a living olive tree, so it cannot be moved, and she knows he is truly her husband.
greek_mythology.explanation: The immovable marriage bed stands for the unbreakable bond between a faithful husband and wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's true householder keeps his bond whole; Homer's rooted bed is the Greek image of that same faithful home.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “So too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says character is built by repeated action: we become temperate by consistently acting with self-control.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural defines the virtuous householder by what he consistently does not desire; Aristotle explains that such character is formed by habit.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Hongzhi Emperor keeps Empress Zhang as his only consort
real_life_example.event: The Hongzhi Emperor of the Ming dynasty, who reigned from 1487 to 1505, kept Empress Zhang as his only wife from his time as a prince until his death, although Chinese emperors customarily kept many consorts. His ministers repeatedly urged him to take more consorts to secure the succession, and he refused. Historians describe him as the only monogamous emperor in Chinese history.
real_life_example.explanation: In a court where an emperor's household was expected to include many women, Hongzhi defined his own household by fidelity to one wife.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural identifies the true householder as the man who does not desire a woman who belongs to another; Hongzhi went further and refused even the consorts his position allowed.

tamil:
பிறன்மனை நோக்காத பேராண்மை சான்றோர்க்கு
அறனொன்றோ ஆன்ற வொழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Piranmanai nokkaadha peraanmai saandrorkku,
Aranondro aandra ozhukku.
meaning: For good people, the great courage of not even looking at another man’s wife with desire is not just goodness. It is the fullness of right living.
elementary: Being truly strong is not about big muscles. This kural says real strength is choosing not even to look at someone else's husband or wife in a wanting way. That kind of self-control is the strongest and best way to behave.
university: The striking term பேராண்மை ('great manliness' or 'supreme valour') redefines heroism: in a culture that prized martial courage, Valluvar says the greatest valour is the self-mastery not to look (நோக்காத) at another's wife with desire. The couplet moves the moral line from the act to the gaze, the same shift found in the Sermon on the Mount and in the Qur'anic command to lower the gaze. The second line says this restraint is not just one virtue (அறன் ஒன்றோ, 'is it only virtue?') but ஆன்ற ஒழுக்கு, complete or mature conduct, linking this chapter back to the preceding chapter on ஒழுக்கமுடைமை (right conduct). For the சான்றோர் (the noble or accomplished), then, this restraint is the crown of character.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, when Rama shows Lakshmana ornaments dropped by the kidnapped Sita, Lakshmana says he cannot recognise her bracelets or earrings, only her anklets, because he bowed at her feet every day and never raised his eyes to look at her.
hinduism.explanation: Lakshmana, a great warrior, had lived beside his brother's wife for years and never once looked at her face with any desire.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'great manliness that does not look at another's wife' in its most famous Indian example.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that the wrong begins with the desiring look, not only with the act.
christianity.tie_back: Same move as the Kural: the line is drawn at the gaze itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an commands believing men to lower their gaze and guard their chastity.
islam.tie_back: The Kural praises the man who does not look; the Qur'an commands exactly this lowering of the gaze.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?”
judaism.explanation: Job says he has made a solemn promise with his own eyes not to look at a woman with desire.
judaism.tie_back: Job's 'covenant with the eyes' is the Kural's refusal to look, framed as a sacred vow.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Come now, monks: with regard to women who are old enough to be your mother, establish the attitude you would have toward your mother. With regard to women who are old enough to be your sister, establish the attitude you'd have toward a sister.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches young monks to look at women as they would at their own mother or sister, so that desire does not arise.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural praises not looking at another's wife with desire; the Buddha trains the eye to see such a woman as family.
