buddhism.source: Bharadvaja Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.127 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “While his loving wife dwells in his home, the tender one whom he espoused, — seeking (out an auspicious) day, and sounding the drum, for many folks to know,—and whom he guards as his own, what means a man's glance at another's wife?”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār asks why a man who has publicly married a loving wife should even look at another man's wife, so the restraint begins with the eyes.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls the man who does not even look (நோக்கா) at another's wife the possessor of 'great manliness', and the Nālaṭiyār likewise puts the moral line at the glance.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār 86 (ch. 9, 'The Not Desiring Other Men's Wives'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai

sikhism.quote_or_event: “whose eyes do not gaze upon the beauty of others' wives,”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan lists not looking at other men's wives with desire among the marks of the rare, truly pure person.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural moves the line from the act to the gaze and calls this restraint the fullness of conduct; Guru Arjan likewise makes the undesiring eye a mark of holiness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 274, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 9, Pauri 1, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad (Book 6), the hero Bellerophon stays as a guest with King Proetus. The king's wife Anteia desires him, but Bellerophon, being honourable, refuses her. She falsely accuses him, and he is sent on deadly quests, which he survives with the gods' help.
greek_mythology.explanation: Bellerophon, famed for his courage, showed an even greater courage by refusing his host's wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'great manliness': heroism shown not in battle but in refusing another's wife.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “To-day when I saw a handsome person, I did not say to myself, I wish I could lie with her, and Happy is her husband; for he who says this says, Happy is her adulterer also. Nor do I picture the rest to my mind.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus describes the victory of seeing a beautiful woman and refusing even to let desire or fantasy begin.
philosophy.tie_back: Almost a commentary on the Kural: true strength is not letting the look turn into desire at all.

real_life_example.event_title: Goethe leaves Wetzlar and Charlotte Buff
real_life_example.event: In the summer of 1772 the young Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, then a trainee at the Imperial Chamber Court in Wetzlar, fell in love with Charlotte Buff, who was already engaged to Johann Christian Kestner. After a few months Goethe left Wetzlar abruptly in September 1772 without saying goodbye, and Charlotte married Kestner the following spring. Goethe drew on the experience for his novel The Sorrows of Young Werther, published in 1774, in which Lotte was modelled on Charlotte and her fiance on Kestner.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than press his feelings on a woman promised to another man, Goethe withdrew, and the episode became the seed of one of the most influential novels of the age.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls it the greatest manliness not even to look with desire at another's wife; Goethe's departure from Wetzlar was a withdrawal from a woman who belonged to another.

tamil:
நலக்குரியார் யாரெனின் நாமநீர் வைப்பின்
பிறர்க்குரியாள் தோள்தோயா தார்.
transliteration:
Nalakkuriyaar yaarenin naamaneer vaippin,
Pirarkkuriyaal tholthoyaa thaar.
meaning: In this world circled by the fearsome sea, who truly deserves every good thing? Those who do not touch a woman who belongs to another man.
elementary: If you asked, 'Who deserves all the best things in the whole wide world?', this kural has an answer: the people who stay loyal and never go after someone else's husband or wife. Being faithful makes you worthy of good things.
university: The couplet is framed as a question and answer, a device Valluvar uses to give his verdict extra force. The phrase நாமநீர் வைப்பு ('the world set within fearsome waters') is a classical Tamil epithet for the earth encircled by the ocean, so the claim is universal: anywhere in the world. The one worthy of நலம் (goodness, blessing, well-being) is identified by a concrete image, தோள் தோயாதார் ('those whose shoulders do not touch'), an embrace withheld. After several couplets on the ruin that follows adultery, this one reverses the angle and promises reward, showing that the chapter aims to encourage as well as warn.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A widely quoted Sanskrit maxim, usually attributed to Chanakya's Niti, says: one who regards other men's wives as his mother, others' wealth as a lump of clay, and all beings as his own self, is truly wise (a pandita).
hinduism.explanation: This popular saying names respect for other men's wives as the first mark of a truly wise and worthy person.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts answer the question 'who is truly worthy?' by pointing to the person who keeps away from another's wife.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti (maxim 'matrvat paradareshu'; paraphrase; verse numbering and attribution vary between editions)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says the pure-hearted are blessed, and promises them the vision of God.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural says the faithful deserve every good; the Beatitude promises the greatest good to the pure in heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever can guarantee (the chastity of) what is between his two jaw-bones and what is between his two legs (i.e. his tongue and his private parts), I guarantee Paradise for him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet promised Paradise to anyone who guards his speech and his chastity.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says the chaste deserve all good in the world; the Prophet promises them the highest good of all.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned? Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned? So he that goeth in to his neighbour's wife; whosoever toucheth her shall not be innocent.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares touching a neighbour's wife to carrying fire against one's chest: no one can do it and stay unharmed or innocent.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural praises those who do not 'touch the shoulder' of another's wife; Proverbs says whoever does touch her cannot remain innocent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To support mother and father, to cherish wife and children, and to be engaged in peaceful occupation — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists caring for one's own spouse and family among the greatest blessings of life.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural ties worthiness of good to faithfulness; the Buddha calls cherishing one's own wife a supreme blessing.
buddhism.source: Maha-mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Virtue, praise, friendship, greatness, all these four draw not anigh the men who covet their neighbour's wife.”
jainism.explanation: The first half of this Nālaṭiyār quatrain says that virtue, good name, friendship and greatness all stay away from the man who covets another's wife. Turned around, they belong to the man who does not.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that those who do not embrace another's wife deserve every good thing in the sea-girt world, and the Nālaṭiyār makes the same point in reverse: virtue, fame, friendship and greatness avoid the man who covets.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār 82, first half (ch. 9, 'The Not Desiring Other Men's Wives'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai

sikhism.quote_or_event: “whose eyes do not gaze upon the beauty of others' wives, … - O Nanak, among millions, there is scarcely one such 'touch-nothing Saint'.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan closes his portrait of the truly pure person, whose eyes do not covet others' wives, by saying such a one is rare among millions.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks who in the whole sea-girt world deserves every good and answers: those who do not embrace another's wife; Guru Arjan likewise singles out such a person as rare and honoured.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 274, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 9, Pauri 1, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar tells how the hero Peleus, while a guest of King Acastus, was pursued by the king's wife. He refused her out of reverence for Zeus, god of hospitality. After surviving her false accusations, Peleus was rewarded by the gods with marriage to the sea-goddess Thetis, a wedding the gods themselves attended.
greek_mythology.explanation: Peleus refused another man's wife and was rewarded with the greatest honour a mortal could receive.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's promise exactly: the one who does not embrace another's wife is the one who deserves every good thing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the man who abstains from bodily pleasures and delights in this very fact is temperate, while the man who is annoyed at it is self-indulgent.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the truly temperate person is the one who takes joy in holding back from wrong pleasures.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural promises good to those who refrain; Aristotle says the refraining itself becomes a source of joy for the virtuous.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Charles and Emma Darwin's marriage at Down House
real_life_example.event: Charles Darwin married his cousin Emma Wedgwood on 29 January 1839, and in 1842 they moved to Down House in Kent, where they raised their children and lived for the rest of his life. Emma supported his scientific work, handled correspondence for him, and nursed him through long periods of ill health. Their marriage lasted 43 years, until his death at Down House in 1882, and English Heritage describes it as very happy and loving.
real_life_example.explanation: Darwin's steady family life at Down gave him the security in which he carried out decades of research, and his marriage is remembered as a model of companionship.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who do not embrace another's wife are worthy of every good thing; Darwin's long, faithful marriage was accompanied by a full family life and a lifetime of honoured work.

tamil:
அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும் பிறன்வரையாள்
பெண்மை நயவாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Aranvaraiyaan alla seyinum piranvaraiyaal,
Penmai nayavaamai nandru.
meaning: Even if a man does not live by what is right and does many wrong things, it is still good if he does not desire another man’s wife.
elementary: Imagine someone who breaks lots of rules. This kural says: even if they have not been good at many things, they should at least keep this one rule and never go after someone else's husband or wife. It is the one line everyone must never cross.
university: The closing couplet makes a realistic concession: even a man who does not stay within virtue's limits (அறன் வரையான்) and does what should not be done (அல்ல செயினும்) should at least not desire one who lives within another's limits (பிறன் வரையாள்). The repetition of வரை ('boundary') creates a pointed wordplay: he may cross the bounds of virtue, but must not cross the bounds of another's marriage. By holding this line even for the imperfect, Valluvar marks adultery as a floor below which no one should fall, not merely an ideal for saints. The move is pastoral as well as moral, offering even the flawed a place to begin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Vibhishana, the brother of the demon-king Ravana, belongs to a race known for wrongdoing, yet he repeatedly urges Ravana to return Sita to Rama. When Ravana refuses, Vibhishana leaves him and joins Rama.
hinduism.explanation: Even within a household known for evil deeds, one voice insists that taking another's wife is the line that must not be crossed.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says even those who do wrong should hold this one line; Vibhishana holds it amid a family of wrongdoers.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.”
christianity.explanation: Paul singles out sexual sin as different from all other sins, because it is a sin against one's own body.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat this sin as special: whatever else a person does, this one must be fled.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah will give shade, to seven, on the Day when there will be no shade but His. (These seven persons are) ... a man who refuses the call of a charming woman of noble birth for illicit intercourse with her and says: I am afraid of Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet listed, among seven people God will shelter on Judgement Day, a man who refuses a tempting invitation to sin out of fear of God.
islam.tie_back: Both texts show that holding this one line brings great good, whatever else a person's record may be.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not commit adultery.”
judaism.explanation: The seventh commandment states the ban on adultery as an absolute, with no conditions or exceptions.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural sets this as the one line even the imperfect must keep; the Torah states it as a basic, unconditional commandment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Such a man acquires demerit and an unhappy birth in the future. Brief is the pleasure of the frightened man and woman, and the king imposes heavy punishment. Hence, let no man consort with another's wife.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ends its warning with a plain rule for everyone: no one should go to another man's wife.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's closing verse, this sets a universal minimum rule that applies to every person.

jainism.quote_or_event: In Vimalasūri's Jain Rāmāyaṇa (Paumacariya), Rāvaṇa once paid homage to the omniscient monk Anantavīrya and took a vow never to force himself on any unwilling woman. Even after abducting Sītā, he refuses his queen Mandodarī's urging to use force, because of that vow.
jainism.explanation: The Jain tradition portrays Rāvaṇa as a great but flawed man who commits grave wrongs, including the abduction itself, yet keeps this one vow about another man's wife. His remaining desire for Sītā still leads to his downfall.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar concedes that even a man who does many wrongs should at least not desire another's wife, and the Jain Rāvaṇa is that kind of man: a wrongdoer who still holds a line he has vowed not to cross, though by desiring Sītā at all he falls short of the Kural's ideal.
jainism.source: Vimalasūri, Paumacariya 14.1–153 (Rāvaṇa's vow) and 46 (Sītā in Laṅkā); summarised in K. R. Chandra, 'A Critical Study of Paumacariyam' (1970), wisdomlib.org

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Abandoning his own wife, he is engrossed in sexual desire; his thoughts are on the wives of others.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes a man who has left his wife for a renunciant's life only to find his mind fixed on other men's wives.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural holds that even a man who fails at much else must keep this one boundary; Guru Nanak shows a man who has given up much and still fails at this very point.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1013, Raag Maru, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad (Book 7), during the war, the Trojan elder Antenor urges his own people to give Helen and her treasure back to the Greeks. Paris agrees to return the treasure but refuses to give up the woman, and the war goes on.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even in the middle of a war, a wise Trojan saw that keeping another man's wife was the wrong at the root of all their suffering.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural marks another's wife as the line not to cross whatever else one does; Antenor saw the same, even though his city did not listen.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nor does goodness or badness with regard to such things depend on committing adultery with the right woman, at the right time, and in the right way, but simply to do any of them is to go wrong.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says adultery can never be done 'the right way': it is always wrong, whatever the situation.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts treat adultery as an absolute line: the Kural says even the imperfect must keep it, and Aristotle says no circumstance makes it right.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Ulysses S. Grant's lifelong devotion to Julia Dent Grant
real_life_example.place: St. Louis, Missouri, and elsewhere, United States
real_life_example.event: Ulysses S. Grant married Julia Dent in 1848 after an engagement of four years delayed by the Mexican-American War, during which he wrote her many letters. In 1854 he resigned suddenly from the army amid reports that he had begun drinking heavily while separated from his family, and he then failed as a farmer and in several other jobs before the Civil War. Through these setbacks and his later fame as general and president, the couple remained devoted; the National Park Service describes their long marriage as marked by love, trust and respect.
real_life_example.explanation: Grant's career included real failures and a reputation for drinking, yet his loyalty to his wife was never in question, and his letters to her are preserved at the Library of Congress.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even a man who falls short in many ways should at least not desire another's wife; Grant, whatever his failings, held firmly to that line.

tamil:
அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்போலத் தம்மை
இகழ்வார்ப் பொறுத்தல் தலை.
transliteration:
Agazhvaaraith thaangum nilampoalath thammai,
Igazhvaarp poruththal thalai.
meaning: The ground holds up even the people who dig into it. In the same way, the best thing you can do is calmly put up with people who insult you and look down on you.
elementary: Think about the ground under your feet. People dig holes in it, stomp on it and poke it with shovels, and it still holds everybody up without complaining. This kural says the best kind of person is like that ground: when someone is mean to you, you stay steady and kind instead of hitting back.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with one of the most famous images in Tamil ethics: the earth (நிலம்) that supports the very people who dig into it (அகழ்வார்). The two verbs are set side by side on purpose. அகழ் (to dig, to wound the ground) matches இகழ் (to scorn, to wound with words), so an insult is pictured as digging into a person, and the patient person takes it in the way soil does, without caving in. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah point out that the earth doesn't just put up with the digger; it keeps holding him up so he doesn't fall, which makes endurance an active kind of support. The last word, தலை ('the foremost'), puts forbearance at the head of the virtues and sets up the thesis the rest of the chapter develops. Other traditions reach for the same metaphor: the Sanskrit kṣamā means both 'earth' and 'forgiveness,' and the Buddha compares abusive speech to a man trying to dig away the whole earth with a hoe.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And because it is seen that there are in the world men who are forgiving like the Earth, it is therefore that creatures derive their life and prosperity.”
hinduism.explanation: In exile, Draupadi urges Yudhishthira to take revenge on the Kauravas. He refuses, arguing that the world survives only because some people forgive the way the earth does.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the kural's own image: forbearance modeled on the ground, which endures injury and keeps supporting others.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section XXIX (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.”
christianity.explanation: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his followers not to strike back when they are hit, and to take the next blow instead of returning it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the earth holding up the one who digs it, the disciple takes the injury without hitting back.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth easily, and when the ignorant address them [harshly], they say [words of] peace,”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes God's true servants as people who walk gently on the earth and answer rude or ignorant speech with peace instead of insults.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link a humble relationship with the earth to a calm, non-retaliating answer when someone insults you.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men that were upon the face of the earth.”
judaism.explanation: Miriam and Aaron have just spoken against Moses (Numbers 12:1-2). He doesn't defend himself, and the Torah praises his meekness above everyone on earth.
judaism.tie_back: Moses quietly bears the people who belittle him, which is the kural's ideal of putting up with those who scorn us.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Suppose that a man were to come along carrying a hoe & a basket, saying, ‘I will make this great earth be without earth.’”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares abusive speech aimed at a trained mind to a man trying to dig away the whole earth with a hoe. He only wears himself out. Monks are told to keep goodwill 'equal to the great earth' whatever others say to them.
buddhism.tie_back: The image is almost the same as the kural's: a digger with a tool against an earth that can't be used up, standing for a patient mind under insult.
buddhism.source: Kakacūpama Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 21 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “…steady and firm like Mount Mandara, deep like the ocean, mild like the moon, refulgent like the sun, pure like excellent gold; like the earth he patiently bore everything; like a well-kindled fire he shone in his splendour.”
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sūtra describes Mahāvīra during his years as a wandering ascetic with a string of similes, and patient endurance is given the image of the earth, which bears everything.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar opens his chapter on patience with the earth that holds up even those who dig into it, and Jain scripture uses the same image, 'like the earth he patiently bore everything', for Mahāvīra's forbearance.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra § 118 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The God-conscious being has a steady patience, like the earth, which is dug up by one, and anointed with sandal paste by another.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan compares the patience of the God-conscious person to the earth, which stays the same whether it is dug into or honoured with sandalwood.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's image is the earth that keeps holding up those who dig into it; Guru Arjan uses the very same image of the dug-up earth for steady forbearance.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 272, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 8, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Ulysses stood firm as a rock and the blow did not even stagger him”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus comes home disguised as a beggar, and the suitor Antinous throws a footstool at him. He doesn't flinch or strike back, although Homer adds that he silently thought about revenge.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus stands like rock or earth under the insult and blow, the way the kural's ideal person bears whoever wounds him.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XVII (trans. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius tells himself to be like a headland that the waves keep hitting. It doesn't move, and in the end it calms the water around it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Stoic uses a landform as his model of patience, just as Valluvar uses the earth.

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi declines to prosecute the Durban mob that assaulted him
real_life_example.event: When Mohandas Gandhi, then a lawyer campaigning for the rights of Indians in Natal, landed at Durban in January 1897, a white mob inflamed by distorted reports of his speeches in India assaulted him and nearly lynched him. The British Colonial Secretary, Joseph Chamberlain, cabled the Natal government asking it to prosecute the attackers, and the colony's Attorney General offered to act if Gandhi would identify them. Gandhi declined, saying the attackers had been misled and that it was his principle not to seek redress of a personal wrong in a court of law.
real_life_example.explanation: By refusing to retaliate through the courts, Gandhi turned public opinion: by his own account the local press declared him innocent and condemned the mob.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural pictures the earth holding up even those who dig into it; Gandhi went on supporting the community that had attacked him rather than striking back at those who wounded him.

tamil:
பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும் அதனை
மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று.
transliteration:
Poruththal irappinai endrum adhanai,
Maraththal adhaninum nandru.
meaning: Always put up with the wrongs people do to you, even when they go too far. Forgetting those wrongs completely is even better.
elementary: If a friend breaks your favorite toy, being patient about it is good. This kural says something is even better: letting it go so completely that you stop thinking about it. Holding onto a hurt is like carrying a heavy rock in your pocket, and forgetting it is like finally throwing the rock away.
university: The couplet sets up two steps: பொறுத்தல் (bearing a wrong) and, higher still, மறத்தல் (forgetting it). The key word இறப்பு here means 'transgression, going beyond bounds.' Traditional commentators such as Parimelazhagan and Mu. Varadarasan read it as an excessive wrong, not as 'death,' although some popular modern glosses take it as 'until death.' Valluvar's point is psychological: if you endure a wrong but still keep a record of it, the endurance is incomplete, because the remembered wrong keeps feeding resentment. Real forbearance lets the grievance go altogether. Rabbinic law draws a similar line between taking vengeance and bearing a grudge (Leviticus 19:18, discussed in Talmud Yoma 23a), and Nietzsche later observed that some strong natures 'forgive' simply by forgetting.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who beareth not malice towards others but is kind to all, who being weak disputeth not with others, who speaketh not arrogantly, and forgeteth a quarrel, is praised everywhere.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura advises King Dhritarashtra that the person everyone praises holds no malice and actually forgets his quarrels instead of keeping them alive.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, it puts forgetting a dispute above merely putting up with it.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIII, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; … is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;”
christianity.explanation: Paul says love is long-suffering and 'thinketh no evil.' The Greek phrase (ou logizetai to kakon) means love doesn't keep a record of wrongs done to it.
christianity.tie_back: 'Suffereth long' corresponds to the kural's bearing, and 'thinketh no evil' (not keeping a ledger of injuries) to its forgetting.

islam.quote_or_event: “and let them pardon and overlook. Would you not like that Allāh should forgive you? And Allāh is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: According to the classical exegetes, this verse was revealed after Abu Bakr swore to stop supporting a relative who had joined in slandering his daughter Aisha. The Qur'an tells him to pardon (ʿafw) and also to overlook (ṣafḥ), that is, to turn the page completely.
islam.tie_back: Pardoning and then overlooking follows the same two steps as the kural's bearing and then forgetting.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids two separate things: taking revenge, and bearing a grudge. The Talmud (Yoma 23a) explains that even helping someone while reminding them of their past wrong counts as bearing a grudge.
judaism.tie_back: Not taking vengeance matches the kural's bearing; not bearing a grudge, not even keeping the memory alive, matches its forgetting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who do not harbor such thoughts still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's opening verses teach that hatred ends only when we stop going over the wrongs done to us.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the kural's 'forgetting': letting go of the memory of the injury so it no longer controls the mind.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
jainism.explanation: Among the twenty-two hardships (parīṣaha) a Jain monk must bear, abuse is met not only with silence but by refusing to let the words lodge in the mind.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to bear even wrongs that go beyond all limits and, better still, to forget them, and the Uttarādhyayana likewise moves from bearing ('silently overlook') to letting go ('not take them to heart').
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So erase your duality and hold tight to forgiveness,”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir tells the seeker to give up the divided, restless mind and hold firmly to forgiveness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks us to bear even extreme wrongs and better still to forget them; Kabir likewise asks for a forgiveness held fast, not grudgingly.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 343, Raag Gauri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Ajax, will you not forget and forgive even in death, but must the judgement about that hateful armour still rankle with you?”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Underworld, Odysseus meets the ghost of Ajax, who is still furious about losing the armour of Achilles to him. Odysseus begs him to forget. Ajax turns away without a word.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the mirror image of the kural: a grievance held even past death shows what refusing to forget costs.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XI (trans. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Mirabeau, who had no memory for any insults and meannesses which were practised on him, and who was only incapable of forgiving because he forgot.”
philosophy.explanation: Nietzsche praises strong natures who can't take their enemies' offences seriously for long. His example is Mirabeau, who didn't need to forgive because he simply forgot.
philosophy.tie_back: Nietzsche arrives at the kural's conclusion, that forgetting a wrong goes beyond forgiving it, though for a different reason.
philosophy.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Genealogy of Morals, First Essay, §10 (trans. Horace B. Samuel)

real_life_example.event_title: Eric Lomax meets and forgives his wartime interrogator Nagase Takashi
real_life_example.event: Eric Lomax, a British signals officer captured at the fall of Singapore, was tortured by his captors while working as a prisoner on the Siam-Burma railway after prisoners were found to have built a radio. For decades he was haunted by the memory of the interpreter at his interrogations, Nagase Takashi, who after the war devoted himself to acts of atonement and paid for a temple of peace near the River Kwai bridge. In 1993 the two men met at Kanchanaburi, and Lomax later gave Nagase a letter saying that, although he could never forget, he offered him total forgiveness; he told the story in his memoir The Railway Man.
real_life_example.explanation: Lomax had lived for nearly fifty years with bitterness, and the meeting is remembered as a rare personal reconciliation between a victim and one of those who had wronged him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural urges bearing even wrongs that go beyond all limits and, better still, letting them go; Lomax moved from enduring a grave wrong to releasing it through forgiveness.

tamil:
இன்மையுள் இன்மை விருந்தொரால் வன்மையுள்
வன்மை மடவார்ப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Inmaiyul inmai virundhoraal vanmaiyul,
Vanmai madavaarp porai.
meaning: The worst kind of being poor is turning away a guest. The greatest kind of strength is staying patient with foolish people.
elementary: Being poor isn't only about having little money. This kural says the saddest kind of poor is not being able to share even a snack with a friend who visits. Being strong isn't only about big muscles either: the strongest kind of strong is staying calm when someone acts silly or rude to you.
university: Valluvar builds the couplet on a double superlative, இன்மையுள் இன்மை ('the poverty within poverty') and வன்மையுள் வன்மை ('the strength within strength'), and uses it to pair two virtues that seem unrelated. The first half looks back to the chapter on hospitality (விருந்தோம்பல், ch. 9), where turning away a guest is the gravest failure of a household. The second half redefines might as the ability to bear the provocations of மடவார், 'the ignorant' or 'foolish.' Setting them side by side suggests a shared logic: hospitality and forbearance both measure inner abundance, not outward resources. Redefining strength as self-mastery is one of the most widely shared moral reversals across traditions, from the Mishnah's 'Who is mighty?' to the hadith about the strong man who controls his anger.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “These two, O king, live (as it were) in a region higher than heaven itself, viz., a man of power endued with forgiveness, and poor man that is charitable.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura names two people who stand above heaven itself: a powerful man who forgives, and a poor man who still gives.
hinduism.tie_back: It pairs the same two ideas as the kural, generosity in poverty and forbearance in power, in one saying.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIII, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy that a servant of God must not quarrel but stay gentle and patient. The next verse applies this to people who oppose him and need instruction.
christianity.tie_back: Being patient and gentle with the contentious and unteaching is the kural's 'strength of strengths,' bearing with the foolish.

islam.quote_or_event: “The strong is not the one who overcomes the people by his strength, but the strong is the one who controls himself while in anger.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet redefines strength: the truly strong person is not the wrestler who throws others down but the one who masters himself when provoked.
islam.tie_back: This is the kural's 'strength within strength' exactly: real power is holding back, not fighting.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’ (Proverbs 16:32).”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma's famous teaching redefines might as control over one's own impulses, and backs it with the proverb that the slow-to-anger outrank warriors.
judaism.tie_back: The same reversal as the kural: the greatest strength is restraint in the face of provocation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who without resentment endures abuse, beating and punishment; whose power, real might, is patience — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the true holy man as someone whose real power is patience under abuse.
buddhism.tie_back: 'Real might is patience' is almost a translation of the kural's வன்மையுள் வன்மை ... பொறை.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a layman abuses a monk, he should not grow angry against him; because he would be like a child, a monk should not grow angry.”
jainism.explanation: Jacobi notes that the word translated 'child' (bāla) also means an ignorant man. Mahāvīra's teaching is that one who answers a fool's abuse with anger becomes a fool too, so patience is the stronger course.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls bearing with fools the greatest strength of all, and the Uttarādhyayana gives the same rule of not raging at the ignorant, though it has no counterpart to the Kural's first half on failing a guest.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “if you are powerful, be weak; … How rare is one who is known as such a devotee.”
sikhism.explanation: A salok in the Guru Granth Sahib describes the rare devotee who, though strong, lives as if powerless; the same salok also praises sharing with others even when one has little.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls bearing with fools the strength within strength and failing a guest the poverty within poverty; this salok joins strength held back with generosity in the same way.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Salok 128 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as travelers, are turned away from a thousand wealthy homes. The poor old couple Baucis and Philemon welcome them and share the little food they have.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid's tale the gods reward the poor couple's hospitality and punish the stingy neighbors. However poor they were, Baucis and Philemon never fell into the 'poverty' of refusing a guest.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It illustrates the kural's first half: the real poverty is being unable to welcome a guest, not a lack of means.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VIII (Baucis and Philemon)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius starts each day expecting to meet difficult people, and reminds himself that their faults come from ignorance, so he shouldn't be angry with them.
philosophy.tie_back: Bearing with the foolish (மடவார்) because they are ignorant is the kural's picture of real strength.

real_life_example.event_title: Lincoln appoints Edwin Stanton despite Stanton's earlier snub
real_life_example.place: Cincinnati, Ohio, and Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: In 1855 Abraham Lincoln, then an Illinois lawyer, was retained for the defence in the McCormick v. Manny reaper patent case and prepared a brief, but when the trial moved to Cincinnati the eastern lawyers leading the defence, including the eminent attorney Edwin M. Stanton, kept him from taking part. Lincoln nonetheless supplied the brief he had written. After he became president, Lincoln chose Stanton as his Secretary of War, and Stanton became one of his most important advisers.
real_life_example.explanation: Lincoln's willingness to set aside a personal humiliation and appoint the most capable man available is often cited as an example of his magnanimity.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls patiently bearing with the slights of others the strength within strength; Lincoln bore Stanton's slight and later gave him one of the highest offices in the land.

tamil:
நிறையுடைமை நீங்காமை வேண்டின் பொறையுடைமை
போற்றி யொழுகப் படும்.
transliteration:
Niraiyudaimai neengaamai vendin poraiyudaimai,
Potri yozhugap padum.
meaning: If you never want to lose your good, steady character, you must value patience and live by it every day.
elementary: Imagine your good character is a glass filled to the top with water. Every time you lose your temper, some spills out. This kural says that if you want to keep your glass full, you have to carry it carefully, which means being patient all the time.
university: நிறை is a rich Tamil word meaning fullness, completeness, and also self-restraint or integrity. It describes a wife's guarded constancy in chapter 6 and the sages 'full of word' in chapter 3. Valluvar makes பொறையுடைமை (possessing patience) the precondition for keeping நிறையுடைமை (possessing fullness). The two '-உடைமை' compounds deliberately echo each other, which suggests patience is not one virtue among many but the container that keeps the others from leaking away. The phrase போற்றி ஒழுகுதல் ('to guard and live by') implies constant vigilance, not occasional restraint, and Solomon Pappaiah reads நிறை as சான்றாண்மை, the complete nobility of character treated in chapter 99. The Epistle of James makes almost the same claim, that patience is what makes a person 'perfect and entire.'

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is equal to friends and enemies, who is equipoised in honor and dishonor, heat and cold, happiness and distress, fame and infamy, who is always free from contaminating association, always silent and satisfied with anything, who doesn’t care for any residence, who is fixed in knowledge and who is engaged in devotional service – such a person is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the ideal devotee as someone whose mind stays whole and steady (sthira-matiḥ) through honor and dishonor, praise and blame.
hinduism.tie_back: An even mind under insult or praise is the kind of unbroken inner fullness (நிறை) that the kural says patience protects.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.”
christianity.explanation: James teaches that patience, allowed to do its full work, makes a believer complete and lacking nothing.
christianity.tie_back: 'Perfect and entire, wanting nothing' is almost a definition of நிறை, and both texts make patience its source.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allāh is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents patience (ṣabr) as one of the two supports of the believer's life, together with prayer.
islam.tie_back: Both treat patience as something you must keep hold of to stay upright and whole.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth;”
judaism.explanation: Among the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, God is erech apayim, 'long-suffering.' Rabbinic tradition teaches imitation of God: as He is merciful and patient, so should you be.
judaism.tie_back: Patience is part of the divine fullness of character. To keep that completeness in yourself, you have to practise long-suffering too.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “a monk may be ever so gentle, ever so mild-tempered, ever so calm, as long as he is not touched by disagreeable aspects of speech. But it is only when disagreeable aspects of speech touch him that he can truly be known as gentle, mild-tempered, & calm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells of Lady Vedehikā, famous for her gentleness, who lost that reputation the moment her maid tested her patience. Good character that can't bear provocation was never really secure.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the kural's warning: without patience, your fullness of character leaks away the moment it is tested.
buddhism.source: Kakacūpama Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 21 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Supreme forbearance–uttama kṣamā, supreme modesty–uttama mārdava, supreme straightforwardness–uttama ārjava … constitute ten virtues (dharma).”
jainism.explanation: The Tattvārthasūtra puts forbearance first among the ten virtues that stop new karma from flowing into the soul. Pūjyapāda glosses it as freedom from anger when meeting 'insolent words, ridicule or derision, disgrace, bodily torment' from vicious people.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that whoever wants to keep his completeness of character (நிறை) must cherish patience, and in Jainism forbearance comes first among the virtues that keep the soul's purity whole against incoming karma.
jainism.source: Tattvārthasūtra 9.6, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Let patience be your purpose in life; implant this within your being. In this way, you will grow into a great river; you will not break off into a tiny stream.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid says that patience made firm within turns a person into a great river instead of a broken trickle.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says patience is what keeps one's fullness of character from being lost; Farid's image of the river that grows rather than breaks off makes the same point.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Salok 117 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “at night she would unpick the stitches again by torchlight. She fooled us in this way for three years without our finding it out”
greek_mythology.explanation: For years Penelope endures the pressure of the arrogant suitors. She patiently weaves Laertes' shroud by day and unravels it by night, so that she keeps her faithfulness to Odysseus intact.
greek_mythology.tie_back: நிறை also means constancy and chastity. Penelope's patient endurance is what keeps her integrity from being lost.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XXIV (trans. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you hear unpleasant language, you will find patience.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that for every hard thing we have a matching inner capacity. For insulting words, that capacity is patience, and using it keeps us from being 'hurried away' by events.
philosophy.tie_back: Keeping patience at the ready protects the self-possession that the kural calls நிறை.

real_life_example.event_title: Andrei Sakharov's exile in Gorky
real_life_example.event: After the physicist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Andrei Sakharov denounced the Soviet military intervention in Afghanistan, he was banished in January 1980, without trial, to the closed city of Gorky, and his Soviet honours were taken from him. During nearly seven years of exile he went on several hunger strikes, including ones to win permission for his wife, Yelena Bonner, to travel abroad for medical treatment, which she was granted in 1985. In December 1986 Mikhail Gorbachev telephoned to tell him he could return to Moscow, and Sakharov immediately pressed him to release other political prisoners.
real_life_example.explanation: Through years of isolation and pressure Sakharov neither recanted nor turned to bitterness, and he returned to public life with his convictions and moral authority intact.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that whoever wishes never to lose his fullness of character must cherish patience; Sakharov's long endurance in exile preserved the integrity that had made him a moral voice.

tamil:
ஒறுத்தாரை ஒன்றாக வையாரே வைப்பர்
பொறுத்தாரைப் பொன்போற் பொதிந்து.
transliteration:
Oruththaarai ondraaga vaiyaare vaippar,
Poruththaaraip ponpor podhindhu.
meaning: People think nothing of those who pay back every wrong. But they treasure those who stay patient, like gold kept safe and wrapped up.
elementary: Two kids get pushed in the lunch line. One shoves back hard, and the other says, 'It's okay.' Later, which one do people trust and want as a friend? This kural says people treasure the patient one like a piece of gold kept safe in a box, while the one who always hits back isn't valued at all.
university: ஒறுத்தார் ('those who punished' the offender) and பொறுத்தார் ('those who bore it') differ by a single initial consonant, and Valluvar uses the near-rhyme to make the moral contrast audible. ஒன்றாக வையார் means such people are not counted as anything at all, while பொன்போற் பொதிந்து வைப்பர் ('they wrap and keep like gold') suggests a treasure bundled up and stored with care. The judgement is a social one: honor goes not to the person who wins the exchange of blows but to the one who refuses it. That reverses a warrior-culture instinct that leaving a slight unavenged is shameful. Aristotle is a useful contrast: he praises the good-tempered man who 'tends to make allowances,' but warns that putting up with every insult can look 'slavish.' Valluvar settles that tension firmly on the side of forbearance.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Forgiveness is a virtue of the weak, and an ornament of the strong.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura admits that people sometimes mistake the forgiving for weak, but insists that forgiveness is great power, a jewel worn by the strong.
hinduism.tie_back: 'Ornament' matches the kural's gold. The forbearing person is prized and adorned, not despised.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIII, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells believers that the real glory is patiently enduring mistreatment you didn't deserve.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say where true honor lies: with the one who bears wrong patiently, not the one who hits back.

islam.quote_or_event: “And whoever is patient and forgives - indeed, that is of the matters [worthy] of resolve.”
islam.explanation: Right after allowing proportionate retaliation, the Qur'an praises patience and forgiveness as a higher, more resolute path.
islam.tie_back: Both texts rank the one who forbears above the one who retaliates.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is the discretion of a man to be slow to anger, And it is his glory to pass over a transgression.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs calls overlooking an offence a person's glory, that is, their honor and splendor.
judaism.tie_back: 'His glory' corresponds to the kural's 'treasured like gold': forbearance is what earns honor.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who can blame such a one, as worthy as a coin of refined gold? Even the gods praise him; by Brahma, too, is he praised.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Dhammapada's chapter on anger, the self-controlled person of flawless character is called as precious as refined gold and praised even by the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: It uses the same gold image as the kural for the person who has mastered anger.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The young man's self-restraint is self-restraint. The gift of him who owns no stores of wealth is gift indeed. When man has means and might to punish every fault, if he forbear, call him the patient man.”
jainism.explanation: In its chapter on meekness, the Jain-authored Nālaṭiyār says that real forbearance belongs to the man who has the power to punish and holds back.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar contrasts those who punish (ஒறுத்தார்), whom the world counts as nothing, with those who forbear (பொறுத்தார்), whom it treasures like gold, and the Nālaṭiyār uses the same pair of verbs (ஒறுக்கும் … பொறுக்கும்) to praise the man who could punish but forbears.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār 65 (ch. 7, 'The Absence of Anger: Meekness'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When something is placed on the balancing scale and weighed, the side which descends is heavier.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the scale to show that the one who bows low is found to weigh more.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says people count the punisher as nothing and treasure the forbearing like wrapped gold; Guru Nanak likewise says the one who yields proves the more valuable when weighed.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles, insulted when Agamemnon takes his prize Briseis, withdraws from the war in rage. His unappeased anger brings countless deaths on the Greeks.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad opens by naming Achilles' wrath as its subject, and it shows that refusing to let an insult pass wins the hero no lasting honor, only grief for his friends and for himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A counter-example: the person who must avenge every slight ends up diminished, not treasured.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad, Book I (trans. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the good-tempered man is not revengeful, but rather tends to make allowances.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says good temper is praised, and that the good-tempered man is not vengeful but makes allowances. He also warns that tolerating every insult can look 'slavish.'
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle praises the forbearing over the revengeful, as the kural does, though with more reservations.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.5 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Taizong of Tang makes his rival's adviser Wei Zheng his trusted critic
real_life_example.event: Wei Zheng had served as an adviser to Crown Prince Li Jiancheng and had urged him to strike first against his younger brother Li Shimin. After Li Shimin killed his brothers in 626 and became Emperor Taizong, Wei Zheng was not punished but entered the new emperor's close circle as a counsellor. For years he criticised the emperor frankly, at one point pointing out more than 200 of his mistakes, which Taizong accepted and corrected; after Wei Zheng's death Taizong wrote that, in losing him, he had lost a mirror in which to see his own failings.
real_life_example.explanation: Taizong's tolerance of a former enemy turned blunt critic is one reason he is remembered as one of the greatest emperors in Chinese history, and Wei Zheng became the model of the honest minister.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says people count the punisher as nothing but treasure the forbearing like gold; Taizong's forbearance won him an adviser he valued as a precious mirror and a lasting reputation as a model ruler.

tamil:
ஒறுத்தார்க்கு ஒருநாளை இன்பம் பொறுத்தார்க்குப்
பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்.
transliteration:
Oruththaarkku orunaalai inbam poruththaarkkup,
Pondrun thunaiyum pugazh.
meaning: Getting even brings happiness for just one day. Staying patient brings praise that lasts as long as the world lasts.
elementary: Getting back at someone can feel good, for about one day. Then the good feeling is gone. Being the person who stayed kind is different: people remember it and talk about it for a very, very long time.
university: The couplet sets two time-scales against each other: ஒருநாளை இன்பம் ('one day's pleasure') and பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ் ('fame until [the world] perishes'). Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah read பொன்றும் as the ending of the world, while Kalaignar reads it as 'throughout one's life.' Either way the basic contrast between passing gratification and lasting reputation holds. Valluvar is speaking the language of புகழ், the enduring renown he devotes chapter 24 to, where reputation is treated as the only thing that outlives the body. The psychological point is sharp: Aristotle also observes that revenge 'relieves' anger by 'producing ... pleasure instead of pain,' but Valluvar insists that this pleasure is the shortest-lived of goods.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man may attain renown in this world by doing two things, viz., by refraining from harsh speech, and by disregarding those that are wicked.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura names renown as the reward for not answering harshly and for disregarding the provocations of the wicked.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, it makes lasting fame the fruit of forbearance.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIII, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.”
christianity.explanation: James points to Job, whose patience became proverbial and is still remembered long after his trials ended.
christianity.tie_back: Job's lasting fame for endurance illustrates the kural's claim that praise for the patient outlives them.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account [i.e., limit].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an promises the patient a reward so large it can't be measured.
islam.tie_back: The unlimited reward of the patient matches the kural's everlasting praise, set against revenge's one day.

judaism.quote_or_event: “whoever forgoes his reckonings with others for injustices done to him, the heavenly court in turn forgoes punishment for all his sins”
judaism.explanation: Rava teaches that a person who lets injustices against him pass is himself treated with lasting divine mercy.
judaism.tie_back: Forgoing retaliation brings a lasting reward, while insisting on your due brings nothing that endures.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Rosh Hashanah 17a (William Davidson/Koren translation)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that returning hatred never brings lasting peace, and that only non-hatred does so, as an eternal law.
buddhism.tie_back: Revenge brings only a short relief, while forbearance produces something lasting, which is the kural's contrast.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Leave off the causes of sin, acquire fame through patience! (A man who acts up to this) will rise to the upper regions after having left this body of clay.”
jainism.explanation: In the lecture on the four rare requisites of the spiritual life, Mahāvīra's disciples are told directly that patience is how lasting fame is won, and that it carries the soul upward after death.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar sets the one-day pleasure of revenge against the fame that lasts as long as the world, and the Uttarādhyayana likewise says that fame comes through patience and its reward outlasts this body.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 3.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, is remembered as Sikhism's first martyr: ordered by the emperor Jahangir to remove supposedly offensive passages from the Adi Granth, he refused and was tortured to death at Lahore in 1606.
sikhism.explanation: Sikhs honour Guru Arjan's endurance of torture without yielding as one of the defining moments of their history.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the pleasure of revenge lasts a day while the fame of the forbearing lasts as long as the world; the Guru's endured suffering has won him lasting honour among Sikhs.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guru Arjan' (Tamanna Nangia, fact-checked by Britannica Editors)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The fame, therefore, of her virtue shall never die, and the immortals shall compose a song that shall be welcome to all mankind in honour of the constancy of Penelope.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Underworld, Agamemnon's ghost declares that Penelope's patient faithfulness through twenty years of pressure will be famous forever.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Patient endurance wins undying fame, just as the kural promises praise until the world ends.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XXIV (trans. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For remember that, if you adhere to the same point, those very persons who at first ridiculed will afterwards admire you.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the new philosopher to expect mockery and to bear it without replying, because steady endurance eventually turns ridicule into admiration.
philosophy.tie_back: Enduring insult earns lasting esteem, while retaliating would forfeit it.

real_life_example.event_title: Saladin's terms for the surrender of Jerusalem
real_life_example.event: After defeating the crusader army at Hattin, Saladin besieged Jerusalem in 1187, and its defender, Balian of Ibelin, negotiated the city's surrender. Saladin allowed the Christian inhabitants to ransom themselves at fixed rates and leave, set free many elderly and poor people who could not pay, and allowed noblewomen to leave without ransom, although thousands who could not be redeemed were enslaved. His treatment of the city contrasted sharply with the massacre that had followed the crusaders' capture of Jerusalem in 1099.
real_life_example.explanation: Saladin's restraint, set against the bloodshed of 1099, inspired a lasting reputation for magnanimity that later writers and historians built upon.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural sets the one day's pleasure of revenge against fame that lasts as long as the world; Saladin passed over the chance to avenge 1099 and won a renown that has endured for more than eight centuries.

tamil:
திறனல்ல தற்பிறர் செய்யினும் நோநொந்து
அறனல்ல செய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Thiranalla tharpirar seyyinum nononthu,
Aranalla seyyaamai nandru.
meaning: Even when others hurt you in ways you did not deserve, it is good to feel sorry for the pain their wrong will bring them, and not to do wrong back.
elementary: When someone is unfair to you, you might want to be unfair back. This kural says don't. Instead, feel a little sad for them, because doing wrong usually comes back to hurt the person who does it, and keep doing the right thing yourself.
university: The key phrase is நோநொந்து. Mu. Varadarasan reads it as grieving over the suffering (நோ) that will fall on the wrongdoer as the fruit of his act, which makes the couplet an ethic of compassion toward the offender rather than mere self-restraint. Solomon Pappaiah offers a slightly different nuance, grieving at the thought that retaliation would hurt him, but both readings end in refusing அறனல்ல, 'what is not dharma.' The couplet therefore goes beyond tolerance to a positive moral stance: being injured doesn't license you to abandon virtue. Socrates states the same principle in the Crito, that it is never right to return wrong for wrong, and Jesus acts it out on the cross by praying for those who crucify him.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That which is antagonistic to one's own self, should never be applied in respect of another. Briefly even this is virtue.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura sums up dharma in one rule: never do to another what you would find hurtful yourself.
hinduism.tie_back: Because you know how injury feels, you refuse to inflict it back even when you've been wronged, which is the kural's refusal of 'what is not dharma'.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIX, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
christianity.explanation: While being crucified, Jesus prays for his executioners and feels for their spiritual danger instead of cursing them.
christianity.tie_back: Grieving for the wrongdoer instead of retaliating is exactly the kural's நோநொந்து.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the retribution for an evil act is an evil one like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation - his reward is [due] from Allāh. Indeed, He does not like wrongdoers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an allows equal retribution but holds up pardon and reconciliation as the better way, rewarded by God.
islam.tie_back: Both texts steer the injured person away from answering wrong with wrong.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not: ‘I will do so to him as he hath done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.’”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs explicitly forbids the tit-for-tat reasoning of paying someone back for what he did to you.
judaism.tie_back: This is the kural's அறனல்ல செய்யாமை: don't answer wrong with wrong.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever returns insult to one who is insulting, returns taunts to one who is taunting, returns a berating to one who is berating, is said to be eating together, sharing company, with that person.”
buddhism.explanation: When the brahman Akkosaka abuses him, the Buddha refuses the 'meal' of insults, explaining that anyone who returns abuse joins in the offender's wrongdoing.
buddhism.tie_back: Returning wrong for wrong makes you a partner in it, which is why the kural says not to act against dharma even when wronged.
buddhism.source: Akkosa Sutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya 7.2 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “To bear with those that speak contemptuous words; yea, more, to say, ‘Ah, will these sink in the other world to hell, the place of fire, as fruit of their contemptuous words;’ and to grieve, is duty of the perfect man.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār asks the noble person not only to bear an insult but to grieve over the karmic suffering the insulter is storing up for himself.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that when others wrong us, we should feel sorry for the suffering their wrong will bring them and not retaliate, and the Nālaṭiyār states the same compassion for the wrongdoer's coming fate almost point for point.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār 58 (ch. 6, 'Renunciation'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid teaches not to hit back at those who hurt us, but to answer them with humility and go home at peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even when wronged without cause one should not do anything unrighteous in return; Farid gives the same counsel in concrete form.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Salok 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Old King Priam comes to Achilles' tent to beg for the body of his son Hector. Achilles, who killed Hector and has been abusing his corpse, is moved by Priam, weeps with him, and returns the body.
greek_mythology.explanation: At the end of the Iliad, Achilles finally feels for his enemy's grief and stops trying to punish him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Feeling for the enemy's suffering instead of continuing to strike at him reflects the kural's நோநொந்து.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad, Book XXIV (trans. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
philosophy.explanation: In prison awaiting execution, Socrates refuses to escape unjustly and states that wronging someone in return is never right, however badly you've been treated.
philosophy.tie_back: Almost a restatement of the kural: however unfitting the harm received, do nothing unrighteous in return.

real_life_example.event_title: Martin Luther King Jr. bears no ill will toward the woman who stabbed him
real_life_example.place: Harlem, New York City, United States
real_life_example.event: While signing copies of his book Stride Toward Freedom at Blumstein's department store in Harlem, Martin Luther King Jr. was stabbed in the chest with a letter opener by Izola Ware Curry, a woman who was later judged to be mentally ill. Surgeons at Harlem Hospital removed the blade, which had come close to his aorta. King later stated publicly that he felt no ill will toward Curry and hoped she would receive the help she needed, and he reaffirmed his commitment to nonviolence.
real_life_example.explanation: Instead of anger, King answered a near-fatal attack with concern for his attacker's well-being, and he described the experience as deepening his faith in nonviolence.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural counsels feeling sorrow for the suffering that awaits the wrongdoer and not returning wrong for wrong; King's response was compassion for the woman who had nearly killed him.

tamil:
மிகுதியான் மிக்கவை செய்தாரைத் தாந்தம்
தகுதியான் வென்று விடல்.
transliteration:
Migudhiyaan mikkavai seydhaaraith thaandham,
Thagudhiyaan vendru vidal.
meaning: When proud people do you great wrongs because they think they are above you, beat them with your own goodness, which means your patience.
elementary: Sometimes a bully acts big and mean, and you might think the only way to win is to be even meaner. This kural says you can beat them another way: by staying calm and good. Your patience works like a superpower that makes their meanness look small.
university: The couplet plays on மிகுதி ('excess, arrogance') and தகுதி ('fitness, worth'). The aggressor acts out of surplus (மிகுதியான் மிக்கவை, 'excessive deeds out of excess'), and is to be overcome by the victim's own proper measure (தாந்தம் தகுதியான்). Commentators consistently identify this தகுதி with பொறை, patience itself, so forbearance becomes a strategy for victory rather than passive defeat. The verb, வென்று விடல் ('conquer'), is deliberately martial: Valluvar claims the vocabulary of winning for the person who doesn't retaliate. The same logic appears in Paul's 'overcome evil with good,' in the Qur'an's 'repel evil with what is better,' and in Vidura's maxim that anger is conquered by forgiveness, a maxim that reappears almost word for word in the Dhammapada (v. 223).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Anger must be conquered by forgiveness; and the wicked must be conquered by honesty; the miser must be conquered by liberality, and falsehood must be conquered by truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura teaches that each vice is defeated by its opposite virtue, and anger above all by forgiveness.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the kural, the aggressor is 'conquered' not by force but by one's own virtue of forbearance.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIX, Vidura's counsel (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul closes his teaching on non-retaliation by telling believers to defeat evil by doing good, not by answering in kind.
christianity.tie_back: The same reversal of victory: the wronged person wins through goodness, not counter-attack.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon, the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells believers to push back evil with something better, and promises that this can turn an enemy into a close friend.
islam.tie_back: Repelling the aggressor with better conduct is the kural's victory through one's own worth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Others say: [Who is mighty?] Who turns an enemy into his friend.”
judaism.explanation: Expanding Ben Zoma's 'Who is mighty?', Avot de-Rabbi Natan records the view that the mightiest person is the one who wins over his enemy and makes him a friend.
judaism.tie_back: Victory through character rather than force is the kural's 'conquer them by your own worth'.
judaism.source: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 23:1 (trans. A. Cohen, Soncino)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that every kind of wrongdoer is defeated by the opposite virtue, the angry by non-anger.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the kural's teaching exactly: conquer the aggressor with your own virtue. It also echoes Vidura's Mahabharata maxim almost word for word.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When persons not our equals say unfitting things, to bear and to be still is worthy conduct. The world girt by foaming waters regards not a contrary course as praise-worthy, but as discreditable.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār's chapter on patience says that the fitting answer to insolence is to bear it calmly, and that striking back only brings discredit in the world's eyes.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to overcome the arrogant through our own worth (தகுதி), meaning patience, and the Nālaṭiyār uses the same word: bearing such insults quietly is 'worthy conduct' (தகுதி).
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār 72 (ch. 8, 'Patience'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Humility is my spiked club. … No evil-doer can withstand these weapons.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes humility as a weapon before which no wrongdoer can stand.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to conquer the arrogant by our own worth, that is, by patience, and uses the language of victory; Guru Arjan likewise turns humility into a weapon that defeats the evil-doer.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 628, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus' Eumenides, the raging Furies threaten to poison Athens after Orestes is acquitted. Athena doesn't fight them. She calms them with patient persuasion and offers them honor, until they become the 'Kindly Ones.'
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena wins over the enraged goddesses through patience and persuasion (Peitho), not force, and turns them from enemies into protectors.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Overcoming aggressors through one's own character rather than retaliation is the kural's victory by தகுதி.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that a person who lives by reason tries, as far as possible, to repay others' hatred, anger and contempt with love and generosity, because hatred grows when returned and can be destroyed by love.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, answering hostility with love is not weakness but the rational way to defeat hatred.
philosophy.tie_back: Defeating the aggressor through one's own better disposition is the kural's தகுதியான் வென்று விடல்.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Proposition 46 and proof

real_life_example.event_title: The satyagrahis at the Dharasana salt works
real_life_example.event: After Gandhi was arrested for announcing a march on the Dharasana salt works, the poet and Congress leader Sarojini Naidu led about 2,500 volunteers there on 21 May 1930. Column after column of marchers walked toward the police guarding the works and were beaten down with lathis, but as instructed they did not strike back or even raise their arms to ward off the blows. The American journalist Webb Miller's eyewitness report was carried by newspapers around the world and prompted an international outcry against British policy in India.
real_life_example.explanation: The marchers lost the confrontation physically but won it morally, because their refusal to retaliate exposed the force used against them to the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural urges overcoming those who heap outrageous wrongs on us through our own worth, that is, through patience; the satyagrahis turned forbearance into a form of victory.

tamil:
துறந்தாரின் தூய்மை உடையர் இறந்தார்வாய்
இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்கிற் பவர்.
transliteration:
Thurandhaarin thooimai udaiyar irandhaarvaai,
Innaachchol norkir pavar.
meaning: People who can calmly take the harsh words of those who go too far are as pure as those who have given up the world.
elementary: Monks and nuns who give up everything are often thought of as very pure. This kural says you don't have to leave home to be that pure. If someone yells nasty words at you and you stay calm, your heart is just as clean as theirs.
university: இறந்தார் here doesn't mean 'the dead.' It means 'those who have transgressed' (from இற, to go beyond), the same root as இறப்பு in Kural 152. Mu. Varadarasan and Kalaignar confirm this sense, though some popular glosses take it literally. The comparison with துறந்தார் ('renunciants') matters because these chapters belong to இல்லறவியல், the section on the householder's life: Valluvar claims that a householder who endures insult reaches the purity normally reserved for ascetics. Solomon Pappaiah makes this explicit, saying that even living a household life, such a person is as pure as a renunciant. The verb நோற்றல் ('to endure as an austerity') anticipates the next couplet's comparison with fasting and recasts patience itself as a form of tapas.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him patiently bear hard words, let him not insult anybody, and let him not become anybody's enemy for the sake of this (perishable) body. Against an angry man let him not in return show anger, let him bless when he is cursed”
hinduism.explanation: Among the rules for the wandering renunciant (sannyāsin), Manu requires him to bear harsh words patiently and to bless those who curse him.
hinduism.tie_back: Bearing harsh words is a defining discipline of the renunciant. The kural says a householder who does the same is equally pure.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:”
christianity.explanation: Peter holds up Christ, who did not answer insult with insult, as the model of holy conduct under abuse.
christianity.tie_back: Bearing abusive words without answering is the mark of the purest life, as in the kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “You will surely be tested in your possessions and in yourselves. And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with Allāh much abuse. But if you are patient and fear Allāh - indeed, that is of the matters [worthy] of resolve.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an warns believers that they will hear much hurtful speech, and says that patience with it, joined with God-consciousness, is a mark of true resolve.
islam.tie_back: Enduring hurtful words (இன்னாச்சொல்) is treated as a high spiritual achievement, as in the kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “About those who are insulted and do not insult, who hear their shame and do not respond, who act out of love and are joyful in suffering, the verse says: ‘And they that love Him are as the sun going forth in its might’ (Judges 5:31).”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud praises those who hear themselves shamed without answering, comparing them to the radiant rising sun.
judaism.tie_back: Shining like the sun, the silent bearer of insult has a purity like the kural's renunciant.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as when people throw what is clean or unclean on the earth — feces, urine, saliva, pus, or blood — the earth is not horrified, humiliated, or disgusted by it”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches the young monk Rahula to make his mind like the earth, which isn't defiled by whatever filth is thrown on it.
buddhism.tie_back: A mind that foul words can't stain is the renunciant's purity the kural describes.
buddhism.source: Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 62 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Ceasing to use the stick (i.e. cruelty) against living beings, abandoning the care of the body, the houseless (Mahâvîra), the Venerable One, endures the thorns of the villages (i.e. the abusive language of the peasants), (being) perfectly enlightened.”
jainism.explanation: The Ācārāṅga's account of Mahāvīra's wanderings in the rough country of Lāḍha shows the great renunciant meeting abuse with endurance instead of retaliation.
