jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that those who bear the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renunciants, and the Ācārāṅga shows the model renunciant himself enduring the 'thorns' of abusive speech.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.8.3.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are patient abide in patience; in this way, they burn their bodies. They are close to the Lord, but they do not reveal their secret to anyone.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid says the patient make patience itself their austerity, and so come close to God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who bear insults from transgressors are as pure as renunciants; Farid likewise treats patience as an inner austerity that brings one near the divine.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Salok 116 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “he resolved, however, to endure it and keep himself in check”
greek_mythology.explanation: On the road home, the goatherd Melanthius reviles the disguised Odysseus with outrageous language and kicks him. Odysseus considers striking back but chooses to endure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Bearing the insolent words of a man who overstepped all bounds reflects the kural's இறந்தார்வாய் இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்றல்.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XVII (trans. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Remember, that not he who gives ill language or a blow insults, but the principle which represents these things as insulting.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that harsh words have power over us only if we accept them as injuries. The disciplined mind stays untouched.
philosophy.tie_back: A mind that insulting words can't stain has the inner purity the kural credits to those who bear harsh speech.

real_life_example.event_title: Haile Selassie addresses the League of Nations
real_life_example.event: Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia, driven into exile by Italy's invasion of his country, came to address the Assembly of the League of Nations. As he was introduced, Italian journalists in the press gallery jeered and shouted insults and had to be removed; the emperor waited for them to be ejected and then delivered his speech in Amharic. He described the invasion, including the use of chemical weapons against his people, and asked what the League intended to do; the League took no effective action.
real_life_example.explanation: The speech became one of the most remembered appeals of the interwar years, and the emperor's composure in the face of jeering contrasted with the collapse of collective security it exposed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who patiently bear the harsh words of people who overstep every limit are as pure as renunciants; Haile Selassie bore the insults of his invaders' supporters without answering in kind.

tamil:
உண்ணாது நோற்பார் பெரியர் பிறர்சொல்லும்
இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்பாரின் பின்.
transliteration:
Unnaadhu norpaar periyar pirarsollum,
Innaachchol norpaarin pin.
meaning: People who go without food to train themselves are great. But they come second to people who put up with the cruel words others say to them.
elementary: Going without food for a whole day to be good is really hard, and people admire it. This kural says something is even harder and better: when someone says mean things to you and you swallow your anger and stay kind, you are the real champion.
university: Valluvar closes the chapter by ranking two kinds of நோன்பு (austerity): உண்ணாது நோற்றல், enduring hunger by fasting, and இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்றல், enduring cruel speech. By placing the faster 'after' (பின்) the one who bears insult, he puts the most visible ascetic practice of his time, prominent in both Jain and Brahmanical asceticism, below an inner, social virtue. Repeating நோற்பார் in both lines insists that patience is itself tapas, completing the argument begun in Kural 159. The ranking resonates with the Dhammapada's 'Enduring patience is the highest austerity,' with the hadith that tells a fasting person to answer abuse by saying 'I am fasting,' and with Isaiah's prophetic critique that a true fast is measured by ethical conduct.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “forgiveness is stored ascetic merit; forgiveness protecteth the ascetic merit of the future; forgiveness is asceticism; forgiveness is holiness”
hinduism.explanation: In the verses Yudhishthira attributes to the sage Kashyapa, forgiveness is declared to be asceticism (tapas) itself and the guardian of all ascetic merit.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, it counts forbearance as the true austerity, above physical penances.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section XXIX (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus pronounces those who are reviled and slandered 'blessed.' In the same sermon (Matthew 6:16-18) he warns that fasting done for show has no value.
christianity.tie_back: Enduring others' evil words is blessed, while external fasting is played down, which comes close to the kural's ranking.

islam.quote_or_event: “Fasting is a shield (or a screen or a shelter). So, the person observing fasting should avoid sexual relation with his wife and should not behave foolishly and impudently, and if somebody fights with him or abuses him, he should tell him twice, 'I am fasting.'”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that a fast is only complete if the faster also refuses to return abuse. Bearing insult is part of the fast's real substance.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link fasting and enduring abusive speech, and make patience under insult the deeper discipline.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Is not this the fast that I have chosen? To loose the fetters of wickedness, To undo the bands of the yoke, And to let the oppressed go free, And that ye break every yoke?”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah rebukes people who fast while behaving badly. God values ethical conduct above abstaining from food.
judaism.tie_back: Like the kural, it ranks moral virtue above fasting as the true austerity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Enduring patience is the highest austerity. ‘Nibbana is supreme,’ say the Buddhas. He is not a true monk who harms another, nor a true renunciate who oppresses others.”
buddhism.explanation: In the verses known as the Ovāda Pātimokkha, the Buddhas declare patient endurance (khanti) the supreme form of tapas.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a direct statement of the kural: patient endurance ranks above every other austerity, fasting included.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk should not be angry if beaten, nor should he therefore entertain sinful thoughts; knowing patience to be the highest good, a monk should meditate on the Law.”
jainism.explanation: The same Uttarādhyayana lecture that begins its list of hardships with hunger calls patience under abuse and violence 'the highest good'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks those who fast below those who endure cruel words, and the Uttarādhyayana, which counts hunger among the hardships a monk must bear, likewise names patience the highest good.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.26 (cf. 2.2–3 on hunger) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To practice forgiveness is the true fast, good conduct and contentment.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak redefines fasting: the real vow is forgiveness, together with good conduct and contentment.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks those who fast below those who endure cruel words; Guru Nanak likewise puts forbearance in the place of the outward fast.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 223, Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He endured both being struck and insulted without a word, though he was in his own house”
greek_mythology.explanation: The dead suitor Amphimedon recalls how the disguised Odysseus, a starving beggar in his own hall, silently bore their blows and insults.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus endures hunger and insult together, and Homer presents his silent endurance of abuse as his greatest test.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XXIV (trans. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for the most part he was despised and laughed at, yet bore all this ill-usage patiently.”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes Laertius reports that Socrates was famous for plain living and endurance of hunger and cold, but even more for calmly bearing mockery and abuse, including Xanthippe's scolding.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates combines bodily austerity with patience under insult, and it is the patience his biographer dwells on, much as the kural ranks it higher.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers II.21 (trans. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: Michael Faraday bears Humphry Davy's opposition to his election to the Royal Society
real_life_example.event: Michael Faraday had begun his scientific career in 1813 as an assistant to Humphry Davy, the leading chemist of his day, at the Royal Institution. When Faraday was put forward for Fellowship of the Royal Society, Davy opposed his election, and Faraday's own papers record that Davy was angry with him at the time. Faraday did not respond with hostility; he consulted the chemist William Wollaston and called on Davy, and he was elected a Fellow in 1824.
real_life_example.explanation: Faraday's restraint toward the patron who tried to block him allowed him to keep working within the scientific establishment, where he went on to become one of the greatest experimental scientists in history.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks those who endure cruel words above even those who endure fasting; Faraday endured the hostility of his own mentor without retaliating, an austerity of the inner life rather than the body.

tamil:
ஒழுக்காறாக் கொள்க ஒருவன்தன் நெஞ்சத்து
அழுக்காறு இலாத இயல்பு.
transliteration:
Ozhukkaaraak kolga oruvanthan nenjathu
Azhukkaaru ilaadha iyalbu.
meaning: Make it a rule of your life to keep your heart free of jealousy.
elementary: Some families have house rules, like “always say please.” This kural says: make “never be jealous of anyone” one of your own rules, as important as any other rule for being good.
university: Valluvar builds the chapter on a pun: ஒழுக்காறு (ozhukkaaru, “the path of right conduct”) and அழுக்காறு (azhukkaaru, “the path of impurity,” i.e., envy) differ by a single sound, so the couplet sets the right road against the soiled road. He places the absence of envy inside the heart (நெஞ்சத்து), not just in outward behavior, which treats envy as a flaw of character rather than a wrong act. Commentators from Parimelazhagar to Mu. Varadarasanar read the couplet as saying freedom from envy should be held as seriously as the formal rules of ozhukkam (Chapter 14). The view is close to Aristotle's, who counted envy among the passions whose very names imply badness, and to the Buddhist idea that a disposition must be trained, not merely a deed avoided.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but who is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor, who is free from false ego and equal both in happiness and distress, who is always satisfied and engaged in devotional service with determination and whose mind and intelligence are in agreement with Me-he is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the character traits of the ideal devotee, and “not envious” (adveṣṭā) comes first.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make freedom from envy a settled trait of character, the foundation of a good life rather than one rule among many.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul closes his list of the “fruit of the Spirit” by telling the community that people who live by the Spirit should not envy each other.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul makes not envying a standing rule of conduct for anyone who wants to live rightly.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not hate one another, and do not be jealous of one another, and do not desert each other, and O, Allah's worshipers! Be brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet lists envy (tahāsud) among the things believers must never do to each other if they are to live as brothers.
islam.tie_back: Both texts turn “do not envy” into a basic rule of how a good person relates to others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good eye, a humble spirit and a moderate appetite he is of the disciples of Abraham, our father. An evil eye, a haughty spirit and a limitless appetite he is of the disciples of Balaam, the wicked.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah marks the followers of Abraham by a “good eye” (ayin tovah), a generous way of seeing others' good, and the followers of Balaam by an “evil eye,” a grudging one.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Avot treats a heart without envy as the sign of a whole way of life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Asked why beings who wish to live without hostility still live in hostility, the Buddha answers that devas, humans, and all other beings “are fettered with envy & stinginess.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Sakka-pañha Sutta, envy (issā) and stinginess (macchariya) are named as the two fetters behind all conflict between beings.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see envy as a basic flaw of the heart that must be removed for a good life, not a minor fault.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 21 (Sakka-pañha Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “Benevolence (maitrī) towards all living-beings (sattva), joy (pramoda) at the sight of the virtuous (guṇādhika), compassion and sympathy (kāruṇya) for the afflicted (kliśyamāna), and tolerance (mādhyasthya) towards the insolent and ill-behaved (avineya) are the other observances.”
jainism.explanation: Umāsvāti names four standing attitudes a vow-holder must cultivate, and the second, pramoda, is gladness at another's excellence, which is the exact inner opposite of envy; Pūjyapāda's commentary glosses it as fervent affection and veneration in the presence of the virtuous.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks that an envy-free heart be adopted as the very rule of conduct, and the Tattvārtha makes joy at others' virtue a fixed observance (bhāvanā) that supports every vow.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.11, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Gurmukh eliminates hate and envy.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sidh Gosht, his dialogue with the yogis, Guru Nanak describes the Gurmukh, the person oriented to the Guru, as one whose way of life clears hatred and envy out of the heart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks us to make a heart free of envy the very rule of conduct; Guru Nanak makes freedom from envy a defining mark of the Gurmukh's way of living.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 942, Raag Raamkalee, Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says there are two Strifes on earth: one “a man would praise,” which spurs neighbour to compete with neighbour in honest work, and one that is “blameworthy,” fostering war and cruelty.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet separates healthy rivalry, which pushes a person to work harder, from the destructive strife that wants only to harm.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar's choice between the “right path” and the “impure path” matches Hesiod's choice between the good Strife and the bad one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is therefore a good feeling felt by good persons, whereas envy is a bad feeling felt by bad persons.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle compares emulation (wanting to earn what another has) with envy (wanting the other not to have it), and calls envy a mark of a bad character.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Aristotle treats the presence or absence of envy as a test of the kind of person one is.

real_life_example.event_title: Robert Schumann hails the young Chopin and the young Brahms
real_life_example.event: In 1831 the young Robert Schumann, himself an aspiring composer, published his first piece of music criticism in the Leipzig Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung, a review that greeted the unknown Frederic Chopin as a genius. In 1853, after the twenty-year-old Johannes Brahms visited the Schumanns in Dusseldorf and played them his unpublished works, Schumann wrote the article New Paths in the Neue Zeitschrift fur Musik, presenting Brahms to the musical world. Yale University Library notes that his two best-remembered reviews, the first and last of his critical career, each hailed the arrival of a young genius.
real_life_example.explanation: Schumann, a leading composer and the most influential music critic of his day, repeatedly used his position to lift up younger rivals rather than guard his own standing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks that a heart free of envy be made the settled rule of one's conduct, and Schumann's whole critical career, from first article to last, was built on celebrating others' gifts.

tamil:
விழுப்பேற்றின் அஃதொப்பது இல்லையார் மாட்டும்
அழுக்காற்றின் அன்மை பெறின்.
transliteration:
Vizhuppetrin aqdhoppadhu illaiyaar maattum
Azhukkaatrin anmai perin.
meaning: If you can stop being jealous of anyone at all, no other good thing you could ever gain is equal to that.
elementary: Imagine a treasure chest full of prizes: gold, trophies, toys. This kural says the best prize is a heart that is never jealous of anyone. Better than all the rest.
university: The key phrase is யார் மாட்டும் (“toward anyone at all”): Valluvar asks for complete freedom from envy, not selective freedom. Envy usually targets equals, as Aristotle observed, so envying no one means refusing to compare one's own standing with others'. By calling this the highest of all விழுப்பேறு (excellent attainments), the couplet puts an inner state above wealth, fame, and learning. The point anticipates the Stoic claim that goods in our control are the only true goods, and that once we see this, “there will be no room for envy.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who is satisfied with gain which comes of its own accord, who is free from duality and does not envy, who is steady both in success and failure, is never entangled, although performing actions.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the free person as vimatsara, one without envy, content with whatever comes and steady in both success and failure.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts present freedom from envy as a supreme attainment that frees a person from bondage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,”
christianity.explanation: In the hymn to love, Paul says love “envieth not,” and closes the chapter by calling love the greatest of the three abiding gifts (13:13).
christianity.tie_back: The Kural calls an envy-free heart the greatest attainment; Paul makes the love that “envieth not” the greatest gift.

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes complete faith depend on wanting for others the same good one wants for oneself, which is the opposite of envy.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat a heart that wishes others well, without envy, as the highest attainment of the religious life.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment with one's own portion, not comparison with others.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts put a heart that does not measure itself against others above any outward prize.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A monk who does not despise what he has received, even though it be little, who is pure in livelihood and unremitting in effort — him even the gods praise.”
buddhism.explanation: The verse after the warning against envying others' gains (Dhp 365) praises the monk who is content with his own.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts rank contentment free from envy as an attainment worth more than material gain.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I forgive all living beings and may all living beings forgive me; I cherish feelings of friendship towards all and I harbour enmity towards none.”
jainism.explanation: This is the Prakrit formula (khāmemi savva jīve) recited at the annual Paryuṣaṇa confession, in which the Jain declares friendship with every being and ill-will towards none.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar prizes freedom from envy towards anyone at all (yār māṭṭum) above every other gain, and the Jain formula likewise refuses any exception: friendship towards all, enmity towards none.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam, verse 86 (English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I have totally forgotten my jealousy of others, … No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that in the company of the holy (the Saadh Sangat) all jealousy of others fell away, so that no one remained an enemy or a stranger to him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural prizes being free of envy toward anyone at all above every other gain; Guru Arjan describes exactly that universal release, with envy gone toward everyone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor old couple in Phrygia, share their meager meal with disguised gods whom richer neighbours turned away; they are rewarded while the neighbourhood is drowned.
greek_mythology.explanation: The couple are content with their humble lot and give freely, with no resentment of wealthier neighbours.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their contentment, free of envy, turns out to be worth more than their neighbours' wealth, echoing the Kural's ranking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For, if the essence of good consists in things in our own control, there will be no room for envy or emulation.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus says that once you see real goods as inner ones, no one else's honors or power can make you envious. The only thing worth wanting is to be free.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers see freedom from envy as the sign of the highest good a person can reach.

real_life_example.event_title: Nishida and Oe make the Medals of Friendship
real_life_example.event: At the Berlin Olympic Games, the Japanese pole vaulters Shuhei Nishida and Sueo Oe both cleared 4.25 metres and tied for second place after a final lasting more than five hours. The placings were settled by the Japanese side, with the older Nishida given the silver medal and Oe the bronze. After returning to Japan, the two friends had both medals cut in half and joined, so that each man kept a medal that was half silver and half bronze, which became known in Japan as the Medals of Friendship.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than let a ranking divide them, two rivals in the same event chose to share the honour equally, and Nishida's medal is now displayed by Waseda University.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says no gain equals freedom from envy toward anyone at all, and Nishida and Oe valued their friendship above the difference between silver and bronze.

tamil:
அறன்ஆக்கம் வேண்டாதான் என்பான் பிறனாக்கம்
பேணாது அழுக்கறுப் பான்.
transliteration:
Aran aakkam vendaadhaan enbaan piranaakkam
Penaadhu azhukkaruppaan.
meaning: Someone who is jealous when others do well, instead of being happy for them, is really saying they do not want goodness or success for themselves.
elementary: If your friend wins a prize and you sulk instead of cheering, you're not just being unkind to them. You're blocking your own chance to be good and to do well. Being jealous is like saying “I don't want good things for myself either.”
university: The couplet makes a psychological claim: envy is self-defeating, not just unkind. Parimelazhagar reads அறனாக்கம் as both அறம் (virtue) and ஆக்கம் (prosperity). The envious person's attitude implicitly rejects both, since virtue grows through goodwill and prosperity through good conduct. பேணாது (“without cherishing”) implies the right response to another's good fortune is active appreciation, close to the Buddhist mudita (sympathetic joy). Aristotle's definition fits closely: the envious man “is pained at all good fortune,” even when it is deserved.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At Yudhishthira's Rajasuya sacrifice, Duryodhana sees the Pandavas' wealth and splendour and is consumed with jealousy. He tells his father he cannot bear their prosperity, which leads to the rigged dice game.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana cannot welcome his cousins' success and turns to deceit, abandoning dharma for envy.
hinduism.tie_back: He becomes the Kural's envious man exactly: by resenting another's prosperity he gives up both righteousness and, in the end, his own fortune.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta sub-parva), Ganguli translation

christianity.quote_or_event: “Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to share in others' joy rather than resent it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's ideal of cherishing (பேணுதல்) another's prosperity is what Paul commands here.

islam.quote_or_event: “Or do they envy people for what Allāh has given them of His bounty?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an rebukes those who resent the favor God has given to others.
islam.tie_back: Both texts condemn resentment of another's blessing, which in the Qur'anic frame means resenting God's own gift.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.”
judaism.explanation: The tenth commandment forbids even the inner wanting of what belongs to one's neighbour.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts target the inner reaction to another's prosperity, not just outward acts.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One should not despise what one has received, nor envy the gains of others. The monk who envies the gains of others does not attain to meditative absorption.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that envying others' gains blocks one's own spiritual progress.
buddhism.tie_back: Close to the Kural: envying another's prosperity costs the envier his own highest good.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Spite against knowledge–pradoṣa, concealment of knowledge–nihnava, non-imparting of knowledge out of envy–mātsarya, causing impediment to acquisition of knowledge–antarāya, disregard of knowledge–āsādana, and disparagement of true knowledge–upaghāta, lead to the influx (āsrava) of knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇa) and faith-obscuring (darśanāvaraṇa) karmas.”
jainism.explanation: In Jain karma theory envy (mātsarya) and spite towards another's learning do not harm the other person; they draw in karmic matter that clouds the envier's own knowledge and faith.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the man who envies another's prosperity in effect wants neither virtue nor prosperity for himself, and the Tattvārtha shows the mechanism: envy blocks the envier's own spiritual growth.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.10, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Give up your envy of others, you fool!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan calls envy of other people plain foolishness and tells the mind to drop it, since it profits nothing in a short human life.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the man who envies another's prosperity in effect rejects his own virtue and wealth; Gurbani likewise treats envy as self-defeating folly.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 889, Raag Raamkalee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Aglauros, daughter of Cecrops, is filled with envy by the goddess Envy (Invidia) at her sister Herse's good fortune in being loved by Mercury. She wastes away and blocks the god at her sister's door.
greek_mythology.explanation: Instead of rejoicing in her sister's blessing, Aglauros is eaten up by resentment and tries to stop it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She shows the Kural's point: resenting another's prosperity ruins the resenter's own life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The man who is characterized by righteous indignation is pained at undeserved good fortune, the envious man, going beyond him, is pained at all good fortune.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle separates indignation at undeserved success from envy, which resents any success at all, including deserved success.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's envier resents the prosperity of others whatever its source; Aristotle defines envy the same way.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.7 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Haydn praises Mozart to his father
real_life_example.event: In February 1785 Joseph Haydn, then the most celebrated composer in Europe, heard the last three of Mozart's new string quartets played at a gathering in Vienna where Mozart's father Leopold was present. Haydn told Leopold that his son was the greatest composer he knew either in person or by reputation, and that he had taste and the deepest knowledge of composition; Leopold reported the remark in a letter to his daughter. Mozart dedicated the six quartets to Haydn when they were published later that year, calling him his dear friend.
real_life_example.explanation: Haydn, the established master, openly rejoiced in the rise of a younger composer who could have been seen as his rival, and their mutual admiration enriched both men's music.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural condemns envying another's prosperity instead of welcoming it, and Haydn did the opposite, welcoming Mozart's genius with generous praise.

tamil:
அழுக்காற்றின் அல்லவை செய்யார் இழுக்காற்றின்
ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து.
transliteration:
Azhukkaatrin allavai seyyaar izhukkaatrin
Edham padupaakku arindhu.
meaning: Wise people know the trouble that comes from doing wrong, so they will never do wrong because of jealousy.
elementary: If you know a path has a big muddy pit, you don't walk that way. Wise people know jealousy leads to doing mean things, and mean things lead to trouble, so they don't let jealousy push them into it.
university: The subject, “the wise” (அறிவுடையோர்), is understood from context, as the commentators note. The couplet treats restraint from envy-driven wrongdoing as a matter of knowledge: seeing where the “fault-path” (இழுக்காறு) leads. Valluvar moves from the feeling of envy (azhukkaaru) to the acts it produces (அல்லவை, unrighteous deeds), and the wise stop the chain at the first link. The reasoning is prudential as well as moral, like the Buddha's image of the trader who avoids a dangerous road. It also matches Aristotle's claim that envy, like theft or murder, has no right amount or right occasion; it is always a mistake.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But those who, out of envy, disregard these teachings and do not practice them regularly, are to be considered bereft of all knowledge, befooled, and doomed to ignorance and bondage.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says those who act out of envy (abhyasūyantaḥ) lose their knowledge and are ruined.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts link envy-driven conduct to a lack of wisdom and its ruinous result.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that envy is the soil in which every kind of wrongdoing grows.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's chain from envy to wrongful acts appears here: where envy is, “every evil work” follows.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not wish for that by which Allāh has made some of you exceed others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allāh of His bounty.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an forbids longing for others' advantages and redirects the heart to asking God directly.
islam.tie_back: Both texts stop envy early, before it grows into wrongful acts, by pointing to a better path.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.”
judaism.explanation: God warns Cain, angry that Abel's offering was accepted, that sin is waiting at the door and that he must master it before he acts.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's wise person does what Cain failed to do: sees where envy leads and refuses to act on it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a trader with a small escort and great wealth would avoid a perilous route, or just as one desiring to live avoids poison, even so should one shun evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a wise person avoiding evil to a trader who knows a road is dangerous and takes another.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's wise avoid the envy-path because they know the danger on it; the Dhammapada uses the same logic.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The two sins attachment and aversion lead one to commit sinful acts. That monk who always besieges them will not wander in this mundane existence.”
jainism.explanation: Jainism traces all wrongdoing to the twin passions of rāga (attachment) and dveṣa (aversion), and teaches that one who sees this and checks them escapes the round of suffering in saṃsāra.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's wise man refuses to do wrong out of envy because he knows the suffering it leads to, and the Jain verse likewise sees aversion, of which envy is a form, as the root of sinful acts whose fruit is continued wandering in suffering.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam, verse 130 (Samyamasutra; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Jealousy and envy bring terrible pain, and one is cursed throughout the three worlds.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok in Maaroo ki Vaar, Guru Nanak warns that envy brings deep suffering and spoils a person everywhere.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wise person avoids envy-driven wrong because he knows the suffering it brings; Guru Nanak names that suffering plainly.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1091, Raag Maaroo (Maaroo ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod warns that the bad Strife “fosters evil war and battle, being cruel: her no man loves,” unlike the good Strife of honest rivalry.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet tells his brother Perses to recognize the destructive form of rivalry and turn away from it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's wise, Hesiod's listener must see where destructive rivalry leads and refuse to follow it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Some have names that already imply badness, e.g. spite, shamelessness, envy, and in the case of actions adultery, theft, murder ... It is not possible, then, ever to be right with regard to them; one must always be wrong.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says envy, unlike anger or fear, has no right amount; it is always wrong, just as theft or murder is.
philosophy.tie_back: This is why the Kural's wise never act from envy: there is no case in which envy-driven action is right.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.6 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Darwin refuses to act in a paltry spirit toward Wallace
real_life_example.place: Down House, Kent, and the Linnean Society, London, England
real_life_example.event: In June 1858 Charles Darwin, who had worked on natural selection for about twenty years without publishing, received an essay from Alfred Russel Wallace setting out the same theory. Writing to Charles Lyell on 25 June, Darwin asked whether he could honourably publish his own sketch now and said he would rather burn his whole book than have Wallace or anyone think he had behaved meanly. Lyell and Joseph Hooker arranged for Wallace's essay and extracts from Darwin's earlier writings to be read together at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858.
real_life_example.explanation: Darwin faced the loss of credit for his life's work, yet he refused to suppress or outrun his rival, and the joint reading gave both men their place.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the wise, knowing where wrongdoing leads, will not do wrong out of envy, and Darwin refused to act unfairly toward a rival even when his priority was at stake.

tamil:
அழுக்காறு உடையார்க்கு அதுசாலும் ஒன்னார்
வழுக்காயும் கேடீன் பது.
transliteration:
Azhukkaaru udaiyaarkku adhusaalum onnaar
Vazhukkaayum kedeenbadhu.
meaning: For jealous people, jealousy alone is enough to ruin them. Even if their enemies fail to hurt them, their own jealousy will bring them down.
elementary: Imagine someone who never needs a bully to hurt them, because they keep hurting themselves by feeling jealous all the time. Envy is like a bully that lives inside you.
university: The phrase அது சாலும் (“that is enough”) makes envy a self-sufficient engine of destruction. No external enemy (ஒன்னார்) is needed, and even if enemies falter (வழுக்காயும்), envy does not. The same insight appears across traditions: Proverbs calls envy “the rottenness of the bones,” Ovid pictures Envy gnawing herself, and the Dhammapada compares the depraved man to a creeper that strangles its own host tree. Aristotle's definition explains why: envy is pain at another's good that brings the envier no gain, only suffering.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “These six are always miserable, viz., the envious, the malicious, the discontented, the irascible, the ever-suspicious, and those depending upon the fortunes of others.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells King Dhritarashtra that the envious come first among those who are always unhappy, whatever their outward circumstances.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say envy produces its own misery; the envious need no enemy.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), Ganguli translation

christianity.quote_or_event: “A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says envy rots a person from the inside, while a calm heart gives life.
christianity.tie_back: Envy destroys from within, needing no enemy, just as the Kural says.

islam.quote_or_event: “Avoid envy, for envy devours good deeds just as fire devours fuel or (he said) “grass.””
islam.explanation: The hadith says envy consumes a person's own store of good deeds, as fire eats up wood.
islam.tie_back: Both texts describe envy as a self-consuming fire that destroys the envier.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah names envy (kin'ah) first among three passions that destroy a person.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats envy as enough on its own to ruin someone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a single creeper strangles the tree on which it grows, even so, a man who is exceedingly depraved harms himself as only an enemy might wish.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a corrupt person to a tree choked by a creeper growing on it: he does to himself what an enemy would want to do.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's point that the envious need no enemy because they are their own.

jainism.quote_or_event: The god Saṅgamaka, hearing Śakra praise Mahāvīra's steadfastness, set out to break him: “His jealousy increased greatly when he saw Śrī Vīra standing so, undisturbed, a disinterested friend of the world.” After six months of failed torments he lamented, “how long have I wandered over the earth, alas! deceived by my own stupidity!”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra's account has the envious god throw every terror at Mahāvīra without disturbing his meditation, while Saṅgamaka himself breaks his vow, loses his radiance and is expelled from heaven.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says envy alone suffices to ruin the envier even if his foes do him no harm, and Saṅgamaka's jealousy left its target untouched while destroying Saṅgamaka himself.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. IV, Part 4 “Attacks by Saṅgamaka” (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In jealousy, the body is not at peace; without the Fear of God, multitudes are ruined.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Dakhni Oankar Guru Nanak teaches that jealousy destroys a person's peace from within, and that those without reverence for God are brought to ruin.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says envy alone is enough to ruin a man even if his enemies fail; Guru Nanak likewise places the destruction inside the envious person himself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 933, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “She finds men's successes disagreeable, and pines away at the sight. She gnaws and being gnawed is also her own punishment.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid personifies Envy (Invidia) as a figure who eats vipers' flesh and wastes away at others' success: she is her own torment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ovid pictures exactly what the Kural states: envy punishes the envier without any outside enemy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Envy is pain at the sight of such good fortune as consists of the good things already mentioned; we feel it towards our equals; not with the idea of getting something for ourselves, but because the other people have it.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines envy as pain at another's good that brings no gain to the envier.
philosophy.tie_back: If envy is pain with no gain, it harms only the envier, which is why the Kural calls it “enough” to ruin a person.

real_life_example.event_title: The Bone Wars ruin Cope and Marsh
real_life_example.place: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; New Haven, Connecticut; and the American West, United States
real_life_example.event: The palaeontologists Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh, once friends, spent decades in a bitter competition to find and name dinosaur fossils in the American West. In January 1890 Cope gave a journalist material accusing Marsh of plagiarism and misuse of federal funds, and the New York Herald ran the charges for weeks. Congress then cut the Geological Survey's budget, Marsh lost his paleontology post and had to hand over many fossils, while Cope, who had already lost his fortune, was left with little but his collection and died in 1897.
real_life_example.explanation: PBS and National Geographic describe the feud as ruining both men, who did each other far more damage than any outside opponent.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says envy alone is enough to destroy the envious even if no enemy harms them, and Cope and Marsh's rivalry brought down both of them.

tamil:
கொடுப்பது அழுக்கறுப்பான் சுற்றம் உடுப்பதூஉம்
உண்பதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Koduppadhu azhukkaruppaan sutram uduppadhoovum
Unbadhoovum indrik kedum.
meaning: A person who is jealous when others receive gifts will be ruined, and their family with them, left with no clothes to wear and no food to eat.
elementary: Imagine a kid who gets upset every time a teacher gives stickers to others. Eventually, nobody wants to share with that kid or their friends either. Being jealous of other people's gifts leaves you, and the people around you, with nothing.
university: This couplet narrows envy to a specific form: resentment of generosity itself (கொடுப்பது, “what is given”), whether one objects to a gift going to someone else or tries to stop it. The punishment is social and material: not only the envier but his சுற்றம் (kin, dependents) are left without food or clothing, since the grudging spirit cuts the household off from the web of mutual giving. The idea has a close counterpart in the Buddha's teaching that whoever obstructs another's gift harms three parties, beginning with himself. Pirkei Avot likewise names the giver who wishes others would not give as having an “evil eye” toward what belongs to others.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When King Bali prepares to grant three steps of land to the dwarf Vamana, his preceptor Shukracharya urges him to withhold the gift. Bali refuses, gives anyway, and is ultimately blessed; later retellings add that Shukra lost an eye trying to block the gift.
hinduism.explanation: Shukra tries to stop a gift from being given, and his obstruction fails.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural condemns the one who resents or blocks another's giving; Shukra's attempt is a well-known illustration of that failure.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the vineyard workers, the owner answers those who resent his generosity to latecomers: are they envious (“evil eye”) because he is generous?
christianity.tie_back: Jesus confronts exactly the envy the Kural condemns: resenting what is given to someone else.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who are stingy and enjoin upon [other] people stinginess and conceal what Allāh has given them of His bounty - and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment -”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an condemns those who are stingy themselves and also urge others not to give.
islam.tie_back: Both texts condemn those who obstruct others' generosity and warn of humiliating loss.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are four types of charity givers. He who wishes to give, but that others should not give: his eye is evil to that which belongs to others.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah singles out the person who resents others' giving as having an “evil eye” toward what belongs to them.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact target: resentment of what others give.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever prevents another from giving a gift creates three obstructions, three impediments. Which three? He creates an obstruction to the merit of the giver, an obstruction to the recipient's gains, and prior to that he undermines and harms his own self.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Vacchagotta that blocking someone else's gift harms the giver, the receiver, and, first of all, the one who blocks it.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts teach that begrudging another's giving ends in the begrudger's own ruin.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 3.57 (Vaccha Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “Laying obstacles (vighna) (in way of charity, etc.) is the cause of the influx of obstructive (antarāya) karmas.”
jainism.explanation: Jain doctrine holds that obstructing another's giving, gain or enjoyment binds antarāya karma, which in turn obstructs the obstructer's own future charity, gain, and enjoyment of food, clothing and other goods.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar warns that one who resents what is given to others will end without food or clothing, and the Tattvārtha's karma law says the same: blocking another's gift blocks one's own receiving.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.27, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The True Lord and Master is on the side of the True Guru; and so, all those who oppose Him waste away to death in anger, envy and conflict.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that people who resented the greatness the Lord had given the Guru could not take it away, and wore themselves out in envy and strife.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that one who resents what is given to others perishes along with his kin; Guru Ram Das describes the envious who begrudge God's gift to another wasting themselves away.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 307, Raag Gauree (Gauri ki Vaar), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Envy travels to Athens, “wherever she passes she tramples the flower-filled fields, withers the grass, blasts the highest treetops and poisons homes, cities and peoples with her breath.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's Envy does not stay inside one heart; her breath blights crops and poisons whole communities.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, where the envier's kin lose food and clothing, envy's damage spreads to the people around the envier.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Emulation makes us take steps to secure the good things in question, envy makes us take steps to stop our neighbour having them.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle notes that envy is active: it moves people to stop others from getting good things.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's envier who resents what is given to others is Aristotle's envious man trying to stop his neighbour from receiving.

real_life_example.event_title: Benedict Arnold resents promotions given to others
real_life_example.place: Philadelphia, West Point (New York) and London
real_life_example.event: In February 1777 the Continental Congress promoted five brigadier generals junior to Benedict Arnold to major general and passed him over, and Arnold felt his honour insulted and threatened to resign. Although he was later made a major general, his seniority was not restored, and Mount Vernon and History.com describe his resentment over promotion as a motive for his later treason. In 1780 his plot to hand West Point to the British was discovered; he fled to the British side and spent his last years in England, distrusted on both sides of the Atlantic, dying in London in 1801.
real_life_example.explanation: A brave and gifted commander allowed grievance over honours granted to others to turn into betrayal, and lost both his reputation and his country.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that one who resents what is given to others will perish together with his household, and Arnold's resentment of others' promotions led to his disgrace and exile.

tamil:
அவ்வித்து அழுக்காறு உடையானைச் செய்யவள்
தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்.
transliteration:
Avvithu azhukkaaru udaiyaanaich cheyyaval
Thavvaiyaik kaatti vidum.
meaning: The goddess of good luck turns away from the jealous person and points them out to her older sister, the goddess of bad luck.
elementary: Imagine Good Luck as a friendly person who visits your house. When she sees you're always jealous, she leaves, and on her way out she tells her grumpy sister, Bad Luck, “This house is yours now.”
university: Valluvar here uses a mythological image unusual for a text that mostly avoids sectarian deities. செய்யவள் (“the red/fair one”) is Lakshmi (Tiru), and தவ்வை (“elder sister”) is Mudevi/Jyeshtha, goddess of misfortune, who in the Padma and Linga Puranas rises from the churned ocean before Lakshmi and is told to dwell among the quarrelsome and wicked. அவ்வித்து is read by Parimelazhagar as “being herself envious [of him],” so the goddess answers envy with envy, a measure-for-measure punishment. The image turns an abstract claim, that envy drives away prosperity, into a vivid scene, a technique Valluvar uses sparingly and to strong effect.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Jyeshtha (Mudevi), elder sister and opposite of Lakshmi, emerges from the churning of the ocean before Lakshmi; in the Padma and Linga Puranas she is told to dwell in homes of quarrel, harsh speech, and wicked people.
hinduism.explanation: Hindu myth pairs prosperity (Lakshmi) with her elder sister misfortune (Jyeshtha), who takes over where vice lives.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses this exact pair: Lakshmi leaves the envious man and hands him over to her elder sister.
hinduism.source: Padma Purana and Linga Purana, as summarized in the Wikipedia article on Jyestha (citing Leslie 1992 and Kinsley 1997)

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hasteth to be rich hath an evil eye, and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that the grasping, “evil-eyed” person does not see that poverty is coming for him.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the envious “evil eye” drives prosperity away and invites poverty.

islam.quote_or_event: Iblis refuses to bow to Adam, saying “I am better than him,” and is told: “Descend from it [i.e., Paradise]... So get out; indeed, you are of the debased.”
islam.explanation: Iblis resents the honor given to Adam and is expelled from the place of favor.
islam.tie_back: As Lakshmi abandons the envious man, divine favor is withdrawn from Iblis because he resented another's elevation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Saul eyed David from that day and forward.” ... “And Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with him, and was departed from Saul.”
judaism.explanation: After hearing David praised above him, Saul watches him with an envious eye, and the text notes that God's presence has left Saul and gone to David.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the envious man is abandoned by divine favor, which passes to the one he envies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where a woman or man is envious. He/she envies, begrudges, & broods about others' gains, honor, respect, reverence, salutations, & veneration. ... If instead he/she comes to the human state, then he/she is not influential wherever reborn.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that envy leads to rebirth in bad destinations or, if reborn human, to a life without influence or standing.
buddhism.tie_back: Envy drives good fortune away, which is the Kural's point in karmic rather than mythological terms.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 135 (Cula-kammavibhanga Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: When the envious god Saṅgamaka returned to heaven after failing to shake Mahāvīra, Śakra at once turned his back on him and declared him unfit to be seen; Saṅgamaka, his beauty blurred like a mirror sprinkled with water, was expelled from the Saudharma heaven.
jainism.explanation: In Hemacandra's telling the envious god loses his splendour and his place among the gods, and the king of gods publicly turns away from him and casts him out.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar pictures Fortune turning from the envious man and pointing him out to Misfortune, and the nearest Jain image is Śakra turning his back on the envious Saṅgamaka and driving him from heaven's prosperity.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X, ch. IV, Part 4 “Attacks by Saṅgamaka” (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “All the nine treasures, and the eighteen supernatural powers are held by our Lord and Master in the Palm of His Hand.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that all wealth and power rest in the hand of the one God, not with any separate deity of fortune.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures the goddess of fortune leaving the envious man for her sister Misfortune; Sikh teaching sets aside such goddesses and places all fortune in the One Lord's hand alone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, Rehras (So Dar section), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod's iron age, “Envy, foul-mouthed, delighting in evil, with scowling face, will go along with wretched men one and all. And then Aidos and Nemesis ... will go from the wide-pathed earth.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Envy becomes people's companion, the goddesses of shame and righteous retribution leave the earth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As Lakshmi leaves the envious man, Hesiod's good goddesses abandon a humanity that keeps company with Envy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For jealousy has no place in the celestial choir.”
philosophy.explanation: In Socrates' myth of the soul's journey, the gods move freely through heaven and anyone able may follow, because envy has no place among the divine.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato puts envy outside the divine company; the Kural shows the goddess of fortune leaving the envious.

real_life_example.event_title: Li Si brings down his gifted schoolmate Han Fei
real_life_example.event: Han Fei, a brilliant Legalist thinker whose writings the King of Qin admired, came to the Qin court on a diplomatic mission in 233 BCE. According to Britannica, Li Si, the chief minister and Han Fei's former schoolmate, apparently fearing that Han Fei might win the king's favour with his superior learning, had him imprisoned, and Han Fei died in prison. Li Si rose to great power under the First Emperor, but after the emperor's death he fell out with the eunuch Zhao Gao, who had him executed in 208 BCE.
real_life_example.explanation: Li Si removed a more gifted rival and reached the summit of power, yet his fortune did not last and he ended in ruin.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural pictures fortune deserting the envious and handing him over to misfortune, and Li Si's high fortune ended in disgrace and death.

tamil:
அழுக்காறு எனஒரு பாவி திருச்செற்றுத்
தீயுழி உய்த்து விடும்.
transliteration:
Azhukkaaru ena oru paavi thiruchchetruth
Theeyuzhi uyththu vidum.
meaning: Jealousy is a wicked thing like no other. It wipes out a person's riches and pushes them into a place of terrible suffering.
elementary: Envy is like a sneaky thief who first steals everything you have, then pushes you onto a dangerous road. Once envy moves in, it takes your good things away and leads you somewhere bad.
university: Valluvar personifies envy as a பாவி (sinner, evil being) with no equal (ஒரு), and gives it two acts: it destroys wealth (திருச்செற்று, with திரு again evoking Lakshmi from the previous couplet) and drives its host into தீயுழி. The term means “evil place” or “evil path”; Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as hell, others as a life of wrongdoing. The double sense covers both this-worldly ruin and afterlife punishment, a pattern also seen in the Dhammapada's “suffers here and hereafter.” Parallels such as Korah and Devadatta, whose envy ended with the earth swallowing them, show how widely traditions have linked envy to a downward plunge.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are envious and mischievous, who are the lowest among men, I perpetually cast into the ocean of material existence, into various demoniac species of life.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the envious (dviṣataḥ) and cruel are repeatedly cast into lower, demonic births.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say envy drives a person downward to the worst destination.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one.”
christianity.explanation: Eliphaz tells Job that envy kills the simple person who harbors it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's “sinner without equal,” envy is pictured as a killer of its host.

islam.quote_or_event: “And his soul permitted to him the murder of his brother, so he killed him and became among the losers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells of Adam's son who, after his brother's offering was accepted and his was not, killed him and became “among the losers.”
islam.tie_back: Envy of a brother's acceptance leads to the gravest sin and lasting loss, the path the Kural describes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They, and all that appertained to them, went down alive into the pit, and the earth closed upon them: and they perished from among the congregation.”
judaism.explanation: Korah and his followers, who challenged Moses and Aaron out of jealousy of their position, are swallowed by the earth with all their possessions.
judaism.tie_back: Envy destroys wealth (“all that appertained to them”) and plunges the envier into the pit, as in the Kural.
judaism.source: Numbers 16:33 (KJV); cf. Pirkei Avot 5:17 on Korah's dispute

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The evil-doer suffers here and hereafter; he suffers in both the worlds. The thought, “Evil have I done,” torments him, and he suffers even more when gone to realms of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The commentarial tradition attaches this verse to Devadatta, whose envy of the Buddha led to schism and assassination attempts, and who was swallowed by the earth into hell.
buddhism.tie_back: Envy ruins in this life and drives to hell hereafter, the two-stage fall the Kural describes.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 17 (trans. Buddharakkhita); Devadatta story from the Dhammapada Commentary

jainism.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
jainism.explanation: The young ascetic who calls himself “without a protector” tells King Śreṇika that the worst enemy a person can have is his own perverted disposition, which brings him to grief at death and, as the preceding verses say, to hell.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar personifies envy as a sinner without equal that wrecks a man's wealth and drives him to the fire of hell, and the Jain verse likewise ranks the inner vice above any outward foe as the agent of ruin.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.48 (cf. 20.46) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the worlds of Shiva, Brahma and Indra, I wandered around, burning up with envy.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes wandering even through the heavens of the gods while burning with envy, so that even those exalted realms bring no relief.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls envy a matchless sinner that drives a man into the fire of hell; Guru Arjan's image of a soul burning with envy wherever it goes echoes that fire.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1219, Raag Saarang, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Aglauros, poisoned by Envy, blocks Mercury from reaching her sister; the god turns her into a dark stone statue, stained by her envious mind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Envy destroys Aglauros's life and fortune completely, ending in her punishment by a god.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's “sinner,” Envy wrecks its host and delivers her to a terrible end.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle groups envy with spite and shamelessness, and with adultery, theft, and murder, as things that “imply by their names that they are themselves bad”; for all of them, “one must always be wrong.”
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, envy is not a feeling to moderate but a vice that always leads a person wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's “sinner without equal” and Aristotle's “always wrong” both treat envy as corrupt at its root.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.6 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Pazzi conspiracy against the Medici
real_life_example.event: Members of the Pazzi family, a rival Florentine banking house, joined a plot to overthrow the ruling Medici, and on 26 April 1478 conspirators attacked Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici during Mass in Florence Cathedral, killing Giuliano and wounding Lorenzo. The people of Florence rallied to the Medici, the plot collapsed, and the conspirators were pursued and punished. The Pazzi family was stripped of its riches and banished, while Lorenzo emerged with his power strengthened.
real_life_example.explanation: Instead of competing fairly, the Pazzi tried to seize a rival's position by crime, and the attempt destroyed their own wealth and standing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says envy destroys a man's wealth and drives him onto the path of evil, and the Pazzi lost their fortune after turning to a criminal plot against their rivals.

tamil:
அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் செவ்வியான்
கேடும் நினைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Avviya nenjathaan aakkamum sevviyaan
Kedum ninaikkap padum.
meaning: When a jealous person grows rich and a good, honest person falls into hard times, it is something strange that we should stop and think about.
elementary: Sometimes a mean, jealous kid seems to get everything, while a kind kid has a hard time. That looks unfair, and this kural says: stop and think about it. Things may not stay that way, and there is a deeper reason behind it.
university: Valluvar recognizes the classic problem of theodicy: the wicked sometimes prosper and the good sometimes suffer. He does not deny it. He calls these cases நினைக்கப்படும், “to be reflected upon.” Parimelazhagar resolves the anomaly through karma: the envious man's prosperity comes from past merit now being used up, and the good man's suffering from past deeds now being paid off, so neither lasts. The same wrestling appears in Psalm 73, in Rabbi Yannai's admission in Pirkei Avot, in the Dhammapada's teaching that evil “ripens” late, and in Glaucon's challenge in Plato's Republic, which makes this one of the most widely shared questions in world ethics.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In exile in the forest, Draupadi laments to Yudhishthira that the righteous king suffers while the wicked Duryodhana prospers, and questions divine justice; Yudhishthira answers that one practices dharma for its own sake and that its fruits come in time.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata stages a full debate over why the virtuous suffer and the envious thrive.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the anomaly the Kural says must be pondered: the envious prosper and the upright suffer.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Draupadi–Yudhishthira dialogue), Ganguli translation

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. ... Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist is troubled that the wicked prosper, until reflection in God's sanctuary shows him their final end.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: the prosperity of the wicked is a puzzle to be pondered until one sees how it ends.

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those who disbelieve ever think that [because] We extend their time [of enjoyment] it is better for them. We only extend it for them so that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an explains that the apparent prosperity of wrongdoers is a respite that will end in punishment, not a sign of favor.
islam.tie_back: Both texts ask the reader to think past the surface when the undeserving prosper.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Yannai said: it is not in our hands [to explain the reason] either of the security of the wicked, or even of the afflictions of the righteous.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah admits that the ease of the wicked and the suffering of the righteous are beyond full human explanation.
judaism.tie_back: It names the same two anomalies as the Kural: the wicked's prosperity and the upright's suffering.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It may be well with the evil-doer as long as the evil ripens not. But when it does ripen, then the evil-doer sees (the painful results of) his evil deeds. It may be ill with the doer of good as long as the good ripens not. But when it does ripen, then the doer of good sees (the pleasant results of) his good deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha explains that results of deeds ripen with a delay, so the wicked may prosper and the good suffer for a while.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the karmic resolution that Parimelazhagar gives for the Kural's anomaly.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Mahāvīra broke his fast at the proud, wealthy Abhinava's house, a stream of treasure fell there, while the devout but ruined Jinadatta, who had waited in vain, gained nothing visible; an omniscient disciple of Pārśva then explained that Jinadatta had earned rebirth in the Acyuta heaven, and that “the stream of treasure, fruit in this world of the Arhat’s fast-breaking was obtained by Sheth Abhinava, who is devoid of pure character.”
jainism.explanation: The episode answers why a man of poor character can prosper while a good man stays poor: visible wealth is only a this-worldly fruit, and the real merit lies with the pure-minded, to bear fruit in time.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the prosperity of the envious and the poverty of the upright must be pondered, and this Jain story ponders exactly that case and resolves it through karma and inner disposition.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X, ch. IV, Part 4 (episode of Jīrṇaśreṣṭhin and Abhinava) (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “By His Command, some are high and some are low; by His Written Command, pain and pleasure are obtained.”
sikhism.explanation: In the second pauri of Japji, Guru Nanak teaches that rise and fall, joy and suffering all happen within hukam, the divine order, which is beyond human calculation.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks us to ponder why the envious sometimes prosper and the upright suffer; Japji answers that such reversals of fortune lie within God's hukam.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 2, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the wealthy King Croesus asks Solon who is the happiest of men, Solon refuses to call Croesus happy and says no one should be called fortunate until one has seen how his life ends; Croesus later loses his kingdom.
greek_mythology.explanation: Solon warns that visible prosperity is no sure sign of lasting fortune.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the story invites reflection on why fortune seems to go to the wrong people, and on how it ends.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book II of the Republic, Glaucon challenges Socrates with the case of the perfectly unjust man who enjoys wealth and reputation and the perfectly just man who is thought unjust and suffers torture. Socrates spends the rest of the dialogue showing that justice is still better.
philosophy.explanation: Plato builds his central ethical argument around the anomaly of the prosperous wicked and the suffering righteous.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same anomaly must be pondered; the Republic ponders it at length.

real_life_example.event_title: Aristides the Just is ostracised and then recalled
real_life_example.event: Aristides, an Athenian statesman renowned for his honesty and known as the Just, was ostracised in 482 BCE after political manoeuvring by his rival Themistocles and accusations of sympathy with Persia. When Xerxes invaded, the Athenians recalled the ostracised exiles in 480 BCE, and Aristides led a hoplite force at the battle of Salamis. In 479 BCE he was one of the Athenian commanders at the victory of Plataea.
real_life_example.explanation: An upright man suffered exile while his rival prevailed, yet within two years his city recalled him and gave him high command.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural invites reflection on the puzzle of the upright suffering misfortune, and Aristides' exile, soon reversed, shows such misfortune need not last.

tamil:
அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை அஃதுஇல்லார்
பெருக்கத்தில் தீர்ந்தாரும் இல்.
transliteration:
Azhukkatru akandraarum illai aqdhuillaar
Perukkaththil theerndhaarum il.
meaning: No one has ever become great by being jealous, and no one free of jealousy has ever lost the good things they had.
elementary: Being jealous has never helped anyone become great, not even once. And people who are happy for others never end up losing out because of it. So jealousy has zero upside, and kindness has zero downside.
university: The chapter closes with a balanced pair of universal negatives: அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை (none have grown great through envy; அகன்றார், literally “expanded”) and அஃதில்லார் பெருக்கத்தில் தீர்ந்தாரும் இல் (none without it have been cut off from increase). The form is a complete disjunction: envy never helps and its absence never hurts, so envy is irrational even on purely selfish grounds. Read with Kural 169, the couplet resolves the anomaly: apparent exceptions are temporary and the long-run pattern holds. The prudential argument matches Epictetus: if someone gains an advantage by paying a price you did not pay, “don't imagine that he has gained any advantage over you.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: Duryodhana, whose envy of the Pandavas drives the whole conflict, dies at Kurukshetra with his brothers and allies destroyed, while the Pandavas, whom he tried to ruin, recover the kingdom.
hinduism.explanation: The epic's overall arc shows the envious prince losing everything and his envied cousins restored.
hinduism.tie_back: Its conclusion matches the Kural's: envy raised no one, and those it targeted did not ultimately fall.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata (overall narrative; Shalya and Sauptika Parvas), Ganguli translation

christianity.quote_or_event: “Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the prodigal son, the father answers the elder brother, who resents the feast for his returned brother, that he has lost nothing.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural says the unenvious never lose prosperity; the father tells the envious son he never lacked anything to begin with.

islam.quote_or_event: People envy Qarun's great wealth, saying “Oh, would that we had like what was given to Qārūn.” After the earth swallows him, the same people say, “Oh, how Allāh extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it!”
islam.explanation: Those who envied Qarun's riches realize, after his destruction, that envying him would have brought them nothing but ruin.
islam.tie_back: The story teaches the Kural's lesson: envied prosperity was not real greatness, and envy leads nowhere.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And his brethren envied him; but his father observed the saying.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph's brothers envy him and sell him into slavery, yet Joseph rises to rule Egypt and they end up bowing before him.
judaism.tie_back: The envious brothers gained nothing by their envy, and the envied Joseph was not held down, as the Kural says.
judaism.source: Genesis 37:11 (KJV), with the narrative of Genesis 37-45

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where a woman or man is not envious. He/she does not envy, begrudge, or brood about others' gains, honor, respect, reverence, salutations, or veneration. ... he/she is influential wherever reborn.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that freedom from envy leads to good rebirth and to influence and standing in future lives.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the second half of the Kural: those free from envy never fall from greatness.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 135 (Cula-kammavibhanga Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “Censuring others, praising oneself, concealing good qualities present in others and proclaiming noble qualities absent in oneself, cause the influx (āsrava) of karmas which lead to low-status (nīcagotra).”
jainism.explanation: Jain karma theory holds that belittling others and hiding their merits, the habits of the envious, bind karma that brings low standing in future lives, while the next sutra (6.26) assigns high standing to the reverse disposition.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar concludes that no one ever grew great through envy, and the Tattvārtha makes it a law of karma that the envious habit of concealing others' virtues leads downward, never up.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.25, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One whose heart is filled with jealousy of others, never comes to any good.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das states flatly that a heart full of jealousy of others never prospers.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural closes by saying no one has ever grown great through envy; Guru Ram Das says the envious never come to any good.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 308, Raag Gauree (Gauri ki Vaar), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes the good Strife, under which a man seeing a rich neighbour works harder to plough, plant, and set his own house in order, and says “This Strife is wholesome for men,” unlike the destructive kind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Honest emulation, which works to match a neighbour's success rather than resent it, is what makes people prosper.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As the Kural says, prosperity comes to those without envy, not to the envious.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If another, then, paying fifty cents, takes the lettuce, and you, not paying it, go without them, don't imagine that he has gained any advantage over you. For as he has the lettuce, so you have the fifty cents which you did not give.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus argues that someone else's gain is never really your loss, so envy has no reason to exist.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers argue that envy never helps, and that one who does not envy loses nothing.

real_life_example.event_title: Alfred Russel Wallace, Darwin's greatest champion, is showered with honours
real_life_example.event: After the joint reading of 1858, Charles Darwin's name came to dominate the theory of natural selection that Alfred Russel Wallace had reached independently. The Natural History Museum notes that Wallace expressed no resentment and was Darwin's greatest supporter, and in 1889 he titled his own book on the theory Darwinism. Wallace rose to the highest ranks of science, receiving the Royal Society's Darwin Medal in 1890 and, in 1908, both its Copley Medal and the Order of Merit.
real_life_example.explanation: Wallace's lack of resentment did not cost him: he was honoured throughout his long life as a leading naturalist.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says no one free from envy has ever fallen from prosperity, and Wallace, who never begrudged Darwin his fame, received the highest honours of his day.

tamil:
நடுவின்றி நன்பொருள் வெஃகின் குடிபொன்றிக்
குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்.
transliteration:
Naduvindri nanporul vehkin kudiponrik
Kutramum aange tharum.
meaning: If you stop being fair and long to take someone else's good things, that greed will ruin your family and bring blame on you, right away.
elementary: Imagine wanting your classmate’s new bike so badly that you stop caring what is fair. This kural says that kind of wanting is like a crack in your own house: it doesn’t just get you in trouble, it hurts your whole family too.
university: The chapter opens with its thesis in its strongest form: covetousness (வெஃகுதல், vehkuthal) is condemned not only as an act of seizure but as a desire born of abandoning நடு (nadu), the equity or impartiality Valluvar had already exalted in chapter 12 (நடுவு நிலைமை). The consequences are twofold and immediate: the family line (குடி, kudi) is destroyed and guilt (குற்றம்) accrues, and the word ஆங்கே (aange, “right there, at that moment”) insists that the damage is not deferred to a future birth but arrives simultaneously with the desire. Parimelazhagar reads the kural as addressed to the householder, which explains why the penalty falls on the kudi: the covetous man betrays the very household he is supposed to sustain. The idea that injustice in acquisition corrodes the acquirer’s own house recurs across traditions, from the Hebrew story of Achan to Aristotle’s analysis of pleonexia as a vice of unfairness (anisotes).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Duryodhana, consumed by desire for the kingdom and wealth that rightfully belonged to his Pandava cousins, refused even a compromise of five villages. The war that followed at Kurukshetra annihilated his entire line of brothers, sons, and allies.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana coveted what was not his, ignored every appeal to fairness, and in the end his whole family was wiped out in the war he started to keep it.
