hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says unfair coveting destroys one’s own kudi (family line); the Mahabharata is the epic-scale illustration of exactly that.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva and Stri Parva (narrative)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns Timothy that the very desire to get rich is a trap that leads people into ruin.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates the danger in the desire itself and says it ends in destruction.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly but only [in lawful] business by mutual consent.” … “And whoever does that in aggression and injustice - then We will drive him into a Fire.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids taking other people’s wealth unfairly and warns of punishment for doing it out of injustice.
islam.tie_back: “Unjustly” is the Qur’anic equivalent of the Kural’s naduvindri (without fairness), and both attach guilt to it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight, then I coveted them, and took them.”
judaism.explanation: Achan confesses that he saw forbidden treasure, coveted it, and hid it in his tent. The narrative then records that he was executed together with his sons, daughters, livestock, and tent (Joshua 7:24-25).
judaism.tie_back: Almost a narrative enactment of the Kural: covet what is not yours, and your whole household is destroyed along with you.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Riches ruin only the foolish, not those in quest of the Beyond. By craving for riches the witless man ruins himself as well as others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that craving for wealth destroys not only the person who craves but also the people around him.
buddhism.tie_back: Same double damage as the Kural: the coveter harms himself and those connected to him.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Taking anything that is not given is stealing (steya).” Pūjyapāda adds: “It follows that activity actuated by impure dispositions is stealing (steya), whether external objects are taken or not.”
jainism.explanation: The third Jain vow, asteya, forbids taking what is not given, and the standard commentary extends the fault inward: a passion-driven reaching for another's property is already theft, even before anything is seized.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says merely setting one's heart on another's property brings ruin and guilt at once, and the Jain commentary agrees that the covetous disposition itself counts as stealing.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.15, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak tells both communities of his day that taking what belongs to someone else is as forbidden as their strongest dietary taboo.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that giving up fairness and setting one's heart on another's property brings ruin and guilt at once; Guru Nanak makes another person's rightful due the most forbidden thing of all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eriphyle, bribed with the golden necklace of Harmonia, sent her husband Amphiaraus to his death in the expedition against Thebes; her son Alcmaeon later killed her in revenge. Homer names her among the shades in the underworld as the woman who took gold as the price of her own husband.
greek_mythology.explanation: One woman’s desire for a precious necklace that was not hers set off a chain of death and revenge that destroyed her own family.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Covetousness for a “good thing” (nanporul) led directly to the ruin of the household, just as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 11 (Eriphyle among the shades); fuller story in later mythographers

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle defines the unjust man in the particular sense as “grasping” (pleonektes) and “unfair” (anisos): one who takes more than his share of goods at the expense of others.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, the vice of wanting more than your fair share is precisely what injustice is, and it is a defect of character, not just a bad act.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s link between grasping and unfairness mirrors the Kural’s link between coveting and loss of nadu (equity).

real_life_example.event_title: The fall and Siberian exile of Prince Menshikov
real_life_example.place: St Petersburg and Berezov (Beryozovo), Siberia, Russia
real_life_example.event: Aleksandr Menshikov, Peter the Great's closest associate, had been under almost continuous investigation for corrupt practices while helping to run the state, and after the death of Catherine I he was accused of abuses and embezzlement of state property. In September 1727 a decree of the young Emperor Peter II stripped him of all his offices, honours, titles and property, and he was exiled with his family to Berezov in Siberia. His wife died on the journey, a daughter died in exile in 1728, and Menshikov himself died there in 1729.
real_life_example.explanation: The most powerful man in Russia lost everything at a stroke, and his household shared his ruin.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that coveting what belongs to others brings ruin on one's family and guilt on oneself, and Menshikov's grasping at state wealth ended with his whole family in exile.

tamil:
படுபயன் வெஃகிப் பழிப்படுவ செய்யார்
நடுவன்மை நாணு பவர்.
transliteration:
Padupayan vehkip pazhippaduva seyyaar
Naduvanmai naanu pavar.
meaning: People who are ashamed to be unfair will never do shameful things just because they want the profit those things could bring.
elementary: Suppose you could win a game by quietly peeking at someone’s cards. A person who would feel embarrassed to cheat just won’t do it, even if it means winning. This kural says that feeling of shame protects you from doing wrong for a prize.
university: Where kural 171 threatened consequences, 172 names the internal safeguard: நாண் (naan), a moral sense of shame or modesty, here specifically shame at நடுவன்மை (naduvanmai, “non-equity”). The phrase படுபயன் (padupayan) denotes the gain that “falls” to one, the benefit that would accrue from taking another’s property, and பழிப்படுவ (pazhippaduva) are acts that incur public blame. Valluvar’s psychology is notable: the person of integrity is restrained less by fear of punishment than by an internalised aversion to injustice, a theme developed fully in chapter 102 (நாணுடைமை). This aligns with Gita ethics, in which modesty (Sanskrit hri) and the reflex of weighing gain against righteousness are marks of a mature moral agent.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…compassion and freedom from covetousness; gentleness, modesty and steady determination … these transcendental qualities, O son of Bharata, belong to godly men endowed with divine nature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the qualities of a divinely-natured person; two of them are freedom from covetousness (aloluptvam) and modesty, or a sense of shame at wrongdoing (hri).
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural pairs the same two things: shame at wrongdoing, and therefore no coveting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers that covetousness is so unfitting for holy people that it should not even be mentioned among them.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts appeal to a sense of what is fitting or shameful: good people recoil from covetousness itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly or send it [in bribery] to the rulers in order that [they might aid] you [to] consume a portion of the wealth of the people in sin, while you know [it is unlawful].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids scheming, including bribery, to get other people’s wealth, noting that people do this even while knowing it is wrong.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says the person with a conscience will not do blameworthy deeds for profit; the Qur’an names exactly those blameworthy schemes and forbids them.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, here I am: witness against me before the LORD, and before his anointed: whose ox have I taken? or whose ass have I taken? or whom have I defrauded? whom have I oppressed? or of whose hand have I received any bribe to blind mine eyes therewith?”
judaism.explanation: At the end of his career Samuel publicly challenges the people to name anything he took unjustly; no one can.
judaism.tie_back: Samuel is the portrait of the person the Kural describes: someone so ashamed of injustice that he never profited from it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is indeed virtuous, wise, and righteous who neither for his own sake nor for the sake of another (does any wrong), who does not crave for sons, wealth, or kingdom, and does not desire success by unjust means.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines the righteous person as someone who will not seek wealth or success through unjust means.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s statement: the righteous person does not pursue gain through injustice.

jainism.quote_or_event: Queen Kamalāvatī to King Ishukāra: “A man who returns, as it were, to the vomit, is not praised; but you want to confiscate the property left by the Brâhmaṇa. If the whole world and all treasures were yours, you would still not be satisfied, nor would all this be able to save you.”
jainism.explanation: When the king prepares to seize the estate abandoned by the family that renounced the world, the queen shames him by likening such greed to eating vomit, and the king himself then renounces.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those with a sense of shame at unfairness will not stoop to disgraceful acts for gain, and the queen's rebuke shows shame checking a king who was about to take another's property.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.38–39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They accept bribes, and block justice.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Ramkali ki Vaar, Guru Nanak condemns those who sit in judgment and make a show of piety, but sell justice for a bribe.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who feel shame at unfairness will never do disgraceful things for gain; Guru Nanak shows the shameless opposite, people who trade fairness for a bribe.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 951, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Do not get base gain: base gain is as bad as ruin.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother that dishonest profit is no profit at all; it is equivalent to disaster.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says the honourable will not do blameworthy deeds for gain; Hesiod gives the same rule in one line.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now, suppose a wise man had just such a ring, he would not imagine that he was free to do wrongly any more than if he did not have it; for good men aim to secure not secrecy but the right.”
philosophy.explanation: Retelling Plato’s story of Gyges’ ring of invisibility, Cicero argues that a good person would not use a guarantee of impunity to take what is not his, because what restrains him is the wrongness of the act and not fear of being found out.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s inner safeguard: the person who is ashamed of injustice turns down disgraceful gain even when nothing outside him would stop him.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book III, §38 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))

real_life_example.event_title: The insulin team sells its patent to the University of Toronto for one dollar each
real_life_example.event: After Frederick Banting, Charles Best, James Collip and their colleagues developed insulin at the University of Toronto, Banting objected to taking out patents and charging royalties for its manufacture. Banting, Best and Collip assigned their patent rights on insulin and its method of preparation to the University of Toronto for one dollar each, so that no one could secure a profitable private monopoly. The university then licensed manufacturers and used the royalties to fund further research.
real_life_example.explanation: The discoverers of a life-saving drug could have grown rich from it but chose to place it in public trust.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who feel shame at unfairness will not do disgraceful things for gain, and the insulin team refused to profit privately from the suffering of diabetic patients.

tamil:
சிற்றின்பம் வெஃகி அறனல்ல செய்யாரே
மற்றின்பம் வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Sitrinbam vehki aranalla seyyaare
Matrinbam vendu pavar.
meaning: People who want the other, lasting happiness will never do wrong just to grab a small pleasure that soon passes.
elementary: If you are saving your pocket money for something you really love, you won’t spend it on a cheap sweet that’s gone in a minute. This kural says people who want the big, lasting kind of happiness don’t do bad things for tiny, quick treats.
university: The kural sets up a contrast between சிற்றின்பம் (sitrinbam, “petty pleasure”) and மற்றின்பம் (matrinbam, “the other joy”). Parimelazhagar glosses the latter as the bliss of heaven or liberation, while modern commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan read it as the enduring happiness that flows from aram (virtue); either way, the argument is a rational trade-off, not a prohibition. Covetousness is foolish because it sacrifices a greater, lasting good for a trivial, fleeting one. This is among the most widely shared structures in world ethics: the Buddha’s ‘renounce the lesser happiness for the greater’, Nachiketas refusing Death’s riches, and Socrates rebuking Athens for preferring money to the soul all have the same shape.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “These things last till tomorrow, O Death, for they wear out this vigour of all the senses.” … “No man can be made happy by wealth.”
hinduism.explanation: When Death offers the boy Nachiketas cattle, gold, long life, and a kingdom to stop him asking about the Self, Nachiketas refuses: such pleasures do not last and cannot truly satisfy.
hinduism.tie_back: Nachiketas is the Kural’s model: he wants the ‘other joy’ and so will not trade it for small, passing pleasures.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts earthly treasure, which decays and can be stolen, with heavenly treasure, which lasts.
christianity.tie_back: Same contrast of a perishable lesser good against an imperishable greater one.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not extend your eyes toward that by which We have given enjoyment to [some] categories of them, [its being but] the splendor of worldly life by which We test them. And the provision of your Lord is better and more enduring.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the believer not to look longingly at the worldly enjoyments of others, because God’s provision is better and lasts longer.
islam.tie_back: An almost exact match: don’t covet others’ passing pleasures, because the other joy is better and more enduring.

judaism.quote_or_event: “More precious is one hour in repentance and good deeds in this world, than all the life of the world to come; And more precious is one hour of the tranquility of the world to come, than all the life of this world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah weighs this world’s pleasures against the world to come, and says one hour of that tranquility outweighs a whole lifetime here.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures worldly pleasure against a far greater joy that makes the smaller one not worth sinning for.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If by renouncing a lesser happiness one may realize a greater happiness, let the wise man renounce the lesser, having regard for the greater.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the wise to give up small pleasures when doing so leads to a far greater happiness.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s sitrinbam/matrinbam argument almost word for word.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasures bring only a moment's happiness, but suffering for a very long time, intense suffering, but slight happiness; they are an obstacle to the liberation from existence, and are a very mine of evils.”
jainism.explanation: The two sons of the priest Bhṛgu refuse their father's offer of wealth and pleasures, explaining that momentary enjoyment costs long suffering and blocks the lasting goal of liberation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who seek the other, lasting joy will not do wrong for a petty, passing pleasure, and the Jain verse sets the same contrast between a moment's pleasure and the enduring good of liberation.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Baba, the pleasures of other foods are false.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that sensual enjoyments pursued for their own sake lead to ruin, while the true joy lies in the Lord's Name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who seek the lasting joy will not do wrong for a small passing pleasure; Guru Nanak likewise calls such pleasures false compared with lasting delight in God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stranded on Thrinacia, Odysseus’ starving crew ignored his warning and slaughtered the sacred cattle of Helios for a feast. Zeus destroyed their ship and every one of them lost the homecoming they had struggled ten years to reach.
greek_mythology.explanation: The sailors took something that was not theirs for a few days of feasting and lost their lives and their return home.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They traded the ‘other joy’ (homecoming) for a petty, unlawful pleasure, exactly what the Kural says the wise never do.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “O my friend, why do you who are a citizen of the great and mighty and wise city of Athens, care so much about laying up the greatest amount of money and honor and reputation, and so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul?”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells his jury that he spends his life challenging people who chase money while neglecting the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates, like Valluvar, calls it a bad trade to chase lesser goods at the expense of the greater one.

real_life_example.event_title: Bobby Jones calls a penalty on himself at the U.S. Open
real_life_example.place: Worcester Country Club, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States
real_life_example.event: During the first round of the 1925 U.S. Open, the amateur golfer Bobby Jones's club moved his ball slightly as he addressed it on the 11th hole. No official, playing partner or spectator saw it, but Jones reported it and took a one-stroke penalty. He finished the 72 holes tied with Willie Macfarlane and lost the title in a playoff.
real_life_example.explanation: Jones gave up a national championship rather than take an advantage no one else would have known about, and his integrity became part of golf's tradition.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who seek lasting joy will not do wrong for a small passing gain, and Jones preferred his honour to a title won unfairly.

tamil:
இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார் புலம்வென்ற
புன்மையில் காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Ilamendru vehkuthal seyyaar pulamvendra
Punmaiyil kaatchi yavar.
meaning: People who see clearly and have control over their senses will not long for what belongs to others, even when they think, “We are poor and have nothing.”
elementary: It is easy not to want your friend’s lunch when you already have a big one. This kural is about someone who is really hungry and still doesn’t take what isn’t theirs, because they’ve trained themselves to be strong inside.
university: This kural removes the most sympathetic excuse for covetousness: need. இலம் என்று (ilam endru, “saying ‘we have nothing’”) captures the self-justifying thought of the poor, and Valluvar insists that even this does not license desire for another’s goods among those who are புலம் வென்ற (pulam venra, “sense-conquered”) and of புன்மையில் காட்சி (punmaiyil kaatchi, “vision free from meanness”). The pairing of sense-mastery with non-covetousness is characteristically Indian (compare the Gita’s sthitaprajna), but the insistence that integrity must survive poverty is universal, as Agur’s prayer in Proverbs attests. Valluvar is not romanticising poverty; he is arguing that virtue that fails under pressure was never virtue.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is able to withdraw his senses from sense objects, as the tortoise draws his limbs within the shell, is to be understood as truly situated in knowledge.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the steady-minded sage as someone who can pull his senses back from their objects the way a tortoise pulls in its limbs.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s pulam venra (sense-conquered) person is exactly this tortoise-like sage, who is not pulled toward others’ goods even in want.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound … both to abound and to suffer need.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he has learned to be content whether he has plenty or is going without.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s sage, Paul’s contentment doesn’t collapse when he is poor.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Charity is] for the poor who have been restricted for the cause of Allah … An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint … They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises poor people whose self-restraint is so great that outsiders think they are well-off, since they do not press others for what they have.
islam.tie_back: These are the Kural’s people: genuinely poor, yet with such restraint that they reach for nothing that belongs to others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me: Lest I be full, and deny thee … or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.”
judaism.explanation: Agur asks God to spare him from poverty precisely because he knows poverty tempts people to take what isn’t theirs.
judaism.tie_back: Proverbs names the very temptation the Kural addresses (poverty as an excuse to take), though it asks to be spared the test instead of praising those who pass it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says contentment itself is the greatest wealth, so someone who has it is never truly poor.
buddhism.tie_back: This is why the Kural’s sage does not covet even in want: his real wealth is his contentment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means. Though two mâshas would do to supply your want, still you would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.”
jainism.explanation: In the commentary's frame story, the poor student Kapila set out to earn two pieces of gold; offered any wish by the king, he kept raising his demand until he saw what was happening, renounced on the spot and spoke this verse.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who have mastered their senses will not covet others' goods even when they think 'we have nothing', and Kapila, a needy man, saw through his own rising craving and gave it up.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 8.17, with Jacobi's note summarizing the commentary's story of Kapila (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, if you see someone else's buttered bread, do not envy him for it.”
sikhism.explanation: In this salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sufi Sheikh Farid tells the person of plain means to be content with simple fare and not to hanker after the richer bread on another's plate.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the self-mastered will not covet others' goods even when they think, we are poor; Farid gives the same counsel to the poor man looking at a richer table.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 29 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Fools! They know not how much more the half is than the whole, nor what great advantage there is in mallow and asphodel.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod mocks greedy men who don’t realise that a modest share, even the poor man’s simple food of mallow and asphodel, is worth more than grabbing everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts honour the person who can live on little without reaching for more.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Not even the impudence of my accusers dares to say that I have ever exacted or sought pay of anyone; they have no witness of that. And I have a witness of the truth of what I say; my poverty is a sufficient witness.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial Socrates points to his own poverty as proof that, despite years of teaching, he never took money from anyone, and he had earlier said he lived in utter poverty because of his devotion to the god.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates is the Kural’s person of clear vision who stays poor but does not reach for what is not his.

real_life_example.event_title: Thomas Paine gives up the profits of Common Sense
real_life_example.event: Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense, published in January 1776, sold in enormous numbers and helped turn American opinion toward independence. Paine declined royalties after the first printing so that the pamphlet could be sold cheaply and reprinted freely, and gave his profits to buy mittens for Continental troops. By the end of the Revolution he was penniless and had to ask Congress for reimbursement of his expenses.
real_life_example.explanation: Paine, a man of modest means, chose not to enrich himself from the most successful publication of the age.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the self-mastered do not covet others' wealth even when they think themselves poor, and Paine stayed poor rather than take wealth from his cause.

tamil:
அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவென்னாம் யார்மாட்டும்
வெஃகி வெறிய செயின்.
transliteration:
Ahki akandra arivennaam yaarmaattum
Vehki veriya seyin.
meaning: What good is a sharp and wide-ranging mind if its owner wants other people's things and acts foolishly toward anyone at all?
elementary: Imagine the smartest kid in class who uses their brains to trick friends out of their toys. Being clever doesn’t make that okay; it just makes the cleverness useless. This kural says being smart means nothing if greed makes you act foolishly.
university: The first line is a small masterpiece of sound and sense: அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு (ahki akandra arivu) describes knowledge that is at once narrowed to a fine point (ahku, ‘to become subtle/minute’) and broadened (akal, ‘to spread wide’), in other words both deep and wide. The rhetorical question ‘என்னாம்?’ (ennaam, ‘of what use?’) then cancels that learning entirely if its possessor, driven by covetousness, does வெறிய (veriya, senseless or improper deeds) toward யார்மாட்டும் (yaarmaattum, ‘anyone whatsoever’). The kural anticipates the chapter on learning (40-43) by insisting that intellect is not a moral safeguard; covetousness can hijack it. The Gita’s chain of desire, anger, delusion, and ‘loss of intelligence’ and Plato’s image of reason enslaved to money-making make the same diagnosis.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From anger, delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost, one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Continuing the previous verse (2.62, where attachment breeds desire and desire breeds anger), Krishna traces how unchecked desire ends by destroying the intellect itself.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s point exactly: however great your intelligence, covetous desire can make it useless.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that even total knowledge is worth nothing without love.
christianity.tie_back: Same rhetorical structure as the Kural (‘what use is all knowledge if…?’), although Paul’s condition is lack of love rather than presence of greed.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an compares people who carry knowledge but do not live by it to a donkey loaded with books it cannot use.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares learning useless when conduct contradicts it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids judges to take bribes because the desire for gain blinds even wise people.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts warn that desire for another’s wealth disables even the sharpest mind.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To his own ruin the fool gains knowledge, for it cleaves his head and destroys his innate goodness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that knowledge in the hands of someone without virtue works against him and destroys his goodness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts insist that intelligence alone cannot save someone whose conduct is bad.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Knowledge without right conduct, acceptance of the asceticism without right faith and observance of austerities without self-control are all futile.”
jainism.explanation: Jainism's three jewels must go together: learning that is not joined to right conduct does not lead to liberation and is counted worthless.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks what use a deep and wide intellect is if its owner covets others' goods and acts senselessly, and the Jain verse likewise calls knowledge without right conduct futile.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam, verse 210 (Ratnatrayasutra; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If an educated person is a sinner, then the illiterate holy man is not to be punished.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak teaches that learning does not save a person who does wrong, while a simple person who lives rightly does not suffer for lacking it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use a sharp and wide mind is if its owner covets and acts senselessly; Guru Nanak likewise holds that learning is worth nothing without right conduct.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Erysichthon, wanting timber for his banquet hall, cut down Demeter’s sacred grove despite every warning. Demeter cursed him with insatiable hunger; he devoured his fortune, sold his own daughter, and at last consumed his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: A king with every advantage let greed for what was sacred and not his drive him into total madness and self-destruction.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Erysichthon shows the Kural’s veriya (senseless) conduct: greed turns a powerful man’s judgment into madness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s account of the oligarchic man, the money-loving part of the soul is set on the throne, and reason is made to sit at its feet, permitted only to calculate how more money can be made.
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes a person whose intelligence is still working but is now just a servant of his desire for wealth.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s diagnosis precisely: a sharp, wide intellect made worthless by covetousness.

real_life_example.event_title: The arrest of Nicolas Fouquet after the fete at Vaux-le-Vicomte
real_life_example.event: Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's superintendent of finances and a cultivated patron of writers and artists, built the magnificent chateau of Vaux-le-Vicomte and entertained the king there with a lavish fete on 17 August 1661. On 5 September 1661 he was arrested at Nantes by d'Artagnan and charged with embezzlement of public funds. After a trial lasting about three years the judges voted for banishment, but the king changed the sentence to life imprisonment, and Fouquet died in the fortress of Pignerol in 1680.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the most brilliant and refined men in France ended his life in prison because of the way he had enriched himself from state funds.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use a subtle and broad mind is if its owner covets others' goods, and Fouquet's taste and talent could not save him once he was charged with taking public money.

tamil:
அருள்வெஃகி ஆற்றின்கண் நின்றான் பொருள்வெஃகிப்
பொல்லாத சூழக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Arulvehki aatrinkan nindraan porulvehkip
Pollaadha soozhak kedum.
meaning: Even someone who wants to be kind and has stayed on the right path will be ruined if they start wanting others' riches and plotting evil ways to get them.
elementary: Think of a kid who has always been kind and helpful. If one day they start scheming to take someone else’s things, all that goodness can come crashing down. This kural says no one is so good that greed can’t ruin them.
university: The kural turns on a deliberate repetition: the same verb வெஃகு (vehku, ‘to desire’) is used for the noble desire for அருள் (arul, grace/compassion) and the base desire for பொருள் (porul, wealth). The same faculty of longing can be aimed upward or downward, and a person who has aimed it well can still redirect it disastrously. ஆற்றின்கண் நின்றான் (aatrinkan nindraan, ‘one who stood in the path’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the householder’s path by which grace is attained, and more broadly by modern commentators as the path of virtue; பொல்லாத சூழ (pollaadha soozha) stresses that plotting is itself ruinous, even before any theft. The kural is a warning against spiritual complacency, echoed in the Gita’s admission that the senses carry away even a striving sage, and in the Qur’anic portrait of the man raised by signs who ‘adhered to the earth’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The senses are so strong and impetuous, O Arjuna, that they forcibly carry away the mind even of a man of discrimination who is endeavoring to control them.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that even a wise person who is actively striving can be carried off by desire.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural warns the same: one who has stood on the path of grace can still be ruined by desire for wealth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that some who were once in the faith coveted money, wandered away, and brought great pain on themselves.
christianity.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: people already on the path of faith were ruined by coveting.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if We had willed, we could have elevated him thereby, but he adhered [instead] to the earth and followed his own desire. So his example is like that of the dog: if you chase him, he pants, or if you leave him, he [still] pants.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells of a man who had been given God’s signs and could have been raised high by them, but he clung to worldly things and followed his desire.
islam.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s fallen seeker: someone given grace who throws it away for worldly desire.
islam.source: Qur’an 7:176 (Sahih International; the account begins at 7:175)

judaism.quote_or_event: “But Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, Behold, my master hath spared Naaman this Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought: but, as the LORD liveth, I will run after him, and take somewhat of him.”
judaism.explanation: Gehazi, the servant of the prophet Elisha, schemed to get the gifts his master had refused, lied to cover it, and was struck with leprosy (2 Kings 5:27).
judaism.tie_back: Gehazi lived in a prophet’s household (on the path of grace), coveted another’s wealth, plotted deceit to get it, and was ruined, just as the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is one who, turning away from desire (for household life) takes to the life of the forest (i.e., of a monk). But after being freed from the household, he runs back to it. Behold that man! Though freed, he runs back to that very bondage!”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes someone who had renounced worldly desire but then ran back to it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes the person already on the path who returns to worldly desire and loses what was gained.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When suppressed, passion can bring about the spiritual degeneration of even the most virtuous monk, who in his conduct is akin to Jina himself, what can we say of monks who are under the sway of attachment?”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching warns that passions (kaṣāya), greed among them, merely held down rather than destroyed can bring down even a monk whose conduct resembles a Jina's.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says even one who has longed for grace and stood on virtue's path will be ruined once he covets others' wealth, and the Jain verse warns that passion can make even the most virtuous fall.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam, verse 132 (Samyamasutra; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The man-eaters say their prayers.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak mocks officials who devour people through bribery and oppression while still keeping up the forms of prayer and piety.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that even one who has stood on the path of virtue is ruined once he covets others' wealth and plots to get it; Guru Nanak shows such outward piety emptied by greed.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, so favoured by the gods that he dined at their table, stole their nectar and ambrosia to share with mortals, and was cast down to eternal punishment in the underworld.
greek_mythology.explanation: Someone admitted to the gods’ own company threw it all away by taking what was not his.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s seeker who stood on the path of grace, Tantalus had divine favour and lost it through coveting and theft.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the myth of the Ring of Gyges, a shepherd who finds a ring of invisibility uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king, and seize the kingdom. Glaucon argues that even a supposedly just man would do the same if he could act with impunity.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the story to ask whether anyone’s goodness would survive the chance to take whatever they wanted without consequence.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural answers Glaucon’s challenge: even the person who seemed to stand on the path will be ruined if he lets covetousness plot for him.

real_life_example.event_title: Televangelist Jim Bakker is convicted of fraud
real_life_example.event: Jim Bakker built the PTL television ministry into a large religious enterprise that included the Heritage USA resort in South Carolina. Prosecutors showed that he had sold far more lifetime partnerships, promising yearly lodging at the resort, than could ever be honoured, and diverted the money to other uses. In October 1989 a federal jury convicted him on all 24 counts of fraud and conspiracy, and he was sentenced to 45 years in prison, later reduced; he served almost five years.
real_life_example.explanation: A preacher who had led a large ministry lost his ministry, his freedom and his reputation through greed for his followers' money.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says even one who has stood on the path of virtue and grace will be ruined if he covets others' wealth, and Bakker's fall from ministry to prison shows exactly that.

tamil:
வேண்டற்க வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம் விளைவயின்
மாண்டற் கரிதாம் பயன்.
transliteration:
Vendarka vehkiyaam aakkam vilaivayin
Maandar karithaam payan.
meaning: Do not wish for riches that come from wanting what belongs to others. When those riches finally bear fruit, the result is hardly ever good.
elementary: It’s like planting a seed you stole from your neighbour’s garden. It might grow, but the fruit tastes bitter because you know how you got it. This kural says wealth you got by grabbing others’ things never gives you a truly good harvest.
university: The kural uses an agricultural metaphor: வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம் (vehkiyaam aakkam, ‘increase that comes through coveting’) is a crop, and விளைவயின் (vilaivayin, ‘at the time of its ripening’) its fruit is மாண்டற்கு அரிது (maandarku arithu, ‘hard to be excellent’). The argument concerns delayed consequences: ill-gotten gain may look like prosperity at first, but its maturation reveals its true nature. Some commentators (e.g., Solomon Pappaiah) read maandal as ‘goodness’ in enjoyment, while others read it as ‘glory’; either way the gain proves hollow. The theme of sweet-at-first, bitter-at-the-end fruit links this kural to the Gita’s account of rajasic happiness and to Proverbs’ ‘bread of deceit.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That happiness which is derived from contact of the senses with their objects and which appears like nectar at first but poison at the end is said to be of the nature of passion.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes pleasures of passion (rajas) as sweet at first but poisonous once they have run their course.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same of covetous gain: it looks good at first, but its ripened fruit is bad.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, a rich man plans bigger barns for his harvest, but he dies that night and never enjoys any of it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that gain pursued through greed does not bear good fruit when the time comes.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Hakim! This property is like a sweet fresh fruit; whoever takes it without greediness, he is blessed in it, and whoever takes it with greediness, he is not blessed in it, and he is like a person who eats but is never satisfied.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Hakim ibn Hizam that wealth taken with greed carries no blessing and never satisfies.
islam.tie_back: Almost the same image as the Kural: wealth is a fruit, and when greed is how you get it, the fruit is not good.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says that what you gain dishonestly tastes sweet at first but later turns to gravel in your mouth.
judaism.tie_back: The same arc as the Kural’s ripened fruit: sweet at first, bad when it matures.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no satisfying sensual desires, even with the rain of gold coins. For sensual pleasures give little satisfaction and much pain.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says even a rain of gold could not satisfy desire, and what it brings is more pain than pleasure.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says gain chased by craving yields little good and much harm.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasures are the thorn that rankles, pleasures are poison, pleasures are like a venomous snake; he who is desirous of pleasures will not get them, and will come to a bad end at last.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami tells Indra, who has urged him to multiply his gold and treasury, that grasping after objects of desire ends badly however good it looks at first.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says gain born of coveting will rarely ripen into good fruit, and Nami likewise says the one who covets pleasures comes to a bad end at last.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.53 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “For the sake of this wealth, so many were ruined; because of this wealth, so many have been disgraced.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn on the devastation of Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak reflects that wealth gathered and fought over has brought ruin and disgrace on many.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that prosperity won by coveting rarely bears good fruit when it ripens; Guru Nanak shows that harvest of ruin and disgrace.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asked Dionysus that everything he touched should turn to gold. His wish was granted, but his bread and wine turned to metal as he tried to eat, and he begged the god to take the gift back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas got exactly the riches he craved, and they turned out to be useless, even deadly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s point in myth: greedy gain, once it ‘ripens’, gives no good fruit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes those who take gain from shameful sources, such as petty extortion or exploiting others, as displaying ‘sordid love of gain’ (aischrokerdeia): they endure reproach for the sake of gain, and small gain at that.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that people who profit dishonourably earn disgrace, not honour, and the profit is small anyway.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s maandarku arithu: such gain rarely yields anything excellent or honourable.

real_life_example.event_title: Cicero prosecutes Verres for plundering Sicily
real_life_example.event: Gaius Verres, Roman governor of Sicily from 73 to 71 BCE, exploited the province ruthlessly, seizing money and art from its people. The Sicilians asked Cicero to prosecute him, and in 70 BCE Cicero gathered evidence across the island and opened the case with such force that Verres' defender, Hortensius, abandoned the defence. Before the hearing of evidence was over, Verres left Rome for exile in Massilia (Marseille), was condemned in his absence, and spent the rest of his life in exile.
real_life_example.explanation: The fortune Verres extracted from Sicily brought him not enjoyment but disgrace and a lifetime of exile, and Cicero's speeches made his name a byword for corruption.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that wealth gained by coveting seldom bears good fruit when it ripens, and Verres' plunder ripened into ruin and exile.

tamil:
அஃகாமை செல்வத்திற்கு யாதெனின் வெஃகாமை
வேண்டும் பிறன்கைப் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Ahkaamai selvaththirku yaadhenin vehkaamai
Vendum pirankaip porul.
meaning: If you ask what keeps your riches from shrinking, the answer is this: do not want the things that are in someone else's hands.
elementary: If you want to keep your own toys safe, the best rule is never to grab other people’s toys. Then no one has a reason to take yours, and you stay happy with what you have. This kural says not wanting other people’s things is the secret to keeping your own.
university: The kural is built on a pun that is lost in translation: அஃகாமை (ahkaamai, ‘non-diminishing’) and வெஃகாமை (vehkaamai, ‘non-coveting’) differ by a single consonant, so the grammar of the line enacts its claim that the one secures the other. It is framed as a riddle with its own answer (‘yaadhenin…’, ‘if one asks what…’), a didactic device Valluvar uses often. பிறன் கைப் பொருள் (piran kaip porul, ‘property in another’s hand’) pointedly includes even possessions casually within reach. The ethical logic is both moral and practical: a society in which people do not covet is one in which everyone’s wealth is secure, and a mind that does not covet does not feel its own wealth as insufficient. The kural thus unites the tenth commandment’s social function with the Upanishadic ‘do not covet’ as a spiritual discipline.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “ALL this, whatsoever moves on earth, is to be hidden in the Lord (the Self). When thou hast surrendered all this, then thou mayest enjoy. Do not covet the wealth of any man!”
hinduism.explanation: The Isha Upanishad’s first verse says everything belongs to the Lord; enjoy what is given in that spirit, and do not covet anyone’s wealth.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Do not covet the wealth of any man’ is the Kural’s vehkaamai in the Upanishad’s own words, presented as the basis of rightful enjoyment.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews tells believers to live free of covetousness and be content, because God will never abandon them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties freedom from coveting to the security of what one has.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah of his bounty.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says not to long for what others have been given, but to keep to your own earned share and ask God for more.
islam.tie_back: Same prescription as the Kural: don’t desire what is in another’s hand; your own share is secure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s.”
judaism.explanation: The tenth commandment (lo tachmod) forbids even the inner desire for anything that belongs to one’s neighbour.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Any thing that is thy neighbour’s’ is the Kural’s piran kaip porul, the property in another’s hand.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the fortune of a person of pure, self-controlled, righteous conduct keeps increasing.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links pure, restrained conduct to prosperity that does not decline.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.” And: “One ought to put an end to anger through calmness, pride by modesty, deceit by straight-forwardness and greed by contentment.”
jainism.explanation: This Saman Suttam couplet (a rendering of Daśavaikālika 8.38) ranks greed as the passion that ruins everything, and prescribes contentment (santoṣa) as its cure.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the way to keep one's wealth from dwindling is not to covet another's, and the Jain verses agree that greed destroys everything while contentment overcomes it.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam, verses 135–136 (Samyamasutra; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com); cf. Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.38

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak names kirat karni (honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing) as the true path, in place of living off what belongs to others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one's wealth is kept from dwindling by not coveting what is in another's hands; Guru Nanak's answer is to live on one's own honest labour and share it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In his elegy to the Muses, Solon prays for wealth but refuses to acquire it unjustly: wealth the gods give stays with a man secure from bottom to top, while wealth men chase through outrage (hubris) comes unwillingly and is soon mixed with ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: Solon says that justly gained wealth lasts, while wealth gained by overreaching brings destruction.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Same claim as the Kural: not grasping at what is not yours is what keeps your wealth from dwindling.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Is anything brought around to you? Put out your hand and take your share with moderation. Does it pass by you? Don’t stop it. Is it not yet come? Don’t stretch your desire towards it, but wait till it reaches you. Do this with regard to children, to a wife, to public posts, to riches…”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus compares life to a dinner party: take your own portion politely and don’t reach for dishes that belong to others or haven’t come to you yet.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s rule in Stoic form: do not reach for what is in another’s hand.

real_life_example.event_title: The failure of the Darien scheme
real_life_example.place: Darien, Isthmus of Panama, and Scotland
real_life_example.event: Between 1698 and 1700 the Company of Scotland sent expeditions to found a Scottish colony and trading centre at Darien on the Isthmus of Panama, a region claimed by Spain. The venture collapsed amid disease, Spanish resistance and lack of English support, costing about 2,000 lives. National Museums Scotland estimates that Scotland lost a quarter of its liquid capital, and the National Library of Scotland notes that the loss is thought to have hastened the Union with England in 1707.
real_life_example.explanation: A nation staked a large share of its wealth on seizing a foothold in land others claimed, and the loss shook its economy and independence.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the way to keep one's wealth from dwindling is not to covet what is in another's hands, and Scotland's grab for Spanish-claimed land drained its wealth instead.

tamil:
அறனறிந்து வெஃகா அறிவுடையார்ச் சேரும்
திறன்அறிந் தாங்கே திரு.
transliteration:
Aranarindhu vehkaa arivudaiyaarch serum
Thiranarin thaange thiru.
meaning: The goddess of good fortune knows the worth of wise people who understand what is right and do not want others' things, and she finds her own way to them.
elementary: Imagine good luck as a friend who likes visiting kind, honest people. This kural says if you know what’s right and don’t try to take other people’s things, good fortune will find its way to your door by itself.
university: திரு (thiru), glossed by all traditional commentators as Lakshmi (Thirumagal), the goddess of fortune, is here personified as an agent with judgment: திறன் அறிந்து (thiran arindhu) means she ‘knows the proper way’ or ‘recognises their merit’ and arrives ஆங்கே (aange, ‘right there’). The kural thus reverses the covetous logic: the coveter reaches for wealth and loses it, while the one who does not reach is sought out by wealth itself. Parimelazhagar’s gloss emphasises that these people are அறிவுடையார் (arivudaiyaar) who know aram, so their restraint is a considered moral choice, not mere passivity. The idea that virtue attracts prosperity has close analogues in the Gita’s closing verse (where ‘sri’ accompanies righteousness), Socrates’ ‘from virtue come money and every other good’, and the Buddhist teaching that the righteous non-coveter may reappear among those of ‘great property’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Wherever there is Krsna, the master of all mystics, and wherever there is Arjuna, the supreme archer, there will also certainly be opulence, victory, extraordinary power, and morality.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita ends with Sanjaya declaring that where righteousness is, there Sri (fortune) will be too.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say Sri, fortune, goes to the side of righteousness; the Gita even uses the same goddess-word.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his listeners to seek righteousness first rather than chase material things, and those things will be given to them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s reversal: don’t grasp at wealth, pursue virtue, and provision will come to you.

islam.quote_or_event: “And will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah - then He is sufficient for him.”
islam.explanation: Continuing 65:2 (‘whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out’), the Qur’an promises that the God-conscious will be provided for from unexpected sources.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, provision comes to the righteous of its own accord rather than through their grasping.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says real wealth comes from God’s blessing, and that kind of wealth carries no sorrow with it.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say prosperity is given to the righteous rather than seized by them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Here someone is not covetous: he is not a coveter of another’s chattels and property thus: ‘Oh, that what is another’s were mine!’” … “If a householder who observes conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct, should wish: ‘Oh, that … I might reappear in the company of the warrior-nobles of great property!’ it is possible…”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names non-covetousness as part of righteous conduct and says such a righteous householder can gain rebirth among people of great wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s pairing: the one who does not covet another’s property is the one to whom prosperity comes.

jainism.quote_or_event: After King Nami refused to multiply his treasury, Śakra (Indra) dropped his disguise and praised him: “Bravo! you have conquered anger; bravo! you have vanquished pride; bravo! you have banished delusion; bravo! you have subdued greed.”
jainism.explanation: The king of the gods, who had tested Nami by urging wealth and conquest on him, comes in his true form to honour the one who desired nothing, then pays him reverence and departs.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar pictures Fortune seeking out the wise who do not covet, and in the Jain story it is the king of gods himself who comes to honour the sage who has subdued greed.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.55–56 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Maya is the slave of the Lord's devotees; it works for them.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that worldly wealth, which enslaves the grasping, comes to serve those who are devoted to God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says fortune seeks out, of her own accord, the wise who do not covet; Guru Amar Das says worldly wealth becomes the servant of the devoted.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 231, Raag Gauree, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor elderly couple, gladly shared their meagre food with disguised gods whom richer neighbours had turned away. Zeus and Hermes turned their hut into a temple, made them its priests, and granted their wish to die together.
greek_mythology.explanation: A poor couple who didn’t grasp at anything, and shared what little they had, were richly rewarded by the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s Thiru, divine favour sought out the humble and virtuous rather than those who grasped.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue come money and every other good of man, public as well as private.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says virtue doesn’t come from wealth; it is the other way round, and every good, including wealth, comes from virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s claim in philosophical form: virtue comes first, and fortune follows it.

real_life_example.event_title: American women give Marie Curie a gram of radium
real_life_example.place: The White House, Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: Marie Curie had deliberately chosen not to patent radium or its medical uses, and by 1920 its high price left her without enough for her own research in Paris. The journalist Marie Meloney organised a fund among American women that raised the money to buy a gram of radium for her. On 20 May 1921 President Warren G. Harding presented the gift to Curie at the White House on behalf of the women of America.
real_life_example.explanation: Curie had refused to profit from her discovery, and the resources she needed came to her unasked through the gratitude of others.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says fortune recognises the worth of those who do not covet and seeks them out of her own accord, and the radium Curie would not profit from came to her as a gift.

tamil:
இறலீனும் எண்ணாது வெஃகின் விறல்ஈனும்
வேண்டாமை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Iraleenum ennaadhu vehkin viraleenum
Vendaamai ennum serukku.
meaning: Wanting others’ things without thinking about the result leads to ruin. The great strength of not wanting them leads to victory.
elementary: Grabbing for something that isn’t yours without thinking is like reaching into a fire: you get burned. But being strong enough to say “I don’t need that” is like winning a race. This kural says not wanting is a kind of superpower.
university: The chapter closes with a perfectly balanced antithesis built on a rhyme: இறல் ஈனும் (iral eenum, ‘gives birth to destruction’) against விறல் ஈனும் (viral eenum, ‘gives birth to victory’). The verb ஈன் (een, ‘to bear, as offspring’) makes both outcomes the natural children of their causes. எண்ணாது (ennaadhu, ‘without reflecting’) identifies thoughtlessness about consequences as the root of covetousness, while வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு (vendaamai ennum serukku) calls non-desire a kind of செருக்கு (serukku, ‘pride, exaltation, greatness’). Valluvar reclaims a word usually negative and makes it the dignity of the person who needs nothing from others. The idea that restraint is itself a victory appears in Epictetus, in the Qur’anic promise of success to those saved from their own avarice, and in the Buddhist ‘craving-freed’ who vanquishes all suffering.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell-lust, anger, and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names greed (lobha) as one of three gates to self-destruction and says every sensible person should abandon it.
hinduism.tie_back: Matches the destructive half of the Kural (iral eenum): unreflective greed gives birth to ruin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But godliness with contentment is great gain.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says the real profit in life is godliness combined with contentment.
christianity.tie_back: The positive half of the Kural: not wanting is itself a gain and a victory. The surrounding verses (6:9-10) supply the destructive half.

islam.quote_or_event: “…and find not any want in their breasts of what the emigrants were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the people of Madinah who felt no craving for what others received, and says those protected from their own greed (shuhh) are the successful ones.
islam.tie_back: Close to the Kural’s viral eenum: freedom from inner craving is what yields success and victory.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that hasteth to be rich hath an evil eye, and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says someone in a greedy rush to get rich doesn’t stop to consider that it will bring him to ruin.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ennaadhu (without thinking) is Proverbs’ ‘considereth not’; both say thoughtless greed leads to ruin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The gift of Dhamma excels all gifts; the taste of the Dhamma excels all tastes; the delight in Dhamma excels all delights. The Craving-Freed vanquishes all suffering.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the person free of craving conquers all suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: Victory through non-desire: the Buddhist version of the Kural’s viral eenum vendaamai.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though a man should conquer thousands and thousands of valiant (foes), greater will be his victory if he conquers nobody but himself.”
jainism.explanation: Asked by Indra to subdue rival princes, King Nami replies that victory over one's own self, including the greed he goes on to name, is greater than any outward conquest.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ends by saying that the proud strength of not wanting gives birth to victory, and Nami's teaching names that very self-mastery the greatest victory.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.34 (cf. 9.36) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir sets greed against forgiveness: one leads to spiritual death, the other is where God dwells.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's closing antithesis says coveting gives birth to destruction while the strength of not wanting gives birth to victory; Kabir draws the same contrast between greed and death on one side and the divine presence on the other.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir, Salok 155 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “…as often happens when gain deceives men’s sense and dishonour tramples down honour, the gods soon blot him out and make that man’s house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that a man who seizes wealth when greed clouds his judgment is soon destroyed by the gods, and the wealth doesn’t last.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s iral eenum ennaadhu vehkin: coveting without thought brings destruction.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…bring to your mind both points of time: that in which you will enjoy the pleasure, and that in which you will repent and reproach yourself after you have enjoyed it; and set before you, in opposition to these, how you will be glad and applaud yourself if you abstain … how much better it is to be conscious of having gained so great a victory.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus advises weighing what comes after giving in to a desire against the joy of holding back, and calls holding back a great victory.
philosophy.tie_back: Both halves of the Kural: think of the consequences (the opposite of ennaadhu), and see that abstaining is a victory (viral).

real_life_example.event_title: The Athenian expedition to Sicily ends in disaster
real_life_example.event: In 415 BCE Athens, answering an appeal from Segesta and hoping to extend its power over Sicily, sent a great fleet and army against Syracuse, over the objections of the general Nicias. Syracuse, reinforced by Sparta and Corinth, held out, and in 413 BCE the Athenians lost the decisive naval battle in the harbour of Syracuse. The retreating army surrendered, the generals Nicias and Demosthenes were executed, and Thucydides records that at least 7,000 prisoners were taken.
real_life_example.explanation: Thucydides presents the expedition as an overreach by a city that wanted more than it needed, and its failure was a turning point toward Athens' defeat in the Peloponnesian War.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says coveting without weighing the consequences gives birth to destruction, and Athens' reach for Sicily ended in the loss of its fleet and army.

tamil:
அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும் ஒருவன்
புறங்கூறான் என்றல் இனிது.
transliteration:
Arangooraan alla seyinum oruvan,
Purangooraan endral inidhu.
meaning: A person may never speak about goodness and may do only wrong. Still, it is good if people can say, “At least they do not talk badly about others behind their backs.”
elementary: Imagine a kid who forgets his homework, is messy, and gets into trouble a lot. But everyone says, “He never talks badly about anyone when they’re not around.” That one good thing still shines. This kural says not gossiping about people behind their backs is so important that even someone with lots of faults earns a little praise for it.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a deliberately provocative concession: he imagines a man who neither professes aram (virtue) nor practises it, and still finds one thing worth saying in his favour — that he is not a backbiter (puṟaṅkūṟāṉ, literally “one who speaks at the back”). The rhetorical move establishes a hierarchy of vices before any argument is made: slander is placed so low that merely abstaining from it counts as a redeeming trait. The verb “enṟal” (“that it be said”) is significant; the good in question is reputational, located in what the community can truthfully say of the man, which neatly mirrors the fact that backbiting is itself a crime against another’s reputation. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read the couplet as an argument a fortiori: if non-slander redeems even the unrighteous, how much more is it required of the righteous. The chapter sits in the householder section (Illaraviyal) right after Envy and Covetousness, reflecting a sequence from inner vices to their expression in speech.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…non-violence, truthfulness, absence of anger, renunciation, peacefulness, restraint from fault-finding, compassion toward all living beings…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the qualities of a divine nature, and one of them is apaiśunam — literally “non-paiśunya,” refraining from slander and fault-finding about others.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita counts not backbiting as a core mark of a good person; the Kural says it is so basic that even a bad person gets credit for it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law”
christianity.explanation: James tells the early Christians flatly not to speak against each other, because running someone down makes you a judge in God’s place.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat speaking evil of others as a stand-alone wrong serious enough to be named on its own.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not spy or backbite each other. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when dead? You would detest it.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids ghībah (backbiting) and compares it to eating your dead brother’s flesh — attacking someone who cannot defend himself because he is not there.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an and the Kural both single out speaking about someone behind his back as a uniquely ugly act.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people; neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah’s command against being a rakhil (talebearer) is the root of the whole Jewish law of lashon hara, harmful speech about others.
judaism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the Torah treats carrying tales about others as its own named commandment, set right beside protecting a neighbour’s life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And what is right speech? Abstaining from lying, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from abusive speech, abstaining from idle chatter: This, monks, is called right speech.”
buddhism.explanation: In defining the Eightfold Path, the Buddha makes avoiding divisive speech (pisuṇā vācā, tale-bearing) one of the four parts of Right Speech.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism, like the Kural, puts refusing to talk others down at the foundation of ethical life.

jainism.quote_or_event: “For eight causes discipline is called virtue, viz.: not to be fond of mirth, to control one's self, not to speak evil of others, not to be without discipline, not to be of wrong discipline, not to be covetous, not to be choleric, to love the truth; for their influence discipline is called virtue.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana names refraining from speaking evil of others as one of the eight marks that make a monk's discipline count as virtue.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar grants that a man who does nothing else right still earns one good word for not backbiting, and the Jain text likewise counts not speaking evil of others as a virtue in its own right.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.4–5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “It is not good to slander anyone, but the foolish, self-willed manmukhs still do it.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that slandering anyone at all is never good, and that it is the self-willed manmukh who falls into the habit.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even a man with no other virtue earns some credit if he does not backbite; Guru Amar Das likewise singles out slander as a wrong to be avoided toward anyone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 755, Raag Soohee, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Do not get a name either as lavish or as churlish; as a friend of rogues or as a slanderer of good men.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s farmer-wisdom warns his brother to guard his reputation, and one of the worst names a man can earn is ‘slanderer of good men.’
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod and Valluvar both frame the issue in terms of what people say of you: being known as a non-slanderer is itself a good name.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We may, however, enter, though sparingly, into discourse sometimes when occasion calls for it, but not on any of the common subjects … but principally not of men, so as either to blame, or praise, or make comparisons.”
philosophy.explanation: In his rules for everyday conduct, Epictetus tells the student that talking about other people, and above all finding fault with them, is the first kind of conversation to give up.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar picks out the same habit as the one to drop first, so much so that someone who manages only this much has still done something good.
philosophy.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, ch. 33 (tr. Elizabeth Carter (as edited at the Internet Classics Archive))

real_life_example.event_title: Young Benjamin Franklin resolves to speak ill of no one
real_life_example.place: At sea, on the voyage from London to Philadelphia
real_life_example.event: In 1726, aged twenty and returning from London to Philadelphia after a period of youthful mistakes he later called errata, Benjamin Franklin drew up a written Plan of Conduct for his future life. Its fourth resolution was to speak ill of no one, even when the criticism would be true, and instead to excuse the faults he heard charged against others and to speak all the good he knew of everybody. The original manuscript is lost, but the text survives in an early printed copy reproduced in The Papers of Benjamin Franklin.
real_life_example.explanation: Franklin, who openly admitted his own early failings, singled out refraining from speaking ill of others as one of the few rules he set himself for life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even a man with many faults has something good if it can be said that he does not speak ill of others behind their backs, and Franklin made that one restraint a cornerstone of his self-reform.

tamil:
அறனழீஇ அல்லவை செய்தலின் தீதே
புறனழீஇப் பொய்த்து நகை.
transliteration:
Aranazheei allavai seydhalin theedhe,
Puranazheeip poiththu nagai.
meaning: Saying bad things about someone behind their back and then giving them a fake smile to their face is worse than turning away from goodness and doing wrong.
elementary: Suppose a classmate says mean things about you when you’re gone, then comes up and grins at you like your best friend. That’s worse than someone who is just openly naughty — because the fake smile is a trick. This kural says the two-faced person is worse than the openly bad one.
university: The couplet is built on a pointed parallelism: aṟaṉ-aḻīi (“destroying virtue”) against puṟaṉ-aḻīi (“destroying [someone] at the back”), with the second judged worse (tītē). What tips the scale is the final phrase poyttu nakai, “smiling falsely” — the backbiter compounds slander with a feigned intimacy in the victim’s presence. Valluvar is thus condemning not only malicious speech but hypocrisy as a structure of relationship, a split between the face and the back that corrupts the trust on which the householder’s social world rests. The claim that this is worse than open wickedness anticipates a widely shared intuition across ethical traditions: the open enemy can be guarded against, but the smiling detractor disarms his victim first. The verse also sharpens 181: there, abstaining from slander redeemed a sinner; here, slander joined to false friendliness sinks a man below the sinner.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Parth, the qualities of those who possess a demoniac nature are hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names dambha — hypocrisy, showing a good face while hiding a bad heart — as the very first mark of a demonic nature.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts rank the false face above open vice; the smiling backbiter of the Kural is a textbook case of dambha.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist laments a companion who spoke sweetly to his face while plotting against him.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s smiling backbiter exactly: soft speech in front, a drawn sword behind.

islam.quote_or_event: “The worst people in the Sight of Allah on the Day of Resurrection will be the double faced people who appear to some people with one face and to other people with another face.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet calls the two-faced person (dhu’l-wajhayn) the worst of people before God.
islam.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the hadith ranks the double-faced person at the very bottom — below other kinds of sinners.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Their tongue is a sharpened arrow; it speaks deceit. One speaks peaceably to his neighbor with his mouth, but in his heart he lies in wait for him”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud’s discussion of malicious speech quotes Jeremiah’s picture of the peaceful-mouthed ambusher, and in the same passage the school of Rabbi Yishmael says lashon hara outweighs idolatry, sexual sin, and bloodshed combined.
judaism.tie_back: Both the ranking (worse than the gravest sins) and the peaceful face over a hidden attack match the Kural’s verdict.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who flatters be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he approves of his friend's evil deeds, (ii) he disapproves his friend's good deeds, (iii) he praises him in his presence, (iv) he speaks ill of him in his absence.”
