buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches the layman Sigala to recognise the false friend: praise to your face, slander behind your back.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s ‘foe in the guise of a friend’ is the Kural’s backbiter who smiles falsely — almost word for word.

jainism.quote_or_event: “पिट्ठिमंसं न खाएज्जा” (piṭṭhimaṃsaṃ na khāejjā) — “One should not talk ill of others in their absence.”
jainism.explanation: The Daśavaikālika forbids a monk to 'eat the flesh of the back', its idiom for running people down when they are not there, and the tradition treats such talk as cowardly.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says tearing a man down behind his back and smiling at his face is worse than open wrongdoing, and the Jain sūtra uses the same 'behind the back' image to ban that kind of talk outright.
jainism.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.47, Prakrit line with English rendering as given on tattvagyan.com ('Do not talk ill behind someone's back')

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who have one thing in their heart, and something else in their mouth, are judged to be false.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid says that those whose words do not match their hearts are counted false.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural judges the man who tears others down behind their backs and then smiles falsely to their faces as worse than an open evildoer; Farid names that same split between heart and mouth as falseness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For hateful in my eyes, even as the gates of Hades, is that man that hideth one thing in his mind and sayeth another.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles rebuffs Agamemnon’s envoys, declaring that he loathes a man who says one thing and hides another in his heart.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles and Valluvar share a special loathing for the split between the face and the heart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But of all forms of injustice, none is more flagrant than that of the hypocrite who, at the very moment when he is most false, makes it his business to appear virtuous.”
philosophy.explanation: Having said that wrong is done either by force or by fraud and that fraud is the more contemptible, Cicero ranks the hypocrite who wears a mask of goodness while deceiving as the worst wrongdoer of all.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Cicero says the false friendly face is worse than open wrongdoing.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book I, §41 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))

real_life_example.event_title: Procopius writes the Secret History
real_life_example.event: Procopius of Caesarea served as secretary to the general Belisarius and became the official historian of Emperor Justinian's reign, writing the Wars and a work called Buildings that praised Justinian's building projects. At the same time he secretly composed the Anecdota, or Secret History, a fierce attack on Justinian, Empress Theodora, Belisarius and his wife Antonina, saying it contained what he could not write openly for fear of the rulers. It was not published until after his death.
real_life_example.explanation: The same author praised his rulers in public and savaged them in private, and the Secret History is now a famous example of hidden disparagement behind a flattering front.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural condemns tearing a person down behind his back while showing him a false smile to his face, and Procopius wrote praise for the court in public and invective against it in secret.

tamil:
புறங்கூறிப் பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல்
அறங்கூற்றும் ஆக்கத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Purangoorip poiththuyir vaazhdhalin saadhal,
Arangootrum aakkath tharum.
meaning: It is better to die than to live by saying bad things behind people's backs and being fake to their faces. Dying gives the real gain that the teachings of goodness speak of.
elementary: Imagine you could stay popular only by telling mean secrets about your friends and pretending to be nice to them. This kural says it’s better to lose everything than to live that way — being a good, honest person matters more than anything you could win by gossip.
university: The couplet raises the stakes from comparison of vices to a comparison between a way of life and death itself. Puṟaṅkūṟip poyttu uyir vāḻtal — “living by backbiting and falsehood” — names a whole livelihood, the courtier’s or social climber’s art of advancing by undermining others. Against this Valluvar sets cātal, death, which paradoxically yields ākkam (prosperity, gain) of the kind that aṟam-kūṟṟu, the pronouncements of the moral treatises, recognise. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss the death as dying in poverty for having refused such conduct — a reading that turns the verse into a choice between material survival bought by slander and moral gain secured by refusing it. The structure echoes a theme found across classical ethics: that there are lives not worth living, and that moral ruin is a worse fate than death.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that for an honourable person, living on in disgrace is worse than dying.
hinduism.tie_back: Both say a dishonourable life is worse than death; the Kural names backbiting as one such dishonourable life.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters … they which commit such things are worthy of death”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists backbiters among those whose deeds, by God’s judgment, deserve death.
christianity.tie_back: Paul names backbiting specifically and links it to death; the Kural too weighs a backbiter’s life against death.

islam.quote_or_event: “one of them never saved himself from being soiled with his urine while the other used to go about with calumnies (to make enmity between friends).”
islam.explanation: Passing two graves, the Prophet revealed that one man was being punished after death for spreading tales (namīmah) that set friends against each other.
islam.tie_back: The hadith shows that a life lived by slander carries its cost beyond death — the Kural’s point that such a life is not worth its gains.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Third speech, i.e., malicious speech about a third party, kills three people. It kills the one who speaks malicious speech, and the one who accepts the malicious speech when he hears it, and the one about whom the malicious speech is said.”
judaism.explanation: The Sages of the Land of Israel taught that backbiting is lethal — even to the one who speaks it.
judaism.tie_back: If slander ‘kills’ the slanderer, then, as the Kural says, living by it is already a kind of death, worse than an honest one.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easy is life for the shameless one who is impudent as a crow, is backbiting and forward, arrogant and corrupt.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada notes that the backbiter’s life is easy, while the next verse says the modest, pure life is hard.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts admit slander can make life easier — and both say that easy life is the wrong one to choose.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Indifferent and pure with regard to every kind of control, a Śramaṇa should walk about; he who entertains pure thoughts during his whole life, dies as a worthy and wise man.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga holds that a life kept pure in thought ends in a worthy death, so the quality of a death depends on how the life was lived.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says death is better than a life kept going by backbiting and falsehood, and the Jain verse likewise judges a life by whether it can end in a pure and worthy death.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.2.2.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, no one else is truly alive; those who merely live shall depart in dishonor”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Vaar Maajh, Guru Nanak teaches that only one whose mind holds the Lord is truly alive, and that a life which loses honour is not worth having.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says it is better to die than to stay alive by backbiting and falsehood; Guru Nanak likewise rates a dishonoured life as no true life at all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ajax, shamed after his madness, tells his wife Tecmessa that a man of noble birth must either live with honour or die with honour, and then takes his own life rather than live disgraced.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sophocles’ tragic hero decides that a dishonourable life is not worth keeping.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ajax embodies the Kural’s ‘death is better than a base life,’ though his disgrace comes from madness, not slander.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The difficulty, my friends, is not to avoid death, but to avoid unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.”
philosophy.explanation: Condemned to die, Socrates tells the jury that wrongdoing is the real danger to flee, not death.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates and Valluvar agree: death is a lesser evil than living by injustice such as slander and falsehood.

real_life_example.event_title: Irena Sendler refuses to give the Gestapo any names
real_life_example.event: Irena Sendler, a Warsaw social worker who headed the children's section of the underground Council to Aid Jews (Zegota), helped smuggle Jewish children out of the Warsaw Ghetto and place them in hiding. Arrested by the Gestapo in October 1943, she was interrogated under harsh mistreatment and pressed to give up the names of the organisation's leaders and the hidden children, but she never revealed the names of the children or her colleagues. She was sentenced to death, but Zegota bribed an official to release her, and she resumed her underground work.
real_life_example.explanation: Sendler could have bought her life by speaking against others, and she chose to face death instead.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says it is better to die than to live by speaking against others, and Sendler accepted a death sentence rather than save herself by betraying the people who depended on her.

tamil:
கண்ணின்று கண்ணறச் சொல்லினும் சொல்லற்க
முன்னின்று பின்நோக்காச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Kannindru kannarach chollinum sollarka,
Munnindru pinnokkaach chol.
meaning: You may even say hard, unkind things to a person's face. But never say words behind their back without thinking about the harm those words will do.
elementary: If your friend does something wrong, it’s okay to tell them straight to their face, even if it’s hard to hear. What’s not okay is saying it to others when your friend isn’t there. Say it to their face or don’t say it at all.
university: The couplet turns on a set of spatial and visual puns. Kaṇ niṉṟu (“standing before the eyes”) is paired with kaṇ aṟa (“with the eye cut off,” i.e., without kaṇṇōṭṭam, the courteous regard that Valluvar treats as a virtue in chapter 58), while muṉ niṉṟu (“having stood in front”) contrasts with piṉ nōkkā col, which carries two senses: words that do not look to consequences, and words aimed at someone’s back. Valluvar concedes a real cost — harsh, face-to-face speech is not ideal — but ranks it clearly above secret disparagement, because direct speech leaves the target free to answer, correct, or defend himself. This makes the verse a procedural ethic of speech: criticism is legitimate in principle, but its moral character depends on the presence of the person criticised. The same structure appears in legal ideals of hearing both parties and in religious norms of private, direct rebuke.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the discipline of speech as saying what is true and beneficial without needlessly upsetting others.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s standard of true and beneficial speech rules out consequence-blind talk behind someone’s back, which is exactly what the Kural forbids.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers to take a grievance straight to the person, privately, before involving anyone else.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus, like Valluvar, says to tell a person’s fault to his face rather than to others behind his back.

islam.quote_or_event: “Backbiting implies your talking about your brother in a manner which he does not like.” … “If (that failing) is actually found (in him) what you assert, you in fact backbited him, and if that is not in him it is a slander.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that talking about someone in a way he would dislike is ghībah even when it is true; if false, it is worse — slander.
islam.tie_back: Both texts agree that even true criticism becomes a wrong when it is spoken about the person rather than to him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Any statement that is said in the presence of its master, i.e., if the subject of the statement was there, does not have any prohibition due to malicious speech.”
judaism.explanation: Rabba rules that speech said in the subject’s presence is not lashon hara, citing Rabbi Yosei, who never said anything he would not say to the person himself; Abaye disagrees, calling it both impudence and lashon hara.
judaism.tie_back: Rabba’s rule is the Kural’s rule: saying it to someone’s face is a different and lesser matter than saying it behind his back.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, but unendearing & disagreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha explains that he will say unpleasant truths when they are beneficial, choosing the right time — as he did openly about Devadatta.
buddhism.tie_back: Both allow hard words spoken openly and for a purpose, while ruling out careless words that ignore consequences.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If our intention is to remove the fault of a man, then we should tell his faults in his presence only so that he can reflect on them and eliminate the same. To tell someone's mistake in his presence is an act of bravery; but we should take care to tell him or her in privacy.”
jainism.explanation: Explaining the Daśavaikālika's ban on talking ill of people in their absence, this Jain gloss says a fault should be named to the person's face, privately and kindly, and never behind their back.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar allows even harsh words spoken to a man's face but never thoughtless words behind his back, and the Jain gloss draws the same line between correcting someone to their face and talking about them when they are absent.
jainism.source: Modern explanatory gloss on Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.47, tattvagyan.com ('Do not talk ill behind someone's back')

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid forbids even one harsh word to anyone, since the Lord dwells in every person.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural allows even harsh words spoken to a person's face, so long as one never speaks thoughtlessly behind his back; Farid's verse shares the concern for careful speech but goes further, forbidding harshness altogether.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “needs must I verily speak my word outright, even as I am minded, and as it shall be brought to pass”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles tells Odysseus he will speak bluntly to his face, and goes on to say he hates a man who hides one thing and says another.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles chooses the harsh, open word over hidden speech — the very preference Valluvar states.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Every such person is a skulker and a coward; he will not come into the open; he is an ambuscader shooting from a lurking-place”
philosophy.explanation: Lucian argues that the slanderer is a coward: an honest accuser makes his charge publicly and lets it be examined.
philosophy.tie_back: Lucian and Valluvar both say: if you have a charge, bring it into the open where the person can answer.

real_life_example.event_title: Bishop Ambrose confronts Emperor Theodosius
real_life_example.event: In 390 CE, after Emperor Theodosius I ordered a reprisal at Thessalonica that led to a massacre of its citizens, Bishop Ambrose of Milan wrote to the emperor directly, telling him he could not excuse the act and that he would not celebrate the Eucharist in his presence until the emperor repented. Ambrose required Theodosius to do public penance. After some hesitation the emperor complied and was readmitted to communion at Christmas 390.
real_life_example.explanation: Ambrose rebuked the most powerful man in the empire openly and in his own name, rather than undermining him in secret, and the emperor accepted the rebuke.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says harsh words spoken to a person's face are better than thoughtless words behind his back, and Ambrose chose to confront the emperor directly.

tamil:
அறஞ்சொல்லும் நெஞ்சத்தான் அன்மை புறஞ்சொல்லும்
புன்மையாற் காணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Aranjollum nenjaththaan anmai puranjollum,
Punmaiyaal kaanap padum.
meaning: When someone talks badly about others behind their backs, that small-minded habit shows that their heart is not truly good, no matter how much they talk about goodness.
elementary: Someone might always say, “Be kind! Be fair!” But if you hear them gossiping meanly about people when those people leave, you know they don’t really mean what they say. Gossip is like a window that lets you see what’s really inside a person.
university: Here Valluvar turns backbiting into evidence. The phrase aṟañ-collum neñcattāṉ — one whose heart speaks of virtue, or, as many commentators read it, one who merely talks virtue — sets up a contrast between profession and inner reality, and puṟañ-collum puṉmai (“the meanness of speaking at the back”) becomes the diagnostic sign that exposes the gap. The verse therefore makes slander not only a wrong but a symptom: a person’s habitual talk about the absent is a more reliable index of character than his public moralising. The idea that inner character leaks out through small, unguarded habits is common to many ethical traditions, and it sharpens the chapter’s treatment of hypocrisy begun in 182. Valluvar implicitly invites the listener to read people by what they say about others when those others are not present.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who restrains the senses of action but whose mind dwells on sense objects certainly deludes himself and is called a pretender.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna calls a mithyācāra (pretender) anyone who shows outward restraint while his mind stays attached to what he claims to renounce.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts expose the one whose outward religiosity hides an unchanged inner self; the Kural names backbiting as the giveaway.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man’s religion is vain.”
christianity.explanation: James says an uncontrolled tongue shows that a person’s religion is empty, however devout he appears.
christianity.tie_back: James and Valluvar agree: the tongue reveals whether the claimed virtue is real.

islam.quote_or_event: “O community of people, who believed by their tongue, and belief did not enter their hearts, do not back-bite Muslims, and do not search for their faults”
islam.explanation: The Prophet addresses backbiters as people whose faith is on their tongues but has not reached their hearts.
islam.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s own claim: backbiting shows that professed virtue has not entered the heart.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone who speaks malicious speech is considered as though he denied the fundamental belief in God.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yohanan teaches that the one who speaks lashon hara, whatever he professes, is effectively a denier of God.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say slander cancels out religious profession and shows what the speaker really believes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares someone who recites teachings without living them to a hired cowherd counting cattle that aren’t his.
buddhism.tie_back: Both expose the person who speaks virtue without owning it; the Kural finds the proof in backbiting.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Censuring others, praising oneself, concealing good qualities present in others and proclaiming noble qualities absent in oneself, cause the influx (āsrava) of karmas which lead to low-status (nīcagotra).”
jainism.explanation: Umāsvāti puts running others down and claiming virtues one does not have side by side as causes of karma that leads to rebirth in low status.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says a man's backbiting shows that his talk of virtue is hollow, and the Tattvārtha Sūtra pairs that same censure of others with the false display of virtues one does not have.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.25 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “We are good at talking, but our actions are bad. Mentally, we are impure and black, but outwardly, we appear white.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Sri Raag ki Vaar, Guru Nanak confesses the human gap between fine words and bad conduct, and between a dark inner mind and a clean outward show.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that however much a man talks of virtue, his backbiting shows his heart is not given to it; Guru Nanak exposes that same gap between virtuous talk and the inner heart.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Sri Raag (Sri Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Momus, the god of fault-finding, criticised the maker of man for not setting a door or window in the human breast, so that people’s real thoughts could be seen.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the tale Lucian retells, the carping god wanted people’s hidden intentions made visible.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar suggests there already is such a window: a person’s backbiting shows what his heart is really like.
greek_mythology.source: Lucian, Hermotimus 20 (paraphrase of the Momus fable)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for the highest reach of injustice is, to be deemed just when you are not.”
philosophy.explanation: In Glaucon’s challenge in the Republic, the perfectly unjust man is the one who keeps a reputation for justice while being unjust.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato names the danger the Kural helps us detect: the person who seems virtuous but is not, whose backbiting gives him away.

real_life_example.event_title: Richard Owen's anonymous review of the Origin of Species
real_life_example.event: Richard Owen, Britain's most eminent anatomist and a colleague of Charles Darwin for twenty years, wrote a very long anonymous review attacking On the Origin of Species, published in the Edinburgh Review in 1860. Britannica notes that Owen misquoted passages, altering words inside quotation marks, and that he was moved by a sense that his own preeminence was about to be lost. Darwin privately called the review extremely malignant and clever, and wrote to Charles Lyell of how painful it was to be hated so intensely by Owen.
real_life_example.explanation: A great scientist who stood for impartial learning revealed, through a hidden attack on a colleague, a pettiness that damaged his own lasting reputation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the meanness of backbiting shows that a man's heart is not truly given to virtue, however much he speaks of it, and Owen's anonymous attack exposed the gap between his public standing and his conduct.

tamil:
பிறன்பழி கூறுவான் தன்பழி யுள்ளும்
திறன்தெரிந்து கூறப் படும்.
transliteration:
Piranpazhi kooruvaan thanpazhi yullum,
Thirantherindhu koorap padum.
meaning: A person who spreads other people's faults will have their own faults searched out, and the worst ones will be chosen and told about them.
elementary: If you tell everyone about your friend’s mistakes, soon people start looking for your mistakes too — and they’ll pick the most embarrassing ones to share. Gossip is like a boomerang: it comes back to hit you.
university: The couplet states a law of reciprocity in the economy of reputation. Piṟaṉ paḻi kūṟuvāṉ (“one who speaks another’s blame”) will find that taṉ paḻi uḷḷum (“even among his own blameworthy deeds”) the ones chosen with discernment (tiṟaṉ terintu) will be spoken of. The phrase tiṟaṉ terintu is sharp: people will not merely repeat his faults but select the most damaging, just as the backbiter selected and polished the faults of others. Valluvar therefore presents slander as self-defeating — by making fault-finding normal, the slanderer licenses the same treatment of himself. The passive kūṟappaṭum (“will be spoken”) leaves the agent unspecified, allowing both a social reading (others will retaliate) and a moral-causal one akin to karma. The idea that judgment returns in the same measure is widely shared across ethical traditions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As it does and acts, so it becomes; by doing good it becomes good, and by doing evil it becomes evil”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad states the law of karma: a person becomes what he does.
hinduism.tie_back: The slanderer who deals in faults becomes a man of faults — and, as the Kural says, is spoken of for them.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that the standard you use to judge others will be used to judge you.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s boomerang: pick at others’ faults and your own will be picked at the same way.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed whoever tries to expose his Muslims brother’s secrets, Allah exposes his secrets wide open, even if he were in the depth of his house.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that whoever hunts for and exposes others’ hidden faults will have his own hidden faults exposed by God.
islam.tie_back: Almost the Kural itself: the exposer of others’ faults will see his own faults exposed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What is the meaning of that which is written: ‘This shall be the law of the leper [metzora]’ … This means that this shall be the law of a defamer [motzi shem ra].”
judaism.explanation: Reish Lakish reads metzora (one afflicted with tzara’at) as motzi shem ra, a defamer: the one who hid behind secret speech is publicly marked for it.
judaism.tie_back: In both, the slanderer’s own disgrace becomes public — his hidden fault is put on display.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever harasses an innocent man, a man pure, without blemish: The evil comes right back to the fool like fine dust thrown against the wind.”
buddhism.explanation: Said of the monk Kokālika, who slandered Sāriputta and Moggallāna and came to ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: Slander thrown at others blows back on the slanderer — the Kural’s point in a vivid image.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A man who insults another will long whirl in the Circle of Births; to blame others is not good. Considering this a sage is not conceited.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga warns that insulting and blaming others binds karma that keeps the insulter in the cycle of rebirth for a long time.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the man who spreads others' faults will have his own worst faults spread in turn, and the Jain text likewise says blaming others comes back on the one who blames, here as long bondage to rebirth.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.2.2.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid tells the discerning person to stop recording other people's faults and to look honestly at his own.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that one who spreads others' faults will have his own worst faults picked out and told; Farid turns the same scrutiny back on oneself before others do it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 6 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The best treasure a man can have is a sparing tongue, and the greatest pleasure, one that moves orderly; for if you speak evil, you yourself will soon be worse spoken of.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod advises restraint of speech because evil-speaking comes back as worse talk about oneself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s exact claim: speak ill of others and you will be spoken of worse.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “You look at the pimples of others when you yourselves are covered with a mass of sores”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca turns on the critics who mock philosophers’ faults, reminding them how much worse their own are.
philosophy.tie_back: The fault-finder invites a return inspection that shows his own, larger faults — as the Kural predicts.

real_life_example.event_title: James Callender turns his pen on Thomas Jefferson
real_life_example.event: The journalist James Thomson Callender had attacked John Adams and the Federalists in pamphlets such as The Prospect Before Us (1800), with financial help from Thomas Jefferson, and was jailed under the Sedition Act. After Jefferson became president, Callender expected a reward, including the post of postmaster of Richmond, and when it did not come he felt betrayed. In 1802, writing in the Richmond Recorder, he turned the same invective on Jefferson, publishing damaging allegations about Jefferson's private life and the letters showing Jefferson had given him money.
real_life_example.explanation: Jefferson had helped sponsor a writer whose trade was attacking others' reputations, and that writer ended by selecting and publishing the most damaging charges against Jefferson himself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that one who spreads others' faults will have his own worst faults hunted out and told, and Jefferson's support for Callender's attacks came back on him in exactly that way.

tamil:
பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர் நகச்சொல்லி
நட்பாடல் தேற்றா தவர்.
transliteration:
Pagachchollik kelirp pirippar nagachcholli,
Natpaadal thetraa thavar.
meaning: People who do not know how to make friends through warm, friendly talk will say things that split people apart, even their own close friends.
elementary: Some people know how to make friends by saying kind, fun things. Others only know how to say “Did you hear what she said about you?” — and that makes friends fight. This kural says people who can’t make friends with nice words end up breaking friendships with nasty ones.
university: The verse is built on the chiastic pair paka-c-colli (“speaking so as to split”) and naka-c-colli (“speaking so as to make [people] laugh/rejoice”). Valluvar diagnoses divisive speech as a failure of social skill as much as of morality: those who cannot tēṟṟu (be sure of, master) the art of naṭpāṭal, friendship-making through genial conversation, fall back on the easier currency of tale-bearing. The object kēḷir means kin or intimates, so the damage falls on the speaker’s own circle — Parimelazhagar notes they alienate even their friends from themselves. This connects the chapter to the book’s later treatment of friendship (naṭpu, chapters 79–83) and recalls the Buddhist category of pisuṇā vācā, speech that splits people apart. The couplet implies a positive programme: cultivate the speech that unites, and the temptation to divide loses its hold.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, the maid Manthara whispers to Queen Kaikeyi that Rama’s coronation will ruin her and her son Bharata, turning a queen who loved Rama into the cause of his exile.
hinduism.explanation: Manthara’s poisonous tale-bearing breaks apart a royal family that had been united and loving.
hinduism.tie_back: Manthara is the Kural’s divider: her words split kin who had no quarrel until she spoke.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs observes that a whisperer — a gossip — breaks up even the closest friends.
christianity.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: divisive whispering separates intimates.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not obey every worthless habitual swearer [And] scorner, going about with malicious gossip -”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns against following the one who goes about spreading namīm — tale-bearing that sows discord.
islam.tie_back: Both texts point to the gossip who circulates tales between people as someone to reject.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What is different and notable about a leper, that the Torah states: ‘He shall dwell alone; outside of the camp shall be his dwelling’? He replied: By speaking malicious speech he separated between husband and wife and between one person and another”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud explains that the slanderer is made to live alone because his words had separated spouses and friends.
judaism.tie_back: Both identify the slanderer as one who splits apart people who belong together — and who ends up alone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What he has heard here he tells there to break those people apart from these people here. What he has heard there he tells here to break these people apart from those people there.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines divisive speech (pisuṇā vācā) as carrying tales back and forth to break people apart.
buddhism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s ‘speaking to split’ — the canonical Buddhist description of it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk or a nun, well considering, should not use speech whether truth or untruth, or truth mixed with untruth, if it be sinful, blamable, rough, stinging, coarse, hard, leading to sins, to discord and factions, to grief and outrage, to destruction of living beings.”
jainism.explanation: The Ācārāṅga forbids any speech, even true speech, that leads to discord and factions or causes grief.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar condemns words that split people apart and drive away even close friends, and the Ācārāṅga bans speech that leads to discord and factions even when what it says is true.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.4.1.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, speaking insipid words, the body and mind become insipid.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak teaches that harsh, graceless speech dries up the speaker himself, body and mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who cannot win friends with pleasant talk fall into divisive speech that drives off even their own; Guru Nanak likewise warns that harsh speech leaves the speaker sour and estranged.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But abhorred Strife bare painful Toil and Forgetfulness and Famine and tearful Sorrows, Fightings also, Battles, Murders, Manslaughters, Quarrels, Lying Words, Disputes, Lawlessness and Ruin”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod’s family tree of the gods, Eris (Strife) gives birth to Lying Words and Disputes along with violence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Myth places divisive, lying speech in the family of Strife; the Kural shows that kind of speech tearing friends apart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Many are the friendships that have been cut short, many the households set by the ears, because slander has found ready credence.”
philosophy.explanation: Lucian opens his essay on slander by listing the friendships and families it has destroyed.
philosophy.tie_back: Lucian and Valluvar both describe slander as the force that tears apart friends and kin.

real_life_example.event_title: Rousseau breaks with David Hume
real_life_example.place: Wootton, Staffordshire, England, and Paris, France
real_life_example.event: In 1766 the philosopher David Hume brought Jean-Jacques Rousseau, then facing persecution on the Continent, to England and found him a refuge at Wootton in Staffordshire. Rousseau became convinced, wrongly, that Hume was at the centre of a plot to mock and dishonour him, and spread accounts of Hume's bad faith in letters that circulated in Paris. Hume answered by publishing their correspondence as A Concise and Genuine Account of the Dispute, and the friendship ended in a public quarrel.
real_life_example.explanation: Suspicion and accusatory talk turned a protector into an enemy and made the quarrel the talk of literary Europe.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who cannot build friendship through warm, cheerful words fall back on words that divide and drive away even their own friends, and Rousseau's accusations cost him his greatest benefactor.

tamil:
துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும் மரபினார்
என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Thunniyaar kutramum thootrum marabinaar,
Ennaikol ethilaar maattu.
meaning: If people make a habit of telling everyone the faults of those closest to them, what will they not do to strangers?
elementary: If someone spreads secrets about their own best friend, imagine what they’d say about you! This kural says: watch how people talk about their closest friends — that’s how they’ll treat everyone else.
university: The couplet argues a fortiori from intimacy. Tuṉṉiyār (“those who are close”) are the people whom affection, obligation, and self-interest should all protect; if the slanderer’s marapu (settled disposition, habit) leads him to tūṟṟu (scatter abroad, as chaff is winnowed) even their faults, then no restraint can be expected toward ētilār, those who are unconnected to him. The rhetorical question ennaikol (“what indeed?”) leaves the outcome to the listener’s imagination. Valluvar is making a practical point about trust: how a person speaks of his intimates is the best predictor of how he will treat everyone else. The verse also implies that backbiting is not an occasional lapse but a trait, marapu, which, once formed, spares no one.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As the honest are always pained at speaking ill of others, so do the wicked always rejoice in doing the same thing.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala says this after King Dushyanta, her own husband, publicly reviles her as a lewd woman and denies their son.
hinduism.tie_back: The king who slanders his own wife and child shows the Kural’s point: one who defames his intimates will spare no one.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva §74 (K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother; thou slanderest thine own mother’s son.”
christianity.explanation: God rebukes the wicked man who slanders even his own brother.
christianity.tie_back: The same outrage as the Kural: slander aimed at the closest of kin.

islam.quote_or_event: “whoever screened a Muslim, Allah will screen him on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that a Muslim is a brother to be protected, and that covering a brother’s faults earns God’s covering of one’s own.
islam.tie_back: Islam sets the opposite ideal: those close to you are owed concealment of their faults, not exposure.

judaism.quote_or_event: Miriam and Aaron spoke against their own brother Moses; Miriam was struck with tzara’at and shut outside the camp for seven days.
judaism.explanation: The Torah’s example of lashon hara is aimed at a sibling, and later tradition treats it as the model case of the sin.
judaism.tie_back: Even a prophetess who spoke against her own brother was punished, showing how serious it is to disparage intimates.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “For a liar who has violated the one law (of truthfulness) who holds in scorn the hereafter, there is no evil that he cannot do.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that once a person abandons truthful speech, no evil is beyond him.
buddhism.tie_back: Both argue from one proven vice to unlimited danger: if he does this, what won’t he do?

jainism.quote_or_event: “If he is frequently angry; if he perseveres in his wrath; if he spurns friendly advice; if he is proud of his learning; if he finds fault with others; if he is angry even with friends; if he speaks evil even of a good friend behind his back; ... then he is called ill-behaved.”
jainism.explanation: Among the fourteen faults that mark an ill-behaved monk who cannot reach nirvāṇa, the Uttarādhyayana lists speaking evil even of a good friend behind his back.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks what a man who spreads the faults even of those closest to him would not do to strangers, and the Jain text singles out exactly this, slandering even a good friend behind his back, as a sign of bad character.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.7–9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He slanders others, and pollutes himself with his own filth.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that the habit of slandering others dirties the slanderer's own mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what a person who habitually broadcasts even his intimates' faults will not do to strangers; Guru Amar Das shows how deeply such a habit corrupts the one who has it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 88, Sri Raag (Sri Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “paying this penalty, they say, for the shameful weakness he displayed in failing to keep a bridle on his lips, when admitted by gods, though he was but mortal, to share the honours of their feasts like one of them.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Tantalus was welcomed to the gods’ own table and then betrayed their confidences with an unbridled tongue.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tantalus fits the Kural’s type: one who exposes even those who took him into their inner circle.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “When he is sitting with others, he loves to criticise one who has just left the circle; nay, if he has found an occasion, he will not abstain from abusing his own relations.”
philosophy.explanation: Theophrastus sketches the Evil-Speaker, who attacks whoever has just left the room and does not spare his own family.
philosophy.tie_back: Theophrastus draws the Kural’s portrait exactly: a backbiter who spares not even his kin.

real_life_example.event_title: Truman Capote publishes La Cote Basque 1965
real_life_example.event: In November 1975 Esquire magazine published La Cote Basque 1965, a chapter from Truman Capote's unfinished novel Answered Prayers. Capote's wealthy society friends, whom he called his swans, recognised themselves as thinly disguised characters whose private secrets, confided to him over years of friendship, were exposed. Most of them cut him off, and Babe Paley, his closest friend among them, never spoke to him again.
real_life_example.explanation: Capote treated the confidences of his closest friends as material to broadcast, and in doing so lost nearly all of them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what a person who broadcasts the faults even of his intimates will not do to strangers, and Capote's friends, seeing their own secrets in print, drew exactly that conclusion.

tamil:
அறன்நோக்கி ஆற்றுங்கொல் வையம் புறன்நோக்கிப்
புன்சொல் உரைப்பான் பொறை.
transliteration:
Arannokki aatrungol vaiyam purannokkip,
Punsol uraippaan porai.
meaning: The earth still carries the person who waits until someone is gone and then says mean things about them. Is that only because the earth cares about being good?
elementary: The ground holds up everyone who walks on it — good people and mean people. This kural jokes that the Earth must be very patient and kind to keep carrying a gossip who waits for people to leave so he can say nasty things about them.
university: The couplet is one of Valluvar’s sharpest ironies. Vaiyam, the earth, is imagined as a moral agent who bears (āṟṟu) the poṟai (burden, weight) of the slanderer, and the poet wonders whether it does so only aṟaṉ nōkki — out of regard for dharma, since bearing all beings is its duty. The mirrored phrases aṟaṉ nōkki and puṟaṉ nōkki are carefully placed: the earth looks toward virtue, while the slanderer looks toward the back, watching for his victim’s absence before he speaks puṉ col, base words. The image draws on the Indian idea of the earth as the patient bearer of all beings, whose forbearance (poṟai also means patience) contrasts with the slanderer’s impatience to wound. Valluvar thus makes the slanderer a dead weight on the world, tolerated only by a patience he does not deserve.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, the Earth (Bhūmi), weighed down by the burden of wicked kings, takes the form of a cow and goes weeping to Brahmā to ask for relief.
hinduism.explanation: Hindu myth pictures the Earth as a patient mother who carries the weight of the wicked until it becomes too much.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image: the earth patiently bearing the slanderer’s weight, only out of dharma.

christianity.quote_or_event: “for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points to God’s patience, which sustains even the wicked, as the model for loving enemies.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts marvel at a forbearance that keeps supporting even those who don’t deserve it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if Allah were to impose blame on the people for what they have earned, He would not leave upon the earth any creature. But He defers them for a specified term.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says only God’s forbearance keeps wrongdoers on the earth at all.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the wrongdoer stays on the earth only because of a patience he has not earned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He and I cannot dwell together in the world.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Hisda, citing Mar Ukva, says God declares this about anyone who speaks lashon hara, reading Psalm 101:5.
judaism.tie_back: The Talmud and the Kural are equally astonished that the world has room for the slanderer at all.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as when people throw what is clean or unclean on the earth — feces, urine, saliva, pus, or blood — the earth is not horrified, humiliated, or disgusted by it”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Rahula to make his mind like the earth, which accepts whatever is thrown on it without disgust.
buddhism.tie_back: Both use the earth as the model of boundless forbearance; the Kural ironically applies it to carrying the slanderer.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though life cannot be prolonged, as the saying is, still foolish people sin recklessly; a foolish man is filled to the brim (as it were) with sins. Considering this a sage is not conceited.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga pictures the reckless fool as a vessel filled to the brim with sin, a heavy load of karma he has made for himself.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar wonders whether the earth bears the slanderer's weight only out of duty, and the Jain verse likewise pictures the reckless sinner as loaded to the brim with sin.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.2.2.21 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The mythical bull is Dharma, the son of compassion; this is what patiently holds the earth in its place.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak reinterprets the myth of the bull that carries the earth: what really holds the world up is dharma, born of compassion.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural wonders whether the earth bears the weight of the backbiter only out of regard for dharma; Japji says it is dharma itself that patiently holds the earth up.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib, Pauri 16, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the gods by means of Helen's loveliness embroiled Troy and Hellas, causing death thereby, that they might lighten mother Earth of the outrage done her by the increase of man's number.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollo explains that the Trojan War was sent to relieve Mother Earth of the weight of too many mortals.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Greek myth, like the Kural, imagines the earth as burdened by humans who weigh on her.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Orestes (Apollo’s closing speech) (E. P. Coleridge)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “falling upon that earth out of which my father collected the seed … which bears me when I tread on it and abuse it for so many purposes.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius reflects with gratitude on the earth that patiently bears him even as he misuses it.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts marvel at the earth’s endurance of those who abuse it.

real_life_example.event_title: Pietro Aretino, the scourge of princes
real_life_example.event: The writer Pietro Aretino settled in Venice in 1527 after making many enemies in Rome. His satirical attacks on the powerful often amounted to blackmail, and he called himself the scourge of princes. Kings and nobles who feared his satire or wanted his praise sent him gifts, and he grew wealthy and lived in style in Venice until his death in 1556.
real_life_example.explanation: Aretino prospered for decades by trading on what he might say about people, a puzzle that his contemporaries and later historians have noted.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural wonders whether the earth bears the weight of the man who speaks base words of others only out of its own patience, and Aretino lived comfortably for decades on such words.

tamil:
ஏதிலார் குற்றம்போல் தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்
தீதுண்டோ மன்னும் உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Ethilaar kutrampol thankutrang kaankirpin,
Theedhundo mannum uyirkku.
meaning: If people could see their own faults the way they see the faults of others, could any harm ever come to anyone?
elementary: It’s easy to notice when a friend makes a mistake, but hard to notice our own. If everyone checked their own mistakes as carefully as they check others’, there would be much less gossip — and much less trouble for everyone.
university: Valluvar closes the chapter by moving from prohibition to cure. The comparison ētilār kuṟṟampōl (“like the faults of strangers”) captures the ease and even pleasure with which we see others’ failings; if that same clear sight were turned on taṉ kuṟṟam, one’s own faults, the rhetorical question asks, would any harm (tītu) remain for mannum uyir — beings who endure, or, in some commentaries, the soul that persists? The logic is psychological: backbiting feeds on an asymmetry of attention, and self-examination removes both the motive and the moral standing for it. Mu. Karunanidhi’s gloss draws out the practical point — the habit of slander disappears and life becomes peaceful. The ending thus turns the chapter’s condemnation of the slanderer into a discipline for the reader, echoing a strikingly wide range of traditions that contrast the tiny flaw in others with the large one in oneself.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Thou seest, O king, the fault of others, even though they be as small as a mustard seed. But seeing, thou noticest not thy own faults even though they be as large as the Vilwa fruit.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala rebukes King Dushyanta, who slanders her while blind to his own wrong in denying her.
hinduism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s exact image: others’ tiny faults seen, one’s own huge faults ignored.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva §74 (K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus mocks the person who picks at a speck in someone else’s eye while ignoring a plank in his own.
christianity.tie_back: The same lesson as the Kural: look at your own faults as sharply as you look at others’.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of you looks at the mote in his brother's eye while forgetting the stump in his own eye.”
islam.explanation: Abu Hurayra warns against seeing a speck in a brother’s eye while forgetting the stump in one’s own.
islam.tie_back: Same imbalance of sight that the Kural asks us to correct.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I would be surprised if there is anyone in this generation who can receive rebuke. Why? Because if the one rebuking says to him: Remove the splinter from between your eyes, … the other says to him: Remove the beam from between your eyes”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon laments that people tell a critic to deal with his own bigger faults first.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts note how differently we see small faults in others and large ones in ourselves.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one's own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another's faults, but hides one's own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says we winnow others’ faults like chaff in the wind while hiding our own.
buddhism.tie_back: An almost exact statement of the Kural’s point — and the winnowing image matches the Tamil tūṟṟu of kural 188.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The opposites of those mentioned in the previous sūtra and humility (namravṛtti) and modesty (anutseka) cause the influx (āsrava) of karmas that lead to high-status (uccagotra).”
jainism.explanation: Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi, given with the sūtra, explains the opposites as censuring oneself, praising others, proclaiming the real qualities of others and not claiming qualities one lacks.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks what harm could come if people saw their own faults as clearly as others' faults, and the Tattvārtha Sūtra praises exactly that reversal: blaming oneself instead of others.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.26, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, I am the worst of all. Everyone else is good.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, models a humility that looks first at one's own faults and sees others as good.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether any harm could come to living beings if people saw their own faults as clearly as others'; Kabir turns that clear sight wholly on himself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1364, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Hence it is that men are quick to see the faults of others, and yet are often blind to their own failings.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aesop’s fable, every person carries two bags: a small one in front holding the neighbours’ faults and a large one behind holding their own.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The fable explains the very blindness that the Kural asks us to overcome.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We have other men's vices before our eyes, and our own behind our backs.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca says anger at other people grows from this lopsided vision, and gives the example of a father, worse than his son, who scolds the son for the very extravagance he once indulged in himself.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca names the same blindness as the Kural, and like Valluvar treats it as the root of the harm people do to one another.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Of Anger (De Ira), Book II, ch. 28 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: Willy Brandt kneels at the Warsaw Ghetto memorial
real_life_example.event: On 7 December 1970, the day West Germany signed the Treaty of Warsaw with Poland, Chancellor Willy Brandt laid a wreath at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising and then, unplanned, knelt in silence before it. Brandt, who had himself opposed the Nazis from exile, later said he had wanted to ask forgiveness in the name of the German people. The Nobel Committee cited the gesture when it awarded him the 1971 Nobel Peace Prize.
real_life_example.explanation: Instead of dwelling on others' wrongs, a German leader publicly acknowledged his own nation's guilt, and the gesture became a lasting symbol of reconciliation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks whether any harm could remain if people saw their own faults as clearly as others', and Brandt's gesture shows how facing one's own faults can open the way to healing.

tamil:
பல்லார் முனியப் பயனில சொல்லுவான்
எல்லாரும் எள்ளப் படும்.
transliteration:
Pallaar muniyap payanila solluvaan,
Ellaarum ellap padum.
meaning: A person who keeps talking about useless things until many listeners are fed up will be looked down on by everyone.
elementary: Imagine someone in class who keeps talking and talking about nothing while everyone is trying to listen to the teacher. Soon nobody wants to sit next to them. This kural says that people who chatter about useless things make everyone tired of them, and then everyone stops respecting them.
university: The chapter opens with a social rather than a metaphysical sanction: the idle talker is punished by the listening community itself. The verb முனிய (muniya, “to be vexed, to loathe”) names the listeners’ reaction, and எள்ளப்படும் (ellappadum, “will be scorned”) names the outcome, so the couplet traces a causal chain from speech to irritation to contempt. The contrast of பல்லார் (“the many” who hear him) with எல்லாரும் (“everyone”) is deliberate: annoyance starts with the immediate audience but reputation spreads to the whole world. Coming straight after the chapter on backbiting (புறங்கூறாமை), the kural widens the ethics of speech from malicious words to merely empty ones, treating wasted words as a real, if quieter, wrong. Plutarch’s essay on garrulousness makes the same diagnosis, that the chatterer seeks affection and wins hatred.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him not seek after many words, for that is mere weariness of the tongue.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad tells the seeker who has found the Self to practise wisdom instead of piling up words, which only tire the tongue.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat piling up words as fruitless. The Kural stresses how it wears on the listeners, and the Upanishad how it wears out the speaker.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad IV.4.21 (trans. F. Max Müller, SBE 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious; but the lips of a fool will swallow up himself. … A fool also is full of words.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher contrasts gracious speech with a fool’s endless words, which end up destroying the fool himself.
christianity.tie_back: In both texts the babbler is the one who pays: the Kural’s talker ends up scorned, and the Preacher’s fool is swallowed by his own lips.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah has hated for you three things: -1. Vain talks, (useless talk) that you talk too much or about others.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet lists qīla wa qāla (‘it was said and he said’, meaning idle chatter) first among three things God dislikes for people.
islam.tie_back: In the Kural the whole world scorns the idle talker, and in the hadith God himself dislikes idle talk. Both condemn it plainly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that useth many words shall be abhorred; and he that taketh to himself authority therein shall be hated.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira, a Second-Temple Jewish sage, warns that the person who talks too much will be loathed by those around him.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own claim: too many words lead to being abhorred, just as the Kural’s talker is scorned by all.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “They blame those who remain silent, they blame those who speak much, they blame those who speak in moderation. There is none in the world who is not blamed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Atula that people criticise everyone, including those who talk too much.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say that the heavy talker is criticised. The Buddha, however, adds that the silent are blamed too, which softens the Kural’s sharp contrast.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a bitch with sore ears is driven away everywhere, thus a bad, insubordinate, and talkative (pupil) is turned out.”
jainism.explanation: The opening lecture of the Uttarādhyayana compares the talkative, unruly pupil to a mangy dog that is chased away from every door.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the man who keeps up useless talk until his listeners are sick of him ends up scorned by everyone, and the Jain simile shows the talkative pupil driven out wherever he goes.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, speaking insipid words, the body and mind become insipid. He is called the most insipid of the insipid; the most insipid of the insipid is his reputation.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Asa ki Vaar, Guru Nanak warns that fikaa (tasteless, graceless) speech hollows out the speaker and leaves him with a reputation as hollow as his words.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the man who keeps pouring out useless talk ends up scorned by everyone; Guru Nanak likewise says the insipid talker becomes known to all by that insipidness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A man of many words, and those unseemly; a monger of sedition, a railer against all who were in authority, who cared not what he said, so that he might set the Achaeans in a laugh.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Thersites harangues the Greek assembly at Troy. The soldiers are ‘angry and disgusted’, and when Odysseus beats him, the whole army laughs at him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural in narrative form: a man whose many words disgust the many is scorned by all.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In the case of babblers … they are hated when they wish to be liked, that they cause annoyance when they wish to please, that they are laughed at when they think they are admired.”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch diagnoses garrulousness as a disease whose sufferers get the opposite of what they want from their audience.
philosophy.tie_back: Plutarch’s babbler, like the Kural’s, annoys his listeners and is despised by them.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On Talkativeness (De garrulitate) 16, 510c-d (trans. W. C. Helmbold, Loeb)

real_life_example.event_title: The Senate censures Senator Joseph McCarthy
real_life_example.event: In spring 1954 the Army-McCarthy hearings, carried in full on national television, showed Senator Joseph McCarthy badgering witnesses and ignoring procedure and ordinary courtesy, and the Senate Historical Office records that by June he had greatly damaged his image with the American people. The Senate, which its historians describe as weary of his embarrassing antics, then referred a censure resolution to a bipartisan select committee. On 2 December 1954 it voted 67 to 22 to censure him for his conduct towards two Senate committees, and after the vote he lost his power and standing.
real_life_example.explanation: A senator who had dominated the press and the Senate for four years lost his influence once the public had watched him at length and grown tired of him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural traces a chain from wearying talk to the irritation of the many listeners and then to contempt from everyone, which is close to the path from the televised hearings to the Senate's formal censure.

tamil:
பயனில பல்லார்முன் சொல்லல் நயனில
நட்டார்கண் செய்தலிற் றீது.
transliteration:
Payanila pallaarmun sollal nayanila,
Nattaarkan seydhalir reedhu.
meaning: Talking about pointless things in front of many people is worse than being unkind to your own friends.
elementary: If you are rude to one friend, that hurts one person. But if you stand up in front of the whole school and waste everyone’s time with silly talk, you hurt everyone’s time at once. This kural says doing that in front of many people is even worse than being unkind to a friend.
university: The couplet works through a startling comparison. Doing நயனில (nayanila, “what is devoid of goodness/propriety”) to நட்டார் (nattaar, “friends”), which is a real ethical fault, is ranked below speaking பயனில (payanila, “what is devoid of benefit”) before பல்லார் (“the many”). The two phrases rhyme (nayanila / payanila), and the parallel sound makes the ranking stick in the ear. The argument depends on scale and publicity: an unkind act toward a friend stays in a private relationship that can be repaired, while empty talk before an assembly wastes the attention of many people at once and fixes one’s public character. Modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all keep this ‘worse than’ reading, which shows how seriously Valluvar takes the public squandering of speech.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrihari’s Nītiśataka calls silence the ornament that the unlearned can wear in an assembly of the wise, a covering for their lack of knowledge.
hinduism.explanation: The gnomic poet advises that in a learned gathering the unqualified are better off saying nothing than exposing themselves.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts see the assembly as the place where empty talk does the most damage, and both advise silence there.
hinduism.source: Bhartrihari, Nītiśataka (verse on silence as the ornament of the unlearned; numbering varies by edition)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that even ‘idle’ (argos, workless) words are weighed at the final judgment.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts insist that careless words weigh more than people assume. The Kural ranks them above unkind deeds, and Jesus makes them answerable before God.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [they are] those who do not testify to falsehood, and when they pass near ill speech, they pass by with dignity.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes God’s true servants as refusing to join in laghw (vain, idle speech) when they come across it.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link dignity with keeping out of vain talk when others are present.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If two sit together and there are no words of Torah [spoken] between them, then this is a session of scorners.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradion says that a gathering filled only with empty talk turns into a ‘seat of the scornful’.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts judge talk by its social setting: empty words in company harm the whole gathering.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:2 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It isn’t right, monks, that sons of good families, on having gone forth out of faith from home to the homeless life, should get engaged in such topics of conversation.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha finds monks gathered in the assembly hall chatting about kings, food, gossip and so on, and tells them to discuss ten wholesome topics instead.
buddhism.tie_back: Here idle talk in an assembly is corrected at once, which reflects the Kural’s concern about pointless words before many.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 10.69, Kathavatthu Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk should not tell stories, nor ask idle questions, nor gossip. But, knowing the highest Law, he should perform his religious duties, and regard nothing his own.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga tells the monk to give up story-telling, idle questions and gossip and to spend himself on his religious duties instead.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks pointless talk before many people as worse than unkindness to friends, and the Jain rule likewise treats idle talk and gossip as a real fault to be given up, not a harmless habit.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.2.2.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To speak too much and babble is useless.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Nanak dismisses endless talk and babbling as worthless.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks pointless talk before many people as worse than wronging one's friends; Guru Nanak shares the low estimate of babble, though he makes no such comparison.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 661, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, the mortal favoured with a seat at the gods’ table, falls by an ‘unbridled tongue’ in Euripides’ telling: he betrays the confidences of his divine hosts by talking.
greek_mythology.explanation: Several versions put Tantalus’s crime in his mouth (leaking the gods’ secrets) rather than in a deed, and he suffers eternal punishment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Tantalus tradition, like the Kural, rates reckless speech as worse than a wrong done by hand to one’s friends.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Orestes 4-10 (the ‘unbridled tongue’ of Tantalus); cf. Pindar, Olympian 1

philosophy.quote_or_event: Theophrastus’s sketch of ‘The Garrulous Man’ shows a man who sits beside strangers and pours out his dreams, dinners and trivial opinions to anyone within earshot.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle’s successor catalogues the chatterer as a recognisable social type whose talk burdens every company he enters.
philosophy.tie_back: Theophrastus shows how public idle talk imposes on many people at once, which is why the Kural judges it so harshly.

real_life_example.event_title: Khrushchev's intemperate speech at the farewell reception for Gomulka
real_life_example.event: At a Kremlin-attended farewell reception in Moscow for the visiting Polish leader Wladyslaw Gomulka, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev turned to the Western diplomats present and delivered a long, boastful, off-the-cuff harangue about the capitalist countries, Hungary and the Suez crisis. TIME reported that by the time he finished, the Western diplomats had left the room. One line from the speech, rendered in English as a declaration that the Soviets would bury the West, became one of the most widely remembered remarks of the Cold War.
real_life_example.explanation: Unplanned words spoken before a large gathering of foreign envoys did lasting damage to the speaker's image abroad, far beyond the occasion itself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that pointless talk before many people does more harm than an unkind act among friends, and Khrushchev's rambling remarks before the diplomatic corps were repeated around the world for decades.

tamil:
நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும் பயனில
பாரித் துரைக்கும் உரை.
transliteration:
Nayanilan enbadhu sollum payanila,
Paarith thuraikkum urai.
meaning: When a person goes on and on about useless things, their talk itself shows everyone that they are not a good person.
elementary: You can often tell what kind of person someone is just by listening to them. If a person keeps talking on and on about useless things, their own words are like a sign on their back that says, “I am not a good person.” They don’t even need anyone else to say it.
university: The grammar is striking: the subject of சொல்லும் (“will declare”) is the talk itself (உரை, urai), so speech bears witness against the speaker. பாரித்து (paarittu, “spreading out, amplifying”) condemns not a single slip but the habit of stretching trivial matter into long discourse. The key term நயனிலன் (nayanilan, “one without nayan”) is glossed differently by modern commentators: Mu. Varadarasan reads it as lacking virtue (aram), Solomon Pappaiah as lacking justice (neethi), and Kalaignar as simply a ‘useless person’. All of these readings agree that speech works as a public index of inner character. The same idea appears in Solon’s maxim that speech is the image of actions, and in the Buddha’s teaching that discernment is revealed through conversation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Keshav, what is the disposition of one who is situated in divine consciousness? How does an enlightened person talk? How does he sit? How does he walk?”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna asks how inner realisation shows outwardly, and the first sign he asks about is speech.
hinduism.tie_back: Both assume that speech shows a person’s inner state. The Kural uses the idea negatively (empty talk exposes a lack of virtue), and the Gita positively.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool’s voice is known by multitude of words.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher says a fool can be recognised by the sheer quantity of his words.
christianity.tie_back: In both texts, piling up empty words identifies the kind of person who speaks them.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed among the excellence of a person’s Islam is that he leaves what does not concern him.”
islam.explanation: This widely taught saying (also no. 12 in al-Nawawi’s Forty Hadith) makes leaving aside irrelevant matters, including irrelevant talk, a measure of how good someone’s faith is.
islam.tie_back: Both texts read engagement with trivial matters as a measure of inner quality.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A small coin in an empty barrel calls: Kish, kish.”
judaism.explanation: Ulla quotes a folk proverb: one coin in an empty jar rattles loudly, while a full jar makes no noise. (The words ‘small’ and ‘empty’ are the translator’s clarifying additions.)
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say that noisy talk shows inner emptiness.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 85b (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz trans., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It’s through discussion that a person’s discernment may be known, and then only after a long period, not a short period.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a small fish can be told from the ripples it makes, and in the same way a dull mind can be told from how a person talks.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts treat speech as the window through which others read what a person is like inside.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.192, Thana Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Indulging in meaningless and unrestrained talk out of self-importance is maukharya.”
jainism.explanation: Pūjyapāda's commentary defines maukharya (garrulity), which Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.32 lists as a lapse in the layperson's vow to avoid purposeless harm (anarthadaṇḍa-virati).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says long talk about worthless things itself announces the speaker's lack of goodness, and Jain lay ethics names that very habit, meaningless talk born of self-importance, as a breach of a vow.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.32, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever is in the mind, comes forth; spoken words by themselves are just wind.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok preserved in Asa ki Vaar, Guru Angad teaches that what a person truly is inside will show itself, while words on their own are only air.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that long talk about worthless things itself announces the speaker's lack of goodness; Guru Angad likewise holds that the inner self comes out and that mere words are empty wind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Oho, my friend, it’s you, is it? I, too, should have been afraid if I hadn’t heard your voice.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aesop’s fable an ass dressed in a lion’s skin scares everyone until he brays, and the fox recognises him at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Speech gives the speaker away. In the Kural, empty talk exposes a man without worth just as the bray exposes the ass.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, ‘The Ass in the Lion’s Skin’ (trans. V. S. Vernon Jones, 1912)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He used to say, too, that speech was the image of actions.”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes Laertius records Solon’s maxim that a man’s words mirror his deeds and character.
philosophy.tie_back: Solon’s ‘speech is the image’ is the Kural’s point in general terms: empty speech reflects an empty moral life.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 1.58 (Solon) (trans. C. D. Yonge)

real_life_example.event_title: The Tichborne Claimant undone by his own testimony
real_life_example.event: A man who came from Australia claiming to be Sir Roger Tichborne, the lost heir to an English baronetcy, sued for the family estates in a civil trial that opened in May 1871 and ran for 102 days. Under a cross-examination by Sir John Coleridge that lasted more than three weeks, his long testimony failed to hold up, and his case collapsed in March 1872 after evidence of tattoos that the real Roger had and he did not. He was then tried for perjury, found to be Arthur Orton, a butcher's son from Wapping, and sentenced on 28 February 1874 to fourteen years' penal servitude.
real_life_example.explanation: The claimant's own words, poured out at enormous length in court, were what exposed him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that long talk spread over worthless matter itself announces the speaker's lack of worth, and the claimant's weeks of testimony are what proved him an impostor.

tamil:
நயன்சாரா நன்மையின் நீக்கும் பயன்சாராப்
பண்பில்சொல் பல்லா ரகத்து.
transliteration:
Nayansaaraa nanmaiyin neekkum payansaaraap,
Panbilsol pallaa rakaththu.
meaning: Useless, rude words spoken in front of many people pull a person away from goodness and take away the good in them.
elementary: Think of a garden. Every time you throw rubbish into it, the flowers have less room to grow. Rude, useless talk in front of others is like throwing rubbish into your own heart’s garden. Bit by bit, it pushes the good things out.
university: The couplet is built on two paired negatives, பயன்சாரா (“not joined to benefit”) and நயன்சாரா (“not joined to nayan”, i.e., virtue or propriety), with பண்பில் (panpil, “uncultured, graceless”) in between. The claim is about moral formation, not reputation: such speech நன்மையின் நீக்கும் (“removes one from goodness”), gradually alienating the speaker from his own better character. Mu. Varadarasan reads the result as ‘not joining with aram and being removed from good’, while Kalaignar stresses that it also destroys the listeners’ pleasure. The setting பல்லாரகத்து (“among many”) again marks public speech as the place where habits of character are formed. The same point appears in Paul’s warning that ‘vain babblings’ ‘increase unto more ungodliness’ and in the Buddha’s listing of idle chatter among unrighteous conduct.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Words that do not cause distress, are truthful, inoffensive, and beneficial, as well as regular recitation of the Vedic scriptures—these are declared as austerity of speech.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines disciplined speech as words that are both pleasing (priya) and beneficial (hita), among other qualities.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s priya-hita pairing mirrors the Kural’s nayan-payan pairing. Speech lacking both falls short of dharma, and the Kural adds that it removes one from goodness.
