christianity.quote_or_event: “But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns Timothy that empty, irreverent chatter has a snowballing corrupting effect.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say vain speech actively carries the speaker away from goodness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he who buys the amusement of speech to mislead [others] from the way of Allah without knowledge and who takes it in ridicule.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an condemns lahw al-ḥadīth, idle or diverting talk, as a means of leading people away from God’s path.
islam.tie_back: Both texts say frivolous speech pulls people away from the good path, whether the speaker’s own or other people’s.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Merriment and frivolity accustom one to sexual licentiousness.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Akiva warns that light-headed, jesting talk slowly accustoms a person to serious transgression.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see frivolous words as a slope that carries a person away from virtue.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:13 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is a gossip: as one who tells that which is unseasonable … and he speaks out of season speech not worth recording, which is unreasoned, indefinite, and unconnected with good.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists idle chatter (samphappalāpa) as one of four kinds of ‘verbal conduct not in accordance with the Dhamma, unrighteous conduct’.
buddhism.tie_back: In both texts, speech ‘unconnected with good’ is a form of unrighteousness in its own right, not merely bad manners.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 41, Saleyyaka Sutta (trans. Ñanamoli Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not tell anything sinful or meaningless or hurtful, neither for his own sake nor for anybody else's, nor without such a motive.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana puts meaningless speech in the same forbidden class as sinful and hurtful speech, whatever the speaker's motive.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says useless, graceless words cut a person off from virtue, and the Jain rule likewise treats meaningless speech as a moral fault on a level with sinful and hurtful words.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “By mere talk, people do not earn passage to Heaven. Salvation comes only from the practice of Truth.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Vaar Maajh, Guru Nanak insists that talking gets no one to the goal; only truth lived in action does.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says useless, graceless words cut a person off from virtue and goodness; Guru Nanak likewise separates mere talk from the lived truth that alone carries a person forward.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “So long as he was silent, they never suspected that he was not a pigeon like themselves. But one day he was unwise enough to start chattering.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Aesop’s jackdaw disguises itself among the pigeons, gives itself away by chattering, and is driven out by both pigeons and jackdaws.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Chattering cuts the jackdaw off from both flocks, as the Kural says graceless talk cuts a person off from goodness.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, ‘The Jackdaw and the Pigeons’ (trans. V. S. Vernon Jones, 1912)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The buffoon, on the other hand, is the slave of his sense of humour, and spares neither himself nor others if he can raise a laugh, and says things none of which a man of refinement would say.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle describes the vice of excess in conversation: the buffoon’s tasteless talk departs from the mean of ready wit.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s buffoon speaks what ‘a man of refinement’ would not, which is the Kural’s பண்பில்சொல் (graceless words). Both writers call such speech a vice.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.8 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Lysenko's report to the August 1948 session of the Soviet agricultural academy
real_life_example.event: At a session of the Lenin All-Union Academy of Agricultural Sciences approved by Joseph Stalin, its president Trofim Lysenko delivered a report denouncing Mendelian genetics and its supporters, and announced that the Communist Party's Central Committee had approved it. After the session, classical genetics was officially condemned, and many scientists working in it were dismissed or moved to other fields. Teaching and research in standard genetics stayed effectively banned in the Soviet Union into the 1960s, and Lysenko is now remembered as a symbol of science corrupted by politics.
real_life_example.explanation: Rhetoric with no scientific substance, delivered before a large assembly with state backing, set back a whole field of science and harmed many careers.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that graceless words with no benefit, spoken before many, cut a person off from goodness, and Lysenko's speeches put his name to the persecution of honest scientists.

tamil:
சீர்மை சிறப்பொடு நீங்கும் பயனில
நீர்மை யுடையார் சொலின்.
transliteration:
Seermai sirappodu neengum payanila,
Neermai yudaiyaar solin.
meaning: If even good people speak empty, useless words, they lose both their good name and the respect it earned them.
elementary: Imagine a famous, respected captain of a sports team. If she starts saying silly, pointless things all the time, the team slowly stops looking up to her. This kural says that even good people lose their respect if they fill the air with useless words.
university: This kural turns from the habitual babbler to the virtuous person who lapses. நீர்மையுடையார் (neermaiyudaiyaar) means those who have fine nature, literally a ‘watery’ or gentle disposition. The couplet warns that they are not immune: their சீர்மை (seermai, ‘excellence, eminence’) departs together with its சிறப்பு (sirappu, ‘honour, distinction’). Solomon Pappaiah adds ‘அப்பொழுதே’ (‘at that very moment’), stressing how suddenly the loss comes. The point is that reputation is a fragile social credit, and vain talk spends it faster than virtue earns it. Ecclesiastes’ image of dead flies spoiling the perfumer’s ointment is perhaps the closest cross-cultural parallel.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the Pandavas’ Maya Sabha, Duryodhana stumbles in the illusory hall and is laughed at, and the humiliation feeds the enmity behind the dice game and the war. (Popular retellings give Draupadi a cutting jibe, but this line is not found in the critical text.)
hinduism.explanation: The Pandavas were exemplary figures, yet a moment of careless mockery by them had consequences out of all proportion.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the noble are not exempt: a few idle, mocking words can undo the standing that virtue has built.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Duryodhana’s account of the Maya Sabha; trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour.”
christianity.explanation: A tiny contaminant spoils a costly perfume, and a little folly in the same way spoils the name of a respected sage.
christianity.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s exact thought: a person reputed for wisdom and honour loses both through a small lapse.

islam.quote_or_event: “May your mother grieve your loss O Mu’adh! Are the people tossed into the Fire upon their faces, or upon their noses, except because of what their tongues have wrought.”
islam.explanation: Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal, one of the most learned Companions, is surprised to learn that people are held accountable for speech. The Prophet grasps his own tongue and says ‘Restrain this’.
islam.tie_back: Even a righteous, eminent believer is warned that the tongue can undo everything else, just as the Kural warns even people of good character.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Silence is fitting for the wise, and a fortiori the same is true for fools.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud cites this saying of the Sages, followed by Proverbs 17:28 (‘even a fool, when he holds his peace, is considered wise’).
judaism.tie_back: Both texts begin with the wise. The Kural warns that the good lose standing through idle talk, and the Talmud says restraint suits even the wise.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 99a (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz trans., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Surely, when a person is born, an axe is born in his mouth, with which he cuts himself— the fool saying a bad statement.”
buddhism.explanation: The monk Kokālika, despite having gone forth, keeps speaking against Sāriputta and Moggallāna and suffers a terrible fall.
buddhism.tie_back: A man in a revered position destroys himself with his own words, much as the Kural’s person of good character loses excellence and honour.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 3.10, Kokālika Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “When a monk quarrels and uses very bad language, he will suffer great spiritual loss; therefore a wise man should not quarrel.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga warns that even a monk who has taken the vows loses much of his spiritual gain through careless, bad speech.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar warns that even people of fine character lose their excellence and honour if they speak empty words, and the Jain verse likewise says a monk's own words can cost him great spiritual loss.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.2.2.19 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The insipid person is discarded in the Court of the Lord, and the insipid one's face is spat upon.”
sikhism.explanation: Continuing the same salok of Asa ki Vaar, Guru Nanak says the person given to fikaa speech is cast out of the divine Court and disgraced.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that even people of fine character lose their excellence and honour when they speak empty words; Guru Nanak likewise says such speech costs a person all honour, before God as well as people.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Thamyris “boasted that he would surpass even the Muses, daughters of aegis-bearing Jove, if they should sing against him; whereon they were angry, and maimed him. They robbed him of his divine power of song.”
greek_mythology.explanation: A gifted singer loses the very excellence he was famous for because of a vain, boastful claim.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, a person of real excellence loses that excellence and its fame through empty words.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Avoid, likewise, an endeavor to excite laughter. For this is a slippery point, which may throw you into vulgar manners, and, besides, may be apt to lessen you in the esteem of your acquaintance.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus advises the aspiring philosopher that trivial, attention-seeking talk costs dignity.
philosophy.tie_back: Epictetus says it directly: frivolous talk will ‘lessen you in the esteem’ of others, even if you are a serious person. That is the Kural’s point.

real_life_example.event_title: Neville Chamberlain's return from Munich
real_life_example.event: Returning from Munich, where Britain, France, Germany and Italy had agreed that Czechoslovakia must give up the Sudetenland to Germany, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain displayed an Anglo-German declaration signed by himself and Hitler and told the crowd at Downing Street that he believed he had brought back peace for our time. Germany went on to occupy the rest of Czech lands in March 1939 and invaded Poland in September 1939, and Britain declared war. Chamberlain's phrase became a lasting byword for political naivety.
real_life_example.explanation: Chamberlain was a respected, hard-working statesman, yet one confident public pronouncement that proved empty did lasting damage to how he is remembered.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that when even people of good character speak empty words, their eminence and honour slip away, and Chamberlain's reputation has never fully recovered from his promise of peace.

tamil:
பயனில்சொல் பாராட்டு வானை மகன்எனல்
மக்கட் பதடி யெனல்.
transliteration:
Payanilsol paaraattu vaanai makanenal,
Makkat padhadi yenal.
meaning: Do not call someone who loves to show off with empty words a real person. Call them the useless husk among people.
elementary: When farmers harvest rice, the good grain is kept and the light, empty husks called chaff blow away in the wind. This kural says a person who only talks empty talk is like that chaff: they look like a person on the outside, but inside there is nothing useful.
university: Valluvar here turns from consequence to classification. பாராட்டுவான் (paaraattuvaan) means one who displays, cherishes or keeps repeating; Mu. Varadarasan glosses it as ‘saying many times’. The one who does this with பயனில்சொல் (empty words) is denied the name மகன் (makan, ‘man, human being’) and given instead மக்கட்பதடி (makkat-padhadi, ‘the chaff of humanity’). The agricultural metaphor is precise: chaff (பதர்) has the outward form of grain without its kernel, so the babbler has the form of a person without the substance that makes speech human. (One web edition prints ‘பராட்டு’ here, evidently a typo; the standard reading ‘பாராட்டு’ is followed.) The image anticipates later critiques of inauthentic ‘idle talk’, such as Heidegger’s Gerede, in which speech circulates without anyone really grasping what it is about.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrihari’s Nītiśataka says that a man without literature, music and the arts is a beast in plain sight, lacking only a tail and horns.
hinduism.explanation: The poet argues that what makes someone fully human is cultivated inner substance, not mere bodily form.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts deny full humanity to one who has the outward human form but lacks inner substance: the Kural calls him chaff, Bhartrihari a hornless beast.
hinduism.source: Bhartrihari, Nītiśataka (verse ‘sāhitya-saṅgīta-kalā-vihīnaḥ’; numbering varies by edition)

christianity.quote_or_event: “The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD.”
christianity.explanation: God contrasts the empty words of false prophets (chaff) with the true word (wheat).
christianity.tie_back: Both texts use chaff as the image for words without substance, and in both the speakers of such words are judged hollow.

islam.quote_or_event: “The most disliked among you to me, and the one sitting furthest from me on the Day of Judgement are the Thartharun, and the Mutashaddiqun and the Muthafaihiqun.”
islam.explanation: Tirmidhi explains that al-tharthār is ‘the one who talks a great deal’. The prophet ranks such chatterers among those furthest from him.
islam.tie_back: Both texts assign the compulsive talker the lowest rank: chaff among men, or furthest from the Prophet.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Morning sleep, midday wine, children’s talk and sitting in the assemblies of the ignorant put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas lists habits, including idle ‘children’s talk’, that drain a grown person’s life of substance.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see adult idle talk as a way of losing one’s standing as a full person.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:10 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Sweep away the sweepings, throw away the trash, then remove the chaff: non-contemplatives who think they’re contemplatives.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the Sangha to winnow out harsh-mouthed, deluded monks who have the outward form of monks but none of the substance.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts call people chaff when they have the outward form (a man, a monk) without the inner grain.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 2.6, Dhammacariya Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is ignorant of the truth, egoistical, greedy, without self-discipline, and who talks loosely, is called ill-behaved and void of learning.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana counts loose talk among the marks that strip a monk of the name of a disciplined and learned person.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar refuses to call the man who parades empty words a real man and calls him chaff, and the Jain text likewise denies the loose talker the standing of a disciplined, learned person.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, those people are really donkeys; they have no virtue or merit, but still, they are very proud.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok, Guru Nanak refuses the dignity of the name human to people who show off with no virtue behind it, calling them donkeys.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural will not call the man who delights in displaying empty words a real man, but the chaff among human beings; Guru Nanak likewise demotes the hollow show-off below the human.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1411, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Salok 15, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Echo, punished by Juno for distracting her with endless chatter, loses her own speech and can only repeat others’ last words. Pining for Narcissus, she wastes away until nothing remains but her voice.
greek_mythology.explanation: A nymph whose talk had no purpose of its own is reduced to a voice with no substance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echo’s fate turns the Kural’s ‘chaff’ into a story: a person reduced to empty sound without a kernel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heidegger describes ‘idle talk’ (Gerede) as speech that passes along what ‘one says’ without any real grasp of its subject, and he links it to an inauthentic, ‘fallen’ mode of human existence.
philosophy.explanation: For Heidegger, chatter is a symptom of losing oneself in the anonymous ‘they’ (das Man), existing as a person without being truly oneself.
philosophy.tie_back: Heidegger’s idle talker, like the Kural’s ‘chaff among men’, has the form of a speaking human but is hollow at the core.
philosophy.source: Martin Heidegger, Being and Time §35 (‘Idle Talk’)

real_life_example.event_title: The Sokal hoax
real_life_example.event: Physicist Alan Sokal of New York University submitted an article titled Transgressing the Boundaries: Towards a Transformative Hermeneutics of Quantum Gravity to the cultural studies journal Social Text, which published it in its spring/summer 1996 issue without any review by a physicist. Shortly afterwards Sokal revealed in the magazine Lingua Franca that the article was a parody, deliberately filled with impressive-sounding jargon and nonsense. The affair set off a worldwide debate about standards of rigour in academic writing.
real_life_example.explanation: The hoax showed that language can have all the outward form of learned argument while containing nothing of substance.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls the person who shows off empty words the chaff of humanity, grain-shaped but without a kernel, and Sokal's article was built to be exactly such a husk, to show how easily it could pass for the real thing.

tamil:
நயனில சொல்லினுஞ் சொல்லுக சான்றோர்
பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Nayanila sollinum solluka saandror,
Payanila sollaamai nandru.
meaning: Good people may say things that are not pleasant if they must. But it is good for them never to say things that are useless.
elementary: A good coach may sometimes say something that stings, like “You need to practise harder!” That isn’t nice to hear, but it helps. What a good coach should never do is waste the team’s time with pointless chatter. This kural says: a hard word that helps is okay, but a useless word is not.
university: This is the chapter’s most philosophically daring couplet, because it ranks the two standards of speech against each other. நயனில (nayanila) is glossed by Kalaignar as ‘not sweet or pleasant’, by Pappaiah as ‘unjust’ and by Mu. Varadarasan as ‘lacking aram’. On the milder reading, Valluvar concedes that the சான்றோர் (saandror, the noble or accomplished) may speak unpleasantly, but insists that they must never speak uselessly. So usefulness (பயன்) is made the non-negotiable floor of speech, and pleasantness (நயன்) is a desirable but negotiable quality. This differs from Manu’s well-known rule against ‘disagreeable truth’, and it lines up closely with the Buddha’s criteria in the Abhaya Sutta, where beneficial but unwelcome words may be spoken at the right time and unbeneficial words never.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him say what is true, let him say what is pleasing, let him utter no disagreeable truth, and let him utter no agreeable falsehood; that is the eternal law.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu’s famous rule makes pleasantness a requirement of dharmic speech alongside truth.
hinduism.tie_back: This is an instructive contrast. Manu forbids ‘disagreeable truth’, while the Kural permits unpleasant words if they are useful. Both refuse to let empty pleasantness replace substance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs values honest words that hurt over flattering ones that betray.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts accept painful words when they serve a real purpose.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asks believers for qawlan sadīdan, speech that is straight, sound and on target.
islam.tie_back: Both texts define good speech by soundness and aim rather than by softness. A straight word may not please, but it is never empty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands tochacha (rebuke), which is unwelcome speech that is still a duty because it benefits the hearer.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts license unpleasant words when they are genuinely beneficial.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, unbeneficial, unendearing & disagreeable to others, he does not say them. … In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, but unendearing & disagreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha sets out a grid of truth, benefit and pleasantness: unbeneficial words are never spoken, while beneficial but unpleasant words may be spoken at the right time.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s ranking: unpleasant words may be spoken if they are beneficial, and unbeneficial words are never spoken.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhaya Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wise, fearless monks consider even a rough instruction as a benefit, but the fools hate it, though it produces patience and purity of mind.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana teaches that a teacher's harsh but useful words are a real benefit to the wise, even if fools resent them.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar allows the worthy to say unpleasant things if they must but never useless ones, and the Jain text values rough words that do real good over pleasant ones that do none.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Nanak speaks the Word of Truth; he proclaims the Truth at this, the right time.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Tilang, sung during Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak openly voiced painful and unwelcome truths about the violence he saw, and closes by saying he speaks the truth because the hour requires it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural allows the worthy to say what is not pleasing, but never what is useless; Guru Nanak's hymn is a model of speech that is hard to hear yet full of purpose.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The blind seer Tiresias at first refuses to speak, then tells King Oedipus the painful truth that he himself is the polluter of Thebes, and is abused for it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Tiresias’ words are deeply unwelcome, but they are the only words that can save the city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tiresias shows the Kural’s concession in action: the wise may say what is unpleasant, provided it carries real weight.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I am that gadfly which God has given the state and all day long and in all places am always fastening upon you, arousing and persuading and reproaching you.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates defends his irritating questions as a benefit to Athens, like a gadfly stinging a sluggish horse.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates’ speech is famously unpleasant yet purposeful, which fits the Kural’s ideal of the sage who may sting but never babble.

real_life_example.event_title: Ignaz Semmelweis orders doctors to wash their hands
real_life_example.event: At the First Obstetrical Clinic of Vienna General Hospital, where women attended by doctors and medical students died of childbed fever far more often than those in the midwives' clinic, the Hungarian physician Ignaz Semmelweis concluded that doctors coming from autopsies were carrying the cause on their hands. In 1847 he required doctors and students to disinfect their hands with a chlorinated lime solution before examining patients, and the death rate fell sharply. His message was unwelcome to many colleagues, his ideas were largely rejected during his lifetime, and he returned to Pest in 1850; they were accepted only after his death.
real_life_example.explanation: Semmelweis told his profession something it did not want to hear, and it saved lives wherever it was put into practice.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural allows the worthy to say what is unpleasant but never what is useless, and Semmelweis's unpopular instruction was entirely unpleasant to its hearers and entirely useful.

tamil:
அரும்பயன் ஆயும் அறிவினார் சொல்லார்
பெரும்பயன் இல்லாத சொல்.
transliteration:
Arumpayan aayum arivinaar sollaar,
Perumpayan illaadha sol.
meaning: Wise people who look for rare and valuable benefits never say words that do not bring great benefit.
elementary: If you are hunting for gold, you don’t fill your bag with ordinary pebbles. Wise people are like gold-hunters with their words: they only say things that are really valuable, and they don’t waste words on things that don’t matter.
university: The couplet raises the standard. It is not enough for words to have some பயன் (benefit): the wise refuse words lacking பெரும்பயன் (perumpayan, ‘great benefit’). The rhyme of அரும்பயன் (arumpayan, ‘rare benefit’) with பெரும்பயன் binds the two halves together: those who investigate (ஆயும், aayum) rare and valuable ends apply the same selectiveness to their own speech. This describes an intellectual temperament as much as an ethical rule, since the discerning mind that weighs what is worth pursuing also weighs what is worth saying. The Upanishadic command to ‘leave off other words’, Shammai’s ‘speak little’ and Homer’s portrait of Menelaus as ‘a man of few words’ all praise the same economy of speech.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Know him alone as the Self, and leave off other words! He is the bridge of the Immortal.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad points the seeker to the one supremely valuable truth and tells him to drop all other talk.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts link devotion to the highest good with abandoning lesser speech. The Kural’s ‘rare benefit’ is here the Self.
hinduism.source: Mundaka Upanishad II.2.5 (trans. F. Max Müller, SBE 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs equates wisdom with restraint in speech.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts define the wise by what they do not say.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they who turn away from ill speech.”
islam.explanation: Among the defining marks of the successful believers is that they turn away from laghw, vain and pointless talk.
islam.tie_back: Both texts make refusing worthless speech a trait of those who pursue the highest good.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shammai used to say: make your [study of the] Torah a fixed practice; speak little, but do much.”
judaism.explanation: Shammai teaches that a serious person keeps words few and deeds many.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts describe the person devoted to what matters as sparing with words.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 1:15 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is not wise because one speaks much. He who is peaceable, friendly and fearless is called wise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada separates wisdom from talkativeness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts define wisdom against mere volume of speech.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One should always be meek, and not be talkative in the presence of the wise; one should acquire valuable knowledge, and avoid what is worthless.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana joins restraint in speech with the pursuit of valuable knowledge and the avoidance of what is worthless.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the wise who seek rare benefits never speak words without great benefit, and the Jain verse likewise pairs holding back talk with seeking what is valuable and leaving the worthless aside.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, only one thing is of any account: everything else is useless babbling and idle talk in ego.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Asa ki Vaar, Guru Nanak says that only the praise and remembrance of the One counts, and all other talk is the idle babble of haumai (ego).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the wise, who seek rare and great benefit, never speak words lacking great benefit; Guru Nanak likewise holds that only words of the highest worth count and the rest is ego's chatter.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The speech of Menelaus ran trippingly on the tongue; he did not say much, for he was a man of few words, but he spoke very clearly and to the point.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Antenor recalls the Greek embassy to Troy: Menelaus said little, but every word counted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Menelaus embodies the Kural’s ideal: few words, each carrying real weight.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The garrulous listen to nobody, for they are always talking. And this is the first symptom of their ailment: looseness of the tongue become impotence of the ears.”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch notes that the chatterer, whom Nature gave one tongue but two ears, has stopped listening and so has stopped learning.
philosophy.tie_back: In the Kural, the wise who seek rare benefit weigh their words, and in Plutarch the babbler has stopped weighing and listening at all.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On Talkativeness (De garrulitate) 1, 502b-c (trans. W. C. Helmbold, Loeb)

real_life_example.event_title: Einstein's short paper on mass and energy
real_life_example.event: Albert Einstein, then working at the Swiss patent office in Bern, sent the journal Annalen der Physik a brief follow-up to his paper on special relativity, titled Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content? In only a few pages he argued that a body that gives off energy as radiation loses mass in proportion, the result now written as E = mc squared, although the paper does not set out the equation in that form. It became one of the most consequential short papers in the history of science.
real_life_example.explanation: A handful of pages carried an idea that reshaped physics and later underpinned both nuclear energy and our understanding of how stars shine.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who seek rare and precious benefits speak only words of great benefit, and Einstein's brief paper contained almost nothing but its essential argument.

tamil:
பொருள்தீர்ந்த பொச்சாந்துஞ் சொல்லார் மருள்தீர்ந்த
மாசறு காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Poruldheerndha pochchaandhum sollaar maruldheerndha,
Maasaru kaatchi yavar.
meaning: People who see clearly, with no confusion or fault in their thinking, will not speak meaningless words, not even by mistake.
elementary: Some people are so careful and clear-headed that even when they are tired or distracted, they don’t blurt out silly things. This kural says that people whose minds are truly clean and clear don’t say empty words even by accident.
university: The couplet balances two phrases built on தீர்ந்த (theerndha, ‘ended, freed of’). The speech is பொருள்தீர்ந்த (‘emptied of meaning’), and the speakers are மருள்தீர்ந்த (‘freed of delusion’). The symmetry suggests that meaningless words can only come from a mind that still holds some confusion. பொச்சாந்தும் (pochchaandhum, ‘even through forgetfulness/heedlessness’) raises the standard from deliberate restraint to spontaneous purity: the மாசறு காட்சியவர் (maasaru kaatchiyavar, ‘those of flawless insight’) do not need to police their tongues, because nothing empty is left in them to come out. Pochchaappu (heedlessness) later gets a chapter of its own (ch. 54, பொச்சாவாமை), which shows how central vigilance is to Valluvar’s ethics. There is a close parallel in the Buddhist portrait of the freed person whose ‘speech is calm’ and in James’s ‘perfect man’ who ‘offends not in word’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Serenity of thought, gentleness, silence, self-control, and purity of purpose—all these are declared as austerity of the mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna places mauna (silence) among the disciplines of a purified mind, not just of the tongue.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts trace restrained speech back to a purified, clear mind. Where the mind is clear, silence comes naturally.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.”
christianity.explanation: James makes perfect control of speech the mark of spiritual maturity.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts describe a rare perfection in which one does not slip in speech at all.

islam.quote_or_event: “A slave of Allah may utter a word without thinking whether it is right or wrong, he may slip down in the Fire as far away a distance equal to that between the east.”
islam.explanation: The hadith warns about the unconsidered word spoken carelessly.
islam.tie_back: The Kural praises the clear-minded, who do not slip even through heedlessness, and the hadith shows the danger of the heedless word they avoid.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One who wakes up at night, or walks on the way alone and turns his heart to idle matters, behold, this man is mortally guilty.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hananiah ben Hakinai holds that even unguarded, solitary moments must not drift into idleness.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts require vigilance even in unguarded moments; the Kural says the clear-minded do not lapse even in forgetfulness.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:4 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Calm is his thought, calm his speech, and calm his deed, who, truly knowing, is wholly freed, perfectly tranquil and wise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada describes the arahant, freed by true knowledge, whose speech has become calm.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts describe a mind freed of delusion, from which calm, meaningful speech follows without effort.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Possessing perfect wisdom, a sage always vanquishes (his passions); he correctly expounds the Law; he never neglects even the smallest (duty); he is neither angry nor proud.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga describes the sage of perfect wisdom as one whose teaching is always correct and who never slips even in the smallest duty.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those whose vision is free of delusion never speak meaningless words, even by a slip, and the Jain sage of perfect wisdom likewise speaks the Law correctly and never neglects even the smallest duty.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.2.2.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without the Name, all other praise and speech is insipid and tasteless.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Gauree, Guru Ram Das teaches that to one who knows the Naam, every other kind of talk loses its taste.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those whose vision is free of delusion will not speak meaningless words even by a slip; Guru Ram Das likewise says the awakened find all speech without the Name empty.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 301, Raag Gauree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pythagorean tradition held that new disciples kept a strict silence (echemythia) for up to five years before they could speak in the school, training the mind before the tongue.
greek_mythology.explanation: The semi-legendary Pythagorean discipline treated long silence as purification that prepared a person for wise speech.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both traditions make disciplined speech the product of long mental purification, so that careless words no longer arise.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives 8.10 (Pythagoras); cf. Iamblichus, Life of Pythagoras

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The world would be much happier, if men were as fully able to keep silence as they are to speak. Experience abundantly shows that men can govern anything more easily than their tongues.”
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza notes how rarely people control their speech, as evidence of how far they are from real freedom.
philosophy.tie_back: Spinoza says ordinary minds cannot govern their tongues, and the Kural says the delusion-free do so effortlessly. Both link command of speech to clarity of mind.
philosophy.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics III, Prop. 2, Scholium (trans. R. H. M. Elwes)

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi's weekly day of silence
real_life_example.date: Weekly, over many years of his public life (died 1948)
real_life_example.event: For many years Mohandas Gandhi kept every Monday as a day of silence, during which he did not speak and, when he had to communicate, wrote notes instead, even when a meeting with an official could not be avoided. He kept the practice through the busiest years of the independence struggle and used the day for writing and other work. Gandhi himself allowed only rare exceptions, such as severe pain or comforting someone in distress.
real_life_example.explanation: The weekly silence was a deliberate discipline of speech, kept by one of the busiest public figures of his age.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes people of clear vision who never utter meaningless words even through heedlessness, and Gandhi's silent Mondays were a regular training in saying nothing that was not needed.

tamil:
சொல்லுக சொல்லிற் பயனுடைய சொல்லற்க
சொல்லிற் பயனிலாச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Solluka sollir payanudaiya sollarka,
Sollir payanilaach sol.
meaning: Of all the words you could say, say only the useful ones. Never say the ones that are useless.
elementary: Before you speak, ask yourself one simple question: “Will this help?” If the answer is yes, say it. If the answer is no, don’t. That’s the whole rule, and this kural says it in the simplest way possible.
university: The chapter closes with one of the most famous sound-patterns in the Kural. Forms of சொல் (sol, ‘word/speak’) occur five times: சொல்லுக (‘speak’), சொல்லில் (‘among words’, twice), சொல்லற்க (‘do not speak’) and சொல் (‘word’). The only thing that changes between the positive and negative halves is பயனுடைய / பயனிலா (‘useful / useless’). The form enacts the content: a couplet made almost entirely of the word ‘word’ shows perfect economy, with nothing wasted. Solomon Pappaiah reads பயன் as the three classical aims of life (aram, porul, inbam), which ties the rule to the whole structure of the Kural. The maxim sums up the chapter as a single test that can be applied to every utterance, much like Epictetus’s ‘speak merely what is necessary’ and the hadith ‘speak good or keep quiet’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Silence, it is said, is better than speech, if speak you must, then it is better to say the truth; if truth is to be said, it is better to say what is agreeable; and if what is agreeable is to be said, then it is better to say what is consistent with morality.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura, quoting the sage Atreya, sets out a graded ladder in which silence is the baseline and each kind of speech must improve on it.
hinduism.tie_back: In both texts, speech is only justified when it adds value that silence would not. The Kural makes benefit the test, and Vidura adds truth, agreeableness and dharma.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, section 36 (Vidura Niti) (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes the hearer’s benefit (edification) the test of Christian speech.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts give the same two-part rule: speak only what builds up and withhold everything else.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet gives a simple binary test for all speech: say what is good (khayr) or stay silent.
islam.tie_back: The hadith and the Kural state the same two-part rule: speak the beneficial and never the rest.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One who engages in idle chatter … violates a positive commandment, as it is stated: And you shall talk of them; talk of them and not of other matters.”
judaism.explanation: Rava reads Deuteronomy 6:7 (‘you shall talk of them’) as a command to fill speech with Torah and a prohibition of devarim beteilim (idle words).
judaism.tie_back: Both texts give a positive command to speak what is valuable and a matching ban on idle words.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 19b (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz trans., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better than a thousand useless words is one useful word, hearing which one attains peace.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada measures words entirely by their usefulness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts rest on the same useful/useless contrast.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Well considering (what one is to say), speaking with precision, one should employ language in moderation and restraint.”
jainism.explanation: The Ācārāṅga's lecture on modes of speech requires that every word be thought over first and spoken precisely, sparingly and with restraint.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar closes the chapter with the rule to speak only useful words and never useless ones, and the Ācārāṅga sets out the same rule for monks: think first, then speak precisely, sparingly and with restraint.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.4.1.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor. Harsh words bring only grief. Listen, O foolish and ignorant mind!”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Sri Raag, Guru Nanak sets two kinds of speech side by side: words that bring honour are approved, while fikaa words bring only ruin and grief.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural closes the chapter by pairing a command to speak only useful words with a ban on useless ones; Guru Nanak builds the same two-sided rule, approving one kind of speech and rejecting the other.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The best treasure a man can have is a sparing tongue, and the greatest pleasure, one that moves orderly; for if you speak evil, you yourself will soon be worse spoken of.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s farmer-poet counts a sparing, well-ordered tongue as a person’s best possession.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts praise economy and order in speech as the governing rule.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 719-721 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be for the most part silent, or speak merely what is necessary, and in few words.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus gives the Stoic student a rule for speech: silence by default, with only necessary words.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts lay down a rule of speech governed by necessity and usefulness.

real_life_example.event_title: Winston Churchill's memorandum on Brevity
real_life_example.event: In the middle of the Battle of Britain, Prime Minister Winston Churchill issued a War Cabinet memorandum titled Brevity, now held at the UK National Archives as CAB 67/8/11. He asked ministers and officials to make their reports much shorter and to set out the real point concisely. He argued that the time saved would be great and that the discipline of stating the real point briefly would help clearer thinking.
real_life_example.explanation: At a moment of national danger, Churchill treated wasted words as a real cost to the war effort.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's rule is to speak only the words that are useful and never those that are useless, which is almost exactly what Churchill ordered his officials to do.

tamil:
தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்
தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Theevinaiyaar anjaar vizhumiyaar anjuvar,
Theevinai ennum serukku.
meaning: Bad people are not afraid of the pride that comes from doing wrong. Truly good people are afraid of it.
elementary: Imagine two kids near a hot stove. One has touched it so many times he doesn’t even flinch anymore. The other is careful and keeps her hands away. This kural says good people are like the careful kid — they are scared of doing bad things, while people who do bad things all the time have stopped being scared at all.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a paradox: fear, usually a mark of weakness, is here the mark of excellence (விழுமியார், “the eminent”). The object of dread is not punishment but “the pride called evil-doing” (தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு) — Parimelazhagar reads செருக்கு as the intoxication or swagger that evil deeds produce, which dulls conscience the more one indulges it. The couplet thus describes moral desensitization: habitual wrongdoers lose the very faculty of dread that protects the noble. This anticipates what Buddhist ethics calls hiri-ottappa (moral shame and moral dread) and Jewish ethics calls yirat cheit (fear of sin) — fear reconceived as a moral sense rather than cowardice.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Janārdana, although these men, overtaken by greed, see no fault in killing one’s family or quarreling with friends, why should we, with knowledge of the sin, engage in these acts?”
hinduism.explanation: On the battlefield Arjuna contrasts the Kauravas, whose greed has blinded them to sin, with himself and his brothers, who can still see the wrongness of what they are about to do and recoil from it.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly Valluvar’s split: the wrongdoers feel no dread, while those with moral sight fear the sin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate.”
christianity.explanation: Wisdom speaks in Proverbs, defining true reverence as a hatred of evil — and naming pride and arrogance first among the things hated.
christianity.tie_back: Links holy fear, the avoidance of evil, and the rejection of pride — the same triad as the Kural’s “dread of the pride of evil.”

islam.quote_or_event: “Only those fear Allah, from among His servants, who have knowledge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an ties genuine fear of God (khashyah) to knowledge: the more one truly understands, the more one is moved to reverent caution about wrongdoing.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes fear a sign of the elevated, not the base — those with understanding fear; the heedless do not.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone whose fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom is enduring, but anyone whose wisdom precedes his fear of sin, his wisdom is not enduring.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa makes yirat cheit — fear of sin — the foundation on which lasting wisdom must stand.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts treat fear of wrongdoing as the defining trait of the truly excellent person.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, these two bright qualities guard the world. Which two? Conscience & concern.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names hiri (conscience/moral shame) and ottappa (concern/moral dread of the results of wrong action) as the ‘guardians of the world’ that hold society together.
buddhism.tie_back: Ottappa is almost a technical name for Valluvar’s theme: the dread of evil deeds that the noble keep and the corrupt have lost.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.9, Lokapala Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Papabhiru : Apprehensive of sin.”
jainism.explanation: Among the thirty-five qualities Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra lists for the ideal Jain householder is being afraid of sin; Sangave notes that one who keeps these rules becomes, among other things, 'afraid of sinning.'
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar makes dread of evil the mark of the noble, and the Jain ideal householder is defined in the same way, by his apprehension of sin.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of thirty-five qualities of the ideal householder, item 3, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, Jaina Ethics (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You people are unconscious; you should be afraid of sin.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Gauree, Guru Tegh Bahadur tells the heedless that what they lack is a healthy dread of wrongdoing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those steeped in evil feel no fear of it while the truly noble do; Guru Tegh Bahadur likewise treats fearlessness about sin as a sign of being spiritually asleep.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 220, Raag Gauree, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod’s account of the degenerate Iron Age, the goddesses Aidos (Shame) and Nemesis (Righteous Indignation) wrap themselves in white robes and abandon humankind for Olympus, leaving mortals with bitter sorrows and no defense against evil.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Hesiod, a healthy society depends on Aidos and Nemesis — an inner shame at wrongdoing and a dread of the retribution it provokes. When people stop feeling them, moral collapse follows.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s point that losing the dread of evil is itself the sign of the wicked; the noble keep Aidos.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “This sign, which is a kind of voice, first began to come to me when I was a child; it always forbids but never commands me to do anything which I am going to do.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates describes his daimonion, an inner warning that checks him before wrong or unwise action — an early philosophical image of conscience as a restraining dread.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s noble person is one whose inner alarm still sounds; Socrates is the classic example of such a person.

real_life_example.event_title: Andrei Sakharov turns against nuclear testing
real_life_example.event: Andrei Sakharov, a physicist who had played a leading part in building the Soviet hydrogen bomb, became concerned in 1957 about the biological hazards of radioactive fallout from nuclear tests and began campaigning to halt or limit testing, which brought him into conflict with Nikita Khrushchev in 1961. He later said he had helped promote the 1963 treaty banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and under water. After a 1968 essay of his was published abroad he was removed from weapons work, and in 1975 he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, which the Soviet authorities did not allow him to travel to Oslo to receive.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the people best placed to understand the harm his work could do was the one who grew most alarmed by it, at real cost to his own career and safety.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the noble dread evil deeds while hardened wrongdoers feel no fear, and Sakharov's growing dread of the harm his weapons could cause marked him out among those around him.

tamil:
தீயவை தீய பயத்தலால் தீயவை
தீயினும் அஞ்சப் படும்.
transliteration:
Theeyavai theeya payaththalaal theeyavai,
Theeyinum anjap padum.
meaning: Bad deeds lead to more bad things, so we should fear bad deeds even more than we fear fire.
elementary: Fire can burn you, so you keep away from it. But a bad deed is even worse than fire — one bad deed leads to another bad deed, and then another, like sparks starting more fires. So we should be even more careful about doing bad things than about touching fire.
university: The couplet is built on a deliberate pun: தீ means both “evil” and “fire,” and தீயவை (“evil things”) sounds like “fiery things.” Valluvar’s argument is comparative — fire burns only what it touches and can be put out, but evil propagates, generating consequences for both the victim and the doer (Pulavar Kesigan: ‘to others and to oneself’). Evil is therefore self-replicating in a way fire only resembles. The same insight — that wrongdoing breeds more wrongdoing — appears in the rabbinic dictum that ‘one transgression leads to another’ and in Aeschylus’s image of the evil deed that begets its own offspring.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Thus the wise living entity’s pure consciousness becomes covered by his eternal enemy in the form of lust, which is never satisfied and which burns like fire.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names desire (kāma) as the root that drives people to sin, likening it to a fire that only grows the more it is fed.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts use fire as the image of evil’s self-feeding growth; the Kural goes further, saying evil is worse than fire.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James describes a chain of generation: desire gives birth to sin, and sin, fully grown, gives birth to death.
christianity.tie_back: Same logic as ‘evil yields evil’ — wrongdoing is fertile and its offspring are destructive.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, those who devour the property of orphans unjustly are only consuming into their bellies fire. And they will be burned in a Blaze.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes an evil deed as literally being fire in disguise: the unjust gain that seems like nourishment is burning the wrongdoer from within.
islam.tie_back: Like Valluvar, it equates evil with fire — and implies that evil is the more dangerous because it is not recognized as fire.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For one commandment leads to another commandment, and transgression leads to another transgression; For the reward for performing a commandment is another commandment and the reward for committing a transgression is a transgression.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Azzai observes that sin has momentum: each transgression makes the next one easier, so the ‘wage’ of sin is simply more sin.
judaism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s reasoning — evil is to be feared because it produces more evil.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, an evil deed committed does not immediately bear fruit, like milk that does not turn sour all at once. But smoldering, it follows the fool like fire covered by ashes.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares an unripened evil deed to embers hidden under ash — quiet for now, but still burning and certain to scorch the one who carries it.
buddhism.tie_back: Fire and evil are fused in one image, and the danger is precisely that evil keeps burning after the act.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Even such a thing as ghee when approached by the flame of fire will cause intolerable pain by fierce burning; of many bad actions will they become guilty who, though not crooked, become so, and associate with those who are bad.”
jainism.explanation: In its chapter titled 'The fear of misconduct', the Tamil Jain Nālaṭiyār uses the image of fire to warn that one wrong step, here keeping bad company, draws a person into many more bad actions.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says evil should be feared more than fire because it breeds more evil; the Nālaṭiyār also pairs fire with the way wrongdoing multiplies.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 13 ('The fear of misconduct'), st. 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Virtue and vice do not come by mere words; actions repeated, over and over again, are engraved on the soul. You shall harvest what you plant.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak teaches that each deed leaves its mark on the soul, so that repeated actions shape a person and bear their own harvest.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says evil must be feared more than fire because evil gives rise to further evil; Guru Nanak likewise shows deeds engraving themselves and growing into their own crop.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 20, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “It is the evil deed that afterwards begets more iniquity like its own breed; but when a house is righteous, the lot of its children is blessed always.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The chorus of Agamemnon reflects on the curse of the house of Atreus, in which each crime (Atreus’s feast, Iphigenia’s sacrifice) breeds the next murder.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same principle as ‘evil yields evil’, dramatized across generations.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Socrates defends the startling thesis that doing injustice is the greatest of evils — worse even than suffering it — because it corrupts the soul of the doer.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, physical harms like burns or wounds damage only the body, while wrongdoing damages the soul, the most precious thing a person has.
philosophy.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s ranking: evil is to be feared more than fire because its harm is deeper and self-inflicted.

real_life_example.event_title: The Watergate cover-up brings down President Nixon
real_life_example.event: After men connected to President Richard Nixon's re-election committee were caught breaking into the Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate complex in June 1972, Nixon and his aides worked to hide the White House's links to the break-in. A recording of 23 June 1972 captured Nixon approving a plan to have the CIA ask the FBI to halt its investigation. When the Supreme Court ordered the tapes released, this conversation became public in August 1974, his remaining support collapsed, and he resigned on 9 August 1974, the only US president to do so.
real_life_example.explanation: Watergate is the classic example of a cover-up doing more damage than the original wrongdoing, as each new concealment created new offences.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says evil must be feared more than fire because it gives birth to further evil, and the Watergate break-in led step by step to obstruction of justice and the downfall of a presidency.

tamil:
அறிவினுள் எல்லாந் தலையென்ப தீய
செறுவார்க்கும் செய்யா விடல்.
transliteration:
Arivinul ellaan thalaiyenba theeya,
Seruvaarkkum seyyaa vidal.
meaning: Wise people say the highest wisdom of all is not doing bad things even to those who hurt us.
elementary: If someone knocks down your sandcastle, you might want to knock down theirs. But the smartest thing — smarter than anything in any book — is to not do something bad back. Being kind even to someone who was mean to you is the cleverest thing of all.
university: Here Valluvar relocates the virtue of non-retaliation from the realm of emotion (forgiveness) into the realm of intellect: it is the ‘head’ (தலை) of all knowledge. செறுவார் means those who actively hurt or oppress one — genuine enemies, not mere irritants. The claim is that true intelligence sees what the vengeful cannot: that returning evil only multiplies it (the logic of 202) and binds the retaliator to the same consequences. The idea stands in striking agreement with Socrates in the Crito, who argues on rational grounds that one must never return wrong for wrong.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant, always satisfied, self-controlled… such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the ideal devotee as without hatred toward any being (adveṣṭā sarva-bhūtānām) and tolerant (kṣamī) — a person who does not return hostility.
hinduism.tie_back: Shares the ideal of non-hostility toward all, including those who harm; less explicit about enemies than the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Recompense to no man evil for evil… Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul instructs believers never to repay wrong with wrong, but to defeat evil by doing good.
christianity.tie_back: A direct parallel: do no evil even to those who have done evil to you.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches responding to hostility with something better than the offense, promising that enmity can turn into friendship.
islam.tie_back: Same refusal to answer harm with harm, plus a practical wisdom about its effects.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids taking revenge or even nursing a grudge, grounding the command in love of neighbour.
judaism.tie_back: Forbids retaliation, the core of the Kural; Torah’s scope is framed around one’s own people.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha presents non-retaliation as a law of nature: returning hatred only perpetuates it; only non-hatred ends it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, frames non-retaliation as insight into how things work — the highest wisdom.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk should not be angry if beaten, nor should he therefore entertain sinful thoughts; knowing patience to be the highest good, a monk should meditate on the Law. If somebody strikes a restrained, resigned Śramaṇa somewhere, he should think: ‘I have not lost my life.’”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's teaching on the 'troubles' (parīṣaha) a monk must bear includes being beaten. He must not answer with anger, or even with sinful thoughts, toward the one who strikes him.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls refusing to harm even those who harm us the highest wisdom; the Jain canon likewise calls patience under attack 'the highest good' and forbids returning evil even in thought.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.26–27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the seeker to repay those who do evil with good and to keep anger out of the heart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls refraining from evil even toward those who harm us the highest of all wisdom; Farid gives the same counsel, and goes further by asking for active good in return.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the close of the Oresteia, Athena persuades the Furies to abandon the endless blood-for-blood vendetta of the house of Atreus and accept a court of justice, transforming them into the ‘Kindly Ones’.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth mostly celebrates vengeance; the Eumenides is its famous turning point, where wisdom (Athena) breaks the cycle of retaliation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Next-best match: wisdom ending retaliation, though via public justice rather than personal non-retaliation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to any one, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
philosophy.explanation: In prison, Socrates reasons with Crito that since doing wrong is never right, returning wrong for wrong can never be right either.
philosophy.tie_back: Exact parallel, reached — as in the Kural — through reason rather than sentiment.

real_life_example.event_title: Herbert Hoover's American Relief Administration feeds famine-stricken Soviet Russia
real_life_example.event: In 1921, after the writer Maxim Gorky appealed abroad for help with a severe famine in Soviet Russia, Herbert Hoover, head of the American Relief Administration, negotiated an agreement to organise relief inside the country, even though the United States and the Soviet government were deeply hostile to each other. Funded by voluntary contributions and a 20 million dollar appropriation from the US Congress, the ARA's kitchens were feeding nearly 11 million people a day by the summer of 1922, and it also supplied medicine to thousands of hospitals. Historians still debate the mission's politics, but its scale is well documented.
real_life_example.explanation: A country that regarded the Soviet regime as an enemy nevertheless fed millions of its people in their time of need.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls it the highest wisdom to refrain from doing harm even to those who are hostile to us, and the ARA went further, doing large-scale good in a country whose government the United States opposed.

tamil:
மறந்தும் பிறன்கேடு சூழற்க சூழின்
அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு.
transliteration:
Marandhum pirankedu soozharka soozhin,
Aransoozhum soozhndhavan kedu.
meaning: Do not plan someone else's ruin, not even without thinking. If you do, goodness itself will plan the ruin of the one who planned it.
elementary: It’s like throwing a boomerang at someone — it comes flying back at you. This kural says even thinking up a plan to hurt someone is like that boomerang: goodness itself will turn the plan around so it lands on you.
university: The verb சூழ் (‘to plan, surround, encompass’) is repeated three times, mirroring the plot and counter-plot: the schemer ‘surrounds’ another’s ruin, and Aram (Virtue, personified by Solomon Pappaiah as அறக்கடவுள், the deity of Virtue) ‘surrounds’ the schemer’s ruin in turn. Note the extreme standard set by மறந்தும் (‘even in forgetfulness’): not merely the deed but even a passing intention to harm is forbidden. The textual tradition is worth noting — Project Madurai and thirukkural.net print அறஞ்சூழம், but the standard reading followed by commentators and kuraltheni.com is அறஞ்சூழும் (‘will plot’). The ‘plot that recoils on the plotter’ is a near-universal motif, from Haman’s gallows to Hesiod’s ‘evil planned harms the plotter most’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata’s lac-house episode, Duryodhana sends his agent Purochana to build a flammable house at Varanavata and burn the Pandavas alive; forewarned by Vidura, the Pandavas escape through a tunnel, and Purochana perishes in the very fire prepared for them.
hinduism.explanation: The agent of the murderous plot is consumed by his own scheme, while the intended victims survive.
hinduism.tie_back: A narrative illustration of the Kural: the plot to ruin others encompasses the plotter.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha Parva (Ganguli; paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that schemes meant to trap others become traps for the schemer.
christianity.tie_back: Direct parallel to the plot rebounding on the plotter.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Due to] arrogance in the land and plotting of evil; but the evil plot does not encompass except its own people.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an states as a divine law that evil scheming closes in on those who devise it.
islam.tie_back: Even the verb matches: the Arabic yaḥīqu (‘encompasses’) corresponds to Valluvar’s சூழ் (‘surround, encompass’).

judaism.quote_or_event: “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai.”
judaism.explanation: Haman plotted to destroy Mordecai and the Jews of Persia; his plan was reversed and he died on the gallows he had built for his enemy.
judaism.tie_back: The classic Jewish story of the plot recoiling on the plotter.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like fine dust thrown against the wind, evil falls back upon that fool who offends an inoffensive, pure and guiltless man.”
buddhism.explanation: Harm aimed at the innocent blows back into the face of the one who threw it.
buddhism.tie_back: Same boomerang structure as the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to kill. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to tyrannise over. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to torment… The righteous man who lives up to these sentiments, does therefore neither kill nor cause others to kill (living beings). He should not intentionally cause the same punishment for himself.”
jainism.explanation: The Ācārāṅga tells the would-be harmer that his intended victim is like himself. Jacobi's note explains that the pain one causes others in this life one will suffer in the next.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar warns that whoever plots another's ruin brings ruin on himself; the Ācārāṅga addresses the person who 'intends' harm and says the punishment comes back to the plotter.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.5.5.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not harbor evil intentions against others in your mind, and you shall not be troubled, O Siblings of Destiny, O friends.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan forbids even keeping thoughts of harm toward others in the mind, and says that one who does not will be spared trouble himself.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural forbids plotting another's ruin even absent-mindedly, warning that Virtue will plot the plotter's ruin; Guru Arjan likewise bans evil intent at the level of thought and ties one's own peace to it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He does mischief to himself who does mischief to another, and evil planned harms the plotter most.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that unjust scheming damages the schemer above all.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost a translation of the Kural’s second line.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 265–266 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He who does wrong does wrong against himself. He who acts unjustly acts unjustly to himself, because he makes himself bad.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius argues that the primary victim of wrongdoing is the wrongdoer, whose character is degraded by the act.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the conclusion that harm aimed at others lands on oneself, though via inner corruption rather than cosmic retribution.

real_life_example.event_title: Titus Oates and the invented Popish Plot
real_life_example.event: In 1678 Titus Oates, a former Anglican clergyman, swore to a fictitious Jesuit plot to assassinate King Charles II and put his Catholic brother James, Duke of York, on the throne. In the panic that followed, about 35 innocent people were put to death on the strength of the accusations before inconsistencies in his story came to light. In 1684 the Duke of York won 100,000 pounds in damages from Oates for libel, and after James became king in 1685 Oates was convicted of perjury and severely punished, including the pillory and imprisonment.
real_life_example.explanation: The man who manufactured a plot to destroy others was eventually ruined by the exposure of his own lies.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that whoever plots another's ruin will find virtue itself plotting his ruin in turn, and Oates's invented conspiracy ended in his own conviction and disgrace.

tamil:
இலன்என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க செய்யின்
இலனாகும் மற்றும் பெயர்த்து.
transliteration:
Ilan endru theeyavai seyyarka seyyin,
Ilanaagum matrum peyarththu.
meaning: Do not do bad things because you are poor. If you do, you will only end up even poorer.
elementary: Suppose you have no snacks and you take someone else’s lunch. Now nobody trusts you, nobody shares with you, and you might get in big trouble. You end up with even less than before! Being poor is never a good reason to do bad things — it just makes things worse.
university: Valluvar anticipates the most sympathetic excuse for wrongdoing — need — and refuses it. இலன் (‘one who has not’) is echoed in the second line (இலனாகும், ‘becomes one who has not’) with பெயர்த்து (‘again, once more’), producing a circular structure that mirrors the poverty trap itself: evil committed to escape want returns one to want. Most commentators (Mu. Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read இலன் as ‘poor’; Pulavar Kesigan offers an alternative — ‘do not harm someone because he is without support’ — which shifts the focus to exploiting the weak. On the dominant reading, the couplet makes a hard-headed point: ill-gotten means destroy trust, reputation and future prosperity, and so perpetuate the very lack they were meant to cure.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Being bound by hundreds and thousands of desires, by lust and anger, they secure money by illegal means for sense gratification.”
hinduism.explanation: In describing the ‘demoniac’ nature, the Gita names acquiring wealth by unjust means as a mark of those who then sink into ever-lower states.
hinduism.tie_back: Condemns the unjust pursuit of wealth and links it to downfall; does not address poverty as an excuse.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul redirects the thief — often driven by want — to honest labour, which not only meets need but produces surplus to give away.
christianity.tie_back: Rejects wrongdoing as a remedy for need; honest work, not theft, is the way out of lack.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to immorality, while Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an identifies the fear of poverty as a tool Satan uses to push people into wrongdoing, while God’s promise is abundance.
islam.tie_back: Exposes poverty-as-excuse for evil as a deception; the path of evil does not lead to plenty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me: Lest I be full, and deny thee… or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.”
judaism.explanation: Agur prays to be spared extreme poverty precisely because he knows it tempts a person to steal and so to dishonour God.
judaism.tie_back: Recognizes poverty’s pull toward wrongdoing — the very temptation the Kural forbids yielding to.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta, a king neglects to give to the needy; poverty spreads, a poor man steals, and the king’s response sets off a cascade — theft, violence, lying — in which society grows ever poorer and human life-span declines.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha narrates a spiral in which poverty leads to theft, and theft leads to further degradation and deprivation.
buddhism.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s trap on a social scale: wrongdoing born of want produces more want.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana warns that wealth gained through evil deeds does not last: the one who gains it loses it and is trapped by his own passions.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar refuses poverty as an excuse for evil because the evil-doer only ends up poorer; the Jain text likewise says wealth won by evil is lost.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Aasaa from the time of Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak says of the riches that ruined their owners that such wealth is never gathered without sin and never goes with anyone at death.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural forbids doing evil to escape poverty, warning that it only makes one poorer still; Guru Nanak likewise shows wealth won through sin as a loss in the end.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Wealth should not be seized: god-given wealth is much better; for if a man take great wealth violently and perforce, or if he steal it through his tongue… the gods soon blot him out and make that man’s house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother that riches got by force or fraud are short-lived; the gods reduce such a man’s household.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Same economic moral: unjust gain ends in greater loss.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 320–326 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Polus cites Archelaus, who rose from a slave woman’s son to king of Macedon through murder and treachery, as proof that injustice pays. Socrates replies that Archelaus, far from being enviable, is the most wretched of men.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates rejects the idea that wrongdoing is a rational escape from low estate: the unjust man gains power but loses the true good of his soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Next-best: rejects the excuse of lowly circumstance for evil, and argues the wrongdoer ends up poorer in what matters.

real_life_example.event_title: Nick Leeson's hidden losses break Barings Bank
real_life_example.event: Nick Leeson, a trader for Britain's Barings Bank in Singapore, used a secret error account numbered 88888 to hide his trading losses, which had reached hundreds of millions of Singapore dollars by December 1994. After the Kobe earthquake in January 1995 sent the Tokyo market sharply lower, he kept making larger bets in an attempt to recover, and he fled Singapore on 23 February 1995, after which auditors found losses of about 2.2 billion Singapore dollars.
