Barings, one of Britain's oldest merchant banks, collapsed and was sold to the Dutch group ING for a token one pound, and Leeson was sentenced in Singapore to six and a half years in prison.
real_life_example.explanation: Each attempt to escape a hole by concealment and further risk made the hole deeper, until it swallowed the bank.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that evil done to escape want only makes a person poorer still, and Leeson's hidden trades, made to recover losses, turned a loss into the ruin of the whole bank and of himself.

tamil:
தீப்பால தான்பிறர்கண் செய்யற்க நோய்ப்பால
தன்னை அடல்வேண்டா தான்.
transliteration:
Theeppaala thaanpirarkan seyyarka noippaala,
Thannai adalvendaa thaan.
meaning: If you do not want pain and trouble to hurt you, never do bad things to others.
elementary: If you don’t want anyone to pull your hair, don’t pull anyone else’s hair. This kural says: if you don’t want bad things to happen to you, don’t do bad things to other people.
university: The couplet is built on a pair of parallel compounds — தீப்பால (‘things of the evil kind’) done to others, and நோய்ப்பால (‘things of the suffering kind’) that might afflict oneself — so that the grammar itself enacts reciprocity. Commentators agree the sense is causal: suffering that ‘attacks’ (அடல்) a person is the return of the evil he has done. The argument is prudential and universal — anyone who does not want pain has a reason not to inflict it — which makes this Valluvar’s version of the negative Golden Rule. That rule appears independently in the Mahabharata, in Hillel, in Isocrates, in the Buddha and in the Gospels, one of the most striking convergences in world ethics.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One should never do that to another which one regards as injurious to one’s own self. This, in brief, is the rule of Righteousness.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati tells Yudhishthira that all dharma can be summed up in this one principle, adding that when one injures another, the injured turns and injures the injurer.
hinduism.tie_back: The negative Golden Rule plus the reciprocal consequence — both halves of the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus states the Golden Rule in positive form as the summary of the Law and the Prophets.
christianity.tie_back: Same reciprocity principle, phrased positively where the Kural is negative.

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes wishing for others what one wishes for oneself a condition of true faith.
islam.tie_back: Reciprocity principle at the heart of both; the hadith is framed as faith, the Kural as consequence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation.”
judaism.explanation: Asked to teach the whole Torah on one foot, Hillel summarizes it as the negative Golden Rule.
judaism.tie_back: Same negative formulation as the Kural: don’t do to others what you don’t want to suffer.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; all fear death. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha grounds non-harming in empathy: since everyone fears pain as I do, I should not inflict it.
buddhism.tie_back: Same self-comparison logic underlying the Kural’s reciprocity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “All beings hate pains; therefore one should not kill them. This is the quintessence of wisdom: not to kill anything. Know this to be the legitimate conclusion from the principle of the reciprocity with regard to non-killing.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga bases ahiṃsā on reciprocity: every being shrinks from pain as one does oneself, and the same lecture tells the monk to treat all creatures 'so as he himself would be treated'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells whoever does not want suffering to stop inflicting it on others; the Jain reciprocity principle reasons the same way, from one's own hatred of pain to harming no one.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.9–10, cf. I.11.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, the farmer plants acacia trees, and wishes for grapes. He is spinning wool, but he wishes to wear silk.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid mocks the person who sows thorny deeds and still expects sweet fruit.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says whoever does not wish to be tormented by suffering should never do evil to others; Farid's farmer shows the same folly of wanting a good harvest from a bad sowing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 23 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On his journey to Athens, Theseus defeats a series of brigands by giving each the fate he inflicted on travellers — Sciron is hurled off his own cliff, Procrustes is fitted to his own bed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Plutarch notes that Theseus punished the violent by the very violence they had used on others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Dramatizes the reciprocity the Kural warns of: what you do to others comes back upon you.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Do not do to others that which angers you when they do it to you.”
philosophy.explanation: Isocrates, writing in the voice of King Nicocles, gives his subjects this compact rule of conduct.
philosophy.tie_back: A classical Greek statement of the negative Golden Rule, nearly identical in form to the Kural.

real_life_example.event_title: The fall of Robespierre
real_life_example.event: Maximilien Robespierre was the dominant figure on the Committee of Public Safety during the Reign of Terror of 1793-1794, when many thousands of people were executed as enemies of the Revolution. As opposition to the Terror grew, the National Convention ordered his arrest on 9 Thermidor (27 July 1794). The next day he and 21 of his followers were executed by guillotine at the Place de la Revolution, and his fall opened the Thermidorian Reaction against the Terror.
real_life_example.explanation: The leader most identified with sending others to the scaffold was himself sent there by the same revolutionary machinery.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that whoever does not want suffering should never inflict it on others, and Robespierre met the very fate the Terror had dealt out to so many.

tamil:
எனைப்பகை யுற்றாரும் உய்வர் வினைப்பகை
வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்.
transliteration:
Enaippakai yutraarum uyvar vinaippakai,
Veeyaadhu pinsendru adum.
meaning: People can escape even the worst enemies. But the enemy made by their own bad deeds never goes away. It follows them and destroys them.
elementary: You can hide from a bully, run away, or make friends again. But the bad things you did are like a shadow-monster that follows you everywhere. You can’t hide from it or run away from it, because it comes from you.
university: The contrast is between பகை (enmity) from others and வினைப்பகை (‘the enmity of deeds’) — Valluvar’s striking personification of karma as a relentless personal foe. Human enemies can be escaped, appeased or outlived (உய்வர், ‘they survive’); the enemy that is one’s own past action ‘does not perish’ (வீயாது), ‘goes behind’ (பின்சென்று) and ‘kills’ (அடும்). The image of pursuit is shared with the Greek Erinyes, who hound Orestes across the world, and with the Mahabharata’s calf that unfailingly finds its mother among a thousand cows. The couplet thus answers a common hope of wrongdoers — that they might outrun consequences.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As the young calf is able to recognise its dam from among a thousand cows, so does the previous acts of a man pursue him (in all his different transformations).”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma teaches Yudhishthira that past deeds track down their doer as unerringly as a calf finds its mother.
hinduism.tie_back: Same image of deeds pursuing their doer without fail.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if ye will not do so, behold, ye have sinned against the LORD: and be sure your sin will find you out.”
christianity.explanation: Moses warns the tribes that a broken commitment will not stay hidden: the sin itself will track them down.
christianity.tie_back: Sin as a pursuer that will find the sinner — the Kural’s ‘enmity of deeds’.

islam.quote_or_event: “Paradise is not [obtained] by your wishful thinking nor by that of the People of the Scripture. Whoever does a wrong will be recompensed for it, and he will not find besides Allah a protector or a helper.”
islam.explanation: No identity or wishful hope shields a wrongdoer from the consequences of his wrong.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, denies any escape from the recompense of one’s deeds.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Moreover he saw a skull floating on the face of the water. He said to it: because you drowned others, they drowned you. And in the end, they that drowned you will be drowned.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel reads a floating skull as proof that violent deeds pursue their doers through a chain of consequences.
judaism.tie_back: Deeds track down those who commit them, generation after generation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither in the sky nor in mid-ocean, nor by entering into mountain clefts, nowhere in the world is there a place where one may escape from the results of evil deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists every conceivable hiding place and declares none of them safe from the fruit of evil kamma.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s claim: one may escape anything except one’s own evil deeds.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
jainism.explanation: The burglar is crushed in the very hole he dug. In the same way, the Uttarādhyayana says no one escapes the results of his own deeds, in this life or the next.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says other enmities can be survived but the enmity of one's own evil deeds never dies; the Jain verse makes the same point with a man destroyed by his own handiwork.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever you yourself plant, that is what you shall have to eat; nothing else can be said about this.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Soohee, Guru Amar Das states that a person must eat the fruit of his own planting, and that there is no arguing with this law.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one may survive any human enmity, but the enmity of one's own evil deeds never dies; Guru Amar Das likewise presents the return of one's deeds as a law from which there is no escape.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 755, Raag Soohee, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After killing his mother Clytemnestra, Orestes is hunted across Greece by the Erinyes (Furies), who track him by the scent of blood and will not relent until his case is judged at Athens.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Furies are the Greek personification of guilt’s relentless pursuit of a wrongdoer.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A living image of Valluvar’s ‘enmity of deeds’ that follows and destroys.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The difficulty, my friends, is not in avoiding death, but in avoiding unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.”
philosophy.explanation: Condemned, Socrates says death — the slower runner — has caught him, but unrighteousness — the faster — has overtaken his accusers.
philosophy.tie_back: Wrongdoing as a swift pursuer that overtakes its doers — close to the Kural’s image.

real_life_example.event_title: Adolf Eichmann is found in Argentina and brought to trial
real_life_example.event: Adolf Eichmann, the SS officer who had organised the deportation of Jews to the Nazi camps, escaped justice after the Second World War and was living in Argentina under the name Ricardo Klement. Israeli agents seized him near his home in Buenos Aires on 11 May 1960 and flew him to Israel. His trial in Jerusalem began on 11 April 1961, he was found guilty on all counts in December 1961, and he was executed in 1962.
real_life_example.explanation: Fifteen years of hiding on another continent did not end the consequences of what Eichmann had done.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says people may escape any human enmity, but the enmity of their own evil deeds never dies and follows them to destroy them, and Eichmann's past pursued him across the world.

tamil:
தீயவை செய்தார் கெடுதல் நிழல்தன்னை
வீயாது அடிஉறைந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Theeyavai seydhaar kedudhal nizhaldhannai,
Veeyaadhu adiyuraindh thatru.
meaning: Ruin stays with people who do bad things, just as a person's shadow never leaves them and stays right at their feet.
elementary: Try running away from your shadow — you can’t! It sticks to your feet wherever you go. This kural says trouble sticks to people who do bad things in the same way. It follows them everywhere.
university: Valluvar sharpens the pursuit image of 207 into a simile of inseparability: the shadow does not merely follow but ‘dwells at the feet’ (அடியுறை) — the phrase also evokes a servant or dependent who lives at one’s feet. A shadow is produced by the person himself, so the image implies that ruin is not an external punishment but a by-product of one’s own action, as inseparable as it is self-generated. The text itself shows a scribal wrinkle: Project Madurai and thirukkural.net read ‘அஇஉறைந்’, an evident typographical corruption; ytamizh.com and kuruvirotti.com give அடிஉறைந் (‘dwelling at the feet’), the reading adopted here. The shadow simile famously also appears in the second verse of the Dhammapada, but applied to good deeds.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “According as one acts, according as one behaves, so does he become. The doer of good becomes good, the doer of evil becomes evil.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that deeds do not merely earn outcomes but reshape the very being of the doer.
hinduism.tie_back: Ruin is inseparable from the evil-doer because he becomes what he does — the inner logic behind Valluvar’s shadow.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that consequences are bound to actions as a harvest is bound to its seed.
christianity.tie_back: Like the shadow, the harvest is produced by the doer himself and cannot be separated from him.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [for] every person We have imposed his fate upon his neck, and We will produce for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will encounter spread open.”
islam.explanation: Each person’s deeds and their outcomes are fastened to him like a collar at the neck — impossible to shake off.
islam.tie_back: Close to the shadow image: consequences are attached to the person’s own body.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He who performs one commandment acquires for himself one advocate, and he who commits one transgression acquires for himself one accuser.”
judaism.explanation: Each sin creates a lasting ‘accuser’ that stays with the sinner until judgment.
judaism.tie_back: Each evil act generates a constant companion of ill — a moral shadow.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada opens with a pair of verses: suffering follows evil like the cart-wheel follows the ox, and (verse 2) happiness follows good like a never-departing shadow.
buddhism.tie_back: The same simile family — inseparable following at the feet — used for exactly the same point.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a young calf when let loose among a number of cows naturally seeks out and attaches itself to its own mother, so does the act of a former state of existence seek out and attach itself to him who has performed it.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Nālaṭiyār pictures past karma as a calf that unerringly finds its own mother in a herd: a deed finds and clings to the one who did it.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's shadow that never leaves the evil-doer's feet and the Nālaṭiyār's calf that seeks out its mother are both images of a deed's result that cannot be separated from its doer.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 11 ('The effect of actions done in a former birth'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Dadda: Do not blame anyone else; blame instead your own actions. Whatever I did, for that I have suffered; I do not blame anyone else.”
sikhism.explanation: In the acrostic Patti of Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak teaches that suffering comes from one's own actions and that it is wrong to blame others for it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures ruin clinging to evildoers like a shadow, something produced by the person himself; Guru Nanak likewise traces a person's suffering back to his own deeds.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Aasaa (Patti), Pauri 21, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the opening of the Odyssey, Zeus complains that mortals blame the gods for their misfortunes, when in truth their sorrows beyond fate come from their own reckless folly — citing Aegisthus, who was warned yet did evil and was destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s Zeus insists that much human ruin is self-generated, flowing from one’s own wrongdoing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the shadow, ruin is produced by the person himself, not imposed from outside.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, souls are shown receiving, for every wrong they did in life, a penalty ten times over, before choosing their next lives — carrying their characters with them.
philosophy.explanation: Plato portrays the consequences of injustice as following the soul even beyond death.
philosophy.tie_back: Next-best: consequences cannot be shed, even at death.

real_life_example.event_title: The forged Hitler Diaries
real_life_example.event: In April 1983 the West German magazine Stern announced that it had obtained Adolf Hitler's secret diaries, for which it had paid 9.3 million marks through its reporter Gerd Heidemann. Within weeks the West German Federal Archives established that the notebooks had been produced after the war; they had been forged by Konrad Kujau, and Heidemann had kept millions of marks of the payments for himself. In 1985 a Hamburg court sentenced both men to more than four years in prison.
real_life_example.explanation: A forgery and a fraud that promised fortune and fame brought prison and lasting disgrace on the men who carried them out.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares ruin to a shadow that never leaves the evildoer's feet, and the forgery and fraud brought both men a disgrace that stayed with them for the rest of their lives.

tamil:
தன்னைத்தான் காதல னாயின் எனைத்தொன்றும்
துன்னற்க தீவினைப் பால்.
transliteration:
Thannaiththaan kaadhala naayin enaiththondrum,
Thunnarka theevinaip paal.
meaning: If you truly love yourself, do not go near any bad deed at all, even a small one.
elementary: If you love yourself, you take care of yourself — you brush your teeth and wear a helmet on your bike. This kural says that taking care of yourself also means staying away from bad deeds, even tiny ones, because they end up hurting you.
university: Valluvar here turns self-love (தன்னைத்தான் காதலன்) — often treated as a vice — into the very motive for virtue: anyone who genuinely wishes himself well will keep away from evil. The key intensifier is எனைத்தொன்றும் (‘any whatsoever, however slight’), and the verb துன்னற்க means ‘do not approach or come near’, implying avoidance of the whole territory of evil (தீவினைப் பால், ‘the side/portion of evil’) rather than only its grave acts. This is a form of ‘enlightened self-interest’: properly understood, self-love and morality coincide. Aristotle makes the same argument in Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, and the Dhammapada puts it in almost the same words: ‘If one holds oneself dear, one should diligently watch oneself.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One must deliver himself with the help of his mind, and not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that a person can be his own friend or his own enemy; true self-friendship means raising oneself rather than sinking into what degrades.
hinduism.tie_back: Same idea that genuine self-regard requires restraining oneself from what harms.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Abstain from all appearance of evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to keep away from every form of evil, not only its gross expressions.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘however small’ and ‘do not go near’ — avoiding the whole range of evil.

islam.quote_or_event: “So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, And whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”
islam.explanation: Nothing is too small to count: even an atom’s weight of evil will be shown to its doer.
islam.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s warning against evil ‘however small’ — every speck returns to oneself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And be careful with a light commandment as with a grave one… reckon… the gain [that may be obtained through the committing] of a transgression against the loss [entailed] thereby.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince advises weighing any apparent gain from a sin against the loss it brings, and treating light matters as seriously as grave ones.
judaism.tie_back: Same prudential self-interest and refusal to treat any wrong as trivial.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If one holds oneself dear, one should diligently watch oneself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that genuine self-love expresses itself as vigilant self-guarding against wrong.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a verbatim counterpart of ‘if one loves oneself’ in the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Man! Thou art thy own friend; why wishest thou for a friend beyond thyself? … Man! restraining thyself (from the outward world) ‘thou wilt get free from pain.’”
jainism.explanation: The Ācārāṅga tells each person that he is his own friend, and that restraint, not outside help, frees one from pain.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says anyone who truly loves himself will keep away from every evil; the Ācārāṅga likewise makes the self its own friend, and self-restraint the way to escape suffering.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.3.3.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Why do you do such evil deeds, that you shall have to suffer so? Do not do any evil at all; look ahead to the future with foresight.”
sikhism.explanation: In a pauri of Asa ki Vaar, the Guru argues from plain self-interest: since one must suffer for one's deeds, one should do no evil at all and look ahead.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that anyone who truly loves himself should not go near evil of any kind, however small; the pauri makes the same appeal to self-interest and demands no evil at all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, Pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus’s fable, the young Heracles at a crossroads is approached by Vice, who offers an easy road of pleasure, and Virtue, who offers a steep road; he chooses Virtue as the path that truly benefits him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles’ choice treats virtue as what is genuinely good for oneself, and vice as a flattering path to self-harm.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Next-best: choosing virtue out of true regard for one’s own good.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus, ‘The Choice of Heracles’ in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21–34 (paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Therefore the good man should be a lover of self (for he will both himself profit by doing noble acts, and will benefit his fellows), but the wicked man should not; for he will hurt both himself and his neighbours, following as he does evil passions.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes true self-love, which seeks the noble, from the vulgar kind that grasps at pleasures and harms the self.
philosophy.tie_back: Same insight: rightly understood, loving oneself means keeping away from evil.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, 1169a (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Hansie Cronje is banned from cricket for life
real_life_example.event: Hansie Cronje, the widely admired captain of South Africa's cricket team, initially denied allegations made by New Delhi police in April 2000 that he had taken money from a bookmaker, but then admitted wrongdoing and lost the captaincy. In June 2000 he told the government-appointed King Commission that he had received thousands of dollars from gamblers and bookmakers on five separate occasions between 1996 and 2000, and that he had offered teammates money to underperform. In October 2000 the United Cricket Board of South Africa banned him for life from all its cricket activities.
real_life_example.explanation: Payments that may have seemed small and private ended a celebrated career and turned a national hero into a byword for corruption in sport.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that anyone who truly loves himself will not go near even the smallest evil, and Cronje's acceptance of bookmakers' money destroyed everything he had built for himself.

tamil:
அருங்கேடன் என்பது அறிக மருங்கோடித்
தீவினை செய்யான் எனின்.
transliteration:
Arungedan enbadhu arika marungodith,
Theevinai seyyaan enin.
meaning: Know this: a person who never steps off the right path to do wrong will be safe from ruin.
elementary: When you walk on a narrow bridge, you’re safe as long as you don’t step off the sides. This kural says life is like that bridge: if you never wander off the good path to do bad things, nothing can really ruin you.
university: The chapter closes on a note of assurance rather than warning. அருங்கேடன் combines அரு (‘rare/absent’) with கேடு (‘ruin’): ‘one for whom ruin is rare or impossible’. The pivotal image is மருங்கோடி — ‘running off to the side’ — which pictures righteousness as a straight road and evil as a swerve off it; Parimelazhagar and later commentators read it as ‘deviating from the proper path’. After nine couplets on the consequences of evil, Valluvar states the positive corollary: since ruin comes from one’s own deeds, the one who does not swerve has nothing to fear. The swerve metaphor has close parallels in Proverbs (‘turn not to the right hand nor to the left’), in the Isha Upanishad’s prayer against ‘crooked’ sin, and in Aristotle’s virtue as a mean between deviations.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O god Agni, knowing all things that are manifested, lead us by the good path to the felicity; remove from us the devious attraction of sin.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad’s closing prayer asks the divine to keep us on the good path (supathā) and away from ‘crooked’ (juhurāṇam) sin.
hinduism.tie_back: Same picture of a straight good path and evil as a crooked deviation from it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Turn not to the right hand nor to the left: remove thy foot from evil.”
christianity.explanation: The father in Proverbs urges his son to keep a straight path, since swerving to either side leads into evil.
christianity.tie_back: Nearly identical to மருங்கோடி — evil as a sideways deviation from the straight road.

islam.quote_or_event: “And, [moreover], this is My path, which is straight, so follow it; and do not follow [other] ways, for you will be separated from His way.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an presents righteousness as one straight path and wrongdoing as side-roads that lead away from it.
islam.tie_back: Same straight-path imagery; not straying is the key to safety.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall observe to do therefore as the LORD your God hath commanded you: ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.”
judaism.explanation: Moses commands Israel to keep exactly to the way of the commandments without deviation, followed by the promise that it may go well with them.
judaism.tie_back: Non-deviation leading to well-being — the Kural’s formula.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If on the hand there is no wound, one may carry even poison in it. Poison does not affect one who is free from wounds. For him who does no evil, there is no ill.”
buddhism.explanation: Just as poison cannot enter unbroken skin, harm finds no entry into the life of one who commits no evil.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s assurance: the one who does no evil is safe from ruin.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A careful man who does not injure living beings, is called ‘circumspect’ (samita). The sinful Karman will quit him as water quits raised ground. In thoughts, words, and acts he should do nothing injurious to beings who people the world, whether they move or not.”
jainism.explanation: Kapila's verses promise that sinful karma runs off the careful, harmless person as water runs off high ground, provided he does no harm in thought, word or deed.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar assures the one who never strays from the right path into evil that he is safe from ruin; the Jain text says sinful karma cannot settle on such a person.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 8.9–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The path of the faithful shall never be blocked.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak says that one whose mind accepts and trusts the Name meets no obstacle on life's path.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural assures that one who never swerves from the straight road into evil is safe from ruin; Guru Nanak likewise promises an unblocked road to those who keep faith.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib, Pauri 14, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus warns his son Icarus to fly a middle course between sea and sun; Icarus, exhilarated, swerves upward toward the sun, the wax of his wings melts, and he falls into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes safety depend on keeping to the prescribed course, and ruin the result of veering off it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A vivid picture of மருங்கோடி — ruin comes from swerving from the right path.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Virtue, then, is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean, i.e. the mean relative to us, this being determined by a rational principle.”
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, virtue is a middle course, and vices are deviations to one side (excess) or the other (deficiency).
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the geometry of the Kural: goodness as a line, evil as a veering off it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6, 1106b–1107a (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Lal Bahadur Shastri resigns as Railways Minister
real_life_example.event: Lal Bahadur Shastri, India's Minister for Railways, resigned in 1956 after a major railway accident in Madras state (at Ariyalur) caused heavy loss of life, taking responsibility although he was not personally at fault. His biographer in the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography calls this a demonstration, rare in post-independence Indian politics, of strict responsibility and accountability. He was brought back into the government in 1957, became Home Minister in 1961, and was chosen as India's second Prime Minister on 9 June 1964.
real_life_example.explanation: Shastri's refusal to evade responsibility, and his reputation for simple, honest living, did not end his career but became the foundation of the trust that later made him Prime Minister.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural assures that one who never swerves from the right path is safe from ruin, and Shastri's resignation, far from ruining him, raised him in public esteem.

tamil:
கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு மாரிமாட்டு
என்ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ உலகு.
transliteration:
Kaimmaaru vendaa kadappaadu maarimaattu
En aatrung kollo ulagu.
meaning: Real helping does not expect anything back. What does the world ever give back to the rain cloud that waters it?
elementary: The rain falls on everyone's fields and never sends a bill. Nobody pays the clouds back, and the clouds never ask. This kural says good people help others the same way — just because it is right, not to get something back.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter by naming the virtue kadappaadu — literally ‘what is owed, what cannot be set aside’ — and then startles the reader by saying this obligation expects no repayment. The rhetorical question (en aatrum kollo, ‘what does it do?’) is read by Parimelazhagar as an emphatic ‘nothing at all’: living beings return nothing to the clouds, so those who resemble clouds do not calculate returns either. Manakkudavar glosses kadappaadu directly as oppuravu, defining it as giving suited to one's means to the deserving without seeking recompense. The image deliberately recalls Chapter 2 (Vaan Sirappu, the Excellence of Rain), turning a cosmological fact into an ethical model: the benefactor is a natural force of sustenance, not a party to a contract. The paradox — a duty that is binding yet unrepaid — anticipates later debates about whether generosity can be obligatory without becoming exchange.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, without being attached to the fruits of activities, one should act as a matter of duty, for by working without attachment one attains the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna to do what is right because it is his duty, not because of what he will get out of it.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's kadappaadu, duty here is binding precisely because it ignores any reward.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers to do good and lend without expecting to be paid back, imitating God who is kind even to the ungrateful.
christianity.tie_back: Same ethic of giving that ‘hopes for nothing again,’ modeled on a divine generosity that, like rain, falls on all.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Saying], ‘We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We wish not from you reward or gratitude.’”
islam.explanation: The righteous who feed the poor, orphan, and captive say they want neither payment nor even thanks from the people they help.
islam.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural's cloud that asks nothing back — not even gratitude — from those it nourishes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Do not be like servants who serve the master in the expectation of receiving a reward, but be like servants who serve the master without the expectation of receiving a reward, and let the fear of Heaven be upon you.”
judaism.explanation: Antigonus of Socho teaches that right action should be done for its own sake, not for a payoff.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural's insistence that genuine duty does not bargain for recompense.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A person responsive to requests, sympathetic to all beings, delighting in distributing alms ... As a cloud—resounding, thundering—rains, filling with water, drenching the plateaus & gullies: a person like this is like that.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha sorts people into three kinds: a cloud that never rains, one that rains only in some places, and one that rains everywhere. The best giver is like the cloud that soaks the whole land.
buddhism.tie_back: Uses the very same rain-cloud image as the Kural to describe the ideal, all-embracing benefactor.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Man's duty is to give to those who are unable to bear (their distresses), not driving them away, nor turning away from the extended hands … to give to those who will pay it back again--has the name of a loan at interest.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār's chapter on liberality says true giving goes to the distressed who cannot repay, and that giving in expectation of a return is only lending at interest.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says duty to others expects nothing back, as the world repays nothing to the rain-cloud; the Nālaṭiyār makes the same point by calling a gift that expects repayment a loan at interest.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 8 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who performs selfless service, without thought of reward, shall attain his Lord and Master.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan describes true seva as service done with no desire for any return.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says true duty toward others looks for nothing in return, as the world gives nothing back to the rain-cloud; Guru Arjan likewise defines real service as service that seeks no reward.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Demeter gives Triptolemus a chariot drawn by winged dragons and wheat, with which he travels the inhabited earth sowing grain for all humankind.
greek_mythology.explanation: In myth, the gift of agriculture is spread freely across the world by the goddess's messenger.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like rain, the gift of grain is given to everyone, and no one repays Demeter in kind.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the immortal gods ... help all alike, among them even those who so ill appreciate their bounty. Let us take them for our guides as far as the weakness of our mortal nature permits; let us bestow benefits, not put them out at interest.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that people should give like the gods, who help everyone, even the ungrateful, rather than treating gifts as loans that earn interest.
philosophy.tie_back: Same model: the benefactor imitates a universal, unpaid bounty, as the Kural's rain does.

real_life_example.event_title: Jonas Salk's polio vaccine is released without a patent
real_life_example.event: On 12 April 1955 the polio vaccine developed by Jonas Salk's team at the University of Pittsburgh, with funding from the public donations of the March of Dimes, was announced as safe and effective. Asked in a television interview with Edward R. Murrow who owned the patent, Salk answered that there was no patent and that the vaccine belonged to the people. He declined to patent it or profit from it, and the vaccine was soon used around the world.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the twentieth century's most important medical advances was given to the public rather than treated as private property.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that true duty to others expects nothing in return, as the world gives nothing back to the rain-cloud, and Salk's vaccine reached the world with no return sought for him.

tamil:
தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருளெல்லாம் தக்கார்க்கு
வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு.
transliteration:
Thaalaatrith thandha porulellaam thakkaarkku
Velaanmai seydhar poruttu.
meaning: All the money a person earns through hard work is meant for one thing: helping people who deserve help.
elementary: Imagine you worked all summer and saved up money. This kural says the best reason to work hard and earn is so that you have something to share with people who really need it.
university: The first line honours effort (thaal aatri, ‘exerting one's foot/strength’), so the kural is not a critique of wealth but a statement of its telos. Velaanmai here does not mean agriculture but ubakaram, beneficence — Parimelazhagar glosses it as oppuravu seydhal, adding that wealth is not meant for eating alone or for hoarding until it is lost. Thakkaar, ‘the worthy,’ introduces discernment: Manakkudavar defines oppuravu as giving to fitting recipients in proportion to one's income, which distinguishes it from the indiscriminate almsgiving of the next chapter (Eekai). The couplet thus rejects both the miser and the ascetic view of wealth, proposing instead a stewardship model in which earnings are held in trust for the community.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Charity given out of duty, without expectation of return, at the proper time and place, and to a worthy person is considered to be in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the highest kind of charity: given as a duty, at the right time and place, to someone who deserves it.
hinduism.tie_back: Matches the Kural's thakkaar (the worthy) and its sense that giving is the proper use of what one has.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to work honestly so that they will have something to give to people in need.
christianity.tie_back: Almost the same logic: the purpose of one's labour is to be able to help others.

islam.quote_or_event: “Believe in Allah and His Messenger and spend out of that in which He has made you successors. For those who have believed among you and spent, there will be a great reward.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents wealth as a trust from God, which believers are to spend for good.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, wealth is not simply owned but held for the purpose of beneficial spending.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the poor shall never cease out of the land: therefore I command thee, saying, Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor, and to thy needy, in thy land.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands generosity as a permanent duty, since need will always exist in society.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes helping others the proper, commanded use of one's means.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “the disciple of the noble ones — using the wealth earned through his efforts & enterprise, amassed through the strength of his arm, and piled up through the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained — provides his friends & associates with pleasure & satisfaction, and maintains that pleasure rightly.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the good uses of honestly earned wealth, including supporting friends, relatives, guests, and the virtuous.
buddhism.tie_back: Echoes the Kural's ‘wealth earned by effort’ and its purpose of benefiting others.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.41, Adiya Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Nyayasampannavibhavah : Possessed of honestly earned wealth.” … “Yathavat atithau sadhau dine cha pratipatti-krt : Diligent in succoring the ascetics, the righteous and the needy.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra's model Jain householder earns his wealth honestly and uses it to support ascetics, the righteous and the needy.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says wealth earned by hard effort exists to help the deserving; Hemacandra's ideal householder pairs honest earning with diligent support of worthy recipients.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of thirty-five qualities of the ideal householder, items 1 and 19, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, Jaina Ethics (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Sarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak joins honest labour (kirat karni) to sharing its fruits (vand chhakna) as the mark of one who knows the true way.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says all the wealth earned through hard, persistent effort exists to help those who deserve help; Guru Nanak likewise ties hard-earned livelihood directly to giving.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Sarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Give to one who gives, but do not give to one who does not give. A man gives to the free-handed, but no one gives to the close-fisted. Give is a good girl, but Take is bad and she brings death.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's farmer's wisdom praises giving but ties it to reciprocity among neighbours.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the Kural's praise of giving and its concern with choosing recipients, but grounds it in exchange rather than duty.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 352–369 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the liberal man, like other virtuous men, will give for the sake of the noble, and rightly; for he will give to the right people, the right amounts, and at the right time, with all the other qualifications that accompany right giving”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle describes the virtue of liberality: using wealth well by giving it rightly to the right people.
philosophy.tie_back: Same idea as the Kural's velaanmai to the thakkaar — wealth's proper use is fitting generosity.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Alfred Nobel leaves his fortune to fund the Nobel Prizes
real_life_example.event: Alfred Nobel, the Swedish chemist and industrialist who had built a fortune from dynamite and other inventions, signed his last will at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris on 27 November 1895. It directed that most of his estate be invested and the income awarded each year as prizes to those who had conferred the greatest benefit on humankind in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and peace. After Nobel's death in 1896 the will met opposition from relatives and others, and the first prizes were awarded in 1901.
real_life_example.explanation: A fortune built over a lifetime of industrial work was turned, by one document, into a permanent reward for those who benefit the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that wealth earned by hard and persistent effort exists to help the deserving, and Nobel's will directed his earnings to the people who most benefit humanity.

tamil:
புத்தே ளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும் பெறலரிதே
ஒப்புரவின் நல்ல பிற.
transliteration:
Puththe lulagaththum eendum peralaridhe
Oppuravin nalla pira.
meaning: Neither in the world of the gods nor here on earth is it easy to find anything as good as helping others.
elementary: If you searched every place — here and even up in heaven — for the very best thing a person can do, you would find nothing better than helping others. It is the top prize of all good deeds.
university: Parimelazhagar gives an ingenious reason for why oppuravu is rare even in heaven: in the world of the gods all are equal, so there are neither givers nor receivers and the virtue cannot be practised; on earth nothing else benefits everyone so equally. He also records a variant reading, peRaRkaridhu, which some commentators took to mean ‘the means to obtain it is rare.’ With 211 and 212, he notes, this couplet completes the chapter's praise of oppuravu before Valluvar turns to its practice. The comparison of heaven and earth is a recurring Tamil device (cf. Kural 23) for asserting a value's absolute primacy, here placing social beneficence above ritual or ascetic merit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are beyond the dualities that arise from doubts, whose minds are engaged within, who are always busy working for the welfare of all living beings and who are free from all sins achieve liberation in the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names working for the good of all beings (sarva-bhuta-hite ratah) as a mark of those who reach the highest spiritual goal.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks devotion to the welfare of all among the highest goods, reaching beyond this world.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.”
christianity.explanation: Paul ranks love (charity) above even faith and hope as the greatest virtue.
christianity.tie_back: Same move of ranking love-in-action above all other goods, as the Kural ranks oppuravu.

islam.quote_or_event: “Never will you attain the good [reward] until you spend [in the way of Allah] from that which you love. And whatever you spend - indeed, Allah is Knowing of it.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says true righteousness (al-birr) is not reached until one gives away what one values.
islam.tie_back: Makes generous giving the gateway to the highest good, as the Kural does.

judaism.quote_or_event: “the world stands upon three things: the Torah, the Temple service, and the practice of acts of piety.”
judaism.explanation: Simeon the Just names gemilut chasadim — acts of loving-kindness — as one of the three pillars holding up the world.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats kindness to others as foundational to the world, not optional.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, if beings knew, as I know, the results of giving & sharing, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of selfishness overcome their minds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that if people understood how great the fruit of sharing is, they would never eat without sharing first, even their last bite.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural's claim that the good of sharing is unmatched, in this world and after.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who are ten miles distant can hear the sound of the wide drum beaten with the stick; those a yojana distant, can hear the hoarse thunder; but all who live in the three worlds piled up will hear the report that some of the excellent have given alms.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār ends its chapter on liberality by saying the fame of generous giving reaches the whole three-tiered Jain universe, further than any drum or thunder.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says nothing in the world of the gods or on earth equals beneficence; the Nālaṭiyār likewise gives charity a renown that spans all three worlds.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak teaches that service done here in the world is what earns honour in the divine Court.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says no good in the world of the gods or on earth equals helping others; Guru Nanak likewise places worldly seva at the centre of what is honoured both here and hereafter.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Stranger, though a still poorer man should come here, it would not be right for me to insult him, for all strangers and beggars are from Jove.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Eumaeus the swineherd explains that care for strangers and beggars is sacred because Zeus himself protects them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Places helping the needy under divine sanction, echoing the Kural's heaven-and-earth esteem for oppuravu.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “we are not born for ourselves alone, but our country claims a share of our being, and our friends a share; and since, as the Stoics hold, everything that the earth produces is created for man's use; and as men, too, are born for the sake of men, that they may be able mutually to help one another”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero, citing Plato and the Stoics, argues that humans exist partly for one another and should strengthen society through exchanging kindnesses.
philosophy.tie_back: Articulates the same civic-reciprocity ideal the Kural calls oppuravu and places at the summit of virtue.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.22 (trans. Walter Miller)

real_life_example.event_title: Edward Jenner's free vaccinations in the Temple of Vaccinia
real_life_example.event: After his first vaccination experiment against smallpox on 14 May 1796, the country doctor Edward Jenner used a small rustic hut in the garden of his home at Berkeley, which he named the Temple of Vaccinia, to vaccinate the poor of the district free of charge. He did not patent his discovery, and he shared cowpox material and his findings widely with other doctors. The Wellcome Collection describes the hut as the world's first free vaccination clinic, and vaccination eventually led to the global eradication of smallpox, declared in 1980.
real_life_example.explanation: Jenner's discovery and his free clinic began a chain of benefit that reached every part of the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says no good on earth or in heaven equals helping others as the world rightly expects, and few acts of help have spread as widely as vaccination freely given.

tamil:
ஒத்த தறிவான் உயிர்வாழ்வான் மற்றையான்
செத்தாருள் வைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Oththa tharivaan uyirvaazhvaan matraiyaan
Seththaarul vaikkap padum.
meaning: Only a person who knows how to help others in the right way is truly alive. Anyone else, though still breathing, counts as dead.
elementary: A person who never helps anyone is like a statue — they are there, but they do not really take part in life. This kural says being truly alive means knowing how to help the people around you.
university: The text reproduced here follows the reading ஒத்த தறிவான் (oththadhu arivaan, ‘one who knows what is fitting’) given with Parimelazhagar's commentary; some modern editions print ஒத்த தறவோன் (‘one of fitting virtue’), a variant worth noting. Parimelazhagar glosses oththadhu as ulaga nadai, ‘the conduct of the world,’ and explains that a person who lacks its knowledge and practice shows no sign of the soul's intelligence and action, and so is reckoned dead. He adds a striking remark: a lapse in worldly conduct, unlike a lapse in Vedic rite, has no expiation. The kural thus defines life socially rather than biologically — a theme with parallels from Aristotle's political animal to rabbinic sayings about the ‘living dead.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: “My dear Arjuna, one who does not follow in human life the cycle of sacrifice thus established by the Vedas certainly leads a life full of sin. Living only for the satisfaction of the senses, such a person lives in vain.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that someone who takes from the cosmic cycle of giving without taking part in it lives a wasted life.
hinduism.tie_back: Same verdict as the Kural: a life that ignores reciprocal duty is not really lived (mogham jivati, ‘lives in vain’).

christianity.quote_or_event: “We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren. He that loveth not his brother abideth in death.”
christianity.explanation: John says that love for others is the sign of real life, and lack of love is a kind of death.
christianity.tie_back: Same life/death contrast defined by one's relationship to others.

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that faith is incomplete without genuinely wanting good for others as for oneself.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes regard for others the test of whether one's inner life is real.

judaism.quote_or_event: “These are the wicked, who even during their lives are called dead”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud teaches that the righteous are called living even after death, while the wicked are called dead even while alive.
judaism.tie_back: Uses the same paradox as the Kural: moral failure makes a living person count as dead.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 18b (Sefaria, William Davidson ed.)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Among the dead they do not die, those who, like fellow travelers on the road, are happy to provide, though they have but little. This is an ancient teaching.”
buddhism.explanation: A deity tells the Buddha that those who share even when they have little do not die among the dead.
buddhism.tie_back: Strikingly parallel: generosity is what separates the truly living from the dead.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 1.32, Macchari Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The function of the souls (jīva) is to help one another.”
jainism.explanation: Umāsvāti's sūtra parasparopagraho jīvānām, now the motto of Jainism, defines what living beings do as mutual help; Pūjyapāda's commentary gives master and servant, teacher and pupil as examples.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says only the one who knows and does what is fitting toward the world is truly alive; Umāsvāti likewise defines the activity of living souls as helping one another.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.21 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak teaches that learning truly reflected upon shows itself in doing good to others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says only the person who understands what is fitting toward the world, and acts on it, is truly alive; Guru Nanak likewise measures real understanding by whether it makes one a benefactor.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “They have no laws nor assemblies of the people, but live in caves on the tops of high mountains; each is lord and master in his family, and they take no account of their neighbours.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus describes the Cyclopes as monstrous precisely because they live without community or care for neighbours.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Presents those who ignore social obligation as less than human — a mythic version of the Kural's verdict.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “he who is unable to live in society, or who has no need because he is sufficient for himself, must be either a beast or a god: he is no part of a state.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that humans are by nature political animals; one who stands outside the shared life of the community is not fully human.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it defines real human life by participation in the community.

real_life_example.event_title: Ida Scudder builds a hospital and medical school for women at Vellore
real_life_example.event: Ida Scudder, born in India to an American missionary family, qualified in medicine at Cornell in 1899 and returned to Vellore, where after her father's death she began treating women in a small room of the mission bungalow. With money she had raised in America she opened a small hospital in 1902, started training nurses by 1909, ran roadside clinics for villages, and in 1918 opened the Union Mission Medical School for Women. The school became the Christian Medical College, Vellore, which was affiliated to the University of Madras by 1950 and grew into one of India's leading medical institutions.
real_life_example.explanation: Scudder spent five decades building institutions shaped around the needs of the society she lived in, especially women who could not be treated by male doctors.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that only the person who understands what is fitting towards the world, and acts on it, is truly alive, and Scudder's life was spent doing exactly what her community most needed.

tamil:
ஊருணி நீர்நிறைந் தற்றே உலகவாம்
பேரறி வாளன் திரு.
transliteration:
Ooruni neernirain thatre ulagavaam
Perari vaalan thiru.
meaning: The riches of a wise person who loves to help the world are like a village pond filled to the top, there for everyone to use.
elementary: Think of a big water tank in the middle of a village that everyone fills their pots from. When a wise, kind person becomes rich, their money is like that full tank: the whole village benefits.
university: Ooruni is specifically the common tank from which a village draws its drinking water, a piece of shared infrastructure in Tamil rural life. Parimelazhagar notes the figure of speech — ‘filling’ really belongs to the water but is attributed to the tank — and explains the point: such wealth does not go to waste but lasts long and unfailingly supplies everyone's needs. Ulagu avaam (‘desiring the world’) is read by Parimelazhagar as loving and practising ulaga nadai, while Manakkudavar reads it as ‘desired by the whole world.’ The kural begins a triad (215-217) of public-good images — tank, fruit tree, medicinal tree — that together treat private wealth in virtuous hands as a quasi-public resource.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The riches of the liberal never waste away, while he who will not give finds none to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Rig Veda's hymn on liberality says generous wealth never runs dry, while the miser ends up alone.
hinduism.tie_back: Echoes Parimelazhagar's point that the generous person's wealth, like the village tank, does not go to waste.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.1 (trans. R. T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But by an equality, that now at this time your abundance may be a supply for their want, that their abundance also may be a supply for your want: that there may be equality”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks one community to share its surplus with another in need, so that resources flow where they are needed.
christianity.tie_back: Like the full tank, one person's abundance becomes the supply for others' needs.

islam.quote_or_event: “And from their properties was [given] the right of the [needy] petitioner and the deprived.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the righteous as those whose wealth contained a rightful share (haqq) for the poor.
islam.tie_back: Treats private wealth as carrying a public claim, as the Kural's tank belongs to the whole village.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs promises that the generous person, who ‘waters’ others, will be refreshed in turn.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the water imagery and the idea that generous wealth keeps on supplying.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Planters of parks or groves, those who build a bridge, a drinking place and well, and those who give monastic quarters. Their merit always grows by day and by night.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises those who build public goods — wells, drinking places, bridges, groves — for the whole community.
buddhism.tie_back: Names the very kind of public water source the Kural uses as its image of virtuous wealth.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 1.47, Vanaropa Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He quitted and rejected his real, valuable property, such as riches, gold, precious stones, jewels, pearls, conches, stones, corals, rubies, &c.; he distributed presents through proper persons, he distributed presents among indigent persons.”
jainism.explanation: Before his renunciation Mahāvīra gave away his riches, distributing them through proper persons and to the poor.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar compares a wise benefactor's wealth to a full village tank open to all; Mahāvīra's great giving before renunciation shows wealth turned into a common supply for the needy.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §112 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: During a siege of Anandpur, Bhai Kanhaiya went among the wounded on the battlefield giving water from his water-skin to men of both armies alike. When some Sikhs complained to Guru Gobind Singh, Bhai Kanhaiya said he saw the Guru in every face, and the Guru praised him and gave him salve to treat all the wounded.
sikhism.explanation: Sikhs remember Bhai Kanhaiya as the model of seva offered to all without distinction, even to enemies.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural likens the wise benefactor's wealth to a brimming village drinking-pond from which everyone may draw; Bhai Kanhaiya's water was given to all who were thirsty, friend or foe.
sikhism.source: SikhNet, The Story of Bhai Kanhaiya Ji (paraphrase of the Sikh tradition)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A bad neighbour is as great a plague as a good one is a great blessing; he who enjoys a good neighbour has a precious possession.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod advises that a good neighbour is one of the most valuable things a person can have.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Recognises, like the Kural, that a good person's resources are a blessing for the whole neighbourhood.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 342–351 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is clearly better that property should be private, but the use of it common; and the special business of the legislator is to create in men this benevolent disposition.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that property should be owned privately, but good people should let it be used for the common benefit.
philosophy.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's model: privately held wealth that functions like the village's common tank.

real_life_example.event_title: Queen Udayamati's stepwell, the Rani-ki-Vav
real_life_example.event: The Rani-ki-Vav, or Queen's Stepwell, on the banks of the Saraswati River at Patan, was built in the 11th century and is traditionally attributed to Queen Udayamati as a memorial to the Chaulukya king Bhima I. UNESCO describes it as a memorial that also functions as a single water management system, designed as an inverted temple with seven levels of stairs leading down to an underground reservoir and decorated with hundreds of sculptures. Silted over for centuries, it was excavated and restored by the Archaeological Survey of India and inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2014.
real_life_example.explanation: Royal wealth was turned into a monumental public reservoir, combining remembrance of a king with a store of water for the community.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the wealth of a wise person who loves the world to the village tank filled to the brim, and the stepwell is literally royal wealth turned into a great public store of water.

tamil:
பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்றால் செல்வம்
நயனுடை யான்கண் படின்.
transliteration:
Payanmaram ulloorp pazhuththatraal selvam
Nayanudai yaankan padin.
meaning: When riches come to a kind, generous person, it is like a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the village, where everyone can pick its fruit.
elementary: A fruit tree deep in a forest helps almost no one, but a mango tree in the middle of town feeds everyone who walks by. A kind person's money is like that town tree.
university: The emphasis falls on ul-oor, ‘inside the village’: the same fruit tree in a distant forest would be of little use, so location stands for accessibility. Parimelazhagar explains nayan (courtesy, kindly propriety) as oppuravu itself, ‘since among the many forms of worldly justice oppuravu is pre-eminent,’ and says the point is that such wealth yields benefit easily to all. Manakkudavar reads nayanudaiyaan as ‘one who is loved by others’ and adds that such wealth benefits even those who dislike him. The couplet moves beyond the tank of 215 to an image of organic, seasonal abundance, suggesting that generosity in the right person is as natural as ripening.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Bounteous is he who gives unto the beggar who comes to him in want of food and feeble. Success attends him in the shout of battle. He makes a friend of him in future troubles.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn praises the giver who feeds the needy, saying such generosity creates lasting bonds.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the village fruit tree, the bountiful person's wealth is open to whoever comes in need.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.3 (trans. R. T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to do good to everyone whenever they get the chance.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural's ideal that a good person's resources should be open to all.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is none amongst the Muslims who plants a tree or sows seeds, and then a bird, or a person or an animal eats from it, but is regarded as a charitable gift for him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says that whenever anyone — even an animal — eats from a tree you planted, it counts as charity from you.
islam.tie_back: Uses the same image of a fruit tree whose produce benefits all comers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “That man himself found a world full of carob trees. Just as my ancestors planted for me, I too am planting for my descendants.”
judaism.explanation: A man planting a carob tree that will take seventy years to bear fruit tells Honi he is planting for future generations, as others once did for him.
judaism.tie_back: Presents the fruit tree as a shared gift to the community across time, as in the Kural.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a (Sefaria, William Davidson ed.)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who gives, who is a master of giving, is dear & charming to people at large.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells General Siha that one visible fruit of generosity is being loved by people in general.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches Manakkudavar's reading of nayanudaiyaan as ‘one loved by others’ — the generous person is the village's beloved tree.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.34, Siha Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who give are like the female palm tree surrounded by the terrace in the midst of the village, they live beloved by many. Men who eat without giving to others, though their family be flourishing, are like the male palm in a burning-ground.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār contrasts the generous person, like a fruit-bearing palm in the middle of the village, with the miser, like a barren palm in a cremation ground.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar likens the generous man's wealth to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the village; the Nālaṭiyār uses almost the same image of a fruitful tree at the village centre.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 6 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: The Sikh langar is a communal kitchen kept in every gurdwara, where free food is served to all who come. Under Guru Amar Das everyone ate together in the casteless langar, and in it all sit in one straight line so that no one claims higher or lower status.
sikhism.explanation: The langar puts shared resources where anyone can reach them, regardless of caste, creed or rank.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures the generous person's wealth as a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the village, where everyone can pick its fruit; the langar is that kind of open, central provision for all.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, langar (and linked coverage in Guru Amar Das and Sikhism: The rejection of caste)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the contest for Athens, Athena plants the first olive tree on the Acropolis as her gift to the city, and the city is awarded to her.
greek_mythology.explanation: The olive, giving fruit, oil, and wood to the whole city, was remembered as Athena's great public gift.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A fruit tree planted at the heart of the city for everyone's benefit — close to the Kural's image.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “he is like a vine which has produced grapes, and seeks for nothing more after it has once produced its proper fruit ... so a man when he has done a good act, does not call out for others to come and see, but he goes on to another act, as a vine goes on to produce again the grapes in season.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius compares the good person to a vine that simply bears fruit, season after season, without seeking credit.
philosophy.tie_back: Same fruit-bearing image for the good person whose benefits flow naturally to others.

real_life_example.event_title: George Peabody founds the Peabody Donation Fund for London's poor
real_life_example.event: George Peabody, an American-born banker who had made his fortune in London, wrote to The Times in March 1862 announcing a gift of 150,000 pounds, later increased, to improve the condition of the poor of London. The trustees of the Peabody Donation Fund used it to build model dwellings for working people, with running water and decent sanitation at affordable rents, and the first block opened in Spitalfields in 1864. The trust he founded still exists today as one of London's oldest and largest housing associations.
real_life_example.explanation: A private fortune was set up as a lasting public resource in the heart of the city, where the people who needed it could reach it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the wealth of a generous person to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the village, where everyone can pick its fruit, and Peabody placed his wealth in the midst of London's working poor.

tamil:
மருந்தாகித் தப்பா மரத்தற்றால் செல்வம்
பெருந்தகை யான்கண் படின்.
transliteration:
Marundhaagith thappaa maraththatraal selvam
Perundhagai yaankan padin.
meaning: When riches belong to a truly good person, they are like a healing tree that always works, with every part of it used as medicine for others.
elementary: Some trees, like the neem tree, can be used as medicine — the leaves, the bark, even the roots. A great-hearted person's money is like that tree: every part of it helps someone feel better.
university: Parimelazhagar spells out what thappaa (‘not failing’) excludes: a tree fails if it grows where it is hard to reach, if it is hidden, if it bears only in some seasons, or if it is useless — so the ideal benefactor is accessible, open, reliable, and helpful in every part. He adds that such a person relieves everyone's distress without regard to his own lack. Manakkudavar glosses thapputhal as ‘hiding’: the medicinal tree does not conceal itself from those who seek it. With this third image Parimelazhagar closes the triad on how the benefactor's wealth is used, escalating from water (sustenance) to fruit (nourishment) to medicine (healing).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just see how these trees are maintaining every living entity! Their birth is successful. Their behavior is just like that of great personalities, for anyone who asks anything from a tree never goes away disappointed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna praises trees for supporting all creatures, comparing them to great souls who never send a seeker away empty-handed.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the Kural's image in reverse: the tree is like a great person, just as the great person's wealth is like the tree.

christianity.quote_or_event: “and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.”
christianity.explanation: In John's vision of the new Jerusalem, the tree of life bears fruit every month and its leaves heal the nations.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the image of a tree whose parts are medicine for all people.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you not considered how Allah presents an example, [making] a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches [high] in the sky? It produces its fruit all the time, by permission of its Lord.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an compares a good word to a firmly rooted tree that yields fruit at all times.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's thappaa maram, the good tree never fails to give.

judaism.quote_or_event: “and the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine.”
judaism.explanation: Ezekiel foresees trees along a sacred river whose fruit feeds and whose leaves heal.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural's image of a tree whose parts serve as food and medicine for others.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “For all those ailing in the world, Until their every sickness has been healed, May I myself become for them The doctor, nurse, the medicine itself.”
buddhism.explanation: Shantideva's bodhisattva vows to become the very medicine that cures the world's sick.
buddhism.tie_back: Same idea as the Kural: the great-hearted person becomes medicine for all.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Charity (dāna) is the giving of one's objects to another for mutual benefit–anugraha.”
jainism.explanation: Umāsvāti defines charity as giving one's own wealth so that both sides benefit: the giver gains merit (puṇya) and the receiver is helped toward right knowledge and the like.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar pictures a noble person's wealth as a healing tree that never fails others; the Jain definition of dāna also treats a good person's possessions as given out for others' benefit.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.38 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Britannica records that Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, had apparently once assisted the Mughal prince Dara Shikoh, possibly curing him of poisoning; the Guru consistently sought peaceful relations with the Mughal dynasty.
sikhism.explanation: Sikh memory of Guru Har Rai includes his help in healing someone from outside the community.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural likens the wealth of a noble person to a medicinal tree whose every part is a cure for others; Guru Har Rai's reported help to Dara Shikoh is an example of healing offered beyond one's own circle.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Guru Har Rai (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Chiron, the wise centaur renowned for his skill in healing, taught medicine to Asclepius; when wounded incurably by Heracles' arrow, he gave up his immortality, which passed to Prometheus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Chiron is the mythic healer-teacher whose knowledge benefited humanity through his pupils, and who finally gave away even his immortality.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A noble figure whose whole being serves healing, close to the Kural's medicinal tree.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “no physician, in so far as he is a physician, considers his own good in what he prescribes, but the good of his patient”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that a true art, like medicine, serves the good of those it cares for, not the practitioner's own gain.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's healing tree, true skill or wealth exists for the benefit of others.

real_life_example.event_title: Nicolas Rolin and Guigone de Salins found the Hotel-Dieu of Beaune
real_life_example.event: In 1443 Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to Duke Philip the Good of Burgundy, and his wife Guigone de Salins founded the Hotel-Dieu at Beaune as a hospital for the poor, at a time when much of the town's population was destitute and the area had recently suffered an outbreak of plague. The building was dedicated on 31 December 1451 and received its first patients the next day, cared for by a community of nursing sisters, and Guigone de Salins continued to direct it after her husband's death until her own death in 1470. The hospital went on caring for patients for more than five centuries before becoming a museum.
real_life_example.explanation: The fortune of one of the most powerful men in Burgundy was turned into a hospital that served the sick poor for over five hundred years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the wealth of a noble person to a medicinal tree that never fails to heal, and the Hotel-Dieu turned the Rolins' wealth into healing for generation after generation.

tamil:
இடனில் பருவத்தும் ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார்
கடனறி காட்சி யவர்.
