transliteration:
Idanil paruvaththum oppuravirku olkaar
Kadanari kaatchi yavar.
meaning: People who clearly understand their duty do not stop helping others, even when they themselves have very little.
elementary: Even when you have only one cookie left, you can still break it in half for a friend. This kural says people who truly understand duty keep helping, even when they do not have much.
university: Idan il paruvam, literally ‘a season without room,’ refers to a time when wealth has contracted; Parimelazhagar glosses it as selvam surungiya kaalam. Kadan ari kaatchi — ‘the vision that knows what is owed’ — is described by him as natural discernment of what one ought to do, so that even when everything else is given up, this is not. Manakkudavar makes the practical point that oppuravu must be done even when wealth is not abundant. Together with 219, this couplet (Parimelazhagar notes) argues that poverty is no reason to abandon oppuravu, moving the virtue from a function of surplus to a function of character.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Rantideva, after fasting for forty-eight days, gives away the food and water he finally receives to a brahmana, a shudra, a man with dogs, and an outcaste, keeping nothing for himself.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata Purana, Rantideva, reduced to poverty and hunger, still gives his last food and drink to whoever asks.
hinduism.tie_back: An exact narrative illustration of not slackening in beneficence even in extreme want.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus praises a poor widow who gave two small coins — everything she had — above the rich who gave from surplus.
christianity.tie_back: Same lesson: true generosity continues even when one's means are nearly gone.

islam.quote_or_event: “but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises the Ansar of Medina who put the needs of the emigrants before their own even while they themselves were poor.
islam.tie_back: Directly matches the Kural's ‘even in a season without means.’

judaism.quote_or_event: “even a poor person who is sustained from charity must also perform charity.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud rules that even someone who lives on charity is still obligated to give charity to others.
judaism.tie_back: Same principle: lack of means does not cancel the duty to help.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 7b (Sefaria, William Davidson ed.)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Some who have little are happy to provide, while some who have much don't wish to give. An offering given from little is multiplied a thousand times.”
buddhism.explanation: A deity tells the Buddha that giving from little is worth far more than giving from plenty.
buddhism.tie_back: Affirms the Kural's praise for those who keep giving when their means are small.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 1.32, Macchari Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Master said compassionately: “Now I have abandoned all associations. Nevertheless, take half of this garment around my shoulder, sir.”
jainism.explanation: After giving away his wealth and becoming a monk, Mahāvīra is approached by Soma, a poor Brahman who missed the year of gifts, and gives him half of the only garment he has left.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who know their duty keep helping even when their means have shrunk; Mahāvīra, with nothing left but one cloth, still gives half of it.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. III, part 1 'Loss of half of his garment' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition as told by Macauliffe, the young Nanak was sent by his father Kalu with money to trade at Chuharkana. On the way he met holy men who had not eaten for days, and he spent his father's money on food for them, saying he had spent it to the best advantage.
sikhism.explanation: This story, remembered as the true bargain, shows Guru Nanak giving away what he had been given even at cost to himself and in the face of his father's displeasure.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who understand their duty do not slacken in helping others even when their own means have shrunk; the young Nanak helped the hungry with the only money he had, though it left him empty-handed.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak (paraphrase of the Janamsakhi account)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “we have not many spare cloaks nor shirts up here, but every man has only one.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Eumaeus the poor swineherd, with barely enough for himself, still kills his best pig for the disguised Odysseus and covers him with his own heavy cloak for the night.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A poor man who does not slacken in hospitality despite having little — the Kural's ideal.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “liberality resides not in the multitude of the gifts but in the state of character of the giver, and this is relative to the giver's substance. There is therefore nothing to prevent the man who gives less from being the more liberal man, if he has less to give.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that generosity is measured by character and proportion to one's means, not by the size of the gift.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural's claim that the dutiful stay generous even when their means are small.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Pestalozzi keeps serving poor children after his Neuhof school fails
real_life_example.event: In the 1770s the Swiss educator Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi and his wife Anna took poor children into their farm, the Neuhof, teaching them spinning, weaving and farming alongside their lessons, but the farm could not support them and the venture never brought him much money. Pestalozzi did not abandon the work: after French troops invaded Switzerland, he gathered more than eighty orphaned and destitute children at Stans in 1799, caring for them himself in a deserted convent until the French reclaimed the building in June 1799. He went on to become one of the founders of modern education.
real_life_example.explanation: Financial failure did not end Pestalozzi's commitment to poor children; it continued in even harder conditions.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who understand their duty do not slacken in helping others even when their means have shrunk, and Pestalozzi returned to caring for destitute children after his own resources had failed.

tamil:
நயனுடையான் நல்கூர்ந்தா னாதல் செயும்நீர
செய்யாது அமைகலா வாறு.
transliteration:
Nayanudaiyaan nalkoorndhaa naadhal seyumneera
Seyyaadhu amaigalaa vaaru.
meaning: For a kind person, being poor means only one thing: the pain of not being able to do the good things they always do.
elementary: Imagine a kid who loves sharing snacks with everyone. If one day there are no snacks to share, the kid feels sad — not because they are hungry, but because they cannot give. That sadness is what ‘being poor’ means to a kind person.
university: Valluvar redefines poverty (nalkooral) from the benefactor's point of view: it is not the loss of personal comforts but the anguish of being unable to perform the benefactions that are his nature (seyum neera). Parimelazhagar underlines this: poverty for such a person is ‘not the inability to enjoy what he would enjoy.’ The verb amaigalaa (‘cannot rest content’) captures a moral restlessness, turning the absence of means into a spiritual rather than material deprivation. Paired with 218, the couplet completes Parimelazhagar's point that oppuravu is not to be abandoned because of want.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I do not pray to the Supreme Personality of Godhead for the eight perfections of mystic yoga, nor for salvation from repeated birth and death. I want only to stay among all the living entities and suffer all distresses on their behalf, so that they may be freed from suffering.”
hinduism.explanation: Rantideva, having given away his last food and water, prays only to share and relieve the sufferings of all beings.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's nayanudaiyaan, his only real want is the ability to relieve others.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says what counts is the willing heart; gifts are judged by what a person has, not by what they lack.
christianity.tie_back: Both locate generosity in the inner disposition that persists when means run out.

islam.quote_or_event: “Every Muslim has to give in charity.” The people asked, “O Allah's Prophet! If someone has nothing to give, what will he do?” He said, “He should work with his hands and benefit himself and also give in charity (from what he earns).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that even someone with nothing must find a way to give — by working, helping the needy, or doing good deeds.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats the inability to give as a problem the good person must still address.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone who gives a peruta to a poor person receives six blessings, and whoever consoles him with words of comfort and encouragement receives eleven blessings.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yitzhak teaches that comforting the poor with words is even greater than giving money.
judaism.tie_back: Offers the person without means a way to still do good, answering the Kural's anguish of inability.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 9b (Sefaria, William Davidson ed.)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sasa Jataka, the Bodhisatta born as a hare eats only grass and reflects that he has no oil, rice, or beans to give any beggar who might come; when Sakka arrives disguised as a hungry brahmin, the hare offers his own body by leaping into the fire.
buddhism.explanation: The hare's one concern is that he lacks anything fit to give a hungry guest, so he gives himself.
buddhism.tie_back: Dramatises the Kural's idea that a kind being's true poverty is the inability to give.
buddhism.source: Jataka No. 316, Sasa Jataka (trans. H. T. Francis and R. A. Neil, ed. E. B. Cowell)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Let a man who regards both this world and the next, give what he can as he gets it; and if, through poverty, giving be impossible, to abstain from begging will be to give twice.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār tells the generous to give whatever they can, and counts it as a double gift when someone too poor to give at least does not burden others by begging.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that for the kind, poverty means only being unable to give; the Nālaṭiyār also treats poverty as the point where giving becomes impossible, and finds a form of giving even there.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 5 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The God-conscious being delights in doing good to others.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan describes the brahm giani, the one who knows God, as someone whose joy lies in doing good to others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that for the kind-hearted, poverty means only the pain of being unable to do good; Guru Arjan likewise makes doing good to others the very delight of the awakened person.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 273, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor old couple, welcome disguised Zeus and Hermes with the little they have and even try to kill their only goose to feed them.
greek_mythology.explanation: The couple's poverty does not stop them; they strain to give more than they have.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the ache of the kind-hearted to give despite want, as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is not, therefore, the thing which is done or given, but the spirit in which it is done or given, that must be considered, because a benefit exists, not in that which is done or given, but in the mind of the doer or giver.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that a benefit lies in the giver's intention, not in the material gift.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural's view that the benefactor's identity lies in the will to give, which persists even without means.

real_life_example.event_title: Oseola McCarty gives her life savings for scholarships
real_life_example.event: Oseola McCarty, who left school in the sixth grade and spent most of her life washing and ironing other people's clothes by hand, gave 150,000 dollars, most of her life savings, to the University of Southern Mississippi in 1995 to fund scholarships for students in financial need. Asked about the gift, she said she did not regret any of it and only wished she had more to give. Local businesses and donors around the world added to the fund, and she received the Presidential Citizens Medal from President Bill Clinton that year.
real_life_example.explanation: A woman of very small means measured her life not by what she owned but by how much good she could do with it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for a kind-hearted person the only real poverty is being unable to do the good deeds that are his nature, and McCarty's one regret was that she did not have more to give.

tamil:
ஒப்புரவி னால்வரும் கேடெனின் அஃதொருவன்
விற்றுக்கோள் தக்க துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Oppuravi naalvarum kedenin aqdhoruvan
Vitrukkol thakka thudaiththu.
meaning: If helping others leads to ruin, that ruin is worth having, even if you had to sell yourself to get it.
elementary: Some people say, ‘If you keep giving, you will end up with nothing!’ This kural answers: even if that happens, it is worth it — being someone who helps is worth more than anything you could lose.
university: The closing couplet answers a prudential objection: oppuravu may lead to kedu, material loss. Valluvar's reply is deliberately extreme — such loss is worth acquiring by selling oneself — and Parimelazhagar notes the logic: nothing is normally bought by selling oneself, so this loss is valued above everything, because it yields lasting renown; hence ‘ruin through oppuravu is not ruin.’ Manakkudavar reframes it as a trade in which one thing is sold to buy a greater, so the apparent loss should be counted as gain. The hyperbole caps the chapter's argument: from rain (211) through wealth (212-217) and poverty (218-219) to self-sacrifice (220), oppuravu is presented as a value that no calculation of self-interest can outweigh.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, to honour his promise of a gift to the sage Vishvamitra, gives away his kingdom, sells his wife and son, and finally sells himself into servitude at a cremation ground.
hinduism.explanation: In the Markandeya Purana, Harishchandra literally sells himself rather than go back on his pledged gift, and is ultimately exalted by the gods.
hinduism.tie_back: A literal enactment of the Kural's ‘worth buying by selling oneself.’
hinduism.source: Markandeya Purana, Harishchandra legend (chs. 7–8), as summarised in secondary sources

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells a rich young man to sell everything he owns and give to the poor.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural's verdict that material ruin for the sake of others is a worthwhile exchange.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he who sells himself, seeking means to the approval of Allah. And Allah is kind to [His] servants.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises the one who ‘sells himself’ — gives up his very self — to seek God's pleasure.
islam.tie_back: Uses the same language of selling oneself as the Kural for a supremely worthwhile sacrifice.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In Usha the Sages instituted that one who dispenses his money to charity should not dispense more than one-fifth ... lest he render himself destitute and need the help of other people.”
judaism.explanation: The rabbis limited charitable giving to a fifth of one's assets so that the giver would not become dependent on others.
judaism.tie_back: An honest contrast: Jewish law praises charity but deliberately guards against the self-ruin the Kural welcomes.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 50a (Sefaria, William Davidson ed.)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If it so happens that, when a disciple of the noble ones obtains these five benefits from wealth, his wealth goes to depletion, the thought occurs to him, ‘Even though my wealth has gone to depletion, I have obtained the five benefits that can be obtained from wealth,’ and he feels no remorse.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that if wealth runs out because it was used well — for family, friends, guests, and the virtuous — the wise feel no regret.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats loss that comes from good use of wealth as no real loss.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.41, Adiya Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: The king said to him, “I will give you my own flesh, weighing it with the dove. Be satisfied. Do not die.” … When the king saw that the dove kept increasing in weight, he himself got on the scales with unequaled courage.
jainism.explanation: King Megharatha, in a former birth of the sixteenth Tīrthaṅkara Śāntinātha, protects a dove from a hawk by offering his own flesh and finally his whole body, while his ministers protest at the loss.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that if helping others brings ruin, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself; Megharatha literally puts himself on the scales to save another being.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book V (Śāntināthacaritra), ch. IV, part 7 'Story of the dove and hawk' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, was executed by the Mughal authorities in Delhi in 1675. He became the second Sikh martyr and is remembered particularly for his stand for religious freedom.
sikhism.explanation: Sikhs honour Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom as giving his own life in defence of the freedom of conscience of others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that if helping others leads to ruin, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself; Guru Tegh Bahadur paid with his own life for others' freedom of faith.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Guru Tegh Bahadur (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus steals fire from the gods and gives it to humankind, and Zeus punishes him by chaining him to a rock where an eagle eats his liver each day.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prometheus accepts terrible suffering as the price of benefiting humanity.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Embodies the Kural's idea that ruin incurred for others' good is worth bearing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I should not have neglected all my own concerns or patiently seen the neglect of them during all these years, and have been doing yours ... And I have a sufficient witness to the truth of what I say—my poverty.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells the jury that he neglected his own affairs to serve Athens, and his poverty proves it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's benefactor, Socrates accepts material ruin as the price of serving others.

real_life_example.event_title: Oskar Schindler spends his fortune to protect his Jewish workers
real_life_example.event: Oskar Schindler, a German businessman and Nazi Party member who had grown rich in occupied Krakow, moved his armaments factory to Brunnlitz in 1944 and devoted himself until liberation in May 1945 to protecting its roughly 1,000 Jewish prisoners, paying for scarce food and medicine himself and deceiving the SS with false production figures. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum records that this required him to spend the fortune he had made in Krakow; he later claimed to have spent 2.64 million Reichsmarks. After the war he struggled financially and failed in business, and in 1993 Yad Vashem named him and his wife Emilie Righteous Among the Nations.
real_life_example.explanation: Schindler gave up a fortune and ended his life in financial hardship, but the more than 1,000 people he helped are why he is remembered.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that if helping others brings ruin, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself, and Schindler exchanged his wealth for the survival of the people in his care.

tamil:
வறியார்க்கொன்று ஈவதே ஈகைமற் றெல்லாம்
குறியெதிர்ப்பை நீர துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Variyaarkku ondru eevadhe eekai matru ellaam
Kuriyedhirppai neeradhu udaiththu.
meaning: Only giving to people who have nothing is true giving. Every other gift is like a trade that expects something back.
elementary: If you give your friend a sticker because you hope they will give you one back, that is really a trade. But if you give your lunch to a kid who has no lunch at all and can never pay you back, that is real giving. This kural says only the second kind counts as true giving.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition by exclusion: ஈகை (eekai) is giving to the வறியார் (the destitute), and everything else is குறியெதிர்ப்பை — a gift made with a ‘measured return’ in view, which the old commentators read as something close to a loan or a reciprocal obligation. The move sharply separates philanthropy from the neighbouring virtue of ஒப்புரவு (social beneficence, Chapter 22) and from ordinary gift exchange, which anthropologists since Marcel Mauss have shown to be governed by expectations of return. The criterion is not the size of the gift but the incapacity of the recipient to repay; that incapacity is what guarantees the purity of the motive. The same test appears in Jesus’ advice to invite those who ‘cannot recompense thee’ and in the Gita’s definition of sattvic gifts given ‘without expectation of return’, making this one of the most widely shared ethical intuitions across traditions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That gift which is given out of duty, at the proper time and place, to a worthy person, and without expectation of return, is considered to be charity in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna ranks gifts by motive; the highest (sattvic) gift is given simply because it ought to be given, with no return expected from the recipient.
hinduism.tie_back: Same core test as the Kural: a gift that expects a return is not the highest kind of giving. The Gita adds conditions of time, place and a ‘worthy’ recipient, whereas Valluvar makes need itself the qualification.

christianity.quote_or_event: “When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours; lest they also bid thee again, and a recompence be made thee. But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his host that feeding people who can invite you back is just an exchange; feeding the poor, who cannot repay, is what is truly blessed.
christianity.tie_back: Almost a paraphrase of the Kural: giving to those who can return the favour is reciprocity, giving to the needy is real generosity.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they give food in spite of love for it to the needy, the orphan, and the captive, [Saying], ‘We feed you only for the face [i.e., approval] of Allāh. We wish not from you reward or gratitude.’”
islam.explanation: The righteous feed the poor, orphans and captives while explicitly refusing any reward or even thanks from them.
islam.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s two elements: the recipient is the needy, and nothing is expected back from them.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A lower level than this is one who gives charity to the poor without knowing to whom he gave and without the poor person knowing from whom he received. For this is an observance of the mitzvah for its sake alone.”
judaism.explanation: In his ladder of eight levels of charity, Maimonides ranks anonymous giving very high because no relationship, gratitude or debt can form between giver and receiver.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Maimonides values the gift that cannot turn into an exchange; anonymity removes any chance of repayment.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Matanot Aniyim 10:8 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He gives a gift with the thought, ‘I am well-off. These are not well-off. It would not be right for me, being well-off, not to give a gift to those who are not well-off.’”
buddhism.explanation: In the Dana Sutta the Buddha ranks motives for giving; giving because others are in need ranks above giving to store up rewards for oneself after death.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s focus on need as the reason to give and its low view of gifts made for personal profit.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.49, Dana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The effect of giving of the gift–dāna–has distinctions based on the specific manner in which it is given–vidhiviśeṣa, the specific thing given–dravyaviśeṣa, the specific nature of the giver–dātṛviśeṣa, and the specific nature of the recipient–pātraviśeṣa.” … “The presence of qualities which lead to salvation indicates the superiority of the recipient–pātraviśeṣa.”
jainism.explanation: Umāsvāti's sūtra, with Pūjyapāda's commentary, says that what a gift is worth depends partly on who receives it. For Pūjyapāda the best recipient is one whose qualities lead toward liberation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar also defines true giving by its recipient, though for him that recipient is the destitute person who cannot repay. Jain dāna theory ranks recipients by spiritual worth instead, so the two agree on the principle and differ on who should receive.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In that place where the lowly are cared for-there, the Blessings of Your Glance of Grace rain down.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak closes this Siree Raag hymn by saying that God's grace falls precisely where the lowest and poorest are looked after.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar defines true giving as giving to those who have nothing, and Guru Nanak locates divine favour exactly where the destitute are cared for.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Give to one who gives, but do not give to one who does not give. A man gives to the free-handed, but no one gives to the close-fisted.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s farmer’s wisdom treats giving as a system of reciprocity: you give to those who will give back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An instructive contrast. Hesiod describes exactly the ‘measured return’ kind of giving that Valluvar says does not count as ஈகை at all.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 353-355 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Therefore the liberal man, like other virtuous men, will give for the sake of the noble, and rightly; for he will give to the right people, the right amounts, and at the right time.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the generous person gives because giving well is noble, not to gain something, and gives to the right recipients.
philosophy.tie_back: Agrees with the Kural that true giving is not motivated by return; Aristotle leaves ‘the right people’ open, while Valluvar specifies the destitute.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Thomas Coram wins a royal charter for the Foundling Hospital
real_life_example.event: Thomas Coram, a retired sea captain of modest background, campaigned for about seventeen years for a home for babies abandoned on London's streets, gathering petitions from aristocrats, artists and scientists. King George II signed the Royal Charter for the Foundling Hospital on 17 October 1739, and the first children were admitted in temporary premises in Hatton Garden in 1741. Coram's memorial at the hospital records that he died in 1751 poor in worldly estate.
real_life_example.explanation: Britain's first dedicated children's charity was built for infants who could never repay anyone, and over two centuries it cared for more than 25,000 children.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines true giving as giving to those who have nothing, and abandoned newborns were the clearest case of recipients who could offer no return.

tamil:
நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல்தீது மேலுலகம்
இல்லெனினும் ஈதலே நன்று.
transliteration:
Nallaaru eninum kolal theedhu melulagam
Illeninum eedhale nandru.
meaning: Even if someone says taking from others is a good way, taking is still bad. And even if giving did not get you into heaven, giving would still be good.
elementary: Imagine someone says, “It’s fine to always ask for other people’s snacks.” It still isn’t a good habit. And imagine someone says, “Sharing won’t win you any prize.” Sharing is still the right thing to do. Giving is good even if nobody rewards you for it.
university: The couplet is built on two concessive clauses (எனினும், ‘even if’) that strip away the usual religious sanctions: receiving is wrong even if called a நல்லாறு (good path), and giving is right even if there is no மேலுலகம் (heaven above). Parimelazhagar reads the first line as rejecting the idea that accepting alms could be meritorious, which touches a live debate in Indian thought where receiving gifts was a recognised livelihood for some groups. The second line is philosophically bolder: it makes the value of giving independent of any afterlife reward, anticipating the distinction between acting from duty and acting from hope of reward. Valluvar thus grounds generosity in its intrinsic goodness rather than in cosmic bookkeeping.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You have a right to perform your prescribed duty, but you are not entitled to the fruits of action. Never consider yourself to be the cause of the results of your activities, and never be attached to not doing your duty.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that right action should be done for its own sake, without attachment to what it will bring you.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle to giving: give because it is good, not because it earns heaven.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
christianity.explanation: Paul quotes Jesus to say that giving is a greater good than receiving.
christianity.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s ranking: receiving is lesser, giving is better.

islam.quote_or_event: “The upper hand is better than the lower hand. The upper hand is that of the giver and the lower (hand) is that of the beggar.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet, speaking about charity and about refraining from begging, said the hand that gives is better than the hand that asks.
islam.tie_back: Same judgement as the Kural’s first line: asking and taking are lower; giving is better.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person should always construct [sic] himself and bear hardship rather than appeal to people at large and make himself a burden on the community.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides urges people to endure hardship rather than depend on others’ charity if they can possibly avoid it.
judaism.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s first line that taking from others is to be avoided even when it seems acceptable.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Matanot Aniyim 10:18 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A person gives a gift seeking his own profit, with a mind attached [to the reward], seeking to store up for himself [with the thought], ‘I’ll enjoy this after death.’”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes this as the lowest motive for giving; higher gifts are given without calculating an afterlife reward.
buddhism.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s second line: giving aimed at securing heaven is inferior to giving done because it is good.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.49, Dana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Is it, therefore, a reproach to a man if he starve and keep his integrity inviolate, rather than fill his stomach by the disgraceful practice of mendicity?”
jainism.explanation: In its chapter on the dread of begging, the Nālaṭiyār says it is better to go hungry with one's integrity intact than to live by asking others for food.
jainism.tie_back: This matches the first half of Valluvar's couplet: taking from others stays bad even when it is called a good path.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 31 ('Dread of mendicity'), st. 2 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself a guru or a spiritual teacher, while he goes around begging - don't ever touch his feet. One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: In this salok Guru Nanak rejects holy men who live by begging, however spiritual their title, and holds up instead the person who earns honestly and shares part of it.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, which says taking is bad even if called a good path and giving is good in itself, Guru Nanak refuses to honour begging dressed up as religion and praises earning and giving.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Saarang ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Give is a good girl, but Take is bad and she brings death.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod personifies Giving and Taking as two women: one good, the other deadly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Same verdict as the Kural: taking is bad, giving is good.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 356 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be tardy in coming forward to be the objects of their kindness; for it is not noble to be keen to receive benefits.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says a good person should be slow to accept favours, since eagerness to receive is not noble.
philosophy.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s claim that receiving is ignoble even when socially accepted.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.11 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Banting, Best and Collip sell the insulin patent for a dollar each
real_life_example.event: After insulin was developed at the University of Toronto, Frederick Banting, Charles Best and James Collip assigned their patent rights on insulin to the university for a token payment of one dollar each. Their stated purpose in patenting was to prevent anyone else from taking out a patent and claiming a monopoly. The university then licensed drug companies to manufacture insulin and used the royalties to fund further research.
real_life_example.explanation: The discoverers of a life-saving treatment declined to take personal profit from it, choosing to place it in public trust instead.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural holds that taking is wrong even when it looks respectable and that giving is good without any reward, and the insulin team refused a legitimate-looking fortune in order to give their discovery away.

tamil:
இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை ஈதல்
குலனுடையான் கண்ணே யுள.
transliteration:
Ilan ennum evvam uraiyaamai eedhal
Kulanudaiyaan kanne ula.
meaning: Not saying the sad words “I have nothing,” and giving anyway, is found only in a person from a truly good family.
elementary: When someone asks for help, it is easy to say, “Sorry, I don’t have anything.” A truly good person doesn’t hide behind that excuse. Even when they have only a little, they find something to share.
university: The couplet turns on the phrase இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம், ‘the misery of saying “I have not”’. Commentators divide on whose words these are: Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan read it as giving before the needy person has to humiliate himself by declaring his poverty, while others (e.g. Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read it as the giver not pleading poverty himself even when he is in straitened circumstances. Both readings put the burden of dignity on the giver: generosity is shown most clearly when one’s means are small or the asker’s shame can be spared. குலன் (kulan), usually glossed ‘noble birth’, is best understood as nobility of character and upbringing, in line with the Kural’s repeated view that conduct, not birth, defines a person (cf. Kural 972).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata’s Ashvamedhika Parva, a starving Brahmin family who live by gleaning grain give their only meal of barley flour to a hungry guest, one after another, rather than turn him away. A mongoose that rolls in the spilled flour finds half its body turned to gold, and later declares that Yudhishthira’s grand horse-sacrifice was not equal to this poor family’s gift.
hinduism.explanation: The story teaches that a small gift given from poverty outweighs lavish gifts given from abundance.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s ideal: a household with almost nothing does not plead poverty, but gives.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva (Anugita section), story of the mongoose and the Brahmin’s flour

christianity.quote_or_event: “Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus praises a poor widow whose two small coins, given out of her poverty, were worth more than the large gifts of the rich.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it honours the person who gives despite having little, instead of pleading poverty.

islam.quote_or_event: “They love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what they [i.e., the emigrants] were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the Ansar of Medina, who shared with the refugees from Mecca and put them first even while poor themselves.
islam.tie_back: Same ideal of giving from one’s own want rather than pleading it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother: But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands that one must not close one’s hand to a poor person but give generously for his need.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s refusal to turn away the asker; the ‘shut hand’ corresponds to the evasive ‘I have nothing’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak the truth; yield not to anger; when asked, give even if you only have a little. By these three means can one reach the presence of the gods.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada tells people to give when asked even if they have only a little.
buddhism.tie_back: Directly parallels the Kural: when someone asks, don’t say ‘I have nothing’; give from the little you have.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Not saying they have very little, not saying they have not anything, let them ever exercise fruitful charity to all. Like the pitcher of the mendicant who enters the house-door for alms, it will, in due course, gradually become full.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār tells people never to excuse themselves with 'I have little' or 'I have nothing', and to keep giving. Small gifts add up, it says, the way a mendicant's pitcher slowly fills.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar finds nobility in giving without first uttering the miserable words 'I have nothing', and this stanza turns down exactly that excuse.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 9 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “His Blessings are so abundant that there can be no written account of them. The Great Giver does not hold back anything.”
sikhism.explanation: Japji's twenty-fifth pauri praises God as the Great Giver whose gifts are beyond counting and who withholds nothing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the noble person who never says 'I have nothing' and gives anyway; Guru Nanak presents the ideal giver as one who holds nothing back.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib, Pauri 25, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey Book 14, the swineherd Eumaeus, a poor servant, welcomes the disguised Odysseus as a ragged stranger, kills two of his own pigs to feed him, and tells him that strangers and beggars come from Zeus and that even a small gift is welcome.
greek_mythology.explanation: A man of humble means makes no excuse of poverty and shares what he has with a beggar.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Eumaeus shows the Kural’s nobility of character: giving generously from little, without pleading want.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I can find nothing to give you which is worthy of you; I feel my poverty in this respect alone. Therefore I present you with the only thing I possess, myself.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells how Aeschines, a poor pupil of Socrates, gave himself when he had no money, and how Socrates valued this above the rich pupils’ gifts.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it praises the person who does not use poverty as an excuse but finds something to give.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Benefits I.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: The Maasai of Enoosaen give fourteen cows to the United States
real_life_example.event: After the September 11 attacks, Kimeli Naiyomah, a Maasai student who had been in New York, asked the elders of his village in western Kenya to let him give a cow to the American people, and the community responded with fourteen cattle from the small herds of local herdsmen. At a ceremony on 2 June 2002 the cows were blessed and presented to the deputy chief of mission of the U.S. Embassy in Nairobi. The cattle remained in Kenya in the care of Maasai herdsmen.
real_life_example.explanation: A village with little material wealth made one of its most valued possessions into a gift of sympathy for the richest country in the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises those who do not plead that they have nothing but give anyway, as the herdsmen of Enoosaen did from their own small stocks.

tamil:
இன்னாது இரக்கப் படுதல் இரந்தவர்
இன்முகங் காணும் அளவு.
transliteration:
Innaadhu irakkap padudhal irandhavar
Inmugam kaanum alavu.
meaning: Being asked for help is painful for a giving person, but only until they see the face of the one who asked light up with joy.
elementary: When a friend is sad and asks for help, you feel a little sad too. But when you help them and they smile, your sadness melts away. This kural says the giver’s pain lasts only until they see that smile.
university: The verb இரக்கப்படுதல், ‘to be begged of’, frames the scene from the giver’s side: Parimelazhagar explains that the sight of a suppliant’s distress is itself painful to a compassionate person. That pain ends at a precise moment — அளவு, ‘up to the point’ — when the giver sees the இன்முகம், the pleasant face, of the one who has been helped. The couplet therefore locates the reward of giving in shared emotion rather than in merit, reputation or return. It also implies a standard for how to give: the gift must be large and gracious enough to change the receiver’s face, which links it with teachings such as Maimonides’ rule that charity must be given with a pleasant countenance.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But charity performed with the expectation of some return, or with a desire for fruitive results, or in a grudging mood, is said to be charity in the mode of passion.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classes grudging, reluctant giving as a lower (rajasic) kind of charity.
hinduism.tie_back: By implication the right way to give is gladly; the Kural pictures the giver’s joy when the receiver brightens.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks Christians to give willingly and cheerfully rather than reluctantly.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s emotional picture of giving: sorrow gives way to gladness in the act of giving.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders [of it] or injury as does one who spends his wealth [only] to be seen by the people.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says charity is cancelled if the giver hurts the receiver by reminding them of it or humiliating them.
islam.tie_back: Both texts care about the receiver’s feelings; a gift is complete only when it leaves the receiver glad, not wounded.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whenever a person gives charity to a poor person with an unpleasant countenance and with his face buried in the earth, he loses and destroys his merit even if he gives him 1000 gold pieces.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides rules that charity given with a sour face loses its merit; it must be given with a pleasant face and with joy, sympathising with the poor person.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of the receiver’s இன்முகம் (pleasant face); Maimonides insists on the giver’s. Both make faces and feelings central to true giving.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Matanot Aniyim 10:4 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Before giving, glad; while giving, the mind is bright & clear; having given, one is gratified: This is the consummation of the sacrifice.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the ideal donor’s state of mind as joyful before, during and after the gift.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it puts joy at the end of a true act of giving.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 6.37, Dana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “To those men the gates of heaven shall never be closed, who with tender hearts and with a mind in accordance with their alms, greatly rejoicing, give even in poverty according to their ability, even as they did in the day of prosperity.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār praises givers who give gladly, with tender hearts, and keep giving even when they have become poor.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar describes the generous person's discomfort at being asked, which ends in joy once the asker is satisfied. The Nālaṭiyār likewise places the giver's joy and tender-heartedness at the centre of a true gift.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Great Giver keeps on giving, while those who receive grow weary of receiving.”
sikhism.explanation: In the third pauri of Japji Guru Nanak contrasts the tireless generosity of God with the limited capacity of those who receive.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures a generous person whose discomfort at being asked ends in the asker's joy; Gurbani's image of the Giver who never tires of giving is the nearest Sikh picture of giving as glad and unforced.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib, Pauri 3, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey Book 17, the suitor Antinous refuses the disguised Odysseus, who is begging for food, insults him, and throws a footstool at him, while others at the feast give him scraps. Even the other suitors warn that the gods sometimes walk among men disguised as strangers.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antinous is the anti-model of a giver: he meets a beggar’s plea with contempt and violence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A contrast to the Kural: instead of sharing the suppliant’s pain and ending it by giving, Antinous adds to it — and later dies first when Odysseus takes revenge.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Above all we should give willingly, quickly, and without any hesitation; a benefit commands no gratitude if it has hung for a long time in the hands of the giver, if he seems unwilling to part with it, and gives it as though he were being robbed of it.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that the manner of giving matters: a gift given reluctantly loses its value.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s picture of a giver who hurries to end the asker’s pain and delights in the result.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Benefits II.1 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: Chris Greicius's wish and the birth of Make-A-Wish
real_life_example.event: In 1980 Chris Greicius, a seven-year-old boy with leukemia in the Phoenix area, wished to become a police officer. Arizona Department of Public Safety officers and family friends gave him a helicopter ride, a tailored uniform and an honorary swearing-in, and he died days later. The people who granted his wish went on to found the Make-A-Wish organisation, which has since granted hundreds of thousands of wishes to seriously ill children.
real_life_example.explanation: A small, spontaneous act of kindness grew into a worldwide charity built entirely around the joy of the child who receives.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural locates the giver's reward in the moment the asker's face lights up, and the whole Make-A-Wish idea rests on bringing that joy to a child's face.

tamil:
ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பசிஆற்றல் அப்பசியை
மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின்.
transliteration:
Aatruvaar aatral pasi aatral appasiyai
Maatruvaar aatralin pin.
meaning: People who train themselves by going hungry are strong. But they are less strong than people who take away the hunger of others.
elementary: Going without food on purpose takes a lot of strength. But this kural says there is an even greater strength: giving food to someone who is hungry. Helping others beats showing how tough you are.
university: The couplet plays on the word ஆற்றல் (power, strength) and the verb ஆற்று (to endure, to perform): the ascetics’ power is பசி ஆற்றல், the power to endure hunger, whereas the philanthropist’s power is to மாற்று (change, remove) hunger. Valluvar deliberately ranks the householder’s charity above the ascetic’s self-mortification — a notable claim in a culture that deeply honoured tapas, and consistent with the Kural’s high regard for the householder (Chapter 5). The same contrast between self-denial and feeding the hungry is made by Isaiah, who says the fast God wants is to ‘deal thy bread to the hungry’. The couplet effectively redefines spiritual strength in social terms.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I do not pray to the Supreme Personality of Godhead for the eight perfections of mystic yoga, nor for salvation from repeated birth and death. I want only to stay among all the living entities and suffer all distresses on their behalf, so that they may be freed from suffering.”
hinduism.explanation: King Rantideva, after fasting for forty-eight days, gives away his food and water to hungry visitors and declares that he wants neither yogic powers nor liberation, only to relieve others’ suffering.
hinduism.tie_back: Rantideva puts relieving others’ hunger above mystic attainments won by austerity — the same ranking as the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink... Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the Last Judgement, Jesus identifies himself with the hungry and says feeding them is serving him.
christianity.tie_back: Feeding the hungry is treated as the highest religious act, as in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “But he has not broken through the difficult pass. And what can make you know what is [breaking through] the difficult pass? It is the freeing of a slave Or feeding on a day of severe hunger An orphan of near relationship Or a needy person in misery.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an calls feeding the hungry in a time of famine ‘the difficult pass’, a steep and demanding climb.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it frames relieving hunger as the true test of strength.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah tells people who fast that God prefers them to share their bread with the hungry.
judaism.tie_back: Near-identical ranking to the Kural: feeding the hungry is valued above going hungry oneself.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sasa Jataka, the Bodhisatta is born as a hare who, having no food to offer a hungry brahmin visitor (the god Sakka in disguise), leaps into a fire so that his own body may be eaten. Sakka honours the gift by painting the hare’s image on the moon.
buddhism.explanation: The hare offers the ultimate gift, its own body, to relieve a stranger’s hunger.
buddhism.tie_back: Relieving hunger is shown as the highest act of virtue, beyond any feat of self-control.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By austerities he cuts off the Karman.” … “By doing service he acquires the Karman which brings about for him the nâman and gôtra of a Tîrthakara.”
jainism.explanation: In Mahāvīra's list of the fruits of religious practice, austerity (tapas) wears away karma. Service to others (vaiyāvṛttya) is said to earn the karma that makes one a future Tīrthaṅkara, the highest rank Jain tradition recognises.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks relieving others' hunger above the ascetic's power to endure hunger. This passage likewise gives service to others a spiritual fruit that austerity alone does not bring.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.27 and 29.43 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without this grain, time does not pass in peace. Forsaking this grain, one does not meet the Lord of the World.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn that opens by calling those who give up food hypocrites, Bhagat Kabir insists that food sustains life and that abandoning it does not bring anyone to God.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks relieving hunger above the ascetic's power to endure it, and Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib likewise refuses to treat fasting and self-starvation as a path to God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 873, Raag Gond, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus steals fire from the gods and gives it to mortals so that they can cook food and survive, and is punished by Zeus by being chained to a rock where an eagle eats his liver.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prometheus uses his power not for himself but to meet human need, at great cost.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it honours power used to relieve others’ want above power used for oneself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If it is in our power to prevent something bad from happening, without thereby sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought, morally, to do it.”
philosophy.explanation: Peter Singer argues that people who can relieve starvation at modest cost are morally obliged to do so.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Singer makes the relief of hunger a central moral demand and a measure of moral strength.

real_life_example.event_title: The Ramakrishna Mission's monks begin famine relief at Mahula
real_life_example.event: In 1897 Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission near Calcutta, with the twofold aim of spreading Vedanta and improving social conditions in India. That May, Swami Akhandananda, a monk of the order who had found famine-stricken villages in Murshidabad district, opened the Mission's first famine relief centre at Mahula, obtaining rice and distributing it to the hungry, with fellow monks and funds sent to help. The relief work lasted about a year.
real_life_example.explanation: An order of renunciant monks made the feeding of the hungry a central part of their religious life rather than devoting themselves only to personal austerity.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks the strength of those who relieve others' hunger above the ascetic's strength to endure hunger, and here ascetics themselves turned to relieving hunger.

tamil:
அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல் அஃதொருவன்
பெற்றான் பொருள்வைப் புழி.
transliteration:
Atraar azhipasi theerththal agdhoruvan
Petraan porul vaippuzhi.
meaning: Feeding the poor whose hunger is crushing them is the best place for a person with money to store it.
elementary: People keep money in a piggy bank or a bank to keep it safe. This kural says the safest place to keep your money is in a hungry person’s full stomach. When you feed someone, your wealth becomes goodness that can never be stolen.
university: The couplet takes the image of a treasury (பொருள் வைப்புழி, ‘the place where wealth is deposited’) and relocates it: the proper strongroom for wealth is the relief of அழிபசி, ‘destroying hunger’, suffered by those who have nothing (அற்றார்). The metaphor inverts ordinary prudence, which stores wealth by withholding it, and claims that wealth is truly secured only by giving it away. Commentators read this both as moral merit that follows the giver into future lives and as social security in this life. The same ‘treasury’ inversion appears in Jesus’ ‘treasures in heaven’, in King Munbaz’s reply in the Talmud and in the Buddhist ‘well-stored fund’ of Khp 8, showing a widely shared intuition that generosity is the only wealth immune to loss.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let the rich satisfy the poor implorer, and bend his eye upon a longer pathway. Riches come now to one, now to another, and like the wheels of cars are ever rolling.”
hinduism.explanation: The Rig Vedic hymn on Liberality urges the rich to feed the poor and look to the long run, since wealth never stays in one place.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats feeding the poor as the far-sighted use of wealth that cannot be kept anyway.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.5 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts perishable earthly treasure with lasting heavenly treasure.
christianity.tie_back: Same ‘true storehouse’ inversion as the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allāh is like a seed [of grain] which grows seven spikes; in each spike is a hundred grains. And Allāh multiplies [His reward] for whom He wills.”
islam.explanation: Wealth spent in God’s way is compared to a seed that multiplies many times over.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, giving is presented not as loss but as the best investment of wealth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My ancestors stored up below, whereas I am storing above... My ancestors stored up treasures in a place where the human hand can reach, and so their treasures could have been robbed, whereas I am storing up treasures in a place where the human hand cannot reach.”
judaism.explanation: King Munbaz, criticised for spending his family treasure on the poor during a drought, replies that he is storing it in a safer place.
judaism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: relieving hunger in famine is the true treasury of wealth.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 11a (William Davidson/Koren translation)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “But when a man or woman has laid aside a well-stored fund of generosity, virtue, restraint, & self-control... That’s a well-stored fund. It can’t be wrested away. It follows you along.”
buddhism.explanation: The Reserve Fund discourse compares buried treasure, which can be lost, with the ‘fund’ of generosity, which cannot.
buddhism.tie_back: Same idea as the Kural: generosity is where wealth is kept safe.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When by blameless means thou hast acquired great wealth, then eat with others rice imported by oxen, for wealth never remaineth in the centre with anyone, but changes its position like a cart-wheel.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār's chapter on unstable wealth says that wealth, once honestly gained, should be shared at the table, because riches never stay with anyone for long.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells the person who has gained wealth to 'store' it in relieving others' hunger; the Nālaṭiyār gives the same advice for the same reason, that wealth kept to oneself does not last.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 1 ('Unstable Wealth'), st. 2 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition recorded by Macauliffe, Guru Nanak visited Duni Chand, a millionaire of Lahore who flew a flag for every lakh of rupees he owned. The Guru gave him a needle to return in the next world; when Duni Chand realised that not even a needle could go with him, the Guru told him to give some of his wealth in God's name and feed the poor so that it would accompany him, and Duni Chand distributed his treasure.
sikhism.explanation: The story teaches that wealth hoarded stays behind at death, while wealth used to feed the poor goes with the giver.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural names relief of the destitute's hunger as the proper place to deposit wealth, and the Guru's counsel to Duni Chand, feed the poor and your wealth shall accompany you, makes exactly that point.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter XI, pp. 129-130 (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s tale, the poor elderly couple Baucis and Philemon share their meagre meal with two disguised gods whom everyone else in the village had turned away. The gods flood the village but turn the couple’s cottage into a temple and grant their wish to serve there together and to die at the same moment.
greek_mythology.explanation: The couple’s generosity from poverty becomes their lasting reward.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their small gift of food turns out to be the safest ‘deposit’ they ever made, as the Kural suggests.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “These fine things show their quality better in the spending than in the hoarding... money is only precious when it is given away.”
philosophy.explanation: Lady Philosophy tells Boethius that riches have value only when they are spent or given, not when they are piled up.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it relocates the value of wealth from keeping it to giving it.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy II, Prose 5 (tr. W. V. Cooper)

real_life_example.event_title: Quaker soup kitchens in the Great Irish Famine
real_life_example.event: In late 1846, as famine spread in Ireland, Quakers led by Joseph Bewley formed the Central Relief Committee of the Society of Friends in Dublin, with a sister committee in London. Although Irish Quakers numbered only about 3,000, they set up soup kitchens in towns such as Waterford, Limerick, Clonmel and Cork, supplied large boilers, and distributed thousands of tons of food and seed. When the government adopted soup kitchens as its main relief in 1847, the Quakers provided boilers and cauldrons for them.
real_life_example.explanation: A small religious community poured its resources into feeding the starving and pioneered the method the state then adopted.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the proper place to store wealth is in relieving the killing hunger of the destitute, which is exactly where the Quakers put theirs.

tamil:
பாத்தூண் மரீஇ யவனைப் பசியென்னும்
தீப்பிணி தீண்டல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Paaththoon mareeiyavanaip pasiyennum
Theeppini theendal aridhu.
meaning: The burning sickness called hunger will hardly ever touch someone who makes a habit of sharing their food.
elementary: Imagine a kid who always shares their snacks at school. When that kid forgets their lunch one day, everyone is happy to share with them. People who share food are rarely left hungry.
university: பாத்தூண் (pāththūṇ) means ‘divided food’, food portioned out and shared, and மரீஇ indicates something practised until it is second nature. Hunger is called தீப்பிணி, a ‘fiery disease’ or ‘evil illness’, strengthening the medical image in which sharing works as a kind of immunity. The claim can be read at three levels: morally, as merit protecting the giver; socially, as a web of reciprocity in which those who share are shared with; and economically, as the observation that shared resources are used more efficiently. The Dhammapada’s ‘Hunger is the worst disease’ and the hadith that ‘food for two is sufficient for three’ show how widespread both the disease image and the sufficiency claim are.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “THE Gods have not ordained hunger to be our death: even to the well-fed man comes death in varied shape. The riches of the liberal never waste away, while he who will not give finds none to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Rig Vedic hymn to Liberality says the generous never run out, while the stingy are left without help.
hinduism.tie_back: Same promise as the Kural: those who share will not be abandoned to want.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.1 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises that those who give will receive generously in return.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, generosity is said to protect the giver from want.

islam.quote_or_event: “The food for two persons is sufficient for three, and the food of three persons is sufficient for four persons.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that food, when shared, stretches to feed more people.
islam.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s claim that sharing food, far from leaving one hungry, provides enough for all.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person will never become impoverished from giving charity. No harm nor damage will ever be caused because of charity.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides states as a principle that giving charity never makes anyone poor.
judaism.tie_back: The same assurance as the Kural: the habitual giver is protected from want.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Matanot Aniyim 10:2 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hunger is the worst disease, conditioned things the worst suffering. Knowing this as it really is, the wise realize Nibbana, the highest bliss.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada calls hunger the worst of diseases.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s striking image of hunger as a disease (தீப்பிணி), though it uses it to point to spiritual release rather than sharing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Give what you are able, even though you have not the thousandth part of a measure of rice in the house, and then eat your meal; the wise call those in this birth wandering beggars whose chimneys smoke not in this earth, surrounded by the deep sea, who gave not alms in a former birth.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār says to share some food before eating, however little one has. It explains present-day hunger and beggary as the karmic result of not giving in a former birth.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says hunger will hardly touch one who habitually shares food; the Nālaṭiyār makes the same link from the other side, since those who never shared become those whose cooking fires go out.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Siblings of Destiny meet together, and eat and spend, but these resources do not diminish; they continue to increase.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes a treasure inherited from the Father that grows rather than shrinks as the community shares and spends it together.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural promises that the habit of sharing food keeps the fiery disease of hunger away; Guru Arjan likewise teaches that what is shared in common is never exhausted.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 186, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, King Erysichthon cuts down a sacred oak of Ceres and scorns the gods. Ceres sends Famine (Fames) to breathe insatiable hunger into him; he eats away his whole fortune, sells his daughter, and finally devours his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hunger is portrayed as a personified curse that consumes a greedy, impious man.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The mirror image of the Kural: the man who respects nothing and shares nothing is the one the ‘fiery disease’ of hunger devours.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant’s fourth example in the Groundwork imagines a prosperous man who refuses to help others in hardship. Kant argues that he cannot will this as a universal law, because many situations may arise in which he himself would need the love and sympathy of others and would then have robbed himself of all hope of help.
philosophy.explanation: Kant shows that a world without mutual help is one nobody could rationally choose, because everyone may one day be in need.
philosophy.tie_back: Offers a rational basis for the Kural’s claim: those who share are part of a practice of mutual aid that protects them too.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, Section II (Ak. 4:423)

real_life_example.event_title: Raiffeisen's bread association in the hunger winter
real_life_example.event: During the hunger winter of 1846-47, when crop failures drove up food prices in the Westerwald, Friedrich Wilhelm Raiffeisen, the local mayor of Weyerbusch, founded an association to obtain bread and grain for the community. It bought flour, partly with private donations, baked bread in its own bakery and gave it to needy people on credit. The association is regarded as a forerunner of the cooperative movement that Raiffeisen later developed.
real_life_example.explanation: Pooling and sharing resources carried a poor rural district through famine and grew into a worldwide model of mutual self-help.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says hunger rarely touches those who make sharing food a habit, and Raiffeisen's community kept hunger at bay by sharing its bread.

tamil:
ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம் அறியார்கொல் தாமுடைமை
வைத்திழக்கும் வன்க ணவர்.
transliteration:
Eeththuvakkum inbam ariyaarkol thaamudaimai
Vaiththizhakkum vankanavar.
meaning: People with hard hearts keep their things to themselves, only to lose them in the end. Do they not know the joy of giving and of being glad about it?
elementary: Imagine a kid who hides all his toys in a box so nobody else can play with them. The toys get old, break, or get lost, and he never had fun sharing them. This kural asks: doesn’t he know how happy it feels to give?
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question (அறியார்கொல், ‘do they not know?’) directed at the வன்கணவர், literally ‘the hard-eyed’, a Tamil idiom for the pitiless and miserly. Its irony lies in the verb pair வைத்து இழக்கும், ‘keep and lose’: the miser keeps wealth in order not to lose it, yet loses it anyway, through death, theft or decay, having missed the one pleasure it could have given. ஈத்து உவக்கும் இன்பம், ‘the joy of giving and delighting’, is presented as a real and distinct pleasure available only to the giver. The argument is almost psychological rather than moral: miserliness is not only wrong but self-defeating.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Isha Upanishad opens by teaching that everything in the world is pervaded by the Lord; one should enjoy it through renunciation and not covet anyone’s wealth, since wealth truly belongs to no one.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that clinging to possessions misunderstands their nature, since nothing we hold is ultimately ours.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it exposes the futility of hoarding what cannot be kept; joy comes from letting go.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the Rich Fool, a man hoards his harvest for himself and dies that very night, losing everything.
christianity.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s ‘keep and lose’: the hoarder stores up wealth only to lose it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those who [greedily] withhold what Allāh has given them of His bounty ever think that it is better for them. Rather, it is worse for them. Their necks will be encircled by what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns misers that their hoarded wealth will become a burden around their necks.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says hoarding does not benefit the hoarder, even though he thinks it does.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt. But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes laments wealth that is hoarded, then lost, leaving nothing behind.
judaism.tie_back: Close parallel to the Kural’s ‘hoard and lose’ (வைத்திழக்கும்).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada contrasts misers with the wise person who rejoices in giving.
buddhism.tie_back: Same contrast as the Kural: the miser misses the joy that the giver knows.

jainism.quote_or_event: “They who, vexing their own bodies by stinting them in food and raiment, perform not acts of that goodly charity which never faileth, but avariciously hoard up what they have gathered together, will lose it all. O Lord of the mountain land which toucheth the sky! the bees which are driven from the honey they have collected bear witness.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār compares misers who neither give nor enjoy their wealth to bees driven from the honey they stored. Like the bees, such hoarders lose everything in the end.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar mocks the hard-hearted who hoard only to lose it all, unaware of the joy of giving, and this stanza makes the same charge with the image of the robbed honeycomb.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 1 ('Unstable Wealth'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He hoards gold and silver, but this wealth is false and poisonous, nothing more than ashes.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Dakhni Oankar Guru Nanak warns that the gold and silver a person piles up is false wealth that turns to ash.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar mocks the hard-hearted who keep wealth only to lose it, and Guru Nanak says the same of hoarding: what is kept back is worthless in the end.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 937, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For the man who gives willingly, even though he gives a great thing, rejoices in his gift and is glad in heart; but whoever gives way to shamelessness and takes something himself, even though it be a small thing, it freezes his heart.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says willing givers feel gladness while grasping takers feel their hearts go cold.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names a real joy that belongs only to the giver.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 357-360 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.”
philosophy.explanation: Andrew Carnegie argued that the wealthy should give away their surplus fortunes during their lifetime rather than hold on to them until death.
philosophy.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s charge that the hoarder only keeps his wealth to lose it at death, missing the chance to give.

real_life_example.event_title: Alexander empties the Persian treasury at Persepolis
real_life_example.event: After defeating Darius III, Alexander the Great seized the vast Achaemenid treasuries, finding enormous reserves at Susa and then at Persepolis, where ancient writers say the stores of gold and silver had accumulated from the revenues of the Persian kings since Cyrus. Alexander carried the treasure away and used the wealth to pay and sustain his army.
real_life_example.explanation: Riches stored up by generations of kings passed in a single campaign to a conqueror, without ever having served the people from whom they were gathered.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks whether hoarders know that they keep their wealth only to lose it, and the Persian royal hoard was kept for centuries only to be lost at a stroke.

tamil:
இரத்தலின் இன்னாது மன்ற நிரப்பிய
தாமே தமியர் உணல்.
transliteration:
Iraththalin innaadhu mandra nirappiya
Thaame thamiyar unal.
meaning: Eating alone, without sharing, just to keep your shelves full is surely worse than begging.
elementary: Begging for food feels bad. But this kural says something feels even worse: sitting alone with a big pile of food and never sharing any of it. Being lonely and greedy is sadder than being poor.
university: The comparison is deliberately shocking. In Chapter 106 (இரவு) and elsewhere, begging is treated as the lowest and most painful condition, yet here Valluvar says solitary eating is more இன்னாது (painful, wretched) than begging, and seals it with மன்ற, ‘certainly’. நிரப்பிய is read by Parimelazhagar as ‘in order to fill up’ one’s wealth, so the target is not eating as such but the miser who refuses to share lest his stores shrink. தமியர் உணல் (eating alone) stands for a whole social failure; the Rig Veda makes the same point when it says the man who eats without a companion is ‘all guilt’, and Epicurus says a meal without a friend is the life of a lion or wolf.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The foolish man wins food with fruitless labour: that food -I speak the truth- shall be his ruin. He feeds no trusty friend, no man to love him. All guilt is he who eats with no partaker.”
hinduism.explanation: The Rig Vedic hymn to Liberality condemns the man who eats alone without sharing, saying he is nothing but sin.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-exact parallel to the Kural’s condemnation of solitary eating (see also Gita 3.13: those who cook only for themselves ‘eat only sin’).
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.6 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
