christianity.quote_or_event: “There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day: And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores, And desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man’s table.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus, the rich man feasts alone while a beggar starves at his gate; after death their fates are reversed.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the parable judges the solitary feaster’s state to be worse than the beggar’s.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense? For that is the one who drives away the orphan And does not encourage the feeding of the poor.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an links refusing to feed the poor with denying the Day of Judgement.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats refusal to share food as a serious moral failure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are four types of character in human beings: One that says: ‘mine is mine, and yours is yours’: this is a commonplace type; and some say this is a sodom-type of character.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah says the attitude ‘what’s mine is mine’ is, according to some, the character of Sodom, the city proverbial for refusing hospitality.
judaism.tie_back: The solitary eater of the Kural is exactly this ‘mine is mine’ person, judged harshly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If beings knew, as I know, the results of giving & sharing, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of selfishness overcome their minds. Even if it were their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat without having shared, if there were someone to receive their gift.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that anyone who understood the fruits of sharing would never eat without first giving.
buddhism.tie_back: Directly parallels the Kural’s condemnation of eating alone and unshared.

jainism.quote_or_event: “To give a part of their meal to the extent of their ability, both to the friendly and unfriendly, and after that to eat, is truly to eat a meal. To those who refuse their food to the needy, and so live and eat and pass on, the door of heaven will be closed.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār's chapter on illiberality says that only a meal shared first with others, whether friend or not, truly counts as eating. Those who eat without sharing have heaven closed to them.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls solitary eating, done to keep one's stores full, more wretched than begging; the Nālaṭiyār likewise denies that unshared eating is a real meal at all.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, those houses in which neither the Holy nor the Lord are served - those houses are like cremation grounds; demons dwell within them.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir says that a household which serves neither holy people nor God is as desolate as a cremation ground.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls eating alone to keep one's stores full more wretched than begging; Kabir likewise judges the closed, unsharing household as worse than poor, a place of death.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Bhagat Kabir 192 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asks Dionysus that everything he touches become gold. His wish is granted, but his bread and wine turn to gold as he touches them, and he sits alone amid his treasure, starving, until he begs the god to take the gift back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas’ greed for gold leaves him hungry and isolated in the middle of great riches.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s point that hoarding for oneself can be more wretched than poverty.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “You must reflect carefully beforehand with whom you are to eat and drink, rather than what you are to eat and drink. For a dinner of meats without the company of a friend is like the life of a lion or a wolf.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca quotes Epicurus, who held that eating without companions reduces a human being to the level of a solitary predator.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats solitary eating as a degradation of human life.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 19.10, quoting Epicurus (tr. R. M. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Spartan citizens share their meals in the common messes
real_life_example.event: Adult male citizens of Sparta were required to belong to a common mess, the syssitia, of about fifteen men, where they ate together daily. Each member had to contribute a fixed amount of barley, cheese, figs, wine and other food, and a citizen who could not or would not make his contribution was expelled and lost his full civic rights.
real_life_example.explanation: Sparta made shared eating a condition of belonging to the community, treating a man outside the common table as no longer a full citizen.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls eating alone to keep one's stores full more wretched than begging, and Sparta built its whole citizen life around the shared table.

tamil:
சாதலின் இன்னாத தில்லை இனிததூஉம்
ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Saadhalin innaadhadhu illai inidhadhooum
Eedhal iyaiyaak kadai.
meaning: Nothing is more painful than dying. But even dying feels sweet when a person can no longer give to others.
elementary: Everyone thinks the worst thing in the world is dying. But this kural says a truly kind person would feel even worse if they could never help anyone again. For them, being unable to give is the saddest thing of all.
university: The final couplet of the chapter uses a hyperbolic reversal: death, the ultimate இன்னாதது (painful thing), becomes இனிது (sweet) — the emphatic அதூஉம், ‘even that’ — at the point where giving is no longer possible (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). The claim measures the worth of a life by its capacity to give: a life without that capacity is, for the generous person, worse than no life. Commentators read it as describing either the giver who has lost his means or one who faces a suppliant with nothing left to offer. The closing hyperbole makes giving not merely a virtue among others but the very thing that makes life worth living, bringing the chapter to a climax.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, King Shibi is tested by gods who take the form of a hawk chasing a dove. When the dove seeks refuge with him, Shibi refuses to give it up and instead offers the hawk an equal weight of his own flesh, finally placing his whole body on the scales rather than fail to give protection.
hinduism.explanation: Shibi would rather give up his life than fail to give what is asked of him.
hinduism.tie_back: Embodies the Kural’s claim that for the generous, being unable to give is worse than death.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, story of King Shibi (Sivi)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if I live in the flesh, this is the fruit of my labour... Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says death would be gain for him; the only reason to go on living is to serve others.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, life’s value is measured by what one can give to others; without that, death is preferable.

islam.quote_or_event: “And spend [in the way of Allāh] from what We have provided you before death approaches one of you and he says, ‘My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I would give charity and be of the righteous.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an pictures a dying person whose deepest regret is not having given charity while they could.
islam.tie_back: Links death and the lost chance to give, as the Kural does.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says that righteousness (tzedakah, a word later used for charity) saves from death, while ill-gotten treasure is useless.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties giving and death together, treating righteousness/charity as what gives life its value.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sivi Jataka, King Sivi, who gives alms daily, longs to give something from his own body. When a blind brahmin (Sakka in disguise) asks for an eye, he gladly gives both eyes, and is later rewarded with divine sight.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta king values the chance to give more than his own body and sight.
buddhism.tie_back: Shows the Kural’s attitude that for a true giver, giving outweighs even the greatest personal loss.

jainism.quote_or_event: Samantabhadra defines sallekhanā, the Jain practice of voluntarily giving up the body by gradual fasting, as something undertaken for the sake of dharma. It is permitted only when calamity, famine, old age or incurable disease makes it impossible to go on living righteously.
jainism.explanation: In Jain householder ethics, a person may calmly accept death when life can no longer be used to practise dharma. This 'wise death' is treated as a final religious act, not as a defeat.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says death becomes sweet when one can no longer give. Jainism also accepts death once a life can no longer serve its moral purpose, but for Jains that purpose is self-purification rather than giving.
jainism.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra 122 (cf. tr. Champat Rai Jain, 1917)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without meditating in remembrance on the Lord, one's life is like that of a snake. This is how the faithless cynic lives, forgetting the Naam, the Name of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan compares a life without remembrance of God to a snake's long but harmful life.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says death becomes sweet when one can no longer give, measuring life by its usefulness; Guru Arjan likewise judges a long life empty of its true purpose as no better than a snake's.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 239, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Alcestis, when no one else will die in place of King Admetus, his wife Alcestis gives her own life for him, choosing death over a life in which she could not give him the gift of survival.
greek_mythology.explanation: Alcestis treats giving, even of her own life, as more important than living.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Reflects the Kural’s scale of values in which giving outweighs life itself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He would prefer a short period of intense pleasure to a long one of mild enjoyment, a twelvemonth of noble life to many years of humdrum existence, and one great and noble action to many trivial ones.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the good person will give up wealth and even life for friends and country, because a short noble life beats a long empty one.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures life by the noble giving it makes possible, not by its length.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.8 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Julius Rosenwald's fund is required to spend itself out
real_life_example.event: Julius Rosenwald, president of Sears, Roebuck and Company, established the Julius Rosenwald Fund in 1917, chiefly to improve education for African American students, and gave much of his fortune during his lifetime. He opposed permanent endowments and stipulated that the fund spend its assets within 25 years of his death. After he died in 1932 the fund continued its work and closed in 1948.
real_life_example.explanation: Rosenwald treated wealth as something to be given away within a lifetime and a generation, not preserved for its own sake.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural measures a life by its capacity to give, and Rosenwald arranged his fortune so that its whole purpose would be exhausted in giving.

tamil:
ஈதல் இசைபட வாழ்தல் அதுவல்லது
ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Eedhal isaipada vaazhdhal adhuvalladhu
Oodhiyam illai uyirkku.
meaning: Give to people in need, and live so that people speak well of you. There is no other real gain a person can get from life.
elementary: Imagine a piggy bank you can’t take with you when you leave. The only things you really keep from life are what you gave away and the kind words people say about you because of it. Giving, and being remembered well for it, is the real prize of being alive.
university: The chapter on Renown opens by fusing it with the preceding chapter on Giving (ஈகை): ஈதல் (giving) and இசைபட வாழ்தல் (living so that isai, praise, arises) are presented as one achievement, gathered by the demonstrative அது (‘that’). The pivotal word is ஊதியம் (wages, income, profit), a commercial term deliberately applied to the உயிர் (the living soul): life is framed as a venture whose only true yield is renown generated by generosity. Classical commentary (Parimelazhagan, echoed by Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah) specifies giving to the poor, which anchors புகழ் in ethical action rather than mere celebrity. The couplet thus redefines ‘gain’: wealth hoarded is not profit; wealth converted into others’ welfare, and the esteem that follows, is. The same link between liberality and lasting worth appears in the Vedic hymn to Liberality and in Aristotle’s remark that the liberal are loved precisely because they give.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The riches of the liberal never waste away, while he who will not give finds none to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Rig Vedic hymn titled ‘Liberality’ says wealth that is shared is never really lost, while the person who refuses to give ends up alone and friendless.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats giving as the one ‘income’ that does not evaporate: the giver’s wealth survives by being given.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, taking leave of the Ephesian elders, tells them to support the weak and cites Jesus’ saying that giving is more blessed than receiving.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts relocate life’s real gain from what one takes in to what one gives out.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allāh is like a seed [of grain] which grows seven spikes; in each spike is a hundred grains.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an pictures charity as a seed that multiplies many hundredfold, so that what is given is not lost but increased.
islam.tie_back: The Kural calls giving the soul’s only profit; the Qur’an likewise frames spending on others as the most fruitful investment a person can make.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold.”
judaism.explanation: Hebrew wisdom literature ranks a good reputation and people’s goodwill above any amount of money.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar says renown is the only real profit; Proverbs says a good name outranks riches. Both place reputation above wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts the miser, who gains nothing lasting, with the wise giver, whose generosity alone secures future happiness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts make giving the single act that yields a real, lasting return for a life.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Three merchants set out on their travels, each with his capital; one of them gained there much, the second returned with his capital, and the third merchant came home after having lost his capital. … The capital is human life, the gain is heaven; through the loss of that capital man must be born as a denizen of hell or a brute animal.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's parable of the three merchants treats human life as capital: virtue earns a profit, mere decency only preserves the capital, and sin loses it.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says giving and a praiseworthy life are the only real profit a person can earn from living. The Jain parable likewise treats a human life as an investment whose only true gain is a good life's reward, not wealth.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.14–16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who serve are content. They meditate on the Truest of the True. They do not place their feet in sin, but do good deeds and live righteously in Dharma.”
sikhism.explanation: This pauri of Asa di Vaar describes those whose lives consist of service, remembrance of God and good deeds.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar says giving and living so that praise gathers round one's name is the only real profit of life; the Sikh Gurus likewise define a well-spent life as service and good deeds, though without making praise the goal.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466-467, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (pauri), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor elderly couple, alone in their Phrygian village welcome the disguised Jupiter and Mercury and share their meagre food. The gods flood the inhospitable neighbourhood, turn the couple’s cottage into a temple, and at death change them into an oak and a linden that later visitors honour with garlands.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their small act of hospitality is the only thing that distinguishes them, and it becomes the reason they are remembered and honoured ever after.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, humble giving is what converts an ordinary life into an honoured name.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The liberal are almost the most loved of all virtuous characters, since they are useful; and this depends on their giving.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle observes that generous people win exceptional affection from others, and that this esteem springs directly from their giving.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle and Valluvar both trace a person’s good standing among others back to the act of giving.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W.D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Sir Thomas Bodley reopens Oxford's university library
real_life_example.event: Oxford's old university library had been stripped of its books and furniture in the mid-sixteenth century. The retired diplomat Thomas Bodley offered to restore it, personally paying for and directing its refurbishment from 1598 and giving books of his own, and the library opened on 8 November 1602. In 1610 he secured an agreement under which the Stationers' Company would give the library a copy of every book printed in England.
real_life_example.explanation: A private fortune given to a public institution made Bodley's name permanent: the library has been called the Bodleian ever since.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the only real profit of life is to give and to live so that praise gathers around one's name, and Bodley's gift turned his wealth into a name that has lasted four centuries.

tamil:
உரைப்பார் உரைப்பவை எல்லாம் இரப்பார்க்கொன்று
ஈவார்மேல் நிற்கும் புகழ்.
transliteration:
Uraippaar uraippavai ellaam irappaarkku ondru
Eevaarmel nirkum pukazh.
meaning: All the praise that people speak comes to rest on those who give something to people who ask for help.
elementary: When grown-ups tell stories about great people, the ones everyone loves to talk about are usually the helpers, the ones who shared. Kindness is what people remember and keep talking about.
university: உரைப்பார் உரைப்பவை, ‘what those who speak speak’, is read by Parimelazhagan as the praise uttered by poets and eulogists; the couplet claims that all of it ultimately ‘stands upon’ (மேல் நிற்கும்) givers. Renown is thus a social fact: it lives in the mouths of others and is conferred, not seized. The verb நிற்கும் (‘stands, abides’) implies durability; the praise settles and remains. Classical Tamil culture institutionalised exactly this in the bardic economy of Sangam patronage, where poets immortalised generous chieftains such as Pari in verse. The couplet therefore doubles as a sociology of reputation: fame follows the flow of gifts, a pattern echoed in the Buddha’s list of the visible fruits of generosity and in the Psalmist’s praise of the one who ‘hath given to the poor’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is for this, O king, that they who have great intelligence say that there is nothing higher and greater in the three worlds than gift!”
hinduism.explanation: The sage Markandeya, instructing Yudhishthira on charity, concludes that the wise unanimously declare giving to be the highest thing in all the worlds.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says all that speakers praise rests on givers; the Mahabharata likewise reports the verdict of the wise converging on the giver.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 199 (trans. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her.”
christianity.explanation: When a woman pours costly ointment on Jesus and is criticised for waste, he declares that her generous act will be told everywhere in her memory.
christianity.tie_back: A single act of lavish giving becomes what people everywhere speak of, just as the Kural says all praise settles on the giver.

islam.quote_or_event: “You people are Allah's witnesses on earth.”
islam.explanation: When a funeral passed and people praised the deceased, the Prophet said Paradise was affirmed for him, explaining that the community’s testimony about a person carries real weight.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat what people say about someone as a meaningful verdict on that life; the Kural adds that such praise gathers around givers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He hath dispersed, he hath given to the poor; his righteousness endureth for ever; his horn shall be exalted with honour.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalm describes the righteous person who distributes to the poor, promising that his righteousness lasts and his standing is raised in honour.
judaism.tie_back: Giving to the poor leads to enduring honour: nearly the same chain of cause and effect as the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The fine reputation of one who gives, who is a master of giving, is spread far & wide.”
buddhism.explanation: Asked by General Siha for a fruit of generosity visible in this life, the Buddha lists, among others, that the generous person’s good reputation travels widely.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a restatement of the Kural: renown is the visible, spoken-about fruit that settles on the giver.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.34, Siha Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the sky sounded drums, intoxicating by their echoes, like bards proclaiming Śreyāṃsa’s happiness.” … The kings, townsmen, and the other people … said to Śreyāṃsa: “O Prince, you are fortunate, a crest-jewel of men, since you persuaded the Master to accept even a little cane-juice.”
jainism.explanation: When Prince Śreyāṃsa offered sugar-cane juice to break the first Tīrthaṅkara Ṛṣabha's year-long fast, gods and men together celebrated the giver. Jain tradition holds that the duty of giving on earth began with this act.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says all the praise that speakers utter comes to rest on those who give; in this Jain story, the praise of gods, kings and townspeople likewise gathers on the giver Śreyāṃsa.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book I (Ādīśvaracaritra), ch. III, part 7 'The fast-breaking of Ṛṣabha' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “DADDA: The One Lord is the Great Giver; He is the Giver to all.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Bavan Akhri Guru Arjan teaches that there is only one true Giver, who provides for every being.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says all the praise of poets comes to rest on those who give; Guru Arjan directs that praise to the One who is the Giver of all, so the Sikh parallel moves the givers' glory to God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 257, Raag Gauree, Bavan Akhri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He that is righteous and deals righteously, the people tell of his praise among all lands, and many shall call him blessed.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope, preparing to honour a ragged stranger (the disguised Odysseus), reflects that the harsh are cursed while the righteous are praised everywhere.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts describe praise spreading through people’s speech; Penelope says this while practising generous hospitality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The prize appointed for the noblest deeds; and this is honour; that is surely the greatest of external goods.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle identifies honour as the greatest of the external goods, the recognition that is awarded for the finest actions.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle treats honour as conferred by others for noble deeds, just as the Kural says praise settles on those who give.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (trans. W.D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Maecenas becomes the patron of Virgil and Horace
real_life_example.event: Gaius Maecenas, a wealthy adviser to Augustus who remained an equestrian and never held high office, supported a circle of poets that included Virgil and Horace. Virgil dedicated the Georgics to him, Horace dedicated several works to him, and Maecenas gave Horace an estate in the Sabine hills. His name became proverbial for a generous patron of the arts.
real_life_example.explanation: The praise of the greatest poets of the age settled on the man who supported them, so lastingly that his name became a common word for a patron.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that all the praise that poets utter comes to rest on those who give, and in Maecenas the poets' praise literally became the giver's name.

tamil:
ஒன்றா உலகத்து உயர்ந்த புகழல்லால்
பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன் றில்.
transliteration:
Ondraa ulagaththu uyarndha pukazhallaal
Pondraadhu nirpadhu ondril.
meaning: In this world, nothing lasts forever except a great good name, which has no equal.
elementary: Toys break, houses get old, and even mountains slowly wear down. But a story about someone who was truly good can be told again and again for a thousand years. Good fame is the one thing that doesn’t wear out.
university: The syntax hinges on ஒன்றா, which commentators read two ways: as qualifying புகழ் (‘peerless, matchless renown’) or as describing உலகு (‘this world, where nothing stays constant’). Either way, the couplet sets renown against the Indian commonplace of impermanence (நிலையாமை), which Valluvar treats in its own chapter (34): bodies, riches and kingdoms are பொன்றும் (perishable), but உயர்ந்த புகழ், exalted renown, alone stands. This is Valluvar’s this-worldly answer to the question of immortality: not the soul’s survival, but the survival of a good name in human memory. The claim parallels the Greek heroic ideal of kleos aphthiton (‘imperishable fame’), though Valluvar grounds renown in giving rather than martial glory. Philosophers such as the Stoics would dispute it, counting reputation among things outside our control and therefore not a true good.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for one who has been honored, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that fleeing battle would earn him a disgrace that people would talk about forever (the Sanskrit calls the ill-fame avyayā, ‘imperishable’).
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita presupposes the Kural’s point from the negative side: reputation, good or bad, outlasts the person and is what endures.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts perishable earthly wealth with imperishable treasure stored with God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts sort things into the perishable and the imperishable, but Jesus locates the imperishable in heaven, Valluvar in renown on earth.

islam.quote_or_event: “And grant me a mention [i.e., reputation] of honor among later generations.”
islam.explanation: Abraham prays that he will be remembered with honour by the generations who come after him.
islam.tie_back: A prophet explicitly asks for the very thing the Kural calls the one imperishable possession: an honoured name that outlives him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says a righteous person’s memory remains a blessing, while the wicked person’s name decays.
judaism.tie_back: Only the good name survives decay: the same contrast between lasting renown and everything that rots away.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even gorgeous royal chariots wear out, and indeed this body too wears out. But the Dhamma of the Good does not age; thus the Good make it known to the good.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that splendid possessions and the body itself decay, but the teaching and way of the good do not grow old.
buddhism.tie_back: Both divide the world into what wears out and the one thing that does not; for Valluvar it is renown, for the Dhammapada the Dhamma of the good.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.”
jainism.explanation: Queen Kamalāvatī reminds King Iṣukāra that at death every possession is left behind, and only dharma goes with a person.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says nothing in this world lasts except matchless renown. The Jain text also picks out one thing that survives impermanence, but that thing is dharma, not fame.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Raam Chand passed away, as did Raawan, even though he had lots of relatives. Says Nanak, nothing lasts forever; the world is like a dream.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur reminds the reader that even the most celebrated figures of legend, hero and villain alike, passed away, and that nothing in the world is permanent.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says nothing in the world endures except peerless renown; Guru Tegh Bahadur agrees that everything perishes but does not exempt fame, pointing instead to God alone as lasting.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahala 9, Salok 50, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Thus even in death your fame, Achilles, has not been lost, and your name lives evermore among all mankind.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the underworld, Agamemnon’s shade tells Achilles that his fame survived his death and lives on among all people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is kleos aphthiton, imperishable fame, the Greek counterpart of Valluvar’s புகழ் that alone does not perish.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Things not in our control are body, property, reputation, command, and, in one word, whatever are not our own actions.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus lists reputation among external things that are not truly ours and should not be treated as goods.
philosophy.tie_back: A deliberate counterpoint: where the Kural calls renown the one lasting possession, the Stoic calls it something never really possessed at all.

real_life_example.event_title: James Prinsep deciphers the edicts of Ashoka
real_life_example.event: Before the 1830s the Mauryan emperor Ashoka was known almost only from Buddhist chronicles. In 1837 the British scholar James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script of inscriptions on pillars and rocks, revealing edicts issued by a king who called himself Beloved of the Gods, Piyadasi. These edicts were identified as Ashoka's, restoring a major ruler to history after some two thousand years.
real_life_example.explanation: An emperor whose empire, cities and dynasty had all vanished was brought back to the world's memory through the record of his moral teaching carved in stone.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says nothing in this world stands except exalted renown, and Ashoka's palaces perished while the edicts recording his ideals survived to restore his name.

tamil:
நிலவரை நீள்புகழ் ஆற்றின் புலவரைப்
போற்றாது புத்தேள் உலகு.
transliteration:
Nilavarai neelpukazh aatrin pulavaraip
Potraadhu puththel ulagu.
meaning: If someone earns a good name that spreads across the earth and lasts, the world of the gods will honor that person even more than its own wise beings.
elementary: Imagine a class in the sky where the angels usually cheer for their own star students. But if someone down on earth does something so good that the whole world talks about it for ages, even the sky-class stops and cheers for that person instead.
university: The couplet is deliberately audacious: earthly renown outranks celestial status. Its key term is contested. புலவர் ordinarily means ‘learned ones’ or ‘poets’, but Parimelazhagan glosses it here as the devas, so that the heavenly world (புத்தேள் உலகு) ‘does not praise’ its own gods but the person whose fame fills the earth (நிலவரை, ‘to the bounds of the land’); Mu. Varadarasan follows this, and Pope renders it as heaven ceasing to laud the sage. Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi read புலவர் as scholars or learned men. On any reading, Valluvar inverts the usual hierarchy in which heaven confers worth on earth: here the earth’s verdict, expressed as lasting renown, is what heaven itself acknowledges. A striking parallel is the Mahabharata story of King Indradyumna, who fell from heaven when his earthly reputation faded and regained it once living memory of his generosity was found.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The report of virtuous deeds spreadeth over the earth and ascendeth to heaven. As long as that report lasts, so long is the doer said to be in heaven.”
hinduism.explanation: King Indradyumna falls from heaven because no one remembers him; when an ancient tortoise recalls his lavish gifts, a celestial car returns him to heaven with these verses.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s claim: a person’s standing in heaven depends on the endurance of their renown on earth.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 198 (trans. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat.”
christianity.explanation: In the judgment scene, the King welcomes into the kingdom those who fed the hungry and cared for strangers.
christianity.tie_back: Heaven honours people for what they did on earth for others, echoing the Kural’s heaven that honours the earthly giver.

islam.quote_or_event: “All the inhabitants of the Heaven would love him, and then he is granted the pleasure of the people on the earth.”
islam.explanation: When God loves a servant, Gabriel announces it in heaven, all heaven’s inhabitants love that person, and then acceptance is placed for him among people on earth.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link heavenly esteem and earthly esteem for a person; the direction is reversed (heaven first in the hadith, earth first in the Kural).

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are three crowns: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of royalty, but the crown of a good name supersedes them all.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shimon ranks a good name above the most sacred and powerful distinctions in Jewish life.
judaism.tie_back: Just as the Kural places earthly renown above even celestial sages, the Mishnah places a good name above priesthood and Torah learning.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:13 (trans. Joshua Kulp; numbered 4:17 in some editions)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As kinsmen welcome a dear one on arrival, even so his own good deeds will welcome the doer of good who has gone from this world to the next.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says a doer of good is greeted in the next world by his own good deeds, like a traveller welcomed home by relatives.
buddhism.tie_back: In both, what a person did on earth determines the welcome they receive in the higher world.

jainism.quote_or_event: “…because he stands fast in midst of dangers and fears, patiently bears hardships and calamities, adheres to the chosen rules of penance, is wise, indifferent to pleasure and pain, rich in control, and gifted with fortitude, the name Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra has been given him by the gods.”
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sūtra says the gods themselves gave Vardhamāna the name 'Mahāvīra' because of his human virtues. In Jain cosmology the gods honour and serve the Tīrthaṅkaras, and liberation can only be reached from a human birth.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar imagines the celestial world honouring a renowned human above its own sages. Jain tradition holds something similar, with gods naming, praising and serving a human Jina whose achievement exceeds their own.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §108 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “with a good name and reputation, with praise and fame throughout the world- still, if the Lord does not bless you with His Glance of Grace, then who cares? What is the use?”
sikhism.explanation: In the seventh pauri of Japji Guru Nanak imagines a person famed across the world and asks what such fame is worth without God's grace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural claims that worldwide, lasting renown wins honour even above the celestials; Guru Nanak takes up the same picture of world-wide fame and subordinates it to the divine glance.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib, Pauri 7, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “After him I saw mighty Hercules, but it was his phantom only, for he is feasting ever with the immortal gods, and has lovely Hebe to wife.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus sees only Heracles’ shade in Hades, because the hero himself, after his earthly labours, was taken up to live among the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles’ renowned deeds on earth won him a seat of honour among the immortals, much as Valluvar’s earthly renown wins heaven’s praise.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “What would not a man give if he might converse with Orpheus and Musaeus and Hesiod and Homer?”
philosophy.explanation: Facing death, Socrates imagines an afterlife where he could meet the renowned figures of the past, and counts that prospect a great good.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates pictures the next world as a place where the famous of the earth are sought out and honoured, loosely echoing the Kural’s heaven that honours the earthly renowned.

real_life_example.event_title: Yuri Gagarin's world tour after the first human spaceflight
real_life_example.place: Moscow, Soviet Union, and cities around the world
real_life_example.event: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human to travel into space, orbiting the Earth once in Vostok 1. Two days later he appeared beside Premier Khrushchev in Moscow, and he then made a worldwide tour, greeted by cheering crowds; in July 1961 he visited London and Manchester at the invitation of a trade union, meeting dignitaries and royalty, and he also met India's Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.
real_life_example.explanation: At the height of the Cold War, a single achievement made one man's name celebrated across rival blocs and continents.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of renown that reaches the ends of the earth and is honoured even above the celestials, and Gagarin, who had himself gone beyond the sky, was acclaimed across the whole globe.

tamil:
நத்தம்போல் கேடும் உளதாகும் சாக்காடும்
வித்தகர்க் கல்லால் அரிது.
transliteration:
Naththampol kedum uladhaakum saakkaadum
Viththakarkku allaal aridhu.
meaning: A loss that is really a gain, and a death that lets you live on in people's memory, are hard for anyone except the truly wise to achieve.
elementary: A candle gets smaller as it burns, but it lights up the whole room. Some very wise people are like that. When they give away their time, money, or even their life for others, they seem to lose, but their goodness grows and people remember them forever.
university: This is the chapter’s most paradoxical and textually difficult couplet. நத்தம் is glossed by Parimelazhagan as ஆக்கம் (increase), giving ‘a ruin that is like gain’: the loss suffered by the physical body (poverty through giving, hardship) that enlarges the ‘body of fame’ (புகழுடம்பு). சாக்காடும் உளதாகும், ‘death that becomes existence’, refers to dying in such a way that one’s renown is fixed for ever. Only the வித்தகர் (the skilled, the wise) manage this conversion of loss into gain. Commentators including Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah explain it through the Tamil idea of two bodies, the perishing body of flesh and the enduring body of renown. Cross-culturally it matches the logic of heroic or sacrificial death: Achilles’ choice at Troy, Diotima’s account of those who die ‘for the sake of leaving behind them a name’, and the grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, either you will be killed on the battlefield and attain the heavenly planets, or you will conquer and enjoy the earthly kingdom.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that a righteous warrior cannot lose: death in duty brings heaven, and victory brings the kingdom.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a rightly met death not as loss but as a form of gain.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a seed that must die in the soil in order to produce a harvest, pointing to his own death.
christianity.tie_back: The same paradox as the Kural: an apparent loss or death that is actually increase.

islam.quote_or_event: “And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allāh as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision,”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an declares that those who die in God’s cause are not truly dead but living and provided for.
islam.tie_back: Both describe a death that is actually a continued life, ‘death that becomes existence’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one’s birth.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth pairs the value of a good name with the claim that the day of death surpasses the day of birth, since only at death is a life’s name complete.
judaism.tie_back: Death that seals a good name is better than a beginning: close to the Kural’s death that establishes lasting renown.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sasa Jataka the Bodhisatta, born as a hare with nothing else to give, leaps into a fire to offer his own body as food to a brahmin, who is Sakka in disguise. The fire turns icy and does not burn him, and Sakka marks the sign of a hare on the moon so that the hare’s virtue will be known throughout the aeon.
buddhism.explanation: The hare’s willingness to give up his life is converted into an everlasting sign in the sky.
buddhism.tie_back: A self-sacrifice that should have been pure loss becomes lasting renown, the very conversion the Kural credits to the wise.
buddhism.source: Jataka No. 316, Sasa-Jataka (ed. E.B. Cowell, Vol. III)

jainism.quote_or_event: “These two ways of life ending with death have been declared: death with one's will, and death against one's will. Death against one's will is that of ignorant men, and it happens (to the same individual) many times. Death with one's will is that of wise men, and at best it happens but once.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's lecture on death contrasts the fool's repeated, unwilling deaths with the wise person's single, willing death, which can bring the cycle of rebirth to an end.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says a loss that is really gain, and a death that is really living on, are within reach only of the wise. The Jain text likewise reserves a death that is a victory rather than a loss for the wise alone.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.2–3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The death of brave heroes is blessed, if it is approved by God.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Alahanian, hymns sung in mourning, Guru Nanak says that the death of the truly brave is blessed when it is accepted by God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of a death that is really a way of living on, achieved only by the wise; Guru Nanak likewise calls a death approved by God not a loss but a blessing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 579, Raag Vadhans, Alahanian, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “If I stay here and fight, I shall not return alive but my name will live for ever: whereas if I go home my name will die, but it will be long ere death shall take me.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles explains his two possible fates: early death at Troy with undying fame, or a long, obscure life at home.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The classic statement of trading the body’s life for a name that lives forever, the Kural’s ‘death that becomes existence’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They are ready to run all risks greater far than they would have for their children, and to spend money and undergo any sort of toil, and even to die, for the sake of leaving behind them a name which shall be eternal.”
philosophy.explanation: Diotima tells Socrates that the love of immortal fame drives people to spend, toil and even die, citing Alcestis, Achilles and Codrus.
philosophy.tie_back: Both identify the paradoxical exchange of wealth and even life for an undying name.

real_life_example.event_title: Joan of Arc is executed, rehabilitated and canonised
real_life_example.event: Joan of Arc, the peasant girl who led French forces to relieve Orleans during the Hundred Years' War, was tried by an ecclesiastical court and executed at Rouen on 30 May 1431. On the order of Pope Callixtus III, proceedings in 1455-56 annulled her conviction, and in 1920 she was canonised by Pope Benedict XV, while the French parliament decreed a yearly national festival in her honour.
real_life_example.explanation: A death meant to discredit her became the foundation of a renown that has grown for nearly six centuries; she is honoured as France's national heroine and patron saint.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of a death that is really a way of living on, and Joan's execution became the beginning of her enduring life in the memory of her nation.

tamil:
தோன்றின் புகழொடு தோன்றுக அஃதிலார்
தோன்றலின் தோன்றாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Thondrin pukazhodu thondruka aqdhilaar
Thondralin thondraamai nandru.
meaning: If you are born into the world, be born with the qualities that earn a good name. If you do not have them, it would be better not to be born.
elementary: If you’re going to step onto the stage in the school play, practise hard and do your best. Showing up and doing nothing good can be worse than not showing up at all. Whatever you take part in, do it in a way people can be proud of.
university: The verb தோன்று (‘to appear, arise, be born’) occurs five times, giving the couplet an incantatory force. Two readings exist. Parimelazhagan and Pope take it as ‘being born’: if one is born, one should be born with qualities that bring renown, and for those without them it were better not to be born (Pope: ‘’twere better hide your face’). Mu. Varadarasan and Karunanidhi read it as ‘appearing in a field’: whatever role or arena one enters, one should enter it with distinction, or not at all. The first reading is existential, the second vocational; both insist that visibility without merit is a net negative. The thought has sharp parallels: Jesus’ ‘good for that man if he had not been born’, Qoheleth’s preference for an untimely birth over a life empty of good, and the Mahabharata heroine Vidula’s maxim that it is ‘better to blaze up for a moment than smoke for ever’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is better to blaze up for a moment than smoke for ever and ever.”
hinduism.explanation: Queen Vidula rebukes her son Sanjaya, who lies despondent after defeat, urging him to win distinction by his deeds rather than live on without honour.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it prefers a brief appearance with glory to a long existence without it.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 133 (trans. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “It had been good for that man if he had not been born.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says this of the one who would betray him, Judas.
christianity.tie_back: The same judgement form as the Kural: some lives would have been better never begun.

islam.quote_or_event: “The disbeliever will say, “Oh, I wish that I were dust!””
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment, seeing what his own hands have sent forth, the disbeliever wishes he had never existed as a person at all.
islam.tie_back: A life lived without worth leads to the wish for non-existence, echoing the Kural’s ‘better not to appear’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years be many, and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth says that a long, prolific life that never attains good, and ends without honourable burial, is worse than never having been born.
judaism.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: existence without the good (and without honour at the end) is worse than non-appearance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada lists the qualities by which a person’s glory steadily increases.
buddhism.tie_back: It names the qualities with which one should ‘appear’: those that naturally produce renown.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Death devours your days, using the sun from which they originate as the measure by which he metes them. Practise therefore virtue and be compassionate, for such as do not act thus, though they are born, must be esteemed as unborn.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār says that those who live without virtue and compassion may as well never have been born.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that if one is born, one should be born with the qualities that bring renown, and that otherwise it is better not to be born. The Nālaṭiyār passes the same verdict, that a birth without virtue counts as no birth.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 1 ('Unstable Wealth'), st. 7 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That family, whose son has no spiritual wisdom or contemplation - why didn't his mother just become a widow?”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir asks why a mother should have borne a son who lives without spiritual wisdom, implying it would have been better had he never been born.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that those without the qualities that bring renown would do better not to be born at all, and Kabir makes the same harsh judgement about a life empty of wisdom.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 328, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “It becomes us, therefore, to take our stand at the head of all the Lycians and bear the brunt of the fight.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Sarpedon tells Glaucus that because they enjoy honour and privilege as princes, they must justify it by fighting in the front ranks.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Those who appear in a prominent place must appear with deeds worthy of renown, or their position is empty.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Honour is the prize of virtue, and it is to the good that it is rendered.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle, discussing the great-souled person, says honour is properly given only to the genuinely good.
philosophy.tie_back: Renown should accompany real excellence; one who seeks the stage without virtue has no claim to it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (trans. W.D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Abebe Bikila wins the Olympic marathon barefoot
real_life_example.event: Abebe Bikila, a late addition to Ethiopia's team, ran the Rome Olympic marathon barefoot and won in a world-best time of 2 hours 15 minutes 16.2 seconds. He became the first Black African to win an Olympic gold medal, and in Tokyo in 1964 he became the first person to win two Olympic marathons.
real_life_example.explanation: Bikila's first appearance on the world stage was so distinguished that it changed how the world saw African athletes.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that whoever appears before the world should appear with qualities that bring renown, and Bikila's first Olympic appearance did exactly that.

tamil:
புகழ்பட வாழாதார் தந்நோவார் தம்மை
இகழ்வாரை நோவது எவன்.
transliteration:
Pukazhpada vaazhaadhaar thannovaar thammai
Ikazhvaarai novadhu evan?
meaning: People who do not live in a way that earns a good name should be upset with themselves. Why are they upset with the people who look down on them?
elementary: If you didn’t study and got a bad grade, being angry at the teacher doesn’t help. It’s better to look at what you could do differently. The same goes for what people think of you: if they don’t think well of you, first check your own actions.
university: Valluvar turns from praising renown to diagnosing a common evasion: blaming one’s critics instead of oneself. The couplet sets தந்நோவார் (‘they do not grieve over themselves’) against இகழ்வாரை நோவது (‘resenting those who scorn them’) and ends in the rhetorical எவன், ‘why?’. The ethical claim is that reputation, though it lives in others’ mouths (Kural 232), is earned by one’s own conduct, so responsibility lies within. Commentators from Parimelazhagan to Karunanidhi read it as a call to self-correction rather than to resentment. The insight is widely shared: Jesus’ mote and beam, Lamentations’ question why a living man should complain of the punishment of his own sins, Zeus’s complaint in the Odyssey that mortals blame the gods for their own folly, and Epictetus’ portrait of the uninstructed person who lays the fault of his condition on others.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man must elevate himself by his own mind, not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that each person is responsible for lifting or lowering themselves; the self is its own friend or enemy.
hinduism.tie_back: Both locate the cause of one’s standing within oneself, not in others.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus rebukes those who fixate on others’ small faults while ignoring their own large ones.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s renownless person resents critics instead of examining himself: the same misplaced focus.

islam.quote_or_event: “And whatever strikes you of disaster - it is for what your hands have earned; but He pardons much.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that misfortunes people suffer are largely the result of their own deeds.
islam.tie_back: The Kural traces a poor reputation to one’s own conduct; the Qur’an traces misfortune to one’s own hands.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?”
judaism.explanation: The poet of Lamentations asks why anyone should complain about suffering that follows from their own wrongdoing, and urges self-examination instead.
judaism.tie_back: Nearly the same rhetorical question as the Kural’s எவன் (‘why?’): why resent consequences you brought on yourself?

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one’s own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells people to stop scrutinising others’ failures and to look at their own deeds, both done and left undone.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s advice exactly: look at what you failed to do, not at those who criticise you.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By repenting of one's sins to oneself the soul obtains repentance, and becoming indifferent by repentance he prepares for himself an (ascending) scale of virtues, by which he destroys the Karman resulting from delusion.”
jainism.explanation: In Jain practice, self-reproach for one's own faults (nindā) and confessing them before a teacher (garhā) are regular disciplines that purify the soul.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells those who lack renown to grieve over themselves instead of resenting their critics; Jainism likewise makes blaming oneself, not others, a path to moral growth.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.6 (cf. 29.7) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Slander me, slander me - go ahead, people, and slander me. Slander is pleasing to the Lord's humble servant.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir welcomes the criticism of others, saying that the devotee is glad to be slandered because it humbles and cleanses him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks why those who fail to earn renown resent their critics instead of grieving over themselves; Kabir models the opposite of resentment, accepting criticism without anger.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “See now, how men lay blame upon us gods for what is after all nothing but their own folly.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Opening the Odyssey, Zeus complains that mortals blame the gods for troubles they bring on themselves, citing Aegisthus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same diagnosis as the Kural: people blame outside forces for what their own conduct produced.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “An uninstructed person will lay the fault of his own bad condition upon others. Someone just starting instruction will lay the fault on himself.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus describes stages of moral progress: blaming others, then blaming oneself, and finally blaming no one.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar asks the renownless to take Epictetus’ second step: turn the blame inward rather than on critics.

real_life_example.event_title: President Kennedy takes responsibility for the Bay of Pigs
real_life_example.event: In April 1961 an invasion of Cuba by CIA-trained Cuban exiles at the Bay of Pigs failed within days. At his news conference on 21 April, President John F. Kennedy, pressed about the failure, noted the old saying that victory has a hundred fathers and defeat is an orphan, and stated that he was the responsible officer of the government. His public approval rating rose to 83 percent in the weeks that followed.
real_life_example.explanation: Instead of blaming advisers, agencies or critics, Kennedy publicly owned the failure, and the public respected him for it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks why those who fall short resent their critics instead of grieving over themselves, and Kennedy answered a defeat by taking the blame on himself.

tamil:
வசையென்ப வையத்தார்க் கெல்லாம் இசையென்னும்
எச்சம் பெறாஅ விடின்.
transliteration:
Vasaiyenba vaiyaththaarkku ellaam isaiyennum
Echcham peraaa vidin.
meaning: Wise people say that for anyone on earth, it is a shame not to leave behind a good name.
elementary: A good camper leaves the campsite better than they found it, maybe with a helpful sign for the next visitors. Life is similar: it’s a shame to leave without leaving behind something good that people remember you by.
university: The pivotal word is எச்சம்: ‘remainder, residue, what is left over’, and by extension ‘offspring’ or ‘legacy’. Renown (இசை) is defined as the proper residue of a life; to fail to obtain it (பெறாஅ, with the poetic vowel-lengthening called அளபெடை) is வசை, reproach, and the plural subject வையத்தார்க் கெல்லாம் makes the standard universal. Pope captured the offspring sense: ‘Fame is virtue’s child, they say; if, then, / You childless live, you live the scorn of men.’ The idea that a person’s true progeny is their good name has a remarkable parallel in Isaiah 56:5, where the childless are promised ‘a name better than of sons and of daughters’, and in Diotima’s speech in Plato’s Symposium, where the ‘children’ of Homer and Lycurgus are their works. The Islamic teaching on what continues after death (ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge, a righteous child) offers a devotional analogue: what a person leaves behind continues to count.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Your enemies will describe you in many unkind words and scorn your ability. What could be more painful for you?”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that abandoning his duty would leave him an object of public scorn, the most painful outcome of all.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat the world’s reproach, for failing to achieve what earns honour, as a real and bitter disgrace.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews says that Abel’s righteous offering still ‘speaks’ long after his death.
christianity.tie_back: A good deed as the part of a person that remains and keeps speaking: the Kural’s எச்சம் of renown.

islam.quote_or_event: “When a man dies, his acts come to an end, but three, recurring charity, or knowledge (by which people) benefit, or a pious child, who prays for him (for the deceased).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet names three things that keep benefiting a person after death: ongoing charity (sadaqah jariyah), useful knowledge, and a righteous child.
islam.tie_back: An exact counterpart to எச்சம், the ‘remainder’ a life leaves behind, even including the offspring sense of the word.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off.”
judaism.explanation: God promises faithful eunuchs, who can have no children, an everlasting name that is better than descendants.
judaism.tie_back: Precisely Pope’s reading of the Kural: renown is the offspring that outlasts a life, better than sons and daughters.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As from a great heap of flowers many garlands can be made, even so should many good deeds be done by one born a mortal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada urges every mortal to make the most of the material of life by producing many good deeds.
buddhism.tie_back: Both treat a human life as something that ought to leave a worthy product behind.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Neither his kinsmen, nor his friends, nor his sons, nor his relations will share his suffering, he alone has to bear it; for the Karman follows the doer.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra tells King Brahmadatta that at death nothing goes with a person except the karma they have earned.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls renown the proper legacy (eccam) that a life leaves behind. The Jain answer is that what remains of a life is the karma it carries forward, not a name left among others.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.23 (cf. 13.24) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who lack the Naam wander around lost, with their noses cut off; without the Name, they sit and cry.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das says that those without the Name live in disgrace, using the Punjabi idiom of a cut-off nose for public shame.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says it is a disgrace to leave no legacy of renown; Guru Amar Das likewise calls the life that lacks its true treasure a life of shame.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1414, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Let me not then die ingloriously and without a struggle, but let me first do some great thing that shall be told among men hereafter.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Realising he is doomed before Achilles, Hector resolves to leave behind at least a deed that will be told in the future.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hector’s last wish is the Kural’s எச்சம்: not to leave the world without a remainder of renown.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Who, when he thinks of Homer and Hesiod and other great poets, would not rather have their children than ordinary human ones?”
philosophy.explanation: Diotima argues that great works and laws are ‘children of the soul’ that bring their parents everlasting glory, more precious than physical offspring.
philosophy.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s ‘offspring called renown’: a legacy of fame as a truer child than any bodily heir.

real_life_example.event_title: James Smithson's bequest founds the Smithsonian Institution
real_life_example.place: London, England, and Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: James Smithson, a British scientist and the illegitimate son of Hugh Smithson, 1st Duke of Northumberland, never visited the United States and had no children. His will of 1826 provided that if his nephew died without heirs, his estate should go to the United States to found at Washington an institution bearing his name for the increase and diffusion of knowledge. The nephew died childless in 1835, Congress accepted the gift in 1836, and the Smithsonian Institution was established by an Act signed on 10 August 1846.
real_life_example.explanation: A childless man denied his father's name left a legacy that made his own name one of the best known in the world of learning.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls renown the legacy every life should leave behind, and Smithson, with no children, left a name that has outlived any line of descendants.

tamil:
வசையிலா வண்பயன் குன்றும் இசையிலா
யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்.
transliteration:
Vasaiyilaa vanpayan kundrum isaiyilaa
Yaakkai poruththa nilam.
meaning: When the land carries the body of a person with no good name, its rich, healthy harvest will grow smaller.
elementary: Think of a garden where one plant takes all the water and sunshine but never gives flowers or fruit. The whole garden does a little worse because of it. A person who takes from the world but gives nothing good back is a bit like that plant.
university: Here Valluvar moves from social reproach to cosmic consequence: the earth (நிலம்) that ‘bears’ (பொறுத்த) a renownless body (இசையிலா யாக்கை) suffers a decline (குன்றும்) in its bountiful, faultless yield (வசையிலா வண்பயன்). The choice of யாக்கை, the bare physical frame, pointedly denies such a person any fuller identity: they are mere body, a burden on the ground. The underlying belief, common to many ancient cultures, links moral quality to fertility: righteous people and rulers bring rain and harvest, the unrighteous bring dearth, an idea found in the Gita’s cycle of rain and sacrifice, the Buddha’s discourse on unprincipled kings, and Homer’s blameless king under whom the earth yields abundantly. Modern readers may take it as a vivid image of free-riding: a life that consumes without contributing diminishes the common stock, close to Cicero’s charge that the self-absorbed are ‘traitors to social life’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “All living bodies subsist on food grains, which are produced from rain. Rains are produced by performance of yajña [sacrifice], and yajña is born of prescribed duties.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a cycle in which rightful action sustains the rain that feeds the crops that feed all beings.
hinduism.tie_back: In both, the fertility of the land depends on how human beings conduct themselves.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, an owner finds a fig tree barren for three years and asks why it should keep taking up the soil.
christianity.tie_back: The fruitless tree ‘cumbers the ground’ just as the renownless body burdens the land in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “Corruption has appeared throughout the land and sea by [reason of] what the hands of people have earned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an attributes disorder and ruin on land and sea to human wrongdoing.
islam.tie_back: Both texts see the earth’s well-being as damaged by the moral failures of those who live on it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.”
judaism.explanation: After Cain murders Abel, God tells him the ground will no longer give him its strength.
judaism.tie_back: The land’s yield diminishes because of the moral state of the one who lives on it, as in the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When the people of town and country are unprincipled, the courses of the moon and sun become erratic.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a chain in which unprincipled rulers and people lead to erratic seasons, insufficient rain, badly ripening crops and sickly people, and the reverse when people are principled.
buddhism.tie_back: Human moral quality directly affects the land’s produce, exactly as the Kural claims.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.70, Adhammika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “From the moment that this our boy has been begotten, our silver increased, our gold increased, &c. … Now our wishes have been fulfilled, therefore shall the name of our boy be Vardhamâna.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's parents named him Vardhamāna, 'the Increaser', because their household prospered from the moment he was conceived.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the land that carries a renownless person sees its harvest fail. The Kalpa Sūtra tells the reverse story, in which a virtuous soul's presence makes the family's wealth and grain increase.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §§106–107 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who forget the Naam, the Name of the Lord, are a burden on the earth.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, in a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that people who forget God are only a weight on the earth that carries them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the land that bears a body without renown loses its yield; Farid uses the same image of the earth burdened by an empty life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The earth yields its wheat and barley, the trees are loaded with fruit, the ewes bring forth lambs, and the sea abounds with fish by reason of his virtues.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The disguised Odysseus tells Penelope that her fame reaches heaven like that of a blameless king whose virtue makes land and sea abundant.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The positive mirror image of the Kural: virtue and renown make the land fruitful, so their absence would make it fail.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They are traitors to social life, for they contribute to it none of their interest, none of their effort, none of their means.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero condemns those who, absorbed in their own affairs, give nothing to the common life of society.
philosophy.tie_back: The rationalist version of the Kural: a life that takes but contributes nothing diminishes the shared stock.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.29 (trans. Walter Miller)

real_life_example.event_title: Norman Borlaug's wheat transforms harvests in Mexico and South Asia
real_life_example.event: From 1944 Norman Borlaug worked on a Rockefeller Foundation programme in Mexico, where he developed high-yielding, disease-resistant wheat varieties, and Mexico became self-sufficient in wheat in 1956. In the 1960s these varieties were introduced to India and Pakistan, where wheat yields nearly doubled between 1965 and 1970. Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.
real_life_example.explanation: The work of one renowned scientist and his colleagues changed the yield of whole countries' land and averted famines that had been widely predicted.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the land bearing a person without renown sees its harvest decline; Borlaug shows the converse, a person of lasting renown under whose work the land's yield multiplied.

tamil:
வசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார் இசையொழிய
வாழ்வாரே வாழா தவர்.
transliteration:
Vasaiyozhiya vaazhvaare vaazhvaar isaiyozhiya
Vaazhvaare vaazhaa thavar.
meaning: People who live without blame are the ones who truly live. People who live without a good name are not really living at all.
elementary: Being alive is like being given a notebook. Some people fill it with kind, brave, helpful stories. Others leave it empty or scribble unkind things. Valluvar says only the first kind are really ‘living’; the others just have the notebook.
university: The chapter closes with a chiastic couplet built on repetition: வசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார் / இசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழாதவர். The halves pivot on a near-rhyme, வசை (blame) and இசை (renown), so that ‘living without blame’ and ‘living without renown’ sound almost identical yet lead to opposite verdicts. The emphatic particle ஏ marks exclusivity: only the blameless truly live; the renownless are precisely the not-living. Life is thus redefined qualitatively rather than biologically. Similar ideas appear in the Talmudic teaching that the wicked are called dead even in their lifetimes, the Dhammapada’s ‘the heedless are as if dead already’, the Gita’s verdict that the self-indulgent person ‘lives in vain’, and Revelation’s church that has ‘a name that thou livest, and art dead’. Valluvar’s distinctive move is to make renown, the social trace of virtue, the test of whether one has lived at all.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man who does not follow this prescribed Vedic system of sacrifice certainly leads a life of sin, for a person delighting only in the senses lives in vain.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the self-indulgent person who ignores the cycle of duty and sacrifice ‘lives in vain’ (moghaṁ jīvati).
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts deny that mere biological life counts as living; a life empty of worth is in vain.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.”
christianity.explanation: The risen Christ tells the church in Sardis that despite its reputation for being alive, it is spiritually dead.
christianity.tie_back: Both separate true life from mere appearance of life; Revelation warns that a name must reflect real works.

islam.quote_or_event: “And is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him light by which to walk among the people like one who is in darkness, never to emerge therefrom?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the guided person as someone brought from death to life, contrasted with one who stays in darkness.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats true life as a moral and spiritual state rather than mere breath.

judaism.quote_or_event: “These are the wicked, who even during their lives are called dead.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud contrasts the righteous, called living even after death, with the wicked, who are called dead while still alive.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s exact verdict: the blameless truly live, and those without worth are the ‘not-living’ even while alive.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless. Heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful die not. The heedless are as if dead already.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that careless, unmindful people are effectively dead even while living, while the heedful do not die.
buddhism.tie_back: The same redefinition of life and death by quality of living that the Kural makes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse without profit to him who acts contrary to the Law.” “The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse with much profit to him who acts up to the Law.”
jainism.explanation: The young sons of the priest Bhṛgu tell their father that every passing day is lost for good, and that its worth depends on whether it was lived righteously.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar separates those who truly live from those who merely stay alive. The Jain verses draw the same line, saying that only days lived by the Law bear fruit.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.24–25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, no one else is truly alive; those who merely live shall depart in dishonor; everything they eat is impure.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says that only those in whom God dwells truly live; others merely exist and leave the world in dishonour.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural closes by saying that those who live without renown, though alive, do not really live; Guru Nanak makes the same distinction between true life and mere living in dishonour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I would rather be a paid servant in a poor man's house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the underworld, Achilles, the very emblem of undying glory, tells Odysseus that even the humblest life on earth is better than all his fame among the dead.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A deliberate counterpoint: Homer lets his greatest hero question whether renown can compensate for life itself, the opposite of the Kural’s verdict.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The life which is unexamined is not worth living.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial, Socrates says a life without moral self-examination is not worth living.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Socrates sets a qualitative test for whether a life counts; the test is self-examination rather than renown.

real_life_example.event_title: Socrates refuses to escape before his execution
real_life_example.event: In 399 BCE Socrates was tried in Athens on charges of impiety and corrupting the young, convicted and sentenced to death. While he awaited execution, his friend Crito urged him to escape into exile, which was a realistic option, but Socrates refused, arguing that escape would be a wrong against the laws he had lived under. He drank the poison, most likely hemlock, and died calmly among his friends.
real_life_example.explanation: Socrates chose a blameless death over a compromised life, and his example has been treated ever since as a model of integrity.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that only those who live free of reproach truly live, and Socrates judged that a life bought by doing wrong would not be worth living.

tamil:
