அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம் பொருட்செல்வம்
பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள.
transliteration:
Arutchelvam selvaththul selvam porutchelvam,
Pooriyaar kannum ula.
meaning: Kindness is the richest of all riches. Money and things can be found even in the hands of low, mean people.
elementary: Anyone can end up with a big pile of money, even a bully or a cheat. But a kind heart that cares about every living thing is something only good people have. So kindness is the richest treasure there is.
university: The chapter opens by reversing the ordinary hierarchy of value with a pun on selvam (wealth): arul-selvam, the wealth of grace, is ‘the wealth among wealths’, while porul-selvam, material wealth, is disqualified precisely because it is morally indiscriminate — it collects even with the pooriyaar, the base or vile. The argument is not that money is evil (Valluvar devotes the whole Book of Porul to acquiring it, and Kural 757 calls arul the child of love nursed by wealth) but that a good which the wicked can own equally well cannot be the highest good. Parimelazhagar, placing this chapter at the head of the ascetic section (Thuravaraviyal), glosses arul as compassion that flows to all living beings without any tie of kinship — the matured, universalised form of the anbu (love for one’s own) praised in Chapter 8. The logic echoes Socrates’ claim that virtue is not produced by wealth, and the Stoic and Buddhist ranking of inner goods above external ones.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “nonviolence, truthfulness, freedom from anger; renunciation, tranquility, aversion to faultfinding, compassion and freedom from covetousness”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists compassion (dayā bhūteṣu, ‘compassion toward beings’) among the qualities that make up the daivī sampad — literally the ‘divine wealth’ or endowment — of the godly person, in contrast to the demonic endowment described next.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita, like the Kural, frames compassion as a kind of wealth (sampad) that outranks ordinary possessions, and places it next to freedom from covetousness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts perishable earthly wealth with a lasting treasure, and the surrounding Sermon on the Mount identifies that treasure with mercy, almsgiving and love.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts demote material riches in favour of an inner, moral treasure, though Jesus stresses impermanence while Valluvar stresses that even the wicked can own money.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth is not in having many possessions, but rather (true) wealth is feeling sufficiency in the soul.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet redefines ghinā (richness) as an inner state rather than a quantity of goods.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hadith relocates true wealth from possessions to the soul; the Kural names that inner wealth as compassion, the hadith as contentment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “let not the rich man glory in his riches: But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah rejects wealth as a ground of pride and points instead to chesed (lovingkindness), the very quality God exercises in the world.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts set riches below lovingkindness; Jeremiah adds that chesed is a divine attribute, matching the ‘almost divine’ register of arul.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All the grounds for making merit leading to spontaneously arising (in heaven) do not equal one-sixteenth of the awareness-release through good will.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says every other form of merit, however great, is outshone by a mind of boundless good will (mettā), as the stars are outshone by the moon.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts rank a universal, compassionate disposition as the supreme ‘wealth’ above every other kind of accumulation.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I have horses, elephants, and subjects, a town and a seraglio, power and command … how could he be without protection? Reverend sir, you speak untruth.” … “You are the protector of all unprotected beings, O ascetic.”
jainism.explanation: King Srenika boasts that his riches make him secure, but the young monk shows him that wealth protects no one, and the humbled king ends by calling the compassionate monk the protector of every unprotected being.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks the wealth of compassion above material wealth, which even the basest can hold; the Uttaradhyayana likewise sets a king's treasure below the monk's care for all beings.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.14-15, 20.56 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Compassion is wealth, want of compassion useless.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Nasihat Nama (Instruction), which Macauliffe records as uttered by Guru Nanak to Mian Mitha, compassion is set among other virtues as the true wealth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls the wealth of compassion the wealth of all wealths, and this line says simply that compassion is wealth and its absence worthless.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter X, p. 129 (Nasihat Nama)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor elderly couple, take in Jupiter and Mercury after a thousand wealthier households bar their doors; the rich neighbourhood is drowned while the couple’s hut becomes a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: The only household that shows kindness to the disguised strangers is the poorest one, and it is the one the gods honour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An illustration of the Kural’s claim: material wealth sat with the uncaring neighbours, while the true wealth was the poor couple’s compassion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue come money and every other good of man, public as well as private.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells the Athenian jury that his whole mission has been to persuade them to care for the soul before wealth, since money cannot produce goodness.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers subordinate material wealth to moral excellence; Valluvar makes the excellence specifically compassion.

real_life_example.event_title: Abdul Sattar Edhi builds Pakistan's largest welfare network while living with almost nothing
real_life_example.event: In 1951 Abdul Sattar Edhi established a charitable service in Karachi, funded by private donations, to provide basic emergency care, starting with a single ambulance that he drove himself. The Edhi Foundation grew into a nationwide network of ambulances, maternity centres, orphan care and shelters, and in 1997 it entered Guinness World Records as the largest volunteer ambulance organisation. Edhi never took a salary from the foundation, owned only a couple of sets of clothes and lived in a small room beside his office.
real_life_example.explanation: Edhi became one of the most honoured people in his country through compassion alone, while deliberately possessing almost nothing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls compassion the wealth of all wealths and notes that money is found even among the base, and Edhi's life showed a person rich only in compassion yet esteemed above the wealthy.

tamil:
நல்லாற்றாள் நாடி அருளாள்க பல்லாற்றால்
தேரினும் அஃதே துணை.
transliteration:
Nallaatraal naadi arulaalga pallaatraal,
Therinum aqdhe thunai.
meaning: Think things through the right way and make kindness your rule for living. However many ways you test it, kindness is the one thing that truly helps you.
elementary: Imagine trying every road on a map to find the safest way home. Valluvar says that whichever road you test, the one that always gets you there safely is being kind. Kindness is the friend that never lets you down.
university: The couplet is epistemological as well as ethical: naadi (having searched) and pallaatraal therinum (even if you examine by many methods) describe a process of inquiry whose result is always the same — arul is the only thunai, the companion or aid, that holds. Parimelazhagar reads pallaatraal as the conflicting doctrines of the various schools (samayams), so the kural makes a strikingly ecumenical claim: whatever creed one tests, compassion is the point on which all converge. This anticipates later comparative ethics, which often finds compassion to be the common denominator of otherwise divergent religious systems. It also sets up the chapter’s practical thesis — that arul is not one virtue among many but the reliable guide when theories disagree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Prajapati answers gods, humans and asuras with the single syllable ‘Da’, which they hear as damyata (control yourselves), datta (give) and dayadhvam (be compassionate); the thunder repeats ‘Da Da Da’ as a teaching for all.
hinduism.explanation: One divine utterance yields three disciplines, and compassion (dayā) is the one required of the asuras, the beings most prone to cruelty.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Upanishad treats compassion as a teaching that remains valid however the instruction is heard or interpreted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.”
christianity.explanation: Asked how to inherit eternal life, Jesus lets the lawyer test three candidates (a priest, a Levite and a Samaritan); the answer that survives is the one who showed mercy.
christianity.tie_back: A near-dramatisation of ‘test it by many paths and mercy alone is the guide’: religious status fails the test and compassion passes.

islam.quote_or_event: “and—above all—to be one of those who have faith and urge each other to perseverance and urge each other to compassion.”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Balad describes the ‘challenging path’ (freeing slaves, feeding orphans and the destitute) and crowns it with a community that urges compassion (marḥama) on one another.
islam.tie_back: Both texts present compassion as the path that holds when the harder, steeper ways of virtue are weighed.
islam.source: Quran 90:17 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?”
judaism.explanation: Micah reduces the many demands of religion to three, and the Talmud (Sukkah 49b) reads ‘to love mercy’ as gemilut chasadim, acts of lovingkindness.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts sift many religious options and arrive at mercy or kindness as the essential requirement.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Kalamas, confused by rival teachers, are told not to rely on tradition, scripture or logic alone but to see for themselves which states lead to harm; the Buddha then describes the disciple who pervades the whole world with a mind imbued with good will and compassion.
buddhism.explanation: After a method of personal testing, the conclusion reached is the cultivation of boundless good will and compassion.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s structure: examine by many paths, and compassion is what stands.

jainism.quote_or_event: “First the persuasion of every one should be ascertained, and then we will ask them severally: Ye professors! is pain pleasant to you, or unpleasant? If they give the right answer, reply: For all sorts of living beings pain is unpleasant, disagreeable. and greatly feared.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga answers rival teachers who claim to have examined the matter in every way and found killing harmless: tested properly, every inquiry leads back to the fact that all beings fear pain, so none should be harmed.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that however many ways one examines the paths, compassion alone proves the true support; the Acaranga likewise says that honest inquiry from every side always arrives at non-harm.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.4.2.3-6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Be kind to all beings-this is more meritorious than bathing at the sixty-eight sacred shrines of pilgrimage and the giving of charity.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Baarah Maah of Raag Maajh Guru Arjan weighs kindness to living beings against the most valued religious acts, pilgrimage and charity, and finds kindness greater.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that however many paths one examines, compassion proves the only true support; Guru Arjan likewise sets compassion above all the other recognised forms of merit.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 136, Raag Maajh, Baarah Maah, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “an altar to Eleos (Mercy), of all divinities the most useful in the life of mortals and in the vicissitudes of fortune”
greek_mythology.explanation: Pausanias describes the Athenian Altar of Pity, where suppliants such as the children of Heracles and Adrastus sought refuge.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Among all the gods, the one judged most useful through life’s changes is Mercy — close to the Kural’s claim that compassion is the one reliable aid.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Boundless compassion for all living beings is the surest and most certain guarantee of pure moral conduct, and needs no casuistry.”
philosophy.explanation: Schopenhauer argues that compassion, not rational rule-following, is the real foundation of morality.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘Needs no casuistry’ is the Kural’s ‘however many ways you examine it’: when theories multiply, compassion is still the sure guide.
philosophy.source: Arthur Schopenhauer, On the Basis of Morality, Part III, ch. 8 (trans. A. B. Bullock)

real_life_example.event_title: Akbar's debates in the Ibadat Khana
real_life_example.event: In 1575 the Mughal emperor Akbar began building the Ibadat Khana, a hall of worship at Fatehpur Sikri, where weekly debates were held. From 1578 he opened the discussions to Hindu pandits, Jain teachers, Zoroastrian priests and Jesuit missionaries as well as Muslim scholars. Britannica records that this comparative study convinced him that there was truth in all religions but that none possessed the whole truth, and his court developed the policy of sulh-i kul, universal peace and tolerance among creeds.
real_life_example.explanation: An emperor deliberately examined many rival doctrines side by side and arrived at a policy of tolerance and protection for all his subjects.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that whatever paths one examines, compassion alone proves the true support, and Akbar's testing of many creeds led him to a policy of goodwill toward all.

tamil:
அருள்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்க் கில்லை இருள்சேர்ந்த
இன்னா உலகம் புகல்.
transliteration:
Arulserndha nenjinaark killai irulserndha,
Innaa ulagam pugal.
meaning: People whose hearts are full of kindness will never enter the dark world of suffering.
elementary: Think of kindness as a lamp you carry inside you. Wherever you go, it keeps the dark away. Valluvar says people with kind hearts will never end up in the dark, sad place.
university: The couplet is built on a sound-and-image rhyme: arul serndha (joined with grace) against irul serndha (joined with darkness). Traditional commentators such as Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read the ‘dark world of pain’ as naragam (hell); modern commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan and Kalaignar take it as the darkness of ignorance and misery in this life. The two readings are compatible: on either view a compassionate heart is inherently protected from darkness, whether that darkness is a place one goes after death or a state one lives in now. The line compresses a moral cosmology found widely, in which a being’s inner quality decides its destination, as in the karmic ‘happy and unhappy destinations’ of the Pali canon or the Isles of the Blessed and Tartarus in Plato.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The transcendental qualities are conducive to liberation, whereas the demonic qualities make for bondage.”
hinduism.explanation: Having listed compassion among the divine qualities (16.2), Krishna says those qualities lead to freedom while their opposites lead to bondage.
hinduism.tie_back: Same moral cosmology: a compassionate nature leads away from darkness and bondage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.”
christianity.explanation: The Beatitude promises that those who show mercy will themselves receive mercy.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts promise the merciful a protected destiny; the Kural phrases it negatively, as exemption from the dark world.

islam.quote_or_event: “The merciful are shown mercy by Ar-Rahman. Be merciful on the earth, and you will be shown mercy from Who is above the heavens.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet links human mercy directly to receiving the mercy of God, whose name Ar-Rahman is built on the same root.
islam.tie_back: The merciful are shielded by divine mercy, just as the compassionate heart is kept from the world of pain.

judaism.quote_or_event: “anyone who has compassion for God’s creatures will receive compassion from Heaven, and anyone who does not have compassion for God’s creatures will not receive compassion from Heaven.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, derives this from Deuteronomy 13:18.
judaism.tie_back: Heaven’s treatment of a person mirrors their compassion toward creatures, echoing the Kural’s promise to the compassionate heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “some woman or man is a killer of living beings, murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, merciless to living beings... he reappears in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts this with one who ‘dwells compassionate for the welfare of all living beings’, who reappears ‘in a happy destination, in the heavenly world’.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a commentary on the Kural: mercilessness leads to hell, compassion keeps one out of it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who despises the Law that enjoins compassion, and praises the Law that permits slaughter, and who feeds but a single unprincipled man, even if he be a king, will go to darkness, and not to the gods.”
jainism.explanation: In his debate with a Vedic priest, the Jain monk Ardraka says that whoever rejects the law of compassion goes to darkness (Jacobi notes the original word literally means 'night').
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those whose hearts hold compassion never enter the dark world of suffering; Ardraka states the same truth from the other side, that those who scorn compassion go to darkness.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga II.6.45 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Where there is awesome and terrible heat and blazing sunshine, there, the Name of the Lord will give you shade.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan promises that in the terrifying passages after death the Name of God will shelter the soul.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those filled with compassion never enter the dark world of suffering; the nearest Sikh assurance is that the Name shields the soul in that fearful realm.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 264, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 2, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Socrates’ closing myth in the Gorgias: under Zeus’s law, souls who lived justly and piously go to the Isles of the Blessed, while the unjust are sent to Tartarus, the prison of punishment.
greek_mythology.explanation: Judges of the dead examine the naked soul, and its moral character decides where it goes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s idea that inner character decides whether one enters the dark world, though the Greek criterion is justice rather than compassion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Until he extends the circle of his compassion to all living things, man will not himself find peace.”
philosophy.explanation: Schweitzer argues that an ethic limited to human relations leaves people inwardly unsettled.
philosophy.tie_back: Read with Varadarasan’s this-worldly interpretation of the kural, the compassionate heart escapes the darkness of inner misery.
philosophy.source: Albert Schweitzer, The Philosophy of Civilization (trans. C. T. Campion)

real_life_example.event_title: Corrie ten Boom survives Ravensbruck and turns to healing work
real_life_example.event: Corrie ten Boom and her family hid Jews and resistance workers in their home in Haarlem until it was raided on 28 February 1944; the six people in the hiding place were not found. Corrie was imprisoned and deported with her sister Betsie to the Ravensbruck concentration camp, where Betsie died in December 1944, and Corrie was released at the end of that month. After the war she helped run a home for camp survivors and worked at rehabilitation with former Dutch collaborators.
real_life_example.explanation: Her compassion took her into one of the darkest places of the century, yet she came out of it devoted to healing rather than to bitterness.
real_life_example.tie_back: On the modern commentators' reading of the kural, the darkness the compassionate never enter is inner misery, and ten Boom passed through a camp without being swallowed by hatred.

tamil:
மன்னுயிர் ஓம்பி அருளாள்வார்க்கு இல்லென்ப
தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை.
transliteration:
Mannuyir oambi arulaalvaarkku illenba,
Thannuyir anjum vinai.
meaning: Wise people say that those who protect all living things and live with kindness will never have to fear what their own actions bring back to them.
elementary: If you spend your life looking after others — feeding a stray cat, helping a friend who fell, being gentle to little creatures — you will never have to lie awake worrying about the bad things you did. Protecting others makes your own heart safe.
university: Mannuyir means ‘the enduring lives’, the whole population of living beings that fills the world, and oambi (protecting, cherishing) describes an active guardianship, not mere harmlessness. The second line allows two readings. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasan take thannuyir anjum vinai as ‘evil deeds whose results one’s own soul would dread’, so the protector of life accumulates no karmic cause for fear. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take it more psychologically: such a person does not fear for their own life. Either way, the kural states a principle of moral reciprocity: fearlessness is earned by protecting others. The verb enba (‘they say’) presents this as received wisdom, and it has parallels in Jain and Buddhist teaching on abhaya-dāna, the ‘gift of fearlessness’ given to all beings.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Rantideva, after forty-eight days of fasting, gives away his food and water to a succession of hungry guests, including an outcaste with his dogs, and declares that he seeks neither mystic powers nor liberation, only to take on the sufferings of all beings so that they may be free of pain.
hinduism.explanation: Rantideva is the Bhagavata’s model of compassion that protects every living being, even at the cost of his own life.
hinduism.tie_back: A living picture of mannuyir oambi, cherishing all lives; the Bhagavata says the gods then reveal themselves to him, and he has nothing to fear.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.”
christianity.explanation: In the Last Judgment, those who fed, clothed and visited the vulnerable are welcomed without fear.
christianity.tie_back: Protecting the weakest leaves one with nothing to fear at the final reckoning, just as the kural promises.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah thanked him for his (good) deed and forgave him.” The people asked, “Is there a reward for us in serving (the) animals?” He replied, “Yes, there is a reward for serving any animate.”
islam.explanation: A thirsty traveller climbs back down a well and carries up water in his shoe for a dying dog, and is forgiven his sins for it.
islam.tie_back: Compassion toward any living thing removes the burden of past sins, which is the kural’s ‘no deed to fear’, and it extends explicitly beyond humans.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi suffered for years after he dismissed a calf being led to slaughter with the words ‘Go, for this you were created’; his suffering ended when he stopped his maidservant from sweeping away young weasels, citing “The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud presents the rabbi’s affliction and his release as mirrors of his lack of compassion and then his compassion for creatures.
judaism.tie_back: Protecting even the smallest lives removes the suffering one’s soul dreads, exactly as the kural teaches.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even as a mother protects with her life / Her child, her only child, / So with a boundless heart / Should one cherish all living beings”
buddhism.explanation: The Metta Sutta asks for protective, maternal love toward every being, ‘whether they are weak or strong, omitting none’.
buddhism.tie_back: Oambi, protecting and cherishing, is exactly the mother’s guardianship the sutta describes, extended to all lives.
buddhism.source: Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (trans. Amaravati Sangha)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Be without fear, O king; but grant safety to others also; in this transient world of living beings, why are you addicted to cruelty?”
jainism.explanation: King Sanjaya, out hunting, kills a frightened deer, then trembles before the meditating monk Gardabhali, who tells him he need not fear but must give the same safety to every creature; the king renounces his throne.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who protect all living beings need never fear for themselves; Gardabhali links the king's own freedom from fear to his giving safety to all beings.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 18.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They are kind to all beings; they have overpowered the five thieves.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Salok Sahaskriti Guru Arjan describes the holy as those who are kind to every living being and have mastered the five passions.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises those who cherish all living beings and so need not fear the consequences of their deeds; Guru Arjan joins universal kindness with victory over the inner thieves that produce wrongdoing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1357, Salok Sahaskriti, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Nausicaa tells her maids that strangers and beggars come under the protection of Zeus, so the shipwrecked Odysseus must be fed, washed and clothed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Protecting the helpless stranger was a religious duty under Zeus Xenios, and neglecting it risked divine anger.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Protecting the vulnerable keeps one right with the gods; the Greek scope is human strangers rather than all beings.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A man is really ethical only when he obeys the constraint laid on him to help all life which he is able to succor, and when he goes out of his way to avoid injuring anything living.”
philosophy.explanation: Schweitzer’s ‘reverence for life’ asks for active help as well as abstention from harm toward every living being.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches oambi exactly: an active, universal protection of life as the mark of the ethical person.
philosophy.source: Albert Schweitzer, Civilization and Ethics (The Philosophy of Civilization, vol. 2, trans. C. T. Campion)

real_life_example.event_title: The founding of the world's first animal protection society
real_life_example.event: In 1822 Parliament passed the Cruel Treatment of Cattle Act, promoted by the MP Richard Martin and often called Martin's Act, the first law protecting animals. On 16 June 1824 Martin, the Reverend Arthur Broome, William Wilberforce and others met at Old Slaughter's Coffee House in London and founded the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, the first national animal protection society in the world. In 1840 Queen Victoria allowed it to add Royal to its name.
real_life_example.explanation: Protection of living beings was extended beyond humans into law and organised public action for the first time.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises those who protect all living beings and live by compassion, and the founders of the society made the protection of animals a public cause.

tamil:
அல்லல் அருளாள்வார்க்கு இல்லை வளிவழங்கும்
மல்லன்மா ஞாலங் கரி.
transliteration:
Allal arulaalvaarkku illai valivazhangum,
Mallanmaa gnaalang kari.
meaning: Suffering never comes to people who live with kindness. This great, rich earth, where the wind blows, is the proof.
elementary: Look around the whole wide world, where the wind blows over every field and sea. Valluvar says the whole world can see that kind people are not the ones who end up miserable. The earth itself is the witness.
university: Valluvar calls the whole wind-swept earth as a witness (kari), a legal image in which the world itself testifies to a moral regularity. Parimelazhagar understands the witness as the people of the world, who can see for themselves that the compassionate do not suffer. Kalaignar offers a physical metaphor instead: as the moving wind sustains the vast earth, so the inner movement of arul sustains a person through hardship. The claim, that the kind escape sorrow, is empirically bold and can be read two ways: as an external promise of protection, or as an internal truth that allal (inner affliction) cannot take root in a mind at peace with all beings. The second reading brings the kural close to the Stoic claim that genuine benevolence is invincible and to the Buddhist list of the benefits of mettā.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those devotees are very dear to Me who are free from malice toward all living beings, who are friendly, and compassionate... equipoised in happiness and distress, and ever-forgiving.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna links the compassionate temperament (karuṇa) with evenness of mind in joy and sorrow.
hinduism.tie_back: The compassionate are not overthrown by sorrow, which is a psychological version of the kural’s allal illai.

christianity.quote_or_event: “for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points to sun and rain, the ordinary workings of nature, as evidence of God’s impartial kindness, which disciples should imitate.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s wind-swept earth, nature itself bears witness to universal benevolence; Jesus stresses God’s generosity rather than the compassionate being spared sorrow.

islam.quote_or_event: “But My mercy encompasses everything.”
islam.explanation: God tells Moses that divine mercy extends over all creation, and that He will ordain it for those who shun evil.
islam.tie_back: The whole of creation is held within mercy, a cosmic backdrop like the earth that witnesses to the security of the compassionate.
islam.source: Quran 7:156 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “For I have said, Mercy shall be built up for ever”
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew olam chesed yibaneh is read in Jewish tradition as ‘the world is built by lovingkindness’, making chesed the structure on which the world stands.
judaism.tie_back: The world itself rests on and testifies to lovingkindness, much as the kural calls the great earth to witness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One sleeps easily, wakes easily, dreams no evil dreams. One is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings. The devas protect one. Neither fire, poison, nor weapons can touch one.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists eleven benefits for one who cultivates the release of mind through good will.
buddhism.tie_back: An explicit catalogue of the kural’s promise: the one who lives by compassion is shielded from affliction.

jainism.quote_or_event: Umasvati's Tattvartha Sutra lists compassion (anukampa) for all living beings and for those who keep vows, together with charity, self-restraint with some attachment, forbearance and purity, as the causes of the inflow of pleasant-feeling (sata-vedaniya) karma.
jainism.explanation: In Jain karma theory, compassion attracts the karma that later ripens as pleasant experience, while causing pain to others attracts karma that ripens as suffering.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says sorrow does not come to those who live by compassion; the Tattvartha Sutra gives the Jain mechanism, in which compassion binds karma whose fruit is pleasant feeling rather than pain.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 6.12 (Digambara numbering; 6.13 in the Svetambara recension), as given with commentary by Vijay K. Jain (wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The mythical bull is Dharma, the son of compassion; this is what patiently holds the earth in its place.”
sikhism.explanation: Japji reinterprets the myth of the bull that bears the world: what really holds up the earth is dharma, born of compassion.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar calls the wind-swept earth to witness that the compassionate do not suffer; Guru Nanak goes further and makes compassion, through dharma, the very support of the earth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib, Pauri 16, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that where people deal straight judgements to strangers and citizens alike, the city flourishes: peace settles on the land, the earth bears plenty, oaks bear acorns, and flocks are heavy with wool.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod the fertility of the land visibly reflects the righteousness of its people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The abundant earth bears witness to virtue, a close echo of mallanmaa gnaalam (the great, fertile world) as witness; Hesiod’s virtue is justice rather than compassion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “a good disposition is invincible, if it be genuine, and not an affected smile and acting a part.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus asks what even the most violent man can do to someone who remains kind toward him.
philosophy.tie_back: Genuine benevolence cannot be defeated by others’ harm, a Stoic form of ‘sorrow does not come to the compassionate’.

real_life_example.event_title: The public rallies to Mary Seacole after her bankruptcy
real_life_example.event: Mary Seacole, a Jamaican-born businesswoman and healer, ran a hotel and store near the front in the Crimean War, where she fed and cared for British soldiers. At the war's end she returned to England destitute and was declared bankrupt. Military admirers raised funds for her, a benefit festival in 1857 attracted thousands of people, and her memoir Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands, published the same year, sold well.
real_life_example.explanation: The kindness she had shown to others was publicly remembered, and the public's support lifted her out of ruin.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says sorrow does not stay with those who live by compassion and that the wide world stands witness, and in Seacole's case the people of the world themselves came to her aid.

tamil:
பொருள்நீங்கிப் பொச்சாந்தார் என்பர் அருள்நீங்கி
அல்லவை செய்தொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Porulneengip pochchaandhaar enbar arulneengi,
Allavai seidhozhugu vaar.
meaning: Wise people say that those who give up kindness and live by doing wrong have lost sight of life's real purpose and forgotten the pain they once suffered.
elementary: Imagine someone who once got badly hurt, forgets how much it hurt, and then starts hurting others. Valluvar says people who throw away kindness and do mean things have forgotten what really matters, as if they lost the map of their own life.
university: The kural turns on the word porul, which can mean ‘wealth’, ‘meaning’ or ‘the real object (of life)’. Varadarasan and Pulavar Kesikan read porul neengi as ‘having left the true end, that is, virtue’, and pochchaandhaar as ‘those who have forgotten their life’s purpose’. Parimelazhagar reads it karmically: such people neglected virtue in an earlier life and have now forgotten the sufferings it brought. Solomon Pappaiah combines the two senses: they lose their wealth and also forget the pain they once endured. The unifying idea is moral amnesia. Cruelty is presented less as malice than as a forgetting, of one’s purpose and of the fellow-feeling one’s own suffering should have taught. This anticipates the reciprocal logic of Kural 250.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Parth, the qualities of those who possess a demoniac nature are hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita’s list of demonic qualities includes pāruṣya (harshness) and ends with ajñāna (ignorance).
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, the Gita pairs pitilessness with a kind of ignorance or forgetting of the real goal.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that someone can gain everything while losing the one thing that gives life its worth.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts describe losing the true porul, life’s real object, while pursuing the wrong things.

islam.quote_or_event: “A woman entered the (Hell) Fire because of a cat which she had tied, neither giving it food nor setting it free to eat from the vermin of the earth.”
islam.explanation: A single sustained act of cruelty to a helpless animal was enough to ruin the woman.
islam.tie_back: Abandoning compassion and persisting in cruelty (seidhozhugu, ‘continually doing’) means losing the true gain of life.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs presents cruelty as self-harm and mercy as self-benefit.
judaism.tie_back: The cruel person in the kural has likewise lost their own true good; they are their own chief victim.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who inflicts violence on those who are unarmed, and offends those who are inoffensive, will soon come upon one of these ten states”, among them “loss of wealth, or houses destroyed by ravaging fire”.
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada lists the calamities that follow cruelty toward the harmless, ending with rebirth in hell.
buddhism.tie_back: Includes the literal loss of porul (wealth), matching the double meaning in the kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
jainism.explanation: The sage warns that a man without pity is ruined by his own perversity more surely than by any enemy, and will know it only at death.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who abandon compassion and do wrong have lost sight of life's real purpose; the Uttaradhyayana likewise says the pitiless man is ruined by his own perversity and learns too late what he has lost.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Creation is in the Creator, and the Creator is in the Creation, totally pervading and permeating all places.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir teaches that God dwells in all creatures and all creatures dwell in God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who abandon compassion and do wrong have lost sight of life's true purpose; Kabir supplies the Sikh reason such cruelty is a forgetting, since the one harmed carries the same divine presence.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1350, Raag Prabhaatee, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Even so has Achilles flung aside all pity, and all that conscience which at once so greatly banes yet greatly boons him that will heed it.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollo rebukes the gods for tolerating Achilles, who drags Hector’s corpse daily and ‘knows neither right nor ruth’.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles, having cast off pity and persisting in outrage, has lost his true self, until Priam reminds him of his father (see Kural 250).

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And, generally, we feel pity whenever we are in the condition of remembering that similar misfortunes have happened to us or ours, or expecting them to happen in the future.”
philosophy.explanation: In his analysis of the emotions, Aristotle says pity depends on remembering or expecting suffering of one’s own, so those who think themselves beyond harm feel little of it.
philosophy.tie_back: This gives the psychology behind the Kural’s charge: those who drop compassion have forgotten what they themselves have suffered.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric, Book II, ch. 8 (1386a) (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)

real_life_example.event_title: Massachusetts Bay banishes Roger Williams
real_life_example.place: Massachusetts Bay Colony and Providence, New England
real_life_example.event: The Puritan colony of Massachusetts Bay, founded by people who had left England in search of freedom to worship in their own way, banished the minister Roger Williams in October 1635 for his dangerous opinions, including his view that magistrates had no right to interfere in matters of religion. Williams fled and in 1636 founded Providence on land from the Narragansett, as a refuge for people troubled in conscience. It became a haven for Baptists, Quakers, Jews and other dissenters.
real_life_example.explanation: A community shaped by the experience of religious pressure imposed the same pressure on a dissenter in its midst, while the man it expelled built a refuge for others.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who abandon compassion have forgotten what they themselves suffered, and the colony's leaders treated a dissenter as they had once complained of being treated.

tamil:
அருளில்லார்க்கு அவ்வுலகம் இல்லை பொருளில்லார்க்கு
இவ்வுலகம் இல்லாகி யாங்கு.
transliteration:
Arulillaarkku avvulagam illai porulillaarkku,
Ivvulagam illaagi yaangu.
meaning: The next world has nothing for people without kindness, just as this world has nothing for people without money.
elementary: You need money to buy things in this world, like a ticket for the bus. Valluvar says kindness is the ticket for the next world. Without it, you can’t get on.
university: This is one of the Kural’s most quoted parallelisms, built on the matched pairs arul and porul (grace and wealth) and avvulagam and ivvulagam (that world and this world). It is also notably realistic: Valluvar does not pretend that poverty is irrelevant here; he concedes that this world is closed to the destitute (compare the chapter on poverty, 105). That concession makes the second claim sharper, because compassion is to be treated as the currency of the hereafter. Kalaignar gives a non-metaphysical reading: wealth is essential to the householder’s life (illaram) and compassion to the renunciate’s (thuravaram), fitting this chapter’s place at the start of the ascetic section. The couplet shows the Kural’s characteristic balance between worldly realism and spiritual priority.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the gate of heaven, Yudhishthira refuses Indra’s demand that he leave behind the dog that has followed him, saying he will not abandon a devoted and helpless creature even to enter heaven; the dog is revealed as Dharma, who praises his compassion for all creatures.
hinduism.explanation: Heaven is opened to Yudhishthira precisely because he would not give up compassion to get there.
hinduism.tie_back: A story version of ‘without compassion there is no other world’: compassion is literally what admits him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that those who show no mercy will receive none at the judgment.
christianity.tie_back: The merciless have no share in the world to come, which is the kural’s claim almost word for word.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah will not be merciful to those who are not merciful to mankind.”
islam.explanation: Divine mercy, on which salvation depends, is withheld from those who withhold mercy from others.
islam.tie_back: Same claim: without compassion there is no share in the other world.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The wealthy Jews of Babylonia will descend to Gehenna because they do not have compassion on others.” ... “anyone who does not have compassion for God’s creatures, it is known that he is not of the descendants of Abraham, our father.”
judaism.explanation: Rav condemns rich men who refused both a loan and food to a visitor in need.
judaism.tie_back: Striking parallel: having porul (wealth) but lacking arul (compassion) still means losing the world to come.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who, while himself seeking happiness, oppresses with violence other beings who also desire happiness, will not attain happiness hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The next verse gives the converse: whoever does not oppress others will find happiness hereafter.
buddhism.tie_back: Lack of compassion closes off happiness in the hereafter, as in the kural’s avvulagam illai.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In vain he adopts nakedness, who errs about matters of paramount interest; neither this world nor the next will be his; he is a loser in both respects in the world.”
jainism.explanation: The sage says a false ascetic who goes wrong on what matters most loses both this world and the next.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar matches this world, closed to the poor, with the other world, closed to the pitiless; the Uttaradhyayana uses the same this-world/next-world pairing for one who errs in what matters most, which in the passage includes being 'without pity' (20.48).
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.49 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, to use force is tyranny, even if you call it legal. When your account is called for in the Court of the Lord, what will your condition be then?”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir warns that oppression remains tyranny whatever justification it is given, and that it will be judged in the divine court.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the other world holds nothing for those without compassion; Kabir asks what will become of the pitiless when their account is called for hereafter.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Bhagat Kabir 187 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phoenix tells Achilles that the Prayers (Litai) are daughters of Zeus, lame and wrinkled, who follow behind Ruin (Ate); whoever respects them is helped, but whoever rejects them is followed by Ruin until he pays the penalty.
greek_mythology.explanation: Refusing a suppliant’s plea for mercy brings ruin on the person who refuses.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Rejecting compassion closes off divine favour, a this-worldly Greek counterpart to the lost ‘other world’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle concedes that happiness needs external goods, since it is impossible, or at least not easy, to act nobly without resources such as friends, wealth and political power.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle is candid that virtue alone does not secure a flourishing life in this world.
philosophy.tie_back: This parallels the first half of the kural (without wealth there is no ‘this world’), and shares Valluvar’s realism about material conditions.

real_life_example.event_title: Enrico Scrovegni builds the Arena Chapel painted by Giotto
real_life_example.event: Reginaldo Scrovegni of Padua was a notorious moneylender whom Dante placed among the usurers in the Inferno. His son Enrico, also a banker, founded a chapel on the site of the Roman arena in Padua around 1303, which was consecrated in 1305 and decorated by Giotto with a celebrated fresco cycle. In its Last Judgment Enrico is shown kneeling and presenting the chapel to the Virgin, while usurers appear among the damned.
real_life_example.explanation: Art historians often read the chapel as an attempt by a rich banking family to secure spiritual standing that wealth alone could not buy.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says wealth rules this world but compassion is the currency of the next, and the Scrovegni chapel shows a fortune made in this world being spent in hope of the other.

tamil:
பொருளற்றார் பூப்பர் ஒருகால் அருளற்றார்
அற்றார்மற் றாதல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Porulatraar pooppar orukaal arulatraar,
Atraarmat raadhal aridhu.
meaning: People who lose their money may do well again one day. But people who lose their kindness are truly poor, and they almost never get it back.
elementary: A tree can lose all its leaves in winter and still bloom again in spring. But if the tree’s roots die, it cannot grow back. Losing money is like losing leaves. Losing kindness is like losing the roots.
university: The verb pooppar, ‘they will blossom’, turns poverty into a season: the poor are like a plant between flowerings, and fortune may return orukaal, at some time. The loss of arul is described with a deliberate repetition, arul atraar atraar, ‘those bereft of grace are bereft’: they are destitute in the absolute sense, and a change in their state (maTru aadhal) is aridhu, rare or difficult. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar stress this asymmetry: wealth can be recovered, but compassion, once lost, rarely returns. Philosophically the kural makes a claim about character, that compassion is a root disposition and not a possession, so its loss changes who a person is rather than what they have. The word ‘rare’ rather than ‘impossible’ leaves room for moral recovery.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Attaining repeated birth amongst the species of demoniac life, such persons can never approach Me. Gradually they sink down to the most abominable type of existence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes those of demonic, pitiless nature as falling ever further, birth after birth.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts describe a pitiless state that tends to reinforce itself rather than recover.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?”
christianity.explanation: John asks how anyone with possessions who closes his heart to the needy can have the love of God in him.
christianity.tie_back: Possessing wealth but lacking compassion is true poverty, the kural’s arul atraar atraar.

islam.quote_or_event: “Mercy is not removed (from anyone) except from a wicked one.”
islam.explanation: The Arabic shaqī means one who is wretched or damned, so losing mercy is a mark of ultimate misfortune.
islam.tie_back: Losing compassion is the sign of true wretchedness, the kural’s ‘truly destitute’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Due to [biglal] this thing means that it is a wheel [galgal] that turns in the world, upon which people continuously rise and fall.”
judaism.explanation: The same Talmudic passage adds that ‘anyone who has compassion for God’s creatures will receive compassion from Heaven’, and that anyone who lacks it will not.
judaism.tie_back: Poverty is a turning wheel, so the poor may rise again, which is the kural’s pooppar orukaal; lack of compassion is what Heaven does not overlook.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, who repeatedly tried to kill the Buddha and split the Sangha, is described by the Buddha as bound for hell for an aeon and ‘incurable’ (atekiccho).
buddhism.explanation: His persistent cruelty is presented as having carried him beyond easy remedy.
buddhism.tie_back: An example of the ‘rarely recovers’ state of one who has lost compassion; commentarial tradition does, however, foresee his eventual awakening in the distant future.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The capital is human life, the gain is heaven; through the loss of that capital man must be born as a denizen of hell or a brute animal. … Having once forfeited them, he will have to endure these two states of misery; it will be difficult for him to attain an upward course for a long time to come.”
jainism.explanation: In the parable of three merchants, the one who loses his capital stands for the sinner who wastes human life, and the Sutra warns that such a loss is very hard to recover.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who lose wealth may flourish again, but those who lose compassion rarely recover; the Uttaradhyayana likewise sets ordinary loss against a moral loss from which the way back is long and hard.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 7.16-18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “How can anyone know the pain of another, if there is no compassion and sympathy within? The discarded bride is miserable, and loses both worlds”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas says that one with no feeling within cannot know another's pain, and that such a soul loses both this world and the next.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who have lost compassion are truly destitute and seldom recover; Ravidas likewise describes the heart without sympathy as wretched and bereft in both worlds.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 793, Raag Soohee, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon, a wealthy Thessalian, ignores the pleas of a dryad and cuts down Ceres’ sacred oak; the goddess sends Famine into him, and his insatiable hunger devours his whole fortune until, having even sold his daughter, he consumes his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: His pitiless act leads to a ruin that no amount of wealth can halt.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A rich man who lost compassion loses everything, beyond recovery, while the kural suggests mere poverty would have been survivable.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “if it often happens, this kind of separation, it makes it difficult for that which detaches itself to be brought to unity and to be restored to its former condition.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus compares a person who cuts himself off from others through hatred to a branch cut from a tree: it can be grafted back, but repeated separation makes restoration hard.
philosophy.tie_back: The same asymmetry as the kural: estrangement from fellow-feeling, once habitual, is rarely reversed.

real_life_example.event_title: Henri Dunant, ruined and forgotten, receives the first Nobel Peace Prize
real_life_example.event: Henri Dunant, whose efforts after the Battle of Solferino led to the founding of the Red Cross, went bankrupt in 1867, left Geneva and spent years in poverty and obscurity. A journalist found him living in a hospice in the village of Heiden in 1895, and in 1901 he shared the first Nobel Peace Prize with Frederic Passy, honoured for his humanitarian efforts to help wounded soldiers. The prize money was kept from his creditors and remained untouched in a Norwegian bank when he died in 1910.
real_life_example.explanation: Dunant lost his fortune but never his compassion, and it was the compassion that the world finally honoured.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who lose wealth may flourish again, but those who lose compassion are truly destitute, and Dunant, poor but rich in compassion, flourished again in the world's esteem.

tamil:
தெருளாதான் மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டற்றால் தேரின்
அருளாதான் செய்யும் அறம்.
transliteration:
Therulaadhaan meypporul kandatraal therin,
Arulaadhaan seyyum aram.
meaning: If you look closely, the good deeds of an unkind person are like a confused person claiming to understand the deepest truth. They are not real.
elementary: Imagine someone who has never understood maths saying they solved the hardest puzzle in the book. You would not believe them. Valluvar says good deeds done by someone who does not care about others are just like that: they look right, but there is nothing real inside.
university: The comparison is carefully chosen: therulaadhaan is one whose mind is not clear, and meypporul is ultimate reality or the true meaning of scripture. Such a person may recite the words, but cannot genuinely grasp the truth. In the same way, aram (dharma, virtuous action) performed by one who does not have arul may copy the outward form (gifts, rituals, observances) without the inner substance. The kural thus makes compassion the condition of authenticity for all other virtue, a thesis found in Paul’s ‘if I have not charity’ and in the Talmudic teaching that charity is rewarded only according to the kindness in it. Kant offers a pointed contrast: he held that acts done from sympathy alone lack moral worth and that only acts done from duty have it. Valluvar’s position is closer to virtue and sentiment theorists such as Hume and Schopenhauer, for whom the motive of fellow-feeling is what makes an act good.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And that charity, which is given at the wrong place and wrong time to unworthy persons, without showing respect, or with contempt, is held to be of the nature of nescience.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classifies giving done with contempt as tāmasic, the lowest grade, belonging to ignorance.
hinduism.tie_back: Charity without inner regard for the recipient is, as in the kural, a kind of ignorance dressed up as virtue.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says even the most extreme acts of generosity are worthless without agapē (love).
christianity.tie_back: Almost exactly the kural: aram performed without arul is empty.

islam.quote_or_event: “O believers! Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺ or hurtful words, like those who donate their wealth just to show off”
islam.explanation: The verse compares such charity to soil on a bare rock that is washed away by rain.
islam.tie_back: Giving without inner goodwill has no substance, like the unclear mind’s ‘vision’ of truth.
islam.source: Quran 2:264 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “The reward for charity is paid from Heaven only in accordance with the kindness and generosity included therein”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar also teaches that gemilut chasadim (acts of lovingkindness) are greater than tzedakah (charity) in three respects.
judaism.tie_back: The value of a virtuous act is measured by the compassion inside it, which is the kural’s thesis.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even though he be well-attired, yet if he is poised, calm, controlled and established in the holy life, having set aside violence towards all beings — he, truly, is a holy man, a renunciate, a monk.”
buddhism.explanation: The preceding verse (141) says nakedness, matted hair, fasting and ash-smearing cannot purify one who has not overcome inner defilement.
buddhism.tie_back: Outward religious practice is empty without the inner disposition of harmlessness, matching the kural’s view of aram without arul.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who do not know this (Law), are not awakened, though they fancy themselves awakened; believing themselves awakened, they are beyond the boundary of right faith.”
jainism.explanation: Having just called non-killing 'the quintessence of wisdom', the Sutrakritanga says that those who miss this law only imagine they are enlightened and are in fact outside right faith.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar likens virtue without compassion to a confused mind claiming to see the truth; the Sutrakritanga likewise says that those ignorant of the law of non-harm only fancy themselves awakened.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.11.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You kill living beings, and call it a righteous action. Tell me, brother, what would you call an unrighteous action?”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir challenges those who sacrifice animals and call it dharma, asking what could count as sin if that is righteousness.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar says the virtue of someone without compassion is no more real than a muddled mind's claim to have seen truth; Kabir likewise exposes religious acts done without compassion as false righteousness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1103, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Lycaon receives the disguised Jupiter with a show of hospitality, but secretly serves him the flesh of a slaughtered hostage and plots to kill him in his sleep; Jupiter destroys his house and turns him into a wolf, still thirsting for blood.
greek_mythology.explanation: A sacred duty, hospitality to a guest, is performed in outward form by a man with no pity.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The ‘virtue’ of the pitiless is a hollow performance, as the kural warns; Lycaon’s case is an extreme one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant argues that a philanthropist who helps others out of sympathy acts amiably but without true moral worth; only if sympathy were extinguished and he helped purely from duty would the act have moral worth.
philosophy.explanation: For Kant, the moral value of an act lies in its maxim of duty, not in the feeling behind it.
philosophy.tie_back: A direct counterpoint: Valluvar holds that virtue without compassion is hollow, whereas Kant holds that virtue from compassion alone is not yet moral. The contrast shows what is distinctive in the Kural’s sentiment-centred ethics.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals 4:398

real_life_example.event_title: The Spanish Requerimiento is read to Indigenous peoples
real_life_example.place: Spanish Americas (first read on the coast of present-day Colombia)
real_life_example.event: Around 1510-1513 the Council of Castile drew up the Requerimiento, a formal text to be read aloud to Indigenous peoples before conquest, asserting the authority of the pope and the Spanish crown and demanding their submission and acceptance of Christian preaching. It was often read only in Spanish, sometimes from a distance, so that its hearers could not understand it, and translation was merely recommended. Historians describe it as a legal formality that served chiefly to justify conquest to the Spanish themselves.
real_life_example.explanation: An outward ritual of legality and religion was performed without any real concern for the people it addressed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says virtue practised without compassion is as unreal as a confused mind claiming to see the truth, and the Requerimiento was a show of righteousness emptied of any regard for its hearers.

tamil:
வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்கதான் தன்னின்
மெலியார்மேல் செல்லு மிடத்து.
transliteration:
Valiyaarmun thannai ninaikkadhaan thannin,
Meliyaarmel sellu midaththu.
meaning: When you go to bully someone weaker than you, remember how you yourself felt standing scared before someone stronger than you.
elementary: Before you push around a smaller kid, remember how scared you felt when a bigger kid picked on you. That memory is a key that unlocks kindness.
university: The chapter closes with a practical technique rather than a doctrine: a deliberate act of imagination (ninaikka, ‘let him think’) timed for the moment of temptation (sellumidaththu, ‘when he goes against’). Compassion is produced by recalling one’s own vulnerability, so the powerful person is asked to see themselves in the position of the weak. This is the reflective, perspective-taking root of the Golden Rule, and it matches Aristotle’s analysis of pity (eleos) as pain at undeserved suffering that one could imagine befalling oneself. Placing this couplet last grounds the lofty arul of the opening kurals in ordinary moral psychology: universal compassion begins with a remembered fear.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I regard them to be perfect yogis who see the true equality of all living beings and respond to the joys and sorrows of others as if they were their own.”
hinduism.explanation: Ātmaupamya, judging others by analogy with oneself, is presented as the mark of the highest yogi.
hinduism.tie_back: The same self-analogy the kural recommends: feel another’s fear as your own.

christianity.quote_or_event: “O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me: Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, a servant forgiven a vast debt by his master then chokes a fellow servant over a small one.
christianity.tie_back: Exactly the kural’s scenario: someone who once stood helpless before a stronger party forgets it when facing someone weaker.

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The hadith makes self-reference the measure of how one should treat others.
islam.tie_back: Both rely on putting oneself in the other’s place; the kural specifically invokes the memory of one’s own weakness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Also thou shalt not oppress a stranger: for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.”
judaism.explanation: Israel is told to remember its own powerlessness in Egypt when dealing with the vulnerable.
judaism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: recall your own weakness before the strong when you are tempted to oppress the weak.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; all fear death. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha grounds non-violence in the shared fear of all beings and the practice of self-comparison.
buddhism.tie_back: The kural’s method exactly: recall your own trembling and so spare the weaker.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to kill. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to tyrannise over. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to torment.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga tells the would-be oppressor to put himself in his victim's place, and concludes that the righteous man therefore neither kills nor causes killing.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks the strong to remember how they once trembled before someone stronger when they turn on the weak; the Acaranga gives the same exercise of imagined reversal at the moment one means to harm or tyrannise.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.5.5.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “But if a powerful tiger attacks a flock of sheep and kills them, then its master must answer for it.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn on Babar's invasion Guru Nanak contrasts fights between equals with the strong falling on the defenceless, which the Lord who owns the flock must answer for.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks the powerful to remember their own fear before the stronger when they move against the weak; Guru Nanak likewise singles out the attack of the strong on the defenceless as the wrong that calls for an account.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 360, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Fear, O Achilles, the wrath of heaven; think on your own father and have compassion upon me”
greek_mythology.explanation: Priam kisses the hands that killed his son, and Achilles weeps as he thinks of his own father, then releases Hector’s body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Compassion comes through self-reference: Achilles softens when he pictures his own father in Priam’s helpless position.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Let pity then be a kind of pain excited by the sight of evil, deadly or painful, which befalls one who does not deserve it; an evil which one might expect to come upon himself or one of his friends”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle adds that ‘all that men fear in regard to themselves excites their pity when others are the victims.’
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s psychology of eleos is the kural’s technique made theory: pity arises from imagining oneself in the sufferer’s place.

real_life_example.event_title: West Germany's Basic Law guarantees asylum to the politically persecuted
real_life_example.event: The Basic Law of the Federal Republic of Germany, drafted by the Parliamentary Council and proclaimed on 23 May 1949, stated in Article 16 that persons persecuted on political grounds enjoy the right of asylum. Germany's Federal Agency for Civic Education explains that the right was included because many people persecuted for racial or political reasons under the Nazi regime had survived only by finding refuge abroad, while others had been refused such protection. The provision was deliberately worded without restrictions; it was later narrowed by an amendment in 1993.
real_life_example.explanation: A new state wrote the memory of its own citizens' flight and vulnerability into a protection for the weak of other nations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks the strong to remember how they once stood helpless before the stronger, and the framers of the Basic Law turned the memory of persecution and exile into a guarantee for the persecuted.

tamil:
தன்னூன் பெருக்கற்குத் தான்பிறிது ஊனுண்பான்
எங்ஙனம் ஆளும் அருள்.
transliteration:
Thannoon perukkarkuth thaanpirithu oonunpaan,
Enganam aalum arul.
meaning: How can someone who eats another creature's flesh just to grow their own body ever be truly kind?
elementary: Imagine someone who says they love animals, but eats one just to grow bigger themselves. That doesn’t fit together, does it? This kural asks exactly that: how can you be truly kind if you make your own body grow by using up another living body?
university: The chapter opens with a rhetorical question built on a stark bodily symmetry: ஊன் (flesh) appears on both sides of the transaction — தன்னூன் (one’s own flesh) is enlarged by பிறிது ஊன் (another’s flesh). The verb ஆளும் (“rule, govern”) is telling: Valluvar does not ask whether the meat-eater can feel pity occasionally, but whether அருள் (universal compassion, the virtue of the preceding chapter 25) can be the governing principle of his life. Placed in the துறவறவியல் (the section on renunciation), the argument is addressed first to those aspiring to the ascetic ideal, though commentators from Parimelazhagar onward read it as binding on all who claim arul. The logic of feeding self at the cost of other anticipates the Mahabharata’s Anushasana Parva and Ovid’s Pythagoras almost word for word, making this one of the most cross-culturally echoed couplets in the Kural.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That man who seeks to increase his own flesh by (eating) the flesh of others, has to live in this world in great anxiety and after death has to take birth in indifferent races and families.”
hinduism.explanation: In Bhishma’s discourse on abstaining from meat, the Mahabharata condemns exactly the person who grows his own body by consuming other bodies, and says he pays for it in this life and the next.
hinduism.tie_back: Nearly identical wording to the Kural’s “தன்னூன் பெருக்கற்கு… பிறிது ஊனுண்பான்” — the same flesh-for-flesh image, with the same moral verdict.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anusasana Parva, Section CXV (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh: For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns against people who stuff themselves with meat and wine, saying such self-indulgence ruins a person.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see meat-eating for bodily gratification as morally corrosive, though Proverbs targets gluttony rather than the killing itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “Beware of meat. It has addictiveness like the addictiveness of wine.”
islam.explanation: Caliph Umar warned people that meat can become a craving as hard to control as alcohol.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, Umar treats meat as something that enslaves the eater’s appetite, though he counsels moderation rather than abstention.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells how a calf being led to slaughter hid its head in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s garment and wept; he said, “Go, for this you were created.” Because he showed no compassion, heaven decreed years of suffering on him, which ended only when he later showed mercy to small animals.
judaism.explanation: Even the greatest sage was held accountable for brushing off the fear of an animal about to be killed for food.
judaism.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s claim that one cannot be governed by compassion while treating another creature’s life as simply food for oneself.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; all fear death. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha asks us to imagine ourselves in the other creature’s place — since all fear death, we should neither kill nor make others kill.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s question presupposes this same act of empathy: the eater’s flesh and the eaten one’s flesh are alike.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He eats crisp goats’ meat, his belly grows, and his veins swell with blood--but he gains nothing but life in hell, just as the ram is only fed to be killed for the sake of a guest.”
jainism.explanation: In the parable of the ram, the meat-eater who fattens his body on other creatures' flesh is compared to a ram fattened for slaughter: all his feeding only readies him for hell.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks how one who eats another's flesh to fatten his own can be ruled by compassion; the Uttaradhyayana uses the same image of a body swelling on another creature's meat and calls it ripening for hell.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 7.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, the dinner of beans and rice is excellent, if it is flavored with salt. Who would cut his throat, to have meat with his bread?”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir says a plain meal of khichri and salt is good food, and asks who would slit a throat just to have meat with his bread.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural condemns taking another creature's flesh to fatten one's own body; Kabir sets the same choice before the eater, simple food against a life taken for the sake of the palate.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Bhagat Kabir 188 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Erysichthon cut down Ceres’ sacred oak and was cursed with a hunger that no food could fill; after devouring all his wealth he finally began to tear and eat his own limbs.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows appetite without restraint turning on the eater himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic picture of the Kural’s “feeding one’s own flesh” gone to its end-point: a body fattened by consuming leads to self-destruction.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Oh, how wrong it is for flesh to be made from flesh; for a greedy body to fatten, by swallowing another body; for one creature to live by the death of another creature!”
philosophy.explanation: Ovid puts into Pythagoras’ mouth the core Pythagorean argument for vegetarianism: it is wrong to build one body out of another’s death.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s image — one’s own flesh enlarged by another’s flesh — and the same moral outrage.
philosophy.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV (Pythagoras’ teaching; trans. A. S. Kline)

real_life_example.event_title: Tolstoy writes The First Step on giving up meat
real_life_example.event: Leo Tolstoy wrote the essay The First Step as the preface to the Russian edition of Howard Williams's book The Ethics of Diet. In it he argued that a good life must begin with self-control, and that the first thing to give up is eating meat, because it requires killing animals against our moral feeling. He closed the essay with a first-person account of his visits to the slaughterhouse at Tula, which he had long put off because he felt ashamed to watch suffering he could not prevent.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the world's most admired moral writers argued publicly that a compassionate life and the killing of animals for the table cannot sit together.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks how compassion can rule a person who fattens his own flesh on another's, and Tolstoy's essay made the same argument that real kindness has to begin by refusing that flesh.

tamil:
பொருளாட்சி போற்றாதார்க்கு இல்லை அருளாட்சி
ஆங்கில்லை ஊன்தின் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Porulaatchi potraathaarkku illai arulaatchi,
Aangillai oonthin pavarkku.
meaning: People who do not take care of their money cannot enjoy having it. In the same way, people who eat meat cannot enjoy the gift of kindness.
elementary: If you leave your bicycle out in the rain and never look after it, soon you won’t really have a bike worth riding. In the same way, if you eat animals, you can’t really keep the treasure called kindness — it slips away because you haven’t looked after it.
university: The couplet works through a precisely balanced parallel: பொருளாட்சி (the enjoyment or sovereignty of wealth) is matched with அருளாட்சி (the sovereignty of grace), and போற்றாதார் (those who do not protect) with ஊன்தின்பவர் (flesh-eaters). The comparison is instructive: wealth is not lost in a single act, but eroded by neglect; likewise compassion is not denied by one meal but hollowed out by a habit that treats life as consumable. The adverb ஆங்கு (“likewise, in that manner”) makes the analogy explicit, a typical Valluvar move from the practical sphere of porul (wealth) to the spiritual sphere of arul. The couplet thus frames compassion as a possession requiring active guarding, a theme found in Buddhist and Mahayana insistence that meat-eating corrodes karuna itself.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The life-breaths of other creatures are as dear to them as those of one's to one's own self.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma reminds Yudhishthira that every creature values its life exactly as we value ours.
hinduism.tie_back: This recognition is what the Kural calls arul; eating flesh means disregarding it, and so losing the possession of compassion.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anusasana Parva, Section CXV (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says a good person cares about the life of his animals, while even the ‘mercy’ of the wicked is really cruelty.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures a person’s mercy by how they treat animal life — and warns that claimed mercy can be empty.

islam.quote_or_event: “The merciful are shown mercy by Ar-Rahman. Be merciful on the earth, and you will be shown mercy from Who is above the heavens.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that mercy works like a circuit: those who show mercy to what is on earth receive God’s mercy.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat mercy as something one keeps only by practising it; the Kural adds that flesh-eating breaks the practice.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud (Chullin 84a) derives from the Torah’s wording that a person should not eat meat except when he has a real appetite for it, treating meat as a concession to be used sparingly and not as an everyday entitlement.
