judaism.explanation: Rabbinic teaching limits casual meat-eating, treating it as something requiring restraint.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s sense that habitual flesh-eating is a moral hazard, though it stops far short of renunciation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “the eating of meat extinguishes the seed of Great Kindness”
buddhism.explanation: In this Mahayana sutra, the Buddha forbids meat to his followers because eating it destroys the root of compassion.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s thesis in Buddhist terms: flesh-eaters cannot keep possession of compassion.
buddhism.source: Mahayana Mahaparinirvana Sutra (as quoted in scholarly summaries; other renderings read “Great Compassion”)

jainism.quote_or_event: “In compassion to all beings, the seers, the Gñâtriputras, avoid what is sinful; afraid of it, they abstain from food especially prepared for them.”
jainism.explanation: Answering Buddhists who defend eating meat prepared for monks, Ardraka says the followers of Mahavira refuse such food because of their compassion for all beings.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says flesh-eaters cannot enjoy the possession of compassion; Ardraka presents refusing meat-dishes as the natural working of compassion for all beings.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga II.6.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You say that the One Lord is in all, so why do you kill chickens?”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Prabhaatee, Kabir challenges a cleric: if he truly believes God lives in every creature, killing one goes against his own faith.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar says a flesh-eater cannot hold on to the wealth of compassion; Kabir says that killing empties out the very belief in God's presence in every life that compassion rests on.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1350, Raag Prabhaatee, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But that former age, that we call golden, was happy with the fruit from the trees, and the herbs the earth produced, and did not defile its lips with blood.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek and Roman myth remembered a Golden Age when humans ate only plants and lived in peace with animals.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The loss of that bloodless age mirrors the Kural’s loss of arul: once flesh is eaten, the gentler state is forfeited.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV (trans. A. S. Kline)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Who could wrong a human being when he found himself so gently and humanely disposed toward other non-human creatures?”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch argues that gentleness toward animals trains a gentle character toward people too.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Plutarch treats compassion as one disposition that must be protected in every sphere, including diet.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On the Eating of Flesh I.7 (996A; Loeb trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: Benjamin Franklin abandons his vegetarian resolution over fried cod
real_life_example.place: Off Block Island, Rhode Island, North America
real_life_example.event: As a teenager Benjamin Franklin adopted a vegetable diet after reading the writer Thomas Tryon, and he regarded the killing of fish as a kind of unprovoked murder. On a voyage from Boston, becalmed off Block Island, the crew caught cod, and the smell of the frying fish tempted him. Recalling that smaller fish had been found in the cod's stomachs, he reasoned that if fish ate one another he could eat them, dined heartily, and afterwards returned to a vegetable diet only now and then; in his Autobiography he remarked wryly on how conveniently reason supplies excuses for what one already wants.
real_life_example.explanation: Franklin's honest account shows how a principle of kindness to animals can slip away through a single unguarded moment of appetite.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that, as unguarded wealth is lost, compassion is not kept by those who eat flesh, and Franklin's resolve gave way exactly when he stopped guarding it.

tamil:
படைகொண்டார் நெஞ்சம்போல் நன்னூக்காது ஒன்றன்
உடல்சுவை உண்டார் மனம்.
transliteration:
Padaikondaar nenjampol nannookkaathu ondran,
Udalsuvai undaar manam.
meaning: Like the heart of someone holding a weapon, the mind of someone who enjoys eating another creature's body does not turn toward goodness.
elementary: When someone is holding a sword ready to fight, they are not thinking gentle thoughts. The Kural says that someone who enjoys eating another animal’s body is in a similar mood inside — their heart is not turned toward kindness.
university: Valluvar here moves from action to psychology: the claim is about the state of the மனம் (mind) and நெஞ்சம் (heart). படைகொண்டார் — those who have taken up weapons — is a vivid image of a mind already committed to harm; the flesh-eater who has “tasted the body” (உடல்சுவை) is said to share that orientation. The key word நன்னூக்காது (“does not look toward the good”) implies a turning of attention: pleasure in flesh habituates the mind away from arul. The comparison is striking in a text that elsewhere honours warriors (Porutpaal), showing that Valluvar is describing a disposition, not condemning soldiers; it parallels the Upanishadic idea that food shapes the mind, and the Lankavatara Sutra’s claim that animals fear the meat-eater as they fear a hunter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Chandogya Upanishad teaches that when food is pure, the mind (sattva) becomes pure, and from a purified mind comes steady remembrance of the Self (āhāra-śuddhau sattva-śuddhiḥ).
hinduism.explanation: What we eat shapes the quality of our mind.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly claims that relishing flesh shapes the mind, turning it away from goodness like a weapon-bearer’s.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth, and upon every fowl of the air, upon all that moveth upon the earth, and upon all the fishes of the sea; into your hand are they delivered.”
christianity.explanation: When God first permits meat after the Flood, the same passage says that animals will now fear and dread humans.
christianity.tie_back: The Bible links the start of meat-eating to a new relationship of fear — the same weapon-like stance toward other creatures the Kural describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah has enjoined goodness to everything; so when you kill, kill in a good way and when you slaughter, slaughter in a good way. So every one of you should sharpen his knife, and let the slaughtered animal die comfortably.”
islam.explanation: Islam permits slaughter but demands ihsan (excellence and kindness) even when the knife is in hand.
islam.tie_back: Both texts worry about the heart of the one holding the blade; Islam answers by disciplining the slaughterer with mercy, the Kural by renouncing flesh altogether.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man; he that sacrificeth a lamb, as if he cut off a dog’s neck”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah condemns those who kill animals in ritual while their hearts are far from God, equating it with violence against humans.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Isaiah refuses to separate killing animals from the violent disposition it reveals.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Lankavatara Sutra (chapter 8) argues that the Bodhisattva should not eat meat, because living beings sense the odour of death on the meat-eater and fear him, and because meat-eating is incompatible with the compassion a Bodhisattva must cultivate.
buddhism.explanation: The meat-eater becomes, in the eyes of animals, like a hunter — a figure of threat.
buddhism.tie_back: A striking echo of the Kural’s comparison of the flesh-eater’s mind to that of a weapon-bearer.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A man who always feeds two thousand worthy monks, does not control himself, and will be blamed in this world like a man with bloody hands. They kill a fattened sheep, and prepare food for the sake of a particular person; they season the meat with salt and oil, and dress it with pepper.”
jainism.explanation: Ardraka says that a patron who has a sheep killed and its meat seasoned to feed monks stands, for all his piety, like a man with bloody hands.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar compares the mind of one who relishes flesh to the heart of one who holds a weapon; Ardraka likewise puts the provider of a meat feast alongside a man with blood on his hands.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga II.6.36-37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If one's clothes are stained with blood, the garment becomes polluted. Those who suck the blood of human beings-how can their consciousness be pure?”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Vaar Maajh, Guru Nanak points out that people call a bloodstained garment impure, and asks how the mind of someone who lives off other people's blood can ever be clean.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a mind that has relished another body cannot turn toward goodness, like the mind of one holding a weapon; Guru Nanak likewise holds that feeding on others' blood leaves the consciousness impure.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Vaar Maajh (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the Athenian Bouphonia (“ox-slaying”) festival, after the sacrificial ox was killed the priest fled, and the axe itself was put on trial and condemned — a ritual acknowledgement of guilt for the killing.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Athenians felt that killing a working ox was close to murder, so they ritually blamed the weapon.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The festival treats the weapon and the killing as morally charged — the same link between blade and heart that the Kural draws.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Note that the eating of flesh is not only physically against nature, but it also makes us spiritually coarse and gross by reason of satiety and surfeit.”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch argues that meat-eating dulls and coarsens the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s claim that relishing flesh turns the mind away from goodness.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On the Eating of Flesh I.6 (995E; Loeb trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: William Hogarth publishes The Four Stages of Cruelty
real_life_example.event: William Hogarth published a series of four prints, The Four Stages of Cruelty, following the fictional Tom Nero from a boy who torments animals in the street to an adult who harms people and is finally punished by the law. Hogarth wrote that the prints were meant to reduce the cruel treatment of animals that was common on London's streets, and he had them priced cheaply so that ordinary people could buy them. The series argued that cruelty tolerated in small things, even in children, grows into greater cruelty later.
real_life_example.explanation: Hogarth's prints became a classic statement of the idea that harming animals hardens the heart and turns it away from goodness.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the heart of one who relishes another creature's body to that of a man holding a weapon, and Hogarth's series showed the same hardening of the mind toward harm.

tamil:
அருளல்ல தியாதெனிற் கொல்லாமை கோறல்
பொருளல்ல தவ்வூன் தினல்.
transliteration:
Arulalla thiyaathenir kollaamai koral,
Porulalla thavvoon thinal.
meaning: If you ask what kindness is and what it is not: not killing is kindness, and killing is not. Eating the flesh of what was killed is wrong.
elementary: What is kindness? Not hurting or killing. What is unkindness? Killing. So eating the meat that came from killing isn’t right either — because it depends on the unkind act.
university: This couplet has a compressed catechism structure that Parimelazhagar unpacks as: அருள் யாது? கொல்லாமை; அருளல்லது யாது? கோறல் — “What is grace? Non-killing. What is not grace? Killing.” The final clause, பொருளல்லது அவ்வூன் தினல் (“eating that flesh is not porul”), extends the moral judgement from the act of killing to the act of eating, closing the loophole that the eater is innocent because someone else killed. பொருள் here is best read as “righteousness, what is proper” (Varadarasan: அறம் அல்லாதது). The argument prefigures chapter 33 (கொல்லாமை, Non-killing), making flesh-renunciation the dietary corollary of ahimsa.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Meat can never be obtained without injury to living creatures, and injury to sentient beings is detrimental to (the attainment of) heavenly bliss; let him therefore shun (the use of) meat.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu reasons that because meat always requires harming a living being, and harm blocks spiritual reward, one should avoid meat.
hinduism.tie_back: Same syllogism as the Kural: killing is contrary to virtue, meat requires killing, so eating meat is not right.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat. And to every beast of the earth… I have given every green herb for meat: and it was so.”
christianity.explanation: In the original creation, God gives humans and animals plants — not each other — as food.
christianity.tie_back: The Edenic ideal of a world without killing for food reflects the Kural’s identification of non-killing with goodness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And there is no creature on [or within] the earth or bird that flies with its wings except [that they are] communities like you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran declares that animals and birds form communities just like human ones.
islam.tie_back: Recognising animals as fellow communities grounds the Kural’s claim that killing them is the opposite of compassion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Meat was not permitted to Adam, the first man, for consumption”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud reads Genesis 1:29-30 as meaning that the first human was vegetarian; meat was permitted only after the Flood.
judaism.tie_back: Rabbinic tradition thus preserves the ideal that a world without killing for food was the original good — the Kural’s standard.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “I undertake the precept to refrain from taking life”
buddhism.explanation: The first of the Five Precepts binds every Buddhist not to kill living beings.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s definition of compassion as non-killing; whether it extends to eating meat is debated within Buddhism.
buddhism.source: Five Precepts (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī), as summarised in scholarship on Buddhist vegetarianism

jainism.quote_or_event: “A wise man should study them with all means of philosophical research. All beings hate pains; therefore one should not kill them. This is the quintessence of wisdom: not to kill anything.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga sums up the whole path in one rule: because every being hates pain, wisdom comes down to not killing anything.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar answers 'what is compassion?' with 'not killing'; the Sutrakritanga answers 'what is wisdom?' with the same reply.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.11.9-10 (also at I.1.4.10) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, they oppress living beings and kill them, and call it proper. When the Lord calls for their account, what will their condition be?”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir rejects the claim that killing a creature by force becomes acceptable because it is labelled proper, and warns that God will call such killers to account.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural flatly calls killing the opposite of grace and says eating what was killed is not right; Kabir likewise refuses to let any label turn killing into righteousness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1375, Salok Bhagat Kabir 199 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For the son of Cronos has ordained this law for men, that fishes and beasts and winged fowls should devour one another, for right is not in them; but to mankind he gave right which proves far the best.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says animals eat each other because they lack justice, while Zeus gave justice to humans.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hesiod separates the human moral order from the law of devouring — though he applies it to human conduct generally, not to diet.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 276-280 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Will ye not cease from this ill-sounding slaughter? See ye not that ye are devouring one another in the thoughtlessness of your hearts?”
philosophy.explanation: Empedocles, believing souls pass between humans and animals, calls animal slaughter and eating a form of cannibalism.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he treats killing and eating as one continuous wrong born of a heedless heart.

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Wu of Liang requires Chinese Buddhist monks to give up all meat
real_life_example.event: Emperor Wu of Liang, a devoted Buddhist patron, called assemblies of monks and pressed on them a rule that monastics must abstain from all meat, citing the Nirvana Sutra. Earlier monastic rules had allowed monks to eat so-called clean meat, from animals not killed specifically for them, and some monks objected that the old discipline did not forbid meat. The emperor's rule was enforced and became the lasting norm for Chinese Buddhist monks and nuns.
real_life_example.explanation: The decree closed the loophole that eating meat is innocent so long as someone else did the killing, and it shaped Chinese Buddhist practice for the following fifteen centuries.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says not killing is compassion and adds that eating the flesh of what was killed is also not right, which is exactly the loophole Emperor Wu's rule closed.

tamil:
உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை ஊனுண்ண
அண்ணாத்தல் செய்யாது அளறு.
transliteration:
Unnaamai ulladhu uyirnilai oonunna,
Annaaththal seyyaathu alaru.
meaning: Life is kept safe by not eating meat. If a person eats meat, a place of terrible suffering will swallow them and never let them out.
elementary: Many animals stay alive because people choose not to eat them. But the Kural gives a warning too: eating flesh is like falling into a deep, sticky pit that closes its mouth and won’t let you climb back out.
university: The first line, உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை, is read by Parimelazhagar and Varadarasan as “the continued life of beings depends on not eating flesh,” while Karunanidhi reads it socially: because some refrain, many creatures are spared. The second line uses a vivid image: அளறு (literally “mire, bog,” conventionally “hell”) will not perform அண்ணாத்தல் — opening the mouth — to release the one it has swallowed. The mire-image suggests a moral trap from which there is no easy exit, a consequence proportional to the finality of the death inflicted. Comparable ideas of unending or long-lasting punishment for bloodshed appear in Manu’s “mamsah” etymology and in Empedocles’ exile of the blood-polluted daimon.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “'Me he (mam sah)' will devour in the next (world), whose flesh I eat in this (life); the wise declare this (to be) the real meaning of the word 'flesh' (mamsah).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu derives the word for meat (māṃsa) from “me he (will eat)”: the animal you eat now will eat you in the next life.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts warn that eating flesh sets up a consequence that swallows the eater in return.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the rich man, who “fared sumptuously every day” and ignored suffering at his gate, the rich man ends in torment and cannot cross back.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s image of a place of punishment that does not let its captive go, earned by self-indulgence without mercy.

islam.quote_or_event: “A lady was punished because of a cat which she had imprisoned till it died. She entered the (Hell) Fire because of it”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that cruelty to a single animal can lead a person into Hell.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties the death of an animal at human hands to a hellish consequence for the human.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And while the flesh was yet between their teeth, ere it was chewed, the wrath of the LORD was kindled against the people, and the LORD smote the people with a very great plague.”
judaism.explanation: When the Israelites in the wilderness demanded meat, they were struck down while still eating the quail; the place was named Kibroth-hattaavah, “graves of craving.”
judaism.tie_back: The craving for flesh leads directly to a pit of death — close to the Kural’s image of the swallowing mire.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who, while himself seeking happiness, oppresses with violence other beings who also desire happiness, will not attain happiness hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says harming others for one’s own happiness blocks happiness in future lives.
buddhism.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s warning that the flesh-eater’s future is closed off.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You like meat minced or roasted; I have been made to eat, ever so many times, poisoned meat, and red-hot to boot.” … “Always frightened, trembling, distressed, and suffering, I have experienced the most exquisite pain and misery.”
jainism.explanation: Prince Mrigaputra recalls his past lives in hell for his parents, setting the meat they enjoy beside the poisoned, red-hot meat he was forced to eat there.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar warns that hell will swallow the flesh-eater and not let him go; Mrigaputra's account of the hells pairs the taste for meat with its endless repayment there.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 19.69, 19.71 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, those mortals who consume marijuana, fish and wine - no matter what pilgrimages, fasts and rituals they follow, they will all go to hell.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir warns that people who eat fish and take intoxicants are not saved by their pilgrimages, fasts or rituals, but go down to hell.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar says hell swallows the flesh-eater and does not let him go; Kabir's salok also sends the eater of flesh to hell, whatever religious merit he claims.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1377, Salok Bhagat Kabir 233 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus’ crew, starving, slaughtered and ate the sacred cattle of the Sun; as punishment they all died and never returned home.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic picture of the Kural’s warning: eating forbidden flesh brings a doom from which there is no return.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “whenever one of the daemons, whose portion is length of days, has sinfully polluted his hands with blood… he must wander thrice ten thousand seasons from the abodes of the blessed”
philosophy.explanation: Empedocles taught that a soul stained by bloodshed is exiled through countless lifetimes before it can return to bliss.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts describe a long captivity for those who shed blood; the Kural’s mire “will not open its mouth.”

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Tenmu bans the eating of certain meats in Japan
real_life_example.event: In 675 Emperor Tenmu, a devout Buddhist, issued a decree forbidding the eating of cattle, horses, dogs, monkeys and chickens, at first during the farming months of the year. Later rulers strengthened the restriction and it hardened into a broad taboo on meat that lasted in some form for about 1,200 years. The ban was formally ended in 1872 when Emperor Meiji publicly began eating meat.
real_life_example.explanation: A single act of restraint, rooted in Buddhist respect for life, spared animals across Japanese society for more than a thousand years.
real_life_example.tie_back: One reading of the kural is that the life of creatures is preserved because people refrain from eating flesh, and Japan's long meat taboo is a large-scale example of that preservation.

tamil:
தினற்பொருட்டால் கொல்லாது உலகெனின் யாரும்
விலைப்பொருட்டால் ஊன்றருவா ரில்.
transliteration:
Thinarporuttaal kollaathu ulagenin yaarum,
Vilaipporuttaal oondraruvaar il.
meaning: If the world did not kill animals to eat them, no one would kill animals and sell their meat for money.
elementary: Why does a shop sell something? Because people buy it. If nobody bought meat, nobody would kill animals to sell it. So the person who buys is part of the reason the animal was killed.
university: This is the most analytical couplet of the chapter, and it answers a specific excuse: “I did not kill; I only bought meat already killed.” Valluvar identifies the causal chain — தினற்பொருட்டு (for the sake of eating) generates விலைப்பொருட்டு (for the sake of price) — so that the consumer’s demand is the root cause of the butcher’s act. G. U. Pope’s translation makes the rebuttal explicit (“Who’d kill and sell, I pray, if none came there the flesh to buy?”). The argument is strikingly modern, anticipating demand-side ethics, and directly contests the Theravada allowance of meat not seen, heard or suspected to be killed for oneself; it closely matches Manu 5.51, which counts the buyer among the slayers.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who permits (the slaughter of an animal), he who cuts it up, he who kills it, he who buys or sells (meat), he who cooks it, he who serves it up, and he who eats it, (must all be considered as) the slayers (of the animal).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu spreads the guilt of the killing across the whole chain, including buyer, seller and eater.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s point: buying and eating make one a participant in the slaughter.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says it is better to give up meat if eating it harms others.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul holds the eater responsible for the wider effects of his eating — though his concern is fellow believers, not animals.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is no person who kills a small bird or anything larger, for no just reason, but Allah will ask him about it.”
islam.explanation: Every killing of an animal must have a legitimate purpose, and each will be accounted for before God.
islam.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s insistence that the purpose behind killing matters morally; Islam accepts eating as a just purpose, the Kural does not.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When the LORD thy God shall enlarge thy border… and thou shalt say, I will eat flesh, because thy soul longeth to eat flesh; thou mayest eat flesh, whatsoever thy soul lusteth after.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah frames ordinary meat-eating as a permission granted to human craving, which many rabbinic and later thinkers (e.g., Rav Kook) read as a concession rather than an ideal.
judaism.tie_back: The text itself locates the origin of killing in the eater’s desire — the same causal root the Kural identifies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, a lay follower should not engage in five types of business. Which five? Business in weapons, business in human beings, business in meat, business in intoxicants, and business in poison.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha forbids lay followers from trading in meat as a livelihood.
buddhism.tie_back: Targets the same “killing for price” the Kural names; but the Jivaka Sutta permits monks to eat meat not killed specifically for them, which the Kural’s demand argument implicitly rejects.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A true monk should not accept such food and drink as has been especially prepared for him along with slaughter of living beings.” … “Those who praise the gift, are accessory to the killing of beings.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga holds that whoever consumes food or approves of gifts that involve killing shares in the guilt of the killing.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar answers the buyer who says 'I did not kill' by showing that demand creates the killing; Jain teaching likewise makes the one who accepts or praises slaughtered food an accessory to the slaughter.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.11.14, I.11.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, it is tyranny to use force; the Lord shall call you to account.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir says that any use of force against another living being is oppression, and God will demand an answer for it.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar refuses to let the buyer of meat shift the blame to the butcher; the nearest Sikh teaching is that everyone who takes part in violence answers for it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1375, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Mecone, Prometheus divided a slaughtered ox so that humans kept the meat and the gods received only bones wrapped in fat; from then on sacrifice fed human appetite while appearing to honour the gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth explains why sacrificial meat ends up on human tables.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It exposes how human appetite drives the killing behind a respectable pretext — as the Kural exposes the buyer’s excuse.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “What a terrible thing it is to look on when the tables of the rich are spread… And it is even more terrible to look on when they are taken away, for more is left than has been eaten. So the beasts died for nothing!”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch points out that the killing is driven by the appetite and display of diners, who waste much of what was slaughtered.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he places responsibility for the slaughter on the consumers whose demand causes it.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On the Eating of Flesh I.4 (994F; Loeb trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: CITES bans the international ivory trade
real_life_example.event: After the 1970s and 1980s, when demand for ivory drove the poaching of hundreds of thousands of African elephants, the parties to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species met in Lausanne in 1989 and moved the African elephant to Appendix I. This effectively banned international commercial trade in ivory, with the listing taking effect in January 1990. In the years that followed, ivory markets shrank and prices fell, and poaching declined in many areas, though later one-off sales and continuing illegal trade weakened the ban's effect.
real_life_example.explanation: The ban showed in practice that cutting off the buyers' market is one of the most effective ways to stop the killing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural argues that no one would kill for money if no one wanted to buy, and the ivory ban put that reasoning into international law.

tamil:
உண்ணாமை வேண்டும் புலாஅல் பிறிதொன்றன்
புண்ணது உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Unnaamai vendum pulaaal pirithondran,
Punnathu unarvaarp perin.
meaning: If people understood that meat is really the wound of another living creature, they would stop eating it.
elementary: If you saw a hurt animal with a sore, you would never want to eat that sore. The Kural says meat is really just that — a wound cut from another living creature. If we remembered that, we wouldn’t want to eat it.
university: The force of the couplet lies in a single noun, புண் (wound, sore, ulcer). By renaming meat as “another creature’s wound,” Valluvar strips away the culinary vocabulary that disguises its origin, a technique of moral re-description. The conditional உணர்வார்ப் பெறின் (“if one gains those who perceive / if one comes to perceive”) makes the argument depend on clear perception: the problem is not ignorance of a rule but a failure to see what is in front of us. The metrical lengthening in புலாஅல் (alapedai) lingers on the word “flesh,” as if forcing the reader to look at it. Plutarch and Ovid’s Pythagoras make the very same move, calling meat “sores” and “pitiful wounds.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Having well considered the (disgusting) origin of flesh and the (cruelty of) fettering and slaying corporeal beings, let him entirely abstain from eating flesh.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the reader to reflect on where meat comes from — the binding and killing of living beings — and then to give it up entirely.
hinduism.tie_back: Same method as the Kural: once one sees the true origin of flesh, the desire to eat it should end.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink.”
christianity.explanation: Daniel and his friends refuse the Babylonian king’s meat and wine and ask for vegetables and water instead, and emerge healthier.
christianity.tie_back: An example of deliberate refusal of meat as a matter of conscience, though Daniel’s concern is ritual purity rather than the animal’s wound.

islam.quote_or_event: “Prohibited to you are dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, and [those animals] killed by strangling or by a violent blow or by a head-long fall or by the goring of horns…”
islam.explanation: The Quran forbids blood, carrion and animals killed violently, focusing attention on how an animal died.
islam.tie_back: Both texts ask the eater to look at the death and bleeding behind the meat; Islam responds with purity laws, the Kural with abstention.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat.”
judaism.explanation: Even when meat is permitted, the Torah forbids eating it with its blood, because the blood is the animal’s life.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it insists that meat is bound up with another creature’s life and must not be eaten as if it were mere food.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Taking life, beating, wounding, binding, stealing, lying, deceiving, worthless knowledge, adultery; this is stench. Not the eating of meat.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Amagandha Sutta, a Buddha answers a vegetarian Brahmin by saying true impurity lies in evil deeds, not in eating meat.
buddhism.tie_back: An honest counterpoint: this early text denies that meat itself defiles, whereas the Kural insists meat is inherently a wound — yet it still lists wounding and taking life as the real impurity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “all beings, those with two, three, four senses, plants, those with five senses, and the rest of creation, (experience) individually pleasure or displeasure, pain, great terror, and unhappiness.” … “some kill (them) for the sake of their flesh, some kill them for the sake of their blood”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga first insists that every creature feels pain and terror, then lists the killing of animals for their flesh and blood among the sinful acts a wise man must give up.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that if people truly saw flesh as another creature's wound they would not eat it; the Acaranga likewise asks the reader to see the pain and terror behind every piece of flesh taken.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.1.6.2, I.1.6.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You seize a living creature, and then bring it home and kill its body; you have killed only the clay.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir strips away the religious language around ritual slaughter and describes what actually happens: a living creature is caught and its body destroyed, and he adds that this 'offering' gains the slayer nothing.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar makes people see meat for what it is, another creature's wound; Kabir similarly describes the slaughter in plain words so it can no longer be dressed up as piety.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1350, Raag Prabhaatee, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Pythagoras compares flesh-eaters to the Cyclops Polyphemus, who devoured Odysseus’ companions raw: people “tear, with cruel teeth, at pitiful wounds, recalling Cyclops’s practice.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The monstrous cannibal Cyclops becomes a mirror for ordinary meat-eating.
greek_mythology.tie_back: By invoking the Cyclops, the myth makes the eater see the torn body in front of him — the Kural’s ‘wound.’
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV (trans. A. S. Kline); Homer, Odyssey 9

philosophy.quote_or_event: “How was it that the pollution did not turn away his taste, which made contact with the sores of others and sucked juices and serums from mortal wounds?”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch asks how the first meat-eater could bear to put the sores and wounds of another creature to his lips.
philosophy.tie_back: Precisely the Kural’s image: flesh is another creature’s wound, and seeing it so should end the appetite.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On the Eating of Flesh I.1 (993B; Loeb trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: Upton Sinclair's The Jungle exposes the meatpacking industry
real_life_example.place: Chicago, Illinois, and Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle, first serialised in 1905 and published as a book in 1906, described the conditions inside Chicago's meatpacking plants. Sinclair wrote it to draw attention to the workers, but readers were most shocked by what it revealed about how meat was produced. President Theodore Roosevelt ordered an investigation, and in 1906 Congress passed the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act.
real_life_example.explanation: When the public was made to see clearly where its meat came from, it recoiled and demanded change.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says people would stop eating flesh if they truly perceived it as another creature's wound, and The Jungle showed how strongly people react when the reality behind meat is laid bare.

tamil:
செயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த காட்சியார் உண்ணார்
உயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த ஊன்.
transliteration:
Seyirin thalaippirindha kaatchiyaar unnaar,
Uyirin thalaippirindha oon.
meaning: People who see clearly, free of confusion and fault, will not eat the flesh of a body that has lost its life.
elementary: When your eyes are clear, you see things as they really are. People whose minds are clear and free from wrong ideas look at meat and see a body that was once alive — so they don’t eat it.
university: The couplet is built on an elegant repetition: தலைப்பிரிந்த (“separated from”) occurs in both lines — the wise are separated from செயிர் (fault, delusion), while the flesh is separated from உயிர் (life). The parallel suggests a moral symmetry: purity of vision is achieved by the same act of separation that, done to a living being, produces flesh. காட்சியார் (“those of vision”) links the virtue to perception, continuing kural 257’s theme that seeing clearly ends the desire for meat. Parimelazhagar glosses செயிர் as the delusion (mayakkam) that makes one mistake the body for the self, placing this couplet within the ascetic epistemology of the துறவறவியல்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is beyond duality and doubt, whose mind is engaged within, who is always busy working for the welfare of all sentient beings, and who is free from all sins, achieves liberation in the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita describes sages whose impurities are destroyed (kṣīṇa-kalmaṣāḥ) and who delight in the welfare of all beings (sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ).
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s “those freed from fault” are the same figures, and their concern for all beings excludes eating them.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But let all except the very weak and the sick abstain altogether from eating the flesh of four-footed animals.”
christianity.explanation: St Benedict’s monastic rule forbids monks the meat of four-footed animals, a practice kept for centuries in Western monasticism.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, those who commit to purity of life and vision renounce flesh.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram.”
islam.explanation: Pilgrims in the consecrated state of ihram are forbidden to hunt or kill game.
islam.tie_back: Islam links a heightened state of purity with refraining from killing animals — a limited echo of the Kural’s pure-sighted who refuse flesh.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud records Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s teaching that an ignoramus is prohibited from eating meat, deriving from Leviticus 11:46 (“This is the torah of the beast and of the fowl”) that only one who engages in Torah study may eat animals and fowl.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic tradition ties the permission to eat meat to spiritual knowledge and discipline.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts connect meat and wisdom — but in opposite directions: the Talmud limits meat to the learned; the Kural says the truly wise abstain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is not noble who injures living beings. He is called noble because he is harmless towards all living beings.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines the noble one (ariya) by harmlessness toward all beings.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, spiritual excellence is defined by refusing to harm living creatures.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You are irreligious, unworthy men, devoted to foolish pleasures, who say that partaking heartily of this meat you are not soiled by sin. All who partake of such food, commit sins in their ignorance; but the wise do nothing of the kind.”
jainism.explanation: Ardraka rejects the claim that one can eat meat without moral stain, saying meat-eating comes from ignorance and the wise do not do it.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those whose vision is free of delusion will not eat lifeless flesh; Ardraka likewise contrasts the ignorance of meat-eaters with the wise, who abstain.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga II.6.38-39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The fools argue about flesh and meat, but they know nothing about meditation and spiritual wisdom. What is called meat, and what is called green vegetables? What leads to sin?”
sikhism.explanation: In Vaar Malaar Guru Nanak mocks those who make meat-eating the test of holiness while knowing nothing of meditation or spiritual wisdom.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those whose vision is free of delusion will not eat flesh; Guru Nanak agrees that clear vision is what matters but places it in spiritual wisdom, not in avoiding meat.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1289, Vaar Malaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod’s golden race of mortals lived “like gods,” free from toil and grief, while the fruitful earth gave them its harvest unforced; later Pythagorean writers took this age as a model of bloodless living.
greek_mythology.explanation: The first, purest human race lived on what the earth freely gave.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The purest humans of myth, like the Kural’s fault-free sages, live without killing for food.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Can you really ask what reason Pythagoras had for abstaining from flesh? For my part I rather wonder both by what accident and in what state of soul or mind the first man who did so, touched his mouth to gore”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch reverses the burden of proof: it is not the abstainer but the meat-eater whose state of mind needs explaining.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s assumption that a clear, undeluded mind naturally refuses flesh.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On the Eating of Flesh I.1 (993A-B; Loeb trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: Plutarch delivers his discourses On the Eating of Flesh
real_life_example.event: The Greek writer Plutarch composed two discourses, On the Eating of Flesh, preserved in his Moralia, which argue for abstaining from meat. He asked why people find it strange that Pythagoras refused flesh, argued that the human body is not built like a carnivore's, and condemned the cruelty of killing animals for luxurious meals. The Loeb editors note that these speeches probably date from his youth.
real_life_example.explanation: Plutarch's essay is one of the earliest surviving arguments in the West that clear thinking about what meat is should lead a person to refuse it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those whose vision is freed from delusion will not eat flesh separated from life, and Plutarch argued that only habit and blindness keep people eating it.

tamil:
அவிசொரிந் தாயிரம் வேட்டலின் ஒன்றன்
உயிர்செகுத் துண்ணாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Avisorindh thaayiram vettalin ondran,
Uyirsekuth thunnaamai nandru.
meaning: Not killing a single creature to eat it is better than making a thousand offerings by pouring ghee (melted butter) into a holy fire.
elementary: Some people think doing big, fancy religious ceremonies makes them very good. The Kural says: sparing just one animal’s life, and not eating it, is better than a thousand of those ceremonies.
university: This couplet makes a pointed comparison with Vedic ritual: அவி (havis, oblations such as ghee) poured into the fire in a thousand வேள்வி (yajñas, sacrifices). By ranking the simple restraint of not killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices, Valluvar subordinates ritual merit to ethical conduct — a critique shared with the Jain and Buddhist movements and with the later Upanishadic interiorisation of sacrifice. The numerical contrast (ஆயிரம் versus ஒன்றன் — “a thousand” versus “one”) is characteristic of Valluvar’s rhetoric of disproportion. Manu 5.53 offers a strikingly similar valuation, equating lifelong abstention from meat with a century of horse-sacrifices, while the Hebrew prophets and Jesus prefer “mercy, and not sacrifice.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who during a hundred years annually offers a horse-sacrifice, and he who entirely abstains from meat, obtain the same reward for their meritorious (conduct).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu equates lifelong abstinence from meat with a hundred years of the grandest Vedic sacrifice.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the same comparison as the Kural: abstention from flesh outweighs vast ritual offerings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice”
christianity.explanation: Jesus quotes Hosea to say God values mercy over ritual offerings.
christianity.tie_back: Same ranking as the Kural: compassion outweighs sacrifice.

islam.quote_or_event: “Their meat will not reach Allah, nor will their blood, but what reaches Him is piety from you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran says God receives none of the sacrificial animal’s meat or blood — only the worshipper’s inner devotion.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares that the outward offering is worthless compared with the inner moral state.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.”
judaism.explanation: Hosea says God prefers loving-kindness (ḥesed) to animal offerings.
judaism.tie_back: The same prophetic ranking of compassion above ritual that the Kural expresses.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, the Buddha tells a Brahmin of a great ancient sacrifice in which no oxen, goats, fowl or pigs were slain and no trees cut; only ghee, oil, butter, curds and honey were offered — and then teaches that giving, virtue and the precepts are still greater sacrifices.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines sacrifice as bloodless and ultimately ethical.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks not killing above ritual offerings.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You (use) Kusa-grass, sacrificial poles, straw and wood, you touch water in the evening and in the morning; thereby you injure living beings, and in your ignorance you commit sins again and again.” … “Penance is my fire; life my fireplace; right exertion is my sacrificial ladle; the body the dried cowdung; Karman is my fuel; self-control, right exertion, and tranquillity are the oblations, praised by the sages, which I offer.”
jainism.explanation: The outcaste-born monk Harikesa tells Brahmin sacrificers that their fire rites injure living beings, and redefines true sacrifice as inner discipline whose first rule is 'doing no injury to living beings' (12.41).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks not killing a single creature above a thousand fire sacrifices; Harikesa likewise sets non-injury and inner penance above, and against, the Vedic fire offering.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.39, 12.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You kill living beings, and call it a righteous action. Tell me, brother, what would you call an unrighteous action?”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Maaroo Kabir asks a priest who kills animals in sacrificial rites how he can call that dharma, and what then he would call sin.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks not killing a single creature above a thousand fire-sacrifices; Kabir likewise rejects killing done in the name of sacred rites.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1103, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “It is not enough to have committed such wickedness: they involve the gods in crime, and believe that the gods above delight in the slaughter of suffering oxen!”
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Pythagoras attacks animal sacrifice as dragging the gods into human cruelty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s rejection of the idea that killing for ritual can be meritorious.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV (trans. A. S. Kline)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And the altar did not reek with pure bull's blood, but this was held in the greatest abomination among men, to eat the goodly limbs after tearing out the life.”
philosophy.explanation: Empedocles describes a golden age when worship was bloodless and killing to eat was the worst abomination.
philosophy.tie_back: Joins sacrifice and meat-eating in one condemnation, as the Kural does.

real_life_example.event_title: Ashoka's First Rock Edict forbids animal sacrifice
real_life_example.place: Mauryan Empire (Girnar and other edict sites), India
real_life_example.event: In the first of his Major Rock Edicts, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka proclaimed that in his domain no living beings were to be slaughtered or offered in sacrifice. The same edict recorded that his royal kitchen, where many thousands of animals had once been killed for food, now killed only two peacocks and a deer, and the deer not always, and that in time even these would not be killed.
real_life_example.explanation: A great king publicly placed sparing animal life above the sacrificial rites that were then a mark of royal piety.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks not killing one creature above a thousand fire sacrifices, and Ashoka's edict set aside sacrifice itself in favour of not killing.

tamil:
கொல்லான் புலாலை மறுத்தானைக் கைகூப்பி
எல்லா உயிருந் தொழும்.
transliteration:
Kollaan pulaalai maruththaanaik kaikooppi,
Ellaa uyirum thozhum.
meaning: All living creatures will put their hands together and honor the one who does not kill and refuses to eat meat.
elementary: Imagine every animal in the world putting its paws together to say “thank you” to one person. That’s the picture here: the person who never kills and never eats animals is loved and honoured by every living thing.
university: The chapter closes with an image of cosmic reverence: எல்லா உயிரும் (all living beings) perform கைகூப்பித் தொழுதல் — the joined-palm gesture of worship. The two qualifications, கொல்லான் (one who does not kill) and புலாலை மறுத்தான் (one who has refused flesh), sum up the chapter and anticipate the next section on கொல்லாமை. The hyperbole of animals folding hands is deliberate: the one who renounces power over other lives receives from them the honour usually given to gods. Parallel visions appear in Isaiah’s peaceable kingdom, Empedocles’ age when “all things were tame and gentle to man,” and the Buddhist teaching that one who cultivates goodwill is dear to human and non-human beings alike.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He for whom no one is put into difficulty … is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the person who causes no living being distress is especially beloved of God.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the one who harms no creature receives the highest honour.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the Little Flowers of St Francis, birds gather around Francis as he preaches to them, stretching their necks and bowing their heads, and do not fly away until he blesses them; later tradition tells of the wolf of Gubbio made gentle by him.
christianity.explanation: Christian legend pictures creatures responding with reverence to a saint of radical gentleness.
christianity.tie_back: A near-literal image of the Kural’s “all living beings worship him.”
christianity.source: The Little Flowers of St Francis (Fioretti), ch. 16 and ch. 21

islam.quote_or_event: “Yes, there is a reward for serving any animate (living being).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet told of a man forgiven by God for giving water to a thirsty dog, and taught that kindness to any living creature is rewarded.
islam.tie_back: Both texts see kindness to all living beings as earning the highest esteem; in Islam the honour comes from God.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid… They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah envisions a messianic age when no creature harms another.
judaism.tie_back: The peaceable kingdom is the social form of the Kural’s ideal: a world where no one kills, honoured by all creatures.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings. The devas protect one.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the eleven benefits of cultivating goodwill (metta), the Buddha lists being beloved by humans and non-humans and protected by the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: Very close to the Kural’s promise that the non-harming person is revered by all living beings.

jainism.quote_or_event: The opening verse of the Dasavaikalika Sutra, placed in the Saman Suttam's Dharmasutra, calls dharma the highest good, names its essence as non-violence (ahimsa), self-control (samyama) and penance (tapas), and says that even the gods bow down to one whose mind is always set on dharma.
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition holds that one whose life is grounded in non-violence wins the reverence even of the gods.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says all living beings will join their palms in worship of the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; the Dasavaikalika says the gods themselves bow to the one whose dharma is rooted in ahimsa.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 1.1, as Saman Suttam v. 82 (Dharmasutra)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “And when, O Nanak, he is merciful to all beings, only then shall he be called a Muslim.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Vaar Maajh Guru Nanak lists the real marks of a believer and ends by saying that only someone merciful to all living beings has earned the name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural promises the reverence of all living beings to the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; Guru Nanak likewise makes mercy toward all beings the condition for true religious honour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Vaar Maajh (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orpheus, the legendary singer linked to the Orphic way of life that abstained from killing, drew wild beasts, birds, trees and stones to gather around him in peace when he sang.
greek_mythology.explanation: Myth pictures all nature gathering in rapt attention around the gentle Orpheus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An image of all creatures honouring one figure of harmlessness, as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For all things were tame and gentle to man, both beasts and birds, and friendly feelings were kindled everywhere.”
philosophy.explanation: Empedocles recalls an age of Love when humans did not kill, and in return every creature was friendly toward them.
philosophy.tie_back: The same reciprocal harmony the Kural promises: renounce killing, and all creatures become your friends.

real_life_example.event_title: Francis of Assisi is proclaimed patron of those who promote ecology
real_life_example.event: In the apostolic letter Inter Sanctos, Pope John Paul II declared Saint Francis of Assisi the heavenly patron of those who promote ecology. The letter praised Francis for revering nature as a gift of God and pointed to his Canticle of the Creatures. Francis, who died in 1226, had long been remembered for his gentleness toward animals and all living things.
real_life_example.explanation: Nearly eight centuries after his death, Francis's reputation for kindness to every creature made him a figure honoured around the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says all living beings will revere the one who harms none, and Francis, remembered for his gentleness to creatures, became a universally honoured symbol of that ideal.

tamil:
உற்றநோய் நோன்றல் உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை
அற்றே தவத்திற் குரு.
transliteration:
Utra noi nondral uyirkku urukan seyyaamai
Atre thavaththirku uru.
meaning: Patiently bearing the pain that comes to you, and never hurting any other living thing: this is what true penance (a life of strict self-control) really is.
elementary: Imagine someone bumps into you and it hurts. Penance, says Valluvar, is two simple things: you put up with the hurt without making a fuss, and you never hurt anyone back or hurt anyone at all. That is what being a real ‘tapas’ person looks like.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition that is striking for what it leaves out: no fire rituals, no fasting regimens, no forest hermitage, only a two-part ethical formula — endurance (நோன்றல், noṉṟal) of suffering that befalls oneself, and non-infliction (செய்யாமை) of suffering on other lives. The emphatic அற்றே (‘just that much’) deliberately reduces tapas from spectacle to disposition. Parimelazhagar notes that the suffering endured includes both what arises naturally (hunger, cold, illness) and what others inflict, which aligns the verse closely with the Jain and Buddhist redefinition of austerity as patience plus ahiṃsā. The move is thus both conservative (it keeps the prestigious word ‘tapas’) and reformist (it ethicizes it), and it frames every later claim in the chapter about the ‘power’ of tapas as resting on this moral foundation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of the body consists in worship of the Supreme Lord, the brāhmaṇas, the spiritual master, and superiors like the father and mother, and in cleanliness, simplicity, celibacy and nonviolence.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita breaks tapas into bodily, verbal and mental kinds, and places nonviolence (ahiṃsā) inside the very definition of bodily austerity.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita makes not-harming part of what tapas is; Valluvar goes further by making it half the whole definition and pairing it with endurance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells believers that patiently enduring undeserved suffering, without striking back, is what pleases God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts define spiritual worth as bearing pain patiently while refusing to retaliate.

islam.quote_or_event: “Fasting is a shield (or a screen or a shelter). So, the person observing fasting should avoid sexual relation with his wife and should not behave foolishly and impudently, and if somebody fights with him or abuses him, he should tell him twice, ‘I am fasting.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes sawm not merely as going hungry but as a discipline in which the faster absorbs provocation without answering it with harm.
islam.tie_back: The Islamic fast, like Valluvar’s tapas, joins bodily endurance with a refusal to hurt others even when provoked.

judaism.quote_or_event: “About those who are insulted and do not insult, who hear their shame and do not respond, who act out of love and are joyful in suffering, the verse says: ‘And they that love Him are as the sun going forth in its might’.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud praises those who absorb insult without returning it and who accept suffering with joy, likening them to the rising sun.
judaism.tie_back: Endure what comes, harm no one in return — the same two pillars Valluvar names as the whole of tapas.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Enduring patience is the highest austerity. ‘Nibbana is supreme,’ say the Buddhas. He is not a true monk who harms another, nor a true renunciate who oppresses others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines tapas as patient endurance and declares that anyone who harms others is not a genuine renunciant.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a restatement of the Kural: austerity = patience + not harming others.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Suffering from insects a great sage remains undisturbed. … Tolerate living beings, do not kill them, though they eat your flesh and blood.”
jainism.explanation: In the lecture on the twenty-two troubles (parīṣaha) a monk must bear, Mahavira tells him to endure even the bites of insects without driving them off or harming them.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar defines penance as bearing one's own suffering while causing none to others; this verse joins exactly those two halves, patient endurance and refusal to injure even the creatures causing the pain.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.10-11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
sikhism.explanation: Shaikh Farid, whose saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, tells the seeker to take blows without hitting back, to answer them with humility, and to return to inner peace.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar defines true penance as bearing what one suffers while causing no suffering to others; Farid asks for exactly that, patience under blows and no retaliation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus, disguised as a beggar in his own house, bears the suitors’ insults and blows night after night, commanding his own heart to endure rather than lash out.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s hero is celebrated for polytlas — much-enduring — self-command under humiliation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Mirrors the endurance half of Valluvar’s definition; the non-harm half fails, since Odysseus later slaughters the suitors.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “These two words, he said, are ἀνέχου (bear) and ἀπέχου (forbear).”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus taught that the two worst faults are failing to endure what must be endured and failing to refrain from what must be avoided; ‘bear and forbear’ would make a person almost sinless.
philosophy.tie_back: The Stoic two-word rule is a near twin of Valluvar’s two-part definition of tapas.
philosophy.source: Epictetus in Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 17.19.5-6 (trans. J. C. Rolfe)

real_life_example.event_title: The Doukhobors burn their weapons and bear persecution without resistance
real_life_example.place: Transcaucasus, Russian Empire (now Georgia, Azerbaijan and Turkey), and Saskatchewan, Canada
real_life_example.event: In 1895 thousands of Doukhobors, a Russian Christian sect committed to pacifism, piled up their own weapons in their villages in the Transcaucasus and burned them, refusing to bear arms or do military service. The Russian authorities responded with renewed persecution, and the Doukhobors did not take up arms in return. With help from Leo Tolstoy and from English Quakers, about 7,500 of them emigrated to Canada in 1899 and settled in what became Saskatchewan.
real_life_example.explanation: The Burning of Arms has been called one of the first mass pacifist protests of modern times, and the community chose to absorb punishment and exile rather than harm anyone.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines true penance as bearing whatever suffering comes to oneself while inflicting none on others, which is exactly the two-part stance the Doukhobors took.

tamil:
தவமும் தவமுடையார்க்கு ஆகும் அதனை
அஃதிலார் மேற்கொள் வது.
transliteration:
Thavamum thavamudaiyaarkku aagum adhanai
Aqdhilaar merkolvadhu.
meaning: Penance (a life of strict self-control) works only for those who truly have its inner strength. For others, just going through the motions of it is useless.
elementary: Wearing a doctor’s coat does not make you a doctor. In the same way, putting on the clothes and habits of a holy person does not work unless you really have the patience and goodness inside.
university: The couplet turns on a pun-like repetition: தவம் (tapas) comes only to those who have தவம். Commentators split on what the second ‘tapas’ means. Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read it karmically — only those who accumulated tapas in earlier births can undertake it now — while Mu. Varadarasan reads it as a warning against தவக்கோலம், the ascetic costume adopted without ascetic conduct. The second reading anticipates the very next chapter, கூடாவொழுக்கம் (‘Imposture’), and fits Valluvar’s habitual suspicion of form without substance. Either way, the verse asserts that tapas is not a technique anyone can pick up but the outward expression of an already-formed inner capacity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who undergo severe austerities and penances not recommended in the scriptures, performing them out of pride and egoism, who are impelled by lust and attachment, who are foolish and who torture the material elements of the body as well as the Supersoul dwelling within, are to be known as demons.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna condemns austerity performed by those whose inner disposition is proud and desirous — the outward act is present but the right nature is not.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts insist that tapas without the proper inner quality is worthless or worse.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns against fasting as a public performance; the show earns only human notice, not God’s reward.
christianity.tie_back: Matches Varadarasan’s reading: the ascetic ‘look’ without the ascetic reality is empty.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever does not give up forged speech and evil actions, Allah is not in need of his leaving his food and drink.”
islam.explanation: A fast that leaves the character unchanged is declared meaningless in God’s sight.
islam.tie_back: The outward discipline without the inner reality is futile — Valluvar’s exact verdict.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the LORD?”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah mocks ritual fasting and sackcloth performed by people whose conduct stays unjust, and redefines the true fast as freeing the oppressed.
judaism.tie_back: Both reject the costume of penance when the substance is missing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the use of your matted hair, O witless man? What of your garment of antelope’s hide? Within you is the tangle (of passion); only outwardly do you cleanse yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha ridicules the ascetic whose matted locks and deerskin conceal an untamed mind.
buddhism.tie_back: Precisely the ‘tavakkōlam’ critique: the ascetic garb is useless without the inner tapas.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If an ignorant man should eat but a blade of Kusa-grass every month, (the merit of his penance) will not equal the sixteenth part of his who possesses the Law as it has been taught.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami tells Indra that even the most extreme fasting by one who lacks right understanding is worth almost nothing beside the inner possession of the true Law.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says outward tapas is futile for those who lack its inner quality; Nami makes the same point by ranking the severest fast of an ignorant man below a sixteenth of true inner discipline.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Yoga is not the patched coat, Yoga is not the walking stick. Yoga is not smearing the body with ashes.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Soohee Guru Nanak tells the yogis that the ascetic's coat, staff and ash do not make a person one with God; union comes from living purely in the midst of the world.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says putting on the outward form of penance is futile without the inner quality; Guru Nanak likewise empties the ascetic's outfit of any value.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 730, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon begs his father Helios to let him drive the sun-chariot; lacking the strength and skill for it, he loses control, scorches the earth, and is struck down by Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A task suited only to one with the proper power ends in ruin when attempted by one without it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s principle that a discipline belongs only to those with the capacity for it; others who take it up fail.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus warns that whoever takes up the Cynic’s cloak, wallet and staff without the inner preparation and divine calling undertakes a great matter in vain and makes himself ridiculous.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus the Cynic life is a vocation for the rare person fitted for it, not a costume anyone may wear.
philosophy.tie_back: A close philosophical parallel: the ascetic life ‘belongs to’ those who possess its inner qualification.
philosophy.source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.22 (On the Calling of a Cynic)

real_life_example.event_title: Pope Clement VI condemns the flagellant processions
real_life_example.place: Avignon, France (papal court), with the processions spreading across Germany and the Low Countries
real_life_example.event: During the Black Death, bands of flagellants travelled from town to town in Germany and neighbouring lands, performing public penance by scourging themselves in organised processions. As the movement spread and grew hostile to church authority, the University of Paris appealed to the pope. In letters dated 20 October 1349, Pope Clement VI condemned the movement and forbade the processions, and it soon dwindled into a small, hunted sect.
real_life_example.explanation: The church judged that a dramatic outward display of penance, cut loose from inner discipline and authority, had become a danger rather than a virtue.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that taking up the outward form of penance is futile for those who lack its inner quality, and the flagellant episode shows outward austerity being rejected as hollow.

tamil:
துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி மறந்தார்கொல்
மற்றை யவர்கள் தவம்.
transliteration:
Thurandhaarkku thuppuravu vendi marandhaarkol
Matraiyavargal thavam.
meaning: Is it because others wanted to give food and help to the people who gave up the world that they forgot to practice self-control themselves?
elementary: Picture a whole village cooking lunch for a few hermits on the hill. Valluvar jokes: maybe everyone got so busy packing lunches for the hermits that they forgot to become good and disciplined themselves!
university: This is one of Valluvar’s rare ironic rhetorical questions (கொல் marks doubt). Read straightforwardly, it offers an indulgent explanation for why so few undertake tapas: society needs householders to feed the ascetics. Read more sharply — as Kalaignar does — it is a rebuke: supporting renunciants is no substitute for one’s own discipline. The verse also documents a real economic structure of early Indian religion, in which Jain, Buddhist and Brahmanical renouncers depended on lay donation, and in which donors believed they shared the merit of those they supported. Valluvar gently punctures the complacency that such a division of spiritual labour could produce.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu declares that just as all creatures live by depending on air, so the members of all the other orders of life (students, forest-dwellers, renunciants) subsist by the support of the householder, who is therefore the most excellent order.
hinduism.explanation: Brahmanical law explicitly makes the householder the economic base on which ascetics rely.
hinduism.tie_back: Describes the very arrangement Valluvar is teasing — householders feeding renunciants.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that receiveth a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he that receiveth a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward.”
christianity.explanation: Those who host and support God’s messengers share in their reward.
christianity.tie_back: Supports the ‘merit through support’ logic that Valluvar suggests has made householders forget their own tapas.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Charity is] for the poor who have been restricted for the cause of Allah, unable to move about in the land. An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an directs charity to those wholly devoted to God’s cause who cannot earn for themselves.
islam.tie_back: Parallels lay support of renunciants as a religious duty.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rashi explains that the tribe of Zebulun engaged in sea-trade and provided for Issachar, who devoted himself to Torah study, and so Moses blessed Zebulun first — the supporter shares in the scholar’s merit.
judaism.explanation: The ‘Issachar–Zebulun’ partnership became the classic Jewish model of lay support for full-time religious devotion.
judaism.tie_back: A direct counterpart to householders feeding ascetics; Valluvar’s question probes whether the Zebulun role lets one neglect one’s own discipline.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Sangha is praised as the ‘incomparable field of merit for the world’; monks on the dhutanga and alms-round path depend entirely on lay donors, who earn merit by giving.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism formalized the monk–lay relationship: renunciants practise, householders feed them and gain merit.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the arrangement behind Valluvar’s question about why ‘others’ forgot tapas.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You have left the dreadful âsrama (that of the householder) and are wanting to enter another; (remain what you were), O king, and be content with observing the Pôsaha-days.”
jainism.explanation: Indra, testing Nami, suggests he stay a householder and keep only the lay fasting days (pōṣadha), reflecting the Jain arrangement in which lay people support monks with alms while practising lesser austerities themselves.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ironically asks whether householders forgot penance because they were busy feeding renunciants; the Jain scheme answers differently, expecting even householders to keep periodic fasts alongside their almsgiving.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.42 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself a guru or a spiritual teacher, while he goes around begging - don't ever touch his feet. One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: In Vaar Saarang Guru Nanak refuses honour to holy men who live by begging and gives it instead to the householder who earns by his own labour and shares what he has.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar wonders, perhaps ironically, whether householders have stopped doing penance because they are busy feeding renunciants; Guru Nanak answers that honest work and sharing (kirat karni, vand chhakna) is itself the true path.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Vaar Saarang (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor old couple Baucis and Philemon feed two disguised gods from their meagre store and are rewarded by being made priests of a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hospitality to the sacred visitor is rewarded with sacred status.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Weak parallel: support of the holy earns merit, but there is no ascetic class or critique.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s ideal city the guardians own no property and receive their sustenance from the producing citizens as a wage for their guardianship.
philosophy.explanation: Plato builds a division of labour in which a disciplined, propertyless elite is maintained by others.
philosophy.tie_back: Resembles the lay–ascetic economy Valluvar describes, though Plato’s guardians are rulers, not penitents.

real_life_example.event_title: Duke William of Aquitaine founds the Abbey of Cluny
real_life_example.event: William I, Duke of Aquitaine, signed a charter founding a Benedictine monastery at Cluny and endowed it with land. The charter says he gave part of his worldly goods for the benefit of his soul, and it requires the monks to pray for him, his family and others while living under the Rule of Saint Benedict. Cluny was placed under the protection of the pope, free from the duke's own control.
real_life_example.explanation: Cluny became one of the most influential monasteries in medieval Europe, and its charter shows the common arrangement in which lay patrons supported monks and counted on their prayers for their own salvation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural wryly asks whether people neglect their own penance because they are busy supplying the renunciants, and Cluny's founder openly paid monks to do the praying for his soul.

tamil:
ஒன்னார்த் தெறலும் உவந்தாரை ஆக்கலும்
எண்ணின் தவத்தான் வரும்.
transliteration:
Onnaar theralum uvandhaarai aakkalum
Ennin thavaththaan varum.
meaning: If a person who practices strict self-control wishes it, that power alone can defeat enemies and lift up friends.
elementary: In old stories, people who did very long and sincere penance got special powers — like a superhero who trained for years. Valluvar says such a person could, just by wishing it, stop bad people and help good friends.
university: Here Valluvar adopts the widespread Indian belief that tapas generates real, even cosmic, power — the power to curse (சாபம்) and to bless (அருள்), as Parimelazhagar glosses ஆற்றல் in the neighbouring verse. The conditional எண்ணின் (‘if he wills’) is crucial: after 261 defined the ascetic as one who harms no one, the implication is that such power exists but is normally left unused. The verse thus holds a tension typical of Indian ascetic literature, where rishis like Vishvamitra or Durvasa possess destructive capacity that their own ethic ought to restrain.
