Modern commentators such as Kalaignar demythologize it as the practical power of resolve and self-control.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Vishvamitra, having amassed great tapas, uses its power to raise his devotee King Trishanku bodily toward heaven and, when the gods cast him down, creates a new constellation of heavens for him.
hinduism.explanation: The Ramayana’s famous episode shows tapas as a force that can uplift a friend in defiance even of the gods.
hinduism.tie_back: A textbook illustration of ‘uplifting those who love him’ through tapas; Vishvamitra elsewhere also curses his foes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Elijah answered and said to the captain of fifty, If I be a man of God, then let fire come down from heaven, and consume thee and thy fifty. And there came down fire from heaven, and consumed him and his fifty.”
christianity.explanation: The ascetic prophet Elijah calls down fire on the soldiers sent to seize him.
christianity.tie_back: A holy man’s spiritual standing directly destroys his enemies, as the Kural says tapas can.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah said, ‘I will declare war against him who shows hostility to a pious worshipper of Mine… and if he asks Me, I will give him, and if he asks My protection (Refuge), I will protect him.’”
islam.explanation: One who draws near through extra devotions gains God’s protection against enemies and has requests granted.
islam.tie_back: Devotional discipline yields both defeat of foes and fulfilment of wishes, though the agent is God, not the ascetic’s own power.

judaism.quote_or_event: After twelve years hiding in a cave in study and deprivation, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his son emerged with such spiritual intensity that whatever they gazed upon was burned, until a heavenly voice sent them back.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud portrays ascetic withdrawal as generating a dangerous, destructive spiritual force.
judaism.tie_back: Close to the Kural’s claim that tapas can destroy; the story also criticizes its unrestrained use.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists supernormal powers (iddhi) — multiplying the body, passing through walls, walking on water — as fruits of the concentrated mind of the disciplined monk, while elsewhere forbidding their display.
buddhism.explanation: Early Buddhism accepts that meditative discipline yields extraordinary powers but treats them as secondary and potentially dangerous.
buddhism.tie_back: Agrees that discipline yields power; differs in never endorsing its use to destroy enemies.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He is the man of great fame and might, of awful piety and power; do not injure him who cannot be injured, lest he consume you all by the fire (of his virtue).”
jainism.explanation: When Brahmin youths beat the outcaste-born monk Harikesa, Bhadra warns them of his ascetic power and Yakshas strike them down, yet Harikesa himself declares, 'There is not the least hatred in me' (12.32).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural credits tapas with power to crush foes and raise up friends; the Harikesa story shows that power vividly, though in Jain telling the monk himself wills no harm.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He Himself is the Supreme Master of all; wealth and miraculous spiritual powers, and all other external tastes and pleasures, are all like beads on a string.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak tells the yogis that God alone is Master, and that the occult powers (siddhis) they seek through austerity are only side pleasures.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural credits the ascetic with power to destroy enemies and raise friends; Guru Nanak places all such power in God and treats yogic powers as distractions.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib, Pauri 29, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Chryses, priest of Apollo, is insulted by Agamemnon; he prays to Apollo, who sends a plague of arrows upon the Greek army.
greek_mythology.explanation: A holy man’s standing with a god becomes a weapon against those who wrong him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Resembles the ‘destruction of enemies’ power of the Kural’s ascetic, but grounded in priestly service, not austerity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plotinus argues that the sage who has turned inward to contemplation cannot be touched by magic spells and that only the irrational part of a person is subject to such forces.
philosophy.explanation: Neoplatonism grants the contemplative a kind of invulnerability but not active power over others.
philosophy.tie_back: A distant parallel: the disciplined soul gains power, but only defensive, never used to harm or promote others.

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi's fast brings calm to Calcutta
real_life_example.event: When communal rioting broke out again in Calcutta soon after Independence, Gandhi began a fast on the evening of 1 September 1947, saying he would continue until the violence stopped. Within days the rioting cooled, and leaders of Hindu, Muslim, Sikh and other groups came to him pledging to prevent further violence. He broke the fast on the evening of 4 September.
real_life_example.explanation: A single old man's voluntary self-denial achieved a peace that force had not, which is why the episode is often cited as an example of the practical power of fasting and self-discipline.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the power of penance, if the ascetic wills it, can subdue what opposes him and raise up those he loves, and Gandhi's fast subdued the riots and protected the people he cared for.

tamil:
வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங் கெய்தலால் செய்தவம்
ஈண்டு முயலப் படும்.
transliteration:
Vendiya vendiyaangu eydhalaal seydhavam
Eendu muyalap padum.
meaning: Strict self-control lets a person get whatever they want, just as they want it. So it should be worked at with effort, here and now.
elementary: If you practise the piano every day, one day you can play any song you want, just the way you want. Valluvar says tapas is like that for your whole life — so start practising now, not later.
university: The verse gives the motivational logic of tapas: it is effective, delivering desired ends ‘as desired’ (வேண்டியாங்கு). ஈண்டு (‘here’) is read by Parimelazhagar as ‘in this birth’, urging urgency, while Mu. Varadarasan reads it as ‘even in the householder’s state’, democratizing tapas beyond the forest. The claim sits in tension with the Gita’s ideal of desireless action and with Valluvar’s own later chapter on the destruction of desire (அவா அறுத்தல்); commentators resolve this by noting that for the truly austere the highest ‘desire’ is liberation itself. The couplet thus captures tapas at its most instrumental while quietly pointing beyond instrumentality.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The child Dhruva, rejected by his father, performs severe tapas in the forest of Madhuvana; Vishnu appears and grants him a kingdom and ultimately the eternal pole-star position.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana’s Dhruva story is the paradigm of tapas yielding exactly what the practitioner sought, and more.
hinduism.tie_back: Embodies ‘obtaining what one desires, as one desires’ through tapas.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus assures that sincere, hidden fasting will be rewarded by God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts affirm that real austerity produces real results; Jesus stresses secrecy.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah said, ‘All the deeds of Adam’s sons (people) are for them, except fasting which is for Me, and I will give the reward for it.’”
islam.explanation: Fasting is singled out as the act whose reward God personally bestows, beyond ordinary measure.
islam.tie_back: Affirms the unique efficacy of ascetic discipline that motivates the Kural’s call to pursue it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then said he unto me, Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words.”
judaism.explanation: After three weeks of fasting and mourning, Daniel is told his self-affliction secured an answer from heaven.
judaism.tie_back: Self-chastening directly obtains what was sought — the logic of this Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In his first sermon the Buddha rejects both indulgence in sense pleasures and devotion to self-mortification as extremes, teaching the Middle Way after his own years of extreme austerity failed to bring awakening.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism explicitly denies that harsh bodily austerity reliably delivers the highest goal.
buddhism.tie_back: An instructive contrast: Buddhism shares the goal-orientation but disputes that severe tapas is the means.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a large tank, when its supply of water has been stopped, gradually dries up by the consumption of the water and by evaporation, so the Karman of a monk, which he acquired in millions of births, is annihilated by austerities, if there is no influx of bad Karman.”
jainism.explanation: Jain doctrine holds that tapas, once new karmic inflow is stopped, burns away accumulated karma (nirjarā), and so is the decisive means to liberation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar urges penance now because it obtains what one desires; the Jain text also presents tapas as supremely effective, but its goal is the shedding of karma rather than the fulfilment of wishes.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 30.5-6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the remembrance of God, hopes are fulfilled.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan lists the fruits of simran, meditative remembrance of God, and among them says that a person's hopes are fulfilled.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar urges penance now because it gives whatever one desires; Guru Arjan makes the same promise for remembering God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 263, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows; long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod teaches that excellence and prosperity are gained only through hard toil, which becomes easy once the summit is reached.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s conviction that strenuous discipline is the reliable road to what one seeks.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 289-291 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For of all things good and fair, the gods give nothing to man without toil and effort.”
philosophy.explanation: In Prodicus’ fable of Heracles at the crossroads, Virtue tells the young hero that every good thing is earned by labour.
philosophy.tie_back: Same principle as the Kural: disciplined effort is the price and the guarantee of every desired good.

real_life_example.event_title: Charles Goodyear discovers vulcanization after years of hardship
real_life_example.event: Charles Goodyear spent years experimenting to make rubber stable in heat and cold, during which his family lived in poverty and he was jailed for debt. In 1839 he found that rubber mixed with sulfur and heated became strong and stable, the process later called vulcanization, and he patented it in 1844. Others made fortunes from the process, and Goodyear himself died in debt.
real_life_example.explanation: Goodyear's discovery transformed industry, and his story is often told as an example of single-minded persistence through hardship.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural urges people to take up disciplined effort now because it delivers what one seeks, and Goodyear's years of privation did deliver the exact result he had been pursuing.

tamil:
தவஞ்செய்வார் தங்கருமஞ் செய்வார்மற் றல்லார்
அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு.
transliteration:
Thavanjeyvaar thangarumanj seyvaar matru allaar
Avanjeyvaar aasaiyut pattu.
meaning: People who practice strict self-control are doing their own true work. Everyone else is caught in the trap of wanting things and only works toward their own harm.
elementary: Think of a fly stuck in a spider’s web — the more it wriggles, the more stuck it gets. Valluvar says people who chase every want are like that fly, while people who practise self-control are doing the one job that really helps them.
university: The couplet rests on a sonic antithesis — தவம் (tavam, penance) against அவம் (avam, futility or self-harm) — so that tapas and its absence differ by a single consonant. தம் கருமம் (‘their own work’) implies that spiritual self-cultivation is a person’s genuine duty, while the ‘busy’ worldly life is in fact a failure to act for oneself. Parimelazhagar glosses அவம் as bringing harm upon oneself, since desire-driven action produces karmic bondage. The verse inverts ordinary valuations: the ascetic who seems idle is the only one truly working, and the striving householder, if driven by desire, is idle in the deepest sense.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names desire (kāma) as the root enemy that devours those it entangles.
hinduism.tie_back: Same diagnosis: desire (ஆசை) turns human effort into self-destruction.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that worldly gain pursued at the soul’s expense is ultimate loss.
christianity.tie_back: Mirrors தவம்/அவம்: desire-driven success is really self-ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: Restraining the self from its desires (the basis of Sufi riyāḍa, self-discipline) is the path to salvation.
islam.tie_back: The self-restrained do their true work; the desire-led lose — the Kural’s dichotomy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that appetites and ambitions drive a person to ruin.
judaism.tie_back: Same verdict as the Kural on those ‘caught in desire’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are lust-infatuated fall back into the swirling current (of samsara) like a spider on its self-spun web. This, too, the wise cut off. Without any longing, they abandon all suffering and renounce the world.”
buddhism.explanation: Desire is a self-spun trap; the wise cut it and renounce.
buddhism.tie_back: The same two paths: renunciation as true work, desire as self-made entanglement (ஆசையுட் பட்டு).

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasures are the thorn that rankles, pleasures are poison, pleasures are like a venomous snake; he who is desirous of pleasures will not get them, and will come to a bad end at last.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami, renouncing his throne, warns Indra that the pursuit of pleasure is self-destructive and ends in ruin.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar contrasts ascetics doing their true work with those who, caught in the net of desire, labour for their own ruin; Nami's verse gives the second half of that contrast in the strongest terms.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.53 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe. Nothing else will work.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan tells the listener that human birth is the one opportunity to meet God, and that every other pursuit is useless for that purpose.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who practise penance alone do their real work while everyone else labours for their own ruin; Guru Arjan likewise calls seeking God the one work that counts and the rest useless.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa (So Purakh section; also at Ang 378), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon, cursed with insatiable hunger for cutting down Demeter’s sacred grove, devours all his wealth, sells his own daughter, and finally eats his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s grim tale shows appetite consuming its owner.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A vivid image of desire-driven activity that is ultimately self-destruction (அவம்).

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates asks his fellow Athenians whether they are not ashamed to care so much about wealth, reputation and honour while giving no thought to wisdom, truth and the improvement of their souls.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates redefines a person’s real business as care of the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches தம் கருமம் — the self-cultivator alone does his proper work; the acquisitive neglect it.

real_life_example.event_title: Pope Celestine V resigns the papacy for the life of a hermit
real_life_example.place: Italy (Papal States and Kingdom of Naples)
real_life_example.event: Pietro da Morrone, an elderly hermit from the Abruzzi mountains, was elected pope in July 1294 and took the name Celestine V. After about five months he issued a decree that a pope could abdicate and then resigned, because he lacked administrative skill and believed the office endangered his soul. He hoped to return to his hermitage but was held under supervision by his successor, Boniface VIII, until his death.
real_life_example.explanation: Celestine was the first pope to resign of his own free will, and he chose the life of prayer over the highest office in the Western church.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who practise penance are doing their own true work while others labour for their own ruin, and Celestine judged the busy papacy a danger and the hermit's life his real task.

tamil:
சுடச்சுடரும் பொன்போல் ஒளிவிடும் துன்பஞ்
சுடச்சுட நோற்கிற் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Sudachchudarum ponpol olividum thunbanj
Sudachchuda notkirpavarkku.
meaning: Gold shines brighter the more it is heated in fire. In the same way, people who practice self-control shine brighter the more suffering burns them.
elementary: When gold is put in a very hot fire, the dirt burns away and it becomes shinier. Valluvar says hard times do the same for a patient, disciplined person: every difficulty makes them shine brighter.
university: Among the most celebrated images in the Kural, the verse exploits the reduplicated சுடச்சுட (‘as it burns and burns’) twice — once for the goldsmith’s crucible and once for suffering — binding metaphor and meaning through sound. The figure also restores the etymological heart of tapas, from the Sanskrit root tap, ‘to heat, burn’, a notion also present in the Tamil நோன்பு/நோற்றல் of endurance. Commentators differ on what ‘shines’: Varadarasan and Pappaiah say true knowledge (மெய்யுணர்வு, ஞானம்), Kalaignar says reputation. The refining-fire metaphor is one of the most widely shared images in world religious literature, making this verse unusually rich in parallels.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Rig Veda’s creation hymns describe Order (ṛta) and Truth (satya), and even the first stirring of being, as born from kindled tapas — heat — making ascetic ‘heat’ a cosmogonic force.
hinduism.explanation: In Vedic thought tapas is literally a creative, purifying heat.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s gold-in-fire image recovers this primal sense of tapas as burning that produces brilliance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ.”
christianity.explanation: Peter likens believers’ trials to the fire that tests gold, producing glory.
christianity.tie_back: Almost the same image: suffering as fire, the sufferer as gold that shines.

islam.quote_or_event: “No fatigue, nor disease, nor sorrow, nor sadness, nor hurt, nor distress befalls a Muslim, even if it were the prick he receives from a thorn, but that Allah expiates some of his sins for that.”
islam.explanation: Every suffering, however small, purifies the believer of sin.
islam.tie_back: Suffering as purification — the refining function of the Kural’s fire.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights; he did neither eat bread, nor drink water… Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone while he talked with him.”
judaism.explanation: After forty days of total fasting on Sinai, Moses descends with a face literally radiant.
judaism.tie_back: Austerity endured leads to shining — a striking literal counterpart to ‘shines like gold’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One by one, little by little, moment by moment, a wise man should remove his own impurities, as a smith removes his dross from silver.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the metalworker’s refining as the model of gradual self-purification.
buddhism.tie_back: Same smithing metaphor for spiritual refinement.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is exempt from love, hatred, and fear, (and who shines forth) like burnished gold, purified in fire, him we call a Brâhmana.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha describes the true holy man as one whose passions have been burnt away, so that he shines like gold refined in fire.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's image of gold that shines brighter the more it is heated is matched here by the same goldsmith's image for the ascetic purified of passion.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.21 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Let self-control be the furnace, and patience the goldsmith. … With the Fear of God as the bellows, fan the flames of tapa, the body's inner heat.”
sikhism.explanation: The closing pauri of Japji describes the spiritual life as a goldsmith's workshop, where self-control is the furnace and tapa the fire in which the true Word is forged.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar compares the ascetic to gold that shines brighter the more it burns; Guru Nanak also uses the goldsmith's fire and names tapa as the heat that does the work.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib, Pauri 38, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Demeter, nursing the infant Demophon, secretly places him in the fire each night to burn away his mortality and make him immortal, until his frightened mother interrupts her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Fire here refines a mortal into something divine and deathless.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic counterpart to fire as the agent of transformation into radiance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Ignis aurum probat, miseria fortes viros.” (Fire tests gold, misfortune brave men.)
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that God trains good people through hardship, as fire proves gold.
philosophy.tie_back: Nearly identical image and moral: adversity reveals and refines the worthy.

real_life_example.event_title: Beethoven writes the Heiligenstadt Testament
real_life_example.event: Convinced that his deafness was permanent and worsening, Ludwig van Beethoven wrote a long letter to his brothers at Heiligenstadt describing his despair and his isolation from others. He wrote that only his art held him back, and that he could not leave the world before producing all he felt called to create. The letter was never sent and was found among his papers after his death, and in the following years he composed works such as the Eroica Symphony.
real_life_example.explanation: The document marks the turning point at which Beethoven resolved to keep working through his affliction, and much of his greatest music came after it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the ascetic to gold that shines brighter the more it is burned, and Beethoven's suffering was followed by the most brilliant period of his work.

tamil:
தன்னுயிர் தான்அறப் பெற்றானை ஏனைய
மன்னுயி ரெல்லாந் தொழும்.
transliteration:
Thannuyir thaan arap petraanai enaiya
Mannuyir ellaam thozhum.
meaning: A person who has fully let go of thinking about “me” and “my life” is honored by every other living being in the world.
elementary: Most of us think ‘me first’. A person who, after lots of practice, stops thinking ‘me, me, me’ becomes so good and gentle that everyone — people and even animals — looks up to them.
university: The first line is famously compressed: தன்னுயிர் தான் அறப் பெற்றான் can be read as ‘one who has become rid of [attachment to] his own life and of the ego “I”’ (Parimelazhagar, Varadarasan) or as ‘one who has fully gained possession of his own self’ (Pope’s ‘utter self-control’). Both readings converge on self-mastery culminating in egolessness. The consequence — ‘all other enduring lives worship him’ — echoes the Indian belief, also found in Jain and yogic texts, that the ahiṃsā-perfected sage commands the reverence even of animals. Placed after 267, the verse presents egolessness as the gold that emerges from the refining fire.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Patañjali teaches that when a yogi is firmly established in non-violence, hostility is abandoned by all beings in his presence.
hinduism.explanation: The perfected ascetic radiates a peace that transforms how all creatures relate to him.
hinduism.tie_back: Close to ‘all living beings worship him’ — the universal response to the perfected self.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow.”
christianity.explanation: Christ’s total self-emptying (kenosis) is followed by universal homage.
christianity.tie_back: Same arc: complete surrender of self leads to worship by all beings.

islam.quote_or_event: “Charity does not decrease wealth, no one forgives another except that Allah increases his honor, and no one humbles himself for the sake of Allah except that Allah raises his status.”
islam.explanation: Self-effacement before God leads to exaltation.
islam.tie_back: Egolessness brings honour, as in the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.”
judaism.explanation: Self-mastery is ranked above military conquest.
judaism.tie_back: Affirms the supreme worth of the self-conquered person that the Kural celebrates.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even the gods hold dear the wise one, whose senses are subdued like horses well trained by a charioteer, whose pride is destroyed and who is free from the cankers.”
buddhism.explanation: The arahant whose pride is gone is cherished even by the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: Near-exact match: pride (ego) destroyed → revered by all beings, even divine ones.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
jainism.explanation: Nami, having given up his kingdom, is free of every sense of 'mine'; at the end of the dialogue Indra himself reveals his true form and pays reverence to him again and again (9.59).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says one free of 'I' and 'mine' is worshipped by all beings; Nami shows that freedom from possession, and the king of the gods bows before him.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Among all persons, the supreme person is the one who gives up his egotistical pride in the Company of the Holy.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan says the greatest of all people is the one whose ego (haumai) has been erased in holy company.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the one who has lost the sense of 'I' and 'mine' is worshipped by all; Guru Arjan likewise ranks the ego-free person above everyone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 266, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, after completing his grievous labours, is received among the immortals on Olympus, given Hebe as wife, and honoured as a god.
greek_mythology.explanation: Endured toil ends in apotheosis and worship.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Endurance leading to universal honour; but Heracles’ path is heroic, not ego-renouncing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But verily, if I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes.”
philosophy.explanation: After the self-denying Cynic asks the world-conqueror merely to stand out of his sun, Alexander confesses his admiration.
philosophy.tie_back: The man who wants nothing commands the reverence even of the most powerful — the Kural’s point in miniature.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 14 (trans. B. Perrin)

real_life_example.event_title: A million mourners honour Brother André, the humble doorkeeper
real_life_example.event: Alfred Bessette, known as Brother André, was a lay brother of the Congregation of Holy Cross who served for decades as doorkeeper of the Collège Notre-Dame in Montreal, welcoming the sick and troubled who came to him. He was the driving force behind the building of Saint Joseph's Oratory on Mount Royal. When he died on 6 January 1937, more than a million people came to pay their respects, and he was canonized in 2010.
real_life_example.explanation: A man with no rank, wealth or education beyond the basics drew one of the largest outpourings of public reverence in Canadian history.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the one who has let go of the sense of I and mine is worshipped by all, and a self-effacing porter was honoured by multitudes.

tamil:
கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும் நோற்றலின்
ஆற்றல் தலைப்பட் டவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Kootram kudhiththalum kaikoodum notralin
Aatral thalaippattavarkku.
meaning: People who have gained the power that comes from strict self-control can even escape death itself.
elementary: Everyone is scared of death, like a giant monster nobody can beat. Valluvar says a person who has become really strong through tapas can even jump right over that monster.
university: கூற்றம் (Kūṟṟam), ‘the one who separates [soul from body]’, is the Tamil personification of Death, identified with Yama; குதித்தல் means to leap over or escape. The inclusive உம் (‘even’) signals this as the ultimate limit case of tapas-power, following the curse-and-blessing powers of 264. The medieval commentator Manakkudavar explicitly glosses the verse with the legend of Markandeya, the boy-devotee who escaped Yama’s noose, while Parimelazhagar identifies ஆற்றல் as the power of curse and grace. Philosophically, the verse can also be read as conquest of the fear of death, or as liberation from the cycle of births — interpretations that let the verse speak beyond its mythological frame.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Markandeya, destined to die at sixteen, clings to the Shiva linga in devotion and austerity; when Yama casts his noose, Shiva emerges, kicks Yama away, and grants the boy eternal youth.
hinduism.explanation: Manakkudavar’s own commentary on this Kural cites Markandeya’s escape from death.
hinduism.tie_back: The traditional illustration of ‘leaping beyond Kūṟṟam’ through tapas.
hinduism.source: Markandeya legend (Shaiva Puranas; Tirukkadavur tradition), cited by Manakkudavar on Kural 269

christianity.quote_or_event: “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”
christianity.explanation: Paul proclaims death conquered for the faithful through resurrection.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the claim that death can be overcome; in Christianity through grace rather than accumulated austerity.

islam.quote_or_event: “And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision.”
islam.explanation: Those who give themselves wholly for God are not truly subject to death.
islam.tie_back: Supreme self-sacrifice transcends death, a partial echo of the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud relates that the Angel of Death could not take King David because his mouth never ceased from Torah study; only by distracting him for a moment could it approach.
judaism.explanation: Unbroken spiritual discipline held death itself at bay.
judaism.tie_back: Close to the Kural’s image of disciplined power holding off Death.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless. Heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful die not. The heedless are as if dead already.”
buddhism.explanation: Sustained vigilance leads to the Deathless (amata), Nibbana.
buddhism.tie_back: Discipline conquers death — understood as release from the round of rebirth.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a sage truly performs these two kinds of austerities, he will soon be thoroughly released from the Circle of Births.”
jainism.explanation: After listing the six external and six internal austerities, the lecture promises that their true practice frees the soul entirely from repeated birth and death.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the power of tapas lets one leap even beyond Death; for Jainism, austerity ends the cycle of birth and death altogether, so death no longer has a hold.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 30.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Remembering God, death is eliminated.”
sikhism.explanation: In the opening section of the Sukhmani Guru Arjan says that remembering God drives death away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those with the power of penance can leap even beyond Death; Guru Arjan says the same for one who remembers God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 1, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles wrestles Thanatos (Death) at the tomb of Alcestis and forces him to give her back to life.
greek_mythology.explanation: The much-enduring hero physically overpowers Death.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic ‘leap over Death’ by one whose strength was forged through labours.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Other people are likely not to be aware that those who pursue philosophy aright study nothing but dying and being dead.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says the philosopher’s discipline of detaching soul from body is a rehearsal for death, leaving him unafraid of it.
philosophy.tie_back: The disciplined life overcomes death by mastering it in advance.

real_life_example.event_title: Shackleton brings every man of the Endurance expedition home alive
real_life_example.place: Weddell Sea, Elephant Island and South Georgia, Southern Ocean
real_life_example.event: After the ship Endurance was crushed by Antarctic pack ice, Ernest Shackleton's 28 men camped on the ice and reached Elephant Island in lifeboats. Shackleton and five companions sailed the small boat James Caird about 800 miles to South Georgia, and three of them crossed the island's mountains on foot to reach the Stromness whaling station on 20 May 1916. On 30 August 1916 the Chilean tug Yelcho rescued the 22 men left on Elephant Island, and not one member of the ship's crew died.
real_life_example.explanation: The expedition became a classic example of endurance and self-discipline defeating seemingly certain death.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who gain the strength of disciplined endurance can leap even beyond Death, and Shackleton's men survived an ordeal that should have killed them.

tamil:
இலர்பல ராகிய காரணம் நோற்பார்
சிலர்பலர் நோலா தவர்.
transliteration:
Ilar palar aagiya kaaranam norpaar
Silar palar nolaadhavar.
meaning: Many people in the world have nothing because only a few practice strict self-control, while most do not.
elementary: In a class, only a few kids practise every day, and most don’t. That is why only a few become really good. Valluvar says the same about the whole world: most people are ‘poor’ inside because only a few do the hard work of tapas.
university: The closing couplet uses a neat chiastic arithmetic — இலர் பலர் (the have-nots are many) because நோற்பார் சிலர், பலர் நோலாதவர் (the practisers are few, the non-practisers many). இலர் is ambiguous: Solomon Pappaiah reads material poverty, Varadarasan and Kalaignar read lack of strength, and Puliyur Kesikan reads lack of true knowledge. The choice matters: a literal economic reading makes tapas a cause of prosperity, while the spiritual reading makes it the cause of inner wealth. Either way the verse ends the chapter with a sober sociology of virtue — excellence is rare because discipline is rare — and turns the whole chapter into an exhortation to join the few.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Out of many thousands among men, one may endeavor for perfection, and of those who have achieved perfection, hardly one knows Me in truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna observes how rare the serious spiritual aspirant is.
hinduism.tie_back: The same ‘few strive, many don’t’ observation that grounds the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts the many on the easy road with the few on the hard road to life.
christianity.tie_back: Same arithmetic of many and few, with the hard path as the source of true wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the forerunners, the forerunners - … A [large] company of the former peoples And a few of the later peoples.”
islam.explanation: The foremost in devotion, brought nearest to God, are few among later generations.
islam.tie_back: The spiritually foremost are few, as the Kural’s practisers are few.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai remarks that he has seen the ‘people of ascent’ — those of the highest spiritual rank — and they are few.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud acknowledges that those who reach the highest spiritual level are a small minority.
judaism.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s ‘the practisers are few’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Few among men are those who cross to the farther shore. The rest, the bulk of men, only run up and down the hither bank.”
buddhism.explanation: Only a few achieve liberation; the majority stay in the round of existence.
buddhism.tie_back: Near-identical picture of the few who strive and the many who do not.

jainism.quote_or_event: “And though they have heard the Law and believe in it, it is difficult for them to fulfill it strenuously; many who approve of the religion, do not adopt it.”
jainism.explanation: The 'four requisites' lecture says that human birth, hearing the Law, faith and strenuous practice are each rare, so very few actually carry the discipline through.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the many are destitute because those who practise penance are few; the Jain text likewise laments that many approve the path but few take it up.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 3.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Out of millions, hardly anyone is a servant of the Lord. All the others are mere traders.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Gujri Guru Arjan observes that among millions there is scarcely one true devotee, while the rest practise religion as a bargain for their own gain.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar explains the world's want by noting that those who practise are few and those who do not are many; Guru Arjan makes the same observation about true devotees and the many who only trade.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 495, Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sparta’s agoge subjected boys to hunger, cold, one cloak a year and harsh discipline; the few full citizens so trained dominated a far larger population of helots.
greek_mythology.explanation: Rigorous austerity produced a small elite of exceptional capability.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s claim that the disciplined few hold what the undisciplined many lack; but the Spartan aim was military, not spiritual.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For as they say in the mysteries, ‘the thyrsus-bearers are many, but the mystics few’; and these mystics are, I believe, those who have been true philosophers.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates distinguishes the many who carry the outward emblems from the few who are genuinely initiated through philosophical purification.
philosophy.tie_back: The many/few contrast between those who merely participate and those who truly undergo the discipline.

real_life_example.event_title: Ninomiya Sontoku revives impoverished villages through diligence and thrift
real_life_example.event: Ninomiya Sontoku, a farmer who had rebuilt his own family's ruined farm, was engaged to restore struggling villages and estates. He taught sincerity, diligence, living within one's means and giving back, and he preferred loans repaid from the villagers' own harvests to outright grants. The districts he developed suffered very little in the great famine of 1836, and his teachings grew into the Hotoku movement.
real_life_example.explanation: Sontoku showed that the poverty of many villages could be reversed when people adopted steady self-discipline, and he became a national model of diligence.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says so many are destitute because few practise disciplined effort, and Sontoku's work turned poor villages around by teaching exactly that discipline.

tamil:
வஞ்ச மனத்தான் படிற்றொழுக்கம் பூதங்கள்
ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்.
transliteration:
Vanja manaththaan padittrozhukkam boodhangal
Aindhum agaththe nagum.
meaning: When someone with a deceitful mind pretends to live a holy life, the five elements (earth, water, fire, air and sky) that make up their own body laugh at them from inside.
elementary: Imagine someone pretending to be very good while secretly cheating. People outside might be fooled, but the earth, water, fire, air and sky that his body is made of can see everything — and they giggle at the silly act. You can’t hide a lie from the stuff you are made of.
university: The chapter opens with a striking image: the five great elements (pancha bhutas — earth, water, fire, air, ether) that compose the hypocrite’s body are themselves the witnesses who see through his sham piety and laugh inwardly. The word படிற்றொழுக்கம் (padittrozhukkam) denotes counterfeit or disguised conduct, and அகத்தே (agaththe) plays on “inside” — both inside the body and inside themselves. The point is that concealment is metaphysically impossible: the deceiver carries his witnesses with him. Parimelazhagar’s tradition reads the elements’ laughter as mockery of a man who thinks he can fool the world while his own substance knows the truth — a theme paralleled by Manu’s list of cosmic witnesses and the Qur’anic image of skins testifying.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The wicked, indeed, say in their hearts, ‘Nobody sees us;’ but the gods distinctly see them and the male within their own breasts. The sky, the earth, the waters, (the male in) the heart, the moon, the sun, the fire, Yama and the wind, the night, the two twilights, and justice know the conduct of all corporeal beings.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells witnesses that no one lies unseen: the sky, earth, waters, fire, wind and the inner self are all watching everything a person does.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the same list as the Kural’s five elements: the physical world itself is the witness that knows the hypocrite’s real conduct.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns his disciples against hypocrisy and says that whatever is hidden will eventually come out into the open.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats religious pretence as ultimately transparent: what the hypocrite hides is already known.

islam.quote_or_event: “Until, when they reach it, their hearing and their eyes and their skins will testify against them of what they used to do.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement, the Qur’an says a person’s own body parts — ears, eyes, skin — will speak up and report what that person did.
islam.tie_back: The same idea as the Kural: the hypocrite’s own body is the witness against him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him… Whose hatred is covered by deceit, his wickedness shall be shewed before the whole congregation.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs describes a person who hides malice behind pleasant words and says his wickedness will eventually be exposed publicly.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s conviction that a deceitful inner life cannot stay covered; exposure and shame follow.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever being depraved, devoid of self-control and truthfulness, should don the monk’s yellow robe, he surely is not worthy of the robe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a person who is corrupt and untruthful gains nothing by wearing a monk’s robe — he simply does not deserve it.
buddhism.tie_back: Names the exact sin of the chapter — holy dress over a deceitful mind — though without the image of the elements mocking him.

jainism.quote_or_event: “My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
jainism.explanation: The monk tells King Srenika that no outside agent protects or condemns a person; the self itself is the author and witness of its own good and evil.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar pictures the hypocrite's own bodily elements laughing at him from within; the Jain verse likewise places the true judge of conduct inside the self rather than in outward appearances.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Outwardly, they wear religious robes, but within is the filth of Maya. They cannot conceal this, no matter how hard they try.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan describes people who wear holy dress over a mind full of worldly filth, and says the truth cannot be hidden however much they try.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar pictures the hypocrite's own five elements laughing at his sham holiness; Guru Arjan likewise says the inner corruption under the robe cannot be concealed.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 267, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the song of Demodocus, Aphrodite and Ares carry on a secret affair in Hephaestus’ house; Helios the Sun, who sees everything, reports it, Hephaestus traps them in an invisible net, and the assembled gods burst into laughter at the exposed pair.
greek_mythology.explanation: A hidden wrongdoing is seen by a cosmic power (the Sun), exposed, and met with the gods’ mocking laughter.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s picture of a natural, all-seeing element exposing concealed misconduct and laughing at it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Hypocrisy is the homage vice pays to virtue.”
philosophy.explanation: La Rochefoucauld observes that hypocrites pretend to be good precisely because goodness is admired; their disguise is a backhanded compliment to virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Diagnoses the same phenomenon the Kural mocks — vice dressed up as virtue — with a similarly ironic, laughing tone.

real_life_example.event_title: Margaret Fox confesses that the spirit rappings were a hoax
real_life_example.place: Academy of Music, New York City, United States
real_life_example.event: In 1848 the young sisters Margaret and Kate Fox of Hydesville, New York, began producing rapping sounds that they presented as messages from spirits, and their seances helped launch the Spiritualist movement. In October 1888 Margaret told the New York World, and then a public audience at the New York Academy of Music, that the raps had been a fraud produced chiefly by movements of the joints of their toes. She retracted the confession the following year.
real_life_example.explanation: Four decades of claimed contact with the spirit world turned out to have come from the sisters' own bodies.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the five elements of the hypocrite's own body laugh at his false show of holiness, and in the Fox case the deceivers' own bodies were the secret source of the sham.

tamil:
வானுயர் தோற்றம் எவன்செய்யும் தன்னெஞ்சம்
தான்அறி குற்றப் படின்.
transliteration:
Vaanuyar thotram evanseyyum thannenjam
Thaanari kutrap padin.
meaning: What good is looking as holy as the sky is high, if your own heart knows the wrong you have done?
elementary: Suppose you wear a shiny superhero costume, but inside you know you just took your friend’s toy without asking. The costume doesn’t make you a hero. What you know about yourself matters more than how you look.
university: வானுயர் தோற்றம் (“a sky-high appearance”) refers to the imposing garb and bearing of the ascetic, and Valluvar poses a rhetorical question: of what use is it? The criterion he sets is not public exposure but self-knowledge — தன்னெஞ்சம் தான் அறி குற்றம், the fault the heart itself is aware of. Valluvar thus locates moral judgement in conscience rather than reputation, a remarkably interior standard for an ancient ethical text. The kural parallels the Gita’s notion of mithyācāra (the pretender whose mind dwells on what his outward restraint pretends to renounce), and Stoic ideas of conscience as the one witness who cannot be deceived.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who restrains the senses and organs of action, but whose mind dwells on sense objects, certainly deludes himself and is called a pretender.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that someone who outwardly acts restrained but inwardly keeps craving is a mithyācāra — a fake.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s case: impressive outer discipline is worthless when the heart knowingly clings to what it pretends to have given up.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things.”
christianity.explanation: John says that when our own heart accuses us, God — who knows even more than our heart — sees the whole truth.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the decisive verdict comes from the heart’s own knowledge of its guilt, not from outward appearance.

islam.quote_or_event: “Rather, man, against himself, will be a witness, Even if he presents his excuses.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says each person is a witness against himself and knows the truth about his own deeds, whatever excuses he offers.
islam.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘fault the heart itself knows’: no outward show can override inner self-knowledge.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me…”
judaism.explanation: God complains through Isaiah that the people honour him outwardly with words while their hearts are elsewhere.
judaism.tie_back: Same gap the Kural exposes — splendid outward devotion, empty or guilty heart — and the same verdict that the outward form is worthless.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The evil-doer suffers here and hereafter; he suffers in both the worlds. The thought, ‘Evil have I done,’ torments him…”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the wrongdoer is tormented by his own awareness of what he has done.
buddhism.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s focus on the self-known fault as what really counts, whatever the outward show.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One who for a long time wears a shaven crown and mortifies himself, but who is careless with regard to the vows, and neglects penance and self-control, will not be a winner in the battle (of life).”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's tradition warns that a monk may keep the outward marks of asceticism for years while inwardly neglecting the vows that make it real.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks what use a sky-high appearance of holiness is when the heart knows its own faults; this verse makes the same point about a shaven head worn over a careless inner life.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.41 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Mentally, we are impure and black, but outwardly, we appear white.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Vaar Sri Raag Guru Nanak speaks in the first person for all of us, admitting that our minds are impure and black while we look white and clean outside.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use a sky-high holy appearance is when one's own heart knows its faults; Guru Nanak's confession is exactly that inner knowledge of the gap between how we look and what we are.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Vaar Sri Raag (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After killing his mother, Orestes is hounded by the Furies (Erinyes) — spirits of guilt and vengeance whom he cannot escape even at Apollo’s shrine, until he is tried before Athena’s court.
greek_mythology.explanation: Orestes’ protected status at a holy place cannot silence the pursuit of his guilt.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, sacred surroundings and status do not neutralise a known wrong; guilt follows the doer.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If your deeds are honourable, let everybody know them; if base, what matters it that no one knows them, as long as you yourself know them? How wretched you are if you despise such a witness!”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells Lucilius that hiding a shameful act is pointless, because you yourself are always a witness to it.
philosophy.tie_back: Almost Valluvar’s exact point: reputation is irrelevant when the self knows its own fault.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 43.5 (tr. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Rousseau, author of a famous book on education, gives up his own children
real_life_example.event: By his own account, Jean-Jacques Rousseau and his partner Therese Levasseur had five children, and each was left at the Paris foundling hospital shortly after birth. In 1762 Rousseau published Emile, or On Education, which became one of the most influential works ever written on bringing up children. His abandonment of his children was later used against him by Voltaire, and in his Confessions Rousseau acknowledged and tried to justify what he had done.
real_life_example.explanation: The gap between Rousseau's celebrated public teaching and his private conduct became one of the best-known examples of a moral authority undercut by what he knew of himself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use a sky-high appearance of virtue is when the heart knows its own faults, and Rousseau's own Confessions record the fault behind his lofty reputation.

tamil:
வலியில் நிலைமையான் வல்லுருவம் பெற்றம்
புலியின்தோல் போர்த்துமேய்ந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Valiyil nilaimaiyaan valluruvam petram
Puliyinthol porththumeindh thatru.
meaning: Someone with no control over themselves who dresses up like a strict holy person is like a cow eating crops while wearing a tiger's skin.
elementary: Picture a cow wearing a tiger costume so it can sneak into a farm and eat the crops. It looks scary, but it’s still just a cow munching grass. A person who dresses like a strong holy person but can’t control himself is the same — a costume on the outside, the same old habits inside.
university: The simile is doubly pointed: the cow is weak, not fierce, and the tiger-skin lends it a borrowed terror that lets it graze unchallenged on another’s field. வலியில் நிலைமையான் (“one lacking the strength” — traditionally, strength to restrain the senses) contrasts with வல்லுருவம் (“a mighty form”), the forbidding garb of tapas. The target is not ordinary weakness but the exploitation of a sacred appearance to feed appetite. The same fable circulated widely in the ancient world — the Panchatantra’s ass in the tiger-skin and Aesop’s ass in the lion’s skin — and in both the disguise ultimately betrays itself.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra story “The Ass in the Tiger-Skin,” a washerman dresses his donkey in a tiger’s skin and turns it loose in the farmers’ fields at night; everyone flees from the ‘tiger’ while it eats the grain, until it brays and is recognised and killed.
hinduism.explanation: A weak animal wearing a fearsome skin feeds on others’ crops until its real voice gives it away.
hinduism.tie_back: This is essentially the Kural’s image told as a story — the borrowed skin, the grazing on crops, and the inevitable exposure.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book 4, “The Ass in the Tiger-Skin” (tr. Arthur W. Ryder)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns of religious teachers whose gentle outward appearance hides a predatory nature.
christianity.tie_back: The same animal-disguise logic as the Kural, inverted: here the predator wears the harmless skin, but in both the costume misrepresents the real creature.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up…”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes hypocrites whose impressive outward forms hide inner hollowness, like dry timber propped up to look solid.
islam.tie_back: Like the tiger-skinned cow, the hypocrite’s imposing exterior has nothing strong behind it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Do not be afraid of the Pharisees, and neither [should you fear] from those who are not Pharisees; rather, beware of the hypocrites who appear like Pharisees, as their actions are like the act of the wicked Zimri and they request a reward like that of the righteous Pinehas.”
judaism.explanation: King Yannai warns his wife that the real danger is people who look like pious Pharisees but act like sinners while demanding a saint’s reward.
judaism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s type: someone borrowing the appearance of the devout while their deeds belong to a weaker, baser nature.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 22b (William Davidson / Koren–Steinsaltz translation)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are many evil characters and uncontrolled men wearing the saffron robe. These wicked men will be born in states of woe because of their evil deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that plenty of undisciplined people wear the monk’s robe, and their robe will not save them.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘weak in self-control but strong in appearance’ figure.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the poison Kâlakûta kills him who drinks it; as a weapon cuts him who awkwardly handles it; as a Vêtâla kills him who does not lay him; so the Law harms him who mixes it up with sensuality.”
jainism.explanation: The text warns that taking up the monk's discipline while still giving in to the senses turns the discipline itself into a danger to the false monk.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's cow grazing in a tiger's skin is a weakling hiding sensual appetite under a fierce ascetic guise; the Jain verse condemns the same mixture of religious garb and unmastered senses.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, you wear your prayer shawl on your shoulders and the robes of a Sufi; your words are sweet, but there is a dagger in your heart.”
sikhism.explanation: Shaikh Farid rebukes the false holy man who puts on the prayer shawl and robe of a Sufi and talks sweetly while hiding a dagger in his heart.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar likens the weak-willed man in an ascetic's fierce form to a cow in a tiger's skin grazing another's crop; Farid's false Sufi likewise uses borrowed holy dress to cover what he really is.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1380, Salok Sheikh Farid 50 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “An Ass found a Lion’s Skin, and dressed himself up in it. Then he went about frightening every one he met… Elated by the success of his trick, he loudly brayed in triumph.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The ass in the lion’s skin scares everyone until its own braying reveals what it really is.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Greek twin of Valluvar’s simile: a weak animal in a predator’s skin, exposed by its true nature.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, “The Ass in the Lion’s Skin” (tr. V. S. Vernon Jones)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The boastful man, then, is thought to be apt to claim the things that bring glory, when he has not got them, or to claim more of them than he has…”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines the boaster as someone who claims admirable qualities he does not possess.
philosophy.tie_back: The tiger-skinned cow is a boaster in Aristotle’s sense: claiming the strength of austerity without having it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.7 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Captain of Kopenick
real_life_example.place: Kopenick, near Berlin, German Empire (now Germany)
real_life_example.event: Wilhelm Voigt, an unemployed shoemaker with a criminal record, put together a Prussian army captain's uniform from second-hand pieces. Wearing it, he ordered a squad of about ten real soldiers to follow him to the town hall of Kopenick, where they arrested the mayor and the treasurer on his orders and he took about 4,000 marks from the town treasury. He was arrested ten days later and sentenced to four years in prison.
real_life_example.explanation: The episode became a byword for how a borrowed uniform could make soldiers and officials obey a man with no real authority at all.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the weak man in the imposing garb of an ascetic to a cow grazing on crops in a tiger's skin, and Voigt fed himself from the town's treasury by wearing a captain's borrowed form.

tamil:
தவமறைந்து அல்லவை செய்தல் புதல்மறைந்து
வேட்டுவன் புள்சிமிழ்த் தற்று.
transliteration:
Thavamaraindhu allavai seydhal pudhalmaraindhu
Vettuvan pulsimizhth thatru.
meaning: Hiding behind a holy look while doing wrong is like a hunter hiding behind a bush to trap birds.
elementary: A bird hunter hides in a bush so the birds think it’s just a plant, and then — snap! — he catches them. Someone who pretends to be holy so people trust him, and then tricks them, is doing the same thing. The holy look is just his hiding bush.
university: Valluvar here turns from the hypocrite’s inner weakness to his active predation. The verb மறைந்து (“hiding”) appears twice in parallel — தவம் மறைந்து / புதல் மறைந்து — making tapas itself the thicket, the camouflage that renders the trapper invisible to his prey. The trusting public are the birds (புள்), drawn close precisely because the cover looks harmless and natural. This anticipates the widespread Indian motif of the “cat-ascetic” (baiḍāla-vratika) who adopts vows to lure victims — condemned in both the Mahabharata and Manu — and resonates with Jesus’ charge that the Pharisees ‘for a pretence make long prayer’ while devouring widows’ houses.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A wicked cat, O king, once on a time took up his abode on the banks of the Ganges, abandoning all work and with his hands upraised (after the manner of a devotee). Pretending to have purified his heart, he said unto all creatures… I am now practising virtue.”
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata the ‘ascetic cat’ wins the trust of the mice with a show of austerity and then eats them one by one until an old mouse sees through him.
hinduism.tie_back: A precise match: austerities used as a hiding place from which to trap trusting victims — Valluvar’s hunter in the bush.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 161 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows’ houses, and for a pretence make long prayer: therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus accuses religious leaders of using long public prayers as a front while cheating vulnerable widows.
christianity.tie_back: Same structure as the Kural: piety as a blind behind which the vulnerable are caught.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the hypocrites [think to] deceive Allah, but He is deceiving them. And when they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing [themselves to] the people and not remembering Allah except a little.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says hypocrites use prayer as a public display to deceive, while their hearts are not in it.
islam.tie_back: Worship becomes a screen for deception, as tapas does in the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For among my people are found wicked men: they lay wait, as he that setteth snares; they set a trap, they catch men. As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit…”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah compares deceivers among God’s people to bird-trappers lying in wait, their houses crammed with loot like a cage full of birds.
judaism.tie_back: Uses the very same fowler-and-birds image as the Kural for those who prey on others from concealment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It would be better to swallow a red-hot iron ball, blazing like fire, than as an immoral and uncontrolled monk to eat the alms of the people.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says an immoral monk living on people’s trusting donations does something worse than swallowing burning iron.
buddhism.tie_back: Condemns the same abuse: living off public trust earned by a religious appearance.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who has the character of a sinner, though he lays great stress on the outward signs of his calling as a means of living; he who does not control himself, though he pretends to do so; will come to grief for a long time.”
jainism.explanation: The verse condemns the monk who uses the outward emblems of his order, such as the broom, as a means of livelihood while living sinfully.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar likens doing wrong under cover of penance to a hunter hiding behind a bush to snare birds; the Jain text condemns exactly this use of the ascetic's signs as cover for self-serving conduct.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.43 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage. They tear apart and eat the living beings, and so they are not called white.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Soohee Guru Nanak points to herons that live at holy bathing places in spotless white while seizing and devouring living creatures.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar compares the predator hiding behind the garb of penance to a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds; Guru Nanak's heron likewise uses a pure-looking appearance in a holy place to catch its prey.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Greeks leave the Wooden Horse — presented as a sacred offering — outside Troy; the Trojans bring it into the city, and the warriors hidden inside emerge at night to sack it.
greek_mythology.explanation: An apparently holy gift conceals armed men waiting to strike.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the hunter behind the bush, danger hides inside something that looks sacred and harmless.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Glaucon’s tale, the shepherd Gyges finds a ring that makes him invisible; using it, he commits adultery, murders the king and seizes the throne — Glaucon argues that anyone who could act unseen would do the same.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the ring to ask whether people are just only because they fear being seen.
philosophy.tie_back: The false ascetic’s robe works like Gyges’ ring: it makes his wrongdoing invisible, exactly as the bush hides the hunter.

real_life_example.event_title: Ferdinand Waldo Demara serves as a naval surgeon under a false name
real_life_example.place: HMCS Cayuga, off the coast of Korea
real_life_example.event: Ferdinand Waldo Demara, an American who had earlier passed himself off in several religious orders, took the identity of a real doctor, Joseph Cyr, whom he had met while living with a religious order in Maine. In March 1951 he offered his services to the Royal Canadian Navy as Dr Cyr, was commissioned as a surgeon-lieutenant without his credentials being checked, and served aboard the destroyer HMCS Cayuga in Korean waters, where he treated wounded men. He was exposed as an impostor some months later.
real_life_example.explanation: Demara repeatedly hid behind trusted roles, from monk to doctor, which led people to accept him without question.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural likens the man who hides behind a sacred garb to a hunter hidden in a bush, and Demara used respected roles as cover in just that way.

tamil:
பற்றற்றேம் என்பார் படிற்றொழுக்கம் எற்றெற்றென்று
ஏதம் பலவுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Patratrem enbaar padittrozhukkam etretrendru
Edham palavum tharum.
meaning: People who say, “We have given up all wanting,” but live falsely will face many troubles that make them cry, “What have we done! What have we done!”
elementary: If you tell everyone you gave up sweets, but secretly eat them all, one day you’ll be caught — and you’ll feel terrible and say, “Why did I do that?” Pretending costs more in the end than being honest.
university: The kural records the hypocrite’s own claim — பற்றற்றேம் (“we are free of attachment”) — and sets against it his eventual cry, எற்று எற்று (“what [have we done], what!”), an onomatopoeic doubled lament unusual in the Kural. Valluvar’s focus is on consequences: படிற்றொழுக்கம் (disguised conduct) produces ஏதம் பலவும், “many evils,” culminating in bitter self-reproach. The phrase may refer both to worldly ruin when the imposture is exposed and to karmic suffering afterwards. The pattern — pretended renunciation leading to anguished regret — is echoed in Manu’s consignment of ‘cat’ and ‘heron’ ascetics to hell and in Jesus’ ‘weeping and gnashing of teeth’ for hypocrites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those Brahmanas who act like herons, and those who display the characteristics of cats, fall in consequence of that wicked mode of acting into (the hell called) Andhatamisra.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu says religious pretenders who behave like the ‘cat’ or the ‘heron’ (feigning piety to catch prey) fall into a dark hell.
hinduism.tie_back: Same moral arithmetic as the Kural: sham renunciation leads to great suffering for the pretender.

christianity.quote_or_event: “…and appoint him his portion with the hypocrites: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, the unfaithful servant is sent to share the fate of hypocrites, a place of weeping and grinding teeth.
christianity.tie_back: The hypocrite’s end is anguished lament — the Kural’s cry of ‘What have we done!’

islam.quote_or_event: “The hypocrites will call to the believers, ‘Were we not with you?’ They will say, ‘Yes, but you afflicted yourselves and awaited [misfortune for us] and doubted, and wishful thinking deluded you…’”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement the hypocrites plead that they were outwardly with the believers, and are told that their self-deception ruined them.
islam.tie_back: Captures the Kural’s scene of the pretender’s too-late realisation that his false show has destroyed him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire?”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah describes hypocrites suddenly seized with terror when judgement arrives.
judaism.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s picture of the pretender overtaken by distress and crying out in dismay.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as kusa grass wrongly handled cuts the hand, even so, a recluse’s life wrongly lived drags one to states of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a monk’s life lived falsely injures the one who lives it, like grass grabbed the wrong way slicing the hand.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s warning: the renunciant’s life, when faked, turns against the faker and brings him grief.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Thus the self-willed sinner who leaves the road of the highest Ginas, who with the appetite of an osprey is desirous of pleasure, will grieve in useless sorrow.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture's verdict on the false monk is that his hidden craving for pleasure ends in bitter and fruitless grief.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who falsely claim to be free of attachment will end crying 'What have we done!'; the Jain text likewise foresees useless sorrow for the monk who hides his appetites.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.50 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He dyes his robes with saffron dye, and wearing these robes, he goes out begging. … From house to house he goes begging, and tries to teach the world; but his mind is blind, and so he loses his honor.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Maaroo Guru Nanak describes a man who puts on the saffron robe of renunciation and begs from door to door, preaching to others while his own mind stays blind, until he loses his honour.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that those who falsely claim to have given up all attachment will end up crying 'what have we done!'; Guru Nanak likewise shows the false renunciant ending in disgrace.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1012, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A Wolf resolved to disguise himself in order that he might prey upon a flock of sheep without fear of detection. So he clothed himself in a sheepskin… But that very night… the shepherd… laid hands on the Wolf in mistake for a Sheep, and killed him with his knife on the spot.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The wolf’s disguise works — so well that it gets him slaughtered as a sheep.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The disguise itself becomes the source of the deceiver’s ruin, as the Kural predicts of false renunciation.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, “The Wolf in Sheep’s Clothing” (tr. V. S. Vernon Jones)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A good conscience welcomes the crowd, but a bad conscience, even in solitude, is disturbed and troubled.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca says a person living falsely is haunted and uneasy even when alone.
philosophy.tie_back: Describes the inner torment that the Kural’s ‘What have we done!’ expresses.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 43.5 (tr. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: The fall of Cardinal Wolsey
real_life_example.place: Hampton Court, London and Leicester, England
real_life_example.event: Thomas Wolsey, a cardinal of the Church and Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor, accumulated enormous wealth, with an income at its peak estimated at many times that of the richest nobleman, and built Hampton Court Palace. When he failed to obtain the pope's annulment of Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon, he fell from favour in 1529 and was stripped of his offices except the archbishopric of York. In November 1530 he was arrested on a charge of treason and died at Leicester Abbey on his way south to face it.
real_life_example.explanation: A churchman vowed to spiritual service who had amassed worldly power and riches lost all of it within a single year.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that those who claim to have renounced attachment while clinging to the world will meet many sorrows, and Wolsey's sudden ruin fits that warning.

tamil:
நெஞ்சின் துறவார் துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து
வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்.
transliteration:
Nenjin thuravaar thurandhaarpol vanjiththu
Vaazhvaarin vankanaar il.
meaning: No one is more hard-hearted than people who have not truly given up the world in their hearts, yet trick others by acting as if they have.
elementary: Some people pretend to be kind helpers who need nothing, so others trust them and give them things — but secretly they are greedy. Valluvar says that tricking people who trust you like this is about the meanest thing a person can do.
university: Valluvar’s strongest verdict in the chapter uses வன்கணார் — literally “the hard-eyed,” those without compassion — and makes it superlative: none are worse (இல்). The contrast நெஞ்சின் துறவார் / துறந்தார்போல் (“not renounced in heart” / “like those who renounced”) sharpens the gap between inner reality and outward role. The special cruelty lies in exploiting the reverence and generosity that society extends to genuine renunciants, and so corrupting the very institution of trust. Plato made the same ranking when Adeimantus and Glaucon called seeming-just-while-being-unjust the ‘highest reach’ of injustice, and Manu classes such pretenders as ‘cats’ bent on doing injury.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “(A man) who, ever covetous, displays the flag of virtue, (who is) a hypocrite, a deceiver of the people, intent on doing injury, (and) a detractor (from the merits) of all men, one must know to be one who acts like a cat.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu describes the ‘cat-like’ pretender: greedy inside, flying the banner of virtue outside, deceiving people and bent on harm.
hinduism.tie_back: A point-by-point match: inner craving, outward show of virtue, deceit, and cruelty toward others.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus closes his denunciation of the hypocritical scribes and Pharisees with his harshest words anywhere in the Gospels.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats religious hypocrisy as the worst category of wrongdoing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire – and never will you find for them a helper.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an places hypocrites in the very lowest level of Hell, below open disbelievers.
islam.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s superlative judgement: those who feign faith are worse than any other sinners.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes a betrayer whose gentle words hide a heart set on violence.
judaism.tie_back: Captures the cruelty the Kural sees in soft outward piety covering a hostile, grasping heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by shaven head does a man who is indisciplined and untruthful become a monk. How can he who is full of desire and greed be a monk?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha asks how anyone still full of craving could truly be a monk, whatever his shaved head suggests.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘not renounced in heart yet appearing renounced’.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
jainism.explanation: Speaking of monks who break their vows, the text calls such a man pitiless and says his own perversity harms him more than any murderer could.
