jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls those who pose as renunciants while deceiving others the most hard-hearted of all; the Jain verse likewise labels the false monk 'without pity' and says his perversity will turn on him.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The man-eaters say their prayers. Those who wield the knife wear the sacred thread around their necks.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak attacks officials of his day who devoured the people and preyed on the poor while making a show of prayer and wearing the sacred thread.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar calls none more hard-hearted than those who live by deceiving others while posing as holy; Guru Nanak's man-eaters at prayer show the same cruelty under a religious surface.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Lycaon receives Zeus (Jupiter) as a guest with an outward show of hospitality, but secretly plans to murder him and serves him human flesh; Zeus destroys his house and turns him into a wolf.
greek_mythology.explanation: A sacred duty — hospitality to a guest — is used as a cover for murderous cruelty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the false renunciant, Lycaon exploits a sacred role to harm the trusting, and is shown to be a beast within.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…for the highest reach of injustice is: to be deemed just when you are not.”
philosophy.explanation: In the Republic, Glaucon argues that the perfectly unjust man is the one who does wrong while enjoying a reputation for justice.
philosophy.tie_back: The same ranking as the Kural: the person who does wrong behind a reputation for goodness is the worst of all.

real_life_example.event_title: Moliere's Tartuffe is banned
real_life_example.event: Moliere's comedy Tartuffe, about a man who feigns intense piety in order to gain control of a trusting family's household and fortune, was first performed before Louis XIV at Versailles on 12 May 1664. After attacks from devout critics, the king banned public performances, and a revised version was banned again in Paris in 1667. Public performance was finally permitted on 5 February 1669, and the play became one of the most successful in the French repertoire.
real_life_example.explanation: Tartuffe's name became a byword in French and English for the religious hypocrite who preys on the trust of the devout.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says none are more hard-hearted than those who live by deceiving others while posing as renunciants, which is precisely the character Moliere put on the stage.

tamil:
புறங்குன்றி கண்டனைய ரேனும் அகங்குன்றி
முக்கிற் கரியார் உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Purangundri kandanaiya renum agangundri
Mukkir kariyaar udaiththu.
meaning: Some people are bright red on the outside like the kundri seed (a small red seed), but inside they are as black as the seed's dark tip.
elementary: There’s a tiny seed that is shiny red all over — except for one small black spot. Some people are like that: they look bright and good on the outside, but they hide a dark spot inside. Don’t judge only by the shiny part.
university: The kundri (குன்றி, Abrus precatorius) is a brilliant scarlet seed with a black spot at its ‘nose’ (மூக்கு); Valluvar makes it an emblem of the hypocrite, crimson-bright in outward piety, black at the core. The line plays on the repeated குன்றி in புறம் (outer) and அகம் (inner) — the fundamental Tamil poetic pair — so that the seed embodies both states at once. The seed was also used as a jeweller’s weight and is poisonous, which adds a latent irony: something small, attractive and valued conceals toxicity. The image anticipates Jesus’ ‘whited sepulchres’ and Hesiod’s Pandora — beauty outside, deceit within.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That Brahmana, who with downcast look, of a cruel disposition, is solely intent on attaining his own ends, dishonest and falsely gentle, is one who acts like a heron.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu describes the ‘heron’ pretender who keeps his eyes lowered like a meditating saint but is cruel and selfish inside.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kundri seed, the heron-ascetic shows a gentle surface and a dark interior.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus likens hypocrites to whitewashed tombs — bright outside, full of corruption inside.
christianity.tie_back: The Christian twin of the kundri seed: a beautiful exterior with darkness at the core.

islam.quote_or_event: “The signs of a hypocrite are three: 1. Whenever he speaks, he tells a lie. 2. Whenever he promises, he always breaks it… 3. If you trust him, he proves to be dishonest.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet lists the hidden traits by which someone who looks like a believer can be recognised as a hypocrite.
islam.tie_back: Tells us how to find the ‘black tip’ behind the bright exterior: look at speech, promises and trust.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Burning lips and a wicked heart are like a potsherd covered with silver dross.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares warm, fervent speech covering a wicked heart to a cheap clay pot coated with a silvery glaze.
judaism.tie_back: A shiny surface over something base — the same contrast as the kundri’s red body and black tip.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by mere eloquence nor by beauty of form does a man become accomplished, if he is jealous, selfish and deceitful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says fine speech and good looks mean nothing if the person inside is envious, selfish and deceptive.
buddhism.tie_back: Same contrast as the Kural: a fine exterior cannot redeem a dark interior.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He is empty like a clenched fist, (of no value) like an uncoined false Kârshâpana or like a piece of glass resembling turquoise, he is held lightly by men of discernment.”
jainism.explanation: The false monk is compared to things that look valuable but are hollow or counterfeit, which discerning people see through.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's kundri seed, bright red outside but black at the tip, matches this Jain image of coloured glass passing for a gem and a false coin passing for real money.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.42 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Bronze is bright and shiny, but when it is rubbed, its blackness appears.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak opens a hymn in Raag Soohee with the image of polished bronze, bright on the surface but leaving black marks once it is rubbed, as a picture of a person who only looks good.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar's kundri seed is bright red outside with a black tip; Guru Nanak's bronze is likewise bright outside and black underneath.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Also the Guide, the Slayer of Argus, contrived within her lies and crafty words and a deceitful nature at the will of loud thundering Zeus…”
greek_mythology.explanation: The gods adorn Pandora with beauty and finery, but Hermes places lies and a deceitful nature inside her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Pandora is the mythic kundri seed: dazzling outside, deceit within.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 69–82 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But the affectation of simplicity is like a crooked stick. Nothing is more disgraceful than a wolfish friendship (false friendship). Avoid this most of all. The good and simple and benevolent show all these things in the eyes, and there is no mistaking.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius says pretended goodness is twisted and false friendship is the worst disgrace; real goodness shows plainly.
philosophy.tie_back: Condemns the same split between an appealing outside and a hidden, predatory inside.

real_life_example.event_title: The collapse of Ivar Kreuger, the Match King
real_life_example.event: The Swedish financier Ivar Kreuger built a business empire that controlled much of the world's match production and lent large sums to governments, and he was widely admired as a financial genius. After his death in Paris in March 1932, auditors from Price Waterhouse found that many of the assets and profits recorded by his companies were fictitious and that he had forged Italian government bonds. His group of companies collapsed and many of them went bankrupt.
real_life_example.explanation: Kreuger's dazzling reputation concealed a hollow and fraudulent core that was revealed only when he was gone.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of people who look as bright red outside as the kundri seed but are black within like its tip, and Kreuger's empire was exactly such a bright surface over a dark centre.

tamil:
மனத்தது மாசாக மாண்டார் நீராடி
மறைந்தொழுகு மாந்தர் பலர்.
transliteration:
Manaththadhu maasaaga maandaar neeraadi
Maraindhozhugu maandhar palar.
meaning: Many people with dirty minds bathe in holy waters, just like truly great people do, and hide their bad lives behind that show.
elementary: Taking a bath gets the dirt off your skin — but it can’t wash away a mean or dishonest thought. Some people make a big show of holy bathing so everyone thinks they’re pure, but inside they’re still dirty. Clean hands don’t mean a clean heart.
university: Ritual bathing (நீராடல்) was the most visible sign of purity in both Brahmanical and Tamil religious life; Valluvar turns it into an instrument of concealment. The phrase மாண்டார் நீராடி can be read ‘bathing like the great (மாண்டார்)’ — imitating the ablutions of true sages — and மறைந்தொழுகு (‘conduct in hiding’) suggests that the water itself becomes a screen, as Kalaignar’s gloss has it: submerged, the bather disappears. The mind (மனம்) is the site of மாசு (impurity), echoing Kural 34’s definition of dharma as a mind free of stain. Across traditions, from Isaiah’s ‘Wash you, make you clean’ to Heraclitus mocking blood-purification, the same protest is made: outward ablution cannot cleanse inward defilement.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Hitopadesha, an old tiger sits “newly bathed on the bank of a pool, like a Brahman, and with holy kuskus-grass in his paws,” offering a golden bangle and assuring a traveller, “I am strict at ablutions and alms”; the greedy traveller wades in, sticks in the mud, and is eaten.
hinduism.explanation: The tiger uses the marks of ritual purity — bathing, holy grass, charity — to lure a victim into his reach.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s figure: ritual bathing performed as a disguise for a predatory mind.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Book 1, “The Story of the Tiger and the Traveller” (tr. Edwin Arnold)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess. Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within…”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says hypocrites wash the outside of the cup while leaving the inside filthy, and tells them to clean the inside first.
christianity.tie_back: The same contrast as the Kural between outward washing and inner impurity.

islam.quote_or_event: “So woe to those who pray, [But] who are heedless of their prayer – Those who make show [of their deeds].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns worshippers who go through the motions of prayer only to be seen.
islam.tie_back: Ritual acts done for display while the heart is absent — the Kural’s showy bather.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And when ye spread forth your hands, I will hide mine eyes from you… your hands are full of blood. Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil.”
judaism.explanation: God tells worshippers that their prayers are rejected because their hands are bloody; real washing means stopping their evil deeds.
judaism.tie_back: Makes the Kural’s point directly: ritual washing is empty without cleansing one’s conduct.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the use of your matted hair, O witless man? What of your garment of antelope’s hide? Within you is the tangle (of passion); only outwardly do you cleanse yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha mocks an ascetic who keeps the outward marks and washes his body while his mind is tangled with passion.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: outward cleansing by someone whose mind remains defiled.

jainism.quote_or_event: “O Brâhmanas, why do you tend the fire, and seek external purity by water? The clever ones say that external purity which you seek for, is not the right thing.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Harikesa tells the sacrificing priests that ritual bathing gives only outward purity, and later calls the Law his pond and celibacy his true bathing-place (12.46).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar mocks those who bathe in sacred waters to hide minds full of filth; Harikesa likewise rejects water-purity in favour of inner purity.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “With filth within the heart, even if one bathes at sacred places of pilgrimage, still, he shall not go to heaven.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir declares that a person whose heart is full of filth gains nothing from bathing at holy places of pilgrimage.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar mocks those who bathe in sacred waters with filth in their minds and live hidden behind that show; Kabir says the same, that ritual bathing cannot wash an inner filth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 484, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Mecone, Prometheus divides a sacrificial ox: he hides the meat inside the stomach and wraps the bare bones in glistening fat, and invites Zeus to choose; Zeus picks the attractive portion, and ever after the gods receive bones wrapped in fat at sacrifices.
greek_mythology.explanation: A sacred rite is turned into a trick, with a pleasing surface covering something worthless.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s bather, religious ritual is used as a cover, its fine surface hiding the reality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They vainly purify themselves by defiling themselves with blood, just as if one who had stepped into the mud were to wash his feet in mud. Any man who marked him doing thus, would deem him mad.”
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus ridicules people who think blood-rituals can make them pure.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s scepticism that outward purification rites can cleanse real impurity.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, fragments 129–130 (Burnet numbering; tr. John Burnet)

real_life_example.event_title: Rasputin gains influence at the Russian court as a holy man
real_life_example.event: Grigori Rasputin, a Siberian peasant who presented himself as a wandering holy man, reached St Petersburg in 1903 and from 1905 became close to Tsar Nicholas II and Empress Alexandra, largely because he appeared able to ease the suffering of their son Alexei, who had haemophilia. Reports of his debauched private conduct caused repeated scandal, and in 1911 the prime minister sent the tsar a report on his behaviour. His influence over appointments grew during the First World War until a group of noblemen killed him in December 1916.
real_life_example.explanation: Rasputin's reputation for holiness opened the doors of the palace even as reports of his conduct away from it became a national scandal.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of those with impurity in their minds who live hidden behind an outward show of holiness, a description that fits how Rasputin's critics saw him.

tamil:
கணைகொடிது யாழ்கோடு செவ்விதுஆங் கன்ன
வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Kanaikodidhu yaazhkodu sevvidhuaang kanna
Vinaipadu paalaal kolal.
meaning: An arrow is straight but does harm. A lute (a stringed instrument) is bent but makes sweet music. So judge people by what they do, not by how they look.
elementary: An arrow looks perfectly straight, but it’s made for hurting. A guitar has a curvy neck, but it makes lovely music. So don’t decide who is good just by how they look — watch what they actually do.
university: Here Valluvar moves from condemnation to method: how can one tell the hypocrite from the saint? The paired images turn the usual metaphors upside down — கணை (arrow) is straight yet கொடிது (cruel), while யாழ்கோடு (the curved neck of the yazh, the ancient Tamil harp-lute) is bent yet செவ்விது (upright, good). Since செம்மை and கொடுமை mean both ‘straight/crooked’ and ‘good/cruel’, the kural exploits the double meaning to show that visual straightness and moral straightness are different things. The conclusion — வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல், ‘assess by the quality of deeds’ — is a pragmatic epistemology of character that parallels Jesus’ ‘by their fruits ye shall know them’ and the Yaksha’s answer that conduct, not birth or learning, makes a Brahmin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is neither birth, nor study, nor learning, that is the cause of Brahmanahood, without doubt, it is behaviour that constitutes it.”
hinduism.explanation: Yudhishthira tells the Yaksha that a person is truly a Brahmin by conduct alone, not by birth or scholarship.
hinduism.tie_back: Same standard as the Kural: judge people by their actions, not by outward markers of status.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 311 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?”
christianity.explanation: Right after warning about wolves in sheep’s clothing, Jesus says people are known by what they produce.
christianity.tie_back: Almost identical rule to the Kural’s: ignore the look, judge by the results.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says God judges by hearts and actions, not by appearance or riches.
islam.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s rejection of appearance as a measure; adds the heart alongside deeds.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi said: don’t look at the container but at that which is in it: there is a new container full of old wine, and an old [container] in which there is not even new [wine].”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that the vessel’s look tells you nothing about its contents.
judaism.tie_back: Like the straight arrow and curved lute, the outward shape misleads; what matters is what the thing really holds and does.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even though he be well-attired, yet if he is poised, calm, controlled and established in the holy life, having set aside violence towards all beings — he, truly, is a holy man, a renunciate, a monk.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says someone dressed like an ordinary layperson can still be a true holy man if his conduct is right.
buddhism.tie_back: The ‘curved lute’ case: the wrong look, but the right deeds — judge by conduct.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By one's actions one becomes a Brâhmana, or a Kshattriya, or a Vaisya, or a Sûdra.”
jainism.explanation: Jayaghosha teaches that a person's real standing comes from conduct, not from birth or outward marks.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says to judge people by their deeds and not by appearance, as the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute sweet; the Jain verse likewise makes deeds, not outward signs, the measure of a person.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The simmal tree is straight as an arrow; it is very tall, and very thick. … Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak notes that the silk-cotton tree is straight, tall and imposing, yet birds that come to it leave disappointed, and concludes that sweetness and humility are what make a person good.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar says the arrow is straight but cruel and the lute bent but sweet, so people must be judged by their deeds, not their looks; Guru Nanak's straight-as-an-arrow tree yields nothing, while humble sweetness is the real worth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus returns to Ithaca, Athena disguises him as a ragged old beggar; the suitors mock and abuse him, but he is in fact the rightful king, revealed by his deeds when he strings the great bow.
greek_mythology.explanation: A shabby appearance hides a hero, whose true identity is shown by what he does.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The ‘bent lute’ half of the Kural: an unimpressive look that hides real worth, known only through action.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Alcibiades compares Socrates to the statues of Silenus sold in shops — grotesque figures that open up to reveal images of the gods inside — saying that Socrates’ ugly, satyr-like exterior hides divine virtue within.
philosophy.explanation: Plato presents Socrates as proof that an unappealing outside can contain the finest character.
philosophy.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s curved lute: a crooked-looking form that produces something beautiful.

real_life_example.event_title: Joseph Merrick, the Elephant Man, finds a home at the London Hospital
real_life_example.event: Joseph Merrick was born with severe physical deformities and was exhibited in a freak show before the surgeon Frederick Treves arranged for him to live at the London Hospital in 1886. Treves at first assumed from his appearance and difficult speech that he was mentally impaired, but came to recognise him as intelligent and sensitive; Merrick could read and write and enjoyed books. Public donations allowed him to remain at the hospital until his death in April 1890 at the age of 27.
real_life_example.explanation: Merrick's story is a lasting lesson that a person's appearance can mislead even an expert observer about the person within.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the bent-necked lute is sweet while the straight arrow is cruel, so people must be judged by their deeds and not their looks, and Merrick's life taught that lesson to Victorian London.

tamil:
மழித்தலும் நீட்டலும் வேண்டா உலகம்
பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்.
transliteration:
Mazhiththalum neettalum vendaa ulagam
Pazhiththadhu ozhiththu vidin.
meaning: There is no need to shave your head or to grow your hair long, if you simply give up what the world says is wrong.
elementary: Some holy people shave their heads and some grow their hair really long. Valluvar says: your haircut doesn’t make you good! If you stop doing bad things, you’re already on the right path — hair or no hair.
university: The chapter closes with its most famous and most radical line. மழித்தல் (shaving the head, as Jain and Buddhist monks did) and நீட்டல் (growing matted locks, as Shaiva and Vedic ascetics did) were the defining visual signs of rival renunciant orders; Valluvar dismisses both in a single breath, declaring them unnecessary (வேண்டா). The only real requirement is ethical: உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்தல் — abandoning what the wise of the world condemn. This non-sectarian move, placing conduct above every order’s insignia, is characteristic of the Kural as a whole and parallels the Dhammapada’s dismissal of tonsure and matted hair, Manu’s ‘the external mark is not the cause of merit’, and Seneca’s warning against the philosopher’s unkempt beard.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…let him, though blemished (by a want of the external marks), fulfil his duty, equal-minded towards all creatures; (for) the external mark (of the order) is not the cause of (the acquisition of) merit.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the renunciant that the outward signs of his order do not produce spiritual merit; right conduct does.
hinduism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s own claim: ascetic insignia are unnecessary; ethical conduct is what counts.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus criticises people who make their fasting visible on their faces so others will admire them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s shaved or matted heads, visible ascetic signs are rejected as mere display.

islam.quote_or_event: “Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but [true] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah… and gives wealth… [and who] establishes prayer and gives zakah; [those who] fulfill their promise…”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says righteousness isn’t about outward ritual forms like the direction you face, but about faith and good conduct.
islam.tie_back: Same move as the Kural: outward religious form is secondary; ethical life is what matters.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God…”
judaism.explanation: Joel calls people to real inner repentance instead of the outward sign of tearing their clothes.
judaism.tie_back: Replaces an outward religious gesture with inner change — as the Kural replaces tonsure and matted locks with giving up wrongdoing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by shaven head does a man who is indisciplined and untruthful become a monk.” / “Not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth does one become a holy man. But he in whom truth and righteousness exist — he is pure, he is a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha rejects both tonsure and matted hair as marks of holiness; only truth and righteousness count.
buddhism.tie_back: Names the same two hairstyles as the Kural (shaving and long locks) and reaches the same verdict.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One does not become a Sramana by the tonsure, nor a Brâhmana by the sacred syllable ôm, nor a Muni by living in the woods, nor a Tâpasa by wearing (clothes of) Kusa-grass and bark. One becomes a Sramana by equanimity, a Brâhmana by chastity, a Muni by knowledge, and a Tâpasa by penance.”
jainism.explanation: Jayaghosha says that no outward sign, whether a shaven head, a sacred word or forest dress, makes someone holy; only inner virtue does.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says there is no need to shave the head or grow matted hair if one gives up what the world condemns; the Jain verse likewise denies that tonsure or ascetic dress make a renunciant.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.31-32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, you have not shaved your mind, so why do you shave your head?”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir tells the shaven-headed ascetic that unless the mind itself has been cleared of vice, shaving the head means nothing.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar says neither shaving the head nor growing matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Kabir likewise says the outward mark is useless without a changed mind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads the young Heracles meets two women: Vice, dressed and made up to show off her charms, and Virtue, plainly and modestly clothed; Heracles chooses Virtue’s hard road of good deeds.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prodicus’ allegory contrasts glamorous outward appearance with genuine virtue shown in action.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it tells us that real goodness is chosen in conduct, not in how one is dressed or adorned.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Repellent attire, unkempt hair, slovenly beard, open scorn of silver dishes, a couch on the bare earth, and any other perverted forms of self-display, are to be avoided.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells Lucilius not to advertise his philosophy through scruffy hair and ostentatious poverty; the real difference should be inward.
philosophy.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: long hair and showy austerity are unnecessary; inner reform is what matters.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 5.2 (tr. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Erasmus publishes The Praise of Folly
real_life_example.place: Western Europe (work of the Dutch humanist Erasmus)
real_life_example.event: The Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus published The Praise of Folly, a satire in which Folly herself mocks theologians, monks and rulers, including the monks' pride in their habits, rules and ceremonies. In his earlier Enchiridion of 1503 he had argued that true piety consists not in outward ceremonies but in inward conversion. The satire provoked strong resentment among theologians, and in 1564 it was among his works placed on the Church's index of prohibited books.
real_life_example.explanation: Erasmus became the most famous voice of his age for the view that outward religious forms count for nothing without an inward change of life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says there is no need to shave the head or grow long hair if one simply gives up what the world condemns, and Erasmus mocked the monks' outward marks while urging inner reform.

tamil:
எள்ளாமை வேண்டுவான் என்பான் எனைத்தொன்றும்
கள்ளாமை காக்கதன் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Ellaamai venduvaan enbaan enaiththondrum,
Kallaamai kaakkathan nenju.
meaning: If you never want to be looked down on, guard your heart so it never even thinks of stealing anything from anyone, however small.
elementary: Nobody wants to be laughed at or called a cheat. The way to make sure that never happens is to keep a guard at the door of your own mind, so that even the idea of sneaking away something that isn’t yours — even a pencil — never gets in.
university: The chapter opens by locating fraud (kaḷavu) not in the hand but in the heart (neñcu): the verb is kākka, “let him guard,” and its object is the mind itself. Valluvar’s motive clause is social and reputational — eḷḷāmai, “not being scorned” — which fits the householder-and-ascetic audience of the Tuṟavaṟaviyal section, where public trust is the currency of a moral life. The word eṉaittoṉṟum (“anything whatsoever”) forecloses the familiar rationalisation that small frauds do not count, anticipating the Aristotelian claim that theft admits no virtuous mean. Commentators from Parimēlaḻakar to Mu. Varadarasan read kaḷḷāmai as covering not only burglary but every covert appropriation, including short-changing and deceit in dealings.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do not covet the wealth of any man!”
hinduism.explanation: The very first verse of the Isha Upanishad tells the seeker to see everything as belonging to the Lord and, on that basis, never to hanker after anyone else’s property.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts place the prohibition at the level of desire and extend it to any wealth at all, not just large thefts.
hinduism.source: Isha Upanishad 1 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE vol. 1)

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that honesty is tested in trivial matters; a person who cheats in small things reveals a character that will cheat in large ones.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s “anything whatsoever” (eṉaittoṉṟum): no fraud is too small to matter.

islam.quote_or_event: “So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, And whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”
islam.explanation: Surat az-Zalzalah teaches that on the Day of Judgement even the tiniest deed, good or bad, will be brought to light.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it denies that any wrong is too small to count, and ties wrongdoing to eventual exposure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let the property of your fellow be as precious unto you as your own”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yose’s maxim in the Mishnah asks a person to value a neighbour’s possessions exactly as he values his own, which rules out any scheme to take them.
judaism.tie_back: Both locate honesty in an inner disposition toward others’ property, cultivated before any act.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who in this world takes nothing that is not given to him, be it long or short, small or big, good or bad — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines the truly noble person as one who never takes what is not freely given, regardless of its size or value.
buddhism.tie_back: The Dhammapada’s “small or big” is the same sweep as the Kural’s eṉaittoṉṟum — honesty admits no exceptions.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I renounce all taking of anything not given, either in a village or a town or a wood, either of little or much, of small or great, of living or lifeless things.”
jainism.explanation: This is the opening of the third great vow (asteya) that every Jain monk takes. It renounces taking anything not given, whatever its size or value.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells the man who wants to avoid contempt to guard his heart against taking “anything at all” by fraud. The Jain vow likewise allows no exception for small things: “of little or much, of small or great.”
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.15, the third great vow (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, pp. 205-206)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of the Vaar in Raag Maajh, Guru Nanak takes what each community holds most forbidden and says that taking another's due is just as forbidden. Sikh teaching sets this beside kirat karni, earning by honest work.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells anyone who wants to avoid contempt to guard against taking anything of another's by stealth. Guru Nanak's comparison makes such taking the deepest kind of defilement.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how the old herdsman Battus saw Mercury driving off Apollo’s stolen cattle and was bribed with a cow to keep silent. Mercury returned in disguise, offered a cow and a bull for information, and Battus betrayed the secret at once; Mercury turned him into a stone, a lasting emblem of the informer.
greek_mythology.explanation: A small, greedy gain made through complicity in theft and double-dealing leaves Battus a permanent object of scorn.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s warning that even a petty fraudulent gain leads to lasting disgrace.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “in the case of actions adultery, theft, murder; for all of these and suchlike things imply by their names that they are themselves bad”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle, having defined virtue as a mean, stops to insist that some acts, theft among them, have no right amount; any instance of them is simply wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: Supplies the philosophical logic behind “anything whatsoever”: there is no acceptable quantity of fraud.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Rosie Ruiz is stripped of the Boston Marathon title
real_life_example.event: Rosie Ruiz crossed the finish line first among women at the 1980 Boston Marathon on 21 April. Runners and officials quickly grew suspicious because no checkpoint had recorded her and race photographs showed her only near the end, and witnesses said they saw her join the course close to the finish. On 29 April officials stripped her of the title and named Canada's Jacqueline Gareau the winner; Ruiz always maintained that she had run the whole race.
real_life_example.explanation: One shortcut turned a moment of glory into lasting public ridicule, and 'pulling a Rosie' became slang for cheating one's way to success.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that anyone who wishes never to be scorned must guard the heart against taking anything by stealth, and Ruiz's finish became a byword for exactly that scorn.

tamil:
உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும் தீதே பிறன்பொருளைக்
கள்ளத்தால் கள்வேம் எனல்.
transliteration:
Ullaththaal ullalum theethe piranporulaik,
Kallaththaal kalvem enal.
meaning: Even thinking in your mind, “I will sneakily steal what belongs to someone else,” is wrong.
elementary: Imagine thinking, “When no one is looking, I’ll trick my friend out of his toy.” Even if you never do it, just planning it is already a bad step, because every wrong action begins as a thought.
university: Valluvar moves culpability upstream from act to intention: uḷḷattāl uḷḷalum tītē — “even the thinking with the mind is evil.” The phrase kaḷḷattāl kaḷvēm (“we shall steal by craft”) specifies the content of the forbidden thought as a deliberate scheme, not a passing temptation, which is important for the ethical claim. This parallels the Tenth Commandment’s ban on coveting, the Buddhist teaching that mind precedes action, and the Gita’s account of how dwelling on objects breeds desire. Commentators note the psychological realism: fraud requires premeditation, so the only reliable defence is to refuse the premeditation itself.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain from mere contemplation of desirable things to attachment and then to consuming desire.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say the danger starts in thought; dwelling on another’s wealth is the first link in the chain toward fraud.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, Thefts, covetousness, wickedness, deceit…”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that what defiles a person comes from inside the heart, listing thefts, covetousness and deceit among evils that start as inner thoughts.
christianity.tie_back: Same claim as the Kural: theft and deceit are born in the heart before the hand.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whether you show what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allāh will bring you to account for it.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that God judges what lies hidden within a person as well as what is displayed.
islam.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s claim that a concealed intention to defraud is already morally weighed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house; thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife, nor his man-servant, nor his maid-servant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s.”
judaism.explanation: The last of the Ten Commandments forbids not an act but a desire directed at a neighbour’s property.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the inner wish to take another’s goods itself a transgression.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada’s opening verse makes mind the source of every action and its consequences.
buddhism.tie_back: Grounds the Kural’s claim that the fraudulent plan in the mind is already the root of the harm.

jainism.quote_or_event: “It follows that activity actuated by impure dispositions is stealing (steya), whether external objects are taken or not.”
jainism.explanation: Commenting on the sutra that defines stealing as taking what is not given, Pūjyapāda holds that the guilt lies in the passion (pramatta-yoga) behind the act. A theft-minded disposition is therefore already stealing, even if nothing is actually taken.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that merely thinking “I will take his property by cunning” is already a wrong. Pūjyapāda likewise places stealing in the impure disposition itself, whether or not anything is taken.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.15, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “False is the mind which covets the wealth of others.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan names each faculty that goes astray: the hands that steal, the ears that slander, and here the mind that covets another's wealth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural finds wrong in merely thinking of taking another's property by cunning. Guru Arjan likewise condemns the coveting mind itself, before any act.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 269, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Glaucon’s tale in Plato’s Republic, the shepherd Gyges finds a ring that makes him invisible; secure from detection, he uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king and seize the kingdom.
greek_mythology.explanation: The legend asks what a person would do if he could take anything without being seen, exposing whether honesty is inner or merely fear of exposure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural answers Gyges: the scheme formed in the unseen mind is already the wrong, detection or not.
greek_mythology.source: Plato, Republic II, 359c-360b (legend of the Ring of Gyges)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will.”
philosophy.explanation: Kant opens the Groundwork by locating moral worth entirely in the will, not in outcomes.
philosophy.tie_back: Converse of the Kural: if goodness lies in the will, a will set on fraud is already bad before it acts.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section (tr. T. K. Abbott)

real_life_example.event_title: Judge Landis bans the Black Sox, including a player who took no money
real_life_example.event: Eight Chicago White Sox players were accused of conspiring with gamblers to lose the 1919 World Series, and on 2 August 1921 a jury acquitted them. The next day baseball commissioner Kenesaw Mountain Landis banned all eight for life, declaring that this applied regardless of the jury's verdict and also to any player who sat in meetings where throwing games was discussed and did not tell his club. Third baseman Buck Weaver had accepted none of the money, but he had known of the scheme and kept silent, and his ban was never lifted.
real_life_example.explanation: Landis treated involvement in planning a fraud, even without taking the reward, as disqualifying, which set the standard for integrity in American professional sport.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even forming the intention to take another's property by cunning is already a wrong, and Landis's ruling punished involvement in the scheme itself, not only the payoff.

tamil:
களவினால் ஆகிய ஆக்கம் அளவிறந்து
ஆவது போலக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kalavinaal aakiya aakkam alavirandhu,
Aavadhu polak kedum.
meaning: What is gained by stealing may seem to grow beyond all limits, but it will all be lost.
elementary: It’s like a soap bubble: a stolen treasure puffs up bigger and bigger and looks amazing, and then — pop! — it’s gone, and it can even splash away the things you already had.
university: The couplet turns on the paradox of āvatu pōla, “as if growing”: fraudulent gain has the appearance of prosperity but not its substance. The phrase aḷaviṟantu is read two ways by commentators — as “beyond measure” describing the apparent growth, or (with Mu. Varadarasan and Kalaignar) as the ruin exceeding its natural limit and consuming even legitimately held wealth. Either way, Valluvar denies the fraudster even a prudential victory. The same instability of ill-gotten wealth is a commonplace across Hesiod, Proverbs, Jeremiah and the Qur’an, suggesting a widely shared moral-economic intuition that dishonest gain lacks durable foundations.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Held in bondage by hundreds of desires, and driven by lust and anger, they strive to accumulate wealth by unjust means, all for the gratification of their senses.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the demoniac character as heaping up wealth by unlawful means; the surrounding verses trace this path to ruin and lower births.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts expose unjust accumulation as a false prosperity that ends in downfall.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool.”
christianity.explanation: Jeremiah compares wrongly gained wealth to eggs a bird broods over but never hatches: the promise of increase never comes to fruition.
christianity.tie_back: Identical logic to “as if growing, it perishes”: the apparent increase of unjust riches is illusory.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allāh destroys interest and gives increase for charities.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an contrasts usury, which seems to multiply wealth, with charity, which seems to reduce it; God reverses both appearances.
islam.tie_back: Same paradox as the Kural: exploitative gain that looks like growth is actually headed for destruction.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished; But he that gathereth little by little shall increase.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts wealth gained through emptiness or dishonesty, which dwindles, with patiently earned wealth, which grows.
judaism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s claim that fraud-wealth decays while honest wealth endures.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as rust arising from iron eats away the base from which it arises, even so, their own deeds lead transgressors to states of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares wrongdoing to rust that grows out of iron and then consumes the very metal that produced it.
buddhism.tie_back: Mirrors the reading of aḷaviṟantu in which fraud-wealth destroys even the wealth one already had.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana warns that wealth gained by evil means does not last. Its owners lose it and are left bound by their own passions.
jainism.tie_back: In the Kural, fraudulent wealth seems to swell but perishes and takes more with it. Here wealth acquired by evil deeds is lost and the acquirer is caught in further snares.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
sikhism.explanation: In one of the Babar hymns in Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak reflects on the wealth of rulers ruined by invasion. It was piled up through wrongdoing, and it could not save them or go with them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says wealth gained by fraud seems to grow but will perish. Guru Nanak describes wealth gained through sin that cannot last and abandons its owner at death.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Wealth should not be seized: god-given wealth is much better; for if a man take great wealth violently and perforce, or if he steal it through his tongue, as often happens when gain deceives men’s sense and dishonour tramples down honour, the gods soon blot him out and make that man’s house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that wealth taken by force or by deceitful speech is quickly withdrawn by the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost a paraphrase of the Kural: fraudulent wealth stays only a little while and brings the house down with it.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 320-326 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Consolation of Philosophy, Lady Philosophy argues that riches are never truly a person’s own: they belong to Fortune, who hands them out and takes them back as she pleases, so no one should rest security or identity on them.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius stresses how unstable external wealth is and how foolish it is to trust it.
philosophy.tie_back: Strengthens the Kural’s point: if even honest wealth is unstable, wealth gained by fraud rests on nothing at all.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II

real_life_example.event_title: The South Sea Bubble bursts
real_life_example.event: Shares in the South Sea Company rose from about 128 pounds in January 1720 to around 1,000 pounds by June, then collapsed to about 124 pounds by December, ruining thousands of investors and many landed and merchant families. The company had given gifts of its new stock, in effect bribes, to leading politicians and to the king's mistress. Parliament held an inquiry, and the estates of the company's directors were later sold under official authority.
real_life_example.explanation: The bubble became the classic warning of how wealth built on manipulation and corruption can swell rapidly and then destroy far more than it ever produced.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says wealth gained by fraud may seem to grow beyond measure but perishes and takes more with it, which is exactly the arc of the South Sea Company.

tamil:
களவின்கண் கன்றிய காதல் விளைவின்கண்
வீயா விழுமம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Kalavinkan kandriya kaadhal vilaivinkan,
Veeyaa vizhumam tharum.
meaning: A strong wish to gain by stealing will, in the end, bring sorrow that never ends.
elementary: Wanting to cheat is like planting a thorn bush because its flowers look pretty. When it grows up, the thorns keep poking you, and you can never get rid of them.
university: Kaṉṟiya kātal — a desire that has become hardened or habitual — is the subject, and the agricultural verb viḷaivu (ripening, harvest) sets up the karmic metaphor: fraud is a seed whose fruit is vīyā viḻumam, “unperishing affliction.” The emphasis on habit links this couplet to 286 and 288, where Valluvar treats fraud as a character formed by repetition. The imagery of delayed but certain ripening is close to the Dhammapada’s description of evil deeds that seem sweet until they ripen. Commentators split between reading the sorrow as this-worldly (disgrace, punishment) and as extending into later births; the adjective vīyā allows both.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names greed among the three doors to hell and says these passions degrade the self.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘hardened craving’ for fraudulent gain is exactly lobha (greed), and its fruit is lasting ruin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs describes deceitful gain as sweet at first and painful in its aftertaste.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s movement from desire to a bitter harvest (viḷaivu).

islam.quote_or_event: “And whoever betrays, [taking unlawfully], will come with what he took on the Day of Resurrection. Then will every soul be [fully] compensated for what it earned, and they will not be wronged.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that whoever misappropriates goods will carry them to Judgement, where every soul receives its due.
islam.tie_back: The fraudulent gain becomes a lasting burden, like the Kural’s ‘unperishing affliction’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For all that do such things, even all that do unrighteously, are an abomination unto the LORD thy God.”
judaism.explanation: After commanding honest weights and measures, the Torah declares that anyone who deals dishonestly is an abomination to God.
judaism.tie_back: The lasting harm of the Kural is framed here as enduring estrangement from God.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “So long as an evil deed has not ripened, the fool thinks it as sweet as honey. But when the evil deed ripens, the fool comes to grief.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the consequences of an evil deed stay hidden until they ripen, and then they bring grief.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s harvest metaphor: wrong ‘ripens’ (viḷaivu) into sorrow.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Thus when he takes another's property, and is (after all) not satisfied by the 'colours' (he has obtained), he becomes unhappy, and nobody will protect him.”
jainism.explanation: Lecture 32 traces a chain: craving grows, greed leads a man to take another's property, and the theft brings only deeper misery and no protection. The lecture adds that passion accumulates karman, which in the end produces further misery.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says an ingrained craving for fraudulent gain ripens into endless sorrow. The Jain text likewise shows craving that ends in theft bearing fruit only in unhappiness, with no one to protect the thief.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.29-31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are attached to the poison of greed and sin grab at the wealth of others; they only bring pain on themselves.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan says that people held by greed seize others' wealth and harvest only suffering. Sikh teaching names greed (lobh) as one of the five thieves within.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a hardened craving for gain by fraud bears fruit in endless sorrow. Guru Arjan likewise traces the grabbing of others' wealth to greed and says it ends in pain for the grabber.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 408, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Pindar’s version, Tantalus, a guest at the gods’ table, stole nectar and ambrosia and gave them to his mortal drinking companions; for this he was punished forever, with a huge stone hanging over his head.
greek_mythology.explanation: A theft driven by craving and pride is repaid with punishment that never ends.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic image of the Kural’s vīyā viḻumam — sorrow that does not die — as the harvest of theft.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Socrates argues that doing injustice is worse than suffering it, and that the wrongdoer who escapes punishment is the most wretched of all, because his soul stays diseased.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the real harm of wrongdoing is inside the wrongdoer: a lasting corruption of the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Gives a philosophical account of why the Kural’s sorrow is ‘undying’: the damage is to the self, not just to fortune.

real_life_example.event_title: Cassie Chadwick's lifetime of fraud ends in prison
real_life_example.place: Cleveland and Columbus, Ohio, United States
real_life_example.event: Elizabeth Bigley, later known as Cassie Chadwick, began forging documents as a girl and served a prison term in Ohio for forgery before being released early. From the late 1890s she borrowed large sums from banks, using forged securities bearing Andrew Carnegie's name and letting it be believed she was his secret daughter. Her scheme was exposed in November 1904, she was convicted in March 1905 of conspiracy, including against a bank in Oberlin that collapsed, and she died in the Ohio Penitentiary in 1907.
real_life_example.explanation: Her career shows a habit of deception repeated over decades until it ended in disgrace, imprisonment and death behind bars.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says an ingrained craving for gain by fraud, when it ripens, yields sorrow without end, and Chadwick's long habit ripened into ruin for her and her victims.

tamil:
அருள்கருதி அன்புடைய ராதல் பொருள்கருதிப்
பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Arulkarudhi anbudaiya raadhal porulkarudhip,
Pochchaappup paarppaarkan il.
meaning: People who only want other people's things, and wait for them to look away, cannot have real kindness or love.
elementary: A real friend helps you when you drop your lunch money. Someone who waits for you to drop it so they can grab it can’t be kind at the same time — the waiting-to-grab heart pushes the kindness out.
university: The couplet contrasts two inner orientations: aruḷ karuti, “holding grace (compassion) in regard,” and poruḷ karuti, “holding another’s wealth in regard.” The fraudster’s signature act is poccāppu pārttal — watching for the other person’s forgetfulness or unguardedness — which Valluvar treats as incompatible with aṉpu (love). The couplet ties this chapter to the preceding ones on Aruḷuṭaimai (compassion), showing that for Valluvar honesty in dealings is not a separate commercial rule but a consequence of compassion. Kant’s shopkeeper, the hadith of the wet grain, and Micah’s schemers lying awake all describe the same failure: treating another person’s vulnerability as an opportunity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…compassion for all living entities; freedom from covetousness; gentleness; modesty…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists compassion and freedom from covetousness side by side among the divine qualities.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita pairs exactly what the Kural pairs: compassion (aruḷ) and the absence of coveting others’ wealth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, after citing ‘Thou shalt not steal’ among the commandments, sums them all up as love, which cannot harm a neighbour.
christianity.tie_back: Same logic as the Kural: love and scheming against a neighbour’s goods cannot coexist.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Prophet put his hand into a heap of grain and found the lower part wet, he said: “Why did you not place this (the drenched part of the heap) over other eatables so that the people could see it? He who deceives is not of me (is not my follower).”
islam.explanation: The seller hid damaged grain where buyers would not notice, relying on their lack of vigilance; the Prophet declared such deception outside his community.
islam.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s target: profiting from the other party’s unguarded moment (poccāppu).

judaism.quote_or_event: “Woe to them that devise iniquity And work evil upon their beds! When the morning is light, they execute it, Because it is in the power of their hand. And they covet fields, and seize them…”
judaism.explanation: Micah condemns those who lie awake plotting to seize others’ property and act as soon as the chance comes.
judaism.tie_back: Captures the Kural’s schemer who covets and waits for the right moment to take.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Abandoning the taking of what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given. He takes only what is given, accepts only what is given, lives not by stealth but by means of a self that has become pure.”
buddhism.explanation: Describing the virtue of a monk, the Buddha contrasts a life of stealth with one lived by a purified self.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s stealthy watcher and the Buddha’s ‘life by stealth’ are the same figure; purity of heart excludes both.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A thief feels neither pity nor shame, nor does he possess discipline and faith. There is no evil that he cannot do for wealth.”
jainism.explanation: Śivārya's Digambara manual on monastic discipline says that the thief's mind has no room for compassion. Its fixation on wealth crowds out pity, shame and faith.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who covet another's goods and wait for his careless moment cannot be people of compassion (aruḷ). The Jain verse says the same thing directly: “A thief feels neither pity nor shame.”
jainism.source: Bhagavatī Ārādhanā 862 (Śivārya), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Bronze is bright and shiny, but when it is rubbed, its blackness appears.”
sikhism.explanation: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, Guru Nanak sang this hymn at the inn of Sajjan. Sajjan seemed a pious host to travellers but robbed them once they were off guard, and he repented on hearing it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who covet others' goods and wait for a moment of carelessness cannot have loving compassion. Sajjan's polished hospitality hiding a predator's watchfulness is exactly that bright surface over darkness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Mecone, when gods and mortals were settling their portions, Prometheus divided an ox deceptively: the meat and fat innards hidden in the ox’s stomach, and the bare bones wrapped in glistening fat. He invited Zeus to choose, hoping he would be fooled by appearances; Zeus in anger withheld fire from mankind.
greek_mythology.explanation: A trick in the dividing of shares, relying on the other party taking the surface at face value, poisons the relationship between gods and humans.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the Kural’s point that a dealer who counts on the other side’s oversight destroys goodwill.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is always a matter of duty that a dealer should not over charge an inexperienced purchaser”
philosophy.explanation: Kant’s example of the honest shopkeeper: exploiting a buyer who cannot judge the price is the plain wrong that honesty forbids.
philosophy.tie_back: The inexperienced purchaser is the person whose unguarded moment the Kural’s fraudster is waiting for.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section (tr. T. K. Abbott)

real_life_example.event_title: Colonel Blood's attempt to steal the Crown Jewels
real_life_example.place: Tower of London, London, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Thomas Blood, an Irish adventurer, disguised himself as a clergyman and visited the Crown Jewels at the Tower of London, gradually winning the trust and friendship of their elderly keeper, Talbot Edwards, and his family. On 9 May 1671 he returned with accomplices, and once Edwards had unlocked the jewel room they overpowered him and seized the crown, orb and sceptre. The alarm was raised and Blood was caught before he could leave the Tower, but King Charles II later pardoned him.
real_life_example.explanation: The plot is remembered as one of history's most audacious thefts, carried out by exploiting the goodwill of a man who had befriended the thief.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who covet another's goods and wait for his unguarded moment cannot be people of love, and Blood cultivated a friendship precisely to catch his keeper off guard.

tamil:
அளவின்கண் நின்றொழுகல் ஆற்றார் களவின்கண்
கன்றிய காத லவர்.
transliteration:
Alavinkan nindrozhugal aatraar kalavinkan,
Kandriya kaadha lavar.
meaning: People with a deep-rooted desire for stealing cannot live within proper limits.
elementary: A scale in a shop is supposed to measure fairly. Someone who loves cheating is like a scale with a broken spring — it can’t stay steady, and it keeps tipping the wrong way.
university: Aḷavu (“measure, limit”) is the key term of the second half of the chapter (286-289), and Valluvar plays on its near-rhyme with kaḷavu (“fraud, theft”). Commentators differ on what aḷavu means: Parimēlaḻakar takes it as the ascetic’s limited livelihood, Mu. Varadarasan as thrift or contentment, others as the rule of right conduct. The rhyme itself makes the point that fraud is a failure of measure, which is why honest weights and measures are the concrete test in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, the Qur’an and the Buddhist suttas. The couplet repeats kaṉṟiya kātal from 284, presenting fraud as a habit that eats away the ability to keep within limits.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who is regulated in his habits of eating, sleeping, recreation and work can mitigate all material pains by practicing the yoga system.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches moderation (yukta) — a measured life — as the foundation of spiritual discipline.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s ‘regulated’ person is the one who keeps within aḷavu; the Kural says the fraud-lover cannot.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that a set determination to become rich traps people in desires that drag them beyond all restraint.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes an entrenched desire for gain that destroys a person’s ability to live within bounds.

islam.quote_or_event: “Woe to those who give less [than due], Who, when they take a measure from people, take in full. But if they give by measure or by weight to them, they cause loss.”
islam.explanation: Surat al-Mutaffifin condemns traders who demand full measure for themselves but short-change others.
islam.tie_back: The literal failure of measure (aḷavu) through fraud in weights, the concrete form of the Kural’s abstract point.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not have in thy bag diverse weights, a great and a small. Thou shalt not have in thy house diverse measures, a great and a small. A perfect and just weight shalt thou have; a perfect and just measure shalt thou have…”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids even keeping two sets of weights, one for buying and one for selling.
judaism.tie_back: The fraudster’s ‘great and small’ weights are exactly a refusal to stand by a single, fixed measure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He abstains from running messages… from buying and selling… from dealing with false scales, false metals, and false measures… from bribery, deception, and fraud.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the virtues of the monk, the Buddha lists refusal to use false scales and measures and refusal of deception and fraud.
buddhism.tie_back: Makes honest measure part of the definition of virtue, as the Kural does.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “If there were numberless mountains of gold and silver, as big as Kailâsa, they would not satisfy a greedy man; for his avidity is boundless like space.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami, renouncing his kingdom, tells Indra that greed has no natural limit. No amount of wealth can satisfy it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says those in whom the love of fraudulent gain has hardened cannot keep within measure (aḷavu). Nami's verse describes the same measureless quality of greed, “boundless like space.”
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without contentment, no one is satisfied.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan describes a person who heaps up Maya and pleasures but never feels satisfied. He wears himself out chasing more, and only contentment (santokh) brings rest.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those hardened in love of fraudulent gain cannot keep within measure. Guru Arjan names contentment as the missing measure, without which desire knows no limit.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon cut down Ceres’ sacred oak for his own use. Ceres sent Famine to him, and he became insatiably hungry: he consumed all his wealth, repeatedly sold his daughter Mestra, and in the end devoured his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Someone who seized what was not his is punished with an appetite that has no limit.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An image of the Kural’s point that the fraud-lover cannot remain within any measure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…virtue must have the quality of aiming at the intermediate.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines moral virtue as hitting the mean between excess and deficiency.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s mean is a close counterpart to Valluvar’s aḷavu; the fraud-lover has lost the ability to aim at it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Bre-X gold fraud collapses
real_life_example.place: Busang, East Kalimantan, Indonesia, and Calgary and Toronto, Canada
real_life_example.event: The Canadian company Bre-X Minerals claimed an enormous gold deposit at Busang in Indonesia, and its stock became a star of the Toronto Stock Exchange. In March 1997 tests by the mining company Freeport found insignificant amounts of gold, and an independent review by Strathcona Mineral Services concluded that the core samples had been tampered with by adding gold from elsewhere. Billions of dollars in market value vanished, Bre-X went bankrupt in November 1997, and no one was ever criminally convicted of the fraud.
real_life_example.explanation: Called the biggest fraud in mining history, Bre-X showed how a deception can keep inflating its claims far beyond any natural limit until it collapses.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those hardened in the love of fraud cannot keep their conduct within measure, and the Busang claims swelled without limit until they burst.

tamil:
களவென்னும் காரறி வாண்மை அளவென்னும்
ஆற்றல் புரிந்தார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Kalavennum kaarari vaanmai alavennum,
Aatral purindhaarkan il.
meaning: Stealing is a dark, sneaky skill. People who have chosen the strength of living within proper limits do not have it.
elementary: Some people are clever in a sneaky, shadowy way. But a person who has learned to be happy with a fair share has a brighter kind of strength, and the sneaky cleverness simply has no room to live in them.
university: Kār aṟivu — literally “black knowledge” — is Valluvar’s striking name for fraud: an intelligence that is real but darkened, directed at deception rather than understanding. He opposes to it aḷavu eṉṉum āṟṟal, “the power called measure,” so that restraint is framed not as weakness but as a form of strength. The contrast anticipates Aristotle’s distinction between practical wisdom and mere cleverness (deinotēs), which can serve bad ends. Textual note: some online editions print the last word-group as புரிந்தார்கண்ட இல்; the reading புரிந்தார்கண் இல் given here follows Tamil Surangam and thirukkural-thamizh.org and fits the metre.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Among all modes of purification, purity in (the acquisition of) wealth is declared to be the best; for he is pure who gains wealth with clean hands, not he who purifies himself with earth and water.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu ranks honesty in acquiring wealth above every kind of ritual purity.
hinduism.tie_back: The person of ‘measure’ in the Kural is the one with clean hands in money matters; dark cleverness has no place there.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But godliness with contentment is great gain.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says true profit is godliness joined to contentment, not accumulation.
christianity.tie_back: Contentment is the ‘strength of measure’; it removes the motive for the dark cleverness of fraud.

islam.quote_or_event: “And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an even [i.e., honest] balance. That is the best [way] and best in result.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an commands honest measure and calls it both morally best and best in its outcome.
islam.tie_back: Affirms, like the Kural, that honest measure is a strength rather than a loss.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment with one’s portion.
judaism.tie_back: The contented person has the ‘strength of measure’ and so no use for fraud’s dark cleverness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ranks contentment above every material possession.
buddhism.tie_back: Contentment is the Kural’s aḷavu; where it is present, the urge to defraud does not arise.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Nirgrantha who has taken possession of some ground, should always take possession of a limited part of it and for a fixed time. The Kevalin says: If a Nirgrantha who has taken possession of some ground, should take possession of an unlimited part of it and for an unfixed time, he might take what is not given.”
jainism.explanation: One of the five clauses that protect the vow against stealing requires the monk to keep a strict limit on what he occupies and for how long. Going beyond that limit is treated as sliding into theft.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar sets 'measure' (aḷavu) against the dark cleverness of fraud. The Jain clause makes the same link institutional: keeping to a fixed measure is what keeps one from taking what is not given.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.15, third great vow, third clause (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, p. 206)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Hundreds of thousands of clever tricks, but not even one of them will go along with you in the end.”
sikhism.explanation: In the first pauri of Japji, Guru Nanak dismisses cleverness (siaanap) as a way to reach truth. Only walking in the Hukam, God's order, removes the wall of falsehood.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls fraud a 'dark cleverness' that is absent in those who have chosen the strength of measure. Japji likewise sets worldly cunning against the true discipline it can never replace.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, the newborn god uses his cunning to steal Apollo’s cattle and lie about it. When Zeus orders a reconciliation, Hermes gives Apollo the lyre, receives honours over herds in exchange, and swears he will never steal from Apollo again.
greek_mythology.explanation: The trickster’s dark cleverness is turned into lawful exchange once he accepts a fixed and agreed share.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the Kural’s point from the other side: fraudulent cunning ends once someone accepts measure (an agreed, fair portion).

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus tells his students to behave in life as at a banquet: when a dish is passed to you, reach out and take a moderate share; if it passes you by, do not grab after it; if it has not yet reached you, do not send your desire ahead of it.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic ideal is a disciplined measure in taking, grounded in accepting one’s portion.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s aḷavu is the banquet-guest’s moderation, which leaves no room for grabbing by stealth.

real_life_example.event_title: Ishida Baigan teaches honest dealing to Kyoto's merchants
real_life_example.event: Ishida Baigan, a farmer's son who had worked as an apprentice in a Kyoto merchant house, began giving public lectures in his home in 1729, founding the Shingaku (heart learning) movement. He taught that merchants' fairly earned profit was legitimate, that a true merchant must benefit his customer as well as himself, and that honesty and frugality were linked virtues. After his death, disciples spread his teaching to schools across Japan.
real_life_example.explanation: Baigan gave Japan's merchant class an ethic that treated honest restraint, not clever deception, as the source of a merchant's strength and standing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the dark cleverness of fraud is not found in those who have chosen the strength of measure, and Baigan taught merchants to choose exactly that measured honesty.

tamil:
அளவறிந்தார் நெஞ்சத் தறம்போல நிற்கும்
களவறிந்தார் நெஞ்சில் கரவு.
transliteration:
Alavarindhaar nenjath tharampola nirkum,
Kalavarindhaar nenjil karavu.
meaning: Goodness stays firmly in the hearts of people who know proper limits. In the same way, sneaky deceit stays in the hearts of people who know stealing.
elementary: Your heart is like a room. If you practise being fair, fairness moves in and makes itself at home. If you practise cheating, sneakiness moves in instead — and whoever lives there decides how you act.
university: The couplet is built on precise parallelism — aḷavu aṟintār / kaḷavu aṟintār (“those who know measure / those who know fraud”) — with the verb niṟkum (“stands, abides”) serving both halves. The point is that virtue and deceit (karavu, “concealment”) are both settled dispositions formed by what one has come to “know” through practice. This is close to Aristotle’s claim that we become just or unjust through our dealings with others, and to the Gospel image of the heart as a treasury from which good or evil is brought out. It also explains 284 and 286: once fraud is ‘known’ in this habitual sense, concealment becomes the heart’s standing condition.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Among them, the open rogues (are those) who subsist by (cheating in the sale of) various marketable commodities, but the concealed rogues are burglars, robbers in forests, and so forth.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu classifies thieves the king must restrain and puts dishonest traders among them, treating fraud in the market as a settled way of life.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu’s ‘rogues who subsist by cheating’ are the Kural’s kaḷavu aṟintār, people for whom deceit has become a livelihood and a habit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A good man out of the good treasure of the heart bringeth forth good things: and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth evil things.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus describes the heart as a storehouse whose contents determine a person’s words and deeds.
christianity.tie_back: Same two-sided structure as the Kural: virtue dwells in one kind of heart, deceit in the other.

islam.quote_or_event: “…and when a thief steals, then he is not a believer at the time of stealing…”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that faith and theft cannot occupy the heart at the same moment.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats the heart as holding either faith/virtue or deceit, but not both together.

judaism.quote_or_event: “This is as Shmuel said: It is prohibited to deceive people, and even to deceive a gentile.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud’s principle of geneivat da’at (‘theft of the mind’) treats creating false impressions as a form of theft, and lists many everyday examples.
judaism.tie_back: The rabbis, like Valluvar, see deceit (karavu) as fraud’s inner form, forbidden even when no goods change hands.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Chullin 94a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Think not lightly of evil, saying, ‘It will not come to me.’ Drop by drop is the water pot filled. Likewise, the fool, gathering it little by little, fills himself with evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says character fills up gradually, one small deed at a time.
buddhism.tie_back: Explains how kaḷavu aṟintār come to have deceit settled in the heart: little by little, through repeated practice.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When he is overcome by violent desire, takes another's property, and is not satisfied with those 'colours' and their possession, then his deceit and falsehood increase on account of his greed; yet he will not get rid of his misery.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana describes how one act of taking another's property leads to settled habits of deceit and falsehood, fed by greed.
