jainism.tie_back: The Kural says deceit lives steadily in the hearts of those who have learned fraud. The Jain verse shows how deceit grows and takes root in the one who takes what belongs to others.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who have one thing in their heart, and something else in their mouth, are judged to be false.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid contrasts those whose love is true in the heart with those whose inner mind and outward words do not match.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says virtue abides in the hearts of those who know measure, while deceit abides in the hearts of those who have learned fraud. Farid likewise judges people by what is settled in the heart, not by what they show.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus’ maternal grandfather Autolycus is said to have surpassed all men in thievery and in the oath, a skill given to him by Hermes, whom he honoured with sacrifices.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents skill in theft and tricky oaths as a settled excellence of character, almost a gift of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An example of the Kural’s kaḷavu aṟintār: for Autolycus deceit has become a stable second nature.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “by doing the acts that we do in our transactions with other men we become just or unjust”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle teaches that moral character is formed by habit, and that justice or injustice is built up through how we deal with others.
philosophy.tie_back: The same two-sided account of habituation as the Kural: repeated honest dealing makes virtue settle in, and repeated fraud makes deceit settle in.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Hwang Woo-suk's stem cell papers are found to be fabricated
real_life_example.place: Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea
real_life_example.event: Korean scientist Hwang Woo-suk had published two celebrated papers in Science, in 2004 and 2005, claiming breakthroughs in cloned human embryonic stem cells. Investigations by Seoul National University found that a significant amount of the data in both papers had been fabricated, and Science retracted them. Hwang was dismissed from the university in March 2006.
real_life_example.explanation: The scandal revealed not a single lapse but deception repeated across separate papers, and it became one of the best-known cases of research fraud.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says deceit settles permanently in the hearts of those who have learned fraud, and Hwang's fabrication recurred from one paper to the next.

tamil:
அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர் களவல்ல
மற்றைய தேற்றா தவர்.
transliteration:
Alavalla seydhaange veevar kalavalla,
Matraiya thetraa thavar.
meaning: People who know nothing but stealing will be destroyed right there, while doing things that go beyond proper limits.
elementary: If the only trick you know is cheating, it’s like a player who only knows how to foul — sooner or later, right in the middle of the game, they get caught and sent off.
university: The couplet says the fraudster’s ruin is not deferred but comes āṅkē — “right there,” in the act itself. The phrase kaḷavu alla maṟṟaiya tēṟṟātavar (“those who do not understand anything other than fraud”) describes a person whose repertoire has narrowed to one method, which completes the habituation argument of 288. Plato gives a striking parallel: a completely unjust person could not act at all, because cooperation depends on some remnant of justice. Acts 5’s account of Ananias, struck down while misrepresenting a sale, is the most literal illustration of perishing ‘right there.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But he who enjoys such gifts without offering them to the demigods in return is certainly a thief.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna calls anyone who only takes and never gives back a thief, cut off from the cycle of reciprocity that sustains life.
hinduism.tie_back: The person who knows nothing but taking has broken the order that sustains him, which parallels the Kural’s self-destroying fraudster.

christianity.quote_or_event: Ananias and Sapphira sold a property, secretly kept back part of the price, and presented the rest as the whole. When Peter confronted him, “Ananias hearing these words fell down, and gave up the ghost”.
christianity.explanation: A deception about the price of a sale is followed at once by death.
christianity.tie_back: The most literal parallel to āṅkē vīvar — the fraudster perishes ‘right there,’ in the act.

islam.quote_or_event: “And O my people, give full measure and weight in justice and do not deprive the people of their due and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption.”
islam.explanation: The prophet Shu’ayb warns the people of Madyan, notorious for short-weighting, to stop; the Qur’an goes on to tell how they persisted and were destroyed (11:94).
islam.tie_back: A community that knew nothing but fraud in measure perished in its measureless deeds, as the Kural warns.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The getting of treasures by a lying tongue Is a vapour driven to and fro; they [that seek them] seek death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says treasure gained by lies is a passing vapour, and those who pursue it are in effect pursuing their own death.
judaism.tie_back: Matches the Kural: those committed to deceitful gain are destroyed by the very pursuit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who destroys life, utters lies, takes what is not given, goes to another man’s wife, and is addicted to intoxicating drinks — such a man digs up his own root even in this world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that one who takes what is not given destroys his own foundations in this very life.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Digs up his own root even in this world’ matches the Kural’s ruin āṅkē — here and now.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
jainism.explanation: Jacobi's note gives the commentator Devendra's story. A burglar is caught by the feet in the hole he dug, and as his companion pulls him from the other side, the wall falls and crushes him: he dies in the very breach he made.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who know nothing but fraud are ruined 'right there' (āṅkē), in the act itself. The Jain image of the burglar killed in his own breach is almost exactly that picture.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3, with Jacobi's note citing Devendra's commentary (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O my mind, do not practice deception, even inadvertently. In the end, your own soul shall have to answer for its account.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir describes a man who brings home others' wealth through many deceptions. He warns that the deceiver's own soul must render the account, and none of those he fed will help him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who know no way of living but fraud are destroyed by their own measureless deeds. Kabir likewise makes the deceiver's ruin the direct reckoning of his own deception.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 656, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sisyphus, remembered as the craftiest of men for his many deceptions (including cheating death), is seen by Odysseus in the underworld endlessly pushing a huge stone uphill, only for it to roll back each time.
greek_mythology.explanation: A life built entirely on trickery ends in labour that achieves nothing and never ends.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘those who know nothing but fraud’ find their cleverness turned into futile, self-defeating action.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for had they been whole villains, and utterly unjust, they would have been utterly incapable of action.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that even a band of thieves needs some justice among its members to act; total injustice would make action impossible.
philosophy.tie_back: A philosophical form of the Kural’s claim: someone who knows only fraud undermines the very conditions for successful action and fails in the act.

real_life_example.event_title: The Mona Lisa thief is caught trying to sell it
real_life_example.event: Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian former worker at the Louvre, took the Mona Lisa from the museum in August 1911 and hid it in his Paris room for more than two years. In late 1913 he wrote to Florentine art dealer Alfredo Geri offering to sell it, and Geri, together with Uffizi director Giovanni Poggi, examined the painting and alerted the police. Peruggia was arrested at his hotel in Florence on 11 December 1913 and the painting was returned to the Louvre.
real_life_example.explanation: After two years of perfect concealment, the theft unravelled at the very moment the thief tried to profit from it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who know no way but fraud are destroyed in the very act, and Peruggia was undone in the act of trying to cash in on his theft.

tamil:
கள்வார்க்குத் தள்ளும் உயிர்நிலை கள்ளார்க்குத்
தள்ளாது புத்தேள் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kalvaarkkuth thallum uyirnilai kallaarkkuth,
Thallaadhu puththel ulagu.
meaning: Thieves lose even their own lives. People who never steal will not miss out on heaven (the world of the gods).
elementary: Cheaters can lose even the simple things everyone needs, like a safe life. People who stay honest are promised the biggest prize of all, like a door to heaven that will always open for them.
university: The chapter ends with an antithesis built on one verb, taḷḷu (“to fail, to reject”): life itself (uyirnilai, the soul’s stay in the body) ‘fails’ the kaḷvār, while the world of the gods (puttēḷ ulaku) ‘does not fail’ the kaḷḷār. Solomon Pappaiah reads the first clause vividly as ‘even their own life shuns the thief.’ Textual note: some online editions repeat கள்வார்க்குத் in the second line, but the antithesis requires கள்ளார்க்குத் (“to those who do not defraud”), which is the reading of Tamil Surangam, thirukkural-thamizh.org and the standard commentaries. The contrast of this-worldly collapse with heavenly reward parallels 1 Corinthians 6:10, the Chandogya Upanishad’s list of those who ‘fall,’ and the Talmud’s first question at the heavenly court.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who steals gold, or drinks liquor, or goes to bed with his teacher’s wife, or kills a brāhmin—these four are lost. Also lost is the fifth—one who keeps company with such people.”
hinduism.explanation: In its teaching on the paths of souls after death, the Chandogya lists the thief of gold among the gravest sinners, who are ‘lost’ (patanti, ‘fall’).
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties theft to the soul’s downfall, in contrast to the higher worlds reached by the virtuous (5.10.7).

christianity.quote_or_event: “Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists thieves, the covetous and extortioners among those shut out of God’s kingdom.
christianity.tie_back: The negative mirror of the Kural’s second line: heaven fails the defrauder and, by implication, stays open to the honest.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do they not think that they will be resurrected For a tremendous Day - The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds?”
islam.explanation: Straight after condemning those who give short measure, the Qur’an reminds them of the Day of Judgement.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sets fraud in dealings against one’s final destiny.

judaism.quote_or_event: “…when a person is brought to judgment for the life he lived in this world, they say to him in the order of that verse: Did you conduct business faithfully?”
judaism.explanation: Rava teaches that the first question asked at the heavenly court is whether one dealt honestly in business.
judaism.tie_back: Makes honesty in dealings the first key to the world beyond, as the Kural makes non-fraud the guarantee of the gods’ world.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Some are born in the womb; the wicked are born in hell; the devout go to heaven; the stainless pass into Nibbana.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada sets out the different destinies that follow different kinds of conduct.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s two-way contrast of downfall for wrongdoers and heaven for the upright.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A sinner, though he be a mendicant (friar), will not escape hell; but a pious man, whether monk or householder, ascends to heaven.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's sermon on two kinds of death says that destiny follows conduct, not status. Sinners fall to hell, while the virtuous, lay or monastic, rise to the heavens of the gods.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural closes the chapter by contrasting the fraudster, whom even bodily life fails, with the honest person, for whom the world of the gods does not fail. The Jain verse draws the same contrast between the sinner and the pious person who reaches heaven.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who does not steal the wealth of others, who does not commit evil deeds or sinful acts - the Messenger of Death does not even approach him.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan says that one who sings God's praises and keeps clear of others' wealth is beyond the reach of Death's messenger.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ends by saying the world of the gods will not fail those who never defraud. Guru Arjan likewise promises that one who never takes others' wealth is safe from Death's messenger.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 684, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But they who give straight judgements to strangers and to the men of the land, and go not aside from what is just, their city flourishes, and the people prosper in it”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod contrasts the prosperity and peace the gods grant the just with the ruin they send on the crooked.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sets divine favour for the straight dealer against collapse for the crooked one.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225-227 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial Socrates declares that the gods do not neglect the good, in this life or the next.
philosophy.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s confidence that the honest will not be failed, even beyond death.

real_life_example.event_title: Forger Han van Meegeren is convicted and dies weeks later
real_life_example.event: After the Second World War a supposed Vermeer was found in Hermann Goering's collection and traced to the Dutch painter Han van Meegeren, who was arrested on suspicion of collaboration. He declared that the painting was his own forgery and proved it by painting another 'Vermeer' under supervision, and chemical analysis confirmed modern materials in his works. On 12 November 1947 he was convicted of forgery and fraud and sentenced to one year in prison, but he died on 30 December 1947 before serving it.
real_life_example.explanation: Van Meegeren's career of deception ended in public exposure, conviction and, within weeks, the end of his life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those who defraud even life in the body fails them, and van Meegeren did not outlive his conviction for long.

tamil:
வாய்மை எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும்
தீமை இலாத சொலல்.
transliteration:
Vaaymai enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhondrum
Theemai ilaadha solal.
meaning: If you ask what truthfulness is, it is speaking words that cause no harm of any kind to anyone.
elementary: Being truthful isn’t only about not telling lies. Imagine your words are like gifts you hand to people — a truthful gift is one that never hurts anybody. So truth means saying things that are real AND that don’t cause harm.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a deliberately surprising definition: vaaymai is not defined by correspondence to fact (the usual Western criterion) but by its effect — speech ‘without even the least evil’ (yaadhondrum theemai ilaadha). The standard commentators (Parimelazhagar, Mu. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah) all read theemai as harm to others, so truth becomes an ethical rather than merely epistemic category. This places the Kural within the broader Indian tradition that fuses satya with ahimsa, and it sets up the controversial next couplet (292) on beneficial untruth. The verse’s rhetorical form — a question answered in a definition (enappaduvadhu yaadhenin, ‘if one asks what is called…’) — marks it as the chapter’s thesis statement.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Words that do not cause distress, are truthful, inoffensive, and beneficial, as well as regular recitation of the Vedic scriptures—these are declared as austerity of speech.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines the discipline of speech as words that are true AND do not upset or harm the listener. The commentary on this verse also cites Manu 4.138: speak the truth, speak what is pleasing, do not speak an unpleasant truth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita builds harmlessness into the very definition of right, truthful speech.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers that every word should build people up and do them good, never tear them down.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts judge speech by its effect on the hearer: good speech ‘ministers grace,’ never harm.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allāh and speak words of appropriate justice.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asks believers to speak ‘qawlan sadīdan’ — speech that is straight, true, and right, the next verse promising that God will set their deeds right in return.
islam.tie_back: ‘Appropriate, just’ speech unites truth with rightness toward others, echoing the Kural’s harmless truth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour; execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates.”
judaism.explanation: The prophet Zechariah joins truth and peace as a pair: speaking truth is meant to build a peaceful community.
judaism.tie_back: Truth in Zechariah is always paired with peace, just as the Kural pairs it with harmlessness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak only the speech that neither torments self nor does harm to others. That speech is truly well spoken.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Subhasita Sutta, Vangisa praises the Buddha’s teaching that good speech must hurt neither the speaker nor anyone else; the same verses call truth ‘deathless speech.’
buddhism.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s definition: right speech is speech free of harm, grounded in truth.
buddhism.source: Subhasita Sutta, Sutta Nipata 3.3 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Speaking what is not commendable–asat–is falsehood (anṛta).” … “What is not laudable? That which causes pain and suffering to the living beings is not commendable. It does not matter whether it refers to the actual fact or not.”
jainism.explanation: Umāsvāti's definition of falsehood, as explained by Pūjyapāda, rests on harm rather than on factual accuracy. Speech that causes pain to living beings counts as untruth because every Jain vow serves ahiṃsā.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar defines truthfulness as speech that harms no one in any way. Pūjyapāda defines its opposite as speech that causes pain to living beings, 'whether it refers to the actual fact or not.' The two definitions mirror each other almost exactly.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.14, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all.”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks Sheikh Farid tells the seeker never to wound anyone with speech, because God dwells in every heart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines truthful speech as speech that harms no one in any way. Farid grounds the same ideal of harmless speech in God's presence in all beings.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And Sea begat Nereus, the eldest of his children, who is true and lies not: and men call him the Old Man because he is trusty and gentle and does not forget the laws of righteousness, but thinks just and kindly thoughts.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s Nereus, the ‘Old Man of the Sea,’ is the Greek god famed for never lying — and Hesiod pairs his truthfulness with gentleness and kindly thoughts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Nereus embodies truth that is also gentle and kind — truth without harm.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Immanuel Kant, in his 1797 essay ‘On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy,’ argued that truthfulness in all statements is an unconditional duty of reason — one may not lie even to a murderer asking where a friend is hiding.
philosophy.explanation: Kant defines truthfulness purely as not asserting falsehood, whatever the consequences to others.
philosophy.tie_back: An instructive contrast: Kant defines truth by the statement, Valluvar by its effect on others — and would likely judge Kant’s truthful answer to the murderer as not vaaymai at all.
philosophy.source: Kant, On a Supposed Right to Lie (1797)

real_life_example.event_title: Elisabeth Kubler-Ross talks honestly with dying patients
real_life_example.place: University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, United States
real_life_example.event: In 1965 the psychiatrist Elisabeth Kubler-Ross joined the University of Chicago and began a series of seminars in which terminally ill patients were interviewed and allowed to speak openly about their illness and their care. At the time many doctors avoided telling patients that their condition was terminal, and some colleagues thought her seminars cruel, but she found that patients wanted to be treated as people and spoken to frankly. Her book On Death and Dying (1969), drawn from these interviews, helped change the medical approach to the care of the dying.
real_life_example.explanation: Kubler-Ross showed that honest speech, offered with compassion, relieved the isolation of the dying rather than harming them, and her work helped make truthful, caring conversation part of end-of-life medicine.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines truthfulness as speech that brings no harm to anyone, and Kubler-Ross demonstrated that even the hardest truths could be spoken in a way that comforted rather than wounded.

tamil:
பொய்மையும் வாய்மை யிடத்த புரைதீர்ந்த
நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்.
transliteration:
Poymaiyum vaaymai yidaththa puraitheerndha
Nanmai payakkum enin.
meaning: Even a lie can count as the truth if it brings about pure good with no harm in it.
elementary: Imagine a friend is scared before a big test and asks if they look nervous. Saying “You look calm and ready!” — to help them, not to trick them for your own gain — is the kind of “kind untruth” this kural talks about. But it only counts if it does real good and hurts no one.
university: This is one of the most debated couplets in the Kural. Having defined truth by harmlessness in 291, Valluvar draws the logical consequence: a statement that is factually false but yields ‘faultless good’ (puraitheerndha nanmai) occupies ‘the place of truth’ (vaaymai idaththa). The qualifier purai theerndha — ‘with the defect removed’ — is strict: the good must be free of any taint, not merely useful to the speaker. Commentators diverge on scope: Varadarasan says such words ‘obtain the place’ of truth; Pappaiah reads it as permission to speak falsely where truth would otherwise be required. The verse places the Kural in a consequentialist line of Indian ethics (compare Krishna’s teaching in the Mahabharata) rather than the absolutism of Kant or of Buddhist precept.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Truth may be unutterable, and even falsehood may be utterable where falsehood would become truth and truth would become falsehood.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna the story of the ascetic Kausika, who had vowed always to speak the truth. When robbers asked him which way their fleeing victims had gone, he told them truthfully; the victims were killed, and Kausika fell into hell for the harm his ‘truth’ caused.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s logic: a harmful ‘truth’ ceases to be truth, and a harmless untruth can take truth’s place.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Karna Parva, Section 69 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way?”
christianity.explanation: Rahab hid Israel’s spies and misled the king’s men to save their lives (Joshua 2); the New Testament praises her as justified by her deed.
christianity.tie_back: A deception that saved innocent lives is honoured — close to the Kural’s ‘faultless good.’

islam.quote_or_event: “He who makes peace between the people by inventing good information or saying good things, is not a liar.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that someone who carries good (even embellished) words between quarrelling people to reconcile them is not counted a liar.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, Islam allows a narrowly bounded untruth when its fruit is pure good — here, peace.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is permitted for a person to depart from the truth in a matter that will bring peace.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud cites Joseph’s brothers, and even God’s softened report of Sarah’s words to Abraham, as examples of altering the truth to preserve peace. Rabbi Natan calls it a mitzvah.
judaism.tie_back: Jewish law, like the Kural, lets a peace-making untruth stand in truth’s place.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 65b (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz tr.)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be unfactual, untrue, unbeneficial, but endearing & agreeable to others, he does not say them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists which words he will speak: only what is true and beneficial, with a sense of the proper time. As the translator notes, the possibility of saying something untrue but beneficial is not even considered.
buddhism.tie_back: An honest contrast: early Buddhism shares the Kural’s concern for benefit, but will never allow falsehood to take truth’s place.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mendicant should not tell it, nor show it, he should not comply with their request, but look on silently, or, though knowing it, he should say that he did not know.”
jainism.explanation: If travellers ask a wandering monk whether he has seen a man or an animal on the road, the Ācārāṅga tells him not to give them away. He should stay silent or, though he knows, say that he does not know, so that no living being comes to harm.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar allows that even a falsehood stands in place of truth when it produces faultless good. The Jain monk is likewise permitted to say 'I do not know', against the literal facts, in order to protect life.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.3.3.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, pp. 146-147)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, where there is spiritual wisdom, there is righteousness and Dharma. Where there is falsehood, there is sin.”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks Bhagat Kabir sets falsehood plainly on the side of sin. Gurbani as a whole treats kooR (falsehood) as the wall between the soul and God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural allows that a falsehood can stand in the place of truth if it produces faultless good. Gurbani offers no such exception, which makes this verse a point of contrast rather than agreement.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “We know how to speak many false things as though they were true; but we know, when we will, to utter true things.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The Muses tell Hesiod that they can speak convincing falsehoods as well as truth — the divine source of poetry itself deals in both.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Greek myth, like the Kural, recognises that falsehood can wear truth’s clothing — though the Muses do not limit it to ‘faultless good.’

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic (389b), Socrates says falsehood is useless to the gods but may be useful to humans ‘as a medicine,’ and that only the rulers may use it, for the good of the city.
philosophy.explanation: Plato accepts a ‘medicinal lie’ for the common good, while condemning the ‘true lie’ of self-deception in the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Both Plato and Valluvar allow falsehood when it heals rather than harms — though Plato restricts it to rulers.

real_life_example.event_title: Doctors at Rome's Fatebenefratelli Hospital invent K Syndrome
real_life_example.place: Fatebenefratelli Hospital, Tiber Island, Rome, Italy
real_life_example.event: After the Nazi round-up of Jews in Rome on 16 October 1943, doctors at the Fatebenefratelli Hospital, led by head physician Giovanni Borromeo, admitted Jewish and anti-fascist refugees as patients and listed them in official records as suffering from K Syndrome, an invented and supposedly contagious disease. Occupying soldiers who searched the hospital avoided the wards said to hold these patients, and the hospital continued sheltering refugees until the Allies entered Rome in June 1944. In 2004 Yad Vashem recognised Borromeo as Righteous Among the Nations.
real_life_example.explanation: The doctors deliberately told a falsehood whose only purpose and effect was to save innocent lives, at serious risk to themselves.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says even a falsehood takes the place of truth when it yields good wholly free of fault, and the invented disease that protected refugees is about as clear a case of such a blameless lie as history offers.

tamil:
தன்நெஞ் சறிவது பொய்யற்க பொய்த்தபின்
தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்.
transliteration:
Than nenju arivadhu poyyarka poyththapin
Than nenjae thannaich chudum.
meaning: Do not lie about what your own heart knows is true. Once you lie, your own heart will burn you with guilt.
elementary: Have you ever told a fib and then felt a hot, uncomfortable feeling inside, even if no one found out? That feeling is your own heart “burning” you. This kural says: don’t lie against what you know is true, because your conscience will punish you.
university: The couplet moves truthfulness from the social sphere into the interior. ‘Than nenju arivadhu’ — what one’s own heart knows — specifies a deliberate lie, one told against one’s own knowledge. The punishment is not external: ‘than nenjae thannaich chudum,’ the self’s own heart scorches the self. The repetition of than (self) three times across two lines enacts the reflexive structure of conscience. Kalaignar explicitly glosses nenju as manachaatchi, ‘conscience,’ and Pappaiah adds that the burning intensifies when the world discovers the lie — combining inner guilt with outer shame.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Soul itself is the witness of the Soul, and the Soul is the refuge of the Soul; despise not thy own Soul, the supreme witness of men.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu warns witnesses in court not to lie, because their own inner self is the highest witness; the next verse says the wicked think no one sees them, but the gods and ‘the male within their own breasts’ see them.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make the inner self the witness and judge of every lie.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God.”
christianity.explanation: John describes the heart as an inner court that condemns or acquits us, with God knowing even more than our heart.
christianity.tie_back: The self-accusing heart is the Kural’s burning heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “Leave what makes you in doubt for what does not make you in doubt. The truth brings tranquility while falsehood sows doubt.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that truth settles the heart while lying leaves it restless and troubled.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘burning heart’ after a lie is Islam’s ‘doubt’ that falsehood sows within.

judaism.quote_or_event: “LORD, who shall abide in thy tabernacle? who shall dwell in thy holy hill? He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist says the one fit to stand before God speaks truth ‘in his heart’ — inner words agreeing with outer ones.
judaism.tie_back: Both demand that speech never betray what the heart knows.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When anyone feels no shame in telling a deliberate lie, there is no evil, I tell you, he will not do.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches his young son Rahula that shamelessness about deliberate lies empties a person of spiritual worth, and tells him to reflect on every action like looking in a mirror.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s burning heart is exactly the healthy shame the Buddha wants Rahula to keep.
buddhism.source: Ambalatthika-rahulovada Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 61 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “After and before he has lied, and when he is on the point of lying, he feels infinitely unhappy.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana describes the inner torment that surrounds a lie: before it, while it is being told, and after it.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar warns that once you lie against what your own heart knows, your heart will burn you. The Jain verse likewise places the punishment for lying inside the liar, as 'infinite' unhappiness.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Speaking lies, one eats poison; the self-willed manmukh departs, crying out in pain.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of the Vaar in Raag Raamkalee, Guru Amar Das says that the liar feeds himself poison. The self-willed person (manmukh) who lives by falsehood leaves the world in anguish.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a lie told against what one's own heart knows will burn that heart. Guru Amar Das likewise makes the lie a poison taken by the liar himself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 948, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For hateful in my eyes, even as the gates of Hades, is that man that hideth one thing in his mind and sayeth another.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles tells Odysseus he despises anyone whose words differ from what is in his mind.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles condemns the same split the Kural forbids: saying what the heart knows is false.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic (382a-c), Socrates distinguishes the ‘true lie’ — falsehood lodged in the soul about the most important things — which gods and men hate above all, from the mere lie in words.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, the worst harm of falsehood is to the liar’s own soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers locate the deepest damage of lying inside the liar.

real_life_example.event_title: Thomas More refuses to swear the oath his conscience rejected
real_life_example.place: Lambeth Palace and the Tower of London, London, England
real_life_example.event: On 13 April 1534 Sir Thomas More, the former Lord Chancellor, appeared before the king's commissioners at Lambeth and said he would accept the royal succession but refused to swear the Oath of Succession, whose preamble renounced papal authority and affirmed Henry VIII's supremacy over the Church. He was imprisoned in the Tower of London, where he was interrogated several times and continued to refuse to affirm what he did not believe. He was convicted of treason on 1 July 1535 and beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535.
real_life_example.explanation: More chose imprisonment and death rather than state on oath something his own conscience held to be false.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns never to lie about what one's own heart knows to be true, and More would not utter such a lie even to save his life.

tamil:
உள்ளத்தாற் பொய்யா தொழுகின் உலகத்தார்
உள்ளத்து ளெல்லாம் உளன்.
transliteration:
Ullaththaal poyyaadhu ozhukin ulagaththaar
Ullaththul ellaam ulan.
meaning: A person who lives without lying, even inside their own heart, will have a place in the hearts of everyone in the world.
elementary: Think of someone you completely trust — a grandparent or a teacher who never tricks you. You carry them in your heart, don’t you? This kural says that if you are honest even inside your own thoughts, everyone will keep you in their hearts too.
university: The couplet is built on an elegant chiasmus of ullam (heart/mind): one who does not lie ‘with the heart’ (ullaththaal) comes to live ‘in the hearts’ (ullaththul) of all. Truthfulness here extends past speech to conduct (ozhukin, ‘if one conducts oneself’) and even to thought — Kalaignar reads it as not even thinking falsehood. The reward is not wealth or heaven but a permanent place in human regard, which links this chapter to the preceding chapter on fame (புகழ், ch. 24). Pappaiah narrows ‘ulagaththaar’ to the noble (uyarndhavar), following the classical reading of ulagam as ‘the worthy.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, who kept his word at the cost of his kingdom, his family and his freedom, is remembered across India as ‘Satya Harishchandra’ — the very name a byword for truthfulness. Gandhi wrote that the play about him shaped his lifelong devotion to truth.
hinduism.explanation: The Puranic king who refused to break his word even in utter ruin became a permanent hero in the popular imagination.
hinduism.tie_back: Harishchandra is the Kural’s promise fulfilled: truthfulness made him dwell in the hearts of all people.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!”
christianity.explanation: Jesus singles out Nathanael for praise because there is no deceit in him at all.
christianity.tie_back: A heart without guile wins the highest regard — the Kural’s reward.

islam.quote_or_event: “And grant me a mention [i.e., reputation] of honor among later generations.”
islam.explanation: Abraham prays for a good name among later generations; the Arabic is ‘lisāna ṣidqin,’ literally ‘a tongue of truth.’
islam.tie_back: The truthful prophet asks for exactly the Kural’s reward: to live on in the regard of all people.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue is but for a moment.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says truthful speech lasts forever, while lies pass away quickly.
judaism.tie_back: Truth gives a lasting place in the world; lies vanish — the same contrast as the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “People hold dear him who embodies virtue and insight, who is principled, has realized the truth, and who himself does what he ought to be doing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the one people cherish is virtuous and truthful (the Pali saccavādin also means ‘truth-speaker’).
buddhism.tie_back: Being held dear by all people is the Kural’s ‘dwelling in their hearts.’

jainism.quote_or_event: “A truthful man is treated as reliable as the mother, as venerable as the guru (preceptor) and as beloved as the one who commands knowledge.”
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic teaching holds that truthfulness earns a person the trust, reverence and affection of everyone around them.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural promises that one who never lies even in the heart will live in the hearts of all people. The Jain verse says the truthful man becomes trusted like a mother and beloved by all.
jainism.source: Mūlācāra 837 (Vaṭṭakera), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One knows the Truth only when the Truth is in his heart.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak says truth is real only when it lives in the heart, not merely on the tongue.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural promises that one who is free of falsehood even in the heart will live in the hearts of all people. Guru Nanak shares the first half: truth must first dwell in one's own heart.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Whoever deliberately lies in his witness and forswears himself… that man’s generation is left obscure thereafter. But the generation of the man who swears truly is better thenceforward.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod teaches his brother that the liar’s family sinks into obscurity, while the truthful man’s line prospers and is remembered.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Truthfulness earns a lasting good name among people; lies bring oblivion.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 280-285 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes the truthful man as one who is true in word and in life even where nothing is at stake, simply because his character is such — and who will therefore be all the more truthful where much is at stake.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, truthfulness is a settled state of character, not a calculation.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘not lying with the heart’ is Aristotle’s truthfulness rooted in character.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.7 (paraphrase of W. D. Ross tr.)

real_life_example.event_title: Walter Cronkite is named the most trusted man in America
real_life_example.event: Walter Cronkite anchored the CBS Evening News from the early 1960s until 1981 and was known for his adherence to journalistic integrity, reporting events from the Kennedy assassination to the Moon landing. In 1972 an Oliver Quayle poll named him the most trusted man in America, ranking him above the president, the vice-president and members of Congress. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1981.
real_life_example.explanation: Cronkite's standing rested on a public belief that he would not knowingly deceive his audience, and that trust gave him lasting affection across a divided country.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who lives without falsehood dwells in the hearts of all people, and Cronkite's reputation for truthfulness won him a place in the regard of a whole nation.

tamil:
மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின் தவத்தொடு
தானஞ்செய் வாரின் தலை.
transliteration:
Manaththodu vaaymai mozhiyin thavaththodu
Thaanam seyvaarin thalai.
meaning: A person whose words are true and match their heart is greater than people who practice both strict self-control and giving to others.
elementary: Some people do hard things to look holy, like fasting, and some give lots of gifts. This kural says that someone who simply speaks the truth from the heart, every day, is even greater than people who do both of those big things.
university: Here Valluvar ranks truthfulness above the two most prestigious religious practices of his world: thavam (tapas, ascetic austerity, the subject of chapter 27) and dhaanam (charity/gift-giving). The qualifier manaththodu — ‘together with the mind’ — is decisive: only truth that agrees with inner conviction counts, not lip-truth (Kalaignar: ‘udhattalavil indri ulamaara,’ ‘not just from the lips but from the heart’). The couplet belongs to a broad pan-Indian and wider religious critique of ritualism, in which inner integrity outweighs outer observance. Its hierarchy — truth above tapas — is stated almost verbatim in the Mahabharata’s image of truth outweighing a hundred horse-sacrifices.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A hundred horse-sacrifices had once been weighed against Truth, and Truth was found heavier than a hundred horse-sacrifices.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala, rejected by King Dushmanta, reminds him that truth outweighs even the greatest Vedic rituals — equal, she says, to studying all the Vedas and bathing at every holy place.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s ranking: truthfulness weighs more than the grandest religious works.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 74 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that true worship is not about the right mountain or temple, but about spirit and truth.
christianity.tie_back: Inner truth, not outward religious performance, is what counts most.

islam.quote_or_event: “Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but [true] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allāh… Those are the ones who have been true, and it is those who are the righteous.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says real righteousness is not the direction you face in prayer, but faith, generosity, keeping promises and patience — and it calls such people ‘the ones who have been true.’
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the verse places inner truthfulness above outward ritual form.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.”
judaism.explanation: In his psalm of repentance David says God wants truth deep inside a person; a few verses later he adds that God does not delight in burnt offerings but in a broken and contrite heart (51:16-17).
judaism.tie_back: Inner truth over sacrifice — the Kural’s ‘truth with the heart’ above austerity and gifts.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth does one become a holy man. But he in whom truth and righteousness exist — he is pure, he is a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha rejects the outward marks of ascetics; the next verse mocks the man in antelope skins who ‘only outwardly’ cleanses himself.
buddhism.tie_back: Truth, not ascetic show, makes a person holy — the Kural’s point about austerity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One may have a tuft or matted hair on the head or a shaven head, remain naked or wear a rag. But if he tells a lie, all this is futile or fruitless.”
jainism.explanation: Śivārya says that all the outward marks of asceticism count for nothing if the ascetic is untruthful. In this text, truth outranks the visible practices of tapas.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks the one who speaks truth from the heart above those who practise both austerity and charity. The Jain verse makes the same ranking from the other side: without truth, austerity is fruitless.
jainism.source: Bhagavatī Ārādhanā 843 (Śivārya), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Pilgrimages, austere discipline, compassion and charity - these, by themselves, bring only an iota of merit.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak says that the recognised religious works, including austerity and charity, earn only a sesame-seed's worth of honour. What counts is hearing, believing and loving the Name within.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks truthful speech that agrees with the heart above those who practise both austerity and charity. Japji likewise puts austerity and charity below the inner relation with the True One.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 21, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Mecone, Prometheus tricked Zeus into choosing bones wrapped in fat rather than meat, and Hesiod explains this deception as the origin of how humans offer sacrifice — the ritual itself is born from a lie.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth the central religious ritual, animal sacrifice, is rooted in a trick played on the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A sideways contrast: Greek myth shows ritual without truth at its origin, while the Kural insists truth outranks ritual.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He who lies is guilty of impiety to the same divinity; for the universal nature is the nature of things that are.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius argues that because Nature itself is truth, lying is a sin against the divine — honesty is the true piety.
philosophy.tie_back: For the Stoic, as for Valluvar, truthfulness is itself the highest religious act.

real_life_example.event_title: Martin Luther refuses to recant at the Diet of Worms
real_life_example.event: Martin Luther, whose Ninety-five Theses of 1517 had condemned the sale of indulgences, was summoned before the Diet of the Holy Roman Empire at Worms under a safe-conduct. On 18 April 1521 he refused to repudiate his writings unless convinced of error by Scripture or by reason, declaring that his conscience was bound by the Word of God. The Edict of Worms then banned his writings and declared him a heretic and outlaw.
real_life_example.explanation: Luther's protest began as a challenge to the idea that religious merit could be bought through payments, and at Worms he placed sincere conviction above every outward religious authority.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks truth spoken in harmony with one's heart above both austerity and charity, and Luther, who had attacked purchased indulgences, insisted at Worms that he could speak only what his conscience held true.

tamil:
பொய்யாமை அன்ன புகழில்லை எய்யாமை
எல்லா அறமுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Poyyaamai anna pugazhillai eyyaamai
Ellaa aramum tharum.
meaning: No praise is as great as the praise for never lying. Without any extra effort, it brings every other good quality with it.
elementary: Being known as someone who never lies is the best reputation you can have. And it’s like a magnet — once you are truthful, other good habits, like fairness and kindness, come to you easily, without you even trying hard.
university: The couplet makes two claims: truthfulness is the supreme source of pugazh (fame, cf. ch. 24), and it ‘yields every dharma’ (ellaa aramum tharum). The pivot word eyyaamai is read in two ways: Parimelazhagar-line commentators take it as ‘without suffering/strain’ — truthfulness produces all virtue effortlessly, unlike painful austerity; Varadarasan and Pappaiah read it as ‘without one’s knowing it,’ i.e., the virtues accrue unnoticed. Either way the claim is that veracity is a generative, master virtue from which the others follow — a thesis close to the Islamic hadith that truthfulness leads to righteousness.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The true prevails, not the untrue; by the true the path is laid out, the way of the gods.”
hinduism.explanation: The Mundaka Upanishad — source of India’s national motto ‘Satyameva Jayate’ — says truth wins, and that truth itself lays down the road to the divine.
hinduism.tie_back: Truth that triumphs and opens the path to every good echoes the Kural’s truth that brings unmatched fame and all virtues.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes truth-telling the first step of the new life, because believers belong to one another like parts of one body.
christianity.tie_back: Truthfulness as the foundation from which the rest of the moral life grows.

islam.quote_or_event: “…the truthful men and truthful women… for them Allāh has prepared forgiveness and a great reward.”
islam.explanation: Among the qualities God praises in believing men and women, truthfulness appears alongside patience, charity and fasting, all promised a great reward.
islam.tie_back: Truthfulness earns the highest honour — divine praise and reward.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel used to say: on three things does the world stand: On justice, on truth and on peace.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah names truth as one of the three pillars that hold up the whole world.
judaism.tie_back: Truth as a foundation supporting everything else — the Kural’s ‘brings all virtues.’

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who utters gentle, instructive and truthful words, who imprecates none — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha gives truthful, gentle speech as one mark of the true brahmin, the person worthy of the highest honour.
buddhism.tie_back: Truthful speech earns the highest title of respect.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Truthfulness indeed is tapa (penance). In truthfulness do reside self-restraint and all other virtues. Just as the fish can live only in the sea, so can all other virtues reside in Truthfulness alone.”
jainism.explanation: The Bhagavatī Ārādhanā calls truthfulness the element that all the other virtues live in, as fish live in the sea.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that never lying brings every other virtue with it, without any strain. The Jain verse says that all virtues live in truthfulness, which is the same claim.
jainism.source: Bhagavatī Ārādhanā 842 (Śivārya), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Truth is the medicine for all; it removes and washes away our sins.”
sikhism.explanation: In the same salok of Asa di Vaar on what true living means, Guru Nanak calls Truth a cure for every ill, cleansing the person of wrongdoing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says truthfulness brings every other virtue with it, without strain. Guru Nanak makes truth the single remedy that heals everything else.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Muse, you and the daughter of Zeus, unforgetting Truth: with the hand that puts things right, keep from me the blame for lying, for wronging my friend.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar calls on Aletheia (Truth), daughter of Zeus, to protect his reputation from the blame of a broken promise.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In Greek thought Truth is a goddess who guards a person’s good name — the Kural’s link between truth and fame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And falsehood is in itself mean and culpable, and truth noble and worthy of praise.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle states that truthfulness is by its very nature noble and deserves praise.
philosophy.tie_back: Truth is ‘worthy of praise’ in itself — the Kural’s ‘no fame like truthfulness.’
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.7 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Raja Harishchandra, the story of the truthful king, opens India's film industry
real_life_example.event: Dadasaheb Phalke's silent film Raja Harishchandra, widely regarded as the first full-length Indian feature film, was released at the Coronation Cinema in Bombay on 3 May 1913. It told the legend of King Harishchandra, who gave up his kingdom and family to keep his word to the sage Vishwamitra and was finally restored. Because no women would take the roles, Phalke cast men in the female parts, and the film was a great success; only fragments survive today.
real_life_example.explanation: When India's first feature film needed a story that every audience would know and honour, it turned to the legend of a king remembered above all for never breaking faith with the truth.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says there is no fame like that of never lying, and the enduring fame of the truthful Harishchandra was strong enough to launch an entire national cinema.

tamil:
பொய்யாமை பொய்யாமை ஆற்றின் அறம்பிற
செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Poyyaamai poyyaamai aatrin aram pira
Seyyaamai seyyaamai nandru.
meaning: If you are truthful and never fail at it, that is enough, even if you do no other good deed.
elementary: Imagine a report card where one subject counts so much that getting it right is enough to pass everything. For Valluvar, truthfulness is that subject: if you never fail at being honest, you’re doing well even if you haven’t done any other good deeds yet.
university: A celebrated example of Valluvar’s wordplay: poyyaamai poyyaamai (literally ‘non-lying, not failing’) and seyyaamai seyyaamai (‘not doing, not doing’). The first pair means practising non-falsehood unfailingly; the second is read by most commentators (Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah) as ‘not doing [other virtues] is itself not a lack’ — truth alone suffices. Varadarasan offers a softer reading (‘practising other virtues also becomes good’), and Kalaignar reads it as truthfulness surpassing the merit of mere abstentions. The dominant reading makes veracity a sufficient condition of the good life, the strongest claim in the chapter after 300.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “satya-pratiṣṭhāyāṁ kriyā-phala-āśrayatvam”
hinduism.explanation: Patanjali teaches that when a person is firmly established in truthfulness, actions and their fruits come to rest on him — commentators say his words and deeds become effective by truth alone.
hinduism.tie_back: Truthfulness alone, fully established, makes all action bear fruit — like the Kural’s claim that truth alone suffices.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises that living in the truth brings freedom from sin and bondage.
christianity.tie_back: Truth alone has the power to liberate — close to the Kural’s truth that is enough by itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “Truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise. And a man keeps on telling the truth until he becomes a truthful person.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that steady truthfulness leads step by step to all righteousness and finally to Paradise, while lying leads to wickedness and the Fire.
islam.tie_back: Keep truthfulness unfailingly, and the rest of goodness follows — the Kural’s point exactly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Keep thee far from a false matter; and the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah does not merely forbid falsehood — it commands keeping far away from it, an unusually strong phrasing rabbinic tradition often notes.
judaism.tie_back: Unfailing distance from falsehood as a core command echoes the Kural’s unfailing non-lying.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “For a liar who has violated the one law (of truthfulness) who holds in scorn the hereafter, there is no evil that he cannot do.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada calls truthfulness ‘the one law’: break it, and every other evil becomes possible.
buddhism.tie_back: The mirror image of the Kural: keep this one virtue and all is well; break it and all is lost.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Man, understand well the truth! exerting himself in the rule of truth a wise man overcomes Mâra.”
jainism.explanation: In the Ācārāṅga, Mahāvīra urges the seeker to hold to truth, saying that by exerting himself in truth the wise man overcomes death (Māra). Jainworld renders the same passage as “O Self! Practice Truth, and nothing but Truth.”
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that unbroken truthfulness is enough even without any other virtuous deed. The Ācārāṅga makes the rule of truth by itself sufficient to overcome death.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.3.3.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, p. 33); cf. the Jainworld rendering of the same passage

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So how can you become truthful? And how can the veil of illusion be torn away? O Nanak, it is written that you shall obey the Hukam of His Command, and walk in the Way of His Will.”
sikhism.explanation: Japji's first pauri rejects ritual bathing, silence, fasting and cleverness as paths to becoming truthful (sachiaara). It names one way only: living in the divine order.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that if one practises truthfulness unfailingly, it is well even without other virtuous deeds. Japji likewise treats becoming truthful as the one thing needed and finds the many other practices unnecessary.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that when a god swears falsely by the waters of Styx he lies breathless for a year, is barred from nectar and ambrosia, and is cut off from the gods’ councils and feasts for nine more years.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even immortals keep one law above all: their sworn word by the Styx must never be false.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Among the gods, truthfulness to one’s oath is the one indispensable law, as truthfulness is for Valluvar.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “From me you shall hear the whole truth.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial Socrates refuses flattery and rhetoric, offering only the truth — and dies rather than abandon it.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates staked his whole life on one commitment, truth, and considered it enough.

real_life_example.event_title: Solzhenitsyn publishes Live Not by Lies on the day of his arrest
real_life_example.event: On 12 February 1974, the day KGB officers arrested him at his Moscow flat, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn released his essay Live Not by Lies. It urged Soviet citizens not to attempt heroic protest but simply to refuse personal participation in lies, by not writing, signing, saying or voting for anything they did not believe. The next day he was stripped of his Soviet citizenship and deported to West Germany.
real_life_example.explanation: Solzhenitsyn argued that an ordinary person who did nothing else but steadfastly refuse to lie could help bring down a system that depended on lies.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that if one practises truthfulness without ever failing, it is well even if one does no other virtuous deed, which is almost exactly the programme Solzhenitsyn set out in his essay.

tamil:
புறந்தூய்மை நீரான் அமையும் அகந்தூய்மை
வாய்மையால் காணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Purandhooymai neeraan amaiyum agandhooymai
Vaaymaiyaal kaanap padum.
meaning: Water makes a person clean on the outside. Being truthful shows that a person is clean on the inside.
elementary: When you get muddy, you take a bath and you’re clean on the outside. But how do you get clean on the inside? This kural says water can’t reach there — only telling the truth can wash your mind and heart.
university: The couplet sets up a clean binary: puram / agam (outer / inner), a pairing that also names the two great genres of classical Tamil poetry. Outer purity ‘is achieved’ (amaiyum) by water; inner purity ‘is seen / made manifest’ (kaanappadum) by truthfulness — truth both produces and reveals a clean mind. This is a pointed comment on ritual bathing (neeraadal) in holy waters. Textual note: several popular web editions print the first word as ‘புறள்தூய்மை’; the grammatically regular form ‘புறந்தூய்மை’ (puram + thooymai), used here, is attested in other editions and fits the parallel with அகந்தூய்மை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The body is cleansed by water, the internal organ is purified by truthfulness, the individual soul by sacred learning and austerities, the intellect by (true) knowledge.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists what purifies each part of a person: water for the body, truthfulness for the mind.
hinduism.tie_back: Practically word for word the Kural’s claim: water cleans the outside, truth cleans the inside.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus rebukes religious leaders for washing the outside of cups while their hearts are full of greed and deceit.
christianity.tie_back: Inner cleansing matters more than outer washing — the Kural’s agam/puram contrast.

islam.quote_or_event: “But only one who comes to Allāh with a sound heart.”
islam.explanation: Abraham says that on Judgment Day neither wealth nor children will help — only a sound, pure heart.
islam.tie_back: Inner soundness of heart is what truly counts, beyond outward purity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm says entry to God’s presence requires clean hands AND a pure heart — and defines the pure heart as one that has not sworn deceitfully.
judaism.tie_back: Outer cleanness (hands) and inner purity (truthfulness) — exactly the Kural’s two purities.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It is here, O brahman, that you should bathe to make yourself a safe refuge for all beings. And if you speak no untruth, nor work any harm for breathing things… To Gaya gone, what would it do for you? Let any well your Gaya be!”
buddhism.explanation: When a brahmin asks whether the Buddha bathes in sacred rivers to wash away sin, the Buddha replies that true bathing is not lying and not harming — then any ordinary well is as holy as Gaya.
buddhism.tie_back: Truthfulness, not river water, is the real purifying bath — the Kural’s exact point.
buddhism.source: Vatthupama Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 7 (tr. Nyanaponika Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “O Brâhmaṇas, why do you tend the fire, and seek external purity by water? The clever ones say that external purity which you seek for, is not the right thing.” … “The Law is my pond, celibacy my holy bathing-place … there I make ablutions; pure, clean, and thoroughly cooled I get rid of hatred (or impurity).”
jainism.explanation: The low-born monk Harikeśa tells the sacrificing priests that bathing in water gives only outward purity. True cleansing is an inner bath in the Law and in self-restraint, which includes 'abstaining from lying'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar contrasts outer purity from water with inner purity shown through truthfulness. Harikeśa sets the same contrast between washing in water and an inward ethical bath.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.38, 12.46 (cf. 12.41) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One knows the Truth only when the Truth is in his heart. The filth of falsehood departs, and the body is washed clean.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak describes true cleansing as truth entering the heart and washing out the filth of falsehood. Elsewhere Gurbani repeatedly rejects ritual bathing as a means of purity.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says water purifies outwardly but truthfulness shows inner purity. Guru Nanak makes the same contrast: falsehood is the real dirt, and truth is what washes it away.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Into an odorous temple, he who goes / Should pure and holy be; but to be wise / In what to sanctity pertains, is to be pure.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Porphyry quotes the inscription on the doors of the temple of Asclepius at Epidaurus: real purity is holiness of mind, not just a washed body and clean clothes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Greek temple, like the Kural, ranks inner purity above outer cleansing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Beloved Pan, and all ye other gods who haunt this place, give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates closes the Phaedrus praying that his inner soul be beautiful and that his outer self match it.
philosophy.tie_back: Inner beauty first, and outer and inner in harmony — the Kural’s concern for agam over puram.

real_life_example.event_title: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission
real_life_example.event: The Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act of 1995 created South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, to uncover the truth about gross human rights violations committed between 1960 and 1994. Victims gave testimony, and the Commission's Amnesty Committee could grant amnesty for politically motivated acts only to applicants who made full disclosure of the relevant facts. Of 7,112 people who applied, 849 were granted amnesty.
real_life_example.explanation: The Commission made full and truthful disclosure, rather than punishment alone, the path by which a divided country sought to cleanse itself of its past.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says outer cleanliness comes from water but inner purity is seen only through truthfulness, and the Commission tried to purify a nation's conscience by requiring the whole truth to be told.

tamil:
எல்லா விளக்கும் விளக்கல்ல சான்றோர்க்குப்
பொய்யா விளக்கே விளக்கு.
transliteration:
Ellaa vilakkum vilakkalla saandrorkkup
Poyyaa vilakke vilakku.
meaning: Not every lamp is a real lamp. For people of good character, the lamp of truthfulness is the only real lamp.
elementary: A flashlight helps you see in a dark room. But what helps you see the right thing to do when you are confused inside? This kural says truthfulness is that special inner flashlight — and for wise people, it’s the only lamp that really matters.
university: The couplet repeats vilakku (lamp) four times, playing on its meanings: ordinary lamps dispel outer darkness, but ‘the lamp that does not lie’ (poyyaa vilakku) dispels inner darkness. Varadarasan’s gloss adds the parenthetical contrast explicitly: lamps that remove darkness outside versus the lamp of non-falsehood that removes darkness within. Saandror — the noble, the wise — is a key Kural term (cf. ch. 99, Saandraanmai), suggesting truthfulness is the defining light of the fully mature person. The truth-as-light metaphor is among the most widely shared images across religious traditions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From evil lead me to good, From darkness lead me to light, From death lead me to immortality.”
hinduism.explanation: This ancient prayer (‘asato mā sad gamaya, tamaso mā jyotir gamaya’) pairs moving from untruth (asat) to truth (sat) with moving from darkness to light.
hinduism.tie_back: Truth and light are one movement — the Kural’s lamp of truth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If we say that we have fellowship with him, and walk in darkness, we lie, and do not the truth.”
christianity.explanation: John says that walking in darkness while claiming to be close to God is itself a lie; ‘God is light’ (1:5), and walking in the light means living in truth.
christianity.tie_back: Truth and light belong together, falsehood and darkness together — the Kural’s image.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allāh is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The example of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp… Light upon light.”
islam.explanation: The famous Verse of Light describes God’s guidance as a perfect lamp lighting the heart of the believer.
islam.tie_back: A lamp of divine truth that outshines every ordinary lamp — close to the Kural’s image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “O send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist asks God’s light and truth to guide him like lamps on the way.
judaism.tie_back: Truth as a guiding light — the Kural’s ‘lamp that does not lie.’

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When this world is ever ablaze, why this laughter, why this jubilation? Shrouded in darkness, will you not see the light?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada urges people wrapped in the darkness of ignorance to look for the true light of the Dhamma.
buddhism.tie_back: An inner light beyond ordinary lamps, sought by the wise — the Kural’s lamp.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Enlightened by the light of Truth, the wise transcends death.”
jainism.explanation: This Jainworld rendering of an Ācārāṅga passage pictures truth as a light that lets the wise go beyond death. The same text calls the great vows, which include truthfulness, a 'light, illumining the three worlds'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the lamp of truthfulness is the only real lamp for the wise. The Jain text likewise speaks of 'the light of Truth' as what truly illuminates the wise.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.3.3 (Jainworld cites 3/3/66), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'; cf. Ācārāṅga II.16.6 (tr. Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns appeared, even with such light, there would still be pitch darkness without the Guru.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok in Asa di Vaar, Guru Angad says that no amount of outward light can lift inner darkness. Only the Guru's light can do that.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says not every lamp is a true lamp, and for the wise only the lamp of truthfulness is real. Guru Angad likewise sets countless outer lights against the one inner light that truly dispels darkness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He does not grasp falsehood, and he is deceived by neither god nor man, neither in deeds nor in thoughts.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar describes Apollo (Loxias), the shining god of light and prophecy, as one who never touches falsehood and cannot be deceived.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In Greek myth the god of light is also the god of truth — light and truthfulness are one, as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He lit a lamp in broad daylight and said, as he went about, ‘I am looking for a man.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes the Cynic carried a lamp in daylight to show that ordinary light could not find a genuine human being — later retold as searching for an honest man.
philosophy.tie_back: An ordinary lamp cannot reveal the true person; only honesty does — close to the Kural’s ‘not every lamp is a lamp.’
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.41 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: Nehru's broadcast after Gandhi's death: the light that shone was no ordinary light
real_life_example.event: On the evening of 30 January 1948, after Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated, Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru spoke to the nation over All India Radio without a prepared text. He began by saying that the light had gone out of their lives, then corrected himself, saying that the light that had shone in India was no ordinary light and would still be seen a thousand years later, because it represented the living, eternal truths. He urged his listeners not to respond to the killing with violence.
real_life_example.explanation: Nehru described Gandhi's lifelong devotion to truth as a light that death could not put out.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says ordinary lamps are not true lamps and that for the wise only the lamp of truthfulness is the real lamp, which is the very image Nehru reached for when he spoke of Gandhi.

tamil:
யாமெய்யாக் கண்டவற்றுள் இல்லை எனைத்தொன்றும்
வாய்மையின் நல்ல பிற.
transliteration:
Yaam meyyaak kandavatrul illai enaiththondrum
Vaaymaiyin nalla pira.
meaning: Of all the things we have found to be truly real, there is nothing at all that is better than truthfulness.
elementary: Imagine you searched the whole world and all the best books for the most precious treasure. Valluvar says he did that kind of search — and the greatest treasure he found was simply telling the truth.
university: The chapter closes with a personal verdict — one of the rare places Valluvar speaks in the first person (yaam, ‘we’). ‘Meyyaak kandavai’ means ‘things seen/found as real,’ and there is a deliberate play between mey (reality, truth) and vaaymai (truthful speech): among all that is mey, nothing surpasses vaaymai. Pappaiah reads kandavai as ‘the books I have examined,’ making this a survey of all moral literature; Kalaignar takes it as the conclusion of research into what is true. Either way, the couplet sets veracity at the summit of all virtues, bringing the chapter full circle from its opening definition.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There is no virtue equal to Truth: there is nothing superior to Truth. O king, Truth is God himself; Truth is the highest vow.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala tells King Dushmanta that nothing is higher than truth — it is God himself.
hinduism.tie_back: The same verdict as the Kural: nothing in existence is better than truth.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 74 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus identifies himself with truth itself, the one path to God.
christianity.tie_back: Truth placed at the very summit of reality, as in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allāh will say, ‘This is the Day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness.’ For them are gardens [in Paradise] beneath which rivers flow… That is the great attainment.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment, truthfulness is named as the quality that brings the ‘great attainment.’
islam.tie_back: Truthfulness as the final, decisive good — the Kural’s verdict.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Ḥanina said: The seal of the Holy One, Blessed be He, is truth [emet].”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud says God’s own signature — the mark he sets on all things — is truth (emet, spelled with the first, middle and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet).
judaism.tie_back: If God’s own seal is truth, nothing can be higher — the Kural’s conclusion.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 55a (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz tr.)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truth is the highest of savors.”
buddhism.explanation: Asked by the demon Alavaka what is the highest of all tastes, the Buddha answers ‘truth,’ and adds: go and ask others if anything better than truth, self-control, endurance and relinquishment can be found.
buddhism.tie_back: After surveying all good things, truth stands at the top — the Kural’s verdict.
buddhism.source: Alavaka Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.10 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Truth alone is the essence in the world.”
jainism.explanation: The Praśnavyākaraṇa, a Śvetāmbara Aṅga that sets out the five vows, praises truth as the very essence of the world.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ends the chapter by saying that among all the real things he has found, none is better than truthfulness. The Jain Aṅga makes the same supreme claim: truth alone is the essence of the world.
jainism.source: Praśnavyākaraṇa Sūtra 2.2, English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Siree Raag, Guru Nanak gives his verdict that Truth surpasses all else and that living truthfully (sach aachaar) ranks higher still. This is one of the best-known lines in Sikh ethics.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural closes with Valluvar's own verdict that among all things found to be real, nothing is better than truthfulness. Guru Nanak gives the same judgement: nothing ranks above truth lived out.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
