greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I have escaped. There is strength in my truth.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The blind prophet Teiresias, threatened by King Oedipus, answers that the truth he holds is his whole protection — and the truth indeed prevails over the king.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Truth as the strongest possession, stronger even than a king’s power.
greek_mythology.source: Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus 356 (tr. R. C. Jebb, rev. Alex Sens)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Truth is the beginning of every good thing, both to Gods and men.”
philosophy.explanation: In the Laws, Plato’s Athenian says truth leads all goods, and that anyone who would be blessed should share in truth from the start of life.
philosophy.tie_back: Truth at the head of all goods — Valluvar’s closing verdict.

real_life_example.event_title: Truth Prevails becomes the motto on the Czechoslovak and Czech presidential flag
real_life_example.event: After Czechoslovakia became independent in 1918, its first president, Tomas Garrigue Masaryk, drew on the heritage of the reformer Jan Hus and placed a version of the Hussite motto Truth Prevails on the presidential flag. When the Czech Republic was established, its law on state symbols retained the words Pravda vitezi (Truth Prevails) on the flag of the president, where they remain.
real_life_example.explanation: A modern state chose truth, above power or glory, as the single watchword to fly over its head of state.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural concludes that among all things found to be real, nothing surpasses truthfulness, a verdict a whole nation echoed by making Truth Prevails the motto of its highest office.

tamil:
செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான் சினங்காப்பான் அல்லிடத்துக்
காக்கின்என் காவாக்கா லென்.
transliteration:
Sellidaththuk kaappaan sinangaappaan allidaththuk
Kaakkin en kaavaakkaal en.
meaning: Holding back anger only counts when you could actually hurt someone with it. If your anger has no power to do harm anyway, what does it matter whether you hold it back or not?
elementary: Imagine a big kid who could easily push a small kid, but chooses not to. That is real self-control. If a small kid can't push a big kid anyway, 'not pushing' isn't really a choice. This kural says being calm only counts when you really could have hurt someone and you don't.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter by redefining the virtue itself: restraint of anger (sinam kaaththal) is morally meaningful only where one has the power (sellidam, literally 'the place where it goes through') to make the anger effective. Classical commentators such as Parimelazhagar read sellidam as the case of anger toward those weaker than oneself, where retaliation would succeed; restraint toward the stronger is mere prudence or fear. The couplet thus locates virtue in the gap between capacity and action, anticipating the Aristotelian and Stoic view that a virtue is shown only where its opposite is genuinely available. The rhetorical question of the second line ('what if he guards it, what if he does not?') dismisses 'restraint' that costs nothing as morally empty.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata's Adi Parva, the sage Vasishtha, who possessed immense spiritual power, suffered the killing of his hundred sons through the machinations tied to his rival Vishvamitra, yet he did not use that power to destroy Vishvamitra; instead he bore his grief without retaliation.
hinduism.explanation: Vasishtha is the classic Indian image of a sage who could have annihilated his enemy but chose not to unleash his wrath.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the kural's 'restraint where anger would take effect': Vasishtha's patience matters because his power to punish was real.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Chaitraratha Parva, the Vasishtha–Vishvamitra episode)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?”
christianity.explanation: At his arrest, Jesus tells Peter to put away his sword and points out that he could summon overwhelming force, yet he chooses not to.
christianity.tie_back: Like the kural, the restraint is meaningful precisely because the power to retaliate is fully available.

islam.quote_or_event: “If anyone suppresses anger when he is in a position to give vent to it, Allah, the Exalted, will call him on the Day of Resurrection over the heads of all creatures...”
islam.explanation: The Prophet singles out for special honour the person who swallows anger at the very moment he is able to act on it.
islam.tie_back: Near one-to-one with the kural: the merit lies in restraining anger 'when in a position to give vent to it', which is exactly Valluvar's sellidam.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4777 (graded hasan by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’ (Proverbs 16:32).”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines strength: real might is mastery over one's own impulses, and he grounds this in the verse praising the one who is slow to anger.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say that the real test of power is turning it inward to master one's own anger rather than outward against others.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who checks rising anger as a charioteer checks a rolling chariot, him I call a true charioteer. Others only hold the reins.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares controlling anger to reining in a chariot already in motion; merely holding the reins when nothing is moving is not mastery.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the kural, only restraint at the moment of real momentum counts; 'others only hold the reins' parallels Valluvar's dismissal of costless restraint.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Suddenly he stopped, like the ocean at the earth as a boundary and, noble, thought to himself: ‘Shame on a brother’s murder which I, as well as he, greedy for a kingdom, more wicked even than a hunter, have undertaken.’”
jainism.explanation: In Hemacandra's account of the duel, Bāhubali has already beaten Bharata in every contest and has just had the cakra hurled at him. He raises his fist to crush his brother, then stops in mid-charge, condemns his own fury, and renounces the kingdom to become a monk.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says restraint only counts where anger could actually do harm. Bāhubali's fist was raised against a brother he had already defeated, so holding back meant giving up a blow that would surely have landed.
jainism.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book I (Ādīśvaracaritra), ch. 5, part 11, 'The fight between Bharata and Bāhubali' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: According to Sikh tradition, Datu, the son of Guru Angad, resented that Amar Das had been made Guru in his place. He came to Goindwal, taunted Amar Das as a former water-carrier, and kicked him off his seat. Guru Amar Das did not retaliate. He humbly asked Datu's pardon, saying his foot must have been hurt, and then withdrew quietly to his home village.
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das was by then Guru with a following of his own, yet he answered a public insult and a physical assault with humility. Sikh tradition remembers the episode as a model of forbearance.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says true restraint of anger is restraint where one has the power to act on it. Guru Amar Das held back his anger exactly where his position would have let it take effect.
sikhism.source: Wikipedia, 'Guru Amar Das' (paraphrase of traditional accounts)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He stayed his hand on the silver hilt of his sword, and thrust it back into the scabbard as Minerva bade him.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Insulted by Agamemnon, Achilles is already drawing his sword to kill him when Athena (Minerva) intervenes and he sheathes it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A picture of anger checked at the moment it could take effect, though in Homer the restraint comes from a goddess rather than from Achilles' own virtue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Am I more powerful than Philip? yet he allowed a man to curse him with impunity. Have I more authority in my own house than the Emperor Augustus possessed throughout the world?”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca advises that whenever we are provoked we should recall rulers who had total power to punish yet chose to let insults pass.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca, like Valluvar, measures self-control by what one could do with one's power and refrains from doing.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book III (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)

real_life_example.event_title: Grant offers generous terms to Lee's army at Appomattox
real_life_example.place: McLean House, Appomattox Court House, Virginia, United States
real_life_example.event: With the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia surrounded, General Robert E. Lee met General Ulysses S. Grant in Wilmer McLean's parlour to surrender. Grant's terms paroled the Confederate soldiers and sent them home rather than to prison camps, allowed officers to keep their side arms, horses and baggage, and permitted men who owned horses or mules to take them home. Grant also offered 25,000 rations for Lee's hungry troops, and at the end of the meeting he and his staff raised their hats to Lee as he rode away.
real_life_example.explanation: At the moment when Grant held complete power over a defeated enemy that had cost his side dearly, he chose restraint and generosity instead of punishment.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the true test of restraining anger comes where one has the power to make it effective, and Grant, with Lee's army at his mercy, showed exactly that restraint.

tamil:
செல்லா இடத்துச் சினந்தீது செல்லிடத்தும்
இல்அதனின் தீய பிற.
transliteration:
Sellaa idaththuch sinandheedhu sellidaththum
Il adhanin theeya pira.
meaning: Anger at people stronger than you, where it can do nothing, is bad. Anger at people weaker than you, where it can do harm, is worse than anything else.
elementary: If you get angry at a much bigger kid, you will probably get hurt. If you get angry at a much smaller kid, you might hurt them, and that is even worse. So anger is bad either way: it hurts you, or it makes you hurt someone who can't fight back.
university: This couplet completes the argument of 301 by closing every escape route: anger is bad where it is ineffective (sellaa idam, anger toward the powerful, which rebounds on oneself) and worst of all where it is effective (sellidam, anger toward the weak, which inflicts real injury). Mu. Varadarasanar's gloss makes the two cases explicit as 'stronger' and 'weaker' persons. The ethical weight falls on the second line: power over others magnifies the moral gravity of anger rather than licensing it. The structure anticipates modern concerns about abuse of authority in households, workplaces, and states, where anger combined with power becomes cruelty.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, the ascetic Kaushika burns a crane to death with an angry glance after it soils him; later, when a devoted housewife keeps him waiting, his anger has no effect on her, and she rebukes him with the words that she is not a crane, directing him to learn true dharma from a humble meat-seller.
hinduism.explanation: Kaushika's anger kills a helpless bird but is powerless against a righteous woman, and the story treats both as evidence of his spiritual failure.
hinduism.tie_back: The two halves of the kural in narrative form: anger at the weak is destructive evil, and anger at the strong is futile and humiliating.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Markandeya-Samasya Parva, the tale of Kaushika, the devoted wife, and the Dharmavyadha)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells those who hold power over servants to give up threats, reminding them that they themselves answer to a higher Master.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the kural's second line: where you have power over the weak, harsh anger and threats are especially wrong.

islam.quote_or_event: “Bear in mind, Abu Mas'ud; verily Allah has more dominance upon you than you have upon your slave.”
islam.explanation: Abu Mas'ud was whipping his slave in intense anger when the Prophet stopped him with this reminder; he dropped the whip and vowed never to beat a servant again.
islam.tie_back: Directly illustrates the kural's warning that anger toward those under your power is the worst evil, and that you yourself stand under a greater power.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person should never impose excessive fear upon the members of his household, as the husband of the concubine of Gibeah imposed excessive fear upon her and this ultimately caused the downfall of many tens of thousands of Jews.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Hisda warns that intimidating those under your authority at home can spiral into catastrophe, citing the story in Judges 19–20.
judaism.tie_back: Like the kural, the Talmud singles out anger and intimidation directed at dependents as especially destructive.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 6b (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz trans., via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Angered & displeased, she grabbed hold of a rolling pin and gave her a whack over the head, cutting it open.”
buddhism.explanation: Lady Vedehika was famed for gentleness, but her slave Kali tested her; when provoked, the mistress struck her only slave, and her reputation became 'vicious' and 'violent'.
buddhism.tie_back: The story shows that anger vented on someone powerless is the true test of character and the worst of evils, just as the kural says.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He will sink through anger; he will go down through pride; delusion will block up his path; through greed he will incur dangers in both worlds.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami tells the disguised Indra that each of the four passions (kaṣāyas) drags down the person who harbours it, and anger comes first.
jainism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's first half: anger harms the one who feels it, even when it cannot touch its target. It does not match the second half, which says anger against the weak is the worst evil of all.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.54 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O anger, you are the root of conflict; compassion never rises up in you.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Salok Sahaskriti, Guru Arjan addresses anger directly as the source of strife and as wholly without compassion. Anger (krodh) is one of the five thieves in Sikh teaching.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says anger harms oneself when vented on the strong and is the worst evil when vented on the weak. Guru Arjan names what makes it so evil against the weak: it has no compassion.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sahaskriti, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A plain man cannot stand against the anger of a king, who if he swallow his displeasure now, will yet nurse revenge till he has wreaked it.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The seer Calchas fears Agamemnon's anger, and indeed Agamemnon's harsh treatment of the helpless priest Chryses brings a plague on the army, while his quarrel with the stronger Achilles brings disaster on the Greeks.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Iliad Book 1 shows both halves: anger at the powerless (Chryses) is cruelty, and anger at the powerful (Achilles) rebounds on oneself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Why should I make my slave atone by stripes and manacles for having answered me too loudly or having put on a stubborn look, or muttered something which I did not catch? Who am I, that it should be a crime to shock my ears?”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues against anger at dependents, and elsewhere in the same book praises Augustus for stopping Vedius Pollio from feeding a slave to lampreys over a broken cup.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca, like the kural, finds anger most shameful where one has total power over its victim.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book III (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)

real_life_example.event_title: John McEnroe is defaulted from the Australian Open
real_life_example.event: Playing Mikael Pernfors in the fourth round of the 1990 Australian Open, John McEnroe received a warning for glaring at a lineswoman and then a point penalty for cracking his racket. When he protested and swore at the Grand Slam chief of supervisors, the umpire defaulted him from the match. He became the first player since 1963 to be disqualified from a Grand Slam tournament for misconduct, and afterwards accepted that he had himself to blame.
real_life_example.explanation: McEnroe's anger was aimed at officials he had no power to overrule, so it could change nothing except the outcome for himself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says anger directed where it cannot prevail only harms oneself, and McEnroe's outburst against the officials cost him the match he had been leading.

tamil:
மறத்தல் வெகுளியை யார்மாட்டும் தீய
பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்.
transliteration:
Maraththal vekuliyai yaarmaattum theeya
Piraththal adhanaan varum.
meaning: Forget your anger toward anyone at all, because every kind of harm grows out of anger.
elementary: Anger is like a seed that grows weeds. If you keep it, bad things grow out of it: mean words, fights, broken friendships. So the kural says: let go of anger, no matter who made you angry.
university: The verb maraththal ('forgetting', 'letting go') is significant: Valluvar does not ask merely for suppression but for the anger to be dropped from memory, since resentment that is stored continues to generate harm. Yaarmaattum ('toward anyone whatsoever') universalises the precept, removing the distinctions of power drawn in 301 and 302. The second line offers a causal claim: evils (theeya) are 'born' (piraththal) from anger, making it a root vice rather than one fault among many. This genealogical view of anger as a source of other wrongs parallels the Buddhist treatment of dosa as one of the three roots of unwholesome action and the Gita's chain from desire to anger to ruin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names anger as one of three gateways to ruin and commands that it be abandoned.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, the Gita calls for giving anger up entirely because destruction flows from it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath: Neither give place to the devil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows that anger may arise but insists it not be kept overnight, since lingering wrath gives the devil a foothold.
christianity.tie_back: Parallels the kural's 'forget anger': do not hold on to it, because harm grows from it.

islam.quote_or_event: “A man said to the Prophet, ‘Advise me!’ The Prophet said, ‘Do not become angry.’ The man asked (the same) again and again, and the Prophet said in each case, ‘Do not become angry.’”
islam.explanation: Asked for comprehensive advice, the Prophet gives a single repeated instruction to avoid anger.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, this treats giving up anger as a master key, since so much wrongdoing springs from it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids both revenge and holding a grudge, pairing this with the command to love one's neighbour.
judaism.tie_back: The ban on 'bearing a grudge' is close to the kural's 'forget anger'; both demand that resentment be released, not stored.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who do not harbor such thoughts still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that rehearsing grievances keeps hatred alive, while letting them go ends it.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly the kural's own advice: forgetting the offence is how anger, and the evils it breeds, are ended.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a layman abuses a monk, he should not grow angry against him; because he would be like a child, a monk should not grow angry. If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
jainism.explanation: Abuse (ākrośa) is one of the twenty-two hardships (parīṣaha) a Jain monk must learn to bear. He is told neither to answer it with anger nor to store it up in his mind.
jainism.tie_back: 'Not take them to heart' is close to Valluvar's 'forget' (maraththal): the offence is to be dropped from the mind, not merely held back for the moment.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.24–25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks Bhagat Kabir sets forgiveness (khima) at the very centre of the spiritual life: where it is present, God is present.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks us to let go of anger toward anyone at all, because every evil is born of it. Kabir treats that letting go, forgiveness, as the place where God dwells.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Western literature's first epic opens by naming its subject as one man's wrath and the endless suffering it caused.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer and Valluvar agree that anger is a fountain of evils; the Iliad is effectively a narrative proof of the kural's second line.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad, Book 1, opening lines (trans. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Next, if you choose to view its results and the mischief that it does, no plague has cost the human race more dear.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca lists the slaughters, poisonings, and ruined cities that anger has produced.
philosophy.tie_back: A direct philosophical counterpart to 'evils are born of anger'.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book I (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)

real_life_example.event_title: The Peace of Westphalia declares perpetual oblivion and amnesty
real_life_example.place: Munster and Osnabruck, Westphalia, Germany (Holy Roman Empire)
real_life_example.event: The treaties of Munster and Osnabruck, together known as the Peace of Westphalia, ended the Thirty Years' War. Their second articles declared that there should be on both sides a perpetual oblivion and amnesty for all hostile acts committed since the beginning of the troubles. Grievances and claims arising from the war were to be buried in perpetual oblivion so that they could not be used against the other side.
real_life_example.explanation: After decades of devastating war, the peacemakers wrote into law that past injuries must be forgotten, recognising that remembered grievances would only breed new conflict.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks us to let go of anger toward anyone and forget it, because every evil is born from anger, and the Westphalian treaties made such forgetting a binding legal duty.

tamil:
நகையும் உவகையும் கொல்லும் சினத்தின்
பகையும் உளவோ பிற.
transliteration:
Nagaiyum uvagaiyum kollum sinaththin
Pagaiyum ulavo pira.
meaning: Anger kills the smile on your face and the joy in your heart. Is there any enemy worse than that?
elementary: When you are really angry, you can't laugh and you can't feel happy. It's like a thief that steals your smile. The kural asks: what enemy could be worse than one that takes away all your happiness?
university: Valluvar pairs nagai (laughter, the outward cheerfulness of the face) with uvagai (inner delight), a pairing the commentators render as 'face-blossoming and heart-blossoming'. Anger 'kills' both, so the damage is not only social but inward. The rhetorical question reframes anger as a pagai (enemy) that lives within, which is more dangerous than any external foe because it cannot be escaped. The idea of anger as an internal enemy runs through Indian thought (the 'six inner enemies', including krodha) and has close parallels in the Buddhist teaching that an angry person does to himself what an enemy would wish on him.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna identifies desire turned into wrath as the 'all-devouring' enemy that must be known and conquered.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, the Gita names anger as the greatest enemy, one that consumes a person from within.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife ... But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,”
christianity.explanation: Paul sets wrath among the 'works of the flesh' and sets joy and peace among the fruits of the Spirit.
christianity.tie_back: The contrast shows wrath and joy as opposites, as in the kural, where anger kills joy.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anger is an ember in the heart of the son of Adam, as you see it in the redness of his eyes and the bulge of his jugular veins. So whoever senses something from that, then let him cling to the ground.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes anger as a burning coal that visibly disfigures the face and body.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, this shows anger taking over the face and heart, replacing calm cheer with burning.

judaism.quote_or_event: When God accepted Abel's offering and not his, Cain became very angry and his face fell; God asked him why he was angry and why his face had fallen, warning that sin was crouching at the door.
judaism.explanation: In the Torah's first account of anger, the emotion shows immediately on Cain's face and leads him to kill his brother.
judaism.tie_back: Cain's 'fallen countenance' is the kural's lost smile: anger strips the face of light before it does any other harm.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Having killed anger you sleep in ease. Having killed anger you do not grieve. The noble ones praise the slaying of anger — with its honeyed crest & poison root —”
buddhism.explanation: Asked what one thing should be killed, the Buddha answers: anger, because killing it brings ease and ends grief.
buddhism.tie_back: The reverse of the kural: anger kills joy, and killing anger restores it.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 1.71, Ghatva Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Self is the one invincible foe, (together with the four) cardinal passions, (viz. anger, pride, deceit, and greed, they are five) and the (five) senses (make ten). These (foes), O great sage, I have regularly vanquished.”
jainism.explanation: Asked by Keśi who the real enemies are, Gautama names the unconquered self and the four passions, with anger listed first, as the foes to be defeated.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks whether there is any enemy greater than anger. Gautama's answer places anger among the very few enemies that count, ranked above any outward foe.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Emotional attachment to Maya, sexual desire, anger and egotism are demons.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Gujri, Guru Amar Das calls anger and the other passions demons that possess a person from within.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether there is any enemy greater than anger, which kills both the smile and the joy within. Guru Amar Das likewise counts anger among the inner demons that are a person's real foes.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 513, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But Achilles abode at his ships and nursed his anger. He went not to the honourable assembly, and sallied not forth to fight, but gnawed at his own heart, pining for battle and the war-cry.”
greek_mythology.explanation: After his quarrel, Achilles withdraws from everything he loves and consumes himself with resentment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles 'gnawing at his own heart' is anger killing the angry man's own joy, as the kural says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Eighth, consider how much more pain is brought on us by the anger and vexation caused by such acts than by the acts themselves, at which we are angry and vexed.”
philosophy.explanation: Among his rules for handling offence, Marcus observes that our own anger hurts us more than the offence did.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the kural, Marcus treats anger as the real enemy of our peace of mind, worse than any outside wrong.

real_life_example.event_title: Seneca writes On Anger for his brother Novatus
real_life_example.event: The Stoic philosopher Lucius Annaeus Seneca wrote the treatise De Ira (On Anger), addressed to his elder brother Novatus, who had asked how anger might be soothed. In it Seneca described anger as a kind of brief madness, more conspicuous than other passions because it shows in the face and boils forth the more plainly the greater it is. He argued that anger cannot be moderated and must be eliminated rather than managed.
real_life_example.explanation: Seneca's treatise is one of the earliest sustained arguments that anger disfigures the person who feels it and is an enemy to be removed entirely.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says anger kills both the smile on the face and the joy in the heart and asks whether there is any greater enemy, and Seneca likewise portrayed anger as visibly ruining the face and overthrowing the mind.

tamil:
தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின் சினங்காக்க காவாக்கால்
தன்னையே கொல்லுஞ் சினம்.
transliteration:
Thannaiththaan kaakkin sinangaakka kaavaakkaal
Thannaiye kollum sinam.
meaning: If you want to protect yourself, keep your anger in check. If you don’t, your own anger will destroy you.
elementary: Anger is like a fire you carry in your own pocket. If you don't put it out, it burns you first. So the best way to keep yourself safe is to keep anger away.
university: The couplet turns on the reflexive thannai ('oneself'), which frames it: the whole argument is about self-preservation, not the protection of others. Valluvar's point is strategic as much as moral: anger, left unguarded, turns back on its owner, destroying health, judgment, reputation, and eventually life. The repetition of kaa ('guard') across both lines makes guarding anger identical with guarding the self. This self-interested argument against anger complements the altruistic ones elsewhere in the chapter and matches Stoic and Buddhist analyses that anger harms its owner before its target.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From anger, complete delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain of self-destruction: anger leads to delusion, loss of memory, and loss of intelligence, ending in ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's final step, 'praṇaśyati' ('one perishes'), is the kural's 'anger will kill you'.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one.”
christianity.explanation: Eliphaz, speaking in Job, states a proverb that wrath is fatal to the one who harbours it.
christianity.tie_back: Almost a restatement of the kural's second line: anger kills its own owner.

islam.quote_or_event: “The strong is not the one who overcomes the people by his strength, but the strong is the one who controls himself while in anger.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet redefines strength as self-control at the moment of anger.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, the emphasis is on guarding oneself (yamliku nafsahu, 'controls himself') against one's own anger.

judaism.quote_or_event: At Meribah, Moses, angered by the people, addressed them as 'rebels' and struck the rock instead of speaking to it; as a result God decreed that he would not bring Israel into the Promised Land.
judaism.explanation: Jewish tradition (for example Maimonides in his Eight Chapters) identifies Moses' failing here as anger, which cost the greatest prophet his life's goal.
judaism.tie_back: Even for Moses, failing to guard against anger turned it against himself, as the kural warns.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like oneself, all beings hold themselves most dear, yet an angry person, deranged, can kill himself in many ways: with a sword, taking poison, hanging himself by a rope in a mountain glen.”
buddhism.explanation: The verses of the Kodhana Sutta describe how anger can drive a person to destroy even himself.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost literally the kural's 'anger will kill you yourself'.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.60, Kodhana Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The passions are the fire; knowledge, a virtuous life, and penances are the water; sprinkled with the drops of knowledge the fire of the passions is extinguished and does not burn me.”
jainism.explanation: Keśi asks how Gautama puts out the frightful fire that burns embodied beings. Gautama explains that the fire is the passions (Jacobi notes that the plural 'fires' stands for the four kaṣāyas), and that he protects himself by constantly dousing them with knowledge and discipline.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells anyone who wants to protect himself to guard against anger, or it will consume him. Gautama describes exactly that kind of guarding: he keeps the fire of passion from burning him by constantly dousing it.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.50–53 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Unfulfilled sexual desire and unresolved anger waste the body away,”
sikhism.explanation: In the Dakhni Oankar Guru Nanak compares anger and lust to borax that melts gold: they consume the person who harbours them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that if you do not guard against anger, it will destroy you. Guru Nanak likewise describes anger wearing away the very one who keeps it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 932, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Denied the armour of the dead Achilles, Ajax sets out in rage to kill the Greek commanders; Athena drives him mad so that he slaughters livestock instead, and on waking in shame he falls on his own sword.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sophocles' tragedy shows unchecked wrath ending in the self-destruction of the greatest warrior after Achilles.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A literal enactment of 'if you do not guard against anger, it will kill you'.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...careless of itself provided it hurts another, rushing upon the very point of the sword, and greedy for revenge even when it drags the avenger to ruin with itself.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca opens De Ira by describing anger as a passion that will wreck its owner so long as it can harm someone else.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's 'drags the avenger to ruin with itself' is the kural's point exactly.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book I.1 (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)

real_life_example.event_title: Surgeon John Hunter collapses during a heated hospital board meeting
real_life_example.event: John Hunter, the leading surgeon and anatomist of his day, had long suffered from angina pectoris. On 16 October 1793, during a meeting of the board of governors of St George's Hospital, he was engaged in a heated discussion over the admission of students when he collapsed and died. His collections later passed to the Royal College of Surgeons, and he was reburied in Westminster Abbey in 1859.
real_life_example.explanation: Hunter's death in the middle of a heated quarrel has long been cited as an example of how anger can endanger the person who gives way to it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that if you do not guard yourself against anger it will destroy you yourself, and Hunter's life ended in the very moment of a bitter dispute.

tamil:
சினமென்னும் சேர்ந்தாரைக் கொல்லி இனமென்னும்
ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்.
transliteration:
Sinamennum serndhaaraik kolli inamennum
Emap punaiyaich sudum.
meaning: Anger is a fire that kills anyone who comes near it. It even burns up your family and friends, who are like a raft that carries you safely through life.
elementary: Think of your family and friends as a raft that keeps you floating in a big river. Anger is like a fire on that raft. If you let it burn, it destroys the very thing that keeps you safe.
university: The couplet is built on a compound metaphor. Sinam is called serndhaaraik kolli, 'the killer of those who come close', a traditional kenning for fire, which destroys whatever touches it. Inam, one's kin and circle of friends, is called an emap punai, a 'safe raft' that carries one across the dangerous sea of life. Anger, being fire, burns the very raft that was meant to save its owner: it isolates the angry person by consuming the relationships that sustain them. Valluvar thus extends the self-harm argument of 305 to its social dimension.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After setting Lanka ablaze in fury, Hanuman is struck with horror that his fire may have burned Sita herself; he reproaches his own anger and praises those great souls who, by their wisdom, quench anger as it rises, as fire is put out with water.
hinduism.explanation: Hanuman's rage, turned into literal fire, threatens the very person he came to save.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost exactly the kural's image: anger is a fire that burns what we hold dear, the raft that was meant to save us.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns a quarrelling community that mutual hostility will consume them all.
christianity.tie_back: Like the kural, anger among companions destroys the community that sustains each member.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anger comes from the devil, the devil was created of fire, and fire is extinguished only with water; so when one of you becomes angry, he should perform ablution.”
islam.explanation: This narration describes anger as a fire and prescribes water (ablution) to put it out.
islam.tie_back: Shares the kural's core metaphor of anger as a consuming fire.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4784 (graded da'if by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce, And their wrath, for it was cruel; I will divide them in Jacob, And scatter them in Israel.”
judaism.explanation: On his deathbed Jacob condemns the violent anger of his sons Simeon and Levi and foretells that their tribes will be scattered.
judaism.tie_back: The anger of Simeon and Levi ends up breaking apart their own tribes: the kural's burning of the 'raft of kin'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Now, when a person is angry — overcome with anger, oppressed with anger — his friends, companions, & relatives will avoid him from afar, all because he is overcome with anger.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the seven things an enemy wishes on an enemy is friendlessness, and anger brings it about.
buddhism.tie_back: Direct parallel: anger drives away the kin and friends who form one's safe raft.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.60, Kodhana Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys humility, deceit or cheating destroys friends; but greed destroys all.”
jainism.explanation: The Daśavaikālika lists what each passion ruins and gives anger as the destroyer of love (prīti) between people.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's anger burns up 'the raft of kinsmen and friends'. The Jain verse names the same casualty: the bonds of affection that hold a person's circle together.
jainism.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.38 (English rendering as given on tattvagyan.com, 'Greed destroys all')

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The fire of anger is the outcaste who burns dead bodies at the crematorium.”
sikhism.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak lists the inner outcastes that make a person impure. He names anger as a fire that burns as a cremation fire does.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls anger a fire that kills whoever comes near and burns up the raft of kin and friends. Guru Nanak shares the image of anger as a consuming, death-dealing fire.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Consumed by rage at Jason's betrayal, Medea kills their own children to wound him, destroying her family and her own future.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides' Medea is the Greek archetype of anger turning against the angry person's own kin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Medea's fury burns the very family that bound her life together, as the kural's fire burns the raft of kin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Such people are most troublesome to themselves and to their dearest friends.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle, describing the sulky temperament that nurses anger for a long time, notes that it torments both the person and those closest to him.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the kural, Aristotle sees lasting anger damaging one's closest relationships as well as oneself.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.5 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: William Bligh is cast adrift after the mutiny on the Bounty
real_life_example.event: Lieutenant William Bligh, commander of HMS Bounty, had become enraged at his crew's seamanship and had fallen out with his first mate and longtime friend Fletcher Christian. On 28 April 1789 Christian and his supporters seized the ship and set Bligh and 18 loyal men adrift in a small open launch. Bligh navigated about 3,600 miles to Timor, but historians note that while he used physical punishment less than other captains, he was verbally and personally abusive, and later he faced a court-martial (and acquittal) for abusive language.
real_life_example.explanation: Bligh's skill and courage were never in doubt, but his abusive temper turned his own officers and crew, the people who should have carried him safely home, against him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says anger is a fire that burns even the raft of kinsmen and friends that would carry a person through life, and Bligh's anger literally cost him his ship and left him adrift in an open boat.

tamil:
சினத்தைப் பொருளென்று கொண்டவன் கேடு
நிலத்தறைந்தான் கைபிழையா தற்று.
transliteration:
Sinaththaip porulendru kondavan kedu
Nilaththaraindhaan kai pizhaiyaadhatru.
meaning: A person who treats anger as something precious will surely be ruined, just as someone who hits the ground with their hand will surely hurt that hand.
elementary: If you slap the floor as hard as you can, the floor doesn't feel anything, but your hand really hurts. Using anger as your 'power' is the same: the person who uses it gets hurt the most.
university: The target here is a specific attitude: treating anger as porul, a thing of worth or a useful tool, whether as a mark of strength, a way to command respect, or a means of getting results. The simile of striking the ground (nilaththu araindhaan) is precise: the ground is unharmed while the striker's hand is certain to be injured, so anger's force rebounds on its user. Kai pizhaiyaadhu ('the hand does not escape') stresses certainty, not mere probability. The couplet enters a long-running debate, found in Aristotle and Seneca, about whether anger is a useful servant of virtue; Valluvar sides firmly with those who deny it any value.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The sage Durvasa, enraged that King Ambarisha broke his fast before Durvasa returned, creates a fiery demon to kill the king; Vishnu's discus destroys the demon and then pursues Durvasa through all the worlds until he humbly seeks the forgiveness of the very king he attacked.
hinduism.explanation: Durvasa, famous for wielding anger as power, finds his own wrath turned back upon himself.
hinduism.tie_back: A narrative version of the struck ground: the anger he valued as a weapon rebounds on its user.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb states that harm aimed at others returns to its author.
christianity.tie_back: The same rebound logic as the kural's hand striking the ground.

islam.quote_or_event: “...but the evil plot does not encompass except its own people.”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that malicious scheming ultimately surrounds and ruins those who devise it.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, harm that springs from hostility returns upon its originator.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry; For anger resteth in the bosom of fools.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet warns against quick anger, saying it 'rests' or is cherished in the bosom of fools.
judaism.tie_back: The fool who keeps anger in his bosom is the one who 'takes anger as a treasure' in the kural, and both texts expect his undoing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like fine dust thrown against the wind, evil falls back upon that fool who offends an inoffensive, pure and guiltless man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares harming the innocent to throwing dust into the wind, where it blows back into the thrower's face.
buddhism.tie_back: A near-identical physical image to the hand striking the ground: the force returns to its source.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The ascetic jumped up angrily, thinking, ‘I’ll kill the young disciple,’ and began to run. Blind with anger, he ran against a pillar and was killed.” … “Flaming with anger like a fire with an oblation, he seized an axe with a sharp edge and ran forward … As he fell, the sharp axe fell on him and split his head in two.”
jainism.explanation: This is the back-story of the serpent Caṇḍakauśika. In two successive lives a man who treated his rage as a weapon was killed by it: first he ran into a pillar, then his own axe split his head. Hemacandra comments that 'anger which has a sharp continuity goes along into another birth.'
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar compares the man who prizes anger to someone who strikes the ground and only hurts his own hand. In Hemacandra's story the angry man wields his anger, and in the end his own axe, and the blow comes back on him.
jainism.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. 3, part 10, 'Episode of Caṇḍakauśika' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists.”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks Sheikh Farid advises against answering blows with blows. He counsels humility instead of retaliation.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one who treats anger as useful will be hurt as surely as a hand that strikes the ground. Farid's advice not to strike back rejects anger as a tool of response.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles nurses his wrath against Agamemnon as a matter of honour and refuses to fight; the result is the death of his dearest friend Patroclus, after which he bitterly curses strife and anger.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles treats his anger as something precious, a defence of his honour, and it destroys what he loved most.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The anger he valued rebounds on him, as the hand striking the earth cannot escape pain.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...and very like a falling rock which breaks itself to pieces upon the very thing which it crushes.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca's opening description of anger compares it to a falling rock that shatters on what it hits; later he rejects Aristotle's view that anger is a useful 'weapon' for virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Both the image (force that shatters its source) and the argument (anger has no real value) match the kural.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book I.1 (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)

real_life_example.event_title: General Patton's slapping incidents in Sicily
real_life_example.event: During the Sicily campaign, Lieutenant General George S. Patton visited army hospitals and struck two soldiers suffering from what would today be diagnosed as combat stress, accusing them of cowardice. When the incidents became known, General Eisenhower reprimanded him and he was ordered to apologise personally to the two soldiers and to his entire Seventh Army. He lost his Mediterranean command and was passed over for command of American ground forces in the Normandy invasion, which went instead to Omar Bradley.
real_life_example.explanation: Patton treated harsh anger as a tool of leadership, and the episode badly damaged the career of one of the most gifted commanders of the war.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says ruin surely comes to one who treats anger as something valuable, just as the hand that strikes the ground cannot escape injury, and Patton's blows rebounded on his own career.

tamil:
இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன இன்னா செயினும்
புணரின் வெகுளாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Inar eri thoivanna innaa seyinum
Punarin vekulaamai nandru.
meaning: Even if someone hurts you as badly as throwing you into a blazing fire, it is good, if you possibly can, not to get angry with them.
elementary: Sometimes people are so mean it feels like being burned. The kural says: even then, if you can, try not to become angry back. It is really hard, but it is the best and bravest thing to do.
university: This is the chapter's high-water mark of demand: inar eri, a fire of many clustered flames, is the image of the worst possible injury. The concessive punarin ('if it is possible', or in some readings 'if the offender seeks reconciliation') is realistic, acknowledging that non-anger in such extremity may exceed ordinary capacity, but it does not lower the ideal. Kalaignar's gloss takes punarin as the wrongdoer returning to seek friendship, making the couplet about accepting reconciliation without resentment. Either way, the teaching approaches the most radical ethics of non-retaliation found across traditions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The boy Prahlada is subjected by his own father, Hiranyakashipu, to repeated attempts on his life, including poison, serpents, being thrown from heights, and fire, yet he keeps his devotion and shows no hatred toward his father.
hinduism.explanation: Prahlada becomes the Puranic model of a person who suffers extreme cruelty without answering in anger.
hinduism.tie_back: A living example of the kural's ideal: meeting fire-like torment without wrath.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
christianity.explanation: On the cross, in extreme agony, Jesus prays for those who are crucifying him.
christianity.tie_back: The fullest Christian expression of the kural's ideal: no anger even under torment 'like fire'.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Quran instructs believers to answer harm with good, promising that this can turn an enemy into a close friend.
islam.tie_back: Matches both the non-anger ideal and Kalaignar's reading of punarin as reconciliation with the offender.

judaism.quote_or_event: “About those who are insulted and do not insult, who hear their shame and do not respond, who act out of love and are joyful in suffering, the verse says: ‘And they that love Him are as the sun going forth in its might’ (Judges 5:31).”
judaism.explanation: The Sages praise those who absorb humiliation without striking back, comparing them to the rising sun in its strength.
judaism.tie_back: Like the kural, the Talmud treats not answering injury with anger as a sign of greatness.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 88b (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz trans., via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, even if bandits were to carve you up savagely, limb by limb, with a two-handled saw, he among you who let his heart get angered even at that would not be doing my bidding.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Simile of the Saw, the Buddha sets the most extreme standard of non-anger imaginable.
buddhism.tie_back: Near one-to-one with the kural's 'even if they plunge you into fire', and even stricter, since it drops the 'if possible' qualification.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Angry at this thought, Somaśarman, malevolent, stood the neck of a water-jar, filled with blazing coals from a funeral-pyre, on his head. Though burned severely by it, absorbed in meditation, he endured it. The fuel of karma being consumed, omniscience having arisen, he went to emancipation.”
jainism.explanation: The newly ordained monk Gajasukumāla, Kṛṣṇa's younger brother, is standing in meditation in a cemetery when his father-in-law places live coals on his head. He bears it without breaking his meditation and attains liberation. Afterwards Neminātha tells the grieving Kṛṣṇa, 'Do not be angry at Somaśarman.'
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks us to hold back anger even when the harm done to us is like being plunged into blazing fire. In Gajasukumāla's case the fire was literal, and he endured it without retaliating.
jainism.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book VIII (Nemināthacaritra), ch. 10, part 3, 'Gajasukumāla' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, was summoned by the Mughal emperor Jahangir and ordered to remove passages of the Adi Granth. He refused and was tortured to death at Lahore in 1606. Sikh tradition holds that he was made to sit on a red-hot iron plate while burning sand was poured over him. Through it he remained calm and without hatred, accepting God's will as sweet.
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan is Sikhism's first martyr. His serenity under torture is remembered in Sikh tradition as the supreme example of bearing extreme injury without anger.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even if someone does you harm like plunging you into a blazing fire, it is good to refrain from anger. Guru Arjan's martyrdom is almost a literal enactment of that teaching.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'How did Guru Arjan die?' (paraphrase); hot-plate details from Sikh tradition

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Priam goes alone to the tent of Achilles, who has killed his son Hector and defiled his body, and kisses the hands of his son's killer to beg for the corpse; Achilles, moved, puts aside his wrath and returns the body.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad ends not with victory but with two enemies setting aside anger in the face of unbearable loss.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Priam's restraint before the man who burned his life to ashes reflects the kural's ideal of non-anger after the worst injury.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
philosophy.explanation: In prison awaiting execution, Socrates holds that retaliation is never just, no matter how much one has suffered.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates' 'whatever evil we may have suffered' is the Greek counterpart of the kural's 'even if they harm you like fire'.

real_life_example.event_title: Eva Mozes Kor forgives her Nazi persecutors at Auschwitz
real_life_example.event: As a ten-year-old twin, Eva Mozes Kor had been subjected to Josef Mengele's experiments at Auschwitz, where her parents and two older sisters were killed. On the 50th anniversary of the camp's liberation, she returned to Auschwitz with Dr. Hans Munch, a former camp doctor who signed a document attesting to the operation of the gas chambers, and she read and signed her own declaration forgiving the Nazis. Her decision drew criticism from some fellow survivors, but she said it freed her from the pain she had carried for fifty years.
real_life_example.explanation: Kor chose to give up resentment toward those who had inflicted the worst imaginable suffering on her family, and she described the act as her own liberation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even when someone does you harm as painful as being plunged into a blazing fire, it is good, if you can, to refrain from anger toward them, and Kor did so after enduring one of history's greatest injuries.

tamil:
உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும் உள்ளத்தால்
உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின்.
transliteration:
Ulliyadhellaam udaneydhum ullaththaal
Ullaan vekuli enin.
meaning: If a person never lets even a thought of anger into their mind, they will right away get everything they hope for.
elementary: When your mind isn't full of angry thoughts, it has lots of room for good ideas and plans. People also like to help calm, kind people. So a mind without anger can reach its goals much more easily.
university: The couplet plays on the root ul- ('to think', 'the mind'): ulliyadhu ('what one has thought of'), ullaththaal ('in the mind'), and ullaan ('does not think of'). Valluvar sets the standard at the level of thought itself: it is not enough to avoid angry acts or words; one must not entertain (ullaan) anger inwardly. The promised reward, attaining all one intends 'at once' (udan), is striking, and commentators variously read it as worldly success (a clear mind and goodwill from others) or spiritual attainment. The couplet thus links inner purity from anger to efficacy in the world, a pattern also found in the Gita's promise of liberation for those free of desire and anger.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are free from anger and all material desires, who are self-realized, self-disciplined and constantly endeavoring for perfection, are assured of liberation in the Supreme in the very near future.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna promises that freedom from anger and desire brings the highest goal near at hand.
hinduism.tie_back: Close to the kural: the one free of anger in mind attains what is sought, and attains it soon ('abhitaḥ', 'near at hand', like Valluvar's 'udan', 'at once').

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.”
christianity.explanation: In the Beatitudes, Jesus promises the whole earth to the meek, those gentle and slow to anger.
christianity.tie_back: Like the kural, the non-angry are promised a surprisingly large reward.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a garden as wide as the heavens and earth, prepared for the righteous ... who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Quran lists restraining anger and pardoning others among the qualities of those promised a vast paradise.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, freedom from anger is tied directly to receiving the greatest reward.

judaism.quote_or_event: “With regard to whoever forgoes his reckonings with others for injustices done to him, the heavenly court in turn forgoes punishment for all his sins.”
judaism.explanation: Rava teaches that one who lets go of grievances receives complete forgiveness; the passage then tells of Rav Huna recovering from near-death because he never insisted on his rights.
judaism.tie_back: Like the kural, the person who does not hold anger in mind receives an extraordinary, all-encompassing reward.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 17a (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz trans., via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One should give up anger, renounce pride, and overcome all fetters. Suffering never befalls him who clings not to mind and body and is detached.”
buddhism.explanation: The opening verse of the Dhammapada's chapter on anger promises freedom from suffering to one who gives up anger and clinging.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the kural, giving up anger leads to the fulfilment one seeks.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By conquering anger he obtains patience; he acquires no Karman productive of anger, and destroys the Karman he had acquired before.”
jainism.explanation: In the catalogue of spiritual exertions, Mahāvīra says that overcoming anger (krodhavijaya) produces patience, stops new anger-producing karma, and wears away the old.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar promises that someone who never lets anger into his mind will gain whatever he desires. The Jain text also promises a reward for conquering anger, but the reward is freedom from karma rather than fulfilled wishes.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.67 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger. Your body shall not suffer from any disease, and you shall obtain everything.”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks Sheikh Farid tells the seeker to repay harm with good and keep anger out of the mind, promising wholeness and fulfilment in return.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural promises that one who never lets even the thought of anger into the mind will attain everything he sets his heart on. Farid makes the same promise in nearly the same terms.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381-1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Back in his own house in disguise, Odysseus sees the suitors and disloyal maids and is seized with fury, but he strikes his breast and commands his heart to endure, recalling that it endured worse in the Cyclops' cave; this restraint lets him eventually regain his home and family.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus' mastery of rage at the critical moment is what makes his homecoming possible.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Keeping anger from ruling the mind leads to attaining what the heart has long desired, as the kural promises.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Ninth, consider that a good disposition is invincible, if it be genuine, and not an affected smile and acting a part.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus argues that true gentleness cannot be defeated, since the aggressor only harms himself.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the kural, a mind genuinely free of anger is presented as unstoppable in achieving its ends.

real_life_example.event_title: Bjorn Borg, the Ice Man of tennis, wins five straight Wimbledon titles
real_life_example.event: Swedish player Bjorn Borg won the Wimbledon singles championship five years in a row from 1976 to 1980 and six French Open titles, and was known as the Ice Man for never letting opponents see what he was feeling on court. Borg later recalled that he had been suspended as a 13-year-old for bad behaviour and afterwards kept his emotions inside, receiving penalty points only once in his professional career. He retired at 26 with 11 major singles titles.
real_life_example.explanation: Borg's refusal to let anger take hold during matches was regarded by himself and others as a central strength of his game.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural promises that one who never lets anger enter the mind will attain what he sets his heart on, and Borg's famous composure accompanied one of the most successful careers in tennis.

tamil:
இறந்தார் இறந்தார் அனையர் சினத்தைத்
துறந்தார் துறந்தார் துணை.
transliteration:
Irandhaar irandhaar anaiyar sinaththaith
Thurandhaar thurandhaar thunai.
meaning: People who let their anger go beyond all limits are as good as dead. People who have given up anger completely are as great as holy people who have left the world behind.
elementary: A person who is always furious is like someone who isn't really alive: there's no joy, kindness, or peace inside. But a person who has given up anger is like a wise holy person. Letting go of anger makes you truly alive.
university: The closing couplet is a celebrated piece of Tamil wordplay built on two repeated verbs. Irandhaar can mean 'those who have exceeded (all limits)' and 'those who have died'; thurandhaar can mean 'those who have renounced (anger)' and 'those who have renounced (the world)', that is, ascetics. Hence: the excessively angry are like the dead; those who give up anger equal the renunciants. Solomon Pappaiah's gloss offers an alternative reading, that those free of anger are like those who have escaped death, which neatly mirrors the first line. Placed in the Thuravaraviyal (the section on ascetic virtue), the couplet makes giving up anger itself a form of renunciation available to everyone.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who neither hates nor desires the fruits of his activities is known to be always renounced. Such a person, free from all dualities, easily overcomes material bondage and is completely liberated, O mighty-armed Arjuna.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that true renunciation (nitya-sannyasa) is an inner condition, being free of hatred and craving, not an outward vow.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the kural's second line: the person who gives up hostility is equal to the renunciant.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill ... But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment:”
christianity.explanation: Jesus places anger in the same moral category as killing, linking wrath to the realm of death and judgment.
christianity.tie_back: Like the kural's first line, anger is associated with death itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, and when they are angry, they forgive,”
islam.explanation: The Quran lists forgiving while angry among the defining qualities of believers devoted to God.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, letting go of anger is counted among the marks of the spiritually committed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The Sages taught: There are three types of people whose lives are not lives, due to their constant suffering: The compassionate, the hot tempered, and the delicate.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud counts the hot-tempered among those whose lives are 'not lives'.
judaism.tie_back: Almost exactly the kural's first line: the excessively angry are as good as dead.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 113b (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz trans., via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who is free from anger, is devout, virtuous, without craving, self-subdued and bears his final body — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: In the chapter on the true brahmin, freedom from anger is listed first among the marks of the holy person.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the kural's second line, being free of anger places one among the renunciant saints.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Bravo! you have conquered anger; bravo! you have vanquished pride; bravo! you have banished delusion; bravo! you have subdued greed. … Here (on earth) you are the highest man, Reverend sir, and hereafter you will be the highest; exempt from all blemishes you will reach Perfection.”
jainism.explanation: Indra drops his disguise and praises the renouncing king Nami, first of all for having conquered anger, and declares him the highest of men, bound for Perfection.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who have wholly given up anger are equal to renunciants. Here the renunciant is praised precisely for having conquered anger, so the conquest of anger and renunciation are presented together.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.56–58 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “who is not touched by sexual desire or anger - within his heart, God dwells.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person who stays even-minded in pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour. Because anger does not touch such a person, God abides in their heart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who have wholly given up anger are equal to those who have renounced the world. Guru Tegh Bahadur finds the true saint not in renunciation but in the one whom anger cannot touch.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the close of Aeschylus' Oresteia, the Furies, ancient spirits of vengeful wrath, are persuaded by Athena to give up their rage against Athens and are transformed into honoured guardians, the Eumenides ('Kindly Ones').
greek_mythology.explanation: The trilogy ends with wrath itself being renounced and turned into a blessing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Renouncing anger raises the Furies to a sacred, honoured status, echoing the kural's claim that those who give up anger equal the holy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For which reason also, I am not angry with my accusers, or my condemners; they have done me no harm...”
philosophy.explanation: Sentenced to death, Socrates declares that he holds no anger toward those who condemned him.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates facing death without anger embodies the kural's anger-renouncer, who stands above both anger and death.

real_life_example.event_title: Tolstoy makes Do not be angry the first commandment of his faith
real_life_example.event: In What I Believe, written in 1884, Leo Tolstoy set out the teaching he drew from the Sermon on the Mount, naming as Jesus' first commandment that one must live in peace with all and never regard anger as justified. His later Christianity stressed five tenets, beginning with be not angry and including do not resist evil and love your enemies, and his doctrine of nonviolent nonresistance went on to inspire Gandhi. Tolstoy renounced the church's rituals and was excommunicated by the Russian Orthodox Church in 1901.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the world's great novelists placed the complete renunciation of anger at the head of a moral teaching that he presented as a renunciant's way of life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who have wholly renounced anger are equal to those who have renounced the world, and Tolstoy built a renouncer's creed whose very first rule was to give up anger.

tamil:
சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும் பிறர்க்குஇன்னா
செய்யாமை மாசற்றார் கோள்.
transliteration:
Sirappeenum selvam perinum pirarkku innaa
Seyyaamai maasatraar kol.
meaning: Even if hurting someone would bring them great riches and fame, people with pure minds keep firmly to their rule of never causing pain to others.
elementary: Imagine someone offers you a huge treasure chest, but only if you push another kid down to get it. A truly good person says “no thanks” every time. Valluvar says the pure-hearted never hurt anyone, not even for the biggest prize in the world.
university: The chapter opens by testing the principle of non-harm against its strongest temptation: sirappu eenum selvam, wealth that “gives birth to” distinction and social standing. The word kol (settled principle, fixed resolve) matters: non-harm is presented not as a mood or a calculation but as a standing commitment of the maasatraar, “those without stain,” whose minds are clear of the anger and greed that make harm seem attractive. Placed in the turavaraviyal (the section on the renunciant’s virtues), the couplet implies that the refusal to profit from another’s suffering is a defining mark of spiritual maturity, not merely of good manners. The same structure appears in Cicero’s Stoic claim that profiting by a neighbour’s loss is more contrary to nature than death or poverty, and in Plato’s thought-experiment of the Ring of Gyges, which asks whether anyone would stay just if injustice were profitable and safe. Valluvar’s answer is that the stainless would.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him avoid (the acquisition of) wealth and (the gratification of his) desires, if they are opposed to the sacred law, and even lawful acts which may cause pain in the future or are offensive to men.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the householder to give up wealth and pleasures whenever getting them would go against dharma, and even to avoid legal acts that would cause pain or offend others.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Manu ranks not-causing-pain above getting rich: wealth gained against righteousness or at others’ cost is to be refused.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that no amount of worldly gain is worth the loss of one’s inner life.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts set the greatest possible riches against moral integrity and find the riches not worth it. Valluvar names harming others as the price the pure refuse to pay.

islam.quote_or_event: “O believers! Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally, but rather trade by mutual consent.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids enriching yourself at another person’s expense by unjust means; wealth must change hands only by fair, willing exchange.
islam.tie_back: Both forbid seeking wealth through another’s loss or pain. The Kural adds that the pure refuse such gain even when it would bring prestige.
islam.source: Qur’an 4:29 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that a small, honest income is worth more than a fortune gained unjustly.
judaism.tie_back: Same weighing as the Kural: great revenue on one side, righteousness on the other, and righteousness wins.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is indeed virtuous, wise, and righteous who neither for his own sake nor for the sake of another (does any wrong), who does not crave for sons, wealth, or kingdom, and does not desire success by unjust means.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the truly wise person as one who will do no wrong for any reason, and who does not seek wealth or success by unjust means.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s own claim: the pure person will not do wrong even when wealth or success is the reward.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana warns that wealth gained by harmful deeds does not last and leaves its owner bound by his own passions and hatred.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's stainless people refuse to cause pain even for wealth that would bring them distinction. The Jain verse explains why: wealth gained by evil deeds is lost, and the hatred behind it remains.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Macauliffe records that at Saiyidpur (Eminabad) Guru Nanak lodged with Lalo, a low-caste carpenter, and declined the great feast of Malik Bhago, the local steward. When Malik Bhago demanded why, the Guru took Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Bhago's rich bread in the other and squeezed them: it is said milk came from Lalo's bread and blood from Bhago's, because Bhago's wealth had been gained by bribery and oppression.
sikhism.explanation: The story, from the Janamsakhi tradition as Macauliffe retells it, sets honest poverty above lavish wealth that was squeezed out of other people's suffering. Guru Nanak refuses the rich man's hospitality outright.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the stainless will not cause pain even for wealth that brings great prestige; Guru Nanak turned away from just such prestigious wealth because it had been gained by hurting others.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter IV, pp. 43-44 (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato’s retelling of the myth, the shepherd Gyges finds a gold ring that makes him invisible. Freed from all consequences, he seduces the queen, kills the king, and takes the throne. Glaucon uses the tale to ask whether anyone would stay just if injustice were profitable and could never be discovered.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Ring of Gyges tests whether people avoid harming others only because they fear getting caught.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural gives the answer Socrates goes on to defend: the truly pure refuse to harm others for gain even when the gain is huge and the harm would go unpunished.
greek_mythology.source: Plato, Republic II, 359c–360d (the Ring of Gyges)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Well then, for a man to take something from his neighbour and to profit by his neighbour's loss is more contrary to Nature than is death or poverty or pain or anything else that can affect either our person or our property.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero argues that gaining at another’s expense is worse, and more against human nature, than suffering any personal loss.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero and Valluvar both say the good person would rather stay poor than get rich by hurting someone else.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis III.21 (trans. Walter Miller, Loeb 1913)

real_life_example.event_title: John Woolman refuses to write wills that bequeath enslaved people
real_life_example.event: As a young clerk in the early 1740s, the Quaker John Woolman was asked to write a bill of sale for an enslaved woman; he did so against his conscience but told his employer he believed slavery was inconsistent with Christianity. Afterwards, working as a tailor and scrivener who depended on the goodwill of his customers, he refused to draw up wills in which enslaved people would be passed on to heirs, telling one respected neighbour that he could not write his will without breaking his own peace. He went on to spend much of his life persuading Quakers to free those they held in slavery, and his Journal was published in 1775.
real_life_example.explanation: Woolman chose to lose business and risk offending respected customers rather than earn fees from documents that would keep human beings in bondage.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the stainless hold firmly to the rule of never causing pain, even when harming others would bring wealth and standing, and Woolman turned away paid work rather than lend his pen to slavery.

tamil:
கறுத்துஇன்னா செய்தவக் கண்ணும் மறுத்தின்னா
செய்யாமை மாசற்றார் கோள்.
transliteration:
Karuththu innaa seydhavak kannum maruththu innaa
Seyyaamai maasatraar kol.
meaning: Even when someone hurts them out of anger, people with pure minds make it their rule not to hurt that person back.
elementary: If a kid on the playground knocks over your sandcastle on purpose, it is tempting to knock over theirs too. This kural says good-hearted people don’t pay back hurt with more hurt, even when the other person started it.
university: Where Kural 311 tested non-harm against greed, 312 tests it against the stronger pull of justified grievance.
