Karuththu describes the other party’s grudging, hostile intent, while maruththu (in return, in retort) names the retaliatory impulse the stainless decline. The couplet repeats the closing phrase of 311 word for word (seyyaamai maasatraar kol), binding the two into a pair: neither profit nor provocation licenses harm. This places Valluvar alongside Socrates in the Crito, who startled his friend by insisting that one must not return injury for injury, and alongside the Sermon on the Mount and the Buddha’s Simile of the Saw. It also stands in contrast to the older Greek ethic of helping friends and harming enemies, which Plato’s Socrates set out to dismantle.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant … such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna praises the person who bears no hatred toward any being, stays friendly and compassionate, and is patient and forgiving.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s stainless person and the Gita’s dear devotee share the same trait: no hostility toward anyone, even those who give cause.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers never to pay back evil with evil.
christianity.tie_back: Almost the Kural in one line: do not return harm, even to one who harmed you first.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you raise your hand to kill me, I will not raise mine to kill you, because I fear Allah—the Lord of all worlds.”
islam.explanation: One of Adam’s two sons, threatened by his jealous brother, says he will not strike back even to defend himself.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s stainless person, Adam’s son refuses to answer hostility with hostility, even under the gravest threat.
islam.source: Qur’an 5:28 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids taking revenge or even holding a grudge, and commands love of neighbour instead.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts forbid repaying the one who wronged you. Leviticus adds that the grudge itself must go.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, even if bandits were to carve you up savagely into pieces with a two-handled saw, he among you who let his heart get angered even at that would not be doing my bidding.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Simile of the Saw, the Buddha tells his monks that even under the most brutal attack they must not give way to anger or ill will toward the attackers.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural forbids returning harm to a malicious attacker. The Buddha goes further and forbids even the inner anger that would motivate it.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk should not be angry if beaten, nor should he therefore entertain sinful thoughts; knowing patience to be the highest good, a monk should meditate on the Law. If somebody strikes a restrained, resigned Śramaṇa somewhere, he should think: ‘I have not lost my life.’”
jainism.explanation: Corporal punishment (vadha) is one of the hardships a Jain monk must bear. When struck, he answers with patience and not even a thought of retaliation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the stainless will not hurt in return even someone who has spitefully harmed them. Mahāvīra gives the same rule and extends it to the thought of revenge.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.26–27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
sikhism.explanation: In one of his saloks preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the seeker not to hit back at those who strike him, but to answer with humility and return to inner peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks the stainless not to hurt in return even those who have spitefully hurt them; Farid gives the same rule in its most physical form, a blow received and not returned.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Ajax, Odysseus has been Ajax’s bitterest enemy, and Ajax tried to kill him. After Ajax’s suicide, Agamemnon and Menelaus want to leave the body unburied as revenge. Odysseus, the injured party, overrules them and insists his enemy be buried with honour.
greek_mythology.explanation: The man with the most reason to seek revenge is the one who refuses it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus acts as the Kural’s stainless person: wronged by a hostile man, he will not harm him in return, even in death.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates, in prison awaiting execution, insists that wronging someone is never right, even as payback for a wrong done to us.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates and Valluvar state the same rule in almost the same words: no harm in return, whatever harm was suffered.

real_life_example.event_title: Six-year-old Ruby Bridges prays for the crowds who jeered her
real_life_example.place: William Frantz Elementary School, New Orleans, Louisiana, United States
real_life_example.event: On 14 November 1960 six-year-old Ruby Bridges, escorted by federal marshals, became the only Black pupil at William Frantz Elementary School under a federal desegregation order. Crowds gathered daily to shout slurs and threats at her, and white parents withdrew their children, so she was taught alone by the one teacher who stayed. The child psychiatrist Robert Coles, who met her every week, reported that she told him she prayed for the people in the street, asking God to forgive them because they did not know what they were doing.
real_life_example.explanation: Faced with daily hostility she had done nothing to provoke, a small child answered with prayer for her tormentors rather than resentment.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the stainless make it their rule not to hurt in return even those who have spitefully harmed them, and Ruby Bridges met spite with prayers for the very people who abused her.

tamil:
செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும் இன்னாத செய்தபின்
உய்யா விழுமந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Seyyaamal setraarkkum innaadha seydhapin
Uyyaa vizhumam tharum.
meaning: Even if people hate and hurt you when you did nothing to them, hurting them back will later bring you sorrow you cannot escape.
elementary: Suppose someone is mean to you for no reason at all, and you get them back. It might feel fair for a minute, but later you end up feeling awful and stuck in a big fight. The kural says hitting back, even when you didn’t start it, brings trouble you can’t get out of.
university: This couplet sharpens 312 by removing every excuse: the victim did nothing (seyyaamal) to provoke the enmity (setraar, those who hate). Even so, retaliating yields uyyaa vizhumam, a grief from which there is no escape. Because the chapter belongs to the section on the renunciant, older commentators and Pope’s translation read it as addressed to the ascetic, for whom retaliation undoes the discipline of years; the ‘inescapable sorrow’ is at once moral self-damage and the karmic consequence of the act. The logic is prudential as well as ethical: revenge draws the avenger into the cycle of harm. Greek tragedy dramatises exactly this spiral in the house of Atreus, and the Gospel compresses it into the saying that those who take the sword perish by it.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If (the punishment falls) not on (the offender) himself, (it falls) on his sons, if not on the sons, (at least) on his grandsons; but an iniquity (once) committed, never fails to produce fruit to him who wrought it.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches that a wrong, once done, always bears fruit for the one who did it, even if the result is delayed.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘inescapable sorrow’ is this law applied to retaliation: harm done in revenge is still harm, and its fruit cannot be avoided.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.”
christianity.explanation: When Peter strikes one of the men arresting Jesus, Jesus orders him to stop, warning that violence returns on those who use it.
christianity.tie_back: Peter is retaliating against men who came against an innocent Jesus, the Kural’s exact situation, and Jesus warns that such retaliation brings ruin on the one who strikes.

islam.quote_or_event: “The reward of an evil deed is its equivalent. But whoever pardons and seeks reconciliation, then their reward is with Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an allows proportionate response to a wrong, but holds up pardon and reconciliation as the better and more rewarded path.
islam.tie_back: Both texts steer the wronged person away from retaliation. The Kural warns of the sorrow revenge brings; the Qur’an promises reward for forgiving instead.
islam.source: Qur’an 42:40 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not thou, I will recompense evil; but wait on the LORD, and he shall save thee.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs tells the wronged person not to plan revenge but to leave the matter to God.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts tell the victim of unprovoked harm not to repay it; Proverbs adds that deliverance lies in restraint, not in revenge.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that answering hatred with hatred only keeps it alive; only non-hatred ends it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says retaliation traps the avenger in lasting sorrow; the Dhammapada explains why: hatred returned only feeds the cycle.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When he who is free from desires approached the village, the inhabitants met him on the outside, and attacked him, saying, ‘Get away from here.’ He was struck with a stick, the fist, a lance, hit with a fruit, a clod, a potsherd. … abandoning the care of his body, the Venerable One humbled himself and bore pain, free from desire.”
jainism.explanation: During his wanderings in the wild Lāḍha country, Mahāvīra, who had done the villagers no wrong, was beaten, cut and set upon by dogs. He bore it without striking back, 'ceasing to use the stick against living beings.'
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar warns against retaliating even against people who hate you without any provocation. Mahāvīra's conduct in Lāḍha is the Jain model of exactly that restraint toward unprovoked enemies.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I, Lecture 8 ('The Pillow of Righteousness'), Lesson 3, vv. 7–12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org numbering)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and I am no one's enemy.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the state reached in the company of the holy: enmity has gone from both sides, because he no longer answers hostility with hostility.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that striking back even at those who hated us without cause brings sorrow; Guru Arjan describes the freedom of one who has stopped being anyone's enemy.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 671, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the myth behind Aeschylus’ Agamemnon, Thyestes wrongs his brother Atreus, and Atreus takes revenge by serving Thyestes his own children at a feast. The revenge does not end the feud; it plants a curse that brings murder upon murder through the next generations of the house.
greek_mythology.explanation: Atreus answers a real wrong with revenge, and the revenge brings disaster on his own family for generations.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘inescapable sorrow’ made into a family history: harm returned for harm becomes a curse on the avenger’s own line.
greek_mythology.source: Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1583–1602 (Aegisthus’ account of the feast of Thyestes)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius advises that the real victory over someone who wrongs you is refusing to become like them.
philosophy.tie_back: Both see revenge as a trap: the Kural warns that it brings inescapable sorrow, and Marcus says it turns you into the very wrongdoer you resent.

real_life_example.event_title: Henry II does public penance at Canterbury after Becket's murder
real_life_example.event: King Henry II and Archbishop Thomas Becket, once close friends, quarrelled bitterly for years over the rights of the Church, and Becket spent six years in exile. Soon after Becket's return, four of Henry's knights, reportedly acting on the king's angry words although there is no evidence he ordered it, killed the archbishop in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170. Becket was declared a saint in 1173, and in 1174 Henry walked barefoot through Canterbury, submitted to beatings by bishops and monks, and kept an overnight vigil at the shrine as penance.
real_life_example.explanation: The king's anger at an opponent who had defied him led to a crime that shocked Europe and left a stain on his reign that he could not escape.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that striking back with harm at those who opposed and hated you brings sorrow that cannot be escaped, and Henry's angry outburst against his adversary ended in public humiliation and lasting disgrace.

tamil:
இன்னாசெய் தாரை ஒறுத்தல் அவர்நாண
நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்.
transliteration:
Innaa seydhaarai oruththal avar naana
Nannayam seydhu vidal.
meaning: The best way to punish people who hurt you is to be so kind to them that they feel ashamed, and then to let the matter go.
elementary: If your brother breaks your toy and you share your snack with him anyway, he will probably feel really sorry about the toy. Valluvar says that is the best “punishment”: being so kind that the person feels ashamed of being mean, and then forgetting about it.
university: Perhaps the most quoted couplet of the chapter, 314 redefines punishment itself. Oruththal (to punish, chastise) is kept as the goal, but the means is nannayam (goodness, benefit), and its effect is naanam, the wrongdoer’s shame. The closing word vidal (to leave off, let go) led Parimelazhagar and later commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan to read the couplet as requiring one to forget both the injury received and the good returned, so that the kindness does not become a hidden weapon. The idea is found across traditions: Proverbs and Paul speak of heaping coals of fire on an enemy’s head by feeding him, and the Qur’an promises that repelling evil with what is better can turn an enemy into a close friend. What Valluvar adds is the paradox that the gentlest act is the most effective sanction.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When One injures another, the injured turns round and injures the injurer. Similarly, when one cherishes another, that other cherishes the cherisher. One should frame one's rule of conduct according to this.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati tells Yudhishthira that harm invites harm in return while kindness invites kindness, and that one should build one’s conduct on this.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s strategy of answering harm with kindness uses this same principle: goodness shown draws goodness out of the other person.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section 113 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to meet an enemy’s need with kindness, which will bring the enemy to burning shame, and so to overcome evil with good.
christianity.tie_back: This is almost the Kural itself: the ‘coals of fire’ are the shame the kindness produces, and the punishment is goodness.

islam.quote_or_event: “Good and evil cannot be equal. Respond ˹to evil˺ with what is best, then the one you are in a feud with will be like a close friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells believers to answer wrongdoing with the finest possible conduct, which can turn a bitter enemy into a devoted friend.
islam.tie_back: Both texts answer harm with goodness and expect it to change the wrongdoer. The Kural stresses the enemy’s shame, the Qur’an the enemy’s transformation into a friend.
islam.source: Qur’an 41:34 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs advises feeding a hungry enemy, which will heap burning shame on him, and promises that God will reward the kindness.
judaism.tie_back: The source of Paul’s later saying, and a close match to the Kural: kindness to one who harmed you produces shame in him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that each vice is best conquered by its opposite virtue, so wickedness is conquered by goodness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts treat goodness as the true way to defeat someone who does wrong.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Knowing that he was near, the Blessed One said, ‘Caṇḍakauśika, wake up! wake up! Do not be confused.’ When he heard the Lord’s words, the recollection of his former births arose in the serpent … Then, after he had circumambulated the Lord of Three Worlds three times, free from passions, he undertook a fast of his own accord.”
jainism.explanation: The poison-eyed serpent Caṇḍakauśika burns and bites Mahāvīra repeatedly. Mahāvīra answers with compassion and a word of awakening, and the serpent, transformed, gives up violence entirely; Mahāvīra stays on 'from compassion for him.'
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the way to punish a wrongdoer is to do him good until he is ashamed, and then let it go. Mahāvīra meets venom with kindness, and that kindness, not a counter-blow, is what turns the serpent away from violence.
jainism.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. 3, part 10, 'Episode of Caṇḍakauśika' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “A noble person does not adopt demerits in his heart and does good to the evil doer.”
sikhism.explanation: In a stanza titled 'good and bad', Bhai Gurdas compares the noble person to madder, which bears the heat yet dyes others fast, and to sugarcane, which grows sweeter the more it is crushed. Bhai Gurdas's Vaaran are early and authoritative Sikh exegesis, not scripture.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's way to punish wrongdoers is to do them good and let the matter go; Bhai Gurdas likewise praises the one who answers evil with good and keeps no grievance in the heart.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 31, Pauri 15 (English translation as given in the BaniDB database)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the close of Aeschylus’ Eumenides, the Furies threaten to poison Athens after Orestes is acquitted. Athena does not fight or punish them. She answers their rage with patient persuasion and offers of honour and a home in the city, until they give up their anger and become the Kindly Ones.
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena defeats the hostile Furies not by force but by generosity and respect.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ideal, Athena answers hostility with kindness, and the kindness, not punishment, ends the conflict.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “One thing here is worth a great deal, to pass thy life in truth and justice, with a benevolent disposition even to liars and unjust men.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius says the one thing of real worth is to live truly and justly while keeping goodwill even toward liars and the unjust.
philosophy.tie_back: Both call for positive goodwill toward those who do wrong, not just the absence of revenge.

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi gives Jan Smuts a pair of sandals he made himself
real_life_example.event: In South Africa Mohandas Gandhi led nonviolent campaigns against discriminatory laws enforced by General Jan Smuts and was imprisoned several times. Before leaving for India in 1914, after the two men reached an agreement, Gandhi sent Smuts a pair of leather sandals he had made with his own hands. In 1939, in a tribute written for Gandhi's 70th birthday, Smuts recalled that he had worn the sandals for many summers, though he felt he was not worthy to stand in the shoes of so great a man.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi answered his adversary not with bitterness but with a personal gift, and the gesture eventually drew from Smuts a public tribute of humility and respect.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the true way to punish those who have harmed you is to do them such kindness that they feel ashamed, and Gandhi's handmade gift led his old opponent to declare himself unworthy to stand in his shoes.

tamil:
அறிவினான் ஆகுவ துண்டோ பிறிதின்நோய்
தந்நோய்போல் போற்றாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Arivinaan aaguvadhu undo piridhin noy
Thannoy pol potraak kadai.
meaning: What good is all your learning if you do not feel another creature’s pain as your own and protect it from suffering?
elementary: You might know lots of facts, like all the planets or every dinosaur. But if your friend falls and scrapes their knee and you don’t care, what good are all those facts? Valluvar says being smart only matters if you feel other people’s hurt like it’s your own.
university: Valluvar here makes empathy the test of knowledge. Arivu (knowledge, understanding) is asked to justify itself, and the only acceptable answer is that it leads one to regard piridhin noy, the pain of another (piridhu can mean any other being, not only humans), as thannoy, one’s own pain. The verb potru (to guard, protect, cherish) makes the demand active: it is not enough to feel sympathy, one must protect the other from harm as one protects oneself. This anticipates a recurring theme in the Kural that learning without moral application is barren. Comparable ideas appear in the Bhagavad Gita’s claim that true knowledge produces equal vision of all beings, in the Buddha’s reflection that since everyone holds themselves dear no one should harm another, and in the Stoic doctrine of oikeiosis, which asks us to draw the circle of concern outward until strangers are treated as kin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The humble sages, by virtue of true knowledge, see with equal vision a learned and gentle brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater [outcaste].”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says real knowledge shows itself in seeing all beings, high or low, human or animal, with the same eye.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts judge knowledge by its moral fruit: the truly wise see every being as equal, and so cannot treat another’s pain as less real than their own.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him,”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, a priest and a Levite, both religious experts, walk past a wounded man, but a despised Samaritan feels his pain and cares for him.
christianity.tie_back: The parable makes the Kural’s point in story form: religious learning is useless if it does not lead you to treat another’s pain as your own.
christianity.source: Luke 10:33 (KJV), Parable of the Good Samaritan

islam.quote_or_event: “The similitude of believers in regard to mutual love, affection, fellow-feeling is that of one body; when any limb of it aches, the whole body aches, because of sleeplessness and fever.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares the community of believers to a single body in which one part’s pain is felt by all.
islam.tie_back: Both call for feeling another’s pain as your own; the hadith makes it literal through the image of one body.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eliezer said: Let the honor of your friend be as dear to you as your own”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer teaches that another person’s dignity should matter to you as much as your own.
judaism.tie_back: Both require treating what belongs to another, whether honour or well-being, as if it were your own.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:10 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Searching all directions with your awareness, you find no one dearer than yourself. In the same way, others are thickly dear to themselves. So you shouldn't hurt others if you love yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: After King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika agree that no one is dearer to them than themselves, the Buddha draws the conclusion: others feel the same, so do not harm them.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural and the Buddha reason the same way: understanding how precious you are to yourself should make you protect others as you protect yourself.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Knowing what is bad, he who knows it with regard to himself, knows it with regard to (the world) outside; and he who knows it with regard to (the world) outside, knows it with regard to himself: this reciprocity (between himself and) others (one should mind).”
jainism.explanation: At the close of its first lecture on the 'weapon' that harms living beings, the Ācārāṅga makes true knowledge depend on recognising that what hurts oneself hurts others too.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks what use knowledge is if it does not treat another's pain as one's own. The Ācārāṅga makes the same equation: real knowledge of suffering runs both ways between self and other.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.1.7.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The God-conscious being delights in doing good to others.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan describes the brahm giani, the person of true spiritual knowledge, and makes active kindness to others one of the marks of that knowledge.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use knowledge is if it does not make another's pain one's own; for Guru Arjan the highest knowledge shows itself precisely in doing good to others.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 273, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 8, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the opening of Sophocles’ Ajax, Athena shows Odysseus his enemy Ajax, driven mad and humiliated. She invites him to gloat, but Odysseus says he pities Ajax though he is a foe, because in Ajax’s ruin he sees his own fate and that of all mortals.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus recognises his enemy’s suffering as the kind of suffering that could be his own.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s insight in action: true understanding shows up as feeling another’s pain as one’s own, even an enemy’s.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The Stoic Hierocles pictures each person at the centre of concentric circles (self, family, fellow citizens, all humanity) and urges us to keep drawing the outer circles inward, treating those far away as if they were near.
philosophy.explanation: Stoic oikeiosis teaches that moral progress means extending to others the care we naturally feel for ourselves.
philosophy.tie_back: Hierocles offers a method for the Kural’s demand: widen self-concern until another’s pain is guarded as one’s own.
philosophy.source: Hierocles the Stoic, fragment in Stobaeus, Anthology 4.27.23

real_life_example.event_title: Joseph Rotblat leaves the Manhattan Project
real_life_example.place: Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States
real_life_example.event: The Polish-born physicist Joseph Rotblat worked on atomic bomb research at Liverpool and from 1944 at Los Alamos, having joined because he feared Nazi Germany might build such a weapon. In late 1944, when it became clear that Germany was not close to developing an atomic bomb, he left the Manhattan Project on grounds of conscience. He turned his research toward the medical uses of radiation, co-founded the Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs in 1957, and shared the 1995 Nobel Peace Prize with Pugwash for efforts to eliminate nuclear weapons.
real_life_example.explanation: Rotblat refused to let his scientific knowledge serve a weapon whose purpose he could no longer justify, and spent the rest of his life using science to reduce suffering.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what good knowledge is if one does not treat others' pain as one's own and guard them from it, and Rotblat chose to put his learning to protecting people rather than harming them.

tamil:
இன்னா எனத்தான் உணர்ந்தவை துன்னாமை
வேண்டும் பிறன்கண் செயல்.
transliteration:
Innaa enaththaan unarndhavai thunnaamai
Vendum piran kan seyal.
meaning: Whatever you have learned is painful from your own experience, never do that to anyone else.
elementary: Remember how much it hurt when someone left you out of a game? Then you already know not to leave anyone else out. This kural says: if something hurt you, don’t do it to others.
university: This is Valluvar’s clearest statement of the negative Golden Rule, and it is regularly cited alongside Hillel and the Mahabharata in comparative discussions of that principle. The phrase thaan unarndhavai, ‘what one has oneself felt or known,’ grounds the rule in lived experience rather than abstract principle: each person’s own suffering is a textbook of what not to do. Thunnaamai (not approaching, not engaging in) makes the prohibition wide enough to cover even drawing near to such acts. Unlike the positive form (‘do unto others’), the negative form sets a minimum that anyone can meet, and so needs no guesswork about what others want. It closely matches Brihaspati’s summary of dharma in the Mahabharata, Hillel’s one-sentence Torah, and Isocrates’ advice to the Cyprians.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One should never do that to another which one regards as injurious to one's own self. This, in brief, is the rule of Righteousness.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati sums up all of dharma for Yudhishthira in one rule: never do to others what you would find harmful to yourself.
hinduism.tie_back: An almost word-for-word counterpart of the Kural: what you know hurts you, do not do to others.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section 113 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sums up the Law and the Prophets as treating others the way you want to be treated.
christianity.tie_back: The positive form of the Kural’s rule; both use one’s own experience as the measure of how to treat others.

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes wishing for others what you wish for yourself a condition of true faith.
islam.tie_back: Both use one’s own desires and aversions as the standard for how to treat others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Go study.”
judaism.explanation: Asked to teach the whole Torah while standing on one foot, Hillel gives the negative Golden Rule.
judaism.tie_back: Hillel and Valluvar give the same rule in the same negative form: do not do to others what you yourself find painful.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (William Davidson Edition, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hurt not others in ways that you yourself would find hurtful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Udanavarga states the negative Golden Rule directly.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: let your own experience of hurt tell you what never to do to others.
buddhism.source: Udanavarga 5.18 (as quoted in comparative Golden Rule literature)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to kill. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to tyrannise over. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to torment. … The righteous man who lives up to these sentiments, does therefore neither kill nor cause others to kill (living beings).”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra grounds non-violence in direct identification with the victim: whatever you would feel is what the other feels.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's negative Golden Rule says never to do to another what you have learned to be painful. The Ācārāṅga's 'as it would be unto thee' rests on the same experiential ground.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.5.5.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “As you see yourself, see others as well; only then will you become a partner in heaven.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, addressing the religious authorities of his day, makes seeing others as oneself the condition of true religion.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's rule is not to do to others what one has felt as painful oneself; Kabir grounds the same rule in seeing others exactly as one sees oneself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 480, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Homer’s Odyssey, when the nymph Calypso finally agrees to let Odysseus leave, he suspects a trap. She swears she is planning for him only what she would plan for herself in the same need, since her mind is just and her heart is not made of iron.
greek_mythology.explanation: Calypso uses her own needs as the measure of how she treats Odysseus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An early Greek example of the Golden Rule: treat another as you would want to be treated in their place, the principle behind the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Do not do to others that which angers you when they do it to you.”
philosophy.explanation: Isocrates, writing as King Nicocles, advises his subjects to use their own resentment as a guide to how they should treat others.
philosophy.tie_back: A classical Greek statement of the same negative rule as the Kural.
philosophy.source: Isocrates, Nicocles (or The Cyprians) 61 (trans. George Norlin)

real_life_example.event_title: Hiroshima unveils the Cenotaph and its vow never to repeat the evil
real_life_example.place: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park, Hiroshima, Japan
real_life_example.event: On 6 August 1952 the Cenotaph for the A-bomb Victims, designed by Kenzo Tange, was unveiled at Hiroshima's Peace Memorial Ceremony; its stone chest holds the register of those who died from the bombing, regardless of nationality. Its inscription was written by Tadayoshi Saika, a Hiroshima University professor and himself an A-bomb survivor, after Mayor Shinzo Hamai asked for words expressing both a prayer and a vow. The English reads: "Let all the souls here rest in peace; For we shall not repeat the evil." Saika intended the vow to be made by all human beings.
real_life_example.explanation: A city that had suffered the first atomic bombing chose to answer its own experience of pain with a vow that no one should inflict such suffering again.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that whatever you have learned through your own experience to be painful, you must never do to another, and Hiroshima's survivors turned what they had suffered into a public vow never to repeat it.

tamil:
எனைத்தானும் எஞ்ஞான்றும் யார்க்கும் மனத்தானாம்
மாணாசெய் யாமை தலை.
transliteration:
Enaiththaanum ennaandrum yaarkkum manaththaanaam
Maanaa seyyaamai thalai.
meaning: The highest goodness is never to do anything low or hurtful to anyone, however small, at any time, not even in your thoughts.
elementary: Some people only stop themselves from hitting. This kural asks for much more: don’t hurt anyone, not a little bit, not ever, and don’t even plan mean things in your head. That, it says, is the very best kind of goodness.
university: The couplet universalises the prohibition along every axis at once: degree (enaiththaanum, in any measure however small), time (ennaandrum, at any time), and person (yaarkkum, to anyone). The fourth axis is inward: manaththaan aam, ‘that which arises from the mind,’ which commentators read either as deliberate, knowing harm or as harm committed even in intention. Maanaa means base or ignoble acts. Calling this thalai (the head, the foremost virtue) places total non-harm at the top of the chapter’s ethical hierarchy. Similar demands to extend the prohibition into the inner life appear in Leviticus’ command not to hate one’s brother in the heart, in the First Letter of John, where hatred is equated with murder, and in the Metta Sutta’s wish that no one should even desire harm for another.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him not, even though in pain, (speak words) cutting (others) to the quick; let him not injure others in thought or deed; let him not utter speeches which make (others) afraid of him, since that will prevent him from gaining heaven.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu forbids injuring others by word, thought, or deed, even when one is suffering oneself.
hinduism.tie_back: Both extend the ban on harm to the mind itself: no injury in thought, word, or act.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.”
christianity.explanation: The letter of John teaches that hatred in the heart is already murder in God’s eyes.
christianity.tie_back: Both move the line of harm from the hand to the mind: hostile intent is itself a wrong.

islam.quote_or_event: “There should be neither harming (darar) nor reciprocating harm (dirar).”
islam.explanation: This hadith lays down a general rule of Islamic ethics and law: no one may harm another, and harm may not be answered with harm.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it states a rule of non-harm without exceptions of person or occasion.
islam.source: An-Nawawi’s Forty Hadith, no. 32 (Ibn Majah; sunnah.com)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids hatred even when it stays hidden in the heart.
judaism.tie_back: Both forbid harm at the level of the mind, not just outward acts.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none deceive another, or despise any being in any state. Let none through anger or ill-will wish harm upon another.”
buddhism.explanation: The Metta Sutta asks that no one deceive, despise, or even wish harm on any being.
buddhism.tie_back: Both reach from deed into wish: harming anyone, even in the mind, is ruled out.
buddhism.source: Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (trans. Amaravati Sangha)

jainism.quote_or_event: “(E. g. big creatures) have one form of bodily existence and then another. But all are subject to pain; hence they should not be killed. This is the quintessence of wisdom: not to kill anything. Know this to be the legitimate conclusion from the principle of the reciprocity with regard to non-killing.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga calls non-harm toward every being the very core of wisdom, a verse it repeats at I.11.10.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls not harming anyone, in any degree, at any time, even in thought, the highest virtue. The Jain verse likewise sets universal non-harm at the summit, as the 'quintessence' of wisdom.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.1.4.9–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all. Do not break anyone's heart; these are all priceless jewels.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid forbids even the smallest hurt, a single harsh word, because God dwells in every person and every heart is precious.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls it the highest virtue never to cause harm to anyone, however slight; Farid likewise forbids harm down to one unkind word, to anyone at all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 129 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus tells of Glaucus of Sparta, famed for honesty, who was holding money in trust and asked the Delphic oracle whether he might keep it by swearing a false oath. The Pythia answered that tempting the god with the question was as bad as doing the deed. Though he returned the money, his whole family line was later wiped out.
greek_mythology.explanation: The legend teaches that merely intending a wrong is already a serious wrong in the eyes of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural forbids harm ‘even in the mind’; the Glaucus story shows the Greek conviction that intending harm already carries guilt.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book I of the Republic, Socrates leads Polemarchus to abandon the traditional view that justice means helping friends and harming enemies. He argues that harming anyone makes them worse, and that it cannot be the work of the just man to harm anyone at all, friend or enemy.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates concludes that the just person harms no one, under any circumstances.
philosophy.tie_back: Both reject every exception to non-harm, including the traditional exception for enemies.

real_life_example.event_title: The Nuremberg Code sets limits on human experimentation
real_life_example.event: On 19 August 1947 the judges of the American military tribunal in the Doctors' Trial at Nuremberg, which tried German physicians for crimes committed in the concentration camps, delivered their verdict. In a section titled Permissible Medical Experiments they set out ten principles, later known as the Nuremberg Code. These require that the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential and that experiments be conducted so as to avoid all unnecessary physical and mental suffering and injury.
real_life_example.explanation: After revelations of terrible abuses, the Code became a landmark statement that medical research must not inflict needless suffering on any person.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls it the highest virtue never to do any harm, however small, to anyone at any time, and the Nuremberg Code wrote a version of that principle into the foundations of modern medical ethics.

tamil:
தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை தானறிவான் என்கொலோ
மன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னா செயல்.
transliteration:
Thannuyirkku innaamai thaan arivaan en kolo
Mannuyirkku innaa seyal.
meaning: A person knows well how pain feels in their own life. So why do they cause that same pain to other living beings?
elementary: You know how much a bee sting hurts, because it happened to you. So why would anyone go around stinging others? This kural asks: if you know how pain feels, how can you give it to someone else?
university: Kural 318 turns the rule of 316 into a question, and the rhetorical form (en kolo, ‘why, then?’) exposes a contradiction in the person who harms. The contrast between thannuyir (one’s own life or self) and mannuyir (the lives that dwell on earth, all living beings) widens the circle beyond humans, in keeping with the Kural’s broad concern for all creatures, developed further in the next chapter on not killing. The argument is essentially one of consistency: whoever knows pain from the inside cannot claim not to know what they are doing when they cause it. Similar appeals to self-knowledge appear in the Gita’s ‘comparison to one’s own self,’ the Dhammapada’s instruction to put oneself in another’s place, and the Torah’s reminder that Israel knows the heart of the stranger because it was once a stranger.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He is a perfect yogī who, by comparison to his own self, sees the true equality of all beings, in both their happiness and their distress, O Arjuna!”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the highest yogi uses his own experience of joy and sorrow to understand everyone else’s.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts ground concern for others in self-knowledge: your own distress tells you what others feel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers to treat others exactly as they would want to be treated.
christianity.tie_back: Both make one’s own experience the measure of right treatment of others.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever wishes to be delivered from the fire and enter the garden should die with faith in Allah and the Last Day and should treat the people as he wishes to be treated by them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes treating people as you wish to be treated a condition for salvation.
islam.tie_back: Both appeal to what one knows one wants, or does not want, for oneself as the guide for treating others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Also thou shalt not oppress a stranger: for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids oppressing strangers because Israel knows from its own history exactly how a stranger feels.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s argument: you know this pain yourself, so how can you inflict it on another?

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; life is dear to all. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha reminds us that every being fears violence and loves life, so we should put ourselves in their place and never harm them.
buddhism.tie_back: Both reason from one’s own fear of harm to the duty not to harm any living being.

jainism.quote_or_event: “All beings are fond of life, like pleasure, hate pain, shun destruction, like life, long to live. To all life is dear.”
jainism.explanation: The Ācārāṅga states the universal fact on which ahiṃsā rests: every living being values its own life and recoils from pain.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks why someone who knows his own pain inflicts it on other lives (mannuyir). The Jain sutra answers from the other side: every one of those lives feels what he feels.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.2.3.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You say that the One Lord is in all, so why do you kill chickens?”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir exposes the contradiction in someone who professes that God dwells in every creature yet takes a creature's life.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks why one who knows pain in one's own life inflicts it on other lives; Kabir's question likewise exposes the self-contradiction in harming beings one admits are like oneself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1350, Raag Prabhaatee, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the last book of the Iliad, old King Priam comes to Achilles to beg for the body of his son Hector. He asks Achilles to think of his own aged father. Achilles, remembering his father and his own grief, weeps with Priam and gives back the body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles stops abusing Hector’s body once he recognises Priam’s grief as the same grief his own father will feel.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles moves from inflicting pain to showing mercy exactly when he realises he knows that pain from the inside, the Kural’s point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “When asked how men might live most virtuously and most justly, he said, ‘If we never do ourselves what we blame in others.’”
philosophy.explanation: Thales, one of the Seven Sages, sums up the just life as never doing what we condemn when others do it.
philosophy.tie_back: Both expose the inconsistency of the one who harms: we know what we object to, so we must not do it ourselves.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 1.36 (Thales) (trans. C. D. Yonge)

real_life_example.event_title: Anna Sewell writes Black Beauty to win kindness for horses
real_life_example.event: Anna Sewell, who was disabled from a young age and had difficulty walking, spent the last years of her life confined to her house as an invalid while writing Black Beauty, a fictional autobiography of a horse. She stated that one of her aims was to induce kindness, sympathy and an understanding treatment of horses. The book, first published in 1877 by Jarrold of Norwich, is said to have been instrumental in ending the cruel use of the checkrein, or bearing rein.
real_life_example.explanation: Sewell used her final years to make readers feel the suffering of animals from the inside, by telling the story in the horse's own voice.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks why anyone who knows pain in his own life would inflict it on other living beings, and Sewell's book made readers recognise in a horse's suffering the same pain they knew themselves.

tamil:
பிறர்க்கின்னா முற்பகல் செய்யின் தமக்குஇன்னா
பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்.
transliteration:
Pirarkku innaa murpagal seyyin thamakku innaa
Pirpagal thaame varum.
meaning: If you harm others in the morning, harm will come back to you on its own by the afternoon.
elementary: It’s like throwing a ball hard against a wall: it bounces right back at you. This kural says being mean to someone in the morning means trouble will come bouncing back to you by the afternoon.
university: This is among the best-known couplets in Tamil, often quoted as a proverb. Its power lies in its compression of time: murpagal (forenoon) and pirpagal (afternoon) shrink the karmic interval, usually imagined across lifetimes, to a single day. The word thaame (of their own accord) makes the return automatic; no avenger or judge is named, and the consequence seems built into the act. The couplet thus combines a moral law with a psychological one, since harm tends to provoke retaliation and hostility quickly. Parallels range from the Mahabharata’s observation that the injured turns round and injures the injurer, to Proverbs’ image of the stone that rolls back on the one who pushes it, to Theseus giving each bandit on the road to Athens the death he dealt to others.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When One injures another, the injured turns round and injures the injurer.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati warns Yudhishthira that harm done to another comes back to the one who did it.
hinduism.tie_back: The same law of return as the Kural: the harm you send out comes back to you.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section 113 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that everyone harvests exactly what they have planted.
christianity.tie_back: Both teach that harm returns to its author; the Kural adds that the harvest comes fast.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you act rightly, it is for your own good, but if you do wrong, it is to your own loss.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that the effects of one’s good and evil deeds fall back on oneself.
islam.tie_back: Both say that wrongdoing ultimately harms the wrongdoer.
islam.source: Qur’an 17:7 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs pictures harm as a pit that swallows the one who dug it, or a stone that rolls back on the one who pushed it.
judaism.tie_back: Both use the image of harm rebounding naturally on its maker, without any outside avenger.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like fine dust thrown against the wind, evil falls back upon that fool who offends an inoffensive, pure and guiltless man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares harming an innocent person to throwing dust into the wind: it blows straight back into your own face.
buddhism.tie_back: Both picture harm flying straight back at the one who sends it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
jainism.explanation: Jacobi's commentator explains the image: a burglar caught halfway through the hole he dug in a wall is crushed when the wall he undermined collapses on him.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says harm done in the morning returns by itself before evening. The burglar is destroyed by his own handiwork almost at once, which shows the same automatic and swift return of one's deeds.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You shall harvest what you plant.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Japji, Guru Nanak states the law of action plainly: what a person sows in deeds, that same person reaps.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that harm done in the morning returns to the doer by afternoon; Guru Nanak teaches the same return of one's deeds to oneself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 20, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On his journey to Athens, the young Theseus meets a series of bandits who torment travellers. He kills each one by the same method they used on their victims, bending Sinis’ pine trees, hurling Sciron off his cliff, and fitting Procrustes to his own bed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Each bandit suffers exactly the harm he used to inflict on others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s law played out as myth: the harm each villain inflicted comes back to him in the same form.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book IV of the Consolation of Philosophy, Lady Philosophy argues that goodness is what makes us human, so whoever abandons it stops being fully human and sinks into the likeness of a beast. Wickedness therefore is its own punishment and falls on the wicked at once.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius argues that evildoers are punished by their very wickedness, immediately and unavoidably.
philosophy.tie_back: Both see the harm done to others turning back on the doer without delay; Boethius places the punishment inside the soul.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book IV, prose 3

real_life_example.event_title: Danton is tried and executed by the Revolutionary Tribunal he helped create
real_life_example.event: In March 1793 Georges Danton played an instrumental role in establishing the Revolutionary Tribunal, and the following month he helped create the Committee of Public Safety, laying groundwork for the Reign of Terror. When he later opposed the Terror, he was arrested on the night of 29-30 March 1794 and tried before that same Revolutionary Tribunal from 2 to 4 April. He was executed by guillotine in Paris on 5 April 1794.
real_life_example.explanation: Within about a year, the instrument of harm that Danton had helped build was turned against him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that if you harm others in the morning, harm will come back to you by the afternoon, and Danton was condemned by the very tribunal he had helped set up barely a year earlier.

tamil:
நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம் நோய்செய்யார்
நோயின்மை வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Noyellaam noy seydhaar melavaam noy seyyaar
Noyinmai vendu pavar.
meaning: All suffering comes back to those who cause suffering. So people who want to be free of suffering do not cause it to others.
elementary: If you plant thorns, you will get pricked walking through your own garden. If you never want to get pricked, don’t plant thorns. This kural says: if you want a life without pain, don’t give pain to anyone.
university: The chapter closes with a verbal tour de force: the word noy (pain, affliction, disease) appears four times in seven words, so that the sound of the couplet enacts its argument that pain circles back to its source. The first line states a law (all affliction settles on those who afflict), and the second draws the practical conclusion for anyone who wants noyinmai, freedom from suffering. The ethics of non-harm is here grounded partly in enlightened self-interest, rounding off a chapter that has moved from the stainless person’s principle (311–312), through empathy (315–318), to consequence (319–320). The idea is widely shared: Hesiod’s warning that the evil plotter harms himself most, the Qur’an’s statement that evil plotting backfires on the plotters, Marcus Aurelius’ remark that the wrongdoer wrongs himself, and the Dhammapada’s assurance that for one who does no evil there is no ill.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He by whom no one is put into difficulty and who is not disturbed by anyone, who is equipoised in happiness and distress, fear and anxiety, is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the ideal devotee as one who troubles no one and is troubled by no one.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita pairs the two halves of the Kural: the one who causes no distress is also the one free of distress.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that the standard we apply to others will be applied to us.
christianity.tie_back: Both teach that what we deal out comes back to us, so the way to avoid harm is not to deal it.

islam.quote_or_event: “But evil plotting only backfires on those who plot.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an declares that evil schemes end up harming only the schemers.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s first line in Qur’anic form: harm settles on those who cause it.
islam.source: Qur’an 35:43 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made. His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist says the evildoer falls into his own trap and his violence comes down on his own head.
judaism.tie_back: Both declare that the pain one causes lands on oneself.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If on the hand there is no wound, one may carry even poison in it. Poison does not affect one who is free from wounds. For him who does no evil, there is no ill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the one who does no evil to a hand without cuts: poison cannot harm it.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s second line: the person who does no harm stays free of harm.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Whatever cruelty he has done in a former birth, the same will be inflicted on him in the Circle of Births. Having been born in an extremely miserable state of life, the sufferer experiences infinite pain. A wise man hearing of these hells should not kill any living being in the whole world.”
jainism.explanation: At the end of its description of the hells, the Sūtrakṛtāṅga states that the pain one inflicts is the pain one will suffer, and draws the practical conclusion of non-violence.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says all suffering falls on those who cause it, so those who wish to be free of suffering do not cause it. The Jain verses state both halves, the law and the conclusion, in the same order.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.5.2.23–24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not harbor evil intentions against others in your mind, and you shall not be troubled, O Siblings of Destiny, O friends.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan ties freedom from one's own trouble directly to not wishing harm on others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural concludes that those who wish to be free of suffering do not cause it to others; Guru Arjan gives the same practical counsel: wish no one harm, and harm will not trouble you.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He does mischief to himself who does mischief to another, and evil planned harms the plotter most.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that anyone who harms another is really harming himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s central claim in Greek form: pain caused to others falls on the one who causes it.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 265–266 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Does any one do wrong? It is to himself that he does the wrong.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that the wrongdoer is the real victim of his own wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: Both place the harm of wrongdoing on the one who commits it.

real_life_example.event_title: Vidkun Quisling's collaboration ends in his trial and execution
real_life_example.event: During the German invasion of Norway in April 1940, Vidkun Quisling proclaimed himself head of a new government, and from 1942 he served as Minister President of a Nazi-controlled puppet government. He signed laws that enabled the arrest of Norway's Jewish men and the confiscation of Jewish property, and 772 Norwegian Jews were deported, most to their deaths at Auschwitz. After Norway's liberation in May 1945 he was arrested, convicted of treason and other crimes, and executed at Akershus Fortress in Oslo on 24 October 1945; his name became a synonym for traitor.
real_life_example.explanation: The man who helped bring great suffering on his own country ended his life condemned by it, his very name turned into a word of disgrace.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says all suffering falls upon those who cause suffering, and Quisling's betrayal of his people returned on him as condemnation and a lasting byword for treachery.

tamil:
அறவினை யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை கோறல்
பிறவினை எல்லாந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Aravinai yaadhenin kollaamai koral
Piravinai ellaam tharum.
meaning: If you ask what doing good means, it is not killing any living thing. Killing brings every other kind of evil deed along with it.
elementary: Imagine a row of dominoes. If you knock over the first one, all the others fall too. Valluvar says killing is that first domino: once someone is willing to take a life, every other bad act becomes easy. Not killing keeps the whole row standing.
university: Valluvar answers the question “what is aram (virtue)?” with a single negative act — kollaamai, abstention from killing — and then gives its mirror image: kōṟal (killing) “yields all other deeds” (piṟavinai), which the classical commentators, including Mu. Varadarasan, read as all non-virtuous deeds. The couplet therefore makes non-killing not merely one virtue among many but the generative root of the moral life, with killing as the root of vice. This places the Kural squarely within the broad śramaṇic and Brahmanical consensus of early-first-millennium India that ahiṃsā is the highest dharma, a position shared by Jain, Buddhist and epic Hindu sources. The structure of the verse — definition followed by its contrary — is typical of Valluvar’s aphoristic logic, compressing an entire ethical theory into seven words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Abstention from injury is the highest religion.”
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata’s Anushasana Parva, Bhishma teaches Yudhishthira that ahimsa (non-injury) is the supreme dharma — the famous formula ahimsa paramo dharmah.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s answer to “what is virtue?”: non-killing is virtue in its highest form.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section CXV (K. M. Ganguli trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not kill.”
christianity.explanation: The sixth commandment in the Decalogue given at Sinai forbids the unlawful taking of human life.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it places the prohibition on killing at the foundation of the moral law.

islam.quote_or_event: “whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption [done] in the land - it is as if he had slain mankind entirely. And whoever saves one - it is as if he had saved mankind entirely.”
islam.explanation: After the story of Adam’s two sons, the Qur’an declares that unjustly killing one person is morally equivalent to killing all humanity.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat killing as the gravest of wrongs, one that contains the seed of every other evil.

judaism.quote_or_event: “if any man has caused a single life to perish from Israel, he is deemed by Scripture as if he had caused a whole world to perish; and anyone who saves a single soul from Israel, he is deemed by Scripture as if he had saved a whole world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah explains why God created a single human first: to teach that each life is an entire world.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s conviction that taking a life is not one wrong among many but a total, world-destroying wrong.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; all fear death. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha grounds the precept against killing in empathy: every creature fears death just as we do.
buddhism.tie_back: Same core teaching as the Kural — non-killing is the basic ethical act from which the rest of goodness flows.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The Arhats and Bhagavats of the past, present, and future, all say thus, speak thus, declare thus, explain thus: all breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures should not be slain, nor treated with violence, nor abused, nor tormented, nor driven away. This is the pure, unchangeable, eternal law…”
jainism.explanation: The lecture of the Ācārāṅga called 'Righteousness' defines the eternal law of all the Jinas as non-injury to every living being.
jainism.tie_back: Asked what aram is, Valluvar answers 'not killing'; the Ācārāṅga likewise makes non-killing the very definition of the eternal dharma.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.4.1.1–2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You kill living beings, and call it a righteous action. Tell me, brother, what would you call an unrighteous action?”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir confronts those who kill animals in sacrifice and call it dharma, turning the question back on them: if killing is righteousness, what is left to call sin?
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural answers 'what is virtue?' with 'not killing'; Kabir reaches the same point from the other side, insisting that killing cannot be called righteousness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1103, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orestes, having killed his mother Clytemnestra, is hounded across Greece by the Furies (Erinyes), who pursue bloodguilt relentlessly until he is tried at Athens.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aeschylus’ Eumenides the spilling of kindred blood unleashes a chain of pursuit, madness and pollution that no one can escape by ordinary means.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s second line: one killing sets in motion a whole train of further evils.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Porphyry’s treatise On Abstinence from Animal Food argues that justice extends to all sentient creatures and that the philosopher who seeks purity must refrain from killing them.
philosophy.explanation: The Neoplatonist Porphyry (3rd c. CE) built a sustained philosophical case that harming living beings is incompatible with the virtuous, god-like life.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, he makes non-killing a defining mark of virtue rather than an optional scruple.
philosophy.source: Porphyry, On Abstinence from Animal Food, Books 1–3

real_life_example.event_title: Tuscany becomes the first European state to abolish the death penalty
real_life_example.event: Grand Duke Peter Leopold of Tuscany, later Holy Roman Emperor Leopold II, promulgated a new penal code that abolished the death penalty, the first such code in Europe. The reform followed the debate opened by Cesare Beccaria's 1764 book On Crimes and Punishments. Capital punishment was later reintroduced in Tuscany, but 30 November is now marked each year as Cities for Life Day in memory of the 1786 abolition.
real_life_example.explanation: For the first time a European state wrote into its law that the state itself would not kill, and the date is still commemorated by campaigners worldwide.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural answers the question of what virtue is with one act, not killing, and Tuscany made that refusal the foundation of its criminal law.

tamil:
பகுத்துண்டு பல்லுயிர் ஓம்புதல் நூலோர்
தொகுத்தவற்றுள் எல்லாந் தலை.
transliteration:
Pakuththundu palluyir oampudhal nooloar
Thokuththavatrul ellaam thalai.
meaning: Sharing your food with others and protecting all kinds of living things is the greatest of all the good deeds that writers of books on right living have listed.
elementary: If you have a lunchbox and a hungry friend, you split your sandwich. If you see a bird with a hurt wing, you help it. Valluvar says that sharing and taking care of every living thing is the number-one rule in all the good books ever written.
university: The couplet fuses two duties — sharing food (pakuttuṇṭal) and protecting the manifold life of creatures (palluyir ōmputal) — and ranks them as “the head” (talai) of everything the authors of moral treatises (nūlōr) have compiled. Its placement in the chapter on non-killing shows that for Valluvar non-violence is not merely a prohibition but has a positive face: actively sustaining life. The appeal to the collected wisdom of the nūlōr is also a characteristic move, presenting the Kural as a distillation of an entire ethical literature. The pairing of generosity and care for life anticipates modern ethics of care that see nurture, not only abstention from harm, as the core of morality.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The devotees of the Lord are released from all kinds of sins because they eat food which is offered first for sacrifice. Others, who prepare food for personal sense enjoyment, verily eat only sin.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that food must first be offered and shared within the cycle of sacrifice; eating only for oneself is itself sinful.
hinduism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s first half — sharing food (pakuttuṇṭal) is a central religious duty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise.”
christianity.explanation: John the Baptist tells the crowds that true repentance means sharing clothing and food with those who lack them.
christianity.tie_back: Same instruction as the Kural’s pakuttuṇṭal — divide what you have to eat with those in need.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they give food in spite of love for it to the needy, the orphan, and the captive,”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the righteous as those who give away food they themselves desire, seeking only God’s face.
islam.tie_back: Both texts rank sharing food with the vulnerable among the highest virtues.

judaism.quote_or_event: “That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Go study.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel summarizes the whole Torah for a would-be convert in a single ethical principle.
judaism.tie_back: Like Valluvar ranking one virtue as the head of all that the learned have compiled, Hillel names one principle as the sum of all scripture.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If beings knew, as I know, the results of giving & sharing, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of selfishness overcome their minds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that even one’s last mouthful should be shared if there is someone to receive it.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a direct echo of pakuttuṇṭal — eating only after sharing.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain householder ethics joins sharing food with protecting life: the vow of sharing with guests (atithi-saṃvibhāga) is one of the householder's supplementary vows, and the classical Jain list of gifts places the gift of food (āhāra-dāna) alongside the gift of fearlessness or protection of life (abhaya-dāna).
jainism.explanation: For the Jain layperson, generosity with food and active protection of living beings are the positive counterparts of the vow of non-violence.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural ranks sharing one's food and protecting many lives as the chief of all virtues; Jain lay ethics pairs exactly these two, food-giving and life-protecting, as core duties.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.21 (Digambara numbering; atithi-saṃvibhāga vow), with the traditional fourfold dāna scheme in later Jain śrāvakācāra literature

sikhism.quote_or_event: Every gurdwara keeps a langar, a free communal kitchen where food is served to all who come, seated together in a line so that no one claims higher or lower status. Britannica notes that under Guru Amar Das visitors ate in the casteless langar, and that the langar originated as a protest against the caste system.
sikhism.explanation: The langar puts vand chhakna, sharing what one has, at the centre of Sikh worship: no one who comes is turned away hungry.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks sharing one's food first among the virtues the learned have gathered; the Sikh langar makes that sharing a permanent institution open to all.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'langar' (with linked coverage in 'Guru Amar Das' and 'Sikhism: The rejection of caste') (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Triptolemus, who received grain from Demeter and spread agriculture to humankind, was credited with three laws: honour your parents, honour the gods with fruits, and spare animals.
greek_mythology.explanation: Porphyry reports this Eleusinian tradition, linking the gift of shared grain with a command not to harm animals.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Combines the Kural’s two themes — sharing food and protecting living creatures — in a single mythic lawgiver.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch, in On the Eating of Flesh, protests that for the sake of a little flesh humans deprive animals of the sun, of light, and of the span of life that is theirs by nature.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch argues that sustaining our own lives does not justify cutting short the lives of other creatures.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s palluyir ōmputal — the duty to preserve the many lives around us.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, De esu carnium I.4 (994E)

real_life_example.event_title: The Oxford Committee for Famine Relief is founded
real_life_example.place: University Church of St Mary the Virgin, Oxford, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: A group of Oxford citizens, including the vicar T. R. Milford and Professor Gilbert Murray, met in the Old Library of the University Church and formed the Oxford Committee for Famine Relief. They acted because famine in German-occupied Greece could not be relieved while an Allied naval blockade stopped food imports. The committee raised money for relief through the Greek Red Cross and campaigned for food to be allowed through; it later broadened its work and became Oxfam.
real_life_example.explanation: A small local committee grew into one of the world's best-known relief organisations, built on the idea that feeding the hungry is a duty that crosses the lines of war.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks sharing one's food and protecting the many forms of life as the highest of virtues, and the committee was founded to do exactly that for starving strangers.

tamil:
ஒன்றாக நல்லது கொல்லாமை மற்றதன்
பின்சாரப் பொய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Ondraaka nalladhu kollaamai matradhan
Pinsaarap poiyaamai nandru.
meaning: Not killing stands alone as the greatest good. Right behind it, in second place, comes not lying.
elementary: Think of a race where first prize is gold and second is silver. Valluvar gives the gold medal to “never kill” and the silver medal to “never lie.” Both are winners, but not hurting any living thing comes first.
university: Here Valluvar explicitly ranks two virtues he has treated separately: kollaamai (non-killing) is good “as one” (oṉṟāka) — unique and incomparable — and poyyāmai (truthfulness, the subject of chapter 30) is good “following behind it.” This is notable because in chapter 30 he had praised truth in superlative terms; the commentators reconcile the two by saying truth is supreme among virtues of speech, but non-killing is supreme absolutely. The ordering precisely mirrors Patañjali’s list of yamas, where ahiṃsā precedes satya, and the Buddhist precepts, where abstaining from killing is first and false speech fourth. It also contrasts with Gandhi, who, while treating the two as inseparable, made Truth the end and ahimsa the means.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “ahiṃsā-satya-asteya-brahmacarya-aparigrahā yamāḥ” — non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, continence and non-possessiveness are the restraints.
hinduism.explanation: Patañjali lists the five yamas (ethical restraints) of yoga, with ahimsa first and satya second.
hinduism.tie_back: Identical ranking to the Kural: non-killing first, truthfulness immediately after.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt do no murder, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness,”
christianity.explanation: When asked which commandments lead to life, Jesus lists them beginning with the prohibition on murder.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it places not killing at the head of the list, with honesty (no false witness) following.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who do not invoke with Allāh another deity or kill the soul which Allāh has forbidden [to be killed], except by right, and do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse.”
islam.explanation: Among the qualities of the servants of the Most Merciful, refraining from unjust killing is named immediately after refusing idolatry.
islam.tie_back: Shows unjust killing ranked among the very gravest sins, near the top of the moral order as in the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Keep thee far from a false matter; and the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah’s law of justice places the command to shun falsehood and the command not to kill the innocent in a single verse.
judaism.tie_back: Binds together exactly the two virtues the Kural ranks — not lying and not killing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Pāṇātipātā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi” — I undertake the training rule to abstain from taking life.
buddhism.explanation: The first of the five lay precepts is abstaining from killing; abstaining from false speech (musāvādā) is the fourth.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, non-killing is the first and foundational precept, with non-lying following among the core rules.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain list of the five great vows (mahāvratas) taken by monks and the five lesser vows (aṇuvratas) of laypeople, the vow of non-killing (ahiṃsā) always stands first and the vow of truthfulness (satya) second, as in the account of Mahāvīra's five great vows and their clauses.
jainism.explanation: Jainism orders its vows with non-injury at the head and abstention from falsehood immediately after it.
