jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks non-killing as the peerless good with not-lying following close behind; the Jain sequence of vows gives precisely this order.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.15 (the five great vows; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak places truth, and above all a life lived in truth, at the very top of the spiritual life.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks non-killing first and truthfulness second; Guru Nanak's ranking differs, placing truthful living above everything, so the parallel lies in the shared high esteem for truth rather than in the order.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod names Horkos (Oath), who most afflicts men who knowingly swear falsely, while the avenging Erinyes, born from the blood of the wounded Ouranos, punish bloodshed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Early Greek myth assigns divine punishers to both the perjurer and the shedder of blood.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows falsehood and bloodshed as twin cosmic offences, though without the Kural’s explicit ranking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Ahimsa and Truth are so intertwined that it is practically impossible to disentangle and separate them.”
philosophy.explanation: Gandhi likens the two to two sides of a coin, but calls ahimsa the means and Truth the end.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Gandhi ranks and pairs non-violence and truth; interestingly he inverts the Kural’s order, placing Truth highest.
philosophy.source: M. K. Gandhi, From Yeravda Mandir, ch. 2 “Ahimsa or Love”

real_life_example.event_title: Miep Gies hides the Frank family and saves Anne Frank's diary
real_life_example.event: In July 1942 Otto Frank asked his employee Miep Gies to help hide his family from deportation, and she agreed. For more than two years she, her husband Jan and several colleagues secretly brought food, supplies and news to the eight people hiding in the Secret Annex, concealing their presence from the authorities. After the hiding place was raided on 4 August 1944, Gies gathered Anne Frank's diary and papers, kept them in her desk, and later gave them to Otto Frank, the only survivor.
real_life_example.explanation: Gies and her colleagues risked their own lives and lived a long concealment to protect others, and her rescue of the diary preserved one of the most widely read books of the twentieth century.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks not killing first and not lying second, and Gies's two years of necessary concealment were in the service of protecting life.

tamil:
நல்லாறு எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும்
கொல்லாமை சூழும் நெறி.
transliteration:
Nallaaru enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhondrum
Kollaamai soozhum neri.
meaning: If you ask what the good path is, it is the way of life that takes care never to kill any creature at all.
elementary: When you walk in a garden, you watch where you step so you don’t squash the ants or crush the flowers. Valluvar says the “good road” in life is exactly that: always looking out so that you don’t hurt even the smallest living thing.
university: The couplet defines nallāṟu, “the good path,” not by a doctrine or ritual but by a disposition: the neṟi (way of conduct) that “deliberates upon” (cūḻum) not killing “anything at all” (yātoṉṟum). The verb cūḻ suggests active, careful forethought — non-killing is not passive but a vigilant attentiveness in every act. The phrase yātoṉṟum explicitly extends the scope to all living beings, however small, aligning the Kural with the rigorous ahiṃsā of Jain and Buddhist ethics. This conception of ethics as an attentive way of moving through the world anticipates Albert Schweitzer’s “reverence for life.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…austerity; simplicity; nonviolence; truthfulness; freedom from anger; renunciation; tranquillity; aversion to faultfinding; compassion for all living entities…” — these “belong to godly men endowed with divine nature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the divine qualities that lead toward liberation, including ahimsa and compassion for all beings.
hinduism.tie_back: Marks non-violence toward all creatures as a defining feature of the good, liberating path.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs identifies care for the life even of one’s animals as a mark of the righteous person.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the good way is shown by concern for the lives of all creatures, not only humans.

islam.quote_or_event: “And there is no creature on [or within] the earth or bird that flies with its wings except [that they are] communities like you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes animals and birds as communities like human beings, all known to and gathered by God.
islam.tie_back: Grounds the Kural’s regard for “any creature whatsoever” in the dignity of all living communities.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace.”
judaism.explanation: Said of Wisdom, and applied by the rabbis to the Torah as a whole, which they held exists “for the sake of the ways of peace.”
judaism.tie_back: Defines the good path, as the Kural does, as a way of non-harm and peace.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And what, monks, is right action? Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from stealing, abstaining from unchastity: This, monks, is called right action.”
buddhism.explanation: In analysing the Noble Eightfold Path, the Buddha defines right action beginning with abstention from taking life.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: the good path (magga / nallāṟu) is defined first by not killing.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 45.8, Magga-vibhanga Sutta (Thanissaro Bhikkhu trans.)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A wise man should study them with all means of philosophical research. All beings hate pains; therefore one should not kill them. This is the quintessence of wisdom: not to kill anything.”
jainism.explanation: In the lecture titled 'The Path', the Sūtrakṛtāṅga answers 'what is the path?' by enumerating all classes of living beings and concluding that the essence of wisdom is to kill nothing.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural defines the good path as the way that takes thought to kill nothing at all; Mahāvīra's 'Path' lecture likewise makes 'not to kill anything' its core after careful study of every form of life.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.9–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “And when, O Nanak, he is merciful to all beings, only then shall he be called a Muslim.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak redefines what makes a person truly religious: not outward forms but mercy towards every living being.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines the good path as the way that takes care not to kill any creature; Guru Nanak likewise makes mercy to all beings the defining mark of the true religious path.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plato recalls the so-called “Orphic life” of old, in which people abstained from animal sacrifice and from everything that has life, keeping to what is lifeless.
greek_mythology.explanation: Followers of the mythic singer Orpheus were remembered for a way of life defined by refusal to kill.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An ancient Greek “good path” defined, like the Kural’s, by abstaining from killing any creature.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is good to maintain and cherish life; it is evil to destroy and to check life.”
philosophy.explanation: Albert Schweitzer’s ethic of reverence for life holds that every living thing has a will-to-live that the ethical person must respect.
philosophy.tie_back: A modern restatement of the Kural’s good path: careful attention never to destroy any life.
philosophy.source: Albert Schweitzer, Civilization and Ethics (The Philosophy of Civilization, Part II)

real_life_example.event_title: Shogun Tsunayoshi's Edicts on Compassion for Living Things
real_life_example.event: Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, the fifth Tokugawa shogun, issued a long series of decrees known as the Edicts on Compassion for Living Things. They protected a wide range of creatures, including dogs, cats, horses, birds, fish, shellfish and even insects, with many edicts forbidding the abandonment or mistreatment of dogs. Because of these laws he became known as the Dog Shogun, and the edicts remained in force for more than two decades of his rule.
real_life_example.explanation: It was one of the most sweeping attempts by any government to make care for animal life a matter of law, and it remains famous and much debated in Japan.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines the good path as a way of life that carefully considers how to avoid killing anything at all, and Tsunayoshi's edicts tried to extend that care even to insects and shellfish.

tamil:
நிலைஅஞ்சி நீத்தாருள் எல்லாம் கொலைஅஞ்சிக்
கொல்லாமை சூழ்வான் தலை.
transliteration:
Nilaianji neeththaarul ellaam kolaianjik
Kollaamai soozhvaan thalai.
meaning: Many people give up the world because they fear the endless cycle of life and death. The greatest of them is the one who fears the wrong of killing and carefully keeps from it.
elementary: Some people give up their toys, their fancy food and their comfy beds to become monks. That’s hard! But Valluvar says the very best of them is the one who is most careful never to hurt a living thing. Being gentle matters more than giving things up.
university: Valluvar compares two kinds of fear: nilai añci — fear of the “state” of worldly existence and rebirth that drives ascetics to renounce (nīttār) — and kolai añci, fear of the guilt of killing. He declares that among all renunciants, the one moved by the second fear and who deliberates on non-killing is talai, the head. This subordinates the whole apparatus of asceticism to a single ethical commitment, a characteristic Kural move that ranks inner moral conduct over outward religious status. The same move appears in the Mahabharata’s claim that ahimsa is itself the highest penance, and in the Dhammapada’s definition of the true monk as one who has laid down violence toward all beings.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Abstention from injury is the highest religion. It is, again, the highest penance.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma declares that ahimsa is not only the highest dharma but also the highest form of tapas (austerity).
hinduism.tie_back: Directly supports the Kural: non-killing ranks above every other austerity practised by renunciants.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section CXV (K. M. Ganguli trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that even the most extreme renunciation is worthless without love.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it subordinates outward renunciation to an inner ethical disposition — here love, there non-killing.

islam.quote_or_event: “The cases which will be decided first (on the Day of Resurrection) will be the cases of blood-shedding.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that bloodshed is the first matter between people that God will judge.
islam.tie_back: Reflects the Kural’s kolai añci — the fear of bloodguilt as the gravest concern of a God-fearing person.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?”
judaism.explanation: After asking whether God wants thousands of rams or even one’s firstborn, Micah answers that God wants justice and mercy instead.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks ethical mercy above elaborate religious self-sacrifice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even though he be well-attired, yet if he is poised, calm, controlled and established in the holy life, having set aside violence towards all beings — he, truly, is a holy man, a renunciate, a monk.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the true renunciant is marked not by outward austerities but by having laid down violence toward all beings.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural: among renunciants, the truest is the one who has renounced harming life.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who thoroughly knows living beings, whether they move or not, and does not injure them in any of the three ways, him we call a Brâhmana.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha tells a sacrificing priest that the true holy man is defined not by birth or ritual but by knowing all living beings and injuring none in thought, word or act.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar places at the head of all renunciants the one who dreads killing; the Uttarādhyayana likewise makes non-injury the mark of the true ascetic.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 25.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You call yourself the most excellent sage; then who would you call a butcher?”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir mocks those who kill in religious sacrifice yet claim the rank of the highest sages: by their deeds they are no different from butchers.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks highest among renunciants the one who fears the sin of killing; Kabir denies the title of great sage to anyone who kills, whatever his religious standing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1103, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Apollo killed the Cyclopes, Zeus required even this god to atone by serving a mortal, Admetus, as a herdsman for a year; Heracles likewise served Omphale in expiation for killing Iphitus.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth even gods and the greatest heroes had to submit to humiliating servitude to cleanse bloodguilt.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Reflects kolai añci — the dread of bloodguilt is so great that it outranks divine or heroic status.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Empedocles, in his Purifications, portrays himself as an exiled daimon and calls on mortals to cease from the harsh-sounding slaughter by which, unknowingly, they devour one another.
philosophy.explanation: The philosopher-purifier treated abstention from bloodshed as the core of the purified, god-like life.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes refusal to kill the heart of the path of spiritual purification.

real_life_example.event_title: The Swiss Brethren adopt the Schleitheim Confession
real_life_example.event: Leaders of the Swiss Brethren, an early Anabaptist movement, met at Schleitheim and agreed seven articles of faith, with Michael Sattler as their main author. The articles called for separation from the world and rejected the use of weapons of violence, treating the sword as belonging outside the perfection of Christ. The Swiss Brethren refused military service and were harshly persecuted, and Sattler was executed later that year.
real_life_example.explanation: Schleitheim became a founding statement for the nonresistance later kept by Mennonite and Hutterite communities.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the foremost of all who renounce the world is the one who fears the guilt of killing, and these separatists made the refusal to wield the sword central to their renunciation.

tamil:
கொல்லாமை மேற்கொண் டொழுகுவான் வாழ்நாள்மேல்
செல்லாது உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று.
transliteration:
Kollaamai merkon dozhuguvaan vaazhnaalmel
Sellaadhu uyirunnum kootru.
meaning: Death, which eats up all lives, will not come to cut short the days of someone who has made not killing the rule they live by.
elementary: In old stories, Death is like a hunter who comes to take people away. Valluvar says that hunter holds back from someone who never hurts any creature — as if even Death respects a person who protects life.
university: Kūṟṟu, “the one who divides” (Yama, Death), is here personified as “the eater of lives” (uyiruṇṇum). Valluvar claims that it “will not go” (cellātu) against the life-span of one who lives by non-killing. Commentators differ: some read this literally as a promise of long life, others (like Kalaignar) as a poetic image of Death hesitating in awe, and still others spiritually, as freedom from the cycle of rebirth. The idea of karmic reciprocity — sparing life earns life — is explicit in Buddhist teaching on the karmic causes of long and short lives, and has echoes in the biblical promise of prolonged days for sparing the mother bird.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who does not seek to cause the sufferings of bonds and death to living creatures, (but) desires the good of all (beings), obtains endless bliss.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu promise unending happiness to one who never inflicts captivity or death on living beings.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it promises a reward beyond death’s reach to the one who refuses to kill.

christianity.quote_or_event: “What man is he that desireth life, and loveth many days, that he may see good? Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile. Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.”
christianity.explanation: The Psalmist teaches that long and good life belongs to those who turn from evil and pursue peace.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s link between a harmless, peaceful life and many days of life.

islam.quote_or_event: “The merciful are shown mercy by Ar-Rahman. Be merciful on the earth, and you will be shown mercy from Who is above the heavens.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that mercy shown to those on earth is answered by divine mercy.
islam.tie_back: Reciprocity as in the Kural: one who spares and shows mercy to life is spared in turn.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But thou shalt in any wise let the dam go, and take the young to thee; that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands sparing the mother bird when taking from a nest, promising long life in return.
judaism.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: sparing animal life is explicitly rewarded with prolonged days.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “…having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstains from killing living beings, lays aside the rod and lays aside the knife… If… he comes to the human state, he is long-lived wherever he is reborn.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha explains to Subha that abstaining from killing is the karmic cause of long life.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: non-killing keeps death at bay.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 135, Cula-kammavibhanga Sutta (Ñanamoli Thera trans.)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should cease to injure living beings whether they move or not, on high, below, and on earth. For this has been called the Nirvâna, which consists in peace.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga identifies complete cessation of injury with nirvāṇa, the deathless peace beyond the round of births.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says death will not overtake the one who lives by non-killing; the Jain text gives a spiritual version, equating non-injury with the peace of liberation, beyond death's reach.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Messenger of Death does not approach those who are pleasing to the Lord God.”
sikhism.explanation: Gurbani repeatedly promises that Death's messenger cannot come near those who live in God's favour; Sikh commentators usually read this as freedom from spiritual death and the fear of death.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says devouring Death will not advance on the days of one who keeps to non-killing; Guru Arjan makes a similar promise of protection from Death for the one pleasing to God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 401, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor couple Baucis and Philemon try to kill their only goose to feed their disguised divine guests; the gods forbid its slaughter, then spare the couple from the flood and grant them to die together at the same hour.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s tale the gods stop the killing and reward the couple with protection from death’s disaster.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An image of divine favour holding death back from the gentle and hospitable.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial, Socrates tells his judges that the gods do not neglect the good, so death holds no terror for them.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it suggests death has no real power over the one who lives rightly.

real_life_example.event_title: The Christmas Truce on the Western Front
real_life_example.place: Western Front, Belgium and northern France
real_life_example.event: On Christmas Eve 1914 British troops heard German soldiers singing carols and saw lights and small trees along the German trenches, and soldiers began calling greetings across the lines. On Christmas Day men from both sides met in no man's land, exchanged food, tobacco and souvenirs, buried their dead and in some places played football. The truce was unofficial and not observed everywhere, and commanders issued strict orders against repeating it.
real_life_example.explanation: For a short time ordinary soldiers stopped killing one another, and the truce has become an enduring symbol of shared humanity in war.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says Death will not advance on those who keep to non-killing, and while the men laid down their killing, the dying in those sectors paused too.

tamil:
தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க தான்பிறிது
இன்னுயிர் நீக்கும் வினை.
transliteration:
Thannuyir neeppinum seyyarka thaanpiridhu
Innuyir neekkum vinai.
meaning: Even if it costs you your own life, do not do anything that takes away the precious life of another being.
elementary: Suppose a bully says, “Hurt that puppy or I’ll hurt you.” Valluvar says: don’t hurt the puppy, even if you get hurt yourself. The puppy’s life is just as sweet to it as yours is to you.
university: This is one of the most uncompromising couplets in the Kural: one must not perform “the act that removes another’s sweet life” (piṟitu iṉṉuyir nīkkum viṉai) even if it means losing one’s own. The adjective iṉ (sweet) applied to the other’s life insists on its equal preciousness. Varadarasan explicitly reads it as forbidding killing even to save oneself — a stance close to Jain absolutism and more radical than most legal traditions, which permit self-defence. The Talmud reaches a similar conclusion for the case of being forced to kill an innocent person under threat, reasoning that one cannot know one’s own blood is “redder” than another’s.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Shibi, asked by a hawk to surrender a dove that had taken refuge with him, offered his own flesh — finally his whole body — rather than let the dove be killed.
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata’s tale, the gods Indra and Agni test Shibi, who chooses self-sacrifice over allowing a life to be taken.
hinduism.tie_back: Enacts the Kural precisely: give up your own life rather than cause another being’s death.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (story of Shibi, the hawk and the dove)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.”
christianity.explanation: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus teaches non-retaliation, accepting harm rather than inflicting it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it asks one to bear harm to oneself rather than harm another.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you should raise your hand toward me to kill me - I shall not raise my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allāh, Lord of the worlds.”
islam.explanation: Abel (Habil), threatened with murder by his brother, refuses to kill even to defend himself.
islam.tie_back: Nearly the Kural in narrative form: better to be killed than to kill.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is preferable that he should kill you and you should not kill. What did you think, that your blood is redder and more precious than his? Perhaps that man’s blood is redder.”
judaism.explanation: Rava rules that a man ordered to kill another on pain of death must let himself be killed rather than murder.
judaism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s teaching: even to save your own life, do not take another’s.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 25b (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says that even if bandits were to saw a monk limb from limb with a two-handled saw, one who let his mind turn to hatred would not be following his teaching.
buddhism.explanation: In the Simile of the Saw the Buddha demands non-hatred and non-retaliation even under mortal attack.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it forbids answering even a threat to one’s own life with harm to another.

jainism.quote_or_event: The monk Dharmaruci was given a bitter, poisonous gourd dish as alms by the Brahmin woman Nāgaśrī. Told by his teacher to discard it, he saw ants die after tasting a single drop, and rather than let more creatures perish he ate the whole dish himself and died.
jainism.explanation: This celebrated canonical story presents a monk who gave up his own life rather than cause the death of even tiny creatures.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says one must not take another's precious life even at the cost of one's own; Dharmaruci literally chose his own death over killing ants.
jainism.source: Jñātādharmakathāṅga, ch. 16 (Draupadī's former birth as Nāgaśrī); retold in 'Dharmaruchi Muni', Jain stories, jainworld.com

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the spiritually wise person as one who neither threatens others nor is cowed by threats. He himself chose execution in 1675 rather than yield, accepting death rather than inflicting it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural forbids taking another's life even at the cost of one's own; Guru Tegh Bahadur's ideal of never terrorising others, and his own martyrdom, come close to that self-sacrificing non-violence.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Oedipus kills Laius at a crossroads after being struck by him on the road, yet this killing — done in what he saw as self-defence — brings pollution and plague on Thebes and ruin on himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Sophocles, a killing provoked by a threat to oneself still carries full bloodguilt.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s point that saving or defending oneself does not make killing innocent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Asked by Polus whether he would rather suffer injustice or do it, Socrates answers that he would want neither, but if forced to choose he would rather suffer it than do it.
philosophy.explanation: The exchange arises in a discussion of tyrants who kill whom they please; Socrates holds that doing wrong harms the soul more than suffering it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it prefers suffering harm — even death — to inflicting it.

real_life_example.event_title: Franz Jagerstatter refuses to fight and is executed
real_life_example.event: Franz Jagerstatter, an Austrian Catholic farmer who was married with three children, refused to serve as a soldier in Hitler's army because he believed the war was unjust and incompatible with his faith. He offered to serve as a medic instead, but this was refused. He was convicted of undermining military morale and executed on 9 August 1943, and the Catholic Church beatified him as a martyr in 2007.
real_life_example.explanation: Jagerstatter chose to die rather than take part in killing he believed was wrong.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says do not take another's precious life even if it costs your own, and Jagerstatter gave his life rather than fight in an unjust war.

tamil:
நன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் பெரிதெனினும் சான்றோர்க்குக்
கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கங் கடை.
transliteration:
Nandraakum aakkam peridheninum saandrorkkuk
Kondraakum aakkam kadai.
meaning: Even if killing brings a gain that is great and seems good, people of good character see any gain that comes from killing as the lowest of things.
elementary: Imagine someone says, “If you trap and kill this bird, you’ll win a huge prize.” A good person says “No, thanks.” Valluvar says a prize that costs a life isn’t a prize at all — it’s the worst kind of win.
university: Valluvar concedes his opponent’s premise — the prosperity (ākkam) gained may indeed be “great” and even called “good” — and still pronounces it kaṭai, the very lowest, in the eyes of the cāṉṟōr (the noble, perfected ones). Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read the verse as targeting Vedic animal sacrifice (vēḷvi), which promised wealth and heaven through ritual killing; the Kural thus sides with the Jain and Buddhist critique of sacrificial violence. More broadly the couplet rejects consequentialist justifications for killing: no outcome, however beneficial, can redeem the means. The same refusal to let ends justify the taking of life underlies Kant’s formula that persons may never be used merely as means.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It would be better to live in this world by begging than to live at the cost of the lives of great souls who are my teachers. … If they are killed, everything we enjoy will be tainted with blood.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna, facing battle, refuses a kingdom won by killing his elders, calling such enjoyment blood-stained.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna voices the Kural’s judgement that gain through killing is contemptible — though Krishna goes on to overrule him on grounds of duty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice”
christianity.explanation: Jesus quotes Hosea to teach that God desires mercy rather than ritual offerings.
christianity.tie_back: Echoes the commentators’ reading of the Kural as rejecting the promised benefits of sacrificial killing in favour of mercy.

islam.quote_or_event: “…do not say to one who gives you [a greeting of] peace, “You are not a believer,” aspiring for the goods of worldly life; for with Allāh are many acquisitions.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids killing someone who offers peace for the sake of worldly spoils, reminding believers that God’s rewards are greater.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it condemns gain obtained through killing, however tempting.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns against joining those who ambush and kill for plunder, noting that greed for gain destroys life.
judaism.tie_back: Directly condemns, as the Kural does, prosperity sought through killing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Advising the brahmin Kutadanta, the Buddha describes a great sacrifice of an ancient king in which no oxen, goats, fowl or other creatures were slain, and all was offered with ghee, oil and honey; Kutadanta then releases the animals he had gathered for slaughter.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines sacrifice so that its benefits come without killing.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches the commentarial reading of the Kural as rejecting the promised gains of animal sacrifice.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The binding of animals (to the sacrificial pole), all the Vêdas, and sacrifices, being causes of sin, cannot save the sinner; for his works (or Karman) are very powerful.”
jainism.explanation: Jayaghosha rejects animal sacrifice: whatever rewards it promises, ritual killing is a cause of sin and binds the sacrificer with karma.
jainism.tie_back: Parimelazhagar reads the Kural as condemning the 'great gain' promised by sacrificial killing; this verse makes the same anti-sacrificial judgement from the Jain canon.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 25.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Macauliffe tells of Shaikh Sajjan, a robber who built a temple and a mosque for travellers, then threw his guests into a well at night and kept their property. After hearing Guru Nanak's hymn he confessed his murders; the Guru had him bring out all the goods of his victims and give them to the poor, and he became the Guru's follower.
sikhism.explanation: The story shows wealth gained through killing as wholly worthless: it cannot be kept, only given away in repentance.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that however great the gain, profit won by killing is the lowest of things to the noble; Guru Nanak made Sajjan give up every coin he had gained that way.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter IV, pp. 45-47 (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon sacrifices his daughter Iphigenia to gain favourable winds for the fleet to Troy; the ‘gain’ is won, but the killing brings his own murder on his return.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aeschylus the great advantage bought with a life is shown to be ruinous and shameful.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural: even a great gain won through killing is the lowest of things.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant’s formula of humanity: always treat humanity, in yourself or in another, as an end, and never merely as a means.
philosophy.explanation: Kant holds that persons have dignity, not a price, so no advantage can justify sacrificing one for an outcome.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s refusal to weigh a life against any gain, however great.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 4:429

real_life_example.event_title: The International Whaling Commission adopts a moratorium on commercial whaling
real_life_example.event: In 1982 the International Whaling Commission decided that catch limits for all commercial whaling would be set to zero, a moratorium that came fully into force for the 1986 and 1985-86 seasons. The decision followed disagreement among members over the acceptability of whaling and uncertainty about whale stocks. The moratorium remains in place, though a few countries have objected to it or continue whaling under exceptions.
real_life_example.explanation: Nations gave up a long-established and profitable industry built on killing, choosing to protect whale populations instead.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that gain through killing, however great, is the lowest of things to the noble, and the moratorium turned away from profits made by killing whales.

tamil:
கொலைவினைய ராகிய மாக்கள் புலைவினையர்
புன்மை தெரிவா ரகத்து.
transliteration:
Kolaivinaiya raagiya maakkal pulaivinaiyar
Punmai therivaa ragaththu.
meaning: People who kill for a living are seen as doers of shameful deeds by those who understand what truly low behavior is.
elementary: Some jobs make you proud, like helping people or growing food. Valluvar says that a job built on killing living things makes wise people think less of you, because they can see how it hardens the heart.
university: The couplet names the kolaiviṉaiyar, those whose “occupation” (viṉai) is killing, and uses the word mākkaḷ — often reserved for people who have lost human discernment — to describe them. In the minds of those who discern baseness (puṉmai terivār), they are pulaiviṉaiyar, doers of polluted, degraded work. The verse is a moral judgement rather than a caste statement, though the vocabulary of pulai (pollution) reflects the social idiom of its time and should be read critically today. Its underlying insight — that habitual killing corrodes compassion — is shared by the Buddha’s list of wrong livelihoods and by Thomas More’s Utopians, who kept citizens from butchery lest it destroy the feeling of mercy.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who permits (the slaughter of an animal), he who cuts it up, he who kills it, he who buys or sells (meat), he who cooks it, he who serves it up, and he who eats it, (must all be considered as) the slayers (of the animal).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu extends the guilt of killing to everyone in the chain of slaughter and trade.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it condemns those whose work is bound up with killing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.”
christianity.explanation: John teaches that the murderer, and even the hater, is cut off from the life of God.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s verdict that the killer is spiritually degraded.

islam.quote_or_event: “But whoever kills a believer intentionally - his recompense is Hell, wherein he will abide eternally, and Allāh has become angry with him and has cursed him and has prepared for him a great punishment.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an pronounces a curse and severe punishment on the deliberate killer of a believer.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it marks the killer as degraded and cursed in the eyes of the just.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.”
judaism.explanation: After Cain murders Abel, God curses him to be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.
judaism.tie_back: The first killer becomes the first outcast — the degradation the Kural attributes to killers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, a lay follower should not engage in five types of business. Which five? Business in weapons, business in human beings, business in meat, business in intoxicants, and business in poison.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists trades that are wrong livelihood because they depend on harming or killing.
buddhism.tie_back: Directly parallels the Kural’s kolaiviṉaiyar — those whose livelihood is killing are on the wrong path.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.177, Vanijja Sutta (Thanissaro Bhikkhu trans.)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Be without fear, O king; but grant safety to others also; in this transient world of living beings, why are you addicted to cruelty?”
jainism.explanation: King Sañjaya, out hunting, killed a frightened deer and then met the monk Gardabhāli, who rebuked his habit of killing; the king renounced his throne.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural brands those who make killing their pursuit as doers of base deeds; the monk names the hunting king's killing 'cruelty' and turns him from it.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 18.2 and 18.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who suck the blood of human beings-how can their consciousness be pure?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak declares that those who live by preying on others cannot have a pure mind, whatever outward rituals they keep.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls those who make killing their work doers of base deeds in the eyes of the discerning; Guru Nanak likewise judges those who live off others' blood as inwardly impure.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ixion, remembered as the first mortal to shed kindred blood, was shunned by gods and men so completely that no one would purify him, until Zeus himself did — and Ixion later ended bound on a fiery wheel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar makes Ixion the archetype of the killer who becomes an outcast.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the killer as vile and shunned in the eyes of the discerning, as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In More’s Utopia, citizens are not allowed to slaughter animals themselves, because the Utopians believe that butchery gradually kills the feeling of mercy, the gentlest affection of human nature.
philosophy.explanation: Thomas More imagines a society that protects its citizens’ compassion by keeping them away from killing as a trade.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s insight that the work of killing degrades the one who does it.

real_life_example.event_title: Constantine issues a law against gladiatorial shows
real_life_example.event: In 325 the emperor Constantine issued a law, preserved in the Theodosian Code, stating that bloody spectacles had no place in a time of civil peace and domestic quiet and prohibiting gladiators. Criminals who would previously have been condemned to fight as gladiators were to be sent to work in the mines instead. The law was not fully enforced, and gladiatorial games continued in some places until they were finally suppressed decades later.
real_life_example.explanation: An emperor publicly declared the trade of killing for entertainment unfit for a peaceful society, even though the games took decades more to disappear.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who make killing their work are seen as base by the discerning, and Constantine's law declared the gladiator's bloody trade unfit for a civilised peace.

tamil:
உயிருடம்பின் நீக்கியா ரென்ப செயிருடம்பின்
செல்லாத்தீ வாழ்க்கை யவர்.
transliteration:
Uyirudambin neekkiyaa renba seyirudambin
Sellaaththee vaazhkkai yavar.
meaning: People say that those who now live poor, miserable lives in sick bodies are the ones who once took the lives of other beings.
elementary: It’s like planting seeds: if you plant thorns, you get thorns later. Valluvar says that hurting and killing are like planting thorn seeds — sooner or later, sickness and hard times grow back toward the one who planted them.
university: The final couplet adopts the voice of received wisdom (eṉpa, “they say”): those with diseased bodies (ceyir uṭampu) living a miserable, impoverished life (cellāt tī vāḻkkai) are those who “removed life from bodies” (uyir uṭampiṉ nīkkiyār). All the major commentators read this karmically, as the fruit of killing in a former birth. The couplet closes the chapter by grounding the ethics of non-killing in moral causation; it has parallels in Manu and in the Buddha’s teaching that harming beings leads to sickliness. Modern readers will note that such teaching can be misused to blame the sick and poor — a danger also recognised within other traditions, as when Jesus rejects the idea that a man’s blindness was caused by sin (John 9:3).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “injury (to sentient beings) is punished by general sickliness”
hinduism.explanation: In its catalogue of the bodily marks of past sins, Manu assigns chronic illness as the consequence of harming living beings, stating earlier that some suffer for crimes “committed in a former (existence).”
hinduism.tie_back: Almost identical to the Kural: harming life in a former existence yields a diseased body now.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells Peter to sheathe his sword at the arrest, warning that violence returns upon the violent.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s principle that those who take life reap suffering in return — though within one lifetime, not across births.

islam.quote_or_event: “And whatever strikes you of disaster - it is for what your hands have earned; but He pardons much.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that misfortunes are linked to one’s own deeds, though God forgives much.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it traces present suffering to past wrongdoing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “because you drowned others, they drowned you. And in the end, they that drowned you will be drowned.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel, seeing a skull floating on the water, reflects that those who kill are killed in turn.
judaism.tie_back: Expresses the Kural’s logic of measure-for-measure consequence for taking life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who inflicts violence on those who are unarmed, and offends those who are inoffensive, will soon come upon one of these ten states: Sharp pain, or disaster, bodily injury, serious illness, or derangement of mind, … or loss of wealth…”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada lists the painful consequences — including illness and poverty — that befall those who harm the harmless.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural: illness and a ruined life follow from violence against living beings (cf. MN 135 on sickliness).

jainism.quote_or_event: “Carefully conducting himself, he should mind this: blindness, deafness, dumbness, one-eyedness, hunchbackedness, blackness, variety of colour (he will always experience); because of his carelessness he is born in many births, he experiences various feelings.”
jainism.explanation: The Ācārāṅga teaches that bodily afflictions in later births follow from careless conduct, which in Jain terms (pramāda) is the root of injury to living beings.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural traces diseased bodies and wretched lives to past killing; the Ācārāṅga likewise attributes bodily defects in rebirth to careless, injurious conduct.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.2.3.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, they oppress living beings and kill them, and call it proper. When the Lord calls for their account, what will their condition be?”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir warns that those who kill living beings by force and justify it as lawful must still answer for it when their deeds are reckoned.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the wise see wretched, diseased lives as the fruit of having taken life from bodies; Kabir likewise warns that killing is entered in the account and its consequence will come.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1375, Salok Bhagat Kabir, Salok 199 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, who in later tradition killed his son Pelops and served him to the gods, is shown by Odysseus in the underworld standing in a pool under fruit trees, forever hungry and thirsty as water and fruit recede from him.
greek_mythology.explanation: His endless deprivation is the archetypal Greek image of punishment for an abominable killing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s “wretched life” of want as the fruit of having taken life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato cites an ancient teaching that the murderer is punished in Hades and, when born again on earth, must suffer the very thing he did, dying at the hands of another.
philosophy.explanation: In the Laws, Plato uses this tale of reincarnational justice to deter killing.
philosophy.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: killing in one life brings suffering in the next.

real_life_example.event_title: Charles Myers brings shell shock into the medical literature
real_life_example.place: Le Touquet, France, and London, England (published in The Lancet)
real_life_example.event: Charles Myers, a British psychologist, published in The Lancet an account of three soldiers admitted to a war hospital at Le Touquet who had lost memory, vision, smell and taste. His paper introduced the term shell shock into medical literature; soldiers had already been using it, as large numbers of men were being sent home with nervous and mental breakdown. Shell shock went on to affect very large numbers of soldiers during the First World War.
real_life_example.explanation: Myers's work began the medical recognition that war leaves lasting injuries of the mind and body on those who take part in it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who live wretched lives in afflicted bodies are those who once took life, and shell shock showed how the work of killing in war could leave its participants broken.

tamil:
நில்லாத வற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்
புல்லறி வாண்மை கடை.
transliteration:
Nillaadha vatrai nilaiyina endru unarum
Pullarivu aanmai kadai.
meaning: Believing that things which cannot last will last forever is the worst kind of foolishness.
elementary: Imagine building a sandcastle and believing it will stay on the beach forever, even though the waves always come. This kural says that treating things that will surely change or go away as if they will last forever is the silliest mistake a person can make.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter on impermanence not with a description of transience but with an epistemic judgement: the root error is a false cognition, mistaking the non-abiding (nillaadhavai) for the abiding (nilaiyina). The phrase “pullarivaanmai” (petty-mindedness, a paltry intelligence that presumes itself competent) frames the problem as a defect of understanding rather than of morals, and “kadai” (the lowest, the most base) ranks it at the bottom of human conditions. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward read the chapter as the doorway of the renunciate section (thuravaraviyal), since recognising impermanence (nilaiyaamai) is what loosens attachment and makes renunciation (the next chapter, thuravu) intelligible. The idea sits close to the Buddhist and Jain analysis of avidya/moha, where suffering follows from treating the impermanent as permanent, and to the Stoic insistence that disturbance comes from our judgements about things rather than from the things themselves.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kunti, the contact between the senses and the sense objects gives rise to fleeting perceptions of happiness and distress. These are non-permanent, and come and go like the winter and summer seasons.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that the pleasures and pains people cling to are passing like the seasons, and a wise person does not treat them as solid or lasting.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita labels these experiences anitya (non-permanent), which is the same diagnosis the Kural makes: the mistake is treating the non-lasting as lasting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to fix their attention on what lasts rather than on visible things, which are only temporary.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural condemns mistaking the temporary for the permanent; Paul teaches the right way to tell the temporal from the eternal.

islam.quote_or_event: “Everyone upon the earth will perish, And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.”
islam.explanation: The Quran says everything on earth will pass away and only God remains.
islam.tie_back: Only one thing truly abides, so treating anything worldly as permanent is exactly the error the Kural calls the lowest foolishness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) opens by calling everything under the sun hevel, a breath or vapour that does not last.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts start from the same claim: worldly things are fleeting, and seeing them as solid is a mistake.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All conditioned things are impermanent” — when one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. This is the path to purification.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names impermanence (anicca) as a mark of all conditioned things; seeing it clearly frees a person from suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's ‘lowest foolishness’ is the reverse of this wisdom: the fool sees permanence where the Buddha teaches there is only anicca.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As you must, of necessity, one day part with everything, in this transient world of living beings, why do you cling to kingly power?”
jainism.explanation: The monk Gardabhāli confronts King Sañjaya with the folly of clinging to power and possessions in a world where everything must be given up.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls it the lowest folly to take the impermanent for the permanent; the monk asks why the king clings to what he must inevitably lose.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 18.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The world and its affairs are totally false; know this well, my friend. Says Nanak, it is like a wall of sand; it shall not endure.”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks Guru Tegh Bahadur warns that everything built in the world is as unstable as a wall of sand, and that recognising this is the beginning of wisdom.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls it the lowest folly to take passing things for permanent; Guru Tegh Bahadur urges us to know clearly that the world's affairs will not endure.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahala 9, Salok 49, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eos, goddess of the dawn, asked Zeus to make her mortal lover Tithonus immortal but forgot to ask for eternal youth; he went on living while shrivelling with age until he could not move.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows the danger of assuming that what belongs to a mortal, like youth, can simply be made to last.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Eos treated youth as if it were permanent, the very mistake the Kural calls the lowest kind of understanding.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Heracleitus is supposed to say that all things are in motion and nothing at rest; he compares them to the stream of a river, and says that you cannot go into the same water twice.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates reports Heraclitus' view that everything is constantly changing, like a flowing river.
philosophy.tie_back: If everything flows, then believing things are fixed and permanent is exactly the misperception the Kural condemns.

real_life_example.event_title: The Dutch tulip mania collapses
real_life_example.event: In the 1630s prices for rare tulip bulbs in Holland rose to extraordinary heights, and ordinary families were drawn into buying bulbs for resale, with bulbs sold and resold many times without ever leaving the ground. Early in 1637 doubts arose as to whether prices would keep rising, and the price structure collapsed almost overnight, ruining many who had bought at the top. Historians still debate how widespread the damage was, but the boom and sudden crash of early 1637 are well documented.
real_life_example.explanation: Buyers acted as if the high value of a flower bulb was a lasting fact rather than a passing mood of the market. The episode became one of history's best-known warnings about treating a temporary condition as permanent.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar calls it the lowest folly to take what cannot last as if it will endure, which is exactly the mistake the tulip buyers made about bulb prices.

tamil:
கூத்தாட்டு அவைக்குழாத் தற்றே பெருஞ்செல்வம்
போக்கும் அதுவிளிந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Koothaattu avaikkuzhaath thatre perunjelvam
Pokkum adhu vilindhatru.
meaning: Great riches come together like a crowd gathering to watch a show, and they leave like that crowd going home when the show is over.
elementary: Think of people crowding in to watch a street show. When the show ends, everyone walks away at once and the place is empty. This kural says money is like that crowd: it comes in bit by bit, and it can leave all at once.
university: Valluvar builds the couplet on a single theatrical simile with two halves: the assembling of an audience (koothaattu avaik kuzhaam) and its dispersal when the performance ends (adhu vilindhatru). Commentators note the asymmetry the image implies: an audience trickles in gradually but leaves together, just as wealth is accumulated slowly and can vanish in a single reversal. The theatre is also suggestive, since the crowd was never attached to the patron but to the spectacle, much as wealth is never truly bound to its holder. The kural therefore relocates wealth from the category of possession to that of event, something that happens around a person for a time. Comparable ideas appear in the Greek theme of the reversal of fortune (Solon and Croesus) and in the Stoic teaching that external goods are on loan.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Offered wealth, long life, horses, and dancing and singing by Yama, the boy Nachiketas refuses, saying such things last only until tomorrow and wear out the senses, and tells Death to keep his dances and songs.
hinduism.explanation: In the Katha Upanishad, a young seeker rejects every worldly prize because it is short-lived and asks instead for knowledge of what lies beyond death.
hinduism.tie_back: Nachiketas sees wealth and entertainment for what the Kural says they are, a show that ends and a crowd that disperses.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to warn the rich not to rely on wealth, because riches are uncertain.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Uncertain riches’ is the Kural's point in a phrase: wealth can leave as quickly as a crowd after a show.

islam.quote_or_event: “Know that the life of this world is but amusement and diversion and adornment and boasting to one another and competition in increase of wealth and children - like the example of a rain whose [resulting] plant growth pleases the tillers; then it dries and you see it turned yellow; then it becomes [scattered] debris.”
islam.explanation: The Quran compares worldly life and the race for wealth to entertainment and to crops that flourish and then dry up and scatter.
islam.tie_back: Both texts use the language of amusement and spectacle, and both say the gathering of wealth ends in scattering.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wilt thou set thine eyes upon that which is not? for riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns against fixing your gaze on riches, which suddenly grow wings and fly away.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's crowd scatters and Proverbs' riches fly off; both describe how suddenly wealth can leave.

buddhism.quote_or_event: One who looks upon the world as a bubble and a mirage, him the King of Death sees not.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches seeing the world, and the things in it, as a bubble or mirage: real enough to appear, too fleeting to hold.
buddhism.tie_back: A bubble and a theatre crowd are both brief gatherings that vanish; the wise, in both texts, are not taken in by them.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Then at one time, his manifold savings are a large treasure. Then at another time, his heirs divide it, or those who are without a living steal it, or the king takes it away, or it is ruined in some way or other, or it is consumed by the conflagration of the house.”
jainism.explanation: The Ācārāṅga describes wealth that accumulates into a great treasure and then scatters through heirs, thieves, the king, ruin or fire.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural likens wealth to a crowd that gathers for a show and disperses when it ends; the Ācārāṅga traces the same gathering and dispersal of riches.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.2.3.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That wealth, which he believes to be his own, in an instant, belongs to another.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur observes how quickly possessions that seem securely one's own pass to someone else.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures great wealth arriving like a gathering crowd and leaving like the crowd after the show; Guru Tegh Bahadur makes the same point about how suddenly wealth departs.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1008, Raag Maaroo, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Athenian sage Solon refused to call the fabulously rich King Croesus the happiest of men, saying no one should be called happy until his life has ended well. Croesus later lost his kingdom to Cyrus and, on the pyre, cried out Solon's name.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus' story shows the richest man in the world losing everything in a single reversal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus' treasure gathered over a lifetime and scattered in a day, just as the Kural's crowd leaves when the show ends.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never say of anything, "I have lost it"; but, "I have returned it." ... Is your estate taken away? Well, and is not that likewise returned?”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that property is never truly ours: it is lent for a while and eventually given back.
philosophy.tie_back: If wealth is only on loan, its leaving is as natural as an audience going home after the show, which is the Kural's point.

real_life_example.event_title: John Law's Mississippi Bubble bursts
real_life_example.event: The Scottish financier John Law founded a note-issuing bank in Paris and merged it with the company holding France's trading rights in the Mississippi Valley; as controller general of finances in 1720 he presided over intense speculation that drove the company's shares from about 500 livres to many times that value. In the summer of 1720, as shareholders rushed to turn their paper into gold and silver, share prices collapsed and the bank notes lost their value. Law, politically isolated, left France in December 1720.
real_life_example.explanation: Fortunes built up over months of speculation vanished within weeks once the crowd of investors turned and left together. The crash destroyed public confidence in paper money and companies in France for a generation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares great wealth to a theatre crowd that gathers gradually and scatters all at once when the show ends, just as the Mississippi investors poured in and then fled together.

tamil:
அற்கா இயல்பிற்றுச் செல்வம் அதுபெற்றால்
அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்.
transliteration:
Arkaa iyalbitruch selvam adhu petraal
Arkupa aange seyal.
meaning: Riches never stay for long. So when you have them, use them right away to do good deeds that will last.
elementary: If you are given ice cream on a hot day, you should share it right away before it melts. This kural says money is like that ice cream: it won't stay, so use it for good things now, while you still have it.
university: The couplet turns on a deliberate play between “arkaa” (that which does not stay) and “arkupa” (things that do stay, that is, enduring deeds), both drawn from the verb ‘ar’, to abide. Valluvar thus converts a descriptive claim about wealth into an imperative: since wealth is non-abiding, use it for what abides, and do so “aange” (then and there, at once). Commentators identify the enduring deeds with the householder virtues discussed earlier in the work, such as hospitality, charity and helpfulness (oppuravu). The logic is an ethical economics: a perishable asset should be exchanged immediately for an imperishable one before it spoils. The same move, turning transient riches into lasting merit, appears in the Gospel's ‘treasures in heaven’, the Quran's ‘enduring good deeds’, and Bhartrhari's teaching that wealth has only three destinies.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari teaches that wealth has only three possible destinies: it is given away, it is enjoyed, or it is destroyed. Whoever neither gives nor enjoys it is left with the third.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit poet says wealth that is not given away or used will simply be lost.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts start from wealth's instability and conclude that it should be turned into giving before it disappears.
hinduism.source: Bhartrhari, Nitishataka, v. 43 (numbering varies by edition)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his listeners to stop hoarding wealth that decays and to store up lasting treasure through a godly life.
christianity.tie_back: Swap perishable treasure for imperishable treasure: this is exactly the Kural's ‘arkaa’ turned into ‘arkupa’.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one's] hope.”
islam.explanation: The Quran contrasts wealth, which is decoration for this life, with ‘al-baqiyat as-salihat’, good deeds that endure.
islam.tie_back: The Quran's ‘enduring good deeds’ are the Kural's ‘arkupa’ (things that last), set against wealth that does not.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that wealth is useless at the decisive moment, while righteousness (tzedakah, which also came to mean charity) saves.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts rank righteous action above wealth because only the former survives the final reckoning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that hoarding leads nowhere good, while giving brings lasting happiness.
buddhism.tie_back: Giving turns passing wealth into lasting benefit, which is what the Kural urges.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.”
jainism.explanation: Queen Kamalāvatī tells King Ishukāra that riches are left behind at death and only dharma endures.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural urges using unstable wealth at once for lasting deeds; the Uttarādhyayana likewise contrasts possessions that must be left with the Law that alone endures.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak names the person who earns honestly and shares part of it as the one who knows the true path; this is the Sikh pillar of vand chhakna, sharing one's earnings.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that since wealth does not stay, it should be used at once for good deeds that last; Guru Nanak likewise points the householder's wealth towards giving.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Saarang ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor old couple Baucis and Philemon gladly share their meagre food and wine with two disguised strangers who turn out to be Zeus and Hermes; the gods save them from a flood and turn their hut into a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's tale rewards a couple who used what little they had for hospitality right away, without holding back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Giving at once from what you have, rather than clinging to it, is the Kural's instruction for using unstable wealth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy asks Boethius whether riches are precious by their own nature, and argues that money shines more brightly when it is spent on others than when it is hoarded, since avarice makes people hated and generosity makes them honoured.
philosophy.explanation: In Boethius' dialogue, Philosophy shows that wealth only has real value when it is given away.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts say the only good use of passing wealth is to put it at once into generous action.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, prose 5

real_life_example.event_title: Jamsetji Tata endows half his fortune for the Indian Institute of Science
real_life_example.event: In 1898 the industrialist Jamsetji Tata set aside 14 buildings and four landed properties in Bombay, worth about 30 lakh rupees and roughly half his wealth, as an endowment for a research university of science. He kept the offer open through years of negotiation with the colonial government and reaffirmed it in a codicil to his will shortly before he died in 1904. The Indian Institute of Science was established in Bangalore by a vesting order in 1909 and admitted its first students in 1911.
real_life_example.explanation: Tata turned a large part of a fortune that could have been lost or spent into an institution that has trained generations of Indian scientists. The gift has outlasted him by more than a century.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar says that since wealth does not stay, one should at once turn it into deeds that do stay, and Tata converted half his fortune into a lasting institution of learning.

tamil:
நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி உயிர்ஈரும்
வாளது உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Naal ena ondru pol kaatti uyir eerum
Vaal adhu unarvaar perin.
meaning: A day looks like just a stretch of time. But people who understand know it is really a saw, cutting away at your life bit by bit.
elementary: Each day feels like just another day: you wake up, play, and sleep. But every day that passes is one less day you have left, like a saw slowly cutting through a log. This kural says wise people notice this.
university: The couplet turns on an unmasking: “naal” (the day) displays itself (kaatti) as a neutral thing, an ordinary measure of time, but its real nature is a “vaal” (blade, commonly understood as a saw) that “eerum” (cleaves, saws through) life. The verb eer suggests the slow back-and-forth of a saw rather than a single cut, so life is shown being worn away in daily strokes. The conditional “unarvaarp perin” (if one finds those who understand) implies that such people are rare; most take the passing day at face value. Philosophically the kural anticipates Seneca's remark that we die daily and the Psalmist's prayer to ‘number our days’: time is not a container in which life takes place, but the very process by which life is used up.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari laments that with every rising and setting of the sun, life is shortened day by day, yet people, busy with their many affairs, do not notice time slipping away.
hinduism.explanation: The poet observes that each passing day quietly takes something off a person's lifespan.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own image: the ordinary day, marked by sunrise and sunset, is secretly cutting away at life.
hinduism.source: Bhartrhari, Vairagyashataka (verse beginning ādityasya gatāgatair; numbering varies by edition)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.”
christianity.explanation: James reminds his readers that life is a brief vapour and tomorrow is never guaranteed.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts correct the illusion that time is plentiful: life is being used up day by day.

islam.quote_or_event: “By time, Indeed, mankind is in loss, Except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience.”
islam.explanation: Surat al-Asr swears by time and declares that people are in loss as time passes, unless they fill it with faith and good deeds.
islam.tie_back: Time as a steady loss of life is the Kural's point; al-Asr adds the remedy the chapter goes on to give: good deeds.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalm asks God to help people count their days so they grow wise.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's ‘those who understand’ are exactly those who have learned to number their days.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Just as a cowherd drives the cattle to pasture with a staff, so do old age and death drive the life force of beings (from existence to existence).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures aging and death steadily driving life onward, as a herdsman drives cattle with a stick.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts show time as an active force wearing life away, not a harmless backdrop.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Mankind is harassed by Death; it is taken hold of by Old Age; the days are called unfailing… The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse without profit to him who acts contrary to the Law.”
jainism.explanation: Bhṛgu's sons explain that the days pass unfailingly while death and old age seize humanity, and each lost day is gone for ever.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar unmasks the ordinary day as a saw cutting away life; the Jain verses likewise reveal each passing day as irrecoverable life lost.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.23–24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Day by day, hour by hour, life runs its course, and the body withers away.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir describes life being whittled away unit by unit of time, days into watches and watches into hours, until the body is spent.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural unmasks the day as a saw that cuts away at life; Kabir sees the same steady erosion of life in each passing day and hour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 692, Raag Dhanaasree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod names the three Fates, Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos, who spin, measure out and finally cut the thread of each mortal life.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, every life is a thread that is spun, measured, and in the end cut by Atropos, ‘the one who cannot be turned’.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Fates' shears and the Kural's saw both picture time as a blade working on the length of a life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “What man can you show me who places any value on his time, who reckons the worth of each day, who understands that he is dying daily?”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells Lucilius that most people waste their days without noticing that each one is a part of their death already lived.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's ‘dying daily’ is the Kural's day-saw, and his rare person who ‘understands’ matches Valluvar's ‘those who understand’.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 1.2 (Gummere translation)

real_life_example.event_title: Steve Jobs's Stanford commencement address on mortality
real_life_example.event: Apple co-founder Steve Jobs gave the commencement address at Stanford University and devoted the third of his three stories to death. He told the graduates that for 33 years he had looked in the mirror each morning and asked whether he would want to do what he was about to do if it were the last day of his life, and that when the answer was no for too many days in a row he knew he needed to change something. He described a recent brush with a serious illness and urged them not to waste their limited time.
real_life_example.explanation: The speech became one of the most widely shared commencement addresses because it treated each ordinary day as a measured part of a limited life. It shows a practical habit of noticing that every day spent is a day used up.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the day only looks like a harmless unit of time, while the wise see it as a saw cutting away at life, and Jobs described a daily practice built on exactly that awareness.

tamil:
நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன் நல்வினை
மேற்சென்று செய்யப் படும்.
transliteration:
Naachchetru vikkul mel vaaraamun nalvinai
Mersendru seyyap padum.
meaning: Before your tongue stops working and the death rattle (the last breathing sound of a dying person) rises in your throat, hurry to do good deeds.
elementary: If you want to say sorry or help someone, don't wait for ‘someday’, because someday might not come. This kural says do your good deeds now, while you still can talk and act.
university: Valluvar gives the chapter's abstract point a stark physical image: “naa chetru” (the tongue locked or stilled) and “vikkul mel vaaraa mun” (before the hiccup, the death rattle, rises), which are the classical signs of the last moments of life. The imperative “mersendru” (going forward, pressing ahead) carries the sense of taking the initiative and not waiting for circumstances. The image of a silenced tongue also implies that at the end one cannot even speak one's intentions, let alone carry them out. The kural thus moves from recognising impermanence to acting urgently, an ethic of timeliness found in Rabbi Eliezer's ‘repent one day before your death’, the Quran's warning against wishing for a reprieve at death, and Marcus Aurelius' ‘while it is in thy power, be good’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who relinquish the body while remembering Me at the moment of death will come to Me. There is certainly no doubt about this.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that a person's state of mind at death shapes what follows, which implies preparing throughout life for that moment.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat the moment of death as decisive and urge preparation well before it arrives.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says good works must be done while there is still daylight, because night is coming when no one can work.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's silenced tongue is Jesus' ‘night’: the point after which good deeds can no longer be done.

islam.quote_or_event: “And spend [in the way of Allah] from what We have provided you before death approaches one of you and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I would give charity and be among the righteous."”
islam.explanation: The Quran urges believers to give now, before death comes and they beg in vain for a little more time to do good.
islam.tie_back: The same urgency: act before the final moment, when the chance to do good is gone.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eliezer said: ... And repent one day before your death.”
judaism.explanation: Since no one knows the day of their death, the Talmud explains, this means repenting every day.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts tell people to act before death while hiding its date, so the only safe time is now.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:10 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp)

buddhism.quote_or_event: For him who is assailed by death there is no protection by kinsmen. None there are to save him — no sons, nor father, nor relatives. Realizing this fact, let the wise man, restrained by morality, hasten to clear the path leading to Nibbana.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the wise to hurry along the moral path, since nothing can protect a person once death arrives.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Hasten’ is the Kural's ‘mersendru’: the certainty of death is a reason to act on the good without delay.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who can call Death his friend, or who can escape him, or who knows that he will not die, might perhaps decide: this shall be done tomorrow.”
jainism.explanation: The young men refuse to postpone the religious life, since no one can count on escaping death until tomorrow.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural urges doing good before the tongue fails and the death rattle comes; this verse likewise forbids putting off dharma to an uncertain tomorrow.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately! Later on, you will not be able to do anything, when death hangs over your head.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir urges the seeker to stop postponing what matters, because once death arrives the chance to act is gone.
