sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to hurry to do good before the tongue is stilled and the death rattle comes; Kabir gives the same urgent counsel not to wait until death is upon us.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir, Salok 138 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Say not a word in death's favour; I would rather be a paid servant in a poor man's house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the underworld the great hero Achilles tells Odysseus that even the humblest living life is better than glory among the dead, where nothing more can be done.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles' regret shows why the Kural insists on acting now: once life ends, no deed remains possible.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that death is always near, so the time to be good is now.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘While it is in thy power’ matches the Kural's ‘before the tongue is stilled’: goodness must be done while one still can.

real_life_example.event_title: Thomas Guy builds Guy's Hospital in the last years of his life
real_life_example.event: Thomas Guy, a London bookseller and governor of St Thomas' Hospital who had grown very rich by selling his South Sea Company shares in 1720, decided in 1721, at about the age of 76, to build a new hospital for patients who could not be helped elsewhere. Construction began in 1722, and the building was roofed before he died on 27 December 1724. His will left most of his remaining fortune, over 200,000 pounds, to complete and maintain the hospital, which opened soon after his death.
real_life_example.explanation: Guy did not postpone his great charity to a distant future but began it in old age and pushed it forward while he still could. Guy's Hospital remains one of London's major teaching hospitals.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar urges people to hurry and do good before the tongue is stilled at death, and Guy raced to build his hospital in the final years of his life.

tamil:
நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை என்னும்
பெருமை உடைத்துஇவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Nerunal ulan oruvan indru illai ennum
Perumai udaiththu ivvulagu.
meaning: This world has a strange kind of greatness: someone who was here yesterday is gone today.
elementary: Sometimes we hear, ‘I just saw him yesterday, and now he's gone.’ This kural says that is simply how the world works: people can be here one day and gone the next.
university: The couplet is famous for its irony. “Perumai” (greatness, glory) is normally praise, but Valluvar awards it to the world for the most unsettling of distinctions, that a man alive “nerunal” (yesterday) is not there “indru” (today). Commentators such as the thirukkural-thamizh gloss explicitly read perumai here as a mocking word for the world's instability. The unit of time is only a single day, which heightens the sense of suddenness. The world's one reliable ‘achievement’ is the constant disappearance of its inhabitants. The observation echoes the Yaksha's question in the Mahabharata about the wonder of human denial of death, and Marcus Aurelius' remark about yesterday's mucus becoming tomorrow's ashes.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Asked by the Yaksha what is the most wonderful thing in the world, Yudhishthira answers that every day countless beings go to the abode of Yama, yet those who remain act as though they will live forever.
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata, the wisest of the Pandavas names humanity's denial of death, in the face of daily deaths, as the greatest wonder.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's ‘greatness’ of a world where yesterday's man is gone today is the same ironic wonder Yudhishthira points to.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Aranyaka (Vana) Parva, Yaksha Prashna (ch. 313 in Ganguli's numbering)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away:”
christianity.explanation: Peter, quoting Isaiah, says human life and glory wither like grass and flowers.
christianity.tie_back: Peter speaks of the ‘glory of man’ withering; the Kural ironically calls the world's constant loss its ‘glory’.

islam.quote_or_event: “Every soul will taste death, and you will only be given your [full] compensation on the Day of Resurrection. ... And what is the life of this world except the enjoyment of delusion.”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that every living soul will die and that worldly life is a deceptive enjoyment.
islam.tie_back: Both texts present death as the world's universal and reliable feature, which exposes the world's promise of permanence as a delusion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth. For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalm says a person flourishes like a wildflower, then a wind passes and they are gone, and even their place forgets them.
judaism.tie_back: ‘It is gone, and the place thereof shall know it no more’ is the Kural's ‘here yesterday, not here today’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: As a mighty flood sweeps away the sleeping village, so death carries away the person of distracted mind who only plucks the flowers (of pleasure).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares death to a sudden flood that sweeps away a sleeping village overnight.
buddhism.tie_back: Overnight disappearance is the Kural's image: those present yesterday are swept away by today.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra tells Gautama that human life ends as suddenly as a withered leaf drops from its tree.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's ironic 'greatness' of the world, where one alive yesterday is gone today, matches Mahāvīra's image of lives falling like leaves.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever has been created shall be destroyed; everyone shall perish, today or tomorrow.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur states the universal law that all that is born must pass, the only question being whether it is today or tomorrow.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ironically praises the world's 'greatness', that one who was here yesterday is gone today; Guru Tegh Bahadur states the same sudden passing as a plain law.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahala 9, Salok 52, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Men come and go as leaves year by year upon the trees. Those of autumn the wind sheds upon the ground, but when spring returns the forest buds forth with fresh ones. Even so is it with the generations of mankind, the new spring up as the old are passing away.”
greek_mythology.explanation: On the battlefield, Glaucus tells Diomedes that human generations fall and replace one another like leaves.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The world's constant coming and going of people, which the Kural wryly calls its ‘greatness’, is Homer's falling of leaves.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Always observe how ephemeral and worthless human things are, and what was yesterday a little mucus to-morrow will be a mummy or ashes.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself how quickly human life passes from beginning to end.
philosophy.tie_back: Marcus' ‘yesterday ... to-morrow’ matches the Kural's ‘yesterday ... today’, both stressing how short the interval is.

real_life_example.event_title: The eruption of Vesuvius buries Pompeii
real_life_example.event: In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the thriving Roman town of Pompeii under a deep layer of volcanic ash and pumice, while nearby Herculaneum disappeared under volcanic flows. Busy towns full of people, shops and homes were lost in a single eruption. The buried ruins were rediscovered centuries later and now give a detailed picture of Roman daily life frozen at one moment.
real_life_example.explanation: Pompeii has become the classic image of how suddenly ordinary life can vanish. Its preserved streets show a world that was going about its business one day and gone the next.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's ironic 'greatness' of the world is that one who was here yesterday is gone today, and Pompeii shows a whole town undergoing that change in a single day.

tamil:
ஒருபொழுதும் வாழ்வது அறியார் கருதுப
கோடியும் அல்ல பல.
transliteration:
Oru pozhudhum vaazhvadhu ariyaar karudhupa
Kodiyum alla pala.
meaning: People cannot know if they will live even one more moment, yet they make countless plans, more than ten million of them.
elementary: Someone might plan what they'll do next week, next year, and in ten years, even though nobody knows for sure what will happen tomorrow. This kural gently laughs at how many plans we make when we can't even be sure of the next hour.
university: The couplet's force comes from the mismatch of scale: “oru pozhudhu” (a single moment or watch of the day) against “kodiyum alla pala” (not a crore, i.e. ten million, but more). People who cannot guarantee a single stretch of time still carry countless projects, desires and calculations. Commentators note the progression within the chapter from “yesterday/today” (336) to an even smaller unit, “one moment” (337), tightening the frame of uncertainty. The critique is not of planning as such but of a mind that lives in imagined futures while forgetting its own fragility. The Gita's portrait of the deluded man counting his gains ‘today’ and ‘tomorrow’, Jesus' parable of the rich fool, and Aeschylus' ‘blind hopes’ all diagnose the same condition.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The demoniac persons think, "I have gained so much wealth today, and I shall now fulfill this desire of mine. This is mine, and tomorrow I shall have even more."”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes deluded people who endlessly plan their gains for today and tomorrow, as though their lives were secure.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘more than ten million’ calculations, made by people who cannot be sure of the next moment.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus' parable, a rich man plans years of comfort and dies that very night.
christianity.tie_back: The rich fool is the Kural's planner: many years of plans, not even one secure night.

islam.quote_or_event: “And no soul perceives what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul perceives in what land it will die.”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that no one knows what tomorrow will bring or where they will die.
islam.tie_back: Both texts point to the basic uncertainty of the future that makes endless planning foolish.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns against confident talk about tomorrow, since no one knows what a single day will bring.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts set human certainty about the future against ignorance of even one day ahead.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Here shall I live during the rains, here in winter and summer” — thus thinks the fool. He does not realize the danger (that death might intervene).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures a fool making plans for every season without realising death may come first.
buddhism.tie_back: The fool's seasonal planning is the Kural's ‘more than ten million’ thoughts in someone unsure of a single moment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I have this, and I have not that; I must do this, and I should not do that! While he talks in this strain, the robbers (viz. time) drag him away. What foolishness is this!”
jainism.explanation: A man busy reckoning his possessions and plans is carried off by time before he finishes.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar mocks those who cannot be sure of one moment yet make endless plans; the Jain verse shows the planner dragged away by time mid-sentence.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The self-willed manmukhs make their calculations and plans, but only the actions of the Creator come to pass.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak contrasts the endless schemes of the self-centred person with the reality that events unfold by the Creator's will (hukam).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural mocks those who cannot be sure of one more moment yet make countless plans; Guru Nanak likewise sets human plan-making against our real powerlessness over what will happen.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 60, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I caused mortals to cease foreseeing their doom. ... I caused blind hopes to dwell within their breasts.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Prometheus says he stopped humans from foreseeing their deaths by giving them ‘blind hopes’.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In both texts, people forget how fragile life is and fill their minds with countless hopes and plans.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Paulinus that people live as if destined to live forever, never thinking of their own frailty or of how much time has already gone, and put off real living to their fiftieth or sixtieth year.
philosophy.explanation: In On the Shortness of Life, Seneca criticises people who put off living and make distant plans while forgetting that they are mortal.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's forgetful planners are the Kural's people who cannot secure one moment yet plan without end.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life (De Brevitate Vitae) 3

real_life_example.event_title: Antoni Gaudi dies with the Sagrada Familia unfinished
real_life_example.event: The architect Antoni Gaudi, who had devoted more than four decades to designing and building the Sagrada Familia basilica, was struck by a tram in Barcelona on 7 June 1926 while walking to church. He died at the Hospital de la Santa Creu on 10 June and was buried in the crypt of the basilica. The building, planned to take generations, was still far from complete and construction continued long after his death.
real_life_example.explanation: Gaudi's vast, long-range design stands in sharp contrast to the sudden, ordinary accident that ended his life. His plans outlived him by a century, carried on by others.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar remarks that people who cannot be sure of the next moment still carry countless plans, and Gaudi's enormous project was cut short in an instant by a passing tram.

tamil:
குடம்பை தனித்துஒழியப் புள்பறந் தற்றே
உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு.
transliteration:
Kudambai thaniththu ozhiyap pul parandhatre
Udambodu uyiridai natpu.
meaning: The friendship between the body and the soul is like a bird that flies away and leaves its egg (or nest) behind, empty and alone.
elementary: A baby bird grows inside an egg, but one day it breaks out and flies off, leaving the empty shell behind. This kural says our life and our body are like that: one day life flies off, and the body is left behind like the shell.
university: The meaning turns on the word “kudambai”, which Parimelazhagar and many commentators gloss as ‘egg’ (so the chick breaks out and leaves the shell), while others read it as ‘nest’ (so a grown bird abandons its home); both readings agree that the container is left “thaniththu ozhiya” (abandoned, alone). Calling the relationship “natpu” (friendship) is pointed, since it is a friendship of convenience that ends the moment the occupant departs. The egg reading adds the idea that the body was the soul's place of formation, not its permanent home, which prepares for kural 340. The image of soul and body as distinct, one of them leaving the other, parallels the Gita's worn-out garments, Ecclesiastes' spirit returning to God, and Plato's definition of death in the Phaedo as the separation of soul from body.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a person sheds worn-out garments and wears new ones, likewise, at the time of death, the soul casts off its worn-out body and enters a new one.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna explains that the soul discards the body at death as one discards old clothes.
hinduism.tie_back: In both images the soul leaves and the body is left behind like an empty covering: garments in the Gita, shell or nest in the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.”
christianity.explanation: Paul speaks of leaving the body behind at death to be with Christ.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see the body as something the self eventually leaves, not the self's permanent place.

islam.quote_or_event: “No! When the soul has reached the collar bones ... And the dying one is certain that it is the [time of] separation”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes the soul rising in the dying body, and the dying person knowing it is time for separation.
islam.tie_back: ‘Separation’ (al-firaq) is the Kural's parting of bird and shell, soul and body.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes describes death as the body returning to dust and the spirit returning to God.
judaism.tie_back: Body and spirit part ways at death: the body stays behind like the Kural's empty shell, while the spirit goes on.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Ere long, alas! this body will lie upon the earth, unheeded and lifeless, like a useless log.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha reminds his followers that the body will soon lie lifeless and ignored, like a discarded log.
buddhism.tie_back: The abandoned body, left alone and useless, is the Kural's deserted shell or nest.

jainism.quote_or_event: “(The soul) cannot be apprehended by the senses, because it possesses no corporeal form, and since it possesses no corporeal form it is eternal. The fetter of the soul has been ascertained to be caused by its bad qualities, and this fetter is called the cause of worldly existence.”
jainism.explanation: Answering the materialist claim that the soul is produced by and perishes with the body, Bhṛgu's sons say the soul is formless and eternal, only temporarily bound to embodiment by karma.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural pictures body and soul as egg (or nest) and bird, the one abandoned when the other leaves; the Jain verse likewise holds the soul to be distinct from the body and only temporarily joined to it.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.19 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When the soul-swan flies away, by the Command of the Lord, her dust mingles with dust.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak pictures death as the soul, imagined as a swan, flying off at God's command while the body it leaves behind returns to dust.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares the bond of body and soul to a bird leaving its egg or nest empty behind it; Guru Nanak uses the same image of a bird flying from an abandoned body.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1111, Raag Tukhaari, Chhant, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Patroclus is struck down by Hector, his soul leaves his limbs and flies down to the house of Hades, mourning its fate and the youth and strength it leaves behind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer pictures the psyche flying out of the body at the moment of death.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The soul flying away and leaving the body behind is the Kural's bird deserting its shell.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And is this anything but the separation of soul and body? And being dead is the attainment of this separation; when the soul exists in herself, and is parted from the body and the body is parted from the soul-that is death?”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates defines death as the soul and the body parting from each other.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato's definition is the philosophical form of the Kural's image: two companions whose ‘friendship’ ends when one departs.

real_life_example.event_title: Benjamin Franklin writes his own mock epitaph
real_life_example.event: As a young printer of about 22, Benjamin Franklin wrote a humorous epitaph for himself, describing his body in the grave as the cover of an old book whose contents had been torn out and whose lettering and gilding had been stripped away. He added that the work itself would not be lost but would appear again in a new and better edition. Several autograph copies survive, and in his will he asked for a simple inscription on his actual gravestone instead.
real_life_example.explanation: Franklin's famous image treats the body as an outer case that is left empty once its real contents depart. It became one of the best-known epitaphs in American literature.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares body and life to an egg or nest left empty and alone when the bird flies off, and Franklin pictured his own body as an empty book cover left behind.

tamil:
உறங்கு வதுபோலுஞ் சாக்காடு உறங்கி
விழிப்பது போலும் பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Urangu vadhu polum saakkaadu urangi
Vizhippadhu polum pirappu.
meaning: Death is like falling asleep, and being born is like waking up after sleep.
elementary: Every night you fall asleep, and every morning you wake up again. This kural says dying is like falling asleep, and being born is like waking up.
university: The couplet is the chapter's most compressed statement: “saakkaadu” (death) is like “uranguvadhu” (sleeping), and “pirappu” (birth) is like “urangi vizhippadhu” (waking after sleep). Most traditional commentators read it within the Indian framework of rebirth: death and birth follow one another as naturally as sleep and waking, so the cycle is familiar rather than terrifying, and the real goal is to escape it (veedu). Some modern readers, including Kalaignar's gloss, take a more secular line, stressing that death is a sleep from which one does not wake. The analogy is found across traditions: the Greek twins Hypnos and Thanatos, Socrates' ‘dreamless sleep’, the biblical ‘those who sleep in the dust’ shall awake, and the Quran's teaching that God takes souls both in death and in sleep.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Death is certain for one who has been born, and rebirth is inevitable for one who has died. Therefore, you should not lament over the inevitable.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that death and rebirth follow each other as surely as night and day.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's sleep-and-waking cycle is the Gita's cycle of death and rebirth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus speaks of the dead Lazarus as asleep and of raising him as waking him.
christianity.tie_back: Death as sleep and return to life as waking is exactly the Kural's pair of images.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die [He takes] during their sleep. Then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others for a specified term.”
islam.explanation: The Quran teaches that sleep and death are the same kind of event: in both, God takes the soul, returning it only to those who wake.
islam.tie_back: Both texts see sleep and death as closely related, and waking as a return of life.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.”
judaism.explanation: Daniel speaks of the dead as sleepers in the dust who will one day wake.
judaism.tie_back: The same metaphor: death as sleep and a return to life as waking.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary. Long is worldly existence to fools who know not the Sublime Truth.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha likens the long round of births and deaths (samsara) to a long night for those who do not understand the Dhamma.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts use night and sleep imagery for the round of birth and death.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain doctrine describes passing from one birth to the next as almost instantaneous: at death the soul, carrying its karmic body, moves to its next embodiment in at most a few moments (vigraha-gati), so death and rebirth follow each other continuously, like falling asleep and waking.
jainism.explanation: In Jain cosmology there is no long gap between lives; the embodied soul leaves one body and takes the next almost at once until liberation ends the cycle.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural likens death to sleep and birth to waking; Jain teaching on transmigration likewise treats death and rebirth as one continuous passage, though it uses no sleep metaphor.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 2.25–30 (on vigraha-gati, the soul's transit between births)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Death would not be called bad, O people, if one knew how to truly die.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Alahanian, his hymns of mourning, Guru Nanak teaches that death is not to be dreaded by one who has learned to die to ego while living.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural makes death as natural as falling asleep and birth as waking; Guru Nanak likewise strips death of its terror, though by a different route.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 579, Raag Vadhans, Alahanian, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod makes Hypnos (Sleep) and Thanatos (Death) the twin children of Night, dwelling together at the edge of the world: Sleep gentle to men, Death with a heart of iron.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, Sleep and Death are brothers, twin sons of Night.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Making Sleep and Death twins is the mythic form of the Kural's claim that death is like sleep.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “... but a sleep like the sleep of him who is undisturbed even by the sight of dreams, death will be an unspeakable gain.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells his jurors that if death is like a dreamless sleep, it is nothing to fear and may even be a gain.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates and the Kural both remove death's terror by comparing it to ordinary sleep.

real_life_example.event_title: Socrates compares death to a dreamless sleep at his trial
real_life_example.event: In 399 BCE an Athenian jury found the philosopher Socrates guilty and sentenced him to death. In Plato's account of his defence speech, the Apology, Socrates told the jurors that death must be either a dreamless sleep, which he would count as a gain, or a migration of the soul to another place, which would be even better. He therefore argued that death was not something to be feared.
real_life_example.explanation: The speech is one of the founding texts of Western philosophy's reflection on death, and it uses the familiar experience of deep sleep to make death less frightening.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar likens death to falling asleep and birth to waking, and Socrates, facing execution, likewise reasoned about death through the image of sleep and a passage to another life.

tamil:
புக்கில் அமைந்தின்று கொல்லோ உடம்பினுள்
துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Pukkil amaindhindru kollo udambinul
Thuchchil irundha uyirkku.
meaning: The soul only stays for a while in a corner of the body. It seems it has not yet found a lasting home of its own.
elementary: Imagine a traveller who keeps staying in borrowed rooms, moving from one to the next, never having a house of their own. This kural says the soul is like that traveller: the body is only a temporary room, and it is still looking for its true home.
university: Valluvar closes the chapter with a question rather than a statement. “Pukkil” (a settled dwelling, a home one enters to stay) is contrasted with “thuchchil” (a temporary lodging, a borrowed corner), and the particle “kollo” (is it perhaps that...?) gives the line a tone of wondering. The soul is pictured as a tenant in a rented corner of the body, which explains why it keeps moving from body to body: it has not yet reached its true home, which traditional commentators identify with veedu (liberation). The chapter thus moves from wealth (332-333), to time (334-337), to the body (338-339), and finally to the homelessness of the soul, handing on to the next chapter on renunciation. Parallels include the Gita's ‘transient world’ from which liberated souls do not return, Paul's ‘earthly house of this tabernacle’, the hadith of being a ‘stranger or traveller’, and Marcus Aurelius' ‘stranger's sojourn’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Having attained Me, the great souls are no more subject to rebirth in this world, which is transient and full of misery, because they have attained the highest perfection.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the soul keeps returning to this impermanent world until it reaches God, its final home.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's lodger who has not yet found a home is the soul still in this transient world; the Gita names the home it seeks.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.”
christianity.explanation: Paul calls the body a temporary tent, contrasted with the eternal home God provides.
christianity.tie_back: The body as a tent (tabernacle) rather than a permanent house is the Kural's ‘thuchchil’ versus ‘pukkil’.

islam.quote_or_event: “Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler.” Ibn `Umar used to say, “If you survive till the evening, do not expect to be alive in the morning.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Ibn Umar to live in this world like a stranger or traveller passing through.
islam.tie_back: The traveller who has not settled is the Kural's soul lodging in a borrowed corner, with no permanent home here.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as were all our fathers: our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is none abiding.”
judaism.explanation: King David prays that humans are strangers and temporary residents on earth, with no lasting place.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Sojourners’ with ‘none abiding’ matches the Kural's soul as a temporary lodger without a settled home.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Through many a birth in samsara have I wandered in vain, seeking the builder of this house (of life). Repeated birth is indeed suffering! O house-builder, you are seen! You will not build this house again.
buddhism.explanation: At his awakening, the Buddha describes wandering through countless births, each a new ‘house’, until he ends the cycle.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts picture life moving from one temporary house to another without a lasting home, and point to an end of that wandering.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Going through the same religious practices as perfected saints, you will reach the world of perfection, Gautama, where there is safety and perfect happiness.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra points Gautama to Siddha-loka, the abode of the perfected at the summit of the universe, the soul's only permanent home.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural suggests the soul only lodges in the body because it has not yet found a lasting home; Jainism names that home as the world of perfection reached at liberation.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Burn away your hopes and desires, and live like a guest in this world.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das counsels living in the world as a visitor who knows the stay is temporary, not as an owner settling in for good.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural wonders whether the soul, lodging for a while in the body, has yet found a permanent home; Guru Amar Das likewise teaches that here we are only guests.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 646, Raag Sorath (Sorath ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After the fall of Troy, Odysseus wanders for ten years, lodging as a guest or captive in one strange place after another and longing for his home in Ithaca.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Odyssey is the story of a man who stays everywhere but belongs nowhere until he finally reaches home.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus as a guest in foreign houses loosely mirrors the Kural's soul lodging in a body while seeking its true home.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Everything which belongs to the body is a stream, and what belongs to the soul is a dream and vapour, and life is a warfare and a stranger's sojourn, and after-fame is oblivion.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius calls life a stranger's temporary stay, with the body constantly flowing away.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘A stranger's sojourn’ is almost the Kural's image of the soul as a temporary lodger in the body.

real_life_example.event_title: Basho sells his home and sets out on the Narrow Road to the Deep North
real_life_example.event: In 1689 the haiku poet Matsuo Basho sold his home outside Edo and set out on foot, with a companion, on a journey of about five months through the remote northern provinces of Japan. He recorded the journey in prose and haiku in Oku no Hosomichi (The Narrow Road to the Deep North), published in 1694. Basho died in 1694 while on another journey.
real_life_example.explanation: Basho chose to live as a lifelong traveller without a fixed home, and his travel diary became a classic of Japanese literature. His life embodies the idea of existence as a passage rather than a settled dwelling.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural pictures the soul as a lodger in a borrowed corner that has not yet found its permanent home, and Basho gave up his own house to live as a wanderer between temporary lodgings.

tamil:
யாதனின் யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல்
அதனின் அதனின் இலன்.
transliteration:
Yaadhanin yaadhanin neengiyaan nodhal
Adhanin adhanin ilan.
meaning: Whatever a person has let go of, whatever it may be, that thing can no longer cause them pain.
elementary: If you stop caring about keeping a certain toy, you won't cry when it breaks. This kural says every single thing you stop clinging to is one less thing that can make you sad.
university: The doubled pronouns (yaadhanin yaadhanin … adhanin adhanin, “from whatever, whatever … from that, that”) set up an exact one-to-one ledger: each object released cancels the suffering tied to that particular object. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as the gradualist justification for renunciation — one need not abandon everything at once to begin reaping relief, since each detachment pays its own dividend; Karunanidhi likewise glosses it as “whichever single attachment one gives up.” The chapter therefore opens not with an ascetic command but with a near-empirical observation about the mechanics of grief: pain travels along the line of attachment. The same causal claim underlies the Buddhist analysis of suffering as arising from clinging (upādāna) and the Stoic insistence that distress comes from our relation to externals rather than from the externals themselves.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who neither hates nor desires the fruits of his activities is known to be always renounced. Such a person, liberated from all dualities, easily overcomes material bondage and is completely liberated, O mighty-armed Arjuna.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines the true renunciate not by outward robes but by an inner state: someone who neither craves nor resents outcomes, and who therefore slips easily out of bondage.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says what you have let go of can no longer hurt you; the Gita says the one who no longer craves is freed from the bondage that craving creates.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that earthly treasure is always exposed to decay and theft, and urges his hearers to invest where nothing can be lost.
christianity.tie_back: Both locate vulnerability in what we hold: release the earthly treasure and moth, rust and thief lose their power to wound you.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you. And Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful -”
islam.explanation: The Quran teaches that events are decreed so that believers neither collapse over what they lose nor grow proud over what they gain.
islam.tie_back: The same equanimity the Kural describes: loss cannot wound a person whose heart is not bound to the thing lost.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: Stripped in one day of his wealth and his children, Job answers that he arrived with nothing and will leave with nothing, and blesses God.
judaism.tie_back: Job's un-possessive stance lets him face catastrophic loss without collapse — the Kural's principle tested at its most extreme.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief and fear directly to what we hold dear, and declares that one wholly free of such attachment has no grief at all.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly identical logic to the Kural: grief follows attachment, so where attachment is removed, the grief tied to it is gone.

jainism.quote_or_event: “But a man who is indifferent to ‘colours,’ is free from sorrows; though still in the Saṃsâra, he is not affected by that long succession of pains, just as the leaf of the Lotus (is not moistened) by water.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's sermon on the causes of carelessness goes through the senses one by one. For each object (colours, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, feelings) it shows that passion for it brings pain and indifference to it ends that pain.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's doubled 'from whatever, from that' sets up the same one-to-one ledger: each object a person becomes indifferent to stops causing that person pain.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 189)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “As long as I walked along, carrying the load, I continued to pay the fine. But I threw away that bundle, when I met the Perfect Guru; O Nanak, then I became fearless.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes attachment to Maya as a bundle carried on the head: as long as it is carried, its penalty is paid, and once it is set down, fear and burden go with it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that from whatever one has let go, one suffers no more pain; Guru Arjan says the same of the bundle he threw down, whose fine he no longer pays.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 214, Raag Gauree (Gauree Maalaa), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “It would be absurd, if Manes can live without Diogenes, but Diogenes cannot get on without Manes.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Diogenes the Cynic's slave Manes ran away and friends urged him to chase him, Diogenes refused with this reply.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Diogenes simply declines to let the loss hurt him, because he never made his contentment depend on Manes — the Kural's point made as a joke.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.55 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never say of anything, "I have lost it"; but, "I have returned it." Is your child dead? It is returned. Is your wife dead? She is returned. Is your estate taken away? Well, and is not that likewise returned?”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus trains his students to treat everything external as on loan, so that its loss is experienced as a return rather than a theft.
philosophy.tie_back: Once a thing is no longer held as 'mine', its departure causes no pain — exactly the Kural's claim.

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi adopts the loincloth at Madurai
real_life_example.event: During a tour of South India, Mohandas Gandhi was troubled by the poverty of peasants he saw working in loincloths and by the point that many people were too poor to buy enough khadi to replace the foreign cloth they were being asked to give up. On the night of 22 September 1921 in Madurai he decided to wear only a loincloth, at first until the end of October, and he appeared in it in public in Madurai shortly afterwards. The change became permanent and remained his dress for the rest of his life.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi gave up his customary clothing one step at a time, having considered and set aside the idea on earlier occasions before acting on it. The loincloth became a lasting symbol of his identification with India's poor.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural teaches that each single thing a person lets go of is one less source of suffering, and Gandhi's gradual shedding of possessions, of which the Madurai decision was one step, shows renunciation proceeding item by item.

tamil:
வேண்டின்உண் டாகத் துறக்க துறந்தபின்
ஈண்டுஇயற் பால பல.
transliteration:
Vendin undaagath thurakka thurandhapin
Eendu iyarpaala pala.
meaning: If you want lasting good, give things up while you still have them. Once you have given them up, many joys come to you even in this life.
elementary: Taking a heavy backpack off before a long hike isn't losing anything — it's how you get to enjoy the walk. This kural says give things up while you still have them, and you'll find lots of happiness right away.
university: The phrase undaaga (“while [they] exist”) is read by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan as a timing instruction: renounce while wealth, strength and opportunity are still in hand, not after they have already slipped away — giving up what one no longer has is not renunciation at all. The second line's eendu (“here”, in this world) is striking: Valluvar promises not only a post-mortem reward but many present goods (iyarpaala pala), countering the caricature of renunciation as pure deprivation. This anticipates the famous Upanishadic paradox that one enjoys by relinquishing. Placed after the Kural's earlier praise of the householder (ch. 5, Ilvaazhkai), the couplet presents thuravu as a voluntary, later-chosen stage rather than a universal command.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “All this, whatsoever moves on earth, is to be hidden in the Lord (the Self). When thou hast surrendered all this, then thou mayest enjoy. Do not covet the wealth of any man!”
hinduism.explanation: The opening verse of the Isha Upanishad teaches that the world belongs to the Lord, and that true enjoyment comes only after surrendering one's claim to it.
hinduism.tie_back: Same paradox as the Kural: renounce first, and then the joys follow — even in this life.
hinduism.source: Isha (Vajasaneyi-samhita) Upanishad 1 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE vol. 1)

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my sake, and the gospel’s, But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises those who leave everything for him a hundredfold return 'now in this time', as well as eternal life hereafter.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's eendu (here), Jesus insists the rewards of renunciation begin in this life, not only after death.

islam.quote_or_event: “Be indifferent towards this world, and Allah will love you. Be indifferent to what is in people’s hands, and they will love you.”
islam.explanation: Asked for a deed that would win the love of God and people, the Prophet recommends zuhd — detachment from worldly goods.
islam.tie_back: Zuhd brings concrete goods in return — divine and human love — echoing the Kural's promise of many joys after renouncing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot, as it is said: ‘You shall enjoy the fruit of your labors, you shall be happy and you shall prosper’ (Psalms 128:2) ‘You shall be happy’ in this world, ‘and you shall prosper’ in the world to come.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment, and reads the psalm as promising happiness in this world and prosperity in the next.
judaism.tie_back: Contentment rather than accumulation is the path to joy 'in this world' — close to the Kural's promise of joys 'here'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If by renouncing a lesser happiness one may realize a greater happiness, let the wise man renounce the lesser, having regard for the greater.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha frames renunciation as a rational exchange: give up a smaller pleasure to gain a larger one.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's bargain — if you want the many joys, renounce.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You are now a king of great power and prosperity, enjoying the reward of your good actions; put from you the transitory pleasures, and enter the order for the sake of the highest good!”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra urges his former brother, now the universal monarch Brahmadatta, to renounce while he is still at the height of his wealth and power. The king cannot let go, and the lecture records the bad end that follows.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says to renounce while there is still something to renounce. Citra gives exactly that advice to a man who holds everything.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 59)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately!”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks Bhagat Kabir urges that the turn to God must not be postponed, because the time to act is now.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks for renunciation while one still has things to renounce, not after they have slipped away; Kabir likewise insists that the spiritual turn be made today, not tomorrow.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Crates of Thebes, born wealthy, is said to have turned his property into money and distributed it among his fellow citizens, then lived as a cheerful Cynic beggar-philosopher.
greek_mythology.explanation: According to Diogenes Laertius, Crates gave away a large inheritance and embraced the Cynic life, becoming known for his good humour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Crates renounced while he still had much to give up, and found joy in the renounced life — the Kural's timing and promise in one biography.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.87 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that wealth is measured by the limit of one's wants, not by the size of one's possessions.
philosophy.tie_back: Letting go of craving is what makes one rich — a Stoic version of the Kural's claim that renunciation brings many goods.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 2 (tr. R. M. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Julius Nyerere steps down as president of Tanzania
real_life_example.place: Dar es Salaam and Butiama, Tanzania
real_life_example.event: Julius Nyerere, who had led Tanganyika and then Tanzania since independence, voluntarily stepped down as president in 1985 and was succeeded by Ali Hassan Mwinyi. He was one of very few African leaders of his era to give up the presidency without being forced out. He retired to his home village of Butiama, where he farmed, while remaining active in diplomacy, including as a mediator in Burundi's peace talks in the 1990s.
real_life_example.explanation: Nyerere let go of supreme power while he still held it firmly, rather than waiting until it was taken from him. His retirement set an example of peaceful handover that earned him lasting respect.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar says to renounce while one still has things to renounce and promises many goods even in this life, and Nyerere gave up office at the height of his authority and lived on in useful retirement.

tamil:
அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை விடல்வேண்டும்
வேண்டிய வெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு.
transliteration:
Adalvendum aindhan pulaththai vidalvendum
Vendiya vellaam orungu.
meaning: You must conquer your five senses and, at the same time, give up everything you desire.
elementary: Imagine five puppies each pulling you toward a different treat. You need to hold all five leashes AND put all the treats away. This kural says control all five senses and let go of everything they want, all at once.
university: The couplet is built on two parallel imperatives (adalvendum … vidalvendum, “must conquer … must abandon”): conquest of the five sense-fields (aindhan pulam — sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch) and the simultaneous relinquishing of all that they desire. The final word orungu (“together, all at once”) is decisive; Parimelazhagar stresses that a partial abandonment leaves a foothold from which desire regrows. Pairing inner control with outer relinquishment mirrors the Indic scheme of indriya-nigraha and tyaga, and recalls Kural 6's praise of the one who has quenched the five sense-gates. Across traditions the senses appear as the doorways through which the world lays claim to the self — the Gita's tortoise, Plato's unruly horse, Odysseus's wax-stopped crew.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is able to withdraw his senses from sense objects, as the tortoise draws his limbs within the shell, is to be understood as truly situated in knowledge.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares the steady sage to a tortoise that can pull all its limbs inside its shell at will.
hinduism.tie_back: The tortoise withdraws all its limbs together — the Kural's 'conquer the five senses' and 'orungu' (all at once) in a single image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world. And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.”
christianity.explanation: John names the cravings of the body and the eyes as belonging to a passing world, and contrasts them with doing God's will.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see sense-desire as the channel that binds us to the world, and call for turning away from it.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Quran promises Paradise to the one who restrains the self (nafs) from its unlawful desires out of reverence for God.
islam.tie_back: Restraint of the desiring self is the gateway to the highest state — parallel to the Kural's call to conquer the senses.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’ (Proverbs 16:32).”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines strength as the conquest of one's own impulses rather than of other people.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's 'adal' (conquest) is turned inward in exactly the same way: the real victory is over one's own desires.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Good is restraint over the eye; good is restraint over the ear; good is restraint over the nose; good is restraint over the tongue. Good is restraint in the body; good is restraint in speech; good is restraint in thought. Restraint everywhere is good. The monk restrained in every way is freed from all suffering.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists restraint over each sense in turn and concludes that total restraint frees the monk from suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: A sense-by-sense version of the Kural's command to conquer all five senses together.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not desire (pleasant) sounds and colours, but conquer his longing for all kinds of pleasures. A monk should avoid every attachment and bear every pain, be full (of wisdom), not greedy, wander about homeless, give assurance of safety (to all beings), and be free from passions.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga tells the monk to master the pull of the sense-objects and, at the same time, to give up every attachment, living homeless and free of passion.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar pairs conquering the five senses with giving up 'together' everything they crave. These verses join the same two duties: overcome the longing for sounds and colours, and avoid every attachment.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.7.27-28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 296)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They conquer the five thieves, and enshrine the True Lord in the heart.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the way of life that leads to God as overcoming the five thieves (kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankar) and keeping the True One in the heart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks that the five senses be subdued and everything they crave be given up together; Guru Nanak asks for the five inner thieves to be conquered and the heart given to God instead.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 223, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sailing past the Sirens, Odysseus stops his crew's ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast so their song cannot draw him to ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: Warned by Circe, Odysseus uses physical restraint to overcome a sensory lure that has destroyed every sailor before him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Sirens personify the pull of sense-objects; blocking the senses entirely is how Odysseus survives — a mythic image of the Kural's command.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates pictures the soul as a charioteer driving two horses, one noble and one unruly, and describes the struggle to rein in the unruly horse of appetite.
philosophy.explanation: Plato's allegory makes self-mastery a matter of reason forcibly controlling the appetites that pull toward sensual objects.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats the appetites as forces that must be conquered, not negotiated with.

real_life_example.event_title: Simeon Stylites lives atop a pillar in Syria
real_life_example.event: The Christian ascetic Simeon Stylites climbed onto a pillar near Telanissa in northern Syria and spent the rest of his life, more than thirty-five years, on its top, exposed to the weather, with only a railing and a ladder by which visitors could approach. Pilgrims came for counsel and help, and his influence reached even the emperor. After his death in 459 a great church complex, now known as Qal'at Sim'an, was built around the base of his column.
real_life_example.explanation: Simeon became the founder of the stylite tradition, an extreme example of withdrawing from every comfort the senses seek. The ruins built around his pillar are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage property.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls for mastering all five senses and giving up together everything they crave, and Simeon's life on the pillar was a total renunciation of comfort, food, shelter and ease.

tamil:
இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கொன்று இன்மை உடைமை
மயலாகும் மற்றும் பெயர்த்து.
transliteration:
Iyalbaagum nonbirkondru inmai udaimai
Mayalaagum matrum peyarththu.
meaning: Owning nothing at all is natural for someone who has truly given up the world. Owning even one thing pulls them back into the false thinking they had left behind.
elementary: If you are trying to stop eating sweets, keeping 'just one piece' in your pocket makes it very hard to stop thinking about sweets. This kural says someone who has given things up should keep nothing, because even one thing can pull them back.
university: Inmai (having nothing) is called the iyalbu — the natural, defining character — of nonbu (austerity, tapas). The second line's peyarththu (“turning back, reversing”) suggests that possession does not merely distract but undoes progress, returning the renunciant to mayal, bewilderment; Karunanidhi glosses that even one attachment multiplies into many. This is a stricter standard than Kural 341's gradualism, and it applies specifically to one who has already taken up the ascetic life. Comparable rules shaped the Buddhist monk's short list of requisites, the Jain ideal of aparigraha, and the apostolic mission charge in Matthew 10; the Cynic Diogenes made the same point theatrically.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Such a man of understanding acts with mind and intelligence perfectly controlled, gives up all sense of proprietorship over his possessions and acts only for the bare necessities of life. Thus working, he is not affected by sinful reactions.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the sage who has abandoned all possessiveness (tyakta-sarva-parigraha) and keeps only what bare survival needs.
hinduism.tie_back: Both identify non-possession as the defining mark of the renunciate.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses, Nor scrip for your journey, neither two coats, neither shoes, nor yet staves: for the workman is worthy of his meat.”
christianity.explanation: Sending out the twelve apostles, Jesus forbids them to carry money, spare clothing or supplies.
christianity.tie_back: The missionary is to own nothing, like the Kural's ascetic, depending entirely on God and on others' hospitality.

islam.quote_or_event: “Your wealth and your children are but a trial, and Allah has with Him a great reward.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes possessions and family as a test that can distract the believer from God.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's warning that possession brings back delusion, the Quran treats wealth as a trial that can lead the heart astray.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The more property, the more anxiety”
judaism.explanation: Hillel's saying lists the hidden costs that come with each kind of increase — including more worry with more possessions.
judaism.tie_back: Possession breeds a disturbed mind — a Jewish echo of the Kural's 'possession brings bewilderment'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, we who possess nothing. Feeders on joy we shall be, like the Radiant Gods.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the monks' happiness as flowing from owning nothing at all.
buddhism.tie_back: Owning nothing is not a hardship but the natural condition of the joyful renunciate — the Kural's 'inmai' as 'iyalbu'.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who owns even a small property in living or lifeless things, or consents to others holding it, will not be delivered from misery.”
jainism.explanation: In the opening answer of the Sūtrakṛtāṅga, Sudharman gives Mahāvīra's account of what binds the soul. Possessing even a little property, or approving of others holding it, is named first.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says owning even one thing drags the ascetic back into delusion. The Jain canon makes the same uncompromising claim: even a small property blocks deliverance. This is the root of the monastic vow of aparigraha.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.1.1.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 235)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “As the lotus flower floats unaffected in the water, so does he remain detached in his own household.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das gives the classic Sikh image of detachment: the lotus lives in water without being wetted, and the Gurmukh lives in the family home without being bound by it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural makes owning nothing the very nature of austerity; Sikh teaching answers that detachment lies in the mind, so one may keep a household and possessions and still be free of them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 949, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A child has beaten me in plainness of living.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Seeing a child drink water from his cupped hands, Diogenes threw away the cup from his bag, saying this.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Even one small possession was one too many for Diogenes — the Kural's point that the ascetic should keep nothing.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.37 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For to that which once exceeds a due measure, there is no bound.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus warns that once one goes beyond what the body actually needs, desire has no natural stopping point — the shoe becomes gilded, then purple, then jewelled.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's 'possession brings delusion again', even one step beyond need restarts an endless cycle of wanting.

real_life_example.event_title: Clare of Assisi wins papal approval for a Rule of absolute poverty
real_life_example.event: Clare of Assisi, founder of the order of Poor Clares, insisted that her community own nothing, either individually or in common, and in 1228 Pope Gregory IX granted her community the privilege of poverty. When later popes pressed the sisters to accept property, Clare wrote her own Rule enjoining absolute poverty. Pope Innocent IV approved her definitive Rule on 9 August 1253, two days before she died.
real_life_example.explanation: Clare spent decades defending the right of her sisters to hold no property at all, against well-meaning pressure from church authorities. She treated even shared ownership as a step away from the life she had chosen.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar says owning nothing is the very nature of austerity and that possessing even one thing pulls the renunciant back into delusion, which is exactly why Clare refused even communal property.

tamil:
மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல் பிறப்பறுக்கல்
உற்றார்க்கு உடம்பும் மிகை.
transliteration:
Matrum thodarppaadu evankol pirapparukkal
Utraarkku udambum migai.
meaning: For people working to end the cycle of being born again and again, even their own body is one thing too many. So why take on any more ties?
elementary: If you are trying to swim across a river, even your shoes feel heavy. Why would you carry a suitcase too? This kural says someone trying to be truly free finds even their own body a load, so they shouldn't add extra burdens.
university: The couplet argues a fortiori: if even the body — the one attachment that cannot simply be discarded — is migai (excess, surplus) to someone who has set out to cut off births (pirappu arukkal), then every additional bond (thodarppaadu) is indefensible. Parimelazhagar notes that the body is retained only as the instrument through which austerity is practised, not valued for its own sake. The verse does not counsel harming the body; it relocates the body from 'self' to 'tool'. The idea resonates with Plato's Phaedo, where philosophy is a rehearsal for the soul's release from the body, with Paul's groaning 'in this tabernacle', and with the Buddha's house-builder verse, in which the body is the house craving keeps rebuilding.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When the embodied being is able to transcend these three modes, he can become free from birth, death, old age and their distresses and can enjoy nectar even in this life.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the soul, by rising above the qualities that arise from the body, escapes the cycle of birth, death and ageing.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts aim at ending rebirth by loosening identification with the body and what grows from it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes the present body as a tent in which believers groan under a burden while longing for a greater, immortal life.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul experiences the body itself as a burden for one set on a higher life.

islam.quote_or_event: “Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler.”
islam.explanation: Taking Ibn Umar by the shoulder, the Prophet told him to live in the world as a passing traveller, not a settler.
islam.tie_back: A traveller carries only what the road requires; the Kural likewise asks the seeker to add no ties beyond the bare vehicle of the journey.

judaism.quote_or_event: “This world is like a vestibule before the world to come; prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the banqueting-hall.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Jacob compares this life to an entry hall whose purpose is preparation for what lies beyond.
judaism.tie_back: Both treat present existence as a passage whose only value is to prepare for release beyond it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Through many a birth in samsara have I wandered in vain, seeking the builder of this house (of life). Repeated birth is indeed suffering! O house-builder, you are seen! You will not build this house again.”
buddhism.explanation: At his awakening the Buddha declares that he has found craving, the builder of the body-house, and that it will build no more.
buddhism.tie_back: The body is the 'house' that craving keeps rebuilding; for one cutting off births, it is to be ended, not added to.

jainism.quote_or_event: “(In order to be able) to practise control a monk should eat; he should desire to get rid of sin … he should wait for the advent of death; having annihilated his Karman he should not again mix with the world, but be rather like a car whose axle is broken.”
jainism.explanation: The monk keeps up the body only as an instrument of self-control. Freed of karma, he never re-enters the round of worldly existence, like a cart whose axle is broken.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar treats the body as surplus to someone set on ending births. The Jain text likewise allows food only so that control can be practised, and points beyond the body to a soul that never again 'mixes with the world'.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.7.29-30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, pp. 296-297)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan treats the human body as a precious opportunity, the one chance in which a soul can meet God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls even the body one thing too many for those who seek to end rebirth; Sikh teaching shares the goal of ending rebirth but values the body as the very means of reaching it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa (in the So Purakh section of Rehras), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plato reports an Orphic teaching that the body (soma) is the soul's tomb or prison-enclosure (sema), in which the soul pays a penalty until it is released.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Orphic religious tradition, as Plato relays it, saw embodiment as a confinement to be escaped.
greek_mythology.tie_back: If the body itself is a prison, adding further ties is only building more walls — the Kural's reasoning in mythic-religious dress.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedo, Socrates argues that true philosophers practise dying, striving throughout life to separate the soul as far as possible from the body and its demands.
philosophy.explanation: Facing execution, Socrates treats the body as an obstacle to wisdom and philosophy as training for the soul's release.
philosophy.tie_back: For Socrates as for Valluvar, the body is a necessary but excess encumbrance for one seeking release, so nothing further should be added to it.

real_life_example.event_title: Anthony of Egypt withdraws into the desert
real_life_example.event: Anthony, a young Egyptian Christian from a prosperous family, gave away his possessions and took up an ascetic life, eventually living in solitude in the desert near Pispir from about 286 to 305. Disciples gathered around him, and he is regarded as the founder of Christian monasticism.
real_life_example.explanation: Anthony reduced his life to the bare minimum the body needed, and his example inspired the monastic movement that spread across the Christian world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those seeking release even the body is one thing too many, so no further ties should be added, and Anthony kept only the body itself as a tool for his spiritual practice.

tamil:
யானென தென்னுஞ் செருக்கறுப்பான் வானோர்க்
குயர்ந்த உலகம் புகும்.
transliteration:
Yaanenadhu ennum serukkaruppaan vaanork
kuyarndha ulagam pugum.
meaning: A person who cuts away the pride of thinking “I” and “mine” will reach a world higher even than the world of the gods.
elementary: Imagine a kid who stops shouting 'Mine! Mine!' about every toy and stops acting like everything is about them. This kural says a person who drops 'me' and 'mine' reaches a place even better than heaven.
university: Yaan (“I”) and enadhu (“mine”) are the Tamil counterparts of ahankara and mamakara; Parimelazhagar glosses them as mistaking the body for the self and taking unconnected things as one's own, and calls this pairing serukku — pride or delusion. The reward, vaanorkku uyarndha ulagam (“a world higher than the gods'”), is read by traditional commentators as liberation (veedu), which lies beyond even the heavens, themselves impermanent. Karunanidhi, consistent with his rationalist reading, renders it instead as a renown surpassing heaven's. The couplet thus makes ego itself, not property, the root to be severed — property is simply 'mine' extended outward. The parallel with Gita 2.71 (nirmamo nirahankarah, 'without mine, without ego') is almost verbatim.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who has given up all desires for sense gratification, who lives free from desires, who has given up all sense of proprietorship and is devoid of false ego—he alone can attain real peace.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names the pair nirmama (without 'mine') and nirahankara (without 'I') as the conditions for supreme peace.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's yaan/enadhu is the exact Tamil counterpart of the Gita's ahankara/mamata; both promise the highest state to the one who cuts them.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes the death of his old, self-centred ego and its replacement by Christ living within him.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see the dissolution of the ego-'I' as the doorway to a higher life.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, "I was only given it because of knowledge I have."”
islam.explanation: Qarun, fabulously rich, credits his wealth to himself; the Quran recounts his arrogance and his destruction.
islam.tie_back: A negative mirror of the Kural: Qarun's 'I' and 'mine' is exactly the pride the Kural says must be cut away.

judaism.quote_or_event: “be exceeding humble spirit, for the end of man is the worm.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Levitas of Yavneh urges extreme humility, grounded in the reminder of mortality.
judaism.tie_back: Humility here is the Jewish counterpart to cutting off the pride of 'I' and 'mine'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The fool worries, thinking, "I have sons, I have wealth." Indeed, when he himself is not his own, whence are sons, whence is wealth?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha mocks the anxious claim to own sons and wealth, pointing out that the self does not even own itself.
buddhism.tie_back: Both expose the 'I' and the 'mine' as the root delusion; the Buddha adds that the 'I' is not even one's own.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who ceasing from acts relinquishes the idea of property, relinquishes property itself. That sage has seen the path (to final liberation) for whom there exists no property.”
jainism.explanation: The Ācārāṅga puts the root of possession in the mind. The real renunciation is giving up the idea of 'mine', and the sage for whom nothing is 'his' has found the road to liberation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that cutting away the pride of 'I' and 'mine' leads to a world above the gods. The Ācārāṅga likewise makes dropping the sense of 'mine' the doorway to final liberation, which in Jain cosmology lies above every heaven.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.2.6.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, pp. 25-26)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “As long as I claimed, ‘Mine, mine!’, I was surrounded by wickedness and corruption. But when I dedicated my mind, body and intellect to my Lord and Master, then I began to sleep in peace.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan names possessiveness, the cry of mine, as the cause of entanglement, and says peace came only when mind, body and intellect were offered to God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural promises a world beyond the gods to one who cuts off the pride of I and mine; Guru Arjan describes the same cutting off of mine as the passage from corruption into peace.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 214, Raag Gauree (Gauree Maalaa), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, the soul of Odysseus, cured of ambition by the memory of his former toils, chooses last and searches out the neglected life of a private man with no cares.
greek_mythology.explanation: At the close of the Republic, souls choose their next lives; Odysseus, remembering his past, gladly takes a humble, obscure one.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus's rejection of glory and self-importance is a Greek image of cutting away pride — though in Plato he still returns to earth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But you, after all, are neither property nor style.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus corrects the reasoning 'I am richer, so I am better', insisting that a person is not identical with what he owns or displays.
philosophy.tie_back: Separating the self from 'mine' is exactly the cut the Kural demands.

real_life_example.event_title: Pierre and Marie Curie decline to patent the radium process
real_life_example.event: After discovering radium, Pierre and Marie Curie published in detail the methods they had used to isolate it, without patenting any of them. When industrial production of radium began and the question arose whether they should patent the production process, both opposed it, holding that research should be done for its own sake and not mixed with commercial profit. A large radium industry grew up, from which they did not profit by patents.
real_life_example.explanation: The Curies chose not to claim as their own property a discovery that could have made them rich. Their decision kept the method open to all researchers and industries.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises cutting away the pride of 'I' and 'mine', and the Curies refused to treat their discovery as 'mine' to be owned and sold.

tamil:
பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள் பற்றினைப்
பற்றி விடாஅ தவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Patri vidaaa idumbaigal patrinaip
Patri vidaaa thavarkku.
meaning: Sorrows grab hold and never let go of people who hold tightly to the things they are attached to and will not let them go.
elementary: If you grab a cactus and refuse to let go, it keeps hurting you. This kural says when you hang on tightly to things, troubles hang on tightly to you.
university: One of the Kural's most celebrated pieces of wordplay: the phrase patri vidaaa (“seizing, not releasing”) appears twice, first describing sorrows (idumbaigal) and then describing people who hold on to patru (attachment). The mirror structure enacts the moral — the grip we exert is the grip exerted upon us. Mu. Varadarasan specifies the attachments as the twofold 'I' and 'mine' of the previous couplet, making this verse the causal explanation of Kural 346. The same self-reinforcing loop is analysed in Buddhist accounts of craving, in the Gita's chain from dwelling on objects to attachment to desire, and in Spinoza's description of human bondage to the passions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain reaction: dwelling on objects breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, and desire breeds anger (and, in the next verse, ruin).
hinduism.tie_back: Both show attachment generating its own suffering in a chain that tightens around the one who clings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that clinging to wealth traps people in a snare and ends with them piercing themselves with many sorrows.
christianity.tie_back: 'Pierced themselves through with many sorrows' is the Kural's image exactly: the one who clings is held fast by grief of his own making.

islam.quote_or_event: “Competition in [worldly] increase diverts you Until you visit the graveyards.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes people so gripped by the race for more that it holds them until death.
islam.tie_back: The grip of acquisitiveness never lets go until the grave — the Kural's picture of attachment holding its holder fast.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth observes that loving wealth produces endless dissatisfaction rather than contentment.
judaism.tie_back: Clinging to wealth produces a restless dissatisfaction that never releases its grip.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever is overcome by this wretched and sticky craving, his sorrows grow like grass after the rains.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls craving 'sticky' and says the sorrows of one it overcomes multiply like grass after rain.
buddhism.tie_back: 'Sticky' craving and multiplying sorrows mirror the Kural's image of attachment and grief each refusing to let go.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the crane is produced from an egg, and the egg is produced from a crane, so they call desire the origin of delusion, and delusion the origin of desire.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra describes a closed loop: desire produces delusion, and delusion produces desire again, like crane and egg. Elsewhere in the same lecture this cycle is shown to generate karma and misery.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's mirrored phrase, sorrows that seize and never let go of those who seize and never let go, enacts the same self-feeding cycle that the crane-and-egg image describes.
