jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 185)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In that pool, people have made their homes, but the water there is as hot as fire! In the swamp of emotional attachment, their feet cannot move. I have seen them drowning there.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak pictures the world as a burning pool and emotional attachment (moh) as a swamp that holds the feet fast until people drown.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says sorrows grip and never release those who grip their attachments; Guru Nanak shows the same grip from the other side, a swamp of attachment that will not let the feet go.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa (in the So Purakh section of Rehras), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Granted his wish that everything he touched should turn to gold, King Midas finds that his food, drink and everything he holds turns to metal, and he begs to be freed from the gift he craved.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid's telling, Midas's greed becomes a curse that clings to his very hands until the god releases him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Midas grasps at gold, and the thing he grasps grasps back — the Kural's 'clinging clings to you' in mythic form.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza names human weakness in moderating and restraining the emotions 'bondage', explaining that a person ruled by passions is not his own master but is subject to fortune.
philosophy.explanation: In Part IV of the Ethics, Spinoza analyses how passive affects — attachments to external things — hold people captive.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Spinoza sees our attachments as the very chains by which we are held.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Preface (tr. R. H. M. Elwes)

real_life_example.event_title: Qin Shi Huang's search for an elixir of immortality
real_life_example.event: Qin Shi Huang, who unified China in 221 BCE and became its first emperor, became preoccupied with escaping death. In 219 BCE he sent an expedition to the islands of the Eastern Sea to find an elixir of immortality, and when it failed he repeatedly summoned magicians to his court. He died in 210 BCE while on an inspection tour, and his dynasty collapsed within a few years.
real_life_example.explanation: The most powerful man in China could not loosen his grip on life and power, and his fear of losing them drove years of anxious and fruitless searching.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar warns that sorrows cling to those who cling to their attachments, and the First Emperor's grasping after endless life brought him restless anxiety rather than peace.

tamil:
தலைப்பட்டார் தீரத் துறந்தார் மயங்கி
வலைப்பட்டார் மற்றை யவர்.
transliteration:
Thalaippattaar theerath thurandhaar mayangi
Valaippattaar matrai yavar.
meaning: People who have given up everything completely have reached the highest goal. All others are confused and caught in a net.
elementary: A fish that swims completely clear of the net stays free, but a fish that stays near it 'just a little' gets caught. This kural says people who give up everything are truly free, while the rest get tangled up.
university: Theera (“wholly, to the very end”) is the key word: Valluvar contrasts complete renunciants, who have thalaippattaar — 'reached the head', attained the goal — with the rest, who, bewildered (mayangi), are valaippattaar, 'netted'. The rhyming pair thalaippattaar/valaippattaar sharpens the stark binary. Commentators differ over the net: Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as the net of repeated births, Mu. Varadarasan and Karunanidhi as the net of ignorance. The couplet refuses any comfortable middle position — a half-renunciation still counts as capture — in line with Luke 9:62's warning against looking back from the plough and the Gita's 'mesh of delusion'.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Possessed and led astray by such imaginings, enveloped in a mesh of delusion, and addicted to the gratification of sensuous pleasures, they descend to the murkiest hell.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes those driven by endless desires as caught in a 'moha-jala' — a net of delusion — that drags them downward.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's moha-jala (net of delusion) is precisely the Kural's mayangi valaippattaar, 'bewildered and netted'.

christianity.quote_or_event: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus answers a would-be follower who wants first to say goodbye to his family: discipleship admits no looking back.
christianity.tie_back: Both insist that renunciation must be total; divided attention disqualifies.

islam.quote_or_event: “And what is the life of this world except the enjoyment of delusion.”
islam.explanation: The Quran closes a verse about death and judgment by calling worldly life an enjoyment that deceives.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's 'mayangi' (bewildered) corresponds to the Quran's delusion: those who remain attached to worldly life are deceived by it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For man also knoweth not his time: as the fishes that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare; so are the sons of men snared in an evil time, when it falleth suddenly upon them.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth compares humans to fish and birds suddenly caught in nets and snares.
judaism.tie_back: The same image of human beings caught in a net, though Ecclesiastes speaks of sudden misfortune rather than attachment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are lust-infatuated fall back into the swirling current (of samsara) like a spider on its self-spun web. This, too, the wise cut off. Without any longing, they abandon all suffering and renounce the world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures the passionate as trapped in a web of their own making, while the wise cut it and renounce the world.
buddhism.tie_back: The same two outcomes as the Kural: the renunciants go free; the infatuated remain entangled in a self-spun net.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As an elephant, sinking down in a quagmire, sees the raised ground but does not get to the shore, so do we who long for sensual pleasures, not follow the path of monks.” … “But Kitra the great sage, of excellent conduct and penance, was indifferent to pleasure; after he had practised the highest self-control, he reached the highest place of perfection.”
jainism.explanation: King Brahmadatta admits that he is stuck like an elephant in a swamp and cannot leave his pleasures, and he ends in hell. His brother Citra renounces fully and reaches perfection.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's sharp contrast between those who renounce completely and reach the goal and those caught in the net is acted out by the two brothers. One is mired, the other reaches the summit.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.30 and 13.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, pp. 60-61)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The fish did not notice the net in the deep and salty sea.”
sikhism.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak uses the fish caught unawares in the fisherman's net as an image of the heedless soul trapped by Maya and death.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that those who have not wholly renounced are bewildered and netted; Guru Nanak's fish, which never saw the net, is the same bewildered captive.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 55, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hephaestus forges an invisible, unbreakable net and traps Ares and Aphrodite in it in the very act of their illicit passion, exposing them to the laughter of the gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the song of Demodocus, the lovers' desire leads them straight into a finely wrought trap.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Those led by desire end up caught in a net — a vivid mythic counterpart to the Kural's valaippattaar.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the allegory of the cave, prisoners chained since birth mistake shadows for reality; only one who is freed and turns fully around can climb out to the sunlight.
philosophy.explanation: Plato depicts ordinary human life as bondage to illusion, from which only a complete turning of the soul releases one.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato's chained, deluded prisoners correspond to the Kural's 'bewildered, netted' majority; the freed philosopher to the one who has reached the height.

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Shirakawa abdicates but keeps ruling as a cloistered emperor
real_life_example.event: Emperor Shirakawa of Japan abdicated in 1086 in favour of his young son, and he later took Buddhist vows. Rather than withdrawing from public life, he set up his own administrative centre with judicial functions and a military guard, and as retired emperor he dominated his successors and the government for decades. His example created the insei or cloister government, through which later emperors exercised power after abdicating until 1185.
real_life_example.explanation: Shirakawa outwardly renounced the throne and took religious vows, yet remained fully entangled in politics. The system he founded shows how a partial renunciation can leave a person as bound as before.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says only those who renounce completely reach the goal while the rest remain caught in the net, and Shirakawa's half-renunciation left him more entangled in power than ever.

tamil:
பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும் மற்று
நிலையாமை காணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Patratra kanne pirapparukkum matru
Nilaiyaamai kaanap padum.
meaning: The moment a person lets go of all attachments, the cycle of rebirth is cut. Otherwise, they keep going round and round in an endless, unsteady cycle of birth and death.
elementary: A spinning top keeps going as long as you keep flicking it; stop flicking, and it finally rests. This kural says once you stop clinging, the cycle of being born again and again stops — and if you don't, everything keeps wobbling and changing.
university: Kanne (“at that very point”) stresses immediacy: liberation coincides with the cessation of patru rather than following it as a later reward. The second line is read in two ways. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan take matru as 'otherwise': without detachment, instability — the alternation of births and deaths — will be seen. Puliyur Kesikan reads it as 'moreover': with detachment, the impermanence of the world is then clearly seen. Either way the couplet binds this chapter to the preceding one, Nilaiyaamai (Impermanence, ch. 34). The claim that the end of desire is the end of rebirth is shared almost word for word by the Katha Upanishad and the Dhammapada, and appears inverted in the Orphic hope of escaping the 'wheel'.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When all desires that dwell in his heart cease, then the mortal becomes immortal, and obtains Brahman.”
hinduism.explanation: Death himself (Yama) teaches Nachiketas that the cessation of all desires is the moment the mortal becomes immortal.
hinduism.tie_back: Same claim and same immediacy as the Kural: when attachment ends, birth-and-death ends.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad II.6.14 (2.3.14) (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE vol. 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.”
christianity.explanation: Paul directs believers' attention away from visible, temporary things to invisible, eternal ones.
christianity.tie_back: Both contrast the instability of what is clung to with the permanence gained by looking beyond it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And present to them the example of the life of this world, [its being] like rain which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it and [then] it becomes dry remnants, scattered by the winds.”
islam.explanation: The Quran likens worldly life to vegetation that flourishes after rain and is soon blown away as dry debris.
islam.tie_back: The instability (nilaiyaamai) the Kural says is seen by those still attached is here pictured as vegetation scattered by the wind.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth opens by declaring all worldly striving to be hevel — vapour, fleeting breath.
judaism.tie_back: The same insight into the instability of everything grasped, without the Kural's promise of release.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let go of the past, let go of the future, let go of the present, and cross over to the farther shore of existence. With mind wholly liberated, you shall come no more to birth and death.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges total letting-go and promises that the wholly liberated mind will not return to birth and death.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's claim: complete release from clinging ends the cycle of birth.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Misery ceases on the absence of delusion, delusion ceases on the absence of desire, desire ceases on the absence of greed, greed ceases on the absence of property.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana traces misery back through delusion, desire and greed to possession. Remove the last link and the whole chain collapses.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that births are cut at the very moment attachment ceases. The Jain chain likewise makes the end of misery depend directly on the end of grasping.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 185)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Coming and going in reincarnation is ended, O Nanak, for those whose minds are filled with the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that the round of birth and death ends for those in whose minds God dwells.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the cycle of birth is cut the moment attachment ceases, and otherwise the round of coming and going continues; Gurbani uses the same coming and going and ties its end to a mind filled with God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 251, Raag Gauree (Bavan Akhree, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On gold tablets buried with Orphic initiates, the soul declares to the underworld powers that it has flown out of the grievous, weary circle (or wheel) of existence and asks to be admitted among the blessed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Orphic initiates hoped to escape a cycle of reincarnation through purification and ritual.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Orphic 'wheel' is the Greek counterpart to the cycle of births the Kural says is cut when attachment ends.
greek_mythology.source: Orphic gold tablet from Thurii (4th century BCE)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Consolation of Philosophy, Lady Philosophy shows Boethius that Fortune turns her wheel ceaselessly, so anyone who ties his happiness to her gifts must expect to be thrown down.
philosophy.explanation: Imprisoned and ruined, Boethius learns that clinging to the goods of Fortune binds one to her endless instability.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's 'otherwise, instability is seen', Boethius shows attachment to worldly goods locking one into perpetual change.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2

real_life_example.event_title: Bill Wilson and Dr Bob Smith found Alcoholics Anonymous
real_life_example.event: In May 1935 the New York stockbroker Bill Wilson, who had stopped drinking, met the Akron surgeon Dr Robert Smith, and the two men began helping each other and other alcoholics to stay sober. Dr Smith's last drink, on 10 June 1935, is celebrated as the founding date of Alcoholics Anonymous. The fellowship, built on mutual support and reliance on a spiritual power greater than oneself, published its basic text in 1939 and spread around the world.
real_life_example.explanation: The movement helped millions break a cycle of craving, relapse and harm that had seemed endless. Its founders found that the cycle stopped only when the craving itself was surrendered.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar says that at the very moment attachment ceases the cycle is cut, while otherwise endless instability is seen, and AA's founders found that ending the craving was what ended the cycle of relapse.

tamil:
பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை அப்பற்றைப்
பற்றுக பற்று விடற்கு.
transliteration:
Patruga patratraan patrinai appatraip
Patruga patru vidarku.
meaning: Hold on to the One who is free of all attachment. Hold on to that one bond alone, so that you can let go of all others.
elementary: When you're learning to swim, you hold on to the edge of the pool so you can stop being scared of the water. This kural says hold on to God — the one who clings to nothing — so you can let go of everything else.
university: The chapter's closing couplet repeats forms of patru (“attachment, clinging”) six times, a virtuoso climax. It resolves a paradox the chapter has built up: desire cannot simply be willed away, so Valluvar prescribes a single counter-attachment — to patratraan, 'the One without attachment', whom Parimelazhagar and most commentators identify as God, whose feet are to be held — as the instrument for dropping all other attachments. Karunanidhi, in keeping with his secular reading, takes patratraan to mean any truly detached person, making the verse a counsel to cling to the company of the detached. The strategy of replacing a lower attachment with a higher one parallels the Gita's 'higher taste', while the Buddha's raft simile adds the caution that even the means is finally to be let go.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The embodied soul may be restricted from sense enjoyment, though the taste for sense objects remains. But, ceasing such engagements by experiencing a higher taste, he is fixed in consciousness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna notes that forced abstinence leaves the craving intact; only the experience of something higher makes the lower taste fall away.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's 'higher taste' is the Kural's strategy exactly: cling to the higher attachment in order to release the lower ones.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that holding on to Christ has made everything else he once valued worthless by comparison.
christianity.tie_back: Clinging to Christ is what enables Paul to let go of everything else — the Kural's single, liberating attachment.

islam.quote_or_event: “And remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him with [complete] devotion.”
islam.explanation: The Arabic 'tabattal ilayhi tabtila' literally suggests cutting oneself off from all else in order to devote oneself wholly to God.
islam.tie_back: Tabattul — severing from everything to cleave to God alone — is the Kural's formula of one attachment used to cut all others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist declares that God is his only desire and his lasting portion, even as everything else fails.
judaism.tie_back: A single, all-absorbing attachment to God that renders every other desire unnecessary — the heart of the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the same way, monks, I have taught the Dhamma compared to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of holding onto.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares his teaching to a raft: something to hold on to while crossing the flood, and then to leave behind.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's single permitted attachment, the Dhamma is grasped as a means to let go — though the Buddha adds that even it must finally be released.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: Samantabhadra's hymn to the twelfth Tīrthaṅkara, Vāsupūjya, says that worship serves no purpose for the Jina, who is free from attachment, and that blame means nothing to one who has cast off enmity. Yet remembering his pure qualities cleanses the devotee's mind of the stains of sin.
jainism.explanation: Jain devotion is directed to the vītarāga, 'one free of attachment'. Since the Jina grants nothing, the benefit of devotion comes entirely from fixing the mind on detachment itself.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to cling to the One who is without attachment so that every other attachment falls away. Jain worship of the passionless Jina works by exactly this method, although the Jina is a liberated soul, not a creator God.
jainism.source: Svayambhūstotra of Samantabhadra, verse 57 (Vāsupūjya-stuti), Sanskrit text at sanskritdocuments.org

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I am joined with You, and I have broken with all others.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas tells God that by joining himself to the Lord in love he has broken his bond with everything else.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural resolves its chapter by prescribing one attachment, to the One without attachment, so that every other may be let go; Ravidas states exactly that exchange of one bond for all others.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 659, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When his raft is sucked into Charybdis, Odysseus leaps up and clings to a fig tree growing over the whirlpool, holding on until the wreckage is thrown back up and he can escape.
greek_mythology.explanation: Everything else is swallowed by the whirlpool; holding one fixed point is what saves him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A loose image of the Kural's counsel: amid the whirlpool, cling to the one stable thing in order to be freed from everything else.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plotinus ends the Enneads by describing the soul's ascent as a withdrawal from all things of this world toward the One, famously characterised as the flight of the alone to the Alone.
philosophy.explanation: For Plotinus, the soul must turn away from multiplicity and cleave to the One, which is itself beyond need and attachment.
philosophy.tie_back: Clinging to the One that clings to nothing, in order to shed every lower tie, is close to the Kural's paradox.

real_life_example.event_title: Ignatius of Loyola lays down his sword at Montserrat
real_life_example.event: Ignatius of Loyola, a Basque soldier who had been seriously wounded at Pamplona and turned to religion during his recovery, went to the Benedictine abbey of Montserrat in March 1522. He hung up his sword and dagger before the shrine of the Virgin, kept an all-night vigil, gave away his fine clothes to a poor man and put on rough pilgrim's garb. He went on to found the Society of Jesus.
real_life_example.explanation: By binding himself wholly to God, Ignatius found the strength to drop the military ambitions and worldly honour that had ruled his early life. The moment at Montserrat became a turning point in the history of the Jesuits.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises holding fast to the One who is free of attachment so as to let go of every other attachment, and Ignatius gave up his sword and finery by committing himself entirely to God.

tamil:
பொருளல்ல வற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும்
மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Porulalla vatraip porulendru unarum
Marulaanaam maanaap pirappu.
meaning: Thinking that things which are not real are real is a mistake of the mind. From this mistake come unhappy births, again and again.
elementary: Imagine chasing a shiny puddle on a hot road, sure it’s water, when it’s only a mirage. You’d run and run, get more and more thirsty, and never drink. This kural says that when we treat things that don’t last as if they were the real treasure, we keep chasing mirages again and again, life after life.
university: The chapter opens with a diagnosis rather than a prescription: the root of bondage is marul (delusion, confusion), specifically the cognitive error of taking porul-alladhu (what is not the real) for porul (the real). Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read maanaa-p-pirappu (‘inglorious birth’) as the whole cycle of transmigration, which turns the couplet into an epistemological account of samsara: rebirth is caused less by particular sins than by misperception. This closely matches the Advaita Vedanta analysis of adhyasa (superimposition, the classic rope mistaken for a snake) and the Buddhist teaching that avijja (ignorance) is the first link of dependent origination. Because the Tamil ‘porul’ is richly ambiguous (thing, wealth, meaning, reality), the couplet also carries an ethical undertone: whoever treats wealth and possessions as the ultimate ‘thing’ has mistaken the counterfeit for the coin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From the unreal lead me to the real! From the darkness lead me to the light! From death lead me to immortality!”
hinduism.explanation: This ancient Upanishadic prayer asks to be led away from what is unreal toward what is truly real. The Upanishad itself explains that the ‘unreal’ and ‘darkness’ mean death, and the ‘real’ and ‘light’ mean immortality.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar names the same wrong turn (taking the unreal for the real) and the same cost: being caught in death and birth again and again.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28 (Pavamana Mantra), trans. Patrick Olivelle

christianity.quote_or_event: “While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Christians not to fix their eyes on visible things, which pass away, but on unseen realities, which last forever.
christianity.tie_back: Same distinction the Kural draws between passing things wrongly treated as ‘real’ and the lasting reality; the Kural adds rebirth as the consequence of getting it wrong.

islam.quote_or_event: “Know that the life of this world is but amusement and diversion and adornment and boasting to one another and competition in increase of wealth and children … And what is the worldly life except the enjoyment of delusion.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes worldly life as a passing show, like a plant that flourishes after rain and then dries into debris, and calls its enjoyment ‘delusion’.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘marul’ (delusion) and the Qur’an’s ‘enjoyment of delusion’ both describe treating the fleeting world as the real prize.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.”
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew word translated ‘vanity’ (hevel) literally means vapor or breath. Ecclesiastes says that what people chase as solid and lasting is really as thin as breath.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Ecclesiastes warns that what looks substantial is not the real thing; unlike the Kural, it does not tie this mistake to rebirth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who mistake the unessential to be essential and the essential to be unessential, dwelling in wrong thoughts, never arrive at the essential.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that people who confuse the worthless with the valuable, and the valuable with the worthless, are stuck in wrong thinking and never reach what truly matters.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost the same sentence as the Kural: mistaking the non-essential for the essential is the error that keeps beings in bondage.

jainism.quote_or_event: “But they do not cross the Flood of Life, who, ignoring the true relation of things, and not versed in the true Law, hold the above heretical opinions.” … “They do not put an end to birth, who, &c.”
jainism.explanation: After surveying views it considers false, the Sūtrakṛtāṅga concludes that anyone who misreads the true nature of things stays in the flood of saṃsāra and cannot end birth. In Jain terms, wrong view (mithyātva) heads the causes of bondage.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural traces inglorious birth to the delusion that takes the unreal for the real. The Jain text likewise ties the failure to end birth to ignorance of 'the true relation of things'.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.1.1.20 and 23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 239)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “False doubts and dream objects - man believes them to be true.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Namdev says that people take illusions and the objects of a dream for real things, which is the root of their bondage.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural names taking what is not real for the real as the delusion from which lowly birth arises; Namdev names the same error of believing false things to be true.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 485, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ixion, invited to dine among the gods, desired Hera. Zeus shaped a cloud (Nephele) into Hera’s likeness; Ixion embraced the phantom as if it were real and was punished by being bound to an ever-turning wheel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ixion fell for an illusion made to look like the real thing, and his punishment was an endless, spinning wheel.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s picture of mistaking a phantom for reality and being trapped in an endless cycle is strikingly mirrored in Ixion’s cloud and wheel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “To them, I said, the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images.”
philosophy.explanation: In Plato’s Allegory of the Cave, prisoners chained since birth see only shadows on a wall and take them for the whole of reality.
philosophy.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s diagnosis: people take what is not real (shadows) for the real, and that mistake defines the whole condition they live in.

real_life_example.event_title: Piltdown Man is exposed as a forgery
real_life_example.place: Piltdown, Sussex, and the Natural History Museum, London, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: In 1912 the amateur geologist Charles Dawson and the palaeontologist Arthur Smith Woodward announced skull and jaw fragments from a gravel pit at Piltdown as an early human ancestor, and many leading scientists accepted it as a missing link between apes and humans. For about forty years the find shaped debate about human origins, and it was one reason why Raymond Dart's genuine 1925 Taung fossil from South Africa was widely doubted. In November 1953 Joseph Weiner, Kenneth Oakley and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark showed that the jaw came from a modern ape, that its teeth had been filed down and that the bones had been stained to look ancient.
real_life_example.explanation: A counterfeit taken for the real thing did more than fool individuals: it sent a whole field of research down a false path for decades and caused genuine evidence to be dismissed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that mistaking what is not real for the real is the delusion from which an unworthy chain of consequences is born, and the Piltdown forgery, accepted as real, produced forty years of misdirected science.

tamil:
இருள்நீங்கி இன்பம் பயக்கும் மருள்நீங்கி
மாசறு காட்சி யவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Irulneengi inbam payakkum marulneengi
Maasaru kaatchi yavarkku.
meaning: For people who are free from confusion and see the truth clearly, that clear sight drives away darkness and brings true joy.
elementary: When you switch on the light in a dark room, the scary shape in the corner turns out to be just a coat on a chair, and suddenly you feel safe and happy. People who see the truth clearly are like that: the light of truth chases away the darkness and fear, and joy comes in.
university: The couplet is built on a matched pair: irul neengi (darkness departs) and marul neengi (delusion departs). When inner confusion (marul) is removed, outer darkness (irul, which commentators gloss as the darkness of hell or of future births) also lifts. The key phrase maasaru kaatchi, ‘stainless seeing’, frames liberation as a kind of vision (compare the Sanskrit darshana) rather than mere intellectual agreement, and Parimelazhagar takes the resulting inbam (bliss) as the bliss of release (veedu). The light/darkness metaphor for knowledge and ignorance is shared with the Upanishads (tamaso ma jyotir gamaya), with the Buddha’s first sermon (‘illumination arose’), and with Plato’s ascent from the cave. What stands out in Valluvar is the ethical precondition built into the seeing itself: the vision must be free of stain (maasu).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When, however, one is enlightened with the knowledge by which nescience is destroyed, then his knowledge reveals everything, as the sun lights up everything in the daytime.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares true knowledge to the rising sun: once ignorance is destroyed, everything is seen clearly, as objects become visible at dawn.
hinduism.tie_back: Same movement as the Kural: when ignorance (marul) is removed, darkness (irul) goes and clear vision takes its place.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.”
christianity.explanation: In the Beatitudes, Jesus promises that people whose hearts are pure and undivided will see God.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘maasaru kaatchi’ (stainless seeing) and ‘inbam’ (bliss) match the Beatitude’s purity, seeing, and blessedness almost exactly.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allāh is the Ally of those who believe. He brings them out from darknesses into the light.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes God leading believers out of layers of darkness into light, while false guides lead people the other way.
islam.tie_back: The same passage from darkness to light that the Kural promises to those freed from delusion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist says that true sight is only possible within God’s own light, which is also the source of life.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Psalm links clear seeing, light, and the fullness of life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Vision arose, insight arose, discernment arose, knowledge arose, illumination arose within me with regard to things never heard before: ‘This is the noble truth of stress.’”
buddhism.explanation: In his first sermon the Buddha describes his awakening to the Four Noble Truths as vision and illumination, ending with the certainty that there would be no further birth.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘stainless seeing’ that removes darkness corresponds to the Buddha’s ‘vision… illumination’; both ground liberation in seeing truth directly.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “By the teaching of true knowledge, by the avoidance of ignorance and delusion, and by the destruction of love and hatred, one arrives at final deliverance which is nothing but bliss.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's sermon opens by naming the path: true knowledge, the removal of ignorance and delusion, and the end of passion lead to a liberation that is pure bliss.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar promises that when delusion departs and stainless vision arises, darkness lifts and bliss follows. The Jain verse makes the same sequence explicit: delusion avoided, knowledge gained, 'final deliverance which is nothing but bliss'.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 184)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Divine Light shines in their hearts, and like the sun which removes the darkness of night, it dispels the darkness of ignorance.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das says that when the Guru's teaching is taken to heart, divine light dawns within and drives out ignorance as the sun drives out night.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that for those freed from delusion, a clear vision drives away the darkness; Guru Amar Das uses the same image of inner light dispelling the dark.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 87, Siree Raag (Sri Raag ki Vaar), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter closes by declaring blessed the person on earth who has seen the Eleusinian Mysteries, while the uninitiated has no such good lot after death, down in the darkness and gloom.
greek_mythology.explanation: Initiates at Eleusis were promised a happier fate after death because of what they had ‘seen’ in the secret rites.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, a saving ‘sight’ separates those who reach bliss from those left in darkness.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn to Demeter, lines c. 480–482

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The instrument of knowledge can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being, and learn by degrees to endure the sight of being, and of the brightest and best of being, or in other words, of the good.”
philosophy.explanation: Plato says education is not putting sight into blind eyes but turning the whole soul away from shifting appearances toward true being, which it learns to look at directly.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘marul neengi… maasaru kaatchi’ (delusion gone, pure vision gained) is Plato’s turn from becoming to being, from shadow to light.

real_life_example.event_title: Wang Yangming's awakening in exile in Guizhou
real_life_example.event: After protesting against the imprisonment of officials by a powerful court eunuch, the Ming official and scholar Wang Yangming was beaten and banished in 1506-1507 to a minor post in remote Guizhou. There, in hardship and isolation, he reached in 1508 a sudden philosophical awakening: that the principles of things are to be sought within one's own mind rather than in external objects, as the school of Zhu Xi had taught. He went on to teach the unity of knowing and acting, and his ideas became one of the most influential schools of thought in China and Japan.
real_life_example.explanation: Wang's years of confusion about how to find truth ended not through more outward study but through a clear inner insight, which he then spent his life teaching.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural promises that for those freed of delusion and granted stainless sight, darkness gives way to joy, much as Wang's awakening in a bleak exile cleared his long confusion and set the course of his life.

tamil:
ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு வையத்தின்
வானம் நணிய துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Aiyaththin neengith thelindhaarkku vaiyaththin
Vaanam naniya thudaiththu.
meaning: For people who have moved past doubt and become truly certain, heaven is closer than the earth they stand on.
elementary: When you’re not sure which path leads home, even a short walk feels long and scary. But once you know the way for certain, home feels close. This kural says that people who have cleared away all doubt about what is true feel heaven is closer to them than the ground under their feet.
university: Aiyam (doubt) is here a technical term: Indian epistemology treats samshaya (doubt) as one of the defects of cognition that block liberation, alongside viparyaya (error), which Kural 351 addressed. Thelivu (clarity, settled understanding) is the positive term, and Valluvar’s hyperbole (vaanam naniyadhu, ‘the sky/heaven is nearer’) turns ordinary spatial logic upside down: the earth we stand on becomes the distant, precarious thing, while the spiritual goal becomes immediate. Commentators take vaanam as the higher world or liberation (veedu). The inversion echoes the Gita’s warning that the doubting soul finds happiness neither here nor hereafter, and the Mundaka Upanishad’s ‘all doubts are solved’ when the Real is seen. Comparative readers may also note Deuteronomy’s insistence that the divine word is ‘not in heaven’ but ‘very nigh unto thee’, a similar collapsing of distance, though grounded in revelation rather than insight.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But ignorant and faithless persons who doubt the revealed scriptures do not attain God consciousness. For the doubting soul there is happiness neither in this world nor in the next.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a mind stuck in doubt gains nothing, neither happiness in this life nor in the next.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the mirror image of the Kural: doubt closes off both worlds, while freedom from doubt brings heaven closer than earth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells people not to look for God’s kingdom as some distant place or future event: it is already present, within or among them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it collapses the distance to ‘heaven’: for the one who understands, it is nearer than anything outside.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We have already created man and know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than [his] jugular vein.”
islam.explanation: God declares that He is nearer to each person than their own jugular vein. Islamic spirituality pairs this nearness with yaqin, firm certainty, as the state in which that nearness is actually known.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘heaven is nearer than earth’ finds a strong echo in God being nearer than one’s own vein.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.”
judaism.explanation: Moses tells Israel that God’s teaching is ‘not in heaven’ or beyond the sea, where someone would have to fetch it, but very near, in their own mouth and heart.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts remove the imagined distance between a person and the highest truth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better than sole sovereignty over the earth, better than going to heaven, better even than lordship over all the worlds is the supramundane Fruition of Stream Entrance.”
buddhism.explanation: Stream-entry, the first stage of awakening, is reached partly by abandoning doubt (vicikiccha), one of the first three fetters. The Dhammapada says this attainment is worth more than ruling the earth or going to heaven.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the one freed from doubt gains something that outranks all earthly possession.

jainism.quote_or_event: “(The excellence of faith depends on the following) eight points: 1. that one has no doubts (about the truth of the tenets); 2. that one has no preference (for heterodox tenets); 3. that one does not doubt its saving qualities; 4. that one is not shaken in the right belief …”
jainism.explanation: In Jain teaching, freedom from doubt (niḥśaṅkita) is the first limb of right faith (samyag-darśana), the starting point of the path to liberation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that heaven is nearer than earth for those who have passed beyond doubt into clarity. Jainism likewise puts freedom from doubt first among the marks of the right faith that opens the road to liberation.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, pp. 156-157)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Doubt is dispelled, and the Lord of the Universe is met.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir teaches that when doubt (bharam) is dispelled, God is met.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that for those beyond doubt heaven is nearer than the earth; Kabir likewise puts the meeting with God immediately on the far side of doubt.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 344, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The sea-god Proteus foretells that Menelaus will not die in Argos, but the gods will carry him to the Elysian plain at the ends of the earth, where life is easiest for men.
greek_mythology.explanation: Elysium is a paradise where a favored few go instead of the gloomy underworld.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A heavenly destination opened to a few, but it is not reached through freedom from doubt.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Boethius’s Consolation of Philosophy, Lady Philosophy finds the imprisoned narrator’s mind clouded by confusion. She wipes his eyes, the night is scattered, and he recognizes her; she then leads him by argument from doubt to settled insight.
philosophy.explanation: Philosophy cures the narrator’s blindness and confusion step by step until he sees his true situation clearly.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘aiyaththin neengi thelindhaar’ (those who have left doubt and become clear) describes exactly the journey Boethius dramatizes.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book I

real_life_example.event_title: Augustine's conversion in the garden at Milan
real_life_example.event: In the summer of 386 Augustine, a teacher of rhetoric in Milan who had spent years torn between philosophies and his old way of life, was sitting in a garden with his friend Alypius when he heard a child's voice that seemed to tell him to take up and read. He opened Paul's letters at random, read a passage from Romans, and in his Confessions wrote that at the end of that sentence all the darkness of doubt fled away. He gave up his teaching post and was baptised by Bishop Ambrose at Easter 387.
real_life_example.explanation: Augustine's own account presents the end of doubt, not the acquisition of new information, as the turning point after which his whole life changed direction.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those who have passed beyond doubt into clarity, heaven is nearer than the earth, and Augustine describes exactly such a moment when doubt fell away and he set his life toward God.

tamil:
ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும் பயமின்றே
மெய்யுணர்வு இல்லா தவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Aiyunarvu eydhiyak kannum payamindre
Meyyunarvu illaa thavarkku.
meaning: Even if someone has fully learned everything the five senses can tell them, it is of no real use if they do not truly know what is real.
elementary: A person could have perfect eyes, sharp ears and a great nose, and still walk right past a treasure because they don’t know what it is. This kural says the five senses are like a camera: very useful, but you need a wise mind to understand what the pictures really mean.
university: Aiyunarvu, ‘five-fold awareness’, has two classical readings, both preserved in the commentary tradition. Mu. Varadarasanar and others take it as the complete knowledge gathered through the five senses, while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as the ascetic’s mastery or restraint of the five senses. Either way the claim is striking: neither sensory knowledge nor sensory discipline is enough without meyyunarvu, knowledge of the real. The second reading turns the couplet into a pointed warning to renunciants (the chapter sits in the Thuravaraviyal, the section on the ascetic life) that austerity without insight is barren. Philosophically it anticipates the argument of Plato’s Theaetetus that knowledge cannot simply be perception, and it parallels Heraclitus’s remark that eyes and ears are bad witnesses for souls that cannot interpret them.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But, Sir, with all this I know the Mantras only, the sacred books, I do not know the Self. I have heard from men like you, that he who knows the Self overcomes grief.”
hinduism.explanation: The sage Narada lists every science he has mastered (the Vedas, grammar, logic, astronomy, the arts) and then admits to his teacher that he still does not know the Self and is in grief.
hinduism.tie_back: The same point as the Kural: vast learning and perception bring no real benefit without knowledge of the ultimate truth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says many people have working eyes and ears but miss the meaning of what they see and hear.
christianity.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s paradox: full use of the senses, yet no real perception of truth.

islam.quote_or_event: “They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes people who have every faculty of perception but fail to grasp the truth, so their senses bring them no benefit.
islam.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: complete sensory equipment is useless without true understanding.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hear now this, O foolish people, and without understanding; which have eyes, and see not; which have ears, and hear not.”
judaism.explanation: The prophet Jeremiah rebukes people who have functioning senses but no understanding of God and of what is right.
judaism.tie_back: The same contrast the Kural draws between sensory capacity and true knowing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a person who knows many texts but doesn’t realize them to a herdsman counting cows that belong to someone else.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, accumulated knowledge without realization of truth yields no real benefit.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Without (right) faith there is no (right) knowledge, without (right) knowledge there is no virtuous conduct, without virtues there is no deliverance, and without deliverance there is no perfection.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana sets out a strict chain: every later attainment depends on right faith and right knowledge, and nothing else can stand in for them.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that even complete mastery of the five senses brings no benefit without knowledge of the real. The Jain chain likewise makes all discipline and virtue fruitless without right knowledge of reality.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 156)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You may read and read boat-loads of books; you may read and read and fill pits with them. ... O Nanak, only one thing is of any account: everything else is useless babbling and idle talk in ego.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak says that any amount of reading and learning is worthless without the one thing that counts, the Lord's Name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even complete knowledge gathered through the senses brings no benefit without true knowledge of reality; Guru Nanak dismisses boat-loads of learning in the same way.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Oedipus legend, the blind seer Tiresias knows the terrible truth, while King Oedipus, clear-sighted and famous for solving the Sphinx’s riddle, cannot see his own situation. When the truth finally comes out, Oedipus blinds himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth deliberately flips sight and insight: the man with perfect eyes is blind to reality, and the blind man sees it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A dramatic illustration of the Kural: perfect senses bring no benefit without perception of the truth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Eyes and ears are bad witnesses to men if they have souls that understand not their language.”
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus says the senses only report; without a soul able to interpret them, their testimony misleads.
philosophy.tie_back: A near-exact philosophical restatement of the Kural: sense-knowledge is worthless without understanding of the real.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, Fragment 107 (DK B107; trans. John Burnet)

real_life_example.event_title: Al-Ghazali's crisis of certainty and departure from Baghdad
real_life_example.event: Al-Ghazali, appointed chief professor at the Nizamiyya college in Baghdad in 1091 and one of the most celebrated scholars of his day, fell into a spiritual crisis in 1095 in which his voice failed and he could no longer lecture. He left his post and Baghdad, travelled to Damascus and Jerusalem, and turned to the Sufi path. In his later book The Deliverer from Error he described how he had come to doubt whether the senses, and even reason, could give certain knowledge, and how certainty returned only as a gift of God rather than through argument.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the most learned men of the medieval Islamic world concluded that neither sense-knowledge nor scholarship was enough without a deeper grasp of the truth.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even full mastery of what the five senses can know brings no benefit without knowledge of reality, which is close to the conclusion al-Ghazali reached when he found sense perception and learning alone could not give him certainty.

tamil:
எப்பொருள் எத்தன்மைத் தாயினும் அப்பொருள்
மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு.
transliteration:
Epporul eththanmaith thaayinum apporul
Meypporul kaanpadhu arivu.
meaning: Whatever a thing is, and however it looks, wisdom is seeing the real truth inside it.
elementary: Two chocolates can look exactly the same, but one might have caramel inside and the other a nut. You only know by looking inside. This kural says a wise person doesn’t stop at how things look on the outside but finds out what they really are.
university: This is the chapter’s most quoted couplet, and it works as a definition: arivu (wisdom) is meypporul kaanpadhu, ‘seeing the true thing’ in every porul, whatever its apparent nature (eththanmaith thaayinum). The chain of repetitions (epporul, apporul, meypporul) performs the act it describes, peeling ‘thing’ back to ‘true thing’. Mu. Varadarasanar’s gloss makes the point explicit: one must not be dazzled by how a thing appears but know its real nature. Modern readers often extend it to critical thinking in general, meaning not being taken in by surface, reputation, or rhetoric. The ideal is close to the Buddhist yathabhuta-ñanadassana (‘knowing and seeing things as they really are’) and to the Greek project, from Heraclitus to Plato, of distinguishing a thing’s real nature (phusis) from how it seems (doxa).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The door of the True is covered with a golden disk. Open that, O Pûshan, that we may see the nature of the True.”
hinduism.explanation: The seeker prays that the dazzling golden covering over reality be removed so that the truth behind it can be seen.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s demand to look past a thing’s appearance to its ‘meypporul’ matches the prayer to remove the golden lid and see the True.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his critics not to judge by surface impressions but by what is truly right.
christianity.tie_back: Same principle as the Kural: see through appearance to reality.

islam.quote_or_event: “But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allāh knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an reminds believers that how something seems to them can be the opposite of what it really is; only God knows its true nature.
islam.tie_back: Both texts insist that a thing’s appearance can mislead and its true nature must be sought.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
judaism.explanation: When Samuel is about to anoint the impressive-looking Eliab, God tells him that outward appearance is not the measure: God sees the inner reality.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural asks human wisdom to see as God sees here, past the outward form to the true substance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘All conditioned things are impermanent’ — when one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. This is the path to purification.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that wisdom means seeing the real characteristics of things (impermanent, unsatisfactory, not-self) behind their seeming permanence. The tradition calls this yathabhuta, seeing things as they really are.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘meypporul kaanpadhu arivu’ is essentially the Buddhist definition of wisdom as seeing things as they truly are.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who understands the true nature of all substances by means of all proofs (pramâṇa) and nayas, believes by a complete course of study.”
jainism.explanation: Jain epistemology examines every object through valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and partial standpoints (naya). No single appearance or angle is taken for the whole truth of a thing.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar defines wisdom as seeing the true reality in each thing, however it appears. The Jain method of pramāṇa and naya, the basis of anekāntavāda, is a disciplined way of getting past appearances to a thing's true nature.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 155)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Wherever I look, there I see the Lord pervading.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the vision of one who has been taught by the Guru: God is seen pervading everything.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines wisdom as seeing the true reality within each thing, whatever it appears to be; Guru Arjan describes seeing the Lord within whatever he looks at.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 193, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: To learn the truth, Menelaus must seize the shape-shifting sea-god Proteus and hold on while he turns into a lion, a serpent, a leopard, a boar, running water and a tree. Only when Proteus returns to his own form does he speak truly.
greek_mythology.explanation: The truth is available only to the one who refuses to be fooled by changing appearances and holds on until the real form shows itself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A perfect myth of the Kural’s teaching: whatever form a thing takes, wisdom grasps its true nature.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For, though all things come to pass in accordance with this Word, men seem as if they had no experience of them, when they make trial of words and deeds such as I set forth, dividing each thing according to its kind and showing how it truly is.”
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus describes his philosophical task as showing ‘how each thing truly is’, something most people miss even though it is all around them. (He also says, in Fragment 123, that ‘Nature loves to hide.’)
philosophy.tie_back: Heraclitus’s aim of showing ‘how it truly is’ is the Kural’s ‘meypporul kaanpadhu’ almost word for word.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, Fragment 1 (DK B1; trans. John Burnet)

real_life_example.event_title: Oskar Pfungst discovers the secret of Clever Hans
real_life_example.event: Clever Hans, a horse owned by the Berlin schoolteacher Wilhelm von Osten, appeared to answer arithmetic and other questions by tapping his hoof, and in 1904 a group of experts who examined him found no deliberate trickery. The psychology student Oskar Pfungst then ran careful experiments and showed that the horse answered correctly only when the questioner knew the answer and was visible to him. In his 1907 report Pfungst concluded that Hans was reacting to tiny, unintentional movements of the questioner rather than doing sums.
real_life_example.explanation: Pfungst succeeded where expert observers had failed because he tested what was really happening instead of trusting how the performance looked; the Clever Hans effect is still taught as a warning in science.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines wisdom as seeing the true reality within a thing, whatever it appears to be, and Pfungst looked past the appearance of a counting horse to the real cause of its answers.

tamil:
கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார் தலைப்படுவர்
மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி.
transliteration:
Katreendu meypporul kandaar thalaippaduvar
Matreendu vaaraa neri.
meaning: People who have learned and seen what is truly real, here in this life, take the path that never leads back to this world. They are never born here again.
elementary: When you finally solve a really hard maze, you don’t have to go back into it: you’ve found the way out. This kural says that people who learn deeply and truly understand what is real find the way out of the maze of being born again and again.
university: Two emphases distinguish this couplet: kattru (having learned) and eendu (here, in this very life). Valluvar insists that realization must happen within embodied existence, a ‘liberation while living’ close to the Vedantic jivanmukti and to the Buddhist arahant who knows ‘this is the last birth’. Learning is the necessary first step, but the verb is kandaar (they saw), not merely ‘they studied’: scholarship must end in direct seeing, and Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss stresses learning from the great as the start of that process. Vaaraa neri, ‘the path of no return’, closely echoes the Gita’s ‘one who reaches it never returns’. The formula reaches across traditions: Revelation’s ‘he shall go no more out’ and the Orphic initiate’s escape from the ‘circle’ of births voice the same idea of a final exit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That abode of Mine is not illumined by the sun or moon, nor by electricity. One who reaches it never returns to this material world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the supreme state as self-luminous and final: whoever reaches it is never born into this world again.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘vaaraa neri’ (the path that does not come back) is almost a translation of the Gita’s ‘never returns’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out.”
christianity.explanation: The risen Christ promises that the faithful will be made permanent in God’s presence and will never be sent away again.
christianity.tie_back: A final, irreversible arrival parallels the Kural’s path of no return.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wherein they abide eternally. They will not desire from it any transfer.”
islam.explanation: Speaking of the gardens of Paradise, the Qur’an says their dwellers remain forever and never wish to leave.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘vaaraa neri’, the destination is final: no departure and no return to the former state.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Jacob said: this world is like a vestibule before the world to come; prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the banqueting-hall.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that this life is an entrance hall where one prepares (through Torah study and good deeds) to enter the lasting world to come.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘kattru eendu’ (having learned here) likewise treats this life as the place where one prepares for the final destination.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who has reached the goal, is fearless, free from craving, passionless, and has plucked out the thorns of existence — for him this is the last body.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the one who has fully realized the goal will never take another body: this life is their last.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘matreendu vaaraa’ (never coming here again) is the Buddhist ‘last body’.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Then he knows and sees all things, he is free from delusion and hindrances, his Âsravas have gone, and he is proficient in meditation and concentration of thoughts, and being pure he will arrive at beatitude when his life is spent.”
jainism.explanation: The dispassionate sage reaches omniscience (kevala-jñāna) while still alive, knowing and seeing all things. At the end of that life he passes into liberation, from which, in Jain teaching, a soul never returns.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's learned ones who have 'seen' the truth 'here' and take the path of no return match the Jain kevalin, who knows and sees in this very life and then reaches final release when his life ends.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.109 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, pp. 191-192)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “How rare are those who, as Gurmukh, become Jivan Mukta - liberated while yet alive.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das speaks of jivan mukti, liberation while still living, as the rare attainment of the Gurmukh who follows the Guru.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who have learned and seen the truth here, in this life, set out on the path of no return; Guru Amar Das likewise places liberation within this life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 232, Raag Gauree, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Gold leaves buried with Orphic-Bacchic initiates in southern Italy (4th century BCE) have the dead person declare to the underworld queen that they are pure and have escaped the grievous, weary circle, hoping to become a god instead of a mortal.
greek_mythology.explanation: Initiates believed that sacred knowledge and purification let the soul break out of the cycle of births for good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Striking parallel: a Greek belief that knowledge and purity end the ‘circle’ of rebirth, the Kural’s path of no return.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the closing myth of the Phaedo, Socrates says that those who have sufficiently purified themselves through philosophy live thereafter entirely without bodies and reach dwellings fairer still.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato’s Socrates, the true philosopher’s lifelong pursuit of wisdom ends in the soul’s release from the cycle of embodiment.
philosophy.tie_back: The same sequence as the Kural: learning and seeing the truth in this life leads to not coming back into a body.

real_life_example.event_title: Thomas Merton enters the Abbey of Gethsemani
real_life_example.place: Abbey of Gethsemani, Trappist, Kentucky, United States
real_life_example.event: Thomas Merton, who graduated from Columbia University in 1938 and was received into the Catholic Church that same year, taught at Columbia's extension school and at St. Bonaventure College before making a retreat at the Trappist Abbey of Gethsemani in 1941. On 10 December 1941 he entered the abbey as a monk, and he remained a member of the community until his death in 1968. His autobiography The Seven Storey Mountain, published in 1948, described his path from a restless student life to the monastery.
real_life_example.explanation: Merton's path ran from wide academic learning to a decision to give his life wholly to contemplation, a step he never reversed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of those who have learned and, in this life, seen the truth, setting out on a path from which they do not return, and Merton's move from the university to a lifelong monastic vow follows that pattern.

tamil:
ஓர்த்துள்ளம் உள்ளது உணரின் ஒருதலையாப்
பேர்த்துள்ள வேண்டா பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Orththullam ulladhu unarin orudhalaiyaap
Perththulla vendaa pirappu.
meaning: If the mind has carefully studied and firmly understood what is truly real, there is no need to think about being born again.
elementary: Once you truly understand that the monster under the bed was only a shadow, you don’t have to be scared of it again tomorrow night. This kural says that once your mind really and firmly understands what is real, you don’t have to worry about coming back to be born again.
university: Ulladhu, literally ‘that which is’, is one of the most philosophically loaded words in the chapter. It corresponds to the Sanskrit sat (Being) and later gave its name to Ramana Maharshi’s Tamil work Ulladhu Narpadhu (‘Forty Verses on That Which Is’). Orththu (having reflected or investigated) and oru-thalaiyaa (with complete, one-pointed certainty) spell out the method: truth is reached by sustained inquiry until conviction is total. Traditional glosses (Solomon Pappaiah speaks of holding fully in mind ‘what was heard from the great’) connect this to the Vedantic sequence of hearing, reflection and contemplation (shravana, manana, nididhyasana). The language of ‘what is’ invites comparison with Parmenides, for whom Being is ‘uncreated and indestructible’, and with Maimonides, for whom knowing the Primary Being is ‘the foundation of all foundations’. Valluvar’s distinctive claim is soteriological: to grasp Being is to end becoming.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The fetter of the heart is broken, all doubts are solved, all his works (and their effects) perish when He has been beheld who is high and low.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad says that when the ultimate Reality is directly seen, every bond, every doubt, and all karma that would cause future births fall away.
hinduism.tie_back: Just as the Kural says, firm realization of ‘ulladhu’ removes the karmic cause of rebirth; the same Upanishad describes aiming the mind ‘at that which is’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.”
christianity.explanation: In his prayer before his arrest, Jesus defines eternal life itself as knowing the one true God.
christianity.tie_back: Both teach that knowing the ultimate Reality is itself the deathless state.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who remember Allāh while standing or sitting or [lying] on their sides and give thought to the creation of the heavens and the earth, [saying], ‘Our Lord, You did not create this aimlessly; exalted are You [above such a thing]; then protect us from the punishment of the Fire.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who reflect deeply on creation, reach certainty of its purpose and its Creator, and so seek salvation.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘orththu’ (having reflected), careful contemplation leads to grasping the Real and being saved from a dreaded fate.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The foundation of all foundations and the pillar of wisdom is to know that there is a Primary Being who brought into being all existence.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides opens his code of Jewish law by making knowledge of the one true Being, from whose truth everything exists, the first commandment and the basis of wisdom.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘ulladhu’ (That Which Is) and Maimonides’s ‘Primary Being’ both place knowing true Being at the summit of wisdom.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:1 (trans. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is, monks, an unborn — unbecome — unmade — unfabricated. If there were not that unborn — unbecome — unmade — unfabricated, there would not be the case that escape from the born — become — made — fabricated would be discerned.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha affirms that there really is an unborn, unconditioned reality, and that because it exists, escape from birth is possible.
buddhism.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s logic: realizing what truly ‘is’ (the unborn) removes the need to be born again.

jainism.quote_or_event: “1. jîva, Soul; 2. ajîva, the inanimate things; 3. bandha, the binding of the soul by Karman; 4. puṇya, merit; 5. pâpa, demerit; 6. âsrava … 7. saṃvara … 8. the annihilation of Karman; 9. final deliverance: these are the nine truths (or categories). He who verily believes the true teaching of the (above nine) fundamental truths, possesses righteousness.”
jainism.explanation: For Jainism, 'that which is' is spelled out as the nine tattvas, and firm conviction in them is the right view with which the path to the end of rebirth begins.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that once the mind has examined and firmly grasped That Which Is, no further birth need be feared. The Jain counterpart is firm conviction in the real categories (tattvārtha), which is where the soteriological path starts.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.14-15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 154)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “True In The Primal Beginning. True Throughout The Ages. True Here And Now. O Nanak, Forever And Ever True.”
sikhism.explanation: The opening salok of Japji Sahib declares that the One is Sat, true and real, in the beginning, through the ages, now and forever.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of the mind that has examined and grasped That Which Truly Is; the Japji salok names that Ulladhu, the One who simply is, in every time.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, opening salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, souls about to be reborn must drink from the River of Unmindfulness (Lethe) on the Plain of Forgetfulness. Those not protected by wisdom drink more than the measure and forget everything before entering a new life.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this Greek picture of reincarnation, forgetting the truth goes hand in hand with being reborn; wisdom is what limits that forgetting.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Inverse parallel: in the Kural, firmly remembering and knowing the truth is what makes rebirth unnecessary.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In this path are very many tokens that what is is uncreated and indestructible; for it is complete, immovable, and without end.”
philosophy.explanation: Parmenides argues that true Being (‘what is’) never comes into being or passes away; birth and death belong only to mortal opinion.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘ulladhu’ is Parmenides’s ‘what is’: to grasp the ungenerated is to stand outside birth.
philosophy.source: Parmenides, Fragment 8 (DK B8; trans. John Burnet)

real_life_example.event_title: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry in Madurai
real_life_example.event: In 1896 the teenage student Venkataraman, later known as Ramana Maharshi, was overcome in his uncle's house in Madurai by a sudden fear of death. Lying still as if dead, he inquired into what it was that dies and concluded that his true self was not the body; Britannica describes this as the experience from which he derived his method of self-inquiry, vichara. About six weeks later he left home for the holy hill of Arunachala at Tiruvannamalai, where he lived until his death in 1950.
real_life_example.explanation: By his own account the fear of death never returned after that single inquiry, and the rest of his life and teaching grew from it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that once the mind has examined and firmly grasped That Which Is, there is no more need to think of birth, and Ramana's inquiry into the self, the root of his later teaching, is perhaps the closest documented illustration.

tamil:
பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை நீங்கச் சிறப்பென்னும்
செம்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு.
transliteration:
Pirappennum pedhaimai neengach sirappennum
Semporul kaanpadhu arivu.
meaning: True wisdom is seeing the perfect truth, the highest good, so that the foolishness that causes us to be born again and again is taken away.
elementary: Imagine being stuck on a merry-go-round that never stops because you forgot there’s an exit. The moment you notice the exit sign, you can step off. This kural says being born again and again is like forgetting the exit, and seeing what is truly real is the exit sign.
university: The couplet makes a bold equation: pirappu ennum pedhaimai, ‘the folly called birth’. Birth is not only caused by ignorance (as in 351); it is itself named a form of ignorance. Against it stands sirappu ennum semporul, ‘the perfect Truth called excellence’, which commentators read as the Supreme Being or the state of release (Mu. Varadarasanar glosses sirappu as mukti). Semporul (‘the fine, perfect substance’) is the same term used in 359 for the support of all things. Buddhism offers the closest structural parallel: in dependent origination, ignorance (avijja) is the first condition and rebirth (jati) the eleventh, so the fading of ignorance ends birth. Hindu parallels such as Gita 4.9 make knowledge of the divine the reason one ‘does not take birth again’, while John’s ‘the truth shall make you free’ expresses liberation through knowing within a linear rather than cyclical cosmology.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who knows the transcendental nature of My appearance and activities does not, upon leaving the body, take his birth again in this material world, but attains My eternal abode, O Arjuna.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that truly knowing the divine reality ends rebirth: at death such a knower goes to the eternal abode instead.
hinduism.tie_back: Just as the Kural says, seeing the supreme Truth (semporul) removes the ‘folly called birth’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that knowing the truth frees a person from bondage (in context, the bondage of sin).
christianity.tie_back: Same core claim as the Kural: seeing the Truth is what liberates.

islam.quote_or_event: “That is because Allāh is the True Reality, and that which they call upon other than Him is falsehood, and because Allāh is the Most High, the Grand.”
islam.explanation: One of God’s names is al-Haqq, ‘the Truth’ or ‘the True Reality’. Everything else people cling to as ultimate is, by comparison, falsehood.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘semporul’ (the perfect Truth) corresponds closely to al-Haqq as the one Reality to be recognized.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth.”
judaism.explanation: Through Jeremiah, God says that the only thing worth boasting of is not wisdom, strength or riches but understanding and knowing Him (da’at).
judaism.tie_back: Both texts set knowledge of the ultimate Truth above every other kind of knowing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ignorance is a requirement for choices. … Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth. … When ignorance fades away and ceases no residue left behind, choices cease. … When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.”
buddhism.explanation: Dependent origination traces rebirth back, link by link, to ignorance; when ignorance ends completely, rebirth and all its suffering end too.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim spelled out step by step: birth is rooted in ignorance, and removing ignorance removes birth.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Love and hatred are caused by Karman, and they say that Karman has its origin in delusion; Karman is the root of birth and death, and birth and death they call misery.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana traces birth and death to karma and karma to delusion, and then calls birth and death themselves misery.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar names 'the folly called birth'. The Jain verse also roots birth in delusion and treats birth as the very affliction that true insight removes.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 185)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One whom the Creator Lord unites with Himself, is not consigned to reincarnation.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Patti (acrostic) of Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak says that whoever the Creator unites with Himself is not born again.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that seeing the perfect Truth removes the folly called birth; Guru Nanak says that union with the Creator likewise ends rebirth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Aasaa (Patti), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
