greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In a Greek legend, King Midas captured the satyr Silenus and asked what is best for mankind; Silenus answered that it is best never to be born, and next best to die soon. Sophocles’ chorus in Oedipus at Colonus echoes this: not to be born is best of all.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tragic wisdom saw human birth itself as a misfortune.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s startling view of birth as something to be escaped, but offers no path of knowledge out of it.
greek_mythology.source: Sophocles, Oedipus at Colonus 1224–1227; Silenus legend

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plotinus urges the soul to withdraw from the world of images and ‘flee to the beloved Fatherland’, turning inward to behold the One, the source of all being, from which the soul came and to which it can return.
philosophy.explanation: For Plotinus, the soul’s descent into bodies is a kind of forgetting, and contemplative vision of the One reverses it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, embodiment is tied to ignorance, and seeing the supreme Reality is the way home.

real_life_example.event_title: Pasteur's swan-neck flasks refute spontaneous generation
real_life_example.event: From 1859 Louis Pasteur set out to settle whether living microbes could arise on their own from nonliving matter, a belief defended by the naturalist Felix Pouchet. Pasteur boiled broth in flasks whose long, curved necks let in air but trapped dust; the broth stayed clear, but when the neck was broken off it soon swarmed with microbes. In an 1862 paper he argued that the microbes came from germs in the air, not from spontaneous generation.
real_life_example.explanation: A careful look at what was really happening removed a long-standing false belief about how life is born and opened the way to germ theory.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls birth a folly that true seeing removes; Pasteur's experiments removed a folly about birth itself, the belief that life springs spontaneously from decay, by seeing the true cause.

tamil:
சார்புணர்ந்து சார்பு கெடஒழுகின் மற்றழித்துச்
சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய்.
transliteration:
Saarbunarndhu saarbu keda ozhukin matrazhiththuch
Saardharaa saardharu noi.
meaning: Whoever understands what truly supports all things, and lives so that all other attachments fall away, will never be touched by the sorrows that would otherwise cling to them.
elementary: If you’re holding a hundred balloons, the wind can drag you anywhere. But if you let go of them and hold on to one strong railing, you stay safe. This kural says: know what is truly worth holding on to, let the other things go, and troubles can’t grab hold of you.
university: The couplet is built on a remarkable pun: the root saar- (‘to lean on, cling to, attach’) appears four times: saarbu unarndhu (knowing the true support), saarbu keda (so that attachments perish), saardharaa (will not cling) and saardharu noi (the afflictions that would cling). Commentators read the first saarbu as the Supreme Truth (semporul), the support of all things, and the second as worldly attachment (pattru). The wordplay thus contrasts one legitimate ‘leaning’ with many illegitimate ones. The logic, that attachment is the channel through which suffering ‘attaches’, is shared with Buddhist teaching on upadana (grasping) and with the Gita’s call to cut the world-tree ‘with the weapon of detachment’ while taking refuge in its root. Islam’s divine name as-Samad, the One on whom all depend, offers an especially close lexical parallel to the first saarbu.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But with determination one must cut down this tree with the weapon of detachment. So doing, one must seek that place from which, having once gone, one never returns, and there surrender to that Supreme Personality of Godhead from whom everything has begun and in whom everything is abiding since time immemorial.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna pictures worldly existence as a deep-rooted tree to be cut with detachment, while the seeker takes refuge in the Supreme in whom everything rests.
hinduism.tie_back: The same double movement as the Kural: cut false attachments (saarbu keda) and rest in the true Support of all (saarbu unarndhu).

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal … For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns against clinging to perishable possessions and tells his hearers to anchor their hearts in heaven instead.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, what we cling to decides whether loss and sorrow can reach us.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allāh, the Eternal Refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Arabic as-Samad describes God as the One on whom all things depend and to whom everyone turns, while He depends on nothing.
islam.tie_back: As-Samad is a close equivalent of the Kural’s first ‘saarbu’, the true Support of all things, which the wise must recognize.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. … Happy is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the LORD his God.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist warns against leaning on mortal powers that fail, and blesses the one whose support is God alone.
judaism.tie_back: Same contrast as the Kural: false supports that fail versus the one true Support.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From attachment springs grief, from attachment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from attachment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief and fear to attachment: remove the attachment and they have nothing to hold on to.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s logic: when attachment perishes, the afflictions that would cling can no longer cling.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Thus the objects of the senses and of the mind cause pain to passionate men, but they never in the least cause any pain to the dispassionate.”
jainism.explanation: After surveying all six sense-fields, the sermon concludes that pain can attach only where passion gives it something to hold. The dispassionate person offers no foothold.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's wordplay on saar- (clinging) says that afflictions which would cling will not cling to one whose attachments have perished. The Jain verse states the same: objects that hurt the passionate cannot touch the dispassionate.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.100 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 190)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Meditate on the One, O my mind, who is the Support of all.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan tells the mind to meditate on the One God, the support of all beings.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that whoever understands the true Support of all things will be free of the sorrows that cling; Guru Arjan names that Support and asks the mind to rest on it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 51, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe, Odysseus has his crew plug their ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast so that he can hear the Sirens’ song without being pulled to destruction by it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Knowing in advance what the lure really is, Odysseus holds fast to something firm and passes by the danger unharmed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, knowledge plus refusal to be seized by attraction keeps ruin from taking hold.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus opens his Handbook by dividing everything into what is up to us (our judgments, desires and aversions) and what is not (body, property, reputation), teaching that suffering comes from attaching ourselves to what is not ours.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoics, clearly knowing what one’s good actually depends on, and detaching from everything else, makes a person unshakable.
philosophy.tie_back: Parallel to the Kural: know the true support, drop false dependencies, and misfortune can no longer grip you.

real_life_example.event_title: Kamo no Chomei writes An Account of My Hut
real_life_example.event: Kamo no Chomei, a poet from a family of Shinto shrine officials, became a Buddhist monk at about fifty and withdrew from the capital, living first at Ohara and then in a tiny hut he built in the hills of Hino, southeast of Kyoto. In 1212 he wrote the Hojoki, An Account of My Hut, named for the hut's size of ten feet square. The work first describes the fires, whirlwind, famine and earthquake that had struck Kyoto in his lifetime, then contrasts them with the quiet of his simple life in the hills.
real_life_example.explanation: Chomei set the instability of worldly things beside the peace he found once he had let go of house, rank and possessions, and the Hojoki became a classic of Japanese literature on that theme.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that one who knows the true support and lets lesser attachments fall away is no longer gripped by sorrows, and Chomei's record of disasters followed by contentment in a ten-foot hut illustrates that loosening of attachment.

tamil:
காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் இவ்மூன்றன்
நாமம் கெடக்கெடும் நோய்.
transliteration:
Kaamam vekuli mayakkam ivmoondran
Naamam kedakkedum noi.
meaning: When desire, anger and confusion are destroyed so completely that even their names are gone, the suffering they cause is destroyed too.
elementary: Weeds keep coming back if you only snip off the tops. You have to pull them out by the roots so nothing is left. This kural says greed, anger and confusion are like three weeds: pull them out so completely that even their names are forgotten, and the trouble they cause disappears.
university: The chapter closes by naming a triad: kaamam, vekuli, mayakkam (desire, anger, delusion). Its correspondence with the Buddhist ‘three roots’ or ‘three poisons’ (raga, dosa, moha: greed, hatred, delusion) is nearly exact, and it overlaps substantially with the Gita’s ‘three gates of hell’ (lust, anger, greed). Valluvar’s hyperbole, that the very names must perish (naamam keda), insists on eradication rather than suppression: not even the latent tendency or memory may remain. Because the chapter began with delusion (marul) as the cause of birth, ending with mayakkam as the third root closes the argument in a ring. True knowledge removes the delusion that fuels desire and anger, and with all three gone, the ‘disease’ (noi) of suffering and rebirth ends.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell — lust, anger, and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names three inner forces as the doorways to self-destruction and tells every sensible person to abandon them.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-parallel triad to the Kural’s kaamam–vekuli–mayakkam, with the same call to be rid of them completely.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.”
christianity.explanation: John names a threefold root of worldly corruption, and says none of it comes from God.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, a triad of inner drives is identified as the source of spiritual sickness to be overcome.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an promises Paradise to the one who holds back the lower self (nafs) from its passions.
islam.tie_back: Both texts make victory over passion the condition for escaping suffering.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah names three inner vices that destroy a person’s life in this world and the next.
judaism.tie_back: A striking triad parallel: three passions that ruin a person, which the Kural says must be destroyed down to their names.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Reverend, the ending of greed, hate, and delusion is called extinguishment.”
buddhism.explanation: Asked what Nibbana (extinguishment) is, Sariputta defines it simply as the ending of the three roots: greed, hate and delusion.
buddhism.tie_back: An almost exact match: the Kural’s kaamam–vekuli–mayakkam are the Buddhist raga–dosa–moha, and their destruction is liberation.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I shall explain in due order the means which must be adopted by him who wants to thoroughly uproot love, hatred, and delusion.” … “He will get rid of all misery which always afflicts mankind; recovered from the long illness, as it were, and glorious, he becomes infinitely happy, and obtains the (final) aim.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's sermon sets out to uproot completely the triad of rāga, dveṣa and moha (love, hatred and delusion). It ends with the liberated sage cured of all misery 'as from a long illness'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's triad of desire, anger and delusion, destroyed so completely that even their names are gone, and the suffering (noi, 'disease') ending with it, corresponds almost term for term to the Jain uprooting of love, hatred and delusion and the cure of the 'long illness'.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.9 and 32.110 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, pp. 185, 192)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I have brought the ten sensory organs under my control, and erased every trace of the five thieves.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Namdev says he has mastered the senses and wiped out the five thieves (kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankar); the Gurmukhi says even their name (naavau) is erased.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that when desire, anger and delusion are destroyed so completely that even their names are gone, suffering ends; Namdev claims to have erased the very name of the passions.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 693, Raag Dhanaasree, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Heracles fought the Lernaean Hydra, each head he cut off grew back as two, until his companion Iolaus burned the stumps so that none could regrow; the immortal head was buried under a heavy rock.
greek_mythology.explanation: The monster could only be defeated by destroying it at the root so nothing could grow back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘even the names must perish’, cutting off passions superficially fails; they must be destroyed at the source.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that a passion ceases to be a passion as soon as we form a clear and distinct idea of it, and that the more we understand our emotions, the less we are ruled by them.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, true understanding does not merely restrain destructive emotions; it dissolves them as passions.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the chapter’s whole logic: knowledge of the truth is what destroys desire, anger and confusion at the root.

real_life_example.event_title: The World Health Assembly declares smallpox eradicated
real_life_example.event: After a global vaccination and case-finding campaign led by the World Health Organization from 1967, the world's last naturally occurring case of smallpox was found in Somalia in October 1977. Following two further years of searching for cases, a global commission certified eradication in December 1979. On 8 May 1980 the World Health Assembly, in resolution WHA33.3, formally declared that the world was free of smallpox.
real_life_example.explanation: Smallpox is the only human disease ever eradicated, which was possible only because the campaign aimed at complete removal of the disease rather than control.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the suffering caused by desire, anger and delusion ends only when they are destroyed so completely that even their names are gone, and smallpox ended only when it was rooted out everywhere rather than merely reduced.

tamil:
அவாஎன்ப எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து.
transliteration:
Avaa enba ellaa uyirkkum egnaandrum
Thavaaap pirappeenum viththu.
meaning: People say that desire is the seed that, for every living being and at all times, never fails to cause one birth after another.
elementary: A seed falls into the ground and grows into a plant, and that plant drops more seeds that grow again and again. Valluvar says wanting things is like that seed: as long as we keep wanting, we keep getting planted into new lives, over and over.
university: The chapter that closes the ascetic section (Thuravaraviyal) opens by naming avaa (craving) as the vittu, the seed, of an unbroken chain of births (thavaap pirappu). The agricultural metaphor is exact: a seed holds the whole future plant, and craving holds the whole future of embodied existence, so destroying the seed leaves the cycle nothing to grow from. The word “enba” (“they say”) shows Valluvar reporting a consensus of the wise rather than inventing a doctrine, and the idea is indeed shared across Indian soteriologies: the Upanishadic teaching that desire determines rebirth, the Buddhist second noble truth that craving leads to renewed existence, and the Jain account of passions binding karma. Placed right after “Knowledge of Truth” (Meyyunarthal) and just before “Destiny” (Oozh), the chapter that ends Book 1, this chapter makes the uprooting of desire the practical summit of the renunciant’s path.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who forms desires in his mind, is born again through his desires here and there. But to him whose desires are fulfilled and who is conscious of the true Self (within himself) all desires vanish, even here on earth.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that it is desire itself that pulls a person back into birth again and again, and that desire falls away only when the true Self is known.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts name desire as the thing that keeps producing new births. The verse just before it in the Mundaka even calls this the “seed” that the wise go beyond.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James describes desire as something that conceives and gives birth: lust gives birth to sin, and sin grows up into death.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘seed’, James treats desire as the thing everything else grows from. Here it produces sin and death, not rebirth.

islam.quote_or_event: “And I do not acquit myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the lower self (nafs) as constantly urging a person toward wrongdoing unless God’s mercy restrains it.
islam.tie_back: Both locate the root of trouble inside a person’s own urges. Islam sees the result as sin, not a cycle of rebirth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah names three forms of craving that drive a person out of a good life in this world and out of the world to come.
judaism.tie_back: Both treat desire as the root of a person’s ruin. The Kural says desire keeps producing births, while the Mishnah says it drives a person out of the world.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:21 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The origin of suffering, as a noble truth, is this: It is the craving that produces renewal of being accompanied by enjoyment and lust, and enjoying this and that; in other words, craving for sensual desires, craving for being, craving for non-being.”
buddhism.explanation: In his first sermon, the Buddha teaches that craving (tanha) is what produces renewed existence, which is rebirth.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the same statement as the Kural: craving is the seed that keeps producing new births.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (trans. Ñanamoli Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the crane is produced from an egg, and the egg is produced from a crane, so they call desire the origin of delusion, and delusion the origin of desire. Love and hatred are caused by Karman, and they say that Karman has its origin in delusion; Karman is the root of birth and death, and birth and death they call misery.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana sets out a chain in which desire (Jacobi notes the original word is tṛṣṇā, craving) and delusion breed each other, delusion binds karmic matter to the soul, and that karma is the root of repeated birth and death.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls desire the seed that unfailingly yields birth after birth for every being, and the Jain text traces the same line from craving through karma to the 'root of birth and death'.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.6–7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Some are happy, and some are sad. Caught in the desires of the mind, they perish.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says that people, whether happy or sad, are destroyed by being caught in the desires and attachments of the mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls desire the seed that unfailingly produces birth after birth; Guru Nanak says desire is what destroys people, though he does not here call it the seed of rebirth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 152, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Eros (Love), fairest among the deathless gods, who unnerves the limbs and overcomes the mind and wise counsels of all gods and all men within them.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod’s creation story, Eros (Desire) is one of the very first powers to exist, and it drives all the later pairings and births of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In both texts desire comes first and generations grow out of it. Hesiod honors that power, while Valluvar wants it removed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Schopenhauer argues that the world is driven by a blind “will-to-live”, a restless striving. All willing springs from lack and so from suffering. Each satisfied wish only makes room for new ones, and the only real deliverance is for the will to deny itself.
philosophy.explanation: For Schopenhauer, endless wanting is the engine that keeps life and suffering going. Peace comes only when wanting itself is given up.
philosophy.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that desire is the seed of ceaseless existence. Schopenhauer himself pointed to Indian thought as a parallel.
philosophy.source: Arthur Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, §§ 56-57, 68 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: The Klondike Gold Rush
real_life_example.place: Klondike region and Dawson City, Yukon, Canada
real_life_example.event: Gold was found on Bonanza Creek, a tributary of the Klondike River, in August 1896, and when news reached the United States in July 1897 it set off a stampede. More than 100,000 people set out for the Klondike, but only some 30,000 to 40,000 actually reached Dawson City, many after brutal journeys over the Chilkoot and White passes. According to the US National Park Service, only a few of those who arrived obtained the wealth they had dreamed of along the way.
real_life_example.explanation: A single report of riches drew tens of thousands into hardship, and the hope of gain kept pulling new waves of people north long after the best claims had been taken.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls desire the seed that unfailingly produces birth after birth, and the gold rush shows on a human scale how one seed of craving keeps generating new journeys, new hardships and new disappointments.

tamil:
வேண்டுங்கால் வேண்டும் பிறவாமை மற்றது
வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்.
transliteration:
Vendungaal vendum piravaamai matradhu
Vendaamai venda varum.
meaning: If you must want something, want to be free from being born again. That freedom comes only when you want to be free of wanting.
elementary: Imagine you get just one wish. The smartest wish would be: “I wish I didn’t need any more wishes.” Valluvar says that is the one wish worth making, because it is the wish that sets you free.
university: The couplet repeats the verb vendu (“to want”) four times: vendungaal vendum … vendaamai venda. The verbal knot mirrors the paradox it describes. Valluvar admits that a person cannot simply switch off wanting, so he turns the power of desire against itself and makes piravaamai (non-birth, liberation) its one proper object. Parimelazhagar reads vendaamai as the settled state of desirelessness, so the means (wanting not to want) and the goal (not being born again) are joined. The same ‘desire for desirelessness’ paradox appears in the Buddhist distinction between wholesome aspiration (chanda) and craving (tanha), and in the Gita’s call to act without craving the fruits of action.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “No man can be made happy by wealth. Shall we possess wealth, when we see thee? Shall we live, as long as thou rulest? Only that boon (which I have chosen) is to be chosen by me.”
hinduism.explanation: Death offers the boy Nachiketas wealth, long life, kingdoms and pleasures. He refuses them all and insists on the one thing worth wanting: knowledge of what lies beyond death.
hinduism.tie_back: Nachiketas acts out the Kural’s advice. If you must want something, want the one thing that frees you from death and birth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to point their desires toward heavenly things rather than earthly ones.
christianity.tie_back: Both redirect desire instead of simply crushing it: if you must want, want the highest thing.

islam.quote_or_event: “But you prefer the worldly life, While the Hereafter is better and more enduring.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an criticizes people for chasing the passing world instead of the lasting life to come.
islam.tie_back: Both urge that desire be spent only on what is final and lasting, not on what passes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says God is the only thing he truly desires, in heaven or on earth.
judaism.tie_back: Both narrow all wanting down to a single highest object. For the psalmist that object is God, and for Valluvar it is freedom from birth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Beset by craving, people run about like an entrapped hare. Therefore, one who yearns to be passion-free should destroy his own craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada speaks of a person who yearns to be free of passion and who reaches that goal by destroying craving.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the same paradox: a yearning for passionlessness is the one legitimate desire, and it works by ending desire.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Sir, what does the soul obtain by the longing for liberation? By the longing for liberation the soul obtains an intense desire of the Law; by an intense desire of the Law he quickly arrives at an (increased) longing for liberation; he destroys anger, pride, deceit, and greed, which reproduce themselves infinitely.”
jainism.explanation: Saṃvega, the longing for liberation, is the first item in Mahāvīra's lecture on exertion in righteousness. It is the one desire Jainism encourages, because it feeds on itself and destroys the passions, greed included, that otherwise keep reproducing themselves.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that if one must desire, one should desire freedom from birth, which comes through wanting to be free of wanting. Saṃvega is exactly that kind of redirected desire: a longing that wears away greed and leads toward the end of rebirth.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the midst of hope, the Guru teaches us to live above hope and desire.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says the Guru teaches a person to live among hopes and wants while remaining free of them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural turns desire against itself, asking us to desire freedom from desire; Guru Nanak's niraas, being free of hope in the midst of hope, is the same paradox lived out.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 154, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As a young man, Heracles meets two women at a crossroads. Vice promises him an easy road of every pleasure. Virtue promises hard work that leads to true and lasting good, and Heracles chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable shows a hero turning down a life of gratified desires in favor of one higher goal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it is about choosing what to want. The wise choice gives up the many pleasures for the one lasting good.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus’ ‘Choice of Heracles’, in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34 (paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But, for the present, totally suppress desire: for, if you desire any of the things which are not in your own control, you must necessarily be disappointed; and of those which are, and which it would be laudable to desire, nothing is yet in your possession.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the beginner to set desire aside entirely. Wanting external things brings disappointment, and he is not yet able to want the right things properly.
philosophy.tie_back: Both treat suspending desire as the doorway to freedom. The only thing worth pursuing is the state that no longer craves.

real_life_example.event_title: Tolstoy leaves Yasnaya Polyana
real_life_example.place: Yasnaya Polyana and Astapovo, Russian Empire (now Russia)
real_life_example.event: In his later decades Leo Tolstoy preached a life of simplicity and renunciation, while still living on his family estate at Yasnaya Polyana. On the night of 27-28 October 1910 (Old Style), aged 82, he secretly left the estate with his doctor, leaving a letter saying he was going away for good. He fell ill on the train and died of pneumonia at the small railway station of Astapovo on 7 November 1910 (20 November in the modern calendar).
real_life_example.explanation: At the end of his life Tolstoy chose to abandon home and comfort to live out the detachment he had long written about, even though he did not live to carry it through.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that if one must desire anything it should be freedom itself, the desire to be free of desire, and Tolstoy's final flight was the act of a man whose one remaining wish was to leave his worldly life behind.

tamil:
வேண்டாமை அன்ன விழுச்செல்வம் ஈண்டில்லை
ஆண்டும் அஃதொப்பது இல்.
transliteration:
Vendaamai anna vizhuchchelvam eendillai
Aandum aqdhoppadhu il.
meaning: There is no treasure in this world as precious as being free from desire. Even in the next world, nothing is equal to it.
elementary: A kid with a giant pile of toys who always wants more still feels poor. A kid who is happy with what they have feels rich. Valluvar says not wanting is the biggest treasure there is, bigger than anything here or even in heaven.
university: Vizhuchchelvam (“choicest wealth”) turns the idea of wealth inside out: a chapter on renunciation borrows the language of ownership to describe the absence of wanting. The pair eendu (“here”) and aandu (“there”) covers both this world and the heavenly worlds that ritual religion promised as rewards. Valluvar therefore ranks desirelessness above celestial pleasures, in line with the Upanishadic and Buddhist view that heaven is only a finer object of desire. The paradox that wanting less makes one richer shows up almost word for word in Seneca, in the Hadith on ‘richness of the soul’ and in Ben Zoma’s “Who is rich?”, which makes this one of the most cross-culturally shared couplets in the chapter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Pārtha, when a man gives up all varieties of desire for sense gratification, which arise from mental concoction, and when his mind, thus purified, finds satisfaction in the self alone, then he is said to be in pure transcendental consciousness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the person of steady wisdom as one who has dropped all desires and is fully content within himself.
hinduism.tie_back: Both say that being content without desire is the real fullness. It needs nothing outside itself, which is the very definition of wealth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But godliness with contentment is great gain.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy that the real profit in life is godliness joined with contentment, not riches.
christianity.tie_back: Both reverse the usual idea of gain. Not wanting more is itself the greatest wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth is not in having many possessions, but rather (true) wealth is feeling sufficiency in the soul.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that real richness is inner sufficiency (ghina al-nafs), not a large amount of property.
islam.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s exact claim. The greatest wealth is a soul that no longer craves.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma teaches that the truly rich person is the one who is content with what he has.
judaism.tie_back: Both redefine riches as freedom from wanting more.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth. A trustworthy person is the best kinsman, Nibbana the highest bliss.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names contentment as the greatest wealth a person can have.
buddhism.tie_back: This is a direct parallel: the absence of craving is the supreme treasure.

jainism.quote_or_event: “There is much happiness for the sage, for the houseless monk, who is free from all ties, and knows himself to be single and unconnected (with the rest of the world).” … “Here (on earth) you are the highest man, Reverend sir, and hereafter you will be the highest; exempt from all blemishes you will reach Perfection, a higher state than which there is none in this world.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami renounces Mithilā. When Indra, disguised as a Brāhmaṇa, urges him to fill his treasury with gold, silver and jewels, he refuses, saying that freedom from ties is true happiness. Indra then reveals himself and declares Nami the highest of men both here and hereafter.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls freedom from desire a treasure without equal 'here' and 'there'. Nami turns down an actual treasury for that freedom and is praised as supreme in this world and the next.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.16 and 9.58 (context 9.46–49) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without contentment, no one is satisfied. Like the objects in a dream, all his efforts are in vain. Through the love of the Naam, all peace is obtained.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Guru Arjan says that without contentment nothing satisfies, and that every kind of peace is found in love of the Name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls freedom from desire the choicest wealth in this world and the next; Guru Arjan says that without contentment no possession satisfies and that all peace comes from the Name.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor old couple, live contentedly in a humble cottage and gladly share what little they have with disguised gods. Their hut is turned into a temple, and they ask only to serve there and to die together.
greek_mythology.explanation: The couple’s happiness comes from contentment, not from possessions. Even when the gods reward them, they ask for almost nothing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They live out the Kural’s idea that not wanting is the richest state. They are poor in goods but lack nothing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that poverty is measured by craving, not by possessions.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the mirror image of the Kural: if craving is poverty, then being free of craving is the greatest wealth.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 2.6 (trans. R. M. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Diocletian gives up the throne and retires to Split
real_life_example.place: Nicomedia (now Izmit, Turkey) and Split, Croatia (Roman Empire)
real_life_example.event: On 1 May 305 the Roman emperor Diocletian, who had ruled for more than twenty years, voluntarily abdicated, an almost unheard-of step for a Roman emperor. He retired to the great palace he had built on the Adriatic coast at what is now Split, in Croatia. Apart from a brief appearance at an imperial conference at Carnuntum in 308, he stayed in his palace for the rest of his life while rivals fought over the empire.
real_life_example.explanation: Diocletian walked away from supreme power at a time when most emperors kept it until violent death, and did not take it back while the empire's rulers fought for it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks freedom from wanting above any treasure of this world, and Diocletian's choice of a quiet palace over the throne of the Roman world shows the highest worldly prize being let go.

tamil:
தூஉய்மை என்பது அவாவின்மை மற்றது
வாஅய்மை வேண்ட வரும்.
transliteration:
Thoouymai enbadhu avaavinmai matradhu
Vaaaimai venda varum.
meaning: Being pure means nothing other than being free from desire, and that freedom comes from longing for the truth.
elementary: A glass of water looks clear when nothing is stirring it up. Your heart is “clean” when wanting isn’t stirring it. The way to keep it calm is to love what is true more than what is shiny.
university: Valluvar defines thooymai (purity) psychologically rather than ritually, not by baths, diet or caste observances but as avaavinmai, the absence of craving. The second line adds a cause: freedom from craving arises from desiring vaaymai. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss vaaymai as meipporul, ultimate Reality, while Karunanidhi reads it as truthfulness. Either way the chapter keeps its strategy of redirecting desire, letting one longing, for truth, push out all lesser ones. The lengthened forms thoouymai and vaaaymai (alapedai, a metrical lengthening) bind the two key terms by sound as well as sense.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror is covered by dust, or as the embryo is covered by the womb, the living entity is similarly covered by different degrees of this lust.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares desire to smoke over a fire or dust on a mirror, something that clouds the soul’s natural clarity.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat purity as what remains when desire is removed. Take away the dust of craving and the mirror is clean.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently:”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells believers that their souls have been purified by obeying the truth.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s causal chain very closely: purity comes by way of truth.

islam.quote_or_event: “He has succeeded who purifies it, And he has failed who instills it [with corruption].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says success belongs to the one who purifies the soul (tazkiyat al-nafs) of its base inclinations.
islam.tie_back: Both make purity an inner cleansing of the self, not an outward ritual.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm defines the pure person as one who has not set his soul on empty things and has not sworn falsely.
judaism.tie_back: Both tie purity to not craving empty things and to truthfulness, which are the two halves of the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘All conditioned things are impermanent’ — when one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. This is the path to purification.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that seeing the truth about impermanence makes a person turn away from craving, and that this is purification.
buddhism.tie_back: This has the same logic as the Kural: seeing truth leads to the end of craving, and that is purity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Purity–śauca–is freedom from greed (lobha).”
jainism.explanation: Among the ten supreme virtues (daśa-dharma) in Tattvārtha Sūtra 9.6, Pūjyapāda's classic commentary defines purity not as ritual cleanness but simply as the absence of greed. Supreme truthfulness (uttama satya) is listed as a companion virtue in the same sūtra.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar defines purity as freedom from desire rather than as ritual washing. The Jain commentary gives almost the same definition, making śauca identical with freedom from lobha (greed).
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 9.6, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They are not called pure, who sit down after merely washing their bodies. Only they are pure, O Nanak, within whose minds the Lord abides.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak rejects ritual bathing as the test of purity and says only those in whose minds God dwells are pure.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines purity as freedom from desire rather than bathing, diet or caste rule; Guru Nanak likewise moves purity from the washed body to the inner mind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 472, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Socrates’ myth of the winged soul, souls follow the gods to gaze on true Being in the ‘plain of truth’, and their wings are nourished by it. Souls weighed down by base appetite lose their wings and fall.
greek_mythology.explanation: The soul stays pure and winged by feeding on truth, and it falls when appetite drags it down.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links a pure soul to longing for truth and a fallen soul to craving.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedo, Socrates describes philosophy as a “purification” (katharsis). The lover of wisdom separates the soul from bodily pleasures and desires, which ‘nail’ the soul to the body, so that it can grasp truth itself.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, purity means freedom from bodily cravings, and it comes through the love of wisdom and truth.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s formula: purity is freedom from desire, and it is reached by desiring truth.

real_life_example.event_title: Ludwig Wittgenstein gives away his inherited fortune
real_life_example.event: Ludwig Wittgenstein, son of one of the richest industrial families in Austria-Hungary, inherited a fortune when his father died in 1913. After serving in the First World War, during which he completed the work later published as the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, he gave away his share of the family fortune. He then trained as a teacher and worked in village schools in Lower Austria in the early 1920s, living very simply.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the great philosophers of the twentieth century chose plain living over wealth as he devoted himself to questions of truth and meaning.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says purity is freedom from desire, and that this freedom comes from longing for truth; Wittgenstein's giving up of riches alongside his single-minded search for clarity offers a modern parallel.

tamil:
அற்றவர் என்பார் அவாஅற்றார் மற்றையார்
அற்றாக அற்றது இலர்.
transliteration:
Atravar enbaar avaaatraar matraiyaar
Atraaga atradhu ilar.
meaning: Only people who have cut off desire truly deserve to be called people who have given up the world. Others, whatever they have given up, are not fully free like them.
elementary: Throwing your candy away doesn’t really count if you keep thinking about candy all day. Valluvar says the real “giver-upper” is the person who stopped wanting, not just the person who stopped having.
university: The couplet plays on atravar (“those who are cut off”, the renunciants) and avaa atraar (“those cut off from desire”), and ends by saying that others are not free in that full sense (atraaga atradhu ilar). Valluvar draws a sharp line between outward renunciation (robes, poverty, leaving home, the themes of the earlier chapter Thuravu) and inward renunciation. This extends his critique of the false ascetic in Chapter 28 (Koodaavozhukkam, “Imposture”). For Valluvar, freedom is measured by what one no longer wants, not by what one no longer owns.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who has given up all desires for sense gratification, who lives free from desires, who has given up all sense of proprietorship and is devoid of false ego – he alone can attain real peace.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that only the one who has given up desires inwardly, not just outwardly, reaches real peace.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s “he alone” matches the Kural’s claim that only the desire-free are truly renunciants.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.”
christianity.explanation: Paul defines true belonging to Christ as having put to death the desires themselves, not just outward behavior.
christianity.tie_back: Both locate true renunciation in the death of inner desire.

islam.quote_or_event: “Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Ibn ‘Umar to hold the world loosely, like a traveler passing through who doesn’t cling to anything.
islam.tie_back: Both describe detachment as an inner stance toward the world. The hadith does not spell out the Kural’s contrast between inner and outer renunciation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma teaches that real strength is mastering one’s own desires (the yetzer), not conquering others.
judaism.tie_back: Both redefine an honored title (the ‘mighty’, the ‘renunciant’) so that it belongs to whoever has mastered inner desire.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is one who, turning away from desire (for household life) takes to the life of the forest (i.e., of a monk). But after being freed from the household, he runs back to it. Behold that man! Though freed, he runs back to that very bondage!”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a man who outwardly renounces home life but, with his craving still intact, runs straight back to it.
buddhism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s point: outward renunciation without cutting off craving is not true freedom.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If an ordained monk, through carelessness, does not strictly keep the great vows, if he does not restrain himself, but desires pleasure, then his fetters will not be completely cut off.”
jainism.explanation: The ascetic in the Twentieth Lecture warns that taking orders is not enough. A monk who keeps the outward form but still desires pleasure remains bound, and the next verses call him 'empty like a clenched fist'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says only those who have cut off desire are truly renunciants, and that others are not fully 'cut free'. The Jain verse says the same: a monk who still desires pleasure does not have his fetters completely cut off.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When you abandon hope and desire, then you become a true Sannyaasi.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak redefines the renunciant: the true sannyasi is not one who wears the robe but one who has given up hope and desire.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says only those who have cut off desire deserve to be called true renunciants, whatever else others have given up; Guru Nanak says exactly this.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After washing away his golden touch, King Midas comes to hate riches and goes to live in the woods and fields as a worshipper of Pan. But his foolish mind stays unchanged, and he soon earns a pair of ass’s ears for judging Pan’s music above Apollo’s.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas outwardly gives up wealth, but he has not been inwardly transformed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He loosely illustrates the Kural’s warning that outward renunciation is not the same as true inner freedom.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Whoever, then, would be free, let him wish nothing, let him decline nothing, which depends on others else he must necessarily be a slave.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus defines freedom as wanting nothing that depends on things outside oneself. Anyone who still wants such things remains a slave.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a direct parallel. Only the one who has cut off desire is truly free, and everyone else is still bound.

real_life_example.event_title: Queen Christina abdicates but seeks other crowns
real_life_example.event: Queen Christina of Sweden abdicated on 6 June 1654, the day her cousin Charles X Gustav was crowned, and left Sweden at once; she had secretly become a Roman Catholic and settled in Rome. Within a few years she was negotiating with Cardinal Mazarin of France in a scheme to make herself queen of Naples, which collapsed in 1657. About ten years later, with the support of Pope Clement IX, she tried without success to be chosen for the throne of Poland.
real_life_example.explanation: Christina gave up a throne in outward form, yet her later schemes show that the wish to reign had not left her.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says only those who have cut off desire are truly renunciants, and that others, whatever they have given up, are not free in the same way, which is precisely the contrast between Christina's abdication and her later pursuit of crowns.

tamil:
அஞ்சுவ தோரும் அறனே ஒருவனை
வஞ்சிப்ப தோரும் அவா.
transliteration:
Anjuva dhoorum arane oruvanai
Vanjippa dhoorum avaa.
meaning: Being afraid of desire is itself goodness, because it is desire that tricks a person.
elementary: Some joke toys look like candy but have a spring inside that jumps out at you, so you learn to be careful of them. Valluvar says wanting things is a trick like that. It fools us, so being careful of it is part of being good.
university: The couplet frames the ethical life as vigilance: aran (virtue) here simply is the fearing (anjuvadhu) of avaa, because avaa is what vanjippadhu, what cheats and betrays a person. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan add that desire waits for a moment of weakness (sorvu) to strike, much as a thief waits for the watchman to nod off. The repeated expletive oorum gives the line a proverbial, almost incantatory rhythm. This picture of desire as a cunning inner enemy parallels the Gita’s portrait of kama as an “all-devouring” foe and the biblical image of sin crouching at the door.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names desire (kama) as the great enemy that drives people into wrongdoing even against their will.
hinduism.tie_back: Both portray desire as an inner enemy to be feared and guarded against.

christianity.quote_or_event: “That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts;”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes lusts as “deceitful”: they promise good but corrupt the person who follows them.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s key claim that desire is the thing that deceives.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the one who, out of fear of God, holds the soul back from its desires (hawa).
islam.tie_back: Both join fear and the restraint of desire as the heart of righteousness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.”
judaism.explanation: God warns Cain that sin crouches at the door like a predator waiting for its chance, and that he must master it.
judaism.tie_back: Both picture a lurking inner force waiting to ambush a person, and both urge vigilance against it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are lust-infatuated fall back into the swirling current (of samsara) like a spider on its self-spun web. This, too, the wise cut off. Without any longing, they abandon all suffering and renounce the world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares people trapped by lust to a spider caught in the web it spun itself.
buddhism.tie_back: Both show desire as a self-made trap that fools its victim, which is why the wise watch out for it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The kimpāka fruit, a recurring Jain image, tastes and looks sweet but is poison. Desire works the same way: it attracts at first and destroys afterwards, so the monk must stay on guard against it.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that fearing desire is itself virtue because desire deceives and ruins a person. The kimpāka fruit is a picture of that deception, sweet on the tongue and deadly once swallowed.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Maya is a serpent, clinging to the world. Whoever serves her, she ultimately devours.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das calls Maya, the lure of worldly desire, a serpent wrapped around the world that in the end devours those who serve it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that to fear desire is itself virtue because desire deceives and ruins; Guru Amar Das gives that fear its reason, a serpent that destroys its own servants.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 510, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe that the Sirens’ sweet song lures sailors to their death, Odysseus stops his crew’s ears with wax and has himself tied to the mast. When he begs to be set free, his men only tie him tighter.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus knows the song of desire will fool him, so he fears it wisely and guards himself ahead of time.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural in story form: fear desire, because it deceives even the wise.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Human infirmity in moderating and checking the emotions I name bondage: for, when a man is a prey to his emotions, he is not his own master, but lies at the mercy of fortune: so much so, that he is often compelled, while seeing that which is better for him, to follow that which is worse.”
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza calls the power of passions over us “bondage”. They mislead us into following the worse even when we can see the better.
philosophy.tie_back: Both describe desire as something that tricks a person against their own good, which is why it must be guarded against.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Preface (trans. R. H. M. Elwes)

real_life_example.event_title: John Wesley holds his spending fixed as his income rises
real_life_example.event: As a young fellow at Oxford, John Wesley found he could live on about 28 pounds a year, and as his income rose over the following years from 30 to about 120 pounds, he kept his own expenses at that same level and gave the rest away. In his sermon The Use of Money he urged Methodists to gain all they could, save all they could and give all they could, and he warned them repeatedly about the danger of riches.
real_life_example.explanation: Wesley treated rising income not as a chance to live better but as a danger to be guarded against, and built a rule into his life to keep wanting from growing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that standing in fear of desire is itself virtue, because desire deceives, and Wesley's fixed allowance was a deliberate guard against the way more money tends to create more wants.

tamil:
அவாவினை ஆற்ற அறுப்பின் தவாவினை
தான்வேண்டு மாற்றான் வரும்.
transliteration:
Avaavinai aatra aruppin thavaavinai
Thaan vendum aatraan varum.
meaning: If a person cuts off desire completely, the good deeds that lead to a life free from death will come to them just as they wish.
elementary: When you stop grabbing at every toy in the store, your hands are finally free to hold what really matters. Valluvar says that when you drop all your wants, good deeds that last forever come to you easily.
university: Aatra aruppin, “if one cuts utterly”, insists on total rather than partial removal and echoes the chapter title’s aruththal (“cutting”). Thavaa vinai, “unfailing” or “imperishable action”, is glossed by commentators as the deeds that bring deathlessness, that is, liberation. The promise that these deeds arrive thaan vendum aatraan (“in the way he wishes”) holds a quiet irony: the person who has stopped wanting finally gets what he wants. The same paradox, that giving up self-will lines the will up with the good, appears in Stoic acceptance of fate, in the rabbinic “do His will as though it were your will”, and in the Katha Upanishad’s promise that the desireless mortal becomes immortal.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When all desires that dwell in his heart cease, then the mortal becomes immortal, and obtains Brahman.”
hinduism.explanation: Death teaches Nachiketas that the complete ending of all desires is what makes a mortal immortal.
hinduism.tie_back: Both promise that cutting off desire completely yields what does not perish.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad 2.3.14 (numbered II.6.14 in trans. Max Müller, SBE 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.”
christianity.explanation: John contrasts the passing world and its desires with the one who does God’s will and so lasts forever.
christianity.tie_back: In both, leaving desire behind leads to deeds and a life that endure forever.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one’s] hope.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an sets the fleeting objects of worldly desire against “the enduring good deeds” (al-baqiyat al-salihat).
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an’s “enduring good deeds” closely echo the Kural’s thavaa vinai, the deeds that do not perish.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He used to say: do His will as though it were your will, so that He will do your will as though it were His. Set aside your will in the face of His will, so that he may set aside the will of others for the sake of your will.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel teaches that the one who sets aside his own will finds his will fulfilled.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same paradox as the Kural: give up your wants, and what is good comes “as you wish”.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:4 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let go of the past, let go of the future, let go of the present, and cross over to the farther shore of existence. With mind wholly liberated, you shall come no more to birth and death.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges total letting go, which brings the deathless state beyond birth and death.
buddhism.tie_back: Both promise that complete relinquishment leads to the undying.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who endeavours to recognise the vanity of all desires, will arrive at perfect indifference. When he ceases to desire the objects (of the senses), his desire for pleasures will become extinct.” … “He will get rid of all misery which always afflicts mankind; recovered from the long illness, as it were, and glorious, he becomes infinitely happy, and obtains the (final) aim.”
jainism.explanation: The closing verses of the lecture on carelessness describe a sequence. Desire is fully extinguished, the obstructing karmas fall away, and the soul reaches its final aim, liberation, likened to recovery from a long illness.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar promises that once desire is cut off completely, the deeds that lead to deathless life follow as one wishes. The Jain text likewise makes total extinction of desire the threshold beyond which the final aim is reached.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.107 and 32.110 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “who renounces all hopes and desires and remains desireless in the world; who is not touched by sexual desire or anger - within his heart, God dwells.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person who has given up all hopes and desires and is untouched by lust and anger; in that heart God dwells, and the hymn ends with such a person merging in God like water in water.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural promises that one who cuts off desire completely will gain the deeds that lead to undying life; Guru Tegh Bahadur promises that the desireless heart becomes God's dwelling.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles reveals that his mother foretold two fates for him: a long but inglorious life at home, or death at Troy with glory that will never perish (kleos aphthiton).
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles weighs the comforts of a long life against deeds whose fame will not die.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a loose echo of the Kural’s thavaa vinai, “imperishable deeds”. Achilles, however, trades comfort for glory, which is itself a desire.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Don’t demand that things happen as you wish, but wish that they happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that when you give up demanding outcomes, things turn out “well”, because your will now matches reality.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s paradox: cut off desire, and things come as you wish.

real_life_example.event_title: Vinoba Bhave receives the first Bhoodan land gift
real_life_example.place: Pochampalli, Nalgonda district, Hyderabad State (now Telangana), India
real_life_example.event: Vinoba Bhave, a disciple of Gandhi who lived as an ascetic, was walking through Telangana in 1951 when landless Dalit families in the village of Pochampalli asked him for land. On 18 April 1951 a local landowner, Ramachandra Reddy, offered 100 acres in response to his appeal. Vinoba went on to walk across India for years asking landowners to give land to the landless, launching the Bhoodan (land-gift) movement, and in 1958 he received the first Ramon Magsaysay Award for Community Leadership.
real_life_example.explanation: A man who owned nothing and asked nothing for himself was able to persuade others to give away land on a scale no law had achieved.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when desire is cut off completely, the deeds that lead to lasting good come of their own accord, and Vinoba's desireless life became the source of a movement of giving.

tamil:
அவாஇல்லார்க் கில்லாகுந் துன்பம் அஃதுண்டேல்
தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்.
transliteration:
Avaa illaarkku illaagum thunbam aqdhundel
Thavaaadhu menmel varum.
meaning: People without desire have no sorrow. Wherever desire exists, sorrow keeps coming, one after another, without fail.
elementary: Every time you want something you can’t have, you feel a little sad. If you want a hundred things, you get a hundred little sads. Want nothing, and the sads have nowhere to come from.
university: The couplet is a strict pair of conditions. For those without desire (avaa illaarkku), suffering ceases to exist (illaagum); if desire exists (aqdhundel), suffering comes thavaaadhu menmel, without fail, one upon another. The doubled menmel (“more and more, upon and upon”) imitates the way craving compounds, since each satisfied desire breeds new ones. This is the Kural’s closest approach to a formal statement of the Buddhist second noble truth, but Valluvar stays practical rather than metaphysical: he describes the lived economy of wanting, not a theory of dependent origination.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises. From anger, complete delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain reaction: attachment breeds desire, desire breeds anger, and each stage brings a further downfall.
hinduism.tie_back: Both show desire setting off an unending cascade of suffering, each trouble bringing the next.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that craving riches leads into snares and “many sorrows”.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the Kural closely: where desire is, sorrows pile up.

islam.quote_or_event: “So as for he who transgressed And preferred the life of the world, Then indeed, Hellfire will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that the one who prefers worldly desires ends in suffering.
islam.tie_back: Both link giving in to worldly desire with inevitable suffering. The Qur’an places that suffering in the hereafter, the Kural in this life.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that greed brings trouble on one’s own household, while the one who rejects bribes will live.
judaism.tie_back: Both say that desire itself produces trouble and that freedom from it brings life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a tree, though cut down, sprouts up again if its roots remain uncut and firm, even so, until the craving that lies dormant is rooted out, suffering springs up again and again.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that as long as the root of craving remains, suffering keeps growing back.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost identical to the Kural: where craving remains, suffering comes “again and again” (menmel).

jainism.quote_or_event: “Thus the objects of the senses and of the mind cause pain to passionate men, but they never in the least cause any pain to the dispassionate.”
jainism.explanation: After going through each of the senses in turn, the lecture concludes that suffering comes not from the objects themselves but from passionate attachment to them. The dispassionate meet the same objects and feel no pain.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those without desire have no sorrow, while for those with desire sorrow comes without fail. The Jain verse states the same two-sided rule: pain for the passionate, none for the dispassionate.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.100 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The fire of desire is deep within; unsatisfied, people remain hungry and thirsty.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad says that desire is a fire burning inside, and that those who carry it stay hungry and thirsty however much they get.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that where desire exists sorrow comes without fail, one upon another; Guru Angad describes the same endless hunger and thirst that desire brings.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 138, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld, Tantalus stands in a pool beneath fruit-laden trees. Whenever he stoops to drink the water drains away, and whenever he reaches for fruit the wind whirls the branches out of reach, so his torment never ends.
greek_mythology.explanation: Tantalus suffers forever because his desire is endless and never satisfied.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He embodies the second half of the Kural: where desire remains, suffering keeps coming without end.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates tells a parable in which the craving part of a foolish soul is like a leaky jar or sieve. It must be filled again and again and is never satisfied, so its owner lives in constant distress, unlike the orderly person whose jars are sound and full.
philosophy.explanation: Plato argues that a life of ever-renewed desire is a life of ceaseless labor and pain.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s claim that where desire exists, suffering keeps coming, while the desire-free are at rest.

real_life_example.event_title: Ludwig II of Bavaria's building debts and deposition
real_life_example.place: Neuschwanstein, Linderhof and Herrenchiemsee, Bavaria, Germany
real_life_example.event: King Ludwig II of Bavaria poured vast sums into fantastic palaces, including Linderhof, Herrenchiemsee, modelled on Versailles, and the fairy-tale castle of Neuschwanstein. Although heavily in debt, he kept on building, and from 1885 foreign banks threatened to seize his property. In June 1886 the Bavarian government had him declared unfit to rule and deposed him, a step not provided for in the Bavarian constitution, and his uncle Luitpold became regent.
real_life_example.explanation: Each new project led to more debt and more conflict with his ministers, until the king lost his throne and his castles were opened to paying visitors.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that where desire exists, sorrow follows without fail, one upon another, and Ludwig's unending building brought a chain of debts, crises and finally the loss of his crown.

tamil:
இன்பம் இடையறா தீண்டும் அவாவென்னும்
துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்.
transliteration:
Inbam idaiyaraa theendum avaavennum
Thunbaththul thunbam kedin.
meaning: When desire, the worst of all sorrows, is destroyed, joy flows without stopping, even in this life.
elementary: Imagine an itch you’ve had for so long that you forgot it was there. When it finally stops, you feel wonderful all the time. Valluvar says wanting is that itch, and when it’s gone, happiness just keeps going.
university: Valluvar calls avaa “thunbaththul thunbam”, the sorrow among sorrows, the one that gives rise to all the others. Removing it therefore does more than take away one pain: it dries up the source of every pain. The promised result, inbam idaiyaraadhu eendum, is unbroken joy “even here” (eendum), a this-worldly liberation comparable to the Upanishadic jivanmukta and to the Buddhist realization of nibbana in this very life. The joy is defined negatively, as what remains when craving stops. That lines up closely with the Buddhist third noble truth and with Epicurus’s definition of pleasure as freedom from disturbance.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who is not disturbed by the incessant flow of desires – that enter like rivers into the ocean, which is ever being filled but is always still – can alone achieve peace, and not the man who strives to satisfy such desires.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares the desire-free sage to the ocean: rivers pour in, but it stays full and still, at lasting peace.
hinduism.tie_back: Both promise an unbroken inner peace once craving no longer stirs a person.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes a steady contentment that no change of circumstance can break.
christianity.tie_back: Both describe a lasting happiness that no longer depends on getting what one wants.

islam.quote_or_event: “O reassured soul, Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him],”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an speaks of the soul at rest (al-nafs al-mutma’innah), the opposite of the restless, evil-urging self.
islam.tie_back: Both describe a settled joy that follows once the restless self is calmed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist compares his quieted soul to a weaned child that no longer craves its mother’s milk and rests content.
judaism.tie_back: Both picture a soul weaned from craving that finds calm, lasting peace.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Cessation of suffering, as a noble truth, is this: It is remainderless fading and ceasing, giving up, relinquishing, letting go and rejecting, of that same craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Third Noble Truth teaches that suffering ends when craving ends completely.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the most central possible match: when craving, the source of suffering, is destroyed, what remains is lasting peace.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (trans. Ñanamoli Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “From desire of pleasure arises the misery of the whole world, the gods included; whatever misery of body and mind there is, the dispassionate will put an end to it.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana treats desire for pleasure as the single source of all suffering, even that of the gods, and teaches that freedom from passion ends every bodily and mental misery.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls desire the sorrow of sorrows, whose destruction brings unbroken joy even in this life. The Jain verse likewise makes desire the source of all the world's misery and dispassion its complete cure.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.19 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The mind and body are cooled and soothed; peace ensues, and the fire of desire is quenched.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das says that through the Guru's Word the fire of desire is put out and body and mind become cool and peaceful.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that when desire, the sorrow of sorrows, is destroyed, joy flows without break even in this life; Guru Amar Das describes the peace that follows once desire's fire is quenched.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 588, Raag Vadhans (Vadhans ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells of a race of heroes whom Zeus settled after death in the Islands of the Blessed at the ends of the earth. They live there untouched by sorrow while the fertile land bears fruit for them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth imagines a state of unbroken happiness free from sorrow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a distant parallel to the Kural’s unbroken joy. In the myth it is a reward granted by the gods, not the result of ending desire.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “By pleasure we mean the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the soul.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus defines the highest pleasure as tranquility (ataraxia), which is reached by cutting away needless desires.
philosophy.tie_back: Both define the highest joy negatively, as what remains when the disturbance of desire is gone.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus 131 (trans. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: Thoreau's two years at Walden Pond
real_life_example.place: Walden Pond, Concord, Massachusetts, United States
real_life_example.event: On 4 July 1845 Henry David Thoreau moved into a small cabin he had built on land owned by Ralph Waldo Emerson beside Walden Pond, where he lived until September 1847. He strictly limited his spending and possessions to test how simply and cheaply a person could live, while writing and studying nature. His account of the experiment, Walden; or, Life in the Woods, was published in 1854 and became a classic of American literature.
real_life_example.explanation: Thoreau set out to show that cutting wants down to essentials left more time and freedom for what made life worth living.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural promises that when desire, the sorrow of sorrows, is removed, joy flows unbroken even in this life, and Thoreau's Walden is a famous record of finding contentment by needing less.

tamil:
ஆரா இயற்கை அவாநீப்பின் அந்நிலையே
பேரா இயற்கை தரும்.
transliteration:
Aaraa iyarkai avaa neeppin annilaiye
Peraa iyarkai tharum.
meaning: Desire by its nature can never be satisfied. Whoever throws it away gains, at that very moment, a lasting happiness that never changes.
elementary: Trying to fill a bucket that has a hole in the bottom never works. You pour and pour, and it’s never full. Valluvar says wanting is that leaky bucket. Stop pouring into it, and you find a calm that never runs out.
university: The final couplet crowns the chapter with a mirrored wordplay: aaraa iyarkai (a nature that is never filled) against peraa iyarkai (a nature that never departs). Insatiability is what defines desire, and permanence is the reward for giving it up, the unchanging state that commentators identify with liberation (veedu). The word annilaiye (“in that very state” or “at that very moment”) suggests the reward is not postponed to some later heaven but is the same thing as the act of letting go. As the last couplet on renunciation before the chapter on Destiny that closes the Book of Virtue, it sums up Valluvar’s whole ascetic path: the endlessly hungry becomes the endlessly at peace.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Thus the wise living entity’s pure consciousness becomes covered by his eternal enemy in the form of lust, which is never satisfied and which burns like fire.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes desire (kama) as duspura, “never to be satisfied”, a fire that only grows the more it is fed.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s “never satisfied” matches the Kural’s aaraa iyarkai, the nature that is never filled.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus answered and said unto her, Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts water that leaves people thirsty again with “living water” that ends thirst forever.
christianity.tie_back: Both contrast an endless thirst with an everlasting, unchanging fullness.

islam.quote_or_event: “If Adam’s son had a valley full of gold, he would like to have two valleys, for nothing fills his mouth except dust. And Allah forgives him who repents to Him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that human greed is bottomless and only death (“dust”) finally fills it.
