islam.tie_back: This is a direct parallel to the Kural’s aaraa iyarkai: desire is by nature never full.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet observes that the lover of wealth is never satisfied, however much he gains.
judaism.tie_back: Both identify never being satisfied as the defining nature of desire.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no satisfying sensual desires, even with the rain of gold coins. For sensual pleasures give little satisfaction and much pain. Having understood this, the wise man finds no delight even in heavenly pleasures. The disciple of the Supreme Buddha delights in the destruction of craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that even a rain of gold cannot satisfy desire, and that the wise delight in the destruction of craving.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches both halves of the Kural: desire is insatiable, and joy lies in ending it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means. Though two mâshas would do to supply your want, still you would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.”
jainism.explanation: In the story Jacobi summarises from the commentary, the student Kapila is offered whatever he asks by a king. He keeps raising the sum in his mind until it reaches ten thousand millions. Then he suddenly sees that desire can never be filled, renounces on the spot as a self-enlightened sage, and speaks this verse.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says desire is by nature never satisfied, and whoever casts it off at once gains a nature that never changes. Kapila's verse states the insatiability, and his sudden enlightenment on giving desire up acts out the second line.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 8.17, with Jacobi's note on the Kapila legend (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Earning a thousand, he runs after a hundred thousand. Satisfaction is not obtained by chasing after Maya.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Guru Arjan shows the endless escalation of wanting: every gain only starts the chase for more, and no satisfaction comes from Maya.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says desire by nature can never be filled; Guru Arjan pictures exactly that insatiable nature, and the same passage goes on to place lasting peace in the Name.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278-279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon cuts down Ceres’ sacred oak and is punished with Famine. The more he eats, the hungrier he becomes. He spends his wealth, sells his daughter, and finally devours his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: His curse is an appetite that can never be filled and only grows as it is fed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is a mythic picture of the Kural’s aaraa iyarkai, the nature that is never satisfied.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The wealth required by nature is limited and is easy to procure; but the wealth required by vain ideals extends to infinity.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus distinguishes natural needs, which have limits, from vain desires, which have no limit and can never be satisfied.
philosophy.tie_back: Both identify limitless, insatiable desire as the problem, and both locate peace in stepping out of it.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, Principal Doctrines 15 (trans. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: Bhutan adopts Gross National Happiness
real_life_example.event: In the 1970s Bhutan's fourth king, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, coined the term Gross National Happiness and asserted that it mattered more than measures of economic output such as gross national or domestic product. Bhutan's development plans have since been guided by this idea, which weighs material growth alongside wellbeing, culture and the environment. The government later developed a Gross National Happiness Index to measure it.
real_life_example.explanation: Bhutan made it national policy that endless growth in output is not the goal, setting a lasting kind of wellbeing above ever-rising consumption.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says desire by its nature can never be satisfied and that lasting contentment comes only when it is set aside, an idea Bhutan applied to a whole economy by refusing to make ever-greater output its highest aim.

tamil:
ஆகூழால் தோன்றும் அசைவின்மை கைப்பொருள்
போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி.
transliteration:
Aakoozhaal thondrum asaivinmai kaipporul
Pokoozhaal thondrum madi.
meaning: When fate is ready to bring you riches, it makes you work hard without tiring. When fate is ready to take riches away, it makes you lazy.
elementary: Imagine two kids with the same homework. One suddenly feels full of energy and finishes it; the other feels sleepy and gives up. This kural says that even the energy or the sleepiness you feel can be part of your fate: good fortune shows up as hard work, and bad fortune shows up as laziness.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a subtle psychological claim: fate (ஊழ், uzh) does not merely deliver outcomes from outside but works through the agent’s own dispositions. ஆகூழ் (aakuzh, ‘fate of gaining’) manifests as அசைவின்மை (unflagging perseverance), while போகூழ் (pokuzh, ‘fate of losing’) manifests as மடி (sloth). This neatly reconciles the chapter with the Kural’s many praises of effort elsewhere (e.g. the later chapters on ஆள்வினையுடைமை): effort is praised, yet the very capacity to make effort is itself read as a sign of a favourable destiny. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar treat ஊழ் as the ripened fruit of past deeds (பழவினை), which makes the idea closer to karmic causation than to arbitrary luck. The structure anticipates the Stoic ‘co-fated’ reply to the Lazy Argument: outcome and effort are fated together, so fatalism is no excuse for idleness.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The body, the doer (soul), the various senses, the many kinds of efforts, and Divine Providence—these are the five factors of action.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists five causes behind every action; human effort is one of them, but daiva (Providence or fate) is named as the decisive fifth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita places effort and fate side by side: effort is real, but it operates inside a larger, destined frame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers that even their wanting to act and their actual doing are worked in them by God.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural says fate shows up as inner energy; Paul says the very will to act is given from above.

islam.quote_or_event: “As for he who gives and fears Allāh and believes in the best [reward], We will ease him toward ease. But as for he who withholds and considers himself free of need and denies the best [reward], We will ease him toward difficulty.”
islam.explanation: God ‘eases’ each person along the path matching their disposition, making one path smooth and the other hard.
islam.tie_back: Both texts describe a higher power smoothing a person’s road toward either flourishing or decline.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven.
judaism.explanation: The Sages hold that circumstances such as wealth and fortune are set by Heaven, while a person’s reverence and moral choice remain their own.
judaism.tie_back: A partial contrast: the Kural puts even effort and sloth under fate, whereas the Talmud keeps inner moral choice outside it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha rejects the view that whatever a person experiences is entirely caused by what was done in the past, arguing that such a view would leave no room for desire, effort, or the sense of what should and should not be done.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha argues that pure past-action determinism destroys the motivation to act rightly now, so he rejects it.
buddhism.tie_back: A deliberate contrast: the Kural lets fate produce effort or sloth, while the Buddha refuses to let past karma explain away present effort.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The second–lābha antarāya–hinders him from attaining any gain even though he sets his heart on it. … The fifth–vīrya antarāya–prevents effort or exertion, although he wants to make an effort or exert himself.”
jainism.explanation: Jain karma theory has an 'obstructive' karma (antarāya), one subtype of which blocks gain and another blocks energy or exertion. When it ripens, a person can want to strive and still find the effort will not come. In Jainism this karma is subtle matter the soul itself has bound, not a decree from outside.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the fate of gain shows itself as tireless effort and the fate of loss as idleness. Pūjyapāda likewise explains failures of both gain and exertion by karma working within the person's own capacities.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.13, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Gujri ki Vaar Guru Arjan urges udam, steady effort on the path of the Name, and promises that such effort brings true life and peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a fortune bent on giving shows itself as tireless effort; Guru Arjan likewise treats unflagging effort as the way blessings arrive, though he presents it as a duty to take up rather than a sign that fortune has already decided.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes the three Moirai, Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos, as the powers who give mortals at their birth both good and evil to have.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, each person’s share (moira) of good and bad is spun and allotted at birth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like ஆகூழ் and போகூழ், the Moirai hand out a lot of gain or loss before any effort is made.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero reports the ‘Lazy Argument’: if recovering from illness is fated, calling the doctor is pointless. Chrysippus answered that some events are ‘co-fated’: recovery and calling the doctor are fated together.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoics held that fate works through human actions, not around them, so fate is no excuse for doing nothing.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar makes the same move: fate comes to pass through effort (or through its absence).

real_life_example.event_title: Ino Tadataka begins his survey of Japan at fifty-five
real_life_example.place: Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, Japan
real_life_example.event: In 1800, at the age of 55, Ino Tadataka obtained the shogunate's permission to survey the southeastern coast of Hokkaido, partly in order to work out the length of a degree of latitude. His maps impressed the shogunate, which sent him on survey after survey along the coasts of Japan over the next sixteen years, during which he spent more than 3,700 days on the road and covered tens of thousands of kilometres on foot. He died in 1818, and the completed map of Japan based on his surveys was presented to the shogunate in 1821.
real_life_example.explanation: Ino began the work for which he is remembered at an age when most men of his time had retired, and his tireless persistence produced the first accurate map of Japan.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when fortune is set on bringing gain it shows itself as unflagging effort, and Ino's late-life energy, which carried him around the whole country, is the kind of perseverance the couplet describes.

tamil:
பேதைப் படுக்கும் இழவூழ் அறிவகற்றும்
ஆகலூழ் உற்றக் கடை.
transliteration:
Pedhaip padukkum izhavoozh arivagatrum
Aagaloozh utrak kadai.
meaning: When fate brings loss, it makes even a clever person act foolishly. When fate brings gain, it opens up a person’s mind and makes it wider.
elementary: Have you ever had a day when you kept making silly mistakes, and another day when every answer just clicked? This kural says bad fortune can make even smart people act silly, and good fortune can make people seem wiser than usual.
university: The couplet extends the previous one from will to intellect: இழவூழ் (izhavuzh, ‘the fate of loss’) makes one பேதை (a fool), while ஆகலூழ் (aagaluzh, ‘the fate of increase’) அறிவு அகற்றும், widening or enlarging understanding. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan read அகற்றும் as ‘to expand’, not ‘to remove’. The idea is that judgement itself is vulnerable to fortune: brilliant people make ruinous decisions when their luck is turning. The same intuition appears across cultures as the sense that those heading for ruin are first robbed of good judgement, and in the biblical account of Ahithophel’s wise counsel being ‘defeated’ by divine design. Philosophically, it raises the question of moral luck: how far our rationality depends on circumstances we do not control.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna traces a downward chain: attachment breeds desire, desire breeds anger, anger breeds delusion, delusion bewilders memory, and when memory is bewildered intelligence is lost and one falls.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita shows how a person’s intelligence (buddhi) can be lost step by step, leading to ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: Both describe a loss of reason that comes before a fall, though the Gita blames passion rather than fate.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, quoting Isaiah, says God can overturn human cleverness whenever He chooses.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural says a fate of loss makes the wise foolish; here a higher power voids the understanding of the prudent.

islam.quote_or_event: “He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever has been given wisdom has certainly been given much good.”
islam.explanation: Wisdom is described as a gift God grants to whomever He chooses.
islam.tie_back: Matches the second half of the Kural: a favourable decree enlarges understanding.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil upon Absalom.”
judaism.explanation: Absalom rejects the sound advice of Ahithophel for worse advice because God has decreed his downfall.
judaism.tie_back: A near-perfect narrative example: a ruler bound for loss is led to choose foolishly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To his own ruin the fool gains knowledge, for it cleaves his head and destroys his innate goodness.”
buddhism.explanation: In the wrong person, knowledge itself becomes a tool of self-destruction.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see that intelligence can end in ruin, though the Dhammapada blames character rather than fate.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Gñânâvaranîya (which acts as an obstruction to right knowledge)” … “Obstruction of knowledge is fivefold (viz. obstruction to): a. Sruta, knowledge derived from the sacred books; b. Âbhinibôdhika, perception; c. Avadhigñâna, supernatural knowledge; d. Manahparyâya, knowledge of the thoughts of other people; e. Kêvala, the highest, unlimited knowledge.”
jainism.explanation: The first of the eight karmas is knowledge-obscuring karma. It clouds every level of understanding, from book learning up to omniscience, so that how clear or dull a person's mind is depends partly on how much of this karma is active.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says a fate of loss makes even a clever person foolish while a fate of gain widens understanding. Jainism likewise explains the dulling and widening of intellect by the rise or loosening of a particular karma.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 33.2 and 33.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those, whom the Creator Lord would destroy - first He strips them of virtue.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of the Babarvani, reflecting on the ruin of the rich and powerful in Babar's invasion, Guru Nanak observes that before the Creator brings someone down, He first takes away their goodness and judgement.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a fate of loss makes even the clever act foolishly; Guru Nanak names the same pattern, in which ruin begins by stripping a person of the qualities that would have saved them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The chorus in Sophocles’ Antigone sings that evil comes to seem good to the one whose mind a god is leading toward ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tragedy often shows ruin arriving through a god-sent blindness of judgement (atē).
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same pattern as இழவூழ் making a person foolish: judgement fails first, then fortune follows.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, the soul that draws the first lot hastily chooses the life of a great tyrant through folly and greed, and only later discovers that it includes the fate of devouring his own children.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows how a lack of wisdom at the decisive moment locks a soul into a disastrous destiny.
philosophy.tie_back: Folly and ruin travel together in both texts, though Plato stresses the soul’s own responsibility.

real_life_example.event_title: Napoleon waits in Moscow
real_life_example.place: Moscow and the road from Moscow to the Niemen River, Russian Empire
real_life_example.event: In June 1812 Napoleon, then the most successful general in Europe, invaded Russia with a force usually estimated at between 450,000 and 600,000 men. The Russian armies retreated, and after the costly Battle of Borodino in September he entered a largely deserted Moscow, much of which was soon destroyed by fire. He waited there about five weeks for Tsar Alexander I to offer peace, which never came, and left on 19 October; by the end of the winter retreat only a small fraction of his army remained.
real_life_example.explanation: The campaign is a classic example of a commander with an unmatched record of victories making a series of misjudgements that destroyed his army and began the end of his empire.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a fate of loss makes even the clever act foolishly, and Napoleon's long, fruitless wait in Moscow as winter approached is often cited as the moment his famous judgement failed him.

tamil:
நுண்ணிய நூல்பல கற்பினும் மற்றுந்தன்
உண்மை யறிவே மிகும்.
transliteration:
Nunniya noolpala karpinum matrundhan
Unmai yarive migum.
meaning: However many deep books a person studies, in the end the understanding that fate has given them is what wins out.
elementary: You can give a pencil to every child in class, but each one will still draw in their own way. This kural says that reading many clever books helps, but in the end a person’s own natural understanding decides how they really think and act.
university: The key phrase is உண்மை அறிவு (unmai arivu): literally ‘the knowledge that truly is’ one’s own, which commentators gloss as the understanding given by ஊழ், as opposed to what is acquired from books (நூல்). Valluvar is not dismissing learning; he devotes whole chapters to கல்வி (learning). He is noting that learning is filtered through an innate capacity it cannot fully override. The Gita makes a parallel claim that even the learned act according to their own nature (prakṛti), and Heraclitus’ fragment that character is a person’s daimon points the same way. Modern debates on nature versus nurture, and on the limits of education, are a secular version of the same observation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Even a man of knowledge acts according to his own nature, for everyone follows the nature he has acquired from the three modes. What can repression accomplish?”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that learning does not override the nature (prakṛti) a person has acquired.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the same claim as the Kural: however learned, a person’s own innate nature wins out.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit … dividing to every man severally as he will.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that wisdom and knowledge are distributed as gifts, each person receiving a different share.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘own true understanding’, wisdom here is a given portion, not something merely studied into existence.

islam.quote_or_event: “We raise in degrees whom We will, but over every possessor of knowledge is one [more] knowing.”
islam.explanation: Degrees of knowledge are raised by God’s will, and no one’s learning is final.
islam.tie_back: Knowledge levels are set from above, which echoes the Kural’s view that one’s true understanding is allotted.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud relates that the angel appointed over conception brings the drop before God and asks whether it will become strong or weak, wise or foolish, rich or poor, but does not ask whether it will be righteous or wicked.
judaism.explanation: Wisdom, strength and wealth are fixed before birth; only moral character is left to free choice.
judaism.tie_back: It directly supports the Kural: wisdom (or foolishness) is set before any study begins.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: Being around wisdom does not give understanding to someone who lacks the capacity for it.
buddhism.tie_back: Exposure to wisdom, like reading many books, cannot replace the understanding that is truly one’s own.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The dispassionate man who has performed all duties will quickly remove the obstructions to right knowledge and to right faith, and whatever Karman produces obstruction (to righteousness). Then he knows and sees all things, he is free from delusion and hindrances.”
jainism.explanation: In Jainism, perfect knowledge (kevala jñāna) is the soul's own nature. It is not built up from study but revealed once the obstructing karmas are removed, and book learning (śruta) is only one limited, partly covered form of it.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that however many subtle books one studies, the knowledge that is truly one's own prevails in the end. The Jain idea of an innate knowledge, uncovered rather than acquired, offers a parallel to that 'true knowledge' (unmai arivu).
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.108–109 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You may read and read loads of books; you may read and study vast multitudes of books.” … “O Nanak, only one thing is of any account: everything else is useless babbling and idle talk in ego.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak says that no quantity of reading counts in the end; only one thing, the Lord's Name and praise, is of account, and the rest is ego talking.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that however many subtle books one studies, only the understanding truly one's own prevails; Guru Nanak likewise ranks bookish learning below the one thing that really counts.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Prometheus Bound, Prometheus, the giver of all human arts, admits that craft is far weaker than Necessity, and says Necessity is steered by the three Fates and the Furies.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even the god of forethought and skill cannot out-think what is fated.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Learning and skill, however subtle, are weaker than the portion fate assigns, which is the Kural’s point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heraclitus’ fragment ‘ēthos anthrōpōi daimōn’ is usually rendered ‘character is a person’s destiny’.
philosophy.explanation: A person’s inner character, not outside instruction, is what shapes their fate.
philosophy.tie_back: Both put a person’s inner, given nature above what is learned from outside.

real_life_example.event_title: Ramanujan writes to G. H. Hardy
real_life_example.place: Madras (Chennai), India, and Trinity College, Cambridge, England
real_life_example.event: Srinivasa Ramanujan, who had no university degree, taught himself higher mathematics largely from G. S. Carr's Synopsis, a dated book that listed thousands of results with only the briefest proofs, and then went far beyond it with his own discoveries. On 16 January 1913, while working as a clerk in Madras, he wrote to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy, enclosing around 120 theorems. Hardy, though puzzled by the absence of conventional proofs, recognised his genius and arranged for him to come to Cambridge, where Ramanujan was later elected a Fellow of Trinity College.
real_life_example.explanation: Ramanujan's mathematics came from a powerful insight of his own that no textbook had given him, and it astonished scholars trained in far more learning.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that however many subtle books a person studies, it is the understanding that is truly their own that prevails, and Ramanujan's original genius, nourished by a single old book, outran what formal learning could teach.

tamil:
இருவேறு உலகத்து இயற்கை திருவேறு
தெள்ளிய ராதலும் வேறு.
transliteration:
Iruveru ulagaththu iyarkai thiruveru
Thelliya raadhalum veru.
meaning: Fate works in two different ways in the world. Becoming rich is one thing, and becoming wise is quite another.
elementary: Some kids are great at sports and others are great at math, and being good at one doesn’t make you good at the other. This kural says money and wisdom work the same way: being rich and being wise come from different kinds of luck, so one doesn’t guarantee the other.
university: The couplet makes an observation anyone can check: wealth (திரு, thiru, also the name of the goddess of fortune) and clear wisdom (தெள்ளியர் ஆதல்) are handed out on separate tracks. The rich are often not wise, and the wise are often not rich. Commentators read இருவேறு இயற்கை as two distinct operations of ஊழ். Indian folk tradition expresses the same idea as the old rivalry between Lakshmi (wealth) and Saraswati (learning). Ecclesiastes’ remark that bread is not always to the wise nor riches to the understanding, the Talmudic teaching on sustenance depending on mazal rather than merit, and Aristotle’s puzzle about fortunate fools all record the same gap between intelligence and worldly reward.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Among women I am fame, fortune, fine speech, memory, intelligence, steadfastness and patience.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists fortune (śrī) and intelligence (medhā) as separate divine manifestations.
hinduism.tie_back: Wealth and wisdom appear as distinct gifts, matching the Kural’s ‘two different natures’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher notes that wisdom and understanding do not guarantee bread or riches.
christianity.tie_back: An almost exact match: riches and wisdom are separate lots, and one does not bring the other.

islam.quote_or_event: “It is We who have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world and have raised some of them above others in degrees [of rank].”
islam.explanation: God Himself apportions people’s livelihoods and ranks.
islam.tie_back: Worldly wealth is a separately apportioned lot, as the Kural says.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rava teaches that life, children and sustenance depend not on merit but on mazal (fortune). The Talmud illustrates this with two righteous sages, Rabba and Rav Ḥisda: one household enjoyed plenty while the other struggled for bread.
judaism.explanation: Equal virtue and learning did not produce equal prosperity, because sustenance follows fortune.
judaism.tie_back: A vivid illustration of the Kural: being wise and being rich are separate lots.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Shorter Exposition of Kamma, the Buddha explains that beings are owners and heirs of their kamma, and that kamma is what separates beings into rich and poor, and into wise and foolish, each through its own specific causes.
buddhism.explanation: Wealth comes from one kind of past action (generosity) and wisdom from another (inquiry), so the two are distributed separately.
buddhism.tie_back: Close to the Kural: wealth and wisdom come from two different workings of past deeds.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Antarâya is fivefold as preventing: 1. gifts; 2. profit; 3. momentary enjoyment; 4. continuous enjoyment; and 5. power.”
jainism.explanation: Jainism keeps the karma that blocks profit and enjoyment (antarāya) separate from the karma that obscures knowledge (jñānāvaraṇīya, 33.4). Because they are distinct karmas, a person's share of wealth and share of wisdom are governed separately.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar observes that fate works in two different ways, one making people rich and the other making them wise. The Jain list of karmas likewise assigns gain and understanding to two different karmic causes.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 33.15 (cf. 33.2–4) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “By His Command, some are high and some are low; by His Written Command, pain and pleasure are obtained.”
sikhism.explanation: In the second pauri of Japji Guru Nanak teaches that hukam, the divine order, assigns people different stations and different shares of pain and pleasure.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural observes that fate deals out wealth and wisdom on two separate tracks; Japji likewise sees people's unequal portions as handed out by the one divine order rather than earned by merit alone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 2, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the myth Protagoras tells, Epimetheus hands out distinct endowments to each creature: speed to some, strength to others. He runs out before reaching humans, so Prometheus steals craft-wisdom and fire for them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Gifts are handed out one at a time, and no creature receives everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s two separate operations of fate, endowments are allotted separately rather than all together.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that some foolish people succeed in many things where luck is in control, and asks whether good fortune (eutuchia) is a natural gift quite separate from practical wisdom.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle notices that success often lands on the unwise, and he tries to explain luck as something other than intelligence.
philosophy.tie_back: The same observation as the Kural: fortune and wisdom run on different tracks.

real_life_example.event_title: Spinoza declines the chair of philosophy at Heidelberg
real_life_example.place: The Hague, Dutch Republic (now the Netherlands)
real_life_example.event: Baruch (Benedict de) Spinoza, expelled from Amsterdam's Jewish community in 1656, supported himself by grinding optical lenses and lived in modest rented rooms. In 1673 he was offered the chair of philosophy at the University of Heidelberg but declined it, out of concern that he would not have complete freedom to teach as he wished. He died in 1677, and his Ethics, published after his death, became one of the most influential works of Western philosophy.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the great minds of the seventeenth century lived and died with very little money, while his ideas proved far more valuable than any fortune.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says fate works in two different ways, so that becoming wealthy is one thing and becoming wise is another, and Spinoza's life of modest lens-grinding alongside his towering philosophy shows how separate the two can be.

tamil:
நல்லவை எல்லாஅந் தீயவாம் தீயவும்
நல்லவாம் செல்வம் செயற்கு.
transliteration:
Nallavai ellaaan theeyavaam theeyavum
Nallavaam selvam seyarku.
meaning: When you are trying to get rich, fate can turn every good chance into a bad one, and every bad chance into a good one.
elementary: Sometimes you plan a picnic on a sunny day and it rains anyway. Other times you get stuck indoors and end up finding something wonderful. This kural says that when it comes to making money, luck can flip good chances into bad ones and bad chances into good ones.
university: Commentators take நல்லவை and தீயவை here as circumstances favourable or unfavourable to earning, such as the right time, place, means and partners, rather than moral good and evil. Solomon Pappaiah glosses the kural this way: even with the right time, place and trade, an adverse fate brings loss, and even without them a favourable fate brings profit. The couplet warns against over-confidence in planning, since the same conditions can produce opposite results depending on forces beyond calculation. Across traditions this becomes the theme of reversal: the Qur'an’s ‘perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you’, Rabbi Akiva’s night journey, and Boethius’ turning wheel of Fortune.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That which in the beginning may be just like poison but at the end is just like nectar and which awakens one to self-realization is said to be happiness in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita notes that what feels bitter at first can prove sweet in the end, and the reverse.
hinduism.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s theme of reversal: things that seem bad can turn out good.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.”
christianity.explanation: Paul assures believers that even apparent misfortunes are turned to good by God’s purpose.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the ‘bad becomes good’ half of the Kural under a higher governing power.

islam.quote_or_event: “But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allāh knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: Human judgements of good and bad can be reversed by what God alone knows.
islam.tie_back: An almost exact two-way match: the favourable can prove harmful and the unfavourable beneficial.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Akiva, turned away from a town, sleeps in a field; wind blows out his lamp, a cat eats his rooster and a lion his donkey. That night an army captures the town, and his lack of light and noise saves him. He teaches that all the Merciful One does is for the good.
judaism.explanation: A string of misfortunes turns out to be what saved his life.
judaism.tie_back: Circumstances that looked disastrous turn out favourable, which is exactly the Kural’s reversal.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It may be well with the evil-doer as long as the evil ripens not. But when it does ripen, then the evil-doer sees (the painful results of) his evil deeds. It may be ill with the doer of good as long as the good ripens not. But when it does ripen, then the doer of good sees (the pleasant results of) his good deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: Present circumstances can be misleading, because the results of past action ripen later and may reverse them.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts describe good and bad conditions flipping because of a hidden force that ripens over time.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The Karman in question brings about an obstruction to the enjoyment, &c., though all other circumstances be favourable.”
jainism.explanation: Explaining the obstructive karma, Jacobi, following the commentators, notes that it blocks enjoyment and gain even when every outward condition is right. Karma can override good circumstances.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that in getting wealth, fate can turn every favourable circumstance against a person. The Jain gloss makes the same point: obstructive karma defeats gain 'though all other circumstances be favourable'.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 33.15, Jacobi's footnote (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Suffering is the medicine, and pleasure the disease, because where there is pleasure, there is no desire for God.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak turns the usual valuation upside down: hardship heals by turning the mind to God, while comfort sickens by making one forget Him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says fate can turn every favourable circumstance unfavourable and every unfavourable one favourable; Guru Nanak shows the same reversal, with good fortune becoming harmful and misfortune becoming a cure.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Croesus asks the Delphic oracle whether to attack Persia and is told that if he does he will destroy a great empire. Taking this as a promise, he attacks, and the empire he destroys is his own.
greek_mythology.explanation: What looked like the most favourable sign possible became the cause of his ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Good omens and good conditions turn bad, the first half of the Kural in dramatic form.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy tells Boethius that Fortune turns her wheel without pause, and that adverse fortune is often more useful than prosperous fortune, because it reveals true friends and false goods.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius shows that good and bad fortune are always turning and can swap their value.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that favourable and unfavourable circumstances readily change places.
philosophy.source: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, Book II (Prose 1-2, 8)

real_life_example.event_title: William Perkin's failed quinine experiment produces mauve
real_life_example.event: In 1856 the eighteen-year-old chemistry student William Henry Perkin was trying, in a home laboratory in London, to make quinine, the costly anti-malaria drug, from coal-tar chemicals. The experiment failed, but it left a dark residue from which he extracted a brilliant purple substance that could dye silk. He patented it in August 1856 as mauve, the first synthetic dye, set up a factory with his father's help, and the success of his dyes made him rich enough to retire from business in his thirties.
real_life_example.explanation: Perkin's discovery turned coal tar, a waste product, into the raw material of a vast new chemical industry.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that in the pursuit of wealth fortune can turn unfavourable circumstances into favourable ones, and Perkin's failed attempt at a medicine became the source of his fortune and of the synthetic dye industry.

tamil:
பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல உய்த்துச்
சொரியினும் போகா தம.
transliteration:
Pariyinum aagaavaam paalalla uyththuch
Choriyinum pogaa thama.
meaning: What fate has not made yours will not stay, however carefully you guard it. What fate has made yours will not leave, even if you throw it away.
elementary: Imagine holding sand tightly in your fist: it still slips out. Now imagine a boomerang: you throw it away and it comes back. This kural says things that aren’t meant for you slip away however hard you hold on, and things that are meant for you come back even if you throw them away.
university: The couplet turns on பால் (paal), ‘share’ or ‘portion’, the same word used for the three books of the Kural. Things outside one’s allotted share (பாலல்ல) cannot be kept even with painful guarding (பரியினும்), and things within it (தம) will not leave even if deliberately poured out (உய்த்துச் சொரியினும்). It is an extreme statement of possession as destiny. Greek tradition gives a near-perfect illustration in Polycrates’ ring, which was thrown into the sea and came back inside a fish. The ethical point, drawn out by Stoics like Epictetus, is that anxious clinging is irrational: one should hold possessions loosely, as things on loan.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You have a right to perform your prescribed duty, but you are not entitled to the fruits of action.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita teaches that results are not within a person’s control or ownership.
hinduism.tie_back: Both teach that what comes to you is not secured by grasping; results belong to a higher order.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that wealth can simply vanish however much one fixes one’s eyes on it.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the first half of the Kural: riches not truly yours fly off despite careful watching.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Allāh, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will.”
islam.explanation: Power and possession are given and taken by God, whatever the holder does.
islam.tie_back: Both say that keeping or losing possessions depends on a higher decree, not on the owner’s grip.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt. But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth describes carefully hoarded wealth that is lost anyway, leaving the heir with nothing.
judaism.tie_back: Close to the first half of the Kural: guarding wealth cannot keep what is not truly one’s portion.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The fool worries, thinking, ‘I have sons, I have wealth.’ Indeed, when he himself is not his own, whence are sons, whence is wealth?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the fool clings to possessions, not seeing that even the self is not truly owned.
buddhism.tie_back: Both expose the futility of anxious clinging to possessions.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Time elapses and quickly pass the days; the pleasures of men are not permanent; they come to a man and leave him just as a bird leaves a tree void of fruit.”
jainism.explanation: King Brahmadatta, enjoying the rewards of past merit, admits to the monk Citra that worldly pleasures cannot be held: they settle on a person and then leave, like birds deserting a tree once its fruit is gone. Citra had already told him that every deed bears its fruit (13.10).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says what is not one's allotted share will not stay however carefully guarded. The Jain image of pleasures leaving a man as birds leave a fruitless tree expresses the same idea: when the karmic fruit is spent, possessions go.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.31 (cf. 13.10) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He obtains ten things, and puts them behind him; for the sake of one thing withheld, he forfeits his faith. But what if that one thing were not given, and the ten were taken away? Then, what could the fool say or do?”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Guru Arjan reminds the ungrateful person that everything they hold was given by God and can be taken back at will, and that nothing they do can then keep it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says what is not one's allotted share cannot be kept however carefully it is guarded; Guru Arjan likewise teaches that what the Giver withholds or takes back cannot be held on to.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 268, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib (Ashtpadi 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The tyrant Polycrates, warned that his luck was too perfect, throws his most treasured ring into the sea to ward off misfortune. Days later a fisherman brings him a large fish, and the ring is found inside it. His ally Amasis breaks off their friendship, sensing that Polycrates is doomed.
greek_mythology.explanation: What fate has assigned cannot be thrown away, and a doom that is fated cannot be bought off.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An almost literal picture of the second half of the Kural: what is yours comes back even when you throw it away.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never say of anything, ‘I have lost it,’ but, ‘I have restored it.’”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that possessions are only on loan and return to the one who gave them.
philosophy.tie_back: Both remove the anxiety of loss: what is not truly yours goes back, whatever you do.

real_life_example.event_title: Steve Jobs leaves Apple and returns
real_life_example.event: In 1985 Steve Jobs, who had co-founded Apple Computer in 1976, lost a boardroom power struggle with chief executive John Sculley, was removed from running the Macintosh division and left the company to found NeXT. In early 1997 Apple, which needed a new operating system, bought NeXT, and Jobs returned, becoming interim chief executive later that year. Under his leadership the struggling company recovered and went on to become one of the most valuable companies in the world.
real_life_example.explanation: Jobs lost the company he had founded, yet a decade later Apple came back to him through the very company he had started after being pushed out.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that what is truly one's own will not leave even if it is carried off and thrown away, and Apple, lost by Jobs in 1985, returned to him in 1997.

tamil:
வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் கோடி
தொகுத்தார்க்கு துய்த்தல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Vaguththaan vaguththa vagaiyallaal kodi
Thoguththaarkku thuyththal aridhu.
meaning: Even people who pile up crores (tens of millions) of money can enjoy it only as much as the One who decides fate allows. Beyond that, they cannot enjoy it.
elementary: You could fill a whole room with candy, but if you have a toothache you can’t eat any of it. This kural says that piling up huge amounts of money doesn’t mean you’ll get to enjoy it; how much you actually enjoy is decided by fate.
university: The striking phrase வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை (‘the way apportioned by the Apportioner’) is one of the few places where Valluvar speaks of fate through an agent. Commentators differ on whether வகுத்தான் means God or the impersonal law of past deeds. The kural separates possession from enjoyment (துய்த்தல்): accumulation is within human reach, but the capacity to enjoy is allotted. The same gap appears in Ecclesiastes’ rich man to whom God does not give ‘power to eat thereof’, in Jesus’ parable of the rich fool, and in the myth of Midas starving amid gold. This makes the couplet a critique of hoarding as well as a statement about fate.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The opening verse of the Isha Upanishad teaches that all this is pervaded by the Lord, that one should enjoy through renunciation, and that one should not covet anyone’s wealth.
hinduism.explanation: True enjoyment comes only by accepting what is allotted by the Lord, not by grasping more.
hinduism.tie_back: Both tie enjoyment (bhoga/துய்த்தல்) to what is apportioned, not to what is accumulated.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, a rich man plans to build bigger barns and enjoy his stores, but dies that very night.
christianity.tie_back: Wealth gathered is not wealth enjoyed; the decision lies with God, just as in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: Qārūn is given treasures whose keys alone would burden a band of strong men. He boasts that he earned them by his own knowledge, and the earth swallows him with his home. Onlookers then exclaim that Allāh extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it.
islam.explanation: Enormous wealth could not protect Qārūn or be enjoyed, because it was not his by divine allotment.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows that hoarded riches are enjoyed only as far as the Apportioner allows.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A man to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth describes a man with all the wealth he wants but without God-given power to enjoy it.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the Kural itself: possession without the allotted power to enjoy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no satisfying sensual desires, even with the rain of gold coins.”
buddhism.explanation: Even a shower of gold cannot bring real satisfaction to a craving mind.
buddhism.tie_back: Both separate the amount of wealth from the enjoyment actually obtained.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The third–bhoga antarāya–hinders the enjoyment of consumable things, though he is desirous of enjoyment. The fourth–upabhoga antarāya–prevents the enjoyment of non-consumable things, although he is eager after enjoyment of such things.”
jainism.explanation: Jainism separates owning things from being able to enjoy them. Two subtypes of obstructive karma block the enjoyment of consumables and of lasting goods, even when the person has them and wants to enjoy them.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says even those who amass crores can enjoy only as much as has been apportioned to them. The Jain account of enjoyment-obstructing karma makes the same distinction between possessing and enjoying.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.13, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Why, O mind, do you plot and plan, when the Dear Lord Himself provides for your care? From rocks and stones He created living beings; He places their nourishment before them.”
sikhism.explanation: In this hymn, recited daily in the evening prayer So Dar (Rehras), Guru Arjan tells the anxious mind that sustenance (rizak) is set out by God for every creature, even those born inside rock.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says even those who amass crores enjoy only what the Ordainer has apportioned; Guru Arjan likewise teaches that each creature's portion is arranged by the Lord, so scheming adds nothing to it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asks Dionysus that everything he touches turn to gold. His bread and wine harden into gold in his mouth, and he begs to be freed from the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: Limitless gold becomes a curse because he cannot actually enjoy anything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The most vivid picture of the Kural: endless wealth, yet enjoyment is impossible.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca writes to Lucilius that the poor man is not the one who has too little, but the one who craves more.
philosophy.explanation: Wealth is measured by contentment, not by the size of one’s store.
philosophy.tie_back: Both deny that heaping up riches secures their enjoyment.

real_life_example.event_title: Alexander the Great dies at Babylon
real_life_example.event: By 323 BCE Alexander the Great had conquered the Persian Empire, taking possession of its royal treasuries, and ruled lands stretching from Greece to the Indus. In Babylon, while planning an expedition to Arabia and new projects for irrigation and sea routes, he fell ill after a banquet and died in June 323 BCE at the age of 32. He left no clear successor, and his generals soon fought one another and divided his empire.
real_life_example.explanation: The ruler who had gathered more wealth and territory than anyone before him had almost no time to enjoy any of it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even those who amass vast wealth can enjoy it only to the extent fate allows, and Alexander, master of the treasures of Persia, died within a few years of winning them.

tamil:
துறப்பார்மன் துப்புர வில்லார் உறற்பால
ஊட்டா கழியு மெனின்.
transliteration:
Thurappaarman thuppura villaar urarpaala
Oottaa kazhiyu menin.
meaning: Poor people, who have nothing to enjoy, would give up the world, if only fate let the sufferings meant for them pass by without making them go through them.
elementary: Imagine someone with an empty lunchbox. You might think it would be easy for them to say ‘I don’t need lunch.’ But they still feel hungry. This kural says poor people would give up wanting things and become monks, but fate still makes them feel the troubles they are meant to go through, so they can’t let go.
university: This is the chapter’s most compressed and most debated couplet. துப்புரவு (thuppuravu) means the means of enjoyment; those without it (the destitute) would seem to be natural renunciants, since they have nothing to give up. The particle மன் signals an unrealised possibility: they *would* renounce, *if* the sufferings that are theirs to experience (உறற்பால) passed away without being fed to them (ஊட்டா கழியும்). The implication is ironic: poverty does not automatically produce detachment, because fate still insists that its allotted pains be tasted. This fits the karmic principle, shared with Buddhism and Jainism, that ripened deeds must be experienced and cannot simply be skipped.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who has taken his birth is sure to die, and after death one is sure to take birth again. Therefore, in the unavoidable discharge of your duty, you should not lament.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names certain things as aparihārya, unavoidable, and something that must simply be passed through.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts speak of experiences that cannot be skipped and must be undergone.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass.”
christianity.explanation: Job says each human life runs within limits God has fixed.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘sufferings that are one’s portion’, Job’s troubles run within set bounds.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘Never will we be struck except by what Allāh has decreed for us; He is our protector.’ And upon Allāh let the believers rely.”
islam.explanation: Every affliction that reaches a person has already been decreed.
islam.tie_back: Both hold that the troubles meant for someone will reach them.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For against your will were you formed, against your will were you born, against your will you live, against your will you will die.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah reminds people that the basic course of life is imposed on them, not chosen.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say a person cannot opt out of the experiences allotted to them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha states that intentional deeds that have been done and accumulated do not come to an end without their results being experienced, whether in this life or later.
buddhism.explanation: Ripened kamma must be lived through; it cannot be cancelled simply by wishing.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the very principle behind the Kural: the sufferings due to a person must be ‘fed’ to them before they pass.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By pondering (on what he has learned) he loosens the firm hold which the seven kinds of Karman, except the Âyushka (have upon the soul); he shortens their duration when it was to be a long one; he mitigates their power when it was intense.” … “By austerities he cuts off the Karman.”
jainism.explanation: Jainism agrees that bound karma has to come to fruition, but holds that reflection and austerity (tapas) can shorten it, weaken it, and wear it away before it ripens in full. That process, nirjarā, is the purpose of renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar suggests the destitute would renounce if destined suffering did not still have to be lived through. Jainism accepts that karma must be dealt with but answers differently: renunciation and austerity are how destined suffering is cut short.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.22 and 29.27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So many endure distress, deprivation and constant abuse. Even these are Your Gifts, O Great Giver!”
sikhism.explanation: In the twenty-fifth pauri of Japji Guru Nanak says that the hunger and suffering many people endure are also part of what the Giver hands out.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural, in its most debated couplet, says the destitute would renounce the world if fate did not make them live through their allotted sufferings; Japji also sees such suffering as allotted, though as a gift to be accepted rather than a debt fate collects.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib, Pauri 25, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Pandora lifts the lid of the jar, countless ills fly out to roam among mortals, and only Hope stays inside. Hesiod says there is no way to escape the will of Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Troubles are released into human life by divine design and cannot be avoided.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both portray sufferings as a destined portion that mortals cannot escape.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Demand not that events should happen as you wish; but wish them to happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches peace through accepting whatever comes rather than demanding escape from it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural observes that the poor cannot reach detachment while fated sufferings press on them; Epictetus offers acceptance as the way through.

real_life_example.event_title: Carolina Maria de Jesus publishes her favela diary
real_life_example.event: Carolina Maria de Jesus, a Black single mother of three, lived in a shack in a Sao Paulo favela and supported her children by collecting paper and scrap to sell, writing a diary in notebooks she found in the rubbish. Her diary of the years 1955 to 1960 was published in Sao Paulo in 1960 as Quarto de Despejo, later translated into English as Child of the Dark. It described hunger and daily struggle in plain terms and became one of the best-selling books in Brazilian history.
real_life_example.explanation: Her diary showed readers that poverty is not a peaceful simplicity but a daily round of hunger, worry and hard labour.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural observes that the destitute, who have nothing, would seem ready to renounce the world, yet fate still makes them taste the hardships allotted to them, and de Jesus's diary records how having little brought not detachment but constant struggle.

tamil:
நன்றாங்கால் நல்லவாக் காண்பவர் அன்றாங்கால்
அல்லற் படுவ தெவன்.
transliteration:
Nandraangaal nallavaak kaanbavar andraangaal
Allar paduva thevan.
meaning: People who happily accept good times as good, why should they get upset when bad times come? Both come from the same fate.
elementary: When you win a game you say ‘Yay, lucky me!’ So when you lose, why get so upset? Both winning and losing come from the same luck. This kural asks us to take the bad days as calmly as we enjoy the good ones.
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question with a Stoic edge. If good fortune (நன்று) and misfortune (அன்று) both come from ஊழ், then welcoming one and lamenting the other is inconsistent. Mu. Varadarasan glosses it as good deeds and evil deeds ripening, which ties the couplet to karmic reasoning. The ethical advice is equanimity (சமநிலை): accept both outcomes as coming from one source. It is closely echoed in Job’s reply to his wife, in the Mishnah’s rule to bless God for the bad as for the good, in the Gita’s teaching on bearing pleasure and pain alike, in the Buddha’s eight worldly conditions, and in Nietzsche’s amor fati.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, the nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons … one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares joy and sorrow to seasons that come and go and should be borne calmly.
hinduism.tie_back: The same counsel as the Kural: take good and bad with equal composure.

christianity.quote_or_event: “What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?”
christianity.explanation: Job refuses to curse God after catastrophe, reasoning that good and ill come from the same hand.
christianity.tie_back: Nearly word for word the Kural’s question: if you accept the good, why protest the bad?

islam.quote_or_event: “No disaster strikes upon the earth or among yourselves except that it is in a register before We bring it into being … In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: Because both loss and gain are pre-recorded, believers should neither despair nor exult.
islam.tie_back: The same logic as the Kural: one decree governs gain and loss, so meet both evenly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good that befalls him.”
judaism.explanation: Jewish law requires blessing God for misfortune as well as for good fortune.
judaism.tie_back: It puts the Kural’s question into practice: respond to bad as you would to good.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha names eight worldly conditions: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. They come to everyone, and the instructed disciple is neither carried away by the pleasant nor crushed by the unpleasant.
buddhism.explanation: Good and bad fortune are paired features of every life and should be met with the same composure.
buddhism.tie_back: A close parallel to the Kural’s challenge to meet misfortune as calmly as fortune.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By conquering his passions he becomes free from passions; thereby he becomes indifferent to happiness and pains.”
jainism.explanation: In Mahāvīra's lecture on exertion in righteousness, conquering the passions (kaṣāya) brings an evenness in which pleasure and pain, both seen as the ripening of karma, no longer cause elation or distress.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks why those who welcome good fortune should grieve at misfortune, since both come from the same source. The Jain ideal of being indifferent to happiness and pain gives that even-mindedness a practical basis.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That man, who in the midst of pain, does not feel pain, who is not affected by pleasure, affection or fear, and who looks alike upon gold and dust;”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person in whom God dwells as one who is not shaken by pain and not carried away by pleasure, holding gold and dust alike.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks why one who welcomes good fortune should grieve at misfortune, since both come from the same source; Guru Tegh Bahadur portrays the person who meets pleasure and pain with exactly that evenness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles tells the grieving Priam that two jars stand on Zeus’ threshold, one of good gifts and one of evil. Zeus gives some men a mixture and others only evil, so mortals must endure what is given.
greek_mythology.explanation: Good and bad fortune are dispensed by the same god, so grief must be borne.
greek_mythology.tie_back: One source for both good and ill, and so a call to endure the bad: the same reasoning as the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Nietzsche resolves to learn to see what is necessary in things as beautiful, and names this ‘amor fati’, love of fate: to be one day only a Yes-sayer.
philosophy.explanation: Rather than resenting misfortune, one should embrace the whole of what is fated.
philosophy.tie_back: It goes a step beyond the Kural: not just avoiding distress at misfortune but loving the fate that brings it.

real_life_example.event_title: Shackleton's men survive the loss of the Endurance
real_life_example.place: Weddell Sea, Elephant Island and South Georgia, Antarctica and the South Atlantic
real_life_example.event: Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance, carrying his expedition to cross Antarctica, was trapped in the Weddell Sea ice in January 1915 and slowly crushed, and the crew abandoned her in October 1915. Shackleton gave up the original goal and turned the expedition into an effort to save every man: they camped on the ice for months, sailed in open boats to Elephant Island, and Shackleton and five others then crossed some 800 miles of ocean to South Georgia to fetch help. After several attempts he rescued the men left on Elephant Island in August 1916, and none of the Endurance crew died.
real_life_example.explanation: Shackleton accepted the collapse of his great ambition without despair and put all his energy into the new task that misfortune had handed him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks why those who welcome good fortune should be distressed by bad, since both come from the same fate, and Shackleton met the loss of his ship and his goal with the same steady purpose he had brought to the expedition's hopeful start.

tamil:
ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள மற்றொன்று
சூழினுந் தான்முந் துறும்.
transliteration:
Oozhir peruvali yaavula matrondru
Soozhinun thaanmun thurum.
meaning: What is stronger than fate? Even when a person finds another way to escape it, fate gets there first.
elementary: Imagine playing tag with someone who always knows which way you’ll run and is already waiting there. That’s how this kural describes fate: whatever clever path you choose to avoid it, fate is already there ahead of you.
university: The chapter, and with it the whole Book of Virtue (அறத்துப்பால்), ends on a rhetorical question: ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள, ‘what is of greater strength than fate?’ The second line gives the reason: even if one plans (சூழினும்) another course, fate itself arrives first (தான் முந்துறும்). The positioning matters. After thirty-seven chapters on virtue, Valluvar closes by acknowledging the limits of human agency. Book 2 (Porul) then opens with vigorous chapters on effort, and later ones such as ஆள்வினையுடைமை (e.g. Kural 620) even assert that tireless striving can push fate aside. The tension is intended, and it mirrors the Stoic formula that fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling, as well as the Oedipus myth, in which the flight from prophecy is what fulfils it.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Under illusion you are now declining to act according to My direction. But, compelled by the work born of your own nature, you will act all the same, O son of Kuntī.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that his refusal to fight is futile; his own nature will drive him to it anyway.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that whatever path you choose instead, the destined course still overtakes you.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There are many devices in a man’s heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.”
christianity.explanation: Whatever plans people make, God’s purpose is what finally prevails.
christianity.tie_back: It closely mirrors the Kural: human schemes (சூழினும்) are overtaken by a stronger decree.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you should be within towers of lofty construction.”
islam.explanation: No fortress or plan can keep off what God has decreed.
islam.tie_back: The decree ‘arrives first’ wherever one hides, just as fate does in the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Everything is foreseen yet freedom of choice is granted.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Akiva holds together God’s total foreknowledge and genuine human free will.
judaism.tie_back: A contrastive entry: it agrees nothing escapes God’s knowledge but, unlike the Kural, keeps real room for choice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither in the sky nor in mid-ocean, nor by entering into mountain clefts, nowhere in the world is there a place where one may escape from the results of evil deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: No hiding place allows escape from the ripening of one’s past actions.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says every attempt to escape is met by what is already on its way.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Every good deed will bear its fruit to men; there is no escape from the effect of one's actions.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra tells King Brahmadatta that both of their present lives, one a monk and the other a king, are the unavoidable results of earlier deeds. In Jainism the force no plan can outrun is the ripening of one's own karma, not an external fate.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ends the Book of Virtue by asking what is mightier than fate, which gets there first whatever way of escape one plans. The Jain answer is that 'there is no escape from the effect of one's actions'.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, whatever I wish for does not happen. What can I accomplish by merely thinking? The Lord does whatever He wishes; it is not up to me at all.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir admits that his own plans count for nothing, because the Lord carries out His own will, which is often beyond what one has even imagined.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural closes the Book of Virtue by asking what is mightier than fate, which arrives first even when one plans another way; Kabir likewise says the Lord's will prevails over whatever we plan.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1376, Salok Bhagat Kabir 219 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Told by the Delphic oracle that he will kill his father and marry his mother, Oedipus flees Corinth to avoid it. On the road he kills a stranger, Laius, his real father, and in Thebes he marries the widowed queen, his mother.
greek_mythology.explanation: The very plan made to escape the prophecy is what brings it about.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The perfect illustration of the Kural: devise another way, and fate is there first.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca quotes Cleanthes’ prayer to Zeus and Destiny, whose closing thought is that the Fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoics taught that fate will be fulfilled either way; one can only choose whether to go willingly.
philosophy.tie_back: Resistance does not change the destination, which is the Kural’s point about fate’s supremacy.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 107.10-11 (quoting Cleanthes)

real_life_example.event_title: The royal family's flight to Varennes
real_life_example.event: On the night of 20-21 June 1791 King Louis XVI, Queen Marie Antoinette and their children left the Tuileries palace in Paris in disguise, hoping to reach loyal troops near the eastern frontier. At Sainte-Menehould the postmaster's son, Jean-Baptiste Drouet, recognised the travellers and took steps that led to the royal party being stopped and arrested when they reached Varennes. They were escorted back to Paris, arriving on 25 June, and the failed escape destroyed much of the public's remaining trust in the monarchy.
real_life_example.explanation: A carefully planned escape not only failed but hastened the very downfall it was meant to avoid.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what is mightier than fate, since even when a person devises another way out, fate arrives first, and at Varennes the king's planned escape was overtaken a short distance from safety.

tamil:
படைகுடி கூழ்அமைச்சு நட்பரண் ஆறும்
உடையான் அரசருள் ஏறு.
transliteration:
Padai kudi koozh amaichu natparan aarum
Udaiyaan arasarul eru.
meaning: A ruler who has all six parts of a strong country (an army, loyal people, plenty of food and money, ministers, friendly allies and strong forts) is like a lion among kings.
elementary: Think of a strong table that needs all its legs to stand. A kingdom needs six “legs”: soldiers, happy people, food and money, good helpers, friends, and strong walls. A king who has all six is like the lion — the strongest of all the kings.
university: Valluvar opens the Book of Polity not with the king’s personality but with a structural inventory of the state: padai (army), kudi (citizenry), koozh (food/revenue), amaichu (ministry), natpu (alliances), and aran (fortification). This six-limbed model closely parallels the saptanga (“seven-limbed”) theory of the state found in Kautilya’s Arthashastra, minus the king himself — who in the Kural is the one who ‘possesses’ the six, making him the integrating seventh element. The image of the ‘eru’ (a male lion or bull, the pre-eminent male of its kind) frames kingship as excellence in a competitive field of rulers rather than divine right. The chapter structure of the Porutpaal then follows this list, with later chapters devoted to each limb (army, fortress, friendship, ministers), so this kural functions as a table of contents for the whole book of statecraft.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya lists the constituent elements of sovereignty as the king, the minister, the country, the fort, the treasury, the army, and the ally (Arthashastra 6.1, the saptanga theory).
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya’s classic Indian theory says a state is made of seven parts that must all be healthy for the kingdom to survive.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s six possessions of a great king are almost exactly Kautilya’s list once the king himself is set aside.

christianity.quote_or_event: “In the multitude of people is the king’s honour: but in the want of people is the destruction of the prince.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says a king’s glory depends on having many people under him; without them his rule collapses.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘kudi’ (the people) as a core limb of royal greatness, though it names only one of the six elements.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an instructs the community to prepare whatever strength and war-horses it can muster so that enemies are deterred (Qur’an 8:60).
islam.explanation: Muslims are told to be ready with military strength so that enemies think twice about attacking.
islam.tie_back: Parallels the ‘padai’ (army) and ‘aran’ (defence) limbs of the Kural’s strong state.

judaism.quote_or_event: Solomon’s reign is described with an organised cabinet of officials (1 Kings 4:1-7), district officers supplying provisions (4:7, 4:22-23), vast stables of horses and chariots (4:26), and a treaty of friendship with Hiram of Tyre (5:12).
judaism.explanation: The Bible pictures Solomon’s kingdom as great because it had ministers, food supplies, an army, and allies all at once.
judaism.tie_back: Solomon’s kingdom is a narrative illustration of nearly every limb the Kural names: ministers, provisions, army, and alliance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) is said to possess seven ‘treasures’, including the elephant and horse treasures (military might), the householder treasure (wealth), and the counsellor treasure (wise minister) (e.g. Mahasudassana Sutta, DN 17).
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist texts imagine the ideal world-ruler as owning seven special treasures that make his rule complete.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it defines the supreme king by a checklist of possessions — army, wealth, and counsel among them.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a universal monarch with his fourfold army and great power, the possessor of the fourteen attributes of a king, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana uses the cakravartin (universal monarch), with his fourfold army and fourteen royal treasures, as a byword for unmatched sovereign strength. A few verses earlier (11.20) it uses the other image found in this kural: the proud lion that is 'superior to all animals'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's king with all six limbs of state stands among rulers like a lion among beasts. The Jain text draws on the same picture of the fully equipped monarch who has no equal, though it uses it to praise the learned monk.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.22 (cf. 11.20) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: After the martyrdom of his father Guru Arjan, Guru Hargobind took up two swords at his succession, standing for temporal (miri) and spiritual (piri) authority. He trained in arms, built up a Sikh army, fortified his towns, built the Lohgarh fort near Amritsar, and in 1609 founded the Akal Takht as a seat where both the spiritual and the temporal affairs of the community could be settled.
sikhism.explanation: Guru Hargobind gave the Sikh community the means of a self-governing body, with an army, fortifications and a seat of authority, alongside its spiritual life.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural lists army, people, resources, counsel, allies and fortification as the parts of a strong state; Guru Hargobind's miri-piri reforms gave the young Panth several of these same limbs.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guru Hargobind' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod’s account, Zeus wins and keeps his kingship over the gods only by gathering allies — the Cyclopes who forge his thunderbolt and the Hundred-Handed ones who fight beside him against the Titans.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even Zeus needed weapons, fighters, and friends to become and stay king of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s point that a ruler’s supremacy rests on army and allies, not on personal power alone.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “First, there must be food; secondly, arts, for life requires many instruments; thirdly, there must be arms … fourthly, there must be a certain amount of revenue, both for internal needs, and for the purposes of war; fifthly, or rather first, there must be a care of religion … sixthly, and most necessary of all …”
philosophy.explanation: Setting out what a state cannot exist without, Aristotle lists six requisites, among them food, arms, revenue and, last and most necessary, a power of deciding what is just and expedient among citizens.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s six limbs of the state, Aristotle’s list gives six things a polity must have, including the army and the treasury, though the two lists differ item by item.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics, Book VII, ch. 8 (1328b) (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: R. Shamasastry rediscovers Kautilya's Arthashastra
real_life_example.event: In 1905 the Sanskrit scholar Rudrapatna Shamasastry, working as a librarian at the Oriental Library in Mysore, identified a manuscript of the Arthashastra, the ancient Indian treatise on statecraft attributed to Kautilya, which had been known only through later references and was thought to be lost. He published the Sanskrit text in 1909 and an English translation in 1915. The publication brought the treatise to the attention of scholars around the world.
real_life_example.explanation: The rediscovery gave historians a detailed ancient Indian account of how a state should be built and run, including its army, revenue, ministers, alliances and fortifications. It transformed the study of early Indian political thought.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural lists the parts a ruler must possess, army, people, resources, ministers, allies and forts, and the rediscovered Arthashastra is the classic Indian treatise that analyses the state through closely similar elements.

tamil:
