அஞ்சாமை ஈகை அறிவூக்கம் இந்நான்கும்
எஞ்சாமை வேந்தர்க் கியல்பு.
transliteration:
Anjaamai eegai arivookkam innaankum
Enjaamai vendhark kiyalbu.
meaning: Courage, generosity, wisdom and energy: never lacking these four is the true nature of a king.
elementary: A good team captain is brave, shares with everyone, knows what to do, and never gets lazy. This kural says a real king must have all four of these — and never run out of any of them.
university: Having described the external assets of the state, Valluvar now names the four inner qualities of the ruler: anjaamai (fearlessness), eegai (liberality), arivu (wisdom), and ookkam (energy or zeal). The key word is enjaamai — ‘without deficiency’ — which makes the standard one of constancy: a king who is brave in one crisis but timid in the next, or generous only when convenient, does not meet it. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar pair the qualities functionally: courage and energy to act, wisdom to decide rightly, and generosity to bind people to the ruler. The list resembles the Bhagavad Gita’s catalogue of kshatriya traits and Plato’s requirements for the philosopher-ruler, suggesting a widely shared intuition that rulership needs both a warrior’s nerve and a sage’s judgment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Heroism, power, determination, resourcefulness, courage in battle, generosity and leadership are the natural qualities of work for the kṣatriyas.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the natural qualities of the warrior-ruler class: bravery, strength, firmness, skill, generosity, and the ability to lead.
hinduism.tie_back: Heroism and courage match anjaamai, generosity matches eegai, and determination/resourcefulness match ookkam and arivu.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD;”
christianity.explanation: Isaiah describes the coming ideal king, whom Christians identify with Christ, as filled with wisdom, good counsel, and strength.
christianity.tie_back: Wisdom and might together echo the Kural’s pairing of arivu with courage and energy.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and has increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature.”
islam.explanation: When the Israelites doubted Talut (Saul) as king because he was not rich, their prophet replied that God had given him more knowledge and strength.
islam.tie_back: Kingship is justified by wisdom and physical/moral strength — two of the Kural’s four royal qualities.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.”
judaism.explanation: God tells Joshua, the new leader of Israel, to be strong and fearless as he takes command.
judaism.tie_back: Echoes anjaamai — fearlessness as the first requirement of leadership.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The ‘ten royal virtues’ (dasa raja dhamma) listed in the Jataka tradition begin with dana (generosity) and include sila (morality), pariccaga (self-sacrifice), and tapa (self-discipline/energy).
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist stories give kings a list of ten virtues, starting with generosity.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s idea of a fixed set of royal virtues with generosity central, though Buddhist lists stress gentleness over fearlessness.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He (bears everything) like the earth; he annihilates (his Karman); he is free from greed; he, the Omniscient, does not keep store (of anything); he has crossed the ocean of life like the sea: he, the Hero, who grants protection to all, and whose perception is infinite.”
jainism.explanation: In the hymn to Mahavira, the ideal person is called the Hero (Vira), who gives protection, the gift of fearlessness (abhaya), to all beings, and whose knowledge has no limit. The same lecture ranks 'giving safety' as the best of gifts.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's four royal qualities are fearlessness, liberality, wisdom and energy. The Jain praise of Mahavira joins heroism, the giving of protection and boundless wisdom in a single figure, though it describes a spiritual hero rather than a king.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.6.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else - says Nanak, listen, mind: call him spiritually wise.”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks Guru Tegh Bahadur defines the truly wise person as one who neither intimidates others nor is intimidated by them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural names fearlessness and wisdom among the four qualities a ruler must never lack; Guru Tegh Bahadur joins the same two, making fearlessness itself a mark of wisdom.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9, Salok 16, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sarpedon tells Glaucus that kings are honoured with the best seats, meat, and lands only because they must fight in the front ranks; privilege is earned by courage.
greek_mythology.explanation: A Trojan-allied prince explains that kings get special honours only because they are the bravest in battle.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Links royal standing to fearlessness, just as the Kural makes anjaamai a permanent kingly trait.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato has Socrates list the natural gifts required in the philosopher who would rule: good memory, quickness to learn, magnificence (greatness of spirit), graciousness, and kinship with truth, justice, courage, and temperance.
philosophy.explanation: Plato says the ideal ruler must be quick-minded, big-hearted, and brave.
philosophy.tie_back: Wisdom, greatness of spirit, and courage correspond to arivu, eegai, and anjaamai.

real_life_example.event_title: Elizabeth I addresses her troops at Tilbury
real_life_example.event: As the Spanish Armada threatened England in the summer of 1588, Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, commander of the land forces, arranged for Queen Elizabeth I to visit the army camp at Tilbury on the Thames. In early August she reviewed the troops and delivered a speech meant to encourage the men to stand firm against a possible invasion led by the Duke of Parma. The speech became one of the most celebrated in English history.
real_life_example.explanation: At a moment of national danger the queen went in person among her soldiers rather than remaining safe in London. Her visit became a lasting symbol of a ruler's courage and energy in a crisis.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar names fearlessness and energetic drive among the qualities a ruler must never lack, and Elizabeth showed both by going to the front to rally her army.

tamil:
தூங்காமை கல்வி துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றும்
நீங்கா நிலனான் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Thoongaamai kalvi thunivudaimai immoondrum
Neengaa nilanaan bavarkku.
meaning: Being alert and never slow, being learned, and being brave and firm: these three must never leave those who rule a land.
elementary: A good lifeguard never falls asleep on duty, knows how to swim and rescue, and jumps in bravely when needed. A ruler needs the same three things: stay awake, keep learning, and be brave enough to act.
university: Thoongaamai literally means ‘not sleeping’, and the commentators read it as freedom from sloth and delay — prompt action when action is due. Kalvi (learning) and thunivu (decisive courage) complete the triad, and the verb neengaa (‘must not depart’) again stresses that these are permanent dispositions, not occasional performances. The combination is significant: learning without resolve produces a hesitant ruler, and resolve without learning produces a reckless one, while both fail without vigilance. Kautilya’s Arthashastra makes the same point in its timetable for the king, which divides the day and night into tasks and insists that the king ‘shall ever be wakeful’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “IF a king is energetic, his subjects will be equally energetic. If he is reckless, they will not only be reckless likewise, but also eat into his works. Besides, a reckless king will easily fall into the hands of his enemies. Hence the king shall ever be wakeful.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya says the people copy the king’s energy or laziness, so the king must always stay alert.
hinduism.tie_back: “Ever be wakeful” is almost a literal rendering of the Kural’s thoongaamai (sleeplessness/vigilance).

christianity.quote_or_event: “...he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the church that whoever has the gift of leading must lead diligently, not lazily.
christianity.tie_back: Diligence in ruling parallels thoongaamai — the ruler’s refusal to be slothful.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that the strong believer is better and more beloved to God than the weak one, and urged believers to strive eagerly for what benefits them, seek God’s help, and not give in to helplessness (Sahih Muslim 2664).
islam.explanation: Muslims are told to be strong and keen, and never to give up or become passive.
islam.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s pairing of unflagging effort with firm resolve.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:”
judaism.explanation: The Torah requires Israel’s king to write his own copy of the law and study it every day of his life.
judaism.tie_back: Makes lifelong learning (kalvi) a legal duty of kingship, as the Kural makes it a quality that must never leave the ruler.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “I am never content with exerting myself or with despatching business. Truly, I consider the welfare of all to be my duty, and the root of this is exertion and the prompt despatch of business.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist emperor Ashoka says he never stops working hard and dealing quickly with the business of state, because the welfare of all depends on it.
buddhism.tie_back: “Prompt despatch of business” is exactly the no-delay alertness that thoongaamai demands.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict VI (tr. S. Dhammika)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's sermon to his chief disciple Gautama repeats 'be careful all the while' (do not be heedless, pramada, even for a moment) as a refrain for all thirty-six verses. Sloth and delay are the danger he warns against most.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's first requirement is thoongaamai, a wakefulness that never puts off what must be done. Mahavira's refrain is the Jain version of the same never-sleeping vigilance, though he aims it at the soul's liberation rather than at governing a land.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who remain awake and aware are saved, while those who sleep are plundered.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das warns that only those who stay alert are protected, while the careless sleeper is robbed of everything of value.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says sleepless vigilance must never leave those who rule; Guru Amar Das gives the same warning that whoever stops keeping watch loses what they hold.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 34, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “To sleep the whole night through beseemeth not a man that is a counsellor, to whom a host is entrusted, and upon whom rest so many cares.”
greek_mythology.explanation: A dream sent by Zeus scolds King Agamemnon: a leader responsible for an army should not sleep all night.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A near-literal statement of thoongaamai — a ruler must not ‘sleep’ on his responsibilities.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy, and political greatness and wisdom meet in one... cities will never have rest from their evils.”
philosophy.explanation: Plato argues that cities will suffer until rulers become truly learned and wise.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s insistence that kalvi (learning) must never depart from those who rule.

real_life_example.event_title: Peter the Great works in foreign shipyards during the Grand Embassy
real_life_example.place: Zaandam and Amsterdam, Dutch Republic; Deptford, England
real_life_example.event: In 1697 Tsar Peter I of Russia travelled west with a large diplomatic mission, the Grand Embassy, under the assumed name of Pyotr Mikhailov. In the Dutch Republic he studied shipbuilding and worked as a ship's carpenter in the Dutch East India Company's yard, and in England he worked at the Royal Navy dockyard at Deptford and visited factories, arsenals and other institutions. On his return he began sweeping reforms and built up a Russian navy.
real_life_example.explanation: Peter combined a tireless drive to act with a determination to learn practical skills himself, and then had the resolve to impose far-reaching changes on his country.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a ruler must never lose alertness, learning and firm resolve, and Peter's hands-on study abroad followed by bold reform displays all three.

tamil:
அறனிழுக்கா தல்லவை நீக்கி மறனிழுக்கா
மானம் உடைய தரசு.
transliteration:
Aranizhukkaa thallavai neekki maranizhukkaa
Maanam udaiya tharasu.
meaning: A true king never turns away from what is right, removes what is wrong from the land, and keeps a brave sense of honor that never falls short.
elementary: A good referee always follows the rules, sends off players who cheat, and is brave enough to make hard calls. This kural says a real ruler is like that: always fair, stops wrongdoing, and never loses courage or self-respect.
university: The couplet is built on a pair of parallel negatives: aran izhukkaa (not slipping from dharma) and maran izhukkaa (not slipping from martial valour), bound together by maanam — honour or self-respect. Between them sits the positive duty allavai neekki, ‘removing what is not right’, which commentators read both as the king avoiding vice himself and as his suppressing wrongdoing in the realm. The effect is to insist that courage and justice must travel together: valour without righteousness becomes tyranny, while righteousness without valour cannot protect anyone. This coupling of justice and courage has a close analogue in Cicero’s claim that greatness of spirit divorced from justice is a vice rather than a virtue.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If the king did not, without tiring, inflict punishment on those worthy to be punished, the stronger would roast the weaker, like fish on a spit;”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu say that if the king fails to punish wrongdoers, the strong will destroy the weak.
hinduism.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s ‘allavai neekki’ — the king’s duty to remove unrighteousness from the land.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says a king’s rule becomes secure when wicked people are removed from his presence.
christianity.tie_back: Directly parallels ‘allavai neekki’ — removing the unrighteous so that rule rests on justice.

islam.quote_or_event: “O David, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow [your own] desire, as it will lead you astray from the way of Allah.”
islam.explanation: God tells King David to rule with truth and not follow his own wishes.
islam.tie_back: Matches ‘aran izhukkaa’ — a ruler who never slips from righteousness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thus saith the LORD; Execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor: and do no wrong, do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless, nor the widow...”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah tells the king of Judah to do justice, rescue the oppressed, and never do wrong himself.
judaism.tie_back: Combines the Kural’s two duties: staying righteous oneself and actively removing oppression.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that when kings are unrighteous, their ministers, officials, and people become unrighteous too, and even nature falls out of order; when kings are righteous, righteousness spreads downward through the whole realm (AN 4.70).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a king’s goodness or badness flows down to everyone in the kingdom.
buddhism.tie_back: Explains why the Kural requires the king to never slip from dharma — his conduct sets the moral tone of the land.

jainism.quote_or_event: Indra: “Punishing thieves and robbers, cut-purses and burglars, you should establish public safety; thus you will be a Kshattriya.” Nami: “Men frequently apply punishment wrongly: the innocent are put in prison, and the perpetrator of the crime is set at liberty.”
jainism.explanation: Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, tests the renouncing king Nami by pressing royal duties on him, including rooting out wrongdoers. Nami answers that outward justice often misfires, and turns instead to conquering the passions within.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar praises the king who never slips from dharma and removes what is unrighteous from the land. The Jain dialogue accepts that this is the warrior's duty but questions how reliable punishment is, and puts the deeper removal of wrong inside the self.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.28–30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, in a hymn included in the Guru Granth Sahib, says the true hero is one who fights for righteousness and does not abandon the field even when cut to pieces.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural joins never swerving from righteousness with a valour and honour that never falls short; Kabir's hero is defined by exactly that union of dharma and unyielding courage.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On his way to Athens, the young Theseus deliberately takes the dangerous land route and kills a series of bandits (Sinis, Sciron, Procrustes and others) who preyed on travellers, before becoming king.
greek_mythology.explanation: Theseus bravely clears the road of robbers and murderers, making it safe for everyone, and later becomes a respected king.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows courage harnessed to justice — removing wrongdoers — which is the Kural’s joining of maram with aram.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that the loftiness of spirit shown in danger and toil, if it lacks justice and fights for selfish ends rather than the common good, is a vice rather than a virtue.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero says bravery is only good when it serves justice; bravery for selfish ends is actually bad.
philosophy.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s insistence that valour (maram) and righteousness (aram) must both remain unbroken together.

real_life_example.event_title: King Haakon VII refuses to appoint Quisling
real_life_example.event: After Germany invaded Norway, the German envoy Curt Brauer met King Haakon VII on 10 April 1940 and demanded that he dismiss the lawful government and appoint a government headed by the collaborator Vidkun Quisling. At an extraordinary Council of State the king said he could not comply and would rather abdicate than appoint Quisling, while leaving the decision to his ministers, who supported him. German aircraft then bombed Nybergsund, and the king later continued the resistance from exile in Britain.
real_life_example.explanation: Haakon refused to lend royal authority to an illegitimate regime even under direct military threat. His refusal became a rallying point for Norwegian resistance throughout the occupation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes a king who never swerves from righteousness, removes what is wrong and never loses courage or honour, and Haakon's refusal joined justice and courage at the cost of great personal danger.

tamil:
இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலுங் காத்தலும் காத்த
வகுத்தலும் வல்ல தரசு.
transliteration:
Iyatralum eettalung kaaththalum kaaththa
Vaguththalum valla tharasu.
meaning: A good ruler knows how to create sources of money, collect it, keep it safe, and then share out what was kept safe in a wise way.
elementary: Think of a farmer who plants seeds, harvests the crop, stores it safely in a barn, and then shares it out so everyone has food all year. A good ruler does the same with the country’s wealth: make it, collect it, protect it, and share it fairly.
university: This is the Kural’s compact theory of public finance, expressed as four verbs: iyatral (generating new sources of revenue), eettal (collecting), kaaththal (guarding), and vaguththal (apportioning or allocating). The sequence is cyclical — well-allocated spending produces the prosperity from which new revenue is generated — and it treats wealth as a means of governance rather than a royal possession. Commentators note that vaguththal implies planned allocation among competing ends (defence, welfare, religious and civic works), not merely generosity. The same logic appears in Kalidasa’s praise of King Dilipa, who taxed his people only as the sun draws up water, in order to return it a thousandfold as rain.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa says King Dilipa collected taxes from his subjects only for their own welfare, just as the sun draws up moisture only to return it a thousandfold as rain.
hinduism.explanation: A famous Sanskrit poem compares a good king to the sun, which takes water from the earth only to give it back as much more rain.
hinduism.tie_back: Captures the Kural’s full cycle: gathering wealth (eettal) only in order to distribute it wisely (vaguththal).

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the Lord said, Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his lord shall make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of meat in due season?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus praises the wise manager who distributes food to the household at the right time.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the guarding (kaaththal) and timely distribution (vaguththal) of resources.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Joseph] said, ‘Appoint me over the storehouses of the land. Indeed, I will be a knowing guardian.’”
islam.explanation: Prophet Joseph asks the king of Egypt to put him in charge of the nation’s storehouses, promising to guard them wisely.
islam.tie_back: ‘Knowing guardian’ of the storehouses is precisely the Kural’s kaaththal (safeguarding) joined to wise management.

judaism.quote_or_event: Joseph advises Pharaoh to collect a fifth of the harvest during seven years of plenty, store it in the cities under guard, and distribute it during the seven years of famine (Genesis 41:34-36, 41:47-57).
judaism.explanation: Joseph saves Egypt by collecting grain in good years, keeping it safe, and handing it out during the famine.
judaism.tie_back: Enacts all of the Kural’s stages — gathering, storing, guarding, and distributing wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, a king troubled by banditry is advised not to raise taxes or punish, but to give seed and fodder to farmers, capital to traders, and wages to officials; the country then prospers and the treasury fills.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells of a king who fixed crime and poverty by investing in farmers, merchants, and workers, which made the whole kingdom richer.
buddhism.tie_back: Illustrates iyatral — generating new sources of wealth — and wise allocation (vaguththal).

jainism.quote_or_event: “If there were numberless mountains of gold and silver, as big as Kailâsa, they would not satisfy a greedy man; for his avidity is boundless like space.”
jainism.explanation: When Indra tells King Nami to multiply his gold, jewels and treasury 'then you will be a true Kshattriya', Nami answers that no amount of wealth can satisfy craving. For laypeople, Jainism directs wealth through the vow of limiting possessions (parigraha-parimana) rather than through endless accumulation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar sets out how a government should create, collect, guard and distribute wealth. The Jain text, taking the renunciant's view, warns about the greed that a full treasury can feed, which is a counterweight to this kural, not a parallel.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.46–48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says the true path is to live by honest labour and to share part of what one earns, the basis of the Sikh ideals of kirat karni and vand chhakna.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's theory of government runs from producing and gathering wealth to distributing it wisely; Guru Nanak gives the same cycle of earning and sharing at the level of the individual householder.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas wishes that everything he touches turn to gold, and nearly starves because his wealth cannot be used; he begs Dionysus to undo the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: A king who only wanted to pile up gold found that wealth that cannot be used is worthless.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A cautionary contrast: acquisition without right use fails, whereas the Kural demands that gathered wealth be distributed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The Aristotelian Oeconomica holds that the manager of a household or estate must be able to acquire wealth, to preserve it, and to make proper use of it.
philosophy.explanation: An ancient Greek treatise on management says good managers must know how to earn, keep, and use wealth.
philosophy.tie_back: Nearly the same sequence of competences as the Kural’s generate-gather-guard-distribute.

real_life_example.event_title: The Inca state's network of storehouses
real_life_example.event: The Inca Empire built large numbers of state storehouses, called qollqa or colcas, along its road network and near administrative centres. Surplus food, cloth, raw materials and other goods produced through labour owed to the state were stored in them and recorded by officials using knotted-string quipu. The stores supplied armies and state workers and were used to support communities when harvests failed.
real_life_example.explanation: The storehouse system turned the empire's production into a reserve that could be protected and redistributed where it was needed. It helped the empire survive poor harvests and sustain its armies across great distances.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar describes good government as creating wealth, collecting it, guarding it and distributing it wisely, and the Inca storehouses carried out each of these four tasks.

tamil:
காட்சிக் கெளியன் கடுஞ்சொல்லன் அல்லனேல்
மீக்கூறும் மன்னன் நிலம்.
transliteration:
Kaatchik keliyan kadunjollan allanel
Meekkoorum mannan nilam.
meaning: If a king is easy for his people to meet and never speaks harshly, the whole world will praise his land.
elementary: Imagine a school principal whose door is always open and who speaks kindly to every student. Everyone would say that’s a great school! A king who is easy to meet and never speaks rudely makes his whole country admired.
university: Kaatchikku eliyan — ‘easy to be seen’ — names the political virtue of accessibility: a ruler who can be reached by ordinary petitioners without layers of gatekeepers. The second condition, not being kadunjollan (a speaker of harsh words), concerns the manner of the encounter once access is granted. The reward is striking: it is the land (nilam), not merely the king, that the world exalts, implying that a ruler’s approachability shapes the reputation of the whole polity. Kautilya warns in almost identical terms that a king who makes himself inaccessible breeds confusion and public disaffection, and Islamic tradition records a hadith threatening divine seclusion from the ruler who secludes himself from his people.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When in the court, he shall never cause his petitioners to wait at the door, for when a king makes himself inaccessible to his people and entrusts his work to his immediate officers, he may be sure to engender confusion in business, and to cause thereby public disaffection, and himself a prey to his enemies.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya warns that a king who keeps people waiting and hides behind officials will make his people unhappy and his kingdom weak.
hinduism.tie_back: The exact virtue of ‘kaatchikku eliyan’ — being easy for subjects to reach.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus invites everyone who is tired or burdened to come to him, describing himself as gentle and humble.
christianity.tie_back: Christ as king is openly approachable and gentle — both halves of the Kural’s ideal.

islam.quote_or_event: “If Allah puts anyone in the position of authority over the affairs of the Muslims, and he secludes himself (from them), not fulfilling their needs, wants, and poverty, Allah will keep Himself away from him, not fulfilling his need, want and poverty.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warned that a ruler who hides from his people and ignores their needs will find God hiding from him.
islam.tie_back: A direct religious sanction for the Kural’s demand that a ruler be easy to approach.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God’s:”
judaism.explanation: Moses instructs Israel’s judges to listen to ordinary people just as carefully as to important ones.
judaism.tie_back: Hearing ‘the small as well as the great’ is the practical meaning of a ruler being easy to approach.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “...at any time, whether I am eating, in the women’s quarters, the bed chamber, the chariot, the palanquin, in the park or wherever, reporters are to be posted with instructions to report to me the affairs of the people so that I might attend to these affairs wherever I am.”
buddhism.explanation: Emperor Ashoka ordered that the people’s concerns be brought to him at any hour, wherever he was.
buddhism.tie_back: An actual Buddhist king institutionalising the Kural’s ideal of being always reachable.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict VI (tr. S. Dhammika)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As giving safety is the best of gifts, as the best of true speeches is that which causes no distress, as chastity is the highest of austerities, so is the Śramaṇa Jñātṛputra the highest of men.”
jainism.explanation: In the hymn to Mahavira, the best speech is defined as true speech that causes no pain to others. This reflects the Jain vow of truthfulness, which is bound up with non-harm (ahimsa).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's beloved king is one who is not kadunjollan, a speaker of harsh words. The Jain ideal of truthful speech that causes no distress is the same standard of gentle speech, though the verse says nothing about how accessible a ruler is.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.6.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak names sweetness of manner and humility as the very essence of every good quality.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the king who is never harsh of speech; Guru Nanak makes the same gentleness of manner the essence of virtue.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the opening of Sophocles’ Oedipus the King, Oedipus comes out in person to the suppliants at his palace, saying he did not think it right to hear of their troubles from messengers but came himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: King Oedipus goes out to meet his suffering people personally instead of sending servants.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Dramatises the approachable king the Kural praises — though the play then shows his temper toward Teiresias and Creon.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A readiness to listen to those who had anything to propose for the common weal … He was also easy in conversation, and he made himself agreeable without any offensive affectation … There was in him nothing harsh, nor implacable, nor violent.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius describes his adoptive father, the emperor Antoninus Pius, as a ruler who listened to anyone with something useful to propose, was easy to talk to, and had nothing harsh about him.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s praiseworthy king drawn from life: easy to approach and never harsh in speech.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book I, §16 (tr. George Long)

real_life_example.event_title: King Christian X's daily rides through occupied Copenhagen
real_life_example.event: During the German occupation of Denmark, King Christian X rode on horseback through the streets of Copenhagen every day, where citizens could see and greet him. The rides became a public sign that he had not abandoned his claim to Danish sovereignty and won him great popular support. Later legends, such as the story that he wore a yellow star, are not true, but the daily rides are well documented.
real_life_example.explanation: By making himself visible and approachable to ordinary people at a time of national humiliation, the king strengthened the morale and unity of the country.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises a king who is easy for his people to see and approach, and Christian X's daily appearance among Copenhagen's citizens made the whole land admired for its quiet steadfastness.

tamil:
இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்குத் தன்சொலால்
தான்கண் டனைத்திவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Insolaal eeththalikka vallaarkkuth thansolaal
Thaankan danaiththiv vulagu.
meaning: For a ruler who gives with kind words and protects the people, the world will praise him and follow his word, just as he wishes.
elementary: When a friend shares their snacks and says something nice while doing it, everyone wants to be on their team. A king who gives generously, speaks kindly, and protects people finds that the whole world is happy to follow him.
university: The kural joins three verbs — speaking sweetly (insol), giving (eeththal), and protecting (alittal) — and makes their combination the source of consent. The second line is compressed: ‘the world becomes as he sees it by his word’, which commentators such as Parimelazhagar read as the world both praising him and conforming to his intentions. The insight is that legitimacy is earned through the manner as well as the substance of benefaction: gifts given with contempt create resentment, whereas gifts with kind words create loyalty. This closely matches the Buddhist ‘bases of fellowship’ (generosity, kind speech, beneficial help, consistency) and the counsel Rehoboam’s elders gave him — ‘speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Valmiki describes Rama as one who always spoke gently, was the first to speak and greet others kindly, and was devoted to the welfare of his people, which is why the citizens longed for him to be crowned (Ayodhya Kanda 1-2).
hinduism.explanation: Rama was loved by everyone because he spoke kindly first and cared for the people, so they wanted him to be king.
hinduism.tie_back: Sweet speech plus care for the people wins the world’s consent — the Kural’s formula for a ruler whom all follow.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Many will intreat the favour of the prince: and every man is a friend to him that giveth gifts.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs notes that people seek the favour of a generous ruler and befriend those who give.
christianity.tie_back: Generosity (eeththal) draws people to the ruler, as the Kural says the world follows the giving king.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allah, [O Muhammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: God tells the Prophet that his gentleness kept his followers close; if he had been harsh they would have left.
islam.tie_back: The same logic as the Kural: gentle speech is what keeps people gathered around a leader.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever.”
judaism.explanation: The old advisers tell King Rehoboam that if he serves the people and speaks kindly, they will serve him forever. He ignores them and loses most of the kingdom.
judaism.tie_back: Almost a restatement of the Kural: good words and service make the people follow the ruler’s will.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are these four grounds for the bonds of fellowship. Which four? Generosity, kind words, beneficial help, consistency.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names four things that hold people together: giving, kind speech, helping, and treating people consistently.
buddhism.tie_back: Generosity, kind words, and beneficial help map precisely onto the Kural’s giving, sweet speech, and protection.

jainism.quote_or_event: Ishukara's queen Kamalavati to the king: “If the whole world and all treasures were yours, you would still not be satisfied, nor would all this be able to save you. Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.”
jainism.explanation: The queen addresses the king gently, as 'O king' and 'O monarch', and points him to the Law (dharma) as the only real protection. In the story the whole court, king included, takes up the Jain path and reaches perfection.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the world comes round to the ruler who joins kind words with giving and protection. In the Jain story it is the king who receives that kind of benevolent counsel, and the 'protection' it values is dharma rather than royal patronage.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.39–40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Lord lovingly embraces whoever comes to the Lord's Sanctuary - this is the way of the Lord and Master.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says it is the innate nature (birad) of the Master to take into His embrace anyone who comes seeking refuge.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the ruler who gives kindly and protects those who come to him; Guru Arjan describes the divine Master whose defining way is exactly such protection of all who seek shelter.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 544, Raag Bihaagraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...for therefore are there princes wise in heart, because when the people are being misguided in their assembly, they set right the matter again with ease, persuading them with gentle words.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says the Muses give good kings the gift of gentle, persuasive speech, which lets them guide their people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A king who wins people by gentle words finds them following his word — the Kural’s second line.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is not easy to say how far an affable and courteous manner in conversation may go toward winning the affections.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero tells his son that a courteous, kindly manner of speech wins people over in ways that are hard to measure, and points to letters from Philip, Antipater and Antigonus urging their heirs to win the people with kind words.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the ruler who gives with kind words finds the world following him, though Cicero stresses gracious speech more than giving and protection.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book II, §48 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))

real_life_example.event_title: The Jam Sahib of Nawanagar shelters Polish refugee children
real_life_example.event: During the Second World War, Polish children, many of them orphans, who had been released from the Soviet Union with nowhere to go were brought to India. Maharaja Digvijaysinhji, the Jam Sahib of Nawanagar, set up a camp for them near his summer palace at Balachadi from 1942 and maintained it largely at his own expense, with a school, a Polish library and activities that kept their culture alive. Hundreds of children lived under his protection until the camp closed and they were moved on after the war, and he is remembered in Poland as the Good Maharaja.
real_life_example.explanation: The maharaja's generosity was matched by personal warmth toward children far from home, and his care earned lasting gratitude between two distant nations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world follows a ruler who gives with kind words and protects those who come to him, and the Jam Sahib gave refuge and care to children who had lost everything.

tamil:
முறைசெய்து காப்பாற்றும் மன்னவன் மக்கட்கு
இறையென்று வைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Muraiseydhu kaappaatrum mannavan makkatku
Iraiyendru vaikkap padum.
meaning: A king who rules fairly and protects his people will be seen by them as a god.
elementary: When a lifeguard keeps everyone safe and is always fair, the swimmers look up to them like a hero. This kural says a ruler who is fair and protects everyone is looked up to by the people almost like God.
university: The word irai carries a deliberate double meaning — both ‘lord/king’ and ‘God’ — and the chapter title Iraimaatchi itself plays on it. Crucially, Valluvar makes divinity conditional: the king is ‘placed’ (vaikkappadum) as god by the people only because he does murai (justice, due order) and protects them. This inverts the claim of inherent divine kingship found in texts like the Laws of Manu, grounding sacral status in performance rather than birth. Aristotle’s remark that a person of pre-eminent virtue ‘may truly be deemed a God among men’ and Psalm 82’s address to judges as ‘gods’ who must defend the poor show the same conditional logic.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Even an infant king must not be despised, (from an idea) that he is a (mere) mortal; for he is a great deity in human form.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu say that the king, even a child king, is a god in human form and must be respected.
hinduism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s king-as-god image, but Manu makes divinity inherent, while the Kural makes it earned by justice and protection.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For he is the minister of God to thee for good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that a ruler who punishes wrong and protects the good is acting as God’s servant.
christianity.tie_back: The ruler who does justice stands in God’s place for the people, close to the Kural’s claim.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet listed a just ruler first among the seven whom God will shade on the Day when there is no shade but His (Sahih al-Bukhari 660).
islam.explanation: Islam teaches that a just ruler will receive God’s special protection on Judgment Day.
islam.tie_back: A just, protecting ruler holds a uniquely exalted status — though Islam strictly denies any divinity to humans.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.”
judaism.explanation: In Psalm 82, God calls the rulers and judges ‘gods’, but only after demanding that they ‘defend the poor and fatherless’ — and warns that the unjust among them will die like men.
judaism.tie_back: Rulers are called ‘gods’ precisely in their role of doing justice and protecting the weak, as in the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Agganna Sutta, the first king is called Mahasammata, ‘the Great Elect’, chosen by the people to judge and punish wrongdoers in return for a share of rice (DN 27).
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist texts say the first king was simply chosen by the people to keep order, not sent by the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it grounds kingship in doing justice for the people — but it deliberately denies the king divine status.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Here (on earth) you are the highest man, Reverend sir, and hereafter you will be the highest; exempt from all blemishes you will reach Perfection, a higher state than which there is none in this world.”
jainism.explanation: Sakra, king of the gods, throws off his disguise and worships King Nami, who has renounced his throne and mastered his passions. In Jainism even the gods bow to the perfected soul, and no ruler is divine by office.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the just protector-king will be held by his people as a god. Jainism also ranks a royal figure above the gods, but only Nami, who has conquered himself, earns that honour, and a reigning king does not.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.58 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That king sits upon the throne, who is worthy of that throne.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that a throne belongs only to the one who is worthy of it; Sikh thought reserves the title of True King (sacha patshah) for God alone.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a king who rules justly and protects his people is regarded as divine; Guru Nanak likewise makes the right to rule depend on worthiness, though he does not grant any king divine status.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1088, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And when he passes through a gathering, they greet him as a god with gentle reverence, and he is conspicuous amongst the assembled.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says a king who judges fairly is greeted by the people like a god.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural: the just king is ‘placed as god’ by his people.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Such an one may truly be deemed a God among men.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says a person whose virtue far surpasses everyone else’s would be like a god among humans and should rule.
philosophy.tie_back: Divine regard grounded in pre-eminent virtue — the same conditional deification as the Kural.

real_life_example.event_title: The Roman Senate deifies Augustus
real_life_example.event: Augustus, the first Roman emperor, died on 19 August 14 CE, and on 17 September the Senate enrolled him among the gods of the Roman state with the title divus, the deified one. Ancient accounts credit the honour to his achievements, including restoring peace after decades of civil war and maintaining law and order. A temple to the Divine Augustus was built in Rome, and the deification set a precedent for later emperors.
real_life_example.explanation: Augustus had resisted being named a god while alive, but after his death the state honoured the ruler who had brought order and security as divine. His case shows how rulers who were seen to protect their people could be raised to sacred status.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the king who rules justly and protects his people will be regarded as a god, and Rome formally deified Augustus for bringing peace and order.

tamil:
செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும் பண்புடை வேந்தன்
கவிகைக்கீழ்த் தங்கும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Sevikaippach sorporukkum panbudai vendhan
Kavigaikkeezhth thangum ulagu.
meaning: The whole world will live safely under the royal umbrella (the sign of his rule) of a king with the good character to put up with words that are bitter to hear.
elementary: Good medicine often tastes bad, but it makes you better. A wise king listens even when someone tells him an unpleasant truth. Because of that, everyone feels safe living under his rule.
university: Sevi kaippa — ‘so that the ear tastes bitterness’ — is a vivid synaesthetic image for criticism that is unpleasant to hear. The commentators specify that these are the admonitions of wise elders and ministers, whose duty (developed in the later chapter on ‘Seeking the Help of the Great’) is to rebuke the king when needed. The kavigai (royal parasol) is the symbol of sovereign protection, so the kural’s claim is that tolerance of criticism is not a weakness but the condition under which the whole world will rest securely under the ruler’s shade. Vidura’s warning in the Mahabharata that speakers and hearers of unpleasant but healing words are rare, and Marcus Aurelius’ readiness to be corrected, express the same insight.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “They are abundant, O king, that can always speak agreeable words. The speaker, however, is rare, as also the hearer, of words that are disagreeable but medicinal.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells King Dhritarashtra that flatterers are everywhere, but people who speak or accept bitter-but-healing truth are rare.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Disagreeable but medicinal’ words are exactly the Kural’s ear-bittering speech that a great king must bear.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 37 (Vidura Niti), tr. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says a fool hates correction, but a wise person loves the one who corrects him.
christianity.tie_back: The wise ruler of the Kural is the ‘wise man’ who welcomes rebuke rather than resenting it.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best fighting (jihad) in the path of Allah is (to speak) a word of justice to an oppressive ruler.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet said one of the greatest acts of striving is to tell a truth to an unjust ruler’s face.
islam.tie_back: Presents the other side of the Kural’s relationship: speaking hard truth to power is a sacred duty, which the good king must bear.

judaism.quote_or_event: The prophet Nathan confronts King David with the parable of the poor man’s lamb and declares “Thou art the man”; David, rather than punishing him, answers “I have sinned against the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: When the prophet Nathan boldly accused King David of a terrible wrong, David accepted the rebuke instead of getting angry.
judaism.tie_back: A king who bears words bitter to the ear — the exact virtue this kural praises.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says someone who points out your faults is as valuable as a guide to buried treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: Reproof as treasure — the reason the Kural’s king should bear bitter words.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A man who returns, as it were, to the vomit, is not praised; but you want to confiscate the property left by the Brâhmaṇa.”
jainism.explanation: Queen Kamalavati sharply rebukes King Ishukara for planning to seize an heirless Brahmin's estate. The king takes this bitter criticism to heart: he renounces his kingdom, and the narrator reports that 'the king and the queen … they all reached perfection.'
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar promises that the world will shelter under the umbrella of the king who can bear words bitter to the ear. Ishukara is a Jain example of such a king, who accepts a stinging reproof and is raised by it.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.38, 14.53 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The kings are tigers, and their officials are dogs; they go out and awaken the sleeping people to harass them.”
sikhism.explanation: In Vaar Malaar Guru Nanak speaks a famously bitter truth about the rulers of his day, comparing kings to tigers and their officials to dogs that prey on ordinary people.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the king gracious enough to bear words that are bitter to his ears; Guru Nanak's verse is an example of the bitter, unwelcome truth that a good ruler ought to be able to hear.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar (Vaar Malaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Nestor tells Agamemnon that because Zeus has given him the sceptre and the right to judge, it is his duty above all to speak and also to listen, and to act on another man’s good counsel — urging him to repair his quarrel with Achilles.
greek_mythology.explanation: The wise old Nestor reminds King Agamemnon that a king must listen to advice, even advice he does not want to hear.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The duty of a sceptred king to hear hard counsel is the Kural’s central point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If any man is able to convince me and show me that I do not think or act right, I will gladly change. For I seek the truth by which no man was ever injured.”
philosophy.explanation: The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius writes that he will gladly change if anyone shows him he is wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: A ruling emperor embracing correction — the Kural’s king who bears bitter words.

real_life_example.event_title: Frederick Douglass confronts Abraham Lincoln about Black soldiers
real_life_example.place: The White House, Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: The abolitionist Frederick Douglass, who had been recruiting Black soldiers for the Union Army, went to the White House on 10 August 1863 and told President Lincoln he could no longer recruit because Black soldiers received less pay than white soldiers, had no chance of promotion and were not protected when captured. Lincoln received him, listened seriously and explained his reasons, and Douglass later recalled that the president was serious and even troubled by what he had said. Although not all his demands were met, Douglass came away with lasting respect for Lincoln's openness.
real_life_example.explanation: A president in the middle of a civil war gave his full attention to blunt criticism from a man born into slavery, and the meeting began a relationship of mutual respect.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises a ruler gracious enough to bear words that are bitter to hear, and Lincoln received Douglass's sharp complaints with patience and seriousness.

tamil:
கொடையளி செங்கோல் குடியோம்பல் நான்கும்
உடையானாம் வேந்தர்க் கொளி.
transliteration:
Kodaiyali sengol kudiyombal naangum
Udaiyaanaam vendhark koli.
meaning: A king who has these four things, generosity, kindness, fair rule and care for his people, is the light among kings.
elementary: In a dark room, a lamp helps everyone see. This kural says the best king is like a lamp for all other kings, because he gives generously, is kind, rules fairly, and takes care of his people.
university: The chapter closes with a second set of four, this time outward-facing: kodai (gifts), ali (grace or compassion), sengol (the ‘straight sceptre’, i.e., just rule), and kudi ombal (nurturing the people). Where 382 described the king’s inner capacities, this kural describes their effects on subjects, and it crowns the one who has them as oli — the lamp or radiance — of kings, a model by which other rulers are measured. The sengol (straight sceptre) is a central symbol of Tamil political thought, contrasted with the kodungol (crooked sceptre) of the tyrant in later chapters. The image of the just ruler as light recurs in David’s last words in 2 Samuel, and the Hebrew Bible’s ‘sceptre of righteousness’ offers a remarkably close verbal parallel.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa says King Dilipa was the true father of his subjects, because he educated, protected, and sustained them, while their own fathers were merely the cause of their birth.
hinduism.explanation: A Sanskrit poem praises a king who cared for his people so completely that he was more of a father to them than their real fathers.
hinduism.tie_back: Embodies kudi ombal (nurturing the people) and ali (compassion), the heart of the Kural’s ‘light of kings’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom.”
christianity.explanation: The Letter to the Hebrews describes Christ’s kingdom as ruled by a ‘sceptre of righteousness’.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Sceptre of righteousness’ is almost a word-for-word equivalent of the Kural’s sengol (the straight sceptre).

islam.quote_or_event: “The Imam (ruler) is the guardian of his subjects and is responsible for them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that a ruler is like a shepherd who must answer for how he cared for his people.
islam.tie_back: Matches kudi ombal — the ruler’s duty to nurture and protect the people.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God. And he shall be as the light of the morning, when the sun riseth, even a morning without clouds;”
judaism.explanation: In his last words, King David says a just ruler is like the light of a clear sunrise.
judaism.tie_back: Just rule producing radiance — the same image as the Kural’s ‘light of kings’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta, the wheel-turning monarch is told to rely on the Dhamma, provide protection for all his people, allow no crime in his realm, and give wealth to the poor; a later king’s failure to give to the needy sets off a spiral of theft and violence (DN 26).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells of an ideal king who protects everyone and gives to the poor; when a later king stops giving, crime spreads and society collapses.
buddhism.tie_back: Combines generosity, just rule, and protection of the people — the Kural’s four qualities of the model king.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain tradition remembers Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara, as the first king. Before he renounced, he ruled from Vinita (Ayodhya) and taught his people six means of livelihood: asi (arms for protection), masi (writing), krishi (agriculture), vidya (knowledge), vanijya (trade) and shilpa (crafts).
jainism.explanation: In the Jain account, the ideal first ruler protects his people and also equips them to live: he gives them arts, livelihoods and order. Only after that does he give up the throne for the ascetic path.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's 'light among kings' has generosity, compassion, a just sceptre and care for his people. Rishabha as first king is the Jain picture of exactly this kind of nurturing, protecting ruler.
jainism.source: Jain tradition on Rishabhanatha (Adipurana and Svetambara accounts), as summarised in Wikipedia, 'Rishabhanatha'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Now, the Merciful Lord has issued His Command. Let no one chase after and attack anyone else. Let all abide in peace, under this Benevolent Rule.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes halemi raj, a gentle and benevolent rule under the merciful Lord's command, in which no one harasses another and all live in peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls the ruler who joins generosity, compassion, just rule and care for the people the light among kings; Guru Arjan's halemi raj is Sikhism's picture of such compassionate, peaceful rule.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 74, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...like that of some blameless king, who upholds righteousness, as the monarch over a great and valiant nation: the earth yields its wheat and barley, the trees are loaded with fruit, the ewes bring forth lambs, and the sea abounds with fish by reason of his virtues, and his people do good deeds under him.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus compares Penelope’s fame to that of a just king, under whose rule the land flourishes and the people do good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The just king whose virtue nourishes his whole people is the Greek image of the Kural’s ‘light of kings’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...there is no one in any rule who, in so far as he is a ruler, considers or enjoins what is for his own interest, but always what is for the interest of his subject or suitable to his art;”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that a true ruler always acts for the good of those he rules, not for himself.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s ideal of the king defined by care for his people (kudi ombal).

real_life_example.event_title: King Sejong creates the Korean alphabet for his people
real_life_example.event: King Sejong, the fourth ruler of Korea's Joseon dynasty, oversaw the creation of a new phonetic alphabet, completed around 1443, so that ordinary people who could not master Chinese characters could learn to read and write. In 1446 he promulgated it as Hunminjeongeum, the Proper Sounds to Instruct the People, with an explanatory text. That 1446 text is now inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register, and the alphabet, Hangul, is used throughout Korea today.
real_life_example.explanation: Sejong used royal power not to glorify himself but to give literacy to common people, and his reign is remembered as a golden age of Korean culture and science.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural crowns as the light among kings the ruler who combines generosity, compassion, just rule and care for his people, and Sejong's alphabet was a gift of care to all his subjects.

tamil:
கற்க கசடறக் கற்பவை கற்றபின்
நிற்க அதற்குத் தக.
transliteration:
Karka kasadarak karpavai katrapin
Nirka adharkuth thaga.
meaning: Learn what is worth learning, and learn it fully, without gaps. Then live in a way that matches what you have learned.
elementary: Imagine learning all the rules of football perfectly but then cheating in the game. That would make the learning pointless. This kural says two things: learn good things properly, then actually live by them.
university: The chapter on Kalvi opens with a two-step command. The first is கற்க கசடற: learn so that no flaw (kasadu) is left, which traditional commentators such as Parimelazhagar read as choosing the right texts and also removing one's own mental faults through study. The second is நிற்க அதற்குத் தக: stand, or remain, in conduct fitting to that learning. The verb நிற்க (to stand) is significant, because it pictures learning as a place one lives in and not only a set of facts one holds. Because the chapter sits in the Porul section, just after the chapter on kingship, this is also advice to rulers: a king's learning is shown in how he governs, not in how much he can recite. The same link between knowing and doing appears across many traditions, from the Epistle of James to the Stoic Epictetus.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the teacher's farewell address to graduating students in the Taittiriya Upanishad, the student is told to speak the truth, practise dharma, and never neglect study (svadhyaya).
hinduism.explanation: This is a traditional convocation charge. When formal study ends, the teacher says learning must now become right conduct and must also continue as lifelong self-study.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats finishing one's studies as the start of living by them. Both parts are there: study faithfully, then act accordingly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.”
christianity.explanation: James warns believers that hearing or knowing God's teaching is not enough. Anyone who does not act on it is fooling themselves.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the second half of the Kural: once you have learned, stand by it in action.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Greatly hateful in the sight of Allāh is that you say what you do not do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an condemns a gap between what people profess and what they practise. Knowing and saying the right thing without doing it is called hateful to God.
islam.tie_back: It gives the negative side of the Kural's command. Once you know what is right, your conduct has to match it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone whose deeds exceed his wisdom, his wisdom is enduring, but anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, his wisdom is not enduring.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa teaches that learning lasts only when it is rooted in and outweighed by action. Wisdom without deeds withers away.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost a Jewish twin of the Kural: learning is real only when conduct stands in line with it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares someone who knows many texts but does not practise them to a hired cowherd. He counts cattle that are not his own and never gets their milk.
buddhism.tie_back: Same point as the Kural: learning that is not lived gives nothing to the learner.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One does not attain liberation (merely) by the (study of) scripture, if he has no faith with regard to the nature of reality; or one who has faith cannot attain Nirvana if he is devoid of moral discipline.”
jainism.explanation: Kundakunda insists that scriptural learning is necessary but not enough. Knowledge has to be joined with right faith and lived out as right conduct, the three jewels of the Jain path.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to learn flawlessly and then to stand firm in conduct worthy of what we have learned. Kundakunda says the same: learning without matching conduct does not reach the goal.
jainism.source: Pravacanasara III.237 (Kundakunda, tr. A.N. Upadhye; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that knowing the Truth is supreme, but living it out in one's conduct ranks higher still.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks us to learn flawlessly and then to stand by what we have learned; Guru Nanak places conduct that matches the truth above knowledge of it, which is the second half of the couplet.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Athena is at once the goddess of wisdom (metis) and the patron of practical crafts such as weaving, shipbuilding and strategy. In Greek myth her wisdom always shows itself in skilled action.
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena's wisdom is never idle. It appears in finished work, sound counsel and well-fought battles.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Loosely parallel: Greek myth pictures true wisdom as knowledge expressed in deeds, as the Kural asks.
greek_mythology.source: General Greek mythology (Homeric Hymn 28 to Athena; Hesiod, Theogony 886–900 on Metis)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never call yourself a philosopher, nor talk a great deal among the unlearned about theorems, but act conformably to them.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells his students that philosophy is proven by behaviour, not by talk. At a dinner party, do not lecture on how people should eat. Simply eat as one should.
philosophy.tie_back: This echoes the Kural's second line, where learning must be shown by standing in conduct that fits it.

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi reads Unto This Last and founds the Phoenix Settlement
real_life_example.place: Johannesburg to Durban, and Phoenix, Natal, South Africa
real_life_example.event: In 1904 Mohandas Gandhi's friend Henry Polak gave him John Ruskin's Unto This Last to read on the overnight train from Johannesburg to Durban. Gandhi later wrote that he could not put the book down, could not sleep that night, and resolved to change his life according to its ideals. Within weeks he moved the press of his newspaper Indian Opinion to a farm near Durban, the Phoenix Settlement, where he and co-workers such as Albert West lived and worked together as equals.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi did not treat the book as information to be admired; he reorganised his work and daily life around it almost at once, and later translated it into Gujarati as Sarvodaya.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks that one learn what is worth learning thoroughly and then stand in conduct that fits it, which is exactly what Gandhi did after one night's reading.

tamil:
எண்ணென்ப ஏனை எழுத்தென்ப இவ்விரண்டும்
கண்ணென்ப வாழும் உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Ennenba enai ezhuthenba ivvirandum
Kannenba vaazhum uyirkku.
meaning: What we call numbers and what we call letters are said to be the two eyes of every living person.
elementary: You have two eyes to see the world. Valluvar says your mind also has two eyes: numbers and letters. Maths and reading let you understand things you could never see without them.
university: This kural reduces the whole of learning to two basic disciplines, எண் (en, number and calculation) and எழுத்து (ezhuthu, letters and literacy), and calls them the two eyes of human life. Commentators widened the terms. Parimelazhagar took en to cover arithmetic and the sciences such as astronomy, and ezhuthu to cover grammar and literature. The modern commentator Solomon Pappaiah even glosses them as science and the arts. The repeated என்ப ('they say') presents this as settled wisdom, not personal opinion. The image of eyes prepares for the next kural, where lacking learning is compared to having sores instead of eyes. Remarkably, Aeschylus' Prometheus names the very same pair, numbers and the combining of letters, as the founding gifts of civilization.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Mundaka Upanishad teaches that two kinds of knowledge must be known, the higher (para) and the lower (apara). The lower includes the four Vedas together with phonetics, grammar, etymology, metre, ritual and astronomy.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad sorts all learning into a twofold scheme. The 'lower' disciplines, which include the sciences of letters (phonetics and grammar) and of calculation (astronomy), are the tools that come before and serve the higher knowledge.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats learning as a pair of essential faculties. Its lower knowledge includes exactly the letter-based and number-based sciences that Valluvar calls the two eyes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes God's written word as the light that lets him see where he is walking.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's image of learning as eyes, the organs of sight, matches the Psalm's image of the written word as light for the path.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who taught by the pen - Taught man that which he knew not.”
islam.explanation: In the first verses revealed to the Prophet, God is praised as the One who taught humanity through the pen, meaning through writing. Literacy is presented as a divine gift that opens up knowledge.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an honours ezhuthu, letters and writing, as the channel by which people come to know what they did not know. This mirrors the Kural's claim that letters are an eye of life.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The calculation of the equinoxes and gematria are the desserts of wisdom.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer Hisma names astronomical calculation and gematria (the numerical values of letters) as the delightful extras that round out Torah learning.
judaism.tie_back: Here numbers and letters meet, since gematria is literally letters read as numbers. The Mishnah treats both as part of complete wisdom, though as supplements rather than 'eyes'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To have much learning, to be skillful in handicraft, well-trained in discipline, and to be of good speech — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Discourse on Blessings, the Buddha lists extensive learning (bahusacca) and practical skill (sippa) among the highest blessings of a good life.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats basic learning and skills as essential to living well, not as optional ornaments.
buddhism.source: Mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain texts say that Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara and first king, taught his daughter Brahmi the art of writing, so that the Brahmi script bears her name. He taught his other daughter Sundari the science of numbers (anka-vidya).
jainism.explanation: In Jain sacred history, letters and numbers are the first gifts of civilisation, handed down together by the first teacher of humankind to his two daughters.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls numbers and letters the two eyes of every living person. The Jain story of Rishabha teaching Brahmi letters and Sundari numbers makes the same pair the foundation of all human learning.
jainism.source: Jain tradition on Rishabhanatha, Brahmi and Sundari, as summarised in Wikipedia, 'Rishabhanatha'

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Angad, the second Sikh Guru, is remembered as the standardizer of the Gurmukhi script in which much of the Adi Granth is written, and Sikh tradition credits him with setting up schools to teach young people to read and write in their own language, Punjabi, rather than classical Sanskrit.
sikhism.explanation: By fixing a script for the people's own language, Guru Angad made literacy and direct access to the Gurus' hymns possible for ordinary Sikhs.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls letters and numbers the two eyes of every living person; Guru Angad's work on Gurmukhi and the schools linked to him reflect the same conviction that basic literacy belongs to everyone.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guru Angad' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Aye, and numbers, too, chiefest of sciences, I invented for them, and the combining of letters, creative mother of the Muses' arts, wherewith to hold all things in memory.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Chained to his rock, the Titan Prometheus lists the gifts he gave to helpless early humans. Numbers and writing come near the top as the foundations of all other arts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An exact pairing: Aeschylus names numbers and letters as the twin gifts that made human life truly human, just as Valluvar calls them life's two eyes.
greek_mythology.source: Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 459–461 (trans. H. W. Smyth)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Galileo writes that philosophy is written in the great book of the universe. That book cannot be understood unless one first learns its language and reads its letters, and it is written in the language of mathematics.
philosophy.explanation: For Galileo, reading and mathematics together are the only way to 'see' nature. Without them a person wanders as if in a dark labyrinth.
philosophy.tie_back: This parallels the Kural closely: letters and numbers are the faculties through which reality becomes visible.

real_life_example.event_title: Al-Khwarizmi writes on the Hindu art of reckoning
real_life_example.event: Working at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad under the caliph al-Ma'mun, the mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a treatise explaining the Hindu place-value numerals, including zero as a placeholder, and how to calculate with them. The Arabic original is lost, but a Latin translation, Algoritmi de numero Indorum, carried these numerals and methods into Europe. The Latin form of his name, Algoritmi, is the origin of the word algorithm.
real_life_example.explanation: A single book on how to write and work with numbers gave much of the world the counting system it still uses for trade, science and computing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls number one of the two eyes of human life, and al-Khwarizmi's treatise opened that eye for whole civilisations.

tamil:
கண்ணுடையர் என்பவர் கற்றோர் முகத்திரண்டு
புண்ணுடையர் கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Kannudaiyar enbavar katror mugaththirandu
Punnudaiyar kallaa thavar.
meaning: Only educated people can truly be said to have eyes. People without learning just have two sores on their face.
elementary: Two holes in your face are not the same as seeing. If you never learn anything, your eyes look at the world but understand nothing. Valluvar says a person who learns has real eyes.
university: Continuing the eye metaphor of Kural 392, Valluvar reaches one of the harshest images in the chapter. The unlearned person's eyes are புண் (pun), wounds or sores: openings in the face that do nothing and may even be painful. The contrast rests on the difference between physical sight and understanding. Kalaignar's commentary draws the corollary that a learned person without physical sight still 'has eyes', while an unlearned person with sight does not. The rhetoric is deliberately provocative. It belongs to a statecraft section meant to push kings and citizens toward education, and the following chapter, Kallaamai (Ignorance), develops the same harshness. Similar contrasts between seeing eyes and a seeing mind run through the Gospels, the Qur'an and Plato.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A famous verse of Bhartrhari's Nitishataka says that a person without literature, music and the arts is a beast in plain sight, only lacking a tail and horns.
hinduism.explanation: Bhartrhari, the Sanskrit poet-grammarian, uses shock imagery to insist that culture and learning are what make someone fully human.
hinduism.tie_back: Same rhetorical strategy as the Kural: the unlearned person keeps an outwardly human form but lacks what that form is for, just as a face may carry 'sores' instead of eyes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus describes people whose eyes work perfectly but who still fail to perceive the truth in front of them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it separates having eyes from truly seeing. Understanding is what turns sight into vision.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says that true blindness is in the heart and mind that fail to understand, not in the physical eyes.
islam.tie_back: This strongly parallels the Kural: physical eyes do not count as sight without inner understanding.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A brute is not sin-fearing, nor is an ignorant person pious.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel teaches that a person with no learning at all (bur, 'empty field') cannot even reach basic moral seriousness, and an unlettered person cannot be truly pious.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees ignorance as a real deficiency in the person, not a neutral state. Its focus is on piety rather than 'sight'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man of little learning grows old like a bull. He grows only in bulk, but, his wisdom does not grow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares an unlearned person to an ox that gets bigger with age but never gets wiser.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it uses a blunt image to show that a body without learning is a diminished life.
