jainism.quote_or_event: “The saints have scriptures as their eyes; all the living beings have sense-organs as their eyes; the gods have clairvoyance as their eyes; and the Siddhas have eyes in every way.”
jainism.explanation: Kundakunda ranks kinds of 'eyes'. Ordinary beings see only with the senses, while the ascetic sees through scripture (agama-cakshu). The previous verse adds that a monk who lacks scriptural study 'does not know his self'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says only the learned truly have eyes, and the unlearned carry two sores in their face. Kundakunda likewise treats learning as the real eye and sense-sight as the lowest kind of seeing.
jainism.source: Pravacanasara III.234 (cf. III.233) (Kundakunda, tr. A.N. Upadhye; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not call them blind, who have no eyes in their face. They alone are blind, O Nanak, who wander away from their Lord and Master.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok in Ramkali ki Vaar Guru Angad redefines blindness: the truly blind are not those without physical sight but those who have strayed from the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says only the learned truly have eyes and the unlearned merely carry two sores on their face; Guru Angad makes the same move of denying that physical eyes are real sight.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles' Oedipus the King, the blind prophet Tiresias sees the truth, while Oedipus, with perfect eyesight, is blind to who he is. When Oedipus finally understands, he puts out his own eyes.
greek_mythology.explanation: The tragedy is built on the reversal of sight and insight. The man with eyes cannot see, and the eyeless seer knows everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This closely parallels the Kural. Eyes without understanding are useless or even wounds, and understanding is the real sight. Oedipus literally turns his eyes into wounds.
greek_mythology.source: Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus (esp. the Tiresias scene, lines 300–462, and the self-blinding)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's Allegory of the Cave, prisoners watch shadows on a wall and take them for reality. Education is the painful turning of the soul toward the light, so that it finally sees what is real.
philosophy.explanation: Plato defines education not as putting sight into blind eyes but as turning the soul's existing 'eye' toward the truth.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Plato holds that the uneducated have eyes that do not truly see. Learning is what makes vision real.

real_life_example.event_title: Louis Braille devises a reading system for the blind
real_life_example.place: Royal Institute for Blind Youth, Paris, France
real_life_example.event: Louis Braille, blinded as a small child, entered the Royal Institute for Blind Youth in Paris in 1819, where the library held only a few cumbersome books in embossed letters. Adapting a raised-dot system shown to the school by Charles Barbier, he worked out by the age of 15 a code of six-dot cells that blind people could read quickly with their fingertips and write with a simple tool. He published the system in 1829, and it was later adopted around the world.
real_life_example.explanation: Braille's code gave blind people direct access to reading and writing, showing that the power to learn does not depend on physical sight.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that only the learned truly have eyes, and Braille, who could not see, gave countless blind people those eyes of learning.

tamil:
உவப்பத் தலைக்கூடி உள்ளப் பிரிதல்
அனைத்தே புலவர் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Uvappath thalaikkoodi ullap piridhal
Anaiththe pulavar thozhil.
meaning: This is the sign of learned people: others are happy to meet them, and when they leave, others keep thinking of them and want to meet them again.
elementary: Think of a teacher or grandparent whose stories you love. When they come, you are happy. When they leave, you wish they could stay longer. Valluvar says that is how learned people make everyone feel.
university: Here Valluvar moves from the value of learning to its social effect. The புலவர் (pulavar, the learned or poet-scholar) is defined by an experience they create in others: உவப்ப, gladness at meeting, and உள்ளப் பிரிதல், parting in a way that leaves people thinking of them. The word தொழில் (thozhil, occupation or characteristic work) suggests that bringing joy through conversation is the scholar's real 'profession'. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan gloss the second half as others wondering when they will see such a person again. The kural implicitly contrasts true learning, which is generous and delightful, with pedantry that makes people glad to leave. Greek tradition offers vivid parallels, from Odysseus spellbinding the Phaeacians to Alcibiades' account of being enchanted by Socrates' words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhaja Govindam, Adi Shankaracharya teaches that the company of the good (satsanga) leads to non-attachment, then freedom from delusion, then steadiness of mind, and finally liberation.
hinduism.explanation: The tradition of satsang holds that simply being in the company of wise people transforms and uplifts the listener.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats time with the learned as a treasured, transforming experience. Shankara stresses spiritual effect rather than delight and longing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs describes how the meeting of wise minds leaves each person brighter and sharper.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes the benefit of meeting a wise person. The Proverb's emphasis is mutual improvement, while the Kural's is delight and longing.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of a good pious companion and an evil one is that of a person carrying musk and another blowing a pair of bellows.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a good companion to a perfume seller. Even if you buy nothing, you leave carrying a pleasant fragrance.
islam.tie_back: The musk image matches the Kural well: time with a good, learned person leaves something pleasant that stays with you after you part.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If two sit together and there are words of Torah [spoken] between them, then the Shekhinah abides among them.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradion teaches that when people meet and share words of learning, the Divine Presence rests among them.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes a learned meeting a blessed, uplifting event. It focuses on sacred presence rather than personal delight.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To be patient and obedient, to associate with monks and to have religious discussions on due occasions — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Mangala Sutta counts meeting and discussing the Dhamma with learned, disciplined people among life's highest blessings.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats meeting the learned as a real joy and blessing.
buddhism.source: Mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Sramanas, skilled in the interpretation of sacred texts and rich in moral discipline, austerities and right knowledge, should be welcomed with a stand-up, should be served and be bowed down to by other ascetics.”
jainism.explanation: Kundakunda tells monks to rise to their feet, serve and bow when a learned ascetic arrives. Meeting someone rich in knowledge is treated as an occasion for warm and respectful welcome.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar describes the learned as those whose company gladdens others and whose parting leaves people longing to meet again. The Jain rule of joyful, reverent welcome expresses the same regard, although it does not mention the longing after they leave.
jainism.source: Pravacanasara III.263 (Kundakunda, tr. A.N. Upadhye; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The sight of them banishes my evil-mindedness; they are my only true friends.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Gujri ki Vaar Guru Arjan says his true friends are those whose very presence drives away his bad thoughts.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines the learned by the gladness people feel on meeting them and the longing they feel on parting; Guru Arjan likewise names his true friends by the good their mere presence works in him.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 520, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus pauses in telling his adventures at the Phaeacian court, his audience sits spellbound in silence. King Alcinous begs him to go on, saying they would listen until dawn.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus' learning, gained through long travel and hardship, makes his company so delightful that his hosts cannot bear to let him stop.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This fits the Kural closely: the listeners rejoice in his company and do not want it to end.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's Symposium, Alcibiades says that when Socrates speaks, listeners are overwhelmed and enchanted. He compares Socrates to the satyr Marsyas, whose music held everyone spellbound, except that Socrates does it with bare words.
philosophy.explanation: Alcibiades testifies that Socrates' conversation stays in the soul long after it ends and keeps drawing him back.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's pulavar, Socrates makes others glad to meet him and unable to forget him afterward.

real_life_example.event_title: Einstein's lecture tour of Japan
real_life_example.place: Kobe, Tokyo, Kyoto and other cities, Japan
real_life_example.event: At the invitation of the publisher Kaizosha, Albert Einstein toured Japan from 17 November 1922, having learned during the voyage that he had been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Crowds and journalists met him at Kobe, and audiences packed auditoriums in several cities to hear him lecture on relativity for three or four hours at a time through an interpreter. At Keio University in Tokyo on 19 November about 2,000 people filled the lecture hall.
real_life_example.explanation: The tour shows how a great scholar's presence and talk could draw and delight ordinary people far beyond the circle of specialists.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the mark of the learned is that people rejoice to meet them and think of them after they part, and Japan's welcome to Einstein shows that gladness.

tamil:
உடையார்முன் இல்லார்போல் ஏக்கற்றுங் கற்றார்
கடையரே கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Udaiyaarmun illaarpol ekkatrum katraar
Kadaiyare kallaa thavar.
meaning: People who learn by standing humbly before their teachers, like the poor before the rich, are truly great. Those who do not learn are the lowest of all.
elementary: A hungry child waits eagerly for food. A good student waits just as eagerly to learn from a teacher, and is not too proud to ask. The kural says being too proud to learn is what really makes you low.
university: The kural draws on a social image any reader would recognize: the needy person standing anxiously (ஏக்கற்று) before the wealthy. It applies that image to the student before the teacher. What looks like humiliation is really the road to greatness, since those who learn this way are the truly elevated (கற்றார்), while those who refuse to learn are கடையர், the lowest. Solomon Pappaiah reads the second line as condemning those who are ashamed to stand and learn, which makes pride the real barrier to education. The inversion of rank is typical of Valluvar: outward humility produces inner eminence. Many traditions make the same point, from the Gita's call to approach a teacher with submission (echoed in the Sanskrit maxim vidyā dadāti vinayam, 'learning gives humility') to the Mishnah's warning that the shy or ashamed cannot learn.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just try to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him submissively and render service unto him. The self-realized souls can impart knowledge unto you because they have seen the truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that real knowledge is gained by approaching a teacher with humility (pranipata), sincere questioning and service.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-exact match to the Kural's picture of the student standing humbly before the teacher as a precondition for learning.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs teaches that those who welcome instruction grow in knowledge, while those too proud to be corrected sink to the level of beasts.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks the teachable above the proud and unteachable, whom it calls 'brutish', much as the Kural calls them the lowest.

islam.quote_or_event: “Moses said to him, “May I follow you on [the condition] that you teach me from what you have been taught of sound judgement?””
islam.explanation: Even the prophet Moses humbly asks the mysterious servant of God (traditionally al-Khidr) to be allowed to follow him as a student.
islam.tie_back: A strong match for the Kural's first line: even the greatest must stand as seekers before those who know more.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ben Zoma said: Who is wise? He who learns from every man.”
judaism.explanation: True wisdom, Ben Zoma teaches, belongs to the person humble enough to learn from anyone at all. Elsewhere in Avot (2:5), Hillel warns that 'a timid person [cannot] learn', meaning one ashamed to ask questions.
judaism.tie_back: Both teachings match the Kural: wisdom belongs to those who humbly seek it, and pride or shame keeps people ignorant.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges disciples to follow a wise teacher eagerly, as someone would follow a person who knew where treasure was buried.
buddhism.tie_back: The treasure-seeker image mirrors the Kural's 'poor before the rich'. The learner approaches the teacher as the needy approach wealth.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who always acknowledges his allegiance to his teacher, who has religious zeal and ardour for study, who is kind in words and actions, deserves to be instructed.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana makes humble devotion to one's teacher, and staying in the teacher's lineage (kula), the condition for receiving learning. Its first lecture is devoted entirely to a disciple's humility (vinaya).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who stand humbly before their teachers, eager as the poor before the rich, are the superior ones. The Jain text likewise names lowly allegiance to the teacher as what makes a student worthy of instruction.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Bowing down, again and again, I fall at the Feet of my Guru; through Him, I have seen the Lord, the Divine Self, within.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes humbly bowing again and again before the Guru, through whose teaching he came to see the Lord within himself.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who stand humbly before their teachers, like the needy before the rich, are truly superior; Guru Nanak shows the same humility before the teacher as the way to the highest understanding.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 353, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Young Telemachus, sent to seek news from old King Nestor, confesses he feels ashamed and inexperienced about questioning an elder. Athena, disguised as Mentor, tells him to take courage and ask.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess of wisdom herself pushes the young man past his shyness so that he can learn from an experienced elder.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This fits the Kural closely. The learner must humbly approach the one who knows, and shame about asking is the obstacle to overcome.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates explains that the Delphic oracle called him wisest only because, unlike others, he knew that he did not know. His wisdom began with admitting his own poverty of knowledge.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, recognizing one's ignorance, the stance of the 'poor' before knowledge, is the starting point of all real learning.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes humble awareness of one's own need the basis of true superiority in learning.

real_life_example.event_title: Frederick Douglass trades bread for reading lessons
real_life_example.event: As an enslaved boy in Baltimore, Frederick Douglass was taught the alphabet by Sophia Auld until her husband forbade the lessons. In his 1845 Narrative, Douglass recorded that he then made friends with the white boys he met in the street and turned as many as he could into teachers, giving bread to the hungry ones in return for lessons. He also taught himself to write by copying letters from ship timbers and a schoolboy's copy-books.
real_life_example.explanation: Douglass sought learning from anyone who could give it, however young or humble, and his literacy became the foundation of his later life as a writer and abolitionist leader.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises those who eagerly seek learning, like the needy before the rich, and Douglass begged lessons from street children with whatever he had to offer.

tamil:
தொட்டனைத் தூறும் மணற்கேணி மாந்தர்க்குக்
கற்றனைத் தூறும் அறிவு.
transliteration:
Thottanaith thoorum manarkeni maandharkkuk
Katranaith thoorum arivu.
meaning: A well dug in sand gives more water the deeper it is dug. In the same way, a person’s understanding grows the more they learn.
elementary: When you dig a hole at the beach, water starts to seep in, and the deeper you dig, the more water comes. Your mind works the same way: the more you learn, the more wisdom flows out of you.
university: This is perhaps the most quoted kural of the chapter. It rests on a precise agricultural image from the Tamil landscape: the மணற்கேணி, a shallow well dug in sandy riverbed or soil, where groundwater seeps in more strongly the deeper one digs. The parallel verbs தொட்டனை ('as much as dug') and கற்றனை ('as much as learned') set up an exact proportion, and the shared verb ஊறும் ('springs, oozes up') links the two halves. The point is that wisdom (அறிவு, arivu) is not poured in from outside but springs up from within, released by the labour of study. It also implies that learning has no fixed end, since there is always more water below. Parallels range from Proverbs' 'wellspring of wisdom' and the Mishnah's 'ever-flowing spring' to Pope's 'Pierian spring'.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Taittiriya Upanishad, young Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him Brahman. Each time, he is told to go and practise tapas (disciplined inquiry). He comes to understand Brahman step by step as food, breath, mind, understanding, and finally bliss.
hinduism.explanation: Bhrigu's knowledge deepens in stages. Each round of effort 'digs' further and reveals a deeper layer of truth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's sand-well, understanding grows exactly as far as the seeker keeps digging through sustained effort.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs pictures wisdom as a spring that keeps flowing, deep water that wells up and never runs dry.
christianity.tie_back: A strong image match: both texts picture wisdom as water welling up from a deep source.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, “If the sea were ink for [writing] the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it in [continual] supplement.””
islam.explanation: The Qur'an uses an ocean image to show that divine knowledge has no limit. There is always more to learn.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's sand-well, it pictures knowledge as a water source that is never used up.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eleazar ben Arach is like a spring that [ever] gathers force.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai praises his disciple as a spring whose flow keeps increasing, in contrast to another disciple who is 'a plastered cistern which loses not a drop' (retaining learning but not producing new insight).
judaism.tie_back: A striking parallel: the ideal scholar is an ever-growing spring, just as the Kural's learner is a well whose water rises with every bit of digging.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Wisdom springs from meditation; without meditation wisdom wanes. Having known these two paths of progress and decline, let a man so conduct himself that his wisdom may increase.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that wisdom 'springs up' in proportion to cultivation and dries up when practice stops.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, wisdom rises in proportion to effort. Here the effort is meditation rather than study.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By study he destroys the Karman which obstructs right knowledge.”
jainism.explanation: In Jain doctrine, knowledge is the soul's own nature, only covered over by knowledge-obscuring karma (jnanavaraniya). Study wears that covering away, so understanding grows as more of the soul's latent knowledge is uncovered.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's well in the sand yields water the deeper it is dug, and knowledge wells up in proportion to learning. In the Jain picture, too, knowledge is already present and comes out more fully the more one studies.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The seeker comes forth, and the debater dies down; I am a sacrifice, a sacrifice to the Guru, the Creator Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says that the one who keeps searching grows in spiritual life, while the one who only argues withers away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says understanding wells up in proportion to how deeply one digs into learning; Guru Nanak likewise says that it is the persistent seeker, not the disputer, who comes to flourish.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1255, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes the Muses of Mount Helicon bathing in the Hippocrene, the 'Horse's Spring' said to have been struck from the rock by Pegasus' hoof. Along with the Pierian spring, it became the classical symbol of the source of poetic and intellectual inspiration.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, wisdom and inspiration flow from sacred springs, and poets 'drink' from them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it pictures knowledge as water rising from a spring, though Greek myth stresses divine gift more than human digging.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A little learning is a dang'rous thing; / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring: / There shallow draughts intoxicate the brain, / And drinking largely sobers us again.”
philosophy.explanation: Pope warns that shallow learning breeds arrogance, while deep learning brings sober wisdom. The depth of study decides the quality of understanding.
philosophy.tie_back: An excellent match: like Valluvar, Pope ties the benefit of learning to its depth, using the image of a spring.
philosophy.source: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism, Part II, lines 215–218 (1711)

real_life_example.event_title: Michael Ventris deciphers Linear B
real_life_example.event: Michael Ventris became fascinated by the undeciphered Linear B script at the age of 14, after visiting a 1936 London exhibition of finds from Crete and meeting Sir Arthur Evans there. Though he trained as an architect, he kept studying the tablets for years and from 1949 worked intensively on them, using careful analysis of how signs recurred and combined. In June 1952 he announced on British radio that the script recorded a very early form of Greek, a result confirmed with the linguist John Chadwick.
real_life_example.explanation: Years of patient study let Ventris see what experts had missed, pushing written Greek back centuries before Homer.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares understanding to water in a sand well that rises as one digs deeper, and Ventris's insight came only after about sixteen years of steady digging into the problem.

tamil:
யாதானும் நாடாமால் ஊராமால் என்னொருவன்
சாந்துணையுங் கல்லாத வாறு.
transliteration:
Yaadhaanum naadaamaal ooraamaal ennoruvan
Saanthunaiyum kallaadha vaaru.
meaning: For a learned person, every country and every town becomes their own. So why does anyone stay without learning right up to the day they die?
elementary: A good doctor or teacher can move to any town and still be welcomed and needed. What you learn goes with you everywhere and makes you at home anywhere. So why would anyone ever stop learning?
university: The kural is built as a rhetorical question. Its premise is that for the learned, யாதானும் நாடாம், ஊராம் (any land is their land, any town is their town), because learning makes a person welcome and useful anywhere. Its conclusion asks why anyone would remain unlearned சாந்துணையும், 'even until death'. That phrase quietly adds the idea of lifelong learning: there is no age at which study becomes pointless. In the Porul section's concern with the practical world, this is an argument from utility. Land and local status can be lost, but learning is portable citizenship. The first idea matches the Sanskrit maxim that a scholar is honoured everywhere, and the second matches Solon's line about growing old while always learning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A well-known Sanskrit subhashita states: “svadeśe pūjyate rājā, vidvān sarvatra pūjyate”. A king is honoured in his own land, but a learned person is honoured everywhere.
hinduism.explanation: The proverb contrasts the local, limited honour of political power with the universal honour of learning.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-perfect match to the Kural's first half: the learned person is at home and respected in every land and town.
hinduism.source: Sanskrit subhashita (traditionally included in Chanakya Niti collections; attribution varies)

christianity.quote_or_event: “As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.”
christianity.explanation: Daniel and his friends, exiles in a foreign empire, rise to high honour in the Babylonian court purely because of their learning and wisdom.
christianity.tie_back: A narrative example of the Kural's claim: through learning, the exile makes a foreign land his own.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Joseph] said, “Appoint me over the storehouses of the land. Indeed, I will be a knowing guardian.””
islam.explanation: Joseph (Yusuf), sold as a slave into Egypt, becomes the trusted steward of a foreign kingdom because of his knowledge.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows knowledge turning a stranger's land into the place where he is honoured and entrusted.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not: ‘when I shall have leisure I shall study;’ perhaps you will not have leisure.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel warns against putting off study to a later time that may never come, since life is uncertain.
judaism.tie_back: This parallels the Kural's second half, its challenge to anyone who stays unlearned until death: do not postpone learning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better it is to live one day wise and meditative than to live a hundred years foolish and uncontrolled.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that a long life without wisdom is worth less than a single day lived wisely.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's rebuke of those who stay unlearned until death, it counts a lifetime without wisdom as wasted.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The enlightened and liberated monk should control himself, whether he be in a village or a town, and he should preach to all the road of peace; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk is homeless and keeps moving. Wherever his wandering takes him, village or town, he lives by the same discipline and shares his learning with everyone, and the refrain urges him to stay vigilant all his life.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says every land and every town belongs to the learned, so no one should stop learning until death. The Jain ideal of the wandering learned monk, at home and of use in any village or town, matches the first half of the kural.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that since he found the company of the holy, no one seems an enemy or a stranger to him and he is at home with all.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that to the learned every land and every town becomes their own; Guru Arjan describes the same freedom from foreignness, in which no one is a stranger.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Odyssey opens by describing its hero as a man who saw the cities of many peoples and learned their minds.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus' defining trait is knowledge gained through wandering. It lets him survive, and even win honour, in one foreign land after another.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's learned person, Odysseus becomes a citizen of many cities through what he knows.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Solon, the Athenian lawgiver, is reported in Plato's Laches as saying that he grew old always learning many things. The Cynic Diogenes, asked where he came from, called himself 'a citizen of the world' (kosmopolitēs).
philosophy.explanation: Solon models lifelong learning right up to old age. Diogenes models the thinker whose home is the whole world rather than one city.
philosophy.tie_back: Together they cover both halves of the Kural: every land is the learned person's home, and learning should never stop until death.
philosophy.source: Plato, Laches 188b (Solon); Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.63 (Diogenes)

real_life_example.event_title: Al-Idrisi makes his home at the court of Roger II of Sicily
real_life_example.event: Muhammad al-Idrisi, a Muslim scholar born in Ceuta in North Africa and educated in Cordoba, entered the service of the Norman Christian king Roger II of Sicily around 1145. He lived and worked at the court in Palermo for the rest of his life, gathering reports from travellers and earlier geographers. Shortly before Roger's death in 1154 he completed a world map with an accompanying geography, known in Arabic as the Book of Roger.
real_life_example.explanation: Al-Idrisi's learning made him welcome and honoured in a foreign kingdom of a different faith, where he produced one of the great geographical works of the Middle Ages.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says every land becomes the learned person's own land, and al-Idrisi found a lasting home at a foreign court because of what he knew.

tamil:
ஒருமைக்கண் தான்கற்ற கல்வி ஒருவற்கு
எழுமையும் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Orumaikkan thaankatra kalvi oruvarku
Ezhumaiyum emaap pudaiththu.
meaning: The learning a person gains in one life can protect and help them for seven lives to come.
elementary: Planting a tree helps you, your children and your grandchildren long after you have gone. Valluvar says learning is even bigger than that: what you learn now keeps helping you far into the future, even into future lives.
university: This kural draws on the Indian framework of rebirth. ஒருமை (orumai, 'one birth') is set against எழுமை (ezhumai, 'seven births'), a conventional expression for a long chain of future lives. The key word ஏமாப்பு (emaappu) means protection, security or support, so learning is pictured as a lasting safeguard that goes with the soul. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow the traditional rebirth reading. Kalaignar reinterprets it more secularly as learning that protects seven generations of a family. The kural fits the chapter's larger claim that learning, unlike other goods, is not used up or lost. Similar ideas appear in the Gita's teaching that a yogi's progress carries over into the next life and in Plato's theory that learning is recollection from earlier existence.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “On taking such a birth, he revives the divine consciousness of his previous life, and he again tries to make further progress in order to achieve complete success, O son of Kuru.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna assures Arjuna that spiritual progress and understanding are never lost at death. They carry into the next birth and continue from there.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-exact match to the Kural: what is gained in one life protects and advances a person in later lives.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.”
christianity.explanation: Daniel's vision promises that the wise will shine for ever, so that their wisdom has an eternal result beyond this life.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the benefit of wisdom reaches past one lifetime. The framework is resurrection and eternity rather than rebirth.

islam.quote_or_event: “When a man dies, his acts come to an end, but three, recurring charity, or knowledge (by which people) benefit, or a pious child, who prays for him (for the deceased).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that beneficial knowledge is one of only three things that keep earning reward for a person after death.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats learning as one of the few goods whose benefit outlasts a single lifetime.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For when a man passes away there accompany him neither gold nor silver, nor precious stones nor pearls, but Torah and good deeds alone.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yose ben Kisma refuses a fortune to live away from a place of learning, explaining that only Torah and good deeds go with a person beyond death.
judaism.tie_back: A very close match: learning is the possession that goes with a person past the end of this life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Buddhavamsa, the ascetic Sumedha resolves at the feet of the Buddha Dipankara to become a Buddha, then spends countless lives perfecting the paramis, including the perfection of wisdom (pañña). What he builds in each life carries forward to the next.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism teaches that cultivated wisdom and virtue are carried from life to life until they reach full Buddhahood.
buddhism.tie_back: A strong conceptual match: learning and wisdom gained in one birth protect and lift a person through many later births.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By possession of knowledge he acquires an understanding of words and their meaning; thereby he will not perish in the forest of the fourfold Saṃsâra; as a needle with its thread will not be lost, thus the soul possessing the sacred lore will not be lost in the Saṃsâra.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's teaching plays on sutta, meaning both 'thread' and 'scripture'. A needle with a thread is not lost, and a soul that holds sacred knowledge is not lost in the cycle of rebirths.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says learning gained in one birth protects a person through seven births to come. The Jain image of the threaded needle makes the same promise: knowledge keeps the soul safe across the round of rebirth.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.59 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Where there is no mother, father, children, friends or siblings - O my mind, there, only the Naam, the Name of the Lord, shall be with you as your help and support.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Guru Arjan says that where no family or friend can follow, beyond this life, only the Name goes with a person as their support.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says learning gained in one life protects a person through seven lives to come; Guru Arjan names the Naam as the one possession that goes with the soul beyond this life and keeps protecting it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 264, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib (Ashtpadi 2), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, souls choose their next lives. Plato's Socrates says the soul that has practised philosophy chooses wisely, while unphilosophical souls pick disastrous lives out of ignorance.
greek_mythology.explanation: Wisdom gained in one life shapes the quality of the next life a soul chooses.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, learning in one life gives protection across future lives.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Meno, Socrates argues that the soul is immortal and has been born many times, so that what we call 'learning' is really recollection (anamnesis) of knowledge gained before.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, knowledge is carried across lives. The soul brings it into each new birth, and inquiry draws it out again.
philosophy.tie_back: A close conceptual parallel: learning is not confined to one lifetime but runs through many.

real_life_example.event_title: Avicenna's Canon of Medicine teaches doctors for six centuries
real_life_example.place: Persia (now Iran), and universities across Europe
real_life_example.event: The Persian physician and philosopher Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, compiled al-Qanun fi al-tibb, the Canon of Medicine, in the early 11th century. Translated into Latin in the 12th century, it became a standard medical textbook in European universities and was still used at Montpellier, France, as late as about 1650. It also remained central to medicine in the Islamic world.
real_life_example.explanation: The learning gathered in one lifetime went on guiding and protecting physicians and patients for many generations after its author's death.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the learning of one life protects through seven more, and Ibn Sina's Canon kept serving long after him, much as Kalaignar reads it of later generations.

tamil:
தாமின் புறுவது உலகின் புறக்கண்டு
காமுறுவர் கற்றறிந் தார்.
transliteration:
Thaaminburuvadhu ulaginburak kandu
Kaamuruvar katrarindhaar.
meaning: When learned people see that the learning that brings them joy also brings joy to the whole world, they love learning even more.
elementary: When you discover a great story and tell your friends, they love it too, and that makes you want to find even more stories. Learning works like that. Sharing it makes everyone happy, so you want to learn more.
university: The kural describes a self-reinforcing cycle of joy. The learned find pleasure (இன்புறுவது) in their own knowledge, then see that the same knowledge brings pleasure to the world (உலகு இன்புற). That discovery makes them desire (காமுறுவர்) learning all the more. Valluvar's use of kaamam, a word more often tied to love and desire, is striking: learning becomes a passion. The kural suggests that the highest motive for study is neither prestige nor profit but shared delight, which makes knowledge a social good. The idea is echoed in Seneca's statement that he learns only in order to teach, and in the Mishnah and hadith traditions that praise those who learn in order to share.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Gita describes the liberated sages as sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ, those who delight in the welfare of all beings, and says such people attain liberation.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna portrays the truly wise as people whose own inner fulfilment overflows into joyful work for the good of all living beings.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links the joy of the wise with the joy of the world. The Gita's focus is spiritual realization more than learning as such.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples not to hide the light they have received, but to let it shine for the benefit of all.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats what one has received as something to share with the world. The Gospel does not describe the learner's growing desire for learning.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best among you (Muslims) are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet joins learning and teaching into a single excellence. The highest rank goes to those who both acquire knowledge and pass it on.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes learning and delighting others with it inseparable parts of one noble activity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He who learns in order to teach, it is granted to him to study and to teach.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Ishmael teaches that someone who studies with the aim of sharing knowledge is rewarded with further opportunities to learn and to teach.
judaism.tie_back: A good match for the Kural's cycle: sharing learning leads to more learning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The gift of Dhamma excels all gifts; the taste of the Dhamma excels all tastes; the delight in Dhamma excels all delights.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls the sharing of true teaching the greatest gift and delight in the Dhamma the greatest delight.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it joins personal delight in wisdom with giving wisdom to others.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, seeker after the highest truth, study the sacred lore, in order to cause yourself and others to attain perfection.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on 'the very learned' ends by saying that learning is pursued for one's own good and for the good of others alike. What perfects the learner should also benefit the world.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the learned love learning all the more when they see that it delights the world as well as themselves. The Jain verse likewise ties one's own study to the good it brings to others.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that knowledge truly reflected upon makes a person a benefactor of others (paropkari).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the learned love learning more when they see it delight the whole world; Guru Nanak likewise sees the proof of real learning in the good it does for others.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod sings of the Muses, whose songs gladden the great mind of Zeus. When a person loved by the Muses sings, people weighed down with grief forget their sorrows.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, the gifts of the Muses (poetry, song and learning) delight both gods and humans and relieve the world's sorrow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows learning and art spreading joy outward to the whole world.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Lucilius that he is glad to learn so that he may teach. No knowledge, however excellent, would please him if he had to keep it to himself, and he would refuse wisdom itself if it came on condition of never sharing it.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, the joy of learning cannot be separated from the joy of sharing it. Knowledge kept to oneself loses its pleasure.
philosophy.tie_back: An excellent match: the learner's delight grows through the delight of others, which is the Kural's exact cycle.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 6.4

real_life_example.event_title: Rabindranath Tagore founds Visva-Bharati
real_life_example.event: Rabindranath Tagore, who had won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, started an experimental school at Santiniketan in 1901. In 1921 he expanded it into Visva-Bharati, a world university whose stated aim was a meeting of the cultures of East and West. The institution became a central university of India in 1951, and Santiniketan was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
real_life_example.explanation: Tagore turned his own delight in literature, music and art into an institution meant to share that delight with students from across the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the learned love learning all the more when they see it delight the world, and Tagore built a university to spread to the world the learning that delighted him.

tamil:
கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி யொருவற்கு
மாடல்ல மற்றை யவை.
transliteration:
Kedil vizhuchchelvam kalvi oruvarku
Maadalla matraiyavai.
meaning: Learning is the one great treasure that can never be destroyed. Compared with it, all the other things people own are not real treasure at all.
elementary: Toys can break, money can be lost, and a house can burn down. What you have learned stays in your head, and no one can steal it. That is why Valluvar calls learning the best treasure of all.
university: The chapter ends with its thesis. Learning is கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம், 'imperishable, excellent wealth', and all other things are மாடு அல்ல, 'not wealth'. மாடு (maadu) is an old Tamil word for wealth that originally meant cattle, the earliest form of property, which gives the claim an archaic force. The argument works on two levels. Materially, learning cannot be stolen, taxed, destroyed or divided. Evaluatively, only learning deserves the name 'wealth' at all. Placing this conclusion in the Porul (Wealth) section is pointed, since Valluvar redefines the very wealth that section is about. The same claim appears almost word for word in the Sanskrit verse on vidyā-dhana, the wealth of knowledge that thieves cannot steal and kings cannot seize.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A famous Sanskrit subhashita says: “na cora-hāryaṃ na ca rāja-hāryaṃ na bhrātṛ-bhājyaṃ na ca bhāra-kāri; vyaye kṛte vardhata eva nityaṃ vidyā-dhanaṃ sarva-dhana-pradhānam.” Thieves cannot steal it, kings cannot seize it, brothers cannot divide it, and it is no burden to carry. When spent, it only grows. The wealth of knowledge is the foremost of all wealth.
hinduism.explanation: The verse lists every way ordinary wealth can be lost and shows that none of them applies to learning.
hinduism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: learning is imperishable wealth, and it is the chief of all wealth.
hinduism.source: Traditional Sanskrit subhashita on vidyā-dhana (widely cited; exact textual origin uncertain)

christianity.quote_or_event: “How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs ranks wisdom and understanding far above precious metals as the truly valuable possession.
christianity.tie_back: A strong match: learning outranks material wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “The learned are the heirs of the Prophets, and the Prophets leave neither dinar nor dirham, leaving only knowledge, and he who takes it takes an abundant portion.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that the real inheritance of the prophets is knowledge, not money, and that whoever gains it has received a rich share.
islam.tie_back: An excellent match: knowledge is the true wealth, and coins are not the inheritance worth having.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 3641 (graded sahih by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: Midrash Tanchuma tells of a scholar on a ship full of merchants. They mock him for carrying no goods, and he says his merchandise is greater than theirs. Pirates seize everything the merchants own. When they land, the destitute merchants are ignored, while the scholar is welcomed and honoured by the townspeople for his learning.
judaism.explanation: The story shows in narrative form that learning is the one possession pirates cannot take and the one that provides for its owner anywhere.
judaism.tie_back: A perfect narrative parallel: all other wealth disappears, and learning alone remains indestructible and valuable.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Nidhikanda Sutta contrasts treasure buried in the ground, which can be lost, stolen or forgotten, with a 'treasure' of generosity, virtue, restraint and self-control. That inner treasure goes with its owner, cannot be taken by others, and cannot be stolen by thieves.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines real treasure as inner qualities that no loss can touch.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares ordinary wealth perishable and inner wealth imperishable. Its treasure is merit and virtue rather than learning as such.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the ocean of inexhaustible water, the delight of Svayambhû, which is full of precious things of many kinds, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana ends its praise of the learned by comparing them to an inexhaustible ocean full of precious things. An earlier verse in the same lecture (11.26) compares them to 'a well-guarded storehouse … filled with grain of many kinds'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls learning the one imperishable wealth, beside which all else is not wealth. The Jain images of an inexhaustible, treasure-filled ocean and a well-guarded storehouse present learning as unequalled and undiminishing riches in the same way.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.30 (cf. 11.26) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Siblings of Destiny meet together, and eat and spend, but these resources do not diminish; they continue to increase.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan speaks of the spiritual treasure of the Name: however much those who gather in holy company use and share it, it never runs out and only grows.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls learning the one imperishable wealth beside which nothing else is wealth; Guru Arjan describes a spiritual treasure with the same quality of never being used up.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 186, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asks Dionysus that everything he touches should turn to gold. When even his food and drink turn to metal, he begs to be freed from the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows that material wealth, however great, cannot sustain life and may even destroy it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It supports the negative half of the Kural: other possessions are not true wealth. It says nothing directly about learning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells of the philosopher Stilpo. His city was captured and he lost his wife, children and property, yet when the conqueror asked whether he had lost anything, he answered that all his goods were with him, meaning his wisdom and virtue.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoics, the only true possessions are those of the mind, which no conqueror can take.
philosophy.tie_back: An excellent match: everything else can be lost, but the wealth of the mind is imperishable and alone deserves to be called wealth.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 9.18–19

real_life_example.event_title: China's universities carry their learning to Kunming in wartime
real_life_example.event: After the outbreak of war with Japan in 1937, Peking University, Tsinghua University and Nankai University left their campuses in the north, regrouped first in Changsha and then moved to Kunming in the far southwest. There they operated together as the National Southwest Associated University in poor, makeshift buildings until 1946. Among its students were Chen-Ning Yang and Tsung-Dao Lee, who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1957.
real_life_example.explanation: The universities lost their buildings, libraries and homes, yet the knowledge of their teachers and students survived and produced some of the century's great scientists.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls learning the one wealth that cannot be destroyed, and the wartime university showed that when everything else was left behind, learning travelled on intact.

tamil:
அரங்கின்றி வட்டாடி யற்றே நிரம்பிய
நூலின்றிக் கோட்டி கொளல்.
transliteration:
Arangindri vattaadi yatre nirampiya
Noolindrik kotti kolal.
meaning: Speaking in a gathering of learned people without having fully learned your subject is like playing dice without a game board.
elementary: Imagine trying to play a board game when nobody has drawn the board. You can roll the dice, but none of your moves mean anything. This kural says that speaking in front of wise people when you haven’t really studied is exactly like that: lots of movement, no real game.
university: The image is precise: vattu (dice or game pieces) moved without an arangu (the ruled board or square) produce motion without rules, and therefore without meaning or result. Kotti (an assembly, a learned gathering) is the arena of debate, and nirampiya nool (complete, fully mastered texts) is the board that gives structure to every move. Parimelazhagar reads the verse as a warning to one who enters discussion with no framework of learning: his words, however energetic, have nothing to be scored against. The chapter thus opens by defining ignorance not as silence but as ungrounded speech. Across traditions, the parallel concern is the would-be teacher or debater who speaks confidently while ‘understanding neither what they say’ (1 Timothy), the Qur’anic ban on pursuing what one has no knowledge of, and Plato’s critique of the rhetorician who persuades without knowing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhagavad Gita 4.40 teaches that the ignorant person who lacks faith in the revealed scriptures and is full of doubt falls away, finding happiness neither in this world nor the next.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a person who has neither learned the scriptures nor trusts them; such a person has no stable ground to stand on and so cannot progress.
hinduism.tie_back: Both describe the person without a foundation of learning as having no framework — the Kural’s ‘board’ — so that nothing he does adds up.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns Timothy about people who want the status of teachers even though they don’t understand the very things they speak about so confidently.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s figure exactly: someone who takes the floor in a learned setting without the learning that would give his words meaning.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids following or asserting things one has no knowledge of, because every faculty used will be held to account.
islam.tie_back: Both condemn acting and speaking as if one knew, when there is no knowledge underneath.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that jumping in to answer before one has properly heard and understood the matter is both foolish and shameful.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes speaking without the necessary grounding — and the public embarrassment that follows.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Simile of the Snake, the Buddha describes people who learn the teaching poorly and use it only to criticize others and win debates, comparing them to someone who grabs a water snake by the tail and is bitten.
buddhism.explanation: Learning grasped badly and used for argument doesn’t help the arguer — it harms him, like picking up a snake the wrong way.
buddhism.tie_back: Both picture debate conducted without real mastery of the texts as a game that cannot be won.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The simpleton, not being able to acquire any learning for himself, goes into the assembly of the learned, and reciting as his own a stanza which he has learned from some schoolboy, exposes thereby his own ignorance.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain didactic quatrains mock the person who walks into a gathering of scholars with no learning of his own. Whatever he says there only shows how little he knows.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's player throwing dice with no board drawn is the same unprepared speaker. With nothing mastered, his attempt in the learned assembly can only fail.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 32 'Experience in (conducting of) assemblies', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Wisdom which leads to arguments is not called wisdom. Wisdom leads us to serve our Lord and Master; through wisdom, honor is obtained.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of the Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak denies the name of wisdom to cleverness spent in disputation and says that real wisdom serves God and is what earns honour.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural mocks the man who enters a learned assembly to argue without having mastered his texts; Guru Nanak likewise says that argument without true understanding is not wisdom and brings no honour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon insists on driving his father Helios’s sun-chariot without the skill for it; he loses control of the horses and scorches the earth before Zeus strikes him down.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaethon takes on a role that needs mastery he doesn’t have, and his confident attempt turns into chaos.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like dice moved without a board, action without mastery produces motion with no order or good result.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Gorgias, Socrates gets Gorgias to admit that the orator, who has no knowledge of medicine, can seem more convincing than the doctor to an ignorant audience — one who does not know persuading those who do not know.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates shows that rhetoric without knowledge only works in front of people who also don’t know; before experts it collapses.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the same point about the unlearned speaker in an assembly of the learned: his performance has nothing to rest on.

real_life_example.event_title: Bishop Wilberforce argues against Darwin at the 1860 Oxford meeting
real_life_example.place: University Museum, Oxford, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: At the British Association for the Advancement of Science meeting held in Oxford's new University Museum, Samuel Wilberforce, Bishop of Oxford and a celebrated orator, spoke at length against Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection, published seven months earlier, before a noisy crowd of several hundred. The biologist Thomas Henry Huxley replied, and the botanist Joseph Hooker then rose and, as he reported in a letter to Darwin two days later, argued that the bishop could not have read Darwin's book and did not know the basics of botany. No verbatim record was kept, and the famous exchange about ape ancestry survives only in differing later accounts.
real_life_example.explanation: The meeting became a lasting symbol of the gap between confident public eloquence and real command of the subject under debate before a learned audience.
real_life_example.tie_back: Like dice moved without a marked board, Wilberforce's polished rhetoric, in the judgement of the scientists present, had no grounding in the science it addressed, so they found no real argument in it to answer.

tamil:
கல்லாதான் சொற்கா முறுதல் முலையிரண்டும்
இல்லாதாள் பெண்காமுற் றற்று.
transliteration:
Kallaadhaan sorkaa murudhal mulaiyirandum
Illaadhaal penkaamut rattru.
meaning: An uneducated person who wants to be admired as a speaker is like a woman with no breasts wishing to be desired as a woman.
elementary: Some people want everyone to listen to them, but they haven’t learned anything worth saying. Valluvar uses a blunt comparison from his own time: it’s like wanting to be admired for something you simply don’t have. The wish is there, but the thing that would make it come true is missing.
university: Sorkaamurudhal is a craving for speech — specifically the desire to be admired for eloquence in an assembly. Valluvar’s simile, jarring to modern ears, is built on the conventions of classical Tamil poetics, where breasts are a standard marker of feminine attractiveness; the point is structural rather than a comment on women: a desire whose necessary basis is absent is futile and invites ridicule. Learning is to speech what that physical attribute is to erotic appeal in the poetic code. Parallel traditions frame the same pathology as the fool who ‘hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself’ (Proverbs 18:2), the Gita’s ‘men of small knowledge’ attached to flowery words, and the Dhammapada’s reminder that one is not wise because one speaks much. Modern readers may note the simile’s gendered framing as a product of its poetic era.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhagavad Gita 2.42–43 describes people of little understanding who delight in the flowery words of the Vedas and declare that there is nothing beyond them.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna criticizes those who love impressive-sounding language but lack the understanding behind it.
hinduism.tie_back: Both portray a hunger for fine speech in someone who has not acquired the knowledge that would give it substance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself.”
christianity.explanation: The fool isn’t interested in learning anything; he only wants a chance to show off what he thinks.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s unlearned man: all desire to be heard, no desire to learn.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he who disputes about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an enlightening book [from Him].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an criticizes those who eagerly argue about the most serious matters even though they have no knowledge, no guidance, and no scripture behind them.
islam.tie_back: Both describe the urge to hold forth that is not matched by any learning.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A fool also is full of words.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes observes that the fool multiplies words, talking at length about things he cannot know.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s unlearned man likewise wants to fill the room with speech that has nothing behind it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is not wise because one speaks much. He who is peaceable, friendly and fearless is called wise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada separates wisdom from talkativeness: speaking a lot is not what makes a person wise.
buddhism.tie_back: Both deny that eagerness to speak is any sign of learning.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is ignorant of the truth, egoistical, greedy, without self-discipline, and who talks loosely, is called ill-behaved and void of learning.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's lecture on the very learned puts loose talk among the marks of the person without learning. It sits next to ignorance and egoism.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural mocks the unlearned man who longs to be heard as an orator. Jain teaching likewise treats eagerness to talk without learning as a sign of the empty, ill-disciplined person.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “We are good at talking, but our actions are bad.”
sikhism.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak, speaking as the soul-bride, admits the gap between fine words and poor conduct.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ridicules the unlearned man who longs to be admired for his speech; Guru Nanak likewise exposes speech that has nothing real behind it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The satyr Marsyas picks up the flute Athena had thrown away, becomes proud of his playing, and challenges Apollo to a musical contest; he loses and is flayed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Marsyas wanted to be admired as a master musician on the strength of a borrowed instrument and a little practice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s unlearned speaker, he craves the standing of the accomplished without the full accomplishment, and is publicly humiliated.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Apology, Socrates says he examined the poets and found that they could not explain their own poems, yet because of their poetry they believed themselves wise in other matters as well.
philosophy.explanation: The poets had fine words and wanted the reputation of wisdom, but their knowledge did not match their speech.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker likewise wants to be admired for words that are not backed by learning.

real_life_example.event_title: Florence Foster Jenkins sings at Carnegie Hall
real_life_example.place: Carnegie Hall, New York City, United States
real_life_example.event: Florence Foster Jenkins, a wealthy New York socialite whom audiences and critics regarded as one of the worst singers of her day, had for years performed at the Waldorf Astoria and other New York venues, where people came largely to enjoy her mistakes. Urged on by friends, she made her Carnegie Hall debut on 25 October 1944; the recital sold out within about two hours, and she appeared in elaborate costumes she had made herself while the audience laughed and cheered. She died a month and a day later, on 26 November 1944, aged 76.
real_life_example.explanation: Her story is remembered as the classic case of a performer whose longing to be admired far outran the ability on which such admiration must rest.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the unlearned man who longs to be admired as a speaker to one who longs to be desired while lacking what desire depends on, and Jenkins's eager pursuit of acclaim as a singer without a singing voice shows that same mismatch between craving and foundation.

tamil:
கல்லா தவரும் நனிநல்லர் கற்றார்முன்
சொல்லா திருக்கப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Kallaa thavarum naninallar katraarmun
Sollaa thirukkap perin.
meaning: Even uneducated people will be thought of as very good, as long as they stay quiet in front of learned people.
elementary: If you don’t know much about a subject and you’re with experts, the smartest thing you can do is stay quiet and listen. People will actually think well of you for it. Talking would show what you don’t know; silence protects you and lets you learn.
university: The irony of nani nallar (‘exceedingly good’) is gentle but pointed: the unlearned person’s one available virtue is restraint. Parimelazhagar notes that silence both conceals the defect and avoids the harm of error. The verse inverts the previous kural — where the unlearned craved speech, here he is redeemed by abstaining from it. This is one of the most widely shared moral intuitions across cultures: Proverbs 17:28 (‘Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise’), Rabbi Akiva’s ‘a fence for wisdom is silence’, and the famous Sanskrit maxim of Bhartrhari that silence is the ornament of the unlearned in an assembly of scholars, which is an almost exact parallel. The Buddhist corpus adds the self-knowledge dimension: the fool who knows he is a fool is to that extent wise.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka says the Creator gave ignorance a covering that is entirely in one’s own control — silence — and that, especially in an assembly of the learned, silence is the ornament of the unlearned (vibhūṣaṇaṃ maunam apaṇḍitānām).
hinduism.explanation: The unlearned always have a way to hide their ignorance: simply to stay quiet, above all among scholars.
hinduism.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural word for word: among the learned, the unlearned are best off silent.
hinduism.source: Bhartrhari, Nitishataka, verse 7 (numbering varies by edition)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding.”
christianity.explanation: A foolish person who keeps quiet will be taken for wise, because no one hears anything foolish from him.
christianity.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s claim: the unlearned become ‘very good’ by staying silent.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that a believer should either say something good or stay silent.
islam.tie_back: Both treat silence as the right course when one has nothing sound to contribute.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Akiva teaches that silence is a protective fence around wisdom.
judaism.explanation: Just as a fence protects a field, keeping quiet protects and preserves wisdom.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes silence the safeguard of the person who lacks learning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: Recognizing one’s own ignorance is already a kind of wisdom; the real fool is the one who thinks he knows.
buddhism.tie_back: The unlearned person who stays quiet before the learned shows exactly this self-awareness, and so earns the Kural’s praise.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One should always be meek, and not be talkative in the presence of the wise; one should acquire valuable knowledge, and avoid what is worthless.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's first lecture on discipline tells the pupil to stay meek and quiet before the wise and to spend his effort gaining real knowledge.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the unlearned can still be counted good if they keep silent before the learned. The Jain rule of discipline asks for exactly that silence in the presence of the wise.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To speak too much and babble is useless.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Dhanaasree Guru Nanak warns that much talking turns into idle babble.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the unlearned keep their worth only by keeping quiet before the learned; Guru Nanak likewise counts excess speech as worthless.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 661, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Diogenes Laertius reports that Pythagoras’s new pupils had to keep silence for five years, only listening to his discourses, before they were admitted to see him.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Pythagorean school, beginners earned the right to speak by first listening in silence for a long time.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same principle as the Kural: those who have not yet learned should be silent in the presence of those who have.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 8.10

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”
philosophy.explanation: Wittgenstein ends his Tractatus by saying that where language cannot meaningfully reach, one should not try to speak.
philosophy.tie_back: Both counsel silence at the boundary of what one can responsibly say, though Wittgenstein’s boundary is logical, not personal learning.
philosophy.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 7 (tr. C. K. Ogden)

real_life_example.event_title: George Washington stays almost silent at the Constitutional Convention
real_life_example.event: George Washington, whose formal schooling appears to have ended at about fifteen and who never attended college, was chosen to preside over the Constitutional Convention, where many delegates were college-educated men trained in law and the classics. As presiding officer he called on speakers but took almost no part in the substantive debates; according to the record, he first spoke on the issues on the final day, 17 September 1787, to support reducing the number of people each member of the House of Representatives would represent from 40,000 to 30,000. His presence is generally credited with lending the convention prestige and authority.
real_life_example.explanation: Washington, who privately described himself as conscious of a defective education, let the convention's legal theorists argue while he presided, and his reputation for judgement rose rather than fell.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says even the unlearned are counted very good if they keep from speaking in the presence of the learned, and Washington's near-silence among more formally educated colleagues only enhanced his standing.

tamil:
கல்லாதான் ஒட்பம் கழியநன் றாயினும்
கொள்ளார் அறிவுடை யார்.
transliteration:
Kallaadhaan otpam kazhiyanan raayinum
Kollaar arivudai yaar.
meaning: Even if an uneducated person’s cleverness happens to be very good, wise people will not accept it as reliable.
elementary: Sometimes a person who never studied says something that sounds really smart. Wise people still don’t rely on it, because it’s a lucky hit, not something the person truly understands. Next time the same person may be completely wrong, and they won’t know the difference.
university: Otpam denotes native sharpness or cleverness; kazhiya nandru (‘exceedingly good’) concedes that it may even be impressive. Yet the wise (arivudaiyaar) do not ‘take’ (kollaar) it. Parimelazhagar’s explanation is epistemic: insight not grounded in learning is accidental and unreliable, so it cannot be built upon. This anticipates Plato’s distinction in the Meno between true opinion and knowledge — right opinions are valuable but ‘run away’ unless tied down by reasoning, like the statues of Daedalus. The kural is harder-edged than some traditions would allow: Pirkei Avot’s ‘look not at the vessel but at what is in it’ pushes the other way, and Cassandra’s myth dramatizes the tragedy of truth rejected because of its source. The accuracy notes below mark these as contrasts.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhagavad Gita 4.34 instructs the seeker to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master with humility, inquiry and service, because those who have seen the truth can impart knowledge.
hinduism.explanation: Real knowledge is to be received from those who have studied and realized it, not picked up from anyone who sounds clever.
hinduism.tie_back: Both locate reliable insight in those grounded in learning, which is why the wise do not rely on the unlearned.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The legs of the lame are not equal: so is a parable in the mouth of fools.”
christianity.explanation: A wise saying in the mouth of a fool is as unsteady as a lame person’s walk; it doesn’t carry him anywhere.
christianity.tie_back: Even a good saying from one without understanding is not something to lean on — the Kural’s very point.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.”
islam.explanation: Information from an unreliable source is not to be accepted at face value; it must be checked first.
islam.tie_back: Both teach that the reliability of the source matters, and the wise do not simply accept what comes from an unqualified one.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Meir says: look not at the vessel but at what is in it — a new jug may be full of old wine, and an old jug may not even contain new wine.
judaism.explanation: Judge a teaching by its content rather than by the status of the one who delivers it.
judaism.tie_back: This is a contrast: the Mishnah urges weighing content on its merits, while the Kural says the wise will not trust even good-seeming insight from the unlearned.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavour of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: A fool may be surrounded by wisdom and even handle it, as a spoon handles soup, without ever tasting its meaning.
buddhism.tie_back: The unlearned person’s clever-sounding insight is like soup on a spoon: present, but not understood — so the wise do not rely on it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it? Fools, though sinking lower and lower through their sins, believe themselves to be wise men.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on the false ascetic warns that clever words do not make a person wise. Fools mistake their own cleverness for wisdom.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the wise will not accept an unlearned man's cleverness, however fine it looks. The Jain verse likewise refuses to count mere cleverness as wisdom.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 6.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Hundreds of thousands of clever tricks, but not even one of them will go along with you in the end.”
sikhism.explanation: In the first pauri of Japji Sahib Guru Nanak says that no amount of cleverness carries a person through to God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the wise will not accept the cleverness of the unlearned, however striking; Guru Nanak says cleverness without true understanding does not hold up at all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib (pauri 1), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cassandra is given the gift of prophecy by Apollo but cursed so that no one believes her; her true warnings about Troy and Agamemnon’s murder are ignored.
greek_mythology.explanation: Cassandra speaks the truth, but her hearers dismiss it because of who she is and how she speaks.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A cautionary counterpoint: the Kural says the wise will not trust the unlearned even when they are right; Cassandra shows the cost when a true word is rejected for its source.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Meno, Socrates says true opinions are like the statues of Daedalus: valuable while they stay, but they run away unless tied down by reasoning, and once tied they become knowledge.
philosophy.explanation: Someone can be right by luck, but without the understanding that fixes it in place, their correct opinion cannot be relied upon.
philosophy.tie_back: This is precisely why the wise do not ‘take’ the unlearned man’s cleverness: it is right opinion without the tether of learning.

real_life_example.event_title: The Royal Society tests Leeuwenhoek's reports of tiny animals
real_life_example.place: Delft, Dutch Republic, and London, England
real_life_example.event: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Delft draper with no university education who knew no language other than Dutch, wrote to the Royal Society in October 1676 describing vast numbers of tiny living creatures he had seen in water through his home-made lenses. The Society did not accept the claims on his word: it asked for his methods, received testimonials from respected Delft citizens, and had the botanist Nehemiah Grew and then Robert Hooke try to reproduce the observations, which Hooke eventually succeeded in doing. Only after this verification was Leeuwenhoek elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1680.
real_life_example.explanation: The episode shows learned scientists declining to accept even a brilliant outsider's findings until trained observers had confirmed them, a caution that in this case ended by vindicating him.
