real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the wise will not accept the cleverness of an unlearned man as sound, however good it may be, and the Royal Society withheld acceptance of Leeuwenhoek's genuine discoveries until learned members had checked them for themselves.

tamil:
கல்லா ஒருவன் தகைமை தலைப்பெய்து
சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்.
transliteration:
Kallaa oruvan thagaimai thalaippeydhu
Sollaadach chorvu padum.
meaning: An uneducated person’s high opinion of themselves fades away as soon as they meet and talk with learned people.
elementary: Someone might think they’re very smart — until they start talking with people who have actually studied. Then, very quickly, it becomes clear how little they know, and their proud image falls apart.
university: Thagaimai is estimation or worth — here the self-estimation (or reputation) that the unlearned man carries; thalaippeydhu means ‘meeting, coming face to face’ (with the learned), and chorvu padum ‘will droop, fail’. The kural completes the logic of 402–403: the man who does not keep silent will be exposed in conversation. This is the drama of the Socratic elenchus, where confident interlocutors are shown in dialogue to lack what they claimed; Plato’s Phaedrus names the result ‘the show of wisdom without the reality’. The Mundaka and Katha Upanishads describe fools ‘wise in their own conceit’, and 1 Corinthians 8:2 compresses the diagnosis into a sentence. Dhammapada 63’s ‘fool who thinks himself wise’ is exactly the figure whose pride collapses here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Mundaka Upanishad describes fools who live in ignorance yet consider themselves wise and learned; they wander about, afflicted, like the blind led by the blind.
hinduism.explanation: People who believe themselves learned while remaining ignorant stumble from one error to another.
hinduism.tie_back: Both portray the false self-estimation of the unlearned, which cannot survive contact with reality.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that the person who is sure of his own knowledge has not yet begun to know as he should.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s unlearned man thinks highly of himself; Paul explains why that confidence is empty.

islam.quote_or_event: “Here you are - those who have argued about that of which you have [some] knowledge, but why do you argue about that of which you have no knowledge? And Allah knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an rebukes people who push their arguments into areas where they have no knowledge at all.
islam.tie_back: Both picture the unlearned entering debate and being shown up for lacking the knowledge they pretend to.

judaism.quote_or_event: Pirkei Avot lists seven marks of the wise person — among them, he does not speak before one greater in wisdom, does not interrupt, is not hasty to answer, and admits when he has not heard something — while the unformed person (golem) does the opposite.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah contrasts how the wise and the unformed behave in conversation with the learned.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s unlearned man behaves like the golem and is exposed in the very kind of conversation the Mishnah describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The worst kind of fool is the one who believes he is wise.
buddhism.tie_back: That self-believing fool is exactly the man whose esteem collapses when he talks with the learned.

jainism.quote_or_event: Indrabhuti Gautama, a renowned Vedic scholar with 500 disciples, went with bruised pride to debate Mahavira. Mahavira greeted him by name and answered his unspoken doubt about the existence of the soul. Indrabhuti's pride gave way, and he became Mahavira's first and chief disciple, Gautamaswami.
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition remembers the chief ganadhara's conversion as the moment a proud man's self-esteem melted in the presence of one who truly knew.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says an unlearned man's self-esteem withers once he talks with the learned. Indrabhuti's pride likewise dissolved the moment he spoke with Mahavira.
jainism.source: Jain narrative tradition of Indrabhuti Gautama's conversion, as retold in 'Gautamswami' (jainworld.com Jain stories)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, egotism is eliminated.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan lists the fruits of the Saadh Sangat and says pride dissolves in the company of the holy.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the unlearned man's self-esteem withers when he meets the learned; Guru Arjan says self-importance is undone in the company of the truly wise and holy.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When King Midas, judging a music contest, loudly declared Pan’s rustic piping superior to Apollo’s lyre, Apollo gave him the ears of an ass to show the quality of his judgment.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas spoke up confidently among those who truly knew music, and his lack of understanding was made visible to all.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s unlearned man, Midas’s standing collapses the moment he offers his opinion in a company of experts.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They will appear to be omniscient and will generally know nothing; they will be tiresome company, having the show of wisdom without the reality.”
philosophy.explanation: King Thamus warns that writing will let people seem knowledgeable without real understanding.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘The show of wisdom without the reality’ is exactly the unlearned man’s self-image that wilts in real conversation — which, for Plato, is where real knowledge is tested.

real_life_example.event_title: A royal commission tests Mesmer's animal magnetism
real_life_example.event: Franz Anton Mesmer, a physician who had moved his practice from Vienna to Paris, drew crowds of patients with treatments based on an invisible fluid he called animal magnetism. In 1784 King Louis XVI appointed a commission whose members included Benjamin Franklin and Antoine Lavoisier; after tests that included what is probably the first blind trial, it reported that the effects came from the patients' imagination and not from any magnetic fluid. Some 20,000 copies of the report were published, the mesmerist movement declined, and Mesmer left Paris.
real_life_example.explanation: The investigation is remembered as a landmark in testing medical claims, and it showed how quickly a fashionable reputation could collapse once examined by the learned.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the self-esteem of the unlearned withers as soon as they meet the learned, and Mesmer's celebrated standing faded once Franklin, Lavoisier and their colleagues examined his claims.

tamil:
உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர் அல்லால் பயவாக்
களரனையர் கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Ularennum maaththiraiyar allaal payavaak
Kalaranaiyar kallaa thavar.
meaning: Uneducated people can only be said to exist. Beyond that, they are like salty land where nothing grows.
elementary: Some land is so salty that nothing grows on it, no matter how much rain falls. Valluvar says a person who never learns is like that land: they are there, alive, but nothing useful grows from them for themselves or anyone else.
university: Ularennum maaththiraiyar — ‘mere measure of existing’ — reduces the unlearned to bare presence. Kalar is saline or alkaline soil, proverbial in Tamil for barrenness; payavaa (‘unyielding’) insists on the absence of any fruit. The agricultural image makes learning the cultivation that turns land into field. Striking parallels exist: the Buddha’s Desana Sutta (SN 42.7) speaks of a field that is ‘salty’ and poor as the worst kind of soil; the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 79 compares recipients of knowledge to types of land, including barren land that neither holds water nor grows anything; Jeremiah 17:6 speaks of ‘a salt land and not inhabited’; Hesiod calls the man who neither thinks nor learns ‘unprofitable’; and Seneca’s ‘leisure without study is death… a tomb for the living man’ matches the Kural’s reduction of such a life to mere existence.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Hitopadesha asks what use is a son who is born but is neither learned nor virtuous — like a blind eye, which brings only pain.
hinduism.explanation: A life without learning, even in a family, is compared to an organ that is present but useless.
hinduism.tie_back: Both reduce the unlearned person to mere presence without benefit — existing, but yielding nothing.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Prastavika (Introduction), verse on the unlearned son

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’s parable, a fig tree that bears no fruit year after year is judged to be merely taking up space.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s unlearned person likewise merely occupies the ground, yielding nothing.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet compared the guidance and knowledge sent through him to abundant rain falling on land: some fertile soil absorbs it and grows vegetation, some holds water for others, and “a portion of it was barren which could neither hold the water nor bring forth vegetation.”
islam.explanation: People respond to knowledge like different kinds of land; some benefit themselves and others, while some remain barren.
islam.tie_back: An almost identical image: the one who takes in no knowledge is barren land that yields nothing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah compares a spiritually cut-off person to a shrub in salty, barren ground where nothing good comes.
judaism.tie_back: The same ‘salt land’ image the Kural uses for the unlearned.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Desana Sutta the Buddha compares three fields — excellent, middling, and one that is poor, hard, salty, with bad soil — to three kinds of listeners to his teaching.
buddhism.explanation: The same seed does very differently depending on the ground; the salty, poor field yields least.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image of saline, unproductive soil for the person who has not taken in learning.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though great stones do not understand the speech of men, yet since they do what is required of them, as standing, sitting, lying down, or moving, they are far more useful than a fool (as it is impossible to induce a fool to act as we wish him).”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar's chapter on ignorance ranks the fool below even dead stones. Stones are at least of some use, while the fool yields nothing.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the unlearned merely exist, like barren saline land that bears nothing. The Naladiyar similarly calls the fool more useless than lifeless stone.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 34 'Ignorance', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The evil-minded ones plant their seed in the barren soil; such is the sign of those who have no Guru.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Malaar Guru Nanak uses the image of seed sown in barren, saline soil for the effort of those without the Guru's guidance.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares the unlearned to barren saline land that yields nothing; Guru Nanak uses the same image of barren soil (kalar) for a life without the Guru's teaching.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1275, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says the best man thinks things through for himself, the next best listens to good advice, but the man who neither thinks for himself nor takes to heart what another tells him is an unprofitable man.
greek_mythology.explanation: The person who neither reasons nor learns from others is of no use.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both call the unlearned person ‘unyielding’ or ‘unprofitable’ — present but without fruit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Leisure without study is death; it is a tomb for the living man.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca says a life with free time but no study is not truly living — it is a kind of burial while still alive.
philosophy.tie_back: Just as the Kural says the unlearned merely ‘exist’, Seneca says a life without learning is death in life.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 82.3 (tr. R. M. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Japan's Education System Order aims for no illiterate household
real_life_example.event: In 1872 the Meiji government issued the Gakusei, Japan's first comprehensive national education system, which divided the country into school districts and in principle required all children to attend elementary school regardless of sex, family occupation or social status. Its preamble declared that learning was the key to success in life and set the goal that no community should contain an illiterate family and no family an illiterate member. Lack of money, teachers and facilities meant the plan was only partly realised, and it was replaced by a new Education Order in 1879.
real_life_example.explanation: The order treated universal learning as the soil from which productive lives and a modern nation would grow.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural likens the unlearned to barren saline land that yields nothing, and the Gakusei rested on the same conviction that only learning makes a person's life fruitful.

tamil:
நுண்மாண் நுழைபுலம் இல்லான் எழில்நலம்
மண்மாண் புனைபாவை யற்று.
transliteration:
Nunmaan nuzhaipulam illaan ezhilnalam
Manmaan punaipaavai yattru.
meaning: The good looks of a person who lacks deep, sharp understanding are like the beauty of a painted clay doll.
elementary: A clay doll can be painted to look wonderful, but there is nothing inside it — it can’t think. Valluvar says a good-looking person who hasn’t developed a sharp, curious mind is like that doll: nice to look at, but empty.
university: Nunmaan nuzhaipulam — ‘subtle, excellent, penetrating intellect’ — names the kind of understanding that learning produces, able to enter into (nuzhai) fine distinctions. Its absence makes ezhil nalam (beauty, handsomeness) into manmaan punai paavai: a clay figure elaborately decorated. The contrast is surface versus interior. Aesop’s fox, finding an actor’s mask, puts it memorably: a beautiful head, but no brains. Chanakya Niti 3.8 is an almost perfect Sanskrit parallel — beauty, youth and noble birth without learning are like scentless kimshuka flowers. The Qur’an describes those whose ‘forms please you’ as ‘pieces of wood propped up’, and Proverbs likens beauty without discretion to a gold ring in a swine’s snout.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Chanakya Niti says that those endowed with beauty and youth and born in great families, if devoid of learning, do not shine — like kimshuka flowers that have no fragrance.
hinduism.explanation: Looks, youth and noble birth are not enough; without learning, a person is like a bright flower with no scent.
hinduism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: outward beauty without learning is hollow.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus condemns those who look impressive outside while being empty or corrupt inside.
christianity.tie_back: Both contrast a beautiful exterior with a lifeless interior.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes people whose appearance impresses, but who are inwardly like lifeless timber leaning against a wall.
islam.tie_back: Very close to the Kural’s decorated clay doll: an attractive form with nothing living inside.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As a jewel of gold in a swine’s snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion.”
judaism.explanation: Beauty without good sense is as incongruous and wasted as a gold ring in a pig’s nose.
judaism.tie_back: Both say that outward beauty is worthless without inner understanding.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada asks us to look at the body as a painted image, a mass of sores held together, sickly and full of plans that do not last.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges looking past the attractive, decorated surface of the body to see how fragile it really is.
buddhism.tie_back: The same ‘painted image’ idea as the Kural’s decorated clay doll: outward beauty that hides emptiness.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the seagirt earth merit is various. The sensible should be great. Those who are foolish, and are like unbeaten steel and the thorny brinjâl, will flourish in silk and gay apparel.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar notes that fools may be dressed in silk and finery while staying as crude and useless as unworked steel or a thorny plant.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural compares the good looks of someone without understanding to a painted clay doll. The Naladiyar likewise sees only fine outer show over an unformed, empty inside.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 27 'Riches without goodness', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The simmal tree is straight as an arrow; it is very tall, and very thick. But those birds which visit it hopefully, depart disappointed. Its fruits are tasteless, its flowers are nauseating, and its leaves are useless.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak describes the simmal (silk-cotton) tree, impressive to look at but giving nothing of use.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural likens a handsome person without subtle understanding to a painted clay doll; Guru Nanak's tall, fine-looking but fruitless simmal tree makes the same point about outward show without inner worth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a fox rummaging in an actor’s house finds a beautifully made mask and remarks that it is a fine head, but it has no brains.
greek_mythology.explanation: The mask looks perfect, but there’s nothing inside it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s exact image: a beautiful crafted head, empty of mind.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Fox and the Mask’ (Perry 27)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Charmides, when everyone admires the young Charmides’ beauty, Socrates asks whether he also has a noble soul, proposing to ‘strip’ and examine that before his body.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates redirects attention from a handsome appearance to the quality of the mind within.
philosophy.tie_back: Both hold that physical beauty is of little worth unless the mind within is refined.

real_life_example.event_title: Kempelen's chess-playing Turk
real_life_example.place: Vienna, Austria, and on tour in Europe and the United States
real_life_example.event: Around 1770 Wolfgang von Kempelen presented to the court of Empress Maria Theresa in Vienna an automaton in the form of a robed Turk seated behind a cabinet, which appeared to play chess on its own. For decades the machine, later owned by Johann Maelzel, toured Europe and from 1826 the United States, astonishing audiences. In reality a skilled human chess player concealed inside the cabinet followed the game on a small board and moved the figure's arm with levers.
real_life_example.explanation: The Turk became a byword for an impressive figure whose apparent intelligence belonged entirely to someone else.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the fine looks of one who lacks penetrating understanding to a beautifully painted clay doll, and the splendid Turk, with no understanding of its own, was exactly such a decorated figure.

tamil:
நல்லார்கண் பட்ட வறுமையின் இன்னாதே
கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு.
transliteration:
Nallaarkan patta varumaiyin innaadhe
Kallaarkan patta thiru.
meaning: Riches in the hands of uneducated people cause more misery than being poor causes for good people.
elementary: It’s sad when good, wise people are poor. But Valluvar says it’s even worse when foolish, unlearned people get lots of money — because they don’t know how to use it well, and they can cause harm to themselves and everyone around them.
university: Innaadhu (painful, harmful) is the operative comparative: both situations are bad, but thiru (wealth, fortune) in the hands of the unlearned (kallaar) is worse than poverty befalling the good (nallaar). Parimelazhagar explains that the learned poor still do good and are not diminished, whereas the unlearned rich use wealth for harm. The verse belongs to Porul’s concern with statecraft: resources without wisdom are a public danger. Plato’s Euthydemus argues that wealth and other ‘goods’ are good only under the guidance of wisdom and become greater evils under ignorance; the Dhammapada says riches ruin the foolish; the Qur’an forbids handing property to the weak-minded; and Ecclesiastes laments folly set in great dignity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Hitopadesha teaches that learning gives humility; from humility comes worthiness; from worthiness, wealth; from wealth, righteous action; and from that, happiness.
hinduism.explanation: In the right order, wealth should come after and through learning, so that it leads to good use and true happiness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural shows what goes wrong when that order is broken and wealth reaches someone without learning.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the rich fool, a man piles up wealth without wisdom about what truly matters, and it does him no good.
christianity.tie_back: Both show wealth in the hands of a fool as something that ends in loss rather than blessing.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not give the weak-minded your property, which Allah has made a means of sustenance for you, but provide for them with it and clothe them and speak to them words of appropriate kindness.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an instructs that wealth should not be handed over to those who lack the judgment to manage it.
islam.tie_back: Both recognize that wealth in the control of the unwise is harmful.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is the poor that walketh in his integrity, than he that is perverse in his lips, and is a fool.”
judaism.explanation: A poor person of integrity is better off than a foolish one who speaks crookedly.
judaism.tie_back: Both set the poverty of the good above the condition of the fool.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Riches ruin only the foolish, not those in quest of the Beyond. By craving for riches the witless man ruins himself as well as others.”
buddhism.explanation: Wealth itself is not the problem; it destroys those who lack wisdom, and they drag others down too.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s concern: wealth in the hands of the unwise causes harm.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you ask what is the reason why, while the good and just are in poverty, the unjust and unlearned are wealthy, O thou who hast eyes elongated like a lance! when one investigates the matter, it is nothing else but the effect of deeds done in, a former birth.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain quatrain faces the same scandal as the Kural, the wealthy unlearned and the poor good, and explains it by karma carried over from earlier births. Its neighbouring stanza (27.7) adds that the wise would desire neither state.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar judges wealth in the hands of the unlearned to be worse than the poverty of the good. The Naladiyar sets out the same pairing and puts it down to karma, not merit.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 27 'Riches without goodness', stanza 5 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Even poverty is bliss, if God comes to mind in the Saadh Sangat, the Company of the Holy.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Soohee Guru Arjan says that poverty is joyful when it is lived in holy company with God in mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says poverty falling on the good is less painful than wealth in the hands of the unlearned; Guru Arjan likewise says poverty with God in mind is bliss.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 745, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas foolishly asks Dionysus that everything he touches turn to gold; soon his food and drink become gold and he begs to be freed of the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas gets unlimited wealth but lacks the wisdom to want it rightly, and it becomes a curse.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The classic picture of wealth becoming misery in the hands of a fool.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Euthydemus, Socrates argues that wealth, health and other so-called goods are not good in themselves: guided by wisdom they are greater goods, but under ignorance they are greater evils.
philosophy.explanation: What makes wealth good or bad is whether it is used with wisdom or without it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the philosophical ground of the Kural: wealth in the hands of the unlearned becomes a greater evil than poverty.

real_life_example.event_title: Nauru's phosphate fortune is lost
real_life_example.place: Nauru (officially renamed Naoero in 2026), Pacific Ocean
real_life_example.event: Phosphate mining made the small Pacific nation of Nauru, independent since 1968, one of the richest countries in the world per head of population in the 1970s and early 1980s. A major part of the mining income was invested abroad to provide for the time when the phosphate ran out, but the investments lost much of their value through risky ventures and fraud; one notorious venture was a London musical about Leonardo da Vinci, funded by the Nauruan government, that closed within about a month in 1993. By the early 2000s the country was on the edge of bankruptcy, heavily in debt and reliant on foreign aid.
real_life_example.explanation: Nauru's story is widely cited as a warning that sudden wealth managed without sound knowledge can leave people worse off than before.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says wealth in the hands of those without learning does more harm than poverty among the good, and Nauru's fortune, invested without sound expertise, ended in debt and hardship.

tamil:
மேற்பிறந்தா ராயினும் கல்லாதார் கீழ்ப்பிறந்தும்
கற்றார் அனைத்திலர் பாடு.
transliteration:
Merpirandhaa raayinum kallaadhaar keezhppirandhum
Katraar anaiththilar paadu.
meaning: Even if they are born into a high family, uneducated people are not worth as much as learned people born into a low one.
elementary: Some people think being born into an important family makes them better than others. Valluvar disagrees: a person from a humble family who has learned a lot is worth more than a high-born person who hasn’t learned anything. What you learn matters more than where you were born.
university: Merpirandhaar/keezhppirandhu (born high/born low) refers to the social hierarchy of birth in Valluvar’s world; paadu is dignity, worth or standing. The kural does not abolish hierarchy in theory but subordinates it to learning in practice, a notable move in a society structured by birth. The closest parallel is Mishnah Horayot 3:8: a mamzer who is a Torah scholar takes precedence over a High Priest who is ignorant. Buddhism’s Dhammapada 393 and the Vasala Sutta reject birth as the measure of a brahmin; the Upanishadic story of Satyakama Jabala shows a boy of unknown lineage accepted for his truthfulness; Plato’s myth of the metals places each child by the quality of soul, not parentage; and Ecclesiastes prefers a poor, wise youth to a foolish king.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Satyakama Jabala, who does not know his father’s lineage, honestly tells the sage Gautama so; Gautama accepts him as a student, saying only a true brahmin would speak such truth, and Satyakama becomes a great teacher.
hinduism.explanation: A boy of unknown and humble birth is admitted to learning because of his character, and rises to eminence through it.
hinduism.tie_back: Both place the worth gained through truth and learning above the accident of birth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished.”
christianity.explanation: A poor but wise young person is worth more than a king who has grown foolish and will not learn.
christianity.tie_back: Both rank wisdom from a low station above folly in a high one.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah will raise those who have believed among you and those who were given knowledge, by degrees.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says true rank before God comes through faith and knowledge.
islam.tie_back: Both locate a person’s real standing in knowledge rather than in lineage.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah sets an order of precedence by lineage — priest, Levite, Israelite, and so on down to the mamzer — but adds that if the mamzer is a Torah scholar and the High Priest is ignorant, the scholar-mamzer takes precedence over the ignorant High Priest.
judaism.explanation: Learning in Torah overrides even the highest birth-based rank.
judaism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: the learned of lowest birth outrank the unlearned of highest birth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth does one become a brahmin. But he in whom truth and righteousness exist, he is pure, he is a brahmin.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines the highest social title as something earned by inner qualities, not inherited.
buddhism.tie_back: Both deny that birth determines worth.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Harikêsa-Bala was born in a family of Svapâkas (Kândâlas); he became a monk and a sage, possessed of the highest virtues, who had subdued his senses.” … “The value of penance has become visible, birth appears of no value! Look at the holy Harikêsa, the son of a Svapâka, whose power is so great.”
jainism.explanation: The Harikesa lecture tells of a monk born an outcaste who outshines the high-born Brahmin priests who mock him. In the end even they admit that birth counts for nothing beside spiritual attainment.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the high-born unlearned are worth less than the learned of low birth. The Harikesa story makes the same point that inner worth outranks birth, with a low-born sage surpassing proud high-born priests.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.1, 12.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one should be proud of his social class and status. He alone is a Brahmin, who knows God.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Bhairao Guru Amar Das rejects pride of caste and says that true standing comes from knowing God, not from birth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the unlearned high-born are worth less than the learned low-born; Guru Amar Das goes further, denying any worth to birth and placing it in knowledge of God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1127, Raag Bhairao, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the ancient Life of Aesop, Aesop is a slave of lowly origin whose wit repeatedly outshines his master, the philosopher Xanthus, and who eventually wins his freedom and advises kings.
greek_mythology.explanation: A man of the lowest social position proves wiser than his socially superior, supposedly learned master.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s point dramatized: worth comes from understanding, not station of birth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic’s ‘noble lie’ of the metals, Socrates says children may be born with a different metal from their parents — gold from bronze or bronze from gold — and each must be placed according to the quality of their soul, not their parentage.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s ideal city ranks people by what they are capable of, not by the family they come from.
philosophy.tie_back: Both subordinate birth to cultivated capacity.

real_life_example.event_title: B. R. Ambedkar rises through learning to chair the drafting of India's Constitution
real_life_example.place: India, the United States and the United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was born in 1891 into a Dalit family, a community then treated as untouchable under India's caste system. He earned degrees, including doctorates, from Columbia University in New York and the London School of Economics, and was called to the bar at Gray's Inn in London. He was elected to India's Constituent Assembly, chaired its drafting committee, and served as independent India's first law minister from 1947 to 1951.
real_life_example.explanation: Ambedkar's learning carried him past the barriers imposed by birth to become one of the most honoured makers of modern India, often called the father of its Constitution.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those born high but unlearned do not have the worth of the learned born low, and Ambedkar, born into the lowest-ranked community of his society, became through learning the chief architect of his nation's founding law.

tamil:
விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர் இலங்குநூல்
கற்றாரோடு ஏனை யவர்.
transliteration:
Vilangodu makkal anaiyar ilangunool
Katraarodu enai yavar.
meaning: Next to people who have studied great books, uneducated people are like animals next to human beings.
elementary: Think of how different a person is from an animal. Valluvar says the difference between someone who has studied great books and someone who hasn’t is just as big. Learning is what makes us fully human.
university: The closing kural states the chapter’s thesis as a proportion: learned : unlearned :: humans : animals. Ilangu nool (‘shining, illustrious texts’) specifies that it is serious learning, not mere literacy, that marks the difference. The analogy draws on a long tradition, shared across cultures, that locates the distinctively human in reason and cultivated understanding. Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka 12 says one devoid of literature, music and art is a beast without tail and horns; Aristotle, asked how the educated differ from the uneducated, replied ‘as much as the living from the dead’; Psalm 49:20 compares the man in honour without understanding to the beasts that perish; the Qur’an (7:179) likens those who do not use their hearts to understand to livestock; and the Dhammapada’s man of little learning grows old ‘like a bull’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari says a man devoid of literature, music and the arts is truly a beast, only without a tail and horns — and it is the animals’ great good fortune that he does not also eat grass.
hinduism.explanation: Without cultivated learning and art, a human being is really an animal in human shape.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s proportion between the learned and the unlearned.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts, in those things they corrupt themselves.”
christianity.explanation: Jude describes people who talk about what they don’t understand and know only what brute beasts know by instinct.
christianity.tie_back: Both compare those without understanding to animals.

islam.quote_or_event: “They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says people who do not use their faculties to understand are like cattle — or even worse off.
islam.tie_back: The same comparison: failing to cultivate understanding reduces a human to the level of animals.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says that a person, even one of high standing, who lacks understanding is no better than an animal.
judaism.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: without understanding, humans are like beasts.
judaism.source: Psalm 49:20 (Hebrew Bible; KJV wording; Ps 49:21 in Hebrew numbering)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man of little learning grows old like a bull. He grows only in bulk, but, his wisdom does not grow.”
buddhism.explanation: Someone who does not learn only gets older and bigger, like an ox — never wiser.
buddhism.tie_back: Both compare the unlearned to an animal.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a pig leaves a trough filled with grain to feed on faeces, so a brute (of a man) turns away from virtue, and takes to evil ways. Hearing a man thus compared to a dog and a pig, he who desires his own welfare, should adhere to good conduct.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's discipline lecture compares the person who turns from good teaching to animals that choose filth over grain.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the unlearned compare with the learned as beasts compare with men. The Jain verse uses the same animal comparison for those who turn away from instruction.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.5–6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They belong to the human species, but they act like animals.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan describes people who are human in form but beast-like in conduct.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the unlearned compare with the learned as beasts with humans; Guru Arjan uses the same human-and-beast contrast.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 267, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe turns Odysseus’s companions into swine, though their minds remain as before; Odysseus alone is protected by the herb moly, which Hermes gives him along with knowledge of how to resist her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Those without the protecting knowledge are reduced to animals; the one who has it remains fully human.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An allegorical parallel: lack of knowledge leaves a person reduced to the level of beasts.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Asked how much the educated are superior to the uneducated, Aristotle replied: “As much as the living are to the dead.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the gap between the educated and the uneducated is as great as the gap between life and death.
philosophy.tie_back: The same proportional form as the Kural, with living/dead in place of humans/animals.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 5.19 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: King Sejong creates the Korean alphabet for ordinary people
real_life_example.event: In fifteenth-century Korea people wrote in Chinese characters, which were very hard for ordinary people to master, so literacy was largely confined to the elite. King Sejong, the fourth ruler of the Joseon dynasty, had a new phonetic alphabet devised in 1443 and promulgated it in 1446 in the book Hunminjeongeum, The Proper Sounds for Instructing the People, whose preface by the king explains his purpose of enabling common people to express themselves in writing. The 1446 book was inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 1997.
real_life_example.explanation: Sejong treated access to letters as something all his subjects should share, opening learning to people who had been shut out of it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural sets the learned above the unlearned as humans above beasts, and Sejong's alphabet was created so that common people, excluded from letters, could share fully in the human life of reading and writing.

tamil:
செல்வத்துள் செல்வம் செவிச்செல்வம் அச்செல்வம்
செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை.
transliteration:
Selvaththul selvam sevichchelvam achchelvam
Selvaththul ellaam thalai.
meaning: The riches you gain through your ears, by listening to good teaching, are the treasure of all treasures. Of all riches, they come first.
elementary: People think of money, gold and houses as riches. Valluvar says the best treasure of all is what you gather by listening carefully to wise people. That kind of treasure goes into your mind, nobody can steal it, and it is worth more than any other.
university: The chapter opens with a deliberately repetitive line — செல்வம் occurs four times — which enacts its claim: among all the ‘wealths’, செவிச்செல்வம் (the wealth of the ear) is தலை, the head or chief. Placed in Porutpaal immediately after the chapters on learning (கல்வி) and its lack (கல்லாமை), this chapter supplements book-learning with கேள்வி, knowledge received orally from the learned — the dominant mode of transmitting knowledge in a largely oral culture. Parimelazhagar notes that hearing is especially valuable because it is available even to those who cannot study texts themselves, and because the ear receives the distilled result of another’s long learning. Calling it the ‘wealth’ of a treatise on polity is pointed: Valluvar ranks a cognitive possession above the material resources the rest of the book is about.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Vedas themselves are called śruti, “that which is heard”; and in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad Yajnavalkya tells Maitreyi that the Self is to be seen, to be heard (śrotavyaḥ), reflected upon and meditated upon — after she has refused his offer of worldly wealth, asking what use riches are that cannot make her immortal.
hinduism.explanation: Maitreyi turns down her husband’s property and asks instead to hear his teaching; Yajnavalkya then names hearing as the first step toward knowing the Self, and the whole Vedic canon is named after the act of hearing.
hinduism.tie_back: Maitreyi’s choice is the Kural’s ranking acted out: the wealth received through the ear is preferred over all material wealth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.”
christianity.explanation: Martha is busy serving while her sister Mary sits at Jesus’ feet listening to his word; Jesus says Mary chose the better portion, one that cannot be taken away.
christianity.tie_back: Mary’s ‘good part’ is precisely a treasure acquired by listening — like the Kural’s ear-wealth, it is the one possession that cannot be lost.

islam.quote_or_event: “…and say, ‘My Lord, increase me in knowledge.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is instructed to ask God for an increase in knowledge — classical commentators note that knowledge is the only thing he is commanded to ask more of. Early Islamic knowledge was transmitted aurally (samāʿ, ‘hearing’ from a teacher).
islam.tie_back: Knowledge, not wealth, is the thing worth seeking more of — echoing the Kural’s ranking of ear-acquired knowledge above all riches.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:”
judaism.explanation: The Shema, recited twice daily, is the central declaration of Jewish faith, and it begins with the imperative ‘Hear’. Jewish tradition treats hearing (shemaʿ, also ‘obey/understand’) as the foundational religious act.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions place hearing at the head of all things — the Shema makes listening the gateway to faith; the Kural makes it the chief of all wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists seven ‘treasures’ (dhana) of a noble disciple: faith, virtue, conscience, concern for wrongdoing, learning (suta-dhana — literally ‘the treasure of what has been heard’), generosity and wisdom — declaring these superior to any worldly treasure.
buddhism.explanation: Suta means ‘heard’; a learned person in early Buddhism is bahussuta, ‘one who has heard much’. The Buddha explicitly calls this a form of wealth that cannot be taken by kings, thieves, fire or flood.
buddhism.tie_back: An almost literal parallel to செவிச்செல்வம்: hearing counted as a treasure, and ranked above material wealth.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Four things of paramount value are difficult to obtain here by a living being: human birth, instruction in the Law, belief in it, and energy in self-control.”
jainism.explanation: Jainism lists hearing the Law (Prakrit sui, Sanskrit sruti, i.e. hearing) among the four rarest and most valuable things a soul can gain. Jacobi translates it as 'instruction in the Law'.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls the wealth of the ear foremost among all kinds of wealth. The Uttaradhyayana likewise ranks hearing the Law among the few gifts of 'paramount value'.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 3.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Listening-truth, contentment and spiritual wisdom.”
sikhism.explanation: In the tenth pauri of Japji Sahib Guru Nanak lists what deep listening to the Name brings, starting with truth, contentment and spiritual wisdom.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls the wealth gained through the ear the foremost of all wealth; Japji says the highest treasures, truth, contentment and wisdom, come through listening.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib (pauri 10), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon, after hearing Nestor’s counsel at Troy, wishes he had ten such counsellors among the Achaeans — then, he says, Priam’s city would soon fall.
greek_mythology.explanation: The commander of the largest Greek host values one man’s spoken advice more than numbers of soldiers or treasure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Nestor’s counsel is wealth received through the ear; the most powerful king in the story ranks it above his other resources.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch opens his essay On Listening by arguing that right listening is the beginning of right living, since the young receive virtue first through the ear, the one sense by which reason enters the soul.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch treats hearing as the principal channel of moral formation, superior to the other senses because speech (logos) arrives through it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Plutarch places the ear first among the means of acquiring what is truly valuable.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, De auditu (On Listening to Lectures) 1–2

real_life_example.event_title: Charlemagne learns by listening at his court
real_life_example.event: According to his courtier and biographer Einhard, Charlemagne had books read aloud to him at meals, especially histories and Augustine's City of God, and took lessons in rhetoric, logic and astronomy from the English scholar Alcuin of York, whom he invited around 781 to lead the circle of learning at his court. Einhard also records that the emperor tried to learn to write late in life, keeping writing tablets under his pillow, but with little success. Charlemagne's patronage of scholars helped launch the revival of learning known as the Carolingian Renaissance.
real_life_example.explanation: The ruler of the largest Western empire since Rome, who never mastered writing, acquired wide learning chiefly through his ears and made the pursuit of learning a priority of his reign.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls the wealth gained through the ear the foremost of all riches, and Charlemagne, master of vast lands and treasure, built much of his knowledge on what he heard read and taught.

tamil:
செவிக்குணவு இல்லாத போழ்து சிறிது
வயிற்றுக்கும் ஈயப் படும்.
transliteration:
Sevikkunavu illaadha pozhdhu siridhu
Vayitrrukkum eeyap padum.
meaning: Only when there is nothing to feed the ears, no good teaching to listen to, should you give a little food to the stomach as well.
elementary: Imagine you are hungry but a wise teacher is speaking. Valluvar says: keep listening first! Feed your ears with good words, and only when there is nothing more to hear, give your tummy a little food.
university: The kural introduces the governing metaphor of the chapter — hearing as food (செவிக்கு உணவு) — and inverts the ordinary priority of bodily needs. The ‘உம்’ in வயிற்றுக்கும் (‘to the stomach too’) and the qualifier சிறிது (‘a little’) make the stomach a secondary and moderate claimant. Commentators read this not as a call to starve but as a hierarchy: instruction, once lost, may not recur, whereas food can be taken any time. The metaphor links this chapter to the Indian notion of the body as sustained by food and the mind by speech, and anticipates 413 (hearers as those who eat ‘ear-food’) and 420 (those who know only the mouth’s taste).

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Parikshit, cursed to die in seven days, sits by the Ganga and listens to the sage Shuka recite the Bhagavata Purana, taking neither food nor water for the entire seven days.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata frames its entire narration as a listening-fast: the king forgoes food to hear the teaching, and later says the nectar of these narrations removed his hunger and thirst.
hinduism.tie_back: A dramatic enactment of the Kural: food for the ear first, the stomach only afterward, if at all.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.”
christianity.explanation: Fasting in the wilderness, Jesus rejects the tempter’s suggestion to turn stones into bread, placing the word of God above physical food.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts rank ‘the word’ as nourishment superior to bread — the Kural’s ear-food over stomach-food.

islam.quote_or_event: During the Friday sermon, a trade caravan arrived and many listeners rushed out to it, leaving the Prophet standing; the Qur’an rebukes them: what is with God is better than diversion and trade, and God is the best of providers.
islam.explanation: Commentators report the caravan carried food during a time of scarcity; the verse censures those who left the sermon for provisions.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an criticises exactly the reverse of the Kural’s order — abandoning ear-food for stomach-food.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:”
judaism.explanation: The prophet Amos threatens a deprivation worse than hunger: the absence of divine words to hear.
judaism.tie_back: Amos treats hearing as a form of food whose lack is a true famine — the Kural’s ‘food for the ear’ in prophetic form.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The gift of Dhamma excels all gifts; the taste of Dhamma excels all tastes; the delight in Dhamma excels all delights.”
buddhism.explanation: The verse ranks the flavour of the teaching above every other taste, including that of food.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it relocates ‘taste’ from the tongue to the teaching received — ear-food over stomach-food.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the first Paurushî he should study, in the second he should meditate, in the third he should go on his begging-tour, and in the fourth he should study again.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk's daily routine puts study first. Looking for food comes only in the third quarter of the day, after study and meditation, and the fourth quarter is again for study.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to give the stomach a little only when there is no food for the ear. The Jain monk's day, in which the alms round waits until study and meditation are done, puts the same order into practice.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 26.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Upon this Plate, three things have been placed: Truth, Contentment and Contemplation. The Ambrosial Nectar of the Naam, the Name of our Lord and Master, has been placed upon it as well; it is the Support of all.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Mundavani at the close of the Granth, Guru Arjan describes the scripture as a plate of spiritual food: truth, contentment, contemplation and the Name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks food for the ear above food for the stomach; Guru Arjan also offers truth, contemplation and the Name as the food that truly sustains.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Mundavani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the Phaeacian feast, Odysseus tells King Alcinous that there is nothing more gracious than a banquet where the whole company sits listening to a bard while tables stand full of bread and meat.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Homeric ideal feast couples listening with eating — and in the Phaeacian episode the guests stay spellbound by stories deep into the night.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer places ear-food beside stomach-food at the feast; the Kural goes further and ranks it above.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates warns young Hippocrates that teachings are food for the soul, and unlike food bought at market they cannot be carried home in a separate vessel and inspected first — one must take them straight into the soul by listening.
philosophy.explanation: Plato explicitly calls instruction the nourishment of the soul (psychē trephetai mathēmasi) and compares teachers to food merchants.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar share the metaphor of heard instruction as food, and both treat it as more consequential than bodily food.

real_life_example.event_title: Marie Sklodowska studies in Paris on a meagre diet
real_life_example.event: In the autumn of 1891 the young Polish student Maria Sklodowska, later Marie Curie, enrolled at the Sorbonne, and after a few months moved to a cold garret in the Latin Quarter to be close to the university. She had enough money for tuition, her room and the cheapest food, and by her own later account her meals were often reduced to bread with chocolate, eggs or fruit while she attended lectures and studied far into the night. Though she arrived less well prepared than her classmates, she finished first in the physics degree examinations in 1893 and second in mathematics in 1894.
real_life_example.explanation: Her student years are remembered as an example of someone who put instruction ahead of comfort and even of a proper diet.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the stomach should be given only a little, when there is no food for the ear, and the young Sklodowska fed her mind on lectures and study while giving her body as little as she could manage.

tamil:
செவியுணவின் கேள்வி உடையார் அவியுணவின்
ஆன்றாரோடு ஒப்பர் நிலத்து.
transliteration:
Seviyunavin kelvi udaiyaar aviyunavin
Aandraarodu oppar nilaththu.
meaning: People who have gained knowledge by listening, which is food for the ears, are equal on earth to the gods, who are fed by offerings in sacred fires.
elementary: In old times people offered food to the gods through a sacred fire. Valluvar says people who ‘eat’ wise words through their ears are like gods living on earth.
university: A carefully balanced pair of compounds: செவியுணவு (ear-food) is set against அவியுணவு (oblation-food, havis), so that ‘those who have hearing’ are matched with ‘the exalted ones who eat oblations’ — the devas. Parimelazhagar glosses ஆன்றார் as the celestials; நிலத்து (‘on earth’) marks the hearers as terrestrial counterparts of the gods. The logic continues the food metaphor of 412: just as the gods are sustained by subtle offerings rather than gross food, the learned are sustained by subtle instruction. The kural thus elevates the listener’s status, not merely the value of what is heard.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna says that even one who merely listens to this teaching with faith and without envy is freed from sin and attains the auspicious worlds of the righteous.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita closes by promising elevated status — the heavenly realms of the virtuous — not only to the one who studies but to the one who simply hears it faithfully.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts raise the attentive hearer to a quasi-divine rank.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But blessed are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear. For verily I say unto you, That many prophets and righteous men have desired to see those things which ye see, and to hear those things which ye hear…”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples that their hearing places them in a privileged position beyond that of prophets and the righteous of old.
christianity.tie_back: Hearing confers exalted status — the Kural likens it to divinity, Jesus to a blessedness surpassing prophets.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that no people gather in a house of God reciting and studying the Book among themselves but that tranquillity descends on them, mercy covers them, the angels surround them, and God mentions them among those who are with Him.
islam.explanation: Those who gather to hear and study revelation are placed in the company of angels and in God’s own presence.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s hearers ‘equal to the gods’, these listeners are drawn into the celestial company while still on earth.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Israel at Sinai said “we will do and we will hear” (naʿaseh ve-nishma), the Talmud relates that a heavenly voice asked, “Who revealed to My children this secret that the ministering angels use?” — and angels crowned each Israelite.
judaism.explanation: By committing themselves to hearing, the people adopted the manner of angels and were honoured as such.
judaism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: devoted hearers are made equal to celestial beings on earth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Mangala Sutta lists among the ‘highest blessings’ much learning (bahusacca — literally ‘much hearing’) and hearing the Dhamma at the proper time (kālena dhammassavanaṃ); the discourse is spoken in reply to a deva, and its close says those who fulfil these blessings are everywhere victorious and go everywhere in safety.
buddhism.explanation: Hearing is counted among the supreme blessings discussed between the Buddha and the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural exalts the hearer to divine rank; the Mangala Sutta, addressed to gods, counts hearing among the highest blessings.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As Sakra the thousand-eyed, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the fortress-destroyer, the king of gods, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's lecture on the very learned (bahussuya, literally 'one who has heard much') ranks such a monk as without equal, like Indra among the gods.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those rich in learning gained by hearing are equal on earth to the gods. The Jain text matches the 'much-heard' monk with the king of the gods.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Listening-Shiva, Brahma and Indra.”
sikhism.explanation: In the ninth pauri of Japji Sahib Guru Nanak says that by listening, ordinary people rise to the standing of the highest beings, here named as Shiva, Brahma and Indra.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those rich in hearing equal the gods on earth; Japji likewise says listening raises a person to the rank of the gods.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib (pauri 9), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes the Muses singing on Olympus and delighting the great mind of Zeus with their song — the gods, who feast on nectar and ambrosia, also feast on what they hear.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, listening to song is itself one of the divine pleasures on Olympus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both imagine the gods as consumers of a subtle ‘food’; the Kural makes human listeners share that divine diet.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pythagoras’ school admitted novices as akousmatikoi, ‘listeners’, who spent years in silence hearing the master’s sayings; the tradition held Pythagoras himself to be a divine or semi-divine figure whose hearers participated in his wisdom.
philosophy.explanation: Listening was the defining activity of the first rank of Pythagorean disciples, and the community treated the teaching as quasi-divine.
philosophy.tie_back: The Pythagorean ‘hearers’ are an institutional version of the Kural’s honoured listeners, drawing near to the divine through the ear.

real_life_example.event_title: UNESCO recognises the oral tradition of Vedic chanting
real_life_example.event: The Vedas, the oldest sacred texts of Hinduism, are classed as shruti, a Sanskrit word meaning what is heard, and were preserved for many centuries through memorisation and recitation before being written down. Their hymns and formulae were chanted at sacred rituals, including sacrifices, and reciters are trained from childhood in exact techniques of pitch accent, pronunciation and word combination so that the sound of every word stays unaltered. In 2008 UNESCO inscribed the Tradition of Vedic Chanting on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
real_life_example.explanation: The recognition honours one of the world's oldest bodies of knowledge, handed down for thousands of years almost entirely by ear and regarded by its tradition as sacred.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural matches those who feed on the food of the ear with the gods who receive sacrificial oblations, and the Vedic tradition, learned by hearing and chanted at those very sacrifices, treats what is received through the ear as holy.

tamil:
கற்றிலன் ஆயினும் கேட்க அஃதொருவற்கு
ஒற்கத்தின் ஊற்றாந் துணை.
transliteration:
Katrilan aayinum ketka aqdhoruvarku
Orkaththin ootraandh thunai.
meaning: Even if you have not studied, listen to learned people. What you hear will hold you up like a walking stick when you are weak or in trouble.
elementary: Maybe you never got to go to school or read many books. That’s okay — just listen to wise people! What you hear will be like a walking stick that holds you up when life gets hard.
university: Here Valluvar extends the chapter’s value to the unlettered: கற்றிலன் ஆயினும் (‘though he has not learned’) concedes lack of formal study, but கேட்க is an imperative — listening remains possible for everyone. ஒற்கம் means weakness, falling, or distress; ஊற்று is a prop or support (the same word recurs in 415 as ஊற்றுக்கோல், ‘supporting staff’). The kural thus democratises knowledge in an oral society: hearing is a route to wisdom for those without access to texts, and its value is practical — it sustains one when fortune slips.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna says there are others who, not knowing the paths of knowledge themselves, hear the teaching from others and worship accordingly; by devotion to what they have heard, they too cross beyond death.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita explicitly accommodates the untrained seeker who relies only on hearing from the wise, and promises that such hearing carries him through.
hinduism.tie_back: Close match: the unlearned who listens is supported and saved by what he hears.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: On trial before the council, two fishermen without formal schooling speak with confidence; their strength came from having heard Jesus.
christianity.tie_back: Unlearned yet sustained in adversity by what they had heard — a vivid enactment of the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet prayed for God to brighten the face of one who hears a saying, memorises it and conveys it — for many a carrier of knowledge is not himself learned, and many carry it to one who understands it better.
islam.explanation: The hadith honours the listener-transmitter even if he is not a scholar, recognising hearing as a path to knowledge open to all.
islam.tie_back: Both texts affirm that the unlearned can still become possessors of knowledge through hearing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then Samuel answered, Speak; for thy servant heareth.”
judaism.explanation: The boy Samuel, of whom the text says he ‘did not yet know the LORD’ (3:7), is taught by Eli simply to listen; his hearing makes him a prophet who later sustains Israel in crisis.
judaism.tie_back: Lack of learning is no barrier: Samuel begins with nothing but a listening ear, which becomes his lifelong support.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Paṭācārā, having lost her husband, children, parents and brother in quick succession, wanders half-mad with grief; on hearing the Buddha’s words she regains her mind and later becomes an arahant and teacher.
buddhism.explanation: The commentary on the Dhammapada tells how a woman with no learning, in the depth of misfortune, was restored by listening to the Buddha.
buddhism.tie_back: Hearing as ஒற்கத்தின் ஊற்று — the prop that held her up when she had fallen.

jainism.quote_or_event: Rauhineya, a thief, had been told by his dying father never to listen to Mahavira. Passing the assembly with his ears covered, he trod on a thorn, took a hand away to pull it out, and briefly heard Mahavira describing the gods: their feet do not touch the ground, their eyes do not blink, they do not sweat, and their garlands do not wither. Later, minister Abhayakumara tried to trick him into confessing by staging a fake heaven. The few words Rauhineya had overheard let him see through the trap, and he went on to become Mahavira's disciple.
jainism.explanation: In this Jain story a few words, heard unwillingly by an unlettered man, saved him in his worst crisis and changed his life.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar urges even someone who has never studied to listen, because what he hears will be a staff to lean on in adversity. Rauhineya's few overheard words served him in exactly that way.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trisastisalakapurusacaritra, Parva X, ch. 11, 'Story of Rauhineya' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Listening-even the blind find the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: In the eleventh pauri of Japji Sahib Guru Nanak says that listening lets even those without sight, read by commentators as the spiritually ignorant, find their way.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the unlettered to listen anyway, since hearing will be their support in hardship; Japji promises that listening guides even the blind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib (pauri 11), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Lost and unable to find his way home, Odysseus is sent by Circe to the underworld to hear the prophet Tiresias, whose words guide him through the dangers that follow.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, for all his cunning, lacks the knowledge he needs; he must go and listen to one who knows.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hearing the wise supplies what one’s own learning lacks, and supports one through adversity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the myth of Theuth, King Thamus warns that writing will give pupils the appearance of wisdom without its reality, since they will have ‘heard many things without instruction’; Socrates argues that living speech exchanged with a knowledgeable teacher is superior to written texts.
philosophy.explanation: Plato privileges oral teaching over book-learning as the true vehicle of understanding.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise reassures the one without book-learning that listening to the learned is itself a reliable path to wisdom.

real_life_example.event_title: Bookbinder's apprentice Michael Faraday attends Humphry Davy's lectures
real_life_example.event: Michael Faraday, who had been apprenticed to a London bookbinder at fourteen and had no university education, was given a ticket in 1812 to hear Humphry Davy's chemistry lectures at the Royal Institution. He took careful notes, bound them into a volume, and presented them to Davy in the hope of scientific work. On 1 March 1813 he was appointed laboratory assistant at the Royal Institution, the beginning of a career that made him one of the greatest experimental scientists of the nineteenth century.
real_life_example.explanation: A few lectures heard by a young tradesman opened the way to discoveries in electricity and magnetism that shaped the modern world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural urges those who have not studied to listen to the learned, since hearing will be a staff to them in adversity, and Faraday, without formal schooling, rose from the bookbinder's bench by listening to Davy.

tamil:
இழுக்கல் உடையுழி ஊற்றுக்கோல் அற்றே
ஒழுக்கம் உடையார்வாய்ச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Izhukkal udaiyuzhi ootrukkol atre
Ozhukkam udaiyaarvaaich chol.
meaning: The words of people who live the right way are like a walking stick for someone walking on slippery ground.
elementary: When you walk on a muddy, slippery path, a strong stick helps you not fall. Advice from good, honest people works the same way — it keeps you steady when life gets slippery.
university: The image is precise: இழுக்கல் is slipperiness (and by extension moral lapse), ஊற்றுக்கோல் a staff one leans on. The kural qualifies the source of hearing — not any speaker, but ஒழுக்கம் உடையார், those of upright conduct. Parimelazhagar emphasises that the words of the virtuous are trustworthy because their conduct confirms them, and that such words prevent a fall before it happens. The kural links the chapter to the earlier chapter on ஒழுக்கமுடைமை (conduct) and grounds the authority of what one hears in the moral character of the speaker.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Arise, awake; approach the great and learn. The path is sharp as a razor’s edge, difficult to cross, hard to tread — so say the wise.”
hinduism.explanation: The Katha Upanishad describes the spiritual path as treacherous and tells the seeker to approach and hear the great teachers.
hinduism.tie_back: A hazardous path and the counsel of the wise as one’s support — the same structure as the Kural’s slippery ground and staff.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:”
christianity.explanation: The one who hears and acts on Jesus’ words stands firm when rain, floods and winds come.
christianity.tie_back: Heard words from a righteous teacher as the stable footing against collapse — the Kural’s staff on slippery ground.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided.”
islam.explanation: Commentators interpret the ‘rope of Allah’ as the Qur’an and the guidance transmitted through it — something to grip to avoid falling.
islam.tie_back: A physical support image (rope / staff) for guidance received from a trustworthy source.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The law of his God is in his heart; none of his steps shall slide.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist says the one who has taken God’s teaching into his heart will not slip.
judaism.tie_back: Teaching received and held keeps one’s steps from sliding — near-identical imagery to the Kural’s slippery ground.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure. It is always better, and never worse, to cultivate such an association.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges following the corrective words of the wise, who save one from error.
buddhism.tie_back: Words of the wise as a guide that prevents a fall — the Kural’s supporting staff.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A needle with a thread (in it) does not get lost even when it falls in a heap of rubbish, so a person endowed with scriptureal knowledge does not lose his self, even if involved in transmigratory cycle.”
jainism.explanation: The Saman Suttam's verses on right knowledge compare scriptural knowledge to the thread that keeps a needle from being lost. Through it the soul keeps hold of itself even in the confusion of samsara.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar compares the words of the virtuous to a staff for someone walking on slippery ground. The Jain image of the threaded needle likewise presents received teaching as what keeps a person from being lost amid danger.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 248 (Samyagjnanasutra) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I am blind; Your Name, O Creator Lord, is my only anchor and support.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Tilang Bhagat Namdev calls God's Name the support of a blind man; the Gurmukhi word tek is glossed by Sahib Singh as a walking stick.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls the words of the upright a staff for one walking on slippery ground; Namdev calls the Name the walking stick of the blind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 727, Raag Tilang, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Odysseus walks toward Circe’s house, Hermes meets him, warns him of her drugs and gives him the herb moly with instructions; heeding this counsel, Odysseus avoids being turned into a swine like his men.
greek_mythology.explanation: A trustworthy divine adviser’s words save the hero at the moment of greatest danger.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Counsel heard at the right moment keeps one from ‘slipping’ into ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca advises Lucilius to choose some man of high character and keep him always before his eyes, living as if he were watching — ‘we need someone against whom our characters can measure themselves’.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that most wrongdoing is prevented when a witness of good character stands near the one about to err.
philosophy.tie_back: The upright person serves as the support that keeps one from slipping — Valluvar’s staff.

real_life_example.event_title: Augustine listens to the sermons of Ambrose in Milan
real_life_example.event: In the mid-380s Augustine, a gifted teacher of rhetoric from North Africa who had followed the Manichaean sect for years, took up a publicly paid professorship in Milan, then the imperial capital of the West. There he became a regular listener at the preaching of the city's bishop, Ambrose, whose allegorical method of interpreting Scripture helped remove his objections to Christianity. In the summer of 386 he gave up his professorship, and Ambrose baptised him at Easter 387.
real_life_example.explanation: The sermons of a respected bishop helped carry one of the most influential thinkers in Western history through a long period of doubt and indecision.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the words of upright people to a staff for one walking on slippery ground, and Ambrose's preaching gave the wavering Augustine something firm to lean on.

tamil:
எனைத்தானும் நல்லவை கேட்க அனைத்தானும்
ஆன்ற பெருமை தரும்.
transliteration:
Enaiththaanum nallavai ketka anaiththaanum
Aandra perumai tharum.
meaning: Listen to good things, even if only a little. Even that little will bring you great honor.
elementary: You don’t have to listen to a huge lecture. Even hearing one small good idea is worth it, because even a little bit of goodness can make you a much better person.
university: The kural balances எனைத்தானும் (‘however little’) against அனைத்தானும் (‘to that very extent’), so that the benefit is proportionate to what is heard, yet always leads to ஆன்ற பெருமை — full, well-rounded greatness. Two conditions are embedded: the content must be நல்லவை (good things), and the act must be real listening. The couplet thus both encourages even small, occasional listening and implicitly warns against hearing what is not good — a selectivity that parallels many traditions’ counsel about what one lets into the ear.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Shanti mantra “bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ śṛṇuyāma devāḥ” — “O gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious.”
hinduism.explanation: Recited at the opening of the Mundaka and Prashna Upanishads, this Rig Vedic prayer asks that the ear receive only what is good.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts direct the ear specifically toward ‘good things’ (நல்லவை / bhadram).
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 1.89.8; peace invocation of the Mundaka and Prashna Upanishads

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take heed what ye hear: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you: and unto you that hear shall more be given.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns his hearers to be careful what they listen to, and promises increase to those who hear rightly.
christianity.tie_back: Selective hearing of what is good leads to growth — the Kural’s ‘however little, it brings greatness’.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who listen to speech and follow the best of it. Those are the ones Allah has guided, and those are people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who listen discerningly and adopt the best of what they hear.
islam.tie_back: Both texts value hearing selectively for the good, and connect it with honour/understanding.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma asks, “Who is wise?” and answers, “One who learns from every person,” citing the Psalm: “From all my teachers I have gained understanding.”
judaism.explanation: Wisdom comes from gathering good teaching from every source, however humble.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it urges taking in good wherever and in whatever measure it is found.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better than a thousand useless words is one useful word, hearing which one attains peace.”
buddhism.explanation: A single beneficial word heard is worth more than any quantity of empty speech.
buddhism.tie_back: Near-identical point: even a small amount of good hearing yields great benefit.

jainism.quote_or_event: “After listening to scriptures, a person comes to know what is good and what is sinful, having thus known through listening one ought to perform what leads to welfare.”
jainism.explanation: This Jain verse (Prakrit 'socca janai kallanam') makes hearing the source of moral knowledge. From listening one learns good and evil and then acts for one's welfare.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar urges us to listen to what is good, however little, because it leads to greatness. The Jain verse likewise traces right action and welfare back to hearing.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 245 (Samyagjnanasutra); the Prakrit is from the Dasavaikalika Sutra 4 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Within the mind are gems, jewels and rubies, if you listen to the Guru's Teachings, even once.”
sikhism.explanation: In the sixth pauri of Japji Sahib Guru Nanak says that hearing even one teaching of the Guru fills the mind with treasures.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to listen to good things, however little, since even a little brings full greatness; Guru Nanak says even a single teaching heard yields jewels.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib (pauri 6), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe, Odysseus stops his crew’s ears with wax so they cannot hear the Sirens, whose beautiful song lures sailors to death; only he listens, bound to the mast.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Sirens are the classic Greek warning that not everything pleasant to hear is good.
