greek_mythology.tie_back: The negative counterpart of the Kural: hear what is good (நல்லவை), and guard the ear against what destroys.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca advises Lucilius to acquire each day something that will fortify him against poverty, death and other misfortunes, and to select one thought daily to digest thoroughly.
philosophy.explanation: Small daily portions of good teaching, well absorbed, build lasting strength of character.
philosophy.tie_back: Even a little good taken in regularly yields greatness — the Kural’s ‘however little’.

real_life_example.event_title: Booker T. Washington overhears talk of Hampton Institute in a coal mine
real_life_example.event: As a teenager working in a coal mine near Malden, West Virginia, Booker T. Washington, who had been born into slavery, overheard two miners talking in the dark about a school in Virginia for Black students where poor students could work to pay for their board while learning a trade. After some months more in the mine and in domestic service, he set out for the Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute in the fall of 1872, arriving with only fifty cents. He graduated and went on to lead Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, becoming one of the most prominent educators in American history.
real_life_example.explanation: A few words overheard in a mine changed the course of a life and, through Tuskegee, the education of thousands.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that listening to good things, however little, brings full greatness, and a single overheard conversation set Washington on the road to national prominence.

tamil:
பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் பேதைமை சொல்லார் இழைத்துணர்ந்து
ஈண்டிய கேள்வி யவர்.
transliteration:
Pizhaiththunarndhum pedhaimai sollaar izhaiththunarndhu
Eendiya kelvi yavar.
meaning: People who have studied things closely and gathered much learning by listening will not say foolish things, even when they have understood something wrongly.
elementary: Everyone makes mistakes sometimes. But a person who has listened carefully to lots of wise people won’t say silly things even when they get confused, because all that good listening keeps them careful.
university: The paired participles பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் (‘even having understood wrongly’) and இழைத்துணர்ந்து (‘having understood finely, as if threading’) frame the couplet. இழை (thread) suggests minute, careful examination; ஈண்டிய (‘amassed’) describes accumulated hearing. The kural is realistic: the learned may still err in perception, but their trained habit of mind prevents error from becoming foolish speech (பேதைமை). Hearing thus functions as a safeguard not of infallibility but of judgment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna to learn the truth by approaching the wise, through reverent submission, thorough questioning (paripraśnena) and service; the knowers of truth will instruct him.
hinduism.explanation: Pariprashna — questioning repeatedly and thoroughly — is the Gita’s equivalent of இழைத்துணர்தல், careful probing examination of what is heard.
hinduism.tie_back: Knowledge carefully examined through hearing and questioning produces sound judgment and speech.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good… for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: What one has stored within shapes what one says.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘amassed hearing’ is such a treasure — it ensures that even in error the speech is not foolish.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said: whoever believes in God and the Last Day should speak what is good or keep silent.
islam.explanation: Restraint in speech — speaking only good or not at all — is framed as a mark of faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s learned hearers, the believer avoids foolish speech even when uncertain, by choosing silence.

judaism.quote_or_event: Among the seven traits of the wise: he does not interrupt, is not hasty to answer, asks and answers to the point, and about what he has not heard he says, “I have not heard.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah’s portrait of the sage emphasises careful listening and restraint in speaking where knowledge is lacking.
judaism.tie_back: The well-heard sage avoids foolish speech — precisely the Kural’s claim about those of amassed hearing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares one who learns the teaching without examining its meaning to a man grasping a water-snake by the tail and being bitten, while one who examines the meaning with wisdom grasps it correctly, like seizing a snake with a forked stick.
buddhism.explanation: Mere hearing is dangerous; hearing coupled with careful examination yields right understanding and right use.
buddhism.tie_back: Corresponds to the Kural’s இழைத்துணர்ந்து — finely examined hearing that prevents foolish error.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Again, under the influence of his (scriptural) knowledge, he becomes firm in his faith, meditation, observance of vows and self-restraint, and lives a life of purity throughout his lifetime without any wavering.”
jainism.explanation: In the Jain view, knowledge received from scripture gives steadiness, so a person stays firm in faith and conduct without wavering.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who have searched deeply and heard much will not speak foolishly even when they have misunderstood something. The Jain verse likewise credits well-absorbed teaching with keeping a person steady.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 246 (Samyagjnanasutra) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Listening-dive deep into the ocean of virtue.”
sikhism.explanation: In the eleventh pauri of Japji Sahib Guru Nanak says that listening lets a person explore the depths of virtue; Sahib Singh glosses it as gaining insight into endless virtues.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who have examined things finely and gathered much learning by hearing will not speak foolishly; Japji says listening gives a deep understanding of virtue.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib (pauri 11), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Nestor, the aged king of Pylos, ‘from whose tongue speech flowed sweeter than honey’, rises to calm the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles, drawing on the counsel of the great men he has heard and lived among.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor’s long experience of listening to heroes of earlier generations makes his speech measured and wise.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Amassed hearing yields speech free of folly, even amid a crisis.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says we ought to attend to the undemonstrated sayings and opinions of experienced and older people, or of people of practical wisdom, no less than to demonstrations, because experience has given them an eye to see aright.
philosophy.explanation: Practical wisdom accumulated through experience produces sound judgment even without formal proof.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it credits accumulated, well-examined learning with reliable judgment and speech.

real_life_example.event_title: Kepler refuses to ignore an eight-minute error in the orbit of Mars
real_life_example.event: Working with Tycho Brahe's precise observations of Mars, Johannes Kepler spent years trying to account for the planet's motion with combinations of circles, as astronomers had done since antiquity. His best circular model still disagreed with Tycho's data by about eight minutes of arc, and because he trusted those observations to about two minutes, he would not accept it. Re-examining the problem from its foundations, he found that Mars moves in an ellipse, and published his first two laws of planetary motion in Astronomia Nova in 1609.
real_life_example.explanation: Kepler's refusal to let a near-miss stand turned a mistaken assumption into one of the great discoveries of science.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who have examined matters minutely will not speak foolishly even when they have misunderstood something, and Kepler's careful checking kept his early, mistaken model from becoming his published conclusion.

tamil:
கேட்பினும் கேளாத் தகையவே கேள்வியால்
தோட்கப் படாத செவி.
transliteration:
Ketpinum kelaath thagaiyave kelviyaal
Thotkap padaadha sevi.
meaning: Ears that have not been pierced (opened up) by good teaching are no better than deaf ears, even though they hear sounds.
elementary: Your ears can hear noises all day, but if you never really listen to wise lessons, it’s almost like your ears don’t work. Real hearing means letting good lessons get inside.
university: The pun turns on கேள் (‘hear’): ears may கேட்பினும் (hear sounds) yet be கேளாத் தகைய (of the nature of not hearing, i.e., deaf) if not தோட்கப்பட்ட — ‘bored, pierced’ — by கேள்வி. The piercing alludes to the ear-boring ritual (and earrings) of Tamil custom: the true ornament and opening of the ear is instruction. The distinction between physiological hearing and receptive understanding is the heart of the kural and finds close echoes in prophetic and philosophical literature on ‘hearing without hearing’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Katha Upanishad says of the Self: many do not even get to hear of it, and many, even hearing of it, do not comprehend it; wonderful is the teacher and wonderful the one who learns it.
hinduism.explanation: Mere hearing is not enough — receptive understanding is rare.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘ears that hear yet are deaf’ in Upanishadic form.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus distinguishes physical hearing from receptive understanding.
christianity.tie_back: Almost verbatim the Kural’s paradox: hearing, yet not hearing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Deaf, dumb and blind — so they will not return [to the right path].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes those who reject guidance as deaf though their physical hearing is intact.
islam.tie_back: Ears untouched by guidance are counted as deaf — as in the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hear now this, O foolish people, and without understanding; which have eyes, and see not; which have ears, and hear not:”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah rebukes a people whose senses function but whose understanding is closed.
judaism.tie_back: Same paradox as the Kural: working ears, no real hearing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: Proximity to teaching does not guarantee reception; the fool is like a spoon that touches soup without tasting it.
buddhism.tie_back: The fool’s ears, like the spoon, contact wisdom without taking it in — the Kural’s ‘unpierced ear’.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though men destitute of rectitude listen to those who are destitute of envy, when they declare the way of virtue, yet they give no heed, just as the chakler's dog, which seizes and devours leather, knows not how to appreciate the taste of rice and milk.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar describes people who physically hear the teaching of virtue yet take none of it in, like a dog used to leather that cannot taste good food.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says ears never pierced by instruction are as good as deaf, even though they hear sounds. The Naladiyar shows the same kind of hearing, where words arrive and nothing enters.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 33 'Defective knowledge', stanza 2 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O my ears, you were created only to hear the Truth.”
sikhism.explanation: In Anand Sahib Guru Amar Das tells his ears that their purpose is to hear the Truth and the Name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says ears not opened by instruction are as good as deaf; Guru Amar Das says ears exist to hear the Truth, so ears that do not are failing their purpose.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 922, Raag Raamkalee, Anand Sahib (pauri 37), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cassandra, cursed by Apollo, prophesies truly the fall of Troy and Agamemnon’s murder, but those who hear her words do not take them in; in Aeschylus the chorus hears her plainly yet cannot understand.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Trojans and later the Argive elders hear the truth but remain effectively deaf to it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic image of ears that hear yet do not hear.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heraclitus: those who do not understand, even when they have heard, are like the deaf; the saying bears witness of them — ‘present, they are absent’.
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus distinguishes hearing the logos from understanding it; the unreceptive are functionally deaf.
philosophy.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: hearing without instruction is deafness.

real_life_example.event_title: Titanic's ice warnings go unheeded
real_life_example.event: On 14 April 1912, during her maiden voyage, RMS Titanic received a series of wireless warnings from other ships about ice ahead; most were passed to the bridge, but a late message from the Mesaba reporting heavy pack ice and many large icebergs was never delivered because the operator was busy sending passengers' messages. The ship did not slow down, struck an iceberg shortly before midnight, and sank early on 15 April with the loss of more than 1,500 lives. The United States inquiry criticised the captain for failing to reduce speed after receiving ice warnings, and the disaster led to round-the-clock radio watches and the International Ice Patrol.
real_life_example.explanation: The disaster showed that warnings which are heard but not heeded give no protection.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says ears that have not been opened by instruction are as good as deaf even though they hear sounds, and the Titanic received warning after warning without letting them change its course or speed.

tamil:
நுணங்கிய கேள்வியர் அல்லார் வணங்கிய
வாயினர் ஆதல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Nunangiya kelviyar allaar vanangiya
Vaayinar aadhal aridhu.
meaning: People who have not gained fine, deep learning by listening find it hard to speak humbly.
elementary: People who have listened a lot to wise teachers usually speak kindly and humbly. People who haven’t listened much often find it hard to speak gently and politely.
university: Two adjectives govern the couplet: நுணங்கிய (fine, subtle) describes the quality of hearing, and வணங்கிய (bowed, humble) the quality of speech. The link is causal: refined hearing produces humility in speech, because the listener becomes aware of how much others know. Parimelazhagar reads வணங்கிய வாய் as speech that is modest and respectful. The kural thus connects the ear and the mouth: good speaking is an outcome of good listening — a theme echoed widely in wisdom literature that advises being quick to hear and slow to speak.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Gita defines austerity of speech as words that cause no distress, that are truthful, pleasant and beneficial, together with regular study and recitation of the scriptures (svādhyāya).
hinduism.explanation: Gentle, truthful speech is paired with regular learning of the sacred texts.
hinduism.tie_back: Both link cultivated learning with courteous, humble speech.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:”
christianity.explanation: James makes hearing the precondition of restrained, gentle speech.
christianity.tie_back: Listening first produces humble speech — the Kural’s causal link between hearing and mouth.

islam.quote_or_event: “And be moderate in your pace and lower your voice; indeed, the most disagreeable of sounds is the voice of donkeys.”
islam.explanation: Part of the counsel of Luqman the Wise to his son; wisdom expresses itself as humble, lowered speech.
islam.tie_back: Wisdom received through a sage’s counsel issues in humble speech.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools… let thy words be few.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes counsels readiness to hear and restraint of speech as marks of wisdom.
judaism.tie_back: Hearing first, then few and humble words — close to the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada praises the monk who controls his tongue, speaks in moderation, is unassuming and explains the teaching in letter and spirit — his speech is pleasing.
buddhism.explanation: Mastery of the teaching produces restrained, modest and sweet speech.
buddhism.tie_back: Refined learning yielding humble speech — as in the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “But for the following fifteen good qualities he is called well-behaved: if he is always humble, steady, free from deceit and curiosity; if he abuses nobody; … if he listens to friendly advice; if he is not proud of his learning; … if he is enlightened, polite, decent, and quiet: then he is called well-behaved.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on the very learned pairs real learning with humility, courtesy and restrained speech. It lists listening to advice, abusing no one, and being polite and quiet among the marks of the well-trained monk.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that without refined learning gained by hearing it is hard to have humble, courteous speech. The Uttaradhyayana likewise sets humility, polite speech and readiness to listen among the qualities that come with learning.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.10–13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak names sweetness and humility, not size or show, as the heart of every virtue.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says only those refined by careful listening can speak humbly; Guru Nanak makes humble, sweet speech and bearing the essence of goodness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Young Telemachus, sent by Athena to question Nestor, protests that he is inexperienced in subtle speech and that it is shameful for a young man to question an elder; Athena encourages him, and he addresses Nestor with deference.
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus’ speech is modest precisely because he knows he has come to listen and learn.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The posture of a hearer produces respectful, humble speech.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Zeno of Citium, rebuking a talkative youth, said that we have two ears and one mouth so that we may listen more and speak less.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic founder makes the proportion of hearing to speaking a matter of wisdom.
philosophy.tie_back: Listening more produces measured, humble speech — the Kural’s link.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 7.23

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi spends a year listening before taking part in Indian politics
real_life_example.event: When Mohandas Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in January 1915, his political mentor Gopal Krishna Gokhale made him promise to spend a year travelling the country to gain experience, keeping his ears open and expressing no opinion on public questions until this period of probation was over. Gandhi kept the promise even after Gokhale died in February 1915, and spent much of the year touring India and meeting people of many regions and communities.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi's later ability to speak to and for India's very diverse people rested partly on this deliberate period of listening before speaking.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those without refined learning gained by hearing can hardly speak with humility, and Gokhale's counsel made Gandhi listen widely before he spoke, grounding his later public speech in what he had heard.

tamil:
செவியிற் சுவையுணரா வாயுணர்வின் மாக்கள்
அவியினும் வாழினும் என்.
transliteration:
Seviyir suvaiyunaraa vaayunarvin maakkal
Aviyinum vaazhinum en.
meaning: Some people know only the tastes of the mouth and not the tastes of the ear, like animals. What does it matter whether they live or die?
elementary: Some people only care about yummy food and never enjoy listening to wise words. Valluvar says, sharply, that such people live like animals — whether they live or die makes little difference to the world.
university: The closing kural returns to the food metaphor of 412–413 with a stinging contrast between செவியிற் சுவை (the ear’s taste) and வாயுணர்வு (mouth-knowledge, i.e., the palate). மாக்கள் denotes people without discernment — often glossed as ‘beast-like men’. The rhetorical question அவியினும் வாழினும் என் (‘whether they perish or live, what of it?’) declares their existence inconsequential. Some commentators take வாயுணர்வு as knowing only what one’s own mouth says, i.e., talkers who never listen; either way the chapter closes by denying full humanity to those who never cultivate hearing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Eating, sleeping, fear and mating are common to humans and animals; dharma alone is the distinguishing feature of humans, and without it they are equal to beasts.
hinduism.explanation: A famous verse in the introduction to the Hitopadesha defines human distinctiveness by something beyond the appetites.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s judgment: those who know only the appetites are மாக்கள், beast-like.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul condemns those governed by appetite and earthly concerns.
christianity.tie_back: Those who know only the mouth’s taste — ‘whose God is their belly’ — are judged as worthless as the Kural’s மாக்கள்.

islam.quote_or_event: “…They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an compares those with unused ears to cattle — even lower.
islam.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural: those without the ‘taste of the ear’ are beast-like.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist says a person without understanding, however prosperous, is no better than an animal.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts equate a life without understanding with that of beasts.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man of little learning grows old like a bull. He grows only in bulk, but his wisdom does not grow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Pali appassuta — ‘one who has heard little’ — is compared to an ox that merely grows fat.
buddhism.tie_back: The one who has not heard lives like a beast — precisely the Kural’s மாக்கள்.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Although they see by numerous examples the way by which their precious life may depart in the twinkling of an eye, yet they do not good even to the extent of a grain of millet. What does it matter whether such stupid, shameless (persons) live, or whether they die?”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar's chapter on defective knowledge dismisses people who learn nothing from what they see and do no good. It asks whether it matters at all if such people live or die.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks what it matters whether people who know only the tastes of the mouth, not of the ear, live or die. The Naladiyar asks the same question, almost word for word, about the stupid who take in nothing.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 33 'Defective knowledge', stanza 3 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Baba, the pleasures of other foods are false. Eating them, the body is ruined, and wickedness and corruption enter into the mind.”
sikhism.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak contrasts the true food of the Name with other foods, whose enjoyment harms the body and fills the mind with corruption.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural scorns beast-like people who know only the tastes of the mouth and not those of the ear; Guru Nanak likewise rejects the palate's pleasures in favour of spiritual nourishment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When King Midas judged Pan’s rustic piping superior to Apollo’s lyre, Apollo would not let such dull ears keep human shape and gave him the ears of an ass.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s myth punishes an ear without taste by making it literally bestial; Midas had earlier shown the same folly in preferring gold, which turned even his food to metal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ears that do not ‘taste’ properly mark a person as beast-like — the Kural’s மாக்கள் image in myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato says those without wisdom and virtue, always occupied with feasting, look downward like cattle, bent over their tables, feeding and fattening and breeding.
philosophy.explanation: The lover of bodily pleasure lives like grazing cattle, never tasting true pleasure.
philosophy.tie_back: A life devoted to the mouth rather than the mind is bestial — the Kural’s verdict.

real_life_example.event_title: Crassus rejects advice before the Battle of Carrhae
real_life_example.event: Marcus Licinius Crassus, one of the richest men in Rome, led a Roman army against the Parthian Empire in 53 BCE. According to Plutarch, he turned down the Armenian king Artavasdes' advice to advance through the hills of Armenia, where Parthian cavalry would be less effective, and instead followed an Arab chieftain, Ariamnes, onto the open plains of Mesopotamia. Near Carrhae the Parthian horse archers under Surena defeated his army, and Crassus was killed soon afterwards.
real_life_example.explanation: The campaign became a classic warning of how a powerful man who would not listen to counsel could bring ruin on himself and his army.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural dismisses those who know only the tastes of the mouth and never those of the ear, and Crassus, famous for his hunger for wealth, would not take in the advice that might have saved him.

tamil:
அறிவற்றங் காக்குங் கருவி செறுவார்க்கும்
உள்ளழிக்க லாகா அரண்.
transliteration:
Arivatrang kaakkum karuvi seruvaarkkum
Ullazhikka laakaa aran.
meaning: Wisdom is a weapon that protects a person from ruin. It is also a fort inside them that enemies cannot break into or destroy.
elementary: Imagine having a shield and a castle that nobody can ever take away from you. Valluvar says good sense is exactly that. It protects you from making ruinous mistakes, and no enemy can break into it, because it lives inside you.
university: The couplet sets up the governing metaphor of the chapter: arivu is both karuvi (an instrument or weapon) and aran (a fortress). The word அற்றம் (atram) means destruction, ruin, or a vulnerable moment of exposure. Parimelazhagan reads arivu as the faculty that keeps a person from falling into ruin. The second line moves the fortress inward: உள் (ul) is 'inside', so this is a stronghold that attackers (செறுவார், 'those who hate') cannot tear down from within. Placing the chapter in Porutpal is significant. For a king, forts, armies, and treasuries are external defences that can be besieged or bribed away, while discernment cannot be captured. The pairing of 'weapon' and 'wall' covers both active and passive defence. Stoic thought makes the same move with Marcus Aurelius's 'inner citadel', and the Dhammapada's image of the mind fortified like a city is similar.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In this endeavor there is no loss or diminution, and a little advancement on this path can protect one from the most dangerous type of fear.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna has just introduced buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding (2.39). He says that even a little of it acts as a protection against the greatest fear.
hinduism.tie_back: In both texts, discernment protects a person from ruin. The Gita stresses that even a small amount protects, while the Kural stresses that no enemy can destroy it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples that when they are hauled before hostile rulers, they will be given wisdom that none of their opponents can overcome.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts present wisdom as a defence that adversaries cannot break down. This matches the Kural's second line closely.

islam.quote_or_event: Joseph (Yusuf) interprets the king's dream of seven fat and seven lean cows. He counsels storing grain during the seven years of plenty so that Egypt survives the seven years of famine.
islam.explanation: Joseph's knowledge and foresight become Egypt's defence. His understanding protects the whole land from a disaster that armies and wealth could not have stopped.
islam.tie_back: This illustrates the Kural's claim that wisdom is a tool that guards against ruin. Here the ruin was a famine rather than an enemy.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ecclesiastes describes a small city besieged by a great king. A poor wise man in it delivered the city by his wisdom, and the Preacher concludes that wisdom is better than strength and better than weapons of war.
judaism.explanation: Kohelet describes a town that walls and soldiers could not save, but one person's wisdom could. Ecclesiastes 7:19 adds that wisdom makes the wise stronger than ten rulers in a city.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts treat wisdom as the true defence of a besieged place, stronger than physical fortification.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Realizing that this body is as fragile as a clay pot, and fortifying this mind like a well-fortified city, fight out Mara with the sword of wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells practitioners to treat the mind as a walled city and wisdom as the weapon used from inside it against Mara, the tempter.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's double image: wisdom as weapon (karuvi) and the mind as an unbreachable fortress (aran).

jainism.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable; making Zeal his bow, its string Carefulness in walking (iriyâ), and its top (where the string is fastened) Content, he should bend (this bow) with Truth, piercing with the arrow, Penance, (the foe's) mail, Karman--(in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Samsâra.”
jainism.explanation: Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, urges King Nami to build walls, gates and moats before renouncing; Nami answers that the sage's real fortress and weapons are inner virtues, guarded by the three guptis (control of mind, speech and body), with which he pierces the armour of karma.
jainism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, who calls wisdom both a weapon and an inner fortress no enemy can breach, Nami turns the king's walls and bow into inward qualities that cannot be besieged.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.20-22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The True Guru has placed the sword of spiritual wisdom in my hands; I have overcome and slain the Messenger of Death.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Vadhans Guru Ram Das describes spiritual wisdom (gian) as a sword given by the Guru, with which the seeker defeats the forces of death.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls wisdom a weapon against ruin and a fortress enemies cannot breach; Guru Ram Das likewise calls wisdom a weapon that defeats the gravest enemy.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 574, Raag Vadhans, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops Polyphemus's cave, Odysseus survives by cunning (metis) rather than force. He tells the giant his name is 'Nobody', blinds him, and escapes clinging beneath the sheep.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus has no strength to match a Cyclops. His mind is the only weapon and defence he has, and it saves him and his men.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Practical intelligence works here as the weapon that guards against ruin, as the Kural describes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The mind which is free from passions is a citadel, for man has nothing more secure to which he can fly for refuge.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius argues that the ruling faculty of reason, kept clear, is an inner stronghold that outside events and enemies cannot capture.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'inner fortress' (ul aran) almost word for word: reason as a citadel that attackers cannot overthrow.

real_life_example.event_title: Archimedes' machines defend Syracuse
real_life_example.event: When a Roman army and fleet under Marcus Claudius Marcellus besieged the Greek city of Syracuse, they faced defences that the mathematician Archimedes had designed at the request of King Hiero II. According to Polybius and Livy, catapults of different ranges and cranes fitted with hooks that could lift attacking ships out of the water broke up the Roman assaults by land and sea, forcing the Romans to settle into a long blockade. The city fell only in 212 or 211 BCE, and Archimedes died in the sack that followed.
real_life_example.explanation: The knowledge of a single scholar held one of the strongest armies of the age at bay for about two years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls wisdom a weapon that guards against ruin and a fortress that enemies cannot breach, and Archimedes' knowledge literally became the weapons and walls of his city.

tamil:
சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா தீதொரீஇ
நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்ப தறிவு.
transliteration:
Sendra idaththaal selavidaa theethoreei
Nandrinpaal uyppa tharivu.
meaning: Wisdom means not letting the mind run wherever it wants. It keeps the mind away from evil and guides it toward good.
elementary: Your mind is a bit like a puppy that wants to run off in every direction. Wisdom is the leash. It stops the puppy from running into trouble and gently pulls it toward good things.
university: Here arivu is defined by its function over the mind (implied as the subject). சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா means 'not letting it go wherever it goes'. தீது ஒரீஇ means 'removing it from evil', and நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது means 'leading it toward the good'. Three movements are involved: restraint, withdrawal, and redirection. Wisdom is therefore not only knowing the good but actively governing attention and desire. Parimelazhagan glosses the object as the mind driven by the five senses. The image matches Indian and Greek charioteer models of the psyche (Katha Upanishad, Plato's Phaedrus), where intelligence holds the reins of the senses. The Buddhist 'fletcher straightening the arrow' image is similar. The Kural is notably positive: wisdom does not simply suppress the mind, it 'leads' it (uyppathu) somewhere better.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Katha Upanishad teaches that the good (shreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both approach a person. The wise examine and distinguish them and choose the good; the fool chooses the pleasant. It then compares the body to a chariot, the senses to horses, and buddhi (discernment) to the charioteer holding the reins of the mind.
hinduism.explanation: Yama tells Nachiketas that discernment must choose between competing pulls and must rein in senses that would otherwise run wild, like untamed horses.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts describe wisdom as the faculty that stops the mind from going wherever it pulls and steers it to the good.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul sums up the Christian moral life as turning away from evil and holding fast to good.
christianity.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's two moves: theethu oreei (removing oneself from evil) and nandrinpaal uyppathu (leading toward the good).

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises the person who holds the nafs (lower self) back from following its desires.
islam.tie_back: Both texts stress restraining the self from going wherever its inclinations lead.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma asks, 'Who is mighty?' and answers, 'One who subdues his (evil) inclination (yetzer).'
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah redefines strength as mastery over one's own impulses rather than power over others.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see the key human capacity as governing the inner drive that pulls toward wrong.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a fletcher straightens an arrow shaft, even so the discerning man straightens his mind — so fickle and unsteady, so difficult to guard.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the discerning person to an arrow-maker who takes a crooked, wavering shaft and makes it straight.
buddhism.tie_back: In both texts the discerning faculty takes a restless, wandering mind and directs it true.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The unruly, dreadful, bad horse, on which you sit, runs about, Gautama! how comes it to pass that it does not run off with you?” … “I govern it well in its course by the bridle of knowledge; it does not go astray with me, it keeps to the right path.” … “The mind is that unruly, dreadful, bad horse; I govern it by the discipline of the Law (so that it becomes a well-) trained Kambôga-steed.”
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue between Kesi (of Parshva's line) and Gautama (Mahavira's disciple), the mind is a runaway horse that knowledge reins in and keeps on the right path, until it becomes a well-trained steed.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar defines wisdom as not letting the mind go wherever it wanders but leading it from evil to the good; Gautama's 'bridle of knowledge' does exactly that: it restrains the mind and steers it onto the right path.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.55-58 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Taking up the sword of spiritual wisdom, she struggles with her mind, and hope and desire are smoothed over in her mind.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Maaroo Guru Nanak describes the soul-bride using spiritual wisdom to fight her own mind until its restless desires are stilled.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines wisdom as not letting the mind run where it likes, holding it from evil and steering it to good; Guru Nanak shows wisdom wrestling the mind and stilling its cravings.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1022, Raag Maaroo (Solhe), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads the young Heracles meets two women, Vice and Virtue. Vice offers an easy road of pleasure; Virtue offers a harder road of toil and honour. Heracles chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prodicus's fable presents the moment of choice when desire pulls toward the easy path and judgment must turn it toward the good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This dramatises the Kural's turning of the mind away from evil and toward good.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus, 'The Choice of Heracles', as retold in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato's Socrates likens the soul to a charioteer driving two winged horses: one noble and obedient, the other unruly and pulled by appetite. The charioteer (reason) must rein in the unruly horse and guide the pair upward.
philosophy.explanation: Reason's job is to stop appetite from dragging the soul wherever it wants and to direct it toward the good.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural: arivu is the charioteer that keeps the mind from bolting and leads it toward the good.

real_life_example.event_title: Ignatius of Loyola learns to read the movements of his mind
real_life_example.event: In 1521 the Basque soldier Inigo de Loyola was badly wounded in the legs by a cannonball while defending Pamplona against the French and was carried to his family's castle at Loyola. During a long convalescence, with only a life of Christ and a book of saints' lives to read, he noticed that daydreams of knightly glory left him empty and unsatisfied, while thoughts of following Christ and the saints left him uplifted. He resolved to change his life, left Loyola in 1522, and the practice of attending to these inner movements, later called discernment, became central to his Spiritual Exercises and to the Society of Jesus he founded.
real_life_example.explanation: Ignatius turned close attention to his own thoughts into a lasting method for steering the mind, still taught worldwide.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines wisdom as not letting the mind go wherever it wanders, but drawing it away from evil and leading it toward the good, which is what Ignatius learned to do by noticing where each kind of thought led him.

tamil:
எப்பொருள் யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும் அப்பொருள்
மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்ப தறிவு.
transliteration:
Epporul yaaryaarvaaik ketpinum apporul
Meipporul kaanpa tharivu.
meaning: Whatever you hear, and whoever you hear it from, wisdom is finding the real truth of it.
elementary: Sometimes people believe something just because a famous or important person said it. Sometimes they ignore something true because someone they don't like said it. Valluvar says a wise person looks at what was said and asks, 'Is this actually true?', no matter who said it.
university: This is among the most frequently quoted Kurals, often cited as an early statement of critical thinking. The repetition யார்யார் ('whoever, whoever') stresses that the speaker's status, reputation, or hostility is irrelevant. The contrast between பொருள் (porul, the thing said or its surface content) and மெய்ப்பொருள் (meipporul, its true substance) separates what is asserted from what is real. Two errors are ruled out. One is deference to authority, accepting a claim because of who said it. The other is the ad hominem, rejecting it for the same reason. The Kural is less radical than modern empiricism, because it assumes the truth can be discerned through judgment. Still, its location of arivu in the evaluation of claims, not in the collecting of them, anticipates the Buddhist Kalama Sutta and Aristotle's 'truth above friends'. For a king in Porutpal, this is also advice about handling the reports of ministers, spies, and flatterers.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Rig Veda prays, 'Let noble thoughts come to us from every side' (ā no bhadrāḥ kratavo yantu viśvataḥ).
hinduism.explanation: This Vedic invocation is widely cited in India as a charter for openness: good insight is welcome whatever its source.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural shares the Vedic openness to wisdom from any quarter, and adds the requirement that it be tested for real truth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Thessalonians not to reject teachings outright or accept them uncritically, but to test everything and keep what holds true.
christianity.tie_back: This is the same method as the Kural: examine whatever you hear and hold onto its true substance.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who listen to speech and follow the best of it. Those are the ones Allah has guided, and those are people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises those who hear what is said, weigh it, and follow the best of it, and calls them ulu al-albab, 'people of understanding'.
islam.tie_back: Both texts define understanding as sifting what one hears to find what is truly best.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma asks, 'Who is wise?' and answers, 'One who learns from every person.'
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah defines the wise person as someone willing to receive truth from anyone, whatever their standing.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost a direct echo of the Kural's 'from whomever you hear it'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells the Kalamas not to accept teachings merely because of report, tradition, scripture, logic, or the speaker's seeming competence, or because 'this contemplative is our teacher'. They should accept a teaching only when they know for themselves that it is skillful and leads to welfare.
buddhism.explanation: The Kalama Sutta is the classic Buddhist charter for evaluating claims on their merits rather than on the authority of the speaker.
buddhism.tie_back: It makes the same point as the Kural: a claim's truth is not settled by who says it; wisdom sees its real substance.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wisdom recognises the truth of the Law and the ascertainment of true things.”
jainism.explanation: The followers of Parshva and of Mahavira were troubled because the two teachers' rules differed (four vows against five, clothing against none). Gautama's answer is that wisdom looks past the outward differences to what is actually true, and Kesi, satisfied, accepts it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks the wise to find the real substance (meipporul) of whatever is said by whoever says it; Gautama likewise tells the disputing disciples to judge by the truth of the matter, not by which master's label a rule carries.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “From the True Guru, I have obtained a discriminating intellect; the Guru has revealed the spiritual wisdom of God.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Todee Guru Ram Das calls the discriminating intellect (bibek budh), the power to tell true from false and good from bad, a gift of the Guru.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines wisdom as seeing the truth of whatever is said, whoever says it; Guru Ram Das prizes the same discernment as bibek budh.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 711, Raag Todee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cassandra, cursed by Apollo so that no one would believe her, foretells the fall of Troy and Agamemnon's murder. Her hearers dismiss her true words because of who she is.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Trojans and the Argive chorus judge the prophecies by the speaker (a 'mad' captive) and not by their content, and ruin follows.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the failure the Kural warns against: failing to see the truth of a claim because of the person saying it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For, while both are dear, piety requires us to honour truth above our friends.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle criticises the Platonic Form of the Good even though Plato was his teacher and friend. He insists that truth outranks loyalty to any person.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts put the truth of a claim above the identity or status of the person who holds it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1.6, 1096a (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Ibn al-Haytham tests the authorities on light and vision
real_life_example.event: Working in Cairo in the early eleventh century, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham wrote the Book of Optics, which used experiment and mathematics to show that vision results from light entering the eye, rejecting the view of Euclid and Ptolemy that the eye sends out rays. He also wrote Doubts Concerning Ptolemy, a critique of inconsistencies in the astronomy and optics of the most respected scientific authority of his age. Translated into Latin, his Optics influenced European scholars for centuries, and UNESCO marked its thousandth anniversary during the International Year of Light in 2015.
real_life_example.explanation: Ibn al-Haytham is celebrated as a pioneer of experimental method because he insisted on testing claims against evidence, whatever the fame of their author.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says wisdom is seeing the true substance of whatever is heard, whoever says it, and Ibn al-Haytham refused to accept even Ptolemy's teaching without checking whether it was true.

tamil:
எண்பொருள வாகச் செலச்சொல்லித் தான்பிறர்வாய்
நுண்பொருள் காண்ப தறிவு.
transliteration:
Enporula vaagach selachcholli thaanpirarvaai
Nunporul kaanpa tharivu.
meaning: Wisdom is speaking so that others easily understand you and remember what you said, and also catching the deeper meaning in what others say.
elementary: A wise person does two things with words. When they talk, they explain things so clearly that others understand easily. When they listen, they catch even the small, hidden points in what others are saying.
university: The couplet describes wisdom in communication as running in two directions. In speaking, எண்பொருள ஆக means 'so that the meaning is easy' and செலச் சொல்லி means 'speaking so that it goes in', that is, lodges in the listener. In listening, நுண்பொருள் காண்பது means 'seeing the subtle or fine meaning' in another's words. The contrast between எண் (easy, simple) and நுண் (subtle, fine) is deliberate. The wise person simplifies when giving and refines when receiving. This is a sophisticated account of communicative intelligence, close to what classical rhetoric called knowing one's audience (Plato's Phaedrus) and to hermeneutic charity in interpreting others. For rulers and ministers, the Porutpal setting, it is practical advice: make your orders clear, and read the unstated intentions of envoys and courtiers.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes disciplined speech as speech shaped for its effect on the listener: true, agreeable, and helpful.
hinduism.tie_back: This covers the speaking half of the Kural, speaking so that words land well with the hearer.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges speech adapted to each listener: gracious, apt, and responsive to the person being answered.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see wise speech as speech tailored to land with the hearer. Knowing 'how to answer every man' requires grasping what each person means.

islam.quote_or_event: “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ties hikmah (wisdom) directly to how one speaks: persuasively, kindly, and in the best manner for the audience.
islam.tie_back: Both texts connect wisdom with speaking in a way that actually reaches the hearer.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah lists seven marks of a wise person: he does not speak before one greater in wisdom, does not interrupt, is not hasty to answer, asks relevant questions and answers to the point, speaks on first things first, admits when he has not understood, and acknowledges the truth.
judaism.explanation: The sage is defined by disciplined conversation: careful listening, fitting replies, and orderly speech.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Avot treats wisdom as skill in both hearing and speaking.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “That monk who has control over his tongue, is moderate in speech, unassuming and who explains the Teaching in both letter and spirit — whatever he says is pleasing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises the monk whose speech conveys both the letter and the inner meaning of the Dhamma, and so is received well.
buddhism.tie_back: Explaining 'in letter and spirit' parallels the Kural's pairing of plain meaning with subtle meaning, and speech that 'pleases' reaches the hearer.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the debate at Sravasti, the monk Kesi puts his questions to Gautama as riddles: a thousand foes attacking him, a poisonous plant in the heart, a raging fire, a runaway horse, a leaking boat. Each time Gautama grasps the hidden meaning and answers in plain, memorable words (the foe is the unsubdued self and the passions, the fire is the passions, the boat is the body), until Kesi and the whole assembly are satisfied.
jainism.explanation: The episode presents an ideal of communication on both sides: Gautama sees the subtle sense in what Kesi says and then gives that sense back in clear, simple terms that his hearers can take in.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's wise person both speaks so that the meaning easily sinks in and sees the subtle meaning in others' words; Gautama shows both skills, decoding Kesi's riddles and answering in a way the whole assembly can follow.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.35-85 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor.”
sikhism.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak says that only speech that earns honour, before people and before God, is true speech.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines wisdom as speaking so that the meaning lands easily in the listener, and grasping subtle meaning in others; Guru Nanak likewise sets a standard for speech worth speaking.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Nestor of Pylos is introduced as the clear-voiced orator 'from whose tongue flowed speech sweeter than honey'. He is repeatedly sent to reconcile quarrelling chiefs because his words reach them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor is Homer's model of the counsellor whose speech persuades because it is well judged for his audience.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He exemplifies the speaking half of the Kural: words that go in and settle in the hearer's mind.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that a true art of speech requires knowing the nature of the soul. The speaker must identify what kind of soul he addresses and fit the speech to it, simple speech to a simple soul and complex speech to a complex one.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, real rhetoric depends on understanding the listener, which in turn requires a subtle perception of other minds.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts see communicative wisdom as fitting speech to the hearer and perceiving what lies within others.

real_life_example.event_title: Kennedy answers Khrushchev's first letter in the Cuban Missile Crisis
real_life_example.place: Washington, D.C., United States, and Moscow, Soviet Union
real_life_example.event: At the height of the Cuban Missile Crisis, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev sent President John F. Kennedy a private letter on 26 October 1962 suggesting that the missiles in Cuba could be removed in return for a U.S. promise not to invade Cuba, followed on 27 October by a second, public message that also demanded the removal of U.S. missiles from Turkey. On the advice of his officials, Kennedy replied to the terms of the first letter, setting out clear steps for removing the missiles under United Nations supervision in exchange for a pledge not to attack Cuba, while Robert Kennedy privately told the Soviet ambassador that the missiles in Turkey would later be withdrawn. On 28 October Khrushchev announced that the missiles would be removed from Cuba.
real_life_example.explanation: Reading the opening in the first, more conciliatory letter and answering it plainly helped end the most dangerous confrontation of the Cold War.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines wisdom as speaking so that one's meaning goes home easily while grasping the subtle meaning in what others say, and Kennedy's team did both, reading the possibility in Khrushchev's first letter and answering it in clear, acceptable terms.

tamil:
உலகம் தழீஇய தொட்பம் மலர்தலும்
கூம்பலும் இல்ல தறிவு.
transliteration:
Ulagam thazheeiya thotpam malarthalum
Koombalum illa tharivu.
meaning: Wisdom is making friends with the great people of the world and keeping that friendship steady, not opening up like a flower at first and closing up later.
elementary: Some people are super friendly one day and cold the next, like a flower that opens in the morning and shuts at night. Valluvar says it is smart to make friends with good people. It is wise to stay the same kind friend every day, not hot one day and cold the next.
university: This is the most debated couplet in the chapter. ஒட்பம் (otpam) means excellence or sagacity, and உலகம் (ulagam, 'the world') is read by Parimelazhagan and most commentators as 'the great ones of the world' (uyarndhor). The first half therefore says that true excellence is to befriend the eminent. The second half uses a flower image: மலர்தல் (blooming, opening) and கூம்பல் (closing, as a flower does at dusk). Wisdom is keeping that friendship constant, neither over-effusive at the start nor withdrawing later. Some modern readers (e.g. Karunanidhi, Mu. Varadarasan) take the flower image more broadly as emotional equanimity in joy and sorrow. Both readings stress stability: arivu produces steadiness of disposition, especially in relationships. Aristotle's view that friendships of the good endure because goodness endures is a close parallel.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not disturbed in mind even amidst the threefold miseries or elated when there is happiness, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the sthita-prajna, the person of steady wisdom, who neither swells in good times nor collapses in bad.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's 'no blooming and no closing', which the equanimity reading takes as the mark of wisdom.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs defines true friendship by its constancy, the same in good times and in hardship.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's steady friendship, neither opening wide nor shutting, is the friend who 'loveth at all times'.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches believers to hold an even keel: not crushed by loss, not puffed up by gain.
islam.tie_back: This parallels the flower image of neither blooming (exulting) nor closing (despairing).

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah teaches that any love dependent on some particular thing ceases when that thing ceases, while love not dependent on anything never ceases. The love of David and Jonathan is its example.
judaism.explanation: Avot distinguishes fickle, conditional attachment from steady love that does not wax and wane with circumstances.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's steady friendship, which does not open and close with changing fortunes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha describes the true-hearted friend as one who is the same in happiness and in sorrow. Such a friend does not desert you in trouble and would even give up his life for you.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the marks of genuine friendship to help a layman tell steady friends from fair-weather ones.
buddhism.tie_back: 'The same in happiness and sorrow' is the Kural's friend who neither blooms nor closes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sûtras.” … “If he does not meet with a clever companion who surpasses or equals him in virtue, he should live by himself, abstaining from sins and not devoted to pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on the causes of carelessness makes the company one keeps part of the road to liberation: serve worthy elders, avoid fools, and choose only a companion who equals or surpasses oneself in virtue, or else live alone.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's first half says excellence lies in befriending the worthy of the world; the Jain text likewise makes association with the wise, and avoidance of fools, a deliberate discipline.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.3, 32.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone are my friends, who travel along with me; and in that place, where the accounts are called for, they appear standing with me.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Soohee Guru Nanak says true friends are those who stay with a person to the very end, even at the final reckoning.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises befriending the worthy and keeping that friendship steady, without blooming and then closing; Guru Nanak names steadfastness to the end as the test of true friendship.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pylades stays with Orestes through exile, madness, and mortal danger. In Iphigenia in Tauris, when only one of them may leave alive, each insists on dying for the other.
greek_mythology.explanation: Orestes and Pylades became the Greek byword for friendship that holds steady whatever the circumstances.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They embody the Kural's friendship that never closes up when fortune turns.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that friendships of utility and pleasure dissolve easily, but the friendship of the good lasts: “their friendship lasts as long as they are good — and goodness is an enduring thing.”
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the best friendship is between good people and is stable because it rests on character, not on changing advantage or pleasure.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts link friendship with the excellent to a constancy that neither blooms nor fades.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.3, 1156b (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The friendship of Goethe and Schiller
real_life_example.event: After a conversation following a meeting of a natural science society in Jena in July 1794, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller began a close friendship and literary partnership. They worked together on Schiller's journal Die Horen, jointly wrote the satirical epigrams known as the Xenien, commented closely on each other's works, and in 1797 wrote a celebrated series of ballads. The friendship lasted until Schiller's death in Weimar in May 1805, after which Goethe wrote that he had lost half of his own existence.
real_life_example.explanation: Their partnership is one of the most celebrated friendships in literary history, remaining steady and productive for more than a decade.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises befriending the worthy and keeping that friendship steady rather than blossoming and then closing, and the bond between Goethe and Schiller stayed constant from its beginning until Schiller's death.

tamil:
எவ்வ துறைவது உலகம் உலகத்தோடு
அவ்வ துறைவ தறிவு.
transliteration:
Evva thuraivathu ulagam ulagaththodu
Avva thuraiva tharivu.
meaning: Wisdom is living in step with the world, behaving the way the best people in the world behave.
elementary: Every place has its own ways of doing things. A wise person notices how good people around them behave and fits in with them, instead of being odd or rude just to stand out.
university: The couplet turns on the parallel எவ்வது / அவ்வது ('in whatever way / in that way') and on the verb உறைதல் (to dwell or abide). Wisdom is to abide with the world in the way the world abides. As in 425, Parimelazhagan takes ulagam to mean the uyarndhor, the worthy or great of the world, not the crowd. The Kural is therefore not a call to conformity with the majority but to conduct in step with the accepted norms of the good. It still carries a real social insight: discernment includes reading context and custom and not acting eccentrically. This complements 423. There, wisdom judges claims independently; here, wisdom adapts one's conduct to the settled ways of good society. Parallels range from the Talmudic 'never deviate from local custom' to Paul's 'all things to all men' and Descartes's provisional maxim of following his country's customs.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “So as not to disrupt the minds of ignorant men attached to the fruitive results of prescribed duties, a learned person should not induce them to stop work. Rather, by working in the spirit of devotion, he should engage them in all sorts of activities.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna advises the wise not to set themselves apart and unsettle ordinary people. They should act alongside them in the accepted way (compare 3.21: whatever the great do, others follow).
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts see wisdom as moving in step with the world instead of standing apart from it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes adapting his conduct to Jews, Gentiles, and the weak alike: living as they live, so as to reach them.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat adapting to the ways of those around you as wise and effective.

islam.quote_or_event: Ali ibn Abi Talib said: speak to people according to what they understand. Do you want Allah and His Messenger to be denied?
islam.explanation: Bukhari records Ali's teaching in the Book of Knowledge: the wise adapt what they say to the capacity and ways of their audience.
islam.tie_back: Both texts see wisdom as fitting oneself to the people among whom one lives and speaks.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge, no. 127 (saying of Ali)

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that a person should never deviate from local custom. When Moses ascended on high he did not eat bread, and when the angels descended to visit Abraham they appeared to eat.
judaism.explanation: Even Moses and the angels adjusted their behaviour to the realm they were in, and the Talmud draws a general rule of wise conduct from this.
judaism.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural's point: live as the world you are in lives.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says: 'I do not dispute with the world; the world disputes with me.' What the wise in the world agree does not exist, he too says does not exist; what they agree exists, he too says exists.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha presents himself as not contrary for its own sake. He aligns his statements with what the wise of the world accept.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural and Parimelazhagan's reading that one should abide as the wise of the world abide.

jainism.quote_or_event: Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra opens its account of lay conduct with the qualities of the mārgānusārī, the householder who is 'following the path' even before taking the vows. Among them are earning wealth honestly and conforming to the proper, approved customs of one's society and country.
jainism.explanation: For Jain teachers, a layperson's spiritual path begins with being a decent and well-adjusted member of society, living by the accepted good customs around them, before any higher discipline is taken up.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's wisdom of 'living as the (worthy) world lives' corresponds to the Jain picture of the householder whose first virtues include fitting in with the sound customs of his land.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, ch. 1 (the mārgānusārī qualities of the householder); paraphrased

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak teaches that the spiritual life is lived in the world through service, not by leaving it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines wisdom as living in harmony with the world as the worthy do; Guru Nanak likewise places the right life within the world, through seva.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus is introduced as polytropos, 'the man of many turns', who 'saw the cities of many men and learned their mind'. He survives by adapting his manner to each people and court he encounters.
greek_mythology.explanation: His defining trait is adaptability: reading each new society and conducting himself accordingly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He illustrates the Kural's wisdom of moving with the world as the world moves.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The first maxim of Descartes's provisional moral code is to obey the laws and customs of his country, and to govern himself by the most moderate opinions of the most sensible people he would live among.
philosophy.explanation: While doubting everything in theory, Descartes decides that in practice a wise person lives by the settled customs of sensible people around him.
philosophy.tie_back: This closely matches the Kural, including its implicit restriction to the sensible or worthy, as Parimelazhagan reads it.
philosophy.source: René Descartes, Discourse on the Method, Part 3

real_life_example.event_title: Matteo Ricci adopts the ways of Chinese scholars
real_life_example.place: Southern China and Beijing, Ming China
real_life_example.event: The Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci entered China in 1583, when the interior was closed to most foreigners. He learned Chinese, studied the Chinese classics, and in the mid-1590s exchanged the robes of a Buddhist monk for the dress of a Chinese scholar, winning a hearing among officials and literati through his learning in mathematics, astronomy and geography. In January 1601 he was allowed to settle in Beijing, where he lived and taught until his death in 1610.
real_life_example.explanation: By living as the respected scholars of China lived, Ricci became one of the first Europeans accepted into Chinese intellectual life, opening a long exchange of knowledge between Europe and China.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines wisdom as conducting oneself as the worthy of the world conduct themselves, and Ricci succeeded by shaping his dress, speech and learning to the ways of China's scholar-officials.

tamil:
அறிவுடையார் ஆவ தறிவார் அறிவிலார்
அஃதறி கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Arivudaiyaar aava tharivaar arivilaar
Aqdhari kallaa thavar.
meaning: Wise people know what is going to happen before it happens. Unwise people cannot know it.
elementary: If you see dark clouds, you know rain is coming and take an umbrella. A wise person is good at spotting what is going to happen next, while a foolish person gets caught by surprise every time.
university: This couplet defines wisdom and its lack by one criterion: foresight. ஆவது அறிவார் means 'they know what will come to be'. The second line mirrors it: the unwise are precisely those who cannot know that (அஃது அறிகல்லாதவர்). Commentators take ஆவது to mean the outcome or consequence of present actions and circumstances, not supernatural prophecy. Arivu here is predictive practical judgment, the ability to read causes forward to their effects. The Talmudic definition 'who is wise? One who sees what will be born' is almost a translation. Aristotle's phronesis includes deliberating well about what conduces to the good in the long run, and Hesiod's Prometheus (forethought) and Epimetheus (afterthought) personify the Kural's opposition. The couplet also prepares for 429, where foresight becomes protection.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That which in the beginning may be just like poison but at the end is just like nectar and which awakens one to self-realization is said to be happiness in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that sattvic understanding looks past immediate appearances to eventual outcomes, choosing what is bitter now but sweet in the end.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts define higher understanding by the ability to see how things will turn out.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points to the ordinary prudence of thinking ahead to where a project will end before starting it. He contrasts this with the builder who is mocked for being unable to finish.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts define good sense as knowing in advance how things will turn out.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said: the wise (al-kayyis) is one who holds himself to account and works for what comes after death. The incapable (al-'ajiz) is one who follows his desires and merely hopes in Allah.
islam.explanation: The hadith defines intelligence by forward-looking action and folly by living only for the moment.
islam.tie_back: Both texts contrast the wise, who look ahead to what is coming, with the foolish, who cannot.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud asks, 'Who is wise?' and answers, 'One who sees what will be born' (ha-ro'eh et ha-nolad), meaning one who foresees the outcome of things.
judaism.explanation: In Alexander the Great's dialogue with the elders of the Negev, the rabbis define wisdom as foresight of consequences.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost identical to the Kural: the wise know what will come to be.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Future Dangers suttas the Buddha urges monks to consider dangers not yet arrived (old age, illness, famine, strife, corruption of the teaching) and to strive now, while conditions are favourable.
buddhism.explanation: The wise practitioner looks ahead to what is coming and acts before it arrives.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see knowing what is coming as the mark of wisdom.

jainism.quote_or_event: “'If he does not get (victory over his will) early, he will get it afterwards;' such reasoning presupposes the eternity of human life. But such a man despairs when his life draws to its close, and the dissolution of his body approaches.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's discourse on carelessness mocks the man who keeps putting off self-conquest as if life will last forever. Such a person fails to see what is coming and is left in despair when death arrives.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the wise know beforehand what will come and the unwise cannot; the Jain verse gives the unwise person's typical mistake, reasoning as if the future will never arrive.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If someone focuses on the Lord beforehand, then why should he be punished?”
sikhism.explanation: In one of the Babarvani hymns on Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak says that people who are mindful beforehand would not suffer such punishment; Sahib Singh reads it as keeping one's duty in mind in good time.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the wise know beforehand what is coming; Guru Nanak says that being mindful in good time spares one the suffering that comes later.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus ('Forethought') warns his brother Epimetheus ('Afterthought') never to accept a gift from Zeus. Epimetheus accepts Pandora anyway and understands the harm only after it has come.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod builds the two brothers' names and fates on the contrast between foresight and hindsight.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This personifies the Kural exactly: the wise know what will come; the unwise know only too late.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is thought to be the mark of a man of practical wisdom to be able to deliberate well about what is good and expedient for himself... about what sorts of thing conduce to the good life in general.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines phronesis as sound deliberation about what leads to good ends, which requires foreseeing consequences.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts see practical wisdom as seeing where actions lead.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6.5, 1140a (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Themistocles persuades Athens to build a fleet from its silver
real_life_example.event: When a rich new vein of silver was found at the state mines of Laurium in about 483 BCE, the Athenians would normally have shared out the income among the citizens. Themistocles persuaded them instead to spend it on a large fleet of warships, officially for the ongoing war with the island of Aegina. When the Persian king Xerxes invaded Greece in 480 BCE, Athens had about 200 triremes, and this fleet played the leading part in the Greek naval victory at Salamis.
real_life_example.explanation: Turning a windfall into a navy before the danger arrived gave Greece the means to defeat the largest invasion it had ever faced.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the wise know beforehand what is going to happen, and Themistocles had Athens build its fleet before the Persian invasion came.

tamil:
அஞ்சுவ தஞ்சாமை பேதைமை அஞ்சுவது
அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Anjuva thanjaamai pethaimai anjuvathu
Anjal arivaar thozhil.
meaning: Not being afraid of what you should be afraid of is foolish. Being afraid of what you should be afraid of is the way of the wise.
elementary: Being brave does not mean being scared of nothing. A person who isn't afraid of touching a hot stove or running across a busy road is not brave, just foolish. Wise people are careful about the things that really are dangerous.
university: The couplet rests on the repeated verb அஞ்சு (to fear) in a tight chiastic pattern. அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை ('not fearing the fearworthy') is பேதைமை (folly), and அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் ('fearing the fearworthy') is the practice (தொழில்) of the wise. Fear is treated not as a weakness to overcome but as an emotion to calibrate. Commentators apply it to wrongdoing, the anger of the powerful, and real dangers. This is almost exactly Aristotle's doctrine of courage as a mean: the brave person fears the right things in the right way, and fearlessness toward everything is rashness. The Dhammapada (317) and Proverbs (14:16) make the same point. In the Porutpal context, a king who fears nothing, not even enemies, public anger, or his own misdeeds, is a danger to the state.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, that understanding by which one knows what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, what is to be feared and what is not to be feared, what is binding and what is liberating, is in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines sattvic buddhi (clear understanding) partly as knowing what is and is not to be feared.
hinduism.tie_back: This is a direct parallel: both texts identify correctly sorting what is fearworthy as a function of true understanding.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus redirects his disciples' fear away from human persecutors and toward what is truly to be feared.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts teach that the issue is not whether to fear but what to fear.

islam.quote_or_event: “Only those fear Allah, from among His servants, who have knowledge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an connects knowledge ('ilm) directly with rightly placed fear (khashya) of God.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link knowledge with fearing what should be feared.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wise man feareth, and departeth from evil; but the fool behaveth overbearingly, and is confident.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the wise man, who is afraid of evil and avoids it, with the fool, who charges ahead full of confidence.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost a paraphrase of the Kural: the wise fear the fearworthy, and the fool fears nothing.
