buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who see something to fear where there is nothing to fear, and see nothing to fear where there is something to fear — upholding false views, they go to the state of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha condemns misplaced fear in both directions, fearing the harmless and ignoring the truly dangerous, as wrong view.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's exact claim, extended to the opposite error as well.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk should step carefully in his walk (i.e. in his life), supposing everything to be a snare for him.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain ideal of vigilance (apramāda) asks the aspirant to move through life as if surrounded by snares: an alert, well-placed caution toward what can bind the soul with karma, not panic.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls it folly not to fear what should be feared; the Jain monk's habit of treating every step as a possible snare is exactly that wise fear of real dangers.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without the Fear of God, no one crosses over the world-ocean. This Fear of God adorns the Love of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Gauree Guru Nanak teaches that reverent fear of God (bhau) is necessary and that it adorns rather than opposes love.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls it folly not to fear what should be feared and wisdom to fear it; Guru Nanak names the one fear that must never be lost, the fear of God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 151, Raag Gauree Gwaarayree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Icarus ignores his father Daedalus's warning not to fly too near the sun. Exulting in flight and without fear, he soars upward until the wax of his wings melts and he falls into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: Icarus's lack of fear of a real danger, which his wiser father rightly feared, destroys him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This illustrates the Kural's first line: not fearing what should be feared is folly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The man, then, who faces and who fears the right things and from the right motive, in the right way and at the right time, and who feels confidence under the corresponding conditions, is brave.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines courage not as fearlessness but as fearing the right things appropriately. Excess of confidence is rashness.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis stated as moral theory: fearing the fearworthy is wisdom, and not fearing it is folly.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 3.7, 1115b (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: John Snow has the Broad Street pump handle removed
real_life_example.event: During a severe cholera outbreak in Soho in 1854, the physician John Snow, who held that cholera spread through contaminated water rather than through bad air as most authorities then believed, analysed the addresses of the dead and interviewed residents, and found that the cases centred on a public water pump in Broad Street. On the evening of 7 September he presented his evidence to the parish Board of Guardians of St James's, and the pump handle was removed the next day. The outbreak was already declining by then, but Snow's investigation became a founding example of modern epidemiology.
real_life_example.explanation: Snow directed fear at the real danger, the water people trusted, at a time when most experts feared the wrong cause.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says it is folly not to fear what ought to be feared and wisdom to fear it, and Snow rightly feared the contaminated water that his neighbours and many authorities did not.

tamil:
எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்க் கில்லை
அதிர வருவதோர் நோய்.
transliteration:
Ethirathaak kaakkum arivinaark killai
Athira varuvathor noi.
meaning: Wise people who prepare ahead for what is coming will never be hit by a disaster that makes them shake with fear.
elementary: If you know a storm is coming and you close the windows and bring in your toys, the storm can't really hurt you. Wise people prepare ahead of time, so when trouble comes it doesn't shake them.
university: Building on 427 (knowing what will come), this couplet adds action: எதிரதாக் காக்கும் means 'guarding against it as something ahead', that is, protecting oneself before a danger arrives. The result: இல்லை அதிர வருவதோர் நோய் ('there is no affliction that comes so as to make them shudder'). நோய் (noi) literally means disease but is used broadly for suffering or calamity, and அதிர (to shake or tremble) vividly describes the shock of being unprepared. The claim is not that the wise escape every misfortune but that nothing catches them off guard. This parallels the Stoic premeditatio malorum, the Panchatantra fable of the three fish, and Jesus's parable of the house built on rock. It links back to 421's image of arivu as a protective weapon.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra, three fish in a pond overhear fishermen planning to return. Anagatavidhata ('Provider-for-the-future') leaves at once for another pond. Pratyutpannamati ('Ready-wit') escapes by playing dead. Yadbhavishya ('What-will-be-will-be') does nothing and is caught.
hinduism.explanation: The fable ranks prudence by foresight. The fish who guards against danger before it arrives survives with no distress at all.
hinduism.tie_back: This dramatises the Kural: the one who guards against what is coming is untouched by calamity.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts the wise builder, who prepared a foundation before the storm, with the foolish builder whose house collapsed.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts teach that the wise prepare beforehand, so the storm does not bring them down.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah. And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow — and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an calls believers to look ahead to 'tomorrow' (the Hereafter) and prepare for it now.
islam.tie_back: Both texts urge guarding in advance against what is coming.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A prudent man seeth the evil, and hideth himself; but the thoughtless pass on, and are punished.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the prudent person, who sees trouble coming and takes cover, with the naive, who walk straight into it.
judaism.tie_back: This is nearly the same thought as the Kural: foresight plus precaution means calamity does not strike.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a border city is closely guarded both within and without, even so, guard yourself. Do not let slip this opportunity (for spiritual growth). For those who let slip this opportunity grieve when consigned to hell.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the image of a frontier city that guards itself before an attack comes. Those who fail to prepare later grieve.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts teach that guarding in advance prevents later suffering.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is careless in all respects, is in danger; he who is not careless in all respects, is free from danger.” … “Faithful according to the commandment (of the Tîrthakaras), wise, and understanding the world according to the commandment--such a man is without danger from anywhere.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga teaches that constant vigilance, together with wisdom and a true understanding of the world, leaves a person without danger from any quarter; carelessness is what exposes one to danger.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar promises that no calamity will shake those who guard in advance against what is coming; the Acaranga likewise says the vigilant and wise man is 'without danger from anywhere.'
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.3.4.1, I.3.4.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The hot wind does not even touch one who is under the Protection of the Supreme Lord God.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Bilaaval Guru Arjan says that one who takes refuge in God is not even touched by the scorching wind of affliction.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says no calamity can make the wise tremble, because they guard against it in advance; Guru Arjan says affliction cannot even touch one sheltered in God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 819, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Forewarned by Circe about the Sirens, Odysseus prepares before reaching them. He seals his crew's ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast, so the ship passes unharmed where others have perished.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus turns foreknowledge into precaution and faces a lethal danger without being destroyed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's claim: guard against what is ahead, and it will not strike you down.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca urges his friend Lucilius to anticipate every misfortune (exile, loss, disaster) in advance. Nothing should be unexpected, and what has been foreseen strikes more lightly.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic practice of premeditatio malorum rehearses possible calamities so that, when they come, they do not overwhelm.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's 'no affliction comes to make them tremble': prepared minds are not shaken.

real_life_example.event_title: Amundsen's carefully prepared journey to the South Pole
real_life_example.place: Framheim, Ross Ice Shelf, and the South Pole, Antarctica
real_life_example.event: Roald Amundsen's Norwegian expedition prepared every detail at its base, Framheim, on the Ross Ice Shelf: before winter it laid about 3,000 kilograms of supplies in depots at 80, 81 and 82 degrees south, and over the winter it lightened its sledges and readied equipment, relying on Greenland dogs and expert skiers. After a first start in September 1911 was abandoned as too early in the season, Amundsen and four companions set out in October, reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911, and returned to Framheim in late January 1912 after about 99 days and some 3,000 kilometres, with all five men safe.
real_life_example.explanation: The expedition is a classic example of how meticulous preparation can make one of the most dangerous journeys on earth succeed without loss of life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says no calamity comes to make the wise tremble when they guard in advance against what lies ahead, and Amundsen's depots, equipment and planning meant the polar journey never caught his party unprepared.

tamil:
அறிவுடையார் எல்லா முடையார் அறிவிலார்
என்னுடைய ரேனும் இலர்.
transliteration:
Arivudaiyaar ellaa mudaiyaar arivilaar
Ennudaiya renum ilar.
meaning: People who have wisdom have everything. People without wisdom have nothing, whatever else they own.
elementary: Imagine someone with a huge pile of money but no sense. They would probably lose it all or use it badly. Someone with good sense can build up whatever they need. Valluvar says good sense is the one thing that counts as having everything.
university: The chapter ends with a sweeping summary built on the verb உடைமை (possession) that gives the chapter its title. அறிவுடையார் எல்லாம் உடையார் means 'the possessors of wisdom are possessors of all'. என்னுடையரேனும் இலர் means 'whatever they possess, they have nothing'. The point is that wisdom is the meta-possession that makes other possessions useful and secure. Without it, wealth, power, and allies are squandered or turned against their holder. It is striking that this appears in Porutpal, the book on wealth and statecraft: Valluvar ranks arivu above porul (wealth) itself. The Talmud's 'if you have acquired knowledge, what do you lack?' and Socrates's argument in the Euthydemus that wisdom is the only unconditional good are close parallels. Solomon's story, in which he chooses wisdom and receives everything else too, dramatises the same claim.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In this world, there is nothing so sublime and pure as transcendental knowledge. Such knowledge is the mature fruit of all mysticism.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna declares that nothing in the world equals knowledge (jnana) in worth or purifying power.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts rank wisdom above every other possession.

christianity.quote_or_event: When Solomon asks God only for “an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad”, God grants it and adds: “I have also given thee that which thou hast not asked, both riches, and honour.”
christianity.explanation: Solomon chooses discernment over wealth, long life, or victory, and receives the rest as well.
christianity.tie_back: This dramatises the Kural: the one who has wisdom has everything.

islam.quote_or_event: “He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever has been given wisdom has certainly been given much good. And none will remember except those of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an calls hikmah (wisdom) a gift containing 'much good' (khayran kathiran).
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat wisdom as the possession that brings abundant good.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud cites a popular saying: if one has acquired knowledge (da'at), what does he lack? If one lacks knowledge, what has he acquired?
judaism.explanation: The rabbis hold that knowledge is the possession that makes every other possession worthwhile, and without it nothing else counts.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural in both halves, with an almost identical structure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better it is to live one day wise and meditative than to live a hundred years foolish and uncontrolled.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada holds that a single day of wisdom outweighs a century of foolish life.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see wisdom as making a life full and its absence as making everything else worthless.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who knows one thing, knows all things; and he who knows all things, knows one thing.”
jainism.explanation: Jacobi's note explains that true knowledge of any one thing cannot be separated from true knowledge of everything. In Jain thought the soul's own nature is knowledge, which reaches its completion in omniscience (kevala-jñāna).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who have wisdom have everything; the Acaranga makes a parallel claim about knowledge itself: whoever truly has it has, in principle, all of it.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.3.4.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, those who do not think of the Guru, and who think of themselves as clever, shall be left abandoned in the field, like the scattered sesame.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak says the self-satisfied who ignore the Guru are like hollow sesame plants left behind in an empty field.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those without wisdom have nothing, whatever else they own; Guru Nanak says those without the Guru's wisdom, however clever they think themselves, are left empty and abandoned.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Zeus swallows Metis, the goddess of wisdom and counsel, so that her wisdom becomes his own. Only then is his rule secure, and Athena is later born from his head.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod, Zeus's supreme and lasting kingship depends on possessing wisdom within himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mythically parallels the Kural: possessing wisdom secures possession of all.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that wealth, health, beauty, and power are neither good nor bad in themselves. Guided by wisdom they become great goods, and guided by ignorance great evils. He concludes that wisdom is the only good and ignorance the only evil.
philosophy.explanation: In this dialogue with young Clinias, Socrates shows that all other possessions depend on wisdom for their value.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's logic exactly: with wisdom one has everything, and without it one has nothing, whatever one owns.

real_life_example.event_title: Japan's Charter Oath pledges to seek knowledge throughout the world
real_life_example.event: Shortly after the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate, the new government issued the Charter Oath in the name of the young Emperor Meiji, a five-article statement of the principles of the new regime. Its final article pledged that knowledge would be sought throughout the world to strengthen the foundations of imperial rule. The pledge became a guiding principle of the Meiji reforms, under which Japan studied and adopted foreign learning in many fields.
real_life_example.explanation: Japan's new leaders treated knowledge itself, rather than any single material resource, as the foundation on which national strength would be built.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who possess wisdom possess everything, and the Charter Oath made the pursuit of knowledge the basis of a whole nation's future.

tamil:
செருக்குஞ் சினமும் சிறுமையும் இல்லார்
பெருக்கம் பெருமித நீர்த்து.
transliteration:
Serukkunj chinamum sirumaiyum illaar
Perukkam perumitha neerththu.
meaning: People who are free from pride, anger and mean, petty ways will grow in success, and that success will be truly honored.
elementary: Some people get rich and then turn bossy, angry, and greedy for low pleasures. This kural says that when someone does well in life but stays humble, calm, and clean-minded, their success is the kind people truly respect.
university: The chapter opens by naming three faults (குற்றம்) a ruler must purge: செருக்கு (arrogance, the swelling of self that success breeds), சினம் (anger), and சிறுமை (literally ‘smallness’; Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss it as காமம், base lust or petty desire). The claim is conditional and political: பெருக்கம் (increase, prosperity) only becomes பெருமிதம் (dignity, honourable greatness) when these three are absent. Wealth and power are morally neutral amplifiers; what they amplify is character. The triadic diagnosis of pride, anger and desire as the roots of ruin is one of the most widely shared moral analyses across ancient traditions, from the Gita’s ‘demoniac’ qualities to the Mishnah’s list of things that ‘put a man out of the world’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Bewildered by false ego, strength, pride, lust and anger, the demons become envious of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is situated in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, and blaspheme against the real religion.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes how people with power and strength are knocked off balance by ego, pride, lust and anger, and turn against what is good.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita and the Kural name nearly the same cluster of faults (pride, lust, anger) as what corrupts the strong; the Kural states the positive side: strength without them is honourable.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.”
christianity.explanation: John names desire and pride as the marks of a worldly life that pulls a person away from God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts single out desire and pride as the faults that spoil a life; the Kural adds anger and applies it to prosperous rulers.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allah] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Quran praises those who stay generous in good and bad times and who hold back their anger and forgive.
islam.tie_back: Restraining anger while prospering is exactly what the Kural says makes success dignified.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: A rabbi of the Mishnah lists three inner drives that drive a person out of a good life.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Mishnah diagnoses character through a triad of faults; lust and craving for honour (a form of arrogance) overlap directly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One should give up anger, renounce pride, and overcome all fetters. Suffering never befalls him who clings not to mind and body and is detached.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches letting go of anger and pride, and cutting the fetters of craving, so that suffering no longer takes hold.
buddhism.tie_back: The same three faults, anger, pride and craving, are named as what must be dropped; the Kural says the reward is dignified prosperity, the Dhammapada says freedom from suffering.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He will sink through anger; he will go down through pride; delusion will block up his path; through greed he will incur dangers in both worlds.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami, renouncing his throne, names the passions (kashāyas) that ruin a person: anger, pride, delusion and greed. Indra then praises him for having conquered each of them.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says only those free of arrogance, anger and base desire turn prosperity into true dignity; Nami, a king himself, names the same cluster of faults as the cause of a person's fall.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.54 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Unfulfilled sexual desire and unresolved anger waste the body away, as gold is dissolved by borax.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Dakhanee Oankaar Guru Nanak names lust (kaam) and anger (krodh), two of the five thieves, as forces that quietly wear a person down from within, as borax melts gold.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says prosperity has dignity only when it is free of lust, anger and arrogance; Guru Nanak shows the same faults eating away at the person who harbours them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 932, Raag Raamkalee (Dakhanee Oankaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Niobe, queen of Thebes, rich in wealth and fourteen children, boasts that she is greater than the goddess Leto and forbids her worship; Apollo and Artemis kill her children and she is turned to weeping stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: A queen with everything turns arrogant about her good fortune, and her pride destroys all she has.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The negative image of the Kural: prosperity joined to arrogance loses its dignity and ends in ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato divides the soul into reason, spirit (the seat of anger) and appetite (desire), and argues that a person, like a city, is just and well-ordered only when reason governs spirit and appetite.
philosophy.explanation: Plato thinks a good life needs your thinking mind in charge of your temper and your cravings.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s absence of anger and base desire is what Plato calls the rule of reason over spirit and appetite; both link inner order to worthy public standing.

real_life_example.event_title: Louis IX hears his subjects' cases himself at Vincennes
real_life_example.event: King Louis IX of France often administered justice in person, and his companion and biographer Jean de Joinville recorded that at Vincennes, after Mass, the king would sit in the open and let anyone with a dispute approach him directly, without ushers in the way. From 1247 he sent out commissions of inquiry to hear complaints against his own royal officials. His reputation for fairness was so great that foreign rulers asked him to arbitrate their disputes, and he was canonised in 1297.
real_life_example.explanation: Louis IX's power and wealth were remembered not as a cause for fear but as a source of honour, because he used them with restraint and approachability.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says prosperity has real dignity only when free of arrogance, anger and base desire, and Louis IX's open, patient justice gave his greatness that dignity.

tamil:
இவறலும் மாண்பிறந்த மானமும் மாணா
உவகையும் ஏதம் இறைக்கு.
transliteration:
Ivaralum maanbirandha maanamum maanaa
Uvakaiyum yedham iraikku.
meaning: Being stingy, having pride about the wrong things, and taking joy in unworthy things are faults that harm a ruler.
elementary: A leader should not be stingy, should not be proud about the wrong things, and should not enjoy things that are low or harmful. This kural says those three habits are dangers for anyone in charge.
university: Valluvar adds a second triad specific to kingship (இறை, ‘the ruler’): இவறல் (miserliness, refusing to give what should be given), மாண்பு இறந்த மானம் (a sense of honour that has ‘died to excellence’, i.e. touchy pride over the wrong things; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as refusing to bow to the worthy out of pride of office), and மாணா உவகை (joy in what is unworthy). ஏதம் means harm or fault. Each is a perversion of a legitimate royal trait: prudence with wealth decays into avarice, dignity into vanity, and a king’s pleasures into indulgence. Miserliness returns in Kurals 437 and 438 as the gravest of all faults, so this couplet frames the chapter’s political core: a ruler’s private vices become public dangers.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Pride, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance – these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the traits of the ‘demoniac’ character, with pride and conceit at the head.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘pride that has lost all worth’ is the Gita’s pride, arrogance and conceit, marked as a fault of character.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists the qualities a church leader must have: not given to drink, not violent, not greedy for money.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts set out the disqualifying faults of a leader, and both put love of money and self-indulgent pleasure among them.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Qārūn was from the people of Moses, but he tyrannized them. And We gave him of treasures whose keys would burden a band of strong men; thereupon his people said to him, "Do not exult. Indeed, Allāh does not like the exultant.”
islam.explanation: Qarun (Korah) was given enormous wealth, grew arrogant and oppressive, and gloated over his riches; his people warned him against this boastful delight.
islam.tie_back: Qarun embodies all three faults of the Kural: hoarded wealth, arrogant pride and unworthy exultation, and his story ends in ruin (28:81).

judaism.quote_or_event: “Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away: neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah’s law of the king forbids him to pile up wives and wealth for himself, and (17:20) warns ‘that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren’.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Torah names the specific faults that endanger a ruler: self-serving wealth, indulgence and a heart lifted up in pride.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The ‘ten royal virtues’ (dasa-rājadhamma) listed in the Jātaka commentary begin with dāna (generosity) and include maddava (gentleness, freedom from haughtiness), tapa (self-restraint in pleasures) and akkodha (non-anger).
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist tradition teaches that a good king must be generous, gentle rather than proud, and restrained in his pleasures.
buddhism.tie_back: Each of the Kural’s three royal faults is the opposite of one of these virtues: avarice versus generosity, false pride versus gentleness, unworthy joy versus restraint.
buddhism.source: Dasa-rājadhamma, Jātaka commentary (e.g. Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka, J 534)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
jainism.explanation: This verse from the Saman Suttam anthology sets out what each of the four passions destroys, and singles out greed as the one that ruins everything.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar names avarice and false pride among the faults that harm a ruler; the Jain verse likewise picks out greed and pride as destroyers, with greed the most sweeping of all.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam 135 (English tr., jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Ego is a chronic disease, but it contains its own cure as well.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Angad calls haumai (ego) a long-lasting disease of the self, yet one that can be cured through the Guru's grace and the Shabad.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural lists misplaced pride among the faults that harm a ruler; Guru Angad treats that same self-swelling as a chronic sickness that must be treated, not indulged.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Croesus of Lydia shows the Athenian sage Solon his treasuries and waits to be called the happiest of men; Solon refuses to call anyone happy before seeing his end, and Croesus later loses his kingdom to Cyrus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A rich king delights in his wealth and his own greatness, ignores a wise warning, and falls.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus shows the Kural’s danger: a ruler’s pride in wealth and misplaced delight in fortune blind him to ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato has Socrates decree that the city’s guardians must own no private property and may not touch or possess gold and silver, so that greed does not turn them from guardians into tyrants.
philosophy.explanation: Plato thought rulers should be kept away from private riches because love of money ruins people in power.
philosophy.tie_back: Both Plato and the Kural treat the ruler’s relationship to wealth as a question of character that decides whether rule helps or harms.

real_life_example.event_title: King Farouk of Egypt is forced to abdicate
real_life_example.event: King Farouk, who came to the throne of Egypt in 1936, became known for a self-indulgent lifestyle, lavish spending and expensive shopping trips abroad, while the army was angered by defeat in the 1948 war and by reports that the king's associates had profited from supplying faulty weapons. On 23 July 1952 the Free Officers, led by Muhammad Naguib and Gamal Abdel Nasser, seized power. Surrounded at Ras el-Tin palace in Alexandria, Farouk abdicated on 26 July in favour of his infant son and sailed into exile; the monarchy was abolished the following year.
real_life_example.explanation: Farouk's personal excesses steadily destroyed the loyalty and respect on which his throne rested.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that avarice, false pride and delight in unworthy things are the faults that harm a ruler, and Farouk's indulgence cost him his crown.

tamil:
தினைத்துணையாங் குற்றம் வரினும் பனைத்துணையாக்
கொள்வர் பழிநாணு வார்.
transliteration:
Thinaiththunaiyaang kutram varinum panaiththunaiyaak
Kolvar pazhinaanu vaar.
meaning: People who are afraid of being blamed treat even a fault as small as a millet seed as if it were as big as a palmyra palm (a very tall tree).
elementary: A millet seed is tiny, and a palm tree is huge. People who really care about doing right treat even a tiny mistake as if it were a giant one, so they fix it straight away instead of letting it grow.
university: The couplet turns on a vivid scale contrast between தினை (foxtail millet, among the smallest grains) and பனை (the palmyra palm, among the tallest trees). பழிநாணுவார், ‘those who are ashamed before blame’, are defined not by having no faults but by how they perceive them: they magnify their own errors in their own eyes. This is a moral psychology of vigilance. Shame (நாண்) works here as a protective faculty, the Tamil counterpart of Greek aidōs, that makes a small lapse feel intolerable before it can grow. The commentators divide on whether the sense is ‘they grieve over it as if it were huge’ (Puliyur Kesikan) or ‘they guard against it as if it were huge’ (Varadarasan, Karunanidhi); both readings share the principle of disproportionate self-scrutiny.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reminds Arjuna that, for someone of honour, a disgraced name is harder to bear than death.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘those who dread disgrace’ are exactly the people for whom, as the Gita says, dishonour weighs more than death, which is why they treat even small faults as huge.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that how someone handles very small things reveals how they will handle big ones.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts refuse to treat small faults as trivial; the millet-sized fault matters because character is built on the least things.

islam.quote_or_event: “A believer sees his sins as if he were sitting under a mountain which, he is afraid, may fall on him; whereas the wicked person considers his sins as flies passing over his nose and he just drives them away like this.”
islam.explanation: Ibn Mas‘ud contrasts the believer, who feels even his sins as a mountain about to fall, with the wicked person, who brushes them off like flies.
islam.tie_back: Almost the same image as the Kural: the conscientious person sees a small fault as a mountain (palmyra) rather than as something tiny (millet, a fly).

judaism.quote_or_event: “And be careful with a light commandment as with a grave one, for you did know not the reward for the fulfillment of the commandments.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince teaches that small duties deserve as much care as big ones, since we cannot know their true weight.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘treat the small as great’ is the Mishnah’s ‘be as careful with the light as with the grave’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Think not lightly of evil, saying, 'It will not come to me.' Drop by drop is the water pot filled. Likewise, the fool, gathering it little by little, fills himself with evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that small wrongdoings, repeated, fill a person with evil just as drops of water fill a pot.
buddhism.tie_back: Both say that no fault is small enough to ignore; the wise person, like the Kural’s shame-sensitive person, treats the drop as seriously as the flood.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One should not be complacent with a small debt, slight wound, spark of fire and slight passion, because what is small (today) may become bigger (later).”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching treats even a slight stirring of passion (kashāya) as dangerous, comparing it to a small debt, wound or spark that grows if neglected.
jainism.tie_back: Those who dread disgrace, says Valluvar, treat a millet-sized fault as if it were as large as a palmyra; the Jain verse gives the same reason for refusing to belittle a small fault: what is small today grows large tomorrow.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam 134 (English tr., jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, I am the worst of all. Everyone else is good.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir models a humility that looks hard at one's own failings and refuses to rank oneself above anyone else.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises those who see a millet-sized fault in themselves as large as a palmyra; Kabir's self-judgement magnifies his own faults in the same spirit.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1364, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes how, in the degenerate Iron Age, Aidōs (Shame) and Nemesis (Righteous Indignation) will abandon humankind and depart to the gods, leaving no defence against evil.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, Shame is a goddess, and when she leaves the human world, people lose what kept them from wrongdoing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s பழிநாணுவார் are those in whom Aidōs still lives: their sense of shame is the faculty that makes even small faults feel large.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Shame should not be described as a virtue; for it is more like a feeling than a state of character. It is defined, at any rate, as a kind of fear of dishonour...”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle analyses shame as a fear of disgrace that restrains people, especially the young, from doing wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘those who dread disgrace’ are defined by exactly this fear of dishonour, which drives them to magnify their own faults.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.9 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Hugh Dalton resigns over a budget leak
real_life_example.place: Palace of Westminster, London, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: On his way into the House of Commons to deliver his budget, Chancellor of the Exchequer Hugh Dalton stopped to talk with a lobby journalist and mentioned some of his tax plans. The journalist's evening paper printed them shortly before Dalton reached that part of his speech. Although the slip was brief and had little practical effect, Dalton apologised to the House and offered his resignation, which Prime Minister Clement Attlee accepted the next day.
real_life_example.explanation: Dalton treated a small indiscretion as a grave breach of his duty to Parliament and gave up one of the highest offices in government because of it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who dread disgrace treat a fault as small as a millet seed as if it were as tall as a palmyra palm, and Dalton resigned over a few leaked lines.

tamil:
குற்றமே காக்க பொருளாகக் குற்றமே
அற்றந் தரூஉம் பகை.
transliteration:
Kutrame kaakka porulaakak kutrame
Atran tharooum pakai.
meaning: Make guarding against faults your main goal, because faults are the very enemy that brings ruin.
elementary: We often worry about enemies outside us. This kural says the most dangerous enemy is a bad habit or mistake inside ourselves, because that is what can truly destroy us. So guarding against our own faults should be our main job.
university: The repetition of குற்றமே (‘fault itself’) in both lines is emphatic: the ēkāram singles out fault, not external foes, as the true enemy. பொருளாக can be read as ‘as the essential aim’ or, with a pun on பொருள் (wealth, the theme of the whole Porutpāl), ‘as though it were your treasure’: guarding against faults is to be protected like wealth. அற்றம் means ruin or destruction, and தரூஉம் is the prolonged (alapedai) form of தரும், ‘that which brings’. (The two digitised editions consulted print ‘த்ரூஉம்’, a typographical slip for தரூஉம்.) The political reading (Solomon Pappaiah) is that a state is destroyed less by invading armies than by the ruler’s own moral failings, which is the governing thesis of this chapter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that the real enemy is not outside him but the desire and anger within.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural and the Gita both locate the decisive enemy inside the self; the Kural calls it fault, the Gita names lust turning into wrath.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.”
christianity.explanation: God warns Cain that sin is crouching at his door like a predator, and that he must master it.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts picture wrongdoing as an enemy lying in wait, and both command vigilant guarding against it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And I do not acquit myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: In the story of Joseph, the speaker admits that his own soul constantly urges him toward evil, and only God’s mercy protects him.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s enemy within is the Quran’s nafs that ‘persistently enjoins evil’; both demand watchfulness over oneself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So too the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Israel: My children, I created an evil inclination, which is the wound, and I created Torah as its antidote.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud describes the evil inclination as a wound inside each person, and Torah study as the bandage that keeps it from festering; it cites Genesis 4:7, ‘Sin crouches at the door’.
judaism.tie_back: The yetzer hara is the Kural’s inner enemy, and the constant remedy of Torah is the constant guarding the Kural commands.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever harm an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater, an ill-directed mind inflicts on oneself a greater harm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that no external enemy can hurt you as badly as your own badly directed mind.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s claim: one’s own fault is a worse enemy than any outside foe.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Self is the one invincible foe, (together with the four) cardinal passions, (viz. anger, pride, deceit, and greed, they are five) and the (five) senses (make ten). These (foes), O great sage, I have regularly vanquished.”
jainism.explanation: Asked who the thousand foes attacking him are, Gautama answers that the real enemies are within: the unsubdued self, the four passions and the five senses.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar insists that it is fault itself that is the enemy bringing ruin; Gautama likewise locates the true enemy in one's own faults rather than in any outside attacker.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Within this body dwell the five thieves: sexual desire, anger, greed, emotional attachment and egotism.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that the real robbers are not outside but within: the five vices that plunder the treasure of the Naam.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says fault itself is the enemy that brings ruin and must be guarded against; Sikh teaching likewise locates the true enemy in the five thieves inside the self.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 600, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon, reconciling with Achilles, says his ruinous insult was the work of Atē, the goddess of blind folly, who walks on men’s heads and brings them to harm.
greek_mythology.explanation: Agamemnon admits a fault of his own nearly destroyed the Greek army, and describes it as a goddess of ruin that seized him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Iliad personifies fault as a destroying power, as the Kural calls fault an enemy that brings ruin; Agamemnon’s near-defeat came from his own error, not from Troy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...know this of a truth - that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.”
philosophy.explanation: Facing execution, Socrates insists that nothing outside can truly harm a good person.
philosophy.tie_back: If no outside evil can ruin the good, then, as the Kural says, the only real enemy is one’s own fault.

real_life_example.event_title: Sakichi Toyoda builds looms that stop themselves at the first fault
real_life_example.event: In 1896 the inventor Sakichi Toyoda produced a power loom with a device that automatically stopped the machine when a weft thread broke, so that it would not go on weaving defective cloth. His Type G automatic loom of 1924 included stopping devices for broken warp or weft threads among its many automatic mechanisms. Toyota later named this principle jidoka, stopping immediately when an abnormality is detected, and made it one of the two pillars of the Toyota Production System.
real_life_example.explanation: Toyoda's idea was that a fault caught at once costs little, while a fault left running multiplies into waste, and the principle became central to modern quality control.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural tells us to make guarding against faults our chief aim because fault itself is the enemy, and Toyoda built that vigilance into the very machine.

tamil:
வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான் வாழ்க்கை எரிமுன்னர்
வைத்தூறு போலக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Varumunnark kaavaathaan vaazhkkai erimunnar
Vaiththooru polak kedum.
meaning: A person who does not guard against faults before they come will see their life destroyed, like a pile of straw in front of a fire.
elementary: Dry straw near a fire catches in a flash. This kural says that if you don’t protect yourself from mistakes before they happen, your life can go up in flames just as quickly.
university: The couplet is built on a pointed parallel of two முன்னர் (‘before’): வருமுன்னர் (before [the fault] comes) and எரிமுன்னர் (before the fire). Failure to act in the first ‘before’ puts one in the second. வைத்தூறு is a stack of straw (வைக்கோல் போர்), the most combustible of village materials, so the image stresses how sudden and total the ruin is once prevention has failed. This is the chapter’s case for preventive rather than corrective vigilance: once a fault has taken hold, correction may already be too late. The same principle appears in Valluvar’s wider political thought on foresight (compare Kural 442 in the next chapter, which praises counsellors who guard against troubles before they arrive).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra fable of the three fish, Anāgatavidhātā (‘Forethought’) leaves the pond as soon as he hears fishermen plan to return, Pratyutpannamati (‘Ready-wit’) escapes by a trick, and Yadbhaviṣya (‘Whatever-will-be’) waits and is caught.
hinduism.explanation: Three fish hear danger coming; only the one who acts before it arrives is fully safe, and the one who waits is destroyed.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘guard before it comes’ is the lesson of Anāgatavidhātā; the fish who waits is the straw before the fire.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book I (fable of the three fish)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the prudent, who see trouble coming and take cover, with the simple, who walk on into it.
christianity.tie_back: Same contrast as the Kural: guarding in advance saves you, carelessness leads to ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allāh. And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow - and fear Allāh. Indeed, Allāh is Aware of what you do.”
islam.explanation: The Quran urges each person to look ahead and consider what their deeds are preparing for the future.
islam.tie_back: Both call for looking ahead at the consequences of one’s conduct before it is too late; this verse is a classic basis for muhāsaba (self-accounting).

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is the wise person? The one who sees and anticipates the consequences of his behavior.”
judaism.explanation: The sages, answering Alexander the Great, define wisdom as foreseeing where one’s actions will lead.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s person who ‘guards before it comes’ is the Talmud’s wise one who sees what is coming from his conduct.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a border city is closely guarded both within and without, even so, guard yourself. Do not let slip this opportunity (for spiritual growth). For those who let slip this opportunity grieve indeed when consigned to hell.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells monks to guard themselves like a frontier town, because those who waste their chance come to grief.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts call for guarding oneself before the danger strikes, and both warn of irreversible ruin for those who neglect it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As in a forest, full of fuel, a fire fanned by the wind cannot be extinguished, so the fire (as it were) of the senses of him who eats as he lists; it does not benefit any chaste man.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on carelessness warns that once indulgence feeds the senses, their fire spreads like a wind-fanned forest blaze that can no longer be put out, so restraint must come first.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's life that fails to guard against faults before they come burns like a straw stack before a fire; the Jain image is the same, ready fuel and a fire that cannot be stopped once it catches.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The self-willed manmukh has forgotten the Naam. He is like straw, burning in the forest fire.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak compares the person who lives by his own will and forgets the divine Name to dry straw consumed by a forest fire.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that one who does not guard against faults beforehand perishes like a heap of straw before fire; Guru Nanak uses the same image of straw in fire for the unguarded, self-willed life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 63, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And Epimetheus did not think on what Prometheus had said to him, bidding him never take a gift of Olympian Zeus... But he took the gift, and afterwards, when the evil thing was already his, he understood.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Epimetheus (‘Afterthought’) ignores his brother Prometheus (‘Forethought’), accepts Pandora, and understands the danger only after the evils are loose.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Epimetheus is the Kural’s man who does not guard ‘before it comes’; understanding after the fact cannot put the fire out.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The best plan is to reject straightway the first incentives to anger, to resist its very beginnings, and to take care not to be betrayed into it: for if once it begins to carry us away, it is hard to get back again into a healthy condition...”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that a passion must be stopped at its first stirring, because once it takes over, reason can no longer control it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural and Seneca share the logic of prevention: stop the fault before it enters, because once it catches, like fire in straw, it is too late.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira (On Anger) I.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: The Chernobyl reactor explodes during a safety test
real_life_example.place: Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant, near Pripyat, Soviet Union (now Ukraine)
real_life_example.event: Early on 26 April 1986, operators at Unit 4 of the Chernobyl plant were running a test, and a series of actions, including disabling automatic shutdown systems, left the reactor in an extremely unstable state. When they tried to shut it down, a design flaw in the control rods caused a sudden power surge, and explosions and fire destroyed the reactor and released large amounts of radioactive material. Later reviews named major design deficiencies, violations of operating procedures and the absence of a safety culture as causes, and many thousands of people had to leave their homes.
real_life_example.explanation: Known weaknesses and lax procedures, left uncorrected beforehand, turned a routine test into one of the worst industrial disasters in history within seconds.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that one who does not guard against faults before they arrive will be destroyed like a heap of straw before a fire, and Chernobyl's unaddressed flaws ended in literal fire.

tamil:
தன்குற்றம் நீக்கிப் பிறர்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்
என்குற்ற மாகும் இறைக்கு.
transliteration:
Thankutram neekkip pirarkutrang kaankirpin
Enkutra maakum iraikku.
meaning: If a ruler first fixes his own faults and only then looks at the faults of others, what fault could ever harm him?
elementary: It is easy to spot what others are doing wrong. This kural says a good leader first looks at and fixes their own mistakes, and only then points out other people’s. A leader who does that has nothing to be blamed for.
university: This is the chapter’s central statement of self-scrutiny and its logic is sequential: தன்குற்றம் நீக்கி (having removed one’s own fault) comes before பிறர்குற்றம் காண் (seeing others’ faults). The verb காண்கிற்பின் (‘if one is able to see’) implies that judging others rightly is a capacity earned by self-correction. The closing rhetorical question, என்குற்றம் ஆகும் இறைக்கு (‘what fault would there be for the king?’), expects the answer ‘none’. For a ruler whose office is to judge, this is the ethics of legitimate authority: the right to correct others rests on having corrected oneself. The couplet is the Tamil counterpart of the ‘mote and beam’ teaching and of the fable of the two wallets, but it is framed positively as a programme for governance rather than as a rebuke to hypocrisy.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Thou seest, O king, the fault of others, even though they be as small as a mustard seed. But seeing, thou noticest not thy own faults even though they be as large as the Vilwa fruit.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala rebukes King Dushyanta, who denies her, for spotting others’ tiny faults while missing his own huge ones.
hinduism.tie_back: Addressed, like the Kural, to a king; it condemns exactly what the Kural says a king must avoid: judging others before seeing one’s own faults.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section LXXIV (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his hearers to remove the plank in their own eye before trying to remove the speck in someone else’s.
christianity.tie_back: Identical order of operations: first remove your own fault, then you can rightly see and correct others’.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of you looks at the mote in his brother's eye while forgetting the stump in his own eye.”
islam.explanation: Abu Hurayra warns against people who notice a speck in a brother’s eye but forget the log in their own.
islam.tie_back: Same insight as the Kural: self-correction must precede correcting others. Elsewhere the Prophet calls the believer ‘the believer’s mirror’ (Abu Dawud 4918), mutual correction resting on sincerity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “...Reish Lakish says concerning this: Adorn [keshot] yourself and afterward adorn others.”
judaism.explanation: Reish Lakish teaches that you must correct your own conduct before requiring others to correct theirs; the Talmud applies it to a rabbi who first cut down his own trees before ruling that others must cut theirs.
judaism.tie_back: Same order as the Kural, and like the Kural it is applied to a person with authority to judge others.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 107b (also Bava Batra 60b)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one's own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another's faults, but hides one's own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that we broadcast others’ faults like chaff in the wind but hide our own, and (Dhp 253) that the fault-finder’s own defilements grow.
buddhism.tie_back: The Dhammapada describes the problem the Kural solves: because one’s own faults are hard to see, they must be looked for and removed first.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Fight with your Self; why fight with external foes? He who conquers himself through himself, will obtain happiness.”
jainism.explanation: When Indra urges King Nami to subdue the princes who do not acknowledge him, Nami answers that the battle that matters is against oneself, and that only self-conquest brings happiness.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells the ruler to remove his own faults before examining others'; Nami, also a king, likewise turns from the faults and hostility of others to the work of correcting himself.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, tells the wise to stop recording others' wrongs and to look first into their own conduct.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks the ruler to remove his own faults first and only then examine others'; Farid gives exactly this order of self-scrutiny before judging anyone else.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Jupiter has loaded us with a couple of Wallets: the one, filled with our own vices, he has placed at our backs, {the other}, heavy with those of others, he has hung before. From this circumstance, we are not able to see our own faults: but as soon as others make a slip, we are ready to censure.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable says Jupiter hung two bags on every person: others’ faults in front, where we always see them, and our own behind, where we never do.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Explains why the Kural must command the reversal: you have to turn the bag round and deal with your own faults before looking at others’.
greek_mythology.source: Phaedrus, Fables IV.10 (tr. H. T. Riley; Aesopic, Perry 266)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The spirit ought to be brought up for examination daily. It was the custom of Sextius when the day was over... to inquire of his spirit: "What bad habit of yours have you cured to-day? what vice have you checked? in what respect are you better?"”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca describes reviewing his whole day every night, judging himself and correcting his own faults before sleep.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca’s nightly tribunal is a practical method for the Kural’s first step: finding and removing one’s own faults.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira (On Anger) III.36 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: Pope John Paul II's Day of Pardon
real_life_example.event: On the first Sunday of Lent in the Jubilee year 2000, Pope John Paul II led a service in St Peter's Basilica in which senior cardinals and bishops confessed categories of sins committed by members of the Catholic Church over the centuries. These included divisions among Christians, the use of violence in the service of truth, hostility toward followers of other religions including Jews, and wrongs against women, the poor and minorities. After each confession the pope asked God's forgiveness.
real_life_example.explanation: The ceremony was an unprecedented public act by a major institution examining and confessing its own past faults before addressing those of others.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a ruler who first removes his own faults and only then examines others' will be free of fault, and the Day of Pardon began with the Church's own record.

tamil:
செயற்பால செய்யா திவறியான் செல்வம்
உயற்பால தன்றிக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Seyarpaala seyyaa thivariyaan selvam
Uyarpaala thandrik kedum.
meaning: The riches of a stingy person who does not use them for what they should be used for will not last. They will be lost without doing any good.
elementary: Money is meant to be used for good things: helping people, caring for family, doing what is right. This kural says that if someone just sits on their money out of stinginess, it ends up wasted and lost anyway.
university: செயற்பால (‘things that ought to be done’) are the proper uses of wealth, which Valluvar elsewhere lists as giving, enjoyment and public works; இவறியான் is the one who clings (from இவறு, to hoard or be miserly). உயற்பாலது அன்றி means ‘without the quality of surviving / being saved’: hoarded wealth has no future. The argument is not only moral but practical: wealth that is not put to use is exposed to theft, confiscation and decay, and so the miser loses both the good he could have done and the wealth itself. The couplet returns to இவறல் from Kural 432 and prepares for 438’s verdict that miserliness is the worst of all faults.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartṛhari teaches that wealth has only three possible fates: giving (dāna), enjoyment (bhoga) and destruction (nāśa); the one who neither gives nor enjoys is left with the third.
hinduism.explanation: A classical Sanskrit verse says money that is not given away or used will simply be destroyed.
hinduism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s argument: wealth not used for its proper ends ‘perishes without being saved’.
hinduism.source: Bhartṛhari, Nītiśataka (verse on the three fates of wealth, c. 43 in common editions)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten. Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as it were fire. Ye have heaped treasure together for the last days.”
christianity.explanation: James warns the hoarding rich that their piled-up wealth is rotting, and that its decay will testify against them.
christianity.tie_back: Both say hoarded wealth decays uselessly and turns against its owner.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who hoard gold and silver and spend it not in the way of Allāh - give them tidings of a painful punishment.”
islam.explanation: The Quran condemns those who pile up gold and silver without spending it for good.
islam.tie_back: Both condemn hoarding in place of using wealth for its proper purposes.
islam.source: Quran 9:34 (Sahih International, latter part of verse)

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt. But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes (Kohelet) describes wealth hoarded to its owner’s harm and then lost in a bad venture, leaving nothing even for his child.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s exact claim: wealth kept back instead of used ‘perishes’ without benefit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When his wealth isn't properly put to use, kings make off with it, or thieves make off with it, or fire burns it, or water sweeps it away, or hateful heirs make off with it. Thus his wealth, not properly put to use, goes to waste and not to any good use.”
buddhism.explanation: After a miserly millionaire dies childless and his fortune goes to the king’s treasury, the Buddha explains that unused wealth is like a pure pond no one drinks from.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s ‘not properly put to use, goes to waste’ is the Kural’s ‘perishes without being saved’.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 3.19, Aputtaka Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Or he heaps up treasures for the benefit of some spendthrifts, by pinching himself.” … “Then at one time, his manifold savings are a large treasure. Then at another time, his heirs divide it, or those who are without a living steal it, or the king takes it away, or it is ruined in some way or other, or it is consumed by the conflagration of the house.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga describes the man who starves himself to pile up wealth, only to have it divided by heirs, stolen, seized by the king, or burnt with his house, so that he gets no good from it.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the miser's wealth, never put to its proper use, will perish without benefit to anyone; the Acaranga lists the very ways in which hoarded wealth slips away.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.2.1.4 and I.2.3.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The bee stores up loads of honey; then someone comes and takes the honey, and throws dust in its mouth.” … “He takes the wealth of Maya, and buries it in the ground.” … “His wealth remains buried in the ground, while his body turns to dust.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Namdev describes the hoarder who toils for wealth and buries it, only to leave it in the ground at death, like the bee whose stored honey is taken by another.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the miser's wealth, never put to its proper use, perishes without benefit; Namdev's buried treasure and robbed honey make the same point.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1252, Raag Saarang, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asks Dionysus that all he touches turn to gold; his food and drink become gold, and he nearly starves amid riches until he begs to be freed from the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas gets endless gold but cannot use it for anything, not even to eat.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Midas pictures the Kural’s point that wealth not usable for life’s proper ends is worthless and ruinous.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The life of money-making is one undertaken under compulsion, and wealth is evidently not the good we are seeking; for it is merely useful and for the sake of something else.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that wealth has no value in itself; it is only worth what it is used for.
philosophy.tie_back: If wealth is only ‘useful for something else’, then the miser who never uses it, as the Kural says, has wealth that comes to nothing.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.5 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Nadir Shah carries off the Mughal treasury and the Peacock Throne
real_life_example.event: In 1739 the Persian ruler Nadir Shah defeated the larger army of the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah at Karnal and then entered Delhi. He took away the Mughal treasury and the jewelled Peacock Throne built for Shah Jahan, and the Koh-i-Noor diamond most likely formed part of the plunder. The loss left the Mughal treasury depleted and the empire greatly weakened.
real_life_example.explanation: Wealth that had been gathered and stored over generations did nothing to protect the empire and was lost to another in a matter of weeks.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the wealth of one who will not put it to its proper use does not endure but perishes without benefit, and the Mughal hoard passed to a foreign conqueror.

tamil:
பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை எற்றுள்ளும்
எண்ணப் படுவதொன் றன்று.
transliteration:
Patrullam ennum ivaranmai etrullum
Ennap paduvathon randru.
meaning: Stinginess, the greedy grip that holds on to everything, is not counted along with other faults. It stands apart as worse than all of them.
elementary: This kural says that stinginess, a heart that grabs and won’t let go, is not just one bad habit on a list. It is in a class of its own, worse than all the others.
university: பற்றுள்ளம் (‘a clinging heart’) defines இவறன்மை (miserliness) as a disposition of attachment, not merely an act of not giving. The phrase எற்றுள்ளும் எண்ணப்படுவது ஒன்று அன்று (‘it is not a thing to be counted among any [faults]’) is deliberately ambiguous: Mu. Varadarasan reads it as ‘a separate fault that cannot be counted along with others’, and Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi read it as ‘the most terrible of all faults’. Either way it is the chapter’s climax on avarice, which has now appeared three times (432, 437, 438). The ruler-centred reading matters: a stingy king starves the gifts, rewards and public works on which loyalty and prosperity depend, so his avarice spreads into every other failure.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names greed as one of the three gateways to hell that must be abandoned.
hinduism.tie_back: Both rank greed among the most destructive faults; the Kural goes further and sets it above all others.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul calls the love of money the root from which all kinds of evil grow.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul sets the grasping attachment to wealth apart from, and beneath, other evils.

islam.quote_or_event: “...be on your guard against stinginess for stinginess destroyed those who were before you, as it incited them to shed blood and make lawful what was unlawful for them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that stinginess (shuḥḥ) destroyed earlier peoples by driving them to bloodshed and lawbreaking.
islam.tie_back: Both treat miserliness not as a small failing but as a master-fault that leads to every other wrong.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are four types of character in human beings: One that says: ‘mine is mine, and yours is yours’: this is a commonplace type; and some say this is a sodom-type of character.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah notes that some sages see the attitude ‘what’s mine is mine’ as the character of Sodom, whose sin (Ezekiel 16:49) was not helping the poor.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see the refusal to share as worse than it looks: the Kural sets it apart from all faults, the Mishnah links it to Sodom.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says misers cannot reach heaven, while the wise find joy in giving.
buddhism.tie_back: Both single out miserliness as a fault with uniquely serious results.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If there were numberless mountains of gold and silver, as big as Kailâsa, they would not satisfy a greedy man; for his avidity is boundless like space.”
jainism.explanation: Refusing Indra's advice to fill his treasury, Nami answers that greed has no limit: no amount of wealth can ever satisfy a grasping heart.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar sets the clinging, miserly heart apart from every other fault; Nami likewise describes avarice as boundless, unlike any fault that can be measured or satisfied.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O mortal, why have you attached yourself to greed, and lost the jewel of life?”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir warns that clinging greed (lobh) squanders the priceless human birth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural sets the grasping, clinging heart of avarice apart as a fault beyond all others; Kabir likewise treats attachment to greed as the loss of life's single jewel.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 481, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon cuts down Demeter’s sacred oak for his own use; she curses him with insatiable hunger, so he consumes all his wealth, sells his daughter, and finally devours his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: A man who grabs for himself is cursed with a craving that can never be satisfied and destroys him completely.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Erysichthon dramatises the Kural’s ‘grasping heart’ as a fault that swallows everything else.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But meanness is both incurable (for old age and every disability is thought to make men mean) and more innate in men than prodigality... for not only is it a greater evil than prodigality, but men err more often in this direction...”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says stinginess is worse than wastefulness: it is incurable, more natural to people, and more common.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like the Kural, gives miserliness a special rank as the worse and more stubborn fault.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Galba refuses the soldiers' promised reward
real_life_example.event: Servius Sulpicius Galba became Roman emperor in 68 CE after the fall of Nero, and Suetonius describes his reputation for stinginess. He refused to pay the Praetorian Guard the donative, a cash reward, that had been promised in his name, and he passed over his ally Otho to name another man as his heir. Otho won the guard over with a promise of payment, and on 15 January 69 the praetorians killed Galba in the Roman Forum after a reign of about seven months.
real_life_example.explanation: Galba's tight grip on money turned the very soldiers who should have protected him into the instrument of his fall.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls a grasping heart a fault beyond all others, and Galba's refusal to part with what he owed undid every other strength he had as emperor.

tamil:
வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை நயவற்க
நன்றி பயவா வினை.
transliteration:
Viyavarka enjnaandrum thannai nayavarka
Nandri payavaa vinai.
meaning: Never, at any time, think too highly of yourself, and never want to do things that bring no good.
elementary: Being impressed with yourself makes you stop noticing your mistakes. This kural gives two simple rules: never be too proud of yourself, and don’t want to do things that don’t do any good.
university: Two prohibitions run in parallel: வியவற்க (do not wonder at, marvel at) with தன்னை (oneself), and நயவற்க (do not desire) with நன்றி பயவா வினை (deeds that yield no good). எஞ்ஞான்றும் (‘at any time’) makes the first absolute: even at the height of success, self-admiration is forbidden. The two are causally linked. Self-admiration blinds a person to their own faults, which undoes the self-scrutiny of Kural 436, and a self-admiring ruler is the one most easily drawn into vain, unprofitable projects. Solomon Pappaiah reads the second clause politically: a ruler should not want to do what does not benefit the country and its governance.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Humility; pridelessness; nonviolence; tolerance; simplicity; approaching a bona fide spiritual master...”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists humility and freedom from pride first among the qualities that make up true knowledge.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘never admire yourself’ is the Gita’s humility and pridelessness, placed at the head of the virtues.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs teaches that praise should come from others, never from yourself.
christianity.tie_back: Same prohibition as the Kural: never admire or praise yourself.

islam.quote_or_event: “So do not claim yourselves to be pure; He is most knowing of who fears Him.”
islam.explanation: The Quran forbids people to declare themselves pure or righteous, since only God truly knows who is God-fearing.
islam.tie_back: Both forbid self-admiration; the Quran grounds it in the fact that only God sees the heart.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If you have learned much Torah, do not claim credit for yourself, because for such a purpose were you created.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai teaches that even great learning is no reason to admire yourself; you have only done what you were made for.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘never, at any time’, it forbids self-admiration even when there is real achievement.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “'Let both laymen and monks think that it was done by me. In every work, great and small, let them follow me' — such is the ambition of the fool; thus his desire and pride increase.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the fool who wants credit and admiration for everything, so his pride and desire keep growing.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts warn that self-admiration feeds itself and spoils one’s aims; the fool’s wish for credit is the opposite of the Kural’s counsel.

jainism.quote_or_event: “'Frequently (I have been born) in a high family, frequently in a low one; I am not mean, nor noble, nor do I desire (social preferment).' Thus reflecting, who would brag about his family or about his glory, or for what should he long?”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga undercuts self-admiration by reminding the aspirant that across countless rebirths each soul has been both high and low, so pride in birth or glory has no ground.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar forbids admiring oneself at any time; the Acaranga gives a distinctly Jain reason for the same rule: through rebirth, every status one might boast of has already been held and lost many times.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.2.3.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself good — goodness shall not draw near him.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan teaches that self-praise is itself a mark of haumai, and that the person who proclaims his own goodness drives goodness away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural forbids admiring oneself at any time; Guru Arjan states that self-congratulation empties a person of the very virtue he claims.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Narcissus, who has scorned all who love him, falls in love with his own reflection in a pool and wastes away gazing at it, unable to turn from himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: A young man who admires only himself is destroyed by that self-admiration.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Narcissus is the extreme image of the Kural’s first warning: self-admiration leads to deeds that yield nothing and finally to ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The marks of a proficient are, that he censures no one, praises no one, blames no one, accuses no one, says nothing concerning himself as being anybody, or knowing anything: when he is, in any instance, hindered or restrained, he accuses himself...”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus says a person making real progress never talks about himself as important, and looks for fault in himself first.
philosophy.tie_back: Epictetus joins the Kural’s ban on self-admiration with the chapter’s central idea of self-accusation (Kural 436).

real_life_example.event_title: Bokassa crowns himself emperor
real_life_example.event: Jean-Bedel Bokassa, who had ruled the Central African Republic since 1966, renamed it the Central African Empire and in December 1977 crowned himself emperor in a lavish ceremony. The event cost more than 20 million dollars, financed largely by France, in one of the world's poorest countries. Bokassa was overthrown in September 1979 in a coup backed by France.
real_life_example.explanation: The coronation became a byword for a ruler's self-glorification at his people's expense, and it brought him ridicule rather than respect.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural forbids a ruler to admire himself or to desire deeds that bring no good, and Bokassa's coronation was both at once.

tamil:
காதல காதல் அறியாமை உய்க்கிற்பின்
ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்.
transliteration:
Kaadhala kaadhal ariyaamai uykkirpin
Edhila edhilaar nool.
meaning: If you can enjoy what you love without letting others know what you want, your enemies’ plans against you will fail.
elementary: If everyone knows exactly what you want most, people who wish you harm can use that to trick you. This kural says a wise leader keeps their wishes private, so enemies have nothing to use against them.
