university: The couplet uses doubled words for effect: காதல காதல் (‘the things one loves, [and] one’s love’) and ஏதில ஏதிலார் (‘come to nothing, [the plans of] strangers/enemies’). ஏதிலார் means those unrelated or hostile, and நூல் here means their ‘science’ or stratagems, the craft by which they plot. உய்க்கிற்பின் (‘if one is able to experience/carry out’) makes the condition discretion, not renunciation: the ruler may pursue his desires, but must not let them be known. The logic ties the chapter together. A known weakness or appetite is itself a fault (குற்றம்) in the strategic sense, a gap in the armour. By closing the chapter this way, Valluvar moves from moral self-correction to political self-guarding: the ruler must hide from enemies the very desires that could be used to exploit him.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya instructs that the king’s deliberations must be held in secret and guarded so that no outsider learns his plans; others should come to know of an undertaking only once it has begun or been completed.
hinduism.explanation: The ancient Indian manual of statecraft teaches that a king must keep his intentions secret so enemies cannot counter them.
hinduism.tie_back: Same political logic as the Kural: hidden intentions defeat enemies’ schemes.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book I, ch. 15 (tr. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the fool who says everything he thinks with the wise person who holds back.
christianity.tie_back: Both praise keeping one’s inner mind to oneself as a mark of wisdom.

islam.quote_or_event: A widely cited hadith (al-Tabarani) says: seek help in accomplishing your needs through keeping them concealed, for everyone who has a blessing is envied.
islam.explanation: The hadith advises keeping your plans and needs private because others may envy and work against them.
islam.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: concealing one’s desires protects them from those who would spoil them.
islam.source: Al-Tabarani, al-Mu‘jam al-Kabir (hadith on concealment of needs)

judaism.quote_or_event: “That he told her all his heart, and said unto her, There hath not come a razor upon mine head; for I have been a Nazarite unto God from my mother's womb: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me, and I shall become weak, and be like any other man.”
judaism.explanation: Samson finally tells Delilah the secret of his strength, and the Philistines use it to capture him.
judaism.tie_back: A negative example of the Kural: once his enemies know what he holds dearest, their scheme succeeds.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kumma Sutta, a tortoise draws its four legs and neck into its shell when a jackal approaches; the jackal waits for any limb to come out, finds no opening, and leaves. The Buddha tells monks to guard their senses the same way so that Māra finds no opening.
buddhism.explanation: By keeping everything tucked away, the tortoise gives its enemy nothing to seize.
buddhism.tie_back: Same strategy as the Kural: by keeping desires hidden and guarded, one gives the enemy no handle, and their schemes fail.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Just as an impassioned fish which is eager to swallow the bait, has its body transfixed by a hook.” … “Just as an impassioned elephant who is inflamed by carnal desires, is turned from his way by a female elephant (and is captured and at last killed in battle).”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on carelessness shows how each creature is trapped through its own known craving: the fish through its appetite for bait, the elephant through desire. Whoever knows the craving can use it to catch the creature.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar warns that desires known to enemies become the means of their schemes; the Jain similes show the same mechanism, though Jainism's remedy is to give up the craving, not to hide it.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.63, 32.89 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They are close to the Lord, but they do not reveal their secret to anyone.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid describes true devotees who keep their inner love for God private rather than displaying it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural advises enjoying what one loves without others knowing one's desires; Farid praises a similar reticence about one's deepest longing, though for spiritual rather than strategic reasons.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus escapes the Cyclops Polyphemus by calling himself ‘Nobody’; but as he sails away he boasts his real name, and Polyphemus uses it to call down Poseidon’s curse on him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hiding his identity saved Odysseus; revealing it gave his enemy what he needed to strike back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both sides of the Kural in one story: concealment defeats the enemy, and self-revelation lets the enemy’s plan succeed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon distinguishes secrecy, dissimulation and simulation, praising secrecy as a virtue that protects a person’s affairs, and advising openness in reputation but secrecy in habit.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon argues that a wise person keeps their inner intentions private, because revealing them exposes them to others.
philosophy.tie_back: Bacon’s ‘secrecy in habit’ is the Kural’s enjoying one’s desires without others knowing them.
philosophy.source: Francis Bacon, Essays, ‘Of Simulation and Dissimulation’

real_life_example.event_title: Henry Kissinger's secret journey to Beijing
real_life_example.event: During an official visit to Pakistan in July 1971, United States National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger let it be known that he was unwell and resting at a hill resort, while in fact he flew secretly from Pakistan to Beijing. There he held long talks with Premier Zhou Enlai to prepare a visit by President Richard Nixon. The trip stayed hidden until 15 July, when both governments announced Nixon's planned visit to China.
real_life_example.explanation: Because the American aim was kept from rivals and from the press until it was achieved, no one had the chance to obstruct the opening to China before it happened.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that if one can pursue what one desires without others knowing, the schemes of rivals come to nothing, and Kissinger's concealed journey achieved its goal unopposed.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tamil:
அறனறிந்து மூத்த அறிவுடையார் கேண்மை
திறனறிந்து தேர்ந்து கொளல்.
transliteration:
Aranarindhu mootha arivudaiyaar kenmai
Thiranarindhu therndhu kolal.
meaning: Think carefully and find the right way to win the friendship of older, wise people who know dharma (the right way to live).
elementary: Some people know what is right and have learned a lot from long experience. This kural says: find people like that, think carefully about who they really are, and then work to make them your friends and helpers.
university: The chapter opens by fixing three qualifications for the ‘great’ (periyar): they know aram (virtue/duty), they are ‘mootha’ (ripened, whether in age or in understanding), and they possess arivu (knowledge). The verb structure is significant: ‘thiran arindhu’ (knowing the method) and ‘therndhu’ (having examined) both precede ‘kolal’ (taking). Friendship with the wise is not an accident of proximity but a deliberate, tested acquisition — a theme Valluvar develops later in the chapters on friendship (79–83). Parimelazhagar notes that this counsel is addressed first to the king, for whom advisers are an instrument of rule, but it generalises readily to anyone: one’s judgment is only as good as the judgment of those one keeps close.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just try to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him submissively and render service unto him. The self-realized souls can impart knowledge unto you because they have seen the truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that real knowledge comes by deliberately approaching those who have already realized it, and by serving and questioning them with humility.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say wisdom is gained by consciously seeking out and cultivating those who are already wise — and both specify a method (‘thiran arindhu’ / humble inquiry and service).

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs teaches that we absorb the character of those we walk with: stay close to wise people and you grow wise; keep company with fools and you share their ruin.
christianity.tie_back: Same premise as the Kural — deliberately choosing wise companions is how one gains wisdom and safety.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of a good companion (who sits with you) in comparison with a bad one, is like that of the musk seller and the blacksmith’s bellows (or furnace); from the first you would either buy musk or enjoy its good smell while the bellows would either burn your clothes or your house, or you get a bad nasty smell thereof.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a good companion to a perfume seller — you benefit just by being near him — and a bad companion to a blacksmith’s furnace, which harms you even if you never touch it.
islam.tie_back: Implies the same discernment the Kural demands: choose one’s companions carefully, because their quality rubs off.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: Joshua ben Perahiah tells each person to actively make someone their teacher (asei lekha rav) and to acquire (k’neh) a companion — both are things you must go out and get.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘therndhu kolal’ (choose and take), the Mishnah treats a wise mentor as something one must deliberately acquire.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not to associate with the foolish, but to associate with the wise; and to honor those who are worthy of honor — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the Buddha’s list of the highest blessings, the very first is to avoid fools, keep company with the wise, and honor those who deserve honor.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s instruction to seek and honor the virtuous and wise as companions.
buddhism.source: Mangala Sutta (Khp 5 / Sn 2.4), tr. Narada Thera

jainism.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sûtras.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's discourse on the causes of carelessness names service of the gurus and the elders as the first step on the road to liberation, paired with avoiding fools.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks the king to weigh carefully and then win the friendship of those mature in wisdom and virtue. The Jain text likewise puts deliberate attachment to the old and learned at the head of the right path.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “How is the Society of the Saints to be known? There, the Name of the One Lord is chanted.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak gives a test for recognising true company (satsangat): it is the gathering where the One Name is praised.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells one to learn the right way, weigh carefully, and then win the friendship of the wise; Guru Nanak likewise gives a criterion for discerning which company is truly worth joining.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 72, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey Book 2, the goddess Athena takes the form and voice of Mentor, an old and trusted friend of Odysseus, to guide the young Telemachus as he sets out to act like a man and a prince.
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus succeeds because he accepts guidance from an elder of proven loyalty and wisdom — so famous an image that ‘mentor’ became the word for a wise guide.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the Kural’s ideal: a young ruler-to-be strengthened by an aged, virtuous and knowing counselor.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca advises Lucilius to be selective about company and to seek those whose influence raises one’s own character.
philosophy.tie_back: Same deliberate selection of improving companions that the Kural commends.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 7 (tr. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Liu Bei wins Zhuge Liang as his adviser
real_life_example.event: Liu Bei, at the time a minor warlord without a secure base, sought out the scholar Zhuge Liang, who was living in retirement at Longzhong, and persuaded him to enter his service as an adviser. Zhuge Liang helped him organise a large army, urged an alliance with Sun Quan that led to victory over Cao Cao at the Red Cliffs in 208, and helped him found the Shu-Han state in 221. On his deathbed Liu Bei urged his son to rely on Zhuge Liang's advice.
real_life_example.explanation: Liu Bei's rise from a wandering commander to an emperor rested heavily on the wise counsellor he had deliberately sought and kept.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises learning the right way to win, and then securing, the friendship of the wise and mature, and Liu Bei's pursuit of Zhuge Liang became the classic Chinese example of doing so.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tamil:
உற்றநோய் நீக்கி உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும்
பெற்றியார்ப் பேணிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Utranoi neekki uraaamai murkaakkum
Petriyaarp penik kolal.
meaning: Care for and keep close the people who can remove troubles that have already come and protect you from troubles still to come.
elementary: Some wise people can help you fix a problem you already have, and can also warn you about problems before they happen. This kural says: treat people like that with great care and keep them close.
university: ‘Noi’ literally means disease, but here it stands for any affliction — political, financial, or personal. The couplet distinguishes two functions of the wise counselor: the remedial (utra noi neekki, removing the affliction already suffered) and the preventive (uraamai murkaakkum, guarding beforehand against what has not yet arrived). The latter is the rarer gift, since it requires foresight. ‘Petriyaar’ denotes those who possess this capacity as a settled quality, and ‘penik kolal’ (cherishing and holding) implies that such people must be honored and maintained, not merely consulted when convenient.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata (Adi Parva), Vidura foresees Duryodhana’s plot to burn the Pandavas in the house of lac at Varanavata; he warns Yudhishthira in a coded message and secretly sends a miner to dig an escape tunnel.
hinduism.explanation: Vidura both anticipates a danger before it strikes and provides the means of escape when it arrives, so the Pandavas survive the fire.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura is exactly the Kural’s ‘petriyaar’: one who guards against harm before it comes and removes it when it does.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Jatugriha episode), tr. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Sirs, ye should have hearkened unto me, and not have loosed from Crete, and to have gained this harm and loss.”
christianity.explanation: Paul had warned the ship’s crew not to sail; ignored, they are caught in a storm. Paul then gives the counsel that saves everyone aboard.
christianity.tie_back: Paul functions first as a preventive counselor (ignored) and then as a remedial one (heeded) — the two roles the Kural names.

islam.quote_or_event: Before the Battle of the Trench (5 AH), the Prophet accepted the counsel of Salman al-Farsi to dig a defensive trench around Medina, a Persian tactic unknown to the Arabs; the besieging confederates could not break through.
islam.explanation: By heeding a knowledgeable companion, the Prophet protected the city from a danger before it arrived.
islam.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s ‘guarding in advance’ through valuing the counsel of a capable adviser.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (tr. A. Guillaume)

judaism.quote_or_event: Joseph interprets Pharaoh’s dreams and counsels him to store grain during seven years of plenty; Pharaoh appoints him over Egypt, and the land survives seven years of famine.
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s foresight lets Egypt prepare for a disaster before it arrives, and his administration carries it through when it does.
judaism.tie_back: Pharaoh ‘cherishes and holds’ the one who wards off disaster in advance — the exact wisdom of the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Sigala that a good-hearted friend who gives good counsel restrains one from doing evil, encourages one to do good, informs one of what one does not know, and points out the path to heaven.
buddhism.explanation: The true friend-counselor is defined by protecting you from wrong before it happens and guiding you toward good.
buddhism.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s protective, forward-looking adviser who must be valued.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As to one who has lost his way in the wood, others who have not, (show it, thus some) teach the path which is salutary to men. Therefore (he should think): this is for my good that those who know put me right.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga compares the person who has strayed to a traveller lost in a forest, and the wise to those who know the road and lead him back to safety.
jainism.tie_back: The kural praises counsellors who remove troubles that have already come and guard against those still to come. The Jain image shows the knowing guide rescuing a person already lost and setting him on a road that keeps him safe from then on.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.14.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, the five passions are brought to rest.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan lists the benefits of the Saadh Sangat, including bringing the five vices under control.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural values those who remove troubles that have come and guard against troubles to come; Guru Arjan presents holy company as the force that subdues the inner afflictions behind them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey 10, Hermes meets Odysseus on the way to Circe’s house, warns him of her drugs, and gives him the herb moly; Odysseus is protected from transformation and forces Circe to restore his men who had been turned into swine.
greek_mythology.explanation: The divine helper both forestalls the danger to Odysseus and enables the rescue of the men already afflicted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An exact dramatization of the Kural’s two functions: removing trouble that has come, preventing trouble yet to come.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle writes that friendship helps the young to keep from error, and aids older people by ministering to their needs and supplementing the activities that are failing from weakness.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, friends both prevent mistakes and make up for losses already suffered.
philosophy.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s protective and remedial roles of the worthy companion.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Koprulu Mehmed Pasha becomes Ottoman grand vizier
real_life_example.event: In 1656, after the Venetians defeated the Ottoman fleet at the Dardanelles and occupied nearby islands, the court of the young sultan Mehmed IV appointed the elderly provincial governor Koprulu Mehmed Pasha as grand vizier, on his condition that he be allowed to govern without interference. He suppressed rebellious governors and rivals, reorganised the army and rebuilt the fleet, which recovered islands lost to Venice in 1657. Members of his family held the office for much of the following half century, and historians credit the first two Koprulu viziers with a temporary revival of Ottoman power.
real_life_example.explanation: Entrusting the state to an able minister both ended an immediate crisis and laid foundations that protected the empire for decades.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural urges a ruler to cherish those who can remove troubles that have come and guard against those still to come, and Koprulu did both for the Ottoman throne.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tamil:
அரியவற்று ளெல்லாம் அரிதே பெரியாரைப்
பேணித் தமராக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Ariyavatru lellaam aridhe periyaaraip
Penith thamaraak kolal.
meaning: Of all rare things, the rarest is to respect great people and make them your own family.
elementary: Many things in life are hard to get. But this kural says the hardest and most precious thing of all is to have truly great people treat you like family, because you have honored and cared for them.
university: The superlative construction ‘ariyavatrul ellaam aridhe’ (rarest among all rare things) places the friendship of the great above wealth, armies, and territory, all of which are also ‘rare’ in the Porutpaal. The key word is ‘thamar’ — one’s own people, kin. Valluvar is not describing hiring an expert but transforming a great person into someone bound to you by affection and loyalty; ‘peni’ (having cherished) marks the reciprocity required. The rarity has two sources: the great are few, and they cannot be commanded — they must be won.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Satsaṅgatve nissaṅgatvaṁ, nissaṅgatve nirmohatvam; nirmohatve niścalatattvaṁ, niścalatattve jīvanmuktiḥ.”
hinduism.explanation: Shankara’s verse says that from the company of the good comes non-attachment, from that freedom from delusion, from that a steady mind, and from that liberation in this life.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat association with the good (satsang) as the rarest and most transformative possession, the root of every higher gain.
hinduism.source: Adi Shankara (attr.), Bhaja Govindam (Moha Mudgara), verse 9

christianity.quote_or_event: “A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says friendship must be cultivated by one’s own conduct, and that the best friend becomes closer than family.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘peni’ (cherishing) and ‘thamar’ (making them kin).

islam.quote_or_event: “And keep yourself patient [by being] with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His countenance.”
islam.explanation: God tells the Prophet to hold himself firmly among the devout and not turn his eyes away from them for worldly glamour.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it values keeping close to the virtuous above worldly advantages.

judaism.quote_or_event: Yose ben Yoezer taught that one’s house should be a meeting place for the sages, that one should sit in the dust of their feet and drink in their words thirstily.
judaism.explanation: Hosting and humbly attending the wise is treated as the way to fill one’s home with blessing.
judaism.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s ideal of honoring the great and drawing them into one’s own household circle (thamar).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie is actually the whole of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: When Ananda calls good friendship ‘half’ the holy life, the Buddha corrects him: it is the whole of it.
buddhism.tie_back: The most emphatic parallel to the Kural’s claim that such friendship is the rarest of all things.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If one can obtain the privilege of living always with men of good disposition in friendship, who constantly perform acts of virtue through a succession of births, though that succession is affliction, no one will despise it when they have considered the matter.”
jainism.explanation: This Tamil Jain quatrain says that the friendship of the virtuous is so precious that it would make even the round of rebirth, which Jainism counts as suffering, worth accepting.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls honouring the great and making them one's own the rarest of rare things. The Naladiyar values that same friendship above even release from the misery of rebirth.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone are relatives, and they alone are friends, who, as Gurmukh, join together in love.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das redefines kinship: one's true relatives and friends are those who live as Gurmukhs, turned towards the Guru, and meet in love.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls it the rarest of rare things to honour the great and make them one's own kin; Guru Amar Das likewise counts the God-oriented as one's real family.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 643, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey 3–4, Telemachus travels to Pylos and Sparta to seek out the aged Nestor and the king Menelaus, who receive him as a guest-friend and give him counsel and news of his father.
greek_mythology.explanation: The young prince must journey to win the counsel and friendship of great elders, and is received as if family.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Reflects the rarity and value of gaining great men as one’s own.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Cherish some man of high character, and keep him ever before your eyes, living as if he were watching you, and ordering all your actions as if he beheld them.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca, quoting Epicurus, advises taking a person of high character as a constant inner companion and model.
philosophy.tie_back: Same verb of cherishing (‘peni’) applied to a great person held close.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 11 (tr. Gummere), quoting Epicurus

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Rudolf II welcomes Tycho Brahe to Prague
real_life_example.place: Prague and Benatky nad Jizerou, Bohemia (now Czech Republic)
real_life_example.event: After the great Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe left Denmark, the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II made him imperial mathematician in 1599, gave him a generous salary and provided the castle of Benatky near Prague for his observatory. In 1600 Tycho invited the young Johannes Kepler to work with him there. When Tycho died in 1601, Rudolf appointed Kepler to succeed him, and Kepler's planetary tables were later named the Rudolphine Tables in the emperor's honour.
real_life_example.explanation: By honouring and providing for great scholars, Rudolf made his court a centre of the astronomy that transformed European science.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls it the rarest of all things to honour great people and make them one's own, and Rudolf drew two of the greatest astronomers of the age into his household.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tamil:
தம்மிற் பெரியார் தமரா ஒழுகுதல்
வன்மையு ளெல்லாந் தலை.
transliteration:
Thammir periyaar thamaraa ozhukudhal
Vanmaiyu lellaan thalai.
meaning: Getting people who are greater than you to treat you as one of their own is the greatest of all strengths.
elementary: Being strong isn’t just about muscles or money. This kural says the best kind of strength is behaving in a way that makes people who are wiser and better than you want to be on your side.
university: ‘Thammil periyaar’ — those greater than oneself — is the pointed phrase. Rulers and the powerful typically surround themselves with inferiors who flatter; Valluvar calls instead for the humility to keep superiors as intimates. ‘Ozhukudhal’ (conducting oneself) makes this a matter of sustained behavior, not a single act. Calling it the chief of all ‘vanmai’ (strengths) reframes power itself: the strength that multiplies other strengths is the ability to attract and retain better minds.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the Kurukshetra war, Arjuna and Duryodhana both come to Krishna; offered a choice between Krishna’s vast Narayani army and Krishna himself, unarmed and non-combatant, Arjuna chooses Krishna, and Duryodhana gladly takes the army.
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna values having the greater being at his side above any quantity of soldiers — and that choice decides the war.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-perfect enactment: making the one greater than oneself one’s own is the supreme strength.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.”
christianity.explanation: Friends shape and strengthen one another the way one iron blade hones another.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s view that one’s strength is multiplied through close companions.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with those who are true.”
islam.explanation: Believers are commanded not only to be truthful but to place themselves in the company of the truthful.
islam.tie_back: Being ‘with’ the righteous is presented as a source of spiritual strength, as the Kural presents alliance with the great.

judaism.quote_or_event: After Honi HaMe’agel awoke from seventy years’ sleep and found no one in the study house recognized him, he prayed for death; the Talmud concludes, “O chavruta o mituta” — “either companionship or death.”
judaism.explanation: Without learned companions who know and receive him, even a great sage finds life unbearable.
judaism.tie_back: Companionship with the learned is treated as the essential strength without which life itself fails.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After his awakening, the Buddha reflected that one who dwells without reverence and deference dwells in suffering; finding no one superior to himself, he resolved to honor and respect the Dhamma itself.
buddhism.explanation: Even the Buddha felt the need to dwell under something greater than himself.
buddhism.tie_back: Affirms the Kural’s insight that honoring and staying close to what surpasses oneself is a source of strength.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Disobedient, rough speaking, ill-behaved pupils will exasperate even a gentle teacher; but those will soon win even a hot-tempered teacher who humour him and are polite.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's lecture on discipline teaches that it is the junior's own conduct, humble and courteous, that wins over a superior and keeps that superior's goodwill.
jainism.tie_back: The kural calls it the greatest strength to conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself become one's own. The Jain verse likewise makes winning the great a matter of one's own humble conduct.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Lehna, while on a pilgrimage to a Hindu goddess's shrine, met Guru Nanak and resolved to follow him; known for his loyalty to the first Guru, he became Nanak's successor as Guru Angad.
sikhism.explanation: Lehna placed himself under one greater than himself and served him with such devotion that Guru Nanak chose him as the second Guru.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls it the foremost strength to conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself become one's own; Lehna's loyal discipleship made the greatest teacher of his age wholly his own.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guru Angad' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 2, after Nestor’s advice, Agamemnon exclaims that if he had ten such counselors among the Achaeans, Priam’s city would soon fall.
greek_mythology.explanation: The supreme commander rates the counsel of the aged Nestor above multitudes of warriors.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Just as the Kural calls such alliance the chief of all strengths.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Friendship “stimulates to noble actions — ‘two going together’ — for with friends men are more able both to think and to act.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that friends increase our capacity for both thought and action.
philosophy.tie_back: Friendship as a multiplier of strength, the Kural’s central claim.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Lincoln appoints his rivals to his cabinet
real_life_example.place: Springfield, Illinois, and Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: After winning the presidency in 1860, Abraham Lincoln filled the most important posts in his cabinet with the men who had competed against him for the Republican nomination. William H. Seward, the front-runner he had defeated, became Secretary of State; Salmon P. Chase became Secretary of the Treasury; Edward Bates became Attorney General; and Simon Cameron became Secretary of War.
real_life_example.explanation: Lincoln chose to surround himself with powerful and experienced figures rather than loyal followers, gaining their abilities for the Union during the Civil War.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls it the foremost strength to conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself become one's own, and Lincoln made his strongest rivals his closest colleagues.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tamil:
சூழ்வார்கண் ணாக ஒழுகலான் மன்னவன்
சூழ்வாரைச் சூழ்ந்து கொளல்.
transliteration:
Soozhvaarkan naaka ozhukalaan mannavan
Soozhvaaraich soozhndhu kolal.
meaning: A king must use his advisers as his eyes, so he should choose them only after thinking very carefully.
elementary: A king can’t see everything himself, so his advisers are like his eyes. If your eyes are bad, you can’t see clearly. So this kural says a leader must think very carefully before choosing advisers.
university: The couplet plays on the root ‘soozh’ (to deliberate, plan): ‘soozhvaar’ are those who deliberate, and the king must ‘soozhndhu’ (deliberate) in choosing them. The wordplay enacts the argument — deliberation is needed to choose the deliberators. ‘Kan aaka’ (as eyes) is the governing metaphor: a king perceives his realm largely through ministers’ reports and judgments, so their quality determines the accuracy of his vision. The later chapter on ministers (Amaichu, ch. 64) builds on this principle.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Sovereignty (rájatva) is possible only with assistance. A single wheel can never move. Hence he shall employ ministers and hear their opinion.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya holds that no ruler can govern alone; he must appoint ministers and listen to them.
hinduism.tie_back: Same premise: the ruler depends on counselors and must choose and heed them.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.”
christianity.explanation: A people whose leaders lack good counsel collapse; many sound advisers bring security.
christianity.tie_back: Affirms the ruler’s dependence on counselors that the Kural expresses.

islam.quote_or_event: “… and whose affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Quran praises believers who settle their affairs by mutual consultation (shura); elsewhere (3:159) it tells the Prophet himself to consult his companions.
islam.tie_back: Consultation as a pillar of rule parallels the Kural’s ruler who sees through his counselors.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jethro sees Moses judging the people alone from morning to evening and counsels him to choose able men, God-fearing, truthful and hating bribes, as judges over the people; Moses heeds him.
judaism.explanation: Moses accepts that a leader cannot see and judge everything himself and must select capable, upright helpers.
judaism.tie_back: Both the need for counselors and the careful criteria for choosing them echo the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Among the conditions of welfare the Buddha gives for the Vajjian republic: they meet often in assembly, and they honor, respect, and revere their elders and deem them worthy of being listened to.
buddhism.explanation: A polity remains strong as long as it deliberates together and heeds its elders.
buddhism.tie_back: Governance through heeded counsel, as in the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “So a novice who has not mastered the Law, does not know the Law, not being awakened; but afterwards he knows it well through the words of the Ginas, as with his eye (the wanderer sees the way) after sunrise.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga says the untrained novice is like a guide in the dark night, and that the teaching of the Jinas becomes his eye, letting him see the road as if the sun had risen.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says a king sees through his counsellors as his eyes and so must choose them with care. The Jain text likewise treats wise instruction as the eye by which one who cannot see finds the way.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.14.12–13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Guru has applied the true ointment of spiritual wisdom to my eyes.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the Guru as the one who gives true sight, anointing the eyes with spiritual wisdom (gian anjan).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a king sees through his counsellors as his eyes and must choose them carefully; in Gurbani the Guru is the one who gives the eyes true vision.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 124, Raag Maajh, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 10, Diomedes, asked to pick a companion for a night raid, chooses Odysseus, observing that when two go together, one sees before the other how profit may be gained.
greek_mythology.explanation: Diomedes deliberately chooses the shrewdest partner as a second pair of eyes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost literally the Kural’s counselor-as-eyes chosen with care.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli writes that the first opinion one forms of a prince and of his understanding comes from observing the men he has around him; if they are capable and faithful, he may be reckoned wise.
philosophy.explanation: A ruler’s own wisdom is judged by the quality of the ministers he chooses.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s view that selecting counselors is itself the test of a ruler.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 22 (tr. W. K. Marriott)

real_life_example.event_title: Elizabeth I chooses William Cecil as her chief minister
real_life_example.event: On her accession to the English throne in November 1558, Elizabeth I appointed William Cecil, an experienced administrator, as her principal secretary of state. Cecil served her for about 40 years until his death in 1598, first as secretary and from 1572 as Lord Treasurer, having been made Baron Burghley in 1571. He handled almost all of the queen's formal correspondence and was her most trusted adviser through most of her reign.
real_life_example.explanation: Elizabeth's first and most lasting decision as queen was the choice of the minister through whose reports and judgement she would see her kingdom.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a king must treat his counsellors as his eyes and therefore choose them with great care, and Elizabeth's careful choice of Cecil served her for four decades.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tamil:
தக்கா ரினத்தனாய்த் தானொழுக வல்லானைச்
செற்றார் செயக்கிடந்த தில்.
transliteration:
Thakkaa rinaththanaaith thaanozhuka vallaanaich
Chetraar seyakkidandha thil.
meaning: Enemies can do nothing against someone who is able to live as one of a group of good and worthy people.
elementary: If you stay close to good and wise people and act like one of them, your enemies will find there is nothing they can do to hurt you.
university: ‘Thakkaar inaththan’ — one who belongs to the fellowship of the worthy — moves from the friendship of individuals to membership in a circle. ‘Thaan ozhuka vallaan’ (one able himself to conduct himself so) implies that belonging requires one’s own discipline; the worthy will not keep company with the unworthy. The consequence is framed in the negative with total scope: ‘setraar seyak kidandhadhu il’ — there remains nothing for enemies to do. The protection is both practical (good advice closes vulnerabilities) and reputational (a ruler surrounded by the virtuous is hard to isolate).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Throughout the Mahabharata, Duryodhana’s schemes against the Pandavas — poisoning Bhima, the house of lac, the dice game and the attempt to disrobe Draupadi — repeatedly fail because the Pandavas are sheltered by Vidura’s counsel and Krishna’s friendship.
hinduism.explanation: Those who kept company with the wise and the divine proved unassailable, despite their enemies’ power.
hinduism.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural: enemies can find no effective harm to do to one who walks among the worthy.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi and Sabha Parvas (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.”
christianity.explanation: Qoheleth observes that a person alone can be overpowered, but companions together withstand attack.
christianity.tie_back: Companionship as protection against enemies, as in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “… when he said to his companion, ‘Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.’”
islam.explanation: During the Hijra, the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid in the cave of Thawr with pursuers at the entrance; the Quran recalls the Prophet reassuring his companion, and the pursuers did not find them.
islam.tie_back: The righteous companionship of the cave, under divine protection, left enemies unable to harm them.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jonathan, son of King Saul, binds himself in covenant to David, warns him of Saul’s intent to kill him, and helps him escape.
judaism.explanation: David’s friendship with the righteous Jonathan shields him from a powerful enemy.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, a worthy ally renders the enemy’s designs ineffective.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that monks who feel fear in lonely places should recollect the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha — the community of the noble ones — and their fear, trembling and dread will pass.
buddhism.explanation: Taking refuge in the noble community dispels fear, like soldiers who take heart looking at their commander’s banner.
buddhism.tie_back: Belonging to the worthy (the Sangha) as protection against threats — a softer, internal version of the Kural’s claim.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The grass near the stump of the tree will not shake with the plough of the ploughman. Feeble though they be, the anger of enemies will not come on those who have joined the society of the good.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar compares a person who stands among the good to grass sheltered by a tree stump, which the plough passes by without uprooting.
jainism.tie_back: This is almost the same thought as the kural, which says enemies can do nothing to one who lives in the fellowship of the worthy. Both promise that even a weak person is safe from enemies inside that circle.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, all one's enemies become friends.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan teaches that within the Saadh Sangat enmity dissolves and even former enemies become friends.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says enemies can do nothing to one who lives in the fellowship of the worthy; Guru Arjan says that in such fellowship enmity itself disappears.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey 22, when Odysseus fights the suitors, Athena appears at his side in the likeness of Mentor and turns aside the spears the suitors throw, so that none can harm him or his companions.
greek_mythology.explanation: The suitors, though many, can do nothing against the hero who stands with his wise ally.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Enemies find nothing they can do to one standing with the worthy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epicurus taught that it is not so much our friends’ help that helps us as the confidence of their help.
philosophy.explanation: The assurance of trustworthy friends is itself a form of security against fortune and enemies.
philosophy.tie_back: Security through reliable, worthy friends, as in the Kural.

real_life_example.event_title: Frederick the Wise shelters Martin Luther at the Wartburg
real_life_example.event: After the Diet of Worms in 1521, Emperor Charles V declared Martin Luther an outlaw. Luther's protector, Frederick III, Elector of Saxony, known as Frederick the Wise, arranged for him to be taken on the road and hidden at the Wartburg castle, where he lived in disguise for nearly a year. There Luther translated the New Testament into German, and it was published in 1522.
real_life_example.explanation: Under the protection of a respected prince and his circle, a man condemned by the most powerful ruler in Europe was able to continue his work unharmed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says enemies can do nothing to one who lives within the company of the worthy, and Luther's protectors made the emperor's sentence powerless against him.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tamil:
இடிக்குந் துணையாரை ஆள்வாரை யாரே
கெடுக்குந் தகைமை யவர்.
transliteration:
Idikkun thunaiyaarai aalvaarai yaare
Kedukkun thakaimai yavar.
meaning: Who can ruin people who keep friends that scold them when they are wrong?
elementary: A good friend will tell you when you are doing something wrong, even if it hurts to hear. This kural asks: if you keep friends like that close, who could ever bring you down?
university: ‘Idikkum’ means to strike or rebuke — Parimelazhagar glosses it as reproving the king when he errs. The couplet is a rhetorical question that assumes its answer: none. What protects the ruler is not deference but correction. The idea is especially pointed in a political treatise, since rulers are the persons least likely to hear criticism. ‘Aalvaar’ (those who rule / keep) suggests the king must actively maintain such critics in his service rather than merely tolerate them.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Sulabhāḥ puruṣā rājan satataṃ priyavādinaḥ; apriyasya ca pathyasya vaktā śrotā ca durlabhaḥ.”
hinduism.explanation: ‘O king, men who always speak pleasantly are easy to find; but one who speaks what is unpleasant yet wholesome, and one who listens to it, are hard to find.’
hinduism.tie_back: Both value the rare counselor who says what the ruler needs rather than wants to hear.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Maricha to Ravana); also Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Vidura Niti)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
christianity.explanation: A friend’s painful honesty is trustworthy; an enemy’s flattery is a trap.
christianity.tie_back: The rebuking friend as a safeguard, as in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that the believer is the mirror of his fellow believer, and his brother who guards him against loss and protects him in his absence.
islam.explanation: A true brother shows you your faults as a mirror does and protects your interests.
islam.tie_back: The corrective companion who shields from ruin mirrors the Kural’s rebuking ally.

judaism.quote_or_event: The prophet Nathan confronts King David over Bathsheba and Uriah with the parable of the poor man’s lamb, declaring “Thou art the man”; David repents, and though punished, his throne is preserved.
judaism.explanation: David keeps a prophet who dares to rebuke even the king, and his acceptance of rebuke saves his dynasty.
judaism.tie_back: A king who keeps a rebuker survives his own error — the Kural’s point exactly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure. It is always better, and never worse, to cultivate such an association.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a person who points out our faults to a guide who leads us to buried treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: Near-identical: the reproving companion is a treasure and a protection.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Any instruction the wise ones may give me in a kind or a rough way, I shall devotedly accept, thinking that it is for my benefit.” … “Wise, fearless monks consider even a rough instruction as a benefit, but the fools hate it, though it produces patience and purity of mind.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's lecture on discipline teaches welcoming correction from the wise, even when it is harsh, because it brings patience and purity, while fools resent it.
jainism.tie_back: The kural asks who could ruin one who keeps companions able to rebuke him. The Jain text counts that rebuke itself as a benefit and marks the wise by their readiness to welcome it.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.27, 1.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If my heart is pure, and I am slandered, then the slanderer washes my clothes.” … “One who slanders me is my friend.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir welcomes those who expose his faults, saying such critics cleanse him and are really his friends.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks who can ruin one who keeps companions able to rebuke him; Kabir likewise treats the one who points out his faults as a friend who keeps him clean.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey 12, Circe warns Odysseus of the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis; heeding her, he has his men stop their ears with wax and bind him to the mast, and passes the Sirens safely.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus survives because he accepts hard, unwelcome instructions — even about his own weakness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Keeping and obeying a counselor who tells one hard truths keeps one from ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch argues that frank speech (parrhesia) is the language of true friendship and a kind of medicine, and that the flatterer who only pleases is the greatest danger to the powerful.
philosophy.explanation: Real friends tell painful truths for our good; flatterers ruin us.
philosophy.tie_back: The same distinction between the rebuking friend and the destructive flatterer.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend (Moralia)

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi answers Tagore's public criticism with respect
real_life_example.event: In 1921 Rabindranath Tagore published an essay, The Call of Truth, in the Modern Review, criticising parts of Mahatma Gandhi's non-cooperation movement as a negative and inward-looking turning away from cooperation with the wider world. Gandhi replied in his journal Young India on 13 October 1921 in an essay he titled The Great Sentinel, engaging Tagore's arguments seriously. The two continued to debate openly in print over the following years while remaining close friends.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi kept the country's most respected critic close and answered him in public rather than dismissing him, and their exchange remains a model of principled disagreement.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks who can ruin one who keeps companions able to rebuke him, and Gandhi honoured Tagore precisely as the friend who would tell him where he was wrong.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tamil:
இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்
கெடுப்பா ரிலானுங் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Idippaarai illaadha emaraa mannan
Keduppaa rilaanung kedum.
meaning: A king without anyone to scold and correct him has no protection, and he will be ruined even when no enemy is there to destroy him.
elementary: A king with nobody brave enough to tell him he’s wrong is like someone walking without looking. Even if no enemy attacks him, he will trip over his own mistakes and fall.
university: This is the converse of 447. ‘Emaraa’ means unprotected or unsafeguarded — the missing protection is precisely the rebuker. The striking phrase ‘keduppaar ilaanum kedum’ (perishes even without destroyers) locates the source of ruin inside: unchecked error compounds until it destroys. Valluvar thus anticipates a well-known insight of political thought — that autocrats surrounded by yes-men fall by their own misjudgments more often than by foreign conquest.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Yuddha Kanda, Vibhishana urges his brother Ravana to return Sita to Rama; Ravana, surrounded by flattering ministers, insults and expels him, and Lanka is destroyed.
hinduism.explanation: Ravana drives away the one counselor willing to correct him and is ruined by his own obstinacy.
hinduism.tie_back: The king who rejects his rebuker brings about his own destruction.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.”
christianity.explanation: One who refuses correction again and again collapses suddenly and beyond repair.
christianity.tie_back: Refusing rebuke leads to self-inflicted ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that the religion is sincere advice (nasihah) — to God, His Book, His Messenger, the leaders of the Muslims and their common folk.
islam.explanation: Sincere counsel to rulers is part of faith itself, implying that leaders deprived of it are endangered.
islam.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s view that a ruler needs honest advisers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is yet one man, Micaiah the son of Imlah, by whom we may enquire of the LORD: but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.”
judaism.explanation: King Ahab prefers four hundred agreeable prophets to the one who tells him the truth; he goes to battle and is killed.
judaism.tie_back: A king who shuts out his only honest critic perishes by his own choice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that the one who admonishes, instructs and shields one from wrong is dear to the good and disliked by the bad.
buddhism.explanation: Only those who are good welcome correction; those who reject the admonisher show their own ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: Implies the fate the Kural states outright for the uncorrected.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If admonished by a young or an old monk, by one above him or one of equal age, he should not retort against him, being perfectly free from passion; for one who is (as it were) carried away (by the stream of the Samsâra), will not get to its opposite shore.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga tells the monk to accept admonition from anyone, of any age or rank, and warns that one who rejects it is carried off by the current and never reaches the far shore.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the king with no one to rebuke him perishes even without enemies. The Jain verse likewise shows ruin coming from within, to one who refuses correction, with no outside destroyer needed.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.14.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who is attached to Maya is totally blind and deaf. He does not listen to the Word of the Shabad; he makes a great uproar and tumult.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the person ruled by Maya as deaf to the Guru's corrective Word, lost in his own noise.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the king with no one to rebuke him perishes even without enemies; Guru Amar Das portrays the one who will not hear correction as destroying himself from within.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 313, Raag Gauree (Gauree ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 18, Polydamas urges Hector to withdraw the Trojans inside the walls now that Achilles has returned; Hector scorns him, the Trojans applaud Hector’s bad plan, and ‘no one praised Polydamas’ good counsel.’ The next day the Trojans are routed and Hector is killed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector rejects his wise critic and brings disaster on himself and Troy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The leader without a heeded rebuker falls through his own error.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice.”
philosophy.explanation: In his chapter on how to avoid flatterers, Machiavelli warns that a prince surrounded by flatterers, and unable to take counsel, is ruined.
philosophy.tie_back: The ruler without honest counsel undoes himself.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 23 (tr. W. K. Marriott)

real_life_example.event_title: Nicholas II takes personal command against his ministers' advice
real_life_example.event: In the late summer of 1915, with Russian armies in retreat, Tsar Nicholas II dismissed the commander in chief, Grand Duke Nicholas, and took supreme command himself, despite objections from his Council of Ministers. With the tsar away at headquarters, power in the capital passed largely to Empress Alexandra, and capable ministers were replaced by weaker figures, many favoured by Grigori Rasputin. The government lost the confidence of the country, and in March 1917 Nicholas was forced to abdicate.
real_life_example.explanation: By overruling and removing those who warned him, Nicholas cut himself off from correction at the moment his throne most needed it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says an unguarded king with no one to rebuke him perishes even without enemies to destroy him, and Nicholas's monarchy collapsed from within.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tamil:
முதலிலார்க் கூதிய மில்லை மதலையாஞ்
சார்பிலார்க் கில்லை நிலை.
transliteration:
Mudhalilaark kooodhiya millai madhalaiyaanj
Chaarbilaark killai nilai.
meaning: Just as there is no profit without money to start with, there is no steadiness for those without good people to support them.
elementary: You can’t earn money from a business if you have no money to start it. In the same way, you can’t stay steady and safe in life if you have no wise people to lean on.
university: An economic analogy fitting the Porutpaal: ‘mudhal’ (capital) is to ‘oodhiyam’ (profit) as ‘saarbu’ (support) is to ‘nilai’ (stability). ‘Madhalai’ is a prop or supporting beam — the support of the great is the load-bearing pillar of a leader’s position. The analogy implies that alliance with the worthy is not an optional extra but the principal on which all further returns are earned.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Sovereignty (rájatva) is possible only with assistance. A single wheel can never move.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya likens rule to a vehicle that cannot move on one wheel; the ruler’s helpers are the other wheel.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s prop (madhalai), assistance is the precondition of stable rule.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus compares the one who hears and does his words to a wise man who built his house on rock, which withstood the storm, and the one who does not to a foolish man who built on sand, whose house fell.
christianity.explanation: Stability depends on the foundation beneath.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, a sound support is what keeps one standing.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided.”
islam.explanation: The community’s stability depends on holding together to a common support.
islam.tie_back: Stability through a shared support, echoing the Kural’s ‘saarbu’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth warns that the person without companions has no one to raise him when he falls.
judaism.tie_back: Without support, there is no standing — the Kural’s ‘no stability’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists admirable friendship as the first prerequisite for the development of the wings to awakening, preceding virtue, right talk, persistence and discernment.
buddhism.explanation: Good friendship is the foundational capital on which all further spiritual progress is built.
buddhism.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s ‘capital’ image: without the support of the worthy, nothing further can be gained.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Just as they carry off a young bird whose wings are not yet grown, so many unprincipled men will seduce a novice who has not yet mastered the Law, thinking that they can get him in their power, when they have made him leave (the Gakkha).”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga compares a novice who leaves the community of his teachers to a fledgling that leaves the nest too early and is snatched by birds of prey.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says there is no stability without the support of the worthy, just as there is no profit without capital. The Jain image of the unfledged bird shows how quickly a person without that support falls.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.14.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, without capital, no one has ever departed with profit.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the language of trade: without the capital of spiritual wisdom and virtue, no one leaves this world with any gain.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says there is no profit without capital and no stability without the support of the worthy; Guru Nanak uses the same capital-and-profit image for the spiritual life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1244, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The giant Antaeus was invincible while touching his mother Earth, who renewed his strength; Heracles defeated him by lifting him off the ground and crushing him in the air.
greek_mythology.explanation: Cut off from his source of support, the mightiest wrestler lost all strength.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An image of the Kural’s point: without one’s prop, there is no standing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says even the rich and powerful need friends most, to preserve and use their prosperity.
philosophy.tie_back: Friends as the foundation that makes other goods stable and useful.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Maximilian of Mexico loses his French support
real_life_example.event: Archduke Maximilian of Austria became emperor of Mexico in 1864, his rule upheld by French troops sent by Napoleon III. Under pressure from the United States, Napoleon agreed in 1866 to withdraw, and the last French forces left in early 1867. Left with only a small army, Maximilian was besieged and captured at Queretaro by the republican forces of Benito Juarez and was executed in June 1867.
real_life_example.explanation: Maximilian's empire had no foundation of its own, and once the outside support that propped it up was removed, it fell within months.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says there is no stability for those without strong support to prop them up, just as there is no profit without capital, and Maximilian's throne collapsed when its prop was withdrawn.

adhikaram.english: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tamil:
பல்லார் பகைகொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்தே
நல்லார் தொடர்கை விடல்.
transliteration:
Pallaar pakaikolalir paththaduththa theemaiththe
Nallaar thodarkai vidal.
meaning: Losing the friendship of good people is ten times worse than making many enemies.
elementary: Having lots of enemies is bad. But this kural says losing the friendship of good people is ten times worse than that.
university: The chapter closes with a calculus: ‘paththu aduththa’ (ten times over) compares two harms. Enmity from many (pallaar) is external and can be countered; abandonment of good friends (nallaar thodarkai vidal) removes the very counsel and support by which enemies are countered — so it multiplies every other danger. The verb ‘vidal’ (letting go) places responsibility on the one who drops such friendships, whether through pride, neglect, or preference for flatterers.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Stung by Vidura’s repeated advice to make peace with the Pandavas, Dhritarashtra angrily tells him to leave; Vidura goes to the Pandavas in the forest, and the king, soon realizing his loss, sends Sanjaya to bring him back.
hinduism.explanation: Casting off the one truly good counselor proves a grave loss even the king immediately feels, and the Kaurava line is later destroyed in the war he tried to prevent.
hinduism.tie_back: Forsaking the good is shown as a self-inflicted wound worse than enmity.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that bad company corrupts good character.
christianity.tie_back: The reverse side of the Kural: leaving good company for bad is corrosive.

islam.quote_or_event: “Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken that one as a friend.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment, the wrongdoer bites his hands in regret for having followed a misleading friend instead of the Messenger’s way.
islam.tie_back: Abandoning the good companion for the wrong one is shown as a supreme, lasting regret.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But he forsook the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him.”
judaism.explanation: Rehoboam rejects the elders who had served Solomon and follows his young peers; ten tribes break away and the kingdom is split.
judaism.tie_back: Forsaking the good counselors costs more than any external enemy could.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada advises not to associate with evil companions or seek the company of the vile, but to associate with good friends and seek the company of noble men.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha directs his followers to cling to good companions and away from bad ones.
buddhism.tie_back: Implicitly treats the loss of good friends as a serious harm, as the Kural does.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A good man should long to live with his teacher in order to perform his duties, knowing that he who does not live with his teacher will not put an end to his mundane existence. Making manifest the conduct of the virtuous, an intelligent (monk) should not leave the (company of his teacher).”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns that leaving the company of the virtuous teacher costs nothing less than liberation itself, so the wise do not leave it.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar judges giving up the friendship of the good to be ten times worse than the enmity of many. The Jain text likewise treats leaving good company as the greatest loss, since it closes the way out of samsara.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.14.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: During the siege of Anandpur in 1705, some Sikhs signed a disclaimer (bedava) disowning Guru Gobind Singh and left; shamed at home and led back by Mai Bhago, they rejoined the Guru and fell fighting at Khidrana (Muktsar), where the Guru tore up the bedava at the dying Mahan Singh's request.
sikhism.explanation: Abandoning the Guru's company proved a far deeper loss to these Sikhs than the danger they fled, and they won back honour only by returning to it at the cost of their lives.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says giving up the friendship of the good is ten times worse than the enmity of many; the deserters found leaving the Guru worse than facing the besieging armies.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University), 'Bedava', as published on thesikhencyclopedia.com (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 1, Agamemnon insults Achilles and takes his prize; Achilles withdraws, and the Greeks suffer more at the Trojans’ hands than at any time in the war. In Iliad 9 Agamemnon admits his folly and offers great gifts to win him back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Alienating his best ally costs Agamemnon more than all the enemy’s efforts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Losing the good friend is worse than the enmity of many.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “You might just as well take the sun out of the sky as friendship from life; for the immortal gods have given us nothing better or more delightful.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius answers philosophers who advise holding friendship loosely to avoid anxiety, or seeking it only for advantage: to remove friendship from life, he says, is like removing the sun from the sky.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Cicero treats the loss of good friends as a darkness that no other good can make up for, though he does not weigh it against the enmity of many.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia (On Friendship), §47 (ch. 13) (tr. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Louis XVI dismisses the reforming minister Turgot
real_life_example.event: Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot, appointed controller general of finances by Louis XVI in 1774, proposed the Six Edicts, which among other things abolished compulsory road labour by peasants and the Paris guilds. The privileged orders, court factions and the Parlement of Paris opposed the reforms strongly. In May 1776 Louis XVI gave way and dismissed Turgot, and most of his reforms were abandoned.
real_life_example.explanation: By giving up an able and honest minister to quiet powerful opponents, Louis XVI lost one of the best chances of reforming France's finances before the crisis that led to the Revolution.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that abandoning the friendship of the good is ten times worse than the hostility of many, and Louis chose to placate many opponents at the cost of his best counsel.

tamil:
சிற்றினம் அஞ்சும் பெருமை சிறுமைதான்
சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும்.
transliteration:
Sitrinam anjum perumai sirumaidhaan
Sutramaach soozhndhu vidum.
meaning: Great people are afraid of mixing with mean, small-minded people. But small-minded people pull such people close and treat them like their own family.
elementary: A truly great person is careful to stay away from petty, mean-spirited people, almost as if afraid of them. A small-minded person does the opposite: they happily pull those same people close and treat them like family.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter by defining two temperaments through a single reaction: அஞ்சும் (‘fears, shrinks from’) versus சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும் (‘surrounds itself with them as kinsfolk’). The சிற்றினம் (‘small/mean kind’) are not necessarily criminals; commentators such as Parimelazhagar gloss them as the base-minded whose company slowly lowers one’s own standard. The chiasmus of பெருமை/சிறுமை (greatness/smallness) makes character a matter of affinity: we show what we are by whom we are comfortable with. This chapter is the deliberate counterweight to chapter 45 (பெரியாரைத் துணைக்கோடல, seeking the help of the great): what one should seek there, one should fear here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Narada Bhakti Sutra (sutra 43) teaches “duḥsaṅgaḥ sarvathaiva tyājyaḥ” — bad company is to be given up in every way.
hinduism.explanation: In the bhakti tradition, dussanga (evil association) is treated as something the serious seeker must avoid completely, not just keep under control.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘greatness fears mean company’ matches the sutra’s call to avoid bad company in every way; both see keeping away as the mark of a serious, elevated person.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to stay out of partnership with sinful conduct and to expose it instead of joining in.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it calls for refusing fellowship with what is base; Paul adds a duty to rebuke, which the Kural does not mention.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see those who engage in [offensive] discourse concerning Our verses, then turn away from them until they enter into another conversation.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the believer to walk away from gatherings where sacred things are mocked, and not to sit on with them.
islam.tie_back: Getting up and leaving low company is the behaviour the Kural credits to greatness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.”
judaism.explanation: The first verse of the Psalms defines the blessed person by the company they refuse, moving from walking to standing to sitting with the wicked.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts measure a person’s worth by the company they keep away from.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not associate with evil companions; do not seek the fellowship of the vile. Associate with the good friends; seek the fellowship of noble men.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers to avoid vile companions and look for noble ones.
buddhism.tie_back: The Pali ‘purisādhame’ (lowest of men) is close to the Kural’s சிற்றினம், and both verses contrast avoiding the low with seeking the noble.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When reprimanded a wise man should not be angry, but he should be of a forbearing mood; he should not associate, laugh, and play with mean men.”
jainism.explanation: In the opening lecture on discipline, the well-trained disciple is told plainly to keep away from the company and pastimes of mean men.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says greatness shrinks from the company of the mean-minded. Here the Jain disciple's discipline likewise includes refusing to keep company with such people.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, I have been ruined and destroyed by bad company, like the banana plant near the thorn bush.” … “The thorn bush waves in the wind, and pierces the banana plant; see this, and do not associate with the faithless cynics.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir pictures bad company as a thorn bush that tears the tender banana plant beside it, and warns the seeker to keep away from the faithless (saakat).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says greatness fears the company of the mean while smallness embraces it; Kabir shows why the wise shrink from such company and urges them to avoid it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus has his crew stop their ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast so he cannot follow the Sirens’ call.
greek_mythology.explanation: The wise hero knows how strong a corrupting pull can be, so he protects himself from it in advance instead of trusting his willpower.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s point that greatness ‘fears’ low company. Being wary of it is wisdom, not weakness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For be assured that if a person be ever so sound himself, yet, if his companion be infected, he who converses with him will be infected likewise.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the student to avoid vulgar gatherings, because even a sound person catches the sickness of the company they keep.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains why the great fear mean company: in both texts, closeness to the base is contagious.

real_life_example.event_title: President Harding and the Ohio Gang
real_life_example.event: After his election in 1920, Warren G. Harding gave high office to a circle of political friends and allies, many from his home state, who became known as the Ohio Gang, among them Attorney General Harry Daugherty, Interior Secretary Albert B. Fall and Veterans Bureau head Charles R. Forbes. Investigations after Harding's death in 1923 exposed widespread corruption: Forbes was imprisoned for fraud and bribery at the Veterans Bureau, and Fall became the first cabinet member sent to prison for crimes in office, over the Teapot Dome oil leases. Harding himself was never charged.
real_life_example.explanation: A president who chose to surround himself with self-serving cronies saw his administration become a byword for corruption, and his own reputation has never recovered.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says smallness gathers the mean-minded round itself as kin, and Harding's comfortable circle of friends is a textbook case of the company a leader chooses defining his rule.

tamil:
நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர்திரிந் தற்றாகும் மாந்தர்க்கு
இனத்தியல்ப தாகும் அறிவு.
transliteration:
Nilaththiyalbaal neerthirindhu atraakum maandharkku
Inaththiyalba thaagum arivu.
meaning: Water changes its color and taste depending on the ground it flows over. In the same way, a person’s understanding takes on the nature of the people they spend time with.
elementary: Rain is pure when it falls, but it turns muddy, salty or sweet depending on the ground it runs over. Our minds work the same way: they pick up the colour and taste of the people we spend time with.
university: The simile works because rain is pure when it falls and only takes on colour, salt or sweetness from the ground (நிலத்தியல்பு) it touches. அறிவு here is not raw intelligence but practical understanding, the judgement a person brings to life. Valluvar’s claim is environmental: the mind is not a sealed container but something that absorbs from its surroundings. The next two couplets (453–454) sharpen this into a paradox: intelligence seems to belong to the mind but is actually supplied by one’s company.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Queen Kaikeyi loves Rama as her own son, until her hunchbacked maid Manthara keeps working on her mind and turns her into the one who demands Rama’s exile.
hinduism.explanation: A noble queen’s judgement is changed not by her own nature but by the constant presence of a petty, scheming companion.
hinduism.tie_back: Kaikeyi is the water and Manthara is the soil. Her ‘arivu’ took on the nature of the company she kept.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.”
christianity.explanation: Paul quotes a proverb (from the Greek poet Menander) warning that bad company corrupts good character.
christianity.tie_back: Both claim that one’s inner character takes on the quality of one’s company, however good it started out.

islam.quote_or_event: “Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken that one as a friend. He led me away from the remembrance after it had come to me.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement the wrongdoer regrets a friendship that pulled him away from guidance he had already received.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point seen from the end: understanding the person once had was reshaped by a bad friend.

judaism.quote_or_event: Maimonides writes that it is human nature to be drawn after the views and deeds of one’s friends and neighbours, so one should keep company with the righteous and the wise and stay away from the wicked.
