judaism.explanation: Maimonides treats social influence as a law of human nature and builds a rule of conduct on it.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s thesis in legal prose: character follows company the way water follows soil.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares following a fool to wrapping a rotten fish in a blade of kusa grass: the grass itself comes to smell rotten. Leaves wrapped around incense, by contrast, come to smell sweet.
buddhism.explanation: What we are wrapped up with passes its quality to us, whether that is foul or fragrant.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the same image-logic as the Kural. The grass, like the water, takes on the character of what it is in contact with.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Water when mixed with milk will become milk, not remaining water. Will it exhibit the appearance of water? In like manner, if you consider it, the meanness of the mean when united with the dignity of the excellent will utterly vanish.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar uses the image of water taking on the nature of the milk it is mixed with to show that a person takes on the character of the company they join.
jainism.tie_back: This is the same liquid image as the kural, where water changes with the soil it runs through and the mind changes with its company. Here it is shown from the hopeful side, as the mean are transformed by the excellent.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 7 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, the mind has become a bird; it soars and flies in the ten directions. According to the company it keeps, so are the fruits it eats.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir compares the restless mind to a bird whose nourishment depends on where it settles, that is, on the company it keeps.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says understanding takes on the nature of one's company as water takes on the nature of the soil; Kabir says the mind feeds on whatever its company offers.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus’s men enter Circe’s hall, share her food and drink, and are turned into swine, keeping only their human minds.
greek_mythology.explanation: Often read allegorically (for example by the Stoics and later moralists) as the way a degrading environment turns people into beasts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In both, the surroundings a person enters change what they become.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For from the good you will learn what is good, but if you mix with the bad you will lose the intelligence which you already have.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates quotes the poet Theognis, who says that good company teaches goodness while bad company destroys the intelligence one already has.
philosophy.tie_back: Theognis’s ‘intelligence’ corresponds exactly to the Kural’s அறிவு, which company can raise or ruin.
philosophy.source: Theognis, as quoted in Plato, Meno 95d (trans. Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Solomon Asch's conformity experiments
real_life_example.event: At Swarthmore College, psychologist Solomon Asch asked students to say which of three lines matched a reference line, a task with an obvious answer. Unknown to each real participant, the others in the room were working with Asch and on certain trials all gave the same wrong answer. A large share of participants, about three-quarters, went along with the group's clearly false answer at least once.
real_life_example.explanation: The experiments became a classic demonstration that even a plain judgement of the senses bends toward the view of the surrounding group.
real_life_example.tie_back: As water takes on the nature of the soil it runs through, Asch's students showed their judgement taking on the colour of the company around them.

tamil:
மனத்தானாம் மாந்தர்க் குணர்ச்சி இனத்தானாம்
இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல்.
transliteration:
Manaththaanaam maandhark kunarchchi inaththaanaam
Innaan enappadunj chol.
meaning: Our power to understand things comes from our own mind. But how others judge us, saying “that is the kind of person they are,” comes from the friends we keep.
elementary: What you think and feel comes from inside you. But what other people say about you, like ‘he’s a good guy’ or ‘he’s trouble’, mostly depends on who your friends are.
university: The couplet sets inner and outer against each other: உணர்ச்சி (perception, awareness) arises from மனம் (mind), while reputation, இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல் (‘the word by which one is called such a man’), arises from இனம் (one’s group). This is a sociological observation: others cannot see into a person’s mind, so they judge by association. Valluvar does not call this judgement unfair. He treats it as a fact the prudent must reckon with, which is why the chapter sits in the Porul (polity) book rather than Aram. Together with 454 it forms a two-step argument: first reputation, then even inner wisdom, turns out to depend on one’s company.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Karna is generous, brave and bound by his word, yet because he stands with Duryodhana’s faction he is remembered as part of the Kaurava wrong and dies on its side.
hinduism.explanation: His personal nobility could not override the name that came from the company he chose.
hinduism.tie_back: Karna’s உணர்ச்சி came from his own mind, but his இன்னான் (‘what kind of man he is’) was settled by his association with Duryodhana.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus’s critics judge him by the people he eats with. Jesus quotes the accusation to show how such people think, and does not accept it.
christianity.tie_back: This confirms the Kural’s observation that society labels a person by their company. The Gospel, however, rejects the verdict when the purpose of the company is redemptive.

islam.quote_or_event: “A man follows the religion of his friend; so each one should consider whom he makes his friend.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says a person’s way of life can be read from their close friends, so friends should be chosen with care.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a person’s identity is judged by, and actually shaped by, their companions.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah’s saying “woe to the wicked, woe to his neighbour” is applied by Rashi to the tribe of Reuben, who camped beside Korah and were drawn into his rebellion.
judaism.explanation: Being near the wicked brings both ruin and a shared name.
judaism.tie_back: Reuben is remembered alongside Korah because of whom they camped beside, which illustrates the Kural’s point about reputation from company.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha warns Sigala that one who associates with evil companions finds that gamblers, libertines, drunkards, cheats, swindlers and ruffians become his friends and companions.
buddhism.explanation: Among the dangers of bad company, the Buddha lists that one’s whole circle, and so one’s standing, is defined by such people.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s point that one comes to be counted as ‘such a man’ by the circle one keeps.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though innocent in intention, persons will be despised on account of the (bad) company they have joined. In the forest both the scent-giving sandal and the teak tree will be burned when the brushwood, which has been cut, has caught fire.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar warns that even a person with a pure inner intention is judged, and suffers, by the company they keep, just as fine sandalwood burns along with the brushwood around it.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar sets inner perception, which comes from the mind, against the verdict 'he is such a man', which comes from one's company. The Naladiyar makes the same split between innocent intention and reputation earned through company.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Of all plants, the sandalwood tree is the most sublime. Everything near the sandalwood tree becomes fragrant like sandalwood.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das uses the sandalwood tree, which perfumes everything growing near it, as an image of the saints whose company transforms those around them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the verdict 'he is such-and-such a man' comes from one's company; Guru Ram Das likewise shows plants taking on the very name and nature of what they stand beside.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 834, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus returns, the goatherd Melanthius and the disloyal maidservants, who had sided with the suitors, share the suitors’ punishment.
greek_mythology.explanation: They are judged not by their rank but by the camp they joined.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s view that the world pronounces its verdict on a person according to their company.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The orator Aeschines reminds the Athenian jury that they put Socrates to death because he was shown to have educated Critias, one of the Thirty Tyrants.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates’s public name was shaped by his association with notorious pupils, whatever his own inner philosophy.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a historical case of the Kural’s claim: people read one’s mind from one’s company.

real_life_example.event_title: Mary, Queen of Scots, marries the Earl of Bothwell
real_life_example.event: In February 1567 Lord Darnley, husband of Mary, Queen of Scots, was killed when the house where he was staying was blown up, and James Hepburn, Earl of Bothwell, was widely held to be the chief suspect. Bothwell was acquitted at a trial with no prosecution case, and in May 1567 Mary married him. The Scottish nobles turned against the couple, Mary surrendered to them at Carberry Hill in June, was held at Lochleven Castle and was forced to abdicate in favour of her infant son in July 1567.
real_life_example.explanation: Whatever Mary herself knew, a question historians still debate, her marriage to the suspected man was enough for her subjects to judge her by him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that others cannot see into the mind and so name a person by the company they keep, and Mary lost her crown largely on the strength of whom she joined herself to.

tamil:
மனத்து ளதுபோலக் காட்டி ஒருவற்கு
இனத்துள தாகும் அறிவு.
transliteration:
Manaththu ladhupolak kaatti oruvarku
Inaththu ladhaagum arivu.
meaning: A person’s good sense seems to live in their own mind. But it really comes from the group of people they spend time with.
elementary: We think our good sense is all our own. But look closely and much of it comes from the people around us: what they talk about, what they value, how they act.
university: காட்டி (‘making it appear’) is the key word. Valluvar grants that wisdom seems to live in one’s own mind, then corrects the appearance: it is actually இனத்துளது, lodged in one’s group. This is a strikingly early statement of what is now called distributed or socially embedded cognition: judgement is sustained by the conversations, norms and examples of a circle. It does not deny individual minds, which 453 affirmed, but it undercuts the pride of thinking oneself self-sufficient. The practical corollary, drawn out in 455–460, is that choosing one’s company is choosing one’s wisdom.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Duryodhana relies on his uncle Shakuni’s counsel. The plan of the rigged dice game, which leads to the Pandavas’ exile and in the end to the war, is Shakuni’s idea.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana’s ‘wisdom’ in the crisis is really his adviser’s cunning working through him.
hinduism.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s claim that what looks like a person’s own mind is supplied by their circle.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The disciple is not above his master: but every one that is perfect shall be as his master.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says a student, once fully trained, becomes like the one he learns from.
christianity.tie_back: In both, a person’s wisdom takes on the shape of the company they learn from.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that the believer is a mirror to his fellow believer.
islam.explanation: A good companion shows you your faults and virtues, so self-knowledge comes through others.
islam.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s claim that clear understanding is received from one’s company rather than produced in isolation.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Hanina says he learned much from his teachers, more from his colleagues, and most of all from his students.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud locates the growth of wisdom in the web of people one studies with.
judaism.tie_back: This confirms the Kural’s point that wisdom lives within one’s company.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: Wisdom is found by keeping company with the wise, who show one what one cannot see alone.
buddhism.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s point that true understanding comes from the company one keeps.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the worthy teachers, who are thoroughly enlightened and from early times well versed in conduct, are satisfied (with a pupil), they will make over to him their extensive and weighty knowledge of the sacred texts.”
jainism.explanation: In Jain monastic life, knowledge of the scriptures passes from teacher to pupil; a disciple's learning is literally handed over by the enlightened company he serves.
jainism.tie_back: The kural holds that wisdom seems to live in one's own mind but really lives in one's company. The Jain verse likewise has the pupil's wisdom come from the worthy teachers whose company he has won.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.46 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, spiritual wisdom is revealed.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan teaches that true wisdom (sugiaan) comes to light within the Saadh Sangat.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says wisdom only seems to live in one's own mind but really resides in one's company; Guru Arjan places the revelation of wisdom in holy company.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Athena, disguised as Mentor, travels with young Telemachus and guides him to Nestor and Menelaus. In their company the hesitant boy grows into a prudent young man.
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus’s new judgement is formed through his companions.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His wisdom seems to be his own but comes from his company, just as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus warns that a person who often talks with others must either become like them or bring them round to his own ways.
philosophy.explanation: Conversation is formative, so an untrained mind is reshaped by the company it keeps.
philosophy.tie_back: This supports the Kural’s claim that what passes for one’s own mind is largely the imprint of one’s circle.

real_life_example.event_title: Young physicists gather at Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen
real_life_example.event: Niels Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics opened at the University of Copenhagen in 1921, and Bohr set out to make it a place where a constantly renewed group of young physicists could work together. Through the 1920s visitors from many countries, including Werner Heisenberg, Wolfgang Pauli and Paul Dirac, spent time there arguing over the problems of the atom. Much of the work that produced the new quantum mechanics in the mid-1920s was done by people who studied or debated in this circle, which they nicknamed Bohr's kindergarten.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the greatest advances in modern science grew out of a community of debate rather than from a single solitary mind.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says wisdom only seems to live in one's own mind but really resides in one's company, and quantum mechanics was in large part the product of the Copenhagen circle.

tamil:
மனந்தூய்மை செய்வினை தூய்மை இரண்டும்
இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும்.
transliteration:
Mananthooimai seivinai thooimai irandum
Inanthooimai thoovaa varum.
meaning: A clean, pure mind and clean, pure actions both come from keeping company with good, pure people.
elementary: Having a clean heart and doing clean, honest things are both easier when the people around you are good. Good friends act like a support that keeps your thoughts and actions straight.
university: தூவா (‘support, prop, means’) is the pivot. Purity of mind (மனம்) and of action (செய்வினை), the two pillars of Aram, are made to depend on a third thing, purity of company (இனம்). This goes a step beyond 452’s simile: company is not just an influence on character but its enabling support. The triple repetition of தூய்மை holds the three purities together in one sound-chain, mirroring the argument. Parimelazhagar notes that although mind and deed seem to be individual possessions, they are sustained by one’s associates.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Narada Bhakti Sutra 44 explains why bad company must be shunned: it gives rise to lust, anger and delusion, then loss of memory and of discernment, and finally utter ruin.
hinduism.explanation: The sutra traces a chain from bad association to the collapse of inner purity and so of right action.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the reverse of the Kural’s claim: impure company corrupts mind and deed, just as pure company supports them.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul.”
christianity.explanation: Friendship with a hot-tempered person teaches you his ways and traps your soul.
christianity.tie_back: The same logic runs through both: the company one keeps shapes one’s inner state (soul) and outer conduct (ways).

islam.quote_or_event: “…the one who is blowing a pair of bellows will either burn your clothes or you will get a bad smell from him.”
islam.explanation: In the Prophet’s parable, an evil companion is like a blacksmith: you come away either scorched or carrying his foul smell.
islam.tie_back: In both, impurity passes from companion to person, staining conduct (the burnt clothes) and inner character (the smell).

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have not sat with vain persons, neither will I go in with dissemblers. I have hated the congregation of evil doers; and will not sit with the wicked. I will wash mine hands in innocency.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist links his ‘clean hands’ (pure deeds) directly to his refusal to sit among evildoers.
judaism.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s logic: purity of action rests on purity of company.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Prince Ajatasattu, won over by the ambitious monk Devadatta, is persuaded to seize the throne from his father, King Bimbisara, who then dies in prison, while Devadatta plots against the Buddha himself.
buddhism.explanation: A royal heir’s mind and deeds are corrupted through one bad association, ending in patricide.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim in its darkest form: impure company brings impurity of mind and of deed.
buddhism.source: Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga VII; cf. Digha Nikaya 2

jainism.quote_or_event: “Living in this (company of the teacher) and protecting (himself or other beings) in the three ways (viz. in thoughts, words, and acts), he (gets) peace and the annihilation (of sins) as they say.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga ties the purification of thought, word and deed, and the destruction of sin, to the monk's staying in the company of his teacher.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says purity of mind and of deeds both come through purity of company. In the Jain verse, too, guarding thought, word and act and wearing away sin happen within that good company.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.14.16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, all filth is removed.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that the Saadh Sangat washes away the filth of vice from the mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says purity of mind and of deeds comes through purity of company; Guru Arjan says holy company is what cleanses a person.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus’s scouts eat the lotus offered by the Lotus-eaters, lose all wish to return home, and have to be dragged back to the ships.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sharing the ways of a certain people dissolves both their purpose (mind) and their duty (action).
greek_mythology.tie_back: This illustrates how company undermines both of the purities the Kural names.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I come home more greedy, more ambitious, more voluptuous, and even more cruel and inhuman, — because I have been among human beings.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca confesses that mixing with the crowd leaves him morally worse in both desire and conduct.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a first-person witness to the Kural’s claim that purity of mind and of action depend on one’s company.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 7 (trans. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: The Clapham Sect campaigns against the slave trade
real_life_example.event: A group of evangelical Christians living near one another in Clapham, south London, including William Wilberforce, the banker Henry Thornton, James Stephen and Zachary Macaulay, centred their lives on shared worship and public causes. Many of them sat in Parliament, where they campaigned for decades against the slave trade and for reforms such as prison reform, while funding schools and missionary and Bible societies. They played a large part in the abolition of the British slave trade in 1807 and of slavery in the British Empire in 1833.
real_life_example.explanation: The members sustained one another through long years of defeat, showing how a close circle of committed people can keep both conviction and action on course.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says purity of mind and purity of deeds are both supported by the purity of one's company, and the Clapham neighbours kept each other's purpose and conduct steady.

tamil:
மனந்தூயார்க் கெச்சம்நன் றாகும் இனந்தூயார்க்
கில்லைநன் றாகா வினை.
transliteration:
Mananthooyaark kechcham nanraagum inanthooyaark
Killai nanraakaa vinai.
meaning: People with pure minds leave behind a good name for those who come after them. People who keep pure company never do anything that is not good.
elementary: People with clean hearts leave good things behind them: good children, a good name. People whose friends are good never end up doing bad things, because their friends keep them on track.
university: எச்சம் (‘that which remains’) is read by Parimelazhagar as good progeny, and by others as the good name that outlives a person; both senses make purity of mind a matter of legacy. The second line is sharper: for those with pure company there is no deed that is not good (இல்லை நன்றாகா வினை). The double negative is emphatic. Good company does not merely encourage good action; it rules out bad action. The couplet divides the labour: the mind decides what one leaves behind, and company decides what one does.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that a sincere seeker who falls short in this life is reborn into a family of the pure and prosperous, or even into a family of wise yogis.
hinduism.explanation: Purity of mind is rewarded with a good lineage and a good circle in which to continue.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s link between a pure mind and a good ‘eccham’ (continuation or posterity).

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit. A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that what a person produces flows from what they are.
christianity.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s claim that a pure source leaves good fruit, and its double negative (‘cannot bring forth evil fruit’).

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that when a person dies, their deeds end except for three: ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge, or a righteous child who prays for them.
islam.explanation: A good legacy (the righteous child, lasting good) continues after death.
islam.tie_back: This corresponds closely to Parimelazhagar’s reading of எச்சம் as good progeny.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Blessed is the man that feareth the LORD… His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed.”
judaism.explanation: The upright leave a blessed posterity behind them.
judaism.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that the pure-minded leave a good எச்சம்.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If with a pure mind a person speaks or acts happiness follows him like his never-departing shadow.”
buddhism.explanation: Deeds done from a pure mind leave an unbroken trail of good results.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see a pure mind as producing lasting good consequences.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who adopts the conduct which the wise ones have attained by their virtues and always practised, will not incur blame.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline promises that one who takes on the conduct practised by the wise will do nothing that deserves blame.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's second line says those whose company is pure do no deed that is not good. The Jain verse likewise says that following the wise keeps one free of blameworthy acts.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.42 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, one's feet do not wander.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that in holy company a person does not step onto crooked paths; commentators gloss the line as not taking a step towards wrongdoing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those whose company is pure do no deed that is not good; Guru Arjan likewise says that in pure company one's steps do not go astray.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The pious old couple Baucis and Philemon welcome disguised gods. Their cottage becomes a temple, and at death they are turned into an intertwined oak and linden that are honoured ever after.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pure hearts leave a lasting and venerated legacy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s ‘eccham’, the good that outlives the pure-minded.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The friendship of good men is good, being augmented by their companionship.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says good men grow better together, taking on from each other the traits they admire, whereas bad men become worse by growing alike.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s second line: those in good company are held to good action.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.12 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The White Rose student resistance in Munich
real_life_example.event: In 1942 a small circle of friends at the University of Munich, including Hans and Sophie Scholl, Alexander Schmorell, Christoph Probst, Willi Graf and their professor Kurt Huber, wrote and secretly distributed leaflets urging Germans to oppose the Nazi regime. On 18 February 1943 Hans and Sophie Scholl were caught distributing the sixth leaflet at the university. They and other members were tried by the People's Court and put to death in 1943, and they are now honoured in Germany as examples of moral courage.
real_life_example.explanation: A group of friends held one another to a standard of conscience at a time when most people stayed silent, and they left a lasting example.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the pure-minded leave a good legacy and those whose company is pure do no deed that is not good, and the White Rose circle acted together and is remembered together.

tamil:
மனநலம் மன்னுயிர்க் காக்கம் இனநலம்
எல்லாப் புகழுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Mananalam mannuyirk kaakkam inanalam
Ellaap pugazhum tharum.
meaning: A good mind brings a person success and plenty. Good friends bring them every kind of praise and fame.
elementary: A good heart helps you do well in life. But good friends give you something extra: they help people everywhere know and respect you.
university: Here the parallelism moves from purity (தூய்மை) to goodness (நலம்), and the rewards from legacy to worldly outcomes: ஆக்கம் (prosperity, growth) from the mind, எல்லாப் புகழும் (every kind of fame) from company. The word எல்லா (‘all’) quietly ranks the second above the first. Prosperity may be private, but fame is by nature social and so depends on one’s circle. The couplet explains why reputation, discussed in 453, is not just vanity: in the Porul context of kingship and public life, renown is a resource, and it flows through association.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Vibhishana, righteous in mind, leaves his brother Ravana’s court and takes refuge with Rama. Through that company he wins the throne of Lanka and lasting honour as a model devotee.
hinduism.explanation: His goodness of mind was real, but his renown came through the company he joined.
hinduism.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s two rewards exactly: mind gives worth, and company gives fame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Ordinary fishermen are recognised and honoured because of the company they had kept.
christianity.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that goodness of company confers renown.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the first forerunners [in the faith] among the Muhajireen and the Ansar and those who followed them with good conduct — Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him.”
islam.explanation: The early community, and those who followed them in goodness, are honoured as a group.
islam.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s idea that honour comes through belonging to a good company.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ruth the Moabite binds herself to Naomi (‘whither thou goest, I will go’), joins Naomi’s people, and becomes the great-grandmother of King David.
judaism.explanation: Her loyal goodness, joined to a good household, led to a renowned lineage.
judaism.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s claim that goodness of company brings renown.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie is actually the whole of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: When Ananda suggests that good friendship is half of the spiritual life, the Buddha corrects him: it is the whole.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats good company as the source of every good, not just a helpful extra.
buddhism.source: Upaddha Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 45.2 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Even the hare in the wide, beauteous, and sublime heavens, since it is seen in the moon with refulgent beams, will be adored (by men). And in like manner even those who are without any dignity (of their own), if they obtain the love of the good, who are as mountains of virtue, will have dignity.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar says that just as the hare seen on the moon is honoured because of the moon, people who have no standing of their own gain dignity through the affection of the good.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says goodness of company brings every kind of renown. The Naladiyar's hare in the moon shows good company conferring honour on someone who would otherwise have none.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 6 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The poor castor oil plant, growing near the sandalwood tree, becomes fragrant; in the same way, the sinner, associating with the Saints, becomes acceptable and approved.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says even the lowly castor plant takes on sandalwood's fragrance, and even a sinner gains honour and acceptance through the company of the saints.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says good company brings every kind of renown; Guru Ram Das shows company raising even the humblest to honour and approval.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 861, Raag Gond, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Patroclus, the companion of Achilles, wins lasting fame in the Iliad; his name is bound up with that of the greatest of the Achaeans.
greek_mythology.explanation: His glory is closely tied to the company he kept.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This illustrates the Kural’s point that renown flows through good association.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells Lucilius to choose companions who raise him up.
philosophy.tie_back: This shares the Kural’s view that goodness of company is a source of advancement.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 7 (trans. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: The first Impressionist exhibition
real_life_example.event: Frustrated by the official Salon, a group of about thirty artists formed a cooperative society and opened their own exhibition in the former studio of the photographer Nadar on the boulevard des Capucines. Among them were Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Camille Pissarro, Paul Cezanne and Berthe Morisot. The show drew few visitors and hostile reviews, and a critic mocked the group as impressionists after Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, but the name stuck and the group went on to hold eight exhibitions by 1886.
real_life_example.explanation: Artists who would have struggled alone gained a shared identity, a platform and eventually world fame by showing together.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says goodness of company brings every kind of renown, and the Impressionists' fame came to them as a group, under a single name.

tamil:
மனநலம் நன்குடைய ராயினும் சான்றோர்க்கு
இனநலம் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Mananalam nankudaiya raayinum saanrorkku
Inanalam emaap pudaiththu.
meaning: Even people of good character who already have a very good mind find that good friends make them safer and stronger.
elementary: Even very good and wise people still need good friends. Good company works like a protective wall that keeps their goodness safe.
university: The concessive ஆயினும் (‘even though’) blocks the obvious objection: surely the already-good (சான்றோர்) do not need company? Valluvar replies that for them too, இனநலம் is ஏமாப்பு, security or fortification. The word suggests protection against the slow wearing-down of virtue by circumstance. Virtue, on this view, is not a fixed possession but a condition to be kept up, and company is part of the upkeep. The couplet guards against the moral self-sufficiency that 454 already undercut.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Arjuna, the greatest archer of his age and a man of dharma, collapses into confusion on the battlefield and is restored only by Krishna, who rides beside him as charioteer and friend.
hinduism.explanation: Even the most capable and righteous hero needs a steadying companion at the decisive moment.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point that good company is a fortress even for the good.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together.”
christianity.explanation: Believers, including the mature, are to keep gathering so they can spur each other to goodness.
christianity.tie_back: In both texts even the virtuous need a good community to support their goodness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And keep yourself patient [by being] with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His countenance.”
islam.explanation: Even the Prophet, the best-minded of men, is told to stay in the company of sincere worshippers and not follow the heedless.
islam.tie_back: This is a direct parallel to ‘even for the wise, good company is a fortress’.

judaism.quote_or_event: Honi the Circle-Maker, a holy man, sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, no one recognises or respects him, and he prays for death. The Talmud concludes: ‘either companionship or death’.
judaism.explanation: Even a saint cannot flourish without a fitting circle.
judaism.tie_back: This makes the Kural’s point in its strongest form: even the virtuous depend on good company.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a seeker not find a companion who is better or equal, let him resolutely pursue a solitary course; there is no fellowship with the fool.”
buddhism.explanation: The committed seeker should look for good or better companions, and prefer solitude to a foolish one.
buddhism.tie_back: This shares the Kural’s high valuation of good company and its rejection of bad. It differs in allowing solitude as an alternative.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Sramana engaged in austerities, who longs for righteousness, should eat the proper quantity of allowed food, should select a companion of right understanding, and should live in a place suited to seclusion.” … “If he does not meet with a clever companion who surpasses or equals him in virtue, he should live by himself, abstaining from sins and not devoted to pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: Even the ascetic already devoted to austerity and righteousness is told to choose a companion of right understanding, ideally one equal or superior in virtue. Jainism also allows him to live alone rather than accept a lesser companion.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says that even for the already virtuous, good company is a source of security. The Jain text likewise has even the advanced ascetic seek a worthy companion, though it qualifies the need more than Valluvar does.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.4–5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, the mind becomes stable.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that the Saadh Sangat steadies the mind so that it stops wandering.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says even the already-virtuous gain security and strength from good company; Guru Arjan presents holy company as the steadying support of the mind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Diomedes volunteers for the night raid on the Trojan camp, he asks for a companion, saying that when two go together one sees before the other what is best. He chooses Odysseus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even the bravest hero knows that a good companion multiplies judgement and safety.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s ‘fortress’ of good company, even for the excellent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that even the supremely happy good man needs friends, since no one would choose to have all goods on condition of being alone. Man is a political creature whose nature is to live with others.
philosophy.explanation: Self-sufficiency does not remove the need for good company, even at the height of virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the same claim as the Kural: even the sanror are fortified by good company.

real_life_example.event_title: Marcel Grossmann helps Einstein with the mathematics of general relativity
real_life_example.event: As students at the Zurich Polytechnic, Albert Einstein often missed lectures and relied on the careful notes of his friend Marcel Grossmann to prepare for exams. In 1912, when Einstein returned to Zurich with the physical ideas for a new theory of gravity but not the mathematics to express it, he turned to Grossmann, by then a professor of geometry, who guided him through the relevant mathematical literature. In 1913 they published a joint paper outlining the theory, with Einstein writing the physics and Grossmann the mathematical part.
real_life_example.explanation: Even one of the most original minds in history needed a trusted friend at crucial moments to make progress.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even for the wise, who already have goodness of mind, good company is a source of security and strength, and Grossmann was that support for Einstein.

tamil:
மனநலத்தின் ஆகும் மறுமைமற் றஃதும்
இனநலத்தின் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Mananalaththin aakum marumaimat rahdhum
Inanalaththin emaap pudaiththu.
meaning: A good mind earns a happy life in the next world. Even that is made safe by keeping good company.
elementary: A good heart earns you happiness after this life. But good friends make that happiness even more certain by helping you stay good all the way through.
university: The previous couplet made good company a fortress for virtue in this life; this one extends the claim to மறுமை, the next world. Even the reward that seems most purely individual, earned by one’s own inner goodness (மனநலம்), is secured (ஏமாப்பு, repeated from 458) by one’s company. The மற்று… அஃதும் (‘and even that’) is emphatic. The pairing of 458 and 459 moves from this world to the next and leaves no domain where company does not matter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “satsaṅgatve nissaṅgatvaṃ nissaṅgatve nirmohatvam | nirmohatve niścalatattvaṃ niścalatattve jīvanmuktiḥ”
hinduism.explanation: Shankara’s verse traces a chain: from good company comes detachment, from detachment freedom from delusion, from that steadiness in truth, and from that liberation.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s claim that the highest spiritual attainment is secured through good company.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.”
christianity.explanation: The repentant thief, crucified next to Jesus, turns to him and receives the promise of paradise in his company.
christianity.tie_back: Salvation here comes through a change of heart and is sealed by the company he is with, which parallels the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: When a man asked the Prophet when the Hour would come, the Prophet asked what he had prepared for it. The man said only his love of Allah and His Messenger, and the Prophet replied that he would be with those he loved.
islam.explanation: The company one loves in this life decides one’s company in the next.
islam.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that good company secures the afterlife.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The fellowship of the God-fearing is itself recorded for their future reward.
judaism.tie_back: This links good company to one’s standing in the world to come, as the Kural does.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not to associate with fools, to associate with the wise, and to honor those who are worthy of honor — this is the highest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Mangala Sutta puts right association first in its ladder of blessings, which ends in the realisation of Nibbana.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the path to the ultimate good begins with and is secured by good company.
buddhism.source: Mangala Sutta, Khuddakapatha 5 / Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “His knowledge will be honoured, his doubts will be removed, he will gladden the heart of his teacher by his good acts; kept in safety by the performance of austerities and by meditation, being as it were a great light, he will keep the five vows.” … “Honoured by gods, Gandharvas, and men, he will, on leaving this body which consists of dirt and impurities, become either an eternal Siddha, or a god of great power and small imperfections.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline ends by following the disciple who has served his teachers beyond death, to rebirth as a powerful god or to final liberation as a Siddha.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says bliss in the world to come is earned by goodness of mind and made secure by good company. The Jain disciple's reward after death likewise comes through his own vows and his bond with his teachers.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.47–48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, one meets the Incomprehensible Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that union with God, the highest spiritual goal, is reached within the Saadh Sangat.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says even bliss in the world to come is made secure by goodness of company; Guru Arjan makes holy company the place where the soul meets God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Proteus tells Menelaus that he will not die in Argos but be taken to the Elysian plain, because he is Helen’s husband and so son-in-law of Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A blessed afterlife granted because of whom one is joined to.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a near-literal case of the next world secured by association, though it is kinship, not moral company.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates, facing death, says that if death leads to a place where he can talk with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod and Homer, he would be willing to die again and again.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, the good of the next world is largely the company of the good and wise.
philosophy.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s link between the afterlife and good company.

real_life_example.event_title: Geert Groote and the Brethren of the Common Life
real_life_example.event: After a religious conversion in 1374, the Dutch preacher Geert Groote gave up his worldly goods and began the movement later called the Devotio Moderna, which stressed meditation and the inner life. With his friend Florentius Radewyns he gathered followers who lived together, copied manuscripts for their living and prayed in common, forming the Brethren of the Common Life. The community shaped later figures such as Thomas a Kempis, the probable author of The Imitation of Christ.
real_life_example.explanation: The movement was built on the idea that a devout life is best sustained by living and working alongside others who share it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even blessedness in the world to come, earned by goodness of mind, is made secure by good company, which is the very principle on which the Brethren lived.

tamil:
நல்லினத்தி னூங்குந் துணையில்லை தீயினத்தின்
அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்.
transliteration:
Nallinaththin oongum thunaiyillai theeyinaththin
Allar paduppadhooum il.
meaning: Nothing helps a person more than good friends, and nothing causes more pain and trouble than bad friends.
elementary: Good friends are the best help you can ever have. Bad friends are the worst trouble you can ever have. Nothing else comes close in either direction.
university: The chapter ends with a symmetrical superlative: nothing surpasses (ஊங்கு) good company as a support (துணை), and nothing causes as much suffering (அல்லல்) as bad company. The emphatic lengthening in படுப்பதூஉம் (an alapedai, or metrical vowel extension) stresses the second half, so the warning weighs more than the praise, in keeping with the chapter title. The couplet sums up the whole adhikaram and connects it to chapter 45: seek the great, avoid the small, because nothing else in life has as much power to help or harm.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Hitopadesha, a deer befriends a smooth-talking jackal against the advice of his true friend, the crow. The jackal leads him into a hunter’s snare, and only the crow’s cleverness saves him.
hinduism.explanation: The fable sets the true friend’s help against the false friend’s harm.
hinduism.tie_back: This illustrates both halves of the Kural: good company is the greatest help and bad company the greatest danger.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb sets out both outcomes: wisdom from wise company and ruin from foolish company.
christianity.tie_back: Its two-part structure mirrors the Kural’s two-part verdict.

islam.quote_or_event: “Close friends, that Day, will be enemies to each other, except for the righteous.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement, friendships built on wrongdoing turn into enmity, while righteous friendships last.
islam.tie_back: Both texts say bad company brings the greatest harm and good company the most lasting support.

judaism.quote_or_event: Nittai of Arbel taught: keep far from an evil neighbour, do not attach yourself to the wicked, and do not give up belief in retribution.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah’s ethical teaching warns against closeness to the wicked because of the calamity it brings.
judaism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s warning that bad company brings more suffering than anything else.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Association with fools is ever painful, like partnership with an enemy. But association with the wise is happy, like meeting one’s own kinsmen.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the pain of foolish company with the joy of wise company.
buddhism.tie_back: This is a two-sided verdict matching the Kural almost exactly.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Like paddy multiplied through the goodness of the soil, persons will become good through the goodness of their respective families. Like the destruction of a good ship on the approach of a strong gale, goodness will be destroyed by bad company.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar sets the growth of goodness through a good setting against the way bad company wrecks goodness, like a ship broken by a gale.
jainism.tie_back: This mirrors the closing superlative of the kural, where nothing helps more than good company and nothing harms more than bad. The Naladiyar sets the same two outcomes side by side.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 9 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, associate with the Holy people, who will take you to Nirvaanaa in the end. Do not associate with the faithless cynics; they would bring you to ruin.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir sets the two kinds of company side by side: holy company stays with you to the end and brings liberation, while the company of the faithless brings destruction.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ends the chapter by saying no help is greater than good company and nothing causes more affliction than bad company; Kabir gives the same two-sided verdict.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stranded on Thrinacia, Odysseus’s crew follow Eurylochus’s bad counsel and slaughter the cattle of Helios. Zeus destroys the ship and all of them; only Odysseus, who refused, survives.
greek_mythology.explanation: Following a bad companion’s lead brings total ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This illustrates the Kural’s second half: nothing afflicts like bad company.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates asks Meletus whether it is not true that the good do good to those near them and the evil do evil, and whether anyone would rather be harmed than helped by those he lives with.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates takes it as obvious that one’s companions are the nearest source of both benefit and harm.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the same two-sided principle as the Kural.

real_life_example.event_title: Narendranath Datta meets Sri Ramakrishna
real_life_example.event: In 1881 Narendranath Datta, a college student troubled by religious doubt, went to meet the teacher Sri Ramakrishna at the Kali temple in Dakshineswar. He became a frequent visitor and disciple, and Ramakrishna chose him as leader of his young followers. After Ramakrishna's death in 1886 Narendranath led them into a monastic brotherhood and, as Swami Vivekananda, went on to found the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.
real_life_example.explanation: One meeting and the friendship that followed turned a doubting student into one of modern India's most influential spiritual leaders.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says there is no greater help than good company, and the company of Ramakrishna shaped the whole course of Vivekananda's life.

tamil:
அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ஆகி வழிபயக்கும்
ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து செயல்.
transliteration:
Azhivadhooum aavadhooum aaki vazhipayakkum,
Oodhiyamum soozhndhu seyal.
meaning: Before you do something, think about what you will lose, what you will gain, and what good will be left in the end. Only then begin.
elementary: Before you start something, ask three questions: What might I lose? What will I get? And after everything is added up, will it really be worth it? Only when you have thought about all three should you begin.
university: The opening couplet sets out a three-part calculus that governs the whole chapter: அழிவது (what is spent or destroyed at the outset — the cost), ஆவது (what comes into being — the gain), and வழிபயக்கும் ஊதியம் (the profit that results in due course — the net yield after costs are subtracted). The verb சூழ் (to deliberate, to survey all round) is the chapter’s keyword. Parimelazhagar reads the triad as capital outlay, return, and eventual surplus, which makes this one of the earliest cost-benefit formulations in world ethical literature. Placed in the Porul (polity) section, the kural is addressed first to rulers, but it is phrased generally enough to apply to any undertaking. The point is not to avoid risk but to see the whole ledger before committing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhagavad Gita 18.25 describes “tamasic” action as action begun out of delusion, without regard to its consequences, the loss it will cause, the injury to others, and one’s own capacity.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna ranks actions by the quality of mind behind them. The lowest kind is the one started blindly, without counting cost, consequence, harm, or whether you are even able to do it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita lists the very factors the Kural tells us to weigh (loss, outcome, capacity) and condemns action that ignores them.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses an everyday picture: no sensible builder starts a tower without first sitting down and working out whether he can afford to finish it.
christianity.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s instruction to reckon cost against outcome before starting.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught his companions the istikhara prayer for every matter of consequence: before deciding, one asks God for the better course, naming whether the matter is good or bad “for my religion, my livelihood and the outcome of my affairs.”
islam.explanation: Muslims are taught to pause before important decisions and ask God to guide them toward what is good in its consequences and away from what is harmful.
islam.tie_back: Istikhara builds a deliberate pause and a weighing of outcomes into the start of any undertaking, as the Kural requires.

judaism.quote_or_event: Alexander the Great asked the Elders of the South who deserves to be called wise. They answered: the one who sees what will result (ha-ro’eh et ha-nolad) — who anticipates the consequences of his conduct.
judaism.explanation: For the rabbis, wisdom isn’t just knowing a lot; it’s seeing ahead to what your actions will produce.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘வழிபயக்கும் ஊதியம்’ — what an action yields down the road — is exactly what the rabbis’ wise man foresees.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells his son Rahula to reflect before any bodily, verbal or mental act: would this lead to my own affliction, to the affliction of others, or both? If so, it is unskillful and should not be done; if not, it may be done.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches a child to use his actions like a mirror — look at them before, during and after, and check whether they will cause harm.
buddhism.tie_back: A formal ‘check before you act’ procedure, weighing results before committing, like the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Three merchants set out on their travels, each with his capital; one of them gained there much, the second returned with his capital, and the third merchant came home after having lost his capital. This parable is taken from common life; learn (to apply it) to the Law.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's sermon uses a merchant's ledger of capital, gain and loss to teach how a human life should be spent, and closes by saying the wise man weighs the outcomes in his mind before choosing his course (7.30).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's three-part reckoning of what is spent, what is gained and the net profit matches the parable's capital, profit and loss almost term for term.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.14–15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not do any evil at all; look ahead to the future with foresight. So throw the dice in such a way, that you shall not lose with your Lord and Master. Do those deeds which shall bring you profit.”
sikhism.explanation: In a pauri of Asa Ki Vaar, Guru Nanak tells the seeker to look far ahead before acting, to play life's game so as not to lose, and to do only what yields profit.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks for a reckoning of cost, gain and final yield before acting; Guru Nanak likewise asks for long foresight and deeds chosen for their profit.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus (‘Forethought’) warned his brother Epimetheus (‘Afterthought’) never to accept a gift from Zeus; Epimetheus accepted Pandora anyway and only understood the harm once it had come.
greek_mythology.explanation: The two brothers’ names say it all: one thinks before, the other thinks after. The one who thinks after lets disaster into the world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural asks us to be Prometheus — to calculate outcomes before acting, not after.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Benjamin Franklin’s “moral or prudential algebra”: divide a sheet into Pro and Con columns, list the reasons on each side over several days, strike out items of equal weight against each other, and see where the balance lies before deciding.
philosophy.explanation: Franklin gave a friend a practical method for hard decisions: write down everything for and against, cancel out equal items, and see what remains.
philosophy.tie_back: A literal written version of the Kural’s ledger of loss, gain, and resulting profit.
philosophy.source: Benjamin Franklin, letter to Joseph Priestley, 19 September 1772

real_life_example.event_title: Disraeli buys Egypt's Suez Canal shares for Britain
real_life_example.event: When Egypt's ruler Isma'il Pasha, deep in debt, put up for sale his country's shares in the Suez Canal Company, nearly half of all its shares, the British government under Benjamin Disraeli bought them for about four million pounds. The Foreign Office had advised against the purchase, and because Parliament was not sitting, Disraeli obtained the money as a loan from the banking house of N. M. Rothschild and Sons, which the government repaid within months.
real_life_example.explanation: A large immediate outlay bought Britain a major stake in the shortest sea route to India, a gain that shaped its policy in the region for decades.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks a ruler to set what will be spent against what will be gained and the yield that follows, and Disraeli's purchase was a case of paying a heavy price now for a lasting strategic return.

tamil:
தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு
அரும்பொருள் யாதொன்றும் இல்.
transliteration:
Therindha inaththotu therndhennich cheyvaarkku,
Arumporul yaadhondrum il.
meaning: Nothing is too hard for people who first talk things over with carefully chosen advisers and then study the matter themselves before they act.
elementary: If you pick good, trustworthy friends, talk your plan over with them, and think it through yourself too, there is almost nothing you cannot get done.
university: The couplet joins two acts of discernment: தெரிந்த இனம் (a circle that has itself been tested and chosen — echoing the preceding chapters on seeking the help of the great and avoiding mean company, 44–46) and தேர்ந்து எண்ணி (having examined and reasoned). Counsel is only as good as the counsellors, so selection comes before consultation. The strong universal claim (‘no object is hard to attain’) is typical of Valluvar’s rhetoric, which states the ideal case to motivate the practice. The idea of the ruler’s council (mantra) was a central institution of classical Indian statecraft, and the Kural places it at the heart of deliberate action.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya opens his chapter on counsel by teaching that all undertakings of state should be preceded by deliberation in a properly constituted council, and that counsel should be kept secret and taken with tested ministers.
hinduism.explanation: India’s classic manual of government says a king should never act on big matters alone: he should first talk them through with carefully chosen, trustworthy advisers.
hinduism.tie_back: Same pairing as the Kural: chosen counsellors plus deliberation before action.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.”
christianity.explanation: Plans fail when people make them alone; they succeed when many wise advisers help shape them.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s promise that consultation makes goals achievable.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an describes the believers as those “whose affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves” (shura).
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises communities that decide their shared matters by talking them over together rather than by one person’s whim.
islam.tie_back: Shura is the Islamic institution of deliberating with others before acting.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.”
judaism.explanation: A nation without good advice collapses; with many wise advisers it stays safe.
judaism.tie_back: Same principle as the Kural, applied to national affairs.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjians, the Buddha says they will prosper and not decline so long as they meet together often, meet in harmony, and conduct their business in harmony.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a people who regularly gather and decide things together, in agreement, will be very hard to defeat.
buddhism.tie_back: Collective, well-ordered deliberation makes a group strong, as in the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sūtras.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's path to deliverance begins with choosing one's company: serve the teachers, shun fools, study, and reflect. The next verses tell the monk to select a companion of right understanding who equals or surpasses him in virtue (32.4–5).
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it joins careful choice of counsellors with one's own examination and reflection as the way to reach what is otherwise hard to attain.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.3 (cf. 32.4–5) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The chosen ones, the self-elect, are accepted and approved. The chosen ones are honored in the Court of the Lord. … The chosen ones meditate single-mindedly on the Guru.”
sikhism.explanation: In the sixteenth pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak praises the panch, the chosen ones whose minds are fixed on the Guru, as accepted and pre-eminent. Later Sikh tradition took the five chosen Sikhs as the model for weighty collective decisions.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says nothing is hard for those who deliberate with a well-chosen circle; Japji Sahib honours just such a tested, chosen company.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib (pauri 16), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Volunteering for the night raid on the Trojan camp, Diomedes asks for a companion, saying that when two go together one sees the advantage before the other, while a man alone has thinner wit; he picks Odysseus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Diomedes chooses the cleverest partner he can find, because two minds notice what one would miss.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Choosing the right companion to think with before a risky action is the Kural’s point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We deliberate not about ends but about means.” Aristotle adds that on important questions we call in others to help us deliberate, distrusting our own ability to decide alone.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says real deliberation is working out how to reach a goal, and for big decisions sensible people ask others for help.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s deliberation with others mirrors the Kural’s deliberation with a chosen circle.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.3 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Delta Committee plans the Netherlands' Delta Works
real_life_example.event: After the North Sea flood of 1 February 1953 killed more than 1,800 people in the Netherlands, the government set up a Delta Committee of experts led by the director-general of Rijkswaterstaat, A. G. Maris, within weeks. Its studies produced the Delta Plan in 1955, which became law in 1958, and over the following decades engineers built a chain of dams, sluices and storm-surge barriers, ending with the Eastern Scheldt barrier in 1986.
real_life_example.explanation: A task once thought impossible, closing off the sea arms of the southwestern delta while keeping key shipping routes open, was achieved through years of study by a chosen body of specialists.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural promises that nothing is too hard for those who deliberate with well-chosen counsellors and examine matters themselves, and the Delta Works grew from exactly such a committee.

tamil:
ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை
ஊக்கார் அறிவுடை யார்.
transliteration:
Aakkam karudhi mudhalizhakkum seyvinai,
Ookkaar arivutai yaar.
meaning: Wise people will not take on a project that risks losing the money they already have just in the hope of making more later.
elementary: Smart people don’t risk everything they already have just because they hope to win something bigger. They protect what they have first.
university: The pairing ஆக்கம் (gain, increase) and முதல் (principal, capital) is commercial vocabulary and continues the ledger of 461. The verb ஊக்கார் (‘they will not be eager to / will not set about’) matters: Valluvar does not ban all risk, but says the wise will not be enthusiastic for ventures where the principal itself is at stake. This is a rule of prudence rather than timidity. It tells a ruler not to gamble the treasury or the kingdom’s security on speculative expansion. Later chapters praise energy and persistence (ஊக்கம், chapter 60), so the teaching is best read as ‘secure the base before seeking growth’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A saying attributed to Chanakya warns that whoever abandons what is certain in pursuit of what is uncertain loses the certain, and the uncertain is lost as well.
hinduism.explanation: If you drop what you surely have to chase something you only might get, you can end up with nothing.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s warning against losing capital while chasing gain.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want.”
christianity.explanation: Careful planners end up with plenty, but people who rush after quick gain end up poor.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it contrasts steady, careful increase with hasty ventures that lead to loss.

islam.quote_or_event: On wine and gambling (maysir) the Qur’an says there is great sin in them and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.
islam.explanation: The Qur’an admits gambling can bring some gain, but says the harm is bigger, so it should be given up.
islam.tie_back: Gambling is the clearest case of risking what one has for hoped-for profit, which the Kural tells the wise to avoid.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Isaac taught that a person should always divide his money into three parts: a third in land, a third in merchandise, and a third kept at hand.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud advises spreading your wealth so no single venture can wipe you out.
judaism.tie_back: Protecting the principal while still seeking gain is the practical heart of the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha advises the householder Sigala to divide his wealth into four parts: one to enjoy, two to invest in his work, and the fourth to keep in reserve against misfortune.
buddhism.explanation: Even the Buddha told lay people to save part of their money for hard times instead of putting it all at risk.
buddhism.tie_back: Keeping a reserve so that the principal survives is the Kural’s concern.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a man for the sake of one Kâkinî (risks and) loses a thousand (Kârshâpaṇas), or as the king lost his kingdom (and life) by eating a mango-fruit which he was strictly forbidden (by his physician)”
jainism.explanation: Two short examples show the folly of staking something great for a trifling gain: a thousand coins thrown away for a copper, a kingdom lost for one forbidden mango.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns the wise not to put their capital at risk for a hoped-for gain, and the Jain verse pictures exactly that bad bargain.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The self-willed manmukhs lose their capital, and still, they demand profits. How can they earn any profit?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das uses the trader's language of capital and profit: the self-willed squander their principal and still expect a return.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns against losing one's capital in the hope of future profit; Guru Amar Das calls it folly to lose the capital and still expect a gain.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1131, Raag Bhairao, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a dog carrying a piece of meat across a stream sees its reflection, snaps at the ‘bigger’ piece in the water, and drops the real one.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greedy dog lost the meat it had by grabbing for a bigger piece that wasn’t real.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A vivid picture of losing capital while reaching for imagined gain.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Dog and Its Reflection’ (Perry 133)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is, therefore, only a madman who, in a calm, would pray for a storm; a wise man's way is, when the storm does come, to withstand it with all the means at his command, and especially, when the advantages to be expected in case of a successful issue are greater than the hazards of the struggle.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero warns against exposing oneself to danger needlessly and says a risk is worth running only when the gain to be expected from success outweighs what is hazarded.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural's rule that the wise weigh what may be lost against what may be gained, and do not court ruin for the sake of a hoped-for profit.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book I, §83 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))

real_life_example.event_title: Long-Term Capital Management's leveraged bets collapse
real_life_example.event: The hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management earned thin margins on each trade and borrowed heavily to magnify them, holding about 30 dollars of debt for every dollar of its own capital by the end of 1997. After Russia's debt default in August 1998 set off market turmoil, the fund lost 44 percent of its value in that month alone. In September the Federal Reserve Bank of New York brought together fourteen banks and brokerages, which put about 3.6 billion dollars into the fund so that its holdings could be wound down in an orderly way.
real_life_example.explanation: The fund's pursuit of extra profit through borrowing put its own capital, and that of its lenders, at risk, and the losses came far faster than the gains had.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the wise will not chase future profit by risking the capital they already hold, which is exactly the risk that heavy borrowing created for this fund.

tamil:
தெளிவி லதனைத் தொடங்கார் இளிவென்னும்
ஏதப்பாடு அஞ்சு பவர்.
transliteration:
Thelivi ladhanaith thotangaar ilivennum,
Edhappaatu anju bavar.
meaning: People who are afraid of being shamed by failure will not start anything whose plan and outcome are not clear to them.
elementary: People who care about their good name don’t start things they don’t fully understand, because failing halfway would make them look foolish.
university: தெளிவு (clarity, certainty) is the key concept: an undertaking is ‘தெளிவு இலது’ when its means, outcome, or one’s own ability to finish it are uncertain. The motive for restraint is இளிவு (humiliation, contempt), described as an ஏதப்பாடு (a harm or calamity). Valluvar treats reputation as a real asset of the ruler, and public failure as damage to it, not just wounded pride. Commentators differ slightly. Parimelazhagar stresses that the doubtful venture ends in ridicule, while modern commentators such as Kalaignar read it more broadly as avoiding dishonourable acts. Both readings rest on the same logic: foreseeable shame is itself a cost to include in deliberation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna warns Arjuna that people will speak of his dishonour forever, and that for one who has been honoured, dishonour is worse than death.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reminds Arjuna that a respected person has a reputation to protect, and losing it is a terrible thing.
hinduism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s view of disgrace as a grave harm that must shape one’s choices.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says the builder who starts without checking his resources will be laughed at when the half-built tower stands unfinished.
christianity.tie_back: The very same motive the Kural gives: fear of public ridicule for an unfinished undertaking.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an commands: do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge; hearing, sight and heart will all be questioned.
islam.explanation: Don’t go after something you don’t really understand, because you will be held responsible for how you used your senses and mind.
islam.tie_back: Forbids acting without clear knowledge, as the Kural does, though the motive is accountability to God rather than fear of shame.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go not forth hastily to strive, lest thou know not what to do in the end thereof, when thy neighbour hath put thee to shame.”
judaism.explanation: Don’t rush into a dispute you aren’t sure how to finish, or you’ll end up embarrassed in front of others.
judaism.tie_back: Same logic as the Kural: an unclear beginning leads to shame at the end.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says a deed is not well done if one regrets it afterwards and reaps its fruit weeping; it is well done if one does not regret it and reaps its fruit with joy.
buddhism.explanation: A good action is one you won’t be sorry for later.
buddhism.tie_back: Thinking ahead to avoid later regret and grief is close to the Kural’s concern with avoiding later disgrace.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Dirgha-darsi : Far-sighted.” … “Salajja : Actuated by a sense of shame.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra's list of the qualities of an ideal Jain layman includes being far-sighted and being moved by a sense of shame, alongside not engaging in a reprehensible occupation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's prudent man avoids unclear ventures because he fears disgrace; Hemacandra's householder combines the same foresight with a lively sense of shame.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of the thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, those deeds which do not bring merit - forget about those deeds. Otherwise, you shall be put to shame, in the Court of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the seeker to drop any undertaking that brings no merit, lest it end in shame.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who fear disgrace will not begin unclear undertakings; Farid likewise steers clear of deeds that lead only to shame.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 59) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Bellerophon, after his triumphs, tried to ride Pegasus up to Olympus; Pegasus threw him, and he ended his life wandering alone and scorned.
greek_mythology.explanation: A hero tried something far beyond his reach and ended up disgraced and alone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An undertaking begun without regard to its real prospects ends in humiliation, as the Kural warns.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises: in every affair consider what comes before and what follows, then undertake it; otherwise you will begin eagerly, and when difficulties appear you will give up shamefully.
philosophy.explanation: Think a project through first, or you’ll start with excitement and quit in embarrassment.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s link between lack of clarity at the start and disgrace at the end.

real_life_example.event_title: The warship Vasa sinks on her maiden voyage
real_life_example.event: A few weeks before the Swedish royal warship Vasa sailed, Admiral Klas Fleming had thirty men run back and forth across her deck to test her stability, and onlookers could see that she failed the test. The ship sailed anyway, and within minutes of setting out on her first voyage a gust of wind heeled her over, water poured in through the open lower gunports, and she sank in Stockholm harbour in front of a large crowd. Around 30 of those on board died, and the wreck was raised in 1961 and is now displayed in the Vasa Museum.
real_life_example.explanation: The most powerful warship in the Baltic became a public humiliation for the Swedish crown because doubts about whether she could sail safely were never resolved before she set out.
