real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that those who fear disgrace do not begin a venture whose outcome is unclear, and the Vasa sailed with exactly such an unresolved doubt and ended in public disgrace.

tamil:
வகையறச் சூழா தெழுதல் பகைவரைப்
பாத்திப் படுப்பதோ ராறு.
transliteration:
Vakaiyarach choozhaa thezhudhal pakaivaraip,
Paaththip patuppadho raaru.
meaning: Rushing to fight enemies without planning every step is like preparing a field for them to grow strong in.
elementary: If you rush to fight someone without planning properly, you actually help them — like planting a seed in good soil and watering it so it grows bigger.
university: The metaphor is agricultural. பாத்தி is a prepared garden bed, and பாத்திப் படுத்தல் means settling a plant in such a bed so it takes root. A poorly planned attack does not just fail. It strengthens the enemy, who gains confidence, allies, and legitimacy from beating back a rash assault. வகையற (exhaustively, covering every category) points to the sixfold considerations of statecraft (strength, place, time, means, allies, and so on) that commentators read into the phrase. Pope renders it: ‘With plans not well matured to rise against your foe, / Is way to plant him out where he is sure to grow!’ It is the chapter’s one explicitly military couplet.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya teaches that before marching, the conqueror must assess his own and the enemy’s relative strength, the suitability of place and time, the season for campaigning, and possible revolts and losses.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra says a king should work out many factors before going to war, not just whether he is angry or brave.
hinduism.tie_back: An itemised version of the Kural’s ‘வகையற’ — deliberating every category before rising against a foe.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: A wise king works out whether his army can win before he marches. If it can’t, he seeks peace instead.
christianity.tie_back: Same scenario as the Kural: deliberate fully before rising against an enemy.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an instructs the believers to prepare against their enemies whatever strength they can, including steeds of war, so as to deter them.
islam.explanation: Muslims are told to get properly ready before facing an enemy, not to rush in unprepared.
islam.tie_back: Preparation before confrontation is the Kural’s point, though the Qur’an stresses deterrence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Every purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war.” And: “For by wise counsel thou shalt make thy war.”
judaism.explanation: The Bible says plans hold up when made with advice, and that war especially should be waged only with good counsel.
judaism.tie_back: Directly applies deliberation before action to going to war.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Before attacking the Vajjians, King Ajatasattu sends his minister Vassakara to ask the Buddha. After hearing the seven conditions that keep the Vajjians strong, the minister concludes they cannot be defeated by force alone.
buddhism.explanation: Even an ambitious king checked first whether his attack could work, and the answer showed him it couldn’t.
buddhism.tie_back: A narrative case of assessing an enemy’s strength before rising against it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable; making Zeal his bow, its string Carefulness in walking (iriyâ), and its top (where the string is fastened) Content, he should bend (this bow) with Truth, piercing with the arrow, Penance, (the foe's) mail, Karman--(in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Saṃsâra.”
jainism.explanation: When Indra urges King Nami to fortify his city, Nami answers that the real campaign is fought against karma, and he lists in detail the fortress, wall, bow, string and arrow it requires.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's warning against attacking a foe without thorough planning, Nami's war against karma is to be fought only once every defence and weapon has been prepared.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.20–22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: After Guru Arjan's execution, Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, bore two swords for temporal and spiritual authority, trained in arms, built up a Sikh army, fortified his towns and in 1609 built the Akal Takht at Amritsar, recognizing that a clash with Mughal power was coming. Britannica records that his Sikhs later defeated Shah Jahan's armies four times.
sikhism.explanation: Guru Hargobind did not rush into conflict after his father's martyrdom. He first prepared, militarily and institutionally, for a confrontation he saw coming.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that rising against foes without full preparation only strengthens them; Guru Hargobind's long preparation before facing Mughal forces shows the opposite course.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Guru Hargobind" (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Adrastus led the Seven against Thebes although the seer Amphiaraus foresaw that the expedition would fail. Six of the seven champions died, and Thebes held.
greek_mythology.explanation: An army marched against a city despite warnings that the plan was doomed, and it was destroyed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A rash, ill-considered attack that failed and left the enemy secure, as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology.source: Apollodorus, Library 3.6; Aeschylus, Seven Against Thebes

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu observes that the general who wins makes many calculations in his temple before the battle is fought, while the general who loses makes but few calculations beforehand.
philosophy.explanation: Battles are mostly won or lost in the planning, before any fighting starts.
philosophy.tie_back: Near-identical doctrine: exhaustive calculation before engaging the enemy.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, ch. 1 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: The Jameson Raid into the Transvaal
real_life_example.event: Leander Starr Jameson led about 500 armed men from the borders of Bechuanaland into the Boer republic of the Transvaal, expecting a rising by foreign residents in Johannesburg that never happened. The column was surrounded and surrendered at Doornkop on 2 January 1896. Cecil Rhodes was forced to resign as prime minister of the Cape Colony, while President Paul Kruger gained international sympathy and won re-election in 1896.
real_life_example.explanation: The badly prepared raid did not weaken Kruger's government but made it stronger and deepened the divisions that led to the South African War of 1899-1902.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says an attack launched without thorough planning settles the enemy in a prepared bed where he grows strong, and the Jameson Raid left Kruger more secure than before.

tamil:
செய்தக்க அல்ல செயக்கெடும் செய்தக்க
செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Seydhakka alla seyak ketum seydhakka,
Seyyaamai yaanung ketum.
meaning: Doing what you should not do ruins you. Not doing what you should do ruins you just as much.
elementary: You can get into trouble in two ways: by doing something you shouldn’t, and by not doing something you should. Both can hurt you just as much.
university: The couplet is built on a chiastic repetition of செய்தக்க (‘what is fit to be done’). It balances sins of commission against sins of omission and treats both as equally ruinous (கெடும் … கெடும்). This keeps the chapter from turning into a counsel of timidity: deliberation is meant to discern the right action, and paralysis is as fatal as rashness. In a political reading, a ruler who neglects necessary measures (defence, justice, relief) falls as surely as one who pursues reckless ones. The same double structure is familiar from moral and legal traditions that separate positive duties from prohibitions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Laws of Manu state that a man who omits a prescribed act, or performs a blameworthy act, or clings to sensual objects, must perform a penance.
hinduism.explanation: In the Hindu law books you can go wrong both by skipping your duties and by doing forbidden things, and both need to be put right.
hinduism.tie_back: Same two-sided account of wrongdoing as the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: The General Confession: “We have left undone those things which we ought to have done; And we have done those things which we ought not to have done.”
christianity.explanation: Anglican worshippers confess both kinds of failure: what they neglected and what they wrongly did.
christianity.tie_back: An almost word-for-word counterpart to the Kural’s two clauses.
christianity.source: Book of Common Prayer (1662), Morning Prayer, General Confession

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an calls for a community “inviting to [all that is] good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong,” and says those are the successful.
islam.explanation: Muslims are asked both to promote what is good and to stop what is wrong. Doing only one isn’t enough.
islam.tie_back: The paired duties of doing right and avoiding wrong echo the Kural’s two-sided rule.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Simlai taught that 613 commandments were given to Moses: 365 prohibitions, matching the days of the year, and 248 positive commands, matching the limbs of the body.
judaism.explanation: Jewish law is built from both ‘do this’ and ‘don’t do that’ commandments, and a person can fail by breaking either kind.
judaism.tie_back: The positive/negative split mirrors the Kural’s ‘what should be done’ and ‘what should not be done’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To avoid all evil, to cultivate good, and to cleanse one’s mind — this is the teaching of the Buddhas.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s teaching in one line: stop doing bad things and start doing good things, and keep your mind pure.
buddhism.tie_back: Avoiding the wrong and doing the right, the Kural’s two clauses in the same order.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One should desist from one thing, and practise another: desist from neglect of self-control, and practise self-control.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on the monk's mode of life opens with a double rule: some things must be given up and others actively practised.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says ruin comes both from doing what should not be done and from failing to do what should; the Jain verse likewise demands both abstaining and acting.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 31.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You have not done what you should have done; you are entangled in the web of greed. Nanak, your time is past and gone; why are you crying now, you blind fool?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur rebukes the person who, caught up in greed, leaves undone what ought to have been done, until the time for it has gone.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one is ruined as much by failing to do what ought to be done as by doing what ought not; Guru Tegh Bahadur lays out the ruin of omission.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1428, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 36), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles withdraws from the fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon and refuses to return even when the Greeks are being routed. His inaction leads to the death of Patroclus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles’ refusal to act when he was needed brought disaster on his own side and on his best friend.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the second half of the Kural: ruin from failing to do what ought to be done.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Mill writes that a person may cause evil to others not only by his actions but by his inaction, and in either case is justly accountable to them for the injury.
philosophy.explanation: Mill says you can harm people by what you fail to do as well as by what you do, and you are responsible either way.
philosophy.tie_back: A modern philosophical statement of the Kural’s parity between commission and omission.
philosophy.source: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859), ch. 1

real_life_example.event_title: The Quebec Bridge collapses during construction
real_life_example.event: The design of the Quebec Bridge's long cantilever span had been enlarged, but its dead load had been calculated using weights for the original, shorter span. In August 1907 the inspector Norman McLure reported that key compression members were bending and the bend was growing, yet the chief engineer insisted that work continue; McLure's urgent advice that no more load be placed on the bridge was relayed only on 27 August, and the south arm collapsed two days later, killing 75 workers. A royal commission found that faulty design and inadequate engineering supervision had caused the disaster.
real_life_example.explanation: The failure came both from what was done wrongly, a miscalculated design, and from what was left undone, halting the work when the warnings appeared.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says ruin comes both from doing what should not be done and from failing to do what should be done, and the Quebec Bridge failed through both kinds of error at once.

tamil:
எண்ணித் துணிக கருமம் துணிந்தபின்
எண்ணுவம் என்பது இழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Ennith thunika karumam thunindhapin,
Ennuvam enbadhu izhukku.
meaning: Think it through first, and then decide what to do. Saying “we will think about it after we start” is a mistake.
elementary: Do your thinking first, then make up your mind and go. Starting first and figuring it out later is a big mistake.
university: Probably the most-quoted couplet of the chapter. Its force comes from the sequence எண்ணி → துணிக (reflect → resolve) and the rejection of the reversed order துணிந்தபின் எண்ணுவம் (‘having resolved, we shall reflect’). Two faults are excluded at once. One is beginning without deliberation. The other, implied, is wavering and reopening the question after committing, which dissipates resolve. துணிவு means both decision and courage, so the couplet unites prudence and boldness: deliberation belongs before action, and firmness belongs after decision. இழுக்கு (a slip, a blemish) casts the failure as a lapse of character, not merely of technique.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After eighteen chapters of dialogue, Arjuna tells Krishna that his delusion is destroyed, his doubts are gone, and he stands firm, ready to act on Krishna’s word.
hinduism.explanation: The whole Gita is one long pause to think before battle. Only when Arjuna’s doubts are cleared does he commit to action.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s structure (deliberation first, then firm resolve) is the Kural’s sequence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: Once you’ve committed to something important, you mustn’t keep looking back and second-guessing.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s condemnation of reconsidering after resolving.

islam.quote_or_event: “…and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah.”
islam.explanation: God tells the Prophet: talk things over with your people first, but once you’ve decided, act with trust and don’t hesitate.
islam.tie_back: An exact counterpart: consult and deliberate, then resolve and proceed firmly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee. Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established.”
judaism.explanation: Think carefully about where you are going, then walk steadily ahead without turning aside.
judaism.tie_back: Pondering first and then holding firmly to the path is the Kural’s order.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes the resolve of a disciple who has set out on the path: willingly let only skin, sinews and bones remain, let flesh and blood dry up; energy will not be relaxed until the goal is attained.
buddhism.explanation: Once a Buddhist practitioner decides to seek awakening, they commit completely and don’t turn back.
buddhism.tie_back: Illustrates the unwavering resolve that should follow deliberation.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Vratas or a vow is a solemn resolve made after deliberation to observe a particular rule of conduct … A vow affords stability to the will and guards its votary from the evils of temptation or of unguarded life”
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics defines the vow, the basic unit of a layman's discipline, as a resolve taken only after deliberation, which then keeps the will steady.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's order (reflect, then resolve, and do not reopen the question afterwards) is how the Jain vow works: deliberation comes first, and steadiness follows.
jainism.source: Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code', section on the twelve vratas (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. When you place your feet on this Path, give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak asks that the full cost be accepted before the first step on the path of love; once the step is taken, there is no holding back.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to think first and then resolve, not to begin and think afterwards; Guru Nanak asks the seeker to settle the price before setting foot on the path, then give without hesitation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran Thay Vadheek (salok 20), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops’s cave, Odysseus first thinks of stabbing Polyphemus as he sleeps, but a second thought stops him: no one could move the boulder from the door. He devises the stake-and-ram plan and carries it out without hesitation.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus thinks through his options before he acts, then sticks to the plan he chooses.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus’s metis is the Kural’s ‘think, then resolve’ in action.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Descartes’s second maxim: be as firm and resolute in action as possible once a course is chosen, like travellers lost in a forest who should walk straight in one direction rather than wander in circles.
philosophy.explanation: Descartes says that once you’ve picked a direction, keep going; changing your mind every few steps gets you nowhere.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s rule against reopening deliberation after resolving.
philosophy.source: René Descartes, Discourse on Method (1637), Part 3

real_life_example.event_title: Construction of the Sydney Opera House begins before the design is resolved
real_life_example.event: Work on the Sydney Opera House began in 1959, pressed forward before a state election, long before Jorn Utzon's design for the roof shells and their supports had been worked out. As each new design was produced the cost rose and the completion date moved back, and the estimated cost of 3.5 million pounds had reached 13.7 million by 1962. After a dispute with the state government over payments, Utzon resigned in 1966, and other architects completed the building, which opened in 1973.
real_life_example.explanation: The building became a world icon, but starting before the plan was settled led to years of delay, a vastly higher cost and the departure of its architect.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls it a disgrace to say we will think it through after we have begun, and the Opera House was begun on precisely that basis.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம் பலர்நின்று
போற்றினும் பொத்துப் படும்.
transliteration:
Aatrin varundhaa varuththam palarnindru,
Potrinum poththup patum.
meaning: Work that is not done the right way will fail, even if many people stand by to help and protect it.
elementary: If you work hard but in the wrong way, the project will fall apart — even if lots of people are trying to help hold it together.
university: ஆறு here means ‘way, proper method’. வருந்தா வருத்தம் (‘toil not toiled [in the right way]’) is effort poured out without a method. The verb போற்று (to guard, cherish, maintain) and பலர்நின்று (many standing together) anticipate the objection that sheer numbers or goodwill can make up for bad method. Valluvar denies it. பொத்துப் படும் means ‘it will spring a leak / be breached’, an image of a vessel or dam giving way. The couplet adds to the chapter’s argument: deliberation must choose not only whether to act but how, and a wrong method cannot be rescued by resources applied afterwards.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna says that one who discards the injunctions of scripture and acts on the impulse of desire attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
hinduism.explanation: If you ignore the proper way and just do what you feel like, your effort won’t bring success.
hinduism.tie_back: Effort outside the proper method (ஆறு) is fruitless, as the Kural says.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus compares the one who hears his words and does not do them to a foolish man who built his house on sand: the rain fell, the floods came, the winds beat on it, and it fell, and great was its fall.
christianity.explanation: However much work goes into a house, it collapses if it isn’t built the right way on a solid foundation.
christianity.tie_back: Labour without the right method ends in collapse, the Kural’s ‘breach’.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an speaks of the greatest losers in their deeds: those whose effort is lost in worldly life while they think they are doing well in their work.
islam.explanation: Some people work very hard and even think they’re doing great, but their effort is wasted because it isn’t on the right path.
islam.tie_back: Effort outside the right way is lost, however sincere, as the Kural says.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct.”
judaism.explanation: Chopping wood with a dull axe takes much more effort; a little wisdom about the right method saves a lot of wasted strength.
judaism.tie_back: Wrong method multiplies toil; right method (wisdom) makes it succeed, as the Kural says.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Bhumija that one who seeks oil by pressing sand will get none, whether he has hopes or not, because that is not the way to get oil; one who presses sesame seeds will get it.
buddhism.explanation: No matter how hard or hopefully you squeeze sand, you won’t get oil. You need the right method.
buddhism.tie_back: An exact parallel: the outcome depends on the method, not on effort or wishes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If an ignorant man should eat but a blade of Kuśa-grass every month, (the merit of his penance) will not equal the sixteenth part of his who possesses the Law as it has been taught.”
jainism.explanation: Nami tells Indra that even the harshest austerity, done without right knowledge, is worth almost nothing next to practice guided by the true teaching.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says effort spent without the proper method will fail however much it is supported; Jainism likewise holds that great toil without the right way yields little.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Hundreds of thousands of clever tricks, but not even one of them will go along with you in the end. … O Nanak, it is written that you shall obey the Hukam of His Command, and walk in the Way of His Will.”
sikhism.explanation: In the first pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak says that endless cleverness achieves nothing; only walking in the way of God's will (hukam) succeeds.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says effort spent in the wrong way fails whatever help it has; Guru Nanak says countless clever efforts fail unless they follow the right way.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib (pauri 1), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld the Danaids are condemned to carry water forever in leaking vessels, so the jar they labour to fill never fills.
greek_mythology.explanation: They work without end, but because their jars have holes, all their effort is wasted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Endless labour through a ‘breached’ vessel echoes the Kural’s பொத்துப் படும் (springs a leak).

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon observes that a lame man who keeps to the right road outstrips a runner who takes the wrong one.
philosophy.explanation: Going the right way matters more than how fast or strong you are.
philosophy.tie_back: Method beats force, the Kural’s core claim.
philosophy.source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum (1620), Book I, Aphorism 61

real_life_example.event_title: The French attempt to build the Panama Canal fails
real_life_example.place: Isthmus of Panama (then part of Colombia)
real_life_example.event: Ferdinand de Lesseps, celebrated for building the Suez Canal, led a French company that began digging a sea-level canal across Panama in 1881, financed by public share subscriptions in France. Landslides, flooding and tropical diseases defeated the method, and an estimated 22,000 workers died; a change to a lock canal came only in 1887. In 1889 the shareholders dissolved the company and all work stopped, with about 40 percent of the excavation done.
real_life_example.explanation: Great prestige, huge sums of money and the backing of many investors could not save a plan built on a method that did not suit the ground.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says effort not spent in the proper way will fail even if many stand by to support it, and the French canal collapsed despite vast public backing because its method was wrong.

tamil:
நன்றாற்ற லுள்ளுந் தவறுண்டு அவரவர்
பண்பறிந் தாற்றாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Nandraatra lullun thavaruntu avaravar,
Panbarin dhaatraak katai.
meaning: Even when you try to do good, you can fail if you do not understand what each person is like and what suits them.
elementary: Even being kind can go wrong if you don’t understand the person you’re helping. What helps one person might upset another.
university: The couplet carries deliberation into benevolence itself. நன்று ஆற்றல் (doing good, conferring benefits) is normally praised without qualification, but Valluvar notes a தவறு (error, failure) that arises when one does not know அவரவர் பண்பு (the respective natures of each person). Parimelazhagar explains that benefits given to those whose nature does not suit them may be misused or may turn them hostile. For a ruler, rewards and favours are tools of policy and must fit their recipients. The reduplicated அவரவர் (‘each respectively’) insists on individual discernment rather than uniform treatment. Some editions spell the verb தவுறுண்டு; the standard reading is தவறுண்டு.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra, a bird in her snug nest advises shivering monkeys in the rain to build shelters for themselves; the offended monkeys tear her nest apart.
hinduism.explanation: The bird meant well, but she gave advice to creatures who couldn’t take it, and she lost her home.
hinduism.tie_back: Doing good without knowing the recipient’s nature backfires, exactly as the Kural warns.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book 1 (‘The Monkeys and the Bird’)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.”
christianity.explanation: Don’t offer something precious to those who can’t value it, or they may trample it and turn on you.
christianity.tie_back: Good things given without regard to the recipient’s nature can do harm, as the Kural says.

islam.quote_or_event: Ali ibn Abi Talib said: speak to people according to what they can understand; do you want Allah and His Messenger to be denied?
islam.explanation: Even true teaching can backfire if it doesn’t fit what the listener can grasp.
islam.tie_back: Doing good (teaching truth) must fit each person’s capacity, as the Kural teaches.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.”
judaism.explanation: The same correction that a wise person welcomes will make a scornful person hate you.
judaism.tie_back: Whether a well-meant act helps or harms depends on the recipient’s character.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha explains to Prince Abhaya that he speaks only what is true and beneficial, and even then he knows the proper time for saying it, taking account of the listener.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha didn’t just say true, helpful things. He chose when and how to say them depending on who was listening.
buddhism.tie_back: Good speech must be adapted to the person and occasion, as the Kural requires of good deeds.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The effect of giving of the gift–dāna–has distinctions based on the specific manner in which it is given–vidhiviśeṣa, the specific thing given–dravyaviśeṣa, the specific nature of the giver–dātṛviśeṣa, and the specific nature of the recipient–pātraviśeṣa.”
jainism.explanation: Umasvati teaches that the fruit of a gift depends on how it is given, what is given, who gives and who receives. Pujyapada's commentary compares this to seed whose harvest depends on the soil.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that even doing good can fail if one ignores each person's nature, and the Jain sutra makes the recipient's nature one of the factors that decide a gift's result.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Wisdom leads us to serve our Lord and Master; through wisdom, honor is obtained. Wisdom does not come by reading textbooks; wisdom inspires us to give in charity.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Saarang Guru Nanak says that true giving is guided by wisdom, the same discernment that leads to serving God and earning honour.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says even doing good can fail without understanding those one deals with; Guru Nanak makes wisdom the guide of charity.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Helios, wishing to prove his love, swears to grant his son Phaethon any gift; Phaethon asks to drive the sun chariot, cannot control the horses, scorches the earth, and is struck down by Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A father’s generous gift, given without thinking about whether his son could handle it, led to disaster.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A kindness given without regard to the recipient’s nature and capacity brings ruin, the Kural’s warning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that giving or spending money is easy and anyone can do it, but doing it to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive and in the right way is neither easy nor for everyone.
philosophy.explanation: Being generous is easy; being generous well — to the right person in the right way — takes wisdom.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s point that good deeds need discernment about the person.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.9 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Macartney Embassy's gifts fail to impress the Qianlong Emperor
real_life_example.event: Britain sent Lord George Macartney to the Qing court with a large retinue and a great quantity of presents, including clocks, carriages and scientific instruments, hoping to open more ports and station an ambassador in China. The Qianlong Emperor treated the presents as tribute and, in edicts addressed to King George III, rejected every British request, stating that China had no need of Britain's manufactures.
real_life_example.explanation: Lavish gifts chosen without understanding how the recipient's court saw the world produced the opposite of the intended effect.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that even well-meant giving can fail when one does not understand the nature of the person receiving it, and Britain's gifts misjudged the emperor and his court.

tamil:
எள்ளாத எண்ணிச் செயல்வேண்டும் தம்மொடு
கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது உலகு.
transliteration:
Ellaadha ennich cheyalventum thammotu,
Kollaadha kollaadhu ulagu.
meaning: Think carefully and do only things the world will not look down on. People do not accept actions that do not fit who you are and your place in life.
elementary: Before you act, ask: will good people respect this, and does it fit who I am? People won’t accept actions that don’t suit the person doing them.
university: The closing couplet adds a social test to the practical tests of the preceding kurals. எள்ளாத (‘what is not despised’) introduces public judgement, and the wordplay கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது (‘the world will not accept what is not accepted with oneself’) sets the criterion of fit. An action must suit the agent’s station, capacity and character (தம்மொடு). Parimelazhagar takes it that the world will not approve deeds out of keeping with one’s status, even when the deeds themselves are not bad. For a ruler, legitimacy depends on acting in ways subjects and peers can recognise as fitting. The chapter thus ends by setting individual calculation inside a community of judgement.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna teaches that it is better to perform one’s own duty (svadharma), even imperfectly, than another’s duty well; and that whatever a great person does, others follow as their standard.
hinduism.explanation: Do what fits your own role and nature, and remember that people watch and copy those in high positions.
hinduism.tie_back: Action fitting one’s own station, judged by the watching world, echoes தம்மொடு கொள்ளாத.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul speaks of “providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says it isn’t enough to be right before God; your conduct should also look honourable to other people.
christianity.tie_back: Acting in ways the world will not scorn is the Kural’s standard too.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said: righteousness is good character, and sin is what wavers in your soul and you would dislike people to find out about.
islam.explanation: One test of wrongdoing is whether you’d be embarrassed for others to learn of it.
islam.tie_back: Uses the imagined judgement of others as a check on action, like the Kural’s ‘what the world will not scorn’.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi said: which is the right path a person should choose? Whatever is an honour to the one who does it and brings him honour from others.
judaism.explanation: Pick the way of acting that you can respect in yourself and that other people will respect too.
judaism.tie_back: The same two tests as the Kural: fitting to oneself, and approved by the world.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kalama Sutta the Buddha tells the Kalamas that when they know for themselves that certain things are unskillful, blameworthy and criticised by the wise, and lead to harm, they should abandon them.
buddhism.explanation: One way to check an action is to ask whether wise people would criticise it.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Criticised by the wise’ is the Buddhist form of the Kural’s ‘what the worthy would not scorn’.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Prasiddham desacharam samacharan : Following the reputable usages of the country.” … “Adsa-kalayoh charyam tyajan : Avoiding action which is inappropriate to time and place.”
jainism.explanation: Among the qualities Hemacandra expects of a Jain householder are keeping to the respected customs of the land and avoiding conduct out of keeping with time and place.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's final test is that an act should be fitting so the world does not scorn it, and Hemacandra's layman measures his conduct by the same standard of social fitness.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of the thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
sikhism.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak puts truthful conduct above even the knowledge of truth, so that how one lives is the final test.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks for conduct that will not earn the world's scorn; Guru Nanak likewise makes conduct the test, though he measures it by truth rather than by public approval.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Arachne, a mortal weaver, challenges the goddess Athena and weaves the gods’ misdeeds; her presumption is punished and she is turned into a spider.
greek_mythology.explanation: Arachne did something that didn’t fit her place in the world, and she was punished for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates action out of keeping with one’s station meeting rejection, the Kural’s கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith argues that we judge our own conduct by imagining how an impartial spectator would view it, and that we naturally desire not only to be praised but to be praiseworthy.
philosophy.explanation: Smith says a good check on our actions is to picture how a fair-minded observer would see them.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘act so that the world will not scorn’ is a version of Smith’s impartial-spectator test.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), Part III

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Nero competes at the Olympic Games
real_life_example.event: During a tour of Greece, the Roman emperor Nero competed in the Greek games, adding contests in music and tragedy to the Olympic programme. At Olympia he drove a ten-horse chariot, fell from it and did not finish the race, yet was proclaimed the winner.
real_life_example.explanation: An emperor performing as a competitor and accepting a victory he had not earned became a lasting example of conduct unworthy of a ruler.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world will not approve what does not suit one's own station, and Nero's games turned his rank into an object of ridicule.

tamil:
வினைவலியும் தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும்
துணைவலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Vinaivaliyum thanvaliyum maatraan valiyum
Thunaivaliyum thookkich cheyal.
meaning: Before you act, compare four strengths: how much strength the job needs, how strong you are, how strong your opponent is, and how strong the helpers on each side are.
elementary: Before you start something big, stop and measure four things: how hard the job is, how strong you are, how strong the other side is, and who will help each of you. Only after weighing all four should you decide to go ahead.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a four-part audit: vinai-vali (the strength the undertaking requires), tan-vali (one’s own strength), maatraan-vali (the adversary’s) and thunai-vali (the strength of allies, which Parimelazhagar reads as the allies of both parties). The verb thookki, ‘weighing as on a balance’, governs all four terms, so action (seyal) is justified only by comparison. Assessing yourself alone is not enough. This is the centre of the Kural’s political realism, and it closely parallels Kautilya’s Arthaśāstra, whose ninth book opens with a chapter on knowing power, place, time, strength and weakness before any campaign. Prudence here is not timidity. It is what makes effective action possible.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthaśāstra opens its book on the conqueror’s campaigns with a chapter on knowing power, place, time, strength and weakness. There the would-be invader compares his own powers with the enemy’s: the power of counsel, the power of treasury and army, and the power of energy and valour. He marches only when that comparison favours him.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya makes assessment of relative strength a formal step that must come before any war. The king has to know both his own resources and the enemy’s, and has to account for place and season too.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost exactly Valluvar’s fourfold weighing. Valluvar even adds allies (thunai-vali) as a separate item on the scale.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book IX, Chapter 1 (tr. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses a king comparing troop numbers to illustrate counting the cost before committing. A king who finds himself outmatched negotiates instead of fighting.
christianity.tie_back: It pairs one’s own strength against the opponent’s before acting, which is the core of the Kural’s weighing. The Kural adds the task’s strength and allies’ strength as further items.

islam.quote_or_event: “Now, Allah has lightened [the hardship] for you, and He knows that among you is weakness. So if there are from you one hundred [who are] steadfast, they will overcome two hundred. And if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast.”
islam.explanation: The verse sets a realistic ratio of strength for the believers’ military obligation. It takes their actual weakness into account and does not demand the impossible.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a sober calculation of one’s own force against the enemy’s as the basis for deciding whether to fight.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Every purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb insists that war, of all undertakings, must be entered only after deliberation and sound advice.
judaism.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s demand that action follow careful weighing, though the four strengths are not spelled out.

buddhism.quote_or_event: King Ajātasattu, planning to attack the Vajjians, sends his minister Vassakāra to ask the Buddha what will happen. The Buddha asks Ānanda whether the Vajjians still keep seven conditions of welfare, including meeting often, acting in concord and honouring their elders. He concludes that while they keep them, they can be expected to prosper and not decline.
buddhism.explanation: The episode is in effect an assessment of the opponent’s real strength. The minister leaves understanding that the Vajjians cannot be conquered by force while they remain united.
buddhism.tie_back: It dramatises maatraan-vali, knowing the enemy’s actual strength before attacking, which is one of the Kural’s four weights.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Balabalam janan : Aware of one's own strength and weakness.”
jainism.explanation: One of the thirty-five marks of the ideal Jain layman in Hemacandra's Yogashastra is knowing one's own strength and weakness. It sits next to far-sightedness and avoiding action unsuited to time and place.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks a person to weigh their own strength against the demands of the task before acting, and Hemacandra names that self-assessment as a basic householder virtue.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of the thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No power to speak, no power to keep silent. … He alone has the Power in His Hands. He watches over all.”
sikhism.explanation: In the thirty-third pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak denies that any human has power of their own, even to speak or keep silent; all power is in God's hand.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the actor to weigh the strengths of task, self, enemy and allies; Guru Nanak teaches that every such strength finally rests with God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7, Japji Sahib (pauri 33), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before the Achaeans march on Troy, old Nestor advises Agamemnon to array the army by tribes and clans so that each group supports its own. That way he will learn which chiefs and men are brave and which are cowards, and whether any failure comes from heaven or from human weakness.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor proposes organising the army so that its real strength, including the reliability of allies and contingents, becomes visible before the decisive fight.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It reflects the Kural’s concern with knowing one’s own strength and one’s allies’ strength (thunai-vali) before acting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu holds that victory follows from accurate knowledge of both one’s own condition and the enemy’s. Ignorance of either brings defeat.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the closest single-sentence analogue to the Kural’s instruction to weigh one’s own and the opponent’s strength before acting.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War III.18 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Japan secures the Anglo-Japanese Alliance before facing Russia
real_life_example.place: London, United Kingdom, and Tokyo, Japan
real_life_example.event: In 1902 Japan concluded an alliance with Britain under which each partner would stay neutral if the other went to war with one power, but would come to its aid if a second power joined in against it. With this safeguard against a coalition, the Japanese government took a firmer line against Russian advances in Manchuria and Korea, and in 1904 it went to war with Russia.
real_life_example.explanation: Japan measured not only its own forces against Russia's but also the allies each side could call upon, and arranged matters so that it would face Russia alone.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural tells a ruler to weigh the task, his own strength, the enemy's strength and the strength of the allies on each side, and the alliance was Japan's way of fixing that last term in its favour before acting.

tamil:
ஒல்வ தறிவது அறிந்ததன் கண்தங்கிச்
செல்வார்க்குச் செல்லாதது இல்.
transliteration:
Olvadhu arivadhu arindhadhan kan thangich
Chelvaarkkuch chellaadhadhu il.
meaning: Nothing is out of reach for people who know what they can do, learn what the job needs, and keep working steadily at it.
elementary: If you know what you’re able to do, learn everything you need for it, and then stick with it without giving up, there’s nothing you can’t reach.
university: This couplet turns the caution of 471 into confidence. It has three stages: olvadhu (discerning what is within one’s power), arivadhu (acquiring the knowledge the task needs) and thangi (settling into the work with steady application). The conclusion, chellaadhadhu il (‘there is nothing that will not go’ for such people), is not a claim to unlimited power. It is conditional: success without limit is promised only inside the field that honest self-assessment has marked out. Knowing your limits is exactly what lets you be effective within them. The verse also defends Valluvar’s realism against the charge of defeatism, since measuring your strength is meant to lead to action, not to paralysis.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna teaches that it is better to perform one’s own duty (svadharma), even imperfectly, than another’s duty well. Work suited to one’s own nature does not bring sin.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita directs each person to the field of action that fits their own nature and capacity, rather than an ambitious role that belongs to someone else.
hinduism.tie_back: This resembles the Kural’s olvadhu, knowing what is truly one’s own to accomplish, as the ground on which steady effort succeeds.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, each servant is entrusted in proportion to his ability. Those who work faithfully with what they have are rewarded.
christianity.tie_back: Capacity is measured first and diligence follows, much like the Kural’s sequence of knowing what one can do and then persisting in it.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do good deeds properly, sincerely and moderately and know that your deeds will not make you enter Paradise, and that the most beloved deed to Allah is the most regular and constant even if it were little.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet commends deeds done within one’s capacity and kept up steadily, over bursts of effort that cannot be sustained.
islam.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s pairing of realistic scope (olvadhu) with steady perseverance (thangi) as the way to reach one’s aim.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.”
judaism.explanation: Moses assures Israel that the commandment is neither too hard nor too far off. It lies within their reach, so they can carry it out.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it frames a task correctly understood as within one’s capacity, and therefore as achievable.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The monk Soṇa, exhausted by excessive striving, thinks of giving up. The Buddha reminds him that a lute plays well only when its strings are neither too taut nor too slack. In the same way, over-aroused persistence leads to restlessness and slack persistence to laziness, so Soṇa should find the right pitch of effort and then pursue his practice. Soṇa does so and attains arahantship.
buddhism.explanation: The lute simile teaches that attainment comes from effort tuned to one’s real capacity and then kept up. Neither strain nor laxity works.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s formula of knowing what one can do and then persisting in it. The result is also the same: the goal Soṇa despaired of turns out to be reachable.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A householder is advised that according to his ability and environment he should proceed stage by stage and that he should observe the rules of discipline that are prescribed for each stage.”
jainism.explanation: The eleven pratimas, or stages of lay discipline, are climbed like rungs of a ladder: one rises according to one's ability and moves up only after standing firm on the step below.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural promises success to those who know what they can do and keep steadily at it, and the graded Jain path follows the same pattern of honest self-measure and steady progress.
jainism.source: Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code', section on the eleven pratimas (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
sikhism.explanation: In Gujri Ki Vaar Guru Arjan praises udam, steady effort, and practice kept up over time as the way to life and peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says nothing is out of reach for those who know what they can do and keep steadily at it; Guru Arjan likewise promises the fruit of sustained effort.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri, Gujri Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops’ cave, Odysseus is about to stab the sleeping Polyphemus. He stops when he realises that he and his men could never move the boulder blocking the entrance. Having recognised what is and is not within their power, he devises a plan that fits it, blinding the giant and escaping under the sheep.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus succeeds because he first identifies the limit of his strength and then pursues only a plan that works within it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s point that knowing what is possible is what makes success possible.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus opens his Handbook by dividing all things into those within our power (judgement, impulse, desire, aversion) and those not within our power (body, property, reputation, office). He holds that someone who attends only to what is within their power cannot be thwarted.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus, correctly identifying the sphere of one’s real power is the precondition of an unhindered life.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it promises that nothing can stop those who understand where their power lies and act inside it. The Stoic version turns inward, while Valluvar’s looks outward to practical tasks.

real_life_example.event_title: Thor Heyerdahl's Kon-Tiki raft crosses the Pacific
real_life_example.place: Callao, Peru, to Raroia, Tuamotu Islands (French Polynesia)
real_life_example.event: To test his theory that South Americans could have reached Polynesia, the Norwegian Thor Heyerdahl and five companions built a raft of balsa logs modelled on early South American designs and set out from Callao, Peru. Critics had predicted the raft would break up within weeks, but after about 101 days and some 4,300 miles it reached the reef of Raroia in the Tuamotu Islands.
real_life_example.explanation: The voyage showed that such a crossing was physically possible, though scholars did not accept Heyerdahl's wider theory of Polynesian origins.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says nothing is out of reach for those who know what they can do, learn what the task needs and keep steadily at it, and the Kon-Tiki crew prepared carefully and held to their course for over three months.

tamil:
உடைத்தம் வலியறியார் ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி
இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்.
transliteration:
Udaiththam valiyariyaar ookkaththin ookki
Idaikkan murindhaar palar.
meaning: Many people did not know how strong they really were. They rushed into a task, driven only by eagerness, and broke down halfway.
elementary: Lots of people get very excited and jump into something big without checking whether they’re strong enough. Halfway through they run out of strength, and it all falls apart.
university: Udaiththam vali, ‘the strength they themselves possess’, is exactly what these people fail to know. Ookkam (zeal, drive) is praised elsewhere in the Kural, with a whole chapter on it (ch. 60, Ookkam Udaimai), so Valluvar is not condemning enthusiasm itself. He condemns enthusiasm cut loose from measurement. The verb murindhaar (‘they snapped’) suggests a branch or axle giving way under strain and looks ahead to the cart-axle image of 475. Palar (‘many’) gives the verse an empirical, historical tone: this is not a hypothetical but a pattern seen across many careers and kingdoms.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Gita calls an action tamasic (of the mode of ignorance) when it is undertaken out of delusion, without regard to consequences, loss, harm to others, or one’s own ability.
hinduism.explanation: Among the marks of deluded action, Krishna names disregard of one’s own capacity (pauruṣam anavekṣya).
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s diagnosis in doctrinal form: action begun without knowing one’s strength belongs to delusion and ends badly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus describes a builder who starts without reckoning his resources and is left with an unfinished tower and public ridicule.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Began to build, and was not able to finish’ closely matches the Kural’s idaikkan murindhaar, ‘broke down midway’.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that religion is easy, and that whoever overburdens himself in it will be overpowered and unable to continue. He advised believers to avoid extremes, to aim at what is right and come close to it, and to take heart.
islam.explanation: The hadith warns that zeal which ignores one’s real capacity cannot be sustained, and the zealous person gives up.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s picture of zeal without self-knowledge collapsing before it reaches the end.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes warns against eagerly undertaking obligations one cannot fulfil. It is wiser not to begin than to begin and fail.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it condemns commitments made in enthusiasm without regard to capacity, which end unfinished.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Before his awakening, the Bodhisatta pushed ascetic practice to the extreme, holding his breath and reducing food until his body wasted and he was near death. He found that these austerities did not lead to awakening, recalled a calmer state of absorption from his childhood, and took up the middle way.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s own story is one of overreaching zeal that nearly destroyed him partway along the path, until he adopted a practice suited to what a human body and mind can bear.
buddhism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s warning that fervour beyond one’s real strength breaks down before reaching the goal.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A man believes himself a hero as long as he does not behold the foe, as did Śiśupāla (before he beheld) the valorously-fighting, great warrior.” … “So a novice, who as yet has not suffered pains and is not yet used to a mendicant's life, believes himself a hero till he practises austerities.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga's lecture on hardships pictures eager novices who rush into the monastic life sure of their courage, then lose heart once cold, heat, hunger and insult test them.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's warning almost exactly: many who did not know their real strength set out in a burst of zeal and broke down halfway.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.3.1.1 and 1.3.1.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My strength is exhausted, and I am in bondage; I cannot do anything at all.”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks Guru Tegh Bahadur gives voice to someone whose strength has run out and who is left helpless and bound.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of those who misjudged their strength and broke down midway; Guru Tegh Bahadur describes that state of spent strength and helplessness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 53), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon begs his father Helios to let him drive the chariot of the Sun. Helios warns him that not even Zeus could control those horses, but Phaethon insists. Partway across the sky he loses control, the horses bolt and scorch the earth, and Zeus strikes him down with a thunderbolt.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaethon’s eagerness overrides his father’s warning about the limits of his strength, and he fails in mid-course.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a mythic version of the Kural: zeal without knowing one’s strength, then collapse midway.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In every affair consider what precedes and follows, and then undertake it.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus continues that someone who does not do this will begin eagerly, without thinking of the consequences, and then give up in disgrace when difficulties appear. He adds: consider first what the matter is and what your own nature can bear.
philosophy.tie_back: It is almost a commentary on the Kural: eager starts without self-assessment end in shameful abandonment midway.

real_life_example.event_title: The Burke and Wills expedition breaks down on the way back
real_life_example.place: Victoria to the Gulf of Carpentaria, Australia
real_life_example.event: The Victorian Exploring Expedition under Robert O'Hara Burke set out to cross Australia from south to north. Burke split his party, pushed ahead from Cooper Creek with a small group and inadequate provisions, and came near the Gulf of Carpentaria in February 1861, but on the return journey the men weakened, missed the depot party at Cooper Creek by hours, and Burke and William Wills died at the end of June 1861. A royal commission later censured Burke for dividing his party and setting out with inadequate supplies.
real_life_example.explanation: The expedition reached its goal but collapsed on the way back, because its leader had not matched the pace of his plans to the strength of his men and supplies.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says many who did not know the measure of their strength have broken down midway, and Burke's party gave out on the homeward stretch of its journey.

tamil:
அமைந்தாங் கொழுகான் அளவறியான் தன்னை
வியந்தான் விரைந்து கெடும்.
transliteration:
Amaindhaangu ozhugaan alavariyaan thannai
Viyandhaan viraindhu kedum.
meaning: A person who does not get along with others, does not know their own limits, and thinks too highly of themselves will soon be ruined.
elementary: Someone who won’t get along with others, doesn’t know how strong they really are, and keeps bragging about how great they are will fall very fast.
university: Three faults are linked here. The first is failing to fit one’s conduct to others (amaindhaangu ozhugaan, which commentators read as refusing to accommodate those around one, especially more powerful neighbours). The second is ignorance of one’s own measure (alavu ariyaan). The third is self-admiration (thannai viyandhaan). The first two are errors of judgement, and the third is the emotional state that keeps them going, because the self-admirer stops checking. Viraindhu (‘swiftly’) matters: pride does not merely lead to ruin eventually, it speeds it up.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Confident in his army and his own prowess, Duryodhana rejects Krishna’s peace embassy and every counsel of Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and his own parents. He refuses to give the Pandavas even five villages, and the war that follows destroys him and his house.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana will not accommodate others, misjudges his real strength, and is swollen with self-regard, the three faults the Kural lists.
hinduism.tie_back: His swift ruin at Kurukshetra illustrates the Kural’s viraindhu kedum.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavad-yana sections; tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns against inflated self-estimation and calls for a sober judgement of oneself according to the measure actually given.
christianity.tie_back: It addresses the Kural’s alavu ariyaan and thannai viyandhaan: not knowing one’s measure, and thinking too highly of oneself.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people and do not walk through the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful.”
islam.explanation: Luqman’s counsel to his son forbids arrogance toward people and conceited self-display.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s pairing of failing to get along with others and self-admiration. The Kural adds the practical consequence of swift ruin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb holds that pride is the prelude to collapse.
judaism.tie_back: It gives the same causal chain as the Kural’s thannai viyandhaan … kedum: self-exaltation leading to ruin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is called a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada treats inflated self-assessment as the deepest form of folly.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s alavu ariyaan and thannai viyandhaan: not knowing one’s real measure and admiring oneself.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain story of Bahubali, son of Rishabhanatha, Bahubali renounces the world after his contest with his brother Bharata, but at first will not go to bow before his younger brothers, who had become monks before him. He stands motionless in meditation for a year, yet omniscience does not come to him until his sisters Brahmi and Sundari tell him to get down from the elephant of pride. When he lets go of his pride, he attains kevala-jnana.
jainism.explanation: The story teaches that even heroic austerity is blocked by pride (mana), one of the four passions that bind karma to the soul.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that self-admiration and refusing to fit in with others bring swift ruin; in the Bahubali story it is exactly such pride that holds back a great soul until he gives it up.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Parva 1 (life of Ṛṣabha; tr. Helen M. Johnson, Gaekwad's Oriental Series)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The humble beings abide in peace; subduing egotism, they are meek. The very proud and arrogant persons, O Nanak, are consumed by their own pride.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan contrasts the humble, who live in peace, with the proud, who are destroyed by their own pride (haumai).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the self-admiring man who ignores his own measure soon comes to ruin; Guru Arjan says the arrogant are consumed by their pride.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib (ashtapadi 12, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Arachne, a gifted weaver, boasts that her skill surpasses Athena’s and refuses to admit any debt to the goddess. She rejects Athena’s warning, delivered in the guise of an old woman, and challenges her to a contest. Enraged, Athena destroys her work, and Arachne is turned into a spider.
greek_mythology.explanation: Arachne’s self-admiration and refusal to accept advice bring swift ruin, even though her skill is real.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s three faults: refusing to accommodate, misjudging one’s standing, and admiring oneself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: After questioning a man reputed to be wise, Socrates concludes that he himself is wiser in one small way: neither of them knows anything fine and good, but the other man thinks he knows when he does not, while Socrates does not think he knows.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates makes accurate knowledge of one’s own limits the beginning of wisdom and exposes self-admiration as ignorance.
philosophy.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s alavu ariyaan and thannai viyandhaan: self-flattery comes from not knowing one’s own measure.

real_life_example.event_title: Charles XII of Sweden is defeated at Poltava
real_life_example.event: After years of victories in the Great Northern War, Charles XII of Sweden invaded Russia and turned south into Ukraine, far from his supplies. Though wounded in the foot, he chose to attack Peter the Great's fortified camp at Poltava, the assault failed, and three days later most of the Swedish army surrendered at Perevolochna. Charles escaped to Ottoman territory, where he spent about five years trying in vain to persuade the Ottomans to attack Russia.
real_life_example.explanation: A king who had won many battles staked his army on one more deep campaign and lost Sweden's standing as a great power.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that one who misjudges his own measure and acts without regard to others is quickly ruined, and Poltava destroyed Charles's army in a single day.

tamil:
பீலிபெய் சாகாடும் அச்சிறும் அப்பண்டஞ்
சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்.
transliteration:
Peelipey saakaadum achchirum appandanj
Chaala miguththup peyin.
meaning: Even peacock feathers, which are very light, will break the axle of a cart if you pile on too many.
elementary: A peacock feather weighs almost nothing. But if you pile far too many onto a cart, even feathers will snap its axle. Lots of small things can add up to too much.
university: This is one of the Kural’s most famous images. The peacock feather (peeli) is the lightest of loads and the cart (saakaadu) a sturdy vehicle, yet when it is loaded chaala miguththu (‘in great excess’), the axle (achchu) breaks. Parimelazhagar applies the verse to kings: even weak enemies can overwhelm a strong ruler if they combine, so a king should not provoke many small foes at once. A broader reading applies it to any capacity. No strength is infinite, and sheer quantity can turn trifles into a fatal burden. The image anticipates the later proverb of the straw that breaks the camel’s back.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who is regulated in his habits of eating, sleeping, recreation and work can mitigate all material pains by practicing the yoga system.”
hinduism.explanation: The verse before it warns that yoga is not for someone who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little. The body has a measure that excess breaks.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats capacity as having a limit that must not be overloaded, even with ordinary, harmless things.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of wineskins that burst when strained beyond what they can hold.
christianity.tie_back: As with the Kural’s axle, a container or carrier fails when made to bear more than its capacity.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity. … Our Lord, and lay not upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us. Our Lord, and burden us not with that which we have no ability to bear.”
islam.explanation: The verse affirms that every soul has a limit of capacity and prays not to be loaded beyond it.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s picture of a burden that must stay within what the bearer can carry.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud repeatedly uses the principle ‘tafasta merubah lo tafasta’: if you grasp too much, you have not grasped anything; if you grasp a little, you have grasped it.
judaism.explanation: The sages use this maxim to choose the smaller of two possible measures, reasoning that overreaching loses everything.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that taking on more than can be held leads to losing it all.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 4b (also Yoma 80a, Chagigah 17a)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not think lightly of evil, saying, ‘It will not come to me.’ Drop by drop is the water pot filled. Likewise, the fool, gathering it little by little, fills himself with evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that small things, each negligible, accumulate until the vessel is full.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s insight that light items (drops, feathers) become decisive in quantity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Do not get into an uneven road like a weak burden-bearer; for you will repent of it afterwards; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: In his sermon to Gautama, Mahavira uses the image of a weak porter who leaves the smooth road for an uneven one under his load, and will regret it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's overloaded cart and the Jain overburdened porter both teach that a load beyond one's capacity ends in breakdown.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You may read and read loads of books; you may read and study vast multitudes of books. … O Nanak, only one thing is of any account: everything else is useless babbling and idle talk in ego.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Nanak imagines learning piled up by the cartload (gadee) and says that without the one thing, the Name, it all counts for nothing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures a cart overloaded even with feathers; Guru Nanak also pictures a cart piled with light things, though his point is their worthlessness, not the breaking axle.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a donkey heavily loaded begs the unburdened horse to take a share. The horse refuses, the donkey collapses and dies under the load, and the master then puts the whole burden, and the donkey’s hide, on the horse.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable shows a carrier failing when loaded beyond its strength, and the burden then falling on others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the same picture as the Kural’s overloaded cart: a bearer breaks when the load exceeds its capacity.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Horse and the Ass’ (tr. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that both excessive and deficient exercise destroy bodily strength, and that too much or too little food or drink destroys health, while the right amount produces, increases and preserves them. The virtues, he argues, are destroyed by excess and deficiency in the same way.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that even good and necessary things become destructive past their proper measure.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives the philosophical form of the Kural’s point that excess of even a light thing breaks what bears it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.2, 1104a (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The cities of the Lombard League defeat Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano
real_life_example.event: Northern Italian cities, among them Milan, Venice, Mantua, Padua and Brescia, formed the Lombard League in 1167 to resist the Holy Roman emperor Frederick I Barbarossa's attempts to curb their self-government. At Legnano in 1176 the League's army, led by Milan, routed the imperial forces. Frederick agreed to a truce and in the Peace of Constance of 1183 granted the cities self-government in return for their allegiance.
real_life_example.explanation: No single city could have defeated the emperor, but together they broke his power in northern Italy.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's cart of peacock feathers shows how many light loads together break a strong axle, and the old commentators read it as a warning that small foes combined can overwhelm a great ruler, as the Lombard cities did.

tamil:
நுனிக்கொம்பர் ஏறினார் அஃதிறந் தூக்கின்
உயிர்க்கிறுதி ஆகி விடும்.
transliteration:
Nunikkombar erinaar ahdhirandhu ookkin
Uyirkkirudhi aagi vidum.
meaning: A person who has climbed to the very tip of a tree branch and tries to climb even higher will fall and lose their life.
elementary: Imagine climbing a tree right out to the thinnest tip of a branch. If you try to go even further, the branch breaks and you fall. You need to know when you’ve gone as high as you safely can.
university: Nunikkombar, the thin end of a branch, marks the exact limit of what one’s strength, and the support one relies on, can bear. Commentators apply it to a ruler who has already stretched his power as far as it will go: any further push (ahdhu irandhu ookkin, ‘if he strives beyond it’) becomes fatal. The verse pairs with 475. There an external load exceeds capacity; here one’s own ambition exceeds the support beneath. The image is precise: the danger is greatest exactly when one is highest.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Triśaṅku wants to ascend to heaven in his own body. Refused by his guru Vasiṣṭha and cursed by Vasiṣṭha’s sons, he turns to Viśvāmitra, whose ascetic power lifts him up. The gods throw him back down, and he is left suspended head-down in a heaven of his own between earth and the gods’ realm.
hinduism.explanation: Triśaṅku has already reached the height of a king’s station and tries to climb beyond the limit set for mortals. He ends suspended, neither risen nor safe.
hinduism.tie_back: It is a mythic version of trying to climb past the branch-tip.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.”
christianity.explanation: Set on the pinnacle of the Temple and urged to throw himself down trusting in rescue, Jesus refuses to go beyond the safe limit on the strength of presumption.
christianity.tie_back: Standing at the highest point, he declines to overreach, which is the restraint the Kural urges on the climber at the branch-tip.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear the earth [apart], and you will never reach the mountains in height.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an reminds human beings of the fixed limits of their stature and strength against pride that imagines no ceiling.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names a height beyond which human striving cannot go.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.”
judaism.explanation: The builders of Babel try to push human achievement past its proper limit. Their project is halted and they are scattered.
judaism.tie_back: It is a biblical form of the Kural’s climbing past the tip: reaching for more than the limit allows ends in collapse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, already a respected monk with psychic powers and the patronage of Prince Ajātasattu, asks to take over leadership of the Saṅgha from the Buddha. When refused, he plots against the Buddha’s life and splits the order. The tradition records that he fell into ruin.
buddhism.explanation: Having reached a high position, Devadatta reaches beyond it and destroys himself.
buddhism.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s warning that striving past the limit one has already reached is fatal.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means. Though two māṣas would do to supply your want, still you would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.”
jainism.explanation: In the commentary's story, the student Kapila needs only two pieces of gold, but once a king offers him whatever he asks, he keeps raising the sum until he suddenly sees his folly and renounces.
jainism.tie_back: Kapila's mounting wish is the Kural's climber who reaches the tip of the branch and still strives higher; in both, going past the proper limit is the danger.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 8.17, with Jacobi's note on the commentary's story of Kapila (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, do not be so proud of your tall mansions. Today or tomorrow, you shall lie beneath the ground, and the grass shall grow above you.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir warns that whatever height one reaches is temporary and the fall to the ground is sure.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that climbing beyond the branch tip is fatal; Kabir warns that those proud of their height will soon lie low.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1366, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 38) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
