greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus makes wings of feathers and wax for himself and his son Icarus and warns him to fly a middle course, neither too low near the sea nor too high near the sun. Icarus, thrilled by flight, soars upward. The sun softens the wax, the feathers fall away, and he plunges into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: Icarus climbs past the height his means can bear and dies for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the closest mythic parallel to the Kural’s climber who goes beyond the branch-tip.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Artabanus warns Xerxes against invading Greece. He points out that the god strikes the tallest creatures, buildings and trees with his thunderbolt, and brings low whatever towers above the rest.
philosophy.explanation: Herodotus’ wise adviser argues that greatness pushed further exposes one to catastrophe.
philosophy.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s insight that danger is greatest at the highest point and that pressing further brings destruction.

real_life_example.event_title: The Ottoman siege of Vienna fails
real_life_example.event: The Ottoman grand vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha led a vast army to besiege Vienna in July 1683. On 12 September a relief army under King John III Sobieski of Poland attacked at the Kahlenberg and routed the besiegers. Kara Mustafa was put to death in Belgrade on the sultan's orders on 25 December 1683, and in the wars that followed the Ottomans lost large territories in central Europe.
real_life_example.explanation: The siege marked the furthest point of a long Ottoman advance, and the attempt to push beyond it began a long retreat.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who climb beyond the tip of the branch fall to their death, and Kara Mustafa's push to Vienna went past the limit his empire could support and cost him his life.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து ஈக அதுபொருள்
போற்றி வழங்கு நெறி.
transliteration:
Aatrin alavarindhu eega adhuporul
Potri vazhangu neri.
meaning: Know how much you have, and give in a sensible way. That is how you keep your money safe while still giving.
elementary: Being generous is good, but give in a way that fits what you actually have. That way you can keep helping people and still keep your household going.
university: Here the chapter turns from military to economic power, since for Valluvar wealth is also a form of vali. Aatrin means ‘in the proper way’, or in some readings ‘according to one’s capacity’. Alavu arindhu means knowing the measure of one’s wealth. The couplet reconciles two duties that could conflict: potri (preserving) and vazhangu (distributing). Measured giving is not stinginess. It is the method (neri) that makes generosity sustainable. Some web editions print aravarindhu here, but the standard Parimelazhagar text and most editions read alavarindhu, ‘knowing the measure’, which fits the chapter’s theme.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Taittirīya Upaniṣad’s parting charge to graduating students, the teacher lays down how gifts are to be given: with faith, not without faith; śriyā deyam (in keeping with one’s prosperity); with modesty, with awe and with understanding.
hinduism.explanation: The Upaniṣad regulates the manner and proportion of giving, not only the act.
hinduism.tie_back: If śriyā deyam is read as ‘give in keeping with one’s means’, it parallels the Kural’s alavu arindhu eega.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not. For I mean not that other men be eased, and ye burdened.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Corinthians that a gift is measured by what the giver has, and that generosity is not meant to relieve others by crushing the giver.
christianity.tie_back: This is very close to the Kural’s instruction to give knowing one’s measure, so that giving and preserving go together.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not make your hand [as] chained to your neck or extend it completely and [thereby] become blamed and insolvent.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids both miserliness (a hand chained to the neck) and giving everything away (a hand fully outstretched) that leaves one destitute.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s path of giving by measure, which preserves one’s wealth while still distributing it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD thy God which he hath given thee.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah ties the festival offering to each person’s actual means.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes one’s own measure the standard for giving.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha advises the young householder Sigāla to divide his earnings into four parts: one for his own use and the support of others, two for investment in his work, and the fourth set aside against misfortune.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist lay ethics sets a budget in which spending and giving are measured shares of income, not unlimited outflows.
buddhism.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s way of giving while preserving wealth: distribution fitted to one’s measure.
buddhism.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (tr. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Charity (dāna) is the giving of one's objects to another for mutual benefit–anugraha.”
jainism.explanation: Pujyapada explains that a gift benefits both sides, bringing merit to the giver and right knowledge to the recipient. He also recalls that charity is to be practised according to one's capacity (sutra 6.24).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural teaches that rightly measured giving preserves the giver's wealth, and the Jain definition of dana likewise sees a properly made gift as good for the giver as well as the receiver.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.38, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak joins honest earning (kirat karni) with sharing (vand chhakna): one gives some of what one has earned, not all of it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to give in the right way, knowing the measure of one's means, so that wealth is preserved while given; Guru Nanak commends giving a part of honest earnings.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor elderly couple Baucis and Philemon welcome disguised Zeus and Hermes with what little they have: cabbage, a bit of smoked pork, simple wine. They give generously within their means and even try to kill their one goose for the guests.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their hospitality is generous yet in proportion to their modest household, and the gods reward it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It illustrates giving from one’s real measure, as the Kural advises.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “liberality resides not in the multitude of the gifts but in the state of character of the giver, and this is relative to the giver’s substance.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines liberality as giving the right amounts to the right people, relative to one’s resources. He adds that the liberal person does not neglect his own property, since he wants to be able to keep helping others.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s doctrine in philosophical terms: generosity measured against one’s means, so that giving and preserving go together.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1, 1120b (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Jakob Fugger founds the Fuggerei
real_life_example.event: The merchant and banker Jakob Fugger endowed a walled settlement of homes for needy Catholic citizens of Augsburg, setting the annual rent at one Rhenish guilder and providing in the foundation deed that it should last forever. Funded by the Fugger foundations' endowment, the Fuggerei still houses about 150 people, and its annual base rent remains the equivalent of one guilder, about 88 euro cents.
real_life_example.explanation: Because the gift was set up within the means of a lasting endowment, it has kept giving for five centuries without being used up.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says giving in the right way and within one's measure is how wealth is preserved even while it is given, and the Fuggerei is a gift that has outlived its giver by 500 years.

tamil:
ஆகாறு அளவிட்டி தாயினுங் கேடில்லை
போகாறு அகலாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Aagaaru alavittidhu aayinum kedillai
Pogaaru agalaak kadai.
meaning: It does no harm if the money coming in is small, as long as the money going out is not bigger.
elementary: It’s OK if you don’t earn much. What matters is that you don’t spend more than you earn. A small income with even smaller spending keeps you safe.
university: Aagaaru (the way wealth comes in) and pogaaru (the way it goes out) are channel metaphors, like the irrigation channels that feed and drain a village tank. Valluvar makes a ratio, not an absolute amount, the test of financial health. A narrow inflow (alavu ittidhu, ‘small in measure’) does no harm provided the outflow does not grow broader (agalaak kadai). The verse is often compared to Mr Micawber’s famous rule in Dickens, but it is well over a thousand years older. Within the chapter, it applies ‘knowledge of power’ to the household: one’s economic strength is the relation between inflow and outflow, not the size of either.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Arthaśāstra has the Collector-General keep accounts under separate heads: receipts (āya), expenditure (vyaya) and net balance (nīvī). The state’s strength is judged by keeping expenditure within revenue.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya institutionalises the comparison of income with outgoings as the basis of a sound treasury.
hinduism.tie_back: Āya and vyaya correspond to the Kural’s aagaaru and pogaaru, and the aim in both is that outflow should not exceed inflow.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book II, Chapter 6 (tr. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches contentment with modest provision rather than an endless pursuit of more.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes a small income sufficient as long as needs and spending stay within it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [they are] those who, when they spend, do so not excessively or sparingly but are ever, between that, [justly] moderate.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the servants of the Merciful as spending in balance, neither extravagantly nor miserly.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s demand that outflow be kept in proportion to means.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma teaches in the Mishnah: Who is rich? The one who rejoices in his portion.
judaism.explanation: Wealth is redefined as contentment with what one has rather than the size of one’s holdings.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that a small income need not mean harm or poverty if desire and spending stay within it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells the householder Dīghajāṇu that balanced livelihood means knowing one’s income and expenditure and living neither too extravagantly nor too meanly, so that income exceeds expenditure. He compares this to a goldsmith holding up a scale who knows exactly how far it dips or rises.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist lay ethics explicitly makes the balance of inflow against outflow a condition of welfare.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural: no harm from small income while outgoings stay smaller.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Vyayam ayochitam kurvan : Spending in proportion to one's income.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra counts keeping spending in proportion to income among the basic qualities of a good Jain householder, next to earning wealth honestly and dressing according to one's means.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's rule in plain terms: a small inflow does no harm as long as the outflow is kept within it.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of the thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I ask for two kilos of flour, and half a pound of ghee, and salt.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Sorath Bhagat Kabir lists the plain needs he asks of God: a little flour, a little ghee and salt, nothing beyond.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a small income does no harm if spending stays within it; Kabir's modest list shows needs kept small.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 656, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod advises his brother Perses on household thrift: be sparing in the middle of the jar, since saving at the dregs comes too late, and observe due measure, because proportion is best in everything.
greek_mythology.explanation: The archaic Greek farmer-poet makes measured use of stores the basis of a household that lasts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s rule that outflow must be kept within what comes in.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 368–369, 694 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure nineteen nineteen and six, result happiness. Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure twenty pounds ought and six, result misery.”
philosophy.explanation: Mr Micawber, himself chronically in debt, gives young David the famous rule that happiness depends not on the size of income but on whether spending stays below it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s aagaaru/pogaaru ratio almost word for word.

real_life_example.event_title: Andrew Jackson's government pays off the national debt
real_life_example.event: Andrew Jackson came to office determined to end the national debt, and his administration used revenue from the sale of federal lands while he vetoed many spending bills. By January 1835 all of the government's interest-bearing debt had been paid off, the only time in United States history, and that year the government ran a large surplus that Congress distributed to the states. Within a short time, an economic downturn led the government to borrow again.
real_life_example.explanation: For a brief period the United States government spent less than it took in, until it had no debt at all.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that a narrow income does no harm so long as outgoings are not wider, and Jackson's government cleared its debts by keeping spending below its revenue.

tamil:
அளவறிந்து வாழாதான் வாழ்க்கை உளபோல
இல்லாகித் தோன்றாக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Alavarindhu vaazhaadhaan vaazhkkai ulapola
Illaagith thondraak kedum.
meaning: A person who does not live within what they can afford may seem to be doing well, but their life will vanish and leave nothing behind.
elementary: Someone who spends as if they have more than they do might look rich for a while. But soon it all disappears, as if it had never been there.
university: The couplet diagnoses an illusion. Ula pola means ‘as if existing’: the spendthrift’s life looks abundant, but it illaagi (becomes nothing) and thondraak kedum (perishes without a trace, not even appearing afterwards). The phrase alavu arindhu vaazhaadhaan ties personal finance back to the chapter’s thesis: living well requires knowledge of one’s measure just as war does. The warning is less about spending itself than about the gap between appearance and substance. Wealth that is not measured is only apparent.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the dice game, Yudhiṣṭhira keeps staking beyond what he can afford to lose: his wealth, his kingdom, his brothers, himself and finally Draupadī. An emperor who has just performed the Rājasūya sacrifice ends the day with nothing.
hinduism.explanation: Yudhiṣṭhira’s vast apparent prosperity vanishes in one sitting because he does not stop within the measure of what he can afford.
hinduism.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural’s ula pola illaagi: a life that seemed full becomes empty.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Sabhā Parva (Dyūta sub-parva; tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.”
christianity.explanation: The prodigal son takes his inheritance, lives as if it were endless, and is soon reduced to feeding pigs.
christianity.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s point that a life not lived within its measure looks rich and then vanishes.

islam.quote_or_event: “…and do not spend wastefully. Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils, and ever has Satan been to his Lord ungrateful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids squandering (tabdhīr) and ranks it as a serious moral failing.
islam.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s condemnation of living beyond one’s measure. The Qur’an stresses the moral gravity, while the Kural stresses the practical collapse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up.”
judaism.explanation: The wise man’s house keeps its stores, while the fool consumes everything.
judaism.tie_back: It gives the Kural’s contrast between living by measure and wasting until nothing remains.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists six channels through which a householder’s wealth drains away: intoxicants, roaming the streets at unseemly hours, frequenting fairs and shows, gambling, bad companions and idleness. Each is described as dissipating what has been earned.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist lay ethics shows how unmeasured habits quietly empty a household.
buddhism.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s picture of a life that seems prosperous while its substance is draining away.
buddhism.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (tr. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “After having enjoyed pleasant seats, beds, carriages, riches, and pleasures, after having squandered his wealth which he had so much trouble in gaining, and after having committed many sins, he will, under the burden of his Karman, and believing only in the visible world, be grieved in the hour of death like the ram at the arrival of a guest.”
jainism.explanation: The parable compares the self-indulgent man to a ram fattened for a guest: it looks well fed and thriving until the day it is slaughtered.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's spendthrift seems to prosper and then vanishes without a trace; the Jain fattened ram gives the same picture of apparent plenty ending suddenly.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.8–9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “As the bubbles in the water well up and disappear again, so is the universe created; says Nanak, listen, O my friend!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur compares worldly existence to a bubble that rises and vanishes on the water.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the life of one who lives beyond his means seems to prosper, then vanishes without a trace; Guru Tegh Bahadur's bubble has the same brief show and quick end.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 25), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cursed by Ceres with insatiable Hunger, King Erysichthon eats through his whole fortune. He sells his daughter Mestra again and again to buy more food, and finally, with nothing left, devours his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Consumption without any measure destroys first a rich king’s wealth and then the king himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is an extreme image of the Kural’s life that becomes nothing through consumption without measure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes the prodigal as someone ruined through his own fault, since wasting one’s substance is a kind of ruining oneself, because life depends on property. He adds that prodigals soon exhaust their means and so are driven to take from wrong sources.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats prodigality as a vice of excess that destroys its possessor’s livelihood.
philosophy.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s claim that one who does not live within his measure is ruined, and by his own doing.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1, 1120a–1121b (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Rembrandt loses his house and collection
real_life_example.event: In 1639 Rembrandt bought a large house on the Jodenbreestraat in Amsterdam, and he spent heavily on paintings, prints, antiquities and studio props. Mounting debts left him unable to keep up the payments, and in 1656 an official inventory was made of his possessions, nearly all of which were then sold at auction. The house was sold in 1658, and Rembrandt moved to a rented home on the Rozengracht, where he died in 1669.
real_life_example.explanation: The most celebrated painter of his city lived in apparent prosperity for years before his household and collection were dispersed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the life of one who does not live within his means seems to flourish and then vanishes, as Rembrandt's grand house and collection did.

tamil:
உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புர வாண்மை
வளவரை வல்லைக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Ulavarai thookkaadha oppuravu aanmai
Valavarai vallaik kedum.
meaning: Giving away money without thinking about how much you really have will soon use up everything you own.
elementary: Helping others is wonderful, but if you give away more than you actually have, soon you’ll have nothing left, not even enough to keep helping.
university: Oppuravu is the civic virtue of beneficence to which Valluvar devotes chapter 22 (Oppuravu Arithal), where he says that even ruin incurred through beneficence is worth buying by selling oneself (220). Here he adds the prudential counterweight. Ulavarai thookkaadha describes beneficence that does not weigh (thookku, the same balance-verb as in 471) the extent of what one has, and it rapidly (vallai) destroys the limits of one’s wealth (valavarai). The chapter thus ends where it began, with weighing. Even virtue has to be measured against capacity if it is to last.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Karṇa, famous for never refusing a request, is approached by Indra disguised as a brahmin, who asks for his natural armour and earrings. Although his father Sūrya has warned him that they make him invulnerable, Karṇa cuts them from his body and gives them away. This leaves him exposed in the war that follows.
hinduism.explanation: Karṇa’s generosity ignores what he himself needs to survive and contributes to his eventual defeat.
hinduism.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s warning about beneficence that does not weigh one’s own limits. The epic, however, honours Karṇa’s gift as noble.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Vana Parva (Kuṇḍalāharaṇa sub-parva; tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: Paul insists that duties to one’s own household come first and may not be sacrificed.
christianity.tie_back: It supports the Kural’s limit on beneficence: generosity that ignores one’s own resources and dependents is a failure. Elsewhere, though, the gospels praise the widow who gave all she had (Mark 12:41–44).

islam.quote_or_event: “And they ask you what they should spend. Say, ‘The excess [beyond needs].’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an answers the question of how much to give by pointing to what is surplus to one’s needs.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ulavarai thookku, weighing what one has before giving.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One who scatters should not scatter more than one-fifth, lest he render himself destitute and need the help of other people.”
judaism.explanation: The rabbis at Usha set an upper limit on charitable giving so that the giver does not become poor himself.
judaism.tie_back: It gives the Kural’s principle as a rule: beneficence that does not weigh one’s means ends in destitution.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Prince Vessantara, perfecting generosity, gives away his kingdom’s auspicious rain-bringing white elephant, which leads to his exile. He then gives away his chariot, his children and even his wife.
buddhism.explanation: The Jātaka presents boundless giving as the Bodhisatta’s perfection (dāna-pāramī), even though it brings exile and loss.
buddhism.tie_back: It is a deliberate counterpoint to the Kural. Vessantara’s giving takes no account of his resources and ruins his estate, which is exactly what Valluvar warns against in a householder, while the Buddhist story praises it as a spiritual ideal.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Tyāga: Charity is of three kinds, namely, gift of pure food (āhāradāna), gift of dispelling fear (abhayadāna), and gift of right knowledge (jñānadāna). The giving of these to others according to one's capacity is charity.”
jainism.explanation: Among the sixteen practices that lead to rebirth as a Tirthankara, Pujyapada's commentary defines charity as giving according to one's capacity, and austerity likewise.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says beneficence must be weighed against one's resources, and the Jain definition builds the same limit into charity itself.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.24, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Sikhs practice dasvandh, setting aside a tenth of their earnings in the Guru's name for the community's common resources. The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism traces the idea to Guru Nanak's line on earning and sharing (Ang 1245) and records that under Guru Ram Das Sikhs were asked to set apart at least ten per cent of their income for the common pool.
sikhism.explanation: Dasvandh gives Sikh generosity a set proportion, so that giving is regular and tied to what one actually earns.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that generosity that does not weigh one's resources soon exhausts wealth; dasvandh ties giving to a fixed share of income.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala), "Dasvandh" by Wazir Singh (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Timon of Athens pours out his fortune on friends, flatterers and hangers-on without counting the cost. When his wealth is gone, those he helped abandon him, and he withdraws in bitterness to live as a labourer outside the city.
greek_mythology.explanation: Timon’s generosity, which never weighed his means, destroys his wealth and leaves him friendless.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a close illustration of the Kural: oppuravu that does not weigh one’s limits ruins one’s wealth quickly.
greek_mythology.source: Lucian, Timon the Misanthrope (tr. H. W. and F. G. Fowler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero lists cautions for acts of kindness: they must not harm the recipient or others, must not exceed our means, and must suit the recipient’s worth. He argues that those who want to be more open-handed than their circumstances allow wrong their own next of kin, and are often tempted into taking wrongly from others to fund their generosity.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero makes the limit of one’s means a strict condition of true liberality.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s ulavarai thookkaadha oppuravu: beneficence that ignores one’s means is self-destructive and ends up being unjust.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.42–44 (tr. Walter Miller)

real_life_example.event_title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage through Cairo
real_life_example.event: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with a very large caravan carrying great quantities of gold. When he stopped in Cairo, he spent and gave away gold so lavishly that its value there fell, and the market had still not recovered some twelve years later.
real_life_example.explanation: Generosity on such a scale became famous across the Mediterranean world but also showed that even vast wealth can be poured out faster than is wise.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that giving without weighing the limits of one's resources quickly exhausts them, and Mansa Musa's journey is the best-known case of giving on a scale beyond measure.

tamil:
பகல்வெல்லும் கூகையைக் காக்கை இகல்வெல்லும்
வேந்தர்க்கு வேண்டும் பொழுது.
transliteration:
Pakalvellum Kookaiyaik Kaakkai Ikalvellum
Vendharkku Ventum Pozhudhu.
meaning: In the daytime even a crow can beat the stronger owl. In the same way, a king who wants to beat his enemies must wait for the right time.
elementary: An owl is bigger and fiercer than a crow, but owls can hardly see in bright daylight. So in the daytime a crow can chase an owl away. If you pick the moment when you are at your best and the other side is at its weakest, even a small player can win.
university: The opening couplet grounds the chapter in natural observation. The kookai (owl) is stronger than the kaakkai (crow), but it is day-blind, so pakal (daytime) reverses their strength. Parimelazhagar draws the lesson for the vendhar (king): an ikal (hostile contest) is won not by strength alone but by the pozhudhu (hour) that suits one’s side. The image has a close Sanskrit parallel in the Panchatantra’s third book, the war of the crows and owls (Kākolūkīya), where the crows burn the owls’ cave by daylight. Both editions consulted (Thirukkural.net and Project Madurai) give the same text, apart from a sandhi spacing in ikalvellum.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Book III of the Panchatantra, the war of the crows and the owls, the owl-king’s army attacks the crows at night and slaughters them. The crow minister Sthirajivin later wins the owls’ trust and lives in their cave. Then, in daylight, when the owls are blind and helpless, he and the crows block the entrance and set it on fire, destroying the whole colony.
hinduism.explanation: The weaker crows cannot win by night, which is the owls’ hour. They win completely by choosing the day, when the owls cannot see.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s crow-and-owl image worked out as a full political fable.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book III (Kākolūkīya, ‘Crows and Owls’), tr. Arthur W. Ryder

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then Jesus said unto them, My time is not yet come: but your time is alway ready.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus’ brothers urge him to show himself publicly in Judea at the feast. He refuses because the moment (kairos) is not yet right for him, though any time suits them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s king, Jesus acts not when pressed to but when the hour favours his purpose.

islam.quote_or_event: At the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq, 627 CE), a much larger confederate army besieged Medina. The Muslims held their defensive line rather than meet it in open field. After weeks, a bitter cold wind at night wrecked the besiegers’ camp and they withdrew. The Qur’an recalls this in Sura 33:9, where God sent a wind and unseen forces against them.
islam.explanation: The weaker side avoided the stronger side’s favoured ground and waited until conditions turned against the besiegers.
islam.tie_back: As with the crow by day, victory came to the weaker side when circumstances were in its favour, not through raw strength.
islam.source: Qur’an 33:9–10 and the sira accounts of the Battle of the Trench

judaism.quote_or_event: “And of the children of Issachar, which were men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do.”
judaism.explanation: When David was gathering support for his kingship, the Chronicler singles out the men of Issachar for one skill: they understood the times and so knew what Israel should do.
judaism.tie_back: The verse makes reading the moment a qualification of royal counsel, just as the Kural says kings need the right time.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dhammaññu Sutta the Buddha lists seven qualities that make a monk worthy of gifts and respect. One of them is being kālaññū, ‘one who knows the right time’: the time for study, questioning, effort and seclusion.
buddhism.explanation: Knowing the proper time is counted as a distinct virtue, next to knowing the teaching, its meaning, oneself, moderation, assemblies and persons.
buddhism.tie_back: Kālaññutā is almost a Pali name for this chapter’s title, kaalam arithal (‘knowing the time’).
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.64 (Dhammaññu Sutta), tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “This mendicant who knows the time, the strength (of himself), the measure (of all things), the practice, the occasion (for begging, &c.), the conduct, the religious precepts, the true condition (of the donor or hearer), … he proceeds securely (on the road to final liberation) after having cut off both (love and hate).”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga describes the wise mendicant as one who knows the right time, his own strength and the occasion, and who therefore moves securely toward liberation.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's crow beats the owl because it knows its hour; the Acaranga likewise pairs knowing the time with knowing one's own strength as the mark of the wise, though its goal is liberation rather than victory.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.2.5.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He could appoint a worm as king, and reduce an army to ashes.”
sikhism.explanation: In Majh Ki Vaar Guru Nanak says that God can raise the weakest creature to a throne and bring the mightiest army to nothing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural shows the weaker crow beating the stronger owl when the hour favours it; Guru Nanak also sees the weak overturning the strong, though by God's will rather than timing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 144, Raag Maajh, Majh Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad Book 10, Odysseus and Diomedes scout the Trojan lines by night, when the Trojans and their new allies are asleep. They kill the Thracian king Rhesus and his men in their sleep and take his famous horses, which Achilles’ absence had left the Greeks unable to win in daylight battle.
greek_mythology.explanation: Having been beaten by day, the Greeks switch to the hour that favours stealth, and two men do what an army could not.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point in reverse lighting. Each side has its hour, and the wise fighter strikes in his own.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad, Book 10 (the Doloneia), tr. Samuel Butler

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There is surely no greater wisdom, than well to time the beginnings, and onsets, of things.”
philosophy.explanation: In his essay on delays, Bacon calls the timing of beginnings the height of practical wisdom. He warns both against missing the moment and against acting before it is ripe.
philosophy.tie_back: Bacon states as a maxim what the Kural shows with the crow: the hour chosen decides the contest.

real_life_example.event_title: Finnish ski troops defeat Soviet divisions at Suomussalmi
real_life_example.event: In the Winter War, the Soviet Union attacked Finland with forces many times larger than the Finnish army. At Suomussalmi, Soviet motorised divisions, many drawn from the milder Ukrainian military district and not equipped for the northern winter, were tied to narrow forest roads, while lightly armed Finnish troops moved quickly on skis. The Finns cut the road-bound columns into isolated pockets and destroyed two Soviet divisions, though Finland was later forced to make peace and give up territory.
real_life_example.explanation: A much smaller force won by fighting in the season and conditions that favoured it and crippled its stronger enemy.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says even a crow beats the stronger owl by day, so the weaker side must wait for the time that favours it, and the northern winter was the Finns' daylight and the Soviets' night.

tamil:
பருவத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் திருவினைத்
தீராமை ஆர்க்குங் கயிறு.
transliteration:
Paruvaththotu Otta Ozhukal Thiruvinaith
Theeraamai Aarkkung Kayiru.
meaning: Acting at the right time is like a rope that ties good fortune down so it cannot slip away from you.
elementary: Farmers plant when the rains come, not whenever they like. If you do things at the right time, good luck stays with you as if tied by a rope. If you ignore the time, it wanders off.
university: Paruvam means season or ripe time, and otta ozhukal means conducting oneself so as to cling to it. The image in the second line is striking: thiru (Fortune, often personified as the goddess Lakshmi or Tirumakal) is fickle by nature, and timely action is the kayiru (rope) that aarkkum (binds) her so that she does not theeraamai, that is, depart. Parimelazhagar glosses paruvam as the time suited to the undertaking. He reads the couplet as a claim that wealth lasts only when action keeps pace with circumstance. Renaissance Europe has a close analogue in Machiavelli’s Fortuna, who favours the man whose conduct matches the times. The Tamil text is identical in both sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let the king undertake his march in the fine month Margasirsha, or towards the months of Phalguna and Kaitra, according to the (condition of his) army.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu’s rules for kings give seasonal windows for campaigns, chosen to suit harvests and the readiness of the army.
hinduism.tie_back: This is paruvam in concrete form: royal success depends on moving with the season, not against it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.”
christianity.explanation: Paul uses the farmer’s image of harvest in its proper season to urge steady good work that will bear fruit at the right time.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul ties reward to season, although his focus is on endurance until the season comes.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that there are two blessings in which many people are cheated: health and free time. People let both pass without using them, and later regret it.
islam.explanation: The hadith treats the right time to act as a gift that is easily wasted, not something always available.
islam.tie_back: The Kural adds that using the season well is exactly what keeps good fortune bound to you.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He [also] used to say: If I am not for myself, who is for me? But if I am for my own self [only], what am I? And if not now, when?”
judaism.explanation: Hillel’s three questions end by insisting that the present moment is the time to act, since postponement has no natural end.
judaism.tie_back: ‘If not now, when?’ is the moral core of keeping in step with the season.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The idler who does not exert himself when he should, who though young and strong is full of sloth, with a mind full of vain thoughts — such an indolent man does not find the path to wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada condemns the one who fails to make an effort at the time for effort (uṭṭhāna-kāla).
buddhism.tie_back: Missing the season for effort loses the prize, which is the Kural’s point about Fortune slipping loose.

jainism.quote_or_event: “At the right time a monk should sally forth, and he should return at the right time; avoiding to do anything out of time, he should do what is appropriate for each period of the day.”
jainism.explanation: The opening lecture on discipline makes timeliness a rule of the monk's whole day: each act has its proper hour and nothing is to be done out of season.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says acting in step with the season binds Fortune; this verse shares the principle of doing each thing at its fitting time, though for a Jain monk the reward is discipline, not wealth.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn recited daily in Rehras, Guru Arjan tells the soul that the human birth is its ripe moment, the opportunity not to be let slip.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says acting in step with the season is the rope that holds Fortune fast; Guru Arjan calls human life the one season in which the highest prize can be won.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa (So Purakh / Rehras), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod’s farmer’s calendar tells Perses to start the harvest when the Pleiades rise and to plough when they set. It fixes each task to a sign in the sky and warns that the man who ploughs late will reap little.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Hesiod, prosperity comes to the one who keeps the gods’ seasons, and ruin to the one who acts out of time.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is paruvaththotu otta ozhukal, living in step with the season, as the path to lasting wealth.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, lines 383–617 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In The Prince, chapter 25, Machiavelli argues that Fortune governs about half of human affairs. He says a prince prospers when his way of acting fits the times and falls when the times change and he does not.
philosophy.explanation: Machiavelli treats Fortune as a force that can be managed by matching one’s conduct to the quality of the times.
philosophy.tie_back: His Fortuna and Valluvar’s Thiru are the same fickle goddess, and both are held by timely conduct.
philosophy.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. XXV (tr. W. K. Marriott)

real_life_example.event_title: Vasco da Gama crosses the Indian Ocean with and against the monsoon
real_life_example.event: Guided by a pilot engaged at Malindi on the East African coast, Vasco da Gama's ships left on 24 April 1498 and, carried by the monsoon winds, reached the Malabar coast near Calicut on 18 May, a crossing of about 24 days. On the way home he left Calicut in late 1498 before the monsoon winds had turned in his favour, and the return crossing of the Arabian Sea took nearly three months, during which many of his crew died of scurvy.
real_life_example.explanation: The same ocean took less than four weeks to cross in the right season and nearly three months in the wrong one, at a terrible cost in lives.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says acting in step with the season is the rope that binds Fortune, and da Gama's two crossings show fortune held by timing on the way out and lost by ignoring it on the way back.

tamil:
அருவினை யென்ப உளவோ கருவியான்
காலம் அறிந்து செயின்.
transliteration:
Aruvinai Yenpa Ulavo Karuviyaan
Kaalam Arindhu Seyin.
meaning: Is any task truly impossible if you do it with the right tools and at the right time?
elementary: Opening a tight jar is hard with bare hands. With the right tool and a little warm water it is easy. Most ‘impossible’ jobs become possible when you have the right tools and choose the right moment.
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: aruvinai enpa ulavo, ‘are there things one could call hard deeds?’ The condition has two parts, karuviyaan (by means of instruments) and kaalam arindhu (knowing the time). Parimelazhagar takes karuvi to mean the resources of the state, such as army and treasury, together with the right methods. Neither timing without means nor means without timing is enough. The printed spelling ‘yenpa’ reflects sandhi with the preceding vowel; the word is enpa.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthaśāstra, Book IX, opens with a chapter on knowing power, place and time before invading. It weighs the strength of counsel, treasury and army against the enemy’s, and also the seasons and terrain in which each force works best.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya treats means (śakti) and time (kāla) as separate variables to be judged together before any undertaking.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s pairing of karuvi (means) and kaalam (time).
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book IX, Chapter 1 (tr. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to be careful and to ‘buy up’ the opportune moment (exagorazomenoi ton kairon) rather than waste it.
christianity.tie_back: Wise, careful use of the moment is half of the Kural’s formula for making hard things achievable.

islam.quote_or_event: A man asked the Prophet whether he should leave his camel untied and trust in God, or tie it and trust. The Prophet told him to tie it and then trust.
islam.explanation: Reliance on God (tawakkul) is not a reason to neglect practical means. The two go together.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s success likewise needs the proper karuvi (means) as well as the favourable moment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing: and a wise man’s heart discerneth both time and judgment. Because to every purpose there is time and judgment…”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet says that every undertaking has its proper time and its proper manner (et u-mishpat), and that the wise person perceives both.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Time and judgment’ is a close Hebrew counterpart to the Kural’s ‘time and means’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bhūmija Sutta the Buddha compares a person who seeks results by the wrong method to someone pressing sand for oil or milking a cow by its horn. With the right method, pressing sesame seeds or milking from the udder, the result comes whether one hopes for it or not.
buddhism.explanation: Results depend on using the right means. Wishing does not bring success and does not block it either.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s claim that nothing is hard for the one with proper karuvi rests on the same logic of fitting method to goal.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra opens by declaring that right faith, right knowledge and right conduct together form the path to liberation. Jain teaching holds that a soul fit for liberation who takes up these three means will in time reach even that hardest of goals.
jainism.explanation: Jainism names the specific means (the three jewels) by which the most difficult of all undertakings, freeing the soul from karma, is accomplished.
jainism.tie_back: The kural asks whether anything is impossible for one who acts with the right means at the right time; Jainism answers similarly about liberation, given the proper means applied over time.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.1 of Umasvati (paraphrase of the sutra's content)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My strength has been restored, and my bonds have been broken; now, I can do everything.”
sikhism.explanation: This salok answers the preceding cry of helplessness: with strength restored through God, every means (upai) becomes possible. Some traditions attribute it to Guru Gobind Singh, though the Guru Granth Sahib places it among Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether anything is impossible for one with the right means at the right time; the salok declares that with strength and means restored, everything can be done.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 54) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops’ cave, Odysseus does not attack at once. He prepares an olive-wood stake, hardens it in the fire, gets Polyphemus drunk on strong wine, and blinds him only once the giant has fallen asleep.
greek_mythology.explanation: An impossible escape becomes possible through the right tools (stake, wine, a false name) used at the right moment (drunken sleep).
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s formula in story form: karuvi and kaalam together overcome a far stronger foe.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Further, there can be no doubt that a work is spoilt when not done at the right time? … the husbandman will not make his own plough or mattock, or other implements of agriculture, if they are to be good for anything.”
philosophy.explanation: Founding the first city in speech, Socrates argues that work is ruined if its moment is let slip, and that each worker needs good implements made by others, so smiths and carpenters must join the city.
philosophy.tie_back: The right time and the right implements, the Kural's kaalam and karuvi, appear together as the two conditions of successful work.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic, Book II, 370b–c (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Eisenhower launches D-Day on Stagg's weather forecast
real_life_example.event: Planners of the Allied invasion of Normandy needed the right combination of moonlight, tides and weather, which limited the possible dates to 5-7 or 18-20 June 1944. On 4 June, forecasts of foul weather led General Dwight D. Eisenhower to postpone the landings by 24 hours, and the chief meteorologist, Group Captain James Stagg, then predicted a brief break in the weather, on which Eisenhower ordered the invasion to go ahead on 6 June. German forecasters, by contrast, expected conditions to remain unsuitable for a landing.
real_life_example.explanation: Vast resources of men, ships and equipment made the invasion possible, but it was the choice of the exact moment that allowed them to succeed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks whether anything is impossible for one who acts with the right means and at the right time, and D-Day joined enormous means to a carefully chosen hour.

tamil:
ஞாலம் கருதினுங் கைகூடுங் காலம்
கருதி இடத்தாற் செயின்.
transliteration:
Gnaalam Karudhinung Kaikootung Kaalam
Karudhi Itaththaar Seyin.
meaning: Even if you aim to win the whole world, you can get it, as long as you choose the right time and the right place to act.
elementary: A surfer can ride a huge wave, but only by paddling out at the right moment and at the right spot. Pick the right time and place, and even very big goals become reachable.
university: Gnaalam karudhinum means ‘even if one sets one’s mind on the earth’, that is, universal dominion, and kaikoodum means ‘it will come into one’s hand’. The condition joins kaalam karudhi (considering the time) with idaththaal seyin (acting by means of the place). This anticipates the next chapter, Idanarithal (Knowing the Place, Kurals 491–500). Parimelazhagar explains that idam here means a place of action favourable to oneself and difficult for the enemy. Time and place are treated as the two coordinates of successful action, as in the kāla and deśa of Sanskrit statecraft. Both sources give identical text; ‘karudhinung’ carries the nasal sandhi of karudhinum before k-.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A widely quoted verse of Chāṇakya Nīti tells a person to think again and again about what the time is, who are friends, what the place is, what income and expenditure are, who one is, and what one’s strength is.
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya’s checklist puts time and place first among the questions to settle before acting.
hinduism.tie_back: The same two coordinates, kaalam and idam, are what the Kural says make even world-conquest possible.

christianity.quote_or_event: Speaking at the Areopagus in Athens, Paul says that God made all nations from one blood and fixed both their appointed times and the boundaries of where they live.
christianity.explanation: Paul presents history as ordered by the right times and the right places, under divine providence.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural gives the same two coordinates, time and place, as the conditions for great achievement.

islam.quote_or_event: After the Quraysh allies broke the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet marched on Mecca in 630 CE. He had gathered a large force secretly and approached from several directions at once. The city surrendered with almost no fighting.
islam.explanation: Years of patience were followed by a move at a well-chosen moment and by well-chosen routes, which won the Prophet’s central goal with little bloodshed.
islam.tie_back: Choosing the moment (the broken treaty) and the approach (several routes into Mecca) brought the greatest aim within reach, as the Kural promises.
islam.source: Qur’an 48 and 110; sira accounts of the Conquest of Mecca (Fath Makka)

judaism.quote_or_event: “…and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”
judaism.explanation: Mordecai urges Esther to act. She is now queen, in the one place (the Persian court) where she can save her people, at the one moment when it matters.
judaism.tie_back: Being in the right place at the right time turns an apparently impossible rescue into a real one.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After his awakening, the Buddha at first hesitated to teach. When Brahmā Sahampati asked him, he surveyed the world and saw beings like lotuses at different stages of emergence from the water. Judging the time right, he went to the Deer Park at Isipatana to give his first sermon to the five ascetics, who were ready to understand.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha chose both the moment and the place and audience for the teaching that would spread across Asia.
buddhism.tie_back: A world-changing aim was achieved by judging kaalam and idam precisely.
buddhism.source: Saṃyutta Nikāya 6.1 (Āyācana Sutta) and the Vinaya Mahāvagga narrative

jainism.quote_or_event: In Hemacandra's account of the first universal monarch, Bharata, son of Rishabhanatha, sets out on his conquest of the six divisions of Bharatavarsha only after the discus-jewel (cakra-ratna) appears in his armoury, and by a long, staged campaign brings the whole land under his rule. Jain tradition then shows him renouncing it all and attaining omniscience.
jainism.explanation: The Jain Puranic tradition does contain a world-conquest that succeeds when the sign of the right moment has appeared, but it treats such dominion as worldly and ultimately to be given up.
jainism.tie_back: The kural promises that even the whole world comes within reach if time and place are rightly chosen; Bharata's digvijaya is the Jain example of exactly such a conquest, though Jainism values his later renunciation more highly.
jainism.source: Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra of Hemacandra, Book 1, Bharata's conquest (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Ranjit Singh rose to pre-eminence among the clans of the Sikh confederacy, captured Lahore in 1799 and went on to extend his rule across the Punjab, founding the Sikh kingdom over which he ruled as maharaja.
sikhism.explanation: Starting as one chief among many, Ranjit Singh built a kingdom out of a divided Punjab by moving at the right moment and from the right base.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says even the whole world can be won by one who picks the right time and place; Ranjit Singh's rise from Lahore to rule of the Punjab is a Sikh historical case of such a gain.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Ranjit Singh" by Khushwant Singh (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Zeus did not challenge Cronus while still a child hidden on Crete. He grew up in secret and freed his swallowed siblings. He then released the Cyclopes and Hundred-Handers from beneath the earth, gaining thunderbolts and allies, before fighting the Titans. He won rule of the cosmos.
greek_mythology.explanation: The eventual lord of the world waited for the time of his strength and chose his ground and allies before fighting.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Dominion over the world came through timing and position, as Valluvar says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Without that opportunity their powers of mind would have been extinguished, and without those powers the opportunity would have come in vain.”
philosophy.explanation: Machiavelli says Moses, Cyrus, Romulus and Theseus owed nothing to fortune but opportunity: Cyrus, for example, had to find the Persians discontented with the Medes and the Medes softened by long peace before he could found his empire.
philosophy.tie_back: As in the Kural, the winning of great kingdoms depends on acting when time and circumstance are right.
philosophy.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. VI (tr. W. K. Marriott)

real_life_example.event_title: The Greek fleet defeats the Persians in the straits of Salamis
real_life_example.event: The Greek allied fleet, smaller than the Persian navy of Xerxes, took position in the narrow strait between the island of Salamis and the Attic coast. The Persian ships moved into position during the night and entered the strait in the early morning, where the confined waters hampered the larger fleet, and the Greek triremes rammed and boarded many of them. The defeat forced Xerxes to postpone his land campaign, giving the Greek city-states time to unite against him.
real_life_example.explanation: By fighting where their smaller numbers counted for most and the enemy's for least, the Greeks turned back the largest empire of their age.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says even the world can be won by one who chooses the right time and acts in the right place, and Salamis was won by forcing the battle into a place of the Greeks' choosing.

tamil:
காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது
ஞாலம் கருது பவர்.
transliteration:
Kaalam Karudhi Iruppar Kalangaadhu
Gnaalam Karudhu Pavar.
meaning: People who want to win the world do not get upset or hasty. They wait calmly and watch for the right time.
elementary: A cat watching a mouse-hole sits very still and doesn’t get upset or jump too early. People with big goals are like that. They stay calm and wait for their chance.
university: The couplet picks up gnaalam karudhu (‘aiming at the world’) from the previous kural and shows the inner attitude that goes with it. Such people iruppar, ‘stay’ or ‘sit still’, and do so kalangaadhu, ‘without being agitated’. Parimelazhagar explains that they are not disturbed by the enemy’s present prosperity or by their own present setbacks, because they know that the favourable time will come. The virtue described is patience that is also watchfulness, an active waiting rather than inertia. The printed division ‘karudhu pavar’ is a metrical split of karudhupavar, and the two sources agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When (the king) knows (that) at some future time his superiority (is) certain, and (that) at the time present (he will suffer) little injury, then let him have recourse to peaceful measures.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu advises a king who is sure to gain the upper hand later to stay at peace for now, since waiting costs him little.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s calm waiting for the right time, written as a rule of royal policy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain.”
christianity.explanation: James uses the farmer who waits calmly for the rains as the model of patience before a great outcome.
christianity.tie_back: The waiting farmer matches the Kural’s unperturbed person who waits for the moment.

islam.quote_or_event: At Hudaybiyyah (628 CE), the Prophet accepted a truce whose terms many companions found humiliating. They could not enter Mecca that year and had to return fugitives. The Qur’an nevertheless called it ‘a clear victory’ (48:1), and within two years Mecca opened to him.
islam.explanation: The Prophet held back from forcing the issue and waited calmly while circumstances turned in his favour.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s waiting ‘without agitation’ by one who aims at the greater goal.
islam.source: Qur’an 48:1; sira accounts of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah

judaism.quote_or_event: David was already anointed king by Samuel, yet he refused to seize the throne from Saul. For years he lived as a fugitive in the wilderness and twice spared Saul’s life when he had the chance to kill him, waiting for the kingship to come in its own time.
judaism.explanation: David’s restraint while marked for kingship is the Bible’s classic picture of patient waiting for one’s hour.
judaism.tie_back: He was one who ‘aimed at the realm’ and waited without panic for the right time.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that as a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, the wise are not moved by praise or blame.
buddhism.explanation: The wise person keeps an inner steadiness whatever happens outside.
buddhism.tie_back: Kalangaadhu, ‘unshaken’, names the same calm that the Kural requires while waiting.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A restrained, very learned, and wise (monk) should accept such alms as are freely given him, being free from passions and waiting for his end. This is the doctrine of the Kêvalin.”
jainism.explanation: The Path lecture closes by describing the sage who lives free of passion and calmly waits for his appointed end.
jainism.tie_back: The kural praises those who wait undisturbed for their time; the Jain sage also waits calmly and without agitation, though what he awaits is the end of life and liberation, not the chance to win the world.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.11.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Within yourself, make patience the bow, and make patience the bowstring. Make patience the arrow, the Creator will not let you miss the target.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, makes patience (sabar) the whole weapon: bow, string and arrow, which God will not let miss.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural shows those who aim at the world waiting calmly and unshaken for their time; Farid teaches that patience itself is the weapon that finds its mark.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 115) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: For years Penelope held off the suitors. She promised to choose one of them after finishing a shroud for Laertes, and each night she secretly unwove what she had woven by day. She kept the household intact until Odysseus returned.
greek_mythology.explanation: She could not overpower the suitors, so she bought time with calm cunning, waiting for the moment when things would change.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope shows the Kural’s patient waiting, steady amid pressure and alert to the coming time.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Sun Tzu said: The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu teaches that security lies in your own hands, while the chance of victory must be waited for, since the enemy provides it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s picture: secure and unshaken, the aspirant waits for the time.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IV.1 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Fabius Maximus, the Delayer, wears down Hannibal
real_life_example.event: After Hannibal's victories in Italy, Quintus Fabius Maximus was made dictator in 217 BCE and refused to meet Hannibal in pitched battle, instead shadowing his army through the hills, harassing his foraging parties and cutting off his supplies. His caution was unpopular in Rome, earning him the nickname Cunctator, the Delayer, and his command was divided with his critic Minucius. After the Romans abandoned the strategy and suffered a disastrous defeat at Cannae in 216 BCE, they returned to his approach.
real_life_example.explanation: Fabius endured public ridicule rather than fight on the enemy's terms, and his patience was later recognised as having saved Rome.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who aim high wait unshaken for their time, undisturbed by the enemy's present success, and Fabius held to his course while Hannibal seemed unstoppable and Rome mocked him.

tamil:
ஊக்க முடையான் ஒடுக்கம் பொருதகர்
தாக்கற்குப் பேருந் தகைத்து.
transliteration:
Ookka Mutaiyaan Otukkam Porudhakar
Thaakkarkup Perun Thakaiththu.
meaning: When a strong, active person holds back for a while, it is like a fighting ram stepping back so it can charge harder.
elementary: When a ram wants to butt, it first walks backward a few steps, then rushes forward with great force. A strong person who waits quietly for a while is not giving up. They are getting ready to charge.
university: Ookkam means energy or zeal, and otukkam means drawing in, withdrawal or restraint. Porudhakar is a fighting ram (poru, ‘fight’, + thakar, ‘ram’), and thaakkal means butting or striking. Perum thakaiththu means ‘is of the nature of drawing back’, which Parimelazhagar reads as backing up to strike harder. The image reassures anyone who might misread the patient man’s restraint as weakness: his pause is how he gathers force. The same logic appears in the feigned retreats of military history and in Sun Tzu’s ‘coyness of a maiden’ followed by the rush of a hare. The printed ‘perun thakaiththu’ shows the nasal sandhi of perum before th-.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Jarasandha besieged Mathura again and again, Krishna and Balarama finally withdrew. They moved the Yadavas to the island fortress of Dwaraka, so that Krishna came to be called Ranchhod, ‘the one who left the battlefield’. From that secure base Krishna later arranged Jarasandha’s death through Bhima.
hinduism.explanation: The withdrawal looked like flight but was a strategic step back that made a decisive later blow possible.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the ram stepping back before the charge: an energetic hero’s retreat that sets up the strike.

christianity.quote_or_event: When the Pharisees plotted to destroy Jesus, Matthew says he knew of it and withdrew from there. Great crowds followed him and he healed them, and he told them not to make him known, since his hour had not yet come.
christianity.explanation: Jesus repeatedly avoided confrontation that would have come too early, and kept his mission going until the appointed time.
christianity.tie_back: His withdrawal is restraint in the service of a later and greater purpose, like the ram’s step back.

islam.quote_or_event: Facing persecution in Mecca, the Prophet and his followers emigrated to Medina in 622 CE (the Hijra). There they built a community and strength. Eight years later they returned to Mecca in triumph.
islam.explanation: The Hijra was a withdrawal that became the base for later success. Islam dates its calendar from it.
islam.tie_back: Like the ram’s backward step, the retreat to Medina gathered the force for the return.
islam.source: Qur’an 9:40; sira accounts of the Hijra

judaism.quote_or_event: At Ai, Joshua set an ambush behind the city and led the main army in a feigned flight. When the men of Ai left their walls to pursue, the ambush took the city, and Israel turned back and struck.
judaism.explanation: The pretended retreat drew the enemy out of his strong position so that Israel’s counter-attack would be decisive.
judaism.tie_back: This is the fighting ram’s step back turned into a battle plan.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kumma Sutta, a tortoise draws its limbs and head into its shell when a jackal comes near. The jackal waits for it to put something out, but the tortoise keeps still until the jackal gives up and leaves. The Buddha tells monks to guard their senses in the same way.
buddhism.explanation: Drawing in at the dangerous moment protects one from a waiting predator.
buddhism.tie_back: Otukkam, drawing in, is shown as strength rather than weakness, though here it protects and does not strike.
buddhism.source: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.199 (Kumma Sutta), tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: When Bahubali, after defeating his elder brother Bharata in the contests that settled their war, raised his fist for a final blow, he stopped, judged that striking his brother would be wrong, and turned the same raised hand on himself, pulling out his hair in the ascetic's renunciation. Jain tradition then shows him standing in unmoving meditation until he gained omniscience.
jainism.explanation: The story turns a blow held back into a greater victory: the energy withdrawn from striking an outward foe is redirected against the passions within.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's ram draws back so that it can strike harder; Bahubali's drawn-back fist also becomes a stronger blow, aimed at his own karma rather than at an enemy.
jainism.source: Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra of Hemacandra, Book 1, Bharata and Bahubali (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The sinner, like the deer hunter, bows down twice as much.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Nanak notes that a hunter stalking deer bends low only to strike, so outward bowing is no proof of humility.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares the energetic man's holding back to a ram stepping back before it charges; Guru Nanak sees the same pattern in the hunter's crouch before the kill.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After ten years of fighting, the Greeks burned their camp and sailed away to hide behind the island of Tenedos, leaving the wooden horse on the shore. When the Trojans had brought it inside, the fleet came back by night and the men in the horse opened the gates.
greek_mythology.explanation: The apparent withdrawal was the preparation for the blow that ended the war.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The ram steps back and then charges. The Greeks retreat and then take Troy.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 8.492–520 (Demodocus’ song); fuller in Virgil, Aeneid II

philosophy.quote_or_event: “At first, then, exhibit the coyness of a maiden, until the enemy gives you an opening; afterwards emulate the rapidity of a running hare, and it will be too late for the enemy to oppose you.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu advises apparent passivity until the enemy exposes himself, then sudden, overwhelming speed.
philosophy.tie_back: Restraint first and then a rush is the ram’s backward step and forward charge.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War XI.68 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Napoleon gives up the Pratzen Heights before striking at Austerlitz
real_life_example.event: Before the Battle of Austerlitz, Napoleon withdrew his troops from the Pratzen Heights and kept his right flank weak, and the Russian and Austrian allies occupied the heights and launched their main attack against that flank. As the morning mist cleared, Napoleon saw that the allies had moved troops away from the heights and weakened their centre, and he sent Marshal Soult's corps up the slope to take it, cutting the allied army in two. His 68,000 troops defeated almost 90,000 Russians and Austrians, and Austria made peace soon afterwards.
real_life_example.explanation: Giving up the high ground at first helped draw the allies into the move that exposed them to Napoleon's decisive attack.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares a strong man's holding back to a fighting ram stepping back to strike harder, and Napoleon's withdrawal from the heights was followed by the blow that won the battle.

tamil:
பொள்ளென ஆங்கே புறம்வேரார் காலம்பார்த்து
உள்வேர்ப்பர் ஒள்ளி யவர்.
transliteration:
Pollena Aange Puramveraar Kaalampaarththu
Ulverppar Olli Yavar.
meaning: Wise people do not burst out in anger right away. They keep it inside and wait for the right time to act.
elementary: If someone is rude to you and you shout back at once, you may make things worse. A wise person stays calm on the outside, remembers what happened, and deals with it later at a better moment.
university: Pollena means suddenly or at once, and aange means right there. Puram veraar means ‘they do not sweat or seethe outwardly’, and ul verppar means ‘they seethe within’. Olliyavar are the bright or clear-minded. Parimelazhagar explains that when the wise are provoked by enemies, they do not show anger immediately, because doing so would warn the enemy. They hold it until kaalam paarththu, ‘watching for the time’. The couplet is about strategy, not ethical renunciation of anger: the feeling is kept and redirected, not dissolved. Commentators contrast it with Chapter 31 (Vekulaamai, ‘Not Being Angry’), where anger is to be given up entirely. The two sources agree; ‘olli yavar’ is a metrical split of olliyavar.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the dice hall, as Draupadi was humiliated, Bhima raged. Yudhishthira’s word, and the Pandavas’ bond to the wager, held him back from attacking the Kauravas then and there. Instead Bhima swore vows he fulfilled thirteen years later at Kurukshetra, breaking Duryodhana’s thigh and drinking Duhshasana’s blood.
hinduism.explanation: Bhima’s anger was not given up but held in until the war, the right time.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘seething within, not without’, kept until the moment for revenge came.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Sabhā Parva (Dyūta sub-parva) and Śalya/Karṇa Parvas (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: James tells believers to be swift to hear, slow to speak and slow to wrath, because human anger does not produce the righteousness of God.
christianity.explanation: Early Christian ethics warns against quick, uncontrolled outbursts of anger.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Slow to wrath’ matches the Kural’s refusal to blaze up on the spot, though James does not advise saving it for later.

islam.quote_or_event: “˹They are˺ those who donate in prosperity and adversity, control their anger, and pardon others. And Allah loves the good-doers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises al-kāẓimīn al-ghayẓ, literally ‘those who hold in their rage’, as a camel swallows back its cud.
islam.tie_back: Kaẓm al-ghayẓ, holding in rage, is almost a literal counterpart of ul verppar, ‘seething within’.
islam.source: Qur’an 3:134 (tr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Joseph made haste; for his bowels did yearn upon his brother: and he sought where to weep; and he entered into his chamber, and wept there. And he washed his face, and went out, and refrained himself, and said, Set on bread.”
judaism.explanation: Overcome by feeling at seeing Benjamin, Joseph hides it, weeps in private, then returns composed. He does not yet reveal himself to the brothers who sold him, and waits until the test is complete.
judaism.tie_back: This is powerful feeling hidden within and held back until the right moment, as the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada calls the one who checks rising anger, as a charioteer checks a rolling chariot, a true charioteer. Others merely hold the reins.
buddhism.explanation: Mastery means stopping anger at the very moment it starts to roll.
buddhism.tie_back: The check on the sudden outburst (pollena) is shared, though Buddhism aims to extinguish anger, not store it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not speak unasked, and asked he should not tell a lie; he should not give way to his anger, and bear with indifference pleasant and unpleasant occurrences.”
jainism.explanation: The monk is told not to give way to anger at all and to meet both pleasant and unpleasant events with equanimity.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's wise man hides his anger and waits for the right time; Jainism agrees that anger should not burst out, but it asks for anger to be given up rather than stored for later.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O anger, you are the root of conflict; compassion never rises up in you.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Salok Sehskritee, Guru Arjan addresses anger (krodh), one of the five thieves, as the root of strife and the enemy of compassion.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural has the wise keep their anger hidden until the right time; Sikh teaching goes further and treats anger itself as a vice to be overcome, not stored up.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sehskritee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Agamemnon takes Briseis, Achilles half-draws his sword to kill him. Athena, visible to him alone, grips his hair and tells him to hold his hand, to use words only, and promises that he will one day receive gifts three times as great for this insult. Achilles pushes the sword back into its sheath.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess of wisdom stops the instant outburst and points Achilles toward a later redress.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural exactly: the wise do not strike on the spot but hold their wrath for the right time.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle praises the man who is angry at the right things and with the right people, and also as he ought, when he ought and for as long as he ought. He blames both irascibility and a slavish lack of spirit.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, anger is not bad in itself. Its virtue is a matter of right measure and right timing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wise man also keeps his anger but lets it out only ‘when he ought’.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.5, 1125b31–1126a3 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The young Kangxi Emperor removes the regent Oboi
real_life_example.event: The Kangxi Emperor came to the Qing throne in 1661 at not quite seven years old, and four senior Manchu advisers, Sonin, Suksaha, Ebilun and Oboi, governed in his name. Although he began formally attending to state affairs in 1667, real power remained with the regents, Oboi chief among them. In 1669, at the age of 15, the emperor had Oboi arrested and removed the regents, taking control of the government himself.
real_life_example.explanation: The young emperor bore the regents' domination for years and acted only when he was able to break it, beginning one of the longest and most successful reigns in Chinese history.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the wise do not flare up at once but hold their resentment inside and wait for the right time, and Kangxi waited until he could act decisively against the man who dominated his court.

tamil:
செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க இறுவரை
காணின் கிழக்காம் தலை.
transliteration:
Serunaraik Kaanin Sumakka Iruvarai
Kaanin Kizhakkaam Thalai.
meaning: When you meet your enemies, put up with them and even show them respect. When their time to fall comes, they will fall headfirst.
elementary: Sometimes you have to put up with someone difficult who is stronger than you right now. If you stay patient, a time will come when they lose their power. Wait for that time instead of starting a fight you can’t win.
university: Serunar are enemies, and sumakka means ‘carry’ or ‘bear’. Parimelazhagar understands this as even showing them deference, carrying them ‘on one’s head’ as it were. Iruvarai is the limit or end-time, the point at which the enemy’s fortune has run out. Kizhakkaam thalai, ‘the head will turn downward’, comes from kizh (below). Parimelazhagar reads kizhakku here as keezh, ‘downward’, not the homonym meaning ‘east’. The advice is openly realpolitik: submit outwardly while weak and strike when the enemy’s time has come. It closely echoes Kanika’s counsel to Dhritarashtra in the Mahābhārata to carry the enemy on one’s shoulder and then smash him like a pot on a stone. Both sources give identical text.
