hinduism.quote_or_event: The minister Kanika advises Dhritarashtra that as long as time is unfavourable, a king should carry his foe on his shoulder. When the right time comes, he should dash the foe to pieces like an earthen pot thrown on a stone.
hinduism.explanation: Kanika’s Machiavellian counsel, given as the Kauravas turn against the Pandavas, recommends outward submission until the moment to destroy.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Carry him on your shoulder’ is sumakka, ‘bear him’. The pot smashed on the stone is the head that falls at iruvarai.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Ādi Parva, Section 142 (Kanika’s counsel; tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the wheat and the tares, the householder refuses to pull up the weeds too early and waits for harvest, when they can be removed safely.
christianity.tie_back: Enduring what is hostile until its appointed end is the Kural’s sumakka … iruvarai.

islam.quote_or_event: In an early Meccan sura, the Prophet is told to bear patiently what his opponents say and to part from them gracefully. God says to leave the wealthy deniers to Him and to give them a little respite.
islam.explanation: The weak early community is told to endure hostility and not to retaliate, because the opponents’ end is fixed.
islam.tie_back: Bearing the enemy now and trusting that his downfall will come in its time is the Kural’s counsel.

judaism.quote_or_event: “David said furthermore, As the LORD liveth, the LORD shall smite him; or his day shall come to die; or he shall descend into battle, and perish.”
judaism.explanation: David, standing over the sleeping Saul, refuses to kill him. He is sure that Saul’s appointed end will come by itself.
judaism.tie_back: ‘His day shall come’ is very nearly the Kural’s iruvarai, the boundary-time of the enemy’s fall.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta repeatedly plotted against the Buddha. He tried to have him killed by assassins, a boulder and a maddened elephant. The Buddha never retaliated. Tradition says Devadatta was finally swallowed by the earth as the result of his own deeds.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha bore his enemy’s hostility, and the enemy fell by the working of his own karma.
buddhism.tie_back: This shares the Kural’s pattern of enduring now until the enemy’s end, without the Kural’s idea of striking back.
buddhism.source: Vinaya, Cullavagga VII; Dhammapada Commentary on verse 17

jainism.quote_or_event: “There is not the least hatred in me, neither now, nor before, nor in future. The Yakshas attend upon me, therefore they have beaten the boys.”
jainism.explanation: The beaten monk Harikesa bears abuse and blows without hatred, and his attackers are nevertheless brought low, not by him but by the guardian spirits.
jainism.tie_back: The kural advises bearing one's foes until their time of downfall comes; in this story the monk too bears his enemies and they fall, but Jainism insists that he wanted no revenge at all.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid tells the seeker not to return blows but to answer aggressors with deference and go home in peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to bear with foes and even honour them until their time of downfall comes; Farid also counsels bearing foes and honouring them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 7) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Returning to Ithaca disguised as a beggar, Odysseus endures the suitors’ insults, a stool thrown at him, and the taunts of his own disloyal servants. He waits until the contest of the bow puts a weapon in his hands. Then he throws off his rags and kills them all.
greek_mythology.explanation: The king bears humiliation from his enemies in his own hall until the moment of their ruin comes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is sumakka followed by the falling heads, in the most famous revenge story of Greek epic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: After Rome’s disasters against Hannibal, Quintus Fabius Maximus refused pitched battle and shadowed the invader from the hills. He endured public mockery as ‘Hannibal’s pedagogue’ and ‘the Delayer’ (Cunctator) while Hannibal’s strength wore down. Plutarch praises his judgment, which Rome’s later victory vindicated.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch holds up Fabius as the model of the statesman who bears an enemy’s presence and his own disgrace until time turns the balance.
philosophy.tie_back: Fabius ‘carried’ Hannibal in Italy for years until the invader’s power ran out, as the Kural advises.

real_life_example.event_title: Tokugawa Ieyasu serves Hideyoshi, then wins Japan
real_life_example.event: After fighting Toyotomi Hideyoshi without success in 1584, Tokugawa Ieyasu agreed to become his vassal and served him for the rest of Hideyoshi's life, strengthening his own domain around Edo and avoiding Hideyoshi's costly invasions of Korea. Hideyoshi died in 1598, leaving a young heir, and in 1600 Ieyasu defeated the rival coalition at the Battle of Sekigahara, becoming the undisputed master of Japan. He received the title of shogun in 1603, founding the Tokugawa shogunate.
real_life_example.explanation: Ieyasu bowed to a stronger rival for more than a decade and moved only when that rival's power had passed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises bearing with one's foes, even showing them deference, until their time runs out, and Ieyasu's long service to Hideyoshi ended in his own supremacy.

tamil:
எய்தற் கரியது இயைந்தக்கால் அந்நிலையே
செய்தற் கரிய செயல்.
transliteration:
Eydhar Kariyadhu Iyaindhakkaal Annilaiye
Seydhar Kariya Seyal.
meaning: When a rare chance comes, grab it at once and do the thing that would be too hard to do at any other time.
elementary: Imagine a gate that opens only for a moment. If you run through right away, you get in. If you wait to think it over, it shuts. When a rare chance comes, use it straight away.
university: The couplet uses a chiasmus of ‘rare’ things: eydhar kariyadhu (what is hard to obtain, the rare opportunity) and seydhar kariya seyal (deeds hard to do). The link is annilaiye, ‘in that very state, at that very moment’. Iyaindhakkaal means ‘when it has come together’ or ‘when it has fallen into place’. Parimelazhagar stresses immediacy: the opportunity will not return, so the difficult act must be done while it lasts. The previous couplets counselled patience, and this one completes them by insisting that patience ends in decisive action. The Greek figure of Kairos, bald behind so that he cannot be grabbed once he has passed, is the classic Western emblem of the same idea. Text identical in both sources; ‘eydhar kariyadhu’ and ‘seydhar kariya’ are metrical splits of eydharkariyadhu and seydharkariya.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that fortunate are the warriors who meet, unsought, a righteous war like this one, which comes as an open door to heaven. To turn away from it would be to lose both duty and honour.
hinduism.explanation: The battle has arrived by itself (yadṛcchayā) as a rare chance for the kshatriya, and to hesitate is to fail.
hinduism.tie_back: A rare, unsought opportunity that must be taken at once matches the Kural’s eydharkariyadhu iyaindhakkaal.

christianity.quote_or_event: “…behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.”
christianity.explanation: Paul quotes Isaiah to insist that the moment of grace is now and should not be put off.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Now is the accepted time’ carries the urgency of the Kural’s annilaiye, ‘at that very moment’.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn ‘Umar, recalling the Prophet’s counsel to live in the world like a stranger, advised: if you reach the evening, do not wait for the morning, and if you reach the morning, do not wait for the evening. Take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death.
islam.explanation: Present opportunities are fleeting and should be used now, before they are gone.
islam.tie_back: Using the chance while it lasts is the Kural’s annilaiye, ‘then and there’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not: ‘when I shall have leisure I shall study;’ perhaps you will not have leisure.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel warns against putting off what matters until a better time that may never arrive.
judaism.tie_back: The chance you have is the one to use, as the Kural says of the rare opportunity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a border city is closely guarded both within and without, even so, guard yourself. Do not let slip this opportunity (for spiritual growth). For those who let slip this opportunity grieve indeed when consigned to hell.”
buddhism.explanation: The Pali khaṇo vo mā upaccagā, ‘let not the moment pass you by’, treats human birth as a rare opportunity that must not be wasted.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s rare moment, eydharkariyadhu, that must be seized annilaiye, then and there.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A rare chance, in the long course of time, is human birth for a living being; hard are the consequences of actions; Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama that human birth is a rare opportunity across vast ages and must be used without a moment's carelessness.
jainism.tie_back: The kural urges seizing a rare opportunity at once to do what would otherwise be impossible; Jainism makes the same demand about the rarest opportunity of all, a human life in which liberation can be pursued.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.4 (refrain from 10.1) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately! Later on, you will not be able to do anything, when death hangs over your head.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir urges acting at once while the chance remains, because the moment, once lost, does not return.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to seize a rare opportunity the moment it comes and do the hard deed; Kabir insists on acting now, before the opening closes.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 138) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Kairos, the god of the opportune moment, was portrayed in Lysippus’ famous bronze. A dialogue epigram attributed to Posidippus describes it. The god stands on tiptoe on a razor’s edge with wings on his feet and a lock of hair over his forehead, while the back of his head is bald. Whoever meets him must grab him from the front, because once he has passed no one can catch him from behind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Kairos personifies the fleeting right moment that must be seized at once or lost forever.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘when the rare thing comes, act then’ is the exact moral of the Kairos statue.
greek_mythology.source: Posidippus, epigram on Lysippus’ Kairos (Greek Anthology 16.275)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar, Brutus argues for marching at once to Philippi. He says there is a tide in human affairs which, if taken at its flood, leads to fortune, and if missed leaves life stranded in shallows and misery.
philosophy.explanation: Brutus insists that a favourable moment, once missed, does not come back.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s rare opportunity is Shakespeare’s flood tide, and both must be taken the moment it comes.
philosophy.source: William Shakespeare, Julius Caesar, Act 4, Scene 3

real_life_example.event_title: American envoys accept Napoleon's offer of all Louisiana
real_life_example.event: President Thomas Jefferson's envoys, Robert Livingston and James Monroe, were authorised to pay up to 10 million dollars for New Orleans and West Florida. On 11 April 1803, the French unexpectedly offered the whole Louisiana Territory, and although this went beyond their instructions, the envoys agreed without waiting the months needed to consult Washington. The treaty, dated 30 April 1803, transferred about 827,000 square miles for 15 million dollars, roughly doubling the size of the United States.
real_life_example.explanation: A chance that arose from Napoleon's sudden change of plans was seized at once and transformed the future of the United States.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when a rare opportunity comes, one must at once do the deed that would otherwise be impossible, and the envoys closed the deal before the opportunity could vanish.

tamil:
கொக்கொக்க கூம்பும் பருவத்து மற்றதன்
குத்தொக்க சீர்த்த இடத்து.
transliteration:
Kokkokka Koompum Paruvaththu Matradhan
Kuththokka Seerththa Itaththu.
meaning: When the time is not right, wait quietly like a heron standing still. When the right moment comes, strike as fast and sure as the heron catches a fish.
elementary: Have you seen a heron fishing? It stands very still in the water for a long time. When a fish swims close, it stabs down in a flash. Be patient like the heron while you wait, and quick like the heron when your chance comes.
university: The chapter ends with a double simile built on the kokku (heron or crane). In the season of koompum, ‘folding in’ or ‘drawing oneself together’, one should kokku okka, ‘be like the heron’, standing motionless and seemingly asleep. When the time is seerththa, ‘excellent’ or ‘fitting’, one should be like its kuththu (stab). Parimelazhagar notes the pairing of stillness and sudden strike as the model of a king’s conduct toward enemies. The heron also appears in Manusmṛti 7.106 and in the Chāṇakya Nīti as a model of patient concentration, which suggests a shared South Asian stock image. Some texts, including the musical setting on Thirukkural.net, read ‘seerththa vidaththu’ with a glide consonant. The two editions consulted print ‘seerththa idaththu’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him plan his undertakings (patiently meditating) like a heron; like a lion, let him put forth his strength; like a wolf, let him snatch (his prey); like a hare, let him double in retreat.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu’s rules for kings use animal models, and the heron stands for patient, concentrated planning before the strike.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s heron-king, still in planning and swift in the snatch.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take ye heed, watch and pray: for ye know not when the time is.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples to stay alert and ready, because the decisive moment will come without warning.
christianity.tie_back: The heron’s watchful stillness before an unpredictable moment is the attitude described here.

islam.quote_or_event: At Uhud (625 CE) the Prophet posted archers on a hill with orders not to leave it. When they abandoned their post to collect spoils, Khalid ibn al-Walid, then fighting for Mecca, who had been watching for exactly that gap, struck the Muslims from the rear. The Qur’an (3:152) reflects on the lapse.
islam.explanation: The episode shows both sides of the heron’s lesson: the cost of leaving watchful stillness too early, and the power of a strike timed to the enemy’s opening.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an’s reproach for abandoning the post and Khalid’s timed charge together illustrate the Kural’s wait-then-strike.
islam.source: Qur’an 3:152; sira accounts of the Battle of Uhud

judaism.quote_or_event: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven… a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet’s poem of times pairs opposite actions, each right in its own season.
judaism.tie_back: The heron’s time of stillness and time of striking are one of Kohelet’s pairs in bird form.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Abhaya Sutta, the Buddha says that the Tathāgata knows the proper time to say even unwelcome things that are true and beneficial. He compares himself to a person who quickly removes a stick or stone from an infant’s mouth, even if it draws blood, when the moment requires it.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha waits for the right time (kālaññū) and then acts decisively, even painfully, for the good of the other.
buddhism.tie_back: Holding back until the right moment and then acting sharply is the heron’s pattern, applied to speech.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikāya 58 (Abhaya Sutta), tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “As dhaṅkas, herons, ospreys, cormorants, and pheasants meditate upon capturing fish, (which is) a sinful and very low meditation, so some heretical, unworthy Sramanas contemplate the pursuit of pleasures; (they are) sinful and very low like herons.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga uses the heron's still, fish-watching posture as an image of false meditation, a show of stillness that hides a predatory aim.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar praises the heron's stillness before it strikes as a model of good timing; the Jain text uses the same bird for the opposite lesson, so it is an honest contrast rather than an agreement.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.11.27-28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, the crane perches on the river bank, playing joyfully. While it is playing, a hawk suddenly pounces on it.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid's crane sits heedless on the riverbank until a hawk falls on it without warning, an image of death striking the careless.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells one to wait like a heron and strike like its beak when the moment comes; Farid uses the same waterside bird, but as the prey of a sudden strike rather than the striker.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1383, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Gaia hid her son Cronus in ambush with a jagged sickle. When Ouranos came at night and lay over the earth, Cronus struck in a single blow and overthrew his father.
greek_mythology.explanation: Cronus waited hidden and motionless for the one moment when his far stronger father was exposed, then struck decisively.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Still in ambush and swift in the strike, Cronus follows the heron’s method.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…it is good, to commit the beginnings of all great actions to Argus, with his hundred eyes, and the ends to Briareus, with his hundred hands; first to watch, and then to speed.”
philosophy.explanation: Bacon divides action into a phase of watchful vigilance and a phase of swift execution. He adds that ‘secrecy in the counsel, and celerity in the execution’ make the statesman effective.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘First to watch, and then to speed’ is the heron’s stillness followed by its stab.

real_life_example.event_title: Muhammad Ali's rope-a-dope in the Rumble in the Jungle
real_life_example.place: Kinshasa, Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo)
real_life_example.event: Muhammad Ali, a heavy underdog, fought the unbeaten heavyweight champion George Foreman in Kinshasa. For several rounds Ali leaned on the ropes, blocking and absorbing Foreman's punches in the tactic he called the rope-a-dope, and by the middle rounds Foreman was visibly tiring. In the eighth round Ali came off the ropes with a rapid combination that knocked Foreman down, and he was counted out, giving Ali back the world heavyweight title.
real_life_example.explanation: Ali's long stillness on the ropes looked like weakness but was the preparation for one sudden, decisive attack.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says to stand still like the heron while the time is not ripe and strike like its beak when it is, and Ali waited on the ropes until Foreman was spent and then struck once, decisively.

tamil:
தொடங்கற்க எவ்வினையும் எள்ளற்க முற்றும்
இடங்கண்ட பின்அல் லது.
transliteration:
Thodangarka evvinaiyum ellarka mutrum
Idanganda pinnal lathu.
meaning: Do not start any action against an enemy, and do not look down on them, until you have found a place from which you can surround and defeat them.
elementary: Before a game of hide-and-seek, a smart player first looks around for the best hiding spot, and never thinks the seeker is too silly to find them. Valluvar says to do the same with any big task: find the right spot first, and never think the other side is weak.
university: The chapter opens the third member of the triad that runs through chapters 48 to 50: strength (vali), time (kaalam) and now place (idam). The key word is ‘mutrum idam’, a place from which one can encircle or besiege (mutruthal, to surround, to lay siege); Parimelazhagar and the modern word-glosses (for example thirukkural-thamizh.org) take it as the ground suited for investing the enemy. The two prohibitions are joined: ‘thodangarka’ (do not begin) and ‘ellarka’ (do not despise), so over-confidence and bad positioning are treated as a single error. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah take ‘ellarka’ as ‘do not scorn the enemy’, whereas Kalaignar reads it as ‘do not treat the undertaking itself as trivial’, a minor interpretive variant. Older printed texts give the sandhi form ‘தொடங்கற்க வெவ்வினையு மெள்ளற்க’, which modern editions split as ‘எவ்வினையும் எள்ளற்க’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya opens Book IX of the Arthashastra by telling the would-be conqueror to weigh his own and his enemy’s power, place and time before marching, and he defines a good place as ground suited to the manoeuvres of one’s own army and unsuited to the enemy’s.
hinduism.explanation: For Kautilya, desha (place) is one of the things a king has to calculate before starting any campaign, together with strength and the right season.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar gives the same order: work out the ground first, and only then begin.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book IX, Chapter 1 (tr. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock… And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts two builders: one picked solid ground and his house stood, the other picked sand and his house fell.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the outcome is decided by choosing the right ground before starting to build.

islam.quote_or_event: Before Badr, the Companion al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir asked the Prophet whether the chosen campsite was fixed by revelation or was a matter of war and strategy. When told it was strategy, he advised moving forward to the wells nearest the enemy, and the Prophet accepted.
islam.explanation: The early biography presents this as a model of choosing a position carefully before fighting begins, by taking control of the water.
islam.tie_back: It fits the Kural’s rule not to begin until the right position has been found.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad), account of Badr

judaism.quote_or_event: “Do not despise any man, and do not discriminate against anything, for there is no man that has not his hour, and there is no thing that has not its place.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Azzai warns that nobody should be dismissed, because every person has a moment and every thing has its place.
judaism.tie_back: The mishnah brings together the Kural’s two concerns, not despising the other side (ellarka) and taking place seriously.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes Himalayan ground where only monkeys can go and level ground where hunters lay tar traps. Wise monkeys see the trap and keep away, while a careless monkey walks onto the hunter’s ground and gets stuck in five places.
buddhism.explanation: He uses the story to warn monks against leaving their proper range (their own territory) for someone else’s ground.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the fatal mistake is acting before judging whether the ground belongs to you or to your enemy.
buddhism.source: Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.7, Makkata Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Fight with your Self; why fight with external foes? He who conquers himself through himself, will obtain happiness. The five senses, anger, pride, delusion, and greed--difficult to conquer is one's self; but when that is conquered, everything is conquered.”
jainism.explanation: Nami tells Indra that the real enemy is within and is hard to defeat, and that victory there carries every other victory with it.
jainism.tie_back: The kural warns against attacking or belittling a foe before securing the right ground; Nami also treats the enemy as difficult and names the self as the only ground from which full victory can be won.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.35-36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: After Guru Gobind Singh sent him to the Punjab in 1708, Banda Singh Bahadur did not strike at once at Sirhind, the seat of the Mughal governor Wazir Khan. He first took Samana, Sadhaura and other towns, following a long, roundabout route while he waited for Sikhs from the Doaba and Majha to join him, and only then attacked Sirhind, which fell after the battle of Chappar Chiri in May 1710.
sikhism.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism records that Banda Singh deliberately delayed his main blow until he had gathered strength and secured the ground around his target.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says not to move against an enemy, or to belittle him, until one has found ground from which to surround and overcome him; Banda Singh likewise waited and built a base before attacking Sirhind.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Banda Singh Bahadur', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Xerxes advanced in 480 BCE, the Greek allies debated where to make their stand, first at Tempe and then at the narrow pass of Thermopylae with the strait of Artemisium beside it, and they chose the pass because the narrows would cancel out Persian numbers.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus shows the Greeks picking the position before committing to battle, having judged that the terrain mattered more than headcount.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s advice in practice: settle the ground first, then begin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you know the enemy and know yourself, your victory will not stand in doubt; if you know Heaven and know Earth, you may make your victory complete.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu ends his chapter on terrain by saying that knowing the ground (Earth) is what makes victory complete.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts treat knowing the ground as something you need before acting, and neither lets you underestimate the enemy.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War X.31 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Hannibal encircles the Roman army at Cannae
real_life_example.event: In the Second Punic War a Roman army of more than 80,000 men under the consuls Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro met Hannibal's smaller Carthaginian army of under 50,000 near the river Aufidus. Hannibal placed his line in a forward-curving crescent with cavalry on the wings, and as his centre gave way the Romans pressed into it. His infantry then closed on their flanks and his cavalry came round behind them, surrounding the Roman army and destroying it.
real_life_example.explanation: Cannae became the classic example of encirclement, studied by commanders for more than two thousand years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns against engaging an enemy before finding ground from which one can surround him, and Hannibal fought only where his formation could close around the larger Roman army.

tamil:
முரண்சேர்ந்த மொய்ம்பி னவர்க்கும் அரண்சேர்ந்தாம்
ஆக்கம் பலவுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Muranserntha moimbi navarkkum aransernthaam
Aakkam palavun tharum.
meaning: Even for people who are already strong in battle, fighting from a safe, well-protected place gives them many extra advantages.
elementary: Even the strongest kid in a snowball fight does better behind a snow wall. Being strong is good, but being strong and in a safe spot is much better.
university: ‘Muran’ means hostility or opposition and ‘moimbu’ means strength, so the first line describes people strong enough to take on an enemy. ‘Aran’ is the fortress, one of the six limbs of the state that later gets its own chapter (74, அரண்), and ‘aakkam’ is gain or prosperity. The ‘-um’ (even) in ‘navarkkum’ is the point: position adds to strength and is no substitute for the lack of it, which is why Parimelazhagar reads the verse as saying that even the mighty gain from a secure base. Modern glosses widen ‘aran’ to any safe place of operation, not only a walled fort (thirukkural-thamizh.org: ‘the place of action is safe’). Older printings show the sandhi ‘மொய்ம்பி னவர்க்கு மரண்சேர்ந்தா மாக்கம்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As enemies do not hurt these (beings, when they are) sheltered by (their) fortresses, even so foes (can) not injure a king who has taken refuge in his fort.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists the kinds of forts (desert, water, forest, earthwork, armed camp, hill) and compares a king in his fort to animals that are safe in their own shelters.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, this makes the aran (fortified position) a source of power beyond the king’s own strength.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says the community he is founding will stand on a rock that no hostile power can overcome.
christianity.tie_back: The image is a secure foundation that makes its occupants hard to overcome, which is the Kural’s aran.

islam.quote_or_event: At the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq, 627 CE), the outnumbered Muslims of Medina dug a trench across the open northern approach on Salman al-Farisi’s advice, and the confederate army could not force its way through.
islam.explanation: A prepared defensive line let a much smaller force hold off a large coalition until the siege fell apart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says a secure position adds advantages even to fighters who are already strong, and the trench did this for Medina.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (tr. A. Guillaume), account of the Trench; cf. Quran 33:9–25

judaism.quote_or_event: “The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs counts the rock-hyrax among creatures that are small but very wise, because it makes up for weakness by living among rocks.
judaism.tie_back: The hyrax is a picture of the Kural’s aran: safety comes from where you are.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares a disciple to a king’s frontier fortress with a deep foundation post, a moat, a patrol road, many weapons, troops, a wise gatekeeper, high walls and ample stores. Such a fortress cannot be taken by enemies from outside.
buddhism.explanation: Each part of the fortress stands for a spiritual quality that keeps the practitioner safe from Mara.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s point that a fortified position multiplies security is the literal basis of this simile.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.63 (7.67 in some editions), Nagara Sutta: The Fortress

jainism.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable; … (in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Saṃsâra.”
jainism.explanation: When Indra urges King Nami to build walls, gates and a moat, Nami replies with a fortress made of virtues, guarded threefold and impregnable.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says even the strong gain greatly by fighting from a fortress; Nami agrees that a fortress brings victory, but his fortress is faith and patience and his battle is against karma.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.20-22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Sanctuary of the Lord's Feet is my fortress and battlement.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan names God's protection as his fort and rampart, the secure position from which he faces every threat.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says even the strong gain much by fighting from a fortified position; Guru Arjan names the one fortress Gurbani trusts above all others.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 742, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Athens asked Delphi about the Persian invasion, the oracle said that a ‘wooden wall’ alone would stay unconquered. Themistocles took this to mean the fleet and persuaded the Athenians to place their hope in the ships and the waters around Salamis.
greek_mythology.explanation: Athens survived by picking the defensive position that suited it best, which was the sea, rather than trusting its city walls.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says the right place of refuge multiplies a people’s strength, and the Athenians found theirs in the ships.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu says securing yourself comes before attacking, and is something within your own control.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s secured base (aran) is exactly this first step of making yourself impossible to defeat.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IV.1 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Constantinople's walls withstand the Arab siege of 717-718
real_life_example.event: Soon after Leo III became Byzantine emperor in 717, a large Umayyad army and fleet laid siege to Constantinople, which was protected by the massive Theodosian land walls and by sea walls. Behind these fortifications, and using the incendiary weapon known as Greek fire against the enemy fleet, the defenders held out through a harsh winter while the besiegers suffered from hunger and disease. With a Bulgar force also attacking them, the Arab army withdrew in August 718.
real_life_example.explanation: The victory checked the Arab advance into southeastern Europe and showed how a fortified capital multiplied the strength of its defenders.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even those already strong in war gain many advantages from a secure fortified position, and Leo's forces held on because they fought from behind Constantinople's walls.

tamil:
ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப இடனறிந்து
போற்றார்கண் போற்றிச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Aatraarum aatri adupa idanarinthu
Potraarkan potrich cheyin.
meaning: Even weak people can become strong enough to win if they pick the right place, protect themselves well, and then act against their enemy.
elementary: A little cat on a high shelf can bat at a big dog that can’t reach it. The cat isn’t stronger, it just picked the right spot. Valluvar says even weak people can win if they choose their spot well and stay safe.
university: The verse turns on the wordplay ‘aatraarum aatri’: those who lack power (aatraar) come to have it (aatri) and destroy the enemy (adupa). ‘Potraar’ literally means ‘those who do not honour us’, a standard Kural word for enemies, and the next word ‘potri’ (having guarded, taken care) repeats the sound with the opposite meaning. Parimelazhagar reads ‘potri’ as the actor protecting himself, so the conditions for success are knowing the place and staying self-protected. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow this reading; Kalaignar adds the idea of choosing the right place for the attack. The kural spells out what 492 implied: the right place can make up for missing strength, and not merely add to strength one already has.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the meditator to set up a firm seat in a clean place, neither too high nor too low, and only then to begin controlling the mind.
hinduism.explanation: Even inner discipline starts with choosing and securing the right spot, because an unsteady position works against the practitioner.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘idan arinthu… potri’ (know the place, guard yourself, then act) matches the yogi’s order of preparation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “After these things Jesus walked in Galilee: for he would not walk in Jewry, because the Jews sought to kill him.”
christianity.explanation: John says Jesus deliberately worked in Galilee and stayed away from Judea while his opponents there were looking for a chance to kill him.
christianity.tie_back: He kept his mission going by choosing a safer place of action, much like the Kural’s ‘potraarkan potri’ (guarding oneself among enemies).

islam.quote_or_event: “[Remember] when you were on the near side of the valley, and they were on the farther side, and the caravan was lower [in position] than you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran recalls where each side stood at Badr, when a small and poorly equipped Muslim force defeated a much larger Quraysh army.
islam.tie_back: The verse points to positioning at a battle where the weaker side won, which is the Kural’s claim.

judaism.quote_or_event: At Michmash, Jonathan and his armour-bearer climbed a narrow crag between two rocky outcrops and attacked a Philistine outpost from a position where the enemy could not bring its numbers to bear. Their success set off a wider Philistine rout.
judaism.explanation: Two men beat a garrison by using a narrow, high approach the enemy did not expect.
judaism.tie_back: The weak defeating the strong by knowing the ground is the Kural’s ‘aatraarum aatri adupa’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If only I had kept to my proper range today, to my own ancestral territory, this hawk would have been no match for me in battle.”
buddhism.explanation: A quail caught by a hawk talks its way free, returns to a ploughed field full of clods, dodges behind one, and the diving hawk breaks its own breast on it.
buddhism.tie_back: The weak bird beats the strong one only because it fights from ground it knows, which is exactly what this kural says.
buddhism.source: Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.6, Sakunagghi Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a tortoise draws its limbs into its own body, so a wise man should cover, as it were, his sins with his own meditation. He should draw in, as it were, his hands and feet, his mind and five organs of sense, the effect of his bad Karman, and every bad use of language.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga uses the tortoise, weak in itself but safe inside its shell, as the model for the monk who guards himself through restraint.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says even the weak can win if they guard themselves well in a safe place; the tortoise image shows Jain self-protection, though the danger guarded against is karma, not an army.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.8.16-17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My True Guru is the power of the powerless.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that those who have no strength of their own become strong once they take shelter with the Guru.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says even the weak overcome their enemies when they take the right position and guard themselves; Gurbani says the powerless gain power by taking the Guru as their refuge.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1142, Raag Bhairao, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before Salamis, Themistocles argued that fighting in the narrow strait favoured the smaller Greek fleet, while open sea favoured the larger Persian one, and the Greeks won by fighting in the narrows.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus records the argument and the victory that followed, which saved Greece.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The weaker side won by picking where to fight, as the Kural says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A Kid standing on the roof of a house, out of harm’s way, saw a Wolf passing by and immediately began to taunt and revile him. The Wolf… said, ‘Sirrah! I hear thee: yet it is not thou who mockest me, but the roof on which thou art standing.’”
philosophy.explanation: The fable ends with the moral that time and place often give the weak an advantage over the strong.
philosophy.tie_back: That moral restates Kural 493, together with the previous chapter’s point about time.
philosophy.source: Aesop, The Kid and the Wolf (tr. G. F. Townsend)

real_life_example.event_title: The Swiss confederates defeat the Habsburg army at Morgarten
real_life_example.event: Duke Leopold I of Habsburg led an army of knights to invade the valley of Schwyz, marching by a narrow route between the shore of Lake Ageri and the steep slopes of Morgarten. The men of Schwyz, joined by fighters from Uri, waited on the heights and attacked the column while it was strung out in the narrow ground. Leopold's army was routed and he escaped, and the confederates renewed their alliance in the Pact of Brunnen less than a month later.
real_life_example.explanation: The victory helped secure the survival of the young Swiss confederation and gave the Swiss a lasting reputation as formidable foot soldiers.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says even the weak can defeat their enemies if they choose the right place and keep themselves safe, and the confederates struck from the heights where the knights could not use their strength.

tamil:
எண்ணியார் எண்ணம் இழப்பர் இடனறிந்து
துன்னியார் துன்னிச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Enniyaar ennam izhappar idanarinthu
Thunniyaar thunnich cheyin.
meaning: Enemies who planned to beat you will lose their plans if you find the right place, stay close to it, and act from there.
elementary: A turtle pulled all the way into its shell makes the curious dog give up and walk away. When you are in the right place and stay there, the other side stops trying.
university: The verse repeats words in pairs: ‘enniyaar ennam’ (the plan of those who planned) and ‘thunniyaar thunni’ (those who reached the place, keeping close to it). ‘Thunnuthal’ means to approach, cling to or stay close; commentators read the second ‘thunni’ as keeping firmly to the chosen ground instead of drifting away from it. Parimelazhagar takes ‘enniyaar’ as enemies who expected to win, and ‘ennam izhappar’ as more than tactical defeat: they give up the intention itself. Kalaignar has the foe not even daring to think of victory, and Pulavar Kesikan takes ‘thunni’ as pressing the battle closely. Where 493 was about winning, this kural is about deterrence: the right position ends the contest before it begins.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Sabha Parva, Krishna tells Yudhishthira that the Yadavas, worn down by Jarasandha’s repeated invasions of Mathura, moved to Kushasthali (Dvaraka), a fortress on the sea. There they felt safe from his attacks.
hinduism.explanation: Instead of fighting on exposed ground, the Yadavas took a position their powerful enemy could not easily reach.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural says, taking and holding the right place frustrates an enemy who planned to win.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Sabhā Parva, Section 14 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sends his disciples into hostile territory and tells them to be shrewd about how they move there.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s idea of knowing where you stand so that enemies’ designs fail is close to the ‘wise as serpents’ half of this saying.

islam.quote_or_event: “And Allāh repelled those who disbelieved, in their rage, not having obtained any good.”
islam.explanation: This verse closes the Quran’s account of the Trench, when the confederate army besieging Medina gave up and left empty-handed.
islam.tie_back: Enemies who ‘planned’ to take Medina ‘lost their plan’ (ennam izhappar) once the defenders held their prepared ground.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the children of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites that inhabited Jerusalem; but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem unto this day.”
judaism.explanation: The Jebusites held their hill-city so firmly that the tribe of Benjamin had to give up trying to expel them.
judaism.tie_back: A people fixed in a strong place outlasted their attackers’ plans, which is Kural 494’s scenario.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Realizing that this body is as fragile as a clay pot, and fortifying this mind like a well-fortified city, fight out Mara with the sword of wisdom. Then, guarding the conquest, remain unattached.”
buddhism.explanation: The verse tells the practitioner to make the mind a fortified city from which Mara, the tempter, can be fought off.
buddhism.tie_back: Holding a fortified position so that the attacker’s design fails is the kural’s point, moved inward.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The Buddhas that were, and the Buddhas that will be, they (as it were) have Peace as their foundation, even as all things have the earth for their foundation. And if any accidents whatever befall him who has gained that (foundation), he will not be overpowered by them as a mountain by the storm.”
jainism.explanation: Here 'Buddhas' means the Tirthankaras; the sage who stands firmly on the ground of peace cannot be overpowered, as a mountain is not moved by a storm.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says that those who hold fast to their chosen ground defeat the plans of their enemies; the Jain sage who holds to the foundation of peace is similarly beyond the reach of every assault.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.11.36-37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My enemies and opponents have grown weary of attacking me, and now, I have become happy, O my friends and Siblings of Destiny.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of thanksgiving, Guru Arjan says that those who set out to harm him have worn themselves out and given up, because he stands under the Lord's protection.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says enemies who planned to win drop their plans when the defender holds firm to the right ground; Guru Arjan describes opponents who grew weary and gave up.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 826, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Behind the walls of Troy, the Trojans held off the Achaean army for ten years. The besiegers never took the city by assault, and in the end had to resort to the trick of the wooden horse.
greek_mythology.explanation: A strong position frustrated a superior coalition for a decade, until the defenders were drawn out of their own security.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As long as the Trojans stayed with their ground (thunni), the attackers’ plans kept failing, which is the Kural’s point.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad (siege narrative), and Odyssey 8.492–520 on the horse

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Hence the skillful fighter puts himself into a position which makes defeat impossible, and does not miss the moment for defeating the enemy.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu says a well-chosen position removes the enemy’s chance of winning.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that holding the right place makes the enemy’s plans come to nothing.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IV.14 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Masséna halts before the Lines of Torres Vedras
real_life_example.event: During the Peninsular War, Wellington had a great network of forts, redoubts and barriers built across the hills north of Lisbon, using the natural terrain and blocking the roads, and laid waste the country in front of them. In October 1810 his Anglo-Portuguese army withdrew behind these Lines, and Marshal Masséna's French army, arriving before them, did not attempt a full assault. After a winter of great hardship and heavy losses from hunger, the French began to retreat from Portugal in March 1811.
real_life_example.explanation: Without a major battle, a well-chosen and fortified position defeated an invasion simply by making the enemy's plan impossible.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that if those who have found the right place hold fast to it, enemies who planned to beat them will have to give up their plans, which is exactly what Masséna did.

tamil:
நெடும்புனலுள் வெல்லும் முதலை அடும்புனலின்
நீங்கின் அதனைப் பிற.
transliteration:
Nedumpunalul vellum muthalai adumpunalin
Neengin athanaip pira.
meaning: In deep water a crocodile can beat other animals. But once it leaves the water, those same animals can beat it.
elementary: A fish is the best swimmer in the pond, but put it on the grass and it can hardly move. The crocodile is the same: a champion in the river, in trouble on dry land.
university: This is the chapter’s best-known image. ‘Nedumpunal’ is deep or wide water; ‘adum’ (kills, overcomes) is placed in the middle so that it can be read with either half. Parimelazhagar’s construction is: in deep water the crocodile defeats others; if it leaves the water, others (pira) kill it. The verse leaves out the verb of the second clause and borrows it from ‘adum’, typical Kural compression. The Sanskrit nīti tradition has the same image in a Pañcatantra verse (nakraḥ svasthānam āsādya gajendram api karṣati), where the crocodile in its own place drags even a lordly elephant but out of it is beaten by a dog. That suggests a shared South Asian stock of proverbs rather than direct borrowing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “nakraḥ svasthānam āsādya gajendram api karṣati | sa eva pracyutaḥ sthānāc chunāpi paribhūyate”
hinduism.explanation: In its own place, the crocodile drags even a king of elephants; the same crocodile, fallen from its place, is overpowered even by a dog.
hinduism.tie_back: This Sanskrit maxim is almost a twin of Kural 495, crocodile included.
hinduism.source: Pañcatantra III (Kākolūkīya), v. 43/46 depending on edition; cited in Apte and Böhtlingk–Roth s.v. nakra (wisdomlib.org)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm says the righteous person does well like a tree planted in its proper place beside water.
christianity.tie_back: It gives the positive side of the crocodile image: in its right element, a living thing is at full strength.

islam.quote_or_event: At Uhud the Prophet told his fifty archers, “Stick to your place, and don’t leave it even if you see birds snatching us, till I send for you.” When most of them left the hill to collect booty, the Quraysh cavalry circled round, and the Muslims were routed.
islam.explanation: The archers were decisive on their hill and became helpless once they left it.
islam.tie_back: Like the crocodile leaving the water, a force that abandons its own place gives its strength away.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If we are afraid in the water, our natural habitat which gives us life, then in a habitat that causes our death, all the more so.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Akiva tells of a fox inviting frightened fish onto dry land, and the fish refuse because leaving their element would kill them for certain. He applies the parable to Israel and Torah.
judaism.tie_back: The same creature-out-of-its-element logic as the crocodile verse.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 61b (William Davidson/Koren translation, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As a fish when pulled out of water and cast on land throbs and quivers, even so is this mind agitated.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares the untrained mind to a fish thrown onto land, helpless and thrashing.
buddhism.tie_back: The water creature that loses its power on land is the Kural’s central image.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain metaphysics holds that souls and matter can move only where dharmastikaya, the medium of motion, is present, and come to rest by means of adharmastikaya, the medium of rest. Commentators illustrate this with the fish, which moves freely only in water, the water being the medium of its movement.
jainism.explanation: In Jain cosmology the power to move depends on being in the right medium; outside that medium, motion is impossible however strong the being is.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's crocodile is mighty in deep water and helpless out of it; the Jain doctrine of the medium of motion, with its fish-in-water illustration, likewise makes a being's power depend on the element it is in.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.17 of Umasvati (paraphrase), with the traditional fish-in-water illustration from the commentaries

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O mind, love the Lord, as the fish loves the water.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the fish, which thrives in water and cannot live outside it even for a moment, as an image of the soul's dependence on God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's crocodile is mighty in deep water and helpless on land; Gurbani's fish likewise has its whole life and strength in its own element.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 60, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The giant Antaeus, son of Earth, could not be beaten while he touched the ground, which kept renewing his strength. Heracles defeated him by lifting him off the earth and crushing him in the air.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antaeus’s strength belonged to his element; taken out of it, he was easily beaten.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the Greek crocodile, invincible in his own place and powerless once removed from it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I well deserve my fate, for what business had I on the land, when by my nature and habits I am only adapted for the sea?”
philosophy.explanation: A crab that leaves the shore to feed in a meadow is eaten by a fox and blames itself as it dies.
philosophy.tie_back: Almost the crocodile kural in fable form: a sea creature is lost on land.
philosophy.source: Aesop, The Crab and the Fox, Perry 116 (tr. G. F. Townsend)

real_life_example.event_title: Tran Hung Dao destroys the Mongol fleet at the Bach Dang River
real_life_example.place: Bach Dang River, near Haiphong, Vietnam
real_life_example.event: During the third Mongol invasion of Dai Viet, the Vietnamese commander Tran Hung Dao avoided pitched battles on land and then chose to fight the withdrawing Yuan fleet on the Bach Dang River. His men drove stakes into the riverbed below the waterline, a tactic used at the same river in 938, and lured the Mongol ships onto them. The fleet was wrecked and destroyed, and the invasion ended in defeat.
real_life_example.explanation: The Mongols, nearly unbeatable on the open plains, were defeated on a tidal river whose conditions their enemy understood far better.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's crocodile is master only in its own element, and the Mongols, masters of land warfare, were overcome once they fought on Vietnamese waters.

tamil:
கடலோடா கால்வல் நெடுந்தேர் கடலோடும்
நாவாயும் ஓடா நிலத்து.
transliteration:
Kadalodaa kaalval nedunther kadalodum
Naavaayum odaa nilaththu.
meaning: A tall chariot with strong wheels cannot run on the sea, and a ship that sails the sea cannot run on land.
elementary: A bicycle is great on the road but useless in a swimming pool, and a boat is great in the pool but useless on the road. Every tool, and every person, has a place where it works best.
university: The kural uses a paired image: ‘kaal val nedunther’, the tall chariot with strong wheels (kaal, literally ‘leg’, here the wheel), and ‘naavaay’, the sea-going ship, a word related to Sanskrit nau and Latin navis, which shows early Tamil familiarity with maritime trade. The repeated verb ‘odaa’ (will not run) connects the two lines. Parimelazhagar reads the verse as an allegory for forces: land armies and naval forces each succeed only in their own element, so a king must match his forces to the terrain. Kalaignar makes it a general lesson that whoever chooses where to act must at least know that a chariot will not cross the sea. The thirukkural-thamizh.org gloss extends it to countries bordered by mountains, forests, sea or desert, each needing its own methods.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya describes different kinds of battlefield and matches each arm of the army to suitable ground: chariots need level, firm, open terrain, elephants can handle uneven and marshy ground, and infantry can fight almost anywhere.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Indian military science treats choosing terrain for each arm as an exact skill.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s chariot-and-ship image is the poetic form of this technical rule.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book X, Chapter 4 (tr. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “They ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves.”
christianity.explanation: In Paul’s shipwreck off Malta, the ship that had carried them across the sea was stuck and broken once it hit land.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ship that ‘does not run on land’, told as an actual event.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs are the ships in the sea, like mountains. If He willed, He could still the wind, and they would remain motionless on its surface.”
islam.explanation: The Quran points to great ships as signs of God, whose power depends on the conditions of the sea and wind.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats the ship’s strength as dependent on its proper element.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And took off their chariot wheels, that they drave them heavily: so that the Egyptians said, Let us flee from the face of Israel.”
judaism.explanation: Pharaoh’s chariots, the best weapon of their time on dry land, got stuck in the seabed and lost their wheels.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s chariot that ‘does not run on the sea’ appears literally in the Exodus story.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the raft simile, the Buddha describes a man who builds a raft to cross a flood and then carries it on his head over dry land. He asks whether that is the right use of a raft, and the monks agree it is not.
buddhism.explanation: A tool built for water becomes a burden on land; the Dhamma is to be used for crossing over, not clung to.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ship that cannot run on land makes the same point: something useful in one element is useless in another.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra teaches that a soul freed from all karma rises to the top of the inhabited universe (loka) and goes no further, because the medium of motion (dharmastikaya) does not exist beyond it. Even a perfected soul cannot move where its medium is absent.
jainism.explanation: Jainism holds that even the highest being's movement is limited by the medium available to it.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says the strong chariot cannot run on the sea nor the ship on land; Jain doctrine gives a cosmic version of the same rule, since no being, however perfect, can travel where its medium of motion is absent.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 10.8 of Umasvati (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If someone embarks on a boat of stone, he shall drown with its cargo.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak warns that a vessel unfit for the water sinks with everything aboard, an image for relying on the wrong support to cross the world-ocean.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the chariot cannot run on the sea nor the ship on land; Guru Nanak likewise shows that a means unsuited to its medium brings only ruin.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 420, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Pylos (425 BCE), Thucydides notes the strange reversal of the Athenians, a sea power, defending from land, while the Spartans, a land power, attacked from ships and tried in vain to force a landing on a rocky shore.
greek_mythology.explanation: Each side was fighting outside the element it was strong in, and the Spartan assault failed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the chariot-at-sea and ship-on-land problem in real Greek history.
greek_mythology.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 4.11–14 (tr. Richard Crawley)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Moor your craft higher up than the enemy, and facing the sun. Do not move up-stream to meet the enemy. So much for river warfare.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu gives separate rules for mountains, rivers, salt-marshes and flat country, because each kind of ground needs its own tactics.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that methods suited to one terrain fail in another.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IX.6 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Napoleon's Army of England waits at Boulogne
real_life_example.event: After war with Britain resumed in 1803, Napoleon gathered more than 150,000 soldiers in camps along the Channel coast around Boulogne and had well over a thousand flat-bottomed boats and barges built to carry them to England. The crossing depended on gaining control of the Channel, but the Royal Navy kept the French fleets away and the invasion never took place. In late August 1805 Napoleon marched the army east against Austria, and on 21 October 1805 the French and Spanish fleet was defeated at Trafalgar.
real_life_example.explanation: The finest land army in Europe could not reach an island enemy that ruled the sea, and Napoleon had to seek his victories on the Continent instead.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a strong chariot cannot run on the sea and a ship cannot run on land, and Napoleon's Grande Armee, unbeatable on land, never crossed twenty miles of water.

tamil:
அஞ்சாமை அல்லால் துணைவேண்டா எஞ்சாமை
எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின்.
transliteration:
Anjaamai allaal thunaivendaa enjaamai
Enni idaththaal seyin.
meaning: If you think everything through carefully and act from the right place, you need no other helper except your own courage.
elementary: If you have practised your speech, checked every page, and are standing in the right spot on stage, the only thing left to bring is courage. This kural says good planning and the right place leave you needing only a brave heart.
university: ‘Enjaamai enni’ means to think things through without remainder (enjuthal, to be left over), so planning comes first. ‘Idaththaal seyin’ means acting from, or by means of, the right place; the instrumental ‘-aal’ makes place the means of action. ‘Anjaamai allaal thunai vendaa’ says no ally is needed except fearlessness, so courage takes the place of all outside help. Parimelazhagar notes that thorough deliberation and the right ground remove the need for allies (thunai), which were discussed earlier under ‘Valiyarithal’ (ch. 48, thunaivali). Kalaignar’s gloss is about thorough method and leaves out place, a lighter reading than the traditional one.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna lists abhayam, fearlessness, first among the divine qualities (daivī sampad) that lead to freedom.
hinduism.explanation: In the Gita, fearlessness heads the list of virtues belonging to a person of divine nature.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes fearlessness the one companion needed once planning and positioning are done.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. Stand therefore…”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to prepare fully, then hold their ground firmly.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Having done all, to stand’ matches the Kural’s thorough preparation followed by steadfast courage in position.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those to whom people said, ‘Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them.’ But it [merely] increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Sufficient for us is Allāh, and [He is] the best Disposer of affairs.’”
islam.explanation: After Uhud, believers who were warned of a gathering enemy answered with fearlessness instead of alarm.
islam.tie_back: The refusal to be frightened by numbers matches the Kural’s ‘no ally but fearlessness’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.”
judaism.explanation: God charges Joshua to be courageous as he leads Israel into the land and its campaigns.
judaism.tie_back: Courage as the leader’s essential quality going into the field fits the Kural’s ‘anjaamai’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fear for an awakened one, whose mind is not sodden (by lust) nor afflicted (by hate), and who has gone beyond both merit and demerit.”
buddhism.explanation: For the Dhammapada, a well-trained mind no longer knows fear.
buddhism.tie_back: The kural’s fearlessness as one’s only needed companion has an inner counterpart here.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Be without fear, O king; but grant safety to others also; in this transient world of living beings, why are you addicted to cruelty?”
jainism.explanation: The sage Gardabhali tells the frightened King Sanjaya, who had killed a deer in the monk's park, to be fearless and to grant fearlessness to all beings.
jainism.tie_back: The kural names fearlessness as the only ally a well-prepared person needs; Jainism also prizes fearlessness, but joins it to the gift of safety to others (abhaya-dana), whereas the kural is about attacking an enemy.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 18.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else”
sikhism.explanation: In this salok Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the truly wise person as one who neither threatens others nor gives way to fear of them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that once a plan is complete and the ground is right, fearlessness is the only ally needed; Guru Tegh Bahadur makes fearlessness the mark of the wise.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Thermopylae, when the Spartan Dieneces was told the Persian arrows were so many they would hide the sun, he answered that this was good news, because they would then fight in the shade.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus records the reply as an example of fearlessness in a well-chosen position against huge odds.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Once the ground was chosen, fearlessness was the only thing the Greeks still needed, as the Kural says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The natural formation of the country is the soldier’s best ally; but a power of estimating the adversary, of controlling the forces of victory, and of shrewdly calculating difficulties, dangers and distances, constitutes the test of a great general.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu calls terrain an ally in itself, provided the general calculates everything carefully.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts treat the right ground plus full calculation as removing the need for other allies.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War X.21 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Admiral Yi Sun-sin's stand at the Myeongnyang Strait
real_life_example.event: During Japan's second invasion of Korea, Admiral Yi Sun-sin, recently restored to command after being demoted, had only about thirteen warships left against a Japanese fleet of more than a hundred and thirty. He chose to fight in the narrow Myeongnyang Strait, whose name means roaring currents, where the channel and fast tidal flow kept many ships from passing at once. The Japanese ships were hampered and fell into confusion, and the Japanese fleet withdrew after heavy losses.
real_life_example.explanation: Careful choice of a battleground that neutralised enemy numbers allowed a tiny fleet to turn back a large one.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that one who thinks everything through and acts from the right place needs no ally but fearlessness, and Yi had no allies, only his plan, the strait and his courage.

tamil:
சிறுபடையான் செல்லிடம் சேரின் உறுபடையான்
ஊக்கம் அழிந்து விடும்.
transliteration:
Sirupadaiyaan sellidam serin urupadaiyaan
Ookkam azhinthu vidum.
meaning: If a leader with a small army stands on ground where it can fight well, a leader with a big army will lose his push and his advantage.
elementary: In a narrow hallway, one kid can block the way even if ten kids are trying to get through, because only one can squeeze in at a time. A small team in the right spot can stop a big team.
university: ‘Sellidam’ is the key word: ‘the place where one’s power prevails’ (sellu, to be current or valid, as with a coin that ‘passes’). Parimelazhagar reads it as ground favourable to the small army, where it can fight on its own terms. ‘Urupadaiyaan’ is the commander of a large or mighty army, and ‘ookkam’, his drive and self-confidence (the subject of chapter 60), is what gets destroyed. Solomon Pappaiah gives a different reading: when the large army goes after the small one into the place where the small one lies, the large army’s prestige is lost. The sense stays the same, but the grammar of ‘sellidam’ is read in another way.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One bowman, placed on a rampart, is a match in battle for one hundred (foes), one hundred for ten thousand; hence it is prescribed (in the Sastras that a king will posses) a fortress.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu puts a number on the advantage of position: a single archer on a wall equals a hundred attackers.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the small force on its own ground overcoming the large one, as the Kural describes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews recalls heroes such as Gideon, Barak and David who, weak in numbers, routed much larger forces.
christianity.tie_back: It celebrates the few defeating the many, the outcome this kural describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allāh. And Allāh is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: Before facing Goliath’s army, the faithful few under Saul (Talut) remind themselves that small forces have often beaten large ones.
islam.tie_back: The Kural gives the practical means, favourable ground, by which a small force can win.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The children of Israel pitched before them like two little flocks of kids; but the Syrians filled the country.”
judaism.explanation: The Arameans thought Israel’s God ruled only the hills and chose to fight on the plain, yet the small Israelite force still won.
judaism.tie_back: The passage is openly about choosing terrain against a small army, though it overturns the Aramean assumption.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Tacchasūkara Jātaka, wild boars terrorised by a tiger are organised by a clever boar (the Bodhisatta). They dig pits and take up positions on prepared ground, so that when the tiger leaps, it falls into a pit and is killed.
buddhism.explanation: Weak animals defeat a far stronger predator by preparing the ground where the fight happens.
buddhism.tie_back: The small force on its own prepared ground breaks the strong one’s spirit, which is the kural’s scenario.
buddhism.source: Jātaka No. 492, Tacchasūkara Jātaka (ed. E. B. Cowell)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though a man should conquer thousands and thousands of valiant (foes), greater will be his victory if he conquers nobody but himself.”
jainism.explanation: Nami tells Indra that a single victory over oneself outweighs the conquest of countless warriors.
jainism.tie_back: The kural shows a small force standing on its own ground defeating a great army; Nami's saying likewise makes the single self, on its own ground, greater than thousands of foes, though Jainism moves the battle inward.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: At Chamkaur in December 1705, Guru Gobind Singh, with only a small band of Sikhs, took shelter in a walled, double-storeyed house with a single entrance. He posted eight Sikhs to guard each of its four sides and two at the gate, and through a whole day the much larger imperial army surrounding it failed to storm it.
sikhism.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism describes how a handful of defenders, using a defensible house as a temporary citadel, held off repeated assaults until their arrows and ammunition ran out.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a small force on ground where its strength counts saps the drive of a large army; at Chamkaur a few Sikhs on well-chosen ground held off a far larger host.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Chamkaur Sahib', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Thermopylae, a few thousand Greeks led by Leonidas and his 300 Spartans held the narrow pass for days against Xerxes’ huge army. Repeated Persian assaults, including the elite Immortals, failed until a traitor showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the narrows, Persian numbers counted for nothing, and the Great King’s confidence was badly shaken.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the classic case of ‘sirupadaiyaan sellidam’, the small army on its own ground ruining the large army’s drive.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “With a superior force, make for easy ground; with an inferior one, make for difficult ground.”
philosophy.explanation: Wu Tzu, quoted by Chang Yu in Giles’s notes, advises the smaller army to seek broken terrain where numbers cannot be deployed.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s rule for the small army put as a maxim.
philosophy.source: Wu Tzu, quoted in Chang Yu’s commentary on Sun Tzu III.17 (Giles, The Art of War, 1910)

real_life_example.event_title: Henry V's smaller army wins at Agincourt
real_life_example.event: Henry V's English army, much smaller than the French force facing it, took position on a recently ploughed field bounded by woods on both sides, which narrowed the front. The English archers drove sharpened stakes into the ground before them, and days of rain had turned the field to deep mud. The heavily armoured French men-at-arms, advancing through the mud and crowded together in the narrow space, lost their advantage of numbers and suffered a disastrous defeat.
real_life_example.explanation: Agincourt is a classic case of a small army choosing ground where the enemy's greater numbers became a burden rather than a strength.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that if a commander with a small army stands on ground where his strength prevails, the commander of a large army loses his drive and advantage, as the French did at Agincourt.

tamil:
சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும் மாந்தர்
உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Sirainalanum seerum ilareninum maanthar
Urainilaththodu ottal arithu.
meaning: Even people with no strong fort and no great power are hard to beat if you attack them in their own homeland.
elementary: Even a small puppy barks bravely and is hard to chase out of its own house, because it knows every corner. People are hardest to beat at home.
university: ‘Sirai nalan’ is the excellence of an enclosure or defensive barrier (sirai also means a moat or a prison-wall), and ‘seer’ is any other kind of distinction or strength. ‘Urainilam’ is the land where people live, their home ground, and ‘ottal’ is read by Parimelazhagar as going there to engage them. The kural balances 492: there the advantage came from fortification, here it comes from simply being at home, with the home fighter’s knowledge of the land and motivation. The thirukkural-thamizh.org gloss makes the psychology explicit: the knowledge that one is defending one’s own place is itself a source of courage. The verse also works as a warning to the invader, who is always at a disadvantage on foreign ground.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In weighing campaigns, Kautilya advises the conqueror to consider whether the ground suits his own forces or the enemy’s. He treats the enemy’s home terrain, where the defender knows the land and the invader does not, as a factor that raises the cost of attack.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Indian statecraft counts the defender’s familiarity with his own land among the things to be calculated.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural states the resulting rule plainly: people are hard to beat in their own land.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book IX, Chapter 1 (tr. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “When a strong man armed keepeth his palace, his goods are in peace.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a householder guarding his own house, who can be overcome only by someone stronger.
christianity.tie_back: The defender in his own dwelling is secure, which fits the Kural’s ‘urainilam’.

islam.quote_or_event: “When Allah’s Messenger (ﷺ) besieged Taif and could not conquer its people, he said, ‘We will return (to Medina) If Allah wills.’”
islam.explanation: After the victory at Hunayn, the Muslim army besieged Taif but could not take it and withdrew.
islam.tie_back: It illustrates how hard it is to dislodge people from their own home ground.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The river of Kishon swept them away, that ancient river, the river Kishon. O my soul, thou hast trodden down strength.”
judaism.explanation: Deborah’s song celebrates Israelite tribes defending their own hill-country, where the invader Sisera’s nine hundred iron chariots were swept away by the local river.
judaism.tie_back: Lightly armed people on their own land beat a far better-equipped invader.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Suṃsumāra Jātaka, a crocodile tricks a monkey onto its back to steal its heart. The monkey says its heart hangs on the fig tree, gets carried back to the bank, leaps into the tree and cannot be caught.
buddhism.explanation: Once the monkey is back in its own tree, the crocodile has no power over it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s people at home, the monkey is safe in its own place.
buddhism.source: Jātaka No. 208, Suṃsumāra Jātaka (ed. E. B. Cowell)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Monks who equal the ocean in depth, who are difficult to overcome, are frightened by nobody (or nothing), and are not easily assailed, who are full of extensive learning and take care of themselves, will go to the highest place, after their Karman has been annihilated.”
jainism.explanation: The very learned monk, who has no fort or army, is described as hard to overcome and not easily attacked because of his depth and self-guarding.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says people without strong forts or special strength are still hard to beat on their home ground; the Jain monk too is unconquerable without walls, because his strength lies in himself.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
