sikhism.quote_or_event: For much of the eighteenth century, after the death of Guru Gobind Singh, the Sikhs of the Punjab were under threat and siege from both Mughal and Afghan armies, yet they could not be put down in their own land, and from about the 1760s they were the de facto rulers of many parts of the Punjab.
sikhism.explanation: The Harvard Pluralism Project summarises how a community without great fortresses endured decades of campaigns against it in its home region and eventually came to rule there.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even people with no strong fort or special strength are hard to beat when attacked in the land where they live; the Sikhs' survival in the Punjab bears this out.
sikhism.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, 'The Struggle for Survival' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Darius invaded Scythia, the Scythians, who had no towns or farmland to defend, kept retreating across their own steppe and refused pitched battle. Their king Idanthyrsus told Darius they had nothing he could force them to defend, and the Persian army eventually had to withdraw.
greek_mythology.explanation: A people without forts or fixed wealth proved impossible to conquer in their own land.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s case: no ‘sirai nalan’, and still ‘ottal arithu’, hard to attack at home.
greek_mythology.source: Herodotus, Histories 4.120–142, esp. 4.127 (tr. A. D. Godley)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Clausewitz argues that the defensive form of war is in itself stronger than the offensive, because the defender benefits from terrain, local support and waiting, while the attacker grows weaker the further he advances into hostile country.
philosophy.explanation: His analysis explains why invading someone’s homeland is so costly.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the theory behind the Kural’s observation that people are hard to beat on their own ground.
philosophy.source: Carl von Clausewitz, On War, Book VI, Chapter 1 (tr. J. J. Graham)

real_life_example.event_title: Ethiopia defeats the Italian invasion at Adwa
real_life_example.event: After Italy claimed Ethiopia as a protectorate, Emperor Menelik II led a large army north to meet the Italian forces advancing from Eritrea. Italian commander Oreste Baratieri ordered a night march into the mountainous country around Adwa, but his brigades became separated in the unfamiliar terrain, and Menelik's forces defeated them one after another. Italy recognised Ethiopia's full independence in the peace that followed.
real_life_example.explanation: Adwa was the first decisive defeat of a European colonial army by an African state and kept Ethiopia independent.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that people are hard to defeat when you attack them in the land where they live, and the invaders lost their way and the battle in Ethiopia's own mountains.

tamil:
காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும் கண்ணஞ்சா
வேலாள் முகத்த களிறு.
transliteration:
Kaalaazh kalaril nariyadum kannanjaa
Velaal mukaththa kaliru.
meaning: A brave war elephant that can pierce spear-carrying soldiers with its tusks can be killed even by jackals when it gets stuck in deep mud.
elementary: A huge elephant is the strongest animal in the forest, but if it gets stuck in deep mud, even small animals can bother it and it can’t fight back. Being big and strong doesn’t help if you’re stuck in the wrong place.
university: The chapter closes with its strongest contrast. ‘Kaal aazh kalar’ is mire or saline swamp where legs sink; ‘kann anjaa’ is ‘unflinching of eye’, never afraid; ‘velaal mukaththa kaliru’ is the tusker that carries spear-bearing warriors (velaal) impaled on its tusks (mukam, the front), which Parimelazhagar explains as an elephant that has gored armed soldiers. The ‘nari’ is the jackal, the most contemptible of predators, so the verse sets the mightiest animal against the meanest. The old continuous text (thirukkural-thamizh.org) shows the sandhi ‘காலாழ் களரி னரியடுங் கண்ணஞ்சா வேலாண் முகத்த களிறு’, where ‘வேலாண்’ is ‘வேலாள்’ joined to ‘முகத்த’. The kural returns to 491’s warning: the greatest strength, put on the wrong ground, falls to the weakest enemy.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Karna Parva, the left wheel of Karna’s chariot sinks into the earth in the middle of his duel with Arjuna. While Karna struggles to lift it free, the peerless warrior is struck down.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata’s great tragic hero is not beaten by lack of skill or courage but by ground that gives way under him.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the fearless war elephant stuck in the mire, told of a human champion.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Karṇa Parva, Sections 90–91 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist thanks God for lifting him out of sinking mud and putting his feet on firm ground.
christianity.tie_back: The contrast between miry clay and a rock underfoot is the Kural’s contrast between the swamp and firm footing.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Remember] when He… sent down upon you from the sky, rain by which to purify you… and to make steadfast your hearts and plant firmly thereby your feet.”
islam.explanation: Before Badr, rain firmed up the sandy ground under the Muslim position. Commentators add that the same rain made the Quraysh side heavy and slippery.
islam.tie_back: Firm footing for one side and bad ground for the other is exactly the kural’s lesson.

judaism.quote_or_event: Sisera, commander of nine hundred iron chariots, the elite weapon of his day, lost the battle by the river Kishon when the ground turned against his chariots. He fled on foot and was killed by Jael, a tent-dwelling woman.
judaism.explanation: The most feared force in Canaan was destroyed by bad ground and finished off by an unlikely hand.
judaism.tie_back: This is the mighty tusker in the mire, killed by the weakest of foes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Delight in heedfulness! Guard well your thoughts! Draw yourself out of this bog of evil, even as an elephant draws himself out of the mud.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada uses the familiar image of an elephant stuck in a bog to urge vigilance.
buddhism.tie_back: Same image as the kural, the mighty elephant helpless in mud, turned into advice to get out of it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As an elephant, sinking down in a quagmire, sees the raised ground but does not get to the shore, so do we who long for sensual pleasures, not follow the path of monks.”
jainism.explanation: King Brahmadatta confesses that his attachment to pleasure leaves him like an elephant stuck in a bog, able to see firm ground but unable to reach it.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's mighty elephant becomes helpless once its feet sink in mud; the Jain text uses the same image of a powerful elephant stuck in a quagmire, here as a picture of the soul trapped by its desires.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Attracted by the lure of sexual desire, the elephant is captured, O crazy mind, and now the halter is placed around its neck.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir recalls how the mighty elephant is drawn onto ground where it can be trapped, and once caught it must bear the goad and halter.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's fearless war elephant is brought down even by jackals once it is stuck in the mire; Kabir's elephant likewise loses all its power once it is lured onto the wrong ground.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 335, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 21, Achilles, unmatched on the plain, fights the river-god Scamander in his own element. The flood breaks down on him, the ground washes away beneath his feet, and the greatest warrior of Troy nearly drowns until the gods step in.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even Achilles is almost undone once he fights in the river’s domain rather than on firm ground.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the tusker in the mire, the mightiest fighter becomes helpless where his footing gives way.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In crossing salt-marshes, your sole concern should be to get over them quickly, without any delay.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu treats marshland as dangerous ground where an army must not linger or give battle if it can avoid it.
philosophy.tie_back: His warning rests on the Kural’s point that boggy ground can destroy even a mighty force.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IX.7 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Flemish townsmen defeat the French knights at the Battle of the Golden Spurs
real_life_example.event: When the towns of Flanders rose against French rule, a French army of professional mounted knights was sent against them. The Flemish army, made up largely of townspeople and craft guildsmen fighting on foot, took a stand on ground bounded by streams and ditches, where marshy soil hampered the horsemen. The French cavalry charge broke down on this ground and the knights were defeated by the foot soldiers, who afterwards collected the fallen knights' spurs as trophies.
real_life_example.explanation: The battle showed that the most prestigious troops of the age could be beaten by ordinary infantry once they were caught on ground that suited the defender.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the fearless war elephant can be killed even by jackals once it is stuck in mud, and the proud French knights were brought down by humble townsmen in the marshes of Courtrai.

tamil:
அறம்பொருள் இன்பம் உயிரச்சம் நான்கின்
திறந்தெரிந்து தேறப் படும்.
transliteration:
Aramporul inbam uyirachcham naankin
Thirandherindhu thaerap padum.
meaning: Give a person an important job only after testing them in four ways: with doing right, with money, with pleasure, and with fear for their own life.
elementary: Before a coach makes someone team captain, she quietly watches: Do they play fair even when cheating would win? Do they share the snacks? Do they get distracted by fun and forget practice? Do they stay brave when things get scary? Only a kid who passes all four gets the armband.
university: The chapter title pairs தெரிதல் (examining, discerning) with தெளிதல் (arriving at clear confidence), and this opening couplet names the method: testing by the four ‘ways’ (திறம்) of அறம், பொருள், இன்பம் and உயிரச்சம். Parimelazhagar reads these as deliberate trials of the candidate’s mind, a reading made vivid by Solomon Pappaiah, who describes staged provocations on grounds of righteousness, money and a woman’s supposed affection, plus a feigned threat to life. This matches almost point for point Kautilya’s four upadhās (religious, monetary, love and fear allurements) in Arthaśāstra 1.10, and commentators have long noted the correspondence. Kalaignar instead turns the tests into positive qualities (firm in dharma, honest in money, not infatuated by pleasure, unafraid for one’s life). Both web sources give the couplet identically; the final verb தேறப்படும் (‘is to be trusted’) sets the key root தேறு that recurs through the chapter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Teachers have decided that, in accordance with ascertained purity, the king shall employ in corresponding works those ministers whose character has been tested under the three pursuits of life, religion, wealth and love, and under fear.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya describes secret tests in which agents tempt each minister with a religious pretext, money, a love intrigue, and fear; only those who refuse are counted pure.
hinduism.tie_back: This names the same four tests as the Kural: dharma, wealth, pleasure and fear.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy that church officers must be tested first and appointed only if found blameless.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the order is fixed: prove first, then entrust.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of the women said, ‘O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy.’”
islam.explanation: The daughter of the old man of Midian recommends hiring Moses after seeing his strength and honest conduct firsthand at the well.
islam.tie_back: Trustworthiness observed in action is the basis for hiring, as the Kural requires.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.”
judaism.explanation: Jethro advises Moses to choose officials by character: capable, God-fearing, truthful and resistant to bribes.
judaism.tie_back: Fear of God and hatred of unjust gain match the Kural’s tests of dharma and of wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It’s through living together that a person’s virtue may be known, and then only after a long period, not a short period; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive; by one who is discerning, not by one who is not discerning.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells King Pasenadi that virtue, purity, endurance and discernment are each revealed by a different test (living together, trading, adversity, discussion) and only over time.
buddhism.tie_back: A four-part examination of character, each in its own arena, closely matches the Kural’s method.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who does not speak untruth from anger or for fun, from greed or from fear, him we call a Brâhmana.”
jainism.explanation: In the sermon of the monk Jayaghosha, the true Brahmana is the one whose truthfulness holds under every pressure: anger, amusement, greed and fear.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tests a candidate through virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear of death; the Jain verse likewise defines worth as integrity that does not give way to greed, pleasure-seeking or fear.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: On Baisakhi 1699 at Anandpur, according to Sikh tradition, Guru Gobind Singh came out of his tent and asked for five Sikhs willing to offer their heads. The crowd fell silent in fear, but five came forward one after another. They were then revealed alive, and these five, the Panj Pyare, became the first members of the Khalsa.
sikhism.explanation: The Harvard Pluralism Project recounts the tradition of the Guru testing his followers by the fear of death before founding a new order on those who passed.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a person should be trusted with office only after being tested in four ways, the last being fear for one's life; the founding of the Khalsa rests on exactly such a test.
sikhism.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, 'The Khalsa' (paraphrase of Sikh tradition)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Returning to Ithaca disguised as a beggar, Odysseus tests the swineherd Eumaeus, the maids, the suitors and even Penelope, watching how each behaves toward a powerless stranger before revealing himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus deliberately hides his identity so that everyone’s true loyalty and greed come out.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a staged test of character before trust is given, as the Kural asks.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates proposes that future guardians be watched from youth and put through labours, pains and conflicts, then through fears and then enchantments of pleasure, like gold tried in the fire, and only those who come out pure are made rulers.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s scheme deliberately exposes candidates to fear and to pleasure to see whether their convictions hold.
philosophy.tie_back: Testing by fear and by pleasure before giving authority is the core of the Kural’s fourfold trial.

real_life_example.event_title: China selects its officials by imperial examination
real_life_example.event: From the Sui and Tang dynasties onward, Chinese governments increasingly filled official posts through competitive written examinations on the classical Chinese texts rather than by birth or recommendation alone. Under the Ming and Qing the examinations ran in three levels, at county, provincial and capital level, and the highest degree, the jinshi, made a candidate eligible for high office. The system lasted until it was abolished in 1905.
real_life_example.explanation: For well over a thousand years one of the world's largest states refused to hand out office until candidates had been examined, and the examinations were meant to test character as well as learning.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural insists that a person be tested before being trusted with office, and imperial China built that principle into a permanent state institution.

tamil:
குடிப்பிறந்து குற்றத்தின் நீங்கி வடுப்பரியும்
நாணுடையான் சுட்டே தெளிவு.
transliteration:
Kudippirandhu kutraththin neengi vaduppariyum
Naanudaiyaan sutte thelivu.
meaning: Trust a person who comes from a good family, has no faults, and is so afraid of shame that they guard their good name.
elementary: Think about who you would let hold the class pet over the weekend. You would pick the kid from a caring home, who does not break rules, and who would feel really bad if people thought they had been careless. Feeling embarrassed about doing wrong is actually a superpower that keeps people honest.
university: Three qualifications are stacked: birth in a good lineage (குடிப்பிறப்பு), freedom from faults (குற்றம்), and நாண், the moral shame that fears a வடு, literally a scar, meaning a stain on one’s reputation. சுட்டே தெளிவு means ‘confidence rests on the one so pointed out’. Varadarasan and Pappaiah read குடி as literal family background, while Kalaignar reverses the logic: one who is faultless and ashamed of wrongdoing is thereby shown to be truly ‘high-born’, a reading that plays down birth in favour of conduct. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the first phrase as removing the faults of one’s birth-group. Both sources agree on the text; the idea of நாண் as a guard against wrongdoing returns at length in chapter 102 (நாணுடைமை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…gentleness; modesty; steady determination; vigor; forgiveness; fortitude; cleanliness; and freedom from envy and from the passion for honor – these transcendental qualities, O son of Bharata, belong to godly men endowed with divine nature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the qualities of a divine nature, including hrī (modesty, shame at doing wrong), and calls such a person abhijāta, ‘well-born’.
hinduism.tie_back: Being well-born and having a sense of shame are paired as marks of a trustworthy nature, as in the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul requires that a church overseer be well regarded even by outsiders, so he does not bring disgrace.
christianity.tie_back: Concern for an unstained reputation matches the Kural’s ‘shame that dreads a stain’.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you don’t feel ashamed (from Haya’: pious shyness from committing religeous indiscretions) do whatever you like.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet quotes an old prophetic saying: without ḥayāʾ (moral shame), nothing holds a person back.
islam.tie_back: The Kural trusts the man of நாண் for the same reason: shame is what keeps him from wrong.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that shame is a good sign in a person, since one who feels shame will not quickly come to sin, and it links a shamefaced disposition with descent from those who stood at Sinai.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic tradition treats bushah (shame) as a moral safeguard and even as a mark of good lineage.
judaism.tie_back: Lineage and shame as a guard against sin are the two anchors of this Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha calls hiri (conscience, shame at wrongdoing) and ottappa (concern for blame) the two bright qualities that guard the world; without them society would fall into confusion.
buddhism.explanation: These two qualities are what stop a person from doing wrong even when unobserved.
buddhism.tie_back: நாண் that fears a stain is almost exactly hiri joined with ottappa.

jainism.quote_or_event: “hence none is either high or low. After knowing this, who will feel proud of taking birth in respectable or high family?”
jainism.explanation: Because every soul has been born many times into high and low families, Jainism holds that family rank confers no real distinction; worth lies in conduct.
jainism.tie_back: The kural looks first to good family as a ground for confidence; the Jain teaching sets family lineage aside and would rest confidence on the faultlessness and moral shame the kural also names.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 90 (Precepts on Religion, uttama-mardava; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Recognize the Lord's Light within all, and do not consider social class or status; there are no classes or castes in the world hereafter.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak tells his hearers to see God's light in everyone and not to ask about anyone's caste or social rank.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks that trust go to someone of good family who fears any stain on his name; Guru Nanak rejects birth and status as a measure of a person, so Sikhism would keep the Kural's sense of shame but not its test of lineage.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 349, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Protagoras’ myth, Zeus fears the human race will destroy itself and sends Hermes to give every person aidōs (shame, respect) and dikē (justice), ordering that anyone lacking them be put to death as a plague to the city.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes shame a precondition for anyone to take part in civic life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes shame a precondition for public trust.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In any office of trust or stewardship, on the other hand, the opposite rule should be observed; for more virtue than ordinary is required in the holder of such an office, but the necessary knowledge is of a sort which all men possess.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle names loyalty to the constitution, administrative capacity and virtue as the qualifications for high office, and says that posts of trust call above all for exceptional virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle makes character, not skill alone, the test of whom a ruler should trust.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics, Book V, ch. 9 (1309a–b) (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Lord Carrington resigns as Foreign Secretary
real_life_example.event: Three days after Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands, Peter Carington, 6th Baron Carrington, resigned as British Foreign Secretary together with two junior ministers. In his resignation letter he said that much of the criticism was unfounded, but that he had been responsible for the conduct of the policy and thought it right to resign. A later official inquiry did not find him at fault, and his acceptance of responsibility was widely praised.
real_life_example.explanation: A minister of old family and long service chose to give up high office rather than let a failure of his department rest on anyone else, an unusually clear example of personal honour in politics.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks for someone of good family who dreads any stain on his name, and Carrington's resignation shows that sense of shame acting as a safeguard of public trust.

tamil:
அரியகற்று ஆசற்றார் கண்ணும் தெரியுங்கால்
இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு.
transliteration:
Ariyakatru aasatraar kannum theriyungaal
Inmai aridhe veliru.
meaning: Even among people who have studied hard books and seem to have no faults, if you look closely, it is rare to find one with no ignorance at all.
elementary: Even the smartest kid in class, the one who knows every dinosaur name, might not know how to tie their shoes. Nobody knows everything. So when you choose someone for a job, check carefully instead of assuming they are perfect.
university: The couplet tempers the previous two: even the learned (அரிய கற்று) and flawless (ஆசு அற்றார்) will, on examination (தெரியுங்கால்), rarely be found without வெளிறு. வெளிறு literally means ‘whiteness’ and is used of weak, pale timber, and commentators gloss it as அறியாமை (ignorance) or a hidden weak spot. The practical lesson is that selection is not a search for a perfect person but a realistic judgment, which sets up the weighing of strengths and faults in the next couplet (504). Varadarasan and Pappaiah stress that no one is wholly free of ignorance, while Kalaignar aims the point at reputation: even those praised as flawless cannot be assumed so without examination. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Every endeavor is covered by some fault, just as fire is covered by smoke.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that no action in the world is entirely free of defect, just as no fire burns without smoke.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural makes the same point about people: some flaw is always there if you look.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.”
christianity.explanation: James admits that everyone stumbles in many ways; only a hypothetical perfect man would not.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it expects some flaw even in the best.

islam.quote_or_event: “We raise in degrees whom We will, but over every possessor of knowledge is one [more] knowing.”
islam.explanation: After Joseph outwits his brothers, the Qur’an notes that above every learned person there is someone who knows more.
islam.tie_back: No learned person has complete knowledge, which is the Kural’s point.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth observes that no one, however righteous, is wholly without fault.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same realism to choosing people.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a person who is wholly blamed or wholly praised.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that no person in any age is entirely praiseworthy or entirely blameworthy.
buddhism.tie_back: Even the best will have something to fault, as the Kural says.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You do not know what is most essential in the Vêdas, nor in sacrifices, nor in the heavenly bodies, nor in duties.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha tells a priest renowned for his Vedic learning that, for all his study, he has missed what is most essential.
jainism.tie_back: The kural warns that even the deeply learned turn out, on close examination, to have some ignorance; here a famously learned man is examined and found lacking in the essential point.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Everyone makes mistakes; only the Guru and the Creator are infallible.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that every human being is liable to err and that freedom from error belongs to God and the Guru alone.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even the learned and seemingly flawless will rarely be found free of some ignorance when closely examined; Guru Nanak says the same of everyone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 61, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Thetis dips the infant Achilles in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, but the heel she holds stays dry, and he is later killed by an arrow there.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest of heroes still has one weak spot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s வெளிறு is exactly this kind of hidden weak spot in someone who seems perfect.
greek_mythology.source: Statius, Achilleid 1 (the Styx dipping); the heel detail belongs to later tradition

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seeking to test the oracle that no one was wiser than he, Socrates questions politicians, poets and craftsmen with great reputations for wisdom, and finds each of them, on examination, ignorant of much they claimed to know.
philosophy.explanation: Close questioning shows that those with the highest reputations still lack real knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s ‘when examined’ (தெரியுங்கால்).

real_life_example.event_title: Vesalius corrects Galen's anatomy in the Fabrica
real_life_example.place: Padua, Republic of Venice (now Italy); printed in Basel, Switzerland
real_life_example.event: Andreas Vesalius, professor of anatomy at Padua, published De humani corporis fabrica in 1543, based on his own dissections of human bodies. It corrected many errors in the work of Galen, the Greek physician whose anatomy had been treated as authoritative for some 1,300 years. Many of Galen's mistakes came from the fact that he had described human anatomy largely from dissections of animals.
real_life_example.explanation: Even the most revered authority in medicine turned out, on close examination, to have hidden gaps in his knowledge.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even the learned and seemingly flawless will rarely be found free of ignorance when closely examined, and Galen's errors show exactly that.

tamil:
குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி அவற்றுள்
மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல்.
transliteration:
Kunamnaadik kutramum naadi avatrul
Migainaadi mikka kolal.
meaning: Look at a person’s good points, then at their faults. See which side is bigger, and judge them by that.
elementary: Imagine a friend who sometimes forgets your birthday but always shares, always helps, and always tells the truth. If you put the good things on one side of a see-saw and the forgetful thing on the other, the good side sinks way down. That’s how the Kural says to judge people: by which side is heavier.
university: The verb நாடு (to seek, look into) occurs three times, giving a three-step procedure: examine குணம் (good qualities), then குற்றம் (faults), then மிகை (which is greater), and finally கொளல், ‘take’ the person according to what is மிக்க (predominant). Following 503’s point that no one is flawless, this is a rule of proportion rather than perfection. Pappaiah narrows it to appointment (choose by the excess of virtues), while Kalaignar keeps it general: a clear judgment about someone comes only after this weighing. Some commentators note the ambiguity of மிக்க கொளல்: judge the person by what predominates, or keep the one in whom virtues predominate; either way the method is the same. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Sometimes the mode of goodness becomes prominent, defeating the modes of passion and ignorance, O son of Bharata. Sometimes the mode of passion defeats goodness and ignorance, and at other times ignorance defeats goodness and passion.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that everyone has all three guṇas, and a person’s character is known by which one is dominant.
hinduism.tie_back: Judging someone by the quality that prevails is the Kural’s rule of மிகை.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.”
christianity.explanation: Peter teaches that great love outweighs and covers many faults.
christianity.tie_back: The idea that a strong virtue can outweigh faults is close to the Kural’s weighing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Then as for one whose scales are heavy [with good deeds], … But as for one whose scales are light, …”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment each person’s deeds are weighed; the fate of each depends on which side is heavier.
islam.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image of a balance: judge by which side tips.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Everything is foreseen yet freedom of choice is granted, And the world is judged with goodness; And everything is in accordance with the preponderance of works.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Akiva teaches that judgment follows the preponderance of a person’s deeds.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Preponderance’ is precisely the Kural’s மிகை.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Salt Crystal discourse the Buddha explains that a small bad deed by someone of great, developed goodness is like a pinch of salt in the Ganges, while the same deed by someone with little goodness is like salt in a cup of water.
buddhism.explanation: The effect of a fault depends on how much good surrounds it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise judges faults in proportion to a person’s virtues.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain epistemology teaches that a thing is known through valid knowledge (pramana) and through partial standpoints (nayas), so that any single viewpoint captures only one aspect of a many-sided reality (anekantavada).
jainism.explanation: Because reality is many-sided, Jain thinkers insist that judgment weigh several aspects together rather than fix on one feature alone.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar asks the examiner to look at a man's virtues and then his faults and judge by what prevails; the Jain doctrine of standpoints similarly warns against a verdict drawn from one side only.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.6 (pramana and naya), with the anekantavada doctrine as generally expounded

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Good deeds and bad deeds-the record is read out in the Presence of the Lord of Dharma.”
sikhism.explanation: In the closing salok of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak pictures a person's good and bad actions both being read out and weighed before the divine judge.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to look into a person's virtues, then his faults, and judge him by whichever prevails; Japji Sahib likewise has both columns of the record read before judgement.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib (closing salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before Achilles and Hector fight, Zeus lifts his golden scales with the fates of both warriors; Hector’s side sinks toward Hades, and Apollo leaves him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The gods decide by weighing and seeing which side is heavier.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s method is a moral version of these scales.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says that someone who strays only a little from the right, whether toward excess or deficiency, is not blamed; only the one who strays far is, and how far is a matter for perception in particular cases.
philosophy.explanation: Moral judgment of a person allows for small deviations and looks at the overall pattern.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too tolerates lesser faults when virtues clearly prevail.

real_life_example.event_title: General Groves chooses Oppenheimer to lead Los Alamos
real_life_example.place: Washington, D.C. and Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States
real_life_example.event: General Leslie Groves, head of the Manhattan Project, chose the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer to direct its new weapons laboratory even though Oppenheimer had almost no administrative experience, had not won a Nobel Prize, and faced security objections over past left-wing associations. Groves ordered that his clearance be issued, calling him essential to the project. Groves later wrote that he had never felt it was a mistake to select and clear Oppenheimer for the post.
real_life_example.explanation: Groves openly listed the candidate's drawbacks and still judged that his breadth of knowledge and drive outweighed them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural tells us to weigh a person's virtues against his faults and judge by whichever prevails, which is what Groves did.

tamil:
பெருமைக்கும் ஏனைச் சிறுமைக்கும் தத்தம்
கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்.
transliteration:
Perumaikkum aenaich chirumaikkum thaththam
Karumame kattalaik kal.
meaning: Whether a person is great or mean and small, their own actions are the test that shows it.
elementary: A jeweller checks whether a ring is real gold by rubbing it on a special black stone and looking at the streak. You can check whether someone is really kind the same way, by looking at what they actually do, not what they say or what they wear.
university: கட்டளைக் கல் is the goldsmith’s touchstone (உரைகல்): gold rubbed on it leaves a streak whose colour shows its purity. The couplet says that deeds (கருமம், from Sanskrit karma) are such a stone for both பெருமை (greatness) and சிறுமை (meanness), and the emphatic ஏ in கருமமே excludes other tests such as birth, wealth or eloquence. It completes the lesson of 502: family is a starting presumption, but conduct is the decisive proof. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads கட்டளைக் கல் as an inscribed ‘edict stone’ that guides conduct, but the touchstone reading of Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Pope (‘touchstone true’) is standard. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…theoretical and practical knowledge, foresight, retentive memory, and affability shall be tested from successful application in works…”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya lists how each quality of a candidate minister is to be verified, and ability is judged by work actually done.
hinduism.tie_back: Work as proof of worth is the Kural’s touchstone.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says people are known by what their lives produce, as trees are known by their fruit.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Fruits’ play the role of the Kural’s touchstone of deeds.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says that tribes and peoples exist so we may know one another, but true nobility is measured by righteousness.
islam.tie_back: Greatness is measured by conduct, not lineage, as the Kural says.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Study is not the most important thing, but actions; whoever indulges in too many words brings about sin.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon ben Gamaliel teaches that deeds, not learning or talk, are what finally count.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too treats action as the decisive test.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by birth is one an outcast; not by birth is one a brahman. By deed one becomes an outcast, by deed one becomes a brahman.”
buddhism.explanation: Insulted as an ‘outcast’, the Buddha replies that high and low status come from conduct, not birth.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that deeds are the touchstone of greatness and meanness.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipāta 1.7, Vasala Sutta, v. 21 (trans. Piyadassi Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “By one's actions one becomes a Brâhmana, or a Kshattriya, or a Vaisya, or a Sûdra.”
jainism.explanation: Jayaghosha teaches that a person's standing is made by deeds, not by birth or outward marks.
jainism.tie_back: The kural makes each person's own deeds the touchstone of greatness or meanness; the Jain verse likewise makes actions alone the measure of what a person is.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Apply the Touchstone of Truth to your mind, and see if it comes up to its full weight.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak borrows the goldsmith's touchstone and scale: a person's inner life is to be tested against truth as gold is tested on the stone.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls a person's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and meanness; Guru Nanak uses the same touchstone image for testing a person's worth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 22, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Instead of taking the safe sea route, the young Theseus walks the bandit-infested road to Athens, defeating Periphetes, Sinis, Sciron and Procrustes, so that his deeds announce him before his father Aegeus recognises him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Theseus proves he is worthy of his royal birth by what he does on the road.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His deeds, not his birth tokens alone, are the touchstone of his greatness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts, so that character is formed and shown in activity.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, virtue is a settled disposition revealed by repeated action.
philosophy.tie_back: If character shows itself in action, then deeds are the fair touchstone the Kural names.

real_life_example.event_title: Bonaparte creates the Legion of Honour
real_life_example.event: As First Consul, Napoleon Bonaparte created the Legion of Honour by a law of 19 May 1802. It was an order of merit for both military and civil service, open to recipients without regard to birth or religion. It remains France's highest order of merit.
real_life_example.explanation: In a society that had long rewarded noble birth, the state chose to honour people for what they had actually done.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls deeds the touchstone of greatness and meanness, and the Legion of Honour made deeds, not birth, the test for honour.

tamil:
அற்றாரைத் தேறுதல் ஓம்புக மற்றவர்
பற்றிலர் நாணார் பழி.
transliteration:
Atraaraith thaerudhal ombuga matravar
Patrilar naanaar pazhi.
meaning: Do not trust people who have no family or community ties. With no one to answer to, they feel no shame about doing wrong.
elementary: Why do people usually behave well? Partly because they don’t want to let down their family, friends and neighbours. Someone who doesn’t care about anyone might not care if they get in trouble either. So the Kural says: be careful before trusting someone who has no one they care about.
university: அற்றார் means ‘those who are cut off’; the standard commentary (followed by Varadarasan, Pappaiah and Pope) takes it as those without kin (சுற்றம்), who are therefore பற்றிலர், without attachments, and so நாணார் பழி, unashamed of blame. The reasoning links back to 502: shame works through the people whose opinion one values, so someone with no such bonds has no brake. Kalaignar reads அற்றார் as the unprincipled (நெறியற்றவர்), and Sivayogi Sivakumar reverses the sense, reading it as a call to raise up those who have nothing, a reading at odds with the chapter’s context. ஓம்புக here means ‘guard against, avoid’. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him appoint seven or eight ministers whose ancestors have been royal servants, who are versed in the sciences, heroes skilled in the use of weapons and descended from (noble) families and who have been tried.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king to choose ministers with deep hereditary ties to the court and to noble families, and who have been tested.
hinduism.tie_back: Ministers rooted in family and loyalty are the opposite of the unattached people the Kural warns against.

christianity.quote_or_event: “One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity; (For if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?)”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes a man’s care for his own household a qualification for leading the church.
christianity.tie_back: Family bonds, well kept, show the kind of person who can be trusted with more.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that the best of people are those who are best to their families, adding that he was the best of them to his own family.
islam.explanation: A person’s treatment of kin is presented as a measure of goodness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise reads a person’s bonds with kin as evidence of trustworthiness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “…one from among thy brethren shalt thou set king over thee; thou mayest not put a foreigner over thee, who is not thy brother.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah requires Israel’s king to be one of their own kin, bound to the people he rules.
judaism.tie_back: Authority goes to someone with ties to the community, as the Kural advises.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Rhinoceros Horn discourse the Buddha praises the renunciant who drops all ties of children, wife, parents, wealth and kin and wanders alone like a rhinoceros horn.
buddhism.explanation: For the seeker of liberation, freedom from attachment is an ideal, not a danger.
buddhism.tie_back: This is a contrast: the Kural is speaking of state service, where the unattached lack the social brake of shame.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who has given up his former connections (with his parents, &c.), with his kinsmen and relations, and who is not given to pleasure, him we call a Brâhmana.”
jainism.explanation: For the Jain monastic ideal, cutting ties with kin is a mark of spiritual worth rather than of untrustworthiness.
jainism.tie_back: The kural distrusts those without kin because they have nothing binding them to shame; Jainism honours the monk who has deliberately given up kin, an honest contrast in values, though it presumes he is bound instead by his vows.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, do not associate with the faithless cynics; run far away from them.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir warns against keeping company with the saakat, the person cut off from God, because such a one has no inner bond to hold him back from wrong.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says not to trust those who are cut off from all ties, since without attachments they feel no shame; Kabir likewise warns against relying on those cut off from the bond that restrains.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Nestor warns the Achaean chiefs that a man who loves the horror of civil strife is clanless, lawless and hearthless (aphrētōr, athemistos, anestios).
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer groups being without clan, without law and without hearth as the marks of a dangerous man.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Being without kin and without restraint go together, just as the Kural says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that man is by nature a political animal, and that one who is by nature without a city is either a bad man or above humanity, like the ‘tribeless, lawless, hearthless one’ Homer condemns.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, ties to household and city are what make ethical life possible.
philosophy.tie_back: The rootless person, lacking these ties, is the one the Kural warns us not to trust.

real_life_example.event_title: The Praetorian Guard sells its support to Didius Julianus
real_life_example.event: After the Praetorian Guard killed the emperor Pertinax in 193, two men sought its backing for the throne, and the wealthy senator Didius Julianus won by promising the soldiers the larger cash payment. The Guard then proclaimed him emperor. Julianus ruled only about two months before he was deposed when Septimius Severus marched on Rome.
real_life_example.explanation: Soldiers whose loyalty was tied to no ruler and no community gave the empire to whoever paid most, with no apparent concern for the disgrace.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns against trusting people with no ties, since having no attachments they feel no shame at blame, and the Guard's sale of its support is a stark case.

tamil:
காதன்மை கந்தா அறிவறியார்த் தேறுதல்
பேதைமை எல்லாந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Kaadhanmai kandhaa arivariyaarth thaerudhal
Paedhaimai ellaan tharum.
meaning: Trusting people who do not have the knowledge they need, just because you like them, will lead to every kind of foolish mistake.
elementary: Your best friend is awesome, but if they’ve never baked anything, you wouldn’t make them in charge of the cake for the whole school fair just because you like them. Liking someone is not the same as them being good at the job.
university: காதன்மை கந்தா means ‘with affection as the post’: கந்து is the post or pillar to which something is tied, so affection becomes the only support of the choice. அறிவு அறியார், ‘those who do not know what should be known’, names the risk, and the result is பேதைமை எல்லாம், every kind of folly. Pappaiah reads it as the folly produced by favouritism in appointments, and Kalaignar adds that such choices bear only useless results. Varadarasan’s printed gloss says the chooser’s ‘ignorance will perish’, which appears to be a typographical slip given his other readings and Pope’s ‘the height of folly’. The text reads எல்லாந் தரும் (sandhi of எல்லாம் + தரும்) in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The blind king Dhritarashtra, out of love for his son Duryodhana, repeatedly sets aside the counsel of Vidura and Bhishma and lets Duryodhana and his companions direct the kingdom, leading to the ruinous Kurukshetra war.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata presents Dhritarashtra’s affection as the root of the Kuru downfall.
hinduism.tie_back: Trusting an unwise person out of love brings ‘every folly’, as the Kural warns.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Vidura’s counsels and Dhritarashtra’s responses)

christianity.quote_or_event: “My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.”
christianity.explanation: James forbids partiality, favouring some people for reasons other than merit.
christianity.tie_back: Favouritism is the trap the Kural names.

islam.quote_or_event: “When honesty is lost, then wait for the Hour (Doomsday).” The Bedouin said, “How will that be lost?” The Prophet (ﷺ) said, “When the power or authority comes in the hands of unfit persons, then wait for the Hour (Doomsday.)”
islam.explanation: Giving authority to people unfit for it is described as a betrayal of trust and a sign of the end times.
islam.tie_back: Entrusting affairs to the unqualified is the ‘folly’ the Kural warns of.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But he forsook the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men that were grown up with him, that stood before him.”
judaism.explanation: Rehoboam rejects experienced advisers in favour of the friends he grew up with, and their harsh advice splits the kingdom of Israel.
judaism.tie_back: Trusting familiar friends over the wise is exactly the folly the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a seeker not find a companion who is better or equal, let him resolutely pursue a solitary course; there is no fellowship with the fool.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha advises going alone rather than attaching oneself to a fool.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns against binding oneself to the unwise, however dear.

jainism.quote_or_event: “But he who puts bad bullocks before his car, will be tired out with beating them; he will feel vexation, and his goad will be broken (at last).”
jainism.explanation: The teacher Garga compares unfit pupils to bad bullocks yoked to a cart: whoever harnesses them reaps only exhaustion and frustration.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says trusting the unfit out of fondness brings every folly; Garga's image shows the same result of yoking unfit helpers to one's work.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 27.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Friendship with a fool never works out right.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok in Asa Ki Vaar, Guru Angad says that a bond formed with someone who lacks understanding cannot succeed, however it began.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that trusting people who lack the needed knowledge, merely out of fondness, brings every kind of folly; Guru Angad says affection for a fool never works out.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Having sworn by the Styx to grant his son Phaethon any wish, the loving sun-god Helios lets the untrained boy drive the chariot of the Sun; Phaethon loses control, scorches the earth, and is struck down by Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A father’s love leads him to hand a great task to someone without the skill for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Affection as the only ‘post’ of trust ends in disaster, just as the Kural predicts.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli writes that the choice of ministers is of no small importance to a prince, and that the first opinion people form of a ruler’s intelligence comes from the men he keeps around him.
philosophy.explanation: A ruler is judged by the quality of those he appoints.
philosophy.tie_back: Choosing incompetent favourites exposes the chooser’s own folly, which is the Kural’s point.

real_life_example.event_title: Charles IV makes the guardsman Manuel Godoy his chief minister
real_life_example.event: Manuel Godoy, a young officer of the royal bodyguard and a protege of Queen Maria Luisa, was raised by King Charles IV to the highest offices and made chief minister in 1792 at about the age of 25. His rule was marked by costly wars, financial strain and growing unpopularity. In March 1808 the Revolt of Aranjuez forced his dismissal and the abdication of Charles IV, which opened the way for Napoleon to take control of Spain.
real_life_example.explanation: A government handed to a royal favourite without proven ability ended in the fall of the king himself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that trusting unqualified people merely because one is fond of them brings every kind of folly, and Godoy's career shows the result.

tamil:
தேரான் பிறனைத் தெளிந்தான் வழிமுறை
தீரா இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Thaeraan piranaith thelindhaan vazhimurai
Theeraa idumbai tharum.
meaning: Someone who trusts a stranger without checking them first brings endless trouble, even to their own children and grandchildren.
elementary: If a stranger at the park says, “Give me your house key and I’ll water your plants,” and you just hand it over, trouble could follow your whole family for a long time. Trust has to be earned before you give it.
university: தேரான் (‘without examining’) and பிறன் (‘another, an outsider’) define the fault, and தெளிந்தான் (‘he who trusted’) the one who commits it. The key phrase வழிமுறை is read by Varadarasan and Kalaignar as ‘those who come after him’, his descendants, so the harm outlives the one who made the mistake; Pope follows this (‘on all his race’). Pappaiah shifts பிறன் to someone indifferent to the nation’s interests, a modern political reading. The second line தீரா இடும்பை தரும் is repeated word for word in 510, framing the chapter’s last three couplets with the same warning. ytamizh prints the couplet without the final full stop; the words are otherwise identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Queen Kaikeyi trusts the counsel of her maid Manthara without examining her motives, demands Rama’s exile and Bharata’s coronation, and so brings grief on Dasharatha, who dies, and on the whole royal house.
hinduism.explanation: One unexamined confidence sets off suffering for a whole dynasty.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural warns that unexamined trust brings sorrow that passes down to one’s line.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that people who look harmless may be dangerous inside, so appearances must be tested.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural too warns against trusting an unexamined outsider on appearances.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.”
islam.explanation: Believers are told to check reports from untrustworthy people before acting on them.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s rule is the same: investigate first or face lasting regret.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the men took of their provision, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Gibeonites pretend to be travellers from far away; Joshua’s leaders make a sworn treaty without proper inquiry, and that oath binds Israel for generations, returning as a famine in David’s time (2 Samuel 21).
judaism.tie_back: An unexamined agreement with strangers brings trouble on later generations, which is the Kural’s வழிமுறை.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by appearance is a man rightly known, nor should trust be based on a quick glance, — for, disguised as well-restrained, the unrestrained go through this world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns King Pasenadi that people who look disciplined may not be, so trust must not be given at a glance.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s தேரான் தெளிவு: trust without examination.
buddhism.source: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.11, verse (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, as given in notes to Udāna 6.2)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Just as a person is free while climbing a tree but once he starts falling then he has no power to check it.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain teaching on karma says a person is free when binding karma but loses control once its consequences begin to unfold.
jainism.tie_back: The kural warns that a careless act of trust lets loose sorrow that cannot be recalled; the Jain image makes the same point that the choice is free but its fall cannot be stopped.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 60 (Precepts on Karma; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not associate with the faithless cynics; they would bring you to ruin.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir warns that close association with those turned away from God ends in ruin for the one who keeps their company.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that putting confidence in someone unexamined brings endless sorrow; Kabir likewise warns that the wrong companion brings ruin.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 93) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Trojans take in Sinon, a Greek stranger with a convincing story, believe him without proper testing, and drag the wooden horse into the city, leading to the fall of Troy and the end of Priam’s line.
greek_mythology.explanation: Laocoön’s warning is ignored and one act of unexamined trust destroys a whole city and dynasty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Trusting an untested stranger brings sorrow that does not end, just as the Kural says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero, following Theophrastus, says one should love after judging, not judge after loving, and notes that people who make friends hastily often come to regret it.
philosophy.explanation: Judgment must come before attachment, or regret follows.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural states the same order and the same cost of reversing it.

real_life_example.event_title: Lobengula signs the Rudd Concession
real_life_example.event: King Lobengula of the Ndebele signed a concession with agents of Cecil Rhodes led by Charles Rudd, believing he was granting limited mining rights. The written document gave the grantees exclusive rights to all metals and minerals in his kingdoms, and Lobengula later repudiated it and sent envoys to London to protest. The British government accepted the concession in 1889 and used it to charter the British South Africa Company, which went on to take over his kingdom.
real_life_example.explanation: Trust placed in outsiders without fully examining what was being signed cost the king his realm and his people their land for generations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that trusting a stranger without examination brings endless sorrow even on one's descendants, which is what followed this signature.

tamil:
தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது தேர்ந்தபின்
தேறுக தேறும் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Thaerarka yaaraiyum thaeraadhu thaerndhapin
Thaeruga thaerum porul.
meaning: Do not trust anyone without checking them first. After checking, trust them with the things they can be trusted with.
elementary: Before you lend your favourite bike, you watch how your cousin treats their own toys. Once you’ve seen they’re careful, you lend it without nagging them every five minutes. Check first, then really trust.
university: The couplet plays on two nearly identical roots: தேர் (to examine, choose) and தேறு (to trust, be confident). Almost every word is built on them, a characteristic Valluvar wordplay that makes the rule easy to remember: தேறற்க … தேராது (do not trust without examining), தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக (after examining, trust). The closing phrase தேறும் பொருள் is read in two ways: Varadarasan and Kalaignar take it as trusting in what deserves trust, while the older commentary followed by Pope takes it as entrusting to each person the duties suited to what the test showed. Pappaiah adds the practical corollary that one should not doubt someone after appointing them, which leads into 510. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Of these tried ministers, those whose character has been tested under religious allurements shall be employed in civil and criminal courts…”
hinduism.explanation: After the four tests, Kautilya assigns each minister to the kind of work his proven integrity suits.
hinduism.tie_back: Examine first, then entrust the matters the person has proved fit for, as the Kural’s தேறும் பொருள் suggests.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men’s sins: keep thyself pure.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns Timothy not to ordain anyone hastily, since he shares responsibility for their faults.
christianity.tie_back: This is the first half of the Kural: trust no one without examination.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and when you judge between people to judge with justice.”
islam.explanation: Trusts, including offices, must be given to those who are properly qualified for them.
islam.tie_back: Giving each trust to its rightful holder is the Kural’s ‘trust him in what he can be trusted with’.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Sira advises that if you want a friend you should acquire him through testing and not be quick to trust him, since some are friends only when it suits them.
judaism.explanation: The Jewish sage makes testing the doorway to trust.
judaism.tie_back: The same sequence as the Kural: test, then trust.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells the Kalamas not to accept teachings on report, tradition or a teacher’s authority, but when they know for themselves, after examination, that something is skilful and leads to welfare, then to take it up and live by it.
buddhism.explanation: Acceptance is to follow personal examination, and once examined it is to be acted on fully.
buddhism.tie_back: The same two-step: examine, then commit.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Jain teacher Haribhadra is remembered for declaring that he had no partiality for Mahavira and no hatred for Kapila, and that whoever's words are reasonable should be accepted.
jainism.explanation: Haribhadra insisted that even religious trust must follow rational examination rather than prior loyalty.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says trust no one without examination and, once examined, trust fittingly; Haribhadra applies the same order of examining first and then trusting to the teachers one follows.
jainism.source: Haribhadra, Lokatattvanirnaya (famous couplet; attribution as summarised in Wikipedia, 'Haribhadra')

sikhism.quote_or_event: “First, examine the merchandise, and then, make the deal.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak gives a trader's rule: test what you are dealing in before you commit to it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to trust no one without examining him and, once he has been examined, to trust him; Guru Nanak's rule puts the testing first and the commitment after.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1410, Salok Vaaran Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a man buying an ass takes it home on trial and turns it loose among his herd; it goes straight to the laziest, greediest animal, so he returns it, saying he can already tell what it is from the company it chose.
greek_mythology.explanation: The buyer tests before committing, and the test reveals the animal’s character.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Examine before you trust, as the Kural’s first line commands.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Ass and His Purchaser’

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Lucilius to consider for a long time whether to admit someone as a friend, but once he has decided, to welcome him wholeheartedly and speak as freely with him as with himself.
philosophy.explanation: Deliberation comes before friendship and full confidence after it.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s two commands almost exactly: do not trust without examination; after examination, trust.

real_life_example.event_title: The Soviet Union selects Yuri Gagarin for Vostok 1
real_life_example.place: Moscow and Star City, Soviet Union (now Russia)
real_life_example.event: In 1960 the Soviet Union chose its first group of 20 cosmonaut candidates from among military pilots after extensive medical and psychological testing. After further training and examinations, managers ranked Yuri Gagarin first, with Gherman Titov as his backup, and on 12 April 1961 Gagarin made the first human spaceflight. The candidates themselves had voted overwhelmingly for Gagarin as the one they wanted to fly first.
real_life_example.explanation: No one was trusted with the first human spaceflight until he had been examined repeatedly, and the trust was then given in full.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says to trust no one without examining him and, once examined, to trust him in what he is fit for, as the Soviet selection did.

tamil:
தேரான் தெளிவும் தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்
தீரா இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Thaeraan thelivum thelindhaankan aiyuravum
Theeraa idumbai tharum.
meaning: Trusting someone you have not checked, and doubting someone you checked and then trusted, both bring endless trouble.
elementary: There are two ways to mess up with friends. One is trusting someone you just met with a big secret. The other is having a friend who has always been loyal and still checking their bag every day. Both make life miserable. Check carefully once, then trust.
university: The closing couplet names two opposite errors: தேரான் தெளிவு, confidence without examination (the fault of 508), and தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு, suspicion toward someone already tested and trusted. Both produce தீரா இடும்பை, ‘unending affliction’, repeating word for word the second line of 508, so the chapter ends by balancing its warnings: examination is required, but once done it must be honoured. Suspicion of a proven servant damages morale, invites real disloyalty, and wastes the effort of testing, points modern commentators such as Pappaiah and Kalaignar make explicit in the setting of appointments. The next chapter (52, தெரிந்து வினையாடல்) goes on to how the trusted person should be employed. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Sita has been rescued and her purity publicly confirmed by the fire ordeal, Rama later sends her into exile in response to gossip in Ayodhya, bringing lasting grief to both of them and to their family.
hinduism.explanation: Doubt revived after a trust has been proven leads to lasting sorrow.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s second error: suspicion toward one already tested and trusted.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 118 and Uttara Kanda 43-45

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then saith he to Thomas, reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus rebukes Thomas for holding on to doubt despite the reliable testimony of the other disciples.
christianity.tie_back: Persisting in doubt when evidence already warrants trust is the error the Kural warns about.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin.”
islam.explanation: Believers are told not to harbour baseless suspicion of one another or spy on each other.
islam.tie_back: Unfounded suspicion toward those already proven trustworthy is the Kural’s ஐயுறவு.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joshua ben Perahiah used to say: appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah pairs choosing a companion with the duty to give people the benefit of the doubt.
judaism.tie_back: Choose carefully, then do not meet the chosen one with suspicion, which is the balance of the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares a mind troubled by doubt (vicikicchā) to muddy water stirred up and set in the dark, in which a person cannot see their own reflection; doubt is one of the five hindrances.
buddhism.explanation: Persistent doubt keeps the mind from seeing clearly and acting well.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise treats needless doubt as a source of lasting affliction.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The persons possessed of Right Faith are free from doubts and are therefore fearless.”
jainism.explanation: Freedom from doubt (nihshankita) is the first of the eight limbs of right faith: once the truth has been tested and accepted, wavering suspicion is a fault.
jainism.tie_back: The kural condemns doubting one already examined and trusted; Jainism likewise counts doubt about what has been rightly accepted as a flaw that brings fear and instability.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 232 (Essential requisites of Right Faith; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who has no faith in the True Guru, and who does not love the Word of the Shabad, shall find no peace, even though he may come and go hundreds of times.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das says that someone who withholds trust from the Guru gains nothing however often he returns, and remains without peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that doubting one who has been tested and trusted brings unending trouble; Gurbani likewise says that withholding faith from the proven Guru leaves one without peace.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 591, Raag Vadhans, Vadhans Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cephalus, doubting his faithful wife Procris, tests her in disguise; their marriage is later poisoned by mutual suspicion, and Procris, secretly following him out of jealousy, is killed by his own javelin.
greek_mythology.explanation: Suspicion toward a proven partner destroys what it was meant to protect.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Doubting the one already proven brings grief that cannot be undone, as the Kural warns.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that only the friendship of good people is proof against slander, because it is not easy to believe anyone speaking against someone we have ourselves tested over a long time; among such friends there is trust and the thought ‘he would never wrong me’.
philosophy.explanation: Long testing produces a trust that should not be shaken by talk.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too says that once someone is tested, doubting them is the error.

real_life_example.event_title: Admiral Yi Sun-sin is removed from command
real_life_example.event: In 1597, during the Japanese invasions of Korea, Admiral Yi Sun-sin, who had already won a series of naval victories, was falsely accused, arrested and reduced to the rank of a common soldier. His replacement, Won Gyun, led the fleet into a defeat at Chilcheollyang in which almost all of its warships were lost. Yi was then restored to command and, with only about a dozen ships, won the Battle of Myeongnyang in October 1597.
real_life_example.explanation: A government that doubted its proven commander lost nearly its entire navy before turning back to him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that doubting someone already tested and trusted brings endless trouble, and Korea's naval disaster of 1597 shows it.

tamil:
நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி நலம்புரிந்த
தன்மையான் ஆளப் படும்.
transliteration:
Nanmaiyum theemaiyum naadi nalampurindha
Thanmaiyaan aalap padum.
meaning: Give the job to the person who weighs the good and the bad in a matter and then naturally chooses to do what is good.
elementary: Imagine picking a team captain. You don’t pick the kid who just does whatever pops into their head. You pick the one who stops, thinks “what could go right, what could go wrong?”, and then chooses the good way. That’s the kind of person you give a job to.
university: The chapter opens by naming the first qualification of a worthy agent: not raw talent but a settled disposition (தன்மை) that examines (நாடி) both benefit and harm and then inclines (புரிந்த) toward the good. Varadarasan and Kalaignar read it as a test of the candidate’s character, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as an instruction to the appointee himself — once entrusted with a task, weigh its good and ill and do only what is good. Both readings converge on judgment joined to moral preference: discernment without a love of the good produces a clever but dangerous servant, and good intentions without discernment produce a well-meaning bungler. The pairing anticipates Aristotle’s prohairesis (deliberate choice) and the Upanishadic distinction between the good (śreyas) and the merely pleasant (preyas).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The good and the pleasant approach man: the wise goes round about them and distinguishes them. Yea, the wise prefers the good to the pleasant, but the fool chooses the pleasant through greed and avarice.”
hinduism.explanation: Yama tells Nachiketas that both options present themselves to everyone; the wise person walks around them, examines them, and deliberately picks the good.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s two-step: examine both sides (நாடி), then prefer the good (நலம்புரிந்த).

christianity.quote_or_event: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Thessalonians to test everything rather than accept it blindly, and then cling to whatever proves good.
christianity.tie_back: Testing plus holding to the good is the disposition the Kural says marks the employable person.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who listen to speech and follow the best of it. Those are the ones Allah has guided, and those are people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who hear all that is said, weigh it, and follow the best part of it.
islam.tie_back: Hearing everything and following the best mirrors weighing good and ill and choosing the good.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Give Thy servant therefore an understanding heart to judge Thy people, that I may discern between good and evil; for who is able to judge this Thy great people?”
judaism.explanation: Young King Solomon asks God not for wealth or long life but for the ability to tell good from evil so he can govern well.
judaism.tie_back: Solomon names the very faculty the Kural treats as the first qualification for anyone who governs or serves the state.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by passing arbitrary judgments does a man become just; a wise man is he who investigates both right and wrong.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a person is truly just and wise only when they carefully investigate both sides before deciding.
buddhism.tie_back: Investigating both right and wrong is the Kural’s நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி.

jainism.quote_or_event: “After listening to scriptures, a person comes to know what is good and what is sinful, having thus known through listening one ought to perform what leads to welfare.”
jainism.explanation: This Dasavaikalika verse, gathered in the Saman Suttam, teaches that one should come to know both the good and the harmful and then choose to do what leads to welfare.
jainism.tie_back: The kural asks for the person who weighs both good and harm and is drawn to the good; the Jain verse describes exactly that act of knowing both sides and then choosing the beneficial.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 245 (Precepts on Right Knowledge; from Dasavaikalika Sutra 4.11; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The swans peck at the diamonds and pearls, while the crane chases after frogs.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan contrasts the swan, which by its nature picks out what is precious, with the crane, which by its nature goes after what is base.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to employ the one who, after weighing good and harm, is by nature drawn to the good; Guru Arjan's swan is exactly such a nature, choosing pearls over frogs.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 960, Raag Raamkalee, Raamkalee Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Choice of Heracles: at a crossroads the young Heracles is approached by two women, Vice offering an easy, pleasant road and Virtue offering a hard but noble one; after hearing both, he chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles listens to both sides before choosing, and the choice shapes the labours he later carries out for others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The hero who weighs both paths and chooses the good is the one fit for great tasks, just as the Kural says.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus’ fable as retold in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...discern between good and evil, and so to choose always and everywhere the better life as he has opportunity.”
philosophy.explanation: At the end of the Republic, Socrates says the most important learning is the ability to tell good from evil and so always pick the better course.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato treats this power of discernment as the key qualification, just as the Kural makes it the first test of a worker.

real_life_example.event_title: The Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting substances is signed
real_life_example.event: Governments meeting in Montreal signed a protocol to cut and eventually phase out the production and use of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other chemicals that deplete the stratospheric ozone layer, even though these chemicals were widely used in refrigeration, aerosols and industry. The treaty came into force in 1989, was strengthened several times, and became the first United Nations treaty to be ratified by every country. CFCs were phased out worldwide by 2010.
real_life_example.explanation: Faced with useful but harmful products, the world's governments weighed the benefit against the damage and chose the course that protected life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the one who weighs both the good and the harm in a matter and is drawn to do the good, which is what the parties to the Montreal Protocol did.

tamil:
வாரி பெருக்கி வளம்படுத்து உற்றவை
ஆராய்வான் செய்க வினை.
transliteration:
Vaari perukki valampaduththu utravai
Aaraaivaan seyga vinai.
meaning: Give the work to someone who can find more ways to bring money in, make it grow, and spot and fix the problems that come up.
