elementary: Think of someone looking after a lemonade stand. A good manager finds more customers, makes the stand earn more, and spots problems early, like running out of cups, and fixes them. That’s the person who should run the stand.
university: Kural 512 defines administrative competence in three verbs: பெருக்கி (expand the வாரி, the channels of revenue), வளம்படுத்து (turn income into lasting prosperity), and உற்றவை ஆராய் (look into whatever befalls, i.e., foresee and remove obstacles). Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all read உற்றவை as the hindrances that threaten wealth, so the ideal agent is productive and protective at once. The couplet is strikingly economic: Valluvar judges the officer by measurable growth, not by birth or favour. Kautilya’s Arthashastra sets out the same standard, promoting superintendents who raise revenue and keeping in permanent service those who increase it loyally.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who increase the king’s revenue instead of eating it up, and are loyally devoted to him, shall be made permanent in service.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya’s manual of statecraft says officials who grow the treasury, rather than skimming it, should be kept on for good.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ideal worker is the one who widens revenue and builds prosperity; Kautilya says that is exactly who should keep the job.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then came the first, saying, Lord, thy pound hath gained ten pounds. And he said unto him, Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the pounds, the servant who multiplied his master’s money is rewarded with authority over ten cities.
christianity.tie_back: The one who increases what he is given is the one trusted with bigger work, which is the Kural’s criterion.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Joseph] said, “Appoint me over the storehouses of the land. Indeed, I will be a knowing guardian.””
islam.explanation: Joseph asks the king of Egypt to put him in charge of the nation’s grain stores, pointing to his knowledge and his ability to guard them.
islam.tie_back: Joseph both builds up reserves and guards against the coming famine, the growth-plus-foresight the Kural asks for.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it came to pass from the time that he appointed him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, that the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; and the blessing of the LORD was upon all that he had, in the house and in the field.”
judaism.explanation: Once Potiphar makes Joseph overseer, his whole household and fields prosper.
judaism.tie_back: The right overseer makes the estate flourish, just as the Kural’s worker makes prosperity grow.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, a wise chaplain advises a king troubled by banditry not to punish harder but to give seed and fodder to farmers, capital to traders, and proper wages to officials; the land then grows prosperous and peaceful.
buddhism.explanation: Growing the country’s sources of income removes the causes of disorder and fills the treasury.
buddhism.tie_back: Widening sources of income and removing what threatens prosperity is exactly the skill Kural 512 wants in an administrator.

jainism.quote_or_event: “During his reign he taught, for the benefit of the people, the seventy-two sciences, of which writing is the first, arithmetic the most important, and the knowledge of omens the last, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men.”
jainism.explanation: Before his renunciation, Rishabha, the first Tirthankara and first king, is credited with giving people the arts, crafts and occupations by which they live.
jainism.tie_back: The kural praises the administrator who widens the sources of income and builds prosperity; Jain tradition gives its first king the role of founding the arts and occupations on which prosperity rests.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha §211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Amar Das organised the Sikh congregations into twenty-two districts (manjis) whose leaders passed on the disciples' offerings. When Guru Ram Das began the costly work of digging the sacred pool at Amritsar and building the Harimandar, Sikhs were asked to set aside a tenth of their income (dasvandh), and masands were appointed to collect it and bring it to the Guru.
sikhism.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism describes how the early Gurus built up regular channels of income for the community and turned them into lasting institutions such as the shrine and the langar.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural wants an administrator who widens the sources of revenue and turns them into growing prosperity; the early Sikh system of districts, tithes and collectors did just that for the community.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Dasvandh' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: While Odysseus is away, his loyal swineherd Eumaeus builds pens and carefully tends and guards his master’s herds, keeping the estate going through twenty years of absence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Eumaeus is the model servant: he looks after and builds up his master’s wealth and guards it against the suitors’ waste.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He grows and protects what he has been given, like the Kural’s ideal worker, though on a small household scale.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle retells how Thales, mocked for his poverty, foresaw a great olive harvest, rented all the olive presses in advance and made a fortune, and adds that statesmen should know such methods because states often need money.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats knowing how to create wealth as a real part of statesmanship.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise treats the ability to open new sources of revenue as a key qualification for public work.

real_life_example.event_title: Sergei Witte's term as Russia's finance minister
real_life_example.event: As Russian minister of finance from 1892 to 1903, Sergei Witte oversaw construction of the Trans-Siberian Railway, encouraged foreign investment and industrial growth, and in 1897 put the ruble on the gold standard. Under him the state monopoly on the sale of spirits became the largest single source of government revenue. He was dismissed in 1903 after palace intrigue.
real_life_example.explanation: Witte was judged by results: he widened the state's income, turned it into railways and industry, and stabilised the currency.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks for someone who can widen the sources of income, turn them into lasting prosperity and deal with obstacles, which describes Witte's work as finance minister.

tamil:
அன்பறிவு தேற்றம் அவாவின்மை இந்நான்கும்
நன்குடையான் கட்டே தெளிவு.
transliteration:
Anbarivu thetram avaavinmai innaankum
Nangudaiyaan katte thelivu.
meaning: You can safely trust a person who fully has these four things: loyal love, knowledge, clear and firm thinking, and freedom from greed.
elementary: If you’re choosing someone to hold the class piggy bank, you want four things: they care about the class, they’re smart, they make clear decisions, and they don’t want the money for themselves. A person with all four is safe to trust.
university: Kural 513 is a compact job specification: அன்பு (attachment or loyalty to the ruler and the enterprise), அறிவு (knowledge), தேற்றம் (clarity and decisiveness; Varadarasan glosses it as the power to decide without doubt, Kalaignar as capacity to act), and அவாவின்மை (freedom from covetousness). நன்குடையான் stresses that the four must be held fully and steadily, not occasionally. Freedom from greed comes last, as the safeguard that keeps loyalty, knowledge and decisiveness from being turned to private gain. Jethro’s advice to Moses in Exodus 18:21, choosing capable men of truth who hate unjust gain, is an almost exact counterpart.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but who is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor, who is free from false ego and equal both in happiness and distress, who is always satisfied and engaged in devotional service with determination and whose mind and intelligence are in agreement with Me—he is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the ideal devotee as friendly and kind, not possessive, content, and firm in determination.
hinduism.tie_back: Kindness (அன்பு), steady intelligence (அறிவு), firm determination (தேற்றம்) and contentment without possessiveness (அவாவின்மை) map closely onto the Kural’s four qualities.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists what a church overseer must be, stressing again and again that he must not love money.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the New Testament makes freedom from greed a condition for being trusted with responsibility.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of the women said, “O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy.””
islam.explanation: One of the daughters of the man of Midian recommends hiring Moses because he has shown both strength and trustworthiness.
islam.tie_back: Capability plus trustworthiness is the Qur’an’s short list; the Kural makes the same point with four qualities.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.”
judaism.explanation: Jethro tells Moses to pick capable, God-fearing, honest men who hate unjust gain, and put them in charge.
judaism.tie_back: Capability, integrity and hatred of gain closely match the Kural’s knowledge, clarity and freedom from greed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha names three roots of wholesome action: non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa, shown as goodwill) and non-delusion (amoha, i.e. wisdom).
buddhism.explanation: Good action grows from being free of greed, full of goodwill, and clear-seeing.
buddhism.tie_back: Goodwill, wisdom and non-greed correspond to three of the Kural’s four qualities (அன்பு, அறிவு, அவாவின்மை).

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
jainism.explanation: Of the four passions (kashayas) that bind karma, greed is singled out as the one that ruins every virtue.
jainism.tie_back: Freedom from greed is one of the four qualities the kural requires before trust; the Jain verse explains why it matters so much, since greed undoes everything else, love included.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 135 (Precepts on Passions; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: As a young man Guru Nanak moved to Sultanpur and worked as a clerk in the Lodi administration. The janamsakhis, the traditional accounts of his life, remember him in these years for his honesty and devotion to truth.
sikhism.explanation: The Harvard Pluralism Project notes Guru Nanak's government post at Sultanpur and the janamsakhi tradition of his honesty in it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural trusts the one who combines loyalty, knowledge, clear judgement and freedom from greed; the janamsakhis present the young Nanak as just such an honest official.
sikhism.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, 'Guru Nanak' (paraphrase; janamsakhi tradition)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before sailing to Troy, Odysseus entrusts his whole household to his old friend Mentor, whose loyalty and good sense make him fit to keep it safe.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus picks a friend known for loyalty and judgment to look after everything he owns.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Trust is given to someone with loyal love and wisdom, as the Kural recommends.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And to this end they ought to be wise and efficient, and to have a special care of the State?”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says the city’s guardians must be wise and capable and must truly care for the city; later he denies them private property so greed cannot corrupt them.
philosophy.tie_back: Wisdom, capability, love of the city and freedom from acquisitiveness are almost exactly the Kural’s four qualities.

real_life_example.event_title: Garibaldi hands southern Italy to Victor Emmanuel and goes home to Caprera
real_life_example.place: Naples, Italy, and the island of Caprera, Sardinia
real_life_example.event: After conquering Sicily and Naples with his volunteers in 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi held plebiscites and handed the whole of southern Italy to King Victor Emmanuel II, meeting him on 26 October 1860 and giving up his dictatorship of the South. He was the first to hail Victor Emmanuel as king of a united Italy. Immediately afterwards he returned to his farm on Caprera, refusing the rewards offered to him.
real_life_example.explanation: Garibaldi combined loyalty to the cause, military skill and decisive action with a striking lack of personal greed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names loyalty, knowledge, decisiveness and freedom from greed as the marks of a trustworthy agent, and Garibaldi's handover and refusal of rewards display all four.

tamil:
எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும் வினைவகையான்
வேறாகும் மாந்தர் பலர்.
transliteration:
Enaivagaiyaan theriyak kannum vinaivagaiyaan
Veraagum maandhar palar.
meaning: Even after being tested and approved in every way, many people turn out to be different once they actually start doing the work.
elementary: Someone can do great in a practice game and then play very differently in the real match. Tests help, but you only really know a person once they’re doing the actual job.
university: Having spent chapter 51 on testing (தெரிந்து தெளிதல்), Valluvar now admits its limits: however thoroughly a man is examined (எனைவகையான் தேறிய), the nature of the work itself (வினைவகையான்) can change him. Parimelazhagar sees here the corrupting pressure of office, wealth and power, and Pappaiah reads it as simple underperformance against expectations. The practical lesson, developed in Kural 520, is that selection must be followed by continuing supervision. The saying of Bias preserved by Aristotle, “rule will show the man,” states the same insight: power reveals what screening could not.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just as it is impossible not to taste the honey or the poison that finds itself at the tip of the tongue, so it is impossible for a government servant not to eat up, at least, a bit of the king’s revenue.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya warns that officials in charge of revenue are constantly tempted, and even tested men may start to skim once the money is in their hands.
hinduism.tie_back: The work itself changes the worker, which is exactly the Kural’s warning.

christianity.quote_or_event: “This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein.”
christianity.explanation: Judas, one of the Twelve chosen by Jesus himself, was trusted with the common purse and stole from it.
christianity.tie_back: Even someone chosen after close personal contact changed once he held the money, as the Kural warns.

islam.quote_or_event: “And recite to them, [O Muhammad], the news of him to whom we gave [knowledge of] Our signs, but he detached himself from them; so Satan pursued him, and he became of the deviators.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells of a man given great knowledge who later turned away and went astray.
islam.tie_back: Being gifted and approved at the start does not guarantee faithfulness later.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It repenteth Me that I have set up Saul to be king; for he is turned back from following Me, and hath not performed My commandments.”
judaism.explanation: Saul, chosen and anointed as king, failed once in power to carry out what he was charged with.
judaism.tie_back: Even a man chosen by the highest authority can turn out differently once in the role.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, a monk who had gained psychic powers, was ruined by the gain, honour and fame that came to him; the Buddha likens this to a plantain that dies after it bears fruit.
buddhism.explanation: Success and position changed Devadatta until he turned against the Buddha.
buddhism.tie_back: The pressures of a role can transform someone who once seemed sound, as Kural 514 observes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “After they have been instructed, admitted into the order, and nourished with food and drink, they disperse in all directions like geese whose wings have grown.”
jainism.explanation: The teacher Garga laments pupils who were instructed, accepted and cared for, yet once in service would not carry out their tasks and scattered.
jainism.tie_back: The kural observes that many people tested and approved still turn out differently once they are doing the work; Garga's pupils, received and trained with care, prove exactly that.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 27.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: The masands, appointed by Guru Arjan to preach and to collect the community's offerings, were at first chosen for their piety and devotion. As time passed many grew neglectful of their office and took to enriching themselves, until Guru Gobind Singh charged them with corruption and oppression, punished the guilty and abolished the institution.
sikhism.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism traces how agents who had been carefully selected were changed by the power and wealth their office brought.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that even people tested in every way often turn out differently once they are doing the work; the masands, chosen for piety, were corrupted by their office.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Masands' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar tells how Tantalus, honoured by the gods and admitted to their table, could not bear his great good fortune and stole nectar and ambrosia to give to mortal companions, and was punished for ever.
greek_mythology.explanation: A man who seemed worthy of the gods’ trust betrayed it once he had it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Trust granted after approval can still be abused, which is the Kural’s point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “This is why the saying of Bias is thought to be true, that ‘rule will show the man’; for a ruler is necessarily in relation to other men and a member of a society.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle quotes the sage Bias: you only discover what a person is really like when he holds power over others.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same: many who passed every test turn out differently once they are actually in the job.

real_life_example.event_title: Thomas Becket turns from royal chancellor to opponent of Henry II
real_life_example.event: Thomas Becket had served Henry II as chancellor and was the king's close friend, and in 1162 Henry had him made Archbishop of Canterbury. Soon afterwards Becket gave up the chancellorship against the king's wishes and began defending the rights of the Church against the crown. The dispute came to a head over the Constitutions of Clarendon of 1164, and Becket went into exile in France until 1170.
real_life_example.explanation: A man the king knew intimately and had tested for years became a very different person once he held the new office.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even people tested and approved in every way often turn out differently once they are actually doing the work, as Becket did after becoming archbishop.

tamil:
அறிந்தாற்றிச் செய்கிற்பாற்கு அல்லால் வினைதான்
சிறந்தானென்று ஏவற்பாற் றன்று.
transliteration:
Arindhaatrich cheygirpaarku allaal vinaidhaan
Sirandhaanendru evarpaat randru.
meaning: Give a job only to someone who knows how to do it and can push through the hard parts to finish it. Never give it to someone just because you like or admire them.
elementary: If the school play needs someone to run the lights, you don’t pick your best friend just because you like them. You pick the kid who knows how the lights work and won’t give up when something goes wrong.
university: The couplet sets competence against favouritism. Its first line gives the positive standard: அறிந்து (knowing the method), ஆற்றி (enduring obstacles) and செய்கிற்பான் (able to carry the task through). Its second line rules out appointing someone because he is சிறந்தான், someone the ruler holds dear or considers excellent in a general way. Pope’s “specious fav’rite” and Pappaiah’s gloss “thinking him one of our own (party, clan)” bring out the anti-nepotism edge. Plato’s ship of state, where sailors who have never learned navigation clamour to steer, dramatises the same danger.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, the blind king Dhritarashtra keeps backing his son Duryodhana out of fatherly attachment, although wiser advisers such as Vidura warn him that Duryodhana is unfit, and the result is the destruction of the Kuru line.
hinduism.explanation: Power is handed to someone because he is beloved, not because he is capable, and it ends in disaster.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural forbids exactly this: giving work to someone because he is dear rather than because he can do it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye know not what ye ask. Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of...?” ... “but to sit on my right hand, and on my left, is not mine to give, but it shall be given to them for whom it is prepared of my Father.”
christianity.explanation: When the mother of James and John asks for places of honour for her sons, Jesus replies that such positions depend on being able to bear the cost, not on a personal request.
christianity.tie_back: Positions go to those prepared and able, not to those with the right connections.

islam.quote_or_event: “Abu Dharr, thou art weak and authority is a trust. and on the Day of judgment it is a cause of humiliation and repentance except for one who fulfils its obligations and (properly) discharges the duties attendant thereon.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet, though fond of his close companion Abu Dharr, declines to appoint him to office because he is not suited to its burdens.
islam.tie_back: Affection does not justify an appointment; only the ability to carry the duty does. This is the Kural exactly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But he forsook the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men that were grown up with him, that stood before him.”
judaism.explanation: King Rehoboam ignores experienced advisers and relies on his childhood friends, and the kingdom splits in two.
judaism.tie_back: Relying on familiar favourites instead of proven competence is the error the Kural warns against.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says that one fit to go on a mission (duteyya) listens, gets others to listen, learns, remembers, understands, helps others understand, knows what is relevant and what is not, and does not stir up quarrels, and names Sariputta as having these qualities.
buddhism.explanation: Envoys are chosen by a list of specific skills.
buddhism.tie_back: Choosing an agent by demonstrated ability, not by rank, matches the Kural’s positive standard.

jainism.quote_or_event: “An excellent pupil needs no express directions, or he is (at least) quickly directed; he always carries out his duties as he is told.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline describes the worthy disciple as one who understands what is required and reliably carries it through.
jainism.tie_back: The kural would give a task only to one who knows how to do it and can see it through, not to a favourite; the Jain verse describes that kind of capable, reliable doer.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Nanak had two sons, yet before he died he appointed one of his faithful followers as his successor in leading the community, naming him Guru Angad, the 'limb' of Guru Nanak.
sikhism.explanation: The Harvard Pluralism Project records that leadership passed to a proven disciple rather than to the Guru's own sons.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a task should go to one who knows how to do it and can see it through, never to someone because he is dear; Guru Nanak passed over his own sons for a faithful disciple.
sikhism.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, 'Guru Nanak' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Helios, bound by an oath and moved by love for his son, lets the inexperienced Phaethon drive the chariot of the sun; Phaethon loses control, scorches the earth, and Zeus strikes him down.
greek_mythology.explanation: A father gives a job to his son out of affection, although the son lacks the skill and strength for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s warning come to life: give the task to one who can do it, not to one you love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The sailors are quarrelling with one another about the steering—every one is of opinion that he has a right to steer, though he has never learned the art of navigation and cannot tell who taught him or when he learned...”
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s ship of state shows people who lack the skill fighting for the helm while the real navigator is ignored.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar agree that the helm belongs to whoever knows the craft, not to the popular or the favoured.

real_life_example.event_title: Prussian reformers open the officer corps to merit
real_life_example.event: After Prussia's crushing defeat by Napoleon in 1806, a reform commission led by Gerhard von Scharnhorst, himself not of Prussian noble birth, reorganised the army. The reformers opened the officer corps, previously drawn almost entirely from the nobility, to middle-class candidates and made advancement depend on merit and education. They also founded military schools and developed the modern general staff.
real_life_example.explanation: A state that had lost a war with officers chosen by birth decided to choose them for knowledge and ability instead.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a task should go to the one who knows how to do it and can see it through, not to someone favoured for other reasons, which is the principle the Prussian reformers adopted.

tamil:
செய்வானை நாடி வினைநாடிக் காலத்தோடு
எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்.
transliteration:
Seyvaanai naadi vinainaadik kaalaththodu
Eydha unarndhu seyal.
meaning: First judge the person who will do the work, then judge the work itself, and then act when the time is right for both.
elementary: To bake a cake you need the right baker, the right recipe, and the right moment, so it’s ready when the party starts. Get all three right and it works.
university: Kural 516 sets out a three-part planning method: examine the doer (செய்வானை நாடி), examine the deed (வினைநாடி), and fit both to the proper time (காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து). Pappaiah reads it as bringing agent and task together and then matching the pair to the moment. The couplet also draws on the earlier chapters on strength (48), time (49) and place (50). Plato’s specialisation principle, that things go best when each person does the one thing natural to him and does it at the right time, runs remarkably parallel.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That gift which is given out of duty, at the proper time and place, to a worthy person, and without expectation of return, is considered to be charity in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says a good action needs the right recipient, the right time and the right place.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s check of person, time and place mirrors the Kural’s check of doer, deed and time.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says a sensible builder works out beforehand whether he has what it takes to finish the job.
christianity.tie_back: Assess the task and your means before you start, as the Kural advises.

islam.quote_or_event: “...and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to consult his people, reach a considered decision, and then act with trust in God.
islam.tie_back: Deliberate first, then act decisively, is the procedure the Kural lays out.

judaism.quote_or_event: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes teaches that every action has its proper time.
judaism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s third element, fitting the work to the right moment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “...a sense of himself, a sense of moderation, a sense of time, a sense of social gatherings, & a sense of distinctions among individuals.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the qualities of a worthy person, among them knowing oneself, knowing the right time, and knowing how individuals differ.
buddhism.tie_back: A sense of time plus a sense of differences between people covers the Kural’s timing and choice of person.

jainism.quote_or_event: “At the right time a monk should sally forth, and he should return at the right time; avoiding to do anything out of time, he should do what is appropriate for each period of the day.”
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic discipline insists that each action be fitted to its proper time.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's third step is to act when doer and deed fit the right time; the Jain rule makes timeliness a matter of discipline, though it does not address sizing up doer and deed.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who reflects upon his allotted span of life, becomes the slave of God.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak praises the person who thinks about the time he has been given and uses it for its true purpose.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks that the doer and the deed be weighed and then matched to the right time; Guru Nanak likewise asks that one's time be considered before it is spent.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 84, Siree Raag, Siree Raag Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Kairos, the Greeks’ personification of the opportune moment, was shown in Lysippus’ statue with a lock of hair in front and bald behind: the moment can be seized as it comes but not once it has passed.
greek_mythology.explanation: The right moment has to be recognised and grasped before it slips away.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This reflects the Kural’s demand to fit the work to the proper time.
greek_mythology.source: Posidippus, epigram on Lysippus’ Kairos (Greek Anthology 16.275)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...we must infer that all things are produced more plentifully and easily and of a better quality when one man does one thing which is natural to him and does it at the right time, and leaves other things.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that work goes best when each person does the task suited to his nature, at the right moment.
philosophy.tie_back: The right person, the right task and the right time is almost exactly the Kural’s formula.

real_life_example.event_title: Ferdinand and Isabella back Columbus after the fall of Granada
real_life_example.event: Christopher Columbus sought support from Ferdinand and Isabella from 1486, and they had a commission examine his proposal while they were fighting the war against Granada. After at least two rejections, he obtained royal support in January 1492, soon after Granada surrendered on 2 January. In April 1492 he was granted the title Admiral of the Ocean Sea, and he sailed in August.
real_life_example.explanation: The monarchs examined both the man and the plan, and committed to it only when their war was over and resources were free.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says to size up the doer, then the deed, and then act when both fit the right time, and the monarchs' long-delayed decision followed that order.

tamil:
இதனை இதனால் இவன்முடிக்கும் என்றாய்ந்து
அதனை அவன்கண் விடல்.
transliteration:
Idhanai idhanaal ivanmudikkum endraaindhu
Adhanai avankan vidal.
meaning: Once you decide that “this person can do this job in this way,” hand the job over to them and leave it in their hands.
elementary: When your teacher knows you’re good at drawing and have the markers you need, she gives you the class poster to make and then lets you do it, without hovering over every line.
university: The couplet is built on demonstratives: இதனை (this task), இதனால் (by these means), இவன் (this man), and then அதனை அவன்கண் விடல் (leave that with him). Delegation follows a specific three-way match of task, resources and person; Varadarasan glosses இதனால் as “by this instrument” and Pappaiah as the manpower and money available. விடல் (to release) implies real handing over, not a nominal assignment followed by micromanagement. Jethro’s advice in Exodus 18, and the master in the parable of the talents who gives each servant a share “according to his several ability” and then departs, express the same trust.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, when the monkey search parties set out for Sita, Rama gives his signet ring to Hanuman alone, judging that he is the one most likely to find her; Hanuman goes on to leap the ocean to Lanka and succeed.
hinduism.explanation: Rama works out who can accomplish the mission and with what, then entrusts it to him completely.
hinduism.tie_back: This man, this task, these means, then leave it to him: exactly the Kural’s formula.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.”
christianity.explanation: The master gives each servant as much as that servant can handle, then leaves them to get on with it.
christianity.tie_back: Allotting by ability and then really leaving is the heart of Kural 517.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and when you judge between people to judge with justice.”
islam.explanation: Classical exegesis applies this verse to giving offices and responsibilities to those who are rightly suited to them.
islam.tie_back: Giving each trust to the person it properly belongs to is the Kural’s entrusting principle.

judaism.quote_or_event: “...every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge themselves; so shall they make it easier for thee and bear the burden with thee.”
judaism.explanation: Jethro tells Moses to let the appointed judges settle ordinary cases themselves and bring him only the hard ones.
judaism.tie_back: Real delegation to proven people, releasing the task to them, is what the Kural commands.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Devadatta leads a group of new monks away to Gayasisa, the Buddha sends Sariputta and Moggallana, his two ablest disciples, to win them back; they succeed.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha matches a delicate mission to the two disciples best suited to it and leaves it to them.
buddhism.tie_back: Choosing the right people for a specific task and trusting them to finish it reflects Kural 517.

jainism.quote_or_event: “'What shall I do now? I want to be employed, sir, in doing some work or in studying.' If he is ordered to do some work, he should do it without tiring; if he is ordered to study, he should do it without allowing himself to be affected by any pains.”
jainism.explanation: In the daily routine of the Jain monk, the superior assigns each disciple either work or study, and the disciple carries out the assigned task fully.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says that once you have decided who will do a task, you should hand it over to him; the Jain routine shows a superior assigning work and the disciple taking it on wholly.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 26.9-10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: When Guru Arjan compiled the first definitive collection of Sikh scripture, he entrusted the writing of the text to Bhai Gurdas, a senior member of his congregation, who served as scribe of the Adi Granth. The work was finished in 1604 and installed in the Darbar Sahib at Amritsar.
sikhism.explanation: The Harvard Pluralism Project records that the Guru chose a learned and trusted disciple for the most important writing task of the early community.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that once one has decided that this person will do this task by these means, the task should be handed over to him; Guru Arjan handed the writing of the scripture to Bhai Gurdas.
sikhism.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, 'The Sikh Scripture' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Asked to pick a partner for a dangerous night raid on the Trojan camp, Diomedes chooses Odysseus for his cleverness and courage, saying that with him they could return even through blazing fire.
greek_mythology.explanation: Diomedes chooses the partner whose skills fit the mission.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Matching a particular person to a particular task by known ability echoes the Kural’s “this man will do this.”

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that masters who can afford it appoint a steward to run the household so that they themselves can devote their time to politics or philosophy.
philosophy.explanation: Once a competent manager is in place, the master hands over management entirely.
philosophy.tie_back: Handing work to a capable agent and leaving it with him is the Kural’s advice.

real_life_example.event_title: Lincoln leaves the 1864 campaign plans to Grant
real_life_example.event: After appointing Ulysses S. Grant general-in-chief of the Union armies in March 1864, President Abraham Lincoln wrote to him on 30 April, the eve of Grant's spring campaign. In the letter Lincoln said he did not know and did not seek to know the details of Grant's plans, and that he was content to leave them to him. Grant crossed the Rapidan River with the Army of the Potomac days later, beginning the campaign that led to the end of the war.
real_life_example.explanation: After years of interfering with generals who failed him, Lincoln found one he trusted and left the work in his hands.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that once you have decided this person will do this task by these means, you should hand the task to him and leave it with him, as Lincoln did with Grant.

tamil:
வினைக்குரிமை நாடிய பின்றை அவனை
அதற்குரிய னாகச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Vinaikkurimai naadiya pindrai avanai
Adharkuriya naagach cheyal.
meaning: After finding out what work a person is good at, put them fully in charge of it and give them the power to do it.
elementary: If you find out your friend is the best goalkeeper, you don’t just let them try out. You make them the goalkeeper for real, with the gloves and everything.
university: The key word is உரிமை, suitability and also rightful ownership. Once fitness for a task (வினைக்குரிமை) has been established, the ruler must make the person its rightful holder (அதற்குரியனாக). Pappaiah stresses the second half: having appointed a man, let him exercise the powers of the post himself. The couplet thus balances Kural 517: 517 is about handing over, 518 about conferring the standing and authority that make the handover real. It is Valluvar’s closest statement of the specialisation principle, which Plato made the definition of justice and the Gita discussed in terms of svadharma.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is better to engage in one’s own occupation, even though one may perform it imperfectly, than to accept another’s occupation and perform it perfectly. Prescribed duties, according to one’s nature, are never affected by sinful reactions.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says each person does best following the duty that fits his own nature.
hinduism.tie_back: Work should match the person’s nature: the Kural’s வினைக்குரிமை (fitness for a task).

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.”
christianity.explanation: The apostles pick seven qualified men and formally put them in charge of the daily food distribution.
christianity.tie_back: Find the qualified people, then formally give them the task: the Kural’s two steps.

islam.quote_or_event: “When honesty is lost, then wait for the Hour (Doomsday).” ... “When the power or authority comes in the hands of unfit persons, then wait for the Hour (Doomsday.)”
islam.explanation: The Prophet counts giving authority to unfit people as a sign that honesty has been lost from the world.
islam.tie_back: Authority belongs to those truly suited to it; the hadith states negatively what the Kural states positively.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Forasmuch as God hath shown thee all this, there is none so discreet and wise as thou. Thou shalt be over my house, and according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled...”
judaism.explanation: Having seen Joseph’s wisdom for himself, Pharaoh gives him full authority over Egypt.
judaism.tie_back: After seeing fitness, Pharaoh makes Joseph the real holder of the office, exactly the Kural’s அதற்குரியனாகச் செயல்.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha publicly named particular disciples as foremost (etadagga) in particular qualities: Sariputta in wisdom, Moggallana in psychic power, Upali in monastic discipline, and so on.
buddhism.explanation: He recognised each disciple’s special strength and gave each a matching role and standing.
buddhism.tie_back: Finding each person’s aptitude and giving them standing in it reflects the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “At last he anointed his hundred sons as kings, and gave each a kingdom.”
jainism.explanation: Before renouncing the world, Rishabha handed over rule by consecrating his sons and giving each a realm of his own.
jainism.tie_back: The kural asks that a man found fit for a task be made its rightful holder with full authority; Rishabha's act of anointing each son over his own kingdom is a formal transfer of authority of exactly that kind.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha §211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: In 1708 at Nanded, Guru Gobind Singh initiated Banda Singh into the Khalsa and, before sending him north to the Punjab, gave him a drum, a banner and five arrows as emblems of authority, with five Sikhs to accompany him.
sikhism.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism records that the Guru gave Banda Singh both a mission and visible signs of the authority needed to carry it out.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that once a person's fitness for a task is known, he should be made fully responsible for it with the authority that goes with it; Guru Gobind Singh gave Banda Singh both.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Banda Singh Bahadur', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Protagoras’ myth, Epimetheus hands out abilities to the animals so that each kind has what suits its way of life, giving speed to some, strength to others, and wings or burrows to others.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth pictures a world in which capacities are matched to roles.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the fit between being and function that the Kural asks rulers to honour.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...one man should practise one thing only, the thing to which his nature was best adapted;—now justice is this principle or a part of it.”
philosophy.explanation: Plato defines justice in the city as each person doing the one task his nature fits him for.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato raises the Kural’s principle, find each person’s fit and make that their work, to the definition of justice.

real_life_example.event_title: Napoleon III makes Haussmann prefect of the Seine
real_life_example.event: Emperor Napoleon III appointed Georges-Eugene Haussmann prefect of the Seine in 1853, in effect the administrator of Paris, with the task of transforming the city. Over the next seventeen years Haussmann cut broad boulevards through old districts, greatly expanded the sewers and water supply, and created new parks. He raised large loans with little oversight and was dismissed in 1870 when a more liberal government came in.
real_life_example.explanation: Napoleon III gave one administrator both the task and the authority and money to carry it out, and Paris was remade as a result.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that once a person's fitness for a task is established he should be made fully responsible for it with the authority that goes with it, which is how Haussmann was empowered.

tamil:
வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் கேண்மைவே றாக
நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு.
transliteration:
Vinaikkan vinaiyudaiyaan kenmaive raaga
Ninaippaanai neengum thiru.
meaning: Good fortune leaves a ruler who wrongly doubts the loyalty of a worker who is truly devoted to the work.
elementary: Imagine a kid who works really hard on a group project and is friendly with the teacher, and the teacher starts thinking “he must be up to something.” If you treat your best helpers that way, you lose them, and everything goes wrong.
university: The couplet warns against a failure of trust after appointment. வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் is the man wholly absorbed in his assigned work; கேண்மை வேறாக நினைத்தல் is to read his familiarity or friendship with the ruler as something else, such as presumption or disloyalty. Pope renders it as failing to bear the informal friendly ways of such servants, and Pappaiah adds the courtly setting of slanderers who poison the ruler’s mind against capable officers. The penalty is that திரு (prosperity, the goddess of fortune) departs, because a ruler who drives away his best workers destroys his own wealth. Saul’s jealousy of David is the classic Hebrew example.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Dhritarashtra repeatedly suspects and rebukes his loyal half-brother and minister Vidura, at one point driving him from court, while listening to Duryodhana and his allies; the kingdom ends in ruin.
hinduism.explanation: A king who distrusts his most faithful counsellor loses everything.
hinduism.tie_back: Suspecting the devoted servant drives away fortune, as the Kural warns.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha and Udyoga Parvas (Ganguli trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season? Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing. Verily I say unto you, That he shall make him ruler over all his goods.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says a wise master rewards the servant he finds faithfully at work by giving him even more.
christianity.tie_back: The positive side of the Kural: honour the devoted worker, don’t suspect him.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.”
islam.explanation: Believers are told to check reports from unreliable people before acting, or they may harm the innocent and regret it.
islam.tie_back: This matches Pappaiah’s reading: a ruler must not turn on a loyal worker because of slanderers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And David had great success in all his ways; and the LORD was with him. And when Saul saw that he had great success, he stood in awe of him.”
judaism.explanation: King Saul grows fearful and suspicious of David, his most successful servant, and tries to kill him; the kingdom passes from Saul’s house.
judaism.tie_back: A ruler who turns on his devoted, effective servant loses his fortune, the Kural’s exact scenario.

buddhism.quote_or_event: According to the Dhammapada commentary, King Pasenadi of Kosala, swayed by jealous courtiers’ slander, had his loyal commander Bandhula and his sons killed; he later learned Bandhula was innocent, and in the end lost his throne with the help of Bandhula’s aggrieved nephew.
buddhism.explanation: A king who distrusts his faithful commander on the word of slanderers brings about his own downfall.
buddhism.tie_back: Fortune leaves the ruler who misreads a loyal worker, as Kural 519 says.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary, story of Vidudabha (Burlingame, Buddhist Legends)

jainism.quote_or_event: “(A bad pupil thinks:) 'I get but knocks and boxes on the ear, hard words and blows;' and he believes a teacher who instructs him well, to be a malevolent man.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline describes the bad pupil who misreads the well-meant care of a devoted teacher as hostility.
jainism.tie_back: The kural warns the ruler who misreads a devoted worker's closeness and grows suspicious of him; the Jain verse shows the same error of turning genuine devotion into imagined ill will, though here it runs from pupil to teacher.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Slandering the Saints, all happiness vanishes. … Slandering the Saints, all one's influence vanishes.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan lists the losses that come to one who speaks ill of the devoted: peace, standing and influence all depart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says fortune leaves the ruler who grows suspicious of a servant devoted to his work; Guru Arjan says influence and happiness leave the one who turns against the devoted.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib (ashtapadi 13), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theseus believes Phaedra’s false accusation against his son Hippolytus without looking into it and curses him; Hippolytus dies, and only then does Theseus learn the truth.
greek_mythology.explanation: A ruler who misjudges a loyal, upright member of his household on false report brings ruin on himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s warning against thinking otherwise of the faithful.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes how tyrants keep power by cutting down anyone who stands out, distrusting good and able men, and preferring flatterers, and he treats these as marks of the worst kind of rule.
philosophy.explanation: Suspicion of excellent subordinates is a defining vice of tyranny.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural counts the same suspicion among the things that drive fortune away.

real_life_example.event_title: Sultan Muhammad III has his minister Mahmud Gawan executed
real_life_example.event: Mahmud Gawan served the Bahmani sultans for many years as chief minister, and under him the sultanate reached its greatest size and degree of central control. Rival nobles falsified evidence, including a forged letter, to make him appear a traitor, and Sultan Muhammad III ordered his execution in 1481. Many nobles then withdrew from the court, and the effective power of the Bahmani state rapidly dissolved.
real_life_example.explanation: A ruler who let others turn him against his most devoted minister lost the support that held his kingdom together.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that fortune leaves the ruler who grows suspicious of a servant devoted to his work, and the Bahmani kingdom's collapse after Gawan's death shows it.

tamil:
நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன் வினைசெய்வான்
கோடாமை கோடா துலகு.
transliteration:
Naadorum naaduga mannan vinaiseyvaan
Kodaamai kodaa thulagu.
meaning: A king should check every day how his workers behave. As long as they do not go wrong, the country will not go wrong either.
elementary: A good coach checks on the team at every practice, not just once at the start of the season. If the players stay on track, the whole team does well.
university: The chapter closes by joining selection to supervision: நாடோறும் நாடுக, examine every day. The logic is causal: if the worker does not swerve (கோடாமை), the world, meaning the realm and its people, will not swerve (கோடாது). Most commentators read it as vigilance over officials, but Kalaignar reads கோடாமை as the worker’s heart not withering, so the king’s daily attention becomes care for the welfare of labour. Kautilya prescribes almost the same thing, that superintendents be examined daily because men are changeable, which gives the Kural a precise parallel in Indian statecraft.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While engaged in work, they shall be daily examined; for men are naturally fickle-minded, and, like horses at work, exhibit constant change in their temper.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya says officials must be checked every day because people’s dispositions shift while they work.
hinduism.tie_back: This is Kural 520’s நாடோறும் நாடுக almost word for word.

christianity.quote_or_event: “After a long time the lord of those servants cometh, and reckoneth with them.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, the master comes back and asks each servant to account for what he did.
christianity.tie_back: Delegation is followed by accountability, though here after a long time rather than every day.

islam.quote_or_event: “All of you are guardians and responsible for your wards and the things under your care. The Imam (i.e. ruler) is the guardian of his subjects and is responsible for them...”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that every ruler answers for those in his care.
islam.tie_back: The ruler’s responsibility for his people requires the constant attention to his agents that the Kural prescribes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, And look well to thy herds;”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs tells the owner to keep close, personal watch over everything in his care.
judaism.tie_back: Diligently knowing the state of your charge is the Kural’s daily examination.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In five ways should a master minister to his servants and employees as the Nadir : (i) by assigning them work according to their ability, (ii) by supplying them with food and with wages, (iii) by tending them in sickness, (iv) by sharing with them any delicacies, (v) by granting them leave at times.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells employers to assign work by ability and look after their workers’ welfare; in return the workers do their duties well.
buddhism.tie_back: This fits the whole chapter’s theme of assigning work by ability, and Kalaignar’s welfare reading of Kural 520.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Then he should, in due order, reflect on all transgressions he has committed during the day, with regard to knowledge, faith, and conduct.”
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic practice prescribes a daily review (pratikramana) in which each monk examines and confesses the day's lapses before his guru.
jainism.tie_back: The kural asks the king to examine his workers' conduct every day so that nothing goes crooked; Jain discipline builds the same daily inspection into every monk's evening routine.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 26.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The kings are tigers, and their officials are dogs; they go out and awaken the sleeping people to harass them.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes a realm where rulers prey on the people and their officials, left unchecked, go out to harass ordinary folk.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a king must watch his officials every day, because the world goes crooked when they do; Guru Nanak shows the world that results when officials are not held straight.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar, Malaar Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says Zeus has countless unseen spirits roaming the earth, watching over human judgments and wrongdoing.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek belief, divine oversight keeps an eye on how people act.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Constant watchfulness over those who act on authority parallels the Kural’s daily review of the king’s agents.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Xenophon’s Oeconomicus, Ischomachus tells the story of the Persian king who asked what fattens a horse fastest and was told “the master’s eye,” and says the master’s own attention is what makes stewards and estates flourish.
philosophy.explanation: The owner’s personal, continuing oversight is what keeps workers diligent.
philosophy.tie_back: The master’s eye is the Kural’s daily examination.

real_life_example.event_title: The Yongzheng Emperor and the palace memorial system
real_life_example.event: The Yongzheng Emperor of the Qing dynasty expanded and regularised the palace memorial system, under which trusted officials across the empire sent confidential reports directly to him. He wrote his replies on them personally in vermilion ink before they were returned to the sender. Britannica describes him as an able ruler who checked corruption and personally scrutinised and directed all important matters of government.
real_life_example.explanation: Yongzheng kept a continual, personal watch on what his officials were doing, and his reign is known for its campaign against corruption.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural tells the ruler to look into the conduct of those doing his work every day, because if they do not go crooked the world will not, and Yongzheng's memorial system was built for that daily scrutiny.

tamil:
பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் பழைமைபா ராட்டுதல்
சுற்றத்தார் கண்ணே உள.
transliteration:
Patratra kannum pazhaimaipaa raattudhal
Sutraththaar kanne ula.
meaning: Even when someone has lost everything, it is only relatives who still honor the old bond they shared.
elementary: When someone’s pockets are full, lots of people want to sit next to them at lunch. But if they lose everything, most of those people drift away. Your family is different: they still remember the good times and stay by your side. That is what makes family special.
university: The chapter title சுற்றம் தழால் means ‘embracing the circle of kin’; Parimelazhagar glosses it as the king holding his kinsmen close so that they never leave him, and he explains that it follows ‘Selection and Employment’ (Ch. 52) because, having spoken of those who do the king’s work, Valluvar now turns to the rest of his ‘surround’. In this opening couplet பற்று means wealth or support, so பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் is ‘even when all holdings are gone’; the concessive உம் implies that such a man is normally no longer honoured by anyone. Parimelazhagar reads பழைமை as the kindnesses the man once did for them in his days of plenty, and the emphatic ஏ in கண்ணே stresses that kin alone keep faith, since others cut ties the moment the wealth is gone. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi all agree on the sense, and Karunanidhi turns it into a definition: those who show this loyalty are the true kin. Editions differ only in sandhi (உள / யுள) at the end of the second line.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama is stripped of his throne and sent into exile, his brother Bharata refuses the crown he has been handed, follows Rama into the forest to beg him to return, and then rules only as a regent, placing Rama’s sandals on the throne.
hinduism.explanation: Bharata stays loyal to Rama at the very moment when Rama has lost every worldly advantage, and he treats their old bond as more important than the kingdom.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the kind of kin the Kural describes, who honour the old tie even when the man has nothing left.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Bharata’s visit to Chitrakuta and the sandals, sargas 100-115)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says that a brother shows his real worth when trouble comes.
christianity.tie_back: Kin prove themselves in adversity, which is exactly the Kural’s point.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Quraysh boycotted the Prophet’s clan and pushed them into the valley of Abu Talib for about three years, his uncle Abu Talib and the Banu Hashim, most of whom did not share his faith, kept protecting him out of kinship and went hungry alongside him.
islam.explanation: The clan stood by its kinsman when he had lost all outside support and was under economic siege.
islam.tie_back: This is kin keeping faith with one of their own when he has nothing, as in the Kural.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad), account of the boycott of Banu Hashim

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Ruth said: ‘Entreat me not to leave thee, and to return from following after thee; for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God;”
judaism.explanation: Naomi has lost her husband, her sons and her livelihood, yet her daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her.
judaism.tie_back: Ruth keeps the family bond alive when Naomi is widowed and has nothing, just as the Kural expects of true kin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “they do not forsake him in his troubles,”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the ways friends and associates repay a clansman who has treated them well; one is that they stand by him in misfortune.
buddhism.tie_back: Those who have been cherished do not abandon the man when trouble comes, which matches the Kural’s kin.

jainism.quote_or_event: “We were brothers once, kind to each other, loving each other, wishing well to each other.”
jainism.explanation: The universal monarch Brahmadatta meets the monk Kitra, his brother in five earlier births, and honours the old bond even though Kitra now owns nothing; Kitra in turn, 'for old friendship's sake', loves the king and counsels him.
jainism.tie_back: Like the kin in the Kural who keep the old bond with a man who has lost everything, the king does not let Kitra's poverty as a monk cancel their ancient tie.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.5 (see also 13.15) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone are my friends, who travel along with me; and in that place, where the accounts are called for, they appear standing with me.”
sikhism.explanation: In a Soohee hymn Guru Nanak defines a true friend (sajan) as one who stays at your side to the very end, even at the final reckoning when everything else has fallen away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says only kin keep faith with a man who has lost everything; Guru Nanak likewise measures a real bond by whether it still holds when nothing else remains.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Polyneices dies attacking Thebes and is refused burial as a traitor, his sister Antigone buries him anyway and accepts death rather than abandon her disgraced brother.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antigone honours her kinship with a brother the whole city has rejected.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Only his kin stand by him once he has lost everything, as the Kural observes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And in poverty and in other misfortunes men think friends are the only refuge.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that philia (the love of friends and family) matters most when fortune turns against us.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural gives this refuge specifically to kin, whose attachment outlasts a man’s wealth.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Napoleon's mother and sister join him in exile on Elba
real_life_example.event: After his first abdication in 1814, Napoleon was sent to the small island of Elba and landed at its capital, Portoferraio, on 4 May 1814. His mother, Letizia Bonaparte, and his sister Pauline came to join him there, his mother living in a house in Portoferraio, while his wife Marie-Louise and their young son, for whom rooms had been prepared, never came. In 1818 his mother wrote to the Allied powers asking for his release from his final exile on Saint Helena, but her letter went unanswered.
real_life_example.explanation: When the emperor had lost his throne and the court that once surrounded him, it was his mother and sister who crossed the sea to share his exile, and his mother kept pleading for him long after his final defeat.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even when a man has lost everything he owned, his kin alone keep honouring the old bond, and Letizia Bonaparte did exactly that for her fallen son.

tamil:
விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம் இயையின் அருப்பறா
ஆக்கம் பலவும் தரும்.
transliteration:
ViruppaRaach chutram iyaiyin aruppaRaa
Aakkam palavum tharum.
meaning: If a person has relatives whose love never fails, they will bring that person many kinds of good fortune that keep on growing.
elementary: Think of a garden where lots of people help water the plants. The plants keep growing new branches and flowers. A family that loves you all the time works like those helpers: with them around, good things keep sprouting in your life.
university: Parimelazhagar notes that விருப்பறா (‘whose affection never ceases’) is there to exclude kin who are secret enemies (உட்பகை), and that அருப்பறா qualifies ஆக்கம் to mean wealth that never stops putting out new shoots (அருப்பு, ‘sprouting’, which he glosses as கிளைத்தல், ‘branching’). This separates it from wealth that grows only by its owner’s own effort. He explains the conditional இயையின் (‘if one should obtain’) as a sign of how rare such kin are, and reads பலவும் (‘all the many’) as pointing to the six limbs of the state (army, subjects, treasury, ministers, allies and fortress), which keep growing because many hands tend them together. The couplet sets out the economic logic of the chapter: kin are the root of expanding prosperity. The text is stable, and the Tamil commentators agree on the meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Relatives, again, in consequence of mutual dependence and mutual aid, grow together, like lotus-stalks in a lake.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura warns Dhritarashtra that relatives who support one another flourish together.
hinduism.tie_back: Loving kin make prosperity grow together, which is the Kural’s அருப்பறா ஆக்கம், wealth that keeps sprouting.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 36 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher praises working together because it multiplies what each person gains and protects each of them.
christianity.tie_back: Bonds that never fail bring greater returns, as the Kural says loving kin bring wealth of many kinds.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever loves that he be granted more wealth and that his lease of life be prolonged then he should keep good relations with his Kith and kin.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ties silat al-rahim, keeping up the bonds of kinship, directly to more provision and a longer life.
islam.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own claim: loving kin bring ever-increasing prosperity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is For brethren to dwell together in unity!”
judaism.explanation: The psalm goes on to compare brothers living in harmony to fragrant oil and to the dew of Hermon, on which God commands blessing.
judaism.tie_back: Brothers united in affection bring down blessing, much as the Kural’s loving kin bring abundance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sammodamana Jataka, a flock of quails caught in a hunter’s net rises together at their leader’s signal, lifts the net and escapes. They thrive while they stay in harmony, but once they start quarrelling they are all caught.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta’s fable teaches that a kin group in harmony prospers and is safe, and that discord ruins it.
buddhism.tie_back: Kin whose love never fails keep the whole group flourishing, which is the Kural’s point.
buddhism.source: Sammodamana Jataka (Jataka No. 33), trans. E. B. Cowell et al.

jainism.quote_or_event: Samantabhadra counts vatsalya, loving and guileless affection toward one's fellow believers, among the eight limbs of right faith; the Jain community treats this mutual affection as what keeps the fellowship strong and flourishing.
jainism.explanation: Vatsalya is the Jain virtue of steady, sincere affection within the community of the faithful, and it is a required limb of samyak darshana.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises kin whose love never fails; vatsalya is the nearest Jain ideal of unfailing affection among one's own, though its circle is the faith community, not blood kin.
jainism.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara, verses on the eight limbs of right faith (vatsalya-anga) (tr. Champat Rai Jain)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You are my Relative, and You are my Brother. You are my Protector everywhere; why should I feel any fear or anxiety?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan addresses God as the kinsman and brother whose care never fails, and finds in that bond freedom from all fear.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural prizes kin whose love never fails; for Guru Arjan the one kinsman whose love truly never fails is God, and the gift is fearlessness rather than ever-growing wealth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 103, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Castor is killed, his brother Polydeuces (Pollux) begs Zeus to let him share his own immortality with him, and the twins end up alternating their days between Olympus and the underworld.
greek_mythology.explanation: A brother’s unfailing love wins the twins a lasting shared blessing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Love between kin that never fails brings lasting gain, as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch argues that nature made brothers the way it made pairs of hands, feet and eyes, so that they could help each other, and that a man who treats his brother as a partner doubles his strength in every undertaking.
philosophy.explanation: For Plutarch, a strong bond between brothers is a practical asset that makes each brother more capable.
philosophy.tie_back: Affectionate kin multiply one’s resources, as the Kural teaches.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, De Fraterno Amore (On Brotherly Love)

real_life_example.event_title: Mayer Amschel Rothschild's five sons build a banking house across Europe
real_life_example.place: Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples
real_life_example.event: Mayer Amschel Rothschild, a Frankfurt dealer and banker, had five sons, all of whom entered the family business. The eldest, Amschel, stayed in Frankfurt, while Nathan established himself in England and founded N M Rothschild in London in 1809, James set up in Paris, Salomon in Vienna and Carl in Naples, and the brothers kept in close touch and worked together on major government loans. In 1810 the father made the Frankfurt firm a partnership with his sons, and in 1822 the Austrian emperor ennobled all five brothers.
real_life_example.explanation: Historians describe the five linked houses as working in effect like a single multinational bank, a strength that no one brother could have built on his own.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says kin whose affection never fails bring prosperity that keeps putting out new shoots, and the Rothschild brothers' cooperation across five cities made their family business grow far beyond its Frankfurt beginnings.

tamil:
அளவளா வில்லாதான் வாழ்க்கை குளவளாக்
கோடின்றி நீர்நிறைந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Alavalaa villaadhaan vaazhkkai kulavalaak
Kotindri neernirain thatru.
meaning: A person who does not share their heart with their relatives is like a big pond with no banks: whatever water comes in just flows away.
elementary: Imagine pouring water into a pond with no edges. The water spreads out and disappears, and the pond never stays full. A person who keeps away from family is like that pond: good things come, but with no one around to help hold on to them, they slip away.
university: The key word அளவளாவு means intimate mingling, literally ‘measuring together’. Parimelazhagar explains that heart-union grows out of exchanging one’s own measure with another’s, so the word stands by metonymy for close intimacy with kin, and ‘with kin’ is supplied from the chapter heading. குளவளா is the broad expanse of a tank and கோடு is its bank. For Parimelazhagar வாழ்க்கை here stands for the wealth that sustains life, and his point is that without kin to ‘hold’ it, a man’s wealth drains outward just as water spills from a tank that has no banks. He groups kurals 522-524 as showing kin to be the cause (ஏது), the fortress (அரண்) and the fruit (பயன்) of wealth, and this couplet shows kin as the fortress. Some printed texts divide the first word as அளவளாவு இல்லாதான், and thirukkural.net prints it with a space as அளவளா வில்லாதான்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And the tree that stands singly, though gigantic and strong and deep-rooted, hath its trunk soon smashed and twisted by a mighty wind. Those trees, however, that grow in close compact are competent owing to mutual dependence to resist winds more violent still.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells the king that a man cut off from his relatives is as easy to destroy as a lone tree in a storm.
hinduism.tie_back: The isolated man in the Kural is the bankless tank, and in Vidura he is the lone tree; both are defenceless without kin.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 36 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is;”
christianity.explanation: The letter to the Hebrews warns believers not to drift away from the fellowship of the community.
christianity.tie_back: Drawing away from one’s own people is the very failure the Kural describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you - when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together and you became, by His favor, brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an calls on believers to hold together and warns against splitting apart, since joined hearts are a divine favour.
islam.tie_back: Hearts joined together, like the Kural’s அளவளாவு, are what hold a community’s strength in place.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hillel said: do not separate yourself from the community,”
judaism.explanation: Hillel’s maxim warns against cutting oneself off from the collective life of one’s people.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural pictures the man who stays apart from his kin as a tank with no banks, and Hillel names the same danger.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:4 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Rukkhadhamma Jataka, the Buddha tells his quarrelling Sakya and Koliya kinsmen about a forest where the trees stood close together and survived a great storm, while a tree growing alone in the open was uprooted. The lesson he draws is that kinsfolk should stay united.
buddhism.explanation: The story shows kin standing together as protection against disaster.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s tank without banks and the Jataka’s lone tree both picture a life without kin as unprotected.
buddhism.source: Rukkhadhamma Jataka (Jataka No. 74), trans. E. B. Cowell et al.

jainism.quote_or_event: “if he is angry even with friends; if he speaks evil even of a good friend behind his back”
jainism.explanation: In the list of the ill-behaved monk, Mahavira includes the man who turns on his own friends and maligns them; the same list ends with the one who 'does not share with others'.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's man who never mingles heart to heart with his kin lives like a tank without banks; the Jain list likewise marks as failed the man who cuts himself off from those closest to him.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the state reached in the company of the holy, in which the heart mixes freely with all and no one remains an outsider.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a life without heart-to-heart mingling with one's people is like a tank without banks; Guru Arjan's open fellowship with everyone is the very opposite of that isolation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the father and his quarrelling sons, the father asks each son to break a bundle of sticks, and none can. He then unties the bundle and shows how easily each stick snaps alone, teaching them that they are strong while united and easy to beat when divided.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable makes family unity the source of strength and separation the source of weakness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The single stick and the bankless tank both picture life without kin.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, The Father and His Sons (Perry Index 53)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for no one would choose the whole world on condition of being alone, since man is a political creature and one whose nature is to live with others.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that even the happiest man needs people to share his life with, because humans are social by nature.
philosophy.tie_back: A life without close ties is empty however much it holds, just as the Kural’s tank stays empty however much water pours in.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.9 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Inca civil war between Huascar and Atahualpa
real_life_example.event: After the Inca ruler Huayna Capac died in an epidemic without a clearly settled successor, his sons Huascar, based at Cuzco, and Atahualpa, based in the north at Quito, fought a long civil war for the throne. The war divided the Inca nobility and armies and was costly to both sides, and Atahualpa's generals finally captured Huascar in 1532. Only months later, in November 1532, a small Spanish force under Francisco Pizarro captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca, and the empire soon fell under Spanish rule.
real_life_example.explanation: Historians count the brothers' war, together with epidemic disease and Spanish weapons, among the reasons the largest empire in the Americas collapsed so quickly.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares a man who does not live heart to heart with his kin to a wide tank without banks, and the quarrel between royal brothers left the Inca realm unable to hold on to what it had built.

tamil:
சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப் படஒழுகல் செல்வந்தான்
பெற்றத்தால் பெற்ற பயன்.
transliteration:
Sutraththaal sutrap pataozhukal selvandhaan
Petraththaal petra payan.
