meaning: The real reward of becoming rich is living in a way that keeps your relatives gathered around you.
elementary: Suppose you have a big box of snacks. If you eat them alone, it’s just snacks. If you share them, your cousins come and sit around you, laughing and talking. That circle of family is the real prize, not the snacks.
university: The couplet repeats sounds on purpose (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட, பெற்றத்தால் பெற்ற) so that the verse itself seems to ‘surround’ its subject. Parimelazhagar glosses it as: the fruit a man gains from having gained wealth is to conduct himself, embracing his kin, so that he is encircled by them. He notes that in பெற்ற the final அ, and in அதனால் the particle அன், have dropped out for the sake of the rhyme. He explains that such conduct counts as the ‘fruit’ of wealth because it lets a king rule without enemies, and he treats it as the third term of the sequence cause–fortress–fruit (kurals 522-524). Pappaiah and Karunanidhi read it the same way. The gloss attributed to Mu. Varadarasan for this kural on thirukkural.net actually belongs to kural 468 and is evidently misplaced there.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The riches of the liberal never waste away, while he who will not give finds none to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn on liberality teaches that shared wealth lasts and wins companions, while hoarded wealth leaves its owner alone.
hinduism.tie_back: Wealth that gathers people round its owner is the Kural’s definition of what wealth is for.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.1 (trans. R. T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes providing for one’s own relatives a basic duty of faith.
christianity.tie_back: Resources are meant to sustain one’s kin, which the Kural calls the very fruit of wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “They ask you, [O Muhammad], what they should spend. Say, ‘Whatever you spend of good is [to be] for parents and relatives and orphans and the needy and the traveler.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an lists parents and relatives first among those on whom wealth should be spent.
islam.tie_back: Kin come first in the proper use of wealth, as the Kural says.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Torah commands that when a brother becomes poor and his hand fails, his kinsman must uphold him and let him live alongside him, lending without interest.
judaism.explanation: The law treats supporting an impoverished relative as a duty of those who have means.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too sees the proper use of wealth as keeping one’s kin close and supported.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “performs the five oblations: to relatives, guests, the dead, kings, & devas. This is the fourth benefit that can be obtained from wealth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika the benefits to be gained from wealth, and offerings to relatives are one of them.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts define the benefit of wealth partly by what it does for one’s kin.

jainism.quote_or_event: After the birth of Mahavira, King Siddhartha and Queen Trisala, whose silver, gold and riches had kept increasing from the time the child was conceived, invite their friends, relations, kinsmen, agnates and cognates, feed them, honour them with flowers, clothes, perfumes and ornaments, and before them name the boy Vardhamana, 'the increasing'.
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra shows a prosperous Jain royal household using its increase to gather and honour the whole circle of its kin.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the fruit of wealth is to be surrounded by one's kin; in the Kalpa Sutra the family's growing wealth is spent precisely on gathering and honouring the kindred.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §§ 104-107 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Every Sikh gurdwara has its langar, a communal refectory, where all who come sit together in one straight line, none placed ahead to claim higher status or behind to mark inferiority; the distinctive Sikh langar arose as a protest against caste.
sikhism.explanation: The community's resources are spent on a common kitchen that gathers everyone, kin and stranger alike, around a shared meal.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the real fruit of wealth is to live surrounded by one's people; the langar turns shared resources into a gathered community, though Sikhism widens that circle to everyone.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Sikhism: Sikh practice” by W. H. McLeod (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Telemachus reaches Pylos, he finds old King Nestor seated among his sons and people at a great sacrifice on the shore. His wealth is spent on feasting, and he is surrounded by a loyal household.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor is the Homeric picture of a prosperous old age: a rich king surrounded by devoted sons.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His wealth takes the form of kin gathered round him, the image the Kural holds up.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “even rich men and those in possession of office and of dominating power are thought to need friends most of all; for what is the use of such prosperity without the opportunity of beneficence, which is exercised chiefly and in its most laudable form towards friends?”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that prosperity is pointless without people on whom to use it for good.
philosophy.tie_back: The value of wealth lies in the people it gathers and serves, which is what the Kural teaches about kin.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Christian IX and Queen Louise gather their family at Fredensborg each summer
real_life_example.event: King Christian IX of Denmark and Queen Louise saw their children marry into many of Europe's royal houses: their daughters included Alexandra, later Queen of the United Kingdom, and Dagmar, Empress of Russia, and their son George became King George I of Greece. Every summer the couple, known as Europe's parents-in-law, gathered their children, their children's spouses and their many grandchildren at Fredensborg Palace. The painter Laurits Tuxen recorded these Fredensborg Days in a group portrait about five by seven metres, made in 1883-1886, which now hangs in Christiansborg Palace in Copenhagen.
real_life_example.explanation: The king of a small country found the true reward of his position in a family circle that stretched across the continent and returned to him year after year.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the real fruit of gaining wealth and standing is to live surrounded by one's kin, and Christian IX's summers at Fredensborg were exactly such a life.

tamil:
கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் அடுக்கிய
சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப் படும்.
transliteration:
Kotuththalum insolum aatrin atukkiya
Sutraththaal sutrap patum.
meaning: A person who gives freely and speaks kindly will be surrounded by relatives, circle after circle of them.
elementary: If you share your crayons and also say nice things to people, everyone wants to be near you. Then their brothers and sisters come too, and soon there’s a big happy circle around you. Sharing plus kind words is like a magnet for family.
university: Parimelazhagar notes that the verb ஆற்றின் (‘if one is able to accomplish’) stresses how hard it is to practise both virtues in due measure. He explains அடுக்கிய சுற்றம் as kin ‘stacked’ in succession: the kin of one’s kin, and then their kin, bound in a widening chain. He explicitly identifies the two means with the Sanskrit statecraft terms dāna (gift) and sāma (conciliation), the first two of the four upāyas, so this kural brings the Arthaśāstra toolkit into the domestic setting of kinship. Kurals 525-528, he says, set out the ‘means of embracing kin’. இன்சொல் (‘sweet speech’) links back to Chapter 10, இனியவை கூறல், and it anticipates the Buddhist saṅgahavatthu of giving and kind speech.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Straw (for a seat), ground (for sitting upon), water (to wash the feet and face), and, fourthly sweet words,--these are never wanting in the houses of the good.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura says that the houses of the good always have simple gifts for guests together with kind words.
hinduism.tie_back: Giving together with sweet speech is the Kural’s formula for drawing people close.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 36 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another; ... Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.”
christianity.explanation: Paul joins brotherly affection and courtesy with material generosity toward the community.
christianity.tie_back: Warmth together with giving is how the community holds together, much as the Kural says.

islam.quote_or_event: “and to parents do good and to relatives, orphans, and the needy. And speak to people good [words] and establish prayer and give zakah.”
islam.explanation: The covenant verse joins material kindness to relatives with the command to speak good words.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s pair of giving and kind speech in one sentence, with relatives named.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone who gives a peruta to a poor person receives six blessings, and whoever consoles him with words of comfort and encouragement receives eleven blessings.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yitzhak ranks kind, comforting words above even the coin that is given.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too joins the gift to the sweet word and treats both as essential.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 9b (William Davidson Edition)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are these four grounds for the bonds of fellowship. Which four? Generosity, kind words, beneficial help, consistency.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the saṅgahavatthu, the qualities that hold a family or community together, and the first two are giving and kind speech.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own formula: generosity and kind words bind kin around you.

jainism.quote_or_event: “if he does not share with others; if he is always unkind: then he is called ill-behaved.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira closes his list of the faults of the ill-behaved monk with two failures: not sharing and unkindness.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural names generosity and kind speech as what draws circle after circle of kin; the Jain text names their opposites, not sharing and unkindness, as the marks of the man who has failed.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak names sweetness and humility as the very core of every good quality.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says kin gather in circle after circle round one who gives freely and speaks kindly; Guru Nanak places that sweetness at the heart of virtue.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before the war with the Titans, Zeus frees the Hundred-Handers, who are children of Earth like the gods themselves, gives them nectar and ambrosia and speaks to them respectfully to ask for their help. Won over, they fight on his side and secure his victory.
greek_mythology.explanation: Zeus wins over powerful relatives by combining gifts with courteous words.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Giving together with kind speech gathers kin as allies, as the Kural says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca insists that the manner of giving matters as much as the gift: a benefit given readily, with a kind face and gracious words, binds the receiver, while one given grudgingly or with harsh words loses its value.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, generosity and courteous speech together are what make a gift create lasting goodwill.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too requires both the gift and the sweet word.

real_life_example.event_title: Moshoeshoe gathers scattered peoples into the Basotho nation
real_life_example.event: During the wars and migrations that convulsed Southern Africa in the early nineteenth century, the chief Moshoeshoe led his people to the nearly impregnable mountain stronghold of Thaba Bosiu. His following grew as other African peoples were drawn by the protection he could provide, and he had a reputation for generous treatment of allies and enemies alike. He united these groups of refugees into the Sotho (Basotho) nation, and he is regarded today as the father of Lesotho.
real_life_example.explanation: Moshoeshoe built a nation not from a single bloodline but by drawing ever more peoples into his circle through protection and generous dealing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who can both give freely and deal kindly will be surrounded by kin, circle upon circle, and Moshoeshoe's generosity turned scattered refugees into one people.

tamil:
பெருங்கொடையான் பேணான் வெகுளி அவனின்
மருங்குடையார் மாநிலத்து இல்.
transliteration:
Perungotaiyaan penaan vekuli avanin
Marungutaiyaar maanilaththu il.
meaning: No one on this wide earth has more relatives around them than a person who gives generously and does not hold on to anger.
elementary: Picture two kids. One shares a lot but gets angry and shouts all the time. The other shares and stays calm and kind. Everyone flocks to the second kid. Giving plus a calm heart brings the biggest family circle.
university: Parimelazhagar glosses பெருங்கொடை as ‘great liberality’ of a kind that never itself leads to want. He takes பேணான் வெகுளி (‘does not cherish anger’) to mean that the king does not indulge anger beyond measure, since he grants that a ruler may sometimes need to show it. மருங்கு (‘side’) here means kin (கிளை), so மருங்குடையார் are ‘those who have people at their side’. This kural adds a negative condition to the positive means of 525: generosity will not keep kin if it comes with an unpredictable temper, a point that looks ahead to Chapter 31 (வெகுளாமை) and to 306, where anger is said to burn the raft of one’s own people (இனம்). The text is stable, and all the main commentators agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O king, anger is a kind of bitter, pungent, acrid, and hot drink, painful in its consequences: ... Do thou, O king, swallow it up and obtain peace.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura urges Dhritarashtra to master his anger so that peace can be restored within the Kuru family.
hinduism.tie_back: Restraining anger keeps kin together, which is the second condition in the Kural.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 36 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another,”
christianity.explanation: Paul pairs putting away anger with active kindness toward others.
christianity.tie_back: Dropping anger and practising generous kindness is the combination the Kural says wins the widest circle of kin.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allah, [O Muhammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an credits the Prophet’s gentleness for keeping his followers around him, and says harshness would have scattered them.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says the same: a leader free of anger keeps his people close.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that a soft answer turns away wrath while a grievous word stirs up anger.
judaism.explanation: The proverb contrasts calm speech that defuses conflict with harsh words that inflame it.
judaism.tie_back: Setting anger aside keeps relationships whole, which is the Kural’s second condition.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that one should overcome the angry person by non-anger, the wicked by goodness, the miser by generosity and the liar by truth.
buddhism.explanation: The verse pairs non-anger and generosity as ways of winning people over.
buddhism.tie_back: Non-anger and liberality are exactly the two qualities the Kural names.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If he is frequently angry; if he perseveres in his wrath; if he spurns friendly advice”
jainism.explanation: These open the list of faults that make a monk ill-behaved, a list that also includes being angry even with friends and not sharing with others.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says no one has more people around him than the generous man who does not nurse anger; the Jain text condemns exactly the nursed anger ('perseveres in his wrath') and the refusal to share.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, tells the listener to repay wrong with good and never let anger settle in the mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says no one has more people at his side than the generous man who does not nurse anger; Farid joins the same two things, doing good and refusing to harbour anger.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phoenix tells Achilles the story of Meleager, who withdrew from battle in anger at his mother and refused the pleas and gifts of elders, priests, friends and even his own family, until his city was nearly lost.
greek_mythology.explanation: Meleager’s nursed anger cuts him off from his kin and nearly destroys his people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the reverse of the Kural: cherished anger drives kin away.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch’s dialogue on controlling anger argues that anger, more than any other passion, makes a man hateful to those around him and drives away household and friends, while mildness makes him loved and approachable.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch treats mastery of anger as the key to keeping one’s household and friends loyal.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too makes freedom from anger a condition for having kin around one.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, De Cohibenda Ira (On the Control of Anger)

real_life_example.event_title: Cyrus the Great lets deported peoples return home
real_life_example.event: After the Persian king Cyrus the Great captured Babylon in 539 BCE, a proclamation inscribed in his name on a clay cylinder recorded how he restored shrines and allowed deported peoples to return to their homes, reversing the policy of earlier Assyrian and Babylonian kings. It is thought to have been at this time that the Judaeans returned to Jerusalem to rebuild their Temple. About a century later the Greek historian Herodotus recorded that the Persians called Cyrus a father, because he was gentle and devised good things for them, while they called his son Cambyses a master.
real_life_example.explanation: Instead of keeping the peoples his predecessors had uprooted in captivity, Cyrus gave them back their homes and gods, and his own people remembered him as a father rather than a master.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says no one on earth has more people at his side than one who gives freely and does not nurse anger, and Cyrus won lasting loyalty through generosity rather than vengeance.

tamil:
காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும் ஆக்கமும்
அன்னநீ ரார்க்கே உள.
transliteration:
Kaakkai karavaa karaindhunnum aakkamum
Annanee raarkke ula.
meaning: A crow does not hide its food. It calls its family with a caw and eats with them. Good fortune comes only to people who are like that.
elementary: When a crow finds food, it doesn’t sneak off with it. It says ‘Caw! Caw!’ so its whole family comes to share. People who share like the crow end up with the most good things in life, because everyone sticks with them.
university: This is the best-known couplet of the chapter. Parimelazhagar explains that when crows find food they do not hide it (கரவா) but caw (கரைந்து) to summon their flock and eat together, and that the ‘prosperities’ (ஆக்கமும்) that come through kin belong only to those who have such a nature (அன்ன நீரார்). He lists those prosperities as freedom from enemies and great wealth. He reads the உம் in ஆக்கமும் as an ‘inclusive’ particle: such people gain not only virtue (அறம்) and pleasure (இன்பம்) but material wealth (பொருள்) as well. He defines the crow-like nature as arranging things so that kin enjoy everything one enjoys oneself. Some modern readers (e.g. Karunanidhi) take ஆக்கம் more broadly as ‘elevation’. The crow’s calling of its kin is proverbial in Tamil culture and is echoed in later didactic literature.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He feeds no trusty friend, no man to love him. All guilt is he who eats with no partaker.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn condemns the man who eats his food alone and shares it with no one.
hinduism.tie_back: The crow that calls others to its food is the opposite of the man who ‘eats with no partaker’.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.6 (trans. R. T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And all that believed were together, and had all things common; And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need.”
christianity.explanation: The first Jerusalem community pooled what it had and gave to each as they needed.
christianity.tie_back: Nothing is hidden and everything is shared, as with the Kural’s crow.

islam.quote_or_event: “They love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what the emigrants were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful.”
islam.explanation: The Ansar of Medina shared their homes and goods with the migrants, and the Qur’an promises success to those saved from stinginess.
islam.tie_back: Open-handed sharing leads to success, which echoes the Kural’s ‘prosperity belongs to such people’.

judaism.quote_or_event: Isaiah describes the fast God desires as sharing one’s bread with the hungry, bringing the homeless poor into one’s house, clothing the naked, and not hiding oneself from one’s own flesh, that is, one’s kin.
judaism.explanation: The prophet treats open sharing with the needy, and never turning away from one’s own kin, as true piety, and promises that light and healing will follow.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Hide not thyself from thine own flesh’ is very close to the Kural’s கரவா, not hiding one’s food from one’s kin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If beings knew, as I know, the results of giving & sharing, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of selfishness overcome their minds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that anyone who understood the fruit of sharing would never eat without first sharing.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the crow’s rule: never eat without first calling others to share.

jainism.quote_or_event: At the naming feast of the infant Mahavira, his parents sit down in the dining hall together with their friends, relations, kinsmen, agnates, cognates and followers, and they partook, ate, tasted, and interchanged (bits) of a large collation of food, drink, spices, and sweetmeats.
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra describes the royal family not keeping its good fortune to itself but calling all its kin to eat and share at one table.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's crow caws to call its kin and eats with them; the Jain royal house likewise calls its whole kindred to share its food in celebration.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira § 104 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: This salok is a scriptural root of kirat karni and vand chhakna: earn by honest work and share what you earn.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the crow that does not hide its food but calls its kin to eat with it; Guru Nanak likewise makes sharing what one has the mark of the right path.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod advises the farmer to invite his friend to his feast, and above all whoever lives near him, because neighbours come running when trouble strikes while more distant kinsmen are slow to arrive.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod treats sharing one’s table with those around one as a practical way of building a circle that will help in need.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the crow, one calls others to share and so builds up support, though Hesiod ranks neighbours above distant kin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For this cause it would seem that we ought to summon our friends readily to share our good fortunes (for the beneficent character is a noble one),”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle advises calling friends in readily to share one’s good fortune.
philosophy.tie_back: Calling others in to share one’s good fortune is exactly what the Kural’s crow does.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.11 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Fan Zhongyan founds the Fan clan charitable estate
real_life_example.event: Fan Zhongyan, a Song-dynasty scholar-official from Suzhou who had been orphaned of his father in infancy, used his own funds late in his career to buy farmland near his home town and set it up as a charitable estate for his clan. Rents from the land supplied grain to members of the Fan lineage and helped them meet the costs of weddings, funerals and schooling. The estate continued for centuries and became a model for later lineage trusts in China.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than keep the fruits of his success for his own household, Fan arranged for the whole clan to share in them, and his example shaped Chinese kinship institutions for generations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the crow that does not hide its food but calls its kin to share it, and Fan Zhongyan's estate turned his own prosperity into a meal for the whole clan.

tamil:
பொதுநோக்கான் வேந்தன் வரிசையா நோக்கின்
அதுநோக்கி வாழ்வார் பலர்.
transliteration:
Podhunokkaan vendhan varisaiyaa nokkin
Adhunokki vaazhvaar palar.
meaning: If a king does not treat everyone the same but gives each person the respect their worth deserves, many people will stay close to him because of it.
elementary: A good coach doesn’t give every player the same job. The fastest runner plays forward, and the one with the best hands becomes goalkeeper. When each person feels truly seen for what they’re good at, they all want to stay on the team.
university: The couplet contrasts பொது நோக்கு (‘common or uniform regard’) with வரிசை நோக்கு (‘regard according to rank or order’). Parimelazhagar reads வரிசை as each person’s own worth (தத்தம் தகுதி). He explains that uniform treatment is rejected because it drives away the superior, who feel slighted, while graded regard is prescribed because it keeps everyone loyal. This makes it a principle of proportional, not arithmetic, equality, very like Aristotle’s distributive justice. With this kural Parimelazhagar closes the four-verse unit (525-528) on the ‘means of embracing kin’. Karunanidhi’s modern gloss softens the hierarchy (‘all people are equal, but use each according to ability’), and Pappaiah places the kural explicitly within the ruler’s treatment of his kin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Laws of Manu list wealth, kindred, age, the performance of sacred rites and sacred learning as grounds for respect, each later one weighing more, so that honour is to be given by graded merit rather than uniformly.
hinduism.explanation: Manu sets out a scale for how much respect each person should receive.
hinduism.tie_back: This is graded regard (வரிசை நோக்கு) rather than uniform treatment (பொது நோக்கு), as the Kural prescribes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability;”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, the master entrusts each servant with a share matched to his ability.
christianity.tie_back: Treating each person according to capacity rather than uniformly is the Kural’s principle.

islam.quote_or_event: “And it is He who has made you successors upon the earth and has raised some of you above others in degrees [of rank] that He may try you through what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an treats differences of rank among people as part of the divine order and a test.
islam.tie_back: People are not all placed alike, so treating them according to rank reflects that order, as in the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: At the end of his life Jacob gathers his twelve sons and blesses each one differently, according to his character and deeds; the text notes that he blessed every one according to his own blessing.
judaism.explanation: The patriarch does not bless his sons all alike but fits each blessing to the son.
judaism.tie_back: Individual rather than uniform regard among kin is exactly the Kural’s வரிசை நோக்கு.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Generosity, sweet speech, Helpfulness to others, Impartiality to all, As the case demands.”
buddhism.explanation: The closing verse of the Sigalovada lists the four ‘winning ways’ and qualifies them as applied ‘as the case demands’.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘As the case demands’ calls for the fitting treatment of each person that the Kural recommends.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra teaches four right attitudes rather than one uniform one: friendliness toward all living beings, joy at the sight of the more virtuous, compassion for the afflicted, and equanimity or tolerance toward the insolent and ill-behaved.
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics asks a person to adjust his inner regard to the condition and merit of each being he meets.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural advises regarding each person according to his worth instead of treating all alike; the Tattvartha's four attitudes likewise grade one's regard by the other's virtue and situation.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.11 (Digambara numbering; English rendering at Jain Square)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Nanak passed over his own two sons and appointed his devoted disciple Lahina, renamed Angad, as his successor, because Lahina's conduct persuaded him that he was the more suitable choice.
sikhism.explanation: Nanak judged by proven worth rather than by family claim when choosing who would lead the community.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the ruler to give each person the regard their merit deserves rather than the same to all; Guru Nanak's choice of a successor by merit rather than birth is a Sikh instance of weighing people by worth.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Sikhism: Guru Angad” by W. H. McLeod (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After defeating the Titans, the gods urge Zeus to rule, and he divides the privileges (timai) among them, giving each god a fitting share of honour, which secures their loyalty to his reign.
greek_mythology.explanation: Zeus keeps his divine kin loyal by giving each a distinct and appropriate honour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is graded regard keeping the circle together, as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “To kinsmen, too, and fellow-tribesmen and fellow-citizens and to every other class one should always try to assign what is appropriate, and to compare the claims of each class with respect to nearness of relation and to virtue or usefulness.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that we owe different things to different people and must weigh each person’s closeness and merit.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s வரிசை நோக்கு, regard given to kin according to their worth.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.2 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Peter the Great issues the Table of Ranks
real_life_example.event: Peter the Great's Table of Ranks arranged Russia's military, naval and civil services into a hierarchy of fourteen grades and based promotion on personal ability and performance rather than on birth and family descent. Anyone who reached the eighth rank gained the status of a hereditary noble, which caused resentment among parts of the old aristocracy that lost its exclusive claim to high office. With minor changes, the system remained in use until 1917.
real_life_example.explanation: By ranking servants of the state according to service and merit, Peter tied capable people of many backgrounds to the throne while keeping a clear order of precedence.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a king who gives each person the regard their merit deserves, rather than treating everyone the same, will have many staying by him, and the Table of Ranks wrote merit-based, graded regard into law.

tamil:
தமராகித் தற்றுறந்தார் சுற்றம் அமராமைக்
காரணம் இன்றி வரும்.
transliteration:
Thamaraakith thatrurandhaar sutram amaraamaik
Kaaranam indri varum.
meaning: Relatives who were once close but left because of some hurt will come back on their own once the cause of the fight is gone.
elementary: Suppose your cousin stopped coming over because you kept teasing him. If you stop teasing, he’ll start coming back all by himself. When you fix the reason someone left, the friendship often heals itself.
university: Parimelazhagar construes the couplet as: when those who were once one’s own (தமர்) have left because of some cause, their becoming kin again ‘comes’ (வரும்) of itself once that cause of discord (அமராமைக் காரணம்) no longer exists in oneself. He infers from the phrase that the cause really did exist before, and names it as the king’s own conduct, such as straying from the right path or doing things that displease. Because the kin were naturally affectionate and the estrangement was artificial, it ends when its cause ends; the ruler need not court them again, since they ‘return’ to their old nature. Pappaiah reads the kural in modern political terms, as members returning to a movement once the leader’s fault is gone. Karunanidhi reads it differently: those who left on some pretext come back once they see the pretext does not hold. Thirukkural.net prints தமராகிக் in the first word, but Parimelazhagar’s text on Wikisource and the standard editions read தமராகித், which is the reading adopted here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let, therefore, thy sons cherish the Pandavas, and the Pandavas also cherish thy sons. O king, let the Kurus and the Pandavas, both having same friends and same foes, live together in happiness and prosperity.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura urges Dhritarashtra to remove the cause of the family rift, his sons’ injustice, so that the estranged cousins can be reunited.
hinduism.tie_back: Remove the cause of the estrangement and the kin come back, as the Kural says.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 36 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.”
christianity.explanation: The estranged son returns home and is welcomed without conditions.
christianity.tie_back: A kinsman who has left comes back and the old bond resumes at once, as the Kural predicts.

islam.quote_or_event: “Al-Wasil is not the one who recompenses the good done to him by his relatives, but Al-Wasil is the one who keeps good relations with those relatives who had severed the bond of kinship with him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet defines the true maintainer of kinship as the one who restores ties with relatives who have broken them off.
islam.tie_back: Keeping the way open for estranged kin to return is the spirit of the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: Twenty years after Jacob fled Esau’s anger over the stolen blessing, the brothers meet again, and Esau runs to meet Jacob, embraces him, falls on his neck and kisses him, and they weep together.
judaism.explanation: Once the old grievance has faded, the estranged brother comes back and the kinship bond is restored.
judaism.tie_back: When the cause of estrangement is gone, kin return, as the Kural says.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the Sakyas and Koliyas, kin connected by marriage, are about to go to war over the waters of the Rohini river, the Buddha removes the cause of the quarrel by asking whether water is worth more than the lives of princes. The kinsmen are reconciled.
buddhism.explanation: Once the cause of the dispute is set aside, the two kin clans return to peace.
buddhism.tie_back: Remove the cause and estranged kin come back together, as the Kural says.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verses 197-199; Kunala Jataka (Jataka No. 536), introduction

jainism.quote_or_event: The brothers Bharata and Bahubali, sons of Rishabhanatha, fall out when Bharata demands his brother's submission and they fight; Bahubali renounces the world, but his omniscience comes only once he lets go of the pride that kept him from bowing to his brothers, and Bharata comes to honour him.
jainism.explanation: In the Jain account the rift between brothers is mended once its cause, pride and possessiveness, has gone.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says kin who left over a grievance return of themselves once the cause of the rift is removed; the Bharata-Bahubali story shows estranged brothers reconciled once the pride between them has gone.
jainism.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra of Hemachandra, Book 1 (Bharata and Bahubali episode) (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS)

sikhism.quote_or_event: During the siege of Anandpur forty Sikhs signed a disclaimer (bedava) renouncing Guru Gobind Singh and went home; shamed by Mai Bhag Kaur (Mai Bhago), they returned to fight beside him at Khidrana in 1705, and the Guru, finding their dying leader Maha Singh, forgave them and tore up the disclaimer. The place was renamed Muktsar, the Pool of Liberation.
sikhism.explanation: Those who had broken away came back of their own accord, and the Guru received them as his own again.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says kin who left over some grievance return by themselves once the cause of the rift is gone; the Forty Liberated Ones returned and were fully restored to their Guru.
sikhism.source: Wikipedia, “Battle of Muktsar” (Forty Liberated Ones), paraphrase of traditional accounts

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles withdraws from the Greek army because Agamemnon has insulted him by taking his prize Briseis. Once Agamemnon admits his fault and the grievance is set right in Book 19, Achilles returns to the fight.
greek_mythology.explanation: An estranged comrade returns once the leader’s wrong that caused his withdrawal has been removed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Remove the leader’s own fault and those who left come back, which is Parimelazhagar’s reading of the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “so to those who have been our friends we ought to make some allowance for our former friendship, when the breach has not been due to excess of wickedness.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that a former bond still has a claim on us after a rift, provided the rift did not come from real wickedness.
philosophy.tie_back: An old bond whose rift has a removable cause can be restored, which is the Kural’s point.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Hungary is reconciled with the Habsburg crown in the Compromise of 1867
real_life_example.event: After the Hungarian revolution of 1848-49 was put down, Hungary was ruled directly from Vienna, and many Hungarians answered with stubborn passive resistance, boycotting the imperial parliament set up in 1861. Led by the moderate Ferenc Deak, who insisted on Hungary's constitutional rights, Hungary negotiated the Compromise (Ausgleich) concluded on 8 February 1867, under which Emperor Franz Joseph gave Hungary full internal self-government with its own responsible ministry, while Hungary accepted that the empire remain a single state for war and foreign affairs. On 8 June 1867 Franz Joseph was crowned King of Hungary in Buda.
real_life_example.explanation: Once the grievance that had driven Hungary away, rule without its constitution, was removed, the estranged kingdom returned to its allegiance to the dynasty.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who left because of a grievance come back of their own accord once its cause is gone, and Hungary returned to its crowned king when its constitution was restored.

tamil:
உழைப்பிரிந்து காரணத்தின் வந்தானை வேந்தன்
இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Uzhaippirindhu kaaranaththin vandhaanai vendhan
Izhaiththirundhu ennik kolal.
meaning: When a relative who left the king for no reason comes back wanting something, the king should give what they need, but wait and judge them carefully before taking them back.
elementary: Imagine a teammate who quit for no reason and now wants to rejoin because he needs something. The captain can help him, but should watch how he behaves for a while before trusting him fully again. Welcome back, but with open eyes.
university: Parimelazhagar takes the bare உழைப் பிரிந்து (‘having left one’s side’) to imply that there was no reason for leaving, and காரணத்தின் வந்தானை as ‘one who came back because of some purpose’. He explains இழைத்திருந்து as ‘having done or supplied that purpose’: if the king does not meet the motive that brought the man back, he may leave again and join the enemy. He explains எண்ணிக் கொளல் as ‘accept him after examination’, because the man left without love and came back out of interest. Taken together with 529, Parimelazhagar sees two cases: the kinsman whom the king’s own fault drove away should be allowed to return freely, while the one who left without cause should be taken back only after scrutiny. Varadarasan similarly says the king should grant the help sought and then examine before re-admitting him, while Pappaiah reads இழைத்திருந்து as ‘waiting patiently’. Karunanidhi instead describes the man as one who left on a pretext and returned for a genuine reason.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Ravana’s brother Vibhishana deserts Lanka and comes to Rama asking for refuge, Rama first holds a council: Sugriva and others suspect a spy, and Hanuman argues from Vibhishana’s conduct and motive that he is sincere. Only after weighing their views does Rama accept him.
hinduism.explanation: Rama hears Vibhishana’s reasons, has him assessed and then takes him in, even promising him Lanka’s throne.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama both meets the man’s purpose and examines him before accepting, which is the Kural’s இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.”
christianity.explanation: Paul had refused to take John Mark on his second journey because Mark had earlier left the mission (Acts 15:37-39); years later, having seen him proven, Paul asks for him again.
christianity.tie_back: Someone who once left is taken back only after a period of testing, as the Kural advises.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘No blame will there be upon you today. Allah will forgive you; and He is the most merciful of the merciful.’”
islam.explanation: Yusuf forgives the brothers who betrayed him, but only after testing them over several visits, including the planted cup, until he sees they have changed.
islam.tie_back: Taking back estranged kin after examining them is the Kural’s method.

judaism.quote_or_event: When the brothers who sold Joseph arrive in Egypt needing grain, Joseph does not reveal himself at once. He tests them, holding Simeon and demanding that Benjamin be brought, and reveals himself and welcomes them only after Judah offers himself in Benjamin’s place.
judaism.explanation: The kin come back out of need, and Joseph examines them before restoring the bond.
judaism.tie_back: They come ‘for a reason’, their need is met with grain, and they are examined before being accepted, which is exactly what the Kural prescribes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The monastic code requires someone who formerly followed another sect and now asks to join the Sangha to live under a four-month probation (titthiya-parivāsa) so that his conduct and sincerity can be observed before he receives full ordination.
buddhism.explanation: The Sangha admits newcomers from rival groups only after a period of examination.
buddhism.tie_back: Accept the one who comes, but only after weighing him, as the Kural advises.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain monastic discipline includes upasthapana, or re-initiation: a monk who has seriously lapsed, or who comes back after leaving, is not simply restored but must undergo expiation and be ordained again.
jainism.explanation: The Tattvartha Sutra lists re-initiation among the kinds of expiation (prayascitta) by which the community deals with a monk who has broken with it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural advises the king to meet the returning kinsman's need but weigh him before taking him back; Jain discipline likewise readmits the returner only after a deliberate process.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.22 (kinds of expiation, including upasthapana) (various translations)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “But one who feels good only when good is done for him, and feels bad when things go badly - do not call him a lover. He trades only for his own account.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad distinguishes true love from a bond kept by calculation, in which a person stays only while things go his way.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the ruler to meet the need of the kinsman who left without cause and came back for his own purpose, and then to weigh him carefully; Guru Angad names exactly that kind of attachment: love that trades on its own account.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus returns after twenty years, Penelope does not take him back at once. She tests him with the secret of their bed, carved from a living olive tree, and embraces him only when he answers correctly.
greek_mythology.explanation: The one who has come back is carefully examined before being fully accepted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s எண்ணிக் கொளல, accepting only after deliberation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Cicero’s dialogue On Friendship, Laelius advises that we should judge people before we give them our affection rather than love first and judge afterwards, and should test a character before trusting it.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero makes careful assessment come before full attachment.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s rule for the returning kinsman: examine first, then embrace.

real_life_example.event_title: Athens takes back Alcibiades
real_life_example.event: In 415 BCE the Athenian general Alcibiades, recalled from the expedition to Sicily to face charges of sacrilege, fled to Sparta, Athens's enemy, and advised the Spartans; he later went over to the Persian governor Tissaphernes. After leading the Athenian fleet to victories in the Hellespont, he returned to Athens in triumph in 407 BCE, the old charges were dropped, and he was given supreme command above all other generals. When a subordinate he had left in charge of the fleet lost a battle to the Spartans at Notium in 406 BCE, Alcibiades was not re-elected general and withdrew to Thrace.
real_life_example.explanation: Athens restored a former defector to the highest command almost at once, without lasting trust on either side, and the arrangement collapsed within about a year.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises a ruler to meet the needs of a kinsman who left and came back for his own purposes, but to weigh him carefully before taking him back, and Athens's haste with Alcibiades shows what happens when that weighing is skipped.

tamil:
இறந்த வெகுளியின் தீதே சிறந்த
உவகை மகிழ்ச்சியிற் சோர்வு.
transliteration:
Irandha vekuliyin theedhe sirandha
Uvakai makizhchchiyir sorvu.
meaning: Becoming careless because you are carried away by great joy does more harm than even anger that has gone out of control.
elementary: Imagine a team that is winning a game by a lot. The players start celebrating early, stop paying attention, and the other team sneaks back and wins. Getting too excited and careless can hurt you even more than losing your temper, because you don't even notice the danger coming.
university: The chapter title பொச்சாவாமை is the negative verbal noun of பொச்சா- (‘to forget, to be negligent’; compare பொச்சாப்பு, ‘forgetfulness, heedlessness’). So it names a positive discipline of not forgetting, and because it sits in the Arasiyal (royal conduct) section, Parimelazhagar reads the whole chapter as advice to a king. In this couplet சோர்வு is the lapse or slackening born of சிறந்த உவகை மகிழ்ச்சி, ‘the delight of surpassing joy’, and இறந்த வெகுளி is anger that has gone past all bounds. Parimelazhagar says that such joy comes from great wealth, great pleasure and great pride. He explains the comparison this way: measured anger is needed to crush enemies and punish the wicked, and even excessive anger may sometimes kill a foe, but forgetfulness born of joy kills only the person who has it, so it is the worse evil. Manakkudavar agrees on the sense but records another way to read the phrase, as the joy one directs towards those one must favour. Pavanar follows Parimelazhagar. The emphatic ஏ in தீதே underlines the surprising verdict that the pleasant fault is worse than the violent one.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He whom neither anger nor joy, nor pride, nor false modesty, nor stupefaction, nor vanity, can draw away from the high ends of life, is considered as wise.”
hinduism.explanation: The anxious king Dhritarashtra cannot sleep, and Vidura counsels him through the night. Vidura says a wise man is someone who is pulled away from his true aims neither by the heat of anger nor by the glow of joy.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural pairs the same two forces, anger and joy, and warns that joy is the more treacherous distraction.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that indulgence and worldly absorption dull the heart, so that the decisive moment arrives while one is unprepared.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats being overfull with pleasure as the thing that makes a person careless.

islam.quote_or_event: “And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing the enemy by His permission until [the time] when you lost courage and fell to disputing about the order [given by the Prophet] and disobeyed after He had shown you that which you love.”
islam.explanation: At Uhud the Muslim archers had been told never to leave their hill. When victory and its spoils seemed certain they left their post, and the enemy cavalry turned the battle against them.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's danger exactly: slackness born of the joy of apparent success, which turns victory into defeat.
islam.source: Qur'an 3:152 (Saheeh International), with the Uhud narrative in the sira literature

judaism.quote_or_event: “lest when thou hast eaten and art satisfied, and hast built goodly houses, and dwelt therein; and when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, and thy silver and thy gold is multiplied, and all that thou hast is multiplied; then thy heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God”
judaism.explanation: Moses warns Israel that prosperity in the promised land will be the moment of greatest danger, because abundance swells the heart and breeds forgetting.
judaism.tie_back: The Torah and the Kural both name forgetfulness born of prosperity and joy as the special peril of the successful.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not give way to heedlessness. Do not indulge in sensual pleasures. Only the heedful and meditative attain great happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha links heedlessness (pamāda) directly to indulgence in pleasure and sets heedfulness against both.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural too finds the root of carelessness in pleasure and delight.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though one believe in the Law, he will rarely practise it; for people are engrossed by pleasures; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira warns Gautama that even those who hold the true teaching fail to act on it because pleasure absorbs them, and the refrain he repeats is 'be careful all the while'.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says carelessness born of great joy does more harm than anger; Mahavira likewise names absorption in pleasure as what makes people neglect what they know.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Forgetting his Lord and Master, the mortal enjoys sensual pleasures; then, disease rises up in his body.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Malaar Guru Nanak traces suffering back to pleasure pursued in forgetfulness of God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the lapse that comes from excessive delight does more harm than unbounded anger; Guru Nanak shows the same sequence, indulgence breeding forgetfulness and forgetfulness breeding harm.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1256, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theseus kills the Minotaur and sails home from Crete. He and his pilot are so overjoyed at their success that they forget to raise the white sail that was meant to signal his safety. His father Aegeus sees the black sail from the cliffs, believes his son is dead, and throws himself to his death.
greek_mythology.explanation: The triumph was complete, but a single lapse caused by the joy of victory turned it into tragedy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's forgetfulness born of great joy, and its cost was worse than any enemy's anger.
greek_mythology.source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 22; also Catullus 64

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the offences which are committed through desire are more blameable than those which are committed through anger”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius approves Theophrastus's view that a fault committed under pleasure is worse than one committed in anger, because anger at least turns from reason with pain, while pleasure carries a person along willingly.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the same counter-intuitive ranking, placing the pleasant failing above the violent one.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 2.10 (trans. George Long), reporting Theophrastus

real_life_example.event_title: The Wall Street boom ends in the Crash of 1929
real_life_example.event: During the prosperous 1920s, share prices on the New York Stock Exchange rose to unprecedented heights, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average increasing about six-fold between 1921 and September 1929, and millions of ordinary people bought stocks, many with borrowed money while putting down only about a tenth of the price. In mid-October 1929 the prominent economist Irving Fisher said that stock prices appeared to have reached a permanently high plateau. Days later the market fell nearly 13 percent on 28 October and nearly 12 percent on 29 October, and by mid-November the Dow had lost almost half its value, a collapse that contributed to the Great Depression.
real_life_example.explanation: The long boom bred an optimism so complete that borrowing replaced caution and warnings were brushed aside, and the fall was all the harder for it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that the carelessness born of great joy does more harm than even boundless anger, and the euphoria of the late 1920s led millions to drop their guard just before the crash.

tamil:
பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை அறிவினை
நிச்ச நிரப்புக்கொன் றாங்கு.
transliteration:
Pochchaappuk kollum pukazhai arivinai
Nichcha nirappuk kon raangu.
meaning: Just as being poor day after day slowly destroys a person’s mind, being careless and forgetful destroys a person’s good name.
elementary: If a child is hungry every single day, it is very hard for them to think clearly at school. In the same way, if someone keeps forgetting their promises and jobs, people slowly stop trusting and admiring them, until their good name is gone.
university: The verb கொல்லும் (‘kills’) does strong work in both halves: பொச்சாப்பு kills புகழ் (fame) just as நிச்ச நிரப்பு kills அறிவு (understanding). Parimelazhagar glosses நிச்ச நிரப்பு as filling one's belly every day by begging. When this happens to a learned man, the humiliation and sin involved bring contempt on him and destroy the regard he enjoyed. In the same way, forgetfulness in a man of fame brings contempt, because he fails to guard himself and his affairs fall apart, and so it destroys his standing. Pavanar notes that நிரப்பு (literally ‘fullness’) is an auspicious euphemism for poverty, and he cross-refers to Kural 1046, where even the sound words of the poor go unheeded. Manakkudavar reads this couplet as part of a set on holding firm in worldly affairs. Parimelazhagar groups 531-532 as the couplets that state the fault of heedlessness. Editions split the final words either as நிரப்புக்கொன் றாங்கு or as நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு; the sense is the same.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Anger leads to clouding of judgment, which results in bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, the intellect gets destroyed; and when the intellect is destroyed, one is ruined.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces the downward chain in which the loss of smṛti (memory, mindfulness) destroys discernment and finally the person.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita treats a failure of remembering as something that kills, not merely inconveniences.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead. Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die”
christianity.explanation: The church at Sardis still has a reputation for life, but through lack of watchfulness it has become spiritually dead, and it is told to wake up before what remains dies too.
christianity.tie_back: This is a good name emptied out by heedlessness, which is exactly the loss the Kural describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “And be not like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves. Those are the defiantly disobedient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents forgetting God as self-destroying: the forgetful end up losing even their own selves and their true standing.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, forgetfulness is not a small slip but something that eats away what a person is worth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “whoever forgets one word of his study, scripture accounts it to him as if he were mortally guilty”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Meir, basing himself on Deuteronomy 4:9, treats the careless forgetting of what one has learned as a matter of life and death, though he excuses forgetting that happens despite real effort.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats forgetfulness as something that can kill.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:8, trans. Joshua Kulp

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ties a person's glory (yasa) directly to heedfulness and mindfulness.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the positive side of the Kural: heedfulness makes glory grow, and heedlessness kills it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “There are five causes which render wholesome discipline impossible: egoism, delusion, carelessness, illness, and idleness”
jainism.explanation: Carelessness (pramada) is named among the forces that destroy a monk's discipline.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says forgetfulness kills a man's fame as poverty kills his intellect; the Jain text says carelessness kills the discipline on which a monk's worth rests.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, they do not forget the Naam from the mind; they are honored in the Court of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das ties true honour to never letting the Name slip from the mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says forgetfulness kills a man's good name; Guru Amar Das states the converse, that unbroken remembrance is what wins honour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Elpenor, the youngest of Odysseus's crew, is heavy with wine and falls asleep on Circe's roof. Woken by the noise of departure, he forgets to use the ladder, falls, and breaks his neck. In the underworld he begs Odysseus for a burial mound so that men to come will know of him.
greek_mythology.explanation: One moment of forgetfulness costs Elpenor his life and nearly his memory among men, which he has to plead for.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's point is that heedlessness kills a person's name, and Elpenor's fate shows it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca opens his letters to Lucilius by observing that some of our time is snatched away and some slips from us, but that the most disgraceful loss of all is the one caused by our own carelessness.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca the losses we cause through negligence are worse than those forced on us, because they were within our power to prevent.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says heedlessness steadily wastes something precious, in this case a good name.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 1 (trans. R. M. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Fred Merkle's base-running lapse
real_life_example.place: Polo Grounds, New York City, United States
real_life_example.event: In a game tied 1-1 between the New York Giants and the Chicago Cubs, the Giants appeared to score the winning run in the bottom of the ninth inning on a single by Al Bridwell. Fred Merkle, the 19-year-old runner on first base, headed off the field without touching second base as fans poured onto the field, the Cubs' Johnny Evers claimed a force-out at second, and the umpire ruled Merkle out, so the game ended in a tie. The two teams finished the season level, the Cubs won the replayed game and the National League pennant, and Merkle, though he went on to play in five World Series, was mocked for years with nicknames such as Bonehead.
real_life_example.explanation: One moment of inattention by a capable player became the thing he was remembered for, overshadowing the rest of a long career.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says forgetfulness kills a person's good name, and one forgotten step to second base shaped Fred Merkle's reputation for the rest of his life.

tamil:
பொச்சாப்பார்க் கில்லை புகழ்மை அதுஉலகத்து
எப்பால்நூ லோர்க்கும் துணிவு.
transliteration:
Pochchaappaark killai pukazhmai adhuulakaththu
Eppaalnoo lorkkum thunivu.
meaning: People who are careless and forgetful never become famous. The writers of every kind of book in the world agree on this.
elementary: Ask a coach, a music teacher, a doctor, or a chef, and they will all tell you the same thing: people who keep forgetting and not paying attention never become great at anything. When everyone agrees on something, it's worth listening!
university: புகழ்மை means ‘the state of having fame’, and துணிவு here means a settled conclusion, not courage. Parimelazhagar takes எப்பால் நூலோர் to mean the authors of treatises of every kind, not only of polity (நீதி நூல்). He explains that the rule holds for everyone, not only kings: anyone pursuing any of the four aims of life (aṟam, poruḷ, iṉpam, vīṭu) will fail if heedless, and so will have no fame. Pavanar agrees that the rule is universal but argues that உலகம் here means the Tamil world and that எப்பால் நூல் refers to the branches of Tamil learning, much of which has since been lost; he points out that Valluvar does not say the northern (Sanskrit) texts agree. Manakkudavar reads the couplet simply as saying that heedlessness brings no fame. Parimelazhagar groups 533-535 as describing the harm (ஏதம்) that comes to the heedless.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The six faults should be avoided by a person who wisheth to attain prosperity, viz., sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, indolence and procrastination.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura's statecraft maxims, in the nīti tradition, list the forms of inattention (sleep, drowsiness, idleness, delay) among the faults that rule out prosperity.
hinduism.tie_back: This confirms the Kural's claim that the treatise writers agree: the nīti texts too hold that the heedless cannot prosper.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping. And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus ends his discourse on the last things by extending the command to watch beyond his disciples to everyone.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it presents watchfulness as a rule that holds universally, not a counsel for a few.

islam.quote_or_event: “They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray. It is they who are the heedless.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an names the heedless (al-ghāfilūn) as the lowest of the low: people who have every faculty and use none.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it places heedlessness (ghaflah) beneath all honour.

judaism.quote_or_event: In Mesillat Yesharim, Moshe Chaim Luzzatto builds his ladder of spiritual ascent on the baraita of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair (Avodah Zarah 20b), which starts from watchfulness (zehirut). He makes watchfulness the first rung and argues that a person who goes through life without examining his ways is like someone walking blind along a riverbank.
judaism.explanation: Luzzatto draws together a classic rabbinic chain of virtues in which careful watchfulness is the foundation for every higher attainment.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's ‘all treatises agree’, the Jewish ethical tradition treats vigilance as the agreed starting point without which nothing worthy is achieved.
judaism.source: Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, Mesillat Yesharim, chs. 1-2 (on Zehirut); Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 20b

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By Heedfulness did Indra become the overlord of the gods. Heedfulness is ever praised, and heedlessness ever despised.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada states a universal verdict: heedfulness is always praised and heedlessness always despised, and it cites even Indra's rise as proof.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's ‘settled conclusion of all’: the heedless get no praise.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: This lecture repeats the single command 'be careful all the while' (do not be heedless, pamaya) at the end of nearly every verse, which makes heedfulness the constant burden of Mahavira's teaching.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says every school of thought agrees that the heedless win no lasting glory; in the Jain canon heedfulness is likewise the teaching the master repeats without exception.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, those who forget the Naam-what will happen when they go to the Court of the Lord?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak asks what standing the forgetful can possibly have at the final reckoning.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the heedless never win lasting fame; Guru Nanak agrees that those who forget have no standing where it finally counts.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 17, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Some of Odysseus's men eat the honey-sweet lotus and forget all thought of home. They want only to stay among the Lotus-eaters, and Odysseus has to drag them weeping back to the ships and tie them down.
greek_mythology.explanation: The lotus stands for any pleasure that wipes out memory of one's purpose. The men who ate it would have lost their homecoming (nostos), and with it any share in the hero's glory.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says the forgetful win no fame, and those who forget their homecoming vanish from the story.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pierre Hadot argued that prosoche, continuous attention to oneself and to the present moment, was the fundamental spiritual attitude of the Stoics, and that practices of vigilance were shared across the ancient schools of philosophy.
philosophy.explanation: Hadot's reading of ancient philosophy as a set of ‘spiritual exercises’ puts attention at the core of the Stoic and wider philosophical way of life.
philosophy.tie_back: Hadot's account supports the Kural's claim that the ‘authors of every kind of treatise’ agree on the value of unforgetting vigilance.
philosophy.source: Pierre Hadot, Philosophy as a Way of Life, ed. Arnold I. Davidson (Blackwell, 1995), essay ‘Spiritual Exercises’

real_life_example.event_title: Henri Becquerel develops the plates he had put away
real_life_example.event: Henri Becquerel was testing whether uranium salts, after exposure to sunlight, gave off rays like the newly discovered X-rays, by placing the salts on photographic plates wrapped in black paper. When cloudy weather in late February 1896 interrupted the experiments, he stored the salts and wrapped plates together in a drawer, and on 1 March he developed the plates anyway and found clear images. Further tests showed that the uranium gave off penetrating rays without any sunlight, the discovery of radioactivity, for which he shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre and Marie Curie.
real_life_example.explanation: Becquerel's lasting fame rests on a careful check of plates that seemed unlikely to show anything at all.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the heedless never win lasting fame, and Becquerel's enduring name shows the reverse: fame that came from refusing to overlook a small, apparently pointless step.

tamil:
அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை ஆங்கில்லை
பொச்சாப் புடையார்க்கு நன்கு.
transliteration:
Achcha mutaiyaarkku aranillai aangillai
Pochchaap putaiyaarkku nanku.
meaning: A fort cannot protect someone who is full of fear. In the same way, nothing good can help someone who is careless.
elementary: A castle with tall walls won't help a guard who is too scared to stand at his post. And a house full of good locks won't help if you forget to lock the door. What really protects you is what's going on inside your own head.
university: The couplet is built on a simile (உவமை) marked by ஆங்கு (‘in the same way’). Fear inside makes outer defences (அரண்) useless, and forgetfulness inside makes outer goods (நன்கு) useless. Parimelazhagar spells out the அரண் as forest, mountain and similar strongholds, and glosses நன்கு as wealth of every kind, called ‘the good’ because it is a means to good. His conclusion is that just as the stronghold of the fearful falls, the riches of the heedless perish. Pavanar adds armies to the list of advantages and derives நன்கு from நல் > நன். Manakkudavar sums the couplet up as saying that the heedless have no protection. By pairing அச்சம் (fear) with பொச்சாப்பு (heedlessness), Valluvar treats both as inner failures of a ruler's mind that no outward resource can make up for.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One must deliver himself with the help of his mind, and not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the decisive ally or enemy is one's own mind, not any outer circumstance.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural too says an inner defect, fear or forgetfulness, cancels every outward protection.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.5 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But know this, that if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken up.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points out that a house is lost not for lack of walls but for lack of watching.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: defences and possessions are useless to someone who is not vigilant.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah has already given you victory in many regions and [even] on the day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you, but it did not avail you at all, and the earth was confining for you with its vastness; then you turned back, fleeing.”
islam.explanation: At Hunayn the Muslim army trusted in its unprecedented size and was ambushed and scattered at first.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, a great outward advantage is worth nothing when the mind is complacent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then the five men departed, and came to Laish, and saw the people that were therein, how they dwelt in security, after the manner of the Zidonians, quiet and secure; for there was none in the land, possessing authority, that might put them to shame in any thing, and they were far from the Zidonians, and had no dealings with any man.”
judaism.explanation: The Danite spies find Laish rich, remote and carelessly at ease. The tribe soon comes against the unsuspecting city and burns it (Judges 18:27-28).
judaism.tie_back: Laish had every natural advantage but no vigilance, and its good fortune did it no good, as the Kural says.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By effort and heedfulness, discipline and self-mastery, let the wise one make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.”
buddhism.explanation: The only true refuge, the Buddha says, is an island built within oneself out of effort and heedfulness.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural too places real security in the inner state, not in outer walls.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that outward advantages are useless to the careless, who lose even the insight they once had.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says no advantage helps the heedless, just as no fortress helps the fearful; the Jain verse likewise says wealth cannot protect the careless.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Raawan made castles and fortresses of gold, but he had to abandon them when he left.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir points to the mythical king Ravana, whose golden fortresses could not hold him or save him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says no fortress helps the fearful and no advantage helps the heedless; Kabir likewise shows outer strongholds failing a ruler whose inner life had gone astray.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1104, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Aeolus gives Odysseus all the adverse winds tied up in an ox-hide bag, and the west wind carries his fleet home. With Ithaca in sight, Odysseus, worn out from steering for nine days, falls asleep. His crew open the bag hoping to find treasure, and the storm blows them all the way back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus had every advantage a sailor could want, and lost it all in one lapse of watchfulness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's heedless man, for whom even the greatest good fortune does no good.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli asks whether fortresses are useful to princes. He concludes that they help or harm according to circumstances, that the best fortress is not to be hated by one's people, and that the Countess of Forlì's citadel did not save her in the end.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli the stone walls matter less than the political condition inside them.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's thought is similar: a stronghold cannot make up for a defect within.
philosophy.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 20 (trans. W. K. Marriott)

real_life_example.event_title: The Dutch raid on the Medway
real_life_example.event: During a war between England and the Dutch Republic, while peace talks were under way at Breda, much of the English fleet lay laid up in the River Medway near the royal dockyard at Chatham, above a defensive chain across the river. In June 1667 a Dutch fleet under Michiel de Ruyter took Sheerness, sailed up the Medway, broke through the chain, burned a number of English ships and towed away the English flagship Royal Charles, while the English sank some of their own large ships to block the channel. The raid put pressure on Charles II, and the Dutch obtained better terms in the Treaty of Breda.
real_life_example.explanation: England possessed one of the strongest navies of its day, yet ships left idle behind a weak boom could not protect even their own home dockyard.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that just as no fortress helps the fearful, no advantage helps the heedless, and England's great warships were of no use while they lay unready in the Medway.

tamil:
முன்னுறக் காவாது இழுக்கியான் தன்பிழை
பின்னூறு இரங்கி விடும்.
transliteration:
Munnurak kaavaadhu izhukkiyaan thanpizhai
Pinnooru irangi vitum.
meaning: Someone who carelessly fails to guard against trouble before it comes will be sorry for their own mistake when the trouble hits.
elementary: If you know a test is coming and you don't study, you'll feel terrible when you see questions you can't answer. Getting ready before trouble comes is much better than feeling sorry afterwards.
university: முன் உற (‘before it arrives’) and பின் ஊறு (‘when the blow has fallen’) frame the couplet in time, and இழுக்கியான் (‘one who slipped, was negligent’) is described by காவாது (‘without guarding’). Parimelazhagar says the troubles in view are those that can be guarded against, namely what enemies do when they spot a lapse. He treats ஊறு as standing for ஊற்றின்கண், with both the case-ending and the linking syllable dropped, and explains இரங்கிவிடும் as ‘will be left to grieve’, because once the trouble has come it can no longer be warded off. Pavanar widens the preventable troubles to include famine and flood, and takes விடும் in the sense of ‘perishing’. Manakkudavar's gloss is almost word for word the same as Parimelazhagar's. This couplet closes Parimelazhagar's group of three (533-535) on the harm that comes to the heedless.
