hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra three fish live in a pond: Anāgatavidhātā (‘Forethought’), Pratyutpannamati (‘Ready-wit’) and Yadbhaviṣya (‘Whatever-will-be’). When fishermen are overheard planning to net the pond, Forethought leaves at once and Ready-wit escapes by playing dead, but Whatever-will-be does nothing and is caught.
hinduism.explanation: This nīti fable, told to princes, contrasts the one who guards in advance with the one who waits and is lost.
hinduism.tie_back: Yadbhaviṣya is exactly the Kural's heedless man, whose failure to act beforehand leaves no remedy afterwards.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book I (Mitrabheda), the fable of the three fish

christianity.quote_or_event: “And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut. Afterward came also the other virgins, saying, Lord, Lord, open to us. But he answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not. Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh.”
christianity.explanation: The foolish virgins brought no spare oil. By the time they had gone to fetch it, the door was shut, and their pleading came too late.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's picture of someone who did not provide beforehand and can only lament afterwards.

islam.quote_or_event: “And spend [in the way of Allah] from what We have provided you before death approaches one of you and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I would give charity and be among the righteous."”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an pictures the person who put off good deeds, begging too late for a little more time.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's pattern: neglect beforehand, then useless lament once the moment has passed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “one should repent today lest he die tomorrow; and by following this advice one will spend his entire life in a state of repentance.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer's advice is to ‘repent one day before your death’. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai adds a parable of a king who invites his servants to a feast without fixing the hour: the wise dress and wait at the door, while the foolish go off to work and are caught unprepared when the call comes.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Talmud teaches that you should be ready before the day of reckoning, because afterwards there is only regret.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a border city is closely guarded both within and without, even so, guard yourself. Do not let slip this opportunity (for spiritual growth). For those who let slip this opportunity grieve indeed when consigned to hell.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the self to a frontier town that has to be guarded before attack, and warns that those who let the moment slip will grieve afterwards.
buddhism.tie_back: It has the same structure as the Kural: guard in advance, or grieve when the harm arrives.

jainism.quote_or_event: “'If he does not get (victory over his will) early, he will get it afterwards;' such reasoning presupposes the eternity of human life. But such a man despairs when his life draws to its close, and the dissolution of his body approaches.”
jainism.explanation: The monk who puts off the work of self-mastery, assuming there is time, ends in despair when the end arrives.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the man who fails to guard against trouble in advance grieves over his mistake when it strikes; Mahavira describes the same belated despair of the procrastinator.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If someone focuses on the Lord beforehand, then why should he be punished?”
sikhism.explanation: In the Babarvani hymns on Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak says the suffering might have been avoided had people kept God in mind before the calamity struck.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one who fails to guard against trouble before it comes is left grieving afterwards; Guru Nanak asks why anyone would suffer if he had paid heed beforehand.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus (‘Forethought’) warned his brother Epimetheus (‘Afterthought’) never to accept a gift from Zeus. Epimetheus forgot the warning and took Pandora, and he understood the evil only once it was already his.
greek_mythology.explanation: The two brothers' names are themselves a lesson: one sees ahead, the other only understands after the damage is done.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Epimetheus is the Kural's man who did not guard beforehand and could only realize his error afterwards.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Explaining why the Italian princes lost their states, Machiavelli says that in quiet times they never thought things could change, which he calls a common human fault of not reckoning on the storm during fair weather. When adversity came, they thought of flight instead of defence.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli, rulers fall less through bad luck than through failing to prepare while they still could.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's heedless ruler, who did not guard in advance and is left lamenting.
philosophy.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 24 (trans. W. K. Marriott)

real_life_example.event_title: The Vajont dam landslide
real_life_example.event: The Vajont dam was built in a gorge known to be geologically unstable, and several geologists and engineers warned of the risk of a single great landslide if the reservoir were filled. When filling began in 1960 the slope of Monte Toc started to move, and in November 1960 a slide of about 700,000 cubic metres fell into the lake, but the reservoir continued to be operated and raised again. On the night of 9 October 1963 a vast landslide fell into the reservoir, sending a wave over the dam that destroyed the town of Longarone below and killed about 2,000 people, although the dam itself survived; several people involved were later convicted in the courts.
real_life_example.explanation: The warning signs were seen and measured for three years, but the danger was not guarded against while there was still time, and once the mountain moved nothing could be done.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who fails to guard against trouble before it comes will be left grieving over his own mistake once it strikes, and Vajont is remembered as a disaster foreseen but not prevented.

tamil:
இழுக்காமை யார்மாட்டும் என்றும் வழுக்காமை
வாயின் அதுவொப்பது இல்.
transliteration:
Izhukkaamai yaarmaattum endrum vazhukkaamai
Vaayin adhuvoppadhu il.
meaning: If a person can stay alert and careful toward everyone and at all times, nothing else is as good as that.
elementary: Being careful once is easy. Being careful with everyone, every day, even when things are going great, is the real superpower. If you can do that, it's better than almost any other gift you could have.
university: The couplet plays on two near-synonyms: இழுக்காமை (‘not slipping’, that is, unforgetfulness) must be present வழுக்காமை (‘without a lapse’). Parimelazhagar explains யார்மாட்டும் as reaching even the king's own people, the servants who do his work and his kin, and என்றும் as meaning ‘in days of growth and of decline alike’. He parses வாயின் as a conditional form built on the verbal-noun stem வாய் (‘to come right, to fall into place’). Pavanar adds that வழுக்காமை means applying this without fail in every task, and he explicitly rejects Parimelazhagar's analysis of வாயின், citing Tolkāppiyam and Kural 737 to argue that வாய் is an intransitive verb. Manakkudavar reads the couplet as a rule for the careful administration of justice. Together with 537, this couplet forms Parimelazhagar's pair on the excellence of unforgetfulness.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, Arjuna, you should always think of Me in the form of Kṛṣṇa and at the same time carry out your prescribed duty of fighting. With your activities dedicated to Me and your mind and intelligence fixed on Me, you will attain Me without doubt.”
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit sarveṣu kāleṣu anusmara means ‘remember at all times’. Krishna asks for unbroken remembrance to go along with, not replace, active duty.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's ideal is likewise remembrance that never lapses, ‘at all times’, while one carries on one's work.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 8.7 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:”
christianity.explanation: Peter calls for constant sobriety and alertness because the danger is always prowling nearby.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats unbroken vigilance as the essential safeguard.

islam.quote_or_event: “And remember your Lord within yourself in humility and in fear without being apparent in speech - in the mornings and the evenings. And do not be among the heedless.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an asks for remembrance (dhikr) morning and evening, as a standing guard against ghaflah, heedlessness.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats unbroken remembrance as the positive virtue that defeats heedlessness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget the things which thine eyes saw, and lest they depart from thy heart all the days of thy life;”
judaism.explanation: Moses commands a watchfulness that lasts ‘all the days of thy life’ so that what has been learned is never forgotten.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's unforgetfulness kept up at all times.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as the footprints of all living beings with legs can be encompassed by the footprint of the elephant, and the elephant's footprint is declared to be supreme among them in terms of its great size; in the same way, heedfulness is the one quality that keeps both kinds of benefit secure — benefits in this life & benefits in lives to come.”
buddhism.explanation: King Pasenadi asks the Buddha whether one quality secures every kind of welfare, and the Buddha names heedfulness (appamāda) as supreme among them all.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘nothing equals it’, stated almost word for word in Buddhist terms.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 3.17 (Appamada Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though others sleep, be thou awake! Like a wise man, trust nobody, but be always on the alert; for dangerous is the time and weak the body. Be always watchful like a Bhârunda bird!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira asks for unbroken vigilance at every moment and toward everyone, comparing it to the mythical two-necked Bharunda bird that can never relax its watch.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises unfailing watchfulness toward everyone and at all times as the highest good; this verse asks for exactly that constant, all-round alertness.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who does not forget the Naam, for a moment or even an instant-how rare is such a person in this world!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak praises remembrance that never lapses even for an instant, and notes how rare it is.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says nothing equals watchfulness kept without a lapse towards everyone and at all times; Guru Nanak prizes the same never-lapsing attention, directed to the Name.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 21, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hera sets Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed watchman, to guard Io. Only some of his eyes ever sleep at a time while the rest keep watch, until Hermes lulls every eye shut with his pipes and a long story and kills him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Argus is the Greek image of constant vigilance. His death shows that one lapse undoes everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural values watchfulness that never lapses at any time, and Argus's end shows why ‘always’ matters.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his discourse on attention (prosoche), Epictetus warns that once you relax your attention you should not imagine you can recover it whenever you like. Each lapse makes the next one easier and builds a habit of neglect, so attention has to be kept up continuously.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus vigilance is not a single act but an unbroken state, and any intermission costs more than it seems to.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's ideal of never slipping, towards anyone, at any time, matches Epictetus's demand exactly.

real_life_example.event_title: Walsingham's watchfulness uncovers the Babington Plot
real_life_example.event: Sir Francis Walsingham, secretary of state to Elizabeth I, kept a network of agents and informers to protect the queen. In 1586, learning through a double agent of a Catholic conspiracy, later named after Anthony Babington, to assassinate Elizabeth and put Mary, Queen of Scots, on the throne, Walsingham had Mary's secret letters, smuggled in beer barrels, intercepted, deciphered by his codebreaker Thomas Phelippes and resealed before delivery. The correspondence exposed the plot, and the conspirators were arrested and tried.
real_life_example.explanation: Watchfulness extended even to letters their writers thought secure protected the queen from a plot that might otherwise have succeeded.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says nothing equals unfailing watchfulness kept towards everyone and at all times, and Walsingham's constant vigilance is a classic example of it in statecraft.

tamil:
அரியஎன்று ஆகாத இல்லைபொச் சாவாக்
கருவியால் போற்றிச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Ariyaendru aakaadha illaipoch chaavaak
Karuviyaal potrich cheyin.
meaning: No job is too hard, however difficult people say it is, if you do it carefully, with a mind that never forgets or slips.
elementary: Building a huge Lego castle sounds impossible. But if you keep the picture in your head, follow each step carefully, and don't lose track, you can finish it. A mind that doesn't forget is like a super-tool that makes hard jobs possible.
university: அரிய என்று ஆகாத இல்லை is a double negative: ‘there is nothing that, being called difficult, cannot be done’. Parimelazhagar takes பொச்சாவாக் கருவி to mean ‘the unforgetting mind’. On his reading, பொச்சாவாத has lost its final syllable by poetic licence, and the mind is called கருவி (‘instrument’) because it is the inner instrument (அந்தக்கரணம்); போற்றிச் செயின் means ‘if one does it with careful thought’. His summary is that people with unbroken attention and sound planning accomplish everything easily. Pavanar calls this gloss over-learned and prefers to read பொச்சாவாக் கருவி as an appositional compound, ‘the instrument that is unforgetfulness’. Manakkudavar likewise glosses it as மறவாமையாகிய கருவி. Modern commentators such as Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah reflect both readings.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O mighty-armed son of Kuntī, it is undoubtedly very difficult to curb the restless mind, but it is possible by suitable practice and by detachment.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna protests that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna grants that it is hard but insists that disciplined practice (abhyāsa) makes it possible.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita says that what is called ‘too hard’ becomes achievable through a steadily disciplined mind.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.35 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
christianity.explanation: In Gethsemane Jesus gives watchfulness joined to prayer as the means by which a weak human nature can hold firm.
christianity.tie_back: Vigilance here is the tool that overcomes weakness, as the Kural's ‘instrument of unforgetfulness’ overcomes difficulty.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who strive for Us - We will surely guide them to Our ways. And indeed, Allah is with the doers of good.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an promises that sustained striving (jihād in its broad sense) will be met with guidance to the way through.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that persistent, careful effort opens paths that seemed closed.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud records Rabbi Yitzḥak's maxim: if someone tells you they laboured and did not find, do not believe them; if they say they found without labouring, do not believe them; but if they say they laboured and found, believe them.
judaism.explanation: The teaching insists that real attainment, especially in Torah, comes only through sustained, careful effort, and that such effort does not fail.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too holds that diligent, attentive work makes even the ‘impossible’ achievable.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The monk who delights in heedfulness and looks with fear at heedlessness advances like fire, burning all fetters, small and large.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures heedfulness as a fire that consumes every obstacle, large or small.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's unforgetting instrument, heedfulness here overcomes every difficulty in its way.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By conquering his will, (a monk) reaches liberation, as a well-broken horse which is clad in harness (goes to battle). Be watchful in your young years; for thereby a monk quickly obtains liberation.”
jainism.explanation: Watchfulness and self-control are the means by which even the hardest goal, liberation, is quickly reached.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says nothing is too hard for one who works with an unforgetting mind as his tool; Mahavira says watchfulness wins even liberation, the hardest goal of all.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Remembering God, one's works are accomplished.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Guru Arjan lists the fruits of simran, among them that one's undertakings are brought to completion.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says nothing is too hard for one who works carefully with an unforgetting mind as his tool; Guru Arjan says that remembrance brings one's works to completion.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 263, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe, Odysseus plugs his crew's ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast, ordering that his bonds be tightened if he begs to be freed. In this way he alone hears the Sirens' song and survives it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus knows his own mind will lapse under the song's spell, so he builds a device that keeps his resolve in force when his memory of it fails.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The mast and ropes are literally an ‘instrument of unforgetfulness’, and with them he achieves what no one had survived before.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Every moment think steadily as a Roman and a man to do what thou hast in hand with perfect and simple dignity, and feeling of affection, and freedom, and justice; and to give thyself relief from all other thoughts.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus urges full, steady attention to whatever task is in hand, putting away carelessness and distraction.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘doing with care through an unforgetting mind’, turned into a daily discipline.

real_life_example.event_title: Amundsen sails the Gjoa through the Northwest Passage
real_life_example.place: Arctic waters of northern Canada, from Norway to Nome, Alaska
real_life_example.event: Many earlier expeditions had sought a sea route through the Arctic waters north of Canada without completing it. After careful preparation Roald Amundsen bought the small 47-ton sloop Gjoa, built in 1872, and left Kristiania (Oslo) on 16 June 1903 with six companions, spending two winters at Gjoa Haven on King William Island, where the party made magnetic observations, and a third winter near Herschel Island. The Gjoa reached Nome, Alaska, in August 1906, the first ship to sail the whole Northwest Passage.
real_life_example.explanation: A small, well-prepared party patiently completed over three years a voyage that larger and better-funded expeditions had failed to achieve.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says no task is too hard if it is done carefully with an unforgetting mind as one's tool, and Amundsen's methodical voyage conquered a route long thought impassable.

tamil:
புகழ்ந்தவை போற்றிச் செயல்வேண்டும் செய்யாது
இகழ்ந்தார்க்கு எழுமையும் இல்.
transliteration:
Pukazhndhavai potrich cheyalventum seyyaadhu
Ikazhndhaarkku ezhumaiyum il.
meaning: Do carefully the things that wise people have praised. Those who ignore them and leave them undone will find no good in any of their seven births (the many lives a person is believed to live).
elementary: Your teachers and parents tell you some things are really worth doing, like being kind, doing homework, and telling the truth. Knowing that isn't enough; you have to actually do them. People who shrug those things off miss out on good things again and again.
university: புகழ்ந்தவை means ‘the things praised’. Parimelazhagar identifies them as the duties that works on polity single out as proper to kings: the three powers, the four expedients (upāya), the five kinds of action, the six policies, and so on. இகழ்ந்தார் here does not mean ‘those who scorned’; all the commentators take it as ‘those who neglected or forgot’, and Parimelazhagar glosses it as மறந்தவர். He reads எழுமையும் இல் as ‘no good in all seven births’, on the ground that those who fall away from their proper duty reap only suffering in hell, and he treats எழுமை (‘sevenfoldness’) as a metonymy. Pavanar rejects Parimelazhagar's appeal to caste duty (சாதி தருமம்) as foreign to the text, lists instead celebrated deeds of the ancient Tamil kings as examples of ‘praised acts’, and reads எழுமை as a conventional number. Parimelazhagar says this couplet sets out what must be done without forgetting.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Perform your prescribed duty, for doing so is better than not working. One cannot even maintain one’s physical body without work.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna urges Arjuna to carry out his prescribed duty (niyataṃ karma) instead of neglecting it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural too insists that recommended duties be actually performed and warns of what follows from neglecting them.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.8 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass: For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was.”
christianity.explanation: James says that hearing what is good without doing it is a kind of forgetting, like glancing in a mirror and walking away.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the Kural closely: the praised deeds must be done, and failing to do them is described as forgetting.

islam.quote_or_event: “There are two blessings that many people are deceived into losing: health and free time.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that many people squander health and leisure, the very means for doing good, and lose them without noticing.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too warns that neglecting to do the praised deeds, while one still can, leaves a person with nothing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Study is not the most important thing, but actions; whoever indulges in too many words brings about sin.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon ben Gamliel teaches that the point of learning is doing: knowledge of the good means nothing unless it is carried out.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural says the same: what the wise praise must be done, not merely admired.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 1:17, trans. Joshua Kulp

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of color but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practice them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that praising the good without practising it is like a showy flower with no scent.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it insists that praised deeds bear fruit only when they are actually done.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who in this life has done no good actions and has not practised the Law, repents of it in the next world when he has become a prey to Death.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Kitra warns King Brahmadatta that failing to do what the Law commends brings regret beyond this life.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who neglect the deeds the wise have praised find no good in any of their births; Kitra likewise warns that neglecting the Law brings suffering in the next existence.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.21 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Meditate in remembrance on the Lord, or else you will regret it in the end, O mind.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir warns that neglecting remembrance now will bring regret when it is too late.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who neglect the deeds the wise have praised will find no good in all their births; Kabir likewise warns that what is neglected now is lamented at the end.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1106, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Oeneus of Calydon offers harvest first-fruits to all the gods but, whether he forgot or failed to notice, leaves out Artemis. In anger she sends the great Calydonian boar, and the ravaging of his land and the strife that follows destroy his house.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phoenix tells this story to Achilles as a warning that neglecting what is due, even through simple forgetfulness, brings ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Oeneus is the Kural's man who ‘failed to perform the praised things’ and found no good afterwards.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But most people do not do these, but take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers and will become good in this way, behaving somewhat like patients who listen attentively to their doctors, but do none of the things they are ordered to do.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle insists that virtue comes only from actually performing virtuous acts, and that those who merely admire the prescriptions are like patients who ignore their doctors.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's demand that praised deeds be done, not merely known.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.4 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Takaki Kanehiro's navy diet defeats beriberi
real_life_example.event: Beriberi was a major disease among Japanese sailors, and on one long voyage of the training ship Ryujo 169 of its 376 crew fell ill and 25 died. Naval surgeon Takaki Kanehiro, who believed the white-rice diet was to blame, had the ship Tsukuba sail a similar route in 1884 with a more varied diet, and only about 14 of its crew developed beriberi and none died, after which the navy changed its rations, adding barley, and beriberi in the navy fell sharply. The army, whose medical leaders doubted the dietary explanation, kept its white-rice ration, and in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-05 more than 27,000 army soldiers died of beriberi.
real_life_example.explanation: The navy acted on a well-tested remedy and was spared, while the army's neglect of the same lesson cost tens of thousands of lives.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that there is no good for those who neglect and leave undone what the wise have shown to be right, and the contrast between Japan's navy and army is a stark example.

tamil:
இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக தாந்தம்
மகிழ்ச்சியின் மைந்துறும் போழ்து.
transliteration:
Ikazhchchiyin kettaarai ulluka thaandham
Makizhchchiyin maindhurum pozhdhu.
meaning: Whenever you feel carried away by your own happiness, remember the people who were ruined because they got careless.
elementary: When you win a prize and feel like the best in the world, it's a good moment to remember the story of the hare who was so sure of winning that he took a nap and lost to the tortoise. Remembering other people's mistakes keeps you careful.
university: இகழ்ச்சி here means heedless disregard (it shares a root with இகழ்ந்தார் in 538), and மைந்துறும் போழ்து means ‘the moment one grows strong or elated’. Parimelazhagar makes kings the subject: when they grow confident in their own pleasures, they should remember those of old who perished through the lapse such pleasure breeds. He explains that the text says ‘their own delight’ because the king owns the means of pleasure, and that it ties elation to ruin because neglect and downfall arise together. The point, he says, is that one who recalls the ruined will think ‘I too shall perish that way’ and will not grow elated. He also records a variant reading, எண்ணுக for உள்ளுக, which Pavanar attributes to Manakkudavar. Manakkudavar gives the couplet a concrete application: kings should have their food, clothing and unguents examined, that is, guard against poisoning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The mortal king Nahusha is raised to the throne of Indra while Indra is in hiding. Intoxicated by his new power, he forces the great sages to carry his palanquin and, in his impatience, kicks Agastya. He is cursed on the spot to fall from heaven as a serpent.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata tells the story as a warning of how quickly exaltation turns into ruin when power makes one careless of what is due.
hinduism.tie_back: Nahusha is exactly the kind of figure the Kural tells rulers to remember when their own delight makes them feel invincible.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Sections 11-17 (the story of Nahusha), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come. Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.”
christianity.explanation: Paul retells Israel's failures in the wilderness and says they were recorded precisely so that the confident would remember them and take heed.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's method: when you feel secure, remember those who fell.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not like the exultant.” … “And We caused the earth to swallow him and his home.”
islam.explanation: Qarun's people warn him against exulting in his vast treasures. He dismisses them, and the earth swallows him, so that those who had envied him the day before learn from his end.
islam.tie_back: Qarun is held up in the Qur'an as exactly the remembered ruin the Kural prescribes for moments of elation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up so that he did corruptly, and he trespassed against the LORD his God; for he went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense.”
judaism.explanation: King Uzziah prospered greatly, but at the height of his strength he grew arrogant and overstepped, and he was struck with leprosy for the rest of his life.
judaism.tie_back: The Chronicler's ‘when he was strong’ is the Kural's மைந்துறும் போழ்து, the very moment it warns about.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Possessions, honor, and popularity came to Devadatta for his own ruin and downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha points to Devadatta as the cautionary example: success and fame swelled him and led to his downfall, like a banana plant killed by its own fruit.
buddhism.tie_back: Devadatta is the kind of ruined figure the Kural tells us to call to mind when success elates us.

jainism.quote_or_event: “And Brahmadatta, king of the Pañkâlas, did not act on the counsel of the saint; he enjoyed the highest pleasure, and (afterwards) sank into the deepest hell.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain canon holds up Brahmadatta, a universal monarch who stayed absorbed in pleasure and ignored all warnings, as an example of ruin through heedlessness.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural tells a man swollen with delight to remember those who perished through heedlessness; Brahmadatta is just such a cautionary figure in Jain tradition.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Many have proclaimed their sovereignty over millions of fortresses on the earth, but they have now departed.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak calls to mind the many rulers who beat the drums of their power and are now gone.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the one swelling with delight to remember those ruined by heedlessness; Guru Nanak recalls vanished rulers for the same sobering purpose.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus fits wings to his son Icarus and warns him to fly a middle course. But the boy delights in his daring flight, abandons his guide and soars higher, until the sun softens the wax and he falls into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: Icarus's fall became the classic Western example of elation making someone forget the limits he had been warned about.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the ruined figure the Kural bids us remember when delight makes us feel we can fly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy reminds the imprisoned Boethius that Fortune's nature is to turn her wheel. She recalls kings brought low, such as Croesus, who was placed on the pyre and saved only by a sudden rain, and tells him that no one should trust prosperity as if it were his own.
philosophy.explanation: For Boethius, remembering the fallen is the cure for the illusion that good fortune is permanent.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's remedy of recalling the ruined when one is swollen with success.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2

real_life_example.event_title: Scipio Aemilianus foresees Rome's own fall at Carthage
real_life_example.event: In 146 BCE, at the end of the Third Punic War, the Roman commander Scipio Aemilianus captured and destroyed Carthage, Rome's great rival. The historian Polybius, who stood beside him, recorded that as Scipio watched the city's fall he took Polybius by the hand and said he felt a dread foreboding that the same fate might one day come to his own country. The later historian Appian wrote that Scipio wept as he looked on the city.
real_life_example.explanation: At the very height of Roman triumph, the victorious general turned his thoughts to how great powers fall rather than to his own glory.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural tells those who feel strong and elated to remember others who were ruined, and Scipio did exactly that in the hour of his greatest victory.

tamil:
உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிதுமன் மற்றுந்தான்
உள்ளியது உள்ளப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Ulliyadhu eydhal elidhuman matrundhaan
Ulliyadhu ullap perin.
meaning: It is easy to get what you set your mind on, as long as you keep thinking about it and never let it slip from your mind.
elementary: If you want to learn to ride a bike, you have to keep that goal in your mind every day, even after you fall. Kids who keep thinking about their goal and don't let it slip away usually get there.
university: The couplet turns on repeating உள்ளியது (‘what was thought of’) together with the verb உள்ளு (‘to think of, keep in mind’): attaining your aim is easy if you can ‘think again what you thought’. Parimelazhagar reads it as advice to a king: he will easily obtain what he intended, exactly as he intended it, if he can keep thinking of that same thing, which he explains as striving towards it without forgetting. He takes மன் as an ஒழியிசை particle, one that implies an unspoken ‘but that is hard to manage’, so the couplet quietly admits that sustained attention is the difficult part. Pavanar rejects this analysis of மன் as unsuitable here and takes மற்று to mean ‘afterwards, further’. Manakkudavar reads the couplet as the requirement to remember, above all, what one first resolved. Parimelazhagar groups 539-540 as the means (உபாயம்) for achieving unforgetfulness.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Drona tests his pupils by setting a wooden bird on a treetop and asking each what he sees. The others describe the tree, the branches, their brothers and their teacher, and are sent away. Arjuna says he sees only the bird's head, is told to shoot, and brings it down.
hinduism.explanation: The episode is the classic Indian image of a mind that holds unwaveringly to what it has aimed at.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna embodies the Kural's formula: to keep thinking of what one has set one's mind on is to attain it easily.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sambhava Parva), Drona's test of the Kuru princes, trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes a life gathered into ‘this one thing’: fixing on the goal ahead and pressing towards it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it presents steady, single-minded attention to the goal as the way to reach it.

islam.quote_or_event: “The reward of deeds depends upon the intentions and every person will get the reward according to what he has intended.”
islam.explanation: The opening hadith of Bukhari makes the intention held in the heart the determining factor in what a person obtains from his deeds.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too ties attainment to what one keeps firmly in mind.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have set the LORD always before me; Surely He is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist describes keeping his focus constantly before his eyes, and finds in that steadiness the source of his firmness.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links continual remembrance of one's aim with unshakeable success.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All compounded things are subject to vanish. Strive with earnestness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha repeats this exhortation near the end of his life, and it is echoed in his final words (appamādena sampādetha, ‘accomplish the goal through heedfulness’). He makes unremitting heedfulness the one thing to hold to until the goal is reached.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's key to attainment is keeping one's aim before the mind without lapse, which is the Buddha's own last counsel.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta) §3.63, trans. Sister Vajira and Francis Story

jainism.quote_or_event: “You have crossed the great ocean; why do you halt so near the shore? make haste to get on the other side; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira urges Gautama not to slacken near the goal but to keep his mind steadily on reaching the far shore.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the goal is easily reached if one keeps thinking of it steadily; Mahavira likewise tells Gautama that sustained, unslackening attention completes the crossing.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Meditate, meditate, meditate in remembrance of Him, and find peace.”
sikhism.explanation: Sukhmani opens by urging repeated, unbroken remembrance as the way to peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says what one has set the mind on is easily reached if one keeps thinking of it; Guru Arjan likewise makes sustained, repeated remembrance the means of reaching what is sought.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Atalanta, the swiftest runner, can beat any suitor. Hippomenes drops three golden apples from Aphrodite during their race, and each time Atalanta turns aside to pick one up. She loses the race she would certainly have won.
greek_mythology.explanation: Atalanta loses not through weakness but because her attention is pulled away from the finish line.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She is the opposite of the Kural's ideal: had she kept her mind on what she aimed at, winning would have been easy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “My experience is what I agree to attend to.”
philosophy.explanation: William James argues that selective, sustained attention shapes what a person's mind and life actually become.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes steady attention to one's aim the decisive condition for achieving it.
philosophy.source: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. 11 ‘Attention’

real_life_example.event_title: Howard Carter's last season in the Valley of the Kings
real_life_example.place: Valley of the Kings, Luxor, Egypt
real_life_example.event: The archaeologist Howard Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, had searched the Valley of the Kings for several seasons from 1917 with little to show for it, and in 1922 Carnarvon agreed to pay for one more season. On 4 November 1922, only days after work resumed, Carter's team uncovered a step cut into the rock, and further digging revealed a stairway leading down to a sealed doorway. It was the almost intact tomb of the pharaoh Tutankhamun, into which Carter and Carnarvon first looked on 26 November 1922.
real_life_example.explanation: Years of fruitless searching ended in one of the most famous archaeological discoveries ever made, because the searcher kept his goal in view when others were ready to stop.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says reaching what you have set your mind on is easy if you keep thinking of it steadily, and Carter's refusal to let go of his search in the Valley of the Kings was rewarded.

tamil:
ஓர்ந்துகண் ணோடாது இறைபுரிந்து யார்மாட்டும்
தேர்ந்துசெய் வஃதே முறை.
transliteration:
Orndhukan Notaadhu Iraipurindhu Yaarmaattum
Therndhusey Vaqdhe Murai.
meaning: Justice means looking into every case carefully, favoring no one, being fair to all, and then thinking it through before acting.
elementary: Imagine a teacher who finds two kids fighting over a broken toy. A fair teacher doesn’t just blame the kid she likes less. She asks questions, listens to both, thinks it over, and then decides. Even if the one who broke it is her favourite helper, the rule is the same for him. That is what “doing it the right way” means.
university: This opening couplet works as a definition: முறை (justice, right order) is a four-step procedure. ஓர்ந்து means investigating what offence was committed; கண்ணோடாது means without கண்ணோட்டம், the soft favour that comes from familiarity or affection (Valluvar gives this quality its own chapter, 58, where it is praised in private life, which is why it has to be ruled out here); இறைபுரிந்து is glossed by Parimelazhagar as holding to impartiality (இறை = நடுவுநிலைமை), though some modern readers take இறை as ‘the ruler’ and the phrase as ‘the king, wishing it’; and தேர்ந்து செய்வது means deciding with those learned in the law books and then giving the fitting penalty. யார்மாட்டும் (‘with anyone at all’) governs the whole sequence, so a kinsman gets no exemption. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow this procedural reading; Kalaignar compresses it to ‘not leaning to either side’. Parimelazhagar notes that the chapter follows பொச்சாவாமை (vigilance) and comes before its opposite, கொடுங்கோன்மை (Ch. 56); செங்கோல், the ‘straight sceptre’, is the standard Tamil metonym for just rule. ytamizh and Thirukkural.net give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A king should, without doubt, look upon his subjects as his own children. In determining their disputes, however, he should not show compassion.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that a king should love his people like a father, but that this love must not tip the scales when he judges their quarrels.
hinduism.tie_back: This is கண்ணோடாது exactly: when judgment is given, affection is set aside.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section LXIX (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels, that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to handle discipline in the church without favouring anyone.
christianity.tie_back: Doing nothing by partiality is the Kural’s ‘showing favour to no one’.

islam.quote_or_event: “What destroyed the nations preceding you, was that if a noble amongst them stole, they would forgive him, and if a poor person amongst them stole, they would inflict Allah's Legal punishment on him. By Allah, if Fatima, the daughter of Muhammad stole, I would cut off her hand.”
islam.explanation: When the Quraysh sent Usama to plead for a noblewoman who had stolen, the Prophet refused and declared that the law would apply even to his own daughter.
islam.tie_back: This is யார்மாட்டும் கண்ணோடாது, favour to no one, however close or high.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; ye shall hear the small and the great alike; ye shall not be afraid of the face of any man; for the judgment is God’s;”
judaism.explanation: Moses tells the judges of Israel to give poor and powerful the same hearing and to fear no one, since justice belongs to God.
judaism.tie_back: Hearing everyone alike and favouring no one is the same rule the Kural sets for the king.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by passing arbitrary judgments does a man become just; a wise man is he who investigates both right and wrong. He who does not judge others arbitrarily, but passes judgment impartially according to the truth, that sagacious man is a guardian of law and is called just.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says a judge is just only if he investigates both sides and decides impartially according to the truth, not on a whim.
buddhism.tie_back: Investigate (ஓர்ந்து), judge impartially (கண்ணோடாது), and so be called just (முறை): the two texts follow the same sequence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men frequently apply punishment wrongly: the innocent are put in prison, and the perpetrator of the crime is set at liberty.”
jainism.explanation: When Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, urges King Nami to punish thieves and robbers so that he may be a true Kshatriya, Nami answers that human punishment often lands on the wrong person.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural defines justice as investigating each case carefully and without favour before acting, and Nami's reply shows what goes wrong when that investigation is skipped: the innocent are jailed and the guilty go free.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “For the king, cleansing is justice; for the scholar, it is true meditation.”
sikhism.explanation: Rejecting ritual purity, Guru Nanak says that what truly purifies each person is the duty of his station, and for a ruler that duty is justice.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines the right sceptre as justice done without favour after careful inquiry; Guru Nanak likewise makes justice the king's essential practice.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1240, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the myth that closes Plato’s Gorgias, Zeus decrees that souls are to be judged after death stripped of body, wealth and rank, by judges who are themselves stripped, because in earlier times the clothed judges had been deceived by fine appearances and false witnesses; Minos, Rhadamanthus and Aeacus are appointed to judge.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows the gods reforming judgment so that nothing (status, beauty, supporters) can sway the verdict.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises கண்ணோடாது: a true verdict must look past whoever the person appears to be.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “to go to the judge is to go to justice; for the nature of the judge is to be a sort of animate justice;”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says people in a dispute go to a judge because the judge is supposed to be justice itself in living form, standing at the fair midpoint between the parties.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural asks the king to be exactly this, the living ‘mean’ who leans to neither side.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.4, 1132a (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Supreme Court orders President Nixon to hand over the Watergate tapes
real_life_example.event: During the Watergate investigation, Special Prosecutor Leon Jaworski subpoenaed tape recordings of conversations in President Richard Nixon's White House, and Nixon refused to hand them over, claiming executive privilege. After hearing argument on 8 July 1974, the Supreme Court ruled 8-0 on 24 July, in an opinion by Chief Justice Warren Burger, that a president's general claim of confidentiality must yield to the demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a criminal trial, with Justice William Rehnquist taking no part. Nixon complied, released transcripts that showed his part in the cover-up, and resigned in August 1974.
real_life_example.explanation: The highest court examined the president's claim on its merits and applied the law to the most powerful man in the country as it would to anyone else.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines justice as examining the matter carefully, showing favour to no one and deciding with those learned in the law, and the Court's unanimous ruling against a sitting president meets every part of that definition.

tamil:
வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகெல்லாம் மன்னவன்
கோல்நோக்கி வாழுங் குடி.
transliteration:
Vaanokki Vaazhum Ulakellaam Mannavan
Kolnokki Vaazhung Kuti.
meaning: All living things on earth look up to the sky for rain. In the same way, the people of a country look to their king’s fair rule in order to live.
elementary: Plants in a garden wait for rain, and without it they dry up. The people of a country are a bit like that garden: they are waiting for their leaders to be fair and kind. When the leader rules well, it is like a good rain, and everyone grows.
university: The couplet is built on an exact parallel: வான் நோக்கி வாழும் உலகு (the world that lives looking to the sky) matches கோல் நோக்கி வாழும் குடி (the citizenry that lives looking to the sceptre). As commentators note, வான் here stands for rain by metonymy, which echoes the opening chapter on rain (வான்சிறப்பு, Ch. 2), where rain sustains all life. Parimelazhagar reads உலகெல்லாம் as ‘all living beings’ and குடி as the settled subjects of the kingdom. Just as he reads கோல் throughout the chapter, the sceptre means just rule, not simply power. Varadarasan and Pappaiah keep the rain comparison; Kalaignar makes it ‘good government is as necessary to citizens as rain is to living things’. The comparison already hints at 545 and 559 (in the next chapter), where just rule and rainfall are causally linked. Both sources agree on the text; வாழுங் is the sandhi form of வாழும் before குடி.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For, when these creatures, being without a king, through fear dispersed in all directions, the Lord created a king for the protection of this whole (creation),”
hinduism.explanation: Manu explains that kingship was created because, without a king, people scattered in fear and could not live securely.
hinduism.tie_back: The subjects ‘live looking to the sceptre’ because, without it, ordinary life cannot go on.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass: as showers that water the earth. In his days shall the righteous flourish; and abundance of peace so long as the moon endureth.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm prays that the just king will be for his people what rain is to the cut grass, bringing new life and peace.
christianity.tie_back: The same picture as the Kural: the righteous ruler is to his people what rain is to the earth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Surely! Everyone of you is a guardian and is responsible for his charges: The Imam (ruler) of the people is a guardian and is responsible for his subjects;”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the ruler as a shepherd whose flock depends on him and for whom he must answer.
islam.tie_back: The flock looking to its shepherd matches the people looking to the sceptre.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When the righteous are increased, the people rejoice; but when the wicked beareth rule, the people sigh.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says the people’s condition follows the character of those who rule them.
judaism.tie_back: Because the people’s welfare hangs on the ruler’s justice, they live ‘looking to the sceptre’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When cattle cross a river, if the bull goes straight, they all go straight, because their leader is straight. So it is for humans: when the one deemed chief does the right thing, what do you expect the rest to do? The whole nation sleeps at ease, when the king is just.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a people to a herd crossing a river that follows the lead bull, straight or crooked.
buddhism.tie_back: The whole nation ‘sleeps at ease’ under a just king, just as the people live by looking to the straight sceptre.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.70, Adhammika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: When, through the fault of time, the power of the wish-fulfilling trees declined and the twins began to break the old laws, the people went to Rishabha, told him of the wrongdoing, and begged him to be their king, saying no one else like him could be found among them.
jainism.explanation: In Jain sacred history, kingship begins when nature's free provision fails. People who once lived from the wishing-trees now have to look to a ruler to keep order and sustain them.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that as all life looks to the sky for rain, subjects look to the king's sceptre. Hemacandra's account describes the moment the people of the first age turned from the failing wishing-trees to Rishabha's rule for their survival.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1, ch. 2, part 8 ‘Coronation as king’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Leaving the water, the fish cannot live; the rainbird cannot live without the raindrops from the clouds.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan uses the rainbird's total dependence on rain from the clouds as an image of the soul's dependence on God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the people live looking to the sceptre as all living things look to the sky for rain; Guru Arjan uses the same picture of life hanging on rain from above, though for him the dependence is on God, not a king.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 708, Raag Jaithsree (Jaithsree ki Vaar), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “All the people look towards him while he settles causes with true judgements:”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the king favoured by the Muses, on whom the whole people fix their eyes as he gives straight verdicts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s own phrase: the people ‘look to’ the king (நோக்கி) as he judges rightly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He is the bond which fastens the commonwealth together, he is the breath of life to all those thousands, who by themselves would become merely an encumbrance and a source of plunder if that directing mind were withdrawn”
philosophy.explanation: Writing to Nero, Seneca compares the ruler to the mind that directs the body and says the great multitude lives by him and would fall into ruin without him.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's image of all life looking to the rain, Seneca makes the ruler the very breath by which the people live.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Of Clemency (De Clementia), Book I, ch. 4 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: Hammurabi sets up his law code on a public stela
real_life_example.event: Toward the end of his reign, King Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 of his legal decisions, covering matters from prices and trade to family and criminal law, inscribed on a diorite stela set up in a temple. In the epilogue, Hammurabi invites any oppressed person who has a case at law to come and stand before his image, read the inscription and learn what is just. The best-preserved stela was found at Susa in 1901 and is now in the Louvre in Paris.
real_life_example.explanation: By placing the law in public view, the king presented justice as something his subjects could look to and rely on, not merely the ruler's private will.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the people of a land look to the king's sceptre as living things look to the sky for rain, and Hammurabi's stela explicitly invited every wronged subject to look to the king's justice.

tamil:
அந்தணர் நூற்கும் அறத்திற்கும் ஆதியாய்
நின்றது மன்னவன் கோல்.
transliteration:
Andhanar Noorkum Araththirkum Aadhiyaai
Nindradhu Mannavan Kol.
meaning: A king’s fair rule is what holds up the holy books of the learned priests and the dharma (the right way of living) that those books teach.
elementary: Think of a town library. The books are wonderful, but if nobody keeps the doors safe and the roof mended, the books get ruined and people stop reading. A fair ruler is like the person who keeps the library safe, so that good teachings and good behaviour can last.
university: Parimelazhagar takes அந்தணர் நூல் as the Vedas and அறம் as the dharma they lay down, and he explains ஆதியாய் நின்றது (‘stood as the origin’) causally: if the sceptre fails, the Veda is forgotten and dharma lapses, so the sceptre is their support, not their source in time. Varadarasan follows him (‘the scripture revered by the Brahmins’). Modern commentators widen the terms: Solomon Pappaiah reads அந்தணர் as ‘those who cultivate wisdom’ and நூல் as their books of knowledge, Kalaignar speaks of ‘the books of the virtuous’, and Sivayogi Sivakumar reads அந்தணர் as ‘those who know the end’. The couplet sets out a characteristic Kural view: learning and morality are not self-sustaining; they need a just political order to protect them. Pope’s ‘Learning and virtue of the sages spring / From all-controlling sceptre of the king’ overstates the idea of origin. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That sceptre on which the well-being and progress of the sciences of Anvikshaki, the triple Vedas, and Varta depend is known as Danda (punishment).”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya says the well-being of philosophy, the three Vedas and economic life all depend on the king’s sceptre of just punishment.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s thesis word for word: the Vedas and the order of life rest on the king’s கோல்.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks Christians to pray for rulers because stable government is what allows a godly and honest life.
christianity.tie_back: Religion and virtue flourish under the ruler’s protection, which is the Kural’s point.

islam.quote_or_event: “We have already sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance that the people may maintain [their affairs] in justice. And We sent down iron, wherein is great military might and benefits for the people,”
islam.explanation: The verse puts scripture, the balance of justice and ‘iron’ (coercive power) side by side as the gifts that keep human society just.
islam.tie_back: Scripture needs the balance and the iron, just as the sages’ books and dharma need the sceptre.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In all matters, his deeds shall be for the sake of heaven. His purpose and intent shall be to elevate the true faith and fill the world with justice, destroying the power of the wicked and waging the wars of God.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides defines the purpose of Jewish kingship as raising up the true faith and filling the world with justice.
judaism.tie_back: The king’s power exists to uphold religion and righteousness, as in the Kural.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 4:10 (trans. E. Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta, the Buddha describes the duty of a wheel-turning monarch: relying on the Dhamma and honouring it, he is to provide righteous protection for his household, troops, nobles, brahmins and householders, town and country people, ascetics and brahmins, and even animals and birds, and to allow no wrongdoing in his realm.
buddhism.explanation: The ideal king’s protective rule makes room for recluses and brahmins to live out their spiritual life.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the righteous ruler the guardian under whom teachers of dharma can flourish.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The example and advice of Samprati induced his vassals to embrace and patronize his creed, so that not only in his own kingdom, but also in the adjacent countries, the monks could practice their religion.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra's history of the Jain elders credits the Mauryan king Samprati with protection and patronage that let the mendicant order and its teaching flourish across and beyond his realm.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the just sceptre is what keeps the sages' scriptures and dharma standing, and the Samprati story makes the same claim from the Jain side: the monks could practise their dharma because a righteous king supported them.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Pariśiṣṭaparvan (Sthavirāvalī) XI, as summarised by Hermann Jacobi; quoted in ‘The Jain Church After Mahavira’, jainworld.com

sikhism.quote_or_event: In 1609 Guru Hargobind built the Akal Takht at Amritsar, a temple and assembly hall where both the spiritual and the temporal affairs of the Sikh community could be settled, and he bore two swords for his twin authority, temporal (miri) and spiritual (piri).
sikhism.explanation: From Hargobind onward Sikh tradition joins temporal authority to the spiritual, with temporal power set to guard the community's faith.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the king's sceptre is the foundation that keeps the sages' scriptures and dharma standing; in Sikh tradition the seat of temporal authority stands to protect the life of the Guru's word.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Guru Hargobind” (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Achilles swears by the sceptre that the sons of the Achaeans carry in their hands when they give judgment, the men who guard the ordinances (themistes) that come from Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer the sceptre is the visible sign that the judge-king holds and protects the god-given laws.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The sceptre as guardian of sacred law is close to the Kural’s கோல் upholding scripture and dharma.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But justice is the bond of men in states, for the administration of justice, which is the determination of what is just, is the principle of order in political society.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that people without law and justice are the most savage of animals, and that the administration of justice is what holds a state together.
philosophy.tie_back: For both writers, justice administered by the ruler is the foundation on which the rest of human goodness stands.

real_life_example.event_title: Goryeo carves the Tripitaka Koreana
real_life_example.place: Goryeo Korea (the woodblocks are now at Haeinsa Temple, South Korea)
real_life_example.event: During the Mongol invasions of Korea, which began in 1231, the Goryeo court under King Gojong undertook to carve the entire Buddhist canon onto wooden printing blocks, in the belief that the Buddha's protection could help drive out the invaders. The work, carried out between 1237 and 1248, produced more than 81,000 blocks. The woodblocks are still kept at Haeinsa Temple, where they are inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register and their storage halls are a World Heritage Site.
real_life_example.explanation: In a time of invasion, royal authority and resources preserved a complete body of sacred learning that has survived for nearly eight centuries.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the king's rule is the foundation that keeps the scriptures of the sages and the dharma they teach standing, and the Goryeo court used its power to preserve the whole Buddhist canon.

tamil:
குடிதழீஇக் கோலோச்சும் மாநில மன்னன்
அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kutidhazheeik Kolochchum Maanila Mannan
Atidhazheei Nirkum Ulaku.
meaning: The whole world holds on to the feet of a great king who rules with love and keeps his people close.
elementary: A team captain who looks after every player, helping the slow ones and cheering up the scared ones, ends up with a team that would follow her anywhere. People hold on to a leader who holds on to them first.
university: The couplet turns on a chiasmus of the verb தழுவு (embrace), used twice in the lengthened form தழீஇ: the king embraces the people (குடி தழீஇ), and the world embraces his feet (அடி தழீஇ). The long vowel (இசைநிறை அளபெடை) fills out the metre and gives the word emphasis. கோல் ஓச்சுதல், ‘wielding the sceptre’, is the idiom for ruling. Parimelazhagar explains ‘embracing the subjects’ as protecting them with love and learning what they lack; ‘clinging to his feet’ means the world will not leave him, so his kingdom stands firm. Varadarasan: ‘the world holds fast to the feet of the king who rules embracing his people with love’. Pappaiah turns it into people living ‘around the feet’ of such a ruler, and Kalaignar has the whole earth honouring the footsteps of a good government. In சுற்றந்தழால் (Ch. 53) Valluvar used the same verb for embracing kin; here the embrace is extended to the whole people. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In the happiness of his subjects lies his happiness; in their welfare his welfare; whatever pleases himself he shall not consider as good, but whatever pleases his subjects he shall consider as good.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya tells the king to treat his people’s happiness and welfare as his own.
hinduism.tie_back: This is what குடி தழீஇ means in practice: the king takes the people’s good as his own.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts rulers who lord it over others with his own rule, that the greatest must be the servant of all.
christianity.tie_back: Greatness that comes from serving the people is the kind the Kural says the world will cling to.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best of your rulers are those whom you love and who love you, who invoke God's blessings upon you and you invoke His blessings upon them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the best rulers as those bound to their people in mutual love and prayer.
islam.tie_back: This is the same two-way embrace: the ruler holds the people and the people hold the ruler.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever.”
judaism.explanation: The elders advise the young king Rehoboam that if he serves the people kindly, they will be loyal to him for ever; he rejects their advice and loses most of the kingdom.
judaism.tie_back: The same promise as the Kural: embrace the people and they will cling to you for good.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All men are my children. What I desire for my own children, and I desire their welfare and happiness both in this world and the next, that I desire for all men.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist emperor Ashoka tells his judicial officers that he wants every subject’s welfare as a father wants his children’s.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka’s paternal embrace of all subjects is the குடி தழீஇ ideal carved in stone.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Kalinga Rock Edict I (trans. S. Dhammika)

jainism.quote_or_event: “During his reign he taught, for the benefit of the people, the seventy-two sciences, of which writing is the first, arithmetic the most important, and the knowledge of omens the last, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men.”
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sūtra presents Rishabha, called ‘First King’ before he became the first Tīrthaṅkara, as a ruler who spent his reign giving his people every skill they needed to live.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural pictures a king who embraces his people and is embraced in return by the whole world, and Rishabha, the Jain model of a king devoted to his subjects' welfare, is still revered by Jains at his feet.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Ṛṣabha §211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Let no one chase after and attack anyone else. Let all abide in peace, under this Benevolent Rule.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan proclaims halemi raj, a gentle and benevolent rule under the merciful Lord's command, in which no one harms another and all live at ease.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the world clings to the feet of the king who rules embracing his people; Guru Arjan's benevolent rule, where all abide in peace, is the Sikh picture of such rule.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 74, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Ithacan assembly, Mentor protests that no one now remembers Odysseus, who ruled his people gently, like a father, and bitterly suggests that kings might as well be harsh and unjust from now on.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus is held up as the model king who treated his people like a father, and the people’s forgetfulness is condemned.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It gives the Kural’s ideal, the king who embraces his people, and complains when the loyalty that should follow is missing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “That man's greatness alone rests upon a secure foundation, whom all men know to be as much on their side as he is above them … at whose approach they do not fly in terror, as though some evil and dangerous animal had sprung out from its den, but flock to him as they would to the bright and health-giving sunshine.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca adds that the subjects of such a ruler guard his sleep, surround and defend him, and offer their own bodies to protect him.
philosophy.tie_back: The ruler who stands on his people's side is held fast by them, as the Kural's world clings to the feet of the king who embraces his people.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Of Clemency (De Clementia), Book I, ch. 3 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: Thailand honours King Chulalongkorn, the Great Beloved King
real_life_example.event: King Chulalongkorn (Rama V) came to the throne of Siam in 1868 and, after his coronation in 1873, carried out sweeping reforms beginning with the abolition of slavery, which was completed by the Slave Abolition Act of 1905, along with new law courts, schools, railways and a system of twelve ministries. He died on 23 October 1910 after ruling for 42 years and became known as Phra Piya Maharaj, the Great Beloved King. The anniversary of his death is a national holiday on which Thais lay wreaths at his equestrian statue in Bangkok's Royal Plaza and at other statues of him, in addition to the flowers that many offer there throughout the year.
real_life_example.explanation: More than a century after his death, his people still gather at the feet of his statue, a lasting sign of the affection earned by a ruler remembered for caring for his subjects.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world clings to the feet of the great king who rules while embracing his people, and Thais still gather at the foot of Chulalongkorn's statue to honour him.

tamil:
இயல்புளிக் கோலோச்சும் மன்னவன் நாட்ட
பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு.
transliteration:
Iyalpulik Kolochchum Mannavan Naatta
Peyalum Vilaiyulum Thokku.
meaning: In the country of a king who rules by fair law, the seasonal rains come and the harvests are rich, both together.
elementary: When a family shares fairly and nobody grabs, dinner time is happy and there is enough for everyone. The old Tamil poets believed a whole country works that way: when the ruler is fair, even the rain and the crops seem to join in.
university: இயல்புளி is இயல்பு with the instrumental ending உளி (= ஆல்), ‘by the proper nature/way’. Parimelazhagar glosses it as ruling according to the method laid down in the books of statecraft (நீதிநூல்), and Varadarasan (‘நீதி முறைப்படி’) and Pappaiah (‘அரச நீதிநூல்கள் கூறியபடி’) follow him. நாட்ட is a genitive plural predicate, ‘belong to his land’. பெயல் is seasonal rainfall and விளையுள் the abundant yield. The final தொக்கு (having gathered together) means the two are always found together there. Behind the couplet lies a belief found across ancient cultures, that the king’s righteousness governs the fertility of the land. Valluvar states the negative in the next chapter: முறைகோடி மன்னவன் செய்யின் உறைகோடி ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல் (559). Kalaignar reads it as a simile, that just government is like timely rain bringing a good harvest, which softens the causal claim. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Whether it is the king that makes the age, or, it is the age that makes the king, is a question about which thou shouldst not entertain any doubt. The truth is that the king makes the age.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma teaches that when the king rules fully by the science of just punishment the Krita age sets in and the earth yields crops in abundance, while under an unjust king the clouds do not pour seasonably and crops fail.
hinduism.tie_back: The same causal chain as the Kural: righteous rule brings rain and harvest together.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section LXIX (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment. … Then judgment shall dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness remain in the fruitful field.”
christianity.explanation: Isaiah foresees a righteous king, and a time when justice and righteousness make even the wilderness fruitful.
christianity.tie_back: Just rule and fruitful land belong together, as the Kural says.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if only the people of the cities had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied [the messengers], so We seized them for what they were earning.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says a community’s faith and God-consciousness would open blessings from sky and earth.
islam.tie_back: Blessings from heaven (rain) and earth (harvest) depend on moral order, as in the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If ye walk in My statutes, and keep My commandments, and do them; then I will give your rains in their season, and the land shall yield her produce, and the trees of the field shall yield their fruit.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah promises rain in season and a full harvest if Israel lives by God’s laws.
judaism.tie_back: Rain in season and yield together, as a reward for living by the law, is the Kural’s பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “At a time when kings are principled, royal officials become principled. … the heavens provide plenty of rain. When the heavens provide plenty of rain, the crops ripen well.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces a chain from righteous kings through officials and people to regular seasons, good rain and ripening crops.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s claim itself: a principled king means good rain and good harvest together.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.70, Adhammika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was brought into the family of the Gñâtris their silver increased, their gold increased; their riches, corn, majesty, and kingdom increased; their army, train, treasure, storehouse, town, seraglio, subjects, and glory increased”
jainism.explanation: Because the realm prospered from the moment the future Tīrthaṅkara was conceived, his parents named him Vardhamāna, ‘the Increaser’.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural links righteous rule to abundant harvests in the land, and the Kalpa Sūtra likewise tells of a royal house whose corn, treasure and subjects multiplied in the presence of great merit.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The rain has fallen; I have found the Transcendent Lord God.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan uses the coming of the rain as an image of grace and fulfilment.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says seasonal rain and rich harvests belong together in the land of a lawful king; Gurbani also links rain with blessing, but the rain is sent by God rather than earned by a ruler's justice.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 105, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But they who give straight judgements to strangers and to the men of the land, and go not aside from what is just, their city flourishes, and the people prosper in it: … The earth bears them victual in plenty, and on the mountains the oak bears acorns upon the top and bees in the midst.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod teaches that Zeus rewards cities whose judges give straight verdicts with peace and a generous earth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: ‘Straight judgements’ are the Greek செங்கோல், and plenty from the earth follows, just as in the Kural.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225–233 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But those officers whose land he sees lying idle and with but few inhabitants, owing either to the harshness of their government, their insolence, or their neglect, he punishes, and making them to cease from their office he appoints other rulers in their place.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells Critobulus that the Persian king rewards governors whose districts are thickly peopled and richly cultivated, and removes those whose land lies waste through harsh or careless rule.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Xenophon ties the fruitfulness of a land to the quality of its government, though through administration rather than seasonal rain.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Oeconomicus (The Economist), ch. IV, 8 (tr. H. G. Dakyns)

real_life_example.event_title: Todar Mal's revenue settlement under Akbar
real_life_example.event: Under the Mughal emperor Akbar, the revenue minister Raja Todar Mal reorganised the land revenue of northern India. Land was carefully measured, using lengths of bamboo joined with iron rings in place of hemp ropes, and the government gathered ten years of local figures on crop yields and prices to set average rates for each crop in each revenue circle.
