Under this system, called zabt, the revenue demand was fixed according to the quality of the soil and the continuity of cultivation, at between one-third and one-half of the value of the produce.
real_life_example.explanation: Assessing taxes on measured land and long-term average harvests replaced arbitrary demands with a known rule, one reason Akbar's administration is remembered for its order.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural links rule by proper law with abundant harvests, and Todar Mal's settlement shows a government binding its demands to the real yield of the land rather than to the ruler's whim.

tamil:
வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது மன்னவன்
கோலதூஉங் கோடா தெனின்.
transliteration:
Velandru Vendri Tharuvadhu Mannavan
Koladhooung Kotaa Thenin.
meaning: A king wins not by his spear but by his scepter (his rule), as long as that rule stays straight and fair.
elementary: A kid who wins a game by cheating doesn’t really win, because soon nobody wants to play with him. A kid who plays fair keeps her friends and keeps winning. For a ruler too, being fair is stronger than being scary.
university: The couplet sets வேல் (spear, the emblem of military force) against கோல் (sceptre, the emblem of justice), two words that differ by a single consonant. அதூஉம், the lengthened form of அதுவும் (‘that too’, with அளபெடை), adds a condition: the sceptre gives victory only if it too does not bend (கோடாது எனின்). The verb கோடு, ‘to bend, be crooked’, is the root of கொடுங்கோல் (tyranny, Ch. 56). Parimelazhagar explains that the spear wins only because the subjects stand loyally with a just king, so victory really comes from the sceptre and the spear is its instrument. Varadarasan and Pappaiah agree; Kalaignar makes the contrast explicit: not the spear that fells enemies, but the unbending sceptre that lets the people live. The point anticipates the chapters on the army (77–78), which treat military strength as dependent on the loyalty that just rule creates. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Thither is victory where righteousness is!”
hinduism.explanation: Vyasa reminds Gandhari that for all eighteen days of the war, when Duryodhana begged her to bless his victory, she replied only that victory lies where righteousness is; the righteous side won.
hinduism.tie_back: Victory follows dharma, not arms: the sceptre, not the spear, as the Kural says.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Stri Parva, Section 14 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist says a king’s safety does not come from the size of his army.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it denies that military force is what secures a king.

islam.quote_or_event: The jurist Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) is widely quoted as teaching that God upholds a just state even if it is unbelieving, and does not uphold an unjust state even if it is Muslim, because the world can endure with justice joined to unbelief but not with injustice joined to faith.
islam.explanation: A major Islamic legal thinker makes justice, rather than power or even religious label, the thing that keeps a state standing.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point: a state’s lasting success depends on a straight sceptre.
islam.source: Ibn Taymiyya, as cited from Majmu‘ al-Fatawa and his writings on public order (hisba)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.”
judaism.explanation: The prophet tells Zerubbabel that the Temple will be rebuilt not by force but by God’s spirit.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts reject force as what really decides success.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Now it is conquest by Dhamma that Beloved-of-the-Gods considers to be the best conquest.”
buddhism.explanation: After the slaughter of the Kalinga war, Ashoka renounced conquest by arms and declared that conquest by righteousness is the best kind.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka discovered in practice what the Kural states: victory by the sceptre, not by the spear.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict XIII (trans. S. Dhammika)

jainism.quote_or_event: When Bharata, the first Cakravartin, and his brother Bāhubali faced each other with their armies, they agreed to settle their dispute through personal contests, beginning with an unblinking eye-fight, instead of a battle that would slaughter their soldiers. Bāhubali won, but at the moment of victory he renounced his kingdom and became a monk.
jainism.explanation: The best-known Jain story about royal conflict refuses to let the spear decide. Armies are set aside, and the real victory turns out to be Bāhubali's conquest of his own pride and anger.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a king's victory comes from his sceptre, not his spear. The Bharata–Bāhubali story likewise declines to let weapons and soldiers settle a royal quarrel.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1, ch. 5, part 11 ‘The fight between Bharata and Bāhubali’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That king sits upon the throne, who is worthy of that throne. Those who realize the True Lord, they alone are the true kings.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says rightful kingship rests on worthiness and truth, not on the mere possession of power.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says victory comes not from the spear but from the sceptre that does not bend; Guru Nanak likewise locates true kingship in worth and truth rather than in force.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1088, Raag Maaroo (Maaroo ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For the son of Cronos has ordained this law for men, that fishes and beasts and winged fowls should devour one another, for right is not in them; but to mankind he gave right which proves far the best.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his brother to give up violence, because Zeus gave humans justice, which proves far better than the rule of force among animals.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Right proving ‘far the best’ over force is the Kural’s preference for the sceptre over the spear.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 276–280 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But, of all motives, none is better adapted to secure influence and hold it fast than love; nothing is more foreign to that end than fear.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero argues that no amount of armed power can withstand the hatred of the many, as the fate of tyrants shows, while the affection won by just rule keeps power safe for ever.
philosophy.tie_back: Lasting victory comes from just rule that wins the people, not from force, which is the Kural's sceptre set above the spear.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book II, §23 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))

real_life_example.event_title: James II's army melts away in the Glorious Revolution
real_life_example.event: James II had alienated many of his subjects through acts such as suspending laws without Parliament's consent and keeping a standing army. When William of Orange landed at Torbay in Devon on 5 November 1688, so many of James's officers deserted, among them Lieutenant-General John Churchill, that James dared not risk a pitched battle, and his own daughter Princess Anne and her husband also abandoned him. Without a major battle, James fled to France in December, and in 1689 the crown was offered to William and Mary together with a Declaration of Rights listing the grievances against him.
real_life_example.explanation: A king with a standing army lost his throne almost without a fight, because those who carried his weapons no longer stood behind his rule.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says it is not the spear that brings a king victory but his sceptre, provided it does not bend, and James II's army was of no use to him once his sceptre had bent.

tamil:
இறைகாக்கும் வையகம் எல்லாம் அவனை
முறைகாக்கும் முட்டாச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Iraikaakkum Vaiyakam Ellaam Avanai
Muraikaakkum Muttaach Cheyin.
meaning: The king protects the whole world, and justice protects the king, as long as he never fails to do justice.
elementary: If you always tell the truth and treat your friends fairly, then when someone spreads a nasty rumour about you, your friends stand up for you. Your fairness becomes your shield. It works the same way for rulers.
university: The two halves mirror each other with the verb காக்கும் (guards): இறை காக்கும் வையகம் எல்லாம் (the lord guards the whole world) and அவனை முறை காக்கும் (justice guards him). The condition முட்டாச் செயின், ‘if he does it without lapse’ (முட்டு = obstruction, failure), is the hinge. Parimelazhagar explains that the merit of just rule protects the king from harm that would otherwise come to him; Varadarasan: ‘if he rules without harming justice, that justice itself protects him’. Pappaiah reads முட்டா as qualifying முறை, i.e. ‘his flawless, upright rule protects him’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the condition oddly (‘even if they err’), which the grammar does not support. The idea is the political counterpart of the Aram principle that dharma protects those who protect it; compare Manu’s ‘dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ’. Both sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Justice, being violated, destroys; justice, being preserved, preserves: therefore justice must not be violated, lest violated justice destroy us.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches the classic principle dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ: justice protects those who protect it and destroys those who violate it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘justice guards him who does not fail it’ is the same maxim.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb promises a lasting throne to the king who judges the poor faithfully.
christianity.tie_back: Just judgment secures the king himself, which is the Kural’s point.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah will give shade, to seven, on the Day when there will be no shade but His. (These seven persons are) a just ruler, …”
islam.explanation: First among the seven whom God shelters on the Day of Judgment is the just ruler.
islam.tie_back: The ruler’s justice becomes his protection, here in the next world.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is an abomination to kings to commit wickedness; For the throne is established by righteousness.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb holds that a king’s throne is made firm by righteousness, not by wickedness.
judaism.tie_back: Righteousness upholding the throne is justice guarding the king.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Dhamma surely protects one who practices Dhamma.”
buddhism.explanation: The elder Dhammika teaches that Dhamma, well practised, protects the one who practises it and brings happiness.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle to the king: practise justice and justice guards you.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.”
jainism.explanation: Queen Kamalāvatī warns King Ishukāra, who is about to seize property, that neither wealth nor power can protect a ruler; only dharma can.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the king guards the world and justice in turn guards the king. The queen tells her king the same thing: the Law alone protects him.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The mythical bull is Dharma, the son of compassion; this is what patiently holds the earth in its place.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak reinterprets the myth of the bull that bears the earth: what really holds the world in place is dharma, born of compassion.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the king guards the world and justice in turn guards the king; Guru Nanak likewise names righteousness as the power that keeps everything standing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib, Pauri 16, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Next he married bright Themis who bare the Horae (Hours), and Eunomia (Order), Dike (Justice), and blooming Eirene (Peace), who mind the works of mortal men,”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod makes Order, Justice and Peace daughters of Zeus and Themis who watch over human affairs.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Justice as a guardian power watching over those who honour it gives the Kural’s idea a mythic form.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that of all means of gaining and keeping power, none is better suited than being loved and none worse than being feared; fear, he says, is a poor guardian of lasting power, while goodwill keeps it safe for ever, and he points to the violent ends of tyrants.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, a ruler’s best protection is the goodwill won by just and generous conduct, not guards or terror.
philosophy.tie_back: The ruler who guards others justly is himself guarded, as the Kural says.

real_life_example.event_title: King Juan Carlos defends Spain's constitution against the 1981 coup
real_life_example.event: On 23 February 1981, Civil Guard officers led by Antonio Tejero stormed Spain's Congress of Deputies during the vote to install a new prime minister and held the deputies and members of the government captive for about 18 hours. That night King Juan Carlos appeared on national television to denounce the uprising and call for loyalty to the democratic constitution and the elected government. The coup collapsed, constitutional order was restored, and its leaders were tried and imprisoned.
real_life_example.explanation: Because the king stood firmly by the constitution, the lawful order he upheld gave him the authority to stop the coup, and the episode strengthened both Spanish democracy and his own position.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the king guards the world and justice guards the king, so long as he upholds it without fail, and Juan Carlos's loyalty to the lawful order protected both his country and his crown in 1981.

tamil:
எண்பதத்தான் ஓரா முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்
தண்பதத்தான் தானே கெடும்.
transliteration:
Enpadhaththaan Oraa Muraiseyyaa Mannavan
Thanpadhaththaan Thaane Ketum.
meaning: A king whom people cannot easily reach, and who does not look into their problems and give fair judgments, will fall low and be ruined, even without an enemy.
elementary: Imagine a class monitor who locks herself away and never listens when kids come to her with a problem. Problems pile up, everyone gets upset, and soon nobody trusts her. She didn’t need an enemy to lose her job. She lost it all by herself.
university: எண்பதம் means ‘easy access’ (எண் = easy, பதம் = occasion or audience; Varadarasan: எளிய செவ்வி); தண்பதம் means a ‘low state’ (Parimelazhagar: தாழ்ந்த நிலை). The two rhyming compounds frame the couplet. Commentators take the negation of ஓரா (not examining) and முறைசெய்யா (not doing justice) as extending back over எண்பதத்தான், so the king is one who is not accessible, does not investigate, and does not give justice; Pope accordingly renders ‘Hard of access, nought searching out’. Pappaiah keeps the positive reading grammatically but gives the same sense. தானே கெடும் (‘perishes of himself’) is taken by Parimelazhagar and Varadarasan to mean ‘even without enemies’ (பகைவரில்லாமலும்): neglect of justice is self-destruction. Kalaignar departs and reads எண்பதம் as pomp or display. The couplet links accessibility to justice, a theme taken up again in வெருவந்தசெய்யாமை (Ch. 57). The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Uttara Kanda of the Valmiki Ramayana, Rama tells Lakshmana the story of King Nriga, who left two brahmins disputing over a cow waiting at his palace gate for days without a hearing; in their anger they cursed him to live as a lizard in a pit, and Rama draws the lesson that a king must never keep those seeking justice waiting.
hinduism.explanation: A king ruined not by an enemy but by his own failure to give petitioners a hearing.
hinduism.tie_back: Nriga is the Kural’s inaccessible king who ‘perishes of himself’.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (the story of Nriga, told by Rama)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that whoever refuses to hear the poor will one day cry out and not be heard himself.
christianity.tie_back: The ruler who shuts out petitioners brings about his own downfall, as in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “If Allah puts anyone in the position of authority over the affairs of the Muslims, and he secludes himself (from them), not fulfilling their needs, wants, and poverty, Allah will keep Himself away from him, not fulfilling his need, want and poverty.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that a ruler who shuts himself off from his people’s needs will find God shut off from his own; on hearing it, Mu‘awiya appointed a man to attend to people’s needs.
islam.tie_back: An almost exact counterpart of the Kural’s inaccessible ruler who ruins himself.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 2948 (graded sahih by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: “See, thy matters are good and right; but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee.”
judaism.explanation: Absalom stood at the city gate telling every litigant that King David had no one to hear his case, and so ‘stole the hearts’ of Israel and raised a revolt.
judaism.tie_back: A king’s failure to hear cases nearly costs David his throne, without any foreign enemy, just as the Kural warns.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore your aim should be to act with impartiality. … Those who are bored with the administration of justice will not be promoted;”
buddhism.explanation: Ashoka warns his judicial officers that indifference, laziness and weariness lead to unjust imprisonment, and that those bored with justice will not advance.
buddhism.tie_back: Neglecting to examine cases and give justice is the fault the Kural condemns.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Kalinga Rock Edict I (trans. S. Dhammika)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
jainism.explanation: The sage tells King Śreṇika that a person's own wrong conduct does more damage than any outside foe, and in the same sermon he says the self is ‘friend and foe’ (20.37).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's king, inaccessible and failing to do justice, is brought down by his own conduct ‘even without an enemy’, which is exactly the Jain claim that one's own perversity outdoes any enemy.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Dark Age of Kali Yuga is the knife, and the kings are butchers; righteousness has sprouted wings and flown away.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak indicts the rulers of his age, who preyed on their subjects instead of giving them justice.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a king who is hard to reach and does not give justice sinks and perishes of himself; Guru Nanak paints that unjust rule, in which righteousness itself has fled.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 145, Raag Maajh (Majh ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Homer compares the rout of the Trojans to the autumn storm that Zeus sends against men who give crooked judgments in the assembly and drive out justice, heedless of the gods, so that the rivers flood and the works of men are ruined.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, a community’s neglect of justice brings destruction without any human enemy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ruin that comes from within, through crooked judgment, is the Kural’s தானே கெடும்.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “An old woman once assailed Demetrius as he was passing by, and demanded many times that he give her a hearing. ‘I have no time,’ said Demetrius. ‘Then don't be king,’ screamed the old woman.”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch says Demetrius was hard to approach, kept embassies waiting for years and threw his subjects' petitions into a river, so that the Macedonians felt insulted rather than ruled; soon afterwards his army deserted him and he lost Macedonia.
philosophy.tie_back: The king who cannot be reached and will not hear complaints undoes his own kingdom, exactly as the Kural warns.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Demetrius, ch. 42 (tr. Bernadotte Perrin)

real_life_example.event_title: The Wanli Emperor withdraws from government
real_life_example.event: The Wanli Emperor of the Ming dynasty, who reigned from 1573 to 1620, increasingly withdrew from government after the death of his able Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng in 1582. For years he neglected daily business, failed to appear at court audiences and refused to read the memorials his officials sent him, while factional quarrels among officials grew and more and more of his responsibilities passed to palace eunuchs. Strained by costly wars and an empty treasury, the Ming dynasty fell in 1644, less than a quarter of a century after his death.
real_life_example.explanation: Historians commonly trace the Ming dynasty's decline to Wanli's long withdrawal, when officials could no longer reach the throne and the empire's problems went unresolved.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a king whom his people cannot reach, and who does not look into their complaints and give justice, sinks low and perishes by his own doing, and the Wanli Emperor's closed court began the ruin of his dynasty.

tamil:
குடிபுறங் காத்தோம்பிக் குற்றம் கடிதல்
வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Kutipurang Kaaththompik Kutram Katidhal
Vatuvandru Vendhan Thozhil.
meaning: Protecting the people from outside harm, caring for them, and punishing crime is not a fault in a king. It is his proper job.
elementary: A lifeguard who blows her whistle at kids running by the pool isn’t being mean. It is her job, keeping everyone safe. A fair ruler who stops people from doing wrong is doing the same kind of job.
university: Parimelazhagar separates two kinds of protection: புறம் காத்து, guarding the people from others (enemies, robbers, grasping officials), and ஓம்பி, protecting them from himself (for example, by not over-taxing). Only then comes குற்றம் கடிதல், removing crime by fitting punishment. வடு அன்று (‘not a scar or blemish’) answers an implied objection that punishment, as a form of harm, conflicts with the ethic of non-injury taught in the Aram section (e.g. Ch. 32–33); வேந்தன் தொழில் (‘the king’s work’) makes it a duty of office. Varadarasan follows Parimelazhagar closely. Pappaiah reads குற்றம் as the people’s grievances (குறைகள்), which shifts the emphasis from punishment to redress. Kalaignar adds that the ruler should punish whoever the offender is, without fearing reproach. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads புறம் as ‘beyond the borders’. The couplet prepares for the harsher 550. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A king who punishes those who do not deserve it, and punishes not those who deserve it, brings great infamy on himself and (after death) sinks into hell.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu says that failing to punish the guilty disgraces a king as much as punishing the innocent.
hinduism.tie_back: The blemish lies in not punishing, which is the reverse side of the Kural’s ‘punishment is no blemish’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. … for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that the ruler’s sword against evildoers is part of his God-given service, not a wrong.
christianity.tie_back: Punishing wrongdoing is the ruler’s proper work, not a stain, as in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and when you judge between people to judge with justice.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an treats authority as a trust and just judgment as a command from God.
islam.tie_back: Judging and correcting wrongdoing is a sacred duty of those in authority, not a fault.

judaism.quote_or_event: “pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear it inspires, every man would swallow his neighbor alive.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina teaches that the fear government inspires is what stops people from devouring one another.
judaism.tie_back: The ruler’s power to restrain wrongdoers is a blessing to pray for, not a blemish.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It is my desire that there should be uniformity in law and uniformity in sentencing. I even go this far, to grant a three-day stay for those in prison who have been tried and sentenced to death.”
buddhism.explanation: Ashoka, a Buddhist king, kept courts and punishments but insisted on uniform law and granted a reprieve for appeals.
buddhism.tie_back: Even a king devoted to non-harm accepts punishment as part of his work, as the Kural says, while tempering it.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Pillar Edict IV (trans. S. Dhammika)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A king will be the punisher of those transgressing boundaries. Seated on a very high throne, consecrated first, having at hand the fourfold army, he should have unbroken commands.”
jainism.explanation: When the earlier laws of reproach fail and people start doing wrong, Rishabha explains that a consecrated king is needed to punish transgressors, and he is then made the first king.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that protecting the people and curbing crime by punishment is a king's proper work, not a blemish. In Jain sacred history the office of king was created for exactly that purpose.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1, ch. 2, part 8 ‘Coronation as king’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Hargobind was both pir, spiritual leader, and mir, chieftain of his people, responsible for protecting them against tyranny with force of arms.
sikhism.explanation: From the sixth Guru onward, armed protection of the community became a recognised duty of Sikh leadership.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says guarding the people and curbing wrongdoing is no blemish on a king but his proper work; Sikh tradition likewise treats protecting the people against tyranny as a duty, not a stain on spiritual authority.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Sikhism: Guru Hargobind” by W. H. McLeod (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Eumenides, Athena founds the court of the Areopagus and urges the Athenians not to banish all fear from their city, since no mortal who fears nothing remains just; the court is to be a guardian of the land, awake while others sleep.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess of wisdom establishes lawful punishment as the city’s protection.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Justice that restrains crime is presented as a gift to the city, not a stain, as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But he who desires to inflict rational punishment does not retaliate for a past wrong which cannot be undone; he has regard to the future, and is desirous that the man who is punished, and he who sees him punished, may be deterred from doing wrong again.”
philosophy.explanation: Protagoras argues that rational punishment is not revenge but a way of protecting the future by deterring wrongdoing.
philosophy.tie_back: Punishment understood as protection is the Kural’s குற்றம் கடிதல் as the king’s duty.

real_life_example.event_title: La Reynie becomes Paris's first lieutenant general of police
real_life_example.event: By an edict of March 1667, Louis XIV created the office of lieutenant of police for Paris, bringing together in one office policing duties that had been divided among many officials, and appointed Gabriel Nicolas de La Reynie, who held it until 1697. The office was responsible for public safety, fires and floods, street cleaning, the food supply and public order. Under La Reynie, streets were lit at night by thousands of lanterns and refuse was collected at fixed hours.
real_life_example.explanation: The crown treated keeping the capital safe, clean and orderly as a regular duty of government rather than an occasional show of force.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says guarding the people from harm, caring for them and curbing crime is no blemish on a king but his proper work, and the new Paris police office joined protection, public care and law enforcement in one royal duty.

tamil:
கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல் பைங்கூழ்
களைகட் டதனொடு நேர்.
transliteration:
Kolaiyir Kotiyaarai Vendhoruththal Paingoozh
Kalaikat Tadhanotu Ner.
meaning: When a king punishes cruel killers with death, it is like a farmer pulling out weeds to protect the young crop.
elementary: A gardener pulls out weeds not because she hates plants but because the weeds would choke the vegetables. The Kural says a ruler must stop people who seriously hurt others, so that everyone else can grow up safe. (Grown-ups still argue about how harsh such punishments should be.)
university: The final couplet puts the chapter’s argument about punishment in an agricultural image: பைங்கூழ் is the young green crop, and களை கட்டல் is weeding. The phrase கொலையிற் கொடியாரை is read in two ways. Varadarasan and Pappaiah take கொலையின் as instrumental, so the king punishes the cruel ‘by death’ (கொலைத்தண்டனையால்). Kalaignar takes it as the offence, so the cruel are ‘those who commit murder and similar cruelties’. Parimelazhagar’s commentary follows the first line of reading and presents capital punishment as the protection of the good, just as the weed is removed for the crop’s sake. Commentators note the tension with the Aram section’s உயிர் கொல்லாமை (not killing, Ch. 33). The usual resolution is that Aram states the individual’s ethic while Porul states the king’s duty. Modern readers such as Kalaignar keep the metaphor but stress that it applies to hardened offenders, not the ordinary wrongdoer. The next chapter, Tyranny, reverses the image. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya calls the whole book of the Arthashastra devoted to criminal justice Kantakasodhana, ‘The Removal of Thorns’, treating the suppression of the wicked, the seizure of criminals and their trial as clearing thorns out of the realm.
hinduism.explanation: Indian statecraft pictured criminals as thorns that a king must root out so that his people can move and work safely.
hinduism.tie_back: Thorns removed from the realm and weeds pulled from the crop are the same kind of image.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book IV, ‘The Removal of Thorns’ (trans. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A wise king scattereth the wicked, and bringeth the wheel over them.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb uses the image of a threshing wheel: a wise king separates out the wicked as grain is separated from chaff.
christianity.tie_back: A farming image for the king’s removal of evildoers, as in the Kural’s weeding.

islam.quote_or_event: “And there is for you in legal retribution [saving of] life, O you [people] of understanding, that you may become righteous.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that lawful retribution for murder actually preserves life in the community.
islam.tie_back: Punishing killers to protect the living is the logic of weeding to save the crop.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Morning by morning will I destroy all the wicked of the land; to cut off all the workers of iniquity from the city of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: In this royal psalm the king vows to purge the land of evildoers every day.
judaism.tie_back: The king ‘cutting off’ the wicked to keep the city whole matches the Kural’s weeding.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, the Buddha tells of a king whose realm was plagued by bandits; his wise chaplain advises that execution, imprisonment and banishment will not end the plague, and that instead the king should give seed and fodder to farmers, capital to traders and proper wages to officials, after which the country became peaceful.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist text answers crime by removing its economic causes rather than by killing offenders.
buddhism.tie_back: It is a deliberate counterpoint: where the Kural pulls the weed, the sutta improves the soil so that weeds do not grow.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Virodhi Himsa is the kind of injury which is necessarily committed in defense of person and property, against thieves, robbers, dacoits, assailants and enemies, in meeting their aggression, and in causing the least possible injury, necessary in the circumstances, in which one may find oneself.”
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics allows a householder only defensive injury against aggressors, and only the least injury the situation requires. Monks must avoid even that.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural approves of a king executing murderers the way a farmer pulls weeds. Jainism will accept force against violent offenders only as minimal, defensive injury and would not call execution a good.
jainism.source: ‘The Concept of Himsa’, jainworld.com (text from V.A. Sangave's Jaina Path of Ahimsa; page also credited to Acharya Mahapragya)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The slanderers are not allowed to stay; they are pulled out by their roots, like useless weeds.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says those who malign the Lord's servants cannot stand, but are uprooted like useless weeds.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural likens punishing the cruel to a farmer pulling weeds to save the young crop; Guru Arjan uses the same weeding image for the removal of wrongdoers.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 683, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And further, make a law by my order, that he who has no part in reverence and justice shall be put to death, for he is a plague of the state.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Protagoras’ myth, Zeus sends Hermes to give reverence and justice to all people, and orders that anyone who cannot share in them be put to death as a disease of the city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Removing one who destroys the community to save the rest is the Kural’s weeding in divine terms.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And the good physician and lawgiver of the State ought, like the wise bee-master, to keep them at a distance and prevent, if possible, their ever coming in; and if they have anyhow found a way in, then he should have them and their cells cut out as speedily as possible.”
philosophy.explanation: Plato likens the lawgiver who removes the city’s destructive ‘drones’ to a beekeeper cutting diseased cells out of the hive.
philosophy.tie_back: Cutting out what harms the hive is the same move as pulling weeds from the crop.

real_life_example.event_title: The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg delivers its verdicts
real_life_example.event: After the Second World War, the Allied powers set up the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg to try leading figures of Nazi Germany for crimes including war crimes and crimes against humanity. On 1 October 1946 the judges convicted 19 of the defendants and acquitted 3. Twelve were sentenced to death, three to life imprisonment and four to prison terms of ten to twenty years.
real_life_example.explanation: The tribunal held those responsible for mass killing to account through a court of law, with evidence and acquittals, rather than through vengeance.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares a king who punishes murderous criminals to a farmer pulling up weeds to save the green crop, and the Nuremberg tribunal removed the chief architects of mass murder so that a peaceful order could grow again.

tamil:
கொலைமேற்கொண் டாரிற் கொடிதே அலைமேற்கொண்டு
அல்லவை செய்தொழுகும் வேந்து.
transliteration:
Kolaimerkon daarir kodithe alaimerkondu
Allavai seythozhukum vendhu.
meaning: A king who keeps troubling his people and doing wrong to them is crueler than a murderer.
elementary: Picture a playground bully who knocks you over once, and then picture a class monitor who is supposed to look after everyone but pushes kids around every single day. The monitor is worse, because the hurt never stops and the one person meant to protect you is the one hurting you. Valluvar says a cruel king is like that monitor, only much bigger.
university: The chapter is the mirror image of the preceding one, செங்கோன்மை (the straight sceptre, ch. 55): கொடுங்கோல் is the ‘bent’ rod of a ruler who governs by oppression. The key word அலை means harassing or tormenting, and Parimelazhagar glosses அலைமேற்கொண்டு as taking up, out of covetousness for wealth (பொருள்வெஃகி), the business of harassing the subjects. His reason for the comparison is that the murderer’s harm lasts a moment, whereas the tyrant’s is lifelong, so ‘harassment is crueller than killing’. He also notes the grammatical point that வேந்து, a neuter-class noun, is used here of a person (திணை/பால் மயக்கம்). Manakkudavar gives substantially the same reading, while Solomon Pappaiah stresses greed for the people’s property. The text is uniform across ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com; the older continuous text on thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the unsplit sandhi forms யலைமேற்கொண் / டல்லவை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kamsa, king of Mathura, imprisoned his own father, persecuted the Yadus and had the infant children of his sister Devaki put to death one after another, until Krishna, the child he feared, grew up and killed him.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata Purana, Kamsa is the classic tyrant whose power is used against the very people and kin he should protect.
hinduism.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s cruel king, Kamsa does more harm than an ordinary killer because the whole kingdom lives under his fear.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As a roaring lion, and a ranging bear; so is a wicked ruler over the poor people.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb compares a wicked ruler to beasts of prey loose among the helpless.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks an unjust ruler alongside the most dangerous killers.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a sector among them, slaughtering their [newborn] sons and keeping their females alive. Indeed, he was of the corrupters.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an’s portrait of Pharaoh is its central image of a ruler who turns state power into ongoing oppression of his own subjects.
islam.tie_back: Pharaoh is the Kural’s tyrant exactly: a king whose rule is itself a form of killing.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ezekiel says that the princes of Jerusalem have become like wolves tearing their prey, shedding blood and destroying lives for the sake of dishonest gain.
judaism.explanation: The prophet accuses the rulers themselves, not outside enemies, of preying on the people for profit.
judaism.tie_back: It matches Parimelazhagar’s reading that the tyrant harasses his subjects out of greed for their wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The whole nation sleeps badly, when the king is unprincipled.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that when the king goes astray, his officials and then the whole people follow, just as a herd follows its lead bull.
buddhism.tie_back: The whole nation suffering day and night echoes Parimelazhagar’s point that the tyrant’s harm never stops, unlike a killer’s single act.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.70, Adhammika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Be without fear, O king; but grant safety to others also; in this transient world of living beings, why are you addicted to cruelty?”
jainism.explanation: The monk Gardabhāli answers King Sañjaya, who has been hunting terrified deer in the royal park, by asking him to give other beings the same safety he wants for himself.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls a ruler who torments his subjects crueler than a murderer, and the Jain sage likewise confronts a king directly with his cruelty toward helpless beings.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 18.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who act like tyrants are accepted and approved - recognize that this is the sign of the Dark Age of Kali Yuga.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak lists the marks of a degenerate age, and one of them is that oppression by the powerful comes to be treated as lawful and normal.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls the ruler who habitually harasses his people crueller than a professional killer; Guru Nanak likewise refuses to let accepted tyranny pass as legitimate and names it a sign of moral darkness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 902, Raag Raamkalee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Lycaon of Arcadia, a cruel ruler, served human flesh to Zeus to test him; Zeus destroyed his house and turned him into a wolf whose savage nature matched his reign.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells the story as the first example of human wickedness that moves the gods to punish the world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A king who becomes a literal wolf pictures the Kural’s claim that a tyrant is worse than an ordinary killer.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates describes how the people’s ‘protector’ becomes a tyrant: once he has tasted the blood of his own citizens through unjust trials and killings, he turns into a wolf, as in the Arcadian legend.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the tyrant is the worst of men because he turns the power of the state against those he rules.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar agree that the ruler who preys on his own people is worse than a common criminal.

real_life_example.event_title: Idi Amin expels Uganda's Asian community
real_life_example.event: On 4 August 1972 Uganda's military ruler Idi Amin ordered the country's Asian population, most of them of Indian and Pakistani descent, to leave within 90 days, claiming they were sabotaging the economy. Tens of thousands were forced out, allowed to take only what they could carry, and received no compensation for their homes and businesses. The community had played a central role in Uganda's commerce, and the expulsion contributed to the country's economic decline in the 1970s.
real_life_example.explanation: A ruler used the power of the state to strip a whole community of its livelihood and property, causing suffering that lasted for years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a king who makes a practice of harassing his people and doing injustice is crueller than a murderer, and Amin's expulsion order harmed tens of thousands for the rest of their lives.

tamil:
வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென் றதுபோலும்
கோலொடு நின்றான் இரவு.
transliteration:
Velodu nindraan iduven rathupolum
Kolodu nindraan iravu.
meaning: When a king, who has the power to punish, asks his people for money, it is like a robber with a spear on a lonely road saying, “Hand it over.”
elementary: If a big kid holding a stick says ‘Can I please have your lunch?’, it isn’t really a question, because you know what happens if you say no. Valluvar says that when a king with power over you ‘asks’ for extra money, it is the same as a robber demanding it.
university: The image is of the solitary highwayman (வேலொடு நின்றான்) and the king ‘standing with the rod’ (கோலொடு நின்றான்), the rod here meaning the power to punish (ஒறுத்தல் தொழில்). Parimelazhagar draws two inferences: ‘standing with a spear’ implies the robber is alone on a deserted road, and the word இரவு (begging, request) shows that what the king asks for is not the lawful revenue (இறைப்பொருள் அன்மை). Because the king’s request carries an unspoken threat to punish anyone who refuses, even ‘asking’ becomes tyranny; he adds that kurals 551-552 together state the fault of tyranny itself. Manakkudavar reads கோலொடு நிற்றல் as standing in the posture of one who administers justice, and adds that even a voluntary-seeming levy above the fixed dues is like robbery on the road. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take the couplet as a comment on extortionate taxation. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu warns that a king who gives no protection yet takes his share of the produce, his taxes, tolls and fines will soon sink into hell, since he takes on the sins of the people he fails to protect.
hinduism.explanation: In the Dharmashastra, taxation is fair only as payment for protection; without it, the levy becomes a sin.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point: a levy without righteous rule is just robbery.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he said unto them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you. … Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.”
christianity.explanation: John the Baptist tells tax collectors and soldiers, the two faces of state power, not to extort beyond what is due.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar, John treats demands backed by force above the lawful due as extortion.

islam.quote_or_event: After the woman of Ghamid was stoned for adultery she had confessed, the Prophet said her repentance was so sincere that even a collector of unjust taxes (ṣāḥib maks) would be forgiven if he repented like that.
islam.explanation: The hadith treats the taker of unjust levies as the extreme case of a grave sinner.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s view that exacting money by the power of office is among the worst wrongs.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Israel asks for a king, Samuel warns that the king will take their sons, their daughters, their best fields and vineyards, and a tenth of their grain and flocks, and they will become his servants.
judaism.explanation: The prophet describes kingship as, by nature, taking from the people.
judaism.tie_back: Samuel’s ‘he will take’ corresponds to the king’s demand in the Kural, which his subjects cannot refuse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: A wise chaplain advises King Mahāvijita that a kingdom plagued by bandits cannot be cured by more levies and punishments; instead the king should give seed to farmers, capital to traders and wages to officials, and the country then becomes prosperous and safe.
buddhism.explanation: The Kūṭadanta Sutta sets out a Buddhist economics of rule that relies on giving, not taking.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the positive counterpart to the Kural’s warning against a king who rules by demanding.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A man who returns, as it were, to the vomit, is not praised; but you want to confiscate the property left by the Brâhmana.”
jainism.explanation: Queen Kamalāvatī shames King Ishukāra for trying to seize the property a Brahmin gave up when he renounced the world. Jacobi notes that confiscating heirless property was then a royal privilege.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural likens a king who demands his subjects' wealth to a highwayman with a spear. The queen likewise condemns a ruler's grab for his subjects' goods as shameful.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Bringing the marriage party of sin, Babar has invaded from Kaabul, demanding our land as his wedding gift, O Lalo.”
sikhism.explanation: Addressing his disciple Bhai Lalo, Guru Nanak describes Babar's invasion as a sinful wedding party that seizes by force what it pretends to receive as a gift.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural likens a sceptred king's demand for money to a highwayman with a spear saying ‘Hand it over’; Guru Nanak likewise exposes armed power that takes wealth by force under a respectable name.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 722, Raag Tilang (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On his road to Athens the young Theseus killed a series of highway robbers, including Sciron, who made travellers wash his feet and then kicked them off the cliff, and Sinis the pine-bender. By clearing the road he showed what kind of king he would be.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Plutarch’s account, a true ruler is the one who ends robbery on the roads, not the one who practises it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar’s image of the road robber stands for the king who has forgotten this duty.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies themselves, but little kingdoms?”
philosophy.explanation: Augustine argues that without justice, the state is simply a robber band on a larger scale.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s simile turned into a general principle: a king without justice is just a robber.
philosophy.source: Augustine, City of God IV.4 (trans. Marcus Dods)

real_life_example.event_title: Charles I's forced loan and the Five Knights' Case
real_life_example.event: Unable to get the taxes he wanted from Parliament, Charles I demanded a forced loan from his subjects in 1626-27 and had more than 70 gentlemen who refused to pay imprisoned. Five of them, led by Sir Thomas Darnel, sought release through the courts in the Five Knights' Case of 1627, but the judges refused bail. In 1628 Parliament answered with the Petition of Right, which declared that no one should be taxed without Parliament's consent or imprisoned without cause shown.
real_life_example.explanation: The king called his demand a loan, but because refusal meant prison it was really taking by force.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when a ruler holding the sceptre asks his subjects for money it is like a robber with a spear saying 'hand it over', which is exactly how Charles I's forced loan worked.

tamil:
நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்
நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்.
transliteration:
Naadorum naadi muraiseyyaa mannavan
Naadorum naadu kedum.
meaning: A king who does not look into wrongs every day and give fair judgments will watch his country grow weaker every day.
elementary: If you never look after a garden, weeds creep in a little each day until the flowers are gone. A king who doesn’t check every day for unfair things happening, and fix them, lets his whole country slowly go to ruin in the same way.
university: The couplet plays on நாள் / நாடு: நாடொறும் (daily, from நாள் + தொறும்) and நாடி (examining, from நாடு-தல்), then நாடு (country). Parimelazhagar glosses: the king who does not daily examine the wrongs occurring in his land and render fitting justice will daily ‘lose’ his country. He explains that since the country is a limb (உறுப்பு) of the king, the verb ‘perish’ is attributed to him, and that ‘losing’ here means failing to enjoy its fruits (பயன் எய்தாமை). He records an alternative construal, ‘the king’s country perishes daily’ (மன்னவன் நாடு நாள்தொறும் கெடும்), which Manakkudavar and Kalaignar adopt. For the first word, thirukkural.com prints the unassimilated form நாள்தொறும், while ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the sandhi form நாடொறும்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya divides the king’s day into eighths and assigns him times to hear the petitions of citizens and country people. He warns that a king who makes petitioners wait at his door, or who is hard to reach, causes confusion in the state and disaffection among the people.
hinduism.explanation: For the Arthashastra, attending daily to the people’s complaints is the core routine of kingship.
hinduism.tie_back: It sets out as a timetable the daily enquiry that Valluvar says keeps the kingdom from decaying.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells of an unjust judge who for a long time ignored a widow pleading for justice, and gave way only because she kept coming back.
christianity.explanation: The parable assumes that a judge who neglects the cries of the weak is unjust.
christianity.tie_back: The judge is the negligent ruler of the Kural, who does not look into wrongs day by day.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that any ruler given charge of people who does not look after them with sincere care will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.
islam.explanation: The hadith makes neglect of one’s subjects a grave moral failure, not just bad administration.
islam.tie_back: It condemns the same inattentive ruler whom the Kural says will slowly lose his realm.

judaism.quote_or_event: “O house of David, thus saith the LORD: Execute justice in the morning, And deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor, Lest My fury go forth like fire…”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah tells the royal house to do justice every morning and to rescue the robbed.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Justice in the morning’ is the Kural’s daily enquiry and justice, with ruin as the price of neglect.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sīhanāda Sutta a king fails to give wealth to the needy; poverty spreads, then theft, then weapons, killing and lying, and the lifespan and beauty of the people decline generation after generation.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta traces how one royal neglect grows step by step into a society’s collapse.
buddhism.tie_back: It is a long-scale version of the Kural’s ‘day by day the country perishes’.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse without profit to him who acts contrary to the Law.”
jainism.explanation: The two Brahmin youths tell their father that every day lived without dharma is lost for good, so dharma cannot be put off.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a king who fails to do justice every day sees his country decline every day, and the Jain verse makes the same day-by-day reckoning of what is lost when dharma is neglected.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They accept bribes, and block justice.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak condemns the man who sits in the seat of judgment but takes bribes and so denies people what is rightfully theirs.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a king who does not examine wrongs and render justice every day loses a little of his country each day; Guru Nanak points to the same failure at the seat of justice.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 951, Raag Raamkalee (Raamkalee ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ play, Thebes is struck by blight and plague because the murder of King Laius was never investigated; Creon admits the Sphinx made the city set aside the unsolved crime.
greek_mythology.explanation: The city suffers because a wrong was never looked into and put right.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatizes the Kural’s warning that unexamined wrongs slowly destroy the land.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle calls the ruler the guardian of justice, and says that for this reason a true ruler does not take more than his share and labours for others.
philosophy.explanation: Rule, for Aristotle, is justified only by constant attention to what is just.
philosophy.tie_back: A ruler who fails at this guardianship is the one the Kural says wears his country away.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.6, 1134b (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Huizong's neglect of government and the fall of Kaifeng
real_life_example.event: Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty, who reigned from 1100, is remembered as a gifted painter, calligrapher and patron of the arts, and Britannica records that he sought escape from affairs of state in the pleasures of arts and letters. When the Jurchen invaded he abdicated in favour of his son in 1125-26. The Jurchen then captured the capital, Kaifeng, and took both Huizong and his son into captivity, ending the Northern Song dynasty in 1127.
real_life_example.explanation: An emperor absorbed in the arts rather than the daily business of ruling saw his realm decline and finally fall.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that a king who does not look into wrongs every day and give justice will see his country decline day by day, as Huizong's did.

tamil:
கூழுங் குடியும் ஒருங்கிழக்கும் கோல்கோடிச்
சூழாது செய்யும் அரசு.
transliteration:
Koozhung kudiyum orungizhakkum kolkodich
Choozhaathu seyyum arasu.
meaning: A king who twists justice and acts without thinking about what will happen will lose both his riches and his people at once.
elementary: Imagine a lemonade stand owner who cheats customers without thinking ahead. Soon the customers stop coming, and with them goes the money. Valluvar says a careless, unfair king loses his treasure and his people together, because the people are where the treasure comes from.
university: கூழ் (literally gruel or food) stands for wealth, and குடி for the subjects. Parimelazhagar makes the pairing precise: கூழ் is the wealth already amassed, and குடி is the people who are the source of wealth yet to be earned, so the tyrant loses past and future income together. சூழாது means ‘without deliberating’ on what will follow, and கோல்கோடி means ‘bending the sceptre’; he notes கோடி stands for the infinitive கோட. He adds that the next couplet gives the cause of losing wealth already amassed. Manakkudavar marks this couplet as stating the fault that comes from acting without deliberation. Kalaignar reads குடி more loosely as ‘the people’s esteem’. The text is the same across the sources consulted, and Pope’s rendering ‘who counsel doth refuse’ follows the sense of சூழாது.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That king who is illiberal, and without affection, who afflicts his subjects by undue chastisements, and who is rash in his acts, soon meets with destruction.”
hinduism.explanation: The sage Vamadeva warns King Vasumanas that harsh, rash rule leads straight to ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: Rash action (சூழாது) and unjust punishment (கோல்கோடி) are the two faults the Kural names.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section XCII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: Thomas Aquinas argues that tyrannical rule cannot last long, because it is hateful to the multitude and rests on fear, which is a weak foundation, so tyrants are soon overthrown.
christianity.explanation: For Aquinas, oppression undermines the very base of the ruler’s power.
christianity.tie_back: It agrees with the Kural that the unjust king loses his people, and with them his hold on power.
christianity.source: Thomas Aquinas, De Regno (On Kingship) I.10

islam.quote_or_event: Of Pharaoh and his people after they pursued the Israelites, the Qur’an says: “So We removed them from gardens and springs” and from treasures and an honoured station.
islam.explanation: Pharaoh’s oppression ends with the loss of all his wealth and power at a single stroke.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘loses both wealth and people at once’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke; my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”
judaism.explanation: King Rehoboam rejects the elders’ advice to lighten the people’s burden, and the ten northern tribes break away from him.
judaism.tie_back: He is exactly the king who ‘does not deliberate’ and bends the rod, and so loses most of his people and revenue in one day.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells King Ajātasattu’s minister that the Vajjians will not decline as long as they meet often, act in harmony, keep their established laws, and honour and listen to their elders.
buddhism.explanation: The ‘conditions of non-decline’ tie a state’s survival to consultation and just custom.
buddhism.tie_back: They are the exact opposite of the Kural’s king, who acts without counsel and bends justice.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In vain he adopts nakedness, who errs about matters of paramount interest; neither this world nor the next will be his; he is a loser in both respects in the world.”
jainism.explanation: The sage tells King Śreṇika that someone who errs about the things that matter most loses on both sides at once, in this life and the next.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's thoughtless, unjust king loses his wealth and his people together, and the Jain verse likewise describes a wrong-doer who loses both things at once.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.49 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Where are the games, the stables, the horses? Where are the drums and the bugles?”
sikhism.explanation: Lamenting the sack of Saidpur by Babar's army, Guru Nanak asks where all the splendour of the ruling class has gone; in the same hymn he says that those who had remembered the Lord beforehand would not have been punished.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a king who bends justice without thought loses wealth and people at once; Guru Nanak pictures a whole order's wealth and pomp vanishing in a single stroke.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Creon, king of Thebes, ignores his son Haemon and the prophet Tiresias and persists in an unjust decree. By the end he has lost his son and his wife, and the city has turned against him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sophocles shows a ruler who refuses counsel and loses everything at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Creon’s fall is the Kural’s king who ‘acts without deliberation’ and loses all together.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that tyranny and oligarchy are the shortest-lived of all constitutions, and that most tyrannies have lasted only a short time.
philosophy.explanation: His survey of Greek history finds oppressive rule unstable by nature.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives historical support to the Kural’s claim that the bent sceptre brings quick and total loss.

real_life_example.event_title: Louis XIV revokes the Edict of Nantes
real_life_example.event: In October 1685 Louis XIV issued the Edict of Fontainebleau, revoking the Edict of Nantes that had given French Protestants (Huguenots) religious toleration since 1598. Although emigration was forbidden, at least 200,000 Huguenots fled to the Netherlands, England, Prussia, America and elsewhere over the following years. Many were skilled craftsmen and merchants, and their departure strengthened the economies of France's rivals while weakening France's own.
real_life_example.explanation: A single unjust decree drove away a large and productive part of the population and with it much of the country's skill and wealth.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a king who bends justice without thinking of the consequences loses wealth and people together, and the revocation did exactly that.

tamil:
அல்லற்பட்டு ஆற்றாது அழுதகண் ணீரன்றே
செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை.
transliteration:
Allarpattu aatraathu azhuthakan neerandre
Selvaththaith theykkum padai.
meaning: The tears of people who are suffering more than they can bear are a weapon that wears away a cruel king’s riches.
elementary: Water dripping on a stone for a long, long time can wear a hole right through it. Valluvar says the tears of people treated unfairly are like that water: drop by drop, they wear away the riches of the ruler who made them cry.
university: அல்லல் is distress, ஆற்றாது ‘unable to bear it’, and படை ‘army’ or ‘weapon’. The verb தேய்க்கும் (wears away, grinds down) has led translators to render படை as a file or saw (Pope has ‘sharp instruments’, and the prose translation ‘a saw’). Parimelazhagar calls the figure ஏகதேச உருவகம் (partial metaphor): Valluvar does not say ‘the tree of wealth’, but the verb implies it. He explains that the destructive work really done by the sin of causing suffering is credited to the tears that are its sign, ‘because nothing is crueller than those tears’, and that the sense is that the wealth wastes away quickly. He groups kurals 553-556 as stating the evils that befall the tyrant himself. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Take care that the eyes of the weak do not burn thee with thy kinsmen. In a race scorched by the eyes of the weak, no children take birth.”
hinduism.explanation: The sage Utathya warns King Mandhatri that the grief of the oppressed has a power that can destroy even the mightiest ruler.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s idea exactly: the suffering of the weak becomes a weapon against the tyrant.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section XCI (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.”
christianity.explanation: James warns oppressive rich men that the cries of those they cheated have reached God, and that their riches are already rotting.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the cry of the wronged is what destroys the oppressor’s wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: When sending Mu‘ādh to Yemen, the Prophet told him to beware of the supplication of the oppressed, for there is no barrier between it and God.
islam.explanation: The cry of the wronged goes straight to God and brings about justice.
islam.tie_back: Like the tears in the Kural, the prayer of the oppressed works as a weapon against the unjust.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child. If thou afflict them in any wise—for if they cry at all unto Me, I will surely hear their cry— My wrath shall wax hot, and I will kill you with the sword…”
judaism.explanation: The Torah promises that God hears the cry of the defenceless and turns it against their oppressor.
judaism.tie_back: The victim’s cry becomes the ‘sword’, just as in the Kural the tears become the army.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like fine dust thrown against the wind, evil falls back upon that fool who offends an inoffensive, pure and guiltless man.”
buddhism.explanation: Harm done to the innocent comes back on the one who does it.
buddhism.tie_back: In the Kural, the suffering a tyrant inflicts comes back to wear away his own wealth.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Suffering, sorrow, agony, moaning, injury and lamentation, in oneself, in others or in both, lead to the influx of karmas which cause unpleasant feeling.”
jainism.explanation: Jain karma theory holds that causing others to grieve, weep and lament draws in karmic matter that later ripens as suffering for the one who caused it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the tears of oppressed subjects are the weapon that wears away a tyrant's wealth. Jain doctrine also turns the victims' weeping back on the oppressor, through karma.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.11, English rendering on jainworld.com (Tattvarth Sutra, Chapter 6)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “But if a powerful tiger attacks a flock of sheep and kills them, then its master must answer for it.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Babar hymns Guru Nanak cries out over the slaughter of the defenceless and insists that the suffering of the weak calls the one responsible for them to account.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the tears of those who can no longer bear their suffering wear away the tyrant's wealth; Guru Nanak likewise makes the cry of the oppressed a demand that power must answer.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 360, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phoenix tells Achilles of the Prayers (Litai), lame and wrinkled daughters of Zeus, who follow after Ruin. If a man rejects them, they go to Zeus and ask that Ruin should dog that man until he pays in full.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, the rejected pleas of suppliants become a force that brings ruin on the hard-hearted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is close to the Kural’s idea that unanswered distress turns into a destructive power.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that fear is a poor guardian of lasting power and goodwill a faithful one, and that no amount of power can withstand the hatred of the many, as the fall of tyrants shows.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, the resentment of the oppressed eventually overthrows even the strongest ruler.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives the Kural’s ‘tears as an army’ a political explanation.

real_life_example.event_title: The Duke of Alba's Tenth Penny and the Dutch Revolt
real_life_example.place: The Low Countries (now the Netherlands and Belgium)
real_life_example.event: Sent by Philip II of Spain to govern the Netherlands, the Duke of Alba ruled through a special tribunal, the Council of Troubles, and in 1569 announced a permanent ten per cent sales tax, the Tenth Penny. The tax united Catholics and Protestants against Spanish rule. When rebels seized the port of Brielle on 1 April 1572 other towns joined the revolt, and Alba left the Netherlands in 1573 without having restored control.
real_life_example.explanation: The suffering caused by harsh rule and heavy taxation turned the population against the crown and began the long process by which Spain lost its richest provinces.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the tears of people who can no longer bear their suffering are the weapon that wears away an oppressive ruler's wealth, and the revolt against Alba wore away Spain's hold on the Netherlands.

tamil:
மன்னர்க்கு மன்னுதல் செங்கோன்மை அஃதின்றேல்
மன்னாவாம் மன்னர்க் கொளி.
transliteration:
Mannarkku mannuthal sengonmai akhthindrel
Mannaavaam mannark koli.
meaning: Fair rule is what makes a king’s fame last. Without it, his glory will not stay.
elementary: A trophy you won by cheating doesn’t feel like yours, and people stop cheering once they find out. Valluvar says a king’s glory is like that: only fair, honest rule keeps it shining, and without fairness it fades away.
university: The couplet repeats the root மன்- ‘to endure’ for effect: மன்னர் (kings), மன்னுதல் (enduring) and மன்னா (will not endure). ஒளி (light, lustre) means renown. Parimelazhagar supplies the instrumental case lost by elision: ‘kings’ fame endures by the straight sceptre’. He cites Nāṉmaṇikkaṭikai 17 (‘if you wish to endure in this world, plant fame’) to show that fame is what makes a person endure. He explains the plural (ஒளி taken as many forms of fame, from victory, generosity and so on) and concludes that if their fame does not last, the kings themselves do not last. Some continuous-text editions read the sandhi form அஃதின்றேன் and மன்னாவா மன்னர்க் for அஃதின்றேல் மன்னாவாம். Manakkudavar puts this couplet first in the ‘faults’ series, taking the loss of glory as the first penalty of misrule.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhishma tells how the first true king, Prithu, was called rājā because he gladdened (rañjana) all the people by protecting them, the earth yielding abundantly under his righteous rule.
hinduism.explanation: The very title ‘king’ is said to come from pleasing and protecting the people.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural says, a king’s standing and fame rest wholly on righteous rule.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section LIX (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb ties the permanence of a throne to just judgement of the powerless.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim: just rule is what makes a king endure.

islam.quote_or_event: “O David, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow [your own] desire, as it will lead you astray from the way of Allah.”
islam.explanation: David’s authority as ruler is given on the condition that he judges with truth.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes just judgement the condition of lasting rule.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are three crowns: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of royalty, but the crown of a good name supersedes them all.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shimon ranks a good name above every office, kingship included.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise holds that royal glory is empty unless the good name that comes from just rule upholds it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Jātakas list ten royal virtues (dasa rāja-dhamma): generosity, moral conduct, self-sacrifice, honesty, gentleness, self-restraint, freedom from anger, non-violence, patience and non-opposition to the right. A king who keeps them is praised and his reign prospers.
buddhism.explanation: In Buddhist tradition, a king’s greatness is measured by these ten virtues.
buddhism.tie_back: They spell out the ‘straight sceptre’ that the Kural says alone makes a king’s fame last.
buddhism.source: Jātaka No. 534, Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka (ed. E. B. Cowell)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Sânti, a universal monarch of great power, the bringer of peace to the world, gave up Bharatavarsha and reached perfection.”
jainism.explanation: Gardabhāli's sermon lists righteous universal monarchs, such as Bharata, Sagara and Śānti, who are remembered for their virtue and for renouncing their power.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says only just rule makes a king's fame endure, and the Jain list keeps the names of kings who brought peace to the world, though it values their renunciation more than their reigns.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 18.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone find peace, and they are the true kings, whose dealings are true.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan defines true kingship not by power or display but by truthful dealing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says only just rule makes a king's glory endure; Guru Arjan likewise grants the title of true king only to those whose dealings are true.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 962, Raag Raamkalee (Raamkalee ki Vaar), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato’s closing myth, Minos, Rhadamanthys and Aeacus, kings remembered for their justice in life, are appointed after death to judge the dead, while the souls of tyrants are the most scarred and incurable.
greek_mythology.explanation: Only just kings gain an honour that lasts forever; unjust rulers become eternal warnings.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s point that only just rule makes a king’s glory endure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Nero that a ruler’s one impregnable defence is the love of his citizens, and that clemency secures a lasting good name where cruelty leaves only a hated memory.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic argues that mercy and justice, not force, make a reign secure and its memory honoured.
philosophy.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s claim that only the straight sceptre makes a ruler’s glory last.

real_life_example.event_title: Stalin's body is removed from Lenin's Mausoleum
real_life_example.event: After Stalin's death in 1953 his embalmed body was placed beside Lenin's in the mausoleum on Red Square. During the de-Stalinization campaign led by Nikita Khrushchev, the body was removed on 31 October 1961 and reburied by the Kremlin Wall. The same year the city of Stalingrad was renamed Volgograd.
real_life_example.explanation: Within a decade of his death, the honours given to one of history's most feared rulers were being taken down by his own successors.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says just rule is what makes a king's fame last and that without it his glory will not endure, and the removal of Stalin from the mausoleum shows such glory fading.

tamil:
துளியின்மை ஞாலத்திற்கு எற்றற்றே வேந்தன்
அளியின்மை வாழும் உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Thuliyinmai gnaalaththirku etratre vendhan
Aliyinmai vaazhum uyirkku.
meaning: A king without kindness is to his people what a lack of rain is to the earth.
elementary: When it doesn’t rain for a long time, plants wilt, rivers shrink, and animals go thirsty. A king without kindness makes his people wilt in just the same way, because his care is like rain to them.
university: துளி (a drop) stands for rain by synecdoche. Parimelazhagar says the word was chosen because a drop is the most telling part of rain. அளி means gracious, tender care, and உயிர் (life, living beings) here stands for the subjects. The construction எற்று… அற்றே (‘of what kind…? just so’) makes a rhetorical comparison. Parimelazhagar notes that this couplet puts negatively what kural 542 had said positively: the whole world lives looking to the sky for rain, and the subjects look to the king’s sceptre. He groups kurals 557-558 as stating the evils that fall on those who live in the tyrant’s land. Solomon Pappaiah reads அளி more broadly as ‘righteous governance’. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu tells the king to act like Indra: as Indra sends plentiful rain in the four months of the rainy season, so the king should shower benefits on his kingdom.
hinduism.explanation: The ‘vow of Indra’ makes the king’s generosity the political counterpart of rain.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the positive form of the Kural’s image: the king’s kindness is rain to his people.

christianity.quote_or_event: “…for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points to God’s rain, given freely to everyone, as the model for goodness that does not pick and choose.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural calls a ruler’s kindness a kind of rain; here God’s rain is the pattern of such kindness.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that whoever is not merciful to people, God will not be merciful to him.
islam.explanation: Mercy toward others is made the condition of receiving God’s mercy.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s merciless king cuts himself off from mercy, and his people from relief.

judaism.quote_or_event: “May he come down like rain upon the mown grass, as showers that water the earth.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm for the king prays that his just rule will refresh the land as rain does.
judaism.tie_back: It is the same image as the Kural: a king’s gracious rule is rain for his people.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha compares his teaching to a great rain cloud that pours down equally on every herb, shrub and tree, each drinking according to its kind.
buddhism.explanation: Compassion is pictured as rain that nourishes every living thing without discrimination.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘kindness as rain’ is the same image, applied to a king.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The customs, taxes, and confiscations were released, buying and selling prohibited, no policemen were allowed to enter houses, great and small fines were remitted, and debts cancelled.”
jainism.explanation: At Mahāvīra's birth King Siddhārtha also freed all prisoners, and the Kalpa Sūtra says the whole population of town and country rejoiced at this display of royal grace.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a king's lack of kindness is like drought to his people. Siddhārtha's festival shows the reverse: a king's kindness falling on his subjects like relief.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §102 (with §100) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When it rains, there is happiness. Water is the key to all life.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak celebrates rain as the source of joy and the sustainer of every living thing.
