sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares a king's lack of kindness to drought on the world; Guru Nanak's verse shows how completely all life hangs on the rain, which is what gives the Kural's comparison its force.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 150, Raag Maajh (Maajh ki Vaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Demeter withdrew in grief and anger, she made the earth bear no crops, and mankind would have perished of famine if Zeus had not brought her daughter back.
greek_mythology.explanation: When the goddess who sustains life holds back her care, the whole world goes hungry.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s drought, the withdrawal of care from above leaves every living being in distress.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Answering Thrasymachus, Socrates argues that a true ruler, like a true shepherd, looks to the good of those in his care, not his own profit.
philosophy.explanation: Rule is defined as care for the ruled.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s king without அளி (gracious care) fails the very definition of ruling.

real_life_example.event_title: Haile Selassie's government and the Wollo famine
real_life_example.event: During a drought in 1972-73, famine struck the province of Wollo in northern Ethiopia, and tens of thousands of people died. The imperial government of Haile Selassie tried to conceal the famine, and its denial became an international scandal after it was exposed in a British television documentary. Famine, unemployment and political stagnation fed the unrest that led army officers to depose the emperor on 12 September 1974.
real_life_example.explanation: The lack of care from the ruler turned a natural drought into a human disaster and cost him his throne.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a king's lack of kindness is to his people what drought is to the world, and in Wollo the two came together.

tamil:
இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை முறைசெய்யா
மன்னவன் கோற்கீழ்ப் படின்.
transliteration:
Inmaiyin innaathu udaimai muraiseyyaa
Mannavan korkeezhp padin.
meaning: Under an unfair king, having money brings more misery than having nothing at all.
elementary: Imagine a class where a mean monitor takes the best toy from anyone who brings one. Soon, the kids who bring nice toys are the most worried ones. Valluvar says that under a greedy king, being rich becomes more dangerous than being poor.
university: The paradox turns on இன்மை (having nothing) and உடைமை (possessing). Parimelazhagar explains it by describing what the covetous king does: those who own property are the ones who suffer seizures, torture and binding ‘till the hands ache’ (கைந்நோவ யாப்புண்டல்), so under such a ruler wealth is worse than poverty. He applies it to everyone (யாவர்க்கும்), not just the rich, and groups kurals 557-558 as stating the evils that fall on those who live in the tyrant’s land. Manakkudavar agrees (‘even the wealthy suffer’) and counts 557-559 as the evils of failing to do justice. கோற்கீழ்ப் படின் means ‘if one falls under the sceptre’. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhishma teaches that a king should draw revenue gently, as a bee gathers honey without harming the flower, or as one milks a cow without cutting the udder, so that the people can go on producing wealth.
hinduism.explanation: Greedy taxation that crushes the producers destroys the source of all wealth.
hinduism.tie_back: Under a king who ignores this, wealth becomes a burden, which is exactly the Kural’s point.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section LXXXVIII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: Naboth refused to sell King Ahab the vineyard he had inherited, so Queen Jezebel had false witnesses accuse him. He was stoned to death and the king took the vineyard.
christianity.explanation: Naboth’s small property was exactly what brought the unjust king’s power down on him.
christianity.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s paradox: under an unjust king, owning something is more dangerous than owning nothing.

islam.quote_or_event: “As for the ship, it belonged to poor people working at sea. So I intended to cause defect in it as there was after them a king who seized every [good] ship by force.”
islam.explanation: Al-Khidr damages the poor men’s boat to save it, because a sound boat would be taken by the tyrant king.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s paradox exactly: under an unjust king, having something good is worse than having less.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And they covet fields, and seize them; And houses, and take them away; Thus they oppress a man and his house, Even a man and his heritage.”
judaism.explanation: Micah condemns the powerful who take land and houses from ordinary people.
judaism.tie_back: Under such rulers, a man’s property is exactly what draws oppression, as the Kural says.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes a man who works hard to gain wealth and then suffers anxiety guarding it, thinking ‘How can I keep kings and thieves from taking it?’, and grieves bitterly when kings seize it.
buddhism.explanation: Among the dangers of wealth, the sutta names seizure by kings as a standard source of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: It spells out why property can hurt more than poverty under a grasping ruler.

jainism.quote_or_event: Kumārapāla, the Caulukya king of Gujarat who became a disciple of the Jain teacher Hemacandra, is remembered for abolishing the royal right to seize the property of people who died without heirs, which had left widows and families destitute.
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition presents the end of this confiscation as an act of compassion inspired by Jain teaching: the king stopped preying on his subjects' property.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that under an unjust king owning wealth is worse than poverty, because the owners are the ones who get stripped. Kumārapāla's reform removed one such predatory practice.
jainism.source: Kumarapala (Chaulukya dynasty), Wikipedia (summarising Jain prabandha sources)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Their wealth and youthful beauty, which gave them so much pleasure, have now become their enemies.”
sikhism.explanation: Describing the households of Saidpur when Babar's soldiers fell on them, Guru Nanak says the very wealth and beauty they had enjoyed now turned against them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that under an unjust sceptre having wealth brings more misery than having nothing; Guru Nanak shows exactly this, wealth becoming the owner's enemy under lawless power.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Asked for advice on ruling, the tyrant Thrasybulus led Periander’s messenger through a cornfield, silently cutting off every ear of grain that stood above the rest. Periander understood that he should do away with the most prominent citizens.
greek_mythology.explanation: Under tyranny, standing out through wealth or distinction makes a person a target.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is a vivid picture of the Kural’s paradox: under the cruel sceptre, the well-off suffer most.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that tyrants deliberately impoverish their subjects, through heavy taxes and great public works like the pyramids of Egypt, so that the people are too busy and poor to plot against them.
philosophy.explanation: He sees stripping people of property as a deliberate tool of tyranny.
philosophy.tie_back: It explains why, as the Kural says, wealth becomes a misery under such a king.

real_life_example.event_title: Sulla's proscriptions
real_life_example.event: After winning the civil war, the dictator Lucius Cornelius Sulla posted public lists of people declared outlaws, and the property of those named was confiscated and sold, often cheaply to his friends and supporters. Britannica describes the victims as some 520 wealthy opponents whose property went to Sulla's veterans, and their sons and grandsons were barred from public office. Ancient writers report that some people were added to the lists simply because others wanted their estates.
real_life_example.explanation: Under Sulla's rule owning property became a danger in itself, since wealth could put a person's name on the lists.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that under an unjust ruler having wealth brings more misery than having nothing, and the proscriptions made riches a reason to be targeted.

tamil:
முறைகோடி மன்னவன் செய்யின் உறைகோடி
ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்.
transliteration:
Muraikodi mannavan seyyin uraikodi
Ollaathu vaanam peyal.
meaning: If a king rules unfairly, the seasons go wrong and the clouds will not give rain.
elementary: Think of a team captain who cheats. Soon nobody plays well, the whole game falls apart, and it feels as if even luck has left. The old poets said that when a king is unfair, even the rain stops coming on time.
university: The couplet repeats கோடி (bending): the king ‘bends’ justice (முறைகோடி) and the rain ‘bends’ from its season (உறைகோடி). Parimelazhagar notes that both forms stand for the infinitive கோட, glosses உறைகோடுதல் as ‘failing to rain at the time for rain’, and says the cause is given in the next couplet. Classical commentators take this as a real cosmic link between royal righteousness and the monsoon, a belief widespread in Indian thought. Kalaignar instead reads உறை as reservoirs and rain-storage works that fall to ruin under misrule, so the rain cannot be stored and used. The text is the same across the sources consulted, apart from sandhi spacing in the older continuous text (செய்யி னுறைகோடி யொல்லாது).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If the deity of the clouds pours rain seasonably and the king acts virtuously, the prosperity that ensues maintain the subjects in felicity.” … “It is the king who constitutes the age.”
hinduism.explanation: The sage Utathya teaches that whether the age is Krita or Kali, a golden age or a dark one, depends on the king’s conduct, and that seasonable rain goes together with a virtuous king.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the same cosmic link the Kural draws between a crooked king and failing rain.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section XCI (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months.”
christianity.explanation: James recalls the drought under King Ahab, whose idolatry and injustice Elijah opposed.
christianity.tie_back: In the biblical story, as in the Kural, an unrighteous king’s reign is marked by the heavens holding back their rain.

islam.quote_or_event: A hadith lists sins that bring collective punishment: when people cheat in weights and measures, they are struck by famine, hardship and the oppression of the ruler, and when they withhold zakat, rain is withheld from the sky.
islam.explanation: Moral corruption and injustice are linked to drought and hardship.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s belief that injustice in a society causes the rain to fail.

judaism.quote_or_event: Moses warns that if Israel turns aside to serve other gods, God will shut up the heaven so that there is no rain and the land will not yield its fruit.
judaism.explanation: In the Shema, seasonable rain depends on the people’s faithfulness.
judaism.tie_back: It is the same moral link between righteousness and rain, though Deuteronomy applies it to the whole people rather than the king.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that when kings are unprincipled, their officials, the householders and the people follow; then the sun, moon, seasons and winds go awry, the deities are angered, the heavens do not give enough rain, and the crops ripen unevenly.
buddhism.explanation: The Adhammika Sutta traces a chain from royal injustice all the way to failed rains and failed harvests.
buddhism.tie_back: It is almost exactly the Kural’s claim that a crooked king makes the seasons fail.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.70, Adhammika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain account of the first age, the wishing-trees that had fed humanity lost their power ‘through the fault of time’, and only after that did people begin to break the laws and need a king to punish them.
jainism.explanation: Jain cosmology puts the decline of nature's bounty in the turning of the cosmic time cycle (avasarpiṇī), not in a ruler's moral failings.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural claims that when a king bends justice the seasons fail and rain stops. Jainism instead attributes natural decline to time itself and makes kings a response to that decline, not its cause.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1, ch. 2, part 8 ‘Coronation as king’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Food and wealth are produced in abundance when it rains, if it is the Will of God.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that rain and the plenty it brings come by the divine Will (hukam).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the seasons fail and rain is withheld when a king rules against justice; Gurbani also links rain to a higher order, but places that order in God's Will rather than in the ruler's conduct.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1282, Raag Malaar (Malaar ki Vaar), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that on a city whose people practise violence and crooked justice, Zeus sends famine and plague together, the people waste away, women bear no children and houses dwindle. Often a whole city suffers for one wicked man.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod, crooked judgements bring natural disaster on the whole community.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Greek counterpart of the Kural’s idea that injustice from above stops the rain.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 238-247 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “… they appeared glorious and blessed at the very time when they were full of avarice and unrighteous power. Zeus, the god of gods, who rules according to law, and is able to see into such things, perceiving that an honourable race was in a woeful plight, and wanting to inflict punishment on them …”
philosophy.explanation: Critias tells how the kings of Atlantis, once just and obedient to law, grew greedy and unjust, so that Zeus resolved to punish them; the dialogue opens by recalling that the island was later sunk by an earthquake.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato links the injustice of rulers to a cosmic punishment of their whole land, a distant parallel to the Kural's failed seasons and rain.

real_life_example.event_title: Soviet irrigation schemes dry up the Aral Sea
real_life_example.place: Aral Sea, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan (then Soviet Union)
real_life_example.event: Soviet planners diverted almost all the water of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton fields in Central Asia, and from the 1960s the Aral Sea, which has no outlet, began to shrink rapidly. By the late 1980s it had split into separate northern and southern seas, rising salinity had destroyed its fishery, and dust from the exposed seabed was degrading farmland. NASA reports that the loss of the water made the region's winters colder and its summers hotter.
real_life_example.explanation: Decisions made by a distant government without regard for the people of the region changed their very climate and ruined their livelihoods.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when a ruler rules against justice the seasons go wrong and the rain fails, and Kalaignar's reading of the neglect of water works fits the Aral Sea's fate.

tamil:
ஆபயன் குன்றும் அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர்
காவலன் காவான் எனின்.
transliteration:
Aapayan kundrum aruthozhilor noolmarappar
Kaavalan kaavaan enin.
meaning: If the ruler does not protect the land, the cows give less milk and the learned priests who do the six sacred duties forget their holy books.
elementary: If a school has no one looking after it, the lunch kitchen stops working and the teachers stop teaching. Soon both food and learning are gone. Valluvar says that when a king doesn’t protect his land, food (milk from cows) and learning (the old books) both start to fade.
university: ஆபயன் is ‘the yield of the cow’ (ஆ, cow, and பயன், fruit), meaning milk and its products. அறுதொழிலோர் are ‘those of the six duties’, which Parimelazhagar lists as the Brahmin’s six duties: studying, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifice, giving and receiving (ஓதல், ஓதுவித்தல், வேட்டல், வேட்பித்தல், ஈதல், ஏற்றல்). He ties the couplet to 559: without milk there is no oblation (அவி), without recitation there are no mantras, so sacrifice stops, and so the rain fails. He groups 559-560 as the evils that befall the tyrant’s land. Modern commentators widen the reference: Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘the wise’ (ஞானியர்), and Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar read ‘productive work and the major occupations decline’. The older continuous text has the sandhi form நூன்மறப்பர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The three kinds of Fire, the three Vedas, and sacrifices with Dakshina, all become lost when the king becomes heedless.” … “Elephants and steeds and kine … all lose their vigour when the king becomes unrighteous.”
hinduism.explanation: Utathya warns Mandhatri that royal neglect brings down both the Vedic order and the vigour of cattle.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches both halves of the Kural, cattle failing and the Vedas forgotten, almost word for word.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section XCI (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts the good shepherd with the hired hand who abandons the flock when danger comes.
christianity.tie_back: The hireling is the Kural’s ‘guardian who does not guard’, and his flock is left exposed.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that every one of you is a shepherd and responsible for his flock: the ruler is a shepherd and responsible for his people.
islam.explanation: Rule is defined as guardianship, for which the ruler will be held to account.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s காவலன் (guardian) is the Prophet’s shepherd, whose neglect harms everyone in his care.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear it inspires, every man would swallow his neighbor alive.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina teaches that without a protecting authority, society collapses into violence.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s point: when the guardian does not guard, the order that sustains everything else falls apart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Buddha’s account of the origin of society, once theft and disorder break out the people choose one of themselves, the ‘Great Elect’ (Mahāsammata), to guard the fields and punish wrongdoers in return for a share of the rice.
buddhism.explanation: Kingship begins as a contract to protect the harvest and keep order.
buddhism.tie_back: A king who does not guard has broken the very agreement that, in the Buddhist story, created kings.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A dreadful dearth prevailing about this time forced the monks to emigrate as far as the seaside. During these unsettled times they neglected their regular studies, so that the sacred lore was on the point of falling into oblivion.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra tells how a great famine in Candragupta's time scattered the Jain monks so that the canon was nearly forgotten, until the Saṅgha met at Pāṭaliputra to gather the eleven Aṅgas again.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that when the land is not protected, the learned forget their scriptures, and Jain history records exactly that: in a time of public distress the monks almost lost their sacred texts.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Pariśiṣṭaparvan IX.55–76, as summarised by Hermann Jacobi; quoted in ‘The Jain Church After Mahavira’, jainworld.com

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They tax the cows and the Brahmins, but the cow-dung they apply to their kitchen will not save them.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak rebukes the officials of his day who levied taxes on cows and Brahmins while still clinging to outward rituals of purity.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that when the guardian fails to protect, the cows yield less and the learned forget their scriptures; Guru Nanak also connects the plight of cows and learned men with failing custodians, though his concern is their hypocrisy rather than the loss of Vedic learning.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus compares Penelope’s fame to that of a blameless king who upholds justice: under such a king the earth bears wheat and barley, the trees are laden with fruit, the flocks bear young without fail, and the sea gives fish.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer ties the fertility of land and flocks to the king’s justice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the positive side of the Kural: where the guardian guards, the herds are fruitful.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hobbes argues that without a common power to keep order, there is no place for industry or agriculture, no arts, no letters and no society, and the life of man is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short.
philosophy.explanation: For Hobbes, the sovereign’s protection is the precondition of all production and learning.
philosophy.tie_back: Both halves of the Kural are here: livelihood fails and ‘letters’ are lost when the guardian does not guard.

real_life_example.event_title: The Nazi book burnings and the purge of German universities
real_life_example.place: Berlin and university towns across Germany
real_life_example.event: On 7 April 1933 the new Nazi government issued the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, which led to the dismissal of Jewish and politically undesirable university teachers, over 1,100 of them by 1935. On 10 May 1933 pro-Nazi student groups burned books by Jewish, pacifist and left-wing authors in university towns, with some 20,000 volumes burned before a crowd of about 40,000 on Berlin's Opernplatz.
real_life_example.explanation: When the state stopped protecting scholars and learning, Germany's universities lost much of the knowledge they had been built to keep.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that when the guardian of the land fails to protect it the learned forget their texts, and the burnings and dismissals of 1933 drove learning out of German universities.

tamil:
தக்காங்கு நாடித் தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால்
ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது வேந்து.
transliteration:
Thakkaangu naadith thalaichchellaa vannaththaal
Oththaangu oruppadhu vaendhu.
meaning: A true king looks into a wrong fairly and carefully, then punishes it in a way that fits the crime, so that it does not happen again.
elementary: Imagine a teacher who finds a broken window. A good teacher first finds out calmly who did it and why, and then gives a fair consequence, not too big and not too small, so it won't happen again. This kural says a good ruler works the same way: find out the truth first, then correct fairly.
university: The chapter title வெருவந்த செய்யாமை means ‘not doing things that cause dread (veru)’, and Valluvar opens it not by forbidding punishment but by defining its right form. Three steps are packed into the couplet: தக்காங்கு நாடி (investigating as is fitting, i.e., impartially), ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுத்தல் (punishing in a measure that matches the offence), and the purpose clause தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால் (so that the wrong does not advance or recur). The traditional commentators, with Parimelazhagar at their head, read this as the positive standard against which the tyranny of the previous chapter (கொடுங்கோன்மை, ch. 56) is measured, and modern glosses (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all stress neutrality in inquiry and proportion in penalty. The definition-style ending ‘… வேந்து’ (‘that is a king’) makes proportionate justice constitutive of kingship itself. Text agrees across ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the latter printing the older sandhi-joined form (வண்ணத்தா / லொத்தாங் கொறுப்பது) with no change in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If (punishment) is properly inflicted after (due) consideration, it makes all people happy; but inflicted without consideration, it destroys everything.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches that danda (punishment) is a blessing only when applied after careful examination; used rashly, it ruins the whole order it is meant to protect.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts insist that investigation must come before punishment, exactly the Kural’s ‘தக்காங்கு நாடி’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?”
christianity.explanation: Nicodemus reminds the council that the law forbids condemning anyone before a hearing and a proper inquiry into what he has done.
christianity.tie_back: Nicodemus’s principle of hearing before judging is the first step the Kural requires of a king.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if you punish [an enemy, O believers], punish with an equivalent of that with which you were harmed. But if you are patient - it is better for those who are patient.”
islam.explanation: The Quran allows retribution only in strict equivalence to the harm done, and praises restraint above even that.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுத்தல்’ (punishing in matching measure) is the same principle of equivalence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the judges shall make diligent inquisition … And those which remain shall hear, and fear, and shall henceforth commit no more any such evil among you.”
judaism.explanation: Deuteronomy requires judges to investigate diligently, and gives the purpose of the penalty as preventing the evil from being repeated.
judaism.tie_back: Diligent inquiry plus a penalty aimed at non-recurrence is almost exactly ‘தக்காங்கு நாடித் தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால்’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It is my desire that there should be uniformity in law and uniformity in sentencing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist emperor Ashoka ordered his judicial officers (rajjukas) to judge consistently and even granted a three-day stay to those sentenced to death so appeals could be heard.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka’s even-handed, reviewable sentencing is a royal program for the Kural’s fair, fitting punishment.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Pillar Edict IV (trans. S. Dhammika)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men frequently apply punishment wrongly: the innocent are put in prison, and the perpetrator of the crime is set at liberty.”
jainism.explanation: When Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, urges King Nami to punish thieves and robbers to prove himself a true Kshatriya, Nami answers that human punishment is often misdirected.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural requires a king to investigate impartially before he punishes; Nami's reply names the injustice that follows when that inquiry is skipped.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Lord and Master is True, and True is His justice. He issues His Commands according to His judgement.”
sikhism.explanation: Closing his hymn on Babar's invasion, Guru Nanak affirms that the Lord's commands follow from true judgement, so that what befalls each person answers to justice.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a true king first inquires fairly and then punishes in due measure; Guru Nanak's model of justice is likewise a command that issues only from true judgement.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Greek myth Rhadamanthys, famed for his strict fairness, judges the dead; Plato’s Gorgias imagines souls judged stripped of rank and finery so that the judge sees each soul exactly as it is.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes the ideal judge one who examines the true character of each case without being swayed by status.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s demand for impartial investigation before punishment is personified in Rhadamanthys.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But he who desires to inflict rational punishment does not retaliate for a past wrong which cannot be undone; he has regard to the future, and is desirous that the man who is punished, and he who sees him punished, may be deterred from doing wrong again.”
philosophy.explanation: Protagoras argues that rational punishment looks forward, aiming to prevent repetition rather than to vent anger over the past.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s purpose clause ‘தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால்’, punishing so that the wrong does not recur.

real_life_example.event_title: John Adams defends the British soldiers after the Boston Massacre
real_life_example.place: Boston, Massachusetts (then a British colony), United States
real_life_example.event: After British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston on 5 March 1770, Captain Thomas Preston and eight soldiers were indicted, and John Adams agreed to serve on their unpopular defence team. Preston was acquitted on 30 October 1770 after a trial lasting longer than a day, and in the soldiers' trial, decided on 5 December 1770, six men were acquitted and two were found guilty of manslaughter rather than murder. The two convicted men avoided the death penalty by pleading benefit of clergy and were branded on the hand instead.
real_life_example.explanation: In a town furious at the army, the case was settled by testimony heard in court, and the verdicts distinguished between the men according to what each had actually done.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a true ruler first inquires impartially and then punishes in measure with the offence, and the Boston trials show inquiry before judgement and a penalty matched to the proven wrong rather than to public anger.

tamil:
கடிதோச்சி மெல்ல எறிக நெடிதாக்கம்
நீங்காமை வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Kadidhoachchi mella eriga nedidhaakkam
Neengaamai vaendu bavar.
meaning: Rulers who want to stay successful for a long time should raise the stick sternly but bring it down gently. They should warn firmly but punish mildly.
elementary: Think of a parent who says in a serious voice, ‘If you do that again, there will be no TV for a month!’, but when it happens, takes away TV for just one evening. The warning is strong, the punishment is gentle. The kural says leaders who do this keep their people’s trust for a long time.
university: The image is of a raised stick: கடிது ஓச்சி (lift it high, severely) but மெல்ல எறிக (bring it down softly). The classical commentary, followed by Mu. Varadarasanar, reads this as appearing to proceed with great severity while in fact not exceeding due measure, while Kalaignar’s modern gloss separates the stages as stern reproof but mild punishment. The reward named is நெடிது ஆக்கம் நீங்காமை, prosperity that does not depart for a long time, so the couplet argues from prudence as much as from mercy. Pope’s ‘raise the rod with brow severe, but let it gently fall’ has become the standard English rendering. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi form ‘மெல்ல வெறிக’, which is the same words as ‘மெல்ல எறிக’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “No,” says Kauṭilya; for whoever imposes severe punishment becomes repulsive to the people; while he who awards mild punishment becomes contemptible. But whoever imposes punishment as deserved becomes respectable.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya rejects his teacher’s advice that a king should always hold the sceptre raised (udyatadaṇḍa), arguing for punishment that is deserved, neither harsh nor lax.
hinduism.tie_back: The raised-but-restrained sceptre in the Arthashastra is the same picture as the Kural’s rod raised high but lowered gently.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.”
christianity.explanation: James teaches that judgment stays real but mercy has the final word over it.
christianity.tie_back: The rod is raised (judgment) but comes down gently (mercy), which is the Kural’s balance.

islam.quote_or_event: “Avert the legal penalties from the Muslims as much as possible, if he has a way out then leave him to his way, for if the Imam makes a mistake in forgiving it would be better than making mistake in punishment.”
islam.explanation: This narration keeps the fixed penalties on the books but urges the ruler to avoid applying them wherever a way out exists.
islam.tie_back: Severe law, lenient application: the rod is raised high but falls softly.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah records that a Sanhedrin which executes someone once in seven years is called destructive; Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says once in seventy years, and Rabbis Tarfon and Akiva say that had they sat on the Sanhedrin no one would ever have been executed.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis kept capital law in the Torah but surrounded it with procedures so demanding that it was almost never carried out.
judaism.tie_back: Stern law held high, applied with extreme restraint, is the Jewish legal form of the Kural’s gentle stroke.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “They are told that despite his remorse Beloved-of-the-Gods has the power to punish them if necessary, so that they should be ashamed of their wrong and not be killed.”
buddhism.explanation: After Kalinga, Ashoka reminded restless forest peoples that he still held the power to punish, precisely so they would reform and he would not have to use it.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka raises the rod as a warning and hopes never to strike, which is the Kural’s strategy.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict XIII (trans. S. Dhammika)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not, in every case, wait for the express command (of the teacher) like an unbroken horse for the whip (of the rider), but like a broken horse which sees the whip (of the rider) he should commit no evil act.”
jainism.explanation: The first lecture on monastic discipline holds up the well-trained horse that needs only to see the whip, not feel it, as the model for a pupil.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's ruler raises the rod sternly but lets it fall gently; the Jain verse likewise says that the visible rod, not the blow, should be what keeps a well-disciplined person from wrongdoing.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Your child makes mistakes again and again, but still, You are pleased with him, O Father of the Universe.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das pictures God as a father who goes on loving his child in spite of repeated faults.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural advises raising the rod sternly but letting it fall gently; Guru Ram Das gives the ideal of a guardian whose correction is always tempered by tender regard.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1321, Raag Kalyaan, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Eumenides, Athena founds the Areopagus court and tells the Athenians to honour neither anarchy nor despotism, yet not to banish fear entirely from the city; the terrifying Furies are then given an honoured, gentler role as the Kindly Ones.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth keeps a measure of awe in the city’s justice but transforms raw vengeance into a restrained, protective institution.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Keep the dread in reserve, soften its actual use: this is the Kural’s raised rod and gentle stroke.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli advises that a prince should make himself feared in such a way that, even if he does not win love, he avoids hatred, chiefly by keeping his hands off his subjects’ property and not being needlessly cruel.
philosophy.explanation: Even the most hard-headed theorist of power holds that the ruler’s severity must be displayed but kept within bounds, or it will destroy him.
philosophy.tie_back: Machiavelli and Valluvar reach the same practical conclusion by different moral routes: show sternness, avoid actual cruelty, and your rule will last.

real_life_example.event_title: The Meiji government pardons the rebel admiral Enomoto Takeaki
real_life_example.event: Enomoto Takeaki, who had led the last forces loyal to the former shogunate, surrendered to the new Meiji government at the fortress of Goryokaku in Hakodate in June 1869. He was sent to Tokyo and held in confinement for about three years, after which he was pardoned. He went on to serve the government as envoy to Russia and held several ministerial posts.
real_life_example.explanation: The new government crushed the armed rebellion completely, but the penalty that followed was limited, and the former rebel became one of its useful servants.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises raising the rod sternly but letting it fall gently, and Enomoto's defeat, brief confinement and pardon show severity in the contest and mildness in the punishment.

tamil:
வெருவந்த செய்தொழுகும் வெங்கோல னாயின்
ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Veruvandha seydhozhugum vengoalan aayin
Oruvandham ollaik kedum.
meaning: A cruel king who keeps doing things that fill his people with fear will surely and quickly be ruined.
elementary: Imagine a team captain who yells and scares everyone all the time. Soon nobody wants to play for them, and the team falls apart. The kural says a ruler who keeps people frightened will quickly lose everything.
university: This couplet supplies the chapter’s title phrase: வெருவந்த செய்து ஒழுகும் describes a ruler whose habitual conduct (ஒழுகுதல், ongoing practice) is to do dread-inducing things. வெங்கோலன், the ‘hot’ or cruel sceptre, is the opposite of the செங்கோல் (straight sceptre) of chapter 55. ஒருவந்தம் means ‘certainly, without doubt’ and ஒல்லை ‘quickly’, so the prediction is doubly emphatic: sure and soon. Commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) agree in glossing ‘veru’ as the fear felt by the subjects (குடிகள் அஞ்சும்படி). The couplet is read identically in both sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He is the best of kings in whose dominions men live fearlessly like sons in the house of their sire.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that the mark of the ideal king is that his subjects live without fear, like children at home.
hinduism.tie_back: Bhishma states positively what the Kural states negatively: rule without dread is the standard, and rule by dread is ruin.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section LVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes legitimate authority as something that only wrongdoers need fear; ordinary good people should not live in dread of it.
christianity.tie_back: A ruler who terrifies the innocent has abandoned what Paul says rulers are for, which is the Kural’s tyrant.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a sector among them, slaughtering their [newborn] sons and keeping their females alive. Indeed, he was of the corrupters.”
islam.explanation: The Quran presents Pharaoh as the archetypal ruler who governs through terror, and whose power is later swept away.
islam.tie_back: Pharaoh’s reign of dread and its destruction is the Kural’s warning in narrative form.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As a roaring lion, and a ranging bear; so is a wicked ruler over the poor people.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares the oppressive ruler to a predator whose very presence terrifies the helpless.
judaism.tie_back: The roaring lion is the image of the வெங்கோலன் who rules by dread.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; all fear death. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha grounds non-violence in the plain fact that every being fears the rod and death, so no one should impose that fear on others.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural forbids a king to rule by dread; the Dhammapada explains why dread is a wrong to inflict.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Be without fear, O king; but grant safety to others also; in this transient world of living beings, why are you addicted to cruelty?”
jainism.explanation: King Sanjaya, out hunting, kills the frightened deer in a park and then is himself seized with fear before the meditating monk Gardabhali, who tells him to give others the safety he wants for himself; the king renounces his throne.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a king who habitually fills his people with dread will swiftly perish; the Jain story makes the same point from inside, showing the inflicter of fear becoming afraid and being told to give up cruelty and grant safety (abhaya) instead.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 18.11 (with 18.3-10) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, to use force is tyranny, even if you call it legal.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose verses the Gurus placed in the scripture, rejects the excuse that violence becomes acceptable once it is given a lawful name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the cruel-sceptred king whose habit is to spread dread will surely and swiftly be ruined; Kabir insists that force remains tyranny whatever legal dress it wears.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the legend retold by Cicero, the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse lets the flatterer Damocles sit on his throne for a day, with a sword hanging over his head by a single horsehair, to show that a ruler who governs by fear lives in constant fear himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: The sword of Damocles pictures the insecurity of a regime built on terror.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says such a ruler perishes swiftly; the legend shows the blade already hanging over him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But, of all motives, none is better adapted to secure influence and hold it fast than love; nothing is more foreign to that end than fear.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero, quoting Ennius (‘whom they fear they hate’), argues that no power can stand against the hatred of the many and that every despot meets a violent end.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s case against ruling by fear is almost a prose commentary on this Kural’s ‘surely and swiftly ruined’.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis 2.23 (trans. W. Miller, Loeb)

real_life_example.event_title: The harsh Qin dynasty collapses soon after the First Emperor's death
real_life_example.event: The state of Qin unified China in 221 BCE, and its ruler, known as Qin Shi Huang, governed through a rigid Legalist legal system with severe punishments, heavy taxation and forced labour on great building projects. After his death in 210 BCE, revolts and fighting broke out across the empire. The dynasty collapsed by 207-206 BCE, less than four years after his death, and was soon replaced by the Han dynasty.
real_life_example.explanation: The first dynasty to unite all China, ruling largely through fear of punishment, lasted only about fifteen years, one of the shortest-lived major dynasties in Chinese history.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural predicts that a cruel-sceptred ruler who habitually fills his people with dread will certainly and swiftly be ruined, and the Qin dynasty fell almost as soon as its founder was gone.

tamil:
இறைகடியன் என்றுரைக்கும் இன்னாச்சொல் வேந்தன்
உறைகடுகி ஒல்லைக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Iraikadiyan endruraikkum innaachchol vaendhan
Uraikadugi ollaik kedum.
meaning: A king whose people call him “our harsh ruler” will have his life cut short and will quickly be destroyed.
elementary: If everyone at school whispers ‘the new class monitor is mean,’ that monitor won’t be monitor for long. The kural says when a whole country calls its king cruel, his time is almost up.
university: The couplet turns from the ruler’s acts to the people’s verdict: இறை கடியன் (‘the lord is harsh’) is the இன்னாச் சொல், the painful word, that the subjects speak. The ruler is thus defined by his reputation, and public opinion becomes a political force. உறை கடுகி is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘his lifespan shrinking’ (ஆயுள் குறைந்து), while Pappaiah reads it as the term of his rule contracting; both readings fit, and Pope’s ‘his age shall dwindle’ follows the first. ஒல்லைக் கெடும் repeats the ‘swiftly perishes’ of 563, binding the two couplets together. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That king who through folly rashly oppresses his kingdom, (will), together with his relatives, ere long be deprived of his life and of his kingdom.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu warns that an oppressive king loses both his life and his throne before long.
hinduism.tie_back: The same double loss (shortened life, quick ruin) that the Kural predicts for the king his people call cruel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them … But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts domineering rulers with the servant-leadership he asks of his disciples.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural condemns the ruler remembered for harshness; Jesus redefines greatness as service.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best of your rulers are those whom you love and who love you … And the worst of your rulers are those whom you hate and who hate you and whom you curse and who curse you.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet measures rulers by the mutual regard between them and their people.
islam.tie_back: A ruler his people curse as cruel is ‘the worst of rulers’, the one the Kural says quickly perishes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the king answered the people roughly … saying, My father made your yoke heavy, and I will add to your yoke: my father also chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”
judaism.explanation: Rehoboam rejects his elders’ counsel and threatens his people with harsher rule; ten tribes immediately break away.
judaism.tie_back: Harsh words and a reputation for cruelty cost Rehoboam most of his kingdom at once, just as the Kural warns.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak not harshly to anyone, for those thus spoken to might retort. Indeed, angry speech hurts, and retaliation may overtake you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that harsh speech rebounds on the speaker.
buddhism.tie_back: The king whose harshness becomes a byword finds it returning on him as the people’s bitter verdict.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a bitch with sore ears is driven away everywhere, thus a bad, insubordinate, and talkative (pupil) is turned out.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana warns that a person whose conduct makes him disliked is rejected wherever he goes.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's king earns the people's bitter name 'cruel' and is cut off; in the Jain verse too, a reputation for bad conduct leads to rejection.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Gathering the wealth of Maya, you earn an evil reputation.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan warns the one who heaps up wealth by pressing on others that what he really earns is the ill name and ill wishes of the people.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a king whom his subjects call ‘cruel’ will have his span cut short; Guru Arjan likewise notes that oppressive gain earns the people's bitter verdict.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 42, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Antigone, Creon’s son Haemon warns him that the whole city is quietly mourning Antigone and condemning his harsh decree, but Creon refuses to listen and soon loses his son and wife.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Theban legend shows a ruler deaf to his people’s murmurs about his cruelty, and destroyed as a result.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Haemon reports exactly the ‘இன்னாச் சொல்’ the Kural describes, and Creon’s ruin follows swiftly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Xenophon’s Hiero, the tyrant Hiero confesses that he knows he is hated, lives in constant fear, and cannot trust anyone; the poet Simonides advises him to win his citizens’ love by kindness instead.
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon portrays the tyrant’s life as shortened and poisoned by the hatred he has earned.
philosophy.tie_back: The ruler known as cruel lives under the shadow the Kural describes; Xenophon offers the same cure the chapter implies.

real_life_example.event_title: Nicolae Ceausescu is shouted down at his last rally
real_life_example.event: On 21 December 1989 Romania's ruler Nicolae Ceausescu addressed a large organised rally in Bucharest, broadcast live, to condemn the unrest in Timisoara. Partway through the speech people in the crowd began shouting against him, the broadcast was briefly cut, and he was unable to continue. The next day he and his wife fled the capital by helicopter, were taken into custody by the army, and on 25 December were tried by a special military tribunal and executed.
real_life_example.explanation: Within four days of the moment the crowd openly voiced its verdict on him, a ruler who had held power for nearly a quarter of a century had lost everything.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a king whom the people call cruel will have his span cut short and perish quickly, and the shouting at Ceausescu's rally was followed in days by the end of his rule and his life.

tamil:
அருஞ்செவ்வி இன்னா முகத்தான் பெருஞ்செல்வம்
பேஎய்கண் டன்னது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Arunjevvi innaa mugaththaan perunjelvam
Paeey kandannadhu udaiththu.
meaning: The great riches of a ruler who is hard to meet and who greets people with an unfriendly face are like treasure guarded by a demon. They are scary and help no one.
elementary: Imagine a huge toy box that belongs to someone who never opens the door and scowls at everyone who knocks. Nobody gets to play with the toys, so it’s as if a monster were sitting on them. The kural says a leader who can’t be reached and always frowns makes his riches useless.
university: Two faults are named: அருஞ்செவ்வி, rare or difficult audience (செவ்வி = an opportune moment of access), and இன்னா முகம், a disagreeable countenance. The simile பேஎய் கண்டு அன்னது is read in the commentarial tradition as wealth that a pēy (demon, ghoul) has seen or seized: it exists but inspires only fear and benefits no one, which is why Pope renders ‘blasted by demon’s glance’ and Pappaiah ‘held by a bhūta’. The couplet widens the chapter’s idea of dread from punishment to everyday demeanour: an unapproachable, scowling ruler terrifies without lifting a rod. The spelling பேஎய் preserves the classical alapedai (vowel prolongation) for metre, and both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When in the court, he shall never cause his petitioners to wait at the door, for when a king makes himself inaccessible to his people and entrusts his work to his immediate officers, he may be sure to engender confusion in business, and to cause thereby public disaffection, and himself a prey to his enemies.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya makes accessibility a core royal duty, warning that an unreachable king breeds disaffection and falls to his enemies.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘அருஞ்செவ்வி’ (rare audience) is precisely the inaccessibility the Arthashastra condemns.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: And there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary. And he would not for a while.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus’ parable describes a judge who has the power to help but will not hear the needy, contrasting him with a God who listens.
christianity.tie_back: The unjust judge who will not give audience is the Kural’s அருஞ்செவ்வி ruler.

islam.quote_or_event: “No Imam closes his door on one in need, dire straits and poverty, except that Allah closes the gates of the Heavens from his dire straits, his needs, and his poverty.”
islam.explanation: On hearing this, Mu‘awiya appointed a man to look after the people’s needs so that access would not be blocked.
islam.tie_back: A ruler who shuts his door is the Kural’s hard-to-reach king, and his wealth becomes spiritually useless to him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Absalom said unto him, See, thy matters are good and right; but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee.”
judaism.explanation: Absalom stands at the city gate exploiting the fact that King David has become hard to reach, and so ‘steals the hearts’ of Israel.
judaism.tie_back: An unreachable king loses his people’s loyalty, which is the danger the Kural points to.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “At any time, whether I am eating, in the women's quarters, the bed chamber, the chariot, the palanquin, in the park or wherever, reporters are to be posted with instructions to report to me the affairs of the people so that I might attend to these affairs wherever I am.”
buddhism.explanation: Ashoka deliberately made himself reachable at every hour so that the people’s business never waited on his convenience.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka is the historical opposite of the Kural’s அருஞ்செவ்வி king.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict VI (trans. S. Dhammika)

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain tradition holds that after attaining omniscience a Tirthankara preaches in the samavasarana, a hall open to all, where gods, humans and animals gather to hear him, each understanding the sermon in their own language.
jainism.explanation: The samavasarana ('refuge to all') presents the ideal teacher as someone everyone can approach, with no being turned away.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar condemns the ruler who is hard to see and scowls at those who come; the Jain image of the Jina's open assembly is its opposite, a presence anyone can reach.
jainism.source: Samavasarana in Jain tradition (summary in Wikipedia, 'Samavasarana')

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Amar Das made it a rule that anyone who wished to see him had first to eat in the casteless langar, sitting with everyone else, and it was said that even the Mughal emperor Akbar ate there and sought his advice.
sikhism.explanation: The Guru's presence was open to all comers on equal terms, through a shared meal rather than through rank or favour.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the wealth of a ruler who is hard to see and harsh of face is like treasure guarded by a demon; the Sikh tradition made access to the Guru open and equal for every visitor, ruler and commoner alike.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, ‘Guru Amar Das’ (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells of the terrible serpent, offspring of Ceto and Phorcys, that guards the golden apples in a secret place at the ends of the earth, a treasure that no one may approach.
greek_mythology.explanation: The dragon-guarded hoard (later named Ladon) is wealth that exists but benefits no one, because terror surrounds it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘wealth seen by a demon’ is the same image: riches made useless by the fearsome guardian sitting on them.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle advises that a ruler who wishes to preserve his rule should appear to his subjects not harsh but dignified, inspiring respect rather than fear, and should seem a guardian of the public treasury rather than its owner.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle links the ruler’s demeanour and his handling of wealth directly to the stability of his rule.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural condemns the harsh face and the hoarded, unusable wealth; Aristotle recommends the dignified face and wealth held in trust.

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Rudolf II withdraws into Prague Castle with his collections
real_life_example.event: Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II moved his court to Prague in 1583, and in later years, subject to severe depression, he lived in seclusion there among his vast collections of art, curiosities and scientific instruments. The Habsburg archdukes, dissatisfied with his government, forced him in 1608 to give up Hungary, Austria and Moravia to his brother Matthias. In 1611 Matthias's army virtually held him prisoner in Prague until he yielded Bohemia as well, and he died there in January 1612.
real_life_example.explanation: Rudolf owned one of the greatest treasure collections in Europe, yet as he grew more withdrawn and hard to reach, his family and subjects turned to his brother and his power slipped away.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural likens the wealth of a ruler who is hard to see to treasure held by a demon, and Rudolf's famous collections, locked away with a secluded emperor, did nothing to keep his crowns.

tamil:
கடுஞ்சொல்லன் கண்ணிலன் ஆயின் நெடுஞ்செல்வம்
நீடின்றி ஆங்கே கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kadunjollan kannilan aayin nedunjelvam
Needindri aangae kedum.
meaning: If a ruler speaks harshly and shows no kindness, his great riches will not last. They will disappear right then.
elementary: A shopkeeper who is rude and never smiles at customers soon has an empty shop, no matter how many goods are on the shelves. The kural says a leader with harsh words and no kindness loses even great riches very quickly.
university: கடுஞ்சொல்லன் is one given to harsh words, and கண்ணிலன், literally ‘eyeless’, means lacking kaṇṇōṭṭam, the gracious, considerate regard that is the subject of the very next chapter (58, கண்ணோட்டம்). The couplet thus bridges two chapters: without kindly regard, even நெடுஞ்செல்வம் (vast, long-accumulated wealth) perishes நீடின்றி ஆங்கே, without delay, on the spot. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses கண்ணிலன் as கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாதவன் and Pappaiah as lacking முகதாட்சண்யம் (considerateness), while Kalaignar renders it as a ‘merciless heart’. The contrast நெடும் (long) and நீடு இன்றி (without lasting) is a deliberate verbal play. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna counts gentle, non-agitating speech as a form of spiritual discipline (tapas).
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s கடுஞ்சொல்லன் fails exactly this discipline of speech, with worldly as well as spiritual cost.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul pairs the rejection of harsh speech with a call to tender-hearted kindness.
christianity.tie_back: The same two faults the Kural names, harsh words and lack of kindly regard, are what Paul tells believers to put away.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allāh, [O Muḥammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells the Prophet that his gentleness held the community together, and that rudeness and hardness of heart would have scattered it.
islam.tie_back: ‘Rude in speech and harsh in heart’ is almost a translation of கடுஞ்சொல்லன் கண்ணிலன், and the loss it brings is immediate.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that harsh words provoke hostility while gentle ones defuse it.
judaism.tie_back: The ruler’s grievous words stir up the anger that quickly undoes his fortune.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who utters gentle, instructive and truthful words, who imprecates none — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada counts gentle, non-cursing speech among the marks of the truly noble person.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s harsh-tongued ruler is the opposite of the Buddha’s gentle speaker.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Disobedient, rough speaking, ill-behaved pupils will exasperate even a gentle teacher; but those will soon win even a hot-tempered teacher who humour him and are polite.”
jainism.explanation: The text sets rough speech, which turns away even the gentle, against courtesy, which wins over even the hot-tempered.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a harsh-tongued ruler without kindly regard loses his wealth at once; the Jain verse likewise treats harsh speech as something that loses goodwill and courtesy as what earns it.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “who speaks insipid words with his tongue, is ruined, again and again.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das warns that the person whose tongue utters harsh, graceless (phikka) words brings ruin on himself again and again.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the vast wealth of a ruler who is harsh in speech and lacks kindly regard will not last; Guru Amar Das likewise ties harsh speech to repeated ruin.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 594, Raag Vadhans, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how King Erysichthon scornfully cut down Ceres’ sacred oak, ignoring pleas for mercy; the goddess cursed him with endless hunger, and he devoured his whole fortune until he was left with nothing.
greek_mythology.explanation: A proud, pitiless king sees his great wealth vanish almost at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Harshness and lack of pity destroy even ‘long wealth’ on the spot, as the Kural warns.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Xenophon’s Cyrus holds his empire together by philanthropia, courteous speech, generous gifts and kindly attention to others, arguing that goodwill is a surer treasure than hoarded gold.
philosophy.explanation: The Cyropaedia presents kindness and pleasant speech as the true foundations of lasting power and wealth.
philosophy.tie_back: The positive image of the Kural: a ruler who is gentle in word and kindly in regard keeps both his people and his riches.

real_life_example.event_title: Sultan Osman II's harsh measures against the Janissaries end his reign
real_life_example.event: After the Ottoman army's failure at Khotin in 1621, the young Sultan Osman II blamed the Janissary corps, cut their pay and closed their coffee shops, and planned to raise a new army to break their power. Hearing of his plans and already resentful of his treatment, the Janissaries revolted in May 1622. They deposed him on 19 May and killed him the following day, restoring his uncle Mustafa I to the throne.
real_life_example.explanation: Osman's reign of about four years ended almost at once when the soldiers he had treated with open contempt turned against him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that a ruler harsh in speech and lacking kindly regard loses even great wealth on the spot, and Osman's treatment of his own troops cost him his throne in a matter of days.

tamil:
கடுமொழியும் கையிகந்த தண்டமும் வேந்தன்
அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்.
transliteration:
Kadumozhiyum kaiyigandha thandamum vaendhan
Adumuran thaeykkum aram.
meaning: Harsh words and punishments that go too far are like a file that slowly wears down a king’s power to beat his enemies.
elementary: A metal file rubs a little bit off a key every time you use it, until one day the key no longer works. The kural says that every cruel word and every too-big punishment rubs away a little of a leader’s strength, until it is gone.
university: கையிகந்த தண்டம் is punishment that has ‘gone beyond the hand’, exceeding its proper limit (Mu. Varadarasanar: முறைகடந்த தண்டனை). அடுமுரண் is the destroying strength, the capacity to crush enemies, and அரம் is a file, so the metaphor is of gradual erosion rather than sudden collapse, complementing the ‘swift ruin’ of 563–566. The couplet echoes 566 (harsh words) and 561 (proportionate punishment), making excess, not punishment itself, the target. The word தண்டம் (Sanskrit daṇḍa) links Valluvar to the wider Indian daṇḍanīti tradition of measured punishment. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi form ‘அடுமுரண் டேய்க்கு மரம்’, identical in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If the king is not wrathful, if he is not addicted to evil practices and not severe in his punishments, if he succeeds in keeping his passions under control, he then becomes an object of confidence unto all like the Himavat mountains.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma teaches that freedom from wrath and from severe punishment makes a king as secure and trusted as the Himalayas.
hinduism.tie_back: The reverse of the Kural’s file: restraint builds the king’s strength where excess wears it down.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section LVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns those in authority at home that excessive harshness breaks the spirit of those under them.
christianity.tie_back: Excessive harshness erodes the bond that gives authority its strength, as the Kural’s file does.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the retribution for an evil act is an evil one like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation - his reward is [due] from Allāh. Indeed, He does not like wrongdoers.”
islam.explanation: The Quran caps retribution at an equal measure and ranks pardon above it; going beyond the measure is itself wrongdoing.
islam.tie_back: ‘கையிகந்த தண்டம்’, punishment beyond measure, is what this verse rules out.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah sets a strict upper limit on corporal punishment to protect the dignity of the one punished.
judaism.tie_back: The Torah forbids exactly the punishment ‘beyond the hand’ that the Kural says erodes a king.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “While being completely law-abiding, some people are imprisoned, treated harshly and even killed without cause so that many people suffer. Therefore your aim should be to act with impartiality.”
buddhism.explanation: Ashoka rebukes his judicial officers for excessive and unjust punishment, naming anger and cruelty as its causes and non-anger and patience as its cure.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka identifies and forbids the excessive punishment that the Kural calls a file on royal power.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Kalinga (Separate) Rock Edict I (trans. S. Dhammika)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra lists nine graded kinds of expiation (prayascitta) for faults, running from confession and repentance through penance and temporary suspension up to expulsion and reinitiation, so that the correction can be matched to the gravity of the fault.
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic discipline uses a graded scale of remedies rather than one severe penalty, starting from the mildest step of confession.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says punishment beyond measure wears down a king's power like a file; the Jain scale of expiation is built on the opposite principle of measured correction.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.22 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, speaking insipid words, the body and mind become insipid.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that harsh, graceless speech gradually drains the speaker himself, body and mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says harsh words and excessive punishment are a file that slowly wears away a king's strength; Guru Nanak likewise sees harsh speech as wearing down the one who uses it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He repealed the laws of Draco, all except those concerning homicide, because they were too severe and their penalties too heavy.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Plutarch reports that Draco’s laws punished almost every offence with death, so harshly that they were said to be written in blood, and Solon swept them away.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Punishment beyond measure could not last; it wore away the authority of the laws themselves.
greek_mythology.source: Plutarch, Life of Solon 17.1 (trans. B. Perrin, Loeb)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues in On Clemency that frequent and cruel punishment does not secure a ruler but multiplies his enemies, since every execution creates new kin who hate him, while mercy makes his power safe.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, cruelty is politically self-defeating: it drains the ruler’s security instead of adding to it.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca’s argument is the Kural’s file metaphor spelled out: excessive severity wears away the ruler’s strength.

real_life_example.event_title: England's Bloody Code is dismantled
real_life_example.event: Between the 1690s and about 1750 Parliament passed many laws making specified crimes, including some thefts of small value, punishable by death, a body of law later known as the Bloody Code. In 1832 opponents of capital punishment argued in Parliament that such severity discouraged victims from prosecuting and juries from convicting, though others disputed this. Robert Peel, as Home Secretary from 1822, carried a broad consolidation and reform of the criminal law between 1825 and 1830, and most of the capital statutes were repealed in the 1820s and 1830s.
real_life_example.explanation: Punishments far beyond the measure of the offence did not strengthen the law; reformers argued that they weakened it, and Parliament eventually abandoned them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls punishment beyond measure a file that slowly wears away a ruler's strength, and the Bloody Code's long, gradual discrediting shows excess eroding rather than reinforcing authority.

tamil:
இனத்தாற்றி எண்ணாத வேந்தன் சினத்தாற்றிச்
சீறிற் சிறுகும் திரு.
transliteration:
Inaththaatri ennaadha vaendhan sinaththaatrich
Seeril sirugum thiru.
meaning: A king who does not think things through with his advisers, and then gets angry and blames them, will see his good fortune shrink.
elementary: Imagine a group leader who never asks the team for ideas, and then, when the project goes wrong, shouts at everyone. The team stops helping, and things get worse and worse. The kural says a leader who skips advice and then explodes in anger loses what they have.
university: The couplet is syntactically compact and has two established readings. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take இனத்து ஆற்றி எண்ணாத as ‘not deliberating together with his circle (ministers)’, so the fault is failure to consult followed by angry outbursts; Pope, following the older commentary, reads it as handing affairs to ministers without himself reflecting, and then raging at them when things fail. On either reading the pattern is the same: neglect of counsel, then சினத்து ஆற்றி சீறுதல், being carried along by anger and flaring at subordinates. The result is that திரு (Śrī, royal fortune) சிறுகும், dwindles. Here ‘dread’ is directed at the king’s own ministers, extending the chapter’s concern from subjects to the inner court. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From anger, complete delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain from anger to delusion to loss of judgment to ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: The raging king of this Kural loses judgment in exactly this chain, and with it his fortune.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.”
christianity.explanation: James urges listening first and restraining anger, because anger does not produce right outcomes.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Swift to hear, slow to wrath’ is the exact reverse of the king who neither deliberates nor restrains his anger.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, and when they are angry, they forgive, … and whose affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves.”
islam.explanation: In consecutive verses the Quran praises believers who forgive when angry and who settle their affairs by consultation (shura).
islam.tie_back: Consultation and restraint of anger are the two virtues whose absence the Kural blames for the shrinking of royal fortune.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that plans made without counsel fail, while those made with many advisers stand.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s king who does not deliberate with his circle is the one whose purposes are disappointed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who checks rising anger as a charioteer checks a rolling chariot, him I call a true charioteer. Others only hold the reins.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises the one who can halt anger as it rises, as a skilled driver stops a runaway chariot.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s king is carried along by anger (சினத்து ஆற்றி); the Buddha calls for the opposite mastery.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
jainism.explanation: This verse, which comes from the Dasavaikalika Sutra, names anger as the passion (kashaya) that destroys affection.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's king who rages at his counsellors instead of deliberating with them sees his fortune shrink; the Jain verse explains the mechanism, since anger destroys the goodwill his rule depends on.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam 135 (English tr., jainworld.com; from Dasavaikalika Sutra 8.38)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Tatta: In anger, you are burnt, you fool. T'hat'ha: That place where you live, is cursed.”
sikhism.explanation: In his acrostic Patti, Guru Amar Das warns the learned man that anger burns him up and spoils the very place where he dwells.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a king who acts without deliberating with his counsellors and lashes out in anger will see his fortune shrink; Guru Amar Das likewise shows anger consuming the angry man and his surroundings.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 435, Raag Aasaa (Patti), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the opening of the Iliad, Agamemnon, stung by the seer Calchas’ advice, rages at Achilles and seizes his prize; Achilles withdraws from the war and the Greeks suffer disaster after disaster.
greek_mythology.explanation: A leader who answers counsel with fury alienates his best ally and brings losses on his whole cause.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agamemnon is the Kural’s king who lashes out at those around him and watches his fortunes shrink.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells of the governor Gnaeus Piso, who in anger ordered a soldier executed, then, when the supposedly murdered comrade turned up alive, condemned the soldier, the returned man, and the centurion as well, turning his own error into three deaths.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca uses the story to show how anger in a ruler refuses correction and multiplies injustice.
philosophy.tie_back: Piso is the Kural’s ruler who does not deliberate, then rages at subordinates, to his own discredit.

real_life_example.event_title: Ibrahim Lodi alienates his nobles and loses the Delhi Sultanate
real_life_example.event: Ibrahim Lodi, sultan of Delhi from 1517, tried to rule more autocratically than his father and became increasingly suspicious and harsh toward his Afghan nobles, some of whom rebelled. Resenting his attempts to curb their authority, Dawlat Khan Lodi, governor of the Punjab, and Alam Khan Lodi, Ibrahim's uncle, appealed to Babur, the ruler of Kabul, for help. Babur invaded, and Ibrahim was defeated and killed at the First Battle of Panipat in April 1526, ending the Lodi dynasty.
real_life_example.explanation: A sultan who ruled without carrying his nobles with him and treated them with suspicion and harshness found his own governors inviting a foreign enemy against him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a king who does not deliberate with his circle and then flares at them in anger will see his fortune shrink, and Ibrahim's quarrels with his nobles led directly to the loss of his kingdom.

tamil:
செருவந்த போழ்திற் சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்
வெருவந்து வெய்து கெடும்.
transliteration:
Seruvandha poazhdhil siraiseyyaa vaendhan
Veruvandhu veydhu kedum.
meaning: A king who does not build a strong fort ahead of time will be filled with fear when war comes, and will quickly fall.
elementary: If you never build a shelter and a big storm comes, you get frightened and soaked. The kural says a ruler who doesn’t prepare protection in peaceful times panics and falls when trouble arrives.
university: சிறை here means a protective barrier or fortification (Mu. Varadarasanar: அரண்), not ‘prison’ in the modern sense; the couplet is about defence made ready before செரு (battle) arrives. The striking reversal is in வெருவந்து: the very dread (veru) the tyrant inflicted on others now falls on him, so the chapter’s key word turns back on its source. Commentators connect this to the preceding couplets: a king who has alienated his people through fear and cruelty lacks the human ‘fortress’ of their loyalty when danger comes, which is why this apparently military verse belongs in a chapter on not ruling by terror. வெய்து கெடும் means ‘perishes swiftly/painfully’. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That king, however, who is of righteous behaviour and who is ever engaged in attracting the hearts of his people, never sinks when attacked by foes. If overcome, he soon regains his position.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma teaches that the loyalty of a king’s people is his real protection when enemies attack.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s unprotected king falls in war; Bhishma names the protection he lacked: the hearts of his people.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section LVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a king who plans before war to teach his followers to count the cost.
christianity.tie_back: Preparation before battle is exactly what the Kural’s doomed king neglected.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allāh and your enemy.”
islam.explanation: The Quran commands the community to be prepared for defence so that aggressors are deterred.
islam.tie_back: Readiness before conflict is what the Kural’s king failed to make; notably, both texts direct deterrence at external enemies, never at one’s own people.
