judaism.quote_or_event: “They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon.”
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah’s people rebuild Jerusalem’s wall while armed, making their defences ready before the enemy strikes.
judaism.tie_back: A people who build their own wall willingly is the opposite of the Kural’s ruler without a fortress.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjians, the Buddha says they cannot be defeated so long as they meet often in harmony, honour their elders, protect the vulnerable and keep their customs; Ajatasattu’s minister concludes they cannot be conquered by force.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha presents a people’s internal harmony and justice as their strongest defence.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s king lacks a protective ‘fortress’; the Vajjians’ fortress is the goodwill and order of their society.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable”
jainism.explanation: When Indra urges the renouncing King Nami to build walls, gates, battlements and a moat, Nami answers that the true fortress is built from faith, self-control and patience.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's king perishes because he has prepared no place of defence; Nami agrees that defence must be prepared in advance but says the fortress that really protects is inner discipline, not stone.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.20-22 (cf. 9.18) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Millions of religious leaders failed to halt the invader, when they heard of the Emperor's invasion.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak records that when Babar's invasion was announced, the Lodi rulers relied on the prayers and charms of holy men instead of real defence, and none of it stopped the invader.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a king who has not prepared his defences beforehand will be seized with fear when war comes and quickly perish; Guru Nanak describes rulers caught unready and falling in just this way.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, the bard Demodocus sings of the wooden horse that the Trojans dragged inside their own walls; with their guard down, Troy fell in a single night.
greek_mythology.explanation: A city that neglected its defence at the decisive moment was destroyed swiftly and completely.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s king without protection, Troy was caught unready and perished quickly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, those who wish to be feared must inevitably be afraid of those whom they intimidate.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero illustrates with Dionysius of Syracuse, who dared not let a barber near his throat, and Alexander of Pherae, who needed armed guards even with his wife.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s word வெருவந்து, the tyrant himself seized by fear, is exactly Cicero’s point.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis 2.24–25 (trans. W. Miller, Loeb)

real_life_example.event_title: France enters the Franco-German War unprepared and the Second Empire falls
real_life_example.event: France declared war on Prussia on 19 July 1870, but its armies were slow to mobilise and not ready to fight when German forces crossed the border, with shortages of equipment reported among the units. One French army was soon bottled up in Metz, and on 1-2 September at Sedan, Emperor Napoleon III was captured and a French army of nearly 100,000 men surrendered. On 4 September, after news of the defeat reached Paris, the Second Empire was overthrown and a republic was proclaimed.
real_life_example.explanation: An empire that went to war without having readied its defences collapsed within about six weeks of the first battles.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that a ruler who has not prepared his defences beforehand will be seized with fear when war comes and quickly perish, and Napoleon III's unready empire fell almost as soon as the fighting began.

tamil:
கல்லார்ப் பிணிக்கும் கடுங்கோல் அதுவல்லது
இல்லை நிலக்குப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Kallaarp pinikkum kadungoal adhuvalladhu
Illai nilakkup porai.
meaning: A cruel ruler who keeps ignorant, unlearned people as his helpers is the heaviest weight the earth has to carry. There is none heavier.
elementary: Picture a bully who gathers other kids who don’t know right from wrong to help him push everyone around. That gang makes the whole playground miserable. The kural says a cruel ruler with foolish helpers is the heaviest weight the world has to carry.
university: The closing couplet names the social mechanism of tyranny: கடுங்கோல் (the harsh sceptre) பிணிக்கும் (binds, attaches) கல்லார் (the unlearned) to itself, meaning it draws in and relies on men without learning or moral training to carry out its will. The traditional commentary, followed by Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar, and Pope (‘Tyrants with fools their counsels share’), reads it this way; Pappaiah’s gloss instead stresses a regime that punishes so as to terrify, propped up by those who have not studied the books of justice. பொறை means a load or burden, and the idea of the earth (நிலம்) groaning under wicked rulers is widespread in Indian thought. The couplet ties back to chapter 41 (கல்லாமை, lack of learning) and closes the chapter by showing that terror is never exercised alone. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi-joined ‘கடுங்கோ லதுவல்ல தில்லை’, identical in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Bhagavata Purana tells how Mother Earth, overburdened by vast armies of demonic rulers posing as kings, took the form of a cow and went weeping to Brahma, who promised that the Lord would descend as Krishna to lift the burden.
hinduism.explanation: The myth pictures tyrannical kings and their forces as a literal weight the earth can no longer bear.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘நிலக்குப் பொறை’ (burden on the earth) is the same image, applied to a cruel regime and its unlearned agents.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let them alone: they be blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that leaders without true understanding, followed by others equally unseeing, bring ruin on all together.
christianity.tie_back: A harsh ruler bound to the unlearned is a case of the blind leading the blind, with everyone falling.

islam.quote_or_event: “So he bluffed his people, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were [themselves] a people defiantly disobedient [of Allāh].”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes Pharaoh deceiving his people into following him, and holds them responsible too.
islam.tie_back: A tyrant who binds the undiscerning to his service is the pairing the Kural calls the earth’s heaviest burden.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear: For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with meat.”
judaism.explanation: Agur lists things the earth itself ‘cannot bear’, including the unfit man who seizes rule and the fool who prospers.
judaism.tie_back: The earth that cannot bear a fool in power is the Kural’s ‘no greater burden on the earth’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Mangala Sutta names ‘not associating with fools, associating with the wise’ as the very first of the highest blessings.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha places the choice of companions at the foundation of a good life.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s tyrant does the opposite, binding the unlearned to himself, and so becomes a curse rather than a blessing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When reprimanded a wise man should not be angry, but he should be of a forbearing mood; he should not associate, laugh, and play with mean men.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana tells the disciplined person to avoid keeping company with base people.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's tyrant binds the unlearned to himself as his helpers; the Jain verse warns against exactly that kind of association.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Deer, falcons and government officials are known to be trained and clever. When the trap is set, they trap their own kind; hereafter they will find no place of rest.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak compares the officials of an oppressive state to decoy deer and hunting falcons, trained creatures used to snare their own kind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the heaviest burden on the earth is a harsh sceptre that binds unlearned men to itself as its helpers; Guru Nanak shows how such rule works through trained servants who prey on their own people.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar (Malaar ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In a fragment of the lost epic Cypria, Zeus pities the Earth, weighed down by the countless and increasingly lawless race of men, and plans the Trojan War to lighten her burden.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth, like Indian myth, imagines the Earth as literally burdened by human wickedness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘பொறை’ on the earth has a direct Greek counterpart in Earth’s plea to Zeus.
greek_mythology.source: Cypria, fragment 1 (preserved in a scholium on Iliad 1.5)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato describes how the tyrant must rid himself of the brave, the high-minded and the wise, and is left to live among the worthless, hiring bodyguards from the worst elements, as a doctor purges the best and keeps the worst.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, tyranny by its nature drives out good and learned men and depends on the base and ignorant.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘கல்லார்ப் பிணிக்கும் கடுங்கோல்’ analysed from the inside.

real_life_example.event_title: Ivan the Terrible's oprichnina
real_life_example.event: In 1565 Tsar Ivan IV set aside a large part of his realm as the oprichnina, a territory under his direct personal control, and formed a personal force, the oprichniki, which grew to several thousand men. Through them he carried out years of terror against boyars, towns and ordinary people, including the devastation of Novgorod in 1570. When the oprichniki failed to defend Moscow against a Crimean Tatar attack in 1571, Ivan abolished the oprichnina in 1572.
real_life_example.explanation: A ruler who governed by terror bound to himself a body of men whose only qualification was loyalty to his will, and they inflicted lasting damage on the country while failing it in a real emergency.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls a harsh sceptre that gathers unworthy helpers the heaviest burden the earth can bear, and the oprichnina shows how such a ruler and his chosen enforcers together weighed upon an entire land.

tamil:
கண்ணோட்டம் என்னும் கழிபெருங் காரிகை
உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Kannottam ennum kazhiperung kaarikai
Unmaiyaan undiv vulagu.
meaning: The world keeps going only because of a very great beauty called kannottam (looking at others with kindness and care).
elementary: Think of a playground where the big kids notice the little ones and help them up when they fall. That kind look makes the whole playground a happy place. Valluvar says the whole world keeps going because people, especially leaders, look at others kindly like that.
university: The chapter title கண்ணோட்டம் literally means ‘the running (ஓட்டம்) of the eye (கண்)’, i.e., the eye going out towards another in consideration; Parimelazhagar defines it as the disposition that, on seeing those one is familiar with, cannot bring itself to refuse or hurt them, and he places the chapter in the Arasiyal (royal) section as a quality of the king. The phrase கழிபெருங் காரிகை (‘exceedingly great beauty’) treats benignity as an ornament rather than a duty, a theme picked up again in kural 575. The second line, உண்மையான் உண்டு இவ்வுலகு (‘because of its existence, this world exists’), is a strong ontological claim: social order itself depends on this quality. Modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah) gloss it as ‘looking at a person’s face’ and softening accordingly, while Kalaignar reads it more broadly as love joined with compassion. The text agrees across ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the latter printing the older sandhi-joined form (கண்ணோட்ட மென்னுங் … யுண்மையா னுண்டிவ்) with no change in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Valmiki Ramayana, Rama is repeatedly praised as priyadarśana, ‘pleasing to behold’, and his rule (Rama-rajya) is remembered as an age in which subjects flourished under a king whose regard for them was constant and kindly.
hinduism.explanation: The Indian ideal of the king includes not only just law but a gracious, approachable presence that makes subjects feel seen and protected.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise makes the ruler’s kindly regard the ‘great beauty’ on which the world rests.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 1 (description of Rama’s qualities); tradition of Rama-rajya

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus grounds human mercy in the character of God, making it the family likeness of all who belong to him.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat kindly regard as the foundational quality, not an optional extra, in ordering human life.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allah, [O Muhammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells the Prophet that his gentleness held the community together, and that harshness would have scattered it.
islam.tie_back: Just as Valluvar says the world stands by kannottam, this verse says a leader’s community stands by his leniency.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.”
judaism.explanation: The Priestly Blessing (Birkat Kohanim) pictures divine favour as a shining, lifted face turned towards the people, and makes that gracious look the source of peace.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘look of the eye’ that sustains the world is closely mirrored in the blessing’s gracious face that grants peace.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After his awakening, the Buddha, moved by compassion for beings, surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha and saw beings with little dust in their eyes, and so decided to teach.
buddhism.explanation: In the Pali account the Buddha’s decision to teach springs from a compassionate look over the whole world.
buddhism.tie_back: Like kannottam, it is a compassionate gaze that sets in motion the good of the world.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The function of the souls (jīva) is to help one another.”
jainism.explanation: Umasvati's aphorism parasparopagraho jivanam, now treated as a motto of Jainism, says that living beings exist in a web of mutual help.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the world keeps going because kindly regard for others exists; the Jain sutra likewise makes mutual help the defining function of every soul.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.21 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Be kind to all beings-this is more meritorious than bathing at the sixty-eight sacred shrines of pilgrimage and the giving of charity.”
sikhism.explanation: In his song of the twelve months, Guru Arjan ranks kindness to every living being above all pilgrimages and formal charity.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls kannottam, kindly regard for others, a surpassing beauty by which the world goes on; Guru Arjan likewise places kindness to all beings above every outward religious act.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 136, Raag Maajh (Baarah Maahaa), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “from whose eyes as they glanced flowed love that unnerves the limbs: and beautiful is their glance beneath their brows.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the three Graces (Charites), daughters of Zeus, whose gracious glance is itself their beauty and pours out love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar’s ‘great beauty’ located in a kindly look is the same idea as the Graces whose beauty lies in their glance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca, addressing the young Nero, argues that clemency befits no one more than a king, because a ruler’s mercy is what binds subjects to him and keeps the state secure.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, mercy is the defining ornament of rightful power and the practical foundation of a stable realm.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Seneca treats the ruler’s gentleness as both his chief beauty and what holds the world together.

real_life_example.event_title: Fridtjof Nansen creates the Nansen passport for stateless refugees
real_life_example.event: After the Soviet government revoked the citizenship of Russians living abroad in 1921, hundreds of thousands of refugees from the Russian civil war were left without any state that would issue them papers. Fridtjof Nansen, the Norwegian explorer serving as the League of Nations' first High Commissioner for Refugees, convened an intergovernmental conference in Geneva in July 1922 that agreed on an identity certificate for these stateless people. The Nansen passport was later extended to Armenian and other refugees, roughly 450,000 were issued, and Nansen received the 1922 Nobel Peace Prize for his refugee and relief work.
real_life_example.explanation: A single act of considerate regard for people who belonged nowhere gave them back the ordinary ability to travel, work and live among nations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world keeps going because of the great beauty of kindly regard, and the Nansen passport shows that regard quite literally reopening the world's doors to people the world had shut out.

tamil:
கண்ணோட்டத் துள்ளது உலகியல் அஃதிலார்
உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Kannottath thulladhu ulagiyal aqdhilaar
Unmai nilakkup porai.
meaning: All the everyday business of the world runs on kindness toward others. People without it are just a burden on the earth.
elementary: Imagine a class where everyone shares pencils and helps each other. One child never helps anyone and only takes. The class works because of the helpers; the one who never helps just makes things heavier for everyone. Valluvar says people without kindness are like extra weight the earth has to carry.
university: உலகியல் means ‘the conduct or course of the world’, i.e., everyday social transactions, and Parimelazhagar takes the first line to mean that all such dealings are sustained by kannottam. The second line’s உண்மை (‘existence’, not ‘truth’ here) and பொறை (‘burden’) make a stark judgement: a person without kindly regard contributes nothing and simply weighs on the land, an image the Tamil tradition also uses of the ungrateful and the idle. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both render பொறை as சுமை/பாரம் (load), while Kalaignar stresses the ‘embracing with love’ that such people lack. The couplet thus moves from the cosmic claim of 571 to its negative corollary. ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org agree; the latter prints the sandhi-joined form (துள்ள துலகிய லஃதிலா / ருண்மை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…nonviolence; truthfulness; freedom from anger; renunciation; tranquillity; aversion to faultfinding; compassion for all living entities; freedom from covetousness; gentleness…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists dayā bhūteṣu (compassion toward all beings) and mārdava (gentleness) among the qualities of the divine nature (daivī sampat).
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita, like the Kural, sees compassion as the mark of a life that upholds the world rather than burdens it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, a fig tree that bears no fruit is said only to take up space and exhaust the soil.
christianity.tie_back: The fruitless tree that ‘cumbers the ground’ is almost exactly the Kural’s person without kindness who is a burden on the earth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah will not be merciful to those who are not merciful to mankind.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes mercy toward people the condition for receiving God’s mercy.
islam.tie_back: Both texts judge the person lacking kindly regard as having no rightful place, whether on earth or before God.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shammai used to say: make your [study of the] Torah a fixed practice; speak little, but do much; and receive all men with a pleasant countenance.”
judaism.explanation: Even the famously strict Shammai required that every person be received with a pleasant face, making warm regard a basic rule of social life.
judaism.tie_back: Receiving everyone with a kindly face is the everyday ‘worldly conduct’ that the Kural says rests on kannottam.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even as a mother protects with her life / Her child, her only child, / So with a boundless heart / Should one cherish all living beings”
buddhism.explanation: The Metta Sutta asks for a boundless, protective kindness toward every being without exception.
buddhism.tie_back: This all-embracing goodwill is what the Kural says the whole world runs on.
buddhism.source: Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (trans. Amaravati Sangha)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Benevolence (maitrī) towards all living-beings (sattva), joy (pramoda) at the sight of the virtuous (guṇādhika), compassion and sympathy (kāruṇya) for the afflicted (kliśyamāna), and tolerance (mādhyasthya) towards the insolent and ill-behaved (avineya) are the other observances.”
jainism.explanation: The four bhavanas (contemplations) of friendliness, joy, compassion and equanimity are given to sustain the vows of non-violence and the rest.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says all the world's business runs on kindly regard; the Jain sutra makes goodwill toward every being a daily discipline underlying all conduct.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.11 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who forget the Naam, the Name of the Lord, are a burden on the earth.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose verses the Gurus included in the scripture, says that a life cut off from the divine Name is mere dead weight on the earth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that people without kindly regard merely exist as a burden on the earth; Farid uses the same image of a worthless life weighing on the earth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Zeus and Hermes, disguised as travellers, are turned away by every house in a Phrygian village except that of the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon; the gods flood the pitiless village and turn the couple’s hut into a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s tale shows the unkind community swept away while the kindly household is preserved and honoured.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The villagers without regard for strangers are, as the Kural says, a burden the earth can do without.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “… as men, too, are born for the sake of men, that they may be able mutually to help one another; in this direction we ought to follow Nature as our guide, to contribute to the general good by an interchange of acts of kindness, by giving and receiving …”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero says human society is held together by mutual kindness, and a few sections later calls those who keep to their own affairs and give society nothing traitors to social life.
philosophy.tie_back: As in the Kural, the world's business runs on kindly regard, and those who withhold it contribute nothing to the life they share.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book I, §§22, 29 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))

real_life_example.event_title: Clara Barton founds the American Red Cross
real_life_example.event: Clara Barton, who had nursed and supplied soldiers during the American Civil War and later ran an office that traced missing soldiers, learned of the European Red Cross movement in Switzerland in 1869 and worked with it during the Franco-Prussian War. On 21 May 1881 she founded the American Red Cross in Washington, D.C., and in 1882 the United States ratified the Geneva Convention. She led the organisation for 23 years, and her push for peacetime disaster relief led the International Red Cross Conference to adopt the so-called American Amendment in 1884.
real_life_example.explanation: Barton made organised compassion a permanent part of everyday national life, so that help after floods, fires and wars no longer depended on chance.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the ordinary business of the world runs on kindly regard, and Barton's Red Cross turned that regard into an institution that ordinary communities still rely on in every disaster.

tamil:
பண்என்னாம் பாடற்கு இயைபின்றேல் கண்என்னாம்
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்.
transliteration:
Pan ennaam paadarku iyaipindrel kan ennaam
Kannottam illaadha kan.
meaning: What use is a tune that does not fit the song? In the same way, what use is an eye that shows no kindness?
elementary: If someone plays a happy tune while you sing a sad lullaby, the music doesn’t help at all; it just sounds wrong. Valluvar says eyes are the same: eyes are meant to look kindly, and eyes without kindness are like music that doesn’t match the song.
university: பண் is the technical term for a melodic mode in Tamil music (roughly comparable to a raga), and இயைபு means ‘concordance’ or ‘fitting together’; the couplet thus draws on the Tamil musical tradition, in which the right pann had to suit the song and its mood. Parimelazhagar explains that just as a pann not matched to its song is useless, an eye not joined to kannottam is useless, so kindness is the eye’s proper ‘accompaniment’. The rhetorical question என்னாம் (‘what will it be?’, i.e., of what use) is repeated to link the two halves. Solomon Pappaiah renders பண் as ராகம், and all four commentaries on ytamizh.com share this reading. thirukkural-thamizh.org has பண்ணென்னாம் … கியைபின்றேற் for ytamizh’s பண்என்னாம் … இயைபின்றேல், which are orthographic and sandhi differences only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bharata’s Natyashastra teaches that music and performance succeed only when they evoke the right rasa (aesthetic emotion) through fitting bhava (feeling); technically correct sound without the fitting emotion fails to move the audience.
hinduism.explanation: Indian aesthetics judges art by whether its form fits and conveys the right inner feeling.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s mismatched pann and song is exactly this failure of fit, and the eye without kindness is form without its proper feeling.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says even the most eloquent gift, if it lacks love, is only empty noise.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s musical image of noise without love matches the Kural’s melody without fit and eye without kindness.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders or injury as does one who spends his wealth [only] to be seen by the people…”
islam.explanation: The Quran warns that a gift given with hurtful words or reminders is emptied of value, like dust washed off a bare rock.
islam.tie_back: An outward act without inner kindness is worthless, just as the Kural says of the eye without kannottam.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols. But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.”
judaism.explanation: Amos declares that temple music is unwelcome to God when it is not matched by justice and righteousness in life.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a melody that does not fit its true purpose is worthless; what gives it value is the moral quality behind it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of color but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practice them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares fine words without practice to a flower that looks lovely but has no scent.
buddhism.tie_back: The scentless flower, like the ill-fitting melody and the unkind eye, has the outward form but lacks its essential quality.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra's maxim padhamam nanam tao daya, 'first knowledge, then compassion', teaches that knowledge exists for the sake of compassion toward living beings.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching sees knowing and seeing as incomplete until they lead to compassion (daya).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use an eye is without kindly regard; the Jain maxim likewise treats knowing without compassion as missing its purpose.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 4.10 (as quoted and translated on the Jainstudy blog)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Among the ragas, Siree Raag is the best, if it inspires you to enshrine love for the True Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das says that even the most honoured musical mode is only truly fine when it carries the singer into love; the scripture itself is arranged by raag.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use a melody is that does not fit the song, and what use an eye without kindly regard; Guru Amar Das likewise judges music by whether its form carries the right inner feeling.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 83, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orpheus’s song in the underworld is so perfectly fitted to his grief that it moves even the pitiless rulers of Hades to pity and to release Eurydice.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the myth music has power because it carries true feeling that softens the hardest hearts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Music matched to feeling moves others to pity; the Kural says eyes, like music, exist to carry that pity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates argues that rhythm and harmony sink deep into the soul and that good music must fit and express good character; music detached from virtue is rejected.
philosophy.explanation: Plato ties the worth of music to its harmony with the moral character it expresses.
philosophy.tie_back: As Plato judges music by its fit with character, Valluvar judges the eye by its fit with kindness.

real_life_example.event_title: Yehudi Menuhin and Benjamin Britten play for the survivors of Bergen-Belsen
real_life_example.event: A few months after British troops liberated the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, the violinist Yehudi Menuhin made a short tour of displaced persons' camps in Germany, with the composer Benjamin Britten as his pianist. On 27 July 1945 they gave two concerts at Belsen for survivors who were still living there. Among the listeners was the cellist Anita Lasker, who had survived Auschwitz and Belsen.
real_life_example.explanation: Two celebrated musicians chose to bring their art to people who had suffered terribly, joining musical skill to human compassion.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use a melody is if it does not fit the song, and what use an eye is without kindness; at Belsen, music was given its fitting purpose by being joined to compassion for those who heard it.

tamil:
உளபோல் முகத்தெவன் செய்யும் அளவினால்
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்.
transliteration:
Ulapol mugaththevan seyyum alavinaal
Kannottam illaadha kan.
meaning: Eyes that do not show the right amount of kindness may sit in a face, but what good do they really do?
elementary: A doll can have beautiful painted eyes, but they never notice when you are sad. They are just there for decoration. Valluvar says eyes that never look kindly at anyone are like doll’s eyes: they are in the face, but they are not really doing an eye’s job.
university: உளபோல் (‘as if they exist’) makes the eyes a mere appearance on the face (முகத்து), and எவன் செய்யும் asks what use they serve. The key qualifier is அளவினால் (‘in due measure’): Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read the kindness required as kannottam within proper limits, i.e., kindness that does not override duty, which anticipates kural 578. Solomon Pappaiah likewise speaks of ‘kannottam within bounds’ (வரம்பிற்கு உட்பட்ட), while Kalaignar reads it as the eyes failing to stir love and pity in the heart. The couplet shares its second line verbatim with 573 (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்), a deliberate repetition that ties the two images together. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints உளபோன் … மளவினாற் (sandhi forms) for ytamizh’s உளபோல் … அளவினால், with no change in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But you cannot see Me with your present eyes. Therefore I give you divine eyes. Behold My mystic opulence!”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that his physical eyes, though working, cannot see what truly matters until he is given a higher kind of sight.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say that physical eyes alone are not enough; the eye has worth only when it sees in the right way.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that the eye’s moral quality (a ‘single’ or generous eye versus an ‘evil’ or grudging eye) determines whether a person is full of light or darkness.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Jesus judges the eye by the disposition it carries, not by its mere presence.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that outward features count for nothing before God; what matters is the heart and what it produces.
islam.tie_back: Eyes that merely sit in the face without kindness are exactly the outward form this hadith says has no value.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eliezer said, a good eye; Rabbi Joshua said, a good companion; Rabbi Yose said, a good neighbor; Rabbi Shimon said, foresight. Rabbi Elazar said, a good heart.”
judaism.explanation: Asked for the right way to cleave to, Rabban Yohanan’s disciples name the ‘good eye’ (ayin tovah), a generous and benevolent way of looking at others, and its opposite, the evil eye, as the way to shun.
judaism.tie_back: The rabbis, like Valluvar, make the moral quality of one’s gaze a central measure of character.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha reminds the over-strenuous monk Sona, a former lute player, that a lute sounds well only when its strings are neither too tight nor too loose, and tells him to set his effort in the same balance.
buddhism.explanation: Right practice, like right tuning, depends on measure rather than excess in either direction.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s அளவினால் (‘in due measure’) asks for kindness tuned in exactly this balanced way.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though he may possess all five organs of sense, still it is a rare chance to be instructed in the best Law; for people follow heretical teachers”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama that having complete senses is not enough unless they lead a person to the true Law.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says eyes without kindly regard only seem to be in the face; the Jain verse likewise says faculties in themselves count for little until they serve something higher.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O my eyes, the Lord has infused His Light into you; do not look upon any other than the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In Anand Sahib Guru Amar Das tells his eyes that their power of sight is a divine light given for a purpose, and must be used for that purpose.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says eyes without kindly regard only seem to be in the face and do no good; Guru Amar Das likewise holds that eyes are worth only what they are used to see.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 922, Raag Raamkalee, Anand Sahib (pauri 36), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Argus Panoptes, the giant with a hundred eyes, is set by Hera to watch Io and never lets all his eyes sleep, yet uses them only for guarding and surveillance, never for pity.
greek_mythology.explanation: The many-eyed watchman sees everything but feels nothing for the captive he guards, and is finally lulled to sleep and slain by Hermes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Argus shows that eyes, however many, are useless as eyes of a person when they carry no kindness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Emmanuel Levinas holds that the face of another person makes an ethical demand on me before anything else; to see a face truly is already to be called to responsibility for the other.
philosophy.explanation: For Levinas, ethics begins in the face-to-face encounter, where looking at someone properly means responding to their vulnerability.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s eyes that merely sit in the face without responding to others fail exactly the encounter Levinas places at the root of ethics.
philosophy.source: Emmanuel Levinas, Totality and Infinity (1961), Section III

real_life_example.event_title: Elizabeth Fry visits the women prisoners of Newgate
real_life_example.event: Early in 1813 a friend urged Elizabeth Fry, a Quaker minister, to visit the women's side of Newgate Prison, and she went in although the jailer warned her that the prisoners were dangerous. She found several hundred women and their children crowded into a few rooms, some sleeping on the floor. Fry kept returning, started a school for the prisoners' children, and with the prisoners and authorities introduced a matron, classification, education and paid sewing work, founding a Ladies' Association for Newgate in 1817.
real_life_example.explanation: Many officials had looked at Newgate for years; Fry was among the first to look at its women with real concern, and her measured, practical kindness changed prison practice in Britain.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says eyes without kindly regard in due measure only seem to be present; the officials' eyes had seen Newgate without effect, while Fry's regard, combined with order and discipline, actually did good.

tamil:
கண்ணிற்கு அணிகலம் கண்ணோட்டம் அஃதின்றேல்
புண்ணென்று உணரப் படும்.
transliteration:
Kannirku anigalam kannottam aqdhindrel
Punnendru unarap padum.
meaning: Kindness is the jewel that makes the eye beautiful. Without it, the eyes will look like nothing more than two sores.
elementary: People wear necklaces and bracelets to look nice. Valluvar says the nicest thing your eyes can ‘wear’ is kindness. If your eyes are always angry or cold, people will not see pretty eyes at all; they will see something that hurts, like a scrape.
university: அணிகலம் (‘ornament, jewel’) recalls the காரிகை (‘beauty’) of 571: kannottam is the eye’s jewellery, not merely its function. The shocking alternative, புண் (‘wound, sore’), plays on the near-rhyme கண்/புண், and the passive உணரப்படும் (‘will be perceived as’) implies the judgement of others; Solomon Pappaiah specifies ‘by the wise’ (பெரியோரால்), as does the Pope/Drew-style English gloss on ytamizh. Parimelazhagar’s point is that eyes are honoured only because they carry grace; without it they are merely openings in the flesh. This is the couplet the chapter is most remembered for, and its imagery of ornament versus wound is found in later Tamil ethical literature. The two sources agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms கண்ணிற் கணிகலங் … மஃதின்றேற் / புண்ணென் றுணரப்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Adi Shankara’s Kanakadhara Stotram, the poet praises the gracious sidelong glance (kaṭākṣa) of the goddess Lakshmi, whose kindly look alone is said to shower prosperity on a poor household.
hinduism.explanation: In Hindu devotion the deity’s kindly glance is itself the gift and the adornment of divine beauty.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hymn treats the kindly look as the eye’s true jewel and source of blessing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest…”
christianity.explanation: Before challenging the rich young man, Jesus looks at him with love, so that even a hard word comes through a kindly gaze.
christianity.tie_back: This is kannottam in action: the eye’s true adornment is the love it carries toward the person it looks at.

islam.quote_or_event: “Your smiling in the face of your brother is charity…”
islam.explanation: The Prophet counts even a smile toward another as an act of charity (sadaqah).
islam.tie_back: A kindly face is itself a gift, just as the Kural calls kindly regard the eye’s jewel.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor.”
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew is tov ayin, literally ‘good of eye’, the biblical idiom for a generous, kindly disposition toward others.
judaism.tie_back: The ‘good eye’ that is blessed is a close Hebrew counterpart to the kindly eye that the Kural calls adorned.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings. The devas protect one. Neither fire, poison, nor weapons can touch one. One’s mind gains concentration quickly. One’s complexion is bright.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the eleven benefits of cultivating goodwill (metta), the Buddha lists being dear to others and having a bright, clear complexion.
buddhism.tie_back: Goodwill brightens the face and makes one beloved, just as kannottam is the ornament of the eye.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 11.16, Metta Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As you look so happy in outward appearance, you must have peace of mind.”
jainism.explanation: A former Kshatriya who has turned monk reads Sanjaya's inner peace from the brightness of his face.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls kindly regard the jewel of the eye; the Jain verse likewise assumes that a person's inner quality shows in, and adorns, the face.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 18.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I am adorned with Truth, and I have applied the mascara of the Fear of God to my eyes.”
sikhism.explanation: Speaking as the bride-soul, Guru Arjan says her true adornment is a virtue, and that what she puts on her eyes is reverence for God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls kindly regard the jewel that adorns the eye, without which eyes are mere sores; Guru Arjan likewise makes a virtue the real ornament of the eyes.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 737, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Cyclops Polyphemus, with his single great eye, looks on Odysseus and his men not as guests but as food; Odysseus blinds that eye with a burning stake and escapes.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s monster embodies the eye without regard for guests, and his punishment falls on the very eye that showed no kindness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Polyphemus’s pitiless eye, turned into a wound, is a vivid picture of the Kural’s eye without kannottam becoming a sore.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes a nameless virtue of social life, a kind of friendliness, the mean between the obsequious flatterer and the quarrelsome, surly person who cares nothing for giving pain to others.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the pleasant, considerate manner in dealings with others is a genuine virtue, and its absence makes one disagreeable.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s friendly mean is close to kannottam as the grace of social interaction, whose lack makes a person offensive to others.

real_life_example.event_title: Audrey Hepburn's UNICEF mission to famine-struck Somalia
real_life_example.event: Audrey Hepburn, the film star, served as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador for a token salary of one dollar a year and had already visited Ethiopia, Sudan and Bangladesh for the agency. In 1992 she spent several days flying around central Somalia during the famine, visiting a feeding centre at Baidoa where starving children were being cared for. She was already seriously ill, underwent surgery in November 1992, and died in January 1993.
real_life_example.explanation: In her last working year, one of the world's most admired faces chose to be seen looking with compassion at suffering that much of the world had ignored.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls kindly regard the jewel of the eye, and Hepburn is remembered less for her famous looks than for the compassionate gaze she turned on Somalia's children.

tamil:
மண்ணோ டியைந்த மரத்தனையர் கண்ணோ
டியைந்துகண் ணோடா தவர்.
transliteration:
Mannodu iyaindha maraththanaiyar kannodu
iyaindhukan nodaa thavar.
meaning: People who have eyes but never look kindly at others are no better than trees standing in the ground.
elementary: A tree stands in one place and can’t notice when someone near it is crying. Valluvar says a person who has eyes but never looks kindly at others is just like that tree: standing there, but not really caring about anyone.
university: The couplet is built on a careful parallel: மண்ணோடு இயைந்த மரம் (‘a tree joined to the soil’) and கண்ணோடு இயைந்து கண்ணோடாதவர் (‘those who, though joined to eyes, do not let the eye run out [in kindness]’). The verb கண்ணோடு is the root of the chapter’s title, so the line plays on having கண் (eyes) but not doing கண்ணோட்டம். Parimelazhagar is usually cited as noting that trees too were said to have ‘eyes’ (buds or nodes), so that the unkind are no better than eyed trees; this pun is reported in commentary tradition and should be treated with some caution. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘like a tree that has eyes but does not see’, while Solomon Pappaiah stresses that such people move about but are as insensible as a tree fixed in the earth. The two texts agree word for word, with the line break falling inside கண்ணோ / டியைந்து in both.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Pride, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance – these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita lists pāruṣya (harshness, hardness) among the traits of the āsurī (demonic) nature, the opposite of the gentle divine nature.
hinduism.tie_back: The hard, unfeeling person the Kural likens to a tree is the Gita’s harsh āsuric type.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not? and do ye not remember?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus rebukes his disciples for having working eyes and ears yet failing to perceive what is before them.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Having eyes yet not seeing’ is the same paradox the Kural sets out: joined to eyes, yet not using them as eyes should be used.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts.”
islam.explanation: The Quran says true blindness lies not in the eyes but in hearts that will not respond.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s tree-like people have seeing eyes but unfeeling hearts, exactly the blindness this verse describes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not… They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalm mocks idols of wood and metal that have eyes without sight, and says their makers become like them.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s people with eyes who are no better than trees resemble the Psalm’s lifeless images with unseeing eyes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man of little learning grows old like a bull. He grows only in bulk, but, his wisdom does not grow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares a person who never develops inwardly to an ox that merely grows bigger.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s tree-like person, this one has bodily existence without the inner quality that makes a human being.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain teaching classes plants among the ekendriya beings, souls that possess only one sense, touch; human birth with all five senses is counted a rare chance that should not be wasted.
jainism.explanation: In Jain cosmology a tree is a living soul limited to a single sense, while a human being has the full faculties needed for right conduct.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural compares people who have eyes but show no kindly regard to trees standing in the soil; on Jain terms, such a person lives with five senses but, morally, no better than a one-sensed being.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.5-9 and 10.17, with Jacobi's note on the ekendriyas (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “What can cold do to a stone?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the stone that feels no cold as an image of the person on whom nothing outside can make an impression.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who have eyes yet never look kindly on others are like trees rooted in the soil, with form but no feeling; Guru Nanak's unfeeling stone makes the same point about outward form with no inner response.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 143, Raag Maajh (Maajh ki Vaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Gorgon Medusa’s gaze turns everyone who meets it to stone, until Perseus beheads her using a mirrored shield.
greek_mythology.explanation: Medusa’s look is the opposite of a kindly regard: it does not warm or soften others but deadens them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A gaze with no warmth is lifeless and makes others lifeless, like the Kural’s eyed yet wooden people.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius writes that a branch cut off from the branch next to it is cut off from the whole tree, and so a person who separates himself from even one fellow human has cut himself off from the whole community.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic emperor, withdrawing one’s goodwill from others amounts to self-amputation from the living body of humanity.
philosophy.tie_back: Both use tree imagery to say that a person without fellow-feeling is cut off from true human life.

real_life_example.event_title: The Evian Conference on refugees from Nazi Germany
real_life_example.event: At President Franklin Roosevelt's initiative, delegates from 32 countries and a number of aid organisations met for nine days at Evian on Lake Geneva to discuss Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Germany and annexed Austria. Nearly all the governments represented declined to open their doors to more refugees, and the Dominican Republic was the only participant that offered to accept significant additional numbers. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum concludes that the conference had very little impact on the refugees' plight.
real_life_example.explanation: The conference is remembered as a moment when the world's governments looked directly at people in danger and, apart from rare exceptions, did not act.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who have eyes but never look kindly are like trees rooted in the soil, having the form of seeing without the feeling, which is what most delegations at Evian displayed.

tamil:
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர் கண்ணுடையார்
கண்ணோட்டம் இன்மையும் இல்.
transliteration:
Kannottam illavar kannilar kannudaiyaar
Kannottam inmaiyum il.
meaning: People without kindness are really without eyes. And people who truly have eyes are never without kindness.
elementary: Imagine your friend drops their lunch and everyone looks away, but one kid runs over to help. Valluvar would say only that kid truly ‘saw’. Having real eyes means noticing people and caring about them; if you never care, it is as if you have no eyes at all.
university: The couplet is a chiasmus built on the single word கண்: those without கண்ணோட்டம் are கண்ணிலர் (‘eyeless’), and those who are கண்ணுடையார் (‘possessed of eyes’) are never without கண்ணோட்டம். Parimelazhagar reads it as a definition by convertibility: in the moral sense, having eyes and having kannottam are one and the same thing, so that physical sight without kindness does not count as sight. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah render it almost identically, while Kalaignar reverses the emphasis, saying the eyes of the compassionate alone deserve the name. With 576 it completes a sequence (573-577) that systematically strips the unkind eye of every value. Both sources agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has sandhi forms கண்ணோட்ட மில்லவர் … மின்மையு மில்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The humble sages, by virtue of true knowledge, see with equal vision a learned and gentle brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater [outcaste].”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita says the truly wise are sama-darśinaḥ, ‘those who see with equal vision’, regarding every being with the same respect.
hinduism.tie_back: For both texts, real seeing is a moral kind of sight; only the one who regards all beings rightly truly has eyes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.”
christianity.explanation: In the Gospels, Jesus’ seeing the crowds leads directly into compassion.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim in narrative form: one who truly sees cannot be without compassion.

islam.quote_or_event: “They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes those who have working senses but do not use them rightly as worse than cattle.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says people with eyes that do not truly see are in effect eyeless.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good eye, a humble spirit and a moderate appetite he is of the disciples of Abraham, our father. An evil eye, a haughty spirit and a limitless appetite he is of the disciples of Balaam, the wicked.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah makes the ‘good eye’, a generous and kindly way of seeing others, the first mark of a true disciple of Abraham.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the eye that counts is the good, benevolent eye; the other kind belongs to the wicked.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha speaks of three eyes: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the eye of discernment, and teaches that the eye of discernment is the highest.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching separates physical sight from the higher ‘eyes’ that see truly.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise separates the physical eye from the true eye, which in his case is the eye of kindness.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Without (right) faith there is no (right) knowledge, without (right) knowledge there is no virtuous conduct, without virtues there is no deliverance, and without deliverance there is no perfection.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's road to deliverance begins with right vision or faith (samyag-darshana), without which nothing else counts as true knowing or right action.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that those without kindly regard are really eyeless; Jainism likewise separates physical sight from right 'seeing' (darshana), which alone counts as true vision.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 28.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not call them blind, who have no eyes in their face. They alone are blind, O Nanak, who wander away from their Lord and Master.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad redefines blindness: the truly blind are not those without physical sight but those who have strayed from God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those without kindly regard are really eyeless, and those who truly have eyes always have it; Guru Angad makes the same move of redefining sight and blindness in moral terms.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Raamkalee (Raamkalee ki Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Oedipus the King, the blind prophet Tiresias sees the truth, while Oedipus, with perfect eyesight, cannot see what he has done until he blinds himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: The play turns on the irony that the sighted man is truly blind and the blind man truly sees.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s paradox that the sighted can be ‘eyeless’ has its Greek counterpart in Oedipus and Tiresias.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He is a runaway, who flies from social reason; he is blind, who shuts the eyes of the understanding; … he is a piece rent asunder from the state, who tears his own soul from that of reasonable animals, which is one.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus lists the ways a person fails his own nature: whoever cuts himself off from the shared reason and fellowship of rational beings is a fugitive, blind, and torn from the whole.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Marcus calls the one who withdraws from fellow-feeling blind, though his blindness is of the understanding rather than a lack of kindly regard.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV, §29 (tr. George Long)

real_life_example.event_title: Bartolome de las Casas gives up his encomienda in Cuba
real_life_example.event: Bartolome de las Casas had come to the Caribbean as a settler, served as a chaplain in the Spanish conquest of Cuba, and was granted land and Indigenous labourers under the encomienda system. Influenced by Dominican friars who denounced the treatment of the Indigenous people, he renounced his encomienda and freed the people assigned to him around 1514, and began preaching that other colonists should do the same. When his preaching in Cuba had little effect he went to Spain to plead the case at court, and he spent the rest of his long life defending the Indigenous peoples of the Americas.
real_life_example.explanation: Las Casas had lived among the same suffering for years before he truly saw it; once he did, he could not look away for the rest of his life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those without kindly regard are really eyeless and those who truly have eyes are never without it, and Las Casas's turning point was the moment his sight became real sight.

tamil:
கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட வல்லார்க்கு
உரிமை உடைத்திவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Karumam sidhaiyaamal kannoda vallaarkku
Urimai udaiththiv vulagu.
meaning: The world truly belongs to those who can show kindness without letting their duty be harmed.
elementary: A good referee is friendly and kind to all the players, but still calls a foul when someone breaks the rules. Valluvar says the best leaders are like that: kind to everyone, but they never let kindness stop them from doing what is right.
university: கருமம் here means one’s proper task, and for a king Parimelazhagar specifies it as the administration of justice (the ytamizh English gloss adds ‘administration of justice’ in brackets); சிதையாமல் means ‘without letting it be spoiled’. The couplet thus sets a limit on kannottam: kindness toward familiar people must never become favouritism that ruins just government, which explains the அளவினால் (‘in due measure’) of 574. உரிமை உடைத்து இவ்வுலகு (‘this world has rightful ownership [for them]’) promises that such rulers are the world’s natural possessors. Modern commentators generalise the principle to anyone who is compassionate without neglecting their duties (Kalaignar: ‘first in not failing duty and in showering mercy’). Both texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms கருமஞ் சிதையாமற் … வல்லார்க் / குரிமை யுடைத்திவ்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya teaches that a king severe with the rod terrifies his subjects, one too mild with it is despised, and one who wields it justly is respected.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra demands a balance: neither harshness nor softness, but punishment measured by justice.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s balance of kindness that does not ruin duty, seen from the side of the king’s rod.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee? She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus shows mercy to the woman accused of adultery while still clearly naming the wrong and calling her to change.
christianity.tie_back: Mercy without abandoning the moral standard is exactly the Kural’s kindness that does not damage duty.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression.”
islam.explanation: The Quran joins ʿadl (justice) and iḥsān (excellence or kindness) in a single command, so that neither is to be sacrificed to the other.
islam.tie_back: Justice held together with kindness is the combination the Kural says wins the world.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that a king’s rule is secured by mercy (ḥesed) together with truth.
judaism.tie_back: As the Kural says the world belongs to the ruler who is kind without neglecting duty, Proverbs says mercy with truth upholds the throne.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Jatakas list ten royal virtues (dasa raja dhamma) for a righteous king, including generosity, gentleness (maddava), patience (khanti) and non-violence, alongside moral conduct and adherence to what is right.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist ideal king combines gentleness and patience with steady righteousness.
buddhism.tie_back: This list of royal virtues pairs kindness with righteousness, just as the Kural does.
buddhism.source: Jataka 534 (Mahahamsa Jataka) and related Jataka tradition of dasa raja dhamma

jainism.quote_or_event: “Virodhi Himsa is the kind of injury which is necessarily committed in defense of person and property, against thieves, robbers, dacoits, assailants and enemies, in meeting their aggression, and in causing the least possible injury, necessary in the circumstances, in which one may find oneself.”
jainism.explanation: Jain lay ethics requires a householder to give up intentional violence but recognises that protecting people and property may require force, always kept to the least possible injury.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the world belongs to those who are kind without letting their duty suffer; Jain ethics likewise lets the householder, or the ruler, do the duty of protection while keeping the injury done to a minimum.
jainism.source: 'The Concept of Himsa', Jain philosophy pages on jainworld.com

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They are kind to all beings; they have overpowered the five thieves.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the holy as joining kindness to all beings with firm mastery over lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the world belongs to those who show kindly regard without letting their duty be spoiled; Guru Arjan likewise pairs kindness with a discipline that it is never allowed to weaken.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1357, Salok Sehskritee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Eumenides, Athena founds the Areopagus court to try Orestes and then persuades the vengeful Furies to accept honour in Athens, turning them into the ‘Kindly Ones’ without abolishing justice.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows justice kept intact while vengeance is softened into benevolence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Athena achieves what the Kural praises: kindness that does not destroy the work of justice.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes equity (epieikeia) as a correction of the law where its generality makes it unjust, and the equitable person as one who takes less than his strict due though the law is on his side.
philosophy.explanation: Equity lets humane judgement soften the law without abandoning justice itself.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s equity is the kind of measured mildness the Kural asks for: kind, yet never spoiling justice.

real_life_example.event_title: George Washington's Newburgh Address to his discontented officers
real_life_example.event: Near the end of the American Revolutionary War, Continental Army officers who had gone months or years without pay or promised pensions circulated an anonymous address threatening to defy Congress. George Washington forbade the meeting they had called and summoned the officers himself on 15 March 1783, where he read a speech that sympathised with their grievances but condemned the methods being proposed. The next day the officers passed a unanimous resolution commending Washington, the threatened mutiny ended, and Washington kept pressing Congress until the officers were granted five years' full pay.
real_life_example.explanation: Washington showed real understanding of his officers' hardship without letting that sympathy override his duty to uphold civilian authority.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world belongs to those who can show kindly regard without letting their duty be damaged, and at Newburgh Washington's sympathy for his men and his duty to the republic stood side by side.

tamil:
ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும்கண் ணோடிப்
பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை.
transliteration:
Oruththaatrum panbinaar kannum kannodip
Poruththaatrum panbe thalai.
meaning: The highest goodness is to show kindness and patiently put up with even those who like to hurt us.
elementary: If a classmate keeps being mean to you, the easy thing is to be mean back. Valluvar says the very best thing is to stay kind and patient with them anyway. That is the hardest kind of kindness, and so it is the greatest.
university: ஒறுத்து ஆற்றும் பண்பினார் means ‘those whose nature is to cause harm/afflict’, and the matching பொறுத்து ஆற்றும் பண்பு is ‘the nature that bears it and carries on’; the verbal rhyme ஒறுத்து/பொறுத்து sets the injurer’s nature against the forbearer’s. கண்ணும் (‘even towards’) extends kannottam from familiar friends to enemies, the chapter’s highest reach. Commentators differ slightly on the object: Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘even those who deserve punishment’, stressing a judge’s leniency, while Solomon Pappaiah and the English gloss read ‘those who grieve or harm us’, stressing personal forbearance; Parimelazhagar’s royal reading allows both. தலை (‘head’, i.e., foremost) ranks this above all other forms of kindness. Both texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has கண்ணுங்கண் for ytamizh’s கண்ணும்கண்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the devotee dear to him as maitraḥ karuṇaḥ (friendly and compassionate) and kṣamī (forgiving) toward all beings.
hinduism.tie_back: Kindness and forbearance toward all, including those who harm us, is the Kural’s supreme virtue.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
christianity.explanation: On the cross, Jesus prays for the very people who are putting him to death.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s highest virtue at its limit: kindly bearing with those who are actively harming one.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Quran commands answering hostility with something better, promising that an enemy may become a close friend.
islam.tie_back: Returning kindness for harm is exactly the forbearing kannottam the Kural ranks highest.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who was plagued by a heretic and waited for the moment of divine anger to curse him, but dozed off; on waking he concluded that cursing people is not proper, since God’s mercy is over all his creatures, even sinners.
judaism.explanation: The sage learns that even toward someone who torments him, the right course is mercy rather than retaliation.
judaism.tie_back: Rabbi Yehoshua’s turn from cursing to forbearance is the Kural’s kindly patience toward those who harm us.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches meeting each vice with its opposite virtue rather than in kind.
buddhism.tie_back: Overcoming the wicked by goodness is the Kural’s forbearing kindness toward those who hurt us.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Ceasing to use the stick (i.e. cruelty) against living beings, abandoning the care of the body, the houseless (Mahâvîra), the Venerable One, endures the thorns of the villages (i.e. the abusive language of the peasants), (being) perfectly enlightened.”
jainism.explanation: In the pathless Ladha country villagers beat Mahavira, set dogs on him and abused him, and he bore it all without retaliating.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural ranks forbearing kindness toward those who hurt us as the highest virtue; Mahavira's patience under the Ladha villagers' blows and insults is the Jain model of that forbearance.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.9.3.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org, where it is numbered Lecture 8, Lesson 3)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir places forgiveness at the highest level, as the very place where God is present.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls it the highest virtue to bear patiently with those whose nature is to hurt us; Kabir likewise exalts forgiveness above all, as the dwelling of God Himself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the aged Priam comes by night to Achilles’ tent to ransom the body of Hector, the son who killed Patroclus, Achilles, moved by pity, weeps with him, returns the body and grants a truce for the funeral.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest warrior of the Iliad extends compassion to the father of his worst enemy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ pity for Priam is kindly regard shown to one bound up with the very person who hurt him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that benevolence is invincible if it is genuine, and that the most insolent man can do nothing to one who stays kind to him and gently corrects him.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, unshakeable goodwill toward offenders is both the highest and the strongest stance.
philosophy.tie_back: Marcus’s invincible kindness toward those who wrong us is the Kural’s supreme forbearance.

real_life_example.event_title: J. R. Jayewardene urges forgiveness of Japan at the San Francisco Peace Conference
real_life_example.event: At the conference called to make peace with Japan after the Second World War, Ceylon's finance minister J. R. Jayewardene addressed the delegates in the War Memorial Opera House. Citing the Buddha's teaching that hatred is ended not by hatred but by love, he argued that Japan should be allowed to rejoin the community of nations as a free country, and Ceylon renounced its claim to reparations. Japanese leaders have repeatedly acknowledged the speech in the decades since.
real_life_example.explanation: A country that had suffered wartime attack chose to answer its former enemy with forbearance rather than retribution.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls it the highest virtue to show kindly regard and patiently bear with even those who have hurt us, and Ceylon's stand at San Francisco extended that regard to a former enemy.

tamil:
பெயக்கண்டும் நஞ்சுண் டமைவர் நயத்தக்க
நாகரிகம் வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Peyakkandum nanjundu amaivar nayaththakka
Naagarigam vendu pavar.
meaning: People who want the kind of politeness everyone admires will even drink poison they watched a friend pour for them, and still stay friends.
elementary: Suppose a friend gives you a cookie that tastes awful, and you know they didn’t make it right. A very gracious person might eat it and still smile, because they care more about the friend than the cookie. Valluvar tells this as an extreme story to show how far true kindness can go.
university: The couplet is deliberately hyperbolic: பெயக் கண்டும் (‘even having seen it poured’) and நஞ்சு உண்டு அமைவர் (‘they drink the poison and remain calm/content’) describe people who knowingly accept harm from someone close rather than break the bond. நாகரிகம் here does not mean modern ‘civilisation’; Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take it as the refined kannottam, the urbane courtesy that is நயத்தக்க (‘worthy of being desired’ by all). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah specify that the poison is offered by those one has long associated with, and the Sangam anthology Natrinai (poem 355) is frequently cited for the closely related idea that the truly refined will drink even poison offered by friends. Commentators treat the couplet as illustrating the extreme limit of kannottam rather than a literal instruction. Both texts agree word for word.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the gods and demons churn the ocean of milk, the deadly poison halahala rises first and threatens all the worlds; out of compassion Shiva drinks it and holds it in his throat, which turns blue, earning him the name Nilakantha.
hinduism.explanation: Shiva knowingly takes poison upon himself for the sake of others, showing the highest kind of grace.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the refined person of the Kural, Shiva drinks poison he has seen, calmly, out of care for others.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He it is, to whom I shall give a sop, when I have dipped it. And when he had dipped the sop, he gave it to Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon.”
christianity.explanation: At the Last Supper Jesus, knowing Judas will betray him, still shares food with him as a sign of fellowship.
christianity.tie_back: Keeping table fellowship with one known to be preparing harm is the Kural’s courtesy that drinks the poison a companion pours.

islam.quote_or_event: “A Jewess brought a poisoned (cooked) sheep for the Prophet (ﷺ) who ate from it. She was brought to the Prophet and he was asked, ‘Shall we kill her?’ He said, ‘No.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet was served poisoned meat, suffered its effects, and still refused to have the woman who served it killed.
islam.tie_back: Enduring poison served by a host and refusing revenge is a striking historical parallel to the Kural’s image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. Now therefore fear ye not: I will nourish you, and your little ones. And he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph, once sold into slavery by his own brothers, forgives them and promises to provide for them.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph swallowed the ‘poison’ his kin gave him and still kept the bond, which is the Kural’s gracious courtesy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: At Pava the smith Cunda serves the Buddha a dish (sukara-maddava) after which he falls gravely ill; the Buddha eats it, then asks Ananda to reassure Cunda that the last meal given to a Buddha brings great merit, so that no one blames him.
buddhism.explanation: Even as the meal leads to his final illness, the Buddha’s concern is to protect his host from remorse and blame.
buddhism.tie_back: Accepting a harmful dish from a devoted host while guarding the bond is close to the Kural’s image of drinking a friend’s poison calmly.

jainism.quote_or_event: The monk Dharmaruchi, breaking a month-long fast, was served a dish of bitter gourd that his teacher recognised as deadly; sent to dispose of it, he saw ants die after touching a drop, and rather than let more creatures die he ate the whole poisonous dish himself and died calmly.
jainism.explanation: This story, from the Jnatadharmakatha tradition, shows a monk knowingly swallowing poison he has seen served to him rather than cause harm.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises those who calmly drink poison they have seen poured; Dharmaruchi does this literally, though his motive is compassion for small beings rather than courtesy toward a friend.
jainism.source: Dharmaruchi Muni story (Jnatadharmakatha tradition), as retold on jainworld.com

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Your Will seems so sweet to me; whatever You do, is pleasing to me.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan prays to accept whatever God sends, bitter or sweet, as pleasing; Sikh tradition remembers him for keeping this acceptance through his torture and martyrdom in 1606.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises those who, for the sake of courtesy, will calmly drink poison poured for them by a friend; Guru Arjan's acceptance of whatever comes as sweet is the Sikh counterpart of such calm endurance.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 713, Raag Todee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The wise centaur Chiron, teacher and friend of heroes, is accidentally struck by one of Heracles’ arrows dipped in the Hydra’s poison; unable to heal, he bears it without enmity toward Heracles and finally gives up his immortality.
greek_mythology.explanation: Chiron endures a poison that came from a friend’s hand without turning against him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Chiron bearing poison from a friend without resentment echoes the Kural’s refined person who drinks poison from a companion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedo, the servant of the Eleven who brings Socrates the hemlock weeps as he says farewell, and Socrates speaks warmly of the man’s kindness before calmly drinking the cup.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates meets the bearer of his poison with graciousness and drinks it with complete composure.
philosophy.tie_back: His calm, courteous acceptance of the cup is a classical image of the Kural’s refinement that drinks poison and stays at peace.

real_life_example.event_title: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson renew their friendship
real_life_example.place: Quincy, Massachusetts, and Monticello, Virginia, United States
real_life_example.event: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson, partners in the American Revolution, became bitter political opponents, and after Jefferson defeated Adams in the 1800 presidential election the two men stopped writing to each other. Their mutual friend Benjamin Rush spent years urging them to make peace, and in 1812 Adams wrote to Jefferson and Jefferson replied. They then corresponded until both died on 4 July 1826, the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.
