real_life_example.explanation: Two men who had wounded each other deeply in public life chose to set the injuries aside and value the friendship above them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises those who, for the sake of courtesy and friendship, will swallow even a bitter injury from a friend and stay at peace with him, as Adams and Jefferson did for the last fourteen years of their lives.

tamil:
ஒற்றும் உரைசான்ற நூலும் இவையிரண்டும்
தெற்றென்க மன்னவன் கண்.
transliteration:
Otrum uraisaandra noolum ivaiyirandum
Thetrenga mannavan kan.
meaning: A ruler should know that he has two eyes: his spies, who show him what is really happening, and the respected books of law, which show him what should be done.
elementary: A captain steering a ship needs two things: a lookout who shouts what he sees on the sea, and a map that shows the right route. With only one, the ship gets lost. This kural says a ruler is the same: he needs people who tell him what is really going on, and good rules that tell him what is right.
university: The chapter title ஒற்றாடல் means ‘the employment (ஆடல், handling) of spies’; one printed text glosses it ஒற்றரை ஆளும் திறம், ‘the skill of managing spies’. It follows directly on கண்ணோட்டம் (ch. 58, ‘the kindly eye’), and Valluvar continues the eye image by naming two organs of royal sight: ஒற்று (the spy, or intelligence generally) and உரைசான்ற நூல் (a treatise ‘full of renown’). Parimelazhagar takes the second to be the science of polity (நீதிநூல்), and the commentators draw the contrast that the treatise shows what should be done while the spy shows what is being done; a king lacking either is half-blind. The verb தெற்றென்க (‘let him know clearly’) turns the saying into a direct order. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it the same way, and the text is identical on ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the last printing it in older sandhi-joined form (ஒற்று முரைசான்ற நூலு மிவையிரண்டுந்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let the king who sees (everything) through his spies, discover the two sorts of thieves who deprive others of their property, both those who (show themselves) openly and those who (lie) concealed.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu describes the ideal king as one who ‘sees through his spies’ (the Sanskrit ideal of the cāra-cakṣus, the spy-eyed ruler) and uses that sight to apply the law against open and hidden wrongdoers.
hinduism.tie_back: Spies as the king’s eyes, working together with the law, is exactly the Kural’s pair of ‘two eyes’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the word of God is quick, and powerful … and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews joins a searching, discerning word to an all-seeing eye from which nothing is hidden.
christianity.tie_back: A discerning word plus a seeing eye mirrors the Kural’s law-book plus spy, though here both belong to God and not to a king.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, We have revealed to you, [O Muḥammad], the Book in truth so you may judge between the people by that which Allāh has shown you. And do not be for the deceitful an advocate.”
islam.explanation: The ruler-judge is to decide by the revealed Book and by what God has let him see, and is warned against being fooled into siding with deceivers.
islam.tie_back: The Book and the ‘showing’ together play the roles of the Kural’s law-text and spy-eye.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs pictures a king on the seat of justice whose watchful sight alone drives wrongdoing away.
judaism.tie_back: Judgment (law) and the king’s eyes are the two instruments of the Kural’s couplet.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti-Sīhanāda Sutta, the righteous wheel-turning king is told to rely on the Dhamma alone, to give lawful protection to all classes, and to go regularly to wise ascetics and ask them what is wholesome and what is not, so that he stays informed and on the right path.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist ideal king governs by two supports: the Dhamma as his law and constant questioning of the wise as his source of knowledge.
buddhism.tie_back: Law plus active inquiry is a gentler Buddhist version of the Kural’s law-book plus spy.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Knowledge is fivefold: 1. Sruta, knowledge derived from the sacred books; 2. Âbhinibôdhika, perception; 3. Avadhi, supernatural knowledge; 4. Manahparyâya, knowledge of the thoughts of other people; 5. Kêvala, the highest, unlimited knowledge.”
jainism.explanation: Jain epistemology begins its list of the ways of knowing with two ordinary sources: what is learned from scripture (śruta) and what is learned by direct observation (mati or perception).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's two eyes, the law-books that show what ought to be done and the spies who report what is actually happening, line up with scripture-knowledge and perception, the first two Jain kinds of knowledge.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Guru has given the healing ointment of spiritual wisdom, and dispelled the darkness of ignorance.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan pictures the Guru's teaching as a salve (anjan) put on the eyes, so that a person can see what the darkness of ignorance had hidden.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural gives the king two eyes, his spies and the books of statecraft; Guru Arjan likewise treats the Guru's wisdom as what gives true sight, though he means the inner eye, not political intelligence.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 293, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that the maiden Dike (Justice) sits beside her father Zeus and tells him of men’s unjust minds, and that the eye of Zeus sees all and understands all.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Greek picture, the king of the gods rules with two helpers: Justice, who reports wrongdoing, and his own all-seeing eye.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Justice and the watching eye beside the throne match the Kural’s law and spy as a king’s two eyes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Xenophon says that Cyrus the Great, by rewarding everyone who brought him useful information, came to have many so-called ‘King’s eyes’ and ‘King’s ears’ spread across his empire, so that people feared to say or do anything against him.
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon presents a network of informants as the sense organs of a well-run empire.
philosophy.tie_back: The ‘King’s eyes’ are the Kural’s ஒற்று almost word for word.

real_life_example.event_title: U-2 photographs and a lawful quarantine in the Cuban Missile Crisis
real_life_example.place: Cuba and Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: On 14 October 1962 an American U-2 reconnaissance aircraft photographed Soviet medium-range and intermediate-range ballistic missile sites under construction in Cuba, and analysts at the National Photographic Interpretation Center identified the missiles the next day. President John F. Kennedy and his advisers chose a naval quarantine rather than an immediate attack, using the word quarantine because a blockade would legally imply a state of war, and they sought the backing of the Organization of American States. Kennedy announced the quarantine on 22 October, and it was lifted on 20 November 1962 after the Soviet Union agreed to remove its missiles and, finally, its IL-28 bombers.
real_life_example.explanation: The crisis was handled with two kinds of sight working together: hard intelligence about what was actually happening, and careful attention to law and treaty about what the United States could rightfully do.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a ruler has two eyes, spies who show what is happening and the respected books of law that show what ought to be done, and in October 1962 both eyes were open at once.

tamil:
எல்லார்க்கும் எல்லாம் நிகழ்பவை எஞ்ஞான்றும்
வல்லறிதல் வேந்தன் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Ellaarkkum ellaam nigazhpavai enjnjaandrum
Vallaridhal vaendhan thozhil.
meaning: A king’s job is to find out quickly, at all times, everything that happens to everyone, whether they are enemies, friends, or neither.
elementary: A good school principal wants to know right away if someone is being bullied, if a pipe is leaking, or if a new student feels lost, not a month later. This kural says a ruler’s real work is the same: always finding out quickly what is happening to everyone.
university: The couplet stacks three universals, எல்லார்க்கும் (to all persons), எல்லாம் (all things) and எஞ்ஞான்றும் (at all times), then adds வல் (‘swiftly’) to அறிதல் (knowing). Parimelazhagar spells out ‘all persons’ as the king’s enemies, friends and neutrals (பகைவர், நட்பினர், நொதுமலர்), and Pappaiah and Kalaignar follow this three-way division, which matches the Arthashastra’s mandala theory of foreign relations. Most commentators add ‘through spies’ in brackets because the chapter context requires it, even though the word ஒற்று is not in the line. The closing தொழில் (‘occupation, duty’) presents knowing as the king’s trade and not something he does now and then. The wording is the same on all three sources consulted; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form எல்லார்க்கு மெல்லா.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As the Wind moves (everywhere), entering (in the shape of the vital air) all created beings, even so let him penetrate (everywhere) through his spies; that is the office in which he resembles the Wind.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu compares the king to the wind god, whose ‘office’ is to reach every being through his spies.
hinduism.tie_back: Getting everywhere, into everyone’s affairs, is the Kural’s ‘all things of all people’; both texts call it the king’s office or duty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning … And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus demands watchfulness at every hour of the night, because what matters may arrive at any time.
christianity.tie_back: Being alert at every hour echoes the Kural’s எஞ்ஞான்றும், ‘at all times’.

islam.quote_or_event: “And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. And He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but that He knows it.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes God’s complete knowledge of everything that happens, down to a single falling leaf.
islam.tie_back: The Kural asks the human king to aim, as far as he can, at the same complete knowledge of events in his realm.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And see the land, what it is; and the people that dwelleth therein, whether they be strong or weak, few or many; And what the land is that they dwell in, whether it be good or bad; and what cities they be that they dwell in, whether in tents, or in strong holds.”
judaism.explanation: Moses gives the twelve spies a full intelligence brief covering people, strength, numbers, land and fortifications.
judaism.tie_back: Moses wants to know ‘everything about everyone’ in Canaan, which is the scope the Kural sets for a king.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka the Bodhisatta, as the sage Mahosadha, sends spies to every royal court, and they bring home reports that let him learn of plots against his king before they happen.
buddhism.explanation: The future Buddha is shown as a wise minister who keeps his king informed by a wide network of agents.
buddhism.tie_back: Reports from every court, arriving continually, are the Kural’s ideal of knowing all things about all parties.
buddhism.source: Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka (Jātaka 546), as summarised in the Dictionary of Pali Proper Names (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He was a Kevalin, omniscient and comprehending all objects, he knew all conditions of the world, of gods, men, and demons; whence they come, where they go … their food, drink, doings, desires, open and secret deeds, their conversation and gossip, and the thoughts of their minds; he saw and knew all conditions in the whole world of all living beings.”
jainism.explanation: On attaining kevala-jñāna Mahavira is described as knowing everything about every being, including their hidden deeds and thoughts, at all times.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks the king to know everything that happens to everyone, at all times; Jainism places that complete, all-encompassing knowledge in the omniscient Jina rather than in any ruler or his spies.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra 2.15.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The recording scribes of the conscious and the unconscious, Chitr and Gupt, know all actions and karma.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan uses the inherited figure of Chitr and Gupt, the recorders who note every deed of every person, to say that nothing anyone does goes unknown.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural makes it the king's trade to know at all times everything that happens to everyone; Gurbani gives such total and constant knowledge only to the divine order and its recorders.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 838, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hera set Argus Panoptes, the ‘all-seeing’ giant with eyes all over his body, to watch without rest, because some of his eyes were always awake while others slept.
greek_mythology.explanation: Argus is Greek myth’s image of a watcher who never stops seeing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His sleepless, many-eyed watch pictures the Kural’s demand for knowing everything at all times.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now this foreknowledge cannot be elicited from spirits; it cannot be obtained inductively from experience, nor by any deductive calculation. Knowledge of the enemy’s dispositions can only be obtained from other men.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu argues that the knowledge a sovereign needs most can come only from living informants.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Sun Tzu makes gathering human intelligence a core duty of the wise ruler.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 13.5-6 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Britain's Room 40 intercepts the Zimmermann Telegram
real_life_example.event: In January 1917 the German foreign secretary Arthur Zimmermann sent a coded telegram proposing that, if the United States entered the war, Mexico should ally with Germany. British naval codebreakers in Room 40 intercepted and decoded it as it passed over British-controlled cable routes. Britain passed the text to the American ambassador Walter Page on 22 February, its publication helped turn American opinion, and the United States declared war on Germany in April 1917.
real_life_example.explanation: Room 40 was reading not only enemy messages but the traffic that touched neutral countries, and so learned an enemy plan aimed at two neutrals before either of them knew of it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural makes it a ruler's duty to learn quickly what is happening with enemies, friends and neutrals alike, and the Zimmermann intercept shows that wide watchfulness turning the course of a war.

tamil:
ஒற்றினான் ஒற்றிப் பொருள்தெரியா மன்னவன்
கொற்றங் கொளக்கிடந்தது இல்.
transliteration:
Otrinaan otrip poruldheriyaa mannavan
Kotrang kolakkidandhadhu il.
meaning: A king who does not collect news through spies and understand what it means has no way to win.
elementary: Imagine a football coach who never watches the other team play and never thinks about what their moves mean. He will keep losing. This kural says a leader has to find out what is going on and then think carefully about what it means.
university: The first line repeats the root ஒற்று (ஒற்றினான் ஒற்றி, ‘spying by means of a spy’), a figure of repetition that runs through the whole chapter. The key phrase is பொருள் தெரியா, ‘not discerning the meaning or import’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as not examining the benefit (பயன்) of what spies report, and Pulavar Kesikan as not working out the significance of events in enemy lands. So Valluvar is not satisfied with collecting data; the king must interpret it. The second line, கொற்றங் கொளக்கிடந்தது இல், says literally that ‘there is nothing lying there for him to take as victory’. Pappaiah widens கொற்றம் from battlefield victory to lasting success of the government. The text agrees on all three sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ஒற்றினா னொற்றிப் பொருடெரியா, with the sandhi shown.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “By spies, by a (pretended) display of energy, and by carrying out (various) undertakings, let the king constantly ascertain his own and his enemy’s strength.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king to measure his own strength and the enemy’s constantly, and spies come first among the means.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Ascertaining strength’ from spy reports is the Kural’s பொருள் தெரிதல், discerning what the intelligence means.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the example of a king who weighs the enemy’s strength against his own before going to war.
christianity.tie_back: Sitting down to weigh the facts is the interpretive step without which, the Kural says, victory is impossible.

islam.quote_or_event: Before Badr, the Prophet’s scouts brought in two water-carriers of the Quraysh. Asked how many camels the army slaughtered each day, they said nine one day and ten the next, and the Prophet concluded that the enemy numbered between nine hundred and a thousand.
islam.explanation: The early biographies show the Prophet turning a small piece of scouting information into an accurate estimate of enemy numbers.
islam.tie_back: Getting information and then reasoning out its meaning is exactly what the Kural means by ஒற்றிப் பொருள் தெரிதல்.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sīrat Rasūl Allāh, Battle of Badr (paraphrase)

judaism.quote_or_event: “And they brought up an evil report of the land which they had searched unto the children of Israel, saying, The land … is a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof; and all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature.”
judaism.explanation: Ten of the twelve spies turned their observations into a fearful, distorted report. The people accepted it without weighing it against Joshua and Caleb’s account and lost their chance to enter the land.
judaism.tie_back: This is a clear case of intelligence gathered but wrongly interpreted, and the promised victory is lost, as the Kural warns.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “No harm, indeed, can be done to the Vajjis in battle by Magadha’s king, Ajatasattu, except through treachery or discord.”
buddhism.explanation: King Ajatasattu sent his chief minister Vassakara to find out the Buddha’s view before attacking the Vajjis. Vassakara drew this strategic conclusion from what he heard.
buddhism.tie_back: The minister gathers information and then works out what it means for victory, which is the two-step process the Kural requires.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta 1.5 (trans. Sister Vajira & Francis Story)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Without (right) faith there is no (right) knowledge, without (right) knowledge there is no virtuous conduct, without virtues there is no deliverance, and without deliverance there is no perfection.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana makes right knowledge a precondition of right conduct, and right conduct a precondition of final success.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural says a king who does not gather and understand reports has no path to victory, Jainism says that without correct knowledge there is no way to the soul's victory.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those mortals whose minds are like deep dark pits do not understand the purpose of life, even when it is explained to them.” … “Some know how to speak, and understand what they are told. They are wise and beautiful.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak contrasts those who hear words without grasping their meaning with those who understand what they are told.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a king who gathers news through spies but does not work out what it means can win nothing; Guru Nanak likewise values not the hearing of reports but the understanding of them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1246, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On a night raid, Odysseus and Diomedes capture the Trojan scout Dolon, question him about where the Trojan allies are camped, and use his answers to reach the newly arrived Thracian king Rhesus and take his famous horses.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Doloneia shows scouting turned straight into success once the Greeks grasp what the information reveals, namely an unguarded new ally.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Greeks’ success comes from reading the intelligence correctly, which is the Kural’s condition for victory.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will also suffer a defeat.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu’s best-known saying makes knowledge of the enemy a condition of reliable victory.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same thing from the negative side: without understood intelligence there is no victory.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.18 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Stalin disregards warnings of the German invasion
real_life_example.event: In the months before June 1941, Soviet intelligence sources in Germany, Japan, Romania and Switzerland, including the spy Richard Sorge in Tokyo, reported that Germany was preparing to invade, and Churchill and Roosevelt also tried to warn Joseph Stalin. Stalin dismissed the reports as provocations or disinformation, kept supplying raw materials to Germany and ordered his forces not to fire on German aircraft crossing the border. On 22 June 1941 Germany launched Operation Barbarossa and inflicted massive early defeats on the unprepared Red Army.
real_life_example.explanation: Stalin did not lack intelligence; he failed to weigh it and draw the obvious conclusion, and his country paid an enormous price for that failure.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a king who gathers news through spies but does not work out what it means has no path to victory, which is exactly what happened when Stalin's many warnings went unheeded.

tamil:
வினைசெய்வார் தம்சுற்றம் வேண்டாதார் என்றாங்கு
அனைவரையும் ஆராய்வது ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Vinaiseyvaar thamsutram vaendaadhaar endraangu
Anaivaraiyum aaraaivadhu otru.
meaning: A true spy watches everyone without exception: the king’s own officers, his relatives, and his enemies too.
elementary: A fair referee watches every player on the field, even the ones from his own town and even his friends. If he only watched one team, the game would be unfair. This kural says a good investigator checks on everyone equally.
university: Valluvar names three groups: வினைசெய்வார் (those who carry out the king’s business, i.e. officials), தம் சுற்றம் (the king’s own kin), and வேண்டாதார் (those who do not wish him well, i.e. enemies). He then sums them up in அனைவரையும் (‘all of them’). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take தம் to mean the king’s own relatives. Kalaignar reads the couplet as a rule of impartiality for the spy, who must not make exceptions for those he likes or dislikes. Pappaiah modernises the groups as civil servants, the ruling party, the opposition and foreigners, and says the spy reads their inner intent (மனக்கருத்து) from their words and deeds. The couplet is also a definition, ending ‘… is a spy’ (ஒற்று), a form repeated in 585-587. The text agrees across sources, with thirukkural-thamizh.org giving the sandhi form தஞ்சுற்றம்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “… shall be sent by the king to espy in his own country the movements of his ministers, priests, commanders of the army, the heir-apparent, the door-keepers, the officer-in-charge of the harem …”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya sends wandering spies to watch the king’s own highest officers, including his heir, as well as foreign kings.
hinduism.tie_back: Watching officials, family and enemies alike is exactly the Kural’s list of ‘officials, kin and those ill-disposed’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And a man’s foes shall be they of his own household.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns, quoting Micah, that opposition can come from one’s closest relatives.
christianity.tie_back: This is why the Kural does not exempt the king’s kin from scrutiny.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon and overlook and forgive - then indeed, Allāh is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells believers that even close family can work against their true interest, and urges watchfulness balanced by forgiveness.
islam.tie_back: Being alert even toward one’s own family is the Kural’s point about including தம் சுற்றம் in the spy’s scope.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Trust ye not in a friend, put ye not confidence in a guide … For the son dishonoureth the father … a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.”
judaism.explanation: Micah, grieving over a corrupt society, warns that friends, advisers and household members may all prove false.
judaism.tie_back: Friends, advisers and family are the same circle the Kural insists must be watched along with open enemies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigālovāda Sutta the Buddha warns of ‘foes in the guise of friends’: the one who only takes, the one who only talks, the flatterer, and the companion in ruin. He teaches how to recognise each by his conduct.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches lay people to test the conduct of those close to them rather than trusting appearances.
buddhism.tie_back: Judging even friends by their words and deeds is the Kural’s impartial ஆராய்தல் (examination) of all.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though others sleep, be thou awake! Like a wise man, trust nobody, but be always on the alert; for dangerous is the time and weak the body. Be always watchful like a Bhârunda bird!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's sermon on carelessness tells the monk to stay vigilant and not rely on anyone, comparing him to the mythical Bhāruṇḍa bird that is always on guard.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's spy must watch officials, kin and enemies alike; this verse gives the same posture of universal, unsleeping watchfulness, though turned inward against spiritual danger.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When Chitr and Gupt, the celestial accountants of the conscious and subconscious, call for your account, who will screen you then?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan warns that when the record of each person's deeds is called for, no one can cover for anyone else; rank and kinship give no shelter.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's spy watches officials, the king's own kin and his enemies without exception; Guru Arjan's account from which no one is screened has the same impartial reach, though it belongs to divine judgment, not a ruler's surveillance.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 616, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Returning to Ithaca disguised as an old beggar, Odysseus secretly tests his own household (the swineherd Eumaeus, the goatherd Melanthius, the maids, and even his son and wife) to learn who has stayed loyal before he acts.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus acts as his own spy, examining servants, family and enemies before trusting anyone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He covers the Kural’s whole range: workers, kin and hostile suitors are all examined alike.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle lists among the devices of tyranny that the ruler tries to know everything his subjects say and do, and employs spies such as the ‘female detectives’ of Syracuse and the eavesdroppers Hiero sent to every gathering.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats blanket surveillance of citizens as a mark of the tyrant who fears his people.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a useful contrast: Valluvar’s universal scrutiny belongs to a just king (ch. 55) and is aimed at officials and threats, while Aristotle warns what it becomes in a tyrant’s hands.

real_life_example.event_title: The Venona project uncovers Soviet agents inside the US government
real_life_example.event: On 1 February 1943 the US Army's Signal Intelligence Service began a small, secret programme at Arlington Hall to study encrypted Soviet diplomatic and intelligence cables that had been collected since 1939. From 1946 the codebreaker Meredith Gardner and colleagues were able to read parts of messages showing that Soviet intelligence had sources inside the War Department, the atomic bomb project and other government agencies. Working with the FBI, the project, which ran until 1980, helped identify Klaus Fuchs, Julius Rosenberg and others, and the FBI says some 350 people connected with Soviet intelligence were identified.
real_life_example.explanation: The most dangerous leaks came not from open enemies but from trusted people inside the government's own offices and laboratories.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a true intelligence service watches everyone without exception, the ruler's own officials as well as his enemies, and Venona found that some of the gravest threats sat among America's own officials.

tamil:
கடாஅ உருவொடு கண்ணஞ்சாது யாண்டும்
உகாஅமை வல்லதே ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Kadaaa uruvodu kannanjaadhu yaandum
Ugaaamai valladhae otru.
meaning: A real spy looks ordinary so no one suspects him, does not get nervous when people stare, and never lets his secret slip anywhere.
elementary: In a game of hide-and-seek in plain sight, the best player looks totally ordinary, stays calm even when someone stares at them, and never giggles and gives themselves away. This kural says a good spy is like that: ordinary-looking, calm and able to keep a secret.
university: The couplet names three qualities, and two of its words use the lengthened vowel (அளபெடை): கடாஅ உரு, ‘a form that does not provoke questioning’ (from கடாவுதல், to interrogate), and உகாஅமை, ‘not spilling’ (from உகுத்தல், to let fall, i.e. to leak a secret). In between comes கண் அஞ்சாது, ‘not fearing the eyes’ of suspicious onlookers. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as not fearing the looks of those who watch him. Pappaiah adds that the spy must hold out whatever method is used on him, naming the four upāyas (sāma, dāna, bheda, daṇḍa: persuasion, bribery, division, force). யாண்டும் (‘anywhere, at any time’) makes the secrecy absolute. The wording agrees across sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi கண்ணஞ்சா தியாண்டு முகாஅமை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Scouting Lanka for Rama, Hanuman shrinks himself to the size of a cat and slips into Ravana’s city at night unnoticed. Later, when he is captured and brought before Ravana, he answers fearlessly and gives away nothing that would harm Rama.
hinduism.explanation: Hanuman is the Indian epic’s model of the ideal scout: disguised, fearless before the enemy king, and loyal.
hinduism.tie_back: An unsuspected form, fearless eyes and a closed mouth are the three marks the Kural lists.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sends his disciples into hostile territory and tells them to combine shrewdness with a harmless appearance.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Harmless as doves’ is the unsuspected appearance and ‘wise as serpents’ is the discretion the Kural asks of a spy.

islam.quote_or_event: “So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city and let him look to which is the best of food and bring you provision from it and let him be cautious. And let no one be aware of you.”
islam.explanation: The Sleepers of the Cave send one of their number into a hostile city on an errand, with orders to be careful and give no one any sign of who they are.
islam.tie_back: Moving among others unnoticed and revealing nothing is the Kural’s spy in miniature.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But if thou return to the city, and say unto Absalom, I will be thy servant, O king; as I have been thy father’s servant hitherto, so will I now also be thy servant: then mayest thou for me defeat the counsel of Ahithophel.”
judaism.explanation: David sends his friend Hushai back into Absalom’s court as a planted agent who looks like a loyal convert and secretly works for David.
judaism.tie_back: Hushai shows the Kural’s qualities: a form that raises no suspicion, calm before the usurper and his advisers, and a secret never revealed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who is friendly amidst the hostile, peaceful amidst the violent, and unattached amidst the attached — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises the person whose calm is not shaken by hostile surroundings.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s spy also has to stay composed and fearless among enemies, though for a worldly purpose.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Living thus he with equanimity bore, endured, sustained, and suffered all calamities arising from divine powers, men, and animals, with undisturbed and unafflicted mind, careful of body, speech, and mind.”
jainism.explanation: During his twelve years as a wandering ascetic Mahavira met every hardship without being shaken, keeping strict guard over body, speech and mind.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's spy does not flinch under anyone's gaze and never lets slip what he holds; Mahavira's unshaken composure and guarded speech give a Jain picture of that steadiness, though without any secret mission.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra 2.15.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He watches over all, but none see Him. How wonderful this is!”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji, Guru Nanak marvels that the Creator sees every being while remaining unseen by all of them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's ideal spy draws no suspicion and is never detected while he observes; Japji's watcher who sees all and is seen by none is the nearest Sikh image, though it is said of God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7, Japji Sahib (Pauri 30), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the day he is born, the infant Hermes steals Apollo’s cattle, disguises the tracks with strange sandals and by driving the herd backwards, then lies in his cradle looking innocent and denies everything to Apollo’s face.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hermes, god of messengers and stealth, shows innocent looks, nerve under questioning, and a refusal to confess.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same three traits make the Kural’s ideal spy, though Hermes uses them for mischief.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli observes that everyone sees what a ruler appears to be, but few feel what he really is, and those few dare not contradict the many.
philosophy.explanation: Machiavelli stresses how far appearance can be separated from inner purpose in political life.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s spy depends on that gap: an unsuspected outward form hiding a fixed inner purpose.

real_life_example.event_title: Virginia Hall, the Limping Lady, works undetected in occupied France
real_life_example.event: Virginia Hall, an American who had lost her lower left leg in a hunting accident and walked with an artificial limb, became the British Special Operations Executive's first female resident agent in France in 1941. The Gestapo circulated wanted posters for her, and when her network was compromised she escaped over the Pyrenees on foot. In 1944 she returned for the American Office of Strategic Services, disguised as an elderly French farmwoman, and organised resistance and sabotage while reporting German troop movements; the Gestapo never caught her.
real_life_example.explanation: Hall's ordinary, unremarkable appearance and her steady nerve let one of the most wanted Allied agents move freely through occupied territory.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes the true spy as having an appearance that draws no suspicion, not flinching under watchful eyes and never letting a secret slip, all of which Hall did in occupied France.

tamil:
துறந்தார் படிவத்த ராகி இறந்தாராய்ந்து
என்செயினும் சோர்விலது ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Thurandhaar padivaththa raagi irandhaaraaindhu
Enseyinum soarviladhu otru.
meaning: A good spy disguises himself as a holy man who has given up the world, goes into places no one else can, learns everything, and never gives himself away, whatever is done to him.
elementary: In old stories, a clever messenger sometimes dresses as a humble traveller so he can pass through the gates. Even if guards question him roughly, he stays in character and keeps his secret. This kural describes that kind of brave, patient spy.
university: துறந்தார் படிவத்தர் ஆகி means ‘taking on the form (படிவம்) of those who have renounced’, that is, dressing as an ascetic or wandering monk. Such figures could travel freely in ancient India. இறந்து ஆராய்ந்து is read by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘going beyond [ordinary limits], into places otherwise unreachable, and examining’. Pappaiah makes it explicit: places one cannot go. என்செயினும் சோர்வு இலது means ‘whatever [the suspicious] may do to him, he does not slip’. Here சோர்வு means a lapse that gives the secret away, not tiredness, and Pappaiah and Kalaignar both read it as holding out under torture. The disguise matches the Arthashastra’s tāpasa (ascetic) spy closely, which is often cited in comparative studies of the Kural. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give identical text; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms ராகி யிறந்தாராய்ந் / தென்செயினுஞ் சோர்வில தொற்று.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man with shaved head (muṇḍa) or braided hair (jaṭila) and desirous to earn livelihood is a spy under the guise of an ascetic practising austerities. Such a spy surrounded by a host of disciples with shaved head or braided hair may take his abode in the suburbs of a city …”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya describes in detail the spy disguised as an ascetic, a figure respected enough to go anywhere and hear everything.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s துறந்தார் படிவம், the guise of a renunciant, almost exactly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that a harmless religious appearance can hide a very different inner purpose.
christianity.tie_back: Seen from the other side, this is the Kural’s spy in a renunciant’s robe. Scripture condemns the deceit, while Valluvar approves of it for the service of a just state.

islam.quote_or_event: On the freezing night of the Battle of the Trench, the Prophet sent Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman into the enemy camp for news, telling him to do nothing that would alarm them. Hudhayfah saw Abu Sufyan warming himself by a fire, held back from shooting him, and returned with his report.
islam.explanation: Hudhayfah went through cold and danger into the enemy’s midst, stayed undetected, and kept strictly to his mission.
islam.tie_back: He entered where others would not go, kept his cover, and did not break discipline, which is the Kural’s இறந்து ஆராய்ந்து … சோர்வு இலது.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And they went, and came unto the mountain, and abode there three days, until the pursuers were returned: and the pursuers sought them throughout all the way, but found them not.”
judaism.explanation: Joshua’s two spies, hunted after their mission in Jericho, hid patiently in the hills until it was safe to return with their report.
judaism.tie_back: Their patience and their refusal to be caught match the Kural’s spy who does not slip whatever happens.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the use of your matted hair, O witless man? What of your garment of antelope’s hide? Within you is the tangle (of passion); only outwardly do you cleanse yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that ascetic dress, such as matted hair and hide garments, can be a mere outward costume over an unrenounced mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The verse shows how common it was for renunciant dress to be only a costume, the very disguise the Kural’s spy uses.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain tradition relates that early in his ascetic wanderings Mahavira came near the village of Corāka, where guards wary of thieves asked who he was. Bound by his vow of silence, he did not answer; the guards took him for a thief or spy, seized him and tormented him, until two women who knew him (Somā and Jayantī) came and had him freed, and the guards begged forgiveness.
jainism.explanation: The story shows how a silent wandering renunciant could be suspected of being a spy, and how Mahavira kept his silence even under torture.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's spy goes about in a renunciant's guise and never gives himself away whatever is done to him; this Jain story turns the image round, showing a real ascetic who was mistaken for a spy and still revealed nothing under torment.
jainism.source: Life of Mahāvīra, episode at Corāka in his fourth year of ascetic practice (HereNow4U, 'Lord Śrī Mahāvīra', as summarised in the wisdomlib.org Jainism glossary s.v. Corāka)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The lazy unemployed has his ears pierced to look like a Yogi. Someone else becomes a pan-handler, and loses his social status.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak mocks those who put on the marks and dress of renunciation, not from inner detachment but to live without honest work.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural approves of a spy who takes the guise of a renunciant to go where others cannot; Gurbani knows the same disguise but condemns it, since for Sikhs the ascetic's outward garb proves nothing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Helen recalls how Odysseus disfigured himself with blows, put on a beggar’s rags like a slave, and slipped into Troy. He went unrecognised by all but her, gathered much knowledge, and got back safely to the Greeks.
greek_mythology.explanation: The master spy of Greek legend takes on the humblest disguise, that of a beggar, to enter the enemy city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A beggar’s disguise in Greece matches the renunciant’s disguise in the Kural: the lowest-status, least-suspected costume to get where others cannot.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus calls the true Cynic philosopher, who wears only a rough cloak and owns nothing, a ‘scout’ (kataskopos) sent ahead by God to spy out what is truly friendly or hostile to human beings and to report back fearlessly, as Diogenes did.
philosophy.explanation: Stoic teaching pictures the ascetic philosopher as a spy who goes into frightening territory and returns with a report that is not distorted by fear.
philosophy.tie_back: An ascetic who is really a scout and cannot be shaken is the Kural’s spy, turned into a moral image.

real_life_example.event_title: Nain Singh surveys Tibet disguised as a Buddhist pilgrim
real_life_example.event: Nain Singh, one of the Indian surveyors known as pundits who were trained by the Survey of India, set out in 1865 to map Tibet, which was then closed to outsiders. Travelling disguised as a Buddhist pilgrim and trader, he counted his paces on a rosary of 100 beads instead of the usual 108, hid notes and a compass in a prayer wheel and concealed instruments in his baggage, reaching Lhasa in 1866. He fixed the position and altitude of Lhasa and mapped a long stretch of the trade route, and the Royal Geographical Society later awarded him its Patron's Medal.
real_life_example.explanation: By taking the outward form of a pilgrim, Nain Singh entered a country that no ordinary surveyor could enter and brought back accurate information without ever being exposed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes the spy who takes on the guise of a renunciant, enters places others cannot reach, examines them thoroughly and never gives himself away, which is almost exactly Nain Singh's journey.

tamil:
மறைந்தவை கேட்கவற் றாகி அறிந்தவை
ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Maraindhavai kaetkavat raagi arindhavai
Aiyappaadu illadhae otru.
meaning: A spy is someone who can uncover hidden secrets and has no doubt at all about what he has found.
elementary: A good detective in a mystery story does two things: she finds the hidden clues, and she checks them until she is sure before she tells anyone. Guessing isn’t enough. This kural says a real investigator uncovers secrets and makes sure they are true.
university: மறைந்தவை கேட்க வற்று ஆகி means ‘being able (வற்று, ‘capable’) to hear what is concealed’. அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லது means ‘having no doubt about what has been learned’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the second half as being able to decide firmly without wavering. Pappaiah adds that the spy draws secrets ‘from the very mouth of those who did the deed’, and Kalaignar that he learns through those who are present at secret meetings. So the couplet sets two standards, access to secrets and certainty about them, and the next two couplets (588-589) add a check on that certainty from the king’s side. The text is identical across the three sources, apart from the sandhi யறிந்தவை / யையப்பா டில்லதே in thirukkural-thamizh.org.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A skilful person capable of guessing the mind of others is a fraudulent disciple. Having encouraged such a spy with honour and money rewards, the minister shall tell him, ‘Sworn to the king and myself, thou shalt inform us of whatever wickedness thou findest in others.’”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya’s first class of spy is chosen for his skill at reading hidden intentions and is bound by oath to report them.
hinduism.tie_back: Reading what others hide is the Kural’s மறைந்தவை கேட்க வற்று.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known. Therefore whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light; and that which ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that whispered secrets will eventually be heard and brought into the open.
christianity.tie_back: Secrets told ‘in the ear in closets’ are exactly the மறைந்தவை the Kural’s spy is able to hear.

islam.quote_or_event: “And a man came from the farthest end of the city, running. He said, ‘O Moses, indeed the eminent ones are conferring over you [intending] to kill you, so leave [the city]; indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisors.’”
islam.explanation: A well-wisher learns of the chiefs’ secret plot and rushes to warn Moses with a clear, certain report.
islam.tie_back: He learns a closed council’s hidden plan and delivers it without hesitation, as the Kural’s ideal informant would.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And one of his servants said, None, my lord, O king: but Elisha, the prophet that is in Israel, telleth the king of Israel the words that thou speakest in thy bedchamber.”
judaism.explanation: The king of Aram suspects a traitor because Israel always knows his plans, and learns that the prophet Elisha reveals even words spoken in his bedchamber.
judaism.tie_back: Knowing ‘the words spoken in the bedchamber’ is the furthest reach of the Kural’s hearing of hidden things.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka, the sage Mahosadha’s trained parrot, sent to the court of King Cūḷani-Brahmadatta, overhears the king and his chaplain Kevaṭṭa secretly plotting to conquer all of India and brings the plan back to his master.
buddhism.explanation: The Jātaka shows a hidden plot being discovered and reported with certainty in time for the wise minister to act.
buddhism.tie_back: The parrot overhears what was meant to stay hidden, which is the Kural’s ideal of hearing the concealed.
buddhism.source: Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka (Jātaka 546), as summarised in the Dictionary of Pali Proper Names (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “(The excellence of faith depends on the following) eight points: 1. that one has no doubts (about the truth of the tenets); 2. that one has no preference (for heterodox tenets); 3. that one does not doubt its saving qualities …”
jainism.explanation: The first limb of right faith in Jainism (niḥśaṅkita) is freedom from doubt about what has been rightly understood.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's ideal spy is left with no doubt about what he has found; Jainism likewise prizes conviction free of doubt as the first mark of sound understanding.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, the Creator knows everything; nothing can be hidden from Him.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Gauree ki Vaar, Guru Ram Das reminds the listener that no concealed act or intention escapes the Creator's knowledge.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's spy can draw out what is hidden and is left with no doubt about it; Gurbani gives such complete and certain knowledge of hidden things to God alone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 302, Raag Gauree (Gauree ki Vaar, salok), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Demeter searches everywhere for her stolen daughter, it is Helios, the Sun who watches over gods and men, who tells her the hidden truth: Zeus had given Persephone to Hades, who carried her off to the underworld.
greek_mythology.explanation: Only the all-seeing Sun knows the concealed deed, and he reports it plainly and with certainty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Helios has what the Kural requires: access to what is hidden and an account free of doubt.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Descartes’ first rule of method is never to accept anything as true that he does not clearly know to be so, and to include nothing in his judgments beyond what is presented to his mind so clearly and distinctly that he has no occasion to doubt it.
philosophy.explanation: Descartes makes freedom from doubt the test for accepting any proposition.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ஐயப்பாடு இல்லது (‘free of doubt’) applies the same standard to a spy’s findings.
philosophy.source: René Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part 2 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Marian Rejewski breaks the German Enigma machine
real_life_example.event: At the end of 1932 Marian Rejewski, a young mathematician in the Polish Cipher Bureau, used mathematical methods to reconstruct the wiring of the German military Enigma machine, and with Jerzy Rozycki and Henryk Zygalski he went on to read German Enigma messages through the 1930s. In 1938 the team built a device called the bomba to help find daily settings. In July 1939, at Pyry near Warsaw, Polish intelligence handed over its methods and reconstructed Enigma machines to British and French representatives.
real_life_example.explanation: Rejewski drew out secrets that Germany believed to be beyond reach, and did so with mathematical rigour that left no doubt about the results.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes the spy who can draw out what is hidden and has no doubt about what he has found, and Rejewski's reconstruction of Enigma met both standards.

tamil:
ஒற்றொற்றித் தந்த பொருளையும் மற்றுமோர்
ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Otrotrith thandha porulaiyum matrumoar
Otrinaal otrik kolal.
meaning: Even news that a spy has brought in should be believed only after another spy has checked it.
elementary: If one friend tells you there is no school tomorrow, you would probably check with another friend or the school website before staying home. This kural says a wise leader always double-checks a report with a second source.
university: The couplet plays on the root ஒற்று, which appears four times (ஒற்று ஒற்றித் தந்த … ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றி): ‘what a spy has spied out and delivered, have it spied out again by another spy, and then accept it’. The உம் in பொருளையும் (‘even the information’) means that even a reliable spy’s report is not exempt. Mu. Varadarasanar says it should be taken as true only after the two accounts are found to agree (ஒப்புமை கண்டபின்). Kalaignar stresses comparing the two reports before deciding. கொளல் is an infinitive-style imperative (‘one should accept’), the same form Valluvar uses for maxims elsewhere. This couplet and 589 together set out a clear doctrine of corroborating intelligence. The text agrees across all three sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The immediate officers of the institutes of espionage (saṃsthānāmantevāsina) shall, by making use of signs or writing (saṃjñā lipibhi), set their own spies in motion (to ascertain the validity of the information).”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya builds a second layer of spies whose job is to check the reports of the first.
hinduism.tie_back: Spies sent to test other spies’ information are the Kural’s மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல் put into practice.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the church to test every claim before holding on to it.
christianity.tie_back: Test first, then accept: the Kural’s rule for spy reports in its most general form.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.”
islam.explanation: The Quran orders that a report from an unreliable source be investigated before anyone acts on it, to avoid harming innocent people.
islam.tie_back: Verify before acting, especially where lives are at stake: the heart of this Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then shalt thou enquire, and make search, and ask diligently; and, behold, if it be truth, and the thing certain …”
judaism.explanation: Deuteronomy says that a rumour of grave wrongdoing in a town must be investigated thoroughly and found true and certain before anything is done.
judaism.tie_back: Enquire, search and ask diligently until it is certain: the Kural’s demand for a second check.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Come, Kalamas. Do not go upon what has been acquired by repeated hearing; nor upon tradition; nor upon rumor; nor upon what is in a scripture; nor upon surmise …”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the Kalamas not to accept a claim just because it was reported to them, but to test it until they know for themselves.
buddhism.tie_back: Refusing to act on a report alone is the Kural’s refusal to accept even one spy’s word unchecked.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 3.65, Kalama Sutta (trans. Soma Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: Samantabhadra opens his Āptamīmāṃsā (also called Devāgamastotra) by refusing to accept even the Jina as an authority because of outward signs such as the arrival of gods, travel through the sky or royal fans, since such marvels are also seen among magicians; he then tests the Jina's teaching by reason and the logic of anekāntavāda before accepting it.
jainism.explanation: This classic Digambara work makes critical examination the ground for trust, even toward the most authoritative source.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says even a trusted spy's report must be re-checked by another spy before it is accepted; Samantabhadra applies the same rule of verification to the highest authority Jainism recognises.
jainism.source: Samantabhadra, Āptamīmāṃsā (Devāgamastotra) v. 1 and overall argument (described in Vijay K. Jain's translation, 2016; PhilArchive record)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “and placed in the Court of our Lord and Master, and there, the genuine and the counterfeit are separated.”
sikhism.explanation: Using the image of coins brought before their master to be assayed, Guru Nanak says that whatever is offered as true is tested in the Lord's court and the false is set apart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the king to accept even a spy's report only after another spy has checked it; Guru Nanak's assay of coins shares the conviction that what is offered as genuine must be tested before it is accepted.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 789, Raag Soohee (salok in Soohee ki Vaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Trojans capture the Greek Sinon, who tells a moving story that the wooden horse is a sacred offering. Without checking his story against any other source, and ignoring Laocoön’s warning, they drag the horse into the city, and Troy falls.
greek_mythology.explanation: The most famous intelligence failure in myth comes from trusting one planted informant.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the disaster the Kural guards against by never accepting a single source unchecked.
greek_mythology.source: Virgil, Aeneid 2 (paraphrase; the story belongs to the Greek Trojan cycle)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Without subtle ingenuity of mind, one cannot make certain of the truth of their reports.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu warns that spy reports cannot simply be taken at face value; the ruler must use his judgment to test them.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts insist that a spy’s report must be tested before it is trusted.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 13.17 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: American codebreakers confirm that AF means Midway
real_life_example.place: Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, and Midway Atoll
real_life_example.event: In spring 1942 US Navy codebreakers at Station Hypo in Pearl Harbor, led by Joseph Rochefort, read Japanese messages referring to an objective called AF and suspected it was Midway, but analysts in Washington doubted this. To test the reading, the Navy had Midway report by secure cable and then broadcast an uncoded message that its fresh-water plant had broken down. When a Japanese intelligence report soon stated that AF was short of water, the identification was confirmed, and the US Navy prepared the ambush that won the Battle of Midway in June 1942.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than act on a single reading of intercepted traffic, the Navy found an independent way to check it before staking the Pacific Fleet on it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even information a spy has brought in should be accepted only after it has been checked by another, and the water-shortage test was exactly such a second check.

tamil:
ஒற்றெற் றுணராமை ஆள்க உடன்மூவர்
சொற்றொக்க தேறப் படும்.
transliteration:
Otret runaraamai aalga udanmoovar
Sotrokka thaerap padum.
meaning: Use spies so that none of them knows about the others. When three such spies report the same thing, you can believe it.
elementary: If three students are each asked separately what happened at recess, and they can’t talk to each other first, but all three tell the same story, the teacher can be pretty sure it is true. This kural says a wise leader checks the truth the same way.
university: The first line says to employ (ஆள்க) spies in a way that one does not become aware (உணராமை) of another. The second says that when the words of three (மூவர் சொல்) agree together (தொக்க), the thing may be trusted (தேறப்படும்). There is a real textual variant in the first word. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print ஒற்றெற் றுணராமை, while thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ஒற்றொற் றுணராமை, i.e. ஒற்று ஒற்று உணராமை, ‘one spy not knowing another spy’. That is the sense every commentator, including Parimelazhagar, gives, and the -எற்று form is best explained as a sandhi or scribal variant. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the second line as ‘if the three agree, take it as true’. Pappaiah is more cautious: even when three agree, examine it before accepting. The rule is strikingly close to Arthashastra 1.12, which requires agreement from three independent sources and says the spy-units must not know one another.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Neither the institutes of espionage nor they (the wandering spies) shall know each other … When the information thus received from these three different sources is exactly of the same version, it shall be held reliable. If they (the three sources) frequently differ, the spies concerned shall either be punished in secret or dismissed.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya requires spy networks that do not know one another and accepts a report only when three independent sources agree.
hinduism.tie_back: Spies unaware of one another and three agreeing sources: both halves of the Kural, point for point.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the story of Susanna, the young Daniel separates the two elders who have falsely accused her and questions each alone about which tree the alleged act happened under. One says a mastic tree and the other a holm oak, their lie is exposed, and Susanna is saved.
christianity.explanation: By keeping the witnesses apart, Daniel makes sure their stories are truly independent, so their disagreement shows the truth.
christianity.tie_back: Keeping informants from knowing one another and then comparing their words is the Kural’s method exactly.
christianity.source: Susanna (Daniel 13 in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; KJV Apocrypha), vv. 51-59 (paraphrase)

islam.quote_or_event: “And bring to witness two witnesses from among your men … That is more just in the sight of Allāh and stronger as evidence and more likely to prevent doubt between you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran requires more than one witness for important transactions, because corroboration strengthens evidence and removes doubt.
islam.tie_back: Several witnesses to remove doubt reflects the Kural’s agreement of three.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And afterward they bring in the second witness and examine him in the same manner. If their statements are found to be congruent the judges then discuss the matter.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah requires witnesses to be questioned one at a time with the others sent out of the room, and their testimony counts only if their separate accounts agree.
judaism.tie_back: Separate examination so that no witness knows another’s answer, followed by a check for agreement, is the Kural’s procedure in a courtroom.
judaism.source: Mishnah Sanhedrin 3:6 (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz translation, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Without approval and without scorn, but carefully studying the sentences word by word, one should trace them in the Discourses and verify them by the Discipline.”
buddhism.explanation: In the ‘four great references’, the Buddha says that any claim to be his teaching must be checked against two independent standards, the Suttas and the Vinaya, before it is accepted.
buddhism.tie_back: Accepting a report only when independent sources agree is the principle behind the Kural’s three agreeing spies.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta 4.8-11 (trans. Sister Vajira & Francis Story)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who understands the true nature of all substances by means of all proofs (pramâna) and nayas, believes by a complete course of study.”
jainism.explanation: Jain epistemology holds that a thing is properly known only when it is examined through valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and from several partial standpoints (naya), which are then brought together.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural trusts a matter only when three independent spies' reports agree; the Jain method likewise reaches confidence by combining several separate lines of evidence and viewpoint rather than relying on one.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Meeting with the council, my doubts were not dispelled. The chiefs did not give me satisfaction.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes turning to the village council (the panch) and to the chiefs, and finding that neither could set his anxious mind at rest.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural trusts a matter once three independent spies agree; Guru Arjan's verse is the nearest Sikh reflection on seeking certainty from several authorities, and it is partly a counterpoint, since their word did not settle his doubt.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 621, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: To test the oracles, King Croesus sent separate messengers to several shrines at once, each to ask on the hundredth day what the king was doing at that moment. Only Delphi (and, by some accounts, Amphiaraus) answered correctly, that he was boiling a tortoise and lamb in a bronze pot.
greek_mythology.explanation: Croesus set up independent, simultaneous inquiries so that the sources could not coordinate, then trusted only those that proved accurate.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Independent informants who cannot confer, judged by whether their answers match reality, is the Kural’s method in legendary form.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Thucydides says he did not rely on the first account he heard or on his own impressions, but tested every report as rigorously as he could, which was hard because different eyewitnesses gave differing accounts of the same events.
philosophy.explanation: The founder of critical history describes his method as cross-examining several independent witnesses.
philosophy.tie_back: Comparing independent reports and accepting only what holds up is what the Kural asks of a king.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 1.22 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Independent reports and air photographs confirm the German rocket site at Peenemunde
real_life_example.place: Peenemunde, Germany, and RAF Medmenham, England
real_life_example.event: From 1939 British intelligence received scattered reports, including the anonymous Oslo Report, that Germany was developing long-range rockets and other secret weapons, but these were at first doubted. Reports from other sources pointed to Peenemunde on the Baltic coast, and photo-reconnaissance flights between 1942 and 1943 were examined by interpreters at RAF Medmenham, where Constance Babington Smith's section searched for secret weapons. When separate lines of intelligence and the aerial photographs agreed, Bomber Command attacked Peenemunde on the night of 17-18 August 1943 in Operation Hydra.
real_life_example.explanation: No single report was trusted on its own; action came only when separate, unconnected sources told the same story.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says to use agents who do not know of one another and to trust a matter when their separate reports agree, which is how Britain confirmed the threat from Peenemunde before striking it.

tamil:
சிறப்பறிய ஒற்றின்கண் செய்யற்க செய்யின்
புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை.
transliteration:
Sirapariya otrinkan seyyarka seyyin
Purappaduththaan aagum marai.
meaning: A king should not reward a spy where others can see. If he does, he gives away his own secret.
elementary: Imagine a secret helper who quietly tells the teacher when someone is being picked on. If the teacher gave that helper a big prize in front of the whole class, everyone would know who the helper was, and the secret would be ruined. This kural says to thank secret helpers quietly.
university: சிறப்பு அறிய means ‘so that the honour is known [to others]’; ஒற்றின்கண் செய்யற்க, ‘do not do it to the spy’; செய்யின் புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை, ‘if you do, you become the one who brought the secret out into the open (புறப்படுத்தல்)’. The irony is that after all the care in 585-589 to keep spies hidden, the king himself becomes the leak by rewarding them publicly. Pappaiah reads the couplet as ‘reward the spy, but reward him secretly’, which fits Sun Tzu’s and Kautilya’s view that spies must be generously paid. Mu. Varadarasanar reads மறை as both the secret information and the spy’s identity. The text agrees across sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form வொற்றின்கட் செய்யற்க செய்யிற் / புறப்படுத்தா னாகு மறை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That king whose secret plans other people, (though) assembled (for the purpose), do not discover, (will) enjoy the whole earth, though he be poor in treasure.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu puts keeping counsel secret above wealth as a source of royal power.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s warning about leaking the secret through public honours protects exactly this kind of secrecy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that good deeds and gifts should be given quietly, without public display.
christianity.tie_back: Giving in secret instead of in public view is the Kural’s advice on how to reward a spy.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you disclose your charitable expenditures, they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you, and He will remove from you some of your misdeeds [thereby].”
islam.explanation: The Quran allows open giving but calls concealed giving better.
islam.tie_back: Its preference for concealed giving matches the Kural’s preference for a spy’s reward given out of sight.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the gossip who exposes secrets with the trustworthy person who keeps them.
judaism.tie_back: A king who honours his spy publicly acts like the ‘talebearer’ who reveals secrets, and the Kural wants him to be the faithful one who keeps them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the standard description of right speech, the disciple does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard in one place in order to divide people, nor repeat here what he has heard there.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist ethics teaches restraint in passing on what one has heard, to avoid causing harm and division.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also asks the king not to let slip, through a public gesture, what should stay unspoken.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 41, Sāleyyaka Sutta, on right speech (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “the divulging from jealousy or other motives of the secret intention of another person as divined by watching his gestures or facial expression”
jainism.explanation: Among the faults that break the layperson's vow of truthfulness (Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.26) is sākāra-mantrabheda; the Digambara interpretation reproduced here defines it as exposing a secret read from outward signs, and Siddhasena's commentary links a related fault to 'divulging affairs of state'.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a king who honours a spy in public betrays the secret through an outward sign; Jain ethics names the leaking of hidden matters through visible signs as a breach of the truth vow.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.26, sākāra-mantrabheda, Digambara interpretation (Cāmuṇḍarāya's Cāritrasāra) as given in R. Williams, Jaina Yoga (1963), quoted in the wisdomlib.org Jainism glossary

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself good, goodness shall not draw near him.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan teaches that goodness put on display and claimed as one's own loses its worth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a king who honours his spy publicly gives away the secret the spy's work depends on; Guru Arjan offers only a distant echo, that worth announced in public is undone by the announcement.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas’s barber, the only one who knew his master had donkey’s ears, could not bear to keep the secret. He whispered it into a hole in the ground and covered it, but reeds grew there and whispered the secret to the wind for everyone to hear.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows that a secret, once let out in any form, finds its way to everyone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural warns the king not to be the one who lets it out, by a gesture as small as a public reward.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Hence it is that which none in the whole army are more intimate relations to be maintained than with spies. None should be more liberally rewarded. In no other business should greater secrecy be preserved.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu joins generous rewards for spies with the strictest secrecy in handling them.
philosophy.tie_back: Reward richly but in secret is exactly the balance this Kural asks for.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 13.14 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Double agent Garbo receives his MBE in secret
real_life_example.event: Juan Pujol Garcia, codenamed Garbo, was a Spanish double agent run by MI5 who fed the Germans false reports from an imaginary network of agents, helping convince them that the main Allied invasion would come at the Pas de Calais rather than Normandy. In July 1944 the Germans awarded him the Iron Cross, still believing he worked for them. In December 1944 the British awarded him the MBE, presented by MI5's Director General, but in secret to avoid exposing him, and his identity as Garbo was not publicly uncovered until 1984.
real_life_example.explanation: Britain honoured one of its most valuable agents while making sure that no one outside a tiny circle knew it, protecting both the man and the deception.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns a ruler not to honour a spy where others can see, lest he himself reveal the secret, and Garbo's private MBE followed that counsel to the letter.

tamil:
உடையர் எனப்படுவது ஊக்கம் அஃதில்லார்
உடையது உடையரோ மற்று.
transliteration:
Udaiyar enappaduvadhu ookkam aqdhillaar
Udaiyadhu udaiyaro matru.
meaning: Inner drive is the only thing a person can truly be said to own. People without it do not really own anything, whatever else they have.
elementary: Imagine two children who are each given a box of paints. One gets excited and paints every day; the other leaves the box closed on a shelf. Only the first one really ‘has’ paints. The Kural says the eager, energetic spirit is the thing that makes anything you own actually yours.
university: The chapter opens by redefining possession itself: “udaiyar enappaduvadhu” (what it is to be called a possessor) is ookkam, which Parimelazhagar glosses as mental elation or upsurge of the will toward action (ullaezhuchi), the drive that animates effort rather than effort itself. The rhetorical question “udaiyadhu udaiyaro” (do they own what they own?) denies that the unenergetic possess even their existing wealth, since without ookkam it will neither be defended nor increased; “matru” is treated by the commentators as an expletive particle (asai). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all paraphrase the line as ‘only the energetic are truly possessors’, and the text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. The adhikaram sits in Arasiyal (royalty), after Espionage and before Unsluggishness (Madiyinmai), Manly Effort (Aalvinaiyudaimai) and Not Despairing in Trouble, forming a cluster on the psychology of exertion that parallels the Sanskrit utsāha-śakti, the ‘power of energy’ that Kautilya lists among a king’s three powers. Thirukkural.net titles the chapter ‘Magnanimity’, while Pope and ytamizh.com use ‘Energy’, reflecting the double sense of ookkam as both drive and largeness of spirit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The performer is said to be in the mode of goodness, when he or she is free from egotism and attachment, endowed with enthusiasm and determination, and equipoised in success and failure.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the best kind of worker as one filled with utsāha (zeal) and dhṛti (resolve), who keeps working steadily whatever the outcome.
hinduism.tie_back: Utsāha is the Sanskrit counterpart of ookkam, and the Gita, like the Kural, makes it a defining trait of the worthy person.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to put their whole heart and energy into every task, treating even ordinary work as service to God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat wholehearted inner energy as what gives a person’s life and work its real value.

islam.quote_or_event: “A strong believer is better and is more lovable to Allah than a weak believer, and there is good in everyone, (but) cherish that which gives you benefit (in the Hereafter) and seek help from Allah and do not lose heart…”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises the strong, active believer and tells people to pursue what benefits them eagerly and never give in to helplessness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ookkam and the hadith’s strength and refusal of ‘ajz (helplessness) both mark the energetic person as the one of real worth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whatsoever thy hand attaineth to do by thy strength, that do; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth urges people to act with all their strength now, because this life is the only arena for effort.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that the energy you bring to action is what counts, more than anything you merely hold.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kasibharadvaja Sutta the Buddha answers a ploughing brahmin by describing his own ‘farming’, in which faith is the seed and energy (viriya) is the draught-ox that carries him forward to freedom from bondage.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells a farmer that his spiritual work has its own plough and oxen, and energy is the beast that pulls everything forward.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, energy is the working asset that makes every other endowment productive.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Four things of paramount value are difficult to obtain here by a living being: human birth, instruction in the Law, belief in it, and energy in self-control.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira names energy or exertion (vīrya) in self-control as one of the four rarest and most valuable possessions; verse 10 adds that many who approve of the religion never fulfil it strenuously.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says energy is the only thing that truly makes one an owner; the Uttaradhyayana likewise ranks energy among the few possessions of real worth.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 3.1 (cf. 3.10) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and chant the Lord's Name. O very fortunate ones, earn this wealth.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan calls for udam, active effort, and names the Lord's Name as the wealth that such effort earns.
