sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says only those with inner energy truly possess anything; Guru Arjan likewise ties real wealth to effort, though the wealth he means is the Name, not property.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 48, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, born with divine strength, wins his lasting fame only through the Twelve Labours, a lifetime of relentless exertion undertaken at Eurystheus’ command.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles’ gifts meant little until he threw himself into one exhausting task after another, and his tireless striving is what made him a hero.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The myth illustrates the Kural’s point that endowment without energetic use is not true possession.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that happiness lies in virtuous activity, not in merely having a good disposition: just as at the Olympic Games it is not the finest and strongest who are crowned but those who actually compete, so in life those who act rightly win the prize.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle a capacity you never use is like a strong athlete who never enters the race; only active exercise (energeia) earns the good.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that what you hold counts only if energy puts it to work.

real_life_example.event_title: Babur loses his homeland and goes on to found the Mughal Empire
real_life_example.place: Fergana and Samarkand (Central Asia), Kabul, and Panipat, India
real_life_example.event: Babur inherited the kingdom of Fergana as a boy in 1494 and spent years trying to hold Samarkand, but in the end lost both Samarkand and his native Fergana. He took Kabul in 1504 and made it his base, and after several raids into India he defeated Sultan Ibrahim Lodi of Delhi at the First Battle of Panipat in April 1526. By his death in 1530 he had laid the foundation of the Mughal Empire.
real_life_example.explanation: Having lost every possession he was born to, Babur still had the drive that let him build something far larger than what he lost.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the only real possession is inner energy and that those without it do not truly own even what they hold, and Babur's life shows energy outlasting the loss of a whole kingdom.

tamil:
உள்ளம் உடைமை உடைமை பொருளுடைமை
நில்லாது நீங்கி விடும்.
transliteration:
Ullam udaimai udaimai poruludaimai
Nillaadhu neengi vidum.
meaning: A strong, eager mind is the thing you own that lasts. Money and things do not stay. They slip away.
elementary: A sandcastle can be washed away by the next wave, but the skill and excitement that built it stay with you, so you can build another one tomorrow. Money and things can disappear, but a strong, eager mind stays yours.
university: The couplet sets two kinds of udaimai (property) against each other: ullam udaimai, possession of ‘mind’, which Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss as ookkam, and porul udaimai, possession of goods. The triple repetition ‘udaimai udaimai … udaimai’ is a deliberate sound-play (sol-pin-varunilai) that forces the reader to ask which ‘having’ deserves the name. The verbs ‘nillaadhu neengi vidum’ (does not stay, departs) echo the Aram-section chapter on impermanence (Nilaiyaamai, ch. 34), but here the lesson is practical rather than renunciatory: since wealth is fugitive, the ruler’s real capital is the energy that can regain it. Solomon Pappaiah renders ullam as mana uruthi (firmness of mind), a slight shift from zeal to resolve. The text agrees verbatim in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Yama offers Nachiketas cattle, gold, horses and long-lived sons in place of the secret of death, the boy refuses, answering that a man cannot be satisfied by wealth and that such things wear away the vigour of the senses.
hinduism.explanation: Nachiketas turns down every treasure Death offers because riches are temporary and cannot give lasting satisfaction.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Upanishad ranks an inner possession above material goods that ‘do not stay’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that earthly riches decay or are stolen, and urges people to invest in the lasting treasure of the spirit.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same contrast between perishable wealth and an inner possession that abides.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth is not in having many possessions, but rather (true) wealth is feeling sufficiency in the soul.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that true richness is an inner state of the soul, not a large pile of goods.
islam.tie_back: Both sayings redefine real wealth as something held within the self.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot…”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines riches as an inner disposition toward one’s portion, not the size of one’s holdings.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Mishnah locates true possession in the mind rather than in property.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists seven ‘noble treasures’ (faith, virtue, conscience, concern, learning, generosity and discernment) and says that, unlike gold, they cannot be taken by kings, thieves, fire or flood.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts qualities of mind that no disaster can seize with material riches that can be lost at any time.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural too says wealth ‘departs’ while a possession of the mind remains.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on carelessness opens by urging exertion and warns that wealth gives no lasting protection to one who lacks vigilance.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's contrast between energy, which endures, and wealth, which slips away, this verse sets the unreliability of riches against the inner alertness that alone keeps a person on the right road.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Your wealth shall not go with you; why do you cling to it, you fool?”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan reminds the listener that riches are left behind and are no fit object of attachment.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural sets the lasting possession of an energetic mind against wealth that slips away; Guru Arjan shares the verdict on wealth, though what he sets against it is the Name rather than drive.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 288, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas is granted the golden touch, but his food and drink turn to gold, and he begs Dionysus to take the gift away, washing it off in the river Pactolus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas learns that a mountain of gold is worthless and even harmful when it cannot sustain life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The story shows the Kural’s point that material wealth is not a true or lasting possession.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy tells the imprisoned Boethius that Fortune’s gifts of wealth and rank were never truly his, since what can be taken away does not belong to a person; only goods of the mind are one’s own.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius, stripped of wealth and office, is taught that external goods are only on loan from Fortune.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s claim that property ‘does not stay but departs’ while the mind’s possession endures.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2

real_life_example.event_title: Thomas Carlyle rewrites The French Revolution after the only manuscript is burned
real_life_example.event: After spending months in 1834 on the first volume of his history of the French Revolution, Thomas Carlyle lent his only draft to the philosopher John Stuart Mill, in whose house it was accidentally burned. When Mill confessed, Carlyle responded generously and began to reconstruct the work at once. The completed three-volume The French Revolution was published in 1837 and established his reputation; a small burnt fragment is kept at Carlyle's House in Chelsea.
real_life_example.explanation: What Carlyle owned, a finished manuscript, vanished overnight, but the power of mind that had produced it remained and produced it again.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says energy of mind is the possession that lasts while other possessions slip away, and Carlyle's lost manuscript and rewritten book are a vivid example.

tamil:
ஆக்கம் இழந்தேமென்று அல்லாவார் ஊக்கம்
ஒருவந்தம் கைத்துடை யார்.
transliteration:
Aakkam izhandhemendru allaavaar ookkam
Oruvandham kaiththudai yaar.
meaning: People who keep a firm hold on their inner drive do not cry, “We have lost our money.”
elementary: If a strong wind knocks down your block tower, you can cry about it, or you can say ‘I still have my hands and my ideas’ and build again. People with real energy don’t sit around moaning about what they lost; they know they can make more.
university: The key image is ‘kaiththu udaiyaar’: those who hold ookkam as kaipporul, ready money in the hand, which Parimelazhagar reads as the secure capital that makes lost aakkam (prosperity) recoverable. ‘Oruvandham’ means certainly or firmly (nichchayamaaga), qualifying the grip on energy; ‘allaavaar’ (will not be distressed) derives from allal, affliction. Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the implied condition ‘even when prosperity has actually been lost’, while Kalaignar stresses that such people do not lose their ookkam along with their wealth. The couplet thus answers 592: if wealth departs, energy remains the seed of its return, which is why the chapter treats ookkam as a king’s fundamental resource. The Tamil text is identical in both base sources, differing only in word-splitting (izhandhemendru vs. izhandhaem endru).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One whose mind remains undisturbed amidst misery, who does not crave for pleasure, and who is free from attachment, fear, and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the steady-minded person who does not fall apart when troubles come.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s energetic person, like the Gita’s sthita-prajña, is not shaken into lament by loss.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he has learned to stay steady whether he has plenty or nothing.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s energetic person, Paul does not collapse into complaint when his resources vanish.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches believers not to be crushed by what they have lost nor puffed up by what they have gained.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the strong-spirited do not lament lost prosperity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, And naked shall I return thither; The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; Blessed be the name of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: Having lost his flocks, servants and children in one day, Job refuses to curse or despair.
judaism.tie_back: Job embodies the Kural’s refusal to cry ‘we have lost our wealth’, though from faith rather than energy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures the wise as a rock that stays put whatever storms of fortune blow against it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s energetic person is similarly unshaken by the storm of lost prosperity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
jainism.explanation: When Indra tells the renouncing King Nami that his city and palace are burning, Nami answers that he grieves at nothing because he no longer claims any of it as his own.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says those who hold energy firmly do not grieve over lost wealth; Nami likewise does not lament the loss of his kingdom, though his calm rests on non-possession rather than on confidence that energy will win wealth back.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That man, who in the midst of pain, does not feel pain, who is not affected by pleasure, affection or fear, and who looks alike upon gold and dust”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person in whose heart God dwells as one who is not shaken by suffering and values gold no more than dust.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who firmly hold energy do not grieve over lost wealth; Guru Tegh Bahadur's steady person likewise does not lament loss, though his steadiness comes from detachment rather than confidence in winning wealth back.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus loses every ship, every companion and all his Trojan treasure, yet he washes up naked on Scheria and still presses on until he regains his home and kingdom.
greek_mythology.explanation: Stripped of everything, Odysseus keeps his resourceful, tireless spirit and uses it to win back all he had.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s idea that energy held ‘in hand’ outlasts lost wealth and can restore it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells how Stilpo, whose city had been captured and his family and property lost, was asked by Demetrius whether he had lost anything, and replied that he had lost nothing, for all his goods were with him.
philosophy.explanation: The philosopher Stilpo insists that real goods live inside a person and cannot be plundered.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ookkam-holder, Stilpo does not say ‘I have lost my wealth’ because his real capital is within.

real_life_example.event_title: Thomas Edison rebuilds after the West Orange factory fire
real_life_example.place: West Orange, New Jersey, United States
real_life_example.event: In December 1914 a fire destroyed much of the factory complex surrounding Thomas Edison's laboratory in West Orange, New Jersey, although the laboratory buildings themselves survived. The loss was very large, but Edison led the rebuilding of the works. He continued his business and research there through the First World War, during which he also chaired the Naval Consulting Board.
real_life_example.explanation: Edison treated the destruction of a great part of his property as a setback to be repaired rather than a disaster to be mourned.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who firmly hold energy do not grieve over lost wealth, and Edison's response to the fire was to rebuild rather than lament.

tamil:
ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் அசைவிலா
ஊக்க முடையா னுழை.
transliteration:
Aakkam adharvinaaich chellum asaivilaa
Ookkam udaiyaan uzhai.
meaning: Good fortune itself asks for directions and goes to the home of a person whose drive never weakens.
elementary: Picture good luck as a little traveller with a map, going around asking, ‘Where does the hardworking kid live?’ The Kural says success goes looking for people who never give up.
university: Valluvar personifies aakkam (prosperity, increase) as a traveller who ‘adhar vinaai’, asks the road (adhar = path), to reach the dwelling (uzhai) of the man of unwavering (asaivilaa) energy. Parimelazhagar notes that prosperity need not be sought by such a person; it seeks him, a reversal of the usual image of the striver chasing fortune. Solomon Pappaiah’s modern rendering, ‘wealth learns his address and goes to him’, keeps the playful personification. The idea closely matches the Sanskrit subhāṣita ‘udyoginaṁ puruṣa-siṁham upaiti lakṣmīḥ’ (Lakshmi approaches the lion-like man of effort), found in the Hitopadesha prologue, showing a shared Indian topos. The two base sources agree on the text; thirukkural.net joins ‘ookka mudaiyaa nuzhai’ as in the metrical manuscripts, which is simply the sandhi form of ‘ookkam udaiyaan uzhai’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Lakshmi, goddess of fortune, approaches the lion-like man of effort; only cowards say that fortune is simply handed out by fate, so set fate aside and exert yourself with your own strength.
hinduism.explanation: The Hitopadesha’s famous verse says prosperity comes to the energetic, not to those who wait on destiny.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own image: fortune travels to the unwavering man of energy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, the servants who actively traded with their money are given far more, while the one who buried his talent loses it.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, increase flows to the one who acts energetically with what he has.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an states that what a person gains corresponds to the effort he puts in.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly ties prosperity to unwavering effort.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that the one who works with a slack hand becomes poor, while the hand of the diligent brings riches.
judaism.explanation: The sages of Proverbs connect wealth directly to diligent, energetic effort and poverty to slackness.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural says the same, adding the image of prosperity actively seeking out the diligent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that the energetic, careful person steadily grows in honour and standing.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it promises increase to the one whose energy does not flag.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Fields and houses, gold, cattle, slaves and servants: where these four goods, the causes of pleasure, are present, in such families he is born. He will have friends and relations, be of good family, of fine complexion, healthy, wise, noble, famous, and powerful.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana says that one who strenuously fulfils the Law and leaves this body rises to heaven and is later reborn into a family where prosperity and every advantage are already present.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural pictures prosperity finding its own way to the door of the steadfast; here too prosperity arrives unsought for the one who has striven, though in Jainism it comes through karmic merit and rebirth.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 3.17–18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Gujri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan promises that sustained effort brings life and that its practice brings peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says prosperity itself asks the way to the home of the person of unwavering energy; Guru Arjan likewise makes good fortune follow from effort.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells his brother Perses that the gods have set sweat before excellence, that work is no disgrace, and that if he works the idle will soon envy him as he grows rich, for fame and renown attend on wealth.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s farming poem teaches that prosperity and honour follow the hardworking person.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s promise that prosperity comes to the one of unfailing energy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Terence’s comedy Phormio, a character declares that fortune helps the brave (fortes fortuna adiuvat), a proverb later repeated by Pliny and Cicero.
philosophy.explanation: The Latin proverb says good fortune sides with the bold and energetic.
philosophy.tie_back: It is a Roman version of the Kural’s image of fortune seeking out the unwavering.

real_life_example.event_title: Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita found the company that became Sony
real_life_example.event: In 1946, in a Tokyo still recovering from the war, Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita founded Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo (Tokyo Telecommunications Engineering Corporation), which began by making devices such as voltmeters. Early consumer products, including an electric rice cooker and Japan's first tape recorder, sold poorly, but the founders licensed the transistor from Bell Laboratories in the early 1950s and built transistor radios. The company renamed itself Sony in 1958 and in 1961 became the first Japanese company to list its shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
real_life_example.explanation: Two engineers with little capital kept working through failures, and prosperity followed their persistence rather than preceding it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says prosperity finds its own way to the home of the person whose energy never wavers, and Sony's growth from a small postwar workshop shows it arriving after years of steady effort.

tamil:
வெள்ளத் தனைய மலர்நீட்டம் மாந்தர்தம்
உள்ளத் தனையது உயர்வு.
transliteration:
Vellath thanaiya malarneettam maandhardham
Ullath thanaiyadhu uyarvu.
meaning: The stem of a water lily grows as tall as the water is deep. In the same way, a person rises only as high as the drive in their mind.
elementary: A lotus in a pond always grows its stem long enough to reach the top of the water. If the pond is deep, the stem is long. The Kural says people are like that: the bigger your spirit and effort, the higher you rise.
university: This is the chapter’s most celebrated image. ‘Vellaththanaiya malar neettam’ means the length of the flower (its stalk) is proportionate to the flood or water-depth; ‘ullaththanaiyadhu uyarvu’ means human height or eminence is proportionate to ullam, which the commentators again take as ookkam. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah speak generally of neerppookkal (water-flowers), while Kalaignar specifies the lotus stalk (thaamarai thandu); the botanical observation that lotus and water-lily stems lengthen to keep the bloom at the surface underlies the comparison. The parallel structure ‘-aththanaiya … -aththanaiyadhu’ is an example of Valluvar’s use of exact grammatical symmetry (ethirnirai) to make the analogy feel like a law. The couplet implies both limit and possibility: stature cannot exceed inner energy, but greater energy raises it. Text identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna urges Arjuna to lift himself up by his own mind and never let himself sink, since the mind can be the self’s best friend or its worst enemy.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita teaches that how high or low a person goes depends on the state of their own mind.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s lotus image says the same: a person’s height matches the level of their inner energy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he:”
christianity.explanation: This proverb, often quoted in Christian teaching, says a person’s true character follows what is in their heart and mind.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures a person by the level of their inner life.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an ties a people’s outward condition to the state of their inner selves.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too makes outer elevation depend on the inner ‘water-level’ of the mind.

judaism.quote_or_event: Maimonides teaches that every person has the power to become as righteous as Moses or as wicked as Jeroboam; no decree fixes one’s level, which depends on one’s own choice and effort.
judaism.explanation: Maimonides insists that a person’s spiritual height is not predetermined but set by their own will.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly makes a person’s ‘height’ a function of their own inner resolve.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 5:2

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By effort and heedfulness, discipline and self-mastery, let the wise one make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says energy and discipline raise a person above the floodwaters of life.
buddhism.tie_back: Both use water imagery: inner effort determines how far a person rises above the flood.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The pious obtain purity, and the pure stand firmly in the Law: (the soul afterwards) reaches the highest Nirvâna, being like unto a fire fed with ghee.”
jainism.explanation: After saying that one must fulfil the Law strenuously, the text compares the purified soul to a fire that blazes higher as ghee is poured on it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's flower-stalk rises as high as the water is deep, and a person as high as his energy; the Jain image likewise ties the height the soul reaches to how fully it is fed by effort and purity.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 3.11–12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O my mind, you are the embodiment of the Divine Light - recognize your own origin.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das tells the mind that its true nature is divine light and calls it to know that source.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a person rises only as high as the mind, as a water-flower's stalk rises with the water; Guru Amar Das likewise places a person's true height in the mind, though in its divine source rather than its drive.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 441, Raag Aasaa, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar advises his patron Hieron to become such as he is, having learned what that is, urging him to rise to the full measure of his own nature.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet tells a king to grow into the full size of the self he truly has.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the lotus rising to the water-line, Pindar’s ideal is to rise exactly to one’s inner measure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “… it makes a material for itself out of that which opposes it, as fire lays hold of what falls into it, by which a small light would have been extinguished: but when the fire is strong, it soon appropriates to itself the matter which is heaped on it, and consumes it, and rises higher by means of this very material.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus says the ruling part of the mind, when it follows nature, turns every obstacle into fuel, as a strong fire feeds on what would smother a weak one.
philosophy.tie_back: Both use an image from nature in which the strength of the inner force decides how high one rises: the stalk with the water, the flame with its own strength.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV, §1 (tr. George Long)

real_life_example.event_title: Wilma Rudolph overcomes childhood polio to win three Olympic golds
real_life_example.event: Wilma Rudolph, born in Tennessee in 1940, contracted polio and other illnesses as a child and for years could not walk without a leg brace or special shoe. With years of treatment and exercise she learned to walk normally and became a sprinter. At the 1960 Rome Olympics she won gold in the 100 metres, the 200 metres and the 4 x 100 metres relay, becoming the first American woman to win three track and field gold medals at a single Games.
real_life_example.explanation: Rudolph's rise was not set by the body she started with but by the strength of her will and effort.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a person rises as high as the energy of their mind, just as a lotus stalk grows as tall as the water is deep, and Rudolph rose from a leg brace to the top of the Olympic podium.

tamil:
உள்ளுவ தெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல் மற்றது
தள்ளினுந் தள்ளாமை நீர்த்து.
transliteration:
Ulluva thellaam uyarvullal matradhu
Thallinum thallaamai neerththu.
meaning: Let all your thoughts be about rising higher. Even if you do not reach your goal, aiming high is as good as reaching it.
elementary: If you aim to jump over a tall bar and only get halfway, you still jumped higher than if you’d aimed low. The Kural says always think big; even when you don’t reach it, the aiming itself counts.
university: The first line is a direct precept: ‘ulluvadhellaam uyarvu ullal’, let all that you think be the thinking of elevation. The second line is compressed and has produced different readings. Parimelazhagar (reflected in Pope’s ‘if it should be thrust from him by fate, it will have the nature of not being thrust from him’) takes ‘matradhu thallinum’ as ‘even if that (aim) is thwarted by fate (ool)’ and ‘thallaamai neerththu’ as ‘it has the nature (neermai) of not being thwarted’, since the nobility of the aim remains. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the line as an imperative, ‘do not abandon such thinking even if it fails’, while Solomon Pappaiah adds that the great will praise the attempt, so it counts as fulfilled. Thirukkural.net compresses this as ‘failure then is as good as success’. The text is identical in the base sources; the interpretive variation lies in whether ‘thallaamai’ is descriptive or prescriptive.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions. Never consider yourself to be the cause of the results of your activities, nor be attached to inaction.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that one’s task is the effort itself, not control of outcomes, and that giving up action is never right.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the lofty aim keeps its worth even when fate blocks the result.

christianity.quote_or_event: “…forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Paul admits he has not yet arrived but keeps straining forward toward the highest goal.
christianity.tie_back: His constant reaching for the ‘high calling’ is the Kural’s ‘let every thought be of rising’.

islam.quote_or_event: A hadith reported by al-Tabarani and others says that Allah loves lofty and noble matters and dislikes base and petty ones.
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that believers should set their sights on noble, elevated aims rather than trivial ones.
islam.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s command to let every thought be a thought of elevation.
islam.source: al-Tabarani, al-Mu‘jam al-Kabir (hadith on ma‘ali al-umur)

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it;”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon teaches that one must keep striving at a great task even if it cannot be completed in one’s lifetime.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it values the pursuit of a high aim even when completion is blocked.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha recalls resolving before his awakening that he would gladly let his flesh and blood dry up, leaving skin, sinews and bones, rather than relax his energy before reaching what can be reached by human strength and effort.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha aimed at the highest goal and vowed never to lower his effort short of it.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘think only of rising’, carried to its utmost.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You have crossed the great ocean; why do you halt so near the shore? make haste to get on the other side; Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira urges his chief disciple Gautama not to settle for what he has achieved but to press on to the highest goal without a moment's slackness.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to let every thought be of rising higher; Mahavira's charge to Gautama is the same refusal to rest short of the highest aim.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.34 (refrain from 10.1) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak asks total commitment, even readiness to give one's life, from anyone who would walk the path of love for God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks that every thought be lofty and says such an aim keeps its worth even if fate defeats it; Guru Nanak's call to set out with head in hand, whatever the cost, is the closest Sikh counterpart.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads the young Heracles is approached by Vice, offering an easy, pleasant road, and Virtue, offering a steep, hard road to true glory; he chooses the harder, higher path.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles deliberately picks the difficult road that leads upward rather than the comfortable one.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His choice embodies the Kural’s rule that one’s aims should always point toward elevation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca defends philosophers who fall short of their ideals, saying one should admire those who attempt great things even when they fail, because the attempt itself is noble.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that striving toward a lofty goal deserves honour even without full success.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s second line: a high aim that is thwarted is as good as one achieved.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On the Happy Life (De Vita Beata) 20

real_life_example.event_title: Scott's party reaches the South Pole and dies on the return
real_life_example.place: South Pole and the Ross Ice Shelf, Antarctica
real_life_example.event: Captain Robert Falcon Scott led the British Antarctic (Terra Nova) Expedition, whose five-man polar party reached the South Pole on 17 January 1912, only to find that Roald Amundsen's Norwegian party had arrived there on 14 December 1911. All five men died on the return journey, Scott himself with Edward Wilson and Henry Bowers in late March, held up by a blizzard about 11 miles from a supply depot. A search party found their tent, bodies, diaries and photographs the following November.
real_life_example.explanation: Scott's party aimed at one of the hardest goals of their age and reached it, but fate denied them both priority and survival; they are still remembered for the height of their aim and their endurance.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural urges people to let every thought be of rising higher, and says that even if fate thwarts that aim, it keeps the worth of not having been thwarted, which is how Scott's expedition has been remembered.

tamil:
சிதைவிடத்து ஒல்கார் உரவோர் புதையம்பிற்
பட்டுப்பா டூன்றுங் களிறு.
transliteration:
Sidhaividaththu olkaar uravor pudhaiyambir
Pattuppaadu oondrum kaliru.
meaning: Strong-minded people do not give up even when they are ruined, just as a war elephant stands firm with pride even when arrows are stuck deep in its body.
elementary: Think of a brave firefighter who keeps going even when they are tired and hurt. The Kural compares strong-hearted people to a huge elephant that stays standing even when arrows hit it. Tough times don’t make them quit.
university: ‘Sidhaividaththu’ means at the place or time of ruin (sidhaivu), and ‘olkaar’ means they do not bend or droop; ‘uravor’ are those with uram, firmness of mind. The simile is from war: ‘pudhai ambu’ are arrows buried in the flesh, and ‘pattup paadu oondrum kaliru’ is the bull elephant that, though struck, plants itself (oondrum) and upholds its paadu, glossed by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar as its perumai (greatness, dignity). The image comes from Sangam battle poetry, where the wounded tusker holding its ground is a stock emblem of valour. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads ‘pudhai’ as arrows that cover the body. The spelling ‘kaliru’ (களிறு) is the standard word for a male elephant; the texts in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhishma, pierced by so many of Arjuna’s arrows that when he falls from his chariot his body does not touch the ground, lies on a bed of arrows for many days, calm and lucid, and teaches the Pandavas until his chosen time of death.
hinduism.explanation: The great warrior, riddled with arrows, keeps his composure and his dignity and continues to act as a teacher.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the human counterpart of the Kural’s elephant that stands firm though pierced by arrows.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (fall of Bhishma), tr. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed;”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes suffering attacks from every side without being crushed in spirit.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s strong-minded, he is struck but does not falter.

islam.quote_or_event: “So do not weaken and do not grieve, and you will be superior if you are [true] believers.”
islam.explanation: After the setback at Uhud, the Qur’an tells the wounded believers not to lose heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too says the strong do not droop even in the hour of ruin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be strong and of good courage; be not affrighted, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.”
judaism.explanation: God tells Joshua, facing hard battles, to stay strong and not be shaken.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same firmness in danger the Kural praises.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As an elephant in the battlefield withstands arrows shot from bows all around, even so shall I endure abuse.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares his patient endurance of insults to a war elephant standing firm under a hail of arrows.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts use the identical image of the arrow-struck war elephant that does not give way.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As an elephant at the head of the battle, so was Mahâvîra there victorious. … As a hero at the head of the battle is surrounded on all sides, so was there Mahâvîra. Bearing all hardships, the Venerable One, undisturbed, proceeded (on the road to Nirvâna).”
jainism.explanation: Describing Mahavira's harsh wanderings in Lāḍha, where he was beaten, cut and set upon by dogs, the Acaranga compares him to a war elephant at the front of battle who stays unshaken.
jainism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own image: the strong-minded do not falter in ruin, just as a war elephant pierced by arrows stands firm.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra 1.8.3.8 and 1.8.3.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose hymns the Gurus included in the Guru Granth Sahib, defines the true hero (soora) as one who fights for what is right and holds his ground even as he is cut down.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's war elephant, pierced deep with arrows, still stands firm; Kabir's hero, cut piece by piece yet never leaving the field, gives the same picture of steadfastness in ruin.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As the Trojans storm the Greek ships, Ajax is battered by missiles until his shoulder aches under his shield and he can barely breathe, yet he keeps his position and does not give ground.
greek_mythology.explanation: The great Greek defender stays at his post even while being hammered from all sides.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ajax holding firm under the barrage mirrors the elephant standing fast though pierced by arrows.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius tells himself to be like the headland against which the waves keep breaking, which stands firm while the water calms around it.
philosophy.explanation: The emperor-philosopher pictures the steady mind as a rock that stays put while trouble crashes against it.
philosophy.tie_back: His headland and the Kural’s elephant are both images of the strong mind that does not yield in disaster.

real_life_example.event_title: Rana Pratap fights on after the defeat at Haldighati
real_life_example.event: In June 1576 Rana Pratap Singh of Mewar was defeated by a Mughal army of the emperor Akbar at the Battle of Haldighati near Gogunda. Instead of submitting, he withdrew to the hills and continued resistance from mountain strongholds, later making Chavand his capital. He kept raiding until his death in 1597, and Mewar did not formally acknowledge Mughal overlordship until 1614.
real_life_example.explanation: Defeat in open battle did not break Pratap's resolve, and he spent the rest of his life standing his ground in the hills.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the strong-minded do not falter even in ruin, like a war elephant that stands firm though pierced by arrows, and Pratap held firm for two decades after Haldighati.

tamil:
உள்ளம் இலாதவர் எய்தார் உலகத்து
வள்ளியம் என்னுஞ் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Ullam ilaadhavar eydhaar ulagaththu
Valliyam ennum serukku.
meaning: People without inner drive will never know the proud joy of saying, “We are the generous givers of the world.”
elementary: To share lots of cookies with your friends, you first have to bake them. The Kural says people without energy never get to feel the happy pride of being the one who gives to everyone, because they never make enough to give.
university: ‘Ullam ilaadhavar’ again uses ullam for ookkam; ‘vallium ennum serukku’ is the elation or proud self-regard (serukku) of being able to say ‘we are liberal’ (valliyam, from vallal, a munificent patron). The logic, drawn out by Parimelazhagar, is that liberality requires wealth, wealth requires effort, and effort requires ookkam, so the unenergetic are cut off from one of the highest satisfactions of kingship and householdership, the role of the vallal celebrated in Sangam poetry (the seven great patrons, kadaiyezhu vallalgal). Solomon Pappaiah calls it ‘mana uyarvu’, uplift of mind, while Kalaignar reads ‘ullam’ as the eager will to give freely. Sivayogi Sivakumar’s reading, ‘pride of having conquered the world’, diverges from the mainstream. Thirukkural.net’s ‘the poor in spirit can never attain the pride of being the generous patrons of the world’ matches the majority view; the Tamil is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The teacher’s parting instruction to graduating students tells them to give with faith, not without faith, to give with liberality (śriyā), with modesty, with awe and with understanding.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad treats generous giving as a mark of a noble, full-hearted life.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural adds that such magnificent giving is only possible for the energetic.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says true giving flows from a willing, glad heart rather than reluctance.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see generous giving as springing from largeness of heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “The upper hand is better than the lower hand. The upper hand is that of the giver and the lower (hand) is that of the beggar.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises the dignity of being the one who gives rather than the one who must ask.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise prizes the honour of being a giver, which the unenergetic never attain.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs observes that one person scatters freely and yet grows richer, while another withholds and comes to want, and that the generous soul will be enriched and the one who waters others will himself be watered.
judaism.explanation: The sages praise the open-handed, large-spirited person who gives freely.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Proverbs treats generosity as the mark of a big spirit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that misers do not reach the heavenly realms and fools do not praise generosity, but the wise rejoice in giving and are happy because of it.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts small-minded misers with the wise, who find joy in giving.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says only the large-spirited taste the joy of generosity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He gave up his gold and silver, his troops and chariots, and distributed, portioned out, and gave away his valuable treasures (consisting of) riches, corn, gold, pearls, &c., and distributed among those who wanted to make presents to others. Thus he gave away during a whole year.”
jainism.explanation: Before renouncing the world Mahavira spent a whole year giving away his wealth, a great gift that Jain tradition says every Tirthankara makes before renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says only those with energy of spirit can know the joy of being the world's generous givers; in Jainism the year of giving comes from the same resolute spirit that leads to renunciation.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra 2.15.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak joins honest labour (kirat karni) to sharing (vand chhakna): one who earns by his own effort can give from his own hand.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those without energy of spirit will never know the joy of being generous givers; Guru Nanak likewise makes one's own labour the basis of true giving.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor elderly couple Baucis and Philemon, who had almost nothing, eagerly served disguised Zeus and Hermes their best food and wine when every rich household had turned the gods away.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poorest couple in the district proved the most generous because their hearts were large.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The story shows that the pride of generosity belongs to the large-hearted, as the Kural says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle’s great-souled (megalopsychos) person is the sort who confers benefits but is ashamed to receive them, and who likes to repay more than he received.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle’s ideal of greatness of soul includes taking pride in being a benefactor.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s ‘pride of being generous’, which belongs only to those with a large spirit.

real_life_example.event_title: Milton Hershey rises from bankruptcy to found a school for orphaned boys
real_life_example.place: Philadelphia, New York and Hershey, Pennsylvania, United States
real_life_example.event: Milton Hershey's first candy business in Philadelphia went bankrupt after six years, and a second attempt in New York also failed. Returning to Lancaster with little money, he built the Lancaster Caramel Company, sold it in 1900 for one million dollars, and went on to build the Hershey Chocolate Company. On 15 November 1909 he and his wife Catherine signed the deed of trust founding the Hershey Industrial School for orphaned boys, and in 1918 he placed his controlling interest in the chocolate company in trust for the school.
real_life_example.explanation: The same drive that carried Hershey through repeated business failures later made him one of the most generous benefactors of his time.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those without energy of spirit will never know the proud joy of being generous givers, and Hershey's school shows the giving that energy made possible.

tamil:
பரியது கூர்ங்கோட்டது ஆயினும் யானை
வெரூஉம் புலிதாக் குறின்.
transliteration:
Pariyadhu koorngottadhu aayinum yaanai
Veruum pulidhaakkurin.
meaning: An elephant is huge and has sharp tusks, yet it gets scared when a tiger attacks.
elementary: A big dog can run away from a small, brave cat that hisses and charges. The Kural says size and weapons don’t decide who wins; the fierce spirit does, like a tiger that can scare an elephant.
university: The couplet is a pure illustration (eduththukkaattu uvamai) with the moral left implicit: ‘pariyadhu’ (bulky) and ‘koorng kottadhu’ (having sharp tusks) list the elephant’s physical advantages, and ‘veruum’ (fears) is an alapedai (vowel-lengthened) form of verum, which heightens the sense of sudden fright. Parimelazhagar explains that the tiger prevails because it has ookkam, and that the verse teaches that energy, not bulk or weaponry, decides contests; Kalaignar makes this explicit, calling ookkam stronger than physique. The pairing with 597, where the elephant is the image of steadfastness, shows Valluvar using the same animal both ways: wounded but energetic it stands, huge but unenergetic it flees. The text is identical in the base sources; transliterations differ only in rendering the alapedai (veru-um / veruum).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya records a debate on whether energy (utsāha-śakti) or material power (prabhāva-śakti) is superior: his teacher argues that an energetic king, brave and skilled, can overcome even a stronger one, while Kautilya himself ranks power, and above both good counsel, higher.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra weighs energy against sheer resources as sources of victory.
hinduism.tie_back: The teacher’s view is the Kural’s tiger-and-elephant lesson; Kautilya’s own view is a candid counterpoint.

christianity.quote_or_event: The young shepherd David, without armour and armed only with a sling, faces the giant Philistine champion Goliath, clad in bronze with a massive spear, and fells him with one stone.
christianity.explanation: The small but fearless fighter overcomes the huge, heavily armed one.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s tiger, David shows that spirit beats size and weapons.

islam.quote_or_event: “How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: Before facing Goliath’s army, Saul’s few steadfast soldiers declare that small, determined forces often defeat larger ones.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s tiger-versus-elephant lesson applied to armies.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be strong as a leopard, and swift as an eagle, and fleet as a gazelle, and brave as a lion, to do the will of your Father who is in heaven.”
judaism.explanation: Judah ben Tema calls for the fierce energy of predators in the service of God.
judaism.tie_back: His leopard and lion are the Jewish counterpart of the Kural’s tiger, symbols of energetic spirit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Heedful among the heedless, wide-awake among the sleepy, the wise man advances like a swift horse leaving behind a weak jade.”
buddhism.explanation: The alert, energetic person pulls far ahead of those who are sluggish.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it teaches that alert energy, not bulk, decides who prevails.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a strong and irresistible elephant of sixty years, surrounded by his females, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk. … As a proud lion with sharp fangs, who brooks no assault, is superior to all animals, so is a very learned monk (superior to all men).”
jainism.explanation: In a chain of similes the Uttaradhyayana praises the accomplished monk through the mightiest animals, setting the lion that brooks no assault above all other beasts.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's point is that the great elephant still fears the attacking tiger, so courage outweighs size; the Jain verses use the same animal world of strength, with the fearless big cat at the top.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.18 and 11.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Lord is like sugar, scattered in the sand; the elephant cannot pick it up. Says Kabeer, the Guru has given me this sublime understanding: become an ant, and feed on it.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir says the great elephant, an image of pride, cannot gather the sugar of the Lord from the sand, while a tiny ant can.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's huge, sharp-tusked elephant takes fright before a tiger, showing that bulk does not decide a contest; Kabir also shows the great elephant beaten by something small, though what wins for him is humility, not energy.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1377, Salok Bhagat Kabir (238), Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the cave of the giant Cyclops Polyphemus, the far smaller Odysseus blinds him with a sharpened stake and escapes with his men under the giant’s sheep.
greek_mythology.explanation: The small but bold hero overcomes a monstrous opponent many times his size.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode matches the Kural’s point that bulk does not guarantee victory over a spirited foe.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Rallying the Greek officers after their generals had been seized by the Persians, Xenophon tells them that it is neither numbers nor strength that wins victories in war: whichever side advances with the stronger spirit, its enemies as a rule will not stand against it.
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon urges the officers to restore the courage of their troops, since morale, not size, decides battles.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the tiger routing the huge, tusked elephant, the side with the stronger spirit prevails over sheer bulk.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Anabasis, Book III, ch. 1, §42 (tr. H. G. Dakyns)

real_life_example.event_title: The Athenians defeat the Persian army at Marathon
real_life_example.event: In 490 BCE a Persian expeditionary force sent by King Darius I landed at the bay of Marathon, northeast of Athens. About 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans, without Spartan help, faced a larger Persian army and, under generals including Miltiades, attacked with a thinned centre and strengthened wings that routed the Persian flanks and then closed on the centre. The Persians withdrew to their ships and sailed away.
real_life_example.explanation: The smaller force won because of its boldness and determination, not its numbers.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the huge, sharp-tusked elephant still takes fright when a tiger attacks, meaning that spirit and energy defeat sheer size, as the Athenians showed at Marathon.

tamil:
உரமொருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கைஅஃ தில்லார்
மரம்மக்க ளாதலே வேறு.
transliteration:
Uram oruvarku ulla verukkai aqdhillaar
Maram makkal aadhale veru.
meaning: A person’s real strength is having lots of inner drive. People without it are just trees that happen to have human shape.
elementary: A tree stands in one place all day and never tries anything new. The Kural says a person with no energy or drive is like a tree that happens to look like a human. What makes us truly alive is our eagerness to act.
university: ‘Uram’ is strength or firmness, and ‘ulla verukkai’ is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar takes verukkai as abundance, hence ‘excess of ookkam is one’s strength’, while others take verukkai in its lexical sense of wealth (selvam), hence ‘energy is the mind’s wealth’, which is Pope’s ‘energy is mental wealth’. Solomon Pappaiah glosses uram as thinniya arivu (firm understanding). The second line’s ‘maram makkal aadhale veru’ is devastating: the only difference (veru) between the energy-less and trees is that they have become human in form. Parimelazhagar notes the chapter closes by returning to 591, where the energy-less were denied possession; here they are denied full humanity. The text is identical in the base sources; the sandhi form ‘verukkaiaqdhillaar’ contains the aaydham (ஃ) of ‘aqdhu’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Queen Vidula rebukes her son Sanjaya, who lies despondent after defeat, telling him it is better to blaze up for a moment than to smoulder for a long time, and urging him to rise and fight.
hinduism.explanation: A mother shames her listless son, saying a life without energy is not worth living.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidula’s contempt for smouldering inertia matches the Kural’s picture of the energy-less as mere trees.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 133-136 (Vidula’s counsel), tr. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists fervour of spirit and freedom from sloth as marks of Christian life.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see spiritual energy as essential and sluggishness as a failure of real life.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up…”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says the hypocrites look impressive but are hollow inside, like timber propped against a wall.
islam.tie_back: The Kural uses the same wood image for people with human form but no inner life of energy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel urges people to step up with energy and responsibility when others do nothing.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats being fully human as a matter of active striving, not mere form.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better it is to live one day strenuous and resolute than to live a hundred years sluggish and dissipated.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada values a single day of energetic life above a century of lazy existence.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say that life without energy is hardly life at all.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the soul has once got into a vegetable-body, it remains long in that state, for an endless time, after which its lot is not much bettered; Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Jain doctrine treats plants as living souls with a single sense; Mahavira warns that a soul which falls into plant-existence through carelessness may stay there for endless time, which is why human birth must not be wasted.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says people without inner energy are mere trees in human form; Jainism makes the warning literal, since slackness can lead the soul into an actual vegetable body.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.9 (refrain from 10.1) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They belong to the human species, but they act like animals.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan says of those who live without the Name that they have human birth but not human worth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those without inner energy differ from trees only in having human shape; Guru Arjan likewise denies full humanity to those who have the form without the substance.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 267, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says both gods and men are angry with the man who lives idle, for he is like the stingless drones that waste the bees’ labour, eating without working.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod compares the idle to drones in a hive, living beings that contribute nothing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s drone and the Kural’s tree are both images of life without energy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle, seeking the distinctive human function, sets aside mere life because it is shared even with plants, and locates the human good in the active exercise of the rational soul.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, a person who only lives and grows is functioning at the level of a plant, not yet as a human being.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own claim: without active energy, humans are trees in human shape.

real_life_example.event_title: The deaf Beethoven completes and premieres his Ninth Symphony
real_life_example.event: Ludwig van Beethoven's hearing had been failing since his late twenties, and by the 1820s he was profoundly deaf. He nevertheless completed his Ninth Symphony, with a choral finale setting Schiller's Ode to Joy, and it was first performed at the Theater am Karntnertor in Vienna on 7 May 1824. Beethoven stood on stage beside the conductor indicating the tempos while the performance was actually directed by others.
real_life_example.explanation: Deprived of the sense on which a composer most depends, Beethoven still produced one of the most celebrated works in Western music.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a person's real strength is abundance of inner energy, and Beethoven's Ninth shows that energy accomplishing what physical loss seemed to forbid.

tamil:
குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம் மடியென்னும்
மாசூர மாய்ந்து கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kudiyennum kundraa vilakkam madiyennum
Maasoora maaindhu kedum.
meaning: A family is like a lamp that should never go out. But when the dirt of laziness builds up on it, its light fades and dies.
elementary: Think of a lamp that has shone in your home for years. If nobody cleans the soot off the glass, the light gets dimmer and dimmer until the room is dark. Laziness is that soot: a family stays bright only if its people keep working and caring.
university: The opening couplet sets up the chapter’s governing image: குடி (family, lineage) is a குன்றா விளக்கம், a lamp or radiance that of itself would never diminish, and மடி (sloth) is the மாசு, the grime or darkness that ‘spreads over’ (ஊர) it until it dims (மாய்ந்து) and perishes (கெடும்). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read மாசு as a film of dirt that accumulates by degrees, whereas Solomon Pappaiah and the Rev. Drew/Pope tradition render it as darkness; either way the point is that decline is gradual and self-inflicted rather than sudden and external. The chapter heading மடியின்மை (‘absence of sloth’) follows ஊக்கமுடைமை (ch. 60, energy) and precedes ஆள்வினையுடைமை (ch. 62, manly effort), so Valluvar moves from the positive virtue to the vice that undoes it before turning to sustained effort. The text agrees across ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org; the latter prints the older sandhi-joined form (விளக்க மடியென்னு / மாசூர) with no change of wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Arjun, tamo guṇa, which is born of ignorance, is the cause of illusion for the embodied souls. It deludes all living beings through negligence, laziness, and sleep.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names tamas, literally ‘darkness’, as the quality that binds people through negligence (pramāda), laziness (ālasya) and sleep (nidrā).
hinduism.tie_back: Tamas as a darkness born of laziness is almost exactly the Kural’s image of sloth as the grime that dims the family lamp.

christianity.quote_or_event: “While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept. … And the foolish said unto the wise, Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the ten virgins, the careless ones let their lamps go out and are shut out of the wedding feast.
christianity.tie_back: A lamp that goes out through neglect is the same picture as the Kural’s family light dying under sloth.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Allah! I seek refuge with you (Allah) from (worries) care and grief, from incapacity and laziness, from miserliness and cowardice, from being heavily in debt and from being overpowered by other men.”
islam.explanation: Anas reports that the Prophet prayed this often, listing laziness (kasal) among the things a believer should seek God’s protection from.
islam.tie_back: Treating laziness as a danger to be warded off matches the Kural’s view of sloth as the stain that ruins a household.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Through slothfulness the ceiling sags, / Through lazy hands the house caves in.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet notes that a house does not collapse all at once; it sags and leaks gradually when its owners are idle.
judaism.tie_back: The slowly failing house is the Hebrew counterpart of the Kural’s slowly dimming family lamp.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 10:18 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Saṅgārava Sutta, the Buddha compares a mind overcome by sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) to a bowl of water covered with moss and water plants, in which a man cannot see the reflection of his own face.
buddhism.explanation: Sloth and torpor is one of the five hindrances; like a film over water, it hides what should be clearly seen, including one’s own good.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s மாசு (grime) spreading over a lamp and the Buddha’s moss spreading over clear water are the same image of sloth as a covering film.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's sermon on carelessness (pramāda) says that a negligent person loses even the light he once had, like a man whose lamp suddenly goes out in the dark.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's family-lamp that sloth dims and puts out has a close counterpart in the Jain image of the careless man whose lamp is put out.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The self-willed manmukh is very lazy; he is trapped in the wilderness.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak names laziness as a mark of the manmukh, the self-willed person, and says it leaves him lost and trapped.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the grime of laziness dims and puts out the lamp of a family; Guru Nanak likewise shows sloth leading to ruin, though of a person's spiritual life rather than a family's standing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1011, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the start of the Odyssey, the house of Odysseus is being eaten up by the suitors while young Telemachus sits passive, until Athena, disguised as Mentes, rouses him to act for his father’s house.
greek_mythology.explanation: The great house is wasting away not because of an outside attack but because its heir has not yet stirred himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s dimming lamp, a noble house fades while its heir stays inactive and revives only when he rouses himself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In The Way to Wealth, Benjamin Franklin’s Poor Richard warns that sloth, like rust, eats away faster than work wears things out, while a key that is used stays bright.
philosophy.explanation: Franklin argues that idleness wears things away more than work does, and that constant use keeps things bright.
philosophy.tie_back: Franklin’s rust on an unused key and the Kural’s grime on a neglected lamp are the same image of sloth tarnishing what should shine.
philosophy.source: Benjamin Franklin, The Way to Wealth (1758)

real_life_example.event_title: The Merovingian 'do-nothing kings' fade before the mayors of the palace
real_life_example.place: Frankish kingdom (now France, Belgium and western Germany)
real_life_example.event: After King Dagobert I died in 639, the later Merovingian kings of the Franks came to be called rois faineants, do-nothing kings, because real authority passed step by step to the mayors of the palace who governed in their name. By the 740s the mayors were placing Merovingians such as Childeric III on the throne only to keep up the appearance of royal rule. In 751 the mayor Pippin, with papal approval, had himself made king, and Childeric was deposed, tonsured and confined to the monastery of Sithiu near Saint-Omer.
real_life_example.explanation: The dynasty that had founded the Frankish kingdom did not fall in a single blow; its authority dimmed over about a century until it could be removed without a struggle.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural pictures a family as a lamp that grows dim as the grime of sloth settles on it, and the Merovingian line faded in exactly this gradual way until its light went out.

tamil:
மடியை மடியா ஒழுகல் குடியைக்
குடியாக வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Madiyai madiyaa ozhugal kudiyaik
Kudiyaaga vendu bavar.
meaning: If you want your family to rise and be truly respected, treat laziness as something deadly and get rid of it in the way you live.
elementary: If you want your team to be a real team, you can’t treat ‘I’ll do it later’ as harmless. You have to see laziness as the thing that breaks teams, and push it out every day. Families work the same way.
university: The couplet is built on a double pun. மடியை மடியா can mean ‘treating sloth as sloth’, recognising it for the vice it is (Varadarasanar: சோம்பலைச் சோம்பலாகக் கொண்டு), or, because மடி also means ‘to die, perish’, ‘treating sloth as something to be killed’ or ‘as death itself’. Kalaignar’s gloss (சோம்பலை ஒழித்து) takes the second sense. The echo குடியைக் குடியாக, ‘to make the family a family’, implies that a lineage only truly exists as a குடி while it keeps its standing; Parimelazhagar takes குடி here as the illustrious family, not the bare kin-group. ஒழுகல், ‘conduct, practice’, makes this a matter of daily habit, not of a single resolution. Both source texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi-joined மடியா வொழுகல்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa’s ‘charaiveti’ (keep moving) verses, Indra tells Rohita that fortune sits still with the one who sits and sleeps with the one who sleeps, and each stanza ends with the refrain: keep moving on.
hinduism.explanation: The god Indra urges the prince Rohita to keep wandering and striving, teaching that stillness and sleep bring decline while effort brings prosperity.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it tells a prince who wants his line to prosper to reject sloth completely and keep acting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists freedom from sloth, together with fervour of spirit, among the marks of a life given over to God.
christianity.tie_back: Paul, like Valluvar, makes rejecting sloth a daily rule of conduct (ஒழுகல்), not an occasional effort.

islam.quote_or_event: In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says the strong believer is better and more beloved to God than the weak one, and tells believers to strive for what benefits them, seek God’s help, and not give way to helplessness.
islam.explanation: The hadith tells believers to strive energetically for what is beneficial and forbids giving in to incapacity or listlessness (ʿajz).
islam.tie_back: Refusing to ‘give up’ matches the Kural’s demand that anyone who wants to raise their family must put sloth to death.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Tarfon said: the day is short, and the work is plentiful, and the laborers are indolent, and the reward is great, and the master of the house is insistent.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon describes the human condition as a short working day with much to do, and names laziness as the workers’ typical failing.
judaism.tie_back: Tarfon’s ‘indolent labourers’ are the people Valluvar warns: a house (bayit / குடி) is only upheld when that laziness is overcome.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:15 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, the Buddha’s last words to his monks are that all conditioned things are subject to decay, and they should strive on with diligence (appamādena sampādetha).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s final teaching makes diligence, the opposite of heedless sloth, the one thing his followers must hold on to.
buddhism.tie_back: Just as the Kural makes killing sloth the condition for a family’s survival, the Buddha makes diligence the condition for the community’s survival after him.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's famous refrain to Gautama (samayaṃ Goyama mā pamāyae, 'do not be careless even for a moment') makes constant vigilance against negligence the core discipline.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's call to treat sloth as sloth and kill it in one's conduct, Mahavira tells his foremost disciple never to let carelessness in for a moment.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O mind, why are you so lazy? Become Gurmukh, and meditate on the Naam.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das challenges the mind's laziness and sets against it the active, Guru-facing life of the gurmukh.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells those who want their family to stand to see laziness for what it is and kill it in their conduct; Guru Amar Das likewise names laziness and answers it with a daily discipline.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 28, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Do not put your work off till to-morrow and the day after; for a sluggish worker does not fill his barn, nor one who puts off his work”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that a household’s stores are filled only by those who refuse to procrastinate.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s full barn, like the Kural’s thriving குடி, belongs only to the one who treats sloth as the enemy.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 410-412 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If, therefore, you will be negligent and slothful, and always add procrastination to procrastination, purpose to purpose, and fix day after day in which you will attend to yourself, you will insensibly continue without proficiency”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus warns that someone who keeps putting off self-reform because of sloth will slide, without noticing, into a life of no progress.
philosophy.tie_back: Epictetus, like Valluvar, says that sloth has to be named and stopped now, not managed later.
philosophy.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 50 in Carter’s numbering (51 in some editions)

real_life_example.event_title: Fourteen-year-old Alfred Krupp takes on his father's failing works
real_life_example.event: When Friedrich Krupp died on 8 October 1826, he left his family a small, heavily indebted steel works in Essen where production had almost come to a standstill. His fourteen-year-old son Alfred, working alongside his widowed mother, took on the management of the workshop and its handful of employees. He became sole proprietor in 1848 and built the firm into one of the largest industrial enterprises in Europe.
real_life_example.explanation: The family's standing was saved not by inheritance, which was nearly worthless, but by years of relentless daily work by a teenage heir.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who want their family to be a family in the full sense must put laziness to death in their daily conduct, and young Alfred Krupp restored his family's fortunes through exactly that kind of unremitting work.

tamil:
மடிமடிக் கொண்டொழுகும் பேதை பிறந்த
குடிமடியும் தன்னினும் முந்து.
transliteration:
Madimadik kondozhugum pedhai pirandha
Kudimadiyum thanninum mundhu.
meaning: When a foolish person holds on to laziness, which destroys everything, the family they were born into is ruined even before they die.
elementary: Imagine a boy who never helps and never learns, and lets his family’s shop fall apart. The sad part is that the shop can close long before he grows old. His laziness hurts his family first.
university: Valluvar makes மடி ring three times: மடி (sloth) … மடி … மடியும் (perishes). The phrase மடிமடிக் கொண்டு is read in two ways. Varadarasanar and Parimelazhagar take the second மடி as an adjective, ‘sloth that destroys’ (அழிக்கும் இயல்புடைய சோம்பல்). Others hear மடி in its everyday sense of ‘lap’, ‘holding sloth in his lap’, cherishing it; Pappaiah’s ‘the sloth that ought to be cast off’ is close to this. பேதை, ‘fool’, is a strong word in the Kural (see ch. 84, பேதைமை): the fault is presented as a failure of understanding, not just of energy. The paradox that the குடி dies ‘before himself’ (தன்னினும் முந்து) means that the family’s standing, its reputation and wealth, can die while its lazy member is still alive to see it. Both source texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms குடிமடியுந் தன்னினு முந்து.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That happiness which covers the nature of the self from beginning to end, and which is derived from sleep, indolence, and negligence, is said to be in the mode of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna classifies the pleasure people get from sleep, laziness and carelessness as tamasic: it deludes a person from start to finish.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘fool’ (பேதை) who holds on to sloth is exactly the person deluded by tamasic pleasure.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.”
christianity.explanation: Paul sets out a blunt rule for the Thessalonian community: whoever refuses to work has no claim on others’ support.
christianity.tie_back: Paul, like Valluvar, treats the person who clings to idleness as someone who has cut himself off from the life of the household that feeds him.

islam.quote_or_event: “There are two blessings that many people are deceived into losing: health and free time.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that people commonly squander health and leisure, not realising what they have until it is gone.
islam.tie_back: The deceived squanderer of free time is the Kural’s பேதை, who wastes his chances until his family’s fortune is gone.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I passed by the field of a lazy man, / By the vineyard of someone lacking sense. / It was all overgrown with thorns; / Its surface was covered with chickweed, / And its stone fence lay in ruins.”
judaism.explanation: The sage describes the estate of a lazy man ‘lacking sense’, now overgrown and with its walls fallen, as a lesson in how sloth ruins what was inherited.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Lazy’ and ‘lacking sense’ appear together here, as in the Kural’s மடி and பேதை, and the ruined estate stands for the family that dies before its owner.
judaism.source: Proverbs 24:30-31 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The idler who does not exert himself when he should, who though young and strong is full of sloth, with a mind full of vain thoughts — such an indolent man does not find the path to wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a man who has youth and strength but wastes them in sloth and idle thinking, and so never reaches wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts pair sloth with folly: the idler never finds wisdom, and the Kural’s பேதை loses his family.
