jainism.quote_or_event: “You cannot prolong your life, therefore be not careless; you are past help when old age approaches. Consider this: what (protection) will careless people get, who kill living beings and do not exert themselves?”
jainism.explanation: The fourth lecture warns that the careless, who will not exert themselves, have no protection when their end comes.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's fool who clings to destructive sloth and perishes is the Jain 'careless' person who does not exert himself and finds no protection.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O my foolish and silly soul, why are you too lazy to serve?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan calls the lazy soul foolish for neglecting service (seva) to the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls the man who clings to laziness a fool whose family perishes even before he does; Guru Arjan likewise links laziness with folly, though the loss he warns of is spiritual.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1095, Raag Maaroo (Maaroo ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the Ant and the Grasshopper, the grasshopper sings away the summer while the ant stores grain, and when winter comes the grasshopper starves.
greek_mythology.explanation: The idler enjoys the present and ignores the season for work, then finds himself with nothing when need arrives.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s fool, the grasshopper pays for his idleness before he expects to.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Ants and the Grasshopper (trans. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book VIII of the Republic, Socrates describes the idle spendthrift as a ‘drone’ in a household, a plague to the house just as a drone is to the hive, who uses up its wealth while contributing nothing.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the drone to picture the member of a family or city who consumes without working and so brings ruin on the whole.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s drone that ruins the house matches the Kural’s idle fool whose family perishes before he does.

real_life_example.event_title: Ahmad Shah, the last Qajar shah, is deposed while living in Europe
real_life_example.event: Ahmad Shah, who had come to the throne of Iran as a boy in 1909, left for Europe in 1923 on a journey of indefinite length and never returned. While he was absent, Iran's national assembly, the Majles, formally deposed him in October 1925, ending the Qajar dynasty, and the crown was conferred on Reza Khan. Ahmad Shah settled permanently in France and died about four years later.
real_life_example.explanation: A ruling house that had governed Iran since the late eighteenth century came to an end while its last ruler, absent from his country, was still a young man.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the family of one who clings to idleness dies before he does, and the Qajar dynasty ended while its absent shah lived on in exile.

tamil:
குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும் மடிமடிந்து
மாண்ட உஞற்றி லவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Kudimadindhu kutram perugum madimadindhu
Maanda unjatri lavarkku.
meaning: When people fall into laziness and make no real effort, their family's good name falls apart and their faults keep growing.
elementary: When you stop doing your homework, it’s not just one problem. Soon you’re behind, you start making excuses, and you get into more trouble. Laziness is like a door that lets many other problems in, and the whole family feels it.
university: The couplet names two consequences: குடி மடிந்து, ‘the family perishing’, and குற்றம் பெருகும், ‘faults multiplying’. It gives one cause: மடி மடிந்து, ‘having fallen into sloth’. Here மடிந்து is used in the sense of ‘sinking’ or ‘being caught’, which Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both gloss as சோம்பலில் அகப்பட்டு / வீழ்வதால். The rare word உஞற்று (effort, exertion) together with மாண்ட (excellent, worthy) specifies what is missing: not activity of any kind but dignified, purposeful effort (Pope’s ‘noble objects’). Parimelazhagar notes that idleness is productive, of vice, which fits a line of Indian moral thought in which inactivity invites other faults. The same second-line phrase recurs in 607 (மாண்ட உஞற்றிலவர்), which ties the two couplets together. Both sources agree; the older text has the sandhi forms பெருகு மடிமடிந்து and மாண்ட வுஞற்றி.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You should thus perform your prescribed Vedic duties, since action is superior to inaction. By ceasing activity, even your bodily maintenance will not be possible.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna argues that action is better than inaction: even keeping the body alive requires work, so giving up activity leads to decline.
hinduism.tie_back: If idleness cannot sustain even one body, it certainly cannot sustain a family, which is the Kural’s குடி மடிந்து.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.”
christianity.explanation: Paul observes that idleness does not stay alone: it soon turns into gossip, meddling and improper speech.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies’ is a precise illustration of குற்றம் பெருகும், faults multiplying from sloth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the hypocrites [think to] deceive Allah, but He is deceiving them. And when they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing [themselves to] the people and not remembering Allah except a little,”
islam.explanation: The Quran links laziness in worship with a cluster of further faults: hypocrisy, showing off, and neglect of the remembrance of God.
islam.tie_back: Laziness appearing alongside several other vices mirrors the Kural’s claim that faults multiply around sloth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eliezer says: Even if she brought him a hundred maidservants, he can compel her to make thread from wool, since idleness leads to licentiousness. … Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: … since idleness leads to idiocy.”
judaism.explanation: In a ruling about household duties, two sages state a general principle: idleness breeds immorality and dulls the mind, so no one in a household should be entirely without work.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Idleness leads to’ further faults is the rabbinic form of the Kural’s குற்றம் பெருகும், and it is also set in the context of the household.
judaism.source: Mishnah Ketubot 5:5 (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man who is fond of sleep and company, inactive and lazy, and manifesting anger —this is the cause of his downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Discourse on Downfall, the Buddha lists sleepiness, idleness and laziness, together with anger, as the third cause of a person’s ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: Laziness appearing next to other faults and leading to downfall parallels both halves of the Kural: faults multiply, and the house declines.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipāta 1.6, Parābhava Sutta (trans. Piyadassi Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “There are five causes which render wholesome discipline impossible: egoism, delusion, carelessness, illness, and idleness.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana counts carelessness and idleness among the causes that make right discipline impossible, so faults multiply where they take hold.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that for those sunk in sloth faults keep multiplying; the Jain text names idleness as one of the roots that block all wholesome discipline.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The lustful, the angry, the clever, the deceitful and the lazy waste their lives in slander, and never remember their Lord in meditation.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir places the lazy beside the lustful, the angry and the deceitful, as people whose lives drain away into faults.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that for those sunk in laziness who make no worthy effort, faults keep multiplying; Kabir likewise counts laziness among the vices that gather together and waste a life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Both gods and men are angry with a man who lives idle, for in nature he is like the stingless drones who waste the labour of the bees, eating without working”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod calls the idle man a drone who eats what others have worked for, and says he earns the anger of gods and men alike.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The drone’s idleness brings both waste and disgrace, which is the Kural’s double outcome of a ruined family and growing fault.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 302-306 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay ‘Of Idleness’, Montaigne compares an idle mind to fallow land that, left alone, grows a mass of wild and useless weeds, and says it produces fantastic ‘chimeras’ unless kept busy with a fixed purpose.
philosophy.explanation: Montaigne observes from his own retirement that an unoccupied mind does not rest but runs wild and breeds disorder.
philosophy.tie_back: Montaigne’s weed-choked field of the mind is a vivid picture of the Kural’s faults multiplying in the absence of worthy effort.
philosophy.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays I.8, ‘Of Idleness’ (trans. C. Cotton)

real_life_example.event_title: Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa withdraws into the arts as the Onin War begins
real_life_example.event: Ashikaga Yoshimasa became shogun in 1449 but proved an ineffective ruler, and the great lords increasingly ignored his orders. A succession dispute between his brother Yoshimi and his son Yoshihisa helped set off the Onin War of 1467-1477, which devastated Kyoto and left shogunal authority badly weakened. Yoshimasa devoted himself to the tea ceremony, painting and patronage of the arts, and in retirement built his villa at Higashiyama, later the temple Ginkakuji.
real_life_example.explanation: Yoshimasa's patronage shaped Japanese culture, but his neglect of government coincided with the collapse of his house's real power and the start of a century of civil war.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those who sink into sloth and make no worthy effort the family collapses and faults multiply, and under Yoshimasa the Ashikaga shogunate declined while disorder spread across Japan.

tamil:
நெடுநீர் மறவி மடிதுயில் நான்கும்
கெடுநீரார் காமக் கலன்.
transliteration:
Neduneer maravi madidhuyil naangum
Keduneeraar kaamak kalan.
meaning: Putting things off, forgetting, laziness and too much sleep are four things people headed for ruin love. They are like a pleasure boat that carries them to disaster.
elementary: Imagine four friends who always say: ‘Do it later’, ‘Oops, I forgot’, ‘I’m too tired’, and ‘Just five more minutes of sleep.’ They feel comfy, like a boat ride, but the boat is floating toward a waterfall. Good habits are how you steer the boat back.
university: This is the chapter’s best-known couplet and its most careful analysis. It lists four linked dispositions: நெடுநீர், literally ‘long-drawn nature’, i.e. procrastination (Varadarasanar: காலம் நீட்டித்தல்); மறவி, forgetfulness or heedlessness (compare ch. 54, பொச்சாவாமை); மடி, sloth; and துயில், excessive sleep. It calls them the காமக் கலன் of the கெடுநீரார், ‘those whose nature is to perish’. Parimelazhagar and most modern commentators take கலன் as a vessel or ship (மரக்கலம்; Pappaiah: சிறு படகு), giving Pope’s ‘pleasure-boat … to ruin’s shore’. Because கலன் can also mean ‘ornament’, some readers take the line as ‘the ornaments the doomed love to wear’, but the vessel reading is standard. The rhyme நெடுநீர் / கெடுநீரார் binds cause to result. Sivayogi Sivakumar’s gloss of நெடுநீர் as ‘long weeping’ is idiosyncratic and not followed by the classical commentators. The text is identical in both sources apart from sandhi (மடிதுயி னான்குங்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The six faults should be avoided by a person who wisheth to attain prosperity, viz., sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, indolence and procrastination.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura advises King Dhritarashtra that anyone who wants prosperity must give up six faults, which include sleep, indolence and procrastination.
hinduism.tie_back: Three of Vidura’s six (sleep, indolence, procrastination) are three of Valluvar’s four, and both are warnings addressed to rulers about ruin.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Udyoga Parva 33 (Vidura Nīti), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour? Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation.”
christianity.explanation: In Gethsemane, the disciples fall asleep at the critical hour, and Jesus warns that sleep and slackness leave them open to failure.
christianity.tie_back: Sleep at the decisive moment, one of the Kural’s four, is shown here as the beginning of the disciples’ collapse that night.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan puts three knots at the back of the head of any of you if he is asleep. On every knot he reads and exhales the following words, ‘The night is long, so stay asleep.’ … otherwise one gets up lazy and with a mischievous heart.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the pull of sleep as Satan whispering ‘the night is long’, which can only be broken by remembering God, washing and prayer.
islam.tie_back: ‘The night is long, so stay asleep’ is the voice of procrastination and sleep together, which is the attraction of the Kural’s pleasure boat.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas said: morning sleep, midday wine, children’s talk and sitting in the assemblies of the ignorant put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Dosa gives a list of four comfortable habits, starting with sleeping late, that together drive a person out of the world.
judaism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the sage gives a list of four pleasant indulgences that carry a person to ruin, and oversleeping comes first.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:10 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada describes the sluggish, gluttonous person who spends his time sleeping and rolling about like a fattened hog, and says such a fool is reborn again and again.
buddhism.explanation: The verse pictures laziness and oversleeping as keeping a person trapped in the cycle of repeated birth.
buddhism.tie_back: Sleep and sloth carrying the fool around the round of rebirth is the Buddhist form of the Kural’s boat bearing the doomed to ruin.

jainism.quote_or_event: “'If he does not get (victory over his will) early, he will get it afterwards;' such reasoning presupposes the eternity of human life. But such a man despairs when his life draws to its close, and the dissolution of his body approaches.”
jainism.explanation: The text attacks procrastination: putting off effort assumes life lasts for ever. The same lecture (4.6) urges, 'Though others sleep, be thou awake!'
jainism.tie_back: Two of the Kural's four vices on the 'pleasure boat' to ruin, procrastination and oversleeping, are exactly what Uttaradhyayana 4 condemns.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.9; cf. 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Wake up, O mind! Wake up! Why are you sleeping unaware?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur calls the heedless (gaafal) mind out of its sleep.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural names procrastination, forgetfulness, laziness and oversleeping as the pleasure boat of those bound for ruin; Guru Tegh Bahadur's cry against heedless sleep addresses two of the four, forgetfulness and sleep, directly.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 726, Raag Tilang, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey Book 10, Odysseus has sailed for nine days within sight of Ithaca with the bag of winds from Aeolus. He falls asleep from exhaustion, his crew open the bag, and the storm drives the ship all the way back.
greek_mythology.explanation: A single sleep at the wrong time, together with the crew’s careless curiosity, wrecks a homecoming that was almost complete.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Sleep literally steers the ship to disaster, a close picture of the Kural’s ‘vessel’ of the doomed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In On the Shortness of Life, Seneca warns that the greatest obstacle to living is expectancy, which hangs on tomorrow and loses today, and that people postpone life while it runs past them.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that habitual postponement wastes the only time we really have, the present.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca’s diagnosis of postponement explains the first and most dangerous passenger in the Kural’s boat, நெடுநீர்.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Brevitate Vitae 9 (trans. J. W. Basore)

real_life_example.event_title: The Swiss watch industry is overtaken by the quartz watch
real_life_example.event: Although quartz timekeeping had been developed in Switzerland, Swiss watchmakers were slow to adopt it, while Seiko of Japan launched the Quartz Astron, the first quartz wristwatch on the market, on 25 December 1969. Cheaper and more accurate quartz watches from Asia then took over the market, and by the late 1970s the two largest Swiss watch groups were close to insolvency. Employment in the Swiss watch industry fell from almost 90,000 at the end of the 1960s to about 30,000 by the mid-1980s, before the Swatch, launched in 1983, helped lead a recovery.
real_life_example.explanation: A world-leading industry that delayed acting on a technology it had helped create lost most of its jobs within about fifteen years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names delay and heedlessness among the pleasant vessels that carry people to ruin, and the Swiss watchmakers' slowness to act on quartz carried a proud industry close to collapse.

tamil:
படியுடையார் பற்றமைந்தக் கண்ணும் மடியுடையார்
மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Padiyudaiyaar patramaindhak kannum madiyudaiyaar
Maanpayan eydhal aridhu.
meaning: Even if lazy people get the riches of kings who ruled the whole earth, they will rarely get any real good out of it.
elementary: Suppose someone gives you the world’s biggest box of Lego but you never open it. You own it, but you never build anything. Having great things doesn’t help if you’re too lazy to use them.
university: படி here means ‘the earth’, so படியுடையார் are ‘those who possess the earth’, world-ruling kings. பற்று அமைதல் is ‘their possessions or support coming to one’. The classical reading (Parimelazhagar, Varadarasanar, Pappaiah) is: even if the whole wealth of such sovereigns comes to the lazy, they will rarely obtain மாண்பயன், its excellent fruit. Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar read படியுடையார் as ‘worthy or powerful persons’ and பற்று as their affection or patronage: even with the favour of the great, the idle will not rise. The two readings share the same moral: fortune and connection are worthless without exertion. The couplet anticipates 610, where the tireless king gains all that Vishnu’s stride covered, and together they frame the second half of the chapter. The text is identical in both sources apart from sandhi (கண்ணு மடியுடையார் / மாண்பய னெய்த லரிது).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Hence the king shall ever be active and discharge his duties; the root of wealth is activity, and of evil its reverse. In the absence of activity acquisitions present and to come will perish”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya concludes his chapter on royal duties by teaching that activity is the root of wealth and inactivity the root of evil: without effort, even what a king already has will perish.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Acquisitions present … will perish’ without activity is the Kural’s point that even a world-ruler’s wealth bears no fruit for the lazy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou wicked and slothful servant … Take therefore the talent from him, and give it unto him which hath ten talents.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, the servant who buries his master’s money out of sloth gains nothing from it and finally loses even what he was given.
christianity.tie_back: A fortune placed in slothful hands that yields no fruit is exactly the Kural’s மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that what a person gains in the end corresponds to his own striving, not to what he merely inherits or is given.
islam.tie_back: If a person gets only what he strives for, the idle heir gains nothing from a king’s wealth, which is what the Kural says.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb contrasts the lazy person, whose wishes produce nothing, with the diligent, who is richly satisfied.
judaism.tie_back: The sluggard who ‘desireth, and hath nothing’ is the Kural’s idle person for whom even great wealth yields no fruit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigālovāda Sutta, the Buddha lists six dangers of idleness: a man will not work because it is too cold, too hot, too late, too early, or because he is too hungry or too full, and so new wealth does not come to him and the wealth he has dwindles away.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha, advising a young householder, shows how the idler’s excuses stop both the gaining of new wealth and the keeping of old.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Acquired wealth dwindles’ in an idler’s hands is the same as the Kural’s claim that possessions bear no fruit for the lazy.
buddhism.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (trans. Nārada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though one believe in the Law, he will rarely practise it; for people are engrossed by pleasures; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: In the 'Leaf of the Tree' sermon, Mahavira lists the rare advantages a soul may gain (human birth, hearing and believing the Law) and warns that even these are wasted by those who will not act on them.
jainism.tie_back: As the lazy heir gets no good from a world-ruler's wealth, the Jain soul handed rare spiritual fortune gains nothing if it will not exert itself.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Before his death in 1539 Guru Nanak appointed his devoted disciple Lahina, renamed Angad, as his successor; Angad's loyal conduct had persuaded Nanak that he would be more suitable than either of the Guru's two sons.
sikhism.explanation: At the first Sikh succession, the Guruship passed not by inheritance but to the disciple whose service and obedience had proved him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who lack exertion get little good even from a world-ruler's inheritance; the first Sikh succession likewise shows the great prize going to proven devotion rather than to birth.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Sikhism: Guru Angad” (W. H. McLeod) (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus’ fable retold by Xenophon, Virtue tells the young Heracles at the crossroads that the gods give nothing good and fine to people without toil and effort, while Vice offers a road of ease.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles must choose between easy pleasure and hard-won goods; Virtue insists that nothing worthwhile comes without labour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: ‘Nothing good without toil’ is the positive side of the Kural’s warning that the idle get no great fruit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the state of mind may exist without producing any good result, as in a man who is asleep or in some other way quite inactive, but the activity cannot … so those who act win, and rightly win, the noble and good things in life.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes possessing a good from using it: a capacity that lies unused, as in a sleeper, produces nothing, and only those who act win the prize.
philosophy.tie_back: Possession without activity producing ‘no good result’ is exactly the Kural’s lazy man holding a king’s wealth but gaining no மாண்பயன்.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.8, 1098b-1099a (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Commodus inherits the Roman Empire from Marcus Aurelius
real_life_example.event: Commodus succeeded his father, Marcus Aurelius, in 180 at the height of the Roman Empire's power and wealth. He showed little interest in the work of government, leaving it to a series of favourites, and devoted himself to appearing in the arena as a gladiator and hunter of wild beasts. He was killed by conspirators from his own household on 31 December 192, and the empire soon fell into civil war.
real_life_example.explanation: Commodus received one of the greatest inheritances any ruler has known, yet his reign is remembered as the end of Rome's most stable era.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even if the idle inherit the wealth of world-ruling kings, they will rarely gain any real good from it, and Commodus came into the whole Roman world and gained nothing worthy from it.

tamil:
இடிபுரிந்து எள்ளுஞ்சொல் கேட்பர் மடிபுரிந்து
மாண்ட உஞற்றி லவர்.
transliteration:
Idipurindhu ellunjol ketpar madipurindhu
Maanda unjatri lavar.
meaning: People who give in to laziness and make no real effort will end up hearing harsh scolding and mocking words.
elementary: When you promise to help clean up and then just lie on the couch, first your friends say, ‘Come on, help!’ If you still don’t, they start to laugh at you or stop counting on you. Laziness turns friends’ nudges into teasing.
university: இடிபுரிந்து எள்ளும் சொல் combines two kinds of speech: இடி, sharp rebuke (the verb இடித்தல் is used elsewhere in the Kural for a true friend’s correction, e.g. ch. 45, 448), and எள்ளல், scornful mockery. Pappaiah and Parimelazhagar read them as a sequence: friends first rebuke the idle man, and when that fails, contempt follows. மடிபுரிந்து, ‘having embraced sloth by choice’, stresses that the laziness is willed, and the second line repeats the மாண்ட உஞற்றிலவர் of 604, so this couplet adds a social consequence (loss of respect) to the material one described there. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads இடிபுரிந்து as ‘slipping and falling’, a minority interpretation. Both sources agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form இடிபுரிந் தெள்ளுஞ்சொற் கேட்பர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Udyoga Parva, the Kshatriya mother Vidulā finds her son Sañjaya lying dejected and inactive after a defeat, and scolds him at length, calling him a coward and urging him to rise, fight and restore his house.
hinduism.explanation: Vidulā’s rebuke of her son is a classic Indian example of a close relative using harsh words to shake someone out of inertia.
hinduism.tie_back: The idle son hearing sharp rebukes from someone close to him is exactly the இடி (rebuke) of the Kural, delivered before scorn from outsiders follows.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Udyoga Parva 133-136 (Vidulā-putra-anuśāsana), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed. Yet count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.”
christianity.explanation: Speaking of members who ‘walk disorderly, working not at all’, Paul tells the church to shame the idle and admonish them as brothers.
christianity.tie_back: Brotherly admonition followed by public shame is the two-stage sequence the commentators find in இடிபுரிந்து எள்ளுஞ்சொல்.

islam.quote_or_event: “They were satisfied to be with those who stay behind, and their hearts were sealed over, so they do not understand.”
islam.explanation: Surat at-Tawbah reproaches the able-bodied who chose to stay at home instead of going out on the Tabuk expedition.
islam.tie_back: The Quran’s reproach of those who chose ease matches the Kural’s ‘words of rebuke’ directed at those who embrace sloth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man.”
judaism.explanation: The father-teacher of Proverbs mocks the sluggard’s ‘little more sleep’ and warns him of the poverty that will overtake him.
judaism.tie_back: The mocking ‘How long wilt thou sleep?’ is itself an example of the rebuke and scorn the Kural says the idle must hear.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Arise! Do not be heedless! Lead a righteous life. The righteous live happily both in this world and the next.”
buddhism.explanation: The verse is a direct command to wake up and stop being heedless, spoken as a teacher’s correction.
buddhism.tie_back: It reads like the ‘rebuke’ (இடி) half of the Kural: a sharp call aimed at someone who has let himself slacken.

jainism.quote_or_event: “'As are bad pupils, so are bad bullocks; I shall leave these lazy donkeys, and shall practise severe austerities.'”
jainism.explanation: The sage Garga compares pupils who 'break down through want of zeal' to stubborn bullocks, then dismisses them in disgust as lazy donkeys.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that the slothful will hear harsh rebuke and scorn; Garga's scornful words for his lazy pupils are exactly that kind of rebuke.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 27.16; cf. 27.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself a guru or a spiritual teacher, while he goes around begging - don't ever touch his feet.”
sikhism.explanation: In the same salok in which he mocks the lazy man who pierces his ears to pass as a yogi, Guru Nanak tells his hearers to deny honour to the idle who live by begging.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the lazy who make no worthy effort will hear rebuke and scorn; Guru Nanak likewise withholds respect from those who will not work.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad Book 6, Hector finds Paris lounging in his chamber polishing his armour while the Trojans die at the walls, and rebukes him bitterly. Paris admits the rebuke is just and arms himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: The prince who idles at home while others fight is shamed by his own brother, and the shame finally stirs him to act.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris hearing a brother’s just rebuke for his idleness is a dramatised version of this Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius opens Book 5 of the Meditations by scolding himself for wanting to stay in bed at dawn: plants, sparrows, ants, spiders and bees all do their work, so why should a human being refuse to do his?
philosophy.explanation: The emperor turns the rebuke on himself, using the example of busy creatures to shame his own reluctance to get up and work.
philosophy.tie_back: Marcus shows the Kural’s rebuke internalised: a person who would rather scold himself than hear others do it.

real_life_example.event_title: Lincoln rebukes General McClellan for his slowness and then removes him
real_life_example.place: Washington, D.C., and Maryland, United States
real_life_example.event: After the Battle of Antietam on 17 September 1862, General George McClellan did not pursue the retreating Confederate army for weeks despite President Lincoln's urging. When McClellan reported in October that his cavalry horses were sore-tongued and fatigued, Lincoln telegraphed back asking what the horses had done since Antietam that could have tired them. On 5 November 1862 Lincoln ordered him relieved of command and replaced by General Ambrose Burnside.
real_life_example.explanation: Repeated urging gave way to open sarcasm and finally to dismissal, and McClellan never received another military command.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who give themselves to idleness will hear sharp rebukes and then scornful words, and McClellan's inaction drew first Lincoln's prodding, then his cutting telegram, and then removal.

tamil:
மடிமை குடிமைக்கண் தங்கின்தன் ஒன்னார்க்கு
அடிமை புகுத்தி விடும்.
transliteration:
Madimai kudimaikkan thangindhan onnaarkku
Adimai pugutthi vidum.
meaning: If laziness settles into someone from a respected family, it will end up making them a slave to their own enemies.
elementary: A castle with strong walls is safe only while its guards stay awake. If the guards get lazy and fall asleep, the enemy walks right in. Being from a great family won’t protect you if laziness moves in.
university: The couplet depends on a rhyme chain: மடிமை (sloth), குடிமை (nobility of birth), அடிமை (slavery). The sound itself follows the slide from high birth through sloth into bondage. தங்கின், ‘if it takes up residence’, presents sloth as a lodger that gradually takes over the house. ஒன்னார், ‘those who are not one with you’, i.e. enemies, and புகுத்திவிடும், ‘will thrust one into’, give the outcome. Pope’s rendering (‘Bondsmen to them that hate them shall they be’) and the Drew-Lazarus gloss both take the subject as a king of high birth, which fits the placement of the chapter in the அரசியல் (polity) section. Parimelazhagar notes that the sloth of a ruler becomes his enemies’ opportunity. The older text shows heavy sandhi (குடிமைக்கட் டங்கிற்றன் னொன்னார்க் / கடிமை) without any change in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If a king is energetic, his subjects will be equally energetic. If he is reckless, they will not only be reckless likewise, but also eat into his works. Besides, a reckless king will easily fall into the hands of his enemies. Hence the king shall ever be wakeful.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya warns that a heedless king corrupts his subjects and ‘easily falls into the hands of his enemies’, so he must always stay alert.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Fall into the hands of his enemies’ is almost word for word the Kural’s ஒன்னார்க்கு அடிமை புகுத்திவிடும்.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But know this, that if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken up.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that a householder who fails to keep watch lets the thief break in, using it as a picture of spiritual vigilance.
christianity.tie_back: An unwatchful master whose house is broken into is a close image of the noble whose sloth hands him to his enemies.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and will replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all.”
islam.explanation: Following the rebuke of those who ‘adhere heavily to the earth’ (9:38), God warns that a people who will not stir will be replaced by others.
islam.tie_back: A people displaced because they clung to ease parallels the noble house handed over to its enemies because of sloth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The hand of the diligent shall bear rule; But the slothful shall be under tribute.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb states a political law: the diligent end up ruling, while the lazy end up paying tribute or doing forced labour for others.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Under tribute’ (lamas, forced labour) is exactly the Kural’s அடிமை: sloth turns the free into subjects.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada opens its chapter on heedfulness by teaching that heedfulness is the path to the Deathless and heedlessness the path to death: the heedful do not die, while the heedless are as if already dead.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats slack heedlessness as a condition that hands a person over to death, the ultimate enemy.
buddhism.tie_back: Heedlessness surrendering a person to death is the spiritual form of sloth surrendering the noble to his foes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Self is the one invincible foe, (together with the four) cardinal passions, (viz. anger, pride, deceit, and greed, they are five) and the (five) senses (make ten). These (foes), O great sage, I have regularly vanquished.”
jainism.explanation: Gautama tells Kesi that the real enemies are the unconquered self, the passions and the senses, and only someone who conquers them is free; the rest are held in their bondage.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar warns that sloth turns the noble-born into slaves of their enemies; in Jainism, the person who does not exert himself stays bound to his inner enemies, the passions.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Within this body dwell the five thieves: sexual desire, anger, greed, emotional attachment and egotism. They plunder the Nectar, but the self-willed manmukh does not realize it; no one hears his complaint.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das warns that the five thieves living inside a person rob him while he is unaware, and that no one answers his cry.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says laziness in one of noble birth makes him a slave to his enemies; Guru Amar Das likewise shows the unwatchful person plundered by enemies, though they are inner vices, not outside foes.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 600, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the very end of Herodotus’ Histories, Cyrus rejects a proposal that the Persians move to richer, softer lands, warning that soft lands breed soft men. The Persians agree and choose to rule a harsh land rather than sow fertile plains as slaves to others.
greek_mythology.explanation: The founding king of Persia teaches that ease and comfort turn rulers into subjects.
greek_mythology.tie_back: ‘Slaves to others’ as the fruit of softness is the Kural’s அடிமை reached through மடிமை.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In chapter 14 of The Prince, Machiavelli observes that princes who have thought more of ease than of arms have lost their states, and that a prince who neglects the art of war is despised and easily undone.
philosophy.explanation: Machiavelli argues that a ruler’s taste for comfort is the most common way states are lost to rivals.
philosophy.tie_back: Machiavelli’s ease-loving prince who loses his state is Valluvar’s noble who, through sloth, becomes his enemies’ subject.
philosophy.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 14 (trans. W. K. Marriott)

real_life_example.event_title: King Charles IV of Spain gives up his crown to Napoleon at Bayonne
real_life_example.place: Madrid and Aranjuez, Spain, and Bayonne, France
real_life_example.event: Charles IV, king of Spain from 1788, lacked leadership qualities and from 1792 left the government largely to the royal favourite Manuel de Godoy, while he preferred hunting to governing. In March 1808 a riot at Aranjuez forced him to abdicate in favour of his son Ferdinand. Napoleon then summoned the royal family to Bayonne, where both father and son gave up the crown, which Napoleon gave to his brother Joseph, and Charles spent his remaining years in exile under French supervision.
real_life_example.explanation: The heir to one of Europe's oldest crowns ended as a pensioner of the foreign ruler whose armies had occupied his country.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that if sloth settles in a person of noble birth it will make him a subject of his enemies, and Charles IV's neglect of rule ended with his kingdom in Napoleon's hands and himself in Napoleon's custody.

tamil:
குடியாண்மை யுள்வந்த குற்றம் ஒருவன்
மடியாண்மை மாற்றக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kudiyaanmai yulvandha kutram oruvan
Madiyaanmai maatrak kedum.
meaning: When a person drives out the laziness that controls them, the faults that have crept into their family and their own life will go away.
elementary: If your room has become a mess because you kept putting things off, you don’t need magic. Start tidying today and the mess goes away. Kick out laziness and good things come back.
university: After the warnings of 601-608, the ninth couplet offers a remedy, built on the parallel compounds குடியாண்மை and மடியாண்மை. The first is read either as குடி + ஆண்மை, ‘family and manly worth’ (Varadarasanar: குடியிலும் ஆண்மையிலும்; Kalaignar: குடிப்பெருமைக்கும் ஆண்மைக்கும்), or as ‘the governing of one’s family’. The second, மடி + ஆண்மை, is ironic: sloth exercising ‘lordship’ (ஆண்மை) over a man, so that he is its subject (Pappaiah: சோம்பலுக்கு அடிமையாவது). மாற்ற, ‘when one changes, reverses’, puts the cure in the person’s own hands. Echoing 608, where sloth makes a man a slave, here overthrowing sloth’s rule restores him. The older text reads குற்ற மொருவன் with no change of sense.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna places the responsibility for rising or falling on the individual: the same self that drags one down can lift one up.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘when one changes the rule of sloth’ is the Gita’s ‘elevate yourself by yourself’ applied to laziness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.”
christianity.explanation: Paul calls on sleepers to wake and rise, promising that light will be restored to them.
christianity.tie_back: Waking from sleep so that light returns reverses the image of 601, and fits the Kural’s promise that faults vanish when sloth is overthrown.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that a community’s fortune changes only when its members first change themselves inwardly.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s மாற்ற, changing one’s slothful habit so that the family’s faults disappear, is the same principle of self-change coming before restored fortune.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.”
judaism.explanation: The sluggard is told to learn from the ant, which works diligently without anyone forcing it, and to change his ways.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Consider her ways, and be wise’ is an invitation to the change of habit the Kural says will remove the family’s faults.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who having been heedless is heedless no more, illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that someone who was once careless but has become diligent shines again, like the moon coming out from behind clouds.
buddhism.tie_back: Former heedlessness cleared away and the light returning is almost exactly the Kural’s faults vanishing when sloth is overthrown.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By conquering his will, (a monk) reaches liberation, as a well-broken horse which is clad in harness (goes to battle). Be watchful in your young years; for thereby a monk quickly obtains liberation.”
jainism.explanation: The text holds that once the will is mastered and vigilance takes the place of negligence, faults fall away and freedom follows.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural says faults vanish when a man throws off sloth's rule over him, the Jain sutra says conquering one's own will, like breaking in a horse, removes what holds a person back.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My mind is lazy and sleepy. The Lord, Har, Har, has led me to meet the Holy Guru; meeting the Holy, the shutters have been opened wide.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das confesses a lazy, drowsy mind and says that meeting the Guru threw open its closed doors.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the faults of family and manhood vanish once a person throws off the rule of laziness; Guru Ram Das describes the same turn from sloth to openness, though he credits the Guru's grace rather than one's own effort.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 697, Raag Jaithsree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of Hercules and the Waggoner, a carter whose wagon is stuck in the mud prays to Hercules without lifting a finger. The god tells him to put his shoulder to the wheel and whip his horses, since the gods help those who help themselves.
greek_mythology.explanation: Divine help comes only after the idle man changes his behaviour and starts working himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The stuck wagon moves only when the carter stops being passive, just as the Kural says a family’s faults end when a person changes his sloth.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, Hercules and the Waggoner (trans. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Nicomachean Ethics Book II, Aristotle argues that moral virtues come about by habituation: we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts, so our characters are formed by the activities we repeat.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, character is not fixed; changing one’s habitual activity changes who one is.
philosophy.tie_back: Because character follows habit, Valluvar’s cure for a family’s faults is to change sloth’s ‘rule’, the habit that governs a person.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1, 1103a-b (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The idle young Charles Darwin becomes a dedicated naturalist
real_life_example.place: Shrewsbury, Edinburgh and Cambridge, England and Scotland, and the voyage of HMS Beagle
real_life_example.event: Darwin's father, a physician, regarded his teenage son as a wastrel interested mainly in shooting, and Darwin later recorded in his autobiography that his father once told him he cared for nothing but shooting, dogs and rat-catching and would be a disgrace to himself and his family. He abandoned medical studies at Edinburgh and was sent to Cambridge to prepare for the church, where he became a keen collector of beetles and a student of the botanist John Henslow. Through Henslow he joined HMS Beagle in 1831, and the five-year voyage turned him into a tireless naturalist whose work culminated in On the Origin of Species in 1859.
real_life_example.explanation: The young man his father feared would disgrace the family became its most celebrated member once he committed himself to sustained work.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when a person throws off the rule of sloth, the faults that had attached to his family and his own worth disappear, and Darwin's transformation turned a feared family disgrace into lasting honour.

tamil:
மடியிலா மன்னவன் எய்தும் அடியளந்தான்
தாஅய தெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு.
transliteration:
Madiyilaa mannavan eydhum adiyalandhaan
Thaaaya thellaam orungu.
meaning: A king who is never lazy will win, all at once, the whole world that the god who measured the worlds with his steps walked across.
elementary: There is an old story about a god who grew so tall that he crossed the whole world in a few giant steps. This kural says a leader who is never lazy can, by working hard, win everything those giant steps covered. Hard work lets small people take giant steps too.
university: The chapter closes with a Puranic allusion. அடியளந்தான், ‘he who measured with his foot’, is Vishnu as Vāmana-Trivikrama, the dwarf who asked King Mahābali for three paces of land and then grew to cover earth and heaven. தாஅயது (with அளபெடை, vowel lengthening, of தாயது, ‘what he strode across’) is therefore the whole cosmos. ஒருங்கு, ‘together, at once’, suggests that the energetic king gains all of it at once rather than piece by piece. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar read it this way; Kalaignar rationalises the image into a king bringing all he traverses under his footprint. The couplet balances 606: there the idle inherit world-rulers’ wealth and gain nothing, here the tireless king gains the world. The older text has the sandhi-joined form அடியளந்தான் றாஅய தெல்லா மொருங்கு, which differs from the ytamizh reading only in how the words are split.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the dwarf Vāmana asks King Bali for three steps of land, then expands into Trivikrama, covering the earth with one stride and the heavens with the second, and leaves no room for the third.
hinduism.explanation: This is the episode the Kural alludes to: the whole of creation measured out in Vishnu’s strides, a feat already celebrated in the Rig Veda (1.154).
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural promises the tireless king everything Trivikrama’s stride covered, so the myth itself is the measure of his reward.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he said unto him, Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the pounds, the servant who worked hard with what he was given is rewarded with rule over cities.
christianity.tie_back: Diligence rewarded with wide dominion matches the Kural’s tireless king gaining the whole world.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed We established him upon the earth, and We gave him to everything a way.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes Dhul-Qarnayn, a righteous ruler who travels to the far west and far east and is given the means to everything.
islam.tie_back: A tireless ruler whose reach extends across the earth is the Quranic parallel to the Kural’s unsluggish king who gains all the land Vishnu strode.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb promises that diligence raises a person to the highest company and honour.
judaism.tie_back: Diligence lifting a person to royal honour is the Kural’s point, that freedom from sloth brings the greatest possible gain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that the glory of one who is energetic, mindful, pure in conduct, discerning, self-controlled, righteous and heedful steadily increases.
buddhism.explanation: The verse promises ever-growing renown to the energetic and heedful person.
buddhism.tie_back: Ever-increasing glory for the energetic is the Buddhist counterpart of the Kural’s tireless king gaining everything.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain narrative tradition has its own version of the three strides. When the minister Namuci, ruling for a few days, threatened to kill the Jain monks, the ascetic Viṣṇukumāra, brother of King Mahāpadma, came in the form of a dwarf, asked for three paces of ground, and by his ascetic powers grew vast enough to cover the world and defeat Namuci.
jainism.explanation: In Jain tellings the three strides belong not to a god but to a monk whose powers came from tireless austerity and who used them to protect the community.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's unsluggish king who gains all that the strider measured has a Jain parallel in the three strides themselves, credited to ascetic striving rather than to Vishnu.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra VI.8 (Mahāpadmacakricaritra), vv. 148-203 (tr. Helen M. Johnson, vol. IV, pp. 99-102); also Vividhatīrthakalpa (Hastināpura-kalpa)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji, Guru Nanak tells the yogis that the real conquest is of one's own mind, and that this is the same as conquering the world.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural promises the tireless king, all at once, the whole world that Vishnu strode across; Guru Nanak also speaks of winning the whole world, but by mastering the mind rather than by conquest.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib (Pauri 28), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, after completing his twelve labours and a lifetime of ceaseless toil, is taken up to Olympus at his death and made a god, receiving Hebe as his bride.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, the hero who never rested from labour is the one mortal rewarded with a place among the immortals.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tireless labour earning the heavens parallels the Kural’s tireless king gaining all that a god’s stride covered.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In The Way to Wealth, Franklin’s Father Abraham quotes Poor Richard that diligence is the mother of good luck and that God gives all things to industry, urging his hearers to plough deep while sluggards sleep.
philosophy.explanation: Franklin presents diligence as the source of fortune itself: what looks like luck is the reward of steady work.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘God gives all things to industry’ is almost a secular summary of the Kural’s promise to the king without sloth.
philosophy.source: Benjamin Franklin, The Way to Wealth (1758)

real_life_example.event_title: Alexander the Great's campaigns from Macedonia to India
real_life_example.place: From Macedonia across Asia Minor, Egypt and Persia to the Indus valley
real_life_example.event: Alexander, king of Macedon from 336 BCE, crossed into Asia in 334 BCE and defeated the Persians at the Granicus, at Issus in 333 BCE and decisively at Gaugamela in 331 BCE. Marching almost continuously, he took Egypt and the Persian capitals and reached the Indus valley, where he defeated King Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BCE. When his exhausted troops refused to go further east he turned back, and he died at Babylon in 323 BCE, ruler of an empire stretching from Greece to northwestern India.
real_life_example.explanation: In about eleven years of almost ceaseless campaigning, one king brought a greater share of the known world under his rule than anyone before him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural promises that a king free of sloth will gain all at once the whole world that Vishnu's strides covered, and Alexander's unresting campaigns are history's most famous example of a ruler winning a vast realm in a single lifetime.

tamil:
அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை வேண்டும்
பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்.
transliteration:
Arumai udaiththendru asaavaamai vendum
Perumai muyarchi tharum.
meaning: Never give up by telling yourself a task is too hard. Effort itself gives you the strength and greatness to get it done.
elementary: Imagine a big hill you have to climb to get home. If you stand at the bottom saying 'it’s too steep,' you never move. But every step you take makes your legs a little stronger, until the hill doesn’t look so big any more. Trying is what makes you able.
university: The chapter title ஆள்வினை (literally ‘man-work’, human exertion) is glossed by the Thirukkural-Thamizh edition as இடைவிடாத முயற்சி, ‘unceasing effort’, and this opening couplet names the first enemy of effort: அசாவு, the despondency that sets in when a task is judged அருமை (difficult). Parimelazhagar takes பெருமை not as fame but as the ‘greatness’ or capacity needed to accomplish the deed, so the claim is causal: capacity is produced by striving rather than being a precondition for it; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah (ytamizh.com) both read it this way, while Kalaignar renders பெருமை as ‘great strength’. Placed immediately after ஊக்கமுடைமை (ch. 60, energy) and மடியின்மை (ch. 61, absence of sloth), the chapter moves from inner zeal to its outward expression in sustained work, culminating in the famous claim of kural 620 that effort can turn back fate itself. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the latter printing the older sandhi-joined form (அருமை யுடைத்தென் றசாவாமை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You should thus perform your prescribed Vedic duties, since action is superior to inaction. By ceasing activity, even your bodily maintenance will not be possible.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells the hesitant Arjuna that withdrawing from action is never the higher path; even keeping the body alive requires work.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita refuses to let the difficulty of a task become an excuse for not acting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges the Galatians not to grow tired of doing good, promising a harvest to those who do not give up.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Faint not’ is almost a translation of the Kural’s அசாவாமை, not sinking into weariness before the work is done.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, with hardship [will be] ease.”
islam.explanation: The short Meccan sura consoles the Prophet in difficulty by twice promising that ease comes together with hardship, then tells him to keep labouring (94:7).
islam.tie_back: Both texts tell the believer that a task’s hardness is not a reason to despair of it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon teaches that the vastness of a task does not release a person from the obligation to work at it.
judaism.tie_back: Tarfon and Valluvar both deny that ‘it is too great for me’ is a valid reason to hold back.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:16 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “You yourselves must strive; the Buddhas only point the way.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers that no teacher can do the work of liberation for them; the effort must be their own.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the verse locates the power to accomplish in one’s own striving, not in circumstances.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One cannot quickly arrive at discernment; therefore one should exert one's self, abstain from pleasures, understand the world, be impartial like a sage, and guard one's self: (thus) never be careless.”
jainism.explanation: The sutra admits the goal is hard and slow to reach, but takes that as a reason to exert oneself, not to give up.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural says never to lose heart by calling a task too hard, because effort brings the strength to finish it, the Jain text answers difficulty with steady self-exertion.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So tell me - how can the fort of doubt and the moat of Maya be overcome? … Worshipping the Perfect Guru, this awesome force is subdued.”
sikhism.explanation: In a pauri of Gujri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan describes the five passions as an army no hero can withstand, asks how such a fortress could ever be breached, and answers that it can be overcome.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says never lose heart because a task looks too hard; Guru Arjan names the hardest of tasks and refuses to call it impossible.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, pauri 15), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first; but when a man has reached the top, then is she easy to reach, though before that she was hard.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his idle brother Perses that excellence lies up a steep road that becomes easy only once one has climbed it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s ‘hard at first, easy at the top’ is the Kural’s point that effort creates the capacity the task seemed to demand.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 286-292 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca remarks to Lucilius that it is not because things are difficult that we do not dare; it is because we do not dare that they are difficult.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic argues that the difficulty we attribute to a task is largely produced by our own timidity toward it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly Valluvar’s warning against calling a thing ‘too hard’ and sinking into despondency.

real_life_example.event_title: Dashrath Manjhi cuts a road through a hill by hand
real_life_example.event: Dashrath Manjhi, a poor labourer from the village of Gehlaur near Gaya, lived on one side of a rocky hill that forced villagers into a long detour to reach the nearest town and its services. After the death of his wife, he set out to cut a passage through the hill himself, working for about twenty-two years with a hammer and chisel. The finished cut, commonly described as about 360 feet long and 30 feet wide, greatly shortened the journey, and the Bihar government later honoured him as the Mountain Man.
real_life_example.explanation: A task that looked impossible for one man with hand tools was completed because he kept working at it year after year, alongside his ordinary labour.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says never to lose heart by calling a task too hard, because effort itself gives the strength to accomplish it, and Manjhi's road was cut by a man who simply refused to treat the hill as too big.

tamil:
வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல் வினைக்குறை
தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு.
transliteration:
Vinaikkan vinaikedal ombal vinaikkurai
Theerndhaarin theerndhandru ulagu.
meaning: Once you start a task, be careful not to let your effort drop. The world leaves behind people who leave their work half-done.
elementary: If you start building a sandcastle and walk away halfway, the waves wash it away and nobody even knows what you were making. Friends want to team up with the kid who finishes things. Keep going until it’s done.
university: The couplet plays on வினை three times: in the course of வினை (the undertaking), guard against கெடல் (the failing) of வினை (the exertion), because the world has already தீர்ந்தது (let go of) those who have let go of வினைக்குறை, the unfinished remainder of the work. Parimelazhagar reads the first வினை as the undertaking and the second as the effort (முயற்சி), which Mu. Varadarasanar follows; Solomon Pappaiah paraphrases the rhetorical jingle of the second line (தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று) as ‘the world lets go of those who let go’. Kalaignar glosses it with the proverb of the man who ‘leapt half-way across the well’, a vivid way of saying that half an effort is no effort at all. The text agrees in both editions consulted, thirukkural-thamizh.org merely printing the sandhi forms வினைகெட லோம்பல் and தீர்ந்தாரிற் றீர்ந்தன் றுலகு.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka sorts people into three kinds: the lowest never begin a task for fear of obstacles, the middling begin but stop when obstacles strike, and the best, though struck again and again by obstacles, never abandon what they have begun.
hinduism.explanation: The famous Sanskrit verse (prārabhyate na khalu vighnabhayena nīcaiḥ) makes persistence through obstruction the mark of the noblest person.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s warning against letting effort fail midway is precisely Bhartrhari’s distinction between the middling and the best.
hinduism.source: Bhartrhari, Nitishataka (verse beginning prārabhyate na khalu)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that a half-built tower makes its builder a public laughing-stock, so one must be ready to see a commitment through.
christianity.tie_back: The mocking onlookers are the Kural’s ‘world’ that turns away from those who leave work unfinished.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do good deeds properly, sincerely and moderately and know that your deeds will not make you enter Paradise, and that the most beloved deed to Allah is the most regular and constant even if it were little.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that steady, continuous action is dearer to God than bursts of effort that are then abandoned.
islam.tie_back: Both texts prize constancy of effort over enthusiastic beginnings that lapse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof; And the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth values the completion of a matter above its start, and patient endurance above proud self-assurance.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise measures a person by whether the work is carried to its end.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha recalls that he resolved: let skin, sinews and bones remain and flesh and blood dry up, but there would be no relaxing of his persistence until he had attained what can be reached by human firmness, human persistence and human striving.
buddhism.explanation: In the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha names ‘not shrinking back in exertion’ as one of the two qualities that brought him to awakening.
buddhism.tie_back: The Pali purisa-viriya, ‘human (literally manly) effort’, is an exact counterpart of ஆள்வினை, and the refusal to relax midway is this kural’s whole point.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You have crossed the great ocean; why do you halt so near the shore? make haste to get on the other side; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama not to slacken when the goal is nearly won: stopping near the shore wastes the whole crossing.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's warning not to let effort slacken halfway, since the world abandons those who leave work unfinished, is matched by Mahavira's rebuke for halting near the shore.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Let self-control be the furnace, and patience the goldsmith.”
sikhism.explanation: In the closing pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak pictures the shaping of a true life as a goldsmith's long work at the furnace, carried out with patience and steady control.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns against letting effort slacken halfway through a task; Japji Sahib makes patience the craftsman who keeps working until the piece is finished.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib (pauri 38), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When some of Odysseus’ men eat the lotus and lose all wish to go home, he drags them weeping back to the ships and ties them under the benches so the voyage can go on.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Odyssey 9 the lotus-eaters’ gift is forgetfulness of the goal; Odysseus refuses to let the homeward labour stop halfway.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The lotus is the Kural’s வினைகெடல, the slackening of effort in mid-course, and Odysseus guards against it by force.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In every affair consider what precedes and follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit; but not having thought of the consequences, when some of them appear you will shamefully desist.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus warns that people who start eagerly without weighing the effort required give up in disgrace when difficulties appear, and compares them to children who play at one role after another but are nothing with their whole soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts call it shameful to drop a task halfway, though Epictetus places the remedy in weighing the work before starting rather than in keeping one's effort up once started.

real_life_example.event_title: Diderot carries the Encyclopedie through to completion after it is banned
real_life_example.event: Denis Diderot was co-editor of the Encyclopedie, whose first volume appeared in 1751. In 1758 his co-editor Jean le Rond d'Alembert withdrew, and in 1759 the royal privilege was revoked, the volumes already published were condemned, and the pope placed the work on the Index. Diderot nevertheless kept working, the last ten volumes of text were issued together in 1765, and the final volumes of plates appeared in 1772.
real_life_example.explanation: Abandoned by his partner and banned by the authorities at the halfway point, Diderot spent more than a decade finishing one of the defining works of the Enlightenment.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns against letting effort slacken in the middle of a task, and Diderot, faced with every reason to stop halfway, carried the Encyclopedie through to its last volume.

tamil:
தாளாண்மை என்னும் தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்றே
வேளாண்மை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Thaalaanmai ennum thagaimaikkan thangitre
Velaanmai ennum serukku.
meaning: Being proud that you can help others depends on one thing only: the good habit of working hard.
elementary: You can only share cookies with your friends if somebody baked them first. People who work hard are the ones who end up with something to give, and giving feels great. So working is what makes kindness possible.
university: தாளாண்மை, literally ‘the rule of the foot’, is Valluvar’s image for vigorous exertion, and வேளாண்மை here means beneficence or generosity to others (Parimelazhagar: உபகாரம்), not ‘agriculture’, its commonest modern sense. செருக்கு, usually ‘arrogance’, is used positively for the lofty eminence or noble pride of a benefactor, and the emphatic particle ஏ in தங்கிற்றே (‘it abides only there’) makes effort the exclusive seat of that eminence. The logic, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both preserve, links this chapter to the Arathuppal chapters on ஒப்புரவறிதல் and ஈகை: generosity is a virtue, but it presupposes the means that only labour produces. Kalaignar reads the couplet as describing people of ‘unceasing effort’ in whom the pride of helping others takes root. Both editions consulted agree on the text, apart from sandhi (தகைமைக்கட் டங்கிற்றே).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Riches and other objects of enjoyment do not follow the stingy, nor the impotent, nor the idler.”
hinduism.explanation: In Bhishma’s discourse on destiny and exertion, Brahma declares that prosperity eludes both the miser and the idle.
hinduism.tie_back: Linking the idler with the miser echoes the Kural’s claim that the power to give depends on the habit of effort.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section VI (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells converts that honest labour has a purpose beyond self-support: it makes giving to the needy possible.
christianity.tie_back: Labour ‘that he may have to give’ is exactly the Kural’s claim that beneficence rests on effort.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, spend from the good things which you have earned”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asks believers to give in charity from their own honest earnings and from the produce of the earth.
islam.tie_back: Charity is spoken of as flowing from what one has earned, as the Kural roots beneficence in labour.

judaism.quote_or_event: The ‘woman of valour’ of Proverbs 31 rises before dawn, works wool and flax with willing hands, buys a field and plants a vineyard from her earnings, and also opens her hand to the poor and needy.
judaism.explanation: The acrostic poem portrays a household sustained by tireless industry that overflows into generosity.
judaism.tie_back: Her open hand to the poor is made possible by her busy hands, as the Kural says generosity lives in effort.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who acquires his wealth in harmless ways like to a bee that honey gathers, riches mount up for him like ant hill’s rapid growth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the householder Sigala to gather wealth industriously and then divide it, keeping portions for use, business and need, and so win friends by liberality.
buddhism.tie_back: Industrious gathering followed by generous sharing mirrors the Kural’s chain from effort to beneficence.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “doing service consists in giving one's assistance as well as one is able.”
jainism.explanation: Vaiyāvṛttya, active service to teachers, the sick, the aged and the community, is one of the internal austerities in Jainism; benefiting others is defined as giving one's own exertion.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural roots the ability to help others in hard work; Jain vaiyāvṛttya likewise defines service as giving active effort as far as one is able.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 30.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok in Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak links giving to honest labour: the person who earns his bread by his own work and shares part of it is the one who has found the right way.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural rests the power to help others on hard work alone; Guru Nanak likewise makes earned livelihood (kirat karni) the ground of sharing (vand chhakna).
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles’ labours, from killing the Nemean lion to clearing the Stymphalian birds, rid Greece of monsters and earned him cult as Alexikakos, ‘averter of evil’, a benefactor of humankind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tradition made Heracles’ glory inseparable from the gruelling toil through which he served others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His honour as benefactor rests on his labours, as the Kural says the pride of helping others dwells in effort.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says the liberal man will not neglect his own property, since he wishes by means of it to help others.
philosophy.explanation: In his account of liberality, Aristotle insists that true generosity requires caring for and maintaining one’s means.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers see generosity as dependent on the diligent management that produces the means to give.

real_life_example.event_title: Tan Kah Kee builds a business empire and founds Xiamen University
real_life_example.event: Tan Kah Kee, a Chinese-born businessman in Singapore with little formal education, built a large business on pineapple canning, rice milling and above all rubber, which by the 1920s employed thousands of people. He used his fortune to found or support many schools in Singapore and China, including Nanyang Chinese High School in 1918. In 1921 he founded Xiamen University, the first university in China established by an overseas Chinese, and he funded it until 1937, when the government took it over.
real_life_example.explanation: Tan Kah Kee's generosity on this scale was possible only because of the fortune his years of hard work had produced, and he spent much of it on education.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the proud distinction of helping others rests on hard work alone, and Tan Kah Kee's schools and university were built from the earnings of a lifetime of labour.

tamil:
தாளாண்மை இல்லாதான் வேளாண்மை பேடிகை
வாளாண்மை போலக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Thaalaanmai illaadhaan velaanmai pedikai
Vaalaanmai polak kedum.
meaning: A person who will not work but wants to give generously will fail, like a sword waved around by a coward who is afraid to fight.
elementary: Holding a toy sword doesn’t make you a knight; you need the courage to use it. In the same way, saying ‘I’ll help everyone!’ doesn’t help anyone unless you are willing to do the work that makes helping possible.
university: The couplet sharpens kural 613 by negation: வேளாண்மை (beneficence) without தாளாண்மை (effort) is like the வாளாண்மை (sword-mastery) of a பேடி. Parimelazhagar and the older commentators take பேடி as a person of indeterminate sex, conventionally assumed in the ancient world to lack a warrior’s daring; Solomon Pappaiah softens this to ‘one who trembles at the sight of an army’, and the image is best read today as ‘a sword in the hand of one who dare not use it’, since the underlying gender assumption reflects its period rather than Valluvar’s point. The logic is that good intentions without the means produced by labour are as useless as a weapon one cannot wield; Mu. Varadarasanar says such generosity ‘will not come to fulfilment’. Both editions consulted agree on the wording; the sandhi form தாளாண்மை யில்லாதான் is purely orthographic.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Prince Uttara boasts to the palace women that he would rout the Kuru army if only he had a charioteer, but when he sees their host he leaps from the chariot and runs; it is his ‘eunuch’ dance-teacher Brihannala, really Arjuna in disguise, who takes up the bow.
hinduism.explanation: The Virata Parva episode contrasts loud promises of valour with the nerve and skill actually needed to act.
hinduism.tie_back: Uttara’s brave words without the grit behind them are the Kural’s empty sword-flourish; the tale’s irony, that the disguised ‘eunuch’ is the true hero, also undercuts the stereotype in the Kural’s image.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Go-harana), Sections XXXVI-XL (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?”
christianity.explanation: James mocks benevolent words that provide nothing real to the needy.
christianity.tie_back: Good wishes without the means to help are the Kural’s generosity that ‘perishes’ for want of effort.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an asks believers why they say what they do not do, and declares it most hateful to God that people should say what they do not do.
islam.explanation: Surat as-Saff condemns a gap between professed intentions and actual deeds.
islam.tie_back: Both texts expose promises of good that are never backed by the work to fulfil them.

judaism.quote_or_event: Shimon ben Gamaliel teaches that it is not study but doing that is the essential thing, and that whoever multiplies words brings on sin.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah places deeds above words or learning that never issue in action.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise judges good intentions worthless unless effort turns them into real help.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada compares fine words that are not put into practice to a beautiful flower that has colour but no scent: they bear no fruit.
buddhism.explanation: Verses 51-52 contrast words that are merely spoken with words that are lived.
buddhism.tie_back: Kindly intent without effort is the Kural’s version of the scentless flower: attractive but fruitless.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A man believes himself a hero as long as he does not behold the foe … So a novice, who as yet has not suffered pains and is not yet used to a mendicant's life, believes himself a hero till he practises austerities.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga mocks those who think themselves heroes until real hardship comes; the weak then 'become disheartened like cowards in the battle' (I.3.1.7).
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's would-be benefactor who will not work is like a coward holding a sword; the Jain novice who boasts until real effort is needed is the same empty heroism.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.3.1.1 and I.3.1.3; cf. I.3.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The thief robs a house, and offers the stolen goods to his ancestors. In the world hereafter, this is recognized, and his ancestors are considered thieves as well.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak mocks charity given out of wealth one did not honestly earn: the gift is recognised for what it is and brings shame instead of merit.
