sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says generosity without one's own effort fails like a sword in timid hands; Guru Nanak says giving that does not come from one's own honest earning is worthless.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 472, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Paris strides out in gleaming armour to challenge the best of the Achaeans, but when Menelaus steps forward he shrinks back into the ranks, and Hector rebukes him as handsome to look at but lacking strength and courage.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Iliad 3 the splendid warrior-costume of Paris is exposed as show without substance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris is the Kural’s sword in an unwilling hand: the outward form of prowess with none of the effort behind it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that most people, instead of doing good acts, take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers, like patients who listen carefully to their doctors but do none of the things prescribed.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that virtue is formed by doing, and that talking about goodness does not make anyone good.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats a will to do good without the effort behind it as ineffective.

real_life_example.event_title: Robert Owen's cooperative community at New Harmony fails
real_life_example.event: In 1825 the British reformer Robert Owen bought the town of Harmony, Indiana, and invited people to join a cooperative community based on shared property and equality. The community attracted many intellectuals and many people with large families or few useful skills, and only a minority of its residents worked in productive trades such as farming, while plans for organising labour remained vague. By 1827 the experiment had failed, and Owen had lost most of his fortune.
real_life_example.explanation: Owen's generous vision of a community that would provide for all could not survive without enough organised, productive work to sustain it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says generosity without the support of hard work fails like a sword in the hand of one who cannot use it, and New Harmony's noble aims collapsed for lack of the labour needed to pay for them.

tamil:
இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான் தன்கேளிர்
துன்பம் துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண்.
transliteration:
Inbam vizhaiyaan vinaivizhaivaan thankelir
Thunbam thudaiththoondrum thoon.
meaning: A person who wants to work more than they want fun becomes like a pillar for their family. They wipe away the family's troubles and hold them up.
elementary: A house stands because of its pillars. They never get to go out and play; they just hold up the roof so everyone inside is safe. A person who chooses to work hard instead of just having fun becomes a pillar like that for their family.
university: The couplet contrasts two desires: இன்பம் விழையான் (one who does not crave his own pleasure) and வினை விழைவான் (one who craves the work). Such a man is a தூண் (pillar) that both துடைத்து (wipes away) and ஊன்றும் (props up) the sorrows of his கேளிர், his kin; Solomon Pappaiah widens கேளிர் to ‘relatives and friends’ and Kalaignar extends it to ‘the people of the country’, a modern civic reading. Parimelazhagar notes that the pillar image implies a household or lineage that would collapse without such a person. The couplet echoes the Arathuppal ideal of the householder (இல்வாழ்க்கை) as the support of all dependants, now reframed as a fruit of personal effort. Both editions agree on the wording, with sandhi-joined forms (வினைவிழைவான் றன்கேளிர்; துன்பந் துடைத்தூன்றுந் தூண்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna points to King Janaka and others who reached perfection through action, and urges Arjuna to work for lokasangraha, the holding-together and welfare of the world, rather than for himself.
hinduism.explanation: Bhagavad Gita 3.20 presents selfless work as the means by which the wise sustain society.
hinduism.tie_back: Work done for others’ sake, not one’s own pleasure, is the Kural’s pillar that holds up the kin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: The pastoral letter makes providing for one’s household a basic duty of faith.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts make supporting one’s kin a central fruit of a working life.

islam.quote_or_event: “The upper hand is better than the lower hand (i.e. he who gives in charity is better than him who takes it). One should start giving first to his dependents.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ranks the giver above the receiver and says generosity begins with those one supports.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s pillar is exactly this ‘upper hand’ that first sustains its own dependants.

judaism.quote_or_event: Joseph, having risen through years of labour in Egypt, tells his brothers he will sustain them in the famine, and then provides bread for his father, his brothers and all their households.
judaism.explanation: Genesis 45 and 47 show Joseph using his position to become the provider for his whole family.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph is the Kural’s pillar who wipes away his kin’s distress and holds them up.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “But he who does not regard cold or heat any more than a blade of grass and who does his duties manfully, does not fall away from happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Sigala that the one who ignores comfort and discomfort alike and does his work well keeps his prosperity, and elsewhere lists supporting one’s parents as a son’s first duty.
buddhism.tie_back: Setting aside personal comfort to do one’s duties is the Kural’s man who desires work, not pleasure.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “During his reign he taught, for the benefit of the people, the seventy-two sciences, of which writing is the first, arithmetic the most important, and the knowledge of omens the last, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men.”
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition honours Rishabha, the first Tirthankara and first king, for teaching people the crafts and occupations that let them make a living, before he renounced the world.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's worker who wants work over pleasure and becomes a pillar holding up his kin is mirrored, on a civilisational scale, by Rishabha's labours that held up his people.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha §211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who performs selfless service, without thought of reward, shall attain his Lord and Master.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan praises seva done for its own sake, with no thought of reward for oneself.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the one who craves the work rather than his own pleasure and so holds up his kin; Guru Arjan praises service done with no thought of reward for oneself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads the young Heracles meets two women: Vice offers him the easy road of pleasure, and Virtue the hard road of toil that brings real honour. He chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prodicus’ allegory, retold by Xenophon, made Heracles the model of choosing labour over ease.
greek_mythology.tie_back: ‘Not desiring pleasure but desiring work’ is exactly the choice of Heracles.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus, The Choice of Heracles, in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius tells himself that when he is reluctant to rise at dawn he should remember he is rising to do the work of a human being, and asks whether he was made to lie warm under the blankets for his own pleasure.
philosophy.explanation: The emperor reminds himself that he exists for action and service, not for comfort.
philosophy.tie_back: Marcus chooses work over pleasure for the sake of others, as the Kural’s pillar does.

real_life_example.event_title: Maria Sklodowska works as a governess to pay for her sister's medical studies
real_life_example.place: Poland (then under Russian rule) and Paris, France
real_life_example.event: As a teenager in Warsaw, Maria Sklodowska, later Marie Curie, made a pact with her elder sister Bronya: Maria would work to support Bronya through medical school in Paris, and Bronya would later help pay for Maria's studies. Maria worked for several years as a governess and tutor, sending money to her sister while studying on her own in her spare time. In 1891 she went to Paris, lived at first in Bronya's home and enrolled at the Sorbonne.
real_life_example.explanation: By putting aside her own ambitions for years and working for her sister, the future double Nobel laureate became the support on which her family's hopes rested.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who prefers work to personal pleasure becomes a pillar who wipes away the troubles of kin and holds them up, and Maria's years as a governess held up her sister's future and then her own.

tamil:
முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும் முயற்றின்மை
இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்.
transliteration:
Muyarchi thiruvinai aakkum muyatrinmai
Inmai puguththi vidum.
meaning: Effort brings riches and success. Not making an effort brings poverty.
elementary: If you water a plant every day, it grows and gives you flowers. If you forget, it dries up. Effort is the water that makes good things grow, and not trying lets things wilt.
university: This is perhaps the most quoted couplet of the chapter, built on the paired opposites முயற்சி / முயற்றின்மை and ஆக்கும் / புகுத்திவிடும். Parimelazhagar reads திருவினை as திரு (wealth, prosperity) plus the empty increment இன் and the accusative ஐ, so ‘effort creates wealth’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this, whereas Sivayogi Sivakumar splits it as திரு + வினை, ‘auspicious deeds’, and Kalaignar as ‘excellent achievements’. இன்மை, ‘non-being’, is the standard Kural word for poverty (compare ch. 105, நல்குரவு), and புகுத்திவிடும் pictures idleness as actively ushering poverty into the house. The text is identical in both editions, thirukkural-thamizh.org printing the sandhi forms திருவினை யாக்கும் and யின்மை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A well-known verse of the Hitopadesha says that tasks are accomplished by effort, not by wishing, just as deer do not walk into the mouth of a sleeping lion.
hinduism.explanation: Even the lion, king of beasts, must hunt; desire alone never produces results (udyamena hi sidhyanti kāryāṇi na manorathaiḥ).
hinduism.tie_back: Both the fable-book and the Kural teach that effort alone brings gain, while idleness brings nothing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.”
christianity.explanation: Paul rebukes idlers in Thessalonica, telling them to work quietly and earn their own bread.
christianity.tie_back: Paul and Valluvar both tie livelihood directly to labour and want to idleness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an lays down that a person’s portion is tied to his own striving (sa‘y).
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that what effort earns is what one has.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In all labour there is profit; But the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb contrasts toil that yields gain with idle talk that leads to want.
judaism.tie_back: The same two-part structure as the Kural: labour brings profit, its absence brings poverty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Living in this way, he leaves many duties undone, new wealth he does not get, and wealth he has acquired dwindles away.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the excuses of the idle man, too cold, too hot, too early, too late, and states the economic result.
buddhism.tie_back: Idleness admitting poverty is the Kural’s second line in the Buddha’s words.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Saddalaputta, is your ware made by dint of exertion and manly strength, or on the other hand, is it made without exertion and manly strength?”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira asks the Ajivika potter Saddalaputta this question to refute Gosala's fatalism (niyati), which denied any role to exertion. The potter's own reactions show that he really does believe effort and conduct make things happen, and he becomes a Jain lay follower.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says effort creates prosperity; Mahavira makes the same point by showing that even the potter's prosperous trade depends on 'exertion and manly strength'.
jainism.source: Uvasagadasao (Upāsakadaśāḥ), ch. 7, Saddalaputta (tr. A.F.R. Hoernle), as quoted in the jainworld.com chapter 'Rival Sects'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace. Meditating, you shall meet God, O Nanak, and your anxiety shall vanish.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Gujri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan uses the word udam (effort, exertion) and promises that the one who makes the effort and keeps practising it will gain life and peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says effort brings prosperity and idleness brings want; Guru Arjan likewise says effort brings life and peace and puts anxiety to flight.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Through work men grow rich in flocks and substance, and working they are much better loved by the immortals.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod urges his brother Perses to work rather than seek wealth through lawsuits and idleness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod and Valluvar give the same economic law: work creates wealth.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 293-319 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: John Locke argues that it is labour that puts the difference of value on everything, reckoning that of the products useful to human life the far greater part is owed to labour rather than to nature.
philosophy.explanation: In his chapter on property, Locke makes labour the main source of wealth and value.
philosophy.tie_back: Locke gives a political-economic version of the Kural’s ‘effort produces wealth’.
philosophy.source: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, ch. 5, §40

real_life_example.event_title: Konosuke Matsushita starts a workshop in his home in Osaka
real_life_example.event: On 7 March 1918, twenty-three-year-old Konosuke Matsushita founded Matsushita Electric Housewares Manufacturing Works in Osaka with his wife Mumeno and her younger brother Toshio Iue. Their first product was an improved attachment plug, made partly with metal parts recycled from used light bulbs, and sales were weak until Matsushita began dealing directly with wholesalers. The business was incorporated in 1935 as Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. and became one of the world's largest electronics makers, renamed Panasonic in 2008.
real_life_example.explanation: A three-person family workshop grew, through persistent effort, into a global company and a source of prosperity for many thousands of employees.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says effort builds up prosperity while lack of effort ushers in poverty, and the Matsushita workshop is a classic case of wealth built from almost nothing by work.

tamil:
மடியுளாள் மாமுகடி என்ப மடியிலான்
தாளுளாள் தாமரையி னாள்.
transliteration:
Madiyulaal maamugadi enba madiyilaan
Thaalulaal thaamaraiyinaal.
meaning: People say the dark goddess of bad luck lives with the lazy. The goddess of good fortune, who sits on a lotus, lives with the hard work of someone who is not lazy.
elementary: Pretend Good Luck and Bad Luck are two visitors looking for a home. Bad Luck loves a messy room where someone is napping all day. Good Luck knocks on the door of the kid who’s busy building and practising. Where you work, good luck moves in.
university: Valluvar borrows two goddesses of popular belief: மாமுகடி, the ‘great dark Mugadi’ (மூதேவி, Sanskrit Jyeṣṭhā or Alakṣmī), goddess of misfortune, and தாமரையினாள், ‘she of the lotus’, Tirumagal or Lakshmi; the verb என்ப (‘they say’) signals that he is citing received wisdom. Parimelazhagar notes that sloth is the ‘dwelling’ of the one and effort (தாள்) the dwelling of the other, so fortune is located not in fate but in conduct; Kalaignar demythologises the pair entirely, treating the goddess names as figures for the industrious and the idle. There is a textual point: ytamizh.com prints தாளுளான் (masculine), but the parallelism with மடியுளாள் and the sandhi form றாளுளா டாமரையி னாள் in thirukkural-thamizh.org (தாளுளாள் + தாமரை) confirm the feminine தாளுளாள், ‘she dwells in the effort’, which is the reading adopted here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A famous Hitopadesha verse says that Lakshmi, goddess of fortune, approaches the lion-like man of effort, and only cowards say that fortune is handed out by fate; so set fate aside and exert yourself with your own strength.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit maxim (udyoginaṃ puruṣasiṃham upaiti lakṣmīḥ) names the same goddess and the same condition for her favour.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural itself: the lotus-goddess comes to dwell with the diligent.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the parable of the talents, the servants who trade with their master’s money double it and are rewarded, while the one who buries his talent out of fear and sloth is called ‘wicked and slothful’ and loses even what he had.
christianity.explanation: Jesus’ parable shows increase coming to the active and loss to the idle.
christianity.tie_back: Blessing dwells with the diligent and deprivation with the lazy, as in Valluvar’s two goddesses.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one’s own hands. The Prophet of Allah, David used to eat from the earnings of his manual labor.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises self-earned sustenance as the best, citing even a prophet-king who lived by his own labour.
islam.tie_back: Blessing is found in one’s own labour, the ‘dwelling’ the Kural gives to the goddess of fortune.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Yitzhak teaches that if someone tells you, ‘I laboured and did not find,’ do not believe him; ‘I did not labour yet found,’ do not believe him; but ‘I laboured and found,’ believe him.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud treats real attainment as something that only comes with toil.
judaism.tie_back: Success lodging only where there is labour is the Kural’s fortune that ‘dwells in effort’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada links steadily increasing glory to energy and heedfulness.
buddhism.tie_back: Glory growing with the energetic parallels fortune taking up residence with the diligent.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain tradition knows the goddess Śrī (Lakṣmī) seated on a lotus: she is the fourth of the fourteen auspicious dreams Queen Triśalā saw before Mahavira's birth. But Jain doctrine credits fortune and misfortune to a person's own karma and conduct, not to goddesses of luck.
jainism.explanation: Jainism keeps Śrī as an auspicious symbol, but in its non-theistic karma theory prosperity and adversity follow one's own deeds, a view close to Valluvar's actual point about effort and sloth.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's image of the lotus goddess living in effort and Misfortune living in sloth fits Jainism only as metaphor: in Jain teaching one's own conduct, not a deity, brings fortune.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §36 (the dream of the goddess Śrī) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Cheated and plundered by Maya, you do not think of God, and you waste your life in laziness.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of Bhagat Trilochan included in the Guru Granth Sahib, the idle person is pictured as robbed and ruined, his life squandered through laziness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says misfortune dwells in sloth; Trilochan's hymn likewise shows laziness leaving a person plundered and his life wasted.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 92, Siree Raag, Bhagat Trilochan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “work, high-born Perses, that Hunger may hate you, and venerable Demeter richly crowned may love you and fill your barn with food; for Hunger is altogether a meet comrade for the sluggard.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod pairs the grain-goddess Demeter, who favours the worker, with Hunger, the sluggard’s companion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Demeter and Hunger are an exact Greek counterpart to the lotus-goddess and the dark Mugadi.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 299-302 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Samuel Smiles opens Self-Help with the maxim ‘Heaven helps those who help themselves’, arguing that the spirit of self-help is the root of all genuine growth in the individual.
philosophy.explanation: The Victorian moralist made personal industry the true source of what people call good fortune.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Smiles says fortune favours the self-reliant worker.

real_life_example.event_title: Alexander Fleming notices the mould that leads to penicillin
real_life_example.place: St Mary's Hospital, London, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Returning from holiday on 3 September 1928, the bacteriologist Alexander Fleming began sorting through culture plates of Staphylococcus bacteria in his laboratory. On one plate contaminated by a mould he saw that the bacteria around the mould had been destroyed, and he went on to show that the mould produced a substance, which he named penicillin, that killed many kinds of bacteria. He published his findings in 1929, and penicillin was later developed into a medicine by Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their Oxford team; the three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.
real_life_example.explanation: A chance contamination became a medical revolution only because an experienced researcher was at work, paying attention, and followed up what he saw.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says good fortune dwells in the effort of the industrious, and Fleming's lucky mould brought its fortune to the world through a working scientist who was ready to recognise it.

tamil:
பொறியின்மை யார்க்கும் பழியன்று அறிவறிந்து
ஆள்வினை இன்மை பழி.
transliteration:
Poriyinmai yaarkkum pazhiyandru arivarindhu
Aalvinai inmai pazhi.
meaning: Having bad luck is nothing to be ashamed of. The real shame is knowing what needs to be done and still not making the effort.
elementary: Nobody laughs at you if it rains on sports day. That’s just bad luck. But if you knew you had a test and didn’t study at all, that’s on you. What matters is whether you tried.
university: The couplet turns on பழி (blame, disgrace) and on the contested word பொறி. Parimelazhagar takes பொறி as ஊழ், favourable destiny, so ‘to lack good fortune is no disgrace’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar follow him, while Solomon Pappaiah (and, differently, Sivayogi Sivakumar) read பொறி in its other sense of bodily organ or faculty, making the point that physical disability is no disgrace but failure to exert oneself is. Both readings yield the same moral: blame attaches only to what lies in our power, namely அறிவறிந்து ஆள்வினை, effort guided by knowing what ought to be known. The chapter title word ஆள்வினை appears here explicitly, and the couplet prepares for 619-620’s direct confrontation with fate. The text is the same in both editions (sandhi: பழியன் றறிவறிந் / தாள்வினை யின்மை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Everything can be secured by Exertion: but nothing can be gained through Destiny alone, by a man that is wanting in personal Exertion.”
hinduism.explanation: Asked whether destiny or exertion is stronger, Bhishma relays Brahma’s answer that destiny is like seed and exertion like the tilled field, and neither yields without the other.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Mahabharata puts responsibility on the exertion that is within a person’s power.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section VI (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him. I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.”
christianity.explanation: Asked whose sin caused a man’s blindness, Jesus denies that the affliction is anyone’s fault and turns at once to the duty of working while there is time.
christianity.tie_back: An unchosen affliction is no disgrace; neglecting the work one should do is what counts, as in the Kural, especially on Pappaiah’s ‘bodily faculty’ reading.

islam.quote_or_event: “A strong believer is better and is more lovable to Allah than a weak believer, and there is good in everyone, (but) cherish that which gives you benefit (in the Hereafter) and seek help from Allah and do not lose heart, and if anything (in the form of trouble) comes to you, don’t say: If I had not done that, it would not have happened so and so, but say: Allah did that what He had ordained to do”
islam.explanation: The Prophet commands striving for what benefits and forbids losing heart, while accepting misfortune as decree rather than as grounds for self-reproach.
islam.tie_back: Misfortune is accepted without disgrace, but slackness in striving is not, which is the Kural’s own division.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For a righteous man falleth seven times, and riseth up again, But the wicked stumble under adversity.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says the righteous are marked not by never falling but by rising again.
judaism.tie_back: Falling (misfortune) brings no shame; what matters is the effort to rise, as in the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The idler who does not exert himself when he should, who though young and strong is full of sloth, with a mind full of vain thoughts — such an indolent man does not find the path to wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha condemns the one who has youth and strength and still will not exert himself at the right time.
buddhism.tie_back: Having capacity and knowing the time yet not striving is exactly the Kural’s ‘disgrace’.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Acknowledging the truth about bondage and liberation, but talking only, not acting (in accordance with these tenets), they seek comfort for themselves in mighty words. Clever talking will not work salvation…”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira condemns those who know the truth but do not act on it; knowledge without exertion saves no one.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's real disgrace, knowing what should be done and not making the effort, is exactly the 'false ascetic' of Uttaradhyayana 6, who knows but does not act.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 6.9-10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Dadda: Do not blame anyone else; blame instead your own actions.”
sikhism.explanation: In his acrostic Patti, Guru Nanak teaches that a person should not lay blame on others but look at the record of his own deeds.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says there is no disgrace in bad luck, only in failing to make the effort; Guru Nanak likewise places responsibility on one's own actions, not on outside causes.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Aasaa (Patti), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Work is no disgrace: it is idleness which is a disgrace.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells Perses that shame belongs not to labour or to poverty itself but to the idle.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod places disgrace precisely where Valluvar does: in the lack of effort.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 311 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus begins his Handbook by dividing things into those within our power, our judgements, impulses and actions, and those not in our power, such as body, property and reputation.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, only what is in our power can be the object of praise or blame.
philosophy.tie_back: Unlucky externals carry no blame; neglecting what is in our power does, as the Kural says.

real_life_example.event_title: Frida Kahlo teaches herself to paint after her bus accident
real_life_example.event: On 17 September 1925, eighteen-year-old Frida Kahlo was severely injured when the bus she was riding in was struck by a streetcar in Mexico City, and she spent months in plaster casts, largely confined to bed. Her mother had a special easel made so she could paint lying down, and a mirror was fixed above her bed so she could study her own face. Teaching herself, she produced her first known work, Self-Portrait Wearing a Velvet Dress, in 1926, and went on to become one of the most celebrated painters of the twentieth century.
real_life_example.explanation: Kahlo did not choose her injuries, which affected her for the rest of her life, but she chose to work within their limits, and that work made her name.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says misfortune is no disgrace, only the failure to make an effort is, and Kahlo's accident brought no shame on her while the effort she made from her bed brought lasting honour.

tamil:
தெய்வத்தான் ஆகா தெனினும் முயற்சிதன்
மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும்.
transliteration:
Theyvaththaan aagaadhu eninum muyarchithan
Meyvaruththak kooli tharum.
meaning: Even if fate stops you from reaching your goal, your effort will still pay you back for all your hard work.
elementary: Say you practise hard for a race and still don’t win because it rained and you slipped. You didn’t get the trophy, but your legs are stronger and you’re faster than before. Hard work always pays something, even when luck says no.
university: Parimelazhagar glosses தெய்வம் as ஊழ் (fate, the fruit of past deeds), so the protasis concedes that destiny may make the full aim unattainable (ஆகாது); even then முயற்சி pays தன் மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி, the wage owed for its own bodily strain. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah keep the fate reading, but Kalaignar takes தெய்வம் literally as God, turning the couplet into a rationalist contrast between calling on God and working, a reading the Tamil can bear but the commentarial tradition does not support. The couplet is a careful concession to chapter 38 (ஊழ்), where kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate: Valluvar grants fate’s power over outcomes while denying it power to cancel the return on labour. Both editions agree, thirukkural-thamizh.org printing தெய்வத்தா னாகா தெனினு முயற்சிதன்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The body, the doer (soul), the various senses, the many kinds of efforts, and Divine Providence—these are the five factors of action.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists effort (ceṣṭā) and providence (daiva) as distinct contributors to any action, so neither alone determines the result.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita, like the Kural, gives effort its own share in outcomes even where fate also plays a part.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.”
christianity.explanation: Paul assures the Corinthians that faithful labour is never wasted, whatever happens.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Not in vain’ is the Kural’s promise that effort always earns its wage.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that his effort is going to be seen - Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense”
islam.explanation: Following the verse that a person has only what he strives for, the Qur’an promises that every effort will be seen and fully repaid.
islam.tie_back: Effort is guaranteed its recompense, exactly the Kural’s ‘wage of toil’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ben He He said: According to the labor is the reward.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah’s terse Aramaic saying (lefum tza‘ara agra) ties reward to the pain of the labour.
judaism.tie_back: ‘According to the labour, the reward’ is the Kural’s ‘wage of the body’s toil’ almost word for word.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 5:23 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: Shipwrecked on his way to recover his kingdom, Prince Mahajanaka swims for seven days with no shore in sight. When the sea-goddess Manimekhala asks why he struggles in vain, he replies that one who strives does his duty and is free of blame even if he fails; moved, she carries him to safety.
buddhism.explanation: The Mahajanaka Jataka, one of the Ten Great Birth Stories, illustrates the perfection of energy (viriya).
buddhism.tie_back: Effort that seems doomed by fate still earns its reward, here literally, as the Kural promises.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra teaches that austerity (tapas) brings about both the stopping of new karma (saṃvara) and the shedding of karma already bound (nirjarā). For Jains, effort always bears fruit at the level of karma, even when an outward aim fails because of past karma that is ripening.
jainism.explanation: In Jain doctrine 'fate' is the ripening of one's own past karma; it may block a present goal, but sincere exertion is never wasted, because it wears away karma.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural says effort pays the wages of the body's toil even when fate denies the goal, Jainism holds that exertion always earns its return in shed karma.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.3 (tapasā nirjarā ca); see Nathmal Tatia, That Which Is (1994)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They receive the wages of their labor, begging at the Door of their Lord and Master.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Soohee ki Vaar, Guru Nanak speaks of devotees who labour and receive the wages of that labour at the Lord's door.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even when fate blocks the goal, effort still pays the wages of the body's toil; Guru Nanak likewise speaks of labour that is paid its wage.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Soohee (Soohee ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: A carter whose wagon is stuck in the mud prays to Heracles for help; the god appears and tells him to put his shoulder to the wheel and goad his oxen, for the gods help only those who help themselves.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Aesopic fable rebukes reliance on the gods in place of one’s own exertion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the fable says that effort, not appeal to heaven, gets results.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, Hercules and the Wagoner (Perry 291; trans. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant writes that even if, through the special disfavour of fortune or the meagre provision of a stepmotherly nature, a good will wholly lacked the power to achieve its purpose, it would still shine like a jewel by its own light, as something having its full worth in itself.
philosophy.explanation: For Kant the worth of a good will does not depend on whether fortune allows it to succeed.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers hold that adverse fortune cannot cancel the value of honest effort.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, Section I

real_life_example.event_title: Dorando Pietri is disqualified from the Olympic marathon and honoured by the Queen
real_life_example.event: In the marathon at the 1908 London Olympic Games, the Italian runner Dorando Pietri entered the stadium first but, exhausted, collapsed several times and went the wrong way, and officials helped him across the finish line. He was disqualified for receiving outside assistance, and the gold medal went to the American Johnny Hayes. The next day Queen Alexandra presented Pietri with a special silver-gilt cup, and his effort made him a popular hero.
real_life_example.explanation: Pietri was denied the victory he had all but reached, yet his extraordinary effort earned a unique royal honour and lasting fame.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even when fate keeps the goal out of reach, effort still pays the wages of one's toil, and Pietri lost the gold but received a reward of his own for what his body had endured.

tamil:
ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர் உலைவின்றித்
தாழாது உஞற்று பவர்.
transliteration:
Oozhaiyum uppakkam kaanbar ulaivindrith
Thaazhaadhu unjatru bavar.
meaning: People who keep working hard without giving up or slowing down will even see fate turn around and run away from them.
elementary: Think of a tiny stream running into a big rock. The rock seems stronger, but the water keeps flowing, day after day, until it carves a path around or even through. People who keep going without giving up can get past even the biggest ‘it’s just meant to be’.
university: The chapter ends with its boldest claim, the one most often quoted: tireless strivers will காண்பர் (see) the உப்பக்கம் (back, rear side) of ஊழ் (fate) itself, a battlefield image of an enemy turning its back in flight (Solomon Pappaiah: விதியையும் புறமுதுகு காட்டக் காண்பர்). The conditions are exacting: உலைவின்றி (without wavering), தாழாது (without delay or slackening) and உஞற்றுபவர் (those who exert themselves, an old verb for effort). Because chapter 38 insists on ஊழின் பெருவலி (fate’s great strength, kural 380), commentators have laboured to reconcile the two; Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar soften the claim so that strivers defeat the fate that obstructs a particular undertaking ‘in time’, while Kalaignar reads it as an outright rejection of fatalism. The couplet stands in the same Indian debate as the Mahabharata’s daiva-versus-puruṣakāra discussions and the Yoga Vasishtha’s praise of paurusha; the text agrees in both editions (sandhi: ஊழையு முப்பக்கங் காண்ப ருலைவின்றித் / தாழா துஞற்று பவர்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Yoga Vasishtha, Vasishtha tells Prince Rama that what people call fate (daiva) is nothing but the fruit of their own past effort, and that vigorous present effort (paurusha) can overcome it, as the stronger of two fighting rams prevails.
hinduism.explanation: The Mumukshu section devotes several chapters to arguing that self-effort, not destiny, is the decisive force in human life.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the fullest Sanskrit statement of the Kural’s claim that relentless effort can put fate to flight.

christianity.quote_or_event: “forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes his life as an unrelenting forward effort that refuses to be defined by the past.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s tireless ‘pressing on’ is the Kural’s உலைவின்றித் தாழாது, striving without faltering or slackening.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an makes a people’s own inner change the condition on which their fortunes are transformed.
islam.tie_back: Human effort as the hinge of changed destiny is the Kural’s point, though framed within divine decree.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel; for thou hast striven with God and with men, and hast prevailed.”
judaism.explanation: After wrestling all night with a mysterious being and refusing to let go, Jacob is renamed for his striving.
judaism.tie_back: Jacob’s victory through unrelenting struggle with a superhuman power is the Kural’s striver who makes fate turn its back.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By effort and heedfulness, discipline and self-mastery, let the wise one make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that effort builds a refuge that the flood of circumstance cannot sweep away.
buddhism.tie_back: An island built by effort that no flood can overwhelm matches the Kural’s effort that stands firm against fate.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a large tank, when its supply of water has been stopped, gradually dries up by the consumption of the water and by evaporation, so the Karman of a monk, which he acquired in millions of births, is annihilated by austerities, if there is no influx of bad Karman.”
jainism.explanation: Jainism teaches that persistent, untiring austerity can wear away even karma built up over countless lives, so no 'destiny' is beyond the reach of effort.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's tireless strivers who see fate turn its back match the Jain teaching that unflagging exertion drains away the accumulated karma that makes up one's fate.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 30.5-6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of Bhagat Kabir in Raag Maaroo, often recited by Sikhs, the true hero is the one who never gives up the fight, whatever it costs him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural promises that those who strive without faltering will see even fate turn its back; Kabir praises the one who never leaves the field, even when cut to pieces.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Although Poseidon pursues him with storms and shipwreck for ten years, Odysseus keeps striving through every disaster and finally reaches Ithaca, winning his homecoming in the teeth of a god’s hostility.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Odyssey shows sustained human endurance prevailing against a hostile divine power.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus is the Greek image of the Kural’s striver who outlasts adverse fate.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli judges that fortune may be arbiter of half our actions but leaves the other half to us, and compares her to a flooding river against which prudent men build dykes and embankments in calm times.
philosophy.explanation: In The Prince, ch. 25, he rejects fatalism and argues that energetic foresight (virtù) can check fortune.
philosophy.tie_back: Machiavelli’s dyke-building against fortune is a Renaissance version of the Kural’s effort that routs fate.

real_life_example.event_title: Lis Hartel wins an Olympic dressage medal after polio
real_life_example.event: In 1944 the Danish rider Lis Hartel, then twenty-three and pregnant, contracted polio and was left paralysed below the knees. After years of rehabilitation she returned to competition, finishing second at the 1947 Scandinavian championships, and at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics, the first Games at which women could compete against men in dressage, she won the silver medal on her horse Jubilee. She needed help to mount and dismount, and the gold medallist Henri Saint Cyr helped her onto the podium; she won silver again in 1956.
real_life_example.explanation: A rider whom illness seemed to have shut out of her sport became the first woman to win an Olympic equestrian medal.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who strive without faltering or slackening will see even fate turn its back, and Hartel's unbroken effort carried her past what polio seemed to have decided for her.

tamil:
இடுக்கண் வருங்கால் நகுக அதனை
அடுத்தூர்வது அஃதொப்ப தில்.
transliteration:
Itukkan varungaal nakuka adhanai
Atuththoorvadhu aqdhoppa thil.
meaning: When trouble comes, smile at it. Nothing beats trouble as well as staying cheerful and calm.
elementary: Imagine your sandcastle gets knocked over by a wave. You can cry, or you can laugh and start building again. The Kural says the laugh is the strongest tool you have: a cheerful heart beats trouble better than anything else.
university: The chapter opens with its most famous imperative, nakuka (laugh, smile), which the commentators do not read as mockery but as the outward sign of a mind that refuses to be shaken; Solomon Pappaiah paraphrases it as rejoicing inwardly, Mu. Varadarasanar as not being agitated. The second line turns on aṭuttūrvatu, literally ‘that which presses close and rides over’, a verbal noun describing what can close in on sorrow and subdue it, and aḥtoppatu il says nothing equals ‘that’ (the laughter or the unperturbed state it expresses). Parimelazhagar, whose commentary frames Idukkan Azhiyaamai as the natural sequel to the preceding chapter on sustained effort (Aalvinaiyudaimai), understands the troubles here as those that arise in the course of undertaking great works, so the king or doer must not lose heart midway. The couplet text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; ytamizh writes the chapter title as one word, இடுக்கணழியாமை, and thirukkural.net renders it ‘Not despairing in afflictive times’, while Pope’s title is ‘Hopefulness in Trouble’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Dhritarashtra, thereafter, in the midst of both the armies, Shree Krishna smilingly spoke the following words to the grief-stricken Arjun.”
hinduism.explanation: At the darkest moment of the Mahabharata, with Arjuna collapsed in despair between two armies, Krishna answers him first with a smile (prahasann iva) before teaching him anything.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s first move against trouble is exactly Krishna’s: meet the crisis with a smile, and the smile itself begins the victory.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience.”
christianity.explanation: James tells believers to greet their trials with joy, because hardship builds steadfast endurance in them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, James makes joy the proper response to trouble and treats that joy as the force that wins through it.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, with hardship [will be] ease. Indeed, with hardship [will be] ease.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an twice assures the Prophet, in a time of pressure, that relief comes together with every difficulty.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s cheerful face toward trouble rests on the same conviction the sura repeats: hardship never comes alone and never has the last word.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells of the sage Nachum Ish Gamzu, who met every misfortune that befell him with the words gam zu le-tovah, ‘this too is for the good’; when a gift he carried to the emperor was stolen and replaced with dirt, he still said it, and the dirt turned out to be miraculous.
judaism.explanation: Nachum became a byword for greeting each blow of fortune with serene confidence instead of lament, and his calm is shown to be vindicated.
judaism.tie_back: His habitual ‘this too is for the good’ is a Jewish form of the Kural’s smile at trouble, an inner stance that disarms misfortune.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A mind unruffled by the vagaries of fortune, from sorrow freed, from defilements cleansed, from fear liberated — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Mangala Sutta the Buddha names a mind that stays untroubled through life’s ups and downs as one of the highest blessings a person can have.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says an unshaken, cheerful mind is the strongest weapon against trouble; the Buddha calls that same mind the greatest blessing.
buddhism.source: Maha-mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (tr. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “If any misfortune happens and he suffers pain, he should cheerfully steady his mind, and bear the ills that attack him.”
jainism.explanation: In Mahavira's teaching on the twenty-two troubles (parishaha) a monk is to meet illness and misfortune with a cheerful, steady mind instead of distress.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's call to smile when trouble comes is matched by the Jain instruction to meet misfortune cheerfully and with a steadied mind.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Your actions seem so sweet to me.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan says that whatever God does tastes sweet to him. Sikh tradition links this acceptance of God's will (bhana manna) with his calm in the face of torture and martyrdom at Lahore in 1606.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to meet trouble with a smile; Guru Arjan meets whatever comes as something sweet, which is the same calm, cheerful acceptance.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Heart, be still, you had worse than this to bear on the day when the terrible Cyclops ate your brave companions; yet you bore it in silence till your cunning got you safe out of the cave, though you made sure of being killed.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Back in his own house disguised as a beggar and surrounded by insults, Odysseus steadies himself by reminding his heart of worse troubles it has already survived.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus shows the Kural’s point that the mind’s own steadiness, not outward force, is what finally masters trouble.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for the mind converts and changes every hindrance to its activity into an aid; and so that which is a hindrance is made a furtherance to an act; and that which is an obstacle on the road helps us on this road.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius argues that a well-ordered mind can turn every obstacle into material for its own progress.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts hold that the right inner response does not just endure trouble but overpowers it and turns it to use.

real_life_example.event_title: Ronald Reagan jokes with his surgeons after being shot
real_life_example.event: On 30 March 1981 President Ronald Reagan was shot outside a Washington hotel; a bullet struck his left lung near his heart and he was rushed to George Washington University Hospital. According to accounts from people who were there, he lifted his oxygen mask moments before surgery and joked to the doctors that he hoped they were all Republicans, and one surgeon replied that today they all were. Reagan recovered and returned to the White House less than four weeks later.
real_life_example.explanation: A light-hearted remark at a moment of real danger steadied the people around him, and the Reagan Foundation has since presented it as a defining example of his calm and optimism.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises meeting trouble with a smile because nothing overpowers sorrow so well, and Reagan's joke on the way into surgery is a vivid example of cheerful calm pressing back against a grave crisis.

tamil:
வெள்ளத் தனைய இடும்பை அறிவுடையான்
உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Vellath thanaiya itumpai arivutaiyaan
Ullaththin ullak ketum.
meaning: Even trouble as huge as a flood goes away once a wise person thinks about it with a steady mind.
elementary: Think of a huge wave rushing at a beach. It looks scary, but when it hits a strong rock it just breaks into foam. A wise, calm mind is like that rock: even a flood of problems falls apart when it meets clear, brave thinking.
university: The flood simile (veḷḷattaṉaiya, ‘flood-like’) stresses both the size and the sudden, overwhelming onrush of trouble (iṭumpai). The second line plays on uḷḷam (mind) and uḷḷa (to think, to resolve): the trouble perishes (keṭum) merely by the wise man’s mind thinking upon it, which Mu. Varadarasanar explains as reflecting on the nature of the trouble, and Solomon Pappaiah as the mind refusing to slacken. Parimelazhagar and later commentators read uḷḷam here as close to ūkkam, the mental elation or resolve praised in chapter 60, so that one act of firm resolve dissolves a whole flood of difficulty. The text agrees in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, and Pope’s rendering (‘When wise men’s mind regards it, it is gone’) follows the same construal.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Having gained that state, one does not consider any attainment to be greater. Being thus established, one is not shaken even in the midst of the greatest calamity.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the yogi whose mind is settled in the Self as one whom even the heaviest sorrow (duḥkhena guruṇāpi) cannot move.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita and the Kural both place victory over the greatest affliction in the state of a steady, wise mind.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus compares the person who hears and practises his teaching to a house on rock that survives the flood.
christianity.tie_back: Both use the flood as the picture of overwhelming trouble and say it breaks harmlessly on a well-founded mind.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity.”
islam.explanation: The closing verses of al-Baqarah assure believers that no burden laid on them exceeds what they are able to bear.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says even a flood of sorrow can be undone by the wise mind; the Qur’an assures that no trial is truly beyond a person’s capacity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee, And through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee; When thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned, Neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah promises Israel that floods and fire will not overwhelm it, because God goes with it through every ordeal.
judaism.tie_back: Isaiah and the Kural share the image of a flood that cannot drown the one who meets it rightly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By effort and heedfulness, discipline and self-mastery, let the wise one make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges the wise to build an inner island of discipline and mindfulness that no rising flood of passion or sorrow can cover.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts picture trouble as a flood and the wise person’s trained mind as the thing that survives it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Is there a shelter, a refuge, a firm ground for the beings carried away by the great flood of water? do you know the island, O Gautama?” … “The flood is old age and death, which carry away living beings; Law is the island, the firm ground, the refuge, the most excellent shelter.”
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, the flood that sweeps beings away is answered by the Law (dharma), an island that the flood cannot cover.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural pictures sorrow as a flood that the wise mind overcomes; the Jain text uses the same flood image and places firm ground against it, though that ground is the Law rather than the mind's own resolve.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.65 and 23.68 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Remembering God, one is not touched by fear. Remembering God, one does not suffer sorrow.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan lists the fruits of simran, among them freedom from fear and from sorrow.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a flood of sorrow vanishes once the wise turn a steady mind on it; Guru Arjan says sorrow cannot afflict a mind turned steadily towards God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Zeus drowned the world in a great flood, only the pious Deucalion and Pyrrha survived; left alone on a devastated earth, they puzzled out the oracle’s riddle to throw ‘the bones of their mother’ behind them, understood it meant the stones of Mother Earth, and so repeopled the world.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s survivors of the flood overcome total catastrophe by keeping their heads and thinking their way to a solution.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, a literal flood of disaster is finally undone by a clear, thoughtful mind.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius tells himself to meet misfortune like a headland that absorbs wave after wave without moving.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wise mind that dissolves a flood of sorrow is the same as Marcus’s promontory that calms the raging water.

real_life_example.event_title: Pombal directs the relief and rebuilding of Lisbon after the 1755 earthquake
real_life_example.event: On the morning of 1 November 1755 a series of earthquakes, followed by a tsunami and fires lasting about six days, devastated Lisbon and killed an estimated 60,000 people in the city. The king's chief minister, Sebastiao de Carvalho, later Marquis of Pombal, organised the aid and reconstruction effort. Rebuilding of the downtown began in 1756 on a new orthogonal street plan drawn up by Manuel da Maia and carried out by the military engineers Eugenio dos Santos and Carlos Mardel, with earthquake-resistant and fire-resistant buildings.
real_life_example.explanation: Instead of being overwhelmed by one of the worst disasters in European history, the government turned to orderly relief and a rational plan, and the rebuilt Baixa district still stands as a model of planned recovery.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says even a flood-like sorrow perishes once a wise person turns a steady mind upon it, and Lisbon's catastrophe was met by deliberate planning that turned ruin into a new city.

tamil:
இடும்பைக்கு இடும்பை படுப்பர் இடும்பைக்கு
இடும்பை படாஅ தவர்.
transliteration:
Itumpaikku itumpai patuppar itumpaikku
Itumpai pataaa thavar.
meaning: People who do not let trouble make them sad turn things around. They end up making trouble itself suffer.
elementary: A bully loves it when you get upset. If you stay calm and cheerful, the bully gets frustrated and gives up. Trouble is like that bully: if you refuse to be sad about it, the trouble is the one that ends up losing.
university: This couplet is a celebrated piece of Valluvar’s wordplay: iṭumpai (sorrow, affliction) occurs four times, arranged chiastically so that ‘those who do not suffer sorrow for sorrow’ are said to ‘cause sorrow to sorrow’. The form paṭā’a in the second line is an alapedai (metrical lengthening, அளபெடை), marked in thirukkural.net’s romanisation as paṭā'a and preserved in both sources consulted. The personification of trouble as an opponent who can itself be defeated recurs in 624 and 625, making the triad the rhetorical centre of the chapter; Parimelazhagar’s line of interpretation, followed by Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar, is that the undaunted person so frustrates misfortune that it withdraws defeated. Pope’s version, ‘From them griefs, put to grief, depart’, keeps the paronomasia.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Arjun, noblest amongst men, that person who is not affected by happiness and distress, and remains steady in both, becomes eligible for liberation.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the dhīra, the steady one whom pleasure and pain do not disturb (na vyathayanti), is fit for immortality.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s person who is not pained by pain is the Gita’s dhīra, and in both texts that refusal to be disturbed is what defeats suffering.

christianity.quote_or_event: “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”
christianity.explanation: Paul taunts death itself, the greatest affliction, declaring it has been robbed of its power.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul turns the tables on the enemy, so that the affliction becomes the defeated party.

islam.quote_or_event: “So do not weaken and do not grieve, and you will be superior if you are [true] believers.”
islam.explanation: After the setback at Uhud, the Qur’an tells believers not to lose heart or sink into grief, promising that they will prevail.
islam.tie_back: The Kural and the Qur’an both link refusing to grieve with gaining the upper hand over misfortune.

judaism.quote_or_event: “the days wherein the Jews had rest from their enemies, and the month which was turned unto them from sorrow to gladness, and from mourning into a good day; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor.”
judaism.explanation: The Purim story ends with a total reversal: the decree meant to destroy the Jews recoils on its author, and their sorrow becomes celebration.
judaism.tie_back: Esther dramatizes the Kural’s reversal, in which the trouble meant to crush people is itself overturned.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Throughout the Mara-samyutta, Mara the Evil One comes to the Buddha again and again in terrifying or tempting forms to shake him; each time the Buddha calmly recognizes him, and Mara, realizing he has been seen through, vanishes sad and disappointed.
buddhism.explanation: The personified force of affliction and temptation fails against a mind that will not be disturbed, and it is Mara who leaves dejected.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s paradox made into a story: the one who is not troubled by trouble leaves trouble itself defeated and grieving.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Suffering from insects a great sage remains undisturbed. As an elephant at the head of the battle kills the enemy, so does a hero (in self-control conquer the internal foe).”
jainism.explanation: Enduring the trouble of biting insects, the sage is compared to a war elephant that turns on and destroys the enemy.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that those who do not grieve at sorrow turn the tables and make sorrow itself suffer; the Jain verse likewise makes the one who endures the attacker who defeats the foe.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That man, who in the midst of pain, does not feel pain, who is not affected by pleasure, affection or fear, and who looks alike upon gold and dust;”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person who is not shaken by pain even in its midst and who stays the same whatever comes.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who do not grieve at sorrow turn the tables on sorrow itself; Guru Tegh Bahadur praises the one who, in the midst of pain, does not feel pain.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops’ cave as Polyphemus devoured his men, Odysseus kept his head, called himself ‘Nobody’, blinded the giant and escaped under the rams, leaving Polyphemus roaring in pain that ‘Nobody’ was hurting him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The monster who meant to destroy Odysseus ends up the one in agony, outwitted by a man who did not panic.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus turns the Cyclops’ threat back on him, just as the Kural says the undaunted inflict trouble on trouble.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that suffering comes from our judgments about events, so changing the judgment removes the disturbance.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s person who is not pained by pain has done what Epictetus urges, taking away trouble’s power over the mind.

real_life_example.event_title: Karoly Takacs wins Olympic gold shooting with his other hand
real_life_example.place: London, United Kingdom, and Helsinki, Finland
real_life_example.event: In 1938 Hungarian army sergeant Karoly Takacs, a world-class pistol shooter, had his right shooting hand shattered when a faulty grenade exploded during army training. He taught himself to shoot with his left hand, won the Hungarian national pistol championship in 1939, and at the 1948 London Olympics won the rapid-fire pistol gold medal with a world record score. Four years later at Helsinki he won the event again, becoming its first repeat Olympic champion.
real_life_example.explanation: Takacs refused to let a career-ending injury end his career, and his comeback is still cited by the Olympic movement as one of its great stories of resilience.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who do not let sorrow grieve them bring grief upon sorrow itself, and Takacs turned the accident that should have finished him into the beginning of two Olympic victories.

tamil:
மடுத்தவா யெல்லாம் பகடன்னான் உற்ற
இடுக்கண் இடர்ப்பாடு உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Matuththavaa yellaam pakatannaan utra
Itukkan itarppaatu utaiththu.
meaning: Some people are like an ox that keeps pulling a cart through every rut and muddy patch. The trouble that meets them is the one that ends up suffering.
elementary: Picture a strong ox pulling a heavy cart down a muddy road. Every time a wheel gets stuck, the ox just leans in and pulls harder until it’s free. If you keep going like that ox, your problems get tired before you do.
university: Maṭuttavāy ellām means ‘in all the places where (the cart) sinks or is blocked’, from maṭu, a pit or deep hollow, and the image is completed by pakaṭu, a draught ox or bull that pulls the cart out without flinching; Pope’s explanation renders pakaṭu as ‘buffalo … through deep mire’, reflecting a traditional alternative gloss for the animal. The second line again personifies trouble: the iṭukkaṇ that such a person meets ‘itself suffers hardship’ (iṭarppāṭu uṭaittu). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both stress persistence without losing heart, while Kalaignar expands the image into success through unbroken effort, linking this couplet to the doctrine of ūkkam and āḷviṉai in chapters 60 and 62. The text is the same in both sources; ytamizh prints the sandhi form மடுத்தவா யெல்லாம் exactly as thirukkural.net does.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Be steadfast in the performance of your duty, O Arjun, abandoning attachment to success and failure. Such equanimity is called Yog.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna asks Arjuna to keep doing his work steadily, unmoved by whether each step succeeds or fails.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ox that keeps pulling through every rut is a picture of the Gita’s steady, unattached worker.

christianity.quote_or_event: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the farmer’s plough to teach that once a task is begun, one must keep pressing forward without looking back.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts borrow the image of plough and draught animal to praise forward-pressing perseverance.

islam.quote_or_event: “O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with [great] exertion and will meet it.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes human life as a hard, toiling journey (kadḥ) that nonetheless arrives at its destination.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ox straining through the mire, the Qur’an pictures life as exertion that pushes steadily to its goal.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it;”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon teaches that one must keep at a vast task even when its completion is out of sight.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ox does not ask how long the road is; it keeps pulling, just as Tarfon forbids setting the burden down.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Delight in heedfulness! Guard well your thoughts! Draw yourself out of this bog of evil, even as an elephant draws himself out of the mud.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the image of a great elephant heaving itself out of a swamp to describe determined spiritual effort.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ox dragging the cart out of the mire and the Dhammapada’s elephant pulling free of the mud are the same picture of strength against being stuck.

jainism.quote_or_event: “… he was free like a bird; he was always waking like the fabulous bird Bhâruṇḍa, valorous like an elephant, strong like a bull, difficult to attack like a lion, steady and firm like Mount Mandara, deep like the ocean … like the earth he patiently bore everything …”
jainism.explanation: During his years as a wandering ascetic, the Kalpa Sutra describes Mahavira with a string of similes, among them the strength of a bull and the earth's patience in bearing everything.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's image of the ox that pulls the cart through every rut is echoed in the Jain portrait of Mahavira as strong like a bull and bearing everything like the earth.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §118 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The mythical bull is Dharma, the son of compassion; this is what patiently holds the earth in its place.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak takes the old myth of a bull bearing the earth and reinterprets it: the bull is dharma, born of compassion, which patiently bears the world's weight.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures the steadfast person as an ox hauling the cart through every rut and mire; Japji Sahib turns the bull that patiently carries the load into an image of dharma.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib (pauri 16), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stranded in the Libyan desert, the Argonauts lifted the Argo onto their shoulders and carried it overland for twelve days and nights across the sand until they reached Lake Tritonis and could sail again.
greek_mythology.explanation: Instead of despairing when their ship could not float, the heroes became beasts of burden and hauled it through the obstacle.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ox dragging the cart through every rut, the Argonauts simply shoulder the load and haul it past the blockage.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus observes that when a lion attacks, it is the bull alone that knows its own strength and charges forward to protect the whole herd, using the bull as a model for the person who rises to hard circumstances.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus, difficulty reveals the strong character that is already in us, as danger reveals the bull’s power.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too takes a bull as its model of strength that shows itself precisely when the road gets hard.

real_life_example.event_title: The Overland Telegraph is pushed through Australia's wet season
real_life_example.event: In 1870 South Australia began building a telegraph line of about 3,200 kilometres (some 2,000 miles) from Port Augusta to Darwin under Superintendent of Telegraphs Charles Todd. In the northern section the tropical wet season flooded creeks, halted the work teams and put the project months behind schedule, and Todd travelled north himself in early 1872 to push the work on. The line, with some 36,000 poles, was completed on 22 August 1872 and was soon linked to the undersea cable from Java, cutting communication time with Europe from months to hours.
real_life_example.explanation: Despite floods, spoiled supplies and a collapsed contract, the builders kept hauling the line forward, and Australia's isolation from the rest of the world ended.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural pictures an ox that drags the cart through every rut and mire until the trouble itself suffers, and the telegraph builders kept dragging their line through every flooded creek until the obstacles gave way.

tamil:
அடுக்கி வரினும் அழிவிலான் உற்ற
இடுக்கண் இடுக்கட் படும்.
transliteration:
Atukki varinum azhivilaan utra
Itukkan itukkat patum.
meaning: Even if troubles come one on top of another, a person who does not break down inside will make those troubles themselves end up in trouble.
elementary: Sometimes bad things come in a row, like missing the bus, then spilling your lunch, then losing your pencil. If you keep your spirit strong and don’t give up, all those troubles run out of steam, one after another.
university: Aṭukki varinum, ‘even if they come stacked’, answers the natural objection to 623 and 624: what if troubles do not come singly but in a relentless series? The subject aḻivilāṉ is literally ‘one without destruction’, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss as one whose mind does not collapse (kalaṅkāmal, maṉam taḷarātavaṉ). The closing iṭukkaṇ iṭukkaṭ paṭum repeats the reversal of 623 with iṭukkaṇ instead of iṭumpai, the sandhi iṭukkaṭ reflecting the following p-. Both sources agree on the text, and the commentarial tradition treats 623-625 as a graded sequence: undaunted by one trouble, dragging through many ruts, and unbroken even by a pile of calamities.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, tested by the sage Vishvamitra, loses his kingdom, sells his wife and son, becomes a servant at a cremation ground, and at last must face his own son’s corpse, yet at every step he refuses to abandon truth; in the end the gods restore everything to him.
hinduism.explanation: The legend heaps calamity upon calamity on a single person to show a spirit that no accumulation of misfortune can break.
hinduism.tie_back: Harishchandra is the Kural’s aḻivilāṉ, the one whom troubles piled one on another cannot destroy, and who outlasts them all.

christianity.quote_or_event: “We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed;”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists affliction after affliction and after each one insists that it has not crushed him.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s ‘cast down, but not destroyed’ is almost a translation of the Kural’s aḻivilāṉ, the one troubles cannot destroy.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits, but give good tidings to the patient, Who, when disaster strikes them, say, ‘Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns of a whole series of trials and promises good news to those who meet them with patient steadfastness (ṣabr).
islam.tie_back: Both texts expect troubles to come in numbers and give the final word to the one who remains unshaken.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the prologue of Job, messenger after messenger arrives, each still speaking when the next comes in: his oxen and asses are taken, his sheep burned, his camels seized, and finally his children killed; yet Job does not curse God or charge him with wrong.
judaism.explanation: Job is the classic figure of a man hit by calamities stacked one upon another who nevertheless is not broken.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘even if they come piled up’ is exactly the Job prologue, where disasters arrive faster than they can be absorbed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The wise person is compared to a rock that the storm beats against without moving it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s aḻivilāṉ is the Dhammapada’s rock, battered by repeated blows and unshaken by them.

jainism.quote_or_event: “All these troubles have been declared by the Kâśyapa. A monk should not be vanquished by them, when attacked by any anywhere.”
jainism.explanation: Having listed twenty-two troubles that may strike a monk, often several at once, the lecture closes by saying he must not be overcome by any of them.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that even when troubles come piled on one another, the one who does not break inside defeats them; the Jain conclusion likewise requires the monk to stay undefeated by every trouble, wherever it attacks.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2, closing verse (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Gobind Singh had to give up Anandpur after a long siege in December 1705, saw his two elder sons die in the battle of Chamkaur, and then learned that his two younger sons had been executed at Sirhind. With only a few companions left, he wrote the Zafarnamah to Emperor Aurangzeb in a mood of unbroken spirit, declaring that the loss of his four children mattered little while the Khalsa still stood.
sikhism.explanation: This run of disasters, coming one after another within a few weeks, is remembered in Sikh history as the supreme test of Guru Gobind Singh's spirit, and his answer was the defiant Zafarnamah rather than despair.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that when troubles come piled one on another, the person who does not break inside makes the troubles themselves suffer; Guru Gobind Singh met a whole cascade of losses without breaking.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Zafarnamah', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles is set labour after labour by Eurystheus, from the Nemean lion and the Hydra to the Augean stables and the descent for Cerberus, each harder than the last and some disallowed so that more had to be added, yet he completes them all.
greek_mythology.explanation: The labours are a mythic catalogue of troubles stacked one on another, deliberately designed to break him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles is the Greek image of the Kural’s unbreakable one, whom an unending pile of trials only makes greater.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Ignis aurum probat, miseria fortes viros.” (Fire tests gold, misfortune brave men.)
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that the gods expose good people to repeated hardships the way fire assays gold, to reveal and strengthen their worth.
philosophy.tie_back: For Seneca as for the Kural, a flood of misfortunes does not destroy the steadfast but proves them.

real_life_example.event_title: Humayun loses his empire and regains Delhi years later
real_life_example.event: The Mughal emperor Humayun was defeated by Sher Shah Sur at Chausa in 1539 and at Kannauj in 1540 and was driven out of India. He took refuge with Shah Tahmasp of Persia, who gave him military aid, and he then took Kandahar and had to seize Kabul three times from his own disloyal brother Kamran. In 1555 he defeated Sikandar Sur at Sirhind and reoccupied Delhi and Agra, regaining his throne after more than a decade, though he died in an accident the following January.
real_life_example.explanation: Humayun suffered defeat, exile and betrayal by his own family one after another, yet he kept going and restored the Mughal dynasty that his son Akbar would make great.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even when troubles come piled one on another, the person who does not break inside makes those troubles suffer, and Humayun's long string of calamities ended in the recovery of his kingdom.

tamil:
அற்றேமென்று அல்லற் படுபவோ பெற்றேமென்று
ஓம்புதல் தேற்றா தவர்.
transliteration:
Atremendru allar patupavo petremendru
Ompudhal thetraa thavar.
meaning: People who never held on tightly to their riches, saying 'we have it,' will not cry 'we have lost it all' when it is gone.
elementary: If you share your toys freely and don’t get too attached to them, you won’t cry much when one breaks. The Kural says people who didn’t cling to their riches don’t fall apart when the riches are gone.
