university: The couplet sets two first-person plural verbs against each other: aṟṟēm, ‘we are bereft’, and peṟṟēm, ‘we have obtained’, the first the cry of the ruined man, the second the self-congratulation of the prosperous. Ōmputal tēṟṟātavar, ‘those who do not know (or care) to hoard and guard’, is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as those who did not greedily cling to wealth when they had it, while Solomon Pappaiah takes it as those who freely gave it away to others, and Kalaignar as those who were not elated by it; the three glosses share the idea that detachment in prosperity prevents despair in loss. The rhetorical question (paṭupavō, ‘would they suffer?’) expects the answer no, and the text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. The couplet shifts the chapter from enduring trouble to preventing it inwardly, preparing for the equanimity teaching of 627-629.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who has given up all desires for sense gratification, who lives free from desires, who has given up all sense of proprietorship and is devoid of false ego – he alone can attain real peace.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the one free of possessiveness (nirmama) and ego finds a peace that no loss can take away.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s person who never said ‘we have got it’ is the Gita’s nirmama, and that lack of possessiveness is why loss cannot make them wail.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.71 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes apostles who, holding nothing tightly, remain joyful even in poverty and grief.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s unclinging person who never cries ‘we are ruined’ matches Paul’s ‘having nothing, and yet possessing all things’.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches believers to hold gains and losses lightly, neither boasting over the one nor despairing over the other.
islam.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s couplet in reverse order: no exulting ‘we have it’, and therefore no despairing ‘we have lost it’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment with what one has rather than the amount one holds.
judaism.tie_back: A person who rejoices in his lot has nothing to wail over when fortune changes, just as the Kural says.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, we who possess nothing. Feeders on joy we shall be, like the Radiant Gods.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha, living without possessions, says his community is happy because it has nothing to lose.
buddhism.tie_back: Those who do not cling to what they own cannot be driven to despair by losing it; the Buddha’s joyful non-possession is the Kural’s point at its extreme.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
jainism.explanation: When Indra tells King Nami, newly turned monk, that his palace and city are on fire, Nami answers that nothing of his is burning, because he calls nothing his own.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether those who never clung to wealth as 'ours' will wail 'we have lost everything'; Nami's reply as Mithila burns is that exact attitude in story form.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If some of this capital is later taken back by the Banker, the ignorant person shows his anger. He himself destroys his own credibility, and he shall not again be trusted.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan compares all we possess to capital lent by God the Banker; the ignorant person who clings to it as his own grows angry when part of it is taken back.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether those who never clung to wealth as their own would wail at its loss; Guru Arjan shows that only the one who treats God's loan as his own rages when it is recalled.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 268, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, an old Phrygian couple, lived in a humble cottage, making their poverty light by owning it openly and bearing it contentedly; when the disguised gods Zeus and Hermes came, they gladly gave them their best, and were rewarded.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s old couple are the model of people who neither clung to goods nor were embittered by lacking them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their calm, generous poverty shows the Kural’s point: those who do not hoard do not despair when they have little.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never say of anything, ‘I have lost it’; but, ‘I have returned it.’ Is your child dead? It is returned. Is your wife dead? She is returned. Is your estate taken away? Well, and is not that likewise returned?”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that nothing external is truly ours, so its loss should be seen as giving back a loan.
philosophy.tie_back: Epictetus forbids the very cry the Kural mocks, ‘I have lost it’, by forbidding the possessive ‘I have it’ that comes before.

real_life_example.event_title: Chuck Feeney gives away his fortune and lives modestly
real_life_example.event: In 1984 Chuck Feeney, co-founder of the airport retailer Duty Free Shoppers, secretly transferred his entire 38.75 per cent stake in the company to his foundation, later known as The Atlantic Philanthropies, leaving himself with only a few million dollars. For the rest of his life he lived modestly in rented apartments, owned no car and flew economy. By the time the foundation closed in 2016 it had given away more than eight billion dollars.
real_life_example.explanation: Feeney treated his wealth as something to give rather than to hold, and he lived without the possessions that usually define a billionaire.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks whether those who never clung to their wealth would ever wail at losing it, and Feeney, who chose to part with almost everything he owned, shows the detachment the couplet praises.

tamil:
இலக்கம் உடம்பிடும்பைக் கென்று கலக்கத்தைக்
கையாறாக் கொள்ளாதாம் மேல்.
transliteration:
Ilakkam utampitumpaik kendru kalakkaththaik
Kaiyaaraak kollaadhaam mel.
meaning: Great people know the body is just a target for pain. So they do not treat the worry that pain brings as a disaster.
elementary: A football goal is made to have balls kicked at it; nobody is shocked when a ball hits it. The Kural says our bodies are a bit like that: bumps, colds and aches are bound to come, so wise people don’t panic when they do.
university: Ilakkam (from ilakku, ‘target’, cognate with Sanskrit lakṣya) makes the body the mark at which afflictions are aimed, an idea the commentators connect with the inevitability of bodily pain for every embodied being. Kalakkam is inner agitation, and kaiyāṟu is a rarer word that the traditional commentary takes as distress or helpless grief, so that the great ‘do not take agitation as (a cause of) distress’; Mu. Varadarasanar instead renders the construction as not adopting agitation as their way of conduct, showing a genuine interpretive divergence. Mēl, ‘the superior ones’, is the subject, with the verb in the honorific-epicene form koḷḷātām. The text is identical in both sources consulted, and Pope’s ‘Man’s frame is sorrow’s target, the noble mind reflects’ keeps the reasoning explicit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kunti, the contact between the senses and the sense objects gives rise to fleeting perceptions of happiness and distress. These are non-permanent, and come and go like the winter and summer seasons. O descendent of Bharat, one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna explains that bodily pleasure and pain are passing sensations like seasons, to be endured with titikṣā (forbearance).
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita and the Kural both hold that because bodily pain is natural and passing, the wise do not let it disturb the mind.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.”
christianity.explanation: Paul accepts that the body is wearing away under hardship while the inner self keeps being renewed.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul separates the body, which takes the blows, from the inner person, who need not lose heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “We have certainly created man into hardship.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an states plainly that toil and difficulty (kabad) are built into the human condition from creation.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s premise that the body is made to be a target of affliction, so hardship should not surprise or unsettle us.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But man is born unto trouble, As the sparks fly upward.”
judaism.explanation: Job’s friend Eliphaz observes that trouble is as natural to human beings as rising sparks are to fire.
judaism.tie_back: Eliphaz states the Kural’s first line, that human life is a natural target for sorrow.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sallatha Sutta the Buddha compares a painful bodily feeling to being struck by an arrow; the untaught person then adds a second arrow of mental distress by worrying and lamenting, while the well-taught disciple feels only the first, bodily arrow.
buddhism.explanation: Bodily pain is unavoidable, but the extra layer of mental agitation about it is optional and can be dropped.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s great ones accept the body as pain’s target yet refuse the kalakkam of the mind, exactly the Buddha’s refusal of the second arrow.

jainism.quote_or_event: “This body is not permanent, it is impure and of impure origin; it is but a transitory residence (of the soul) and a miserable vessel of suffering.”
jainism.explanation: Prince Mrigaputra tells his parents why he wants to renounce: the body is impermanent and by its nature a vessel of suffering for the soul (jiva) that dwells in it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the noble know the body is a target for pain and so are not shaken by it; Mrigaputra likewise sees the body as a natural vessel of suffering.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 19.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, I thought that I was in trouble; the whole world is in trouble!”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Sheikh Farid included in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sufi saint realises that suffering is not his alone but the common lot of everyone in the world.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the noble know the body is simply a target for pain and so do not treat it as a calamity; Farid likewise sees pain as the shared lot of all embodied beings.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles tells grieving Priam that two jars stand on Zeus’ threshold, one of evil gifts and one of good; Zeus gives some men a mixture and others only evil, so that no mortal escapes sorrow and all must endure what comes.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s image makes suffering a built-in portion of every human life handed out by the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ jars express the Kural’s premise that the embodied person is a natural target of trouble and should bear it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Sickness is a hindrance to the body, but not to your ability to choose, unless that is your choice. Lameness is a hindrance to the leg, but not to your ability to choose.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus insists that bodily afflictions touch only the body, not the mind’s own power of choice.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts locate pain in the body and deny it any right to throw the mind into turmoil.

real_life_example.event_title: Matisse turns to paper cut-outs after major surgery
real_life_example.event: In 1941 Henri Matisse underwent serious abdominal surgery that left him in poor health and bedridden much of the time, often working from a bed or a wheelchair. Unable to stand at an easel for long, he turned increasingly to cutting shapes with scissors from paper painted with gouache by his assistants, which were then pinned up as he directed. These cut-outs, made in what he called a second life, became some of the most celebrated works of his career.
real_life_example.explanation: Matisse did not let a failing body become the end of his art; he treated its limits as a condition to work within and found a new form of expression.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the noble know the body is simply a target for pain and so do not treat its distress as a true calamity, and Matisse, confined to bed and chair, went on creating as if his body's suffering were no disaster to his work.

tamil:
இன்பம் விழையான் இடும்பை இயல்பென்பான்
துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்.
transliteration:
Inpam vizhaiyaan itumpai iyalpenpaan
Thunpam urudhal ilan.
meaning: A person who does not chase after pleasure, and who accepts that hard times are a normal part of life, never really falls into misery.
elementary: If you expect every day to be a party, a rainy day feels awful. But if you know that some days are rainy and that’s normal, you just grab an umbrella. The Kural says people who don’t demand fun all the time don’t get crushed when hard times come.
university: The couplet pairs two participial nouns, iṉpam viḻaiyāṉ, ‘one who does not crave pleasure’, and iṭumpai iyalpeṉpāṉ, ‘one who says hardship is natural (iyalpu)’, and concludes that such a person ‘has no falling into sorrow’ (tuṉpam uṟutal ilaṉ). Solomon Pappaiah restricts the pleasure in question to bodily pleasure, in line with 627’s focus on the body, while Kalaignar reads it more broadly as not roaming in search of enjoyment. The shift from iṭumpai (hardship, the event) to tuṉpam (suffering, the experience) is significant: hardship still comes, but it no longer becomes suffering. The text is the same in both sources, and Pope renders it ‘He seeks not joy, to sorrow man is born, he knows’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One whose mind remains undisturbed amidst misery, who does not crave for pleasure, and who is free from attachment, fear, and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines the sthita-prajña, the person of steady wisdom, as one who neither craves pleasure nor is shaken by misery.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s two conditions, no craving for pleasure and no disturbance in misery, are the two halves of this Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples to expect tribulation as a normal part of life in the world, yet to stay cheerful.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus’ ‘ye shall have tribulation’ is the Kural’s iṭumpai iyalpu, and his ‘be of good cheer’ its promise that such a person is not undone.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do the people think that they will be left to say, ‘We believe’ and they will not be tried?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that trial is the normal, expected lot of anyone who claims faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the verse teaches that hardship is part of life’s nature, so no one should be shocked into despair by it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good that befalls him.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah requires Jews to bless God for misfortune as well as for good fortune, treating both as part of life’s ordinary course.
judaism.tie_back: Blessing the bad as one blesses the good is a ritual form of the Kural’s acceptance of hardship as natural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief back to attachment to what is pleasing; without that attachment, grief has no root.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says the one who does not crave pleasure does not fall into sorrow; the Dhammapada gives the reason, since sorrow grows from craving.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Not resentful, having few wants, begging from strangers, and not being dainty, a wise man should not long for pleasant things, nor be sorry afterwards (for not having got them).”
jainism.explanation: Under the trouble of honour and respectful treatment, the monk is told not to crave pleasant things and not to regret their absence.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural describes one who does not chase pleasure and takes hardship as natural, and so never sinks into misery; the Jain verse prescribes both halves, not longing for pleasant things and not grieving at their lack.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Suffering is the medicine, and pleasure the disease, because where there is pleasure, there is no desire for God.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak turns the usual valuation upside down: hardship heals and comfort sickens, because comfort makes a person forget God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the one who does not chase pleasure and accepts hardship as natural; Guru Nanak goes further and calls hardship the medicine and pleasure the disease.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Offered ease and immortality on Calypso’s island, Odysseus chooses instead the hard road home to Ithaca, saying that if some god wrecks him on the sea he will bear it, since he has already endured much on land and sea and can add this to the rest.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus turns down endless pleasure and treats further hardship as simply part of his lot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the Kural’s man who does not crave pleasure and calls hardship natural, and so is not broken by it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nothing happens to any man which he is not formed by nature to bear.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that whatever befalls a human being is within human nature’s capacity to endure.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s view that hardship is iyalpu, natural to us, is Marcus’s view that we are formed by nature to bear it.

real_life_example.event_title: The Zen poet Ryokan chooses a life of poverty in a mountain hut
real_life_example.event: Ryokan (1758-1831), a village headman's son who became a Zen Buddhist priest, never took charge of a temple. After years as a wandering mendicant he returned to his native Echigo province, where he lived mostly as a hermit in a small mountain hut, begging for alms. He is remembered as one of the great poets and calligraphers of the Edo period, and he often wrote with twigs or practised brushstrokes in the air when he could not afford brushes or paper.
real_life_example.explanation: Ryokan accepted hunger, cold and poverty as the ordinary conditions of his chosen life, and his poetry and calligraphy came out of that simplicity rather than in spite of it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who does not chase pleasure and accepts hardship as natural never falls into real misery, and Ryokan, who sought no comfort and lived on alms, is remembered for serenity rather than suffering.

tamil:
இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான் துன்பத்துள்
துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்.
transliteration:
Inpaththul inpam vizhaiyaadhaan thunpaththul
Thunpam urudhal ilan.
meaning: A person who does not chase after pleasure in good times will not be crushed by sadness in bad times.
elementary: If you jump up and down screaming when you win a game, you might cry just as hard when you lose. But if you enjoy the win calmly, you can handle the loss calmly too. The Kural says staying balanced in good times keeps you steady in bad times.
university: The couplet is built as a strict parallel, iṉpattuḷ iṉpam / tuṉpattuḷ tuṉpam, ‘in pleasure, pleasure’ and ‘in sorrow, sorrow’, so that the inner response mirrors the outer situation in each case. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the first half as not cherishing and clinging to pleasure when it comes, and Kalaignar summarises it with a Tamil jingle, not dancing in joy and not wilting in sorrow, as an example of regarding both alike. It differs from 628 in that it concerns one’s attitude within pleasure already present rather than the pursuit of pleasure. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, and Pope’s ‘Mid joys he yields not heart to joys’ control’ captures the sense of inner restraint.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Established in God, having a firm understanding of divine knowledge and not hampered by delusion, they neither rejoice in getting something pleasant nor grieve on experiencing the unpleasant.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the knower of Brahman as one who neither exults (na prahṛṣyet) at the pleasant nor is shaken by the unpleasant.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita gives both halves of the Kural in the same order: no elation in pleasure, and so no grief in pain.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he has learned to stay the same person whether he has plenty or nothing.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s evenness in abundance and need is the Kural’s balance that refuses to be carried away in either direction.

islam.quote_or_event: “Strange are the ways of a believer for there is good in every affair of his … for if he has an occasion to feel delight, he thanks (God), thus there is a good for him in it, and if he gets into trouble and shows resignation (and endures it patiently), there is a good for him in it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the believer who meets good times with gratitude and bad times with patience, so that neither overturns him.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hadith prescribes a measured response in joy that makes a measured response in sorrow possible.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider; God hath made even the one as well as the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth teaches that good and bad days both come from God, so neither should be treated as permanent or ultimate.
judaism.tie_back: Koheleth, like the Kural, pairs prosperity and adversity and asks for a measured, thoughtful response to each.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The good renounce (attachment for) everything. The virtuous do not prattle with a yearning for pleasures. The wise show no elation or depression when touched by happiness or sorrow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada describes the wise as neither lifted up by happiness nor cast down by sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘No elation or depression when touched by happiness or sorrow’ is almost a paraphrase of this Kural’s balanced pair.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He was indifferent to success or failure (in begging), to happiness and misery, to life and death, to blame and praise, to honour and insult.”
jainism.explanation: After renouncing, Mrigaputra is described as unmoved equally by happiness and misery, success and failure.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says one who does not revel in good times will not be sunk in bad times; the Jain ideal of equal indifference to happiness and misery is the same balance.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 19.90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who is not affected by pleasure or pain, who looks upon friend and enemy alike”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks at the close of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the liberated person as one whom neither joy nor sorrow can sway.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one who does not revel in good times will not sink in bad times; Guru Tegh Bahadur praises the one whom neither pleasure nor pain can move.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Niobe, queen of Thebes, exulted so boastfully in her fourteen children that she set herself above the goddess Leto; when Apollo and Artemis struck them all down, her grief was so boundless that she turned to stone and weeps forever.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Niobe is the cautionary opposite of the Kural’s ideal: unrestrained delight in good fortune followed by unrestrained despair in loss.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Her story shows the Kural in reverse: one who revels without measure in joy is drowned without measure in sorrow.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Consolation of Philosophy, Lady Philosophy shows Boethius that Fortune’s nature is to change, so whoever lets himself be lifted up by her gifts has already set himself up to be crushed when she withdraws them.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius learns that attachment to good fortune is what gives bad fortune its sting.
philosophy.tie_back: Philosophy teaches Boethius the Kural’s lesson: restraint in the enjoyment of good fortune is protection against despair in bad.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II

real_life_example.event_title: Su Shi remains cheerful through exile to Huangzhou and Hainan
real_life_example.event: Su Shi, one of China's greatest poets and a successful official, was banished in 1079 to Huangzhou because of his opposition to the reforms of the minister Wang Anshi. There he farmed a plot on an eastern slope, took from it the name Dongpo, by which he is still known, and wrote some of his best-known works, including the Red Cliff rhapsodies of 1082. He showed the same optimism and lack of bitterness when he was banished again to Hainan Island in 1094, and he stayed on friendly terms with Wang Anshi, exchanging poems with him.
real_life_example.explanation: Su Shi's equanimity under disgrace became part of his fame, and the works he wrote in exile are among the best loved in Chinese literature.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the one who does not greedily revel in good times will not be sunk in sorrow in bad times, and Su Shi, who moved from high office to a farmer's life without bitterness, shows the evenness of mind the couplet describes.

tamil:
இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின் ஆகுந்தன்
ஒன்னார் விழையுஞ் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Innaamai inpam enakkolin aakundhan
Onnaar vizhaiyunj chirappu.
meaning: If a person can take hard times as if they were good times, they will win a kind of greatness that even their enemies admire and wish they had.
elementary: Imagine a runner who smiles even while climbing the steepest hill in a race. Even the runners from the other team end up cheering for her. The Kural says if you can treat hard work and hard times as something good, even people who don’t like you will respect you.
university: Iṉṉāmai, ‘the unpleasant, pain’, is the negative of iṉṉā (sweet), so the couplet literally asks one to count the un-sweet as sweet (iṉpam eṉakkoḷiṉ). The reward is ciṟappu, eminence or distinction, qualified as oṉṉār viḻaiyum, ‘which even foes (oṉṉār, those not at one with us) desire or esteem’; ākuntaṉ is ākum taṉ with the final m assimilated, and viḻaiyuñ likewise before ciṟappu. Solomon Pappaiah specifies the hardship as that met while carrying out an undertaking, keeping the chapter’s Parimelazhagar-style link to the king’s or doer’s enterprise, while Mu. Varadarasanar reads it generally. The two sources agree on the text, and the couplet closes the chapter by turning the whole theme outward: inner mastery of trouble becomes public honour.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That which in the beginning may be just like poison but at the end is just like nectar and which awakens one to self-realization is said to be happiness in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the highest kind of happiness often tastes bitter at first and only later proves sweet.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s poison-that-becomes-nectar is the Kural’s pain accepted as pleasure, which in the end yields true distinction.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.37 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ’s sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.”
christianity.explanation: Paul declares that he actually takes pleasure in hardships, because through them he finds real strength.
christianity.tie_back: Paul does what the Kural commends, treating pain as pleasure, and finds in it a strength others cannot take away.

islam.quote_or_event: “But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allāh knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that what feels painful may in fact be good, since God sees its outcome.
islam.tie_back: The Kural asks us to count the painful as pleasant; the Qur’an explains why this can be wise, since the disliked may be the good.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph, once sold into slavery by his brothers, now rules Egypt and tells them the suffering they caused became the means of great good.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph treats his years of pain as a gift, and the brothers who once hated him now bow before his greatness, as the Kural predicts.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though one may conquer a thousand times a thousand men in battle, yet he indeed is the noblest victor who conquers himself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the greatest victory and honour belong to the one who masters his own mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s person who can turn pain into pleasure has won this inner victory, and it earns an honour that outshines conquest over enemies.

jainism.quote_or_event: “For more than twelve years the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira neglected his body and abandoned the care of it; he with equanimity bore, underwent, and suffered all pleasant or unpleasant occurrences arising from divine powers, men, or animals.”
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra says Mahavira bore all hardships, from gods, men and animals, with equanimity for more than twelve years before attaining omniscience (kevala), after which gods and men honoured him.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural promises distinction even enemies admire to one who takes hardship as if it were pleasure; Mahavira's equal acceptance of pleasant and unpleasant ordeals is the Jain model of that, and led to his supreme standing.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §117 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If You will bless me with happiness, then I will worship and adore You. Even in pain, I will meditate on You.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das vows to turn to God in exactly the same way in pain as in happiness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks us to take hardship as if it were pleasure; Guru Ram Das treats pain and happiness alike as occasions to remember God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads, the young Heracles is approached by two women, Vice offering an easy life of pleasure and Virtue offering a hard road of toil; he chooses Virtue’s arduous path, which leads to lasting glory.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prodicus’ fable, retold by Xenophon, makes the willing embrace of hardship the way to true renown.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles chooses toil as the Kural’s person counts pain as pleasure, and both win a fame the world must acknowledge.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Nietzsche resolves to learn more and more to see what is necessary in things as beautiful, calling this amor fati, love of fate, and hoping one day to be only a Yes-sayer.
philosophy.explanation: Nietzsche’s ideal is not merely to endure hardship but to affirm and love it as part of one’s life.
philosophy.tie_back: Amor fati is a modern echo of the Kural’s counsel to take pain itself as pleasure.

real_life_example.event_title: Abdelkader, after defeat and captivity, wins the esteem of Europe
real_life_example.event: Abdelkader, who led Algerian resistance against French conquest, surrendered in December 1847 on the promise of passage to the East but was instead held in France for about four years until Louis-Napoleon allowed his release in 1852. He settled in Damascus, and during the communal violence of July 1860 he and his followers sheltered and protected thousands of Christians at great personal risk. As a result he was highly commended by several European governments.
real_life_example.explanation: A defeated enemy who had endured years of broken promises and captivity emerged with a moral standing that the European powers themselves honoured.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who can take hardship as though it were sweet will win a distinction even enemies admire, and Abdelkader, after defeat and captivity, won praise from the very European world whose armies he had fought.

tamil:
கருவியும் காலமும் செய்கையும் செய்யும்
அருவினையும் மாண்டது அமைச்சு.
transliteration:
Karuviyum kaalamum seykaiyum seyyum
Aruvinaiyum maandadhu amaichchu.
meaning: A good minister (an adviser to the king) is excellent at planning the tools needed, the right time, the way to do it, and the hard task itself.
elementary: Think of a team captain planning a school play. A good captain asks: what props do we need, when should we rehearse, how should we do each scene, and what is the hardest part? This kural says a good adviser always thinks about all four of those things.
university: The couplet opens the Amaichiyal (the section on ministers, chapters 64-73) by defining the minister (amaichu, an abstract noun used for the office-holder) through four objects of deliberation: karuvi (instruments or means, which commentators gloss as troops and wealth), kaalam (the fitting time), seykai (the mode or method of execution) and seyyum aruvinai (the difficult undertaking to be carried out). The verb maandadhu (‘excels, is perfected in’) makes the definition a standard of excellence, not merely a job description. Parimelazhagar and later commentators such as Mu. Varadarasanar read the list as the components of good counsel, which lines up closely with Kautilya’s five limbs of mantra (Arthashastra 1.15). The text is stable across ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and the older-orthography thirukkural-thamizh.org edition, where it appears as ‘karuviyum kaalamum seykaiyum seyyu / maruvinaiyu maanda thamaichchu’. The difference is only in how the words are split; the reading is the same.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Means to carry out works, command of plenty of men and wealth, allotment of time and place, remedies against dangers, and final success are the five constituents of every council deliberation.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya lists what every royal council must weigh: the means, the resources, the right time and place, what could go wrong, and how to finish.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s four items (means, time, method, the hard task) are almost the same checklist.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points out that a sensible king sits down and weighs his resources before starting a war.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural asks the minister to weigh means and difficulty in the same way before acting.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Joseph] said, ‘You will plant for seven years consecutively; and what you harvest leave in its spikes, except a little from which you will eat.’”
islam.explanation: Joseph advises the king of Egypt on what to do (plant), when (seven years), and how (store the grain in the ear) to get through a coming famine.
islam.tie_back: Joseph’s counsel covers the same things the Kural lists: means, timing, method and a hard task.

judaism.quote_or_event: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet teaches that every action has its proper time.
judaism.tie_back: Kaalam, the right time, is one of the four things the Kural’s minister must master.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And how is a monk one with a sense of time? There is the case where a monk knows the time: ‘This is the time for recitation; this, the time for questioning; this, the time for making an effort [in meditation]; this, the time for seclusion.’”
buddhism.explanation: Among seven marks of a worthy person, the Buddha lists knowing the right time for each kind of activity.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the sutta treats knowing the right time as a skill a capable person must have.
buddhism.source: Dhammaññu Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 7.64 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The king of Ujjayinī would be my fight-guest today; yet in a matter to be settled by wit, talk of sword against sword is idle. Therefore, I shall use wit. Verily, wit is a cow of plenty for producing victory.”
jainism.explanation: When Pradyota besieges Rajagriha, King Shrenika turns to his son and minister Abhayakumara, who judges that this crisis calls for strategy rather than battle and picks his means to suit it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural defines the minister by skill in choosing the means, the time and the method for a hard task; Abhaya's reply shows a minister weighing the situation and choosing the right instrument.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: In the Zafarnamah, his Persian verse letter to Emperor Aurangzeb written in 1706, Guru Gobind Singh set out when force may rightly be used. In its often-quoted verse 22 he says, in effect, that it is lawful to take up the sword only when all other means have failed. The letter judges public policy by moral principle and stresses the importance of means over ends.
sikhism.explanation: The Zafarnamah is the nearest thing in Sikh sources to a statement of statecraft: it weighs the right means and the right moment before a grave course of action is taken.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines the minister as one who thinks through the means, the right time and the method; the Zafarnamah likewise ties a grave decision to exhausting other means and choosing the right time.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Zafarnamah', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Kairos, the Greek personification of the opportune moment, was shown by the sculptor Lysippus as a youth with a lock of hair in front and a bald head behind. The point was that the right moment can be grasped as it comes but not once it has passed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greeks made the fleeting right moment into a divine figure that had to be seized at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural lists kaalam, knowing the right time, as a core skill of the counsellor.
greek_mythology.source: Posidippus, epigram on the Kairos of Lysippus (Greek Anthology 16.275), summarized via Theoi Project

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…excellence in deliberation, which is rightness with regard to the expedient-rightness in respect both of the end, the manner, and the time.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines good deliberation (euboulia) as getting right what is useful, including the goal, the way it is done, and the timing.
philosophy.tie_back: End, manner and time closely match the Kural’s task, method and time.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.9 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Cavour wins France as Piedmont's ally against Austria
real_life_example.place: Turin, Paris and Plombieres, France; northern Italy
real_life_example.event: As prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia, Count Camillo di Cavour brought his small state into the Crimean War alongside Britain and France and then secured a place at the Congress of Paris in 1856, where he raised the Italian question before the great powers. At a secret meeting at Plombieres in July 1858 he and Napoleon III agreed on a war against Austria in the following year. When Austria sent Piedmont an ultimatum in 1859, the Franco-Piedmontese alliance came into force, and the war that followed won Lombardy for Piedmont.
real_life_example.explanation: Cavour judged that Piedmont alone could not drive Austria out of Italy, so he spent years acquiring the means (a great-power ally), waiting for the right moment and choosing a method that let Austria appear the aggressor.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines the excellent minister as one who masters the means, the time, the method and the difficult task itself, and Cavour's patient preparation of all four for the hard task of challenging Austria is a clear case of it.

tamil:
வன்கண் குடிகாத்தல் கற்றறிதல் ஆள்வினையோடு
ஐந்துடன் மாண்டது அமைச்சு.
transliteration:
Vankan kudikaaththal katrarithal aalvinaiyodu
Aindhudan maandadhu amaichchu.
meaning: A good minister is also excellent in five more things: firm courage, protecting the people, learning, understanding, and hard work.
elementary: A good class monitor is brave enough to speak up, looks after classmates, keeps learning, and does not give up when a job gets hard. This kural says a good adviser needs all of these together, not just one.
university: The couplet names further qualities: vankan (firmness or fearlessness, literally ‘hard eye’), kudikaaththal (protecting the subjects), katrarithal (knowing through study), and aalvinai (sustained effort, the subject of chapter 62). The phrase aindhudan (‘with the five’) is read in more than one way. In the Parimelazhagar tradition it refers back to the qualities already listed, so the minister has these as well as those. Mu. Varadarasanar splits kudi as noble birth (kudippirappu) and kaaththal as protection so that the verse itself lists five. Puliyur Kesikan instead takes the five as the purity of the five senses. Solomon Pappaiah divides katru and arithal into learning from books and learning by listening to the learned. The older-orthography edition prints ‘katrarithalaalvinaiyo / daindhudan’, which is the same text with a different word division.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…possessed of foresight, wise, of strong memory, bold, eloquent, skilful, intelligent, possessed of enthusiasm, dignity and endurance…”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya gives a long list of qualities for a minister, including wisdom, boldness, learning and staying power.
hinduism.tie_back: Boldness, learning and endurance match the Kural’s vankan, katrarithal and aalvinai almost one for one.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.”
christianity.explanation: The apostles pick administrators to care for the community’s needy, requiring good character and wisdom.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it chooses officials by character and wisdom so that they can look after the people.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of the women said, ‘O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy.’”
islam.explanation: A daughter of Madyan urges her father to employ Moses because he is both strong and trustworthy.
islam.tie_back: Strength and reliability match the Kural’s firmness and dependable protection of those in one’s care.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.”
judaism.explanation: Jethro advises Moses to share his burden by appointing capable, honest men to govern and judge the people.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Jethro sets out the qualities of those who help a leader rule and protect the people.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, the Buddha tells of a wise royal chaplain who advises a king to deal with banditry by giving seed to farmers, capital to traders, and proper wages to officials, rather than by punishment. The kingdom becomes prosperous and safe.
buddhism.explanation: The ideal counsellor here protects the people by fixing the economic causes of disorder.
buddhism.tie_back: This is kudikaaththal, protecting the people, carried out through wise and learned counsel.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Thus I became the protector of myself and of others besides, of all living beings, whether they move or not.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anathi explains to King Shrenika that by renouncing and keeping the vows he became a true protector of all beings, unlike the king with all his wealth and army.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural lists protecting the people among a minister's qualities, with firmness, learning and effort; the Jain verse recasts protection as the ahimsa of the self-controlled person toward all living beings.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: In May 1675 a group of Kashmiri Pandits, persecuted under the Mughal governor of Kashmir, came to Guru Tegh Bahadur at Anandpur for help. According to the Gurbilas account cited in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, the Guru said that the earth's burden would be lifted only if a worthy person gave his head, and the young Gobind Das replied that none was worthier than the Guru himself. Guru Tegh Bahadur took up their cause and was executed in Delhi later that year.
sikhism.explanation: Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur as one who gave his life to protect the freedom of conscience of people who were not even of his own faith.
sikhism.tie_back: Among a minister's qualities the Kural lists firm courage and the protection of the people; Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom is the Sikh model of fearless protection of the vulnerable.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Tegh Bahadur, Guru', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus leaves for Troy he puts his old friend Mentor in charge of his household. In the Ithacan assembly, Mentor boldly rebukes the people for allowing the suitors to waste the absent king’s estate.
greek_mythology.explanation: Mentor is the trusted steward who guards what belongs to his lord and speaks out bravely.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He shows two of the Kural’s qualities, courage (vankan) and protection of those in his charge.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero reminds those who take charge of public affairs of two rules from Plato: to keep the good of the citizens so clearly in view that everything they do serves it, and to care for the whole body politic rather than one part of it.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, the first duty of a statesman is to protect the welfare of all citizens, not a faction.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s kudikaaththal, protecting the people, as a basic mark of a minister.

real_life_example.event_title: Sardar Patel brings the princely states into the Indian Union
real_life_example.event: At independence in 1947, rulers of the princely states, covering about two fifths of India's territory, were free to join India or Pakistan or to stay out of both. Vallabhbhai Patel, as deputy prime minister and minister in charge of the new States Department, worked with its secretary V. P. Menon to bring them in one by one. Over 560 princely states were brought into the Indian Union within a short span of time.
real_life_example.explanation: The work called for firmness with reluctant rulers, steady concern for the security of the people, a knowledge of law and administration, and unbroken effort over many months.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural adds firmness, protection of the people, learning and persevering effort to the minister's qualities, and Patel's integration of the princely states displayed all of them in a single task.

tamil:
பிரித்தலும் பேணிக் கொளலும் பிரிந்தார்ப்
பொருத்தலும் வல்ல தமைச்சு.
transliteration:
Piriththalum paenik kolalum pirindhaarp
Poruththalum valla thamaichchu.
meaning: A good minister knows how to pull allies away from the enemy, keep their own side loyal, and win back people who have left.
elementary: Imagine two teams in a playground game. A clever captain can persuade kids who are thinking of joining the other team to stay neutral, keep his own teammates happy, and make friends again with anyone who left in a huff. This kural says a good adviser has those three skills.
university: The couplet names three diplomatic skills. Piriththal is detaching allies from the enemy. Paenik kolal is keeping one’s own supporters, which Solomon Pappaiah explains as keeping them through gifts and kind words. Pirindhaar poruththal is reconciling those who have left. Commentators link these to the classical upayas (means of statecraft): bheda (division), dana (gifts) and sama (conciliation). Kautilya treats the same means at length. The last words, valla thamaichchu, are an older way of writing valladhu amaichchu (‘the minister is one capable of’), and all three sources agree on the text. Varadarasanar’s gloss and Kalaignar’s specify that those to be divided are the enemy’s helpers, which keeps the verse within fair statecraft rather than general intrigue.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the Kurukshetra war, Krishna travels to Hastinapura as envoy to try to reconcile the Kauravas and the Pandavas. He first appeals for peace and offers a settlement. He also warns Duryodhana’s allies and elders about the cost of war, which works on the loyalties within the Kaurava camp.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna’s embassy uses conciliation, offers and division, the classical upayas, in one mission.
hinduism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s three skills of reconciling, retaining and dividing as the work of a counsellor-envoy.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavat-yana section), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had so said, there arose a dissension between the Pharisees and the Sadducees: and the multitude was divided.”
christianity.explanation: On trial before the council, Paul declares himself a Pharisee on the question of resurrection, which splits his hostile judges into two factions.
christianity.tie_back: This is piriththal, dividing an opposing party, done with a single well-judged word.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you - when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together and you became, by His favor, brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an reminds the believers that once-hostile groups were reconciled into brotherhood and warns them against splitting apart.
islam.tie_back: It praises the Kural’s last two skills, holding one’s own people together and reuniting those who were divided.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Absalom and all the men of Israel said: ‘The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.’—For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil upon Absalom.”
judaism.explanation: David sends his loyal friend Hushai into the rebel Absalom’s council, where Hushai’s advice overturns Ahithophel’s dangerous plan.
judaism.tie_back: Hushai breaks up the enemy’s counsel from within while staying loyal to his king. This is piriththal carried out by a counsellor.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Maha-parinibbana Sutta, King Ajatasattu sends his minister Vassakara to ask the Buddha about attacking the Vajjians. The Buddha lists seven conditions, among them meeting often and in harmony, that keep the Vajjians strong. Vassakara concludes that they cannot be conquered by force, only through diplomacy or by breaking up their unity.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta shows both sides: unity protects a people, and a shrewd minister sees that division is the way to defeat them.
buddhism.tie_back: It sets keeping one’s people together against dividing an opponent, the two poles of the Kural’s verse.

jainism.quote_or_event: “All your princes have been seduced by King Śreṇika. Money has been sent them to make them his; and they, after accepting it, will bind you and deliver you to my father. The money has been buried in their dwellings for their benefit. Dig and look.”
jainism.explanation: Abhayakumara buries money in the camp of Pradyota's allied princes and then warns Pradyota that they have been bribed; Pradyota digs, finds the money and flees, and his allies' army breaks up.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises the minister who can split the enemy's allies away; Abhaya's stratagem does exactly that, turning Pradyota against his own princes without a battle.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: During the long siege of Anandpur a band of Sikhs disowned Guru Gobind Singh and deserted him. Later, repentant, they returned and died fighting for him at Khidrana on 29 December 1705. The Guru tore up their written disclaimer and blessed them as the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated Ones, and the place became Muktsar.
sikhism.explanation: The Chali Mukte are remembered daily in the Sikh Ardas; their story is one of estranged followers taken back and honoured rather than rejected.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural prizes the minister who can bring back those who have broken away; Guru Gobind Singh received the deserters back and erased the record of their desertion.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Chali Mukte', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Achilles withdraws from the fighting in anger, Agamemnon sends Odysseus, Ajax and old Phoenix to him with offers of gifts to win him back to the Greek army.
greek_mythology.explanation: The embassy is a formal attempt to reconcile an estranged ally through gifts and persuasion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is pirindhaar poruththal, bringing back those who have split away, which the Kural counts as a minister’s skill.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu advises that when the enemy’s forces are united they should be separated, and he treats breaking up the enemy’s alliances as better than attacking his army in the field.
philosophy.explanation: Classical Chinese strategy puts diplomatic division before open battle.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s first skill, piriththal, as a doctrine of statecraft.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War I and III (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Talleyrand splits the victorious allies at the Congress of Vienna
real_life_example.event: At the Congress of Vienna the four victorious powers, Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia, negotiated the post-Napoleonic settlement, with defeated France represented by its foreign minister, Talleyrand. When Russia and Prussia pressed claims that alarmed Britain and Austria, Talleyrand proposed a secret treaty of guarantee between Britain, France and Austria. It was signed on 3 January 1815, setting three powers against Russia and Prussia and giving France a seat at the great powers' table.
real_life_example.explanation: Representing a defeated country with no allies, Talleyrand turned the disagreements of the victors to France's advantage by drawing two of them into an alliance with his own country.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the minister who can detach the enemy's allies and bring others over to his side, which is exactly what Talleyrand did to the coalition that had defeated France.

tamil:
தெரிதலும் தேர்ந்து செயலும் ஒருதலையாச்
சொல்லலும் வல்லது அமைச்சு.
transliteration:
Theridhalum thaerndhu seyalum orudhalaiyaach
Sollalum valladhu amaichchu.
meaning: A good minister can study a problem carefully, act only after choosing wisely, and give a firm, clear answer.
elementary: A good referee watches the play closely, thinks for a moment, and then makes a clear call. He does not say “maybe”. This kural says a good adviser looks carefully, chooses wisely, and then speaks clearly.
university: Three abilities are named. Theridhal is examining or understanding the matter. Thaerndhu seyal is acting after deliberate selection of means. Orudhalaiyaach sollal is speaking decisively (orudhalai, ‘one-sided’, i.e. unambiguous). Commentators differ on the last. Varadarasanar and Kesikan take it as boldness and clarity, while Solomon Pappaiah stresses asserting only what is beneficial. The Parimelazhagar tradition ties it to giving the king a settled opinion rather than a list of options, much as Kautilya’s teacher Pishuna asks for counsellors ‘capable of giving decisive opinion’. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read valladhu amaichu, and thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the older form ‘valla thamaichchu’. The two are the same words divided differently.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Hence he shall consult such persons as are believed to be capable of giving decisive opinion regarding those works about which he seeks far advice.”
hinduism.explanation: In the Arthashastra’s debate on counsel, the teacher Pishuna argues that a king should consult men who can give firm, decisive advice rather than half-hearted opinions.
hinduism.tie_back: This is orudhalaiyaach sollal, the decisive word, which the Kural requires of a minister.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that speech should be plain and definite, without evasive hedging or extra oaths.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise praises the minister who can say one clear thing.

islam.quote_or_event: “So pardon them and ask forgiveness for them and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to consult his companions and, once a decision is made, to carry it out with trust in God.
islam.tie_back: This follows the Kural’s order: think it through, decide, then act firmly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Every purpose is established by counsel; and with good advice carry on war.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that plans succeed when built on deliberation, and that even war must be waged by wise guidance.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s thaerndhu seyal: acting only after deliberate choice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kalama Sutta, the Buddha tells the Kalamas not to accept teachings on report, tradition or a teacher’s authority alone. They should examine them, and once they know for themselves what is skilful and beneficial, adopt and practise it.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lays out a method of careful examination followed by committed action.
buddhism.tie_back: It follows the Kural’s sequence of theridhal (examining) and then thaerndhu seyal (acting on what one has chosen).

jainism.quote_or_event: “He, being wise, smelled the food-bag and pronounced this decision, ‘There is here a serpent that poisons by its glance, that originated from the combination of substances. If he had opened the bag, he would have been consumed, certainly. So turn it loose in the forest with your face averted.’”
jainism.explanation: Held captive at Pradyota's court, Abhayakumara is asked about a messenger's food-bag; he examines it, gives a clear diagnosis and a definite instruction, and the danger is shown to be real.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a minister must study a matter, act after careful choice and state a firm conclusion; Abhaya examines the bag and gives a single, decisive verdict.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Wisdom leads us to serve our Lord and Master; through wisdom, honor is obtained.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak praises akal, practical wisdom and discernment, as what guides right action and earns honour.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural wants the minister to understand a matter, act after careful choice and state his conclusion firmly; Guru Nanak likewise makes discerning wisdom the guide of right action.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops’ cave, Odysseus first wants to stab the sleeping Polyphemus. He stops himself when he realizes that his men could never move the huge stone from the doorway. He works out a slower plan (the wine, the blinding stake and the escape under the rams) and carries it through.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus checks his impulse, thinks the situation through, and then acts on a well-chosen plan.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This shows the Kural’s ideal of examining a situation and acting only after careful choice.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Discourse on Method, Descartes’ second provisional maxim is to be as firm and resolute in action as he can. Once he has settled on a course, even a doubtful one, he follows it steadily, like travellers lost in a forest who should walk straight in one direction rather than wander in circles.
philosophy.explanation: Descartes argues that after reasonable deliberation, being decisive is itself a practical virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s thaerndhu seyal and its firm, one-directional conclusion.
philosophy.source: Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part III

real_life_example.event_title: The Beveridge Report sets out a plan against the five giant evils
real_life_example.event: In June 1941 William Beveridge was asked to head a committee of inquiry surveying Britain's patchwork social insurance schemes. His report, Social Insurance and Allied Services, was presented to Parliament on 24 November 1942 and proposed a comprehensive system of social insurance to attack five great evils: want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. More than 600,000 copies of the report and its summaries were sold by February 1944, and after the war Parliament passed the National Insurance Act of 1946 and established the National Health Service in 1948.
real_life_example.explanation: Beveridge's report was valued because it combined a thorough survey of existing provision with a single, clearly argued plan rather than a list of loose options.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names three abilities of a counsellor, examining a matter fully, choosing the course with care and stating a firm, clear conclusion, and the Beveridge Report is a model of all three.

tamil:
அறனறிந்து ஆன்றமைந்த சொல்லான்எஞ் ஞான்றுந்
திறனறிந்தான் தேர்ச்சித் துணை.
transliteration:
Aranarindhu aandramaindha sollaan enjnjaandrum
Thiranarindhaan thaerchchith thunai.
meaning: The best person to plan with is someone who knows what is right, speaks with deep knowledge and care, and always knows how to get things done.
elementary: When you need advice about something hard, you go to the person who knows right from wrong, speaks calmly and carefully, and knows the practical steps. This kural says that kind of person is the best helper for a leader.
university: The couplet sets out three qualifications for a thaerchchith thunai, a ‘companion in deliberation’. The first is aranarindhu, knowing aram (dharma or righteousness). The second is aandramaindha sollaan, one whose speech is full (aandru, ‘abundant, filled with learning’) and measured (amaindha, ‘settled, restrained’). The third is enjnjaandrum thiranarindhaan, one who always knows the method. Commentators differ over whether aandru points to learning, as Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take it, or to maturity. Pappaiah reads amaindha as modest or restrained speech. Parimelazhagar’s reading places moral knowledge first, so the counsellor’s skill serves aram rather than mere expediency. All three editions agree on the text; the older one divides it as ‘aranarindh aandramaindha sollaanenjnjaandrun’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He whom neither anger nor joy, nor pride, nor false modesty, nor stupefaction, nor vanity, can draw away from the high ends of life, is considered as wise.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura, the Mahabharata’s model counsellor, describes the wise man as one whom no passion can pull away from life’s proper aims.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the aranarindhu counsellor, grounded in dharma, whom the Kural calls the best partner in deliberation.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to speak graciously and thoughtfully, fitting each answer to the person addressed.
christianity.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s aandramaindha sol, full and measured speech.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who have responded to their lord and established prayer and whose affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves, and from what We have provided them, they spend.”
islam.explanation: The surah named Ash-Shura (Consultation) lists mutual consultation among the defining traits of the faithful.
islam.tie_back: Shura makes the Kural’s thaerchchith thunai, the partner in deliberation, a religious ideal.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Where no wise direction is, a people falleth; but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that a nation stands or falls by the quality of the guidance it receives.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s point is the same: a ruler needs capable counsellors beside him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak only the speech that neither torments self nor does harm to others. That speech is truly well spoken.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes well-spoken speech as speech that harms no one.
buddhism.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s aandramaindha sol, restrained and weighty speech, as part of a good counsellor’s character.
buddhism.source: Subhasita Sutta, Sutta Nipata 3.3 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “… circumspect in his speaking … guarding his thoughts, guarding his words, guarding his acts, guarding his senses, guarding his chastity; without wrath, without pride, without deceit, without greed …”
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra describes Mahavira as careful in speech (bhasha-samiti) and guarded in word and deed, free from the four passions.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's best counsellor knows what is right and speaks with learning and restraint; the Jain ideal of careful, guarded speech free of passion covers the restraint, though not the giving of counsel.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §118 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Baba, speak only that which will bring you honor.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of Siree Raag, Guru Nanak urges that speech be weighed, so that one says only what is worthy and brings honour.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural wants as a counsellor one whose speech is measured and full of learning; Guru Nanak likewise asks for speech that is weighed and worthy.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Agamemnon and Achilles quarrel, old Nestor of Pylos rises to calm them. Homer calls him the clear-voiced speaker from whose tongue words flowed sweeter than honey, and he draws on his long experience of great men.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor is Homer’s model counsellor: experienced, eloquent and respected by both sides.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He combines the Kural’s learned, measured speech with long practical knowledge.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says that a speaker earns trust through three qualities: practical wisdom (phronesis), virtue (arete) and goodwill (eunoia). A speaker who lacks any one of them gives bad or untrustworthy advice.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, credible counsel needs good judgement, good character and genuine care for the listener.
philosophy.tie_back: Virtue, wisdom and trustworthy speech correspond closely to the Kural’s aram, learned speech and practical skill.

real_life_example.event_title: Nizam al-Mulk founds the Nizamiyya colleges and writes the Book of Government
real_life_example.place: Baghdad and the Seljuq Empire (Iran and Iraq)
real_life_example.event: Nizam al-Mulk, a Persian from Tus, became vizier to the Seljuq sultan Alp Arslan in the 1060s and continued under his son Malik Shah, holding the office for about 30 years. He founded a network of colleges named Nizamiyyas after him, the most famous being the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, founded in 1067, where he appointed scholars such as al-Juwayni and al-Ghazali. He set down his views on government in the Siyasatnama, the Book of Government.
real_life_example.explanation: Nizam al-Mulk is remembered in Persian tradition as the model vizier, a statesman who was also a patron of learning and an author on the right conduct of rulers.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes the ideal counsellor as one who knows what is right, is full of learning and always knows how things are to be done, and Nizam al-Mulk's long vizierate, colleges and treatise on government embody that combination.

tamil:
மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்க்கு அதிநுட்பம்
யாவுள முன்நிற் பவை.
transliteration:
Madhinutpam noolodu udaiyaarkku adhinutpam
Yaavula munnir pavai.
meaning: When a person has a naturally sharp mind and also learning from books, what clever trick could ever beat them?
elementary: Some kids are naturally quick at puzzles, and some have read lots of puzzle books. A kid who is both quick and well-read is very hard to trick. This kural says a good adviser is like that, so no clever trap can fool him.
university: The couplet contrasts madhinutpam, native acuteness of intellect, with nool, learning from texts, and says that someone who has both cannot be outwitted by any adhinutpam, any ‘extreme subtlety’ or stratagem. The rhetorical question yaavula munnirpavai (‘what are there that stand before [him]?’) implies ‘none’. Commentators from Parimelazhagar on distinguish iyarkai arivu (natural intelligence) from seyarkai arivu (acquired or learned intelligence). This pair prepares for kural 637, which uses the same iyarkai and seyarkai vocabulary. Kalaignar and Pappaiah read adhinutpam specifically as hostile schemes (soozhchi). There are small spelling differences, such as முன்நிற் (ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net) against முன்னிற் and the joined ‘மதிநுட்ப நூலோ டுடையார்க்’ in the older-orthography thirukkural-thamizh.org, but the wording is the same.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Duryodhana plots to burn the Pandavas in a house of lac at Varanavata, Vidura sees through the scheme. He warns Yudhishthira in veiled language that only Yudhishthira understands and secretly sends a miner to dig an escape tunnel, so the plot fails.
hinduism.explanation: Vidura’s sharpness and learning defeat an elaborate, carefully hidden conspiracy.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s claim that no stratagem can stand against natural wit joined to learning.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Jatugriha section), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples to combine shrewdness with innocence when facing hostile schemers.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it values a sharpness of mind that cannot be outwitted by others.

islam.quote_or_event: “A believer is not stung twice (by something) out of one and the same hole.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that a believer should be alert and learn from experience so as not to be deceived again the same way.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s minister is similarly too sharp to be caught by any scheme.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Now as for these four youths, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom; and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.”
judaism.explanation: Daniel and his companions, trained for royal service in Babylon, have both learning and a special gift of insight.
judaism.tie_back: Learning plus an inborn gift is the Kural’s nool plus madhinutpam.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Maha-ummagga Jataka, the Bodhisatta is born as Mahosadha, a wise minister to King Vedeha. Again and again he sees through the plots of rival ministers and of the enemy king’s counsellor Kevatta, and turns their stratagems back on them.
buddhism.explanation: Mahosadha is the Buddhist model of a minister whose wisdom no intrigue can defeat.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that no subtle scheme can stand before an intelligent, well-taught minister.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Then the king looked with nectar-sweet glance at the face of Abhayakumāra, the depository of inborn and other kinds of knowledge …”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra calls the minister Abhaya a store of 'inborn and other kinds of knowledge'; Johnson's note explains the four buddhis of Jain tradition: inborn (autpattiki), from deliberation, from training, and from past karma.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says no scheme can outwit one who joins native sharpness with learning; the Jain portrait of Abhaya, who has both inborn intelligence and acquired kinds, is the minister the schemes of Pradyota failed against.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak says that learning becomes valuable only when it is reflected on and inwardly understood, and so put to the service of others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says no scheme can stand against someone who joins native sharpness to book learning; Guru Nanak likewise asks that learning be joined to one's own reflection.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: To avoid going to Troy, Odysseus pretends to be mad and ploughs his field while sowing salt. Palamedes sees through the trick and places Odysseus’s infant son Telemachus in the plough’s path. When Odysseus swerves, the pretence is exposed.
greek_mythology.explanation: One clever man’s scheme is undone by another man’s sharper insight.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This shows the Kural’s point that a sufficiently sharp mind defeats even a subtle stratagem.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Horace asks whether a good poem comes from nature or from art. He answers that he cannot see what study can do without natural talent, or what raw talent can do untrained: each needs the other’s help.
philosophy.explanation: Horace insists that native gift and disciplined learning must work together.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s pairing of madhinutpam (native acuteness) with nool (learning).

real_life_example.event_title: Benjamin Franklin answers the House of Commons on the Stamp Act
real_life_example.place: House of Commons, London, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: While the House of Commons, sitting as a Committee of the Whole, examined witnesses on colonial opposition to the Stamp Act, Benjamin Franklin was the principal witness on 13 February 1766. He answered 174 recorded questions, and by his own later notes 89 of them came from members of the Grenville ministry or other opponents. His answers were printed as The Examination of Doctor Benjamin Franklin, and the Stamp Act was repealed later in 1766.
real_life_example.explanation: Franklin's mix of quick wit and detailed knowledge of the colonies let him parry hostile questions and turn some of them to his own advantage, and the printed examination greatly raised his reputation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what scheme can stand against a person who joins natural sharpness to learning, and Franklin's handling of dozens of hostile questions shows such a person proving hard to outwit.

tamil:
செயற்கை அறிந்தக் கடைத்தும் உலகத்து
இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்.
transliteration:
Seyarkai arindhak kadaiththum ulakaththu
Iyarkai arindhu seyal.
meaning: Even when you know from books how to do something, act only after you understand how the world really works.
elementary: You can read a book about riding a bicycle, but you also need to notice the real road, the bumps and the traffic. This kural says that even after learning the rules, you must look at the real world and act in a way that fits it.
university: The couplet sets seyarkai, the ‘made’ or acquired knowledge of methods found in treatises, against ulakaththu iyarkai, the natural ways of the world. The minister should act (seyal) only after knowing the second as well as the first. Mu. Varadarasanar’s gloss makes seyarkai explicitly nool arivu (book knowledge). Solomon Pappaiah extends it to methods learned from foreign books and applies iyarkai to the character of one’s own land and people. Commentators in Parimelazhagar’s tradition often recall the grammarians’ rule that ulakam, ‘world’, can mean the worthy or experienced people whose conduct sets the norm. There is a small textual variant. ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org read arindhak kadaiththum (with the doubled k), while thirukkural.net prints arindha kadaiththum. The meaning does not change.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Even a man of knowledge acts according to his own nature, for everyone follows the nature he has acquired from the three modes. What can repression accomplish?”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna observes that even the learned must reckon with the nature of beings, which cannot simply be overridden.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that knowledge must take account of how things actually are (iyarkai).
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.33 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes adapting his approach to the character and situation of each audience.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s advice to fit one’s method to the ways of the people one is dealing with.
