islam.quote_or_event: “And We did not send any messenger except [speaking] in the language of his people to state clearly for them, and Allah sends astray [thereby] whom He wills and guides whom He wills.”
islam.explanation: God sends each messenger in his own people’s language so that the message fits those who hear it.
islam.tie_back: Even revealed truth is delivered in a form suited to the world it enters, as the Kural advises.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person should never deviate from the local custom, as Moses ascended to heaven on high and did not eat bread while he was there, whereas the ministering angels descended down to this world, as guests visiting Abraham, and they ate bread.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tanhum bar Hanilai teaches that one should follow the customs of the place one is in, as even Moses and the angels did.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s rule to act in keeping with ulakaththu iyarkai, the ways of the world around you.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 86b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Aranavibhanga Sutta, the Buddha says that one should not insist on one’s own dialect or override ordinary usage. The same bowl is called by different names in different regions, and a wise person uses whatever word is current there instead of insisting on his own.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns against rigidly imposing one standard where local usage differs.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point that correct theory must bend to the real ways of the world.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You, although knowing nīti and well versed in the seventy stories, were caught by her like a parrot by a cat.”
jainism.explanation: Pradyota taunts Abhayakumara, who was captured when a courtesan posing as a pious Jain laywoman drugged him: all his learning in statecraft (niti) did not protect him from a trick of the world.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that knowing methods from books is not enough without knowing how the world actually behaves; Abhaya's capture is a cautionary case of learned policy failing against real-world deceit.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You may read and read loads of books; you may read and study vast multitudes of books. … O Nanak, only one thing is of any account: everything else is useless babbling and idle talk in ego.”
sikhism.explanation: In a famous salok of Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak says that mountains of book learning count for little unless they lead to what truly matters.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the minister to know how the world actually works as well as what the books say; Guru Nanak likewise refuses to treat book learning as enough by itself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Shipwrecked on the Phaeacian shore, Odysseus meets the princess Nausicaa. He decides not to clasp her knees as a formal suppliant might, in case it offends her, and speaks gently from a distance instead.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus knows the formal rules of supplication but adjusts them to the real situation in front of him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s advice: know the rules, then act according to how the world actually is.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nor is practical wisdom concerned with universals only-it must also recognize the particulars; for it is practical, and practice is concerned with particulars. This is why some who do not know, and especially those who have experience, are more practical than others who know…”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that general knowledge is not enough for action; one must also grasp particular circumstances, which experience provides.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s contrast between book methods (seyarkai) and knowing the world (iyarkai).
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.7 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Tanganyika groundnut scheme fails
real_life_example.place: Kongwa and other sites, Tanganyika (now Tanzania)
real_life_example.event: In 1947 Britain's Labour government launched a plan, run by the Overseas Food Corporation, to grow groundnuts on cleared land in Tanganyika to ease a post-war shortage of fats. It was commissioned after a survey completed in only seven weeks, with no pilot scheme, and it failed to allow for the area's soil and rainfall; at Kongwa there was enough rain for a groundnut crop only once between 1947 and 1951. The scheme was abandoned on 9 January 1951, with about 36.5 million pounds written off.
real_life_example.explanation: The planners relied on a plan drawn up on paper and on heavy machinery, while ignoring local conditions and the knowledge of local farmers, and the project collapsed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that even someone who knows from books how a thing should be done must act only after learning how the world actually works, and the groundnut scheme failed for want of exactly that knowledge.

tamil:
அறிகொன்று அறியான் எனினும் உறுதி
உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்.
transliteration:
Arikondru ariyaan eninum urudhi
Uzhaiyirundhaan kooral kadan.
meaning: Even if the king ignores good advice and does not know better himself, the adviser by his side still has the duty to tell him what is truly good.
elementary: Imagine your friend is about to do something unsafe and will not listen. A true friend still tells them the truth, even if they get grumpy. This kural says a leader’s adviser must always tell the leader what is good, even when the leader does not want to hear it.
university: Arikondru (‘having killed knowledge’) is usually taken to mean that the king destroys or ignores the counsel of those who know. Ariyaan eninum (‘even if he himself does not know’) adds that he also lacks knowledge of his own. Even then urudhi (what is truly and lastingly beneficial) must be told (kooral kadan, ‘speaking is a duty’) by the uzhaiyirundhaan, ‘the one who is at his side’, meaning the minister. Solomon Pappaiah stresses that the minister must speak without anger and without fear. Kalaignar applies the verse to those near any ruler. The couplet is the moral centre of the chapter: the minister’s duty to give frank counsel does not depend on whether it will be welcomed. The thirukkural-thamizh.org edition prints ‘arikon rariyaa neninu murudhi / yuzhaiyirundhaan’, a difference of word division only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “They are abundant, O king, that can always speak agreeable words. The speaker, however, is rare, as also the hearer, of words that are disagreeable but medicinal.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells the blind king Dhritarashtra, whose sons are heading for ruin, that honest but unwelcome advice is rare.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura is doing what the Kural requires: telling a king who will not listen what is good for him.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 37 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “For John had said unto Herod, It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother’s wife.”
christianity.explanation: John the Baptist confronts King Herod about his unlawful marriage, and it later costs him his life.
christianity.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s duty to tell a ruler the truth whatever the cost.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Religion is sincerity.” We said, “To whom?” He said “To Allah, to His Book, To His Messenger, and to the leaders of the Muslims and their masses.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet defines religion as nasiha, sincere good counsel, owed even to those in authority.
islam.tie_back: This makes the Kural’s duty to give leaders sincere advice part of faith itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Nathan said to David: ‘Thou art the man.’”
judaism.explanation: After telling David a parable about a rich man who stole a poor man’s lamb, the prophet Nathan confronts the king directly over his sin with Bathsheba and Uriah.
judaism.tie_back: Nathan, a member of David’s court, tells his king the unwelcome truth, as the Kural requires of the one at the ruler’s side.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, but unendearing & disagreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Prince Abhaya that he will speak true and beneficial words even when they are unwelcome, choosing the right moment.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s urudhi, beneficial counsel given even when it will be disliked.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you have no intention of abandoning pleasure, and still long for undertakings and property, my long talk has been to no purpose. I go, king, farewell.” And Brahmadatta, king of the Pañkâlas, did not act on the counsel of the saint …
jainism.explanation: The monk Citta, out of old friendship and concern for the king's welfare, gives the emperor Brahmadatta honest advice again and again; the king admits he knows the Law but will not follow it, and comes to ruin.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that even when the king rejects good counsel and is ignorant himself, the one beside him must still tell him what is truly good; Citta does this to the end, though the king will not listen.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.33-34 (cf. 13.15) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Nanak speaks the Word of Truth; he proclaims the Truth at this, the right time.”
sikhism.explanation: This line closes a hymn of Raag Tilang that belongs to Guru Nanak's Babarvani, his hymns about Babur's invasion, in which he speaks plainly of the cruelty of the powerful.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the one who stands beside the king must still tell him what is truly good, even if the king rejects advice; Guru Nanak insists on proclaiming the truth to the powerful at the very moment it is needed.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before the fighting at the Greek ships, the Trojan counsellor Polydamas urges Hector to withdraw the army inside the city walls now that Achilles has returned. Hector angrily rejects the advice, and the Trojans suffer heavy losses. Hector later admits that he should have listened.
greek_mythology.explanation: Polydamas gives honest counsel to a leader who will not listen.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s situation: a counsellor at the leader’s side whose sound advice is spurned.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch argues that the true friend is known by his frank speech (parrhesia). He is willing to point out a man’s faults for his good, while the flatterer only says what pleases. Plutarch adds that this frankness should be used with tact and at the right moment.
philosophy.explanation: For Plutarch, honest criticism given for the other person’s benefit is the sign of real loyalty.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the minister’s duty in the Kural to speak urudhi, what is truly beneficial.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend (Moralia)

real_life_example.event_title: Hai Rui's memorial rebukes the Jiajing Emperor
real_life_example.event: The Ming Jiajing Emperor had for more than twenty years largely stopped holding court audiences and spent heavily on Daoist rituals and the search for longevity. In 1566 Hai Rui, a secretary in the Ministry of Revenue, submitted a memorial criticising the emperor for this neglect of government, and the emperor had him thrown into prison. Early in 1567, a few days after the emperor's death, Hai Rui was released and restored to his rank, and he was later honoured with the posthumous name Loyal and Incorruptible.
real_life_example.explanation: Hai Rui spoke plainly to a ruler who was known to punish critics, and his courage made him a lasting model of the honest official in China.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even when the ruler rejects wise advice and is ignorant himself, the one at his side must still tell him what is truly good, and Hai Rui did so at the cost of his freedom.

tamil:
பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரியின் பக்கததுள் தெவ்வோர்
எழுபது கோடி உறும்.
transliteration:
Pazhudhennum mandhiriyin pakkadhadhul thevvor
Ezhubadhu kodi urum.
meaning: Seventy crores (seven hundred million) of enemies are better than one minister at your side who secretly plans to harm you.
elementary: A lot of rivals on the other team are easier to handle than one teammate who is secretly trying to make you lose. This kural says a bad adviser close to a leader is more dangerous than a huge army of enemies.
university: Pazhudhennum mandhiri is ‘the minister who contemplates harm’. Mandhiri is from the Sanskrit mantrin; it stands beside the chapter’s Tamil amaichu. Pakkaththul means ‘at one’s side, within one’s own ranks’. Thevvor ezhubadhu kodi (seventy crores of enemies) is hyperbole for a countless host. There is a real textual and grammatical point here. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read mandhiriyin, while the older-orthography thirukkural-thamizh.org reads mandhiriyir (‘mandhiriyir pakkadhadhut tevvo’). Both are forms of the ablative of comparison, ‘than the minister’. That is why Varadarasanar, Kalaignar and Kesikan read ‘seventy crore foes are better than such a minister’. Solomon Pappaiah reads it instead as ‘such a minister equals seventy crore foes’ and glosses pazhudhu as self-interest over the nation’s good.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Shakuni, Duryodhana’s maternal uncle and closest adviser, devises the rigged game of dice through which the Pandavas lose their kingdom. His counsel drives the Kauravas step by step toward the war that destroys them.
hinduism.explanation: Shakuni is the epic’s archetype of the evil counsellor at a prince’s side.
hinduism.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s warning that one adviser who thinks harm can ruin more surely than a host of enemies.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta section), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “I speak not of you all: I know whom I have chosen: but that the scripture may be fulfilled, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.”
christianity.explanation: At the Last Supper, Jesus foretells betrayal by one of his own inner circle, Judas.
christianity.tie_back: The deepest harm comes from one at one’s side, as the Kural warns.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah never sends a prophet or gives the Caliphate to a Caliph but that he (the prophet or the Caliph) has two groups of advisors: A group advising him to do good and exhorts him to do it, and the other group advising him to do evil and exhorts him to do it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that every ruler has an inner circle, and part of it will push him toward evil.
islam.tie_back: This names the Kural’s danger, the harmful adviser at the ruler’s side, as a permanent feature of power.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it was not an enemy that taunted me, then I could have borne it; neither was it mine adversary that did magnify himself against me, then I would have hid myself from him. But it was thou, a man mine equal, my companion, and my familiar friend; We took sweet counsel together…”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says an enemy’s attack could be endured, but betrayal by a trusted companion and fellow counsellor cannot. Tradition often links this to Ahithophel, David’s adviser who joined Absalom’s revolt.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that the enemy within is worse than any number of foes outside.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta befriends Prince Ajatasattu and urges him to kill his father, King Bimbisara, and take the throne while Devadatta takes over the Sangha. The prince follows this counsel, and the kingdom and the Sangha both suffer for it.
buddhism.explanation: Devadatta is the Buddhist figure of the corrupt counsellor whose advice leads a prince to ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s pazhudhennum mandhiri, the adviser at one’s side who plots harm.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anathi warns that harm from within, a person's own wrong conduct, is worse than anything an outside enemy can do.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural judges one treacherous minister at your side worse than seventy crores of open foes; the Jain verse makes the same comparison of an inner enemy with an outer one, though the inner enemy is one's own perversity.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: When Guru Gobind Singh's family was scattered after leaving Anandpur in December 1705, their own cook, Gangu, took the Guru's mother Mata Gujari and his two youngest sons to his house at Kheri. Tempted by the money in their saddlebag, he stole it and betrayed them to the Mughal officials at Morinda. The children were later executed at Sirhind.
sikhism.explanation: Sikh memory holds up Gangu, a trusted member of the household, as the type of the betrayer from within, whose treachery did more harm than the Mughal army that had failed to take them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one treacherous minister at your side is worse than seventy crores of open enemies; the betrayal of the Guru's family by their own household servant is Sikh history's starkest example.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Sahibzada Zorawar Singh', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Greeks pretend to sail away from Troy, they leave Sinon behind. He convinces the Trojans to bring the wooden horse inside their walls, and at night he signals the Greek fleet to return, so the city that had withstood ten years of siege falls from within.
greek_mythology.explanation: One deceiver inside the walls achieved what the whole Greek army could not.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This makes vivid the Kural’s claim that one enemy at your side is worse than a vast host outside.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli writes that a prince can judge a minister simply: when the minister thinks more of his own interests than the prince’s and seeks his own profit in everything, he will never be a good minister and can never be trusted.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli, the self-serving minister is a fundamental danger to the state.
philosophy.tie_back: This follows Solomon Pappaiah’s reading of the Kural’s pazhudhu as self-interest over the nation’s good.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 22 (trans. W. K. Marriott)

real_life_example.event_title: The fall of Sejanus, Tiberius's trusted prefect
real_life_example.event: Sejanus, prefect of the Praetorian Guard, won the complete confidence of the emperor Tiberius and became the chief administrator of the empire, especially after Tiberius withdrew to Capri. He used his position to attack members of the imperial family who stood between him and power. In 31 CE, after Tiberius grew suspicious of his ambitions, a letter from the emperor was read in the Senate, Sejanus was arrested and condemned, and he was executed the same year.
real_life_example.explanation: The most dangerous threat to Tiberius came not from foreign enemies but from the minister he trusted most, who was suspected of plotting to take the throne.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says countless open enemies are better than one minister at one's side who plans one's ruin, and Sejanus is the classic Roman example of such a minister.

tamil:
முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர்
திறப்பாடு இலாஅ தவர்.
transliteration:
Muraippadach soozhndhum mudivilavae seyvar
Thirappaadu ilaaa thavar.
meaning: People without the skill to get things done will leave their work unfinished, even when they have planned it the right way.
elementary: You can draw a perfect plan for a sandcastle, but if you do not know how to pack the sand, it falls apart halfway. This kural says a good plan is not enough; an adviser also needs the skill to finish the job.
university: Muraippadach soozhndhum means ‘even having deliberated in due order’, where soozhchi is the technical term for counsel. Such people mudivilavae seyvar, ‘do only things without completion’, if they are thirappaadu ilaadhavar, lacking executive ability. Ilaaa carries a prosodic lengthening (alapedai) needed for the metre. The thirukkural-thamizh.org edition prints ‘thirappaa delaaa thavar’, the older joined spelling of thirappaadu + ilaaa. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take mudivila to mean half-done or defective work, while Kesikan reads it as ‘endless’, never-concluding activity. Closing the chapter this way balances its stress on deliberation. Counsel without execution fails, which leads into the later chapters on action (vinaiththooimai, vinaiththitpam, vinaiseyalvagai, 66-68).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man engaged in devotional service rids himself of both good and bad reactions even in this life. Therefore strive for yoga, which is the art of all work.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna’s phrase yogah karmasu kaushalam, often rendered ‘yoga is skill in action’, makes skilful execution itself a spiritual ideal.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that without skill in action (thirappaadu) even good planning fails.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.50 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus pictures a builder who lays foundations but cannot complete the tower and becomes a laughing stock.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s mudivila: work begun but never finished.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Great is hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an condemns people whose words and plans are not carried into action.
islam.tie_back: This parallels the Kural’s rebuke of those who plan well but cannot complete the deed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Study is not the most important thing, but actions; whoever indulges in too many words brings about sin.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon ben Gamliel teaches that what counts is doing, not merely learning or talking.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks carrying things out above deliberation alone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of colour but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practise them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares good words that are not practised to a flower that looks fine but has no scent.
buddhism.tie_back: In the same way, well-made plans that are never carried out, as the Kural warns, bear no fruit.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Just as bad bullocks are when put before a car, so are bad pupils when yoked, as it were, to the car of the Law; they break down through want of zeal.”
jainism.explanation: The teacher Garga compares bad pupils to unruly bullocks that break down on the road, failing to carry through what they were set to do.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says those who lack the ability to carry things through leave their work unfinished even after proper planning; Garga's bullocks and pupils likewise break down short of the goal for lack of zeal.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 27.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “We are good at talking, but our actions are bad.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Siree Raag ki Vaar, Guru Nanak confesses the gap between fine words and the deeds that should follow them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those without the skill to carry things through leave their work unfinished even after good planning; Guru Nanak likewise names the gap between fine words and actual deeds.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato’s myth, Epimetheus asks to hand out the gods’ gifts to the animals himself. He shares out speed, strength, fur and claws with careful balance, but uses them all up before he reaches human beings, who are left naked and defenceless until Prometheus steals fire for them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Epimetheus (‘afterthought’) carries out a well-intended plan without the skill to finish it properly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s person who plans properly but leaves the work incomplete.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that virtue has to be active, not just possessed: just as at the Olympic Games it is not the finest and strongest who are crowned but those who compete, so in life it is those who act rightly who win the prize.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, capacity or intention without effective action achieves nothing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly says that right deliberation without skill in execution is worthless.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.8 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Babbage's Difference Engine No. 1 is left unfinished
real_life_example.event: From 1821 Charles Babbage designed Difference Engine No. 1, the first complete design for an automatic calculating engine, and the British government paid for its construction. Only a demonstration section of about 2,000 parts, one-seventh of the whole, was completed in 1832; work halted after a dispute with his engineer Joseph Clement, and the government finally abandoned the project in 1842 after spending about 17,500 pounds. When the Science Museum later built his Difference Engine No. 2 from his drawings, completing the calculating section in 1991, the machine worked.
real_life_example.explanation: Babbage's designs were sound, as the modern reconstruction proved, but the project failed in the practical business of managing the engineer, the costs and the work through to completion.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who lack the skill to carry things through leave their work unfinished even when they have planned it properly, and the brilliantly designed but never-completed Difference Engine is a striking case.

tamil:
நாநலம் என்னும் நலனுடைமை அந்நலம்
யாநலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று.
transliteration:
Naanalam ennum nalanudaimai annalam
Yaanalaththu ulladhooum andru.
meaning: The gift of speaking well is a treasure all by itself. It is not just one of the many other good things a person may have.
elementary: Imagine a treasure box holding gold, toys and books. A kind, clear way of speaking is not just one more thing in the box; it is like a special key that opens many other boxes. This kural says being able to speak well is a treasure all by itself.
university: The chapter opens the minister’s second great qualification after the preceding chapter on the minister (அமைச்சு, ch. 64): nā-nalam, literally “tongue-goodness”, is framed as a nalan-uṭaimai, a possession or wealth in the same grammatical mould as kalvi-uṭaimai or aṟivu-uṭaimai elsewhere in the text. The second line, yā-nalattu uḷḷatūum anṟu, says this good is “not contained within any other good”; the lengthened form uḷḷatūum is an alapeṭai (metrical prolongation). Parimelazhagar explains that eloquence is a distinct excellence because the other goods of a minister (lineage, learning, wealth) cannot be made effective in council without it, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this reading of it as a unique, self-standing merit. Some later commentators, including Kalaignar, read the line more strongly as “the best of all wealth”, a slight shift from “not included among” to “superior to” the other goods. The text is stable across ytamizh.com and the older sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org (நாநல மென்னு நலனுடைமை யந்நலம்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Vak Sukta of the Rigveda, Vāk (divine Speech) speaks of herself as a queen and gatherer of treasures, the power who makes the one she loves mighty, a seer and a sage.
hinduism.explanation: The hymn treats Speech not as a tool but as a sovereign goddess who holds wealth and gives greatness to those she favours; later tradition connects her with Sarasvatī.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hymn counts speech itself as a treasure, not an accessory to other treasures.
hinduism.source: Rigveda 10.125 (Vak Sukta), trans. R. T. H. Griffith

christianity.quote_or_event: “The officers answered, Never man spake like this man.”
christianity.explanation: Temple officers sent to arrest Jesus return empty-handed, giving as their only excuse the unmatched quality of his speech.
christianity.tie_back: The officers treat Jesus’ speech as a power in a class of its own, which is what the Kural means by a good not contained in other goods.

islam.quote_or_event: “[And] taught him eloquence.”
islam.explanation: Surah ar-Rahman lists al-bayān (clear, articulate expression) among God’s first gifts to humankind, right after creating the human being and teaching the Qur’an.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an counts clear speech as a distinct divine gift, much as the Kural counts nā-nalam as its own kind of wealth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A word fitly spoken Is like apples of gold in settings of silver.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb compares a well-placed word to a precious object set in precious metal, a thing of both value and beauty.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts describe good speech as treasure, with value apart from the speaker’s other goods.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Anguttara Nikaya’s list of pre-eminent disciples, the Buddha names the monk Vangīsa as foremost among those gifted with ready, inspired speech (paṭibhāna).
buddhism.explanation: Eloquence is recognised as a separate excellence worth naming, alongside wisdom, psychic power and other distinctions.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also treats eloquence as its own distinct merit, not something absorbed into other virtues.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who having investigated the Law expound it, are awakened and put an end to mundane existence; able to liberate both (themselves and others), they answer the well-deliberated questions.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga's lecture on the ideal monk counts the ability to expound the Law clearly as a gift of its own, one that frees both the speaker and those who hear him.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls goodness of the tongue a wealth in its own right; the Jain verse likewise gives skilled exposition a distinct worth, since it benefits others as well as oneself.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa ki Vaar Guru Nanak names sweetness (mithat), above all in speech and bearing, together with humility as the very essence of every virtue.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls goodness of the tongue a wealth in its own right, not one good among many; Guru Nanak likewise sets sweetness at the core of all goodness rather than treating it as a minor accomplishment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hermes, messenger of the gods, was honoured as Hermes Logios, patron of eloquence and persuasive speech, and the Homeric Hymn to Hermes shows the infant god talking his way out of trouble before Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Greeks gave eloquence its own divine patron, separate from the gods of war, wealth or wisdom.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Giving eloquence its own god reflects the Kural’s view that speech is a good in its own category.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Nicocles, Isocrates delivers his famous praise of logos: speech is what raises humans above animals, lets them found cities, make laws and invent arts, and good speech is the outward sign of a sound mind.
philosophy.explanation: Isocrates argues that the capacity for speech is the source of nearly every civilised good.
philosophy.tie_back: Isocrates, like Valluvar, ranks eloquence as a good of its own order rather than one virtue among many.

real_life_example.event_title: Cicero, a 'new man', wins the consulship through his oratory
real_life_example.event: Marcus Tullius Cicero came from a wealthy equestrian family with no consuls among his ancestors, and he built his career largely on his work as an advocate in the law courts, including his successful prosecution of Verres in 70 BCE. He rose through each office at the minimum legal age and was elected consul for 63 BCE as a novus homo, a 'new man', heading the poll. He is remembered as the greatest Roman orator, and his speeches against Catiline during his consulship are among his best-known works.
real_life_example.explanation: Without noble birth or a military record, Cicero reached the highest office of the Republic mainly through the power of his speech.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls the goodness of the tongue a wealth in its own right, not merely one good among others, and Cicero's rise shows eloquence serving as the capital that a lack of lineage denied him.

tamil:
ஆக்கமுங் கேடும் அதனால் வருதலால்
காத்தோம்பல் சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு.
transliteration:
Aakkamung kedum adhanaal varudhalaal
Kaaththombal sollinkat sorvu.
meaning: Both success and ruin can come from what we say. So be very careful never to make a slip in your speech.
elementary: Words are like the steering wheel of a car: turn it well and you get home safely, jerk it carelessly and you crash. Because words can build things up or break them down, we should be careful never to say the wrong thing.
university: Ākkam (growth, prosperity) and kēṭu (ruin) are the paired outcomes that Valluvar often sets against each other, and here both are said to arrive “by it” (atanāl), meaning speech. The verb phrase kāttu ōmpal, “guarding and protecting”, is a doubled imperative of care, and cōrvu names a lapse, slip or momentary negligence, not deliberate lying. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as advice to the minister, whose words in council can raise or ruin the king’s affairs, and so the lapse to be guarded against is any fault in word choice or timing. Modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar) widen it into a universal maxim of verbal care. The older edition prints the first line in sandhi form (ஆக்கமுங் கேடு மதனால் வருதலாற்), with no difference in meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Udyoga Parva, Vidura warns Dhritarashtra that wounds from arrows and axes heal, but wounds from harsh words do not, and that a wise person never lets such arrows of speech fly.
hinduism.explanation: Vidura’s political counsel treats careless speech as a direct cause of lasting enmity and ruin in a royal household.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Vidura tells a ruler’s counsellor to guard every word because ruin can come from speech.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that a person’s words decide their standing, for good or ill.
christianity.tie_back: Words bring either justification or condemnation, just as the Kural says they bring either gain or ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.”
islam.explanation: The verse commands qawlan sadīdan, straight and well-aimed speech, and the next verse promises that God will then set right the believers’ deeds.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an ties good outcomes to carefully aimed speech, as the Kural ties prosperity to guarding one’s words.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs 18:21 teaches that death and life are in the power of the tongue, and that those who love it will eat its fruit.
judaism.explanation: The sage says the tongue decides between life and death, and people reap the results of how they use it.
judaism.tie_back: Death and life in Proverbs, like ruin and gain in the Kural, both come through speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kokālika Sutta the Buddha says that a person is born with an axe in the mouth, with which the fool cuts himself when he speaks wrongly.
buddhism.explanation: The monk Kokālika slanders the chief disciples and suffers terribly for it; the verses warn that reckless words wound the speaker most of all.
buddhism.tie_back: The axe in the mouth is a vivid picture of the Kural’s warning that ruin can come through one’s own careless speech.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk or a nun, well considering, should not use speech whether truth or untruth, or truth mixed with untruth, if it be sinful, blamable, rough, stinging, coarse, hard, leading to sins, to discord and factions, to grief and outrage, to destruction of living beings.”
jainism.explanation: In the Acaranga's lecture on modes of speech, every word is weighed before it is spoken, because speech can lead to sin, discord, grief and even the destruction of life.
jainism.tie_back: The kural warns that both gain and ruin come through speech, so one must guard against any slip; the Jain rule turns that same care into a discipline of considering each word first.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.4.1.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor. Harsh words bring only grief. Listen, O foolish and ignorant mind!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that speech is the hinge of a person's standing: words that bring honour are accepted, while harsh or insipid words bring only ruin and grief.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says both prosperity and ruin come through speech, so one must guard against any slip of the tongue; Guru Nanak names the same two outcomes, honour and grief, as the fruit of what one says.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Niobe publicly boasts that her many children make her greater than the goddess Leto, and in response Apollo and Artemis kill her children one by one.
greek_mythology.explanation: A single proud speech in front of the people of Thebes brings total ruin on her household.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Niobe’s story shows the ruin side of the Kural: one slip of the tongue destroys everything.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Encomium of Helen, Gorgias calls speech a mighty lord that with a tiny body does divine works, and compares its effect on the soul to drugs on the body: some cure, some kill.
philosophy.explanation: Gorgias argues that speech can bring either healing or harm, depending on how it is used.
philosophy.tie_back: Speech as both cure and poison is Gorgias’ version of the Kural’s gain and ruin.

real_life_example.event_title: A loosely worded order sends the Light Brigade down the wrong valley
real_life_example.event: During the Battle of Balaklava in the Crimean War, Lord Raglan sent a written order for the cavalry to advance rapidly to the front and try to prevent the enemy carrying away the guns. The cavalry commanders could not see which guns he meant from their position, and the Light Brigade charged instead at a Russian battery at the end of a heavily defended valley. Of the roughly 670 men who charged, about 260 were killed or wounded, and the episode became one of the most infamous blunders in British military history.
real_life_example.explanation: The order made perfect sense from Raglan's viewpoint on the heights but was dangerously ambiguous to those who had to carry it out, and no one stopped to clarify it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that both prosperity and ruin come through words, so one must guard against any lapse in speech, and the vague wording of a single order at Balaklava turned into disaster.

tamil:
கேட்டார்ப் பிணிக்கும் தகையவாய்க் கேளாரும்
வேட்ப மொழிவதாம் சொல்.
transliteration:
Kettaarp pinikkum thakaiyavaaik kelaarum
Vetpa mozhivadhaam sol.
meaning: Good speech holds listeners tightly, and it is spoken so well that even people who have not heard it want to hear it.
elementary: Think of a storyteller so good that the children listening can’t look away, and children walking past stop and want to join in. That is what this kural calls real speaking skill.
university: The key verb piṇittal means to bind or tie (as with a rope), so the listener is pictured as captured by the speech, and vēṭpa means “so as to make them desire”. The contrast kēṭṭār / kēḷār, “those who have heard / those who have not heard”, is read two ways. Parimelazhagar takes kēṭṭār as allies or friends (those already listening) and kēḷār as enemies or those who refuse to listen; this is why Pope’s gloss speaks of binding friends and making even enemies desire. Solomon Pappaiah follows this reading but also records the plainer sense of those who heard before and those who have not yet heard. The couplet is effectively the chapter’s definition of sol-vanmai, ending emphatically with -ām col, “that is speech”.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Hanuman first meets Rama and Lakshmana in the Kishkindha Kanda, Rama praises his speech as faultless, well-ordered and pleasing, saying that such words could win over even an enemy with his sword raised.
hinduism.explanation: Rama sees Hanuman’s grammar, tone and order as signs of a learned envoy whose words would charm any listener.
hinduism.tie_back: An enemy won over by speech is the Kural’s picture of even unwilling hearers longing to listen.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And all bare him witness, and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth.”
christianity.explanation: In the synagogue at Nazareth the whole audience is held by the grace of Jesus’ words, even those who were sceptical of him.
christianity.tie_back: Listeners held in wonder are what the Kural means by speech that binds those who hear it.

islam.quote_or_event: “Some eloquent speech has the influence of magic.”
islam.explanation: After two men from the east gave speeches, the Prophet remarked on how eloquence can move people like a spell, even changing the minds of those who had refused.
islam.tie_back: The hadith’s magic-like hold on listeners is the Kural’s power to bind hearers.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ecclesiastes says the Preacher sought out pleasing words and wrote truth rightly, and that the words of the wise are like goads and firmly fixed nails.
judaism.explanation: Kohelet joins pleasing form with true content, speech that both attracts and holds fast in the mind.
judaism.tie_back: Words that please and stick like nails match speech that draws people in and holds them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Brahmāyu Sutta describes the Buddha’s voice as having eight qualities, among them being clear, intelligible, sweet, audible and resonant, so that it reaches the whole assembly and no further.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist texts treat the Buddha’s speech as naturally absorbing to every listener in the assembly.
buddhism.tie_back: A voice made to reach and hold every listener fits the Kural’s ideal of speech that binds its hearers.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The gods, men, Sabaras, and animals took the language of the Lord for their own.”
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition holds that when Mahavira preached, every listener, human or animal, understood him as if he spoke in their own tongue. Jacobi records this from the commentator Devendra in a note on the Uttaradhyayana.
jainism.tie_back: The kural defines true eloquence as speech that binds those who hear it and draws even those who have not heard it; the Jain image of the Jina's sermon captivating every kind of being is an idealised form of that power.
jainism.source: Verse quoted by Devendra's commentary, in Hermann Jacobi's footnote to Uttarādhyayana Sūtra, Lecture 2 (SBE 45, 1895, footnote on p. 8; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Listening-pain and sin are erased.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Suniai (Listening) stanzas of Japji, Guru Nanak praises the transforming power of hearing the divine Word, which holds and changes those who attend to it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises speech that binds its hearers and makes others long to hear it; Japji's refrain shows the Sikh sense of a Word so powerful that hearing it alone transforms the listener.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Jap (Japji Sahib, Pauri 8), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orpheus sings before Hades and Persephone, and his song so enthrals the underworld that the shades weep and the rulers of the dead, who never yield, grant his request.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even the powers most unwilling to listen are captured by Orpheus’ art.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Orpheus moving the unmoved matches the Kural’s speech that makes even those who would not listen long to hear.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In De Oratore, Crassus says nothing seems finer than the power to hold assemblies by speech, win their minds, and move their wills wherever the speaker wishes.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero places the orator’s power to capture an audience at the centre of civic life.
philosophy.tie_back: Holding an assembly and winning its mind is exactly the binding power the Kural describes.

real_life_example.event_title: Swami Vivekananda addresses the World's Parliament of Religions
real_life_example.event: On the opening day of the World's Parliament of Religions, held during the Chicago World's Fair, the Hindu monk Swami Vivekananda began his address by greeting the audience as sisters and brothers of America. The crowd of thousands rose and gave him a long ovation, and his short speech on tolerance and the rejection of fanaticism made him one of the stars of the Parliament. Afterwards he lectured widely across the United States on Hindu philosophy and founded the Vedanta Society in New York.
real_life_example.explanation: An unknown delegate from India won over a large foreign audience in a few minutes, and the demand to hear him again carried him on lecture tours for years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes true eloquence as speech that binds those who hear it and makes even those who have not heard it long to hear it, which is what Vivekananda's Chicago address did.

tamil:
திறனறிந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லை அறனும்
பொருளும் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்.
transliteration:
Thiranarindhu solluka sollai aranum
Porulum adhaninoongu il.
meaning: Speak only after you understand the people listening. Nothing does more good or brings more gain than speech that fits its listeners.
elementary: You explain a game differently to your little cousin than to your teacher. This kural says the smart thing is to know who is listening and choose your words for them, and that doing this is one of the best things you can do.
university: Tiṟan aṟintu, “knowing the tiṟan”, is the interpretive crux. Parimelazhagar takes tiṟan as the qualities of the audience, and Solomon Pappaiah lists them: birth, learning, conduct, wealth, appearance and age. Mu. Varadarasanar reads tiṟan as the right manner or force of the words themselves, and Kalaignar as the underlying reason for speaking. The second line makes a striking claim with the comparative atanin ūungu, “beyond that”, lengthened for metre: neither aṟam (virtue, the first puruṣārtha) nor poruḷ (wealth, the second) exceeds well-fitted speech. The claim makes sense within Porutpal, where the minister’s speech is the means by which both dharma and wealth are secured for the kingdom.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking truthfully and beneficially and in avoiding speech that offends.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines disciplined speech as words that are true, pleasant and beneficial and do not upset the listener.
hinduism.tie_back: Speech shaped to benefit and not agitate the hearer requires the attention to the listener that the Kural demands.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Colossians to speak graciously and fittingly so that they can answer each person appropriately.
christianity.tie_back: Knowing how to answer every person is the Kural’s tiṟan aṟintu, knowing the listener before speaking.

islam.quote_or_event: “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.”
islam.explanation: The verse sets out graded forms of speech (wisdom, good exhortation, gracious argument), which exegetes relate to different kinds of listeners.
islam.tie_back: Choosing among wisdom, exhortation and argument according to the audience is the discernment the Kural asks for.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmudic principle that the Torah speaks in the language of human beings (dibbra Torah ki-lshon benei adam) holds that even divine teaching is expressed in forms its hearers can grasp.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis explain the Torah’s ordinary phrasing as God fitting speech to the human audience.
judaism.tie_back: If even revelation adapts to its listeners, the Kural’s advice to know the hearer before speaking has deep support.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It is spoken at the right time. It is spoken in truth. It is spoken affectionately. It is spoken beneficially. It is spoken with a mind of good-will.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists five factors that make a statement well-spoken and blameless before the wise.
buddhism.tie_back: Right time and benefit to the listener depend on knowing one’s audience, which is the Kural’s point.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.198 (Vaca Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who follows (the instruction) may believe something untrue; (one should) kindly (tell him) 'It is thus or thus.' One should never hurt him by outrageous language, nor give long-winded explanations of difficult passages. (If the pupil does not understand his short explanation), he should explain at greater length. When the pupil has heard it, he will correctly understand the Truth.”
jainism.explanation: The monk who teaches is told to fit his explanation to the hearer: kindly and briefly at first, then at greater length if the pupil has not understood.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says to speak only after knowing the nature of one's hearers; the Sutrakritanga gives a concrete method for shaping speech to what the listener can take in.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.23–24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: At Hardwar, according to the Janamsakhi tradition retold by Macauliffe, Guru Nanak saw pilgrims throwing water eastward to their ancestors and began throwing water westward himself. When the gathered crowd asked why, he said he was watering his fields in the Punjab; when they laughed that it could never reach so far, he asked how their water could then reach ancestors far beyond.
sikhism.explanation: Rather than lecture the pilgrims, the Guru staged a gesture suited to his audience that drew a crowd and let them reach the lesson through their own objection.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the speaker to know the nature of his hearers before speaking, since nothing is more effective than words fitted to them; the Hardwar episode shows Guru Nanak choosing a form of teaching exactly matched to his listeners.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak, ch. IV, pp. 50-51

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Greek army rushes for the ships in Iliad 2, Odysseus turns them back by speaking gently and respectfully to each chieftain but sharply to common soldiers, fitting his words to each listener.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus rescues the expedition by changing how he speaks according to the rank and mood of each person.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a narrative example of the Kural’s rule: know the listener, then speak.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates says a true art of speech must know the kinds of souls and the kinds of speeches, and fit each speech to the soul that will be moved by it.
philosophy.explanation: Plato makes knowledge of the audience the foundation of any real rhetoric.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s matching of speech to soul is almost exactly the Kural’s tiṟan aṟintu.

real_life_example.event_title: John F. Kennedy speaks to West Berliners in their own words
real_life_example.place: Rudolph Wilde Platz, West Berlin, West Germany
real_life_example.event: Two years after the Berlin Wall went up, President John F. Kennedy spoke to a vast crowd of West Berliners outside the Rathaus Schoeneberg. Early in the speech he declared Ich bin ein Berliner, a German phrase he had practised beforehand with his interpreter Robert Lochner in Mayor Willy Brandt's office, to show that the United States stood with the people of the divided city. The line bonded him to his audience and became one of the best-known moments of the Cold War.
real_life_example.explanation: Kennedy's message was not new, but he shaped it to the exact fears, pride and language of the people in front of him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says to speak only after understanding the nature of one's hearers, since nothing is worth more than speech fitted to them, and Kennedy's Berlin speech is a celebrated example of exactly that.

tamil:
சொல்லுக சொல்லைப் பிறிதோர்சொல் அச்சொல்லை
வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து.
transliteration:
Solluka sollaip pirithorsol achchollai
Vellunjol inmai arindhu.
meaning: Say what you have to say only after making sure that no one can say something that beats your words.
elementary: Before you give your answer in a debate, check it from every side, like testing a bridge before you walk on it. If nobody can knock it down, then say it.
university: The couplet is famous for its sound play: col (word) appears five times in two lines, in collu-ka, collai, piṟitōr col, accollai and vellum col, so the verse enacts the verbal skill it recommends. The sense is that before speaking one should know (aṟintu) that no other word (piṟitu ōr col) that would overcome (vellum) that word exists (inmai). Parimelazhagar applies this to the minister in council, whose proposal must be answer-proof before it is offered to the king; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar say the same. The older edition shows sandhi forms (பிறிதோர்சொ லச்சொல்லை / வெல்லுஞ்சொ லின்மை யறிந்து), with no difference in meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At King Janaka’s great debate, the sage Yajnavalkya answers challenger after challenger (Ashvala, Artabhaga, Gargi, Uddalaka and others) until none can refute him, and Gargi declares that no one will defeat him in argument about Brahman.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad presents Yajnavalkya’s answers as so exact that every counter-argument fails.
hinduism.tie_back: Speech that no other speech can defeat is exactly what Yajnavalkya shows in Janaka’s court.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises his disciples that when they are put on trial they will be given words their opponents cannot answer.
christianity.tie_back: Words no adversary can gainsay are the Kural’s speech that no other word can overcome.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom and discernment in speech.”
islam.explanation: David is given faṣl al-khiṭāb, which exegetes understand as decisive, conclusive speech that settles a matter.
islam.tie_back: Decisive speech that ends dispute is the Kural’s speech that cannot be defeated.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Eleazar teaches in Pirkei Avot to be diligent in study and to know what to answer an unbeliever (apikoros).
judaism.explanation: The sage urges preparing answers in advance so that one’s reply to a challenger is sound.
judaism.tie_back: Preparing a reply that will hold against challenge is the discipline the Kural asks for before speaking.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The debater Saccaka boasts that no one could face him in debate without trembling, but when he challenges the Buddha his own theses are refuted, and he is left silent and sweating before the assembly.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta contrasts a boastful debater with the Buddha, whose carefully built answers cannot be overturned.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s unanswerable replies show the kind of speech the Kural means; Saccaka shows what happens without it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Well considering (what one is to say), speaking with precision, one should employ language in moderation and restraint.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga asks the monk to weigh every word, down to number, gender and tense, before speaking, so that what he says is exact and cannot be faulted.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says to speak only after making sure no other word can defeat one's own; the Jain rule of careful, precise speech aims at the same unassailable word.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.4.1.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: At Gorakhmata, Macauliffe relates from the Sikh biographies, Siddhs pressed the young Guru Nanak to put on the yogi's dress; he answered with a hymn saying religion lies not in patched coats, earrings or ashes but in living pure amid the impurities of the world, and the Siddhs, unable to answer him, made obeisance.
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak met the yogis on their own ground with a reply so complete that it ended the dispute, a pattern repeated in his recorded discourses with the Siddhs.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural advises speaking only after making sure no other word can defeat yours; in this account Guru Nanak's answer to the Siddhs left them no rejoinder.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak, ch. V, pp. 59-61

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Achilles dies, Ajax and Ulysses (Odysseus) compete by speech for his armour before the Greek chiefs, and Ulysses’ carefully built argument defeats Ajax’s appeal to his strength.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s retelling, the armour goes to the man whose speech the council cannot answer.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ulysses wins because no counter-speech could overcome his, the Kural’s test for speaking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that the rhetorician must be able to argue both sides of a question, not to argue for the worse, but so that he can see how things stand and refute anyone who argues unfairly.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, good rhetoric means anticipating every counter-argument.
philosophy.tie_back: Knowing the opposing case in advance is how one makes sure that no word can defeat one’s own.

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi pleads guilty at the Great Trial in Ahmedabad
real_life_example.event: Charged with sedition for three articles in his weekly Young India, Mohandas Gandhi pleaded guilty before Judge Robert Broomfield, leaving the prosecution nothing to prove. He then read a written statement explaining how he had turned from loyalty to the British Empire to non-cooperation, and said he was there to submit to the highest penalty the law could impose for what he regarded as the highest duty of a citizen. The judge, acknowledging that many regarded Gandhi as a great patriot, sentenced him to six years and said no one would be better pleased than he if the government later reduced the sentence.
real_life_example.explanation: By admitting the facts and accepting the penalty in advance, Gandhi left no ground for argument against him and turned the trial into an examination of British rule.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises speaking only after making sure no other word can defeat one's own, and Gandhi's carefully prepared statement left the court with nothing to refute.

tamil:
வேட்பத்தாஞ் சொல்லிப் பிறர்சொல் பயன்கோடல்
மாட்சியின் மாசற்றார் கோள்.
transliteration:
Vetpaththaanj sollip pirarsol payankodal
Maatchiyin maasatraar kol.
meaning: Speaking so that others want to listen, and picking out the useful points from what others say, is the way of people with no faults.
elementary: A good friend talks in a way you enjoy hearing, and when you talk, they listen for what you really mean instead of picking on small mistakes. This kural says the best people do both: speak well and listen well.
university: The couplet balances two actions: vēṭpat tām colli (oneself speaking so as to be desired) and piṟar col payan kōṭal (taking the payan, the fruit or meaning, of others’ words). Parimelazhagar adds that in hearing others one should grasp the substance while overlooking faults in their wording, and Solomon Pappaiah follows him. Māṭciyin mācaṟṟār, “those without stain in their excellence”, and kōḷ, “principle or settled practice”, present this as the rule of the most accomplished counsellors. It widens sol-vanmai from speaking to include skilled listening. The older edition reads பிறர்சொற் பயன்கோடன் in sandhi form.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sanskrit tradition praises the haṃsa (swan) for its legendary ability to separate milk from water, and uses the haṃsa-kṣīra-nyāya as a maxim for taking the essence of what one hears and leaving the rest.
hinduism.explanation: The swan is the model of a discerning listener who keeps the worth in others’ words and lets the rest go.
hinduism.tie_back: Taking the fruit of others’ speech while ignoring its faults is the swan’s skill applied to listening.
hinduism.source: Haṃsa-kṣīra-nyāya (Sanskrit maxim), as collected in Wisdom Library

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.”
christianity.explanation: James puts eager listening before speech as the mark of a mature believer.
christianity.tie_back: Being swift to hear matches the Kural’s call to draw the meaning from others’ words.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who listen to speech and follow the best of it. Those are the ones Allah has guided, and those are people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who hear what is said and take up the best of it.
islam.tie_back: Following the best of what one hears is almost the Kural’s piṟar col payan kōṭal.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wise man does not speak before one who is greater than he in wisdom, And does not break into his fellow’s speech; And is not hasty to answer; He asks what is relevant, and he answers to the point.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah lists the habits of a sage, which combine patient listening with relevant, well-aimed speech.
judaism.tie_back: Listening without interrupting and answering to the point is the double skill the Kural credits to the flawless.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “That monk who has control over his tongue, is moderate in speech, unassuming and who explains the Teaching in both letter and spirit — whatever he says is pleasing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada describes a monk whose restrained, clear speech is welcome to all who hear him.
buddhism.tie_back: Speech that is pleasing because of its restraint and meaning matches the first half of the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Will those who are not born of a good family, no matter how much learning they have acquired, will they become sufficiently wise to pass over, without censuring, the faults which occur in the speech of others?”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar's chapter on conduct in assemblies treats overlooking the faults in other people's speech as a mark of the truly cultivated.
jainism.tie_back: Parimelazhagar reads the kural's 'taking the fruit of others' words' as grasping their substance while passing over faults in their wording; the Naladiyar names exactly that generous listening.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 32 'Experience in (conducting of) assemblies', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who has a basket of fragrant virtues, should enjoy its fragrance. If my friends have virtues, I will share in them.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak urges drawing out the fragrance of virtue wherever it is found and sharing in the good qualities of one's companions.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises those who speak so others long to hear and who take the useful meaning from others' words; Guru Nanak likewise asks us to take in the good that others hold.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 765, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus pauses his tale of wanderings at the Phaeacian court, King Alcinous praises how gracefully and wisely he tells it, like a skilled bard, and begs him to keep going through the night.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus speaks so well that his hosts want more, and he in turn has listened carefully to their customs and wishes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A hearer begging for more is exactly vēṭpa, speech that makes people want to hear.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay On Listening, Plutarch advises the young to listen to lectures by looking past a speaker’s style and faults of diction to take hold of what is useful, like a bee drawing honey.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch treats good listening as a skill: taking the benefit and ignoring the flaws.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly Parimelazhagar’s gloss: take the fruit of others’ words, overlook their faults.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, De recta ratione audiendi (On Listening)

real_life_example.event_title: Mahalia Jackson's call and King's dream
real_life_example.place: Lincoln Memorial, Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: Martin Luther King Jr. was the final official speaker at the March on Washington, before a crowd of some 250,000 people, and he began by reading his prepared text. As he neared the end, the singer Mahalia Jackson called out to him to tell the crowd about the dream, a theme he had used at earlier events. King turned aside from his manuscript and spoke extemporaneously about his dream, and these improvised passages became the most celebrated part of the speech.
real_life_example.explanation: King was able both to hold a huge audience and to take in a single call from a friend nearby, seize its value and use it at once.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises those who speak so that others long to hear and who also grasp the useful meaning of what others say, and King's response to Jackson's call shows both skills in one moment.

tamil:
சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான் அவனை
இகல்வெல்லல் யார்க்கும் அரிது.
transliteration:
Solalvallan sorvilan anjaan avanai
Ikalvellal yaarkkum aridhu.
meaning: It is hard for anyone to beat a person in an argument when that person speaks powerfully, never slips up, and is not afraid.
elementary: Picture a class debate. The student who explains clearly, doesn’t forget their points, and isn’t scared to speak up is very hard to beat. This kural says those three things together make someone almost unbeatable.
university: Three predicate nouns build the ideal speaker: colal vallan (strong in speaking), cōrvilan (without lapse; Parimelazhagar glosses cōrvu as forgetfulness of what is to be said, echoing 642) and añcān (one who does not fear, above all fear of the assembly, the theme of chapter 73, Avaiyañcāmai). Ikal means enmity, rivalry or contention, so ikal vellal is victory through opposition; Pope renders it as intrigue or “hostile power”. Solomon Pappaiah expands the three terms to the ability to make others accept one’s thought, persistence even when the message is hard, and fearlessness even before hostile hearers. The older edition prints சோர்வில னஞ்சா னவனை / யிகல்வெல்லல் in sandhi form.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the Kurukshetra war, Krishna goes alone as envoy to the Kaurava court and argues the Pandavas’ case fearlessly and without faltering before Duryodhana and the assembled elders, who cannot answer him even though they reject him.
hinduism.explanation: The peace embassy shows the ideal envoy: articulate, unflinching and not intimidated by a hostile court.
hinduism.tie_back: Krishna has all three of the Kural’s qualities: power of speech, no lapse, and no fear.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavad-yana), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “And they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake.”
christianity.explanation: Stephen’s opponents in the synagogues cannot stand against his words, though they later have him killed.
christianity.tie_back: Stephen is the Kural’s speaker whom no one can overcome in open argument.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Allah] said, “Fear not. Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see.””
islam.explanation: Sent to confront Pharaoh, Moses and Aaron admit their fear, and God tells them to go without fear and speak.
islam.tie_back: Freedom from fear before a hostile power is the añcān (fearless) quality in the Kural’s portrait.

judaism.quote_or_event: The prophet Nathan confronts King David over Bathsheba with a parable about a rich man who takes a poor man’s only lamb, leading David to condemn himself before Nathan says, “You are the man.”
judaism.explanation: Nathan speaks fearlessly to a king, and his carefully built story leaves David with no defence.
judaism.tie_back: Skill, precision and courage together make Nathan’s speech unanswerable, as the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Prince Abhaya is sent by the Jain leader Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta with a two-horned question meant to trap the Buddha, but the Buddha answers calmly and exactly, and the trap fails.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta shows the Buddha as a speaker who cannot be cornered because he is clear, careful and unafraid.
buddhism.tie_back: A speaker no trap can catch fits the Kural’s ideal of one whom no rival can overcome.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk living single should not ridicule heretical doctrines, and should avoid hard words though they be true; he should not be vain, nor brag, but he should without embarrassment and passion (preach the Law). A monk should be modest though he be of a fearless mind.”
jainism.explanation: The ideal Jain preacher speaks without embarrassment and with a fearless mind, yet without hard words, boasting or passion.
jainism.tie_back: The kural describes the speaker who is strong, does not slip and does not fear; the Jain preacher shares the fearlessness and composure, though his goal is to teach, not to defeat rivals.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.21–22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Nanak speaks the Word of Truth; he proclaims the Truth at this, the right time.”
sikhism.explanation: This line closes Guru Nanak's hymn in Tilang on Babur's invasion, in which he openly condemned the violence of the conquest while it was happening.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says no one can overcome a speaker who is forceful, never slips, and does not fear; Guru Nanak's fearless proclamation of truth to power shows that kind of unshaken speaker.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “but when he raised his voice, and the words came driving from his deep chest like winter snow before the wind, then there was none to touch him”
greek_mythology.explanation: Antenor recalls Odysseus’ embassy to Troy: unimpressive at first sight, but when he spoke no one could match him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: “None to touch him” is the Homeric version of the Kural’s “hard for anyone to defeat”.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Quintilian defines the ideal orator, following Cato, as a good man skilled in speaking (vir bonus dicendi peritus), who combines moral steadiness and courage with eloquence.
philosophy.explanation: For Quintilian, eloquence without character and courage is not true oratory.
philosophy.tie_back: Quintilian’s combination of skill, integrity and courage reflects the three qualities of the Kural.

real_life_example.event_title: Nelson Mandela's statement from the dock at the Rivonia Trial
real_life_example.event: Facing charges of sabotage that could carry the death penalty, Nelson Mandela opened the defence case at the Rivonia Trial by making a statement from the dock instead of giving evidence under cross-examination. In a long statement he explained his actions and the cause of a free and democratic society, ending with the declaration that it was an ideal for which he was prepared to die. On 12 June 1964 Judge Quartus de Wet sentenced him and seven others to life imprisonment, saying he had decided not to impose the supreme penalty.
real_life_example.explanation: Mandela spoke without fear, without faltering and with great force in a hostile courtroom, and his statement became one of the most famous speeches of the twentieth century.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says no one can easily overcome a speaker who is powerful, never slips and does not fear, and Mandela's statement from the dock was not defeated even though he lost the case.

tamil:
விரைந்து தொழில்கேட்கும் ஞாலம் நிரந்தினிது
சொல்லுதல் வல்லார்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Viraindhu thozhilkekkum gnaalam nirandhinidhu
Solludhal vallaarp perin.
meaning: If the world finds people who can speak in an orderly and pleasant way, it will quickly do what they ask.
elementary: If a coach explains the plan step by step and in a friendly way, the whole team gets moving straight away. This kural says people are happy to follow someone whose words are clear, well arranged and kind.
university: Nirantu, “in proper sequence, arranged in order”, is the key technical term: it describes dispositio, the arrangement of points in the right order, joined with initu, pleasantly. Toḻil kēṭkum ñālam, “the world that hears or obeys the command”, uses kēḷ in the sense of obedience, and viraintu (swiftly) stresses how quickly the result follows. Parimelazhagar reads ñālam as the people of the world and the couplet as describing the minister whose orderly, sweet speech gets the king’s business done at once. Pope’s rendering, the world gathering round, softens the sense of obedience. The older edition prints கேட்கு ஞால நிரந்தினிது.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Rigvedic hymn to Knowledge says that when the wise fashioned speech with their minds, sifting it as grain is cleaned with a sieve, friends recognised friendship and a blessed mark was set upon their speech.
hinduism.explanation: The hymn pictures good speech as carefully sifted and arranged, producing fellowship among those who hear it.
hinduism.tie_back: Speech sifted and ordered by the mind is the Kural’s nirantu, orderly speech that wins people over.
hinduism.source: Rigveda 10.71.2, trans. R. T. H. Griffith

christianity.quote_or_event: At Pentecost Peter gives a carefully built sermon, moving from prophecy to the resurrection to a call to repentance; the hearers are cut to the heart and about three thousand accept his word that same day.
christianity.explanation: Peter’s orderly argument produces an immediate and large response.
christianity.tie_back: Ordered speech followed by swift response is the pattern the Kural describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those are the ones of whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them but admonish them and speak to them a far-reaching word.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to speak qawlan balīghan, an effective word that reaches deep into the hearers’ souls.
islam.tie_back: Speech that reaches and moves its hearers is the kind the Kural says people act on at once.

judaism.quote_or_event: Abigail meets David on his way to take revenge on her husband Nabal and makes a gracious, well-ordered plea; David at once blesses her good sense and turns back from bloodshed.
judaism.explanation: Her tactful, well-arranged speech changes an armed leader’s course on the spot.
judaism.tie_back: David’s immediate change of course shows the Kural’s point: orderly, pleasant speech gets swift results.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches the householder Upāli by a step-by-step talk (anupubbikathā) on generosity, virtue, heaven, the drawbacks of sensual pleasure and renunciation, then the Four Noble Truths, and Upāli gains the vision of the Dhamma where he sits.
buddhism.explanation: The Pali texts often show this graded, ordered discourse leading to immediate understanding in the listener.
buddhism.tie_back: A talk ordered step by step that brings instant acceptance matches the Kural’s swift response to orderly, sweet speech.

jainism.quote_or_event: “But in that case they should say: 'N. N.! O long-lived one! O long-lived ones! O layman! O pupil! O faithful one! O lover of faith!' Considering well, they should use such sinless, blameless, &c., speech.”
jainism.explanation: Instead of abusive words, the monk is told to address people with courteous, kindly forms of speech that cause no offence.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says the world quickly does the bidding of those who speak in good order and pleasantly; the Jain rule supplies the pleasant, courteous manner, though not the promise of ready obedience.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.4.1.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Humility is the word, forgiveness is the virtue, and sweet speech is the magic mantra. Wear these three robes, O sister, and you will captivate your Husband Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, calls sweet speech a magic mantra that, with humility and forgiveness, wins over even the divine Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that if the world finds those who speak in good order and pleasantly, it will quickly do their bidding; Farid likewise makes sweet speech the spell that brings the one addressed under the speaker's sway.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 127 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that when the Muses honour a king, they pour sweet dew on his tongue, so gentle words flow from his mouth; the people look to him as he settles disputes with straight judgements and quickly ends even a great quarrel.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Muses’ gift of sweet, well-formed speech lets a ruler bring the people along at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Sweet speech that quickly settles affairs and wins the people’s trust is the Kural’s image.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates says every speech should be put together like a living creature, with its own body, head and feet, and a middle and ends that fit each other and the whole.
philosophy.explanation: Plato makes well-ordered structure the mark of a speech worth hearing.
philosophy.tie_back: An organic, well-arranged speech is the Kural’s nirantu, orderly speech.

real_life_example.event_title: Roosevelt's first fireside chat ends the bank panic
