real_life_example.event: After declaring a nationwide bank holiday, President Franklin D. Roosevelt spoke to Americans by radio on 12 March 1933, explaining in plain, orderly terms what had happened to the banks, how the new Emergency Banking Act would work, and when sound banks would reopen. When banks reopened the next day, long lines of customers came to return their hoarded cash, and by the end of March the public had redeposited about two-thirds of the currency withdrawn in the panic. On 15 March the New York Stock Exchange recorded its largest one-day percentage gain.
real_life_example.explanation: The broadcast worked because Roosevelt laid out the situation step by step in a warm, direct manner, and millions of listeners acted on what he asked of them within days.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that if the world finds someone who can speak in good order and pleasantly, it will quickly do what that person asks, and the public's swift return to the banks after Roosevelt's talk is a clear case.

tamil:
பலசொல்லக் காமுறுவர் மன்றமா சற்ற
சிலசொல்லல் தேற்றா தவர்.
transliteration:
Palasollak kaamuruvar mandramaa satra
Silasollal thetraa thavar.
meaning: People who do not know how to say a few words without faults are surely the ones who love to say many words.
elementary: Some people talk and talk because they can’t find the right few words. Someone who knows exactly what to say can say it quickly and clearly, like a good arrow that hits the target in one shot.
university: The couplet sets pala (many) against cila (few), and māc aṟṟa (stainless, faultless) qualifies the few words. Kāmuṟuvar, “they desire”, turns wordiness into a craving. Maṉṟa is an emphatic particle, “certainly, surely”, which Mu. Varadarasanar renders as uṇmaiyāka. Tēṟṟātavar means those who are not able or not skilled: Parimelazhagar takes it as inability to express a matter in few faultless words, so wordiness is a symptom of lacking the skill, not a separate vice. Pope’s rendering (“Who have not skill ten faultless words to utter plain”) adds a number not in the Tamil. In the older edition the second line reads சிலசொல்ல றேற்றா தவர், where sandhi turns collal tēṟṟā into colla ṟēṟṟā.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Sanskrit poet Śrīharṣa defines eloquence (vāgmitā) as speech that is measured and substantial (mitaṃ ca sāraṃ ca), a line that became a common saying.
hinduism.explanation: The epic poem Naiṣadhīyacarita places true eloquence in brief speech full of substance, not in many words.
hinduism.tie_back: Few words full of substance is the Kural’s ideal, and its opposite is the lover of many words.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus rejects the idea that more words make speech more effective.
christianity.tie_back: Trusting in much speaking is the fault the Kural traces to lacking skill with a few good words.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Prophet (ﷺ) used to talk so clearly that if somebody wanted to count the number of his words, he could do so.”
islam.explanation: Aisha describes the Prophet’s speech as measured and distinct, in contrast to someone who rushed through narrations.
islam.tie_back: Countable, deliberate words are the few faultless words the Kural praises.

judaism.quote_or_event: “all my days I grew up among the sages, and I have found nothing better for a person than silence. Study is not the most important thing, but actions; whoever indulges in too many words brings about sin.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon son of Rabban Gamaliel warns that many words lead to fault.
judaism.tie_back: Too many words bringing sin is the reverse of the Kural’s few flawless words.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better than a thousand useless words is one useful word, hearing which one attains peace.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada values one meaningful word above a flood of empty ones.
buddhism.tie_back: One useful word against a thousand useless ones is exactly the Kural’s few against many.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One should always be meek, and not be talkative in the presence of the wise; one should acquire valuable knowledge, and avoid what is worthless.”
jainism.explanation: The opening lecture on discipline warns the pupil against talkativeness and links it to the worthless, as opposed to valuable knowledge.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who love to say many words are those unable to say a few faultless ones; the Jain verse likewise sets idle talk against what has real worth.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To speak too much and babble is useless.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak dismisses much talking as empty babble, since God knows everything without being told.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who cannot speak a few flawless words are the very ones who love to speak many; Guru Nanak likewise rejects wordiness as worthless.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 661, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the speech of Menelaus ran trippingly on the tongue; he did not say much, for he was a man of few words, but he spoke very clearly and to the point”
greek_mythology.explanation: Antenor remembers Menelaus as a speaker who used few words but made each count.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Menelaus is the Kural’s master of few, faultless words.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal ends one of his Provincial Letters by apologising that he made it longer than usual only because he had not had the time to make it shorter.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal’s joke makes the point that brevity takes more skill and effort than length.
philosophy.tie_back: Length as the fallback of one without time or skill is exactly the Kural’s diagnosis.

real_life_example.event_title: Lincoln's two-minute Gettysburg Address follows a two-hour oration
real_life_example.event: At the dedication of the national cemetery at Gettysburg, the main address was a two-hour oration of some 13,000 words by Edward Everett, the best-known orator of the day. President Abraham Lincoln then spoke for barely more than two minutes, delivering 272 words. The next day Everett wrote to Lincoln that he wished he had come as near to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as Lincoln had in two minutes.
real_life_example.explanation: Lincoln's brief, carefully chosen words became one of the most celebrated speeches in history, while the far longer oration is now largely forgotten.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who cannot say a few flawless words are the ones who love to say many, and the contrast at Gettysburg, acknowledged by Everett himself, shows the power of a few faultless words.

tamil:
இணருழ்த்தும் நாறா மலரனையர் கற்றது
உணர விரித்துரையா தார்.
transliteration:
Inaroozhththum naaraa malaranaiyar katradhu
Unara viriththuraiyaa thaar.
meaning: People who cannot explain what they have learned so others understand it are like flowers that bloom in bunches but have no smell.
elementary: Imagine a bunch of beautiful flowers that have no smell at all: nice to look at, but something is missing. A person who knows a lot but can’t explain it to anyone is like that. Learning is meant to be shared.
university: The closing couplet uses an uvamai (simile): iṇar (a cluster or bunch) ūḻttum (though it blossoms) nāṟā malar (a flower that gives no scent). Kaṟṟatu uṇara virittu uraiyātār means those who do not expand (virittu) and state (urai) what they have learned so that others may grasp it (uṇara). Parimelazhagar’s point is that learning (kalvi), however full, is incomplete in a counsellor unless it can be communicated, which links this chapter back to ch. 40 (Kalvi) and ch. 42 (Kēḷvi). The texts differ on the first word: ytamizh.com prints இணருழ்த்தும் with a short u, and the older edition prints இணருழ்த்து நாறா; many standard editions have the expected long-vowel form இணரூழ்த்தும் (iṇar + ūḻttum). The older edition also divides the second line as கற்ற / துணர விரித்துரையா தார் for metre.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Rigvedic hymn to Knowledge describes a man who has learned speech but whose speech is barren, bearing neither fruit nor flower, because he has abandoned the friend who shares knowledge.
hinduism.explanation: The hymn condemns learning that produces nothing for others, using the image of a flowerless, fruitless plant.
hinduism.tie_back: The Vedic image of speech without flower or fruit is very close to the Kural’s flower without fragrance.
hinduism.source: Rigveda 10.71.5-6, trans. R. T. H. Griffith

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that light is meant to be seen and shared, not hidden.
christianity.tie_back: A candle under a bushel, like a scentless flower, is a good thing that fails to reach anyone else.

islam.quote_or_event: “And untie the knot from my tongue / That they may understand my speech.”
islam.explanation: Moses asks God to free his tongue so that his hearers can understand what he has been given to say.
islam.tie_back: Moses’ prayer is for the very skill the Kural requires: explaining what one knows so others grasp it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But Moses said to God, “Please, O my Sovereign, I have never been a man of words, either in times past or now that You have spoken to Your servant; I am slow of speech and slow of tongue.””
judaism.explanation: Moses, who has received God’s message, fears he cannot put it into words for Pharaoh and the people, so God appoints Aaron as his spokesman.
judaism.tie_back: Moses has the knowledge but fears he lacks the expression, the exact gap the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of color but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practice them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada uses the same image of a scentless flower for words that are not matched by practice.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts use the scentless flower, but the Kural applies it to unshared learning and the Dhammapada to unpractised words.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those learned men who collect plenty of books bring them and fill up every room in their houses, and yet understand them not, are of one kind, while those learned men who both understand their purport and are able to explain them to others are of another kind.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar separates the learned who merely hoard books from those who understand them and can explain them to others.
jainism.tie_back: The kural likens those who cannot explain what they have learned to flowers without scent; the Naladiyar draws the same line between learning that stays shut away and learning that can be passed on.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 32 'Experience in (conducting of) assemblies', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that learning proves itself only when, through reflection, it becomes a benefit to others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares those who cannot make their learning understood by others to flowers that bloom without fragrance; Guru Nanak likewise judges knowledge by whether it reaches and helps others.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plutarch tells how the young Demosthenes, though learned and full of ideas, was jeered in the assembly for weak delivery, until the actor Satyrus showed him that the same words spoken with the right expression carried quite different force; he then trained himself into Athens’ greatest orator.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story shows knowledge without the power to convey it being ignored until the skill of expression is gained.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The young Demosthenes was the Kural’s scentless flower, full of learning but unable to reach his hearers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his last speech in Thucydides, Pericles says that a man who knows what is right but cannot explain it clearly is no better off than if he had never thought of it at all.
philosophy.explanation: Pericles lists the ability to explain policy as a basic quality of a statesman, alongside knowing it.
philosophy.tie_back: Knowledge that cannot be expressed is worth no more than ignorance, which is the Kural’s scentless flower.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.60, trans. Richard Crawley

real_life_example.event_title: Fukuzawa Yukichi publishes An Encouragement of Learning in plain Japanese
real_life_example.event: After travelling to the United States and Europe in the 1860s, Fukuzawa Yukichi published Seiyo jijo (Conditions in the West) and then, between 1872 and 1876, the seventeen essays of Gakumon no susume (An Encouragement of Learning). He condensed ideas from Western books into a message of his own and wrote as plainly as possible so that young readers could follow it, and the work was even used as an elementary school textbook. By his own estimate the first essay alone sold about 220,000 copies, many of them pirated, at a time when Japan had about 35 million people.
real_life_example.explanation: Fukuzawa's learning mattered to Meiji Japan because he could unfold it in clear, simple language that ordinary readers understood.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares learned people who cannot explain what they know to flowers that bloom without fragrance, and Fukuzawa is the opposite case, a scholar whose learning spread its fragrance because he explained it so clearly.

tamil:
துணைநலம் ஆக்கம் தரூஉம் வினைநலம்
வேண்டிய எல்லாந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Thunainalam aakkam tharooum vinainalam
Vendiya ellaan tharum.
meaning: Good helpers can bring a person success, but good actions bring everything a person could want.
elementary: Good friends can help you build a bigger sandcastle. But if you build it the right way, patiently and fairly, you get the castle, you keep your friends, and people want to play with you again. Doing things the right way gives you more than any helper can.
university: The chapter opens by ranking two kinds of nalam (goodness, excellence): tuṇai-nalam, the excellence of one’s supporters, the theme of the earlier chapter on seeking the help of the great (ch. 45), and vinai-nalam, the goodness or purity of the action itself, which gives the chapter its name, vinai-t-tūymai. Parimelazhagar reads ākkam narrowly as material increase, while vēṇṭiya ellām (all that is desired) takes in fame and merit in this world and the next, so good allies secure only one good while pure action secures all of them. The line sets the ethical frame for this part of the Amaichiyal (chapters on the minister, 64-73): a minister’s competence (ch. 64) and eloquence (ch. 65) are worthless unless the means he uses are clean. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this contrast closely, while Kalaignar softens it into a partnership in which allies add strength and good deeds done with them bring every benefit. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net both print த்ருஉம், an evident keying error. The sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org has தரூஉம் (tarūum, the alapeṭai lengthening of tarum), and that reading is adopted here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “By worship of the Lord, who is the source of all beings and who is all-pervading, a man can attain perfection through performing his own work.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that one’s own duty, rightly done and offered to God, is itself the path to perfection; nothing outside the right action is needed.
hinduism.tie_back: Like vinai-nalam, rightly performed action is the source from which every good end follows.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.46 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his hearers to put righteousness first and trust that the material needs they worry about will follow.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say that putting rightness first brings ‘all these things’ along with it.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer - We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward [in the Hereafter] according to the best of what they used to do.”
islam.explanation: The Quran promises that righteous action brings a good life now and the best reward later.
islam.tie_back: Righteous deeds yielding both this-worldly and next-worldly good match Parimelazhagar’s gloss of ‘all that is desired’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Study is not the most important thing, but actions”
judaism.explanation: Shimon ben Gamaliel sums up a lifetime among the sages: what counts in the end is not learning or talk but deeds.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise puts the quality of the deed above every outside aid.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If with a pure mind a person speaks or acts happiness follows him like his never-departing shadow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada opens by teaching that action from a pure mind brings happiness that never leaves the doer.
buddhism.tie_back: Pure action (tūymai) as the thing that brings every good matches the Kural’s vinai-nalam.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wilt thou not cease to long for a family? How long wilt thou live in sorrow saying, It is for children? O my heart! there is no advantage that accrues to the soul except the good thou doest, though it be but little.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar's chapter on the fear of misconduct says that no support from family or dependants profits the soul; only the good one does oneself, however small, brings real gain.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ranks the goodness of one's own deeds above the goodness of one's supporters; the Naladiyar likewise sets aside what others can do for us and counts only one's own good action.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 13 'The fear of misconduct', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak ranks truthful conduct (sach aachaar) above everything, even above knowing the truth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says good allies bring increase, but goodness in the deeds themselves brings everything one could wish for; Guru Nanak likewise places the purity of one's own conduct above all else.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus’ fable, told by Socrates in Xenophon, the young Heracles meets Virtue and Vice at a crossroads, and Virtue tells him the gods give nothing truly good without toil and right effort.
greek_mythology.explanation: Vice offers an easy road to pleasure; Virtue promises real goods, honour, friends and a blessed name, only through honest labour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the myth says the right way of acting, not easy help, wins everything worth having.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that at the Olympic Games the crown goes not to the finest or strongest onlookers but to those who compete, and in the same way it is those who act rightly who win the noble and good things in life.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle happiness is found in virtuous activity itself, not in possessions or outside advantages.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too puts the quality of the action ahead of outside supports.

real_life_example.event_title: Johnson & Johnson recalls Tylenol nationwide
real_life_example.event: After seven people in the Chicago area died in September 1982 from Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules that someone had laced with cyanide, Johnson & Johnson's subsidiary McNeil Consumer Products carried out what was then the largest consumer product recall in American history, about 31 million bottles. Chairman James Burke said the recall and replacement would cost over 100 million dollars and that none of it would be passed on to customers. In November 1982 the company became the first to return to the market with the new tamper-resistant packaging required by the Food and Drug Administration, offering to replace any bottle customers had thrown away.
real_life_example.explanation: The poisonings were not the company's fault, yet it chose the costly, public-spirited course, and that conduct rebuilt the trust on which the brand depended.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says good allies bring increase, but goodness in one's own deeds brings everything one could wish for, and Johnson & Johnson set about rebuilding its standing through the integrity of its own response rather than outside help.

tamil:
என்றும் ஒருவுதல் வேண்டும் புகழொடு
நன்றி பயவா வினை.
transliteration:
Endrum oruvudhal vendum pugazhodu
Nandri payavaa vinai.
meaning: Always stay away from any action that brings neither a good name nor any real good.
elementary: Before you do something, ask two questions: will people be proud of me for this, and will it truly help? If the answer to both is no, don’t do it, even if it looks easy or tempting.
university: The couplet gives the test that runs through the whole chapter: a deed must yield pukaḻ (fame, good name) together with naṉṟi (benefit, goodness), and a deed that yields neither is to be avoided (oruvutal, ‘setting aside, shunning’) at all times (eṉṟum). Parimelazhagar and later commentators such as Solomon Pappaiah read the pair as fame in this life and merit (aṟam) for the life to come, so a clean act must be both publicly honourable and morally fruitful. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the rejected deeds as those ‘without purity’ (tūymai aṟṟa), tying the verse to the chapter title. The prose explanation printed with Pope’s translation (‘acts which, in addition to fame, yield no benefit’) reads pukaḻoṭu slightly differently, but all readings agree that honour alone is not enough without real good. The text is stable across all three sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu tells the householder to avoid the pursuit of wealth and pleasure whenever they conflict with dharma, the sacred law.
hinduism.explanation: The lawgiver ranks artha (wealth) and kāma (desire) below dharma and tells the householder to give up any gain that goes against it.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Manu rules out any act that does not also serve the good, however profitable it looks.

christianity.quote_or_event: “whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Philippians to fix their minds on what is both morally good and of good report.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s pairing of virtue and praise mirrors the Kural’s pairing of naṉṟi and pukaḻ.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one’s] hope.”
islam.explanation: The Quran sets passing worldly gains against good deeds whose worth lasts.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too tells the doer to choose only deeds whose good lasts beyond the moment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “which is the straight path that a man should choose for himself? One which is an honor to the person adopting it, and [on account of which] honor [accrues] to him from others.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince defines the right path as one that is honourable in itself and also brings honour from other people.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s double test: a deed must be good in itself and bring an honourable name.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Vanijja Sutta the Buddha names five trades a lay follower should not practise: dealing in weapons, in living beings, in meat, in intoxicants and in poisons.
buddhism.explanation: These livelihoods may be profitable, but they cause harm, so a disciple is told to give them up entirely.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the sutta rules out whole kinds of action because they bring no real good, however much they earn.

jainism.quote_or_event: “An intelligent man who has learned (the sacred texts) takes his duties upon himself, and he becomes renowned in the world; as the earth is the dwelling of all beings, so he will be a dwelling of all duties.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline presents renown as the natural result of taking up one's duties fully and rightly.
jainism.tie_back: The kural requires a deed to bring both good name and real good; the Jain verse joins renown to faithful performance of duty in the same way.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.45 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, those deeds which do not bring merit - forget about those deeds.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, tells the seeker simply to drop any action that yields no good.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one must always give up any deed that brings neither honour nor real good; Farid gives almost the same rule.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that the road to badness is smooth and close at hand, while the gods have set sweat before goodness, on a road that is long and steep at first but easy once the top is reached.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet urges choosing the harder path that leads to real worth over the easy one that leads to ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural too asks for the discipline to turn down easy acts that bring no honour and no good.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that nothing can truly be expedient (utile) that is not also morally right (honestum), and that the appearance of profit in a wrong act is always a delusion.
philosophy.explanation: Book 3 of On Duties is built on the claim that the useful and the honourable can never really conflict.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s refusal to separate profit from honour matches the Kural’s demand for deeds that bring both good name and good.

real_life_example.event_title: Lise Meitner refuses to work on the atomic bomb
real_life_example.event: Lise Meitner, the Austrian physicist who with her nephew Otto Frisch first explained nuclear fission in 1939, was living in exile in Sweden when she was invited in 1942 to join the Manhattan Project. She refused, declaring that she would have nothing to do with a bomb. After the war she continued to avoid any connection between her research and the atomic bomb, and when Otto Hahn alone received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for fission, her own contribution went unrecognised by the prize.
real_life_example.explanation: Meitner turned away from the most consequential scientific project of the war because she judged the deed itself to be one she would not take part in, whatever prestige it might bring.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one must always give up a deed that brings neither honour nor real good, and Meitner, judging bomb-making to be such a deed, refused it outright.

tamil:
ஒஓதல் வேண்டும் ஒளிமாழ்கும் செய்வினை
ஆஅதும் என்னு மவர்.
transliteration:
Oodhal vendum olimaazhkum seyvinai
Aaadhum ennu mavar.
meaning: People who say 'we want to rise higher' must stay away from any action that would dim their good name.
elementary: If you want to become class captain, you wouldn’t cheat on a test, because once people see you cheat they stop trusting you. Anyone who wants to grow greater has to keep their good name bright and stay away from anything that would spoil it.
university: Two alapeṭai (metrical lengthenings) mark the couplet: ஒஓதல் for ஓதல்/ஒருவுதல் (avoiding, shunning), and ஆஅதும் for ஆதும், ‘we shall become (greater)’, which Parimelazhagar takes as the resolve of those who seek to rise ever higher. Oḷi (light, radiance) stands here for reputation and dignity, and oḷi-māḻkum seyviṉai means acts that cause that radiance to fade. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both take oḷi as pukaḻ (fame), linking this verse to the fame-and-good test of 652, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as ‘one’s standing in one’s own lifetime’. The logic is a statesman’s: ambition itself is a reason for scruple, since a stained name blocks the rise one hopes for. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi-joined form ஒஓதல் வேண்டு மொளிமாழ்குஞ் செய்வினை / யாஅது மென்னு மவர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that deserting his duty would bring lasting disgrace, which for a man of standing is worse than dying.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat a dimmed name as a loss too great for someone who aims high to risk.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.34 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells scattered believers to live so honestly that even their critics will be won over by their good works.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Peter treats blameless conduct as the guard of a good name that others are watching.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever desires honor [through power] - then to Allah belongs all honor. To Him ascends good speech, and righteous work raises it. But they who plot evil deeds will have a severe punishment, and the plotting of those - it will perish.”
islam.explanation: The verse tells those who seek honour that only righteous work truly raises a person, while scheming comes to nothing.
islam.tie_back: This fits the Kural closely: people who want to rise must hold to deeds that lift, not ones that disgrace.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are three crowns: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of royalty, but the crown of a good name supersedes them all.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shimon ranks a good name above even learning, priesthood and kingship.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise treats a bright name as the thing an ambitious person must guard above all.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not the sweet smell of flowers, not even the fragrance of sandal, tagara, or jasmine blows against the wind. But the fragrance of the virtuous blows against the wind.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the reputation of the virtuous spreads in every direction, which no ordinary perfume can do.
buddhism.tie_back: The ‘fragrance’ of virtue is the Buddhist image for the same radiance (oḷi) that the Kural says wrong deeds would dim.

jainism.quote_or_event: “His knowledge will be honoured, his doubts will be removed, he will gladden the heart of his teacher by his good acts; kept in safety by the performance of austerities and by meditation, being as it were a great light, he will keep the five vows.”
jainism.explanation: The disciple who rises through good conduct is pictured as a great light, his standing secured by austerity, meditation and keeping the vows.
jainism.tie_back: The kural tells those who mean to rise higher to avoid any deed that dims their radiance; the Jain verse shows the other side, the light that pure conduct and kept vows make shine.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.47 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who have meditated on the Naam, the Name of the Lord, and departed after having worked by the sweat of their brows -O Nanak, their faces are radiant in the Court of the Lord, and many are saved along with them!”
sikhism.explanation: The closing salok of Japji promises radiant faces to those whose lives combined remembrance of God with honest toil.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells those who would rise higher to avoid any deed that dims the light of their good name; Japji likewise links a shining face, a radiant honour, to a life of upright effort.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Jap (Japji Sahib, closing salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hector tells Andromache he would feel dire shame before the Trojan men and women if he shrank from battle like a coward, for he has learned always to stand among the foremost and win glory for his father and himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector chooses danger over any act that would stain the honour he and his house have built.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s aspirant, Hector will not do what dims his name, whatever it costs him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle’s great-souled person (megalopsychos), who is concerned above all with honour, will not stoop to anything base or shameful, since honour is the greatest of external goods and is fitting only to the good.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle real honour can belong only to virtue, so one who seeks it cannot act basely.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s logic that the ambition to rise is itself a reason to avoid tarnishing deeds.

real_life_example.event_title: Rabindranath Tagore renounces his knighthood
real_life_example.event: Rabindranath Tagore, winner of the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature, had been knighted in 1915. After the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in Amritsar in April 1919 and the harsh measures that followed in the Punjab, he wrote to the Viceroy, Lord Chelmsford, on 31 May 1919, asking to be relieved of his knighthood. He wrote that badges of honour had become a mark of shame in that context and that he wished to stand, without special distinctions, beside his countrymen; the letter was published in The Statesman in June 1919.
real_life_example.explanation: Tagore judged that keeping an honour from a government that had acted as it had in the Punjab would tarnish his name, and he gave it up publicly.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who wish to rise must avoid anything that dims the light of their good name, and Tagore chose to give up a title rather than let it dim his standing with his own people.

tamil:
இடுக்கண் படினும் இளிவந்த செய்யார்
நடுக்கற்ற காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Idukkan padinum ilivandha seyyaar
Nadukkatra kaatchi yavar.
meaning: People who see clearly and are not shaken will never do anything shameful, even when they are in deep trouble.
elementary: Imagine you lost your lunch money and saw someone else’s wallet on the floor. A person with a steady, clear mind would still hand it in, even though they’re hungry. Being in trouble doesn’t make a wrong thing right.
university: Iṭukkaṇ is ‘distress, affliction’ (compare the chapter iṭukkaṇ aḻiyāmai, ch. 63), and iḷivanta means ‘what brings disgrace’. Parimelazhagar takes the past-tense participle literally as ‘acts that have (in the past) brought disgrace’, which is why the prose explanation printed with Pope says ‘acts which have brought disgrace (on former ministers)’. The key phrase naṭukku-aṟṟa kāṭci, ‘vision free of trembling’, describes firm, clear discernment that does not waver under pressure, and Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as ‘motionless, clear knowledge’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar add that such people will not act basely even to escape their distress, which prepares for the stronger case of 656. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read இடுக்கண் படினும்; thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the sandhi form இடுக்கட் படினு மிளிவந்த.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, tested by the sage Vishvamitra, loses his kingdom, sells his wife and son, and works as a servant at a cremation ground, yet never breaks his word or his truthfulness.
hinduism.explanation: However deep his suffering, the king refuses to buy relief with a dishonourable act, and in the end the gods restore him.
hinduism.tie_back: Harishchandra is the classic Indian example of the ‘unshaken vision’ that will not stoop even in great distress.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews praises Moses for choosing hardship with his people over the comforts of Pharaoh’s court.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s steady-minded person, Moses accepts affliction rather than take a dishonourable way out.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘My Lord, prison is more to my liking than that to which they invite me. And if You do not avert from me their plan, I might incline toward them and [thus] be of the ignorant.’”
islam.explanation: The prophet Joseph (Yusuf), threatened with prison unless he gives in to wrongdoing, prefers prison.
islam.tie_back: Yusuf is a precise image of the Kural’s ideal: facing real hardship, he still refuses the disgraceful act.

judaism.quote_or_event: Joseph, a slave in Potiphar’s house, refuses the repeated advances of his master’s wife, asking how he could do so great a wickedness and sin against God, and he is thrown into prison on her false charge.
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s refusal costs him his position and freedom, yet the Torah presents it as the root of his later rise.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph shows the Kural’s unshaken discernment: danger does not move him to a dishonourable act.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares the wise to a rock that the winds of fortune cannot move.
buddhism.tie_back: The unshaken rock is a close image for the Kural’s naṭukku-aṟṟa kāṭci, vision that does not tremble.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though overcome by thirst, he should drink no cold water, restrained by shame and aversion (from forbidden things); he should try to get distilled water.”
jainism.explanation: Among the hardships a monk must bear, the Uttaradhyayana says that even when tormented by thirst he must not do what is forbidden, held back by shame and aversion.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says people of steady vision will not do shameful deeds even in deep distress; the Jain monk likewise holds to his rule under thirst, restrained by the same sense of shame.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, took up the cause of those facing forced conversion under Aurangzeb and, refusing to convert himself, was publicly beheaded in Delhi in 1675; Gurdwara Sis Ganj marks the place.
sikhism.explanation: In the greatest personal danger the Guru chose death over an act he held to be dishonourable, and Sikhs remember him for that steadfastness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says people of clear understanding will not do anything shameful even in serious trouble; Guru Tegh Bahadur's refusal to renounce his faith at the cost of his life is a supreme Sikh example of that resolve.
sikhism.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, The Development of the Sikh Community

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Bellerophon, a guest at the court of King Proetus, rejects the queen Anteia’s advances; she falsely accuses him, and he is sent to Lycia carrying a sealed message asking for his death, and made to face the Chimera and other perils.
greek_mythology.explanation: Bellerophon keeps his integrity even though it brings him into mortal danger, and he survives his trials.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s steady-minded person, he will not do the disgraceful thing even when refusing puts him in peril.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates tells the jury that when the Thirty Tyrants ordered him and four others to arrest Leon of Salamis for execution, he alone went home and refused, though it might have cost him his life.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says he cared nothing for death but everything about not doing anything unjust or unholy.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a model case of the Kural: under real threat, a clear mind will not take part in a disgraceful act.

real_life_example.event_title: Mark Twain pays his creditors in full after bankruptcy
real_life_example.place: United States and a world lecture tour
real_life_example.event: Mark Twain's publishing firm, Charles L. Webster and Company, failed in 1894, leaving debts of about 80,000 dollars beyond its assets, and Twain declared personal bankruptcy. Although he was not legally required to repay them in full, he set out from Cleveland on 15 July 1895 on a lecture tour around the world and wrote further books. With the earnings he repaid his creditors every cent, with interest, about a year sooner than he had expected.
real_life_example.explanation: Twain was in serious financial trouble and had a legal way out, but he chose the honourable course of paying in full.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says people of clear, unshaken understanding will not do anything shameful even when in serious trouble, and Twain refused to let bankruptcy become an excuse for leaving his creditors unpaid.

tamil:
எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க செய்வானேல்
மற்றன்ன செய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Etrendru iranguva seyyarka seyvaanel
Matranna seyyaamai nandru.
meaning: Do not do anything that will later make you cry, 'What have I done!' And if you have already done such a thing, it is best not to do it again.
elementary: If you ever do something that makes you think ‘Oh no, why did I do that?’, the best thing is to learn from it and never do it again. Even better is to stop and think first, so you don’t have to feel that way at all.
university: Eṟṟu eṉṟu is an exclamation of dismay (‘what is this!’), and iraṅkuva are deeds one will afterwards lament. The first line forbids such deeds, and the second deals with the case where one has already done one. Here the commentaries split. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read maṟṟu aṉṉa ceyyāmai as ‘not doing such things again’, so repentance means not repeating the fault. The older reading, kept in the Drew-Lazarus prose explanation printed with Pope (‘it were good that he grieved not’) and in Puliyur Kesikan, takes aṉṉa ceyyāmai as ‘not doing that (grieving) again’: a minister should not waste himself in useless regret. This reading is usually traced to Parimelazhagar. The text also varies: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read செய்வானேல் (‘if he does’), while thirukkural-thamizh.org prints செய்வானேன், probably a typographical variant, since the conditional -ēl is needed for the sense.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu teaches that a person who has done a blameworthy deed, knowingly or not, and wishes to be freed from it, must not commit it a second time, and that the resolve ‘I will not do so again’ purifies him.
hinduism.explanation: In the Laws of Manu, the heart of expiation is sincere regret together with a firm resolve never to repeat the deed.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the majority reading of the second line: if one has erred, the good course is never to repeat it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sends away the woman taken in adultery without condemning her, but tells her not to repeat the sin.
christianity.tie_back: This is the same two-step logic as the Kural’s second line: once a wrong is done, the good is never to do it again.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves [by transgression], remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins - and who can forgive sins except Allah? - and [who] do not persist in what they have done while they know.”
islam.explanation: The Quran praises those who, after doing wrong, turn back to God and do not persist in the wrong.
islam.tie_back: ‘Do not persist’ is exactly the Kural’s counsel after a regrettable deed.

judaism.quote_or_event: Maimonides defines complete repentance as the sinner abandoning the sin, removing it from his thoughts and resolving never to do it again, so firmly that God can testify he will not return to it.
judaism.explanation: In the Laws of Repentance, the proof of teshuvah is facing the same situation and not repeating the sin.
judaism.tie_back: Maimonides spells out the Kural’s second line as a full theory of repentance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a person commit evil, let him not do it again and again. Let him not find pleasure therein, for painful is the accumulation of evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada accepts that people may fall into wrong but insists they must not repeat it or take pleasure in it.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost a word-for-word match for the second line of the Kural in its common reading.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not be angry with them nor do them any harm, nor say a single hard word to them, but he should promise not to commit the same sin again; for this is better than to do wrong.”
jainism.explanation: When a monk is corrected for a fault, the Sutrakritanga tells him to accept it calmly and promise not to commit the same sin again.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says to avoid deeds one will regret and, if one has done one, not to do the like again; the Jain verse makes exactly that promise of non-repetition the right response to a fault.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Acting in egotism, so very many have died. After making mistakes, they later repent and regret.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak observes that deeds done from haumai (ego) end in regret and repentance afterwards.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns against doing anything that will later make one cry out in regret; Guru Nanak traces such regret to deeds done in egotism.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 109, Raag Maajh, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ play, Ajax, maddened by Athena, slaughters cattle believing them to be the Greek chiefs; on waking and seeing what he has done, he is overwhelmed with shame and despair.
greek_mythology.explanation: The tragedy dwells on the horror of recognising a deed that cannot be undone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ajax’s awakening is the ‘what have I done!’ moment that the Kural tells us to avoid by never acting that way to begin with.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza holds that repentance is not a virtue and does not arise from reason; one who repents of a deed is twice unhappy or weak, first in the deed and then in the sorrow.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, useless grief over past actions only adds a second weakness to the first.
philosophy.tie_back: This supports the older commentarial reading of the second line, that a minister who has erred should not waste himself in grieving.

real_life_example.event_title: Canada apologises to Japanese Canadians and pledges 'never again'
real_life_example.event: During and after the Second World War, about 22,000 Japanese Canadians were uprooted from their homes, interned or sent to work camps, and had their property confiscated and sold, though not one was charged with disloyalty. On 22 September 1988 Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and Art Miki of the National Association of Japanese Canadians signed the Redress Agreement, and Mulroney apologised in the House of Commons, pledging that the government would ensure, to the limits of its powers, that such injustice would never occur again. The settlement included 21,000 dollars for each survivor and funds to create the Canadian Race Relations Foundation.
real_life_example.explanation: The government acknowledged a wrong that its predecessors had committed and created an institution meant to keep such discrimination from happening again.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says to avoid deeds that one will later lament, and if such a deed has been done, not to do the like again, and Canada's apology joined that admission of regret to a formal pledge against repetition.

tamil:
ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினுஞ் செய்யற்க
சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை.
transliteration:
Eendraal pasikaanbaan aayinum seyyarka
Saandror pazhikkum vinai.
meaning: Even if you have to watch your own mother go hungry, do not do anything that wise people would call wrong.
elementary: Suppose someone you love very much needs help. You would want to do anything for them, but stealing or lying still isn’t the right way. The Kural says even love for your own mother doesn’t make a wrong deed right. You must find an honest way to help.
university: This is the strongest statement in the chapter. Īṉṟāḷ, ‘she who bore (you)’, is the mother; pacikāṇpāṉ āyiṉum means ‘even if he should (have to) see her hunger’. Tamil ethics counts care of parents among the highest duties, so the verse deliberately picks the hardest case: not even that duty justifies deeds the cāṉṟōr (people of perfected character) condemn. Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators read the line without exception clauses, and Kalaignar sharpens it to ‘not even to relieve’ her suffering. This contrasts with the Sanskrit doctrine of āpad-dharma (law in emergencies), where the Mahabharata allows the sage Vishvamitra, in famine, to steal dog’s flesh to survive. The Kural here refuses that concession. The text is identical across sources apart from the sandhi form பசிகாண்பா னாயினுஞ் in thirukkural-thamizh.org. (Solomon Pappaiah’s printed gloss has பெற்றவனின், apparently a slip for பெற்றவளின்.)

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Kaikeyi demands Rama’s exile, his mother Kausalya begs him with tears to stay, yet Rama refuses to break his father’s pledged word, choosing dharma over his mother’s grief and his own claim to the throne.
hinduism.explanation: Rama feels his mother’s anguish deeply but holds that truth and duty cannot be given up even for her.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the epic makes a mother’s suffering the hardest test, and has dharma win.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Rama and Kausalya)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And not rather, (as we be slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say,) Let us do evil, that good may come? whose damnation is just.”
christianity.explanation: Paul flatly rejects the idea that a good end can justify an evil act.
christianity.tie_back: This is the principle behind the Kural: not even the good of feeding one’s mother permits a condemned deed.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives.”
islam.explanation: The Quran requires justice even when it goes against one’s own parents and closest kin.
islam.tie_back: Both texts say that love for parents, however sacred, cannot override the demand of right action.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud rules that for three sins, idolatry, forbidden sexual relations and murder, a person must let himself be killed rather than transgress, even to save his own life.
judaism.explanation: Although saving life normally overrides almost every commandment, the rabbis set limits that not even survival can cross.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Talmud names deeds so condemned that no desperate need, not even life, can justify them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is indeed virtuous, wise, and righteous who neither for his own sake nor for the sake of another (does any wrong), who does not crave for sons, wealth, or kingdom, and does not desire success by unjust means.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada defines the wise person as one who will not do wrong even on behalf of others.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Nor for the sake of another’ is the principle of the Kural, which uses one’s own mother as the hardest example.

jainism.quote_or_event: “'Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife, and sons will not be able to help me, when I suffer for my own deeds.'”
jainism.explanation: Jainism teaches that each soul bears the fruit of its own karma alone, and no relative, not even a mother, can share or lift that burden.
jainism.tie_back: The kural forbids deeds the wise condemn even to relieve a starving mother; the Jain verse gives a reason in its own terms, since the doer alone will suffer for the wrong and the mother cannot help him then.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com); the verse recurs at Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.9.5

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak makes taking another's due (hak paraaia) as abhorrent as the strongest taboo of each community, a line no circumstance excuses.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one must not do what the wise condemn even if it means watching one's own mother go hungry; Guru Nanak likewise treats wrongful gain as absolutely forbidden.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh (Majh ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stranded and starving on Thrinacia, Odysseus’ crew, urged on by Eurylochus, slaughter the forbidden cattle of Helios; Zeus wrecks their ship and all perish except Odysseus, who alone refused to eat.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hunger seemed to justify breaking a divine prohibition, but the forbidden meal destroyed those who ate it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode shows the Kural’s point: dire hunger does not make a condemned deed safe or right.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues against Polus that doing wrong is worse than suffering it, so that if he had to choose, he would rather suffer injustice than commit it.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, wrongdoing harms the soul of the doer, which is a worse evil than any loss he could suffer.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural reaches the same conclusion: better to bear the pain of want than to do a deed the wise condemn.

real_life_example.event_title: The plant scientists of Leningrad guard the seed bank while starving
real_life_example.event: During the siege of Leningrad, staff of the plant-breeding institute founded by Nikolai Vavilov stayed on to protect its collection of about a quarter of a million seed samples, guarding it against rats, looters and their own hunger. Several of them, including the groundnut specialist Aleksandr Shchukin and the head of the rice section, died of starvation at the institute while surrounded by seeds and grain they had refused to eat. Most of the central collection survived the siege, and seeds from it were later used to breed crops grown on a large share of Russia's farmland.
real_life_example.explanation: The scientists believed that eating the collection, the irreplaceable work of many lives, would be a betrayal of their duty to the future, and they held to that even in the most extreme hunger.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says not to do what the wise condemn even if one must watch one's own mother go hungry, and the Leningrad botanists kept to their duty even at the cost of their own lives by starvation.

tamil:
பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கத்தின் சான்றோர்
கழிநல் குரவே தலை.
transliteration:
Pazhimalaindhu eydhiya aakkaththin saandror
Kazhinal kuravae thalai.
meaning: For good people, being very poor is better than getting rich in a shameful way.
elementary: Would you rather have a small lunch you paid for honestly, or a big feast you got by cheating? The Kural says the small honest lunch is worth far more, because you can enjoy it with a clear heart.
university: Paḻi malaintu, ‘having taken on / worn blame’ (malai- as in wearing a garland), describes wealth won by accepting disgrace, and ākkattiṉ is the comparative ablative, ‘than such wealth’. Kaḻi nalkuravu is ‘extreme, excessive poverty’ (kaḻi = beyond measure). Parimelazhagar takes it as the poverty of the cāṉṟōr, and Mu. Varadarasanar adds that they accept it because they keep purity of action (viṉait-tūymai). Talai means ‘head, foremost’, so such poverty ranks first. The couplet restates 656 as a general value judgement and prepares for the fate of tainted wealth in 658-660. All three sources agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the sandhi forms மலைந் தெய்திய வாக்கத்திற்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna describes people of demonic nature who, bound by hundreds of desires and given to lust and anger, strive to pile up wealth by unjust means for their own enjoyment.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita counts gathering wealth through injustice (anyāyena artha-sañcaya) among the marks of a nature bound for ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s tainted wealth is exactly the Gita’s wealth amassed by unjust means, which the wise would never choose over poverty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus asks what any gain could be worth if it costs the self.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural asks the same question in social terms: no fortune is worth one’s honour, so honest poverty is better.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘Not equal are the evil and the good, although the abundance of evil might impress you.’ So fear Allah, O you of understanding, that you may be successful.”
islam.explanation: The Quran warns believers not to be dazzled by the abundance of what is corrupt.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks a little that is good above a great deal gained through wrong.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Psalmist declares that the little a righteous man has is better than the great wealth of many wicked.
judaism.explanation: Psalm 37 comforts the upright, who may see the wicked prosper, with the promise that honest little is worth more.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost the same comparison as the Kural: righteous poverty over wicked plenty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth. A trustworthy person is the best kinsman, Nibbana the highest bliss.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada redefines wealth as contentment, not as possessions.
buddhism.tie_back: The poverty of the good that the Kural praises is rich in the contentment and trustworthiness this verse values.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira warns that wealth won by evil deeds does not last, and that its owners end up caught in the snares of their own passions.
jainism.tie_back: The kural rates the poverty of the good above wealth won through disgrace; the Jain verse explains why such wealth is no prize, since it is lost and leaves its owner bound.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: At Saiyidpur (Eminabad), Macauliffe relates, Guru Nanak stayed with Lalo, a poor carpenter, and declined the feast of the rich steward Malik Bhago. Called to explain, he squeezed Lalo's coarse bread and Bhago's rich bread: milk flowed from the first and blood from the second, showing honest labour against wealth won by bribery and oppression.
sikhism.explanation: The story contrasts the pure food of honest work (kirat karni) with the tainted riches of exploitation, and the Guru openly chose the poor man's bread.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the deepest poverty of good people is better than wealth gained through disgrace; the Guru's preference for Lalo's simple bread over Bhago's feast makes the same choice.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak, ch. IV, pp. 43-44

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor, pious old couple Baucis and Philemon alone welcome Zeus and Hermes in disguise after their rich neighbours turn the gods away; the neighbours’ homes are flooded, and the couple’s hut becomes a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid sets humble goodness against prosperous impiety, and the gods reward the poor couple.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the myth shows the poverty of the good as worth more than the wealth of the unworthy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus says that if he can gain wealth while keeping himself modest, faithful and high-minded, he will; but if he must lose his own goods so that others may gain things that are not good, it is unjust and foolish to ask it.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, integrity is a real good and money is not, so no trade of one for the other makes sense.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s reasoning: better to stay poor than to exchange one’s good name for money.

real_life_example.event_title: Vera Caslavska accepts years of hardship rather than betray her stance
real_life_example.event: The Czech gymnast Vera Caslavska, winner of 22 gold medals at Olympic, world and European level, signed the Two Thousand Words manifesto for democratic reform in June 1968 and, after the Soviet-led invasion that August, went into hiding before winning four golds at the Mexico City Olympics. Because of her political convictions she fell out of favour with the Communist authorities, was refused employment and for two decades was barred from travelling, at times working as a cleaner. After the fall of communism in 1989 she became president of the Czechoslovak Olympic Committee and an adviser to President Vaclav Havel.
real_life_example.explanation: Caslavska could have had the comfortable life of a national sporting hero by bending to the authorities, but she accepted poverty and obscurity instead.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the deepest poverty of good people is better than wealth gained by taking on disgrace, and Caslavska's two decades of hardship rather than giving up her stance is a modern example.

tamil:
கடிந்த கடிந்தொரார் செய்தார்க்கு அவைதாம்
முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும்.
transliteration:
Kadindha kadindhoraar seydhaarkku avaidhaam
Mudindhaalum peezhai tharum.
meaning: People who do the things the wise have told them not to do will suffer for it, even if those things work out.
elementary: If you sneak a cookie from the jar after being told not to, you might get the cookie, but then you feel worried and guilty, and you might get caught later. Even when a wrong plan ‘works’, it ends up making you unhappy.
university: The first line plays on the verb kaṭi- (‘forbid, reject’): kaṭinta, ‘things forbidden (by the great)’, and kaṭintu orār, ‘those who do not reject them and turn away’. Solomon Pappaiah specifies that such people act ‘thinking to gather wealth’, keeping the chapter’s focus on means of gain. The concessive muṭintālum, ‘even if they are accomplished’, is the point: success does not clean a forbidden act, which still brings pīḻai (suffering, affliction). Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes the suffering to come in this life as well as the next, through loss of reputation and later retribution. All sources agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org divides it as செய்தார்க் கவைதா / முடிந்தாலும்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Yama teaches Nachiketas that the good (śreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) are two different things; the wise choose the good, while the foolish choose the pleasant and fall short of the true goal.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad separates what gives immediate satisfaction from what is truly good, warning that success in the pleasant can be failure in the real aim.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s forbidden deed that ‘succeeds’ is a clear case of preyas won and śreyas lost.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says what is gained by fraud tastes sweet at first but turns bitter and painful.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: the wrong deed succeeds, and then brings grief.

islam.quote_or_event: “So when they forgot that by which they had been reminded, We opened to them the doors of every [good] thing until, when they rejoiced in that which they were given, We seized them suddenly, and they were [then] in despair.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes people who ignored warnings and prospered for a time, until their prosperity ended suddenly in ruin.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, success after ignoring what was forbidden only leads to a harder fall.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs says that treasures gained by a lying tongue are a vapour driven to and fro, and that those who seek them are seeking death.
judaism.explanation: Riches obtained by falsehood are pictured as a breath that vanishes and as a snare for the one who pursues them.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too says a forbidden deed that gains its object still ends in suffering.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “So long as an evil deed has not ripened, the fool thinks it as sweet as honey. But when the evil deed ripens, the fool comes to grief.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that the first sweetness of a wrong act hides the pain it will later bring.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the same pattern as the Kural: the forbidden deed may succeed at first, but suffering follows.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
jainism.explanation: The commentator Devendra explains the image: a burglar who had dug his way through a wall is crushed when the wall above the breach comes down, killed by the very work he had completed.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says forbidden deeds bring suffering even when they succeed; the burglar's finished breach, which becomes his death, is a vivid picture of exactly that.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3, with Jacobi's note citing Devendra (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Why do you do such evil deeds, that you shall have to suffer so?”
sikhism.explanation: This pauri of Asa ki Vaar warns that a person must reap the fruit of what they do, so wrong deeds only lead to their own suffering.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says deeds the wise forbid bring suffering even when they succeed; the pauri likewise insists that wrong deeds return as suffering to their doer.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, Pauri 21) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asks Dionysus that everything he touches turn to gold; the wish is granted, but his food and drink turn to metal, and he begs to be freed from the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas gets exactly what his greed asked for, and that success becomes his torment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Midas is the Kural’s warning in myth form: a wrongly sought end, once achieved, brings suffering.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates argues that the tyrant, who seems to have succeeded completely through injustice, is in truth the most wretched of men, enslaved to his desires and living in constant fear.
philosophy.explanation: Against Thrasymachus and Glaucon, Plato argues that injustice harms the one who does it, however well it seems to go.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural states the same idea briefly: wrongful deeds, even when they succeed, bring suffering to the doer.

real_life_example.event_title: The Recruit shares-for-favours scandal brings down Japan's prime minister
real_life_example.event: In the mid-1980s the Recruit company offered cheap, unlisted shares in its real estate subsidiary Recruit Cosmos to nearly 200 politicians, officials and businessmen, who profited when the shares began trading. When the deals came to light, several cabinet ministers resigned, including Finance Minister Kiichi Miyazawa in late 1988, and Recruit's founder Hiromasa Ezoe was indicted in 1989. Prime Minister Noboru Takeshita, who admitted that he and his aides had received stocks, donations and loans from Recruit, announced his resignation on 25 April 1989 and left office in June.
real_life_example.explanation: The share deals did exactly what they were meant to do, enriching those who received them, yet the scheme ended in resignations, indictments and public disgrace.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those who do what the wise forbid, such deeds bring suffering even when they succeed, and the profitable Recruit share deals became the ruin of many who took part in them.

tamil:
அழக்கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம் இழப்பினும்
பிற்பயக்கும் நற்பா லவை.
transliteration:
Azhakkonda ellaam azhappoam izhappinum
Pirpayakkum narpaa lavai.
meaning: Everything gained by making others cry will be lost and leave you crying. Things gained in good ways may be lost for a while, but they will pay off later.
elementary: If you take a toy by making another child cry, that toy will bring you trouble and tears in the end. But if you get something fairly and then lose it, good things will still come back to you later.
university: The first line hinges on the double use of aḻa, ‘so as to weep’: what was taken (koṇṭa) while making others weep will depart (pōm) making the taker weep. It is a compact statement of moral retribution. The second line balances it: naṟ-pālavai, ‘things of a good kind’, meaning wealth obtained by fair means, even if lost (iḻappiṉum), will give fruit afterwards (piṟ-payakkum). Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read this ‘fruit’ as a return of benefit in this life or merit in the next, and Kalaignar says such wealth ‘comes back again’. The verse sharpens the chapter’s theme of means into a law of consequences. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form அழக்கொண்ட வெல்லா மழப்போ மிழப்பினும் / பிற்பயக்கு நற்பா லவை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the rigged dice game the Kauravas win the Pandavas’ kingdom and drag Draupadi into the assembly in tears; her humiliation and curse are later repaid when the Kurukshetra war destroys the Kaurava line, and the Pandavas regain what they lost.
hinduism.explanation: Wealth and power taken through deceit and cruelty lead to the ruin of those who took them, while the wronged side is in the end restored.
hinduism.tie_back: The epic plays out both halves of the Kural: what is taken with tears goes with tears, and what is rightly held, though lost, returns.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (the dice game) and its sequel

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.”
christianity.explanation: James warns rich oppressors that the cries of the workers they cheated have reached God, and that their hoarded riches will rot.
christianity.tie_back: The cries of the wronged, answered by the ruin of the wrongdoer, match the Kural’s ‘taken with tears, gone with tears’.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah destroys interest and gives increase for charities. And Allah does not like every sinning disbeliever.”
islam.explanation: The Quran teaches that gain from exploitation (ribā) will be wiped out, while wealth given away in good faith grows.
islam.tie_back: Both texts set two opposite laws side by side: exploitative gain vanishes, and rightly used wealth brings later increase.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jeremiah compares the one who gets riches unjustly to a partridge that sits on eggs it did not lay: in the middle of his days the riches leave him, and at his end he is a fool.
judaism.explanation: The prophet’s image shows ill-gotten wealth deserting its holder before he can enjoy it.
judaism.tie_back: This matches the first line of the Kural: what was wrongly taken will not stay.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ill done is that action of doing which one repents later, and the fruit of which one, weeping, reaps with tears.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says a wrong action is known by the fruit it bears: the doer later reaps it in tears.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s play on weeping (aḻa) has a close echo in this verse’s ‘weeping, reaps with tears’.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Like as when the glittering spear that he cast is caught by his enemy's hand, the theif's courage is destroyed, so since the gains of sin follow after and destroy the acquirer of these gains in two births, it is good to leave the ignorant altogether.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar teaches that sinful gains turn back on the one who acquired them, like a spear caught and turned by the enemy, and ruin him in this birth and the next.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says what is taken by making others weep will leave the taker weeping; the Naladiyar's spear that comes back on the thrower shows the same return of wrongful gain on its owner.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 13 'The fear of misconduct', stanza 9 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
sikhism.explanation: In his hymns on Babur's invasion Guru Nanak looks at the riches the defeated rulers lost and says that such wealth is gathered only through sin and departs from its owners in the end.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says whatever is taken by making others weep will leave its taker weeping; Guru Nanak watched wealth gained by oppression being stripped from its holders amid lament.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hecuba, the Thracian king Polymestor murders the young Trojan prince Polydorus, entrusted to his care, to keep the boy’s gold; the grieving Hecuba lures him in, kills his sons and blinds him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Gold taken through a mother’s tears ends by bringing the same bereavement to its taker.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a vivid tragic version of the Kural’s first line: what is taken with tears goes with tears.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy tells Boethius that the gifts of Fortune were never truly his, that she takes back what she gives, and that only goods of the mind cannot be taken away.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius separates outside goods, which always slip away, from inner goods, which last.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘good things’ that return after loss are close to Boethius’ goods that Fortune cannot take away.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2

real_life_example.event_title: Napoleon's looted art is returned from the Louvre
real_life_example.event: During his campaigns Napoleon's armies carried off great quantities of art from across Europe, often through treaties imposed on defeated states, to fill the Musee Napoleon at the Louvre, including the Horses of St Mark's from Venice and Raphael's Transfiguration from Rome. After his final defeat in 1815 the Allies, with the Duke of Wellington and the sculptor Antonio Canova as envoy for the Papal States playing leading roles, had much of this art removed from the Louvre and returned to its owners, while Parisians looked on in anger. Roughly half the seized works went back, the bronze horses reaching Venice in December 1815.
real_life_example.explanation: The collection had been gathered by force and to the grief of those who lost it, and it was stripped away again amid the grief of those who had come to see it as a symbol of national glory.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that what is taken by making others weep will go away and leave the taker weeping, and the dismantling of Napoleon's museum in 1815 is a vivid historical case.

tamil:
சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்தே மார்த்தல் பசுமண்
கலத்துள்நீர் பெய்திரீஇ யற்று.
transliteration:
Salaththaal porulseydhe maarththal pasuman
Kalaththulneer peydhireei yatru.
meaning: Trying to keep yourself safe with money gained by cheating is like pouring water into a pot of wet, unbaked clay and hoping it holds.
elementary: If you pour water into a pot made of wet, unbaked clay, the pot softens and falls apart, and the water leaks away. Money gained by cheating is like that: it seems to hold for a moment, but it melts away and takes the ‘pot’ with it.
university: Calam means deceit or crooked means, and poruḷ ceytu ēmārttal (sandhi ceytē mārttal) is ‘to make wealth and guard/secure (with it)’, from ēmam, safety or protection. Parimelazhagar reads the verse in its ministerial setting: a minister who tries to protect his king and realm with wealth gained by fraud. This is why the prose explanation printed with Pope says ‘(For a minister) to protect (his king)’. The image is pacu-maṇ kalam, a pot of green, unfired clay: pouring water in and trying to keep it there (peytu irīi, with irīi an alapeṭai of iruttal, ‘to keep’) destroys both the water and the vessel. The metaphor makes the same point as the rest of the chapter: foul means undo themselves and ruin the very thing they were meant to protect. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms சலத்தாற் … பசுமட் / கலத்துணீர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Isha Upanishad opens by teaching that all this world is pervaded by the Lord, that one should enjoy it through renunciation, and that one must not covet anyone’s wealth.
hinduism.explanation: The verse bases right possession on non-grasping and forbids reaching for what belongs to others.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural shows what happens when that rule is broken: wealth grasped wrongly cannot be held.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell: and great was the fall of it.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus compares a life built without obedience to a house on sand that collapses when the waters come.
christianity.tie_back: Like the unbaked pot, the house on sand is a structure that fails the moment water tests it.

islam.quote_or_event: “O people, Allah is Good and He therefore, accepts only that which is good.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that God accepts nothing gained unlawfully, and describes a man whose food, drink and clothing are unlawful, asking how his prayer could be accepted.
islam.tie_back: Just as the Kural’s clay pot cannot hold water, the hadith says wealth from unlawful sources cannot support even prayer.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud rules that a commandment fulfilled through a transgression (mitzvah ha-ba’ah ba-aveirah), such as waving a stolen lulav on Sukkot, is invalid, citing Isaiah’s ‘I the Lord love justice, I hate robbery with a burnt offering’.
judaism.explanation: Even a sacred purpose cannot be achieved with stolen means; the tainted means cancel the act.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point in legal form: foul means ruin the very purpose they are meant to serve.
