buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Great Forty discourse the Buddha defines wrong livelihood as scheming, persuading, hinting, belittling and using gain to pursue gain, and teaches that right livelihood means abandoning these.
buddhism.explanation: Right livelihood (sammā-ājīva) is a limb of the Noble Eightfold Path, so earning by deceit is itself a departure from the path.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s calam (deceit) as a way of getting wealth is exactly what the Buddha calls wrong livelihood.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that wealth gives no real protection, in this life or the next, to one who has strayed from right conduct.
jainism.tie_back: The kural says that trying to secure oneself with wealth gained by deceit is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot; the Jain verse likewise denies that wealth can be relied on for protection.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Falsehood will come to an end, O Nanak, and Truth will prevail in the end.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that whatever rests on falsehood runs out, and only what rests on truth endures.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares securing oneself with wealth gained by deceit to storing water in an unbaked clay pot; Guru Nanak likewise says that what is built on falsehood cannot last.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 953, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod teaches that wealth should not be seized, since god-given wealth is far better; if a man takes great wealth by violence or by lying tongue, the gods easily bring him low, his house dwindles, and his wealth stays with him only a short time.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet says ill-gotten riches are always unstable, because the gods undo them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim in Greek terms: wealth gathered by fraud will not stay, just as water will not stay in unbaked clay.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle classes those who take from wrong sources, such as usurers, gamblers and robbers, as guilty of ‘sordid love of gain’ (aischrokerdeia), since they accept reproach for the sake of profit.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, where wealth comes from is itself a moral question, and gain bought with disgrace is a vice.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural condemns the same thing, wealth made by crooked means, and adds that it cannot last.

real_life_example.event_title: Regulators close the Bank of Credit and Commerce International
real_life_example.place: London and branches in about 70 countries
real_life_example.event: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), founded by Agha Hasan Abedi, grew into a bank with about 20 billion dollars in assets operating in some 70 countries, but a US Senate investigation later found that it had been built on fraud, concealed losses and a deliberately confusing corporate structure designed to evade regulators. After its auditors documented the fraud, regulators in Britain and other countries shut the bank down worldwide on 5 July 1991. Depositors around the world were left facing heavy losses; in Hong Kong alone some 1.4 billion dollars in local deposits were put in doubt.
real_life_example.explanation: An institution whose apparent strength rested on deceit could not hold its value once the truth came out, and it collapsed taking its depositors' savings with it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares trying to secure oneself with wealth gained by deceit to pouring water into an unbaked clay pot, and BCCI's sudden collapse shows such a vessel failing and losing everything it held.

tamil:
வினைத்திட்பம் என்பது ஒருவன் மனத்திட்பம்
மற்றைய எல்லாம் பிற.
transliteration:
Vinaiththitpam enpadhu oruvan manaththitpam
Matraiya ellaam piRa.
meaning: Being firm in action really means being firm in mind. Every other kind of strength is something different.
elementary: Imagine two kids building a tall block tower. Both have the same blocks, but one gives up when it wobbles and the other keeps going. The blocks are not what made the difference. The strong part was inside the kid who kept going. That inside strength is what gets things done.
university: The chapter title vinai-t-tiṭpam pairs vinai (undertaking, action) with tiṭpam (solidity, firmness), and the opening couplet at once relocates that firmness from the deed to the doer: vinai-t-tiṭpam is maṉa-t-tiṭpam, firmness of mind. Parimelazhagar glosses maṟṟaiya ellām (all the others) as the external supports a minister or king might count on, such as army, fortifications, wealth and allies, and says these are piṟa, other things, not what is meant by the word. The chapter follows directly on vinai-t-tūymai (ch. 66, purity of means), so the Amaichiyal sequence runs: choose clean means, then carry them through with an unshaken mind. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this reading closely (Pappaiah: the resolve not to abandon a task midway), while Kalaignar turns it conditionally: whatever else one has, without firmness of mind there is no firmness in action. The text is identical in ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are on this path are resolute in purpose, and their aim is one. O beloved child of the Kurus, the intelligence of those who are irresolute is many-branched.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna contrasts the single-pointed, resolute intellect (vyavasāyātmikā buddhi) with the scattered mind of the irresolute.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts locate the power to act in a firmly resolved mind rather than in outward means.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.41 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that a divided, wavering mind makes a person unreliable in everything he does.
christianity.tie_back: The negative form of the Kural’s claim: an unsteady mind produces unsteady action.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah" and then remained on a right course - the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve...”
islam.explanation: The verse praises istiqāma, standing firm on a course once it has been professed, and promises divine support to those who do.
islam.tie_back: Steadfastness after the decision, not the decision alone, is what counts, as in the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They are not afraid of evil tidings; their heart is firm, they trust in GOD.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm describes the righteous person whose firm heart keeps him unshaken by bad news.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Their heart is firm’ is almost a translation of maṉa-t-tiṭpam, the firmness of mind the Kural makes central.
judaism.source: Psalms 112:7 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada opens by teaching that every deed and its result flows from the state of the mind behind it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the mind, not outward factors, the true source of what an action becomes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mind is that unruly, dreadful, bad horse; I govern it by the discipline of the Law”
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, Gautama explains that the horse which never runs off with him is his own mind, held in check by the discipline of the Law.
jainism.tie_back: Like the kural, Jainism locates real strength in the steadied mind rather than in any outward power, since everything else follows from whether the mind is mastered.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.58 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak makes mastery of one's own mind the true victory, from which mastery of the world follows.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says firmness in action is really firmness of mind, and all other strength is something else; Guru Nanak likewise places the decisive strength in the conquered mind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Jap (Japji Sahib, Pauri 28), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Heart, be still, you had worse than this to bear on the day when the terrible Cyclops ate your brave companions...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Disguised in his own house, Odysseus holds his anger in check by speaking to his heart, so that his plan against the suitors is not wrecked by impulse.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus’s success comes from mastering his own mind, the firmness the Kural calls the real power in action.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus divides the world into what belongs to our own mind and will, and externals such as body, property and office, which ‘belong to others’.
philosophy.tie_back: His split mirrors the Kural’s: the mind’s firmness is one’s own, and ‘all the others are other’.

real_life_example.event_title: Churchill tells the Commons that Britain will fight on after Dunkirk
real_life_example.place: House of Commons, London, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: After the evacuation of more than 338,000 Allied troops from Dunkirk, which had left much of the British Army's equipment behind in France, Prime Minister Winston Churchill reported on the war situation to the House of Commons on 4 June 1940. He warned that wars are not won by evacuations and prepared the country for a possible invasion. He declared that Britain would fight on the beaches, the landing grounds, the fields, the streets and the hills, and that it would never surrender.
real_life_example.explanation: At a moment when Britain's material strength was at its lowest, the speech made national resolve itself the country's main asset and helped carry Britain through the summer of 1940.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that real firmness in action is firmness of mind and that every other kind of strength is something else, and Churchill rallied a nation that had just lost its army's equipment by appealing to its resolve rather than its resources.

tamil:
ஊறொரால் உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை இவ்விரண்டின்
ஆறென்பர் ஆய்ந்தவர் கோள்.
transliteration:
OoRoraal utrapin olkaamai ivviraNdin
AaRenpar aaindhavar koaL.
meaning: People who have studied this say firm action follows two rules: stay away from harm before it comes, and do not give up when it comes anyway.
elementary: Before riding your bike, you check the tyres and wear a helmet so you don’t get hurt. But if you still fall, you don’t quit biking forever; you get up and keep riding. Being careful first, and being brave after, are the two secrets of finishing things.
university: The couplet sets out a two-part rule: ūṟu orāl, keeping clear of harm (ūṟu, injury or obstacle; orāl, avoidance), and uṟṟa piṉ olkāmai, not flagging (olku, to shrink or slacken) once harm has struck. Parimelazhagar reads the first clause as not undertaking an act likely to come to grief, and the ‘āyntavar’ (those who have investigated) as the authors of the political treatises (nīti nūl), so that the couplet cites a consensus of statecraft; Solomon Pappaiah follows him. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar instead read the first clause as removing an obstacle before it arrives, which puts more weight on foresight than on choice of task. Either way, firmness is shown to include prudence, not mere stubbornness, which links this chapter back to terintu ceyal vakai (ch. 47). The three web texts agree on the wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not disturbed in mind even amidst the threefold miseries or elated when there is happiness, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the sthita-prajña, the person whose mind stays level when suffering arrives.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s second rule, not shrinking once harm has come.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.56 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his hearers to count the cost of an undertaking beforehand, lest they begin and be mocked for failing to finish.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s first rule: foresee the trouble before it comes, so the work can be carried through.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits, but give good tidings to the patient,”
islam.explanation: The Quran says trials will come regardless and praises ṣabr, patient steadfastness, in meeting them.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s second rule, it assumes setbacks will come and makes not buckling under them the virtue.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Seven times a righteous person falls and gets up, While the wicked are tripped by one misfortune.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the righteous, who rise again after repeated falls, with the wicked, whom one blow undoes; elsewhere (22:3) it praises the shrewd person who sees trouble coming and takes cover.
judaism.tie_back: Taken together, the two proverbs give both halves of the Kural’s rule, foresight and refusing to stay down.
judaism.source: Proverbs 24:16 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria); cf. Proverbs 22:3

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sabbāsava Sutta the Buddha lists different ways of abandoning the mental effluents, among them some to be abandoned by avoiding (keeping away from a wild elephant, a thorny place, bad company) and some to be abandoned by enduring (bearing cold, heat, hunger and harsh words).
buddhism.explanation: The discourse treats avoiding and enduring as two distinct, complementary skills in dealing with harm.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s pair: ūṟu orāl (avoid) and olkāmai (endure without giving way).
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 2, Sabbasava Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “twenty-two troubles which a monk must learn and know, bear and conquer, in order not to be vanquished by them when he lives the life of a wandering mendicant.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's teaching on the parisahas (troubles) asks the monk to know the hardships in advance and to bear them without being overcome when they arrive.
jainism.tie_back: This mirrors the kural's two rules of firmness: prepare against harm before it comes, and do not give way once it has come.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra, Lecture 2, prose introduction (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: After Guru Arjan's martyrdom in 1606, the sixth Guru, Hargobind, took up his guruship girded with two swords, following his father's advice to maintain an army; he trained a force, moved his base to the Punjab hills, and later fought several battles with the Mughals.
sikhism.explanation: Guru Hargobind both prepared against further harm and refused to let the community be broken once persecution had struck.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural gives two rules of firmness: guard against harm before it comes, and do not give way when it has come; Guru Hargobind's response to his father's martyrdom shows both.
sikhism.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, The Development of the Sikh Community

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Forewarned by Circe, Odysseus stops his crew’s ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast so the Sirens cannot lure the ship to ruin; soon afterwards, when Scylla seizes six of his men, he grieves but sails on.
greek_mythology.explanation: The episode shows both preventing a known danger before it strikes and pressing on after an unavoidable loss.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus follows the Kural’s two rules in a single voyage.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Writing after a fire destroyed the city of Lugdunum (Lyon) overnight, Seneca urges Lucilius to rehearse possible misfortunes in advance, so that nothing strikes the mind as unexpected and it is not crushed when disaster comes.
philosophy.explanation: Stoic praemeditatio malorum prepares the mind beforehand so that it stays firm afterwards.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca, like the Kural, joins foresight before harm with steadiness after it.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 91 (trans. R. M. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Cook's crew saves the Endeavour after it strikes the Great Barrier Reef
real_life_example.event: Around midnight on 10-11 June 1770 James Cook's ship HMS Endeavour struck a coral reef off the coast of what is now Queensland and began taking on water. Cook had the crew lighten the ship by throwing overboard around 40 to 50 tons of material, including ballast and six of its cannons, and the ship was hauled off the reef on a rising tide. The damaged ship was then taken to a river mouth, now the Endeavour River, where repairs took about six to seven weeks before the voyage continued.
real_life_example.explanation: Faced with the loss of the ship far from any help, Cook and his crew neither panicked nor gave up, and the expedition survived to complete its voyage.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's second rule of firmness is not to give way once harm has struck, and the Endeavour's crew kept working methodically after the grounding until the ship was saved.

tamil:
கடைக்கொட்கச் செய்தக்க தாண்மை இடைக்கொட்கின்
எற்றா விழுமந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Kadaikkotkach seydhakka thaaNmai idaikkotkin
Etraa vizhumanh tharum.
meaning: Real skill means keeping a task quiet until it is finished. If people learn about it halfway, it can cause trouble that cannot be fixed.
elementary: If you are making a surprise birthday card for your mom and you show it to her half-done, the surprise is ruined and you can’t get it back. It is better to work quietly and show it when it’s finished. Some plans work best when they are kept secret until they are done.
university: The key verb is koṭku, to become manifest: kaṭai-k-koṭka, so that it appears at the end, versus iṭai-k-koṭkiṉ, if it appears in the middle. Āṇmai is literally ‘manliness’ but here means competence or mastery in execution (Solomon Pappaiah renders it āḷumai, capability), and eṟṟā vizhumam is sorrow that cannot be removed. Parimelazhagar explains that a plan disclosed before completion lets enemies obstruct it, so secrecy is part of firmness; Kalaignar makes the point explicitly, calling concealment till completion the very ‘firmness of execution’. This couplet echoes the Arthashastra tradition on the secrecy of counsel (mantra-rakṣā) and anticipates the chapter on the conduct of affairs (ch. 68). Some readers print the first line with sandhi, ceytakkatāṇmai; the three sources consulted agree on the wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s chapter on the business of council insists that deliberation be held in secret and that no outsider learn of a plan before it is carried out, since disclosure ruins undertakings and brings disaster to the king.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra makes guarding the secrecy of counsel (mantra) a basic rule of statecraft.
hinduism.tie_back: It gives the political reasoning behind the Kural: a plan revealed midway is exposed to its enemies.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when his brethren were gone up, then went he also up unto the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus declines to go publicly to the feast, saying his time has not yet come, then goes quietly and reveals himself only midway through the festival.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows a purpose that is kept hidden until the right moment for it to be revealed.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers or they will contrive against you a plan...”
islam.explanation: Jacob tells young Joseph to keep his dream of future greatness to himself, since disclosing it early will stir his brothers’ envy and plotting.
islam.tie_back: The same logic as the Kural: revealing a destiny or plan before it is fulfilled invites obstruction.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I got up at night, I and a few men with me, and telling no one what my God had put into my mind to do for Jerusalem...”
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah surveys Jerusalem’s broken walls by night and tells no one his plan (2:16 adds that even the officials knew nothing) until he is ready to begin the rebuilding.
judaism.tie_back: A textbook case of the Kural’s counsel: keep the work hidden until it can go forward, since enemies will try to stop it.
judaism.source: Nehemiah 2:12, 2:16 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka the wise Mahosadha, the Bodhisatta, has a great tunnel dug in secret and lets its existence be known only when it is complete and his king must be rescued.
buddhism.explanation: The Jātaka praises the sage’s concealed preparation, which succeeds because rivals do not learn of it in time.
buddhism.tie_back: The tunnel is revealed only at the end, as the Kural advises.
buddhism.source: Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka (No. 546), summary in Malalasekera’s Dictionary of Pali Proper Names

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk should avoid untruth, nor should he speak positively (about future things, his plans, &c.)”
jainism.explanation: Among the rules of discipline, a monk is told not to make confident declarations about future things or his own plans, as part of guarding his speech from untruth.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's advice that a task should become known only when it is done finds a partial echo in this Jain restraint on announcing one's plans before they are fulfilled.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: On Baisakhi 1699 at Anandpur, according to Sikh tradition, Guru Gobind Singh asked for five Sikhs to offer their heads and took each volunteer into his tent; only at the end did he come out with all five alive in new garments and reveal his purpose, founding the Khalsa.
sikhism.explanation: The Guru kept his design hidden until it was complete, so the meaning of the event became clear only when he presented the five beloved ones (panj pyare).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says true capability carries a task through so it becomes known only when finished; Guru Gobind Singh's founding of the Khalsa was disclosed only at its completion.
sikhism.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, The Khalsa

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus stays disguised as a beggar in his own palace and reveals himself only after he has strung the great bow and his vengeance on the suitors has begun.
greek_mythology.explanation: His return succeeds because his identity and plan stay hidden until the decisive moment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His concealment until the deed is under way is the Kural’s kaṭai-k-koṭka in action.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Let your plans be dark and impenetrable as night, and when you move, fall like a thunderbolt.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu advises that intentions be kept wholly hidden until the moment of action.
philosophy.tie_back: The same strategic rule as the Kural: hide the plan, and let it be seen only in its result.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War VII.19 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: The secret evacuation of Anzac and Suvla at Gallipoli
real_life_example.event: After the failure of the Allied campaign at Gallipoli, a withdrawal plan devised largely by Lieutenant Colonel Brudenell White was carried out in stages and kept hidden from the Ottoman forces facing the Allied trenches. Periods of silence and irregular firing accustomed the enemy to quiet lines, men were taken off by night, and in the last hours self-firing drip rifles kept up occasional shots after the trenches were empty. About 36,000 troops left Anzac and Suvla over several nights ending on 20 December 1915 with very few casualties, and Helles was evacuated in the same way by 9 January 1916.
real_life_example.explanation: Because the plan stayed secret until it was complete, an operation that commanders had feared might cost heavy losses was achieved almost without loss of life, and it is often called the best-planned part of the whole campaign.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says true capability lies in carrying out a task so that it becomes known only when it is finished, and the Gallipoli withdrawal succeeded precisely because the enemy did not learn of it until the last troops had gone.

tamil:
சொல்லுதல் யார்க்கும் எளிய அரியவாம்
சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்.
transliteration:
Solludhal yaarkkum eLiya ariyavaam
Solliya vaNNam seyal.
meaning: Anyone can talk about how to do something. The hard part is doing it exactly the way it was said.
elementary: It is easy to say, “I will clean my whole room today!” It is much harder to actually pick up every sock and toy. Anyone can make a promise; the strong person is the one who does what they said.
university: The couplet balances eḷiya (easy) against ariya (hard, rare), and solludal (saying) against solliya vaṇṇam seyal (acting in the manner that was said). Parimelazhagar takes solludal as stating how a task ought to be carried out, the counsel a minister gives, so the couplet sets planning and advice against execution; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan follow him, while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar widen it to any promise or declaration. The plural eḷiya / ariya (literally ‘easy things’, ‘hard things’) is idiomatic and is normally rendered in the singular. In the chapter’s argument the couplet explains why firmness of mind is needed at all: plans are cheap, and only a firm mind turns word into deed. All three sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The mind is restless, turbulent, obstinate and very strong, O Kṛṣṇa, and to subdue it, I think, is more difficult than controlling the wind.”
hinduism.explanation: After hearing Krishna’s teaching on meditation, Arjuna objects that it is easily described but extremely hard to put into practice.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna voices the Kural’s point: stating the method is easy, carrying it out is hard.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.34 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus criticises teachers whose instructions are sound but who do not practise them themselves.
christianity.tie_back: ‘They say, and do not’ is the failing the Kural has in view.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Great is hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.”
islam.explanation: The Quran rebukes believers who announce intentions or commitments and then fail to act on them.
islam.tie_back: It condemns the very gap between saying and doing that the Kural calls the hard part.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shammai used to say: make your [study of the] Torah a fixed practice; speak little, but do much...”
judaism.explanation: Shammai tells students to promise little and accomplish much, putting deeds ahead of words.
judaism.tie_back: A practical answer to the Kural’s observation that talk is easy and deeds are hard.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:15 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of color but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practice them.”
buddhism.explanation: Fine words not put into practice are compared to a flower that looks lovely but has no scent.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts value the doing over the saying.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Acknowledging the truth about bondage and liberation, but talking only, not acting (in accordance with these tenets), they seek comfort for themselves in mighty words. Clever talking will not work salvation”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira criticises those who can expound the doctrine of bondage and liberation but do not live by it, trusting in words instead of deeds.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's point that saying how a thing should be done is easy while doing it as said is hard is exactly the gap this verse condemns.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.9-10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “We are good at talking, but our actions are bad.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak admits the gap between fine words and actual conduct as a common human failing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says anyone can say how a thing should be done, but doing it as said is hard; Guru Nanak names exactly that gap between speaking well and acting well.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the Boasting Traveler, a man brags of a giant leap he made at Rhodes and offers witnesses; a bystander tells him to suppose this is Rhodes and leap for them.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable punctures boasting by demanding the deed itself, here and now.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The bystander’s challenge makes the Kural’s point: claiming is easy, doing is the test.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, The Boasting Traveler (trans. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never call yourself a philosopher, nor talk a great deal among the unlearned about theorems, but act conformably to them.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells his students to show their philosophy by how they live, not by talking about it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he treats acting in line with one’s words as the real, and harder, achievement.

real_life_example.event_title: Kennedy's Moon goal is carried out as stated
real_life_example.event: On 25 May 1961 President John F. Kennedy asked a joint session of Congress to commit the United States to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the end of the decade. The goal required a huge national effort in funding, engineering and testing through the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo programmes. On 20 July 1969 Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, and its crew returned safely to Earth, within the deadline Kennedy had set.
real_life_example.explanation: Announcing the goal took one speech; meeting it exactly as stated took eight years of sustained work by hundreds of thousands of people.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says anyone can say how a thing should be done but doing it exactly as it was said is hard, and the Moon landing is a rare case of a public declaration fulfilled to the letter.

tamil:
வீறெய்தி மாண்டார் வினைத்திட்பம் வேந்தன்கண்
ஊறெய்தி உள்ளப் படும்.
transliteration:
VeeReydhi maaNdaar vinaiththitpam vaendhankaN
OoReydhi uLLap padum.
meaning: The firm action of people who have become great reaches even the king, and so everyone comes to respect it.
elementary: When a student works hard and finishes a great project, the teacher notices, then the principal hears about it, and soon the whole school knows. Steady, finished work travels up to the people in charge, and everyone respects it.
university: Vīṟu is distinction or excellence and māṇṭār those who are great or eminent; the verb māḷ can also mean ‘to die’, and Sivayogi Sivakumar’s gloss on ytamizh.com reads the phrase as ‘those who died valiantly’, but the mainstream commentators (Parimelazhagar, Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesikan) take māṇṭār as ‘the eminent’. Parimelazhagar specifies that their eminence comes from excellence of counsel (eṇṇam), and that their firmness in execution, by ‘reaching’ the king (vēntaṉkaṇ ūṟu eyti, where ūṟu means contact or effect, not harm as in 662), is then esteemed by everyone (uḷḷappaṭum). The couplet thus explains how a minister’s firmness is rewarded: it becomes visible through the ruler’s regard. Pope’s ‘With king acceptance finds and fame through all the state’ follows the same reading. The three sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Whatever action a great man performs, common men follow. And whatever standards he sets by exemplary acts, all the world pursues.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna notes that the deeds of eminent people become the standard everyone else follows.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the firm action of the great becomes widely known and honoured.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.21 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things...”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, the servant who carried his charge through faithfully is praised and promoted by his master.
christianity.tie_back: Diligent execution reaches the lord’s notice and wins honour, as the Kural says.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will appoint him exclusively for myself." And when he spoke to him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established [in position] and trusted."”
islam.explanation: Having seen Joseph’s wisdom and integrity, the king of Egypt takes him into his own service and gives him high standing.
islam.tie_back: Joseph’s proven worth ‘reaches the king’ and brings him esteem, as the Kural describes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “See a man skilled at his work— He shall attend upon kings; He shall not attend upon the lowly.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs promises that someone who excels at his work will end up serving before kings.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s exact claim: excellence in action reaches the king.
judaism.source: Proverbs 22:29 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the reputation of an energetic, disciplined person keeps growing.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say sustained, disciplined action brings growing renown.

jainism.quote_or_event: “An intelligent man who has learned (the sacred texts) takes his duties upon himself, and he becomes renowned in the world; as the earth is the dwelling of all beings, so he will be a dwelling of all duties.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's lecture on discipline says the pupil who reliably shoulders his duties becomes renowned, and goes on to say he will be honoured by gods, Gandharvas and men.
jainism.tie_back: Just as the kural says the firmness of eminent men reaches the king and wins general esteem, the Jain text makes steadfast discharge of duty the source of a person's renown.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.45 (cf. 1.48) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Nanak proclaimed Lehna's succession - he earned it.”
sikhism.explanation: The bards Satta and Balwand record that Guru Nanak raised his devoted disciple Lehna (Guru Angad) to the Guruship because of his proven, steadfast service.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the firmness in action of the distinguished reaches the king and wins everyone's esteem; Lehna's steadfast service reached Guru Nanak himself and won him the highest seat.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 966, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar), Satta and Balwand (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Then the king knew that he must be the valiant offspring of a god, so he kept him in Lycia, gave him his daughter in marriage, and made him of equal honour in the kingdom with himself...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Sent by the Lycian king on deadly tasks, Bellerophon completes each one (the Chimaera, the Solymi, the Amazons, an ambush), and the king finally honours him instead.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Bellerophon’s firmness in carrying out every task reaches the king and wins him the highest honour.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...honour is the prize of virtue, and it is to the good that it is rendered.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that honour is the proper reward that follows real excellence.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise has esteem follow proven excellence in action.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Engineer M. Visvesvaraya becomes Diwan of Mysore and later receives the Bharat Ratna
real_life_example.event: Mokshagundam Visvesvaraya joined the Mysore State service as Chief Engineer in 1909 and led work on the Krishnaraja Sagara dam, using automatic sluice gates of his own design; the dam created what was then one of the largest reservoirs in Asia. In 1912 the Maharaja's government made him Diwan of Mysore, a post he held until 1918, during which the dam project was given top priority. In 1955 he received the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, and his birthday, 15 September, is observed as Engineers' Day in India.
real_life_example.explanation: Visvesvaraya's record of carrying great works through to completion brought him first the ruler's trust and then the esteem of the whole nation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the firmness in action of the eminent reaches the king and so comes to be held in regard by all, and Visvesvaraya's proven firmness as an engineer won him the Maharaja's highest office and, later, national honour.

tamil:
எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப எண்ணியார்
திண்ணியர் ஆகப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
ENNiya eNNiyaangu eydhupa eNNiyaar
ThiNNiyar aagap peRin.
meaning: If people who make plans stay firm in carrying them out, they will get what they planned, and in just the way they planned it.
elementary: If you decide to learn to ride a bike and you keep practising every day, even after wobbling, you will ride just the way you imagined. Wishing is the start; sticking with it is what makes the wish come true.
university: The couplet plays on eṇṇu (to think, plan) four times: eṇṇiya (what was planned), eṇṇiyāṅku (as it was planned), eṇṇiyār (those who planned), set against tiṇṇiyar (the firm), which chimes with tiṭpam in the chapter title. Parimelazhagar reads it as a promise conditional on firmness in execution: planners who are also firm doers obtain both the object and the manner they intended; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow him. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print eytu (எய்து), but the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org has eytupa (எய்துப, ‘they will attain’, future plural), and thirukkural.net’s own musical setting of the couplet by P. A. Muthukrishnan also quotes எய்துப; that reading, which the metre and grammar need, is adopted here. The couplet is one of the most often quoted in the Porul section, as a maxim that resolve turns intention into result.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Bhagīratha undertakes long austerities to bring the celestial Gaṅgā down to earth for his ancestors, persisting through each obstacle until Śiva agrees to bear her fall and the river reaches its goal.
hinduism.explanation: His persistence is so proverbial that ‘Bhagīratha prayatna’ (Bhagiratha’s effort) is a common Indian phrase for relentless, successful effort.
hinduism.tie_back: Bhagīratha attains exactly what he set out to do because he stays firm, as the Kural promises.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For verily I say unto you, That whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; and shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe that those things which he saith shall come to pass; he shall have whatsoever he saith.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that an undivided, undoubting heart obtains what it asks for.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties getting what one intends to an unwavering inner firmness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that a person gains only what he has actively striven for.
islam.tie_back: Both texts tie attainment to sustained effort toward the intended end.

judaism.quote_or_event: “...along the path a person wishes to proceed, one leads and assists him.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar draws from Torah, Prophets and Writings the principle that a person is helped along whatever path he firmly chooses.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a settled intention is carried to fulfilment along the course it has chosen.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Makkot 10b (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Gladly would I let the flesh & blood in my body dry up, leaving just the skin, tendons, & bones, but if I have not attained what can be reached through human firmness, human persistence, human striving, there will be no relaxing my persistence.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the resolve (adhiṭṭhāna) of a committed disciple, who will not relax effort until the goal is reached, and says such a disciple can expect the fruit.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Human firmness’ leading to attainment is the Kural’s tiṇṇiyar reaching what they planned.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 70, Kitagiri Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “But he who has renounced pleasure, will not miss his aim”
jainism.explanation: In the parable of the ram, the Uttaradhyayana contrasts the one who, though taught the right way, goes astray again and again with the one who has renounced pleasure and therefore does not miss his aim.
jainism.tie_back: Like the kural's promise that the firm will attain what they planned, this verse makes steadiness of purpose the condition for reaching one's goal.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.25-26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that sustained effort (udam) and practice bring the fruit that is sought.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural promises that planners who are firm in carrying out their plans will attain what they aimed at; Guru Arjan likewise ties attainment to steady effort and practice.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Nevertheless, I want to get home, and can think of nothing else. If some god wrecks me when I am on the sea, I will bear it and make the best of it.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Offered immortality by Calypso, Odysseus holds to his single aim of returning home, and in the end he gets there.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His fixed intention, held firmly through every setback, reaches its goal just as he meant it to.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca writes that our plans miscarry because they have no fixed aim, and that when a man does not know which harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, a firmly fixed purpose is the precondition for any course of action to succeed.
philosophy.tie_back: He matches the Kural’s point that attainment follows a settled, firmly held intention.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 71 (trans. R. M. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: The Eiffel Tower is completed in time for the 1889 Exposition
real_life_example.event: For the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centenary of the French Revolution, the organisers chose the design submitted by Gustave Eiffel's firm from more than 100 proposals. Construction began on 26 January 1887 and the tower was finished on 31 March 1889, in two years, two months and five days, with a small workforce and some 2.5 million rivets. It served as the entrance to the Exposition, which opened that May, and was visited by about two million people during the fair.
real_life_example.explanation: An unprecedented iron structure was built exactly to plan and on time, becoming a lasting symbol of engineering achievement.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that planners who are firm in carrying out their plans attain what they aimed at in just the way they aimed at it, and Eiffel's team delivered the tower as designed and in time for the event it was built for.

tamil:
உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை வேண்டும் உருள்பெருந்தேர்க்கு
அச்சாணி அன்னார் உடைத்து.
transliteration:
UruvukaNdu eLLaamai vaeNdum uruLperundhaerkku
AchchaaNi annaar udaiththu.
meaning: Never look down on someone because of how small or plain they look. Some people are like the tiny pin that holds the wheel on a huge rolling chariot.
elementary: A giant temple chariot has huge wheels, but a tiny metal pin keeps each wheel from falling off. Without that little pin, the whole chariot stops! Some people are small or quiet, but they hold everything together, so never laugh at someone for being small.
university: Uru (form, size, appearance) and eḷḷāmai (not despising) open the couplet, and its image is the accāṇi, the small pin driven through the end of the axle (accu) that keeps the wheel of a great rolling temple chariot (uruḷ perun tēr) in place. Parimelazhagar, and Solomon Pappaiah after him, apply it within the chapter’s theme: men of firm mind may be small in body yet great in achievement, so they must not be judged by appearance; Kalaignar and Mu. Varadarasanar give it the wider moral that no one should be belittled for their size. The couplet reverses the usual link between bulk and strength, placing strength once again in firmness rather than outward form, as in 661. The three sources agree on the text; in sandhi form the lines read uruvukaṇ ṭeḷḷāmai vēṇṭu muruḷperuntērk / kaccāṇi yaṉṉā ruṭaittu.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Viṣṇu comes to King Bali’s sacrifice as Vāmana, a dwarf brahmin boy, and asks for just three steps of land; granted it, he grows to cosmic size and covers the earth and heavens in two strides.
hinduism.explanation: The Vāmana avatāra is India’s classic warning that small size can hide immeasurable power.
hinduism.tie_back: Bali’s court, seeing only a dwarf, learns what the Kural teaches: never judge strength by size.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth.”
christianity.explanation: James points out that a huge ship is steered by a tiny rudder, to show how a small thing can control a great one.
christianity.tie_back: The helm and the linchpin make the same point: a small part can govern a great vessel.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that worth is measured by inner disposition and deeds, not by outward appearance or means.
islam.tie_back: Both texts forbid judging people by their outward form.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But GOD said to Samuel, “Pay no attention to his appearance or his stature, for I have rejected him. For [GOD sees] not as humans see; humans see only what is visible, but GOD sees into the heart.””
judaism.explanation: Sent to anoint a king, Samuel is warned not to be impressed by Eliab’s height; the chosen one is the youngest, the overlooked shepherd David.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Pay no attention to his appearance or his stature’ is almost the Kural’s uruvu kaṇṭu eḷḷāmai.
judaism.source: 1 Samuel 16:7 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: Venerable Bhaddiya the Dwarf (Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya), whose small and unattractive body drew mockery, is taken by Sāriputta for a mere learner; the Buddha declares that Bhaddiya has already cut the cycle and reached freedom.
buddhism.explanation: The Udāna records the Buddha correcting a senior disciple who misjudged a small monk’s attainment.
buddhism.tie_back: The dwarf-monk is the Kural’s linchpin: small in form, complete in achievement.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Who is that dandy coming there? he is swarthy, dreadful, with a turned-up nose, miserably clad, a very devil of a dirty man”
jainism.explanation: The Brahmin priests mock the outcaste monk Harikesa for his looks and poverty, until his spiritual power is revealed and they cry that the value of penance has become visible and birth appears of no value.
jainism.tie_back: The story enacts the kural's warning not to despise anyone for small size or plain appearance, for the scorned figure proves to be the one on whom everything turns.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.6 and 12.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Nanak seeks the company of the lowest of the low class, the very lowest of the low.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak deliberately sides with those society despises, rejecting caste and outward status as measures of worth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns against scorning anyone for small size or humble looks, since such people can be the linchpin of a great chariot; Guru Nanak likewise refuses to look down on the lowly.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...now you know that it is possible for even a Mouse to confer benefits on a Lion.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The lion laughs at a mouse’s promise to repay him, but when the lion is caught in hunters’ ropes, the mouse gnaws him free.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The despised small creature proves indispensable, just as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, The Lion and the Mouse (trans. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I say, that he is exactly like the busts of Silenus, which are set up in the statuaries’ shops, holding pipes and flutes in their mouths; and they are made to open in the middle, and have images of gods inside them.”
philosophy.explanation: Alcibiades compares Socrates, notoriously ugly, to cheap satyr figurines that open to reveal golden images of gods inside.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates is the philosopher’s linchpin: unimpressive outside, indispensable within.

real_life_example.event_title: FC Barcelona signs the small thirteen-year-old Lionel Messi
real_life_example.event: As a boy in Argentina Lionel Messi was diagnosed with a growth hormone deficiency, and when his club there stopped paying for his treatment his family sought a club abroad. FC Barcelona's officials hesitated at first over his small size and the cost of the hormone therapy, but the club signed him and paid for his treatment when he arrived at the age of thirteen. He went on to become one of the most successful players in the club's history.
real_life_example.explanation: A player some thought too small became the centre of one of the greatest teams of his era, showing how misleading physical size can be as a measure of ability.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that no one should be scorned for small size, since the world has people like the little linchpin that holds a great chariot wheel, and Barcelona's decision not to judge the young Messi by his height gave the club its linchpin.

tamil:
கலங்காது கண்ட வினைக்கண் துளங்காது
தூக்கங் கடிந்து செயல்.
transliteration:
Kalangaadhu kaNda vinaikkaN thuLangaadhu
ThookkanG kadindhu seyal.
meaning: Once you have clearly decided what to do, do it without wavering and without delay.
elementary: When you and your friends decide to build a treehouse, first think carefully. But once you’ve decided, don’t keep changing your mind or saying “maybe tomorrow.” Grab the hammer and start building!
university: The couplet moves in three steps: kalaṅkātu kaṇṭa vinai, an undertaking seen or decided without confusion (kalaṅku, to be muddied or agitated); tuḷaṅkātu, without wavering (tuḷaṅku, to tremble or sway); and tūkkam kaṭintu, having cast off tūkkam. Parimelazhagar takes tūkkam here as procrastination or delay (nīṭṭittal), not literal sleep, and the modern commentators follow him (Pappaiah: ‘without faltering and without delay’); Pope’s ‘mind unslumbering’ keeps the literal sense. The logic is that deliberation belongs before the decision, and firmness after it, which echoes the rule about deliberating and then acting in terintu ceyal vakai (ch. 47). The sandhi text reads viṉaikkaṭ ṭuḷaṅkātu, the same words written with the sandhi applied.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Arjuna said: My dear Kṛṣṇa, O infallible one, my illusion is now gone. I have regained my memory by Your mercy. I am now firm and free from doubt and am prepared to act according to Your instructions.”
hinduism.explanation: After long deliberation, Arjuna’s confusion clears and he declares himself firm and ready to act.
hinduism.tie_back: Clear decision (kalaṅkātu kaṇṭa) followed by unwavering action is exactly the Kural’s sequence.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.73 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to hold firm and keep working, confident their work is not wasted.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Stedfast, unmoveable’ answers to the Kural’s tuḷaṅkātu, never swaying once the work is begun.

islam.quote_or_event: “...and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah. Indeed, Allah loves those who rely [upon Him].”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to take counsel, and then, once a decision is made, to act on it with trust instead of hesitating.
islam.tie_back: Consultation, then firm and prompt action, is the Kural’s own sequence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He [also] used to say: If I am not for myself, who is for me? But if I am for my own self [only], what am I? And if not now, when?”
judaism.explanation: Hillel’s last question rejects putting off what ought to be done.
judaism.tie_back: ‘If not now, when?’ is the Kural’s tūkkam kaṭintu, casting off delay.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:14 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hasten to do good; restrain your mind from evil. He who is slow in doing good, his mind delights in evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that delay in doing good leaves room for the mind to drift to harm.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts treat delay as the enemy of a good act already decided on.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Now you have entered on the path from which the thorns have been cleared, the great path; walk in the right path; Gautama, &c. Do not get into an uneven road like a weak burden-bearer; for you will repent of it afterwards”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama that, the path now being clear, he should walk it steadily and not stray onto an uneven road, ending each verse with the refrain to be careful all the while.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's counsel to carry out without wavering a course settled with a clear mind matches this call to keep to a path already seen clearly.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.32-33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately!”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, urges acting at once rather than putting off what must be done.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that once a course is settled with a clear mind it should be carried out without wavering or delay; Kabir gives the same call against procrastination.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Gordium, Alexander is shown the famous knot said to promise rule of Asia to whoever undoes it; according to the popular version, he does not hesitate but cuts it through with his sword.
greek_mythology.explanation: The ‘Gordian knot’ has become the byword for decisive action that refuses to be stalled.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Alexander acts without wavering or delay once his course is set, as the Kural urges.
greek_mythology.source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 18 (trans. Bernadotte Perrin)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present- I am rising to the work of a human being.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius argues himself out of lingering in bed by recalling that he exists for action.
philosophy.tie_back: This is tūkkam kaṭintu in its literal and figurative sense: shake off sloth and do the work.

real_life_example.event_title: Julius Caesar crosses the Rubicon
real_life_example.event: In January 49 BCE the Roman Senate, led by Caesar's opponents, demanded that Julius Caesar give up his army and return to Rome as a private citizen. Caesar instead led his troops, reportedly a single legion, across the small river Rubicon, the boundary between his province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy proper, an act that began a civil war. He then advanced rapidly through Italy, and the phrase crossing the Rubicon has since meant passing a point of no return.
real_life_example.explanation: Once Caesar had made his choice he acted at once and without hesitation, and the speed of his advance gave his opponents no time to organise.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that once a course has been settled with a clear mind it should be carried out without wavering or delay, and Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon has become the world's shorthand for exactly such an irreversible, unhesitating commitment.

tamil:
துன்பம் உறவரினும் செய்க துணிவாற்றி
இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை.
transliteration:
Thunpam uRavarinum seyka thuNivaatri
Inpam payakkum vinai.
meaning: Even if a lot of hardship comes your way, keep going bravely with work that will bring happiness in the end.
elementary: Learning to swim can be scary: water gets in your nose and your arms get tired. But if you keep going, one day you’ll zoom across the pool and love it. Some good things feel hard at first and happy at the end, so keep being brave.
university: The couplet sets tuṉpam (suffering) against iṉpam (joy), with the concessive uṟa variṉum, ‘even if it comes in abundance’ (uṟa, intensely), and the command ceyka tuṇivu āṟṟi, ‘act, sustaining courage’. Parimelazhagar explains that the suffering belongs to the beginning or the course of the undertaking while the joy is its fruit at the end, so a firm mind must not judge a task by its first taste; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah add ‘in the end’ (muṭivil) to make this explicit. Kalaignar reverses the emphasis, defining a joy-bringing act as one carried through despite suffering. The couplet sets up the chapter’s conclusion in 670. The three sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That which in the beginning may be just like poison but at the end is just like nectar and which awakens one to self-realization is said to be happiness in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines sāttvika happiness as the kind that is bitter at first and sweet in the end.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost a gloss on the Kural: accept early pain for the joy the deed will yield.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.37 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews admits that discipline is painful while it lasts but says it later bears good fruit.
christianity.tie_back: The same pattern as the Kural, grievous now and fruitful afterward.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, with hardship [will be] ease. Indeed, with hardship [will be] ease.”
islam.explanation: Repeated for emphasis, the verse assures that relief comes with and after hardship.
islam.tie_back: It gives the same encouragement as the Kural, to persist through tuṉpam toward iṉpam.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They who sow in tears shall reap with songs of joy.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm pictures labour done in sorrow that yields a joyful harvest.
judaism.tie_back: Sowing in tears and reaping in joy is the Kural’s arc from tuṉpam to iṉpam.
judaism.source: Psalms 126:5 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the taking on of a practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasure in the future.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha classifies undertakings by their present and future results and commends the path that is hard now but brings happiness later.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the kind of act the Kural tells us to press on with.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 45, Culadhammasamadana Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “If any misfortune happens and he suffers pain, he should cheerfully steady his mind, and bear the ills that attack him.”
jainism.explanation: In the lecture on troubles the monk is told to meet misfortune and pain with a steadied, cheerful mind, bearing it for the sake of the welfare of his soul.
jainism.tie_back: This parallels the kural's call to press on courageously through great hardship toward the work that brings joy at the end.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, describes the true hero as one who holds the field whatever he suffers.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to carry on boldly with a worthy task even when great hardship comes; Kabir's hero who never leaves the field gives the same counsel of perseverance.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first; but when a man has reached the top, then is she easy to reach...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod pictures the path to excellence as steep and rough at first but easy once the summit is reached.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts tell us to accept the early hardship for the good at the end.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 289-292 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Diogenes Laertius reports Aristotle’s saying that the roots of education are bitter but its fruit is sweet.
philosophy.explanation: The maxim, attributed to Aristotle, holds that the hard early stages of learning are repaid by its rewards.
philosophy.tie_back: Bitter root and sweet fruit is the Kural’s suffering-then-joy in another image.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 5.18 (trans. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: Junko Tabei reaches the summit of Everest after an avalanche
real_life_example.event: In 1975 Junko Tabei helped lead a Japanese all-women expedition to Mount Everest. While the team slept at Camp II, an avalanche struck their tents and knocked Tabei unconscious, but the expedition continued. On 16 May 1975 she became the first woman to reach the summit of Everest.
real_life_example.explanation: Tabei's climb opened the highest mountain to women climbers and showed what persistence could achieve after a near-fatal setback.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural urges boldly carrying on with a task that brings joy in the end, even if much hardship comes along the way, and Tabei went on from being buried by an avalanche to a historic summit.

tamil:
எனைத்திட்பம் எய்தியக் கண்ணும் வினைத்திட்பம்
வேண்டாரை வேண்டாது உலகு.
transliteration:
Enaiththitpam eydhiyak kaNNum vinaiththitpam
VaeNdaarai vaeNdaadhu ulagu.
meaning: No matter what other strengths they have, the world does not value people who do not value being firm in action.
elementary: A kid might be the fastest runner, the best drawer and the funniest in class, but if they never finish their part of the group project, nobody wants them on the team. Finishing what you start matters more than all the other talents.
university: The final couplet closes the chapter in a ring: eṉai-t-tiṭpam (firmness of whatever kind) echoes vinai-t-tiṭpam, and the line turns on the repeated vēṇṭu (to want, to value): vēṇṭārai vēṇṭātu, ‘does not want those who do not want’ firmness of action. Parimelazhagar takes eṉai-t-tiṭpam to mean the other strengths listed under 661 (wealth, army, allies and the like), and ulaku (the world) to mean the wise or great, who alone set a proper value on things; Solomon Pappaiah follows this with uyarntōr (the eminent), while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep ‘the world’ at large. The effect is to restate 661 as a judgement of worth: firmness in action outranks every other kind of strength. The three sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, do not yield to this degrading impotence. It does not become you. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O chastiser of the enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna rebukes Arjuna, the greatest archer of his age, whose skill counts for nothing while he refuses to act.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna has every strength but, for a time, lacks resolve to act, which is exactly the person the Kural says the world will not value.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.3 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells a would-be follower that one who starts and then wavers is unfit for the work.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares the unsteady doer unwanted, whatever else he may offer.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row as though they are a [single] structure joined firmly.”
islam.explanation: Coming just after the rebuke of those who say what they do not do (61:2-3), the verse praises solid, unwavering action.
islam.tie_back: The positive side of the Kural: firmness in action is what is truly valued.

judaism.quote_or_event: “...one whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, to what may he be compared? To a tree whose branches are numerous but whose roots are few, so that when the wind comes, it uproots it and overturns it...”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says that wisdom without matching deeds is like a top-heavy tree, easily blown over.
judaism.tie_back: Wisdom without action, like the Kural’s ‘other strengths’ without firmness in action, cannot stand.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The idler who does not exert himself when he should, who though young and strong is full of sloth, with a mind full of vain thoughts — such an indolent man does not find the path to wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says youth and strength are wasted on someone who will not exert himself when it is time to act.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Though young and strong’ is the Kural’s eṉai-t-tiṭpam: strengths that count for nothing without resolve to act.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Just as bad bullocks are when put before a car, so are bad pupils when yoked, as it were, to the car of the Law; they break down through want of zeal.”
jainism.explanation: The teacher Garga, wearied by pupils who balk and wander like unruly bullocks, finally leaves those lazy donkeys and goes his own way in austerity.
jainism.tie_back: As the kural says the world does not value those who do not value firmness in action, the Jain parable shows the zealless being given up as useless by their own teacher.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 27.8 (cf. 27.16) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak demands total, unwavering commitment from anyone who would walk the Sikh path.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the world does not value those who lack firmness in action, whatever else they have; Guru Nanak likewise accepts no half-hearted follower and asks for resolve to the point of giving one's head.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...you fight bravely, and no man with any justice can make light of your doings in battle. But you are careless and wilfully remiss. It grieves me to the heart to hear the ill that the Trojans speak about you...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector tells his brother Paris that his courage and skill are real, but his wilful slackness has made the Trojans despise him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris is the Kural’s case exactly: gifted, yet not esteemed, because he will not apply himself firmly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And as in the Olympic Games it is not the most beautiful and the strongest that are crowned but those who compete (for it is some of these that are victorious), so those who act win, and rightly win, the noble and good things in life.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that virtue as a mere capacity earns nothing; only those who act on it win the prize.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he denies honour to strength that does not act, however great.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.8 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Wright brothers fly days after Langley's well-funded Aerodrome fails
real_life_example.place: Potomac River, Washington, D.C., and Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, United States
real_life_example.event: Samuel Langley, Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, had government funding and great scientific prestige for his piloted Aerodrome, but it plunged into the Potomac on launch on 7 October 1903 and broke up again on 8 December 1903. His request for further funding was refused, he suffered public ridicule, and the project ended. Nine days later, on 17 December 1903, Wilbur and Orville Wright, bicycle makers who had worked on their machine through years of patient trials, made the first powered, controlled airplane flights near Kitty Hawk.
real_life_example.explanation: Prestige, money and official backing did not produce flight; the Wrights' persistent, methodical work did, and history credits them with the achievement.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that whatever other strengths people have, the world does not value those who lack firmness in action, and the Wrights, with far fewer resources than Langley, won the lasting honour because they carried the task through.

tamil:
சூழ்ச்சி முடிவு துணிவெய்தல் அத்துணிவு
தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது.
transliteration:
Soozhchi mudivu thunivu eydhal aththunivu
Thaazhchiyul thangudhal theedhu.
meaning: The goal of thinking things over is to reach a firm decision. Once you have decided, letting that decision sit and wait is harmful.
elementary: Imagine your team spends all of recess deciding which game to play, finally agrees on tag, and then just stands around until the bell rings. All that planning was wasted. This kural says: think carefully, decide, and then actually start.
university: The chapter opens by linking it to the preceding chapters on counsel (soozhchi, deliberation) and firmness in action (vinaith thitpam, ch. 67): the telos (mudivu) of counsel is thunivu, a settled resolve, not endless discussion. Thaazhchi means lowering, lagging or delay, and thangudhal 'to remain, to linger', so the second line pictures a resolve that has sunk into procrastination; theedhu (evil, harm) ranks such delay as a positive fault rather than mere inefficiency. Parimelazhagar glosses the kural as teaching that once the ministers' counsel has concluded in a decision, the king must not let time pass before execution, because delay lets circumstances and the enemy change. Older editions print the couplet with full sandhi (துணிவெய்த லத்துணிவு / தாழ்ச்சியுட் டங்குத றீது), as in thirukkural-thamizh.org, but the words are identical. The maxim closely matches the proverb Aristotle cites in Nicomachean Ethics VI.9: deliberate slowly, execute quickly.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Arjun said: O Infallible One, by Your grace my illusion has been dispelled, and I am situated in knowledge. I am now free from doubts, and I shall act according to Your instructions.”
hinduism.explanation: After eighteen chapters of dialogue, Arjuna announces that his doubts are gone and he will now act, which ends the counsel and begins the battle.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's long deliberation ends exactly as the Kural prescribes: in a doubt-free resolve (thunivu) that is carried straight into action.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: A would-be follower asks to delay his commitment to say goodbye at home, and Jesus answers that someone who starts ploughing and keeps looking back is not ready.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat hesitation after a decision has been made as a real failure, not a harmless pause.

islam.quote_or_event: “So pardon them and ask forgiveness for them and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allāh.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to consult his companions, and once he has made up his mind, to put his trust in God and proceed.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's sequence exactly: consultation (soozhchi), then resolve (azm, thunivu), then action without wavering.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not: ‘when I shall have leisure I shall study;’ perhaps you will not have leisure.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel warns against postponing a good resolution to some later, more convenient time, because that time may never come.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hillel treats a resolve that is left to wait for later as a resolve that will likely fail.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hasten to do good; restrain your mind from evil. He who is slow in doing good, his mind delights in evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges quick action on good intentions, because slowness gives the mind room to slide back into bad habits.
buddhism.tie_back: The Dhammapada and the Kural agree that delay after a good decision is not neutral; it actively opens the way to harm.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You have crossed the great ocean; why do you halt so near the shore? make haste to get on the other side; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira urges Gautama, who has already taken the decisive step of renunciation, not to linger at the last stage but to hasten to completion.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's teaching that once a decision has been reached, delay is a harm is mirrored in this rebuke to halting when the goal is in reach.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately! Later on, you will not be able to do anything, when death hangs over your head.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose saloks the Gurus included in the scripture, warns that putting off what has been resolved is fatal, because the time to act can close without warning.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that once a decision is reached, letting it sink into delay is a positive harm; Kabir likewise treats postponement of a settled duty as the real danger.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Kabir (Salok 138), Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells his brother Perses not to put off work until tomorrow or the day after, because a man who delays never fills his barn and is always wrestling with ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: In his farming poem Hesiod treats postponement as the main enemy of the careful farmer, who must act as soon as the work is due.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod's delaying farmer who wrestles with ruin is the Kural's theedhu: a decision left idle turns into damage.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They say that one should carry out quickly the conclusions of one's deliberation, but should deliberate slowly.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle, discussing excellence in deliberation, cites the common saying that thinking should be slow but carrying out the result should be fast.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost a Greek translation of Kural 671: counsel is meant to end in resolve, and resolve should not lag.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.9 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Bell files his telephone patent hours before Elisha Gray
real_life_example.place: U.S. Patent Office, Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: On 14 February 1876 a patent application for Alexander Graham Bell's telephone was filed at the U.S. Patent Office. A few hours later the same day, the inventor Elisha Gray filed only a caveat, a declaration that he intended to patent a similar device within three months. Bell was granted U.S. Patent No. 174,465 on 7 March 1876, and in the legal disputes that followed, his earlier filing of a full application helped him prevail.
real_life_example.explanation: Gray had worked out a comparable idea, but he had not yet acted on it fully, and a gap of a few hours meant that the patent, and the fame, went to Bell.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that once a decision is reached, letting it sit idle in delay is a harm, and Gray's choice to file a preliminary caveat rather than a full application lost him the race by a matter of hours.

tamil:
தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால தூங்கற்க
தூங்காது செய்யும் வினை.
transliteration:
Thoonguga thoongich cheyarpaala thoongarka
Thoongaadhu seyyum vinai.
meaning: Take your time with tasks that should be done slowly. But never delay tasks that must be done right away.
elementary: Planting a tree is something you can take your time over, choosing the best spot. But if the bathtub is overflowing, you turn off the tap right now. A wise person knows which jobs can wait and which cannot.
university: The couplet is a famous piece of verbal play: the verb thoongu appears five times, in the sense of 'to delay, to be slow, to tarry' (literally to droop or hang, and by extension to sleep). Parimelazhagar explains that some undertakings (such as those whose moment has not yet come) are properly done by waiting, while others (such as those where the opportunity or the enemy will not wait) must be done without any delay; the skill lies in telling the two apart.
