The kural therefore qualifies 671: the rule is not simply 'hurry' but correct timing, echoing the earlier chapter on knowing the right time (kaalam aridhal, ch. 49). Modern commentators Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, and there are no significant textual variants. It pairs naturally with the Latin-Greek motto festina lente and with Francis Bacon's essay on delays.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Gautama orders his son Chirakari (the slow-acting one) to kill his mother in anger; Chirakari, by nature deliberate, weighs the command at length, and by the time he has finished Gautama has repented and rejoices that his son was slow.
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells this story to show that in grave, irreversible matters, slowness can be the wise course.
hinduism.tie_back: Chirakari's story illustrates the first half of the Kural, that some deeds are rightly slept over, while Bhishma's wider teaching insists that urgent duties must not be delayed.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, the story of Chirakari (Ganguli trans., Santi Parva section 266)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.”
christianity.explanation: James tells believers that some responses should be quick and others slow.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, James does not praise speed or slowness in themselves; he assigns each to the right kind of act.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is hesitation in everything except in the actions of the next world.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that careful, unhurried deliberateness (tu'ada) is good in most matters, but deeds that serve the hereafter should be done promptly.
islam.tie_back: The hadith draws exactly the Kural's line between tasks that may wait and tasks that must not.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4810 (graded sahih by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet opens his famous poem by saying that each activity has its own proper time.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's two-speed rule depends on this same idea: each task has its right time, fast or slow.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha explains that even when he has something true and beneficial to say, he waits for the proper time to say it, choosing the moment with care.
buddhism.explanation: In the Abhaya Sutta the Buddha describes his speech as governed by a sense of the right time as well as by truth and benefit.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Buddha treats timing as part of doing an act well: some things are best held back until their moment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “At the right time a monk should sally forth, and he should return at the right time; avoiding to do anything out of time, he should do what is appropriate for each period of the day.”
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic discipline assigns each activity its proper time and forbids doing things out of season.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's rule that some tasks may be done slowly while others must not be delayed is a version of this principle that every act has its due time.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In all ten directions, the branches are green and alive. That which ripens slowly, is sweet.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Baarah Maahaa (song of the twelve months) Guru Nanak observes that fruit which ripens in its own time is the sweet one, an image of patient, unhurried growth toward the Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's first half says some tasks are properly done slowly; Guru Nanak's image of slow ripening honours exactly that kind of patience, while Kabir's call to act at once (see Kural 671) matches the second half.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1109, Raag Tukhaari, Baarah Maahaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The emperor Augustus often repeated the Greek saying speude bradeos, hasten slowly, and held that whatever is done well enough is done quickly enough.
greek_mythology.explanation: Suetonius reports that Augustus disliked rashness in a commander and liked this paradoxical motto.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hasten slowly captures the Kural's balance: urgency where needed, patience where haste would spoil the work.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon advises that the beginnings of great actions be entrusted to Argus with his hundred eyes, and their ends to Briareus with his hundred hands: watch patiently first, then act swiftly.
philosophy.explanation: In his essay on delays Bacon argues that there is a ripe moment for every action, to be waited for patiently and then seized at once.
philosophy.tie_back: Bacon's two giants stand for the two halves of the Kural: slowness where waiting helps, speed where it does not.

real_life_example.event_title: Danes ferry almost all of Denmark's Jews to Sweden within weeks
real_life_example.event: In late September 1943 the German diplomat Georg Ferdinand Duckwitz leaked word of a planned roundup of Denmark's Jews, and Danish contacts quickly warned the Jewish community. When the roundup began on the night of 1 October, most Jews had already gone into hiding, and resistance workers, ordinary citizens and fishermen moved them to the coast and ferried them across the narrow strait to neutral Sweden. Within a few weeks about 7,200 Jews and some 700 non-Jewish relatives reached safety, while fewer than 500 were caught and deported.
real_life_example.explanation: Because the warning was acted on at once rather than debated, almost the whole Jewish population of Denmark survived the Holocaust.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says never to delay tasks that must be done at once, and the Danish rescue succeeded because people acted within hours and days of the warning.

tamil:
ஒல்லும்வா யெல்லாம் வினைநன்றே ஒல்லாக்கால்
செல்லும்வாய் நோக்கிச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Ollumvaai ellaam vinai nandre ollaakkaal
Sellumvaai nokkich cheyal.
meaning: Whenever you can act directly, that is best. When you cannot, find another way that will work and do it that way.
elementary: If the front door is open, you walk straight in. If it is locked, you don't give up; you go round to the back door or ask someone for the key. Pick the way that actually works.
university: Ollum vaai means 'where it is possible (feasible)', and sellum vaai 'the way that will go through, the effective route'. Parimelazhagar reads vinai here in its political sense of open action against an enemy, that is, danda (force), the last of the four classical expedients (sama, dana, bheda, danda); where force can succeed it is best, and where it cannot one must choose among the remaining expedients. Solomon Pappaiah follows this reading explicitly, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the couplet more generally as 'do the work directly where you can, otherwise find a workable way'. The older sandhi text reads வினைநன்றே யொல்லாக்காற் with no difference of meaning. The teaching is pragmatic flexibility of means within a fixed end, a theme shared with the Arthashastra and later Machiavelli.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu teaches that among the four expedients, conciliation, gifts, division and force, the wise commend conciliation and force for the prosperity of a kingdom, choosing the means that suit the situation.
hinduism.explanation: The law code gives the king a menu of methods and expects him to pick whichever will actually work.
hinduism.tie_back: Parimelazhagar reads this Kural within the same fourfold scheme of upayas: use force where it can succeed, otherwise another means.

christianity.quote_or_event: “To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes changing his approach for each audience so that his mission succeeds by whatever route is open.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts hold the goal fixed and treat the method as flexible, choosing whatever way will get through.

islam.quote_or_event: “So, if I forbid you to do something, then keep away from it. And if I order you to do something, then do of it as much as you can.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ties duty to capacity: do what is possible, to the extent it is possible.
islam.tie_back: The hadith shares the Kural's ollum vaai logic: act fully wherever you are able.

judaism.quote_or_event: Before meeting his estranged brother Esau, Jacob prepares on three fronts at once: a gift to appease him, prayer to God, and a plan for battle, dividing his camp so that one part could escape.
judaism.explanation: Rashi draws from the verses that Jacob readied himself for gifts, prayer and war, so that if one means failed another would be at hand.
judaism.tie_back: Jacob embodies the Kural's teaching: prepare the direct way, and have other workable routes ready when it will not serve.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the parable of the burning house, a father cannot get his playing children out by simply calling them, so he promises them wonderful carts outside, and they run out to safety.
buddhism.explanation: The Lotus Sutra uses this story to explain upaya, skilful means: when the direct way fails, a teacher finds another route that works.
buddhism.tie_back: The father does exactly what the Kural says: when the direct approach is not possible, look for the way that gets through.
buddhism.source: Lotus Sutra, chapter 3 (parable of the burning house)

jainism.quote_or_event: In the meeting of Kesi and Gautama, the followers of Parshvanatha (four vows) and of Mahavira (five vows) ask why two Jinas pursuing the same goal prescribed different forms of the Law. Gautama explains that the form was adapted to the people of each age, the earliest of whom could only with difficulty understand the precepts and the latest only with difficulty observe them.
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition holds that the same end may be reached by different prescribed means, chosen according to what will actually work for those concerned.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's advice to act directly where possible and otherwise to find a route that will work has a loose echo in this Jain acceptance of adapting means to circumstances.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23 (Kesi and Gautama), esp. 23.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: In the Zafarnama, the Persian letter Guru Gobind Singh sent to the emperor Aurangzeb in 1705, verse 22 states the principle that when every other means of redressing a wrong has failed, it is lawful and just to take up the sword.
sikhism.explanation: The verse, borrowed almost word for word from Saadi, became a classic summary of the Sikh idea of righteous struggle (dharam yudh): force is legitimate only after other means have been tried and have failed.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural teaches choosing the means that will actually work, direct action where possible and another route where not; the Zafarnama also grades the means, but in the reverse order, putting force last.
sikhism.source: Guru Gobind Singh, Zafarnama, verse 22 (Dasam Granth), as summarised in Wikipedia, Zafarnama (letter)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After ten years of failed assaults on Troy, the Greeks, on Odysseus' plan, build the wooden horse, and the city falls by stratagem where force had not succeeded.
greek_mythology.explanation: The bard Demodocus sings of the horse at the Phaeacian court, celebrating Odysseus' cunning.
greek_mythology.tie_back: When the direct way (siege) proved impossible, the Greeks looked for the route that would get through, just as the Kural advises.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli says a prince must know how to fight both by law and by force, and must imitate both the lion and the fox, since the lion cannot avoid traps and the fox cannot drive off wolves.
philosophy.explanation: He argues that a ruler needs more than one way of acting and must switch according to what the situation allows.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise holds that where one means (force) will not work, the wise agent turns to another.

real_life_example.event_title: The Berlin Airlift supplies a blockaded city by air
real_life_example.event: Beginning on 24 June 1948, Soviet forces blocked rail, road and water access to the western sectors of Berlin, home to about two million people. Lacking the ground forces to break through, the United States and Britain flew in food, fuel and other supplies from airbases in western Germany, starting on 26 June 1948 and eventually landing aircraft every minute or so at the peak. The Soviets lifted the blockade in May 1949, and the airlift, which delivered about 2.3 million tons of cargo, continued until 30 September 1949.
real_life_example.explanation: Instead of forcing the land routes, which risked war, the Western allies found another route that worked, and the city was kept alive without a shot being fired.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says direct action is best where it is possible, and where it is not, one should find a route that will work, and the Berlin Airlift replaced a blocked road with a highway in the sky.

tamil:
வினைபகை என்றிரண்டின் எச்சம் நினையுங்கால்
தீயெச்சம் போலத் தெறும்.
transliteration:
Vinai pagai endru irandin echcham ninaiyungaal
Theeyechcham polath therum.
meaning: Think about it: an unfinished task and an enemy not fully beaten are like leftover sparks of a fire. They can grow back and destroy you.
elementary: When you put out a campfire, you pour water until every last glowing coal is out, because one hidden ember can start a big fire later. A job left half-done, or a quarrel only half-settled, is like that ember.
university: Echcham means 'remainder, leftover', and theeyechcham 'the remnant of a fire'; therum means 'will burn, will destroy'. Parimelazhagar notes that an unfinished undertaking and a partly subdued enemy both look small and harmless, but grow unnoticed, like smouldering embers, until they destroy the one who neglected them; Mu. Varadarasanar stresses this unseen growth. The thought is a commonplace of Indian niti: the Mahabharata's counsel of Kanika (Shanti Parva 12.138.58, critical edition) lists the remnant of a debt, of a fire and of an enemy as things that grow again and again if left unchecked. The older sandhi text reads வினைபகை யென்றிரண்டி னெச்ச நினையுங்காற் / றீயெச்சம் with no change in meaning. Modern readers often apply the enemy half to unresolved conflicts or problems rather than literal foes.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “ṛṇaśeṣo'gniśeṣaśca śatruśeṣastathaiva ca / punaḥ punarvivardheta svalpo'pyanivāritaḥ”
hinduism.explanation: In this Sanskrit verse, Kanika tells King Shatrumtapa that what is left over of a debt, a fire or an enemy, however small, grows again and again if it is not dealt with.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the same image and the same pairing as the Kural: a leftover fire and a leftover enemy both come back to destroy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus describes a builder who starts a tower without the means to complete it and ends up a laughing stock.
christianity.tie_back: Luke shows the cost of the first half of the Kural's warning: an unfinished task does not stay harmless but turns against the one who left it.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet is reported to have said that God loves it when any of you does a piece of work, that you do it with itqan, that is, thoroughly and completely.
islam.explanation: This hadith makes finishing and perfecting a task a quality God loves.
islam.tie_back: It supports the task half of the Kural: work should be taken to completion, not left in pieces.
islam.source: Hadith in al-Bayhaqi, Shu'ab al-Iman (graded hasan by al-Albani, al-Silsila al-Sahiha 1113)

judaism.quote_or_event: King Saul is commanded to finish the war with Amalek but spares King Agag and the best of the spoil; Samuel tells him that because of this incomplete obedience the kingdom will be torn from him.
judaism.explanation: Saul's half-finished campaign becomes the turning point of his downfall, and later tradition links the leftover Agagite line to Haman.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the story treats an enemy left partly dealt with as a smouldering danger that later consumes the one who left it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, an evil deed committed does not immediately bear fruit, like milk that does not turn sour all at once. But smoldering, it follows the fool like fire covered by ashes.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that consequences can lie hidden like embers under ash before flaring up.
buddhism.tie_back: The same image of fire covered by ash carries the Kural's warning about remnants that look dead but are not.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One should not be complacent with a small debt, slight wound, spark of fire and slight passion, because what is small (today) may become bigger (later).”
jainism.explanation: The preceding verse warns that even one who has repressed all his passions may fall again, so one must not be complacent while remnants of passion remain.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's image of an unfinished task and a half-defeated foe as embers that grow back and destroy is matched almost exactly by this Jain warning about a spark of fire and the remnants of passion.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam 134 (cf. 133), English tr. on jainworld.com

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If someone focuses on the Lord beforehand, then why should he be punished? The kings had lost their higher consciousness, reveling in pleasure and sensuality.”
sikhism.explanation: Writing of Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak says the rulers who ignored the gathering danger while absorbed in pleasure were overtaken by disaster that foresight could have prevented.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a half-dealt-with enemy grows unnoticed like embers until it destroys the careless; Guru Nanak's lament shows rulers ruined by exactly such neglect of a danger they should have attended to in time.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Ashtapadi (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Heracles cuts off the heads of the Lernaean Hydra, two grow back for each one; only when Iolaus burns each stump with firebrands can the monster be finished off.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Hydra shows that an enemy only partly destroyed regrows stronger unless the job is completed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Hydra's regrowing heads are the Kural's echcham: a remnant that multiplies unless it is fully dealt with.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli advises that if an injury must be done to an enemy it should be of such a kind that there is no fear of revenge, since men avenge slight injuries but cannot avenge heavy ones.
philosophy.explanation: He argues that half-measures against opponents are the worst policy because they provoke without disabling.
philosophy.tie_back: Machiavelli reaches the Kural's conclusion from political calculation: a half-handled enemy is a future danger.

real_life_example.event_title: Malaria returns to Sri Lanka after near-elimination
real_life_example.event: An intensive spraying campaign cut malaria in Sri Lanka from about 92,000 cases in 1953 to just 17 cases in 1963. In the belief that the disease was nearly gone, control was scaled back: many DDT spraying teams were disbanded when a consolidation phase began in 1964, and surveillance did not react to the rising numbers. Cases grew from 1965 onward into a countrywide epidemic, with more than half a million cases reported in 1969, and the country was not certified malaria-free until 2016.
real_life_example.explanation: Sri Lanka's experience became a classic warning in public health that a disease brought low but not finished can return with great force.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that an unfinished task is like embers left burning that grow back and destroy, and Sri Lanka's malaria, reduced to a handful of cases and then left unwatched, flared back into an epidemic.

tamil:
பொருள்கருவி காலம் வினையிடனொடு ஐந்தும்
இருள்தீர எண்ணிச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Porul karuvi kaalam vinai idanodu aindhum
Irul theera ennich cheyal.
meaning: Before you act, think clearly about five things until nothing is unclear: money, tools, timing, the task itself, and the place.
elementary: Before baking a cake you check: Do I have the ingredients? Do I have a bowl and an oven? Do I have enough time before dinner? Do I know the recipe? Is the kitchen free? Once all five are clear, you start.
university: The kural lists five factors: porul (wealth, resources), karuvi (instruments, which Parimelazhagar extends to the army and other means), kaalam (time), vinai (the nature and method of the act itself) and idam (place). Irul theera, 'until the darkness is dispelled', means until every doubt has been removed. Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah add that each factor must be weighed for both oneself and the enemy, so this is a comparative strategic appraisal and not just a checklist. The structure closely matches the Arthashastra's five limbs of counsel (1.15), which include means, men and materials, and the apportionment of place and time, and it summarises earlier Kural chapters on strength (48), time (49) and place (50). Older editions print the line with full sandhi (வினையிடனொ டைந்து / மிருடீர வெண்ணிச் செயல்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya lists five limbs of counsel: the means of starting an undertaking, the excellence of men and materials, the allotment of place and time, remedies against failure, and the successful completion of the work.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra makes these five points the required agenda of any royal council before an undertaking.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts insist on a fixed five-part review, with resources, instruments, place and time at its core, before any action is begun.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher observes that working with a blunt tool wastes effort, and wisdom lies in preparing the instrument first.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's karuvi point: examining your instruments beforehand is part of acting wisely.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy.”
islam.explanation: The Quran instructs the community to prepare material strength and means before any confrontation.
islam.tie_back: It asks for the same preparation of resources and instruments that the Kural's first two factors describe.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rebuilding Jerusalem's wall under threat, Nehemiah has the builders work with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, posts guards at the exposed places, and sets working hours from dawn until the stars appear.
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah plans resources, tools, place and time together so the work can be finished despite enemies.
judaism.tie_back: His careful planning of means, instruments, time and place is a working example of the Kural's five-fold review.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists five wrong times for striving (old age, illness, famine, danger and a split in the community) and five right times when conditions support effort.
buddhism.explanation: In the Samaya Sutta he teaches that the success of practice depends on choosing favourable times and conditions.
buddhism.tie_back: This reflects the Kural's kaalam factor: an act must be weighed against the time and conditions in which it is attempted.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A person should decide upon fasting after taking into consideration his physical strength, stamina, faith, state of health, place and time.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching on austerity requires that a practice be undertaken only after weighing one's own capacities together with the place and the time.
jainism.tie_back: Like the kural's fivefold review of resources, instruments, time, act and place before acting, this verse makes a deliberate survey of capacity, place and time the precondition of an undertaking.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam 445 (Tapasutra), English tr. on jainworld.com

sikhism.quote_or_event: “First, examine the merchandise, and then, make the deal.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the trader's rule of inspecting goods before buying as a model for judging carefully before committing oneself.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells one to think through resources, means, time, the act and place until no doubt remains before acting; Guru Nanak's saying states the same principle of full appraisal before commitment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1410, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Calypso gives Odysseus a bronze axe, an adze and augers, shows him where the tall dry trees stand, and brings sailcloth; he builds his raft in four days and sets out on the fifth with a fair wind she sends.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus' escape succeeds because materials, tools, place, craft and timing all come together before he sails.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode is almost a story version of the Kural's five factors: resources, instruments, time, the work itself and place.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle lists the circumstances of an action: who acts, what is done, about what or in what it is done, sometimes with what instrument, for what end, and how.
philosophy.explanation: He sets out these particulars to show what a person must know for an act to be truly voluntary and deliberate.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle breaks action into a fixed set of circumstances, including instrument, manner and setting, all of which must be clear before acting well.

real_life_example.event_title: Nansen's Fram is designed to drift with the Arctic ice
real_life_example.event: To test the theory that sea ice drifts from Siberia across the Arctic towards Greenland, Fridtjof Nansen had the ship Fram built with a rounded, wide, shallow hull and almost no keel, so that pressure from the ice would lift it rather than crush it. The ship was insulated and stocked so that its crew could live aboard for up to five years. In September 1893 the Fram was deliberately frozen into the ice off the New Siberian Islands, and it drifted across the Arctic Ocean until it broke free north of Spitsbergen in 1896, bringing back significant scientific data.
real_life_example.explanation: Nansen matched the vessel, the supplies, the time and the route to the nature of the task, and the expedition returned intact from a region where many ships had been crushed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks that resources, instruments, time, the nature of the task and the place all be thought through until no confusion remains, and the Fram expedition was planned around exactly those five factors.

tamil:
முடிவும் இடையூறும் முற்றியாங்கு எய்தும்
படுபயனும் பார்த்துச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Mudivum idaiyoorum mutriyaangu eydhum
Padupayanum paarththuch cheyal.
meaning: Act only after looking at what it takes to finish the task, the problems that may come up along the way, and the gain it will bring at the end.
elementary: Before starting a big jigsaw puzzle, ask: How long will it take to finish? What could go wrong, like the cat scattering pieces? And will the finished picture be worth it? If yes, begin.
university: Mudivu here is read by Parimelazhagar as the effort (muyarchi) required to bring the work to completion, idaiyooru as the hindrances that may come in between, and padupayan as the large yield obtained when it is completed (mutriyaangu eydhum). The kural thus sets out a three-part cost-benefit appraisal: cost of completion, risk, and return. Mu. Varadarasanar reads mudivu more simply as 'the way of completing the task', while Kalaignar reorders the three items but keeps the sense. The older sandhi text reads முடிவு மிடையூறு முற்றியாங் கெய்தும், with no difference of meaning. The idea anticipates the Gospel image of counting the cost before building, and Epictetus' advice to consider what comes before and after any undertaking.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That action is declared to be in the mode of ignorance, which is begun out of delusion, without thought to one’s own ability, and disregarding consequences, loss, and injury to others.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the lowest (tamasic) kind of action as one started without weighing consequences, loss and one's own capacity.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita condemns exactly what the Kural forbids: acting without first looking at effort, obstacles and outcome.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a sensible builder who calculates whether he can complete a tower before laying its foundation.
christianity.tie_back: Counting the cost of finishing is the Kural's mudivu: weighing what completion will demand before beginning.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Messenger of Allah! Shall I tie it and rely (upon Allah), or leave it loose and rely (upon Allah)?” He said: “Tie it and rely (upon Allah).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells a man to take sensible precautions against a foreseeable risk and then trust in God.
islam.tie_back: Tying the camel is guarding against the Kural's idaiyooru, the obstacles that can be foreseen and prevented before acting.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Reckon the loss [that may be sustained through the fulfillment] of a commandment against the reward [accruing] thereby, and the gain [that may be obtained through the committing] of a transgression against the loss [entailed] thereby.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince teaches weighing losses against rewards before acting.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's balance of cost and padupayan (great gain), applied to moral choices.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells his son Rahula to reflect before any action whether it will lead to harm for himself or others, to reflect again while doing it, and again after it is done.
buddhism.explanation: Like looking in a mirror, one checks an act's results at every stage.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha, like the Kural, asks that consequences be looked at before acting rather than discovered afterwards.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Three merchants set out on their travels, each with his capital; one of them gained there much, the second returned with his capital, and the third merchant came home after having lost his capital.”
jainism.explanation: The parable treats human life as capital that can be increased, preserved or lost, and adds that, considering what is at stake, one should weigh the outcomes in one's mind.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's call to weigh the effort, the obstacles and the gain before acting is reflected in this Jain parable of reckoning the stakes and possible returns of a venture.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.14-15 (cf. 7.19) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So throw the dice in such a way, that you shall not lose with your Lord and Master. Do those deeds which shall bring you profit.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa ki Vaar Guru Nanak uses the image of a calculated move in a game, urging that one's efforts be chosen so that they end in gain rather than loss before the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks one to weigh the effort, the obstacles and the great gain of a task before acting; Guru Nanak likewise asks for deeds weighed by their final profit.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (Pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: A thirsty fox falls into a well; a goat jumps in after being told the water is fine; the fox climbs out on the goat's back and leaves it stranded, saying it should have looked for a way out before jumping in.
greek_mythology.explanation: Aesop's fable is traditionally summed up as look before you leap.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The goat fails to weigh the Kural's mudivu: how the venture is to be completed and brought safely to an end.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Fox and the Goat

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In every affair consider what precedes and follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit; but not having thought of the consequences, when some of them appear you will shamefully desist.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus uses the example of the Olympic athlete, who must count the training, hardships and possible defeat before committing.
philosophy.tie_back: His advice lines up item by item with the Kural: effort to completion, obstacles along the way, and whether the gain is worth it.

real_life_example.event_title: Ferdinand de Lesseps builds the Suez Canal
real_life_example.event: In 1854 the Egyptian ruler Said Pasha granted Ferdinand de Lesseps a concession to form a company to dig a canal between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. Despite opposition from Britain, difficulty selling shares outside France, a cholera epidemic in 1865 and labour problems, digging began on 25 April 1859 and the waters of the two seas met in August 1869. The canal was formally opened on 17 November 1869, greatly shortening the sea route between Europe and Asia.
real_life_example.explanation: The project faced heavy costs and repeated obstacles, but the enormous gain it promised for world trade carried it through, and it remains one of the most important waterways in the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks one to weigh the effort needed, the obstacles on the way and the great gain at the end before acting, and the Suez Canal was a venture whose huge eventual return justified a decade of costly struggle.

tamil:
செய்வினை செய்வான் செயன்முறை அவ்வினை
உள்ளறிவான் உள்ளம் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Seyvinai seyvaan seyanmurai avvinai
Ullarivaan ullam kolal.
meaning: The right way to do a task is to find out what someone who knows that task well thinks about it.
elementary: If you want to learn to bake bread, the best first step is to ask a baker who has done it a thousand times. They know the little secrets no recipe tells you.
university: Ullarivaan means 'one who knows the inside' of the work: its hidden difficulties, tricks and secrets. Ullam kolal means 'to take (on) his mind or view'. Parimelazhagar glosses the knower as someone who has already carried out such an undertaking and knows its secret (marmam), and Solomon Pappaiah likewise reads 'one who has done this work before'. The sound pattern (seyvinai seyvaan seyanmurai; ullarivaan ullam) is deliberate and makes the couplet easy to remember. The older sandhi text reads செயன்முறை யவ்வினை / யுள்ளறிவா னுள்ளங் கொளல். The kural extends the earlier chapter on seeking the help of the great (periyaaraith thunaikkodal, ch. 45) to the practical level of expertise.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Learn the Truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him with reverence and render service unto him. Such an enlightened Saint can impart knowledge unto you because he has seen the Truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that real knowledge comes from someone who has seen the truth directly.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's tattva-darshin, one who has seen the reality, is the spiritual counterpart of the Kural's ullarivaan, one who knows a task from within.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest? And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me?”
christianity.explanation: The Ethiopian official admits he cannot understand the scripture alone and invites Philip to explain it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the story holds that a task is best approached by seeking out someone who understands it from inside.

islam.quote_or_event: “So ask the people of the message if you do not know.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells those who lack knowledge to ask those who have it.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's method in one line: whoever does not know, should ask the one who does.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jethro watches Moses judging the people alone from morning to evening, tells him the method is not good and will wear him out, and advises him to appoint capable officers over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens; Moses follows the advice.
judaism.explanation: An experienced outsider who understands the work of governing shows Moses a better method.
judaism.tie_back: Moses does what the Kural recommends: he adopts the view of someone who understands how the work is best done.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a wise adviser to a guide who knows where treasure is buried.
buddhism.tie_back: The guide to hidden treasure is the Kural's ullarivaan, the one who knows what is hidden inside a task.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Guessing the teacher's thoughts and the purport of his words, one should express one's assent, and execute (what he desires to be done).”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline teaches the pupil to grasp the mind of the experienced teacher and act upon it, and promises that satisfied teachers will hand on their weighty knowledge.
jainism.tie_back: The kural's method of learning the mind of one who knows the work from inside is closely paralleled by this Jain rule of taking on the teacher's intention before acting.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.43 (cf. 1.46) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Go and ask the happy, pure soul-brides, how did they obtain their Husband Lord?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak tells the seeker to learn the way from those who have already reached the goal, rather than relying on cleverness of one's own.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the right method is to take the mind of one who knows the task from the inside, having done it before; Guru Nanak sends the seeker to those who have already succeeded.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 722, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe tells Odysseus that before he can find his way home he must go to the house of Hades and consult the seer Tiresias, who alone can tell him the route and the measure of his journey.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus makes the terrible journey because only Tiresias knows the path from within.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Even the resourceful Odysseus follows the Kural's method, seeking out the one who truly knows the task before attempting it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates asks Crito whether a man in athletic training should heed the praise and blame of everyone, or only of the one man who is his doctor or trainer; Crito agrees it is the expert alone.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates uses this to argue that in any matter one should follow the person who has real knowledge of it, not the crowd.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates and the Kural agree that the proper way to act is to take the view of the one who knows the work.

real_life_example.event_title: The Iwakura Mission studies Western institutions at first hand
real_life_example.event: In 1871 Japan's new Meiji government sent a large delegation led by Iwakura Tomomi, with senior leaders including Kido Takayoshi, Okubo Toshimichi and Ito Hirobumi, on a journey of about two years through the United States and Europe. Although it also hoped to prepare for revising Japan's unequal treaties, the mission divided into teams to study education, administration, finance, law and industry in the countries that had already built modern states. Its members returned with ideas that shaped Japan's later reforms, including the conviction that the country needed a constitution.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than guessing how to build a modern state, Japan's leaders went to observe those who had already done it and learned from them directly.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the right way for anyone undertaking a task is to learn the mind of someone who knows that task from the inside, and Japan's leaders crossed the world to study nations that had already done what Japan set out to do.

tamil:
வினையான் வினையாக்கிக் கோடல் நனைகவுள்
யானையால் யானையாத் தற்று.
transliteration:
Vinaiyaan vinaiyaakkik kodal nanaikavul
Yaanaiyaal yaanaiyaath thatru.
meaning: Using one task to get another one done is like using a trained elephant to catch a wild one.
elementary: When you go to the shop to buy milk and also post a letter on the way, one trip does two jobs. Long ago, people caught wild elephants by using a tame elephant to lead them in. Smart people let one job help with the next.
university: Nanaikavul, literally 'wet cheek', refers to an elephant in musth, whose temples stream with fluid; such tame elephants were used as decoys to lure and capture wild ones, a practice well attested in Tamil and Sanskrit sources on elephant-keeping. Vinaiyaan vinai aakkik kodal means 'to bring about a (further) task by means of a task'. Parimelazhagar specifies that the second undertaking should be of the same kind as the first, just as elephant catches elephant, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as completing one task while doing another. The older sandhi text reads கோட னனைகவுள் / யானையால் யானையாத் தற்று. The elephant simile gives a vivid image of turning one achievement into the means of the next.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Rama helps Sugriva win back his throne from Vali, and Sugriva in return sends the monkey armies across the world to find Sita and later to build the bridge to Lanka.
hinduism.explanation: By completing one undertaking (Sugriva's restoration), Rama gains the means for his larger one (the rescue of Sita).
hinduism.tie_back: This is vinaiyaan vinai aakkik kodal on an epic scale: one completed task becomes the tool for the next.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the parable of the unjust steward, a manager about to lose his post uses his remaining authority over his master's accounts to win friends who will take him in later, and Jesus tells his hearers to use worldly wealth to make friends for the future.
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the shrewd steward, Jesus praises using present resources to secure a future end.
christianity.tie_back: The steward uses one piece of business to accomplish another, as the Kural's elephant is used to catch its fellow.

islam.quote_or_event: Joseph, now in charge of Egypt's grain stores, uses the distribution of grain to his visiting brothers to bring about their return with his brother Benjamin, and so to reunite his family.
islam.explanation: Surah Yusuf shows Joseph turning an administrative duty into the means of a deeper purpose.
islam.tie_back: Joseph uses one task (supplying grain) to achieve another (restoring his family), which is the Kural's method.

judaism.quote_or_event: “From and within the forest comes the ax to it,”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud cites this popular saying to explain why Obadiah, said to be an Edomite convert, was chosen to prophesy against Edom: the axe handle that fells the tree is cut from the forest itself.
judaism.tie_back: Like the elephant used to catch an elephant, the forest supplies the tool for its own felling: like is taken by means of like.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 39b (William Davidson trans., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that an unskilful thought can be driven out by focusing on a skilful one, as a skilled carpenter knocks out a coarse peg with a fine one.
buddhism.explanation: In the Vitakkasanthana Sutta the first method of calming the mind uses one thought to displace another.
buddhism.tie_back: The carpenter's peg, like the Kural's elephant, is a tool of the same kind used to accomplish the task.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Just as an impassioned elephant who is inflamed by carnal desires, is turned from his way by a female elephant (and is captured and at last killed in battle).”
jainism.explanation: In the lecture on the causes of carelessness, the elephant lured and captured by a decoy female is an image of how attachment to the senses leads a soul to ruin.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain text knows the same decoy-elephant capture the kural uses, but turns it into a warning about the senses rather than a model of using one undertaking to win another.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.89 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Servant Nanak begs for the dust of the feet of that GurSikh, who himself chants the Naam, and inspires others to chant it.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das honours the Sikh whose own practice becomes the means of drawing others into the same practice.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures one achievement used to secure another, like a tamed elephant luring a wild one; the Gurbani image is of one who, having made the Name his own, draws others to it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 306, Raag Gauree, Gauri ki Vaar (salok), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Set to clean the vast Augean stables in a single day, Heracles breaches the walls and diverts the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through them, letting one force of nature do the work.
greek_mythology.explanation: Instead of doing the labour by hand, Heracles turns existing powers into his tool.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles makes one thing (the rivers' flow) accomplish another (the cleansing), as the Kural's hunter uses one elephant to take another.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon writes that nature, to be commanded, must be obeyed: human power over nature comes from using nature's own laws and forces.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon's programme for science rests on turning natural processes against one another to achieve human ends.
philosophy.tie_back: The idea that nature is mastered by nature matches the Kural's elephant-by-elephant image.
philosophy.source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum I, aphorism 3

real_life_example.event_title: The Great Exhibition's profits build the museums of South Kensington
real_life_example.event: The Great Exhibition of 1851, held in the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, made a surplus of about 186,000 pounds. Prince Albert proposed that the profit be used for educational institutions, and in December 1851 the Royal Commission for the Exhibition of 1851 began buying land in South Kensington. That estate became home to the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Science Museum, the Natural History Museum, Imperial College, the Royal Colleges of Art and Music and the Royal Albert Hall.
real_life_example.explanation: One successful undertaking was deliberately used as the engine for another, and the exhibition of a single summer produced institutions that have lasted more than 170 years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that using one undertaking to achieve another is like using a tamed elephant to capture a wild one, and the Great Exhibition's surplus was harnessed to capture a far larger prize in the museums and colleges of South Kensington.

tamil:
நட்டார்க்கு நல்ல செயலின் விரைந்ததே
ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Nattaarkku nalla seyalin viraindhadhe
Ottaarai ottik kolal.
meaning: Winning over people who are not yet on your side is more urgent than doing good things for people who are already your friends.
elementary: Your friends already like you. But if there is a kid in class who keeps fighting with you, making peace with them first can make everything easier for everyone. Turning a rival into a friend is the urgent job.
university: Nattaar are those already bound in friendship; ottaar are those who do not adhere to one, that is, rivals or foes, and ottik kolal is 'to make them adhere, to bring them round'. Parimelazhagar, followed by the Drew-Lazarus translation reproduced on ytamizh, specifies the foes of one's foes, so that the kural advises quickly securing allies against a common enemy before an undertaking, while modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read it more broadly as reconciling enemies. Viraindhadhu, 'the more urgent', ranks this ahead of kindness to friends because friends are already secure while potential enemies can still change sides. The older sandhi text reads விரைந்ததே / யொட்டாரை யொட்டிக் கொளல். The kural fits the Indian mandala theory of alliances and also anticipates ethical teachings about turning an enemy into a friend.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Trapped between a hunter's net and hunting animals, the mouse Palita makes a timely alliance with his natural enemy, the cat Lomasa, who is caught in the net; each saves the other, and they part with prudent caution.
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira this fable to show that in need a wise king quickly makes allies even of former enemies.
hinduism.tie_back: The mouse follows the Kural exactly: bringing a foe round in time is more urgent than anything else.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, the mouse and the cat (Ganguli trans., Santi Parva section 138)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them. And if ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says kindness to friends is ordinary; the greater work is love toward enemies.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Luke ranks reaching out to those who are not on your side above doing good to those who already are.

islam.quote_or_event: “Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Quran teaches that answering hostility with goodness can turn an enemy into a close friend.
islam.tie_back: This is ottaarai ottik kolal: bringing the hostile one round until he is bound to you.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Others say: [Who is mighty?] Who turns an enemy into his friend.”
judaism.explanation: In a list of true virtues, one opinion defines real strength as making an enemy into a friend.
judaism.tie_back: The rabbis and the Kural both treat winning over a foe as a higher achievement than ordinary good deeds.
judaism.source: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 23 (trans. A. Cohen, Soncino, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that hostility ends only through non-hostility, not by fighting it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Dhammapada gives the ethical basis for the Kural's advice to win over those who are against you.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I forgive all living beings and may all living beings forgive me; I cherish feelings of friendship towards all and I harbour enmity towards none.”
jainism.explanation: This verse, recited at the Jain rite of mutual forgiveness, makes friendship toward every being and enmity toward none a central discipline.
jainism.tie_back: The kural urges winning over those not yet one's friends; the Jain ideal goes further by refusing to regard anyone as a foe at all.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam 86, English tr. on jainworld.com

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the state reached in the company of the holy, in which enmity and estrangement fall away altogether.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks winning over those not yet on one's side above favouring existing friends; Guru Arjan goes further, dissolving the line between friend and foe entirely.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Meeting on the battlefield at Troy, Glaucus and Diomedes discover that their grandfathers were guest-friends, so they refuse to fight, clasp hands and exchange armour as a pledge.
greek_mythology.explanation: Two enemies choose friendship over combat in the middle of a war.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode shows the Kural's ideal: turning someone on the other side into a bound friend.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu holds that the best thing in war is to take the enemy's country whole and intact, and that supreme excellence is to break the enemy's resistance without fighting.
philosophy.explanation: The Art of War ranks winning an opponent over, or disarming him intact, above destroying him.
philosophy.tie_back: Sun Tzu's strategy, like the Kural's, puts bringing the adversary round ahead of other actions.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, ch. 3 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Benjamin Franklin wins France's alliance for the American cause
real_life_example.event: In Paris Benjamin Franklin, with fellow commissioners Silas Deane and Arthur Lee, worked in Paris to win French support for the American Revolution. When news of the British surrender at Saratoga reached France in December 1777, the foreign minister Vergennes decided in favour of an alliance. On 6 February 1778 the commissioners signed a Treaty of Alliance and a Treaty of Amity and Commerce with France, which bound both countries not to make a separate peace with Britain.
real_life_example.explanation: Bringing a great power that was not yet committed onto the American side changed the course of the war, and French aid proved decisive in the years that followed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that winning over those not yet on one's side is more urgent than doing good to existing friends, and Franklin's mission turned France, Britain's rival but not yet America's ally, into a formal partner against a common enemy.

tamil:
உறைசிறியார் உள்நடுங்கல் அஞ்சிக் குறைபெறின்
கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து.
transliteration:
Uraisiriyaar ulnadungal anjik kuraiperin
Kolvar periyaarp panindhu.
meaning: Leaders of a small country, afraid that their own people are scared, will give in to a stronger power and accept peace if they are offered a chance.
elementary: Imagine a small team facing a much bigger, stronger team and all your players are scared. A wise captain might agree to a fair deal instead of a hopeless match, to protect the team. Sometimes the brave choice is to make peace.
university: Uraisiriyaar, 'those whose dwelling (realm) is small', is read by Parimelazhagar as the ministers of weak states; ulnadungal anji means 'fearing the inner trembling' of their own subjects; kurai perin, 'if they obtain an opening' for reconciliation; periyaarp panindhu kolvar, 'they will submit to and embrace the great'. The Drew-Lazarus rendering on ytamizh follows this reading, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it more generally about the weak yielding to the strong for the sake of their people. The older sandhi text reads உண்ணடுங்க லஞ்சிக் குறைபெறிற். Placed at the end of the chapter, the kural completes the method of execution by admitting that sometimes the wise act is timely submission rather than conflict, a principle also central to the Arthashastra's teaching on the weak king and to Luke 14:31-32.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya teaches that a king who is weaker than his rival should make peace with him, and that a weak king attacked by a strong one should submit, bending like a reed, and wait for better times.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra treats timely submission (samdhi) by the weaker side as sound policy, not cowardice.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's advice to the rulers of small realms: accept terms with the stronger party to protect one's people.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus describes a weaker king who, seeing he is outnumbered, sends envoys early to ask for terms.
christianity.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's scene: a smaller ruler seeking terms from a greater one.

islam.quote_or_event: At al-Hudaybiyyah the Prophet accepts a truce with Quraysh on terms many of his companions found humiliating, including turning back from Mecca that year; the Quran later calls the outcome a clear victory.
islam.explanation: Accepting restrictive terms from a stronger party in the moment protected the community and opened the way to later success.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's rulers, the Prophet chose a negotiated settlement over a clash, for his people's sake.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and live.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah urges King Zedekiah to submit to Babylon's greater power rather than rebel and bring ruin on Jerusalem.
judaism.tie_back: The prophet gives the Kural's counsel to a small kingdom: bow to the greater power for the survival of the people.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Victory begets enmity; the defeated dwell in pain. Happily the peaceful live, discarding both victory and defeat.”
buddhism.explanation: Traditionally linked to the war between King Pasenadi and King Ajatasattu, the verse says conflict harms winner and loser alike.
buddhism.tie_back: It gives an ethical reason to prefer peace to fighting on, which supports the Kural's settlement-seeking rulers.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Bharata, eldest son of Rishabha, set out to bring every realm under his rule as chakravartin, his ninety-eight younger brothers, each holding a smaller kingdom, were called on to submit. Jain tradition relates that rather than fight or bow, they became monks and gave up their kingdoms, leaving Bahubali alone to resist.
jainism.explanation: In the Jain universal history the weaker rulers neither wage a hopeless war nor merely submit, but renounce kingship altogether.
jainism.tie_back: The kural observes that small rulers, fearing for their people, will yield to a mightier power when an opening is offered; the Jain story shows lesser kings in the same position choosing renunciation instead.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book I (life of Ṛṣabha and Bharata's conquest), as summarised in Wikipedia, 'Bharata chakravarti'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When something is placed on the balancing scale and weighed, the side which descends is heavier.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa ki Vaar Guru Nanak uses the scale to show that the one who bows is the one of real weight, so humility is strength, not loss.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the rulers of a small realm, fearing for their people, will bow to a greater power when peace is offered; Guru Nanak's scale gives a moral reason why such bowing need not be shameful.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Old King Priam goes by night to the tent of Achilles, who has killed his son, kneels and kisses his hands, and wins back Hector's body so that Troy can mourn.
greek_mythology.explanation: The weaker king humbles himself before the stronger warrior to obtain what his people need.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Priam, like the rulers in the Kural, bows to the greater power when an opening appears, for the sake of his people.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Melian Dialogue the Athenian envoys urge the small island of Melos to yield, arguing that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must; Melos refuses and is destroyed.
philosophy.explanation: Thucydides presents the negative case: a small state that refuses terms from a far stronger power is wiped out.
philosophy.tie_back: The fate of Melos shows, in reverse, the prudence the Kural credits to small states that bow when terms are offered.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 5.84-116 (trans. Richard Crawley)

real_life_example.event_title: Siam accepts France's terms in the crisis of 1893
real_life_example.event: In 1893, after clashes with French forces in the Mekong valley, French gunboats forced their way up the Chao Phraya River and blockaded Bangkok, and France gave Siam an ultimatum. King Chulalongkorn's government accepted the French demands, agreeing to pay an indemnity and withdrawing from the east bank of the Mekong, which France took as part of its protectorate in Laos. The concession was part of a broader policy of yielding territory to Western powers in the hope that Siam could keep its overall independence, and Siam stayed independent while its neighbours fell under colonial rule.
real_life_example.explanation: Facing a far stronger power, Siam chose painful concessions over a war it could not win, and in doing so preserved the kingdom itself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the rulers of a small realm, fearing for their own people, will bow to a mightier power and accept terms when an opening for peace is offered, which is what Chulalongkorn's government did under French guns in 1893.

tamil:
அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல் வேந்தவாம்
பண்புடைமை தூதுரைப்பான் பண்பு.
transliteration:
Anbudaimai aandra kudippiraththal vendhavaam
Panbudaimai thoodhuraippaan panbu.
meaning: An envoy (a messenger sent to speak for a king) should be loving, come from a respected family, and have the good manners that kings value.
elementary: When your class sends someone to ask the principal for a longer break, you pick a kind person who comes from a family everyone trusts and who knows how to be polite to grown-ups. The person carrying a message has to be someone the listener already respects.
university: The chapter on the envoy (tūtu) belongs to the Amaichiyal, the section on ministers (chs. 64-73), and opens with the general qualifications. Parimelazhagar glosses aṉpuṭaimai as affection toward one’s own kin (cuṟṟattār), ‘āṉṟa kuṭi’ as a family fit to bear ministerial office, and ‘vēntu avām paṇpu’ as the qualities royalty desires. He adds that kin-affection means the envoy keeps his relatives from harm, and good lineage means he has heard of envoy-craft from his forebears. Manakkudavar reads the first quality differently, as love for one’s own king, and explains ‘qualities kings desire’ as not coveting what the king covets. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar keep the three-part list, Pappaiah widening the love to people, state and kin. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற; the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org reads அன்புடைமை யான்ற, the same words with the glide written in.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him also appoint an ambassador who is versed in all sciences, who understands hints, expressions of the face and gestures, who is honest, skilful, and of (noble) family.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu tell the king how to choose his envoy, and good family is on the list along with learning, honesty and skill.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Manu makes noble birth one of the envoy’s basic qualifications.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 7.63 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.”
christianity.explanation: When the apostles need people to act on the community’s behalf, they ask for men already known for good reputation and wisdom.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, a person is sent to represent others because of character that people already recognize.

islam.quote_or_event: “I asked you about his family and your reply was that he belonged to a very noble family. In fact all the Apostles come from noble families amongst their respective peoples.”
islam.explanation: Questioning Abu Sufyan about the Prophet, the Byzantine emperor Heraclius treats noble lineage as a mark of a genuine messenger.
islam.tie_back: Heraclius and the Kural both assume that a trustworthy messenger comes from a respected family.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that loveth pureness of heart, for the grace of his lips the king shall be his friend.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says a person with a pure heart and gracious speech wins the friendship of kings.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘quality that kings love’ (vēntu avām paṇpu): good character and pleasant manners.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Among the highest blessings the Buddha lists in the Mangala Sutta are supporting one’s parents, cherishing spouse and children, and helping one’s relatives.
buddhism.explanation: The discourse treats care for one’s own kin as a mark of a well-ordered and admirable life.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches Parimelazhagar’s reading of aṉpuṭaimai as affection for one’s own kin.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who always acknowledges his allegiance to his teacher, who has religious zeal and ardour for study, who is kind in words and actions, deserves to be instructed.”
jainism.explanation: The sutra names loyalty to one's teacher's house, eagerness to learn and kindness in speech and action as what makes a disciple fit to be trusted with instruction.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural asks for a loving nature, good standing and refined conduct in an envoy, the Jain text asks for loyalty, zeal and kind conduct in one who is to be trusted.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Recognize the Lord's Light within all, and do not consider social class or status; there are no classes or castes in the world hereafter.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak rejects birth and social rank as a measure of worth, telling the listener to see the one divine Light in every person.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural counts birth in a family of good standing among an envoy's qualifications; Sikh teaching agrees that a loving nature and refined conduct matter, but explicitly refuses to rank anyone by birth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 349, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Greeks send an embassy to the angry Achilles, Nestor has Phoenix lead it. Phoenix is the old man who raised Achilles, and he later appeals to that bond of love.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phoenix is chosen for his loving relationship with Achilles, which the Greeks hope will make the hearer receptive.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In the Kural too, affection and good standing are what qualify someone to carry a message.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay ‘Of Negotiating’, Francis Bacon advises using agents who have a personal attachment to the business they are sent on, and matching the agent’s temperament to the task.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon argues that a negotiator who cares about the cause works harder at it, and that personal qualities should be chosen to fit the mission.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Bacon judges an envoy first by character and attachment, and only then by skill.

real_life_example.event_title: Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit becomes the first woman to preside over the UN General Assembly
real_life_example.place: United Nations, New York, United States
real_life_example.event: Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit, daughter of the nationalist leader Motilal Nehru and sister of Jawaharlal Nehru, led India's delegation to the United Nations and served as ambassador in Moscow and Washington after independence. In 1953 the member states elected her president of the UN General Assembly, the first woman ever to hold the post. She later served as India's high commissioner in London.
real_life_example.explanation: Her career shows how a diplomat from a family long schooled in public life, with a manner that won the respect of other states, could be entrusted with her country's voice and then chosen to preside over the assembly of nations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names good family standing and the conduct that rulers value as marks of an envoy, and Pandit's background and the trust placed in her by the world's governments reflect both.

tamil:
அன்பறிவு ஆராய்ந்த சொல்வன்மை தூதுரைப்பார்க்கு
இன்றி யமையாத மூன்று.
transliteration:
Anbarivu aaraaindha solvanmai thoodhuraippaarkku
Indri yamaiyaadha moondru.
meaning: Love for the king, good sense, and the skill to speak with carefully chosen words are three things an envoy must have.
elementary: Imagine you are sent to ask the neighbours to give back your family’s ball. You need three things. You have to care about your family, you have to know exactly what to ask for, and you have to pick your words well so the neighbours say yes.
university: The couplet names three indispensable (iṉṟiyamaiyāta) qualities. Parimelazhagar makes each one specific: aṉpu is love for one’s own king, aṟivu is knowing what is good for him, and ārāynta colvaṉmai is careful speech before foreign kings. He explains the ‘examining’ (ārāytal) as choosing words the other side will agree to. From ‘indispensable three’ he infers that the ministerial virtues listed earlier are also needed. He also notes that 681 and 682 give the general marks common to both kinds of envoy the chapter goes on to separate. Solomon Pappaiah reads aṉpu as love of country, and Kalaignar gives a plain list. The couplet looks back to chapter 65 (Colvaṉmai, power of speech). On the text: the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org runs the words together (அன்பறி வாராய்ந்த … தூதுரைப்பார்க் கின்றி யமையாத), with no change of wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On first meeting Hanuman, Rama tells Lakshmana that someone who speaks like this must have mastered the Vedas and grammar, because in a long speech he made not one error, and his words would win over even an enemy with a raised sword.
hinduism.explanation: Hanuman comes to Rama as Sugriva’s envoy. His devotion, knowledge and flawless, well-chosen speech make Rama trust him at once.
hinduism.tie_back: Hanuman has all three of the Kural’s essentials: love for his master, knowledge, and carefully chosen speech.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes apostles as ambassadors who speak on another’s behalf and plead with their hearers to be reconciled.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s envoy, the ambassador is moved by love for the one who sends him (2 Cor 5:14) and has to speak persuasively.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Moses] said, ‘My Lord, expand for me my breast [with assurance] And ease for me my task And untie the knot from my tongue That they may understand my speech.’”
islam.explanation: Before going to Pharaoh as God’s envoy, Moses asks for confidence and clear, understandable speech.
islam.tie_back: Moses treats power of speech as indispensable to the mission, just as the Kural does.

judaism.quote_or_event: Sent to Pharaoh, Moses protests that he is ‘slow of speech’. God appoints his brother Aaron to be his spokesman, so the message is delivered with both Moses’ knowledge and Aaron’s eloquence.
judaism.explanation: The Torah treats the mission to Pharaoh as needing a good speaker, and supplies one when the envoy himself lacks the skill.
judaism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s claim that speaking skill is indispensable, not optional, for an envoy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It’s a mendicant who learns and educates others. They memorize and remember. They understand and help others understand.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the qualities that make a monk fit to go on a mission, and names Sāriputta as having them.
buddhism.tie_back: Learning, understanding and the ability to make others understand match the Kural’s knowledge and discerning speech.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.16, Dūteyya Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Then the King, after giving instructions, despatched a messenger, named Suvega, skilled in polity, eloquent, courageous, to Bāhubali.”
jainism.explanation: When the Chakravartin Bharata sends an envoy to his brother Bahubali, Hemachandra's narrative picks a man described by exactly the qualities a messenger needs: knowledge of statecraft, eloquence and courage.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's three indispensables, love for the king, knowledge of what serves him and skill with words, closely match Suvega's knowledge of polity and eloquence, chosen for his master's mission.
jainism.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Bhai Lehna, who became Guru Angad, is remembered above all for his loyalty to Guru Nanak; having understood his master's ideals, he gave them definite form and, as Guru, standardised the Gurmukhi script in which much of the scripture is written.
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad's devotion to Guru Nanak, joined to an understanding of what his master intended and a gift for setting it down in words and script, made him Guru Nanak's chosen successor.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural names love for one's master, knowledge of what serves him, and skill with words as the envoy's three essentials; Guru Angad's loyalty, understanding and work on the written word together show all three.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Guru Angad

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Trojan elder Antenor recalls how Odysseus came to Troy as an envoy: he stood with his eyes fixed on the ground, but when he spoke, his words fell like winter snowflakes and no mortal could rival him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents Odysseus as the model of an envoy’s eloquence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural’s ārāynta colvaṉmai, carefully weighed speech, at its best.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says a speaker earns trust through three things: practical wisdom (phronēsis), virtue (aretē), and goodwill toward the audience (eunoia).
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, persuasion depends on the speaker’s character as well as the argument.
philosophy.tie_back: His goodwill, wisdom and skilled speech line up closely with the Kural’s love, knowledge and chosen words.

real_life_example.event_title: Sergei Witte secures peace at Portsmouth without an indemnity
real_life_example.event: To end the Russo-Japanese War, President Theodore Roosevelt invited Russia's chief negotiator Sergei Witte and Japan's Baron Komura Jutaro to talks that were held at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard. Under the treaty signed on 5 September 1905, Russia gave up its rights to Port Arthur and the southern half of Sakhalin Island but paid no indemnity to Japan. Witte was made a count for his efforts.
real_life_example.explanation: Witte came out of a lost war having protected the point his government cared about most, refusing any payment, while still finding terms the other side would sign.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks of an envoy loyalty to his ruler, knowledge of what serves him, and words chosen so that the other side will agree, and Witte's settlement at Portsmouth shows those three working together.

tamil:
நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன் ஆகுதல் வேலாருள்
வென்றி வினையுரைப்பான் பண்பு.
transliteration:
Noolaarul noolvallan aagudhal velaarul
Vendri vinaiyuraippaan panbu.
meaning: An envoy who speaks for their own king's victory in front of kings armed with spears must be the most skilled scholar even among learned people.
elementary: If you have to explain your team’s plan to the biggest, toughest team in the playground, you had better know the rules of the game better than anyone there. Knowing more than the clever people is what keeps you safe in front of the strong ones.
university: The couplet contrasts two audiences: nūlār, those learned in the treatises, and vēlār, the spear-bearers. Parimelazhagar identifies the first as the foreign court’s ministers, learned in nīti-nūl (works on polity), and the second as foreign kings. He says Valluvar wrote ‘vēlār’ to evoke their readiness to kill (kōṟal mālaiyar), and ‘veṉṟi viṉai’ to cover both kinds of envoy’s work. To be ‘vallaṉ’ (master) is more than knowing the texts: it is being able to set them out and apply them in front of ministers who only know them. Manakkudavar reads nūlāruḷ nūlvallaṉ as being able to expound all the texts before the learned. Pappaiah stresses knowledge of political ethics in a hostile court. On the text: the sandhi-joined text reads நூலாரு ணூல்வல்ல னாகுதல், the same words as the split form (நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன் ஆகுதல்) in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the war, Krishna goes as the Pandavas’ envoy to the Kaurava court. In front of Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and the assembled warriors, he argues for peace from dharma and statecraft. Duryodhana plots to seize him.
hinduism.explanation: The most learned of counsellors speaks in a hall full of armed kings, pressing his side’s case while in danger himself.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s picture: learning greater than the learned, used among spear-bearers for one’s own side’s success.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Bhagavat-yana sections (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, calling himself an ambassador, defends his message before the Roman governor Festus and King Agrippa, and his learning is so plain that Festus remarks on it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s envoy, Paul stands before men of armed power and is marked out by superior learning.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Quraysh sent envoys to the Negus of Abyssinia to demand the Muslim emigrants, Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib answered for the Muslims before the king and his bishops. He explained their faith and recited from Surat Maryam, and the Negus refused to hand them over.
islam.explanation: Ja‘far’s learned, measured answer in a foreign court won protection for his people against an armed opponent’s embassy.
islam.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s ideal: mastery of one’s own teaching, used among powerful rulers to win the case.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad)

judaism.quote_or_event: “And in all matters of wisdom and understanding, that the king enquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm.”
judaism.explanation: Daniel and his companions, exiles at a foreign court, prove more learned than all of Babylon’s scholars.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s nūlāruḷ nūlvallaṉ: foremost among the learned, in front of a powerful foreign king.
