buddhism.quote_or_event: When the Greek king Milinda invites the monk Nāgasena to debate, Nāgasena agrees only if the king will talk as a scholar does, not as a king does. Kings punish those who disagree; scholars can be refuted without anger.
buddhism.explanation: The learned monk faces a powerful king and relies on learning to set fair terms before answering the king’s hard questions.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s envoy, Nāgasena uses learning to hold his ground before a king who could use force.
buddhism.source: Milindapañha, Book II (trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, The Questions of King Milinda)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a trained Kambôga-steed, whom no noise frightens, exceeds all other horses in speed, so a very learned monk is superior to all others.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on 'the very learned' praises the monk of deep learning as excelling all others, like a war-horse that no noise can frighten.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural wants the envoy to be the most learned among the learned when he faces spear-bearing kings; the Jain image likewise joins superior learning with fearlessness amid clamour.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says that learning becomes real only when it is reflected on and turned to use for others, not when it is merely possessed.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says an envoy among learned ministers and armed kings must be more than learned: he must be able to apply what he knows; Guru Nanak likewise values learning only when it is digested and put to work.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, the infant Hermes steals Apollo’s cattle. Brought before Zeus, he talks his way out with clever speech and wins Apollo over with the lyre he has invented. He becomes the messenger and herald of the gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hermes, the divine herald, is a figure of cleverness and skilled speech who can win over more powerful gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The god of messengers succeeds, as the Kural says an envoy must, by outdoing the clever in wit and learning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero has Crassus argue that no one can be a complete orator without knowledge of all the important subjects and arts, because eloquence without substance is empty noise.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, persuasive speech in public affairs rests on wide learning.
philosophy.tie_back: It fits the Kural’s demand that the envoy be the most learned among the learned.

real_life_example.event_title: Philosopher Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan meets Stalin as India's ambassador
real_life_example.event: Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, professor of Eastern religions and ethics at Oxford and author of works on Indian philosophy, served as India's ambassador to the Soviet Union from 1949 to 1952. Before leaving Moscow he was received by Joseph Stalin, and the Indian record of the conversation shows him explaining India's parliamentary methods and independent foreign policy, correcting Stalin's doubt that Indian women had voted, and raising complaints about Soviet press coverage of India. Stalin agreed to recall the Soviet correspondent concerned.
real_life_example.explanation: A scholar sent among powerful rulers argued his country's case point by point before one of the most feared leaders of the century and came away with a concrete concession.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the one who speaks for his king before spear-bearing rulers must be the most learned among the learned, and Radhakrishnan, an Oxford professor, was exactly such an envoy before Stalin.

tamil:
அறிவுரு வாராய்ந்த கல்விஇம் மூன்றன்
செறிவுடையான் செல்க வினைக்கு.
transliteration:
Arivuru vaaraaindha kalvi-im moondran
Serivudaiyaan selga vinaikku.
meaning: Send a person on the mission only if they have three things together: good sense, a fine appearance, and learning that has been tested.
elementary: To show the new kid around school, the teacher picks someone who is smart, looks neat and friendly, and has learned the school rules properly. Someone with only one of these would not be enough. You need all three together.
university: Parimelazhagar makes each of the three precise. Aṟivu is innate intelligence (iyaṟkai aṟivu). Uru is a presence that viewers find attractive (kaṇṭār virumpum tōṟṟap polivu). Ārāynta kalvi is learning that has been examined ‘with many, over a long time’. The key word is ceṟivu, ‘combination’ or ‘density’: he notes that the three rarely come together in one person, and that together they make the envoy respected, so the mission succeeds. ‘Viṉai’ is the business of embassy to foreign kings. Manakkudavar reads ceṟivu as ‘containment’ (aṭakkam). Pappaiah adds that the person should be able to frame his message himself, which anticipates the ‘self-composing’ envoy of 687. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print கல்விஇம் மூன்றன் (a vowel hiatus); the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org reads கல்வியிம் மூன்றன், with the glide y written in.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “(Such) an ambassador is commended to a king (who is) loyal, honest, skilful, possessing a good memory, who knows the (proper) place and time (for action, who is) handsome, fearless, and eloquent.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists appearance next to memory, skill and eloquence as qualifications for an envoy.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s aṟivu, uru and kalvi, Manu counts a good appearance as a real qualification alongside intelligence and learning.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 7.64 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.”
christianity.explanation: Luke describes the young Jesus growing in wisdom and in bodily stature together, and winning people’s favour.
christianity.tie_back: Wisdom, bearing and the goodwill they earn are the combination the Kural looks for in an envoy.

islam.quote_or_event: Dihya al-Kalbi, whom the Prophet sent with his letter to the Byzantine ruler, was known for his striking good looks. Umm Salama mistook the angel Gabriel for Dihya, calling him ‘a handsome person amongst the companions’.
islam.explanation: The early community’s envoy to the emperor was remembered for his fine appearance.
islam.tie_back: The Kural lists uru, an impressive presence, as part of what makes an envoy respected abroad.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 7 (Dihya carries the letter); Sahih al-Bukhari 3634 (his handsome appearance)

judaism.quote_or_event: “That is cunning in playing, and a mighty valiant man, and a man of war, and prudent in matters, and a comely person, and the LORD is with him.”
judaism.explanation: Saul’s servant recommends David for royal service by listing skill, courage, good judgement and good looks.
judaism.tie_back: Prudence, comeliness and cultivated skill are a close match for the Kural’s aṟivu, uru and kalvi.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Sāriputta was won over to the Dhamma when he saw the monk Assaji on his alms round and was struck by his calm, graceful bearing. He asked him who his teacher was and received a short verse of teaching.
buddhism.explanation: Assaji’s outward bearing opened the way, and his wisdom finished the work.
buddhism.tie_back: Presence first earns respect and learning then carries the message, as the Kural expects of an envoy.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As water put into a shell shines with a doubled brilliancy, so do the piety, fame, and knowledge of a very learned monk.”
jainism.explanation: The sutra says the virtues and knowledge of a learned monk shine out doubly, as water does in a conch shell.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural joins natural sense, an impressive presence and tested learning in its envoy; the Jain verse only partly matches, linking inner learning with an outward radiance others can see.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Wisdom leads us to serve our Lord and Master; through wisdom, honor is obtained.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sarang ki Vaar Guru Nanak praises good sense (akal) as what makes one's service to the Master effective and wins honour.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural wants an envoy with natural good sense, presence and tested learning so that he is respected and succeeds; Guru Nanak likewise links sound judgement to good service and the honour it earns.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before Odysseus appears before the Phaeacians, Athena makes him taller and sturdier-looking so that he will be welcomed, feared and respected, and will succeed in the contests ahead.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer treats appearance as something that decides how a stranger pleading his cause will be received.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This matches Parimelazhagar’s point that uru helps the envoy be well regarded, and so helps the mission succeed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates says the nature fit for the highest training must be quick to learn, have a good memory, and be high-minded and gracious. Such natural gifts, perfected by education and maturity, deserve to be entrusted with the state.
philosophy.explanation: Plato holds that the best public servant joins natural talent with long, tested education.
philosophy.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s pairing of innate aṟivu with ārāynta kalvi, learning examined over time.

real_life_example.event_title: Dag Hammarskjold's mission to Peking for the detained airmen
real_life_example.date: 30 December 1954 to 13 January 1955; airmen released in 1955
real_life_example.event: Asked by the UN General Assembly to seek the release of American airmen who had served under the UN Command in Korea, Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjold travelled to Peking and negotiated directly with Zhou Enlai, since the People's Republic of China was not represented at the United Nations. Hammarskjold, who held a doctorate in economics and had been the outstanding student of his day at Uppsala, kept the talks going by personal correspondence after he left. In 1955 China released all fifteen detained airmen.
real_life_example.explanation: The mission succeeded through a combination of sound judgement, personal standing and deep learning, qualities the Nobel Committee and the UN later credited for what was called his first major victory.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks for an envoy in whom good sense, an impressive presence and tested learning are combined, and Hammarskjold's Peking mission is an example of all three bringing a difficult task to success.

tamil:
தொகச்சொல்லித் தூவாத நீக்கி நகச்சொல்லி
நன்றி பயப்பதாந் தூது.
transliteration:
Thogachchollith thoovaadha neekki nagachcholli
Nandri payappadhaan thoodhu.
meaning: A good envoy sums things up briefly, leaves out harsh words, speaks so pleasantly that people smile, and so brings good to their king.
elementary: If you need to tell a friend they broke your toy, you don’t list every bad thing they ever did. You say it short, you leave out the mean words, and you say it kindly, maybe with a smile. Then they are much more likely to help fix it.
university: Parimelazhagar reads the three verbs as two techniques. Tokac colli is condensing: when many demands must be made, state the one cause from which they all follow, so the other side agrees because the point is short and has to be worked out. Tūvāta nīkki naka colli applies to unwelcome demands: drop the harsh words (veyya col) and put things so pleasantly that the listener agrees without feeling the sting. Both serve naṉṟi payattal, securing benefit for one’s own king. Manakkudavar says the couplet teaches ‘how to speak’. Kalaignar glosses tūvāta as what would provoke anger, and Varadarasanar as what is useless. The couplet repeats the ideals of chapter 65 on speech, applied to diplomacy. On the text: all sources agree; the final தூது follows நன்றி பயப்பதாம் with the m assimilated (பயப்பதாந்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita defines disciplined speech as true, pleasant, helpful, and free of anything that disturbs the listener.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural gives the envoy the same pattern: leave out words that wound, speak pleasantly, and bring benefit.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to speak graciously and aptly to outsiders so that they can answer each person well.
christianity.tie_back: Gracious, well-seasoned speech to outsiders is the envoy’s craft the Kural describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “Go, both of you, to Pharaoh. Indeed, he has transgressed. And speak to him with gentle speech that perhaps he may be reminded or fear [Allah].”
islam.explanation: God sends Moses and Aaron as envoys to a tyrant and tells them to speak gently so that he might listen.
islam.tie_back: Softening a hard message so that a hostile ruler will listen is exactly the Kural’s tūvāta nīkki.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb teaches that patience and gentle speech can persuade a ruler and overcome even the hardest resistance.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s envoy likewise wins over a foreign king with soft words.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says speech with five qualities is well spoken: it is said at the right time, it is true, it is said gently, it is beneficial, and it is said with a mind of goodwill.
buddhism.explanation: Good speech in the Buddha’s teaching is timely, true, gentle and beneficial.
buddhism.tie_back: Gentle and beneficial speech is the Kural’s naka colli … naṉṟi payattal.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Disobedient, rough speaking, ill-behaved pupils will exasperate even a gentle teacher; but those will soon win even a hot-tempered teacher who humour him and are polite.”
jainism.explanation: The verse contrasts rough speech, which alienates even the gentle, with courteous, agreeable speech, which wins over even the irritable.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural's envoy avoids harsh words and speaks pleasantly to win advantage for his master, the Jain text teaches that politeness, not rough speech, wins a superior's goodwill.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are in the Guru Granth Sahib, forbids even one harsh word on the ground that the Lord dwells in every listener.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's true envoy drops harsh words and speaks so pleasantly that listeners agree; Farid's rule against any harsh word gives that diplomatic courtesy a spiritual basis.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon’s offer to Achilles ends with a demand that Achilles yield to him as the more kingly man. When Odysseus repeats the offer to Achilles, he lists the gifts but quietly leaves out that insulting demand.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus edits his king’s message and drops the part that would only anger the hearer, so the offer has a better chance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is tūvāta nīkki, leaving out the harsh words, carried out by Homer’s model envoy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: François de Callières, a French diplomat, advised that a good negotiator should put things agreeably, keep his temper, and never offend a prince with harsh words, because a well-turned phrase wins more than a blunt demand.
philosophy.explanation: Callières’ early handbook of diplomacy treats pleasant, tactful speech as a working tool.
philosophy.tie_back: His advice closely matches the Kural’s envoy, who speaks so as to please while pursuing his master’s gain.
philosophy.source: François de Callières, De la manière de négocier avec les souverains (1716)

real_life_example.event_title: Ralph Bunche negotiates the 1949 armistice agreements on Rhodes
real_life_example.event: After the UN mediator Count Folke Bernadotte was killed in September 1948, his chief aide Ralph Bunche became acting mediator in the Arab-Israeli conflict. Working from the island of Rhodes through eleven months of almost continuous negotiation, he obtained signatures on separate armistice agreements between Israel and the individual Arab states. Time magazine credited the first agreement largely to his ability, patience, tact and unflagging good humour, and in 1950 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
real_life_example.explanation: Bunche kept bitterly opposed parties at the table by tact and humour rather than pressure, and the agreements he secured stood as the framework for nearly two decades.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the envoy who avoids harsh words and speaks so pleasantly that his hearers are won over, and Bunche's tact and good humour at Rhodes are a modern example.

tamil:
கற்றுக்கண் அஞ்சான் செலச்சொல்லிக் காலத்தால்
தக்கது அறிவதாம் தூது.
transliteration:
Katrukkan anjaan selachchollik kaalaththaal
Thakkadhu arivadhaam thoodhu.
meaning: A good envoy is well-learned, is not scared by angry looks, speaks so the message sinks in, and knows what is right for the moment.
elementary: Sometimes when you explain something important, the other person frowns at you. A brave messenger doesn’t run away or start stammering. They keep calm, say it clearly so it is understood, and think about what will work best right then.
university: Parimelazhagar rearranges the clauses: kaṟṟu (having studied the works on polity), cela colli (speaking so the enemy king takes the message to heart), kaṇ añcāṉ (not fearing his glare, ceyirttu nōkku), and kālattāl takkatu aṟivatu (knowing the means suited to the time). He explains why learning comes first: it teaches the means (upāyam), and if the moment calls for another method, the envoy must be able to change course. Manakkudavar gives kaṟṟu a narrower sense, having learned how to calm a foreign king who becomes angry. Pappaiah calls the timely skill a strategic path (tantira vazhi). ‘Kaṇ añcāṉ’ goes back to the Sangam ideal of the unflinching gaze (vaṉkaṇ), which returns in 689. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read காலத்தால் / தக்கது அறிவதாம்; the sandhi-joined text reads கற்றுக்கண் ணஞ்சான் … காலத்தாற் / றக்க தறிவதாந் தூது, the same wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Captured and brought bound before Ravana, Hanuman speaks without fear. He declares himself Rama’s envoy and warns Ravana to return Sita. When Ravana orders his death, Vibhishana objects that an envoy may not be killed.
hinduism.explanation: Hanuman delivers his master’s warning to the face of an enraged king, with learning and nerve.
hinduism.tie_back: He embodies the Kural’s envoy who ‘does not fear the eye’ and makes his words sink in.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel, For which I am an ambassador in bonds: that therein I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.”
christianity.explanation: In prison, Paul calls himself an ‘ambassador in bonds’ and asks for boldness to speak his message as he should.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s bold speech under hostile power is the Kural’s kaṇ añcāṉ, the envoy who does not quail.

islam.quote_or_event: Before the battle of al-Qadisiyya, the Muslim envoy Rib‘i ibn ‘Amir rode into the Persian commander Rustam’s richly carpeted tent. Unimpressed by its splendour, he calmly stated his side’s terms and aims.
islam.explanation: Early histories remember Rib‘i as unafraid of the display and power of the Persian court.
islam.tie_back: He fits the Kural’s envoy who is not cowed by a hostile ruler’s gaze and delivers his message whole.
islam.source: al-Tabari, Tarikh al-rusul wa-l-muluk (History of al-Tabari, vol. 12: The Battle of al-Qadisiyyah)

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Pharaoh said unto him, Get thee from me, take heed to thyself, see my face no more; for in that day thou seest my face thou shalt die. And Moses said, Thou hast spoken well, I will see thy face again no more.”
judaism.explanation: Threatened with death if he appears again, Moses answers Pharaoh calmly and without fear.
judaism.tie_back: Moses does not fear the king’s angry face, which is the Kural’s kaṇ añcāṉ almost word for word.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “They don’t tremble when arriving at an assembly of fierce debaters. … and they don’t tremble when questioned.”
buddhism.explanation: In the verses on the qualified envoy, the Buddha says such a monk is not shaken by a hostile assembly or by hard questions.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Buddhist form of the Kural’s kaṇ añcāṉ: steadiness in front of hostile listeners.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.16, Dūteyya Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Suvega, clinging to his courage though disturbed in mind, got up and left the council-hall, watched by the kings whose eyes were red with anger…”
jainism.explanation: After delivering Bharata's demand, the envoy Suvega leaves Bahubali's court under the furious glares of the princes and bodyguards, keeping hold of his courage.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's envoy 'does not flinch at angry looks'; Suvega delivers his whole message and walks out steady under eyes red with anger.
jainism.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else - says Nanak, listen, mind: call him spiritually wise.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur makes fearlessness, together with not intimidating others, a mark of true wisdom; he himself went to his death in Delhi in 1675 rather than yield.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's envoy does not flinch at angry looks and knows what the moment needs; Guru Tegh Bahadur's ideal is exactly such composed fearlessness grounded in wisdom.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9 (Salok 16), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Priam goes alone to the tent of Achilles, the man who killed his son. He faces Achilles’ temper, kisses his hands, and, choosing his moment and his words, persuades him to give back Hector’s body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Priam, acting as his own envoy, faces a dangerous and angry enemy and wins his request through courage and well-judged speech.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s trio: no fear of the fierce gaze, words that sink in, and a sense of what the moment needs.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At his trial, Socrates refuses to flatter or plead before an angry Athenian jury. He says he would rather die than speak in a way unworthy of himself.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates speaks the truth plainly to a hostile audience and ignores the threat to his life.
philosophy.tie_back: Fearlessness before angry listeners is the Kural’s kaṇ añcāṉ.

real_life_example.event_title: Adlai Stevenson confronts Valerian Zorin at the UN Security Council
real_life_example.place: UN Security Council, New York, United States
real_life_example.event: During the Cuban Missile Crisis, the United States ambassador to the UN, Adlai Stevenson, pressed the Soviet representative Valerian Zorin in an open session of the Security Council to say whether the Soviet Union had placed missiles in Cuba. When Zorin would not answer directly, Stevenson had large reconnaissance photographs of the missile sites displayed to the Council. The JFK Library notes that the normally courteous Stevenson confronted Zorin aggressively that day.
real_life_example.explanation: Stevenson chose the moment and the evidence so that his case reached not only the Soviet delegate but the whole Council and the watching world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks for an envoy who speaks so that his words sink in, who does not flinch under a hostile glare, and who knows what the moment requires, which is what Stevenson did in the Council chamber.

tamil:
கடனறிந்து காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து
எண்ணி உரைப்பான் தலை.
transliteration:
Kadanarindhu kaalang karudhi idanarindhu
Enni uraippaan thalai.
meaning: The best envoy knows their duty, waits for the right time, chooses the right place, and thinks carefully before speaking.
elementary: If you want to ask your parents for a puppy, the smartest way is to wait until they are relaxed, not in the middle of a busy morning. Pick a good spot, and practise what you will say and what they might answer. That is how the best messengers do it.
university: Parimelazhagar glosses kaṭaṉ as the proper conduct toward foreign kings, which comes from weighing their standing, one’s own king’s and one’s own. Kālam is their cevvi, the mood in which they are receptive. Iṭaṉ is a place where one’s supporters are at hand. Eṇṇi means rehearsing in advance one’s own words, the other side’s likely replies, and one’s counter-replies. He says Valluvar chose ‘talai’ (the foremost) because the Sanskrit treatises (vaṭanūlār) rank envoys as first, middle and last, the last being a mere letter-carrier. With this couplet ends the section (681-687) on the envoy who frames his own words (tāṉ vakuttuk kūṟuvāṉ). The following three couplets deal with the envoy who repeats a given message. Manakkudavar likewise calls this the mark of the foremost envoy. On the text: the sandhi-joined text reads கருதி யிடனறிந் / தெண்ணி யுரைப்பான் றலை, the same wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya ranks envoys in three grades: one with full ministerial qualifications who may negotiate on his own judgement (nisṛṣṭārtha), one lacking a quarter of those qualities who is limited to a set commission (parimitārtha), and one lacking half who only carries messages (śāsanahara).
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra grades envoys by how much they may frame the message themselves.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Sanskrit three-grade scheme (talai, iṭai, kaṭai) that Parimelazhagar says Valluvar alludes to with ‘talai’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Sending out his disciples, Jesus tells them to combine shrewd judgement with innocence among hostile hearers.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s foremost envoy is also shrewd about time and place while doing no harm.

islam.quote_or_event: “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the Prophet to deliver his message with wisdom and to argue in the most fitting manner.
islam.tie_back: ‘Wisdom’ and ‘the way that is best’ correspond to the Kural’s careful weighing of duty, moment and manner.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And there was set meat before him to eat: but he said, I will not eat, until I have told mine errand. And he said, Speak on.”
judaism.explanation: Abraham’s servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac, will not eat until he has delivered his mission. He then tells it in a carefully arranged way.
judaism.tie_back: He knows his duty (kaṭaṉ aṟintu) and chooses his moment and words, like the Kural’s foremost envoy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Devadatta split the Sangha and took 500 monks to Gayāsīsa, the Buddha sent Sāriputta and Moggallāna after them. Devadatta invited Sāriputta to teach while he rested and then fell asleep. Sāriputta and Moggallāna took that moment to teach the monks and lead them back.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s two chief disciples, sent as envoys into a hostile assembly, waited for the right time and place before speaking.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s kālam karuti, iṭaṉ aṟintu: choosing the moment and setting before delivering the message.

jainism.quote_or_event: “At the right time a monk should sally forth, and he should return at the right time; avoiding to do anything out of time, he should do what is appropriate for each period of the day.”
jainism.explanation: The discipline lecture asks the monk to do each thing at its proper time and nothing out of season.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's best envoy knows protocol and waits for the right time and place; the Jain rule shares the stress on fitting action to the proper moment.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor. Harsh words bring only grief. Listen, O foolish and ignorant mind!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that speech must be weighed by its effect, since honourable words are accepted and careless or harsh words bring ruin.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's foremost envoy rehearses his words, the other side's replies and his own answers before speaking; Guru Nanak likewise asks that words be judged by what they will bring before they are said.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Shipwrecked and naked, Odysseus wonders whether to clasp the princess Nausicaa’s knees or to plead from a distance with gentle words. He decides to stand apart and speak, so as not to anger her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows Odysseus weighing place, manner and words before speaking to someone whose help he needs.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s eṇṇi uraippāṉ: the speaker who thinks through where and how to speak before he opens his mouth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates tells Phaedrus that a true speaker must first learn the different kinds of soul and which kinds of speech persuade each. He must then be able to recognise them quickly in real life, and must add to this a knowledge of the right times for speaking and for keeping silent before his art is complete.
philosophy.explanation: In the closing discussion of rhetoric, Plato makes knowledge of the listener, together with a sense of the right moment (kairos) for each kind of speech, a condition of any real art of persuasion.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato's speaker, like the Kural's ideal envoy, must judge the audience and the moment before choosing his words.

real_life_example.event_title: John Adams presents his credentials to King George III
real_life_example.event: John Adams, the first United States minister to Britain, presented his credentials to King George III less than a week after arriving in London, following eight years of war between the two countries. The audience followed the formal ceremony of the royal court, and Adams delivered a short address he had rehearsed and committed to memory, assuring the King of his country's wish for friendly relations. He reported the exchange, including the King's reply, to John Jay the next day.
real_life_example.explanation: Adams treated a delicate first meeting between former enemies with careful attention to court protocol and prepared words, and the King answered in kind.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes the best envoy as one who knows the proper protocol, chooses the right moment and place, and thinks his words through before speaking, as Adams did before George III.

tamil:
தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றின்
வாய்மை வழியுரைப்பான் பண்பு.
transliteration:
Thooymai thunaimai thunivudaimai immoondrin
Vaaymai vazhiyuraippaan panbu.
meaning: A person who carries the king's message exactly as given must be honest and clean, have good helpers, be brave, and above all tell the truth.
elementary: When your teacher gives you a note for your parents, you shouldn’t swap the words for a treat, you should have a grown-up nearby who can help, you should be brave enough to deliver it even if it’s bad news, and you must never change what it says.
university: From here Parimelazhagar turns to the second kind of envoy, the vazhi uraippāṉ, who repeats his king’s words exactly as spoken. He gives each quality a job. Tūymai is purity from greed for wealth or women (poruḷ kāmaṅkaḷ), so bribes cannot bend the message. Tuṇaimai is having the foreign ministers’ support, so that if the envoy’s praise of his own king angers them, they can smooth it over by saying ‘that is how our people speak’. Tuṇivuṭaimai is boldness, so he does not hold back out of fear of harm. Vāymai is truthfulness, so everyone can trust him. He reads ‘immūṉṟiṉ’ with the -iṉ in the sense of ‘together with’: truthfulness is a fourth quality alongside the three. Manakkudavar differs: tuṇaimai is having kin, tuṇivu is resolving after inquiry. Pappaiah follows Parimelazhagar closely. On the text: all sources agree; the sandhi-joined text writes யிம்மூன்றின்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the war, Dhritarashtra sends his charioteer Sanjaya to the Pandavas. Sanjaya is trusted on both sides for his honesty. He delivers the king’s message and carries Yudhishthira’s reply faithfully back to the Kaurava court.
hinduism.explanation: Sanjaya is a messenger valued above all for integrity and accurate reporting.
hinduism.tie_back: He fits the Kural’s vazhi uraippāṉ, the envoy whose purity and truthfulness make him trusted by both courts.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Sanjaya-yana sections (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.”
christianity.explanation: Paul insists that he passes on the message entrusted to him without falsifying it, and wins trust through truthfulness.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s tūymai and vāymai: a messenger who does not tamper with what he was given.

islam.quote_or_event: At al-Hudaybiyya, the Prophet chose ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan as envoy to the Quraysh partly because his clan in Mecca could protect him. A kinsman there gave him protection while he delivered the message.
islam.explanation: The envoy was picked in part because he had allies in the other camp.
islam.tie_back: This is Parimelazhagar’s tuṇaimai: supporters at the foreign court who keep the envoy safe and the talks smooth.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (trans. A. Guillaume), account of al-Hudaybiyya

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wicked messenger falleth into mischief: but a faithful ambassador is health.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb contrasts the damage a corrupt messenger causes with the good a faithful envoy brings.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too makes faithfulness and purity the envoy’s defining traits.

buddhism.quote_or_event: King Ajātasattu sends his minister Vassakāra to the Buddha with instructions to repeat his question exactly and bring back exactly what the Buddha says, since Tathāgatas do not speak falsely. Vassakāra does both.
buddhism.explanation: The minister acts as a word-for-word envoy between the king and the Buddha.
buddhism.tie_back: He is a clear example of the Kural’s vazhi uraippāṉ, the one who carries a message exactly as given.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk should avoid untruth, nor should he speak positively (about future things, his plans, &c.); he should avoid sinful speech, and always keep free from deceit.”
jainism.explanation: The sutra requires truthful, guileless speech free of deceit from the monk.
jainism.tie_back: Of the Kural's four qualities for the envoy who repeats his king's words (purity, support, boldness, truthfulness), the Jain verse supports the truthfulness and freedom from deceit.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: After the battle of Chamkaur (1704), Guru Gobind Singh would not trust Mughal couriers with his Zafarnama, a letter rebuking Aurangzeb for breaking his oath of safe passage, so he sent his own Sikhs, Bhai Daya Singh and Bhai Dharam Singh, to carry it to the emperor personally.
sikhism.explanation: The Guru chose envoys whose loyalty and courage he could rely on to deliver a bold, unwelcome message exactly as written, into the hands of a hostile emperor.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's envoy who carries his master's message unchanged must be incorruptible, bold and truthful; Daya Singh and Dharam Singh were chosen precisely because they could be trusted to deliver the Guru's words intact.
sikhism.source: Wikipedia, Zafarnama (letter), citing Isher Singh Nara and Louis E. Fenech

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Answering the embassy, Achilles says he hates like the gates of Hades the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another, and that he will therefore speak plainly.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles demands transparent truthfulness in the envoys’ exchange and practises it himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His ideal is the Kural’s vāymai, truthfulness joined to boldness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Harold Nicolson named truthfulness the first quality of the ideal diplomat, followed by precision, calm, good temper, patience, modesty and loyalty. He argued that a negotiator’s lasting credit rests on never deceiving.
philosophy.explanation: A twentieth-century diplomat’s classic study puts moral reliability at the centre of the envoy’s craft.
philosophy.tie_back: Nicolson’s truthfulness and loyalty match the Kural’s vāymai and tūymai.

real_life_example.event_title: American envoys refuse the bribe demanded in the XYZ Affair
real_life_example.event: President John Adams sent Charles Cotesworth Pinckney, John Marshall and Elbridge Gerry to France to restore relations and protect American shipping. Intermediaries for the French foreign minister Talleyrand told them that negotiations would require a large loan to France and a personal bribe for Talleyrand. The envoys refused, Pinckney and Marshall prepared to leave, and when their dispatches were published in 1798 with the French agents' names replaced by the letters X, Y and Z, the demand caused a public outcry.
real_life_example.explanation: The envoys would not let money bend their mission and reported exactly what had happened, even though it meant failing to reach an agreement.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks of the envoy who carries his master's message a purity that bribes cannot touch, boldness and truthfulness, all of which the American commissioners showed in Paris.

tamil:
விடுமாற்றம் வேந்தர்க்கு உரைப்பான் வடுமாற்றம்
வாய்சேரா வன்க ணவன்.
transliteration:
Vidumaatram vendharkku uraippaan vadumaatram
Vaaysera vankanavan.
meaning: Only a person strong enough never to let a shameful word slip out should carry their king's message to other kings.
elementary: Suppose you are sent to tell a bigger kid that your friend wants his bike back. If the big kid scares you, it’s tempting to say ‘my friend is silly, never mind’. A good messenger stays strong and never says something that makes the person who sent him look bad.
university: Viṭu māṟṟam is ‘the word sent’, the king’s message. Vaṭu māṟṟam is ‘a word that scars’. Parimelazhagar explains this as words that lower one’s own king, which the envoy might say out of fear of harm to himself. Vaṉkaṇ is the firmness never to let such words out, even by a slip of the tongue (vāy cōrntum). He says ‘vaṭu’ (a scar) was chosen because such lowering goes against the duty of one’s station (cāti tarumam). He also notes that ‘vāy cērā’ expresses the result (not speaking) through its cause (firmness). Manakkudavar calls the quality añcāmai, fearlessness. Pappaiah and Kalaignar stress not saying anything wrong or demeaning when danger threatens. On the text: ytamizh.com prints the couplet without a final stop; thirukkural.net and the sandhi-joined text have வன்க ணவன். in the metrical division; thirukkuralvilakkam.blogspot.com joins it as வன்கணவன். Some editions give வாய்சோரா for வாய்சேரா (Parimelazhagar’s gloss uses ‘வாய்சோர்ந்தும்’), but the sources consulted read வாய்சேரா.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya tells the envoy to deliver his king’s message exactly as entrusted, even if weapons are raised against him, and to bear whatever the enemy says without betraying his master. Because envoys are the mouthpieces of kings, they are not to be killed.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra makes faithful, unflinching delivery the envoy’s first duty under threat.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s vaṉkaṇ: the firmness that keeps a message intact and free of any disgrace to the king under pressure.

christianity.quote_or_event: Frightened in the high priest’s courtyard, Peter denies three times that he knows Jesus. When the cock crows he remembers Jesus’ words and weeps bitterly.
christianity.explanation: Under fear, the chief disciple says words that dishonour the master he represents, and he bitterly regrets it.
christianity.tie_back: It is a warning example of the Kural’s vaṭu māṟṟam, the shameful word that slips out when firmness fails.

islam.quote_or_event: “What do you believe yourselves? They said: We believe as he believes. He said: I swear by Allah that were it not that messengers are not killed, I would cut off your heads.”
islam.explanation: Musaylimah’s envoys stand by their master’s claim even in front of the Prophet, and the Prophet spares them because envoys are not to be killed.
islam.tie_back: They do not back away from their sender’s message under pressure. This is the Kural’s firmness, though the cause they served was rejected.

judaism.quote_or_event: Avtalyon warns scholars to be careful with their words. A careless phrase could lead students into error, and in the end the name of Heaven would be profaned.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that a representative’s careless words bring disgrace on the one he represents.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s envoy must likewise never let slip a word that stains the name of the king who sent him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Prince Abhaya that he never speaks words that are untrue or unbeneficial. Even true and beneficial words he speaks only when he knows the time is right, whether or not they are welcome.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha keeps strict control over what leaves his mouth, weighing truth, benefit and timing.
buddhism.tie_back: This kind of self-mastery in speech is what keeps the Kural’s envoy from letting a harmful word slip.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Well done! You alone, messenger, are the first of the eloquent since you are able to utter such a speech before me.”
jainism.explanation: Bahubali, angered by Bharata's demand, still admits that Suvega delivered his master's message in full and with force, without softening it out of fear.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks for an envoy firm enough never to let slip a word that lowers his king; Suvega speaks for Bharata's supremacy in a hostile court, and even his opponent grants his firmness.
jainism.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Summoned by Aurangzeb, Guru Har Rai sent his son Ram Rai to represent him; when the emperor objected to a line of the Adi Granth as disparaging to Muslims, Ram Rai tried to appease him by claiming it had been wrongly transcribed, and Guru Har Rai excommunicated him for it and passed him over for the succession.
sikhism.explanation: Sikh history remembers Ram Rai as the envoy who, under pressure at a foreign court, let slip words that lowered his own Guru's scripture, and was cast off for it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says only one firm enough never to let a shameful word slip out under pressure is fit to carry his master's message to other kings; Ram Rai is the exact counter-example, and the Guru's response shows how seriously the fault was judged.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Guru Har Rai

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Trojan herald Idaeus brings Paris’s offer to the Greek camp. While delivering it, he adds his own wish that Paris had died before causing all this.
greek_mythology.explanation: Idaeus lets words slip that shame the side he represents while he is delivering their official message.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the envoy the Kural rules out: one who lets a vaṭu māṟṟam, a disgraceful word, pass his lips.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But I thought that I ought not to do anything common or mean in the hour of danger: nor do I now repent of the manner of my defence, and I would rather die having spoken after my manner, than speak in your manner and live.”
philosophy.explanation: After being condemned, Socrates explains why he would not weep, plead or bring his children into court to win pity, saying that he would rather die than save himself with words unworthy of him.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's envoy, Socrates holds that no pressure, even the threat of death, should force a shameful word from a man of firm character.

real_life_example.event_title: Busbecq holds firm through years of confinement at Suleiman's court
real_life_example.event: Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, envoy of the Habsburg ruler Ferdinand I to Sultan Suleiman, presented demands at his first audience that he described as full of dignity and independence, and the Sultan received them coldly. On his second mission he and his staff were confined to their lodgings and treated almost as prisoners, and when his colleagues were allowed to leave in 1557 he chose to stay, judging that his departure would signal the end of talks and make war more likely. In 1562 he concluded a truce acceptable to both sides and returned to Vienna.
real_life_example.explanation: Under years of pressure and confinement, Busbecq neither abandoned his post nor gave way on his master's position, and his patience finally produced peace terms.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says only an envoy firm enough never to let a word that lowers his king slip out under pressure is fit to carry his message, and Busbecq's steadiness in Constantinople fits that demand.

tamil:
இறுதி பயப்பினும் எஞ்சாது இறைவற்கு
உறுதி பயப்பதாம் தூது.
transliteration:
Irudhi payappinum enjaadhu iraivarku
Urudhi payappadhaam thoodhu.
meaning: A true envoy delivers the king's whole message and works for the king's good, holding nothing back, even if it costs the envoy their life.
elementary: Think of a lifeguard who swims out to someone in trouble even though the waves are scary. A true messenger is like that. Even when delivering the message is frightening or dangerous, they carry it all the way for the people who trusted them.
university: Iṟuti is ‘end’, meaning death. Eñcātu is ‘without leaving any of it out’. Uṟuti is ‘firm good’ or advantage. Parimelazhagar: even if the words will end the envoy’s life, he does not hold back out of fear, and he speaks his king’s position to foreign kings exactly as told. He adds that by naming death, the worst outcome, Valluvar leaves lesser dangers without need of mention. With 688-690 the chapter completes its account of the envoy who repeats a given message (kūṟiyatu kūṟuvāṉ). The couplet ends the chapter on its highest demand, loyalty to the death, and prepares for chapter 70 on conduct in the king’s presence. All modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read iṟuti as the envoy’s own death. On the text: the sandhi-joined text reads பயப்பினு மெஞ்சா திறைவற் / குறுதி, the same wording as the split form.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sent by Rama to Ravana with a final ultimatum, Angada delivers it in full in the demon king’s own court. When Ravana orders him seized, Angada leaps onto the palace roof carrying his captors and breaks its peak before returning.
hinduism.explanation: Angada carries his master’s ultimatum into the enemy’s hall and gives all of it, knowing he may be killed.
hinduism.tie_back: He fits the Kural’s envoy who holds nothing back even when the embassy may cost his life.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.”
christianity.explanation: Warned that chains await him, Paul says his life matters less than finishing the commission he was given.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s iṟuti payappiṉum eñcātu: carrying out the commission even at the cost of one’s life.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet’s envoy al-Harith ibn ‘Umayr al-Azdi, carrying a letter to the ruler of Busra, was seized and killed by the Ghassanid chief Shurahbil ibn ‘Amr. The killing of this envoy led to the expedition of Mu’ta.
islam.explanation: The sira remembers an envoy who died carrying his master’s letter, and treats killing him as a grave violation.
islam.tie_back: It makes real the Kural’s case in which the embassy ‘yields death’ (iṟuti payappiṉum).
islam.source: al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Maghazi; Ibn Sa‘d, Tabaqat (account of Mu’ta)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me … and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.”
judaism.explanation: Esther goes before the Persian king uninvited to plead for her people, knowing it could mean death.
judaism.tie_back: ‘If I perish, I perish’ is the spirit of the Kural’s envoy, who does not hold back though death may follow.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Before going to teach among the fierce people of Sunāparanta, the monk Puṇṇa tells the Buddha how he will meet each threat, including being killed, without resentment. The Buddha then sends him, and he wins many followers there.
buddhism.explanation: Puṇṇa accepts that his mission may end in his death and goes anyway.
buddhism.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s envoy who does not turn back even when the mission may end his life.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Suvega proceeded, even though knowing these signs unfavorable. Good servants of a master do not falter anywhere, like an arrow.”
jainism.explanation: On the road to Takshashila the envoy meets a string of evil omens yet goes on, and the narrator praises the servant who does not falter in his master's business.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's true envoy delivers his king's message even if it costs him his life; Suvega presses on despite the omens and then speaks his message in a court ready to kill him.
jainism.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak makes readiness to give one's life the condition for entering the path of devotion, a line later embodied in the Sikh martyr tradition.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's true envoy delivers his king's message in full even if it costs him his life; Guru Nanak asks the same readiness to lay down one's head for one's Master.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Sparta killed Persian heralds, two Spartan nobles, Sperthias and Boulis, volunteered to go to Xerxes and give their lives in atonement. Xerxes refused to kill them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tradition held heralds sacred under Hermes, and these envoys went knowingly to their deaths for their city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s envoy, they carried out their mission for their state knowing it would probably kill them.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero tells how Marcus Atilius Regulus, a captive of Carthage, was sent to Rome on oath to negotiate a prisoner exchange. He advised the Senate against it because it harmed Rome, then kept his oath and went back to Carthage to be tortured to death.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero holds Regulus up as the model of an envoy who puts his country’s good and his given word above his life.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s envoy almost exactly: he secures his country’s good (uṟuti) though his own death (iṟuti) follows.

real_life_example.event_title: Zhang Qian completes his mission to the Yuezhi after years of captivity
real_life_example.event: The Han emperor Wudi sent Zhang Qian to seek an alliance with the Yuezhi against the Xiongnu. Zhang was captured by the Xiongnu and held for about ten years, but escaped and continued westward until he reached the Yuezhi in the region of Bactria, then was captured again on his return journey. He finally got back to the court after an absence of about thirteen years and gave the emperor a detailed report on the lands he had seen.
real_life_example.explanation: Although the alliance he sought was refused, Zhang Qian carried his mission through at great personal risk and his full report opened Han China's contacts with Central Asia.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the envoy who fulfils his king's charge to the end even at the risk of his life, and Zhang Qian persisted through two captivities to complete and report on his mission.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tamil:
அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க
இகல்வேந்தர்ச் சேர்ந்தொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Akalaadhu anukaadhu theekkaaivaar polka
Ikalvendharch serndhozhuku vaar.
meaning: People who serve kings who are quick to anger should act like people warming themselves by a fire. They should not go too far away or too close.
elementary: On a cold night you sit near a campfire. Too far away and you shiver; too close and you get burned. Being around a very powerful person is the same: stay close enough to be useful, but never so close that you get burned.
university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of how the minister or courtier (the Amaichiyal section) is to conduct himself with the ruler, and its governing image is the fire (thee) at which one warms oneself (theekkaaivaar). The paired negatives akalaadhu (not withdrawing) and anukaadhu (not approaching) define a calibrated middle distance rather than a fixed rule. Parimelazhagar reads ikalvendhar as kings whose temper easily turns to hostility (ikal = enmity, variance), so the danger is not the king’s wickedness but his volatility: the same fire that warms can burn. The simile closely parallels Kautilya (Arthashastra 5.4), who likens royal service to life in fire, and Dhaumya’s counsel in the Mahabharata that the king is a great fire. The traditional sandhi text reads “அகலா தணுகாது” and “விகல்வேந்தர்”, which divide into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “To dwell with a king is, alas, difficult. ... the king, who is a deity in an embodied form, is as a great fire sanctified with all the mantras.”
hinduism.explanation: Before the Pandavas go into hiding as servants at King Virata’s court, the priest Dhaumya warns them that living near a king is hard, and he compares the king to a great sacred fire.
hinduism.tie_back: Dhaumya and Valluvar use the same image, the king as a fire, to teach the same thing: approach carefully.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Section 4 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him ... But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells guests not to grab the seat nearest the host, because they may be moved down in shame. It is better to be invited closer.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it teaches that pushing too close to the powerful backfires, and that the right nearness is the one you are invited to.

islam.quote_or_event: “He who lives in the desert will become rude; he who pursues the game will be negligent, and he who visits a king will be perverted.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that going to the court of a ruler puts a person’s integrity at risk, because being near power tempts and tests people.
islam.tie_back: The hadith names the burn that the Kural’s fire image warns about: getting too close to rulers is dangerous.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 2859 (graded sahih by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be careful [in your dealings] with the ruling authorities for they do not befriend a person except for their own needs; they seem like friends when it is to their own interest, but they do not stand by a man in the hour of his distress.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel warns that rulers act friendly when it helps them and drop you when it does not, so deal with them warily.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same careful middle distance the Kural asks for. Rulers can be useful, but you cannot safely get close to them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let him prudently keep not too far from the king nor yet too near to him, and let him stand ready before him, telling something for his lord to hear.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Vidhurapandita Jataka, the wise minister Vidhura teaches his family the rules for living at a king’s court, and this is one of them.
buddhism.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s own wording: not too far and not too near.
buddhism.source: Vidhurapandita Jataka (Ja 545), v. 154, The King’s Court (Rājavasati) section

jainism.quote_or_event: “A well-behaved monk should not sit on his hams, nor cross his arms, nor stretch out his legs, nor stand (too) close to his teacher.”
jainism.explanation: The discipline lecture sets out how a disciple keeps a respectful distance and posture before his teacher; a nearby verse (1.34) similarly has the monk stand 'neither too close by nor too far off' when receiving alms.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural pictures courtiers keeping a measured distance from the king, like people warming themselves at a fire; the Jain rule likewise asks for a measured, respectful distance before a superior.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.19 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The kings are tigers, and their officials are dogs; they go out and awaken the sleeping people to harass them.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the rulers and officials of his day as predators whose power falls unpredictably on ordinary people.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that changeable, powerful kings must be approached like a fire, neither too near nor too far; Guru Nanak's tigers make the same point about the danger of royal power, though from the side of its victims.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar, Malaar ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus fits wings to his son Icarus and tells him to fly a middle course: too low and the sea spray will soak the feathers, too high and the sun will melt the wax. Icarus, excited, soars toward the sun and falls into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows that safety lies in a middle distance, and that being carried too close to a blazing power ends in disaster.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Icarus flying at the sun is the mythic version of the courtier who comes too near the fire.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Self-protection shall be the first and constant thought of a wise man; for the life of a man under the service of a king is aptly compared to life in fire.”
philosophy.explanation: Kautilya ends his chapter on a courtier’s conduct by saying that serving a king is like living in fire. Fire burns only the body, but a king can ruin or raise a servant’s whole family.
philosophy.tie_back: Kautilya and Valluvar build their advice on the same metaphor of royal service as fire.
philosophy.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 5.4, The Conduct of a Courtier (trans. R. Shamasastry)

real_life_example.event_title: Voltaire at the court of Frederick the Great
real_life_example.place: Berlin and Potsdam, Prussia (now Germany); Frankfurt
real_life_example.event: After years of admiring correspondence, Voltaire accepted Frederick II's pressing invitation and set out for Berlin on 28 June 1750, at first enchanted by life at the Prussian court in Berlin and Potsdam. Difficulties soon arose, and when he ridiculed Maupertuis, president of Frederick's Berlin Academy, in the pamphlet Diatribe du docteur Akakia (1752), the enraged king had it burned and gave its author a thorough dressing down. Voltaire left Prussia on 26 March 1753 and, on the journey home, was held under house arrest at an inn in Frankfurt by order of the Prussian resident.
real_life_example.explanation: The greatest writer of the age moved from flattering distance into the king's daily circle, and the very closeness that warmed him exposed him to the royal temper.
real_life_example.tie_back: Voltaire found that a powerful and changeable king is like a fire: welcome at a respectful distance, but scorching to one who settles too close and takes liberties beside it.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tamil:
மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை மன்னரால்
மன்னிய ஆக்கந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Mannar vizhaipa vizhaiyaamai mannaraal
Manniya aakkam tharum.
meaning: If you do not want the things the king himself wants, the king will give you success that lasts.
elementary: Picture a class helper who never tries to grab the teacher’s special chair or the teacher’s favourite pen. Because the teacher never has to worry about that helper, the teacher trusts them more and more. Not wanting what belongs to the boss is how you earn lasting trust.
university: The couplet turns on the repeated root vizhai (to desire): the servant must not desire (vizhaiyaamai) what the kings desire (mannar vizhaipa). Parimelazhagar takes the objects to be the king’s own enjoyments, such as his ornaments, pleasures and women, which a courtier must never share or rival. Mu. Varadarasanar instead reads “those whom the king favours”, meaning one should not compete for the king’s favourites. Either way, the reward is manniya aakkam, prosperity that lasts (manniya = enduring), and it comes through the king himself (mannaraal). The play on mannar/manniya is typical of Valluvar’s sound patterning. The older text in thirukkural-thamizh.org reads மன்னரான் for மன்னரால், a dialectal instrumental ending with the same meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bharata refuses the throne his mother schemed to win for him. He goes to the forest to bring back his brother Rama, and when Rama will not return he rules only as regent, with Rama’s sandals placed on the throne.
hinduism.explanation: Bharata will not claim anything that belongs to the rightful king, even when it is handed to him, and he is remembered with lasting honour for it.
hinduism.tie_back: Bharata shows the Kural’s rule in its purest form: he refuses to desire what is the king’s, and that refusal secures his enduring standing.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Bharata and the padukas)

christianity.quote_or_event: “When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee: And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite. Be not desirous of his dainties: for they are deceitful meat.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb tells someone eating at a ruler’s table to hold back and not crave the ruler’s luxuries, because they are a trap.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts tell the courtier not to desire the ruler’s own delights.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not extend your eyes toward that by which We have given enjoyment to [some] categories of them, [its being but] the splendor of worldly life by which We test them. And the provision of your Lord is better and more enduring.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells believers not to gaze longingly at the luxuries of the powerful, because those are a test. What God provides is better and lasts longer.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sets not coveting the splendour of the great against a more enduring reward.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Love work, hate acting the superior, and do not attempt to draw near to the ruling authority.”
judaism.explanation: Shemaiah teaches that one should work honestly, dislike playing the lord, and not court the government.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Hate acting the superior’ is close to the Kural’s point: do not want the powers and pleasures that belong to the ruler.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let him on no account ever enjoy the same pleasures as the king, let him follow behind in everything, such a one may dwell in a king’s court.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura’s rules for courtiers forbid enjoying what the king enjoys. The courtier is always to stay a step behind the king.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s rule almost exactly: do not desire the king’s own pleasures.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Not resentful, having few wants, begging from strangers, and not being dainty, a wise man should not long for pleasant things, nor be sorry afterwards (for not having got them).”
jainism.explanation: In the trouble of 'respectful treatment', the monk is told to want little and not to long for pleasant things.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural advises the courtier not to covet what the king desires; the Jain verse teaches a more general freedom from craving pleasant things, which would keep one from coveting a ruler's enjoyments.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak makes coveting and taking what is another's due as abhorrent as the gravest taboo of one's own faith.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the servant not to covet what the king himself desires; Guru Nanak's rule against taking what belongs to another covers that case as a general principle.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The courtier Damocles praised the wealth of the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse, so Dionysius let him enjoy it for a day. Damocles sat among golden dishes and perfumes, but a sword hung above his head by a single horsehair, and he soon begged to leave.
greek_mythology.explanation: The courtier envied his ruler’s luxury, was given a taste of it, and found out what danger came with it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural tells the servant not to desire the king’s things. Damocles is the classic courtier who did, and learned why.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus says that an invitation to a great man’s dinner is sold at a price, namely flattery and attendance. If you are unwilling to pay it, you should not complain about going without the dinner, because you still have not had to flatter.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic teaches that the privileges of the powerful always come with a price, and that a free person can simply decline to want them.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Epictetus asks us to stop wanting the great man’s goods, although for him the reward is inner freedom rather than royal favour.

real_life_example.event_title: Belisarius refuses the crown the Goths offered him at Ravenna
real_life_example.event: By 540 the hard-pressed Ostrogoths in Italy offered to surrender to the Byzantine general Belisarius if he would rule over them as emperor. Belisarius, who served the emperor Justinian, dissembled: he accepted the Goths' capitulation at Ravenna and then refused the title, claiming the kingdom and its treasury in Justinian's name. Justinian, who had already come to fear that so popular a commander might aim at his throne, recalled him from Italy.
real_life_example.explanation: The one prize a ruler most jealously guards is his own crown, and Belisarius pointedly declined to reach for it even when it was offered to him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises the servant not to covet what the king himself desires, and Belisarius turned down the very throne that Justinian held dear.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tamil:
போற்றின் அரியவை போற்றல் கடுத்தபின்
தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது.
transliteration:
Potrin ariyavai potral kaduththapin
Thetrudhal yaarkkum aridhu.
meaning: If you want to stay safe, avoid serious mistakes. Once the king becomes suspicious of you, no one can make him trust you again.
elementary: A glass vase with a crack can be glued, but you can always see the crack. Trust works the same way. It is much easier to be careful and never break it than to try to fix it after someone starts to doubt you.
university: The first line plays on potru (to guard, to preserve): potrin (if you would guard [yourself]) and potral (guard against). Ariyavai are, in Parimelazhagar’s gloss, grave faults the king will find hard to pardon. The key word is kaduththal, to suspect or to be incensed, and the second line states the psychology bluntly: once suspicion has formed, thetrudhal (reassuring or convincing) is difficult for anyone (yaarkkum). The Kural’s wider theory of trust helps here. Chapter 51 (Therindhu Thelidhal) warns the king against doubting a servant he has tested, so this couplet gives the courtier’s side of the same danger. The sandhi text in older editions runs “போற்றி னரியவை” and “றேற்றுதல் யார்க்கு மரிது.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra’s first book, the jackal Damanaka poisons the friendship between the lion-king Pingalaka and his trusted minister, the bull Sanjivaka, by whispering suspicions to each of them. Once the lion suspects the bull, nothing can undo it, and Sanjivaka is killed.
hinduism.explanation: The frame story of ‘The Loss of Friends’ shows how quickly a ruler’s suspicion, once planted, destroys even a favoured servant.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s warning played out: after suspicion arises, reassurance is almost impossible.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book I (Mitrabheda), frame story of Pingalaka and Sanjivaka

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then the presidents and princes sought to find occasion against Daniel concerning the kingdom; but they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him.”
christianity.explanation: At the Persian court, Daniel’s jealous rivals search for a fault to use against him and cannot find one, because he has been careful and faithful.
christianity.tie_back: Daniel lives out the Kural’s first line: guard against faults so that suspicion has nothing to hold on to.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the king said, ‘Bring him to me.’ But when the messenger came to him, [Joseph] said, ‘Return to your master and ask him what is the case of the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plan.’”
islam.explanation: Joseph has been imprisoned under suspicion. When the king summons him, he refuses to leave until the king has formally investigated the accusation and cleared his name.
islam.tie_back: Joseph knows the Kural’s truth: suspicion at court does not fade by itself, so a full clearing is needed before he can safely serve.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place; for yielding pacifieth great offences.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet advises that when a ruler turns angry with you, you should stay calm at your post and yield, because only calm submission soothes great offences.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see how hard it is to recover once a ruler’s mind turns against you. Kohelet gives the remedy, the Kural the prevention.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let not the wise man, thinking himself to be held in honour, ever venture to speak roughly to the suspicious king.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura warns that kings are naturally suspicious, so a courtier must never give offence, even when he feels secure.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts treat the king’s suspicion as a hazard that the courtier must avoid provoking in the first place.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A weak point in one's lord, even though small, must be guarded against. By means of a hole even small, water destroys a dam.”
jainism.explanation: Suvega warns Bahubali that failing to wait on his elder brother leaves room for informers to poison the king's mind, and that even a small breach in the lord's trust must be guarded against.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that once a king grows suspicious no one can calm him; the Jain narrative likewise says even a small fault in the ruler's eyes must be guarded against before it bursts the dam.
jainism.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Why do you do such evil deeds, that you shall have to suffer so? Do not do any evil at all; look ahead to the future with foresight.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa ki Vaar Guru Nanak warns against any deed whose consequences one will later have to bear, urging foresight before acting.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural advises guarding against grave faults because a ruler's suspicion, once roused, cannot be undone; Guru Nanak likewise counsels avoiding wrong entirely by looking ahead to its consequences.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (Pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the court of King Proetus, the queen falsely accuses the young hero Bellerophon. Proetus believes her and sends Bellerophon away with a sealed tablet asking the king of Lycia to kill him. Bellerophon has to survive monsters and ambushes before he is trusted again.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s story shows how a single suspicion at court can turn a king against a guest and set off a long ordeal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Proetus’s suspicion, once formed, could not be talked away, which is exactly the Kural’s warning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells of a man who had grown old in the service of kings. Asked how he had managed something so rare at court, he replied that it was by accepting injuries and thanking the king for them.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman Stoic uses the anecdote to show how precarious life at a royal court is, where one misstep or show of resentment can be fatal.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts assume that a ruler’s displeasure, once aroused, is almost impossible to undo, so survival means never provoking it.

real_life_example.event_title: Naser al-Din Shah turns against his reforming minister Amir Kabir
real_life_example.event: Mirza Taqi Khan, known as Amir Kabir, helped secure the throne for the young Naser al-Din Shah in 1848 and as chief minister launched sweeping reforms, including the founding of the Dar al-Fonun college. His reforms antagonized excluded notables, who formed a coalition against him in which the queen mother was active, and she convinced the young shah that the minister wanted to usurp the throne. In the autumn of 1851 the shah dismissed him and exiled him to Kashan, where he was put to death on the shah's orders in January 1852.
real_life_example.explanation: The minister's record of service and even his marriage to the shah's sister could not undo the suspicion once it had been planted in the ruler's mind.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that once a king has grown suspicious, no one can set his mind at rest, and no past loyalty saved Amir Kabir once the shah came to believe he sought the throne.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tamil:
செவிச்சொல்லும் சேர்ந்த நகையும் அவித்தொழுகல்
ஆன்ற பெரியா ரகத்து.
transliteration:
Sevichchollum serndha nakaiyum aviththozhukal
Aandra periyaar akaththu.
meaning: When you are with great and powerful people, do not whisper in someone's ear or share a secret smile with anyone.
elementary: Imagine you are speaking to the class and two children in the front row start whispering and giggling. You would wonder whether they were laughing at you. That is why, around important people, you should not whisper or trade secret smiles.
university: Sevichchol is literally ‘ear-speech’, words whispered into another person’s ear, and serndha nakai is ‘joined laughter’, a smile or glance shared with someone else. Solomon Pappaiah glosses it as winking and smiling while looking at another’s face. The verb avi (to extinguish or suppress) asks the courtier to put out these impulses altogether. Aandra periyaar are ‘the great ones who are complete in power’, which Parimelazhagar takes as kings. The rule rests on the suspicion theme of the previous couplet: private signals between courtiers look to a ruler like conspiracy or mockery. Kautilya’s Arthashastra 5.4 lists almost the same prohibitions, secret talk with another in the assembly and loud laughter without cause. The older text reads “செவிச்சொல்லுஞ் சேர்ந்த நகையு மவித்தொழுக / லான்ற பெரியா ரகத்து.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In the presence of even laughable objects, a man should not break out into loud laughter, like a maniac; nor should one show (unreasonable) gravity by containing himself, to the utmost. One should smile modestly, to show his interest.”
hinduism.explanation: Dhaumya teaches the Pandavas to control their laughter at court: neither laughing wildly nor standing stiff, but smiling modestly.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat uncontrolled laughter in the ruler’s presence as a breach of the courtier’s discipline.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Section 4 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers,”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists ‘whisperers’, people who spread talk behind others’ backs, among the vices of a corrupt society.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural bans ear-whispering before great persons, and Paul counts whispering itself as a vice.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, when you converse privately, do not converse about sin and aggression and disobedience to the Messenger but converse about righteousness and piety.”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Mujadila addresses the private conversations (najwa) that some people held in the Prophet’s community, which hurt others and bred suspicion.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Quran treats private whispering in the leader’s circle as a source of harm and mistrust.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet warns that even private talk about the king has a way of reaching him.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural forbids whispers in the king’s presence because whispers always look suspicious and seldom stay secret.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let him not laugh too much, nor keep always silent; he should utter, when the due season comes, a concise and measured speech.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura teaches that a courtier should keep his laughter and speech measured.
