buddhism.tie_back: Both texts ask the servant to rein in laughter and loose talk before the king.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One should always be meek, and not be talkative in the presence of the wise; one should acquire valuable knowledge, and avoid what is worthless.”
jainism.explanation: The sutra asks for meek, restrained behaviour and little talk in the presence of superiors; Uttaradhyayana 11.4 also lists 'not to be fond of mirth' as part of discipline.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural forbids whispering and shared laughter in the presence of the great; the Jain rule asks for quiet, restrained conduct before one's superiors.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “It is not good to slander anyone, but the foolish, self-willed manmukhs still do it.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das condemns slander and talk behind others' backs as the habit of the self-willed (manmukh).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural forbids whispering in another's ear or sharing private smiles in the presence of the great; Gurbani's ban on backbiting covers the moral side of such whispering, though not its court etiquette.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 755, Raag Soohee, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas’s barber discovers that Apollo has given the king ass’s ears. Unable to keep the secret, he whispers it into a hole in the ground, but the reeds that grow there murmur it to everyone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s story shows that whispered words about a king do not stay hidden.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural forbids ear-whispering at court. Midas’s barber shows why: whispers about the powerful always travel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He shall also avoid talking to another in secret, mutual conversation with another in the assembly (of ministers) ... nor loud laughter with no cause for jest.”
philosophy.explanation: Kautilya lists behaviours a courtier must avoid in the king’s assembly, including whispered side-conversations and laughter without cause.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s pair: whispering to another and laughing with another before the king.
philosophy.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 5.4, The Conduct of a Courtier (trans. R. Shamasastry)

real_life_example.event_title: Lord Chesterfield warns his son against audible laughter in polite company
real_life_example.event: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield, a British statesman and diplomat who served as secretary of state from 1746 to 1748, wrote a long series of letters of advice on manners and worldly success to his son Philip. In a letter dated Bath, 9 March 1748, he warned his son that he hoped he would often be seen to smile but never heard to laugh, calling audible laughter ill-bred and a mark of folly. The letters, not written for publication, later appeared as Letters to His Son and became famous as guides to the art of pleasing.
real_life_example.explanation: A seasoned courtier passed on the rule that in polished society the face may show pleasure but must not break into the private, noisy mirth that offends others.
real_life_example.tie_back: Like the kural, which tells the courtier to suppress shared smiles and whispers before the great, Chesterfield counselled restraint of laughter in the company one must please.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tamil:
எப்பொருளும் ஓரார் தொடரார்மற் றப்பொருளை
விட்டக்கால் கேட்க மறை.
transliteration:
Epporulum oraar thodaraarmatru apporulai
Vittakkaal ketka marai.
meaning: When the king is talking in secret, do not try to listen in or ask him about it. Hear the secret only if he chooses to tell you.
elementary: When your parents are talking quietly in the kitchen, it is tempting to sneak up and listen, or to keep asking ‘What were you talking about?’ The polite and trustworthy thing is to wait. If they want you to know, they will tell you.
university: The couplet sets out three stages. Oraar means not listening intently or eavesdropping (oru = to attend closely). Thodaraar means not following up with questions. Vittakkaal ketka means listening only once the king himself lets the matter out. The final word, marai (secret, hidden counsel), is held back to the end, which gives the line a sense of withheld information. Parimelazhagar sets the scene as a king in secret counsel with others, and the logic follows from 693: curiosity about royal secrets is exactly what breeds suspicion. The joined text in older editions reads “எப்பொருளு மோரார் தொடரார்மற் றப்பொருளை / விட்டக்காற் கேட்க மறை.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “No one should keep contact with royal secrets.”
hinduism.explanation: Dhaumya tells the Pandavas that, living at Virata’s court, they must keep clear of the king’s secrets and later never disclose them.
hinduism.tie_back: Dhaumya and Valluvar both make keeping away from royal secrets a basic rule of survival at court.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Section 4 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.”
christianity.explanation: When the disciples press the risen Jesus about when the kingdom will be restored, he tells them that some things are kept by the Father and are not theirs to demand.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the one who holds authority also decides what to reveal, and the follower should not pry.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin. And do not spy or backbite each other.”
islam.explanation: The Quran forbids spying (tajassus), prying into matters others have not chosen to share.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ban on overhearing and interrogating is a court-specific form of this general rule against spying.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says that concealing is God’s prerogative and investigating belongs to the king, so knowledge and secrecy are part of sovereign authority.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural treats the king’s marai (secret) as his to keep or reveal, and Proverbs likewise puts the right to conceal and search with the sovereign.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When the king finds out his moral qualities, his wisdom and his purity of heart, then he learns to trust him and hides not his secrets from him.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura teaches that a courtier comes to share the king’s secrets only when the king chooses to share them, after his character has been proved.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s final clause: the secret should reach you because the king lets it go, not because you took it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “…if he is always humble, steady, free from deceit and curiosity; if he abuses nobody…”
jainism.explanation: Among the fifteen marks of a well-behaved monk the sutra lists being free from curiosity, alongside humility and steadiness.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural forbids prying into the king's private talk or pressing him with questions; the Jain list counts freedom from curiosity as a mark of good discipline.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.10-13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “His limits cannot be perceived. What is the Mystery of His Mind?”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak says the purposes in the mind of the divine King cannot be pried into or exhausted by human effort.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the courtier not to strain after the king's secret counsel but to hear it only if the king reveals it; Guru Nanak treats the Lord's counsel as a mystery beyond human probing, known only as He reveals it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Jap (Japji Sahib, Pauri 24), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The hunter Actaeon strays into the goddess Diana’s hidden grotto and sees her bathing. For seeing what was not meant for him, he is turned into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells the story as a warning about the terrible cost of intruding on what the powerful keep hidden.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural warns against overhearing a sovereign’s secret, and Actaeon is the mythic example of the price of seeing what is reserved.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “‘Which one of my possessions may I share with you?’ ‘Anything, Sire,’ said Philippides, ‘except your secrets.’”
philosophy.explanation: In his essay on curiosity, Plutarch praises the comic poet Philippides, who asked King Lysimachus for any gift except his secrets. Plutarch adds that people who pry into the affairs of the more powerful destroy themselves.
philosophy.tie_back: Philippides is the ideal courtier of this Kural: he positively does not want to know the king’s secrets.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, On Being a Busybody (De curiositate) 4, Moralia 517 (Loeb trans. W. C. Helmbold)

real_life_example.event_title: Senator Truman stops probing the secret Manhattan Project
real_life_example.event: As chairman of a Senate committee reviewing defense spending, Harry Truman noticed large sums flowing into an unexplained wartime project and asked Secretary of War Henry Stimson about it. Stimson told him the matter was secret for reasons of national security, and Truman dropped the inquiry. He learned the details of the atomic bomb project only after becoming president on 12 April 1945, receiving a full briefing from Stimson on 25 April.
real_life_example.explanation: A vigorous investigator accepted that some state secrets were not his to pry into, and waited until the secret was properly entrusted to him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural tells the servant not to eavesdrop or press with questions when the ruler deals in secrets, but to hear them only when they are freely told, which is exactly how Truman came to know of the bomb.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tamil:
குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி வெறுப்பில
வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல்.
transliteration:
Kurippu arindhu kaalam karudhi veruppila
Venduba vetpach cholal.
meaning: Understand the king's mood, wait for the right time, and then say what is needed in a pleasant way he will want to hear.
elementary: If you want to ask for a later bedtime, you would not ask when Mum is rushing or cross. You would wait until she is relaxed, ask kindly, and explain why it is a good idea. Choosing the right moment and the right words makes people ready to listen.
university: The couplet lays out three steps. Kurippu arindhu means reading the ruler’s inner disposition from outward signs, the subject of the very next chapter (71, Kurippu Arithal). Kaalam karudhi means weighing the right time, echoing chapter 49 (Kaalam Arithal). Then comes the manner of speech: veruppila (things not repugnant) and venduba (things needed or useful), spoken vetpa (so that he desires to hear them). Parimelazhagar notes that what is needful must still be said, but framed so that it is welcome. That makes this not flattery but an art of timing and packaging, close to what Greek rhetoric called kairos. The traditional text is the same apart from sandhi.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him say what is true, let him say what is pleasing, let him utter no disagreeable truth, and let him utter no agreeable falsehood; that is the eternal law.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu sets the rule for virtuous speech: it should be both true and pleasant, avoiding harsh truths and sweet lies alike.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s ‘needed and not displeasing, said so he wants to hear it’ is a court-specific form of Manu’s true-and-pleasing ideal.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks that speech always be gracious and well-seasoned, fitted to each listener.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts value truth delivered gracefully and fitted to the listener.

islam.quote_or_event: “And speak to him with gentle speech that perhaps he may be reminded or fear [Allah].”
islam.explanation: God sends Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh, the most powerful and hostile king of their time, and tells them to speak gently so that their message might be received.
islam.tie_back: Even a hard truth to a king should be spoken so that he can hear it, which is the Kural’s ‘so he desires to hear’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And I said unto the king, If it please the king, and if thy servant have found favour in thy sight, that thou wouldest send me unto Judah, unto the city of my fathers’ sepulchres, that I may build it.”
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king, waits until the king notices his sad face and asks what he wants. He silently prays, then makes his request in carefully courteous terms, and it is granted.
judaism.tie_back: Nehemiah reads the moment, waits for the opening, and frames a needed request pleasingly, which is the Kural’s method exactly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, and endearing & agreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Prince Abhaya that even true, beneficial and pleasing words should be spoken only at the right time.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s three tests of true, beneficial and timely match the Kural’s needful, not displeasing, and at the right time.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Guessing the teacher's thoughts and the purport of his words, one should express one's assent, and execute (what he desires to be done).”
jainism.explanation: The disciple is to read the teacher's unspoken intention and respond to it fittingly.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks the courtier to read the king's mood and choose the moment before speaking; the Jain rule likewise asks the disciple to read a superior's mind and respond in a way that fits it.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.43 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So what offering can we place before Him, by which we might see the Darbaar of His Court? What words can we speak to evoke His Love? In the Amrit Vaylaa, the ambrosial hours before dawn, chant the True Name, and contemplate His Glorious Greatness.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak asks how one should approach the divine Court and with what words, and answers with the right time (the hours before dawn) and the right speech (the True Name and His praise).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to read the king's mood, wait for the right moment and then say what he will want to hear; Guru Nanak's question and answer about approaching the heavenly Court turn on the same two things, timing and welcome words.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Jap (Japji Sahib, Pauri 4), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Croesus, captured by Cyrus, first asks whether he may speak or must keep silent. Given leave, he points out that Cyrus’s soldiers are plundering what is now Cyrus’s own property and suggests a tactful remedy. Cyrus is pleased and adopts it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus shows a captive speaking to a conqueror: he asks permission, picks his moment, and offers advice framed around the king’s own interest.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus uses the Kural’s full method of reading the moment and framing useful counsel so that the king wants to hear it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He, therefore, added one more to the number of those who have shown to their bitter cost how little kings care for their friends' good advice.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells how Praexaspes advised King Cambyses to drink less, and the drunken king shot the adviser's son through the heart to prove his hand was steady. Seneca judges that Praexaspes was wiser in holding his tongue afterwards than in offering correction to such a king in the first place.
philosophy.tie_back: The tale shows the danger the Kural guards against, which is giving a king sound but unwelcome advice without reading his mood or waiting for the right moment.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira (Of Anger), III.14 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: Galileo names Jupiter's moons the Medicean Stars
real_life_example.event: In January 1610 Galileo discovered four moons orbiting Jupiter and published the findings in Sidereus Nuncius in March 1610. He had written to his former pupil, Grand Duke Cosimo II de' Medici, about the discoveries and named the moons the Medicean Stars, announcing the name on the book's title page and in a dedication, and he sent the Grand Duke a copy together with the telescope he had used. The Grand Duke was pleased and invited Galileo to become Philosopher and Mathematician to the court in Florence, which Galileo accepted.
real_life_example.explanation: Galileo presented a discovery that challenged the prevailing view of the heavens in a form his prince was glad to receive, and so won the patronage to keep working.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks the counsellor to read the ruler, choose the moment and say what is needful in a way he will want to hear, as Galileo did by offering an important truth wrapped in an honour to the Medici.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tamil:
வேட்பன சொல்லி வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும்
கேட்பினும் சொல்லா விடல்.
transliteration:
Vetpana solli vinaiyila egngnaandrum
Ketpinum sollaa vidal.
meaning: Tell the king things that are useful and good for him. Never talk about useless things, even if he asks you to.
elementary: If your friend asks you to help them copy homework, a good friend says no, even though the friend asked. A good helper suggests things that really help, and stays quiet about bad ideas, even when invited to share them.
university: Vetpana means ‘what is desirable’, which in Parimelazhagar’s reading are things beneficial to the king, not merely things he would like to hear. Vinaiyila means ‘what has no deed’, that is, fruitless or unprofitable matters. The concessive ketpinum (‘even if he asks’) is the moral centre of the couplet: the courtier’s integrity must hold even against a direct royal request, and egngnaandrum (at no time whatever) rules out exceptions. Commentators differ here. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as ‘speak only what the king desires’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘speak useful things even unasked’. Pope’s ‘speak pleasant things’ softens the point. The couplet thus protects 696 from being read as a licence to flatter. The older text reads “வினையில வெஞ்ஞான்றுங் / கேட்பினுஞ் சொல்லா விடல்.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person should set forth before the king those topics that are both profitable and pleasant; but should a subject be profitable without being pleasant, he should still communicate it, despite its disagreeableness. ... and not to indulge in speech that is alike unpleasant and profitless.”
hinduism.explanation: Dhaumya ranks the courtier’s speech by usefulness. Say what is useful and pleasant, say what is useful even if unpleasant, and never say what is both unpleasant and useless.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Dhaumya makes benefit, not the king’s wish, the test of what a courtier should say.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva, Section 4 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that empty, useless words carry moral weight and will be judged.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural bans useless speech even when the king asks for it. Jesus makes every idle word answerable before God.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes useful, good speech or else silence a mark of faith.
islam.tie_back: Speak what is good or say nothing is the Kural’s rule, and the courtier follows it even before the king.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As the LORD liveth, what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak.”
judaism.explanation: When King Ahab’s four hundred prophets all flatter him with promises of victory, the prophet Micaiah is told to agree with them. He refuses and speaks only the unwelcome truth.
judaism.tie_back: Micaiah refuses to say empty, harmful things even when the king’s court demands them, which is the Kural’s ‘even if he asks, do not say it’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, unbeneficial, but endearing & agreeable to others, he does not say them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha will not say even true and pleasant things if they do no good.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s refusal of pleasing but useless speech is exactly the Kural’s refusal to say unprofitable things, whatever the king wants.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not tell anything sinful or meaningless or hurtful, neither for his own sake nor for anybody else's, nor without such a motive.”
jainism.explanation: The sutra forbids sinful, idle or harmful speech whatever the reason, whether for oneself or for another.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says never to speak of useless or harmful things even if the king asks; the Jain rule bars meaningless or hurtful speech even when it is for someone else's sake.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Nanak speaks the Word of Truth; he proclaims the Truth at this, the right time.”
sikhism.explanation: Closing a hymn on the violence of Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak insists on telling the truth about rulers and events, whatever the powerful might prefer to hear.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the counsellor to say only what is truly good for the king and never what is useless, even if the king asks for it; Guru Nanak's resolve to speak only truth at the decisive moment rests on the same integrity.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “O Solon, our converse with kings should be either as rare, or as pleasing as is possible.” “No indeed!” said Solon, “but either as rare or as beneficial as possible.”
greek_mythology.explanation: At King Croesus’s court, the fable-writer Aesop advises Solon to speak to kings pleasantly or not at all. Solon corrects him: speak rarely, or speak what is truly beneficial.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This exchange sets 696 against 697. Aesop voices the ‘pleasing’ side, and Solon voices Valluvar’s final word: benefit over pleasure.
greek_mythology.source: Plutarch, Life of Solon 28 (trans. Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “When asked, he should tell the king what is both good and pleasing, but not what is bad though pleasing; if the king is pleased to listen, he may secretly tell what though unpleasant, is good.”
philosophy.explanation: Kautilya tells the courtier to offer what is good and pleasing, to refuse what is bad even if pleasing, and to say hard truths privately.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘Not what is bad though pleasing’ is the Kural’s refusal to speak unprofitable things even when asked.
philosophy.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 5.4, The Conduct of a Courtier (trans. R. Shamasastry)

real_life_example.event_title: Bismarck persuades King Wilhelm I to make a lenient peace at Nikolsburg
real_life_example.event: After Prussia's victory over Austria at Koniggratz in July 1866, King Wilhelm I wanted to take territory from Austria and from Saxony, which he regarded as a legitimate war trophy, and senior officers pressed to cross the Danube. Bismarck, who had no interest in taking land from Austria and did not want to make it a lasting enemy, opposed these demands; he later claimed he came close to resigning and was saved when the Crown Prince persuaded his father to accept Bismarck's terms. The preliminary peace signed at Nikolsburg on 26 July 1866 took no Austrian territory for Prussia and left Saxony intact.
real_life_example.explanation: Bismarck refused to serve up the trophies his king wanted, and the moderate peace kept the door open to later friendship with Austria.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a counsellor should speak only of what truly benefits the king and never of what is useless or harmful, even when the king himself asks for it, and Bismarck held to that line against his own sovereign.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tamil:
இளையர் இனமுறையர் என்றிகழார் நின்ற
ஒளியோடு ஒழுகப் படும்.
transliteration:
Ilaiyar inamuraiyar endru ikazhaar nindra
Oliyodu ozhukap padum.
meaning: Do not look down on the king, thinking 'he is younger than me' or 'he is my relative.' Act with respect for the high place he holds.
elementary: Suppose your older cousin becomes the team captain. At family dinners they are just your cousin, but on the field you listen to them as captain. The job deserves respect, whoever is doing it.
university: The couplet names two excuses for disrespect: ilaiyar (‘he is our junior’) and inamuraiyar (‘he stands in such-and-such a kinship relation to us’). Ikazhaar forbids the contempt that comes from both. The key phrase is nindra oli, ‘the radiance that abides [in him]’. Parimelazhagar interprets it as the divine light or majesty present in the king, and Pope accordingly translates ‘the glory kingly state doth bring’. Modern readers such as Solomon Pappaiah reduce it to respect for the office (padhavi) rather than the person. The idea that royal dignity belongs to the office, not the age or family of its holder, closely matches Manusmriti 7.8. The couplet is also a warning to royal kinsmen, whose familiarity is the most tempting route to contempt.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Even an infant king must not be despised, (from an idea) that he is a (mere) mortal; for he is a great deity in human form.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches that a king’s youth is no reason to disrespect him, because kingship itself carries divine majesty.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own claim. ‘He is young’ is no excuse, because of the radiance (oli) that resides in the king.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the young church leader Timothy that his youth should not be used to discount his authority.
christianity.tie_back: Paul, like the Kural, rejects ‘he is young’ as a reason to despise someone who holds authority.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran commands obedience to those who hold rightful authority, grounding it in the office rather than personal qualities.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it directs respect to ‘those in authority’ as such, whatever their age or relation to us.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD’S anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the anointed of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: David, hunted by King Saul, who is also his father-in-law, has the chance to kill him in a cave. He refuses because Saul still bears the anointing of kingship.
judaism.tie_back: David honours the anointing, the office’s sacred radiance, over his personal relationship and grievance, which is the Kural’s nindra oli.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The king does not count as a common person, the king must not be paired with anyone else; kings are easily vexed, as the eye is hurt if touched by a barley-awn.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura warns courtiers never to treat the king as an equal or an ordinary man.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts forbid bringing the king down to one’s own level, whether as a junior or as family.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you, fearless at the thought, ‘He is my brother,’ do not come, that is not fitting. Kings, whose essence is command, are not restrained by relationship.”
jainism.explanation: Suvega tells Bahubali that kinship with the Chakravartin is no excuse for failing to honour him as king, because royal authority is not set aside by family ties.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural forbids looking down on the king as 'my relative' or 'younger than me'; Suvega's speech makes the same point that kinship does not cancel the respect owed to the throne.
jainism.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Amar Das (born 1479) became the disciple of Guru Angad (born 1504), a man twenty-five years his junior, and after Guru Angad's death succeeded him as the third Guru at the age of 73.
sikhism.explanation: Sikh tradition remembers Amar Das for years of humble service to his younger Guru, to whose family he was also related by marriage, treating him with full reverence as Guru.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural forbids slighting a ruler on the grounds that 'he is younger than me' or 'he is my relative', and asks respect for the dignity of the office; Amar Das honoured a younger Guru, and a kinsman, entirely for the light of the office he held.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Guru Amar Das and Guru Angad (dates and succession)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Achilles quarrels with Agamemnon, old Nestor tells him not to strive against a sceptred king. Achilles may be the stronger fighter and the son of a goddess, but the king whom Zeus has honoured holds the greater rank.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor argues that personal superiority in strength and birth does not cancel the honour that belongs to the king’s office.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says the same: personal factors such as age or family do not outrank the dignity of the throne.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Duties are universally measured by relations. … In this manner, therefore, you will find, from the idea of a neighbor, a citizen, a general, the corresponding duties if you accustom yourself to contemplate the several relations.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that what we owe someone follows from the role or relation in which they stand to us, such as father, brother, citizen or general, and not from what we think of them personally.
philosophy.tie_back: In the same way the Kural asks that the king be treated according to the office he holds, not according to his age or his kinship with oneself.

real_life_example.event_title: Peter the Great removes his half-sister Sophia from power
real_life_example.event: Sophia Alekseyevna ruled Russia as regent from 1682 for her brother Ivan V and her younger half-brother Peter, who were proclaimed joint tsars, and she used grand royal titles while the boy Peter lived away from the Kremlin. In July 1689 the seventeen-year-old Peter clashed with her publicly in Moscow's Kazan Cathedral, and when Sophia tried to turn the streltsy against his family, many of their colonels supported Peter instead. In September 1689 Peter overthrew her, she was denied her royal titles, and she was confined in the Novodevichy Convent in Moscow.
real_life_example.explanation: Sophia had treated the crowned tsar as a junior relative to be managed, and the young ruler's authority asserted itself the moment he came of age.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns against slighting a ruler because he is younger or a relative, and Sophia lost everything by treating the tsar as merely her younger half-brother.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tamil:
கொளப்பட்டேம் என்றெண்ணிக் கொள்ளாத செய்யார்
துளக்கற்ற காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Kolappattem endru ennik kollaadha seyyaar
Thulakkatra kaatchiyavar.
meaning: People with steady judgment never think 'the king likes us' and then do things the king would not accept.
elementary: Being the teacher’s favourite does not mean you can break the rules. A sensible student knows that being liked is not a free pass, and keeps behaving well so that the trust lasts.
university: The couplet pivots on two forms of kol (to take, to accept). Kolappattem means ‘we have been accepted or esteemed [by the king]’, and kollaadha means ‘things [he] would not accept’. The echo makes the point that acceptance by the king does not make the unacceptable acceptable. Thulakkatra kaatchi, ‘vision without wavering’, marks the wise courtier as one whose judgement does not drift once favour arrives. Parimelazhagar reads the error as a specific psychology: favour breeds presumption, and presumption breeds offence. That links the couplet forward to 700, where old familiarity replaces present favour as the source of self-deception. The couplet also refines 692: not coveting what is the king’s includes not coveting the licence that favour seems to give.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna promises to pardon a hundred offences from his kinsman Shishupala. Relying on that forbearance, Shishupala heaps insults on Krishna at Yudhishthira’s royal consecration, until the hundredth is passed and he is struck down.
hinduism.explanation: Shishupala treats his protected status as permission to offend, and it ruins him.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the clearest mythic case of the person who thinks ‘I am accepted’ and so does what cannot be accepted.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Shishupala-vadha), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that a servant, however faithful, should claim no special standing from his service.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s steady-minded servant likewise never turns favour into a claim to licence.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet or be loud to him in speech like the loudness of some of you to others, lest your deeds become worthless while you perceive not.”
islam.explanation: The Quran warns the Prophet’s own companions, the people closest to him, not to become loud or casual in his presence, or their good deeds could be lost without their noticing.
islam.tie_back: Being close to the leader is no licence for improper conduct, which is the Kural’s point about favoured courtiers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So Haman came in. And the king said unto him, What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour? Now Haman thought in his heart, To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?”
judaism.explanation: Haman, the Persian king’s favourite, is so sure of his standing that he misreads the king’s question, and his presumption leads to his downfall.
judaism.tie_back: Haman is the Kural’s foolish favourite, whose certainty that he is esteemed blinds his judgement.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let him not seat himself on the king’s chair or couch or seat or elephant or chariot; as thinking himself a privileged person, such a one may dwell in a king’s court.”
buddhism.explanation: Vidhura forbids a courtier from taking royal privileges because he believes himself specially favoured.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Thinking himself a privileged person’ is precisely the Kural’s kolappattem endru enni, thinking ‘we are esteemed’.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should never do anything disagreeable to the wise, neither in words nor deeds, neither openly nor secretly.”
jainism.explanation: The sutra says the disciple must never do what displeases his superiors, in word or deed, openly or in secret.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns those who think 'the king favours us' against doing what he would not accept; the Jain rule simply allows no exception, so favour gives no licence for conduct the superior would disapprove.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, one who claims to know everything shall not be decorated in the world hereafter.”
sikhism.explanation: At the end of Japji Pauri 21 Guru Nanak warns that the self-important person who presumes on his own greatness is not honoured in the Lord's Court.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that people of steady judgement never presume on the king's favour to do what he would not accept; Guru Nanak likewise warns that presumption (haumai) loses honour in the Court one thinks one has a claim on.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Jap (Japji Sahib, Pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ixion is invited by Zeus to live among the gods on Olympus and is even purified by him. Presuming on this favour, he tries to seduce Hera, and is bound for ever to a turning wheel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar tells the story as the warning of a guest who could not bear his great good fortune.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ixion is the Kural’s favourite who, sure that he is accepted, does the unacceptable.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that in friendships between unequals, such as ruler and subject, the lesser party must give more honour and love in proportion. The friendship breaks down when the lesser party forgets the difference.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, a friendship between unequals lasts only if the lower party keeps the proper ratio of honour.
philosophy.tie_back: The favoured courtier who stops honouring the difference because he is ‘accepted’ breaks exactly this proportion.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.7 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Earl of Essex deserts his post in Ireland and loses Elizabeth's favour
real_life_example.place: Ireland and London, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex, was Queen Elizabeth I's favourite, and for years she put up with his rashness, even after he turned his back on her during a dispute. Sent to Ireland as lord lieutenant in 1599, he concluded an unfavourable truce and, defying the queen's instructions, suddenly returned to England to justify himself to her privately. She placed him under house arrest and deprived him of his offices in June 1600, and after a failed attempt to raise London in revolt in February 1601 he was tried and executed for treason.
real_life_example.explanation: Essex mistook years of indulgence for licence and did what the queen had forbidden, trusting her affection to cover it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says people of steady judgement never think the king favours them and so do what the king would not accept, the very error that ruined Essex.

adhikaram.english: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tamil:
பழையம் எனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யும்
கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்.
transliteration:
Pazhaiyam enak karudhip panpalla seyyum
Kezhudhakaimai kedu tharum.
meaning: Being too relaxed because 'we are old friends of the king,' and then behaving badly, will lead a person to ruin.
elementary: Suppose your best friend from kindergarten becomes the class president. If you start bossing them around or ignoring the rules because ‘we go way back’, the friendship and your place will both suffer. Old friendship is precious, but it is not permission to misbehave.
university: Pazhaiyam means ‘we are old [associates]’, and panpalla are ‘things that are not proper conduct’. The subject of the sentence is kezhudhakaimai, the intimate familiarity, or the privilege claimed through intimacy, that leads to such conduct, and it is this that tharum (brings) kedu (ruin). The word matters because chapter 81 (Pazhaimai, ‘Old Friendship’) uses kezhudhakaimai approvingly for the easy freedom old friends allow each other. Valluvar deliberately shows that the same freedom, turned toward a king, becomes fatal. The chapter thus ends where it began: the right distance from the fire is not closed by long acquaintance. The older text reads “பழைய மெனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யுங் / கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: Drona, now poor, goes to King Drupada and greets him as a boyhood friend, reminding him of the promises they made as students. Drupada scornfully replies that friendship between a king and a poor man cannot last, and the insulted Drona later takes revenge.
hinduism.explanation: In the Adi Parva, Drona treats old intimacy as a claim on a reigning king, and the encounter ends in humiliation and lasting enmity.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s pazhaiyam, ‘we are old friends’, presumed upon before a throne, with ruin following for both men.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava sub-parva (Drona and Drupada), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house.”
christianity.explanation: In his home town, people who have known Jesus since childhood dismiss him because of their familiarity with his family.
christianity.tie_back: The same force the Kural warns about is at work: long familiarity erodes proper reverence.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not make [your] calling of the Messenger among yourselves as the call of one of you to another.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells the believers, many of them the Prophet’s long-time companions, not to address him as casually as they address one another.
islam.tie_back: Long companionship does not license casual treatment of the one in authority, which is the Kural’s warning against kezhudhakaimai.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that visiting too often turns welcome into weariness and even hatred.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts teach that intimacy pushed too far destroys the relationship it relies on.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Channa, the Buddha’s charioteer from his days as a prince, grows arrogant because of that old bond and treats other monks with contempt. Before his death the Buddha orders the ‘higher penalty’ (brahmadanda): the monks are simply not to speak to him. Channa is shaken into humility.
buddhism.explanation: Channa’s pride rests on his old closeness to the Buddha, and it earns him a formal penalty from the Buddha himself.
buddhism.tie_back: Channa is the Buddhist model of the Kural’s pazhaiyam enak karudhi: presuming on old intimacy, followed by consequences.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 6.4; background in Vinaya commentarial tradition

jainism.quote_or_event: Gosala travelled with Mahavira for six years as a self-declared pupil. He later broke away, proclaimed himself a Tirthankara, and picked a quarrel with his former teacher. He hurled his magic fire (tejolesya) at Mahavira, but it turned back on him, and he died after repenting.
jainism.explanation: In Jain tradition Gosala's long familiarity with Mahavira did not breed reverence. It led to arrogance and open defiance, and that defiance brought about his own ruin.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that the intimacy of 'we are old friends of the king' leads people into improper conduct and destroys them; Gosala's story shows an old companion presuming on the past, with the same result.
jainism.source: Bhagavati Sutra (Vyakhyaprajnapti), Shataka 15, as summarised by T.U. Mehta, The Path of Arhat, 'Association with Gosala' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: According to Sikh tradition, Guru Angad's son Datu, resenting that Amar Das had been made Guru, came to Goindwal, taunted him that only yesterday he had been a water-carrier in their house, and kicked him from his seat; Amar Das humbly asked whether he had hurt his foot, withdrew for a time, and Datu, finding no following, went back to Khadur.
sikhism.explanation: Datu relied on his old family standing and familiarity with the new Guru to act with contempt, and lost all standing as a result.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that the familiarity which says 'we are old acquaintances' and then behaves improperly brings ruin; Datu's appeal to old household ties to justify his insult is exactly that, and it left him without followers.
sikhism.source: Wikipedia, Guru Amar Das (citing Sikh tradition)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, a mortal favoured to dine at the gods’ own table, abuses that intimacy by stealing their nectar and ambrosia for his mortal friends. His punishment is eternal hunger and thirst, with food and water always just out of reach.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar says Tantalus could not digest his great good fortune and turned the gods’ closeness into offence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tantalus turned intimacy with the highest powers into improper liberties, which is exactly the kezhudhakaimai that brings ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “… who with his own hand while at table stabbed Clitus, his dearest friend, who had been brought up with him, because he did not flatter him enough, and was too slow in transforming himself from a free man and a Macedonian into a Persian slave.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca recalls how Alexander killed Clitus, a friend he had grown up with, at a banquet for speaking too freely, and how he caged Lysimachus, another close friend, with a lion.
philosophy.tie_back: Clitus' fate shows the Kural's warning in action: an old intimacy with a king did not protect the friend who took liberties in his presence, and it led to his ruin.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira (Of Anger), III.17 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: The fall of Ibrahim Pasha, Suleyman the Magnificent's boyhood companion
real_life_example.event: Ibrahim, a slave of Christian birth from near Parga, became the inseparable companion of the future Sultan Suleyman before his accession, and in 1523 Suleyman raised him over more senior officials to be grand vizier, later marrying a sister to him. For thirteen years he ran the empire's affairs and led campaigns in Hungary and Persia, but he was unpopular with the Ottoman elite for his reputation for arrogance and was reported to have boasted publicly of his power over the sultan's decisions. Alarmed by his usurpation of the titles of sovereignty, Suleyman had him put to death in March 1536.
real_life_example.explanation: The closeness of a lifelong friendship gave Ibrahim power, but it also led him to behave as an equal of the sultan, and that familiarity ended in his ruin.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that the familiarity which makes a man act improperly because he is an old friend of the king will bring him to ruin, and Ibrahim's story fits it closely.

tamil:
கூறாமை நோக்கக் குறிப்பறிவான் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
மாறாநீர் வையக் கணி.
transliteration:
Kooraamai nokkak kurippu-arivaan enjnjaandrum
Maaraaneer vaiyak kani.
meaning: A person who can look at someone and know what they mean without a word being said is always a jewel to this world surrounded by the sea.
elementary: Imagine your friend comes to school looking quiet and droopy. Nobody says anything, but you notice, sit next to them, and share your snack. You understood without being told. Valluvar says a person who can do that is like a jewel the whole world wears.
university: The chapter opens a sequence in the Amaicciyal (section on ministers) that follows directly on ‘Conduct in the Presence of the King’ (ch. 70): having learned how near to stand, the minister must now learn to read the ruler’s unspoken kurippu (intention, inner purpose shown by outward sign). Parimelazhagar reads the subject as the minister and the object as the king: kooraamai (without his saying it) and nokka (by looking, i.e., at the face and eyes) he knows the intent, and such a man is ani (ornament, jewel) to the vaiyam (earth) whose maaraaneer (never-failing water, the ocean) surrounds it; enjnjaandrum means ‘at all times’. The hyperbole of ‘ornament to the world’ rather than ‘to the court’ signals that this faculty is rare and universally prized. The same title, Kurippu Arithal, reappears as chapter 110 in the Kamattuppal, where lovers read each other’s glances; commentators note the deliberate echo between political and amorous sign-reading. The standard text reads nokka; one online sandhi edition prints நோக்ககிக், evidently a misprint for நோக்கக் (some editions give நோக்கிக், with the same sense).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He shall also endeavour to read the mind and appearance of the king.”
hinduism.explanation: In the chapter on how a courtier serves the ruler, Kautilya makes reading the king’s mood from his looks and movements a standing duty of the minister.
hinduism.tie_back: Kautilya names the same skill Valluvar praises: knowing the ruler’s intent from his appearance before he speaks.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore the king said unto me, Why is thy countenance sad, seeing thou art not sick? this is nothing else but sorrow of heart.”
christianity.explanation: King Artaxerxes sees his cupbearer Nehemiah’s face and correctly reads grief in his heart before Nehemiah has said anything.
christianity.tie_back: A royal court scene in which the unspoken heart is read from the face, as the Kural describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes needy people too dignified to beg; the careless think they are fine, but the perceptive recognise their need from outward signs.
islam.tie_back: The praised person is the one who knows a need that is never spoken, just as the Kural praises reading the unsaid.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Joseph came in unto them in the morning, and saw them, and, behold, they were sad. And he asked Pharaoh’s officers ... saying: ‘Wherefore look ye so sad to-day?’”
judaism.explanation: Joseph, a prisoner, notices from their faces that Pharaoh’s butler and baker are troubled, and that attentiveness leads to his interpreting their dreams and later to his rise at court.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph’s rise begins with reading unspoken trouble on a face, the very skill the Kural says makes a man a jewel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘Such is your thinking, here is where your thinking is, thus is your mind.’ And however much he may read, that’s exactly how it is, and not otherwise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists reading another’s mind, first of all by means of a sign, as one of three recognised wonders, and says the accurate reader is never wrong.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism likewise treats accurately knowing another’s unspoken mind as a rare and admired power.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 3.60, Sangarava Sutta, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk who, on receiving an order from his superior, walks up to him, watching his nods and motions, is called well-behaved.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana opens its lecture on discipline by defining the good disciple as one who attends to his teacher's unspoken nods and gestures, not only to his words.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats reading a superior's silent signs as the mark of the person most worth having in the presence of authority.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is a Sikh, a friend, a relative and a sibling, who walks in the Way of the Guru's Will.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das defines the true disciple as one who lives inside the Guru's bhana (will), already moving with it rather than waiting to be told.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the one who grasps a master's intention without a word being said; Gurbani honours the Sikh who is so attuned that he walks within the Guru's will.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 601, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “No one noticed his distress except Alcinous, who was sitting near him, and heard the heavy sighs that he was heaving.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus hides his tears under his cloak while the bard sings of Troy; only King Alcinous perceives his grief and tactfully ends the song.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Alcinous is the Kural’s ornament in action: he understands a guest’s silent sorrow and acts on it without being asked.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Lucilius that a person’s character can be gathered from the smallest things: the way they walk, move a hand, answer, or carry their face.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, outward signs are constant evidence of the inner man for anyone who pays attention.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca supports the Kural’s premise that the attentive can know a mind without being told.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 52 (trans. R. M. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Jane Goodall watches David Greybeard make and use a tool
real_life_example.event: In mid-1960 Jane Goodall, a 26-year-old without formal scientific training, began a field study of wild chimpanzees at Gombe on Lake Tanganyika for the paleoanthropologist Louis Leakey. After months of patient watching she gained the trust of an older male she named David Greybeard, and late in 1960 she saw him strip a twig and use it to fish termites from a mound, evidence that chimpanzees make and use tools. Her long study went on to reveal chimpanzee personalities, emotions and social bonds, and she became one of the best-known naturalists in the world.
real_life_example.explanation: By reading the gestures and expressions of animals that could tell her nothing in words, Goodall changed how science understood both chimpanzees and humans.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the person who understands what others intend without a word being said as an ornament to the world, and Goodall's wordless understanding of the chimpanzees made her a figure honoured worldwide.

tamil:
ஐயப் படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானைத்
தெய்வத்தோ டொப்பக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Aiyap padaaadhu akaththadhu unarvaanaith
Theyvaththodu oppak kolal.
meaning: A person who can know without any doubt what is inside someone else's mind should be thought of as equal to a god.
elementary: Some grown-ups seem to know exactly what you are feeling before you say it, and they are always right. It can feel almost magical. Valluvar says a person who can truly do that deserves to be honoured almost like a god.
university: Aiyap padaaadhu uses alapedai (metrical vowel lengthening, படாஅது for படாது) to stretch ‘without doubting’, stressing certainty rather than guesswork. Akaththadhu is ‘that which is within’ (akam = interior, mind), and unarvaan ‘one who perceives’. Parimelazhagar explains the comparison theyvaththodu oppa (as equal to a deity): to know the heart directly is a faculty proper to the divine, so a man who has it without error shares a divine attribute, though he remains human (Mu. Varadarasanar adds ‘even though he is a man’). Kalaignar makes the logic explicit: if such knowledge belongs to God, the man who has it may be likened to God. The couplet should be read with 701 as a rising scale: ornament to the world, then peer of the gods. No significant textual variants; the sandhi text reads படாஅ தகத்த துணர்வானைத்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that he knows all beings, past, present and to come, while no one truly knows him.
hinduism.explanation: Complete knowledge of every being’s inner life is presented as a mark of the divine.
hinduism.tie_back: If knowing hearts fully is God’s own trait, the Kural’s claim that such a person is like a god follows naturally.

christianity.quote_or_event: “for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
christianity.explanation: God tells Samuel that humans judge by looks, but God sees the heart directly.
christianity.tie_back: Seeing into the heart is God’s way of seeing, so a person who does it without doubt comes close to the divine, as the Kural says.

islam.quote_or_event: “He knows that which deceives the eyes and what the breasts conceal.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names knowledge of hidden glances and concealed thoughts as one of God’s attributes.
islam.tie_back: Knowing what the breast conceals is described as God’s knowledge, which is why the Kural compares its human possessor to a deity.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud reads Isaiah 11:3 as saying the Messiah will ‘smell and judge’, knowing the truth without evidence, and reports that Bar Koziba was rejected when he could not do this.
judaism.explanation: Knowing guilt or innocence without witnesses is treated as a sign of divinely endowed, messianic status.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, knowing what is inside without doubt raises a person above the ordinary toward the divine.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Among the Tathagata’s powers the Buddha lists knowing, as it really is, the dispositions and faculties of other beings.
buddhism.explanation: Accurate knowledge of others’ inner tendencies is counted among the powers that mark a fully awakened one.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism, like the Kural, places flawless knowledge of other minds among the highest, near-superhuman attainments.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He reached the knowledge called Manaḥparyāya, by which he knew the thoughts of all sentient beings, with five organs, which are not defective, and possess a developed intellect, (living) in the two and a half continents and the two oceans.”
jainism.explanation: When Mahavira took up the ascetic life he gained manaḥparyāya jñāna, the direct knowledge of other beings' minds, which Jainism counts among the higher, supersensory kinds of knowledge.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural sets the one who knows another's mind without doubt beside the divine; Jain scripture likewise treats certain knowledge of other minds as a mark of the most advanced souls.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.15.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You are permeating each and every heart, O Lord, Inner-knower, Searcher of Hearts.”
sikhism.explanation: Antarjami, the Inner-knower who sees what lies within every heart, is one of Gurbani's most frequent names for God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls the one who perceives another's mind without doubt equal to a god; in Gurbani, knowing the heart from within is precisely the mark of the divine.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Delphic oracle tells Croesus’ envoys that Apollo knows the number of the sands and the measure of the sea, understands the mute and hears those who do not speak.
greek_mythology.explanation: The god’s power shows in knowing what is unspoken; Croesus’ test of the oracles turns on it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In Greek myth, hearing the voiceless is exactly what makes a god a god, which is the Kural’s comparison.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aquinas argues that the secret thoughts of the heart, as they are in themselves, are known to God alone; angels and men can only conjecture them from bodily signs such as changes of face.
philosophy.explanation: He separates certain knowledge of hearts, which belongs to God, from inference by signs, which is open to creatures.
philosophy.tie_back: Aquinas sharpens the Kural’s point: to read signs without doubt is to come as close as a creature can to what belongs to God.
philosophy.source: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 57, a. 4

real_life_example.event_title: George Kennan sends the Long Telegram from Moscow
real_life_example.event: After Stalin's speech of 9 February 1946 alarmed American officials, the State Department asked George F. Kennan, its foremost Soviet expert and charge d'affaires in Moscow, to explain Soviet conduct. Kennan wired back a reply of more than 5,000 words, arguing that powerful internal dynamics, not Western incentives, drove Moscow's behaviour. The telegram circulated widely in Washington, and its ideas, developed in his 1947 X article, became the basis of the American policy of containment.
real_life_example.explanation: Kennan read the hidden intentions of a closed regime with such assurance that his analysis guided American policy for decades.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural honours one who perceives without doubt what lies inside another's mind, and Kennan's confident reading of the Soviet leadership's purposes earned him almost oracular standing in Washington.

tamil:
குறிப்பிற் குறிப்புணர் வாரை உறுப்பினுள்
யாது கொடுத்தும் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Kurippir kurippunar vaarai uruppinul
Yaadhu koduththum kolal.
meaning: People who can read what others mean from the signs on their face are worth getting as helpers, whatever you have to give to win them.
elementary: If a football team finds a player who always knows where a teammate will pass before the ball is kicked, the coach will do almost anything to keep that player. Valluvar says a leader should treat people who read signals the same way.
university: The phrase kurippir kurippu unarvaar is the chapter’s technical formula, repeated in 705: ‘those who perceive the kurippu by means of kurippu’. Parimelazhagar takes the first kurippu as the outward signs (of face and eye) and the second as the inner intention they betray; Pope and Drew follow a further gloss in which the reader uses the indications of his own mind as a key to another’s. Uruppu here means the constituent ‘limbs’ of a kingdom (arasu uruppu: army, people, treasury, ministers, allies, forts, as set out in ch. 39), so yaadhu koduththum kolal is ‘secure them by giving whichever of these is asked’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both read it as ‘giving anything among the country’s possessions’. The advice sits in a long Indian tradition of the king paying any price for an able minister. Uruppu will recur in 704 and 705 in the bodily sense (limbs, sense-organs), a deliberate word-play.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On first meeting Hanuman, Rama tells Lakshmana that Hanuman’s speech shows deep learning and discernment, and that a king with such a messenger will have every undertaking succeed.
hinduism.explanation: Rama recognises at once that Hanuman reads situations and people with rare skill and values him accordingly.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Ramayana treats such a perceptive helper as worth securing at any cost.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out.”
christianity.explanation: A person’s real purpose lies deep and hidden, and only a discerning person can bring it to the surface.
christianity.tie_back: The ‘man of understanding’ who draws out hidden purposes is the helper the Kural says to acquire at any price.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the king said, ‘Bring him to me; I will appoint him exclusively for myself.’ And when he spoke to him, he said, ‘Indeed, you are today established [in position] and trusted.’”
islam.explanation: After Joseph reads the meaning hidden in the king’s dream, the king takes him out of prison and appoints him to his personal service.
islam.tie_back: The king does what the Kural advises: when he finds a man who reads hidden meanings, he secures him at once and at great cost.

judaism.quote_or_event: The queen tells Belshazzar about Daniel, a man of excellent spirit who explains riddles and dissolves doubts; the king summons him, offers purple, a gold chain and third rank in the kingdom, and gives them to him.
judaism.explanation: A king faced with an unreadable sign pays the highest price to bring in the one man who can read it.
judaism.tie_back: Belshazzar’s rewards illustrate ‘give whatever it takes’ for a reader of signs.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Maha-Ummagga Jataka, King Vedeha hears of the boy Mahosadha’s uncanny discernment, brings him to court despite his rivals, and makes him his chief adviser.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta as Mahosadha repeatedly reads the hidden intentions of rivals and enemy kings and saves the kingdom.
buddhism.tie_back: The story is the Kural’s advice in narrative form: a king who wins such a discerner at any cost is saved by him.

jainism.quote_or_event: “An intelligent man who has learned (the sacred texts) takes his duties upon himself, and he becomes renowned in the world; as the earth is the dwelling of all beings, so he will be a dwelling of all duties.”
jainism.explanation: The verse follows the praise of the pupil who guesses his teacher's thoughts and needs no express directions (1.43–44), and calls such a person a support on which everything rests.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says such perceptive people should be won at any price, and the Jain text says the same kind of person becomes indispensable, a 'dwelling of all duties'.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.45 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Surrender body, mind, wealth, and everything to the Guru; obey the Order of His Will, and you will find Him.”
sikhism.explanation: In Anand Sahib, Guru Amar Das tells the seeker to hand over body, mind and wealth to the Guru, who knows the inner state, and to live by his hukam.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who read inner intentions should be won whatever part of one's wealth it costs; Anand Sahib says to give everything to the Guru who sees within.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 918, Raag Ramkali, Anand Sahib, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon praises Nestor’s counsel and wishes he had ten such counsellors among the Achaeans, saying Troy would then soon fall.
greek_mythology.explanation: The commander values one wise adviser above many warriors.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agamemnon’s wish is the Greek version of ‘acquire such men whatever it costs’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli says the first judgement of a ruler’s intelligence is the quality of those around him, and distinguishes minds that understand for themselves, minds that grasp what others understand, and useless minds.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli, choosing perceptive ministers is itself the proof of a prince’s wisdom.
philosophy.tie_back: Both Machiavelli and Valluvar make securing perceptive servants a top royal priority.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 22 (trans. W. K. Marriott)

real_life_example.event_title: Churchill orders that the Bletchley codebreakers get all they want
real_life_example.place: Bletchley Park and London, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: On 21 October 1941 four codebreakers working on the German Enigma ciphers at Bletchley Park, Alan Turing, Gordon Welchman, Hugh Alexander and Stuart Milner-Barry, bypassed their managers and wrote directly to Prime Minister Winston Churchill, saying their work was being held up for lack of a few dozen clerks, typists and naval staff. Churchill at once sent a handwritten minute to General Ismay, bearing an Action This Day label, that read: Make sure they have all they want on extreme priority and report to me that this has been done. On 18 November Ismay reported that the staff were being supplied very rapidly.
real_life_example.explanation: Churchill understood that the people who could read the enemy's hidden intentions were worth any price, and he backed them at once.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who can read inner intentions from outward signs must be secured whatever must be given to win them, which is exactly the priority Churchill gave the codebreakers.

tamil:
குறித்தது கூறாமைக் கொள்வாரோ டேனை
உறுப்போ ரனையரால் வேறு.
transliteration:
Kuriththadhu kooraamaik kolvaarodu enai
Uruppor anaiyaraal veru.
meaning: People who understand what others mean without being told, and people who cannot, may look the same, but they are very different.
elementary: Two phones can look exactly the same on the outside, but one has a smart app that understands your voice and the other does not. People are like that too: two people can look alike, but one understands what you mean without words and the other does not.
university: Kuriththadhu is ‘what (someone) has in mind’, and kooraamaik kolvaar ‘those who take it in without its being spoken’. Enai = the others (ஏனை), and uruppu or anaiyar (உறுப்பு ஓர் அனையர்) means ‘alike in limbs’, i.e., in bodily form; aal (ஆல்) is concessive (‘though’), and veru ‘they are different’. Parimelazhagar supplies the implied contrast: they are different in understanding (arivu), so the bodily likeness is misleading. The couplet quietly shifts uruppu from 703’s political ‘limbs of the kingdom’ to the body’s limbs. Commentators link it with the Kural’s repeated claim that the unperceptive are human only in form (compare 993 and the chapter on folly), and with the Sanskrit maxim that intelligence shows itself in grasping what is unsaid. The sandhi text reads ‘யுறுப்போ ரனையரால்’; there are no variants of meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He that understandeth quickly, listeneth patiently, pursueth his objects with judgment and not from desire and spendeth not his breath on the affairs of others without being asked, is said to possess the foremost mark of wisdom”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells King Dhritarashtra that quick understanding is the first sign that separates the wise (pandita) from the rest.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura, like Valluvar, uses quickness of understanding to divide people who otherwise look the same.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.”
christianity.explanation: The letter contrasts spiritual infants with mature people whose perception has been trained by practice.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it divides people not by appearance but by trained powers of discernment.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if We willed, We could show them to you, and you would know them by their mark; but you will surely know them by the tone of [their] speech.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told he will recognise the hypocrites, who look like everyone else, from subtle signs in how they speak.
islam.tie_back: People who look identical are told apart by the perceptive, which is exactly the Kural’s contrast.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah lists seven traits that mark a golem (an uncultivated person) and seven that mark a wise person, such as not interrupting, answering to the point, and knowing what one has not understood.
judaism.explanation: Wisdom is defined by how a person listens and takes in what others say, not by status or appearance.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say that the real difference between people lies in how they understand others, not in how they look.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that a person’s virtue, purity, endurance and discernment can be known only through long association, and only by one who is attentive and discerning, not by one who is not.
buddhism.explanation: The ability to see what others are really like belongs to the discerning person and not to others.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta, like the Kural, draws a line between those who perceive what lies beneath and those who cannot.

jainism.quote_or_event: “An excellent pupil needs no express directions, or he is (at least) quickly directed; he always carries out his duties as he is told.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana sets the pupil who understands without being told against the 'ill-behaved' one who stays insubordinate and inattentive even when given an order (1.3).
jainism.tie_back: Both texts divide people who look alike into two different kinds: those who grasp what is wanted without being told, and those who do not.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.44 (cf. 1.2–3) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Sikh tradition tells how a jug fell into mud and Guru Nanak asked his sons to pick it up; they refused the dirty, menial task, but Bhai Lehna lifted it out, washed it clean and brought it back full of water. Guru Nanak later named Lehna, renamed Angad, as his successor instead of his own sons.
sikhism.explanation: The sons and the disciple stood equally close to the Guru, yet only Lehna understood and carried out what the Guru wanted; the story is one of several told to explain his choice as Guru Angad.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who grasp a master's intent unbidden and those who do not may look alike in body yet are different kinds of people; the Guru's sons and Lehna show exactly this.
sikhism.source: Wikipedia, 'Guru Angad' (summarising W. Owen Cole and Piara Singh Sambhi, The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices, 1978, p. 18)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “so true is it that the gods do not grace all men alike in speech, person, and understanding.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus rebukes the handsome but tactless Euryalus, saying one man may look plain yet be gifted in mind, while another looks like a god but lacks sense.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus makes the Kural’s point: outward form is no guide to the powers of the mind.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle separates understanding (synesis) and considerate judgement (gnome), the capacity to grasp and fairly judge what others say and mean, from other intellectual virtues, noting that people are praised as ‘understanding’ for it.
philosophy.explanation: He treats the grasp of another’s meaning as a distinct excellence that some people have and others lack.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, names the faculty that makes people who look alike very different.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.10-11 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Dr Joseph Bell's powers of observation inspire Sherlock Holmes
real_life_example.event: Joseph Bell, a surgeon who taught at the University of Edinburgh and the Royal Infirmary, taught that keen observation of small details was the key to accurate diagnosis, and reportedly demonstrated this by working out strangers' backgrounds and habits in front of his classes from their clothing and manner. The medical student Arthur Conan Doyle became Bell's assistant at the Infirmary, and when he created Sherlock Holmes in A Study in Scarlet (1887) the detective's powers were widely said to be modelled on Bell's. In a letter of 7 May 1892, now held by the Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh, Doyle told Bell that he owed Sherlock Holmes to him.
real_life_example.explanation: Bell showed that, among people who look alike, the one who notices what others miss is in effect a different kind of person.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who grasp what is unspoken and those who cannot may look alike in body yet are different kinds of people, the very contrast Bell drew between himself and his students, and Doyle between Holmes and Watson.

tamil:
குறிப்பிற் குறிப்புணரா வாயின் உறுப்பினுள்
என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்.
transliteration:
Kurippir kurippunaraa vaayin uruppinul
Enna payaththavo kan.
meaning: If your eyes cannot read what someone means from the signs they give, what use are your eyes among all the parts of your body?
elementary: What good is a flashlight if you never switch it on? Your eyes are for more than seeing colours and shapes. They are meant to notice when someone is sad, worried or happy. If they never notice that, it is as if the flashlight stays off.
university: The couplet repeats 703’s formula kurippir kurippu unar- in the negative (unaraa vaayin, ‘if they do not perceive’) and turns it on the eye itself. Uruppinul (‘among the organs’) now plainly means the body’s members, and enna payaththavo is a rhetorical ‘of what profit are they?’ Parimelazhagar explains that the eyes are the foremost of the sense-organs, and their special excellence is to catch another’s mind through the signs of face and eye; if they cannot do that they are no better than the other limbs. Drew and Pope render ‘if they cannot by their own indications dive those of another’, reflecting the reading that the eye both shows and reads kurippu. The rhetorical question anticipates 710, where the eye becomes the only measuring rod. The sandhi text reads குறிப்புணரா வாயி னுறுப்பினு / ளென்ன பயத்தவோ கண்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that he cannot see Krishna’s true form with his own eyes and grants him a divine eye to see it.
hinduism.explanation: Ordinary sight is shown to be inadequate for seeing what really matters until it is given a deeper power.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say that eyes which only see surfaces fall short of their true purpose.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Why reason ye, because ye have no bread? perceive ye not yet, neither understand? have ye your heart yet hardened? Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns his disciples about the ‘leaven’ of the Pharisees, and they take it literally; he rebukes them for missing his meaning.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus asks the Kural’s own question: what are eyes for if they miss the meaning behind the sign?

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says the real failure of sight lies in the heart’s inability to understand what the eyes see.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, eyes that take in signs without understanding them are no better than blind.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hear now this, O foolish people, and without understanding, that have eyes, and see not, that have ears, and hear not”
judaism.explanation: The prophet rebukes a people who have every faculty of perception yet grasp nothing of what is happening.
judaism.tie_back: Jeremiah and Valluvar both mock eyes that see without understanding.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Shortly before his passing, the Buddha gives Ananda a broad hint that he could remain for an aeon if asked, but Ananda, his mind distracted, fails to grasp the sign and does not ask.
buddhism.explanation: Even the Buddha’s closest attendant misses a plain signal, and the chance is lost.
buddhism.tie_back: The episode shows the Kural’s point: failing to read an intended signal makes one’s eyes and ears useless at the moment they matter most.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not, in every case, wait for the express command (of the teacher) like an unbroken horse for the whip (of the rider), but like a broken horse which sees the whip (of the rider) he should commit no evil act.”
jainism.explanation: The trained horse responds to the sight of the whip and does not need the blow; the good disciple likewise acts on what he sees rather than waiting to be told outright.
jainism.tie_back: The verse turns on the eye's job of reading a sign, which is the faculty the Kural says is worthless if it cannot read intentions.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not call them blind, who have no eyes in their face. They alone are blind, O Nanak, who wander away from their Lord and Master.”
