sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad redefines blindness: having eyes in the face counts for nothing if they do not see what truly matters.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use the eyes are among the body's organs if they cannot read intention; Guru Angad likewise says eyes that do not perceive leave a person blind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Oedipus taunts the blind prophet Tiresias as blind in ears, mind and eyes, while Tiresias answers that Oedipus has sight yet cannot see the evil he is in.
greek_mythology.explanation: The man with working eyes misses every sign, while the blind seer understands everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Sophocles dramatises the Kural’s question: eyes that cannot read the signs are worthless.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heraclitus says that eyes and ears are poor witnesses for people whose souls do not understand their language.
philosophy.explanation: The senses deliver signs, but only an understanding mind can read them.
philosophy.tie_back: Heraclitus states the principle behind the Kural: sight without understanding gives no knowledge.

real_life_example.event_title: The Opana radar sighting before Pearl Harbor is dismissed
real_life_example.place: Opana Point and Fort Shafter, Oahu, Hawaii, United States
real_life_example.event: At 7:02 a.m. on 7 December 1941, Privates Joseph Lockard and George Elliott, practising with the radar set at Opana on Oahu's northern tip, detected an unusually large formation of aircraft approaching from the north and telephoned the information center at Fort Shafter. Lieutenant Kermit Tyler, who was there for training, reasoned that it was an expected flight of American B-17 bombers and told them not to worry about it. The operators tracked the contact until about 7:40, and the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor began at 7:55 a.m.
real_life_example.explanation: The radar saw the attack coming, but no one interpreted what it showed, and the warning was wasted.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use eyes are if they cannot read the meaning behind what they see, and at Opana the new electronic eye saw everything yet the sign went unread.

tamil:
அடுத்தது காட்டும் பளிங்குபோல் நெஞ்சம்
கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்.
transliteration:
Aduththadhu kaattum palingupol nenjam
Kaduththadhu kaattum mukam.
meaning: Just as clear crystal shows the color of whatever is next to it, the face shows whatever is strongest in the heart.
elementary: Put a clear glass marble next to a red flower and the marble looks red. Put it next to a leaf and it looks green. Your face is like that marble. Whatever feeling is strongest inside you shows through it.
university: Palingu (Sanskrit sphatika) is clear rock-crystal, and aduththadhu kaattum means ‘shows what is next to it’: the crystal has no colour of its own but displays the hue of its neighbour. This is the famous Indian sphatika image (the crystal beside a red japa flower) used in Sankhya and Vedanta for how the pure self seems coloured by what it is near; Valluvar turns it into a psychology of expression. Kaduththadhu is glossed by Parimelazhagar as mikkadhu, ‘what is uppermost or abounding’ (from kadu-, to be intense), so the face shows the dominant feeling, not every passing thought. Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘what abounds in the heart’, and Pope renders ‘what’s throbbing in the mind’. The couplet grounds the chapter’s claim that kurippu can be read: the face is an honest medium. Sandhi text: பளிங்குபோ னெஞ்சங் / கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The internal (working of the) mind is perceived through the aspect, the motions, the gait, the gestures, the speech, and the changes in the eye and of the face.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king presiding over a court how to read witnesses and litigants from their outward signs.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu, like Valluvar, treats the face and eyes as reliable displays of the inner mind.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The heart of a man changeth his countenance, whether it be for good or evil: and a merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira observes that the face changes according to the state of the heart, for good or for ill.
christianity.tie_back: Sirach states the Kural’s rule almost word for word: the heart shows on the face.

islam.quote_or_event: “Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration.”
islam.explanation: The inner devotion of the Prophet’s companions is described as visibly marked on their faces.
islam.tie_back: What fills the heart shows on the face, as the Kural’s crystal shows its neighbour’s colour.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs uses the image of a reflection in water to show how one heart mirrors or reveals another.
judaism.tie_back: Both use a reflecting medium to explain how the heart becomes visible.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha illustrates knowledge of others’ minds with the image of a young person checking their face in a clean mirror or a bowl of clear water and seeing at once whether there is a blemish.
buddhism.explanation: A trained mind sees another’s state, passionate or free, as plainly as a face in a mirror.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural and the sutta both use a clear reflecting surface to show how visible an inner state is.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The alteration produced on the soul, just as on a crystal by the presence of black things, &c., is denoted by the word lêsyâ.”
jainism.explanation: In Jacobi's note to the lecture on leśyās he quotes this verse from the Avacūri commentary. It explains the soul's 'colourings' (black through white) as reflections of the karma that accompanies it, the way a clear crystal takes on the colour of what lies beside it.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism uses the same crystal image as the Kural: just as the crystal shows its neighbour's colour, the soul shows the colour of the dispositions that dominate it.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 34, note 1 by Jacobi quoting the Avacūri commentary (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who have meditated on the Naam, the Name of the Lord, and departed after having worked by the sweat of their brows -O Nanak, their faces are radiant in the Court of the Lord, and many are saved along with them!”
sikhism.explanation: The closing salok of Japji Sahib says that the inner labour of remembering the Name shows outwardly as a radiant face.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the face shows whatever is strongest in the heart, as crystal shows its neighbour's colour; Japji says the devotion within becomes visible as radiance on the face.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib (closing salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He sat himself down away from the ships with a face as dark as night, and his silver bow rang death as he shot his arrow in the midst of them.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollo’s anger at the insult to his priest is visible on his face before it is released in the plague.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Even the god’s face shows the rage that fills him, as the Kural says every face shows its heart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero tells orators that the whole effect of delivery depends on the face, since the face is the image of the mind and the eyes its interpreters.
philosophy.explanation: Rhetoric depends on the fact that the face displays the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s ‘image of the mind’ is the Kural’s crystal in Roman form.

real_life_example.event_title: Duchenne de Boulogne photographs the true and false smile
real_life_example.event: The French physician Guillaume Duchenne de Boulogne applied electric currents to the facial muscles of his subjects and used the new technique of photography to record the expressions that resulted, publishing his findings in 1862 as Mecanisme de la physionomie humaine. He was among the first to test empirically the idea that emotional expressions can be understood as movements of particular facial muscles. He noted that a false smile used only the muscles around the mouth, while a genuine smile also caused contractions around the eyes.
real_life_example.explanation: Duchenne showed that the face carries the true state of feeling in ways the will cannot easily counterfeit.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the face to crystal that shows the colour of what lies beside it, and Duchenne demonstrated that a genuine inner feeling shows through on the face in a way a forced expression cannot copy.

tamil:
முகத்தின் முதுக்குறைந்தது உண்டோ உவப்பினும்
காயினும் தான்முந் துறும்.
transliteration:
Mukaththin mudhukkuraindhadhu undo uvappinum
Kaayinum thaanmun thurum.
meaning: Is anything wiser than the face? Whether a person is happy or angry, the face shows it first.
elementary: When you get a present you love, your smile arrives before you can say ‘thank you’. When you are cross, your frown shows up before any words. Your face is like a messenger who always runs ahead of you.
university: Mudhukkuraindhadhu comes from mudhukkurai(mai), a Tamil idiom for mature wisdom or sagacity (literally ‘old-shortened’, an idiom whose sense is ‘wise beyond years’); the question ‘is there anything wiser than the face?’ credits the face with a kind of intelligence. Uvappinum kaayinum (‘whether it rejoices or burns with anger’) names the two poles of emotion, and thaan mun urum means ‘it comes forward first’, before speech or deliberate action. Parimelazhagar comments that the face runs ahead of the mind in disclosing liking and dislike, which is why it is called wise: it seems to know first. The irony is deliberate: the face is ‘wise’ precisely because it cannot keep a secret. Sandhi text: முதுக்குறைந்த துண்டோ வுவப்பினுங் / காயினுந் தான்முந் துறும்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On seeing his kinsmen drawn up for battle, Arjuna says his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles and his hair stands on end.
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna’s inner turmoil shows in his body before he has made any decision.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural says, the body and face announce the mind’s state before words or decisions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell. And the LORD said unto Cain, Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen?”
christianity.explanation: Cain’s anger and resentment show on his face before he acts.
christianity.tie_back: Cain’s fallen face runs ahead of his deed, exactly as the Kural says the face runs ahead of the mind.

islam.quote_or_event: “I know when you are pleased with me or angry with me.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Aisha he can tell her mood from a small change in how she swears: ‘by the Lord of Muhammad’ when pleased, ‘by the Lord of Abraham’ when angry.
islam.tie_back: Pleasure and anger leak out ahead of any declaration, and a loving observer reads them.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Ilai teaches that a person’s character is recognised by three things: his cup, his pocket and his anger (koso, kiso, ka‘aso).
judaism.explanation: How someone behaves when drinking, when paying and when angry reveals what they really are.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Talmud treats moments of strong feeling such as anger as the times when the inner person shows through.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha, seeing Sariputta approach, remarks that his faculties are clear and his complexion pure and bright, and asks what meditation he has been practising.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha reads Sariputta’s inner state from his face before Sariputta says a word.
buddhism.tie_back: Sariputta’s face announces his inner calm first, and the Buddha reads it, as the Kural describes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Perceiving the teacher's anger one should pacify him by kindness, appease him with folded hands, and promise not to do wrong again.”
jainism.explanation: The disciple is expected to notice his teacher's anger as soon as it shows and respond to it at once with humility.
jainism.tie_back: It assumes what the Kural states: anger shows itself before anything is said, so the attentive person can read it.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.41 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who meditates on the Naam is at peace; his face is radiant and bright.” … “The faithless cynic barks out his lies, and his face is blackened.”
sikhism.explanation: In two hymns Guru Arjan describes the inner state showing on the face: the peace of the Name brightens it, while falsehood darkens it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the face is the first to announce whether a person is pleased or angry; Guru Arjan likewise treats the face as the place where the inner condition becomes visible.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 44, Sri Raag, Guru Arjan; and Ang 239, Raag Gauri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “His heart was black with rage, and his eyes flashed fire as he scowled on Calchas”
greek_mythology.explanation: When the seer blames him for the plague, Agamemnon’s fury is visible in his eyes and scowl before he speaks.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agamemnon’s face runs ahead of his words, as the Kural says it always does in anger.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Wittgenstein remarks that the human body is the best picture of the human soul, and elsewhere that we see emotion in a face directly rather than inferring it from facial contortions.
philosophy.explanation: For Wittgenstein, expression is not a clue from which we reason; the feeling is visible in the face itself.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘wise face’: the face presents the feeling immediately, ahead of any report.

real_life_example.event_title: Paul Ekman tests facial expressions among the Fore of Papua New Guinea
real_life_example.place: South East Highlands, Papua New Guinea
real_life_example.event: To test whether facial expressions of emotion are learned or universal, the American psychologist Paul Ekman travelled in 1967 and 1968 to the Fore people, an isolated community with almost no contact with the outside world. He told them simple stories and asked them to choose the photographed face that matched, and also asked them to show the expressions themselves. Ekman found that the Fore expressed emotions such as sadness, fear, surprise, anger and disgust with the same eye and mouth movements seen in Western populations.
real_life_example.explanation: The study suggested that the face announces basic feelings in a common language that crosses cultures.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the face is wiser than anything, announcing pleasure or anger before words can, and Ekman found that faces speak the same emotional language even where no spoken language is shared.

tamil:
முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும் அகம்நோக்கி
உற்ற துணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Mukamnokki nirka amaiyum akamnokki
Utradhu unarvaarp perin.
meaning: If you have people who can look into your heart and understand what has happened to you, it is enough to stand where they can see your face.
elementary: When you come home after a bad day, a good parent can often tell just by looking at you. You don’t have to explain; you just stand there, and they already know you need a hug. Valluvar says that is what great helpers are like.
university: The couplet balances two ‘lookings’: mukam nokki (looking at the face) and akam nokki (looking into the heart). Nirka amaiyum means ‘it suffices to stand’, and utradhu is ‘what has befallen’ (a trouble or need). Parimelazhagar makes the king the one who stands: if he has ministers able to look into his mind and perceive what has occurred, he need not voice his trouble; standing and looking at their faces is enough, and they will understand and remedy it. Some modern readers (e.g., Kalaignar) generalise it to anyone who can read hearts. The couplet is the practical payoff of 701 and 703: the value of the perceptive minister is that the ruler is spared the need to speak, which in court may itself be dangerous. Variant spelling: ytamizh prints முகம்நோக்கி, the sandhi edition முகநோக்கி நிற்க வமையு மகநோக்கி.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The poor Brahmin Sudama visits his boyhood friend Krishna but is too ashamed to ask for help; Krishna understands his need unspoken and sends him home to find his hut turned into a mansion.
hinduism.explanation: Sudama asks for nothing; his presence is enough for Krishna, who reads his heart.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s scene exactly: standing before one who reads hearts is enough.

christianity.quote_or_event: “for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers not to pile up words in prayer, since God already knows their needs.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, one who knows the heart makes spoken requests unnecessary.

islam.quote_or_event: “Finally Abu-l-Qasim (the Prophet) passed by me and he smiled when he saw me, for he knew what was in my heart and on my face.”
islam.explanation: Abu Hurayrah, starving, hints at his hunger to others who miss it; the Prophet reads it on his face and feeds him.
islam.tie_back: Abu Hurayrah only had to stand before the right person; his face was enough, as the Kural says.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it was so, when the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, that she obtained favour in his sight ... Then said the king unto her: ‘What wilt thou, queen Esther? for whatever thy request, even to the half of the kingdom, it shall be given thee.’”
judaism.explanation: Esther risks her life simply by standing uninvited before the king; seeing her, he understands she has an urgent request before she speaks.
judaism.tie_back: Esther only has to stand before the king’s gaze, and her unspoken purpose is recognised.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After his awakening the Buddha inclines not to teach; Brahma Sahampati, knowing the Buddha’s thought with his own mind, appears before him and begs him to teach.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says nothing aloud; the deity perceives his unspoken inclination and responds.
buddhism.tie_back: An unspoken inner state is perceived and answered by one who looks into the mind, as the Kural describes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Guessing the teacher's thoughts and the purport of his words, one should express one's assent, and execute (what he desires to be done).”
jainism.explanation: The ideal disciple reads his teacher's thoughts and acts on them, so the teacher does not have to explain what he needs.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says it is enough to stand before those who read the heart; the Jain verse describes exactly that kind of attendant from the other side.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.43 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You know completely the condition of my mind; who else could I go to tell of it?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan tells God that the whole condition (birtha) of his mind is already known to Him, so there is no need to explain it to anyone.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that before those who look into the heart it is enough simply to stand and be seen; Guru Arjan says the Lord already knows the mind's trouble without being told.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 382, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “You know it; why tell you what you know well already?”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Thetis rises from the sea to her weeping son, Achilles says she already knows his grief without being told.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles only has to be seen by one who knows his heart; explanation is unnecessary.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith argues that we come to feel what another feels by imaginatively placing ourselves in their situation, so that a sympathetic observer grasps a sufferer’s state from their circumstances and looks.
philosophy.explanation: Sympathy is the faculty that lets one person understand another’s condition without full explanation.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s perceptive helper is Smith’s sympathetic spectator at work.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments I.i.1

real_life_example.event_title: Jean-Dominique Bauby dictates a memoir by blinking one eye
real_life_example.place: A naval hospital near Calais, France
real_life_example.event: On 8 December 1995, Jean-Dominique Bauby, editor of the French edition of Elle, suffered a stroke and awoke from a coma about 20 days later unable to speak and able to move only his left eyelid. A therapist devised a system in which the alphabet was read aloud and he blinked at the letter he wanted, and with an assistant writing down each letter he dictated his memoir, The Diving Bell and the Butterfly. The book was published just days before he died of pneumonia at the age of 44.
real_life_example.explanation: Bauby could no longer speak, but the people around him learned to read his eye so well that he could share a whole book of his inner life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that if you have people who can look into your heart, it is enough simply to stand before them, and Bauby's helpers understood him through his face and eye alone.

tamil:
பகைமையும் கேண்மையும் கண்ணுரைக்கும் கண்ணின்
வகைமை உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Pakaimaiyum kenmaiyum kannuraikkum kannin
Vakaimai unarvaarp perin.
meaning: To people who understand the different ways eyes look, the eyes alone will show if someone is an enemy or a friend.
elementary: A dog can tell if you are friendly by the way you look at it. Soft eyes mean ‘friend’, a hard stare means ‘watch out’. Wise people learn to read eyes the same way, and the eyes tell them who is a friend and who is not.
university: Pakaimai (enmity) and kenmai (friendship, intimacy) are the two things kan uraikkum, ‘the eye will declare’. The condition is kannin vakaimai unarvaar, ‘those who perceive the varieties (vakai) of the eye’, i.e., the different kinds of look. Parimelazhagar applies it to foreign policy: if the king has ministers who can read the movements of the eye, the eyes of other kings and their envoys will themselves reveal hostility or friendship. Drew’s translation, following him, adds ‘(of foreign kings)’. Commentators link the verse with the Kural’s treatment of hidden enmity (ch. 89, Utpakai) and false friendship (ch. 83), where a smiling face may cover hostility: the eye is harder to disguise than the mouth. Sandhi text: பகைமையுங் கேண்மையுங் கண்ணுரைக்குங் கண்ணின் / வகைமை யுணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Angry appearance when the courtier is in sight; evading or refusal to hear his speech; no inclination to give him a seat or to see him; change in syllables and accents while talking to him; seeing with one eye; brow-beating ...”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya lists the signs by which a courtier can tell that the king has turned against him, many of them in the eyes and brows.
hinduism.tie_back: Kautilya catalogues the ‘varieties of the eye’ that, as the Kural says, reveal enmity to the trained observer.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.”
christianity.explanation: After Peter’s third denial, a single look from Jesus tells Peter everything, and he goes out and weeps.
christianity.tie_back: A look carries a whole message of relationship without words, as the Kural says eyes speak friendship and estrangement.

islam.quote_or_event: “Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater. We have certainly made clear to you the signs, if you will use reason.”
islam.explanation: Believers are warned that hostile outsiders give away their enmity through outward signs, if one pays attention.
islam.tie_back: Enmity shows through outward signs to the attentive, which is the Kural’s claim about the eye.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Jacob beheld the countenance of Laban, and, behold, it was not toward him as beforetime.”
judaism.explanation: Jacob reads in his father-in-law’s face that friendship has turned to hostility, and decides to leave.
judaism.tie_back: Jacob does exactly what the Kural describes: he reads enmity in a face and acts on it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches Sigala how to tell false friends, such as the flatterer and the one who only talks, from true friends, by the signs in their behaviour.
buddhism.explanation: Friendship and enmity in disguise can be recognised by those who know what to look for.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the sutta teaches that friend and foe can be told apart from their signs.

jainism.quote_or_event: Hemacandra tells how the serpent Caṇḍakauśika, reborn as a snake whose very look was poisonous because of anger carried over from former lives, turned its deadly glare on the wandering Mahavira. Mahavira's calm, unhostile gaze did not change, and the serpent was pacified and awakened.
jainism.explanation: The episode sets the look of hatred against the look of compassion and shows that anger carried in the soul comes out through the eyes.
jainism.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that the eyes declare enmity or friendship to anyone who can read them.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10 (Mahāvīra-caritra), ch. 3, part 10, 'Episode of Caṇḍakauśika' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Bronze is bright and shiny, but when it is rubbed, its blackness appears.”
sikhism.explanation: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, Guru Nanak sang this hymn to Sajjan, a welcoming host who secretly robbed and killed travellers; the shining surface hid an inner blackness, and Sajjan repented.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who understand glances can tell an enemy from a friend; Guru Nanak saw the enemy beneath Sajjan's friendly surface.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Suhi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “whereon Minerva went up to Ulysses and prompted him to beg pieces of bread from each one of the suitors, that he might see what kind of people they were, and tell the good from the bad”
greek_mythology.explanation: Disguised as a beggar, Odysseus goes round the suitors to learn from their looks and conduct which are friendly and which hostile.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus is the Kural’s trained observer, sorting friend from foe by watching them.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is a point of cunning, to wait upon him with whom you speak, with your eye; as the Jesuits give it in precept: for there be many wise men, that have secret hearts, and transparent countenances.”
philosophy.explanation: Bacon advises watching the eyes and face of the person you negotiate with, because even guarded people give themselves away there.
philosophy.tie_back: Bacon’s ‘secret hearts, transparent countenances’ is the Kural’s point that the eye tells what the tongue hides.

real_life_example.event_title: Margaret Thatcher judges Gorbachev a man she can do business with
real_life_example.place: Chequers and London, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: On 16 December 1984, British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher held long talks at Chequers with Mikhail Gorbachev, then a rising Soviet leader who had been mentioned as a possible successor in Moscow. In a BBC interview with John Cole the next day she said: I like Mr Gorbachev. We can do business together. She explained that he had been ready for full, detailed discussion rather than prepared statements, and her assessment became international news, a first Western verdict on the man who became Soviet leader in 1985.
real_life_example.explanation: From a face-to-face meeting Thatcher judged that a Soviet adversary could be dealt with as a partner, a judgement that proved important as the Cold War began to thaw.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that to those who understand the different kinds of glances, the eyes themselves reveal friend or foe, and Thatcher read from a personal encounter that Gorbachev could be a partner rather than simply an enemy.

tamil:
நுண்ணியம் என்பார் அளக்குங்கோல் காணுங்கால்
கண்ணல்லது இல்லை பிற.
transliteration:
Nunniyam enpaar alakkungol kaanungaal
Kannalladhu illai pira.
meaning: If you look closely at people who say they can read others well, you will find their only measuring stick is the eyes. They use nothing else.
elementary: A builder uses a ruler to measure wood. A person who is good at understanding others uses a different ruler: their eyes. By watching carefully, they measure what someone is feeling.
university: Nunniyam enpaar are ‘those who say, we are subtle (nunmai)’, i.e., who claim fine discernment. Alakkungol is ‘the rod with which they measure’ (alakkum kol), and kaanungaal ‘when one examines it’. Parimelazhagar, as usual, applies it to ministers: the measuring rod of those who claim to know others’ minds turns out, on inspection, to be nothing but their eyes. There is a double sense that commentators note: the minister measures by his own eye, and what he measures is the other person’s eye (continuing 709). The closing kan alladhu illai pira (‘there is nothing other than the eye’) sums up the chapter, which moves from praise of the perceptive (701-704) to the face (706-707) and finally the eye (705, 709-710) as the decisive sign. Sandhi text: நுண்ணிய மென்பா ரளக்குங்கோல் காணுங்காற் / கண்ணல்ல தில்லை பிற.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A well-known verse of the Panchatantra (also in the Hitopadesha) says that even an animal understands what is spoken, but the wise infer what is unspoken, for the fruit of intelligence is knowing the gestures of others (parengita-jnana-phala hi buddhayah).
hinduism.explanation: Classical Sanskrit niti literature defines intelligence itself as the ability to read others’ unspoken signs.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make reading signs the real measure of a subtle mind.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus calls the eye the lamp of the body, the organ through which the whole person is lit or darkened.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts give the eye a unique, measuring role over the whole person.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed in that are signs for those who discern.”
islam.explanation: The word translated ‘those who discern’ (al-mutawassimin) means those who read marks, and classical exegetes connected it to firasa, the believer’s insight into people.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an honours those who read signs, the same people the Kural says measure by the eye.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah says that the disciples of Abraham have a good eye, while the disciples of Balaam have an evil eye, making the eye the index of a person’s character.
judaism.explanation: In rabbinic idiom the eye (ayin tovah, ayin ra‘ah) reveals whether a person is generous or grudging.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the rabbis treat the eye as the clearest measure of what lies inside.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha speaks of three eyes: the eye of flesh, the divine eye, and the unsurpassed eye of discernment (pañña-cakkhu).
buddhism.explanation: Real seeing, for the Buddha, is the eye of wisdom that sees things as they are.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts make ‘the eye’, rightly trained, the true instrument of subtle knowledge.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra classes knowledge gained through the senses and mind (mati) and through testimony (śruta) as parokṣa, indirect, and keeps the name pratyakṣa, direct, for knowledge the soul has without the senses: clairvoyance, knowledge of other minds, and omniscience.
jainism.explanation: For Jainism, any judgment that relies on the eye is a mediated and limited instrument. Only the purified soul knows another being directly.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the eye is the only measuring rod even the subtle have, while Jainism agrees that ordinary judges rely on the senses but holds that a higher, eye-free knowing exists.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 1.11–12 (cf. tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, those eyes are different, which behold my Husband Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that truly seeing eyes are of another kind altogether: the eyes that see the Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the only measuring rod of the truly discerning is the eye; Gurbani also makes the quality of one's seeing the real measure, though of the divine rather than of other people.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 577, Raag Vadhans, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Achilles turned in amaze, and by the fire that flashed from her eyes at once knew that she was Minerva.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles recognises the disguised goddess Athena at once by the look of her eyes alone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: For Achilles, as for Valluvar’s discerning minister, the eye is the one sure test.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The ancient Physiognomonics attributed to Aristotle holds that character can be inferred from bodily signs, and that the region around the eyes, forehead, head and face is the most reliable place to look.
philosophy.explanation: Greek physiognomy made the eyes the chief evidence for reading a person.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a systematic version of the Kural’s claim that the eye is the discerner’s only measuring rod.

real_life_example.event_title: Bernard Berenson sets out a connoisseurship of the trained eye
real_life_example.event: The Harvard-educated art critic Bernard Berenson, who lived most of his life near Florence, became one of the most famous connoisseurs of Italian Renaissance painting, known for a discriminating eye and exceptional memory. In 1895 he published his Lorenzo Lotto and the essay The Rudiments of Connoisseurship, setting out his method of attributing pictures through close visual study in the manner of Giovanni Morelli. His opinions were widely sought by collectors, and many masterpieces now in American museums were bought on his recommendation.
real_life_example.explanation: Berenson built a career on the claim that the trained eye, rather than documents alone, could tell one master's hand from another's.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those who claim fine discernment the only true measuring rod is the eye, and Berenson made the eye the measure of artistic judgement.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tamil:
அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லின்
தொகையறிந்த தூய்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Avaiyarindhu aaraaindhu solluka sollin
Thokaiyarindha thooimai yavar.
meaning: People with pure minds who know words well should first understand the group they are speaking to, and then speak with care.
elementary: You talk one way to your baby cousin, another way to your friends, and another way to your teacher. A good speaker first looks at who is listening, then picks the right words for them.
university: The chapter opens by making knowledge of the audience (avai, the assembly or council) a precondition of speech: avaiyarindhu (having known the assembly) comes before aaraaindhu (having deliberated) and solluka (let them speak). Parimelazhagar explains that assemblies are of three grades relative to the speaker, those superior, equal, and inferior in learning (mikkaar, oththaar, thaazhndhaar), and the rest of the chapter works through how to behave before each. Sollin thokai (the aggregate of words) is glossed in the commentarial tradition, and in Solomon Pappaiah’s modern paraphrase, as the three kinds of expressive word: direct (senjol), figurative (ilakkanai-chol), and suggestive (kurippu-chol). Thooimai (purity) is a moral term, not a stylistic one: the speaker must not use this command of language to deceive the hearers. The ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net texts print the first word as “அவையறிநது”, an evident typing slip; the sandhi-joined text “அவையறிந் தாராய்ந்து” confirms the reading அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who desireth to obtain a knowledge of the customs of different countries, and also the languages of different nations, and of the usages of different orders of men, knoweth at once all that is high and low.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells King Dhritarashtra that a wise man studies how different peoples and classes speak and behave, and so understands everyone from the highest to the lowest.
hinduism.tie_back: Knowing “the usages of different orders of men” is exactly the knowledge of the assembly that the Kural requires before a person speaks.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Colossians that their speech should be gracious and carefully seasoned, so that they can give each person the answer that fits that person.
christianity.tie_back: “How ye ought to answer every man” is the Kural’s point: fit your words to the particular hearer.

islam.quote_or_event: “You should preach to the people according to their mental caliber so that they may not convey wrong things about Allah and His Messenger.”
islam.explanation: Ali ibn Abi Talib warned teachers to speak to people at the level they can understand, so that they do not misunderstand what they hear and then spread wrong ideas. Bukhari places it under the heading of choosing some people rather than others for certain teachings.
islam.tie_back: Ali’s rule, speak according to the listener’s capacity, is the Kural’s rule of knowing the assembly before you speak.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb praises a word that fits its setting. The Hebrew phrase behind “fitly” suggests a word spoken in the right circumstances.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker who first studies the assembly is trying to produce exactly this fitting word.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Lotus Sutra the Buddha explains that he teaches through skillful means (upaya), shaping his teaching with many kinds of explanations, parables, and stories to suit the different dispositions and capacities of the beings he addresses.
buddhism.explanation: Mahayana tradition holds that the Buddha adjusted how he taught to the understanding of each audience, while the truth being taught stayed the same.
buddhism.tie_back: Skillful means is the Buddhist form of the Kural’s rule: understand the listeners first, then choose your words.
buddhism.source: Saddharma-pundarika (Lotus Sutra), Chapter 2 ‘Skilfulness’, trans. H. Kern

jainism.quote_or_event: “(If the pupil does not understand his short explanation), he should explain at greater length. When the pupil has heard it, he will correctly understand the Truth.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga tells the preaching monk to fit his explanation to the hearer: briefly at first, then at greater length if the listener needs it, and never with long-winded explanations of difficult passages (1.14.23).
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes judging the audience a precondition of speaking well, so that words are weighed to suit those who hear them.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.24 (cf. I.14.23) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak makes the worth of speech depend on its effect: only words that bring honour are approved.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks the clean-minded speaker to weigh his words before speaking; Guru Nanak likewise says speech must be weighed by whether it brings honour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Greek army rushes for the ships in Iliad Book 2, Odysseus goes through the camp. To every chieftain he speaks courteously and reasons with him, but to every common soldier he speaks sharply and orders him back to his place.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows Odysseus, the master speaker, instantly changing his manner of speech according to the rank of the person in front of him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus reads each audience before he speaks, which is the skill this kural asks for.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Rhetoric may be defined as the faculty of observing in any given case the available means of persuasion.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines rhetoric as the skill of seeing what will persuade in each particular case. In the same chapter he says that persuasion depends partly on putting the hearers into the right frame of mind.
philosophy.tie_back: “In any given case” captures the Kural’s demand to study this particular assembly before speaking.

real_life_example.event_title: John F. Kennedy addresses the Greater Houston Ministerial Association
real_life_example.place: Rice Hotel, Houston, Texas, United States
real_life_example.event: During the 1960 presidential campaign, Senator John F. Kennedy spoke to the Greater Houston Ministerial Association, a gathering of clergy, at the Rice Hotel in Houston, to address concerns about his Catholic faith, noting that no Catholic had ever been elected president. He set out his support for religious tolerance and the absolute separation of church and state, said he was not the Catholic candidate for president but the Democratic Party's candidate who happened also to be a Catholic, and asked to be judged on his record of fourteen years in Congress. He then took questions from the ministers.
real_life_example.explanation: Kennedy chose his audience deliberately and spoke directly to the doubts that this particular assembly of clergy held about him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks speakers to understand the assembly in front of them before weighing their words, and Kennedy shaped his address precisely to the concerns of the ministers he faced.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tamil:
இடைதெரிந்து நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லின்
நடைதெரிந்த நன்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Idaitherindhu nankunarndhu solluka sollin
Nadaitherindha nanmai yavar.
meaning: Good people who know how words work should choose the right moment, understand the subject fully, and only then speak.
elementary: If you want to ask your mom for something, you don’t ask while she is rushing to catch a bus. You wait for a good moment and think it through first. Wise speakers wait for the right time too.
university: Where 711 stressed the audience, this kural stresses the moment: idai (interval, opening) is glossed by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar as the court’s sevvi, its receptive moment, when the hearers are ready and willing to listen. Nankunarndhu (having understood well) requires full command of the matter, and Solomon Pappaiah adds that the speaker must avoid faults of both word and sense (sorkutram, porutkutram). Sollin nadai (the gait or course of words) refers to how each of the three kinds of word conveys its meaning, which parallels sollin thokai in 711. The parallel structure of 711 and 712 (sollin thokaiyarindha thooimaiyavar / sollin nadaitherindha nanmaiyavar) presents purity and goodness as twin moral qualities of the ideal counsellor. The text is the same in all sources consulted, apart from the sandhi joining (“சொல்லி னடைதெரிந்த”).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking truthfully and beneficially and in avoiding speech that offends.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna counts disciplined speech, meaning speech that is true, helpful, and does not upset the listener, as a form of spiritual austerity (tapas).
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker, who waits for the right opening and speaks only what is fully understood, is practising this austerity of speech.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks that speech be measured by its effect on the hearers: it should build them up and do them good.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it keeps the listeners’ good in view when deciding what to say.

islam.quote_or_event: “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the Prophet to call people with wisdom (hikmah) and fine instruction. Commentators understand hikmah here as fitting the message to the hearers and the occasion.
islam.tie_back: Speaking “with wisdom” and “in a way that is best” is the Kural’s discerning, well-timed speech.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth teaches that every action has its proper season, including speech and silence.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s idai, the right opening for speech, is Koheleth’s “time to speak”.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, and endearing & agreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Prince Abhaya that he says only what is true and beneficial, and that even then he chooses the proper time to say it.
buddhism.tie_back: “A sense of the proper time” is the Kural’s idaitherindhu, knowing the moment.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “To give way to: anger, pride, deceit and greed, laughter, fear, loquacity and slander; these eight faults should a well-disciplined monk avoid; he should use blameless and concise speech at the proper time.”
jainism.explanation: Bhāṣā-samiti, carefulness in speech, is one of the five samitis every Jain monk observes. It requires speech that is free of passion, sparing, and timed correctly.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's call to choose the right moment and speak only after understanding fully matches the Jain rule of 'blameless and concise speech at the proper time'.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 24.9–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “First, examine the merchandise, and then, make the deal.”
sikhism.explanation: In a trader's maxim, Guru Nanak says one must first understand what one is dealing with before committing to the transaction.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the speaker should understand the matter fully before speaking; Guru Nanak gives the same order: understand first, then act.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1410, Salok Vaaran Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Shipwrecked and naked, Odysseus meets the princess Nausicaa. He weighs whether to clasp her knees as a suppliant or to plead from a distance, and decides that gentle words spoken from where he stands suit the moment best.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer stops the action to show Odysseus judging what kind of approach the situation calls for before he says a word.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus reads the moment before speaking, as the Kural requires.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They would be sure to ask him whether he knew ‘to whom’ he would give his medicines, and ‘when,’ and ‘how much.’”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that anyone who only knows speech techniques is like a man who knows drugs but does not know which patient to give them to, when, or in what dose. Real rhetoric, like real medicine, requires that knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: “To whom” and “when” are the Kural’s two demands: know the assembly and know the moment.

real_life_example.event_title: Nehru's Tryst with Destiny speech at the midnight of independence
real_life_example.event: The Constituent Assembly of India met at eleven at night on 14 August 1947, and Jawaharlal Nehru moved a resolution that its members take a pledge of service to India after the last stroke of midnight. Introducing it, he said: At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom. As the clock struck twelve, the President and members stood and took the pledge.
real_life_example.explanation: Nehru timed his words to the exact moment of independence, so that the speech and the event it described became one.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural tells good speakers to pick the right moment before they speak, and Nehru delivered his most famous words at the very hour they were meant for.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tamil:
அவையறியார் சொல்லல்மேற் கொள்பவர் சொல்லின்
வகையறியார் வல்லதூஉம் இல்.
transliteration:
Avaiyariyaar sollalmer kolpavar sollin
Vakaiyariyaar valladhooum il.
meaning: People who start speaking without understanding their listeners do not know how words work. They have no real skill at all.
elementary: Imagine telling a scary ghost story at a little kid’s birthday party. The story may be good, but you picked the wrong crowd, and now everyone is crying. Not knowing your listeners can spoil even good words.
university: This kural is the negative of 711. Avaiyariyaar (those who do not know the assembly) who take up speaking (sollal mer kolpavar) are thereby shown to be sollin vakaiyariyaar, ignorant of the kinds of words. Valladhooum il (they have no ability whatever) uses an alapedai, a lengthened vowel (thooum), for emphasis. Parimelazhagar’s point is that eloquence cannot be separated from knowledge of the audience. A speaker who misjudges the assembly proves thereby that he does not know how words work, however learned he may be. The sandhi text reads “சொல்லன்மேற் கொள்பவர்”, and “வல்லதூஉ மில்”, which divide into the same words as சொல்லல்மேற் and வல்லதூஉம் இல்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That worst of men who entereth a place uninvited, and talketh much without being asked, and reposeth trust on untrustworthy wights, is a fool.”
hinduism.explanation: In his list of the marks of a fool, Vidura includes the man who talks at length when no one has asked him.
hinduism.tie_back: Talking “without being asked”, without reading the room, is how the Kural’s avaiyariyaar give themselves away.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that answering before you have listened brings shame on the speaker.
christianity.tie_back: Speaking before you understand the matter or the assembly is the folly the Kural describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids acting or speaking on matters you do not know, and warns that a person will answer for how he used his faculties.
islam.tie_back: The speaker who does not know the assembly is acting without knowledge, which this verse forbids.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious; but the lips of a fool will swallow up himself.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth contrasts the gracious speech of the wise with a fool’s talk, which ruins the fool himself.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker who misreads the assembly is undone by his own words, as the fool is here.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is not wise because one speaks much. He who is peaceable, friendly and fearless is called wise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada separates wisdom from talkativeness: a lot of speech is no evidence of wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise denies real ability to the person who is eager to speak but does not understand the assembly.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who correctly knows the sacred texts, who practises austerities, who understands all details of the Law, who is an authentic interpreter, clever, and learned--such a man is competent to explain the entire creed.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga closes its lecture on the true monk by stating who is qualified to speak on the Law. By implication, one without that understanding should not take it up.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that whoever speaks without the needed understanding has no real ability; the Jain verse sets out the competence a speaker must have.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To speak too much and babble is useless.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak dismisses excessive talk as empty babble.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one who speaks without understanding the assembly shows no real ability; Guru Nanak calls speech that is not grounded in understanding mere useless babble.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 661, Raag Dhanasri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Greek assembly, Thersites, a man of disorderly words, rails at Agamemnon out of turn. Odysseus rebukes him and strikes him with the sceptre, and the assembled army laughs at him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents Thersites as the model of someone who speaks without any sense of place, rank, or occasion, and who is shamed for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Thersites is the avaiyariyaar of this kural: he speaks without knowing the assembly and ends up with no standing at all.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay on talkativeness, Plutarch describes the chatterer who bursts into every conversation regardless of the company, is ignored or laughed at, and finds that nobody believes or values what he says.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch argues that the habitual talker loses the very thing speech exists for, which is being heard and trusted.
philosophy.tie_back: Plutarch reaches the Kural’s verdict: whoever speaks without regard to the listeners has no real power of speech.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, De garrulitate (On Talkativeness), Moralia 502B-515A (trans. W. C. Helmbold)

real_life_example.event_title: Wagner's Tannhauser is whistled off the stage of the Paris Opera
real_life_example.place: Paris Opera (Salle Le Peletier), Paris, France
real_life_example.event: Wagner revised Tannhauser for the Paris Opera and, to meet its convention, agreed to add a ballet, but he placed it in the first act rather than in its traditional place in the second. Members of the Jockey Club, who usually arrived after dinner for the second half of the evening and missed the dancing, disrupted the performances with whistles and catcalls, joined by political opponents of the production's sponsors. After 164 rehearsals, the opera was withdrawn after only three performances.
real_life_example.explanation: However strong the music, Wagner's disregard of what the Paris audience expected turned the premiere into a fiasco.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who speaks without first understanding the assembly shows no real ability, and Wagner's refusal to accommodate the Paris Opera's audience sank the production despite its merits.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tamil:
ஒளியார்முன் ஒள்ளிய ராதல் வெளியார்முன்
வான்சுதை வண்ணம் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Oliyaarmun olliya raadhal veliyaarmun
Vaansudhai vannam kolal.
meaning: Among bright, learned people, show how bright you are. Among dull people, be plain like a white-painted wall and do not show off.
elementary: With your older brother who loves science, you can talk about planets and black holes. With your little sister you just say “the moon is pretty tonight.” You are just as smart either way. You simply show only as much as your listener can use.
university: The kural depends on a pun: oliyaar (the luminous, the learned) is set against veliyaar (the blank or white, the empty-minded), and before the latter one should take on the colour of vaansudhai, pure white lime plaster. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read this as appearing unlearned before the unlearned. Solomon Pappaiah softens it to coming down to the hearers’ level so that they can follow, and Kalaignar keeps the stronger sense of appearing ignorant. Plaster is bright but has no lustre of its own, so the image suggests someone who covers his learning without losing his integrity. This is the key verse of the chapter’s three-way scheme (superior, equal, inferior assemblies), and it is the source of the modern Tamil proverbial advice to “be white lime before fools.” The text agrees in all sources; the sandhi text reads “ஒளியார்முன் னொள்ளிய ராதல்” and “வண்ணங் கொளல்”.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Unless one be asked, one must not explain (anything) to anybody, nor (must one answer) a person who asks improperly; let a wise man, though he knows (the answer), behave among men as (if he were) an idiot.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the learned not to display knowledge unasked or to answer improper questioners, and to behave, when appropriate, as if he knew nothing.
hinduism.tie_back: “Behave … as if he were an idiot” is the Kural’s white plaster: the wise man hides his light among those who cannot receive it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes adapting himself to every kind of listener so as to reach them.
christianity.tie_back: Paul becoming “weak to the weak” is close to the Kural’s speaker who takes on plain white before the plain.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We did not send any messenger except [speaking] in the language of his people to state clearly for them.”
islam.explanation: God sends each prophet to speak in his people’s own language, so that the message will be clear to them.
islam.tie_back: Speaking at the level and in the idiom of your hearers is the Kural’s advice to take on their colour.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the introduction to the Guide for the Perplexed, Maimonides explains that he will present deep matters in scattered hints, so that they reach the prepared reader while remaining hidden from the unprepared multitude. He cites the rabbinic rule that such matters are to be taught only to those fit to receive them.
judaism.explanation: Maimonides deliberately veils his learning when speaking to people who are not ready for it, while revealing it to the qualified.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s double rule: shine before the learned, and wear a plain surface before others.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed, Introduction (trans. M. Friedländer)

buddhism.quote_or_event: According to the Dhammapada commentary, the Buddha travelled to Alavi to teach a poor farmer. The man arrived exhausted and hungry after searching for a lost ox, so the Buddha had him fed before saying a word of Dhamma.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha set aside his teaching until he had met the listener’s actual condition, and remarked that hunger is the greatest of illnesses (Dhammapada 203).
buddhism.tie_back: Adjusting what you say and when you say it to where the listener actually is follows the Kural’s advice.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 203 (story of a lay disciple at Alavi)

jainism.quote_or_event: “If he is not proud of his learning; if he does not find fault with others”
jainism.explanation: Among the fifteen qualities of the well-behaved monk, the Uttaradhyayana lists humility about one's learning; being 'proud of his learning' is among the faults of the ill-behaved (11.7).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's advice to hide one's brilliance like plain white plaster before the dull is close to the Jain ideal of a learned person who does not show off.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.10–13 (excerpt) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you are wise, be simple; if you are powerful, be weak; … How rare is one who is known as such a devotee.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, praises the rare devotee who hides wisdom and strength under simplicity.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the learned to take on the plain colour of white plaster among the dull and keep their brilliance hidden; Farid likewise says the wise should appear simple.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 128) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus returns to his own palace disguised by Athena as a ragged beggar. He hides his identity and cleverness among the insolent suitors, and reveals himself only when the moment and the company are right.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest mind among the Greeks chooses to look like nothing among people who would only abuse what he is.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus in rags is the Kural’s white plaster: brilliance deliberately covered before the unworthy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that uneducated speakers are often more persuasive than educated ones before popular audiences, because they argue from familiar, concrete things. He advises speakers to argue from what the hearers already accept, not from far-fetched premises.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle sees that sophistication can work against a speaker before a plain audience, and that the effective speaker comes down to the hearers’ level.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives the practical logic behind the Kural’s advice to put aside brilliance before the unlearned.

real_life_example.event_title: Faraday gives The Chemical History of a Candle to a young audience
real_life_example.place: Royal Institution, London, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: The Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures for young people began in 1825, and Michael Faraday delivered nineteen series of them. His last, given when he was 70 in late December 1860 and early 1861, was a set of six lectures on The Chemical History of a Candle to an audience averaging about 650 young people, using a simple candle and many demonstrations to explain combustion. In the lectures he spoke of himself and his listeners together as fellow philosophers and even as fellow juveniles, and the lectures were published in 1861 and have never been out of print.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the greatest scientists of his day set aside the language of the laboratory and met children on their own ground, and the result became a classic.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises speakers to shine fully among the learned but to take on a plain colour before those without learning, and Faraday wrapped deep science in the plain language of a candle for his young hearers.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tamil:
நன்றென்ற வற்றுள்ளும் நன்றே முதுவருள்
முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு.
transliteration:
Nandrendra vatrullum nandre mudhuvarul
Mundhu kilavaach cherivu.
meaning: Of all good things, the best is holding back from speaking first when you are among elders who are wiser than you.
elementary: When your grandparents and their friends are talking about the old days, you might know a fun fact too. But the polite and smart thing is to listen first and let them speak. Waiting your turn shows you are growing up.
university: Mudhuvar are elders in knowledge, not just in age. In Parimelazhagar’s scheme this is the conduct suited to an assembly superior to oneself, just as 714’s first half suits an equal one. Mundhu kilavaa means not uttering (kila, to speak) first, not jumping ahead. Cherivu (literally density or closeness) here means self-restraint, what Mu. Varadarasanar calls adakkam, and it links this chapter to ch. 13, Adakkamudaimai. The superlative nandrendravatrullum nandre (good even among the things called good) is strong praise: such restraint is ranked above other virtues of the counsellor. Kalaignar’s paraphrase adds a vivid Tamil idiom, “like a cashew seed” (mundhiri kottai), for a person who pushes forward to speak. The text agrees across sources; the sandhi text reads “நன்றென்ற வற்றுள்ளு நன்றே முதுவருண்”.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For the vital airs of a young man mount upwards to leave his body when an elder approaches; but by rising to meet him and saluting he recovers them.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches that deference to elders is basic to right conduct, so much so that failing to show it is pictured as losing one’s life-breath.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s restraint before elders, letting them speak first, comes from the same culture of respect for seniors.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.”
christianity.explanation: James tells believers to put listening first and to be slow to speak.
christianity.tie_back: “Slow to speak” is the Kural’s mundhu kilavaa, not rushing to speak first.

islam.quote_or_event: “I wanted to say that it was the datepalm tree but as I was the youngest of all (of them) I kept quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet asked his companions a riddle. Young Ibn Umar knew the answer but stayed silent out of deference to the senior companions present.
islam.tie_back: Ibn Umar’s silence is almost a dramatization of this kural: knowing, yet not speaking first among elders.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wise man does not speak before one who is greater than he in wisdom, And does not break into his fellow’s speech; And is not hasty to answer.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah lists seven marks of the wise, and the first is not speaking before someone greater in wisdom.
judaism.tie_back: This is virtually the Kural’s wording: do not speak first before those greater in learning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Tittira Jataka, a partridge, a monkey, and an elephant work out which of them is the eldest so that they can honour him. The Buddha tells the story when senior monks are left without lodging because younger monks took it first, and he rules that respect and precedence go to seniority.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha makes deference to elders a rule of the monastic community.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s restraint before elders applies the same principle of precedence to speech in council.
buddhism.source: Tittira Jataka (Jataka No. 37), in The Jataka, vol. 1, ed. E. B. Cowell

jainism.quote_or_event: “One should always be meek, and not be talkative in the presence of the wise; one should acquire valuable knowledge, and avoid what is worthless.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's discipline also tells the disciple 'He should not speak unasked' (1.14). Restraint of speech before the wise is part of vinaya, the humility that makes learning possible.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's restraint of not rushing to speak first among wiser elders, stated almost word for word as a Jain rule of conduct.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.8 (cf. 1.14) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa ki Vaar, Guru Nanak names sweetness and humility as the very essence of all good qualities.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls the restraint that does not rush to speak first before wiser elders the best of all good things; Guru Nanak names humility the essence of virtue.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Arriving at Pylos, the young Telemachus hesitates to approach the aged king Nestor. He tells Athena, disguised as Mentor, that a young man is shy of questioning an elder.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents Telemachus’s reluctance to speak first before a revered elder as proper modesty, and Athena encourages him gently.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Telemachus’s restraint before Nestor is the Kural’s modesty among elders.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In all cases, then, silence is a safe adornment for the young man, and especially so, when in listening to another he does not get excited or bawl out every minute, but even if the remarks be none too agreeable, puts up with them, and waits for the speaker to pause …”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch advises a young man attending a philosopher's lecture to listen in silence, to wait until the speaker has finished, and not to rush in with objections, recalling the saying that nature gave us two ears and one tongue.
philosophy.tie_back: Plutarch, like the Kural, praises the restraint of a younger person who does not hurry to speak before those wiser than himself.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On Listening to Lectures (De auditu), ch. 4 (tr. F. C. Babbitt)

real_life_example.event_title: Thomas Jefferson's silence in the Continental Congress
real_life_example.event: Thomas Jefferson, a young Virginia delegate in the Continental Congress, rarely spoke in its debates, and John Adams later recalled that during the whole time he sat with him in Congress he never heard him utter three sentences together. Jefferson was nonetheless known for a masterly pen, and in June 1776 he was named to the committee to prepare the Declaration of Independence alongside Adams, the elder Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman and Robert Livingston, which entrusted him with the draft. Adams reflected in his autobiography that eloquence in public assemblies was not the surest road to fame, pointing to the reserve of Washington, Franklin and Jefferson.
real_life_example.explanation: Jefferson let senior and more forceful members carry the floor, and his restraint left him trusted with the most important writing of all.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the restraint that does not rush to speak first among wiser elders, and Jefferson's quiet in Congress earned him the confidence of his seniors.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tamil:
ஆற்றின் நிலைதளர்ந் தற்றே வியன்புலம்
ஏற்றுணர்வார் முன்னர் இழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Aatrin nilaithalarndh thatre viyanpulam
Etrunarvaar munnar izhukku.
meaning: Making a mistake in speech in front of people who understand many subjects is like slipping and falling off the right path.
elementary: A spelling mistake in a note to your friend is no big deal. The same mistake in the final round of a spelling bee, in front of the judges, feels like tripping on stage. Mistakes count most in front of experts.
university: Viyanpulam (wide fields, meaning vast areas of learning) etrunarvaar (those who have received and understood them) are the most demanding audience there is, and an izhukku (slip or lapse) before them is compared to aatrin nilaithalarndhatru, losing one’s footing on the way. Commentators disagree about aaru. Parimelazhagar and most modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) take it as the path of right conduct, so a verbal slip before the learned is as disgraceful as a good man’s moral lapse. Puliyur Kesikan takes aaru as a river and reads the image as a swimmer losing his footing mid-stream, so the lapse is dangerous and hard to recover from. The kural thus explains why 715’s restraint matters: before the learned the cost of error is very high. The text agrees in all sources; the sandhi text reads “ஆற்றி னிலைதளர்ந் தற்றே வியன்புல மேற்றுணர்வார் முன்ன ரிழுக்கு”.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At King Janaka’s sacrifice, the boy-sage Ashtavakra challenges Bandin, the court debater who had defeated and drowned many scholars. In the debate before the learned assembly Ashtavakra wins, and Bandin, now silenced, meets the same fate he had imposed on others.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata tells how a famous debater’s failure before an assembly of the learned brought his complete downfall.
hinduism.tie_back: Bandin’s fall is the Kural’s image made literal: a slip before the learned is a fatal loss of footing.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Sections 132-134 (story of Ashtavakra), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.”
christianity.explanation: James treats stumbling in speech as the hardest failing to avoid, and calls the person who never slips in word perfect.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s izhukku, a slip of speech, is the stumbling James speaks of.

islam.quote_or_event: “A slave of Allah may utter a word without thinking whether it is right or wrong, he may slip down in the Fire as far away a distance equal to that between the east.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that one careless word can make a person slip and fall a great distance.
islam.tie_back: The hadith uses the same picture of a verbal slip as a fall, as the Kural does.

judaism.quote_or_event: “To slip upon a pavement is better than to slip with the tongue: so the fall of the wicked shall come speedily.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira compares a slip of the tongue with a physical fall, and judges the verbal one worse.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s own comparison, a verbal slip likened to losing one’s footing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Saccaka, a famous debater, boasts that he can make the Buddha tremble. In front of a large assembly of Licchavis he is refuted, and then sits silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head bowed, unable to reply.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta shows how a proud speaker’s reputation collapses at once when he stumbles before a discerning audience.
buddhism.tie_back: Saccaka’s humiliation is the Kural’s izhukku before the learned, a public loss of footing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not pervert nor render obscure (the truth); he should fabricate neither text nor meaning, being a saviour; being devoted to the Teacher and considering well his words, he delivers faithfully what he has learned.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain expounder must speak with great care, because a slip in handing on the doctrine distorts the truth that others rely on.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural compares a slip of speech before the deeply learned to falling from the path, and the Jain verse likewise treats error in learned speech as a serious lapse to guard against.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, speaking insipid words, the body and mind become insipid. He is called the most insipid of the insipid; the most insipid of the insipid is his reputation.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak warns that careless, graceless speech spoils the speaker inwardly and ruins his name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares a slip of speech before the deeply learned to losing one's footing on the path; Guru Nanak says bad speech brings a fall in one's whole standing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Thracian singer Thamyris boasted that he could out-sing the Muses themselves. In the contest he failed before them, and they maimed him and took away his gift of song.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s brief story shows how overreaching before the greatest masters of an art ends in disgrace.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Failing before the Muses, the ultimate learned audience, is the Kural’s slip before those of vast learning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates describes questioning men with a reputation for wisdom, first politicians, then poets and craftsmen, and exposing, often in front of listeners, that they did not know what they claimed to know. This earned him their lasting resentment.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows how damaging it is to have one’s claim to knowledge fail under the questioning of someone more discerning.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates’ targets suffered what the Kural warns of: a lapse exposed before a keen examiner.

real_life_example.event_title: Benjamin Disraeli's maiden speech is shouted down in the House of Commons
real_life_example.place: House of Commons, London, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Benjamin Disraeli, elected for Maidstone in 1837, was already ridiculed for his dandified appearance and affected manner when he rose to make his first speech in the House of Commons. Members heckled and mocked him, and he defiantly declared as he sat down that the time would come when they would hear him. He went on to become a celebrated parliamentary debater and, in 1868 and again from 1874, prime minister.
real_life_example.explanation: Before the most demanding audience in the country, a gifted speaker's misjudged first appearance turned into a famous humiliation that took him years to overcome.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares a slip in speech before learned and experienced people to losing one's footing on the path, and Disraeli's maiden speech was just such a fall before the Commons.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tamil:
கற்றறிந்தார் கல்வி விளங்கும் கசடறச்
சொல்தெரிதல் வல்லார் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Katrarindhaar kalvi vilangum kasadarach
Soltheridhal vallaar akaththu.
meaning: The learning of people who have studied deeply shines brightest among those who can judge words without any mistakes.
elementary: A great chess move looks like nothing special to someone who doesn’t know chess. Show it to a chess champion and they gasp, “Wow!” Your best work shines most in front of people who can understand it.
university: Vilangum (will shine, become manifest) is the key verb. Learning does not show its worth in a vacuum. It becomes visible only in the akam (midst, company) of those who are kasadara soltheridhal vallaar, able to examine words kasadara, without flaw or dross. Kasadu (impurity, dross) links back to Valluvar’s famous command in ch. 40, Kalvi (kural 391): “கற்க கசடறக் கற்பவை.” There is a pairing here: flawless study (391) meets flawless hearing (717). Commentators note that this kural balances 716. The expert audience that punishes a slip is also the only audience that can properly recognise real learning. The ytamizh/thirukkural.net text “சொல்தெரிதல்” and the sandhi form “சொற்றெரிதல்” are the same word.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Janaka offers a thousand cows with gold on their horns to the most learned of the Brahmins at his sacrifice. Yajnavalkya claims them, and his learning is tested one after another by the finest scholars of the court, including Asvala, Artabhaga, Uddalaka and Gargi. His answers stand, and the assembly acknowledges his mastery.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad shows a sage’s learning fully displayed only when it is tested by a court of equally learned questioners.
hinduism.tie_back: Yajnavalkya’s learning shines because his hearers can judge flawlessly, which is exactly what the Kural says.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Book 3 (trans. F. Max Müller)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers.”
