christianity.explanation: The twelve-year-old Jesus sits among the teachers in the Temple, listening and asking questions, and those learned men are amazed by his understanding.
christianity.tie_back: His wisdom shows most clearly among the doctors of the law, hearers able to recognise it, as the Kural says.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘Are those who know equal to those who do not know?’ Only they will remember [who are] people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asserts the difference between the knowing and the unknowing, and says only people of understanding will take the lesson to heart.
islam.tie_back: Only “people of understanding” can take in what is said, just as the Kural says learning shines only before skilled judges.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud (Taanit 7a) applies this verse to Torah scholars, who sharpen each other in study. Learning grows keen among peers able to test it.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s learning that shines among skilled judges of words is the rabbinic picture of scholars sharpening scholars.
judaism.source: Proverbs 27:17 (KJV), as applied in Babylonian Talmud Taanit 7a

buddhism.quote_or_event: Before their famous dialogue, the monk Nagasena tells King Milinda that he will discuss only if the king talks as scholars do, where each side is corrected without anger, and not as kings do, who punish anyone who contradicts them. The king agrees, and the dialogue that follows shows Nagasena’s learning at its best.
buddhism.explanation: The Milindapanha makes a discerning, fair-minded partner the condition for real learning to appear.
buddhism.tie_back: Nagasena’s insistence on a “scholar’s” hearing is the Kural’s point: learning shines only before those able to judge words well.
buddhism.source: Milindapanha, Book 2, ch. 1 (trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, The Questions of King Milinda)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As water put into a shell shines with a doubled brilliancy, so do the piety, fame, and knowledge of a very learned monk.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on 'The Very Learned' praises learning that shines all the more because of what holds it, opening a long series of similes for the learned monk.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says learning shines brightest in the company of those who can judge words without flaw, and the Jain image likewise has learning gaining 'doubled brilliancy' from a fitting setting.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone purchase the gem, O Nanak, who have virtue in their purse. Those who do not appreciate the value of the jewels, wander like blind men in the world.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad says the jewel (the Name and the Guru's word) is valued only by those qualified to recognise it; others pass it by like the blind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says learning shines only among those able to judge words flawlessly; Guru Angad says jewels are prized only by those who can appraise them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the court of the Phaeacians, Odysseus tells the story of his wanderings. King Alcinous praises him for telling his tale with the skill of a bard, and the whole hall sits spellbound.
greek_mythology.explanation: Among refined and discerning hosts, Odysseus’s wisdom and eloquence are fully recognised.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus’s gifts shine among hearers able to value them, as the Kural says learning does.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Seventh Letter, Plato writes that real understanding cannot be handed over like other subjects. It flashes out suddenly, like light kindled from a leaping spark, only after long shared inquiry and friendly questioning between capable minds.
philosophy.explanation: Plato holds that insight shows itself only in the company of fit fellow-inquirers.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s vilangum (shines forth) matches Plato’s image of learning lit up among worthy interlocutors.

real_life_example.event_title: Hilbert and Klein bring Emmy Noether to Gottingen
real_life_example.event: In 1915 the leading Gottingen mathematicians David Hilbert and Felix Klein invited Emmy Noether, then working without pay at Erlangen, to help with mathematical problems connected with the theory of relativity, because they needed an expert in invariant theory. She soon proved the result now called Noether's theorem, linking symmetries in physics to conservation laws, which Einstein praised for its penetrating mathematical thinking. Because women could not then obtain the habilitation, her courses were advertised under Hilbert's name while he and Klein fought the university authorities, and in 1919 she was finally made a Privatdozent.
real_life_example.explanation: Noether's brilliance, long unrecognised in its official standing, was recognised and championed by the very people best able to judge it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says real learning shines among those who can judge words flawlessly, and Noether's genius found its proper setting among the greatest mathematicians of Gottingen.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tamil:
உணர்வ துடையார்முன் சொல்லல் வளர்வதன்
பாத்தியுள் நீர்சொரிந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Unarva thudaiyaarmun sollal valarvadhan
Paaththiyul neersorindh thatru.
meaning: Speaking to people who can understand is like watering a garden bed where plants are already growing.
elementary: Watering a plant that is already sprouting makes it shoot up fast. Watering an empty patch of dirt does nothing. Telling good ideas to someone who wants to learn is like watering the sprout.
university: This kural is the positive counterpart of the chapter’s closing image (720). Unarvadhu udaiyaar are people who have understanding, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah stress that they understand for themselves (thaame unargindra), even without being told. Speaking to them is like watering (neer sorindhatru) a paaththi, a small irrigated garden bed, in which the crop is valarvadhu, already growing of its own accord. The image is agricultural and exact: the water does not create growth but speeds up growth that is already under way, so the speaker’s words bear fruit at once. Parimelazhagar takes this as the assembly of equals in learning, and so completes the scheme begun in 714. The text agrees across sources; the sandhi text reads “உணர்வ துடையார்முற் சொல்லல்” and “பாத்தியு ணீர்சொரிந் தற்று”.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Mundaka Upanishad teaches that when a student has approached the teacher properly, with a calm mind and controlled senses, the wise teacher should fully impart to him the knowledge of Brahman, by which the imperishable is known.
hinduism.explanation: Teaching is to be poured out fully on the prepared and receptive student.
hinduism.tie_back: The prepared student is the Kural’s growing crop, and the teacher’s words are the water that makes it flourish.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the sower, the word bears fruit only in the hearer who understands, the good soil.
christianity.tie_back: The same agricultural logic as the Kural: words bear fruit in understanding hearers.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of guidance and knowledge with which Allah has sent me is like abundant rain falling on the earth, some of which was fertile soil that absorbed rain water and brought forth vegetation and grass in abundance.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares his teaching to rain. Fertile ground absorbs it and flourishes, while barren ground gains nothing.
islam.tie_back: The receptive soil that turns rain into growth is the Kural’s bed of growing crops.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah rules that the most profound teachings, such as the Work of the Chariot, may be expounded only to a student who is wise and understands on his own.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic tradition keeps its deepest instruction for hearers who already have the understanding to take it further for themselves.
judaism.tie_back: “Understands on his own” is almost exactly the Kural’s unarvadhu udaiyaar, those whose understanding already grows by itself.
judaism.source: Mishnah Chagigah 2:1 (Sefaria, William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz edition)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the parable of the plants, one great cloud rains equally on all the herbs, shrubs and trees of the earth. Each takes up the water according to its own nature and size and grows accordingly, and in the same way beings receive the Buddha’s single teaching according to their capacity.
buddhism.explanation: The Lotus Sutra pictures teaching as rain whose effect depends on how far each plant has grown.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s water poured on growing crops is the Lotus Sutra’s rain on plants that are ready to take it in.
buddhism.source: Saddharma-pundarika (Lotus Sutra), Chapter 5 ‘On Plants’, trans. H. Kern

jainism.quote_or_event: “(The teacher) takes delight in instructing a clever (pupil), just as the rider (in managing) a well-broken horse; but he tires to instruct a foolish (pupil), just as the rider (tires to manage) an unbroken horse.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana says that teaching depends on the receiver: instruction given to a capable hearer is a pleasure and bears fruit, while instruction given to a dull one wears out the teacher.
jainism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's point that speaking to those who already understand is like watering plants that are already growing.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Word is the tree; the garden of the heart is the farm; tend it, and irrigate it with the Lord's Love.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak pictures the Guru's word as a tree planted in the garden of a receptive heart and watered with love.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural likens speaking to people who understand to watering a bed where plants are already growing; Guru Nanak likewise pictures the word flourishing in a watered, prepared heart.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 354, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Athena, disguised as Mentor, counsels the young Telemachus. Because he is ready to listen, her advice quickly takes root: he calls an assembly, sets sail to seek news of his father, and grows into a man fit to stand beside Odysseus.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess’s words fall on a mind already beginning to mature, and they produce rapid growth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Telemachus is the growing crop, and Athena’s counsel is the water that makes it flourish.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates says the true teacher, like a sensible farmer, chooses a fitting soul and plants in it words joined with knowledge. Such words can defend themselves and bear seed that grows again in other minds.
philosophy.explanation: Plato contrasts this real cultivation of receptive minds with scattering words carelessly, as in writing or in pleasure-gardens that come to nothing.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s farmer sowing in a fit soul is the Kural’s watering of the growing bed.

real_life_example.event_title: Einstein translates and extends Satyendra Nath Bose's paper
real_life_example.place: Dacca (now Dhaka, Bangladesh) and Berlin, Germany
real_life_example.event: In 1924 Satyendra Nath Bose, a physicist at Dacca University, wrote a short paper deriving Planck's radiation law without relying on classical physics; he sent it to Philosophical Magazine but heard nothing back. He then sent it to Albert Einstein, who received it in June 1924, recognised that it solved a problem he had struggled with, translated it into German himself and had it published in Zeitschrift fur Physik in August 1924. Einstein quickly extended Bose's method to material particles, leading to what became known as Bose-Einstein statistics and the prediction of Bose-Einstein condensation.
real_life_example.explanation: Bose's ideas, ignored by one journal, bore fruit almost at once when they reached a mind ready to understand and develop them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural likens speaking to people of understanding to watering a garden bed where the plants are already growing, and Bose's work flourished the moment it reached Einstein.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tamil:
புல்லவையுள் பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லற்க நல்லவையுள்
நன்கு செலச்சொல்லு வார்.
transliteration:
Pullavaiyul pochchaandhum sollarka nallavaiyul
Nanku selach chollu vaar.
meaning: People who can speak good things well to a good group should never, even by mistake, speak about them to a low-minded group.
elementary: You wouldn’t show your best drawing to kids who you know will just scribble on it and laugh. Save it for people who will really look at it. Good words should be shared with good listeners.
university: Pullavai (a low or mean assembly, from pul, grass, meaning petty or base) is set against nallavai (a good assembly). Pochchaandhum (even through forgetfulness) uses the root of ch. 54, Pochchaavaamai (Unforgetfulness): the speaker is not to slip, even for a moment, into speaking before an unworthy audience. Nanku sela sollu (to speak so that it goes in well) describes speech that enters and settles in the hearers’ minds. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as speech that is “fixed in the mind” (manadhil padhiyumaaru). The ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net texts print “நன்குசலச்”, apparently a corruption. The sandhi text “நன்கு செலச்சொல்லு வார்” and P. A. Muthukrishnan’s musical setting (“நன்கு செலச் சொல்லுவார்”, quoted on thirukkural.net) support the reading செல, which Parimelazhagar’s gloss (to cause to enter) also requires.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “This confidential knowledge may not be explained to those who are not austere, or devoted, or engaged in devotional service, nor to one who is envious of Me.”
hinduism.explanation: At the end of the Gita, Krishna forbids Arjuna to pass on its teaching to the undisciplined, the uninterested, or the hostile.
hinduism.tie_back: Krishna’s ban on teaching the unfit hearer is the Kural’s refusal to speak in the pullavai.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.67 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And whosoever shall not receive you, nor hear your words, when ye depart out of that house or city, shake off the dust of your feet.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells the disciples not to keep pressing their message on those who refuse to hear it, but to move on.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it advises withholding speech from an unreceptive audience.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when they hear ill speech, they turn away from it and say, ‘For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace will be upon you; we seek not the ignorant.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises believers who withdraw courteously from vain and hostile talk instead of engaging with it.
islam.tie_back: “We seek not the ignorant” is the Kural’s refusal to hold forth in the mean assembly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb warns that engaging a fool on his own terms lowers the wise to his level.
judaism.tie_back: Speaking in the pullavai risks this lowering, which is why the Kural forbids it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the wanderer Vacchagotta asks the Buddha whether there is a self or not, the Buddha stays silent. He later explains to Ananda that either answer would only have confused Vacchagotta further or confirmed a wrong view.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha holds back even true teaching when the listener is not in a state to receive it properly.
buddhism.tie_back: His silence before an unready hearer is the Kural’s rule: do not speak good words where they cannot take root.
buddhism.source: Ananda Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 44.10 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “When reprimanded a wise man should not be angry, but he should be of a forbearing mood; he should not associate, laugh, and play with mean men.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain disciple is told to keep away from low company and not to take part in its idle talk and amusement.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns the good speaker never, even by forgetting himself, to hold forth before a mean assembly, and the Jain verse likewise keeps the disciplined person out of mean men's company.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Don't argue with fools.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak's brief counsel in Asa ki Vaar is not to waste words in dispute with the foolish.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells those who speak well in good assemblies never, even by forgetfulness, to speak in a mean one; Guru Nanak likewise says not to spend words on fools.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (pauri 19), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a cock scratching for food finds a precious jewel. He says that it may be valuable to someone who prizes it, but he would rather have a single grain of barley.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable shows a treasure wasted on a finder who cannot value it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Good words spoken in a mean assembly are the jewel before the cock, a treasure the hearers will not value.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Cock and the Jewel’ (trans. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never call yourself a philosopher, nor talk a great deal among the unlearned about theorems, but act conformably to them. … Thus, therefore, do you likewise not show theorems to the unlearned, but the actions produced by them after they have been digested.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the student not to lay out philosophical principles before people who cannot receive them, but to keep silent among them and show the fruit of those principles in conduct.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts hold that worthy teaching should not be spoken before an audience unfit to receive it.

real_life_example.event_title: Pablo Casals refuses to perform in countries that recognised Franco's regime
real_life_example.event: The Catalan cellist Pablo Casals, an outspoken opponent of fascism, settled in Prades in French Catalonia and refused to return to Spain after the Spanish Civil War. In 1946 he announced his retirement from public performance in protest at worldwide recognition of the Franco regime, extending his boycott to countries such as the United States and the United Kingdom that maintained relations with Spain. He resumed public performance in 1950 only in Prades, where the Casals Festival was founded, and later made rare exceptions such as his 1961 performance at the White House for President Kennedy.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the world's greatest musicians withheld his art from stages he considered compromised, offering it only where it could serve his convictions.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who can speak good things well in a worthy assembly should never offer them in an unworthy one, and Casals kept his music back from audiences he would not dignify with it.

adhikaram.english: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tamil:
அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்தற்றால் தங்கணத்தார்
அல்லார்முன் கோட்டி கொளல்.
transliteration:
Anganaththul ukka amizhdhatraal thanganaththaar
Allaarmun kotti kolal.
meaning: Speaking to people who are not like-minded is like spilling amrita (the drink that makes gods live forever) into a dirty drain.
elementary: Imagine pouring the most delicious juice in the world down the drain. What a waste! Explaining something wonderful to people who don’t care at all is like that. The juice was good; it just went to the wrong place.
university: The chapter closes with its most memorable image. Amizhdhu (amrita, the nectar of immortality) is ukka (spilled) into an anganam, the drain of a house’s open courtyard: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss it as an unclean courtyard, Solomon Pappaiah as a sewer. Thanganaththaar allaar are those who are not of one’s own gana (group, circle), meaning not one’s equals in learning and outlook. Kotti kolal (to hold a discourse) uses kotti, cognate with Sanskrit goshthi (assembly, learned conversation). The simile, like 718’s, is exact. Nectar is not spoiled by being spilled, but it can never be recovered or drunk, so it is wasted. The sources differ slightly on one form: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read தங்கணத்தார், while the sandhi-joined text reads “தங்கணத்த ரல்லார்முற்” (தங்கணத்தர்). The meaning is unaffected.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Even in times of dire distress a teacher of the Veda should rather die with his knowledge than sow it in barren soil.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the teacher that it is better to take his learning to the grave than to waste it on unfit recipients. The verse before it compares such teaching to good seed thrown on barren land.
hinduism.tie_back: Seed in barren soil and nectar in the gutter are the same waste: precious knowledge poured where it cannot be received.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns against offering sacred things to those who will only trample them, and may turn on the giver.
christianity.tie_back: Pearls before swine and nectar in the gutter are twin images of treasure wasted on the unworthy.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts at what hears nothing but calls and cries … deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not understand.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an likens preaching to those who will not understand to a herdsman shouting at animals that hear only noise.
islam.tie_back: Words wasted on hearers who cannot take them in are the Kural’s spilled nectar.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Speak not in the ears of a fool: for he will despise the wisdom of thy words.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb forbids speaking wisdom to a fool, who will only scorn it.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s conclusion in plain words: wisdom poured before the wrong hearers is wasted.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Just after his awakening, the Buddha at first hesitates to teach. He reflects that the Dhamma is deep and subtle, and that a generation delighting in attachment would not understand it, which would only weary him. He agrees to teach only when he sees that some beings have little dust in their eyes.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha weighs whether his teaching would simply be wasted on listeners unable to receive it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s hesitation is the Kural’s worry about pouring nectar where it will be lost.
buddhism.source: Ayacana Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 6.1 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a pig leaves a trough filled with grain to feed on faeces, so a brute (of a man) turns away from virtue, and takes to evil ways.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana uses this coarse image for the unfit pupil who turns from the good food of instruction to filth, and in the next verses says such a pupil is driven away.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's nectar spilled into a gutter and the Jain pig leaving grain for filth both picture something precious wasted on those unfit to receive it.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you take Ambrosial Nectar and irrigate the neem tree with it, still, says Kabeer, its natural qualities are not changed.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir pictures nectar poured on the bitter neem: the nectar is wasted and the neem stays bitter. Commentators such as Sahib Singh read the hymn as warning against pressing spiritual teaching on the unreceptive.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural likens speaking before those not of one's kind to nectar spilled into a gutter; Kabir likewise shows nectar wasted on something that cannot receive it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 481, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cassandra, given true prophecy by Apollo but cursed never to be believed, foretells the murder of Agamemnon and her own death. The elders of Argos listen, but they cannot grasp or accept her words.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her true and precious speech falls on hearers who cannot receive it, and it is completely lost.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Cassandra’s wasted prophecy is nectar spilled into the gutter, the Kural’s picture of words lost on the wrong audience.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “As Heraclitus says ‘asses would prefer sweepings to gold’; for food is pleasanter than gold to asses.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle quotes Heraclitus to show that different kinds of creatures take pleasure in different things. The unfit cannot value what is precious.
philosophy.tie_back: Gold before asses is the Kural’s nectar before those not of one’s kind: worth that the audience cannot recognise.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10.5 (trans. W. D. Ross), quoting Heraclitus (DK B9)

real_life_example.event_title: Mendel's laws of heredity are presented in Brunn and then overlooked
real_life_example.event: After years of experiments crossing garden peas, the Augustinian monk Gregor Mendel presented his results on the inheritance of traits to the Brunn Natural Science Society in 1865, and they were published in 1866 in the society's relatively obscure proceedings. The work, which laid the mathematical foundation of genetics, remained largely overlooked during his lifetime. It was rediscovered around 1900 by Carl Correns, Hugo de Vries and Erich Tschermak, some fifteen years after Mendel's death.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the most important discoveries in biology was offered to listeners and readers who did not grasp its value, and it lay unused for a generation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares speaking before those who cannot share one's understanding to nectar spilled into a gutter, not spoiled but wasted, much as Mendel's insight lay unused for thirty-five years.

tamil:
வகையறிந்து வல்லவை வாய்சோரார் சொல்லின்
தொகையறிந்த தூய்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Vakaiyarindhu vallavai vaaisoraar sollin
Thokaiyarindha thooimai yavar.
meaning: People with pure minds who know words well and understand their listeners will not stumble when they speak before a powerful group.
elementary: Imagine you know every line of the school play, and you have peeked out to see who is in the audience. Because you know your words and you know who is listening, your voice stays steady. Knowing your words and knowing your listeners keeps you from getting tongue-tied.
university: This couplet opens Avaiyañcāmai (“not fearing the assembly”). It pairs with the chapter before it, Avaiyaṟital (knowing the assembly), inside the Amaicciyal, the section on ministers. Parimelazhagar reads vakai aṟintu (“knowing the kind”) as first working out what sort of assembly one is in. Vallavai is the assembly of the able or powerful, and vāy sōrār means “their mouths will not slip,” that is, they will not falter or make mistakes out of fear. Sollin tokai aṟinda tūymaiyavar are “the pure who know the tokai (range or classification) of words,” which commentators connect with a grammarian’s knowledge of word-classes and how to use them. So the chapter’s first answer to stage fright is skill combined with integrity. The sandhi-joined text reads “சொல்லின் றொகையறிந்த,” where றொ is simply ன் fused with தொ, and the words are unchanged.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking truthfully and beneficially and in avoiding speech that offends. One should also recite the Vedas regularly.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a discipline of speech: words should be true and helpful, should not wound, and should rest on steady study of scripture.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita joins pure speech to learning in the same way the Kural praises “the pure who know the range of words.”
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to speak graciously and with some bite, so that they can give each person a fitting answer.
christianity.tie_back: Knowing how to answer “every man” is close to the Kural’s knowing what kind of assembly one faces.

islam.quote_or_event: “My Lord, expand for me my breast [with assurance] … And untie the knot from my tongue / That they may understand my speech.”
islam.explanation: Before facing Pharaoh’s court, Moses asks God to give him confidence and to free his tongue so that his words will be understood.
islam.tie_back: This is a prayer for exactly what the Kural describes: not stumbling in speech before a powerful gathering.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wise man does not speak before one who is greater than he in wisdom, And does not break into his fellow’s speech; And is not hasty to answer; He asks what is relevant, and he answers to the point”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah lists the traits of a wise person in discussion: he respects rank, does not interrupt, does not rush, and speaks to the point.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that well-ordered speech in learned company depends on knowing the setting and knowing how words work.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The Realized One knows the right time to speak so as to explain what he knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, but which is disliked by others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha sorts speech by whether it is true, whether it helps, and whether it is welcome. He speaks only what is true and beneficial, and he chooses the right moment.
buddhism.tie_back: This amounts to knowing the kinds of words and the kind of occasion, which the Kural says keeps a speaker from faltering.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarājakumāra Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk should be modest though he be of a fearless mind; he should expound the Syâdvâda; he should use the two (permitted) kinds of speech, living among virtuous men, impartial and wise.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga's lecture on the Nirgrantha tells the teaching monk to pair a fearless mind with modesty, to speak in the qualified, many-sided manner of syadvada, and to use only the permitted kinds of speech.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's pure-minded speaker who knows the full range of words and does not stumble before a powerful assembly matches this monk, who is fearless yet modest and weighs every word he speaks among others.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else - says Nanak, listen, mind: call him spiritually wise.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur makes fearlessness, neither inspiring fear nor yielding to it, the mark of the truly wise (giani).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who know the full range of words will not falter before a powerful gathering; Guru Tegh Bahadur says true wisdom is shown precisely by not being afraid of anyone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 16), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says the Muses pour sweet dew on the tongue of a king they favour. His words then flow gently, he speaks surely in the assembly, and he quickly settles even a great quarrel.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod’s picture, a ruler who speaks well in public has been given the gift of the Muses, and the people look to him when he gives judgement.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Speaking steadily and without error before an assembly is the ideal the Kural describes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that a true orator must know the different kinds of souls and the kinds of speech that suit each one, and must be able to see, in the moment, what sort of listener is in front of him.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, the art of speaking rests on classifying both listeners and speeches and matching one to the other.
philosophy.tie_back: This is very close to vakai aṟintu, knowing the kind of assembly, joined with knowing the classes of words.

real_life_example.event_title: Frederick Douglass delivers What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?
real_life_example.place: Corinthian Hall, Rochester, New York, United States
real_life_example.event: At the invitation of the Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society, Frederick Douglass addressed an audience of five to six hundred people, each paying a small admission fee, at Corinthian Hall on 5 July 1852. He praised the signers of the Declaration of Independence as great men and then set out how the freedoms celebrated on Independence Day were denied to enslaved Americans. The address became the most celebrated of his speeches.
real_life_example.explanation: Douglass understood exactly the audience before him, people proud of the nation's founding, and built his argument on their own reverence for its ideals.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who know the full range of words and first take the measure of the assembly will not falter before it, and Douglass's speech is a model of reading an audience and speaking without faltering.

tamil:
கற்றாருள் கற்றார் எனப்படுவர் கற்றார்முன்
கற்ற செலச்சொல்லு வார்.
transliteration:
Katraarul katraar enappaduvar katraarmun
Katra selachchollu vaar.
meaning: People who can share what they have learned with other learned people, in a way that really reaches them, are called the most learned of all.
elementary: Lots of kids can read a book. The one who can explain it clearly to the whole class, even with the teacher listening, is the one everyone calls the real expert.
university: The line repeats kaṟṟār (“the learned”) four times. The word-play mirrors the idea that learning is measured among the learned. The key term is cela-c-colluvār, “those who speak so that it goes (cel-)” into the hearers. Parimelazhagar glosses it as speaking so that the matter enters the listeners’ minds, and Mu. Varadarasanar likewise says “so that it settles in their hearts.” The judgement is about rank: standing among scholars comes from being able to explain things well before one’s peers, not from private learning. The sandhi-joined text reads “கற்றாருட் கற்றா ரெனப்படுவர் கற்றார்முற்,” in which ட் and ற் are sound-changes of ள் and ன் before க.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Janaka offers a thousand cows, with gold on their horns, to the most learned Brahmin at his sacrifice. When the others hesitate, Yajnavalkya claims the cows and then answers one questioner after another from the assembled scholars, including Gargi.
hinduism.explanation: Yajnavalkya’s standing as the foremost knower is settled in public, by answering the learned in front of the learned.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s “most learned of the learned” shown as an actual event.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.1-3.9 (trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions. And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers.”
christianity.explanation: The twelve-year-old Jesus sits among the teachers of the Law, listening, asking and answering, and they are amazed.
christianity.tie_back: A young learner speaks before the learned and is recognised as learned himself.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘O Adam, inform them of their names.’ And when he had informed them of their names, He said, ‘Did I not tell you that I know the unseen [aspects] of the heavens and the earth?’”
islam.explanation: The angels have admitted that they know only what they were taught. Adam, who has been taught the names of things, then lays out that knowledge before them.
islam.tie_back: Knowledge proves its worth when it is set out before a learned assembly, here the angels.

judaism.quote_or_event: The sons of Bathyra, leaders in Jerusalem, could not recall whether the Passover offering overrides the Sabbath. Hillel, a newcomer from Babylonia, proved the answer before them by formal reasoning and tradition, and they appointed him their head (Nasi).
judaism.explanation: Hillel’s leadership was granted because he could lay out his learning convincingly before the learned.
judaism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s claim: those who can explain before scholars are ranked first among scholars.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “That monk who has control over his tongue, is moderate in speech, unassuming and who explains the Teaching in both letter and spirit — whatever he says is pleasing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises the monk who can expound the teaching accurately and pleasingly.
buddhism.tie_back: Its standard of excellence, explaining the teaching so that it is well received, matches the Kural’s cela-c-collutal.

jainism.quote_or_event: “(If the pupil does not understand his short explanation), he should explain at greater length. When the pupil has heard it, he will correctly understand the Truth.”
jainism.explanation: The same lecture tells the teacher to fit his explanation to the hearer and to lengthen it when a short account does not get through, so that the listener really grasps the truth.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises those who speak so that their learning actually reaches the hearers; the Jain teacher is likewise judged by whether his words reach and settle in the listener.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Siddhas formed an assembly; sitting in their Yogic postures, they shouted, ‘Salute this gathering of Saints.’ … I offer my salutation to the One who is true, infinite and incomparably beautiful.”
sikhism.explanation: Siddh Gosht opens with Guru Nanak facing an assembly of learned yogis; he answers their questions one by one, setting out his teaching so that it reaches them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls 'most learned of the learned' those who can set out their learning before the learned so that it reaches them; Siddh Gosht shows Guru Nanak doing this before the Siddhas' assembly.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 938, Raag Ramkali, Siddh Gosht, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “when he raised his voice, and the words came driving from his deep chest like winter snow before the wind, then there was none to touch him, and no man thought further of what he looked like.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Antenor remembers Odysseus coming to Troy as an envoy. At first he stood stiff with his eyes on the ground, but once he began to speak no one could match him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus proved himself foremost by speaking before an assembly of Trojan elders.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Quintilian takes up Cato’s definition of the orator as “a good man skilled in speaking” (vir bonus dicendi peritus) and makes it the goal of his whole course of education.
philosophy.explanation: For Quintilian, the complete man of learning is the one who can bring his knowledge and character to bear in public speech.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats effective speech before an audience as the crown of learning.

real_life_example.event_title: David Hilbert presents his problems to the International Congress of Mathematicians
real_life_example.event: At the second International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris, David Hilbert gave a talk in which he described ten problems from a list of twenty-three unsolved questions he believed would shape mathematics in the coming century. The full list appeared in the published paper. Several of the problems became central to twentieth-century mathematics, and the organisers later placed his paper among the plenary lectures because of its importance.
real_life_example.explanation: Before an audience of the world's leading mathematicians, Hilbert set out his vision so clearly that it directed much of their research for generations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the most learned of the learned are those who can present their learning before the learned so that it truly reaches them, which is what Hilbert's address achieved.

tamil:
பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் அரியர்
அவையகத்து அஞ்சா தவர்.
transliteration:
Pakaiyakaththuch chaavaar eliyar ariyar
Avaiyakaththu anjaa thavar.
meaning: Many people are ready to die fighting among enemies. Few people can stand in front of a group and speak without fear.
elementary: Lots of people are brave in a game or on the playground. Standing up in front of the whole school to say what you really think takes a different kind of courage, and fewer people have it.
university: The couplet is built as a sharp contrast: pakai-y-akattu (“inside the enemy ranks”) against avai-y-akattu (“inside the assembly”), and eḷiyar (“easy to find, many”) against ariyar (“rare”). Parimelazhagar takes the first group as warriors who throw themselves fearlessly among the enemy and die, and the second as those who are unafraid before the learned. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the first as “many in the world.” The couplet ranks civil courage above martial courage, a bold claim in a culture whose puṟam poetry celebrated heroic death. The sandhi-joined text “பகையகத்துச் சாவா ரெளிய ரரிய / ரவையகத் தஞ்சா தவர்” divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Draupadi is dragged into the Kuru assembly hall after the dice game and asks whether she was lawfully staked. The great warriors and elders present, men who would later die bravely at Kurukshetra, sit silent. Only the young Vikarna, and Vidura, speak up for her.
hinduism.explanation: Heroes who feared nothing on the battlefield could not bring themselves to speak for justice in the assembly.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point in dramatic form: many will die in battle, few will speak without fear in council.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta sub-parva), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Brought before the high council, two fishermen speak so boldly that the learned rulers are astonished.
christianity.tie_back: Fearless speech before a council is rare enough to make the members marvel, just as the Kural says such speakers are rare.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best fighting (jihad) in the path of Allah is (to speak) a word of justice to an oppressive ruler.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ranks speaking a just word to a tyrant above other kinds of striving, including armed struggle.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it places courageous speech before power above courage on the battlefield.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4344 (graded sahih by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: “and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law; and if I perish, I perish.”
judaism.explanation: Esther decides to enter the Persian king’s court unsummoned, which could mean death, in order to plead for her people.
judaism.tie_back: Speaking before a throne asks more courage than the Kural’s easy battlefield death, and Esther finds it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Sariputta that there are eight kinds of assembly: nobles, brahmins, householders, ascetics, and four orders of gods. He recalls entering hundreds of assemblies of nobles, sitting and talking with them, and seeing no ground for fear or timidity to arise in him.
buddhism.explanation: Fearlessness in every kind of assembly (vesārajja, self-assurance) is listed among the Buddha’s marks of greatness.
buddhism.tie_back: Being fearless in the assembly is presented as rare and admirable, as the Kural says.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 12, Mahāsīhanāda Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Monks who equal the ocean in depth, who are difficult to overcome, are frightened by nobody (or nothing), and are not easily assailed, who are full of extensive learning and take care of themselves, will go to the highest place, after their Karman has been annihilated.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture 'The Very Learned' compares the learned monk to heroes, kings and the ocean, and closes by naming fearlessness ('frightened by nobody') as a mark of deep learning.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says fearless speakers in an assembly are rarer than men willing to die among enemies; the Jain text also holds fearlessness joined to learning to be a rare and high attainment.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Nanak speaks the Word of Truth; he proclaims the Truth at this, the right time.”
sikhism.explanation: This closes the Tilang hymn in which Guru Nanak openly describes the slaughter of Babur's invasion; Sikh tradition remembers him speaking the truth while armies raged.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says many will die among enemies but few can stand fearless in an assembly; Guru Nanak's courage was to speak the truth openly in a time of terror.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Son of Tydeus, in war your prowess is beyond question, and in council you excel all who are of your own years”
greek_mythology.explanation: Agamemnon proposes to give up and sail home, and everyone sits silent until the young warrior Diomedes rises and rebukes the king. Old Nestor then praises him for being brave both in war and in council.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In a room of silent chieftains, Diomedes shows the rarer courage of the council.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “forsook his post, cast away his arms, and ran away most disgracefully”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch says that Demosthenes, the boldest speaker in the Athenian assembly, fled from the battle of Chaeronea.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the mirror image of the Kural. Courage in council and courage in battle are separate virtues, and a person can have one without the other.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Demosthenes 20 (trans. Bernadotte Perrin)

real_life_example.event_title: Margaret Chase Smith delivers her Declaration of Conscience
real_life_example.place: United States Senate, Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: Senator Margaret Chase Smith of Maine, then the only woman in the Senate and a first-term member of Senator Joseph McCarthy's own party, rose in the Senate chamber to deliver a fifteen-minute speech criticising the use of the Senate for unproved charges and character attacks. McCarthy sat two rows behind her, and on her way to the chamber he had reminded her of his influence over convention votes. Six Republican colleagues joined her Declaration of Conscience, and McCarthy later had her removed from the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.
real_life_example.explanation: At a time when many senators feared McCarthy, Smith chose to speak against him in front of the whole Senate and accepted the political cost.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those willing to face death among enemies are many, but those who stand fearless in an assembly are rare, and Smith's speech is a celebrated example of that rarer courage.

tamil:
கற்றார்முன் கற்ற செலச்சொல்லித் தாம்கற்ற
மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்.
transliteration:
Katraarmun katra selachchollith thaamkatra
Mikkaarul mikka kolal.
meaning: Share what you have learned with learned people so it reaches them. Then, from people who know even more, learn the best of what they know.
elementary: Share what you know in class. Then listen to the teacher and the older kids who know even more. Speaking up and listening both help you grow.
university: The couplet repeats the formula kaṟṟār mun kaṟṟa cela-c-colli from 722 and adds a second duty: mikkāruḷ mikka koḷal, “take the surplus from those who surpass you.” Parimelazhagar reads mikkār as those superior in learning and mikka as whatever their learning holds beyond one’s own. The ytamizh commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) agree. Speaking before the learned is therefore not a performance but one part of a cycle of learning: speak, be tested, learn more. The sandhi-joined text has “தாங்கற்ற” and “மிக்காருண்” for தாம்கற்ற and மிக்காருள்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just try to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him submissively and render service unto him. The self-realized soul can impart knowledge unto you because he has seen the truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna to seek out those who know more and to learn from them through questions and service.
hinduism.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s second half: take the greater knowledge from those who surpass you.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 4.34 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly.”
christianity.explanation: Apollos, eloquent and mighty in the scriptures, preached boldly. Priscilla and Aquila, who understood more, then taught him further.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s cycle almost step by step: speak boldly before the learned, then learn more from those who know more.

islam.quote_or_event: “Moses said to him, ‘May I follow you on [the condition] that you teach me from what you have been taught of sound judgement?’”
islam.explanation: Moses, a prophet already rich in knowledge, asks al-Khidr, who has knowledge Moses lacks, to teach him.
islam.tie_back: The learned take from someone greater the knowledge that goes beyond their own, which is exactly mikkāruḷ mikka koḷal.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma asks, “Who is wise?” and answers that the wise person is one who learns from every person.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah defines wisdom as an openness to keep learning from others, especially from those who know more.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats continued learning from others as the sign of true learning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada urges us to seek out wiser people who will correct us, and to treat them as a treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: Taking correction and more knowledge from those who surpass us is the second half of the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “At the right time he may put a question about living beings to a well-conducted (monk), who will explain the conduct of the virtuous; and what he hears he should follow and treasure up in his heart, thinking that it is the doctrine of the Kêvalins.”
jainism.explanation: The Nirgrantha lecture asks the monk both to teach others (I.14.5) and to go to better-informed monks with his questions, keeping what he learns from them.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's twofold duty, to present one's learning before the learned and then take from those who know more, matches the Jain monk who teaches yet keeps learning from his superiors.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.15; cf. I.14.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Let us form a partnership, and share our virtues; let us abandon our faults, and walk on the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak invites companions to pool their good qualities, each giving and receiving, and to leave their faults behind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to give what one has learned to the learned and take from those who know more; Guru Nanak's partnership of virtues is the same two-way exchange.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 766, Raag Suhi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Telemachus tells Athena, who is disguised as Mentor, that he has no practice in careful speech and that a young man feels shy about questioning an elder. She answers that some things he will think of himself and a god will prompt the rest, and he goes to question old Nestor.
greek_mythology.explanation: A shy youth overcomes his fear in order to speak before, and learn from, a man far wiser than himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He speaks before the learned and draws out knowledge from the one who knows more, both halves of the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Told by the oracle that no one was wiser than he, Socrates went to politicians, poets and craftsmen who were reputed to be wise, and questioned them in order to test the claim and to learn from them.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates’ method is to lay out questions before those with a reputation for learning in the hope of gaining from them.
philosophy.tie_back: He speaks before the learned and looks to learn more from them, even though he often found them lacking.

real_life_example.event_title: Andrew Wiles announces, then repairs, his proof of Fermat's Last Theorem
real_life_example.place: Isaac Newton Institute, Cambridge, England, and Princeton, United States
real_life_example.event: At the end of a series of three lectures at the Isaac Newton Institute in Cambridge on 23 June 1993, Andrew Wiles announced a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. Later in 1993 a referee checking the details found a serious gap. Wiles worked for about a year with his former student Richard Taylor to correct it, and the completed proof, with a companion paper by Taylor and Wiles, was published in the Annals of Mathematics in 1995.
real_life_example.explanation: Wiles put his work before the most expert audience available, accepted the flaw their scrutiny revealed, and drew on a colleague's help to complete it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks the learned to set their knowledge before the learned and then take from others whatever lies beyond their own, which is the cycle Wiles went through between his 1993 lectures and the 1995 proof.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து கற்க அவையஞ்சா
மாற்றங் கொடுத்தற் பொருட்டு.
transliteration:
Aatrin alavarindhu karka avaiyanjaa
Maatrang koduththar poruttu.
meaning: Study the right way to reason and argue, so that you can answer questions in front of a group without fear.
elementary: If you want to answer tricky questions without getting nervous, practise thinking things through step by step. When you know how to reason, a hard question doesn’t scare you.
university: Parimelazhagar reads āṟṟin aḷavu aṟintu kaṟka as “learn, by the proper path (of grammar), the aḷavai-nūl,” that is, the science of pramāṇa (means of valid knowledge), or logic. Solomon Pappaiah paraphrases it as tarka śāstra, the logic of proofs, and Kalaignar as grammar together with logic. Māṟṟam koṭuttal means “giving a reply,” so the purpose of this study is avai añcā, not fearing the assembly, above all when being cross-questioned. Some modern readers take āṟṟin aḷavu more loosely as “the measure of one’s ability” or “the scope of the subject.” The sandhi text “ஆற்றின் னளவறிந்து” shows a metrical doubling, and the words are the same.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Nyaya Sutra opens by listing sixteen subjects whose knowledge leads to the highest good. They include the means of valid knowledge (pramana), the parts of a formal argument, discussion (vada), wrangling, cavil, fallacies, and the ‘points of defeat’ at which a debater loses.
hinduism.explanation: Indian logic was built largely as a discipline for winning and judging debates in learned assemblies.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the aḷavai (pramāṇa) learning that Parimelazhagar says one must master in order to answer fearlessly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells believers to be prepared at any time to explain and defend their faith.
christianity.tie_back: Being ready to give a reasoned answer is the Kural’s māṟṟam koṭuttal.

islam.quote_or_event: “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the believer to argue in the best way, which assumes skill in reasoning and debate.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats well-trained argument as the way to face opponents.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be diligent in the study of the Torah; And know how to answer an epicuros”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar tells students to study hard so that they can reply to a skeptic.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural almost word for word in purpose: study so that you can give an answer.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the same way, when astute aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics come to see me with a question already planned, the answer just strikes me on the spot.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares himself to a charioteer who knows every part of a chariot. Because his understanding is thorough, answers come to him at once, even to questions prepared in advance.
buddhism.tie_back: Thorough learning is what makes a ready, fearless reply possible, which is the Kural’s argument.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarājakumāra Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The knowledge (of the seven categories) is attained by means of pramāṇa and naya.”
jainism.explanation: Umasvati makes valid means of knowledge (pramana) and partial standpoints (naya) the method for knowing reality, and Pujyapada's commentary adds that pramana is 'for oneself' and 'for others', with knowledge put into words serving as pramana for others.
jainism.tie_back: Parimelazhagar reads this Kural as urging study of the science of pramana, logic, so as to answer without fear in an assembly; Jainism makes that same science of pramana and naya the basis of all sound knowledge and argument.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.6, with Pujyapada's Sarvarthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak values learning that has been reflected on (vichar), because it equips a person to serve others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the student to learn the method of reasoning properly so as to answer fearlessly in assembly; Guru Nanak too asks for learning that is reflected on and put to use.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “You knew nothing neither of war nor of the arts whereby men make their mark in council, and he sent me with you to train you in all excellence of speech and action.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Phoenix reminds Achilles that he was sent to train him in speaking in council as well as in fighting.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Greek heroes also had to be trained for the assembly, which is the kind of preparation the Kural recommends.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay on studies, Bacon says that reading makes a full man, conference (discussion) makes a ready man, and writing makes an exact man.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon holds that practice in discussion is what makes a person quick and ready in reply.
philosophy.tie_back: Disciplined preparation is what produces a ready reply, as the Kural argues.

real_life_example.event_title: Thurgood Marshall, trained at Howard, wins Brown v. Board of Education
real_life_example.place: Howard University Law School and the U.S. Supreme Court, Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: Thurgood Marshall graduated first in his class from Howard University Law School in 1933, where his mentor Charles Hamilton Houston encouraged students to use the law for social change. Marshall went on to argue thirty-two cases before the U.S. Supreme Court and win twenty-nine of them. The most famous was Brown v. Board of Education, decided in 1954, in which the Court declared racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional.
real_life_example.explanation: Marshall's long training in legal reasoning allowed him to argue repeatedly and successfully before the highest court in the land.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural urges study of the proper method of reasoning so that one can answer in an assembly without fear, and Marshall's disciplined legal training made him a fearless advocate before the Supreme Court.

tamil:
வாளொடென் வன்கண்ணர் அல்லார்க்கு நூலொடென்
நுண்ணவை அஞ்சு பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Vaalodden vankannar allaarkku noolodden
Nunnavai anju pavarkku.
meaning: What use is a sword to someone who is not brave? What use are books to someone afraid of a group of sharp thinkers?
elementary: A shiny sword is no use to a knight who runs away. In the same way, knowing lots of facts doesn’t help if you’re too scared ever to say them.
university: Two parallel questions, vāḷoṭu eṉ (“what [has he] to do with a sword?”) and nūloṭu eṉ (“what with books?”), set weapons and learning side by side. Vaṉkaṇ, literally “hard eye,” means steady courage. Nuṇ-avai is an assembly of subtle, sharp minds. Solomon Pappaiah takes nūl specifically as books of logic, continuing from 725, while Kalaignar reads it broadly as learning in general. On all readings the logic is the same: just as a sword is useful only to the brave, learning is useful only to someone who can use it before the learned. Owning it without using it is the same as not owning it. The sandhi text reads “வன்கண்ண ரல்லார்க்கு நூலொடெ / னுண்ணவை யஞ்சு பவர்க்கு.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “My whole body is trembling, and my hair is standing on end. My bow Gāṇḍīva is slipping from my hand, and my skin is burning.”
hinduism.explanation: Overwhelmed by dread on the battlefield, Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, feels his famous bow slipping from his grasp.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s image made literal: the best weapon is useless in a hand that shakes with fear.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 1.29 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, the servant who buried his master’s money out of fear is condemned for letting it go unused.
christianity.tie_back: A gift left unused because of fear is worthless, just like books in the hands of someone who fears the assembly.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an likens people who carry scripture but do not act on it to a donkey loaded with books it cannot use.
islam.tie_back: Learning that is carried but never used is as useless as the books the Kural says a timid scholar owns.

judaism.quote_or_event: When God calls him to be a prophet, Jeremiah protests that he cannot speak because he is only a youth. God tells him not to fear their faces, promises to be with him, and puts words in his mouth.
judaism.explanation: The prophet is given his message and still has to overcome his fear of audiences before the message can be of any use.
judaism.tie_back: The word without the courage to speak it goes unused, which is the Kural’s point.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A learned person doesn’t have the insecurities of a person of little learning.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists learning among the qualities that make a trainee self-assured rather than timid.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism holds that learning should remove timidity, so learning that leaves a person afraid has failed at its purpose.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.101, Sārajja Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a trained Kambôga-steed, whom no noise frightens, exceeds all other horses in speed, so a very learned monk is superior to all others.”
jainism.explanation: In praising the very learned monk, the Uttaradhyayana chooses a war-horse that no noise can frighten, so fearlessness becomes part of what makes learning excel.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use books are to someone who fears a sharp assembly; the Jain simile likewise counts learning as excellent only when it comes with steady nerve.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak makes courage, being ready to give one's head, the entry condition for the path of love.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use a sword or books are to one without courage; Guru Nanak likewise says nothing on the path is of use without the courage to stake everything.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Alexandrus quailed as he saw Menelaus come forward, and shrank in fear of his life under cover of his men.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Paris, armed with bow, sword and two spears, shrinks back from Menelaus, and Hector scolds him as someone fair to look at but with neither wit nor courage.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris is the Kural’s man with a sword but without courage.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is absurd to hold that a man ought to be ashamed of being unable to defend himself with his limbs, but not of being unable to defend himself with speech and reason, when the use of rational speech is more distinctive of a human being than the use of his limbs.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that being unable to defend oneself in speech is at least as shameful as being unable to defend oneself physically.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like the Kural, puts armed self-defence and verbal self-defence side by side and counts failure in either as shameful.

real_life_example.event_title: Copernicus withholds On the Revolutions until the end of his life
real_life_example.event: Nicolaus Copernicus privately circulated an outline of his sun-centred system around 1514, but his full work, De revolutionibus, with its mathematical proofs, was not published until 1543, the year of his death. Publication came only after his supporter Georg Joachim Rheticus had printed a summary in 1540 or 1541 and then arranged the printing of the full book. In his dedication to Pope Paul III, Copernicus anticipated many of the objections his ideas would raise.
real_life_example.explanation: Scholars have taken the long delay as a sign that Copernicus was well aware of the furore his work might cause among the learned.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use books are to one who fears an assembly of sharp minds, and for decades Copernicus's knowledge sat largely unused because he hesitated to set it before the learned.

tamil:
பகையகத்துப் பேடிகை ஒள்வாள் அவையகத்து
அஞ்சு மவன்கற்ற நூல்.
transliteration:
Pakaiyakaththup pedikai olvaal avaiyakaththu
Anju mavankatra nool.
meaning: The learning of someone who is afraid to speak in front of a group is like a shiny sword in the hand of a coward facing the enemy.
elementary: Picture a very sharp, shiny sword held by someone who is shaking too hard to lift it. It looks impressive but does nothing. Learning you’re too scared to share is just like that sword.
university: This couplet turns 726 into a single simile: pēṭi kai oḷ vāḷ, “the bright sword in the hand of a pēṭi.” In classical Tamil, pēṭi means a person who is neither man nor woman, traditionally glossed as a eunuch or hermaphrodite. Pope and Drew translate it “hermaphrodite,” and Pope’s verse has “sexless being.” The martial culture of the time used such a person as a stock figure for someone unfit for battle; the image reflects that period’s assumptions, not a judgement the modern reader needs to share. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all stress uselessness: the sword is fine, but the hand fails it. The couplet also repeats 723’s pakai-y-akattu / avai-y-akattu frame. The sandhi text reads “பேடிகை யொள்வா ளவையகத் / தஞ்சு மவன்கற்ற நூல்.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, do not yield to this degrading impotence. It does not become you. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O chastiser of the enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna rebukes Arjuna’s collapse with the word klaibya, the state of a klība, a man unfit for manly action, and tells him to stand up.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita uses the same kind of image as the Kural’s pēṭi, a warrior disarmed by fear, to shame a skilled man into using his skill.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.3 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: In the garden of Gethsemane, Peter draws his sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest’s servant. Hours later, in the high priest’s courtyard, he denies knowing Jesus when a servant girl questions him.
christianity.explanation: Peter’s sword is quick, but his courage fails him the moment he has to speak before those around him.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s pairing of sword and assembly, showing that a drawn blade is no proof of courage to speak.

islam.quote_or_event: “And whoever turns his back to them on such a day, unless swerving [as a strategy] for war or joining [another] company, has certainly returned with anger [upon him] from Allah”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an condemns the fighter who flees the battle line out of fear.
islam.tie_back: An armed man who flees is the first half of the Kural’s simile.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What man is there that is fearful and faint-hearted? let him go and return unto his house, lest his brethren’s heart melt as his heart.”
judaism.explanation: Before battle, the Torah sends fearful soldiers home, because a frightened fighter is of no use and weakens everyone else.
judaism.tie_back: An armed but fearful man is useless, which is the core of the Kural’s simile.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Firstly, one warrior falters and founders at the mere sight of a cloud of dust. He doesn’t stay firm, and fails to plunge into battle.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes five kinds of warrior, the first of whom loses his nerve before the fighting even starts, and compares them to monks who give up.
buddhism.tie_back: An armed man who falters before battle is exactly the pēṭi’s useless sword.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.75, Yodhājīva Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As at the time of the battle the coward looks behind him for a ditch, thicket, or other hiding-place, (thinking that) nobody knows who will win; 'A moment's moment will bring the decision; when we lose, we shall fly.' Thus thinks the coward.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga uses the coward who plans his escape in battle as a picture of weak monks who, when tested, fall back on worldly skills instead of standing firm.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's learned man who fears the assembly is like a sharp sword in a coward's hand before the enemy; the Jain text uses the same coward-in-battle figure for someone whose equipment is wasted by lack of nerve.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.3.3.1-2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir defines the true hero as one who actually stands and fights for the right and never quits the field.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures learning held by the fearful as a bright sword in the hand of one unfit to fight, never used; Kabir's hero is the opposite, one who uses his strength and stays on the field.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maru, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Hector challenges any Achaean champion to single combat, the Greek chiefs sit silent, ashamed to refuse and afraid to accept, until old Nestor shames them and nine warriors finally stand up.
greek_mythology.explanation: Fully armed heroes are frozen by fear until they are reproached.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Weapons in the hands of men gripped by fear are worth nothing until courage returns.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus notes that a lyre player who sings and plays well on his own becomes anxious when he walks into the theatre. The cause is not a lack of skill but his wish for applause, which is not in his control.
philosophy.explanation: Fear of the audience, not lack of ability, is what makes a skilled performer falter.
philosophy.tie_back: The skill is sharp but unusable once the performer is afraid, like the gleaming sword in the Kural.

real_life_example.event_title: Henry Cavendish's electrical discoveries stay unpublished for a century
real_life_example.event: Henry Cavendish published an early version of his theory of electricity in 1771, but although he continued to work on the subject he published nothing more on it. His manuscripts, recording many careful experiments, remained with his family for about a hundred years. James Clerk Maxwell acquired them in 1874 and published an edition in 1879, showing that Cavendish had anticipated results later credited to others.
real_life_example.explanation: Results that could have advanced the science of electricity in Cavendish's lifetime lay hidden, so that others received the credit for rediscovering them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the learning of one who will not use it before the assembly to a gleaming sword in a hand that never strikes, and Cavendish's unpublished electrical work is a vivid case of fine learning left unused.

tamil:
பல்லவை கற்றும் பயமிலரே நல்லவையுள்
நன்கு செலச்சொல்லா தார்.
transliteration:
Pallavai katrum payamilare nallavaiyul
Nanku selachchollaa thaar.
meaning: No matter how many subjects they have studied, people who cannot share good things clearly with a good group are of no use.
elementary: A treasure chest that stays locked forever is no better than an empty box. If you learn lots of things but never share them clearly, nobody gets any good out of them.
university: The couplet plays on the syllable avai: pal-l-avai (“many things”) and nal-l-avai (“a good assembly”) echo each other. Payam ilar means “without benefit.” Here payam is the classical form of payaṉ (use, fruit), not the modern Tamil word for fear, a false friend worth pointing out in a chapter about fear. Nalla avai is the assembly of good or learned people, and naṉku cela-c-collutal again means speech that reaches and persuades (see 722). Solomon Pappaiah adds that such a person is useless to the world, extending the loss from the individual to society. The sandhi text reads “நல்லவையு / ணன்கு.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Taittiriya Upanishad pairs every duty with svādhyāya-pravacana, one’s own study together with teaching it to others. In the graduation address the teacher tells the departing student not to neglect study and teaching.
hinduism.explanation: In the Vedic ideal, learning is incomplete unless it is also passed on to others.
hinduism.tie_back: Learning that is never expounded falls short, which is why the Kural calls the silent scholar useless.
hinduism.source: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.9 and 1.11 (trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says light is meant to be seen; hiding it defeats its purpose.
christianity.tie_back: Hidden learning, like a covered lamp, benefits no one.

islam.quote_or_event: “He who is asked something he knows and conceals it will have a bridle of fire put on him on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that withholding knowledge when asked is a serious fault.
islam.tie_back: Knowledge that is not conveyed fails its purpose, as the Kural says of the learned person who cannot speak.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 3658 (graded hasan sahih by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: Moses tells God that he is slow of speech and slow of tongue. God answers by appointing Aaron as his spokesman, so that what Moses knows can reach the people.
judaism.explanation: Even Moses’ knowledge needed a voice before it could help anyone.
judaism.tie_back: Learning has to be spoken well in order to be of use, which is the Kural’s point.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that a great deal of textual learning brings no benefit if it is never put to use.
buddhism.tie_back: Learning much but gaining nothing from it is the Kural’s verdict on the scholar who cannot speak.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, seeker after the highest truth, study the sacred lore, in order to cause yourself and others to attain perfection.”
jainism.explanation: The closing verse of 'The Very Learned' says the purpose of study is the good of others as well as oneself.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says many subjects studied are useless if one cannot put them well before a good assembly; the Jain verse similarly holds that learning is meant to benefit others, not only its owner.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You may read and read loads of books; you may read and study vast multitudes of books. … O Nanak, only one thing is of any account: everything else is useless babbling and idle talk in ego.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa ki Vaar, Guru Nanak says cartloads of reading count for nothing without the one thing that matters, the Name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says however many subjects one has studied, one is useless without the power to present good things to a good assembly; Guru Nanak too says vast reading alone is of no account.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the gods do not grace all men alike in speech, person, and understanding. One man may be of weak presence, but heaven has adorned this with such a good conversation that he charms every one who sees him; his honeyed moderation carries his hearers with him so that he is leader in all assemblies of his fellows”
