greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus tells Euryalus, who is handsome but tactless, that real standing in the assembly comes from skill in speech.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Only those who can speak well lead in the assembly, and other gifts count for little without that skill.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Isocrates, the most famous teacher of rhetoric in Athens, admits that he lacked a strong voice and the boldness needed to face crowds. So he never addressed the assembly himself and worked through written speeches and teaching instead.
philosophy.explanation: Here is a man of great learning who could not deliver it before the assembly in person.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a real case of the Kural’s learned man unable to speak in the assembly.

real_life_example.event_title: Josiah Willard Gibbs's great work on thermodynamics goes long unappreciated
real_life_example.event: Between 1876 and 1878 Josiah Willard Gibbs of Yale published On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances, a long paper that introduced the phase rule and is now seen as a landmark of physical chemistry. It appeared in the Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences in a dense, highly mathematical form that most contemporaries found very hard to follow. Its value was recognised only gradually, helped by James Clerk Maxwell and by later translations into German in 1892 and French in 1899.
real_life_example.explanation: Gibbs's ideas were among the most important of his century, yet because they were not put in a form most scientists could grasp, years passed before they had their full effect.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that however much a person has learned, it bears no fruit if it is not set persuasively before the assembly, and the slow reception of Gibbs's treatise shows that cost.

tamil:
கல்லா தவரின் கடையென்ப கற்றறிந்தும்
நல்லா ரவையஞ்சு வார்.
transliteration:
Kallaa thavarin kadaiyenba katrarindhum
Nallaa ravaiyanju vaar.
meaning: People who have studied and understood, yet are afraid to speak before a group of good people, are said to be even lower than people who never learned.
elementary: If a kid knows the answer but stays quiet because they’re scared, it’s as if they never knew it. It might even be worse, because a kid who doesn’t know can at least ask a question.
university: Kaṭai means “the lowest,” so kallātavariṉ kaṭai is “lower than the unlearned.” The verb eṉpa (“they say”) presents the judgement as the verdict of the wise. Kaṟṟu aṟintum, “though they have learned and understood,” stresses both study and understanding, so the failure is purely a failure of nerve. Solomon Pappaiah reads avai añcuvār as those so afraid that they do not even go to the assembly. The ranking is harsh because the unlearned at least lack the means, while the learned coward wastes what he has. Variant: thirukkural-thamizh’s sandhi text reads “கல்லா தவரிற் கடையென்ப கற்றறிந்து / நல்லா ரவையஞ்சு வார்,” where the final -um of கற்றறிந்தும் is absorbed before ந; ytamizh prints the separated form கற்றறிந்தும்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Vidura teaches that a gathering without elders is no true assembly, and that elders who do not speak for dharma are not true elders.
hinduism.explanation: Vidura says that seniority and learning lose their worth when their holders stay silent where justice needs to be spoken.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same: learned people who fear the assembly fall below those who have no learning at all.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Vidura Niti (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue: For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.”
christianity.explanation: Educated leaders who privately believed stayed silent in public out of fear of their peers.
christianity.tie_back: The learned who know the truth but fear the assembly are judged harshly, as in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Allah praises] those who convey the messages of Allah and fear Him and do not fear anyone but Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who deliver what they have been given without fearing people.
islam.tie_back: Fear of people is what the Kural condemns in the learned.

judaism.quote_or_event: Moses tells the judges of Israel not to be afraid of any man’s face when they give judgement, because judgement belongs to God.
judaism.explanation: Those entrusted with legal knowledge are commanded not to let fear of people silence or bend them.
judaism.tie_back: Learning betrayed by fear of the audience is exactly what the Kural condemns.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is not wise because one speaks much. He who is peaceable, friendly and fearless is called wise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada includes fearlessness in its definition of the wise.
buddhism.tie_back: If wisdom includes fearlessness, a learned person ruled by fear falls short of it, as the Kural implies.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Weak men who are unable (to bear) these insults in villages or towns, become disheartened like cowards in the battle.”
jainism.explanation: Among the troubles of monastic life, the Sutrakritanga lists public ridicule in villages and towns, and says weak monks give way under it like cowards in battle.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural ranks the learned man who dreads a good assembly below the unlearned; the Jain verse likewise treats losing one's nerve before the public as a real failure in someone who has taken up the higher life.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.3.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That scholar who is full of greed, arrogant pride and egotism, is known to be a fool.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says a learned person ruled by greed and ego is to be counted a fool despite his learning.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the learned who dread a good assembly rank lower than the unlearned; Guru Nanak likewise says a scholar can be ranked among fools because of an inner failing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Raag Maajh, Majh ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Young Telemachus calls the first assembly Ithaca has held in twenty years, takes the speaker’s staff, and openly confronts the suitors who are devouring his house, even though he breaks into tears at the end.
greek_mythology.explanation: An inexperienced youth forces himself to speak before the whole community.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the opposite of the Kural’s coward: someone who masters fear of the assembly despite his youth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “although he had a style of speaking which was most like that of Pericles, he was throwing himself away out of weakness and lack of courage, neither facing the multitude with boldness”
philosophy.explanation: After young Demosthenes was jeered in the assembly, the old man Eunomus scolded him for wasting real ability through timidity.
philosophy.tie_back: Talent and learning wasted by fear of the crowd is precisely the failing the Kural ranks below ignorance.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Demosthenes 6 (trans. Bernadotte Perrin)

real_life_example.event_title: Gauss keeps his ideas on non-Euclidean geometry private
real_life_example.event: Carl Friedrich Gauss, already one of the leading mathematicians of his age, privately discussed the possibility of a non-Euclidean geometry with friends from the early 1800s. He told his correspondent Schumacher that he believed his reputation would suffer if he admitted his belief in such a geometry in public, and he did not publish a single paper on the subject. Nikolai Lobachevsky and Janos Bolyai published their own non-Euclidean geometries first.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the greatest mathematicians of all time held back a revolutionary idea out of concern for how his peers would react, leaving the credit to others.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who have learned and understood yet shrink from the assembly rank below even the unlearned, and Gauss's silence on non-Euclidean geometry is a well-documented case of learning withheld for fear of public reaction.

tamil:
உளரெனினும் இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர் களன்அஞ்சிக்
கற்ற செலச்சொல்லா தார்.
transliteration:
Ulareninum illaarodu oppar kalananjik
Katra selachchollaa thaar.
meaning: People who fear a group and so cannot share what they have learned in a way that reaches others are like the dead, even though they are alive.
elementary: A lamp that is never switched on might as well not be there. When fear stops you from ever sharing what you know, it is as if that part of you isn’t there at all.
university: Uḷar eṉiṉum (“though they exist, are alive”) and illārotu oppar (“they are equal to those who are not”) set being against non-being. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read illār as the dead. Kaḷaṉ (kaḷam, “arena, place of assembly”) stands in for avai for variety, and añci (“fearing”) names the cause. The closing phrase kaṟṟa cela-c-collātār repeats the formula of 722 and 724 and ties the chapter together: to learn but not to pass it on is a kind of death. The sandhi text reads “உளரெனினு மில்லாரொ டொப்பர் களனஞ்சிக்.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for one who has been honored, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that shrinking from his duty out of fear would bring a disgrace worse than dying.
hinduism.tie_back: In the Gita as in the Kural, a failure of nerve leaves a man worse than dead.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.34 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.”
christianity.explanation: The risen Christ tells the church at Sardis that it has the reputation of being alive but is in fact dead.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Alive in name but dead in fact’ is almost the Kural’s own wording for the silent scholar.

islam.quote_or_event: “And is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him light by which to walk among the people like one who is in darkness, never to emerge therefrom?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes someone given life and light to walk among people, in contrast with someone still in darkness.
islam.tie_back: Real life means bringing one’s light among people, and the Kural says those who cannot are like the dead.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jeremiah says that when he decided to stop speaking God’s word, it became like a fire shut up in his bones, and he grew weary of holding it in and could not.
judaism.explanation: For the prophet, keeping a message unspoken is a torment that eats him from inside.
judaism.tie_back: Knowledge held back instead of spoken makes life unbearable, which is close to the Kural’s ‘alive yet like the dead.’

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless. Heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful die not. The heedless are as if dead already.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada calls the heedless as good as dead even while they live.
buddhism.tie_back: It uses the same ‘living yet dead’ judgement the Kural passes on the fearful scholar.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who having investigated the Law expound it, are awakened and put an end to mundane existence; able to liberate both (themselves and others), they answer the well-deliberated questions.”
jainism.explanation: The Nirgrantha lecture praises those who have studied the doctrine and then expound it, answering questions so that both they and others are freed.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says those who cannot pass on what they learned are like the dead; the Jain verse puts the same value the other way round, praising those who do expound their learning as fully awakened.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone are truly alive, whose minds are filled with the Lord. O Nanak, no one else is truly alive;”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says that only those in whom the Lord dwells are really living; the rest only appear to be alive.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who cannot pass on their learning for fear are like the dead though alive; Guru Nanak uses the same living-yet-dead contrast.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Maajh, Majh ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After his quarrel with Agamemnon, Achilles sits by his ships and goes neither to the assembly, where men win glory, nor to war, and he lets his heart waste away.
greek_mythology.explanation: Cut off from both assembly and battle, the greatest hero lives on but wastes away.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Withdrawing from the assembly is a slow death of the self, as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca writes that if wisdom were given to him on condition that he keep it shut up and never declare it, he would refuse it, because no good thing is pleasant to possess unless it can be shared.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, wisdom that can never be passed on is not worth having.
philosophy.tie_back: Learning that is never spoken counts for nothing, the same verdict as the Kural’s.

real_life_example.event_title: Fermat's marginal note and his unpublished mathematics
real_life_example.event: Pierre de Fermat, a lawyer and councillor in Toulouse, wrote in the margin of his copy of Diophantus's Arithmetica that he had found a remarkable proof of what became known as Fermat's Last Theorem, but that the margin was too small to contain it. Attempts to have his work published during his lifetime failed largely because he never wanted to put it into polished form. His marginal notes became known only after his son Samuel published them in an edition of the Arithmetica in 1670, and the theorem was not proved until the 1990s.
real_life_example.explanation: Fermat's methods and proofs, which he rarely set out in full for others, were largely lost to his contemporaries, and mathematicians spent centuries trying to recover what he claimed to know.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who cannot pass on what they have learned so that it reaches others are like the dead though alive, and Fermat's unshared proofs left his contemporaries with little more than tantalising claims.

tamil:
தள்ளா விளையுளும் தக்காரும் தாழ்விலாச்
செல்வரும் சேர்வது நாடு.
transliteration:
Thallaa vilaiyulum thakkaarum thaazhvilaach
chelvarum servadhu naadu.
meaning: A true country has three things together: crops that never fail, good and worthy people, and rich people whose riches do not shrink.
elementary: Think of a good neighbourhood. The gardens always grow food, there are wise grown-ups you can ask for help, and the shopkeepers do well enough to keep their shops open. When all three are there together, it feels like a real home. Valluvar says a country is the same.
university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of naadu (the realm or territory), the third of the six angas (limbs) of kingship listed in kural 381, and it begins with a definition by constituents. Thallaa vilaiyul is literally ‘produce that does not fail’ (thal, to reject or fall off), thakkaar are ‘the worthy’, whom Parimelazhagar glosses as men of virtue and learning, and thaazhvilaa chelvar are ‘the wealthy without decline’, whom he identifies as merchants whose stock never runs out; Pope’s prose gloss follows him in naming merchants. Modern commentators widen the reading: Solomon Pappaiah turns the first term into the labourers who produce the harvest and the third into the unselfish rich, while Kalaignar reads the wealthy as those who do not squander riches on evil ends. The verb servadhu (that in which they gather together) makes the point that a land is defined by the coexistence of these groups, not by any one of them. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘விளையுளுந் தக்காருந்’ and ‘செல்வருஞ்’, which divide into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Valmiki’s opening description of Ayodhya under King Dasaratha paints a city whose people were learned, virtuous and content with their own wealth, where no one was poor, miserly or uneducated, and whose granaries and treasuries were full.
hinduism.explanation: The Ramayana begins its story by showing the ideal kingdom: a place that is rich in goods and also rich in good and learned people.
hinduism.tie_back: Ayodhya brings together the same three things as the Kural: plenty, worthy people and wealth that does not run out.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, Sarga 6 (description of Ayodhya)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to teach wealthy believers not to be proud or rely on riches, but to use them generously for others.
christianity.tie_back: Modern commentators read the Kural’s ‘wealthy without decline’ as the rich who spend well, which is exactly Paul’s ideal of the rich.

islam.quote_or_event: “There was for [the tribe of] Saba’ in their dwelling place a sign: two [fields of] gardens on the right and on the left. [They were told], ‘Eat from the provisions of your Lord and be grateful to Him. A good land [have you], and a forgiving Lord.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an recalls the people of Sheba, who lived between two great gardens and were told they had been given a good land.
islam.tie_back: Saba’s gardens on either side are a picture of the Kural’s unfailing harvest, the first mark of a real country.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the LORD thy God bringeth thee into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and depths that spring out of valleys and hills; A land of wheat, and barley, and vines, and fig trees, and pomegranates; a land of oil olive, and honey; A land wherein thou shalt eat bread without scarceness, thou shalt not lack any thing in it.”
judaism.explanation: Moses describes the promised land to Israel as a place of water, grain and fruit where bread will never be scarce.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Bread without scarceness’ is the Torah’s version of the Kural’s ‘harvest that never fails’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta, the Buddha foretells a future age when India will be rich and prosperous, its villages, towns and royal cities so close together that a cockerel could fly from one to the next, under a righteous wheel-turning king.
buddhism.explanation: After a long decline, people return to good conduct and the land becomes crowded, fertile and wealthy again.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddhist ideal realm, like the Kural’s, is a land where plenty and good people exist together.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was brought into the family of the Gñâtris their silver increased, their gold increased; their riches, corn, majesty, and kingdom increased; their army, train, treasure, storehouse, town, seraglio, subjects, and glory increased”
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra describes King Siddhartha's realm flourishing in grain, riches, stores and subjects from the moment the future Tirthankara entered the family, a sign of the merit attached to his presence.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural defines a true country by unfailing harvests, worthy people and lasting wealth; the Jain text presents the same marks of a flourishing realm as the result of a virtuous presence within it.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: When Guru Arjan completed the pool at Amritsar and built the Harimandar in its midst, he kept a community kitchen open to all castes and creeds, invited traders from different regions to settle and open their businesses around the temple, and had rest houses built for pilgrims, so that a city grew up with the Harimandar as its focus.
sikhism.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism describes how Guru Arjan deliberately built a living town: a shared kitchen that fed everyone, merchants drawn in to trade, and a community of devotees gathered around the shrine.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines a true country as the place where steady food, worthy people and prospering merchants come together, and Guru Arjan's Amritsar was planned around exactly that combination.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Arjan Dev, Guru

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The fruits never rot nor fail all the year round, neither winter nor summer, for the air is so soft that a new crop ripens before the old has dropped.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus reaches the land of the Phaeacians and sees King Alcinous’ orchard, where pears, apples, figs and grapes are always in season.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer’s orchard where fruit ‘never fails’ is the mythic picture of the Kural’s thallaa vilaiyul, the harvest that never fails.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “First, there must be food; secondly, arts, for life requires many instruments; thirdly, there must be arms ... fourthly, there must be a certain amount of revenue, both for internal needs, and for the purposes of war.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle lists the functions a city cannot do without, starting with food and going on to crafts, arms, revenue, worship and justice.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Aristotle defines a state by the things and people it must contain, and food comes first on both lists.

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Zhenzong distributes drought-resistant Champa rice
real_life_example.place: Lower Yangtze and Huai river regions, Song China
real_life_example.event: After a severe drought struck the lower Yangtze and Huai river valleys in 1012, the Song emperor Zhenzong had thirty thousand bushels of early-ripening, drought-resistant rice seed from Champa, in present-day central Vietnam, distributed to farmers in the stricken areas. He also had instructions on how to grow the new rice circulated to the farmers. The fast-maturing variety could be grown on higher ground and, in many places, allowed two harvests a year.
real_life_example.explanation: The new rice made harvests far less vulnerable to drought, and historians link its spread to the growth of population in southern China.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names harvests that never fail as the first mark of a true country, and Zhenzong's distribution of Champa rice was a deliberate effort to make his land's harvests failure-proof.

tamil:
பெரும்பொருளால் பெட்டக்க தாகி அருங்கேட்டால்
ஆற்ற விளைவது நாடு.
transliteration:
Perumporulaal pettakka thaaki arungettaal
aatra vilaivadhu naadu.
meaning: A true country is so rich that others want it, is free from terrible disasters, and grows plenty of crops.
elementary: Imagine a garden so lovely and full of fruit that everyone in town wishes it were theirs. It is not flooded or eaten by pests, and every year it gives more than enough. That is what a good country is like.
university: Perumporul is ‘great wealth’, and pettakkadhu means ‘that which is desirable’; Parimelazhagar takes the desire to be that of other kingdoms, so the kural admits that a rich land will be coveted, which prepares for the next chapter on fortification (Aran). Arungettaal is read by Parimelazhagar as arum-kedu, ‘with destructive causes being absent’ (arumai here meaning scarcity or absence), and Solomon Pappaiah lists the traditional calamities meant: excessive rain, drought, wild beasts, harmful birds and misrule. Aatra vilaivadhu means ‘yielding abundantly’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read pettakkadhu more generally as ‘praised and desired by all’. The sandhi-joined text runs the words together as ‘பெட்டக்க தாகி யருங்கேட்டா லாற்ற’, with no change in meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him settle in a country which is open and has a dry climate, where grain is abundant, which is chiefly (inhabited) by Aryans, not subject to epidemic diseases (or similar troubles), and pleasant, where the vassals are obedient and his own (people easily) find their livelihood.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king what kind of country to make his home: one with plenty of grain, free from disease and other troubles, and pleasant to live in.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu’s abundant, pleasant and trouble-free country matches the Kural’s desirable, calamity-free land of great yield.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Lot lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, even as the garden of the LORD.”
christianity.explanation: When Abraham and Lot must separate, Lot looks at the fertile Jordan plain and chooses it because it is so rich and well watered.
christianity.tie_back: The plain is the kind of land the Kural describes: so rich that others want it for themselves.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if only the people of the cities had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied [the messengers], so We seized them for what they were earning.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says abundance from sky and earth would have come to towns that were faithful, while calamity came to those that were not.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s land of great yield and no calamity is, in Qur’anic terms, a land on which blessings have been opened.

judaism.quote_or_event: “We came unto the land whither thou sentest us, and surely it floweth with milk and honey; and this is the fruit of it.”
judaism.explanation: The spies Moses sent into Canaan come back with huge clusters of fruit and report that the land is wonderfully rich.
judaism.tie_back: Canaan is desired because of its fruit, which is what the Kural means by a land made desirable by its great wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahasudassana Sutta the Buddha describes Kusavati, the royal city of an ancient righteous king, as rich, prosperous, crowded with people and well supplied with food, and never silent with the sounds of festivity.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Ananda that the small town where he is dying was once this splendid capital, and then teaches that all such splendour passes.
buddhism.tie_back: Kusavati is the Buddhist picture of the desirable land the Kural praises, full of wealth and food.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Knowing that the earth with its crops of rice and barley, with its gold and cattle, that all this put together will not satisfy one single man, one should practise austerities.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami, renouncing the kingdom of Mithila, answers Indra's call to enlarge his wealth by saying that even the whole earth's harvests and gold cannot satisfy one person's craving.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises a land so rich that others desire it; the Jain answer is that such desire for land is limitless, so the right response to a rich country is restraint, not covetousness.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.49 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Creator has given me the nine treasures, wealth and spiritual powers, and I do not lack anything. Eating, spending and enjoying, I have found peace; the gifts of the Creator Lord continually increase. … Millions of obstacles have all been removed, and pain does not even approach me.”
sikhism.explanation: In a chhant celebrating the completion of the Amritsar pool, Guru Arjan describes a place overflowing with God's gifts, where abundance keeps growing and harm cannot come near.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's ideal land is rich, untouched by calamity and abundantly fruitful; Guru Arjan's hymn pictures the same unfailing plenty and freedom from trouble, received as divine grace.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 783-784, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “If they had had these they would have colonized the island, for it is a very good one, and would yield everything in due season.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus describes a fertile island near the Cyclopes with meadows, deep soil and a safe harbour, which nobody works because the Cyclopes have no ships.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer’s island is the kind of land others would covet for its yield, which is how Parimelazhagar reads the Kural’s ‘desirable’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates says that once a city wants luxuries beyond its needs, its land will no longer be enough, so it will have to cut off a slice of its neighbours’ land, and the neighbours will want a slice of its land too. That, he says, is the origin of war.
philosophy.explanation: Plato traces war back to one land coveting another land’s wealth.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the danger hidden in the Kural’s word ‘desirable’: a rich land draws envy, which is why the next chapter turns to fortresses.

real_life_example.event_title: Augustus annexes Egypt and makes it Rome's granary
real_life_example.event: After defeating Mark Antony and Cleopatra, Octavian, later called Augustus, arrived in Egypt in 30 BCE, ended the Ptolemaic monarchy and annexed the country as his personal domain, governed by a prefect of his choosing. Egypt's wealth was largely agricultural, and its grain supplied the city of Rome; its revenues were almost equal to those of Gaul. Historians count the addition of Egypt as a major supplier of the capital among Augustus's most important measures for Rome's food supply.
real_life_example.explanation: Egypt's dependable Nile harvests made it so valuable that Rome's ruler kept it under his own direct control.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes a true country as one so rich that others desire it, free of ruinous calamities and yielding abundant harvests, and Egypt was coveted and seized by Rome for exactly that wealth.

tamil:
பொறையொருங்கு மேல்வருங்கால் தாங்கி இறைவற்கு
இறையொருங்கு நேர்வது நாடு.
transliteration:
Poraiyorungu melvarungaal thaangi iraivarku
iraiyorungu nervadhu naadu.
meaning: A true country can carry heavy burdens that fall on it all at once, and still pay its ruler all the taxes it owes.
elementary: Picture a strong family. When cousins suddenly arrive because their house was flooded, the family makes room and shares its food, and it still pays its bills on time. A good country is strong in the same way.
university: Porai is ‘burden’ and orungu ‘all together’, so the first line describes a load that arrives all at once. Parimelazhagar specifies the load as people fleeing from neighbouring lands in distress, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow him, Pappaiah adding refugees from war and natural disaster. The second line plays on the double sense of irai: iraivan is the king and irai is the tax due to him, so a land ‘yields fully the king’s due to the king’ (iraivarku irai orungu nervadhu). The kural therefore measures a country’s strength by its surplus, since only a land with reserves can absorb strangers and still pay its revenue gladly. The sandhi text reads ‘மேல்வருங்காற் றாங்கி யிறைவற் கிறையொருங்கு’, the same words joined.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As the leech, the calf, and the bee take their food little by little, even so must the king draw from his realm moderate annual taxes.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king to take taxes gently, a little at a time, so that the country is never drained.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s land pays its full dues willingly, and Manu explains the other half of that bargain: the king must tax lightly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For for this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God’s ministers, attending continually upon this very thing. Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Christians in Rome to pay taxes and customs to the authorities as a duty.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s ‘render to all their dues’ is the attitude of the Kural’s land, which gives the king his due in full.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [also for] those who were settled in al-Madinah and [adopted] the faith before them. They love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what the emigrants were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the Ansar of Medina, who welcomed the emigrants from Mecca and shared with them even when they themselves were in need.
islam.tie_back: Medina carrying the load of the emigrants is exactly the burden Parimelazhagar sees in this kural: newcomers arriving all at once.

judaism.quote_or_event: Under Solomon, the Book of Kings says, Judah and Israel were as many as the sand of the sea, eating, drinking and rejoicing; twelve district officers each supplied the king’s household for one month of the year, and the people dwelt safely, every man under his vine and fig tree.
judaism.explanation: Solomon’s kingdom is shown as so prosperous that it fed a very large population and also kept the royal court supplied.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s strong land: it carries a great population and still meets the king’s dues in full.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta the Buddha tells of a king whose land is plagued by bandits. His wise chaplain advises him not to raise taxes or punish, but to give seed and fodder to farmers, capital to traders and proper wages to officials. The people prosper, crime ends, and the king’s revenue grows.
buddhism.explanation: The story teaches that a prosperous people is what makes a ruler’s revenue secure, not heavier taxes.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s land pays the king in full because it has surplus; the Kutadanta story shows how that surplus is created.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Karuna-Dana means gifts or offerings made out of compassion to any one who deserves it, being hungry, thirsty, diseased, distressed, disabled, helpless, or the like.”
jainism.explanation: Jain lay ethics urges the householder to give compassionate gifts (karuna-dana), commonly grouped as food, medicine, knowledge and protection from fear, to anyone in need, human or animal.
jainism.tie_back: Commentators read this Kural's sudden burden as people fleeing distress in other lands; the Jain duty of compassionate giving, including protection from fear, is the closest Jain counterpart to a land that can absorb such a burden.
jainism.source: 'Basic Positivity of Ahimsa', in The Jaina Path of Ahimsa (online book, jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Under Guru Amar Das the Guru ka Langar became still more renowned: he expected every visitor to eat in it before seeing him, and Emperor Akbar is said to have eaten there like any other pilgrim. Guru Angad had called Amar Das the home of the homeless and the shelter of the unsheltered, and as Guru he organised twenty-two preaching districts whose leaders transmitted the disciples' offerings to Goindval.
sikhism.explanation: The langar was built to absorb whoever arrived, however many and however suddenly, while the community's offerings still flowed in an orderly way to the centre.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises a land that can carry a sudden influx of people and still pay its ruler's dues in full; Guru Amar Das's langar and offering network did the same for the Sikh community.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Amar Das, Guru

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “We will recoup ourselves by the levy of a general rate; for private individuals cannot be expected to bear the burden of such a handsome present.”
greek_mythology.explanation: King Alcinous of the Phaeacians has his nobles give rich gifts to the stranger Odysseus and says the cost will be met by a levy on the whole people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Phaeacian land shoulders the cost of a stranger and meets it through a common levy, much as the Kural’s land bears a sudden burden and pays its dues.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Productive of subsistence not only to its own people, but also to outsiders on occasions of calamities ... capable of bearing the burden of a vast army and heavy taxation ... these are the qualities of a good country.”
philosophy.explanation: Kautilya lists the marks of a good country (janapada), including feeding outsiders in times of calamity and bearing heavy taxation.
philosophy.tie_back: Kautilya names both halves of this kural: supporting outsiders in their distress and carrying the burden of the king’s taxes.

real_life_example.event_title: The Edict of Potsdam opens Brandenburg to Huguenot refugees
real_life_example.event: After Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, which had protected French Protestants, Elector Frederick William of Brandenburg issued the Edict of Potsdam offering the Huguenots refuge. It promised help with travel, free choice of where to settle, houses and building materials, tax exemptions, the right to practise their trades and their own French-language churches. At least 20,000 Huguenots settled in his lands, which had been thinned by the Thirty Years' War.
real_life_example.explanation: A land with resources to spare took in a sudden wave of refugees and turned them into farmers, artisans and manufacturers who strengthened the state.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the country that can bear a heavy burden that falls on it all at once, which Parimelazhagar explains as people fleeing from neighbouring lands, and Brandenburg's welcome of the Huguenots is a classic example.

tamil:
உறுபசியும் ஓவாப் பிணியும் செறுபகையும்
சேரா தியல்வது நாடு.
transliteration:
Urupasiyum ovaap piniyum serupakaiyum
seraa thiyalvadhu naadu.
meaning: A true country carries on free from terrible hunger, diseases that never end, and enemies that destroy.
elementary: A happy home is one where nobody goes to bed hungry, nobody is sick all the time, and nobody is afraid of bullies breaking in. Valluvar says a good country is a whole land like that.
university: The kural names the classic triad of public calamity: urupasi (severe hunger, famine), ovaap pini (disease that does not cease, that is, epidemic) and serupakai (enemies who destroy). Parimelazhagar notes that the third means enemies who come from outside and attack, since internal enmity is treated separately in the next kural. The verb iyalvadhu (that which goes on, continues) suggests a lasting condition rather than a single lucky year. The same trio of famine, pestilence and war recurs in Sanskrit, biblical and Greek accounts of disaster, which makes this one of the most widely shared ideas in the chapter. The sandhi text reads ‘உறுபசியு மோவாப் பிணியுஞ் செறுபகையுஞ்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the close of the Yuddha Kanda, Valmiki describes Rama’s reign: no widows mourned, there was no fear of wild beasts or disease, no robbers, the rains came in season, trees were always in fruit, and people lived long lives free from sickness.
hinduism.explanation: This description of Rama Rajya became the classic Indian picture of a perfect realm.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama Rajya is a land with no hunger, no sickness and no danger, the three absences the Kural makes the test of a country.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 128 (Rama’s reign)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: And great earthquakes shall be in divers places, and famines, and pestilences.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns his disciples of the calamities to come: war, earthquake, famine and plague.
christianity.tie_back: Luke lists the very evils the Kural’s good country is free from: enemies, famine and pestilence.

islam.quote_or_event: “Let them worship the Lord of this House, Who has fed them, [saving them] from hunger and made them safe, [saving them] from fear.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an reminds the Quraysh of Mecca that God protected their city from hunger and from fear.
islam.tie_back: Freedom from hunger and from the fear of enemies are two of the Kural’s three marks of a good land.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I will grant your rains in their season, so that the earth shall yield its produce and the trees of the field their fruit ... you shall eat your fill of bread and dwell securely in your land. I will grant peace in the land ... and no sword shall cross your land.”
judaism.explanation: God promises Israel that if they keep the covenant, their land will have rain, full harvests, security and peace from invasion.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Eat your fill’ and ‘no sword shall cross your land’ are the Torah’s version of a land free from hunger and enemies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The commentarial tradition says the Ratana Sutta was first taught when the city of Vesali was struck by drought and famine, then by disease, then by harmful spirits drawn by the dead. The Buddha came, the sutta was recited around the city, and the three dangers passed.
buddhism.explanation: The Ratana Sutta is still chanted as a protection because of this story of a city freed from famine, plague and fear.
buddhism.tie_back: Vesali’s three afflictions closely mirror the Kural’s triad of hunger, disease and hostile forces.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 2.1, Ratana Sutta, with its commentary (Piyadassi’s introduction)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Bhadrabahu, the last Srutakevali, predicted at Ujjain a twelve years drought and famine in the north, where upon the Jaina community migrated to the south under his leadership.”
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition, supported by Shravanabelagola inscriptions, holds that a twelve-year famine made the north unlivable for the monastic community, which moved south with Bhadrabahu (traditionally joined by Chandragupta Maurya).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a true country is untouched by crushing hunger; the Bhadrabahu story shows from the Jain side how famine strips a land of its worth, so that even the religious community has to leave it.
jainism.source: Jain Heritage Centres, 'Chandragiri' (Shravanabelagola), jainheritagecentres.com, summarising the Bhadrabahu tradition and Shravanabelagola inscriptions

sikhism.quote_or_event: As Guru Arjan moved from village to village he helped people sink wells and undertake other works of public welfare, especially to relieve the hardship of the famine then gripping the Punjab; a baoli (step-well) he built still stands in Lahore, and at Tarn Taran lepers were treated by the Guru with loving care.
sikhism.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism records the fifth Guru's response to famine and disease as practical seva: water works, relief and care for the sick.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural names crushing hunger and endless disease among the evils a true land must be free of; Guru Arjan's wells, famine relief and leper care were Sikh work against exactly those evils.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Arjan Dev, Guru

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Peace, the nurse of children, is abroad in their land, and all-seeing Zeus never decrees cruel war against them. Neither famine nor disaster ever haunt men who do true justice.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the city whose people judge fairly: it is spared war, famine and disaster, and the earth feeds it richly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s just city is free of war, famine and disaster, which is almost the Kural’s list of hunger, disease and enemies.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225-230 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kautilya devotes a chapter to ‘remedies against national calamities’, naming fire, floods, pestilence, famine, rats, wild beasts, snakes and demons, and prescribing what the state must do against each.
philosophy.explanation: For Kautilya, protecting the land from these disasters is a basic duty of government.
philosophy.tie_back: Kautilya’s list includes the Kural’s famine and pestilence, and treats their absence as a matter of good statecraft.

real_life_example.event_title: War, crowding and plague strike Athens
real_life_example.event: Early in the Peloponnesian War, Pericles allowed the people of the Attic countryside to take refuge inside the walls of Athens while the Spartans raided the land, and the city became severely overcrowded. In 430 BCE a plague broke out in the crowded city and over the following years killed a large part of its population, including both of Pericles' legitimate sons. When the Spartans again invaded and laid waste to the fields in 429 BCE, crops could not be planted, and Pericles himself died of the plague that autumn.
real_life_example.explanation: Athens, the richest city in Greece, was brought low when a destructive enemy, hunger and an unrelenting epidemic struck together.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a true country is one untouched by crushing hunger, endless disease and destructive enemies, and Athens in 430 to 429 BCE shows what befalls a land when all three arrive at once.

tamil:
பல்குழுவும் பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகையும் வேந்தலைக்கும்
கொல்குறும்பும் இல்லது நாடு.
transliteration:
Palkuzhuvum paazhseyyum utpakaiyum vendhalaikkum
kolkurumpum illadhu naadu.
meaning: A true country has no groups fighting each other, no enemies inside who bring ruin, and no killer gangs that trouble the king.
elementary: A sports team can have the best players, but if they split into little groups that fight each other, and some even help the other side, they will lose. A country is the same: it needs its people to pull together.
university: Where kural 734 dealt with dangers from outside, this one turns to dangers from within. Palkuzhu is ‘many groups’, which Parimelazhagar reads as factions that quarrel among themselves, paazhseyyum utpakai is ‘internal enmity that works ruin’, and vendhalaikkum kolkurumpu is ‘murderous petty chiefs (or bands) that harass the king’; kurumpu can mean a small hill-chief or a gang of marauders. Solomon Pappaiah modernises the list as caste, religious and political factions, disloyal party members, and local strongmen. The theme is developed fully in chapter 89 (Utpakai, Internal Enmity). The ytamizh text prints the last word as ‘இல்லத’, which appears to be a typographical slip for the standard ‘இல்லது’ found in the sandhi text and other editions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Protect thyself, O king, from all fears that arise from within. Fears, however, that arise from outside are of little consequence. The first kind of fear, O king, may cut thy roots in a single day.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that quarrels and disunion inside a kingdom are far more dangerous than foreign enemies.
hinduism.tie_back: Bhishma and Valluvar agree that internal enmity is the danger that can destroy a land from its roots.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section 107 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand.”
christianity.explanation: Answering critics, Jesus points out that any kingdom torn by internal division will fall.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Brought to desolation’ is close to the Kural’s paazhseyyum, ‘working ruin’: division inside a land destroys it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute and [thus] lose courage and [then] your strength would depart; and be patient. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns the believers that quarrelling among themselves will drain away their courage and strength.
islam.tie_back: The strength that ‘departs’ through dispute is what the Kural’s land keeps by being free of factions.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud asks why the Second Temple was destroyed when the people of that time studied Torah, kept the commandments and did acts of kindness. It answers that there was baseless hatred among them, and teaches that baseless hatred weighs as much as idolatry, forbidden relations and bloodshed together.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis locate the fall of Jerusalem in hatred among Jews themselves, not only in the Roman armies.
judaism.tie_back: Yoma’s teaching is a historical example of the Kural’s ‘internal enmity that works ruin’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What have you heard, Ananda: do the Vajjis assemble and disperse peacefully and attend to their affairs in concord?” ... “So long, Ananda, as this is the case, the growth of the Vajjis is to be expected, not their decline.”
buddhism.explanation: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjis, the Buddha says they cannot be defeated as long as they meet often and act in harmony.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s point is the Kural’s: a people without factions cannot easily be destroyed.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 1.4 (trans. Sister Vajira and Francis Story)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Punishing thieves and robbers, cut-purses and burglars, you should establish public safety; thus you will be a Kshattriya.” Nami answered: “Men frequently apply punishment wrongly: the innocent are put in prison, and the perpetrator of the crime is set at liberty.”
jainism.explanation: Indra, testing the renouncing King Nami, urges him to secure public safety by punishing criminals, and Nami replies that royal punishment often goes astray.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural wants a land free of internal enemies and murderous gangs; the Jain dialogue accepts that ideal of public safety, voiced by Indra, while doubting that a king's punishments can achieve it justly.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.28 and 9.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Now, the Merciful Lord has issued His Command. Let no one chase after and attack anyone else. Let all abide in peace, under this Benevolent Rule.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan proclaims the halemi raj, a gentle rule under God's command in which no one harasses or preys on another and everyone lives at ease.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's true country is free of quarrelling factions, ruinous internal enemies and gangs that trouble the realm; Guru Arjan's benevolent rule is a land where no one attacks anyone else.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 74, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the end of the Oresteia, Athena calls on the Furies, now called the Kindly Ones, to bless Athens, and the chorus prays that civil strife (stasis) may never roar in the city and that citizens may never shed each other’s blood in revenge.
greek_mythology.explanation: The trilogy ends by turning the spirits of vengeance into guardians against civil war.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The prayer against stasis is the Greek form of the Kural’s wish for a land free of faction and murderous internal enemies.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For indeed any city, however small, is in fact divided into two, one the city of the poor, the other of the rich; these are at war with one another; and in either there are many smaller divisions.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says most cities are not truly one city but many hostile factions, which is why they are weak.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s ‘many cities’ within one city is exactly the Kural’s palkuzhu, the many factions a real land must be free of.

real_life_example.event_title: The Gunpowder Plot is discovered
real_life_example.event: A group of conspirators led by Robert Catesby planned to blow up the House of Lords during the State Opening of Parliament, killing King James I, his family, his chief ministers and the members present. An anonymous letter warned Lord Monteagle to stay away from Parliament, and he passed it to the government. On the night of 4 November 1605 a search of the cellars beneath the House of Lords found Guy Fawkes with 36 barrels of gunpowder, and the plot collapsed.
real_life_example.explanation: The plot showed how a small band of internal enemies could threaten to destroy a kingdom's entire leadership in a single stroke.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a true country is free of internal enemies who work ruin and of murderous bands that trouble the ruler, and the Gunpowder Plot is one of history's best-known examples of exactly such a danger.

tamil:
கேடறியாக் கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா
நாடென்ப நாட்டின் தலை.
transliteration:
Kedariyaak ketta idaththum valangundraa
naadenpa naattin thalai.
meaning: Wise people say the best country is one that never meets ruin, and even when harm does come, does not lose its riches.
elementary: A strong tree is rarely hurt by storms, and even when a branch breaks, it keeps giving fruit. The best country is like that tree: hardly ever harmed, and quick to stay fruitful even when it is.
university: The kural has two degrees of excellence: kedariyaa (‘not knowing ruin’) and, failing that, ketta idaththum valam kundraa (‘even when ruined, its richness does not decline’). Parimelazhagar takes the ruin to be damage from enemies, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow him, while Kalaignar reads it as any kind of harm that the land’s resources are great enough to repair. Enpa (‘they say’) marks the judgment as the view of the learned, and naattin thalai means ‘the head, or foremost, of lands’. The idea is resilience: the best land is judged not only by its good years but by how it comes through bad ones. The ytamizh text reads ‘நாட்டின் தலை’ and the sandhi text ‘நாட்டிற் தலை’, a difference of joining only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Puranic story of King Prithu, the earth withholds her crops during a time of disorder and famine. Prithu pursues the earth, who has taken the form of a cow, and she agrees to yield again; he levels the land, and the earth is ‘milked’ so that grain and plenty return.
hinduism.explanation: The earth is named Prithvi after him, because he restored her fruitfulness after it had failed.
hinduism.tie_back: Prithu’s earth recovers its abundance after ruin, the second and harder test of the Kural’s best land.
hinduism.source: Vishnu Purana 1.13 and Bhagavata Purana 4.18 (story of Prithu)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus compares those who live by his words to a man who built his house on rock, which survived the storm.
christianity.tie_back: The house that is struck but ‘fell not’ is a picture of the Kural’s land that stays whole even when ruin comes.

islam.quote_or_event: “Then will come after that seven difficult [years] which will consume what you saved for them, except a little from which you will store.”
islam.explanation: Joseph interprets the king’s dream and tells Egypt to store the surplus of seven good years, so that the land can survive seven years of famine.
islam.tie_back: Joseph’s Egypt is the Kural’s best land: when disaster strikes, its stores keep its richness from failing.

judaism.quote_or_event: Genesis tells that when famine struck the land, Isaac stayed in Gerar at God’s word, sowed there, and reaped a hundredfold in that same year, and grew very wealthy.
judaism.explanation: Even in a year of famine, Isaac’s fields flourished.
judaism.tie_back: Isaac’s hundredfold harvest in a famine year is an image of a land whose richness does not fail even in bad times.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, Ananda, as far as the Aryan race extends and trade routes spread, this will be the foremost city Pataliputta, a trade-center. But Pataliputta, Ananda, will be assailed by three perils — fire, water, and dissension.”
buddhism.explanation: Seeing the fort being built at Pataligama, the Buddha predicts it will become the greatest city of the region, but also names the dangers it will face.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha, like Valluvar, speaks of a ‘foremost’ land and knows that even the best land will meet danger.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 1.28 (trans. Sister Vajira and Francis Story)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The regions other than these are stable.”
jainism.explanation: Jain cosmology teaches that only Bharata and Airavata pass through cycles of rise and decline, while the other regions (such as Videha) stay in a stable condition; Pujyapada's commentary adds that they have no ascending or descending half-cycles of time.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's best country is one that does not know ruin, or does not lose its richness even when harmed; Jain cosmology likewise imagines lands that never undergo decline.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 3.28, with Pujyapada's Sarvarthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: The Harimandar at Amritsar was demolished by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1762 and its sacred tank filled with debris; when the Sikhs sacked Sirhind in January 1764 they set aside several hundred thousand rupees for its restoration, the foundation of the new sanctum was laid on 19 April 1764, and the temple, bridge, gateway and cleared tank were completed by 1776.
sikhism.explanation: Sikh history remembers the repeated destruction and rebuilding of its central shrine and city; within two years of ruin the community had funded and begun its restoration.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the best land is one that does not lose its richness even when ruin comes; Amritsar, ruined in 1762 and rising again from 1764, is a Sikh example of that resilience.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Des Raj, Bhai (by Sarmukh Singh Amole)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, the grieving goddess makes the earth barren for a year, and famine threatens all mankind. When her daughter Persephone is returned, Demeter lets the fields grow again, and the whole earth is heavy with leaves and flowers.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth explains how the land can be struck barren and then return to full growth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Demeter’s earth, ruined and then made fruitful again, reflects the Kural’s land whose richness comes back even after harm.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn to Demeter (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli argues that a prince whose city is well fortified, stocked with a year’s food, drink and fuel, and whose people are kept at work, cannot easily be taken, because an enemy cannot keep a siege going that long.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli, a city’s strength lies in its reserves as much as in its walls.
philosophy.tie_back: Machiavelli’s well-stocked city is the Kural’s best land: even when it is attacked, its wealth does not fail.

real_life_example.event_title: Tokyo is rebuilt after the Great Kanto Earthquake
real_life_example.event: On 1 September 1923 a magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck the Kanto region, and the fires that followed destroyed much of Tokyo. Within weeks the government set up the Imperial Capital Reconstruction Department under Home Minister Goto Shinpei to plan the city's recovery. Over the following years land readjustment and the rebuilding of streets, bridges, canals and parks were carried out across the burned districts, laying the foundations of modern Tokyo.
real_life_example.explanation: Even after one of the worst disasters of the century, Japan had the resources and organisation to rebuild its capital on a better plan.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the land that, even when ruin comes, does not lose its richness, and the reconstruction of Tokyo after 1923 shows a country recovering its strength after catastrophe.

tamil:
இருபுனலும் வாய்ந்த மலையும் வருபுனலும்
வல்லரணும் நாட்டிற்கு உறுப்பு.
transliteration:
Irupunalum vaaindha malaiyum varupunalum
vallaranum naattirku uruppu.
meaning: The parts of a country are water from rain and from springs, hills in the right places, rivers that flow from them, and a strong fort.
elementary: A castle in a story often sits by a river, with hills behind it, springs nearby and high walls around it. Water keeps people alive, and hills and walls keep them safe. Valluvar says a country needs all of these, like a body needs arms and legs.
university: Uruppu means ‘limb’ or ‘organ’, so the kural presents the natural features of a land as parts of a living body. Parimelazhagar reads irupunal (‘the two waters’) as water from below (springs, wells) and water from above (rain), and varupunal (‘the water that comes’) as rivers flowing from the hills; the hills themselves are vaaindha (well situated) because they feed the rivers and shelter the land. Kalaignar instead reads irupunal as river and sea, and varupunal as rain. Vallaran, the ‘strong fortress’, anticipates the next chapter, Aran, where hills, water and forest reappear as natural defences. The sandhi text reads ‘வல்லரணு நாட்டிற் குறுப்பு’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him build (there) a town, making for his safety a fortress, protected by a desert, or a fortress built of (stone and) earth, or one protected by water or trees, or one (formed by an encampment of armed) men or a hill-fort. Let him make every effort to secure a hill-fort, for amongst all those (fortresses mentioned) a hill-fort is distinguished by many superior qualities.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists the kinds of fortress a king may build, protected by desert, earth, water, forest, men or hills, and says the hill-fort is best.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu’s water, hill and forest forts are the same natural defences the Kural names as limbs of a country.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High. God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist sings of Jerusalem as a city refreshed by a river and made unshakable by God’s presence.
christianity.tie_back: A river that gives life and a city that ‘shall not be moved’ match the Kural’s pairing of water and strong defence.

islam.quote_or_event: “And He has cast into the earth firmly set mountains, lest it shift with you, and [made] rivers and roads, that you may be guided.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names mountains and rivers among the signs of God’s care for people on earth.
islam.tie_back: Mountains and rivers are two of the Kural’s limbs of a land, here presented as God’s gifts.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Psalms say that as the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people from now and for ever.
judaism.explanation: The hills around Jerusalem are used as a picture of God’s protection.
judaism.tie_back: The psalm takes for granted what the Kural says outright: surrounding hills are a land’s natural defence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where the royal frontier fortress has large stores of grass, timber & water for the delight, convenience, & comfort of those within, and to ward off those without.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a royal frontier fortress with a deep moat, high ramparts and stores of water and food, which cannot be taken by enemies. He uses it as a picture of a well-guarded mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The fortress needs water and strong walls together, as the Kural’s country needs its waters and its vallaran.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: Indra: “Erect a wall, gates, and battlements; dig a moat; construct sataghnîs: then you will be a Kshattriya.” Nami: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable”
jainism.explanation: Urged to fortify Mithila with walls, moat and engines, the renouncing King Nami turns the fortress into a picture of the inner life, with faith, penance, self-control and patience as its walls and bolt.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural lists a strong fortress among the limbs of a country; the Jain text knows the same royal ideal of fortification but moves the real stronghold inside the soul.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.18 and 9.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “… wind, water, fire and the nether regions - in the midst of these, He established the earth as a home for Dharma.”
sikhism.explanation: In the thirty-fourth pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak describes the elements and regions of creation and says that God set the earth among them as a dharamsal, a place where righteous living is practised.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural lists the waters, hills and defences that form the limbs of a country; Japji Sahib likewise names the natural elements that frame the earth, but sees in them the setting for dharma.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7, Japji Sahib (pauri 34), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “It is rugged and not a good driving country, but it is by no means a bad island for what there is of it. It grows any quantity of corn and also wine, for it is watered both by rain and dew ... and there are watering places where the water never runs dry.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena, in disguise, describes Ithaca to the returning Odysseus: rocky and hilly, but watered by rain and by springs that never fail.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Rain from above and springs that never run dry are exactly Parimelazhagar’s ‘two waters’, set in a hilly land.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It should afford easy egress to the citizens, and at the same time be inaccessible and difficult of capture to enemies. There should be a natural abundance of springs and fountains in the town, or, if there is a deficiency of them, great reservoirs may be established for the collection of rainwater.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle sets out the ideal site for a city: hard for enemies to reach, with plentiful springs, or cisterns for rainwater.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, names spring water, rain water and natural defence as essentials of a good territory.

real_life_example.event_title: King Kassapa I builds his capital on the rock of Sigiriya
real_life_example.event: King Kassapa I made Sigiriya his capital, building a palace on the summit of a granite rock that rises about 180 metres above the surrounding plain and intending it as a safeguard against his enemies. Visitors entered through a gigantic brick and plaster lion whose paws still frame the stairway. At the foot of the rock lay elaborate water gardens with ponds and terraces, surrounded by a moat.
real_life_example.explanation: Sigiriya combined a natural rock fortress, carefully managed water and surrounding lands into a single royal stronghold that is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural lists water, well-placed hills and a strong fortress as the limbs of a country, and Sigiriya, a hill fortress ringed by water gardens and a moat, brings these features together in one place.

tamil:
பிணியின்மை செல்வம் விளைவின்பம் ஏமம்
அணியென்ப நாட்டிற்கிவ் வைந்து.
transliteration:
Piniyinmai selvam vilaivinpam emam
aniyenpa naattirkiv vaindhu.
meaning: Wise people say a country has five jewels: no disease, riches, good crops, happiness and safety.
elementary: A birthday cake looks best with candles, icing, fruit, sprinkles and a name on top. A country has its own five decorations: healthy people, enough money, good crops, happy faces and safe streets.
university: Ani means ‘ornament’ or ‘jewel’, so where kural 737 listed the land’s limbs (uruppu), this one lists its adornments. The five are piniyinmai (absence of disease), selvam (wealth), vilaivu (produce), inpam (enjoyment, happiness) and emam (safety, protection); Parimelazhagar glosses emam as the protection given to subjects. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pope follow the same five, while some modern readers join vilaivu and inpam as ‘the joy of harvest’. The verse sums up the chapter’s positive ideal in a single list. The ytamizh text prints the second line as ‘அணியென்ப நாட்டிவ் வைந்து’, but the sandhi text and the standard editions read ‘நாட்டிற்கிவ் வைந்து’ (naattirku + iv + aindhu, ‘these five for a land’), which is needed for the metre and is followed here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In consequence again of royal protection, men can everywhere sleep fearlessly and at their case without shutting their houses and doors with bolts and bars.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati tells King Vasumanas that good royal protection lets people live without fear, so that they can sleep with their doors unlocked.
hinduism.tie_back: Sleeping with open doors is a vivid picture of emam, the security that is one of the Kural’s five ornaments of a land.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section 68 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “That our garners may be full, affording all manner of store: that our sheep may bring forth thousands and ten thousands in our streets: That our oxen may be strong to labour; that there be no breaking in, nor going out; that there be no complaining in our streets. Happy is that people, that is in such a case.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist prays for full barns, growing flocks, strong oxen, no invasion and no distress, and calls such a people happy.
christianity.tie_back: Full barns, no breaking in and a happy people are the Kural’s produce, security and joy in one prayer.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [mention] when Abraham said, ‘My Lord, make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits.’”
islam.explanation: Abraham prays for Mecca to be a safe city whose people are fed with fruit.
islam.tie_back: Abraham asks for two of the Kural’s ornaments, security and produce, as the essentials of a good city.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig-tree; And none shall make them afraid.”
judaism.explanation: Micah pictures a time of peace when everyone enjoys the fruit of his own land without fear.
judaism.tie_back: Sitting under one’s own vine without fear joins produce, happiness and security, three of the Kural’s five ornaments.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth. A trustworthy person is the best kinsman, Nibbana the highest bliss.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ranks health first among gains and contentment as the truest wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also puts freedom from disease first among a land’s ornaments, followed by wealth and happiness.

jainism.quote_or_event: “May all subjects prosper, the king be strong and righteous, rains fall timely, diseases be eradicated, and may there be no fear of famine, theft, fire, or illness.”
jainism.explanation: The Shanti Path recited at the end of Digambara worship, addressed to Shantinatha, includes a prayer for the welfare of the whole realm: health, timely rain, plenty and security under a righteous king.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural names freedom from disease, wealth, harvests, happiness and security as a land's five ornaments; this Jain prayer asks for almost exactly the same goods for every country.
jainism.source: Shanti Path (Hindi Shanti Path of Digambara worship), verse 7, English rendering at frontdesk.co.in ('Shanti Path with Meaning', 2025)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Baygumpura, ’the city without sorrow’, is the name of the town. There is no suffering or anxiety there. There are no troubles or taxes on commodities there. There is no fear, blemish or downfall there. … There is lasting peace and safety there, O Siblings of Destiny. … That city is populous and eternally famous. Those who live there are wealthy and contented.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas, whose hymns are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, describes Begampura, the ideal city where suffering, fear and inequality are absent and its citizens are prosperous, secure and at peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural names five ornaments of a land, freedom from disease, wealth, harvests, happiness and security; Ravidas's Begampura is adorned with almost the same list: no suffering, wealth, contentment, peace and safety.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 345, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells that Zeus married Themis, who bore the Horai: Eunomia (Good Order), Dike (Justice) and Eirene (Peace), goddesses who watch over the works of mortal men.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, order, justice and peace are divine sisters who make human communities flourish.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Horai are, in effect, the ornaments of a well-ordered land, as the Kural’s five are.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We may define happiness as prosperity combined with virtue; or as independence of life; or as the secure enjoyment of the maximum of pleasure; or as a good condition of property and body, together with the power of guarding one's property and body and making use of them.”
philosophy.explanation: In his guide for political speakers, Aristotle sets out the commonly agreed parts of happiness, including wealth, health and the secure enjoyment of life, and applies several of them to whole communities as well as to individuals.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle's list of what makes life good overlaps closely with the Kural's ornaments of a country, which are health, wealth, happiness and security.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric, I.5, 1360b (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)

real_life_example.event_title: The first Human Development Report introduces the Human Development Index
real_life_example.place: United Nations Development Programme, New York, United States
real_life_example.event: In 1990 the UN Development Programme published the first Human Development Report, led by the economist Mahbub ul Haq with Amartya Sen as a key collaborator. It introduced the Human Development Index, which ranks countries not by income alone but by an average of longevity, education and standard of living. The report argued that development should be judged by whether people can lead long, healthy and creative lives.
real_life_example.explanation: The index changed how the world measures national success, treating health and knowledge as being as important as wealth.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names freedom from disease, wealth, good harvests, happiness and security as the ornaments of a country, and the Human Development Index similarly judges nations by health and well-being as well as wealth.

tamil:
நாடென்ப நாடா வளத்தன நாடல்ல
நாட வளந்தரு நாடு.
transliteration:
Naadenpa naadaa valaththana naadalla
naada valandharu naadu.
meaning: Wise people say a true country is one whose riches come without having to search for them. A land that gives riches only after hard searching is not a true country.
elementary: Some gardens grow fruit almost by themselves because the soil and rain are just right. Other gardens need you to dig, water and fight weeds every day for a tiny crop. Valluvar says the best country is like the first garden.
university: The kural is built on a pun between naadu (‘country’) and the verb naadu (‘to seek, to search for’): naadaa valaththana are lands ‘whose wealth is not sought’, and naada valandharu naadu is a land ‘that gives wealth only when sought’. Parimelazhagar explains that the best lands produce their riches by natural endowment, without great exertion by the inhabitants, while lands that yield only to heavy labour are not counted as countries in the full sense. The line is not a praise of idleness, since the Kural elsewhere (chapter 62, Aalvinaiyudaimai) insists on effort; it is a judgment on natural endowment. Kalaignar makes this explicit by contrasting lands naturally rich with lands that prosper only through constant struggle.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Mahabharata’s description of the Uttarakurus, the northern land of the blessed, tells of trees that bear fruit and flowers in every season and yield whatever the people need, so that they live in ease without labouring for their food.
hinduism.explanation: Uttarakuru is the Indian image of a land that gives everything by nature.
hinduism.tie_back: Uttarakuru is the extreme case of the Kural’s ideal: a land whose wealth comes without being sought.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Jambu-khanda section (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.”
christianity.explanation: In a parable of the kingdom of God, Jesus describes seed growing by itself while the farmer sleeps, without his knowing how.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Fruit of herself’ is close to the Kural’s naadaa valam, wealth that grows without being laboriously sought.

islam.quote_or_event: “And Allāh presents an example: a city [i.e., Makkah] which was safe and secure, its provision coming to it in abundance from every location, but it denied the favors of Allāh. So Allāh made it taste the envelopment of hunger and fear for what they had been doing.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes a city whose provision came to it plentifully from everywhere, until its ingratitude brought hunger and fear.
islam.tie_back: Provision ‘coming to it’ from every side is the Kural’s land whose wealth arrives without being sought.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the land, whither thou goest in to possess it, is not as the land of Egypt, from whence ye came out, where thou didst sow thy seed, and didst water it with thy foot, as a garden of herbs; but the land, whither ye go over to possess it, is a land of hills and valleys, and drinketh water as the rain of heaven cometh down.”
judaism.explanation: Moses contrasts Egypt, where fields must be watered by hard irrigation work, with the promised land, which is watered by rain from heaven.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s very contrast: a land that yields only through toil versus a land that yields by its own nature.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Agganna Sutta the Buddha tells how, at the beginning of the world, rice grew by itself, clean and ready to eat, and whatever was gathered in the evening grew back by morning. Only when beings began to hoard it did the self-growing rice disappear, so that they had to plough, sow and divide the fields.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta explains the origin of labour, property and kingship as a fall from a time of effortless plenty.
buddhism.tie_back: The self-growing rice is the Buddhist picture of wealth that comes without being sought, the Kural’s ideal.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The others are called the ‘regions of enjoyment’–bhogabhūmi as the objects of enjoyment are provided by the ten kinds of desire-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa).”
jainism.explanation: Pujyapada contrasts the lands of labour (karmabhumi), where agriculture and the other occupations are needed, with the lands of enjoyment (bhogabhumi), where wish-fulfilling trees supply everything without effort.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural ranks highest the lands whose wealth comes without being sought; Jain cosmology has exactly such lands, though it also teaches that liberation can be won only in the lands of labour.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 3.37, with Pujyapada's Sarvarthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
