sikhism.quote_or_event: “Why, O mind, do you plot and plan, when the Dear Lord Himself provides for your care? From rocks and stones He created living beings; He places their nourishment before them.”
sikhism.explanation: In the So Dar portion of the evening prayer, Guru Arjan tells the anxious mind that God has already set sustenance before every creature, even those born among rocks and stones.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural honours the land whose wealth comes without being laboriously sought; Guru Arjan teaches that provision is already laid out by the Creator before it is sought.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For the fruitful earth unforced bare them fruit abundantly and without stint. They dwelt in ease and peace upon their lands with many good things.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the golden race of men under Cronos, who lived without toil because the earth fed them of its own accord.
greek_mythology.tie_back: ‘The earth unforced’ is almost a translation of the Kural’s naadaa valam, wealth that is not sought.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 116-119 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Statesman, Plato’s Stranger tells the myth of the age of Cronus, when people had fruit in plenty from trees and plants that the earth gave of its own accord, without farming, and needed no political constitutions.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the myth to contrast a divinely cared-for age of plenty with the present age, in which people must work and govern themselves.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s myth gives a philosophical frame to the Kural’s contrast between lands rich by nature and lands rich only through toil.

real_life_example.event_title: Oil is struck at Burgan, Kuwait
real_life_example.event: Surface seepages of bitumen at Burgan had long hinted at oil, and in 1934 the ruler of Kuwait granted a concession to the Kuwait Oil Company, a joint venture of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company and Gulf Oil. Burgan No. 1, drilled at a seepage beginning in 1936, struck a high-pressure oil-bearing sandstone in February 1938. Exports began in 1946, and the Great Burgan field became one of the largest in the world, the main source of Kuwait's wealth.
real_life_example.explanation: A small country's prosperity came above all from the riches already lying beneath its soil.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural honours lands whose wealth comes from their natural endowment rather than from endless toil, and Kuwait's fortune from the Burgan field is a modern example of riches given by the land itself.

tamil:
ஆங்கமை வெய்தியக் கண்ணும் பயமின்றே
வேந்தமை வில்லாத நாடு.
transliteration:
Aangamai veydhiyak kannum payamindre
vendhamai villaadha naadu.
meaning: Even if a land has all these good things, it is of no use if it does not have a good king who gets along with his people.
elementary: You can have the best football, the greenest field and the fastest players, but without a good captain who works well with the team, you will not win. A country with every treasure still needs a good leader.
university: The chapter ends by subordinating everything it has praised to kingship. Aangu amaivu eydhiya kannum means ‘even when it has attained all the excellences set out there’ (in the previous nine kurals), and payam indre means ‘it is without fruit’. The key compound vendhamaivu is read by Parimelazhagar as ‘harmony, or fitness, between king and subjects’, which Pope follows with ‘not with its king at peace’; Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar read it more simply as ‘a good king or good government’, and Solomon Pappaiah as a government with love for its citizens. Either way, the verse links this chapter back to the Kural’s section on kingship (Arasiyal) and warns that natural wealth without right rule is wasted. The sandhi text agrees with ytamizh word for word.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The world depends upon agriculture and trade and is protected by the Vedas. All these again are duly protected by the king exercising his principal duty.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati tells King Vasumanas that without royal protection, farming and trade would collapse, the strong would rob the weak and famine would ravage the kingdom.
hinduism.tie_back: Brihaspati makes the Kural’s point: all a land’s wealth depends on a king who fulfils his duty.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section 68 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “The king by judgment establisheth the land: but he that receiveth gifts overthroweth it.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says a just king makes a country stable, while a corrupt one brings it down.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the proverb makes the fate of the land depend on the quality of its ruler.

islam.quote_or_event: “Surely! Everyone of you is a guardian and is responsible for his charges: The Imam (ruler) of the people is a guardian and is responsible for his subjects.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that every person, and above all the ruler, is a guardian answerable for those in his care.
islam.tie_back: The ruler as guardian of his people is the bond (vendhamaivu) without which, the Kural says, a rich land is useless.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Hanina, the vice-high priest said: pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear it inspires, every man would swallow his neighbor alive.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that even an imperfect government is a blessing, because without it society would fall into violence.
judaism.tie_back: Rabbi Hanina, like Valluvar, holds that a land without working rule gains nothing from its other goods.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that when kings are unrighteous, their officials and then the whole people become unrighteous; the sun and moon go astray, the rains fail to come in season, the crops ripen badly, and people become weak and short-lived. When kings are righteous, the reverse happens.
buddhism.explanation: In this teaching, the moral quality of the ruler flows down through the people into nature itself.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s point is the Kural’s: a land’s fertility and well-being are worthless, even lost, without a righteous ruler.

jainism.quote_or_event: “During his reign he taught, for the benefit of the people, the seventy-two sciences, of which writing is the first, arithmetic the most important, and the knowledge of omens the last, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men.”
jainism.explanation: Rishabha, called 'First King' among his five names, is remembered as the ruler who gave his people the arts, sciences and occupations; Jacobi's note adds that the Kulakaras before him were the first kings and founders of families.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says even a land with every excellence is fruitless without a fitting ruler; the Jain account of Rishabha likewise makes a wise king the one who turns a land's potential into a working society.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha §§210-211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The kings had lost their higher consciousness, reveling in pleasure and sensuality. Since Baabar’s rule has been proclaimed, even the princes have no food to eat.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Babarvani hymns, Guru Nanak laments the sack of the Punjab by Babur's armies and lays part of the blame on the rulers, who had squandered their wealth in pleasure and lost their awareness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that even a land with every excellence is fruitless without a fitting ruler; Guru Nanak shows a rich realm brought to hunger because its rulers were unfit.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Ashtapadi, Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “You are like some blameless king, who upholds righteousness, as the monarch over a great and valiant nation: the earth yields its wheat and barley, the trees are loaded with fruit, the ewes bring forth lambs, and the sea abounds with fish by reason of his virtues.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, in disguise, praises Penelope by comparing her to a just king whose goodness makes the whole land fruitful.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer, like Valluvar, makes the land’s abundance depend on the quality of its king.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates says that cities will never have rest from their evils until philosophers become kings, or kings and rulers become true philosophers, so that political power and wisdom meet in one person.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, the right ruler is the one condition without which no city can be good.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar both end their picture of the good city by insisting that everything depends on the right kind of ruler.

real_life_example.event_title: The reign of Charles II, last Habsburg king of Spain
real_life_example.event: Charles II inherited the vast Spanish empire at the age of four in 1665. Chronically ill and widely regarded as unable to govern effectively, he was dominated by court factions while Spain suffered economic troubles and military setbacks against Louis XIV. He fathered no children, and the dispute over his succession after his death in 1700 led to the War of the Spanish Succession and the break-up of Spain's European possessions.
real_life_example.explanation: Spain still ruled one of the largest empires in the world, but without a capable ruler its great resources could not prevent decline.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even a land with every good quality bears no fruit without a fitting ruler, and Spain under Charles II is a well-known case of vast wealth undone by a king unable to rule.

tamil:
ஆற்று பவர்க்கும் அரண்பொருள் அஞ்சித்தற்
போற்று பவர்க்கும் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Aatru pavarkkum aranporul anjiththar
potru pavarkkum porul.
meaning: A fort is a treasure both for a king who goes out to attack and for a king who stays inside it to protect himself out of fear.
elementary: Think of a tree house with a strong ladder. When you want to go out and play a game of tag, it is your safe base to run out from. When it starts to rain or a big dog chases you, it is the place you run back into. Valluvar says a fort is useful in both ways, for going out and for staying safe.
university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of aran (fortification), the last of the six angas (limbs) of the state listed in kural 381 (padai, kudi, koozh, amaichu, natpu, aran). The couplet is built on a balanced contrast: aatrupavar are ‘those who act’, which Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) take as those who go out to make war on others, while anjith than potrupavar are ‘those who, fearing, guard themselves’, the besieged who seek shelter. The word porul is used twice, first as ‘a thing of value’ (aran porul, ‘the fort is a treasure’) and then as the predicate, a deliberate play on the same word that also names the whole second book of the Kural (Porutpaal). The point is that a fortress is not merely defensive: it is a base of operations for offense and a refuge in weakness alike. The sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org reads ‘ஆற்று பவர்க்கு மரண்பொரு ளஞ்சித்தற்’, which divides into the same words as the ytamizh.com text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One bowman, placed on a rampart, is a match in battle for one hundred (foes), one hundred for ten thousand; hence it is prescribed (in the Sastras that a king will posses) a fortress.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king that a fort multiplies the strength of every defender, which is why the law books require a king to have one.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Manu treats the fort as an essential royal asset because of the military advantage it gives.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 7.74 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)

christianity.quote_or_event: “When a strong man armed keepeth his palace, his goods are in peace.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of an armed man guarding a stronghold to describe how security keeps what is inside safe.
christianity.tie_back: The image matches the Kural’s second half: a guarded stronghold is what keeps the fearful safe.

islam.quote_or_event: “They said, ‘O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are [great] corrupters in the land. So may we assign for you an expenditure that you might make between us and them a barrier?’”
islam.explanation: A people suffering from raiders offer to pay Dhul-Qarnayn to build them a protective barrier.
islam.tie_back: Their offer shows what the Kural says: to those who live in fear, a fortification is worth paying for.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He acted with vigor, rebuilding the whole breached wall, raising towers on it, and building another wall outside it.”
judaism.explanation: When the Assyrian king Sennacherib came against Jerusalem, King Hezekiah’s first act was to repair and double the city walls.
judaism.tie_back: Hezekiah, threatened and afraid, turns to the fort as his chief asset, just as the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “With this first requisite of a fortress it is well provided for the protection of those within and to ward off those without.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Nagara Sutta the Buddha lists the parts of a royal frontier fortress, repeating that each one both protects those inside and drives off those outside.
buddhism.tie_back: The refrain has the same two-sided use as the Kural: the fort serves both defense and active resistance.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Erect a wall, gates, and battlements; dig a moat; construct śataghnîs: then you will be a Kshattriya.”
jainism.explanation: In the Uttaradhyayana's dialogue on King Nami's renunciation, Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, urges the departing king that fortifying his city is the very mark of a warrior-ruler; Nami answers that the only fortress worth building is an inner one.
jainism.tie_back: Indra's advice voices exactly the Kural's premise that a fort is the prized possession of a king, while the Jain text then turns that premise toward renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, built up a Sikh army and fortified his cities; he built a fort near Amritsar named Lohgarh, instilled the will to fight and high morale in his followers, and his Sikhs went on to defeat Shah Jahan's armies four times, adding to Sikh ideals the right and duty to defend the faith by the sword if necessary.
sikhism.explanation: After Guru Arjan's martyrdom, Guru Hargobind gave the community both a spiritual and a temporal centre, and a fortress that served as a base for its armed defence.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls a fortress a treasure both for those who march out to fight and for those who shelter in fear; Guru Hargobind's Lohgarh was built for a community that had to do both.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Guru Hargobind

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Poseidon recalls that he and Apollo built the walls of Troy for King Laomedon, and those god-built walls sheltered the Trojans throughout the war while Hector used the city as a base for his attacks on the Greek camp.
greek_mythology.explanation: Troy’s walls served the Trojans both as a refuge when they were driven back and as the starting point for their sallies.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Troy shows both uses the Kural names: a base for those who attack and a shelter for those who defend.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Those who have their cities surrounded by walls may either take advantage of them or not, but cities which are unwalled have no choice.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues against those who scorn walls: walls give a city options, while having none leaves it no choice at all.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, sees the fort as a resource that serves a city whether it attacks or defends.

real_life_example.event_title: Edward I builds his castles in north Wales
real_life_example.event: After conquering the last independent part of Wales, King Edward I of England began building great castles at Conwy, Caernarfon and Harlech in 1283, and later at Beaumaris, largely designed by his chief military architect, James of St George. UNESCO describes them as works of both colonisation and defence. Harlech stood on a crag above the sea with access to a small quay, so that in times of trouble it could be supplied by boat, and it was attacked during the Welsh rising led by Madog ap Llywelyn in 1294-95.
real_life_example.explanation: The castles served Edward both as bases from which his officials and soldiers controlled newly conquered country and as strongholds where garrisons, supplied from the sea, could hold out when the Welsh rose against them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a fortress is precious both to the king who marches out to attack and to the one who shelters behind it in fear, and Edward's castles were built to serve exactly both purposes.

tamil:
மணிநீரும் மண்ணும் மலையும் அணிநிழற்
காடும் உடைய தரண்.
transliteration:
Maninheerum mannum malaiyum aninizhar
kaadum udaiya tharan.
meaning: A true fort has water as clear as a jewel, open land, hills, and a forest with thick shade.
elementary: Imagine building a pillow fort. It is best to put it behind the sofa, beside a blanket ‘river’, with a big armchair ‘mountain’ next to it and lots of cushions like a forest. Anyone sneaking up has to cross all of that first. Valluvar says the best forts use nature in the same way: water, open ground, hills and forest.
university: Here Valluvar lists the natural defenses (iyarkai aran) that should surround a fort: mani neer (water clear as a gem, i.e. a moat or lake that never dries), mann (land, glossed by Varadarasanar and Pappaiah as open ground with no cover for an attacker), malai (hill) and ani nizhal kaadu (forest of beautiful or dense shade). Parimelazhagar and the later commentators read these as four types of fort: neer aran, nila aran, malai aran and kaattu aran. Pappaiah states this directly. The list closely parallels the Sanskrit arthashastra classification into water-fort (audaka), mountain-fort (parvata), desert or open-land fort (dhanvana) and forest-fort (vanadurga), which suggests a shared South Asian military science that the next couplet calls simply ‘the treatise’ (nool). Kalaignar reads mani neer as a deep, wide moat. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘மணிநீரு மண்ணு மலையு மணிநிழற் / காடு முடைய தரண்’, which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “a water-fortification (audaka) such as an island in the midst of a river, or a plain surrounded by low ground; a mountainous fortification (párvata) such as a rocky tract or a cave; a desert (dhánvana) such as a wild tract devoid of water and overgrown with thicket growing in barren soil; or a forest fortification (vanadurga) full of wagtail (khajana), water and thickets.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya names four kinds of natural fortification to be built at the kingdom’s borders: water, mountain, desert and forest.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the same four-part list as the Kural’s water, land, hill and forest.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 2.3 ‘Construction of Forts’ (trans. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “He shall dwell on high: his place of defence shall be the munitions of rocks: bread shall be given him; his waters shall be sure.”
christianity.explanation: Isaiah promises the righteous a high rocky stronghold with guaranteed bread and water.
christianity.tie_back: Isaiah’s ideal refuge combines the height of hills with an assured water supply, two of the Kural’s natural defenses.

islam.quote_or_event: “And Allah has made for you, from that which He has created, shadows and has made for you from the mountains, shelters.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an counts shade and mountain shelters among God’s gifts for human protection.
islam.tie_back: Shade and mountains are two of the natural protections the Kural wants around a fort.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A large force was assembled to stop up all the springs and the wadi that flowed through the land, for otherwise, they thought, the king of Assyria would come and find water in abundance.”
judaism.explanation: Before the Assyrian siege, Hezekiah’s men blocked the springs outside Jerusalem so that the besiegers would have no water.
judaism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s point that controlling water is itself a fortification.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, the royal frontier fortress has a moat, both deep & wide.”
buddhism.explanation: The second requisite of the Buddha’s model fortress is a deep, wide moat.
buddhism.tie_back: The moat is the Kural’s ‘gem-clear water’, the first natural defense on its list.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “At each gate they made a tank with golden lotuses having four gates like the rampart of the samavasaraṇa.” … “In the midst of the samavasaraṇa, a caitya-tree made by the Vyantaras, rising for three kos, indicated the rise of the Three Jewels.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra's description of the samavasarana, the assembly hall the gods raise for a Tirthankara's preaching, sets pools of water at its gates and a great shade-giving sacred tree at its centre within its ramparts.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain sacred enclosure combines clear water and a towering tree inside its walls, a distant echo of the Kural's natural defences of gem-clear water, open ground, hill and shady forest, though its purpose is sermon and refuge, not war.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra 1.3, part 10 ‘Description of a samavasaraṇa’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS, 1931; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “A fortress like that of Sri Lanka, with the ocean as a moat around it - there is no news about that house of Raavan.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir recalls Ravana's island citadel, defended by the sea itself, to show that even the strongest natural defences do not last.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural lists clear water, open ground, hills and forest as a fortress's natural defences; Kabir names the greatest of water-moats, but only to say that it could not keep Ravana's house in being.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 481, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, the princess Nausicaa describes the city of the Phaeacians to Odysseus as surrounded by a high wall, with a fine harbour on either side and a narrow entrance, a site protected by the sea on both flanks.
greek_mythology.explanation: The ideal city of the Phaeacians is protected mainly by its natural setting of water and a narrow approach.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Homer’s ideal city depends on natural surroundings as much as on its wall.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There should be a natural abundance of springs and fountains in the town, or, if there is a deficiency of them, great reservoirs may be established for the collection of rainwater, such as will not fail when the inhabitants are cut off from the country …”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle requires the ideal city’s site to have a water supply that cannot fail even during a war.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, begins good fortification with the natural site, and above all with water.

real_life_example.event_title: Rajput rulers build the hill forts of Rajasthan among hills, rivers, forest and desert
real_life_example.event: Between the 8th and 18th centuries the Rajput states of Rajasthan built a series of great hill forts, six of which, at Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron, Amber and Jaisalmer, now form a single UNESCO World Heritage property. UNESCO notes that the forts use the natural defences offered by the landscape, namely hills, deserts, rivers and dense forests, with Ranthambore set in forest, Gagron protected by a river and Jaisalmer standing in desert, and that they contain extensive water-harvesting structures. Gagron is surrounded on three sides by the waters of the Ahu and Kalisindh rivers.
real_life_example.explanation: The forts show a long South Asian tradition of choosing sites where water, hills, forest and open ground did much of the work of defence, backed by secure water supplies.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar lists clear water, open ground, hills and dense forest as the marks of a true fortress, and the Rajput builders set their forts among exactly these natural defences.

tamil:
உயர்வகலம் திண்மை அருமைஇந் நான்கின்
அமைவரண் என்றுரைக்கும் நூல்.
transliteration:
Uyarvakalam thinmai arumaiin naankin
amaivaran endruraikkum nool.
meaning: Books on this subject say a fort's wall needs four things: it must be high, thick, strong, and hard to reach.
elementary: A good sandcastle wall has to be tall so the waves can’t jump over it, thick so they can’t push through, packed hard so it doesn’t crumble, and hard to reach, maybe behind a ditch. If any one of these is missing, the sea gets in. Valluvar says the old books on forts ask for the same four things.
university: After the natural defenses (742), Valluvar turns to the man-made wall (seyarkai aran, as Pappaiah calls it) and gives its four standard qualities: uyarvu (height, so that it cannot be scaled), akalam (breadth, which Pappaiah explains as room for defenders to stand and move on the rampart), thinmai (solidity, so that it cannot be battered down) and arumai (difficulty or inaccessibility). Parimelazhagar’s tradition explains arumai as the difficulty of approach created by engines and traps (pori) set on the walls, a reading that Pappaiah follows. The phrase endru uraikkum nool, ‘so says the treatise’, is one of the places where Valluvar openly cites earlier military and political science. Commentators link it to the arthashastra tradition, whose fort specifications (for example, a rampart ‘six dandas high and twice as much broad’) are very similar. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘உயர்வகலந் திண்மை யருமையிந் நான்கி / னமைவர ணென்றுரைக்கு நூல்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “a rampart six dandas high and twice as much broad shall be erected by heaping mud upwards and by making it square at the bottom, oval at the centre pressed by the trampling of elephants and bulls, and planted with thorny and poisonous plants in bushes.”
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra gives exact measurements for a fort’s rampart, packed hard by elephants and bulls and planted with thorny bushes.
hinduism.tie_back: It sets out the Kural’s four qualities: height, breadth, strength (packed earth) and inaccessibility (thorns).
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 2.3 ‘Construction of Forts’ (trans. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And had a wall great and high, and had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels.”
christianity.explanation: John’s vision of the New Jerusalem describes a great, high wall with gates guarded by angels.
christianity.tie_back: The ideal heavenly city has the Kural’s height and greatness, with guarded and hard-to-reach entrances.

islam.quote_or_event: “Bring me sheets of iron” - until, when he had leveled [them] between the two mountain walls, he said, “Blow [with bellows],” until when he had made it [like] fire, he said, “Bring me, that I may pour over it molten copper.”
islam.explanation: Dhul-Qarnayn builds his barrier from iron fused with molten copper and fills the gap between two mountains with it.
islam.tie_back: The barrier is as high as the mountains and as solid as metal, showing the Kural’s height and strength.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Walk around Zion, circle it; count its towers, take note of its ramparts; go through its citadels, that you may recount it to a future age.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist invites pilgrims to walk around Jerusalem and admire its towers and ramparts as a sign of God’s protection.
judaism.tie_back: The psalm praises the same features the Kural lists: tall towers and strong ramparts.
judaism.source: Psalms 48:13-14 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 48:12-13)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, the royal frontier fortress has ramparts: high & thick & completely covered with plaster.”
buddhism.explanation: The seventh requisite of the Buddha’s fortress is a high, thick, fully plastered rampart.
buddhism.tie_back: High, thick and sealed is almost the Kural’s height, breadth and strength.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “It may be noted that three gunavratas and four siksavratas are grouped together and are known as silavratas, i.e., supplementary vows because these vows perform the work of supplementing or protecting the five main anuvratas just as towns are protected or guarded by the encircling walls built around them.”
jainism.explanation: Jain householder ethics treats the seven supplementary vows as a protective wall thrown around the five small vows of non-violence, truth, non-stealing, chastity and non-possession.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural specifies the height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility of a town's wall, Jainism borrows the same image of the encircling wall to explain how the supplementary vows guard the core vows.
jainism.source: Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’, section on the twelve vratas (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “How can the beautiful fortress be conquered, O Siblings of Destiny? It has double walls and triple moats.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir pictures the ego-bound self as a fortress with double ramparts and triple moats, defended by the passions, so strong that no ordinary person can take it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines a fort by height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility; Kabir's fortress with its double walls and triple moats has exactly those qualities, though he means the fortress of the mind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1161, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Odysseus sees in the underworld Antiope’s twin sons Amphion and Zethus, who founded seven-gated Thebes and surrounded it with towers, because even with all their strength they could not live in wide Thebes without walls. Later tradition says Amphion’s lyre made the stones move into place by themselves.
greek_mythology.explanation: The founders of Thebes knew that even great strength needs a high, towered wall around it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s tall, strong wall is the same thing the mythic founders of Thebes thought a city could not do without.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “not only should cities have walls, but care should be taken to make them ornamental, as well as useful for warlike purposes, and adapted to resist modern inventions.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle wants city walls that look fine but are above all built to resist the latest siege engines.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s wall ‘adapted to resist’ attack is the Kural’s idea of arumai: a wall made hard to overcome.

real_life_example.event_title: Theodosius II builds the land walls of Constantinople
real_life_example.event: Under Emperor Theodosius II and his prefect Anthemius, a new line of land walls was built across the peninsula of Constantinople, with work dated to about 413 and repeatedly strengthened afterwards. The system combined a massive main wall with 96 towers, a lower outer wall in front of it and a moat. World History Encyclopedia gives the inner wall as almost 5 metres thick and about 12 metres high, with a moat about 20 metres wide that could be flooded, an arrangement that kept enemy siege engines far from the main wall.
real_life_example.explanation: The layered walls protected Constantinople through many sieges over the following centuries and became the classic example of a city defence that height, thickness and obstacles made almost impossible to approach.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility as the four qualities of a fortress wall, and the Theodosian walls combined tall towers, thick masonry and a moat that kept attackers at a distance.

tamil:
சிறுகாப்பிற் பேரிடத்த தாகி உறுபகை
ஊக்கம் அழிப்ப தரண்.
transliteration:
Sirukaappir peridaththa thaaki urupakai
ookkam azhippa tharan.
meaning: A fort should have only a few places that need guarding but lots of room inside, and it should crush the spirit of any enemy that attacks.
elementary: Think of a playground fort with just one small doorway and lots of room inside. You only need one friend at the door to keep watch, while everyone else can play inside. And anyone who tries to get in soon gives up, because the doorway is so hard to rush. That is Valluvar’s kind of fort.
university: The couplet sets two design principles against each other: siru kaappu (small guard-length, i.e. few places that need to be defended) and per idam (large interior space). The commentators all explain this as a narrow, easily held perimeter or entrance around a spacious interior; Kalaignar says that the part to be protected is small while the inside is wide. The second line gives the purpose: urupakai ookkam azhippathu, ‘that which destroys the zeal of the strong enemy who comes against it’. Pappaiah glosses this as filling the besiegers with dismay. The idea is psychological as much as structural: a well-designed fort defeats the attacker’s morale before it defeats his army. Parimelazhagar treats the chapter’s verses from 743 on as a list of the defining marks (ilakkanam) of a man-made fort. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘சிறுகாப்பிற் பேரிடத்த தாகி யுறுபகை / யூக்க மழிப்ப தரண்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him cause to be built for himself, in the centre of it, a spacious palace, (well) protected, habitable in every season, resplendent (with whitewash), supplied with water and trees.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king to build a spacious, well-protected palace at the centre of his fort.
hinduism.tie_back: A roomy interior inside a guarded ring is the Kural’s ‘ample within, small to guard’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs describes God as a tower that anyone righteous can run into and be safe.
christianity.tie_back: A single strong tower with room for all who shelter there echoes the Kural’s small-to-guard, large-within fort.

islam.quote_or_event: “So Gog and Magog were unable to pass over it, nor were they able [to effect] in it any penetration.”
islam.explanation: Once Dhul-Qarnayn’s barrier closed the single gap between the mountains, the raiders could neither climb it nor break through.
islam.tie_back: One narrow gap sealed between natural walls stops a whole hostile people: few points to guard, and an enemy’s drive brought to nothing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is much work and it is spread out; we are scattered over the wall, far from one another. When you hear a trumpet call, gather yourselves to me at that place; our God will fight for us!”
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah, rebuilding Jerusalem’s wall with too few men, sets up a trumpet signal so that the defenders can gather at whatever point is attacked.
judaism.tie_back: Nehemiah faces the very problem the Kural solves: a long wall needs a small number of points that must actually be guarded.
judaism.source: Nehemiah 4:13-14 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 4:19-20)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a border city is closely guarded both within and without, even so, guard yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers to guard themselves as carefully as a frontier city is guarded.
buddhism.tie_back: The closely guarded border city is the Kural’s fort, where careful guarding makes the whole place secure.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anativyakte gupte sthane suprativesmike aneka- nirgamadvaravivarjita-niketana : Dwelling in a place which is not too exposed and not too enclosed, with good neighbors, and few exits.”
jainism.explanation: Among Hemacandra's thirty-five qualities of an ideal Jain householder is living in a well-sited home that is neither too exposed nor too shut in and has only a few ways in and out, the traditional reasoning being security against thieves.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's fort with few points to guard and ample room inside is matched, on a domestic scale, by the Jain householder's dwelling with few exits that is neither too open nor too cramped.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, no. 7, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’ (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “It is defended by the five elements, the twenty-five categories, attachment, pride, jealousy and the awesomely powerful Maya. The poor mortal being does not have the strength to conquer it; what should I do now, O Lord? … The greed that fills their hearts is the arrow; with these things, their fortress is impregnable.”
sikhism.explanation: In the same hymn Kabir describes the garrison and weapons of the fortress of maya, and confesses that its defences break the will of anyone who tries to storm it by his own strength.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's fort crushes the zeal of the enemy that attacks it; Kabir's fortress so daunts the attacker that he cries he has no strength to take it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1161, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus describes the pass of Thermopylae as a narrow way between the mountains and the sea, where the Greeks rebuilt an old wall. There Leonidas and a small Greek force held back Xerxes’ huge army for several days, and even the Persian king’s elite Immortals were driven back.
greek_mythology.explanation: A narrow front let a few defenders hold off many attackers and badly damage their confidence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Thermopylae is a real example of the Kural’s narrow point to guard that ‘destroys the enemy’s zeal’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The general, unable to control his irritation, will launch his men to the assault like swarming ants, with the result that one-third of his men are slain, while the town still remains untaken.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu warns that besieging a well-walled town makes the attacking general reckless and wastes his army.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point seen from the attacker’s side: a good fort wears down the enemy’s spirit as well as his army.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.5 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: The garrison of Kumamoto Castle holds out against the Satsuma army
real_life_example.event: In February 1877, during the Satsuma Rebellion, Saigo Takamori's samurai army attacked Kumamoto Castle, the only Imperial Army base in Kyushu, which was defended by government troops under Major General Tani Tateki. The castle had been built in the early 1600s by Kato Kiyomasa as a formidable fortress, and this was the first time its defences were tested in battle. The garrison held the castle for about two months without the rebels getting in, until government reinforcements arrived in April and the Satsuma forces withdrew.
real_life_example.explanation: Although the Satsuma forces were seasoned fighters and the defenders were less experienced, the castle let the garrison hold out until the rebel offensive lost its momentum and was broken.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises a fort that is easy to guard yet roomy within and that breaks the spirit of any enemy who attacks it, and Kumamoto Castle stalled the rebel army until its campaign collapsed.

tamil:
கொளற்கரிதாய்க் கொண்டகூழ்த் தாகி அகத்தார்
நிலைக்கெளிதாம் நீரது அரண்.
transliteration:
Kolarkarithaaik kondakoozhth thaaki akaththaar
nilaikkelithaam neerathu aran.
meaning: A fort should be hard to capture, full of stored food, and easy for the people inside to defend.
elementary: If you are playing a long game of capture-the-flag, your base needs three things. It should be hard for the other team to get into, it should have snacks and water so you don’t have to leave, and it should be easy for your own team to move around in. Valluvar says a real fort needs the same three things.
university: The couplet names three conditions. Kolarku arithaai means ‘hard to take’; Pappaiah adds ‘even under a siege of many days’. Konda koozhthu aagi means ‘holding provisions’. Koozh (literally gruel or food) is the same word that names the Koozhiyal (the section on wealth and resources) in some divisions of the Porutpaal, and here it means stored food. Akaththaar nilaikku elithaam means ‘easy for those within to hold their position’. Varadarasanar reads this as easy for the defenders to stay in, while Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as convenient for the defenders to fight from. The final neerathu (‘of such a nature’) marks the three conditions as the fort’s defining nature. The ytamizh text reads ‘நிலைக்கெளிதாம் நீரது’, and the sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org reads ‘நிலைக்கெளிதா நீர தரண்’. These are orthographic variants of the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let that (fort) be well supplied with weapons, money, grain and beasts of burden, with Brahmanas, with artisans, with engines, with fodder, and with water.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists everything a royal fort must hold, from grain and water to weapons and skilled people.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu’s well-supplied fort is exactly the Kural’s fort ‘holding provisions’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says that anyone planning to build a tower must first make sure he has the resources to finish it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a stronghold as useless without enough resources behind it.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Joseph] said, ‘You will plant for seven years consecutively; and what you harvest leave in its spikes, except a little from which you will eat.’”
islam.explanation: Joseph advises Egypt to store most of seven years’ harvest in preparation for the famine to come.
islam.tie_back: Stored grain against hard times is the Kural’s ‘konda koozh’, the fort’s food reserve.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He strengthened the fortified towns and put commanders in them, along with stores of food, oil, and wine, and shields and spears in every town.”
judaism.explanation: King Rehoboam fortified the towns of Judah and stocked each one with food, oil, wine and weapons.
judaism.tie_back: A strong fort stocked with food is exactly what this couplet asks for.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, it has large stores of rice & barley for the delight, convenience, & comfort of those within, and to ward off those without.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s ideal fortress keeps large grain stores so that those inside are comfortable and can resist those outside.
buddhism.tie_back: This joins the Kural’s ideas of stored food and a fort that is ‘easy for those within’.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable …”
jainism.explanation: Nami replies to Indra that a sage's true fortress is built from faith, austerity, self-control and patience, and that, guarded by the three guptis of mind, speech and body, it cannot be taken.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks for a fortress that is hard to capture and easy to hold; the Jain sage describes an inner citadel that is impregnable because its gate is barred by self-control and its wall is patience.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.20–22, first half (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: When the Rajput hill chiefs and imperial Mughal contingents laid siege to Guru Gobind Singh's fort at Anandpur, the Guru and his Sikhs withstood their successive assaults over many months despite dire scarcity of food caused by the prolonged blockade, until the besieged were reduced to desperate straits.
sikhism.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism shows that Anandpur held firm against assault, and that the blockade's real weapon was hunger.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a fortress must be hard to take and well stocked with food; Anandpur proved the first, and its ordeal shows why the second matters.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus reports that when Cyrus besieged Babylon, the Babylonians had stored provisions for many years in advance and did not worry about the siege. Cyrus took the city only by diverting the Euphrates and entering along the riverbed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Babylon’s stores made it almost impossible to starve out, so the attacker had to use a trick instead.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Babylon illustrates the Kural’s provisioned fort and hints at its warning, in the next couplets, about stratagem.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “With a view to the latter it should afford easy egress to the citizens, and at the same time be inaccessible and difficult of capture to enemies.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that, for war, a city’s site should make movement easy for its own citizens and approach hard for enemies.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost word for word the Kural’s ‘hard to capture’ yet ‘easy for those within’.

real_life_example.event_title: Hunger forces the surrender of Vicksburg
real_life_example.event: The Confederate army under General John Pemberton had spent more than a year fortifying Vicksburg with a ring of earthen forts and over 170 cannon, and two Union assaults ordered by General Ulysses S. Grant on 19 and 22 May 1863 failed to break through. Grant then laid siege to the city and cut it off from supplies, and the defenders' daily rations shrank to tiny portions of bacon, flour, sugar, peas and molasses. After 47 days of siege, Pemberton's army surrendered on 4 July 1863.
real_life_example.explanation: Vicksburg showed that earthworks and guns could repel direct assault but not hunger; once its food ran short, the stronghold that controlled the Mississippi had to yield.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks that a fort be hard to capture, well stocked with food and easy for its defenders to hold; Vicksburg had the first and third qualities but not the second, and fell for that lack.

tamil:
எல்லாப் பொருளும் உடைத்தாய் இடத்துதவும்
நல்லாள் உடையது அரண்.
transliteration:
Ellaap porulum udaiththaai idaththuthavum
nallaal udaiyathu aran.
meaning: A true fort has everything that may be needed, and good, brave soldiers who will help when danger comes.
elementary: A good school on a stormy day has torches, blankets and food in the cupboard. But it also needs calm grown-ups who know what to do when the lights go out. Supplies alone are not enough; you need good people too. Valluvar says the same about a fort.
university: The first line (ellaap porulum udaiththaai, ‘having all things’) sums up the material requirements of 745, and the second line brings in the human element that the chapter’s last couplet will make decisive: idaththu uthavum nallaal, ‘good men who help at the (critical) place or time’. Idam can mean both the spot where danger arises and the moment of need, and Varadarasanar reads it as the moment of crisis in battle. Nallaal (nal + aal, ‘good person’) is read by all the commentators as brave warriors: Pappaiah speaks of heroes who can defeat enemies trying to destroy the fort from outside, and Kalaignar of strong fighters who leap into battle. The pairing of stores and soldiers reflects the arthashastra and Dharmashastra habit of listing a fort’s supplies and its garrison together. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘எல்லாப் பொருளு முடைத்தா யிடத்துதவு / நல்லா ளுடைய தரண்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him build (there) a town, making for his safety a fortress, protected by a desert, or a fortress built of (stone and) earth, or one protected by water or trees, or one (formed by an encampment of armed) men or a hill-fort.”
hinduism.explanation: Among the six kinds of fort, Manu includes one made of nothing but armed men (the nri-durga).
hinduism.tie_back: Manu treats good fighting men as a fortress in their own right, which is the Kural’s point about ‘good men who help’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says a wise king counts his soldiers before going to war.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats having enough capable fighters as basic to military success.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the believers to prepare every kind of strength and cavalry they can to deter their enemies.
islam.tie_back: Being ready with ‘whatever you are able of power’ matches the Kural’s fort that has all things and able men.

judaism.quote_or_event: “From that day on, half my servants did work and half held lances and shields, bows and armor.”
judaism.explanation: While Jerusalem’s wall was being rebuilt, Nehemiah kept half his men armed and on guard.
judaism.tie_back: A wall needs armed men ready to defend it, which is the Kural’s ‘good men who help in need’.
judaism.source: Nehemiah 4:10 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 4:16)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, the royal frontier fortress has a large army stationed within — elephant soldiers, cavalry, charioteers, bowmen, standard-bearers, billeting officers, soldiers of the supply corps, noted princes, commando heroes, infantry, & slaves.”
buddhism.explanation: The fifth requisite of the Buddha’s fortress is a full garrison of every kind of soldier stationed inside.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘nallaal’, the fighters who make the stored fort useful.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “On both sides of the east gate of the first rampart stood two gold-colored Vaimānika-gods as door-keepers.” … “At the four gates of the second wall, in the same order beginning with the east, stood the goddesses Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā and Aparājitā, all having one hand in the position bestowing fearlessness …”
jainism.explanation: In Hemacandra's account of Rishabha's assembly hall, every gate of every rampart is held by divine guardians, and the goddesses at the second wall raise the hand that grants fearlessness to those within.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's fort is complete only when it has good and valiant defenders to help in danger, and the Jain samavasarana likewise stations guardians at each gate who give security to all inside.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra 1.3, part 10 ‘Description of a samavasaraṇa’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS, 1931; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: At Anandpur, which Guru Gobind Singh had fortified, the Khalsa was given concrete form at the Baisakhi gathering of 1699: the Panj Piare, five Sikhs of different castes and regions, were initiated first, and the Khalsa were enjoined to succour the helpless and fight the oppressor, to have faith in one God and to consider all human beings equal.
sikhism.explanation: Guru Gobind Singh founded a disciplined, casteless fellowship of saint-soldiers whose duty was to stand by the weak in the hour of danger.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a true fortress holds everything needed and good, brave men who help when danger comes; the Khalsa gave the fortress of Anandpur exactly such defenders.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Seven Against Thebes, as seven enemy champions prepare to storm the seven gates of Thebes, King Eteocles chooses a matching Theban champion to hold each gate, himself taking the seventh.
greek_mythology.explanation: The safety of Thebes depends on posting a fit defender at every gate.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The walls of Thebes are only as good as the men who help at each point of danger, which is the Kural’s ‘idaththu uthavum nallaal’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for when men are well prepared no enemy even thinks of attacking them.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle ends his discussion of city defenses by saying that good preparation discourages attack in the first place.
philosophy.tie_back: A fort fully stocked and well manned, as the Kural requires, is one that enemies do not dare to attack.

real_life_example.event_title: King George VI awards the George Cross to the island of Malta
real_life_example.event: From 1940 Malta was under almost constant air attack, and from January to July 1942 there was only one 24-hour period when no bombs fell; food, fuel and ammunition ran so short that the people came close to starvation and spent long periods in underground shelters. On 15 April 1942 King George VI awarded the George Cross to the island and its people in recognition of their courage under repeated attack. Later in 1942 the Operation Pedestal convoy fought its way through to Malta with vital supplies, despite the loss of many of its ships.
real_life_example.explanation: Malta's survival depended on both supplies brought in at great cost and the endurance of the people who held on under bombardment.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar says a true fortress holds every needed thing and has brave people who help when danger comes, and the island fortress of Malta survived only when both came together.

tamil:
முற்றியும் முற்றா தெறிந்தும் அறைப்படுத்தும்
பற்றற் கரியது அரண்.
transliteration:
Mutriyum mutraa therindhum araippaduththum
patrar kariyathu aran.
meaning: A true fort cannot be taken by surrounding it, by attacking it directly, or by tricks from people inside.
elementary: Imagine your best toy locked in a treasure box. Someone might wait outside your room for hours, or try to grab it quickly, or even trick your little brother into opening the box. A really safe box beats all three tricks. Valluvar says a real fort must be safe from waiting, grabbing and tricking.
university: The couplet lists the three ways a fort can be taken and says a true aran resists all of them: mutriyum (by besieging it all round), mutraathu erindhum (by attacking without a full siege, i.e. storming a weak point), and araippaduththum (by araippadal, which Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read as vanjanai, deceit or treachery, and Pappaiah as turning some of those inside into a fifth column). Pope’s English (‘mine beneath the ground’) follows the other old sense of arai as a hollow or underground passage, so there is a real divergence between treachery and undermining; the Tamil commentarial tradition generally prefers treachery. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘முற்றியு முற்றா தெறிந்து மறைப்படுத்தும்’, where ‘எறிந்து மறைப்படுத்தும்’ is the sandhi form of ‘எறிந்தும் அறைப்படுத்தும்’, which confirms the reading araippaduththum. The inclusion of treachery points ahead to 750: the human element can undo even a physically perfect fort.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Book XIII of the Arthashastra, titled Strategic Means to Capture a Fortress, teaches a conqueror to take forts by sowing dissension among the defenders, using spies and secret agents inside the walls, and only then by siege and assault.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya treats subversion from inside as just as important as siege and storm in taking a fort.
hinduism.tie_back: The same three methods (siege, assault and inside treachery) are what the Kural’s fort must resist.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book XIII (trans. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus continues his image: an armed man’s stronghold is safe only until someone stronger overpowers it.
christianity.tie_back: It warns of what the Kural’s fort must prevent: being taken by a stronger assault.

islam.quote_or_event: “they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah; but [the decree of] Allah came upon them from where they had not expected, and He cast terror into their hearts.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes a tribe whose strongholds failed because defeat came from a direction they did not expect and their courage collapsed.
islam.tie_back: It shows why the Kural requires a fort that cannot be taken in any way, including from an unexpected direction or by a collapse inside.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One wise man prevailed over a city of warriors and brought down its mighty stronghold.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that one clever strategist can bring down a stronghold that force could not.
judaism.tie_back: It names the danger in the Kural’s third method: stratagem, which a true fort must be proof against.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, the royal frontier fortress has a gate-keeper — wise, experienced, intelligent — to keep out those he doesn’t know and to let in those he does.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s fortress has a wise gatekeeper who admits only people he knows.
buddhism.tie_back: The gatekeeper guards against the Kural’s third danger, infiltration and treachery.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though others sleep, be thou awake! Like a wise man, trust nobody, but be always on the alert; for dangerous is the time and weak the body.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's sermon on carelessness tells the monk to keep constant watch and not rely on anyone, because danger can come at any moment and the body is frail.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's fortress must withstand siege, assault and betrayal from within; the Jain call to stay awake and trust nobody is the same vigilance against an enemy who strikes when the guard is down, applied to the soul.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: After months of siege, the besiegers of Anandpur offered the Sikhs safe exit on solemn oaths; but as soon as the Guru and his Sikhs came out, the hill rulers and their Mughal allies fell upon them, and Guru Gobind Singh later rebuked Emperor Aurangzeb in his Zafarnamah for commanders who had perjured their oath and treacherously attacked him once he was outside the safety of his fortification.
sikhism.explanation: Anandpur was not taken by blockade or assault; it was emptied by a false promise, and the betrayal is remembered as one of the defining wrongs of Sikh history.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's true fortress cannot be taken by siege, by storming or by treachery; Anandpur resisted the first two and fell only to the third.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After ten years in which neither siege nor battle could take Troy, the Greeks left the wooden horse, filled with hidden warriors, outside the walls. The Trojans drew it into the city themselves, and the men inside opened the gates.
greek_mythology.explanation: Troy withstood blockade and assault but fell to a trick that got enemies inside the walls.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Troy passed the Kural’s first two tests and failed the third: it was taken by deceit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The rule is, not to besiege walled cities if it can possibly be avoided.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu advises against attacking walled cities directly because sieges cost so much.
philosophy.tie_back: The strategist’s rule assumes the Kural’s fort: one so hard to take by siege or storm that attackers should avoid it.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.4 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Krak des Chevaliers falls to Sultan Baybars
real_life_example.event: Krak des Chevaliers, the great Hospitaller castle regarded as virtually impregnable, was besieged by the Mamluk sultan Baybars from early 1271. His army pounded the walls with siege engines and used miners to bring down a tower, breaking into the outer ward, but the defenders held out in the stronger inner castle. On 8 April 1271 the remaining garrison surrendered after receiving a letter ordering them to do so, which the French Ministry of Culture's account describes as forged by Baybars and World History Encyclopedia describes as perhaps forged.
real_life_example.explanation: Where siege and assault had only partly succeeded against one of the finest castles ever built, deception completed the conquest.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural lists the three ways a fort may be taken, by siege, by direct assault and by treachery, and at Krak des Chevaliers all three were used, the last one finishing the work.

tamil:
முற்றாற்றி முற்றி யவரையும் பற்றாற்றிப்
பற்றியார் வெல்வது அரண்.
transliteration:
Mutraatri mutri yavaraiyum patraatrip
patriyaar velvathu aran.
meaning: A true fort lets the people inside, holding their ground, beat even a strong army that is skilled at surrounding forts.
elementary: In a game of king-of-the-hill, the one on top can hold off a crowd of climbers as long as he keeps his footing. Valluvar says a good fort works like that hill. Even when many skilled attackers surround it, the defenders who hold their ground can win.
university: The couplet repeats two roots in a tight pattern. Mutraatri mutriyavar means ‘those who besiege, being skilled (aatri) in besieging’, i.e. an expert siege force, and patraatrip patriyaar means ‘those who hold on, being able to hold (their ground)’, i.e. the defenders who do not let go of the place they occupy. Varadarasanar reads patru as the defenders’ attachment to their position, and Pappaiah as not abandoning their post. The fort is defined by its result: it is that in which the holders defeat (velvathu) even a skilled besieger. The repeated sounds (mutru, patru) make the couplet memorable. It shifts the chapter from the fort’s structure to the fort in action, preparing for 749-750. The sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org is ‘முற்றாற்றி முற்றி யவரையும் பற்றாற்றிப் / பற்றியார் வெல்வ தரண்’, which matches ytamizh.com.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As enemies do not hurt these (beings, when they are) sheltered by (their) fortresses, even so foes (can) not injure a king who has taken refuge in his fort.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu compares a king in his fort to animals safe in their natural shelters, where enemies cannot harm them.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Manu promises that those who hold their fort cannot be overcome by those outside.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There was a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it: Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher tells of a small city with few defenders that was saved from a great king’s siege.
christianity.tie_back: It is the Kural’s scene: a few who hold their ground defeating a powerful besieger.

islam.quote_or_event: At the Battle of the Trench (627 CE), the Muslims of Medina dug a trench across the city’s open approach and held their positions against a much larger confederate army. After a long siege, harsh weather and divisions among them led the besiegers to withdraw; the Qur’an recalls the episode in Surat al-Ahzab.
islam.explanation: Defenders who kept their line behind a prepared defense outlasted a stronger besieging force.
islam.tie_back: It is a clear case of the Kural’s holders who, keeping their ground, defeat the besiegers.
islam.source: Qur’an 33:9-25 and the sira accounts of the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq)

judaism.quote_or_event: The books of Kings, Isaiah and Chronicles tell how Sennacherib of Assyria surrounded Jerusalem in Hezekiah’s day, having already taken the other fortified towns of Judah. Jerusalem did not surrender, and the Assyrian army withdrew without taking the city.
judaism.explanation: Jerusalem, held by its defenders, outlasted the greatest siege army of its age.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s fort in practice: a skilled besieger defeated by those who held firm inside.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “then it is said to be a royal frontier fortress that can't be undone by external foes or duplicitous allies.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that a fully equipped frontier fortress cannot be defeated by enemies outside or false friends inside.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Can’t be undone’ is the Kural’s fort, which beats even skilled besiegers.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “… making Zeal his bow, its string Carefulness in walking (iriyâ), and its top (where the string is fastened) Content, he should bend (this bow) with Truth, piercing with the arrow, Penance, (the foe's) mail, Karman--(in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Saṃsâra.”
jainism.explanation: Continuing his reply to Indra, Nami says that the sage, defending from within his fortress of faith, fights back with the bow of zeal and the arrow of penance and pierces the armour of karma.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural's defenders, holding their ground, defeat even an expert besieging army, the Jain sage holds his inner fortress and from it overcomes the besieging force of karma.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.20–22, second half (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: After the evacuation of Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh reached Chamkaur with barely forty Sikhs and his two elder sons; when the imperial army surrounded them, his sons Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh and all but five of the Sikhs fell in the action, and the five survivors then bade the Guru save himself to reconsolidate the Khalsa.
sikhism.explanation: A handful of Sikhs held a small walled haveli against a far larger besieging force long enough for the Guru to escape.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's true fortress lets those inside, holding firm to their posts, prevail against a skilled besieging army; at Chamkaur the defenders held their ground to the death and secured what mattered most, the Guru's survival.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: For nine years the Achaean army camped before Troy without taking it; in the Iliad the Trojans, holding the city, even drive the Greeks back to their ships during Achilles’ absence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Troy’s defenders held their walls against the largest army of the heroic age for a decade.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Troy long showed the Kural’s point: defenders who held their ground wore down a mighty besieger.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Sun Tzu said: The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu teaches that a commander first makes himself safe from defeat and then waits for the chance to win.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s defenders do the same: they hold firm in their fort and then overcome the besiegers.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 4.1 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: The Rats of Tobruk hold the port against Rommel
real_life_example.event: In April 1941 a German-Italian army under General Erwin Rommel surrounded the Libyan port of Tobruk, which was held by a garrison of mainly Australian troops under Lieutenant General Leslie Morshead, together with British and Indian units. The defenders, supplied by night by Royal Navy and Royal Australian Navy ships, held a long defensive perimeter, patrolled aggressively and repulsed repeated ground assaults under almost constant shelling and bombing. The siege ended in December 1941 without the Axis forces taking the port, and the soldiers adopted as a badge of honour the name Rats of Tobruk, first used as a taunt by German propaganda.
real_life_example.explanation: Holding Tobruk forced the Axis to bring most of their supplies overland across some 1,500 kilometres of desert and helped keep them from Egypt and the Suez Canal.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a true fortress lets defenders who hold fast to their positions defeat even a strong army skilled in siegecraft, and the Tobruk garrison's refusal to give up ground defeated one of the war's most capable commanders.

tamil:
முனைமுகத்து மாற்றலர் சாய வினைமுகத்து
வீறெய்தி மாண்ட தரண்.
transliteration:
Munaimukaththu maatralar saaya vinaimukaththu
veereythi maanda tharan.
meaning: A true fort becomes famous because its fighters are so skilled that they knock down the enemy right at the front line.
elementary: A castle becomes famous not just because its walls are pretty but because of the brave defenders who stopped every attack at the gate. People tell stories about what they did there. Valluvar says a fort gets its greatness from the deeds done in its defense.
university: The couplet sets munaimukam (the battle-front) against vinaimukam (the field of action or operations): the enemy (maatralar) falls (saaya) at the front because of what the defenders do, and through those deeds the fort attains distinction (veeru eythi) and excellence (maanda). Pappaiah notes that the enemy is destroyed ‘as soon as battle begins’, and Kalaignar stresses attacks launched from within. Veeru, ‘pride, distinction, uniqueness’, suggests that a fort’s fame comes from the deeds done in its defense rather than from its stones. The couplet is thus the bridge between the structural couplets (742-747) and the conclusion in 750 that without vinai maatchi (excellence in action) no fort exists at all. The repetition of mukaththu (‘at the face of’) in both halves is a characteristic Kural device. The sandhi-joined text is identical in wording to the ytamizh.com reading.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Considering your specific duty as a kṣatriya, you should know that there is no better engagement for you than fighting on religious principles; and so there is no need for hesitation.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reminds Arjuna that for a warrior, fighting in a righteous battle is the highest duty.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural gives the fort’s glory to the warriors who fight at the front, and the Gita makes such fighting the warrior’s highest calling.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.31 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews praises the heroes of faith who became brave in battle and drove back foreign armies.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it finds honor in defenders whose deeds in battle make the enemy flee.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row as though they are a [single] structure joined firmly.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises believers who stand together in battle as solidly as a well-built wall.
islam.tie_back: The defenders themselves become the fortification, and their firm stand is what earns honor, as in the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As for the builders, each had his sword girded at his side as he was building.”
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah’s builders worked on Jerusalem’s wall with swords at their sides, ready to fight.
judaism.tie_back: The wall’s strength came from men ready to act at once, and it is their readiness that the Kural honors.
judaism.source: Nehemiah 4:12 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 4:18)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Realizing that this body is as fragile as a clay pot, and fortifying this mind like a well-fortified city, fight out Mara with the sword of wisdom. Then, guarding the conquest, remain unattached.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the practitioner to fortify the mind like a city and actively fight Mara from it.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the fortified city is a base for active fighting, not just a place to hide.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though a man should conquer thousands and thousands of valiant (foes), greater will be his victory if he conquers nobody but himself.”
jainism.explanation: Nami answers Indra's call to subdue rival princes by ranking self-conquest above any number of battlefield victories.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises a fort whose defenders win renown by felling the enemy at the battle-front; Jainism accepts that such victories happen but holds that the more glorious victory is won over oneself.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok in Raag Maaroo, Kabir says that true heroism is recognised on the battlefield itself, in the one who fights for the right and never abandons his post.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a fortress wins its fame from the deeds of its defenders at the very front of battle; Kabir likewise locates a warrior's renown in standing firm on the field.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo (Salok), Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Hector is the chief defender of Troy: his infant son is called Astyanax, ‘lord of the city’, because Hector alone protected Ilios, and his attacks from the city drive the Greeks back to their ships.
greek_mythology.explanation: Troy’s glory in the epic rests on Hector’s deeds on the battlefield.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hector is the Kural’s idea in a single hero: the city’s fame comes from its defender’s deeds at the front.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A city will be well fortified which is surrounded by brave men and not by bricks.”
philosophy.explanation: In a saying attributed to Lycurgus, the Spartan lawgiver says that brave men are a better wall than bricks.
philosophy.tie_back: It anticipates the Kural’s conclusion that a fort’s worth lies in its defenders’ deeds.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 19.4 (trans. B. Perrin, LacusCurtius)

real_life_example.event_title: The defence of Rorke's Drift
real_life_example.event: During the British invasion of the Zulu Kingdom, after the British defeat at Isandlwana on 22 January 1879, the small garrison at the mission station of Rorke's Drift, led by Lieutenants John Chard and Gonville Bromhead, chose to stay and fight rather than retreat. They built barricades from bags of maize, biscuit boxes and other stores and held off attacks by a Zulu force several thousand strong from late afternoon until dawn. Eleven Victoria Crosses were awarded to the defenders.
real_life_example.explanation: The improvised post became one of the most celebrated actions in British military memory, remembered far more widely than the larger defeat that came just before it.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar says a fortress wins its fame through the deeds of its defenders at the battle front, and Rorke's Drift, not even a true fort, became famous solely for the stand made there.

tamil:
எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும் வினைமாட்சி
இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்.
transliteration:
Enaimaatchith thaakiyak kannum vinaimaatchi
illaarkan illathu aran.
meaning: No matter how great a fort is, it is no fort at all if the people in it are not skilled and strong in action.
elementary: You could have the best football in the world, but if nobody on your team can kick, you will still lose. A fort is the same. The tallest walls are useless if the people inside don’t know how to defend them. Valluvar ends the chapter by saying that people matter more than walls.
university: The closing couplet undercuts everything before it. Enai maatchiththu aakiya kannum means ‘even when it has every kind of excellence’, summing up the natural defenses, walls, provisions and garrison of 742-749. Yet it is illathu, ‘non-existent’, among those who lack vinai maatchi, excellence in action. Varadarasanar glosses vinai maatchi as skill in the ways of action, Pappaiah as the ability to understand and act against the enemy, and Kalaignar simply says that if those inside are incompetent there is no use at all. The play on maatchi (‘excellence’) in both lines sets the fort’s excellence against its holders’ excellence, and the holders win. Pope’s verse rendering (‘To craven souls no fortress strength supplies’) makes the lack a matter of courage, while the Tamil commentators stress practical competence more broadly. The ytamizh.com Varadarasanar gloss ends with the words ‘பொருள் செயல்வகை’, the title of the next chapter, which appears to be a page artifact rather than part of the commentary. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும் வினைமாட்சி / யில்லார்க ணில்ல தரண்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Hanuman reports to Rama that Lanka is guarded by moats, high walls, four great gates and huge numbers of rakshasa troops, making it seem impregnable. Yet the city falls once Ravana, blinded by pride and deaf to good counsel, loses his brother Vibhishana and fights an unrighteous war.
hinduism.explanation: Lanka had every material advantage but was lost because its master lacked wisdom and right action.
hinduism.tie_back: Lanka proves the Kural’s last word: a fort with every excellence is nothing without excellence in those who hold it.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 3 (Hanuman’s description of Lanka) and following

christianity.quote_or_event: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm says walls and watchmen are useless unless God guards the city.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say the walls themselves are not what protects a city. The psalm points to God, the Kural to capable defenders.

islam.quote_or_event: “They will not fight you all except within fortified cities or from behind walls. Their violence among themselves is severe. You think they are together, but their hearts are diverse.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes enemies who hide behind walls but are divided among themselves, and so are weak despite their fortifications.
islam.tie_back: Walls cannot save a people divided at heart, which is the Kural’s point that a fort is nothing without worthy defenders.
