judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud relates that when Rabbi Yehuda Nesia levied a tax for repairing the city wall even on the Sages, Reish Lakish objected that Torah scholars do not need protection. He cited verses from the Psalms to argue that the merit of the people, not the stones, guards a city.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis ask what really protects a city and put the quality of its people above the wall.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Talmud holds that a wall’s protective power depends on the worth of those within.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “With persistence as his army, the disciple of the noble ones abandons what is unskillful, develops what is skillful, abandons what is blameworthy, develops what is blameless, and looks after himself with purity.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Nagara Sutta’s application, the fortress’s army stands for the disciple’s own persistent effort.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta, like the Kural, makes the active effort of those inside what finally decides whether the fortress stands.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “You cannot prolong your life, therefore be not careless; you are past help when old age approaches. Consider this: what (protection) will careless people get, who kill living beings and do not exert themselves?”
jainism.explanation: The fourth lecture of the Uttaradhyayana warns that nothing can protect those who are careless and do not exert themselves; protection depends on one's own vigilant effort.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural ends by saying even the finest fortress is no fortress for those who lack skill and vigour in action, and the Jain verse likewise denies any protection to people who will not exert themselves.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Millions of religious leaders failed to halt the invader, when they heard of the Emperor’s invasion. He burned the rest-houses and the ancient temples; he cut the princes limb from limb, and cast them into the dust. None of the Moguls went blind, and no one performed any miracle.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes Babur's sack of the Punjab and mocks the defenders who trusted in the spells of holy men rather than in competent action; their strongholds and palaces fell all the same.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says no fortress is a fortress in the hands of people who lack skill in action; Guru Nanak shows a whole realm's defences failing because its holders relied on charms instead of deeds.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417-418, Raag Aasaa (Ashtapadi, Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, the Greeks build a great wall and ditch around their ships. While Achilles withdraws from battle and the other leading Greek heroes are wounded, Hector breaks the gate with a stone and the Trojans pour over the wall.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Greeks’ fortification failed as soon as its best fighters were missing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural’s conclusion in story form: a strong wall is nothing without worthy men to hold it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For men, and not walls or ships in which are no men, constitute a state.”
philosophy.explanation: The Athenian general Nicias tells his defeated army in Sicily that the city is its people, not its walls.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s closing verdict: without capable people, walls count for nothing.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 7.77 (trans. Benjamin Jowett, Perseus Digital Library)

real_life_example.event_title: Fort Douaumont falls almost without a shot
real_life_example.event: Fort Douaumont, the largest and one of the most modern of the forts guarding Verdun, had been stripped of most of its guns and much of its garrison in 1915 on the orders of the French high command. When German troops approached it on 25 February 1916, only a small body of reserve gunners remained inside. A German sergeant found his way in through one of the gun embrasures, other small parties followed, and the fort was taken without a real fight.
real_life_example.explanation: Douaumont showed that even the most modern fortress was worthless once too few capable defenders were left inside to use it, and its easy fall shocked France early in the Battle of Verdun.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ends the chapter by saying that however excellent a fortress may be, it is no fortress at all without people of skill and vigour to hold it, and Douaumont is almost a literal case.

tamil:
பொருளல் லவரைப் பொருளாகச் செய்யும்
பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்.
transliteration:
Porulal lavaraip porulaakach cheyyum
porulalladhu illai porul.
meaning: Nothing but money can make people who count for nothing into people who count for something. There is nothing else like it.
elementary: Imagine a boy nobody picks for the team. One day he brings a brand-new football, and suddenly everyone wants to play with him. He is the same boy, but now people notice him. Valluvar says money works like that ball: it makes people who were ignored get noticed.
university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of koozh (கூழ், treasury or wealth), one of the six limbs of the state named in kural 381, and it begins with a deliberately startling claim. The couplet plays on three senses of porul: ‘thing of account’, ‘worth’, and ‘wealth’, so that porulallavar are ‘those who are no-thing’, and the second line says there is no porul (thing) except porul (wealth). Parimelazhagar treats the verse as a plain statement of how the world behaves rather than a moral endorsement, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar likewise read it as a description of social esteem, not of true merit. The ytamizh text divides பொருளல்லது இல்லை, while the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh reads பொருளல்ல தில்லை; the words are the same.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He that has wealth has friends. He that has wealth has kinsmen. He that has wealth is regarded as a true man in the world. He that has wealth is regarded as a learned man.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna urges the grieving Yudhishthira not to renounce the kingdom, arguing that wealth is what makes a person count in the eyes of the world.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna and Valluvar make the same observation: wealth makes a person be seen as someone of worth.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section VIII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “The poor is hated even of his own neighbour: but the rich hath many friends.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb observes that the poor are shunned even by those nearest them, while the rich attract a crowd of friends.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes how wealth turns an ignored person into a sought-after one.

islam.quote_or_event: “And He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient.”
islam.explanation: God reminds the Prophet that he once lacked means and that God raised him to sufficiency, as one of several favours listed in the sura.
islam.tie_back: The verse shares the Kural’s picture of someone raised from nothing by provision, but it credits God rather than wealth itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They make a banquet for revelry; wine makes life merry, and money answers every need.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet notes, with his usual dry realism, that money is what meets every demand of life.
judaism.tie_back: Kohelet and the Kural share the same unsentimental claim that wealth is the one thing that answers for everything else.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 10:19 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The second thing, having got wealth by legitimate means, is the wish: ‘May fame come to me, together with my family and mentors.’”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that the second hard-won desire of a householder is fame, which follows once wealth has been legitimately gained.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta, like the Kural, sees standing and reputation as things that come after wealth.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.61, Pattakamma Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The value of penance has become visible, birth appears of no value! Look at the holy Harikêśa, the son of a Śvapâka, whose power is so great.”
jainism.explanation: After the outcaste-born monk Harikesa is first despised and then revered, the onlookers conclude that worth comes from austerity and virtue, not from birth or outward standing.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says only wealth can turn people of no account into people of account; the Jain story makes the opposite claim, that it is penance that raised a man counted as nothing into one honoured by all.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Nanak seeks the company of the lowest of the low class, the very lowest of the low. Why should he try to compete with the great?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak deliberately turns away from the esteem the world gives to the wealthy and powerful, and places himself among those whom society counts as nothing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural observes that only wealth turns people of no account into people who count; Guru Nanak answers that observation by choosing the company of those who count for nothing in the world's eyes.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But if you work, the idle will soon envy you as you grow rich, for fame and renown attend on wealth.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his brother Perses that honest work leads to riches, and that riches bring fame and renown with them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod gives the same reason as Valluvar: esteem goes wherever wealth goes.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Adam Smith describes how people are naturally disposed to admire and almost worship the rich and great while neglecting persons of poor and mean condition, and he calls this disposition the great cause of the corruption of our moral sentiments.
philosophy.explanation: Smith explains that we tend to honour the wealthy because we sympathise more easily with their good fortune, even when they do not deserve it.
philosophy.tie_back: Smith explains why the Kural’s observation holds, while warning that the esteem wealth brings is not moral worth.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I, Section III, Chapter 3

real_life_example.event_title: Jacques Coeur, a furrier's son, is ennobled by Charles VII
real_life_example.event: Jacques Coeur, born around 1395 in Bourges as the son of a furrier, built a great trading business that dealt in salt, silks and many other goods. He became argentier (steward of royal expenditure) to King Charles VII, sat on the king's council, was put in charge of tax collection, and was ennobled in 1441. His fortune helped fund the king's reconquest of Normandy in 1450.
real_life_example.explanation: A merchant's son with no rank of his own was raised by his wealth into the king's council and the nobility of France.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says nothing but wealth turns those who count for nothing into people who count, and Coeur's fortune carried him from a furrier's household to the king's side.

tamil:
இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர் செல்வரை
எல்லாரும் செய்வர் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Illaarai ellaarum elluvar selvarai
ellaarum seyvar sirappu.
meaning: Everyone looks down on people who have nothing, and everyone praises people who are rich.
elementary: Two children come to a party. One wears a torn shirt and the other a shiny new outfit. Some people smile at the second child and ignore the first, even though nothing else is different. Valluvar is telling us this happens, so that we notice it and do not treat people unfairly.
university: The couplet is built on a tight parallelism: illaarai (the have-nots) against selvarai (the wealthy), and ellaarum elluvar (all scorn) against ellaarum seyvar sirappu (all do honour). Mu. Varadarasanar adds in parentheses that the poor are scorned even if they have other virtues and the rich honoured even if they have none, which makes the verse a comment on injustice as well as a fact of life. Parimelazhagar reads it, like 751, as a reason for the ruler to gather wealth: a king without a treasury would suffer the same contempt. Kalaignar’s gloss calls this simply the way of the world (உலக நடப்பு). The sandhi-joined text reads இல்லாரை யெல்லாரு மெள்ளுவர், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is seen that a poor man, even when he stands near, is accused falsely. Poverty is a state of sinfulness. It behoveth thee not to applaud poverty, therefore.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna argues that society treats the poor with suspicion and contempt, so poverty should not be praised.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna sees the same contempt for the poor that Valluvar describes.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section VIII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool.”
christianity.explanation: James rebukes a congregation that gives the best seat to a rich visitor and pushes a poor one to the floor.
christianity.tie_back: James shows the very scene the Kural describes, honour for the rich and scorn for the poor, and calls it sinful partiality.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one’s] hope.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an grants that wealth adorns worldly life but says lasting good deeds count for more with God.
islam.tie_back: The verse agrees that wealth brings worldly honour, as the Kural says, while pointing to a truer measure of worth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So I observed: Wisdom is better than valor; but The wisdom of the poor is scorned, And their words are not heeded.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet tells of a poor wise man who saved a city yet was forgotten, and concludes that the poor person’s wisdom is despised.
judaism.tie_back: Kohelet sees the same scorn for the poor as the Kural, even when the poor have real merit.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 9:16 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada calls contentment the greatest wealth, measuring worth by inner qualities rather than possessions.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching places real value in contentment and virtue, not in what a person owns.
buddhism.tie_back: This is a counterweight to the Kural’s observation: the world honours the rich, but the Dhamma honours the content.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When (the priests) saw him coming up, emaciated by austerities, in a miserable condition, and with the poorest outfit, they laughed at him, the ruffians.”
jainism.explanation: The Brahmin priests at a sacrifice mock and then try to drive off the monk Harikesa because he looks destitute, until his spiritual power is revealed and they beg his forgiveness.
jainism.tie_back: The episode dramatises exactly what the Kural observes, that everyone scorns the person who appears to have nothing, though the Jain text condemns that scorn rather than treating it as a reason to get rich.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one respects the poor man. He may make thousands of efforts, but no one pays any attention to him. When the poor man goes to the rich man, and sits right in front of him, the rich man turns his back on him. But when the rich man goes to the poor man, the poor man welcomes him with respect.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir describes how the world slights the poor and honours the rich, then concludes that the two are brothers and that the truly poor one is he who lacks the Name in his heart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says everyone scorns those who have nothing and honours the rich; Kabir paints the very same scene, almost line for line.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “An evil shame is the needy man’s companion, shame which both greatly harms and prospers men: shame is with poverty, but confidence with wealth.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says that poverty brings shame with it and wealth brings confidence and standing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s shame of poverty and confidence of wealth mirror the Kural’s scorn and honour.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Juvenal’s third satire complains that the hardest thing about unhappy poverty is that it makes people ridiculous, and it describes the poor man in Rome mocked for his torn cloak and patched shoes.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman satirist protests that in Rome the poor are laughed at and shut out while the rich are courted.
philosophy.tie_back: Juvenal gives the angry version of the Kural’s calm observation that all scorn the poor.

real_life_example.event_title: Twelve-year-old Charles Dickens works in a blacking factory while his father is in debtors' prison
real_life_example.event: In February 1824 John Dickens was imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea prison in Southwark, and most of his family joined him there. His twelve-year-old son Charles was sent to work at Warren's Blacking warehouse near Hungerford Stairs, pasting labels on pots of boot blacking. The family was released some months later after an inheritance allowed the debt to be paid, and Dickens later drew on the debtors' prison in novels such as Little Dorrit.
real_life_example.explanation: The episode shows how quickly debt stripped a respectable family of its standing in Victorian society, and Dickens spent much of his writing life exposing how the poor were treated.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural observes that everyone looks down on those who have nothing, and the Dickens family's fall into the Marshalsea and a child's labour in a rat-infested warehouse show that contempt in action.

tamil:
பொருளென்னும் பொய்யா விளக்கம் இருளறுக்கும்
எண்ணிய தேயத்துச் சென்று.
transliteration:
Porulennum poyyaa vilakkam irularukkum
enniya theyaththuch chendru.
meaning: Money is a lamp that never fails. Take it to any land you choose, and it will drive away the darkness of trouble there.
elementary: Think of a torch that never runs out of batteries. Wherever you walk at night, it lights the path. Valluvar says money can be like that: when you go to a new place, it can help you make friends and solve problems.
university: The metaphor pairs poyyaa vilakkam (the lamp that does not fail or lie) with iruL (darkness), and the second line sends the lamp to enniya theyam, ‘the country one has in mind’ (theyam from Sanskrit desha). Parimelazhagar glosses the darkness as enmity (பகையாகிய இருள்), and Pope and Drew’s English follows him with ‘the darkness (of enmity)’; Solomon Pappaiah likewise says wealth enters even foreign lands and dispels the darkness of hostility. Mu. Varadarasanar reads iruL more broadly as any obstacle (இடையூறு), and Kalaignar as suffering (துன்பம்). The verse sets up 759, where wealth becomes the sharpest weapon against a foe’s pride. The sandhi-joined text reads விளக்க மிருளறுக்கு மெண்ணிய, which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthashastra lists dana, giving gifts, among the four means (upayas) a ruler uses with other states, alongside conciliation, sowing dissension and force, so that gifts can turn a hostile neighbour into an ally.
hinduism.explanation: Indian statecraft treated well-placed gifts of wealth as a standard way to win over enemies without war.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s lamp at work: wealth sent into another land to dispel the darkness of enmity.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra (four upayas: sama, dana, bheda, danda), trans. R. Shamasastry

christianity.quote_or_event: “I say unto you, Make unto yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into the everlasting habitations.”
christianity.explanation: After the parable of the shrewd steward, Jesus tells his disciples to use worldly wealth to make friends who will welcome them later.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus, like Valluvar, sees wealth as something that turns strangers into friends.
christianity.source: Luke 16:9 (KJV), as quoted in John Wesley, Sermon 50

islam.quote_or_event: “Zakah expenditures are only for the poor and for the needy and for those employed to collect [zakah] and for bringing hearts together [for Islam] and for freeing captives [or slaves] and for those in debt and for the cause of Allah and for the [stranded] traveler.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an sets aside a share of zakat for ‘bringing hearts together’, meaning people whose hostility could be softened and whose goodwill could be won by wealth.
islam.tie_back: This category of zakat recipients is a direct religious use of wealth to dispel enmity, as the Kural describes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A gift in secret subdues anger, A present in private, fierce rage.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that a well-timed private gift calms even fierce anger.
judaism.tie_back: The proverb and the Kural agree that wealth can put out the darkness of hostility.
judaism.source: Proverbs 21:14 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, with his legitimate wealth he defends himself against threats from such things as fire, flood, rulers, bandits, or unloved heirs. He keeps himself safe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists protecting oneself against dangers as the second fitting use of rightly earned wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s lamp, rightly earned wealth here drives off threats wherever they arise.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.61, Pattakamma Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's sermon pairs wealth with the image of a lamp in the dark, but warns that wealth gives no lasting protection and that the careless lose their way as when a lamp goes out.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls wealth an unfailing lamp that dispels darkness wherever its owner goes; the Jain verse uses the same lamp-and-darkness image to deny that wealth can be relied on, a pointed counter-reading.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The One Name is my lamp; I have put the oil of suffering into it.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak names the divine Name as the lamp that lights his way, burning away suffering as its oil.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls wealth an unfailing lamp that cuts through darkness wherever its owner goes; Guru Nanak's unfailing lamp is the Name, which Gurbani treats as the true wealth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 358, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the myth of Danaë, her father Acrisius locks her in a bronze chamber, but Zeus reaches her as a shower of gold that passes through the roof; Roman moralists such as Horace later read the story as showing that gold gets through every barrier.
greek_mythology.explanation: Gold enters the one place that was sealed against every visitor.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s lamp, gold goes wherever it is aimed and gets past whatever stands in the way.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero, writing to Atticus, recalls Philip of Macedon’s saying that any fortress could be taken if only a donkey laden with gold could climb up to it.
philosophy.explanation: Philip’s point was that gold opens gates that armies cannot.
philosophy.tie_back: Philip’s donkey of gold is the Kural’s lamp carried into an enemy’s land to undo its resistance.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Letters to Atticus 1.16.12; also Plutarch, Sayings of Kings

real_life_example.event_title: President Truman signs the Marshall Plan into law
real_life_example.place: Washington, D.C., United States, and Western Europe
real_life_example.event: President Harry Truman signed the Economic Cooperation Act, which created the European Recovery Program known as the Marshall Plan. Over about four years the United States transferred some 13 billion dollars in aid to sixteen Western European countries, including former wartime enemies, to rebuild their economies. Aid was also offered to the Soviet Union and the countries of eastern Europe, which declined to take part.
real_life_example.explanation: American wealth, sent abroad, helped rebuild war-shattered economies and turned recent battlefield enemies into partners.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls wealth an unfailing lamp that dispels the darkness of hostility in any land its owner chooses, and Marshall aid carried that light into a Europe darkened by war.

tamil:
அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும் திறனறிந்து
தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்.
transliteration:
Aran eenum inbamum eenum thiranarindhu
theedhindri vandha porul.
meaning: Money earned the right way, without doing anything wrong, brings both goodness and happiness.
elementary: Imagine two children selling lemonade. One makes it carefully and charges a fair price. The other sneaks sugar from a neighbour and cheats customers. Only the first can enjoy the money without worry and use it to do kind things. Valluvar says honest money brings both goodness and happiness.
university: The verb eenum (ஈனும், ‘brings forth, gives birth to’) is repeated for both aram (virtue) and inbam (pleasure or happiness), so wealth is pictured as the parent of the other two purusharthas. The conditions are thiran arindhu, ‘knowing the proper means’, and theedhu indri, ‘without evil’. Parimelazhagar takes the proper means to be those fitting one’s station and the law, and the absence of evil to mean acquiring without harm or deceit to others. Sivayogi Sivakumar adds that it means seeking wealth with knowledge of one’s own ability and harming no one. The sandhi-joined text reads அறனீனு மின்பமு மீனுந், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Manusmriti opens its rules for the householder by telling him to gain his living by a blameless occupation that causes little or no pain to others, and to gather wealth only enough for his proper needs.
hinduism.explanation: The dharma texts treat earning as a duty that must be carried out without harming other beings.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s theedhindri vandha porul, wealth that comes without harm, as the basis of a righteous household.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the former thief to earn honestly so that he can be generous to people in need.
christianity.tie_back: Paul, like Valluvar, links honestly earned wealth to the ability to do good.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, spend from the good things which you have earned and from that which We have produced for you from the earth.”
islam.explanation: Believers are told to give in charity from the good and lawful things they have earned.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an and the Kural agree that lawfully earned wealth is what virtue is built on.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You shall enjoy the fruit of your labors; you shall be happy and you shall prosper.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm promises that someone who walks in God’s ways will enjoy what their own hands have earned.
judaism.tie_back: Honest labour producing happiness is the inbam half of the Kural’s promise.
judaism.source: Psalm 128:2 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And what is the happiness of ownership? It’s when a gentleman owns legitimate wealth that he has earned by his own efforts and initiative, built up with his own hands, gathered by the sweat of the brow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that a layperson finds real happiness in owning wealth that was legitimately earned, and further happiness in using it to make merit.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta’s legitimate wealth that brings both happiness and merit is the Kural’s wealth that yields both inbam and aram.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Nyayasampannavibhavah : Possessed of honestly earned wealth.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra places honestly earned wealth first among the thirty-five qualities of the ideal Jain householder, so lawful earning is the foundation of lay virtue.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says wealth gained by right means and without wrongdoing gives rise to virtue and happiness, and the Jain householder code makes exactly such honestly earned wealth the first mark of a good layman.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, no. 1, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’ (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Maajh ki Vaar, Guru Nanak declares that wealth taken from another's rightful share is as forbidden as the most abhorrent food in each faith.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says wealth gained by right means and without wrongdoing gives birth to virtue and happiness; Guru Nanak draws the boundary from the other side, condemning wealth taken unjustly as utterly unclean.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh (Maajh ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Through work men grow rich in flocks and substance, and working they are much better loved by the immortals.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod teaches that honest work brings wealth and also the favour of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: For Hesiod as for Valluvar, rightly gained wealth brings prosperity and divine favour together.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In On the Happy Life, Seneca argues that a philosopher may own ample wealth provided it was taken from no one, is not stained with another’s blood, and was gained without wronging anyone.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca answers critics of his riches by saying wealth is no disgrace to a wise man if it was honestly acquired and used well.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca’s conditions match the Kural’s theedhindri, wealth that comes without evil.

real_life_example.event_title: Shibusawa Eiichi publishes his book on ethics and business
real_life_example.event: Shibusawa Eiichi, who helped found Japan's First National Bank in 1873 and went on to help establish hundreds of companies, set out his business philosophy in the book Rongo to Soroban in 1916. Drawing on classical Chinese moral teaching, he argued that morality and economic activity are inseparable. He held that business should make profit by honest means and that its profits should serve the public good.
real_life_example.explanation: Shibusawa, often called the father of Japanese capitalism, insisted that wealth earned without ethics was no true success.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says wealth gained by knowing the right ways and without doing wrong gives birth to both virtue and happiness, which is almost exactly the union of moral teaching and the abacus (soroban) that Shibusawa taught.

tamil:
அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாராப் பொருளாக்கம்
புல்லார் புரள விடல்.
transliteration:
Arulodum anbodum vaaraap porulaakkam
pullaar purala vidal.
meaning: Do not hold on to money that comes without kindness and love. Let it go.
elementary: Suppose you could win a big prize, but only by being mean to a friend. Valluvar says to let that prize go. Money that makes you unkind is like a shiny apple that is rotten inside.
university: The first line names two qualities the earning must carry: arul (அருள், compassion toward all beings, the subject of chapter 25) and anbu (அன்பு, affection toward one’s own, the subject of chapter 8). The second line is vivid: pullaar, ‘not embracing’ (from pullu, to hug or cling), and purala vidal, ‘letting it roll off’, as one lets go of something that slips from the arms. Parimelazhagar applies the verse to the ruler, who should refuse revenue gathered by cruelty to his subjects, and Pope and Drew’s English accordingly begins with ‘(Kings) should rather avoid’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah generalise it to anyone who earns. The sandhi-joined text reads அருளொடு மன்பொடும், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The first verse of the Isha Upanishad teaches that all this is pervaded by the Lord, that one should enjoy by renunciation, and that one should not covet anyone’s wealth (ma gridhah kasya svid dhanam).
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that wealth is to be enjoyed with detachment and never grasped from others.
hinduism.tie_back: The Upanishad’s refusal to grasp at others’ wealth matches the Kural’s advice to let wrongly gained wealth roll away.

christianity.quote_or_event: “We are. Thirdly, to gain all we can without hurting our neighbour. But this we may not, cannot do, if we love our neighbour as ourselves.”
christianity.explanation: Wesley tells Methodists to gain all they can, but never by harming a neighbour’s body, soul or livelihood, since that breaks the law of love.
christianity.tie_back: Wesley’s rule that gain must never break love for one’s neighbour is the Kural’s rule that gain must come with anbu and arul.
christianity.source: John Wesley, Sermon 50, The Use of Money, I.3

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly but only [in lawful] business by mutual consent.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids taking others’ wealth unjustly and allows only fair trade that both sides agree to.
islam.tie_back: Both texts reject wealth that comes at the cost of justice and goodwill toward others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ill-gotten wealth is of no avail, But righteousness saves from death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that treasure gained by wickedness brings no real benefit.
judaism.tie_back: Wealth gained without righteousness is worthless, which is why the Kural says to let it go.
judaism.source: Proverbs 10:2 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Discerning clearly, a clever person knows both kinds of happiness: the other kind is not worth a sixteenth part of the happiness of blamelessness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha ranks the happiness of owning and using wealth far below the happiness of a blameless life.
buddhism.tie_back: Wealth that costs one’s blamelessness is not worth keeping, which is the Kural’s point in letting it roll away.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that wealth gained by wrongful acts will be lost and leaves its owner bound by passion and hatred, binding further karma.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to let go of wealth that comes without compassion and love, and the Jain verse gives the reason: wealth gained by evil deeds does not stay and drags its owner into bondage.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “For the sake of this wealth, so many were ruined; because of this wealth, so many have been disgraced. It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
sikhism.explanation: Reflecting on the fall of the Lodi nobility before Babur, Guru Nanak says that their hoarded wealth brought ruin and disgrace, because it had been gathered through wrongdoing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to let wealth gained without compassion and love roll away rather than embrace it; Guru Nanak shows what such wealth does to those who cling to it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Ashtapadi, Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Wealth should not be seized: god-given wealth is much better; for if a man take great wealth violently and perforce, or if he steal it through his tongue, as often happens when gain deceives men’s sense and dishonour tramples down honour, the gods soon blot him out and make that man’s house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that wealth taken by force or deceit is soon lost and brings the gods’ punishment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod, like Valluvar, tells us to refuse wealth gained without justice or kindness.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, lines 320-326 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There are two sorts of wealth-getting, as I have said; one is a part of household management, the other is retail trade: the former necessary and honorable, while that which consists in exchange is justly censured; for it is unnatural, and a mode by which men gain from one another.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle separates honourable wealth-getting that serves the household from money-making that profits at other people’s expense.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like the Kural, rejects gain made at the cost of others.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I, Part X (trans. B. Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: The Kangxi Emperor freezes China's tax quota permanently
real_life_example.event: In 1712 the Kangxi Emperor of the Qing dynasty decreed that the empire's direct tax quota, tied to the count of adult males liable to tax, would be fixed at its existing level and never increased, even as the population grew. The policy is summed up in the phrase yongbu jiafu, never to add taxes. Economic historians note that the cap was largely observed for more than a century, so the tax burden per person fell as China's population and farmland grew; some scholarly accounts date the measure to 1713.
real_life_example.explanation: The emperor gave up revenue he could have raised, choosing light taxation of a growing population over a fuller treasury.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural tells rulers to let go of wealth that does not come with compassion for the people, and Kangxi's freeze declined the extra revenue that heavier taxing of his subjects would have brought.

tamil:
உறுபொருளும் உல்கு பொருளும்தன் ஒன்னார்த்
தெறுபொருளும் வேந்தன் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Uruporulum ulgu porulumthan onnaarth
theruporulum vendhan porul.
meaning: A king’s money comes from property that has no owner, from taxes on goods and roads, and from payments made by enemies he has beaten.
elementary: Think of a school fund. It gets money from lost-and-found items nobody claims, from small fees for using the playground, and from the prize when the school wins a match against another school. Valluvar lists the kinds of money that belong to a king’s treasury in a similar way.
university: This is the chapter’s one technical verse, listing three lawful sources of royal revenue. Uruporul is ‘wealth that comes of itself’, which Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah explain as ownerless property such as heirless estates and treasure trove, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take it as ordinary tax (இறை, வரி). Ulgu porul is customs or toll revenue on goods, and theru porul is tribute or spoil taken from subdued enemies (onnaar). The verse spells out what 755 means in practice: a king’s legitimate income has clear, lawful channels. The sandhi-joined text reads உறுபொருளு முல்கு பொருளுந்தன் னொன்னார்த், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Manusmriti directs that property whose owner has disappeared be held by the king in trust for three years, after which the king may take it, and elsewhere it sets out duties on merchandise and the king’s share of produce.
hinduism.explanation: The dharma texts set out ownerless property and customs duties as lawful royal income.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu covers two of the Kural’s three categories, unclaimed wealth and customs, almost term for term.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Christians in Rome to pay the government its taxes and customs as rightful dues.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s tribute and custom line up closely with the Kural’s tribute and ulgu (customs) as lawful royal revenue.

islam.quote_or_event: “And know that anything you obtain of war booty - then indeed, for Allah is one fifth of it and for the Messenger and for [his] near relatives and the orphans, the needy, and the [stranded] traveler.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an assigns one fifth of the spoils of war to God and the Messenger, to be used for relatives, orphans, the needy and travellers.
islam.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s third category, wealth taken from enemies, as a lawful share of public revenue.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Israel asks for a king, Samuel warns that the king will take a tenth of their grain, vineyards and flocks, and will take their fields and servants for his own use.
judaism.explanation: Samuel describes royal revenue as a burden the people will bring on themselves by demanding a king.
judaism.tie_back: Samuel describes the same royal revenue the Kural lists, but warns against its excess.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, the Buddha tells of a wise chaplain who advises a king not to raise taxes to fund a sacrifice, but to give seed, capital and wages to farmers, traders and officials, so that the realm grows prosperous and the treasury fills.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta teaches that a ruler’s revenue should grow out of a thriving people, not from heavier taxes.
buddhism.tie_back: It gives a Buddhist view of the royal treasury the Kural lists, with the stress on lawful and non-oppressive revenue.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Multiply your gold and silver, your jewels and pearls, your copper, fine robes, and carriages, and your treasury; then you will be a true Kshattriya.”
jainism.explanation: Indra, testing the renouncing King Nami, tells him that filling the royal treasury is what makes a true king; Nami replies that mountains of gold would not satisfy greed and turns to austerity.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural lists the lawful sources of a king's treasury; the Jain text acknowledges the royal ideal of a full treasury but places it in the tempter's mouth, setting the king's wealth against the renouncer's freedom.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.46 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Under Guru Arjan a cadre of local leaders called masands looked after the Sikh sangats in distant places and collected from the disciples dasvandh, one-tenth of their income, which they were enjoined to give for communal sharing; by encouraging agriculture and trade and introducing this tithe for the common use of the community, a stable economic base was secured. When complaints arose against the masands, Guru Gobind Singh in 1698 told the Sikhs to bring their offerings to him directly.
sikhism.explanation: The early Sikh community had defined, lawful channels of revenue, and when collectors abused them the Guru reformed the system.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural lists the lawful sources of a ruler's treasury; the Sikh Gurus likewise built a common treasury on a clearly defined, voluntary tithe and removed the intermediaries who misused it.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entries Arjan Dev, Guru and Gobind Singh, Guru

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Iliad opens with Achilles and Agamemnon quarrelling over the division of spoils taken from conquered towns, each claiming his share of the prizes as a right of honour.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, wealth taken from defeated enemies was a recognised part of a king’s possessions and status.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This shows the Kural’s theru porul, wealth from subdued foes, as royal income in the heroic world.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book V of The Wealth of Nations, Adam Smith examines the sources of the sovereign’s revenue, discussing income from crown property and from taxes on land, goods and consumption, including customs duties.
philosophy.explanation: Smith analyses where a state’s income should come from and how to raise it fairly.
philosophy.tie_back: Smith gives a modern, systematic version of the Kural’s short list of lawful royal income.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2

real_life_example.event_title: Denmark collects the Sound Dues at Elsinore
real_life_example.event: From 1429 to 1857 the Danish crown required ships passing through the Oresund, the narrow strait between Denmark and Sweden that leads into the Baltic, to stop and pay a toll at Elsinore. Eric of Pomerania built the first fortress there in the 1420s, and Frederik II began the Renaissance castle of Kronborg in 1574. Around 1.8 million passages were recorded, and the toll was both a major source of royal income and a political instrument for Denmark.
real_life_example.explanation: For more than four centuries a single customs toll at a narrow strait helped finance the Danish monarchy.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural lists toll and customs revenue among the lawful wealth of a king, and the Sound Dues are one of history's longest-running examples of exactly that kind of royal income.

tamil:
அருளென்னும் அன்பீன் குழவி பொருளென்னும்
செல்வச் செவிலியால் உண்டு.
transliteration:
Arulennum anbeen kuzhavi porulennum
selvach cheviliyaal undu.
meaning: Kindness is the child born to love, and it is brought up by a rich nanny called money.
elementary: Picture a baby born to a loving mother, cared for by a kind nanny who has plenty of food and warm blankets. Valluvar says kindness is like that baby: love gives birth to it, and money helps it grow, because it is easier to help others when you have something to give.
university: This is one of the Kural’s finest extended metaphors. Arul (compassion for all beings) is the kuzhavi, the infant, born of anbu (love for one’s own; anbeen is anbu plus eenra, ‘borne by love’), and porul is the selvach cheviliyal, the rich wet-nurse or foster-mother (cevili) who raises it. The genealogy reverses the usual worry that wealth corrupts: love begets compassion, but compassion cannot grow into practical kindness without means. It links back to chapter 8, Anbudaimai, which says love begets affection and friendship, and it answers 755 by showing the right relation of wealth to arul and anbu. The sandhi-joined text reads அருளென்னு மன்பீன் குழவி பொருளென்னுஞ், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Taittiriya Upanishad’s parting counsel to graduating students tells them to give with faith, to give in plenty, to give with modesty, with awe, and with sympathy.
hinduism.explanation: The teacher links generous giving to an attitude of reverence and fellow-feeling.
hinduism.tie_back: Giving ‘in plenty’ joined to sympathy echoes the Kural’s picture of wealth nursing compassion.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?”
christianity.explanation: John says that love is real only when a person who has means opens both heart and purse to someone in need.
christianity.tie_back: John links love, compassion and ‘this world’s good’ in the same chain as the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “[True] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah... and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask [for help], and for freeing slaves.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an defines true righteousness as faith shown in the giving of wealth to those in need, even though one loves that wealth.
islam.tie_back: In both texts, compassion takes practical form through wealth given away.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Where there is no bread, there is no Torah; where there is no Torah, there is no bread.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah teaches that spiritual life and material sustenance depend on each other.
judaism.tie_back: As the Kural’s compassion needs a well-provided nurse, Torah needs bread in order to flourish.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And they’d hold on to friends by dividing their wealth in four.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the young householder Sigalaka that a wise person keeps friendships alive by managing wealth well and sharing it.
buddhism.tie_back: Here too, well-kept wealth nourishes bonds of love and care.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Yathavat atithau sadhau dine cha pratipatti-krt : Diligent in succoring the ascetics, the righteous and the needy.” … “Sadaya : Compassionate.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra's ideal householder, who first earns wealth honestly, is to be compassionate and to use his means in supporting ascetics, good people and the poor.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural pictures compassion as a child born of love and nursed by wealth, and the Jain layman's code likewise expects the compassionate householder to sustain the needy and the holy from his resources.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, nos. 19 and 31, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’ (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: When Guru Nanak left his post as storekeeper to the Nawab of Sultanpur, complaints were made of his extravagance; but on investigation the storehouse was found full and his accounts correct, and money was even found due to him from the State, which the Guru refused, asking the Nawab to spend it in relieving the wants of the poor.
sikhism.explanation: Macauliffe, following the Janamsakhi tradition, tells how Nanak's honestly kept wealth, far from being lost, became a means of care for the poor.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures compassion as a child nursed by the rich foster-mother called wealth; in this story honestly earned wealth is turned at once into the nourishment of compassion.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak, pp. 42-43

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Athens set up Kephisodotos’ statue of Eirene (Peace) holding the infant Ploutos (Wealth) in her arms, and Pausanias describes a similar statue at Thebes of Tyche carrying the child Ploutos.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek art pictured wealth as a baby nursed and carried by a goddess.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Greek image uses the same nurse-and-infant figure as the Kural, but reversed: in Athens Peace nurses Wealth, while in the Kural Wealth nurses Compassion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle defines liberality as the virtue of giving to the right people, in the right amounts, at the right time, and notes that the liberal person must also take from the right sources so as to have something to give.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, generosity is a real virtue, but it needs property to work with.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, sees kindness in action as needing wealth to grow.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book IV, Chapter 1

real_life_example.event_title: Zubaydah funds wells and rest stations on the pilgrim road to Mecca
real_life_example.place: Darb Zubaydah, from Kufa (Iraq) to Mecca (Saudi Arabia)
real_life_example.event: Zubaydah bint Jafar, wife of the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, supported charitable works along the pilgrimage road linking Kufa and Baghdad with Mecca. As growing numbers of pilgrims strained the water and food of the Arabian desert, she personally paid for many new intermediate rest stops for pilgrims travelling on foot, along with wells and reservoirs. The road became known as the Darb Zubaydah, and its Iraqi and Saudi sections are on UNESCO's World Heritage tentative list.
real_life_example.explanation: A royal fortune was turned into water and shelter for ordinary travellers, and the whole route came to bear her name.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls compassion the child of love, raised by the wealthy foster-mother called wealth, and Zubaydah's riches gave her care for pilgrims the means to save lives across the desert.

tamil:
குன்றேறி யானைப்போர் கண்டற்றால் தன்கைத்தொன்று
உண்டாகச் செய்வான் வினை.
transliteration:
Kundreri yaanaippor kandatraal thankaiththondru
undaagach cheyvaan vinai.
meaning: Starting a job with money already in hand is like watching an elephant fight from a hilltop. You are safe and can see everything.
elementary: Imagine two huge elephants pushing and fighting in a field. If you stood in the middle, you could get hurt. But if you climb a hill and watch from the top, you are safe and can see everything. Valluvar says that starting a big job with savings in your pocket is like watching from that hill.
university: The simile draws on a familiar sight in Sangam India, the royal elephant fight, which was deadly to anyone on the ground and a pleasure to watch from high up. Thankaiththu ondru undaaga means ‘with something being in one’s own hand’, that is, having one’s own funds, and cheyvaan vinai is ‘the work of one who acts’. Parimelazhagar explains that such a person has no need to depend on others and so can watch the struggle of the undertaking without fear, while Kalaignar adds the image of not being caught between the fighting elephants. The sandhi-joined text reads கண்டற்றாற் றன்கைத்தொன் றுண்டாகச், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Wealth brings about accessions of wealth, like elephants capturing (wild) elephants.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna compares money that brings in more money to trained elephants used to capture wild ones.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts use the elephant to show that someone who starts with wealth in hand is in a position of strength.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section VIII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the builder who checks his funds before starting as an image of counting the cost of discipleship.
christianity.tie_back: The builder with enough in hand is the Kural’s watcher on the hill, while the one without is caught and mocked.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one’s own hands. The Prophet of Allah, David used to eat from the earnings of his manual labor.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises living from one’s own earnings rather than depending on others.
islam.tie_back: The hadith’s pride in self-earned means matches the Kural’s trust in having one’s own wealth in hand.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Rabbi Yitzḥak says: A person should always divide his money into three; he should bury one-third in the ground, and invest one-third in business, and keep one-third in his possession.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud advises keeping part of one’s wealth liquid and at hand, so that one is never left without resources.
judaism.tie_back: Rabbi Yitzhak’s third kept in hand is exactly the Kural’s wealth ‘in one’s own hand’ that makes a venture safe.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 42a (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One portion is to enjoy. Two parts invest in work. And the fourth should be kept for times of trouble.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha advises the householder to invest half his wealth in work and keep a quarter in reserve for hard times.
buddhism.tie_back: Working with capital and a reserve is the secure position the Kural pictures as the hilltop.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Vyayam ayochitam kurvan : Spending in proportion to one's income.” … “Balabalam janan : Aware of one's own strength and weakness.”
jainism.explanation: Among the Jain householder's practical virtues are measuring expenditure against income and knowing one's own strength and weakness before acting.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's man who starts a venture with money already in hand, watching safely as from a hilltop, reflects the same prudence the Jain householder code asks for in matching outlay to means and knowing one's capacity.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, nos. 12 and 23, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’ (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Reliance on mortals is in vain - know this well.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan teaches that leaning on other people for support is futile, and that the one Giver is God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one who undertakes a task with his own means in hand can watch the struggle safely, free of dependence on others; Guru Arjan likewise warns against depending on other people.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 281, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But let it be your care to order your work properly, that in the right season your barns may be full of victual.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells Perses to plan his work so that his stores are full when they are needed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Full barns before the season turns are the Kural’s funds in hand before a venture begins.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle tells how Thales, mocked for his poverty, foresaw a large olive harvest, used a small sum to reserve all the olive presses in Miletus and Chios in advance, and made a fortune when the harvest came.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle uses the story to show that a philosopher can make money easily when he chooses to, by having funds ready at the right moment.
philosophy.tie_back: Thales with deposits in hand, waiting calmly for the harvest, is the Kural’s watcher on the hill.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I, Part XI (trans. B. Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Heinrich Schliemann uses his merchant fortune to excavate Hisarlik
real_life_example.event: Heinrich Schliemann made a large fortune in trade, much of it as a military contractor during the Crimean War, and retired from business in his thirties to devote his money to archaeology. Frank Calvert, who owned part of the mound at Hisarlik and believed it was Troy, lacked the funds for further digging. Beginning in 1870, Schliemann paid for large excavations there himself, employing many workers, and he went on to uncover the remains of the ancient city.
real_life_example.explanation: Because he paid his own way, Schliemann could pursue an expensive, uncertain search that others could not afford to attempt.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that one who starts a venture with money already in hand is like a person watching an elephant fight from a hilltop, and Schliemann's private fortune let him undertake the dig without depending on anyone.

tamil:
செய்க பொருளைச் செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்
எஃகதனிற் கூரிய தில்.
transliteration:
Seyga porulaich cherunar serukkarukkum
eqkadhanir kooriya thil.
meaning: Build up your money. No blade is sharper than money for cutting down the pride of your enemies.
elementary: Imagine a bully who brags that nobody can stand up to him. Then the whole class saves up to build a strong new fence and hire a coach, and suddenly the bully stops bragging. Valluvar says a well-stocked treasury is the sharpest sword against a proud enemy.
university: The verse opens with a blunt imperative, seyga porulai, ‘make wealth!’, which is rare in the Kural and gives the command its force. Cherunar are foes, serukku is their arrogance, and aRukkum (‘that cuts off’) sets up the image of eqku (எஃகு), steel or a sword, of which nothing is sharper (kooriyadhu il). Parimelazhagar explains that wealth lets a king raise and keep armies and allies, and so humbles enemies without his having to strike himself. Solomon Pappaiah addresses the verse to anyone who wants to achieve something. The sandhi-joined text reads செருக்கறுக்கு மெஃகதனிற், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthashastra holds that the army is rooted in the treasury (koshamulo hi dandah), so a king with a full treasury can raise and keep the force needed to subdue enemies.
hinduism.explanation: Indian statecraft ranked the treasury as the source of military power.
hinduism.tie_back: For Kautilya as for Valluvar, wealth is the real weapon behind every other weapon.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VIII (on the elements of sovereignty), trans. R. Shamasastry

christianity.quote_or_event: “For wisdom is a defence, and money is a defence: but the excellency of knowledge is, that wisdom giveth life to them that have it.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher places money beside wisdom as a protection, while ranking wisdom higher.
christianity.tie_back: Money as a defence is the protective side of the Kural’s sharp steel.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy... And whatever you spend in the cause of Allah will be fully repaid to you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the community to prepare strength to deter enemies and promises that spending for this cause will be repaid.
islam.tie_back: In the verse, spending builds the strength that humbles an enemy, much as the Kural’s wealth cuts down a foe’s pride.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For to be in the shelter of wisdom is to be also in the shelter of money, and the advantage of intelligence is that wisdom preserves the life of the one who possesses it.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet says money, like wisdom, gives shelter from life’s threats.
judaism.tie_back: Kohelet’s shelter of money is the defensive side of the Kural’s weapon against enemies.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 7:12 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta, the Buddha tells how a king who failed to give wealth to the poor set off a slide into theft, weapons and violence, showing that neglecting material provision breeds conflict.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta traces social violence back to poverty the ruler failed to relieve.
buddhism.tie_back: Seen from the opposite side, wealth rightly used is what keeps hostility from arising, which is a gentler version of the Kural’s weapon.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Fight with your Self; why fight with external foes? He who conquers himself through himself, will obtain happiness.”
jainism.explanation: Nami tells Indra, who urges him to subdue rival kings, that the real battle is against one's own passions, and in the next verse he names them: the senses, anger, pride, delusion and greed.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls wealth the sharpest steel for cutting down the pride of one's enemies; Jainism points the blade inward, telling one to cut down one's own pride and greed instead of external foes.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “From the Guru, I have obtained the supremely powerful sword of spiritual wisdom.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das names the Guru's wisdom as the sharpest of swords, the weapon with which the enemies within, the passions and ego, are cut down.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says there is no steel sharper than wealth for cutting down a foe's pride; Gurbani names a different sharpest blade, the Guru's wisdom, which cuts down one's own pride.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1087, Raag Maaroo, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Thucydides, the Spartan king Archidamus warns his people before the Peloponnesian War that war is a matter less of arms than of money, which is what makes arms useful.
greek_mythology.explanation: Archidamus argues that Athens’ wealth makes it more dangerous than Sparta’s soldiers alone can handle.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Archidamus and Valluvar agree that wealth is the sharpest weapon in a conflict.
greek_mythology.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 1.83

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero, urging war against Mark Antony, calls unlimited money the sinews of war (nervos belli, pecuniam infinitam), a phrase that became proverbial.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero argues that money is what holds a war effort together.
philosophy.tie_back: The sinews of war and the sharpest steel are the same idea: wealth is what defeats an enemy.

real_life_example.event_title: Jakob Fugger finances the election of Charles V as Holy Roman Emperor
real_life_example.event: After Emperor Maximilian I died in 1519, his grandson Charles of Spain and King Francis I of France competed to be elected Holy Roman Emperor, and the electors sought payments from both. Of election expenses of about 852,000 guilders spent on Charles's behalf, the Augsburg banker Jakob Fugger raised almost 544,000. Charles was elected, and Francis I's bid failed.
real_life_example.explanation: A banker's money, not an army, decided which of Europe's two most powerful kings would wear the imperial crown.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says no steel is sharper than wealth for cutting down an enemy's pride, and Fugger's loans defeated the ambitions of the king of France without a blow being struck.

tamil:
ஒண்பொருள் காழ்ப்ப இயற்றியார்க்கு எண்பொருள்
ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு.
transliteration:
Onporul kaazhppa iyatriyaarkku enporul
enai irandum orungu.
meaning: For people who have earned plenty of money honestly, the other two goals of life, doing good and being happy, come easily.
elementary: Think of a garden. Once the soil is rich and well watered, flowers and vegetables both grow easily. Valluvar says honest wealth is like that rich soil: once you have it, goodness and happiness grow easily too.
university: The closing verse ties the chapter to the three aims of life (muppaal: aram, porul, inbam) that give the Kural its three books. Onporul is ‘bright’ or excellent wealth, which the commentators take to mean wealth gained by good means, echoing 754; kaazhppa (from kaazh, hard core) means firmly and abundantly; enporul is ‘an easy thing’ (en, easy); and enai irandum orungu means ‘the other two, together’. Parimelazhagar explains that for such a person virtue and pleasure are both easily attained, and Kalaignar names the three purusharthas explicitly. The verse repeats the pairing in 754 and closes the chapter’s argument that honestly earned wealth underpins a complete life. The sandhi-joined text reads இயற்றியார்க் கெண்பொரு ளேனை யிரண்டு மொருங்கு, which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Kautilya holds that wealth and wealth alone is important, inasmuch as charity and desire depend upon wealth for their realisation.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya argues that among the three aims of life, artha comes first, because dharma and kama both depend on it.
hinduism.tie_back: Kautilya and Valluvar make the same argument: once wealth is secured, the other two aims follow.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book I, Chapter 7 (trans. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to teach the rich to enjoy God’s gifts and use their wealth for good works.
christianity.tie_back: Paul pairs enjoyment (‘all things to enjoy’) with good works, the same two ends the Kural says wealth makes easy.

islam.quote_or_event: “But seek, through that which Allah has given you, the home of the Hereafter; and [yet], do not forget your share of the world. And do good as Allah has done good to you.”
islam.explanation: Qarun’s people advise him to use his wealth to seek the hereafter and do good, without neglecting his rightful share of worldly enjoyment.
islam.tie_back: The verse joins virtue and lawful enjoyment through wealth, which is the Kural’s ‘other two, together’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Remember that it is the ETERNAL your God who gives you the power to get wealth, in fulfillment of the covenant made on oath with your fathers, as is still the case.”
judaism.explanation: Moses reminds Israel that the ability to prosper comes from God and serves the covenant.
judaism.tie_back: Wealth is placed inside a larger moral purpose, as the Kural places porul in the service of aram and inbam.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 8:18 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “I’ve achieved the goal for which an astute layperson wishes to gain wealth. I don’t regret what I’ve done.”
buddhism.explanation: The householder who has used legitimate wealth to support family, guard against loss, make offerings and give to the virtuous can look back without regret.
buddhism.tie_back: His fulfilled goal, joining enjoyment with merit, is the Kural’s aram and inbam gained through porul.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.61, Pattakamma Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anyonya-pratibandhena trivargam sadhayan : Fulfilling the three-fold aim of life - that is, dharma, artha and kama - without excluding any of its elements.”
jainism.explanation: Hemacandra's ideal Jain householder pursues virtue, wealth and pleasure together in balance, none crowding out the others, alongside the first quality of honestly earned wealth.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural closes by saying that those with abundant honest wealth easily attain the other two aims of virtue and happiness, and the Jain householder code likewise holds the three aims together as one balanced pursuit.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, no. 18, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’ (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak sums up the Sikh householder ideal: earn honestly by one's own labour and share part of it with others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that for those who have gathered honest wealth, virtue and happiness follow easily; Guru Nanak says that the one who earns honestly and shares has found the true path of life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas, granted his wish that everything he touched would turn to gold, found that his food and drink also turned to gold, and he begged Dionysus to take the gift back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas learns that wealth pursued for its own sake destroys the very pleasures it was meant to buy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Midas is the reverse of the Kural: wealth cut off from virtue gives neither happiness nor goodness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle says that happiness also needs external goods, since it is impossible, or not easy, to do noble acts without the proper equipment, and many actions are performed through friends, riches and political power as instruments.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that a complete happy life needs enough external resources to act on one’s virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s riches as the instruments of noble action and happiness state the same idea as Valluvar’s wealth that makes virtue and pleasure easy.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, Chapter 8

real_life_example.event_title: Banker Annamalai Chettiar founds Annamalai University
real_life_example.event: Annamalai Chettiar, from a Nattukottai Chettiar banking family whose business he expanded into South-East Asia, founded Sri Minakshi College and Tamil and Sanskrit colleges at Chidambaram in the early 1920s. In 1928 he agreed with the Madras government to hand these institutions over to form a university, and Annamalai University came into being on 1 January 1929, founded by a private philanthropist. He was knighted in 1923 and later received the hereditary title of Raja of Chettinad.
real_life_example.explanation: A fortune made in banking was turned into a university that promoted Tamil learning and served students across the region.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those who have built up abundant, honestly earned wealth, virtue and happiness come easily, and Annamalai Chettiar's banking wealth made a lasting good work almost a matter of course.

tamil:
உறுப்பமைந்து ஊறஞ்சா வெல்படை வேந்தன்
வெறுக்கையுள் எல்லாம் தலை.
transliteration:
Uruppamaindhu ooranjaa velpadai vendhan
verukkaiyul ellaam thalai.
meaning: An army that has every part it needs and wins without fear of getting hurt is the greatest treasure a king can own.
elementary: Think of a school sports team where every position is filled, everyone has practised, and nobody is scared of a hard game. A coach would say that team is worth more than any trophy cupboard. Valluvar says a king’s well-prepared army is like that: his most precious possession.
university: The chapter opens the Padai-iyal (the section on the army), and its first couplet ranks the army above every other form of veṟukkai (வெறுக்கை, ‘wealth, treasure’). Uṟuppu (உறுப்பு, ‘limb’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the traditional four limbs of an Indian army, elephants, chariots, horse and foot, so uṟuppamaintu means ‘complete in its divisions’; ūṟu (ஊறு) is ‘wound’ or ‘harm’, and ūṟañcā ‘not dreading injury’. The logic echoes kural 381, which lists the army (படை) first among the six limbs of a kingdom, and the Arthashastra’s list of seven elements of sovereignty. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss the line almost identically; Solomon Pappaiah modernizes the ‘limbs’ as land, sea and air forces and police. The ytamizh and thirukkural-thamizh texts agree, differing only in sandhi (உறுப்பமைந் தூறஞ்சா).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “THE king, the minister, the country, the fort, the treasury, the army and the friend are the elements of sovereignty.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya lists the army as one of the seven constituent elements without which a state cannot stand, and then describes the qualities of the best army in detail.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar goes a step further, ranking a complete, fearless army first among a king’s treasures.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VI, Chapter 1 (trans. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses a king weighing the strength of his army as an image of counting the cost before committing to discipleship.
christianity.tie_back: The parable assumes what the Kural states: a king’s real security rests on the army he can actually field.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy and others besides them whom you do not know [but] whom Allah knows.”
islam.explanation: The community is told to keep its forces as fully equipped as it can, both cavalry and every other kind of strength.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a fully equipped, ready force as a primary duty and asset of the polity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Uzziah prepared for them, even for all the host, shields, and spears, and helmets, and coats of mail, and bows, and stones for slinging.”
judaism.explanation: The Chronicler presents Uzziah’s trained army of over three hundred thousand, fully equipped, as a mark of his strength while he sought God.
judaism.tie_back: A complete, well-armed host is pictured as a king’s chief strength, as in the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Excellent are well-trained mules, thoroughbred Sindhu horses and noble tusker elephants. But better still is the man who has subdued himself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha grants that the trained animals of a royal army are excellent, then points to self-mastery as the higher prize.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s admiration for well-trained army ‘limbs’, while redirecting the idea of the greatest treasure inward.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a universal monarch with his fourfold army and great power, the possessor of the fourteen attributes of a king, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana takes the cakravartin, whose fourfold army is the sign of his unmatched power, and uses him as a measure for the learned monk.
jainism.tie_back: The 'fourfold army' is the same four-limbed force (elephants, chariots, horse, foot) that the Kural calls complete in its parts and ranks first among a king's treasures, though the Jain verse in the end prizes the monk above the monarch.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: At his succession in 1606, after his father Guru Arjan's martyrdom, Guru Hargobind is said to have worn two swords, one for temporal authority (miri) and one for spiritual authority (piri). He built up a standing Sikh army and gave the faith a military side it had not had before.
sikhism.explanation: Sikh tradition remembers Guru Hargobind as the Guru who made an organised armed force part of the community's life, with the Akal Takht as the seat of temporal authority facing the Harmandir Sahib.
