sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks a complete, fearless army first among a ruler's treasures; Guru Hargobind's reform is the moment Sikhism decided that the community needed such an army to protect itself, though always beneath the authority of piri, the spiritual sword.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guru Hargobind' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus describes Xerxes’ ten thousand Persian ‘Immortals’, a corps kept always at full strength: whenever a man dropped out, another was chosen to take his place.
greek_mythology.explanation: The elite unit’s prestige came from never being incomplete, and it was the pride of the Persian king’s host.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s uṟuppamaintu, an army complete in all its parts, as a king’s prized possession.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “These are: (1) The Moral Law; (2) Heaven; (3) Earth; (4) The Commander; (5) Method and discipline.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu lists the five constant factors by which a ruler should judge the strength of an army before going to war.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Sun Tzu treats a complete, well-ordered army as something to be assessed and valued with care.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 1.4 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Gustavus Adolphus's reformed Swedish army wins at Breitenfeld
real_life_example.event: At Breitenfeld, the Swedish-Saxon army under King Gustav II Adolf of Sweden met the imperial and Catholic League army under Count Tilly. When the Saxon contingent fled, the Swedes reordered their lines to form a new left flank, outgunned the enemy in the artillery exchange, and destroyed Tilly's army. It was the first major Protestant victory of the Thirty Years' War and established Sweden as a great power.
real_life_example.explanation: Britannica credits the victory to Sweden's flexible, well-drilled linear tactics, the product of Gustavus's reforms of infantry, cavalry and artillery working together.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks first among a king's treasures an army complete in all its parts that wins without fearing harm, and at Breitenfeld a well-integrated Swedish army held firm even when its allies ran.

tamil:
உலைவிடத்து ஊறஞ்சா வன்கண் தொலைவிடத்துத்
தொல்படைக் கல்லால் அரிது.
transliteration:
Ulaividaththu ooranjaa vankan tholaividaththuth
tholpadaik kallaal aridhu.
meaning: Only an army with a long history has the courage to stand firm after losses, unafraid of wounds even when its numbers have shrunk.
elementary: When a team is losing badly, new players often give up, but players who have trained together for years keep going. They have been through hard games before. Valluvar says an old, experienced army is like that: it keeps its courage even when things are going wrong.
university: Ulaivu (உலைவு) means ‘reverse, setback’ and tolaivu (தொலைவு) ‘diminution, loss of numbers’, so the couplet describes valour (vaṉkaṇ, வன்கண்) that survives both defeat and attrition. Tolpaṭai (தொல்படை, ‘ancient army’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the hereditary core force (often called மூலப்படை in the commentarial tradition), as against hired or allied troops, a distinction that closely parallels Kautilya’s preference for hereditary troops. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar follow this reading, while Solomon Pappaiah extends tolpaṭai to native citizen-soldiers whose families have long lived in the land. The text is identical in both sources apart from sandhi (வன்கண் டொலைவிடத்துத் in the joined text).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Coming down directly, from father and grandfather (of the king), ever strong, obedient, happy in keeping their sons and wives well contented, not averse to making a long sojourn, ever and everywhere invincible, endowed with the power of endurance...”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya’s description of the best army begins with its hereditary character and stresses endurance and steadiness.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost exactly Valluvar’s tolpaṭai: a hereditary army whose endurance holds when fortunes turn.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VI, Chapter 1 (trans. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy that the mark of a good soldier is the capacity to endure hardship.
christianity.tie_back: Endurance under hardship is the very valour the Kural assigns to a seasoned army.

islam.quote_or_event: “And how many a prophet [fought and] with him fought many religious scholars. But they never lost assurance due to what afflicted them in the cause of Allah, nor did they weaken or submit. And Allah loves the steadfast.”
islam.explanation: Revealed after the setback at Uhud, the verse holds up earlier companions of prophets who did not weaken when they were struck by losses.
islam.tie_back: It praises the same courage the Kural describes: steadiness when the fight is going badly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hear, O Israel, ye draw nigh this day unto battle against your enemies; let not your heart faint; fear not, nor be alarmed, neither be ye affrighted at them.”
judaism.explanation: Before battle the priest addresses the army, telling it not to lose heart even when the enemy seems stronger.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘fearless valour’ is exactly what this exhortation tries to instil in Israel’s host.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As an elephant in the battlefield withstands arrows shot from bows all around, even so shall I endure abuse.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares his patience to a trained war-elephant that holds its ground under a shower of arrows.
buddhism.tie_back: The image is the Kural’s ūṟañcā vaṉkaṇ, a seasoned fighter unshaken by wounds.

jainism.quote_or_event: “So a novice, who as yet has not suffered pains and is not yet used to a mendicant's life, believes himself a hero till he practises austerities.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga sets the untried novice against the seasoned ascetic: only someone long practised in hardship keeps his courage when trouble comes, while the weak 'become disheartened like cowards in the battle' (1.3.1.7).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says courage that holds through defeat and losses is found only in a long-established army, and the Jain text likewise finds staying power only in those hardened by long endurance.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.3.1.3 (cf. 1.3.1.7) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir's salok, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, defines the true hero as one who holds the field even while being cut down piece by piece.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises courage that stands firm even after defeat and heavy losses; Kabir's hero likewise does not leave the field however much he is cut down.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, when the Trojans drive the Achaeans back to their ships, Ajax son of Telamon stays at the sterns and keeps fighting off the attackers long after others have given way.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ajax is the Iliad’s great picture of defensive steadiness when the battle has turned against his side.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He embodies the Kural’s courage in the hour of defeat.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Laches, the general Laches first defines courage as staying at one’s post and not running away, then refines it to a kind of endurance of the soul; Socrates presses that it must be wise endurance.
philosophy.explanation: The dialogue examines what military courage really is, rooted in steadfast endurance under danger.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar locates exactly this endurance in a veteran army facing defeat.

real_life_example.event_title: The Ten Thousand march home after losing their generals
real_life_example.place: From Cunaxa near Babylon (Iraq) to Trapezus (Trabzon, Turkey)
real_life_example.event: A force of Greek mercenaries known as the Ten Thousand fought for Cyrus the Younger at Cunaxa in 401 BCE, but Cyrus was killed and the expedition failed. Their senior generals were then seized through treachery by the Persian satrap Tissaphernes during a parley. The soldiers elected new leaders, among them the Athenian Xenophon, and marched north through hostile mountains and snow-filled passes until they reached the Black Sea at Trapezus.
real_life_example.explanation: Stranded deep in enemy territory, leaderless and dwindling, the army kept its cohesion and fought its way out, a story Xenophon recorded in the Anabasis.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the courage to hold firm in defeat and loss of numbers is found mainly in a seasoned army, and the veteran Ten Thousand did exactly that after disaster had stripped them of their cause and their commanders.

tamil:
ஒலித்தக்கால் என்னாம் உவரி எலிப்பகை
நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Oliththakkaal ennaam uvari elippakai
naagam uyirppak kedum.
meaning: So what if a crowd of rats roars like the sea? One hiss from a cobra and they all run away and are destroyed.
elementary: Imagine a crowd of mice squeaking very loudly in a barn. It sounds scary, but the moment a snake hisses, they all scurry away. Valluvar says a big, noisy army with no real courage is like those mice, and a small, brave army is like the snake.
university: The couplet is a celebrated uvamai (simile): uvari (உவரி, ‘the salt sea’) describes the roar of a vast but timid enemy, while nākam (நாகம், ‘cobra’) and uyirppa (உயிர்ப்ப, ‘as it breathes, hisses’) picture a small force of real valour. Parimelazhagar reads it as a statement that numbers without courage count for nothing against a brave army, and Solomon Pappaiah explicitly makes the cobra a small army and the rats a large one ‘rat-like in mind’. Kalaignar applies it to a single hero rising in anger. The text is the same in both sources apart from sandhi (ஒலித்தக்கா லென்னா முவரி யெலிப்பகை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, the Pandavas field seven akshauhinis against the Kauravas’ eleven, yet the larger host is defeated at Kurukshetra.
hinduism.explanation: The epic repeatedly stresses that the numerically superior Kaurava army lacked the righteousness and leadership that sustained the smaller force.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s point on an epic scale: a great noisy host gives way before a smaller, stronger one.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga and Bhishma Parvas (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: When the king of Aram surrounds Dothan with horses and chariots, Elisha tells his frightened servant that those with them are more than those with the enemy, and his eyes are opened to see the hills full of horses and chariots of fire.
christianity.explanation: The story teaches that a vast visible host does not decide the outcome.
christianity.tie_back: Like the rats roaring like the sea, the besieging army looks overwhelming yet comes to nothing.

islam.quote_or_event: “How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: As Talut’s (Saul’s) small band faced Jalut (Goliath) and his soldiers, the believers among them affirmed that a small company can overcome a large one.
islam.tie_back: This is the cobra and the rats: size of host matters less than steadfast courage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Come and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised; it may be that the LORD will work for us; for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few.”
judaism.explanation: Jonathan and his armour-bearer alone climb up to a Philistine garrison, and the whole Philistine camp falls into panic and melts away.
judaism.tie_back: A tiny, fearless force scattering a large host is exactly the Kural’s cobra among the rats.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Padhana Sutta, Mara’s ‘army’ of desire, discontent, hunger, craving, sloth and fear gathers around the Bodhisatta, who declares that he will not be driven from his place and defeats it by insight.
buddhism.explanation: A vast and clamorous host is overcome by one steadfast mind.
buddhism.tie_back: It mirrors the Kural’s image: a roaring multitude is undone by a single, truly strong presence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A man believes himself a hero as long as he does not behold the foe, as did Śiśupâla (before he beheld) the valorously-fighting, great warrior.”
jainism.explanation: The verse mocks bravado that lasts only until the real foe appears, and the next verse adds that once the fight begins such men are cut down (1.3.1.2).
jainism.tie_back: Like the rats whose sea-like roar comes to nothing when the cobra hisses, the boaster's courage collapses the moment he faces true valour.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.3.1.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: At Chamkaur in December 1704, after the evacuation of Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh, his two elder sons and about forty Sikhs held a mud fortress against a far larger Mughal-led force. The Guru's elder sons Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh died fighting there.
sikhism.explanation: Sikh memory treats Chamkaur as the classic case of a tiny band of Khalsa holding off a vast besieging army through sheer resolve.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a host of rats roaring like the sea scatters at one breath of the cobra; Chamkaur is remembered in the same terms, with a handful of committed fighters standing against a multitude.
sikhism.source: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Chamkaur' (paraphrase of traditional and historical accounts)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus tells how the Athenians at Marathon, heavily outnumbered, charged the Persian army at a run and put it to flight.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Persians thought the Athenians mad to attack so few against so many, yet the smaller, determined force prevailed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is a historical instance of the Kural’s rats scattered at the cobra’s breath.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Xenophon, rallying the Greek officers after their generals were seized, tells them that it is neither numbers nor strength that wins battles, but that whichever side advances with stouter hearts, the enemy generally will not stand against it.
philosophy.explanation: Stranded deep in Persian territory, Xenophon argues that morale, not size, decides the issue.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s cobra and rats make the same claim about courage versus numbers.

real_life_example.event_title: Robert the Bruce's smaller army defeats Edward II at Bannockburn
real_life_example.place: Bannockburn, near Stirling, Scotland, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Edward II of England led a large army, estimated at some 13,000 infantry and about 3,000 cavalry, to relieve the besieged Stirling Castle. Robert the Bruce met it with a smaller force of perhaps 7,000 infantry, mostly pikemen, and a few hundred light horse, using woodland and dug ditches to channel the attack. Repeated English cavalry charges failed to break the Scottish spear formations, and the English army was routed, with Edward barely escaping.
real_life_example.explanation: A disciplined, determined smaller force overthrew a far larger and more splendid host, in what Britannica calls a decisive battle in Scottish history.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what it matters if a host of rats roars like the sea when a single breath of the cobra scatters them, and at Bannockburn the larger army's numbers counted for little against the resolve of the smaller one.

tamil:
அழிவின்றி அறைபோகா தாகி வழிவந்த
வன்க ணதுவே படை.
transliteration:
Azhivindri araipogaa thaagi vazhivandha
vankanadhuve padai.
meaning: A true army is one that has never been beaten, cannot be bribed by the enemy, and has courage passed down from its fathers.
elementary: Imagine a family that has played in the same village band for generations. Nobody could pay them to play for a rival band, and they never give up halfway through a parade. Valluvar says a true army is like that: loyal, steady, and brave because bravery runs in its history.
university: Three marks define the true army here: aḻiviṉmai (not being broken in battle), aṟaipōkāmai (அறைபோகாமை, not being undermined or won over by enemy intrigue, i.e. free of treachery and desertion), and vaḻivanta vaṉkaṇ (வழிவந்த வன்கண், valour inherited through lineage). Parimelazhagar takes aṟaipōtal as being corrupted by the enemy’s secret approaches, and Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as ‘not falling prey to the enemy’s deceit’. There is a small textual variant: ytamizh prints அழிவின்றி, while the sandhi-joined thirukkural-thamizh text reads அழிவின் றறைபோகா, i.e. அழிவின்று; the sense, ‘without destruction’, is unchanged.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “...ready to share in the weal or woe of the king, and consequently not falling foul with him...”
hinduism.explanation: In Kautilya’s description of the best army, hereditary troops are prized because they share the king’s fortunes and do not turn against him.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s aṟaipōkāmai and vaḻivanta vaṉkaṇ: loyalty and inherited valour.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VI, Chapter 1 (trans. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes the good soldier as one whose loyalty to his commander is not divided by other interests.
christianity.tie_back: An army that cannot be drawn away by other inducements is what the Kural means by one that does not ‘go over’.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an warns believers that when they meet the enemy in battle they must not turn their backs, except to manoeuvre or to rejoin their own company.
islam.explanation: Desertion in the face of the enemy is condemned as a grave fault.
islam.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s demand that a true army never breaks or goes over to the enemy.

judaism.quote_or_event: When David flees Jerusalem during Absalom’s revolt, the foreigner Ittai the Gittite refuses to leave him, vowing that wherever the king is, in death or in life, there his servant will be.
judaism.explanation: Ittai and his men stay loyal to David at the lowest point of his reign, when many others had gone over to Absalom.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s aṟaipōkāmai, troops who will not be won over by the other side.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What have you heard, Ananda: do the Vajjis neither enact new decrees nor abolish existing ones, but proceed in accordance with their ancient constitutions?”
buddhism.explanation: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjis, the Buddha says they cannot be overcome so long as they keep to their ancient ways and remain united.
buddhism.tie_back: Strength drawn from long-held tradition is the Kural’s vaḻivanta vaṉkaṇ, valour that comes down through lineage.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 1.4 (trans. Sister Vajira & Francis Story)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though they tempt him with pleasures, and though they should bind him and carry him home, if he does not care for a (worldly) life, they will not captivate him or make him return to domestic life.”
jainism.explanation: A monk set firmly on the path cannot be won back by pleading relatives, by temptation or even by force; his resolve can be neither bought nor broken.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's true army is one that is not broken and cannot be suborned by the enemy, and the Jain monk shows the same incorruptibility under every kind of pressure.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.2.1.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: After Anandpur was abandoned, Guru Gobind Singh's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were taken before Wazir Khan, governor of Sirhind, and offered rewards and an easy life if they would give up their faith. They refused and were put to death in December 1705; popular tradition says they were bricked up alive.
sikhism.explanation: The younger Sahibzade are honoured in Sikh tradition as children who could not be bought, holding to the courage of their father and their grandfather Guru Tegh Bahadur.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's true army cannot be won over by the enemy and carries a courage handed down through generations; the Sahibzade refused every bribe and showed the inherited resolve of their line.
sikhism.source: Wikipedia, 'Zorawar Singh (Sikhism)' (paraphrase of traditional accounts)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Demaratus tells Xerxes that the Spartans are free but have law as their master, and that law commands them never to flee from battle whatever the size of the enemy, but to stand in their ranks and conquer or die.
greek_mythology.explanation: Spartan steadfastness is presented as an inherited discipline rather than individual bravado.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s army whose courage is handed down and which never breaks.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli argues that a principality without its own arms is never secure, and that mercenary and auxiliary troops are useless and dangerous because they have no loyalty but pay.
philosophy.explanation: He urges rulers to rely on armies composed of their own subjects.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the political-philosophical form of the Kural’s point that only a native, long-established army will not desert.

real_life_example.event_title: The Swiss Guard's stand during the Sack of Rome
real_life_example.place: St Peter's Basilica, Rome (now Vatican City)
real_life_example.event: When the troops of Emperor Charles V stormed Rome, 189 men of the Pontifical Swiss Guard defended Pope Clement VII. Of these, 147 were killed, many on the steps of St Peter's, while the pope escaped to Castel Sant'Angelo. New recruits to the Swiss Guard have been sworn in each year on 6 May in commemoration of that day.
real_life_example.explanation: The Guard held to its duty to the end rather than abandon or betray the pope, and the corps has kept that memory as its living tradition for five centuries.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names as a true army one that cannot be won over by the enemy and that carries courage handed down through generations, and the Swiss Guard's loyalty and its yearly oath on the anniversary embody both.

tamil:
கூற்றுடன்று மேல்வரினும் கூடி எதிர்நிற்கும்
ஆற்ற லதுவே படை.
transliteration:
Kootrudandru melvarinum koodi edhirnirkum
aatraladhuve padai.
meaning: A true army is one that can stand together and fight even if Death himself comes at it in anger.
elementary: Picture a group of friends holding hands in a line during a strong wind on the beach. Alone, each might be pushed over, but together they stay standing. Valluvar says a real army stands together like that, even against the scariest danger.
university: Kūṟṟu (கூற்று) is Death personified, identified by commentators with Yama, and uṭaṉṟu (உடன்று) means ‘having become enraged’. The key word is kūṭi (கூடி, ‘together, united’): the excellence praised is collective resolve rather than individual heroism, and āṟṟal (ஆற்றல்) is the strength to hold. Parimelazhagar notes that even the god of death cannot be resisted by ordinary means, so the hyperbole stresses unity as the army’s defining power. The two sources agree apart from sandhi (கூடி யெதிர்நிற்கு / மாற்ற லதுவே).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do thou fight for the sake of fighting, without considering happiness or distress, loss or gain, victory or defeat—and, by so doing, you shall never incur sin.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna urges Arjuna to face the battle with equanimity, unmoved by fear of loss or even death.
hinduism.tie_back: It reflects the Kural’s resolve to stand firm even when Death advances.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the church, addressed collectively, to be equipped to hold its ground on the worst of days.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Having done all, to stand’ is the Kural’s collective resistance even against Death.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row as though they are a [single] structure joined firmly.”
islam.explanation: The sura named ‘The Ranks’ praises fighters who hold together like a solid building.
islam.tie_back: The firmly joined structure is exactly the Kural’s kūṭi etirniṟkum, standing together against the onslaught.

judaism.quote_or_event: While rebuilding Jerusalem’s walls under threat, Nehemiah arms the builders, tells them not to fear but to remember the LORD, and orders that wherever the trumpet sounds they should rally together there.
judaism.explanation: The scattered workers become a single defensive body ready to meet any attack.
judaism.tie_back: It embodies the Kural’s united stand against a threatening enemy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What have you heard, Ananda: do the Vajjis assemble and disperse peacefully and attend to their affairs in concord?” ... “So long, Ananda, as this is the case, the growth of the Vajjis is to be expected, not their decline.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Ajatasattu’s minister that the Vajjis cannot be conquered while they remain united.
buddhism.tie_back: Concord as the source of invincibility is the heart of the Kural’s kūṭi, ‘standing together’.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 1.4 (trans. Sister Vajira & Francis Story)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard (this) from the venerable men who control themselves and subdue their senses, the virtuous and the learned do not tremble in the hour of death.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's teaching on the two kinds of death says that those trained in self-control meet death calmly and without fear.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises an army that stands firm even when Death himself comes on in fury, and the Jain verse describes the same fearless steadiness before death.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: On Baisakhi in 1699 at Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh asked for volunteers ready to give their heads. Five came forward, and they became the Panj Pyare, the first initiates of the Khalsa, drinking amrit stirred with a double-edged sword from one bowl and all taking the name Singh.
sikhism.explanation: The Khalsa was founded as one body of initiates, of mixed backgrounds, who had shown at the start that they would face death together.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the true army is one that stands together and faces even Death in fury; the Khalsa began with men ready to die, joined by a shared initiation into a single body.
sikhism.source: The Conversation, 'Why Sikhs celebrate the festival of Baisakhi' (2024) (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Divide your men, Agamemnon, into their several tribes and clans, that clans and tribes may stand by and help one another.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor advises Agamemnon to array the Achaeans so that kin stand beside kin and support each other.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His counsel aims at the same mutual support that lets the Kural’s army stand together against Death.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The Moral Law causes the people to be in complete accord with their ruler, so that they will follow him regardless of their lives, undismayed by any danger.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu names moral unity between ruler and people as the first factor in war.
philosophy.tie_back: Complete accord that holds ‘regardless of their lives’ is the Kural’s united stand even against Death.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 1.5–6 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: The Knights of St John hold Malta against the Ottoman siege
real_life_example.event: In May 1565 a large Ottoman force landed on Malta to take the island from the Knights Hospitaller under Grand Master Jean de Valette. The much smaller garrison of knights, soldiers and Maltese defenders held out for nearly four months, losing Fort St Elmo but keeping the main fortifications. When a relief force from Sicily landed in September the Ottomans withdrew, and Malta still marks 8 September as a public holiday.
real_life_example.explanation: Britannica notes that the defence halted the Ottoman advance into the western Mediterranean and shattered their reputation for invincibility.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that is truly an army which can stand together and face the foe even if Death himself comes raging, and Malta's defenders held as one through months when death was daily expected.

tamil:
மறமானம் மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு தேற்றம்
எனநான்கே ஏமம் படைக்கு.
transliteration:
Maramaanam maanda vazhichchelavu thetram
enanaange emam padaikku.
meaning: Bravery, honor, following the good example of earlier soldiers, and being trustworthy are the four things that keep an army safe.
elementary: A good scout troop needs four things: brave members, members who care about doing the right thing, members who follow the good habits of older scouts, and a leader who can trust them. Valluvar says an army needs the same four things to stay safe and strong.
university: The couplet names four qualities: maṟam (மறம், valour), māṉam (மானம், honour, sense of shame at disgrace), māṇṭa vaḻiccelavu (மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு, walking the excellent path of predecessors), and tēṟṟam (தேற்றம்). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take tēṟṟam as ‘being trusted (tested and found reliable) by the king’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar renders it as ‘clear resolve’, a genuine interpretive divergence. Ēmam (ஏமம்) means ‘protection, safeguard’, and the emphatic nāṉkē (‘these four alone’) makes the list exclusive. Both sources agree on the wording (சந்தி: தேற்ற / மெனநான்கே யேமம்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna lists the natural qualities of the kshatriya, the warrior class, as heroism, power, determination, resourcefulness, courage in battle, generosity and leadership.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita defines the warrior by a set of inner virtues rather than by weapons.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s four safeguards, it sees a fighting force’s strength in valour, honour and character.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul describes the Christian’s armour as the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the readiness of the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit.
christianity.explanation: Each piece of protective equipment is matched to an inner virtue.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a soldier’s real safeguard lies in qualities of character.

islam.quote_or_event: “And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute and [thus] lose courage and [then] your strength would depart; and be patient. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: Before battle, believers are told that obedience, unity and patience preserve their courage and strength.
islam.tie_back: It names safeguards of an army, as the Kural does with its four, including trustworthy obedience.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What man is there that is fearful and faint-hearted? let him go and return unto his house, lest his brethren’s heart melt as his heart.”
judaism.explanation: Torah law sends the faint-hearted home before battle so that fear does not spread through the ranks.
judaism.tie_back: Keeping only the valiant protects the army, echoing the Kural’s maṟam as its first safeguard.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says a king’s elephant is fit for royal service when it has four qualities: it listens, it destroys, it endures, and it goes quickly; a monk with the corresponding four qualities is worthy of offerings.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta uses a fourfold standard for a war-elephant as a model of spiritual fitness.
buddhism.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s fourfold list of what makes an army trustworthy and secure.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Therefore a worthy and wise man should be careful, ceasing from sin and being entirely happy. The virtuous heroes of faith (have chosen) the great road, the right and certain path to perfection.”
jainism.explanation: Rishabha's sermon to his sons tells the wise man to follow the 'great road' already taken by earlier heroes of faith.
jainism.tie_back: One of the Kural's four safeguards of an army is walking the excellent path of those who went before, and the Jain verse urges walking the road the heroes of faith have already travelled.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.2.1.21 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If a servant, performing service, obeys the Will of his Master, his honor increases, and he receives double his wages. But if he claims to be equal to his Master, he earns his Master’s displeasure.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad's pauri in Asa di Vaar says that a servant earns honour by faithfully obeying his master's will, and loses it through arrogance.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural lists honour and being trusted by the king among an army's safeguards; Guru Angad ties honour to faithful service under a master's will, though he speaks of the soul serving God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, pauri 22), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plutarch records the Spartan mother who handed her son his shield with the words ‘either this or upon this’, meaning return with it or be carried home on it.
greek_mythology.explanation: The saying captures Spartan honour: to lose one’s shield in flight was the deepest disgrace.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It embodies the Kural’s māṉam, honour, as a safeguard of the army.
greek_mythology.source: Plutarch, Moralia, Sayings of Spartan Women 241F

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The Commander stands for the virtues of wisdom, sincerity, benevolence, courage and strictness.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu defines military excellence in terms of a short list of moral virtues.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, he names a compact set of character qualities as the army’s real protection.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 1.9 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Twenty-one soldiers of the 36th Sikhs defend Saragarhi
real_life_example.place: Saragarhi, Samana Range, North-West Frontier (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
real_life_example.event: Saragarhi was a small signalling post linking Fort Lockhart and Fort Gulistan, held by twenty-one men of the 36th Sikhs under Havildar Ishar Singh. When thousands of Orakzai and Afridi tribesmen attacked, the garrison refused to surrender and fought until all were killed. All twenty-one were posthumously awarded the Indian Order of Merit, then the highest gallantry award open to Indian soldiers, and the Sikh Regiment marks 12 September as Saragarhi Day.
real_life_example.explanation: The defenders were trusted with a vital post and kept that trust with valour and honour that their regiment still commemorates every year.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names valour, honour, following the noble path of predecessors and being trusted as an army's four safeguards, and the Saragarhi garrison displayed all four in a single day.

tamil:
தார்தாங்கிச் செல்வது தானை தலைவந்த
போர்தாங்கும் தன்மை அறிந்து.
transliteration:
Thaarthaangich chelvadhu thaanai thalaivandha
poarthaangum thanmai arindhu.
meaning: A true army knows how to stop an attack, and it moves forward by pushing back the front line of the enemy.
elementary: In a game of tug-of-war, the strongest kids stand at the front where the pull is hardest, and they know how to dig their heels in. Valluvar says a good army is like that: it knows how to take the first hard push and keep moving forward.
university: Tār (தார்) is the vanguard, called tūci (தூசி) in the commentaries, which Pope rendered ‘dust-van’ after the dust raised by an advancing force; tāṉai (தானை) is the army. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as describing an army that, knowing the art of checking an oncoming assault (talaivanta pōr tāṅkum taṉmai), meets and bears the enemy’s vanguard. Solomon Pappaiah reads tār more broadly as the front-line foot soldiers, while Sivayogi Sivakumar takes it as an image of ranks arrayed like a banana bunch, an idiosyncratic reading. Both texts agree (சந்தி: போர்தாங்குந் தன்மை யறிந்து).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Now all of you must give full support to Grandfather Bhīṣma, standing at your respective strategic points in the phalanx of the army.”
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana orders his commanders to hold their positions in the formation so that the line is not broken.
hinduism.tie_back: Holding one’s place in the array to meet the oncoming assault is what the Kural asks of a true army.

christianity.quote_or_event: The apostle Peter urges believers to be watchful because the adversary prowls like a lion, and to resist him steadfast in the faith.
christianity.explanation: The faithful are told to stand their ground against an attack rather than give way.
christianity.tie_back: Meeting the oncoming assault and withstanding it is the Kural’s description of a true army.

islam.quote_or_event: At Uhud the Prophet stationed a company of archers on a hill and ordered them not to leave their post; when most of them left it, the Muslim line was turned, and the Qur’an refers to this disobedience and dispute.
islam.explanation: The episode shows that the outcome depended on holding the assigned position against the enemy’s charge.
islam.tie_back: It illustrates by contrast the Kural’s army that knows how to bear the enemy’s attack.
islam.source: Qur’an 3:152 and the sira accounts of Uhud

judaism.quote_or_event: “And they stood every man in his place round about the camp; and all the host ran; and they shouted, and fled.”
judaism.explanation: Gideon’s three hundred hold their positions around the Midianite camp, and the vast host breaks and flees.
judaism.tie_back: Each man holding his place as the enemy surges is the Kural’s army that bears the assault and advances.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case of a warrior who, on seeing a cloud of dust [stirred up by the enemy army], falters, faints, doesn’t steel himself, can’t engage in the battle.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha ranks warriors by how far they can withstand the stages of an enemy advance, from the dust cloud to hand-to-hand combat.
buddhism.tie_back: The best warrior who bears the ‘cloud of dust’ is exactly the Kural’s army that bears the dust-van of the foe.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.75, Yodhajiva Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Suffering from insects a great sage remains undisturbed. As an elephant at the head of the battle kills the enemy, so does a hero (in self-control conquer the internal foe).”
jainism.explanation: In the list of the twenty-two hardships, the monk who stands firm under stinging insects is compared to a war-elephant at the front of the battle. The next verse forbids him to harm even the insects that bite him (2.11).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's army meets and takes the full weight of the enemy's vanguard, and the Jain hero stands at the 'head of the battle' and bears the assault, though his enemy is inside him.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: During the first siege of Anandpur on 1 September 1700, the hill chiefs sent a drunken, armour-plated elephant to batter down the gate of Lohgarh Fort. Guru Gobind Singh chose Bhai Bachittar Singh to meet it; he rode out and drove his spear through the plate into its forehead, and the wounded elephant turned back into the besiegers' ranks.
sikhism.explanation: The episode is celebrated in Sikh tradition as a single warrior meeting the head of the enemy's assault and turning it back.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's true army knows how to withstand the attack and bears the brunt of the enemy's vanguard; Bachittar Singh met the very spearhead of the assault at the gate and broke it.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Bachittar Singh, Bhai (d. 1705)', citing Gurbilas Patshahi 10 (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Nestor arrays the Pylians with charioteers in front, a mass of brave foot soldiers behind as a bulwark, and the less reliable men placed in the middle so that they must fight.
greek_mythology.explanation: The wise old king shows how an army’s arrangement lets it absorb and repel an attack.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Knowing how to bear the oncoming assault through good order is the Kural’s point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: During the retreat of the Ten Thousand, the Greeks formed a hollow square with baggage in the centre and reorganised their rearguard so that they could keep marching while bearing the Persians’ harassing attacks.
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon describes the practical skill of an army that advances while absorbing pressure.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the Kural’s army that ‘knows how to bear the attack’ and keeps going.

real_life_example.event_title: The 93rd Highlanders' Thin Red Line at Balaklava
real_life_example.event: During the Battle of Balaklava a body of Russian cavalry advanced toward the British base, and the 93rd Highlanders, about 500 men under Sir Colin Campbell, stood in its path. Instead of forming the usual four-deep square, Campbell drew them up in a line two deep, and their disciplined volleys turned the Russian horsemen back. The Times correspondent William Howard Russell's description of them gave rise to the phrase the thin red line.
real_life_example.explanation: A single steady regiment took the full weight of the enemy's leading charge and stopped it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises an army that knows how to withstand an oncoming attack and bears the brunt of the enemy's vanguard, which is precisely what the 93rd did at Balaklava.

tamil:
அடல்தகையும் ஆற்றலும் இல்லெனினும் தானை
படைத்தகையால் பாடு பெறும்.
transliteration:
Adalthagaiyum aatralum illeninum thaanai
padaiththagaiyaal paadu perum.
meaning: Even if an army cannot attack well or hold its ground, it can still win fame by looking strong and well equipped.
elementary: A marching band in smart uniforms, all in step, can make a whole crowd stop and stare, even before it plays a note. Valluvar says an army that is neatly lined up and well equipped can earn respect just by how it looks and moves.
university: Aṭaltakai (அடல்தகை) is the capacity to attack and destroy, āṟṟal (ஆற்றல்) the capacity to withstand; paṭaittakai (படைத்தகை) is the excellence of the army’s equipment and array, and pāṭu (பாடு) means ‘renown, dignity’. Parimelazhagar understands the couplet as saying that order and splendour alone can deter or impress an enemy, and Solomon Pappaiah stresses the disciplined beauty of its formation. Kalaignar reads it slightly differently, as saying the array should be even more excellent than attack and defence. The two sources agree (சந்தி: அடல்தகையு மாற்றலு மில்லெனினுந் தானை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya devotes Book X of the Arthashastra to the arraying of troops (vyuha), naming formations such as the staff, the snake, the circle and the detached array, and how each is to be ordered for battle.
hinduism.explanation: The treatise treats the correct array of an army as a science in itself.
hinduism.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s conviction that an army’s formation and order are a source of strength and prestige.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book X, Chapters 5–6 (trans. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, the weaker king, seeing the size of the advancing army, sues for peace before any battle.
christianity.tie_back: An army can win its ends by its mere appearance and strength, as the Kural says.

islam.quote_or_event: Before the conquest of Mecca, the Muslim army lit many campfires and paraded past Abu Sufyan, whose sight of its numbers and order contributed to the city’s surrender largely without fighting.
islam.explanation: The display of a well-ordered force secured the result that battle might otherwise have decided.
islam.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s claim that an army can win distinction by its array alone.
islam.source: Sira accounts of the conquest of Mecca (Ibn Ishaq)

judaism.quote_or_event: “And he made in Jerusalem engines, invented by skilful men, to be on the towers and upon the corners, wherewith to shoot arrows and great stones. And his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong.”
judaism.explanation: Uzziah’s equipment and engines spread his fame far beyond Judah.
judaism.tie_back: Renown earned through the excellence of an army’s equipment is the Kural’s paṭaittakaiyāl pāṭu.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A tamed elephant is led into a crowd, and the king mounts a tamed elephant. Best among men is the subdued one who endures abuse.”
buddhism.explanation: The trained elephant is the one fit to be shown before crowds and to carry the king.
buddhism.tie_back: Discipline that earns public honour parallels the Kural’s army renowned for its order.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a valiant hero bestriding a trained horse, with heralds singing out to his right and left, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk.”
jainism.explanation: The verse borrows the splendour of a mounted hero with heralds on either side as a picture of a learned monk's dignity.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says an army can win renown by the splendour of its array alone, and the Jain simile likewise treats outward magnificence as something that commands respect.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Gobind Singh held the first Hola Mahalla at Anandpur in February 1701, turning the spring festival of Holi into an organised procession and display of martial skill, with simulated battles near Holgarh Fort.
sikhism.explanation: Hola Mahalla was a public show of the Khalsa's array and training, and Nihangs still lead the procession at Anandpur today.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says an army can win renown by the splendour of its array alone; Hola Mahalla was exactly such a display of ordered strength.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Hola Mahalla' (paraphrase; text as reprinted by Asia Samachar, 2015)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus describes Xerxes reviewing his vast army at Doriscus, riding past nation after nation in their distinctive arms and dress, an array famed throughout Greece.
greek_mythology.explanation: The splendour of the Persian host was itself a weapon, meant to awe the Greeks into submission.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the renown an army can gain by its array alone, though the campaign later failed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Hence to fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu prizes winning through position and strength over actual combat.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s army that wins distinction by its array without fighting is a case of this ideal.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.2 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Zheng He's treasure fleets sail to the Indian Ocean
real_life_example.place: From Nanjing, China, to South-East Asia, India, the Persian Gulf and East Africa
real_life_example.event: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming court sent seven great expeditions under the eunuch admiral Zheng He, with fleets far larger than any then sailing, to South-East Asia, India's Malabar Coast, Hormuz and the coast of East Africa. The fleets carried gifts and were armed, but their chief purpose was diplomatic. On his return in 1415 Zheng He brought envoys of many states of South and South-East Asia to pay homage to the emperor.
real_life_example.explanation: The sheer scale and splendour of the fleets carried Ming prestige across the Indian Ocean and drew many rulers into tributary relations, largely without war.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even without using its strength to attack or defend, a force can win renown by the splendour of its array, and Zheng He's fleets won China honour chiefly by being seen.

tamil:
சிறுமையும் செல்லாத் துனியும் வறுமையும்
இல்லாயின் வெல்லும் படை.
transliteration:
Sirumaiyum sellaath thuniyum varumaiyum
illaayin vellum padai.
meaning: An army will win if its numbers are not shrinking, its soldiers do not hold a lasting grudge, and it is not short of supplies.
elementary: A team does best when nobody keeps quitting, nobody is sulking and angry at the coach, and everyone has enough food and kit. Valluvar says an army is the same: keep it whole, happy and well supplied, and it will win.
university: Three defects are named: ciṟumai (சிறுமை, diminution, a shrinking of numbers or strength), cellāt tuṉi (செல்லாத் துனி, a resentment that will not go away, which Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar direct specifically against the king or commander), and vaṟumai (வறுமை, poverty, i.e. unpaid or ill-supplied troops). Solomon Pappaiah follows this reading, while Sivayogi Sivakumar renders ciṟumai as ‘confusion’, a looser gloss. The couplet’s realism about morale and pay matches Kautilya’s detailed discussion of an army’s ‘calamities’. Both sources agree (சந்தி: சிறுமையுஞ் ... வறுமையு / மில்லாயின்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya discusses the ‘calamities of the army’, among them troops that are unpaid, disaffected, reduced in numbers, or harbouring grievances against the king, and weighs which are hardest to remedy.
hinduism.explanation: The treatise treats pay, morale and strength as conditions without which an army cannot fight well.
hinduism.tie_back: These are the very three defects, dwindling, discontent and want, that the Kural says an army must be free of.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VIII, Chapter 5 (trans. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus answers his critics with a proverb about internal division leading to ruin.
christianity.tie_back: An army eaten by lasting resentment, as the Kural warns, is a house divided against itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “So if there are from you one hundred [who are] steadfast, they will overcome two hundred. And if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast.”
islam.explanation: The verse acknowledges weakness among the believers and sets a realistic ratio for a steadfast force.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links victory to the inner condition of the troops rather than to numbers alone.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My father hath troubled the land; see, I pray you, how mine eyes are brightened, because I tasted a little of this honey. How much more, if haply the people had eaten freely to-day of the spoil of their enemies which they found? had there not been then a much greater slaughter among the Philistines?”
judaism.explanation: Jonathan argues that Saul’s oath forbidding food left the troops faint and blunted their victory.
judaism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s point that an army in want cannot win as it should.

buddhism.quote_or_event: At Kosambi the monks fell into a bitter quarrel that would not be settled; the Buddha urged reconciliation, and when they would not listen he withdrew to dwell alone.
buddhism.explanation: The episode shows how a community paralysed by lasting resentment loses its strength and purpose.
buddhism.tie_back: It is a monastic picture of the Kural’s cellāt tuṉi, the grievance that will not go away.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A houseless and poor monk who wanders from village to village may become tired of ascetic life: he should bear this trouble.”
jainism.explanation: Discontent (arati) is one of the twenty-two hardships, and the monk must overcome it and wander on 'perfectly passionless' (2.15).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural names lasting discontent and want as things that ruin an army. The Jain text also treats discontent as a danger to be overcome, but it accepts poverty instead of curing it.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.14 (cf. 2.15) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I am so hungry, I cannot perform devotional worship. Here, Lord, take back Your mala.”
sikhism.explanation: In this frank hymn Kabir admits that real want undermines even devotion, and asks God for simple food, a bed and a quilt so that he can serve wholeheartedly.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says an army wins if it is free of want and lasting discontent; Kabir makes the same point about the devotee, whose service cannot last on an empty stomach.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 656, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Achilles, aggrieved at Agamemnon for taking his prize, withdraws himself and his Myrmidons from the fighting, and the Achaeans suffer heavy reverses until the quarrel is resolved.
greek_mythology.explanation: The epic is built on the cost of an unresolved grievance between a leader and his best warriors.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the classic illustration of the Kural’s cellāt tuṉi, lasting discontent with the commander.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “By Method and discipline are to be understood the marshalling of the army in its proper subdivisions, the gradations of rank among the officers, the maintenance of roads by which supplies may reach the army, and the control of military expenditure.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu counts supply lines and the control of military spending among the basic factors of war.
philosophy.tie_back: Keeping an army supplied and paid answers the Kural’s warning against vaṟumai.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 1.10 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: The Pennsylvania Line mutinies over pay and enlistments
real_life_example.place: Morristown and Princeton, New Jersey, United States
real_life_example.event: On the night of 1 January 1781 soldiers of the Pennsylvania Line in the Continental Army, long unpaid and poorly supplied and insisting their enlistments had expired, rose in mutiny at their winter camp near Morristown, and an officer was killed in the disorder. Some 1,500 men marched toward Princeton to press their demands on Congress, while rejecting British offers of pardon and back pay to change sides. The mutiny was settled by negotiation, with many men discharged and others furloughed.
real_life_example.explanation: Even loyal troops who refused to desert to the enemy could no longer function as an army once pay, supplies and goodwill toward their government had run out.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says an army wins if it is free from dwindling numbers, lasting discontent and want, and the Pennsylvania Line shows what happens when discontent and poverty take hold.

tamil:
நிலைமக்கள் சால உடைத்தெனினும் தானை
தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்.
transliteration:
Nilaimakkal saala udaiththeninum thaanai
thalaimakkal ilvazhi il.
meaning: Even if an army has many loyal soldiers, it cannot last without good leaders.
elementary: A choir may have lots of good singers, but without a conductor they start and stop at different times and it sounds like a mess. Valluvar says an army is the same: many brave soldiers are not enough without a good leader.
university: Nilaimakkaḷ (நிலைமக்கள்) are ‘steadfast men’, read by Parimelazhagar as long-serving, permanent soldiers, and cāla (சால) means ‘in abundance’; talaimakkaḷ (தலைமக்கள்) are the ‘head-men’, i.e. commanders or generals. The final il vaḻi il (இல்வழி இல்) is a terse play: ‘where they are not, (the army) is not’, which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as the army having no glory and Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as its not being able to hold its ground. The couplet closes the chapter by turning from the troops to their leadership, preparing for the next chapter, Paṭaiccerukku (படைச்செருக்கு, the martial pride of warriors). Both sources agree (சந்தி: சால வுடைத்தெனினுந் ... தலைமக்க ளில்வழி யில்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Our strength is immeasurable, and we are perfectly protected by Grandfather Bhīṣma, whereas the strength of the Pāṇḍavas, carefully protected by Bhīma, is limited.”
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana measures the two armies chiefly by the generals who lead and protect them.
hinduism.tie_back: His reasoning assumes the Kural’s point: an army’s worth depends on its commander.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?”
christianity.explanation: Paul uses the image of an unclear battle signal to argue for clear, intelligible speech in the church.
christianity.tie_back: Without a clear lead, as the Kural says, even willing soldiers cannot act as an army.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”
islam.explanation: The community is commanded to follow rightful authority so that it acts as one body.
islam.tie_back: It assumes, like the Kural, that a body of people needs recognised leaders to be effective.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, set a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of the LORD be not as sheep which have no shepherd.”
judaism.explanation: Moses, nearing his death, asks God to appoint a leader for Israel, and Joshua is commissioned.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Go out before them’ is military language: without such a head, as the Kural says, the host is no host.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If, dear sirs, when the devas have gone into battle, there should arise fear, terror, or horripilation, then on that occasion you should catch sight of the top of my standard. For when you have caught sight of the top of my standard, whatever fear, terror, or horripilation there is will be abandoned.”
buddhism.explanation: Sakka tells the gods’ army that the sight of their leader’s banner will steady them; the Buddha then offers the Triple Gem as a surer refuge.
buddhism.tie_back: An army steadied by sight of its leader is the Kural’s talaimakkaḷ principle.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 11.3, Dhajagga Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “There is now no Gina, but there is a highly esteemed guide to show the way; now being on the right path, Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Even without a living Jina, the community of seekers depends on a respected guide to lead it along the path.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that however many steadfast soldiers there are, an army cannot stand without worthy leaders, and the Jain verse likewise treats a trusted guide as essential to those on the path.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns appeared, even with such light, there would still be pitch darkness without the Guru.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad's salok says that no amount of light is any use without the Guru to guide.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says an army with steadfast soldiers in plenty cannot stand without worthy leaders; Guru Angad says that a hundred moons and a thousand suns still leave darkness without the Guru.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...we cannot all be kings; it is not well that there should be many masters; one man must be supreme—one king to whom the son of scheming Saturn has given the sceptre of sovereignty over you all.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus rallies the Achaeans, who are rushing for the ships, by insisting that an army needs one recognised leader.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The scene shows a host on the point of dissolving for want of command, as the Kural warns.

philosophy.quote_or_event: After the Greek generals are seized, Xenophon tells the remaining officers that without commanders nothing fine or useful can be done anywhere, least of all in war, where good order saves men and disorder has already destroyed many; they elect new generals at once.
philosophy.explanation: The leaderless Ten Thousand recover only by choosing new commanders.
philosophy.tie_back: It is a direct historical demonstration of the Kural: many good soldiers, but no army, until leaders are found.

real_life_example.event_title: Darius III flees and his vast army collapses at Gaugamela
real_life_example.event: At Gaugamela the Persian king Darius III faced Alexander the Great with an army far larger than the Macedonian force, on a plain he had levelled for his chariots and cavalry. When Alexander drove toward Darius's position, Darius fled the field, as he had at Issus two years earlier. The Persian army broke and was routed, and Alexander went on to take Babylon, Susa and Persepolis.
real_life_example.explanation: A huge army of brave soldiers fell apart once its commander abandoned the field, deciding the fate of the Persian Empire.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that however many steadfast soldiers an army has, it cannot stand without worthy leaders, and Gaugamela shows a mighty host dissolving when its leader failed.

tamil:
என்னைமுன் நில்லன்மின் தெவ்விர் பலரென்னை
முன்நின்று கல்நின் றவர்.
transliteration:
Ennaimun nillanmin thevvir palarennai
Munnindru kalnin Ravar.
meaning: A soldier warns the enemy: do not stand against my king. Many who once stood before him are now only stones that mark where they died.
elementary: Imagine a champion team whose fans warn the visitors: “Lots of teams came here thinking they would win, and now their names are just on the list of teams we beat.” The warrior is proud of his leader in the same way, and the proud words themselves are meant to make the other side think twice.
university: The chapter title padaiccherukku joins padai (army) and serukku (pride, exultant spirit), and this opening couplet is cast as a battlefield vaunt addressed to thevvir (“you enemies”). Parimelazhagar takes ennai not as “me” but as en + ai, “my lord” (ai = master, chief), so the soldier boasts of his commander rather than of himself; some modern renderings (e.g., Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh.com) read it as the speaker’s own challenge. The punning repetition of nil- / nin- turns on “standing”: those who stood (nindru) against the lord now stand as kal (stone), alluding to the nadukal, the hero-stone erected for fallen warriors, a custom described in the Tolkappiyam’s Purattinai and attested in Sangam puram poetry. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the couplet identically; the sandhi split “கல்நின் றவர்” = kal ninravar.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore get up. Prepare to fight and win glory. Conquer your enemies and enjoy a flourishing kingdom. They are already put to death by My arrangement, and you, O Savyasācī, can be but an instrument in the fight.”
hinduism.explanation: After revealing his cosmic form, Krishna tells Arjuna that the opposing warriors are as good as fallen already; Arjuna need only step forward.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the soldier’s vaunt that foes who face his lord are already “stones,” Krishna declares the enemy’s fall decided before the battle.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 11.33 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.”
christianity.explanation: When a disciple draws a sword to defend Jesus at his arrest, Jesus orders it sheathed and warns that violence returns on those who use it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural boasts that those who stood against the lord perished; Jesus turns the same observation into a warning against taking up the sword at all, a real divergence from martial pride.

islam.quote_or_event: “So do not weaken and do not grieve, and you will be superior if you are [true] believers.”
islam.explanation: Revealed after the setback at Uhud, the verse tells the believers not to lose heart, promising them the upper hand if their faith holds.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s confident spirit that the righteous side will prevail over those who oppose it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hear, O Israel! You are about to join battle with your enemy. Let not your courage falter. Do not be in fear, or in panic, or in dread of them. For it is the ETERNAL your God who marches with you to do battle for you against your enemy, to bring you victory.”
judaism.explanation: Before battle a priest addresses the army, telling them that their true commander fights at their head.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s soldier, Israel’s fighters draw courage from the one who leads them, not from their own strength.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Victory begets enmity; the defeated dwell in pain. Happily the peaceful live, discarding both victory and defeat.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada observes that every victory plants new hostility and every defeat leaves suffering, so the peaceful let go of both.
buddhism.tie_back: Where the Kural takes pride in a long line of defeated foes, the Buddha sees in that same line a chain of enmity, an honest divergence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though a man should conquer thousands and thousands of valiant (foes), greater will be his victory if he conquers nobody but himself.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami answers Indra's call to subdue rival princes by ranking conquest of the self above any number of battlefield victories.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's warrior boasts of the many foes his lord has turned into memorial stones, and Jainism answers that boast with a greater victory, one won over oneself.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The battle-drum beats in the sky of the mind; aim is taken, and the wound is inflicted. The spiritual warriors enter the field of battle; now is the time to fight!”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir's salok uses the language of the battlefield, with drums, aim and the hero entering the field, to call the seeker to the inner fight.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural gives a warrior's defiant battlefield cry to the enemy; Kabir's salok has the same martial ring of a hero announcing that the hour of battle has come.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Achilles, still unarmed, appears at the trench and shouts three times, the Trojans are thrown into panic and draw back, letting the Greeks recover Patroclus’ body.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Iliad the mere presence and war cry of the great warrior is enough to break the enemy’s nerve.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s warning “do not stand before my lord” rests on the same idea: a hero’s reputation fights before he strikes.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad, Book 18 (paraphrased from the Butler translation)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that the rash man is often a boaster and a pretender to courage, bold before danger but failing in it, while the truly brave are calm beforehand and keen in action.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, loud confidence is not proof of courage; it must be matched by steadiness when danger actually comes.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s vaunt is not empty because it points to deeds already done, the many who fell; Aristotle explains why such a track record matters.

real_life_example.event_title: Darius I carves the Behistun relief over his defeated rivals
real_life_example.event: After winning the Persian throne, Darius I had a great relief and inscription carved high on the cliff at Bisotun, beside the ancient road from Mesopotamia to the Iranian plateau. The relief shows Darius, holding a bow as a sign of sovereignty, with his foot on a figure identified as the usurper Gaumata, and a line of bound captives standing before him. The text, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, records how he overthrew Gaumata, defeated the rebels who claimed the kingdom, and took the throne.
real_life_example.explanation: The monument turned the defeat of a king's opponents into a permanent warning in stone for everyone who travelled the road.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's warrior warns enemies not to stand against his lord, since many who did now stand as stones, and at Behistun those who rose against Darius stand forever carved in stone before him.

tamil:
கான முயலெய்த அம்பினில் யானை
பிழைத்தவேல் ஏந்தல் இனிது.
transliteration:
Kaana muyaleydha ambinil yaanai
Pizhaiththavel endhal inidhu.
meaning: It is better to hold a spear that missed an elephant than an arrow that killed a rabbit in the forest.
elementary: Would you rather say you beat a little kid at chess, or that you lost a close game to the school champion? Trying something truly hard, even if you miss, is more honourable than an easy win over someone weak.
university: The couplet contrasts kaana muyal (the hare of the forest, a small and timid quarry) with yaanai (the elephant, the most formidable target of ancient Tamil warfare), and the arrow (ambu) that succeeded against the hare with the spear (vel) that failed against the elephant (pizhaiththa vel). The key verb endhal, “to hold, to bear,” makes the line about what a warrior is proud to carry: honour belongs to the scale of the attempt, not merely its outcome. Parimelazhagar reads the hare and elephant as figures for weak and mighty enemies, so the teaching concerns the choice of a worthy adversary. Kalaignar’s modern gloss states the point directly: aiming at the strong and missing outranks aiming at the weak and hitting. Both base texts agree on the wording; the sandhi form முயலெய்த = muyal eydha.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Considering your specific duty as a kṣatriya, you should know that there is no better engagement for you than fighting on religious principles; and so there is no need for hesitation.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reminds Arjuna that for a warrior the most worthy engagement is a righteous battle, not a lesser or easier task.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise ranks the worthy, difficult engagement above the easy one.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.31 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.”
christianity.explanation: The young David chooses to face the giant Goliath, the most fearsome opponent on the field, when no one else will.
christianity.tie_back: David goes after the “elephant,” not the hare, which is the Kural’s idea of where honour lies.

islam.quote_or_event: “How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: Facing Goliath’s army, the few faithful soldiers with Saul refuse to be daunted by the enemy’s size.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s warrior who aims at the elephant, they take on the greater foe rather than shrink from it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Come, let us cross over to the outpost of those uncircumcised fellows. Perhaps GOD will act in our behalf, for nothing prevents GOD from winning a victory by many or by few.”
judaism.explanation: Jonathan, with only his armour-bearer, decides to attack a whole Philistine garrison.
judaism.tie_back: Jonathan picks the bold, outsized target, just as the Kural honours the spear raised against an elephant.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though one may conquer a thousand times a thousand men in battle, yet he indeed is the noblest victor who conquers himself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names the hardest of all opponents: one’s own mind.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees that the worthiest contest is the hardest one, but relocates the “elephant” inside the self.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Fight with your Self; why fight with external foes? He who conquers himself through himself, will obtain happiness.” … “difficult to conquer is one's self; but when that is conquered, everything is conquered.”
jainism.explanation: Nami names the self, with the senses, anger, pride, delusion and greed, as the hardest enemy of all and the only one worth fighting.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural honours the warrior who aims at the mighty elephant rather than the easy hare, and Jainism likewise chooses the hardest adversary, the self, over lesser foes.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.35–36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib Guru Nanak names the mind as the real adversary worth defeating; whoever masters it has won everything.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says it is nobler to aim at an elephant and miss than to kill a hare; Guru Nanak points the seeker toward the hardest of all enemies, one's own mind, rather than easy victories.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib, Pauri 28, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sarpedon tells Glaucus that because death awaits all men in any case, they should go forward to the front of the fight and either win glory or give it to another.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Iliad the Lycian prince argues that nobility obliges the noble to take on the greatest danger, not to linger safely behind.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Sarpedon’s reasoning matches the Kural’s: the honourable warrior seeks the great encounter.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that courage is shown chiefly in the noblest dangers, above all death in battle, rather than in trivial risks.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the virtue is measured by the worth of what is faced; facing small dangers is not yet courage in the full sense.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly values the attempt on the elephant over success against the hare.

real_life_example.event_title: Porus fights Alexander at the Hydaspes and keeps his kingdom
real_life_example.event: When Alexander the Great invaded the Punjab, Ambhi, the king of Taxila, submitted, but Porus, who ruled the land between the Hydaspes and Acesines rivers, chose to resist. At the Battle of the Hydaspes his elephants and infantry were outmatched by Alexander's mobile cavalry and mounted archers, and he was defeated. Impressed by his skill and spirit, Alexander allowed Porus to keep his kingdom and may have given him further territory.
real_life_example.explanation: Porus took on the most formidable army of his age and lost, yet his choice to fight earned him a respect that his neighbour's easy submission did not.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says it is better to hold a spear that missed an elephant than an arrow that killed a hare, and Porus, who aimed at the mightiest foe and failed, ended with more honour than one who bowed without a fight.

tamil:
பேராண்மை என்ப தறுகண்ஒன் றுற்றக்கால்
ஊராண்மை மற்றதன் எஃகு.
transliteration:
Peraanmai enba tharukan ondru utrakkaal
Ooraanmai matradhan eqku.
meaning: Having no fear in battle is called great bravery. But helping your enemy when he is in trouble is the sharpest edge of that bravery.
elementary: A good football player plays hard to win. But if a player on the other team falls and gets hurt, the best player stops and helps him up. Being brave is good; being brave and kind is even better.
university: This is the moral centre of the chapter: tharukan (fierceness, unflinching daring) is what people call peraanmai (great manliness or valour), but ooraanmai, helping or showing grace when ondru utrakkaal (“a calamity befalls,” understood as befalling the foe), is its eqku, the keen cutting edge. Parimelazhagar glosses ooraanmai as upakaram (benevolent aid) and the traditional reading takes the misfortune as the enemy’s, so magnanimity to a fallen foe is the sharpest point of heroism. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar both read it this way; Sivayogi Sivakumar paraphrases more broadly as relieving others’ suffering, even enemies’. The metaphor of eqku (steel, blade-edge) is apt: valour without mercy is a blunt weapon.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Yuddha Kanda, when Ravana is exhausted and disarmed in his first duel with Rama, Rama does not kill him but sends him back to Lanka to rest and return to fight another day.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki shows Rama refusing to strike a spent and weaponless opponent, a classic image of dharmic restraint in war.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama’s mercy toward a foe in distress is exactly what the Kural calls the sharp edge of valour.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Sarga 59 in common numbering; paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to answer an enemy’s need with practical help rather than revenge.
christianity.tie_back: Helping an enemy in trouble is the Kural’s highest form of strength, and Paul calls it overcoming evil with good.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah. Then deliver him to his place of safety.”
islam.explanation: Even in a context of hostilities, an enemy who asks for protection must be granted it and escorted to safety.
islam.tie_back: Protecting a vulnerable enemy is the same magnanimity the Kural calls the edge of valour.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat; If he is thirsty, give him water to drink. You will be heaping live coals on his head, And GOD will reward you.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that an enemy’s need is an occasion for kindness, not gloating.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ooraanmai: answering the foe’s misfortune with help.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that enmity ends only when one side answers it with non-hatred.
buddhism.tie_back: Kindness toward a stricken foe is non-hatred in action, the Kural’s sharp edge of valour.

jainism.quote_or_event: In Hemacandra's account of the duel between the brothers Bharata and Bahubali, Bahubali raises his fist for a blow that would have crushed Bharata.
