He then stops himself, turns the same hand to pluck out his own hair in the ascetic's renunciation, and gives up the kingdom instead of striking his defeated brother.
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition makes this moment of restraint toward a beaten rival, not the victory, the climax of Bahubali's heroism; he goes on to become a revered kevalin.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls kindness to an enemy in misfortune the 'sharp edge' of valour, and Bahubali's mercy to the brother at his feet is the best-known Jain example of exactly that.
jainism.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra 1.5 (Ādīśvaracaritra, 'The fight between Bharata and Bāhubali'), tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org

sikhism.quote_or_event: During the siege of Anandpur (1704-05), Bhai Kanhaiya carried water to wounded soldiers of both armies without distinction. When Sikhs complained to Guru Gobind Singh that he was helping the enemy, Kanhaiya said he saw only the Guru's face in every man; the Guru approved and gave him ointment to treat the wounds as well.
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Kanhaiya became the founder of the Sevapanthi order, and his service to wounded enemies is a central Sikh example of seva without enmity.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls help given to an enemy in his misfortune the sharp edge of valour; Bhai Kanhaiya, with the Guru's blessing, gave exactly that help on the battlefield.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Kanhaiya, Bhai (1648-1718)' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the aged Priam comes alone to Achilles’ tent to ransom Hector’s body, Achilles weeps with him, raises him up, and grants a truce for the funeral.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fiercest Greek warrior, faced with his enemy’s grieving father, chooses compassion over rage.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ mercy to a defeated foe is the moment the Iliad itself treats as the height of his greatness, as the Kural would.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues to the young Nero that mercy (clementia) is the virtue that most becomes the powerful, because only the strong are in a position to spare.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, restraint toward those one could crush is a sign of greatness, not weakness.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca’s claim matches the Kural’s ranking of mercy as the keenest edge of strength.

real_life_example.event_title: The captain of the Admiral Hipper rescues Glowworm's crew and praises her commander
real_life_example.place: Norwegian Sea, off the coast of Norway
real_life_example.event: The British destroyer HMS Glowworm, under Lieutenant Commander Gerard Roope, met the much larger German heavy cruiser Admiral Hipper, engaged her and rammed her before Glowworm sank. Hipper's captain, Hellmuth Heye, stopped for over an hour to pick up survivors from the sea. He later sent word to the British through the Red Cross praising Roope's courage in closing with a far stronger ship, and Roope was posthumously awarded the Victoria Cross, gazetted in 1945.
real_life_example.explanation: In the midst of a battle he had just won, an enemy commander used his ship to save his opponents and then made sure their captain's bravery would be honoured.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls fearlessness valour but says helping the enemy when misfortune strikes him is its sharp edge, and Captain Heye's rescue of Glowworm's crew is that edge in action.

tamil:
கைவேல் களிற்றொடு போக்கி வருபவன்
மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும்.
transliteration:
Kaivel kalitrodu pokki varubavan
Meyvel pariyaa nagum.
meaning: A hero throws his only spear at an elephant and looks for another weapon. He finds one stuck in his own body, pulls it out, and smiles.
elementary: A firefighter who has used up all the water in one hose doesn’t give up; he grabs whatever is at hand and keeps going, even laughing at how tough the day is. The warrior in this verse is like that: nothing stops him.
university: Kaivel (the spear in hand) is sent off (pokki) with the kalitru (bull elephant), and the warrior, returning weaponless (varubavan), finds a meyvel, an enemy spear stuck in his own body (mey), which he plucks out (pariyaa) and laughs (nagum). Parimelazhagar and later commentators read the laughter as joy at having found a new weapon, not as indifference to pain, so the image is about undiminished fighting spirit. Solomon Pappaiah adds that he takes the spear to hurl at the next elephant. The couplet belongs to the Sangam puram tradition of the hero who welcomes wounds, and its hyperbole should be read as a literary ideal of morale, not a literal description. The two base texts agree verbatim.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, the nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons. They arise from sense perception, O scion of Bharata, and one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches Arjuna titiksha, the endurance of pain and pleasure as passing sensations.
hinduism.tie_back: The warrior who laughs as he pulls out the spear embodies this calm toleration of pain.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.”
christianity.explanation: Paul uses the soldier’s endurance as a model for Timothy’s perseverance in ministry.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s warrior shows the literal endurance that Paul turns into a spiritual metaphor.

islam.quote_or_event: “And how many a prophet [fought and] with him fought many religious scholars. But they never lost assurance due to what afflicted them in the cause of Allah, nor did they weaken or submit. And Allah loves the steadfast.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises fighters who, though wounded and afflicted, did not lose heart.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s warrior: hurt, but undaunted.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be strong and resolute; be not in fear or in dread of them, for it is indeed the ETERNAL your God who marches with you—who will not fail you or forsake you.”
judaism.explanation: Moses charges Israel before entering the land to remain strong and unafraid.
judaism.tie_back: The resolve not to weaken matches the Kural’s warrior who keeps fighting with the weapon at hand.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As an elephant in the battlefield withstands arrows shot from bows all around, even so shall I endure abuse. There are many, indeed, who lack virtue.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha borrows the war elephant that withstands arrows as an image of patient endurance of insults.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts admire the one who takes the blows and stays composed, but Buddhism turns the battlefield into a lesson in patience.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If any misfortune happens and he suffers pain, he should cheerfully steady his mind, and bear the ills that attack him.”
jainism.explanation: Among the hardships a monk must bear is bodily suffering, which he is to meet calmly and with good cheer instead of complaint.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's hero pulls an enemy spear from his own body and smiles, and the Jain monk is likewise told to meet pain in his body with a cheerful, steady mind.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! The world is afraid of death - that death fills my mind with bliss. It is only by death that perfect, supreme bliss is obtained.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir turns the common fear of death on its head; for one who has died to ego, death holds only joy.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's hero smiles as he pulls a spear out of his own body; Kabir likewise meets what the world fears most with joy rather than dread.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1365, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 22) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Wounded in the shoulder by an arrow from Pandarus, Diomedes has the arrow drawn out, prays to Athena, and returns to the fight with even greater fury.
greek_mythology.explanation: Book 5 of the Iliad shows the wound spurring the hero on instead of stopping him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Diomedes, like the Kural’s warrior, treats the weapon in his own body as no reason to stop.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus teaches that people are disturbed not by things themselves but by their judgments about things.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, the same event can crush or not, depending on how the mind receives it.
philosophy.tie_back: The warrior’s laughter at his wound is a dramatic example of a mind that refuses to judge the pain as defeat.

real_life_example.event_title: Rifleman Lachhiman Gurung fights on one-handed at Taungdaw
real_life_example.place: Taungdaw, west bank of the Irrawaddy, Burma (Myanmar)
real_life_example.event: Rifleman Lachhiman Gurung of the 4th Battalion, 8th Gurkha Rifles, was manning the most forward post of his platoon when it was attacked by a large enemy force at night. He threw back two grenades that landed in his trench, but a third exploded in his right hand, severely wounding him. Alone and disregarding his wounds, he loaded and fired his rifle with his left hand for about four hours, and his example helped his comrades hold their position; he was awarded the Victoria Cross, gazetted in July 1945.
real_life_example.explanation: Badly wounded and with his weapon hand gone, he simply carried on fighting with what he had left.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's hero, having thrown his only spear, finds another in his own wound and smiles, and Lachhiman Gurung, his hand shattered, turned at once to fighting on with the other.

tamil:
விழித்தகண் வேல்கொண டெறிய அழித்திமைப்பின்
ஒட்டன்றோ வன்க ணவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Vizhiththakan velkonda eriya azhiththimaippin
Ottandro vankanavarkku.
meaning: For truly brave soldiers, even blinking when the enemy’s spear comes at their angry eyes counts as running away.
elementary: A goalkeeper facing a penalty kick tries hard not to flinch, because flinching means he can’t see the ball. The verse says a brave person keeps their eyes open and steady even when something scary is coming right at them.
university: Vizhiththa kan, the wide-open, glaring eye fixed on the foe, is set against azhiththu imaippin, “if it gives way and blinks,” when the enemy hurls (eriya) his spear (vel). For the vankanavar (the hard-eyed, stout-hearted), such a blink is ottu, which commentators gloss as tantamount to puRangodai, turning one’s back in flight; Kalaignar makes this equation explicit. The couplet sets an almost impossible standard to show that heroism is first an inner state: the smallest outward sign of fear already counts as defeat. The sandhi forms கொண டெறிய = kondu eriya and வன்க ணவர்க்கு = vankanavarkku; both base sources agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, do not yield to this degrading impotence. It does not become you. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O chastiser of the enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna rebukes Arjuna’s faltering at the start of battle as hrdaya-daurbalya, weakness of heart.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna’s hesitation is the inner “blink” the Kural says a true warrior must not allow.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.3 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews pictures steady, unwavering focus on Christ, who did not turn aside from suffering.
christianity.tie_back: The fixed gaze that does not turn away echoes the Kural’s unblinking eye.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing [for battle], do not turn to them your backs [in flight].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids fleeing when the enemy advances.
islam.tie_back: The Kural pushes the same prohibition inward: even a blink is a kind of turning back.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Is there anyone afraid and disheartened? Let him go back to his home, lest the courage of his comrades flag like his.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah sends the fearful home before battle so that their fear does not spread through the ranks.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts treat a soldier’s inner fear as already a breach in the line.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The wise remain unmoved by the forces that buffet others.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s unblinking warrior and the Buddha’s unshaken rock share the ideal of steadiness, though the Buddha applies it to the mind, not the battlefield.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In a burial-place, or a deserted house, or below a tree he should sit down, alone, without moving, and he should not drive away any one. Sitting there he should brave all dangers; when seized with fear, he should not rise and go to some other place.”
jainism.explanation: A monk meditating alone must not move from his seat even when danger and fear come; leaving it would be a retreat.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that for the truly brave even a blink before a flying spear counts as flight, and the Jain rule likewise treats the smallest yielding to fear as a failure of nerve.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.20–21 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Bhai Mati Das went with Guru Tegh Bahadur to Delhi in 1675 and was arrested with him. When he refused to give up his faith he was sawn in two from the head downwards; Sikh tradition adds that he went on reciting Japji to the end.
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Mati Das is remembered daily in the Sikh Ardas among those who did not waver under the saw.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that for the truly brave even a blink before the enemy's spear counts as retreat; Bhai Mati Das is honoured precisely because he showed no sign of flinching under torture.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Mati Das, Bhai (d. 1675)' (paraphrase); the Japji detail follows devotional tradition

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tyrtaeus urges the Spartan hoplite to stand firm with feet planted and lip bitten, eyes on the enemy, and never to turn away.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Spartan war-poet makes holding one’s ground under the enemy’s charge the defining mark of the good man.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tyrtaeus and the Kural both locate courage in not flinching at the decisive moment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Laches, the general Laches first defines courage as a man’s willingness to remain at his post and face the enemy without running away.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates goes on to show the definition is too narrow, but it captures the popular ideal of steadfastness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s unblinking eye is the most demanding form of “remaining at one’s post.”

real_life_example.event_title: Theodore Roosevelt delivers his speech after being shot
real_life_example.event: While campaigning for president as the Progressive Party candidate, Theodore Roosevelt was shot in the chest by a would-be assassin as he left his hotel in Milwaukee. The bullet passed through his folded speech manuscript and metal glasses case and lodged near his ribs. Refusing to go to hospital first, Roosevelt went on to the auditorium and spoke for about an hour, showing the audience the bullet-pierced manuscript, before he accepted medical treatment.
real_life_example.explanation: Roosevelt treated the attack as no reason to flinch from what he had come to do, and the bullet remained in his body for the rest of his life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for the truly brave even a blink in the face of the enemy's spear counts as retreat, and Roosevelt would not let a bullet make him turn from his audience.

tamil:
விழுப்புண் படாதநாள் எல்லாம் வழுக்கினுள்
வைக்கும்தன் நாளை எடுத்து.
transliteration:
Vizhuppun padaadhanaal ellaam vazhukkinul
Vaikkumdhan naalai eduththu.
meaning: A hero counts his days and calls every day wasted on which he did not get a wound in an honorable fight.
elementary: Some athletes feel a day without practice is a day wasted. The warrior here feels that way about days when he did not stand up bravely for his people. The real lesson is about not letting days slip by without doing something that matters.
university: Vizhuppun is a technical term of puram ethics: a wound of honour, received on the chest or face while facing the enemy, as opposed to a wound in the back (a sign of flight). The warrior “takes up” (eduththu) his days and places (vaikkum) every day without such a wound among vazhukku, lapses or wasted days. Solomon Pappaiah explicitly specifies wounds on face and chest, following the traditional reading. The idea echoes Purananuru poems in which a mother checks that her son’s wounds are on his chest. Modern readers may take the hyperbole as a vivid figure for a life measured by service and risk rather than comfort.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In a Purananuru poem attributed to Kakkaipadiniyar Naccellaiyar, an aged mother, told her son fled the battle, vows to cut off the breast that fed him; searching the field, she finds he fell facing the enemy and rejoices more than at his birth.
hinduism.explanation: Sangam heroic poetry treats a wound received facing the foe as the mark of honour for a warrior and his family.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s vizhuppun, the wound that makes a day count; note this is Tamil puram literature rather than Hindu scripture.

christianity.quote_or_event: “From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Paul points to the scars of his beatings and hardships as proof of his faithful service.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s warrior, Paul treats wounds borne in service as badges of honour, though his are suffered, not inflicted in battle.

islam.quote_or_event: “Fighting has been enjoined upon you while it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an frankly acknowledges that fighting is naturally disliked, even when it is a duty.
islam.tie_back: Unlike the Kural’s warrior who longs for wounds, the Qur’an treats combat as a burden accepted, not desired, an honest divergence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines the gibbor, the mighty hero, as the one who masters himself, citing Proverbs 16:32.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural measures a day by its battle wounds; the rabbis measure might by self-mastery, a meaningful divergence.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The wise show no elation or depression when touched by happiness or sorrow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada counsels equanimity toward whatever each day brings.
buddhism.tie_back: Where the warrior grades his days by wounds, the Buddhist ideal is to stop grading days by such marks at all, a gentle divergence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Acquire perfect knowledge of the Law! why do you not study it? It is difficult to obtain instruction in it after this life. The days (that are gone by) will never return, nor is it easy a second time to obtain human birth.”
jainism.explanation: Rishabha warns his sons that each day not used for the Law is lost for good, because human birth is rare.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's hero counts every day without an honourable wound as wasted, and the Jain teaching likewise reckons each day by whether it was spent in hard spiritual effort.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.2.1.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You fill your belly, and sleep like an animal; you have wasted and lost this human life.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir rebukes a life given to eating and sleeping, saying it squanders the human birth meant for remembering God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's hero counts as wasted every day without an honourable wound; Kabir likewise counts as wasted a life spent in comfort rather than in its true purpose.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the disguised Odysseus returns home, his old nurse Eurycleia recognises him by the scar on his leg from a boar-hunt of his youth.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Odyssey a scar earned in a test of courage becomes the sign of the hero’s true identity.
greek_mythology.tie_back: For the Kural’s warrior too, honourable wounds are what mark him as who he is.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Nietzsche’s maxim holds that what does not kill a person makes them stronger.
philosophy.explanation: The saying treats hardship survived as a source of growth.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s warrior counts days without trial as lost, sharing Nietzsche’s view that struggle is formative.
philosophy.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols, “Maxims and Arrows” 8 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Adrian Carton de Wiart returns to the front again and again
real_life_example.place: Somaliland and the Western Front (France and Belgium)
real_life_example.event: Adrian Carton de Wiart, a British Army officer, lost an eye in Somaliland early in the First World War and later lost his left hand on the Western Front. He kept returning to active service and was wounded many times in that war, by one count eight times. In July 1916 he was awarded the Victoria Cross for his leadership of the 8th Battalion, Gloucestershire Regiment, at La Boisselle during the Battle of the Somme.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than treating each wound as a reason to step back, he treated it as an interruption before returning to the fighting.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's hero counts as wasted every day without an honourable wound, and Carton de Wiart's repeated return to the front shows a man who measured his days by service under fire.

tamil:
சுழலும் இசைவேண்டி வேண்டா உயிரார்
கழல்யாப்புக் காரிகை நீர்த்து.
transliteration:
Suzhalum isaivendi vendaa uyiraar
Kazhalyaappuk kaarigai neerththu.
meaning: For people who want fame that spreads across the world and do not worry about their own lives, wearing the warrior’s ankle ring is a true decoration.
elementary: A medal looks most beautiful on someone who earned it by being brave for others. The warrior’s anklet in this verse is like that medal: it is beautiful because of the courage of the one who wears it.
university: Suzhalum isai is fame that “circles” or spreads around the world; vendaa uyiraar are those who do not desire (cling to) life; kazhal yaappu is the tying on of the kazhal, the heroic anklet worn by warriors in Tamil tradition; and kaarigai neerththu means it has the nature of a true ornament. The point is that the badge of valour is fitting only on those whose courage is real: on others it would be mere decoration. Solomon Pappaiah glosses isai as the fame that stays on earth after death, unlike the hero who departs. Both base texts agree on the wording; the sandhi யாப்புக் = yaappu + k.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that the shame of retreat would follow him forever.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the obverse of the Kural’s fame-seeking warrior who values renown over life.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.34 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness”
christianity.explanation: Near death, Paul looks back on his life as a completed contest and looks forward to a crown from God.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s crown is like the Kural’s anklet, a mark of honour, but it is awarded by God, not by worldly fame.

islam.quote_or_event: “And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision,”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an assures that those who die for God’s cause live on with Him.
islam.tie_back: The Kural promises the fallen hero lasting fame among men; the Qur’an promises life with God instead, a different kind of immortality.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good name is better than fragrant oil, and the day of death than the day of birth.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet values a good name above luxuries and sees its full worth only at death.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks reputation above the ornaments and comforts of life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Self-conquest is far better than the conquest of others. Not even a god, an angel, Mara or Brahma can turn into defeat the victory of a person who is self-subdued and ever restrained in conduct.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada points to the one victory that no one can take away.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural prizes a fame that circles the world; Buddhism prizes a victory that cannot be undone, a different idea of what lasts.

jainism.quote_or_event: “But famous warriors, leaders of heroes at the time of the battle, do not look behind them; (they think) what if all end with death?”
jainism.explanation: Unlike the coward who looks for a hiding-place, the true warrior fights without caring for his life, and the monk is told to 'exert himself in a similar way' (1.3.3.7).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the hero's anklet belongs only to those who do not cling to life, and the Sutrakritanga uses the same warrior's indifference to death as its model of resolve.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.3.3.6 (cf. 1.3.3.7) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. When you place your feet on this Path, give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak asks the seeker to come ready to give up life itself; Sikh tradition links this salok to the Khalsa's founding call for heads in 1699.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the warrior's anklet suits only those who do not cling to life; Guru Nanak says the path is open only to one who comes with his head on his palm.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles tells the embassy that his mother foretold two fates: if he stays at Troy he will die young but his glory (kleos) will be imperishable; if he goes home he will live long without fame.
greek_mythology.explanation: The choice between long life and undying fame is the defining dilemma of the Greek hero.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s warriors who “do not want life” but seek world-wide fame have made Achilles’ choice.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle identifies a “political” or citizen courage, closest to true courage, in which soldiers face danger because of the honours that come to the brave and the disgrace that comes to cowards.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle sees honour-driven courage as admirable but a step below courage chosen purely because it is noble.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s fame-seeking warrior fits this honour-driven courage, and Aristotle helps show both its worth and its limit.

real_life_example.event_title: Queen Victoria institutes the Victoria Cross for valour
real_life_example.event: A royal warrant of 29 January 1856 created the Victoria Cross as Britain's highest award for gallantry in the face of the enemy, backdated to cover acts in the Crimean War. Unlike earlier honours, it was open to all ranks. At the first investiture, in Hyde Park on 26 June 1857, Queen Victoria personally presented the cross to 62 recipients before large crowds.
real_life_example.explanation: The decoration was deliberately reserved for proven courage rather than rank or birth, so that wearing it meant one had risked one's life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the warrior's anklet is a true ornament only on those who seek lasting fame and do not cling to life, and the Victoria Cross was designed as just such a badge, fitting only on those whose valour is real.

tamil:
உறின்உயிர் அஞ்சா மறவர் இறைவன்
செறினும் சீர்குன்றல் இலர்.
transliteration:
Urin uyir anjaa maravar iraivan
Serinum seerkundral ilar.
meaning: Soldiers who do not fear for their lives when war comes do not lose their eagerness to fight, even if the king angrily stops them.
elementary: A team captain may tell an eager player to sit out this game. A truly dedicated player doesn’t sulk or lose heart; they stay ready and keen. The verse says the best soldiers keep their spirit high even when told to wait.
university: Urin (“if it comes,” i.e., if battle arises) uyir anjaa maravar (warriors who do not fear for life) remain seer kundral ilar (without loss of excellence or ardour) even if iraivan serinum, “the king is angry,” which the traditional commentary reads as the king forbidding them to fight. Maravar derives from maram, martial valour, and is the classic Tamil term for the warrior class. Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan read it as the king restraining them; Kalaignar reads it as the king’s displeasure not diminishing their sense of duty. The couplet thus praises discipline without loss of spirit: zeal survives even the leader’s rebuke.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If you do not act according to My direction and do not fight, then you will be falsely directed. By your nature, you will have to be engaged in warfare.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that his warrior nature will drive him to fight even if he resolves otherwise.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s maravar likewise keep their martial spirit even when held back; it is part of their nature.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.59 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.”
christianity.explanation: Ordered by the authorities to stop preaching, the apostles refuse to let the ban dampen their mission.
christianity.tie_back: Their zeal undimmed by a ruler’s prohibition parallels the Kural’s warriors, though the apostles’ cause is non-violent.

islam.quote_or_event: “Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you, but do not exceed the limits. Allah does not like transgressors.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an sets limits even on legitimate fighting.
islam.tie_back: The Kural praises warriors whose zeal survives restraint; the Qur’an insists that zeal must operate within restraint, a complementary emphasis.
islam.source: Qur’an 2:190 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran, via Quran.com)

judaism.quote_or_event: “The Ark and Israel and Judah are located at Succoth, and my master Joab and Your Majesty’s men are camped in the open; how can I go home and eat and drink … ? As you live, by your very life, I will not do this!”
judaism.explanation: King David repeatedly urges the soldier Uriah to leave the front and rest at home; Uriah refuses out of solidarity with his comrades in the field.
judaism.tie_back: Uriah’s soldierly spirit does not slacken even when the king himself tries to turn him aside, as the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A tamed elephant is led into a crowd, and the king mounts a tamed elephant. Best among men is the subdued one who endures abuse.”
buddhism.explanation: The trained royal elephant is the Dhammapada’s image of power held in discipline.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s warriors, keen yet obedient to the king’s check, resemble the tamed war elephant; Buddhism prizes the taming over the fighting.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who always acknowledges his allegiance to his teacher, who has religious zeal and ardour for study, who is kind in words and actions, deserves to be instructed.”
jainism.explanation: The ideal disciple combines steady loyalty to his teacher with zeal of his own that does not fade.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's warriors keep their ardour even when the king angrily holds them back, and the Jain disciple likewise joins obedience to his superior with undimmed zeal.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If my body were afflicted with pain, under the evil influence of unlucky stars; and if the blood-sucking kings were to hold power over me - even if this were my condition, I would still worship and adore You, and my longing to chant Your Praises would not decrease.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak declares that no suffering and no oppressive ruler could lessen his eagerness to praise God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's warriors lose none of their fervour even when the king angrily holds them back; Guru Nanak's longing likewise does not diminish under hostile kings.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Insulted by Agamemnon, who takes his prize Briseis, Achilles withdraws from the fighting and refuses to return despite the Greeks’ losses.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad’s central plot turns on a great warrior whose zeal collapses under his king’s offence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles is the counter-example to the Kural: a hero whose ardour does fail when the king angers him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates tells the jury that, just as he held his post at Potidaea, Amphipolis and Delium where his commanders placed him, he will not abandon the post the god assigned him, even if ordered to stop philosophising.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates uses his soldier’s steadfastness as the model for keeping his calling under pressure from authority.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural’s warriors, Socrates keeps his spirit undiminished even when those in power are angry with him.

real_life_example.event_title: No. 303 Polish Squadron's first victory while still held back from combat
real_life_example.place: RAF Northolt and the skies over Hertfordshire, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: No. 303 Squadron, formed of Polish airmen at RAF Northolt in August 1940, had not yet been declared operational and was flying a training exercise when Pilot Officer Ludwik Paszkiewicz saw enemy aircraft, broke formation and shot down a German Messerschmitt Bf 110. On landing he was reprimanded by his British commander for indiscipline and then congratulated for his success. The squadron was declared operational the next day and became the most successful Fighter Command unit in the Battle of Britain.
real_life_example.explanation: Kept out of the fight by those in authority, the Polish pilots lost none of their eagerness to defend the country that had taken them in.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says warriors who do not fear for their lives keep their fervour even when their king holds them back, and the Polish airmen's zeal survived both official doubt and a reprimand.

tamil:
இழைத்தது இகவாமைச் சாவாரை யாரே
பிழைத்தது ஒறுக்கிற் பவர்.
transliteration:
Izhaiththadhu igavaamaich chaavaarai yaare
Pizhaiththadhu orukkir pavar.
meaning: Who could blame for failure those who die keeping the promise they made?
elementary: If a friend promised to protect you and gave everything trying, no one would say they failed. Keeping your word with all your heart is what counts, even if things don’t turn out perfectly.
university: Izhaiththadhu refers to what one has pledged, the sool or battle-vow sworn before the king; igavaamai is “not transgressing” it; saavaarai are those who die so. The rhetorical question yaare ... orukkirpavar asks “who would punish (or reproach) them” for pizhaiththadhu, the failure. Commentators divide: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as those who die fighting in fulfilment of their vow, whom no one can reproach; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as even if the vow went unfulfilled, death in the attempt removes all blame. Either way, death in fidelity to one’s word places the warrior beyond censure.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, either you will be killed on the battlefield and attain the heavenly planets, or you will conquer and enjoy the earthly kingdom. Therefore, get up with determination and fight.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that a warrior who fights in duty cannot truly lose: death and victory are both honourable outcomes.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural also holds that one who dies keeping his vow cannot be counted a failure.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.37 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer … be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.”
christianity.explanation: The risen Christ encourages the church at Smyrna to remain faithful even if it costs their lives.
christianity.tie_back: Faithfulness to death is honoured, not reproached, just as the Kural says.

islam.quote_or_event: “Among the believers are men true to what they promised Allah. Among them is he who has fulfilled his vow [to the death], and among them is he who awaits [his chance]. And they did not alter [the terms of their commitment] by any alteration”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who kept their pledge even to death.
islam.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s praise of those who die without transgressing their vow.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If anyone makes a vow to GOD or takes an oath imposing an obligation on themselves, they shall not break their pledge; they must carry out all that has crossed their lips.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah makes keeping one’s vow a sacred obligation.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s warrior honours exactly this principle, at the cost of his life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better it is to live one day strenuous and resolute than to live a hundred years sluggish and dissipated.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada prizes resolute effort over a long but slack life.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural honours resolve kept to the end; Buddhism shares the esteem for resolve, though it would direct it to the path rather than the battlefield.

jainism.quote_or_event: “These two ways of life ending with death have been declared: death with one's will, and death against one's will. Death against one's will is that of ignorant men, and it happens (to the same individual) many times. Death with one's will is that of wise men, and at best it happens but once.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira praises the wise man's 'death with one's will', which in Jain practice is the vow of sallekhana kept to the end (5.31–32), and sets it against the fool's frightened death.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says no one can blame those who die keeping the vow they made, and Jainism likewise honours the one who keeps his vow until death as having died the best death.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.2–3 (cf. 5.31–32) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: During the siege of Anandpur some forty Sikhs signed a disclaimer (bedava) renouncing Guru Gobind Singh and went home. Shamed by Mai Bhago, they returned and died fighting the pursuing Mughal force at Khidrana on 29 December 1705. According to tradition, the Guru tore up the disclaimer at the request of the dying Mahan Singh and blessed them as the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated Ones; Khidrana became Muktsar.
sikhism.explanation: Their death in faithful battle wiped out their earlier failure, and they are remembered in the daily Ardas.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks who could blame those who die keeping their vow, even if the vow was not fulfilled; the Chali Mukte had broken faith, yet by dying for the Guru they were freed of all blame.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Chali Mukte' (paraphrase); the torn bedava follows Sikh tradition

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Thermopylae Leonidas and his Spartans hold the pass to the last; their epitaph, attributed to Simonides, tells the passer-by to report to Sparta that they lie there obedient to its laws.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus records the stand and its epitaph as the model of keeping faith with one’s charge to the end.
greek_mythology.tie_back: No one reproaches the Spartans for losing the pass; like the Kural’s warriors, their faithful death is their glory.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Crito, Socrates refuses his friend’s plan of escape, arguing that he must keep his agreement with the laws of Athens even though it means his death.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates holds that breaking a just agreement to save one’s life would be a greater wrong than dying.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural’s warrior, Socrates dies rather than break faith, and history does not count it his failure.

real_life_example.event_title: Leonidas and his Spartans remain at Thermopylae
real_life_example.event: When a Persian force found a mountain path around the Greek position at the pass of Thermopylae, most of the allied Greek army left. The Spartan king Leonidas and his 300 Spartans stayed to hold the pass, together with contingents including some 700 Thespians, and were killed. Herodotus, the main source, reports that Leonidas thought it unfitting for the Spartans to desert the post they had been sent to hold, though he presents some details as hearsay.
real_life_example.explanation: Thermopylae was a military defeat, yet the defenders who died holding their post became one of history's lasting symbols of honour.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks who could blame those who die keeping the vow they made, and no one has ever reproached Leonidas's men for losing a battle they died to keep faith with.

tamil:
புரந்தார்கண் நீர்மல்கச் சாகிற்பின் சாக்காடு
இரந்துகோள் தக்கது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Purandhaarkan neermalgach chaagirpin saakkaadu
Irandhukol thakkadhu udaiththu.
meaning: If a soldier can die in a way that brings tears to the eyes of the king who cared for him, that death is worth begging for.
elementary: When someone gives everything to protect others, the people who loved and led them are deeply moved and never forget them. The verse says the greatest honour is to be so loyal and good that your leader is moved to tears for you.
university: Purandhaar are “those who nurtured or protected” the warrior, chiefly the king who maintained him; the condition is that their kan (eyes) neer malga, brim with tears; such a saakkaadu (death) has a worth that makes it irandhu kol thakkadhu, fit to be obtained even by begging (iravu, the act the Kural elsewhere treats as shameful). The paradox is deliberate: Valluvar, who devotes chapters 106-107 to the shame of begging, says this one thing is worth begging for. The couplet closes the chapter on the bond between ruler and soldier rather than on slaughter: the measure of the death is the grief of the one who knew its worth. Solomon Pappaiah renders the king’s eyes as those that weigh the heroes’ deeds; the other commentators take the tears literally.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Pārtha, happy are the kṣatriyas to whom such fighting opportunities come unsought, opening for them the doors of the heavenly planets.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a righteous battle as a rare opening to heaven for a warrior.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats an honourable death as a prize worth seeking, though it measures the honour by the king’s tears rather than by heaven.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.32 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus wept. Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!”
christianity.explanation: At the tomb of his friend Lazarus, Jesus weeps, and onlookers see in his tears the depth of his love.
christianity.tie_back: The tears of the leader as a sign of how much the departed was valued is the heart of the Kural’s image.

islam.quote_or_event: “Zaid took over the flag and was martyred. Then it was taken by Jafar who was martyred as well. Then `Abdullah bin Rawaha took the flag but he too was martyred and at that time the eyes of Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) were full of tears.”
islam.explanation: Announcing the deaths of three commanders at the battle of Mu’ta, the Prophet wept for them.
islam.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s scene: the leader’s eyes filling with tears for faithful fighters who fell.

judaism.quote_or_event: “How have the mighty fallen In the thick of battle—Jonathan, slain on your heights! I grieve for you, My brother Jonathan, You were most dear to me.”
judaism.explanation: David laments Saul and Jonathan, who died fighting the Philistines on Mount Gilboa.
judaism.tie_back: David’s lament is the grief of a future king for warriors he loved, the very tears the Kural says make such a death precious.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Asked whether warriors slain in battle are reborn among the devas, the Buddha at last answers that a warrior’s mind in battle is set on others’ destruction, so such a death leads to a woeful rebirth, not heaven; the warrior-headman weeps at having been misled.
buddhism.explanation: The Yodhajiva Sutta directly rejects the ancient warrior teaching that death in battle is a path to heaven.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the sharpest divergence from the Kural: the death the Kural calls worth begging for, the Buddha calls a grave danger.
buddhism.source: Yodhajiva Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 42.3 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu; paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A wise man having weighed (both kinds of death) and chosen the better one (taught in) the Law of Compassion, will become calm through patience, with an undisturbed mind (at the time of death).”
jainism.explanation: The wise man deliberately chooses the right kind of death and meets it calmly.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls a hero's death that brings tears to his king's eyes worth begging for, and the Jain text also treats a good death as something to be sought and chosen, though it measures that death by inner calm and compassion rather than by a patron's grief.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The death of brave heroes is blessed, if it is approved by God.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Alahanian (dirges), Guru Nanak says death need not be called bad, and that the hero's death is worthy when it is accepted in God's court.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a death that brings tears to the eyes of the king who cared for the warrior is worth begging for; Guru Nanak likewise honours the hero's death, measuring its worth by the approval of the true Master.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 579, Raag Vadhans, Alahanian, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Achilles learns that Patroclus has fallen, he pours dust on his head and weeps, and later leads the Myrmidons in mourning and holds funeral games in his honour.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad gives some of its most moving scenes to a commander’s grief for his fallen companion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Patroclus’ death is honoured by the tears of the leader who loved him, as the Kural envisions.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Funeral Oration, Pericles honours the Athenian war dead, saying that their memory lives on in the hearts of others and urging the living to imitate them.
philosophy.explanation: Thucydides presents public mourning as the city’s way of declaring what the fallen were worth.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural measures an honourable death by the grief of the one who sustained the warrior; Pericles measures it by the city’s remembrance.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.35-46 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Lincoln weeps for Colonel Elmer Ellsworth
real_life_example.place: Alexandria, Virginia, and the White House, Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: Colonel Elmer Ellsworth, a young officer and close friend of President Abraham Lincoln, was shot and killed in Alexandria, Virginia, after removing a Confederate flag from the roof of the Marshall House inn, becoming one of the first Union officers to die in the Civil War. Lincoln wept at the news. At his order Ellsworth's body lay in state in the East Room of the White House, where both the President and Mary Lincoln wept during the funeral.
real_life_example.explanation: The death of one young officer moved the nation's leader to open grief and made Ellsworth a national symbol in the war's first weeks.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a warrior's death is worth begging for if it brings tears to the eyes of the leader who cared for him, and Ellsworth's death drew exactly such tears from Lincoln.

tamil:
செயற்கரிய யாவுள நட்பின் அதுபோல்
வினைக்கரிய யாவுள காப்பு.
transliteration:
Seyarkariya yaavula natpin adhupol
vinaikkariya yaavula kaappu.
meaning: What is as hard to gain as friendship? And once you have it, what protection is as hard for any enemy to break?
elementary: Making a real friend is like growing a tree from a seed: it takes a long time and lots of care. But once the tree is big, it gives you shade that no storm can easily take away. A true friend is both the hardest thing to grow and the best shelter to have.
university: The chapter opens the Natpiyal (நட்பியல், section on friendship, chapters 79-95) of the Porutpal, where friendship is treated not only as a private good but as one of the supports of a king and of any householder. The couplet is built on two parallel rhetorical questions: seyaRku ariya (செயற்கரிய, hard to make or acquire) and vinaikku ariya kaappu (வினைக்கரிய காப்பு, a guard hard for hostile action to breach). Parimelazhagar reads the second line as ‘what guard is so hard for enemies’ efforts to overcome’, which is why Pope renders it ‘What so sure defence ’gainst all that foe can do?’; Mu. Varadarasanar instead takes vinai as one’s own undertakings, so that friendship is the rare protection for one’s work, and Solomon Pappaiah combines the two senses. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Kishkindha book of the Ramayana, Rama and the exiled monkey-king Sugriva, both having lost kingdom and wife, swear friendship by walking around a sacred fire, each pledging to treat the other’s joys and sorrows as his own.
hinduism.explanation: The pact is formal and costly: Rama must defeat Vali and Sugriva must later marshal the whole monkey army to find Sita.
hinduism.tie_back: The alliance shows the Kural’s two points together: such a friendship is hard to make, and once made it becomes each ally’s strongest defence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says friendship has to be earned by being friendly, and that the best friend holds on more tightly than family.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a true friend as something won with effort and then as an unusually firm support.

islam.quote_or_event: “The believers, both men and women, are guardians of one another.”
islam.explanation: The verse describes the faithful as awliya, protecting allies who stand guard over each other’s welfare.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s word kaappu, guard, is close to the Qur’anic idea of believers as each other’s protectors.
islam.source: Qur’an 9:71 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “A faithful friend is a firm friend; And he that findeth him hath found a treasure. There is no exchange for a faithful friend; Nor price that can be weighed for his goodness.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira calls a faithful friend a treasure, something found rarely and worth more than any price.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts treat a true friend as a rare acquisition and a firm protection once found.
judaism.source: Ben Sira (Ecclesiasticus) 6:14-15 (The Wisdom of Ben Sira, Cambridge, 1899)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie is actually the whole of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: Ananda suggests good friendship is half the spiritual life, and the Buddha corrects him: it is the whole of it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha, like Valluvar, ranks friendship as the hardest-won and most valuable support a person can have.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I am without a protector, O great king; there is nobody to protect me, I know no friend nor any one to have sympathy with me.” … “My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
jainism.explanation: The young monk Anâthi tells King Śreṇika that no friend or kinsman could shield him from suffering, and that in the end only one's own conduct acts as friend or enemy.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls friendship the rarest gain and the surest guard against enemies, while Jainism holds that the last line of defence is the self, which becomes its own friend by acting well.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.9 and 20.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You took pity on me, and blessed me with Your Mercy, and I have met the True Guru, my Friend.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan's closing salok calls the True Guru a friend (sajjan), and says such a friend is met only through God's mercy, not won by one's own merit.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what is as hard to win as friendship; Guru Arjan says the truest friend is so hard to win that he comes only by grace.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahalla 5, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Heracles fought the Hydra, every head he struck off grew back, until his nephew and companion Iolaus seared each stump with fire so that the heads could not regrow.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles could not finish the labour alone; his companion’s help made the impossible task possible.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Iolaus is the Kural’s ‘guard hard to break’: the friend whose help turns back what no single effort can.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “You might just as well take the sun out of the sky as friendship from life; for the immortal gods have given us nothing better or more delightful.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius argues that nothing the gods have given is better than friendship, so taking it from life would be like taking the sun from the sky.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero answers the Kural’s question the same way: nothing is rarer or more precious than friendship.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 13 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: The friendship of the Marquis de Lafayette and George Washington
real_life_example.event: In 1777 the nineteen-year-old Marquis de Lafayette defied King Louis XVI's order to remain in France, sailed to America to join the cause of independence and was made a major general by Congress. Wounded at the Battle of Brandywine in September 1777, he was treated by George Washington's own surgeon, and from then on the two men developed a bond that has been described as more like that of father and son than of commander and officer. Lafayette later returned to France to seek more support for the Americans and, in 1781, harried Cornwallis's army in Virginia before the allied victory at Yorktown.
real_life_example.explanation: A friendship formed in wartime became one of the Revolution's great assets, binding the American commander to a French nobleman who worked to win his own country's help for the cause.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what is as hard to win as friendship and what guards as surely against an enemy's efforts; Lafayette's rare loyalty became a real defence for Washington's cause.

tamil:
நிறைநீர நீரவர் கேண்மை பிறைமதிப்
பின்னீர பேதையார் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Niraineera neeravar kenmai piraimadhip
pinneera pedhaiyaar natpu.
meaning: Friendship with good people grows like the moon getting bigger each night. Friendship with fools shrinks like the moon after it is full.
elementary: Think of the moon. Some nights it starts as a thin smile and gets bigger and brighter every night. Other times it starts big and round and shrinks a little every night. Good friends are like the growing moon: each week you know them, the friendship gets fuller. Silly friends are like the shrinking moon: exciting at first, then less and less.
university: The couplet is one of the Kural’s best-known lunar similes. Niraineera (நிறைநீர) means ‘of the nature of filling up’, that is, the waxing crescent (piRai, பிறை) that grows to fullness; piRaimadhip pinneera (பிறைமதிப் பின்னீர) means ‘of the nature of the moon after fullness’, the waning phase. Neeravar (நீரவர்) are ‘people of good nature’ (from நீர்மை, quality), and Parimelazhagar glosses them as the wise and good, set against pēdhaiyār (பேதையார், fools). Kēṇmai and natpu are near-synonyms for friendship, used for variety. Parimelazhagar notes that the first kind of friendship starts small and grows by the day, while the second starts at its fullest and then declines. The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A widely quoted verse of Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka compares the friendship of the wicked to the morning shadow, long at first and shrinking as the day goes on, and the friendship of the good to the afternoon shadow, short at first and lengthening steadily.
hinduism.explanation: Bhartrhari uses the changing length of a shadow to show that bad friendships start large and fade while good ones start small and grow.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the same image as the Kural’s, with the shadow in place of the moon.
hinduism.source: Bhartrhari, Nitishataka (verse on the two shadows; numbering varies by edition)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb defines a friend by constancy: love that does not rise and fall with circumstances.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s waxing friendship of the worthy is the same constant, ever-growing love the proverb praises.

islam.quote_or_event: “Close friends will be enemies to one another on that Day, except the righteous.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement, friendships not rooted in righteousness turn into enmity, while those of the God-conscious endure.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s waning moon, friendships built on folly decline into nothing, while those of the good last.
islam.source: Qur’an 43:67 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “For there is a friend that is for a season; And that will not (?) continue in the day of affliction.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira warns that some friendships last only for a season and then disappear when trouble comes.
judaism.tie_back: The ‘friend for a season’ is the Kural’s waning-moon friendship of fools.
judaism.source: Ben Sira 6:8 (The Wisdom of Ben Sira, Cambridge, 1899)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever through desire, hate or fear, Or ignorance should transgress the Dhamma, All his glory fades away Like the moon during the waning half. Whoever through desire, hate or fear, Or ignorance never transgresses the Dhamma, All his glory ever increases Like the moon during the waxing half.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Sigala that the wrongdoer’s glory wanes like the moon while the good man’s grows like it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha uses the same waxing and waning moon to separate the wise from the foolish, and the same sutta later uses it of those who keep low company.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Friendship with the wise, whose intelligence divines our thoughts, is like eating a sugar-cane from the top (as its sweetness increases more and more); connexion with persons without sweetness of disposition is like eating it from the opposite end (the flavour decreasing by degrees).”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil quatrain contrasts a friendship with the wise, which grows sweeter over time, with one with ill-natured people, which loses its sweetness bit by bit.
jainism.tie_back: This is the same contrast the Kural draws between the waxing and waning moon: friendship with the good keeps growing, and friendship with fools keeps shrinking.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 1 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Friendship with a fool, and love with a pompous person, are like lines drawn in water, leaving no trace or mark.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad's saloks in Asa di Vaar warn that friendship with a fool never works out right and leaves nothing lasting behind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says friendship with fools wanes like the moon after the full; Guru Angad says it vanishes like a line drawn in water.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pirithous raided Theseus’ cattle to test him; when the two met armed, each so admired the other that they swore friendship instead of fighting, and their bond grew into one of the most famous in myth.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their friendship began with almost nothing, a near-fight, and grew over a lifetime of shared adventures.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the crescent that becomes full: a small beginning that keeps growing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “they cannot know each other till they have ‘eaten salt together’ … for a wish for friendship may arise quickly, but friendship does not.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says true friendship needs time and shared experience, unlike the quick wish to be friends.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s slow-growing friendship of the good is the Kural’s waxing crescent.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Einstein and Michele Besso: from sounding board to collaborator
real_life_example.event: Albert Einstein's 1905 paper on special relativity famously acknowledged the help of his friend and colleague Michele Besso, who served as a sounding board for his ideas. In the following years the friendship grew into active collaboration: between June 1913 and early 1914 the two men worked together on a 54-page manuscript of calculations on the motion of Mercury's perihelion, written partly in Einstein's hand and partly in Besso's. In the same period Besso also acted as a go-between in Einstein's difficult family affairs.
real_life_example.explanation: Their relationship shows a friendship that kept deepening over the years, from conversation partner to working collaborator and family confidant.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares friendship with the worthy to the crescent moon that grows fuller night by night, and Besso's friendship with Einstein grew steadily in depth.

tamil:
நவில்தொறும் நூல்நயம் போலும் பயில்தொறும்
பண்புடை யாளர் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Navildhorum noolnayam polum payildhorum
panpudai yaalar thodarpu.
meaning: Friendship with good people is like a great book. The more often you go back to it, the more you enjoy it.
elementary: Do you have a favourite book you have read many times? Each time, you notice something new and like it even more. Being friends with a kind, good person is like that book: every time you spend time together, the friendship gets sweeter.
university: The couplet sets two verbs of repetition side by side: navil-thoRum (நவில்தொறும், ‘each time it is studied or recited’) and payil-thoRum (பயில்தொறும், ‘each time one associates’). Nūl-nayam (நூல்நயம்) is the excellence or beauty of a learned text, which reveals new depths with every reading; paṇbudaiyāḷar (பண்புடையாளர்) are people of refined character, and thodarpu (தொடர்பு) is their companionship. Parimelazhagar’s point is that good company, unlike pleasures that tire with use, grows sweeter with each meeting, just as a good book does. The comparison fits the Kural’s own high regard for study (chapters 40-42). ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the same text; பண்புடை யாளர் is a metrical split of பண்புடையாளர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The thoughts of My pure devotees dwell in Me, their lives are fully devoted to My service, and they derive great satisfaction and bliss from always enlightening one another and conversing about Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes devotees who find lasting joy in teaching one another and talking together about the divine.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the company of the good is a kind of shared study that keeps giving more delight.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 10.9 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man’s friend by hearty counsel.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb compares a friend’s sincere counsel to perfume that gladdens the heart.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say the company of a good friend keeps bringing fresh sweetness.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of a good pious companion and an evil one is that of a person carrying musk and another blowing a pair of bellows. The one who is carrying musk will either give you some perfume as a present, or you will buy some from him, or you will get a good smell from him”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a good companion to a musk-seller: you always come away with something good, even if only the fragrance.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s good book, every meeting with a good companion leaves you richer.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Honi the Circle-Drawer woke after seventy years, the scholars in the study hall did not believe who he was and gave him no respect, so he prayed for death; Rava explains the episode by the folk saying that it is either friendship or death.
judaism.explanation: For the rabbis, the companionship of fellow learners was so necessary that a scholar without it was better off dead.
judaism.tie_back: The Talmud and the Kural both picture the best friendship as the company of the learned, which feeds the mind as study does.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not associate with evil companions; do not seek the fellowship of the vile. Associate with the good friends; seek the fellowship of noble men.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada tells the reader to choose the company of the noble and avoid the vile.
buddhism.tie_back: Its ‘noble men’ are the Kural’s paṇbudaiyāḷar, whose company is worth seeking out.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The enjoyment of the friendship of men of acute understanding is desirable as the joys of heaven.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar compares the company of discerning friends to heavenly happiness, and in the next sentence calls the company of the unlearned a hell.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the friendship of people of good character gets sweeter each time, like a fine book; the Naladiyar likewise counts the company of the wise among life's highest delights and ties it to learning.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 3 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! The sandalwood tree is good, even though it is surrounded by weeds. Those who dwell near the sandalwood tree, become just like the sandalwood tree.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir uses the sandalwood tree to show how the company of the good gradually passes on its fragrance to those who keep near it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the company of people of fine character gives more delight the longer one keeps it, like a great book; Kabir says those who stay close to the good slowly take on their fragrance.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1365, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 11) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Agamemnon’s envoys reach Achilles’ tent, they find him playing the lyre and singing the deeds of heroes, with Patroclus sitting opposite in silence, waiting for him to finish.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows two friends whose quiet, everyday companionship is pleasure enough.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the long, ever-deepening companionship of two noble friends that the Kural compares to rereading a good book.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Perfect friendship is the friendship of men who are good, and alike in virtue; for these wish well alike to each other qua good, and they are good themselves.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle ranks above all other kinds the friendship between good people who love each other for their character.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s perfect friends are the Kural’s people of fine character, whose bond keeps growing because it rests on lasting virtue.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Inklings read their work aloud in Oxford
real_life_example.event: From about 1933, C. S. Lewis, J. R. R. Tolkien and a circle of Oxford friends met weekly, usually on Thursday evenings in Lewis's rooms at Magdalen College, to read aloud and criticise one another's writing in progress. The group heard and discussed early drafts of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings and Lewis's The Great Divorce, and its members also gathered at the Eagle and Child pub. The Thursday meetings continued until the end of the 1940s.
real_life_example.explanation: Out of these repeated meetings came both lasting friendships and some of the most widely read books of the twentieth century.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar says friendship with people of fine character is like a great book that gives more delight each time one returns to it, and for the Inklings friendship and the rereading of books were the same weekly pleasure.

tamil:
நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல் மிகுதிக்கண்
மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு.
transliteration:
Nagudhar poruttandru nattal migudhikkan
merchendru idiththar poruttu.
meaning: We make friends not just to laugh together, but so that when a friend goes the wrong way, we can step in first and correct them.
elementary: Imagine your friend is about to cross the road without looking. A pretend friend just keeps laughing with them. A real friend grabs their arm and says, ‘Stop! That’s dangerous!’ even if it makes them a bit cross. Friends are for fun, but most of all they are for stopping each other from doing something wrong.
university: This is the chapter’s key statement on the moral purpose of friendship. Nagudhal (நகுதல்) is laughing or merriment; nattal (நட்டல்) is the act of befriending; migudhi (மிகுதி) means excess, that is, a friend’s overstepping or wrongdoing; mēRsenRu (மேற்சென்று) means ‘going ahead, taking the initiative’; and iditthal (இடித்தல், literally ‘striking’) is the classical term for sharp rebuke, related to iḍipparai (இடிப்பார், the rebuking counsellor) in kural 448. Parimelazhagar stresses that the friend must rebuke before the fault grows, without waiting to be asked. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print மேற்செனறு, which looks like a shared typing error; the standard reading மேற்சென்று (as in Mu. Varadarasanar’s ‘முற்பட்டுச் சென்று’ gloss) is given here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “They are abundant, O king, that can always speak agreeable words. The speaker, however, is rare, as also the hearer, of words that are disagreeable but medicinal.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells Dhritarashtra that flatterers are everywhere, but rare is the one who will speak, or listen to, unwelcome words that heal.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura is the friend the Kural describes, who rebukes for the other’s good rather than merely pleasing him.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says a friend’s painful honesty can be trusted, while an enemy’s show of affection cannot.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: a friend is there to strike when needed, not to keep you laughing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or he is an oppressed one. People asked, ‘O Allah’s Messenger! It is all right to help him if he is oppressed, but how should we help him if he is an oppressor?’ The Prophet said, ‘By preventing him from oppressing others.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that helping a brother who does wrong means stopping him.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, true loyalty means stepping in to stop a friend when he goes too far.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You shall not hate your kinsfolk in your heart. Reprove your kindred but incur no guilt on their account.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands open rebuke instead of silent resentment, so that you do not share in another’s wrongdoing.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes rebuke a duty of love rather than a breach of it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure. It is always better, and never worse, to cultivate such an association.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada tells us to value the person who points out our faults as we would a guide to buried treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the rebuking friend of the Kural, and the advice to keep such friends close.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the virtuous Kitra, for old friendship's sake, loved the king who was attached to sensual pleasures, and as he had at heart his welfare, he spoke to him the following words”
jainism.explanation: The monk Kitra, who had been King Brahmadatta's companion through several past births, meets him again and, out of that old friendship, bluntly warns him that his pleasures lead to suffering and urges him to give them up.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says friendship exists to step forward and rebuke a friend who goes too far, and Kitra does exactly that, speaking against his friend's excess because he cares about his welfare.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.15 (Kitra and Sambhûta; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, Guru Nanak stayed at the inn of Sajjan at Tulamba, a man who posed as pious but robbed his guests. Instead of flattering his host, the Guru sang a hymn exposing hollow shininess (now in the Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729); Sajjan confessed, gave away his ill-gotten goods and turned his house into a dharamsala.
sikhism.explanation: The story shows the Guru as a guest who took the initiative to confront a host's wrongdoing, and so saved him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says friendship exists so that we can step in first and rebuke a friend who goes too far; Guru Nanak's hymn to Sajjan was just such a timely rebuke that turned him back.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Sajjan, Shaikh' and 'Tulamba' (paraphrase of the Janamsakhi tradition)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the moment Orestes falters before killing his mother, he turns to his silent friend Pylades and asks what to do; Pylades, speaking for the only time in the play, reminds him of Apollo’s command and tells him to hold all men his enemies rather than the gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pylades says nothing through the whole play until his friend wavers, and then speaks firmly to hold him to his duty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Pylades steps forward at the crucial moment, as the Kural says a friend should.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If we remonstrate, it should be without bitterness; if we reprove, there should be no word of insult. … ‘There are people who owe more to bitter enemies than to apparently pleasant friends: the former often speak the truth, the latter never.’”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius insists that friends must reprove one another, gently but honestly, and quotes Cato on the danger of merely pleasant friends.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero and the Kural agree that a friendship that only pleases has failed its purpose.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 24 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Ezra Pound urges T. S. Eliot to cut The Waste Land
real_life_example.event: Before The Waste Land was published in 1922, T. S. Eliot submitted his drafts to his friend and fellow poet Ezra Pound, who had championed Eliot's work since they met in London in 1914. Pound urged Eliot to cut several long passages, among them a long section in heroic couplets imitating Pope, and Eliot accepted much of his advice, though not all of it. The drafts with Pound's markings were later found among the papers of the New York lawyer John Quinn and published in facsimile in 1971.
real_life_example.explanation: Pound's blunt criticism is widely credited with shaping a sprawling draft into one of the most influential poems of the twentieth century.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says friends are not only for laughing together but for stepping in first to rebuke one another when one goes too far, and Pound did exactly this, cutting away his friend's excesses.

tamil:
புணர்ச்சி பழகுதல் வேண்டா உணர்ச்சிதான்
நட்பாங் கிழமை தரும்.
transliteration:
Punarchchi pazhagudhal vendaa unarchchidhaan
natpaang kizhamai tharum.
meaning: Friendship does not need you to meet often or know each other for long. Thinking and feeling alike is enough to make true friends.
elementary: Sometimes you meet a pen pal or a cousin who lives far away, and even though you rarely see each other, you just ‘get’ each other. You like the same things and feel the same way. Valluvar says that feeling of understanding is what really makes a friend, not how many times you hang out.
university: PuNarchchi (புணர்ச்சி) here means being together or meeting, and pazhaguthal (பழகுதல்) long familiarity; both are declared unnecessary (vēṇdā). What creates friendship is uNarchchi (உணர்ச்சி), which Parimelazhagar glosses as like-mindedness, a mutual understanding of each other’s feelings; this alone gives natpu-ām kizhamai (நட்பாங் கிழமை), the intimate right or claim that belongs to friendship. Commentators traditionally cite the Sangam friendship of the Chola king Kōpperuñcōḻaṉ and the poet Pisirāndaiyār, who were said to have loved each other for years without meeting, and of whom the poet joined the king in his ritual fast unto death (Puranaṉūru 215-217). The text is the same on both web sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Thinking of You as my friend, I have rashly addressed You ‘O Kṛṣṇa,’ ‘O Yādava,’ ‘O my friend,’ not knowing Your glories. … I have dishonored You many times, jesting as we relaxed, lay on the same bed, or sat or ate together”
hinduism.explanation: After seeing Krishna’s cosmic form, Arjuna realises that years of eating, resting and joking together had not shown him who his friend really was.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna learns the Kural’s lesson the other way round: closeness and familiarity alone are not the same as true understanding.
