hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 11.41-42 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.”
christianity.explanation: Jonathan’s friendship with David begins at their first meeting, as soon as David finishes speaking to Saul.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the bond comes from an immediate meeting of souls, not from long acquaintance.

islam.quote_or_event: “Souls are like recruited troops: Those who are like qualities are inclined to each other, but those who have dissimilar qualities, differ.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that souls of a like nature are drawn together from the start, and souls of unlike nature drift apart.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s uNarchchi: an inner kinship of nature that creates friendship before any long acquaintance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For as he is, so is his neighbour; And as his name, so are his works.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira observes that a person’s companion reflects his own character.
judaism.tie_back: The verse rests on the same idea as the Kural, that like natures find each other.
judaism.source: Ben Sira 6:17 (The Wisdom of Ben Sira, Cambridge, 1899)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who sympathises be understood as a warm-hearted friend: (i) he does not rejoice in one’s misfortune, (ii) he rejoices in one’s prosperity, (iii) he restrains others speaking ill of oneself, (iv) he praises those who speak well of oneself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines one kind of true friend by shared feeling: he is glad at your good fortune and grieved at your bad.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s uNarchchi, a sameness of feeling, given as the mark of a real friend.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men cleave not to those to whom their hearts cleave not, within a short space of time; but will the friendship which cherishes the memory of those who are intertwined with one's heart be abandoned, though they are absent from us for a long time?”
jainism.explanation: The stanza says friendship rests on hearts bound together, not on time spent together, and that it lasts through long absence.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says friendship needs neither frequent meetings nor long acquaintance, only a shared understanding of heart, and the Naladiyar likewise grounds friendship in that bond and not in physical presence.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Once united with Him, they will not be separated again, if they are truly united.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says that a union which is real does not come apart, because it rests on inner oneness rather than outward closeness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says friendship needs no constant meetings, only a shared understanding of heart; Guru Nanak likewise makes true union depend on inner oneness, which separation cannot undo.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Meeting on the battlefield as enemies, Glaucus and Diomedes discover that their grandfathers were guest-friends; though they have never met, they refuse to fight, clasp hands, and exchange armour.
greek_mythology.explanation: A bond they had never lived out, but which both recognise, turns enemies into friends on the spot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the scene shows a friendship that needs no previous meetings, only mutual recognition.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In the face of a true friend a man sees as it were a second self. So that where his friend is he is”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius says a true friend is another self, so that wherever the friend is, one is present too.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero, like the Kural, makes friendship a matter of inner identity that distance cannot affect.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 7 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Du Fu's lasting devotion to Li Bai after a brief companionship
real_life_example.event: In 744 the young poet Du Fu met the older and already celebrated Li Bai, probably in Luoyang, and the two travelled together in Henan and, in 745, in Shandong before parting at the end of that year. The standard chronology of Du Fu's life records no later meeting between them. Du Fu went on to write many poems to or about Li Bai, including one describing how his absent friend came to him in a dream.
real_life_example.explanation: Their friendship rested less on time spent together than on a deep mutual understanding of poetry and feeling, which Du Fu kept alive in verse for years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says friendship needs neither frequent meetings nor long acquaintance, since shared feeling alone gives the full claim of friendship, and Du Fu's long remembrance of a companion of barely two years shows this.

tamil:
முகநக நட்பது நட்பன்று நெஞ்சத்து
அகநக நட்பது நட்பு.
transliteration:
Muganaga natpadhu natpandru nenjaththu
aganaga natpadhu natpu.
meaning: Friendship that only makes the face smile is not real friendship. Real friendship makes the heart smile inside.
elementary: Some people smile at you only on the outside, like a mask, but inside they don’t really care. A true friend is happy all the way inside when they see you, even if they don’t make a big show of it. Real friendship is a smile in the heart, not just on the face.
university: The couplet turns on a pair of near-rhyming compounds: muga-naga (முகநக, ‘so that the face smiles’) and aga-naga (அகநக, ‘so that the inside smiles’), with nenjatthu (நெஞ்சத்து, ‘in the heart’) making the inner sense explicit. Naga (நக) means to laugh, smile or blossom, so both commentators and translators often render it as the face or heart ‘blooming’. Parimelazhagar takes the first kind of friendship to be outward courtesy only, and the second to be friendship rooted in love (anbu). The word natpu appears four times in seven words, which gives the verse its proverbial ring. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Chanakya Niti advises avoiding the person who speaks sweetly to your face but works to ruin you behind your back, comparing him to a pot of poison with a layer of milk on top.
hinduism.explanation: The sweet surface hides a poisonous inside, just as a pleasant face can hide ill will.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s face-only friend, whose smile does not reach the heart.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks that love be genuine, with no pretence behind it.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s love ‘without dissimulation’ is the Kural’s smile of the heart rather than of the face.

islam.quote_or_event: “The worst people in the Sight of Allah on the Day of Resurrection will be the double faced people who appear to some people with one face and to other people with another face.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet condemns the two-faced person who shows a different face to different people.
islam.tie_back: Both texts warn against friendship worn on the face but absent from the heart.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many a friend doth a sweet palate make; And gracious lips that greet (?) with peace. Be they that are at peace with thee many; But he that hath thy secret one of a thousand.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira says pleasant speech wins many friends, but the one you can trust with your heart is one in a thousand.
judaism.tie_back: Friends of the lips are many, friends of the heart are rare: the same contrast as the Kural’s face and heart.
judaism.source: Ben Sira 6:5-6 (The Wisdom of Ben Sira, Cambridge, 1899)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is a bottle friend; one says, ‘friend, friend’ only to one’s face; one is a friend and an associate only when it is advantageous.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists false friends, including the one whose friendship exists only in what he says to your face.
buddhism.tie_back: The ‘friend, friend’ only to one’s face is exactly the Kural’s face-smiling friendship that is no friendship.

jainism.quote_or_event: “It is better to be without the love of those who are without sincerity.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar holds that affection that is not sincere is worth less than no affection at all.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural rejects friendship that only makes the face smile and accepts only the kind that gladdens the heart, and the Naladiyar likewise rejects love that lacks inner sincerity.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 9 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone are true, whose love for God is deep and heart-felt. Those who have one thing in their heart, and something else in their mouth, are judged to be false.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose hymns are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, sets heart-felt love against love that lives only on the lips.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says friendship that only makes the face smile is not friendship, while friendship that makes the heart smile is; Farid likewise counts true only the love that is in the heart, not merely on the lips.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the two travellers and the bear, one man scrambles up a tree and leaves his companion to lie still on the ground; when the bear has gone, the one who was left says the bear whispered to him never to travel with a friend who deserts you at the first sign of danger.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable exposes a friendship that was pleasant on the road but empty when it was tested.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The deserter’s friendship was only on the face, never in the heart.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, Fables (trans. G. F. Townsend), ‘The Bear and the Two Travelers’

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In everything false pretence is bad, for it suspends and vitiates our power of discerning the truth. But to nothing it is so hostile as to friendship; for it destroys that frankness without which friendship is an empty name.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius argues that pretence destroys friendship because it takes away the openness that friendship depends on.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s ‘empty name’ is the Kural’s face-only friendship that is not friendship at all.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 25 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Montaigne's friendship with Etienne de La Boetie
real_life_example.event: Around 1559 Michel de Montaigne, then a member of the Parlement of Bordeaux, met Etienne de La Boetie, who also worked for the Parlement, and the two formed a deep friendship that lasted until La Boetie's death at the age of thirty-two in August 1563. Montaigne later oversaw the publication of several of his friend's works. In his essay Of Friendship he set this bond apart from ordinary friendships, which he called mere acquaintances, describing a friendship in which two souls are blended so completely that the seam joining them disappears.
real_life_example.explanation: Montaigne's essay made this friendship the classic European example of a bond rooted in the heart rather than in convenience or outward courtesy.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says friendship that only makes the face smile is not friendship, while friendship that makes the heart smile is, and Montaigne drew the same line between ordinary acquaintance and what he shared with La Boetie.

tamil:
அழிவி னவைநீக்கி ஆறுய்த்து அழிவின்கண்
அல்லல் உழப்பதாம் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Azhivi navainikki aaruyththu azhivinkan
allal uzhappadhaam natpu.
meaning: A friend stops you from doing what would ruin you, guides you onto the right path, and shares your pain when trouble comes anyway.
elementary: A real friend does three things. First, if you’re about to do something that will get you into big trouble, they stop you. Second, they help you find a better thing to do. Third, if something bad happens anyway, they don’t run away; they stay and feel sad with you. That’s what a friend is for.
university: The verse lists three duties in order: azhivinavai nīkki (அழிவினவை நீக்கி, ‘removing the things that lead to ruin’), āRu uytthu (ஆறுய்த்து, ‘sending him along the right way’, from āRu, path), and, if ruin still comes (azhivinkaN, அழிவின்கண்), allal uzhappathu (அல்லல் உழப்பது, ‘toiling in his distress alongside him’). Parimelazhagar takes the first two as prevention and correction, carrying on from the rebuke of kural 784, and the third as the friend’s readiness to share in misfortune he could not prevent. The printed line அழிவி னவைநீக்கி is a metrical split of அழிவினவை நீக்கி. Both web sources give the same text, and Pope’s ‘it weeps with him who weeps’ echoes Romans 12:15.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, when Arjuna throws down his bow in despair, Krishna, serving as his charioteer, talks him out of his paralysis, shows him the path of duty, and stays at his side through the whole war.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna turns Arjuna away from collapse, guides him with the teaching of the Gita, and shares the dangers of the battle with him.
hinduism.tie_back: Krishna carries out all three of the Kural’s duties: steering his friend from ruin, setting him on the right path, and standing with him in hardship.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to share both the joy and the sorrow of others.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s last duty, to share a friend’s grief, and Pope’s English couplet echoes it directly.

islam.quote_or_event: “While they both were in the cave, he reassured his companion, ‘Do not worry; Allah is certainly with us.’”
islam.explanation: During the flight from Mecca, the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid together in the cave of Thawr while their pursuers searched for them.
islam.tie_back: Abu Bakr chose to share the Prophet’s danger in the cave, just as the Kural says a friend shares distress.
islam.source: Qur’an 9:40 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: When Job’s three friends hear of his disasters, they travel to him, weep, tear their robes, and sit with him on the ground for seven days and nights without a word, seeing how great his suffering is.
judaism.explanation: Before their later arguments, Job’s friends simply come and share his grief in silence.
judaism.tie_back: Their silent week is the Kural’s third duty: suffering alongside a friend whose ruin could not be prevented.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he restrains one from doing evil, (ii) he encourages one to do good” … “in misfortune he does not forsake one”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists among the marks of true friends holding one back from evil, urging one toward good, and not deserting one in misfortune.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s three duties appear almost point for point in this list.

jainism.quote_or_event: When the newly ordained prince Meghakumāra, crushed by the burden of self-control, wavered and wanted to give up the monk's life, Mahāvīra stopped him by reminding him of his past birth as an elephant that held its foot in the air to spare a hare. Megha became steady in his vows again, repented and went on with his austerities.
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition presents the Jina as a guide who heads off a follower's fall at the moment of weakness and sets him back on the path.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's friend turns a companion away from ruin and guides him onto the right way, and Mahāvīra does the same for Megha, though the story has no counterpart to the Kural's third duty of sharing in a misfortune that could not be prevented.
jainism.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Parva 10 (Mahāvīracaritra), 'Part 7: Story of Meghakumāra' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org); the episode is first told in Jñātādharmakathā 1

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone are my friends, who travel along with me; and in that place, where the accounts are called for, they appear standing with me.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak's hymn (traditionally sung to Sajjan) defines true friends as those who stay with us right up to the moment of reckoning.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a friend shares our suffering when ruin comes; Guru Nanak's true friends still stand beside us when the account is called and judgement falls.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Orestes is captured in the land of the Taurians and only one of the two friends may go free, Pylades refuses to save himself and leave Orestes to die alone, saying he shared his voyage and will share his fate.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pylades has followed Orestes into exile and danger, and now insists on sharing even death with him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s friend who, when ruin comes, stays to suffer it together.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Such friendship enhances prosperity, and relieves adversity of its burden by halving and sharing it.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius says friendship doubles our good fortune and halves our misfortune by sharing it.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s ‘halving and sharing’ adversity is the Kural’s allal uzhappathu, carrying a friend’s pain with him.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 6 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Friedrich Engels supports Karl Marx for decades
real_life_example.place: Manchester and London, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Friedrich Engels, the son of a cotton manufacturer, first met Karl Marx in 1842 and renewed the contact in 1844. While Marx lived in London and wrote, Engels worked for many years in his family's firm in Manchester and sent him money, support that Smithsonian magazine describes as lasting nearly forty years and beginning even before Engels himself was well off. After Marx died in 1883, Engels devoted much of his remaining time to publishing his friend's unfinished work.
real_life_example.explanation: Engels kept his friend and his family afloat through long years of poverty and then preserved his friend's writings after his death.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says friendship keeps a friend from ruin, helps him along his path and shares his hardship when it comes, and Engels did all of this for Marx over four decades.

tamil:
உடுக்கை இழந்தவன் கைபோல ஆங்கே
இடுக்கண் களைவதாம் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Udukkai izhandhavan kaipola aange
idukkan kalaivadhaam natpu.
meaning: When a person’s clothes slip, the hand rushes to catch them. In the same way, a true friend rushes right away to end a friend’s trouble.
elementary: If your trousers started slipping in front of the whole class, your hand would grab them right away. You wouldn’t stop to think or wait to be asked; your hand just does it. A true friend helps you in trouble that fast and that naturally, as if they were your own hand.
university: This is one of the most quoted images in the Kural. Udukkai (உடுக்கை) is a garment and izhandhavan (இழந்தவன்) the one losing it, so the picture is of clothing slipping, which Solomon Pappaiah and others place ‘in front of many people’ (பலர் முன்னே) to bring out the urgency of shame. The key word is āngē (ஆங்கே, ‘there and then, at once’): the hand acts by reflex, without being asked and without thinking. Parimelazhagar notes that the hand acts before the mind decides, and so friendship should remove idukkaN (இடுக்கண், distress) before the friend has to ask. The image also implies that a friend is part of one’s own body. Both web sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Draupadi is dragged into the Kuru assembly and Duhshasana begins to strip off her garment, she calls on Krishna, and in the popular and later textual tradition her sari is miraculously and endlessly extended so that she cannot be stripped.
hinduism.explanation: Draupadi, who calls herself ‘the friend of Vasudeva’ in the same scene, is rescued at the very moment her garment is being pulled away.
hinduism.tie_back: The image is almost the same as the Kural’s, a garment slipping in public and instant help, with Krishna as the friend who acts at once.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Section LXVIII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher says two are better than one because, when one falls, the other is there to lift him up straight away.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s hand, the companion is right there to catch his fellow at the moment of falling.

islam.quote_or_event: “The similitude of believers in regard to mutual love, affection, fellow-feeling is that of one body; when any limb of it aches, the whole body aches, because of sleeplessness and fever.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares believers to one body that reacts as a whole when any part is hurt.
islam.tie_back: Both texts use the body’s instinctive response to describe how friends respond to each other’s pain without stopping to think.

judaism.quote_or_event: As soon as Abram hears that his kinsman Lot has been taken captive, he arms his 318 trained men, pursues the raiding kings through the night as far as Dan, and brings Lot back.
judaism.explanation: Abram acts the moment the news reaches him, without waiting or being asked.
judaism.tie_back: Abram’s instant rescue is the hand flying to the slipping garment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should a helpmate be understood as a warm-hearted friend: (i) he guards the heedless, (ii) he protects the wealth of the heedless, (iii) he becomes a refuge when you are in danger”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the true friend as one who protects you when you are off guard and becomes your refuge in danger.
buddhism.tie_back: Guarding the heedless is just what the hand does for the man who does not notice his garment slipping.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If I stretch not out my hand and deliver my whole soul without hesitation to my friend who is in distress, may I be cast into the hell where the wretch is punished who has violated the chaste wife of his friend, and may I be scoffed at throughout the far-famed earth!”
jainism.explanation: The speaker swears a solemn oath that he will reach out at once, without hesitating, to a friend in distress, and calls down the worst punishment on himself if he fails.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural pictures friendship as a hand that flies to catch a slipping garment, and the Naladiyar's friend likewise stretches out his hand without hesitation to relieve a friend's distress.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Great is His greatness, as He gives without being asked.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak praises God as the giver who meets our needs before we ask.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's friendship, like a hand catching a slipping garment, removes a friend's distress at once, without being asked; Guru Nanak praises the same unasked help in God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Heracles goes down to Hades, he finds his friend Theseus held fast to the Chair of Forgetfulness and, taking him by the hand, pulls him free and brings him back to the living.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles takes the chance to free his friend the moment he finds him trapped.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The rescuing hand of Heracles is the Kural’s hand reaching out to remove a friend’s distress.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods … Or how can prosperity be guarded and preserved without friends? The greater it is, the more exposed is it to risk.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle opens his discussion of friendship by saying no one would choose life without friends, since friends are what guard us in fortune and in danger.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle sees friends as the protection that keeps a life from coming apart, the role the hand plays in the Kural.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Joshua Speed offers Abraham Lincoln a place to sleep
real_life_example.event: On 15 April 1837 Abraham Lincoln, newly arrived in Springfield to practise law, walked into Joshua Speed's store and asked the price of bedding, but found he could not afford it and asked for credit. Speed, taken with the stranger, at once offered to share his own living quarters above the store, and Lincoln accepted on the spot. The two shared those quarters for several years and became close and lasting friends.
real_life_example.explanation: A moment of spontaneous generosity began one of the most important friendships of Lincoln's life, one that later helped him through a period of deep despair.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares friendship to the hand that flies to catch a slipping garment without being asked, and Speed solved a stranger's embarrassment immediately, before Lincoln could even finish asking for credit.

tamil:
நட்பிற்கு வீற்றிருக்கை யாதெனின் கொட்பின்றி
ஒல்லும்வாய் ஊன்றும் நிலை.
transliteration:
Natpirku veetrirukkai yaadhenin kotpindri
ollumvaai oondrum nilai.
meaning: Where does friendship sit like a king on a throne? In always being ready to hold up a friend in every way you can.
elementary: Think of a walking stick that an old person leans on. It doesn’t move around or give up; it’s always there to take their weight. Valluvar says the very best friendship is like that stick: steady, never changing its mind, and always ready to hold you up however it can.
university: VīRRirukkai (வீற்றிருக்கை) means a throne or seat of majesty, so the question is ‘where is friendship’s throne?’, that is, what is its highest state. The answer has three parts: kotpu inRi (கொட்பின்றி, ‘without kotpu’, a word meaning whirling or wavering, so ‘without change of heart’); ollum vāy (ஒல்லும்வாய், ‘wherever and however possible’); and ūnRum nilai (ஊன்றும் நிலை, ‘the state of propping up, supporting’, as a staff supports). Parimelazhagar explains ollumvāy as helping in every way available toward the friend’s virtue and wealth, and kotpinri as never wavering in mind, whatever the times. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss kotpinri as ‘always, without change’. Both web sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a father tolerates the impudence of his son, a friend the impertinence of a friend, or a husband the familiarity of his wife, please tolerate the wrongs I may have done You.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna asks Krishna for the patient, unwavering forbearance that a friend shows toward a friend.
hinduism.tie_back: The friend’s steady tolerance is the Kural’s kotpinri, a support that does not waver or change its mind.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 11.44 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus calls giving one’s life for one’s friends the greatest love.
christianity.tie_back: Laying down one’s life is the furthest limit of the Kural’s support ‘in every way one can’.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Emigrants arrived in Medina, the Prophet paired each with a Helper as a brother; the Helper Sa‘d ibn al-Rabi‘ offered to share half of all his property with ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf, who thanked him and asked only to be shown the market.
islam.explanation: The Helpers supported newly arrived strangers with everything they had, steadily and without being asked.
islam.tie_back: Sa‘d’s offer is the Kural’s ‘holding up in every way one can’, offered as a settled commitment.

judaism.quote_or_event: Though his father Saul is trying to kill David, Jonathan keeps faith with his friend, warns him of the danger, renews their covenant, and sends him away safely with the signal of the arrows.
judaism.explanation: Jonathan supports David at great cost to his own position as heir.
judaism.tie_back: Jonathan’s loyalty does not waver even under pressure from his own father, and he helps by every means he can.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who is the same in happiness and sorrow be understood as a warm-hearted friend: (i) he reveals his secrets, (ii) he conceals one’s own secrets, (iii) in misfortune he does not forsake one, (iv) his life even he sacrifices for one’s sake.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the friend who stays the same in good times and bad, even to the point of giving his life.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘The same in happiness and sorrow’ is the Kural’s kotpinri, friendship without wavering.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When affection continues affection, then is friendship preserved, like the flower on the stalk, which, being full-blown, closes not again. Those who resemble the lotus, which, having once blown, closes again its petals, know neither affection nor friendship.”
jainism.explanation: The stanza says true friendship stays constant like a flower that never closes once it opens, unlike the lotus that opens and closes again.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural places friendship's throne in steady support that never wavers, and the Naladiyar likewise makes constancy without wavering the test of genuine friendship.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 5 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My associates and companions have all deserted me; no one remains with me. Says Nanak, in this tragedy, the Lord alone is my Support.”
sikhism.explanation: In this salok attributed to Guru Tegh Bahadur, human companions fall away in adversity, and only God stays as an unwavering support.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural places friendship's throne in steady, unwavering support; this salok shows by contrast how worldly companions waver, and finds that steady prop in God alone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 55), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the tyrant Dionysius condemned the Pythagorean Phintias (Pythias) to death, Damon stood surety for his life so that Phintias could settle his affairs; Phintias returned on the appointed day, and the tyrant, amazed, asked to be admitted as a third friend.
greek_mythology.explanation: Damon offered his own life as a pledge, and Phintias kept faith by returning to die.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s enthroned friendship: support given without hesitation and kept without wavering.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “there is nothing which so fits in with our nature, or is so exactly what we want in prosperity or adversity.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius says friendship suits human nature better than anything else and is what we need in both good times and bad.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s friendship for ‘prosperity or adversity’ is the Kural’s support that holds steady in all seasons.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 5 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Anne Sullivan's decades of support for Helen Keller
real_life_example.place: Tuscumbia, Alabama, and elsewhere in the United States
real_life_example.event: On 3 March 1887 Anne Sullivan, a former pupil of the Perkins Institution, arrived at the Keller home in Tuscumbia to teach six-year-old Helen Keller, who could neither see nor hear, by spelling words into her hand. Sullivan stayed with Keller long after the famous breakthrough at the water pump, and when Keller entered Radcliffe College in 1900 Sullivan spelled out all the lectures and unbrailled texts for her, at great cost to her own weak eyesight. Keller graduated with honours in 1904, and Sullivan remained her interpreter and constant companion for decades afterwards.
real_life_example.explanation: Sullivan's steady, many-sided support made possible Keller's education and her later life as an author and public figure.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural places friendship on its throne when it stands firm without wavering and holds the other up in every way it can, and Sullivan's decades of unwavering support are as complete an example as history offers.

tamil:
இனையர் இவரெமக்கு இன்னம்யாம் என்று
புனையினும் புல்லென்னும் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Inaiyar ivaremakku innamyaam endru
punaiyinum pullennum natpu.
meaning: When friends go around saying, “He means this much to me, and I mean that much to him,” the friendship becomes cheap, however nicely they praise it.
elementary: Imagine two kids who keep telling everyone, ‘I’m her best friend, and I gave her THREE presents, and she’s SO lucky to have me!’ It starts to sound like showing off, and the friendship feels less special. Real friends don’t keep score or brag about it; they just are friends.
university: Inaiyar (இனையர்) means ‘such-and-such persons’ and innam (இன்னம்) ‘such-and-such’; the friend who says ‘he is so much to us, we are so much to him’ is measuring and advertising the friendship. Punaiyinum (புனையினும், ‘even if one adorns or praises it’) and pullennum (புல்லென்னும், ‘it looks mean or paltry’, from pul, grass, a common figure for worthlessness) complete the thought. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as a warning that true friends do not set their mutual services side by side or display their closeness, because keeping such accounts belongs to traders, not friends. The chapter thus ends where it began, by setting real friendship above any outward show. Both web sources give the same text; இவரெமக்கு is இவர் எமக்கு joined by sandhi.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Sudama, Krishna’s poor boyhood friend, visits him at Dwaraka, he is too shy to ask for anything and offers only a handful of flattened rice; Krishna receives him with great love, mentions no favour, and Sudama returns home to find his hut quietly turned into a palace.
hinduism.explanation: Neither friend counts or announces what the other means to him: Sudama asks for nothing, and Krishna gives without a word.
hinduism.tie_back: Their unspoken, unmeasured friendship is the opposite of the boasting the Kural warns against.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says loud, showy praise of a friend backfires and is taken as a curse.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: advertising a friendship cheapens it.

islam.quote_or_event: “A man praised another man in front of the Prophet. The Prophet said to him, ‘Woe to you, you have cut off your companion’s neck, you have cut off your companion’s neck,’ repeating it several times”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that lavish praise of a companion harms him, and that such praise should be cautious and modest.
islam.tie_back: Both texts teach that over-praising a friend does damage rather than honour.

judaism.quote_or_event: Shammai teaches that one should say little and do much, and receive everyone with a cheerful face.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah prefers quiet deeds to many words.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s true friendship is likewise shown in deeds rather than declared in words.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who renders lip-service be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he makes friendly profession as regards the past, (ii) he makes friendly profession as regards the future, (iii) he tries to gain one’s favor by empty words, (iv) when opportunity for service has arisen, he expresses his inability.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls the person who keeps declaring friendship, past and future, but fails when needed, a foe dressed as a friend.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s talking-up of friendship, shown to be hollow.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If after contracting a firm friendship with any one, I set myself to note his good and bad qualities, may I be cast into the hell where the traitor who discovers the secrets of his friend is punished, and may I be scoffed at by the whole world!”
jainism.explanation: The speaker swears never to audit a friend once a firm friendship has been formed, treating such reckoning as a betrayal.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says friendship becomes cheap when friends go around measuring what each is to the other, and the Naladiyar likewise treats keeping score inside a friendship as unworthy of it.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak! He alone is called a lover, who remains forever immersed in absorption. But one who feels good only when good is done for him, and feels bad when things go badly - do not call him a lover. He trades only for his own account.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad says that love which keeps track of what it receives is not love but trade.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says friendship cheapens when friends measure and advertise what each is to the other; Guru Angad likewise calls love that keeps accounts mere trading.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Homer never has Achilles and Patroclus boast of what they are to each other; their bond shows in deeds, as when Patroclus puts on Achilles’ armour to save the Greeks, and Achilles speaks of it only in grief, after Patroclus is dead.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest friendship in Greek epic is told almost entirely through action, not through declarations.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ideal: a friendship that needs no announcing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “there can be nothing more utterly subversive of friendship than flattery, adulation, and base compliance.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius names flattery and empty praise as the greatest destroyers of friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero agrees with the Kural that the decorated words of friends cheapen what they praise.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 25 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Hardy and Littlewood agree never to keep score
real_life_example.event: From about 1911 the Cambridge mathematicians G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood began a collaboration that lasted some 35 years. According to their colleague Harald Bohr, they agreed on a set of informal rules, which Mary Cartwright believed date from 1912: neither was obliged to answer or even read the other's letters, it did not matter whether what they wrote to each other was right or wrong, and every joint paper would carry both names regardless of whether one of them had contributed anything to it.
real_life_example.explanation: By refusing to keep accounts of who did what, the two built one of the most productive partnerships in the history of mathematics.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that friends who keep count of what each is to the other cheapen their friendship, and Hardy and Littlewood made not keeping count a formal rule.

tamil:
நாடாது நட்டலிற் கேடில்லை நட்டபின்
வீடில்லை நட்பாள் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Naadaadhu nattalir kedillai nattapin
veedillai natpaal bavarkku.
meaning: Nothing is more harmful than making friends without first checking a person carefully. For loyal people, once a friendship is made, they cannot walk away from it.
elementary: Imagine tying your shoelace to a friend’s shoelace for a three-legged race. Once the knot is tight, you have to run together wherever the other person goes. So before you tie the knot, make sure your partner is someone who runs the right way.
university: The chapter opens on a paradox: the very loyalty that makes a person a good friend is what makes a careless friendship dangerous. Natpaalbavar (நட்பாள்பவர்) are ‘those who maintain friendship’, people for whom a friend once made cannot be dropped; veedu (வீடு) here means ‘release’ or ‘leaving off’, not ‘house’. Parimelazhagar draws the inference the couplet implies: since the good never abandon a friend, there is no evil equal to friendship formed without naadal (நாடல், inquiry), and so the examination must come before, not after. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, while Kalaignar paraphrases it as ‘a bad friendship taken up without inquiry brings harm one cannot escape’. The text is the same in ytamizh, thirukkural.net and the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do not put your trust in a bad companion nor even trust an ordinary friend, for if he should get angry with you, he may bring all your secrets to light.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya warns that trust given too freely, even to an ordinary friend, can be turned against you once the relationship sours.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts counsel caution before intimacy, because a bond once given cannot simply be taken back.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 2.6 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “If thou wouldst get a friend, try him before thou takest him, and do not credit him easily. For there is a friend for his own occasion, and he will not abide in the day of thy trouble.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira tells his student to test a would-be friend before accepting him, because some friends stay only while it suits them. Sirach is deuterocanonical: it is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians but not part of the Protestant or Jewish canon.
christianity.tie_back: Ben Sira and Valluvar give the same order of operations: test first, then befriend.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not take as intimates those other than yourselves, for they will not spare you [any] ruin.”
islam.explanation: The verse warns believers against taking as close confidants people whose hostility has already shown itself.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a badly chosen intimate as a source of ruin and urges discernment before closeness.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jonathan and David bind themselves in a covenant of friendship, and the bond outlives Jonathan: years later David, now king, seeks out Jonathan’s lame son Mephibosheth and keeps him at his table for Jonathan’s sake.
judaism.explanation: In 1 Samuel 18 and 20 the two men swear a lasting covenant, and in 2 Samuel 9 David honours it even after Jonathan’s death.
judaism.tie_back: The story shows Valluvar’s premise from the positive side: a true friendship, once formed, is never released, which is exactly why it must be formed with care.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “these four as enemies the wise behold, avoid them from afar as paths of peril.”
buddhism.explanation: After listing four kinds of foes who look like friends, the Buddha tells Sigala to recognise them and keep them at a distance.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha, like Valluvar, puts the discernment before the relationship: spot the false friend and avoid him from afar.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “To join oneself to many, and strive many days and examine dispositions, and take (for friends) those who are worthy, is proper. Even with a deadly serpent, to associate and afterwards to part from it will be painful.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar tells the reader to examine people's dispositions over many days before taking them as friends, because once a bond is formed, even with something as deadly as a serpent, breaking it is painful.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that nothing is worse than friendship formed without inquiry, since a loyal person cannot get free of it afterwards, and the Naladiyar makes the same point that examination must come first because parting later hurts.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! Associate with the Holy people, who will take you to Nirvana in the end. Do not associate with the faithless cynics; they would bring you to ruin.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir's salok treats companionship as something that carries a person all the way to the end, for good or ill: the company of the holy stays with you to the last, while the company of the saakat (the faithless cynic) brings ruin.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a friendship, once made, cannot be shaken off, so choosing badly is the worst harm; Kabir likewise says the company you take up decides where you end, so it must be chosen before it binds you.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir 93 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with your brother smile—and get a witness; for trust and mistrust, alike ruin men.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod advises his brother Perses to keep clear terms even with friends and kin, because misplaced trust can ruin a man as surely as suspicion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod shares the Kural’s practical caution about giving trust before it has been earned.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 370-372 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, I must again and again repeat, you must satisfy your judgment before engaging your affections: not love first and judge afterwards.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius complains that people choose friends carelessly and then have to break off friendships later, when it is painful to do so.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero states Valluvar’s rule almost word for word: judge first, then love.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia §22 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: The eunuch Wang Zhen leads the Zhengtong Emperor into disaster at Tumu
real_life_example.place: Tumu, near present-day Huailai, Hebei, China
real_life_example.event: The young Zhengtong Emperor of the Ming dynasty placed his complete trust in the eunuch Wang Zhen, his first teacher, who came to dominate the government. In 1449, when the Oirat Mongol leader Esen invaded, Wang Zhen persuaded the emperor to lead an army against him in person, overriding the objections of senior ministers and officers. At the Tumu post station the ill-prepared Ming army was surrounded and largely destroyed, and the emperor was captured and held by the Mongols for about a year.
real_life_example.explanation: The disaster weakened the Ming dynasty and showed how costly a ruler's unexamined trust in a favourite could be.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that nothing is more harmful than friendship formed without careful examination, because a loyal person cannot afterwards break free of it, and the emperor's unquestioning bond with Wang Zhen led him straight into captivity.

tamil:
ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான் கேண்மை கடைமுறை
தான்சாம் துயரம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Aaindhaaindhu kollaadhaan kenmai kadaimurai
thaansaam thuyaram tharum.
meaning: If you make a friend without checking that person again and again, the friendship will bring you pain so bitter it could kill you in the end.
elementary: If you eat a mushroom from the woods without checking it, it might look fine today and make you very sick tomorrow. Friends are like that too. Look carefully, and then look again, before you let someone become your close friend.
university: The doubling aaindhu-aaindhu (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து, ‘having examined and examined’) insists that a single check is not enough; Parimelazhagar understands it as examining a person by many means and on many occasions. Kenmai (கேண்மை) is intimate friendship, and kadaimurai (கடைமுறை) means ‘at the last’ or ‘in the final course’, so the harm is delayed, which is why it is so easily ignored. Thaan saam thuyaram (தான்சாம் துயரம்) is ‘a sorrow from which he himself dies’; most modern commentators, including Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar, take this as hyperbole for grief that can bring a person to death. The sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org reads தான்சாந் துயரந் தரும், a purely orthographic difference from the ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Hitopadesha’s opening book, a deer befriends a smooth-talking jackal against the warning of his old friend the crow, who objects that one should not trust a newcomer whose nature is unknown; the jackal later lures the deer into a hunter’s snare hoping to feast on him, and only the crow’s cleverness saves the deer.
hinduism.explanation: The fable, part of the Mitralabha (‘Winning of Friends’), turns on a friendship accepted on a stranger’s pleasant words without any examination.
hinduism.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural’s warning that an unexamined friendship ends in mortal danger.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Book I (Mitralabha), the deer, the crow and the jackal

christianity.quote_or_event: “Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns against close friendship with a hot-tempered person because his ways become a trap for those who stay with him.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see a poorly chosen friendship as a trap whose damage arrives later.

islam.quote_or_event: “Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken that one as a friend. He led me away from the remembrance after it had come to me. And ever is Satan, to man, a deserter.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment, the wrongdoer bites his hands and laments the friend who led him astray.
islam.tie_back: The verse paints exactly the Kural’s ‘grief at the last’: bitter regret over a friendship that should never have been formed.

judaism.quote_or_event: Amnon, son of King David, has a friend named Jonadab, described as a very shrewd man, who devises the scheme by which Amnon wrongs his half-sister Tamar; two years later Absalom has Amnon killed in revenge.
judaism.explanation: The narrative in 2 Samuel 13 traces Amnon’s ruin back to the counsel of a clever but unscrupulous friend.
judaism.tie_back: It is a biblical case of the Kural’s point: a friend not judged by character leads at last to death.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man who has evil comrades and friends is given to evil ways, to ruin does he fall in both worlds — here and the next.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the young householder Sigala that bad companions drag a person into ruin in this life and the next.
buddhism.tie_back: The verse matches the Kural’s picture of a bad friendship ending in destruction.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: According to the Bhagavatī Sūtra, the wandering ascetic Gośāla attached himself to Mahāvīra and travelled with him as a disciple for about six years. He then broke away, founded the rival Ājīvika sect, and years later came to denounce Mahāvīra, killing two of his monks with a blast of fiery power (tejoleśyā) and hurling it at Mahāvīra himself, though it turned back on Gośāla.
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition remembers Gośāla as the companion whose long association ended in bitter enmity and death, a cautionary tale about close bonds with someone of unsound character.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that intimacy with someone who was not examined again and again brings deadly grief in the end, and the Gośāla episode is Jainism's best-known story of a close companionship that turned lethal.
jainism.source: Bhagavatī Sūtra (Vyākhyāprajñapti) 15, as retold in 'Association with Gosala' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! I have been ruined and destroyed by bad company, like the banana plant near the thorn bush. The thorn bush waves in the wind, and pierces the banana plant; see this, and do not associate with the faithless cynics.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir pictures a soft banana plant growing beside a thorny beri bush: every gust of wind drives the thorns into it, so the damage of bad company comes slowly, again and again, until it destroys.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says friendship formed without repeated examination brings, in the end, grief that can kill; Kabir's banana plant is that slow, fatal wounding by a companion who was never tested.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir 88 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pirithous, king of the Lapiths, meets Theseus and the two swear friendship on the spot. Bound by that oath, Theseus joins Pirithous’ reckless plan to carry off Persephone from the underworld; both are trapped in Hades, and while Heracles later frees Theseus, Pirithous is left there for ever.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth, told by Apollodorus and others, is the classic Greek case of a friendship sworn at first meeting and kept at ruinous cost.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows how a friendship formed without scrutiny ends in deadly sorrow.
greek_mythology.source: Apollodorus, Library, Epitome 1.23-24; Plutarch, Life of Theseus 30-35

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Further, such friendship requires time and familiarity; as the proverb says, men cannot know each other till they have ‘eaten salt together’ … for a wish for friendship may arise quickly, but friendship does not.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the best kind of friendship takes long acquaintance, because only time shows whether each person really deserves the other’s trust.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s ‘eating salt together’ is the long, repeated testing that the Kural’s aaindhu-aaindhu demands.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Pompey seeks refuge with the court of Ptolemy XIII
real_life_example.event: After his defeat by Julius Caesar at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BC, Pompey the Great fled to Egypt, seeking refuge with the young king Ptolemy XIII, whose family had long-standing ties to him. The king's courtiers, wishing to win the favour of the victorious Caesar, decided to be rid of their guest, and Pompey was killed as he came ashore by men sent to meet him.
real_life_example.explanation: Pompey relied on an old connection without weighing the men who now held power at the Egyptian court, and that misplaced trust cost him his life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that a friendship not examined again and again can bring, in the end, sorrow enough to kill, and Pompey's untested reliance on his Egyptian ties did exactly that.

tamil:
குணமும் குடிமையும் குற்றமும் குன்றா
இனனும் அறிந்தியாக்க நட்பு.
transliteration:
Gunamum kudimaiyum kutramum kundraa
inanum arindhiyaakka natpu.
meaning: Make someone your friend only after you know their character, their family, their faults, and the people they spend time with.
elementary: Before you join a new team, you watch how the players behave, who their coach is, what mistakes they make, and who they hang out with. Valluvar says to do the same four checks before you choose a close friend.
university: This couplet supplies the checklist for the chapter’s ‘investigation’: gunam (குணம், disposition or character), kudimai (குடிமை, lineage, the family in which one is raised), kutram (குற்றம், faults), and kundraa inam (குன்றா இனம், one’s abiding associates or kin). Parimelazhagar takes inam as the circle of relatives and companions who stand by a person, on the principle, developed in chapter 46 (Sitrinam Seraamai), that a person takes on the quality of the company he keeps; Puliyur Kesigan accordingly glosses it as ‘the companions who stay with him’. Arindhu yaakka (அறிந்து யாக்க) means ‘form it having known’. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts read குணமும், while the sandhi-joined edition reads குணனுங் குடிமையுங், an older spelling with the same meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Ravana’s brother Vibhishana comes to Rama asking for refuge and friendship, Rama asks his counsellors for their views; Sugriva and others suspect a spy because of his lineage, while Hanuman argues from Vibhishana’s conduct and speech that he is sincere, and only after weighing these views does Rama accept him.
hinduism.explanation: The episode in the Yuddha Kanda is a formal inquiry into a would-be ally’s family, character and motives before a bond is formed.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama’s council examines exactly what the Kural lists: nature, lineage, possible faults and associations.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that a person’s true nature shows in what he produces, as a tree is known by its fruit.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say a person’s character must be read from evidence before you trust him.

islam.quote_or_event: “A man follows the religion of his friend; so each one should consider whom he makes his friend.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that a person takes on the ways of his close friend, so the choice of friend must be weighed carefully.
islam.tie_back: This hadith gives the reason for Valluvar’s checklist: you become like the people you befriend.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4833 (graded hasan by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Joshua said, a good companion; Rabbi Yose said, a good neighbor … Rabbi Joshua said, an evil companion; Rabbi Yose said, an evil neighbor”
judaism.explanation: Asked which path a person should cleave to and which he should shun, Rabban Yohanan’s disciples name the good or evil companion and neighbour among the deciding factors.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Mishnah treats the people around a person as something to examine and choose with care.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “These four, young householder, should be understood as foes in the guise of friends: (1) he who appropriates a friend’s possessions, (2) he who renders lip-service, (3) he who flatters, (4) he who brings ruin.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha gives Sigala a list of signs that reveal a false friend, each broken down into four observable behaviours.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the sutta turns friendship into something to be checked against specific marks of character.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Sramana engaged in austerities, who longs for righteousness, should eat the proper quantity of allowed food, should select a companion of right understanding, and should live in a place suited to seclusion.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's teaching on the path to liberation tells the monk to choose his companion deliberately, for that companion's sound understanding.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to make friends only after weighing a person's character, family, faults and associates, and the Jain canon likewise makes the careful choice of a companion part of the disciplined life.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! The mind has become a bird; it soars and flies in the ten directions. According to the company it keeps, so are the fruits it eats.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir says the restless mind settles wherever its company is, and what it becomes depends on that company, so the people around a person are a true index of what that person will become.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to check a would-be friend's character, faults and the circle he keeps close; Kabir explains why the circle matters, since a person takes the fruit of the company he keeps.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir 86 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the battlefield before Troy, Diomedes asks the Lycian Glaucus who he is; Glaucus recites his lineage back to Bellerophon, and Diomedes realises their grandfathers were guest-friends, so instead of fighting they clasp hands, renew the friendship and exchange armour.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Iliad 6 an enemy becomes a friend only after his family and ancestral ties are laid out.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode shows the Kural’s concern with kudimai and inam: lineage and associations are checked before friendship is sealed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now the qualities we ought to look out for in making our selection are firmness, stability, constancy. There is a plentiful lack of men so endowed, and it is difficult to form a judgment without testing.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero’s Laelius complains that people count their sheep carefully but choose friends with no criteria, and he names the qualities to look for.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero, like Valluvar, gives a checklist of character traits to verify before friendship.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia §17 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Britain introduces positive vetting after the Burgess and Maclean defections
real_life_example.event: In 1951 the British diplomats Guy Burgess and Donald Maclean, who had been recruited by Soviet intelligence before the Second World War, defected to the Soviet Union. In response, the British government in 1952 introduced positive vetting, a procedure intended to establish the integrity of civil servants doing exceptionally secret work. Earlier screening had focused on Communist or Fascist sympathies and associations, but positive vetting widened the inquiry to a person's character, and in 1956 the government declared publicly that character defects could affect a civil servant's posting or promotion.
real_life_example.explanation: The reform reflected a hard lesson: trusted men had been given access to vital secrets without anyone examining closely their character and associations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises learning a person's character, background, faults and associates before admitting him to close friendship, and positive vetting applied that same examination before admitting a person to the state's secrets.

tamil:
குடிப்பிறந்து தன்கண் பழிநாணு வானைக்
கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Kudippirandhu thankan pazhinaanu vaanaik
koduththum kolalvendum natpu.
meaning: Make friends with someone from a good family who feels ashamed of doing wrong, even if it costs you something.
elementary: Some friends are like a good umbrella: worth saving your pocket money for. A friend who comes from a caring home and feels bad if he does something wrong is that kind of friend, so it is worth giving up something to have him.
university: Kudippirandhu (குடிப்பிறந்து) means ‘born into a good family’, the kudi of chapter 96 (Kudimai), and pazhi naanuvaan (பழிநாணுவான்) is ‘one who feels shame at blame’, that is, someone whose sense of honour keeps him from disgraceful acts. Koduththum (கொடுத்தும், ‘even by giving’) carries the force of ‘even at a price’. Parimelazhagar takes it literally as giving wealth to secure such a friend, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah likewise say ‘even by paying a price’, while Kalaignar softens it to ‘by any means’. After three couplets of warning, the chapter turns here to the positive: some friendships are worth paying for. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition reads தன்கட் and கொடுத்துங் … வேண்டு, orthographic variants only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man’s descent may be discerned by his conduct, his country by his pronunciation of language, his friendship by his warmth and glow”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya says that good birth shows itself in conduct, and true friendship in warmth.
hinduism.tie_back: Both link good family to visible good conduct; the Kural adds that such a person is worth acquiring as a friend.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 3.2 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A faithful friend is a strong defence: and he that hath found him, hath found a treasure. Nothing can be compared to a faithful friend, and no weight of gold and silver is able to countervail the goodness of his fidelity.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira says a loyal friend is worth more than any amount of gold or silver. (Sirach is deuterocanonical, accepted by Catholic and Orthodox but not Protestant Christians.)
christianity.tie_back: Ben Sira and Valluvar both say a good friend is worth any price.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with those who are true.”
islam.explanation: The verse tells believers to keep company with the truthful.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s instruction to actively seek out people of integrity as companions.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joshua ben Perahiah used to say: appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew verb here, k’neh, means ‘acquire’ or ‘buy’, and the rabbinic tradition (for example Avot de-Rabbi Natan) reads it as telling a person to obtain a good companion even at personal cost.
judaism.tie_back: This is the closest Jewish parallel to koduththum: a true companion is worth buying.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, a friend endowed with seven qualities is worth associating with. Which seven? He gives what is hard to give. He does what is hard to do. He endures what is hard to endure. He reveals his secrets to you. He keeps your secrets. When misfortunes strike, he doesn’t abandon you. When you’re down & out, he doesn’t look down on you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists seven qualities that make a person worth cultivating as a friend.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta and the Kural agree that a friend of proven character is worth going out of your way to keep.
buddhism.source: Mitta Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 7.35 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, though the friendship of those who, like the channel which fructifies the rice-field, be ever so far away, we must nevertheless go to obtain it.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar says the friendship of truly helpful people is worth going to great lengths for, however far away they are.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the friendship of a well-born person who fears blame is worth securing even at a price, and the Naladiyar likewise counts the right friend worth whatever effort it takes to win them.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The sight of them banishes my evil-mindedness; they are my only true friends. I have searched the whole world; O servant Nanak! How rare are such persons!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says the true friend is the one whose very presence drives out one's evil-mindedness, and such friends are so rare that he had to search the whole world for them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the friendship of a person with a living sense of shame at wrongdoing is worth winning even at a price; Guru Arjan agrees that such a friend, who turns one away from wrong, is rare and worth any search.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 520, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pylades, a prince of Phocis raised alongside Orestes, stays with him through exile, madness and danger; in Euripides’ Iphigenia among the Taurians each insists on dying so that the other may live.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pylades was the Greek byword for the high-born, honourable friend who would pay any price for his companion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the kind of well-born, honour-bound friend the Kural says is worth securing at any cost.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Iphigenia among the Taurians; Aeschylus, Libation Bearers

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But it is natural that such friendships should be infrequent; for such men are rare.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says friendship between good people is the best kind but is scarce, because good people themselves are scarce.
philosophy.tie_back: If such friends are rare, it follows, as the Kural says, that they are worth a high price.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Catherine the Great buys Diderot's library and leaves it with him
real_life_example.place: Paris, France, and St Petersburg, Russia
real_life_example.event: In 1765 Catherine the Great learned that the French philosopher Denis Diderot, editor of the Encyclopedie, was about to sell his library to provide a dowry for his daughter. She bought the collection for 15,000 livres on condition that the books remain with Diderot for the rest of his life, and paid him a yearly sum as librarian of his own books. Diderot afterwards recruited scholars and artists on her behalf and, in 1773, travelled to St Petersburg, where he met the empress for long conversations.
real_life_example.explanation: Catherine was willing to pay generously to win the friendship and goodwill of one of the most respected thinkers in Europe.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises securing, even at a price, the friendship of a worthy person who shrinks from disgrace, and Catherine quite literally paid to gain Diderot's friendship.

tamil:
அழச்சொல்லி அல்லது இடித்து வழக்கறிய
வல்லார்நட்பு ஆய்ந்து கொளல்.
transliteration:
Azhachcholli alladhu idiththu vazhakkariya
vallaarnatpu aaindhu kolal.
meaning: Find and keep friends who can make you cry with hard truths, scold you sharply when you are wrong, and understand how the world works.
elementary: A good coach sometimes tells you, ‘That was wrong, do it again,’ and it can make you want to cry. But that coach makes you better. Valluvar says to choose friends like that coach, not friends who only say nice things.
university: Azhach cholli (அழச்சொல்லி) is ‘speaking so as to make one weep’ and idiththu (இடித்து) is ‘striking’, that is, rebuking hard; the same verb appears in kural 448 of the idikkum thunai, the counsellor who rebukes a king. Parimelazhagar distinguishes the two: the friend makes you weep with counsel before a wrong is done, and rebukes you sharply after it is done; Solomon Pappaiah follows this two-step reading. Vazhakku ariya valla (வழக்கறிய வல்ல) means ‘able to make one know the ways of the world’, adding practical wisdom to frankness. Both ytamizh and thirukkural.net print வல்லார்நடபு, which is missing its pulli; the sandhi-joined edition’s வல்லார்நட் பாய்ந்து confirms the reading வல்லார்நட்பு used here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “They are abundant, O king, that can always speak agreeable words. The speaker, however, is rare, as also the hearer, of words that are disagreeable but medicinal.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells the blind king Dhritarashtra that flatterers are everywhere, but people who speak painful, healing truth are rare, and so are those willing to hear it.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura’s ‘disagreeable but medicinal’ words are the hard words of the friend the Kural tells you to keep.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says a friend’s painful honesty can be trusted, while an enemy’s affection is a trick.
christianity.tie_back: The ‘wounds of a friend’ are the Kural’s words that make you weep.

islam.quote_or_event: “The believer is the believer’s mirror, and the believer is the believer’s brother who guards him against loss and protects him when he is absent.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says a fellow believer should show you your faults as a mirror does, while also protecting you.
islam.tie_back: The ‘mirror’ friend who shows your faults is the Kural’s friend who rebukes.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4918 (graded hasan by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: “You shall not hate your kinsfolk in your heart. Reprove your kindred but incur no guilt on their account.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah makes rebuke a duty: instead of hating someone silently, you must tell him plainly where he is wrong.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts treat honest reproof as a mark of real love rather than a breach of it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure. It is always better, and never worse, to cultivate such an association.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his hearers to treat someone who points out their faults like a guide to buried treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own advice: seek out and keep the friend who rebukes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wise, fearless monks consider even a rough instruction as a benefit, but the fools hate it, though it produces patience and purity of mind.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana teaches that hard words of correction are to be welcomed as a benefit, and that only fools resent them.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says we should seek friends who can rebuke us sharply enough to make us weep, and the Jain canon likewise values the harsh word that corrects us over pleasant flattery.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: When Guru Gobind Singh, passing through Narayana in Rajasthan, saluted the shrine of the saint Dadu by raising an arrow to his forehead, the Khalsa objected and one Sikh, Man Singh, quoted the Guru's own verse forbidding the worship of tombs. The Guru at once offered to pay a fine; after some debate the Sikhs fixed it at Rs 125, which they spent on a kitchen tent.
sikhism.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism says the Guru did this to test the conviction of his Sikhs, and he welcomed being rebuked by them when he appeared to break his own teaching.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to seek friends who will rebuke us sharply and understand the world's ways; the Khalsa rebuking even its Guru, and the Guru accepting it, is the Sikh model of a fellowship that corrects rather than flatters.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, ed. Harbans Singh (Punjabi University, Patiala), entry 'Dadu Dial (1544-1603)' by Gurnek Singh (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As the Greeks are being driven back to their ships, Patroclus comes to Achilles in tears and rebukes him as pitiless for sitting out the battle in anger while his comrades die, then begs to lead the Myrmidons himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: At the opening of Iliad 16, Achilles’ dearest friend is the one person who confronts him to his face over his wrath.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Patroclus is the friend who speaks hard words to stop a wrong, as the Kural describes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Plain speaking is a cause of trouble, if the result of it is resentment, which is poison of friendship; but compliance is really the cause of much more trouble, because by indulging his faults it lets a friend plunge into headlong ruin.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius argues that a friend who only goes along with you does more harm than one whose frankness stings.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero and Valluvar agree that the stinging, frank friend is the one worth keeping.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia §24 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Clementine Churchill's frank letter to Winston
real_life_example.event: On 27 June 1940, in the weeks after the fall of France, Clementine Churchill wrote to her husband, now Prime Minister, to warn him that he was in danger of becoming unpopular with his colleagues and staff because of his rough, sarcastic and overbearing manner. She told him plainly that she herself had noticed his manner growing worse, and urged him to combine his great power with kindness and calm. The letter is preserved in the Churchill Archives Centre at Churchill College, Cambridge.
real_life_example.explanation: The letter is remembered as a model of loving but unsparing counsel, offered to the most powerful man in Britain at a moment of extreme strain.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar urges us to seek those who can speak hard words that sting and who understand the ways of the world, and Clementine's letter was exactly such counsel.

tamil:
கேட்டினும் உண்டோர் உறுதி கிளைஞரை
நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல்.
transliteration:
Kettinum undor urudhi kilaignarai
neetti alappadhor kol.
meaning: Even bad times have one good side. They are a measuring stick that shows how far your friends and relatives will really go for you.
elementary: When it rains, you find out which umbrellas have holes. When something bad happens to you, you find out which friends stay. That is the one good thing about a bad day: it shows you who your real friends are.
university: Kedu (கேடு) is ruin or misfortune and urudhi (உறுதி) is ‘benefit’ or ‘firm good’; the -um in kettinum gives ‘even in ruin’. Kilaignar (கிளைஞர்) literally means kin, ‘those of the same branch’, but Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators extend it to friends, since the chapter is about friendship. The image of neetti alappadhu oor kol (நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல், ‘a rod that measures by stretching out’) is a surveyor’s measuring rod laid end to end, which measures exactly how far each person’s affection reaches. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both stress the paradox that harm itself becomes the instrument of knowledge. The sandhi-joined text reads கேட்டினு முண்டோ ருறுதி, the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Test a servant while in the discharge of his duty, a relative in difficulty, a friend in adversity, and a wife in misfortune.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya says each kind of relationship has its own testing ground, and for a friend that test is adversity.
hinduism.tie_back: Chanakya makes the same claim as the Kural: hardship is the test that measures a friend.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 1.11 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says real friendship is constant and that hard times are what a brother is for.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say adversity is what reveals and proves a true friend or kinsman.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Prophet left Mecca under threat of death, Abu Bakr alone went with him and hid with him in the cave of Thawr while their pursuers searched nearby; the Qur’an remembers him as ‘the second of two’ to whom the Prophet said, ‘Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.’
islam.explanation: Qur’an 9:40 recalls the Hijra, the moment of greatest danger, when Abu Bakr’s loyalty was proven.
islam.tie_back: The hour of danger showed who the true companion was, just as the Kural says misfortune measures friends.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But Ruth replied, ‘Do not urge me to leave you, to turn back and not follow you. For wherever you go, I will go; wherever you lodge, I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God.’”
