judaism.explanation: Widowed and destitute, Naomi urges her daughters-in-law to go home; Orpah leaves, but Ruth refuses to abandon her.
judaism.tie_back: Naomi’s ruin works as the Kural’s measuring rod: it shows who stays and who goes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who is the same in happiness and sorrow be understood as a warm-hearted friend: (i) he reveals his secrets, (ii) he conceals one’s own secrets, (iii) in misfortune he does not forsake one, (iv) his life even he sacrifices for one’s sake.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the marks of a true friend, the Buddha lists that he does not leave you when misfortune comes.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha and Valluvar both name misfortune as the moment a true friend is recognised.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “men will remain until they have done their work in an old house the thatch of which is untied, keeping out the water br a dam, and being drenched with the rain falling down upon them. Thus will friends! remain with one until their business is finished.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar compares self-interested friends to workers who put up with a leaking house only until their job is done, and then leave.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says misfortune is a measuring rod that shows how far friends really go for you, and the Naladiyar's leaking-house image likewise shows how far a fair-weather friend's loyalty reaches before it runs out.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 1 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In good times, there are many companions around, but in bad times, there is no one at all. Says Nanak, vibrate, and meditate on the Lord; He shall be your only Help and Support in the end.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur observes that prosperity gathers companions and adversity scatters them, and he turns from fair-weather friends to God as the one support who remains.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says even misfortune has one benefit, since it measures exactly how far friends will go for you; Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok records the result of that measurement: many in good times, none in bad.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1428, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 32), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus comes home to Ithaca disguised as a ragged beggar and uses his apparent ruin to test his household: the swineherd Eumaeus shares his meagre food with him, while the goatherd Melanthius kicks and insults him, and the loyalty of each is revealed.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the second half of the Odyssey, Odysseus deliberately takes on the look of misfortune in order to measure who is faithful.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His disguise turns misfortune into exactly the Kural’s measuring rod for friends and dependants.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And though what Ennius says is quite true,—‘the hour of need shews the friend indeed,’—yet it is in these two ways that most people betray their untrustworthiness and inconstancy”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius quotes the poet Ennius’ line, the source of the English proverb ‘a friend in need is a friend indeed’, and adds that prosperity and adversity both expose false friends.
philosophy.tie_back: Ennius’ ‘hour of need’ is the Kural’s measuring rod of misfortune.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia §17, quoting Ennius (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Mark Twain publishes the memoirs of the ruined Ulysses S. Grant
real_life_example.event: In May 1884 the collapse of the Wall Street firm of Grant & Ward, run by his partner Ferdinand Ward, wiped out former President Ulysses S. Grant's savings, and later that year he learned that he had incurable throat cancer. His friend Mark Twain, who had long urged him to write his memoirs, arranged to publish them through his own publishing firm, and Grant raced to finish the manuscript, completing it only days before his death in July 1885. The memoirs sold about 300,000 sets and earned his widow, Julia, more than 400,000 dollars.
real_life_example.explanation: When Grant lost his fortune and faced death, Twain's friendship provided the means by which he saved his family from poverty.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even ruin has one benefit, since it is a measuring rod that shows how far one's friends truly reach, and Grant's ruin showed the full length of Twain's friendship.

tamil:
ஊதியம் என்பது ஒருவற்குப் பேதையார்
கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்.
transliteration:
Oodhiyam enbadhu oruvarkup pedhaiyaar
kenmai oreei vidal.
meaning: The real gain for a person is to give up friendship with fools completely.
elementary: If your kite is tied to a heavy rock, it can never fly. Cutting the string to the rock is not a loss; it is how the kite goes up. Letting go of a friend who keeps pulling you into silly trouble is the same kind of win.
university: Oodhiyam (ஊதியம்) is ‘profit’ or ‘gain’, a deliberately commercial word in a chapter of the Porutpal. Pedhaiyaar (பேதையார்) are fools in the specific Kural sense defined in chapter 84 (Pedhaimai): people who take up what harms them and drop what helps them. Oreei (ஒரீஇ) is an alapedai (sound-lengthened) form of oruvi, ‘having abandoned’, and with vidal (விடல், ‘letting go’) it makes ‘to abandon and let go entirely’. Parimelazhagar and Puliyur Kesigan read the couplet as applying to a friendship already formed with a fool unknowingly: leaving it as soon as the folly is recognised is itself a gain. The sandhi-joined text reads ஊதிய மென்ப தொருவற்குப் … யொரீஇ, the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do not keep company with a fool for as we can see he is a two-legged beast. Like an unseen thorn he pierces the heart with his sharp words.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya warns that a fool’s company wounds you in ways you do not see coming.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say that staying away from fools is to your benefit.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 3.7 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb contrasts the gain of walking with the wise with the loss suffered by the friend of fools.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts frame leaving fools’ company as profit and keeping it as loss.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of a good companion (who sits with you) in comparison with a bad one, is like that of the musk seller and the blacksmith’s bellows (or furnace); from the first you would either buy musk or enjoy its good smell while the bellows would either burn your clothes or your house, or you get a bad nasty smell thereof.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a good companion to a perfume seller whose fragrance you share, and a bad one to a blacksmith whose sparks burn you.
islam.tie_back: Both texts weigh companions in terms of gain and loss.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Keep your distance from a dull man, For you will not learn wise speech.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb advises walking away from a fool, since nothing wise can be gained from him.
judaism.tie_back: Both say that leaving the fool is the sensible, profitable choice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a seeker not find a companion who is better or equal, let him resolutely pursue a solitary course; there is no fellowship with the fool.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says it is better to walk alone than to keep company with a fool.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the verse treats leaving the fool, even for solitude, as the better bargain.

jainism.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sûtras.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra lists keeping away from foolish people as one of the essential steps on the road to final deliverance.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls giving up friendship with fools a person's true gain, and the Jain canon likewise puts avoiding fools among the requirements of the path to liberation.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! Do not associate with the faithless cynics; run far away from them. If you touch a vessel stained with soot, some of the soot will stick to you.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir uses the image of a soot-blackened pot: however careful you are, contact leaves a mark, so the only safe course with a bad companion is to get well away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a person's real gain is to give up completely the friendship of fools; Kabir likewise counsels a clean break, since even slight contact with the wrong company leaves its stain.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir 131 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The Farmer laughed aloud and said, ‘It may be all as you say, I only know this: I have taken you with these robbers, the Cranes, and you must die in their company.’”
greek_mythology.explanation: A stork caught in a net with crop-stealing cranes pleads its good character, but the farmer judges it by the company it was keeping.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The fable shows the cost of not leaving bad company in time, the loss the Kural tells us to avoid.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Farmer and the Stork (trans. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But wicked men have no steadfastness (for they do not remain even like to themselves), but become friends for a short time because they delight in each other’s wickedness.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says friendships among bad people are short and unstable because they rest on shared vice.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle explains why such a friendship is worth nothing and losing it is no loss.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.8 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi breaks with his boyhood companion Sheikh Mehtab
real_life_example.event: As a schoolboy in Rajkot, Mohandas Gandhi formed a close friendship with Sheikh Mehtab, entering it, as he later wrote, in the spirit of a reformer, and he described it in his autobiography in two chapters titled A Tragedy. Mehtab later lived in Gandhi's household in Durban, where Gandhi discovered serious misconduct by him and learned that he had turned Gandhi against an honest clerk with false suspicions. Gandhi told him he would have nothing more to do with him and made him leave the house, later writing that in trying to reform the man he had nearly ruined himself and that the break let him begin a more detached and disciplined life.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi came to see the end of this friendship not as a loss but as a rescue that freed him for his later work.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the real gain for a person is to give up completely the friendship of fools, and Gandhi himself described his break with Mehtab as a deliverance.

tamil:
உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ கொள்ளற்க
அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Ullarka ullam sirukuva kollarka
allarkan aatraruppaar natpu.
meaning: Do not think about things that make your spirit weak, and do not make friends with people who will leave you when trouble comes.
elementary: Some friends are like a bicycle that only works on sunny days: the moment it rains, the chain falls off. Do not count on a friend like that. Pick friends who will still be pedalling with you when the road gets muddy.
university: The couplet sets two prohibitions side by side. Ullarka ullam siruguva (உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ) is ‘do not think the things that make the mind small’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take this as avoiding whatever saps one’s energy and resolve (ookkam), and Parimelazhagar treats the first line as an analogy for the second: just as one should not entertain spirit-shrinking thoughts, one should not take up such friends. Allarkan aatraruppaar (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார்) are ‘those who cut off the way in time of distress’, people who withdraw their support exactly when it is needed. Puliyur Kesigan reads the first line differently, as a warning not to think meanly of a friend, which shows the line is open to more than one interpretation. The sandhi-joined text reads உள்ளற்க வுள்ளஞ் … வல்லற்க ணாற்றறுப்பார், the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He is a true friend who does not forsake us in time of need, misfortune, famine, or war, in a king’s court, or at the crematorium (smasana).”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya lists the hard places where a true friend still stands beside you.
hinduism.tie_back: Chanakya defines the true friend by the same test the Kural uses: he does not leave in times of trouble.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 1.12 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge.”
christianity.explanation: Writing from prison, Paul recalls that at his first hearing his supporters deserted him.
christianity.tie_back: Paul describes the very friends the Kural warns against: those who vanish in the hour of distress.

islam.quote_or_event: “[The hypocrites are] like the example of Satan when he says to man, ‘Disbelieve.’ But when he disbelieves, he says, ‘Indeed, I am disassociated from you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.’”
islam.explanation: The verse compares false allies to Satan, who urges a person into wrongdoing and then disowns him when the consequences arrive.
islam.tie_back: It describes the companion who abandons you at the moment of trouble.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be careful [in your dealings] with the ruling authorities for they do not befriend a person except for their own needs; they seem like friends when it is to their own interest, but they do not stand by a man in the hour of his distress.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel warns that powerful patrons seem friendly while it serves them but are gone when trouble comes.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s deserting friend, described almost in its own words.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who renders lip-service be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he makes friendly profession as regards the past, (ii) he makes friendly profession as regards the future, (iii) he tries to gain one’s favor by empty words, (iv) when opportunity for service has arisen, he expresses his inability.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the false friend who talks warmly but is never available when help is actually needed.
buddhism.tie_back: The lip-service friend is the one who, in the Kural’s words, cuts off the way in time of trouble.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Avoiding the friendship of those who resemble elephants, seek the friendship of those who resemble dogs; for an elephant will kill his driver whom he has known for a long time, but a dog will wag his tail while the spear thrown at him is still in his body.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar warns against friends who, like an elephant turning on its own driver, betray a long companion, and praises those who stay loyal even when wounded.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural forbids taking up the friendship of people who abandon you in trouble, and the Naladiyar likewise tells us to avoid such friends and seek those who stay faithful through suffering.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 3 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The world is entangled in its own pleasures; no one is for anyone else. In good times, many come and sit together, surrounding you on all four sides. But when hard times come, they all leave, and no one comes near you.”
sikhism.explanation: In this Sorath shabad Guru Tegh Bahadur describes companions who crowd around in comfort and vanish in distress, because their attachment was only to their own pleasure.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural forbids taking up the friendship of those who cut off their support in time of trouble; Guru Tegh Bahadur describes exactly those people, who leave as soon as hard times come.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 634, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He gave me this advice,” his companion replied. “Never travel with a friend who deserts you at the approach of danger.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When a bear appears, one traveller scrambles up a tree and leaves his companion to save himself by playing dead.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The fable gives the Kural’s own advice: do not keep a friend who runs at the first sign of danger.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Bear and the Two Travelers (trans. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Those who are friends for the sake of utility part when the advantage is at an end; for they were lovers not of each other but of profit.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle explains that friendships based on usefulness dissolve as soon as one party is no longer useful.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle gives the reason fair-weather friends desert: they never loved the person, only the benefit.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.4 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Charles I abandons the Earl of Strafford
real_life_example.event: Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford, had become King Charles I's chief adviser and in 1641 was impeached by the Long Parliament. When his trial failed to prove treason, his opponents turned to a bill of attainder, and after anguished hesitation Charles, fearing for his own security, gave his assent to it. Strafford was executed on Tower Hill on 12 May 1641.
real_life_example.explanation: Strafford had served the king with total devotion, yet in the crisis Charles let him die to protect himself, a decision the king later came to regard as a grave sin.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns against taking up the friendship of those who will cut you off when trouble comes, and Strafford gave everything to a master who deserted him at the decisive moment.

tamil:
கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார் கேண்மை அடுங்காலை
உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்.
transliteration:
Kedungaalaik kaividuvaar kenmai adungaalai
ullinum ullanj chudum.
meaning: Friends who left you when you were in trouble will burn your heart, even if you only think of them at the hour of your death.
elementary: Have you ever been left alone by a friend when you really needed help? That hurt can stay with you for a very long time, even when you are grown up. Valluvar says this hurt is so strong it can burn even at the very end of life.
university: Kedungaalai (கெடுங்காலை) is ‘at the time when one is being ruined’, and adungaalai (அடுங்காலை) is ‘at the time when one is being slain’, the hour of death; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as the time when Yama comes to kill, and Kalaignar reads it as the moment one is being put to death. Ullinum (உள்ளினும், ‘even if one recalls’) and ullam sudum (உள்ளம் சுடும், ‘the heart burns’) make a play on ul- (‘think’) and ullam (‘mind’). The force of the couplet is psychological: the wound of desertion outlasts every other pain, so one should never form such a friendship in the first place, which ties it back to the chapter’s theme of investigation. The sandhi-joined text reads கேண்மை யடுங்காலை யுள்ளினு முள்ளஞ் சுடும், the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Drona and Drupada were boyhood friends, and Drupada promised to share his kingdom one day; when the impoverished Drona later came to him, King Drupada scorned him, saying friendship is impossible between a king and a poor man. The humiliation burned in Drona for years, until he had his pupils, the Kuru princes, capture Drupada and paid him back by taking half his kingdom.
hinduism.explanation: In the Adi Parva, a friend’s rejection in a time of need leaves a wound that shapes Drona’s whole life and feeds the feud behind the great war.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s burning memory of a friend who abandoned you when you were down.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed from his friend; but he forsaketh the fear of the Almighty. My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, and as the stream of brooks they pass away;”
christianity.explanation: In his suffering, Job complains that his friends have failed him like seasonal streams that dry up just when they are needed.
christianity.tie_back: Job voices the burning pain of friends who fail in the time of ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “Close friends, that Day, will be enemies to each other, except for the righteous”
islam.explanation: The verse says that on the Day of Judgment friendships not built on righteousness will turn into hostility.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it looks ahead to the final hour, when unworthy friendships are remembered with bitterness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All love that depends on a something, [when the] thing ceases, [the] love ceases; and [all love] that does not depend on anything, will never cease. What is an example of love that depended on a something? Such was the love of Amnon for Tamar. And what is an example of love that did not depend on anything? Such was the love of David and Jonathan.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah explains that love based on some benefit vanishes when the benefit does, while unconditional love lasts.
judaism.tie_back: It explains why the deserting friend left: his love depended on your good fortune, and when that ended, so did he.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is a bottle friend; one says, ‘friend, friend’ only to one’s face; one is a friend and an associate only when it is advantageous.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes friends who are present only for drinking, flattery or advantage.
buddhism.tie_back: These are the friends who leave when ruin comes, whom the Kural says will burn in memory.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “if friends from whom it is difficult to separate, possess not virtuous dispositions, they are as a fire kindled to burn our hearts.”
jainism.explanation: The stanza says close friends who lack good character become a fire that burns the heart, because the bond is too close to break easily.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the memory of friends who deserted you in ruin burns the heart even at the hour of death, and the Naladiyar uses the same image of the heart burning because of unworthy friends.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My teeth, feet, eyes and ears have stopped working. My body cries out, “Those whom I knew have left me!””
sikhism.explanation: In this salok Sheikh Farid, whose verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, speaks in the voice of an old man near death whose body laments that the people close to him have gone.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the memory of friends who left you as you were falling burns the heart even at the hour of death; Farid's dying body likewise cries out over those who have left it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid 77 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the way to Troy, the Greek leaders abandon the wounded archer Philoctetes alone on the island of Lemnos because his festering wound is unbearable to them; in Sophocles’ play, ten years later, his bitterness toward Odysseus and the sons of Atreus is still so fierce that he would rather die than help them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sophocles’ Philoctetes is an extended study of the lasting resentment of a man deserted by his comrades in his worst hour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His undying anger is the Kural’s burning heart, kindled by friends who left him when he was falling.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is in these two ways that most people betray their untrustworthiness and inconstancy, by looking down on friends when they are themselves prosperous, or deserting them in their distress.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius names deserting a friend in distress as one of the two commonest betrayals of friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero names the very betrayal whose memory, the Kural says, burns at the last.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia §17 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Napoleon names Marmont's betrayal in his last will
real_life_example.event: Auguste Marmont had been one of Napoleon's closest companions since meeting him at the siege of Toulon in 1793, serving as his aide-de-camp and later becoming a marshal. In April 1814, with Napoleon's position collapsing, Marmont went over to the Allies with his army corps, a defection that helped force Napoleon's abdication and made the word ragusade, from Marmont's title of duke of Ragusa, a byword for treachery. In exile on St Helena, as his strength was failing, Napoleon wrote out his will on 15 April 1821, and in it he named Marmont first among those whose treason he blamed for the invasions of France, while declaring that he forgave them.
real_life_example.explanation: Even in his final weeks, Napoleon's mind returned to the old friend who had abandoned him at his fall.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the memory of friends who abandoned you when you were falling will burn the heart even at the hour of death, and Napoleon named Marmont's desertion in his last will.

tamil:
மருவுக மாசற்றார் கேண்மைஒன் றீத்தும்
ஒருவுக ஒப்பிலார் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Maruvuka maasatraar kenmaion reeththum
oruvuka oppilaar natpu.
meaning: Stay close to good people who have no faults. Leave the friendship of unworthy people, even if it costs you something to get away.
elementary: Think of friends like food. Keep eating the fresh fruit. If something in your lunchbox has gone bad, throw it away, even if you paid for it. Keep good friends close, and let the bad ones go even if that costs you something.
university: The closing couplet balances two imperatives in parallel: maruvuka (மருவுக, ‘cling to, embrace’) and oruvuka (ஒருவுக, ‘leave, shun’). Maasatraar (மாசற்றார்) are ‘those without stain’, while oppilaar (ஒப்பிலார்) is ambiguous: Parimelazhagar takes it as those who do not accord with the world’s good ways, Solomon Pappaiah follows with ‘those who do not fit with the world’, and Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘those who lack matching virtue’. Onru eeththum (ஒன்று ஈத்தும், ‘even by giving something’) mirrors koduththum in kural 794: just as a good friend is worth buying, a bad one is worth paying to be rid of. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts read ஈத்தும், while the sandhi-joined edition divides the line as கேண்மையொன் றீத்து மொருவுக, which reads the same once the sandhi is undone.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Old age killeth beauty; patience, hope; death, life; the practice of virtue, worldly enjoyments; lust, modesty; companionship with the wicked, good behaviour; anger, prosperity; and pride, everything.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura lists things that destroy other things, including bad company destroying good conduct.
hinduism.tie_back: It gives the reason the Kural says to leave unsuitable friends at any cost: bad company eats away at good conduct.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.”
christianity.explanation: Paul quotes a proverb, found earlier in the Greek poet Menander, warning that bad company corrupts good character.
christianity.tie_back: Paul and Valluvar both warn that the wrong friends corrupt, so they must be left behind.

islam.quote_or_event: “And keep yourself patient [by being] with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His countenance … and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance and who follows his desire and whose affair is ever [in] neglect.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to stay with the sincere worshippers and not to follow the heedless.
islam.tie_back: The verse has the same two halves as the Kural: hold fast to the pure, turn from the unworthy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Nittai the Arbelite used to say: keep a distance from an evil neighbor, do not become attached to the wicked, and do not abandon faith in [divine] retribution.”
judaism.explanation: Nittai of Arbel tells his students to keep away from bad neighbours and not to bind themselves to the wicked.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s second imperative, ‘shun the unsuitable’, in rabbinic form.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not associate with evil companions; do not seek the fellowship of the vile. Associate with the good friends; seek the fellowship of noble men.”
buddhism.explanation: The verse sets avoidance of evil companions directly beside the seeking of noble friends.
buddhism.tie_back: Its two halves mirror the Kural’s maruvuka and oruvuka almost exactly.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If he does not meet with a clever companion who surpasses or equals him in virtue, he should live by himself, abstaining from sins and not devoted to pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's teaching sets a high bar for companionship: a companion equal or superior in virtue, and otherwise solitude rather than company with someone unworthy.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to cling to the friendship of the blameless and to leave unfit friends whatever it costs, and the Jain canon likewise accepts only virtuous companions and prefers solitude to unworthy company.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! I will remain in the Saadh Sangat, the Company of the Holy, even if I have only coarse bread to eat. Whatever will be, will be. I will not associate with the faithless cynics.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir resolves to hold to good company at any material cost, even a diet of coarse bread, and to refuse the company of faithless people whatever the consequences.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to cling to the friendship of the blameless and leave the unsuitable even if it costs you something; Kabir accepts poverty as the price of keeping good company and shunning bad.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir 99 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A bad neighbour is as great a plague as a good one is a great blessing; he who enjoys a good neighbour has a precious possession. Not even an ox would die but for a bad neighbour.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells Perses that the people living closest to you are either a blessing or a plague.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hesiod puts the good associate and the bad one side by side and counts the first as a treasure.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 346-348 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Perfect friendship is the friendship of men who are good, and alike in virtue; for these wish well alike to each other qua good, and they are good themselves.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the highest friendship exists only between good people who are alike in virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s ‘alike in virtue’ is the opposite of the Kural’s oppilaar, the unlike or unfit whose friendship should be left.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Eisenhower accepts the resignation of Sherman Adams
real_life_example.event: In 1958 a congressional subcommittee revealed that Sherman Adams, President Dwight D. Eisenhower's chief of staff, had accepted gifts, including a vicuna coat and an oriental rug, as well as hotel bills from his old friend Bernard Goldfine, a New England textile manufacturer in trouble with federal regulators, and that Adams had contacted those agencies about Goldfine's cases. Eisenhower at first defended Adams publicly, but as pressure from his own party mounted before the 1958 elections, Adams resigned, and Eisenhower accepted the resignation with deep regret on 22 September 1958.
real_life_example.explanation: Adams's career was lost to an unwise friendship, and Eisenhower had to give up his most valued aide to protect his administration.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural urges us to cling to the blameless and to let go of unsuitable associations even at a cost, and Eisenhower paid the price of losing an aide he greatly valued because of Adams's ties to Goldfine.

tamil:
பழைமை எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதும்
கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு.
transliteration:
Pazhaimai enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhum
kizhamaiyaik keezhndhidaa natpu.
meaning: What is an old friendship? It is one where you never get upset, in any way, when an old friend acts freely with you because you are close.
elementary: A brand-new classmate has to knock before borrowing your pencil. Your oldest friend just picks it up, and you don’t mind at all. That not-minding is what a really old friendship looks like.
university: The chapter opens with a definition. Pazhaimai (பழைமை, ‘oldness’) is the friendship that has grown old, and kizhamai (கிழமை) is the ‘right’ or ‘claim’ (urimai, உரிமை) that such long intimacy creates; keezhndhidaa (கீழ்ந்திடா) means ‘does not cut down, belittle or set aside’. Read with yaadhum (‘in anything at all’), the couplet says that true old friendship never treats the friend’s presumptions as offences. Parimelazhagar places the chapter directly after Natpaaraaydhal (testing a friend before befriending) and the commentarial tradition reads it as the next stage: once a friend has been tested and kept, the bond should bear the freedoms that time brings. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss the couplet as accepting what the old friend does by right of intimacy, while Puliyur Kesigan reads it more broadly as a friendship that lets nothing damage the established bond. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a father tolerates his son, a friend forgives his friend, and a lover pardons the beloved, please forgive me for my offences.”
hinduism.explanation: After seeing Krishna’s cosmic form, Arjuna asks to be forgiven for years of easy familiarity, appealing to the forbearance a friend naturally shows a friend.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita takes for granted exactly what the Kural defines: a true friend does not hold the liberties of intimacy against the other.

christianity.quote_or_event: Ben Sira advises his student not to forsake an old friend, because a new friend cannot compare with him: a new friend is like new wine, which is enjoyed best once it has aged.
christianity.explanation: Sirach ranks the long-tested friend above any newcomer and compares maturing friendship to wine that improves with age. Sirach is deuterocanonical, part of Catholic and Orthodox Scripture but not the Protestant canon.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Ben Sira gives the old friend a standing that a new acquaintance cannot claim.

islam.quote_or_event: “the Prophet (ﷺ) used to mention her very often, and when ever he slaughtered a sheep, he would cut its parts and send them to the women friends of Khadija.”
islam.explanation: Aisha recalls that, years after Khadija died, the Prophet kept honouring the friends of his first wife.
islam.tie_back: This shows the faithfulness to old ties that the Kural calls pazhaimai, kept up long after the relationship began.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All love that depends on a something, [when the] thing ceases, [the] love ceases; and [all love] that does not depend on anything, will never cease. … And what is an example of love that did not depend on anything? Such was the love of David and Jonathan.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah says that love which depends on some benefit ends when the benefit ends, but love that depends on nothing lasts forever, as David and Jonathan’s did.
judaism.tie_back: Love that ‘depends on nothing’ does not keep accounts of slights, so it fits Valluvar’s definition of a friendship that nothing diminishes.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:16 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He gives what is hard to give. He does what is hard to do. He endures what is hard to endure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists qualities that make a friend worth keeping, starting with generosity, effort and endurance on the friend’s behalf.
buddhism.tie_back: Enduring what is hard to endure includes putting up with what an intimate friend does, which is the forbearance the Kural describes.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.35, Mitta Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “If after contracting a firm friendship with any one, I set myself to note his good and bad qualities, may I be cast into the hell where the traitor who discovers the secrets of his friend is punished, and may I be scoffed at by the whole world!”
jainism.explanation: The Jain didactic poet binds himself by an oath never to sit in judgement on a friend once the friendship is firmly made.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural defines old friendship as the bond that never belittles the freedoms an intimate friend takes, and the Naladiyar treats auditing a settled friend's conduct as a kind of treachery.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Bhai Mardana, a Muslim minstrel of Guru Nanak's own village and ten years older than him, went to Sultanpur and, in the words of the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, never parted company with Guru Nanak again; he played the rabab as the Guru sang through all his long journeys until his death at Kartarpur in 1534.
sikhism.explanation: Mardana is the classic Sikh example of a lifelong companion: a friend from childhood who stayed with Guru Nanak across decades of travel and hardship.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines old friendship as a bond that has grown through long closeness and bears the freedoms that time brings; the decades-long companionship of Guru Nanak and Mardana is the Sikh tradition's picture of such a friendship.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, ed. Harbans Singh (Punjabi University, Patiala), entry 'Mardana, Bhai (1459-1534)' by Satbir Singh (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus comes home in disguise after twenty years, his old hound Argos, neglected and lying on a dung heap, recognizes him at once, wags his tail and drops his ears, and then dies.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer gives the first recognition of the returning hero to an old companion whose attachment twenty years of absence had not worn away.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Argos is a picture of the bond the Kural praises, one that time and changed circumstances do not reduce.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The older the sweeter, as in wines that keep well. And the proverb is a true one, "You must eat many a peck of salt with a man to be thorough friends with him."”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius argues that, other things being equal, old friendships should be preferred to new ones, since friendship grows richer with age.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero and Valluvar agree that time is what gives friendship its value and its rights.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 19 (§67), trans. E. S. Shuckburgh

real_life_example.event_title: Theo van Gogh refuses to treat his brother's requests as a debt
real_life_example.event: From about 1880 until 1890, Theo van Gogh, an art dealer in Paris, sent his brother Vincent regular remittances, estimated at around 17,500 francs in total, that made Vincent's career as a painter possible. Vincent often asked for more and wrote of the money as something he owed. In letters of 1888 and 1889 Theo replied that he knew nothing of any debt and that Vincent had repaid him several times over through his work and his brotherly affection.
real_life_example.explanation: Theo's support was one of the main reasons Vincent could keep painting through ten years with almost no sales, and Theo consistently treated Vincent's constant claims on him as a natural part of their bond rather than as impositions.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines long-standing closeness as the bond that never belittles the claims an intimate makes on it, and Theo answered Vincent's repeated requests by denying there was any debt at all.

tamil:
நட்பிற் குறுப்புக் கெழுதகைமை மற்றதற்கு
உப்பாதல் சான்றோர் கடன்.
transliteration:
Natpir kuruppuk kezhudhakaimai matradharku
uppaadhal saandror kadan.
meaning: The freedoms friends take with each other are part of friendship. Good people should welcome those freedoms and enjoy them.
elementary: Salt makes food taste right. In a friendship, the little freedoms friends take, like finishing your sentences or grabbing a fry off your plate, are the salt. A good person does not complain about the salt; they enjoy the meal.
university: Uruppu (உறுப்பு, ‘limb, constituent part’) makes kezhudhakaimai (கெழுதகைமை, ‘the quality of intimate right’) a structural part of friendship, not an extra. The second line turns on uppu (உப்பு, ‘salt’), which the commentators read figuratively as relish or sweetness: the wise should be the salt to that intimacy, accepting it and taking pleasure in it. Mu. Varadarasanar reads uppaadhal as ‘agreeing to’ the friend’s act of right, Solomon Pappaiah as ‘rejoicing at it’, and Puliyur Kesigan as ‘acting as the very model of that intimacy’. G. U. Pope’s ‘to be its savour sweet is duty of the wise’ keeps the image of salt. Saandror (சான்றோர்) are the cultivated people whose kadan (கடன், ‘duty, obligation’) this is. Both base sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the poor Brahmin Sudama visits his childhood friend Krishna, now a king, he is too ashamed to offer the handful of flattened rice he has brought. Krishna pulls the bundle from him himself and eats it with delight.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna takes an old friend’s liberty, grabbing a gift that was not offered, and treats the humble rice as a treasure.
hinduism.tie_back: The episode shows familiarity working as the ‘salt’ of friendship: freedom taken and freedom received with joy on both sides.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells his disciples that he no longer calls them servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing, but calls them friends, because he has made known to them everything he heard from the Father.
christianity.explanation: The relationship moves from formal service to the openness of friendship, defined by shared confidence.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, intimacy and its freedoms are what separate friendship from a mere formal tie.

islam.quote_or_event: After the emigration to Medina, the Prophet paired emigrants with Medinan helpers as brothers. Sa‘d ibn al-Rabi‘ offered his new brother ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf half of his property; ‘Abd al-Rahman thanked him, declined, and asked only to be shown the market.
islam.explanation: The early brotherhood (mu’akhat) was a bond of such familiarity that each could claim from the other what strangers could not.
islam.tie_back: Islamic tradition treats such claims between bonded friends as natural and generous, which is the urimai the Kural calls part of friendship itself.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Merits of the Helpers (Ansar), report of Sa‘d ibn al-Rabi‘ and ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf

judaism.quote_or_event: “appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: Joshua ben Perahiah tells each person to make the effort to gain a companion and to read others’ actions charitably.
judaism.tie_back: Gaining a companion and judging generously together come close to the Kural’s view that taking friends’ freedoms in good part is a duty.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:6 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the advice to Sigala, the Buddha says a lay follower should treat friends with generosity, kind speech, helpfulness, impartiality and sincerity, and lists among the marks of a true friend one who is the same in happiness and in sorrow.
buddhism.explanation: Friendship is described as a set of mutual, reciprocal duties.
buddhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the Buddha makes friendship a duty for good people, not just a pleasure.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though they do evil exceedingly, is it not fitting to be patient with one's friend? … the forbearance of one is the friendship of both.”
jainism.explanation: The poet makes forbearance the thing that holds a friendship together: when one friend bears with the other, both keep the bond.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls the freedoms of intimacy a structural part of friendship that the wise should welcome, and the Naladiyar likewise treats bearing with a friend as what friendship is made of.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 3 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: According to the Puratan Janamsakhi, soon after leaving Sultanpur Mardana complained of hunger, went to a nearby village on the Guru's suggestion, and came back loaded with a bundle of gifts; Guru Nanak rolled on the ground laughing, and Mardana, seeing the oddity of what he had done, threw the bundle away.
sikhism.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism notes that the biographers tell several such humorous stories of Mardana's amiable faux pas, which the Guru met with laughter and patience rather than reproach.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the freedoms friends take are part of friendship and the good should welcome and relish them; Guru Nanak's laughter at Mardana's blunder shows that kind of easy, affectionate tolerance between old companions.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, ed. Harbans Singh (Punjabi University, Patiala), entry 'Mardana, Bhai (1459-1534)' by Satbir Singh, citing the Puratan Janamsakhi (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles and Patroclus grew up together in Peleus’ house and share a tent, food and armour at Troy; Patroclus’ ghost asks that their bones lie together in one urn.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad presents their companionship as shared life and shared possessions, built up from childhood.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their total familiarity, with nothing held back, is the kind of bond in which the Kural says liberties are part of friendship.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “to comrades and brothers one should allow freedom of speech and common use of all things.”
philosophy.explanation: Discussing what is owed to different kinds of people, Aristotle says close companions are owed frankness and shared use of possessions.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly Valluvar’s point: the freedoms of intimacy belong to friendship, and allowing them is a duty.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.2 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Elgar's Enigma Variations portray his friends with affectionate humour
real_life_example.event: Between October 1898 and February 1899 Edward Elgar composed a set of orchestral variations in which each variation is a musical portrait of one of his circle, often built on a friend's quirks or on humorous incidents, such as an organist's bulldog falling into a river and paddling out. He dedicated the work to the friends pictured in it, and his publisher and close friend August Jaeger appeared as Nimrod. The work was first performed under Hans Richter on 19 June 1899 and became Elgar's breakthrough.
real_life_example.explanation: The Enigma Variations turned the teasing familiarity of a circle of friends into one of the best-loved works of English music, with the affectionate Nimrod variation now used at national commemorations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the freedoms friends take with one another are part of friendship itself and that the wise relish them, and Elgar's friends were immortalised precisely through the playful liberties he took with their foibles.

tamil:
பழகிய நட்பெவன் செய்யுங் கெழுதகைமை
செய்தாங்கு அமையாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Pazhakiya natpevan seyyung kezhudhakaimai
seydhaangu amaiyaak kadai.
meaning: What good is a friendship of many years if you will not accept what your close friend does, as if you had done it yourself?
elementary: Imagine your best friend signs both your names on a birthday card for your teacher without asking. If you get cross, what was all that friendship for? A real friend says, ‘Good idea, that’s what I would have done.’
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: evan seyyum (எவன் செய்யும், ‘what will it do?’) asks what use a long-practised friendship (pazhakiya natpu) has if one does not seydhaangu amaidhal (செய்தாங்கு அமைதல்), ‘acquiesce as though one had done it oneself’, in what the friend did by kezhudhakaimai (intimate right). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take this as owning the friend’s act; Solomon Pappaiah adds that this holds even when one does not personally agree with it. Puliyur Kesigan reads the line from the other side: if the same intimacy is not present in the friend too, the long acquaintance is useless. That reading shows the couplet can be taken as a statement about reciprocity. The text is the same in both base sources (with the sandhi form seyyung).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And if, jestfully, I treated You with disrespect, while playing, resting, sitting, eating, when alone, or before others—for all that I crave forgiveness.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna remembers years of casual companionship with Krishna, joking, eating and resting together, and Krishna never took offence.
hinduism.tie_back: Krishna accepted his friend’s familiar behaviour without complaint, which is the acceptance the Kural says gives an old friendship its value.

christianity.quote_or_event: Writing to his friend Philemon, Paul sends back the runaway Onesimus, now a Christian, and asks Philemon to receive him as he would receive Paul himself, offering to repay any debt and noting that Philemon owes Paul his own self.
christianity.explanation: Paul uses the freedom of an old friendship to ask a great deal and trusts Philemon to treat the request as his own.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ideal in practice: a friend’s act of familiarity received as if one had done it oneself.

islam.quote_or_event: When Abu Bakr and ‘Umar fell out, the Prophet told those present not to leave his companion exposed to blame, reminding them that Abu Bakr had believed in him when others called him a liar.
islam.explanation: The Prophet defended the standing of a long-standing companion against criticism of his conduct.
islam.tie_back: He treated an old friend’s place as his own concern, which is close to the Kural’s ideal of owning a friend’s acts.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Companions, narration of Abu al-Darda’

judaism.quote_or_event: On the day David kills Goliath, Jonathan’s soul is bound to David’s. Jonathan makes a covenant with him and, without being asked, gives David his own robe, armour, sword, bow and belt.
judaism.explanation: The prince hands over the symbols of his rank to the friend he loves.
judaism.tie_back: Jonathan treats what is his as David’s, the complete identification of interests the Kural asks of old friends.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He reveals his secrets to you. He keeps your secrets.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the marks of a friend worth keeping, the Buddha lists mutual confidence: sharing secrets and guarding the other’s.
buddhism.tie_back: That kind of mutual trust is what lets a friend act for you and have it accepted as your own act.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.35, Mitta Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Is it right utterly to abandon friends, who ought not to be forsaken though guilty of evil deeds? … will men cut off their hand because it has struck the eye?”
jainism.explanation: The poet compares a friend's offence to one's own hand striking one's own eye: nobody cuts off the hand, because it is part of oneself.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use an old friendship is if one will not accept a friend's act as though one had done it oneself, and the Naladiyar's image of the hand and the eye makes the friend's act literally one's own.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 6 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My Guru is always with me, near at hand. … Your actions seem so sweet to me.”
sikhism.explanation: In this Aasaa shabad Guru Arjan speaks of the Guru as an ever-present companion and says that whatever the Beloved does is sweet to him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use long friendship is if one will not accept what the friend does by right of closeness as though one had done it oneself; Guru Arjan's line shows that attitude of owning and welcoming whatever the closest companion does.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Iphigenia among the Taurians, Orestes and Pylades each insist on dying in the other’s place, and each treats the other’s fate as his own.
greek_mythology.explanation: The two cousins and companions are so close that neither will accept survival at the other’s cost.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their friendship makes no distinction between ‘his act’ and ‘mine’, which is the identification the Kural requires.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Every one likes ceteris paribus to use the horse to which he has been accustomed, rather than one that is untried and new.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero argues that habit and long familiarity give old friendships a weight that new ones do not have.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar asks what long familiarity is worth, and Cicero answers that its worth lies in the ease that habit brings.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 19 (§68), trans. E. S. Shuckburgh

real_life_example.event_title: Louis Howe writes and speaks for Franklin Roosevelt during his illness
real_life_example.event: After Franklin Roosevelt was paralysed by illness in 1921, his old friend and adviser Louis Howe kept Roosevelt before the public by meeting supporters, attending meetings on his behalf and writing editorials and magazine articles, some published under Roosevelt's own byline. Roosevelt kept Howe as his closest counsellor, valued his frank advice and, after winning the presidency, made him his personal secretary with a room in the White House. Howe continued to speak bluntly to Roosevelt until his death in 1936.
real_life_example.explanation: Howe's work in Roosevelt's name helped carry him from apparent political ruin to the governorship of New York and the presidency.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use a long friendship is if one will not accept what the friend does by right of closeness as though one had done it oneself, and Roosevelt allowed Howe's words to go out under his own name.

tamil:
விழைதகையான் வேண்டி இருப்பர் கெழுதகையாற்
கேளாது நட்டார் செயின்.
transliteration:
Vizhaidhakaiyaan vendi iruppar kezhudhakaiyaar
kelaadhu nattaar seyin.
meaning: When close friends do something for you without asking, wise people are happy about it, because it came from someone they love.
elementary: Your friend sees your bike tyre is flat and pumps it up while you are at lunch, without asking. You don’t say, ‘Who gave you permission?’ You say, ‘Thanks!’ That is how old friends treat each other.
university: The key phrase is kelaadhu (கேளாது, ‘without asking’): the friend acts for us kezhudhakaiyaal, ‘by the right of intimacy’. The wise respond vizhaidhakaiyaan (விழைதகையான், ‘because of its desirability’), and vendi iruppar, ‘remain as those who wanted it’. Mu. Varadarasanar emphasises honouring the right itself, while Solomon Pappaiah says the wise accept the act even when they already knew of it, because it was done willingly by a friend. Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesigan make the same point more plainly: a good friend accepts what was done unasked. The couplet assumes a household culture in which a close friend may lawfully use or dispose of what is ours. Both base texts agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sudama leaves Krishna’s palace without having asked for anything. When he gets home, he finds that Krishna has already, without a word, turned his hut into a mansion and ended his poverty, and Sudama accepts the gift with humility and gratitude.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna acts for his old friend without being asked, and the friend receives it as an act of love, not an intrusion.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s situation: a friend acts unasked out of intimacy, and the other welcomes it.

christianity.quote_or_event: In a parable, Jesus describes a man who goes to his friend at midnight and asks to borrow three loaves for an unexpected guest, sure that friendship gives him the right to ask even at that hour.
christianity.explanation: The parable assumes that a friend may make demands that would be unthinkable from a stranger.
christianity.tie_back: It reflects the same culture of intimate claims the Kural assumes, though here the friend asks and is grudgingly answered.

islam.quote_or_event: “or [from houses] whose keys you possess or [from the house] of your friend. There is no blame upon you whether you eat together or separately.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an lists a friend’s house among the places where a believer may eat without blame, alongside the homes of close relatives.
islam.tie_back: This makes into law the liberty the Kural describes: a close friend may take from what is ours without a formal request.

judaism.quote_or_event: Years after Jonathan’s death, King David asks whether anyone of Saul’s house is left to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan’s sake. He brings Jonathan’s lame son Mephibosheth to his table for life and restores Saul’s lands to him, though no one had asked him to.
judaism.explanation: David acts unprompted on the strength of an old friendship.
judaism.tie_back: This is friendship acting without being asked; Mephibosheth’s humble acceptance mirrors the welcome the Kural expects.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The monastic code allows a monk to take an item ‘on trust’ (vissāsa) from a friend when five conditions are met: they are acquainted, intimate, the friend has spoken of it, the friend is alive, and the monk knows the friend will be pleased when the item is taken.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist monastic law recognises that among intimates, taking without asking is not theft if the friend would be pleased.
buddhism.tie_back: It is almost the Kural’s exact situation: an act done unasked by right of intimacy, and accepted because the friend wanted it.
buddhism.source: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga VIII (rule on taking on trust)

jainism.quote_or_event: “In a thing done by strangers, though in itself exceeding bad, what is there fitted to give pain? Considered rightly, it is the acts of those who are affectionately attached; which, O lord of the land where the waterfalls murmur! will be esteemed excellent, abiding in the mind.”
jainism.explanation: The poet holds that the acts of those bound to us by affection are, rightly considered, treasured in the mind as excellent, unlike the acts of strangers.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the wise welcome what a close friend does unasked as something they wanted, and the Naladiyar similarly says a loving friend's acts are prized for the love behind them.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: When Mardana lay dying at Kartarpur in 1534, Guru Nanak asked how he wished his body to be disposed of; Mardana replied that by the Guru's teaching he had overcome pride in the body, and whatever remained should be disposed of as the Guru wished. He declined a tomb, and the Guru consigned his body to the River Ravi.
sikhism.explanation: Mardana left the most personal decision of all to his old companion without asking for anything, trusting that whatever Guru Nanak chose would be right.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the wise welcome what a close friend does for them unasked, as though they had wanted it; Mardana's leaving his own last rites to Guru Nanak shows that complete trust in an old friend's choices.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, ed. Harbans Singh (Punjabi University, Patiala), entry 'Mardana, Bhai (1459-1534)' by Satbir Singh (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pirithous raids Theseus’ cattle to test his famous strength. When the two men meet, each is so taken with the other that Pirithous offers to pay whatever penalty Theseus names, and Theseus instead forgives the raid and offers friendship.
greek_mythology.explanation: As Plutarch tells it, a liberty taken without leave becomes the start of a lifelong friendship rather than a quarrel.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Theseus welcomes an unasked act instead of resenting it, as the Kural advises, though here the friendship begins rather than having aged.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is fitting to go unasked and readily to the aid of those in adversity (for it is characteristic of a friend to render services, and especially to those who are in need and have not demanded them; such action is nobler and pleasanter for both persons)”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle praises the friend who helps without being asked, and says such help is more pleasant for both sides.
philosophy.tie_back: He shares Valluvar’s view that friendship works best through unasked acts that both sides welcome.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.11 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Emerson's friends rebuild his house and send him abroad after a fire
real_life_example.event: On 24 July 1872 a fire badly damaged Ralph Waldo Emerson's house in Concord, destroying the roof and much of the second floor. Without being asked, Emerson's friends raised money to restore the house; his Harvard classmate Francis Cabot Lowell personally delivered a gift of 5,000 dollars from himself and other friends, and Judge Ebenezer Hoar presented a further sum collected to pay for a journey to Europe and Egypt. Emerson accepted, travelled with his daughter Ellen, and returned on 27 May 1873 to find the house restored and the town waiting to welcome him.
real_life_example.explanation: The episode shows a community of old friends acting on its own initiative to rescue a dispirited friend, and Emerson's grateful acceptance of what they had arranged.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the wise welcome what close friends do for them unasked, as if they had wanted it themselves, and Emerson accepted both the rebuilding and the journey his friends had planned without consulting him.

tamil:
பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க
நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்.
transliteration:
Pedhaimai ondro perungizhamai endrunarka
nodhakka nattaar seyin.
meaning: If a friend does something that hurts you, think that it came either from not knowing better or from being so close that they felt free to do it.
elementary: If your best friend borrows your favourite book and spills juice on it, think: ‘Maybe they didn’t know it mattered so much, or maybe they just felt at home with my things.’ Don’t decide straight away that they meant to hurt you.
university: Pedhaimai (பேதைமை, ‘ignorance, folly’) and perungizhamai (பெருங்கிழமை, ‘great intimacy, strong right of friendship’) are the two charitable explanations the couplet offers for an act that is nodhakka (நோதக்க, ‘fit to cause pain’). The particle ondro (ஒன்றோ) divides the commentators. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as ‘either … or’: ignorance or intimacy. Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘not ignorance only, but also great intimacy’. Puliyur Kesigan reads it as rejecting ignorance altogether: think of it as intimacy, not ignorance. The pairing is close to Arjuna’s pramādāt praṇayena vā (‘through carelessness or through affection’) in Bhagavad Gita 11.41, a parallel worth noting even though no direct influence can be shown. The text is the same in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I was ignorant of Your majesty, showing negligence and undue affection.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna explains his past familiarity with Krishna by two causes: pramāda (negligence) and praṇaya (affection).
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita offers the same two explanations as the Kural, pedhaimai and perungizhamai: an offence comes either from not knowing or from too much closeness.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 11.41 (trans. Swami Mukundananda; Sanskrit pramādāt praṇayena vāpi)

christianity.quote_or_event: From the cross, Jesus prays for those crucifying him, asking the Father to forgive them because they do not know what they are doing.
christianity.explanation: Jesus treats even a grave wrong as coming from ignorance and asks for pardon on that ground.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s first explanation, pedhaimai, ignorance becomes the reason for charity.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet warned believers against suspicion, calling it the most untruthful kind of talk, and told them not to spy on one another.
islam.explanation: Hadith literature urges believers to think well of one another (husn al-zann) instead of assuming bad intent.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise tells us to assume harmless causes when a friend’s act stings.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Good Manners (Adab), hadith on suspicion

judaism.quote_or_event: “appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches dan le-khaf zekhut: judging others favourably by tipping the scale toward innocence.
judaism.tie_back: Reading a hurtful act as ignorance or intimacy is this favourable judgement applied to a friend.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:6 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada advises attending to one’s own deeds, done and undone, rather than to the faults of others and what they have or have not done.
buddhism.explanation: The verse moves attention away from cataloguing others’ wrongs.
buddhism.tie_back: Declining to dwell on a friend’s offence is the habit of mind the Kural recommends.

jainism.quote_or_event: “But for the following fifteen good qualities he is called well-behaved: if he is always humble, steady, free from deceit and curiosity; if he abuses nobody; … if he listens to friendly advice; … if he is not angry with friends; if he speaks well even of a bad friend behind his back …”
jainism.explanation: Among the marks of a well-disciplined monk, the Uttaradhyayana lists not being angry with friends, not holding on to wrath, and speaking well even of a bad friend.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks us to put a friend's hurtful act down to ignorance or intimacy, not malice, and the Jain canon likewise asks the disciplined person not to be angry with friends and to speak kindly even of a friend who errs.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.10–13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! Where there is spiritual wisdom, there is righteousness and Dharma. Where there is falsehood, there is sin. Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir ranks forgiveness (khima) as the highest of the virtues he lists, the place where God Himself is present.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to excuse a friend's hurtful act as ignorance or the freedom of great intimacy; Kabir's salok gives the Sikh ground for that charity, since forgiveness is where God dwells.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir 155 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles lets Patroclus fight in his armour but warns him only to drive the Trojans from the ships. Carried away, Patroclus pursues them to the walls of Troy and is killed, bringing Achilles terrible grief, yet Achilles never blames him and mourns him above everyone.
greek_mythology.explanation: The disobedience that cost Achilles his dearest friend came from eagerness and loyalty, not malice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles reads his friend’s fatal act as zeal, not betrayal, much as the Kural asks.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises that when someone treats you badly or speaks ill of you, you should remember that they act from what seems right to them, and that they, not you, bear the harm of their mistaken view.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic method is to explain another’s wrong by their own mistaken judgement, which takes the sting out of personal offence.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s first explanation, pedhaimai, turned into a mental discipline.

real_life_example.event_title: Carlyle forgives John Stuart Mill after the French Revolution manuscript is burned
real_life_example.event: Thomas Carlyle gave his friend John Stuart Mill the only complete manuscript of the first volume of his history of the French Revolution for comment. While it was in Mill's household it was burned by a maid who mistook it for waste paper and used it to light a fire. Mill, distressed, paid Carlyle compensation; Carlyle rewrote the volume, the book was published in 1837, and Mill was one of the first to praise it.
real_life_example.explanation: Carlyle's response turned a disaster that could have ended the friendship into one of the most famous examples of literary forbearance, and the rewritten book made his reputation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks us to put down a hurtful act by a friend to ignorance or to the closeness that made them careless, and Carlyle treated the loss caused by Mill's household as an accident rather than an offence.

tamil:
எல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் துறவார் தொலைவிடத்தும்
தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Ellaikkan nindraar thuravaar tholaividaththum
thollaikkan nindraar thodarpu.
meaning: People who keep to the rules of true friendship will not leave old friends, even when that friendship causes them loss.
elementary: Suppose your oldest friend accidentally makes your team lose the big game. A true friend doesn’t say, ‘We’re done.’ They say, ‘We’ve been friends forever, and one bad game won’t change that.’
university: The couplet balances ellai (எல்லை, ‘limit, boundary’) against tholl-ai (தொல்லை, ‘antiquity’): ellaikkan nindraar are those who stand within the limit (of friendship’s ethic), and thollaikkan nindraar are those who have stood with us from long ago. Tholaividaththum (தொலைவிடத்தும்) is read by most commentators as ‘even in loss or ruin’, from tholai- ‘to be destroyed’. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all take it as ‘even when the old friend’s acts bring harm’. Puliyur Kesigan reads it spatially, ‘even when they have gone to distant places’, and also takes thollai in its modern sense of ‘trouble’, giving ‘those who stood by us in our troubles’. The two readings change the image but keep the ethic of not abandoning old friends. Both base sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the war, Krishna tells Karna that he is Kunti’s eldest son and could be king of the Pandavas. Karna refuses: Duryodhana gave him honour and friendship when others mocked his birth, and he will not desert him now, even knowing the Kaurava side will lose.
hinduism.explanation: In the Udyoga Parva, Karna chooses an old friend’s cause over a throne, knowing it will cost him his life.
hinduism.tie_back: He embodies the Kural’s ‘those who will not give up long-standing ties even in ruin’.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Karna’s reply to Krishna), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul blesses the household of Onesiphorus, who often refreshed him, was not ashamed of his chains, and searched Rome diligently until he found him, while others in Asia turned away.
christianity.explanation: Onesiphorus stayed loyal when association with the imprisoned Paul was costly.
christianity.tie_back: He kept the bond when others broke it, as the Kural’s friend keeps faith in loss.

islam.quote_or_event: During the flight from Mecca, Abu Bakr hid with the Prophet in the cave of Thawr while their enemies searched for them; the Qur’an remembers him as ‘the second of the two’ to whom the Prophet said not to grieve, for God was with them.
islam.explanation: Abu Bakr stayed with his long-time companion at the moment of greatest danger.
islam.tie_back: His steadfastness is the Kural’s refusal to give up an old bond when it brings peril.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not; neither go into thy brother's house in the day of thy calamity: for better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs urges loyalty to one’s own friends and to friends inherited from one’s father, even above distant kin.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Forsake not’ is the Kural’s thuravaar (‘they will not give up’) applied to old, even inherited, friendships.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When misfortunes strike, he doesn't abandon you. When you're down & out, he doesn't look down on you.”
buddhism.explanation: Two of the seven marks of a friend worth keeping are loyalty in misfortune and respect in decline.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s friend who does not let go even in loss.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.35, Mitta Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Even though they do what is disagreeable, one should preserve as gold those who ought not to be forsaken. Daily do men seek for fire and keep it in their house, though it has consnmed both their good house and gold.”
jainism.explanation: The poet says that a true friend should be kept like gold even when he causes harm, just as people keep fire in the house though fire has burned houses and gold.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says those who keep within friendship's bounds will not give up old friends even when the bond brings them loss, and the Naladiyar's fire that has cost house and gold yet is still kept is the same teaching.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 5 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! If the mortal continues to love the Lord in the end, as he pledged in the beginning, no poor diamond, not even millions of jewels, can equal him.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir praises love that stays the same at the end as it was at the beginning, and says such constancy is worth more than any treasure.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who keep to the true bounds of friendship never give up long-standing friends even when it costs them; Kabir prizes the same constancy of a love kept to the end as it was pledged.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir 153 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Through twenty years of Odysseus’ absence, the swineherd Eumaeus keeps faith with his master, refuses to serve the suitors’ interests, and welcomes the disguised stranger kindly, at cost and risk to himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: Eumaeus’ loyalty to an old bond holds up through loss, hardship and pressure from those in power.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the Kural’s ‘one who stands within the bounds’ and does not give up an old tie.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Surely he should keep a remembrance of their former intimacy, and as we think we ought to oblige friends rather than strangers, so to those who have been our friends we ought to make some allowance for our former friendship, when the breach has not been due to excess of wickedness.”
philosophy.explanation: Even where a friendship can no longer continue, Aristotle says past intimacy still creates obligations.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, holds that old friendship keeps its claim even after the friend has changed.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Vice President Truman attends the funeral of Tom Pendergast
real_life_example.event: Tom Pendergast, the Kansas City political boss who had backed Harry Truman's early career, was convicted of income tax evasion in 1939 and died on 26 January 1945. Truman, Vice President of the United States for little more than a week, attended the funeral despite considerable public controversy. In a statement he said that Pendergast had always been his friend and that he had always been Pendergast's.
real_life_example.explanation: Truman accepted damage to his own reputation at the start of his national career rather than abandon an old friend who had fallen into disgrace.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who keep to the true bounds of friendship will not give up a long-standing bond even when it brings them loss, and Truman stood by Pendergast's memory at real political cost.

tamil:
அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார் அன்பின்
வழிவந்த கேண்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Azhivandha seyyinum anbaraar anbin
vazhivandha kenmai yavar.
meaning: People whose friendship has grown through many years of love do not stop loving, even when their friends do things that cause them great harm.
elementary: Think of a very old tree with deep roots. A storm can break some branches, but the tree is still standing the next day. A friendship that has grown for years is like that: even a big hurt doesn’t pull it out of the ground.
university: Azhivandha (அழிவந்த) are ‘things that bring destruction’, and the concessive seyyinum (‘even if they do’) leads to anbaraar (அன்பறார், ‘they do not cut off love’). The subject is anbin vazhivandha kenmaiyavar, ‘those whose kenmai (கேண்மை, friendship) has come along the way of love’, which commentators take as long-standing, inherited affection. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as friendship come down ‘from of old’ (தொன்றுதொட்டு), and Solomon Pappaiah as long-standing friendship. Puliyur Kesigan alone shifts the subject, reading it as ‘our love for them will not be cut off’. The couplet is the strongest statement of the chapter’s ideal and has been criticised by modern readers as possibly encouraging tolerance of harm; the traditional commentators keep it within the framework of a tested, virtuous friendship (compare chapter 80). The text is identical in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Rama helps him win back his kingdom, Sugriva forgets his promise to search for Sita while he enjoys his restored court. Rama is angered and sends Lakshmana to warn him, but when Sugriva repents, Rama receives him back and the alliance holds.
hinduism.explanation: In the Kishkindha Kanda, a friend’s neglect threatens Rama’s whole cause, yet Rama does not abandon the friendship.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama keeps his affection despite an act that threatened ruin, though his initial anger is greater than the Kural’s ideal allows.
