christianity.quote_or_event: Peter, one of Jesus’ closest companions, denies him three times on the night of his arrest. After the resurrection, Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him and entrusts him with feeding his sheep.
christianity.explanation: The betrayal is answered with restored intimacy and trust, not rejection.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus’ love for Peter does not end even after the deepest failure, the Kural’s anbaraar in Gospel form.

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those of virtue among you and wealth swear not to give [aid] to their relatives and the needy and the emigrants for the cause of Allāh, and let them pardon and overlook. Would you not like that Allāh should forgive you?”
islam.explanation: Classical commentators link this verse to Abu Bakr, who had vowed to stop supporting his relative Mistah after Mistah joined in slandering Aisha. After the verse came down, Abu Bakr resumed the support.
islam.tie_back: A long-standing bond survives a grievous injury, which is what the Kural asks of those whose friendship comes down the path of love.
islam.source: Qur’an 24:22 (Sahih International); occasion of revelation per Ibn Kathir

judaism.quote_or_event: When Saul rages at Jonathan that as long as David lives Jonathan will never be king, Jonathan still defends David, warns him, and renews their covenant, giving up his own claim to the throne.
judaism.explanation: Jonathan’s loyalty to David costs him his inheritance and his father’s favour.
judaism.tie_back: His love continues even though the friendship ruins his prospects, as the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, the Buddha’s cousin and an early follower, tries to split the Sangha and to have the Buddha killed. The Buddha meets him without hatred, and later tradition says Devadatta will himself eventually attain awakening.
buddhism.explanation: Even repeated attempts at destruction by a kinsman and former companion do not turn the Buddha to enmity.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the outer limit of the Kural’s ideal: love not cut off despite ruinous acts.
buddhism.source: Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga VII; later commentarial tradition

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men will not be angry, but be patient concerning the friendship of those whom they themselves have courted, though these persons act towards them with constant hate.”
jainism.explanation: The poet compares friends to good water that keeps bursting the bank yet is still drawn up: those who have chosen a friend stay patient even when the friend treats them harshly.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says those whose friendship has come a long way through love do not stop loving even when friends bring them ruin, and the Naladiyar likewise asks patience toward chosen friends who repeatedly do harm.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 2 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger. Your body shall not suffer from any disease, and you shall obtain everything.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, counsels returning good for harm and refusing to let anger take root in the mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those whose friendship has come down a long road of love do not stop loving even when their friends bring them ruin; Farid's counsel to answer evil with goodness is the disposition that makes such love possible.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381-1382, Salok Sheikh Farid 78 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theseus joins Pirithous on his reckless plan to carry off Persephone from the underworld, though he knows it is folly, and both are trapped on enchanted seats in Hades until Heracles frees Theseus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Theseus stays loyal to his friend’s ruinous plan and pays for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He keeps the bond even when the friend leads him to ruin, a vivid if cautionary version of the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If they are capable of being reformed one should rather come to the assistance of their character or their property, inasmuch as this is better and more characteristic of friendship.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that when a friend goes wrong, the friendly response is to help him recover rather than to break off at once.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar he favours keeping faith with an erring friend, though he allows a break with the incurable.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Joachim keeps playing Brahms and accepts the Double Concerto after their rift
real_life_example.event: During the breakdown of violinist Joseph Joachim's marriage, Johannes Brahms wrote a private letter of support to Amalie Joachim that was later read in the divorce proceedings, and Joachim broke off their long friendship. Joachim nevertheless kept performing Brahms's music, and in 1887 Brahms wrote the Double Concerto for violin and cello as a gesture of reconciliation. Joachim rehearsed it with Brahms at Baden-Baden, played it at the premiere in Cologne in October 1887, and received the manuscript inscribed to him for whom it was written.
real_life_example.explanation: A friendship of more than thirty years survived a deep personal injury, and the reconciliation produced one of the great works of the violin repertoire.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those whose friendship has come down a long road of love do not stop loving even when friends do things that bring them ruin, and Joachim went on championing Brahms's music after Brahms's letter had harmed him in court.

tamil:
கேளிழுக்கம் கேளாக் கெழுதகைமை வல்லார்க்கு
நாளிழுக்கம் நட்டார் செயின்.
transliteration:
Kelizhukkam kelaak kezhudhakaimai vallaarkku
naalizhukkam nattaar seyin.
meaning: Some people trust a close friend so much that they will not listen when others talk about that friend’s faults. For them, the day the friend really does wrong is a good day, because it proves their trust.
elementary: Someone at school whispers, ‘Your best friend said something mean about you.’ You say, ‘I don’t believe it.’ Later your friend really does make a mistake, and you work it out together. Your trust was strong enough to survive both the gossip and the mistake.
university: The couplet plays on repeated sounds: kel (கேள், ‘friend, kin’) + izhukkam (இழுக்கம், ‘fault’) is ‘a friend’s fault’, and kelaa (கேளா) is ‘not listening’. Its subject is the person vallaar (வல்லார், ‘skilled, strong’) in kezhudhakaimai who refuses to hear of a friend’s faults. The difficulty is naalizhukkam (நாளிழுக்கம்). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah, following the older interpretation, take the day the friend errs as a fruitful or useful day (பயனுள்ள நாள்) for such a person. Kalaignar reverses it: if friends wrong someone of such trust, all the days of that friendship are wasted. Puliyur Kesigan reads it as the friend’s fault seeming to be merely the fault of the day. G. U. Pope (‘The day his friend offends will day of grace to him appear’) follows the first reading. The text is the same in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Bharata arrives at Chitrakuta with an army, Lakshmana suspects he has come to kill Rama and secure the throne, and urges Rama to fight. Rama refuses to believe ill of his brother and rebukes Lakshmana, and Bharata comes in fact to beg Rama to return.
hinduism.explanation: In the Ayodhya Kanda, Rama will not listen to a suspicion against someone bound to him by long love.
hinduism.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s kelizhukkam kelaa: refusing to hear accusations against an intimate.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Bharata’s arrival at Chitrakuta)

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul writes that love thinks no evil, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things and endures all things, and Peter adds that love covers a multitude of sins.
christianity.explanation: The New Testament describes love as slow to suspect and quick to cover a fault.
christianity.tie_back: This is the posture of the Kural’s friend, who will not hear accusations and takes a real fault calmly.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an tells believers that if an untrustworthy person brings them news, they should verify it, lest they harm people in ignorance and come to regret what they did.
islam.explanation: Reports against others are not to be acted on until verified.
islam.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s refusal to take on trust others’ stories about a friend’s faults.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the person who covers an offence for love’s sake with the one who keeps repeating it and so divides close friends.
judaism.tie_back: Refusing to repeat or hear of a friend’s fault keeps the friendship, as the Kural teaches.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Describing right speech, the Buddha says the disciple does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to divide people, but reconciles those who are divided and encourages those who are united.
buddhism.explanation: Divisive tale-bearing (pisuna vaca) is listed among the kinds of wrong speech.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural approaches the same evil from the listener’s side, by refusing to hear the tale.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Lord of the cool land where the waters brightly shine! the good will not look upon the faults of others after mixing with them (in friendship), though they act disagreeably. Persons destitute of strength of mind who take up evil things and speak of them after mixing (in friendship), are themselves inferior to those of whom they speak.”
jainism.explanation: The poet says that good people will not dwell on a friend's faults, and that those who gossip about a friend's failings are lower than the friend they talk about.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises the friend so secure in intimacy that he will not even listen to talk of his friend's faults, and the Naladiyar similarly puts the one who talks of a friend's faults below the friend himself.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', stanza 7 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
sikhism.explanation: Farid tells the wise not to keep a record of other people's faults but to examine their own.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the person so secure in friendship that he will not even listen to talk of his friend's faults; Farid's refusal to write black marks against others is the same refusal to dwell on a companion's failings.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid 6 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the legend of Damon and Pythias (Phintias), Pythias is condemned by the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse, and Damon stands surety for his life. When others mock him for trusting that Pythias will return, Damon refuses to doubt his friend, and Pythias does come back in time.
greek_mythology.explanation: Damon will not listen to the scorn and suspicion of others about his friend’s faithfulness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His trust is the Kural’s refusal to hear of a friend’s faults.
greek_mythology.source: Legend of Damon and Pythias, reported by Cicero and Valerius Maximus

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch’s essay on telling a flatterer from a friend warns that flatterers often try to slander a man’s true friends to him, and that a wise person guards against such whispering.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch treats slander against one’s friends as a typical tactic of the false companion.
philosophy.tie_back: This is why the Kural praises the friend who will not even listen.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend (Moralia)

real_life_example.event_title: Queen Victoria defends Abdul Karim against her household
real_life_example.event: Abdul Karim arrived from Agra in 1887 to serve Queen Victoria, became her munshi, or teacher, in 1889, taught her Urdu and was later named her Indian Secretary. His rise caused turmoil within the royal household and among government officials, who tried to separate them and accused him of having access to political papers. The Queen supported him in every case, insisted he did not read political papers, and provided for him until her death in 1901.
real_life_example.explanation: The episode shows a monarch refusing to let courtiers' complaints undermine a trusted friendship, in a court where many of the objections reflected prejudice.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the person so secure in an intimate friendship that they will not even listen to talk of the friend's faults, and Victoria refused to hear her household's charges against Abdul Karim.

tamil:
கெடாஅ வழிவந்த கேண்மையார் கேண்மை
விடாஅர் விழையும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kedaaa vazhivandha kenmaiyaar kenmai
vidaaar vizhaiyum ulagu.
meaning: The world loves people who never leave friends whose friendship has lasted, unbroken, for many years.
elementary: People trust the kid who has had the same best friend since kindergarten. If you stick with old friends, others think, ‘I would like a friend like that too.’
university: Kedaaa (கெடாஅ) and vidaaar (விடாஅர்) carry isai-nirai alapedai, a metrical lengthening that also adds emphasis: ‘never ruined’ and ‘never letting go’. Vazhivandha kenmaiyaar are ‘those whose friendship has come down along an unbroken path’. The main verb vizhaiyum ulagu, ‘the world desires or loves’, makes loyalty to old friends a source of public esteem. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read ‘the world praises’, while Puliyur Kesigan reads ‘everyone in the world will want such a person as a friend’. Solomon Pappaiah adds the qualification ‘even if the old friend does harm’, linking this couplet to 807. The text is the same in both base sources; the sandhi-split ytamizh form keeps the alapedai spellings.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Hitopadesha’s first book, Mitralabha, tells how a crow, a mouse, a tortoise and a deer become firm friends and rescue one another again and again from hunters and snares; their steadfastness is held up as the model of winning friends.
hinduism.explanation: The fable collection offers lasting friendship as practical wisdom that everyone admires.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the world loves the faithful friend, and the Hitopadesha teaches that faithfulness as a model.

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that a friend loves at all times and that a brother is born for adversity.
christianity.explanation: Constant love in every season is presented as the mark of the true friend.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s unbroken friendship is this ‘love at all times’, and it wins admiration.

islam.quote_or_event: In a hadith qudsi, God asks on the Day of Resurrection where those are who loved one another for His glory, and promises to shade them on the day when there is no shade but His.
islam.explanation: Friendship kept for the sake of God is promised the highest honour.
islam.tie_back: The Kural promises the world’s love to the steadfast friend; the hadith promises divine honour.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim, Book of Virtue, Good Manners and Joining of Ties

judaism.quote_or_event: After the story of Honi the Circle-Drawer, who slept seventy years and woke to find no one who knew him, the Talmud records the saying ‘either companionship or death’ (o chavruta o mituta).
judaism.explanation: Life without one’s long-known companions is portrayed as not worth living.
judaism.tie_back: This shows how much is lost when old bonds are broken, and so why the Kural honours those who keep them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Sigala that a true friend is the same in happiness and in sorrow: he shares one’s troubles and is ready even to give up his life for one’s sake.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta portrays the loyal companion as someone to be cherished as a mother cherishes her child.
buddhism.tie_back: Cherishing the steadfast friend parallels the Kural’s ‘the world loves’ the loyal.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men cleave not to those to whom their hearts cleave not, within a short space of time; but will the friendship which cherishes the memory of those who are intertwined with one's heart be abandoned, though they are absent from us for a long time?”
jainism.explanation: The poet contrasts quick attachments with the deep friendship that holds on to the memory of a friend even through long absence.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says the world loves those who never let go of friends whose bond has come down unbroken through the years, and the Naladiyar likewise praises a friendship that is not abandoned over long years apart.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Bhai (later Baba) Buddha met Guru Nanak as a boy and served the Gurus for the rest of a very long life: he applied the tilak at the installation of Guru Angad and of the four Gurus after him, helped dig the tank at Amritsar, became the first granthi of the Harimandar in 1604, and trained the young Hargobind. When he died in 1631, Guru Hargobind was at his bedside and gave his shoulder to the bier.
sikhism.explanation: Baba Buddha's unbroken loyalty across six Gurus made him one of the most venerated figures of early Sikhism, honoured by the Guru himself at his death.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the world loves those who never let go of friendships handed down through the years; Baba Buddha, who kept faith with the Gurus' house for over a century, is remembered with exactly that love and honour.
sikhism.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, ed. Harbans Singh (Punjabi University, Patiala), entry 'Buddha, Baba (1506-1631)' by Gurdip Singh Randhawa (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orestes and Pylades, companions from childhood who stand together through exile, matricide and danger in Tauris, became the proverbial pair of perfect friends for later Greek and Roman writers.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their unbroken loyalty earned them lasting fame as the model of friendship.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The world’s admiration of them is exactly the Kural’s vizhaiyum ulagu.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Iphigenia in Tauris; later classical reception

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And the proverb is a true one, "You must eat many a peck of salt with a man to be thorough friends with him."”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius quotes the proverb that only long shared life makes a complete friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘friendship come down an unbroken path’ is a friendship of many pecks of salt.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 19 (§67), trans. E. S. Shuckburgh

real_life_example.event_title: Lafayette's farewell tour and his visit to Washington's tomb
real_life_example.place: United States, including Mount Vernon, Virginia
real_life_example.event: At President James Monroe's invitation, the Marquis de Lafayette returned to the United States in August 1824 and over the next year visited all twenty-four states, greeted by parades and crowds, including an estimated two-thirds of New York City on his arrival. On 17 October 1824 he visited the tomb of his old friend and mentor George Washington at Mount Vernon, leaving it in tears, and he renewed friendships with Jefferson, Madison and other veterans of the Revolution. Congress granted him 200,000 dollars and land, and towns and squares across the country were named in his honour.
real_life_example.explanation: Nearly fifty years after the Revolution, Lafayette's unbroken loyalty to Washington and to his American comrades made him the most celebrated guest the young nation had ever received.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world loves those who never let go of friendships that have come down unbroken through the years, and a whole nation turned out to honour Lafayette's lifelong fidelity to Washington and his old companions.

tamil:
விழையார் விழையப் படுப பழையார்கண்
பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியா தார்.
transliteration:
Vizhaiyaar vizhaiyap paduba pazhaiyaarkan
panbin thalaippiriyaa thaar.
meaning: People who never lose their good feelings for old friends, even when those friends make mistakes, are loved even by their enemies.
elementary: There is a kid in class who is always loyal to friends, even when they mess up. Even the kids who don’t like them much have to admit, ‘Well, they’re a really good friend.’ Loyalty earns respect even from rivals.
university: Vizhaiyaar (விழையார், ‘those who do not wish one well’, i.e. enemies) becomes the agent of vizhaiyappaduba (‘are desired, loved’), a chiasmus: the unloving come to love. Pazhaiyaarkan (பழையார்கண்) is ‘toward old friends’, and panbin thalaippiriyaadhaar are ‘those who do not part from their disposition of goodwill’. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all supply ‘even though the friends do wrong’, carrying over the theme of 805-808. Puliyur Kesigan reads the reward as enemies wanting such a person as a friend. Closing the chapter with enemies’ esteem completes an arc from defining pazhaimai (801) to its social reward (809-810). Both base texts agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the battle at Kurukshetra, Yudhishthira lays down his weapons, walks across to the opposing army and bows to Bhishma, who is fighting for the Kauravas out of old loyalty to the Kuru throne. Bhishma blesses him, and both sides revere the old patriarch throughout the war.
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma’s steadfast loyalty to his old bonds wins the reverence of the side he is fighting against.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that even those on the other side honour the one who does not depart from old ties.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (Yudhishthira seeks blessings before battle), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul urges believers, quoting Proverbs, that if an enemy hungers they should feed him, for by doing so they heap coals of fire on his head, and he tells them to overcome evil with good.
christianity.explanation: Steadfast goodness is presented as the way to change an enemy’s heart.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise expects goodness that does not waver to win over those who wish one ill.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon, the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that answering evil with good can turn an enemy into a devoted friend.
islam.tie_back: As the Kural says of the loyal friend, unwavering goodness makes those who wished ill come to love.

judaism.quote_or_event: Avot de-Rabbi Natan asks who is the mightiest of the mighty and answers: one who makes his enemy into his friend.
judaism.explanation: The rabbinic text treats turning an enemy into a friend as the highest strength.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural describes the same transformation, enemies coming to love, as the reward of steadfast friendship.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world; it is appeased only by non-hatred, and this is an eternal law.
buddhism.explanation: Lasting goodwill, not retaliation, is what ends enmity.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s unwavering goodwill likewise wins over those who wish one ill.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the virtuous Kitra, for old friendship's sake, loved the king who was attached to sensual pleasures, and as he had at heart his welfare, he spoke to him the following words”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citta, meeting King Brahmadatta, his brother and companion through several past births, keeps his old affection for him and seeks his good even though the king has given himself to sensual pleasures.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises those who never part from their goodwill toward old friends even when the friends go wrong, and Citta's continued love for a straying old companion is a canonical Jain example of that loyalty.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.15, 'Citta and Sambhūta' (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
sikhism.explanation: Farid counsels meeting hostility with humility instead of retaliation.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who never fall from goodwill toward old friends, even when the friends err, are loved even by those who wish them ill; Farid's refusal to strike back is the kind of steady goodwill that can disarm ill-wishers.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the battlefield at Troy, the Greek Diomedes and the Lycian Glaucus discover that their grandfathers were guest-friends. Though on opposite sides, they refuse to fight each other, exchange armour, and part as friends, honouring the ancient bond.
greek_mythology.explanation: An inherited friendship from earlier generations is respected even in the middle of war.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Loyalty to pazhaiyaar, old ties, turns enemies into friends, as the Kural’s last couplet says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They should, as I have been told that Cato used to say, rather be unstitched than torn in twain”
philosophy.explanation: Even when a friendship must end, Cicero advises letting it fade gently rather than breaking it violently, out of respect for what it was.
philosophy.tie_back: Both writers keep goodwill toward old friends; Cicero applies it to parting, Valluvar to never parting.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 21 (§76), trans. E. S. Shuckburgh

real_life_example.event_title: Simon Buckner, Grant's old friend and former enemy, honours him at the end
real_life_example.place: New York and Mount McGregor, New York, United States; Fort Donelson, Tennessee
real_life_example.event: In 1854 Simon Bolivar Buckner, Ulysses Grant's friend from West Point and the Mexican War, vouched for the penniless Grant's hotel bill in New York. When Buckner surrendered Fort Donelson to Grant in 1862, Grant demanded unconditional surrender but, remembering his old friend's kindness, offered him money for his captivity. In July 1885 Buckner, a former Confederate general, made a personal visit to the dying Grant at Mount McGregor and served as one of his pallbearers in New York in August 1885 alongside Union generals Sherman and Sheridan.
real_life_example.explanation: Grant's refusal to let war erase an old friendship was answered by a former enemy who chose to honour him, and the funeral became a symbol of reconciliation after the Civil War.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who never fall away from goodwill toward old friends are loved even by those who were against them, and Buckner, a general of the opposing army, came to honour Grant at his deathbed and his funeral.

tamil:
பருகுவார் போலினும் பண்பிலார் கேண்மை
பெருகலிற் குன்றல் இனிது.
transliteration:
Parukuvaar poalinum panpilaar kenmai
perukalir kundral inidhu.
meaning: Even when people with bad character act so loving that they seem to want to drink you up, it is better for that friendship to shrink than to grow.
elementary: Some people hug you so tightly and say so many nice things that it feels wonderful. But if they are not kind or honest underneath, it is better to let that friendship get smaller instead of bigger, just like you would slowly back away from a puppy that wags its tail and also bites.
university: The chapter on tee natpu (தீ நட்பு, ‘evil friendship’) opens with its sharpest image: parukuvaar (பருகுவார்), ‘those who would drink you up’, describing a show of affection so intense it seems to swallow the friend whole. The defect is panpu-ilaar (பண்பிலார்), ‘those without good character’, so the warmth is not the test; character is. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both stress that the excess is appearance (‘தோன்றினாலும்’, ‘நடிக்கும்’), and Kalaignar speaks of being drowned in a flood of affection; all agree the right course is kundral (குன்றல்), letting the bond dwindle, rather than an abrupt break. This sets the chapter’s practical tone: Valluvar is less interested in condemning bad friends than in teaching how to reduce their hold. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net; the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ‘குன்ற லினிது’, a difference of word division only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Hitopadesha’s first book, a jackal makes friends with a deer, flattering him and staying close, because he hopes to eat the deer’s flesh; he leads the deer into a farmer’s snare, and only the deer’s old friend, a crow, saves him.
hinduism.explanation: The jackal’s friendship is all warmth on the surface and appetite underneath, and the deer nearly dies of it.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘friend who would drink you up’ made literal: affection masking a wish to consume.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Book I (Mitralabha), the deer, the crow and the jackal

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him; When he speaketh fair, believe him not: for there are seven abominations in his heart.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that pleasant speech can be a cover for hostility, so fair words alone should not win trust.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it tells the reader to judge by the heart, not by the show of warmth.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he whose speech pleases you in worldly life, and he calls Allah to witness as to what is in his heart, yet he is the fiercest of opponents.”
islam.explanation: The verse describes a person whose words charm and who swears to his sincerity, yet who is in fact a bitter adversary.
islam.tie_back: Both texts warn that pleasing, affectionate speech can hide a character that works against you.

judaism.quote_or_event: Absalom, plotting against his father King David, would take the hand of anyone who came to bow before him and kiss him, and so, the narrator says, he stole the hearts of the men of Israel.
judaism.explanation: Absalom’s overflowing affection was a political tool in service of a rebellion, not a sign of good character.
judaism.tie_back: It shows exactly the Kural’s danger: lavish closeness from someone whose character does not deserve trust.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The friend who appropriates, the friend who renders lip-service, the friend that flatters, the friend who brings ruin, these four as enemies the wise behold, avoid them from afar as paths of peril.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the young Sigala that some who look like friends are really foes and should be kept at a distance.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise refuses to let the appearance of friendship decide the matter and counsels reducing contact.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Our intimacy with those to whom we are not bound by the chain of f'riendship, O king of the hills, the sides of which are covered with groves of tall sandal-trees! though it seem day by day to increase, will be dissolved as instantaneously as fire catches straw.”
jainism.explanation: The poet warns that an intimacy not grounded in real friendship may seem to grow day by day, yet it vanishes as fast as straw catches fire.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says it is sweeter for the effusive friendship of people of poor character to shrink than to grow, and the Naladiyar likewise sees no value in such growing intimacy, since it will burn away at once.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Friendship with the self-willed Manmukhs lasts for only a few short days. This friendship is broken in an instant; this friendship leads to corruption.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das warns that friendship with the manmukh, the person ruled by his own ego, is short-lived and drags one toward vice however warm it seems.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even when people of poor character seem fond enough to drink you in, it is better for that friendship to shrink than grow; Guru Amar Das explains why, since such friendship is brittle and corrupting.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 587, Raag Vadhans (Vadhans ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “How handsome is the Crow,” he exclaimed, “in the beauty of her shape and in the fairness of her complexion!”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aesop’s fable the Fox praises the Crow lavishly only to make her open her beak and drop the meat he wants.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Fox’s gushing praise is the Kural’s ‘as though they would drink you up’: warmth that serves an appetite.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Fox and the Crow (tr. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for the flatterer is a friend in an inferior position, or pretends to be such and to love more than he is loved”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle notes that the flatterer performs a love greater than he receives, and that most people enjoy this because they want to be loved.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s friend of poor character likewise wins us by an excess of displayed love, which is exactly why it must be watched.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.8 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Ferdinand Ward's firm ruins Ulysses S. Grant
real_life_example.event: After his presidency, Ulysses S. Grant became a partner in Grant & Ward, the Wall Street firm of his son Buck and the young financier Ferdinand Ward, whose apparent ability to produce large returns Grant admired, and the Grant family put most of its savings into it. Ward was secretly running what would now be called a Ponzi scheme, and in May 1884 the firm collapsed, leaving Grant nearly penniless and owing a $150,000 personal loan from William Vanderbilt. Ward was convicted of fraud and sent to Sing Sing prison, while Grant, already ill with cancer, wrote his Personal Memoirs to provide for his family.
real_life_example.explanation: Grant's warm trust in a charming partner of bad character grew year by year until it destroyed his fortune, and his memoirs were written in the shadow of that ruin.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when people of poor character seem to love you intensely, it is better for that friendship to shrink than to grow, and Grant's closeness to Ward grew until it consumed nearly everything he had.

tamil:
உறின்நட்டு அறினொருஉம் ஒப்பிலார் கேண்மை
பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என்.
transliteration:
Urinnattu arinoruum oppilaar kenmai
perinum izhappinum en.
meaning: People who are not worth having as friends become close when they can get something and leave when they cannot. It makes no difference whether you gain or lose such friends.
elementary: Imagine a classmate who sits with you only on days you bring cookies, and walks away when you don’t. Having that ‘friend’ or not having them is really the same, because they were only ever friends with the cookies.
university: The couplet is built on two paired verbs: urin nattu (உறின் நட்டு), ‘when there is gain, befriending’, and arin oruum (அறின் ஒரூஉம்), ‘when it ends, departing’; ar- here means ‘to cease or be cut off’, and oruu is the lengthened (alapedai) form of ‘leave’. The subjects are oppilaar (ஒப்பிலார்), which Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take as ‘the unworthy’ or ‘those of unequal nature’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it with a twist, ‘those who have no equal in doing this’. The closing ‘en’ (என், ‘what of it?’) is a rhetorical shrug: such friendship is neither gain nor loss. Texts differ in spelling the second word: ytamizh has ‘அறினொருஉம்’, thirukkural.net prints ‘அறின்ஙருஉம்’ (apparently a typographic slip), and the sandhi-joined edition gives ‘உறினட் டறின்னொரூஉ’; the meaning is unaffected.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who loses his money is forsaken by his friends, his wife, his servants and his relations; yet when he regains his riches those who have forsaken him come back to him.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya observes, with some cynicism, that many relationships simply follow wealth, leaving when it goes and returning when it comes back.
hinduism.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural’s friend who comes with gain and leaves with loss.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 15.5 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wealth maketh many friends; but the poor is separated from his neighbour.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs notes that prosperity attracts friends and poverty drives them off.
christianity.tie_back: Both describe friendship that tracks advantage, which is why the Kural says losing it costs nothing.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he who worships Allah on an edge. If he is touched by good, he is reassured by it; but if he is struck by trial, he turns on his face [to the other direction].”
islam.explanation: The verse describes loyalty that holds only while things go well and turns away at the first trial.
islam.tie_back: The same fair-weather pattern the Kural sees in unworthy friends: present in gain, gone in loss.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All love that depends on a something, [when the] thing ceases, [the] love ceases; and [all love] that does not depend on anything, will never cease.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah distinguishes love tied to some benefit, which ends when the benefit ends, from love that depends on nothing and lasts, citing David and Jonathan as the lasting kind.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s gain-based friendship exactly, and it explains why its loss is no loss.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is a bottle friend; one says, ‘friend, friend’ only to one’s face; one is a friend and an associate only when it is advantageous.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha lists kinds of hollow companions, including the one who is a friend only when it pays.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s urin nattu, arin oruum: friend while there is advantage, gone when there is none.

jainism.quote_or_event: “men will remain until they have done their work in an old house the thatch of which is untied, keeping out the water br a dam, and being drenched with the rain falling down upon them. Thus will friends! remain with one until their business is finished.”
jainism.explanation: The poet compares self-serving friends to men who put up with a leaking old house only until their work there is finished, and then leave.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural describes the unworthy who befriend you while there is gain and leave when it ends, and the Naladiyar's friends who stay only until their business is done describe the same thing.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 1 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The true society is the company of those who meditate on the Name of the Lord. Do not associate with those, O Nanak! Who look out only for their own interests.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan contrasts true company, built around the Name, with association with people who are only after their own advantage, and tells the Sikh to avoid the latter.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural describes unworthy people who befriend you when there is gain and leave when it ends; Guru Arjan names the same self-interested companions and says not to keep their company at all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 520, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He who shares the danger ought to share the prize.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aesop’s fable of the Two Travelers and the Axe, one man says ‘I have found an axe’, not ‘we’, but when the owner gives chase he cries ‘we are undone’; his companion tells him to keep saying ‘I’.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The finder wants partnership only in loss, the mirror image of the Kural’s friend who wants it only in gain; both are the same selfish calculation.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Two Travelers and the Axe (tr. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Lucilius that a friendship entered for one’s own advantage is a bargain, and that the man who begins to be your friend because it pays will also stop being your friend because it pays.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, friendship made for profit carries its own ending inside it, because the reason for it can disappear.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar draws the same conclusion: since such friendship comes and goes with gain, having it or losing it is all one.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 9

real_life_example.event_title: Marshal Marmont takes his corps over to the Allies
real_life_example.event: Auguste Marmont had first met Napoleon at Toulon, served as his aide-de-camp, sailed back with him from Egypt and rose under him to become a marshal and duke of Ragusa. In 1814, as the Allied armies closed in, Marmont capitulated at Paris on 30 March and on 5 April went over to the Allied side with his army corps, which had been guarding the road to Fontainebleau. Napoleon abdicated the next day, and under the restored Bourbon king Marmont was made a peer of France, while his title gave French the verb raguser, meaning to betray.
real_life_example.explanation: Marmont had shared in Napoleon's rise for twenty years, but when there was no more to be gained from him he left at the moment of greatest need.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes those who befriend you while there is gain and leave when the gain is gone, and Marmont's change of sides came exactly when Napoleon's fortunes collapsed.

tamil:
உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பும் பெறுவது
கொள்வாரும் கள்வரும் நேர்.
transliteration:
Uruvadhu seerthookkum natpum peruvadhu
kolvaarum kalvarum ner.
meaning: A friend who weighs what they can get from you, a person who loves only for money, and a thief are all alike.
elementary: If someone is your friend only after checking what they can get from you, they are a bit like a person who takes things without asking. A real friend doesn’t keep a price list.
university: Valluvar sets three figures in a row and declares them ner (நேர், ‘equal’): the friend who does seerthookkal (சீர்தூக்கல், ‘weighing on a balance’) of uruvadhu (உறுவது, ‘what will come to him’); those who take only peruvadhu (பெறுவது, ‘what they receive’); and kalvar (கள்வர், ‘thieves’). The middle phrase, peruvadhu kolvaar, is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesigan and Kalaignar, following the traditional gloss, as women who sell their company for payment; Solomon Pappaiah renders it as sex workers. The point is not to single anyone out but to define calculating friendship as a transaction for gain and to class it with taking what is not freely given. All three web texts agree on the wording; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘சீர்தூக்கு நட்பும்’ and ‘கள்வரு நேர்’, a matter of spelling convention.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The prostitute has to forsake a man who has no money, the subject a king that cannot defend him, the birds a tree that bears no fruit, and the guests a house after they have finished their meals.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya lists relationships that last only as long as there is something to take from them.
hinduism.tie_back: The list even begins with the same figure as the Kural, and makes the same point: such attachment is calculation, not friendship.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 2.17 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein.”
christianity.explanation: John explains that Judas objected to an act of generosity not out of concern for the poor but because he kept the common purse and stole from it.
christianity.tie_back: A disciple who measured everything by what he could take is the Kural’s gain-weighing friend, and John, like Valluvar, calls him a thief.

islam.quote_or_event: “And among them are some who criticize you concerning the [distribution of] charities. If they are given from them, they approve; but if they are not given from them, at once they become angry.”
islam.explanation: The verse describes people whose approval of the Prophet rose and fell with what they personally received.
islam.tie_back: Their goodwill is the Kural’s seerthookkum natpu, friendship weighed against personal gain.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many will intreat the favour of the prince: and every man is a friend to him that giveth gifts.”
judaism.explanation: This proverb in the Hebrew Bible observes that friendliness flows toward whoever has something to give.
judaism.tie_back: Friendship that follows gifts is the calculated kind the Kural classes with taking for gain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he appropriates his friend’s wealth, (ii) he gives little and asks much, (iii) he does his duty out of fear, (iv) he associates for his own advantage.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the ‘appropriator’, a foe disguised as a friend whose companionship is a way of taking.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s gain-weighing friend and the Buddha’s appropriator are the same person, and both texts treat him as a taker rather than a friend.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you impartially investigate the two things, it will be found that there is no difference between the shining light of a lamp and the love of courtesans. When the oil is exhausted, the light of the lamp vanishes, and when the money of their lovers is gone, their love also evaporates.”
jainism.explanation: The poet compares mercenary affection to a lamp that shines only while there is oil, so that the love ends as soon as the money runs out.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural puts the calculating friend on a level with those who love only for what they receive, whom the commentators identify as courtesans, and the Naladiyar's lamp image shows exactly that love which lasts only as long as the payment.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 38 'Courtesans', stanza 1 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, when there is greed, what love can there be? When there is greed, love is false. How long can one remain in a thatched hut which leaks when it rains?”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that love mixed with greed (lab) is false and gives no lasting shelter, like a leaking hut in the rain.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural puts the friend who weighs what he stands to gain in the same class as the hired companion and the thief; Farid likewise says love that calculates its profit is not love at all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid 18 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hecuba, King Priam sends his youngest son Polydorus, with a store of gold, to his guest-friend Polymestor of Thrace for safekeeping; when Troy falls, Polymestor murders the boy and keeps the gold.
greek_mythology.explanation: A sworn bond of guest-friendship is weighed against profit, and profit wins.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Polymestor is the Kural’s calculating friend who turns out to be no better than a thief.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now those who love each other for their utility do not love each other for themselves but in virtue of some good which they get from each other.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines friendship of utility as love directed not at the person but at the benefit.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the analytical version of the Kural’s friend who weighs what he will gain.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Bessus seizes Darius III and claims the Persian throne
real_life_example.event: After his defeat by Alexander the Great at Gaugamela, the Persian king Darius III retreated east, accompanied by Bessus, his relative and satrap of Bactria. In 330 BCE Bessus and other satraps arrested the king, and as Alexander's forces closed in, Darius was killed by his captors. Bessus then proclaimed himself king under the name Artaxerxes V, but within a year his own officers handed him over to Alexander, who had him executed.
real_life_example.explanation: A kinsman and trusted governor treated his fallen king as a prize to be used for his own advancement, and his gain lasted barely a year.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural sets the friend who weighs up what he stands to get beside the thief, and Bessus weighed his king's misfortune as a chance to seize the crown for himself.

tamil:
அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா அன்னார்
தமரின் தனிமை தலை.
transliteration:
Amarakaththu aatrarukkum kallaamaa annaar
thamarin thanimai thalai.
meaning: It is better to be alone than to have friends who are like an untrained horse that throws its rider off in the middle of a battle.
elementary: If you ride a bike with wobbly brakes, it might fail just when you’re going downhill. A friend who leaves you at the scariest moment is like that bike, and it’s safer to walk on your own.
university: The image is martial: amarakam (அமரகம்) is ‘the battlefield’, kallaa maa (கல்லா மா) ‘a horse that has not been trained’, and aatrarukkum (ஆற்றறுக்கும்) describes it cutting the rider off midway, whether by throwing him (Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar) or bolting from the field (Puliyur Kesigan, who widens maa to ‘an untaught beast’). Thamar (தமர்) means ‘one’s own people, intimates’, and the verdict is thanimai thalai (தனிமை தலை): solitude is supreme. The couplet sharpens the chapter’s logic: a bad friend is not merely useless but dangerous at exactly the moment you depend on him. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘அமரகத் தாற்றறுக்குங் கல்லாமா வன்னார் தமரிற் றனிமை தலை’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is better to be without a kingdom than to rule over a petty one; better to be without a friend than to befriend a rascal”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya ranks having no friend above having a bad one, in a series of ‘better without’ comparisons.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s thanimai thalai, solitude over unworthy company, stated almost word for word.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 6.13 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs compares trusting an unfaithful person in a crisis to leaning on a body part that gives way under load.
christianity.tie_back: Like the untrained horse in battle, the unfaithful man fails exactly when you put your weight on him.

islam.quote_or_event: “But when the two armies sighted each other, he turned on his heels and said, ‘Indeed, I am disassociated from you.’”
islam.explanation: The verse describes Satan encouraging the Quraysh before Badr and promising to protect them, then abandoning them as battle was joined.
islam.tie_back: A protector who vanishes when the armies meet is the Kural’s horse that throws its rider on the battlefield.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Nittai the Arbelite used to say: keep a distance from an evil neighbor, do not become attached to the wicked, and do not abandon faith in [divine] retribution.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah advises keeping one’s distance from bad neighbours and not attaching oneself to the wicked.
judaism.tie_back: Both teach that distance, even isolation, is better than attachment to people who will fail or harm you.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If for company you cannot find a wise and prudent friend who leads a good life, then, like a king who leaves behind a conquered kingdom, or like a lone elephant in the elephant forest, you should go your way alone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada advises walking alone rather than settling for unworthy companions.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s thanimai thalai in Buddhist form: solitude over bad company.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If he does not meet with a clever companion who surpasses or equals him in virtue, he should live by himself, abstaining from sins and not devoted to pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain canon tells the monk to choose a companion at least his equal in virtue, and to live alone if none can be found.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says it is better to be alone than to have companions who, like an untrained horse, throw you in the midst of battle, and the Uttaradhyayana likewise prefers solitude to an unworthy companion.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Before the battle of Bhangani (1686 or 1688), a body of Pathans who had taken service with Guru Gobind Singh on the recommendation of Pir Buddhu Shah were bought over by the hill raja Bhim Chand with promises of plunder, and most of the Udasis also deserted. Hearing of this, Pir Buddhu Shah came with his sons and several hundred followers to fight at the Guru's side, and two of his sons were killed.
sikhism.explanation: The episode sets companions who abandoned the Guru on the eve of battle against an ally who arrived when it mattered and paid for it with his sons' lives.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says it is better to be alone than to have companions like an untrained horse that throws its rider in mid-battle; the hired Pathans at Bhangani were exactly such companions, while Pir Buddhu Shah showed what a true ally is.
sikhism.source: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Bhangani', citing Harjinder Singh Dilgeer and the Bachittar Natak (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Never travel with a friend who deserts you at the approach of danger.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aesop’s fable, one traveler climbs a tree and leaves his companion to face a bear alone; the survivor says the bear ‘whispered’ this advice to him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The deserting friend is the untrained horse of the Kural, and the moral is the same: better to go alone.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Bear and the Two Travelers (tr. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca urges Lucilius to withdraw into himself as far as he can and to associate only with people who will make him better, since bad company infects the character.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, keeping one’s own company is preferable to company that weakens or corrupts.
philosophy.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s preference for solitude over unreliable companions, though on moral rather than practical grounds.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 7

real_life_example.event_title: Mir Jafar's cavalry stands aside at the Battle of Plassey
real_life_example.event: Before the battle, Robert Clive of the East India Company and the Jagat Seth bankers secretly promised Mir Jafar, one of the commanders of Siraj-ud-Daulah, nawab of Bengal, that he would become nawab if Siraj were defeated. At Plassey the nawab's army greatly outnumbered Clive's, but Mir Jafar, commanding a large body of the nawab's cavalry, kept his troops out of the fighting. Clive won, and Mir Jafar was installed as nawab, ruling largely as a puppet of the British.
real_life_example.explanation: Plassey was decided less by fighting than by a commander who abandoned his own side in the middle of the battle, and it opened the way to British rule in Bengal.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns against companions who are like an untrained horse that throws its rider in the midst of battle, and Mir Jafar left his nawab exposed at the very moment of combat.

tamil:
செய்தேமஞ் சாராச் சிறியவர் புன்கேண்மை
எய்தலின் எய்தாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Seydhemanj saaraach chiriyavar punkenmai
eydhalin eydhaamai nandru.
meaning: Small-minded people will not protect you, even after you have done a lot for them. It is better never to have their poor friendship than to have it.
elementary: Think of an umbrella with holes in it. You can carry it, take care of it and open it every time, but it still won’t keep you dry. Some friends are like that, and it’s better not to count on them at all.
university: The key compound is seydhemam saaraa (செய்தேமம் சாரா): ēmam (ஏமம்) is ‘protection, safety’, and the phrase means ‘not coming to be a protection even when it has been made one’. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as ‘though set to guard, they do not guard’, Solomon Pappaiah as ‘though we help them in many ways, they are no protection to us’, and Puliyur Kesigan as ‘they do not come to rescue us when trouble arrives’. Chiriyavar (சிறியவர்) are ‘the small’, people mean in mind, and their bond is pun-kenmai (புன்கேண்மை), ‘paltry friendship’. The conclusion, eydhalin eydhaamai nandru, ‘not attaining is better than attaining’, extends 814: such friendship is not neutral but a net loss. The text is uniform across the three sources, the sandhi-joined edition writing ‘யெய்தலி னெய்தாமை’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He is a true friend who does not forsake us in time of need, misfortune, famine, or war, in a king’s court, or at the crematorium (smasana).”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya defines a true friend by presence in hardship, listing the moments when friends are most needed.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s petty friends are the negative of this definition: they fail to be a protection when it counts.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 1.12 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge.”
christianity.explanation: Paul recalls that at his first defence before the court, none of his companions stood by him.
christianity.tie_back: It is the experience the Kural warns of: companions who are no protection in the hour of need.

islam.quote_or_event: “Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken that one as a friend.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement the wrongdoer regrets the companion who led him astray.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s eydhalin eydhaamai nandru voiced as regret: better never to have had that friend.

judaism.quote_or_event: “To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed from his friend … My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, and as the stream of brooks they pass away”
judaism.explanation: Job complains that his friends, like seasonal streams, ran dry just when he needed them.
judaism.tie_back: Job’s friends are the Kural’s pun-kenmai: no protection when it matters.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he guards the heedless, (ii) he protects the wealth of the heedless, (iii) he becomes a refuge when you are in danger, (iv) when there are commitments he provides you with double the supply needed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the true ‘helpmate’ friend as one who protects and becomes a refuge in danger.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s petty friends are the exact opposite: they never become the refuge (ēmam) a friend should be.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The friendship of illustrious men is eminently valuable, and is productive of benefit as timely rain. But the f'riendship of the mean, even in the time of their prosperity, resembles, O lord of the land of clear water! the failure of rain in its due season.”
jainism.explanation: The poet contrasts the friendship of noble people, which helps like timely rain, with the friendship of the mean, which fails you like rain that does not come when it is due.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls the friendship of small-minded people who will not protect you, even when you have done everything for them, better never gained, and the Naladiyar likewise says the friendship of the mean fails when it is most needed.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 2 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In this world, I have seen love to be false. Whether spouses or friends, all are concerned only with their own happiness. All say, “Mine! mine!”, and attach their consciousness to you with love. But at the very last moment, none shall go along with you. How strange are the ways of the world!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur observes that those who profess love and call us their own are moved by their own comfort, and none of them stands by us when it finally counts.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the paltry friendship of small-minded people, who give no protection even when you have done everything for them, is better never gained; Guru Tegh Bahadur describes those who claim us lovingly yet are not there at the decisive moment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 536, Raag Devgandhari, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Philoctetes was bitten by a snake on the way to Troy and his wound festered, his Greek comrades marooned him alone on the island of Lemnos, though he carried the bow of Heracles they would later need.
greek_mythology.explanation: The companions he had joined in a common cause abandoned him at the moment he most needed protection.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Philoctetes’ comrades are the Kural’s small-minded friends, who give no protection when it is due.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero has Laelius quote Ennius’s line that a sure friend is discerned in an unsure situation, and observes that many fail this test, deserting friends in adversity.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, adversity is the touchstone of friendship, and those who desert in hardship were never true friends.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural applies the same touchstone and concludes that friends who fail it are better not had.

real_life_example.event_title: Pompey is killed on arriving in Egypt
real_life_example.place: Off the coast of Egypt near Pelusium
real_life_example.event: After his defeat by Julius Caesar at Pharsalus, Pompey the Great sailed to Egypt, expecting help from the court of the young king Ptolemy XIII, whose father Ptolemy XII had been his ally and client. The king's advisers, including Pothinus and the general Achillas, feared offending the victorious Caesar. Pompey was killed in a small boat as he was brought ashore, before he could set foot in Egypt.
real_life_example.explanation: Pompey had supported the Ptolemaic house in its time of need, but when he came seeking protection, those he had helped gave him none.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the friendship of small-minded people who will not protect you even after you have done everything for them is better never gained, and Pompey met his end at the hands of the court he had long supported.

tamil:
பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பின் அறிவுடையார்
ஏதின்மை கோடி உறும்.
transliteration:
Pedhai perungezheei natpin arivudaiyaar
edhinmai kodi urum.
meaning: Being a stranger, or even an enemy, to wise people is worth ten million times more than being a very close friend of a fool.
elementary: If you’re building a sandcastle, a careful kid who doesn’t like you will still not knock it over, but a clumsy best friend might jump right on it while trying to help. Sometimes a sensible rival is safer than a silly friend.
university: The couplet sets pedhai perung kezheei natpu (பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பு), ‘the greatly intimate friendship of a fool’, against arivudaiyaar edhinmai (அறிவுடையார் ஏதின்மை), and the reading of edhinmai divides commentators. Edhilaar means ‘strangers, outsiders’, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take edhinmai as ‘the absence of friendship’, being unconnected to the wise; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar sharpen it to ‘enmity’ (பகை), giving the more striking proverb ‘a wise enemy is better than a foolish friend’. Kezheei (கெழீஇ) is the alapedai form of kezhu-, ‘to be closely joined’. ‘Kodi urum’ (கோடி உறும்) means ‘is worth a crore’, i.e., ten million times over. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘நட்பி னறிவுடையா ரேதின்மை’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In a Panchatantra story, a king appoints his pet monkey as bodyguard; when a fly settles on the sleeping king, the monkey swings a sword at it and kills the king, and the tale is set beside one in which a wise thief saves a life, to teach that a wise enemy is better than a foolish friend.
hinduism.explanation: The monkey’s devotion is real, but its foolishness makes its closeness deadly.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s comparison in story form: the fool’s intimacy does more harm than the wise man’s enmity.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book I (Mitrabheda), the king and the foolish monkey

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the gains of walking with the wise against the ruin that comes from keeping company with fools.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts judge friendship with fools as harmful and closeness to the wise as valuable.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of a good pious companion and an evil one is that of a person carrying musk and another blowing a pair of bellows.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a good companion to a perfume seller whose scent rubs off on you, and a bad one to a blacksmith whose bellows burn your clothes or leave a foul smell.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, simply being near the wrong person damages you, however close the bond.

judaism.quote_or_event: King Rehoboam rejected the counsel of the elders who had served his father Solomon and followed the young men who had grown up with him; their advice to answer the people harshly led ten tribes to break away.
judaism.explanation: Rehoboam preferred the familiar intimacy of foolish peers to the counsel of the wise, and lost most of his kingdom.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s warning in history: a fool’s close friendship costs far more than distance from the wise.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better it is to live alone; there is no fellowship with a fool. Live alone and do no evil; be carefree like an elephant in the elephant forest.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada declares that there is no real companionship to be had with a fool.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar and the Buddha agree that a fool’s intimacy is worth less than none.

jainism.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sûtras.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana names avoiding foolish people, together with serving one's teachers and study, as part of the road to liberation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural ranks even distance from the wise far above close friendship with a fool, and the Jain canon likewise makes keeping away from fools part of the path itself.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Friendship with a fool never works out right. As he knows, he acts; behold, and see that it is so.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad says that however close one becomes to a fool, the fool still acts only according to his own limited understanding, so the friendship can never come right.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says being a stranger to the wise is worth ten million times more than the closest friendship with a fool; Guru Angad gives the reason, since intimacy cannot change how a fool acts.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a Mouse ‘formed an intimate acquaintance with a Frog’, who tied their feet together and dragged him into the pond, where the Mouse drowned and a Hawk carried off both.
greek_mythology.explanation: A tie of close friendship with a heedless partner brings death to one and ruin to both.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural’s perung kezheei natpu, the tightly bound friendship that destroys.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Mouse, the Frog, and the Hawk (tr. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Fontaine’s fable of the Bear and the Garden-Lover ends with the moral that nothing is as dangerous as an ignorant friend and that a wise enemy would be better: the bear, guarding his sleeping friend, kills him with a paving stone while trying to swat a fly.
philosophy.explanation: The bear’s loyalty is sincere; its stupidity is what kills.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s proverb: a fool’s close friendship is worse than a wise man’s enmity.
philosophy.source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables VIII.10, L’Ours et l’Amateur des jardins

real_life_example.event_title: Charles I shields his favourite, the Duke of Buckingham
real_life_example.event: George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham, was the closest friend and chief minister of King Charles I, and he led England's war policy. A naval expedition against Cadiz in 1625 failed, and in 1626 the House of Commons blamed Buckingham and tried to impeach him, but Charles imprisoned one of the impeachment managers, Sir John Eliot, and dissolved Parliament rather than give up his favourite. Buckingham's landing on the Ile de Re in 1627 also ended in failure, and the king's quarrels with Parliament over money and his favourite deepened.
real_life_example.explanation: Charles's intimacy with an unsuccessful favourite cost him the cooperation of Parliament at the start of his reign, beginning the conflict that later led to civil war.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that distance, or even enmity, with the wise is worth far more than close friendship with a fool, and Charles chose his favourite over the counsel of Parliament at great cost.

tamil:
நகைவகைய ராகிய நட்பின் பகைவரால்
பத்தடுத்த கோடி உறும்.
transliteration:
Nakaivakaiya raakiya natpin pakaivaraal
paththaduththa kodi urum.
meaning: What you get from your enemies is worth a hundred million times more than the friendship of people who only laugh along with you.
elementary: A friend who just giggles at everything never tells you there’s spinach in your teeth. Even someone who doesn’t like you might point it out. Sometimes honest criticism helps more than easy laughter.
university: Nakaivakaiyar (நகைவகையர்) are ‘those of the laughing kind’: Mu. Varadarasanar adds ‘laughing outwardly without love within’, Kalaignar ‘those who laugh and talk as a performance’, and Puliyur Kesigan ‘those useful only for idle talk and merriment’. Against them stands what comes from pakaivar (பகைவர், ‘enemies’), worth paththaduththa kodi (பத்தடுத்த கோடி), ‘ten crore’ or a hundred million times more. The exaggeration escalates the kodi of 816. Commentators differ on what an enemy provides: most modern glosses say ‘benefit’, while Kalaignar paradoxically says even the suffering enemies cause is worth more, because it at least makes one alert. The wording agrees across ytamizh and thirukkural.net; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘நட்பிற் பகைவராற்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Of a rascal and a serpent, the serpent is the better of the two, for he strikes only at the time he is destined to kill, while the former at every step.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya prefers an open, predictable danger to the constant harm of a bad person close at hand.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks the obvious enemy above the false companion.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 3.4 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?”
christianity.explanation: Judas leads the arresting crowd to Jesus and identifies him with a friendly kiss.
christianity.tie_back: The open enemies with swords were less treacherous than the friendly gesture; the Kural likewise ranks enemies above friendship that is all surface.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Religion is sincerity.” We said, “To whom?” He said “To Allah, to His Book, To His Messenger, and to the leaders of the Muslims and their masses.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes sincere goodwill, nasiha (often rendered sincere counsel), the core of religion in every relationship.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s laughing friends offer the opposite of nasiha: pleasant noise without honest concern.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs holds that honest wounds from a true friend are worth more than an enemy’s pleasant kisses.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts value painful honesty over pleasant surface affection, though they assign the roles differently.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(iii) he tries to gain one’s favor by empty words”
buddhism.explanation: Among the marks of the ‘lip-service’ friend, a foe in the guise of a friend, the Buddha lists courting favour with empty talk.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s nakaivakaiyar, whose friendship is laughter and talk with nothing inside.

jainism.quote_or_event: “It is better to be without the love of those who are without sincerity. Death is preferable to an incurable disease. To kill him at once is more desirable than to vex a man so that he becomes sore at heart, and to abuse is better than to praise one for that which we do not possess.”
jainism.explanation: In a string of 'better than' sayings, the poet holds that it is better to have no love at all than insincere love, and better to be abused than falsely praised.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says what comes from enemies is worth far more than the friendship of those who only laugh along with you, and the Naladiyar likewise prefers open hostility to hollow affection and flattery.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 9 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If my heart is pure, and I am slandered, then the slanderer washes my clothes. One who slanders me is my friend”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir says the person who attacks him with slander actually does him good, washing away his faults, so he counts such a critic as a friend.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says what comes to you from enemies is worth far more than the friendship of those who only laugh along with you; Kabir likewise finds real benefit in his detractors, which no flattering companion can give.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Diogenes Laertius reports that Antisthenes, the follower of Socrates, advised paying attention to one’s enemies, because they are the first to notice one’s mistakes.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Antisthenes an enemy’s hostile attention is a kind of free audit.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It gives a reason for the Kural’s paradox: an enemy’s scrutiny serves you better than friends who only laugh.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book 6 (Antisthenes)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay How to Profit by One’s Enemies, Plutarch argues that an enemy’s constant watchfulness keeps a person careful and self-correcting in ways that indulgent friends do not.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch turns enmity into a moral tool: those who hunt for your faults make you guard against them.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains why Valluvar says enemies yield far more than friends who only share a laugh.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, How to Profit by One’s Enemies

real_life_example.event_title: Peter the Great rebuilds his army after defeat at Narva
real_life_example.event: In November 1700 Charles XII of Sweden routed Peter the Great's much larger Russian army at the Battle of Narva. In the following years Peter regrouped his troops and carried out sweeping military reforms, forming new regiments with modern weapons, uniforms and tactics, often with the help of foreign officers and engineers, and building up foundries and arms works. Russia retook Narva by siege in 1704 and decisively defeated Sweden at Poltava in 1709.
real_life_example.explanation: The harsh lesson of defeat by an enemy did more to make Russia a military power than years of comfortable court life had done.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that what comes from enemies is worth far more than the friendship of those who only laugh along with you, and what Peter learned from the Swedes at Narva became the foundation of his later victories.

tamil:
ஒல்லும் கருமம் உடற்று பவர்கேண்மை
சொல்லாடார் சோர விடல்.
transliteration:
Ollum karumam udatru pavarkenmai
sollaadaar sora vidal.
meaning: Some people pretend they cannot help and so spoil a job that could easily be done. Let your friendship with them quietly fade without saying anything.
elementary: If a friend always says ‘I can’t’ whenever you need a small hand, even when they easily could, you don’t need to have a big fight. You can just slowly spend more time with friends who do help.
university: Ollum karumam (ஒல்லும் கருமம்) is ‘a task that can be done’; udatrupavar (உடற்றுபவர்) are those who ‘harass’ or ruin it, which Solomon Pappaiah and the classical English versions read as feigning inability to do what they could, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar as making the possible impossible. The remedy is notably mild: sollaadaar (சொல்லாடார்), ‘without speaking of it’, sora vidal (சோர விடல்), ‘let it slacken’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read sollaadaar as ‘without letting them know’, Puliyur Kesigan as ‘by ceasing to talk with them’. The counsel is gradual disengagement rather than confrontation, a tactful way to avoid making a fresh enemy. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘ஒல்லுங் கரும முடற்று பவர்கேண்மை’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Shalya agrees to serve as Karna’s charioteer at Kurukshetra but, having privately promised Yudhishthira to weaken Karna, belittles him throughout the battle and undermines his morale.
hinduism.explanation: The man whose job was to carry Karna’s chariot to victory uses his position to spoil the very task he was given.
hinduism.tie_back: Shalya is the Kural’s udatrupavar, the companion who ruins a doable task from the inside.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva and Karna Parva (Shalya as Karna’s charioteer)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?”
christianity.explanation: James mocks those who offer warm words to someone in need while doing nothing they could easily do.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s friend who could help but finds a way not to.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they will swear by Allah, ‘If we were able, we would have gone forth with you,’ destroying themselves [through false oaths], and Allah knows that indeed they are liars.”
islam.explanation: The hypocrites excuse themselves from the expedition by claiming they were unable, when in truth they did not want the hardship.
islam.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s pretended inability over a task that could be done.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it. Say not unto thy neighbour, Go, and come again, and to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee.”
