judaism.explanation: Proverbs forbids putting off a neighbour with excuses when one is perfectly able to help now.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural describes the friend who does exactly this; Proverbs names it as a fault.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(iv) when opportunity for service has arisen, he expresses his inability.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists this as a mark of the ‘lip-service’ friend, a foe in the guise of a friend.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s udatrupavar almost word for word: the friend who pleads inability when the chance to help arrives.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though they adhere to one in friendship as closely as the small toes of a dog to one another, yet of what benefit is the love of those who do not help one even to the extent of the leg of a fly?”
jainism.explanation: The poet asks what use there is in the love of friends who cling closely yet will not help even in the smallest way.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to let friendship quietly slacken with those who spoil a task they could easily do, and the Naladiyar likewise questions the worth of close friends who will not lift a finger to help.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If a fool does a job, he cannot do it right. Even if he does something right, he does the next thing wrong.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad observes that a foolish person spoils whatever task he takes up, so his help cannot be relied on.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of those who ruin a task that could easily be done and advises letting their friendship slacken quietly; Guru Angad describes the same unreliable helper who spoils what he is given to do.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Greek leaders came to recruit Odysseus for the war against Troy, he pretended to be mad, ploughing a field with an ill-matched team; Palamedes exposed him by placing the infant Telemachus in the plough’s path.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus feigned incapacity to escape a duty he was fully able to perform.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural’s pretended inability in mythic form.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero has Laelius endorse Cato’s advice that friendships which have gone wrong should be unstitched gradually rather than torn apart, unless some intolerable wrong makes an immediate break unavoidable.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero prefers a gradual, quiet loosening to a public rupture that might turn a friend into an enemy.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s sollaadaar sora vidal, let it slacken without speaking of it, very closely.

real_life_example.event_title: Bernadotte's corps takes part in neither Jena nor Auerstedt
real_life_example.event: On the day Napoleon defeated the Prussians at Jena, Marshal Davout's single corps fought and beat the main Prussian army at nearby Auerstedt. Marshal Bernadotte's I Corps, positioned between the two battlefields, took part in neither battle, despite requests from Davout for support. Napoleon blamed Bernadotte for failing to help, but did not bring him to a court-martial; historians still debate whether Bernadotte disobeyed or was following ambiguous orders.
real_life_example.explanation: A capable marshal's corps stood idle while a colleague fought against heavy odds, and Napoleon's trust in him was never the same, though he made no public break.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises letting friendship quietly slacken, without announcement, with those who fail to do what they could easily have done, and Napoleon set aside formal punishment while his confidence in Bernadotte waned.

tamil:
கனவினும் இன்னாது மன்னோ வினைவேறு
சொல்வேறு பட்டார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Kanavinum innaadhu manno vinaiveru
solveru pattaar thodarpu.
meaning: Friendship with people whose actions and words do not match hurts you even in a dream.
elementary: If a friend promises to save you a seat and then gives it to someone else, and does it again and again, you start feeling uneasy even when you’re just thinking about them. A friend’s words and actions should match.
university: The couplet names the fault precisely: vinai veru, sol veru (வினை வேறு, சொல் வேறு), ‘deed apart, word apart’, the divorce of action from speech. Kanavinum (கனவினும், ‘even in a dream’) intensifies: such a connection hurts not only in waking life, as Puliyur Kesigan spells out, but even in sleep. Manno (மன்னோ) is an emotive particle of emphasis or lament, which Sivayogi Sivakumar renders as a rhetorical question, ‘will it not give pain even in a dream?’ The word here is thodarpu (தொடர்பு, ‘connection, association’) rather than natpu, perhaps suggesting such people never achieve true friendship. All three texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition prints ‘கனவினு மின்னாது’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Duryodhana’s side invites the Pandavas to Varanavata with gracious words and builds them a fine house there, secretly made of lac and other flammable materials so that it can be set on fire while they sleep.
hinduism.explanation: The gracious invitation and the deadly intent are the starkest split between word and deed in the epic.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s vinai veru, sol veru, and a reason such ties haunt even one’s dreams.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (the house of lac, Jatugriha)

christianity.quote_or_event: “My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.”
christianity.explanation: John insists that love must be shown in action, not only spoken.
christianity.tie_back: This is the positive form of the Kural’s complaint against those whose words and deeds diverge.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Great is hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an condemns the gap between what people say and what they actually do.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s vinai veru, sol veru is exactly the fault these verses denounce.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes a former companion whose gentle speech covered hostile intent.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s split between word and deed, and the anguish of the psalm matches ‘painful even in a dream’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he makes friendly profession as regards the past, (ii) he makes friendly profession as regards the future, (iii) he tries to gain one’s favor by empty words, (iv) when opportunity for service has arisen, he expresses his inability.”
buddhism.explanation: The ‘lip-service’ friend is all professions of goodwill about past and future, with nothing done now.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s friend whose words go one way and deeds another.

jainism.quote_or_event: “माया मित्ताणि नासेइ” (māyā mittāṇi nāsei), “Deception destroys friendship”
jainism.explanation: The Dasavaikalika names deceit (maya), one of the four passions (kashayas) that bind karma to the soul, as the passion that specifically destroys friendship.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says friendship with people whose deeds differ from their words is painful even in a dream, and the Jain canon names this kind of double-dealing as the very thing that destroys friendship.
jainism.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.38, Prakrit text with English rendering on tattvagyan.com ('Destroyer of friends')

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, there are dozens who say they are friends; I search, but I cannot find even one.”
sikhism.explanation: Farid laments that many claim friendship in words, but when he looks for one who is a friend in deed, he cannot find any.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says friendship with those whose deeds differ from their words is painful even in a dream; Farid names the same gap between people who call themselves friends and the friendship that is actually there.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Salok Sheikh Farid 87 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Achilles tells the embassy sent by Agamemnon that he hates like the gates of Hades the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles names the gap between inner intent and outward speech as the thing he most despises.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ loathing echoes the Kural’s judgment that such people are a torment even in dreams.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “… when he has been deceived by the pretences of the other person, it is just that he should complain against his deceiver; he will complain with more justice than one does against people who counterfeit the currency, inasmuch as the wrongdoing is concerned with something more valuable.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the bitterest complaints between friends arise when one pretended to love the other for his character while really loving him for profit or pleasure, and he ranks this deception above counterfeiting money.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like the Kural, treats a friendship in which outward profession differs from the real disposition as a grievous wrong.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, IX.3, 1165b (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Pizarro takes Atahualpa's ransom and executes him
real_life_example.event: In November 1532 the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca. Atahualpa offered to fill a large room with gold, and twice over with silver, in exchange for his release, and over the following months his people delivered the treasure. In 1533, having received the ransom, Pizarro had Atahualpa tried on a series of charges and executed, and the treasure was melted down and shared among the Spaniards.
real_life_example.explanation: The ransom agreement showed how worthless Pizarro's undertakings were once he had what he wanted.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that ties with people whose deeds are one thing and whose words another are painful even in a dream, and Atahualpa kept his side of the bargain only to find that Pizarro's deeds bore no relation to the terms agreed.

tamil:
எனைத்தும் குறுகுதல் ஓம்பல் மனைக்கெழீஇ
மன்றில் பழிப்பார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Enaiththum kurukudhal ombal manaikkezheei
mandril pazhippaar thodarpu.
meaning: Do not get even a little close to people who are friendly with you in private but say bad things about you in public.
elementary: Imagine someone who plays nicely with you at your house but makes fun of you in front of the whole class. That’s not a real friend, and it’s wise to keep your distance from them.
university: The chapter closes on the double-faced friend: manaik kezheei (மனைக் கெழீஇ), ‘intimate in the house’, and mandril pazhippaar (மன்றில் பழிப்பார்), ‘those who revile in the manram’, the public hall or assembly where reputations are made. The prescription is the strongest in the chapter: enaiththum kurukudhal ombal (எனைத்தும் குறுகுதல் ஓம்பல்), ‘guard against approaching in any measure at all’. Where 811 and 818 allowed a gradual waning, here even the slightest contact is to be avoided, since such a person turns private trust into public damage. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan all read manai literally as ‘home’, while Kalaignar’s gloss refers to private moments. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘எனைத்துங் குறுகுத லோம்பன்’ and ‘மன்றிற் பழிப்பார்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Avoid him who talks sweetly before you but tries to ruin you behind your back, for he is like a pitcher of poison with milk on top.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya warns against the person who is sweet in your presence and destructive in your absence.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s home-friend and public slanderer, and both texts prescribe avoidance.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 2.5 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I speak not of you all: I know whom I have chosen: but that the scripture may be fulfilled, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.”
christianity.explanation: At the Last Supper Jesus applies Psalm 41:9 to Judas, the table companion who will betray him.
christianity.tie_back: Sharing bread at home and turning on someone outside is the pattern the Kural tells us to avoid.

islam.quote_or_event: “The worst people in the Sight of Allah on the Day of Resurrection will be the double faced people who appear to some people with one face and to other people with another face.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet names the two-faced person, who shows different faces in different company, as among the worst of people.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s friend at home and slanderer in the assembly is exactly this double-faced person.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it … But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says he could have endured an enemy’s reproach, but the one shaming him is a close companion who once shared his confidence.
judaism.tie_back: This is the pain of the Kural’s friend who is intimate in private and reviles in public.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he approves of his friend’s evil deeds, (ii) he disapproves his friend’s good deeds, (iii) he praises him in his presence, (iv) he speaks ill of him in his absence.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the flatterer, a foe in the guise of a friend, as one who praises to your face and disparages you behind your back.
buddhism.tie_back: Items (iii) and (iv) are the Kural’s couplet almost exactly, and the Sutta’s remedy, to avoid such people from afar, matches its counsel.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If he is frequently angry; if he perseveres in his wrath; if he spurns friendly advice; if he is proud of his learning; if he finds fault with others; if he is angry even with friends; if he speaks evil even of a good friend behind his back … then he is called ill-behaved.”
jainism.explanation: Among the faults that mark a monk as ill-behaved and keep him from Nirvana, the Uttaradhyayana lists speaking evil of a good friend behind his back.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns against coming even slightly close to those who are friendly at home but run you down in public, and the Jain canon condemns that same two-faced disparaging of a friend as a fault that blocks liberation.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.7–9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! I have seen a person who is as shiny as washed wax. He seems very clever and very virtuous, but in reality, he is without understanding, and corrupt.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir describes a person whose polished outward show of virtue hides a corrupt nature within.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns against even slight contact with those who are friendly in private but revile you in public; Kabir's polished but corrupt man shows the same split between the face he presents and what he is.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir 139 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In one strand of the myth (Euripides’ Orestes; Diodorus Siculus 4.74), Tantalus, honoured as a guest at the gods’ own table, repaid their intimacy by blurting their secrets to mortals, and was punished eternally.
greek_mythology.explanation: Tantalus turned the privileges of private friendship into public exposure of his hosts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He fits the Kural’s pattern of intimacy at home turned against the host in public.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Orestes; Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 4.74

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The dissembler is a man, for instance, who accosts his enemies and engages readily in talk with them, to show that he bears no grudge, and who praises to their faces the very men he slanders behind their backs …”
philosophy.explanation: In the first of his character sketches, Theophrastus describes the dissembler, who is friendly in private encounters while running the same people down elsewhere.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the person the Kural warns against: friendly in private and disparaging in public.
philosophy.source: Theophrastus, Characters, I (The Dissembler) (tr. Charles E. Bennett and William A. Hammond)

real_life_example.event_title: Dickens portrays his friend Leigh Hunt as Harold Skimpole
real_life_example.event: Charles Dickens and the poet and essayist Leigh Hunt were friends of long standing. In Bleak House, published in monthly parts in 1852-53, Dickens created Harold Skimpole, a charming but irresponsible sponger, and readers who knew Hunt recognised him in the character. In a letter to John Forster in 1853 Dickens called Skimpole an exact portrait of a real man, the caricature caused Hunt much distress, and Dickens later apologised.
real_life_example.explanation: A friendship kept up in private was damaged when one friend held the other up to public ridicule in a widely read novel.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns against coming close to those who are friendly at home but run you down in public, and Dickens's private friendship with Hunt sat beside a public caricature that all their acquaintances recognised.

tamil:
சீரிடம் காணின் எறிதற்குப் பட்டடை
நேரா நிரந்தவர் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Seeridam kaanin erithar̲kup pattadai
neraa niranthavar natpu.
meaning: The friendship of people who spend time with you but are not with you in heart is like an anvil, the iron block a blacksmith hammers on. When they get the chance, they will strike you down on it.
elementary: A blacksmith’s anvil looks like a strong, steady table, but its real job is to hold the metal still so the hammer can hit it. A fake friend can feel like solid support, but they are only holding you in place until it suits them to let you get hurt.
university: The chapter title kooḍaa naṭpu (கூடா நட்பு) means ‘friendship that does not truly join’, and this opening couplet defines it: those who are neraa (நேரா, not inwardly agreeing) yet niranthavar (நிரந்தவர், outwardly close). Paṭṭaḍai (பட்டடை) is the smith’s anvil, the block on which metal is laid to be cut; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read the simile this way, Pappaiah adding that it looks like support while really serving the cutting. Seer-idam (சீரிடம்) is ‘the fitting place or occasion’, so the danger lies in timing: the false friend waits for an opening. Parimelazhagar places this chapter after Thee Natpu (82, evil friendship) as a treatment of friendship that is enmity in disguise, a theme he reads in a royal-political frame. The couplet is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After the war, the blind king Dhritarashtra asks to embrace Bhima. Krishna, sensing his grief-driven rage, pushes forward an iron statue of Bhima instead, and the old king crushes it to pieces in what was meant to look like a loving embrace.
hinduism.explanation: An embrace, the most intimate sign of affection, is turned into the very means of destruction once the chance appears.
hinduism.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s anvil, the embrace looks like support but is the place where the blow is meant to fall.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And from that time he sought opportunity to betray him.”
christianity.explanation: Judas remains among the twelve, sharing their life, while secretly waiting for the right moment to hand Jesus over.
christianity.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s ‘when they find the fitting moment’: closeness kept up while waiting for the chance to strike.

islam.quote_or_event: “How [can there be a treaty] while, if they gain dominance over you, they do not observe concerning you any pact of kinship or covenant of protection? They satisfy you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse [compliance], and most of them are defiantly disobedient.”
islam.explanation: The verse describes allies whose words please while their hearts refuse, and who will honour no bond once they gain the upper hand.
islam.tie_back: Pleasing outwardly, hostile inwardly, and waiting for the advantage: the same anatomy as the Kural’s false friend.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Their tongue is a sharpened arrow, / They use their mouths to deceive. / They speak to their fellows in friendship, / But lay an ambush for them in their hearts.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah describes a society where friendly speech covers a heart that is lying in wait.
judaism.tie_back: Friendly speech outside, an ambush inside: Valluvar’s anvil waiting for its moment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “These four, young householder, should be understood as foes in the guise of friends: (1) he who appropriates a friend's possessions, (2) he who renders lip-service, (3) he who flatters, (4) he who brings ruin.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches the layman Sigala to recognise four kinds of people who look like friends but act as enemies.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Foes in the guise of friends’ is almost a definition of the Kural’s kooḍaa naṭpu.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Avoiding the friendship of those who resemble elephants, seek the friendship of those who resemble dogs; for an elephant will kill his driver whom he has known for a long time, but a dog will wag his tail while the spear thrown at him is still in his body.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain didactic anthology warns that some companions, like a war elephant, stay docile for years and then turn on the very person who has handled them longest.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's anvil, which seems to hold you up until the moment comes to strike, is the same danger as the Nālaṭiyār's elephant that kills the driver it has long known.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 22 ('The choice of friends'), st. 3 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “False is friendship with the false and greedy. False is its foundation. O Moollah, no one knows where death shall strike.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok added after the vaars, Guru Nanak warns that a bond formed with the false and greedy rests on a false foundation, and sets it beside the unpredictability of death's blow.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures false friendship as an anvil that looks like support but is the base for a blow; Guru Nanak likewise calls such friendship false at its very foundation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Saloks Vaaran Te Vadheek (salok 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He asked me to his house, feasted me, and then butchered me most miserably as though I were a fat beast in a slaughter house”
greek_mythology.explanation: Agamemnon’s ghost tells Odysseus how Aegisthus welcomed him home with a feast, the very act of hospitality becoming the trap.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The feast is the anvil: a show of welcome that is really the place prepared for the blow.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “when he has been deceived by the pretences of the other person, it is just that he should complain against his deceiver; he will complain with more justice than one does against people who counterfeit the currency, inasmuch as the wrongdoing is concerned with something more valuable.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats pretended friendship as worse than forging money, because what is counterfeited is more precious.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers see feigned friendship as a counterfeit that does its harm precisely because it is trusted.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Germany breaks the Nazi-Soviet Pact and invades the Soviet Union
real_life_example.place: Moscow and the western Soviet Union
real_life_example.event: On 23 August 1939 Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union signed a ten-year non-aggression pact in Moscow, negotiated by their foreign ministers Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov, with a secret protocol dividing eastern Europe into spheres of influence. Hitler regarded the pact as a temporary tactical move, and in July 1940 he decided to attack the Soviet Union within the following year. On 22 June 1941 more than three million German soldiers invaded the Soviet Union, ending the pact after less than two years.
real_life_example.explanation: The pact gave each side what it wanted for a time, but for Germany it was only a platform from which to prepare the attack it had always intended.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the friendship of those who are outwardly close but not one at heart to an anvil, a seeming support that is really the base on which you will be struck when the moment comes, and the pact served Germany in exactly that way.

tamil:
இனம்போன்று இனமல்லார் கேண்மை மகளிர்
மனம்போல வேறு படும்.
transliteration:
Inampondru inamallaar kenmai magalir
manampola veru padum.
meaning: The friendship of people who act like your own family but are not will keep changing, like the heart of someone whose love depends on being paid.
elementary: Some kids are your friend only when you have the best snack at lunch. The day you have nothing to share, they sit somewhere else. Their friendship changes shape depending on what they can get.
university: Inam (இனம்) means one’s own circle or kin; inam-pondru inam-allaar are those who resemble kin but are not. Kenmai (கேண்மை) is intimacy or friendship. The comparison with magalir manam (மகளிர் மனம்) is read by Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesigan) specifically as the mind of courtesans (பொதுமகளிர் / விலைமகளிர்), whose affection follows payment, not as a judgment on women in general; Puliyur Kesigan glosses the point as changing ‘according to the gain received’. The comparison reflects the social assumptions of its age, but its logical point is clear: an attachment driven by gain changes when the gain changes. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Hitopadesha’s first book, a jackal makes friends with a deer by flattering it, while really hoping to feed on it; the deer ignores the warnings of its old friend the crow until it is caught in a snare, and the jackal waits for it to die.
hinduism.explanation: The fable shows a newcomer who copies the language of friendship but is moved only by what he can gain.
hinduism.tie_back: The jackal is ‘like kin but not kin’, and his friendship turns as soon as profit points elsewhere.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Book I (Mitralabha), the deer, the crow and the jackal

christianity.quote_or_event: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that a divided heart produces a life with no fixed direction.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s false friend is ‘double-minded’ in just this sense, so his friendship keeps shifting.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with their evil ones, they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we were only mockers."”
islam.explanation: The hypocrites present themselves as one with the believers but change their words as soon as the company changes.
islam.tie_back: They ‘seem like our own people but are not’, and their loyalty shifts with the room, as the Kural says.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Each of you, beware of your friend! / Trust not even your kinsfolk! / For every sibling takes advantage, / Every friend deals basely.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah laments a time when even those who look like family and friends seek their own advantage.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts warn that the look of kinship guarantees nothing when advantage rules the heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is a bottle friend; one says, 'friend, friend' only to one's face; one is a friend and an associate only when it is advantageous.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists kinds of companions whose friendship lasts only as long as it is convenient or profitable.
buddhism.tie_back: A friend ‘only when it is advantageous’ is the Kural’s gain-driven friendship that changes form.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men will remain until they have done their work in an old house the thatch of which is untied, keeping out the water by a dam, and being drenched with the rain falling down upon them. Thus will friends remain with one until their business is finished.”
jainism.explanation: The chapter on improper friendship in the Nālaṭiyār describes friends who stay only as long as they have something to gain, like workmen who put up with a leaking house until their job is done.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says friendship with those who only seem to be one's own shifts with what they can get; the Nālaṭiyār's friends who stay only 'until their business is finished' are the same gain-driven bond.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 24 ('Improper Friendship'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I thought that he was a great swan, so I associated with him. If I had known that he was only a wretched heron from birth, I would not have touched him.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das uses the swan and heron (a bird that only looks like a swan) to describe one who passes for a true companion but is of another nature altogether.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of people who seem like one's own kind but are not; Guru Amar Das's heron that looked like a swan is the same kind of false likeness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 585, Raag Vadahans, Vadahans Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 1), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the bat and the weasels, a bat caught by one weasel claims to be a mouse, and caught by another that hates mice claims to be a bird, changing what it is to suit whoever holds it.
greek_mythology.explanation: The bat survives by switching sides, belonging fully to no one.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s false kin likewise change their colours according to what each moment offers.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Bat and the Weasels’ (Townsend translation)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the essence of friendship being that two minds become as one, how can that ever take place if the mind of each of the separate parties to it is not single and uniform, but variable, changeable, and complex?”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero argues that friendship requires a steady, single-minded character, and that a changeable mind makes it impossible.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s point is the same: a heart that ‘changes’ cannot hold a real friendship.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 25 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Warwick the Kingmaker turns against Edward IV
real_life_example.event: Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, Edward IV's cousin, had been the chief supporter who helped make him king in 1461. After quarrels over Edward's marriage to Elizabeth Woodville and his growing independence, Warwick rebelled, fled to France in 1470, and was reconciled there with his former enemy Margaret of Anjou, wife of the Lancastrian king Henry VI. Returning to England in September 1470, he drove Edward into exile and put Henry VI back on the throne, but Edward returned and Warwick was killed at the Battle of Barnet in April 1471.
real_life_example.explanation: Warwick moved from kinsman and kingmaker to enemy as his own influence rose and fell, showing how little a kin-like bond meant when interests changed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the friendship of those who seem like your own people but are not will shift with what they can gain, and Warwick, Edward's own cousin and chief ally, changed sides when his standing at court declined.

tamil:
பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்து மனநல்லர்
ஆகுதல் மாணார்க் கரிது.
transliteration:
Palanalla kat̲rak kadaiththu mananallar
aaguthal maanaark karithu.
meaning: Even after studying many good books, people with a bad nature find it hard to become good at heart.
elementary: You can read every book about kindness and still be unkind. Knowing the rules of a game does not make you a fair player. A person who doesn’t care about you can learn lots of nice words without their heart changing.
university: Pala nalla katrak kadaiththu (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்து) means ‘even when it happens that they have learned many good things’; mana-nallar (மனநல்லர்) are the good-hearted. Maanaar (மாணார்) literally means ‘those who are not excellent’; Varadarasanar glosses it as those who have not attained greatness through inner affection, while Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as those hostile at heart (பகையுணர்வு படைத்தோர்), and Pope’s gloss ‘enemies’ follows the latter. The couplet thus warns against assuming that a learned enemy has been softened by learning: knowledge of virtue is not virtue. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Vasishtha Dharmasutra teaches that the Vedas, even learned in full with their auxiliary sciences, do not purify a person who lacks good conduct.
hinduism.explanation: The dharma tradition holds that sacred learning is no substitute for character.
hinduism.tie_back: Same claim as the Kural: much learning does not make a bad heart good.
hinduism.source: Vasishtha Dharmasutra 6.3 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 14)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul insists that knowledge without love has no worth.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts separate knowing much from being good at heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an compares those who carry scripture without living by it to a donkey loaded with books.
islam.tie_back: Learning carried but not taken to heart is the Kural’s learned man who stays unkind.

judaism.quote_or_event: “one whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, to what may he be compared? To a tree whose branches are numerous but whose roots are few, so that when the wind comes, it uproots it and overturns it”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah teaches that wisdom without matching deeds has no roots.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s learned but ill-hearted person is a tree of many branches with no root of goodness.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that reciting scripture without practising it leaves a person outside its benefits.
buddhism.tie_back: Same insight: many good texts studied do not make a good heart.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though they wash it with milk and put it to dry many days, charcoal has not the property of becoming white. Though they strike with a stick, and thrust too, understanding will not enter into the body void of virtue.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār says that someone whose nature lacks goodness is not changed by instruction, just as charcoal stays black however often it is washed in milk.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar warns that a hostile person who has studied many good books still does not become good at heart; the Nālaṭiyār's charcoal that milk cannot whiten makes the same point, that learning poured over a bad nature does not change it.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 26 ('The want of understanding'), st. 8 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That scholar who is full of greed, arrogant pride and egotism, is known to be a fool.”
sikhism.explanation: In Majh Ki Vaar Guru Nanak denies that learning by itself makes a person good: a scholar ruled by greed and ego is still counted a fool.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that those hostile at heart are not made good-hearted by much study; Guru Nanak likewise says learning does not cure a corrupt heart.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Raag Majh, Majh Ki Vaar (pauri 6), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus, the most gifted craftsman of Athens, grew jealous of his nephew and pupil Perdix (also called Talos), who had invented the saw, and threw him from the Acropolis.
greek_mythology.explanation: Supreme skill and knowledge did not prevent envy from ruling Daedalus’s heart.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s learned enemy, great learning left the heart unchanged.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heraclitus says that much learning does not teach understanding, otherwise it would have taught Hesiod and Pythagoras, Xenophanes and Hecataeus.
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus mocks famous learned men for amassing information without insight.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise denies that wide reading produces a sound heart.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, fragment DK 22 B40 (preserved in Diogenes Laertius 9.1)

real_life_example.event_title: Seneca's teaching fails to make Nero good
real_life_example.event: The Stoic philosopher Seneca became tutor to the young Nero in 49 CE and, after Nero became emperor in 54, served as one of his chief advisers. Nero relied less and less on Seneca's counsel, and around 62 Seneca withdrew from public life and devoted himself to writing philosophy. In 65, after Seneca's enemies accused him of a part in the Pisonian conspiracy against Nero, the emperor ordered his death.
real_life_example.explanation: Years of instruction by one of Rome's leading moral philosophers did not make Nero a good ruler, and in the end he turned against his own teacher.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even after studying many good books, those who lack inner nobility rarely become truly good-hearted toward you, and Nero, schooled by Seneca himself, ended by condemning him.

tamil:
முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா
வஞ்சரை அஞ்சப் படும்.
transliteration:
Mugaththin iniya nagaaa agaththinnaa
vanjarai anjap padum.
meaning: Be afraid of two-faced people who smile sweetly with their faces while their hearts mean you harm.
elementary: A shiny red apple can still have a worm inside. A big smile on the outside does not always mean kindness on the inside, so it is wise to watch what people do, not just how they smile.
university: The couplet sets mugam (முகம், face) against agam (அகம், the inner self), a pairing that will return in Kural 830. Nagaaa (நகாஅ, ‘smiling’) shows alapeḍai, the metrical lengthening of a vowel, and akaththinnaa (அகத்து இன்னா) means ‘bitter or harmful within’. Vanjar (வஞ்சர்) are deceivers, and anjappaḍum (அஞ்சப்படும்) is the impersonal ‘is to be feared’; Varadarasanar reads it as fearing to make friends with them, Kalaignar as fearing them and keeping away. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kamsa sends the demoness Putana to kill the infant Krishna. She comes as a beautiful, affectionate woman, takes the child lovingly and offers him her breast, which she has smeared with poison; Krishna draws out her life instead.
hinduism.explanation: A face of tenderness hides a murderous purpose.
hinduism.tie_back: Putana is the Kural’s sweet face over a bitter heart, in its most vivid form.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns of people whose gentle appearance hides a predatory heart.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Beware’ of the gentle outside and the wolf inside is exactly the Kural’s ‘fear those who smile but are bitter within’.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he whose speech pleases you in worldly life, and he calls Allah to witness as to what is in his heart, yet he is the fiercest of opponents.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes a man whose pleasant words and pious oaths cover deep hostility.
islam.tie_back: Pleasing on the surface, the fiercest opponent beneath: the Kural’s smiling deceiver.

judaism.quote_or_event: “with talk smoother than butter, / yet with a mind set on war; / with words that were softer than oil, / yet in fact were drawn swords.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes a former companion whose soft words hid a mind bent on war.
judaism.tie_back: Smooth words outside, swords within: the same split the Kural tells us to fear.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the use of your matted hair, O witless man? What of your garment of antelope's hide? Within you is the tangle (of passion); only outwardly do you cleanse yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha rebukes a man whose outward ascetic appearance hides inner corruption.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts warn that a pleasing outside can conceal what is tangled within.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching names deceit (māyā) as one of the four passions (kaṣāya) that bind karma, and says that deceit in particular destroys friendship.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to fear those who smile with the face while bitter within; the Jain verse explains why: such deceit is exactly the passion that destroys friendship.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam, v. 135 (from the Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.38), English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit, via jainworld.com

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, you wear your prayer shawl on your shoulders and the robes of a Sufi; your words are sweet, but there is a dagger in your heart. Outwardly, you look bright, but your heart is dark as night.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid exposes the person whose outward look and sweet words hide a dagger within.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to fear deceivers who smile with the face while the heart is bitter; Farid's sweet words with a dagger in the heart are the same split between face and heart.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1380, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 50) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe welcomes Odysseus’s men graciously into her hall and serves them a pleasant mixture of cheese, barley, honey and wine, into which she has put drugs; then she strikes them with her wand and turns them into swine.
greek_mythology.explanation: Warm hospitality is the vehicle of the harm.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Circe’s gracious welcome over a harmful purpose is the sweet face and bitter heart of the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Republic, Glaucon argues that the height of injustice is to seem just without being just, so that the unjust man wears a reputation for goodness while doing harm.
philosophy.explanation: Plato poses the problem of the person whose appearance of virtue is a mask.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s deceiver is the person who seems good to our face but is not good to us.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic, Book II (trans. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: An Lushan, the emperor's favourite, rebels against the Tang
real_life_example.event: An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkish origin, rose in the 740s to command all three northeastern military regions, with about 160,000 troops, and on his frequent visits to the capital became a personal favourite of Emperor Xuanzong and his consort Yang Guifei. Toward the end of 755, claiming a secret order from the emperor to remove the chief minister Yang Guozhong, he marched his army on the capital. He took Luoyang, proclaimed himself emperor in 756 and captured Chang'an, forcing Xuanzong to flee to Sichuan.
real_life_example.explanation: The general who had won the emperor's warm personal favour became the leader of a rebellion that shook the Tang dynasty for eight years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns against deceivers whose faces smile sweetly while their hearts are bitter, and An Lushan rose as a court favourite before turning his army against the emperor who had trusted him.

tamil:
மனத்தின் அமையா தவரை எனைத்தொன்றும்
சொல்லினால் தேறற்பாற்று அன்று.
transliteration:
Manaththin amaiyaa thavarai enaiththondrum
sollinaal ther̲ar̲paat̲ru andru.
meaning: Never trust, in anything at all, the words of people who are not with you in their hearts.
elementary: If someone keeps promising to share their toys but never does, you learn to stop believing the promise. Words are easy to say. When someone does not really care about you, what they say is not something to lean on.
university: Manaththin amaiyaathavar (மனத்தின் அமையாதவர்) are ‘those not settled with us in mind’; enaiththondrum (எனைத்தொன்றும்) means ‘in anything at all’. Theraṟpaaṯru anru (தேறற்பாற்று அன்று) means ‘it is not fit to be trusted or relied upon’, using theṟal (தேறல், clear conviction), the same root as the chapter Therindhu Thelidhal (51) on testing before trusting. Varadarasanar reads it as not trusting their words in any undertaking, and Kalaignar as not being able to reach any clear decision on such people’s words. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who trusts the words, true or false, of a foe, meets with destruction like a seeker of honey, in a pit covered with dry grass.”
hinduism.explanation: In Bhishma’s tale of the bird Pujani and King Brahmadatta, the bird refuses to trust the king’s soothing words after enmity has arisen.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘The words, true or false, of a foe’ are not to be relied on: the Kural’s exact rule.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.”
christianity.explanation: John teaches that real love is shown in action and truth, not in speech alone.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts refuse to treat words as proof of a loving heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up - they think that every shout is against them. They are the enemy, so beware of them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that the hypocrites’ appearance and speech are attractive but hollow, and that they are to be guarded against.
islam.tie_back: Attractive speech from those not one with you in heart is not to be trusted, as the Kural says.

judaism.quote_or_event: “An enemy dissembles with his speech, / Inwardly he harbors deceit. / Though he be fair-spoken do not trust him, / For seven abominations are in his mind.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that fair speech from someone hostile within must not be trusted.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Though he be fair-spoken do not trust him’ is virtually the Kural restated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who renders lip-service be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he makes friendly profession as regards the past, (ii) he makes friendly profession as regards the future, (iii) he tries to gain one's favor by empty words, (iv) when opportunity for service has arisen, he expresses his inability.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the friend whose friendship lives only in words.
buddhism.tie_back: The lip-service friend’s ‘empty words’ are exactly what the Kural says not to rely on.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Our intimacy with those to whom we are not bound by the chain of friendship, O king of the hills, the sides of which are covered with groves of tall sandal-trees! though it seem day by day to increase, will be dissolved as instantaneously as fire catches straw.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār warns that closeness with people who are not truly bound to us can look as if it is growing, yet it vanishes in an instant.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says nothing at all should be trusted from those not one with us in heart; the Nālaṭiyār agrees that a bond without a real 'chain of friendship' cannot be relied on, however warm it seems.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 24 ('Improper Friendship'), st. 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever is in the mind, comes forth; spoken words by themselves are just wind.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok in Asa Ki Vaar, Guru Angad teaches that what counts is what is in the mind, while words cut off from it are only air.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the words of those not one with you in heart cannot be relied on; Guru Angad likewise calls words empty when the heart is not behind them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 22), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Him do I hate even as the gates of hell who says one thing while he hides another in his heart”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles rejects Agamemnon’s gift-laden embassy, refusing to be won over by words that do not match the heart behind them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles, like Valluvar, will not rely on the words of one whose heart is elsewhere.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Friendship, in which, unless you both see and show an open breast, to use a common expression, you can neither trust nor be certain of anything--no, not even of mutual affection, since you cannot be sure of its sincerity.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero says that without openness of heart, nothing a friend says can be relied on.
philosophy.tie_back: Where the heart is not open and one with ours, the Kural likewise says words cannot be trusted.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 26 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Shivaji escapes from Aurangzeb's detention at Agra
real_life_example.event: Under the Treaty of Purandar, made after his defeat by the Mughal general Jai Singh, the Maratha leader Shivaji agreed to visit the court of Emperor Aurangzeb, and he arrived at Agra in May 1666 with Jai Singh's promise that he would be allowed to return home safely. The audience went badly, and Shivaji was kept under guard rather than allowed to leave. Later that year he escaped with his son Sambhaji, reached his own territory again and resumed his struggle against the Mughals.
real_life_example.explanation: Shivaji learned that the assurances given in a treaty with an opponent counted for little once he was in that opponent's power.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the words of those who are not one with you in heart should not be relied on in any matter, and Shivaji's trust in the promises of safe conduct ended in detention at Agra.

tamil:
நட்டார்போல் நல்லவை சொல்லினும் ஒட்டார்சொல்
ஒல்லை உணரப் படும்.
transliteration:
Nattaarpol nallavai sollinum ottaarsol
ollai unarap padum.
meaning: Even when enemies say good things as if they were friends, people soon see what their words really mean.
elementary: A wolf can try to sound like a sheep, but sooner or later it growls. When someone who doesn’t like you starts talking sweetly, listen carefully; the truth usually shows up quickly.
university: Naṭṭaar (நட்டார்) are friends, those who have made friendship, and oṭṭaar (ஒட்டார்) are those who do not ‘stick’ or join with us, that is, foes. Nallavai sollinum (நல்லவை சொல்லினும்) concedes that the words themselves may be good, and ollai (ஒல்லை) means ‘quickly’. The couplet is partly reassurance: false friendship tends to betray itself in speech, and Kalaignar says the meanness in such words will come out without fail. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the ‘understanding’ as recognising quickly that the words are not truly meant for our good. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the golden deer (the demon Maricha in disguise) is shot by Rama and cries out for help in Rama’s voice, Sita is frightened, but Lakshmana at once recognises the call as a demon’s trick and insists that no one could harm Rama.
hinduism.explanation: The enemy’s imitation of a beloved voice is seen through by the alert listener.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s point that hostile words dressed as friendly ones are quickly understood by the discerning.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that what people really are becomes evident from what they produce.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts trust that hidden hostility reveals itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if We willed, We could show them to you, and you would know them by their mark; but you will surely know them by the tone of [their] speech.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says the hypocrites will be recognised by the very way they speak.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the foe’s words, however friendly, quickly give him away.

judaism.quote_or_event: “His hatred may be concealed by dissimulation, / But his evil will be exposed to public view.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs promises that disguised hatred will come into the open.
judaism.tie_back: Same confidence as the Kural that false friendliness is soon unmasked.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It's through dealing with a person that his purity may be known, and then only after a long period, not a short period; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive; by one who is discerning, not by one who is not discerning.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that integrity is revealed through dealings, to an attentive and discerning observer.
buddhism.tie_back: Both say a false friend’s nature can be read; the Buddha adds that it takes time and attention.

jainism.quote_or_event: “To join oneself to many, and strive many days and examine dispositions, and take (for friends) those who are worthy, is proper. Even with a deadly serpent, to associate and afterwards to part from it will be painful.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār advises testing people's natures over many days before taking them as friends, because it is painful to part even from a bad companion once a bond has formed.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar is confident that a foe's friendly words are soon seen through; the Nālaṭiyār sets out the practical discipline behind this, a long examination of character before any friendship is accepted.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 22 ('The choice of friends'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! I have seen a person who is as shiny as washed wax. He seems very clever and very virtuous, but in reality, he is without understanding, and corrupt.”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks, Kabir describes seeing through a person who looks polished, clever and virtuous but is corrupt underneath.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the good words of foes posing as friends are quickly seen for what they are; Kabir likewise sees through the shiny surface to what lies beneath.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 139) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, the infant Hermes steals Apollo’s cattle and then denies it with innocent, sweet-sounding speeches, but Apollo sees through the lies at once and drags him before Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Charming, innocent words do not hide the truth from a discerning listener.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As the Kural says, the real meaning behind fair words is soon understood.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But if we only take reasonable care, it is as easy to separate and distinguish a genuine from a specious friend as anything else that is coloured and artificial from what is sincere and genuine.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero holds that, with reasonable care, a false friend is as easy to detect as anything counterfeit.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero and Valluvar share the confidence that the specious friend is readily seen through.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 25 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Menelik II rejects Italy's reading of the Treaty of Wuchale
real_life_example.event: In 1889 Emperor Menelik II of Ethiopia signed a treaty of friendship with Italy, known as the Treaty of Wuchale (Wichale). Article 17 in the Amharic text allowed Ethiopia to use Italy's good offices in dealing with other powers, while the Italian text made this obligatory, and Italy used its version to proclaim a protectorate over Ethiopia. Menelik rejected the claim in 1890, denounced the whole treaty in 1893, and after his victory at Adwa in 1896 Italy accepted the treaty's annulment and recognised Ethiopia's independence.
real_life_example.explanation: A treaty presented as friendship concealed a claim to control, and Menelik saw through it and refused to accept it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even when enemies speak good words as if they were friends, their real nature is soon seen, and the friendly treaty's hidden meaning was quickly recognised and repudiated by Menelik.

tamil:
சொல்வணக்கம் ஒன்னார்கண் கொள்ளற்க வில்வணக்கம்
தீங்கு குறித்தமை யான்.
transliteration:
Solvanakkam onnaarkan kollar̲ka vilvanakkam
theengu kur̲iththamai yaan.
meaning: Do not trust an enemy’s polite, bowing words. A bow bends low only so it can shoot and do harm.
elementary: When an archer pulls back a bow, it bends down low, almost like it is bowing politely. But that bend is what sends the arrow flying. Sometimes people who don’t like you act extra polite right before they try to hurt you.
university: The couplet turns on a pun in vaṇakkam (வணக்கம்), which means both ‘bowing, reverence’ and ‘bending’: sol-vaṇakkam is ‘humility in speech’, vil-vaṇakkam ‘the bending of a bow’. Onnaar (ஒன்னார்) are those who are not one with us, enemies. Since the bow’s bend ‘signals harm’ (theengu kuṟiththamaiyaan, தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்), a foe’s deferential words should be read the same way; Pappaiah and Kalaignar draw out the simile in this sense, and Pope translates ‘pliant speech’ and ‘pliant bow’. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Ravana, planning to abduct Sita, approaches her hermitage disguised as a gentle wandering ascetic, praising her with courteous and reverent words until she offers him hospitality; then he reveals his true form and carries her off.
hinduism.explanation: Humble, respectful speech is the opening move of an act of violence.
hinduism.tie_back: Ravana’s bowing words are the bent bow of the Kural, curved for harm.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?”
christianity.explanation: Judas greets Jesus with a disciple’s kiss of respect, the agreed signal for his arrest.
christianity.tie_back: A gesture of reverence used as the trigger for harm is the Kural’s bending bow.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not take as intimates those other than yourselves, for they will not spare you [any] ruin. They wish you would have hardship. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns against taking as intimates those whose words already betray hostility and whose hearts hide more.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it tells believers not to accept hostile people’s outward speech as friendship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wounds by a loved one are long lasting; / The kisses of an enemy are profuse.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts a true friend’s honest blows with an enemy’s lavish shows of affection.
judaism.tie_back: An enemy’s profuse kisses are the foe’s humble words that the Kural says not to accept.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who flatters be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he approves of his friend's evil deeds, (ii) he disapproves his friend's good deeds, (iii) he praises him in his presence, (iv) he speaks ill of him in his absence.”
buddhism.explanation: The flatterer praises to your face and undermines you behind your back.
buddhism.tie_back: His praise is the respectful ‘bowing’ speech that the Kural says hides harm.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The absence of benevolence of disposition in him whose form is beautiful is like water mixed with milk, that is pleasant to drink. For those who are wise, to become companions of the wicked is like the nâgâ playing with the female cobra.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār's chapter on improper friendship says a pleasing exterior can hide a lack of goodwill, and that the wise who keep company with the wicked are like a snake playing with a deadly cobra.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says a foe's humble, bowing speech is like the bend of a bow, which signals harm; the Nālaṭiyār similarly warns that a pleasant surface and playful closeness can hide venom.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 24 ('Improper Friendship'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Everyone bows down to himself; no one bows down to another. … The sinner, like the deer hunter, bows down twice as much. But what can be achieved by bowing the head, when the heart is impure?”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Nanak observes that the hunter stalking a deer bends lowest of all, so deep bowing can serve harm, and bowing means nothing when the heart is impure.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a foe's humble speech is like the bending of a bow, which bends only to harm; Guru Nanak's sinner who bows twice as much, like the hunter, makes the same point.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok 1 before pauri 14), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Agamemnon returns from Troy, Clytemnestra greets him with an elaborate, flattering speech of welcome and has rich purple tapestries spread for him to walk on into the palace, where she then kills him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Extravagant reverence is the prelude to murder.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Clytemnestra’s bowing welcome is the Kural’s bent bow: deference that signals harm.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu advises that when the enemy’s envoys use humble words while the enemy steps up its preparations, it is a sign that he is about to advance.
philosophy.explanation: Strategic thought reads humility from a foe as a warning, not a reassurance.
philosophy.tie_back: Sun Tzu and Valluvar both read a foe’s humble speech the way one reads a drawn bow.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Chapter IX (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Japan's envoys keep negotiating in Washington as the Pearl Harbor fleet sails
real_life_example.place: Washington, D.C., and Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, United States
real_life_example.event: Through late 1941 Ambassador Kichisaburo Nomura and special envoy Saburo Kurusu held talks in Washington with Secretary of State Cordell Hull, holding out hope of a negotiated settlement. On 26 November 1941 a Japanese carrier fleet secretly left the Kuril Islands for Hawaii while the talks continued. On 7 December the envoys reached Hull's office with Japan's reply shortly after 2 p.m. Washington time, after the attack on Pearl Harbor had already begun.
real_life_example.explanation: Courteous diplomacy continued in Washington while a striking force was already on its way, so the talks gave no warning of what was coming.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a foe's humble, bowing speech should not be trusted, just as a bow bends only to do harm, and the polite negotiations ran side by side with the preparation of the attack.

tamil:
தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும் ஒன்னார்
அழுதகண் ணீரும் அனைத்து.
transliteration:
Thozhuthagai yullum padaiyodungum onnaar
azhuthagan neerum anaiththu.
meaning: An enemy may hide a weapon in the hands they fold before you in respect. Their tears hide harm in the same way.
elementary: Imagine someone bowing to you with hands pressed together, but hiding a water balloon behind them. Pretend sadness can be a trick too. If someone has been mean to you, a show of respect or tears doesn’t always mean they have changed.
university: Thozhuthagai (தொழுதகை) is the hand joined in worship or salutation, and paḍai oḍungum (படை ஒடுங்கும்) means ‘a weapon lies concealed’. The second line extends the image: onnaar azhutha kaṇṇeer (ஒன்னார் அழுத கண்ணீர், the tears foes have wept) is anaiththu (அனைத்து, of that same kind). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the couplet literally as a weapon concealed in the worshipping hand, and Kalaignar adds that even in weeping their hearts are full of plotting. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; thirukkural.net prints the words as தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் and கண் ணீரும் with the same metrical division.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And O Bharata, speak soft words before thou smitest and even while thou art smiting! After the smiting is over, pity the victim, and grieve for him, and even shed tears.”
hinduism.explanation: The minister Kanika gives Dhritarashtra a cynical lesson in statecraft: gentle words and tears can be used as cover for violence.
hinduism.tie_back: Kanika’s counsel is the exact practice the Kural warns about: a foe’s tears that are part of the weapon.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 142, Kanika’s counsel (Ganguli translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he sent them to Bethlehem, and said, Go and search diligently for the young child; and when ye have found him, bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also.”
christianity.explanation: Herod claims he wants to worship the child, while planning to kill him.
christianity.tie_back: Herod’s ‘worship’ is the worshipping hand with a weapon hidden inside.

islam.quote_or_event: “Here you are loving them but they are not loving you, while you believe in the Scripture - all of it. And when they meet you, they say, "We believe." But when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you in rage.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes people who profess faith to the believers’ faces but rage against them in private.
islam.tie_back: Their profession of belief is the joined hand, and their private rage the hidden weapon.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joab said to Amasa, “How are you, brother?” and with his right hand Joab took hold of Amasa’s beard as if to kiss him. Amasa was not on his guard against the sword in Joab’s [left] hand, and [Joab] drove it into his belly”
judaism.explanation: Joab greets his rival with a brotherly embrace while holding a sword in his other hand.
judaism.tie_back: A hand of greeting with a weapon hidden in the other is the Kural’s image made into history.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bilara Jataka, a jackal poses as a holy ascetic, standing on one leg and facing the sun in apparent worship. Rats come to pay him respect, and as they leave he seizes and eats the last of them each day, until the Bodhisatta, king of the rats, exposes him.
buddhism.explanation: A posture of worship is used as the cover for killing.
buddhism.tie_back: The jackal’s devotion is the worshipping hand that hides the weapon.
buddhism.source: Bilara Jataka (Jataka No. 128), trans. in E. B. Cowell (ed.), The Jataka

jainism.quote_or_event: “A little monkey breaking into a fruit with its finger, will strike and seize its own father, though coming to meet it. Lord of the hills! the friendship of those who are without unity (of mind) is not pleasant.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār uses the image of a young monkey that strikes even its own father as he comes toward it, to show that closeness without unity of mind is dangerous.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says a weapon may hide in the very hands a foe joins in worship; the Nālaṭiyār's monkey that strikes the one approaching it likewise shows harm arriving through a gesture of closeness.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 24 ('Improper Friendship'), st. 7 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The man-eaters say their prayers. Those who wield the knife wear the sacred thread around their necks. … in their hands they hold the knives - they are the butchers of the world!”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Nanak attacks oppressors of his day who perform prayers and wear religious marks while holding the knife against others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a weapon may lie hidden in hands joined in worship; Guru Nanak likewise shows the knife held by those who make a show of prayer.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 16), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “others were for letting it remain as an offering and propitiation for the gods. And this was how they settled it in the end, for the city was doomed when it took in that horse, within which were all the bravest of the Argives waiting to bring death and destruction on the Trojans.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The Greeks’ apparent religious offering hides an army inside it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The wooden horse is a weapon hidden inside an act of worship, as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The great advantages of simulation and dissimulation are three. First, to lay asleep opposition, and to surprise.”
philosophy.explanation: Bacon notes coolly that a show which hides one’s true intent serves to disarm others and take them by surprise.
philosophy.tie_back: This is why the Kural warns of foes’ worship and tears: such shows are designed to lull us before the blow.
philosophy.source: Francis Bacon, Essays, ‘Of Simulation and Dissimulation’

real_life_example.event_title: The Great Seal gift hides a Soviet listening device
real_life_example.place: U.S. ambassador's residence, Moscow, Soviet Union
real_life_example.event: On 4 August 1945 a group of Soviet schoolchildren presented a hand-carved wooden replica of the Great Seal of the United States to the American ambassador, Averell Harriman, as a gesture of friendship between wartime allies. The carving hung in the ambassador's residence until 1952, when U.S. security officers discovered a hidden passive listening device, later called The Thing, inside it. In May 1960 Ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. displayed the seal at the United Nations Security Council to show how it had been used for spying.
real_life_example.explanation: A gift offered in friendship, by children and in a time of alliance, turned out to conceal an instrument used against the recipient.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a weapon may lie hidden even in hands joined in worship, and the friendly gift of the Great Seal concealed a device for spying on the very people it honoured.

tamil:
மிகச்செய்து தம்மெள்ளு வாரை நகச்செய்து
நட்பினுள் சாப்புல்லற் பாற்று.
transliteration:
Migachcheythu thammellu vaarai nagachcheythu
natpinul saappullar̲ paat̲ru.
meaning: When people make a big show of friendship but secretly look down on you, smile back at them on the outside, but let that friendship die inside you.
elementary: If a classmate is super-friendly to your face but laughs at you behind your back, you don’t have to start a fight. You can stay polite and friendly when you meet, but quietly stop trusting them and stop sharing your secrets.
university: Migachcheythu (மிகச்செய்து) is ‘making much of (friendship)’, and thammeḷḷuvaar (தம் எள்ளுவார்) are ‘those who scorn us’ within. The difficult phrase saappullaṟpaaṯru (சாப்புல்லற்பாற்று) is read by the commentators as ‘one should embrace (pullal) in such a way that it dies (saa)’: Varadarasanar says one should make them laugh in that friendship while acting so that the bond dies, and Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as answering pretence with pretence. Pope’s explanation, in the tradition of Parimelazhagar’s royal-political reading, presents this as the duty of kings toward such foes. Whether read as defensive policy or as cynicism, the couplet assumes a political setting where open rupture is costly; ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give identical text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If thou art angry, show thyself as if thou art not so, speaking even then with a smile on thy lips.”
hinduism.explanation: Kanika counsels Dhritarashtra to hide hostility behind a smiling manner in dealing with rivals.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s strategy of keeping the false friend smiling while one’s own inner friendship has ended.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 142, Kanika’s counsel (Ganguli translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples to combine shrewdness about hostile people with innocence of conduct.
christianity.tie_back: Both counsel staying outwardly peaceable while inwardly alert to those who mean harm.

islam.quote_or_event: “Let not believers take disbelievers as allies rather than believers. And whoever [of you] does that has nothing with Allah, except when taking precaution against them in prudence.”
islam.explanation: The verse forbids real alliance with hostile parties, while permitting outward caution in prudence.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly permits outward civility toward the scornful while withholding real friendship.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Absalom rebels against David, David’s loyal friend Hushai goes to Absalom, greets him warmly and appears to join him, but inwardly remains David’s man and defeats the dangerous advice of Ahithophel.
judaism.explanation: Outward friendship is offered to a hostile party while inner loyalty lies elsewhere.
judaism.tie_back: Hushai keeps Absalom pleased on the surface while the ‘friendship’ is dead within, as the Kural advises.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that hostility is ended only by non-hostility.
buddhism.tie_back: A contrast: the Kural answers pretence with pretence, while the Dhammapada asks one to drop hostility altogether.

jainism.quote_or_event: “It is better to be without the love of those who are without sincerity. Death is preferable to an incurable disease. To kill him at once is more desirable than to vex a man so that he becomes sore at heart, and to abuse is better than to praise one for that which we do not possess.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār says that affection from insincere people is worth less than having no affection at all, and that false praise is worse than open abuse.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar advises letting a pretender's friendship die inwardly while keeping him smiling; the Nālaṭiyār agrees that insincere love is better done without, though it does not recommend answering pretence with pretence.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 22 ('The choice of friends'), st. 9 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who offers both respectful greetings and rude refusal to his master, has gone wrong from the very beginning. O Nanak! Both of his actions are false; he obtains no place in the Court of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Angad condemns double conduct, outward respect together with inner refusal, as false from the start.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural advises answering a scornful false friend with an outward smile while letting the friendship die inside; Guru Angad treats any such split between outward show and inner stance as falsehood.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 21), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Back in Ithaca disguised as a beggar, Odysseus endures the suitors’ mockery in his own house, keeping a calm face and even smiling grimly to himself, while he quietly prepares their destruction.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus answers scorn with outward composure while his inward attitude toward the suitors is settled.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Outward ease toward those who scorn you, inner withdrawal: the Kural’s strategy in epic form.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The best composition and temperature, is to have openness in fame and opinion; secrecy in habit; dissimulation in seasonable use; and a power to feign, if there be no remedy.”
philosophy.explanation: Bacon allows dissimulation and even feigning as a last resort, used only in season.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Bacon treats measured counter-pretence as legitimate prudence against those who deceive.
philosophy.source: Francis Bacon, Essays, ‘Of Simulation and Dissimulation’

real_life_example.event_title: Cesare Borgia's reconciliation with his captains at Senigallia
real_life_example.event: In October 1502 several of Cesare Borgia's own condottieri met at Magione and conspired against him, and over the following weeks they negotiated a reconciliation and returned to his service. At the end of December, Vitellozzo Vitelli, Oliverotto da Fermo and two members of the Orsini family met Borgia at Senigallia, which they had just taken in his name. Borgia separated them from their troops, arrested them, and had them put to death, an episode described by Machiavelli, who was then an envoy at Borgia's side.
real_life_example.explanation: Both sides made a show of renewed friendship while neither trusted the other, and the reconciliation ended in Borgia's sudden blow.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes those who make a great show of friendship while secretly despising you, and advises answering with outward cordiality while letting the bond die within, which is how Borgia treated the captains who had plotted against him.

tamil:
பகைநட்பாம் காலம் வருங்கால் முகநட்டு
அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்.
transliteration:
Paganatpaam kaalam varungaal muganattu
aganatpu oreei vidal.
meaning: When the time comes that you must treat an enemy like a friend, be friendly on your face but keep them out of your heart, and drop them when you can.
elementary: Sometimes you have to work on a group project with someone who has been unkind to you. You can be polite and work together, but you don’t have to hand them your diary. Be friendly on the outside and careful on the inside.
university: Pagai-naṭpaam kaalam (பகை நட்பாம் காலம்) is ‘a time when enmity turns into friendship’, for instance an alliance forced by circumstances. The couplet resolves the chapter with the face/heart pair already used in Kural 824: muga-naṭṭu (முகநட்டு, befriending with the face) but aga-naṭpu oreei (அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ, removing friendship from the heart). Oreei (ஒரீஇ) is the alapeḍai-lengthened form of oree, ‘leaving’, and viḍal (விடல்) means ‘one should give it up’. Varadarasanar reads the final word as giving up even the outward friendship when the chance comes, Pappaiah as letting go of it in the mind, and Pope follows the first reading with ‘give up (even the former)’. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.
