hinduism.quote_or_event: “A weak person having made a compact with a stronger one when both are threatened by foes, should (when that common danger passes away) conduct himself heedfully and by considerations of policy. Having gained his object, the weaker of the two parties should not again repose confidence on the stronger.”
hinduism.explanation: The mouse Palita, who made a temporary alliance with the cat Lomasa to escape a hunter, refuses the cat’s invitations to continued friendship once the danger has passed.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s counsel: accept a necessary friendship with a foe, but never let it into the heart.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section 138, the cat and the mouse (Ganguli translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to keep the peace with everyone so far as it depends on them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural too keeps outward peace with a former enemy, though it adds a caution Paul does not.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if they incline to peace, then incline to it [also] and rely upon Allah. Indeed, it is He who is the Hearing, the Knowing. But if they intend to deceive you - then sufficient for you is Allah.”
islam.explanation: Believers are to accept a hostile party’s offer of peace, while recognising it may be a deception.
islam.tie_back: Accept the enemy’s turn to friendship outwardly, but keep your reliance elsewhere: the Kural’s balance.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Jacob meets Esau after twenty years of enmity, they embrace and weep, and Esau offers to travel with him. Jacob graciously declines, sending Esau on ahead, and then settles in a different direction at Succoth.
judaism.explanation: Jacob accepts the reconciliation outwardly but does not put himself in his brother’s power.
judaism.tie_back: Friendly in face, guarded in heart: Jacob’s conduct matches the Kural’s advice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who is friendly amidst the hostile, peaceful amidst the violent, and unattached amidst the attached — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises one who stays friendly and unattached in the midst of hostility.
buddhism.tie_back: Friendliness among the hostile without attachment loosely mirrors the Kural’s friendly face with an uncommitted heart.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Benevolence (maitrī) towards all living-beings (sattva), joy (pramoda) at the sight of the virtuous (guṇādhika), compassion and sympathy (kāruṇya) for the afflicted (kliśyamāna), and tolerance (mādhyasthya) towards the insolent and ill-behaved (avineya) are the other observances.”
jainism.explanation: The Tattvārtha Sūtra prescribes four attitudes to support the vows; toward the ill-disposed the Jain response is mādhyasthya, a detached equanimity free from both attachment and aversion.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar advises being friendly in face but withholding friendship in the heart when a foe must be treated as a friend; the Jain answer is also inner detachment from the hostile, but grounded in goodwill to all beings rather than political calculation.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.11 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: During the siege of Anandpur in 1704, the Mughal commanders and the allied hill chiefs offered Guru Gobind Singh safe passage, backed by an assurance sworn on the Quran and an oath by the cow. The Guru had advised staying, but under starvation the Sikhs left the fort, and they were attacked near the Sarsa river with all the oaths broken.
sikhism.explanation: Sikh historical memory treats the broken oaths of Anandpur as the classic case of enemies offering friendship that was never meant, and Guru Gobind Singh's Zafarnama later rebuked Aurangzeb for them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that when an enemy turns friendly one may be friendly in face but must keep friendship out of the heart; the Guru's distrust of the oaths at Anandpur shows why.
sikhism.source: Wikipedia, 'Second siege of Anandpur' (citing Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 5, and J. S. Grewal, Guru Gobind Singh, 2019)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After their single combat ends undecided at nightfall, Hector and Ajax exchange gifts, a sword and a belt, and part as men who fought in hatred but separated in friendship, yet they remain on opposite sides of the war.
greek_mythology.explanation: Enemies show each other the courtesies of friendship while remaining enemies.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A friendly face between foes without real alliance is the situation the Kural addresses.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “they neither love warmly nor hate bitterly, but following the hint of Bias they love as though they will some day hate and hate as though they will some day love.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle describes the guarded attitude of the experienced, following the sage Bias of Priene.
philosophy.tie_back: Loving ‘as though they will some day hate’ is the inner reserve the Kural advises toward a foe turned friend.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric II.13 (trans. W. Rhys Roberts)

real_life_example.event_title: Alexander I's alliance with Napoleon after Tilsit
real_life_example.place: Tilsit, East Prussia (now Sovetsk, Russia), and Russia
real_life_example.event: After Russia's defeat at Friedland, Tsar Alexander I met Napoleon on a raft in the Neman River, and in July 1807 the Treaty of Tilsit made Russia France's ally and committed it to Napoleon's Continental Blockade against British trade. Russia's economy depended heavily on British trade, and its support for the blockade was half-hearted. On 31 December 1810 Alexander issued a decree reopening Russian ports to neutral shipping, which in effect readmitted British trade, and in June 1812 Napoleon invaded Russia.
real_life_example.explanation: An alliance forced on Alexander by defeat was kept up in public for a time and then allowed to lapse once Russia was ready to stand on its own.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when an enemy must for a time be treated as a friend, one should be friendly in face, keep friendship out of the heart, and let it go when one can, which is the course the Tilsit alliance followed.

tamil:
பேதைமை என்பதொன்று யாதெனின் ஏதங்கொண்டு
ஊதியம் போக விடல்.
transliteration:
Pedhaimai enbadhondru yaadhenin edhangkondu
oodhiyam poga vidal.
meaning: What is foolishness? It is grabbing what hurts you and letting go of what would help you.
elementary: Imagine someone offers you a choice between a shiny toy that will break in a day and a bicycle you could ride for years, and you pick the toy and walk away from the bike. That swap, keeping the bad thing and dropping the good one, is exactly what the poet calls being foolish.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition rather than an example: pedhaimai (பேதைமை) is the act of taking up edham (ஏதம், harm, loss) and letting oodhiyam (ஊதியம், gain, profit) go. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read the pair as a ledger of consequences: the fool does not merely fail to gain, he actively trades gain for loss, which is why folly is placed in the Natpiyal section right after the chapters on bad friendship. Puliyur Kesigan sharpens this into a cost-benefit reading (accepting the trouble that comes with a task while throwing away the profit it would bring), whereas Sivayogi Sivakumar reads edhangkondu as ‘out of fear of a small hardship’, a softer psychological gloss. Kalaignar stresses the failure of discernment: the fool never clarifies which is harmful and which is beneficial. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Katha Upanishad, Yama tells Nachiketas that the good (shreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both approach a person; the wise examine and choose the good, while the dull-witted choose the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad frames life’s basic test as a choice between what truly benefits and what merely attracts, and calls the person who picks wrongly a fool.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar defines folly the same way: choosing what harms over what profits.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.”
christianity.explanation: The letter to the Hebrews holds up Esau as a warning: a man who traded something of lasting worth for a moment’s appetite.
christianity.tie_back: Esau is the textbook case of taking the small harm and letting the great gain go.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those are the ones who have purchased error [in exchange] for guidance, so their transaction has brought no profit, nor were they guided.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the self-deceived as bad traders who swap guidance for error and walk away with no profit.
islam.tie_back: Both texts use the language of profit and loss to define the fool’s bargain.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then Jacob gave Esau bread and pottage of lentiles; and he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright.”
judaism.explanation: Genesis tells how Esau, hungry from the field, sold his birthright for a bowl of stew and walked off unconcerned.
judaism.tie_back: The story dramatizes the Kural’s definition: grabbing a passing want and letting a lasting good go.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If by renouncing a lesser happiness one may realize a greater happiness, let the wise man renounce the lesser, having regard for the greater.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada advises giving up a small pleasure when doing so secures a larger one.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the wise mirror image of the fool in the Kural, who gives up the greater gain for the lesser.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a man for the sake of one Kâkinî (risks and) loses a thousand (Kârshâpanas), or as the king lost his kingdom (and life) by eating a mango-fruit which he was strictly forbidden (by his physician)”
jainism.explanation: In the 'Parable of the Ram' Mahāvīra's teaching shows the fool trading something vast for a trifle, like a man who loses a thousand coins for a single small one, or a king who loses his kingdom for a forbidden mango.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar defines folly as grasping what harms you and letting real gain slip away; the Uttarādhyayana's man who loses a thousand coins for one small coin shows that very trade.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The nights are wasted sleeping, and the days are wasted eating. Human life is such a precious jewel, but it is being lost in exchange for a mere shell. … You fool - you shall regret and repent in the end!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak calls it folly to trade the jewel of human life for a worthless shell, and warns that the fool will regret it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines folly as grabbing what harms you and letting gain slip away; Guru Nanak's fool who swaps a jewel for a shell makes exactly this losing trade.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 156, Raag Gauri Bairagan, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells how Epimetheus, though warned by Prometheus never to accept a gift from Zeus, took in Pandora and understood the harm only after it was already his.
greek_mythology.explanation: Epimetheus, whose name means ‘afterthought’, accepts the gift that carries every evil into the world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s fool, he takes in the harm and loses the good he had been warned to keep.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Protagoras, Socrates argues that people choose worse over better because they mismeasure pleasures and pains, and that the remedy is an art of measurement; the failure he calls ignorance.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, choosing the larger harm for the smaller benefit is a failure of knowledge, not of desire.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise defines folly as a mistaken weighing of harm against gain.

real_life_example.event_title: Decca Records turns down the Beatles
real_life_example.event: Through their manager Brian Epstein, the Beatles were given an audition at Decca Records' studios in north London on New Year's Day 1962, recording about fifteen songs. Decca turned them down and instead signed Brian Poole and the Tremeloes, another group that auditioned that day. Later in 1962 the Beatles were signed by EMI's Parlophone label under producer George Martin and went on to become the most successful band in popular music.
real_life_example.explanation: The decision became one of the best-known missed opportunities in business history, though Decca's executives acted on their judgement of a young, unproven group.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines folly as taking hold of what brings loss and letting slip what would bring profit, and Decca chose the lesser act and let the Beatles go to a rival.

tamil:
பேதைமையுள் எல்லாம் பேதைமை காதன்மை
கையல்ல தன்கட் செயல்.
transliteration:
Pedhaimaiyul ellaam pedhaimai kaadhanmai
kaiyalla thankat seyal.
meaning: The worst foolishness of all is wanting to do things you should not do.
elementary: A goldfish might dream of climbing trees like a squirrel, but if it jumps out of its bowl to try, it will only get hurt. The silliest mistake is wanting badly to do things that are not right for who you are.
university: The couplet ranks follies and puts at the top kaadhanmai (காதன்மை, fond desire, love) for kaiyalla (கையல்ல, what is not within one’s proper hand or conduct). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take kaiyalla as acts unsuited to one’s own moral conduct (ஒழுக்கம்), which matches G. U. Pope’s ‘deeds which to your station unbefitting prove’ and Drew’s ‘delight in doing what is forbidden’. Kalaignar instead reads it as deeds beyond one’s ability, Solomon Pappaiah as desiring things that do one no good, and Puliyur Kesigan as both choosing an undesirable act and doing it unfittingly; the line thus spans a moral reading (forbidden) and a prudential one (beyond one’s scope). The wording is the same in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is far better to discharge one’s prescribed duties, even though faultily, than another’s duties perfectly. Destruction in the course of performing one’s own duty is better than engaging in another’s duties, for to follow another’s path is dangerous.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna against taking up a role that is not his own, however attractive it seems.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly calls it the height of folly to love deeds that do not belong to one’s own path.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James traces wrongdoing back to a desire that pulls a person toward what he should not do.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar likewise locates the worst folly in desire (kaadhanmai) fixed on unfitting deeds.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear the earth [apart], and you will never reach the mountains in height.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an rebukes the person who strides about as though he could do what is far beyond his measure.
islam.tie_back: Both warn against reaching for what lies outside one’s rightful scope.

judaism.quote_or_event: “LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist claims a quiet humility that does not grasp at matters beyond his reach.
judaism.tie_back: It describes the wise opposite of the Kural’s fool, who sets his heart on what does not befit him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The fool seeks undeserved reputation, precedence among monks, authority over monasteries, and honor among householders.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada’s chapter on the fool describes him as hungry for positions and honours that do not fit him.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool, too, sets his heart on what is not properly his.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The presumptuously saying, We are those who will do what should not be done, and the deferring and putting aside that which ought to be done at once, verily these two things will cause affliction instantly, even to ascetics, who have renounced the pleasures of the domestic state.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār names two ruinous habits: boldly taking up what should not be done, and putting off what should be done at once, and it says they bring trouble even to renunciants.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls the greatest folly a fond desire for deeds unfitting for oneself; the Nālaṭiyār likewise puts eagerness to do 'what should not be done' first among the habits that bring swift affliction.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 24 ('Improper Friendship'), st. 5 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Like the monkey with a handful of grain, who will not let go because of greed - just so, all the deeds committed in greed ultimately become a noose around one’s neck.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir uses the monkey trapped because it will not let go of a fistful of grain to show how deeds done from greed tighten into a noose.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls it the worst folly to set one's heart on unfitting deeds; Kabir's monkey clinging to what traps it shows that attachment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 336, Raag Gauri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Bellerophon, after his victories, tried to ride the winged horse Pegasus up to the dwelling of the gods and was thrown back down to earth.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar uses the story to warn that reaching for what belongs to the gods ends in a fall.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It pictures the Kural’s chief folly: desiring a deed that is not one’s own to do.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates defines justice as each person doing his own work and not meddling in what belongs to another.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats staying within one’s proper task as the basis of a well-ordered soul and city.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise counts it the worst folly to love deeds that are not one’s own.

real_life_example.event_title: Muhammad ibn Tughluq moves his capital to Daulatabad
real_life_example.event: Sultan Muhammad ibn Tughluq of Delhi moved his capital to Deogiri in the western Deccan, renamed Daulatabad, in order to strengthen his hold on the south, and large numbers of people from Delhi were moved there. Soon after he was established in the Deccan, rebellions broke out in the north, on the western frontier and in Bengal, and he had to return to Delhi. His transfer of the capital and his introduction of a token currency are both counted among his ambitious schemes that failed and caused great hardship.
real_life_example.explanation: The sultan's projects were bold, but they were poorly executed and beyond what his government could carry out, and they stirred opposition across his realm.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls it the worst folly to set one's heart on deeds that are not fitting for oneself, read by some commentators as deeds beyond one's ability, and the forced move of the capital was such an undertaking.

tamil:
நாணாமை நாடாமை நாரின்மை யாதொன்றும்
பேணாமை பேதை தொழில்.
transliteration:
Naanaamai naadaamai naarinmai yaadhondrum
penaamai pedhai thozhil.
meaning: Feeling no shame, not looking for what is worth having, having no love, and caring about nothing: these are the habits of a fool.
elementary: Think of a kid who breaks a window and doesn’t feel sorry, never tries to learn anything, isn’t kind to friends, and leaves their toys out in the rain. Each of those things on its own is a warning sign; together they are what the poet calls a fool.
university: The couplet is a fourfold catalogue built on negative nouns ending in -aamai/-inmai: naanaamai (நாணாமை, shamelessness at what deserves shame), naadaamai (நாடாமை, not seeking out what deserves seeking), naarinmai (நாரின்மை, lack of naar, ‘fibre’, a metaphor for the affection that binds people), and penaamai (பேணாமை, not cherishing or protecting anything). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss naar as anbu (love), and the commentators agree the list describes a whole disposition rather than isolated faults; Pope renders it ‘Ashamed of nothing, searching nothing out, of loveless heart, / Nought cherishing’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads naarinmai as lacking sweetness of manner, a minor variation. The text is identical in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are demoniac do not know what is to be done and what is not to be done. Neither cleanliness nor proper behavior nor truth is found in them.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita’s portrait of the demoniac nature is a list of absences: no sense of right action, no purity, no truth.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise defines the fool by what is missing in him: shame, seeking, love and care.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes people who boast of what ought to embarrass them and care only for appetite.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s first mark of the fool, shamelessness at what deserves shame.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of the sayings of the early Prophets which the people have got is: If you don't feel ashamed … do whatever you like.”
islam.explanation: The hadith treats haya’ (a sense of shame) as the brake on bad conduct: once it is gone, anything goes.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar puts naanaamai, absence of shame, first among the fool’s traits for the same reason.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6120 (sunnah.com; translator’s parenthetical gloss elided)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore they shall fall among them that fall.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah condemns a people who have lost the ability to blush at their own wrongdoing.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see the loss of shame as a sign of ruin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are ashamed of what they should not be ashamed of, and are not ashamed of what they should be ashamed of — upholding false views, they go to states of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says misplaced shame, especially no shame where it is due, leads to suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s naanaamai is exactly shamelessness at what should shame us.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If he is frequently angry; if he perseveres in his wrath; if he spurns friendly advice; if he is proud of his learning; if he finds fault with others; if he is angry even with friends; if he speaks evil even of a good friend behind his back; if he is positive in his assertions; if he is malicious, egoistical, greedy, without self-discipline; if he does not share with others; if he is always unkind: then he is called ill-behaved.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana lists the marks of an 'ill-behaved' monk, a whole disposition of anger, ingratitude, greed and unkindness that keeps him from Nirvāṇa.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar sketches the fool through a catalogue of lacks (no shame, no seeking, no affection, no care); the Uttarādhyayana similarly defines the ill-behaved by a list of traits, including lacking kindness and not sharing with others.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.7-9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are totally blind in their minds, do not have the integrity to keep their word. … Some do not know the Sound-current of the Naad, spiritual wisdom or the joy of song. They do not even understand good and bad.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak lists the marks of the inwardly blind: no integrity in keeping their word, no taste for wisdom or song, and no grasp of good and bad.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural catalogues the habits of the fool, shamelessness, not seeking, lacking affection and cherishing nothing; Guru Nanak gives a similar list of inner lacks.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1411, Saloks Vaaran Te Vadheek (salok 15), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod foresees a degenerate age in which Aidos (Shame) and Nemesis (Righteous Indignation) wrap themselves in white robes and leave the earth, abandoning humankind to grief.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth shame is a goddess, and her departure marks the moral collapse of a whole generation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise treats the absence of shame as the root mark of the fool.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says shame (aidos) befits the young, who live by feeling and make mistakes, because it holds them back; and he calls the person who would feel no shame at disgraceful acts base.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats a sense of shame as a safeguard for those not yet fully virtuous.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool lacks exactly this safeguard.

real_life_example.event_title: The six-month reign of Tsar Peter III
real_life_example.event: Peter III became emperor of Russia in January 1762, while Russia was fighting Prussia in the Seven Years' War, and in May he made peace with Frederick II of Prussia and withdrew Russia from the war, giving up its gains. He planned a war against Denmark on behalf of his German duchy of Holstein, offended the Orthodox Church by pressing changes in its practices, and alienated the imperial guards by threatening to disband them. In July 1762, about six months after his accession, his wife Catherine and the guards overthrew him, and she took the throne as Catherine II.
real_life_example.explanation: Peter III showed little regard for his subjects' feelings or his country's interests, and in a few months he lost the support of every group that mattered.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural lists the fool's habits as shamelessness, not seeking what is worth seeking, lack of affection and caring for nothing, and Peter III's brief reign showed indifference to the Russia he had been given to rule.

tamil:
ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் பிறர்க்குரைத்தும் தானடங்காப்
பேதையின் பேதையார் இல்.
transliteration:
Odhi unarndhum pirarkkuraiththum thaanadangaap
pedhaiyin pedhaiyaar il.
meaning: No one is a bigger fool than someone who has studied, understood, and even taught others, yet does not live by what they learned.
elementary: Imagine a swimming coach who teaches everyone how to stay safe in the pool but then jumps into the deep end without looking. Knowing the rules and telling others is not enough; the biggest silliness is not following them yourself.
university: The couplet climbs three steps, odhi (ஓதி, having recited or studied), unarndhum (உணர்ந்தும், having understood) and pirarkku uraiththum (பிறர்க்கு உரைத்தும், having explained to others), and then collapses on thaan adangaa (தான் அடங்கா, himself not restrained, not conforming). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take adangudhal as living within the discipline the texts teach, and the superlative pedhaiyin pedhaiyaar il (‘there is no fool beyond this fool’) makes the learned hypocrite the extreme case of the chapter. Puliyur Kesigan glosses adangaa as lacking self-restraint (adakkam), linking the couplet to the chapter on Adakkamudaimai. All four commentaries and the two base texts agree on the reading.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A well-known verse of the Hitopadesha says that people remain fools even after studying the scriptures, and that the one who acts on them is the truly learned person.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit fable collection holds that learning proves itself only in practice.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar makes the same point: knowing and teaching without living it is the deepest folly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells the crowds to follow what the teachers of the law teach but not to copy their conduct, because they do not practise it.
christianity.tie_back: ‘They say, and do not’ is Valluvar’s learned fool in four words.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do you order righteousness of the people and forget yourselves while you recite the Scripture? Then will you not reason?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an rebukes those who preach goodness and recite scripture but neglect it in their own lives, and calls this a failure of reason.
islam.tie_back: Both texts name reciting, preaching, and not practising as the height of unreason.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Study is not the most important thing, but actions.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon son of Rabban Gamaliel teaches that learning finds its purpose in deeds.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise judges study worthless, even foolish, without conduct to match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the learned non-practitioner to a hired herdsman counting cattle that are not his.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say that reciting without practising gains a person nothing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Acknowledging the truth about bondage and liberation, but talking only, not acting (in accordance with these tenets), they seek comfort for themselves in mighty words. Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it? Fools, though sinking lower and lower through their sins, believe themselves to be wise men.”
jainism.explanation: In 'The False Ascetic' Mahāvīra rebukes those who know and speak the doctrine but do not live by it, calling them fools who think themselves wise.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says no fool is greater than one who has studied, understood and taught, yet does not himself conform; the Uttarādhyayana likewise calls those who talk the truth without acting on it 'fools' who sink while believing themselves wise.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.9-10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He says one thing, and does something else. There is no love in his heart, and yet with his mouth he talks tall. … One who does not practice what he preaches to others, shall come and go in reincarnation, through birth and death.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan condemns the person who teaches others but does not live by it, and says such a one stays bound to birth and death.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls the person who studies, understands and teaches others but does not live by it the greatest fool; Guru Arjan names the same failure and its cost.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 269, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib (ashtapadi 5, stanza 7), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plato recounts the story of Thales, who fell into a well while gazing at the stars, and a Thracian servant girl joked that he was eager to know the heavens but could not see what lay at his feet.
greek_mythology.explanation: The anecdote mocks learning that never reaches one’s own steps.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s fool, the scholar knows much but fails in his own conduct.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises never to call yourself a philosopher or talk about principles among ordinary people, but to act on them, just as sheep show how much they have eaten not by bringing up grass but by producing wool and milk.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus, philosophy is proven by conduct, not by lecturing.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar equally scorns the one who teaches but does not live the teaching.

real_life_example.event_title: Charles Van Doren admits the quiz show Twenty-One was rigged
real_life_example.event: Charles Van Doren, an English instructor at Columbia University from a celebrated literary family, became a national celebrity by winning $129,000 on the NBC quiz show Twenty-One in 1956-57. After denying the rigging to the press, the public and a grand jury, he testified before a congressional committee in November 1959 that he had been given the answers in advance and coached on how to perform. Columbia accepted his resignation, NBC ended his contract, and he later pleaded guilty to perjury and received a suspended sentence.
real_life_example.explanation: A scholar who taught literature and was celebrated as a model of learning had taken part in a deception watched by millions.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says no fool is greater than one who has studied, understood and taught others yet does not live by what he learned, and Van Doren, a university teacher, lived for years in a public lie.

tamil:
ஒருமைச் செயலாற்றும் பேதை எழுமையும்
தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு.
transliteration:
Orumaich cheyalaatrum pedhai ezhumaiyum
thaanpuk kazhundhum alaru.
meaning: In just one life, a fool can do enough wrong to fall into a hell of suffering that lasts through seven future lives.
elementary: A few minutes of scribbling with permanent marker on your bedroom wall can leave a mess that takes weeks to clean. The poet says the foolish person can make, in one life, a mess so big it sticks to him for a very long time.
university: The couplet sets orumai (ஒருமை, one birth) against ezhumai (எழுமை, the seven births), and alaru (அளறு, literally ‘mire’ or ‘mud’) is the traditional word for naragam, hell. Parimelazhagar, Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah all read it eschatologically: in one life the fool is able to make (ஆற்றும்) the hell he will enter and sink into across seven births. Kalaignar departs from this, reading orumaich cheyal as ‘self-willed action’ and alaru as a mire of suffering in this world, a deliberately non-theological gloss; Puliyur Kesigan’s note on thirukkural.net is truncated. Pope’s ‘The fool will merit hell in one brief life on earth’ follows the traditional reading. The text is the same in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are envious and mischievous, who are the lowest among men, I perpetually cast into the ocean of material existence, into various demoniac species of life.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes how persistent wrong conduct leads to repeated low births within samsara.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool likewise builds, in one life, a hell that follows him through many births.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that what a person sows in this life decides what he reaps, even into eternity.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly says the fool’s one life sows a harvest of long suffering.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they will say, ‘If only we had been listening or reasoning, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze.’”
islam.explanation: The people of the Fire confess that their failure to listen and to reason in this life is what put them there.
islam.tie_back: Both texts tie unreason in one life to lasting punishment after it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that a path chosen without wisdom can lead to ruin even when it looks right.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool likewise walks confidently into a lasting downfall.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Fools of little wit are enemies unto themselves as they move about doing evil deeds, the fruits of which are bitter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the fool is his own worst enemy, planting deeds whose fruit is bitter.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool, too, digs his own hell by his own actions.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The capital is human life, the gain is heaven; through the loss of that capital man must be born as a denizen of hell or a brute animal. ... Having once forfeited them, he will have to endure these two states of misery; it will be difficult for him to attain an upward course for a long time to come.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's parable of the three merchants treats a human life as capital; the fool who squanders it in one life falls into hell or animal birth and struggles for a very long time to rise again.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the fool in one birth makes the hell he will sink into for seven; the Uttarādhyayana likewise has one wasted human life bring rebirth in hell from which an 'upward course' is hard to win 'for a long time to come'.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.16, 7.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Vibrate, and meditate on the Lord of the Universe, and never forget Him. This is the blessed opportunity of this human incarnation. … Otherwise, you shall regret and repent afterwards, and you shall not be carried across to the other side.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir teaches that this one human birth is the chance to be freed from the round of births; wasted, it leads to regret and to staying in that round.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the fool can make in one life the suffering of seven births; Kabir likewise says the chance of this single life, once wasted, keeps one bound to rebirth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld Odysseus sees Tityos, Tantalus and Sisyphus undergoing endless punishments for wrongs committed in their lifetimes.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer pictures the afterlife as the place where one life’s misdeeds become unending suffering.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural similarly makes one lifetime’s folly the cause of long-lasting torment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, the soul that drew the first lot hastily chose the life of a great tyrant without examining it, and only afterwards discovered it was fated to devour its own children; Plato notes he had lived his previous life in a well-ordered city by habit, without philosophy.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows how an unexamined choice can doom a soul across its next life.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool likewise sets the course of many births by one life’s foolish deeds.

real_life_example.event_title: Thomas Austin releases rabbits at Barwon Park
real_life_example.place: Barwon Park, near Geelong, Victoria, Australia
real_life_example.event: Shortly after Christmas 1859, twenty-four European wild rabbits imported from England by the grazier Thomas Austin arrived in Melbourne, and Austin released some of them on his Barwon Park property so that he and his friends could hunt them. The rabbits multiplied rapidly, crossing into New South Wales by 1880, reaching Queensland in 1886 and Western Australia in 1894. Genetic research has traced most of Australia's rabbits to this release, and they became one of the country's most destructive pests, damaging crops, pasture and native plants for generations.
real_life_example.explanation: A single act done for one man's sport created a problem that has cost Australia's land and farmers dearly for more than a century and a half.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the fool can in one lifetime create a hell that lasts through seven births, and Austin's release of a few rabbits caused harm that has lasted through many generations.

tamil:
பொய்படும் ஒன்றோ புனைபூணும் கையறியாப்
பேதை வினைமேற் கொளின்.
transliteration:
Poipadum ondro punaipoonum kaiyariyaap
pedhai vinaimer kolin.
meaning: When a fool takes on a job they do not know how to do, the job fails, and they also end up in chains.
elementary: If someone who has never cooked tries to make a big dinner alone, the food gets burnt, and they might also burn their hand. Taking on a job you don’t know how to do can spoil the job and hurt you too.
university: Kaiyariyaa (கையறியா) means ‘not knowing the method’ (kai here is the way of doing), and the couplet’s rhetorical ondro (ஒன்றோ, ‘is it only one thing?’) introduces a double penalty: the work poipadum (பொய்படும், comes to nothing) and the doer punai poonum (புனைபூணும், wears fetters). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take punai literally as the shackles of a man held culpable, which Pope follows (‘himself he binds with chains’), while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar soften it to ‘he too is ruined’ or ‘punishes himself’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss kaiyariyaa morally (not knowing the right way of conduct), whereas Pappaiah reads it practically (not knowing how to do the work). Both base sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That action performed in illusion, in disregard of scriptural injunctions, and without concern for future bondage or for violence or distress caused to others is said to be in the mode of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classes as tamasic any work begun in delusion without weighing its consequences, including future bondage.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s ignorant undertaker likewise ruins the work and binds himself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that starting a project without weighing one’s ability leads to failure and public shame.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts describe a task begun without competence that ends in failure and harm to the doer.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids acting on what one does not know and warns that one will be held accountable.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool takes up work he does not understand and pays for it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins. He shall die without instruction; and in the greatness of his folly he shall go astray.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs pictures the wrongdoer caught and bound by the cords of his own actions, led astray by folly.
judaism.tie_back: The image of being bound by one’s own folly mirrors the Kural’s self-imposed fetters.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Aramadusaka Jataka, monkeys left to water a king’s garden pull up every sapling to check the length of its roots so they can measure the water, and the whole garden withers.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta remarks that fools, trying to do good, end up doing harm.
buddhism.tie_back: It is a vivid picture of the Kural’s fool who takes on work he does not understand and ruins it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana pictures a burglar trapped and crushed in the very hole he dug, as an image of how a person's own deeds catch and bind him.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the fool who takes up work he does not understand not only fails but puts himself in fetters; the Uttarādhyayana's burglar caught in his own breach is likewise undone by his own handiwork.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If a fool does a job, he cannot do it right. Even if he does something right, he does the next thing wrong.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Angad observes that whatever task a fool takes up goes wrong, and even a success is followed by a fresh mistake.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that when a fool who does not know the way takes up a task, the work fails; Guru Angad says the same of the fool's undertakings.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok 5 before pauri 22), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon begged to drive the chariot of the Sun for one day, could not control the horses, set the earth on fire, and was struck down by Zeus’s thunderbolt.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells it as the tale of a youth who took on a task far beyond his skill.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the work is ruined and the doer is destroyed with it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Apology, Socrates reports that the craftsmen he questioned truly knew their crafts, but because of that skill thought themselves wise in other weighty matters too, and this error overshadowed their wisdom.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates exposes people who act as experts beyond the reach of their real knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool likewise takes on work whose method he does not know.

real_life_example.event_title: Francis I is defeated and captured at Pavia
real_life_example.event: During his war with Emperor Charles V, King Francis I of France laid siege to Pavia, and in the battle against the imperial relief army he led his armoured cavalry in a charge with couched lances. The charge put his horsemen where his own artillery could no longer fire on the enemy, and Spanish arquebusiers inflicted heavy losses on the French. Francis was captured, taken to Spain and held in Madrid for more than a year, and was released only after signing the Treaty of Madrid in January 1526.
real_life_example.explanation: The king's old-fashioned tactics against an army using firearms not only lost the battle but made him a prisoner of his rival.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when one who does not know how to do a thing takes it on, the work fails and he ends up putting himself in chains, and Francis's ill-judged charge lost the battle and his own freedom.

tamil:
ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர்பசிப்பர் பேதை
பெருஞ்செல்வம் உற்றக் கடை.
transliteration:
Edhilaar aarath thamarpasippar pedhai
perunjelvam utrak kadai.
meaning: When a fool becomes very rich, strangers eat their fill while the fool's own family goes hungry.
elementary: Imagine a boy who wins a huge bag of candy and hands it all out to kids he barely knows, while his little sister at home gets none. Having lots of something doesn’t help your family if you don’t know how to share it wisely.
university: The couplet contrasts edhilaar (ஏதிலார், strangers, those with no tie) who aara (ஆர, eat their fill) with thamar (தமர், one’s own kin) who pasippar (பசிப்பர், go hungry). Puliyur Kesigan follows the traditional explanation that the fool’s wealth comes from past merit (munvinai), while the lack of judgment in spending it is his own; Parimelazhagar’s tradition reads the strangers as flatterers and parasites who gather round new wealth. Kalaignar’s gloss stresses that outsiders ‘roll up’ the money while affectionate kin go without. Pope renders edhilaar as ‘foes’, a stronger word than the Tamil requires; Drew’s ‘neighbours’ is closer. The text is the same in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And charity performed at an impure place, at an improper time, to unworthy persons, or without proper attention and respect is said to be in the mode of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classes giving to the wrong people, at the wrong time and place, as charity in ignorance.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool likewise lavishes his wealth on the wrong people while his own go short.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that neglecting one’s own household is a basic moral failure.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s fool commits exactly this failure, feeding strangers and starving kin.

islam.quote_or_event: “And give the relative his right, and [also] the poor and the traveler, and do not spend wastefully.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an puts relatives first among those with a claim on one’s wealth and forbids squandering it.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool reverses this order, wasting wealth on outsiders while kin go hungry.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A man to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it: this is vanity, and it is an evil disease.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes laments the man whose great wealth ends up feeding a stranger rather than himself.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts picture abundant wealth consumed by strangers instead of those it should serve.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta, the Buddha warns young Sigala of the channels through which wealth is squandered, such as drink, gambling and bad companions, and teaches that one should support friends and relatives with gifts and kindly care.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta pairs wise use of wealth with duties to one’s own circle.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool fails at both: his wealth leaks to outsiders and his kin go hungry.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The bat will not go to the rough-stemmed wood-apple tree, though near and fruitful. So the riches of those who, though they be very near to one, have no greatness of soul, have not the excellence of being considered as profitable.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār says the wealth of small-souled people is of no use even to those closest to them, like a fruitful tree that the bat will not visit.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that when a fool gets great wealth his own people go hungry; the Nālaṭiyār similarly observes that riches in the hands of those without greatness of soul do nothing for those near them.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 27 ('Riches without goodness'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Your wealth shall not go with you; why do you cling to it, you fool? Children, friends, family and spouse - who of these shall accompany you? … The fool does not acknowledge the One who gave this; forgetting the Naam, O Nanak! He will repent in the end.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan asks the fool why he clings to wealth that will not stay with him and forgets the One who gave it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that when a fool gains great wealth, strangers enjoy it while his own go hungry; Guru Arjan also shows the fool's wealth slipping away from him and his family.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 288, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib (ashtapadi 19, stanza 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odysseus’s absence, the suitors occupy his house and feast day after day on his herds and wine, while Penelope and Telemachus look on helplessly.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer makes the wasting of a household’s wealth by outsiders a central wrong of the Odyssey.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It mirrors the Kural’s picture of strangers feasting while the family suffers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says the prodigal gives to the wrong people, enriching flatterers and others who deserve nothing, while failing to give to those who should receive.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, prodigality is a failure to give to the right people in the right amounts.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool shows exactly this vice: outsiders grow fat while kin go hungry.

real_life_example.event_title: Khedive Ismail's debts bring Egypt under European financial control
real_life_example.event: Khedive Ismail of Egypt financed costly modernisation projects and other ambitions largely with loans from European financiers, and the national debt rose many times over during his reign. In 1875 he sold Egypt's Suez Canal shares to Britain, and in 1876, unable to meet payments, Egypt's finances were placed under the supervision of a European debt commission and British and French controllers. In June 1879 the Ottoman sultan, pressed by Britain and France, deposed Ismail in favour of his son Tawfiq.
real_life_example.explanation: Ismail's borrowing enriched foreign bondholders while the burden of repayment fell on Egypt, and it ended in the loss of control over the country's own finances.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when a fool comes into great wealth, strangers feast while his own people go hungry, and Egypt's wealth under Ismail flowed to foreign creditors while Egyptians bore the cost.

tamil:
மையல் ஒருவன் களித்தற்றால் பேதைதன்
கையொன்று உடைமை பெறின்.
transliteration:
Maiyal oruvan kaliththatraal pedhaidhan
kaiyondru udaimai perin.
meaning: When a fool gets hold of something valuable, they are like a person who is already out of their mind and then gets drunk too.
elementary: Picture a kid who is already running wild at a party and then gets a big bag of sugar. Things go from silly to much worse! Giving power or money to someone who doesn’t think clearly only makes their foolishness bigger.
university: The simile doubles the condition: maiyal (மையல், bewilderment, madness) is a man already deranged, and kaliththal (களித்தல்) is intoxication by toddy, so the fool who gains udaimai (உடைமை, possession) is a madman who is also drunk. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss maiyal as piththu (பித்து, madness) and kaliththal as being dazed by kal (கள், toddy), and Puliyur Kesigan adds that such a man drinks more and more and strays from his course. Kai ondru (கை ஒன்று) is read as ‘anything in his hand’, so the point holds for any wealth or authority, not only great fortune. Pope (‘as when a mad man raves in drunken glee’) and Drew follow the same reading, and the two base sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The demoniac person thinks: ‘So much wealth do I have today, and I will gain more according to my schemes. So much is mine now, and it will increase in the future, more and more…’ In this way, such persons are deluded by ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita shows wealth swelling the deluded person’s arrogance into a kind of intoxication.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise says possession makes an already confused mind drunk.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the rich fool, abundance makes a man complacent and heedless of what matters.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts show possessions intoxicating the fool rather than steadying him.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not give the weak-minded your property, which Allāh has made a means of sustenance for you, but provide for them with it and clothe them and speak to them words of appropriate kindness.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids handing control of property to those who lack sound judgment, while still providing for them.
islam.tie_back: It rests on the same insight as the Kural: wealth in a fool’s hands does harm.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear: For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with meat;”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs lists a fool who has plenty among the things the world cannot bear.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise says a fool with possessions becomes worse, like a madman made drunk.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Riches ruin only the foolish, not those in quest of the Beyond. By craving for riches the witless man ruins himself as well as others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says wealth is dangerous only in the hands of the foolish.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say possession magnifies the fool’s folly into ruin.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana says possessions do not save the heedless person; his judgment goes dark, as when a lamp is suddenly put out.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar compares a fool who gets possessions to a madman who is also drunk; the Uttarādhyayana likewise shows wealth failing the heedless man and his sight of the right way vanishing.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One person brings a full bottle, and another fills his cup. Drinking the wine, his intelligence departs, and madness enters his mind; he cannot distinguish between his own and others, and he is struck down by his Lord and Master.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes how wine drives out intelligence and brings in madness, so a man can no longer tell his own from others; Sikh teaching rejects intoxicants.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural likens a fool who gains something to a madman who is also drunk; Guru Amar Das's picture of drink bringing madness gives the same image of reason lost.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 554, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre Ki Vaar (salok 1 before pauri 16), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas, granted any wish by Dionysus, foolishly asked that everything he touched turn to gold, and soon found he could not eat or drink.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows a foolish man given power turning a gift into a curse.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s fool, Midas is made worse, not better, by what comes into his hands.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes the character that wealth produces as insolent and arrogant, as if possessed by their riches, behaving like people who think they have every good thing; he calls this a prosperous fool.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle observes that sudden wealth distorts character, especially in those without judgment.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar says the same: possession intoxicates the foolish.

real_life_example.event_title: Ceausescu builds the House of the People
real_life_example.event: From 1984 the Romanian leader Nicolae Ceausescu had an enormous government palace, the House of the People, built in Bucharest, and the project required clearing large areas of the historic city centre. Thousands of workers and hundreds of architects worked on it during the 1980s, a time when Romania was struggling to feed its own people and the costs were enormous. The building was still unfinished when Ceausescu fell in December 1989, and it now houses Romania's Parliament.
real_life_example.explanation: Absolute power let one man pour a struggling nation's resources into a monument to himself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares a fool who comes into possession of something to a madman who is also drunk, and unchecked control of a country led Ceausescu into one of the most extravagant building projects of the century.

tamil:
பெரிதினிது பேதையார் கேண்மை பிரிவின்கண்
பீழை தருவதொன் றில்.
transliteration:
Peridhinidhu pedhaiyaar kenmai pirivinkan
peezhai tharuvadhon ril.
meaning: Friendship with fools is very sweet, because when it ends, saying goodbye causes no pain at all.
elementary: Some friends are like a balloon on a string: it is fun for a while, but when it floats away you don’t really miss it. The poet is joking that friends who are foolish are ‘lovely’, because losing them doesn’t hurt at all.
university: The couplet is ironic praise: peridhu inidhu (பெரிது இனிது, ‘exceedingly sweet’) is applied to pedhaiyaar kenmai (பேதையார் கேண்மை, friendship with fools), and the reason given is that at pirivu (பிரிவு, separation) there is no peezhai (பீழை, pain, affliction). Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesigan all read it as saying that a fool’s friendship is ‘sweet’ only in that losing it costs nothing, so its real worth is zero; Kesigan hedges with ‘in one way’. Solomon Pappaiah reads it slightly differently, as friendship among fools themselves, whose partings cause them no grief, which matches Drew’s ‘the friendship between fools’. The text is the same in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka says one might pull a jewel from a crocodile’s jaws or wear a raging serpent like a flower, but one cannot win over a fool whose mind is set wrong.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit poet treats the fool as someone no real bond can be formed with.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s irony makes a similar point: friendship with a fool has so little in it that losing it costs nothing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, quoting a Greek proverb, warns that bad company damages character.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts imply that friendship with fools is worth little and well lost.

islam.quote_or_event: “Close friends, that Day, will be enemies to each other, except for the righteous”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says friendships not grounded in righteousness will fall apart on the Day of Judgment.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar likewise implies that friendships without wisdom have nothing in them that lasts.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go from the presence of a foolish man, when thou perceivest not in him the lips of knowledge.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs advises simply leaving the company of a fool once you see he has no wisdom to offer.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s irony points the same way: walking away from a fool costs nothing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Good is it to see the Noble Ones; to live with them is ever blissful. One will always be happy by not encountering fools.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says plainly that life is happier without fools in it.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s joke rests on the same truth: separation from a fool brings no grief.

jainism.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sûtras.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana counts keeping clear of foolish people among the steps on the road to final deliverance.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar jokes that friendship with fools is sweet because parting from them costs nothing; the Uttarādhyayana states the same lesson plainly, that fools are to be avoided altogether.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Friendship with a fool never works out right. As he knows, he acts; behold, and see that it is so. … Friendship with a fool, and love with a pompous person, are like lines drawn in water, leaving no trace or mark.”
sikhism.explanation: In two saloks of Asa Ki Vaar Guru Angad says friendship with a fool never works out, and that it is like a line drawn in water, gone without a trace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's ironic praise is that friendship with fools is sweet because parting from it leaves no pain; Guru Angad's line drawn in water leaves the same lack of any mark.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (saloks 3 and 4 before pauri 22), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the travellers and the bear, one companion scrambles up a tree and leaves his friend to face the bear; the bear seems to whisper to the man on the ground never to travel with a friend who deserts at the first sign of danger.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable shows a friendship that proves worthless the moment it is tested.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s fool’s friendship, it is one whose loss is no loss.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle explains that friendships based on pleasure or usefulness are easily dissolved, since when the pleasure or use ends, the friendship ends too.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, only friendship grounded in virtue endures; the rest come apart without much loss.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s fool’s friendship is the shallow kind whose ending leaves no wound.

real_life_example.event_title: General Charles Lee is suspended and then dismissed from the Continental Army
real_life_example.place: Monmouth, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, United States
real_life_example.event: Major General Charles Lee, second in rank in the Continental Army, led the advance at the Battle of Monmouth in June 1778, but his attack faltered and his troops fell back in disorder until George Washington rallied them. At his own request Lee was court-martialed and was found guilty of disobeying orders, misbehaviour before the enemy and disrespect to Washington, and was suspended for a year. He continued to attack his accusers and Congress, was dismissed from the army in January 1780, and the army carried on under Washington without him.
real_life_example.explanation: Lee's departure removed a quarrelsome and unreliable senior officer, and it cost the American cause nothing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says ironically that friendship with fools is sweet because nothing is lost when it ends, and the army's parting with Lee caused no loss at all.

tamil:
கழாஅக்கால் பள்ளியுள் வைத்தற்றால் சான்றோர்
குழாஅத்துப் பேதை புகல்.
transliteration:
Kazhaaakkaal palliyul vaiththatraal saandror
kuzhaaaththup pedhai pugal.
meaning: A fool walking into a gathering of good and worthy people is like putting unwashed feet on a clean bed.
elementary: Imagine coming in from a muddy football field and climbing straight into a freshly made bed with dirty feet. Everything gets messy. The poet says a fool barging into a group of wise people spoils things in the same way.
university: The closing simile sets kazhaaak kaal (கழாஅக்கால், unwashed foot) in palli (பள்ளி) against the fool’s pugal (புகல், entering) into saandror kuzhaaam (சான்றோர் குழாஅம், the gathering of the noble). The lengthened forms kazhaaa- and kuzhaaa- are isai-nirai alapedai (இசைநிறை அளபெடை), vowel prolongation that fills out the metre. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take palli as a bed (as do Pope and Drew), but Puliyur Kesigan reads it as a place of worship (‘தொழுகைக்குரிய பள்ளி’), making the image one of defiling a sanctuary; both senses of palli are attested in Tamil. The text is identical in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka calls silence the cover the Creator gave to hide ignorance, and says it is the ornament of the unlearned above all in an assembly of the learned.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit verse advises the ignorant to keep quiet when among the wise.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar sees the fool’s presence in a learned gathering as a defilement; Bhartrhari offers the fool his only remedy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment: And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the wedding feast, a guest who enters unprepared is challenged and has no answer.
christianity.tie_back: Like the unwashed foot on the bed, he brings into a pure gathering what does not belong there.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, when you rise to [perform] prayer, wash your faces and your forearms to the elbows and wipe over your heads and wash your feet to the ankles.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an requires washing, including the feet, before standing in prayer.
islam.tie_back: On Kesigan’s reading of palli as a place of worship, the Kural’s image is the very impurity this washing prevents.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Therefore the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.”
judaism.explanation: The first psalm says the wicked have no place in the gathering of the righteous.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise sees the fool as out of place in the assembly of the wise.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says a fool can sit among the wise for a lifetime and absorb nothing.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see the fool in wise company as out of place and unchanged.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If one who has grown up in ignorance enter the assembly of the excellent in learning, in the earth, and sits down, it will be like the sitting down of a dog; and though, not remaining quiet, he should say anything, it will be like the barking of a dog.”
jainism.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār mocks the ignorant man who enters a gathering of the learned: his sitting there is like a dog's, and his speech is like barking.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar compares a fool entering the assembly of the wise to putting unwashed feet on a clean bed; the Nālaṭiyār uses an equally earthy image for the same intrusion, a dog sitting and barking among the learned.
jainism.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 26 ('The want of understanding'), st. 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Seeing the swans swimming, the herons became envious. But the poor herons drowned and died, and floated with their heads down, and their feet above.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das tells of herons who envied the swans and tried to swim among them, only to drown in disgrace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a fool entering the assembly of the wise is like unwashed feet on a clean bed; Guru Amar Das's herons venturing among the swans are likewise out of place.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 585, Raag Vadahans, Vadahans Ki Vaar (salok 3 before pauri 1), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the mountain god Tmolus judged the music contest between Apollo and Pan and gave the prize to Apollo, Midas alone objected; Apollo gave him the ears of an ass for his dull hearing.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows a fool pushing his opinion into a contest judged by the divine and the wise, and being marked for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s fool entering the assembly of the wise, Midas spoils the gathering and disgraces himself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedo, Socrates says that it is not permitted for the impure to lay hold of the pure, which is why the soul must be cleansed before it can grasp truth.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats purification as a precondition for entering into contact with what is pure.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s unwashed foot on a clean bed is a homely image of the same incompatibility.

real_life_example.event_title: George Psalmanazar's false Formosa deceives learned London
real_life_example.event: A young Frenchman who called himself George Psalmanazar arrived in London around 1703 claiming to be a native of Formosa (Taiwan), and in 1704 published a description of the island, which he had never visited, complete with an invented alphabet and language. He was received in learned circles, including the Royal Society and the Bishop of London, until other experts showed his claims to be false and he became a target of satire. In his memoirs, published in 1764 after his death, he admitted the imposture.
real_life_example.explanation: An impostor with no real knowledge entered the gatherings of scholars and, once exposed, became a byword for fraud.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural likens a fool entering an assembly of the wise to setting unwashed feet on a clean bed, and Psalmanazar's appearance among London's learned societies brought falsehood into a place meant for knowledge.

tamil:
அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை பிறிதின்மை
இன்மையா வையா துலகு.
transliteration:
Arivinmai inmaiyul inmai piridhinmai
inmaiyaa vaiyaa thulagu.
meaning: Of all the things a person can lack, lacking good sense is the real poverty. The world does not count lacking other things, like money, as real poverty.
elementary: Imagine two kids: one has an empty piggy bank but knows how to read, count and solve problems; the other has a full piggy bank but can’t figure anything out. The first one can earn coins again, but the second one will keep losing them. That is why the poet says not knowing is the emptiest pocket of all.
university: The chapter opens with a paradox built on the repeated word inmai (இன்மை, lack, poverty): arivinmai (அறிவின்மை, absence of understanding) is ‘the poverty among poverties’, while piridhinmai (other lacks, chiefly of wealth) the world will not reckon as poverty at all. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render it as ‘the famine of knowledge is the cruelest famine’, and Solomon Pappaiah shifts the evaluator from ‘the world’ (ulagu) to ‘the great ones’ (periyor), reflecting the classical commentary habit of reading ulagu as ‘the wise of the world’. Puliyur Kesigan adds that material poverty is not regarded as lasting poverty, since it can be remedied, whereas folly cannot. Placed in the Natpiyal after Pedhaimai (ch. 84), Pullarivaanmai shifts the focus from simple folly to the conceited, perverse ignorance (pull-arivu, ‘petty knowledge’) of one who thinks himself wise. Text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the second line is printed in its traditional sandhi-split form ‘inmaiyaa vaiyaa thulagu’ (for vaiyaadhu ulagu).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In this world, there is nothing so sublime and pure as transcendental knowledge.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna ranks knowledge above every other purifying possession or practice.
hinduism.tie_back: If knowledge is the greatest possession, its absence is the greatest poverty, exactly Valluvar’s claim.

christianity.quote_or_event: “How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs weighs wisdom against money and finds money the lesser treasure.
christianity.tie_back: Lacking gold is a small want; lacking wisdom is the real one.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" Only they will remember [who are] people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an poses a rhetorical question whose answer is plainly no: knowledge separates people more than anything else.
islam.tie_back: Both texts make the lack of knowledge the decisive deficiency in a person.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If he acquired this, what else is lacking? If he has not acquired this, what has he acquired?”
judaism.explanation: In the same passage Abaye cites a tradition that a poor person is only one lacking in intelligence, and the saying from the West follows: whoever has understanding has everything.
judaism.tie_back: Almost Valluvar’s exact thought: the only true poverty is poverty of understanding.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A worse taint than these is ignorance, the worst of all taints.”
buddhism.explanation: After listing many stains on a person’s life, the Buddha names ignorance as the deepest of them.
buddhism.tie_back: Both rank ignorance as the worst among a whole list of deficiencies.

jainism.quote_or_event: “All men who are ignorant of the Truth are subject to pain; in the endless Samsâra they suffer in many ways.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on the false ascetic opens by making ignorance of the truth the root of every kind of suffering across endless rebirth, and goes on to urge the wise to search for the truth themselves.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls lack of understanding the real poverty among all poverties, and Mahavira's sermon likewise treats ignorance, not any lack of goods, as the want that causes all other suffering.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one respects the poor man. … Says Kabir, he alone is poor, who does not have the Naam, the Name of the Lord, in his heart.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir starts from the world's contempt for the poor and turns it round: the only real poverty is lacking the Name in one's heart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the lack of understanding is the real poverty and the world should not count other lacks as want; Kabir likewise moves true poverty from money to the inner life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas, already rich, asks Bacchus that everything he touches turn to gold; his food and drink harden into metal and he begs to be freed from the gift, and later he earns ass’s ears for his poor judgment in the contest between Pan and Apollo.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas has endless wealth but no sense, and the wealth does him no good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Gold could not cure his real poverty, which was a poverty of judgment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Diogenes Laertius reports Socrates as saying that there is only one good, knowledge, and only one evil, ignorance.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates reduces all good and evil to the presence or absence of knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise treats the absence of knowledge as the only lack that truly matters.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 2.31

real_life_example.event_title: Paulo Freire's forty-hour literacy programme at Angicos
real_life_example.place: Angicos, Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil
real_life_example.event: In 1963 the educator Paulo Freire led a government-funded pilot programme in the small town of Angicos in north-eastern Brazil, in which nearly 300 poor rural workers and adolescents were taught to read and write in about forty hours of instruction. Teachers built lessons around words and images drawn from the learners' own lives, aiming at political awareness as well as literacy. The pilot was meant to lead to a national literacy programme, but that plan was halted after the military coup of 1964 and Freire left Brazil.
real_life_example.explanation: Angicos became the founding example of Freire's view that illiteracy, more than lack of money, kept the poor powerless, and his methods were later used in literacy campaigns around the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the lack of understanding is the real poverty, and Freire's programme treated the workers' want of literacy, rather than their want of wealth, as the deprivation to be overcome first.

tamil:
அறிவிலான் நெஞ்சுவந்து ஈதல் பிறிதியாதும்
இல்லை பெறுவான் தவம்.
transliteration:
Arivilaan nenjuvandhu eedhal piridhiyaadhum
illai peruvaan thavam.
meaning: When a fool happily gives something away, it is only because of the good luck the receiver earned from past good deeds.
elementary: Suppose a kid who never shares suddenly hands you his best sandwich with a big smile. You didn’t earn it from his good sense; you were just lucky that day. The poet says a fool’s gift is like that: it comes from the receiver’s good luck, not the giver’s wisdom.
