university: The kural is ironic: a person without understanding (arivilaan, அறிவிலான்) does not give wisely, so if he gives nenjuvandhu (நெஞ்சுவந்து, with a gladdened heart), the explanation must lie outside him, in the thavam (தவம், austerity, accumulated merit) of the recipient (peruvaan). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss thavam as nalvinai (good karma), and the old English rendering speaks of ‘the receiver’s merit (in a former birth)’, reflecting the karmic reading of the classical commentators. Kalaignar softens it to ‘the receiver’s good fortune’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as the receiver’s own spiritual quality drawing the gift. The underlying point is that the fool’s generosity is unreliable and unearned, an accident of providence rather than a virtue. No textual variants appear between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And charity performed at an impure place, at an improper time, to unworthy persons, or without proper attention and respect is said to be in the mode of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classifies giving by the understanding behind it, and gift without discernment belongs to tamas, the mode of ignorance.
hinduism.tie_back: A fool’s gift has no wisdom behind it; any good it does is not the giver’s doing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And it shall be, that thou shalt drink of the brook; and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there.”
christianity.explanation: God feeds Elijah through ravens, creatures that give without any understanding of what they do.
christianity.tie_back: The gift reaches the receiver because of who he is before God, not because of the giver’s wisdom.

islam.quote_or_event: “And there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision, and He knows its place of dwelling and place of storage.”
islam.explanation: Provision (rizq) is assigned by God; whoever hands it over is only the channel.
islam.tie_back: As in the kural, what the receiver gets is due to what was allotted to him, not the giver’s sense.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the Book of Esther, the fickle King Ahasuerus, who earlier approved Haman’s decree, is moved after a sleepless night to heap honor on Mordecai and later grants Esther’s plea.
judaism.explanation: Jewish tradition reads the turn of events as hidden providence working through an unreliable ruler.
judaism.tie_back: The king’s generosity came not from his wisdom but from the merit and destiny of those who received it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta the Buddha describes four kinds of purification of an offering, including one purified by the recipient but not by the giver: the giver lacks virtue, yet the gift bears fruit because the recipient is virtuous.
buddhism.explanation: The worth of a gift can come entirely from the person who receives it.
buddhism.tie_back: Very close to Valluvar: a gift from an unworthy giver yields good because of the receiver’s merit.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvārtha Sūtra teaches that the merit of a gift is not fixed. It varies with four things: the manner of giving, the thing given, the giver, and the worthiness of the recipient (pātra).
jainism.explanation: In Jain teaching on charity (dāna), a gift's fruit depends partly on who receives it, which is why a worthy recipient such as a restrained monk adds to the merit of the offering.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural ironically credits a fool's glad gift to the recipient's own merit, and Jain dāna theory likewise counts the recipient's worthiness as one of the things that decide what a gift is worth.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39 (Digambara numbering; 7.34 in the Śvetāmbara recension), Umāsvāti; cf. tr. Vijay K. Jain, wisdomlib.org

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He Himself is the Creator, and He Himself is the Enjoyer; He Himself gives, and causes others to give.”
sikhism.explanation: In a pauri of Bihaagre Ki Vaar, Guru Ram Das says that God is the real Giver and is the one who moves others to give.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural explains a fool's glad giving by the receiver's merit, not the giver's virtue; Gurbani likewise traces any gift beyond the human giver, to God who causes others to give.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 554, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre Ki Vaar (pauri 15), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aristophanes’ comedy Plutus, the god of wealth is blind, which is why riches fall to people at random rather than to the deserving.
greek_mythology.explanation: Wealth flows without discernment; who gets it is not decided by anyone’s wisdom.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The fool’s gift is similarly blind; its landing on someone reflects their luck.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says the generous person gives to the right people, the right amounts and at the right time, whereas the prodigal gives without discrimination, often to those who should not receive.
philosophy.explanation: Real generosity needs practical wisdom; giving without it is not a virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise refuses to credit the fool’s gift as virtue; any benefit is the receiver’s good fortune.

real_life_example.event_title: The Boston Red Sox sell Babe Ruth to the New York Yankees
real_life_example.place: Boston and New York, United States
real_life_example.event: In late December 1919 Boston Red Sox owner Harry Frazee, who was short of money, agreed to sell the contract of his star player Babe Ruth to the New York Yankees owners Jacob Ruppert and Tillinghast Huston. The Yankees paid 25,000 dollars in cash and three promissory notes, about 100,000 dollars in all, and the sale was announced in January 1920. Ruth went on to his greatest years with the Yankees.
real_life_example.explanation: The sale is remembered as one of the most lopsided deals in sports history, transforming the Yankees and stripping Boston of its best player.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says ironically that when a fool gives something away gladly, the cause lies in the good fortune of the receiver, and the Yankees owed their great prize to Frazee's willingness to part with it rather than to any skill of their own.

tamil:
அறிவிலார் தாந்தம்மைப் பீழிக்கும் பீழை
செறுவார்க்கும் செய்தல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Arivilaar thaandhammaip peezhikkum peezhai
seruvaarkkum seydhal aridhu.
meaning: Fools bring more suffering on themselves than even their enemies could cause them.
elementary: Think of a kid who won’t wear a coat in the snow, eats all the candy at once and then skips homework. No bully could make his day as miserable as he has made it himself. The poet says fools are their own worst enemies.
university: Valluvar uses the doubled noun-verb peezhikkum peezhai (பீழிக்கும் பீழை, the affliction with which they afflict) to stress self-made misery, and seruvaar (செறுவார், those who hate, enemies) to set up the comparison. All the modern commentators agree on the sense: the harm fools do to themselves exceeds what an enemy could achieve (Mu. Varadarasanar: ‘of a measure even their foes cannot inflict’; Kalaignar: ‘the torment enemies could not deliver, fools give themselves’). Puliyur Kesigan notes the distress-causing nature (varuththam) of such self-inflicted suffering. The thought links this chapter to the Natpiyal’s concern with enemies: for the fool, the most dangerous enemy is internal. Both web texts read identically.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For him who has conquered the mind, the mind is the best of friends; but for one who has failed to do so, his mind will remain the greatest enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that an uncontrolled mind becomes a person’s worst adversary.
hinduism.tie_back: The fool’s own mind does him more harm than any outside enemy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A fool’s mouth is his destruction, and his lips are the snare of his soul.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs shows the fool trapping himself with his own words.
christianity.tie_back: The fool’s ruin comes from inside, not from his enemies.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all, but it is the people who are wronging themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an places the source of human ruin in people’s own choices.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, it says the deepest harm is self-inflicted.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Fools fold their hands together / And have to eat their own flesh.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet pictures the idle fool as devouring himself.
judaism.tie_back: A vivid image of the self-inflicted affliction Valluvar describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever harm an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater, an ill-directed mind inflicts on oneself a greater harm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares enemy harm with self-harm and finds the latter greater.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the same comparison the kural makes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
jainism.explanation: In the commentarial story, the burglar is crushed by the very wall he dug through, an image of how each soul's own deeds (karma) come back on it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says fools hurt themselves more than any enemy could, and the Jain burglar dies in the hole he cut himself, so the ruin is his own work and no enemy's.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Dadda: Do not blame anyone else; blame instead your own actions. Whatever I did, for that I have suffered; I do not blame anyone else.”
sikhism.explanation: In his acrostic Patti, Guru Nanak teaches that the suffering one meets comes from one's own deeds, not from others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says fools hurt themselves more than any enemy could; Guru Nanak likewise finds the source of suffering in one's own actions, not in others.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Aasaa, Patti Likhi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon cuts down Ceres’ sacred oak despite warnings, is cursed with insatiable hunger, sells everything he owns and finally begins to devour his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: His own reckless choice becomes a hunger that destroys him from within.
greek_mythology.tie_back: No enemy could have ruined him as thoroughly as his own folly did.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus teaches that people are disturbed not by things but by their judgments about things, and that the uninstructed blame others for their troubles while the instructed look to themselves.
philosophy.explanation: Our suffering is largely produced by our own faulty judgments.
philosophy.tie_back: The fool’s self-made pain matches the Stoic diagnosis of self-caused distress.

real_life_example.event_title: Muhammad ibn Tughluq's token currency ends in mass forgery
real_life_example.event: Between about 1329 and 1332 Sultan Muhammad ibn Tughluq of Delhi attempted a fiduciary currency, issuing brass and copper tokens that were meant to pass at the value of silver tankas. The tokens were forged on a massive scale, and the experiment became a total failure. The sultan then redeemed all the tokens, forged and genuine alike, in gold and silver at the treasury's expense.
real_life_example.explanation: The scheme, imposed without safeguards against forgery, inflicted on the sultan's own treasury a loss that no rival had managed to cause and became a byword for ill-judged policy.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the suffering fools bring on themselves exceeds anything their enemies could inflict, and the sultan's ill-planned currency drained his own treasury more effectively than any foe.

tamil:
வெண்மை எனப்படுவ தியாதெனின் ஒண்மை
உடையம்யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Venmai enappaduva dhiyaadhenin onmai
udaiyamyaam ennum serukku.
meaning: What is stupidity? It is the proud belief that says, “We are the wise ones.”
elementary: A kid who says “I already know everything, I don’t need to listen” stops learning right there. The poet says that feeling of being sure you are the smartest is exactly what being foolish means.
university: The kural defines folly by a pair of light-words: venmai (வெண்மை, literally ‘whiteness’, i.e. blankness, emptiness of mind) is set against onmai (ஒண்மை, ‘brightness’, i.e. keen intelligence). Folly is not mere blankness but the serukku (செருக்கு, conceit, intoxicated pride) that claims brightness: ‘udaiyam yaam’, ‘we possess it’, with the royal or self-inflating plural. Mu. Varadarasanar equates venmai with pullarivu, the chapter’s key term; Pappaiah calls it a ‘delusion’ (mayakkam) and Kalaignar ‘arrogance’ (aanavam). Structurally the kural mirrors 831 in the preceding chapter (‘pedhaimai enbadhondru yaadhenin…’), giving a definition in question-and-answer form. Text identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Fools dwelling in darkness, wise in their own conceit, and puffed up with vain knowledge, go round and round, staggering to and fro, like blind men led by the blind.”
hinduism.explanation: Yama describes those who think themselves learned while remaining in ignorance.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Wise in their own conceit’ is precisely Valluvar’s definition of folly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs ranks the self-satisfied ‘wise man’ below even the plain fool.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts locate the worst folly in thinking oneself wise.

islam.quote_or_event: “[They are] those whose effort is lost in worldly life, while they think that they are doing well in work.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes people who are confidently wrong about the worth of their own deeds.
islam.tie_back: Their false certainty is the same conceit the kural names as folly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ah, / Those who are so wise— / In their own opinion; / So clever— / In their own judgment!”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah pronounces woe on those whose wisdom exists only in their own eyes.
judaism.tie_back: Self-assessed brilliance is exactly the serukku Valluvar condemns.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that self-awareness redeems a fool, but the conceit of wisdom seals his folly.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the same definition: real folly is believing oneself wise.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it? Fools, though sinking lower and lower through their sins, believe themselves to be wise men.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira mocks people who rely on fine words and doctrine without right conduct, and names as the mark of the fool his belief that he is wise.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar defines folly as the conceit that says 'we are wise', and the Uttarādhyayana gives the same definition: the fool sinks while he believes himself wise.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak! Everyone speaks of Him, each one wiser than the rest. … O Nanak! One who claims to know everything shall not be decorated in the world hereafter.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib Guru Nanak notes that everyone holds forth as wiser than the next, and warns that whoever claims to know everything will not be honoured hereafter.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines folly as the conceit that says 'we are the wise ones'; Guru Nanak likewise names the claim to know everything as the mark that disgraces.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib (pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Arachne, a gifted weaver, boasts that her skill surpasses Minerva’s and refuses the goddess’s warning to be humble; she loses the contest of pride and is turned into a spider.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her downfall comes from overrating herself and dismissing counsel.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The pride that says ‘we are the wise ones’ is the folly Valluvar defines.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows. I neither know nor think that I know.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates finds that his only advantage over a reputed wise man is that he does not mistake ignorance for knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: The kural’s folly is the reputed wise man’s condition: claiming a wisdom he lacks.

real_life_example.event_title: General Braddock spurns Native allies and is defeated at the Monongahela
real_life_example.place: Monongahela River, near present-day Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States
real_life_example.event: In 1755 General Edward Braddock led a British army trained in European parade-ground drill against the French at Fort Duquesne. He had very few Native American guides, a shortage sources link to his own treatment of the Native leaders he met, and he appears to have ignored intelligence on the French position offered through a Mohawk ally. On 9 July 1755 his advance column was attacked near the Monongahela River by a smaller French and Native force, more than half his men were killed or wounded, and Braddock was mortally wounded.
real_life_example.explanation: The defeat kept the Ohio Valley in French hands for three more years and made Braddock a lasting example of a commander undone by confidence in his own methods.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural defines folly as the arrogance that says we are the wise ones, and Braddock's reliance on his own European ways over local knowledge led his army into disaster.

tamil:
கல்லாத மேற்கொண் டொழுகல் கசடற
வல்லதூஉம் ஐயம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Kallaadha merkon dozhugal kasadara
valladhooum aiyam tharum.
meaning: Pretending to know things you never learned makes people doubt even the things you really do know well.
elementary: If a boy who is great at football starts bragging that he is also a chess champion, and everyone sees he can’t play chess, they start wondering whether he is really good at football either. Faking one thing makes people doubt the real things too.
university: Kallaadha (கல்லாத, what one has not learned) set against kasadara valladhu (கசடற வல்லது, what one has mastered without flaw) gives the kural its hinge, and the emphatic -ooum (‘even that’) shows the reach of the damage: aiyam (ஐயம், doubt) spreads from the pretended to the genuine. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read kallaadha as unread books (nool), so the fool pretends to scholarship; Kalaignar widens it to any field one pretends to know. Puliyur Kesigan reads merkondu ozhugal more actively as rashly undertaking a task one has not learned, which casts doubt even on work one could do perfectly. The kural is a pointed observation about credibility: a single exposed pretense devalues an entire reputation. Both sources give identical text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra a jackal who falls into a vat of indigo dye passes himself off as a new king of the beasts; when he hears other jackals howl and howls back, his true nature is exposed and he loses everything.
hinduism.explanation: The fable mocks the impostor whose pretense is found out by a single slip.
hinduism.tie_back: Once the pretense is exposed, nothing he claimed is believed any more.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes would-be teachers who claim expertise they do not have.
christianity.tie_back: This is the posture Valluvar warns against: acting learned in what one has not learned.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids claiming or acting on what one does not know.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar gives the worldly cost of the same fault: lost trust.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And concerning that which he has not heard, he says: I have not heard; And he acknowledges the truth.”
judaism.explanation: Among the seven marks of the wise person, the Mishnah lists honestly admitting what one has not learned.
judaism.tie_back: The wise admit gaps; the fool pretends and so loses credit for what he does know.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sihacamma Jataka a merchant’s donkey, dressed in a lion’s skin, is left to graze in fields; villagers fear it until it brays, revealing itself, and it is beaten.
buddhism.explanation: The borrowed image of strength collapses the moment the true voice is heard.
buddhism.tie_back: Pretended mastery, once exposed, brings disgrace instead of respect.

jainism.quote_or_event: In its chapter on purity of speech, the Daśavaikālika Sūtra tells the monk that where there is doubt about a matter, he must not declare 'it is just so'. He may speak with certainty only about what he truly knows.
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic rules on speech forbid asserting as certain anything one does not know, because false certainty breaks the vow of truthfulness (satya).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that pretending to know what one never learned makes people doubt even one's real knowledge, and the Jain rule removes the cause by forbidding any confident claim beyond what one knows.
jainism.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra ch. 7 (Vākyaśuddhi, 'purity of speech'), Prakrit 'jattha saṃkā bhave taṃ tu, evameyaṃ ti no vae'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak! The blind man may go to appraise the jewels, but he will not know their value; he will return home after exposing his ignorance.”
sikhism.explanation: In Ramkali Ki Vaar Guru Angad describes the blind man who sets himself up to value jewels and only shows how little he knows.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says pretending to know what you never learned destroys your credibility; Guru Angad's blind appraiser exposes his own ignorance the same way.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Raamkalee, Ramkali Ki Vaar (salok 1 before pauri 15), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon insists on driving his father Helios’ sun chariot though he has never learned how; he loses control, scorches the earth and is struck down.
greek_mythology.explanation: He takes up a task he has not mastered, with disastrous results.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Undertaking what one has not learned, as Puliyur Kesigan reads the kural, brings ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Because they were good workmen they thought that they also knew all sorts of high matters, and this defect in them overshadowed their wisdom.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates found that skilled craftsmen spoiled their real expertise by claiming knowledge beyond it.
philosophy.tie_back: Exactly the kural: pretending to unlearned knowledge clouds even real mastery.

real_life_example.event_title: Henry Ford's ignorance of history is exposed at his libel trial
real_life_example.event: Henry Ford sued the Chicago Tribune for libel after it called him an ignorant idealist and an anarchist. At the 1919 trial in Mount Clemens, the newspaper's lawyers questioned him on subjects outside his expertise, and he mangled basic facts of American history, placing the American Revolution in 1812 and describing Benedict Arnold as a writer. The jury found in Ford's favour but awarded him only six cents in damages.
real_life_example.explanation: The trial made the world's most famous industrialist an object of ridicule on subjects he had pronounced on publicly, even as his genius in manufacturing remained undisputed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that pretending to know what one never learned makes people doubt even what one has mastered, and Ford's public pronouncements beyond his field brought scorn that touched his whole reputation.

tamil:
அற்றம் மறைத்தலோ புல்லறிவு தம்வயின்
குற்றம் மறையா வழி.
transliteration:
Atram maraiththalo pullarivu thamvayin
kutram maraiyaa vazhi.
meaning: If you do not get rid of your faults, then carefully covering your body with clothes is just foolishness.
elementary: Imagine someone who irons a perfect shirt every morning but is mean to everyone all day. Looking neat on the outside doesn’t hide the meanness. The poet says hiding your body but not fixing your faults is silly.
university: Atram (அற்றம்) here means the parts of the body to be covered, nakedness; maraiththal is covering it. Valluvar sets this against kutram (குற்றம், fault, moral defect) that remains unhidden (maraiyaa), arguing that modesty about the body while one’s faults stay on display is pullarivu, the very ‘petty understanding’ the chapter is named for. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all take ‘covering faults’ to mean removing them (neekkuthal), not concealing them, and Puliyur Kesigan adds the image of the hypocrite fully clothed and walking about ‘as though good’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads atram differently, as ‘ruin’ or ‘loss’, giving a minority interpretation that concealing one’s downfall is the petty act. Text identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who restrains the senses of action but whose mind dwells on sense objects certainly deludes himself and is called a pretender.”
hinduism.explanation: Outward restraint without inner change is called self-deception.
hinduism.tie_back: Like clothing the body while keeping one’s faults, it is surface without substance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus condemns those who keep the outside polished while the inside stays corrupt.
christianity.tie_back: The kural’s well-dressed fool with uncorrected faults is a whited sepulchre.

islam.quote_or_event: “O children of Adam, We have bestowed upon you clothing to conceal your private parts and as adornment. But the clothing of righteousness - that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names bodily clothing and then points to righteousness as the better covering.
islam.tie_back: Almost Valluvar’s exact contrast: covering nakedness matters less than covering oneself with virtue.

judaism.quote_or_event: After eating from the forbidden tree, Adam and Eve sew fig leaves to cover their nakedness and hide among the trees, then each shifts the blame for the wrongdoing to another.
judaism.explanation: Their first instinct is to cover the body and hide, not to admit and set right the fault.
judaism.tie_back: They hide nakedness while leaving the real fault uncorrected, the folly the kural names.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the use of your matted hair, O witless man? What of your garment of antelope’s hide? Within you is the tangle (of passion); only outwardly do you cleanse yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha mocks the ascetic whose outward dress is perfect while his mind stays tangled.
buddhism.tie_back: Same folly: tending the outer covering and leaving the inner fault.

jainism.quote_or_event: Kundakunda's Liṅga-pāhuḍa teaches that what makes a true mendicant is the inner disposition (bhāva-liṅga), and that the outward form (dravya-liṅga), even the Digambara monk's total nudity, does not make anyone a true monk.
jainism.explanation: For the Digambara master, how the body is presented, clothed or naked, is worthless unless the inner faults of passion are removed.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls it folly to cover the body carefully while leaving one's faults exposed, and Kundakunda, from the other side, says that even giving up all clothing achieves nothing while those inner faults remain.
jainism.source: Kundakunda, Liṅga-pāhuḍa (with Bhāva-pāhuḍa), as summarised by Jainpedia, 'Kundakunda'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “What should I account as the rewards of this human life, if one does not feel love and devotion to the Lord? Wearing clothes and eating food is useless, if the mind is filled with the love of duality.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says that the outward routines of life, even dressing and eating, are worthless while the mind remains full of duality.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls it foolish to cover the body carefully while leaving one's faults uncured; Guru Nanak likewise says wearing clothes is useless when the mind is not set right.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1411, Saloks Vaaran Te Vadheek (salok 11), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Republic, Glaucon tells of the shepherd Gyges, whose ring makes him invisible and who then commits injustice freely, to argue that people value seeming just more than being just.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth separates outward reputation from inner character.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The kural rejects caring for appearances while the fault underneath is untouched.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At the close of the Phaedrus, Socrates prays to Pan to be made beautiful in the inner man and that his outward and inward selves be at one.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates asks for inner beauty first and outer agreement with it.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise demands that the inner person be set right, not just the outer covering.

real_life_example.event_title: Richard Whitney, former head of the Stock Exchange, is exposed as an embezzler
real_life_example.event: Richard Whitney, president of the New York Stock Exchange from 1930 to 1935 and a model of Wall Street respectability, secretly took money entrusted to him, including funds from the Exchange's Gratuity Fund for members' families, the New York Yacht Club, of which he was treasurer, and bonds from his father-in-law's estate. In March 1938 the Exchange discovered that his firm was insolvent and Manhattan District Attorney Thomas E. Dewey charged him with embezzlement. Whitney pleaded guilty and was sentenced to five to ten years in Sing Sing prison.
real_life_example.explanation: The fall of the man who had stood for the Exchange's integrity captivated a nation still struggling through the Great Depression.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls it folly to cover the body carefully while leaving one's faults uncorrected, and Whitney's immaculate public respectability concealed wrongs that he never put right.

tamil:
அருமறை சோரும் அறிவிலான் செய்யும்
பெருமிறை தானே தனக்கு.
transliteration:
Arumarai sorum arivilaan seyyum
perumirai thaane thanakku.
meaning: A fool who does not keep good advice, or lets an important secret slip, does great harm to themselves.
elementary: If your coach gives you a secret play and you shout it across the field, or you just forget it because you weren’t listening, your own team loses. The poet says the fool who lets good advice slip away hurts himself most.
university: The crux is arumarai sorum (அருமறை சோரும்): arumarai is ‘a rare/precious marai’, where marai may mean a secret, a hidden counsel, or a sacred teaching, and sorum means ‘lets slip, lets go loose’. Mu. Varadarasanar follows the traditional reading: the fool fails to keep a precious secret in his mind and blurts it out. Pappaiah and Kalaignar instead read it as failing to accept or follow precious advice, Puliyur Kesigan as studying the rare scriptures yet growing slack and missing their true sense, and Sivayogi Sivakumar as abandoning rare insights. All converge on the second line: perumirai (பெருமிறை, great harm or affliction) is done by the fool thaane thanakku, ‘himself to himself’, echoing 843. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Udyoga Parva, Duryodhana repeatedly rejects the counsel of Vidura, Bhishma, Drona and finally Krishna himself to make peace with the Pandavas, and the war that follows destroys him and his house.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata presents Duryodhana as the archetype of the ruler who throws away wise advice.
hinduism.tie_back: Letting precious counsel slip brought on him a ruin no enemy could have engineered alone.

christianity.quote_or_event: “They would none of my counsel: they despised all my reproof. Therefore shall they eat of the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices.”
christianity.explanation: Wisdom warns that those who refuse counsel will reap the results of their own choices.
christianity.tie_back: The harm falls on the fool himself, just as the kural says.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they will say, "If only we had been listening or reasoning, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze."”
islam.explanation: The damned confess that their ruin came from failing to listen and reflect.
islam.tie_back: Their great harm was self-made by letting the warning slip.

judaism.quote_or_event: King Rehoboam rejects the counsel of the elders who served his father Solomon to lighten the people’s burden and follows his young companions instead; the ten northern tribes break away from him.
judaism.explanation: The narrative shows a ruler losing most of his kingdom by discarding wise advice.
judaism.tie_back: Rehoboam’s loss was the perumirai he did to himself by letting good counsel go.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a wise adviser to a guide to buried treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool lets that precious ‘hidden’ counsel slip, losing the treasure.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wise, fearless monks consider even a rough instruction as a benefit, but the fools hate it, though it produces patience and purity of mind.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline contrasts the wise pupil who values a teacher's correction with the fool who rejects the very counsel that would help him.
jainism.tie_back: On the reading of the Kural in which the fool lets precious counsel slip and so harms himself, the Uttarādhyayana gives the same picture: the fool hates the instruction that would have made him patient and pure.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Take the Guru’s advice, you ignorant fool; without devotion, even the clever have drowned.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan tells the ignorant to take the Guru's counsel, warning that even clever people sink without it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the fool who lets precious counsel slip does great harm to himself; Guru Arjan urges the fool to hold fast to the Guru's advice for the same reason.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 288, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib (ashtapadi 19, stanza 6), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus warns his son Icarus to fly a middle course, neither too low nor too near the sun; Icarus ignores the advice, the wax melts and he falls into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: Clear instructions are given and thrown away in a moment of thrill.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Icarus’ fall is harm done by himself to himself through neglected counsel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If any man is able to convince me and show me that I do not think or act right, I will gladly change; for I seek the truth by which no man was ever injured. But he is injured who abides in his error and ignorance.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus welcomes correction and notes that the person who refuses it harms himself.
philosophy.tie_back: The one who rejects counsel and stays in error is injured by his own hand, as the kural says.

real_life_example.event_title: Russian armies send uncoded radio orders before Tannenberg
real_life_example.event: In August 1914 two Russian armies invaded East Prussia but transmitted many of their orders over open radio without encoding them. German forces intercepted the messages, learning the location and direction of march of the Russian Second Army and that the First Army was not coming to its aid. Using this knowledge, the German Eighth Army encircled and almost destroyed the Russian Second Army at the Battle of Tannenberg at the end of August.
real_life_example.explanation: Tannenberg became a classic lesson in the cost of failing to guard vital information, as the Russians handed their enemy the secret that decided the battle.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the fool who lets a precious secret slip does great harm to himself, and the Russian commands broadcast their own plans to the enemy who then defeated them.

tamil:
ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான்தேறான் அவ்வுயிர்
போஒம் அளவுமோர் நோய்.
transliteration:
Evavum seygalaan thaandheraan avvuyir
poom alavumor noi.
meaning: A person who will not do what is right when told, and cannot figure it out alone, is like a sickness that lasts until the day they die.
elementary: Some kids can figure out on their own to pack their bag; others at least do it when Mum reminds them. But a kid who won’t think of it and won’t listen when told stays stuck forever. The poet says that kind of stubbornness is like a sickness that never goes away.
university: Valluvar names two routes to right action, being told (evavum, ஏவவும், ‘even when commanded’) and working it out oneself (thaan theral, தான் தேறல், self-ascertainment), and condemns the person who has neither. Such a life is ‘or noi’ (ஓர் நோய், a disease) until the soul departs (poom, the poetic lengthened form of pogum, marked by the alapedai -oom). Commentators differ on whose disease: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar make it a lifelong affliction for the person himself, while Pappaiah, like the classical gloss reflected in the English ‘a burden (to the earth)’, makes him a disease to the world. Kalaignar’s idiom ‘neither sondha-puththi nor sol-puththi’ (neither one’s own wit nor heeding others’ words) neatly captures the double failure. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But ignorant and faithless persons who doubt the revealed scriptures do not attain God consciousness; they fall down. For the doubting soul there is happiness neither in this world nor in the next.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a person who neither knows nor trusts the teaching given to him.
hinduism.tie_back: Having neither insight nor willingness to be taught leaves a person without relief, a lifelong affliction.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that someone who keeps rejecting correction ends beyond cure.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Without remedy’ echoes the incurable lifelong noi of the kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “Deaf, dumb and blind - so they will not return [to the right path].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes people closed to guidance from every direction.
islam.tie_back: Neither hearing advice nor seeing for themselves, they remain stuck, as in the kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is wise? He who learns from every man.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma defines wisdom as the readiness to learn from anyone.
judaism.tie_back: The kural’s fool is the exact opposite: he learns from no one and cannot teach himself.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: Even lifelong contact with a teacher does not help someone who cannot take in what is offered.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘All his life’ matches the kural’s ‘until the soul departs’: the fool stays unchanged to the end.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Whether he know the pith of the Law by intuition or through instruction, a houseless (monk) should exert himself and abstain from sins.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching recognises two routes to right understanding, one's own insight and being taught by others, and expects right effort to follow from either.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar condemns the person who neither acts when told nor works things out himself, and the Sūtrakṛtāṅga names exactly those two routes, intuition and instruction, as the ways the earnest seeker comes to know the Law.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.8.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One whom the Lord has made blind - the Lord can make him see again. He acts only as he knows, although he may be spoken to a hundred times.”
sikhism.explanation: In Ramkali Ki Vaar Guru Angad describes a person who goes on acting by his own lights even when told a hundred times, until God opens his eyes.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of the one who will not do right even when told and cannot work it out himself; Guru Angad's man who ignores a hundred warnings is the same case.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Raamkalee, Ramkali Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 16), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus warns his brother Epimetheus never to accept a gift from Zeus; Epimetheus, whose name means ‘afterthought’, accepts Pandora anyway and understands his mistake only after the harm is done.
greek_mythology.explanation: Epimetheus neither foresees danger himself nor heeds the warning he was given.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the kural’s double failure: no insight of his own and no obedience to counsel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle quotes Hesiod: the best man thinks things through himself, the next best listens to one who advises well, but the man who neither understands for himself nor takes to heart what another says is useless.
philosophy.explanation: This three-tier ranking of people by how they come to know what to do is a classic in Greek ethics.
philosophy.tie_back: The kural describes exactly the third, worthless tier, adding that it lasts a lifetime.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.4, quoting Hesiod, Works and Days 293–297

real_life_example.event_title: Challenger is launched despite engineers' warnings
real_life_example.place: Kennedy Space Center, Florida, United States
real_life_example.event: On the evening of 27 January 1986, engineers at the booster manufacturer Morton Thiokol, including Roger Boisjoly, argued that the space shuttle Challenger should not be launched in the forecast cold because the rubber O-ring seals in the booster joints might fail. After a teleconference with NASA, Thiokol managers reversed the engineers' no-launch recommendation. Challenger broke apart shortly after lift-off the next morning, killing all seven crew members, and the Rogers Commission found that O-ring failure in the cold had caused the accident and that flawed decision-making was a contributing cause.
real_life_example.explanation: The disaster became a standard case study in engineering ethics, showing how an organisation can refuse a clear warning from those who know the facts.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural condemns the one who will not do right even when told and cannot see it for himself, and the managers who overrode the engineers neither heeded the warning nor recognised the danger on their own.

tamil:
காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான் காணாதான்
கண்டானாம் தான்கண்ட வாறு.
transliteration:
Kaanaadhaan kaattuvaan thaankaanaan kaanaadhaan
kandaanaam thaankanda vaaru.
meaning: If you try to make a fool see the truth, you end up looking like the fool, because the fool is sure they already see everything their own way.
elementary: Try explaining to a little brother who is sure the moon follows his car that it only looks that way. He just laughs at you and says you don’t understand. The poet says that when you try to teach someone who is sure he’s right, you end up looking silly.
university: The kural is a wordplay on kaan (காண், to see): kaanaadhaan (one who does not see) is set against kaattuvaan (one who shows) and kandaan (one who has seen), and the line turns on ‘thaankanda vaaru’ (in the way he himself saw). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: one who tries to enlighten a fool becomes a fool himself, while the fool appears wise by his own lights; Pappaiah adds that the fool regards his teacher as the fool. Kalaignar sharpens the second half: the fool shows himself off as wise on the strength of what he alone knows. Puliyur Kesigan gives a different construal: the fool who shows others only what he saw remains one who never saw the truth. The density of the kaan-roots makes the kural famous for its sound-play. Both sources give identical text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And that knowledge by which one is attached to one kind of work as the all in all, without knowledge of the truth, and which is very meager, is said to be in the mode of darkness.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita defines the lowest knowledge as a narrow view mistaken for the whole.
hinduism.tie_back: The fool ‘sees as he has seen’ and takes his small view for everything.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Speak not in the ears of a fool: for he will despise the wisdom of thy words.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs advises against trying to teach a fool, who will only scorn the teaching.
christianity.tie_back: The kural’s would-be teacher is scorned and made to look the fool.

islam.quote_or_event: “Take what is given freely, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to urge what is right but not to get entangled with the obstinately ignorant.
islam.tie_back: Arguing with the fool only makes the teacher look foolish, so wisdom turns away.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs warns that whoever corrects a scoffer brings shame on himself, and advises not to rebuke a scoffer lest he hate you, but to rebuke a wise man who will love you for it.
judaism.explanation: Instruction helps only those willing to receive it; aimed at the scoffer, it rebounds on the teacher.
judaism.tie_back: This is the kural’s first half: the teacher of the fool is the one who ends up disgraced.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Udana, a king has blind men touch different parts of an elephant; each declares the elephant is like a pot, a fan, a pillar or a brush according to the part he felt, and they come to blows over it.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the parable for teachers who cling to partial views and quarrel over them.
buddhism.tie_back: Each blind man ‘sees as he has seen’ and cannot be taught otherwise, exactly kandaanaam thaankanda vaaru.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Now this driver (viz. Garga), who had to deal with bad bullocks, thought: 'What have I to do with bad pupils? I am disheartened. 'As are bad pupils, so are bad bullocks; I shall leave these lazy donkeys, and shall practise severe austerities.'”
jainism.explanation: The learned elder Garga, worn out by pupils who argue and will not be convinced by reasons, finally gives up teaching them and turns to his own austerities.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that whoever tries to show the truth to a fool ends up looking foolish himself, and Garga's story shows the same trap: the teacher tires himself out and has to walk away.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 27.15–16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I do not understand myself, and yet I try to teach others. Such is the guide I am! O Nanak! The one who is blind shows others the way, and misleads all his companions.”
sikhism.explanation: In Majh Ki Vaar Guru Nanak, speaking humbly in his own voice, describes the guide who lacks understanding yet teaches others and leads them astray.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the fool shows others only what he himself saw and remains one who never saw the truth; Guru Nanak's blind guide does the same.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Raag Majh, Majh Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 6), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cassandra, given true prophecy but cursed by Apollo never to be believed, foresees the fall of Troy and Agamemnon’s murder, yet those around her dismiss her as raving.
greek_mythology.explanation: The one who truly sees is taken for mad by those who cannot see.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the kural’s teacher, the seer is made to look the fool by the unseeing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the allegory of the cave, the prisoner who has seen the sun returns to free the others; with eyes unused to the dark he seems ridiculous to them, and they would rather kill him than be led up.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows the cave-dwellers mocking the one who tries to show them reality.
philosophy.tie_back: The teacher looks the fool, while the prisoners trust what they themselves have seen.

real_life_example.event_title: Geologists dismiss Alfred Wegener's continental drift
real_life_example.event: On 6 January 1912 the German scientist Alfred Wegener presented his theory that the continents had once been joined and had drifted apart to a geological meeting in Frankfurt, and he expanded it in later books. Most geologists of his day reacted with hostility, attacked Wegener personally as an outsider, and dismissed the idea as a fairy tale. Only decades later, in the 1960s, did new evidence lead to the theory of plate tectonics and the acceptance of his central idea.
real_life_example.explanation: Wegener's case shows how a person who presents an unwelcome truth can be treated as the foolish one by those who are sure of their own view.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says whoever tries to show the truth to those who will not see ends up looking like the fool, because they are certain they already see everything their own way, and Wegener was ridiculed by geologists who were the ones in error.

tamil:
உலகத்தார் உண்டென்பது இல்லென்பான் வையத்து
அலகையா வைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Ulagaththaar undenbadhu illenbaan vaiyaththu
alagaiyaa vaikkap padum.
meaning: A person who says no to what the wise people of the world say is true will be thought of as a demon on earth.
elementary: If everyone has seen the sun rise every morning and one boy keeps insisting “There is no sun!”, people stop taking him seriously and leave him out of games. The poet says that someone who denies what everyone knows is true gets treated like a spooky outsider.
university: Ulagaththaar (உலகத்தார்) here, as often in the Kural, means not the crowd but the learned of the world (Pappaiah: ‘the great ones’, uyarndhor), and their ‘undu’ (it exists) is denied by the fool’s ‘il’ (it does not). The traditional commentators gloss what is denied as established truths such as the other world, merit and the divine, attested by the learned; Kalaignar gives a modern secular reading: denying what has been clearly shown with evidence. Such a person is placed (vaikkappadum) as an alagai (அலகை, a demon, ghost or pey) on earth, that is, shunned as something not quite human. Sivayogi Sivakumar and Mu. Varadarasanar both stress exclusion (oduhukkappaduvaan, vilakkappaduvaan). The chapter thus ends with perverse denial as the extreme of pullarivu. Text identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “They say that this world is unreal, with no foundation, no God in control. They say it is produced of sex desire and has no cause other than lust.”
hinduism.explanation: In the chapter on divine and demoniac natures, Krishna lists the denial of the world’s divine order as a mark of the asuric (demonic) person.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise brands the denier of what the wise affirm as an alagai, a demon on earth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools,”
christianity.explanation: Paul says those who refuse to acknowledge what is plainly evident in creation became fools while claiming wisdom.
christianity.tie_back: Denial of what is evident marks the fool, as in the kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they rejected them, while their [inner] selves were convinced thereof, out of injustice and haughtiness. So see how was the end of the corrupters.”
islam.explanation: Pharaoh’s people deny Moses’ clear signs out of arrogance, though inwardly convinced.
islam.tie_back: This is the perverse denial of evident truth Kalaignar reads into the kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The scoundrel thinks, “God does not care.””
judaism.explanation: The Psalm’s naval (often rendered ‘fool’) says in his heart what the JPS note gives literally as ‘There is no God’.
judaism.tie_back: The denier of what the world affirms is the Psalmist’s naval, a morally corrupt fool.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Payasi Sutta, Prince Payasi insists there is no other world, no spontaneously reborn beings and no fruit of good or bad deeds, and the monk Kumara Kassapa answers him with a long series of parables until he relents.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta treats denial of the other world and of karmic results as a wrong view to be patiently corrected.
buddhism.tie_back: Payasi denies exactly what the traditional commentators say the kural’s fool denies.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A monk should not think: 'There is, indeed, no life to come, nor an exalted state to be acquired by penances; in short, I have been deceived.'”
jainism.explanation: Among the twenty-two troubles a monk must overcome, the last is the temptation to deny what the Jinas taught: the next life, the fruit of austerity, and the Jinas themselves.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's fool flatly denies what the wise affirm, such as the other world and the fruit of deeds, and the Uttarādhyayana lists exactly this denial as a failing of right faith to be overcome.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.44 (cf. 2.45) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabir! Do not associate with the faithless cynics; run far away from them. If you touch a vessel stained with soot, some of the soot will stick to you.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir tells the seeker to keep well away from the saakat, the faithless cynic who turns from God, since such company stains like soot.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one who denies what the wise affirm is set apart like a demon; Kabir likewise sets the faithless cynic apart and tells the seeker to keep away.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 131) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Pentheus of Thebes refuses to accept the divinity of Dionysus that the women and elders of the city acknowledge, imprisons the god in disguise, and is torn apart by the maenads.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides presents Pentheus’ obstinate denial as a fatal madness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The man who denies what all around him affirm ends as an outcast and horror.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle holds that what everyone believes is so, and that someone who attacks this common belief will hardly have anything more credible to put in its place.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, shared reputable opinion (endoxa) carries real evidential weight.
philosophy.tie_back: The kural likewise treats flat denial of what the world affirms as a mark of folly.

real_life_example.event_title: Alfred Russel Wallace wins the flat-earth wager on the Bedford Level
real_life_example.place: Old Bedford River, the Fens, England
real_life_example.event: In January 1870 John Hampden, who maintained that the Earth was flat, offered a wager of up to 500 pounds to anyone who could prove its curvature. The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace accepted, and in March 1870, using markers along a six-mile straight stretch of the Old Bedford River, showed the curvature to the satisfaction of the referee, John Henry Walsh, editor of The Field. Hampden refused to accept the verdict and pursued Wallace with abusive letters and attacks for years afterwards, and was widely regarded as a crank.
real_life_example.explanation: The episode is remembered as a case of a man who flatly denied an established fact even after it was demonstrated before an agreed referee.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says whoever flatly denies what the wise of the world affirm will be regarded as a demon and kept apart, and Hampden's denial of the Earth's curvature after it had been shown to him left him a byword for obstinate folly.

tamil:
இகலென்ப எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் பகலென்னும்
பண்பின்மை பாரிக்கும் நோய்.
transliteration:
Ikalenba ellaa uyirkkum pakalennum
panbinmai paarikkum noi.
meaning: Hostility (the wish to fight and oppose others) is called a disease. In every living being, it spreads the bad habit of not getting along with others.
elementary: Think of a bad cold that spreads from one kid in class to everyone. Grudges work the same way: one person stops getting along with another, and soon nobody can play together. The poet says that kind of falling-out is a sickness, and it can catch anyone.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition: ikal (இகல், hostility, mental antagonism) is a noi (நோய், disease) that ‘spreads out’ or ‘nourishes’ (paarikkum, பாரிக்கும்) pakal (பகல், separation, non-union) in all creatures. The wordplay is deliberate: pakal normally means ‘daytime’ but here carries its older sense of ‘division’, which Puliyur Kesigan glosses as kūdāmai (கூடாமை, not coming together) and Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘failing to harmonise with other lives’. The traditional commentators following Parimelazhagar treat ikal as the inner root from which outward enmity (pagai, the subject of the next chapter, Pagaimaatchi) grows, which explains why this chapter sits in the Natpiyal (friendship) section of Porutpal. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads ikal unusually as ‘contempt’ (இகழ்ச்சி) that resists another’s nature; Kalaignar emphasises its social result, people unable to live together. The couplet text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names desire-turned-wrath as the one enemy that devours everything in the world.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise names a single inner disease, hostility, as the common affliction of all living beings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if a kingdom be divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points out that any household or realm torn by internal division destroys itself.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s pakal, disunion, is exactly the division Jesus says no house can survive.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you - when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together and you became, by His favor, brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an commands unity and recalls how enemies were turned into brothers by God’s grace.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat division between hearts as the core danger and union as the remedy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Joshua said: an evil eye, the evil inclination, and hatred for humankind put a person out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah lists hatred of people (sinat ha-briyot) among the three traits that destroy a person.
judaism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the rabbis see hatred of others as a ruinous inner condition rather than a passing mood.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fire like lust and no crime like hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ranks hatred as the worst of wrongs, alongside lust as the worst fire.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts single out hostility as the gravest affliction of living beings.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain passions (kaṣāyas) are presented as forces that eat away at the bonds between beings, with anger first destroying love.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls hostility a disease that breeds separation in every creature, and the Jain verse likewise makes the passions destroyers of love and friendship, the very bonds hostility breaks.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 135 (Samyamasūtra; drawn from Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I have totally forgotten my jealousy of others, since I found the Saadh Sangat, the Company of the Holy. … No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes a mind cured of jealousy in the company of the holy: it no longer counts anyone as enemy or stranger, and it gets along with all.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines hostility as the disease that breeds the habit of not getting along with others; Guru Arjan describes the healthy opposite state, in which one gets along with everyone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eris, goddess of Strife, uninvited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, tossed a golden apple marked for the fairest among the guests, setting Hera, Athena and Aphrodite against each other and, through the Judgement of Paris, starting the Trojan War.
greek_mythology.explanation: One act of spiteful discord spread until it engulfed gods, heroes and whole cities.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The myth dramatizes the Kural’s idea that discord is a contagion that spreads to all.
greek_mythology.source: Eris and the Apple of Discord (Cypria, summarized by Proclus; Theoi)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Republic, Socrates argues that injustice breeds factions, hatreds and quarrels that make any group, and even a single soul, incapable of acting together and an enemy to itself.
philosophy.explanation: Plato holds that internal division paralyses both cities and individuals.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s ‘disease that breeds disunion’ is the same diagnosis of self-defeating division.

real_life_example.event_title: Florence's Guelfs split into Blacks and Whites and Dante is exiled
real_life_example.event: Around 1300 the Guelf party that governed Florence divided into two hostile factions, the Blacks led by Corso Donati and the Whites, to which the poet Dante Alighieri belonged. In 1302 the Blacks, allied with Pope Boniface VIII, took control of the city and expelled the Whites. Dante, who was away on a diplomatic mission, was condemned and banished, and spent the rest of his life in exile, during which he wrote the Divine Comedy.
real_life_example.explanation: The feud shows how hostility within a single ruling party could tear a prosperous city apart and drive out even its greatest poet.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls hostility a disease that feeds the refusal to live together, and in Florence it split even former allies of one party into factions that could no longer share the city.

tamil:
பகல்கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும் இகல்கருதி
இன்னாசெய் யாமை தலை.
transliteration:
Pakalkarudhip patraa seyinum ikalkarudhi
innaasey yaamai thalai.
meaning: Even if someone who wants to break away from you does things that hurt you, the best thing is not to hurt them back out of hostility.
elementary: Suppose a classmate stops being your friend and does mean little things to you. You could plan to get back at them, but the poet says the best thing is not to. Not paying back meanness with meanness is what a really strong person does.
university: The couplet is built on a symmetry of motives: the other person acts pakal karudhi (பகல் கருதி, intending separation) and does patraa (பற்றா, unloving or disagreeable things), while you are warned against acting ikal karudhi (இகல் கருதி, out of hostility) and doing innaa (இன்னா, harmful things). The final word thalai (தலை, ‘head’, foremost) marks this restraint as the supreme course. Puliyur Kesigan and Mu. Varadarasanar both read it as forbearance under provocation; Solomon Pappaiah calls it a ‘superior quality’ (சிறந்த குணம்). The thought echoes the Aram chapters on Innaa Seyyaamai (ch. 32), especially Kural 314, but here it is set in Porutpal as practical statecraft: retaliation turns disagreement into lasting enmity. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant ... such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the ideal devotee as without hatred (adveṣṭā), friendly and forgiving toward all.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural asks the same refusal of hatred even toward those who wrong us.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers never to repay harm with harm.
christianity.tie_back: This is nearly a word-for-word restatement of the Kural’s counsel.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the retribution for an evil act is an evil one like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation - his reward is [due] from Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an permits equal retaliation but ranks pardon and reconciliation higher.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names restraint, not retaliation, as the better path.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart ... Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids both inner hatred and outward revenge.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly forbids acting on hostility even when provoked.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who do not harbor such thoughts still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that letting go of the record of wrongs is how hatred ends.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise asks us not to let another’s offences become our motive to harm.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a layman abuses a monk, he should not grow angry against him; because he would be like a child, a monk should not grow angry. … A monk should not be angry if beaten, nor should he therefore entertain sinful thoughts; knowing patience to be the highest good, a monk should meditate on the Law.”
jainism.explanation: Among the troubles a monk must bear, being abused and being struck are to be met with patience and without any thought of retaliation, since patience is the highest good.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that even when someone deliberately does you harm, the highest course is not to strike back in hostility, and Mahavira's rule for abuse and blows says the same.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.24 and 2.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the seeker not to hit back at those who hit him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even when someone does you harm out of a wish to break with you, the best course is not to harm them in return; Farid gives the same rule of non-retaliation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 7), Bhagat Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 24, Achilles, whose friend Patroclus was killed by Hector, receives Hector’s grieving father Priam, weeps with him, and gives back Hector’s body instead of continuing to dishonour it.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest warrior finally sets aside his rage against an enemy who wronged him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles shows, late and at great cost, the restraint the Kural asks for from the start.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Crito, Socrates argues that one must never do wrong, and therefore must never return wrong for wrong or do evil to anyone, whatever one has suffered from them.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates rejects retaliation as itself a form of wrongdoing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural reaches the same conclusion: provocation never licenses harm.

real_life_example.event_title: The Greensboro sit-in at the Woolworth lunch counter
real_life_example.event: On 1 February 1960 four students from North Carolina A&T, Ezell Blair Jr., Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil and David Richmond, sat down at the whites-only lunch counter of the Woolworth store in Greensboro and politely asked to be served. When they were refused and asked to leave, they stayed quietly in their seats. Over the following six months hundreds of students and community members joined the protest and a boycott, and the counter was desegregated on 25 July 1960.
real_life_example.explanation: The sit-in sparked a wave of nonviolent sit-ins across the South and showed the power of patient, peaceful refusal in the face of injustice.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural teaches that even when others do us wrong, the highest course is not to hurt them in return, and the students answered refusal and exclusion with calm, nonviolent persistence.

tamil:
இகலென்னும் எவ்வநோய் நீக்கின் தவலில்லாத்
தாவில் விளக்கம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Ikalennum evvanoi neekkin thavalillaath
thaavil vilakkam tharum.
meaning: If you get rid of the painful disease called hostility, you will win a spotless fame that never fades.
elementary: Imagine carrying a heavy, smelly bag of grudges everywhere you go. When you finally drop it, you feel lighter, and people start to remember you as the kind one. The poet says letting go of hostility makes you shine in a way that lasts.
university: Evvanoi (எவ்வநோய்) is a compound of evvam (எவ்வம், distress, affliction) and noi (disease): hostility is a sickness that torments its host. Its removal yields vilakkam (விளக்கம், literally ‘light, clarity’, here ‘renown, distinction’) qualified twice: thaval illaa (தவல் இல்லா, undiminishing) and thaavil (தாவில், flawless or unfailing). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the outcome as imperishable fame (அழியாத புகழ்), Kalaignar as ‘stainless, lasting fame’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar takes vilakkam more literally as inner clarity. The image of illness and cure continues from 851, so the chapter treats hostility medically: diagnosis (851), restraint (852), cure and its fruit (853). Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Among the divine qualities (daivī sampad) Krishna lists in Gita 16.1-3 are freedom from anger, freedom from malice (adroha) and forgiveness, which he says lead toward liberation, while the demonic qualities bind.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita treats freedom from hostility as part of the radiant, divine nature.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural promises a lasting radiance (vilakkam) to those who remove hostility.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts a healthy heart with envy that rots a person from within.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts picture ill will as a disease and its absence as health and life.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allah] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who swallow their anger and forgive, calling them beloved of God.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it promises honour to those who rid themselves of hostile feeling.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What man is he that desireth life, and loveth many days, that he may see good? ... Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalm promises long life and good to the one who leaves evil and actively pursues peace.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly promises an unfading reward to those who put away hostility.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha declares that only the removal of hatred ends hatred, as a timeless law.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts present the removal of hostility as the one cure, with a lasting result.

jainism.quote_or_event: In Hemacandra's life of Pārśvanātha, Kamaṭha nurses a hatred for his brother Marubhūti that lasts through many births. In the last of them, as the god Meghamālin, he attacks the meditating Pārśva with storm and flood, while Pārśva never answers with hostility. The Kalpa Sūtra gives Pārśva the lasting epithet 'the people's favourite' (puruṣādānīya).
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition contrasts the enemy whose rage drags him through birth after birth with the Tīrthaṅkara who, free of enmity, becomes the most beloved and honoured of teachers.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural promises unfading renown to whoever rids himself of the disease of hostility, and Pārśva, who never returned Kamaṭha's enmity, is remembered with a lasting title of affection.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book IX (Pārśvanāthacaritra), tr. Helen M. Johnson; Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Pārśva (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger. Your body shall not suffer from any disease, and you shall obtain everything.”
sikhism.explanation: Farid promises that one who returns good for evil and keeps anger out of the mind will be free of disease and will gain everything.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls hostility a painful disease whose removal brings undying renown; Farid likewise ties the giving up of anger to freedom from disease and a full reward.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381-1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 78), Bhagat Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Eumenides, Athena persuades the vengeful Furies to give up their wrath against Athens; they become the Eumenides, ‘Kindly Ones’, and receive an honoured, permanent home and worship in the city.
greek_mythology.explanation: Spirits of hostility, once they lay aside their anger, gain lasting honour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s promise of unfading distinction to whoever casts out hostility.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca closes On Anger by urging that, since life is short, we should spend it not in hostility but in cultivating humanity, so that no one fears us and we leave a gentle memory.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that freedom from anger is the path to a calm life and a good name.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise links ending hostility with lasting good repute.

real_life_example.event_title: Robert Schuman proposes pooling French and German coal and steel
real_life_example.event: On 9 May 1950 French Foreign Minister Robert Schuman proposed that French and German coal and steel production be placed under a common High Authority open to other European countries, so that war between France and Germany would become not merely unthinkable but materially impossible. The proposal led to the Treaty of Paris of 1951, which created the European Coal and Steel Community of six countries. In 1985 the date of the declaration was made Europe Day.
real_life_example.explanation: After three wars between France and Germany in seventy years, the declaration began the reconciliation that grew into the European Union, and Schuman is honoured as one of its founders.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural promises unfading renown to those who rid themselves of the disease of hostility, and Schuman's turn away from Franco-German enmity is still commemorated every year on Europe Day.

tamil:
இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் பயக்கும் இகலென்னும்
துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்.
transliteration:
Inbaththul inbam payakkum ikalennum
thunbaththul thunbang kedin.
meaning: When hostility, the worst of all pains, is gone, the greatest of all joys comes.
elementary: Have you ever made up with a friend after a big fight? That warm, happy feeling afterwards is one of the best feelings there is. The poet says being angry at someone is the worst kind of unhappy, so ending it brings the best kind of happy.
university: The couplet is a chiasmus of superlatives: inbaththul inbam (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம், joy among joys) answers thunbaththul thunbam (துன்பத்துள் துன்பம், sorrow among sorrows). The verb payakkum (பயக்கும், yields, produces) makes joy the direct fruit of hostility’s destruction (kedin, கெடின், ‘if it perishes’). Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it straightforwardly as ‘the greatest misery gone, the greatest delight comes’. The same formula ‘துன்பத்துள் துன்பம் கெடின்’ appears in Kural 369 on desire (avaa), so Valluvar ranks hostility alongside craving as the chief sources of suffering. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not connected with the Supreme ... can have neither transcendental intelligence nor a steady mind, without which there is no possibility of peace. And how can there be any happiness without peace?”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna argues that real happiness depends on inner peace.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same: once the turmoil of hostility ends, the greatest joy follows.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus declares a special blessedness for those who end enmity.
christianity.tie_back: Both promise the highest happiness to those who end hostility.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not hate one another, and do not be jealous of one another, and do not desert each other, and O, Allah's worshipers! Be brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet forbids mutual hatred and calls believers to live as brothers.
islam.tie_back: Brotherhood in place of hatred is the joy the Kural describes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist celebrates the sweetness of people living together without strife.
judaism.tie_back: This is the ‘joy among joys’ that follows when hostility is gone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, friendly amidst the hostile. Amidst hostile men we dwell free from hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the happiness of those who stay free of hatred even among enemies.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts tie the highest happiness to freedom from hostility.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By begging forgiveness he obtains happiness of mind; thereby he acquires a kind disposition towards all kinds of living beings; by this kind disposition he obtains purity of character and freedom from fear.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana traces a chain of fruits from the practice of asking forgiveness (kṣamāpana): first happiness of mind, then goodwill toward all beings, then purity and freedom from fear.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that once hostility, the sorrow of sorrows, is destroyed, it yields the joy of joys, and the Jain text likewise makes happiness of mind the first fruit of ending hostility through forgiveness.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not harbor evil intentions against others in your mind, and you shall not be troubled, O Siblings of Destiny, O friends.”
