sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that whoever keeps ill will toward others out of the mind is spared trouble in his own life.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that destroying hostility, the worst of sorrows, yields the greatest joy; Guru Arjan likewise links the absence of ill will with freedom from trouble.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the end of the Odyssey, Athena halts the feud between Odysseus and the kinsmen of the slain suitors, and Zeus wills that they make a solemn peace so that friendship, wealth and peace may return to Ithaca.
greek_mythology.explanation: The epic ends not with victory but with the end of a blood feud and the return of prosperity.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The poem’s happy ending is precisely the end of hostility the Kural praises.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza writes that one who seeks to overcome hatred with love fights joyfully and confidently, while one who avenges wrongs with reciprocal hatred lives in misery.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, answering hatred with love is itself a source of joy.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise links ending hostility to the highest delight.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics IV, Prop. 46 and Scholium

real_life_example.event_title: The Berlin Wall opens and Berliners celebrate
real_life_example.event: On the evening of 9 November 1989 an unclear announcement of new travel rules by East German official Gunter Schabowski sent thousands of East Berliners to the border crossings. At Bornholmer Strasse the overwhelmed guards opened the checkpoint, and people poured through to be greeted by West Berliners with flowers and champagne, while others climbed onto the Wall and began chipping pieces from it. More than two million East Berliners visited West Berlin that weekend.
real_life_example.explanation: The opening of the Wall ended nearly three decades of division in Berlin and opened the way to German reunification in 1990.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when hostility, the worst of miseries, is destroyed it yields the greatest of joys, and the night the symbol of Cold War enmity was breached became one of the most joyful public celebrations of the century.

tamil:
இகலெதிர் சாய்ந்தொழுக வல்லாரை யாரே
மிக்லூக்கும் தன்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Ikaledhir saaindhozhuka vallaarai yaare
mikalookkum thanmai yavar.
meaning: Who could ever beat people who can turn away from hostility whenever it rises inside them?
elementary: Picture someone trying to start a fight with a kid who just smiles and won’t fight back. After a while, there is nothing to fight about, and the bully gives up. The poet says nobody can beat a person who never lets anger take over.
university: The key phrase is ikal edhir saaindhu ozhuga (இகல் எதிர் சாய்ந்து ஒழுக): to ‘lean away against’ hostility, i.e. to recoil from it and conduct oneself in the opposite direction when it arises within. Puliyur Kesigan specifies ‘when hostility arises in one’s own heart’, so the victory is first over oneself; mikal ūkkum (to aspire to overcome) then describes would-be conquerors, of whom ‘who’ (yaare) implies none. Textual note: both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the second line as ‘மிக்லூக்கும்’ while their own romanizations read ‘mikalookkum’ and thirukkural.net’s song version prints ‘மிகலூக்கும்’; the word is mikal + ūkkum, and the printed form appears to be a shared digital orthographic slip. The same form recurs in 858. The text is otherwise identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Before giving up this present body, if one is able to tolerate the urges of the material senses and check the force of desire and anger, he is well situated and is happy in this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the one who can check the force of anger becomes steady and secure.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural calls such a person unconquerable.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says the way to win against evil is not to be dragged into it but to answer with good.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes refusal of hostility the secret of being unconquered.

islam.quote_or_event: “The strong is not the one who overcomes the people by his strength, but the strong is the one who controls himself while in anger.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet redefines strength as mastery over one’s own anger.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar’s unconquerable person is exactly this kind of strong one.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city.’”
judaism.explanation: The sage Ben Zoma defines true might as self-mastery, quoting Proverbs on slowness to anger.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts place real power in conquering one’s own hostility.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria), citing Proverbs 16:32

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that non-anger is itself the means of victory.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s unconquerable person wins by the same non-anger.

jainism.quote_or_event: “They indeed had no effect whatever on the Lord whose power was great. Is a wind, even great, able to shake Meru?”
jainism.explanation: The furious serpent Caṇḍakauśika burns Mahavira with its poisonous gaze and bites him again and again. The Lord stays unmoved and without hostility, and the serpent, overcome by his calm, gives up its anger altogether.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks who could ever defeat those who turn away from hostility, and Caṇḍakauśika's venom cannot even shake Mahavira, who wins not by fighting back but by staying free of enmity.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. III, part 10 'Episode of Caṇḍakauśika' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib Guru Nanak makes kinship with all people the true spiritual order and says that whoever conquers his own mind has conquered the world.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks who could ever defeat those who turn away from hostility when it rises within; Guru Nanak likewise makes victory over one's own mind, held in brotherhood with all, the victory over the world.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib (pauri 28), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the North Wind and the Sun, the Wind blows harder and harder but cannot strip a traveller of his cloak, while the Sun’s gentle warmth makes him take it off.
greek_mythology.explanation: Gentleness succeeds where force and aggression fail.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the one who refuses hostility cannot be overcome.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The North Wind and the Sun (Townsend tr.)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius writes that kindness is invincible if it is genuine, since even the most insolent person can do nothing to one who stays kind and gently corrects him.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic emperor holds that sincere goodwill disarms every attacker.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s ‘who could overcome them?’ makes the same claim.

real_life_example.event_title: Martin Luther King Jr. calms the crowd after his home is bombed
real_life_example.event: During the Montgomery bus boycott, Martin Luther King Jr.'s home was bombed on the evening of 30 January 1956 while he was speaking at a mass meeting; his wife Coretta and their baby daughter were unhurt. He returned to find a large, angry crowd, many of them armed, gathered outside and refusing police orders to leave. Standing on his damaged porch, King urged them to love their enemies and to go home calmly, and what could have become a riot ended peacefully.
real_life_example.explanation: King's refusal to answer violence with violence kept the boycott nonviolent, and the movement went on to win the desegregation of Montgomery's buses later that year.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks who could ever overcome those who turn away from hostility whenever it rises, and King turned himself and his supporters away from retaliation at the very moment it was most provoked, making the movement unbeatable.

tamil:
இகலின் மிகலினிது என்பவன் வாழ்க்கை
தவலும் கெடலும் நணித்து.
transliteration:
Ikalin mikalinidhu enbavan vaazhkkai
thavalum kedalum naniththu.
meaning: A person who thinks it is sweet to get ahead by fighting with others will soon see their life fail and fall apart.
elementary: Some people enjoy picking fights because winning feels good. But someone who always looks for a fight soon has no friends and lots of enemies, and things start to go wrong fast. The poet warns that loving fights leads to falling down.
university: Ikalin mikal inidhu (இகலின் மிகல் இனிது): ‘to excel (mikal) by means of hostility is sweet’ is the boast of the quarrelsome man. Valluvar answers that for him thavalum (தவலும், failing, slipping) and kedalum (கெடலும், perishing) are naniththu (நணித்து, near). Puliyur Kesigan reads mikal as ‘exceeding others in hostility’, Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘victory through hostility’, and Kalaignar as ‘thinking victory easy through opposition’. Pappaiah gives a distinctive reading: such a life’s survival is brief, and its ruin also comes within a brief time. The couplet turns from the inner disease to its social consequence. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata, Shishupala heaps insult after insult on Krishna at Yudhishthira’s Rajasuya sacrifice, delighting in his hostility, until Krishna, having forborne a hundred offences, slays him in the assembly.
hinduism.explanation: A king who revelled in hostility met swift destruction.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural’s man who found hostility sweet and found ruin near.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that a community that feeds on infighting will consume itself.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts warn that relish for hostility ends in self-destruction.

islam.quote_or_event: “And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute and [thus] lose courage and [then] your strength would depart; and be patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that quarrelling saps courage and makes strength vanish.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly says hostility brings swift failure.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells of a host who, out of personal hatred, threw a man named Bar Kamsa out of his feast; the humiliated guest’s revenge set in motion events the sages connect with the destruction of Jerusalem.
judaism.explanation: A private grudge, enjoyed and indulged, escalated into national catastrophe.
judaism.tie_back: This shows how near ruin is to those who indulge hostility.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Victory begets enmity; the defeated dwell in pain. Happily the peaceful live, discarding both victory and defeat.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that winning by conflict only breeds more enmity.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise exposes the sweetness of victory through hostility as a trap.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He stumbled and fell into a pit that was like the mouth of hell. As he fell, the sharp axe fell on him and split his head in two. For there was maturing of bad karma.”
jainism.explanation: In a former birth, the hot-tempered ascetic Kauśika rushes with an axe at men breaking into his woods. His own fury throws him into a pit, where his own axe kills him, and the text adds that anger carries on into the next birth.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that for whoever thinks it sweet to get ahead through hostility, failure and ruin are close at hand, and Kauśika's charge ends in his destruction within moments.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. III, part 10 'Episode of Caṇḍakauśika' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not speak ill of others, or get involved in arguments.”
sikhism.explanation: In a chhant in Raag Vadhans Guru Nanak warns against calling others bad and stirring up quarrels.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that one who finds it sweet to get ahead through hostility is close to ruin; Guru Nanak likewise steers the seeker away from picking quarrels.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 566, Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 18, after Patroclus dies because of his quarrel with Agamemnon, Achilles wishes that strife would perish from gods and men, along with the anger that grows sweeter than honey in a man’s heart.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles recognises too late that the sweetness of his anger brought ruin on those he loved.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s warning: hostility tastes sweet, but ruin is near.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Thucydides describes how, during the civil strife at Corcyra, factions came to prize revenge over self-preservation and admired the violent, until the whole Greek world was convulsed and its character corrupted.
philosophy.explanation: The historian shows that a culture which comes to love conflict quickly destroys itself.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural states the same law for a single life.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 3.82-83

real_life_example.event_title: Charles the Bold's wars end in his death at Nancy
real_life_example.place: Grandson and Morat, Switzerland; Nancy, Lorraine, France
real_life_example.event: Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, pursued constant wars of expansion, and after a failed siege of Neuss he went to war against the Swiss confederates and the Duke of Lorraine. In 1476 the Swiss defeated him at Grandson and again at Morat. On 5 January 1477 he was killed in battle at Nancy against Rene II of Lorraine and his Swiss allies, and his Burgundian state was then divided between the King of France and the Habsburgs.
real_life_example.explanation: Within three years of his greatest power, Charles's appetite for war had destroyed both himself and the independent Burgundian state he had sought to enlarge.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that for one who thinks it sweet to get ahead through hostility, failure and ruin are near, and Charles's relentless warring brought defeat, death and the break-up of his realm within a few years.

tamil:
மிகல்மேவல் மெய்ப்பொருள் காணார் இகல்மேவல்
இன்னா அறிவி னவர்.
transliteration:
Mikalmeval meypporul kaanaar ikalmeval
innaa arivi navar.
meaning: People whose harmful minds are set on fighting can never see the true way that leads to success.
elementary: When you are really angry at someone, it is hard to think clearly, a bit like trying to read with foggy glasses. The poet says people who love fighting have foggy minds, so they miss the smart, true way to win.
university: The couplet balances two uses of mēval (மேவல், attaching to, desiring): ikal mēval (attachment to hostility) and mikal mēval (attaining victory). Those with innaa arivu (இன்னா அறிவு, a harmful or grievous intellect) who cling to hostility cannot see meypporul (மெய்ப்பொருள், the true substance or principle) of success. Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah identify this ‘true substance’ with nīti nūl porul, the teaching of the treatises on statecraft, so hostility blinds a ruler to sound policy; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it more generally as ‘the truth that leads to victory’. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead splits the couplet into two statements about pride and hostility. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From anger, complete delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain from anger to delusion to the loss of discernment.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural describes the endpoint: a mind given to hostility cannot see the truth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But he that hateth his brother is in darkness, and walketh in darkness, and knoweth not whither he goeth, because that darkness hath blinded his eyes.”
christianity.explanation: John says that hatred blinds a person so that he cannot see his own way.
christianity.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s claim that hostility hides the true path.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that hatred can derail one’s sense of justice.
islam.tie_back: Both texts see hostility as distorting judgement.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s brothers, consumed by hatred, could no longer even speak to him calmly, and went on to sell him.
judaism.tie_back: Their story shows how hostility clouds judgement, the Kural’s point.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who mistake the unessential to be essential and the essential to be unessential, dwelling in wrong thoughts, never arrive at the essential.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that minds caught in wrong thoughts never reach what truly matters.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says hostile minds never see the meypporul, the essential truth.

jainism.quote_or_event: After his duel with his brother Bharata, Bāhubali renounces the kingdom and stands so long in motionless meditation that vines grow over him. Yet omniscience (kevala-jñāna) does not come until his sisters Brāhmī and Sundarī tell him to get down from the elephant, meaning the pride left over from the rivalry. Once he lets it go, he attains omniscience.
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition uses Bāhubali to show that even immense austerity cannot reveal the highest truth while a trace of passion born of rivalry remains in the mind.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that minds attached to hostility can never see the true principle, and Bāhubali, rival of his brother, cannot reach omniscience until the last remnant of that rivalry is gone.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book I (Ādīśvaracaritra), tr. Helen M. Johnson; widely retold in Śvetāmbara tradition

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, where there is spiritual wisdom, there is righteousness and Dharma. Where there is falsehood, there is sin. Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir sets wisdom, righteousness and forgiveness against falsehood, greed and sin, placing God himself where forgiveness is.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says minds bent on hostility cannot see the true principle; Kabir likewise places the truth, God himself, with forgiveness, and sin and death with its opposites.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 155), Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Ajax, the hero, consumed by resentment after Achilles’ armour is awarded to Odysseus, sets out to kill the Greek leaders, but Athena clouds his mind and he slaughters cattle instead, believing them his enemies.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ajax’s grudge literally makes him unable to see what is in front of him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a vivid image of a hostile mind blind to reality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus teaches that when someone provokes you, it is your own judgement that has provoked you, and urges us not to be carried away by the first impression so as to gain time to see clearly.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, clear perception requires refusing to be seized by hostile impressions.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says hostility prevents one from seeing the truth.

real_life_example.event_title: The Royal Society's one-sided verdict in the calculus priority dispute
real_life_example.event: After Newton's supporter John Keill suggested in 1708 that Gottfried Leibniz had plagiarised Newton's calculus, Leibniz appealed to the Royal Society, of which Newton was president. Newton chose a committee of his supporters, which published the Commercium Epistolicum in 1712 favouring Newton's priority, and Newton himself wrote an anonymous review of it in the Philosophical Transactions. Historians now credit both men with inventing the calculus independently.
real_life_example.explanation: The bitter dispute is remembered as a case in which personal rivalry overrode fair judgement in one of the greatest scientific institutions of the age.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those whose minds are bent on hostility cannot see the true principle that leads to success, and the quarrel led even Newton to abandon impartial inquiry in favour of winning the fight.

tamil:
இகலிற்கு எதிர்சாய்தல் ஆக்கம் அதனை
மிக்லூக்கின் ஊக்குமாம் கேடு.
transliteration:
Ikalirku edhirsaaidhal aakkam adhanai
mikalookkin ookkumaam kedu.
meaning: Turning away from hostility brings good things. If you push it further, harm comes rushing toward you.
elementary: A small fire can be stamped out, but if you keep feeding it sticks it grows until it burns the house. The poet says anger is like that: put it out and good things grow, feed it and trouble comes running.
university: The first line repeats the key verb of 855, edhir saaidhal (எதிர் சாய்தல், to lean away from), now naming its reward: aakkam (ஆக்கம், prosperity, growth). The second line plays on ūkkam (ஊக்கம், urging, zeal): if one urges hostility on (mikal ūkkin), ruin ‘urges itself’ (ūkkumaam kēdu) toward that person, an elegant mirroring. Puliyur Kesigan reads the first line as checking hostility before it rises in one’s own heart; Pappaiah as ‘not welcoming’ it; Kalaignar as confronting and removing it. Textual note: as in 855, both base sources print ‘மிக்லூக்கின்’ while ytamizh romanizes ‘miklookkin’; the morphology is mikal + ūkkin, and the printed cluster looks like a shared digital slip. Otherwise identical.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names anger as one of three doors to ruin and urges renouncing it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says giving up hostility brings gain, while feeding it brings ruin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace.”
christianity.explanation: James teaches that peace is the soil from which good fruit grows.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly says turning away from hostility yields prosperity.

islam.quote_or_event: Muslims are urged not to cut off a brother for more than three days and to restrain anger, since the Prophet taught that ‘the strong is the one who controls himself while in anger’; the tradition treats unchecked quarrel as self-harming.
islam.explanation: Islamic ethics sets limits on how long estrangement may be fed.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats nursing hostility as harmful and checking it as beneficial.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs promises reward to the one who meets an enemy with kindness instead of hostility.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says turning from hostility brings gain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever harm an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater, an ill-directed mind inflicts on oneself a greater harm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a mind turned toward hatred hurts its owner more than any enemy could.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s second line: feed hostility and ruin comes to you.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A cruel man does cruel acts and is thereby involved in other cruelties; but sinful undertakings will in the end bring about misery.”
jainism.explanation: Jacobi's note glosses the 'cruel man' (Prakrit vêri, Sanskrit vairin) as one who is hostile and hurts living beings. The verse teaches that such enmity drags a person into further enmity and ends in misery.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that whoever pushes hostility further invites ruin to hurry toward him, and the Sūtrakṛtāṅga describes the same spiral: the hostile man's cruelties breed more cruelties and end in misery.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.8.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not be angry with anyone else; look within your own self instead. Be humble in this world, O Nanak! And by His Grace you shall be carried across.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Bavan Akhri Guru Arjan turns the seeker from anger at others to self-examination and humility, promising that grace will carry him across.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that turning away from hostility brings prosperity while pressing it on brings ruin; Guru Arjan likewise tells the seeker to turn from anger at others and promises a good end.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 259, Raag Gauree, Bavan Akhri (salok before pauri 44), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Seven Against Thebes, the brothers Eteocles and Polynices, cursed by their father and unwilling to yield, nurse their quarrel over the throne until they kill each other at the seventh gate.
greek_mythology.explanation: Neither brother would turn away from hostility, and both were destroyed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They embody the Kural’s warning that whoever urges hostility on is met by ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that hatred is increased by being returned, and can on the other hand be destroyed by love.
philosophy.explanation: Feeding hatred makes it grow; meeting it with love dissolves it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the same two-way law the Kural states.

real_life_example.event_title: The Rush-Bagot Agreement disarms the Great Lakes
real_life_example.event: Less than three years after the War of 1812, acting U.S. Secretary of State Richard Rush and the British minister Sir Charles Bagot concluded an agreement by exchange of notes limiting naval forces on the Great Lakes and Lake Champlain. Each side was allowed only a few small vessels of no more than 100 tons, each armed with a single 18-pound cannon. The U.S. Senate approved it in April 1818.
real_life_example.explanation: The agreement is regarded as one of the most successful disarmament agreements in history and helped lower tensions between the United States and British North America after the war.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says turning away from hostility brings prosperity while pushing it further invites ruin, and the two former enemies chose to stand down their warships on the lakes rather than continue a naval race.

tamil:
இகல்காணான் ஆக்கம் வருங்கால் அதனை
மிகல்காணும் கேடு தரற்கு.
transliteration:
Ikalkaanaan aakkam varungaal adhanai
mikalkaanum kedu thararku.
meaning: When good times are coming, a person does not even look at hostility. When harm is coming to them, they try to make their hostility bigger.
elementary: When you are having a great day, a small bump does not bother you. But on a bad day, you might turn a tiny bump into a huge fight that makes everything worse. The poet says growing a quarrel is a sign that trouble is on its way.
university: The couplet reads hostility as a symptom of one’s turning fortune. Ikal kaanaan (இகல் காணான், ‘does not regard hostility’) when aakkam (prosperity) is coming; but to bring on kēdu (கேடு, ruin) he mikal kaanum (மிகல் காணும், ‘sees its increase’, magnifies it). Puliyur Kesigan and Pappaiah add that the fortunate man ignores hostility even with cause, while the one heading for ruin seeks it even without cause. Mu. Varadarasanar reads mikal as ‘seeking to win against it’. The underlying idea, that a mind inclines toward quarrel when its own fall is approaching, resembles the Sanskrit maxim vināśa-kāle viparīta-buddhi (‘at the time of ruin the mind turns perverse’), though Valluvar states it without fatalism. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Udyoga Parva, Krishna travels to Hastinapura as envoy and offers Duryodhana peace for as little as five villages for the Pandavas; Duryodhana, on the brink of disaster, rejects every counsel of peace and even tries to seize Krishna, choosing the war that destroys his line.
hinduism.explanation: On the eve of ruin, Duryodhana magnifies the quarrel instead of ending it.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural’s man who ‘looks to its increase’ when bringing ruin on himself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that choosing to escalate conflict leads to one’s own destruction.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly ties the escalation of hostility to self-made ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “Shall I not inform you of what is more virtuous than the rank of fasting, Salat, and charity? ... Making peace between each other. For indeed spoiling relations with each other is the Haliqah.”
islam.explanation: The hadith calls the corruption of relationships ‘the shaver’, something that strips away what one has.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats magnifying discord as a mark and cause of ruin.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the Second Temple was destroyed, although its generation studied Torah and did good deeds, because of baseless hatred (sinat chinam), which it weighs as equal to idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed together.
judaism.explanation: A society on the verge of catastrophe was marked by unprovoked hatred.
judaism.tie_back: This echoes the Kural: hostility without cause accompanies approaching ruin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that a corrupted mind brings suffering after it as surely as a cart follows an ox.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly sees the turn toward hostility as the mind bringing its own ruin.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on impurity warns that wealth gained wrongly is lost once a person falls under the power of his passions and hatred.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural ties a person's rising or falling fortune to whether he ignores or magnifies hostility, and the Uttarādhyayana likewise links losing one's wealth to being held captive by hatred.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those, whom the Creator Lord would destroy - first He strips them of virtue.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak observes that those headed for destruction first lose their goodness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that a man bringing ruin on himself looks to magnify hostility; Guru Nanak likewise reads the loss of good judgment and virtue as the first sign of coming ruin.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Antigone, the Chorus recalls the ancient saying that evil comes to seem good to the one whose mind a god is leading toward ruin, as Creon stubbornly hardens his quarrel with Antigone and Haemon.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Greeks saw stubborn, worsening quarrel as a sign that doom was near.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s observation that ruin-bound minds magnify hostility.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca opens On Anger by describing anger as heedless of itself, eager to harm another, rushing onto weapons and greedy for a vengeance that drags the avenger down with it.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca portrays hostile passion as a drive toward one’s own destruction.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly sees magnified hostility as the means by which a person brings on ruin.

real_life_example.event_title: Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia
real_life_example.event: After the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the Austro-Hungarian government in July 1914 drafted an ultimatum to Serbia in terms intended to be impossible to accept, and delivered it on 23 July. Serbia replied on time on 25 July, accepting all but two of the demands and offering international arbitration, but Austria-Hungary declared the reply insufficient and declared war on 28 July. The war that followed ended in 1918 with the collapse of the Habsburg monarchy.
real_life_example.explanation: By choosing to escalate rather than accept a largely conciliatory reply, the Habsburg government began the war that destroyed its own empire.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that a person heading for ruin looks to magnify hostility, and Austria-Hungary deliberately enlarged a dispute that Serbia had offered to settle, setting off its own downfall.

tamil:
இகலானாம் இன்னாத எல்லாம் நகலானாம்
நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Ikalaanaam innaadha ellaam nakalaanaam
nannayam ennum serukku.
meaning: All painful things come from hostility. Friendliness brings the proud joy of true goodness.
elementary: Grumpy, fighting groups have lots of problems, while friendly groups share, help, and feel proud of each other. The poet ends the chapter simply: fighting brings every kind of trouble, and friendship brings goodness you can be proud of.
university: The closing couplet sets ikal against nakal (நகல், literally ‘laughing together’, hence friendship, cordiality). From ikal come innaadha ellaam (இன்னாத எல்லாம், all that is painful); from nakal comes nannayam ennum serukku (நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு), ‘the elation called great good’. Puliyur Kesigan and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss nannayam as nalla nīti (good justice or policy) and serukku as perumidha nilai (a state of dignified pride); Pappaiah renders it ‘the wealth-pride of justice’, while Kalaignar reads it as ‘great joy’. Serukku usually means arrogance in the Kural, so its positive use here is notable: the only pride worth having is the dignity friendship confers. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The closing hymn of the Rig Veda (10.191, the Samjñāna Sūkta) calls on people to assemble together, speak together, and let their minds and purposes be in harmony, so that they may dwell well together.
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic tradition ends its oldest collection with a prayer for concord.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s close, it names unity of heart as the source of all good.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.”
christianity.explanation: James teaches that strife is the breeding ground of every kind of evil.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s first line almost exactly: from hostility comes everything painful.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that answering evil with good turns an enemy into a devoted friend.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise sets enmity’s harms against friendship’s goodness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hillel used to say: be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving mankind and drawing them close to the Torah.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel holds up Aaron, the peacemaker, as the model to follow.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s closing praise of friendliness matches this ideal of loving peace and people.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with a pure mind a person speaks or acts happiness follows him like his never-departing shadow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that a pure, well-disposed mind brings happiness that never leaves.
buddhism.tie_back: Paired with verse 1, it mirrors the Kural’s two paths: hostility brings pain, goodwill brings good.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I forgive all living beings and may all living beings forgive me; I cherish feelings of friendship towards all and I harbour enmity towards none.”
jainism.explanation: This verse, recited in the Jain rite of forgiveness (Khāmemi savva jīve), pairs friendship (metti) toward all beings with enmity (vera) toward none as the heart of the religious life.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's closing couplet sets hostility, the source of all painful things, against friendliness, the source of true good, and the Jain verse makes the same pairing of friendship toward all and enmity toward none.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam v. 86 (Dharmasūtra; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com); Prakrit 'Khammāmi savvajīvāṇaṃ … mittī me savvabhūdesu, veraṃ majjhaṃ na keṇa vi'

sikhism.quote_or_event: “WAWWA: Do not harbor hatred against anyone. In each and every heart, God is contained. … Hatred and alienation depart from those who, as Gurmukh, listen to the Kirtan of the Lord’s Praises.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan forbids hatred toward anyone because God lives in every heart, and says that hatred and estrangement leave those who follow the Guru and sing God's praises.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural closes by setting hostility, the source of every pain, against friendliness, the source of true goodness; Guru Arjan likewise roots the end of hatred and estrangement in seeing God in every heart.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 259, Raag Gauree, Bavan Akhri (pauri 46), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But abhorred Strife bare painful Toil and Forgetfulness and Famine and tearful Sorrows, Fightings also, Battles, Murders, Manslaughters, Quarrels, Lying Words, Disputes, Lawlessness and Ruin, all of one nature.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod makes Strife (Eris) the mother of nearly every human misery.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s first line as a genealogy: all painful things are born of hostility.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes concord (homonoia) as political friendship: citizens of one mind about their common interests, which good people achieve and bad people cannot, since they are always seeking advantage and so fall into faction.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, friendship between citizens is the foundation of a good city, and faction its ruin.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly closes by setting friendship’s goodness against hostility’s harms.

real_life_example.event_title: Argentina and Chile dedicate the Christ of the Andes
real_life_example.place: Uspallata (Bermejo) Pass, on the Argentina-Chile border
real_life_example.event: Argentina and Chile, long in dispute over their Andean border and preparing for possible war, agreed in 1902 to settle their claims by arbitration and to limit their armaments. The boundary was settled by an arbitral award that both sides accepted. In 1904 the colossal statue known as the Christ of the Andes, sculpted by Mateo Alonso, was dedicated high on the border pass to commemorate the peace and boundary settlements between the two countries.
real_life_example.explanation: The settlement turned a likely war into a lasting peace, and the statue became one of the world's best-known monuments to friendship between nations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that from hostility come all painful things while from friendliness comes true goodness, and the two republics chose arbitration and friendship over war, marking the choice with a monument of peace.

tamil:
வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக ஓம்பா
மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை.
transliteration:
Valiyaarkku maaretral ombuka ombaa
meliyaarmel meka pakai.
meaning: Do not pick fights with people stronger than you. But do not be slow to stand against people who are weaker.
elementary: Imagine a small boat and a giant ship. A smart small boat does not try to bump the giant ship, because it would sink. Valluvar says: pick your contests wisely, and never start a fight you cannot possibly win.
university: The chapter title pakai maatchi (பகை மாட்சி) means the ‘excellence’ or right conduct of enmity: not whether a ruler will have enemies, but which enmities are worth having. The couplet turns on a deliberate wordplay between ombuka (ஓம்புக, ‘guard against, avoid’) and ombaa (ஓம்பா, ‘without avoiding’), and on meka (மேக, from mevu, ‘desire, take up’). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read it as plain statecraft: avoid opposing the stronger, and willingly take up enmity against the weaker; Solomon Pappaiah sharpens it to ‘if weaker, attack at once’. Mu. Karunanidhi (Kalaignar) notably inverts the moral, praising the one who spares the weak and fights the strong as the true glory of enmity, a modern ethical rereading rather than the traditional gloss. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthashastra (Book 7) lays down the basic rule of interstate policy: a king who is inferior in power to another should make peace with him, while one who is superior should make war.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra treats war and peace as calculations of relative strength rather than matters of pride.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the same rule as the Kural: avoid the stronger, take on the weaker.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a sensible king who measures his strength before battle and seeks peace if he is outnumbered.
christianity.tie_back: The weaker king in the parable does exactly what Valluvar advises: he does not challenge the stronger.

islam.quote_or_event: At Hudaybiyyah (628 CE) the Prophet Muhammad accepted a treaty with the Quraysh on terms many of his companions felt were unfavourable, choosing a truce over a confrontation at that moment.
islam.explanation: The early Muslim community, not yet in a position to prevail at Mecca, accepted peace, and the truce later opened the way to its growth.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows the wisdom of not pressing a contest at an unfavourable moment.
islam.source: Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari 2731-2732 (Book of Conditions)

judaism.quote_or_event: Jeremiah urges King Zedekiah to submit to the yoke of the king of Babylon and live, rather than rebel against an overwhelmingly stronger empire; Zedekiah’s revolt ends in the fall of Jerusalem.
judaism.explanation: The prophet counsels against defying a power that cannot be resisted, and the king who ignored him brought ruin on his city.
judaism.tie_back: It is a tragic illustration of the first half of the Kural: do not set yourself against the stronger.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that victory breeds enmity and the defeated live in pain, while the peaceful live happily, having given up both victory and defeat.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha looks past the calculation of winning and losing to the suffering that every conflict produces.
buddhism.tie_back: It offers a contrasting view: where Valluvar teaches which fights to pick, the Buddha questions picking fights at all.

jainism.quote_or_event: “O king, bring into subjection all princes who do not acknowledge you; thus you will be a true Kshattriya.” … “Though a man should conquer thousands and thousands of valiant (foes), greater will be his victory if he conquers nobody but himself.”
jainism.explanation: Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, urges the renouncing King Nami to subdue the weaker princes around him as a true warrior should. Nami refuses and says the only conquest worth seeking is conquest of oneself.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural advises a ruler to pick fights only with weaker foes, and the Jain text puts that same advice in Indra's mouth and has the saint reject it, so the passage answers the Kural's strategy rather than echoing it.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.32 and 9.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir defines the true hero not by the strength of the foe he chooses but by the cause he fights for.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural advises avoiding stronger foes and taking on weaker ones; Gurbani measures the warrior instead by the righteousness of his cause, whatever the odds.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Melian Dialogue the Athenian envoys tell the people of Melos that, between unequal powers, the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must; Melos resists and is destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Thucydides dramatises the harsh logic of power: a small state that defies a great one is crushed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Melos is the classic case of a weaker party ignoring the Kural’s first warning.
greek_mythology.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 5.84-116

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu advises that a general equal in strength may give battle, one slightly inferior should avoid the enemy, and one unequal in every way should withdraw.
philosophy.explanation: The Art of War makes the decision to fight depend entirely on a sober comparison of forces.
philosophy.tie_back: Sun Tzu and Valluvar give the same rule: never engage a stronger foe.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War III.9-10 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Ranjit Singh accepts the Sutlej frontier with the British
real_life_example.event: Ranjit Singh, ruler of the Sikh kingdom of Punjab, at first rejected the East India Company's terms and crossed the Sutlej to take territory on its southern bank, and both sides began preparing for war when the British sent a force under David Ochterlony to Ludhiana. He then signed the Treaty of Amritsar, which fixed his frontier broadly along the Sutlej while leaving him free to act north of the river. Britannica notes that the episode gave him great respect for the Company's disciplined troops and a determination never to fight them, and that his later conquests were to the west and north.
real_life_example.explanation: A rising ruler chose not to fight a stronger power, and used the security of that frontier to expand where his rivals were weaker.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises avoiding enmity with the stronger while not shrinking from contests with the weaker, which is exactly the course Ranjit Singh followed after 1809.

tamil:
அன்பிலன் ஆன்ற துணையிலன் தான்துவ்வான்
என்பரியும் ஏதிலான் துப்பு.
transliteration:
Anbilan aandra thunaiyilan thaanthuvvaan
enpariyum edhilaan thuppu.
meaning: A person who has no love for their own people, no strong friends to help, and no strength of their own, how could they ever beat a strong enemy?
elementary: Think of a team captain who is mean to his teammates, has no friends on other teams to help, and is not a strong player himself. When a tough team shows up, how can he possibly win? Kindness, friends and your own strength are what keep you safe.
university: The couplet lists three deficits: anbilan (அன்பிலன், without love, which Pappaiah and Varadarasanar read as lacking affection for kin and subjects), aandra thunaiyilan (ஆன்ற துணையிலன், without worthy or powerful allies) and thaan thuvvaan (தான் துவ்வான், himself lacking strength). The closing phrase enpariyum edhilaan thuppu (என் பரியும் ஏதிலான் துப்பு) asks how such a man could destroy (pari) the strength (thuppu) of a stranger-foe (edhilaan). Parimelazhagar reads the verse as the converse of 861: such a person is himself the ‘weak’ party whom others may safely oppose. The trio of affection, alliance and own strength mirrors the Arthashastra’s concern with internal loyalty and allies (mitra) as elements of royal power. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Arthashastra names the seven constituent elements of a state (the king, ministers, country, fort, treasury, army and ally) and treats a ruler lacking loyal subjects and allies as easily overthrown.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya sees power as a combination of personal capacity, popular loyalty and alliances.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s three deficits (no love, no allies, no strength) are the same missing elements.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul writes that even if he had prophecy, all knowledge and faith to move mountains, without charity (love) he would be nothing.
christianity.explanation: For Paul, love is not an extra but the thing that gives every other gift its worth.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar likewise puts love (anbu) first among the things without which a person is powerless.

islam.quote_or_event: “And obey Allāh and His Messenger, and do not dispute and [thus] lose courage and [then] your strength would depart; and be patient. Indeed, Allāh is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns a community facing enemies that internal quarrelling drains away both courage and strength.
islam.tie_back: Both texts tie a group’s power against foes to the bonds within it.

judaism.quote_or_event: Kohelet observes that two are better than one, that woe comes to the one who falls alone with no one to lift him, and that a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
judaism.explanation: The sage notes, in simple human terms, that a person without companions is vulnerable.
judaism.tie_back: It echoes Valluvar’s friendless man who cannot withstand an enemy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Ananda suggests that admirable friendship is half the holy life, the Buddha corrects him: it is the whole of the holy life.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats good companionship as essential, not optional, for spiritual progress.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar too treats worthy companions as indispensable, though for worldly survival.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife, and sons will not be able to help me, when I suffer for my own deeds.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana teaches that no kinsman or ally can shield a soul from the fruit of its own karma, so the seeker must rely on his own conduct.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a man without loving kin, strong allies or strength of his own cannot break an enemy. The Jain verse agrees that relying on others fails, but it moves the struggle inward, where only one's own strength counts.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: In 1699 Guru Gobind Singh instituted the Khalsa, a purified and reconstituted Sikh community bound together as a disciplined order of saint-soldiers committed to courage and to Sikh ideals.
sikhism.explanation: By founding the Khalsa the tenth Guru joined his followers in one loyal brotherhood and gave it the strength to defend itself.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a man without love for his own people, without allies and without strength cannot break an enemy; Guru Gobind Singh's Khalsa built exactly those three things, a devoted people, a brotherhood and armed strength.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, articles Khalsa and Guru Gobind Singh (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the father and his quarrelling sons, he shows them that a bundle of sticks cannot be broken while single sticks snap easily.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable teaches that unity makes a family strong and division makes each member easy to defeat.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar’s loveless, ally-less man is the single stick.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Father and His Sons’

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli advises that the best fortress a prince can have is not to be hated by his people, since walls will not save a ruler whose subjects turn against him.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli, the loyalty of one’s own people is a more reliable defence than any fortification.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise makes affection for one’s own people the first line of defence.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 20 (tr. W. K. Marriott)

real_life_example.event_title: Maximilian's Mexican empire falls once French troops leave
real_life_example.event: Maximilian, an Austrian archduke, became emperor of Mexico in 1864 with the backing of French troops sent by Napoleon III. Under diplomatic pressure from the United States and rising costs at home, Napoleon withdrew the French army, which had fully embarked by March 1867, leaving Maximilian with a small force of foreign volunteers and largely untrained Mexican draftees. Besieged by republican forces at Querétaro, his army surrendered in May 1867, and he was executed in June.
real_life_example.explanation: A regime that lacked broad support among its own subjects, lost its only powerful ally and had little strength of its own collapsed within months.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks how one without the affection of his people, without strong allies and without strength of his own could ever overcome his enemy, and Maximilian's fall answers it.

tamil:
அஞ்சும் அறியான் அமைவிலன் ஈகலான்
தஞ்சம் எளியன் பகைக்கு.
transliteration:
Anjum ariyaan amaivilan eekalaan
thanjam eliyan pakaikku.
meaning: A person who is fearful, does not know what they should know, cannot get along with others, and will not give is very easy for enemies to beat.
elementary: Picture a kid who is scared of everything, doesn’t learn the rules of the game, won’t cooperate with anyone, and never shares. When trouble comes, nobody stands with him and he doesn’t know what to do. Being brave, learning, getting along and sharing are what make you strong.
university: Four faults are stacked in quick succession: anjum (அஞ்சும், he who fears, which Pappaiah glosses as fearing what need not be feared), ariyaan (அறியான், one who does not know what should be known), amaivilan (அமைவிலன், lacking accord or adaptability with others) and eekalaan (ஈகலான், one who does not give). Thanjam (தஞ்சம்) is read by the commentators as an intensifier, ‘very easily’ (Varadarasanar: மிக எளியவன்). Parimelazhagar’s logic is cumulative: fear loses battles, ignorance loses policy, unsociability loses allies and stinginess loses the army, so the foe has little left to overcome. Kalaignar renders amaivilan as lacking the habit of living in harmony and eekalaan as lacking compassion. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the opening of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna rebukes the despondent Arjuna, urging him not to yield to unmanliness and to cast off his petty faint-heartedness and rise.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna treats Arjuna’s fear and confusion on the battlefield as a weakness that must be overcome before anything else.
hinduism.tie_back: Fear and not-knowing, the first two faults in the Kural, are exactly what Krishna addresses.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul tells Timothy that God has not given a spirit of fear, but of power, love and a sound mind.
christianity.explanation: Paul sets fear against three positive qualities that a leader of the church should have.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s fearful, unloving, ignorant man is the opposite of Paul’s ideal of power, love and a sound mind.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Allah! I seek refuge with You from miserliness; and seek refuge with You from cowardice; and seek refuge with You from being sent back to geriatric old age...”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught a supplication that names miserliness and cowardice side by side as evils to be protected from.
islam.tie_back: Two of the Kural’s four faults, fear and not giving, are paired in the same breath.

judaism.quote_or_event: Before battle, the officers of Israel are told to send home any man who is fearful and fainthearted, lest his brothers’ hearts melt like his.
judaism.explanation: Deuteronomy treats fear as contagious and dangerous to the whole army.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural places fear first among the faults that make one easy prey.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha names four bases of social solidarity (generosity, kind speech, beneficial help and impartiality) and says they hold the world together like the linchpin of a moving chariot.
buddhism.explanation: Without these qualities, the Buddha says, people would not respect or support one another.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ungenerous, unaccommodating man lacks exactly these bonds, which is why he stands alone.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Weak men who are unable (to bear) these insults in villages or towns, become disheartened like cowards in the battle.”
jainism.explanation: In its chapter on the hardships of monastic life, the Sūtrakṛtāṅga compares the faint-hearted novice, who breaks under insult and hardship, to a coward who loses heart once the battle begins.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls the fearful man easy prey for his enemies, and the Jain verse likewise shows timidity defeating a man before any real foe has to strike.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.3.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else - says Nanak, listen, mind: call him spiritually wise.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur names fearlessness, joined to never making others afraid, as the mark of the spiritually wise.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the man who is fearful and ignorant is easy prey for enemies; Guru Tegh Bahadur makes the opposite, fearlessness joined to wisdom, the ideal.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 16), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Paris shrinks back into the ranks in fear when Menelaus steps forward, and Hector rebukes him for his cowardice.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows how a prince’s fear shames him before both armies.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris embodies the first fault of the Kural: the fearful man who cannot face his foe.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness, and liberality as the mean between meanness and prodigality.
philosophy.explanation: Cowardice and meanness are, for Aristotle, vices that undermine a person’s character and standing.
philosophy.tie_back: Two of Valluvar’s four faults appear in Aristotle’s list of vices.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.6-9 and IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Ethelred the Unready flees to Normandy
real_life_example.event: Ethelred II, whose byname Unready meant ill-advised or lacking counsel, failed to keep the loyalty of many of his subjects and tried to protect England from Viking raids by paying the Danes large sums of tribute known as the Danegeld. The payments did not stop the raids, and by 1012 some 48,000 pounds of silver was being paid to Danes camped in London. In 1013 King Sweyn of Denmark invaded, was accepted as king, and Ethelred fled to Normandy.
real_life_example.explanation: A king remembered for poor counsel, weak military leadership and the loss of his subjects' allegiance was easily displaced by a determined foe.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural lists fear, lack of understanding, inability to keep others in accord and failure to give as the marks of one who is easy prey, and Ethelred's reign shows several of these at once.

tamil:
நீங்கான் வெகுளி நிறையிலன் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
யாங்கணும் யார்க்கும் எளிது.
transliteration:
Neengaan vekuli niraiyilan enjnaandrum
yaanganum yaarkkum elidhu.
meaning: A person whose anger never goes away and who cannot control themselves is easy for anyone to beat, at any time and in any place.
elementary: If a player gets angry every time and can’t keep the team’s plan a secret, the other team just has to tease him and listen in. He makes himself easy to beat. Staying calm and keeping your plans to yourself is a kind of armour.
university: Neengaan vekuli (நீங்கான் வெகுளி) is anger that does not depart, a settled irascibility rather than a passing flare. Nirai (நிறை) is the key term: Varadarasanar glosses it as the capacity to hold and govern one’s own mind, while Parimelazhagar’s tradition, followed by Solomon Pappaiah and the classic English rendering (‘neither refrains from anger nor keeps his secrets’), reads it as guarding secrets. Both senses describe a leak in self-command through which the enemy can enter. The triple universal of the second line, enjnaandrum yaanganum yaarkkum (எஞ்ஞான்றும் யாங்கணும் யார்க்கும், at all times, in all places, to all), makes the vulnerability total. This anticipates chapter 31 (vekulaamai, avoiding anger), here recast as political danger. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna traces a chain of ruin: from anger comes delusion, from delusion confusion of memory, from that the loss of intelligence, and with intelligence lost, a person is destroyed.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita shows anger as the first link in a collapse of judgement.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s permanently angry man has lost exactly the judgement that would protect him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb compares a person without self-control to an undefended city that anyone can enter.
christianity.tie_back: It is almost the Kural’s image: the man without nirai is open to any attacker.

islam.quote_or_event: “The strong is not the one who overcomes the people by his strength, but the strong is the one who controls himself while in anger.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet redefines strength as mastery of one’s own anger.
islam.tie_back: By that measure, Valluvar’s ever-angry man is the weakest of all.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma asks, ‘Who is mighty?’ and answers: the one who conquers his own impulse.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah locates true power in self-mastery rather than in force.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar’s man without nirai has failed at exactly this kind of might.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada calls the one who checks rising anger as a charioteer checks a speeding chariot a true charioteer; others merely hold the reins.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises active control of anger as real mastery.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s man whose anger never leaves has let go of the reins.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not give way to his anger, and bear with indifference pleasant and unpleasant occurrences. Subdue your Self, for the Self is difficult to subdue; if your Self is subdued, you will be happy in this world and in the next. Better it is that I should subdue my Self by self-control and penance, than be subdued by others with fetters and corporal punishment.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's discipline joins the curbing of anger with mastery of the self, and warns that whoever does not subdue himself will be subdued by others.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a man of lasting anger and no inner restraint (nirai) can be beaten by anyone, and these verses give the same pairing, adding that the self-mastered person cannot be overpowered from outside.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.14–16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O anger, you are the root of conflict; compassion never rises up in you. You take the corrupt, sinful beings in your power, and make them dance like monkeys.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Salok Sahaskriti Guru Arjan addresses anger directly: it breeds strife and takes control of those it possesses, making them dance like performing monkeys.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the man whose anger never leaves him and who lacks self-restraint is easy for anyone to defeat; Guru Arjan likewise shows the angry man as no longer his own master but led about by his passion.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sahaskriti (salok 47), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Ajax, the hero’s rage at losing Achilles’ armour drives him into a delusion in which he slaughters livestock, believing them to be his enemies, and ends in disgrace.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ajax’s unrelenting anger destroys him more completely than any enemy could.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the Kural’s man of unrelenting anger, undone without a battle.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca calls anger a brief madness, an emotion that cannot govern itself, forgets decency and is deaf to reason.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, the angry man has handed control of himself to a passion.
philosophy.tie_back: This is why Valluvar says the angry man is easy prey: he is no longer in command.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira I.1 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: Zinedine Zidane is sent off in the World Cup final
real_life_example.event: In extra time of the 2006 FIFA World Cup final between France and Italy, French captain Zinedine Zidane head-butted Italian defender Marco Materazzi in the chest after an exchange of words, and the referee sent him off. The match ended 1-1 and Italy won the penalty shoot-out 5-3, with France's David Trezeguet missing his kick. It was the last match of Zidane's playing career, and FIFA later fined and banned both players.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the greatest players of his era ended his career not in defeat by skill but by a moment of uncontrolled anger, removing France's leader before the decisive shoot-out.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one whose anger never leaves him and who lacks inner restraint can be overcome by anyone, anywhere, and a single provoked outburst cost Zidane his final match.

tamil:
வழிநோக்கான் வாய்ப்பன செய்யான் பழிநோக்கான்
பண்பிலன் பற்றார்க்கு இனிது.
transliteration:
Vazhinokkaan vaayppana seyyaan pazhinokkaan
panbilan patraarkku inidhu.
meaning: A person who does not look for the right way, does not do what is fitting, does not care about shame, and has no good character is a joy to their enemies.
elementary: A kid who never reads the rules, doesn’t do his homework, doesn’t care if people think badly of him and isn’t kind is very easy for a rival to beat. His rival is actually happy to face him! Learning the right way and caring about your good name make you hard to beat.
university: Vazhi nokkaan (வழிநோக்கான்) is glossed by Parimelazhagar’s tradition, and by Puliyur Kesigan and Pappaiah, as one who does not study the treatises of right conduct (neethi nool); Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it more broadly as not seeking the good path. Vaayppana seyyaan (வாய்ப்பன செய்யான்) is one who fails to do what those texts enjoin or what is fitting; pazhi nokkaan (பழிநோக்கான்) disregards blame or disgrace; panbilan (பண்பிலன்) lacks character. Patraar (பற்றார்) are ‘those who do not hold to him’, that is, enemies, and inidhu (இனிது, sweet) is deliberately ironic: such a man is a pleasure to fight. The sequence moves from knowledge to action to reputation to character. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna warns that one who casts aside the injunctions of scripture and acts on impulse attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal, and therefore scripture should be one’s guide in what to do and what to avoid.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita insists that right action must be guided by authoritative teaching, not whim.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s vazhi nokkaan and vaayppana seyyaan are exactly the man who ignores such guidance.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus compares the one who hears his sayings but does not do them to a foolish man who built his house on sand; when the storm came, it fell, and great was its fall.
christianity.explanation: Knowing what is right without doing it leaves a person with no foundation in a crisis.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s man who neither seeks nor does what is fitting will likewise collapse when an enemy strikes.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an speaks of those who have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see and ears with which they do not hear, calling them heedless.
islam.explanation: The verse condemns people who possess every faculty for guidance but refuse to use it.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar’s man who will not look to the right path is heedless in the same way.

judaism.quote_or_event: Hosea proclaims that the people are destroyed for lack of knowledge, because they have rejected knowledge and forgotten the teaching of their God.
judaism.explanation: The prophet links national ruin directly to the neglect of instruction.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, refusing to learn the right way leaves one open to destruction.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada likens fine words not put into practice to a beautiful flower that has colour but no fragrance.
buddhism.explanation: Teaching is fruitless unless it is lived.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s man who does not do what is fitting is all colour and no fragrance.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Benighted men of wrong faith, (though) they be renowned as heroes, exert themselves in a bad way, which will have, in all respects, evil consequences for them.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga contrasts the effort of those who lack right faith and follow a wrong path, which brings them only ruin, with the effort of the wise who follow the right path.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a man who does not look to the right path or do what is fitting delights his enemies, and the Jain verse likewise says that effort cut off from the right path brings about its own downfall.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.8.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Greed and sin are the king and prime minister; falsehood is the treasurer.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak pictures a corrupt age as a court in which greed rules, sin advises and falsehood keeps the treasury.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a ruler who ignores the right path, does what is unfitting, has no shame and no good character is a delight to his enemies; Guru Nanak pictures the same rule by vice in place of right conduct.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (salok, Guru Nanak) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says the best man is he who thinks things out for himself, the good man is he who listens to good advice, but the one who neither thinks for himself nor heeds another is useless.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod ranks people by how they relate to wisdom, and puts the one who ignores all counsel at the bottom.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar’s man who does not look to the path is Hesiod’s useless man.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Your enemy, wide awake, is constantly lying in wait to take advantage of your actions, and seeking to gain some hold on you, and keeping a constant patrol about your life …”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch says an enemy watches every action for a fault to seize on, and he urges that this watchfulness be turned to profit by living so carefully that the enemy finds nothing to use.
philosophy.tie_back: Read from the other side, Plutarch's point matches the Kural's: a person who neglects right conduct, propriety and shame hands his watching enemies exactly what they want.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, How to Profit by One's Enemies (De capienda ex inimicis utilitate), ch. 3 (tr. F. C. Babbitt)

real_life_example.event_title: Honorius refuses terms and Alaric sacks Rome
real_life_example.event: The Western Roman emperor Honorius, based in Ravenna, had his leading general Stilicho arrested and executed in 408, after which many soldiers of barbarian origin defected to the Visigothic leader Alaric. Honorius repeatedly refused Alaric's demands during sieges of Rome in 408 and 409. In August 410 Alaric's forces entered Rome, which had not been taken by a foreign enemy for nearly 800 years, and occupied it for three days.
real_life_example.explanation: An emperor who removed his ablest defender and would neither fight effectively nor negotiate gave his enemy an opportunity it could hardly have hoped for.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who does not follow the right path, does not do what is fitting and has no care for disgrace is a delight to his enemies, and Honorius's conduct handed Alaric the city.

tamil:
காணாச் சினத்தான் கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்
பேணாமை பேணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Kaanaach chinaththaan kazhiperung kaamaththaan
penaamai penap padum.
meaning: A person who is blinded by anger and full of endless desire is a good enemy to have, because they will bring themselves down.
elementary: Imagine a rival who gets so angry he can’t see straight and wants everything he sees, right now. He runs around grabbing and shouting and forgets to defend himself. Having a rival like that is almost lucky, because his own temper and greed trip him up.
university: Kaanaach chinam (காணாச் சினம்) is anger that does not see, which Puliyur Kesigan explains as anger that blinds one to oneself and to others, and Varadarasanar as anger that does not see the truth. Kazhi perung kaamam (கழிபெருங் காமம்) is desire grown beyond all measure; Pappaiah specifies it as lust for women, while Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep the broader sense of greed or great desire. The second line plays on the root penu (to cherish): penaamai (பேணாமை, non-cherishing, i.e. enmity) penap padum (பேணப் படும், will be cherished), so his hostility is ‘to be prized’ by others. The pairing of krodha and kama as twin enemies of self-government is common to classical Indian thought. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Arjuna asks what drives a man to sin against his will; Krishna answers that it is desire (kama), which turns into anger (krodha), all-devouring and the great enemy here in this world.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita names desire and anger together as the inner enemy that overpowers a person.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar names the same pair, anger and boundless desire, as what makes a man an easy foe.

christianity.quote_or_event: James teaches that each person is tempted when drawn away by his own lust, and that lust, when it has conceived, brings forth sin, and sin brings forth death.
christianity.explanation: Unchecked desire leads step by step to self-destruction.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar’s man of boundless desire is on that same downward path, which is why his enmity is no threat.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an asks the Prophet whether he has seen the one who takes his own desire as his god, asking whether he can be a guardian over such a person.
islam.explanation: The verse portrays a person wholly ruled by desire as beyond help.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar’s man of boundless desire is likewise ruled from within, and so is easily overcome from without.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Philistine lords, unable to overcome Samson by force, use his passion for Delilah to learn the secret of his strength, and so capture him.
judaism.explanation: Samson’s enemies win not by strength but by exploiting his desire.
judaism.tie_back: This is exactly why the Kural says such a man’s enmity is to be welcomed: his passions hand his foes the victory.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says there is no fire like lust, no grip like hatred, no net like delusion and no river like craving.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures desire and hatred as forces that seize and drag a person along.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s blind anger and boundless desire are the fire and the grip that leave a man defenceless.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If there were numberless mountains of gold and silver, as big as Kailâsa, they would not satisfy a greedy man; for his avidity is boundless like space. … He will sink through anger; he will go down through pride; delusion will block up his path; through greed he will incur dangers in both worlds.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami describes desire as boundless as space and says that the person ruled by anger, pride, delusion and greed brings about his own fall.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural welcomes as an enemy the man blinded by anger and swollen with boundless desire because he will destroy himself, and Nami describes exactly that self-ruin through anger and limitless craving.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.48 and 9.54 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Unfulfilled sexual desire and unresolved anger waste the body away, as gold is dissolved by borax.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Dakhni Oankar Guru Nanak says lust and anger eat away the person who harbours them, as borax melts gold.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the enmity of a man blinded by anger and swollen with desire is welcome because he destroys himself; Guru Nanak likewise shows kaam and krodh consuming their own host.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 932, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar (pauri 18), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Paris’s desire for Helen leads him to carry her off from Sparta, bringing the Greek armies down on Troy and destroying his own city.
greek_mythology.explanation: One prince’s unchecked desire brings ruin on his whole people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris is the Kural’s man of boundless desire whose enmity his foes could welcome.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad (background) and the Trojan cycle

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book IX of the Republic, Plato describes the tyrannical man as ruled by a master passion, a slave to desires that multiply without limit, and therefore the most wretched and least free of men.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, the person governed by unlimited appetite is inwardly enslaved, however powerful he seems.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar sees the same inner slavery as an outward weakness enemies can exploit.

real_life_example.event_title: The Otrar incident provokes Genghis Khan against Khwarezm
real_life_example.place: Otrar, Kazakhstan, and Khwarezm, Central Asia
