real_life_example.event: The governor of the Khwarezmian frontier city of Otrar seized a caravan of Muslim merchants travelling under Genghis Khan's protection and had them killed. The Khwarezm-Shah Ala al-Din Muhammad refused to give satisfaction and ordered the execution of Mongol envoys. Genghis Khan then invaded, and between 1218 and 1220 his armies overran the Khwarezmian empire across what is now Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Iran.
real_life_example.explanation: Greed for a caravan's goods and an angry rejection of diplomacy drew a far more dangerous enemy into a war that destroyed the shah's empire.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the enmity of one blinded by anger and swollen with desire is welcome to his foes, since he brings about his own defeat, as the shah and his governor did at Otrar.

tamil:
கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் மன்ற அடுத்திருந்து
மாணாத செய்வான் பகை.
transliteration:
Koduththum kolalvendum mandra aduththirundhu
maanaadha seyvaan pakai.
meaning: If someone stays close to you but does bad things, you should certainly make them your enemy, even if it costs you something.
elementary: Suppose someone on your own team keeps quietly messing up every play. It would honestly be better if he went over to the other team, even if you had to give up something to make that happen. A clear opponent is safer than a teammate who harms you from inside.
university: The commentators divide on aduththirundhu (அடுத்திருந்து). Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as ‘staying close by’: one who remains near you as an associate yet does unworthy things (maanaadha, மாணாத) should be turned into an open enemy, even at the cost of wealth. The older line represented by Parimelazhagar, followed by Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan and by the classic English version (‘having begun a work, does what is not conducive’), reads it as ‘having undertaken’ an action: the enmity of a foe who mismanages his own undertakings is so advantageous that it is worth buying. Mandra (மன்ற) means ‘certainly’. Either way the paradox is that some enmity is a gain worth paying for. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata war, Shalya agrees to serve as Karna’s charioteer but undermines him throughout with discouraging and belittling speech, weakening him from within his own chariot.
hinduism.explanation: An ally placed at Karna’s side becomes a source of harm rather than help.
hinduism.tie_back: Shalya is the close companion who does unworthy things, of whom the Kural says an open enemy would be better.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Karna Parva (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: Judas, one of the twelve, leads the arresting party to Gethsemane and identifies Jesus with a kiss; Jesus asks whether he betrays the Son of man with a kiss.
christianity.explanation: The betrayal comes from inside the closest circle, under the sign of friendship.
christianity.tie_back: Judas is the archetype of the one who stays close yet does harm.

islam.quote_or_event: “Had they gone forth with you, they would not have increased you except in confusion, and they would have been active among you, seeking [to cause] you fitnah [i.e., chaos and dissension]. And among you are avid listeners to them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says it was better that the hypocrites stayed behind, since inside the army they would only have spread disorder.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it judges a harmful insider to be worse than his absence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it: neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; then I would have hid myself from him: But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says an open enemy can be endured or avoided, but harm from a close companion cannot.
judaism.tie_back: This is the heart of the Kural’s logic: an open foe is easier to deal with than a harmful intimate.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, the Buddha’s cousin and a monk within the Sangha, plotted against the Buddha and caused a schism by leading away a group of monks.
buddhism.explanation: The most dangerous opposition to the Buddha arose from inside his own community.
buddhism.tie_back: Devadatta is the insider whose ‘unworthy deeds’ did more harm than any outside foe.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Now this driver (viz. Garga), who had to deal with bad bullocks, thought: 'What have I to do with bad pupils? I am disheartened. As are bad pupils, so are bad bullocks; I shall leave these lazy donkeys, and shall practise severe austerities.'”
jainism.explanation: The elder Garga, worn out by disciples who stayed close to him yet behaved unworthily, breaks with them completely and goes on alone, accepting the loss of his following.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says one should break even at a cost with someone who stays close yet acts unworthily, and Garga does this by giving up his whole following rather than keep company with bad pupils.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 27.15–16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, there are dozens who say they are friends; I search, but I cannot find even one.”
sikhism.explanation: Farid laments that many claim friendship, but a true friend is hard to find.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns against one who stays close as a friend yet does unworthy things; Farid likewise exposes the gap between those who call themselves friends and real friendship.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 87), Bhagat Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Trojans bring the great wooden horse inside their walls as a gift, and the Greek warriors hidden within open the gates by night, so Troy falls.
greek_mythology.explanation: What the Trojans welcomed into their city destroyed them from within.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The horse is the danger the Kural warns of: harm lodged close by is worse than an enemy outside the walls.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli warns that auxiliary troops borrowed from another power are useless and dangerous, because if they lose you are ruined and if they win you are their captive.
philosophy.explanation: Forces that stand beside you without real loyalty are more dangerous than open enemies.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise prefers a clear enemy to a companion whose conduct harms you.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 13 (tr. W. K. Marriott)

real_life_example.event_title: Truman relieves General MacArthur of his commands
real_life_example.event: During the Korean War, General Douglas MacArthur publicly called for a wider war, despite a December 1950 directive requiring that statements on military and foreign policy be cleared first. After a letter of his criticising the administration's limited-war policy was read in Congress in April 1951, President Harry Truman relieved him of his commands, stating that MacArthur could not give wholehearted support to the policies of the United States and the United Nations. The public and congressional reaction against Truman was overwhelming, with some calling for his impeachment.
real_life_example.explanation: Truman chose open conflict with a celebrated subordinate who kept acting against policy, accepting a heavy political price to restore civilian control.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the enmity of one who stays close to you yet acts unworthily should be taken on even at a cost, and Truman paid in popularity to make that break.

tamil:
குணனிலனாய்க் குற்றம் பலவாயின் மாற்றார்க்கு
இனனிலனாம் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Gunanilanaayk kutram palavaayin maatraarkku
inanilanaam emaap pudaiththu.
meaning: A person with no good qualities and many faults ends up with no friends to help, and that makes it easy for enemies to win.
elementary: If someone is never kind and always does mean things, little by little all his friends leave. When a problem comes, he is alone, and that makes it easy for anyone against him. Good habits are what keep friends by your side.
university: The couplet is a causal chain: gunanilan (குணனிலன், without good qualities) plus kutram pala (குற்றம் பல, many faults) yields inanilan (இனனிலன், one without kin or allies, from inam, ‘one’s own group’), and that condition is emaappu (ஏமாப்பு, security or advantage) for the maatraar (மாற்றார், adversaries). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both stress that it is the friendlessness itself, not any action of the foe, that becomes the enemy’s strength. Kalaignar condenses this to ‘he loses his supporters and is easily brought down’. The verse links this chapter back to the Natpiyal chapters on friendship that precede it. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Ravana scorns his brother Vibhishana’s counsel to return Sita and insults him; Vibhishana leaves Lanka and joins Rama, bringing vital knowledge of Lanka’s defences.
hinduism.explanation: Ravana’s arrogance and wrongdoing drive away his own wise kinsman, who becomes a decisive asset to the enemy.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural exactly: a faulty man loses his own people, and his loss is the foe’s gain.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus says that if a kingdom is divided against itself it cannot stand, and if a house is divided against itself it cannot stand.
christianity.explanation: A community that loses its inner cohesion collapses.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s man who has driven away his allies stands in just such a divided house.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allāh, [O Muḥammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the Prophet that his gentleness kept his followers together, and harshness would have scattered them.
islam.tie_back: It is the positive mirror of the Kural: good character keeps allies, bad character loses them.

judaism.quote_or_event: When the people ask Rehoboam to lighten their burden, he rejects the elders’ advice and answers harshly; the ten northern tribes break away and the kingdom is split.
judaism.explanation: A king’s harshness and poor judgement cost him most of his own people.
judaism.tie_back: Rehoboam shows how faults, not enemies, can leave a ruler without allies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjians, the Buddha says they cannot be conquered so long as they meet in harmony, honour their elders and keep their customs.
buddhism.explanation: The Vajjians’ strength lies in their unity and good conduct, not in their armies.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar describes the reverse: a man whose faults have stripped him of allies has lost exactly this protection.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a bitch with sore ears is driven away everywhere, thus a bad, insubordinate, and talkative (pupil) is turned out.”
jainism.explanation: The opening lecture of the Uttarādhyayana says that a monk of bad character finds no welcome anywhere and is driven out of every community.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a man with no virtues and many faults ends up without allies, and the Jain simile shows the same result: faults leave a man unwanted and alone.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Simmal tree is straight as an arrow; it is very tall, and very thick. But those birds which visit it hopefully, depart disappointed. Its fruits are tasteless, its flowers are nauseating, and its leaves are useless.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak's image of the silk-cotton tree shows something imposing but without any good quality, so that those who come to it go away and do not stay.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a man with no virtues and many faults ends up with no allies; the Simmal tree, tall but fruitless, likewise keeps no one who comes to it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (salok before pauri 14), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Agamemnon insults Achilles by seizing his prize Briseis; Achilles withdraws from the fighting and the Trojans drive the Greeks back to their ships.
greek_mythology.explanation: A leader’s arrogance drives away his greatest ally, to the great benefit of the enemy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agamemnon’s fault turns his own camp’s loss into Troy’s advantage, as the Kural predicts.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Therefore the bad man does not seem to be amicably disposed even to himself, because there is nothing in him to love; so that if to be thus is the height of wretchedness, we should strain every nerve to avoid wickedness and should endeavour to be good; for so and only so can one be either friendly to oneself or a friend to another.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that a wicked man, having nothing lovable in him, is at odds with himself and cannot be a true friend to others. In the next chapter he adds that bad men cannot hold together in common purpose.
philosophy.tie_back: This supports the Kural's claim that a man without virtues and full of faults ends up without allies.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, IX.4, 1166b (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Richard II is deserted and deposed
real_life_example.event: Richard II's authoritarian rule and reliance on favourites alienated many nobles, and in 1399, on the death of John of Gaunt, he confiscated the vast Lancaster estates that should have passed to his exiled cousin Henry Bolingbroke. While Richard was in Ireland, Henry landed in England, and leading nobles and many others joined him, while many of the soldiers Richard brought back to Wales deserted. Richard surrendered in August and was deposed, and Henry was crowned as Henry IV.
real_life_example.explanation: A king who had alienated those around him found, at the moment of need, that almost no one would stand with him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a man of many faults ends up without allies, and that very friendlessness becomes his enemy's strength, as Richard's isolation became Henry's opportunity.

tamil:
செறுவார்க்குச் சேணிகவா இன்பம் அறிவிலா
அஞ்சும் பகைவர்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Seruvaarkkuch chenikavaa inbam arivilaa
anjum pakaivarp perin.
meaning: People who fight will never be far from joy if their enemies are both foolish and scared.
elementary: If you are playing a game and your opponent doesn’t understand the rules and is scared to make any move, winning becomes easy and fun. Valluvar says a foolish, frightened enemy is really a stroke of luck for the other side.
university: Seruvaar (செறுவார்) are those who attack or contend; sen ikavaa inbam (சேண் இகவா இன்பம்) is joy that does not go far away, i.e. abiding delight. Varadarasanar keeps this sense (pleasures will not depart), while Puliyur Kesigan reads it as ‘all lofty pleasures remain with them’. The enemy’s two qualities, arivilaa (அறிவிலா, without understanding, which Pappaiah specifies as without knowledge of what is just) and anjum (அஞ்சும், fearing), recapitulate the first two faults of 863. Kalaignar renders the joy specifically as the joy of victory. The verse is the offensive counterpart to the chapter’s earlier defensive lists. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Virata Parva, Prince Uttara boasts that he will defeat the Kaurava army alone, but on seeing it he panics and tries to flee, until Arjuna, disguised as Brihannala, takes the reins and wins the battle.
hinduism.explanation: The episode contrasts the boastful, frightened prince with the skilled warrior who routs the host.
hinduism.tie_back: Uttara is the ignorant, fearful kind of opponent whom the Kural says is a joy to face.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Go-harana) (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus says of the blind guides of his day: if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.
christianity.explanation: Ignorance in those who lead brings ruin on them and their followers.
christianity.tie_back: A foe led by such blindness is, as the Kural says, easy to overcome.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Prophet, urge the believers to battle. If there are among you twenty [who are] steadfast, they will overcome two hundred. And if there are among you one hundred [who are steadfast], they will overcome a thousand of those who have disbelieved because they are a people who do not understand.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an promises that steadfast fighters will overcome much larger forces who lack understanding.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, an enemy without understanding becomes easy to defeat.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the covenant curses of Leviticus, God warns that a disobedient people will be so faint-hearted in the lands of their enemies that the sound of a driven leaf will put them to flight.
judaism.explanation: Fear can so paralyse a people that they flee when no one is pursuing.
judaism.tie_back: Such a fearful foe is exactly what the Kural calls a joy to the attacker.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes five kinds of warriors, including one who loses heart at the mere sight of the cloud of dust raised by the enemy and cannot go into battle.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta uses these timid warriors as an image for monks who give up their practice at the first sign of temptation.
buddhism.tie_back: The warrior who falters at the dust cloud is the fearful foe of the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A man believes himself a hero as long as he does not behold the foe, as did Śiśupāla (before he beheld) the valorously-fighting, great warrior. They go forward to the head of the battle; but when the fight has begun the mother will not recognise her son, and he will be mangled by his foe.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga uses the image of a boastful but untried fighter who collapses once he faces a real opponent, as a warning to novice monks who overrate their own strength.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says those who fight are glad to meet foes who are foolish and fearful, and the Jain image of the vain warrior who is crushed in his first real encounter shows exactly that kind of foe.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.3.1.1–2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, in the midst of this beautiful earth, there is a garden of thorns. Those humble beings who are blessed by their spiritual teacher, do not suffer even a scratch.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok added to Farid's by Guru Arjan, the world is full of thorns, but those blessed by their spiritual teacher pass through unharmed.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who fight will not lack joy if their enemies are foolish and fearful; Gurbani instead places the safety of the righteous in the Guru's blessing, not in the weakness of their foes.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 82, Mahalla 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus outwits the brutish Cyclops Polyphemus by telling him his name is ‘Nobody’, getting him drunk and blinding him, so that when Polyphemus cries for help his neighbours hear that ‘Nobody’ is hurting him.
greek_mythology.explanation: A powerful but witless enemy is overcome by cunning.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Polyphemus is the arivilaa, the foe without understanding whose defeat is a delight.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu teaches that if you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles.
philosophy.explanation: Victory follows from knowledge, and an enemy without it is at a decisive disadvantage.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s ignorant foe is the one who knows neither, and so delivers victory to his opponent.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War III.18 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Frederick the Great routs a divided army at Rossbach
real_life_example.event: During the Seven Years' War, Frederick II of Prussia, with about 21,000 men, faced a combined French and Imperial army of at least 41,000 whose commanders, Soubise and Saxe-Hildburghausen, were at odds with each other. As the allied army marched in columns to outflank him, Prussian cavalry under Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz struck from behind cover and the allied force broke. In less than two hours the allies suffered thousands of casualties and many prisoners, while Prussian losses were around 550.
real_life_example.explanation: A much smaller but well-led army won one of the most lopsided victories of the century against a larger force hampered by divided and poorly judged command.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who fight will never lack joy if their enemies lack understanding, and Rossbach shows how an opponent's poor judgment hands victory to the attacker.

tamil:
கல்லான் வெகுளும் சிறுபொருள் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
ஒல்லானை ஒல்லா தொளி.
transliteration:
Kallaan vekulum siruporul enjnaandrum
ollaanai ollaa tholi.
meaning: A person who will not take even the small, easy win of fighting an enemy with no learning will never become famous.
elementary: If you won’t even try an easy level of a game, how will you ever beat the hard ones and earn a trophy? Valluvar says that someone who shies away from small, easy challenges never earns a great name.
university: The syntax is compressed: kallaan vekulum siruporul (கல்லான் வெகுளும் சிறுபொருள்) is ‘the small gain of being angry with (fighting) the unlearned man’, and ollaanai ollaadhu oli (ஒல்லானை ஒல்லாது ஒளி) says that light, i.e. fame, will not unite with the one who does not obtain it. Varadarasanar on thirukkural.net reads: one who cannot do the easy thing of opposing the unlearned will never gain glory; Pappaiah adds that the gain from fighting one ignorant of the treatises is small, yet the king who disdains it earns no renown; Kalaignar has fame mock such a man for hesitating even before untrained foes. Note: ytamizh.com’s Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar glosses for 870 are misplaced (they discuss forgiving old friends, the theme of kural 810); the couplet text itself is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that if he refuses to fight this righteous battle he will abandon his duty and his good name, and people will speak of his dishonour for ever.
hinduism.explanation: For a warrior, shrinking from a fight he ought to take means the loss of glory.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that glory never comes to one who will not take up a fight within his reach.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus teaches that the one who is faithful in what is least is faithful also in much, and the one unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
christianity.explanation: Small tasks are the test that qualifies a person for greater ones.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar’s man who will not take the small gain shows he is unfit for great glory.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, what is [the matter] with you that, when you are told to go forth in the cause of Allāh, you adhere heavily to the earth?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an rebukes those who hang back when called to act.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it faults the reluctance that forfeits honour.

judaism.quote_or_event: Hillel teaches that in a place where there are no worthy men, one should strive to be one.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah urges a person to step up when the situation calls for it, rather than hold back.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise expects the capable to take up what lies before them, or forfeit their standing.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:5 (Hillel; numbered 2:6 in some editions)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that one who conquers himself is a greater victor than one who conquers a thousand times a thousand men in battle.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redirects the idea of glory from outer victories to inner mastery.
buddhism.tie_back: It offers a counterpoint to the Kural’s worldly calculus of fame through victory.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Penance is of no good if performed by noble men who have turned monks (for the sake of fame); but that penance of which nobody else knows anything (is meritorious). Do not spread your own fame!”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga denies that seeking glory has any spiritual worth and says that hidden, unadvertised effort is the only kind that counts.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says glory never comes to the man who will not take the easy gain of opposing an unlearned foe, while the Jain verse tells the seeker not to pursue glory at all, an honest contrast rather than a parallel.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.8.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That wretched being, whom no one knows - chanting the Naam, the Name of the Lord, he is honored in the four directions.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that even an unknown, lowly person wins honour everywhere through the Name of God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says glory never comes to one who will not take even the easy gain of opposing an unlearned foe; Gurbani locates the source of lasting honour elsewhere, in the Naam.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles tells the embassy that his mother foretold two fates: if he stays and fights at Troy he will die young but win undying glory; if he goes home he will live long without fame.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, glory (kleos) is won only by those who accept the fight.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar likewise says fame never comes to one who declines the contest.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu says that what the ancients called a clever fighter is one who not only wins but wins with ease, by defeating an enemy already defeated.
philosophy.explanation: Strategy consists in seizing victories that are within easy reach.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise faults the man who will not take the easy win over an unlearned foe.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IV.11-13 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Howe halts after Long Island and Washington's army escapes
real_life_example.event: After defeating the inexperienced Continental Army at the Battle of Long Island on 27 August 1776, British General William Howe halted his attack and began siege works rather than pressing the assault, overruling subordinates who argued for a renewed attack. On the night of 29-30 August, George Washington ferried about 9,000 troops across the East River to Manhattan, helped at dawn by fog. Howe did not pursue, and the American army survived to fight on.
real_life_example.explanation: A commander who held every advantage over a raw, untrained army let the chance of a decisive victory slip away.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who will not take even the easy gain of opposing an untrained foe will never win glory, and Howe's pause at Brooklyn is remembered as just such a missed opportunity.

tamil:
பகைஎன்னும் பண்பி லதனை ஒருவன்
நகையேயும் வேண்டற்பாற்று அன்று.
transliteration:
Pakaiennum panpi ladhanai oruvan
nakaiyeyum ventarpaatru andru.
meaning: Being enemies with others has nothing good in it. No one should want it, not even as a game or a joke.
elementary: Some kids pretend to be enemies just for fun, teasing and picking fights as a joke. The poet says even pretend enmity is a bad game, because a joke fight can quickly turn into a real one that nobody can stop.
university: The chapter opens by naming its subject with a moral label: pakai (பகை, enmity) is panpiladhu (பண்பிலது), ‘that which is devoid of good quality’. The emphatic nakaiyeyum (நகையேயும், ‘even in jest / even in play’) carries the force of the couplet: enmity is not to be courted even in sport, still less in earnest. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as an evil without merit that should not be desired even as a pastime, and Kalaignar explains that enmity runs contrary to good character; Puliyur Kesigan adds that this is the settled conclusion of the ethical treatises. The placement is notable: in a chapter that goes on to give hard-headed advice about handling enemies, Valluvar first insists that enmity itself is never desirable. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net, which titles the chapter பகைத்திறந் தெரிதல் with a word break.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavad Gita’s list of divine qualities, Krishna includes adroha, freedom from malice or hostility, alongside forgiveness, fortitude, and purity.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita treats freedom from hostility as part of the character of one born to a divine nature, not just a matter of policy.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats enmity as a lack of good character, something never to be cultivated.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Roman believers to do everything in their power to avoid hostility with anyone.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts make avoiding enmity a standing rule, not an occasional courtesy.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allāh and from prayer. So will you not desist?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that pastimes such as gambling are a doorway through which enmity and hatred enter a community.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise warns that enmity can creep in through play and should not be invited even there.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares the person who harms a neighbour and then claims it was only a joke to a madman throwing deadly missiles.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts refuse to excuse hostility on the grounds that it was meant in fun.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the opening chapter of the Dhammapada the Buddha teaches that hatred is never appeased by hatred, but only by non-hatred, and calls this an eternal law.
buddhism.explanation: Enmity feeds on itself; once started, it only grows by being answered in kind.
buddhism.tie_back: This explains why the Kural says not to start enmity even playfully: it does not end easily once begun.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Everything that happens to somebody, affects him personally; therefore, knowing the creatures' love of their own self, do not deprive them of their life, but cease from endangering and combating them.”
jainism.explanation: Because every being cherishes its own life, Mahāvīra's teaching forbids not only killing but all hostility toward other creatures. The daily Jain confession (pratikramaṇa) says the same in its well-known formula: friendship toward all beings and enmity toward none.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls enmity a thing with no goodness in it, not to be wanted even in jest, and the Jain teaching rules out enmity toward any creature in any form at all.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com); cf. the Prakrit kṣamāpanā verse ‘khāmemi savve jīvā’ of the Āvaśyaka/pratikramaṇa liturgy

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, the Creator is in the Creation, and the Creation abides in God. Whom can we call bad? There is none without Him.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok placed among Farid's, Guru Arjan reasons that since God dwells in every creature, there is no one we may write off as bad.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says enmity has no good in it and should not be courted even in jest; Guru Arjan removes the ground for enmity altogether, since no one is without God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 75, Mahalla 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eris, goddess of strife, threw a golden apple inscribed for the fairest among the goddesses at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis; the contest it provoked led to the Judgment of Paris and ultimately the Trojan War.
greek_mythology.explanation: A mischievous gesture, almost a prank, set off rivalries that ended in a ten-year war.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is a mythic warning that enmity started lightly can grow beyond anyone’s control, as the Kural implies.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes the buffoon as one who will not spare himself or anyone else if he can raise a laugh, and who says things a refined person would never say.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, humour that wounds others is a vice of excess, not harmless fun.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly refuses to treat hostility as acceptable just because it is done in jest.

real_life_example.event_title: The Pig War on San Juan Island
real_life_example.place: San Juan Island, Washington Territory, United States
real_life_example.event: On 15 June 1859 the American settler Lyman Cutlar shot a pig belonging to the British Hudson's Bay Company that was rooting in his garden on San Juan Island, whose ownership both Britain and the United States claimed. When British authorities threatened to arrest him, American troops under Captain George Pickett landed, British warships arrived, and by the end of August hundreds of soldiers and dozens of guns faced each other. General Winfield Scott and Governor James Douglas agreed a joint military occupation, and the dispute was settled peacefully by arbitration in 1872, with the pig as the only casualty.
real_life_example.explanation: A petty quarrel over a garden and a pig came close to dragging two great powers into war, showing how easily trifling hostility can grow beyond anyone's control.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that enmity has no good in it and should not be courted even in jest, and the Pig War shows how a trivial grievance nearly became a real war.

tamil:
வில்லேர் உழவர் பகைகொளினும் கொள்ளற்க
சொல்லேர் உழவர் பகை.
transliteration:
Viller uzhavar pakaikolinum kollarka
soller uzhavar pakai.
meaning: Even if you make enemies of soldiers who use the bow as their plow, never make enemies of learned people who use words as their plow.
elementary: A bully with big muscles can only hurt you while he is near you. But a clever person who writes and speaks well can tell your story to the whole town and to people years from now. So the poet says: if you must quarrel with anyone, never quarrel with the people who are good with words.
university: The couplet is built on a celebrated agricultural metaphor: villēr uḻavar (வில்லேர் உழவர்) are ‘ploughmen whose plough is the bow’, that is, warriors, while collēr uḻavar (சொல்லேர் உழவர்) are ‘ploughmen whose plough is the word’. Mu. Varadarasanar reads the latter as scholars, Solomon Pappaiah as writers, Kalaignar as learned people of verbal power; the older commentarial tradition, reflected in Pope’s gloss ‘ministers whose ploughs are words’, takes them as counsellors skilled in policy. The concessive kolinum (‘even if you incur’) does not recommend war with soldiers; it ranks dangers, implying that the harm of hostile counsel, satire or reputation outlasts and outreaches the harm of arms. The metaphor also suggests that both kinds of men ‘cultivate’ a harvest, and the harvest of words is wider. No variant readings appear between ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Parikshit, irritated while hunting, draped a dead snake on the silent sage Shamika; the sage’s young son Shringi, hearing of the insult, pronounced a curse that the king would die by the serpent Takshaka within seven days, and it came to pass.
hinduism.explanation: A mighty king who could command armies was undone by the spoken word of a sage’s son.
hinduism.tie_back: It dramatizes the Kural’s ranking: the enmity of those whose weapon is the word is more dangerous than that of armed men.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!”
christianity.explanation: James warns that the tongue, though small, can set a whole forest ablaze.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts recognise that words can do more damage than their size suggests.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satirise against the (non-believing amongst the) Quraish, for (the satire) is more grievous to them than the hurt of an arrow.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet asked the poet Hassan ibn Thabit to answer the Quraysh in verse, saying satire wounded them more than arrows.
islam.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s comparison: the word cuts deeper than the bow.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit.
judaism.explanation: Speech is presented as carrying literal life-and-death power.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s caution about enemies who wield words rests on the same recognition.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak not harshly to anyone, for those thus spoken to might retort. Indeed, angry speech hurts, and retaliation may overtake you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that hostile speech provokes hostile speech in return and brings harm back on the speaker.
buddhism.tie_back: Provoking those who answer in words invites a retaliation the Kural warns is especially costly.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You may as well dig rocks with your nails, or eat iron with your teeth, or kick fire with your feet, as treat contemptuously a monk.”
jainism.explanation: When the priests' young men beat the sage Harikeśa, Bhadrā warns them that to make an enemy of a holy man of disciplined mind is like attacking rock, iron and fire: only the attacker is hurt.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns never to make enemies of those whose plough is the word, and Bhadrā's warning likewise makes the wise sage the one opponent it is ruinous to provoke.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Slandering the Saints, one’s life is cut short.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan warns that turning against the holy by slandering them shortens one's very life.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns never to make enemies of the wise whose plough is the word; Guru Arjan likewise warns that turning against the saints, people of the Word, brings ruin on oneself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Achilles’ death, Ajax the mighty warrior and Ulysses the eloquent speaker both claimed his armour; the Greek leaders, swayed by Ulysses’ speech, awarded it to him, and the power of eloquence was shown to outweigh strength of arm.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid stages a contest between the man of the sword and the man of words, and the man of words wins.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s point that the one who ploughs with words is the more formidable opponent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At his trial Socrates says he fears his old accusers, including a comic poet, more than his present prosecutors, because their talk had filled the jurors’ minds with slander since childhood.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates recognised that reputations shaped by skilled talkers and writers are harder to fight than any formal charge.
philosophy.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s warning that the enmity of wordsmiths is the most damaging kind.

real_life_example.event_title: Voltaire's campaign for Jean Calas
real_life_example.event: In March 1762 the Parlement of Toulouse condemned and executed the Huguenot merchant Jean Calas, convicted of murdering his son to stop him converting to Catholicism. Voltaire took up the case and, through a vigorous campaign of letters and pamphlets, including his Treatise on Tolerance of 1763, convinced much of European opinion that the judges had been swayed by anti-Protestant prejudice. A 50-judge royal panel reversed the conviction on 9 March 1765 and the government paid the family an indemnity.
real_life_example.explanation: One writer armed only with a pen discredited a powerful court before all of Europe and helped launch the movement for religious toleration and legal reform in France.
real_life_example.tie_back: The Toulouse judges learned that the hostility of a man whose plough is the word reaches further and lasts longer than that of any warrior.

tamil:
ஏமுற் றவரினும் ஏழை தமியனாய்ப்
பல்லார் பகைகொள் பவன்.
transliteration:
Emur ravarinum ezhai thamiyanaaip
pallaar pakaikol pavan.
meaning: A person who is alone and still makes enemies of many people is more foolish than someone who has lost their mind.
elementary: Picture one kid on the playground who has no friends on his side, yet goes around picking fights with every group. Even someone who is not thinking clearly would not do that. The poet says this is the silliest thing a person can do.
university: The comparison turns on ēmuṟṟavar (ஏமுற்றவர்), ‘those who are deluded or deranged’: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss them as the mad (பித்தர்), Kalaignar as the arrogant, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads ‘the despised’. Ēḻai (ஏழை) here means ‘senseless, witless’, not ‘poor’, as all the commentators agree. Tamiyaṉāy (‘being alone’) and pallār (‘many’) set up the arithmetic: a man without allies who collects many enemies has made the one choice even a madman might avoid. Pappaiah applies it directly to a ruler (ஆட்சியாளன்), in keeping with the Porutpal setting. The text matches in both ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Ravana rejected the counsel of his brother Vibhishana to return Sita, insulted him, and drove him out; Vibhishana went over to Rama, leaving Ravana isolated against a growing alliance.
hinduism.explanation: Ravana’s pride turned his own kin into enemies while he already faced a powerful foe.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural’s figure of folly: alone, and multiplying his enemies.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a prudent king who counts his forces before taking on a stronger enemy.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural condemns exactly the one who skips this reckoning and takes on many while alone.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an tells believers not to fall into disputes among themselves, lest they lose courage and their strength depart.
islam.explanation: Internal quarrels are presented as a direct cause of weakness and defeat.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link isolation and many quarrels with the loss of strength.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet observes that the solitary person has no one to rely on when trouble comes.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s lone man facing many enemies is exactly the one Kohelet pities.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sammodamana Jataka, a flock of quail escape a fowler’s net by lifting it together, but once they begin quarrelling they no longer cooperate and the fowler catches them.
buddhism.explanation: Unity protects; quarrelling leaves each bird alone and easily caught.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s lone man with many enemies is in the position of the quarrelling quail.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A cruel man does cruel acts and is thereby involved in other cruelties; but sinful undertakings will in the end bring about misery.”
jainism.explanation: Jacobi's note glosses the 'cruel man' (veri) as vairin, literally 'one who bears enmity'. The verse says such a man becomes caught in ever-widening hostility that ends in his own misery.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls the lone man who makes many enemies worse than a madman, and the Jain verse shows how the man of enmity piles up further hostilities until they ruin him.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.8.7, with Jacobi's note (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O egotism, you are the root of birth and death and the cycle of reincarnation; you are the very soul of sin. You forsake friends, and hold tight to enemies.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan addresses ahankar, pride, as the root of sin that makes a person drop friends and cling to enemies.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls the man who stands alone yet makes many enemies more foolish than a madman; Guru Arjan names the ego as the folly that drives friends away and gathers enemies.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sahaskriti (salok 49), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the father and his sons, a bundle of sticks cannot be broken while bound together, but each stick snaps easily on its own.
greek_mythology.explanation: Strength lies in having others with you; alone, anyone is easily broken.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s solitary man who takes on many is the single stick.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, The Father and His Sons (tr. G. F. Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that even a band of thieves cannot accomplish anything if its members wrong one another, and that injustice makes a person at odds with others and even with himself.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows that hostility on all sides makes effective action impossible.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats making enemies everywhere as self-defeating folly.

real_life_example.event_title: Paraguay fights the Triple Alliance
real_life_example.place: Paraguay and the Rio de la Plata region, South America
real_life_example.event: Under Francisco Solano Lopez, Paraguay became entangled in disputes with Brazil and Argentina and in Uruguay's civil war, seized Brazilian vessels, attacked Brazilian territory and declared war on Argentina. Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay then formed an alliance against Paraguay in 1865, and the small country fought all three for five years. By the war's end in 1870 Paraguay lay in ruins, having lost more than half of its population and large areas of territory.
real_life_example.explanation: A small state without allies that turned three neighbours against it at once suffered one of the most devastating defeats in modern history.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls the one who stands alone yet makes enemies of many more senseless than a madman, and Paraguay's war against three neighbours shows the cost of that choice.

tamil:
பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் பண்புடை யாளன்
தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்று உலகு.
transliteration:
Pakainatpaak kontozhukum panputai yaalan
thakaimaikkan thangitru ulaku.
meaning: The world holds together because of the greatness of a person of good character who makes enemies into friends and lives that way.
elementary: Imagine a kid who gets pushed by someone, and instead of pushing back, invites that person to play and they become best friends. The poet says people like that are so great that the whole world is held together by them.
university: After three couplets warning against enmity, Valluvar names the ideal: the paṇpuṭaiyāḷaṉ (பண்புடையாளன், ‘man of noble character’) who conducts himself (oḻukum) by making pakai into naṭpu (நட்பு, friendship). Takaimai (தகைமை) is greatness or excellence, and taṅkiṟṟu ulaku (‘the world abides’) is a strong claim: the stability of the world itself depends on such people. Mu. Varadarasanar speaks of the world resting in his magnanimity; Solomon Pappaiah reads it of a ruler who converts enemies and lives with them, so that the world falls within his greatness; Kalaignar has the whole world praising such a person; Sivayogi Sivakumar says the world endures through such honoured conduct. Pope renders it as ‘worthy rule can change his foes to friends’, keeping the political frame. The couplet links back to Chapter 87 and forward to the strategic advice in 875.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Vibhishana, brother of the enemy king Ravana, came seeking refuge, Rama overruled his advisers’ suspicions, accepted him as an ally, and declared that he would give protection to anyone who sought it.
hinduism.explanation: Rama turned a member of the enemy household into a trusted friend and partner.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s gracious person who makes friends of foes, and on whom the right order of the world rests.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;”
christianity.explanation: Jesus commands active goodwill toward enemies rather than retaliation.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts hold up treating an enemy with friendship as the mark of the highest character.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon, the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an promises that answering hostility with goodness can turn an enemy into a close friend.
islam.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s ideal of turning enmity into friendship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Others say: [Who is mighty?] Who turns an enemy into his friend.”
judaism.explanation: Avot de-Rabbi Natan records the view that true might is the ability to make an enemy into a friend.
judaism.tie_back: The rabbis and Valluvar both place the highest strength and greatness in converting enemies to friends.
judaism.source: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 23:1 (tr. A. Cohen, Soncino)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha walked toward the feared bandit Angulimala, who was trying to kill him; through his words Angulimala laid down his weapons, became a monk, and later attained liberation.
buddhism.explanation: The most dangerous enemy of the region was transformed into a disciple and a friend of the Sangha.
buddhism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s ideal at its most dramatic: a deadly foe made into a friend.

jainism.quote_or_event: “There is not the least hatred in me, neither now, nor before, nor in future. …” ‘You know the truth and the Law; you are not angry, compassionate sage; we take refuge at your feet, we together with all of them.’
jainism.explanation: After the priests and their followers have beaten him, the sage Harikeśa declares that he has no hatred at all, and his former attackers become his devotees and take refuge with him.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises the noble person who turns enemies into friends, and Harikeśa, holding no enmity, turns his attackers into people who seek refuge at his feet.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.32–33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition retold by Macauliffe, robbers (thags) on the road surrounded Guru Nanak meaning to rob him; he gave them spiritual instruction, and they gave up their trade, began to repeat the Name, and reformed their lives.
sikhism.explanation: Instead of fleeing or fighting, Guru Nanak turned men who came as his attackers into followers of the Name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the noble person who turns enemies into friends; in this story Guru Nanak does exactly that with men who came to rob him.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak, ch. V, pp. 71-72 (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the end of Aeschylus’ Eumenides, Athena persuades the angry Furies, who threaten to blight Athens, to accept honour in the city; they become the Kindly Ones and bless the land instead.
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena turns implacable avengers into protectors through persuasion rather than force.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The city’s safety rests on this conversion, just as the Kural says the world rests on those who make foes into friends.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Diogenes Laertius records the sage Cleobulus as advising that one should do good to friends to keep them friends, and to enemies to make them friends.
philosophy.explanation: One of the Seven Sages makes winning over enemies a deliberate aim of kindness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural praises exactly this practice of turning enemies into friends.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 1.91 (Cleobulus)

real_life_example.event_title: De Gaulle and Adenauer sign the Elysee Treaty
real_life_example.event: On 22 January 1963 French President Charles de Gaulle and West German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer signed a treaty of friendship between their two countries, long-standing enemies. The treaty set up regular consultations at every level of government on foreign, defence and youth policy and led to the Franco-German Youth Office. The two leaders had begun their rapprochement at Colombey-les-Deux-Eglises in 1958 and marked it publicly at a reconciliation mass in Reims Cathedral.
real_life_example.explanation: Two long-standing enemies became the closest of partners, and their friendship became a foundation of European integration and peace.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world rests on the greatness of those who turn enemies into friends, and the Elysee Treaty turned Europe's oldest rivalry into a lasting friendship.

tamil:
தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால் தான்ஒருவன்
இன்துணையாக் கொள்கவற்றின் ஒன்று.
transliteration:
Thandhunai indraal pakaiyirantaal thaanoruvan
indhunaiyaak kolkavatrin ondru.
meaning: If you have no one to help you and you face two enemies alone, make one of them your friend.
elementary: Suppose two bigger kids are both upset with you and nobody is on your side. Instead of fighting both, you make peace with one of them, and suddenly it is two against one in your favour. That is the smart move the poet recommends.
university: This is the most explicitly strategic couplet of the chapter. Three conditions are stacked in clipped clauses: taṉtuṇai iṉṟāl (‘if one has no support’), pakai iraṇṭāl (‘if the enemies are two’), tāṉ oruvaṉ (‘and one is alone’). The remedy is to take one of the two as iṉtuṇai (இன்துணை), a ‘sweet’ or agreeable ally. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as a general maxim, while Solomon Pappaiah again frames it for a ruler; Sivayogi Sivakumar keeps it close to the text. It complements 874: where that couplet praised turning enemies into friends as a virtue, this one treats it as a necessity of statecraft, in line with the Indian political tradition of alliances among neighbouring powers. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthashastra treats foreign policy as a circle of kings and recommends that a weaker king make peace or alliance (sandhi) with one power when he cannot stand against several.
hinduism.explanation: The classical Indian manual of statecraft makes alliance with one party a standard response to weakness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural gives the same advice in miniature: alone against two, ally with one.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.”
christianity.explanation: A king who sees he is outmatched sends envoys to make peace before battle.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise advises turning a foe into a friend when one cannot win alone.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if they incline to peace, then incline to it [also] and rely upon Allāh. Indeed, it is He who is the Hearing, the Knowing.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the Prophet to accept peace when an adversary offers it.
islam.tie_back: Both texts endorse turning an adversary into a partner in peace when possible.

judaism.quote_or_event: Hunted by King Saul and without support in Israel, David went over to Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, and lived under his protection.
judaism.explanation: Facing a deadly pursuer, David found safety by allying himself with another of Israel’s enemies.
judaism.tie_back: He acts out the Kural’s advice: alone and threatened, take one hostile power as an ally.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the account of the Buddha’s last days, King Ajatasattu’s minister Vassakara is sent to ask about attacking the Vajjians; the Buddha explains they cannot be defeated while united, and the tradition later relates that they were overcome after being divided.
buddhism.explanation: The story shows how dividing a set of opponents changes the balance of power.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the reverse side of the Kural’s strategy: separating two hostile parties so one can be won over.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Knowing the thoughts of their pupils, both Keśi and Gautama made up their minds to meet each other. Gautama, knowing what is proper and what is due to the older section (of the church), went to the Tinduka park, accompanied by the crowd, his pupils. When Keśi, the young monk, saw Gautama approach, he received him with all becoming attention.”
jainism.explanation: The followers of Pārśva and of Mahāvīra were uneasy about their differences, so the two leaders met and turned a possible rivalry into union, and Keśi in the end adopted Mahāvīra's five vows.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural advises a man facing two adversaries to make one of them a friendly ally, and Gautama's courteous approach to Keśi turns a potential rival community into an ally.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.14–16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Britannica records that the Mughal emperor Jahangir, who had imprisoned Guru Hargobind in Gwalior fort, finally released him, apparently seeking the Sikhs' favour as possible allies against the Indian states still defying Mughal rule.
sikhism.explanation: Facing several opponents at once, the emperor chose to turn one adversary, the Sikhs, into a potential ally rather than keep fighting on every front.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural advises one who faces two enemies alone to make one of them an ally; Jahangir's release of Guru Hargobind is an instance of that same calculation.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Guru Hargobind (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the war against the Titans, Zeus freed the Hundred-Handers whom their father had imprisoned, and with them as allies he defeated the Titans.
greek_mythology.explanation: Zeus won a war he could not win alone by bringing estranged powers to his side.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It reflects the Kural’s strategy of gaining an ally to tip the balance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli argues that a prince gains respect by declaring himself openly for one side, and warns that neutrality usually leaves one prey to the winner.
philosophy.explanation: He advises taking an ally rather than standing alone between rival powers.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he sees lone neutrality between two threats as dangerous and alliance as the remedy.

real_life_example.event_title: President Nixon visits China
real_life_example.event: Facing a Cold War rivalry with the Soviet Union and two decades of hostility with the People's Republic of China, the Nixon administration opened a secret channel to Beijing through Pakistan. Nixon travelled to China from 21 to 28 February 1972, becoming the first US president to visit the mainland while in office, and the visit ended with the Shanghai Communique. The State Department's historians record that the administration saw the Sino-Soviet split as an opportunity to build a relationship with Beijing that would counterweigh Moscow, and a US-Soviet summit followed in May 1972.
real_life_example.explanation: By reaching out to one of its two great adversaries, the United States changed the balance of the Cold War and gained leverage with the other.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises that one facing two enemies should make one of them an ally, which is exactly the strategy of the opening to China.

tamil:
தேறினும் தேறா விடினும் அழிவின்கண்
தேறான் பகாஅன் விடல்.
transliteration:
Therinum theraa vitinum azhivinkan
theraan pakaaan vital.
meaning: In a time of trouble, whether you have tested a person before or not, do not get too close to them and do not cut them off. Keep a careful distance.
elementary: When something big goes wrong, it is not the time to suddenly make a new best friend or to start a new fight. The poet says: stay polite and keep a bit of distance, and wait until things are calm before deciding who to trust.
university: This is among the most compressed and debated couplets of the chapter. The verb tēṟu (தேறு, ‘to trust, be convinced about’) appears three times: tēṟiṉum tēṟā viṭiṉum (‘whether one has trusted him or not’), then tēṟāṉ (‘not trusting’) paired with pakāaṉ (பகாஅன், ‘not separating’, with the alapedai lengthening), ending in viṭal (‘leave him so’). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: whether you had earlier assessed a man or not, in a time of ruin neither trust him nor drop him; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar apply it specifically to an enemy, advising neither closeness nor open rupture; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as ‘do not approach the untrustworthy in ruinous times’. Pope’s verse is loose, and his explanation ‘neither to join nor separate’ follows the traditional reading. The thirukkural.net English summary, ‘be wary of joining or opposing any’, captures the consensus: in crisis, keep a guarded neutrality. The text matches in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the Kurukshetra war, Balarama, bound by affection to both the Pandavas and Duryodhana, refused to fight for either side and left on pilgrimage along the Sarasvati.
hinduism.explanation: In the greatest crisis of his family, Balarama neither joined nor broke with either party.
hinduism.tie_back: It is a living example of the Kural’s guarded middle course in a time of ruin.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva and Shalya Parva

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus counsels his disciples to combine wariness with harmlessness in a hostile world.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s advice is the same blend: neither trust blindly nor provoke a break.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, take your precaution and [either] go forth in companies or go forth all together.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an instructs believers facing danger to stay alert and take precautions.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly counsels caution rather than hasty trust in dangerous times.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah warns to be careful with the ruling powers, since they draw people close only for their own needs, seem like friends when it suits them, and do not stand by a person in the hour of distress.
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel’s teaching warns that apparent friends may vanish exactly when trouble comes.
judaism.tie_back: This is why the Kural advises not committing to anyone untested in a time of ruin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha describes false friends, including the one who is a companion only in pleasure and the one who helps only out of self-interest, and contrasts them with the friend who stands by you in misfortune.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha gives criteria for telling true friends from false ones.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural assumes the same problem: in crisis one cannot yet know who is true, so one should stay guarded.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Benevolence (maitrī) towards all living-beings (sattva), joy (pramoda) at the sight of the virtuous (guṇādhika), compassion and sympathy (kāruṇya) for the afflicted (kliśyamāna), and tolerance (mādhyasthya) towards the insolent and ill-behaved (avineya) are the other observances.”
jainism.explanation: Umāsvāti's sūtra prescribes mādhyasthya, a neutral stance toward the insolent. Pūjyapāda's commentary defines it as freedom from both attachment and revulsion.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural advises keeping a careful middle distance in a crisis, neither committing to a doubtful person nor breaking with him, and Jain mādhyasthya is a stance of neither embrace nor rejection.
jainism.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.11, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who is not affected by pleasure or pain, who looks upon friend and enemy alike - says Nanak, listen, mind: know that such a person is liberated.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the liberated person as one whose mind does not swing between friend and enemy.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural advises keeping a careful middle distance in a crisis, neither committing to nor breaking with a person; Gurbani also holds friend and enemy in the same even regard, though for a different reason.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 15), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Trojans found the great wooden horse left by the Greeks, the priest Laocoön urged them not to trust it, saying he feared the Greeks even when they brought gifts.
greek_mythology.explanation: At the decisive moment, an untested offer from a former enemy was the most dangerous thing in Troy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural warns against committing to the untested in a time of danger, which is what Troy failed to heed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that the wish to be friends comes quickly but friendship does not; people cannot know each other until they have shared much over time.
philosophy.explanation: Trust has to be tested by time and experience, not assumed.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural applies this to crisis: trust that has not been tested should not be relied on when ruin looms.

real_life_example.event_title: The first Non-Aligned summit meets in Belgrade
real_life_example.event: In September 1961 leaders of about two dozen countries met in Belgrade for the first conference of the Non-Aligned Movement, founded by Josip Broz Tito of Yugoslavia, Jawaharlal Nehru of India, Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt, Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana and Sukarno of Indonesia. At the height of the Cold War, the member states declined to join either the American-led or the Soviet-led bloc. The conference adopted a declaration against colonialism and an appeal for peace addressed to both superpowers.
real_life_example.explanation: Newly independent nations chose to keep a careful distance from both rival blocs, neither binding themselves to one nor making an open enemy of the other.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural counsels that in a time of crisis one should neither commit to nor break with either side, which is the stance non-alignment took during the Cold War.

tamil:
நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு மேவற்க
மென்மை பகைவர் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Novarka nondhadhu ariyaarkku mevarka
menmai pakaivar akaththu.
meaning: Do not tell your troubles to people who do not already know about them, and do not show your weak points to your enemies.
elementary: If you are feeling hurt, you do not have to tell everyone you meet. And if someone is being mean to you, try not to show them where it hurts, because they might poke you there again. Share your worries with the people who really care and already understand.
university: The couplet has two prohibitions in parallel: nōvaṟka (‘do not lament’) to those who do not know one’s suffering, and mēvaṟka (‘do not take on, display’) meṉmai (மென்மை, ‘softness, weakness’) in the presence of enemies. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take the first line as referring to friends who have not themselves perceived one’s distress: to complain to them is undignified and spreads knowledge of one’s weakness. Solomon Pappaiah reads the hidden object of both lines as ‘our lack of strength’, which should neither be told to unaware friends nor shown to enemies. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the lines quite differently: do not grieve over those who do not understand grief, and do not covet the soft spot of enemies. Pope’s ‘To those who know them not, complain not of your woes; nor to your foeman’s eyes infirmities disclose’ follows the majority reading. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: During their thirteenth year of exile, the Pandavas lived in disguise at King Virata’s court, enduring hardships and insults in silence so that the Kauravas could not discover them.
hinduism.explanation: Revealing themselves before the year ended would have handed their enemies the advantage.
hinduism.tie_back: They lived out the Kural’s rule: keep your suffering hidden and give your enemies no glimpse of weakness.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus warns not to give what is holy to dogs or throw pearls before swine, lest they trample them and turn and tear you.
christianity.explanation: What is precious and vulnerable should not be exposed to those who will misuse it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural applies the same caution to one’s sorrows and weaknesses.

islam.quote_or_event: “I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allāh, and I know from Allāh that which you do not know.”
islam.explanation: The prophet Jacob, grieving for Joseph, refuses to pour out his sorrow to those around him and takes it only to God; earlier in the same sura he warns Joseph not to tell his dream to his brothers lest they plot against him (12:5).
islam.tie_back: Together the verses mirror both halves of the Kural: do not air your grief to the unknowing, and do not expose yourself to hostile people.

judaism.quote_or_event: “That he told her all his heart, and said unto her. There hath not come a razor upon mine head; for I have been a Nazarite unto God from my mother’s womb: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me, and I shall become weak, and be like any other man.”
judaism.explanation: Samson revealed the secret of his weakness to Delilah, who was working for his Philistine enemies, and was captured.
judaism.tie_back: This is the classic disaster the Kural warns against: disclosing one’s weakness where enemies can use it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kacchapa Jataka, a talkative tortoise carried through the air on a stick by two geese cannot resist answering the mocking children below, opens his mouth, and falls.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta uses the tale to teach a king the danger of speaking at the wrong moment.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that speaking out in front of those who mock you can be one’s undoing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If he suffers from the heat of hot things, or from the heat of his body, or from the heat of summer, he should not lament the loss of comfort. … All these troubles have been declared by the Kāśyapa. A monk should not be vanquished by them, when attacked by any anywhere.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's teaching on the twenty-two hardships (parīṣaha) asks the monk to bear them without complaint and never to let them defeat him.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says not to pour out one's troubles or show weakness before enemies, and the Jain discipline likewise forbids lamenting one's sufferings and calls for firmness against every attack.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.8 and closing passage (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Tell your troubles to the One who is the Source of all comfort.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that one's sorrows should be laid before God, the giver of all comfort, rather than spread before others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says not to tell your troubles to those who do not already know them, nor show weakness before enemies; Guru Nanak likewise directs the telling of troubles to God alone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus wakes on Ithaca, Athena disguises him as an old beggar and advises him to tell no one who he is and to endure in silence the insults of the suitors until the time is right.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus keeps his identity and his grief hidden from both enemies and most of his household.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He follows the Kural to the letter, concealing pain and vulnerability from his foes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises that in company one should avoid frequently and at length talking about one’s own actions and dangers, since others do not enjoy hearing them as much as one enjoys telling them.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic counsels reserve about one’s own troubles in ordinary society.
philosophy.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s first line about not airing sorrows to those who do not already know.

real_life_example.event_title: The Ghost Army deceives the enemy in Europe
real_life_example.event: The US Army's 23rd Headquarters Special Troops, a secret unit of about 1,100 men later called the Ghost Army, used inflatable tanks and vehicles, recorded battle sounds played through huge speakers, and fake radio traffic to make the enemy believe that large forces stood where there were few or none. In its largest operation, Operation Viersen in March 1945, it inflated more than 600 dummy vehicles to simulate two divisions while the Ninth Army crossed the Rhine. Its work stayed classified for decades, and its veterans were later awarded the Congressional Gold Medal.
real_life_example.explanation: By hiding gaps in the line and never letting the enemy see where it was thin, the Allies kept their opponents from exploiting their real weak points.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says never to show weakness before enemies, and the Ghost Army made a whole craft of hiding where Allied lines were weak.

tamil:
வகையறிந்து தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப மாயும்
பகைவர்கண் பட்ட செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Vakaiyarindhu tharseydhu tharkaappa maayum
pakaivarkan patta serukku.
meaning: Know the right way to act, build up your strength, and protect yourself well. Then your enemies’ pride will fade away by itself.
elementary: If a team keeps teasing yours, the best answer is not to shout back but to practise, get stronger, and play smart. When they see how ready you are, their boasting stops on its own.
university: Three participial steps lead to the result: vakai aṟintu (‘knowing the method’), taṟceytu (‘making oneself strong’), taṟkāppa (‘guarding oneself’); then māyum (‘will perish’) the cerukku (செருக்கு, ‘pride, arrogance, exultation’) that has arisen in the enemies. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read cerukku as the enemy’s pride, which collapses without a blow once one is prepared; Solomon Pappaiah adds that taṟkāppa includes guarding one’s secrets, linking back to 877; Pope’s explanation renders cerukku as the foes’ ‘joy’ and taṟceytu as ‘securing assistance’, a reading that ties the couplet to 875. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as knowing one’s qualifications and self-protection. The point is deterrence: preparation defeats an enemy’s confidence before any conflict. The text matches in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthashastra teaches that a king should first strengthen the constituent elements of his own state, such as treasury, army, fort and allies, since a well-fortified kingdom deters attack.
hinduism.explanation: Indian statecraft makes self-strengthening the foundation of security against enemies.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s sequence of knowing the method, strengthening oneself, and self-protection follows the same logic.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to be fully equipped so that they can stand firm against their adversary.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts teach that preparation and self-protection are what defeat an enemy’s schemes.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allāh and your enemy...”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an commands believers to build up their strength so that enemies are deterred.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: preparation itself breaks the enemy’s confidence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon.”
judaism.explanation: Mocked and threatened by Sanballat and his allies, Nehemiah’s builders worked and stood guard at once until the wall was finished, and their enemies lost heart.
judaism.tie_back: They did what the Kural advises: knew what to do, made themselves strong, and guarded themselves, and the enemies’ arrogance collapsed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada urges one to see the body as fragile as a clay pot, to make the mind secure like a fortified city, and to fight Mara with the weapon of wisdom.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the image of a well-defended city for inner preparedness against the adversary.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s self-fortification against outer foes has an inner counterpart here.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable; making Zeal his bow, its string Carefulness in walking (iriyâ), and its top (where the string is fastened) Content, he should bend (this bow) with Truth, piercing with the arrow, Penance, (the foe's) mail, Karman--(in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Samsâra.”
jainism.explanation: Asked by Indra to fortify his city, King Nami describes instead an inner fortress and an inner bow, built from the virtues, with which the sage defeats karma.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says to know the method, build up your strength and guard yourself so that the enemy's pride withers, and Nami's fortress-and-bow image gives the same three steps in Jain form, aimed against karma.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.20–22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: After the execution of Guru Arjan, Guru Hargobind trained in arms, built up a Sikh army and fortified his cities, built the Akal Takht at Amritsar in 1609 and the fort of Lohgarh, and later defeated Shah Jahan's forces four times.
sikhism.explanation: Under pressure from Mughal power, the sixth Guru made his community strong and well defended, and is believed to have borne two swords at his succession for temporal (miri) and spiritual (piri) authority.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says to know the right method, build up your strength and guard yourself, and the enemy's arrogance will fade; Guru Hargobind's build-up of Sikh strength and defences shows that strategy at work.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Guru Hargobind (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before facing Medusa, Perseus learned the way from the Graeae and the nymphs and equipped himself with winged sandals, a cap of invisibility, a pouch and a sickle, so that he could approach and escape safely.
greek_mythology.explanation: Perseus succeeded because he first learned the method and armed himself well.
