greek_mythology.tie_back: This follows the Kural’s order: know the way, make yourself ready, protect yourself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu teaches that skilled warriors of old first made themselves invincible and then waited for the enemy to become vulnerable; securing against defeat lies in one’s own hands.
philosophy.explanation: Strategy begins with one’s own preparation, not with attacking.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise places victory over an enemy’s arrogance in one’s own readiness.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, ch. 4 (tr. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Meiji Japan ends the unequal treaties
real_life_example.place: Tokyo, Japan, and London, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: From the 1850s Western powers imposed treaties on Japan that gave their citizens extraterritorial legal privileges and fixed Japan's customs duties, and they refused revision until Japan's institutions matched Western models. The Meiji government built modern legal codes, a constitution, an army and a navy, and in 1894 Britain signed a treaty agreeing to end extraterritoriality, which was abolished in 1899. Japan regained full tariff autonomy in 1911.
real_life_example.explanation: Japan won equal treatment not by a single blow against the treaty powers but by patiently building its own strength until their claims of superiority could no longer be sustained.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that knowing the right method, making oneself strong and guarding oneself will make the enemy's arrogance fade by itself, which is how Japan ended the unequal treaties.

tamil:
இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க களையுநர்
கைகொல்லும் காழ்த்த இடத்து.
transliteration:
Ilaidhaaka mulmaram kolka kalaiyunar
kaikollum kaazhththa itaththu.
meaning: Cut down a thorny tree while it is still young. Once it grows hard, it will hurt the hand of the person who tries to cut it.
elementary: A tiny thorny weed in the garden can be pulled out with two fingers. If you leave it for a year, it grows big, tough thorns that scratch your hands when you finally try to pull it. Problems are the same: deal with them while they are small.
university: The couplet is a pure agricultural image applied to enmity, as all the commentators make explicit: iḷaitāka (‘while young’) muḷmaram (முள்மரம், ‘thorn tree’) kolka (‘destroy’); otherwise, kāḻtta iṭattu (‘when it has hardened’, from kāḻ, the hard heartwood) it kai kollum (‘destroys the hand’) of the kaḷaiyunar (களையுநர், ‘those who weed it out’). Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the literal image; Kalaignar draws the lesson that enmity must be put down before it matures; Sivayogi Sivakumar adds the explicit note that enmity must not be allowed to grow. Solomon Pappaiah reads the thorn tree as one who intends to destroy us. The verb kol- (‘kill’) appears in both lines, giving a pointed reversal: kill it, or it kills your hand. The text matches in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At Duryodhana’s birth, ill omens appeared, and Vidura and the Brahmins advised Dhritarashtra to abandon the child for the sake of the family; out of affection he refused, and the conflict that followed destroyed the Kuru line.
hinduism.explanation: The epic presents a danger recognised early and left to grow until it consumed everyone.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s thorn tree left uncut, wounding the very hands that later tried to remove it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James traces how a small inner impulse grows step by step into something deadly.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts warn that what is small and manageable now becomes lethal once full grown.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not follow the footsteps of Satan.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns against the first small steps of wrongdoing, which lead on to greater harm.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it urges stopping a danger at its first stage.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the evil inclination is at first like a spider’s thread, but in the end it becomes like the thick ropes of a wagon.
judaism.explanation: What begins as something easily broken becomes, if left alone, something that cannot be broken.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same image of early weakness and later strength as the Kural’s young and hardened thorn tree.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a tree, though cut down, sprouts up again if its roots remain uncut and firm, even so, until the craving that lies dormant is rooted out, suffering springs up again and again.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses a tree image to teach that a danger must be removed at the root or it returns.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also uses a tree to teach thorough, timely removal of what will harm you.

jainism.quote_or_event: ‘O Gautama, in the innermost heart there grows a plant which brings forth poisonous fruit; how have you torn it out?’ “I have thoroughly clipped that plant, and torn it out altogether with its roots; thus I have got rid of the poisonous fruit.” … “Love of existence is that dreadful plant which brings forth dreadful fruit; having regularly torn it out, I live pleasantly.”
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue between Keśi and Gautama, craving for existence is pictured as a poisonous plant growing in the heart, which the sage must pull out by the roots.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to cut down the thorn tree while it is young, before it can wound the hand, and Gautama likewise speaks of uprooting a harmful growth completely before it bears its poisonous fruit.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.45–46, 48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, the farmer plants acacia trees, and wishes for grapes.”
sikhism.explanation: Farid uses the image of a farmer who sows thorny acacia yet hopes to harvest grapes, to show that what one lets take root decides what one later reaps.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural uses a thorn tree to teach that enmity must be cut while young before it hardens; Farid's thorny acacia makes the related point that what is allowed to grow determines the harvest.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 23), Bhagat Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before Paris was born, Hecuba dreamed she gave birth to a firebrand that set Troy ablaze; the seer warned of the danger, but the child survived, grew up, and his abduction of Helen brought about the city’s destruction.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows a foretold danger not dealt with in time, which grows into the ruin of all.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s warning that what is left to mature will destroy those who later try to handle it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli compares political troubles to a wasting fever, which at first is easy to cure but hard to detect, and later easy to detect but hard to cure; the Romans, he says, dealt with troubles as soon as they foresaw them.
philosophy.explanation: A wise ruler acts on dangers early, while they are still small.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s thorn tree turned into a theory of statecraft.

real_life_example.event_title: Germany remilitarizes the Rhineland
real_life_example.event: On 7 March 1936 Hitler repudiated the Locarno agreements and ordered German troops into the Rhineland, which had been demilitarized under the post-war settlement. Britain and France condemned the move but did not intervene; after consulting the British, the French cabinet decided not to risk a confrontation. Germany then fortified the Rhine frontier, and the Imperial War Museum notes that the success encouraged Hitler to pursue an even more aggressive foreign policy.
real_life_example.explanation: Historians widely see the failure to act in 1936, while German forces were still weak, as a missed chance to stop a danger that later cost far more to remove.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns to cut down the thorn tree while it is young, and the Rhineland crisis is the classic case of a threat left to harden.

tamil:
உயிர்ப்ப உளரல்லர் மன்ற செயிர்ப்பவர்
செம்மல் சிதைக்கலா தார்.
transliteration:
Uyirppa ularallar mandra seyirppavar
semmal sidhaikkalaa thaar.
meaning: People who do not break the pride of enemies who hurt them are not truly alive, even though they still breathe.
elementary: If someone keeps bullying a group and nobody ever stands up to them, the bully only gets bolder. The poet says that people who never stand up to proud, hostile enemies are not really living freely at all.
university: The closing couplet is the chapter’s sharpest. Uyirppa (உயிர்ப்ப, ‘so much as to breathe’) uḷar allar (‘they do not exist’) maṉṟa (மன்ற, ‘certainly’): such people are not alive even to breathe. The condition is that they cannot citaikkal (‘shatter’) the cemmal (செம்மல், ‘pride, eminence, haughtiness’) of ceyirppavar (செயிர்ப்பவர், ‘those who are hostile or offend’). Kalaignar reads it as: those who cannot break the enemies’ arrogance cannot truly be called alive just because they breathe; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a prediction that such people will be destroyed within a breath; Mu. Varadarasanar’s printed gloss on ytamizh reads ‘தலைமையைக் கொடுக்க’, which appears to be a typographic slip for கெடுக்க (‘destroy’). Sivayogi Sivakumar takes ceyirppavar as open wrongdoers. Read with 871 and 874, the chapter’s logic is clear: never seek enmity, convert it where possible, but where it persists, deal with it decisively. The text matches in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, do not yield to this degrading impotence. It does not become you. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O chastiser of the enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna rouses Arjuna from paralysis on the battlefield and tells him to face his opponents.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats failure to confront hostile pride as a kind of living death.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the Magnificat, Mary praises God who has shown strength with his arm and scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.
christianity.explanation: The song celebrates the overthrow of the arrogant.
christianity.tie_back: It echoes the Kural’s concern with breaking the pride of the hostile, though as God’s act rather than a human duty.

islam.quote_or_event: “Permission [to fight] has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged. And indeed, Allāh is competent to give them victory.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an permits the wronged to defend themselves against those who attack them.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it accepts that aggressive enemies sometimes must be confronted.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the Philistine said, I defy the armies of Israel this day; give me a man, that we may fight together.”
judaism.explanation: For forty days Goliath’s challenge paralysed Israel, until young David went out and brought down his pride.
judaism.tie_back: Israel’s paralysis before Goliath is the condition the Kural calls not truly living, and David’s act is its remedy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that one who conquers himself is a greater victor than one who conquers a thousand times a thousand men in battle.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism relocates the real battle from outer enemies to one’s own mind.
buddhism.tie_back: It offers a contrasting view to the Kural’s call to break the enemy’s pride: the pride to break first is one’s own.

jainism.quote_or_event: ‘Gautama, you stand in the midst of many thousand (foes) who make an attack on you; how have you vanquished them?’ “By vanquishing one, five are vanquished; by vanquishing five, ten are vanquished; by this tenfold victory, I vanquish all foes.”
jainism.explanation: Gautama goes on to explain that these foes are the unconquered self, the four passions (anger, pride, deceit and greed) and the five senses, and that crushing them is the only victory that counts.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says those who cannot break the pride of hostile foes do not truly live, and the Jain sage claims a complete victory over every foe, pride among them, by conquering them within.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.35–36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone are truly alive, whose minds are filled with the Lord. O Nanak, no one else is truly alive; those who merely live shall depart in dishonor; everything they eat is impure.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Majh ki Vaar Guru Nanak says that only those filled with God are truly alive, and that those who merely live will leave the world without honour.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who cannot break the pride of hostile enemies are not alive even to breathe; Guru Nanak shares the claim that mere breathing is not life and links life to honour, but places true life in the remembrance of God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Maajh, Majh ki Vaar (salok, Guru Nanak) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Returning home after twenty years, Odysseus strings his bow and, with Telemachus, overcomes the arrogant suitors who had been consuming his household and plotting against his son.
greek_mythology.explanation: The epic’s climax is the breaking of the suitors’ insolence by the rightful master.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It enacts the Kural’s demand that the pride of hostile enemies must be broken.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli advises that men should either be treated well or be crushed, because they can avenge slight injuries but not serious ones.
philosophy.explanation: He warns that half-measures against enemies leave them able to strike back.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns that those who leave hostile pride intact will not survive.

real_life_example.event_title: The Holy League defeats the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto
real_life_example.place: Gulf of Patras, near Lepanto (Nafpaktos), Greece
real_life_example.event: After the Ottomans attacked Venetian Cyprus, the pope brought Spain, Venice and other states together in a Holy League, whose fleet under Don John of Austria met the Ottoman fleet near Lepanto on 7 October 1571. In about four hours of fighting the allies captured 117 galleys and virtually destroyed the Ottoman force. Britannica notes that the battle destroyed the myth of Turkish naval invincibility, even though Venice later surrendered Cyprus in 1573.
real_life_example.explanation: Lepanto mattered less for the territory it won than for breaking the confidence of a power that had seemed unbeatable at sea.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who cannot break the pride of hostile foes hardly live, and Lepanto is remembered above all as the day that pride was broken.

tamil:
நிழல்நீரும் இன்னாத இன்னா தமர்நீரும்
இன்னாவாம் இன்னா செயின்.
transliteration:
Nizhalneerum innaadha innaa thamarneerum
innaavaam innaa seyin.
meaning: Shade and water are pleasant, but they are bad when they make you sick. In the same way, your own relatives become painful when they do you harm.
elementary: A shady tree and a cool drink are lovely on a hot day, but if the water is dirty it can make you sick. Family and friends are meant to be like shade and water, so when someone close to us starts hurting us, it feels even worse than a stranger doing it.
university: The chapter opens with a paired simile: nizhal-neer (நிழல்நீர், shade and water), the archetypal comforts of a hot land, are innaadha (இன்னாத, painful) when innaa (இன்னா, harmful, i.e. disease-bearing); so too thamar-neer (தமர்நீர், the 'nature' or disposition of one's kin) becomes innaavaam when it does harm. The wordplay on neer, meaning both 'water' and 'nature/quality', is deliberate and is reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar's and Kalaignar's glosses, which read thamar-neer as the qualities of kinsfolk. Solomon Pappaiah extends thamar to one's own party or faction, showing how modern commentators read utpakai (உட்பகை, enmity from within) politically as well as domestically. In the traditional reading framed by Parimelazhagar, the Porul section addresses a ruler, so the 'kin' include courtiers and relations around the throne. Text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Queen Kaikeyi, a member of Dasharatha's own household and once his favourite, uses two old boons to force Rama's exile, breaking the king's heart.
hinduism.explanation: The person closest to the king, whose presence should have been a comfort, becomes the source of the household's greatest grief.
hinduism.tie_back: Like shade and water turned harmful, a beloved relative turned hostile brings pain precisely because she was trusted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist laments betrayal by an intimate who shared his table, a verse the Gospel of John later applies to Judas.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that harm from those who should sustain us, like food and shade, is uniquely bitter.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, among your wives and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon and overlook and forgive - then indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an warns that even the nearest family can, at times, work against one's good, while still urging forgiveness.
islam.tie_back: Both texts recognize that those meant to be our comfort can become a source of harm.

judaism.quote_or_event: Absalom, King David's own son, wins the hearts of the people at the city gate and then raises a rebellion that drives his father out of Jerusalem.
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew Bible presents the revolt as a tragedy precisely because it comes from David's own child.
judaism.tie_back: As the Kural warns, kin who turn to harm become a deeper misery than strangers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, the Buddha's own cousin and a monk in his order, plotted against the Buddha's life and tried to split the Sangha.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist tradition remembers Devadatta as the danger that arose from inside the Buddha's own family and community.
buddhism.tie_back: He embodies the Kural's point that a relative who turns harmful is like refreshment that has turned to sickness.

jainism.quote_or_event: “What is this evil whim of warriors for persistence in heroism in which there is such a quarrel between brothers ending in destruction? If my elder brother does not live, enough of life for me.”
jainism.explanation: In Hemacandra's telling, Bāhubali has just felled his elder brother Bharata in their duel over the kingdom, and he fans the unconscious man with his garment, weeping, appalled at what the quarrel has made of two sons of Ṛṣabha.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that kin, like shade and water, are a comfort that turns to pain once they turn harmful, and the duel of Bharata and Bāhubali is the classic Jain case of brothers whose closeness became the source of their deepest injury.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1 (Ādīśvara-caritra), ch. 5, part 11 'The fight between Bharata and Bāhubali' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS, 1931; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: When Guru Ram Das installed his youngest son Arjan as the fifth Guru in 1581, his eldest son Prithi Chand resented being passed over, and the succession caused lasting discord among the brothers.
sikhism.explanation: The Guru's own household, which should have been his chief support, became a source of rivalry and grief, and Prithi Chand's opposition dogged Guru Arjan's early years.
sikhism.tie_back: As the Kural says that shade and water turn harmful when they breed sickness, the closeness of kin became painful here precisely because the hostility came from within the family.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Why was Guru Arjan's installation as Guru disputed?' (Britannica Editors)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Deianira sends her husband Heracles a robe smeared with what she believes is a love charm from the centaur Nessus; it is poison, and it burns him to death.
greek_mythology.explanation: A gift meant to bind and comfort becomes deadly, delivered by the hero's own wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's image of comforts that turn harmful and of harm arriving through one's own household.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Paracelsus argued that all things can be poison and that only the dose decides whether a thing heals or harms.
philosophy.explanation: The principle holds that even beneficial substances become harmful under the wrong conditions.
philosophy.tie_back: It echoes the first half of the Kural, where shade and water, ordinarily good, become harmful.

real_life_example.event_title: Aurangzeb confines his father Shah Jahan in Agra Fort
real_life_example.event: After the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan fell ill in 1657, his sons fought a war of succession, and his son Aurangzeb emerged victorious and took the throne in 1658. Aurangzeb had his father confined in Agra Fort, where Shah Jahan remained for about eight years until his death in January 1666. He was buried in the Taj Mahal beside his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
real_life_example.explanation: The emperor who had built the most famous monument of devotion to family spent his last years a prisoner of his own son.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the closeness of one's own people, like shade and water, becomes painful when it turns harmful, as Shah Jahan found when his son became his jailer.

tamil:
வாள்போல பகைவரை அஞ்சற்க அஞ்சுக
கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Vaalpola pakaivarai anjarka anjuka
kelpol pakaivar thotarpu.
meaning: Do not fear enemies who come at you openly like a drawn sword. Fear enemies who pretend to be your relatives or friends.
elementary: A bully who shouts at you from across the playground is easy to spot and avoid. The trickier problem is someone who pretends to be your friend while secretly trying to get you in trouble, so that is the person to be careful about.
university: The couplet sets two kinds of foe against each other: vaal-pola pakaivar (வாள்போல பகைவர், foes like a sword), whose hostility is open and therefore manageable, and kel-pol pakaivar (கேள்போல் பகைவர், foes who appear as kel, 'kin' or intimates). The imperative pair anjarka / anjuka (அஞ்சற்க / அஞ்சுக, 'fear not' / 'fear') gives the verse its antithetical snap. What is to be feared is their thodarpu (தொடர்பு), the ongoing association, since closeness is the very channel through which the hidden enemy works. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the second group as those who behave like relatives while harbouring utpakai, and Pope renders them 'foes who seem like kinsmen'. The text agrees in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Duryodhana, outwardly welcoming his Pandava cousins, has a mansion of lac built at Varanavata for them, planning to burn them inside it.
hinduism.explanation: The plot hides lethal enmity behind the forms of family hospitality; the Pandavas escape only through Vidura's warning.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's 'enemy who appears as kin', more dangerous than any open swordsman.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha sub-parva (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him; When he speaketh fair, believe him not: for there are seven abominations in his heart.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that the hater often hides behind gracious speech.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts tell us to fear the pleasant-faced foe more than the open one.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he whose speech pleases you in worldly life, and he calls Allah to witness as to what is in his heart, yet he is the fiercest of opponents.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the person whose agreeable words mask the most bitter hostility.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks the smooth-tongued hidden opponent as the most dangerous.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it ... But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says he could have endured or hidden from an open enemy, but betrayal by a close companion is unbearable.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's contrast exactly: the open foe is bearable, the intimate foe is the one to fear.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha teaches young Sigala to recognize four kinds of foes who come in the guise of friends: the taker, the flatterer, the one who only talks, and the companion in ruin.
buddhism.explanation: The discourse gives practical signs for detecting enemies who present themselves as friends.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's warning to fear foes who wear the face of a friend or relative.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A little monkey breaking into a fruit with its finger, will strike and seize its own father … the friendship of those who are without unity (of mind) is not pleasant.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain-authored Tamil Nāladiyār, in its chapter on improper friendship, pictures the young monkey that turns on its own father as he comes to meet it, and says that closeness without real unity of mind brings no pleasure.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural tells us to fear the foe who comes in the guise of kin more than the open swordsman, and the quatrain's monkey striking the father who comes to greet it is exactly that danger inside an intimate bond.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār 24.7 (English translation serialised in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Bronze is bright and shiny, but when it is rubbed, its blackness appears.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak contrasts a gleaming outward surface with the darkness it hides; in the Janamsakhi tradition this shabad is linked to his meeting with Sajjan, a host who welcomed travellers with a show of piety and then robbed them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that the foe who looks like a friend is more to be feared than an open enemy, and Guru Nanak likewise exposes the friendly surface that hides harm.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Demodocus sings of the wooden horse: the Trojans, deceived, drag the gift into their own city, and the Greeks hidden inside sack Troy from within.
greek_mythology.explanation: A city that withstood ten years of open siege falls to an enemy it welcomed inside its walls.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The open army was survivable; the enemy taken in as a friend proved fatal, as the Kural warns.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There are no intrigues more difficult to guard against than those which are concealed under a pretence of duty, or under the name of some intimate connection. For you can easily avoid one who is openly an adversary, by guarding against him; but this secret, internal, and domestic evil not only exists, but even overwhelms you before you can foresee it or examine into it.”
philosophy.explanation: Accusing Verres of betraying the consul he served as quaestor, Cicero argues that the treachery of a trusted associate is far more dangerous than open hostility.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero makes the Kural's own contrast: an open enemy can be guarded against, while an enemy in the guise of a friend or kinsman strikes before he is detected.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Against Verres (In Verrem), II.1.39 (tr. C. D. Yonge)

real_life_example.event_title: Kim Philby is exposed as a Soviet agent inside British intelligence
real_life_example.event: Kim Philby became a Soviet agent while at Cambridge in the 1930s, joined Britain's Secret Intelligence Service (MI6) in 1940, rose to head its counter-espionage section, and in 1949 became its chief liaison officer in Washington, passing detailed information about British and American intelligence to Moscow. Suspected after two fellow agents fled in 1951, he was eventually confronted in Beirut in January 1963 by his old friend and MI6 colleague Nicholas Elliott and gave a partial confession. Within days he fled to the Soviet Union, where he lived until his death in 1988.
real_life_example.explanation: The most damaging enemy of British intelligence was not a foreign agent kept at arm's length but a trusted colleague and friend at its heart.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says to fear not the open enemy like a drawn sword but the one who poses as one's own, and Philby did his harm precisely through the trust of his colleagues.

tamil:
உட்பகை அஞ்சித்தற் காக்க உலைவிடத்து
மட்பகையின் மாணத் தெறும்.
transliteration:
Utpakai anjiththar kaakka ulaivitaththu
matpakaiyin maanath therum.
meaning: Fear the enemy within your own circle and protect yourself. When you are weak, it will cut you down as surely as a potter’s tool cuts clay.
elementary: A potter uses a thin wire or blade to slice through soft clay in one easy stroke. Hidden enemies wait for a time when you are tired or in trouble, and then they can hurt you just as easily, so it is wise to watch out for them early.
university: The verse pairs a command, utpakai anji thar kaakka (உட்பகை அஞ்சித் தற்காக்க, 'fearing internal enmity, guard yourself'), with a warning about timing: ulaividaththu (உலைவிடத்து), 'at the time of tottering' or decline. The image matpakai (மட்பகை), literally 'clay-enemy', is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as the potter's cutting tool that slices clay vessels, so that maana therum (மாணத் தெறும்) means 'will destroy thoroughly'. Pope's 'potter's knife' follows the same reading. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads the second line as setting a cooking pot on an unfired clay vessel, an interpretive variant rather than a textual one. The Tamil text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Protect thyself, O king, from all fears that arise from within. Fears, however, that arise from outside are of little consequence. The first kind of fear, O king, may cut thy roots in a single day.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that internal dissension is the real danger to a ruler, able to destroy him suddenly.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural almost point for point: guard against the enemy within, which strikes all at once.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section CVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: In Gethsemane, while Jesus' disciples sleep, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrives with an armed crowd and betrays him with a kiss.
christianity.explanation: The betrayal comes from inside the inner circle and at the hour of greatest vulnerability.
christianity.tie_back: As the Kural warns, the internal enemy strikes when one is weakest.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are the enemy, so beware of them.”
islam.explanation: Describing the hypocrites inside the Medinan community, whose appearance and speech are pleasing, the Qur'an names them the real enemy.
islam.tie_back: Both texts urge vigilance against the foe who lives within one's own community.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ahithophel, David's trusted counsellor, joins Absalom's rebellion; David prays that his counsel be turned to foolishness, and Ahithophel urges an immediate strike while David is weary and weak-handed.
judaism.explanation: The trusted insider knows exactly when the king is most vulnerable.
judaism.tie_back: This illustrates the Kural's warning that an internal enemy strikes in a time of weakness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever harm an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater, an ill-directed mind inflicts on oneself a greater harm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that the most damaging enemy is the one inside oneself.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of a hostile insider, the Dhammapada of a hostile mind, but both rank the inner foe above the outer one.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Self is the one invincible foe, (together with the four) cardinal passions, (viz. anger, pride, deceit, and greed, they are five) and the (five) senses (make ten). These (foes), O great sage, I have regularly vanquished.”
jainism.explanation: Asked by Keśi how he withstands the thousands of foes that attack him, Gautama names the true enemies as the unsubdued self, the four passions and the five senses, all of them inside the person.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural urges a man to fear the enemy within and guard himself, and Gautama's answer turns the same vigilance on the foes that live inside one's own camp.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Within this body dwell the five thieves: sexual desire, anger, greed, emotional attachment and egotism.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das locates the most dangerous enemies inside the person, as thieves already living within the house of the body who plunder its true wealth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural urges guarding oneself against the enemy within before it strikes at a moment of weakness, and Gurbani names that inner enemy as the five thieves.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 600, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld, Agamemnon's shade tells Odysseus how he survived the Trojan War only to be killed at his own homecoming feast by his wife Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus.
greek_mythology.explanation: The victor of a ten-year war dies in his own house, at the moment he lets down his guard.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The enemy within strikes when defences are down, just as the Kural warns.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his 1838 Lyceum Address, Abraham Lincoln argued that danger to the American republic would not come from abroad but would spring up from among its own people.
philosophy.explanation: Lincoln held that no external power could crush the nation, and that only internal disorder could destroy it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he identifies the internal enemy as the one to fear and guard against.
philosophy.source: Abraham Lincoln, Address before the Young Men's Lyceum of Springfield (1838)

real_life_example.event_title: Kobayakawa Hideaki changes sides at Sekigahara
real_life_example.event: At the Battle of Sekigahara the western coalition led by Ishida Mitsunari faced the eastern army of Tokugawa Ieyasu. Kobayakawa Hideaki, whose troops were posted on Mount Matsuo as part of the western army, had secretly promised to support Ieyasu; during the battle he led his forces down the mountain against his nominal ally Otani Yoshitsugu, and other commanders switched sides with him. The collapse that followed destroyed the western army and opened the way for Tokugawa rule.
real_life_example.explanation: The western coalition was undone not by the enemy facing it but by a commander standing within its own lines.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that the enemy within strikes at the moment of weakness and cuts as surely as the potter's tool, as Kobayakawa's turn did at the battle's turning point.

tamil:
மனமாணா உட்பகை தோன்றின் இனமாணா
ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்.
transliteration:
Manamaanaa utpakai thondrin inamaanaa
edham palavum tharum.
meaning: If hidden hostility grows from a mind that is not good, it brings many troubles and turns a person's own people against them.
elementary: If a person keeps a secret grudge and refuses to let it go, it slowly spoils everything around them. Soon brothers, sisters and friends are arguing and taking sides, and the whole group stops getting along.
university: The verse balances two negated compounds: mana-maanaa (மனமாணா, 'mind not made excellent', i.e. unreformed or unreconciled) and ina-maanaa (இனமாணா, 'kin not made excellent', i.e. kinsfolk who fall out of harmony). When utpakai arises in the first, it yields edham palavum (ஏதம் பலவும், many faults or evils) of the second kind. Mu. Varadarasanar reads the result as many faults that keep one's kin from being set right, while Kalaignar says such a disposition makes one's own people into enemies. Pope's 'secret enmities ... that minds pervert' and the thirukkural.net rendering 'myriad miseries manifest among kin' both preserve the link between inner hostility and outer estrangement. No textual variant is attested between ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For him who has conquered the mind, the mind is the best of friends; but for one who has failed to do so, his very mind will be the greatest enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that an unmastered mind becomes one's own worst enemy.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural traces the troubles of utpakai back to an unreformed mind, just as the Gita locates the enemy in the uncontrolled mind.

christianity.quote_or_event: “From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?”
christianity.explanation: James traces quarrels within the community back to disordered desires inside each person.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees outward discord among one's own people as the fruit of inner hostility.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet Muhammad told believers not to hate one another, envy one another or turn their backs on one another, but to be servants of God as brothers.
islam.explanation: The hadith treats hidden hatred and envy as the forces that break a community apart.
islam.tie_back: Both texts warn that concealed rancour destroys the bonds among one's own people.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids nursing silent hatred and requires open, honest correction instead.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's 'unreformed' hidden enmity is exactly the hatred in the heart that Leviticus forbids.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who harbor such thoughts do not still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada observes that nursing grievances keeps hatred alive.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the 'unreformed mind' of the Kural, from which hidden enmity and its many troubles keep arising.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
jainism.explanation: The Saman Suttam, gathering canonical Jain verses, names how each of the four passions (kaṣāyas) unravels a particular bond: anger kills affection and deceit kills friendship.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that when hidden enmity takes root in an unreformed mind it turns one's own people against one, and the Jain verse shows how the untamed passions of such a mind destroy love and friendship.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam 135 (English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the mind reformed in the company of the holy, from which enmity has gone so that no one, kin or stranger, seems hostile.
sikhism.tie_back: Where the Kural says hidden enmity in an unreformed mind turns one's own people against one, Gurbani shows the reformed mind in which that enmity cannot take root.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod lists the children of Eris (Strife): Toil, Forgetfulness, Famine, Sorrows, Fightings, Battles, Murders, Quarrels, Lies, Disputes, Lawlessness and Ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth a single strife gives birth to a whole brood of evils.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that one hidden enmity yields 'many evils'.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself each morning that he will meet difficult people, but that all are made for cooperation, like hands, feet and eyelids, so that acting against one another is contrary to nature.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic emperor treats resentment toward one's fellows as a self-inflicted distortion of the mind.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he links an unreformed, resentful mind to the breakdown of a community meant to work as one body.

real_life_example.event_title: The sons of Louis the Pious rise against their father
real_life_example.place: Frankish Empire (near Colmar and at Compiegne and Soissons, present-day France)
real_life_example.event: Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, faced a revolt by his older sons in 830 after he sought to provide a kingdom for Charles, his son by a second marriage. In 833 his sons Lothar, Pippin and Louis met him near Colmar at the place later called the Field of Lies, where his own followers deserted him; he was deposed and made to perform public penance. He was restored in 834 when the younger sons turned against Lothar, but the quarrels continued, and after his death the empire was divided among his sons by the Treaty of Verdun in 843.
real_life_example.explanation: The family quarrel at the top of the Carolingian empire turned father against sons and brother against brother, and ended in the division of Charlemagne's realm.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says hidden enmity in an unreconciled mind brings troubles that turn one's own people against one, as it did within Louis the Pious's family.

tamil:
உறல்முறையான் உட்பகை தோன்றின் இறல்முறையான்
ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்.
transliteration:
Uralmuraiyaan utpakai thondrin iralmuraiyaan
edham palavum tharum.
meaning: If hidden hostility grows among relatives, it brings many deadly troubles.
elementary: When a family has a big fight that nobody fixes, it can grow worse and worse until it breaks the family apart. The poet says a quarrel inside the family can be the most dangerous kind of all.
university: The couplet turns on a chiming pair: ural-muraiyaan (உறல்முறையான், 'by way of relationship') and iral-muraiyaan (இறல்முறையான், 'by way of death'). Where enmity springs from kinship, it yields evils of a deadly kind. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as 'many sufferings of the kind that kill', and Solomon Pappaiah as 'many faults joined with death'. Pope's explanation speaks of internal hatred 'in a (king's) family' leading to 'fatal crime', showing the royal framing of the traditional commentary, where kin-enmity means dynastic feud. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads iral-muraiyaan differently, as harm extending even to those outside the kin, an interpretive variant. The Tamil text agrees in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On the field of Kurukshetra, Arjuna sees grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons and friends arrayed on both sides and despairs that the destruction of the family will ruin its ancient traditions.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata war is the great Indian epic of kin-enmity ending in near-total destruction.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural's warning writ large: enmity within a family brings deadly ruin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And a man’s foes shall be they of his own household.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus, echoing Micah 7:6, warns that the deepest divisions may run through one's own home.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts recognize that hostility within the family is especially grave.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an tells of the two sons of Adam: one's offering is accepted, the other's is not, and the jealous brother kills his brother, becoming one of the regretful.
islam.explanation: The first murder in the Qur'anic story arises from rivalry between brothers.
islam.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural's teaching that enmity among kin leads to deadly harm.

judaism.quote_or_event: Cain, resentful that his brother Abel's offering is accepted and his is not, rises up against Abel in the field and kills him.
judaism.explanation: In Genesis the first killing in human history is fratricide born of jealousy.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's 'enmity by relationship' that brings 'evils by death' is embodied in Cain and Abel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: King Ajatasattu of Magadha, the son of King Bimbisara, had his own father killed to seize the throne, and later confessed this wrong before the Buddha.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist texts remember the patricide as a grave evil born of ambition within the royal family.
buddhism.tie_back: It exemplifies the Kural's warning about deadly enmity inside a dynasty.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When Marbhuti, out of love for his brother, went to bring Kamatha back, the wretched fellow hurled a stone slab on his brother Marubhuti; consequently he died then and there”
jainism.explanation: In the Jain account of Pārśvanātha's former lives, Kamaṭha's hatred for his brother Marubhūti did not end with that murder: across later births he kept tormenting the soul that would become Pārśva, while Marubhūti's soul kept forgiving.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that enmity born within the bond of kinship brings evils of a deadly kind, and Kamaṭha's fratricide, renewed birth after birth, is Jainism's best-known picture of exactly that.
jainism.source: Story of Kamaṭha and Marubhūti (previous lives of Pārśvanātha), as retold on Jain Square, 'Kamatha and Marabhuti' (jainsquare.wordpress.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O anger, you are the root of conflict; compassion never rises up in you.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan addresses anger directly as the root of strife and a force that leaves no room for compassion.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says enmity springing up among kin brings deadly evils, and Gurbani traces such conflict back to anger, which shuts out the compassion that holds a family together.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sehskritee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eteocles and Polynices, the sons of Oedipus, quarrel over the throne of Thebes; Polynices leads seven champions against the city, and the brothers kill each other at the seventh gate.
greek_mythology.explanation: The feud between brothers ends in mutual destruction, fulfilling their father's curse.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'enmity within kinship bringing deadly evils' in its starkest form.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Describing the civil strife at Corcyra, Thucydides observes that kinship became a weaker tie than party, and that fathers killed their sons in the violence.
philosophy.explanation: Thucydides analyses stasis, internal faction, as a force that dissolves even family bonds and unleashes every kind of death.
philosophy.tie_back: He confirms the Kural's insight that enmity within one's own people brings deadly evils.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 3.81-82

real_life_example.event_title: Kublai Khan and his brother Ariq Boke fight for the Mongol throne
real_life_example.event: After the death of the Great Khan Mongke in 1259, his brothers Kublai and Ariq Boke each had himself proclaimed Great Khan in 1260, Kublai at Shangdu and Ariq Boke at Karakorum. The brothers fought a four-year civil war that ended when Ariq Boke submitted in 1264; he died in captivity two years later. The struggle left the Mongol empire effectively split into separate khanates, and Kublai concentrated on China, where he founded the Yuan dynasty.
real_life_example.explanation: A war between brothers broke the unity of the largest land empire in history, which never again acted as one.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says enmity that springs from kinship brings deadly evils, and the brothers' war cost the Mongol empire its unity.

tamil:
ஒன்றாமை ஒன்றியார் கட்படின் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
பொன்றாமை ஒன்றல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Ondraamai ondriyaar katpatin egngnaandrum
pondraamai ondral aridhu.
meaning: Once people who were united start to split apart, it is always hard for them to escape being destroyed.
elementary: Think of a team that always played together well. If the players start secretly disliking each other, they stop passing the ball and stop helping, and soon even an easy match is lost. Once a group splits, it is very hard to stop it from falling apart.
university: The couplet is a study in the root ondru (ஒன்று, 'to be one, to unite'): ondraamai (ஒன்றாமை, disunity) arises among ondriyaar (ஒன்றியார், those who were united), and then pondraamai ondral (பொன்றாமை ஒன்றல், 'attaining non-perishing', i.e. escaping ruin) becomes aridhu (அரிது, difficult) egngnaandrum (எஞ்ஞான்றும், at any time). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: when enmity arises among one's own people, it is always hard to avoid perishing through that internal enmity; Solomon Pappaiah applies it to a government whose fall cannot then be prevented. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as the difficulty of ever reuniting once a group is split by another's intrigue. Both sources print the same text, and thirukkural.net transliterates katpatin, reflecting the sandhi of kan + padin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra's first book, 'The Separation of Friends', the jackal Damanaka sows mistrust between the lion king Pingalaka and his close friend, the bull Sanjivaka, until the lion kills the bull.
hinduism.explanation: The frame story shows how a strong alliance is destroyed once suspicion is planted between its members.
hinduism.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural's teaching that discord among the united makes ruin almost inescapable.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus states it as a general law: a divided kingdom, city or household cannot survive.
christianity.tie_back: This is nearly a restatement of the Kural's claim that disunity among the united leads to ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you - when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together and you became, by His favor, brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an commands the community to stay united and reminds it that it was once divided by enmity.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat unity as survival and division as the road to ruin.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the Second Temple fell, though its generation studied Torah and did good deeds, because of sinat chinam, baseless hatred among Jews, which it weighs as equal to idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed combined.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic tradition locates the cause of national catastrophe in internal enmity rather than in the Roman army.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's lesson: once the united fall into enmity, destruction follows.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjians, the Buddha says they will prosper as long as they meet often and meet, act and disperse in harmony; tradition holds that they were later conquered only after their unity was broken by a planted agent.
buddhism.explanation: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta makes concord the first condition of a people's survival.
buddhism.tie_back: It mirrors the Kural: the united are safe until discord enters, after which ruin is hard to avoid.

jainism.quote_or_event: “But when Mahavira refused to admit his claim, Jamali felt humiliated and finally left him to establish his own order. His order, however, does not appear to have lasted for long.”
jainism.explanation: Jamāli, a monk of Mahāvīra's own order and by tradition his kinsman, caused the first schism (nihnava). His following fell away, and the breakaway group did not survive him.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that once discord arises among those who were united, escaping ruin is hard, and the first Jain schism shows a split from within a united community ending in the dissenter's own decline.
jainism.source: Jain community history, 'Rival Sects' (Nihnavas section), jainworld.com

sikhism.quote_or_event: After Maharaja Ranjit Singh died in 1839, the Sikh state he had built broke down within six years through palace revolutions and assassinations, and after two wars with the British the Punjab was annexed in 1849.
sikhism.explanation: A kingdom that had been a formidable power under one ruler fell quickly once its own leaders turned against each other.
sikhism.tie_back: This bears out the Kural's warning that once discord takes hold among those who were united, escaping destruction becomes very hard.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sikh Wars' (Britannica Editors)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the close of the Eumenides, Athena prays that civil strife, insatiable of evil, may never roar in Athens and that citizens may not drink one another's blood in vengeance.
greek_mythology.explanation: The trilogy ends by naming civil discord as the gravest threat to the newly founded city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees internal division as the deadliest danger to a united people.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates asks whether there is any greater evil for a city than what tears it apart and makes it many instead of one, or any greater good than what binds it together and makes it one.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats the unity of the city as its highest good and division as its worst evil.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly sees disunity among those once united as the gravest danger.

real_life_example.event_title: Athens and Sparta fight the Peloponnesian War
real_life_example.event: Athens and Sparta had fought together against the Persian invasions, but rivalry over Athenian power in the Delian League led to the Peloponnesian War, fought from 431 to 404 BCE and ending in Athens' defeat. The Greek city-states continued fighting among themselves for decades afterwards. Weakened by this infighting, they were defeated by Philip II of Macedon at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, after which they lost their independence.
real_life_example.explanation: The cities that had united to save Greece from Persia wore each other down until an outside power could master them all.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that once discord takes hold among those who were united, it is ever hard to escape destruction, as the Greek city-states found.

tamil:
செப்பின் புணர்ச்சிபோல் கூடினும் கூடாதே
உட்பகை உற்ற குடி.
transliteration:
Seppin punarchchipol kootinum kootaadhe
utpakai utra kuti.
meaning: A family with hidden hostility inside may look joined together like a box and its lid, but it is never truly united.
elementary: A box and its lid fit together neatly, but they are still two separate pieces that can be pulled apart at any moment. A family that is secretly angry inside may look together at dinner, but deep down they are not really united.
university: The governing image is seppin punarchchi (செப்பின் புணர்ச்சி, 'the joining of a seppu'), a small casket whose lid sits flush on its body so that the two look like one object. A kudi (குடி, family, clan or community) that has suffered utpakai may koodinum (கூடினும், even though it comes together) yet kootaadhu (கூடாதே, will surely not unite). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read seppu as a lidded casket, and Pope translates 'casket with its cover'. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads seppu as copper used to join two different metals, an interpretive variant. Pappaiah extends kudi to the party and the state. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The asura brothers Sunda and Upasunda, inseparable in everything and sharing one kingdom, fall into rivalry over the celestial maiden Tilottama and kill each other.
hinduism.explanation: Their seeming oneness hid a fault line that a single provocation split open.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the casket and lid, their union looked complete but did not hold once rivalry entered.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sunda-Upasunda episode, trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Burning lips and a wicked heart are like a potsherd covered with silver dross.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs compares warm words over a hostile heart to cheap clay given a shiny coating.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts use a crafted-object image for outward togetherness covering inner hostility.

islam.quote_or_event: “Their violence among themselves is severe. You think they are together, but their hearts are diverse.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes a group that looks united from outside but is divided within.
islam.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's casket-and-lid image of apparent but unreal union.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph's brothers live under one roof as one family while hatred divides them.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's family, they are together in form but not in heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: At Kosambi, monks of a single community fell into a bitter dispute; they went on living in one monastery but refused to reconcile even when the Buddha himself urged them, and he finally withdrew to the forest alone.
buddhism.explanation: The community remained outwardly one Sangha while being split within.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's picture of a group joined in form but not in spirit.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 128, Upakkilesa Sutta (opening); Vinaya, Mahavagga X

jainism.quote_or_event: “He started as a pupil and ended as a frustrated rival of Mahavira.”
jainism.explanation: Gośāla lived and wandered with Mahāvīra for six years as a self-declared disciple, then broke away, founded the Ājīvika order, and finally attacked Mahāvīra and two of his monks with his fiery power (tejolesyā).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's casket and lid look like one object without being one, and Gośāla's six years at Mahāvīra's side, outwardly together but never one in mind, ending in open attack, illustrate that false union.
jainism.source: T.U. Mehta, The Path of Arhat, 'Association with Gosala' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those who have one thing in their heart, and something else in their mouth, are judged to be false.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, condemns those whose words and inner feelings do not match.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the casket whose lid sits flush yet remains a separate piece, people whose hearts and mouths differ may seem united while being divided inside, as the Kural says.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Atreus, pretending to be reconciled with his brother Thyestes, invites him to a feast of welcome and secretly serves him the flesh of his own sons.
greek_mythology.explanation: A show of family reunion conceals the most savage enmity in Greek myth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's casket and lid in tragic form: apparent union, total inner hostility.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that friendships based on utility or pleasure dissolve easily once the advantage ends, because the partners never loved each other for who they were.
philosophy.explanation: Such friendships look like friendship but lack its inner substance.
philosophy.tie_back: This loosely matches the Kural's union that looks complete but is not real.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The United Arab Republic of Egypt and Syria breaks apart
real_life_example.event: On 1 February 1958 Egypt and Syria proclaimed their union as the United Arab Republic under Gamal Abdel Nasser, and the union was approved by plebiscites later that month. Egyptian dominance of the union antagonized many Syrians, and on 28 September 1961, after a military coup in Damascus, Syria declared itself independent again. Egypt kept the name United Arab Republic until 1971.
real_life_example.explanation: A union that looked complete on paper never became one in spirit and came apart within three and a half years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a group divided by hidden enmity may look joined like a casket and its lid yet never truly unite, which describes the brief union of Egypt and Syria.

tamil:
அரம்பொருத பொன்போலத் தேயும் உரம்பொருது
உட்பகை உற்ற குடி.
transliteration:
Aramporudha ponpolath theyum uramporudhu
utpakai utra kuti.
meaning: A family with hostility inside wears itself down and loses its strength, like metal worn away by a file.
elementary: When you rub a file back and forth on a piece of metal, a little dust falls off each time until the metal gets thinner and thinner. A family that keeps fighting inside loses a little strength every day in the same way, until there is not much left.
university: The image is aram porudha pon (அரம் பொருத பொன், metal struck by a file), which theyum (தேயும், wears away). The second line, uram porudhu (உரம் பொருது), means that the family's own strength (uram) is ground away by the friction of utpakai. Pon usually means gold, as Pope and thirukkural.net render it, but Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss it as iron (இரும்பு), reflecting the wider sense of pon as metal. The echo of porudha / porudhu (struck / striking) emphasises that the family is both the file and the metal, wearing itself down. The text agrees in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Samba, cursed by sages his kinsmen had mocked, produces an iron bolt, King Ugrasena has it ground into fine powder and cast into the sea; the Vrishnis and Andhakas later destroy one another, and the Mahabharata says they were consumed by that iron bolt.
hinduism.explanation: The Yadava clan, invincible to outsiders, perishes in a drunken quarrel among its own members.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the clan's strength is ground away from within, and the epic even uses the image of iron filed to powder.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, Section 1 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns the Galatian church that infighting will wear the community away.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts picture internal friction slowly consuming a group's strength.

islam.quote_or_event: “And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute and [thus] lose courage and [then] your strength would depart; and be patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches that internal disputes sap a community's courage and strength.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says quarrelling within makes a group's strength wear away.

judaism.quote_or_event: After Solomon's death, the people quarrel with his son Rehoboam, and the ten northern tribes break away, leaving Israel split into two rival kingdoms.
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew Bible presents the division as a lasting weakening of the nation.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's image of strength worn down by internal friction fits the divided kingdom.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After the death of the Jain leader Nigantha Nataputta, his followers split into factions and attacked one another with sharp words; the Buddha then taught Ananda ways of settling disputes so that his own Sangha would not suffer the same fate.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses a neighbouring community's decay through infighting as a warning.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's picture of a group wearing itself away through internal enmity is exactly what the sutta describes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Even one who has subsided or repressed all his passions, once more experiences a terrible spiritual degeneration, hence one ought not to become complacent when some remnants of passions still continue.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching warns that passions which have only been suppressed, not destroyed, keep working on the soul and can bring about a steep fall from spiritual heights already reached.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural pictures a family worn down by internal enmity as metal ground away by a file, and the Jain verse likewise describes a hidden remnant that keeps wearing away what has been won.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam 133 (English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The five thieves plunder their homes, and egotism breaks in.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das pictures the home of the heart being robbed from the inside by the vices, with ego breaking through its walls.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures a family worn away by enmity within, like metal under a file, and Gurbani likewise shows a house emptied from within rather than by an outside attacker.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 854, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles over a captive woman leads Achilles to withdraw from battle, and the Greek army suffers heavy losses at Trojan hands.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad opens with internal discord that weakens the Greeks more than any enemy has.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's filed metal, the army loses its strength through friction within its own ranks.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nam concordia parvae res crescunt, discordia maximae dilabuntur.”
philosophy.explanation: The dying King Micipsa tells his sons that through harmony small states grow, while through discord the greatest fall apart.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's principle in Latin: internal discord wears down even the greatest strength.

real_life_example.event_title: The Byzantine civil war of 1341-1347
real_life_example.event: After Emperor Andronicus III died in 1341, John Cantacuzenus, who claimed the regency, and the court of the young John V, led by the empress Anna of Savoy, fell into civil war, and Cantacuzenus proclaimed himself emperor. During the war he allied with the Ottoman Turks and in 1347 retook Constantinople with Turkish help, becoming co-emperor. The fighting ruined much of what remained of the Byzantine economy, allowed the Serbian ruler Stefan Dushan to seize large territories, and helped the Ottomans gain their first foothold in Europe at Gallipoli in 1354.
real_life_example.explanation: Six years of fighting between rival factions within the court wore away the strength of an empire already in decline and invited in the power that would later conquer it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural pictures a house afflicted by internal enmity wearing itself away like metal under a file, which is what the civil war did to Byzantium.

tamil:
எட்பக வன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்
உட்பகை உள்ளதாங் கேடு.
transliteration:
Etpaka vanna sirumaiththe aayinum
utpakai ulladhaang ketu.
meaning: Even if hostility inside a group is as small as half a sesame seed, ruin is hiding inside it.
elementary: A sesame seed is one of the tiniest seeds there is, and half a seed is smaller still. The poet says even a grudge that small, kept hidden inside a group, can grow until it breaks everything apart.
university: The measure of smallness is etpakavu (எட்பகவு, the split half of a sesame seed), among the tiniest units in Tamil idiom; anna (அன்ன) means 'like'. However sirumaiththu (சிறுமைத்து, slight) the utpakai is, ketu (கேடு, ruin) is ulladhu (உள்ளது, present) within it. Mu. Varadarasanar says that even at that size it carries ruin able to destroy a whole family, and Solomon Pappaiah reads it as destruction already present inside the faction. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads 'ulladhu' as 'all that exists', giving 'ruin to everything', a reading the word order allows. The thirukkural.net rendering ('even a dissent as small as a seed') and Pope ('slight as shred of sesame seed') agree with the dominant reading. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Maya Sabha, Duryodhana mistakes a crystal floor for water and falls into a pool he took for solid floor, and Bhima and others laugh at him; the humiliation feeds the envy behind the dice game and the war.
hinduism.explanation: A small moment of mockery within the extended family helps set off the Kurukshetra catastrophe.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural warns, a slight internal grievance can hold ruin within it.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Duryodhana's account of the palace)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!”
christianity.explanation: James warns that a tiny spark, like a careless word, can set a whole forest ablaze.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts insist that a small seed of discord carries vast destructive power.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that Satan has despaired of being worshipped by the believers in Arabia, but has not given up on sowing dissension among them.
islam.explanation: The hadith presents internal discord as the opening through which harm still enters a community.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats even small internal division as dangerous.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud says Jerusalem was destroyed because of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza: a host's servant invited the wrong man to a feast, the host publicly threw out his enemy, the sages present stayed silent, and the humiliated guest went to Rome and informed against the Jews.
judaism.explanation: A trivial mix-up between two similar names, combined with an existing grudge, sets off national catastrophe.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's sesame-seed enmity: tiny in origin, ruinous in effect.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Think not lightly of evil, saying, ‘It will not come to me.’ Drop by drop is the water pot filled. Likewise, the fool, gathering it little by little, fills himself with evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that small wrongs, ignored, accumulate into great harm.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly refuses to treat small enmity as harmless.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One should not be complacent with a small debt, slight wound, spark of fire and slight passion, because what is small (today) may become bigger (later).”
jainism.explanation: This well-known Jain maxim sets a small passion beside a small debt, wound and spark: none of them may be trusted to stay small.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that enmity within, even as slight as half a sesame seed, holds ruin inside it, and the Jain maxim makes the same point that a trifling inner fault must never be dismissed.
jainism.source: Saman Suttam 134 (English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Even if the poisonous snake is fed large amounts of milk, it will still yield only poison.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das observes that a poisonous nature stays poisonous however much it is nourished, so that the harm remains hidden within.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural holds that even enmity as small as half a sesame seed contains ruin, and Gurbani likewise says that poison held inside is never made harmless.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 171, Raag Gauree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eris, the goddess of Strife, throws a golden apple inscribed for the fairest among the goddesses at a wedding feast; the quarrel between Hera, Athena and Aphrodite leads to the judgement of Paris and the Trojan War.
greek_mythology.explanation: A single apple becomes the seed of the most famous war in Greek myth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As the Kural says, strife no bigger than a seed can hold enormous ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In revolutions the occasions may be trifling, but great interests are at stake. Even trifles are most important when they concern the rulers.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle cites how the constitution of Syracuse was overturned by a love-quarrel between two young men in the government.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he warns that the smallest internal dispute among those in power can bring down the state.

real_life_example.event_title: A single deputy's objection breaks up the Polish Sejm
real_life_example.event: In 1652 a single deputy, Wladyslaw Sicinski, objected to extending the session of the Sejm, and his lone protest ended it, the first time the principle known as the liberum veto was used to break up a parliament. Under the practice, any one member could defeat a measure or dissolve a session and nullify its acts, and it was later used so often that business was frequently paralysed and foreign powers bribed deputies to use it. The veto was abolished only in the Constitution of 3 May 1791, shortly before the Commonwealth was partitioned out of existence in 1795.
real_life_example.explanation: A rule that let the smallest dissent paralyse the whole state became one of the main weaknesses of the Commonwealth.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even internal enmity as small as a split sesame seed holds ruin within it, and the liberum veto let a single objection undo a whole parliament.

tamil:
உடம்பாடு இலாதவர் வாழ்க்கை குடங்கருள்
பாம்போடு உடனுறைந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Utampaatu ilaadhavar vaazhkkai kutangarul
paampotu utanurain thatru.
meaning: Living with people who do not truly agree with you is like sharing a small hut with a snake.
elementary: Imagine sleeping in a tiny tent with a snake curled up in the corner. You could never relax, because you would always be wondering when it might bite. Living with someone who secretly dislikes you feels the same way.
university: The closing couplet gives the chapter its most vivid image. Utampaatu ilaadhavar (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) are 'those without inner agreement', people who share one's life without sharing one's mind. To live with them is kutangarul paampotu utanurainthatru (குடங்கருள் பாம்போடு உடனுறைந்தற்று), 'like dwelling together with a snake inside a kutangar'. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss kutangar as a small hut (குடிசை), and Kalaignar stresses the moment-by-moment fear of such a life. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as a dark cave, an interpretive variant. Pope's 'dwelling in a shed with snake for company' and thirukkural.net's 'share a hut with a cobra' agree on the hut reading. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “internal troubles like the fear from a lurking snake are more serious than external troubles.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya advises a king to deal with internal danger first, comparing it to a snake hidden close by.
hinduism.tie_back: The Arthashastra and the Kural use the same image: an internal enemy is a snake inside one's own dwelling.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book IX (trans. R. Shamasastry)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?”
christianity.explanation: The prophet Amos asks a rhetorical question: true companionship requires real agreement.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts hold that a shared life without inner accord cannot be safe or real.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that a believer is not stung twice from the same hole.
islam.explanation: The hadith uses the image of a snake or scorpion hole to teach vigilance against a known source of harm.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural's snake imagery and its counsel to stay alert to danger close at hand.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs values a peaceful home with little over a rich home full of conflict.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts hold that sharing a home without harmony makes life unbearable.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a seeker not find a companion who is better or equal, let him resolutely pursue a solitary course; there is no fellowship with the fool.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada advises going alone rather than living with an unsuitable companion.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats companionship without real accord as worse than solitude.

jainism.quote_or_event: “For those who are wise, to become companions of the wicked is like the nâgâ playing with the female cobra.”
jainism.explanation: The closing quatrain of the Nāladiyār's chapter on improper friendship says that for a wise person, keeping close company with the wicked is as dangerous as sporting with a cobra.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural likens living with those who do not share one's mind to sharing a small hut with a snake, and the Jain Tamil quatrain uses the same serpent image for intimacy with the ill-disposed.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār 24.10 (English translation serialised in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, do not associate with the faithless cynics; run far away from them.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, warns against close company with those cut off from God, whose influence is harmful.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares living with people who do not truly agree with you to sharing a hut with a snake, and Kabir's counsel is to keep away from such company.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Kabeer, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop's fable, a farmer finds a snake frozen with cold, warms it in his bosom, and is bitten to death once it revives.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable warns that taking a hostile nature into one's closest space invites a deadly bite.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's snake in the hut: closeness with a hostile companion is mortal danger.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, The Farmer and the Snake (Perry 176)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca advises Lucilius to avoid crowds and keep company with those who will make him better, because close association with others' vices does harm.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic letter treats one's companions as a decisive influence on peace of mind and character.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that sharing life with the wrong people costs one's safety and peace.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 7

real_life_example.event_title: The First Triumvirate of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus
real_life_example.event: Around 60 BCE Julius Caesar, Pompey and Crassus formed an unofficial and at first secret political alliance, now called the First Triumvirate, each seeking his own ends. The partnership was renewed at Luca in 56 BCE, but the death of Julia, Caesar's daughter and Pompey's wife, in 54 BCE and of Crassus in 53 BCE removed its bonds, and Pompey drew closer to Caesar's opponents in the Senate. In January 49 BCE the Senate decreed a state of emergency against Caesar, and he crossed the Rubicon, beginning a civil war in which Pompey was defeated and killed.
real_life_example.explanation: The three men shared power without sharing purpose, and their uneasy partnership ended in war between two of them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural likens living with those who lack inner agreement to sharing a hut with a snake, which describes the alliance that ended with Caesar and Pompey at war.

tamil:
ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் இகழாமை போற்றுவார்
போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை.
transliteration:
Aatruvaar aatral ikazhaamai potruvaar
potraluL ellaam thalai.
