meaning: Of all the ways a careful person can protect themselves, the first is never to look down on people who have the power to do whatever they set out to do.
elementary: Imagine a small puppy barking and nipping at a big, calm elephant. The safest thing the puppy can do is simply not tease the elephant. Being respectful to people who are strong and capable is the best way to keep yourself out of trouble.
university: The opening couplet frames the whole adhikaram as a matter of self-protection: poatruvaar (போற்றுவார், those who guard themselves) have many kinds of poatral (போற்றல், guarding, watchfulness), but the thalai (தலை, head, foremost) of them all is ikazhaamai (இகழாமை, not despising) the aatral (ஆற்றல், power, capability) of aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், those able to carry out what they undertake). Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary associated with Parimelazhagar, reads the chapter in the setting of statecraft: having discussed internal enmity (Ch. 89), Valluvar now warns the king and his men against offending two classes of the great, the mighty in worldly power and the great in spiritual power (ascetics). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both gloss aatruvaar as one able to complete a chosen task, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as those who lead and guide. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Udyoga Parva, when Krishna comes to the Kaurava court as an envoy of peace, Duryodhana and his allies scheme to seize him, underestimating him; Krishna reveals his overwhelming divine form and the plot collapses.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana treated a being of immense power as an ordinary messenger who could be bound, and the episode foreshadows the ruin that followed his contempt.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s first safeguard is exactly what Duryodhana neglected: never despise the power of those able to act.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavat-yana sub-parva), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “And we beseech you, brethren, to know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you; And to esteem them very highly in love for their work’s sake.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks the Thessalonian church to recognize and highly esteem those who labour and lead among them, precisely because of the work they do.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties respect to the capacity and accomplishment of those who do the work, though without the Kural’s warning of danger.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”
islam.explanation: The verse commands believers to give due obedience and regard to the Prophet and to those holding rightful authority.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly counsels not to slight those who hold real power, though it frames this as wise caution rather than obedience.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let the honor of your student be as dear to you as your own, and the honor of your colleague as the reverence for your teacher, and the reverence for your teacher as the reverence of heaven.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua sets up a ladder of honor in which reverence for one’s teacher approaches reverence for God.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s chapter likewise places due regard for the great among the highest of duties.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To one ever eager to revere and serve the elders, these four blessing accrue: long life and beauty, happiness and power.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that steady reverence for elders brings concrete benefits to the one who shows it.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts present respect for the great as something that protects and benefits the respectful person.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should never do anything disagreeable to the wise, neither in words nor deeds, neither openly nor secretly.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's first lecture on discipline (vinaya) makes giving no offence to the wise, in word, deed, public or private, a basic rule for anyone who wishes to prosper.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural makes not belittling the great the first of all self-protections, and the Uttarādhyayana likewise puts care never to offend the wise at the foundation of right conduct.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not slander the dust”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib, warns against looking down on the dust underfoot, since in the end it covers everyone; traditional commentary reads the dust as the humble saint.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's first safeguard is never to belittle those who have real strength, and Farid likewise warns that what seems low and easy to despise is greater than it looks.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Fareed (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Arachne boasts that her weaving surpasses that of Athena, refuses the goddess’s warning, and after the contest is transformed into a spider.
greek_mythology.explanation: A mortal who scorned the skill and power of a goddess lost her own human form as a result.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Arachne did exactly what the Kural warns against: she made light of the power of one far more capable.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now slighting is the actively entertained opinion of something as obviously of no importance. … clearly you do not think that he can do you harm, for then you would be afraid of him instead of slighting him …”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines anger as a painful impulse to revenge for an unjustified slight, and observes that we slight only those we judge unable to harm us; if we thought them capable, we would fear them instead.
philosophy.tie_back: To belittle someone is to misjudge his power, and the Kural's first safeguard is never to make that error about people who are able to act.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric, II.2, 1378b (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)

real_life_example.event_title: Japan destroys the Russian fleet at Tsushima
real_life_example.place: Tsushima Strait, between Korea and Japan
real_life_example.event: During the Russo-Japanese War, Russia sent its Baltic Fleet on a voyage of nearly 20,000 nautical miles to the Far East. In the Tsushima Strait the Japanese fleet under Admiral Togo Heihachiro crossed the Russian line of advance and destroyed or captured almost the entire Russian force. Britannica describes it as the first occasion in the modern era on which an Asian power defeated a European nation, and Russia soon accepted peace in the Treaty of Portsmouth.
real_life_example.explanation: A great European empire that had treated Japan as a minor power was decisively defeated by it, changing how the world saw Japan.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the first safeguard is never to belittle the strength of those able to carry out what they undertake, a lesson Russia learned at Tsushima.

tamil:
பெரியாரைப் பேணாது ஒழுகிற் பெரியாரால்
பேரா இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Periyaaraip penaadhu ozhukir periyaaraal
peraa itumpai tharum.
meaning: If you act without respect for great people, they will bring you trouble that never goes away.
elementary: If you keep ignoring your coach and being rude, you might find yourself benched for the whole season. Not treating important people with respect can bring trouble that doesn’t go away quickly.
university: The couplet turns on the repeated periyaar (பெரியார், the great): conduct (ozhugal, ஒழுகல்) that does not penu (பேணு, cherish, honour) the great yields, through those same great ones, peraa idumbai (பேரா இடும்பை, affliction that does not depart). The adjective peraa (from pe-, to move away) stresses permanence, which Mu. Varadarasanar renders as நீங்காத துன்பம். Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it simply as disrespect to elders or great persons, while the traditional reading behind Pope’s explanation glosses periyaar as powerful rulers. The phrase periyaaraal (by the great) shows that the harm is not mere fate but the active response of the offended party. Both sources agree on the text, including the sandhi form ஒழுகிற்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Abhijnanashakuntalam, Shakuntala, lost in thoughts of Dushyanta, fails to greet the visiting sage Durvasa, who curses her that her beloved will forget her; much of the play’s suffering follows.
hinduism.explanation: A single lapse in honouring a great ascetic brings a long chain of sorrow that is only lifted much later.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s peraa idumbai: lasting trouble that comes from the very great one who was neglected.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that opposing rightful authority brings judgment upon the one who resists.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that defying those in power returns as heavy consequence on oneself.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet or be loud to him in speech like the loudness of some of you to others, lest your deeds become worthless while you perceive not.”
islam.explanation: Believers are warned that even careless disrespect toward the Prophet can quietly nullify their good deeds.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, failing to honour the great carries a serious and lasting loss, sometimes unnoticed until too late.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet advises against even private contempt for the powerful, since word of it will reach them.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise warns that disregard for the great returns as trouble from the great themselves.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not to associate with the foolish, but to associate with the wise; and to honor those who are worthy of honor — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists honouring those worthy of honour among the highest blessings of life.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural states the reverse side: failing to honour the great invites lasting harm.
buddhism.source: Maha-mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “O lord of the fair hill-land resounding with streams! we should not, thinking they will forgive us, do what is hateful to the guiltless, for none can remove their anger when once they are provoked.”
jainism.explanation: The first quatrain of the Nāladiyār's chapter 'Against reproaching the great' warns against wronging the worthy on the assumption that they will forgive, because their anger once roused cannot be undone.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says disregard for the great brings affliction that will not leave, and the Jain Tamil quatrain names the same lasting, irremovable consequence.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār 17.1 (English translation serialised in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who slanders the Saints, O Nanak! Shall be reincarnated over and over again.”
sikhism.explanation: The shalok opening the thirteenth ashtapadi of Sukhmani Sahib says that contempt for the holy brings suffering that keeps returning, birth after birth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says disregard for the great brings lasting trouble that will not go away, and Guru Arjan likewise describes a penalty that keeps coming back.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa, as given on srigranth.org)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Agamemnon rudely dismisses Chryses, priest of Apollo, who comes to ransom his daughter; Apollo answers the priest’s prayer with a plague on the Greek camp.
greek_mythology.explanation: Insulting a man under divine protection brought sustained disaster on the whole army until the wrong was put right.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agamemnon’s contempt for a great one’s claim produced the Kural’s trouble that comes through the great.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Apology, Socrates tells the Athenian jurors that if they put him to death they will harm themselves more than him, and will not easily find another like him.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that a city which mistreats its wisest citizen injures itself most of all.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly holds that disregarding the great rebounds as lasting harm on the offender.

real_life_example.event_title: Einstein signs the letter warning Roosevelt about atomic bombs
real_life_example.place: Long Island, New York, United States
real_life_example.event: Albert Einstein left Germany after the Nazis came to power in 1933 and settled in the United States, and the Hungarian-born physicist Leo Szilard also left Germany in 1933 because of rising anti-Semitism. In 1939, fearing that Germany might build an atomic bomb, Szilard drafted a letter dated 2 August 1939 that Einstein signed, warning President Franklin D. Roosevelt that uranium fission could lead to extremely powerful bombs. Delivered by Alexander Sachs in October, the letter led Roosevelt to set up the Advisory Committee on Uranium, a step towards the Manhattan Project.
real_life_example.explanation: Scientists whom Nazi Germany had driven out played a key part in starting the effort that gave its enemies the decisive weapon of the war.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that disregarding the great brings lasting trouble at their hands, and Germany's treatment of its own scientists turned their talents to the service of its foes.

tamil:
கெடல்வேண்டின் கேளாது செய்க அடல்வேண்டின்
ஆற்று பவர்கண் இழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Ketalventin kelaadhu seyka atalventin
aatru pavarkan izhukku.
meaning: If you want to ruin yourself, act without listening to advice. If you want to be destroyed, do wrong to people who have great power.
elementary: If you poke a sleeping bear with a stick and ignore everyone shouting stop, you are asking for trouble. Valluvar says, with a wink: if you want to get hurt, go ahead and annoy the strongest one around.
university: This couplet uses irony: keDal veNDin (கெடல் வேண்டின், if you desire ruin), keLaadhu seyga (கேளாது செய்க, do it without listening), izhukku (இழுக்கு, offence, fault) toward aatrupavar (ஆற்றுபவர், those able) aDal veNDin (அடல் வேண்டின், when they wish to slay). The phrase keLaadhu is read differently: Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, takes it as not listening to the righteous dictates of law or the nīti texts, and Solomon Pappaiah likewise speaks of ignoring what the moral treatises say; Kalaignar reads it as not listening to anyone’s advice; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the first half more freely as a separate clause. The pairing keDal/aDal is a typical Valluvar sound-echo. The text is identical in both sources, which print ஆற்று பவர்கண் with the metrical split.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Yuddha Kanda, Ravana rejects the repeated counsel of his brother Vibhishana to return Sita to Rama, insults him, and drives him away, then goes on to his destruction.
hinduism.explanation: Ravana refused to listen to wise advice and persisted in offending a far mightier opponent until his kingdom fell.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s formula for ruin exactly: do not listen, and wrong the one who can destroy you.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that one who keeps refusing correction will meet sudden and irreparable ruin.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s keLaadhu, refusing to listen, is the same road to ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they will say, ‘If only we had been listening or reasoning, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze.’”
islam.explanation: The people of the Fire lament too late that they refused to listen and reason when warned.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it traces ruin to the refusal to heed.

judaism.quote_or_event: King Rehoboam rejects the counsel of the elders who served his father Solomon, follows the harsh advice of his young companions, and ten tribes break away from his kingdom.
judaism.explanation: By refusing to heed experienced counsellors and provoking the people, Rehoboam lost most of his realm.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s path to self-ruin, acting without listening, is exactly Rehoboam’s choice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever, on account of perverted views, scorns the Teaching of the Perfected Ones, the Noble and Righteous Ones — that fool, like the bamboo, produces fruits only for self destruction.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares one who scorns the noble ones to a bamboo whose own fruiting kills it.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, scorning the great is described as a self-chosen path to ruin.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Like a poisonous snake is a great sage of severe austerities, of tremendous piety and power; like a swarm of moths you will rush into a fire, if you beat a monk on his begging tour.”
jainism.explanation: When brahmin youths beat the outcaste-born monk Harikeśa, Bhadrā warns them that assaulting such a sage is like moths rushing into a flame, a ruin they bring on themselves.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that whoever wants to be ruined need only offend those able to destroy, and Bhadrā's image of moths flying into the fire is that same self-chosen destruction.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He himself must eat what he has planted.”
sikhism.explanation: In the same passage on slandering the Saint, Guru Arjan says the slanderer reaps exactly the harvest he has sown.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ironically says that whoever wants ruin need only offend the able, and Gurbani agrees that such a person brings ruin on himself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 280, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Bacchae, King Pentheus ignores the warnings of the seer Tiresias and of his grandfather Cadmus, persecutes the god Dionysus, and is destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pentheus refused all counsel and made war on a power far greater than his own.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He follows the Kural’s ironic recipe for ruin to the letter.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Plato describes a ship whose quarrelling sailors ignore and mock the true navigator, so that the voyage is ruined.
philosophy.explanation: A community that will not listen to those with real skill steers itself toward disaster.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly links ruin to refusing to heed and disrespecting the capable.

real_life_example.event_title: Iraq ignores the UN deadline to leave Kuwait
real_life_example.event: Iraqi forces invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990, and the UN Security Council at once demanded their immediate and unconditional withdrawal, then imposed sanctions. In November 1990 Resolution 678 authorized member states to use all necessary means unless Iraq withdrew by 15 January 1991. Iraq did not withdraw, and a coalition of forces from more than 30 nations began air attacks on 16-17 January and a ground offensive on 24 February that liberated Kuwait within about four days.
real_life_example.explanation: Iraq's leadership defied repeated warnings from a coalition with overwhelming power and saw its army driven out of Kuwait in days.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that one who wants ruin need only offend, without heeding anyone, those able to destroy whenever they wish, which Iraq did by ignoring every warning.

tamil:
கூற்றத்தைக் கையால் விளித்தற்றால் ஆற்றுவார்க்கு
ஆற்றாதார் இன்னா செயல்.
transliteration:
Kootraththaik kaiyaal viliththatraal aatruvaarkku
aatraadhaar innaa seyal.
meaning: When weak people harm strong people, it is like waving to Death with their own hand to come and take them.
elementary: A tiny mouse that pulls a lion’s tail is basically waving and calling, Come and get me! When someone weak picks a fight with someone much stronger, they are inviting their own trouble.
university: The image is vivid: kootram (கூற்றம், Death, Yama, the god who divides life from body) is summoned kaiyaal viLiththu (கையால் விளித்து, by beckoning with the hand). The comparison applies to aatraadhaar (ஆற்றாதார், those without power) doing innaa (இன்னா, harm) to aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், the powerful). Solomon Pappaiah specifies the three kinds of power, of wisdom, wealth and army, and adds that it is the weak who strike first; Mu. Varadarasanar stresses that Yama would come of himself anyway, so the weak only hasten it. The couplet carries forward kural 891’s key word aatruvaar, binding the chapter together. Text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Sabha Parva, Shishupala heaps insults on Krishna at Yudhishthira’s Rajasuya sacrifice; after his hundredth offence Krishna’s discus slays him.
hinduism.explanation: A ruler who kept provoking a far greater power, despite warnings, called his own death upon himself.
hinduism.tie_back: Shishupala is the Kural’s weak man beckoning Death with his own hand.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Sisupala-badha), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points to the common sense of a king who weighs his strength before going to war against a stronger foe.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural warns of what happens when the weaker side skips that reckoning and strikes anyway.

islam.quote_or_event: Surah al-Fil recalls how the army of the elephant marched to destroy the Kaaba and was struck down, made like eaten straw.
islam.explanation: A force that attacked what God protected was destroyed despite its apparent might.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, assaulting a far greater power brings one’s own destruction.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The wrath of a king is as messengers of death: but a wise man will pacify it.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says that provoking a ruler’s anger is like sending for death, and the wise avoid it.
judaism.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s own image of summoning Death by provoking the powerful.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Nidanakatha tells how Mara and his army assailed the Bodhisatta beneath the Bodhi tree with storms and weapons, and were utterly routed.
buddhism.explanation: Even a host of attackers could not prevail against one of supreme spiritual strength.
buddhism.tie_back: It shows the futility of the weaker attacking the truly mighty that the Kural describes.
buddhism.source: Jataka Nidanakatha (trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Birth Stories)

jainism.quote_or_event: “You may as well dig rocks with your nails, or eat iron with your teeth, or kick fire with your feet, as treat contemptuously a monk.”
jainism.explanation: Bhadrā lists three absurd, self-wounding acts to show how futile and harmful it is for ordinary people to scorn a monk of great spiritual power.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that when the powerless harm the powerful they are beckoning Death with their own hand, and Bhadrā's picture of kicking fire is the same harm turned back on oneself.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Slandering the Saints, one's life is cut short.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan opens his catalogue of the slanderer's fate with the shortening of life itself.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the weak who harm the strong are beckoning Death with their own hand, and Gurbani likewise links offending the holy with an early end.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The satyr Marsyas challenges Apollo to a musical contest, loses, and is flayed alive as punishment.
greek_mythology.explanation: A lesser being who challenged a god paid for it with his life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Marsyas beckoned his own doom by provoking a far stronger power, as the Kural warns.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Hence, though an obstinate fight may be made by a small force, in the end it must be captured by the larger force.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu observes that a weaker force that insists on fighting a stronger one will in the end be overwhelmed.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the strategic version of the Kural’s warning that the weak who strike the strong invite their own end.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.10 (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: The Anglo-Zanzibar War
real_life_example.event: When the Sultan of Zanzibar died on 25 August 1896, Khalid ibn Barghash seized the palace and proclaimed himself sultan against the wishes of Britain, which had declared a protectorate over Zanzibar. Britain issued an ultimatum to stand down by 9 am on 27 August, and when Khalid refused, British warships bombarded the palace. The war was over in under an hour, the shortest on record; Khalid fled to the German consulate and Britain installed its own candidate as sultan.
real_life_example.explanation: A ruler with a handful of guns defied the strongest navy in the world and lost everything in less than an hour.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when the powerless provoke the powerful it is like beckoning Death with one's own hand, as Khalid's defiance of the Royal Navy shows.

tamil:
யாண்டுச்சென்று யாண்டும் உளராகார் வெந்துப்பின்
வேந்து செறப்பட் டவர்.
transliteration:
Yaantuchchendru yaantum ularaakaar vendhuppin
vendhu serappat tavar.
meaning: People who make a fierce and powerful king angry will not survive, wherever they run to.
elementary: Playing hide-and-seek with someone who can see everywhere is no fun, because there is nowhere to hide. If you make a very powerful ruler angry, no hiding place is safe.
university: Here the great one is a vendhu (வேந்து, king) of vem-thuppu (வெந்துப்பு, fierce strength); those seRappaTTavar (செறப்பட்டவர், who have incurred his wrath, from seRu, to be angry) will be uLar aakaar (உளர் ஆகார், will not exist, will not live) yaaNDu senRu yaaNDum (wherever they go, anywhere). Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Varadarasanar agree that the offender cannot live anywhere; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads uLar aakaar more psychologically, as being unable to settle. Pope’s rendering notes they will not prosper wherever they go. The two sources agree on the text; thirukkural.net’s transliteration shows the metrical division வெந்துப்பின் / வேந்து, with the split செறப்பட் டவர் in both.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sita recalls how a crow (Kakasura) that wounded her was pursued by a grass blade Rama charged as a missile; the crow fled through the worlds, but no god would shelter it, until it returned to Rama himself for refuge.
hinduism.explanation: No place in any world offered protection from the wrath of the one it had offended.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: wherever the offender flees, there is no refuge from a mighty ruler’s anger.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (the crow episode recounted by Sita)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb.”
christianity.explanation: John’s vision shows all ranks of people trying in vain to hide from divine wrath.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, there is no hiding place from the anger of the supreme ruler.

islam.quote_or_event: “Man will say on that Day, ‘Where is the [place of] escape?’ No! There is no refuge.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment people search for an escape and find none.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the one who angers the mighty finds no place to survive.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jonah tries to flee from God’s command by sailing to Tarshish, but a storm and a great fish bring him back.
judaism.explanation: The prophet learns that there is no running away from the Sovereign he tried to evade.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s offender, Jonah found that flight to distant places does not escape a mighty ruler.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither in the sky nor in mid-ocean, nor by entering into mountain clefts, nowhere in the world is there a place where one may escape from the results of evil deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that no place in the world shelters one from the fruit of one’s evil acts.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same no-escape logic to the wrath of a mighty king.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Like as the golden-coloured serpent trembles, though in Patala, if he hear the sound of the fierce anger of the thunder in the heavens, so enemies, though they have shut themselves up in a fort difficult of access, will not be able to escape when the great are angry.”
jainism.explanation: In the Nāladiyār's chapter against reproaching the great, a serpent deep in the underworld still trembles at thunder, and so enemies cannot hide even in a strong fort once the great are angry.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says those who incur a mighty king's anger will not survive wherever they flee, and the quatrain makes the same point that no refuge holds when the great are roused.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār 17.4 (English translation serialised in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The slanderer of the Saint has no place of rest.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that one who sets himself against the holy finds no refuge anywhere.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who incur a mighty king's anger will not survive wherever they flee, and Gurbani describes the same homelessness for the enemy of the Saint.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 280, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After killing his mother, Orestes is hounded from land to land by the Furies and finds no rest until he reaches Athens.
greek_mythology.explanation: The avenging powers pursue him wherever he goes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s image of one who can find no place to live after angering a great power.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Boethius, once a high official, fell foul of King Theodoric, was imprisoned and condemned, and wrote The Consolation of Philosophy while awaiting execution.
philosophy.explanation: Even a man of great standing could not escape once he had lost the favour of a powerful king.
philosophy.tie_back: His fate illustrates the Kural’s warning about incurring a mighty ruler’s anger, though Boethius protested his innocence.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book I (author’s circumstances)

real_life_example.event_title: Rome pursues Hannibal into exile
real_life_example.place: Carthage, Ephesus and Bithynia (present-day Tunisia and Turkey)
real_life_example.event: After his defeat at Zama, Hannibal was denounced to Rome by rivals in Carthage and fled in 195 BCE to the court of Antiochus III. When Rome defeated Antiochus, one of its peace terms was that Hannibal be surrendered, and he fled again, eventually taking refuge with King Prusias of Bithynia. When the Romans demanded him there too, he took poison at Libyssa around 183 BCE rather than be handed over.
real_life_example.explanation: For more than a decade Rome's enmity followed Hannibal from one kingdom to the next until no refuge remained.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who earn the wrath of a fiercely strong power will not survive wherever they flee, which matches Hannibal's last years.

tamil:
எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்யார்
பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்தொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Eriyaal sutappatinum uyvuntaam uyyaar
periyaarp pizhaiththozhuku vaar.
meaning: A person caught in a fire may still survive, but people who keep doing wrong to the great will not escape.
elementary: Getting burnt by a campfire hurts, but you can heal. Valluvar says that hurting truly great people is even more dangerous than fire, because there may be no getting better from it.
university: The comparison is a fortiori: eri (எரி, fire) can burn a man and still uyvu uNDaam (உய்வு உண்டாம், there may be escape, survival), but uyyaar (உய்யார், they will not survive) who periyaarp pizhaiththu ozhuguvaar (பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்து ஒழுகுவார், live in offence against the great). The chapter title itself comes from this root, pizhai (பிழை, fault, offence). Pope’s explanation, reflecting the traditional commentary, glosses the fire as a forest fire and the great as devotees or ascetics, whose spiritual power is pictured as more consuming than physical flame. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the great as those of surpassing power generally. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The sixty thousand sons of King Sagara, searching for the sacrificial horse, accuse and assault the sage Kapila in his hermitage, and are reduced to ashes by his power.
hinduism.explanation: Their offence against a great sage destroyed them instantly and completely.
hinduism.tie_back: Here the sage’s power literally acts as fire, matching the Kural’s claim that offending the great is deadlier than fire.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (sargas 39-40, the sons of Sagara)

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”
christianity.explanation: The writer warns that those who scorn what is holy face a judgment more terrible than any human punishment.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural also ranks offending the great as worse than being burnt by fire.

islam.quote_or_event: When Abraham’s people cast him into a fire for opposing their idols, God commanded the fire to be coolness and safety for him, and he came out unharmed.
islam.explanation: Abraham survived literal fire because he stood with God, while those who opposed him failed.
islam.tie_back: It echoes the Kural’s point that fire can be survived, while the real danger lies in opposing the truly great.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Warm yourself before the fire of the wise, but beware of being singed by their glowing coals, for their bite is the bite of a fox, and their sting is the sting of a scorpion, and their hiss is the hiss of a serpent, and all their words are like coals of fire.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer teaches that the sages give warmth to those who approach rightly but burn those who offend them.
judaism.tie_back: This is a remarkably close parallel: the great are like fire, and offending them burns worse than flame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like fine dust thrown against the wind, evil falls back upon that fool who offends an inoffensive, pure and guiltless man.”
buddhism.explanation: Harm aimed at a pure person blows back on the one who throws it.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, offending the virtuous great is a fault from which the offender does not escape.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He is the man of great fame and might, of awful piety and power; do not injure him who cannot be injured, lest he consume you all by the fire (of his virtue).”
jainism.explanation: Bhadrā tells the youths attacking Harikeśa that a sage of such power cannot truly be harmed, and that wronging him risks being consumed by the fire of his virtue.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says a man burnt by fire may survive but those who offend the great will not escape, and the Jain verse pictures offending a sage as calling down a fire that would consume them all.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Slandering the Saints, one shall not escape the Messenger of Death.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says there is no escape for one who wrongs the holy.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one burnt by fire may survive but those who offend the great will not escape, and Gurbani uses the same language of no escape.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ajax the Lesser, hated by Athena, escapes shipwreck with Poseidon’s help, but when he boasts that he has escaped despite the gods, Poseidon splits the rock and he drowns.
greek_mythology.explanation: He survived the physical danger of the sea but not his defiance of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s man who survives fire, Ajax survived the storm but could not survive offending the great.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates recalls that the poet Stesichorus was struck blind for speaking ill of Helen and regained his sight only after composing a recantation.
philosophy.explanation: Even a famous poet suffered for defaming a revered figure, and was restored only by making amends.
philosophy.tie_back: It reflects the Kural’s warning that offending the great brings a penalty one cannot simply walk away from.

real_life_example.event_title: Galileo is tried by the Inquisition
real_life_example.event: In 1624 Pope Urban VIII allowed Galileo to write about systems of the universe on condition that the Copernican theory be treated only as a hypothesis. Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, published in 1632, did not do so, and the pope convened a commission that found he had disobeyed a 1616 injunction. Tried by the Inquisition in 1633, Galileo was condemned, the Dialogue was banned, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest near Florence until his death in 1642.
real_life_example.explanation: Even the most famous scientist in Europe could not escape the consequences of crossing the conditions set by the most powerful authority of his world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one may survive a fire but not the anger of the great one has offended, and Galileo, though spared harsher punishment, never regained his freedom.

tamil:
வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கையும் வான்பொருளும் என்னாம்
தகைமாண்ட தக்கார் செறின்.
transliteration:
Vakaimaanta vaazhkkaiyum vaanporulum ennaam
thakaimaanta thakkaar serin.
meaning: If truly great people with fine character become angry with someone, what good are that person’s grand life and great riches?
elementary: You could have the biggest toy collection in the world, but if you are mean to the kindest, wisest grown-up in town, everyone will stop trusting you. All your toys can’t fix that. Good people’s goodwill is worth more than riches.
university: Two pairs balance each other: vagai maaNDa vaazhkkai (வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கை, a life excellent in every kind) and vaan poruL (வான்பொருள், sky-high wealth) are worth ennaam (என்னாம், what will they become?) if thagai maaNDa thakkaar (தகைமாண்ட தக்கார், the worthy, distinguished in noble quality) seRin (செறின், are angered). Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, applies this to a king whose government with all its auxiliaries and untold wealth is useless before the wrath of the righteous great; Solomon Pappaiah glosses the great as those excellent in character. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the couplet differently, as saying that wealth and splendour cannot equal the richness of the worthy, showing an alternative interpretation of seRin. Both sources print the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Indra carelessly lets his elephant trample a garland given by the sage Durvasa, the sage curses him, and Indra and the gods lose their prosperity and fortune until the churning of the ocean restores it.
hinduism.explanation: All the wealth and splendour of the king of the gods vanished when he slighted a great sage.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim exactly: splendid life and vast wealth are worthless once the worthy great are angered.
hinduism.source: Vishnu Purana, Book 1, Chapter 9 (trans. H. H. Wilson)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that worldly gain is worthless if the deepest good is lost.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s question, what use are life and wealth, has the same rhetorical shape.

islam.quote_or_event: “His wealth will not avail him or that which he gained.”
islam.explanation: Said of Abu Lahab, who opposed and insulted the Prophet: his riches could not protect him.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares wealth useless to one who sets himself against the great.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb teaches that wealth gives no protection when wrath arrives.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says riches count for nothing once the worthy are angered.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who inflicts violence on those who are unarmed, and offends those who are inoffensive, will soon come upon one of these ten states: Sharp pain, or disaster, bodily injury, serious illness, or derangement of mind, trouble from the government, or grave charges, loss of relatives, or loss of wealth, or houses destroyed by ravaging fire.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the calamities, including loss of wealth and property, that befall one who offends the harmless.
buddhism.tie_back: It echoes the Kural’s point that wealth and a fine life collapse when one wrongs the virtuous.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Prostrate yourself before him for protection, you together with all of them, if you want to save your life and your property; for in his wrath he might reduce the world to ashes.”
jainism.explanation: Bhadrā urges the priest and his household to seek the offended monk's forgiveness at once, since life and property alike are forfeit if such a sage is roused.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks what good a splendid life and great wealth are once the truly worthy turn their anger on someone, and the Jain verse puts life and property at stake before an offended sage in the same way.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The slanderer of the Saint becomes miserable and poor.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that wronging the holy strips away both happiness and wealth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use a splendid life and great wealth are once the truly worthy are angered, and Gurbani says such a person is left miserable and poor.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 280, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon, a wealthy man, cuts down Demeter’s sacred oak despite warnings, and is cursed with insatiable hunger that devours all his riches.
greek_mythology.explanation: His great wealth was consumed entirely after he offended a goddess.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, prosperity proves worthless once the great are angered.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Apology, Socrates urges the Athenians to care for virtue above wealth, saying that wealth does not bring excellence, but excellence makes wealth and everything else good.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, riches have no value apart from goodness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly subordinates wealth to the regard of the virtuous.

real_life_example.event_title: Ida Tarbell's exposé and the break-up of Standard Oil
real_life_example.place: New York and Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: From November 1902 to October 1904 the journalist Ida Tarbell published a 19-part series in McClure's Magazine documenting the unfair tactics and railroad rebates through which John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil had come to control nearly all oil refining and marketing in the United States. The federal government brought an antitrust suit against the company, and in May 1911 the Supreme Court ordered the Standard Oil trust dissolved, splitting it into 34 independent companies. The Library of Congress and Britannica both credit Tarbell's reporting as a major influence on the outcome.
real_life_example.explanation: The richest business in the world could not protect itself once a determined, principled investigator had laid out the truth before the public and the courts.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use splendid wealth is once the truly worthy turn against its holder, and Standard Oil's vast fortune did not save the trust.

tamil:
குன்றன்னார் குன்ற மதிப்பின் குடியொடு
நின்றன்னார் மாய்வர் நிலத்து.
transliteration:
Kundrannaar kundra madhippin kutiyotu
nindrannaar maaivar nilaththu.
meaning: If great people, firm as mountains, are looked down on, even those who seemed firmly settled on earth will be wiped out along with their families.
elementary: Think of a mountain: it is big, steady and old. If you try to knock a mountain down, you will only hurt yourself. People who are great like mountains deserve respect, and those who treat them badly can lose everything, even their family’s good name.
university: The couplet plays on kunRu (குன்று, hill, mountain) and kunRa (குன்ற, to diminish): if kunRannaar (குன்றன்னார், those like mountains) are kunRa madhikkap paDin (thought of as diminished, slighted), or, in another reading, if they madhi (மதி, resolve) on diminishing someone, then even ninRannaar (நின்றன்னார், those who seem to stand forever) maaivar (மாய்வர், will perish) kuDiyoDu (குடியொடு, along with their lineage) nilaththu (நிலத்து, on earth). The two readings are visible in the commentaries: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as the mountain-like great resolving on destruction, while Sivayogi Sivakumar and Kalaignar take it as others belittling the great. Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, identifies the mountain-like ones as devotees. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Young Yadavas mock the visiting sages Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada by dressing Samba as a pregnant woman; the sages curse that an iron bolt will destroy the race, and the Yadava clan later perishes in fratricidal slaughter.
hinduism.explanation: A jest against great sages led to the destruction of an entire, seemingly invincible dynasty.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s image of seemingly permanent people perishing with their whole kin for slighting the mountain-like great.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, Section 1, trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “And whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus speaks of the rejected cornerstone that breaks those who stumble on it and crushes those it falls upon.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s mountain-like great similarly crush those who set themselves against them.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. And there was for him no company to aid him other than Allah, nor was he of those who [could] defend themselves.”
islam.explanation: Qarun, arrogant in his wealth and defiant toward Moses, was swallowed by the earth along with his house.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, one who seemed firmly established perished from the earth together with his household.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up, and their houses, and all the men that appertained unto Korah, and all their goods.”
judaism.explanation: Korah and his followers, who rebelled against Moses and Aaron, were swallowed by the earth with their households and possessions.
judaism.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s warning that those who belittle the great perish from the earth with their whole family.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Upali Sutta, the Buddha asks whether Upali has heard how the Dandaka, Kalinga, Mejjha and Matanga forests came to be wilderness, and Upali answers that it was through the mental anger of seers.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta recalls a tradition that whole inhabited realms were laid waste because seers were offended.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s picture of established peoples wiped from the earth by the wrath of the great.

jainism.quote_or_event: Kṛṣṇa, learning that his drunken sons and nephews had beaten the meditating ascetic Dvaipāyana almost to death, thought: “Oh! this lack of restraint on the part of these princes will be the death of the family.” Dvaipāyana, reborn as a fire-deity, later burned Dvārakā with its people.
jainism.explanation: In Hemacandra's Neminātha-caritra the Yādava clan, which seemed securely established, perishes with its city because its princes assaulted an ascetic.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that when those great as mountains are slighted, even people who seemed permanently established perish with their families, and the destruction of the Yādavas and Dvārakā is that fate told in full.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 8 (Neminātha-caritra), ch. 11, part 2 'Beating of Dvaipāyana' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The slanderer of the Saint has no heritage at all.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says the slanderer is left with no roots and no lasting line.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that slighting the mountain-like great uproots even those who seemed permanent, together with their families, and Gurbani likewise speaks of a life left with no roots.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 280, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Queen Niobe boasts that her many children make her greater than the goddess Leto; Apollo and Artemis slay her children, and she is turned to weeping stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her pride against a divine mother destroyed her entire family.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, belittling the great brings ruin upon oneself together with one’s kin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Melian Dialogue, the Melians refuse to yield to the far stronger Athenians, and the city is captured, its men killed and its women and children enslaved.
philosophy.explanation: Thucydides shows a small city destroyed as a community after defying a superior power.
philosophy.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s warning that whole households perish when the mighty are slighted, though Thucydides invites sympathy for Melos.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 5.84-116

real_life_example.event_title: The last Qing emperor abdicates
real_life_example.event: In October 1911 a revolt broke out in Wuchang (Wuhan) and spread across China, and the revolutionary leader Sun Yat-sen was chosen as provisional president of the new republic. On 12 February 1912 the six-year-old emperor Puyi was forced to abdicate, ending 267 years of Qing rule and China's imperial system of some 2,000 years. Under the settlement Sun handed the presidency to Yuan Shikai, and Puyi was allowed to live on in the palace.
real_life_example.explanation: A dynasty that had ruled China for centuries and seemed permanent fell within months once the revolution gathered strength.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even those who seem permanently established will perish together with their lineage when the mountain-like great resolve against them, and the Qing dynasty fell along with the imperial system itself.

tamil:
ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின் இடைமுரிந்து
வேந்தனும் வேந்து கெடும்.
transliteration:
Endhiya kolkaiyaar seerin itaimurindhu
vendhanum vendhu ketum.
meaning: When people with high ideals rise up in anger, even a king will be broken in the middle of his rule and lose his kingdom.
elementary: Imagine a team captain who bullies the fairest, most honest player. When the whole team sees it and stands with that honest player, the captain loses the job. Even powerful people can fall if they anger those who live by high principles.
university: Eendhiya koLgaiyaar (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார்) are those who bear aloft high principles or vows; if they seeRin (சீறின், flare up in anger), even the vendhan (வேந்தன், king) will iDai murindhu (இடை முரிந்து, be broken midway) and vendhu keDum (வேந்து கெடும், his kingship will perish). Pope’s explanation glosses the king as Indra and the great as those of exalted vows, reflecting the traditional commentary’s allusion to Nahusha, who was cast down from Indra’s throne by the curse of the sage Agastya. Modern commentators generalize: Solomon Pappaiah speaks of a ruler losing office midway, and Kalaignar reads it politically as tyranny collapsing when principled people rise up. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Nahusha, raised to the throne of Indra, grows arrogant, makes the great sages carry his palanquin, and kicks Agastya; the sage’s curse hurls him from heaven to earth as a serpent.
hinduism.explanation: A king at the summit of power fell in the middle of his reign because he offended a sage of great vows.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the story traditionally linked to this very couplet: even the king of the gods is broken midway when the great flare up.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Sections XI-XVII (Nahusha), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.”
christianity.explanation: Mary’s song praises God who topples the powerful from their thrones.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise says even kings can be brought down from their seats.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will. You honor whom You will and You humble whom You will.’”
islam.explanation: The verse affirms that kingship is given and withdrawn by God.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, no king’s rule is so secure that it cannot be taken away.

judaism.quote_or_event: King Uzziah, grown proud, enters the Temple to burn incense, defying the priests who withstand him; he is struck with leprosy while still raging, and lives apart while his son governs.
judaism.explanation: A powerful and successful king was cut off from rule after defying those consecrated to holy service.
judaism.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s king who is broken midway when he opposes those of high vows.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sarabhanga Jataka, King Dandaki insults the ascetic Kisavaccha, and his kingdom is destroyed, becoming the wilderness later known as the Dandaka forest.
buddhism.explanation: A ruling king lost his realm because he offended an ascetic.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s warning that a king falls when those of lofty vows are provoked.
buddhism.source: Jataka 522, Sarabhanga Jataka (trans. ed. E. B. Cowell)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Enough of this conciliatory talk of yours, Kṛṣṇa. Beaten by your sons, I have made a nidāna—to burn Dvārakā with its people. There is no escape from that, except of you.”
jainism.explanation: When Kṛṣṇa, king of Dvārakā, begs the injured ascetic for pardon, Dvaipāyana refuses and vows to burn the royal city, and Kṛṣṇa loses his capital and kingdom.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that when those who hold high vows flare up in anger even a king is broken midway and loses his kingdom, and Kṛṣṇa, unable to appease an angered ascetic, sees his city destroyed.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 8 (Neminātha-caritra), ch. 11, part 2 (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The slanderer of the Saint breaks down mid-way.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says the slanderer is broken in mid-course, and elsewhere in the same passage that he has no kingdom.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that when those of lofty principle flare up, even a king is broken midway and loses his kingdom, and Gurbani uses the same image of breaking midway.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 280, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Diomedes recalls how Lycurgus, king of the Edonians, attacked the nurses of the young Dionysus; Zeus blinded him and he did not live long, hated by all the gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: A king who assaulted the sacred was cut down in the midst of his life and rule.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, even a king is broken midway when he provokes those under divine protection.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes in Politics V that many monarchies have been overthrown because of insult and contempt shown toward subjects, which provoke attacks on the ruler.
philosophy.explanation: Rulers who treat people with outrage invite their own overthrow.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly says that even kings fall when the high-minded are provoked to anger.

real_life_example.event_title: The Seven Bishops are acquitted
real_life_example.event: In 1688 King James II ordered his Declaration of Indulgence to be read in churches, and the Archbishop of Canterbury and six other bishops petitioned him to withdraw the order, arguing that the royal power to suspend laws on which it rested was illegal. The king had them imprisoned in the Tower and tried for seditious libel, but on 30 June 1688 a jury acquitted them amid public celebration. That same day seven leading Englishmen invited William of Orange to intervene, and by the end of the year William had landed and James had fled the country.
real_life_example.explanation: By prosecuting the bishops, the king turned respected men of principle into public heroes and lost the confidence of the nation within months.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when those of lofty principle are roused, even a king is broken midway and loses his kingdom, which describes James II's fall in 1688.

tamil:
இறந்தமைந்த சார்புடையர் ஆயினும் உய்யார்
சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார் செறின்.
transliteration:
Irandhamaindha saarputaiyar aayinum uyyaar
sirandhamaindha seeraar serin.
meaning: Even people with endless support and powerful friends cannot escape if truly great people become angry with them.
elementary: Having lots of friends to stick up for you is great, but if you do something really wrong to a truly good and respected person, even all those friends can’t save you. Being respectful is better protection than having a big gang.
university: The final couplet sets iRandhu amaindha saarbu (இறந்தமைந்த சார்பு, supports exceeding all measure, from iRa, to go beyond) against siRandhu amaindha seeraar (சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார், those whose glory is excellently formed). The verb uyyaar (உய்யார், they will not survive) echoes kural 896, and seRin (செறின், if angered) echoes 895 and 897, rounding off the chapter. Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, glosses the great here as the noble whose penance is boundless, so the chapter ends where it began, with the two kinds of greatness, worldly and spiritual. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads iRandhamaindha as like the dead, that is renunciants, a markedly different interpretation of the first phrase. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Vishvamitra, with his whole army, tries to seize the wish-granting cow of the sage Vasishtha; Vasishtha’s spiritual power destroys his forces and sons, and the king concludes that a warrior’s might is nothing beside a sage’s power.
hinduism.explanation: All the king’s armies and resources could not prevail against the anger of a great sage.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s conclusion: boundless support does not save one who angers the truly great.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (sargas 52-56, Vishvamitra and Vasishtha)

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist declares that neither great armies nor personal strength can secure deliverance.
christianity.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s own claim that vast support cannot save the offender.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Day when there will not benefit [anyone] wealth or children”
islam.explanation: Abraham’s prayer describes the Day when the usual supports of wealth and family avail nothing.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, one’s supports, however great, cannot save one in the decisive hour.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah warns against trusting wisdom, might or riches as one’s security.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly teaches that worldly supports offer no safety against the anger of the great.

buddhism.quote_or_event: According to the Dhammapada Commentary, Devadatta, despite the backing of the powerful prince Ajatasattu, plotted repeatedly against the Buddha and was finally swallowed by the earth.
buddhism.explanation: Royal patronage could not save one who set himself against the Buddha.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, mighty allies do not protect one who offends the truly great.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary, story for verse 17 (trans. E. W. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends)

jainism.quote_or_event: “What is this delusion of yours? You were told earlier, indeed, that there was no escape for any one here, except you two.”
jainism.explanation: As Dvārakā burns, Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa, the mightiest heroes of their age, haul their parents' chariot to the gate by their own strength, but the fire-god Dvaipāyana tells them no one else can be saved.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says that even those with boundless support and powerful allies cannot escape once the truly great are angered, and the Yādavas, protected by Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma themselves, still perish.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 8 (Neminātha-caritra), ch. 11, part 2 (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The slanderer of the Saint cannot be saved by anyone else.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says no outside protector can rescue one who sets himself against the holy, though the same verse adds that the Saint himself may forgive.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says even those with boundless support and powerful allies will not survive if the truly great are angered, and Gurbani likewise says no other protector can save them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 280, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Capaneus, one of the Seven against Thebes, boasts that not even Zeus can stop him scaling the walls, and is struck down by Zeus’s thunderbolt despite the great army around him.
greek_mythology.explanation: His boast against a supreme power destroyed him in the midst of a mighty host.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s point that great allies do not save one who provokes the great.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In a note on Sun Tzu, the commentator Li Ch’uan recalls Fu Chien, who was warned not to despise his enemy but boasted of a million troops, and was soon disastrously routed at the Fei River.
philosophy.explanation: A ruler confident in vast forces fell after scorning a capable opponent.
philosophy.tie_back: This joins the Kural’s last couplet to its first: despising the able cannot be redeemed by numbers.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.18, with Li Ch’uan’s commentary (trans. Lionel Giles)

real_life_example.event_title: Syngman Rhee resigns after the April Revolution
real_life_example.event: After government claims that South Korea's March 1960 election had given President Syngman Rhee more than 90 percent of the vote, student protests against electoral fraud spread across the country, culminating in mass demonstrations on 19 April. On 25 April university professors marched in Seoul in support of the students. Under pressure that included a unanimous vote of the National Assembly and the views of the United States government, Rhee resigned on 27 April 1960 and went into exile in Hawaii.
real_life_example.explanation: A president who controlled the police, the ruling party and a powerful foreign alliance could not survive once students and their teachers stood together against him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even those with boundless support cannot escape when people of outstanding worth are roused against them, and Rhee's support melted away in weeks.

tamil:
மனைவிழைவார் மாண்பயன் எய்தார் வினைவிழைவார்
வேண்டாப் பொருளும் அது.
transliteration:
Manaivizhaivaar maanpayan eydhaar vinaivizhaivaar
ventaap porulum adhu.
meaning: Men who are ruled by desire for their wives miss the greatest reward in life. People who want to get real work done stay away from this very habit.
elementary: Imagine a team captain who stops practising because he only wants to hang out at home all day. He may be comfortable, but the team never wins. People who want to do big things keep their comfort in balance with their work.
university: The chapter title penvazhich seral (பெண்வழிச் சேறல்) literally means 'going by a woman's way', and Parimelazhagar frames the whole chapter as advice to a ruler or man of affairs within the Porul (polity) section, placed among other vices to be avoided (chapters 92-94 on wanton women, drink and gambling). In this opening couplet manai-vizhaivaar (மனைவிழைவார், those who crave the wife or household pleasure) fail to reach maan-payan (மாண்பயன், the excellent fruit), which Parimelazhagar glosses as aram (virtue), while vinai-vizhaivaar (வினைவிழைவார், those who desire action) reject such indulgence as a hindrance to porul (wealth-making). Textual note: ytamizh and thirukkural.net read the third word as vinaivizhaiyaar (வினைவிழையார், 'those who do not desire action'), while thirukkural.com, kuraltheni.com and Parimelazhagar's own gloss read vinaivizhaivaar; we follow the latter. Also note that thirukkural.com wrongly prints Kalaignar's gloss for Kural 801 under this verse. Modern critics point out that the chapter assumes a male, elite reader and a patriarchal household; many contemporary readers (including Mu. Varadarasanar's 'considering domestic comfort paramount') take its target to be infatuation and neglect of duty rather than women as such, a reading supported by Valluvar's high praise of the wife in chapter 6 (வாழ்க்கைத் துணைநலம்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces how fixing the mind on pleasing objects grows into attachment and craving that cloud judgment.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's doting husband is a case of this chain: absorption in domestic pleasure crowds out the higher aim.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But he that is married careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please his wife.”
christianity.explanation: Paul observes that marriage naturally turns a man's attention toward pleasing his spouse and worldly concerns, as against undivided devotion to God.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it notes that preoccupation with pleasing a wife can draw energy away from a higher calling, though Paul does not condemn marriage.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, let not your wealth and your children divert you from the remembrance of Allāh. And whoever does that - then those are the losers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an warns that even legitimate attachments to family and property can distract from the highest purpose.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns that domestic attachment can cost a person the 'excellent fruit' of life.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Torah exempts a newly married man from military service and public duties for one year so that he may stay home and bring joy to his wife.
judaism.explanation: Jewish law sanctifies a period of devoted attention to a new spouse, but bounds it in time before public obligations resume.
judaism.tie_back: This offers a counterpoint: devotion to a wife is honored, yet the Kural's concern is with such devotion swallowing a person's duties permanently.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “That is not a strong fetter, the wise say, which is made of iron, wood or hemp. But the infatuation and longing for jewels and ornaments, children and wives — that, they say, is a far stronger fetter, which pulls one downward and, though seemingly loose, is hard to remove.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada calls infatuation with family and possessions a fetter stronger than any chain.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's doting husband is held by just such a 'loose but strong' fetter that keeps him from higher attainment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “For a fool who is bound in the fetters of sensuality will be subject to delusion again and again.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga's lecture on women says that a man bound by sensual attachment keeps falling back into delusion (moha), which in Jain terms binds fresh karma and blocks liberation.
jainism.tie_back: Like Kural 901, it says that a man given over to desire for a woman loses life's highest goal, which for Jainism is moksha.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In this world, I have seen love to be false. Whether they are spouses or friends, all are concerned only with their own happiness.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur warns that attachment (moh) to spouse and friends cannot be life's goal, since worldly ties are bound up with self-interest and do not lead to God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that doting on a wife costs a man life's highest fruit; Gurbani agrees that attachment can pull one from the highest aim, but it applies this to every worldly tie and to both partners.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 536, Raag Dayv Gandhaaree, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus lingers a full year feasting in Circe's palace until his crew remind him of home and he resumes his journey.
greek_mythology.explanation: The hero's comfortable stay with an enchantress delays his true task until his companions rouse him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, absorption in pleasure with a woman stalls the man of action until he recalls his purpose.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle analyzes akrasia, the condition of the person who knows what is best but is overcome by desire for pleasure and acts against it.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, the incontinent person's reason is overpowered by appetite, so his choices fail his own better judgment.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's man who chooses domestic pleasure over his duties fits Aristotle's portrait of a will weakened by pleasure.

real_life_example.event_title: Edward VIII gives up the throne to marry Wallis Simpson
real_life_example.place: Fort Belvedere and London, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: Edward VIII succeeded to the throne in January 1936 and made clear that he intended to marry Wallis Simpson, an American who had divorced twice and who the government held would not be acceptable as queen. After Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin rejected a proposed morganatic marriage, Edward signed an Instrument of Abdication on 10 December 1936, witnessed by his three brothers, and it took legal effect the next day. In a radio broadcast he said he could not carry the burden of kingship without the help and support of the woman he loved, and he married her in France in 1937.
real_life_example.explanation: A reigning monarch gave up the highest office in the land rather than give up the woman he wished to marry.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those wholly given over to desire for a wife miss life's highest fruit, while those intent on their duties avoid that path; Edward chose the marriage over the crown.

tamil:
பேணாது பெண்விழைவான் ஆக்கம் பெரியதோர்
நாணாக நாணுத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Penaadhu penvizhaivaan aakkam periyadhor
naanaaka naanuth tharum.
meaning: If a man forgets his duties and lives only for his desire for his wife, whatever success he has will bring him great shame that everyone can see.
elementary: If a class president stops doing the job and just lets his best friend decide everything, the whole class feels let down, and he ends up embarrassed too. Holding a job means doing it yourself.
university: Penaadhu (பேணாது, 'without guarding/caring for') is read by Parimelazhagar as neglecting one's own aanmai (ஆண்மை, manliness, i.e. capacity for independent action), while pen-vizhaivaan (பெண்விழைவான்) is one who desires the 'femininity' of his wife. The aakkam (ஆக்கம், prosperity) he holds becomes a periyadhor naan (பெரியதோர் நாண், a great shame) first for men generally and then for himself; Parimelazhagar explains that because the wife effectively controls the giving and enjoyment of that wealth, the public sees the man's agency as transferred to her. Manakkudavar reads penaadhu as neglecting aram and porul (virtue and wealth). Kalaignar's modern gloss shifts the emphasis to a man who abandons his principles to chase a woman, illustrating the trend among twentieth-century commentators to recast the chapter as a critique of infatuation rather than of women's agency. The text is uniform across ytamizh, thirukkural.net, thirukkural.com and kuraltheni. Contemporary critics note that the verse's notion of 'shame to all men' reflects a gendered honour code of its era.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Dasharatha, bound by boons he had granted his beloved queen Kaikeyi, is compelled to exile his heir Rama, to the dismay of his court and people.
hinduism.explanation: A king's indulgence of a favoured queen leads him to act against his own judgment and his kingdom's welfare.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural warns, the king's power becomes a source of grief and public dismay when it is steered by private attachment.

christianity.quote_or_event: King Lemuel records his mother's counsel not to give his strength to women nor his ways to that which destroys kings.
christianity.explanation: A queen mother advises her royal son that dissipated attachments ruin rulers.
christianity.tie_back: The same concern as the Kural's address to the ruler; notably, here the warning itself comes from a woman.

islam.quote_or_event: “Beautified for people is the love of that which they desire - of women and sons, heaped-up sums of gold and silver, fine branded horses, and cattle and tilled land. That is the enjoyment of worldly life, but Allāh has with Him the best return.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an lists attractions of worldly life that people naturally love, while pointing to a higher return.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's man is captured by one such attraction to the point of neglecting his responsibilities.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.”
judaism.explanation: The narrator of Kings attributes Solomon's decline to his attachment to his many foreign wives.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a powerful man's attachment to his wives leads to the loss of his integrity and standing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are lust-infatuated fall back into the swirling current (of samsara) like a spider on its self-spun web.”
buddhism.explanation: Infatuation traps a person in a web of his own making.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's man is likewise caught in a predicament he spun himself, ending in shame.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Getting up in the night they lull the baby asleep like nurses; and though they are ashamed of themselves, they wash the clothes like washermen.”
jainism.explanation: The text pictures a man who fell for a woman and now does every household chore, aware of his own shame but unable to stop.
jainism.tie_back: This matches Kural 902, where a man who neglects his own standing out of desire for his wife ends up publicly ashamed.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.2.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O sexual desire, you lead the mortals to hell; you make them wander in reincarnation through countless species.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan addresses kaam (lust), one of the five thieves, as a force that drags people away from their true purpose.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the man who drops his duties out of desire for his wife brings shame on himself, and Gurbani likewise treats being ruled by desire as a downfall.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sehskritee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hector rebukes his brother Paris, who prefers Helen's chamber to the battlefield, as a disgrace to his family and city.
greek_mythology.explanation: Paris's devotion to Helen while his people fight makes him an object of reproach even to his own brother.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's picture of a man whose attachment brings shame on himself and others.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch portrays Mark Antony neglecting command and statecraft for Cleopatra, culminating in his flight after her at Actium.
philosophy.explanation: The moralist-biographer presents Antony as a capable man whose judgment was captured by passion.
philosophy.tie_back: Antony is a classical example of the Kural's warning that power steered by attachment ends in shame.

real_life_example.event_title: Nur Jahan's name appears on Mughal coins
real_life_example.event: The Mughal emperor Jahangir married Nur Jahan in 1611, and in the later years of his reign she took charge of many of his duties and issued farmans, or sovereign orders, in her own name. She was the only Mughal queen to have coins issued in her name, and museum and reference sources describe her as the power behind the throne while Jahangir was frequently incapacitated.
real_life_example.explanation: The emperor's wealth and authority came to be seen, even on the coinage, as directed by his wife rather than by himself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the prosperity of a man who abandons his own responsibilities to his wife becomes a public matter of shame, and Nur Jahan's coins made that transfer of agency visible across the empire.

tamil:
இல்லாள்கண் தாழ்ந்த இயல்பின்மை எஞ்ஞான்றும்
நல்லாருள் நாணுத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Illaalkan thaazhndha iyalpinmai egngnaandrum
nallaarul naanuth tharum.
meaning: A man who always gives in and bows low to his wife will feel ashamed whenever he is among good people.
elementary: If you are always too scared to say what you think, even to someone you love, you may feel awkward around friends who speak up honestly. Love works best when both people can speak freely.
