university: Iyalpinmai (இயல்பின்மை) means 'that which is not natural', and Parimelazhagar glosses the whole phrase as the fear (achcham) that makes a man stoop (thaazh) before his wife; within his patriarchal frame, it is 'unnatural' because he expects the wife to be the deferential one. He adds that when a husband is so cowed, no one guides the household and every fault follows, so he is ashamed among the nallaar (நல்லார், the good) at all times (எஞ்ஞான்றும்). Manakkudavar reads it simply as the ruinous habit of stooping to the wife. Kalaignar narrows it to a husband who fails to correct a wife lacking good character, and Solomon Pappaiah stresses fear, showing modern commentators softening the verse toward a critique of timidity. The text is identical in all four sources consulted. Modern readers rightly note that the assumption that deference is natural only for wives is a historical norm, not a universal truth, while the verse's underlying point about a fear-driven partnership remains discussable.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa ends the Raghu dynasty's story with King Agnivarna, who abandons governance for pleasures in the inner palace and dies of his excesses, leaving a pregnant queen to rule.
hinduism.explanation: The epic poet presents the last king's absorption in the women's quarters as the ruin of a glorious line.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's shame before the good is mirrored in the disgrace of a king who neglected his realm for private pleasure.

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs says it is better to live in a corner of the housetop than to share a wide house with a quarrelsome woman.
christianity.explanation: Wisdom literature acknowledges the misery of a household dominated by strife.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural it recognizes an unhealthy domestic dynamic, though it advises distance rather than warning of shame.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon and overlook and forgive - then indeed, Allāh is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an cautions that family members can pull a believer away from what is right, while urging forgiveness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns that yielding to a spouse against one's better judgment brings harm.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Queen Vashti refuses King Ahasuerus's summons, his counsellors fear that all wives will despise their husbands, and a decree is sent that every man should rule his own house.
judaism.explanation: The court treats one queen's independence as a threat to every husband's honour.
judaism.tie_back: The same anxiety about a husband's public standing drives the Kural; many readers find the Esther episode deliberately satirical of that anxiety.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes seven kinds of wives to Anathapindika's daughter-in-law, from a 'murderous' wife to a 'mother-like', 'sister-like' or 'friend-like' wife, judging each by conduct.
buddhism.explanation: Rather than condemning deference either way, the Buddha evaluates marital relationships by kindness and good character.
buddhism.tie_back: This offers a counterpoint: the problem in the Kural is better understood as an unhealthy relationship than as any submission to a wife as such.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.59 (Bhariya Sutta; numbered 7.63 in some editions)

jainism.quote_or_event: “When a monk breaks the law, dotes (on a woman), and is absorbed by that passion, she afterwards scolds him, lifts her foot, and tramples on his head.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga shows what doting leads to: the infatuated man ends up humbled and dominated by the woman he gave way to.
jainism.tie_back: It closely matches Kural 903's 'unnatural' stooping in fear before one's wife, which shames a man among good people.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.2.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So why call her bad? From her, kings are born.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak rejects the low view of women common in his time, pointing out that every person, kings included, is born of woman.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls a husband's deference to his wife unnatural and shameful; Guru Nanak's verse offers a counterpoint, refusing to treat women as inferior.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Xenophon has Socrates explain that he lives with the famously difficult Xanthippe as a horseman trains on a spirited horse, to learn to deal with all people.
greek_mythology.explanation: Socrates treats patience with a strong-willed wife as training in self-mastery rather than as disgrace.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A counterpoint to the Kural: what one tradition calls shameful submission another frames as composure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle criticizes Sparta, arguing that much of its affairs were managed by women and that this contributed to the state's love of wealth and decline.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle views women's influence over men in public life as a structural weakness of a polity.
philosophy.tie_back: This parallels the Kural's political frame, while modern scholars treat Aristotle's account as a product of his gender theory.

real_life_example.event_title: Empress Alexandra directs Russia's government while Nicholas II is at the front
real_life_example.event: In August-September 1915 Tsar Nicholas II took personal command of the Russian army and left his wife, Empress Alexandra, in charge of internal affairs, with Grigory Rasputin as her closest adviser. Over the following months many capable ministers were dismissed and replaced in rapid succession, a pattern mocked as ministerial leapfrog, and the administration was widely discredited. By early 1917 most Russians had lost faith in the tsarist regime.
real_life_example.explanation: The tsar's deference to his wife in affairs of state damaged his standing among the very people whose support his government needed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the habit of yielding to one's wife will make a man ashamed before good people, and Nicholas's reliance on Alexandra badly hurt his reputation among Russia's leaders and public.

tamil:
மனையாளை அஞ்சும் மறுமையி லாளன்
வினையாண்மை வீறெய்த லின்று.
transliteration:
Manaiyaalai anjum marumaiyi laalan
vinaiyaanmai veereydha lindru.
meaning: A man who is afraid of his wife loses the good that leads to a happy next life. Even if he is skilled at his work, it will never win him praise.
elementary: A painter who is too afraid of anyone's opinion to paint what he really sees will never make a great painting. Fear holds back good work.
university: Marumai-ilaalan (மறுமையிலாளன்) means 'one without (merit for) the next world'; Parimelazhagar explains that such a man cannot perform the duties of the householder (illaram) properly and so loses the reward of the hereafter. Vinai-aanmai (வினையாண்மை, the capacity to direct undertakings) may exist, but it will not attain veeru (வீறு, distinction, acclaim) among the good, because one who lacks his own nature cannot bring work to completion. Manakkudavar adds that this verse means such a man will not create wealth. Textual note: ytamizh, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com divide the line as 'வீறெய்த லின்று' while kuraltheni prints 'வீறெய்தல் இன்று'; this is a difference of word-spacing (சீர் division vs. word division), not wording. Kalaignar gives a distinctive modern reading, taking the man as one who fears to undertake married life at all, a reinterpretation that avoids the gendered fear. Contemporary critics observe that the verse links domestic authority to public efficacy in a way typical of premodern political ethics.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Shantanu, smitten by Satyavati, accepts her father's condition that her sons inherit the throne, leading his heir Devavrata to renounce kingship and marriage forever as Bhishma.
hinduism.explanation: A king's infatuation leads him to a concession with far-reaching consequences for the dynasty.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural warns, a ruler's judgment bent by attachment compromises his work and legacy.

christianity.quote_or_event: Pilate's wife sends him a message during Jesus' trial urging him to have nothing to do with that just man, but Pilate yields to the crowd instead.
christianity.explanation: Here the wife gives the righteous counsel and the husband's failure is in not heeding her.
christianity.tie_back: A counterpoint to the Kural: in this story a man's worth would have been served by listening to his wife.

islam.quote_or_event: “Your wealth and your children are but a trial, and Allāh has with Him a great reward.”
islam.explanation: Family and possessions are described as tests whose handling determines one's reward with God.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly ties a man's handling of domestic life to his merit in the next world.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But there was none like unto Ahab, which did sell himself to work wickedness in the sight of the LORD, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up.”
judaism.explanation: The book of Kings presents Ahab as a king whose deeds were driven by his wife's instigation.
judaism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's view that a ruler led by his wife forfeits a good name and a good hereafter.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “For a person tormented by evil thoughts, who is passion-dominated and given to the pursuit of pleasure, his craving steadily grows. He makes the fetter strong, indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: Domination by passion strengthens the bonds that hold one back.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's man, dominated within his household, similarly cannot achieve distinction.

jainism.quote_or_event: “His father and mother, his children and wife who claim him, will admonish him: 'See, you are our supporter; care not for the next world in order to support us.'”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns that family, wife included, can pull a person away from the merit and discipline that shape his next existence.
jainism.tie_back: Kural 904 says the man ruled by fear of his wife becomes marumai-ilaalan, 'one without the next world', and this verse shows that same pull from the Jain side.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.2.1.19 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “While laughing, playing, dressing and eating, he is liberated.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that liberation is reached within ordinary household life, by one who has met the True Guru, not by leaving it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural fears that a man ruled by his wife fails as a householder and loses the merit of the next world; Sikhism agrees the household is where one earns spiritual reward, though it does not make the wife the threat.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The seer Amphiaraus foresees his death in the war of the Seven against Thebes, but his wife Eriphyle, bribed with the necklace of Harmonia, compels him to go.
greek_mythology.explanation: Bound by an agreement to abide by his wife's decision, a wise man is forced into a doomed undertaking.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's man whose actions are governed by his wife cannot bring his work to a good end.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus begins his handbook by distinguishing what is in our power from what is not, warning that one who fears what others control becomes a slave.
philosophy.explanation: Freedom, for the Stoic, lies in governing one's own judgments rather than being ruled by fear of others.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's fearful husband lacks the inner freedom that the Stoics thought necessary for good action.

real_life_example.event_title: Mark Antony follows Cleopatra out of the Battle of Actium
real_life_example.place: Actium, off the west coast of Greece
real_life_example.event: At the naval Battle of Actium, Mark Antony and Cleopatra's fleet fought Octavian's forces under Agrippa. During the battle Cleopatra withdrew with her Egyptian ships, and Antony broke away with a small number of ships and followed her. The rest of his fleet surrendered to Octavian, and his land army surrendered about a week later, leaving Octavian master of the Roman world.
real_life_example.explanation: One of Rome's most experienced generals abandoned his own fleet and army in mid-battle to follow his partner, and his military reputation never recovered.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a man ruled by his wife will not win acclaim for his work however capable he is, and Antony's long record as a commander was overshadowed by his departure from Actium.

tamil:
இல்லாளை அஞ்சுவான் அஞ்சுமற் றெஞ்ஞான்றும்
நல்லார்க்கு நல்ல செயல்.
transliteration:
Illaalai anjuvaan anjumat regngnaandrum
nallaarkku nalla seyal.
meaning: A man who is afraid of his wife will always be afraid even to do good things for good people.
elementary: If you are scared to share your snack with a hungry classmate because someone might be cross with you, fear is stopping you from being kind. Kindness needs a little courage.
university: Parimelazhagar glosses nallaar (நல்லார், the good) as gods, ascetics, the wise, one's two elders (parents) and worthy guests, and nalla seyal (நல்ல செயல்) as giving them what they need; even when the wealth is his own earning, the fearful husband hesitates. He supports the reading with a parallel from the Jain Tamil epic Civaka Cintamani (மண்மகள் 217): 'illaalai anji virunthin mugam kondra nenjin pullaalan', a man who, fearing his wife, turned away the face of a guest. Manakkudavar sums the verse as meaning such a man cannot practise aram (virtue). Kalaignar inverts the sense, reading that a man anxious not to err in doing good will heed a watchful wife, a strikingly egalitarian modern reinterpretation. The text is identical across the four sources. Critics note that the verse presumes hospitality and charity are the husband's prerogative, a presumption that modern readers can retain as a call to generosity without its gendered frame.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Taittiriya Upanishad's parting instruction to students includes treating mother, father, teacher and guest as divine.
hinduism.explanation: Honouring and serving guests and elders is part of the householder's sacred duty.
hinduism.tie_back: The 'good deeds to the good' that the fearful husband neglects are precisely these duties of hospitality and reverence.

christianity.quote_or_event: Herod, who feared John the Baptist as a just and holy man, has him beheaded after a promise made at a banquet, at the request of Herodias through her daughter, though he was exceedingly sorry.
christianity.explanation: A ruler who respected a righteous man nonetheless harms him rather than lose face and displease his wife's faction.
christianity.tie_back: This is close to the Kural: fear of displeasing those at home overrides doing right by the good.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an condemns Abu Lahab together with his wife, the 'carrier of firewood', for their joint hostility to the Prophet.
islam.explanation: A husband and wife are portrayed as reinforcing each other in opposing a righteous messenger.
islam.tie_back: Loosely parallels the Kural's concern that domestic influence can turn a man against the good.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Job's wife urges him to curse God and die, Job answers that she speaks foolishly, and he does not sin with his lips.
judaism.explanation: Job holds to integrity even against the counsel of his closest companion.
judaism.tie_back: Job is the opposite of the Kural's fearful husband: he will not let domestic pressure divert him from righteousness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Vessantara Jataka, Prince Vessantara gives away everything in perfect generosity, and his wife Maddi supports and shares his gifts and exile.
buddhism.explanation: Husband and wife together embody unstinting generosity.
buddhism.tie_back: A counterpoint to the Kural: a spouse can strengthen rather than inhibit good deeds to others.

jainism.quote_or_event: Among Hemachandra's thirty-five qualities of an ideal Jain householder is 'Yathavat atithau sadhau dine cha pratipatti-krt', rendered by Sangave as diligent in helping ascetics, the righteous and the needy. It goes with the lay vow of atithi-samvibhaga, sharing one's food with ascetics.
jainism.explanation: In Jainism, a householder is expected to look after ascetics, good people and guests freely and as a regular duty.
jainism.tie_back: Kural 905 condemns the wife-fearing man who hesitates to do good to good people (the commentator lists ascetics and guests), which is exactly the duty Hemachandra's householder must not neglect.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Yogashastra, list of 35 householder qualities, no. 19, as rendered in V.A. Sangave, 'Jaina ethics' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the true way as honest work (kirat karni) and sharing its fruits with others (vand chhakna).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural regrets a man too afraid of his wife to give from his own earnings to the deserving; for Sikhs, sharing what one honestly earns is a basic duty.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Vaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The aged couple Baucis and Philemon together welcome disguised gods into their humble home and are rewarded.
greek_mythology.explanation: A husband and wife share in generous hospitality toward strangers.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This shows the alternative to the Kural's scenario: a marriage in which good deeds to the worthy are done jointly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes liberality as the virtue of giving the right amounts to the right people at the right time, with pleasure rather than pain.
philosophy.explanation: A generous person gives readily and gladly to worthy recipients.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's fearful husband lacks this readiness, giving to the good with fear rather than gladness.

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Gaozong's senior statesmen are removed after Wu Zetian becomes empress
real_life_example.event: In 655 the Tang emperor Gaozong had his empress Wang deposed and appointed Wu Zetian in her place, against the opposition of senior court officials who objected that she did not come from one of the great noble families. Within a few years those officials were dismissed, exiled or put to death, among them the emperor's own uncle Zhangsun Wuji, who had been one of the dynasty's leading statesmen. By 660 the empress had triumphed over all her opponents.
real_life_example.explanation: The emperor did not protect the experienced counsellors who had served his family, once they stood in the way of his wife.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a man who fears his wife will be afraid even to do good to good people, and Gaozong's failure to shield his loyal elder statesmen illustrates that loss of nerve.

tamil:
இமையாரின் வாழினும் பாடிலரே இல்லாள்
அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சு பவர்.
transliteration:
Imaiyaarin vaazhinum paatilare illaal
amaiyaardhol anju pavar.
meaning: Even if they live as grandly as the gods, men who fear their wife's slender, bamboo-like arms have no real honour.
elementary: A superhero with amazing powers is not much of a hero if he is too scared to act. What makes someone admirable is courage, not just strength or riches.
university: Imaiyaar (இமையார், 'the unblinking ones') is a classical Tamil epithet for the gods; paatu (பாடு) here means dignity or worth, and paatilar those lacking it. Amai-aar-thol (அமையார்தோள்) compares the wife's shoulders or arms to amai (bamboo), a conventional image of feminine grace; Parimelazhagar notes that the slender image heightens the irony: a warrior who conquered heroes' arms yet fears these gentle ones has no aanmai (manliness). He reads 'living like the gods' as the life of heroes who reached heaven through valour, and says this verse closes a group of four (903-906) on the fault of fearing the wife. Manakkudavar takes it to mean that even the wealthy are not respected by others. Kalaignar again reinterprets, aiming the criticism at men who submit to a wife merely for beauty, not for wisdom or character. The text is uniform across sources. Modern critics note the verse's equation of dignity with masculine dominance as a historically situated value.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Pururavas, after the apsara Urvashi leaves him, wanders distraught and pleads with her to return, while she counsels him to recover himself.
hinduism.explanation: A great king is reduced to helplessness by his attachment to a celestial woman.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's man who lives like the gods yet lacks dignity, Pururavas's royal splendour cannot hide his dependence.

christianity.quote_or_event: Samson, the strongest man in Israel, yields his secret to Delilah's persistent pleading and loses his strength and freedom.
christianity.explanation: Extraordinary power proves useless once a man cannot stand firm against the woman he loves.
christianity.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's point that even godlike strength is worthless when a man is governed by a woman's will.

islam.quote_or_event: When the governor's wife falsely accuses Joseph, her husband, though he sees the truth, merely tells Joseph to overlook the matter and asks his wife to seek forgiveness.
islam.explanation: A powerful official acknowledges wrongdoing at home but lacks the resolve to act on it.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's dignified-seeming man who will not stand up within his own household finds a parallel in the governor's weak response.

judaism.quote_or_event: God tells Abraham to listen to Sarah in all that she says regarding Hagar and Ishmael.
judaism.explanation: Here divine instruction explicitly directs a patriarch to follow his wife's counsel.
judaism.tie_back: A counterpoint to the Kural: in Genesis, heeding one's wife can be the path God endorses.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha's half-brother Nanda, newly ordained, pines for the beauty he left at home, until the Buddha shows him a higher aim and he becomes an arahant.
buddhism.explanation: A prince-turned-monk is held back by longing for a woman until he redirects his aspiration.
buddhism.tie_back: As with the Kural's godlike man without dignity, Nanda's status means little until he masters his attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “This has been done by many men who for the sake of pleasures have stooped so low; they become the equals of slaves, animals, servants, beasts of burden--mere nobodies.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga says men who give themselves over to a woman for pleasure lose every bit of standing and become 'mere nobodies'.
jainism.tie_back: This is Kural 906's point that men who fear their wife's arms have no paatu, no real dignity, however splendidly they live.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.2.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They are not said to be husband and wife, who merely sit together. They alone are called husband and wife, who have one light in two bodies.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das defines true marriage as a spiritual partnership of two people sharing one divine light, not a relationship of domination or fear.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural mocks men who live in fear of their wives; Gurbani replaces that picture of rule and fear with partnership between equals.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Soohee (Vaar), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ares, the god of war, is caught in Hephaestus's net with Aphrodite and becomes a laughing stock before the assembled gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: The mightiest warrior-god is rendered ridiculous by his passion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's man living like the gods yet lacking dignity, Ares's divinity cannot save him from humiliation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch advises that a husband should govern his household not as a master over property but as the soul over the body, through sympathy and goodwill.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch's ideal marriage combines partnership and affection with the husband's responsible leadership.
philosophy.tie_back: This reflects the same ancient household ideal behind the Kural, while emphasising mutual goodwill rather than fear in either direction.

real_life_example.event_title: Madame de Pompadour's influence at the court of Louis XV
real_life_example.event: Louis XV declared he would rule without a chief minister, but Britannica records that his indolence and lack of self-confidence produced a court of rival ministers and mistresses, among whom Madame de Pompadour exerted considerable influence. She helped bring her protege the Duke de Choiseul into the ministry, and in 1756 the king, prompted by her, set aside his secret foreign policy. His reign saw reverses in foreign and military affairs, and he became unpopular with his subjects.
real_life_example.explanation: A king who presided over the most splendid court in Europe came to be seen as yielding his authority to a favourite, and lost the respect of his people.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even those who live as splendidly as the gods have no real dignity if they fear the arms of a woman, and Louis XV's grandeur at Versailles did not protect his reputation.

tamil:
பெண்ணேவல் செய்தொழுகும் ஆண்மையின் நாணுடைப்
பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Penneval seydhozhukum aanmaiyin naanutaip
penne perumai utaiththu.
meaning: A woman who has modesty and self-respect is worth far more than a man whose so-called manliness is spent doing whatever his wife orders.
elementary: Being a grown-up does not mean being bossy, and it does not mean just following orders either. A person with self-respect, whoever they are, deserves more admiration than someone who has given up thinking for themselves.
university: Pen-eval (பெண்ணேவல்) is 'a woman's command', and the man who 'conducts himself doing it' (seydhu ozhugum) is contrasted with naanutaip penne (நாணுடைப் பெண்ணே), the woman possessed of naan (நாண், modesty, sense of shame). Parimelazhagar notes that 'modest woman' is added deliberately as the opposite of the shameless man: the wife who issues commands is not the point of comparison, but rather womanhood marked by naan, which he regards as superior to such manhood. He also observes the emphatic separation of 'penne' at the line's start. Manakkudavar reads that such men are not respected by others. The verse is notable because, within its gendered frame, it affirms that a woman's perumai (பெருமை, greatness) can exceed a man's; modern feminist readers note, however, that it values women for modesty while denying men the role of following a woman. Text is identical across sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the forest exile, Draupadi rebukes Yudhishthira for his passivity after the dice game and urges him to reclaim his kingdom by righteous force.
hinduism.explanation: The epic gives a woman the voice of spirited dignity against a husband's resignation.
hinduism.tie_back: This supports the Kural's second half: a woman's dignity can surpass a man's, while complicating the first by showing a wife's counsel as valuable.

christianity.quote_or_event: Barak refuses to go into battle unless the prophetess Deborah goes with him, and she tells him the honour will therefore go to a woman, as Jael later kills Sisera.
christianity.explanation: A commander's dependence on a woman means the glory of victory passes to women.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, a woman's dignity outshines that of a man who will not act on his own, though the text honours Deborah and Jael rather than shaming women's leadership.

islam.quote_or_event: The Queen of Sheba consults her chiefs, who defer to her judgment, and she chooses a wise and peaceful course before submitting to God with Solomon.
islam.explanation: The Qur'an portrays a woman ruler as prudent and her counsellors as rightly deferring to her.
islam.tie_back: A counterpoint: following a woman's lead here is wise, and her dignity is affirmed.

judaism.quote_or_event: Abigail, wife of the boorish Nabal, wisely intercedes with David and averts bloodshed, earning his praise for her discretion.
judaism.explanation: A wife's good judgment far exceeds her husband's, and the narrative honours her.
judaism.tie_back: This agrees with the Kural that a woman's dignity can surpass a man's, while showing a woman's initiative as praiseworthy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Therigatha preserves the verses of early Buddhist nuns who attained liberation, celebrating their insight and resolve.
buddhism.explanation: Early Buddhism records women's spiritual accomplishment in their own voices.
buddhism.tie_back: It affirms, as the Kural's second line does, that a woman's greatness can be real and exemplary.

jainism.quote_or_event: “But when they have captured him, they send him on all sorts of errands.”
jainism.explanation: A long passage of the Sutrakritanga then lists the woman's orders (fetch fruit, rub my back, bring the mirror) and says such women 'order their husbands about like slaves' (1.4.2.15).
jainism.tie_back: It is nearly a one-to-one match for Kural 907's man who 'conducts himself doing a woman's errands' (pen-eval).
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.2.4, cf. 1.4.2.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Mai Bhago (Mata Bhag Kaur) openly rebuked forty Sikhs who had deserted Guru Gobind Singh during the siege of Anandpur; shamed, they followed her back, and they fought beside her at Khidrana (Muktsar) in 1705, where the Guru honoured the fallen as the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated Ones.
sikhism.explanation: A woman's courage and sense of honour exposed and then redeemed the failure of men who had abandoned their duty.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a modest woman's dignity is worth more than the so-called manhood of a man who has lost his own; Mai Bhago's story shows a woman's honour shaming and restoring men who had faltered.
sikhism.source: Wikipedia, 'Mai Bhago' (drawing on the Oxford Encyclopedia of Women in World History and other works)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, as penance, serves Queen Omphale of Lydia, and later tradition depicts him spinning wool in women's dress while she wears his lion-skin and club.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest hero, performing a woman's commands, becomes a classical emblem of reversed roles.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the closest mythic image of the Kural's 'manhood that does a woman's bidding'.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates argues that women of the guardian class should receive the same education and share the same duties as men.
philosophy.explanation: Plato's Socrates holds that capacity, not sex, should determine one's role in the city.
philosophy.tie_back: A counterpoint: Plato's argument undercuts the assumption that a man following a woman is inherently shameful.

real_life_example.event_title: Empress Theodora counsels Justinian to stand firm in the Nika revolt
real_life_example.event: During the Nika riots in Constantinople, the emperor Justinian's advisers urged him to flee the city. His wife, Empress Theodora, advised him to stay and defend his throne, and Justinian remained. His general Belisarius then crushed the revolt, and Justinian went on to rule for more than three decades.
real_life_example.explanation: At the decisive moment the empress showed more resolve and sense of honour than the emperor and his counsellors.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the dignity of a woman of honour is worthier than the manhood of a man who has lost his own, and Theodora's firmness outshone the counsel to flee.

tamil:
நட்டார் குறைமுடியார் நன்றாற்றார் நன்னுதலாள்
பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகு பவர்.
transliteration:
Nattaar kuraimutiyaar nandraatraar nannudhalaal
pettaangu ozhuku pavar.
meaning: Men who live only as their lovely wife wishes will not help their friends in need, and they will not do any good deeds.
elementary: If you only ever do what one person wants, you might forget to help your other friends when they need you. Good friends keep room in their life for everyone who counts on them.
university: Nattaar (நட்டார்) are those who have formed friendship (natpu), and kurai mudiyaar (குறைமுடியார்) means they will not fulfil their friends' needs; nandru aatraar (நன்றாற்றார்) means they will not perform good deeds, which Parimelazhagar specifies as aram that aids the next world. Nan-nudhalaal (நன்னுதலாள், 'she of the fair forehead') is a conventional epithet he compares with 'bamboo-like shoulders' in 906, and pettaangu (பெட்டாங்கு) means 'as she desires'. His reasoning is that the wife cannot herself command and give wealth for these purposes, so both this-worldly and other-worldly duties lapse. Fitting the chapter's place in the Natpiyal (friendship) section, the verse highlights obligations to friends. The text is uniform across sources; Sivayogi Sivakumar's playful gloss reading pettaangu as 'like a pottu (forehead mark)' is a modern pun, not the classical sense. Modern readers may take the general point that any single relationship which crowds out duties to friends and community is unhealthy.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sugriva, restored to his throne with Rama's help, forgets his promise to search for Sita while enjoying pleasures with Tara and Ruma, until Lakshmana confronts him in anger.
hinduism.explanation: A king indulging in the women's quarters neglects a debt to the friend who helped him.
hinduism.tie_back: This is a near-exact illustration of the Kural: absorbed in pleasure, a man fails to meet his friend's need.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And another said, I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus' parable of the great supper, invited guests offer excuses, one citing his new marriage, and the host fills his table with the poor instead.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, attachment to a wife becomes an excuse to neglect a higher call and a host's invitation.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an warns believers that if fathers, sons, brothers, spouses, relatives, wealth, trade and homes are dearer to them than God, His Messenger and striving in His cause, they should await God's decision.
islam.explanation: Family attachments, including to spouses, must not outrank one's higher obligations.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns that devotion to a wife must not displace duties to friends and to virtue.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let thy house be wide open, and let the poor be members of thy household. Engage not in too much conversation with women. They said this with regard to one’s own wife, how much more [does the rule apply] with regard to another man’s wife.”
judaism.explanation: Yose ben Yochanan pairs open-handed hospitality with a caution against excessive absorption in conversation with women, including one's wife.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts link a man's generosity to others with not letting domestic intimacy consume his attention.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In his advice to the young householder Sigala, the Buddha lists reciprocal duties of husband and wife and also the duties one owes to friends and companions, such as generosity and help in need.
buddhism.explanation: The ideal householder balances obligations to spouse with obligations to friends and to religious teachers.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's man fails exactly this balance, letting one relationship eclipse friendship and good works.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Some people are (foolishly) attached to others, and are thereby deluded; the unrighteous make them adopt unrighteousness, and they exult in their wickedness.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns that foolish attachment to another person can draw a man away from right conduct altogether.
jainism.tie_back: Kural 908 says men who live only as their wives wish neither help their friends nor do good deeds, and this verse gives the general Jain diagnosis behind that failure.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.2.1.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that selfless service in ordinary life is what earns honour before God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a man who lives only to please his wife neither helps his friends nor does good deeds; Gurbani calls everyone to active service of others.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Mercury rebukes Aeneas for building Carthage for Dido while forgetting his destined kingdom and his people's future, and Aeneas departs.
greek_mythology.explanation: A leader absorbed in a queen's affairs neglects his obligations to his companions and his son.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, devotion to a beloved leads a man to fail those who depend on him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle holds that friendship is among the greatest external goods and that the good person must act for his friends' sake, even at cost to himself.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, a flourishing life requires active care for friends.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's man who neglects his friends' needs forfeits this essential good.

real_life_example.event_title: Edward IV's secret marriage to Elizabeth Woodville
real_life_example.event: While his chief supporter, Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, was negotiating a marriage for him with a French princess to secure an alliance with France, Edward IV secretly married Elizabeth Woodville, a young widow of no great rank, and disclosed the marriage later in 1464. The Woodville family then rose into positions of trust near the king, further estranging Warwick. The rift widened until Warwick turned against Edward and in 1470 drove him from the throne.
real_life_example.explanation: The king's marriage cut across the plans and interests of the ally who had done most to put him on the throne, and the friendship never recovered.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who live only as their wife wishes will not meet the needs of their friends, and Edward's marriage and favour to his wife's family cost him his greatest friend.

tamil:
அறவினையும் ஆன்ற பொருளும் பிறவினையும்
பெண்ஏவல் செய்வார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Aravinaiyum aandra porulum piravinaiyum
peneval seyvaarkan il.
meaning: Men who simply do whatever their wives command will have no good deeds, no real riches, and none of life's other joys either.
elementary: A good life has three parts: being kind, working hard, and having fun. If someone lets another person run every part of their life, they can end up missing all three.
university: This verse maps directly onto the three aims of the Kural itself: aram (அறம், virtue), porul (பொருள், wealth) and, as Parimelazhagar glosses pira-vinai (பிறவினை, 'other deeds'), inbam (இன்பம், pleasure). He explains that once virtue and wealth are gone, even pleasure is lost because its direction lies with the wife, and he notes that verses 907-909 together treat the fault of doing the wife's bidding (eval). Manakkudavar adds that even men without fear, if they simply obey, lose all three. Textual note: some editions print pen-eval as one word (பெண்ணேவல்), as in 907, while all four sources consulted print 'பெண்ஏவல்' here. Kalaignar narrows the target to men enslaved by arrogant women's orders, a reading that limits the claim. Contemporary scholars stress that Valluvar's ideal of the wife elsewhere (chapter 6) is a partner who safeguards the household, and that the chapter's real target is the abdication of one's own judgment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya teaches that a king should pursue dharma, artha and kama in balance without neglecting any, and separately advises vigilance about dangers that can arise in the royal women's quarters.
hinduism.explanation: The statecraft manual treats balance of life's aims and guarding against palace intrigue as essential to rule.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's triad of virtue, wealth and pleasure, all lost by the man who abdicates judgment, echoes Kautilya's balance.

christianity.quote_or_event: God tells Adam that because he listened to his wife's voice and ate of the forbidden tree, the ground is cursed and he will toil for his bread.
christianity.explanation: In Genesis, heeding one's wife against God's command brings loss of ease and abundance.
christianity.tie_back: This is the classic biblical text behind the Kural's theme, though modern scholars and feminist theologians stress Adam's own responsibility and the shared nature of the fault.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an describes spouses as garments for one another.
islam.explanation: Husband and wife are presented as mutual protection, comfort and covering.
islam.tie_back: A counterpoint: the Qur'an's image of mutuality offers an alternative to the Kural's binary of commanding and obeying.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Rav says: Nevertheless, anyone who follows the counsel of his wife descends into Gehenna... Rav Pappa said to Abaye: But don’t people say a popular proverb: If your wife is short, stoop and whisper to her and consult with her?”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud records a harsh dictum against following a wife's counsel, immediately challenges it with a proverb urging consultation, and resolves that each applies to different spheres.
judaism.tie_back: This parallels the Kural's warning while showing a tradition debating and limiting it, which models a critical reading of the chapter.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59a (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz translation)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Flowing in (from all objects) and watered by craving, feelings of pleasure arise in beings. Bent on pleasures and seeking enjoyment, these men fall prey to birth and decay.”
buddhism.explanation: Pleasure-seeking, watered by craving, binds beings to suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural adds that the man ruled by another's will loses even the pleasures he sought.

jainism.quote_or_event: Hemachandra lists as a quality of the ideal Jain householder 'Anyonya-pratibandhena trivargam sadhayan', which Sangave renders as fulfilling the three-fold aim of life (dharma, artha and kama) without excluding any of its elements.
jainism.explanation: Jain lay ethics asks a householder to pursue virtue, wealth and pleasure in balance so that none crowds out the others.
jainism.tie_back: Kural 909 says the man who obeys his wife in everything loses all three, aram, porul and inbam, which is the same trivarga the Jain householder is told to keep in balance.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Yogashastra, list of 35 householder qualities, no. 18, as rendered in V.A. Sangave, 'Jaina ethics' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The four cardinal blessings are obtained by serving the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says the four traditional aims of life (dharma, wealth, desire and liberation) come through devotion to God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says virtue, wealth and pleasure all slip away from a man who obeys his wife in everything; Gurbani names the same aims but says they are secured by right devotion.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 108, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus's allegory, the young Heracles at a crossroads is approached by two women, Vice offering easy pleasure and Virtue offering toil and lasting good, and he chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: The allegory frames life's direction as a choice of which voice to follow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's man who follows another's commands rather than his own judgment fails the choice Heracles made well.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus, The Choice of Heracles (in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1)

philosophy.quote_or_event: John Stuart Mill argues that the legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong in itself and corrupts both, and that marriage should be a partnership of equals.
philosophy.explanation: Mill's critique rejects the whole framework of command and obedience within marriage.
philosophy.tie_back: A modern counterpoint: Mill would see the Kural's problem as hierarchy itself, in either direction, rather than a husband's submission.
philosophy.source: John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women (1869)

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Xuanzong loses his capital, his throne and Yang Guifei
real_life_example.event: Late in his long reign the Tang emperor Xuanzong withdrew increasingly from government and came under the influence of his consort Yang Guifei, whose relatives dominated the court. When the An Lushan rebellion took Chang'an in 756, the emperor fled toward Sichuan, and at Mawei his mutinous escort killed members of the Yang faction and demanded Yang Guifei's death, which he was unable to refuse. He then abdicated in favour of his son.
real_life_example.explanation: An emperor who had once presided over a golden age lost his government, his capital and in the end the woman he loved.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who do whatever their wives command lose virtue, wealth and even pleasure, and Xuanzong lost all three in a single year.

tamil:
எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சத் திடனுடையார்க்கு எஞ்ஞான்றும்
பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை இல்.
transliteration:
Enserndha nenjath thitanutaiyaarkku egngnaandrum
penserndhaam pedhaimai il.
meaning: People whose minds are full of careful thought and who are strong inside will never fall into the foolishness of being ruled by a woman.
elementary: When you think things through and stay steady inside, you do not get swept away by any one wish or person. A calm, thoughtful mind keeps you in charge of your own choices.
university: En-serndha nenjam (எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சம்) is 'a mind joined to deliberation'; Parimelazhagar takes it as a mind engaged in planning affairs of state, and reads idan (இடன்) not as 'firmness' (as some modern glosses do) but as 'wealth/means', citing Kural 218 ('இடனில் பருவத்தும்') and Kalittokai to establish that sense. Ytamizh's 'thitan' transliteration reflects the sandhi 'நெஞ்சத் திடன்', which modern commentators such as Kalaignar and Mu. Varadarasanar also read as thidan (திடன், firmness of mind), so both readings circulate. Pen-serndhaam pedhaimai (பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை) is the folly arising from attachment to the wife; Parimelazhagar says this folly is the root of all three faults treated earlier, namely desiring, fearing and obeying, so the closing verse sums up the chapter negatively. Manakkudavar explains en-serdhal as discerning the faults that arise from such attachment. Read today, the chapter's enduring core is this closing ideal of deliberative self-command, while its gendered framing belongs to its historical setting.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Katha Upanishad compares the self to the rider of a chariot, the body to the chariot, the intellect to the charioteer, the mind to the reins and the senses to the horses.
hinduism.explanation: One whose intellect holds the reins firmly reaches the goal, while one with unruly senses does not.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's thoughtful, steady-minded person is the well-reined charioteer who is not dragged off course.

christianity.quote_or_event: Joseph, in Egypt, refuses the repeated advances of his master Potiphar's wife and flees, leaving his garment behind.
christianity.explanation: Joseph's steadfast integrity keeps him from yielding, at great personal cost.
christianity.tie_back: He embodies the Kural's firm-minded person who does not fall into folly.

islam.quote_or_event: Yusuf resists the governor's wife, seeking refuge in God, and later says prison is dearer to him than what he is invited to.
islam.explanation: The Qur'anic Joseph shows steadfast resolve rooted in faith.
islam.tie_back: His firmness mirrors the Kural's steady-minded person free of folly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city.’”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma defines true strength as mastery over one's own impulses.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise places real strength in a mind governed by deliberation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who delights in subduing evil thoughts, who meditates on the impurities and is ever mindful — it is he who will make an end of craving and rend asunder Mara's fetter.”
buddhism.explanation: Mindful, disciplined thought breaks the bonds of craving.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's deliberative mind similarly stays free of attachment's folly.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Restraining himself by the thought that these dangerous (pleasures) will not be to his benefit, a monk should abstain from women.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga's remedy is reflection: a man who thinks clearly about what harms him keeps himself from falling under a woman's sway.
jainism.tie_back: Kural 910 likewise says that people whose minds are joined to deliberation (en-serndha nenjam) never fall into the folly of being ruled by a woman.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.2.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak teaches that mastering one's own mind is the real victory.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a mind given to careful thought will never be wholly ruled by attachment, and Japji likewise makes self-mastery the foundation of every other success.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib (Pauri 28), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus has himself bound to the mast so he can hear the Sirens' song without steering his ship to ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: Foresight lets the hero experience temptation without being ruled by it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's ideal: forethought that keeps one from folly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato's Socrates likens the soul to a charioteer driving two horses, one noble and one unruly, and says the well-ordered soul is one in which reason guides the team.
philosophy.explanation: Reason must govern appetite for a soul to rise to the good.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's 'mind joined to deliberation' is the charioteer in command.

real_life_example.event_title: Titus sends Queen Berenice away from Rome
real_life_example.event: Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian, lived openly with Berenice, sister of the Judean king Agrippa II, who hoped to become his wife, but the relationship was unpopular in Rome. Not daring to marry her, he sent her away, probably on his accession as emperor in 79 CE. The Roman biographer Suetonius records that he sent her from Rome at once, against her will and his own.
real_life_example.explanation: On taking power, Titus placed the duties of his office and public confidence above his personal attachment.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those whose minds are joined to careful thought will not fall into the folly of being ruled by attachment to a woman, and Titus made exactly that choice when he became emperor.

tamil:
அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ஆய்தொடியார்
இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Anbin vizhaiyaar porulvizhaiyum aaydhodiyaar
insol izhukkuth tharum.
meaning: The sweet words of bangle-wearing women who want a man's money, not his love, will in the end bring him shame and trouble.
elementary: Imagine a kid who suddenly calls you their best friend every day you bring a big bag of candy, and ignores you on days you bring nothing. Their nice words feel good, but they were never about you, and trusting them only ends with hurt feelings. Real friendship is liking someone, not liking what they can give you.
university: The opening couplet sets the chapter’s key contrast between anbu (அன்பு, love) and porul (பொருள், wealth): the women described here vizhaiyaar, ‘do not desire’, out of love but porul-vizhaiyum, ‘desire wealth’. Aaydhodiyaar (ஆய்தொடியார், ‘those wearing choice bangles’) is a conventional ornamental epithet, and the danger lies in their insol (இன்சொல், sweet speech), the same virtue Valluvar praises in chapter 10, here turned into a tool of profit. Izhukku (இழுக்கு) means both moral lapse and resulting disgrace; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah render it as ‘suffering’, Sivayogi Sivakumar as ‘degradation’. Parimelazhagar places the chapter in the Natpiyal (section on friendship) right after Penvazhicheral (being led by one’s wife), and reads it as a warning against an intimacy that only imitates friendship. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Happiness is said to be in the mode of passion when it is derived from the contact of the senses with their objects. Such happiness is like nectar at first but poison at the end.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes rajasic pleasure as sweet at the start and bitter at the end.
hinduism.tie_back: The insincere sweet words of Kural 911 are nectar at first, and the izhukku they bring is the poison at the end.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns about people who use pleasant language to deceive the naive while serving only their own appetite.
christianity.tie_back: Same picture as the Kural: fair speech covering pure self-interest.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up...”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes hypocrites whose looks and words are attractive but who are hollow inside.
islam.tie_back: Like the women of Kural 911, they please the eye and ear while having no real heart for you.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All love that depends on a something, [when the] thing ceases, [the] love ceases; and [all love] that does not depend on anything, will never cease.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah separates love that depends on some benefit from love that stands on its own, and says the first ends when the benefit ends.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar’s women love the porul, not the person, which is exactly the love that ‘depends on a something’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Among the ‘foes in the guise of friends’, the Buddha lists the one who renders lip-service, who among other things “tries to gain one’s favor by empty words.”
buddhism.explanation: The Sigalovada Sutta teaches a layman to recognize false friends whose kind words have no substance behind them.
buddhism.tie_back: Kural 911’s insol is the same kind of empty, favor-seeking speech.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Meekly and politely they approach him with their manifold arts to win his heart; and talking sweetly in confidential conversation they make him do (what they like).”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns that sweet, intimate talk is the tool by which a man is led wherever the woman wants.
jainism.tie_back: Kural 911 also warns that the sweet words of women who want a man's money, not the man, end in disgrace and grief.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Listen, madman: you have been trapped by false love, which is transitory, like the fading color of the safflower.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan warns the mind that the love it has fallen into is false, bright for a moment like safflower dye and then gone. In Gurbani the safflower stands for any attachment that looks like love but cannot last.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s mercenary sweet words, this love is real only in appearance, and the one who trusts it is left with grief.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 777, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod’s myth of Pandora, the gods dress the first woman in beauty and grace, and Hermes puts lies, crafty words and a deceitful nature in her heart, so that she becomes a lovely gift that brings men trouble.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s story is about a beautiful surface hiding deceit and harm.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 911 likewise warns of an adorned figure whose sweet words bring ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Therefore those who love for the sake of utility love for the sake of what is good for themselves... and not in so far as the other is the person loved but in so far as he is useful or pleasant.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says friendships of utility are not really about the other person but about what one gets.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the porul-vizhaiyum (wealth-desiring) affection of Kural 911, described as philosophy.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Louise de Kéroualle wins the favour and fortune of Charles II
real_life_example.event: Louise de Kéroualle came to England in 1670 in the household of Charles II's sister and, with the encouragement of the French government, which hoped she would be a diplomatic asset, became the king's mistress. She received titles and gifts, including the English dukedom of Portsmouth and the French duchy of Aubigny from Louis XIV, and acted as an intermediary for French interests at court. Britannica notes her unequalled rapacity and records that she was the least popular of the king's mistresses with his subjects.
real_life_example.explanation: A favourite whose position brought her great wealth and served a foreign court made the king's attachment a lasting source of public resentment.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that the sweet words of women who seek a man for his wealth rather than for love bring him disgrace, and this attachment damaged Charles II's standing with his own people.

tamil:
பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும் பண்பின் மகளிர்
நயன்தூக்கி நள்ளா விடல்.
transliteration:
Payandhookkip panburaikkum panbin magalir
nayandhookki nallaa vidal.
meaning: Some women of bad character first weigh what they can get from a man, then speak sweetly to him. Think about what they are really like, and stay away.
elementary: Some people check how much pocket money you have before deciding how friendly to be, and then talk about how loyal they are. Valluvar says: notice that pattern, think about it, and do not get close to someone who measures you by your wallet.
university: The couplet rests on a play of the verb thookku (தூக்கு, ‘to weigh, to measure’): the women payan-thookki, ‘weigh the profit’, so the wise man must nayan-thookki, ‘weigh their character’, and then nallaa vidal (நள்ளா விடல்), ‘leave without joining’. There is also deliberate irony in panburaikkum panbin magalir, ‘women of no virtue (panbu) who speak of virtue’: the speech is a performance tuned to the size of the purse. Puliyur Kesigan reads nayan as their behaviour, while Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as the ‘pleasure’ they offer, which the wise man evaluates and declines. Parimelazhagar treats the couplet as a practical rule of discernment rather than a moral sermon, in keeping with the Porutpal’s concern with prudent conduct. No textual variants appear between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Kathasaritsagara’s tale of Lohajangha, the courtesan Rupinika’s mother Makaradamshtra drives away the penniless young man her daughter genuinely loves, insisting that affection must follow money; the story then shows how calculation and greed undo themselves.
hinduism.explanation: Somadeva’s story collection uses this tale to satirize affection that is weighed against wealth.
hinduism.tie_back: Makaradamshtra is a portrait of payan-thookki, weighing the gain before the man.
hinduism.source: Somadeva, Kathasaritsagara, Book II (tale of Lohajangha), tr. C. H. Tawney

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the Prodigal Son, the companions of the young man’s wasteful days disappear once his money is gone; the story adds that ‘no man gave unto him’.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s mercenary friends likewise last only as long as the purse does.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he whose speech pleases you in worldly life, and he calls Allah to witness as to what is in his heart, yet he is the fiercest of opponents.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns of people who speak pleasantly and even swear to their sincerity while being enemies at heart.
islam.tie_back: Kural 912’s women ‘speak of virtue’ while weighing gain, the same gap between pleasing words and real intent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “With her much fair speech she causeth him to yield, With the blandishment of her lips she enticeth him away.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs describes the enticing woman whose skilled talk leads a simple young man astray.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts warn against flattering speech that is a means to an end.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is a bottle friend; one says, ‘friend, friend’ only to one’s face; one is a friend and an associate only when it is advantageous.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes people whose friendship lasts only while there is something in it for them.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the friendship Kural 912 says to weigh and walk away from.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A young woman, putting on fine ornaments and clothes, will say to a Sramana: 'I shall give up (my former way of life) and practise the rough (viz. control). Reverend sir, teach me the Law!'”
jainism.explanation: The text describes a woman who talks piously of religion in order to win over a monk, and it warns him not to trust that show of virtue.
jainism.tie_back: This fits Kural 912's women who first weigh their profit and then 'speak of virtue' (panburaikkum), so that the wise man must weigh their character and stay away.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Bronze is bright and shiny, but when it is rubbed, its blackness appears.”
sikhism.explanation: This shabad opens with the image of polished bronze that leaves black marks when rubbed: a fine surface hiding a dark interior. According to the Janamsakhi tradition Guru Nanak sang it to Sajjan, a man who kept a pious-looking rest-house for travellers and robbed them, and who repented on hearing it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the wise to weigh the character behind sweet talk of virtue, and Guru Nanak’s bronze shows exactly what such testing reveals.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eriphyle, wife of the seer Amphiaraus, was bribed by Polynices with the golden necklace of Harmonia and in return persuaded her husband to join the doomed expedition against Thebes, where he died.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth became the Greek byword for affection and loyalty sold for a jewel.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Eriphyle weighs gold against the man, as the women of Kural 912 weigh profit before speaking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...there is a dishonour in being overcome by the love of money, or of wealth, or of political power... For none of these things are of a permanent or lasting nature; not to mention that no generous friendship ever sprang from them.”
philosophy.explanation: Pausanias’ speech holds that attachments bought by money are shameful and cannot produce real friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise tells the wise to weigh such attachments and refuse them.

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi vows to avoid wine, women and meat before sailing to England
real_life_example.event: When the young Mohandas Gandhi planned to study law in London, his mother feared he would be led astray, since she had heard that young men in England took to meat and liquor. A family adviser administered an oath, and Gandhi vowed not to touch wine, women or meat, after which his mother gave her permission. He sailed for England on 4 September 1888, and he kept the vow while he was abroad.
real_life_example.explanation: Before entering a world of new temptations, he weighed the dangers in advance and bound himself to keep away from them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises weighing the conduct of those who seek gain and keeping away from them, and Gandhi's vow was a decision to stay clear of such attachments before he ever met them.

tamil:
பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம் இருட்டறையில்
ஏதில் பிணந்தழீஇ அற்று.
transliteration:
Porutpendir poimmai muyakkam iruttaraiyil
edhil pinandhazheei atru.
meaning: The fake hug of a woman who wants only money is like hugging a stranger's dead body in a dark room.
elementary: Think of hugging a big cardboard cut-out of a friend in the dark. It is shaped like a person, but nobody is really there to hug you back. Valluvar says that affection bought with money is like that: it looks like love, but there is no real heart inside it.
university: Kural 913 is the chapter’s most startling simile. Porut-pendir (பொருட்பெண்டிர், ‘women of wealth’, i.e. women who are for wealth) offer a poimmai muyakkam (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், false embrace), compared to clasping an edhil pinam (ஏதில் பிணம், a stranger’s corpse) in an iruttarai (இருட்டறை, dark room). Parimelazhagar’s gloss, followed by Puliyur Kesigan and by the bracketed ‘(hired men)’ in the standard English explanation, explains the image: it is the hired corpse-bearer who handles an unknown body in the dark for pay, without any bond, so the transaction is equally loveless on both sides. Kalaignar reads it as acting out love purely for money. The form thazheei (தழீஇ) is an alapedai (lengthened vowel) form of thazhuvi, ‘having embraced’. Both base sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The pleasures that arise from contact with the sense objects, though appearing as enjoyable to worldly-minded people, are verily a source of misery... so the wise do not delight in them.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that pleasures born only of sense contact are empty and end in sorrow.
hinduism.tie_back: Kural 913 shows the same emptiness in its most vivid form: an embrace with no living heart in it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James traces a path from desire to sin to death.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar puts death at the very center of the embrace itself, which is cold as a corpse.

islam.quote_or_event: “But those who disbelieved - their deeds are like a mirage in a lowland which a thirsty one thinks is water until, when he comes to it, he finds it is nothing...”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an compares empty deeds to a mirage that promises water and gives nothing.
islam.tie_back: The false embrace in Kural 913 also looks like love up close and turns out to hold nothing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Her house is the way to the nether-world, Going down to the chambers of death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs ends its warning about the enticing woman by linking her house to death.
judaism.tie_back: Kural 913 also ties this intimacy to death, through the corpse in the dark room.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Behold this body — a painted image, a mass of heaped up sores, infirm, full of hankering — of which nothing is lasting or stable!”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada asks the reader to see the attractive body as a painted surface over decay.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise strips the purchased embrace down to what it really is: a lifeless body.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain monks and devout lay people meditate on twelve reflections (anupreksha). The sixth is asuchi, the impurity of the body, which Sangave renders as the body being impure and dirty.
jainism.explanation: Jainism weakens physical desire by meditating on the body as perishable and impure, not as a source of real joy.
jainism.tie_back: Kural 913 likens the false embrace of a woman who wants only money to clasping a stranger's corpse in a dark room, a shock image of the same kind as the Jain reflection on the body's impurity.
jainism.source: Asuchi anupreksha, as described in V.A. Sangave, 'Jaina ethics' (jainworld.com); cf. Tattvartha Sutra ch. 9 on the twelve reflections

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Beholding an illusion, you are deceived, and on your bed, you enjoy a false lover.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan pictures the deluded soul as a bride taken in by a mirage, lying on her bed with a lover who is not real. The false lover is Maya: an embrace that gives nothing true back.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural’s stranger’s corpse in a dark room and Guru Arjan’s false lover on the bed both describe an embrace with no living love in it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 460, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Underworld, Odysseus tries three times to embrace the shade of his mother Anticleia, and three times she slips through his arms like a shadow or a dream.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s scene shows an embrace that holds nothing living.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 913’s embrace of a corpse is also contact without any real presence, though Homer’s scene is tender rather than mercenary.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that self-indulgence in the pleasures of touch is especially open to reproach because it belongs to us not as human beings but as animals.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, pleasure cut off from reason and relationship is the least human kind.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s corpse simile makes the same point more harshly: a purely bought embrace has nothing human in it.

real_life_example.event_title: Madame du Barry becomes Louis XV's official favourite
real_life_example.event: Jeanne Bécu, a Paris shop assistant, became the companion of Jean du Barry, a nobleman who had made a fortune as a war contractor and who introduced her into high society. Because the position of official royal favourite required a noble husband, a nominal marriage was arranged to his brother, and in 1769 she was presented at the court of Louis XV. When the king died in May 1774, his successor Louis XVI had her sent away from Versailles to a convent.
real_life_example.explanation: Her rise was arranged through a marriage of convenience and ended the moment the king who had favoured her was gone.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares a relationship sought for wealth and position to an embrace without feeling, and the purely formal arrangements that brought du Barry to court show how little of genuine bond such a connection could hold.

tamil:
பொருட்பொருளார் புன்னலந் தோயார் அருட்பொருள்
ஆயும் அறிவி னவர்.
transliteration:
Porutporulaar punnalan thoyaar arutporul
aayum arivi navar.
meaning: Wise people, who look for the true treasure of kindness, will not touch the cheap charms of women whose only goal is money.
elementary: If you are saving up for something really valuable, like a bicycle, you do not spend it all on sweets that are gone in a minute. Wise people treat their hearts the same way: they look for real kindness, not for ‘friendships’ that are only about money.
university: The couplet turns on a pun on porul: porut-porulaar (பொருட்பொருளார்) are ‘those whose object (porul) is wealth (porul)’, set against arut-porul (அருட்பொருள்), ‘the wealth that is arul (grace, compassion)’, which the wise aayum (ஆயும், examine and pursue). Punnalam (புன்னலம், ‘petty or base beauty’) is the low pleasure they decline, and thoyaar (தோயார்) means ‘will not immerse themselves in or touch’. Mu. Varadarasanar treats arul itself as the highest wealth, while Solomon Pappaiah reads arut-porul as ‘wealth sought together with compassion’, a reading in keeping with Parimelazhagar’s concern that riches be earned and used with arul. The echo of chapter 25 (Aruludaimai) is deliberate. Ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, with punnalan(th) sandhi spelled புன்னலந்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Katha Upanishad, Yama teaches Nachiketas that the good (shreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both come to a person; the wise examine them and choose the good, while the foolish choose the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad says real wisdom is discerning lasting good from passing pleasure.
hinduism.tie_back: The aayum arivinar of Kural 914 are exactly those who examine and choose shreyas (arut-porul) over preyas (punnalam).

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt... But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven...”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts perishable earthly wealth with lasting spiritual treasure.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar’s wise man prefers arut-porul, the wealth of grace, to the petty pleasures money can buy.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one's] hope.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an ranks lasting righteous deeds above worldly adornments.
islam.tie_back: The same choice of lasting good (arut-porul) over passing charm runs through Kural 914.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot...”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment rather than possessions.
judaism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the Mishnah moves true wealth from money to an inner good.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Riches ruin only the foolish, not those in quest of the Beyond. By craving for riches the witless man ruins himself as well as others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says wealth harms only those who crave it, not those seeking the higher goal.
buddhism.tie_back: In Kural 914 the money-minded ruin themselves, while the seekers of arul stay untouched.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain tradition remembers the monk Sthulabhadra, who had once loved the courtesan Kosha. As a monk he asked to spend the rainy season in her house, and at its end his teacher Sambhutavijaya praised him above two disciples who had spent it in a lion's cave and on a wheel.
jainism.explanation: The story is told to show that a man devoted to the spiritual path can stand amid a courtesan's charms without being moved by them.
jainism.tie_back: It illustrates Kural 914: the wise, who seek the wealth of grace (arut-porul), will not touch the cheap charms (punnalam) of women for whom money is everything.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Parisistaparvan VIII.109-169, as summarised from Jinaprabhasuri's Vividhatirthakalpa (OpenEdition / wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Sovereign Lord is the nine treasures for me.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir says that the Lord alone is his whole wealth, while the possessions and spouse people cling to belong to God and go with no one at death. Real riches, for Kabir, are the divine treasure, not what the senses chase.
sikhism.tie_back: As the Kural’s wise seek the wealth of grace and ignore cheap charms, Kabir counts the Lord as his true treasure and lets lesser attractions go.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1158, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads the young Heracles meets two women: Vice, who promises an easy road of pleasures, and Virtue, who offers a harder road to lasting honor; he chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prodicus’ fable, retold by Xenophon, became the classic Greek picture of a moral choice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 914’s wise man makes the same choice, turning from punnalam toward arut-porul.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his defense speech, Socrates says his whole mission was to persuade Athenians, young and old, not to care first for their bodies or property but for the greatest improvement of the soul.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates ranks the soul’s good above wealth and bodily comfort.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s aayum arivinar likewise put the soul’s wealth, arul, above money-bought pleasure.

real_life_example.event_title: Augustine's conversion in the garden at Milan
real_life_example.event: Augustine, then a teacher of rhetoric in Milan, had long struggled to give up what his Confessions describe as the slavery of the desires of the flesh. In a garden in Milan he heard a child's voice chanting take up and read, opened the letters of Paul and read the passage in Romans 13 that warns against revelling and wantonness and urges putting on Christ. He resolved to change his life and was baptised by Ambrose at Easter 387.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the most influential thinkers in Western history turned decisively from a life of pleasure to the pursuit of spiritual grace.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the wise who seek the true wealth of grace will not touch cheap pleasures, and Augustine's conversion is a famous example of choosing grace over such pleasures.

tamil:
பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார் மதிநலத்தின்
மாண்ட அறிவி னவர்.
transliteration:
Podhunalaththaar punnalam thoyaar madhinalaththin
maanda arivi navar.
meaning: People whose wisdom has been made strong by good sense will not go after the cheap pleasures of women who give themselves to anyone who pays.
elementary: A smart kid who knows what real friendship is will not chase someone who is ‘best friends’ with whoever gives the most presents that day. Good sense helps you see that kind of friendship is not really for you at all.
university: Podhu-nalaththaar (பொதுநலத்தார்) means ‘those whose charms (nalam) are common (podhu)’, available to all who pay. Valluvar sets this against mathi-nalam (மதிநலம்), ‘the excellence of natural intelligence’, which makes knowledge maandu (மாண்ட, perfected, excellent). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan distinguish iyarkai arivu (inborn sense) from acquired learning, and Kalaignar explicitly names both ‘natural intelligence and learned knowledge’, following Parimelazhagar’s distinction between mathi (native wit) and arivu (learning). The couplet is built parallel to 914 (punnalam thoyaar repeats), so the pair should be read together: 914 names the motive of the wise (arul), 915 the faculty (mathi). Both base sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is able to withdraw the senses from their objects, just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs into its shell, is established in divine wisdom.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the steady-minded person who can pull the senses back from their objects.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s person of perfected understanding likewise draws back from common, purchased pleasure.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to turn away from youthful passions and pursue virtue.
christianity.tie_back: The wise of Kural 915 likewise turn from low pleasure toward what is excellent.
