islam.quote_or_event: “Beautified for people is the love of that which they desire - of women and sons, heaped-up sums of gold and silver... That is the enjoyment of worldly life, but Allah has with Him the best return.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an notes that worldly desires are made attractive, but that a better return lies with God.
islam.tie_back: Kural 915’s wise man sees past what is made attractive, toward what is truly better.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Lust not after her beauty in thy heart; Neither let her captivate thee with her eyelids.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns the young man not to let outward beauty capture him, and adds that such a woman reduces a man to a loaf of bread.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise tells the wise not to sink into podhu-nalam, beauty offered to all.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Weeds are the bane of fields, lust is the bane of mankind. Therefore, what is offered to those free of lust yields abundant fruit.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares lust to weeds choking a field.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s wise keep their field clear by refusing common, purchased pleasure.

jainism.quote_or_event: “...cohabitation with a harlot–itvarikā aparigṛhītāgamana... are the five transgressions of the fourth minor vow of contentment with one’s wife (svadārasantoṣa aṇuvrata).”
jainism.explanation: Umasvati's Tattvartha Sutra makes going to a prostitute a formal breach of the Jain householder's vow of sexual restraint.
jainism.tie_back: Kural 915 says those of mature understanding will not seek the 'common' charms (podhu-nalam) of paid women, and Jain lay ethics makes this a vow.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.28 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018, wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You gaze upon the wives of others, O my soul; you steal and commit evil deeds.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak speaks to his own soul and lists its faults: a wandering eye for other men’s wives, theft and wrongdoing. Self-examination of this kind, done with the Guru’s understanding, is how Sikhism expects a person to check desire before it acts.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a mind perfected by good sense will not seek low pleasures, and Guru Nanak shows that understanding at work by naming the craving and rebuking it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 155, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus, held for years by the nymph Calypso, refuses her offer to make him immortal and ageless, choosing instead to return home to Ithaca and Penelope.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows his hero choosing what is truly his own over an easy, enchanting comfort.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 915’s discerning man likewise refuses tempting pleasure in favor of what his good sense values.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The Love who is the offspring of the common Aphrodite is essentially common, and has no discrimination, being such as the meaner sort of men feel...”
philosophy.explanation: Pausanias separates common (Pandemos) love, which is indiscriminate and bodily, from heavenly love, which looks to the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s ‘common’ love echoes Valluvar’s podhu-nalam, and both say the wise prefer the higher kind.

real_life_example.event_title: Scipio returns a captive young woman to her father at New Carthage
real_life_example.event: After the Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio captured New Carthage during the Second Punic War, some young soldiers brought him a captive young woman of great beauty. The Greek historian Polybius records that Scipio thanked them, summoned the young woman's father and handed her over to him to be married to whomever he chose. Polybius adds that this display of self-restraint won Scipio the warm respect of his men, and the episode later became the famous artistic subject known as the Continence of Scipio.
real_life_example.explanation: A young commander at the height of victory chose restraint, and was admired for it by his own soldiers and by later generations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those whose understanding has been perfected by good sense will not seek pleasures that are merely offered to them, and Scipio's restraint at New Carthage became a lasting model of that judgment.

tamil:
தந்நலம் பாரிப்பார் தோயார் தகைசெருக்கிப்
புன்னலம் பாரிப்பார் தோள்.
transliteration:
Thannalam paarippaar thoyaar thagaiserukkip
punnalam paarippaar thol.
meaning: People who care about their own good name will not go to the arms of women who show off their charm and sell cheap pleasures to anyone.
elementary: If you care about being known as honest and kind, you will be careful about who you spend your time with. You would not team up with someone who sells their ‘friendship’ to anyone, because you value your good name.
university: The couplet repeats the verb paarippaar (பாரிப்பார்) in two senses: those who paarippaar thannalam, ‘cherish or spread their own goodness (or fame)’, will not touch the shoulders of those who paarippaar punnalam, ‘spread their petty charms abroad’. Thagai-serukki (தகைசெருக்கி) is ‘being proud of their attractiveness or skill’. Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan take thannalam as one’s own fame, Mu. Varadarasanar as one’s ‘good conduct’, and Parimelazhagar as the reputation that comes from virtue. Textual note: thirukkural.net prints the first verb as பாரப்பார் (paarappaar), whereas ytamizh.com and the standard Parimelazhagar text read பாரிப்பார்; the repeated verb and all four commentaries support பாரிப்பார், so the variant looks like a typographical slip.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna places the responsibility for one’s rise or fall on oneself.
hinduism.tie_back: Kural 916’s thannalam paarippaar are those who choose to raise themselves and not to lower their own worth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs ranks reputation above wealth.
christianity.tie_back: Those who guard their thannalam (good name) in Kural 916 make exactly this choice.

islam.quote_or_event: In Surah Yusuf, the wife of al-Aziz tries to seduce the young Joseph behind closed doors; he refuses, seeking refuge in God and saying he will not betray his master’s trust, and he flees.
islam.explanation: Yusuf’s refusal is the Qur’an’s model of a person who guards his integrity under pressure.
islam.tie_back: He is the type of the thannalam paarippaar who will not touch what would stain him.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Potiphar’s wife urges Joseph to be with her, he refuses, asking how he could do such a great wickedness and sin against God, and when she seizes his garment he leaves it and flees.
judaism.explanation: Genesis presents Joseph as the young man who protects his integrity even at personal cost.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph embodies Kural 916: one who values his own goodness does not take what is offered.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not to be contented with one's own wife, and to be seen with harlots and the wives of others — this is a cause of one's downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: The Parabhava Sutta lists such conduct among the causes of a person’s decline.
buddhism.tie_back: Kural 916 states the positive side: those who protect their standing stay away.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the assembly he pronounces holy (words), yet secretly he commits sins; but the wise know him to be a deceiver and great rogue.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga says that a man who hides his sexual lapses still loses his good name among the discerning.
jainism.tie_back: Kural 916 says that those who care about their own good name stay away from women who sell their favours, and this verse shows how such a lapse destroys that reputation.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Sikh ought to treat beautiful women of others as his mothers, sisters, and daughters.”
sikhism.explanation: In a pauri describing the Gursikh’s daily conduct, Bhai Gurdas sets the standard for how a Sikh looks at women who are not his wife: as mother, sister or daughter. This became a widely cited rule of Sikh sexual ethics.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who guard their good name will not seek the arms of women offering cheap favours, and Bhai Gurdas gives the Sikh form of that same self-respecting restraint.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 29, Pauri 11 (English translation as published on BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax and searchgurbani.com)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Queen Anteia tries to win the young hero Bellerophon, but he refuses her because he is upright of heart; in revenge she falsely accuses him to her husband.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents Bellerophon as the noble-minded young man who would not compromise his honor.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is an early Greek picture of the thannalam paarippaar of Kural 916.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If I can get them with the preservation of my own honor and fidelity and greatness of mind, show me the way and I will get them; but if you require me to lose my own proper good that you may gain what is not good, consider how inequitable and foolish you are.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus refuses any gain that would cost him his integrity.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s self-respecting man likewise refuses pleasure that would cost him his good name.

real_life_example.event_title: John Profumo resigns after misleading Parliament
real_life_example.event: John Profumo, Britain's Secretary of State for War, had a brief relationship in 1961 with Christine Keeler, who was also involved with a Soviet naval attaché, Yevgeny Ivanov. In March 1963 Profumo told the House of Commons there had been no impropriety in the relationship, but in June he admitted that this statement was untrue and resigned from the government and from Parliament. The scandal contributed to the fall of Harold Macmillan's government later that year, and Profumo spent the rest of his life in charity work in London's East End.
real_life_example.explanation: A senior minister lost his office and political reputation because of an association he first tried to deny.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who care for their good name will not seek such company, and Profumo's case shows how quickly a public reputation can be lost through it.

tamil:
நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர் தோய்வார் பிறநெஞ்சிற்
பேணிப் புணர்பவர் தோள்.
transliteration:
Nirainenjam illavar thoyvaar piranenjir
penip punarpavar thol.
meaning: Only people without a steady, self-controlled heart will go to the arms of women who hug them while their own hearts are set on someone else.
elementary: Someone who is pretending to be your friend while really thinking about your video games is not giving you their heart. Valluvar says only a person who cannot control their own wishes keeps running after friends like that.
university: Nirai-nenjam (நிறைநெஞ்சம்) is ‘a full or restrained heart’; nirai is the classical virtue of self-control, the power to hold the mind in check, which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as ‘the strength to rule one’s heart’. The women are those who embrace while pira-nenjil peni (பிறநெஞ்சிற் பேணி), ‘cherishing something else in their heart’, which Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah identify as the money they want. The couplet thus contrasts two divided states: the women’s hearts are elsewhere, and the men lack a governed heart of their own. Parimelazhagar connects nirai with the self-mastery praised in chapter 13 (Adakkamudaimai). Both base sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Katha Upanishad’s chariot image, the senses are horses and the mind the reins; for one who lacks understanding and whose mind is never held firm, the senses run wild like a charioteer’s vicious horses.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that an unrestrained mind lets the senses drag a person wherever they go.
hinduism.tie_back: Kural 917’s men without nirai-nenjam are exactly such charioteers who have lost the reins.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs compares a person without self-control to a city with no defenses.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar’s nirai-nenjam illavar are this undefended city.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination,” (the next verse adds: then Paradise will be his refuge).
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the one who restrains the self from its desires.
islam.tie_back: This is the nirai-nenjam that Kural 917 says the weak lack.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma defines true strength as mastery of one’s own impulses.
judaism.tie_back: Kural 917 measures a man the same way: those without that mastery are the ones who fall.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “For a person tormented by evil thoughts, who is passion-dominated and given to the pursuit of pleasure, his craving steadily grows. He makes the fetter strong, indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says an undisciplined mind makes the fetter of craving stronger.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s men without a governed heart tighten that fetter by seeking such company.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One man (women) have in their heart, another in their words, and another still in their actions. Therefore a monk should not trust women, knowing that they are full of deceit.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns that the one whose embrace a man receives may have her heart set on someone else.
jainism.tie_back: This mirrors Kural 917's women who embrace while 'cherishing another in their hearts' (pira-nenjil peni), and the steady, self-governed heart (nirai-nenjam) needed to resist them.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Dark Age of Kali Yuga is the vessel, filled with the wine of sexual desire; the mind is the drunkard.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok addressed to Mardana, Guru Nanak pictures sexual desire as wine and the unruly mind as the one who keeps drinking it. The cure he offers is to make truth, good deeds and modesty the mind’s real food and drink.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says only a heart without self-mastery seeks arms that belong elsewhere, and this salok locates the problem in a mind that cannot stop drinking desire.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 553, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre ki Vaar, Salok (Mardana 1), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe turns Odysseus’ companions into swine with her enchanted food, but Odysseus, protected by the herb moly from Hermes, keeps his mind and is not changed.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth separates those overcome by enchantment from the one who keeps control of himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 917’s nirai-nenjam is Odysseus’ moly: without it, men are transformed by seduction.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you see an attractive person, you will find that self-restraint is the ability you have against your desire.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that each temptation calls on a matching inner capacity.
philosophy.tie_back: That capacity is Valluvar’s nirai, and those who lack it are the ones Kural 917 describes.

real_life_example.event_title: The Countess of Castiglione is sent to win Napoleon III for Italy
real_life_example.event: Virginia Oldoini, Countess of Castiglione, a cousin of the Piedmontese statesman Count Cavour, was sent to Paris to win the French emperor Napoleon III over to the cause of Italian unification. She caused a sensation at the French court and soon, though briefly, became the emperor's mistress. The relationship ended around 1857, after she was ordered to leave Paris for a time following an attack on the emperor in which she had no part.
real_life_example.explanation: Her attachment to the emperor was, by the account of her own sponsors, a means to a political end.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of women who embrace a man while their hearts are set on something else, and the Countess's mission for Italy is a documented case of exactly that.

tamil:
ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்க்கு அணங்கென்ப
மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு.
transliteration:
Aayum arivinar allaarkku anangenba
maaya magalir muyakku.
meaning: For people without the sense to look closely, the hug of tricky, false women is said to be like being grabbed by a demon that leads them to harm.
elementary: In fairy tales, a magic song can make people forget who they are and walk into trouble. Valluvar says that people who do not stop to think can be ‘enchanted’ by false affection in the same way, while thoughtful people can see the trick.
university: Anangu (அணங்கு) in Sangam usage is a dangerous divine power, often a female spirit that seizes and afflicts; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as anangu-thaakku, ‘the attack of an anangu’, and as ‘Mohini’s bewitchment’, and Solomon Pappaiah as ‘a deity who stirs desire and takes life’. Maaya magalir (மாய மகளிர்) are women skilled in maayam (மாயம், deception, illusion). The decisive phrase is aayum arivinar allaar (ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்), ‘those who are not of examining intelligence’: only they experience this as a supernatural seizure, whereas the discerning see an ordinary deception. Enba (என்ப, ‘they say’) marks this as received opinion. Sivayogi Sivakumar alone reads anangu in the positive sense of ‘divine’, as what the foolish mistake such embraces for. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the churning of the ocean, Vishnu takes the form of the enchantress Mohini; the asuras, dazzled by her beauty, hand her the pot of amrita to share out, and she gives it to the devas while the asuras are left with nothing.
hinduism.explanation: The Mohini episode shows how enchantment makes the undiscerning give away what matters most.
hinduism.tie_back: Kalaignar and Mu. Varadarasanar themselves gloss Kural 918’s anangu as ‘Mohini mayakkam’, the Mohini bewitchment.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.”
christianity.explanation: James locates the power of temptation in a person’s own desire.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar likewise implies that the ‘spirit’ works only on those who do not examine themselves.

islam.quote_or_event: “...And what is the worldly life except the enjoyment of delusion.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an calls worldly attractions a pleasure that deceives.
islam.tie_back: Kural 918’s maayam (illusion) is one form of that deceiving enjoyment.

judaism.quote_or_event: Delilah is paid in silver by the Philistine lords to discover the secret of Samson’s strength; she presses him with claims of love until he tells her, and he is captured and blinded.
judaism.explanation: The story is the Hebrew Bible’s classic example of a strong man undone by paid, deceptive affection.
judaism.tie_back: Samson, mighty but undiscerning, is the man of Kural 918 who cannot see through maaya affection.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are lust-infatuated fall back into the swirling current (of samsara) like a spider on its self-spun web.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says infatuation traps a person in a web of their own making.
buddhism.tie_back: In Kural 918, the ‘spell’ that grips the undiscerning is likewise partly their own doing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As (men by baiting) with a piece of flesh a fearless single lion get him into a trap, so women may capture an ascetic though he be careful.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga presents seduction as a snare that catches even the strong and wary.
jainism.tie_back: Kural 918 compares the embrace of deceitful women to seizure by an enchanting spirit (anangu) that ruins those who do not look closely, the same image of a man captured.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The mad-man’s mind is enticed by Maya, the enticer; he has taken the intoxicating drug of falsehood.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan calls Maya mohani, the enchantress who bewitches the mind until it acts as though drugged. The word is the same one the Tamil commentators reach for when they gloss the Kural’s anangu as Mohini’s spell.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares the deceitful embrace to seizure by an enchanting spirit, and Guru Arjan’s enchantress Maya, who leaves the mind drugged and foolish, is a close Sikh counterpart.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1213, Raag Saarang, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “First you will come to the Sirens who enchant all who come near them. If any one unwarily draws in too close and hears the singing of the Sirens, his wife and children will never welcome him home again...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Circe warns Odysseus that the Sirens’ sweet song draws careless sailors to their death; he survives by having himself bound to the mast.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Sirens are a Greek anangu: fatal only to those who come close ‘unwarily’, without the foresight Valluvar calls aayum arivu.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you are struck by the appearance of any promised pleasure, guard yourself against being hurried away by it; but let the affair wait your leisure, and procure yourself some delay.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus advises pausing to examine a tempting impression before acting on it.
philosophy.tie_back: This pause is precisely the aayum arivu (examining intelligence) that Kural 918 says protects against enchantment.

real_life_example.event_title: Ludwig I of Bavaria's infatuation with Lola Montez ends his reign
real_life_example.event: In 1846 the dancer and adventuress Lola Montez performed in Munich, and King Ludwig I became so attached to her that he made her Countess of Landsfeld. Her influence on the government was such that the cabinet was nicknamed the Lola ministry, and the affair further reduced the king's popularity. When the revolutions of 1848 broke out, Ludwig abdicated in favour of his son in March 1848.
real_life_example.explanation: A king who had reigned for more than twenty years lost his throne in part because of an infatuation his subjects would not accept.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those who lack discerning judgment, attachment to such women is like being seized by a spirit that leads to ruin, and Ludwig's attachment helped cost him his crown.

tamil:
வரைவிலா மாணிழையார் மென்தோள் புரையிலாப்
பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு.
transliteration:
Varaivilaa maanizhaiyaar mendhol puraiyilaap
pooriyargal aazhum alaru.
meaning: The soft arms of jewel-wearing women who keep no limits are like a deep, hellish swamp that low and foolish men sink into.
elementary: Picture a pretty field that is really a deep mud bog. It looks soft and inviting, but anyone who walks in without thinking gets stuck and sinks. Valluvar says that ‘love’ that is only bought and sold is like that bog.
university: This couplet supplies the chapter’s title word: varaivilaa (வரைவிலா), ‘without varaivu’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses varaivu as ‘a moral limit’ (ozhukka varaiyarai), and Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah as ‘not distinguishing between high and low’ among those who pay; in akam poetry varaivu also means ‘marriage’, which yields the reading ‘women outside wedlock’. Maanizhaiyaar (மாணிழையார்) is ‘those with fine jewels’. Alaru (அளறு) means both mire or mud and naraka (hell), and the commentators exploit both: Kalaignar speaks of ‘the mire called hell’. Puraiyilaa pooriyargal (புரையிலாப் பூரியர்கள்) are ‘base men without worth’; Sivayogi Sivakumar takes purai as ‘fault’, so ‘those who do not know what is wrong’. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to the hell of self-destruction for the soul—lust, anger, and greed. Therefore, one should abandon all three.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names lust and greed among the gates to hell.
hinduism.tie_back: Kural 919 pictures the place where lust on one side and greed on the other meet as alaru, a hell-mire.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Her feet go down to death; her steps take hold on hell.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs describes the path of the ‘strange woman’ as leading down to death and hell.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar’s alaru is the same downward destination.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an tells believers not even to come near zina (unlawful intimacy), calling it a shameful deed and an evil way.
islam.explanation: The command is to keep clear of the path altogether, not merely to avoid the final act.
islam.tie_back: Kural 919 likewise treats the path itself as a mire that swallows those who enter.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A prostitute is a deep pit; A forbidden woman is a narrow well.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares such company to a deep pit that is hard to climb out of.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the same image as Valluvar’s alaru, the mire in which base men sink.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever is overcome by this wretched and sticky craving, his sorrows grow like grass after the rains.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada calls craving ‘sticky’, something that clings and spreads sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s mire is also sticky: those who step in sink further.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As an elephant, sinking down in a quagmire, sees the raised ground but does not get to the shore, so do we who long for sensual pleasures, not follow the path of monks.”
jainism.explanation: King Brahmadatta admits to the sage Citra that he is stuck in sensual pleasure like an elephant in mud, and the lecture ends with him sinking into the deepest hell.
jainism.tie_back: It closely matches Kural 919's picture of the soft arms of women without limits as a hell-like mire into which undiscerning men sink.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.30, cf. 13.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those fools, who drink in the wine of evil-mindedness, become the husbands of prostitutes.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that people who drink the wine of bad counsel become fools in the company of prostitutes. Elsewhere Gurbani holds out the hope that even the prostitute Ganika was saved by remembering the Name, so no one is beyond grace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls such company a hell-like mire for base, undiscerning men, and Guru Arjan likewise names the evil-minded fool as the one who sinks into it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 399, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus’ scouts in the land of the Lotus-Eaters taste the honey-sweet lotus and lose all wish to return home; he has to drag them back to the ships by force.
greek_mythology.explanation: The episode shows pleasure that makes people forget their purpose and stay stuck.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 919’s base men likewise sink into a sweet-seeming mire they cannot leave.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...he who passes unsanctified and uninitiated into the world below will live in a slough, but that he who arrives there after initiation and purification will dwell with the gods.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates cites the mystery teaching that the impure soul ends in a slough, a muddy swamp, in the afterlife.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s slough and Valluvar’s alaru are the same image: an unpurified life sinks into mire.

real_life_example.event_title: Jahandar Shah's brief reign and devotion to Lal Kunwar
real_life_example.event: Jahandar Shah became Mughal emperor in 1712 after a war of succession. Britannica describes him as a weak and degenerate ruler who raised the courtesan Lal Kunwar, a former dancing girl, to the position of empress-consort and lavished riches on her while failing to pay his soldiers. Within a year his nephew Farrukh-Siyar, backed by the Sayyid brothers, defeated him, and he was put to death in 1713.
real_life_example.explanation: An emperor's indulgence and neglect of his army brought a swift end to his reign and his life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes a hell-like mire into which undiscerning men sink through women who keep no limits, and contemporary historians saw Jahandar Shah's reign as just such a descent.

tamil:
இருமனப் பெண்டிரும் கள்ளும் கவறும்
திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Irumanap pendirum kallum kavarum
thiruneekkap pattaar thodarbu.
meaning: Two-faced women, alcohol and gambling are the friends of people whom good luck has left behind.
elementary: Imagine a kid who spends all their allowance on silly gambling games at the fair, sugary junk, and ‘friends’ who only like them for their money. Soon the money is gone and so are the ‘friends’. Valluvar says these habits are a sign that someone’s good luck is slipping away.
university: The closing couplet groups three ruinous attachments: irumanap pendir (இருமனப் பெண்டிர், ‘women of two minds’, whose heart is in one place and body in another, as Solomon Pappaiah explains), kal (கள், toddy or liquor) and kavaru (கவறு, dice). Their thodarbu (தொடர்பு, ‘association’) belongs to those thiru-neekkap-pattaar (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார்), ‘those from whom Thiru has been removed’; Thiru is both fortune and the goddess Lakshmi (Thirumagal), which is how Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan read it. Parimelazhagar notes that the couplet links this chapter to the next two, Kallunnaamai (93, not drinking) and Soodhu (94, gambling), so it works as a hinge for the whole cluster of vices. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Drinking, dice, women, and hunting, these four (which have been enumerated) in succession, he must know to be the most pernicious in the set that springs from love of pleasure.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu warns a king that these are the worst of the vices born of love of pleasure.
hinduism.tie_back: Three of Manu’s four (drink, dice, women) are exactly Valluvar’s triad of ruin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.”
christianity.explanation: The Prodigal Son loses his inheritance through careless living; his brother later accuses him of spending it on harlots (Luke 15:30).
christianity.tie_back: The prodigal is the thiru-neekkap-pattaan, the man whose fortune leaves him through such company.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allah], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an groups intoxicants and gambling as works of Satan to be avoided for success.
islam.tie_back: Two of Valluvar’s three ruinous companions appear here, set against ‘success’ (falah), close to Valluvar’s thiru.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that loveth pleasure shall be a poor man; He that loveth wine and oil shall not be rich.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs links the love of pleasure and wine to poverty.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise says such loves are the company of those whom fortune has left.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Dice, women, liquor, dancing, singing, sleeping by day, sauntering at unseemly hours, evil companions, avarice — these nine causes ruin a man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists, among causes of ruin, the very triad Valluvar names.
buddhism.tie_back: Dice, women, liquor appear at the head of the list, mirroring Kural 920’s triad of lost fortune.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain codes of lay conduct (shravakachara texts) list seven vices (vyasanas) that a layman must give up completely: gambling, drinking alcohol, eating meat, sexual promiscuity (visiting prostitutes), hunting, theft and adultery.
jainism.explanation: The seven-vice list ties prostitution, drink and gambling together as addictions that ruin a householder.
jainism.tie_back: Kural 920 groups exactly these, double-minded women, liquor and dice, as the companions of those whom fortune has abandoned.
jainism.source: Saptavyasana (seven vices) of the Jain shravakachara literature; glossary entry 'Vyasana', JAINpedia (Institute of Jainology)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The drunkards gamble and look at the wives of others.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas puts drink, gambling and lust for other men’s wives in one line as a single cluster of sins, before saying that even these are less grave than turning one’s back on the Guru. The same three ruinous habits recur together in Sikh moral teaching.
sikhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s own triad, double-minded women, liquor and dice, named together as the companions of the ruined.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 34, Pauri 16 (English translation as published on BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax and searchgurbani.com)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Elpenor, the youngest of Odysseus’ crew, drinks heavily in Circe’s house, sleeps on the roof, and in the morning stumbles off it and breaks his neck.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s small tragedy shows indulgence bringing sudden, pointless ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Elpenor is a minor Greek example of the drink in Kural 920’s triad of misfortune.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epicurus writes that a pleasant life is produced not by continuous drinking and revelry, nor by sensual indulgence or luxurious tables, but by sober reasoning that examines every choice and avoidance.
philosophy.explanation: Even the philosopher of pleasure rejects drinking, revelry and indulgence as the path to happiness.
philosophy.tie_back: Kural 920’s ruinous companions are the very things Epicurus says do not make life good.

real_life_example.event_title: Hogarth publishes A Rake's Progress
real_life_example.event: William Hogarth painted a series of eight pictures, now in Sir John Soane's Museum, and published engravings of them in 1735, after Parliament passed the copyright act known as Hogarth's Act. The series follows Tom Rakewell, a young heir who squanders his inheritance on a dissolute life, including a night of revelry at the Rose Tavern and the loss of a second fortune at the gaming table. He ends in debtors' prison and finally in Bethlem Hospital, known as Bedlam.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the most famous moral satires in British art traces how drink, dissolute company and gambling together ruin a young man of fortune.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names double-minded women, strong drink and dice as the companions of those whom good fortune has abandoned, and Hogarth's series shows all three leading his hero to ruin.

tamil:
உட்கப் படாஅர் ஒளியிழப்பர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Utkap pataaar oliyizhappar enjnjaandrum
katkaadhal kondozhugu vaar.
meaning: People who always crave alcohol will never be feared by their enemies, and they will lose the good name they once had.
elementary: Imagine a strong, respected team captain who starts doing something silly every day. Soon nobody on the other team worries about him any more, and even his own friends stop looking up to him. The Kural says a love of strong drink does exactly that: it makes a person look small.
university: The chapter opens with two losses: the drinker is not utkappadaar (உட்கப்படாஅர், 'not feared', from உட்கு, awe or dread, with an alapedai lengthening) and he oliyizhappar (ஒளியிழப்பர், 'loses his lustre'), where oli (ஒளி) means both brightness and reputation. The habitual sense comes from katkaadhal kondozhuguvaar (கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகுவார்), 'those who conduct themselves holding a love of toddy', so the target is addiction rather than a single lapse. Because the chapter sits in Porutpaal beside Varaivin Magalir (92) and Soothu (94), the traditional reading inherited from Parimelazhagar treats it as one of the vices a ruler must shun; Puliyur Kesikan's gloss on thirukkural.net explicitly makes the subject 'kings' whose enemies no longer fear them and who lose the fame won by their ancestors. Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the subject general. The couplet is identical on ytamizh and thirukkural.net, though the two sites attach the Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar glosses in opposite order.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Son killed sire, and sire killed son, O Bharata. Inebriated with wine, they rushed and fell upon one another.”
hinduism.explanation: At Prabhasa the invincible Vrishni and Andhaka heroes begin a drinking revel, quarrel, and destroy their own clan before Krishna's eyes.
hinduism.tie_back: A warrior people who were once feared lose all their glory through drink, as the Kural warns.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, Section 3 (K. M. Ganguli trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them! … but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.”
christianity.explanation: Isaiah condemns the leaders of Judah who spend their days drinking and lose sight of what truly matters.
christianity.tie_back: The prophet's ‘woe’ on habitual drinkers matches the Kural's picture of a person whose constant craving ruins his standing.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allāh], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ties avoiding intoxicants directly to falah, true success and flourishing.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's drinker loses his lustre; the Qur'an promises success to those who abstain.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wine is not for kings, O Lemuel; Not for kings to drink, Nor any strong drink for princes, Lest they drink and forget what has been ordained, And infringe on the rights of the poor.”
judaism.explanation: The queen mother of King Lemuel warns that rulers who drink forget the law and fail in justice.
judaism.tie_back: Like the traditional royal reading of this Kural, Proverbs says drink is unworthy of a ruler and destroys his authority.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who plays with dice and drinks intoxicants, goes to women who are dear unto others as their own lives, associates with the mean and not with elders — he declines just as the moon during the waning half.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the young householder Sigala that drink is among the habits that make a man's fortunes wane.
buddhism.tie_back: The waning moon is a direct image of the Kural's oliyizhappar, the drinker who loses his light.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He is desirous of women and pleasures, he enters on undertakings and business, drinks liquor, eats meat, becomes strong, a subduer of foes. He eats crisp goats’ meat, his belly grows, and his veins swell with blood--but he gains nothing but life in hell, just as the ram is only fed to be killed for the sake of a guest.”
jainism.explanation: In the Parable of the Ram, Mahāvīra describes the ignorant sinner who drinks and feasts and seems strong and victorious over his enemies, but is only being fattened for ruin, like a ram raised for slaughter.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the habitual drinker loses the awe of his enemies and the lustre of his name; the Jain text grants that the drinker may look strong and fearsome for a while, but says the real outcome is the same downfall.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.6–7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the code of conduct issued by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, forbids Sikhs to take any intoxicant, naming hemp, opium, liquor and tobacco among them.
sikhism.explanation: In Sikh practice abstaining from intoxicants is part of the discipline of a Sikh life, which is meant to keep the Sikh alert, self-governed and fit to serve. Drinking is treated as a breach of that discipline, not a private matter.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the habitual drinker loses the awe of enemies and the lustre of his name, and the Rehat Maryada treats sobriety as part of the dignity a Sikh must keep.
sikhism.source: Sikh Rehat Maryada (Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, Amritsar), English edition on sgpc.net (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The man-eating Cyclops Polyphemus, terror of Odysseus' crew, accepts strong wine, drinks himself into a stupor and is blinded by the very men he had trapped.
greek_mythology.explanation: A monster everyone feared becomes helpless as soon as wine takes hold of him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Wine strips Polyphemus of the dread he inspired, as the Kural says the drinker is no longer feared.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “This evil has betrayed to their enemies the most spirited and warlike races; … this evil has conquered by the wine-cup those who in the field were invincible.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca lists the military disasters drunkenness has brought on peoples and leaders, Alexander among them.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's point is the Kural's: the drinker stops being a threat to his enemies.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 83.22 (Gummere trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: General Mahabat Khan seizes the heavy-drinking Emperor Jahangir on the Jhelum
real_life_example.place: Imperial camp on the Jhelum River, Mughal Empire (now Pakistan)
real_life_example.event: The Mughal emperor Jahangir was a heavy drinker and opium user who, even in the settled middle years of his reign, kept a court official whose charge was the care of the imperial intoxicants. In March 1626 the general Mahabat Khan, summoned to court to answer charges, arrived at the imperial camp on the Jhelum River with about 5,000 Rajput soldiers and, finding the imperial household isolated on one bank, took the emperor captive. Nur Jahan's attempt to rescue her husband failed, and the royal couple remained in Mahabat Khan's hands for months before they managed to slip free later that year.
real_life_example.explanation: An emperor of the richest state in South Asia was seized in his own camp by one of his own commanders, a public humiliation that showed how little awe the throne then commanded.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that those who live in love with drink are not feared by their enemies and lose their lustre, and the habitually intoxicated Jahangir was captured by his own general and had to be rescued by his wife.

tamil:
உண்ணற்க கள்ளை உணில்உண்க சான்றோரான்
எண்ணப் படவேண்டா தார்.
transliteration:
Unnarka kallai unilunka saandroraan
ennap padavendaa thaar.
meaning: Do not drink alcohol. If anyone wants to drink, let it be only those who do not care whether good and wise people respect them.
elementary: Suppose a teacher says, ‘Don't cheat on the test. Well, if you really want to cheat, go ahead, but only if you don't care whether anyone ever trusts you again.’ The teacher isn't giving permission. She is showing how much it costs. The Kural speaks about drinking the same way.
university: The first clause is a flat prohibition, unnarka kallai (உண்ணற்க கள்ளை, 'drink not toddy'). The second, unil unka (உணில் உண்க, 'if you would drink, drink'), is an ironic concession, a figure the commentators call igazhchchi (இகழ்ச்சி, scorn). It limits the 'permission' to those who are saandroraan ennappada vendaathaar (சான்றோரான் எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்), people who do not wish to be esteemed by the saandror (சான்றோர், the noble and learned). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all keep this ironic reading. Puliyur Kesikan adds that the first clause is addressed to arivudaiyor (the wise), since toddy clouds the mind. The structure foreshadows Kural 923, where the saandror again sit in judgment. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The wretched Brahmana who from this day, unable to resist the temptation, will drink wine shall be regarded as having lost his virtue, shall be reckoned to have committed the sin of slaying a Brahmana, shall be hated both in this and the other worlds.”
hinduism.explanation: After unknowingly drinking his disciple Kacha's ashes mixed in his wine, the sage Shukra bans drink for Brahmanas.
hinduism.tie_back: Shukra's decree states the Kural's price outright: whoever drinks gives up the esteem of the virtuous.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 76 (K. M. Ganguli trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to refuse drunkenness and seek a better kind of fullness.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's opening clause, it is a direct command not to give oneself to drink.

islam.quote_or_event: “If a large amount of anything causes intoxication, a small amount of it is prohibited.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet closes the loophole of drinking ‘only a little’.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's mock permission and this hadith both refuse any respectable middle ground for drinking.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Drink no wine or other intoxicant, you or your sons, when you enter the Tent of Meeting, that you may not die. This is a law for all time throughout the ages, for you must distinguish between the sacred and the profane, and between the impure and the pure;”
judaism.explanation: Priests must be sober to keep the clear judgment their sacred role requires.
judaism.tie_back: Those who hope to be counted among the worthy must abstain, which is the Kural's implied ideal.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who destroys life, utters lies, takes what is not given, goes to another man's wife, and is addicted to intoxicating drinks — such a man digs up his own root even in this world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada puts addiction to drink alongside the gravest moral failings.
buddhism.tie_back: Choosing drink means choosing to stand outside the company of the good, just as the Kural implies.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The Most Excellent saints call abstinence from the consumption of wine (madya), flesh (māñsa) and honey (madhu), together with the observance of five small vows (aṇuvrata), as the eight fundamental virtues (mūlaguṇa) of the householder.”
jainism.explanation: Samantabhadra counts giving up wine among the eight root virtues (mūlaguṇa) that every Jain householder must keep, alongside the five small vows.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar's flat command 'drink not toddy' has a direct Jain counterpart in the householder's basic vows, where abstaining from wine is a foundation of a respectable life and not an optional refinement.
jainism.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 66 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018 per wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not drink the false wine at all, if it is in your power.”
sikhism.explanation: After describing how wine drives out sense and makes a man forget his Lord, Guru Amar Das gives a flat command not to drink it at all. He then says that, by the True Guru’s grace, one receives the true wine of the Lord’s love instead.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural’s opening command, drink not, matches Guru Amar Das’s, though the Guru gives no ironic permission to those who do not care about the good.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 554, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Scythian sage Anacharsis is reported to have said that the vine bears three clusters: the first of pleasure, the second of drunkenness, the third of disgust.
greek_mythology.explanation: Anacharsis traces how drinking moves from pleasure to drunkenness to disgust.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, he points to where drinking ends: in the contempt of others.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 1.103 (Hicks trans.)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato's Socrates says the guardians of the ideal city must avoid drunkenness above all, since a guardian is the last person who should be drunk and not know where he is.
philosophy.explanation: Those trusted with the city must keep sober judgment.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato, like the Kural, makes sobriety the condition for being counted among the worthy.

real_life_example.event_title: Babur publicly renounces wine before the Battle of Khanwa
real_life_example.place: Near Sikri and Khanwa, northern India
real_life_example.event: As the Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga of Mewar advanced against him, and his men were losing heart after early setbacks, the Mughal founder Babur publicly forswore wine, which had been one of the great pleasures of his life. About 300 of his nobles and household joined him in the vow, and he also declared the coming fight a holy war, with his men swearing on the Quran not to turn back. Babur then defeated Rana Sanga's much larger army at Khanwa in March 1527, a victory that secured Mughal rule in northern India.
real_life_example.explanation: At the moment when he most needed the trust and respect of his followers, Babur chose to give up drink openly, and the gesture was part of what restored his army's morale.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural bids people not to drink, leaving liquor only to those who do not care for the esteem of the worthy, and Babur gave up wine precisely when he needed the respect of the men who would follow him into battle.

tamil:
ஈன்றாள் முகத்தேயும் இன்னாதால் என்மற்றுச்
சான்றோர் முகத்துக் களி.
transliteration:
Eendraal mugaththeyum innaadhaal enmatruch
chaandror mugaththuk kali.
meaning: Being drunk is painful to see even for the mother who gave birth to you. How much worse must it look to good and wise people?
elementary: Your mom loves you no matter what, even after you spill juice on the carpet. But some behaviour makes even a loving mom sad and embarrassed. If something upsets the person who forgives you most, imagine how it looks to a strict teacher or a respected elder.
university: The couplet argues from the lesser to the greater. Eendraal (ஈன்றாள், 'she who bore') is the most forgiving witness a person has; Puliyur Kesikan glosses her as the one who rejoices whatever her child does. Even 'in her face' (mugaththeyum, முகத்தேயும்) kali (களி, intoxication) is innaadhu (இன்னாது, painful). The question en matru (என் மற்று, 'what, then?') carries the argument to the saandror (சான்றோர்), whom Mu. Varadarasanar describes as having the nature of rebuking faults (குற்றம் கடியும் இயல்பு). The repeated mugam (முகம், face) presents shame as something seen. Kalaignar reads the subject as the son his mother cannot bear to look at. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Chandogya Upanishad names the one who drinks liquor among four great sinners who ‘fall’, along with the thief of gold, the violator of the teacher's bed and the slayer of a Brahmin, and adds as a fifth whoever keeps company with them.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad treats drinking as a fall so grave that it stains even those around the drinker.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, drink brings grief and disgrace not only to the drinker but to those near him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father, and told his two brethren without. And Shem and Japheth took a garment, … and covered the nakedness of their father; and their faces were backward, and they saw not their father's nakedness.”
christianity.explanation: After Noah gets drunk, his own sons cannot bear to look at him and cover his shame.
christianity.tie_back: As with the mother in the Kural, it is the closest family who find the drunkard painful to see.

islam.quote_or_event: “Hamza was drunk and his eyes were red. … and then said, ‘You are not but my father's slaves.’ When the Prophet (ﷺ) understood that Hamza was drunk, he retreated, walking backwards went out and we left with him.”
islam.explanation: Before Islam forbade wine, the Prophet's own uncle Hamza, drunk, insults the Prophet, who quietly withdraws.
islam.tie_back: Drunkenness in the presence of the most honoured person turns into a painful scene of dishonour, as the Kural says.

judaism.quote_or_event: “his father and mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his town at the public place of his community. They shall say to the elders of his town, ‘This son of ours is disloyal and defiant; he does not heed us. He is a glutton and a drunkard.’”
judaism.explanation: The law of the wayward son has the parents themselves bring their drunkard son before the town's elders.
judaism.tie_back: The pain begins with the mother and father and ends before the elders, the same movement as the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In five ways, young householder, the parents thus ministered to as the East by their children, show their compassion: (i) they restrain them from evil, (ii) they encourage them to do good, …”
buddhism.explanation: In the Sigalovada the parents' love shows itself in holding their children back from wrong, intoxicants included, which the same sutta lists as a ruinous habit.
buddhism.tie_back: A parent's grief at a child's drinking comes from this protective love, which the Kural appeals to.

jainism.quote_or_event: “An ignorant man kills, lies, deceives, calumniates, dissembles, drinks liquor, and eats meat, thinking that this is the right thing to do.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra's lecture on 'death against one's will' lists drinking liquor among the habits of the ignorant man (bāla), the opposite of the wise, who brings himself to grief.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that if even a mother cannot bear the sight of her drunken son, the wise will find it far worse; the Uttarādhyayana likewise puts the drinker firmly among the ignorant whom the wise reject.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, those mortals who consume marijuana, fish and wine”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir’s salok goes on to say that whatever pilgrimages, fasts and rituals such people keep, they are lost. For him piety does not excuse intoxication; the wise judge the drinker strictly.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural argues that if drunkenness pains even a forgiving mother, the wise who excuse no fault will see it as worse still, and Kabir is that unforgiving wise judge.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1377, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides' Alcestis, Heracles drinks and sings in King Admetus' house without knowing it is in mourning; a household servant is appalled, and Heracles is ashamed once he learns the truth.
greek_mythology.explanation: The revelry of a hero who is loved and honoured becomes painful to the house that welcomed him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Even friends and household are hurt by the sight of someone in drink, as the Kural says of a mother.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Show how base it is to pour down more liquor than one can carry, and not to know the capacity of one's own stomach; show how often the drunkard does things which make him blush when he is sober; state that drunkenness is nothing but a condition of insanity purposely assumed.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca sets aside Zeno's clever syllogisms against drink and says the honest case against drunkenness is simply to show how shameful it is. He adds that it strips away the sense of shame that otherwise holds men back from wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Seneca makes the drunkard's shame, seen through the eyes of others and of his own sober self, the main charge against drink.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 83.18-19 (tr. Richard Mott Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: The Women's Crusade against the saloons begins at Hillsboro, Ohio
real_life_example.event: After the lecturer Dio Lewis told audiences how his own mother had prayed with other wives of drinking men until a saloon keeper closed his business, women in Hillsboro, Ohio, formed a committee led by Eliza Jane Thompson and from 26 December 1873 went into saloons and drug stores to pray, sing and ask sellers to sign pledges to stop selling liquor. Similar bands spread across the Midwest and Northeast in the winter of 1873-74, drawing tens of thousands of women, most of whom had until then confined themselves to the roles of wives and mothers. The movement led directly to the founding of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union in Cleveland in November 1874.
real_life_example.explanation: The Crusade showed how deeply drunkenness wounded the women closest to drinkers, enough to bring wives and mothers out of their homes into public protest for the first time on such a scale.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that drunkenness is painful to see even for a mother, the most forgiving of witnesses, and the Women's Crusade was born from the grief of mothers and wives watching the men of their families drink.

tamil:
நாண்என்னும் நல்லாள் புறங்கொடுக்கும் கள்ளென்னும்
பேணாப் பெருங்குற்றத் தார்க்கு.
transliteration:
Naanennum nallaal purangodukkum kallennum
penaap perungutrath thaarkku.
meaning: The good lady called Shame (the feeling that stops us from doing wrong) turns her back on those who commit the great wrong of drinking, a wrong no one should welcome.
elementary: Picture Modesty as a kind lady who walks beside you and whispers ‘don't do that, it's embarrassing.’ The Kural says that when someone gets drunk she turns around and walks away, so there's no one left to stop him doing shameful things.
university: Naan (நாண், modesty, the sense of shame) is personified as a nallaal (நல்லாள், a good woman). Purangodukkum (புறங்கொடுக்கும்), literally 'gives the back', is a battlefield term for retreat, so Modesty flees from the drinker as a beaten warrior flees. The parallel compounds naanennum nallaal / kallennum penaap perungutram (கள்ளென்னும் பேணாப் பெருங்குற்றம், 'the great fault called toddy, which none would cherish') set a personified virtue against a personified vice. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses that she will not stand before the drinker; Solomon Pappaiah renders it as Modesty showing her back and going away. The idea looks ahead to Naanudaimai (chapter 102). The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Manusmriti counts drinking sura among the mahapatakas, the great sins, together with killing a Brahmin, stealing gold and violating the teacher's bed, and prescribes severe penances for it.
hinduism.explanation: Dharma law ranks drinking among the gravest offences a twice-born person can commit.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's perungutram, ‘great fault’, has a formal counterpart in Manu's ‘great sin’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.”
christianity.explanation: Paul sets decent, honest conduct against drunkenness and the shameless behaviour that comes with it.
christianity.tie_back: In both texts drunkenness is where decency and modesty give way.

islam.quote_or_event: “An adulterer, at the time he is committing illegal sexual intercourse is not a believer; and a person, at the time of drinking an alcoholic drink is not a believer; …”
islam.explanation: At the moment of drinking, faith is said to leave the drinker.
islam.tie_back: As the Kural's Modesty turns her back, faith (which other hadith pair with modesty) steps away from the drinker.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You shall be sated with shame Rather than glory: Drink in your turn and stagger! The cup in GOD's right hand Shall come around to you, And disgrace to your glory.”
judaism.explanation: Habakkuk pronounces that the one who makes others drunk will himself drink and stagger into disgrace.
judaism.tie_back: Drink brings disgrace in place of dignity, the same exchange the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are, young householder, these six evil consequences in indulging in intoxicants which cause infatuation and heedlessness: (i) loss of wealth, (ii) increase of quarrels, (iii) susceptibility to disease, (iv) earning an evil reputation, (v) shameless exposure of body, (vi) weakening of intellect.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists shamelessness among the direct results of intoxicants.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Shameless exposure’ is the Buddhist way of saying Modesty has left the drinker.

jainism.quote_or_event: Hemacandra's list of the thirty-five qualities of an ideal Jain householder includes salajja, being moved by a sense of shame, alongside such virtues as fearing sin and mastering the senses, while abstinence from wine is counted among the householder's eight root virtues.
jainism.explanation: Jain lay ethics treats a living sense of shame (lajjā) as a mark of the good householder, and renouncing wine as one of his basic vows.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar pictures Modesty as a noble woman who turns her back on the drinker; in the Jain householder's code, shame and abstinence from wine likewise go together as signs of the same upright character.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of thirty-five śrāvaka-guṇas (no. 30, salajja) and the eight mūlaguṇas, as summarised in V.A. Sangave, 'Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make virtue your bread, good conduct the ghee, and modesty the meat to eat.”
sikhism.explanation: Having pictured desire as wine and the mind as a drunkard, Guru Nanak offers a different meal: virtue, good conduct and modesty (saram). The Gurmukh who lives on these is cleansed of sin.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the lady Modesty turns her back on the drinker, and Guru Nanak puts modesty at the very place where the drinker puts his wine.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 553, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre ki Vaar, Salok (Mardana 1), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “When the wine had got into his head he went mad and did ill deeds about the house of Peirithous; this angered the heroes who were there assembled, …”
greek_mythology.explanation: The centaur Eurytion, drunk at a wedding feast, behaves disgracefully in his host's house and is punished.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Once wine took hold, all restraint and sense of shame left Eurytion, as the Kural says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Drunkenness kindles and discloses every kind of vice, and removes the sense of shame that veils our evil undertakings. For more men abstain from forbidden actions because they are ashamed of sinning than because their inclinations are good.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca says drink takes away the shame that usually keeps people from wrongdoing.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's picture of Modesty leaving the drinker.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 83.19 (Gummere trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: Andrew Johnson's intoxicated vice-presidential inaugural speech
real_life_example.place: Senate Chamber, United States Capitol, Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: Before being sworn in as vice president, Andrew Johnson, who had spent the previous evening drinking and reportedly took three glasses of whiskey that morning against fatigue and a cold, rose to address a Senate Chamber filled with senators, justices, diplomats and President Lincoln. He rambled for about twenty minutes about his humble origins, ignored outgoing vice president Hannibal Hamlin's tugs on his coat, and was too disoriented to swear in the new senators, a task a clerk completed. Senators were mortified, reporters wired the story across the country, and both Massachusetts senators introduced a resolution calling for his resignation.
real_life_example.explanation: In one morning of drink a man about to stand next in line for the presidency publicly shamed himself before the nation's leaders.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the noble lady Modesty turns her back on those who drink, and on that morning Johnson's sense of shame deserted him in front of the whole Senate.

tamil:
கையறி யாமை உடைத்தே பொருள்கொடுத்து
மெய்யறி யாமை கொளல்.
transliteration:
Kaiyari yaamai udaiththe porulkoduththu
meyyari yaamai kolal.
meaning: Paying money just to buy a state where you no longer know yourself shows that you do not understand what you are doing.
elementary: Imagine spending all your pocket money on a ticket for a ride that makes you so dizzy you can't remember your own name, and then trips you over. You'd be paying to lose yourself. The Kural says buying liquor is that kind of bad deal.
university: The couplet balances two forms of ignorance: kaiyariyaamai (கையறியாமை) and meyyariyaamai (மெய்யறியாமை). The second clearly means not knowing one's own body or self, the stupor that porul koduththu (பொருள்கொடுத்து, 'by giving wealth') one kolal (கொளல், 'takes on'). The first is read in two ways. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as not knowing what to do, a failure of practical sense. Puliyur Kesikan (thirukkural.net) reads it as having one's past karma as its cause, so only an ill-fated person would make such a bargain. Kalaignar calls it folly beyond words. The Kural's irony is economic: wealth, the subject of Porutpaal, is spent to buy unawareness. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From anger, delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost, one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces how a clouded mind loses memory and then understanding.
hinduism.tie_back: The drinker in the Kural pays for the same sequence of delusion, lost self-awareness and downfall.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh: For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that heavy drinking leads to stupor and poverty.
christianity.tie_back: The bad bargain is the same: money goes out, and stupor and ruin come back.

islam.quote_or_event: “They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, ‘In them is great sin and [yet, some] benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an weighs wine's small gain against its far greater harm.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it judges drinking a losing bargain.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas said: morning sleep, midday wine, children's talk and sitting in the assemblies of the ignorant put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: Wine in the middle of the day is listed among the habits that waste a person's life.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, drinking is something a person chooses that takes him out of his own life and purpose.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The fifth lay precept is to refrain from surā-meraya-majja, intoxicants that are a ground for pamāda, heedlessness.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist ethics defines intoxicants by what they do: they produce heedlessness.
buddhism.tie_back: Pamāda is the Kural's meyyariyaamai, not knowing oneself.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Wine deludes the mind and a deluded person tends to forget piety; the person who forgets piety commits hiṃsā without hesitation.”
jainism.explanation: Amṛtacandra explains that wine clouds the mind, a clouded mind forgets dharma, and a person who has forgotten dharma harms living beings without a second thought.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar mocks the man who pays good money to buy a state in which he no longer knows himself; Amṛtacandra traces what that self-forgetting leads to, from the clouded mind to forgotten dharma and then to violence.
jainism.source: Amṛtacandra, Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya v. 62 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2012), as quoted in the explanatory note to Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 66 on wisdomlib.org

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One person brings a full bottle, and another fills his cup. Drinking the wine, his intelligence departs, and madness enters his mind; he cannot distinguish between his own and others”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the drinking party itself: one brings the bottle, another pours, and the drink takes away the drinker’s mind until he no longer knows his own from what is someone else’s. It also makes him forget his Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural mocks the one who pays to buy a state where he no longer knows himself, and Guru Amar Das describes that same self-loss in detail.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 554, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe gives Odysseus' men a mixture with Pramnian wine laced with drugs; they forget their homeland and are turned into swine.
greek_mythology.explanation: The men eagerly take a drink that robs them of memory and of their human selves.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They take a drink and receive self-forgetting in return, the Kural's meyyariyaamai.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “penalties are doubled in the case of drunkenness; for the moving principle is in the man himself, since he had the power of not getting drunk and his getting drunk was the cause of his ignorance.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that ignorance a person brings on himself through drink does not excuse him; it makes him more blameworthy.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's argument exactly: whoever pays for his own ignorance chose his folly.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.5 (W. D. Ross trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: Hogarth's Gin Lane and the Gin Act end London's Gin Craze
real_life_example.event: In the first half of the eighteenth century cheap, unlicensed gin became so widely sold in London that by 1723 Londoners were estimated to drink on average a pint a week, and people addicted to it spent their wages on drink and sold or pawned their possessions to buy more. In 1751 William Hogarth published Gin Lane, set in St Giles, where a sign over a gin cellar advertised that a customer could be drunk for a penny and dead drunk for twopence, and where the pawnbroker, distiller and undertaker thrive while the poor decay. The print supported the Gin Act of 1751, which restricted who could sell gin and raised its cost, after which gin drinking declined.
real_life_example.explanation: The Gin Craze is a famous case of a whole city paying away its earnings and goods to buy oblivion.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural mocks those who pay good money to buy a state in which they no longer know themselves, and the gin sellers of St Giles literally priced unconsciousness at a penny or twopence.

tamil:
துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
நஞ்சுண்பார் கள்ளுண் பவர்.
transliteration:
Thunjinaar seththaarin verallar enjnjaandrum
nanjunpaar kallun pavar.
meaning: People who are asleep are no different from the dead. In the same way, people who drink alcohol are always no different from people who drink poison.
elementary: When someone is fast asleep, they can't see, hear or help anyone, almost as if they weren't there at all. The Kural says drinking liquor is like taking a little poison: it switches off your mind the same way.
university: The couplet is an udhaaranam (உதாரணம், exemplum) built on two equations. Thunjinaar (துஞ்சினார், those asleep) are 'not different from' (verallar, வேறல்லர்) seththaar (செத்தார், the dead), because both lack awareness. Likewise kallunbavar (கள்ளுண்பவர், toddy-drinkers) are always nanjunbaar (நஞ்சுண்பார், poison-eaters). Mu. Varadarasanar gives the shared term as arivu mayangudhal (அறிவு மயங்குதல், clouding of understanding). Puliyur Kesikan applies enjnjaandrum (எஞ்ஞான்றும், 'always') to the second clause: the drinker is permanently poisoned, while the sleeper only appears dead for a while. Kalaignar reverses the order and reads it as a hyperbole. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “What Kshatriya is there who, armed with weapons, will slay men locked in the embraces of sleep and, therefore, already dead?”
hinduism.explanation: At the drunken revel before the Yadavas' self-destruction, Satyaki taunts Kritavarma for killing sleeping warriors, men he calls ‘already dead’.
hinduism.tie_back: The epic uses the Kural's own equation of the sleeper with the dead, spoken in a scene where drink is the poison.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, Section 3 (K. M. Ganguli trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober. For they that sleep sleep in the night; and they that be drunken are drunken in the night.”
christianity.explanation: Paul puts sleep and drunkenness side by side as two kinds of unawareness that belong to the night.
christianity.tie_back: This is the same pairing the Kural makes: the sleeper and the drinker are both absent from life.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allāh and from prayer. So will you not desist?”
islam.explanation: Intoxicants cut a person off from remembering God and from prayer.
islam.tie_back: The drinker is spiritually ‘asleep’, as the Kural's drinker is as good as poisoned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They taught that an intoxicated person is responsible for all his actions only in a case where he did not reach the state of intoxication of Lot; however, if he reached the state of intoxication of Lot, so that he is altogether unaware of his actions, he is exempt from all liability.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud describes a level of drunkenness so deep that a person counts as no longer present as a moral agent.
judaism.tie_back: Lot's state is the Kural's sleeper-as-dead: there, but not aware.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 65a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that heedfulness is the path to the Deathless and heedlessness the path to death; the heedful do not die, while the heedless are as if dead already.
buddhism.explanation: Heedlessness (pamāda), which intoxicants produce, is treated as a living death.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that losing awareness is already a kind of dying.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana compares sense pleasures to the kimpāka fruit, which tastes sweet but is a deadly poison once it is digested.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says toddy-drinkers are always no different from those who swallow poison; the Jain sūtra makes the same equation between a pleasant indulgence and poison, though it speaks of pleasures in general.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Great Giver has given the intoxicating drug of falsehood. The people are intoxicated; they have forgotten death, and they have fun for a few days.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says that worldly attachment works on people like a narcotic: under its influence they forget that they must die and enjoy themselves for a few short days. Intoxication here is the state of a life heading toward death without knowing it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says drinkers are always like people swallowing poison, and Guru Nanak’s intoxicated crowd, revelling while they forget death, is the same picture.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Elpenor, youngest of Odysseus' crew, gets drunk at Circe's house, sleeps on the roof, and on waking falls and breaks his neck; his shade later meets Odysseus in the underworld.
greek_mythology.explanation: A drunken sleep becomes real death.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's chain of sleep, death and drink-as-poison happens literally to Elpenor.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For if you try to prove that the wise man can souse himself with much wine and yet keep his course straight, … you may go on to infer by syllogisms that he will not die if he swallows poison, that he will not sleep if he takes a sleeping-potion, …”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca mocks the idea that the wise can drink heavily unharmed, placing wine beside poison and sleeping draughts.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca puts wine, poison and sleep together just as the Kural does.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 83.27 (Gummere trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: Repin paints the dying Modest Mussorgsky
real_life_example.event: After the triumphs of Boris Godunov and Pictures at an Exhibition in 1874, the composer Modest Mussorgsky fell into drinking bouts in St Petersburg taverns that could last for days, and his worsening alcoholism eventually made him unemployable in the government posts that supported him. In early 1881 he was hospitalised with chronic alcoholism, and the collector Pavel Tretyakov sent Ilya Repin to paint him; Repin's red-nosed portrait, made over a few sittings, now hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery. Mussorgsky died on 28 March 1881, aged only forty-two, before Repin could return for a final sitting.
real_life_example.explanation: One of Russia's most original composers was destroyed by drink at forty-two, and the portrait painted in his last days became one of the most famous images of a ruined genius.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that drinkers are no different from those who swallow poison, and Mussorgsky's drinking worked on him like a slow poison that killed him in his prime.

tamil:
உள்ளொற்றி உள்ளூர் நகப்படுவர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
கள்ளொற்றிக் கண்சாய் பவர்.
transliteration:
Ullotri ulloor nagappaduvar enjnjaandrum
kallotrik kansaai pavar.
meaning: People who drink in secret until their eyes droop will have their secret found out by the people of their town, who will always laugh at them.
elementary: If you sneak cookies before dinner, the crumbs on your shirt give you away. The Kural says people who drink in secret are the same: their sleepy, drooping eyes tell everyone, and the whole neighbourhood ends up laughing.
university: The verb otri (ஒற்றி, 'in hiding') is used twice. Kal otri (கள்ளொற்றி) is drinking toddy secretly, and ul otri (உள்ளொற்றி) is the townsfolk spying out what is inside. Kansaaibavar (கண்சாய்பவர்) are 'those whose eyes droop', the physical sign that betrays them. Ulloor (உள்ளூர், one's own town) makes the mockery (nagappaduvar, நகப்படுவர், 'will be laughed at') come from neighbours, not strangers. Mu. Varadarasanar reads ul otri as the townsfolk probing into hidden matters. Kalaignar stresses that the reeling eyes cannot be hidden. thirukkural.net prints the couplet without the closing full stop; the wording is otherwise identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Manusmriti prescribes that a twice-born man convicted of drinking sura be branded on the forehead with the sign of a tavern flag, so that his offence is publicly visible and he is shunned.
