hinduism.explanation: Drinking is made permanently public, so everyone in the community knows.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the drinker's secret ends in public exposure and scorn.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti, Chapter 9 (punishments for the great sins) (Bühler trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they also have erred through wine, and through strong drink are out of the way; the priest and the prophet have erred through strong drink, they are swallowed up of wine, … they err in vision, they stumble in judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Isaiah publicly exposes priests and prophets whose drinking shows in their failing sight and judgment.
christianity.tie_back: Even respected men cannot hide drink; it shows in the eyes and steps, as the Kural says.

islam.quote_or_event: When a man who had drunk wine was brought to the Prophet and beaten as a penalty, some onlookers cursed him; the Prophet forbade them, saying not to help Satan against their brother.
islam.explanation: The drinker's exposure brings the community's scorn, which the Prophet himself checks.
islam.tie_back: The townsfolk's ridicule the Kural describes is real, though Islam here restrains it with mercy.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Hudud (the drinker brought for punishment)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who cries, ‘Woe!’ who, ‘Alas!’; Who has quarrels, who complaints; Who has wounds without cause; Who has bleary eyes? Those whom wine keeps till the small hours, Those who gather to drain the cups.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs names the drinker's tell-tale bleary eyes, earned in late-night drinking.
judaism.tie_back: The ‘bleary eyes’ are the Kural's kansaai, drooping eyes that give the secret away.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The monk Sāgata, famed for taming a fierce nāga, was given strong drink by admiring lay followers and was found lying drunk at the town gate; the Buddha rebuked him before the Sangha and laid down the rule against intoxicants.
buddhism.explanation: A celebrated monk is exposed in public, and his fall brings the whole order into disrepute.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, drink exposed at the town gate turns respect into public shame.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Daśavaikālika Sūtra warns the monk not to drink surā or other intoxicants, and describes one who drinks alone in secret, thinking that nobody knows, whose faults and deceit nonetheless become plain for others to see, so that his disgrace grows.
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic teaching treats secret drinking as a double fault, the drinking and the deceit of hiding it, and says such a monk is found out and loses his good standing.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who drink in secret until their eyes droop will be found out and laughed at in their own town; the Daśavaikālika makes the same point, that the secret drinker who thinks no one sees him is exposed.
jainism.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra 5.2 (second part of the chapter on alms-seeking, Piṇḍaiṣaṇā; vv. 36 ff. in standard numbering)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Their falsehood and fraud cannot remain concealed; their false appearances fall off in the end.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that people who live behind a false front are found out in the end, when the coating wears off. What is done in secret does not stay hidden.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural’s secret drinker, betrayed by his drooping eyes and laughed at by his own town, is one case of the exposure Guru Ram Das describes.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 303, Raag Gauree, Gauree ki Vaar, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phrygian peasants find old Silenus wandering drunk, bind him with garlands and lead him to King Midas.
greek_mythology.explanation: Dionysus' companion is caught in drink and paraded before a king.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The drunk who stumbles is found out and made a spectacle by the locals, as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Besides, we forget who we are, we utter words that are halting and poorly enunciated, the glance is unsteady, the step falters, the head is dizzy, …”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca lists the bodily signs that give drunkenness away.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘The glance is unsteady’ is the Kural's kansaai: the eyes betray the hidden drinker.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 83.21 (Gummere trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: George Cassiday, the Man in the Green Hat, exposes Congress's secret drinking
real_life_example.place: United States Capitol, Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: Throughout Prohibition, a bootlegger named George Cassiday quietly delivered liquor in a leather briefcase to the offices of members of the House and Senate, beginning with two House members who had voted for Prohibition. After a 1925 arrest in the House office building made him famous as the Man in the Green Hat, he moved his trade to the Senate side, until Prohibition agents caught him with six bottles of gin in the senators' parking lot on 18 February 1930. He then wrote a front-page series for the Washington Post describing how he had helped about 80 percent of lawmakers break the law, and senators demanded in vain that his client list be published to clear their names.
real_life_example.explanation: Lawmakers who publicly supported Prohibition while drinking in private became a national symbol of hypocrisy once their supplier told his story.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that those who drink in secret will have their secret found out and be laughed at by their own townspeople, and Congress's hidden drinking was exposed and mocked across the nation.

tamil:
களித்தறியேன் என்பது கைவிடுக நெஞ்சத்து
ஒளித்ததூஉம் ஆங்கே மிகும்.
transliteration:
Kaliththariyen enbadhu kaividuka nenjaththu
oliththadhooum aange migum.
meaning: A drinker should stop saying, 'I have never been drunk.' When they drink, whatever they hid in their heart comes out even more.
elementary: It's like a shaken bottle of fizzy drink: open it and everything inside comes spraying out. The Kural says drink opens people up the same way, so pretending you never drink doesn't work. Your secrets fizz out the moment you do.
university: Kaliththariyen (களித்தறியேன்) is the drinker's own denial: 'I have never known intoxication.' Kaividuka (கைவிடுக, 'give it up') tells him to drop the lie. The reason is nenjaththu oliththadhooum (நெஞ்சத்து ஒளித்ததூஉம், 'even what was hidden in the heart'; the -ooum is an alapedai of -um, 'even') aange migum (ஆங்கே மிகும், 'there and then increases', that is, comes out all the more). Mu. Varadarasanar reads the hidden thing as the hidden fault; Puliyur Kesikan as the earlier concealment of drinking itself; Kalaignar as the truth that the drunk man blurts out. The idea is close to the Graeco-Roman proverb 'in wine, truth'. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the Prabhasa revel the drunken Yadava heroes bring up old, buried grievances: Satyaki's contempt for Kritavarma's night massacre, Kritavarma's taunt about Bhurishrava, and the affair of the Syamantaka gem. The quarrel turns into slaughter.
hinduism.explanation: Resentments hidden for years come out the moment wine loosens the heroes' tongues.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's warning in narrative form: drink brings out what was hidden in the heart.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva, Section 3 (K. M. Ganguli trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that under wine the heart speaks out its distortions.
christianity.tie_back: The ‘heart’ that ‘utters’ is the Kural's nenjaththu oliththadhu, what is hidden in the heart, coming out.

islam.quote_or_event: “Avoid Khamr for it is the mother of all evils. … He said: ‘Pour me a cup of this wine.’ So she poured him a cup. He said: ‘Give me more.’ And soon he had intercourse with her and killed the boy.”
islam.explanation: Uthman tells of a devout worshipper who chose wine as the ‘least’ of three sins, and drink then led him into the other two.
islam.tie_back: The cup lets out every evil the man had held back, as the Kural warns.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wine [yayin] was given in seventy letters, … Similarly, the word secret [sod] was given in seventy letters, … Typically, when wine entered the body, a secret emerged.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud notes that 'wine' and 'secret' have the same numerical value of seventy: when wine goes in, the secret comes out.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost word for word the Kural's claim that drink brings out what the heart hid.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 65a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one's own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another's faults, but hides one's own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada describes the habit of hiding one's own faults.
buddhism.tie_back: The drinker who denies drinking is hiding his fault, which the Kural says cannot stay hidden.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pride, fear, disgust, laughter, disliking, grief, sex-passion, and anger etc., are bywords for hiṃsā; and all these go together with wine.”
jainism.explanation: Amṛtacandra teaches that the passions (kaṣāya) and quasi-passions that make up inner violence all go along with wine and come out under its influence.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that once a man drinks, whatever he has hidden in his heart comes out all the more; Amṛtacandra likewise holds that wine brings to the surface the pride, anger, lust and other passions a person carries within.
jainism.source: Amṛtacandra, Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya v. 64 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2012), as quoted in the explanatory note to Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 66 on wisdomlib.org

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That which is within them, comes out; it cannot be concealed by concealment.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak observes that whatever lies inside a person sooner or later shows itself, however hard they try to hide it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the drinker to stop denying it, since whatever is hidden in his heart comes out the moment he drinks, and Guru Nanak states the same law in general form.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1243, Raag Saarang, Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The lyric poet Alcaeus is credited with the saying that wine and truth go together, the origin of the Latin proverb in vino veritas.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tradition held that wine strips away pretence and lets the truth out.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: whatever is hidden comes out with wine.
greek_mythology.source: Alcaeus, fragment (via the proverb ‘in vino veritas’)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “When the strength of wine has become too great and has gained control over the mind, every lurking evil comes forth from its hiding-place. Drunkenness does not create vice, it merely brings it into view; …”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca says drink does not create vices but exposes those already present.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's nenjaththu oliththadhooum aange migum almost exactly.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 83.20 (Gummere trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: Cleitus speaks his grievances at a drinking party and is killed by Alexander
real_life_example.event: At a banquet in Maracanda, the officer Cleitus, who had saved Alexander's life at the Granicus and had just been named governor of Bactria, heard courtiers flatter Alexander at the expense of his father Philip and the older generation of commanders. Heated with wine, Cleitus answered with insolent words, praising Philip and saying that soldiers win the victories for which generals take the glory. Alexander, also in a drunken rage, seized a weapon and killed him, and when sober again was overcome with remorse for days.
real_life_example.explanation: Wine drew out resentments that Cleitus had kept to himself and stripped away the restraint of both men, turning a feast into a tragedy that Alexander bitterly regretted.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that the moment a man drinks, whatever he has hidden in his heart comes out all the more, as Cleitus's long-held grievances burst out at the drinking party.

tamil:
களித்தானைக் காரணம் காட்டுதல் கீழ்நீர்க்
குளித்தானைத் தீத்துரீஇ அற்று.
transliteration:
Kaliththaanaik kaaranam kaattudhal keezhneerk
kuliththaanaith theeththureei atru.
meaning: Trying to reason with a drunk person is like taking a burning torch under deep water to look for someone who has sunk.
elementary: Imagine your friend has dived to the bottom of a pool and you try to find him by shining a candle from the side. The water puts the flame out and you can't reach him. The Kural says giving good reasons to someone who is drunk is like that: your words can't get through.
university: Kaaranam kaattudhal (காரணம் காட்டுதல், 'showing reasons') is set against keezhneer kuliththaan (கீழ்நீர்க் குளித்தான், 'one who has plunged into deep water'), and the attempt is theeththureei atru (தீத்துரீஇ அற்று, 'like searching with fire'). Thuru (துருவுதல்) means to probe or search, and the -eei is an alapedai lengthening. The image works twice over: fire cannot burn under water, and a drowned man is beyond help. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as trying to sober or reform the drinker with arguments. Puliyur Kesikan takes kaaranam kaattudhal as pointing to another drunk as a warning, which leads into Kural 930. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Kishkindha Kanda, Sugriva, restored to his throne, sinks into drink and pleasure and forgets his promise to Rama; earlier counsel has no effect, and only Lakshmana's furious arrival at the gates rouses him.
hinduism.explanation: Reasoning cannot reach a king lost in revelry; only a shock brings him back.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural says, reasons do not reach someone sunk in drink.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoredom and wine and new wine take away the heart.”
christianity.explanation: Hosea says wine takes away the ‘heart’, which in Hebrew thought is the seat of understanding.
christianity.tie_back: Once understanding is gone, there is nothing left for reasons to work on, which is why the Kural's torch is useless.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying …”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an recognises that an intoxicated person does not know what he is saying, so prayer has to wait until he is sober.
islam.tie_back: If the drinker cannot follow his own words, others' reasons will not reach him either, as the Kural says.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You will be like one lying in bed on high seas, Like one lying on top of the rigging. ‘They struck me, but I felt no hurt; They beat me, but I was unaware; …’”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs pictures the drunkard as someone lost at sea who feels nothing.
judaism.tie_back: The sea image matches the Kural's man under water whom no light or reason can reach.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who is drunk, poor, destitute, still thirsty whilst drinking, frequents the bars, sinks in debt as a stone in water, swiftly brings disrepute to his family.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the drinker sinking ‘as a stone in water’, still thirsty even while drinking.
buddhism.tie_back: The sinking stone matches the Kural's drowned man, beyond reach.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who has not renounced pleasure, will miss his aim (i.e. the true end of his soul); for though he has been taught the right way, he will go astray again and again.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana observes that a person still held by pleasure keeps going astray even after being shown the right path, so instruction alone cannot save him.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says reasoning with a drunk man is like searching with a torch for someone sunk deep under water; the Jain text likewise says that teaching cannot reach one who is still bound to his pleasures.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Don't argue with fools.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak’s salok ends with plain advice not to quarrel with a fool, since argument does not reach a mind that has lost its judgment.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says reasoning with a drunk is like searching with a torch under deep water, and Guru Nanak likewise judges argument with the senseless to be wasted effort.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1 (before Pauri 19), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the wedding of Pirithous, the drunken centaurs led by Eurytus try to carry off the bride; no appeal stops them, and the feast becomes the battle of the Lapiths and Centaurs.
greek_mythology.explanation: Once the centaurs are drunk, only force can stop them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As the Kural says, reasoning is useless against the drunk.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that people in a state like drunkenness can repeat proofs or recite verses of Empedocles without their knowledge actually working, like those asleep, mad or drunk.
philosophy.explanation: The drunk may hear words, even repeat them, but the reasoning does not engage.
philosophy.tie_back: The torch is lit, but it cannot work under water.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VII.3 (W. D. Ross trans.)

real_life_example.event_title: The Bronte family fails to rescue Branwell Bronte from drink
real_life_example.event: After he was dismissed from his post as a tutor at Thorp Green in July 1845, Branwell Bronte, the only brother of Charlotte, Emily and Anne, returned to Haworth and over the next three years sank into dependence on alcohol and opium. His family's distress is recorded in Charlotte's letters, the local doctor recommended only that he abstain from alcohol, and in his last year his father, the Reverend Patrick Bronte, took him into his own room to watch over him at night. Branwell's health collapsed and he died on 24 September 1848, aged thirty-one, probably of tuberculosis.
real_life_example.explanation: A family of exceptional intelligence and devotion could neither argue nor watch Branwell out of his addiction.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares reasoning with a drunkard to searching with a torch for someone sunk deep under water, and all the advice and care of Branwell's family could not reach him.

tamil:
கள்ளுண்ணாப் போழ்திற் களித்தானைக் காணுங்கால்
உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு.
transliteration:
Kallunnaap pozhdhir kaliththaanaik kaanungaal
ullaankol undadhan sorvu.
meaning: When a drinker is sober and sees someone else who is drunk, do they not think that they look just as bad when they drink?
elementary: Have you ever laughed at someone acting silly, then realised you act just like that sometimes? The Kural asks why a drinker, seeing another person drunk and stumbling, doesn't think, ‘Oh no, that's me when I drink!’
university: The closing couplet is a rhetorical question marked by kol (கொல்). When the drinker, in kallunnaap pozhdhu (கள்ளுண்ணாப் போழ்து, 'the time he is not drinking'), sees a kaliththaan (களித்தான், a drunk man), will he not reflect, ullaan (உள்ளான், 'will he not consider'), on the sorvu (சோர்வு, slackness, lapse) that comes from his own drinking? The appeal is to self-recognition. Commentators agree on this reading: Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesikan all take it as a sober drinker seeing his own condition in another. Mu. Varadarasanar's printed gloss reads மயங்கினவளை ('the intoxicated woman') on both base sites, apparently a typographical slip for மயங்கினவனை. The text is identical on ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The learned Sukra, having been deceived while under the influence of wine, and remembering the total loss of consciousness that is one of the terrible consequences of drink, and beholding too before him the handsome Kacha whom he had, in a state of unconsciousness, drunk with his wine, then thought of effecting a reform in the manners of Brahmanas.”
hinduism.explanation: Once sober, Shukra looks back at what drink made him do and acts on it.
hinduism.tie_back: Shukra does what the Kural hopes every sober drinker will do: reflect and change.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 76 (K. M. Ganguli trans.)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus calls on his hearers to watch themselves so that drunkenness does not catch them unprepared.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Take heed to yourselves’ is the same self-examination the Kural asks of the sober drinker.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allāh and from prayer. So will you not desist?”
islam.explanation: After setting out the harms of intoxicants, the Qur'an ends with a pointed question.
islam.tie_back: ‘So will you not desist?’ has the same rhetorical form as the Kural's ‘will he not reflect?’

judaism.quote_or_event: “‘They struck me, but I felt no hurt; They beat me, but I was unaware; As often as I wake, I go after it again.’”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs gives the drinker's own voice: he wakes, feels nothing, and goes straight back to the cup.
judaism.tie_back: This is the failure the Kural laments: the drinker who, even when sober, will not reflect.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kumbha Jataka, Sakka appears before King Sabbamitta carrying a jar of liquor and describes in verse everything the drink will do to him; the king, seeing the effects laid out before he drinks, gives up liquor.
buddhism.explanation: A vivid picture of drunkenness's effects leads a king to renounce it while still sober.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the reflection the Kural hopes for: seeing the effects and applying them to oneself.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When one thus knows that a (virtuous) monk or householder will be gladdened (by his gain), how, then, should a man, whilst he is losing (his chance), not be conscious of his losing it?”
jainism.explanation: After the parable of the three merchants, the Uttarādhyayana asks how a person who sees others gaining by virtue can fail to notice his own loss.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar closes by asking whether the drinker who sees another man reeling drunk does not recognise his own state; the Jain verse asks the same kind of question, urging a person to see his own loss by comparison with others.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid tells the clever person not to keep a record of other people’s faults but to bow his head and look at his own. Seeing someone else’s failing is meant to send a person back to examine himself.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether the sober drinker, seeing a drunk man, will think he looks the same himself, and Farid’s ‘look underneath your own collar’ is that same turn to self-examination.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid 6 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the wine must have been doing you a mischief, as it does with all those drink immoderately. It was wine that inflamed the Centaur Eurytion …”
greek_mythology.explanation: The suitor Antinous lectures the disguised Odysseus on the ruin wine brings, while drinking heavily himself; in the next book he is shot down with the cup at his lips.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Antinous sees drink's folly in others but never in himself, the blindness the Kural asks about.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch reports that the Spartans would make helots drink unmixed wine and bring them into the common messes, to show the young men what drunkenness looked like.
philosophy.explanation: Spartan education used the sight of a drunk man to teach sobriety.
philosophy.tie_back: This puts into practice the Kural's hope that seeing another drunk will make a person reflect.

real_life_example.event_title: Bill Wilson seeks out a fellow alcoholic in Akron and Alcoholics Anonymous begins
real_life_example.event: Bill Wilson, a New York stockbroker who had stopped drinking after a hospital stay in late 1934, found himself alone and tempted to drink in an Akron hotel in 1935 after a business deal failed. Having learned that talking with other alcoholics kept him sober, he telephoned a local clergyman and was put in touch with Robert Smith, a physician who was still drinking, and Wilson stayed on in Smith's house for several months. Smith stopped drinking soon after, and the two men's work with other alcoholics grew into Alcoholics Anonymous.
real_life_example.explanation: Wilson discovered that facing another drinker's condition was what kept him from returning to his own, and that insight became the basis of a worldwide movement.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks whether a sober drinker, seeing another man drunk, does not recognise his own state when drinking, and Wilson kept himself sober precisely by seeing his own condition in another alcoholic.

tamil:
வேண்டற்க வென்றிடினும் சூதினை வென்றதூஉம்
தூண்டிற்பொன் மீன்விழுங்கி அற்று.
transliteration:
Vendarka vendridinum soodhinai vendradhooum
thoondirpon meenvizhungi atru.
meaning: Do not go after gambling, even if you can win. Winning at gambling is like a fish swallowing bait with an iron hook hidden in it.
elementary: A fish sees a tasty worm and gulps it, happy for one second, but the worm hides a sharp hook. Valluvar says winning at gambling is that worm: it feels like a prize, but it pulls you in and you cannot get away.
university: The chapter opens by closing the most tempting loophole: vendridinum (வென்றிடினும், 'even should you win') concedes the gambler's best case and still forbids the desire (vendarka, வேண்டற்க). The simile turns on thoondirpon (தூண்டிற்பொன்), where pon (பொன்), usually 'gold', is read by the commentators as 'metal, iron': Mu. Varadarasanar on both ytamizh and thirukkural.net glosses it as தூண்டில் இரும்பு, 'the iron of the hook', and Kalaignar speaks of the iron barb (இரும்பு முள்). The alapedai in vendradhooum (வென்றதூஉம்) gives emphasis: even the thing won. The tradition descending from Parimelazhagar reads this chapter, like the two before it (Varaivin Magalir and Kallunnaamai), as a list of pleasures a ruler and a householder must shun, and the opening couplet sets the theme that gambling's gains are themselves the trap. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Dice, verily, are armed with goads and driving-hooks, deceiving and tormenting, causing grievous woe. They give frail gifts and then destroy the man who wins, thickly anointed with the player's fairest good.”
hinduism.explanation: In the Vedic Gambler's Hymn the speaker describes dice as hooked weapons that hand out small gifts only to ruin even the winner.
hinduism.tie_back: The hymn's hooks that destroy the man who wins match the Kural's hook hidden in the fish's bait.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.34.7 (Gambler's Hymn), trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus asks what any gain is worth if it costs a person their very self.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a win can be a loss in disguise.

islam.quote_or_event: “They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, ‘In them is great sin and [yet, some] benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an admits that gambling can bring some gain but judges the harm to be greater.
islam.tie_back: Both texts grant that one may win and still say: do not want it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And as an asmakhta does not effect acquisition, the one who wins takes money that is not legally his, and is considered a robber.”
judaism.explanation: In the Talmud, Rami bar Hama argues that a dice-player's winnings are not truly his, so even the winner counts as a kind of robber.
judaism.tie_back: The Talmud, like the Kural, denies that the gambler's win is a real gain.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 24b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He bolts the die quite boldly,--knowing not / What burning poison thereon lurks unseen.”
buddhism.explanation: In this Jataka a cheating dice-player keeps swallowing a die to escape losing, not knowing the Bodhisatta has coated the dice with poison.
buddhism.tie_back: A gambler swallowing what hides poison is close to the Kural's fish swallowing what hides a hook.
buddhism.source: Litta Jataka (No. 91), The Jataka vol. I, ed. E. B. Cowell

jainism.quote_or_event: “Just as an impassioned fish which is eager to swallow the bait, has its body transfixed by a hook.”
jainism.explanation: In the lecture on the causes of carelessness, the man who is passionately attached to tastes is compared to a fish that, greedy for the bait, is pierced by the hook hidden inside it.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar warns that even gambling's winnings are like the bait a fish swallows with the iron hook inside; the Uttarādhyayana uses the same image of the baited hook for the pleasure that hides its own ruin.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.63 (the comparison line of the verses on taste, 32.61–73) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Trying to taste the flavor, you swallow the hook.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Namdev uses the old image of the fish: drawn by the taste of the bait, it swallows the iron hook (loh) hidden inside and is caught. For him the lure of the senses always hides the hook.
sikhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s simile, where the gambler’s winnings are the bait a fish swallows together with the iron hook.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1252, Raag Saarang, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...because by a sad spite I had killed the son of Amphidamas- not of set purpose, but in childish quarrel over the dice.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The ghost of Patroclus recalls that a boyhood quarrel over dice made him a killer and sent him into exile.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A small game that seemed harmless carried a hidden cost, as the Kural warns.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But the gamester and the footpad (and the highwayman) belong to the class of the mean, since they have a sordid love of gain.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle classes the gambler with the robber because both love gain from the wrong source.
philosophy.tie_back: For Aristotle, as for Valluvar, even successful gambling gains are something not worth wanting.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Francois Blanc turns big wins into bait at the Monte Carlo casino
real_life_example.event: Facing bankruptcy, Prince Charles III of Monaco in 1863 gave the casino concession to Francois Blanc, who had already run a successful casino at Bad Homburg. Since every casino game is weighted in favour of the house, most players lost in the long run, but Blanc made a public ceremony of any player who broke the bank, covering the table with a black cloth while fresh money was fetched, because he knew that news of a big win drew in crowds of new gamblers hoping to repeat it. The casino soon made Monaco rich, and the principality's own residents have ever since been forbidden to gamble in its casinos.
real_life_example.explanation: The business of Monte Carlo rested on the fact that a well-publicised win costs the house little and lures many more people into losing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says not to desire gambling even when you can win, because the winnings are like the bait a fish swallows with the hook inside, and Blanc deliberately used other people's winnings as bait.

tamil:
ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும் சூதர்க்கும் உண்டாங்கொல்
நன்றெய்தி வாழ்வதோர் ஆறு.
transliteration:
Ondreydhi noorizhakkum soodharkkum undaangol
nandreydhi vaazhvadhor aaru.
meaning: Gamblers win one and lose a hundred. Can such people ever find a way to live a good life?
elementary: Imagine trading a hundred of your marbles for the chance to win one. You would soon have none left. Valluvar asks: if someone keeps doing that, how could life ever go well for them?
university: The couplet works through a stark ratio, ondreydhi noorizhakkum (ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும், 'gaining one, losing a hundred'), and then a rhetorical question ending in -kol (உண்டாங்கொல், 'will there be?'), which expects the answer no. Soodhar (சூதர்) means gamblers; aaru (ஆறு) is 'way, path', so nandreydhi vaazhvadhor aaru is 'a path of living that attains good'. The particle -um in soodharkkum ('even for gamblers') implies that other sinners may still find such a path, but gamblers, as a class, are shut out. Puliyur Kesikan on thirukkural.net softens the arithmetic to 'losing by hundreds out of the hope of gain', and Kalaignar reads it psychologically: a single win lures the player on into a hundred losses. Both base-text sites agree on the wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As of a costly horse grown old and feeble, I find not any profit of the gamester.”
hinduism.explanation: The repentant gambler of the Rig Veda admits his habit has yielded no profit, only decline.
hinduism.tie_back: Both say the gambler's way of life never arrives at any good.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.34.3, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that a craving to get rich leads people into traps that end in ruin.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's gambler, chasing one gain, is the person who falls into this snare.

islam.quote_or_event: “...In them is great sin and [yet, some] benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an sets the small benefit of gambling against its much larger harm.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's one-gained-hundred-lost reckoning in moral terms.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wealth may dwindle to less than nothing, / But one who gathers little by little increases it.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts wealth that vanishes with wealth built slowly through steady effort.
judaism.tie_back: The gambler's path leads to nothing, while the patient path the Kural implies leads to a good life.
judaism.source: Proverbs 13:11 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, on Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are, young householder, these six evil consequences in indulging in gambling: (i) the winner begets hate, (ii) the loser grieves for lost wealth, (iii) loss of wealth...”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists what gambling brings: hatred if you win, grief and loss if you lose.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows that neither winning nor losing gives the gambler a good life.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a man for the sake of one Kâkinî (risks and) loses a thousand (Kârshâpaṇas), or as the king lost his kingdom (and life) by eating a mango-fruit which he was strictly forbidden (by his physician)”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra compares the fool who trades lasting goods for petty pleasures to a man who loses a thousand coins for the sake of a single tiny one.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says gamblers gain one and lose a hundred; the Uttarādhyayana's man who stakes and loses a thousand coins for one kākiṇī expresses the same ruinous arithmetic.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I have seen the world to be such a gambler; all beg for peace, but they forget the Naam, the Name of the Lord. ... People beg for peace, but they receive severe pain.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak looks at the whole world and sees a gambler: everyone stakes their life on winning happiness, forgets the Name that actually gives it, and ends up with far more pain than they began with.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural’s gambler gains one and loses a hundred and never reaches anything good, and Guru Nanak’s gambling world asks for peace and receives great pain.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 222, Raag Gauree Gwaarayree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Patroclus, as a boy, killed a playmate in a quarrel over dice and had to leave his home for exile at the house of Peleus.
greek_mythology.explanation: One small game cost Patroclus his home and set the course of his life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A tiny stake leading to a huge loss echoes the Kural's one gained, a hundred lost.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Both, then, since they are willing to make gain from wrong sources, are sordid lovers of gain...”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the gambler and the robber both look for gain where it should not be sought.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural asks whether such a source of gain can ever lead to a good life, and Aristotle answers no.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Lord Holland agrees to pay the gambling debts of his son Charles James Fox
real_life_example.event: Charles James Fox, the brilliant young member of Parliament and later Britain's first foreign secretary, became notorious in his early twenties for reckless gambling, which caused his parents great unhappiness; within a month of reaching Oxford he had written to his father that he hoped never to play again but could not promise it. In November 1773 his father, Lord Holland, agreed to pay his son's debts up to one hundred thousand pounds, and an Eton College account records that on one occasion his father paid debts of 140,000 pounds. Even after a year in which he won enormously, Fox was soon in debt again, and in 1781 bailiffs were in his house while he was running a faro bank at Brooks's club.
real_life_example.explanation: Fox's occasional large wins never changed the overall result: his gambling consumed sums his family and friends repeatedly had to make good.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says gamblers gain one and lose a hundred, and Fox's winning seasons were swallowed by losses so large that his father had to pay debts of over a hundred thousand pounds.

tamil:
உருளாயம் ஓவாது கூறின் பொருளாயம்
போஒய்ப் புறமே படும்.
transliteration:
Urulaayam oovaadhu koorin porulaayam
pooip purame padum.
meaning: If a person keeps betting on the rolling dice without stopping, their money and everything it brings in will leave them and go to others.
elementary: A king who spends all day shouting bets at a dice board has no time left to look after his kingdom. Little by little, his treasure and his lands end up in other people's hands.
university: The couplet plays two compounds against each other: urulaayam (உருளாயம், 'gain from what rolls', i.e. the die, கவறு) and porulaayam (பொருளாயம், 'wealth and its revenue'). Oovaadhu koorin (ஓவாது கூறின்) means 'if one ceaselessly calls', which Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar take as calling out the stake, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as boasting of one's winnings. Pooip (போஒய், alapedai of போய்) purame padum says the wealth 'goes and lands outside', which Mu. Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss as 'reaches the enemies' (பகைவர்). Pope's English ('If prince unceasing speak of nought but play') and his prose gloss follow the traditional Parimelazhagar reading, which takes the subject to be a king, in keeping with the chapter's place in Porutpaal. The text is identical on both base sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira plays dice against Shakuni, staking and losing his treasury, his kingdom and finally his brothers to Duryodhana.
hinduism.explanation: A righteous king who could not stop calling out stakes handed his whole realm to his rivals in one sitting.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's picture of a king's wealth and revenue passing to his enemies.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (dice-game episode), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, the prodigal son quickly squanders the property his father gave him.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's gambler, he lets his wealth drain away into others' hands.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allah], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an commands believers to avoid gambling so that they can prosper.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows the reverse case: a ruler who will not avoid it loses his wealth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “...those who play dice are disqualified because they are not involved in settling the world, i.e., in productive occupations that demand hard work.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Sheshet says the habitual dice-player is not trusted because he contributes nothing to the productive life of society.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's player who does nothing but call stakes earns nothing, so his income drains away.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 24b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who brings ruin be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: ... (iv) he is a companion in indulging in gambling which causes heedlessness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that a gambling companion is really an enemy dressed up as a friend.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's gambler likewise ends up handing his wealth to the very people across the board from him.

jainism.quote_or_event: “After a man has done acts which cause the death of living beings, his pleasure-seeking relations take possession of his wealth, whilst the doer of the acts must suffer for them.”
jainism.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga warns that the wealth a person gathers by sinful acts passes into other hands, while he alone bears the karmic consequences.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says the man who keeps calling out stakes on the rolling dice will see his wealth and income go and fall to others; the Jain text likewise shows wealth slipping to others while the doer is left with the loss.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.9.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Like the gambler losing the game of chance, you are held in the power of sensory desires.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan tells the soul that it is losing its life the way a gambler loses at play, because the senses have got hold of it. The image is of someone who keeps playing and keeps losing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that the one who keeps calling stakes on the rolling dice will see his wealth and income pass to others, and Guru Arjan’s losing gambler is that same figure.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 212, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The Athenians from the city had just finished their midday meal, after which they had betaken themselves, some to dice, others to sleep, when Pisistratus with his troops fell upon them and put them to the rout.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus tells how Athens fell to Pisistratus while its defenders were busy at dice and napping.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A city lost to a rival while its men played dice is the Kural's warning on a political scale.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The king is surrounded by persons whose only thought is to divert the king, and to prevent his thinking of self.”
philosophy.explanation: Pascal notes that kings are kept in constant play and amusement so they never stop to reflect.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's king, endlessly calling dice, is the diverted ruler who loses track of his realm.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées §139 (trans. W. F. Trotter)

real_life_example.event_title: The Louisiana Lottery drains money from across the United States until Congress closes the mails to it
real_life_example.event: The Louisiana State Lottery Company, a private corporation chartered in 1868, sold tickets in almost every state, drawing about 90 percent of its sales from outside Louisiana and paying its stockholders dividends of well over 100 percent a year between 1887 and 1890. Other states, unhappy that their citizens' money was flowing to the company, pressed President Benjamin Harrison to act, and in September 1890 he signed a law banning lottery tickets and advertisements from the mail; the Postmaster General soon reported that business at the company's New Orleans office had fallen off by a third. Louisiana refused to renew the company's charter, which expired at the end of 1893.
real_life_example.explanation: Millions of small stakes from players across the country became extraordinary profits for a handful of shareholders, which is why so many states fought to shut the lottery down.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the wealth of one who keeps calling stakes on the rolling dice leaves him and falls into the hands of others, and the Louisiana Lottery's ticket buyers steadily enriched its owners.

tamil:
சிறுமை பலசெய்து சீரழிக்கும் சூதின்
வறுமை தருவதொன்று இல்.
transliteration:
Sirumai palaseydhu seerazhikkum soodhin
varumai tharuvadhondru il.
meaning: Nothing makes a person as poor as gambling. It brings many troubles and destroys a person's good name.
elementary: Some bad habits make you a little poorer. Gambling is the champion of them all: it takes your money, gets you into trouble, and makes people stop trusting you.
university: Sirumai pala seydhu (சிறுமை பல செய்து) means 'causing many miseries' (Mu. Varadarasanar: துன்பம் பலவற்றையும்), though sirumai literally means 'smallness, meanness' and can also suggest degradation. Seer (சீர்) here is renown or good standing, glossed as புகழ் by all four commentators. The superlative construction soodhin ... ondru il ('there is nothing like gambling') makes gambling the paramount cause of varumai (வறுமை, poverty). Textual note: both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the verb as சீரழக்கும், but ytamizh's own transliteration ('seerazhikkum') and every gloss (கெடுக்கும், அழிக்கும்) support the standard சீரழிக்கும், so சீரழக்கும் looks like a shared typographical slip; this reading should be confirmed against a printed edition. Kesikan's gloss adds that gambling does this 'to those who love it' (தன்னை விரும்பியவருக்கு).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The gambler's wife is left forlorn and wretched: the mother mourns the son who wanders homeless. In constant fear, in debt, and seeking riches, he goes by night unto the home of others.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gambler's Hymn describes the gambler sinking into debt, homelessness and disgrace, dragging his family down with him.
hinduism.tie_back: It is a vivid picture of the poverty and lost good name the Kural attributes to gambling.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.34.10, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want.”
christianity.explanation: Having wasted everything, the prodigal son falls into real poverty.
christianity.tie_back: This is the want that the Kural says gambling, above everything else, brings.

islam.quote_or_event: “He who played Nardashir (a game similar to backgammon) is like one who dyed his hand with the flesh and blood of swine.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares playing this game of chance to defiling one's hand with something forbidden.
islam.tie_back: The hadith matches the Kural's sense that gambling degrades a person's standing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And these on the following list are the ones who are disqualified by the Sages from bearing witness due to their unseemly behavior...: One who plays with dice [bekubbiyya] for money...”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah strips the habitual dice-player of the right to testify, a public loss of standing.
judaism.tie_back: The gambler's lost credibility is the Kural's seer azhikkum, the ruin of good name.
judaism.source: Mishnah Sanhedrin 3:3 as given in Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 24b (Koren-Steinsaltz English)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(iii) loss of wealth, (iv) his word is not relied upon in a court of law, (v) he is despised by his friends and associates...”
buddhism.explanation: Among the six evils of gambling, the Buddha names lost wealth, lost credibility and lost respect.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's double damage of poverty and ruined reputation.

jainism.quote_or_event: “After having enjoyed pleasant seats, beds, carriages, riches, and pleasures, after having squandered his wealth which he had so much trouble in gaining, and after having committed many sins, he will, under the burden of his Karman, and believing only in the visible world, be grieved in the hour of death like the ram at the arrival of a guest.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana describes the pleasure-seeker who squanders hard-earned wealth and piles up sins, only to face grief and the weight of his karma at death.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says nothing impoverishes like gambling, which brings many miseries and destroys good standing; the Jain verse likewise shows indulgence squandering hard-won wealth and ending in misery.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.8–9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The position of the losing gambler is similar to the deer caught in a trap.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas compares the gambler who has lost his money (vit haar jooaaree) to a deer caught in a snare, unable to get free and facing ruin.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says nothing brings poverty and misery like gambling, and Bhai Gurdas’s gambler stripped of his wealth and trapped like a deer is that misery made visible.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 36, Pauri 3 (English translation as published on BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax and searchgurbani.com)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After the boy Patroclus killed a playmate in a quarrel over dice, his father Menoetius had to bring him away from Opoeis to live as an exile in the house of Peleus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A game of dice cost the young Patroclus his home and standing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows gambling causing misery and loss of place, as the Kural says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For it is for gain that both of them ply their craft and endure the disgrace of it...”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the gambler and the thief accept public disgrace for the sake of profit.
philosophy.tie_back: The disgrace Aristotle names is the Kural's ruined reputation.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Beau Brummell flees England to escape his gambling debts
real_life_example.place: London, England, and Calais and Caen, France
real_life_example.event: George Bryan Brummell, the leader of London fashion and friend of the Prince Regent, inherited a fortune of about 30,000 pounds in 1799, but gambling and extravagance exhausted it, and on 16 May 1816 he fled to Calais to escape his creditors. He spent the rest of his life in France, hopelessly in debt, was imprisoned for debt in Caen in 1835, and after two strokes was given shelter in the charitable asylum of Bon Sauveur in Caen. He died there in 1840, a pauper.
real_life_example.explanation: The most admired man in Regency society ended his life poor, dishonoured and forgotten abroad.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says nothing brings poverty like gambling, which causes many miseries and destroys a person's good name, and gambling took both Brummell's fortune and his place in society.

tamil:
கவறும் கழகமும் கையும் தருக்கி
இவறியார் இல்லாகி யார்.
transliteration:
Kavarum kazhagamum kaiyum tharukki
ivariyaar illaagi yaar.
meaning: People who were proud of the dice, the gambling hall and their own skill, and would not give them up, have ended up with nothing.
elementary: Some people are very proud of being good at a game, and they love the place where it is played. But if that game is gambling and they never stop, Valluvar says, they finish with empty pockets, as many before them did.
university: The first line names gambling's three parts: kavaru (கவறு, the dice), kazhagam (கழகம், the gaming hall) and kai (கை, the hand, meaning dexterity in throwing). Tharukki (தருக்கி) means 'taking pride in', and ivariyaar (இவறியார்) means 'those who clung to, would not let go'. Illaagiyaar (இல்லாகியார்) is past tense: 'became people who have nothing'. Pope's English brings this out ('the men in other days who came to nought'), and Solomon Pappaiah adds that this 'has happened before too' (முன்பும் உண்டு), so the couplet appeals to historical examples. Kesikan reads it as 'those once wealthy and now destitute', and Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the parenthetical 'even though they had every wealth'. Kesikan's text on thirukkural.net prints the dice as சுவறு, apparently a misprint for கவறு; the couplet itself is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Nalopakhyana of the Mahabharata, King Nala, possessed by Kali, keeps gambling against his brother Pushkara despite his queen's pleas, and loses his entire kingdom and wealth.
hinduism.explanation: A famous and accomplished king clung to the dice until he was left with nothing.
hinduism.tie_back: Nala is a classic case of the Kural's 'those who clung to dice in former days and came to nothing'.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana, trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “They said therefore among themselves, Let us not rend it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be...”
christianity.explanation: At the foot of the cross, the soldiers gamble for Jesus' seamless coat.
christianity.tie_back: It shows how gambling's pull goes on even in the darkest place, the same clinging the Kural condemns.

islam.quote_or_event: “...and whoever says to his companion. ‘Come along, let us gamble’ must give alms (as an expiation).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that even inviting someone to gamble is a wrong that needs expiation.
islam.tie_back: Even the first eager step toward the gaming table that the Kural warns about is treated as a fault.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Yehuda said: When are the people listed above disqualified from bearing witness? It is when they have no occupation but this one.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah singles out those who make dice their whole trade and identity.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's gambler, proud of his dice, his hall and his hand, has made gambling his only occupation.
judaism.source: Mishnah Sanhedrin 3:3 as given in Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 24b (Koren-Steinsaltz English)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To be a rake, a drunkard, a gambler, and to squander all one earns — this is a cause of one's downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names gambling and squandering as a cause of a person's downfall.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's verdict that those devoted to gambling become people with nothing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not learn to play chess, he should not speak anything forbidden by the Law; a wise man should abstain from fights and quarrels. Shoes, an umbrella, dice, chowries, working for another, helping each other: from all this a wise man should abstain.”
jainism.explanation: Among the things a wise monk must give up, the Sūtrakṛtāṅga lists learning board games (aṣṭāpada) and handling dice.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says those who prided themselves on the dice, the gaming hall and their skill of hand ended with nothing; the Sūtrakṛtāṅga tells the wise to give up the dice and the gaming board altogether.
jainism.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.9.17–18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Says Kabeer, think of doing some good deeds. In the end, the gambler shall depart empty-handed.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir reminds the proud that kings, gold forts and elephants at the door go with no one, and closes by saying that a person who stakes everything on wealth leaves this world like a gambler, with nothing in his hands.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who took pride in dice, gaming hall and skilled hands, and would not let them go, end up with nothing, and Kabir’s gambler likewise departs empty-handed.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1158, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Athena finds Penelope's suitors amusing themselves with board games before the doors of Odysseus' hall while they consume his estate; they refuse to leave and are finally destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: The suitors cling to the hall, its games and its pleasures, and it costs them everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's gamblers, they would not let go of the hall and its play, and came to nothing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...and the one faces the greatest dangers for the sake of the booty, while the other makes gain from his friends, to whom he ought to be giving.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats gambling as a craft practised for gain at the expense of friends.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's gambler, proud of his 'hand', is practising exactly this craft.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Charles Wells, the man who broke the bank at Monte Carlo, ends in prison
real_life_example.place: Monte Carlo, Monaco, and London, England
real_life_example.event: In 1891 the Englishman Charles Deville Wells, who had arrived at Monte Carlo with only a few hundred pounds, played roulette every day from opening to closing and broke the bank several times, winning tens of thousands of pounds; he said he had a system, and a popular song made him famous. On a third visit in January 1892 his luck turned, he lost heavily, and he cabled his backers for more money, which he also lost, until he was so short of cash that he was selling coal from his yacht. Arrested at Le Havre, he was convicted in London on 14 March 1893 of obtaining money by false pretences from investors in his worthless inventions, and sentenced to eight years' penal servitude.
real_life_example.explanation: The most celebrated winner of his age was soon left with nothing, and the money he had staked turned out to have been taken from others.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of those who prided themselves on the dice, the gaming hall and their own skill and ended up with nothing, and Wells, who claimed a winning system and lived at the tables, finished bankrupt and in prison.

tamil:
அகடாரார் அல்லல் உழப்பர்சூ தென்னும்
முகடியான் மூடப்பட் டார்.
transliteration:
Agadaaraar allal uzhapparsoo thennum
mugadiyaan moodappat taar.
meaning: People who fall under gambling, which is like the goddess of bad luck, will never even fill their stomachs, and they will suffer many troubles.
elementary: Picture a big dark cloud named 'Bad Luck' that swallows people whole. Once it has you, you never get enough to eat and troubles keep coming. Valluvar says gambling is that cloud.
university: Mugadi (முகடி) is Misfortune personified, the goddess known in Tamil as Moodevi or Jyeshtha (மூதேவி), the inauspicious elder sister of Lakshmi. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss it as மூதேவி, and Pope's verse renders it 'Misfortune's other name'. Moodappattaar (மூடப்பட்டார்) means 'those covered or engulfed', which Mu. Varadarasanar renders as 'swallowed' (விழுங்கப்பட்டவர்). Agadaaraar (அகடாரார்) is 'those whose belly (அகடு) is never filled', and allal uzhappar means 'will toil in affliction'. Following Parimelazhagar's two-world reading, Kesikan and the Pope prose gloss take the second clause to mean suffering in the next world as well. Kesikan's text on thirukkural.net seems to drop the negation ('வயிறார உணவைப் பெறுவதுடன்'), which is likely a transcription slip. The couplet text matches on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Sad is the gambler when he sees a matron, another's wife, and his well-ordered dwelling. He yokes the brown steeds in the early morning, and when the fire is cold sinks down an outcast.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic gambler, gripped by the dice, ends each day cold, homeless and outcast while others prosper.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the endless affliction the Kural says comes to those engulfed by gambling.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.34.11, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him.”
christianity.explanation: The ruined prodigal son is so hungry he envies the pigs' food.
christianity.tie_back: His unfilled belly is almost word for word the Kural's agadaaraar.

islam.quote_or_event: “...intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allah], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan...”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents gambling as the work of a malign spiritual power.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's Mugadi, gambling is pictured as an evil force that takes hold of its victims.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A lover of money is never satisfied with money, nor a lover of wealth, with income. That too is futile.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet observes that chasing money never brings satisfaction.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's gamblers whose bellies are never full show the same insatiable want.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 5:9 (Hebrew numbering; JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, on Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who plays with dice and drinks intoxicants, goes to women who are dear unto others as their own lives, associates with the mean and not with elders — he declines just as the moon during the waning half.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's verse describes the dice-player steadily waning like the moon.
buddhism.tie_back: The waning moon slowly covered by darkness parallels the Kural's gambler covered by Misfortune.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Then when death comes at last, the fool trembles in fear; he dies the 'death against one's will,' (having lost his chance) like a gambler vanquished by Kali.”
jainism.explanation: Mahāvīra compares the fool who dies unprepared to a gambler beaten by Kali, the losing throw of the dice, who has thrown away his chance.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar calls gambling a goddess of misfortune that swallows its victims and leaves them in want and sorrow; the Uttarādhyayana likewise uses the gambler overcome by Kali, the throw of ill luck, as its image of utter defeat.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Thieves, adulterers and gamblers are pressed like seeds in the mill.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak names the gambler with the thief and the adulterer as people whose own deeds grind them, as an oil press crushes seeds.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those swallowed by the misfortune called gambling will suffer many sorrows, and Guru Nanak’s gamblers, crushed in the mill, are suffering exactly that.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar, Malaar ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus reports a Lydian tradition that during a long famine the Lydians invented dice and other games, playing on one day so as not to think of food and eating on the next.
greek_mythology.explanation: The legend links the very origin of dice-games with hunger that could not be satisfied.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Dice and an empty belly go together in both texts, though Herodotus treats the games as a way to cope rather than a cause.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We do not seek that easy and peaceful lot which permits us to think of our unhappy condition, nor the dangers of war, nor the labour of office, but the bustle which averts these thoughts of ours, and amuses us.”
philosophy.explanation: Pascal argues that people chase play and bustle to escape facing their own wretchedness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's gambler, covered by Misfortune, is trapped in this kind of distraction and never filled.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées §139 (trans. W. F. Trotter)

real_life_example.event_title: Girolamo Cardano's gambling sends his family to the poorhouse
real_life_example.place: Gallarate and Milan, Duchy of Milan (now Italy)
real_life_example.event: The physician and mathematician Girolamo Cardano, later famous for the Ars Magna, had squandered his father's small bequest and turned to cards, dice and chess to make a living. In 1533, unable to practise medicine after the Milan College of Physicians refused him, he went back to gambling, and things went so badly that he had to pawn his wife's jewellery and some of their furniture. When the family moved to Milan they fared even worse and had to enter the poorhouse; his biographers note that gambling remained an addiction for many years that cost him time, money and reputation.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the finest minds of the Renaissance, who even wrote the first mathematical study of games of chance, could not keep his family fed while gambling held him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those swallowed by the misfortune called gambling will never have their bellies filled and will suffer many sorrows, and Cardano's gambling brought his household to the poorhouse.

tamil:
பழகிய செல்வமும் பண்பும் கெடுக்கும்
கழகத்துக் காலை புகின்.
transliteration:
Pazhagiya selvamum panbum kedukkum
kazhagaththuk kaalai pugin.
meaning: If a person spends their time in the gambling hall, it destroys both the riches they were born into and their good character.
elementary: Your grandparents may have saved a treasure for your family and taught you good manners. Valluvar says that hanging around a gambling house can waste both: the treasure is lost, and the good manners slowly disappear too.
university: Pazhagiya selvam (பழகிய செல்வம்) is 'long-familiar wealth', which all commentators take as ancestral or inherited property (Kalaignar: மூதாதையர் தேடிவைத்த சொத்து). Panbu (பண்பு) is good character or natural virtue. The second line contains an interpretive crux: kaalai (காலை) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Kesikan as kaalam, 'time' ('if one's time is passed in the gaming hall'), and Kesikan adds 'the time meant for doing good'. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reads it literally as 'morning' ('if one goes to the gaming hall in the morning'), the hour that should belong to work. Kazhagam (கழகம்) also appears in 935 as the gaming place. The couplet is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Drinking, dice, women, and hunting, these four (which have been enumerated) in succession, he must know to be the most pernicious in the set that springs from love of pleasure.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king that dice are among the four most destructive vices born of love of pleasure.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu's grouping (drink, dice, women) is the same as the Kural's sequence of chapters 92 to 94, and both warn that these destroy a ruler's estate and character.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.”
christianity.explanation: The prodigal son takes his share of the family inheritance and wastes it in dissolute living.
christianity.tie_back: A squandered inheritance and a corrupted life are exactly what the Kural says the gaming hall produces.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says gambling turns people away from prayer and remembrance of God, and sows hatred.
islam.tie_back: Time taken by the gaming hall is time stolen from virtue, as the Kural's kaalai reading suggests.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wealth may dwindle to less than nothing, / But one who gathers little by little increases it.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts wealth that dwindles away with wealth that grows through steady care.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's ancestral fortune, lost in the gaming hall, is wealth dwindling to nothing.
judaism.source: Proverbs 13:11 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, on Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What are the six channels for dissipating wealth which he does not pursue? ... (d) indulgence in gambling which causes heedlessness...”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists gambling among the six channels through which a householder's wealth drains away.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts present gambling as a leak that empties a family's fortune and its virtue.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those endowed with excellent knowledge live many nayutas of years; so great a loss suffer the fools in a life of less than a hundred years!”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana laments how much fools throw away when they spend their brief human life on passing pleasures.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says time passed in the gaming hall destroys inherited wealth and good character; the Jain verse likewise grieves over the great loss that comes from wasting a short human life on trifles.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Like a gambler he loses and wastes his precious life.”
sikhism.explanation: In a pauri headed ‘Wasting the life by the gambler’, Bhai Gurdas compares the person who throws away the priceless human birth to a gambler who loses everything at play.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says days spent in the gaming hall destroy both inherited wealth and good character, and Bhai Gurdas makes the stake even larger: the gambler loses life itself.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 37, Pauri 26 (English translation as published on BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax and searchgurbani.com)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope's suitors pass their days in Odysseus' hall playing board games and feasting, eating up the estate of his house until they are destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Day after day spent in idle play and feasting swallows a great household's inherited wealth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's warning about time spent in the gaming hall wasting ancestral wealth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Not that there is in fact any happiness in them, or that men imagine true bliss to consist in money won at play, or in the hare which they hunt; we would not take these as a gift.”
philosophy.explanation: Pascal says people go to gaming not for the money but to fill and escape their time.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's focus on time spent in the gaming hall picks up the same insight: the real cost is the life poured away.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées §139 (trans. W. F. Trotter)

real_life_example.event_title: Young Leo Tolstoy's gambling debts cost him the house where he was born
real_life_example.event: Leo Tolstoy inherited the family estate of Yasnaya Polyana in 1847, but as a young man he gambled heavily, and by the time he married in 1862 he had sold half his land and the estate's main house to pay gambling debts. The large manor house in which he had been born was sold in 1854 while he was away in the army, taken apart and carried off to the village of Dolgoye, about 40 kilometres away, where it stood until it was demolished in 1913. Tolstoy lived the rest of his life in one of the two smaller wings, and a stone marks the spot where the house once stood.
real_life_example.explanation: The ancestral home built by his grandfather and father was lost to the card tables before Tolstoy had written his great novels.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that time spent in the gaming hall destroys a person's inherited wealth, and Tolstoy's gambling literally carried off the family house he had inherited.

tamil:
பொருள்கெடுத்துப் பொய்மேற் கொளீஇ அருள்கெடுத்து
அல்லல் உழப்பிக்கும் சூது.
transliteration:
Porulkeduththup poimer koleei arulkeduththu
allal uzhappikkum soodhu.
meaning: Gambling wastes your money, pushes you to lie, kills your kindness, and makes you suffer.
elementary: First gambling takes your money. Then you start fibbing to cover it up. Then you stop caring about other people. And at the end you are very unhappy. Valluvar lists these four steps like a staircase going down.
university: The couplet is a chain of four causative actions with gambling (soodhu, சூது) held back as the subject until the last word. Porul keduththu (பொருள்கெடுத்து) means 'ruining wealth'; poi mer koleei (பொய்மேற் கொளீஇ) means 'making one take up falsehood', where koleei is the causative alapedai form of kol ('take'); arul keduththu (அருள்கெடுத்து) means 'destroying compassion'. The last verb, uzhappikkum (உழப்பிக்கும், 'causes to toil in affliction'), is also causative. Arul, the compassion celebrated in Arattuppaal's chapter 25 (Aruludaimai), is the highest of the virtues lost. Kesikan follows the Parimelazhagar tradition in reading the misery as belonging to both worlds (இருமையும்), and the Pope prose gloss adds '(here and hereafter)'. Both base sites agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Sabha Parva, Yudhishthira, having lost his wealth, his brothers and himself at dice, stakes and loses Draupadi, who is then dragged into the assembly and humiliated while the court looks on.
hinduism.explanation: The dice game first takes the Pandavas' wealth and then pushes the players past every limit of compassion and decency.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's descent from lost wealth to lost compassion to deep misery.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (dice-game episode), trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says love of money leads people away from faith and into many sorrows.
christianity.tie_back: Losing faith and being 'pierced with many sorrows' parallels the Kural's loss of compassion and the misery that follows.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer...”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says gambling breeds hatred between people and pulls them away from God.
islam.tie_back: Animosity replacing goodwill is the Kural's arul keduththu, the destruction of compassion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Since they do not realize the effort required of most people to earn a living they might not be scrupulous about other people’s money, and their testimony cannot be relied upon.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmudic discussion explains why a dice-player's word cannot be trusted in court.
judaism.tie_back: The gambler's unreliable testimony is the Kural's poi mer koleei, the turn to falsehood.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 24b (Steinsaltz's explanatory gloss on Rav Sheshet, Koren-Steinsaltz English)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) the winner begets hate, (ii) the loser grieves for lost wealth, (iii) loss of wealth, (iv) his word is not relied upon in a court of law...”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's list covers hatred, grief, loss of wealth and loss of credibility.
buddhism.tie_back: This covers nearly every step of the Kural's chain: wealth lost, truthfulness doubted, goodwill gone, and grief.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When he is not satisfied with those 'colours,' and his craving for them grows stronger and stronger, he will become discontented, and unhappy by dint of his discontent; misled by greed he will take another's property. When he is overcome by violent desire, takes another's property, and is not satisfied with those 'colours' and their possession, then his deceit and falsehood increase on account of his greed; yet he will not get rid of his misery.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana traces the chain by which unchecked craving leads to discontent, then to taking others' property, then to growing deceit and falsehood, and still to misery; the preceding verse adds that the passionate man torments living beings.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar lists what gambling does: it ruins wealth, drives a person to lying, kills compassion and leaves him in misery. The Jain verses trace the same chain of craving, lying and lasting misery.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.29–30 (cf. 32.27) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The truth is perfect and the falsehood a loser gambler running from pillar to post.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas sets truth, which is whole and secure, against falsehood, which he pictures as a gambler who has lost and runs here and there. Lying and losing at dice go together in his image.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural lists gambling as the vice that drives a man to lies, and Bhai Gurdas gives falsehood the very face of a losing gambler.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 30, Pauri 5 (English translation as published on BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax and searchgurbani.com)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...I had killed the son of Amphidamas- not of set purpose, but in childish quarrel over the dice.”
greek_mythology.explanation: For the boy Patroclus, a dice game turned into a quarrel and the quarrel into a killing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is gambling destroying compassion and bringing lasting sorrow, as the Kural says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...the other makes gain from his friends, to whom he ought to be giving.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the gambler takes from his friends when he ought to be generous to them.
philosophy.tie_back: Taking from friends where one should give is the Kural's arul keduththu, generosity turned upside down.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Pete Rose is banned from baseball and denies betting on the game for years
real_life_example.place: New York and Cincinnati, United States
