real_life_example.event: After a six-month investigation found that Pete Rose, baseball's all-time hits leader and manager of the Cincinnati Reds, had bet on baseball games including those of his own team between 1985 and 1987, Commissioner Bart Giamatti placed him on the permanently ineligible list on 24 August 1989. For more than a decade Rose publicly insisted he had never bet on baseball, before admitting it privately to Commissioner Bud Selig in 2002 and publicly in his autobiography in January 2004. The ban kept him out of the Baseball Hall of Fame.
real_life_example.explanation: A compulsive gambler who began betting uncontrollably by 1985 lost his place in the game he loved and then spent years living a public lie about it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says gambling ruins wealth and drives a person to lying, and Rose's gambling cost him his career and led him to deny the truth for fifteen years.

tamil:
உடைசெல்வம் ஊண்ஒளி கல்விஎன்று ஐந்தும்
அடையாவாம் ஆயங் கொளின்.
transliteration:
Udaiselvam oon-oli kalvi-endru aindhum
adaiyaavaam aayang kolin.
meaning: If a person takes up gambling, these five things will never come to them: clothes, riches, food, fame and learning.
elementary: Think of five good things: clothes to wear, money, food, a good name, and learning. Valluvar says that if you make gambling your habit, all five walk away from you.
university: The couplet lists five goods: udai (உடை, clothing), selvam (செல்வம், wealth), oon (ஊண், food), oli (ஒளி, 'light', i.e. fame or renown) and kalvi (கல்வி, learning). Aayam (ஆயம்) here means gambling, and aayang kolin means 'if one takes it up'. Adaiyaavaam (அடையாவாம்) says these 'will not come to' him, so the stress is on goods that are never gained, not only goods lost. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kesikan list the five in reverse order (fame, learning, wealth, food, clothing), presumably following Parimelazhagar's ranking from highest to lowest, while Pope keeps the Kural's order. Kesikan adds 'even if one does it thinking it mere sport' (வேடிக்கை), and Sivayogi Sivakumar takes oli as 'self-knowledge'. The text is the same on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Nala loses his kingdom at dice to Pushkara, he wanders into the forest with Damayanti wearing a single cloth; starving, he throws that garment over some birds to catch them, and they fly away with it, leaving him naked, hungry and without a kingdom.
hinduism.explanation: The gambler-king is stripped in turn of wealth, food, clothing and royal glory.
hinduism.tie_back: Nala's fall is almost a list of the Kural's five lost goods.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana, trans. K. M. Ganguli

christianity.quote_or_event: “...They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots. These things therefore the soldiers did.”
christianity.explanation: Soldiers gamble for the clothes of a condemned man.
christianity.tie_back: Clothing changing hands by lot echoes the first of the Kural's five losses, seen from the winners' side.

islam.quote_or_event: “...But their sin is greater than their benefit. And they ask you what they should spend. Say, ‘The excess [beyond needs].’”
islam.explanation: The verse condemns gambling and in the same breath teaches spending only what is beyond one's needs.
islam.tie_back: The contrast protects the basic needs, such as food and clothing, that the Kural says the gambler loses.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rather, those who play dice are disqualified because they are not involved in settling the world, i.e., in productive occupations that demand hard work.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Sheshet sees the dice-player as someone outside productive life.
judaism.tie_back: Someone who produces nothing will not gain the food, clothing and wealth the Kural lists.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(v) he is despised by his friends and associates, (vi) he is not sought after for matrimony; for people would say he is a gambler and is not fit to look after a wife.”
buddhism.explanation: The gambler loses respect and the chance of marriage, because people judge him unable to provide.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's lost renown (oli) and inability to secure basic goods.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He will be born among men where there is wealth, beauty, glory, fame, long life, and eminent happiness.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana says the one who has renounced pleasure will be reborn where wealth, glory, fame and happiness are found.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar says that clothing, wealth, food, renown and learning never come to one who takes up gambling; the Jain verse gives the reverse case, in which a similar list of goods comes to the one who has given up pleasure.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak’s short salok sums up two pillars of Sikh life, kirat karni (honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing). Food, clothing and standing are to come from honest labour, never from chance or someone else’s loss.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the gambler never gets clothing, wealth, food, renown or learning, and Guru Nanak names the honest, sharing path by which a person does gain them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Saarang ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus relates that Pisistratus' army overran the Athenians while some of them had gone off to dice after their midday meal.
greek_mythology.explanation: Men at their dice lost their city and with it their freedom and standing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The loss of everything a citizen has echoes the Kural's sweeping list of goods that will not come.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Both, then, since they are willing to make gain from wrong sources, are sordid lovers of gain; therefore all such forms of taking are mean.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle concludes that the gambler's way of getting is mean and dishonourable.
philosophy.tie_back: Such meanness rules out the renown (oli) that the Kural counts among the five goods.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Dostoevsky gambles away his travel money in Wiesbaden and pawns his belongings in Baden-Baden
real_life_example.event: In August 1865 Fyodor Dostoevsky gambled away all his travel money at the Wiesbaden casino and was stranded at his hotel for two months, where he was eventually given nothing to eat but tea and the staff stopped serving him, until friends and a Russian Orthodox priest sent money for him to leave. In 1867, having just married Anna Snitkina, he went to Baden-Baden hoping to escape his debts by gambling, and by the end of that summer he had pawned many of his and his wife's belongings and lost the gifts sent by friends to rescue them. He stopped gambling altogether only in 1871.
real_life_example.explanation: Even a writer of genius, at work on Crime and Punishment at the time, was reduced by roulette to hunger and pawned possessions.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that clothing, wealth, food, renown and learning never reach one who takes up gambling, and Dostoevsky's gambling left him without food in Wiesbaden and without his and his wife's belongings in Baden-Baden.

tamil:
இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல் துன்பம்
உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்.
transliteration:
Izhaththoruum kaadhalikkum soodhepol thunbam
uzhaththoruum kaadhatru uyir.
meaning: The more a gambler loses, the more they love gambling. In the same way, the more a soul suffers, the more it loves living in the body.
elementary: Have you ever lost a game and immediately shouted, 'One more try!'? The more you lose, the more you want to play. Valluvar says life is like that too: even when it hurts, we hold on to it more tightly.
university: The closing couplet turns a psychological observation about gambling into a general statement about existence. Izhaththoruum (இழத்தொறூஉம்) and uzhaththoruum (உழத்தொறூஉம்), both with alapedai, mean 'every time one loses' and 'every time one suffers', placing loss and pain in parallel. Kaadhalikkum (காதலிக்கும், 'comes to love') and kaadhatru (காதற்று) carry the comparison. Most commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Kesikan, Pope) read kaadhatru as kaadhal + atru, 'has love, is fond': the soul (uyir) loves the body more as it suffers, just as the gambler loves gambling more as he loses. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh instead splits it as kaadhal + atru 'without love', giving the opposite sense that the soul does not love suffering, and adds that gambling can lead to despair. Pappaiah reverses which half is the comparison. The text is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When I resolve to play with these no longer, my friends depart from me and leave me lonely. When the brown dice, thrown on the board, have rattled, like a fond girl I seek the place of meeting.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic gambler confesses that however much he resolves to stop, the rattle of dice pulls him back like a lover to a meeting.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's gambler, who loves the game more with every loss, described in his own words.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.34.5, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes being pulled again and again toward what he knows harms him.
christianity.tie_back: The gambler who loses and keeps playing shows this same divided will.

islam.quote_or_event: “They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, ‘In them is great sin and [yet, some] benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an acknowledges the small benefit that makes gambling attractive while judging its harm greater.
islam.tie_back: That small benefit is the lure that keeps the Kural's gambler loving the game through every loss.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A lover of money is never satisfied with money, nor a lover of wealth, with income. That too is futile.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet notes that desire for money only grows and is never satisfied.
judaism.tie_back: Desire that feeds on itself is the Kural's gambler, whose love grows as he loses.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 5:9 (Hebrew numbering; JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, on Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “...the noble truth of the origination of stress: the craving that makes for further becoming — accompanied by passion & delight, relishing now here & now there — i.e., craving for sensual pleasure, craving for becoming, craving for non-becoming.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's Second Noble Truth names craving for continued existence (bhava-tanha) as what binds beings to suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's soul clinging ever harder to a suffering body is this craving for becoming.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those will reap pains who, in thoughts, words, or acts, are attached to their body, to colours, and to forms.”
jainism.explanation: In the lecture on the false ascetic, Mahāvīra teaches that attachment to the body is itself a source of suffering, and in Jain thought this attachment keeps the soul (jīva) bound in saṃsāra.
jainism.tie_back: Valluvar ends by saying the soul loves the body all the more the more it suffers, as the gambler loves the game the more he loses; the Jain verse reverses the direction, teaching that attachment to the body is what produces the pain.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “as the gambler’s addiction does not leave him, So is this mind of Nanak’s attached to the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In a long list of passionate attachments (the moth to the flame, the elephant to its lust), Guru Arjan includes the gambler whose habit will not let him go. He then turns the image round: let the mind cling to the Lord just as tightly.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural observes that gambling is loved all the more the more one loses, and Guru Arjan names that same unbreakable addiction, though he redirects its force toward God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 838, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus reports a Lydian legend that during an eighteen-year famine the people kept up their dice and games, playing on alternate days so they could endure the hunger.
greek_mythology.explanation: A whole people held on to their games, and to life, through years of suffering.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Clinging to play and to life amid hardship echoes both halves of the Kural's comparison.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Not that there is in fact any happiness in them, or that men imagine true bliss to consist in money won at play, or in the hare which they hunt; we would not take these as a gift. ... Reasons why we like the chase better than the quarry.”
philosophy.explanation: Pascal observes that gamblers do not really want the winnings; they want the play itself, the chase rather than the prize.
philosophy.tie_back: That is why, as the Kural says, losing only deepens the gambler's love for the game.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées §139 (trans. W. F. Trotter)

real_life_example.event_title: The Rigveda's Gambler's Lament is composed
real_life_example.event: Hymn 10.34 of the Rigveda, more than 3,000 years old, is spoken by a compulsive dice player who says that a losing throw has driven away his devoted wife, that her mother hates him and that his own family disowns him while he wanders in debt. He describes how, whenever he swears he will not play again, the sound of the dice falling sends him running back to the gaming place like a lover to a meeting. The hymn ends with the god Savitr's counsel to stop playing with dice and to till his field and value what he has.
real_life_example.explanation: The oldest known poem about gambling addiction already describes the pattern of ruin, resolve and relapse that later gamblers would recognise.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says gambling is loved all the more the more one loses, and the Rigveda's gambler, having lost wife, family and wealth, still runs back to the dice whenever he hears them.

tamil:
மிகினும் குறையினும் நோய்செய்யும் நூலோர்
வளிமுதலா எண்ணிய மூன்று.
transliteration:
Miginum kuraiyinum noiseyyum noolor
valimudhalaa enniya moondru.
meaning: The three forces in the body that medical books name, starting with wind, cause sickness when there is too much or too little of them.
elementary: Think of a bicycle tyre: pump in too much air and it bursts, let out too much and it goes flat. Valluvar says the body has three such forces inside it, and it stays healthy only when each one is just right.
university: The chapter opens with theory before practice: noolor (நூலோர், 'the authors of the treatises') are the medical writers, and vali mudhalaa enniya moondru (வளிமுதலா எண்ணிய மூன்று, 'the three reckoned with wind first') are the three humours that Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss as vaatham, piththam and silethumam (வாதம், பித்தம், சிலேத்துமம்), i.e. the vata-pitta-kapha triad of Ayurveda and Siddha medicine. The decisive words are miginum kuraiyinum (மிகினும் குறையினும், 'whether in excess or in deficiency'): illness is defined not as an invading thing but as loss of proportion. Following Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan add that the humours are disturbed through a person's food and activity (உணவும் செயல்களும்), which is why the following couplets turn at once to eating. The chapter closes the Natpiyal section of Porutpaal in the traditional arrangement, a placement commentators explain by treating bodily health as the last of the things a ruler and householder must secure. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Charaka Samhita defines disease as disequilibrium of the body's constituents and health as their equilibrium, and treats vata, pitta and kapha as the doshas whose increase or decrease produces illness.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Ayurveda makes balance the very definition of health and imbalance, in either direction, the definition of disease.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the medical theory the Kural's noolor are summarising: the three humours harm by being too much or too little.

christianity.quote_or_event: Ecclesiastes counsels against being righteous overmuch or wicked overmuch, urging the one who fears God to avoid both extremes.
christianity.explanation: The Preacher warns that going too far in either direction destroys a person.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats harm as coming from both excess and its opposite, though the subject is conduct rather than the body.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the heaven He raised and imposed the balance That you not transgress within the balance. And establish weight in justice and do not make deficient the balance.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents creation as resting on a divinely set balance that must be neither exceeded nor made deficient.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's rule for the body's three humours mirrors this cosmic warning against both transgressing and short-weighting the balance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Since maintaining a healthy and sound body is among the ways of God - for one cannot understand or have any knowledge of the Creator, if he is ill - therefore, he must avoid that which harms the body and accustom himself to that which is healthful and helps the body become stronger.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides, himself a physician, opens his health code by making bodily soundness a religious duty and framing medicine as avoiding what harms and cultivating what strengthens.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts begin a treatment of health with the principle that the body must be kept from what disturbs it.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:1 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha reminds the over-strenuous monk Sona that a lute sounds well only when its strings are neither too tight nor too slack, and tells him to tune his effort the same way.
buddhism.explanation: The simile teaches that both overstrain and slackness spoil the result; balance is what makes the instrument play.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same neither-too-much-nor-too-little rule to the body's three humours.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Vêdanîya is twofold, pleasure and pain; there are many subdivisions of pleasure and so there are of pain also.”
jainism.explanation: In Jain doctrine the experience of bodily pain and pleasure is the fruition of vedaniya karma, one of the eight kinds of karmic matter binding the soul.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural traces disease to an imbalance of three humours, Jainism traces the felt pain of disease further back, to karma, a different causal account of the same suffering.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 33.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The union of air, water and fire / the body is the play-thing of the fickle and unsteady intellect.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak describes the human body as a compound of the elements, air named first, held together for a while and driven about by a restless mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's physicians count three bodily forces led by wind; Guru Nanak likewise sees the body as a mixture of elements led by air, whose condition depends on how they are held together.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 152, Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus warns Icarus to fly a middle course, neither so low that the sea's damp weighs down his wings nor so high that the sun's heat melts their wax; Icarus soars too high and falls.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes both extremes deadly and only the middle path safe.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that harm comes from too much and from too little alike.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Timaeus, Plato explains that the body is compacted of four elements, and that the unnatural excess or defect of these, or their shifting out of their proper place, is the origin of disorders and diseases.
philosophy.explanation: Plato gives a Greek version of humoral pathology in which disease is the excess or deficiency of the body's constituents.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's thesis, with four elements in place of three humours.

real_life_example.event_title: Christiaan Eijkman traces beriberi to polished rice
real_life_example.place: Batavia, Java, Dutch East Indies (now Jakarta, Indonesia)
real_life_example.event: Working in the Dutch government's medical laboratory in Batavia, Christiaan Eijkman found that chickens fed on polished white rice developed a nerve disease resembling beriberi and recovered when they were given unpolished rice. He at first explained this as a harmful substance in the rice grain that the outer layer counteracted, but the finding was later understood as the lack of a vital substance in the rice's outer layer. The work led to the concept of vitamins and earned Eijkman the 1929 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
real_life_example.explanation: Eijkman's experiment helped show that illness can come not only from something harmful being present but from something necessary being missing, a turning point in medical thinking.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the body's forces cause disease whether they grow too strong or fall too low, and Eijkman's beriberi work moved from a theory of harmful excess to the discovery that a deficiency was to blame.

tamil:
மருந்தென வேண்டாவாம் யாக்கைக்கு அருந்தியது
அற்றது போற்றி உணின்.
transliteration:
Marundhena vendaavaam yaakkaikku arundhiyadhu
atradhu potri unin.
meaning: The body needs no medicine if a person eats only after making sure the last meal has been fully digested.
elementary: You would not pour more water into a glass that is still full; it would spill everywhere. Valluvar says the stomach is like that glass: wait until it has finished the last meal before you fill it again, and you will hardly ever need a doctor.
university: The couplet makes a bold claim, that medicine (marundhu, மருந்து) becomes unnecessary (vendaavaam, வேண்டாவாம்) for the body (yaakkai, யாக்கை), on one condition: arundhiyadhu atradhu potri unin (அருந்தியது அற்றது போற்றி உணின்), 'if one eats after carefully confirming that what was taken has been digested'. Atradhu (அற்றது, literally 'that which has ceased') is the technical verb for complete digestion that recurs in 943 and 944. Potri (போற்றி) means not 'praising' here but 'observing with care'; Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as examining the state of digestion, and Kalaignar as allowing the proper interval between meals. Parimelazhagar's tradition reads the hyperbole as a statement of priority: prevention through regimen ranks above cure. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Among Charaka's rules for eating is that one should eat only after the previous meal has been digested, since food taken on top of undigested food disturbs all the doshas.
hinduism.explanation: Ayurvedic dietetics makes the digestion of the last meal the precondition for the next.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's rule almost word for word: eat only when what you ate before has been digested.
hinduism.source: Charaka Samhita, Vimanasthana 1.24 (rules of eating), paraphrase

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus answers his critics that those who are healthy have no need of a physician, only those who are sick.
christianity.explanation: The saying assumes the plain truth that a sound body does not need the doctor.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural tells how to stay among the healthy who need no medicine.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that there are two blessings in which many people are cheated: health and free time.
islam.explanation: The hadith counts health among God's greatest gifts and warns that people squander it.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows the simple discipline that guards this gift so that medicine is never needed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoever conducts himself in the ways which we have drawn up, I will guarantee that he will not become ill throughout his life, until he reaches advanced age and dies. He will not need a doctor.”
judaism.explanation: After setting out rules of eating, exercise and rest, Maimonides promises that anyone who follows them will never need a physician.
judaism.tie_back: Maimonides makes the Kural's exact promise: right regimen at meals means no need for medicine.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:20 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada names good health as the highest gain and contentment as the greatest wealth.
buddhism.explanation: Among all the things a person can acquire, the verse ranks freedom from illness first.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows how that highest gain is kept: by eating only when the last meal is gone.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mind of those who always live in unfrequented lodgings, who eat low food, and who subdue their senses, will not be attacked by the foe, Love, who is vanquished as disease is by medicine.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana treats plain, restrained eating as itself a remedy that keeps the passions from attacking the monk.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural makes careful eating stand in for medicine for the body, the Jain text makes restrained eating serve as medicine for the soul.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Naam is the panacea, the remedy to cure all ills.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan calls the Name of God the medicine for every ailment, meaning above all the ills of ego, desire and fear that trouble the mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that a well-kept regimen makes medicine unnecessary; Gurbani names the one remedy that, practised daily, keeps the inner life from falling sick.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 274, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that before Pandora opened her jar, the races of men lived on earth free from ills, from hard toil and from the heavy sicknesses that bring death.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth imagines an original human life in which sickness, and so medicine, did not exist.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural holds out a modest version of that sickness-free life, earned by a habit of eating rather than lost by a jar.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 90-92 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White), paraphrase

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates in the Republic scorns the need for medicine that arises not from wounds or epidemics but from idleness and a self-indulgent way of living that fills the body with fluxes and winds.
philosophy.explanation: Plato argues that most need for doctors is self-inflicted by bad habits of life.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural draws the positive conclusion: right habits of eating remove the need for medicine.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic III, 405c-d (tr. Benjamin Jowett), paraphrase

real_life_example.event_title: William Beaumont observes digestion through Alexis St. Martin's stomach
real_life_example.place: Fort Mackinac, Michigan Territory, and other army posts, United States
real_life_example.event: In 1822 army surgeon William Beaumont treated Alexis St. Martin, a young French-Canadian trapper accidentally wounded by a gunshot, whose wound healed leaving a permanent opening into his stomach. From 1825 Beaumont used the opening to observe digestion directly, timing how long different foods took to be digested and having gastric juice analysed, which showed it contained hydrochloric acid. He published his results in 1833 as Experiments and Observations on the Gastric Juice and the Physiology of Digestion; modern historians also note that his treatment of St. Martin raises serious ethical questions.
real_life_example.explanation: Beaumont's work established that digestion is a chemical process that takes measurable time, giving scientific shape to the old advice not to eat before the last meal has been dealt with.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural makes complete digestion of the previous meal the test for eating again, and Beaumont was the first to watch and time that process inside a living human stomach.

tamil:
அற்றால் அறவறிந்து உண்க அஃதுடம்பு
பெற்றான் நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு.
transliteration:
Atraal aravarindhu unga ahdhudambu
petraan nedidhuykkum aaru.
meaning: Once your last meal is digested, eat only the right amount. That is the way to keep the body you were given going for a long time.
elementary: A car runs far if you fill the tank properly and do not overflow it. Valluvar says your body is a gift you have been given, and eating the right amount at the right time is how you make it last a long, long time.
university: Atraal (அற்றால், 'when it has been digested') picks up the condition of 942, and adds aravarindhu (அறவறிந்து, அற + அறிந்து): Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read it as knowing the needed quantity, Puliyur Kesikan simply as eating in measure. The second line names the payoff: udambu petraan (உடம்பு பெற்றான், 'he who has obtained a body') can nedidhu uykkum (நெடிது உய்க்கும், 'carry it on long'). Kesikan glosses the body as 'this human frame so hard to obtain' (பெறுவதற்கரியதான இந்த மானிட யாக்கை), an Indian commonplace that human birth is rare and should not be wasted through gluttony. Parimelazhagar's line of interpretation thus links diet to longevity, not merely to comfort. Some editions print the first line as அற்றால் அளவறிந்து; ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net both read அறவறிந்து.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who is temperate in his habits of eating, sleeping, working and recreation can mitigate all material pains by practicing the yoga system.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that regulated eating (yuktahara), along with regulated sleep and work, is the ground of a pain-free yogic life.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's 'eat knowing the measure' is the Gita's yuktahara, here tied to long life rather than to yoga.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.17 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, As It Is, 1972)

christianity.quote_or_event: “By surfeiting have many perished; but he that taketh heed prolongeth his life.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira warns that overeating has killed many, while the one who is careful about food lengthens his days.
christianity.tie_back: It is a near paraphrase of the Kural: measured eating is the way to keep the body long.

islam.quote_or_event: “O children of Adam, take your adornment [i.e., wear your clothing] at every masjid, and eat and drink, but be not excessive. Indeed, He likes not those who commit excess.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an permits eating and drinking but forbids going beyond measure.
islam.tie_back: Both texts allow food freely while insisting that its measure be known and kept.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One should not eat until his stomach is full. Rather, [he should stop when] he has eaten to close to three quarter's of full satisfaction.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides gives a concrete measure: stop eating at about three quarters of fullness.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'knowing the measure', given an actual number.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:2 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When a man is always mindful, knowing moderation in eating, his discomfort fades, and he ages slowly, taking care of his life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha spoke this verse to King Pasenadi, who was panting after eating rice by the bucketful; the king had it recited at every meal and slimmed down.
buddhism.tie_back: Knowing the measure in eating so that one 'ages slowly, taking care of his life' is the Kural's promise of long life almost exactly.
buddhism.source: Donapaka Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 3.13 (tr. Bhikkhu Sujato)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who takes less food than he usually does, in the extreme case but one mouthful, performs abstinence with regard to substance.”
jainism.explanation: Avamodarika, eating less than one's full measure, is one of the six external austerities in Jain discipline.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism, like the Kural, makes the measure of food a matter of deliberate knowledge, though it sets the measure below fullness to burn off karma rather than to prolong life.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 30.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you.”
sikhism.explanation: In So Purakh, part of the evening prayer Rehras, Guru Arjan reminds the listener that a human body is a rare gift and the chance it offers should not be wasted.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's commentators gloss 'one who has obtained a body' as one granted this hard-won human frame, and urge measured eating so that it lasts; Gurbani shares the sense that the body is a gift to be cared for.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa, So Purakh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The maxim 'Nothing in excess' (meden agan) was inscribed at Apollo's temple at Delphi, which Plato says the sages dedicated as the first fruits of their wisdom.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Delphic god's own precinct carried a warning against excess in all things.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural applies the Delphic rule to the dinner plate.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...both excessive and defective exercise destroys the strength, and similarly drink or food which is above or below a certain amount destroys the health, while that which is proportionate both produces and increases and preserves it.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle uses diet as his model for the mean: the right amount of food produces, increases and preserves health.
philosophy.tie_back: Proportionate food that 'preserves' health is the Kural's measured eating that keeps the body long.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.2 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Alvise Cornaro writes his Treatise on the Sober Life
real_life_example.event: Alvise (Luigi) Cornaro, a businessman and patron of the arts in Padua, became critically ill around the age of forty after years of intemperate living and resolved to follow strict rules on the quantity and quality of what he ate and drank. He recovered, and in 1558 published his Treatise on the Sober Life, describing his measured diet as the source of his health and recommending moderation as the way to live to a great age. He revised and added to the work in the following years, lived into his eighties, and died in 1566; the book became an international success and was translated into English many times.
real_life_example.explanation: Cornaro's book is one of the earliest and most widely read personal accounts of measured eating as a path to long life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that one who eats in the right measure after digestion keeps the body going for a long time, which is exactly the regimen and result Cornaro described.

tamil:
அற்றது அறிந்து கடைப்பிடித்து மாறல்ல
துய்க்க துவரப் பசித்து.
transliteration:
Atradhu arindhu kadaippidiththu maaralla
thuykka thuvarap pasiththu.
meaning: Make sure your last meal is digested. Then stick to foods that suit your body, and eat them only when you are really hungry.
elementary: A plant needs water, but only when its soil has dried, and only clean water, not juice or soda. Valluvar says eat when you are really hungry, and choose the food that suits your body.
university: The couplet adds two refinements to the rule of digestion. Maaralla (மாறல்ல, 'things that are not contrary') are foods that do not disagree with one's constitution; Pappaiah extends this to foods unsuited to the body and to the season (உடம்பிற்கும் காலத்திற்கும் ஒவ்வாத). Kadaippidiththu (கடைப்பிடித்து) means holding firmly to such foods as a fixed practice. Thuvarap pasiththu (துவரப் பசித்து), 'being thoroughly hungry', makes real hunger, not appetite or habit, the signal to eat. Pope's translation renders the sense as 'when hunger prompteth thee, with constant care, the viands choose that well agree'. The idea of wholesome and unwholesome food relative to the person (Sanskrit satmya) is shared with Ayurveda, and the Parimelazhagar tradition reads the couplet as practical dietetics. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Foods in the mode of goodness increase the duration of life, purify one's existence and give strength, health, happiness and satisfaction. Such nourishing foods are sweet, juicy, fattening and palatable.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classes foods by their effect, praising those that are agreeable and promote life, strength and health.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's 'foods that agree with the body' correspond to the Gita's sattvic foods.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.8 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, As It Is, 1972)

christianity.quote_or_event: The Preacher calls a land blessed whose princes eat in due season, for strength and not for drunkenness.
christianity.explanation: Ecclesiastes praises rulers who eat at the proper time and for the right purpose.
christianity.tie_back: Eating in due season for strength parallels the Kural's eating only at true hunger.

islam.quote_or_event: God tells the Children of Israel to eat of the good things He has provided and not to transgress therein.
islam.explanation: The Qur'an pairs eating what is good with a warning against going beyond bounds.
islam.tie_back: Both texts call for wholesome food taken within limits.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They are as follows: a person should never eat unless he is hungry, nor drink unless thirsty.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides' first practical rule of health is to eat only from real hunger.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'eat when thoroughly hungry' stated as law.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:1 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches monks to reflect wisely when they take almsfood: not for fun, intoxication or beautification, but only to sustain the body, to end the discomfort of hunger and to support the spiritual life.
buddhism.explanation: The daily reflection on food makes the relief of hunger and the support of the body the only proper reasons for eating.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes real hunger, not pleasure, the occasion for eating.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Sramana engaged in austerities, who longs for righteousness, should eat the proper quantity of allowed food, should select a companion of right understanding, and should live in a place suited to seclusion.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk is to eat only permitted food, and only in the proper quantity.
jainism.tie_back: Choosing allowed food in proper quantity echoes the Kural's choosing agreeable food at the right time, with the Jain criterion being ahimsa and discipline rather than bodily constitution.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Baba, the pleasures of other foods are false. Eating them, the body is ruined, and wickedness and corruption enter into the mind.”
sikhism.explanation: In a Sri Raag hymn, Guru Nanak warns against eating for pleasure foods that harm the body and disturb the mind, setting them against the true nourishment of the Name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells one to keep firmly to foods that agree with the body; Guru Nanak likewise warns against foods that, once eaten, ruin the body.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Alcinous' palace the grieving Odysseus says there is nothing more shameless than the belly, which commands a man to eat even in his deepest sorrow.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's hero admits that hunger rules even a hero's heart.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural accepts hunger's claim but tames it: eat only when hunger is real, and eat what suits you.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Xenophon reports that Socrates ate only as much as he could eat with relish, and came to his meals so ready that the appetite itself was his sauce.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates let genuine hunger, not rich dishes, make food pleasant.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's rule to eat when thoroughly hungry, lived out by a philosopher.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Memorabilia I.3.5 (tr. E. C. Marchant), paraphrase

real_life_example.event_title: Willem Dicke shows that wheat harms children with coeliac disease
real_life_example.event: Dutch paediatrician Willem Karel Dicke presented a doctoral thesis at the University of Utrecht in 1950 showing that wheat flour and rye flour caused the symptoms of coeliac disease in children, while purified wheat starch did not. He had suspected wheat since the 1930s, and observations during the wartime Dutch famine of 1944-45, when bread was scarce, reinforced his view. His work, followed by the identification of gluten as the harmful part of the grain, made the gluten-free diet the standard treatment.
real_life_example.explanation: Dicke showed that a food that nourishes most people can be harmful to some, so that health depends on choosing foods that suit one's own body.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural tells us to keep firmly to foods that agree with the body, and Dicke's patients recovered once a food that disagreed with their constitution was removed.

tamil:
மாறுபாடு இல்லாத உண்டி மறுத்துண்ணின்
ஊறுபாடு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Maarupaadu illaadha undi maruththunnin
oorupaadu illai uyirkku.
meaning: If you eat food that suits your body and stop before you eat too much, no harm will come to your life.
elementary: Even your favourite ice cream will give you a tummy ache if you eat the whole tub. Valluvar says that even good food must be eaten with a 'no, that's enough' at the right moment.
university: Maarupaadu illaadha undi (மாறுபாடு இல்லாத உண்டி) is food that does not clash with the body, the same category as maaralla in 944. The key word is maruththu (மறுத்து, 'refusing'): Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as refusing more once the measure is reached, and Kesikan as eating not as the mind desires but only as much as causes no illness. Solomon Pappaiah takes a different line, reading maruththu as rejecting unsuitable foods, so that the couplet becomes about selection rather than quantity; this is a genuine interpretive divergence. Oorupaadu (ஊறுபாடு) is injury or harm, and uyirkku (உயிர்க்கு) 'to life' or 'to the soul dwelling in the body'. Parimelazhagar's reading, followed by most modern commentators, stresses restraint even with good food. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Foods that are too bitter, too sour, salty, pungent, dry and hot, are liked by people in the modes of passion. Such foods cause pain, distress, and disease.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita warns that foods chosen for intense taste rather than wholesomeness bring disease.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's 'food without contrariety' is the opposite of these disease-causing rajasic foods.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.9 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, As It Is, 1972)

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs advises that if you find honey you should eat only as much as is sufficient for you, lest you be filled with it and vomit it.
christianity.explanation: Even the sweetest good thing must be taken only up to sufficiency.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's lesson that even agreeable food must be eaten with refusal of excess.

islam.quote_or_event: “The human does not fill any container that is worse than his stomach. It is sufficient for the son of Adam to eat what will support his back. If this is not possible, then a third for food, a third for drink, and third for his breath.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet sets the limit of eating at what keeps one upright, or at most a third of the stomach for food.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hadith asks for deliberate restraint even with lawful, wholesome food.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A man who is wise, overcomes his desires, is not drawn by his appetites and eats nothing of the aforementioned unless he needs them for a medical reason, is [indeed] heroic.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides calls the one who masters his appetite at table a hero.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's maruththu, refusing at the table, is exactly this heroic self-mastery.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:10 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares right eating to parents crossing a desert who must eat the flesh of their dead child to survive: they eat only to get across, without any relish or excess.
buddhism.explanation: The stark simile teaches that food should be taken only for sustenance, never for indulgence.
buddhism.tie_back: It pushes to an extreme the Kural's counsel to eat even good food with refusal of excess.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Abstention from dainty food means abstention from such highly nourishing food and drink as milk, curds, ghee, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Rasaparityaga, giving up rich and tasty foods, is one of the six external Jain austerities.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism, like the Kural, asks the eater to refuse what appetite wants, though it renounces even wholesome rich foods for the soul's sake.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 30.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Sleep little, and eat little; O Nanak, this is the essence of wisdom.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak's dialogue with the yogis, this line ends a stanza describing the disciplined seeker who lives in the world without being ruled by appetite.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says no harm comes to one who holds back from eating too much even of wholesome food; the verse likewise makes eating little part of wisdom.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 939, Raag Ramkali, Sidh Gosht (pauri 8), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stranded on Thrinacia, Odysseus' starving companions slaughter the forbidden cattle of the Sun despite his warnings; Zeus destroys their ship, and only Odysseus, who refused the meat, survives.
greek_mythology.explanation: The men who could not refuse food perished, while the one who held back lived.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's promise, that the one who refuses excess suffers no harm to life, is played out in mythic terms.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epicurus writes to Menoeceus that plain fare gives as much pleasure as a costly diet once the pain of want is removed, and that becoming used to simple food is a full supply of health.
philosophy.explanation: The philosopher of pleasure himself argues that restraint and simple food are the true road to health and lasting pleasure.
philosophy.tie_back: This supports the Kural's claim that wholesome food eaten with restraint keeps life free from harm.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus (Diogenes Laertius X.130-131, tr. R. D. Hicks), paraphrase

real_life_example.event_title: Finland launches the North Karelia Project
real_life_example.event: In the early 1970s the Finnish province of North Karelia had one of the highest rates of death from heart disease in the world, and in 1972 local authorities, working with the World Health Organization, launched a community-wide programme to change how people lived. It encouraged residents to replace butter and whole milk with lower-fat alternatives, eat more vegetables and less salt, and stop smoking, and worked with schools and local food producers to change what was on offer. Over the following decades heart-disease deaths among working-age people in the region fell by roughly 80 percent, though the exact figure varies with the period measured.
real_life_example.explanation: The project became a world model for preventing illness by changing everyday diet across a whole community rather than treating disease after it appears.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural promises that no harm comes to the life of one who eats wholesome food and holds back from excess, and North Karelia showed that promise borne out across a whole population.

tamil:
இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்கண் இன்பம்போல் நிற்கும்
கழிபேர் இரையான்கண் நோய்.
transliteration:
Izhivarindhu unbaankan inbampol nirkum
kazhiper iraiyaankan noi.
meaning: Good health stays with a person who knows to eat a little less. In the same way, sickness stays with a person who eats far too much.
elementary: Two friends go to a party. One eats until he is nicely full and goes home happy. The other stuffs himself and spends the night with a stomach ache. Valluvar says that is how it goes every time.
university: The couplet is a balanced antithesis. Izhivu (இழிவு) here means 'lessness': Varadarasanar glosses izhivarindhu unbaan as one who knows what the lesser measure is, and Kesikan as one who eats a little below the full measure; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it more morally as one who knows that taking more than needed is base, exploiting the word's other sense of 'meanness'. Inbam (இன்பம்) is well-being or pleasure, which nirkum (நிற்கும், 'stays, abides'). Kazhiper iraiyaan (கழிபேர் இரையான்) is a striking phrase: irai (இரை) is the word for an animal's prey or fodder, so the glutton is pictured as a beast gulping feed, and kazhiper (கழிபேர்) intensifies it to 'exceedingly great'. Disease abides with him as surely as health with the moderate eater. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There is no possibility of one's becoming a yogī, O Arjuna, if one eats too much, or eats too little, sleeps too much or does not sleep enough.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna makes moderation in eating a precondition of the disciplined, well-ordered life.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita treats the over-eater as one who has forfeited the good state that the moderate keep.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.16 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, As It Is, 1972)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Sound sleep cometh of moderate eating: he riseth early, and his wits are with him: but the pain of watching, and choler, and pangs of the belly, are with an unsatiable man.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira sets the rested, clear-headed moderate eater against the sleepless, bilious, cramped glutton.
christianity.tie_back: It is the same two-sided picture as the Kural: well-being stays with the moderate and suffering with the insatiable.

islam.quote_or_event: “A believer eats in one intestine (is satisfied with a little food), and a kafir (unbeliever) eats in seven intestines (eats much food).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet contrasts the believer, content with little, with one who eats voraciously.
islam.tie_back: The Kural draws the same contrast between the one who eats little and the one who devours, measured by health rather than faith.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As long as one exercises, exerts himself greatly, does not eat to the point of satiation and has loose bowels, he will not suffer sickness and he will grow in strength.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides promises freedom from sickness and growing strength to one who stops short of satiety.
judaism.tie_back: Eating short of fullness and keeping well is the first half of the Kural's antithesis.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:14 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that Mara overthrows one who lives fixed on pleasant things, with senses unguarded and immoderate in eating, as wind topples a weak tree, but cannot shake one who is moderate in eating and restrained, as wind cannot shake a rocky mountain.
buddhism.explanation: The paired verses set the immoderate eater, easily overthrown, against the moderate one who stands firm.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's twin portrait of the moderate eater and the glutton has the same two-sided form.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant food should not be enjoyed with preference, for it generally makes men over-strong; and desires rush upon the strong, like birds upon a tree with sweet fruits.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana warns that rich eating breeds an excess that attracts the passions as fruit attracts birds.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural sees disease settling on the glutton, the Jain text sees desires swarming on him.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, my bread is made of wood, and hunger is my appetizer. Those who eat buttered bread, will suffer in terrible pain.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose verses the Gurus included in the Granth, contrasts his plain dry bread, made tasty only by hunger, with the rich food of those who indulge and later suffer for it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural sets the well-being of the moderate eater against the disease of the glutton; Farid sets plain food eaten in hunger against rich food that brings pain.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 28) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Homer introduces the beggar Irus as notorious for his insatiable belly, always eating and drinking, big to look at but with no strength or force in him; Odysseus fells him with a single blow.
greek_mythology.explanation: The glutton's bulk hides weakness, and he is easily brought down.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Irus embodies the Kural's kazhiper iraiyaan, the over-eater with whom weakness abides.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca observes that simple food once kept people healthy, and that the multiplying of rich dishes has multiplied diseases, so that one who wonders at the countless diseases should count the cooks.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic ties the growth of disease directly to luxurious overeating.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's cooks and diseases are the Kural's glutton with whom illness stays.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 95.15-23 (tr. R. M. Gummere), paraphrase

real_life_example.event_title: Kaibara Ekiken publishes the Yojokun
real_life_example.event: Kaibara Ekiken, a scholar of the Fukuoka Domain who had also studied medicine, wrote the Yojokun (Lessons on Nourishing Life) at the age of 83, and it was published in 1713. The handbook advised balanced, moderate eating and stopping at about eight-tenths full, alongside exercise, sound sleep and a calm mind. Written in plain Japanese rather than classical Chinese, it became one of the most widely read health books in Japan and is still reprinted today; Kaibara himself lived to 86.
real_life_example.explanation: The Yojokun spread the principle of stopping before one is full, still known in Japan as hara hachi bu, to generations of ordinary readers.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says well-being stays with one who knows to eat a little less, which is the very rule of eating to eight-tenths that Kaibara taught.

tamil:
தீயள வன்றித் தெரியான் பெரிதுண்ணின்
நோயள வின்றிப் படும்.
transliteration:
Theeyala vandrith theriyaan peridhunnin
noyala vindrip padum.
meaning: A person who carelessly eats far more than their stomach's fire (the body's power to digest) can handle will get sicknesses without end.
elementary: A small campfire can cook a small pot. If you pile a whole tree on it, the fire chokes and smoke goes everywhere. Valluvar says your tummy has a little fire too, and if you overload it, troubles pile up.
university: The couplet turns on a wordplay of measure: thee alavu (தீ அளவு, 'the measure of the fire') against noi alavu indri (நோய் அளவின்றி, 'diseases without measure'). The fire is the pasi-thee (பசித்தீ), the 'fire of hunger' or digestive fire, as Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss it; it corresponds to the Ayurvedic jatharagni, whose strength determines how much food can be digested. Theriyaan (தெரியான்) is 'one who does not discern', and Kesikan adds that he ignores both the time and the quantity. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads thee alavu instead as an analogy to one who does not know how to use fire in measure, a minority reading. Parimelazhagar's tradition takes the metaphor medically, so that the couplet states a law: exceed the fire's measure and illness exceeds all measure. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Charaka teaches that one should eat in proper measure, and that the right quantity of food depends on the strength of the digestive fire (agni).
hinduism.explanation: In Ayurveda the digestive fire sets the limit of how much food can be taken without harm.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's thee alavu, the measure of the fire, stated as medical doctrine.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For excess of meats bringeth sickness, and surfeiting will turn into choler.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira states plainly that eating too much produces sickness and biliousness.
christianity.tie_back: Excess of food bringing sickness is the Kural's rule that eating beyond measure brings disease beyond measure.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an describes those who reject faith as enjoying themselves and eating as grazing cattle eat, without thought.
islam.explanation: Thoughtless, animal-like eating is presented as the mark of a heedless life.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's theriyaan, the undiscerning eater, is likewise one who eats without thought of measure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Overeating is like poison to anyone's body. It is the main source of all illness. Most illnesses which afflict a man are caused by harmful foods or by his filling his belly and overeating, even of healthful foods.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides traces most human illness to overeating, even of good food.
judaism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that eating beyond measure brings diseases beyond measure.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:15 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who gets drowsy from overeating, fond of sleep, rolling round the bed like a great hog stuffed with grain: that dullard returns to the womb again and again.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada, traditionally linked to King Pasenadi's overeating, pictures the glutton as a sluggish, stuffed hog.
buddhism.tie_back: The thoughtless over-eater of the Kural is this stuffed, dull figure, though the Buddhist cost is rebirth rather than disease.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As in a forest, full of fuel, a fire fanned by the wind cannot be extinguished, so the fire (as it were) of the senses of him who eats as he lists; it does not benefit any chaste man.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana uses the image of fire fed with too much fuel for the senses inflamed by unrestrained eating.
jainism.tie_back: Both texts reach for fire to describe eating without measure, the Kural for the digestive fire and the Jain text for the fire of the senses.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir names lobh (greed), one of the five thieves of Sikh teaching, as the bringer of death, and sets it against forgiveness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that one who thoughtlessly eats beyond measure will suffer diseases beyond measure; Kabir warns more broadly that wherever greed rules, ruin follows.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 155) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how Erysichthon, cursed by Ceres with Hunger for felling her sacred oak, eats ever more and craves ever more, as fire never refuses fuel, until he consumes his fortune and at last his own flesh.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes boundless eating a self-devouring fire that destroys the eater.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Erysichthon is the extreme of the Kural's man who eats beyond the fire's measure and suffers without measure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Growing bodies have the most innate heat; they therefore require the most food, for otherwise their bodies are wasted. In old persons the heat is feeble, and therefore they require little fuel, as it were, to the flame, for it would be extinguished by much.”
philosophy.explanation: Hippocrates measures how much food a body needs by its inner heat, and warns that too much fuel smothers a weak flame.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's thee alavu exactly: food must match the measure of the body's fire.

real_life_example.event_title: King Henry I of England dies after a meal of lampreys
real_life_example.event: Henry I, king of England and duke of Normandy, fell ill and died at Lyons-la-Forêt in Normandy on 1 December 1135. The chronicler Henry of Huntingdon recorded that the king's last illness followed a meal of lampreys, a fish he was fond of, eaten against medical advice. His death without a surviving legitimate son led to a long succession war between his nephew Stephen and his daughter Matilda.
real_life_example.explanation: The account of the king's last meal became a byword in English history for the danger of indulging an appetite against good advice.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that one who thoughtlessly eats beyond what the body can digest will suffer disease beyond measure, and the chroniclers presented Henry's fatal illness in just those terms.

tamil:
நோய்நாடி நோய்முதல் நாடி அதுதணிக்கும்
வாய்நாடி வாய்ப்பச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Noinaadi noimudhal naadi adhuthanikkum
vaainaadi vaaippach cheyal.
meaning: Find out what the sickness is, find its cause, find the way to ease it, and then treat it in the right way.
elementary: When your bike makes a funny noise, a good mechanic first finds which part is wrong, then why it broke, then how to fix it, and only then gets out the tools. Valluvar says a good doctor does the same with a sick person.
university: The most quoted couplet of the chapter is built on a threefold naadi (நாடி, 'having examined'): the disease (noi), its root or first cause (noi mudhal, நோய் முதல்), and the means (vaai, வாய்) that will abate it (thanikkum, தணிக்கும்). Only then comes vaaippach cheyal (வாய்ப்பச் செயல்), 'act fittingly': Kesikan reads it as treating without error in procedure, Varadarasanar as in a way suited to the body. Commentators note the sequence of diagnosis, aetiology and therapy as a complete clinical method; Kalaignar adds that it applies to the ills of society as well as of the body. The repetition of naadi and of vaai/vaaippa gives the line a deliberate, step-by-step rhythm. The couplet appears in the sung version of the chapter by P. A. Muthukrishnan quoted on thirukkural.net. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Charaka instructs the physician to examine the disease first and only afterwards the medicine, and then to begin treatment with knowledge.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Ayurveda puts diagnosis before any prescription.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's order: know the disease and its cause before choosing the remedy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then give place to the physician, for the Lord hath created him: let him not go from thee, for thou hast need of him. There is a time when in their hands there is good success. For they shall also pray unto the Lord, that he would prosper that, which they give for ease and remedy to prolong life.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira honours the physician and describes him seeking the right remedy and the right moment to bring ease.
christianity.tie_back: It supports the Kural's skilled, careful physician, though without its diagnostic method.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is a remedy for every malady, and when the remedy is applied to the disease it is cured with the permission of Allah, the Exalted and Glorious.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that every disease has its proper remedy, which cures when correctly matched to it.
islam.tie_back: Matching the right remedy to the disease is the Kural's 'find the means that abates it'.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud derives from the words 'and he shall surely heal' that the Torah grants the physician permission to heal, so that medical treatment is a sanctioned and even obligatory act.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic law affirms the physician's work as legitimate rather than an intrusion on God's will.
judaism.tie_back: It provides the religious warrant for the physician the Kural describes, though not his method.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 85a (on Exodus 21:19), paraphrase

buddhism.quote_or_event: Buddhaghosa explains the Four Noble Truths through medicine: suffering is like the disease, its origin like the cause of the disease, its cessation like the cure, and the path like the medicine.
buddhism.explanation: The commentarial tradition reads the Buddha's core teaching as a physician's diagnosis, aetiology, prognosis and prescription.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's sequence of disease, its cause and its remedy, raised to a spiritual method.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Love and hatred are caused by Karman, and they say that Karman has its origin in delusion; Karman is the root of birth and death, and birth and death they call misery. Misery ceases on the absence of delusion, delusion ceases on the absence of desire, desire ceases on the absence of greed, greed ceases on the absence of property.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana traces suffering back through karma and delusion to its roots and shows how removing each root ends it, calling final liberation recovery 'from the long illness'.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's method of finding the disease, then its root cause, then what removes it, applied to the soul's misery.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.7-8, cf. 32.110 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O physician, you are a competent physician, if you first diagnose the disease. Prescribe such a remedy, by which all sorts of illnesses may be cured. Administer that medicine, which will cure the disease, and allow peace to come and dwell in the body.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok in Guru Nanak's Malaar ki Vaar, Guru Angad addresses the physician: first find the disease, then the remedy, then give the medicine that truly cures.
sikhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own three steps: find the disease, find the remedy, then act in the way that fits.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1279, Raag Malaar, Malaar ki Vaar, salok of Guru Angad (Mahala 2) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Menelaus is wounded by an arrow, the healer Machaon, son of Asclepius, comes, draws the arrow, looks at the wound, sucks out the blood and skilfully spreads on it the soothing remedies that Chiron had given his father.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's physician examines the wound first and then applies the proper remedy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Machaon follows the Kural's order: look at the injury, then bring the fitting treatment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato contrasts the slave doctor who prescribes hastily with the free doctor who examines the disease from its origin and according to nature, questions the patient and his friends, and prescribes only after understanding the case.
philosophy.explanation: Plato's model physician investigates the nature and origin of the illness before he treats.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's physician who examines the disease and its cause before acting.
philosophy.source: Plato, Laws IV, 720a-e (tr. Benjamin Jowett), paraphrase

real_life_example.event_title: Walter Reed's commission confirms that mosquitoes spread yellow fever
real_life_example.event: In 1900 the United States Army sent a commission led by Walter Reed to Cuba to study yellow fever, which was killing soldiers and civilians. Testing the hypothesis of the Cuban physician Carlos Finlay, the commission showed that the disease was carried by a mosquito and not spread by contact with patients' clothing or bedding. William Gorgas then directed a campaign in Havana to screen patients and destroy mosquito breeding places, and within months of its start in 1901 the city was freed of yellow fever.
real_life_example.explanation: Identifying the true cause of the disease made an effective remedy possible, and the same methods later protected workers building the Panama Canal.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's method is to find the disease, find its cause, find what will relieve it and then act, and the Reed commission and Gorgas followed that sequence step by step.

tamil:
உற்றான் அளவும் பிணியளவும் காலமும்
கற்றான் கருதிச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Utraan alavum piniyalavum kaalamum
katraan karudhich cheyal.
meaning: A trained doctor should think about the patient, how serious the sickness is, and the time or season before treating it.
elementary: A baby and a grown-up with the same cold do not get the same dose of medicine. Valluvar says a good doctor thinks about who is sick, how sick they are, and what time it is before deciding what to do.
university: Three measures must be weighed: utraan alavu (உற்றான் அளவு), the measure of the one afflicted, which Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss as age and the like, and Kesikan as the patient's strength; pini alavu (பிணியளவு), the extent and nature of the disease; and kaalam (காலம்), which Sivayogi Sivakumar reads as the climate of the season, Kalaignar as the right time for treatment, and Pappaiah as both the duration of the illness and the time needed to cure it. The agent is katraan (கற்றான்), 'the one who has learned', i.e. the physician trained in the medical texts, and karudhi (கருதி) means 'having deliberated'. The couplet thus individualises treatment, echoing Ayurveda's attention to the patient's constitution and to season (ritu). Pope renders it 'the habitudes of patient and disease, the crises of the ill these must the learned leech think over well'. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Charaka lays down a tenfold examination of the patient, including his constitution, strength, body measure, power of digestion, capacity for exercise and age, together with attention to place and season, before any therapy is chosen.
hinduism.explanation: Ayurvedic treatment is tailored to the individual patient, the state of the disease and the time.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's weighing of patient, disease and season before acting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My son, prove thy soul in thy life, and see what is evil for it, and give not that unto it. For all things are not profitable for all men, neither hath every soul pleasure in every thing.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira teaches that what helps one person may harm another, so each must test what suits him.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's attention to the particular patient rests on the same insight that not everything suits everyone.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that whoever practises medicine without being known for medical knowledge is liable for the harm he causes.
islam.explanation: The hadith makes learning the condition for the right to treat.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise entrusts treatment to katraan, the one who has learned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All of these beneficial habits which we have stated apply only to a healthy man. In contrast, a sick person, or one who has a single organ which is not healthy, or one who has followed a harmful way of life for many years, each of these must choose different patterns of behavior in accordance with his [particular] illness as it is explained in the medical literature.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides insists that the sick must be treated according to their own illness and condition, following the medical books.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's rule that treatment must fit the particular patient and disease as the learned texts direct.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:21 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha distinguishes three kinds of sick people: those who recover whether or not they get suitable food, medicine and nursing, those who do not recover either way, and those who recover only if they get them.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta recognises that different patients respond differently to treatment.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it asks the carer to weigh the particular patient rather than treat all alike.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Abstinence is briefly of five kinds: with regard to a. substance; b. place; c. time; d. state of mind; e. development.”
jainism.explanation: Jain discipline calibrates even reduced eating by dravya, kshetra, kala and bhava, the substance, place, time and inner state of the one practising it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's weighing of the person, the measure of the illness and the time follows the same habit of judging every practice by its circumstances.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 30.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The physician was called in; he touched my arm and felt my pulse. The foolish physician did not know that the pain was in the mind.”
sikhism.explanation: In the salok just before Guru Angad's, Guru Nanak describes a physician who takes the pulse but misses the real illness, the pain of separation from God within.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks the learned physician to weigh the patient's real condition before acting; Guru Nanak shows what goes wrong when a physician does not grasp the patient's true state.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1279, Raag Malaar, Malaar ki Vaar, salok of Guru Nanak (Mahala 1) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar sings that Asclepius relieved all who came to him, whether with ulcers, wounds, or bodies wasted by summer heat or winter cold, treating some with gentle incantations, some with soothing potions, some with remedies bound on the limbs, and some with the knife.
greek_mythology.explanation: The divine healer chose a different treatment for each sufferer and condition, including those brought on by the season.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Asclepius fits the Kural's learned healer who weighs patient, disease and season before acting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...if ten pounds are too much for a particular person to eat and two too little, it does not follow that the trainer will order six pounds; for this also is perhaps too much for the person who is to take it, or too little- too little for Milo, too much for the beginner in athletic exercises.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle's trainer sets the right amount relative to the person, not by a fixed rule.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's physician likewise sets treatment by the measure of the particular patient.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Dominique-Jean Larrey introduces flying ambulances and triage
real_life_example.place: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic armies, Europe
real_life_example.event: Dominique-Jean Larrey, a surgeon in the French army, introduced horse-drawn flying ambulances in the 1790s to carry wounded soldiers from the battlefield quickly instead of leaving them until the fighting ended. He also insisted that the wounded be treated in order of how badly they were hurt and how urgently they needed care, not according to their rank. His system of sorting casualties is regarded as the origin of modern triage.
real_life_example.explanation: Larrey made the patient's condition and the urgency of the moment, rather than social standing, the basis for medical decisions.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks the physician to weigh the patient, the extent of the disease and the time before acting, and Larrey's triage did exactly that on the battlefield.

tamil:
உற்றவன் தீர்ப்பான் மருந்துழைச் செல்வானென்று
அப்பால் நாற்கூற்றே மருந்து.
transliteration:
Utravan theerppaan marundhuzhaich chelvaanendru
appaal naarkootre marundhu.
meaning: Medicine has four parts: the patient, the doctor who cures, the medicine, and the helper who stays close to give it.
elementary: Getting better is like a team game. The sick person must follow the plan, the doctor must know what to do, the medicine must be good, and someone like a parent or nurse must help every day. If one player is missing, the team struggles.
university: The chapter ends by defining medicine as naarkootru (நாற்கூற்று, 'fourfold'): utravan (உற்றவன், the one afflicted), theerppaan (தீர்ப்பான், the one who cures), marundhu (மருந்து, the remedy), and marundhuzhaich chelvaan (மருந்துழைச் செல்வான், literally 'he who goes near the medicine'). This last term divides the commentators: Varadarasanar reads it as the one who gives the medicine from close by, Kalaignar as the attendant at the bedside, Pappaiah and Kesikan as the preparer or compounder, and Pope's explanation as the compounder. The words appaal (அப்பால், 'that domain') and the closing marundhu frame the whole. Pope's gloss, following Parimelazhagar, adds that each of the four has four qualities in turn, sixteen in all. The fourfold scheme closely matches the Charaka Samhita's 'four feet' of therapy (physician, drug, attendant, patient), which is strong evidence that Valluvar knew the classical medical tradition. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Charaka names the four feet (pada-chatushtaya) of successful treatment as the physician, the drugs, the attendant and the patient, each of which must have its proper qualities.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Ayurveda rests all therapy on these four pillars.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's fourfold medicine, item for item, including the qualities of each that Parimelazhagar's tradition mentions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “With such doth he heal [men,] and taketh away their pains. Of such doth the apothecary make a confection; and of his works there is no end; and from him is peace over all the earth,”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira describes healing as the joint work of God-given medicines, the physician and the apothecary who compounds them.
christianity.tie_back: The physician, the medicine and the compounder here are three of the Kural's four parts of medicine.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet commanded his followers to feed the hungry, visit the sick and set free the captive.
islam.explanation: Visiting and caring for the sick is made a duty for every Muslim, not just for physicians.
islam.tie_back: It honours the Kural's fourth part, the one who stays near the patient.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A Torah Sage is not permitted to live in a community which does not have the following: a doctor, a bloodletter, a bathhouse, a latrine, an available source of water such as a river or a spring, a synagogue, a teacher of children, a scribe, a charity supervisor, a rabbinical court empowered to impose corporal punishment and jail sentences.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides counts a doctor and a medical practitioner among the minimum institutions of a community fit to live in.
