real_life_example.explanation: Ali gave up his title and his best years as a boxer rather than act against what he held to be his conscience.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even acts one seems unable to live without must be given up if doing them would lower one's dignity, and Ali sacrificed the career that was his livelihood rather than do what he believed was wrong.

tamil:
சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யாரே சீரொடு
பேராண்மை வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Seerinum seeralla seyyaare seerodu
Peraanmai vendu pavar.
meaning: People who want both a good name and true greatness will not do anything shameful, even if it would make them famous.
elementary: Some people will do anything to become famous, even mean or silly things. This kural says that people who want to be both well-known and truly good will never do something shameful just to get noticed.
university: The couplet plays on seer (சீர், renown, excellence): seerinum (சீரினும், 'even for renown') and seeralla (சீரல்ல, 'what is not excellent', unworthy deeds). Those who desire seerodu peraanmai (சீரொடு பேராண்மை), renown together with great 'manliness' or nobility of spirit, do not do such things. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses peraanmai as பெரிய ஆண்மை and the unworthy acts as those unfit for kudi-p-perumai (family honour); Kalaignar reads it as a heroic life that will not chase fame by acts contrary to self-respect. The point sharpens the previous kural: not only necessity but even fame itself cannot justify a lowering act. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Katha Upanishad, Yama teaches Nachiketas that the good (shreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both come to a person; the wise examine them and choose the good, while the foolish choose the pleasant and miss the true goal.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad separates what is truly good from what merely looks attractive, and praises choosing the good.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's noble person likewise refuses an attractive gain (fame) when it requires an unworthy act.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them; And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me. Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan”
christianity.explanation: Jesus is offered all the glory of the world on condition of one unworthy act, and refuses.
christianity.tie_back: A vivid case of the Kural's rule: glory is not worth an act that lowers one.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever desires honor [through power] - then to Allah belongs all honor. To Him ascends good speech, and righteous work raises it. But they who plot evil deeds will have a severe punishment, and the plotting of those - it will perish.”
islam.explanation: The Quran says true honour comes only through good speech and righteous work, while evil schemes come to nothing.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it teaches that real honour cannot be reached by unworthy means.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, And loving favour rather than silver and gold.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs ranks a good name above wealth.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural adds that a good name joined to nobility is not to be bought even with fame won unworthily.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Gains, Offerings, Fame, & Status wrongly gained, and whoever would praise self & disparage others. That, Namuci, is your army, the Dark One's commando force.”
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta names fame and status gained wrongly as part of Mara's army that he must defeat.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural too treats fame won by unworthy deeds as something the noble refuse.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 3.2, Padhana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu; accesstoinsight.org)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The excellent will not do the things which will bring upon them the effects of sin in another birth, or disgrace in this birth, though it should cost them their lives.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain quatrain says the noble avoid any act that brings sin in the next life or disgrace in this one, whatever the cost.
jainism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that the honourable will not do unworthy deeds even for renown.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 30 (மானம், 'Honour'), stanza 5 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “with a good name and reputation, with praise and fame throughout the world- still, if the Lord does not bless you with His Glance of Grace, then who cares? What is the use?”
sikhism.explanation: In the seventh pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak says that even worldwide fame is worth nothing without God's grace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who want true glory will not do unworthy deeds even for fame; Guru Nanak likewise puts fame below something higher.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib (pauri 7), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus' fable, the young Heracles meets two women at a crossroads: Vice offers him an easy, pleasant road, while Virtue offers a hard road of toil that leads to true and lasting glory; he chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles chooses the road where glory is earned honestly over an easier road of pleasure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's seekers of renown with nobility, he wants glory only on worthy terms.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus' Choice of Heracles, in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus says that if he can gain wealth while keeping himself modest, faithful and high-minded, he will; but if he must give up his own proper good so that others can gain what is not truly good, it is unjust and foolish to ask it.
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus will accept outward gains only if they leave his character intact.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural applies the same test to fame: it is welcome only if no unworthy act is needed to get it.

real_life_example.event_title: Lawrence Lemieux stops racing to rescue rival sailors at the Seoul Olympics
real_life_example.place: Off Busan, South Korea (1988 Seoul Olympic Games)
real_life_example.event: During a Finn-class race at the 1988 Olympic sailing regatta, held in strong winds off Busan, Canadian sailor Lawrence Lemieux was running in second place overall when he saw that two sailors from Singapore had been thrown from their capsized boat. He left the course, pulled the injured sailors from the water and stayed with them until a patrol boat arrived, then rejoined the race and finished far back, losing his chance of a medal. The International Olympic Committee awarded him the Pierre de Coubertin Medal for sportsmanship.
real_life_example.explanation: Lemieux showed that an Olympic medal was worth less to him than doing what was right by other competitors in danger.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who want true nobility will not do anything unworthy even if it would win them fame, and Lemieux would not sail on toward a medal while others were in danger.

tamil:
பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல் சிறிய
சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு.
transliteration:
Perukkaththu vendum panidhal siriya
Surukkaththu vendum uyarvu.
meaning: When you have plenty, be modest and gentle. When you have very little, hold your head high.
elementary: When you win a game, it is good to be kind and not show off. When you lose, it is good to stand tall and not beg or sulk. This kural says to bow a little in good times and stand straight in hard times.
university: A perfectly balanced antithesis: perukkam (பெருக்கம், increase, prosperity) is set against surukkam (சுருக்கம், contraction, want), and panidhal (பணிதல், bending, humility) against uyarvu (உயர்வு, height, unbending dignity). Siriya (சிறிய, 'small') intensifies the second half: in a narrow, reduced state. Mu. Varadarasanar reads uyarvu as 'height that does not bow' (பணியாத உயர்வு), and Solomon Pappaiah as not stooping to others in poverty. Maanam here is not pride but a discipline that runs against circumstance: humble when one could afford arrogance, upright when one is tempted to grovel. Pope's version on ytamizh.com: 'Bow down thy soul, with increase blest, in happy hour; / Lift up thy heart, when stript of all by fortune's power.' Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not disturbed in mind even amidst the threefold miseries or elated when there is happiness, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the steady sage, who is neither shaken by misery nor puffed up by happiness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural asks for the same steadiness in fortune and misfortune, expressed as humility and dignity.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.56 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada; vedabase.io)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he has learned how to live rightly both in plenty and in need.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural gives the rule for each state: humility in plenty, dignity in need.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you. And Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful -”
islam.explanation: The Quran teaches neither despair in loss nor pride in gain.
islam.tie_back: This matches both halves of the Kural: no arrogance in prosperity, no collapse in poverty.

judaism.quote_or_event: Moses warns Israel that when they have eaten their fill, built fine houses, and seen their flocks, silver and gold multiply, their hearts may be lifted up and they may forget the LORD who brought them out of Egypt.
judaism.explanation: The Torah warns that prosperity breeds arrogance and forgetfulness.
judaism.tie_back: This supports the first half of the Kural, humility in prosperity, but not the second.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The good renounce (attachment for) everything. The virtuous do not prattle with a yearning for pleasures. The wise show no elation or depression when touched by happiness or sorrow.”
buddhism.explanation: The wise are neither elated by good fortune nor cast down by bad.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural turns this evenness into a rule of conduct: humble in plenty, upright in want.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Among all those who live in this fertile and wide world, those who give not alms to others, amongst the rich, though exceeding rich, are poor indeed; while those who go not to beg alms of the rich, though they have become exceedingly poor, are indeed illustrious.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar says a rich man who does not give is truly poor, while a poor man who will not beg from the rich is truly great.
jainism.tie_back: The second half matches the Kural's dignity in want closely; the first half links right conduct in plenty to generosity rather than humility.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 30 (மானம், 'Honour'), stanza 6 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That man, who in the midst of pain, does not feel pain, who is not affected by pleasure, affection or fear, and who looks alike upon gold and dust;”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person who stays the same in pain and pleasure and sees gold and dust alike.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks for humility in prosperity and an upright head in want; Guru Tegh Bahadur asks that neither fortune nor misfortune change who one is.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus tells how the rich king Croesus asked Solon who was the happiest of men, expecting to be named; Solon refused to call any man happy before his end. Later, defeated and on the pyre, Croesus called out Solon's name and was spared by Cyrus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Croesus' pride in prosperity is humbled, and he learns wisdom in defeat.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the cost of lacking the humility in prosperity that the Kural requires.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book 2 of the Consolation, Lady Philosophy reminds Boethius that Fortune turns her wheel by nature, raising the low and casting down the high, so no one should be puffed up by her gifts or crushed by their loss.
philosophy.explanation: Since fortune always turns, neither rising nor falling should change who a person is.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural draws the practical rule: bow when high, stand tall when low.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2

real_life_example.event_title: Albert Einstein declines the presidency of Israel
real_life_example.event: After Chaim Weizmann, Israel's first president, died on 9 November 1952, Ambassador Abba Eban wrote to Albert Einstein on behalf of Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion to ask whether he would accept the presidency if the Knesset elected him. Einstein declined within days, replying that he was deeply moved by the offer but lacked the natural aptitude and experience to deal with people and carry out official duties. Yitzhak Ben-Zvi was elected president instead.
real_life_example.explanation: At the height of his world fame, Einstein turned down a head of state's office with a modest account of his own limits.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks for humility when fortune swells, and Einstein answered the greatest honour offered to him by declaring himself unfit for it.

tamil:
தலையின் இழிந்த மயிரனையர் மாந்தர்
நிலையின் இழிந்தக் கடை.
transliteration:
Thalaiyin izhindha mayiranaiyar maandhar
Nilaiyin izhindhak kadai.
meaning: When people fall from their honourable place, they become like hair that has fallen from the head: worth nothing.
elementary: Hair on your head is combed and cared for. But once a hair falls on the floor, nobody wants it. This kural says a person who drops their good behaviour and self-respect loses the respect others gave them, just like that fallen hair.
university: The simile works through a single verb, izhi (இழி, to descend, fall, be debased), used twice: hair izhindha from the head (fallen) and people izhindha from their nilai (நிலை, station, standing). On the head, hair is an ornament; once fallen it is swept away. Mu. Varadarasanar reads thalai as both 'head' and 'high place' (தலைமை), so the image doubles as falling from leadership. The Parimelazhagar tradition places this after 963 to show what happens when the discipline of maanam fails. Kalaignar applies it to someone who held a high place in people's hearts. Pope: 'Like hairs from off the head that fall to earth, / When fall'n from high estate are men of noble birth.' Both online texts read இழிந்தக் கடை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Nahusha is raised to the throne of Indra in heaven, but growing arrogant he forces the great sages to carry his palanquin and kicks Agastya; cursed by the sage, he falls from heaven and becomes a serpent on earth.
hinduism.explanation: A man raised to the highest place falls to the lowest because of conduct unworthy of his position.
hinduism.tie_back: Nahusha is the Kural's fallen hair: honoured while he kept his station, cast down when he left it.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, sections 11-17 (the story of Nahusha)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that salt that loses its saltiness is thrown out and walked on.
christianity.tie_back: The same image as the Kural: something valued, once it loses its quality, is discarded underfoot.

islam.quote_or_event: “Then We return him to the lowest of the low,”
islam.explanation: After saying that humanity was created in the best form, the Quran warns that a person can be returned to the lowest state, except those who believe and do good.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes a fall from a high to a debased condition.

judaism.quote_or_event: “How art thou fallen from heaven, O day-star, son of the morning! How art thou cut down to the ground, That didst cast lots over the nations!”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah mocks a proud king who once ruled nations and is now brought down to the ground.
judaism.tie_back: It captures the Kural's contrast between the height one held and the low place one falls to.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, a monk of noble birth and early renown in the Sangha, grows ambitious, asks to lead the order in the Buddha's place, plots against him and splits the community; he ends disgraced.
buddhism.explanation: A respected disciple loses all standing through conduct unworthy of his place.
buddhism.tie_back: He is a Buddhist example of the Kural's fallen hair: honoured while worthy, cast off when he fell.

jainism.quote_or_event: The first lecture of the Uttaradhyayana Sutra compares a disobedient, unruly and talkative pupil to a dog with sore ears that is driven away everywhere, while the well-behaved pupil is honoured.
jainism.explanation: One who abandons proper conduct is pushed away wherever he goes.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's fallen hair and Jainism's driven-off dog both picture a person rejected after falling from right conduct.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.4-5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who has the pride of power within, shall dwell in hell, and become a dog.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan warns that pride in rule and power ends in degradation, pictured as falling to the state of a dog.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says people who fall from their honourable place become as worthless as hair fallen from the head; Guru Arjan likewise pictures the proud as brought down to the lowest state.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Bellerophon, once a favoured hero who slew the Chimaera, later becomes hated by the gods and wanders alone over the Aleian plain, eating out his heart and shunning the paths of men.
greek_mythology.explanation: A celebrated hero ends his life as an outcast.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It pictures the Kural's fall from honoured place to worthlessness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus says a person must weigh what his own character is worth and not sell it cheaply; he compares the man of principle to the purple thread in a garment, the small bright stripe that gives the rest its beauty, and says he will not be like the common threads.
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus urges people to stay true to the role that marks them out, rather than sink to the level of the rest.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural warns what happens to those who do sink from their station.

real_life_example.event_title: Puyi, the last emperor of China, works at the Beijing Botanical Garden
real_life_example.event: Puyi had become emperor of China as a small child, abdicated in 1912, and later served as the Japanese-backed ruler of Manchukuo; after years of imprisonment he was pardoned in December 1959. He was then assigned work at the Beijing Botanical Garden, where he lived among ordinary workers. He later worked as a researcher for a national historical committee, published an autobiography, and died in Beijing in 1967.
real_life_example.explanation: Puyi's life is one of history's sharpest falls, from a throne regarded as sacred to an ordinary job in a public garden.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says people who fall from their high station become like hair fallen from the head, prized while in place and ordinary once fallen, and Puyi's later life showed that change.

tamil:
குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர் குன்றுவ
குன்றி அனைய செயின்.
transliteration:
Kundrin anaiyaarum kundruvar kundruva
Kundri anaiya seyin.
meaning: Even people as great as a mountain become small if they do something low, even something as tiny as a kunri seed (a small red bean).
elementary: A big, beautiful glass of milk can be spoiled by one tiny drop of ink. This kural says even a very great person can lose respect by doing one small mean thing.
university: A celebrated piece of wordplay on the root kundru (குன்று): kundru as noun means 'hill' (kundrin anaiyaar, those like a hill), as verb 'to diminish' (kundruvar, they will be lowered), kundruva are 'diminishing' (debasing) acts, and kundri (குன்றி) is the kunrimani, the small red-and-black seed of Abrus precatorius used as a jeweller's weight. The contrast of hill and seed sets the scale: the smallest dishonour outweighs the largest standing. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both read kundri anaiya as 'even a kunrimani's weight'. Pope keeps the botanical sense: 'If meanness, slight as abrus grain, by men be wrought.' Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At Kurukshetra, Yudhishthira, famed for never lying, tells Drona that Ashvatthama is dead, speaking the words the elephant softly so that Drona believes his son has been killed; his chariot, which had always moved a little above the ground, at once sinks to touch the earth.
hinduism.explanation: A single half-truth from a man renowned for truth brings him down from his elevated state.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's mountain brought low by a seed-sized fault.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Drona Parva (the death of Drona)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that a small amount of corruption spreads through the whole.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say that a small wrong is enough to spoil something great.

islam.quote_or_event: “And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.”
islam.explanation: The Quran says that no evil is too small to be counted.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's seed-sized act, even the smallest wrong matters.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Dead flies make the ointment of the perfumer fetid and putrid; So doth a little folly outweigh wisdom and honour.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet says a small folly spoils a person's wisdom and honour, as dead flies spoil fine perfume.
judaism.tie_back: An almost one-to-one match: a small act outweighs great honour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Think not lightly of evil, saying, ‘It will not come to me.’ Drop by drop is the water pot filled. Likewise, the fool, gathering it little by little, fills himself with evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that small wrongs add up.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts warn against treating a small wrong as harmless.

jainism.quote_or_event: After renouncing his kingdom, Bahubali stands motionless in meditation for a year, but omniscience does not come because a trace of pride remains: he will not bow to his younger brothers who became monks before him. Only when his sisters Brahmi and Sundari tell him to get down from the elephant of pride does he let it go and attain kevala jnana.
jainism.explanation: Even a hero of great austerity is held back by a small remnant of pride (mana).
jainism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a tiny fault in a mountain-like person is enough to bring him down.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra, Book 1 (Bharata and Bahubali; tr. Helen M. Johnson)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Kabeer, the gate of liberation is narrow, less than one-tenth of a mustard seed. The mind has become as big as an elephant; how can it pass through this gate?”
sikhism.explanation: A salok in Guru Amar Das's Gujri ki Vaar, opening with Kabir's name, contrasts a gate smaller than a mustard seed with a mind swollen to the size of an elephant by ego.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural sets a mountain against a tiny kunri seed to show that the smallest debasing act brings the great low; this verse sets the tiny seed against the huge elephant to show how bulk of self blocks the way.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 509, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, salok (attributed to Kabir, in the Vaar of Guru Amar Das) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In later tradition, Thetis dips the infant Achilles in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, holding him by the heel; that one untouched spot is where Paris' arrow later kills the greatest of the Greek warriors.
greek_mythology.explanation: One small weak point brings down the mightiest hero.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It mirrors the Kural's contrast between a mountain-sized man and a seed-sized flaw.
greek_mythology.source: Statius, Achilleid 1.133-134, 268-270 (the Styx dipping); not in Homer

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes shame (aidos) as a kind of fear of disrepute, and says it suits the young; the good man should not need it, because he will not voluntarily do bad actions at all.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the good person avoids every disgraceful act, not just large ones.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural adds the warning that even a small disgraceful act lowers a great person.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.9 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Diego Maradona is sent home from the 1994 World Cup
real_life_example.place: Foxborough, Massachusetts, United States (1994 FIFA World Cup)
real_life_example.event: Diego Maradona, captain of Argentina and one of the most celebrated footballers in history, failed a drug test after a World Cup match against Nigeria on 25 June 1994, when laboratory analysis found ephedrine-related stimulants in his sample. He was withdrawn from the tournament, and in August 1994 FIFA banned him from football for 15 months. Maradona denied taking the substance intentionally, saying he had taken a replacement diet product; he never played in a World Cup again.
real_life_example.explanation: One failed test, involving a substance far smaller in scale than his achievements, ended the World Cup career of a national hero and became the lasting image of his final tournament.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even people as great as a mountain are brought low by a debasing act no bigger than a kunri seed, and Maradona's fall came from a few traces of a banned stimulant.

tamil:
புகழ்இன்றால் புத்தேள்நாட்டு உய்யாதால் என்மற்று
இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று நிலை.
transliteration:
Pugazhindraal puththelnaattu uyyaadhaal enmatru
Ikazhvaarpin sendru nilai.
meaning: Running after people who look down on you brings you no fame here and no place in heaven. So what good is it?
elementary: Some children follow around a bully who laughs at them, hoping to be liked. This kural asks: what do you get from that? Nobody admires it, and it does not make you a better person. Better to keep your self-respect.
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question built on the two goods of classical Tamil ethics: pugazh (புகழ், fame in this world) and puththel naadu (புத்தேள் நாடு, the land of the gods, i.e. heaven, reward in the next). Ikazhvaar pin sendru nilai (இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று நிலை), 'the state of going after those who scorn one', yields neither, hence en matru (என்மற்று), 'what else then?'. Solomon Pappaiah reads it as abandoning honour in order to live by following one's despisers. Kalaignar's gloss pointedly adds 'a heaven that does not exist', a modern rationalist reading; the older commentators take heaven at face value. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: My dear Arjuna, how have these impurities come upon you? They are not at all befitting a man who knows the value of life. They lead not to higher planets but to infamy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that his collapse of spirit is unworthy and leads neither to heaven nor to fame.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's 'not to higher planets but to infamy' matches the Kural's 'no fame, no heaven' almost word for word.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.2 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada; vedabase.io)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.”
christianity.explanation: Paul refuses to live by pleasing people at the cost of his true calling.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise rejects living by currying favour with others.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those who take disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek with them honor [through power]? But indeed, honor belongs to Allah entirely.”
islam.explanation: The Quran asks why anyone would look for honour by attaching themselves to people who do not share or respect their faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says honour cannot be found by following those who hold you in contempt.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And all the king’s servants, that were in the king’s gate, bowed down, and prostrated themselves before Haman; for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not down, nor prostrated himself before him.”
judaism.explanation: Mordecai alone refuses to bow before the arrogant Haman, though everyone else does.
judaism.tie_back: He embodies the Kural's refusal to bow and follow after those who hold one in contempt.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not associate with evil companions; do not seek the fellowship of the vile. Associate with the good friends; seek the fellowship of noble men.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha advises seeking the company of the noble, not the base.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural adds that attaching oneself to those who despise one brings no good at all.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Leave off the causes of sin, acquire fame through patience! (A man who acts up to this) will rise to the upper regions after having left this body of clay.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's teaching names the true way to both goods the Kural mentions: fame in this life and a higher world after death.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says fawning on scorners wins neither fame nor heaven; the Jain verse says patience and abandoning sin win both.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 3.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else - says Nanak, listen, mind: call him spiritually wise.”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks, Guru Tegh Bahadur defines the wise person as one who neither intimidates others nor bows to anyone out of fear.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural scorns those who trail after people who despise them; Guru Tegh Bahadur's ideal neither fears nor fawns on anyone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9 (salok 16), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Agamemnon publicly dishonours him by taking Briseis, Achilles refuses the embassy's offer of vast gifts, cities and a royal marriage, saying he will not be won over by the man who insulted him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles will not return to serve a king who scorned him, whatever the reward.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He refuses exactly what the Kural condemns: going after those who held one in contempt.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus says an invitation to a great man's dinner has a price: flattery and attendance at his door. If you will not pay it, do not complain of going without; you keep instead the dignity of not having flattered.
philosophy.explanation: Courting the powerful costs one's self-respect, and Epictetus advises declining the bargain.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural asks what such following gains; Epictetus answers that refusing it keeps something more valuable.

real_life_example.event_title: Samuel Johnson's letter to Lord Chesterfield
real_life_example.event: Lord Chesterfield had accepted the dedication of Samuel Johnson's plan for a Dictionary of the English Language in 1747 but gave the project almost no further help during the long years Johnson spent compiling it. Shortly before the Dictionary appeared in 1755, Chesterfield published two magazine articles praising it, creating the impression that he had been its patron all along. On 7 February 1755 Johnson wrote to him rejecting his belated patronage, and copies of the letter circulated among Johnson's circle and were later printed by James Boswell.
real_life_example.explanation: The letter became famous as a declaration of an author's independence from aristocratic patronage.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what is gained by trailing after those who scorn you, and Johnson refused to attach himself to a patron who had neglected him once his success made the patron eager.

tamil:
ஒட்டார்பின் சென்றொருவன் வாழ்தலின் அந்நிலையே
கெட்டான் எனப்படுதல் நன்று.
transliteration:
Ottaarpin sendroruvan vaazhdhalin annilaiye
Kettaan enappadudhal nandru.
meaning: It is better to be called a person who has lost everything than to live by running after people who do not respect you.
elementary: Imagine choosing between staying poor but proud, or getting treats every day by doing whatever an unkind person tells you. This kural says it is better to lose the treats and keep your self-respect.
university: Ottaar (ஒட்டார்) are those who do not 'stick' to one: people who do not regard or accept one, or enemies. Living by following them (pin sendru vaazhdhal) is set against being called kettaan (கெட்டான், 'he is ruined', or 'he perished'). The phrase annilaiye (அந்நிலையே), 'in that very state', is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as remaining in one's own condition without stooping, while Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take kettaan more starkly as 'died'. Pope's English, quoted on ytamizh.com, follows the stronger reading: 'Better 'twere said, He's perished! than to gain / The means to live, following in foeman's train.' The couplet expresses a priority of honour over comfort, not an instruction to seek death. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that for a person of standing, disgrace is worse than dying.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same in its own way: better to be called ruined than to live in disgrace.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.34 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada; vedabase.io)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I have used none of these things: neither have I written these things, that it should be so done unto me: for it were better for me to die, than that any man should make my glorying void.”
christianity.explanation: Paul refuses to live off the financial support of his churches, saying he would rather die than lose the honour of preaching freely.
christianity.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: better to perish than to live dependent in a way that empties one's honour.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Charity is] for the poor who have been restricted for the cause of Allah, unable to move about in the land. An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Quran praises the poor whose dignity is so strong that people mistake them for well-off, because they will not beg.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it honours those who would rather endure want than live by depending on others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, He will deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and out of thy hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.”
judaism.explanation: Three young Jews tell the king they will not bow even if it costs them their lives.
judaism.tie_back: They prefer possible death to living by submitting to a power that demands they betray themselves.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do I carry muñja grass? I spit on my life. Death in battle would be better for me than that I, defeated, survive.”
buddhism.explanation: Facing Mara's army, the Bodhisatta says he would rather die fighting than live on in defeat.
buddhism.tie_back: This strikingly echoes the Kural's 'better to be called dead' than to live in surrender.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 3.2, Padhana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu; accesstoinsight.org; the site's text has the typo 'woud')

jainism.quote_or_event: “The honourable, though they become through destitution mere bones and skin, will they follow those who are destitute of proper dispositions, to make known their afflictions to them?”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar says the honourable, even when wasted by poverty, will not go after unworthy people to plead their troubles.
jainism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own image of refusing to live by following those who do not value one.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 30 (மானம், 'Honour'), stanza 2 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir describes the true hero as one who would be cut to pieces rather than leave the field, which Sikh tradition reads as standing firm for righteousness and the weak.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says it is better to be called ruined than to live by trailing after one's foes; Kabir's hero chooses to be cut down rather than give ground.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maru, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Antigone, forbidden by King Creon to bury her brother, does so anyway, telling Creon she knew she must die some day and that if she dies before her time she counts it gain.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antigone chooses death over obeying a command that would dishonour her and her family.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She chooses, like the Kural, to be counted lost rather than live by submitting to one who scorns what she holds sacred.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I thought that I ought not to do anything common or mean in the hour of danger: nor do I now repent of the manner of my defence, and I would rather die having spoken after my manner, than speak in your manner and live.”
philosophy.explanation: Condemned to death, Socrates says he would rather die true to himself than live by pleading in a way unworthy of him.
philosophy.tie_back: A near one-to-one match: better to be called dead than to live by stooping to those who scorn one.

real_life_example.event_title: Arturo Toscanini refuses to serve the Fascist and Nazi regimes
real_life_example.place: Bologna, Italy; Bayreuth, Germany; Salzburg, Austria
real_life_example.event: On 14 May 1931 the conductor Arturo Toscanini refused to open a memorial concert in Bologna with the Fascist anthem Giovinezza, and was struck by a group of Fascist youths outside the theatre; his passport was later taken away for a time. In 1933 he withdrew from the Bayreuth Festival in protest at Nazi treatment of Jewish musicians, and in 1938 he broke with the Salzburg Festival as Austria came under Hitler's control. He refused to conduct in Italy while the Fascist regime lasted and went to the United States, returning to conduct at the rebuilt La Scala in 1946.
real_life_example.explanation: Toscanini gave up the leading stages of Europe and his own country rather than lend his art to regimes he opposed.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says it is better to be called ruined than to live by trailing after those who do not value you, and Toscanini chose exile over serving rulers who demanded his submission.

tamil:
மருந்தோமற்று ஊன்ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை பெருந்தகைமை
பீடழிய வந்த இடத்து.
transliteration:
Marundhomatru oonombum vaazhkkai perundhagaimai
Peedazhiya vandha idaththu.
meaning: When your honor and greatness are being destroyed, why hold on to life just to feed your body? Is that a medicine that will let you live forever?
elementary: Everyone grows old one day, no matter what. This kural asks: if you will not live forever anyway, why trade away your good name just to stay comfortable a little longer?
university: The rhetorical question marundho (மருந்தோ, 'is it a medicine?') implies a medicine against death (saavaamai, deathlessness), as Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both supply. Oon ombum vaazhkkai (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) is a life that merely 'nourishes the flesh', set against perundhagaimai (பெருந்தகைமை, nobility) and peedu (பீடு, dignity, greatness), whose destruction is the occasion. The argument is that since death cannot be escaped, saving the body at the cost of honour gains nothing lasting. Kalaignar makes this explicit: there is no medicine for not dying, so do not lower your worth for a better life. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (some editions divide it மருந்தோமற் றூனோம்பும்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who has taken his birth is sure to die, and after death one is sure to take birth again. Therefore, in the unavoidable discharge of your duty, you should not lament.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reminds Arjuna that death is certain for all who are born, so fear of it should not turn him from duty.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same certainty of death to argue that clinging to bodily life at the cost of honour gains nothing.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.27 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada; vedabase.io)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it. For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that holding on to life at any cost loses what really matters.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly asks what is gained by preserving the body while losing one's worth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘Indeed, the death from which you flee - indeed, it will meet you. Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you about what you used to do.’”
islam.explanation: The Quran reminds those who run from death that it will meet them anyway.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says no amount of self-preservation is a medicine against death.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is no man that hath power over the wind to retain the wind; neither hath he power over the day of death; and there is no discharge in war; neither shall wickedness deliver him that is given to it.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet says no one controls the day of death, and wickedness cannot save the wicked.
judaism.tie_back: This supports the Kural's question: dishonourable survival is no defence against death.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither in the sky nor in mid-ocean, nor by entering into mountain clefts, nowhere in the world is there a place where one will not be overcome by death.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says there is nowhere to hide from death.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural concludes from the same fact that honour should not be traded for a little more life.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a lion takes hold of an antelope, so Death leads off a man in his last hour; neither mother, nor father, nor brother will, at that time, save a particle (of his life).”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra warns King Brahmadatta that death takes everyone and no one can save even a fraction of a life.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same truth to show that clinging to the body at the cost of dignity is pointless.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Death would not be called bad, O people, if one knew how to truly die.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Alahaniyan, songs of mourning in Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak says death is not to be feared by one who knows how to die rightly.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether a life that only keeps the body going can be a medicine against death; Guru Nanak also refuses to treat mere survival as the highest good, since what matters is dying rightly.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 579, Raag Vadhans, Alahaniyan, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Sarpedon tells Glaucus that if they could escape old age and death by avoiding battle he would not fight; but since countless fates of death stand over men and none can escape them, they should go forward and win glory.
greek_mythology.explanation: Because death cannot be avoided, Sarpedon argues, it is better to live and die with honour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same reasoning as the Kural: since there is no medicine against death, do not trade honour for survival.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The difficulty, my friends, is not in avoiding death, but in avoiding unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says the real danger is not death, which comes anyway, but doing wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says saving one's body is no remedy, while losing one's worth is the real loss.

real_life_example.event_title: Dietrich Bonhoeffer returns to Germany from New York
real_life_example.place: New York, United States, and Berlin, Germany
real_life_example.event: In June 1939 the German pastor and theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, an opponent of the Nazi regime, accepted an offer from friends to come to Union Theological Seminary in New York, which would have kept him safe abroad. Within weeks he decided that his place was in Germany and sailed home in July 1939, shortly before the outbreak of war. He joined the resistance to Hitler, was arrested in 1943, and was executed at Flossenburg concentration camp on 9 April 1945.
real_life_example.explanation: Bonhoeffer judged that a safe life abroad would cost him his integrity and his right to help rebuild Germany after the war.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks whether a life that merely keeps the body going is any medicine against death when one's dignity is at stake, and Bonhoeffer gave up safety rather than live with that loss.

tamil:
மயிர்நீப்பின் வாழாக் கவரிமா அன்னார்
உயிர்நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்.
transliteration:
Mayirneeppin vaazhaak kavarimaa annaar
Uyirneeppar maanam varin.
meaning: The yak is said to die if it loses its hair. Like that yak, people of honour would rather give up their life than live without honour.
elementary: An old story says the yak loves its long, beautiful hair so much it cannot live without it. This kural uses that story to say that some people treasure their good name the way the yak treasures its hair: nothing is worth losing it for.
university: The kavarimaa (கவரிமா) is the yak (Bos grunniens), whose tail-hair was prized for the chowrie or royal fly-whisk (chamara); popular Tamil usage later turned it into 'kavarimaan', a deer, though commentators identify it as the yak. The belief that it dies on losing its hair is poetic convention, not natural history; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as losing all its hair. Maanam varin (மானம் வரின்) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as 'if honour is about to be destroyed'. The Parimelazhagar tradition sees here the culmination of the chapter: honour valued above life. This is classical heroic ethics and should be read historically, as a statement of honour's supreme worth, not as a recommendation to end one's life; several traditions compared below explicitly reject taking one's own life. Text identical on both sources; Pope: 'Like the wild ox that, of its tuft bereft, will pine away.'

hinduism.quote_or_event: Warned by his father Surya that Indra will come disguised as a Brahmin to ask for his divine armour and earrings, Karna still gives them away when asked, cutting them from his body, because he has vowed never to refuse a gift and will not break his word even to save his life.
hinduism.explanation: Karna gives up his protection, knowing it may cost him his life, rather than lose his honour as a giver.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's yak, Karna will not keep living at the price of what makes him who he is.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Women received their dead raised to life again: and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection:”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews honours believers who refused release from torture rather than renounce their faith.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's honourable, they valued something above survival.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly but only [in lawful] business by mutual consent. And do not kill yourselves [or one another]. Indeed, Allah is to you ever Merciful.”
islam.explanation: The Quran forbids taking one's own life.
islam.tie_back: This is an honest counterpoint: Islam values honour but rejects the Kural's ideal of giving up life when honour is lost.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud rules that for three sins, idolatry, forbidden sexual relations and murder, a person must let himself be killed rather than commit them: yehareg ve'al ya'avor, let him be killed and not transgress.
judaism.explanation: Jewish law names a few lines that must not be crossed even to save one's life.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sets certain values above life itself, though the trigger is a forced sin, not loss of personal honour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Path of Purification, Buddhaghosa tells the monk to guard his virtue like a hen guarding her eggs, or like a yak (camari) guarding its tail, or like a mother her only child, or a person their only eye.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist commentary uses the very same animal, the yak that guards its tail-hair at any cost, as the image of guarding one's moral purity.
buddhism.tie_back: The same yak image as the Kural, but applied to protecting virtue, not to giving up life.
buddhism.source: Buddhaghosa, Visuddhimagga I (on guarding virtue; tr. Bhikkhu Nanamoli, The Path of Purification)

jainism.quote_or_event: Amritachandra discusses sallekhana, the gradual, vowed giving up of food at the end of life, and argues that it is not suicide because it is undertaken without passion; by contrast, a person who ends their life under the sway of passions such as anger or wounded pride commits himsa against the self.
jainism.explanation: Jainism allows a calm, vowed death only in narrow conditions and treats dying out of injured pride as a form of violence.
jainism.tie_back: This is an honest contrast: Jain teaching would see a death prompted by lost honour (mana) as a passion to be overcome, not an ideal.
jainism.source: Amritachandra, Purusharthasiddhyupaya, verses on sallekhana (c. vv. 175-180; tr. Ajit Prasada)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says the path of love for God asks for complete readiness to give oneself, pictured as carrying one's own head in hand.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of the honourable who would give up life itself rather than live when honour is taken; Guru Nanak asks for the same readiness to give one's life, for love of God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles' Ajax, the hero, shamed after his madness, tells his wife Tecmessa that a man of noble birth must either live with honour or die with honour, and then goes alone to the shore rather than live disgraced.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ajax holds that a noble person cannot go on living once his honour is gone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the tragic Greek counterpart of the Kural's yak: life is not worth keeping without honour.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that to die in order to escape poverty, love or anything painful is not the mark of a brave man but of a coward, because it is running from trouble rather than facing it for a noble end.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, giving up life to flee suffering is not courage.
philosophy.tie_back: An honest counterweight to the Kural: classical philosophy questions dying to escape disgrace.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 3.7, 1116a12-15 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The soldiers of HMS Birkenhead stand fast as the ship sinks
real_life_example.place: Danger Point, near Gansbaai, South Africa
real_life_example.event: The troopship HMS Birkenhead, carrying soldiers and some of their families to the Eastern Cape, struck rocks off Danger Point on 26 February 1852. With only a few lifeboats usable, the officers ordered the soldiers to stand fast rather than rush the boats and swamp them, and the men kept their ranks on deck as the ship went down. All the women and children aboard were saved, but about 445 of the 638 people on board were lost, and the soldiers' conduct gave rise to the phrase the Birkenhead drill.
real_life_example.explanation: The soldiers' discipline became a lasting example of putting honour and duty above one's own survival, and helped establish the rule of women and children first.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says people of honour would give up life itself rather than lose their honour, and the Birkenhead soldiers held their ranks to the end rather than save themselves at others' cost.

tamil:
இளிவரின் வாழாத மானம் உடையார்
ஒளிதொழுது ஏத்தும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Ilivarin vaazhaadha maanam udaiyaar
Olidhozhudhu eththum ulagu.
meaning: The world always bows to and praises the glory of honourable people who would rather die than live in shame.
elementary: People remember and admire heroes who never gave up doing what was right, even when it was very hard. This kural says the whole world keeps honouring such people long after they are gone.
university: Ilivu (இளிவு) is disgrace, humiliation; ilivarin vaazhaadha (இளிவரின் வாழாத) are those who 'do not live on when disgrace comes'. Oli (ஒளி), literally 'light', here means radiant fame, the glory that survives a person; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss it as pugazh (புகழ்) or pugazh vadivu (the form of one's fame). Thozhudhu eththum (தொழுது ஏத்தும்) is the language of worship: folding hands and praising. The chapter closes where Tamil heroic ethics often closes, with lasting fame as the reward of honour. Read today, its lasting point is that the world reveres those who keep their integrity at great cost. Pope: 'Who, when dishonour comes, refuse to live, their honoured memory / Will live in worship and applause of all the world for aye!' Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra keeps his word to the sage Vishvamitra though it costs him his kingdom, his wife and son, and his freedom, working at last as a servant at a cremation ground; the gods finally restore him, and his name became the Indian byword for truthfulness.
hinduism.explanation: Harishchandra suffers every loss rather than break his word, and is remembered and revered for it.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural's honourable person whose glory the world still praises.
hinduism.source: Markandeya Purana, chapters 7-8 (tr. F. E. Pargiter)

christianity.quote_or_event: “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews says Abel's faithfulness still speaks long after his death.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural too says the glory of the honourable outlives them.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We gave them of Our mercy, and We made for them a mention [i.e., reputation] of high honor.”
islam.explanation: Speaking of Abraham and his descendants, the Quran says God gave them an honoured name among later generations.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it promises enduring renown to those who held to what was right.

judaism.quote_or_event: The aged scribe Eleazar, ordered to eat pork, refuses even to pretend, saying it does not befit his years to deceive the young; he goes to his death, and the book says he left his death as an example of noble courage and a memorial of virtue for the young and for the whole nation.
judaism.explanation: Eleazar chooses death over a disgraceful pretence and is remembered as a model.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the Kural's scene: one who would not live in disgrace becomes a lasting memorial honoured by his people.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not the sweet smell of flowers, not even the fragrance of sandal, tagara, or jasmine blows against the wind. But the fragrance of the virtuous blows against the wind. Truly the virtuous man pervades all directions with the fragrance of his virtue.”
buddhism.explanation: The good name of the virtuous spreads everywhere, even against the wind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says the glory of the honourable spreads through the world.

jainism.quote_or_event: The opening verse of the Dasavaikalika Sutra calls dharma the highest good, names non-violence, self-control and austerity as its essence, and says that even the gods bow down to one whose mind is always set on dharma.
jainism.explanation: In Jainism it is the person firm in dharma who receives the homage of gods and humans.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's world bows to the honourable; the Jain verse says even the gods bow to the steadfast in dharma.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 1.1 (as Saman Suttam v. 82, tr. T. K. Tukol and K. K. Dixit)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, was executed by the Mughal authorities in Delhi in 1675 and is remembered above all for his stand for religious freedom; Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib now stands at the place of his martyrdom.
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur chose death over submission to religious coercion, and Sikhs and many others still honour his sacrifice centuries later.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the world forever praises those who would not go on living in disgrace; Guru Tegh Bahadur's memory, kept at Sis Ganj and in Sikh prayer, is exactly such lasting honour.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guru Tegh Bahadur' (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles tells the embassy that his mother foretold two fates: if he stays and fights at Troy he will not return home but his glory (kleos) will never perish; if he goes home he will live long without fame.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles weighs a long life against undying glory.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural promises the same reward, lasting worldly praise, to those who put honour before life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his funeral oration, Pericles says that the fallen gave their lives and in return won praise that never grows old, and that the whole earth is the tomb of famous men, whose memory lives on far from home.
philosophy.explanation: Pericles says those who died rather than accept defeat are remembered everywhere.
philosophy.tie_back: Close to the Kural's world that worships the glory of the honourable.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.43 (tr. Richard Crawley)

real_life_example.event_title: Rani Lakshmi Bai of Jhansi is honoured as a national heroine
real_life_example.event: After the death of her husband, the ruler of Jhansi, the British East India Company refused to recognise their adopted son as heir and annexed the state in 1854, rejecting Lakshmi Bai's petition to rule as regent. During the rebellion of 1857-58 she led the defence of Jhansi, escaped when the city fell in April 1858, joined other leaders in taking Gwalior, and was killed in combat near Gwalior in June 1858. Her British opponent, General Hugh Rose, called her the bravest and best of the rebel leaders, and she became a symbol of courage in India, honoured in poetry, statues and the names of institutions.
real_life_example.explanation: Lakshmi Bai's refusal to accept the loss of her state and her son's rights made her one of the most revered figures in Indian history.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world forever honours those who would not go on living in disgrace, and India's lasting reverence for the Rani of Jhansi shows exactly that.

tamil:
ஒளிஒருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கை இளிஒருவற்கு
அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்.
transliteration:
Olioruvarku ulla verukkai ilioruvarku
ahdhirandhu vaazhdhum enal.
meaning: A person's true glory is a mind full of energy and drive. A person's shame is saying, 'I will get by without it.'
elementary: Some kids say, 'I will try the hard puzzle!' and their faces light up. Others say, 'I'll just skip it and sit.' Valluvar says the first kind of heart is what makes a person shine, and the lazy 'I'll just skip it' is what makes a person small.
university: The chapter opens by defining greatness as an inner quality rather than a rank: oli (ஒளி, 'light, lustre, renown') is ulla verukkai (உள்ள வெறுக்கை), literally 'the wealth/abundance of the mind', which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as ஊக்கமிகுதி ('excess of zeal') and Puliyur Kesikan, following the older commentarial line descending from Parimelazhagar, as the resolve 'I will do what others find hard to do'. Its opposite, ili (இளி, 'disgrace'), is not failure but the attitude ahdhirandhu vaazhdhum enal (அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்), 'saying we shall live having let it go'. Pope's 'The light of life is mental energy' follows the majority reading; Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reads verukkai as வெறுமை ('emptiness of mind'), a contemplative minority interpretation not shared by the classical glosses. Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Maanam (Honour, ch. 97), the chapter moves from guarding one's dignity to the active, self-effacing greatness of the noble. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, do not yield to this degrading impotence. It does not become you. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O chastiser of the enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells the despondent Arjuna that giving up in faintheartedness is beneath him and urges him to rise to his task.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it calls the loss of spirit a disgrace and summons a person back to energetic effort.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.3 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher urges wholehearted effort in every task because life's chance to act is brief.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts prize the full-strength drive to act over a life coasting without it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches that a person's portion is tied to their own striving.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates a person's worth in their own effort rather than in what they happen to have.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Judah ben Tema said: Be strong as a leopard, and swift as an eagle, and fleet as a gazelle, and brave as a lion, to do the will of your Father who is in heaven.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah demands boldness, speed and courage in carrying out what is right.
judaism.tie_back: It pictures exactly the abundance of inner energy that the Kural calls a person's light.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:20 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The idler who does not exert himself when he should, who though young and strong is full of sloth, with a mind full of vain thoughts — such an indolent man does not find the path to wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that one who is able but will not exert himself misses the path.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's disgraced man who thinks he can live without effort.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira repeatedly urges his disciple Gautama never to be slack (apramada), because human life and its rare opportunity pass quickly.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain call to unbroken vigilance matches the Kural's scorn for anyone content to live without striving.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
sikhism.explanation: In this salok Guru Arjan ties real life to udham, the effort a person actually puts in. For Sikhs this effort is both honest work (kirat) and the steady practice of the Name, and the Gurus repeatedly reject the idle hope that life will turn out well without it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls an abundance of inner drive a person's glory and the thought of getting by without it a disgrace, and Guru Arjan likewise makes effort the condition of a life that is really lived.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 5, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Work is no disgrace: it is idleness which is a disgrace.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his idle brother Perses that honour comes from labour and shame from idleness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod uses the Kural's very pairing: effort brings honour and a slack life brings disgrace.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 311 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…let this thought be present—I am rising to the work of a human being. Why then am I dissatisfied if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world?”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius rebukes his own reluctance to get out of bed, reminding himself that he exists for action.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he treats wanting to live without exertion as a betrayal of what makes a person worthy.

real_life_example.event_title: Emil Zatopek wins the 5,000 metres, 10,000 metres and marathon at one Olympics
real_life_example.event: Emil Zatopek, a Czechoslovak runner who had taken up the sport while working in a shoe factory and was nicknamed the Human Locomotive for his relentless training, built his success on a punishing interval-training method that others at first scoffed at. At the 1952 Olympic Games in Helsinki he won the 10,000 metres and then the 5,000 metres, both in Olympic record times, and then entered the marathon, a race he had never run before, and won it by more than two and a half minutes. No athlete before or since has won all three long-distance events at the same Games.
real_life_example.explanation: Zatopek's triple victory is remembered as one of the greatest feats in athletics, and it grew from his drive to train harder than anyone thought sensible.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a person's true glory is an abundance of inner drive and his disgrace is the thought of getting through life without it, and Zatopek's achievement came from exactly that inner zeal.

tamil:
பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் சிறப்பொவ்வா
செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமை யான்.
transliteration:
Pirappokkum ellaa uyirkkum sirappovvaa
seydhozhil vetrumai yaan.
meaning: All living beings are born the same way. They become different in worth only because of the different work they do.
elementary: Every baby is born the same way, crying and tiny, whether in a palace or a hut. What makes people different later is what they choose to do: who helps, who works hard, who is kind. That is where real specialness comes from.
university: The couplet sets piRappu (பிறப்பு, 'birth') against siRappu (சிறப்பு, 'distinction'): the first ஒக்கும் ('is equal') for all, the second ஒவ்வா ('is not equal') because of seydhozhil vetrumai (செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமை, 'difference in the work done'). Commentators differ on the scope of uyir: Puliyur Kesikan restricts it to 'all human lives' (எல்லா மக்களுயிர்க்கும்), the older reading, while modern glosses keep 'all living beings'. They also differ on tozhil: Mu. Varadarasanar speaks of the high and low grades of occupations, whereas Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as one's deeds or skill and make the verse an explicit statement that all are equal by birth. This egalitarian reading has made the couplet one of the most frequently cited in modern Tamil debates on caste. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The humble sages, by virtue of true knowledge, see with equal vision a learned and gentle brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater [outcaste].”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the wise look past outward birth and see the same self in every being.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first half: all beings are alike in birth and essence.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 5.18 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Athenians that all peoples come from a single origin.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it grounds human equality in a shared birth.

islam.quote_or_event: “O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says humanity shares one origin and that nobility is measured by righteousness, not lineage.
islam.tie_back: Both halves of the Kural are here: equal origin, and distinction earned by conduct.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And this was done due to the importance of maintaining peace among people, so that one person will not say to another: My father, i.e., progenitor, is greater than your father.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that humanity was created from a single person so that no one could claim superior ancestry.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it denies that birth can make one person higher than another.
judaism.source: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by birth is one an outcast; not by birth is one a brahman. By deed one becomes an outcast, by deed one becomes a brahman.”
buddhism.explanation: Answering a brahman who insulted him, the Buddha says worth is made by action, not by birth.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural restated: birth does not differ, deeds do.
buddhism.source: Vasala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.7, v. 21 (trans. Piyadassi Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “By one's actions one becomes a Brâhmana, or a Kshattriya, or a Vaisya, or a Sûdra.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha tells a sacrificing priest that a person's class is made by conduct, not by birth or ritual marks.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain canon states the Kural's point directly: distinction comes from what one does.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “First, Allah created the Light; then, by His Creative Power, He made all mortal beings. From the One Light, the entire universe welled up. So who is good, and who is bad?”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, a low-caste weaver whose hymns the Gurus placed in the scripture, says that every person comes from the same divine Light. Birth therefore gives no one superiority, and the Sikh tradition draws from this its rejection of caste.
sikhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar's claim that all are equal at birth, Kabir's verse refuses to rank people by where they come from, which leaves only conduct to tell them apart.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1349, Raag Prabhaati, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides' Electra, Electra has been married off to a poor farmer, who treats her with honour and restraint; Orestes, seeing this, reflects that there is no sure test of a man's nobility, since a man of humble station can prove more noble than the well-born.
greek_mythology.explanation: The play uses a lowly farmer to show that nobility of character does not follow birth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it separates worth from lineage and ties it to conduct.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Electra (Orestes' speech on nobility, c. lines 367-390)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his 44th letter Seneca tells Lucilius that philosophy does not ask about a person's pedigree, citing Plato's remark that every king comes from a race of slaves and every slave from kings, and concluding that it is the mind, not ancestry, that makes a person noble.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that long lines of ancestry mix high and low, so only character can confer nobility.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca, like Valluvar, says birth is common to all and distinction is earned.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 44 (trans. R. M. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Zhu Yuanzhang, an orphaned peasant and beggar monk, founds the Ming dynasty
real_life_example.event: Zhu Yuanzhang was born in 1328 into a poor farming family in Haozhou, and when he was a teenager his parents and brothers died, leaving him to enter a Buddhist monastery to avoid starvation and then to wander as a begging monk when the temple could no longer feed him. He joined a rebel army against the Mongol Yuan dynasty at about twenty-four, rose to command, educated himself with the help of scholars, and defeated rival leaders. In 1368 he proclaimed himself emperor at Nanjing, taking the reign title Hongwu, and founded the Ming dynasty, which ruled China for 276 years.
real_life_example.explanation: A boy with no family, land or schooling rose by his own deeds to found one of China's great dynasties, though his later rule became harsh and despotic.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says all are equal by birth and that distinction differs only by the deeds people do, and Zhu's humble birth did not prevent his deeds from making him emperor.

tamil:
மேலிருந்தும் மேலல்லார் மேலல்லர் கீழிருந்தும்
கீழல்லார் கீழல் லவர்.
transliteration:
Melirundhum melallaar melallar keezhirundhum
keezhallaar keezhal lavar.
meaning: Low people are not great even when they sit in high places. Good people are not low even when they are in low places.
elementary: Imagine a bully sitting on the tallest chair in class, and a kind child sitting on the floor. The tall chair does not make the bully great, and the floor does not make the kind child small. Who you are matters more than where you sit.
university: The verse is a chiasmus built on mel (மேல், 'above, superior') and keezh (கீழ், 'below, base'), each used both for physical or social position and for moral quality: melirundhum melallaar melallar, 'though they be above, those not superior are not superior'. Puliyur Kesikan makes the image literal, 'though they sit on high seats' (உயர்ந்த ஆசனங்களிலே), and ties superiority to having done 'deeds hard to do', linking back to Kural 971; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar render mel as high office or position. Pope's 'men of lofty line' reads it as birth, which carries the theme on from Kural 972. The repeated negatives (அல்லார், அல்லர், அல்லவர்) give the couplet its characteristic Valluvan density. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Yaksha's questioning of Yudhishthira, the Yaksha asks what makes a Brahmana, and Yudhishthira answers that it is neither birth nor study nor learning but conduct alone, which must always be guarded.
hinduism.explanation: Yudhishthira insists that rank is earned by behaviour, not inherited by birth or bought by learning.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it denies that a high station makes one high without the matching character.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana (Aranyaka) Parva, Yaksha Prashna episode (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.”
christianity.explanation: Mary's song proclaims that God overturns the order of high and low.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that sitting in a high seat does not secure true height.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that God's measure of a person ignores appearance and riches and looks to heart and action.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's true height and lowness are measured the same way, by inner quality rather than outward place.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I saw an inverted world. Those above, i.e., those who are considered important in this world, were below, insignificant, while those below, i.e., those who are insignificant in this world, were above. He said to him: My son, you have seen a clear world.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Yosef, returning from near death, reports that the true world reverses this world's rankings, and his father calls that the clear view.
judaism.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that worldly position and true standing do not match.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 50a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A monk is not an elder because his head is gray. He is but ripe in age, and he is called one grown old in vain.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the title of elder means nothing without the virtues that should go with it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it denies that outward rank alone makes one truly senior.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The value of penance has become visible, birth appears of no value! Look at the holy Harikêsa, the son of a Svapâka, whose power is so great.”
jainism.explanation: Priests who mocked the low-born monk Harikesa are humbled, and the onlookers proclaim that his austerities, not his birth, decide his worth.
jainism.tie_back: Harikesa is the Kural's person placed low by birth who is in no way low.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Nanak seeks the company of the lowest of the low class, the very lowest of the low. ... In that place where the lowly are cared for-there, the Blessings of Your Glance of Grace rain down.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak deliberately takes his place among those society ranks lowest and says God's grace falls where the lowly are cared for. The verse overturns the idea that social position measures a person's worth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the base are not high even on a high seat and the noble are not low even when placed low, and Guru Nanak gives the same reversal, siding with the people the world calls low.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Odysseus returns home disguised as a ragged beggar and is mocked in his own hall by the suitors, who occupy the seats of honour while behaving shamefully, until he reveals himself as the true king.
