greek_mythology.explanation: The epic contrasts the low appearance of a noble man with the lofty places held by base men.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The suitors are high without being high, and the beggar-king is low without being low.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “These reasonings are unconnected: ‘I am richer than you, therefore I am better’; ‘I am more eloquent than you, therefore I am better.’ … But you, after all, are neither property nor style.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus says that having more of something outward never makes a person better.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it refuses to let external standing define who is truly superior.

real_life_example.event_title: The former slave Epictetus becomes the most admired Stoic teacher of his age
real_life_example.date: c. 55 to c. 135 CE (school at Nicopolis from about 90 CE)
real_life_example.place: Rome, Italy, and Nicopolis, Epirus, Greece
real_life_example.event: Epictetus was born around 55 CE in Hierapolis in Phrygia and as a boy was brought to Rome as a slave of Epaphroditus, a rich freedman who had served the emperor Nero; while still enslaved he attended the lectures of the Stoic Musonius Rufus. After he was freed, he was expelled from Rome around 89-90 CE when the emperor Domitian banished the philosophers, and he opened a school at Nicopolis in Greece that attracted upper-class Roman students, including Arrian, who wrote down his teachings as the Discourses and the Handbook. Later writers report that he was more popular in his own day than Plato. The tutor of the future emperor Marcus Aurelius, Herodes Atticus, is reported to have called him the greatest of the Stoics.
real_life_example.explanation: Born into the lowest rank of Roman society and lame for much of his life, Epictetus became one of the most influential moral teachers of the ancient world, while the emperor who banished him is remembered as a tyrant.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who are not base are not low even when placed low, and Epictetus, a slave by station, stood morally far above many who sat on high seats.

tamil:
ஒருமை மகளிரே போலப் பெருமையும்
தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின் உண்டு.
transliteration:
Orumai magalire polap perumaiyum
thannaiththaan kondozhugin undu.
meaning: A faithful wife stays true by guarding herself. In the same way, greatness lasts only for a person who guards and controls themselves.
elementary: A promise only stays a promise if you keep it, even when nobody is watching. Valluvar says greatness is the same: it is not a prize someone hands you, it stays with you only while you keep guarding your own good behaviour.
university: The simile turns on orumai magalir (ஒருமை மகளிர், 'women of oneness'), which the commentators uniformly read as women of undivided chastity (கற்பு, karpu): Mu. Varadarasanar says ஒரு தன்மையான கற்புடைய மகளிர், and Puliyur Kesikan describes women whose minds do not waver and who guard themselves without lapsing. The point of comparison is thannaiththaan kondozhugin (தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின், 'if one conducts oneself holding oneself'), that is, self-guarding: greatness, like chastity, cannot be imposed from outside and is lost by a single lapse. The gendered simile reflects the period; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it more inwardly as being true to oneself. Pope's 'Like single-hearted women, greatness too, / Exists while to itself is true' keeps the ambiguity. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One must deliver himself with the help of his mind, and not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that each person must raise himself and guard against bringing himself down.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes a person's elevation depend on his own self-guarding.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.5 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs urges constant guarding of one's inner self as the source of everything one becomes.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise says greatness lasts only while one keeps guard over oneself.

islam.quote_or_event: “He has succeeded who purifies it, And he has failed who instills it [with corruption].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ties success or failure to how a person tends their own soul.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes standing depend on keeping oneself pure and guarded.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’ (Proverbs 16:32).”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines might as mastery over one's own impulses.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates true greatness in holding oneself in check.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One truly is the protector of oneself; who else could the protector be? With oneself fully controlled, one gains a mastery that is hard to gain.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says no one else can guard a person; self-control yields a rare mastery.
buddhism.tie_back: Close to the Kural: greatness exists only for the one who guards himself.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Rathanemi lecture, the nun Rajimati, sheltering in a cave after being caught in rain, is approached by the monk Rathanemi, who loses his composure; she stays firm, rebukes him for wavering in his vows, and her steadfastness brings him back to the discipline.
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, revered in Jain tradition for her constancy, guards herself and even restores another's resolve.
jainism.tie_back: She embodies both halves of the Kural's simile: single-hearted faithfulness and the greatness that comes from guarding oneself.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (Rathanemi) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You search for your Husband Lord; you must have some fault in your body. Those who are known as happy soul-brides, do not look to others.”
sikhism.explanation: In these saloks the faithful soul-bride (suhagan) is the one whose devotion is undivided and who does not look elsewhere. Gurbani uses this image for the disciplined soul that keeps itself wholly for God.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar compares the greatness of the self-guarding person to a woman of single-hearted faithfulness, and the Granth's happy soul-bride who does not look to others is the same image of guarded, undivided loyalty.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, salok 114 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld scene of the Odyssey, the shade of Agamemnon praises Penelope for keeping faith with Odysseus through twenty years of pressure from the suitors, and declares that the fame of her virtue will never die.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope's renown rests entirely on her steady self-keeping.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She is the Greek counterpart of the Kural's single-hearted woman whose honour lasts because she guards herself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Republic IV Socrates explains temperance as an ordering and mastery of pleasures and desires, the condition people point to when they call someone 'master of himself'.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats self-mastery as the inner order on which every other virtue depends.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes excellence a matter of keeping hold of oneself.

real_life_example.event_title: Lou Gehrig plays 2,130 consecutive games and then takes himself out of the lineup
real_life_example.event: From 1 June 1925 the New York Yankees first baseman Lou Gehrig played in every one of his team's games for almost fourteen years, a record of 2,130 consecutive games that stood until 1995. A quiet and modest man often overshadowed by his flamboyant teammate Babe Ruth, he was remembered by a teammate as someone who simply did his job every day. When his play declined badly at the start of the 1939 season because of the illness later diagnosed as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Gehrig himself took his name out of the lineup on 2 May 1939, ending the streak, and he never played again.
real_life_example.explanation: Gehrig's greatness rested on steady self-discipline sustained over years, and he guarded his own standards even to the point of ending his record himself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that greatness, like a woman's single-hearted faithfulness, belongs only to one who guards himself, and Gehrig's record was the fruit of a self-discipline no one else imposed on him.

tamil:
பெருமை யுடையவர் ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றின்
அருமை உடைய செயல்.
transliteration:
Perumai yudaiyavar aatruvaar aatrin
arumai udaiya seyal.
meaning: People who have greatness will do, in the right way, things that are very hard for others to do.
elementary: Some jobs are so hard that most people give up, like building a tall tower of blocks without it falling. A great person keeps going and does it carefully, the right way, until it stands.
university: The verse plays on aatru (ஆற்று), used twice: aatruvaar ('they will accomplish') and aatrin, which commentators take either as 'by the (proper) way' (ஆறு, 'path, method') or as 'if they set about it'. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the first: 'in the way proper to it' (உரிய நெறியில்). Puliyur Kesikan adds 'even when they have fallen into poverty' (வறுமையான போதும்), the traditional gloss also reflected in Pope's explanation '(Though reduced) the great will be able to perform…', which holds that greatness shows itself in rare deeds even without resources. The couplet makes concrete the 'deeds hard for others' that Kural 971 called the light of a person. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man engaged in devotional service rids himself of both good and bad reactions even in this life. Therefore strive for yoga, which is the art of all work.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita's famous phrase yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam calls disciplined action a skill or art in doing work.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's great person does hard things the right way, which is skill in action.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.50 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that, strengthened by Christ, he can face anything, whether plenty or want.
christianity.tie_back: It echoes the Kural's confidence that the great can carry out what others cannot, even in hardship.

islam.quote_or_event: In Surat al-Kahf, Dhul-Qarnayn is asked by a threatened people to build a barrier against Gog and Magog; he organises the work, has iron blocks filled in and molten copper poured over them, completes the barrier, and attributes it to his Lord's mercy.
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents a great ruler who accomplishes an enormous task by careful, proper method.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's great person, he does what others could not, and does it the right way.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel teaches that when no one else steps up, one must take on the task oneself.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's great person, who undertakes what others leave undone.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:5 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easy to do are things that are bad and harmful to oneself. But exceedingly difficult to do are things that are good and beneficial.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada notes that the good path is the hard one.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's great people are those who take up exactly these hard, worthwhile deeds.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga Sutra and Kalpa Sutra describe Mahavira's more than twelve years of austerities after renouncing the world, enduring hardship and hostility with equanimity, until he attained omniscience (kevala jnana).
jainism.explanation: Jain scripture presents Mahavira's long, disciplined ascetic effort as the supreme example of a hard task carried through by the proper path.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows greatness as completing what others cannot, in the right manner.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.8 and Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. ... give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the Sikh path as something only the wholehearted can take up: one must be ready to give one's very head. Sikh tradition later saw this demand fulfilled in the Gurus' and early Sikhs' willingness to face martyrdom.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the truly great accomplish what others find too hard, and Guru Nanak sets exactly such a hard path, open only to those who will give everything.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, salok 20, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Set the labour of cleaning King Augeas' vast and long-neglected cattle yard in a single day, Heracles breached the yard's foundations and diverted the rivers Alpheus and Peneus to wash it out.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles achieves an apparently impossible task by finding the right method rather than by brute effort alone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's rare deed done in the proper way.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At the close of the Ethics Spinoza admits that the way to blessedness he has described is very hard and is rarely found, remarking that all excellent things are as difficult as they are rare.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza links excellence with difficulty and rarity.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the same link: the great are known by deeds that are rare because they are hard.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics V, Prop. 42, Scholium (trans. R. H. M. Elwes)

real_life_example.event_title: Galileo, under house arrest and going blind, completes Two New Sciences
real_life_example.place: Siena and Arcetri, near Florence, Italy, and Leiden, Netherlands
real_life_example.event: After his condemnation by the Inquisition in 1633, Galileo began assembling his Discourses on Two New Sciences while confined in Siena, and continued it under house arrest at his villa in Arcetri, where in 1634 he also lost his beloved daughter Maria Celeste. Because publishing in Italy was closed to him, the Dutch printer Louis Elzevir visited him in 1636 and agreed to print the book in Leiden; by January 1638 Galileo had lost his sight entirely. The book came off the press in July 1638, founding the science of the strength of materials and setting out his laws of motion, the pendulum and the parabolic path of projectiles.
real_life_example.explanation: Stripped of freedom, family and finally sight, the old Galileo still produced the work often regarded as the foundation of modern physics.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the great accomplish, in the proper way, deeds that are hard for others, and Galileo completed his hardest scientific work when his circumstances were at their worst.

tamil:
சிறியார் உணர்ச்சியுள் இல்லை பெரியாரைப்
பேணிக்கொள் வேமென்னும் நோக்கு.
transliteration:
Siriyaar unarchchiyul illai periyaaraip
penikkol vemennum nokku.
meaning: Small-minded people never have the thought, 'Let us respect great people and follow their ways.'
elementary: When a great teacher comes to school, some children run to listen and learn, hoping to become like her. Others just shrug and keep playing. Valluvar says wanting to learn from great people is itself a sign of a big heart.
university: Siriyaar (சிறியார், 'the small') is the counter-term to periyaar (பெரியார், 'the great') throughout this chapter and the next. The key phrase is peNikkoLvem (பேணிக்கொள்வேம், 'we will cherish and take to ourselves'): Puliyur Kesikan reads it as 'we will serve the great and attain their nature ourselves' (அவரியல்பை நாமும் அடைவோம்), Solomon Pappaiah as following them and preserving their tradition, and Mu. Varadarasanar as honouring them, which the small cannot do because they do not perceive the greatness at all. Nokku (நோக்கு, 'aim, outlook') and unarchchi (உணர்ச்சி, 'feeling, awareness') make the point psychological: the lack is in perception, not merely in will. Pope renders 'As votaries of the truly great we will ourselves enroll'. The text matches on both sites, with ytamizh omitting the final full stop.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just try to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him submissively and render service unto him. The self-realized souls can impart knowledge unto you because they have seen the truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna urges Arjuna to approach the wise, serve them and learn from them.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the 'aim to cherish the great' that the Kural says small minds lack.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 4.34 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says that seeking the company of the wise makes one wise.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's great-hearted seek the great; the small do not, and stay small.

islam.quote_or_event: “Moses said to him, ‘May I follow you on [the condition] that you teach me from what you have been taught of sound judgement?’”
islam.explanation: Even the prophet Moses humbly asks to follow and learn from a wiser servant of God.
islam.tie_back: He shows the outlook the Kural finds lacking in small minds: the wish to follow the great and absorb their wisdom.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let thy house be a house of meeting for the Sages and sit in the very dust of their feet, and drink in their words with thirst.”
judaism.explanation: Yose ben Yoezer urges eager, humble attachment to the wise.
judaism.tie_back: This thirst to cherish the great is exactly what the Kural says the small never feel.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:4 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a fool can sit beside the wise for a lifetime and absorb nothing.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point exactly: the small have no inner capacity to take on the nature of the great.

jainism.quote_or_event: The first lecture of the Uttaradhyayana, 'On Discipline' (vinaya), contrasts the well-behaved disciple, who stays near his teacher, carries out his instructions and understands his wishes, with the ill-behaved disciple who neglects the teacher and so gains nothing.
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic teaching treats reverent attachment to the teacher as the gateway to knowledge.
jainism.tie_back: The ill-behaved disciple is the Kural's small person who has no wish to cherish the great.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 1, 'On Discipline' (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: Macauliffe recounts that when Guru Nanak's end drew near he appointed his devoted disciple Angad (Bhai Lehna), who had served him wholeheartedly, as his successor, because the Guru's own sons had not obeyed him: their minds were insincere and they had rebelled and deserted him.
sikhism.explanation: In the Sikh account Lehna's readiness to serve the Guru and make the Guru's way his own is what made him Guru Angad, while the Guru's sons, though close to him by birth, never sought that service. Britannica likewise notes that Angad was known for his loyalty to the first Guru.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the resolve to cherish the great and take on their way never arises in small minds, and the story sets Lehna, who had that resolve, against the sons, who lacked it.
sikhism.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter XVII; corroborated by Encyclopaedia Britannica, Guru Angad

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Urged by Athena, the young Telemachus sails to Pylos and Sparta to seek out the aged Nestor and King Menelaus, learning from them about his father and about how great men act.
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus' coming of age begins with going out to learn from the great.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He shows the outlook the Kural says the small lack: wanting to learn from great men and become like them.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's allegory of the cave, the prisoners who have only ever seen shadows mock the one who returns from the light and would even kill anyone who tried to lead them upward.
philosophy.explanation: Plato portrays people who cannot recognise or welcome a mind greater than their own.
philosophy.tie_back: The prisoners are the Kural's small people, for whom honouring the great is simply not part of their outlook.

real_life_example.event_title: James Boswell seeks out Samuel Johnson and becomes his biographer
real_life_example.place: Thomas Davies's bookshop, Russell Street, Covent Garden, London, England
real_life_example.event: The young Scottish lawyer James Boswell, who had admired Samuel Johnson's writings for years, spent months in London trying to meet him and finally did so on 16 May 1763 in the back parlour of the bookseller Thomas Davies, where Johnson's sharp replies left him embarrassed. Undeterred, Boswell called on Johnson at his lodgings a week later and cultivated the friendship for twenty-one years, recording Johnson's conversation in remarkable detail in his journals. His Life of Samuel Johnson, published in 1791, is regarded as one of the greatest biographies in English.
real_life_example.explanation: Boswell's determination to learn from a great man and preserve his words gave the world its fullest portrait of Johnson.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the resolve to cherish the great and make their way one's own never arises in small minds, and Boswell's persistent pursuit of Johnson is the very resolve the kural says the small lack.

tamil:
இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழிற்றாம் சிறப்புந்தான்
சீரல் லவர்கண் படின்.
transliteration:
Irappe purindha thozhitraam sirappundhaan
seeral lavarkan padin.
meaning: When honor and high position come to people of poor character, it only makes them act in ways that go beyond all limits.
elementary: Give a bossy child the job of class leader and he might start ordering everyone around and showing off. The badge was meant for helping, but in the wrong hands it turns into bullying.
university: Sirappu (சிறப்பு, 'eminence, distinction') here covers whatever raises a person; Solomon Pappaiah lists money, learning and office, and Pope's explanation 'nobility of birth, wealth and learning' reflects the traditional commentarial list. When it reaches seeral lavar (சீரல்லவர், 'those without worth'), it becomes irappe purindha thozhitru (இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழிற்று), 'of the nature of acting only in excess': irappu (இறப்பு) is taken by Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar as 'overstepping the bounds' (வரம்பு மீறிய செயல்) and by Kesikan as being driven into arrogance. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads irappu as 'destruction', a minority gloss. The couplet is the negative counterpart to Kural 975: the same eminence that lets the great do rare deeds makes the small insolent. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Self-complacent and always impudent, deluded by wealth and false prestige, they sometimes proudly perform sacrifices in name only, without following any rules or regulations.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the demoniac as people whom wealth and prestige make impudent and lawless.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows advantages turning into insolence and disregard of every limit in unworthy hands.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.17 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear: For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with meat;”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs names the unfit person suddenly raised to power as something the world cannot bear.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's distinction falling to the unworthy and turning into excess.

islam.quote_or_event: “No! [But] indeed, man transgresses Because he sees himself self-sufficient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says a person oversteps bounds once he feels he needs no one.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's 'deeds that overstep the limit' arise in the same way when the unworthy gain distinction.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When you have eaten your fill, and have built fine houses to live in, and your herds and flocks have multiplied, and your silver and gold have increased, and everything you own has prospered, beware lest your heart grow haughty and you forget the Eternal your God…”
judaism.explanation: Moses warns Israel that prosperity can make the heart haughty.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that advantages can turn into arrogance.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 8:12-14 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To his own ruin the fool gains knowledge, for it cleaves his head and destroys his innate goodness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that in a fool even knowledge becomes destructive.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: a distinction such as learning, held by the unworthy, turns to harm.

jainism.quote_or_event: Samantabhadra's householder manual lists eight kinds of pride (mada) to be given up: pride in knowledge, honour, family, caste, power, attainments, austerity and bodily beauty, warning that one who looks down on others through such pride offends against the faith itself.
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics treats every advantage of birth, learning, power or beauty as a possible source of corrupting pride.
jainism.tie_back: The eight madas are exactly the Kural's distinctions that, in the unworthy, breed overbearing conduct.
jainism.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara of Samantabhadra, vv. 25-26 (tr. Champat Rai Jain)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Royal power, wealth, beauty, social status and youth are the five thieves. These thieves have plundered the world; no one’s honor has been spared.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak lists the very things that raise a person in the world (power, wealth, beauty, status, youth) and calls them thieves. Unless a person is anchored in the Guru, they lead to ruin, and the next line says only those who fall at the Guru's feet rob these robbers.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that distinction falling to the unworthy turns into excess, and Guru Nanak names the same gifts of eminence as forces that plunder anyone who is not inwardly fit to hold them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar, Vaar Malaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ixion, after being purified by Zeus and honoured with a place among the gods on Olympus, repaid the favour by trying to seduce Hera, and was bound for ever to a fiery wheel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar tells the story as a warning about a man who could not bear his good fortune.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ixion is the Kural's unworthy man whose distinction turns at once into outrageous excess.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Rhetoric Aristotle sketches the characters that wealth and power produce, observing that the newly rich in particular become insolent and arrogant, behaving as though they possessed every good.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle analyses how fortune tends to warp the character of those who receive it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he notes that distinction in unfit hands turns into insolence.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric II.16 (trans. W. Rhys Roberts)

real_life_example.event_title: Mobutu Sese Seko builds his palace city at Gbadolite
real_life_example.place: Gbadolite, Zaire (now Democratic Republic of the Congo)
real_life_example.event: Mobutu Sese Seko seized power in Zaire in 1965 and, while corruption and mismanagement led the country into decline, amassed one of the largest personal fortunes in the world. In his home region of Gbadolite he built three palaces lined with Italian marble, guest houses for the world's rich and famous, Chinese pagodas, a private hydroelectric plant and an airstrip for the Concorde airliner he frequently used, a complex nicknamed the Versailles of the Jungle. After he was overthrown in 1997 the palaces were looted and now stand in ruins in one of the poorest countries on earth.
real_life_example.explanation: The highest office in a vast nation became, in Mobutu's hands, a means to lavish excess while its people grew poorer.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that distinction falling to the unworthy turns into deeds that overstep every limit, and supreme office in Mobutu's hands produced the boundless extravagance of Gbadolite.

tamil:
பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை சிறுமை
அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து.
transliteration:
Paniyumaam endrum perumai sirumai
aniyumaam thannai viyandhu.
meaning: Greatness always bows and stays modest. Smallness dresses itself up and admires itself.
elementary: A tree heavy with fruit bends its branches low, while an empty stalk sticks straight up. Valluvar says truly great people are like the fruit tree: they stay humble, while small people keep showing off.
university: The couplet sets two verbs in parallel, paniyum (பணியும், 'bends, submits') and aniyum (அணியும், 'adorns'), with the expletive -aam (ஆம்) giving the tone of a settled maxim and endrum (என்றும், 'always') applying to both. Thannai viyandhu (தன்னை வியந்து, 'admiring itself') explains the adorning: littleness dresses itself up in its own praise. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'greatness walks in humility at all times, littleness praises itself', and Kalaignar adds that the small lie puffed up (இறுமாந்து). Pope's 'Greatness humbly bends, but littleness always / Spreads out its plumes' turns aniyum into a peacock image not in the Tamil. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Humility; pridelessness; nonviolence; tolerance; simplicity; approaching a bona fide spiritual master; cleanliness; steadiness; self-control…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna's list of the marks of true knowledge begins with humility and pridelessness (amānitvam, adambhitvam).
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it puts humility first among the marks of the truly great.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 13.8-12 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that self-exaltation leads down and humility leads up.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts set the humble bow of greatness against the self-promotion of littleness.

islam.quote_or_event: “Charity does not decrease wealth, no one forgives another except that Allah increases his honor, and no one humbles himself for the sake of Allah except that Allah raises his status.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that humility raises a person's standing.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes humble bowing the true sign and source of greatness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “…anyone who humbles himself, the Holy One, Blessed be He, exalts him, and anyone who exalts himself, the Holy One, Blessed be He, humbles him. Anyone who seeks greatness, greatness flees from him, and, conversely, anyone who flees from greatness, greatness seeks him.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud explains that Beit Hillel's rulings prevailed because they were humble, and draws a general lesson about greatness.
judaism.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's pairing of humble greatness with self-exalting smallness.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘Let both laymen and monks think that it was done by me. In every work, great and small, let them follow me’ — such is the ambition of the fool; thus his desire and pride increase.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada portrays the fool who wants credit for everything.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's littleness, decking itself out in self-admiration.

jainism.quote_or_event: After defeating his elder brother Bharata, Bahubali renounced the world and stood in motionless meditation for a year, but omniscience would not come because pride kept him from going to bow to his younger brothers, who had become monks before him; when his sisters made him see this and he resolved to go and bow, he attained kevala jnana.
jainism.explanation: In Jain tradition even the greatest austerity is blocked by pride and completed by humility.
jainism.tie_back: Bahubali's greatness is fulfilled only when it bows, just as the Kural says.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacaritra I (Life of Rishabha) (tr. Helen M. Johnson)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak! Are the essence of virtue and goodness. Everyone bows down to himself; no one bows down to another. When something is placed on the balancing scale and weighed, the side which descends is heavier.”
sikhism.explanation: The salok begins with the simmal tree, tall and showy but with useless fruit, and contrasts it with humility. On a scale the heavier pan sinks lower, so true worth shows itself by bowing.
sikhism.tie_back: Valluvar says greatness always bows while littleness admires and adorns itself, and Guru Nanak's image of the heavier pan sinking makes the same point.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Niobe boasted that with her many children she was more worthy of worship than the goddess Leto, who had only two; Apollo and Artemis killed her children, and the grieving Niobe was turned to weeping stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes self-glorifying boast the classic Greek form of fatal pride.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Niobe is the Kural's littleness that adorns itself with its own praise.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Apology Socrates explains the oracle's verdict by saying that the reputedly wise man he questioned knew nothing yet thought he knew, while he himself neither knew nor thought he knew, and so was wiser only in that small way.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates' wisdom consists in an honest humility that refuses to claim more than it has.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates is the Kural's greatness that bows, and his self-satisfied interlocutors are the littleness that admires itself.

real_life_example.event_title: Hokusai, at seventy-five, declares that nothing he drew before seventy was worth noticing
real_life_example.event: By 1834 Katsushika Hokusai was already famous for his print series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, including the Great Wave, yet in a postscript to the first volume of his illustrated book One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji, written at the age of seventy-five, he declared that nothing he had drawn before seventy was worthy of notice. He wrote that only at seventy-three had he begun to grasp the structure of plants, birds, animals, insects and fish, and that he hoped to keep improving through eighty, ninety and a hundred until, at a hundred and ten, every dot and stroke would be alive. He signed himself the Old Man Mad About Painting, and on his deathbed in 1849 he still wished for a few more years in which to become a true artist.
real_life_example.explanation: Japan's most celebrated artist, at the height of his fame, judged his own work with humility and saw himself as still a learner.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that greatness always bows in humility while littleness decks itself out in self-admiration, and the great Hokusai dismissed his own famous work as only a beginning.

tamil:
பெருமை பெருமிதம் இன்மை சிறுமை
பெருமிதம் ஊர்ந்து விடல்.
transliteration:
Perumai perumidham inmai sirumai
perumidham oorndhu vidal.
meaning: Greatness means not being full of pride. Smallness means riding high on pride and showing off.
elementary: A real champion says, 'Thanks, my team helped me.' Someone who isn't much of a champion struts around shouting, 'I'm the best!' Valluvar says being great means not puffing yourself up at all.
university: The couplet defines both terms through a single word, perumidham (பெருமிதம், 'swagger, pride'), which etymologically contains the same peru- ('great') as perumai: greatness is its absence (inmai, இன்மை), littleness is perumidham oorndhu vidal (பெருமிதம் ஊர்ந்து விடல்), 'mounting and riding on pride'. Mu. Varadarasanar reads oorndhu vidal as 'pride growing until it reaches its limit and stopping there', while Solomon Pappaiah sharpens the contrast: having cause for pride yet not being proud is greatness, being proud without cause is littleness. Pope's 'Riding on car of vanity supreme' keeps the image of mounting a vehicle. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Pride, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance – these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names pride, arrogance and conceit as the first marks of the demoniac nature.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it defines the lower nature by the presence of conceit.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.4 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Philippians to act without vainglory and in humility.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's definition of greatness: the absence of conceit.

islam.quote_or_event: “He who has in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of pride shall not enter Paradise. … Pride is disdaining the truth (out of self-conceit) and contempt for the people.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet condemns even a trace of pride and defines it as self-conceit and contempt for others.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats conceit as the defining mark of the lowly soul.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Now Moses himself was very humble, more so than any other human being on earth.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah singles out the greatest prophet for his humility.
judaism.tie_back: Moses is the Kural's greatness defined by the absence of pride.
judaism.source: Numbers 12:3 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that conceit about one's own wisdom is the surest sign of folly.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes inflated self-regard the mark of littleness.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra teaches that pride (mana) destroys humility (vinaya), and that pride is to be conquered by softness or humility (mardava), just as anger is conquered by calm, deceit by straightforwardness and greed by contentment.
jainism.explanation: In Jain doctrine pride is one of the four passions (kashayas) that bind karma, and its remedy is humility.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain ideal of conquering pride by humility is the Kural's definition of greatness as freedom from conceit.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 8.37-39 (numbering varies by edition)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The humble beings abide in peace; subduing egotism, they are meek. The very proud and arrogant persons, O Nanak! Are consumed by their own pride.”
sikhism.explanation: This salok opens the twelfth ashtapadi of Sukhmani, which goes on to list the pride of power, beauty, wealth and even of good deeds as forms of haumai (ego) that destroy a person. Haumai is the root problem in Sikh teaching.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural defines greatness as the absence of arrogance and littleness as riding on it, and Guru Arjan likewise contrasts the meek who live in peace with the proud who are consumed by their pride.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani, Ashtapadi 12 (opening salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon, eager to prove his divine parentage, insisted on driving the chariot of his father the Sun; unable to control the horses, he scorched the earth until Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows vanity literally mounting a chariot it cannot manage.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Phaethon is a vivid picture of the Kural's littleness 'riding on pride' to ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In discussing greatness of soul, Aristotle describes the vain man as one who thinks himself worthy of great things when he is not, and who parades his supposed merits in dress and display and is shown up by events.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle separates real greatness of soul from the vanity that claims it falsely.
philosophy.tie_back: His vain man is the Kural's littleness riding on pride without any ground for it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Pierre and Marie Curie decline the Legion of Honour
real_life_example.event: Pierre and Marie Curie, who shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics for their work on radioactivity, made it a rule to refuse state decorations, while gladly accepting scientific prizes and memberships for their work. Pierre Curie declined France's Legion of Honour in the years before his death in 1906. In 1910, when the minister of education proposed that Marie Curie receive it, she politely declined as well, keeping to the rule she had adopted with her husband.
real_life_example.explanation: Two of the most celebrated scientists in the world saw no need for ornaments of rank, valuing only the recognition of their work itself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says greatness is the absence of arrogance while littleness rides on pride, and the Curies, with every reason for pride, refused the decorations that others coveted.

tamil:
அற்றம் மறைக்கும் பெருமை சிறுமைதான்
குற்றமே கூறி விடும்.
transliteration:
Atram maraikkum perumai sirumaidhaan
kutrame koori vidum.
meaning: Greatness hides other people's weak points. Smallness talks about nothing but their faults.
elementary: If a friend trips and falls in the playground, a kind person helps them up and doesn't laugh. A mean person runs around telling everyone, 'Did you see him fall?' Valluvar says greatness is the helping hand, and smallness is the tattletale.
university: Atram (அற்றம்) means a weak, exposed or shameful point, literally a gap or defenceless state; maraikkum (மறைக்கும்) is 'conceals'. Against this, sirumai kutrame kooRi vidum (குற்றமே கூறி விடும்): 'littleness will speak out only faults', the emphatic -e (ஏ) on kutram marking that it says nothing else. Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah expand the contrast: the great speak of others' merits and hide their failings, the small hide their merits and broadcast their failings. Pope's 'Greatness will hide a neighbour's shame; / Meanness his faults to all the world proclaim' follows this reading. The chapter thus ends on how the great treat others, after nine couplets on how they hold themselves. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…truthfulness; freedom from anger; renunciation; tranquillity; aversion to faultfinding; compassion for all living entities…”
hinduism.explanation: Among the divine qualities Krishna lists apaiśunam, aversion to faultfinding.
hinduism.tie_back: It names as a godly trait the very restraint the Kural calls greatness.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.1-3 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.”
christianity.explanation: Peter teaches that love covers over others' failings.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes covering others' faults the sign of a large heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “…he who conceals (the faults) of a Muslim, Allah would conceal his faults in the world and in the Hereafter.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet promises that whoever covers a fellow believer's faults will have his own covered by God.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's greatness that hides another's weakness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father’s nakedness and told his two brothers outside. But Shem and Japheth took a cloth, placed it against both their backs and, walking backward, they covered their father’s nakedness…”
judaism.explanation: When Noah lies exposed, Ham broadcasts it while Shem and Japheth cover him without looking.
judaism.tie_back: The story enacts the Kural almost literally: greatness covers the exposed weakness, littleness tells it.
judaism.source: Genesis 9:22-23 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one's own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers to watch their own conduct rather than catalogue others' failings.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it rejects the small habit of dwelling on others' faults.

jainism.quote_or_event: Among the eight limbs of right faith (samyag-darshana), Jain teaching lists upaguhana: covering up the faults that weak or ignorant followers bring upon the path, rather than exposing them to public reproach.
jainism.explanation: Concealing a fellow believer's lapse is treated as a component of right faith itself.
jainism.tie_back: Upaguhana is very close to the Kural's greatness that hides others' weakness.
jainism.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara of Samantabhadra, v. 15 (tr. Champat Rai Jain)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, the Sufi saint whose saloks the Gurus placed in the scripture, tells the wise not to tally other people's faults but to look at their own. Elsewhere Gurbani condemns nindaa (slander) as a sign of the self-willed.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says greatness covers others' weaknesses while littleness speaks only of faults, and Farid gives the same instruction: refuse to blacken others and look inward instead.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, salok 6 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the assembly before Troy, Thersites, described as the ugliest and most foul-mouthed man in the army, rails at Agamemnon and the leaders, listing their failings to the troops, until Odysseus silences him with his staff.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer portrays Thersites as the mean man whose speech consists of finding fault.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Thersites is the Kural's littleness that does nothing but proclaim others' faults.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The marks of a proficient are, that he censures no one, praises no one, blames no one, accuses no one, says nothing concerning himself as being anybody, or knowing anything…”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus lists refusing to censure, blame or accuse others among the signs of moral progress.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it counts restraint from exposing others' faults as a mark of the great.

real_life_example.event_title: Eisenhower writes a note taking all the blame if D-Day fails
real_life_example.place: England, United Kingdom (Allied command for the Normandy invasion)
real_life_example.event: On 5 June 1944, after giving the final order for the Allied invasion of Normandy, General Dwight D. Eisenhower wrote a short statement to be issued if the landings failed, saying that the troops had been withdrawn and that his decision had been based on the best information available. He praised the soldiers, airmen and sailors for their bravery and devotion to duty and ended with the words, "If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone." The invasion succeeded, the note was never issued, and an aide retrieved it after Eisenhower discarded it; in his haste Eisenhower had misdated it July 5.
real_life_example.explanation: The Supreme Allied Commander prepared, in advance, to shield everyone under him and to carry any failure himself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says greatness covers up the weaknesses of others while littleness speaks only of their faults, and Eisenhower was ready to hide any failings of his forces behind his own acceptance of the blame.

tamil:
கடன்என்ப நல்லவை எல்லாம் கடன்அறிந்து
சான்றாண்மை மேற்கொள் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Kadanenpa nallavai ellaam kadanarindhu
saandraanmai merkol pavarkku.
meaning: For people who know their duty and choose to live with perfect character, all good things are said to be simply part of their duty.
elementary: Some children help clear the table only when someone asks and then want a sticker for it. Others just do it every day because that is who they are. Valluvar says truly good people are like the second kind: being kind and helpful is not an extra for them, it is just their everyday job.
university: The chapter title saandraanmai (சான்றாண்மை, from saandror, 'the full, the accomplished', and aanmai, 'mastery, the bearing of a quality') names the fullness of noble character; the related noun saalbu (சால்பு, 'abundance, completeness') recurs throughout the chapter. The opening couplet turns on kadan (கடன், 'debt, duty'): for one who knows his kadan and undertakes (merkol, மேற்கொள்) saandraanmai, all good things (nallavai ellaam) are themselves called duty. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses that for such a person all good things become 'natural duty' (இயல்பான கடமை), and Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan both render it as good qualities becoming one's very nature, the line of interpretation that follows the traditional commentary of Parimelazhagar, in which virtue is no longer a burden chosen case by case but an obligation already accepted. Pope's 'All goodly things are duties to the men, they say' keeps the reported-speech force of enpa (என்ப, 'they say'), marking this as received wisdom. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reverses the predicate ('the obligatory duty is the good things'), a minor variation in emphasis rather than in sense. The chapter follows Perumai (Greatness, ch. 98) in the Kudiyiyal and is followed by Panbudaimai (Courtesy, ch. 100). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, without being attached to the fruits of activities, one should act as a matter of duty, for by working without attachment one attains the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that right action should be done simply because it is one's duty, not for what it brings.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise describes the perfected person as one for whom doing good is simply what is owed, not a bargain.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.19 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples that even after doing everything commanded, they should regard it as no more than their duty.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats all good deeds as simply what is owed, leaving no room for self-congratulation.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression. He admonishes you that perhaps you will be reminded.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents justice, good conduct and generosity as standing obligations upon the believer.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the whole range of good conduct is framed as something owed, not optional.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ben Azzai said: Be quick in performing a minor commandment as in the case of a major one, and flee from transgression; For one commandment leads to another commandment, and transgression leads to another transgression; For the reward for performing a commandment is another commandment and the reward for committing a transgression is a transgression.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Azzai teaches that each good deed done as duty draws the next one after it, so that goodness becomes a way of life.
judaism.tie_back: This is how, in the Kural's words, all good things come to be the natural duty of one who has taken up the noble life.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:2 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As from a great heap of flowers many garlands can be made, even so should many good deeds be done by one born a mortal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges that a human life be used to do as many good deeds as possible, as a garland-maker uses every flower.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats the doing of all good things as what a human being owes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having adopted (the law), one should not hide it, nor forsake it.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga teaches that once the law of non-harm has been taken up, one must hold to it openly and never abandon it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's noble person likewise 'takes up' perfection (merkol) and then treats every good as a binding duty.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.4.1.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak sums up the Sikh way of life in two ordinary habits, kirat karni (living by honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing what one earns). The person who does both as a matter of course is the one who knows the Path.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that for those who know what is due from them every good act is simply duty done as a matter of course, and Guru Nanak likewise finds the true path in goodness made into an everyday habit.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang, Vaar Sarang, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus' fable of the Choice of Heracles, the young hero at a crossroads is approached by Vice, who offers an easy life of pleasure, and by Virtue, who offers a hard path of labour and duty; Heracles chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story presents the noble life as something a person deliberately chooses and then lives out through toil.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles' choice mirrors the Kural's person who knowingly takes up perfection and accepts all good things as duty.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus' Choice of Heracles, as retold in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the things we have to learn before we can do them, we learn by doing them, e.g. men become builders by building and lyreplayers by playing the lyre; so too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that moral virtues are formed by habit, so that doing good repeatedly makes goodness part of one's character.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains how, for the Kural's noble person, all good things become natural duty once perfection has been taken up.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Aristides de Sousa Mendes issues visas to refugees in Bordeaux
real_life_example.event: In June 1940, as German forces advanced through France, Portugal's consul general in Bordeaux, Aristides de Sousa Mendes, defied his government's instructions restricting visas and began issuing transit visas to refugees, many of them Jews, giving them free to those who could not pay. Helped by two of his sons, he worked for days with little rest, and Yad Vashem records 1,575 visas issued between 15 and 22 June alone. Recalled to Lisbon, he was dismissed from the diplomatic service and died in poverty in 1954; Yad Vashem recognised him as Righteous Among the Nations in 1966.
real_life_example.explanation: Sousa Mendes treated helping desperate strangers as something his conscience simply required of him, even though it cost him his career and his family's security.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those of perfected character every good deed is simply a duty owed, and Sousa Mendes acted on that duty as a matter of course rather than as a calculated sacrifice.

tamil:
குணநலம் சான்றோர் நலனே பிறநலம்
எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று.
transliteration:
Kunanalam saandror nalane piranalam
ennalaththu ulladhooum andru.
meaning: The real goodness of good people is the goodness of their character. No other kind of goodness counts as real goodness at all.
elementary: A shiny new bike, a nice haircut or a fancy pair of shoes can look great. But Valluvar says the thing that really makes a person beautiful is a kind and honest heart. Everything else is just wrapping paper.
university: The couplet sets kunanalam (குணநலம், 'the goodness of qualities, beauty of character') against piranalam (பிறநலம், 'other goods'). The noble (saandror) have only one nalam (நலம், 'good, beauty, excellence') worth the name; the other kinds are not counted 'among any good' (ennalaththu ulladhooum andru, எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று), where ulladhooum shows the alapedai (vowel lengthening) that fills out the metre. Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Karunanidhi read nalam as beauty (அழகு), contrasting inner beauty of character with outward beauty of form, while Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the more general 'good'; Pope's prose rendering, following the older commentarial tradition associated with Parimelazhagar, understands the other goods as sensual delights. Both readings make the same claim: for the perfected person only character counts. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Katha Upanishad, Yama tells the boy Naciketas that the good (shreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) are two different things; the wise person chooses the good, while the fool chooses the pleasant for the sake of gain and comfort.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad separates true good from attractive but lesser goods and praises the one who prefers the former.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says that only the good of character is real good, and the rest do not count.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad 1.2.1-2 (cf. tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
christianity.explanation: When Samuel is impressed by a tall, handsome candidate for king, God tells him that what matters is the heart, not appearance.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks inner character above every outward excellence.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that outward looks and riches carry no weight with God; only the heart and conduct do.
islam.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's claim that character is the only real good and other goods do not count.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thus said GOD: Let not the wise glory in their wisdom; Let not the strong glory in their strength; Let not the rich glory in their riches. But only in this should one glory: In being earnestly devoted to Me. For I GOD act with kindness, Justice, and equity in the world; For in these I delight —declares GOD.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah dismisses wisdom, strength and wealth as grounds for pride and points instead to kindness, justice and equity.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sets aside every other excellence in favour of goodness of character.
judaism.source: Jeremiah 9:22-23 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by mere eloquence nor by beauty of form does a man become accomplished, if he is jealous, selfish and deceitful. But he in whom these are wholly destroyed, uprooted and extinct, and who has cast out hatred — that wise man is truly accomplished.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that eloquence and good looks do not make a person accomplished; only freedom from jealousy, selfishness, deceit and hatred does.
buddhism.tie_back: This closely echoes the Kural's view that the accomplished person's only real excellence is character.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One does not become a Sramana by the tonsure, nor a Brâhmana by the sacred syllable ôm, nor a Muni by living in the woods, nor a Tâpasa by wearing (clothes of) Kusa-grass and bark. One becomes a Sramana by equanimity, a Brâhmana by chastity, a Muni by knowledge, and a Tâpasa by penance.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha tells a Brahmin priest that religious status comes from inner qualities, not from outward marks like shaved heads, mantras or forest dwelling.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that only goodness of character makes a person truly noble.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.31-32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak puts lived conduct (sach aachaar) above every other attainment, even above truth held only as an idea. In the Sikh view character shown in life is the excellence that counts.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the only real excellence of the noble is goodness of character and that other excellences do not count, and Guru Nanak likewise ranks truthful living above everything else.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue come money and every other good of man, public as well as private.”
greek_mythology.explanation: At his trial Socrates says that his whole mission has been to urge people to care for the soul before body or property.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes virtue the one real good on which every other good depends.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant opens the First Section of the Groundwork by saying that nothing in the world, or even out of it, can be called good without qualification except a good will; talents, fortune and even health can become bad when the will that uses them is not good.
philosophy.explanation: Kant argues that every other excellence is only conditionally good, while goodness of will is good in itself.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in philosophical form: only goodness of character is good in every case.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section (tr. T. K. Abbott)

real_life_example.event_title: Eric Liddell declines to run the 100 metres on a Sunday
real_life_example.event: Learning months in advance that the heats of the 100 metres at the 1924 Paris Olympics would be run on a Sunday, the Scottish sprinter Eric Liddell, a devout Christian, declined to enter his best event and also withdrew from the relays held on Sundays. He was criticised in the press, but trained instead for the 200 and 400 metres, winning bronze in the 200 metres. On 11 July 1924 he won the 400 metres in an Olympic-record time of 47.6 seconds.
real_life_example.explanation: Liddell set his convictions above the most likely route to a gold medal, and his reputation rests as much on that choice as on his victory.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the true excellence of the noble lies in character, with other kinds of excellence not counted at all, and Liddell ranked his principles above athletic glory.

tamil:
அன்புநாண் ஒப்புரவு கண்ணோட்டம் வாய்மையொடு
ஐந்துசால் ஊன்றிய தூண்.
transliteration:
Anbunaan oppuravu kannottam vaaimaiyodu
aindhusaal oondriya thoon.
meaning: Love, shame at doing wrong, helping everyone, kindness toward others, and truthfulness: these five are the pillars that hold up perfect character.
elementary: Think of a tree house held up by five strong posts. If one post breaks, the house wobbles. Valluvar says a good person is held up by five posts too: loving others, feeling shy about doing wrong, sharing, being kind, and telling the truth.
university: This is the chapter's architectural image: saalbu (perfection) is a load resting on five pillars (aindhu ... oondriya thoon, ஐந்து ... ஊன்றிய தூண்). The five are anbu (அன்பு, 'affection'), naan (நாண், 'shame', specifically recoil from blameworthy deeds, as Pappaiah glosses பழி பாவங்களுக்கு நாணுதல்), oppuravu (ஒப்புரவு, 'benevolence to all, sharing what one has gathered', the subject of ch. 22), kannottam (கண்ணோட்டம், 'kindly regard', literally 'running of the eye', the subject of ch. 58) and vaaimai (வாய்மை, 'truthfulness', ch. 30). Commentators differ on how to parse saal: most take ஐந்து சால்பு ஊன்றிய தூண் as 'the five pillars that bear saalbu', while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as pillars of the 'vessel' of perfection; Pope renders 'pillars five of perfect virtue's resting-place'. Karunanidhi glosses oppuravu as 'honouring the world's conduct' and kannottam as 'compassionate acts', showing how the virtues shade into each other. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Gita 16.1-3 Krishna lists the 'divine qualities' (daivī sampad) of the person born for liberation, among them fearlessness, charity, nonviolence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, compassion for all beings, gentleness, modesty and forgiveness.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita gives a catalogue of virtues that together make up a godly character.
hinduism.tie_back: Several of the Kural's five pillars (love, shame, giving, kindness, truth) appear in this list as the supports of a noble nature.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.1-3 (cf. Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists the qualities that grow in a person led by the Spirit.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's five pillars, it names a set of linked virtues, beginning with love, that together make up a complete character.

islam.quote_or_event: “Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but [true] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask [for help], and for freeing slaves; [and who] establishes prayer and gives zakah; [those who] fulfill their promise when they promise; and [those who] are patient in poverty and hardship and during battle. Those are the ones who have been true, and it is those who are the righteous.”
islam.explanation: The verse defines true righteousness through a set of pillars: faith, generous giving, prayer, keeping promises and patience.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes righteousness as resting on several supports, notably generosity and truthfulness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shimon the Righteous was one of the last of the men of the great assembly. He used to say: the world stands upon three things: the Torah, the Temple service, and the practice of acts of piety.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon the Righteous names the three supports on which the whole world stands.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image of supports, with five pillars bearing up perfect character.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:2 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One in whom there is truthfulness, virtue, inoffensiveness, restraint and self-mastery, who is free from defilements and is wise — he is truly called an Elder.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines the true Elder by a short list of qualities rather than by age.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names a handful of virtues, including truthfulness, as what makes someone truly accomplished.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra defines the vows (vrata) as abstaining from injury, falsehood, stealing, unchastity and possessiveness, and says they are kept partially by householders (anuvrata) and completely by ascetics (mahavrata).
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics rests on five vows, which together form the backbone of a disciplined life for monks and laypeople alike.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's five pillars, the five vows are presented as the supports of a perfected character, with truthfulness common to both lists.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.1-2 (cf. tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Then were created the five elements and five friends (truth, contentment and compassion etc.) and five enemies (the five evil propensities) of the creatures.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh exegete, describes creation as setting five virtues in the human being against the five thieves (lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego). Sikh teaching commonly counts the five friends as truth, contentment, compassion, humility and love.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural rests perfect character on five pillars (love, shame at wrongdoing, generosity, kindliness and truthfulness), and Bhai Gurdas likewise gives the human being five virtues as its support against the five thieves.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 39, Pauri 2 (English translation as given on BaniDB/searchgurbani.com)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Book IV of the Republic, Socrates says that a perfectly good city must be wise, courageous, temperate and just, and then finds the same four virtues in the well-ordered soul.
greek_mythology.explanation: Plato's four cardinal virtues are presented as the components that together make up complete goodness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's five pillars, they name a fixed set of virtues on which a perfect character rests.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The foundation of justice, moreover, is good faith; — that is, truth and fidelity to promises and agreements.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero names the two bonds that hold human society together: justice, and its close kin charity, 'which may also be called kindness or generosity' (I.20). He then rests justice itself on good faith, meaning truth and keeping one's word (I.23).
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Cicero rests good character on a few named supports, among them generosity, kindness and truth.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.20-23 (tr. Walter Miller)

real_life_example.event_title: Ashoka's Second Pillar Edict defines Dhamma
real_life_example.event: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka had a series of edicts inscribed on stone pillars across his empire late in his reign. In the Second Pillar Edict he asks what Dhamma consists of and answers with a short list: little evil, much good, kindness, generosity, truthfulness and purity, in S. Dhammika's rendering (older translations by V. A. Smith and D. R. Bhandarkar give compassion or mercy, liberality or gift, truthfulness and purity). The edict says it was written so that people might follow it and that it might long endure.
real_life_example.explanation: Ashoka set out the foundations of right conduct as a short list of inner qualities and literally carved them onto pillars for public instruction.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names five pillars on which perfect character rests, among them generosity, kindly regard and truthfulness, and Ashoka's pillar edict rests Dhamma on an overlapping set of virtues.

tamil:
கொல்லா நலத்தது நோன்மை பிறர்தீமை
சொல்லா நலத்தது சால்பு.
transliteration:
Kollaa nalaththadhu nonmai pirardheemai
sollaa nalaththadhu saalbu.
meaning: Self-discipline is built on the goodness of not killing. Perfect character is built on the goodness of not talking about other people's wrongs.
elementary: A good person does not hurt any living creature, not even a bug. And a really good person also does not go around telling everyone the bad things someone else did. Valluvar says the first is the heart of being holy, and the second is the heart of being truly good.
university: A balanced couplet built on two parallel phrases: kollaa nalam (கொல்லா நலம், 'the goodness of not killing') grounds nonmai (நோன்மை, 'austerity, penance', glossed as தவம் by Varadarasanar and Kesikan), while sollaa nalam (சொல்லா நலம், 'the goodness of not telling') grounds saalbu. Pirar theemai (பிறர்தீமை) may mean either others' faults or the wrongs others have done; Karunanidhi takes the second ('not pointing out the harm others do'), the majority the first. The pairing ties this chapter to Kollaamai (ch. 33) and Purangooraamai (Not Backbiting, ch. 19), and suggests that just as non-killing is the essence of the ascetic, refusal to broadcast faults is the essence of the noble householder. Pope's 'penitence' for nonmai is archaic; 'austerity' is closer. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads nonmai more broadly as 'sustaining life without destroying'. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of the body consists in worship of the Supreme Lord, the brāhmaṇas, the spiritual master, and superiors like the father and mother, and in cleanliness, simplicity, celibacy and nonviolence.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita counts nonviolence among the elements of bodily austerity (tapas), and the next verse adds truthful, non-agitating speech as austerity of speech.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links tapas with non-harm and, in the following verse, with restraint in speech.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law: but if thou judge the law, thou art not a doer of the law, but a judge.”
christianity.explanation: James forbids believers to speak evil of one another, treating such talk as a usurpation of judgment.
christianity.tie_back: This directly matches the Kural's second clause: perfection lies in not speaking of others' faults.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin. And do not spy or backbite each other. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when dead? You would detest it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an compares backbiting to eating a dead brother's flesh.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats talking about others' faults as a grave failure of character.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Do not deal basely with members of your people. Do not profit by the blood of your fellow: I am GOD.”
judaism.explanation: Leviticus forbids slander and talebearing (the translators note 'deal basely' as, for example, slander) and, in the same verse, standing idly by another's blood.
judaism.tie_back: The verse pairs a ban on harmful speech with a concern for life, much as the Kural pairs not speaking ill with not killing.
judaism.source: Leviticus 19:16 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one's own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers to stop examining other people's failings and to look at their own.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's teaching that perfection lies in not speaking of others' faults.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The Arhats and Bhagavats of the past, present, and future, all say thus, speak thus, declare thus, explain thus: all breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures should not be slain, nor treated with violence, nor abused, nor tormented, nor driven away.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga states the core Jain law of ahimsa: no living being may be killed, harmed or abused.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first clause in its most rigorous form: non-killing as the very ground of ascetic discipline.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.4.1.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “It is not good to slander anyone, but the foolish, self-willed manmukhs still do it.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das condemns nindaa (speaking ill of others) as the mark of the manmukh, the self-willed person turned away from the Guru. Gurbani often treats slander as a serious spiritual fault.
sikhism.tie_back: The second line of the Kural grounds perfection in not speaking of others' faults, and Guru Amar Das likewise counts refusing to slander as part of a good life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 755, Raag Suhi, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Book XV of Ovid's Metamorphoses, the philosopher Pythagoras urges people to stop killing animals for food, arguing that all souls pass between bodies and that slaughter defiles human beings.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pythagoras, a semi-legendary Greek sage, made abstention from killing a central religious discipline.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This echoes the Kural's view that real austerity begins with not killing.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV.60-478 (trans. A. S. Kline)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises keeping silent for the most part and, if one must speak about other people, not to blame them, praise them or compare them.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic teacher counts restraint in speaking about others as part of the disciplined life.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's teaching that the noble do not talk about other people's faults.

real_life_example.event_title: Eisenhower drafts a note taking all blame if D-Day fails
real_life_example.event: On 5 June 1944, hours after giving the final order to launch the Allied invasion of Normandy, General Dwight D. Eisenhower wrote a short statement to be released if the landings failed. In it he praised the troops, the air forces and the navy for doing all that bravery and devotion to duty could do, and declared that any blame or fault for the attempt was his alone. He misdated the note July 5; the invasion succeeded and the statement was never used, and it is now held at the Eisenhower Library.
real_life_example.explanation: Even in imagined defeat Eisenhower refused to place the fault on the men under his command.
