real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says perfection rests on not speaking of other people's faults, and Eisenhower prepared to shoulder all blame himself rather than point to anyone else's failings.

tamil:
ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல் அதுசான்றோர்
மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை.
transliteration:
Aatruvaar aatral panidhal adhusaandror
maatraarai maatrum padai.
meaning: The strength of capable people is their modesty. It is the weapon good people use to turn their enemies into friends.
elementary: When someone is cross with you, shouting back usually makes it worse. But if you speak gently and say sorry, the angry person often calms down and even becomes your friend. Valluvar says being humble is the strongest tool a good person has.
university: The couplet plays on the root aatru (ஆற்று, 'to accomplish, to be able'): aatruvaar aatral (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல்), 'the power of those who can achieve', is panidhal (பணிதல், 'bending, humility'). In the second line maatraar (மாற்றார், 'adversaries') are 'changed' (maatrum, மாற்றும்) by this padai (படை, 'weapon, army'), a deliberate pun. Most modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Karunanidhi) read the second line as humility turning enemies away from enmity; Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan, nearer the older commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, read the first line more concretely as the achiever's skill in winning over helpers by bowing to them. Pope's 'Submission is the might of men of mighty acts; the sage / With that same weapon stills his foeman's rage' captures both senses. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Humility; pridelessness; nonviolence; tolerance; simplicity; approaching a bona fide spiritual master; cleanliness; steadiness; self-control; renunciation of the objects of sense gratification; absence of false ego; ... all these I declare to be knowledge, and besides this whatever there may be is ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna places humility and pridelessness first in his list of the marks of true knowledge.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes humility the first strength of the accomplished person.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 13.8-12 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb observes that gentleness defuses anger while harshness inflames it.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim that humility is the weapon that turns adversaries from hostility.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches that answering hostility with something better can turn an enemy into a close friend.
islam.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that the noble person's weapon changes enemies.

judaism.quote_or_event: Avot de-Rabbi Natan expands the Mishnah's question 'Who is mighty?' by answering that the mightiest of the mighty is the one who makes an enemy into a friend.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic tradition redefines strength as the power to win over one's adversary.
judaism.tie_back: This is close to the Kural's idea of the noble person's power to change enemies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that enmity ends only when it is met without enmity.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the way to end hostility is not counter-force but a gentler disposition.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Bravo! you have conquered anger; bravo! you have vanquished pride; bravo! you have banished delusion; bravo! you have subdued greed. Bravo for your simplicity, O saint! bravo for your humility, O saint! bravo for your perfect patience! bravo for your perfect liberation!”
jainism.explanation: After testing King Nami, who had renounced his throne, the god Sakra praises him for conquering pride and for his humility and patience.
jainism.tie_back: Nami's victory, won by humility rather than armies, parallels the Kural's view that humility is the true strength of the capable.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.56-57 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Humility is my spiked club. My dagger is to be the dust of all men’s feet. No evil-doer can withstand these weapons.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan calls humility his weapon: the club and dagger of the Gurmukh are lowliness and being the dust of everyone's feet, and no evil-doer can stand against them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls humility the strength of the capable and the weapon by which the noble turn enemies from enmity, and Guru Arjan gives the very same image of humility as an unbeatable weapon.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 628, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop's fable of the North Wind and the Sun, the Wind tries to strip a traveller's cloak by force and only makes him clutch it tighter, while the Sun's gentle warmth makes him take it off willingly.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable teaches that gentleness achieves what force cannot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it presents a gentle, unforced approach as the stronger weapon.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, The North Wind and the Sun (Perry Index 46)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “That whereby the rivers and seas are able to receive the homage and tribute of all the valley streams, is their skill in being lower than they;--it is thus that they are the kings of them all.”
philosophy.explanation: Laozi teaches that the sea rules the streams because it lies lower than they do, and that the sage leads by placing himself below others.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's paradox in Daoist form: lowliness is the source of real power.
philosophy.source: Laozi, Tao Te Ching 66 (trans. James Legge)

real_life_example.event_title: Willy Brandt kneels at the Warsaw Ghetto memorial
real_life_example.event: On 7 December 1970, during a visit to Poland to sign the Treaty of Warsaw, West German Chancellor Willy Brandt asked to lay a wreath at the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes. After laying it he knelt silently before the memorial, a gesture he later said had not been planned. The gesture was controversial in West Germany at the time, but the Norwegian Nobel Committee cited it when awarding him the 1971 Nobel Peace Prize, and it became a lasting symbol of German-Polish reconciliation.
real_life_example.explanation: A head of government humbling himself before the victims of his nation's crimes did more to open the way to reconciliation with a former enemy than any show of strength could have done.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls humility the true strength of the capable and the weapon that turns enemies from enmity, and Brandt's kneeling helped change relations between peoples long divided by war.

tamil:
சால்பிற்குக் கட்டளை யாதெனின் தோல்வி
துலையல்லார் கண்ணும் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Saalbirkuk kattalai yaadhenin tholvi
thulaiyallaar kannum kolal.
meaning: If you ask what the test of perfect character is, it is being willing to accept defeat even from people who are not your equals.
elementary: It is easy to say 'You win' to a big champion. It is much harder to say it to a younger child who beat you at a game. Valluvar says being able to lose gracefully, even to someone smaller, is the real test of a good person.
university: Kattalai (கட்டளை) here is the touchstone (உரைகல்) used to test gold, as Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss it: saalbu is gold, and its test is tholvi ... kolal (தோல்வி ... கொளல், 'accepting defeat'). Thulai allaar (துலையல்லார்), literally 'those not of the same balance (thulai, துலை)', are one's inferiors; the particle -um in kannum (கண்ணும், 'even with') makes the point that yielding to a superior is no test at all. Kesikan spells out the contrast: the defeat one would accept from one's betters must be accepted even from lesser people. Pope's verse ('What is perfection's test? The equal mind. / To bear repulse from even meaner men resigned') introduces 'equal mind' as a gloss rather than a translation. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads thulaiyallaar as those 'unfit to accept defeat', a less common construal. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do thou fight for the sake of fighting, without considering happiness or distress, loss or gain, victory or defeat – and by so doing you shall never incur sin.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna asks Arjuna to act with an even mind toward victory and defeat alike.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's touchstone similarly asks for a mind that can accept defeat without wounded pride.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.38 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?”
christianity.explanation: Paul rebukes Christians who sue one another and asks why they do not simply accept being wronged.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats willingness to lose to another as a mark of mature character.

islam.quote_or_event: “I guarantee a house in the surroundings of Paradise for a man who avoids quarrelling even if he were in the right, a house in the middle of Paradise for a man who avoids lying even if he were joking, and a house in the upper part of Paradise for a man who made his character good.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet promises reward to those who give up an argument even when they are right.
islam.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's test of perfection: being willing to yield even when one could win.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4800 (graded hasan by al-Albani; Sunnah.com)

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that those who are insulted but do not insult in return, who hear themselves shamed and do not answer, who act out of love and rejoice in suffering, are the ones of whom Scripture says, 'May those who love Him be like the sun rising in its might.'
judaism.explanation: The sages praise the person who absorbs humiliation without retaliating, comparing them to the rising sun.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees the willingness to take a loss without hitting back as the mark of the truly great.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Victory begets enmity; the defeated dwell in pain. Happily the peaceful live, discarding both victory and defeat.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that winning breeds resentment and losing breeds pain, and that the peaceful let go of both.
buddhism.tie_back: This supports the Kural's view that a noble person does not need to win and can accept defeat calmly.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a layman abuses a monk, he should not grow angry against him; because he would be like a child, a monk should not grow angry. If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira lists abuse (akrosha) among the hardships a monk must bear calmly, without anger or retaliation.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's touchstone, it asks one to accept humiliation even from those who are spiritually beneath one, without answering back.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.24-25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you are wise, be simple; if you are powerful, be weak; and when there is nothing to share, then share with others. How rare is one who is known as such a devotee.”
sikhism.explanation: These saloks ask the strong to choose weakness and the wise to choose simplicity, giving up the advantage they could press. A neighbouring salok of Farid (salok 7, Ang 1378) asks the devotee not to strike back but to kiss the feet of those who strike.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural makes the willingness to accept defeat even from those beneath one the touchstone of perfection, and Farid's counsel that the powerful should be weak describes that same chosen yielding.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, salok 128 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Socrates shocks his hearers by maintaining that it is better to suffer wrong than to do wrong, and that he would choose to be wronged rather than wrong another.
greek_mythology.explanation: Socrates holds that losing to injustice harms only one's fortune, while committing injustice harms one's soul.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This gives a philosophical basis for the Kural's view that accepting defeat is a sign of a well-formed character.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is grievous, when a candidate for public offices, to be defeated by one's inferiors; therefore let him be defeated by Vatinius … That all men may know that these things, which I have deemed Cato worthy to undergo, are not real evils.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca has Nature explain why she put Cato through every hardship, including losing an election to the inferior Vatinius: to show that such defeats are no true evil to a good man.
philosophy.tie_back: Cato's calm acceptance of defeat by a lesser man is just the touchstone of perfection the Kural names.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Of Providence (De Providentia) 3.14 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: Eugenio Monti lends his bolt to his British rivals
real_life_example.event: During the two-man bobsleigh at the 1964 Winter Olympics in Innsbruck, the British pair Tony Nash and Robin Dixon found that a bolt on their sled had broken, and Italy's Eugenio Monti, already a multiple world champion, lent them one from his own sled. Nash and Dixon won the gold medal and Monti finished third; days later he and his mechanics also helped repair the Canadian four-man sled, and Canada won that event while Monti again took bronze. The IOC gave Monti its first Pierre de Coubertin award for fair play.
real_life_example.explanation: Monti, the established master of his sport, accepted being beaten by less decorated rivals rather than profit from their bad luck.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural makes the willingness to accept defeat, even at the hands of those who are not one's equals, the touchstone of perfect character, and Monti chose a fair defeat over an unearned victory.

tamil:
இன்னாசெய் தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்
என்ன பயத்ததோ சால்பு.
transliteration:
Innaasey thaarkkum iniyave seyyaakkaal
enna payaththadho saalbu.
meaning: What use is perfect character if it does not do kind things even to people who have hurt you?
elementary: Being nice to people who are nice to you is easy. Valluvar asks a harder question: what if someone was mean to you? He says that being kind back to them is what really shows you are a good person.
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: if one does not do iniyavai (இனியவை, 'pleasant, kind things') even to those who did innaa (இன்னா, 'painful, harmful things'), of what use (enna payaththadho, என்ன பயத்ததோ) is saalbu? The -um of thaarkkum (தார்க்கும், 'even to those who did') carries the force. It restates for the noble householder the teaching of Innaa Seyyaamai (ch. 32), especially Kural 314 (inna seydhaarai oruththal avar naana nannayam seydhu vidal), and all modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Karunanidhi, Kesikan) agree on the plain sense. Note that the English section for this couplet on ytamizh.com is misaligned: its 'Couplet Explanation' belongs to Kural 946 on overeating and the line printed as the couplet is Pope's prose explanation, so it should not be relied on here. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant, always satisfied, self-controlled, and engaged in devotional service with determination, his mind and intelligence fixed on Me – such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the dear devotee as one who bears no hatred toward any being and is friendly and forgiving.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's call for kindness extended to all, including those who give offence.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 12.13-14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;”
christianity.explanation: Jesus commands his followers to love and do good to those who hate and harm them.
christianity.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's demand to do kindness to those who have done harm.

islam.quote_or_event: “Repel, by [means of] what is best, [their] evil. We are most knowing of what they describe.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells the Prophet to answer the evil done to him with what is best.
islam.tie_back: This matches the Kural's teaching of returning good for harm.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat; If he is thirsty, give him water to drink. You will be heaping live coals on his head, And GOD will reward you.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs instructs that an enemy in need should be fed and given drink.
judaism.tie_back: This is a concrete form of the Kural's demand to do good even to those who have done harm.
judaism.source: Proverbs 25:21-22 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that each kind of wrongdoing should be met with its opposite virtue.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that the wicked are to be met with goodness, not with retaliation.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain account of Mahavira's ascetic years, the venomous serpent Chandakaushika bites the meditating Mahavira; instead of anger, Mahavira responds with calm compassion and words of awakening, and the snake gives up violence.
jainism.explanation: The story shows the Jina returning only compassion to a creature that tried to kill him, and thereby transforming it.
jainism.tie_back: This dramatises the Kural's question: what use is perfection if it does not do good even to one who does harm?
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra, Parva X (Life of Mahavira) (tr. Helen M. Johnson)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid's salok, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, tells the devotee to return good for evil and not to let anger take hold. Sikh tradition honours the same ideal in Bhai Kanhaiya, who gave water to the wounded of both sides.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what perfection is worth if it will not do kindness even to those who have done harm, and Farid's command to answer evil with goodness is that same demand.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Awaiting execution, Socrates tells Crito that it is never right to return wrong for wrong.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This shares the Kural's rejection of retaliation, though the Kural goes further in demanding active kindness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “(It is the way of the Tao) to act without (thinking of) acting; to conduct affairs without (feeling the) trouble of them; to taste without discerning any flavour; to consider what is small as great, and a few as many; and to recompense injury with kindness.”
philosophy.explanation: Laozi lists returning kindness for injury as part of the way of the Tao.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's demand to do good to those who have done harm.
philosophy.source: Laozi, Tao Te Ching 63 (trans. James Legge)

real_life_example.event_title: Nelson Mandela invites his Rivonia Trial prosecutor to lunch
real_life_example.event: Percy Yutar was the chief prosecutor at the 1963-64 Rivonia Trial, at which Nelson Mandela and his co-accused were sentenced to life imprisonment; South African History Online notes that he had wanted the death sentence for Mandela. In November 1995, as President of South Africa, Mandela invited Yutar to lunch at his presidential residence in Pretoria and told him he had only been doing his duty as a prosecutor. Some of Mandela's former co-accused, including Walter Sisulu and Ahmed Kathrada, declined to attend.
real_life_example.explanation: Mandela used the power of his office not to settle scores but to extend hospitality to the man who had sought his destruction.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use perfect character is if it does not do kind things even to those who have done harm, and Mandela offered kindness to the prosecutor who had helped send him to prison for decades.

tamil:
இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று சால்பென்னும்
திண்மைஉண் டாகப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Inmai oruvarku ilivandru saalbennum
thinmaiun daakap perin.
meaning: Being poor is no shame for a person who has the inner strength called perfect character.
elementary: Some people have lots of toys and money, and some have very little. Valluvar says having little is nothing to be ashamed of, as long as you are honest, kind and strong inside. That inner strength is worth more than any treasure.
university: Inmai (இன்மை, 'having nothing, poverty') is not ilivu (இளிவு, 'disgrace') for one who has gained the thinmai (திண்மை, 'firmness, solidity') called saalbu. The image of perfection as a kind of solidity anticipates the stability of Kural 989. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Karunanidhi all read inmai as material poverty, and Karunanidhi adds that such a person treats saalbu itself as wealth; Sivayogi Sivakumar widens inmai to 'hardships'. Textual note: ytamizh.com reads இளிவன்று (ilivandru, 'is not disgrace'), the standard reading supported by the commentaries' gloss இழிவு; thirukkural.net's main text prints இனிவன்று, which appears to be a typographical error (ன for ள), since its own commentaries gloss the word as இழிவு. This edition follows இளிவன்று. Placed just before the chapters on Nalkuravu (Poverty, ch. 105) and Iravu (Begging, ch. 106), the couplet establishes that character, not wealth, sets the limits of dignity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, a poor brahmin friend of Krishna's boyhood (known in later tradition as Sudama or Kuchela), content and self-controlled despite his poverty, visits Krishna at Dvaraka carrying only a handful of flattened rice; Krishna receives him with great honour.
hinduism.explanation: The story shows that the poor man's devotion and contentment made him worthy of the highest honour despite his lack of wealth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it presents poverty as no disgrace to a person of firm character.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness, than he that is perverse in his ways, though he be rich.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb ranks an upright poor person above a rich person of crooked ways.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: integrity removes any shame from poverty.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth is not in having many possessions, but rather (true) wealth is feeling sufficiency in the soul.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that real wealth lies in inner contentment, not in property.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it relocates worth from possessions to inner strength.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot, as it is said: “You shall enjoy the fruit of your labors, you shall be happy and you shall prosper” (Psalms 128:2)”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as being content with what one has.
judaism.tie_back: This supports the Kural's view that lack of possessions does not diminish a person of firm character.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth. A trustworthy person is the best kinsman, Nibbana the highest bliss.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names contentment as the greatest wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it implies that a person rich in inner qualities is not truly poor.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami, having renounced his kingdom, tells the disguised god Indra that he lives happily owning nothing, so even the burning of his former city costs him nothing.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows that having nothing is no disgrace, and even a joy, to one of firm spiritual character.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one respects the poor man. ... Says Kabir, he alone is poor, who does not have the Naam, the Name of the Lord, in his heart.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir begins by describing how the world despises the poor and fawns on the rich. He ends by turning the word around: the only real poverty is to lack the Name of God within.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says poverty is no disgrace to one who has the inner strength of perfect character, and Kabir likewise denies that poverty of goods is real poverty for someone inwardly rich.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “... I have no time to give either to any public matter of interest or to any concern of my own, but I am in utter poverty by reason of my devotion to the god.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Socrates tells the Athenian jury that his philosophical mission has left him in complete poverty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Socrates' poverty, worn without shame, illustrates the Kural's claim that want is no disgrace to the person of real worth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Lucilius that honest poverty is not a bad thing, and that it is not the man who has too little but the man who craves more who is poor.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic argues that poverty is a matter of craving, not of possessions.
philosophy.tie_back: This supports the Kural's view that lack of wealth does not lower a person of firm character.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 2.6 (cf. tr. Richard M. Gummere)

real_life_example.event_title: Spinoza declines the Heidelberg chair and lives by grinding lenses
real_life_example.place: The Hague, Dutch Republic (now the Netherlands)
real_life_example.event: The philosopher Baruch (Benedict de) Spinoza supported himself modestly by grinding optical lenses for spectacles and microscopes. In 1673 he was offered the chair of philosophy at the University of Heidelberg, a prestigious post, and declined it because he feared he would not have full freedom to teach and think as he wished. He continued to live simply in The Hague until his death in 1677.
real_life_example.explanation: Spinoza chose a plain, modest life of independent work over position and comfort, and his modest means did nothing to lessen his standing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that poverty is no disgrace to someone with the firmness called perfect character, and Spinoza's modest circumstances never diminished the respect in which he was held.

tamil:
ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம்பெயரார் சான்றாண்மைக்கு
ஆழி எனப்படு வார்.
transliteration:
Oozhi peyarinum thaampeyaraar saandraanmaikku
aazhi enappadu vaar.
meaning: People who are called the ocean (the deep, steady home) of perfect character will not change, even if the whole world comes to an end.
elementary: A big rock on the beach stays in the same place year after year while the waves, the weather and the people all change around it. Valluvar says truly good people are like that: whatever happens around them, they stay good.
university: Oozhi (ஊழி) is the cosmic age or aeon, and its 'shifting' (peyarinum, பெயரினும், 'even if it moves') evokes the dissolution at the end of an age, when, in Indian cosmology, the seas break their bounds. Against this, those called aazhi (ஆழி) of saandraanmai do not shift (thaam peyaraar, தாம்பெயரார்). Aazhi can mean either 'ocean' or 'shore, boundary', and the commentators divide: Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi take it as ocean ('the ocean of perfection'), while Pappaiah and Kesikan, with Pope ('of perfect virtue's sea the shore'), read it as the shore that holds the sea in, an image which sharpens the contrast, since the shore holds even when the seas of the age-end overflow. Pope's line 'Who, though the fates should fail' renders oozhi loosely as fate. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads oozhi as ordinary change over time. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who is not disturbed by the incessant flow of desires – that enter like rivers into the ocean, which is ever being filled but is always still – can alone achieve peace, and not the man who strives to satisfy such desires.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares the steady sage to the ocean, which stays unmoved though rivers pour into it constantly.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same ocean image for the noble person who stays unchanged through every change.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.70 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not. He that putteth not out his money to usury, nor taketh reward against the innocent. He that doeth these things shall never be moved.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm describes the righteous person who keeps his word even at a cost and promises that he will never be moved.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it portrays the person of integrity as one who 'changeth not' and stands firm.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah" and then remained on a right course - the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve but receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises those who, having professed faith, remain steadfast on the right path.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it honours constancy of character that does not waver.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A song of ascents. Those who trust in GOD are like Mount Zion that cannot be moved, enduring forever.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist likens those who trust in God to a mountain that never moves.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it pictures the faithful as permanently steady amid change.
judaism.source: Psalm 125:1 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the wise person to a rock that the storm cannot shake.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes the perfected person as unmoved by whatever changes around them.

jainism.quote_or_event: “... difficult to attack like a lion, steady and firm like Mount Mandara, deep like the ocean, mild like the moon, refulgent like the sun, pure like excellent gold; like the earth he patiently bore everything; like a well-kindled fire he shone in his splendour.”
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra describes the houseless Mahavira through a series of similes, including the steadiness of Mount Mandara and the depth of the ocean.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's 'ocean of perfection', it pictures the perfected one as deep as the ocean and immovable as the world-mountain.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §118 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The soul becomes steady, and does not waver, by the natural inclination of the Guru's Loving Will.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the Gurmukh whose soul, attuned to the Guru's love, becomes adol, unshakable. Gurbani often praises this steadiness against the swaying of Maya and the five passions.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the ocean-like perfected do not change even when the ages shift, and Guru Amar Das likewise describes a soul made steady so that it does not waver.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 87, Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey XX, Odysseus, disguised as a beggar in his own house and enraged by the suitors' insolence, strikes his breast and tells his heart to endure, reminding it that it endured worse in the Cyclops' cave; he holds firm until the right moment.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus stays steady in purpose through twenty years of upheaval.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His steadfastness under changing fortunes echoes the Kural's noble person who does not change when the age changes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius urges himself to stand firm like a headland that the waves cannot move.
philosophy.tie_back: This is close to the Kural's image, especially in the reading of aazhi as the shore that holds while the seas surge.

real_life_example.event_title: Jan Hus refuses to recant at the Council of Constance
real_life_example.event: The Bohemian reformer Jan Hus travelled to the Council of Constance in 1414 under a safe-conduct, but was arrested soon after arriving and held in confinement. Tried as a heretic, he was repeatedly urged to recant his teachings to save his life and refused to disavow what he believed. He was condemned and put to death on 6 July 1415.
real_life_example.explanation: Hus held to his convictions even when the whole weight of the church and empire pressed on him to change.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who are an ocean of perfect character will not shift even if the ages themselves shift, and Hus would not move from his convictions even at the cost of his life.

tamil:
சான்றவர் சான்றாண்மை குன்றின் இருநிலந்தான்
தாங்காது மன்னோ பொறை.
transliteration:
Saandravar saandraanmai kundrin irunilandhaan
thaangaadhu manno porai.
meaning: If good people ever lost their goodness, even this great earth could not carry its own weight.
elementary: Imagine a big table held up by a few strong legs. If those legs get weak, everything on the table comes crashing down. Valluvar says good people are like those legs for the whole world: if they stop being good, the world cannot hold itself up.
university: The closing couplet extends saandraanmai from personal virtue to cosmic support. If the saandravar (சான்றவர், 'the perfected') should decline (kundrin, குன்றின்) in their saandraanmai, the 'great earth' (irunilam, இருநிலம்) itself could not bear (thaangaadhu, தாங்காது) its porai (பொறை, 'burden'); manno (மன்னோ) is an emphatic particle. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kesikan read porai as the earth's burden, so that the noble become, with the five pillars of Kural 983, the hidden supports of the world; Karunanidhi instead takes porai as 'patience', reading that the world would not patiently tolerate such a decline. Sivayogi Sivakumar's reading of irunilam as the 'two states' of inner and outer life is idiosyncratic. Pope: 'The mighty earth its burthen to sustain must cease, / If perfect virtue of the perfect men decrease.' The idea that the righteous sustain the world appears in many traditions, and here completes the chapter's arc from personal duty (981) to the stability of the world. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If I did not perform prescribed duties, all these worlds would be put to ruination. I would be the cause of creating unwanted population, and I would thereby destroy the peace of all living beings.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that if he, the exemplar, ceased doing his duty, the worlds would fall into ruin, since others follow the example of the great.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties the stability of the world to the continued right conduct of its noblest figures.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.24 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus calls his disciples the salt that preserves the earth and warns of what happens if they lose their quality.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the good the preservers of the world and warns of the consequences if their goodness fails.

islam.quote_or_event: “And your Lord would not have destroyed the cities unjustly while their people were reformers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says that God does not destroy communities while they contain people who work for good.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it suggests that the presence of the righteous keeps the world from ruin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And he said, “Let not my Sovereign be angry if I speak but this last time: What if ten should be found there?” “I will not destroy, for the sake of the ten,” came the reply.”
judaism.explanation: Abraham bargains with God over Sodom, and God agrees to spare the city for the sake of just ten righteous people.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows the fate of a whole community resting on a few righteous people.
judaism.source: Genesis 18:32 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, these two bright qualities guard the world. Which two? Conscience & concern. If these two bright qualities did not guard the world, there would be no recognition of 'mother' here, no recognition of 'mother's sister,' 'uncle's wife,' 'teacher's wife,' or 'wife of those who deserve respect.' ...”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that conscience and concern (hiri and ottappa) are the guardians of the world, without which social order would collapse.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the moral qualities of people are what hold the world together.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.9, Lokapala Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The most excellent twice-born men who possess these good qualities, are able to save themselves and others.”
jainism.explanation: At the end of his account of the true Brahmana, the monk Jayaghosha says that only those with real virtues can save both themselves and others.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the welfare of others depend on the virtue of the perfected few.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The mythical bull is Dharma, the son of compassion; this is what patiently holds the earth in its place. One who understands this becomes truthful. What a great load there is on the bull!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak takes the old Indian image of a bull holding up the earth and reinterprets it: what really bears the world is dharma, born of compassion. The weight of creation rests on righteousness, not on a literal animal.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the earth could not bear its burden if the noble fell short, and Japji likewise makes moral righteousness the support that keeps the earth in place.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib, Pauri 16, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Works and Days, Hesiod contrasts the city of the just, where peace, plenty and healthy children flourish under Zeus' favour, with the city of the unjust, on which Zeus sends famine, plague and ruin, so that even one wicked man can bring suffering on a whole city.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod teaches that the prosperity or ruin of a community follows the justice of its people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties the well-being of the world to the virtue of those in it.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225-247 (trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates argues that until philosophers rule, or rulers become genuine lovers of wisdom, cities and the human race will have no rest from their evils.
philosophy.explanation: Plato holds that the well-being of human society depends on the wise and good being at its centre.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the fate of the world hinge on the presence of perfected people.

real_life_example.event_title: Stanislav Petrov judges a missile alert to be a false alarm
real_life_example.place: Early-warning command centre near Moscow, Soviet Union
real_life_example.event: In the early hours of 26 September 1983, Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov was on duty at a Soviet early-warning centre when the satellite system signalled that the United States had launched intercontinental ballistic missiles. Doubting the alert, partly because only a few missiles were shown, he judged it a false alarm rather than reporting an attack, and no missiles arrived. Later investigation found that sunlight reflecting off clouds had fooled the satellites; the incident stayed secret for years.
real_life_example.explanation: The steadiness of one officer at a single moment may have prevented a catastrophe for the whole world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the great earth could not bear its burden if the noble fell short, and Petrov's sound judgement helped keep the world from a disaster it could not have borne.

tamil:
எண்பதத்தால் எய்தல் எளிதென்ப யார்மாட்டும்
பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு.
transliteration:
Enpadhaththaal eydhal elidhenpa yaarmaattum
panputaimai ennum vazhakku.
meaning: People say that being easy for anyone to approach makes it easy to gain the good way called courtesy (being polite and kind to all).
elementary: Imagine a class helper whose door is always open, who smiles at every kid, big or small, and listens. Being kind and polite is easy for that helper because they already let everyone come close. Valluvar says good manners grow out of being easy to reach.
university: The chapter on panbudaimai (பண்புடைமை, 'possession of refined character, courtesy') opens with a practical claim: the path is easy for the one who has en-padham (எண்பதம்), 'easy access', the quality of being approachable (எளிய செவ்வி) to everyone, yaar-maattum (யார்மாட்டும், 'towards whomsoever'). Puliyur Kesikan on thirukkural.net and Mu. Varadarasanar on ytamizh both gloss en-padham as எளிய செவ்வி, availability to all comers, and vazhakku (வழக்கு) as the established good path or usage; Solomon Pappaiah adds that the claim is reported, 'say the learned' (நூலோர் கூறுவர்), reflecting the verb enpa (என்ப, 'they say'). Sivayogi Sivakumar's reading of en as 'numbers' (speaking in words as plain as numerals) is an idiosyncratic minority interpretation not shared by the classical glosses. Pope renders the couplet 'Who easy access give to every man, they say, / Of kindly courtesy will learn with ease the way', and the same accessibility motif appears in the earlier kural 386 on the king who is kaatchikku eliyan (easy of audience). Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Saanraanmai (ch. 99), the chapter turns from the inner perfection of the noble to its outward social face. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant, always satisfied, self-controlled, and engaged in devotional service with determination, his mind and intelligence fixed on Me – such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the marks of the beloved devotee, beginning with being free of envy and a kindly friend (maitraḥ karuṇaḥ) to every living being.
hinduism.tie_back: Being a friend to all without exception is the same open, easy-to-reach disposition the Kural calls the easy road to courtesy.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 12.13–14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers not to hold themselves aloof but to come down to and associate with ordinary and lowly people.
christianity.tie_back: Refusing to stand on dignity and staying reachable by the lowly is exactly the 'easy access to all' that the Kural sets as the gateway to courtesy.

islam.quote_or_event: “Any of the female slaves of Medina could take hold of the hand of Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) and take him wherever she wished.”
islam.explanation: Anas reports that the Prophet was so approachable that even the humblest slave-girl of Medina could lead him by the hand to attend to her need.
islam.tie_back: This is a living picture of en-padham, the easy accessibility to anyone that the Kural says makes courtesy come naturally.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6072, Book of Good Manners (Al-Adab), chapter on pride and arrogance

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shammai used to say: make your [study of the] Torah a fixed practice; speak little, but do much; and receive all men with a pleasant countenance.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah's ethical tractate teaches that every person, without distinction, should be greeted warmly and graciously.
judaism.tie_back: Receiving all men pleasantly is the open-door manner that, in the Kural, makes the path of courtesy easy.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:15 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who is hospitable, and friendly, / Liberal and unselfish, / A guide, an instructor, a leader, / Such a one to honor may attain.”
buddhism.explanation: In the householder's code the Buddha praises the hospitable and friendly person as one who rises to honour.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes friendliness toward all the ground on which a person's refined standing is built.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Disobedient, rough speaking, ill-behaved pupils will exasperate even a gentle teacher; but those will soon win even a hot-tempered teacher who humour him and are polite.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's lecture on discipline (vinaya) contrasts rough, ill-behaved conduct with polite, accommodating manners that win over even a difficult person.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain text, like the Kural, treats easy, pleasant bearing toward others as what makes good conduct succeed.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the state of one who has found the company of the holy: no one is an enemy or an outsider any more, and he is at ease with everyone. The Sikh institutions of the open langar and the sangat put this openness into practice.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says courtesy comes easily to someone approachable by all, and Guru Arjan describes exactly that state of being on easy terms with everyone, with no one treated as a stranger.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid's tale, Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as mortals, are turned away from a thousand doors until the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon welcome them, and they alone are rewarded when the inhospitable valley is flooded.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story celebrates the humble couple whose door and hearth were open to unknown strangers.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their openness to whoever came is the same easy accessibility that the Kural treats as the doorway to true courtesy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For he will behave so alike towards those he knows and those he does not know, towards intimates and those who are not so, except that in each of these cases he will behave as is befitting.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle describes the nameless social virtue between obsequiousness and churlishness, by which a man is pleasant in the right way toward everyone he meets.
philosophy.tie_back: Treating known and unknown alike with fitting pleasantness is Aristotle's version of the Kural's courtesy toward 'whomsoever'.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.6 (tr. W. D. Ross, Internet Classics Archive)

real_life_example.event_title: King Christian X keeps up his rides through occupied Copenhagen
real_life_example.event: King Christian X of Denmark had long been in the habit of riding on horseback through the streets of Copenhagen, and after Germany occupied Denmark in April 1940 he continued the rides. Britannica notes that he rode frequently through the city during the occupation, showing that he had not given up his claim to national sovereignty. The Royal Danish Collection records that these rides created his image as the equestrian king and that many Danes still remember him riding among them during the occupation.
real_life_example.explanation: By remaining visible and within reach of ordinary citizens in a frightening time, the king became a focus of national loyalty and affection.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says courtesy comes easily to one who is easy for anyone to approach, and Christian X's accessible presence on the streets won him the lasting regard of his people.

tamil:
அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல் இவ்விரண்டும்
பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு.
transliteration:
Anputaimai aandra kutippiraththal ivvirantum
panputaimai ennum vazhakku.
meaning: Love for others and being born into a good family: these two together make up the way called courtesy.
elementary: Think of a kind heart as the seed and a good home as the garden it grows in. When a child has both a loving heart and a family that teaches good ways, gentle manners bloom. Valluvar says courtesy needs both.
university: The second couplet names the two roots of panbudaimai: anbudaimai (அன்புடைமை, 'possession of love', the title of chapter 8) and aandra kudip-piraththal (ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல், 'being born in an eminent, accomplished family'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take aandra kudi as a high or noble family, while Solomon Pappaiah reinterprets it as a family that 'lives in harmony with the world' (உலகத்தோடு ஒத்து வாழும் குடும்பம்), softening the hereditary emphasis; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as living a birth worth reflecting on. Pope's 'Benevolence and high born dignity, / These two are beaten paths of courtesy' preserves vazhakku (வழக்கு) as a 'beaten path' or established usage. The kural links this chapter back to Kudimai (ch. 96, 'Nobility of family'), which places good family upbringing at the base of character; modern readers often stress that the second element is about formation and tradition rather than caste rank. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The unsuccessful yogī, after many, many years of enjoyment on the planets of the pious living entities, is born into a family of righteous people, or into a family of rich aristocracy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna assures Arjuna that one whose spiritual effort was cut short is reborn into a righteous or noble household, where good formation can resume.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita, like the Kural, treats birth into a worthy family as a real support for refined character.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.41 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as patient and kind and as the thing that keeps a person from behaving unseemly, that is, discourteously.
christianity.tie_back: This joins the Kural's first root, love, directly to courteous behaviour, though it omits the role of family.

islam.quote_or_event: “You see that the people are of different natures. Those who were the best in the pre-lslamic period, are also the best in Islam if they comprehend religious knowledge.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares people to mines of differing quality, saying the noble-natured before Islam remain the best within it when they gain understanding.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats inherited good nature as a foundation that, joined with right understanding, yields excellence of character.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 3493, 3494 (Book of Virtues and Merits)

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the people of Israel are known by three family traits, being merciful, being bashful or modest, and performing acts of kindness, and that whoever has these traits is fit to join the people.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis define belonging to the people by inherited moral traits of compassion, modesty and kindness rather than by bloodline alone.
judaism.tie_back: It fuses the Kural's two roots, a kindly heart and the character of a worthy lineage, into one definition of a refined people.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Vasala Sutta the Buddha tells the brahmin Aggika Bharadvaja that one does not become an outcast or a brahmin by birth, but by one's deeds.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha rejects birth as the measure of worth and locates nobility entirely in conduct.
buddhism.tie_back: This stands in tension with the Kural's second root, offering a contrast: for the Buddha, kindness and conduct alone make the noble person.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By one's actions one becomes a Brâhmana, or a Kshattriya, or a Vaisya, or a Sûdra.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Gayaghosha tells a sacrificing priest that a person's station is made by deeds, not by birth.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism, like Buddhism, would ground courtesy in conduct rather than lineage, which qualifies the Kural's appeal to good birth.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Recognize the Lord's Light within all, and do not consider social class or status; there are no classes or castes in the world hereafter.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak tells his hearers to see God's light in everyone and not to ask about anyone's jaati (caste or birth status). Sikh teaching consistently refuses to treat lineage as a source of worth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural names loving kindness and birth in a worthy family as the two roots of courtesy; Guru Nanak affirms the first, in recognising God's light in all, but rejects the second, refusing to weigh anyone by birth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 349, Raag Asa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Telemachus and Pisistratus arrive at Sparta, Menelaus welcomes them before learning their names and remarks that their bearing shows they come of a line of sceptred kings, since base men could not have such sons.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, gracious and noble bearing is read as the visible mark of good birth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It reflects the Kural's assumption that a worthy family shows itself in refined manners.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle distinguishes being well-born (eugenes), the excellence of one's stock, from being noble in character (gennaios), noting that the well-born often degenerate and fail to live up to their ancestry.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle grants that good birth is a real advantage but insists it must be matched by personal excellence.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's pairing: lineage alone is insufficient unless joined to a kindly character.

real_life_example.event_title: Princess Diana shakes hands with an AIDS patient
real_life_example.event: In April 1987 Diana, Princess of Wales, opened Britain's first hospital ward dedicated to patients with HIV/AIDS, at the Middlesex Hospital in London. In front of the press she shook the hand of a patient without wearing gloves, at a time when many people wrongly believed the virus could be passed on by touch. The photograph circulated around the world and is credited with helping to challenge the stigma attached to the disease.
real_life_example.explanation: A member of the royal family used her position to show simple warmth to people who were being shunned.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says courtesy is made of loving kindness joined to birth in a worthy family, and Diana, born into an aristocratic family and married into the royal one, joined her rank to visible compassion.

tamil:
உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்றால் வெறுத்தக்க
பண்பொத்தல் ஒப்பதாம் ஒப்பு.
transliteration:
Uruppoththal makkaloppu andraal veruththakka
panpoththal oppadhaam oppu.
meaning: Having the same body parts does not make people truly alike. Being alike in good, pleasing character is the real likeness.
elementary: Two dolls can look exactly the same on the outside, but one might be stuffed with cotton and the other with sharp pins. People are like that too: having two eyes and two hands like someone does not make you like them. Being kind like them does.
university: Uruppu-oththal (உறுப்பொத்தல், 'sameness of limbs') is denied the status of makkal-oppu (மக்களொப்பு, 'likeness among humans'); true oppu is panb-oththal (பண்பொத்தல்), likeness in qualities. The crux is veruththakka (வெறுத்தக்க): Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as 'fit to be joined' (பொருந்தத்தக்க), Solomon Pappaiah as qualities that unite heart with heart, and Pope as 'kindred quality' ('Similitude of kindred quality makes likeness true'), reflecting the older commentarial reading of வெறு as 'to be close, to cohere'. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads it in the modern sense 'hateful', yielding 'likeness in shunning what deserves shunning', a minority interpretation. Kalaignar draws the strong conclusion that only those alike in good qualities deserve to be counted as human at all, which anticipates kural 997. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, in this world there are two kinds of created beings. One is called divine and the other demoniac. I have already explained to you at length the divine qualities. Now hear from Me of the demoniac.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna divides human beings not by appearance or birth but by whether they bear divine or demonic qualities.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it classes people by their qualities rather than their bodily sameness.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.6 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
christianity.explanation: When Samuel is impressed by Eliab's looks, God tells him that the true measure of a person is the heart, not the body.
christianity.tie_back: This sets aside outward bodily form in favour of inner character, as the Kural does.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that appearance and possessions count for nothing before God compared with the heart and actions.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, a person's real identity lies in qualities and deeds, not in the shape of the face or body.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 2564c (Book of Virtue, Enjoining Good Manners)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi said: don’t look at the container but at that which is in it: there is a new container full of old wine, and an old [container] in which there is not even new [wine].”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince warns that outward vessels deceive and that worth lies in what they hold.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's point is the same: the body is a container, and true likeness lies in the qualities within.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:20 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Vasettha Sutta the Buddha explains that grasses, insects, animals, fish and birds show distinct marks of species by birth, but among human beings there are no such distinguishing bodily marks; distinctions among humans are only by name, and a person is what his deeds make him.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha argues that human bodies are basically alike, so the real differences between people must lie in conduct.
buddhism.tie_back: This is close to the Kural's argument: bodily sameness is shared by all, and what truly distinguishes or unites people is their qualities.
buddhism.source: Vasettha Sutta, Sutta Nipata 3.9 (also Majjhima Nikaya 98)

jainism.quote_or_event: “One does not become a Sramana by the tonsure, nor a Brâhmana by the sacred syllable ôm, nor a Muni by living in the woods, nor a Tâpasa by wearing (clothes of) Kusa-grass and bark. One becomes a Sramana by equanimity, a Brâhmana by chastity, a Muni by knowledge, and a Tâpasa by penance.”
jainism.explanation: Gayaghosha teaches that outward marks such as a shaven head or bark clothing do not make a monk or sage; only the inner qualities do.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it rejects outward resemblance as the measure of a person and locates true likeness in character.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.31–32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you are indeed a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother, then why didn't you come by some other way?”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir mocks the claim of birth-superiority by pointing out that every human body comes into the world in the same way. Bodily sameness proves nobody is higher, and what distinguishes people has to lie elsewhere.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says sameness of limbs does not make people truly alike and that real likeness is likeness of character, and Kabir likewise treats the shared body as settling nothing about a person's worth.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 324, Raag Gauri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Circe turns Odysseus' companions into swine, they take on the heads, voices and bristles of pigs, yet their minds remain as before, and they weep in their sties.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer imagines bodies changed into beasts while the human mind stays intact.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The myth makes the Kural's point from the other side: what makes someone human is not the shape of the limbs but what is within.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He lit a lamp in broad daylight and said, as he went about, ‘I am looking for a man.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes the Cynic mocked the crowds of Athens by implying that among all the human bodies around him he could not find a true human being.
philosophy.tie_back: Diogenes dramatizes the Kural's claim that sharing the human form does not make one truly human.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.41 (tr. R. D. Hicks, via Wikisource)

real_life_example.event_title: Albert Einstein gives Marian Anderson a room when a hotel refuses her
real_life_example.event: After the African American contralto Marian Anderson sang at the McCarter Theatre in Princeton on 16 April 1937, the town's Nassau Inn refused her a room because of her race. Albert Einstein, who had attended the concert, invited her to stay at his home instead. The two became friends, and on later visits to Princeton she stayed with Einstein until his death in 1955.
real_life_example.explanation: Einstein saw in Anderson a kindred spirit and an artist he admired, and treated the colour line that the hotel enforced as meaningless.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that real likeness between people lies in shared qualities of character rather than in bodily sameness, and the friendship between the physicist and the singer rested on exactly such kinship.

tamil:
நயனொடு நன்றி புரிந்த பயனுடையார்
பண்புபா ராட்டும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Nayanotu nandri purindha payanutaiyaar
panpupaa raattum ulaku.
meaning: The world praises the character of people who are useful to others because they are fair and do good.
elementary: When a kid is fair in games and also helps others when they fall, everyone on the playground says, 'She's so nice!' Valluvar says people love and praise those who are both fair and helpful.
university: The couplet pairs nayan (நயன், 'justice, equity, fairness') with nanri (நன்றி, 'beneficence, doing good'), and calls those who 'cherish' (purindha, புரிந்த) both payan-udaiyaar (பயனுடையார்), people who are of real use to others. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the pair as நீதியும் நன்மையும், Pappaiah as நீதியும் அறமும், and Pope's prose 'equity and charity' follows the same traditional line. The result is that ulagu (உலகு, 'the world', i.e. the discerning public) 'praises' (paaraattum, பாராட்டும்) their panbu. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes nayan as conduct that gives delight, a looser reading. The kural shows that courtesy in Valluvar is not mere politeness of speech but includes just and beneficial action. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Whatever action a great man performs, common men follow. And whatever standards he sets by exemplary acts, all the world pursues.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that the conduct of an exemplary person becomes the standard the whole world follows.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes the world responding to the visible good conduct of the worthy, though as imitation rather than praise.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.21 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers that their good deeds, seen by others, will lead people to give glory.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's world that praises the useful and good finds an echo here, though the glory is directed to God.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression. He admonishes you that perhaps you will be reminded.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an commands both justice ('adl) and excellent good conduct (ihsan) together.
islam.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's pairing of nayan and nanri, justice joined with beneficence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart: So shalt thou find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs promises that one who holds fast to kindness and faithfulness will win favour with both God and people.
judaism.tie_back: Kindness and truth winning the favour of men is close to the Kural's justice and goodness winning the world's praise.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “People hold dear him who embodies virtue and insight, who is principled, has realized the truth, and who himself does what he ought to be doing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that people cherish the one who is virtuous, principled and does his duty.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the world's affection and esteem follow genuine virtue in action.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 217 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “An intelligent man who has learned (the sacred texts) takes his duties upon himself, and he becomes renowned in the world; as the earth is the dwelling of all beings, so he will be a dwelling of all duties.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline says the conscientious disciple who shoulders his duties becomes famous and supports others as the earth supports all beings.
jainism.tie_back: Renown that comes from bearing duties for others is close to the Kural's praise for those who are useful through justice and goodness.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.45 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak places seva, selfless service done in the middle of ordinary life, at the centre of the Sikh path and promises it honour before God. Service of others is the Sikh form of being useful to the world.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the world praises those who are useful to others through justice and beneficence, and Guru Nanak likewise promises honour to those who serve in the midst of the world.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Disguised as a beggar, Odysseus tells Penelope that her fame reaches heaven like that of a blameless king who upholds justice, under whom the land bears fruit and the people prosper.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer links just rule and the flourishing it brings with wide renown.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's world praising those whose justice benefits others is reflected in this image of the just king's fame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that people's affection and esteem are won above all by kindness and generosity, and their confidence by a reputation for justice, so that justice joined with beneficence is the surest path to true glory.
philosophy.explanation: In his treatise on duties Cicero analyses how goodwill and glory are earned, naming beneficence and justice as the chief means.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero's analysis closely matches the Kural's claim that justice and doing good win the world's praise.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis II.9–11 and II.32–38

real_life_example.event_title: Wangari Maathai receives the Nobel Peace Prize
real_life_example.place: Oslo, Norway, for work in Kenya
real_life_example.event: Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement in Kenya in 1977, organising women to plant tens of millions of trees while campaigning against deforestation, poverty and abuses of power. On 8 October 2004 the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded her the Nobel Peace Prize for her contribution to sustainable development, democracy and peace. She was the first African woman to receive the prize.
real_life_example.explanation: Maathai's honour came from work that combined practical benefit to ordinary people with a stubborn defence of fairness and good government.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world praises the character of those who are useful to others through love of justice and doing good, and the Nobel committee honoured Maathai for exactly that combination.

tamil:
நகையுள்ளும் இன்னா திகழ்ச்சி பகையுள்ளும்
பண்புள பாடறிவார் மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Nakaiyullum innaa thikazhchchi pakaiyullum
panpula paadarivaar maattu.
meaning: Making fun of someone hurts, even as a joke. So people who understand others stay polite even toward their enemies.
elementary: Calling someone a silly name 'just for fun' can still make them cry inside. Kids who really understand feelings don't do it, not even to a kid they're cross with. Valluvar says being polite even to someone you don't like is a sign of real wisdom.
university: The first line states a psychological fact: igazhchi (இகழ்ச்சி, 'contempt, ridicule') is innaa (இன்னா, 'painful') even within nagai (நகை, 'laughter, jest'). The second draws the ethical conclusion: among paadarivaar (பாடறிவார், 'those who know the nature or proper manner', from பாடு, 'way, condition'), panbu remains even within pagai (பகை, 'enmity'). Mu. Varadarasanar reads the paadarivaar as those who act knowing others' nature; Pappaiah expands that such people do not ridicule even foes; Pope renders 'Contempt is evil though in sport. They who man's nature know, / E'en in their wrath, a courteous mind will show.' The jingle nagaiyullum ... pagaiyullum binds jest and enmity as the two tests of courtesy. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita defines the discipline of speech as words that are true and pleasant and that do not disturb others' minds.
hinduism.tie_back: Speech that never agitates another rules out the hurtful jest the Kural warns against.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs compares the one who harms a neighbour and then says he was only joking to a madman throwing deadly arrows.
christianity.tie_back: This is a near one-to-one match for the Kural's warning that ridicule wounds even in jest.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people; perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule [other] women; perhaps they may be better than them. And do not insult one another and do not call each other by [offensive] nicknames.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an forbids mocking, insulting and name-calling, reminding the mocker that the mocked may be better than he.
islam.tie_back: It directly forbids the ridicule that the Kural says hurts even when meant as fun.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone who humiliates another in public, it is as though he were spilling blood.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud teaches that shaming someone so that the blood drains from his face is comparable to bloodshed.
judaism.tie_back: The rabbis, like Valluvar, treat the wound of contempt as real injury, not a harmless matter.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak not harshly to anyone, for those thus spoken to might retort. Indeed, angry speech hurts, and retaliation may overtake you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that harsh speech wounds others and breeds retaliation.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's insight that wounding words, toward anyone at all, cause real pain.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 133 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not tell anything sinful or meaningless or hurtful, neither for his own sake nor for anybody else's, nor without such a motive.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline forbids hurtful speech for any reason, including speech with no motive at all.
jainism.tie_back: Ruling out hurtful words even 'without a motive' covers the idle or joking ridicule the Kural condemns.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all. Do not break anyone’s heart; these are all priceless jewels.”
sikhism.explanation: Farid's saloks forbid even one harsh word because God lives in every person, and call every heart a priceless jewel that must not be broken. The next salok repeats that harming anyone's mind is never good.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that mockery hurts even in jest and so the wise keep courtesy even toward enemies, and Farid likewise forbids any wounding word to anyone, since God dwells in all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, salok 129 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Thersites jeers at Agamemnon to make the Greek soldiers laugh, and Odysseus beats him with the sceptre while the army laughs at him in turn.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's portrait of Thersites shows mockery used for laughter that ends in humiliation and pain.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode illustrates the Kural's warning that ridicule, even when aimed at a laugh, wounds and breeds hostility.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Those who carry humour to excess are thought to be vulgar buffoons, striving after humour at all costs, and aiming rather at raising a laugh than at saying what is becoming and at avoiding pain to the object of their fun.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle condemns the buffoon whose jokes ignore the pain they cause their target, and praises tactful wit.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle names exactly the Kural's concern: a joke that wounds its object is a failure of good character.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.8 (tr. W. D. Ross, Internet Classics Archive)

real_life_example.event_title: Australian airmen bury the Red Baron with full military honours
real_life_example.event: Manfred von Richthofen, Germany's most famous fighter pilot, known as the Red Baron, was shot down and killed over the Somme on 21 April 1918. The next day men of No. 3 Squadron, Australian Flying Corps, buried him in the cemetery at Bertangles with full military honours: men of the squadron fired a volley over the grave, and wreaths sent by British squadrons were laid on it. The Australian War Memorial holds film and photographs of the funeral.
real_life_example.explanation: In the middle of a bitter war, his enemies chose to honour a fallen opponent rather than celebrate over him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who understand people keep their courtesy even toward enemies, and the Australian airmen showed respect to the enemy airman who had shot down so many of their comrades.

tamil:
பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம் அதுஇன்றேல்
மண்புக்கு மாய்வது மன்.
transliteration:
Panputaiyaarp pattuntu ulakam adhuindrel
manpukku maaivadhu man.
meaning: The world keeps going because good-mannered people live in it. Without them, it would sink into the earth and die away.
elementary: A tent stands up because of its poles. Take the poles away and the whole tent falls flat on the ground. Valluvar says kind, well-mannered people are the poles that hold up the whole world.
university: Ulagam (உலகம்) here means the ongoing life of human society; it 'exists' (undu, உண்டு) because it is pattu (பட்டு, 'resting upon, attached to') the panbudaiyaar (பண்புடையார், 'people of character'). Without that support it would man-pukku maaivadhu (மண்புக்கு மாய்வது), 'enter the earth and perish', the final man (மன்) being an emphatic particle. Mu.
