Varadarasanar glosses pattu as 'by being joined to' the courteous; Kalaignar reads ulagam as 'the conduct of the world'; Pope's prose 'The (way of the) world subsists by contact with the good' follows the traditional line. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes the second line very differently, as 'even supplication would be meaningless', which departs from the classical gloss of man-pukku as 'entering the soil'. The kural echoes kural 571 on kannottam, where the world exists through the gracious. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If I did not perform prescribed duties, all these worlds would be put to ruination. I would be the cause of creating unwanted population, and I would thereby destroy the peace of all living beings.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that if he ceased to act rightly as an example, the worlds would fall into ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties the survival of the world to right conduct, though here the support is divine rather than courteous people.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.24 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the LORD said, If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare all the place for their sakes.”
christianity.explanation: God tells Abraham that a city may be preserved from destruction for the sake of the righteous within it.
christianity.tie_back: The idea that the good keep a whole community from perishing is close to the Kural's image of the world resting on the courteous.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if it were not for Allah checking [some] people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted, but Allah is full of bounty to the worlds.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches that God uses some people to restrain others, and that without this the earth would be ruined.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that the world is kept from ruin through the action of good people.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shimon the Righteous was one of the last of the men of the great assembly. He used to say: the world stands upon three things: the Torah, the Temple service, and the practice of acts of piety.”
judaism.explanation: One of the founding sayings of rabbinic ethics names acts of loving-kindness (gemilut hasadim) as one of the pillars on which the world stands.
judaism.tie_back: The image of the world 'standing upon' kindly conduct is the same as the Kural's world resting on people of good character.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:2 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Generosity, sweet speech, / Helpfulness to others, / Impartiality to all, / As the case demands. / These four winning ways make the world go round, / As the linchpin in a moving car.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's four bases of social harmony (sangaha-vatthu), generosity, kind speech, helpfulness and impartiality, are said to keep the world turning like a linchpin.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's claim: courtesy and kindness are what hold the world together.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The most excellent twice-born men who possess these good qualities, are able to save themselves and others.”
jainism.explanation: Gayaghosha concludes that those who truly possess the virtues he has described can rescue not only themselves but others too.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain text, like the Kural, sees people of real virtue as the ones on whom others' welfare depends.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That mortal who renounces possessiveness, greed, emotional attachment and egotism - says Nanak, he himself is saved, and he saves many others as well.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur teaches that the person who conquers ego and greed does not stop at their own freedom but becomes a means of others' deliverance too. In Sikh thought the Gurmukh's goodness steadies and uplifts those around them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the world keeps going because it rests on people of good character, and Guru Tegh Bahadur likewise describes the selfless person as one who carries many others with them.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9, salok 22, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And then Aidos and Nemesis, with their sweet forms wrapped in white robes, will go from the wide-pathed earth and forsake mankind to join the company of the deathless gods: and bitter sorrows will be left for mortal men, and there will be no help against evil.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod foresees that when the goddesses of shame and righteous indignation abandon humanity, nothing will remain to protect people from ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hesiod imagines a world that collapses once decency and right feeling depart.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 197–201 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White; sacred-texts.com)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Zeus feared that the entire race would be exterminated, and so he sent Hermes to them, bearing reverence and justice to be the ordering principles of cities and the bonds of friendship and conciliation.”
philosophy.explanation: In Protagoras' myth, humans gathered in cities begin to destroy each other until Zeus gives them reverence and justice as the bonds of social life.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis in mythic form: without the qualities of refined character, human society would perish.
philosophy.source: Plato, Protagoras 322c (tr. Benjamin Jowett, Internet Classics Archive)

real_life_example.event_title: Gander shelters the passengers of 38 diverted airliners
real_life_example.event: When United States airspace closed after the attacks of 11 September 2001, 38 airliners carrying roughly 6,600 passengers and crew were diverted to Gander, Newfoundland, a town of about 10,000 people. Schools, churches and halls were turned into shelters, residents took strangers into their own homes, and local businesses and volunteers supplied food, clothing and medicines for several days until flights resumed. The town was later formally thanked by the United States for its help.
real_life_example.explanation: Ordinary people's kindness to strangers held things together at a moment when the world seemed to be coming apart.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world keeps going because it rests on people of courteous character, and the people of Gander showed how much a frightened world depends on such people.

tamil:
அரம்போலும் கூர்மைய ரேனும் மரம்போல்வர்
மக்கட்பண்பு இல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Arampolum koormaiya renum marampolvar
makkatpanpu illaa thavar.
meaning: People without good human qualities are no better than trees, even if their minds are as sharp as a file (a metal tool for sharpening).
elementary: A pencil sharpener is very sharp, but it can't give you a hug or say sorry. Valluvar says a person can be super clever, but if they aren't kind they are like a tree trunk: standing there, but not really acting like a person.
university: The couplet plays on the rhyme aram (அரம், 'file, rasp') and maram (மரம், 'tree'): those who lack makkat-panbu (மக்கட்பண்பு, 'the quality proper to human beings') are 'like trees' even if they have a file's koormai (கூர்மை, 'sharpness'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both gloss maram as ஓரறிவுயிர், 'a one-sensed being', invoking the classical Tamil (and Jain) grading of living beings by the number of their senses, so the insult is precise: an intellect without humanity sinks to the lowest rung of life. Pope renders 'Though sharp their wit as file, as blocks they must remain, / Whose souls are void of courtesy humane'. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads aram as a sharp cutting tool and makkat-panbu as 'humanitarianism'. The kural extends the argument of 993 from likeness to humanity itself. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A well-known verse in the introduction to the Hitopadesha says that eating, sleeping, fear and mating are common to humans and animals; dharma alone is what sets humans apart, and those lacking it are equal to beasts.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit fable collection teaches that what makes a human being more than an animal is moral character, not bodily functions or cleverness.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a person without the qualities proper to humans is reduced to a lower form of life.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that even the greatest knowledge and gifts count for nothing without love.
christianity.tie_back: A mind sharp enough to know all mysteries but empty of love is the Kural's sharp file that is still only a tree.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an likens those who carry knowledge without living by it to a donkey loaded with books.
islam.tie_back: The image of a beast carrying learning it does not embody parallels the Kural's sharp-witted person who is still like a tree.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He used to say: one whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, to what may he be compared? To a tree whose branches are numerous but whose roots are few, so that when the wind comes, it uproots it and overturns it.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah compares the person whose learning outstrips his conduct to a tree that topples in the wind.
judaism.tie_back: By a striking coincidence of imagery, it too likens wisdom without goodness to a tree.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that learning recited but not lived brings no real benefit.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats knowledge cut off from good conduct as empty.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 19 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Acknowledging the truth about bondage and liberation, but talking only, not acting (in accordance with these tenets), they seek comfort for themselves in mighty words. Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it? Fools, though sinking lower and lower through their sins, believe themselves to be wise men.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira rejects those who rely on clever talk and doctrine while failing to act rightly, calling them fools who think themselves wise.
jainism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's sharp-minded person who lacks the conduct that makes one truly human.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 6.9–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He acts like a beast, and does not understand anything. Practicing falsehood, he becomes false.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the manmukh, the self-willed person, as living at the level of an animal despite being human, because he lacks the understanding that makes human life worthwhile. Gurbani often uses the image of the beast for a human life emptied of its proper quality.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those without humane qualities are no better than trees however sharp their minds, and Guru Amar Das likewise says that a person without true understanding sinks to the level of a beast.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1132, Raag Bhairao, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Homer describes the Cyclopes as lawless and overbearing beings who hold no assemblies and have no laws, each ruling his own family without regard for others; Polyphemus later scorns the guest-right of Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Cyclopes are powerful and capable, yet lack the social and moral qualities of civilized humans.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They embody the Kural's being who has capacity but lacks the qualities that make one fully human.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For man, when perfected, is the best of animals, but, when separated from law and justice, he is the worst of all; since armed injustice is the more dangerous, and he is equipped at birth with arms, meant to be used by intelligence and virtue, which he may use for the worst ends.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that human intelligence without virtue makes man not the best but the worst and most savage of animals.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle says that a sharp intellect without humane virtue sinks a person below the human.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics I.2, 1253a (tr. Benjamin Jowett, Internet Classics Archive)

real_life_example.event_title: Fritz Haber, Nobel chemist, directs the first chlorine gas attack
real_life_example.event: The German chemist Fritz Haber developed a practical method of synthesising ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, the basis of modern nitrogen fertiliser, and received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. During the First World War he also led Germany's development of poison gas and supervised its first large-scale use, the chlorine attack at Ypres on 22 April 1915. After the war he was widely criticised, and in some circles shunned, for his part in chemical warfare.
real_life_example.explanation: Haber's career shows that outstanding intellectual brilliance and humane judgement are different things, and that the first does not guarantee the second.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those without humane qualities are no better than trees even if their minds are as sharp as a file, and Haber's brilliance did not prevent him from turning science to the mass killing of soldiers.

tamil:
நண்பாற்றார் ஆகி நயமில செய்வார்க்கும்
பண்பாற்றார் ஆதல் கடை.
transliteration:
Nanpaatraar aaki nayamila seyvaarkkum
panpaatraar aadhal katai.
meaning: Even toward people who are unfriendly and do us wrong, failing to be polite is the lowest thing a person can do.
elementary: If a classmate keeps being mean to you, it is tempting to be mean back. But Valluvar says the really strong thing is to stay polite anyway. Being rude back would make you lose something precious of your own.
university: The couplet carries the chapter's ethic to its hardest case. Nanb-aatraar (நண்பாற்றார்) are those who 'do not practise friendship', and nayam-ila seyvaar (நயமில செய்வார்) those who 'do unpleasant, unjust things'; even toward them, to be panb-aatraar (பண்பாற்றார், 'not practising courtesy') is kadai (கடை), 'the lowest, the worst'. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it as a disgrace (இழிவு) to abandon courtesy in the face of hostility; Kalaignar adds patience (பொறுமை) as the means. Pope's 'Though men with all unfriendly acts and wrongs assail, / 'Tis uttermost disgrace in courtesy to fail' captures the parallel of nanbaatraar ... panbaatraar. The kural echoes kural 314 on 'shaming' wrongdoers by doing them good. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is equal to friends and enemies, who is equipoised in honor and dishonor, heat and cold, happiness and distress, fame and infamy, who is always free from contaminating association, always silent and satisfied with anything, who doesn’t care for any residence, who is fixed in knowledge and who is engaged in devotional service – such a person is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna praises the devotee who treats friend and enemy alike and stays steady under insult.
hinduism.tie_back: Even-mindedness toward enemies parallels the Kural's demand to keep courtesy toward the hostile.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 12.18–19 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus commands active goodwill toward enemies and those who mistreat us.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's teaching in its strongest form: answer hostility with goodness, not rudeness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an instructs believers to answer evil with something better, promising that enmity may turn into friendship.
islam.tie_back: Answering the unfriendly with good conduct is exactly what the Kural asks.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs commands kindness to an enemy in need, promising divine reward.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it requires generous, decent conduct toward those who are hostile.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that only non-hatred, not retaliation, can end enmity.
buddhism.tie_back: Refusing to return hostility for hostility is the inner basis of the Kural's courtesy toward the unfriendly.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 5 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a layman abuses a monk, he should not grow angry against him; because he would be like a child, a monk should not grow angry. If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
jainism.explanation: Among the twenty-two hardships a monk must bear is abuse (akrosa), which he must meet without anger, overlooking cruel words.
jainism.tie_back: This Jain discipline of bearing abuse without retaliation closely matches the Kural's refusal to abandon courtesy toward the hostile.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.24–25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Farid, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
sikhism.explanation: Farid tells the devotee not to strike back even at someone who has struck him, but to answer with a gesture of humility and go home in peace. The Gurus kept this teaching in the scripture as a model of courtesy toward the hostile.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls it the lowest disgrace to fail in courtesy even toward the unfriendly and those who wrong us, and Farid asks for exactly that courtesy, even toward someone using his fists.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, salok 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Returning home disguised as a beggar, Odysseus endures insults, kicks and thrown stools from the goatherd Melanthius and the suitors in his own hall, holding back his anger until the time for vengeance.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus shows great restraint under abuse, though his patience is strategic and ends in slaughter.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His restraint resembles the Kural's composure before the hostile, but his aim is revenge rather than courtesy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates, awaiting execution, insists that no wrong, however grave, justifies doing wrong in return.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the philosophical core of the Kural's teaching that courtesy must hold even toward those who wrong us.
philosophy.source: Plato, Crito 49c (tr. Benjamin Jowett, Internet Classics Archive)

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi gives Jan Smuts a pair of sandals he made himself
real_life_example.event: In South Africa Mohandas Gandhi led years of nonviolent campaigns against laws enforced by the government in which Jan Smuts was a leading minister, and he was jailed several times. Before leaving South Africa in 1914 Gandhi gave Smuts a pair of sandals he had made with his own hands. Smuts kept them for many years, and in 1939, writing for Gandhi's seventieth birthday, he said he had worn them for many summers and did not feel worthy to stand in the shoes of so great a man.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi treated his chief political opponent with personal courtesy and kindness, and the opponent came to respond with respect.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that failing in courtesy even toward those who are unfriendly and do us wrong is the lowest disgrace, and Gandhi kept his courtesy toward the minister whose government had imprisoned him.

tamil:
நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்க்கு மாயிரு ஞாலம்
பகலும்பாற் பட்டன்று இருள்.
transliteration:
Nakalvallar allaarkku maayiru gnaalam
pakalumpaar pattandru irul.
meaning: For people who cannot enjoy friendly, cheerful company, this huge wide world is dark even in the middle of the day.
elementary: Imagine a sunny day at the park, but you won't play, laugh, or talk with anyone. Even with the sun shining, it would feel gloomy. Valluvar says a heart that can't smile and join in makes the whole world feel dark.
university: Nagal vallar allaar (நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்) are 'those not able to laugh', that is, unable to mix with others and share friendly cheer; for them maa-iru gnaalam (மாயிரு ஞாலம், 'the great, vast earth') is, even by day (pagalum), fallen into darkness (paal patta-andru irul, பாற்பட்டன்று இருள்). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses nagal as 'mingling with others and rejoicing' (பிறரோடு கலந்து பழகி மகிழ), Pappaiah ties it explicitly to lack of good character, and Kalaignar to inability to enjoy friends; Pope's prose 'To those who cannot rejoice, the wide world is buried darkness even in (broad) day light' follows this line. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads nagal as 'harmonizing with others' and iru as 'two-fold', an idiosyncratic segmentation. The transliteration of gnaalam varies across sites (Gnaalam on ytamizh, ñālam on thirukkural.net). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not connected with the Supreme [in Kṛṣṇa consciousness] can have neither transcendental intelligence nor a steady mind, without which there is no possibility of peace. And how can there be any happiness without peace?”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that without an inner connection there is no peace, and without peace no happiness.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say that the lack of an inner quality turns life joyless, though the Gita's missing quality is spiritual connection rather than sociable cheer.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.66 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the gloom of the downcast with the cheerful heart that makes every day a feast.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the inner capacity for cheer colours the whole world, turning days to gloom or feast.

islam.quote_or_event: “Your smiling in the face of your brother is charity, commanding good and forbidding evil is charity, your giving directions to a man lost in the land is charity for you.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet counts a smile offered to another as an act of charity.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural's high regard for warm, smiling sociability as a moral good.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They said to him: We are jesters, and we cheer up the depressed. Alternatively, when we see two people who have a quarrel between them, we strive to make peace.”
judaism.explanation: Elijah points out two jesters in the marketplace as destined for the World to Come because they bring cheer to the sad and make peace.
judaism.tie_back: The Talmud prizes the very capacity for shared laughter that the Kural says keeps the world from darkness.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 22a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dhammapada the Buddha's disciples declare that they live happily, possessing nothing, and will feed on joy like the Radiant Gods.
buddhism.explanation: The verse celebrates a joy (piti) that does not depend on possessions.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's sense that joy lights up life, though Buddhist joy is inward and ascetic rather than social.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though emaciated like the joint of a crow's (leg) and covered with a network of veins, he should know the permitted measure of food and drink, and wander about with a cheerful mind.”
jainism.explanation: Even when worn thin by fasting, the Jain monk is told to go about with a cheerful mind.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain stress on cheerfulness in all conditions touches the Kural's point that a joyless mind darkens life, though without its social dimension.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns appeared, even with such light, there would still be pitch darkness without the Guru.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad says that no amount of outer light can lift the darkness of a life without the Guru. Outward brightness and inner darkness can exist together.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the wide world lies in darkness even by day for those who cannot share in friendly cheer, and Guru Angad's verse uses the same paradox of darkness in the midst of light.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 2, Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A long time she sat upon the stool without speaking because of her sorrow, and greeted no one by word or by sign, but rested, never smiling, and tasting neither food nor drinks because she pined with longing for her deep-bosomed daughter, until careful Iambe -- who pleased her moods in aftertime also -- moved the holy lady with many a quip and jest to smile and laugh and cheer her heart.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The grieving Demeter, who has withdrawn from all company, is drawn back into life by Iambe's jokes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Demeter's unsmiling isolation and the light that returns with laughter dramatize the Kural's image of a world dark without shared cheer.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter 198–204 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White; sacred-texts.com)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “While those who can neither make a joke themselves nor put up with those who do are thought to be boorish and unpolished.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle calls the person who can neither joke nor bear joking boorish, lacking a social virtue needed for good company.
philosophy.tie_back: This is Aristotle's name for the Kural's nagal vallar allaar, those unable to share in laughter.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.8 (tr. W. D. Ross, Internet Classics Archive)

real_life_example.event_title: The Christmas Truce on the Western Front
real_life_example.place: Western Front, Belgium and northern France
real_life_example.event: Late on Christmas Eve 1914, British troops in parts of the Western Front heard German soldiers in the opposite trenches singing carols and saw lanterns and small trees along their parapets. On Christmas Day men from both sides walked out into no man's land, exchanged food, tobacco and souvenirs, took photographs, buried their dead and in places played impromptu football. The truces were unofficial and uneven, fighting continued elsewhere, and there was no comparable truce later in the war.
real_life_example.explanation: For a brief moment, sharing simple good cheer with the enemy lifted some of the darkness of the war for the men in the trenches.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those unable to share friendly cheer the wide world is dark even in daylight, and the truce showed the reverse: shared cheer brought light into one of history's darkest settings.

tamil:
பண்பிலான் பெற்ற பெருஞ்செல்வம் நன்பால்
கலந்தீமை யால்திரிந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Panpilaan petra perunjelvam nanpaal
kalandheemai yaaldhirin thatru.
meaning: Great riches that come to a person without good manners are like good milk spoiled by a dirty pot.
elementary: Pour fresh milk into a dirty cup and it turns sour and yucky. Valluvar says money is like that milk: if it goes to a rude, unkind person, it turns sour and does nobody any good.
university: The chapter closes with a domestic simile: the perum-selvam (பெருஞ்செல்வம், 'great wealth') of the panbilaan (பண்பிலான், 'man without courtesy') is like nan-paal (நன்பால், 'good milk') that has 'turned' (thirindhu, திரிந்து) through kalam-theemai (கலந்தீமை, 'defect of the vessel'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read kalan as the container (கலம், பாத்திரம்), Kalaignar specifying a vessel coated with verdigris (களிம்பு); Pope's verse 'Like sweet milk soured because in filthy vessel poured' agrees, while his prose 'will perish like pure milk spoilt by the impurity of the vessel' stresses waste. The segmentation kalan + theemai, rather than kalandhu + theemai ('mixed with evil'), is the standard one; Sivayogi Sivakumar's 'by the evil mixed with it' reflects the alternative split. The kural also bridges to the next chapter, Nanriyil Selvam (ch. 101, 'Useless wealth'). Transliterations differ slightly (yaaldhirinh thatru on ytamizh; yaaldhirin thatru on thirukkural.net), but the Tamil text is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The demoniac person thinks: “So much wealth do I have today, and I will gain more according to my schemes. So much is mine now, and it will increase in the future, more and more. He is my enemy, and I have killed him, and my other enemies will also be killed. I am the lord of everything. I am the enjoyer. I am perfect, powerful and happy. I am the richest man, surrounded by aristocratic relatives. There is none so powerful and happy as I am. I shall perform sacrifices, I shall give some charity, and thus I shall rejoice.” In this way, such persons are deluded by ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna depicts how wealth in the hands of a person of demonic character feeds arrogance, enmity and delusion.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows riches turning to evil in a person without good character.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.13–15 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus' parable warns that a good substance poured into an unfit container is lost along with the container.
christianity.tie_back: It shares the Kural's image of a good thing ruined by an unfit vessel, though Jesus applies it to his new teaching.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders or injury as does one who spends his wealth [only] to be seen by the people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His example is like that of a [large] smooth stone upon which is dust and is hit by a downpour that leaves it bare.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an warns that wealth given with insult or for show is washed away, leaving nothing of value.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows the good of wealth spoiled by the giver's ungracious character.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes observes that wealth can be hoarded only to harm its owner.
judaism.tie_back: This shares the Kural's insight that riches can turn bad in the wrong hands.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Riches ruin only the foolish, not those in quest of the Beyond. By craving for riches the witless man ruins himself as well as others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that wealth destroys the foolish but not the wise.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, whether wealth is good or ruinous depends on the character of its holder.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 355 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.” … “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that wealth gained or held without right conduct is lost and brings no protection.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows wealth becoming useless and ruinous when held by one lacking good character.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.2 and 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Wash the vessel, sit down and anoint it with fragrance; then, go out and get the milk. Add the rennet of clear consciousness to the milk of good deeds, and then, free of desire, let it curdle.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak takes the household work of setting milk to curd as an image of the spiritual life: the vessel, the inner self, must be cleaned first, or the milk of good deeds will not set into anything good.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says great wealth in the hands of a discourteous person is like good milk spoiled by an unclean vessel, and Guru Nanak uses the very same image of a clean vessel needed before good milk can turn out well.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 728, Raag Suhi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Granted his wish that everything he touched would turn to gold, King Midas finds that his food and drink become metal in his mouth, so that his great wealth becomes a curse until he begs to be released from it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas' foolish greed turns the gift of riches into something that cannot nourish him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like milk spoiled in a bad vessel, wealth in the hands of the unwise turns from blessing to curse.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Sincerum est nisi uas, quodcumque infundis acescit.”
philosophy.explanation: Horace tells Lollius that unless the vessel is clean, whatever you pour into it turns sour, meaning that possessions and pleasures cannot benefit a corrupted mind.
philosophy.tie_back: Horace uses the very same image as the Kural, a good liquid spoiled by an impure vessel, to say that wealth is wasted on a flawed character.
philosophy.source: Horace, Epistles 1.2.54 (Latin text, The Latin Library)

real_life_example.event_title: Leona Helmsley is convicted of tax evasion
real_life_example.event: The hotel and property billionaire Leona Helmsley was tried in federal court in New York in 1989, and many of the witnesses were her own former employees, whose testimony portrayed her as harsh and abusive toward staff. On 30 August 1989 she was convicted of evading about 1.2 million dollars in federal income tax by charging more than 4 million dollars of personal expenses, mostly renovations to her Connecticut estate, to her businesses. In December 1989 she was sentenced to four years in prison and heavy fines, and the press had long nicknamed her the Queen of Mean.
real_life_example.explanation: Helmsley's great fortune brought her public contempt rather than honour, largely because of how she treated the people who worked for her.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that great wealth in the hands of someone without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by an unclean vessel, and Helmsley's wealth was soured in the public eye by her treatment of others.

tamil:
வைத்தான்வாய் சான்ற பெரும்பொருள் அஃதுண்ணான்
செத்தான் செயக்கிடந்தது இல்.
transliteration:
Vaiththaanvaai Saandra Perumporul Aqdhunnaan
Seththaan Seyakkitandhadhu Il
meaning: A person who fills their house with huge riches but never uses them is as good as dead, because those riches do nothing at all.
elementary: Imagine a boy who fills his whole room with sweets but never eats one and never shares one. The sweets just sit there until they go stale. Valluvar says a person who piles up money like that and never uses it might as well not be there at all.
university: The chapter title நன்றியில் செல்வம் uses நன்றி in its older sense of 'benefit, good' rather than 'gratitude': this is wealth that does no good to anyone. In vaittaan-vaay (வைத்தான்வாய்) வாய் means 'place', so the wealth 'fills the place where he stored it'; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses இடமெல்லாம் நிறைந்த, and Puliyur Kesikan (thirukkural.net) adds that the man does not eat it 'through avarice' (உலோபத்தால்). The second line is elliptical: seththaan (செத்தான்) can be read either as 'he is (equivalent to) a dead man', as Solomon Pappaiah and Pope take it ('Is dead'), or as 'when he dies, there is nothing left done (by the wealth)', as Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render it; both readings yield the same verdict that unused wealth achieves nothing. The chapter stands in the Kudiyiyal after Panbudaimai (ch. 100), turning from courtesy to the social uselessness of hoarded riches, and complements the earlier chapters on Ithal (ch. 23) and Oppuravu (ch. 22). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Yajnavalkya prepares to divide his property and leave home, his wife Maitreyi asks whether the whole earth full of wealth would make her immortal; he answers that her life would merely be like that of the rich, for there is no hope of immortality through wealth.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that riches, however vast, cannot purchase what matters most and are left behind at death.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it exposes wealth as powerless at the moment of death, so a life spent only storing it accomplishes nothing.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells of a rich man whose land yielded so much that he planned bigger barns to store it all and then take his ease; God calls him a fool, for that very night his soul is required of him, and the question is who will own what he has stored.
christianity.explanation: The parable condemns laying up treasure for oneself without being rich toward God or others.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's hoarder, the rich fool dies beside his full storehouses having done nothing with them.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an urges believers to spend from what God has provided before death comes, when a person will plead to be granted a short delay so that he could give charity and be among the righteous.
islam.explanation: Death ends the chance to make wealth do good, and the hoarder's regret comes too late.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's picture of a man who dies with his wealth untouched and nothing accomplished.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Every person will have to justify himself for everything his eye saw and which he did not eat.”
judaism.explanation: Rav teaches that refusing the lawful good things of life is itself something one must answer for; the Talmud adds that Rabbi Eleazar saved coins so he could taste every kind of food once a year.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise counts it a failure to own abundance and never enjoy it.
judaism.source: Jerusalem Talmud, Kiddushin 4:12 (tr. Heinrich W. Guggenheimer, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just now, lord, a money-lending householder died in Savatthi. I have come from conveying his heirless fortune to the royal palace: eight million in silver, to say nothing of the gold. But even though he was a money-lending householder, his enjoyment of food was like this: he ate broken rice & pickle brine.”
buddhism.explanation: King Pasenadi reports a rich miser who lived like a pauper and died, his fortune passing to the crown; the Buddha says such wealth, not properly used, goes to waste.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's hoarder exactly: immense riches, none enjoyed, and nothing achieved by them at death.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 3.19, Aputtaka Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who employs not his time in enjoying his property, or gives not of it to ascetics, but lays it up (like a miser)--at him, the foolish one, about to perish, his hoarded wealth shall mock, and the favour of the world shall mock.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil quatrain pictures the hoarder's own treasure mocking him as death approaches.
jainism.tie_back: It makes the same point as the Kural: wealth neither enjoyed nor given leaves its dying owner with nothing.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 3 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Gathering in and hoarding what they can, the faithless cynics die, O Nanak, but the wealth of Maya does not go with them in the end.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Bavan Akhri, Guru Arjan describes those who spend their lives piling up wealth, die, and find that none of it goes with them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's hoarder fills his house and dies with nothing done through his wealth; Guru Arjan pictures the same person dying in the middle of his gathering.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 257, Raag Gauri, Bavan Akhri (salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas is granted his wish that whatever he touches turn to gold, and finds that his bread and wine also turn to gold, so that the richest man alive faces starvation amid his treasure until he begs the god to take the gift back.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows that wealth which cannot be used for life's ordinary goods is worthless, even deadly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's miser, Midas is surrounded by riches that do nothing for him and bring him close to death.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Misers, he said, took care of property as if it belonged to them, but derived no more benefit from it than if it belonged to others.”
philosophy.explanation: The Cynic Bion of Borysthenes mocks misers as mere caretakers of goods they never actually use.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the hoarder gets nothing from the wealth he guards, as if he were already dead to it.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 4.50 (Bion), tr. R. D. Hicks (Wikisource)

real_life_example.event_title: Hetty Green, America's richest woman, lives in cheap lodgings
real_life_example.place: New York City and Hoboken, New Jersey, United States
real_life_example.event: Hetty Green inherited about 10 million dollars in 1865 and, through shrewd investment and lending on Wall Street, became reputedly the wealthiest woman in the United States, leaving an estate of more than 100 million dollars when she died in 1916. Despite her fortune she lived with her children in inexpensive rented lodgings, for years in a small apartment in Hoboken, avoiding any display of wealth and virtually all society. Newspapers circulated many stories of her frugality, some of them exaggerated, and she became known as the Witch of Wall Street.
real_life_example.explanation: Green's vast fortune grew year after year while she herself lived as though she had very little of it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that a man who fills his house with vast wealth and never enjoys it is as good as dead, since his wealth does nothing through him, and Green amassed immense riches that she scarcely allowed herself to use.

tamil:
பொருளானாம் எல்லாமென்று ஈயாது இவறும்
மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Porulaanaam Ellaamendru Eeyaadhu Ivarum
Marulaanaam Maanaap Pirappu
meaning: Thinking money can do everything, a person holds it tight and gives nothing away. That foolish mistake leads to a low, worthless birth.
elementary: Some people think, 'If I just have enough money, I'll have everything!' So they grip their money tight and never share. Valluvar says this is a big mistake, like a confused traveller holding the wrong map, and it leads them to a very sad place.
university: The first line reports the miser's creed, poruLaal aam ellaam ('by wealth everything is achieved'), and his conduct, eeyaadhu ivaRum ('not giving, he clings'); ivaRu- denotes tight-fisted holding, the same root as இவறல் (miserliness) condemned among royal faults in Kural 432. The second line names the result: maruL (மருள், 'delusion, bewilderment') produces maaNaap piRappu, 'an un-excellent birth'. Mu. Varadarasanar keeps this general ('a birth without distinction'), Kalaignar reads it this-worldly ('a base creature'), while Solomon Pappaiah and Pope's explanation ('will be born a demon') follow the classical line that specifies a ghost or demon birth (பேய்ப் பிறப்பு); Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as an endless, graceless cycle of births. The phrase மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு also closes Kural 351, where delusion about what is real is said to cause such a birth, so Valluvar here treats the miser's faith in money as a species of metaphysical error. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna describes the demoniac mentality that says, so much wealth is mine today and more will come tomorrow; deluded by such thoughts and bound by attachment, these persons fall into a foul hell and take birth again and again in demoniac wombs.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita traces degraded rebirth to the delusion of treating possessions as the measure of life.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the delusion that wealth is everything produces a debased, even demonic, birth.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells of a rich man who feasted every day while the beggar Lazarus lay starving at his gate; after death Lazarus is comforted while the rich man is in torment, reminded that he received his good things in his lifetime.
christianity.explanation: The parable shows a lifetime of withholding from the needy leading to a terrible state after death.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links refusal to give with a fallen condition in the life to come.

islam.quote_or_event: “Woe to every scorner and mocker / Who collects wealth and [continuously] counts it. / He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal. / No! He will surely be thrown into the Crusher.”
islam.explanation: The surah condemns the man who hoards and counts his money, imagining it makes him invulnerable.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's deluded miser who believes wealth is everything and so earns a degraded destiny.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah lists among human characters the one who says, what is mine is mine and what is yours is yours, calls it an ordinary type, and records that some call it the character of Sodom.
judaism.explanation: Refusing ever to share, even when it costs nothing, is identified with the proverbially wicked city.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's miser who gives nothing displays exactly this Sodom-like closed-handedness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Petavatthu, a canonical collection of ghost stories, repeatedly explains that beings were reborn as hungry ghosts (petas) because in their human lives they were stingy and refused to give, even to ascetics who came for alms.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching makes miserliness (macchariya) a direct cause of rebirth in the ghost realm.
buddhism.tie_back: It closely matches the classical reading of the Kural that the miser's delusion leads to a ghost-like birth.
buddhism.source: Petavatthu (Khuddaka Nikaya), stories of misers reborn as petas

jainism.quote_or_event: “If the whole world and all treasures were yours, you would still not be satisfied, nor would all this be able to save you.”
jainism.explanation: Queen Kamalâvatî rebukes King Ishukâra for wanting to seize a renouncer's abandoned property, teaching that no amount of wealth can satisfy or protect the soul.
jainism.tie_back: It directly contradicts the miser's creed in the Kural that wealth can accomplish everything.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “People gather and hoard their possessions, and give nothing to anyone else - the poor fools think that everything is theirs.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says that the hoarder gives nothing away because he is blind: he thinks everything he holds belongs to him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural blames the delusion that wealth is everything for the miser's refusal to give; Guru Nanak likewise ties the refusal to give to a blind belief that it is all his own.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 155, Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Croesus of Lydia shows Solon his treasuries and asks who is the happiest of men, expecting to be named; Solon instead names obscure Athenians who lived and died well, and warns that no one should be called happy until his end is seen.
greek_mythology.explanation: Croesus's confidence that riches equal happiness is exposed as an illusion, later borne out by his fall.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus embodies the Kural's mistaken belief that wealth is everything.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But meanness is both incurable (for old age and every disability is thought to make men mean) and more innate in men than prodigality; for most men are fonder of getting money than of giving.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle judges stinginess a deeper and harder vice to cure than wastefulness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats tight-fisted clinging to wealth as a deep-rooted error with grave consequences.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross, MIT Internet Classics Archive)

real_life_example.event_title: Didius Julianus buys the support of the Praetorian Guard
real_life_example.event: After the Praetorian Guard killed the emperor Pertinax in March 193, the wealthy senator Didius Julianus competed with Pertinax's father-in-law, Sulpicianus, for the Guard's backing by promising each soldier a cash payment, and won with the larger offer. The Guard proclaimed him emperor, but his rule was insecure from the start, and when the general Septimius Severus marched on Rome with the Danube legions, support for Julianus collapsed. He was put to death on 1 June 193, about two months after his accession.
real_life_example.explanation: Julianus's wealth bought him the title of emperor but none of the loyalty or legitimacy needed to keep it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes the delusion of thinking that wealth can do everything, and Julianus's brief, doomed reign shows how badly that belief can end.

tamil:
ஈட்டம் இவறி இசைவேண்டா ஆடவர்
தோற்றம் நிலக்குப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Eettam Ivari Isaiventaa Aatavar
Thotram Nilakkup Porai
meaning: People who only want to pile up money and do not care about a good name are just a weight on the earth.
elementary: Think of a squirrel that hides a thousand nuts and never lets another animal have one, and no one in the forest has a kind word for it. Valluvar says people who only collect and collect, and never do anything good that others would remember, are just heavy weight on the ground.
university: The couplet sets two objects of desire against each other: eettam (ஈட்டம், 'accumulation', from ஈட்டு- 'to earn, amass') and isai (இசை, 'fame, renown'), which in the Kural is earned chiefly by giving (compare Pugazh, ch. 24, beginning 'ஈதல் இசைபட வாழ்தல்'). Those who 'cling to accumulation and do not want renown' have a thoatram (தோற்றம், 'appearance, birth, existence') that is poRai (பொறை, 'burden, weight') to the earth; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read தோற்றம் as 'being born and living', Pope as appearing 'on the stage of being'. Solomon Pappaiah adds a competitive nuance: they want to amass more than others. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads இசை as 'interest/inclination' (இசைவு) beyond acquiring wealth, a minority interpretation. The 'burden of the earth' image echoes Kural 239, where the land bearing a body without fame loses its yield. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna says that one who does not take part in the cycle of sacrifice and sharing set in motion for the world, but lives only for the satisfaction of the senses, lives in vain.
hinduism.explanation: A life that only takes and never contributes back to the common order is declared futile.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it judges the purely acquisitive life a dead weight on the world.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells of a fig tree that bore no fruit for three years; the owner orders it cut down, asking why it should take up the ground, and the gardener pleads for one more year.
christianity.explanation: A barren life that produces nothing for others merely occupies space.
christianity.tie_back: The parable's tree that only 'cumbers the ground' is the Kural's man who is a burden to the earth.
christianity.source: Luke 13:6–9 (Parable of the Barren Fig Tree)

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an warns that rivalry in piling up worldly increase distracts people until they reach their graves, when they will surely come to know its emptiness.
islam.explanation: Competitive accumulation is portrayed as a diversion that fills a whole life and leaves nothing worthwhile.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's men obsessed with accumulation and indifferent to true honour.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Shimon teaches that there are three crowns, of Torah, of priesthood and of royalty, but the crown of a good name surpasses them all.
judaism.explanation: A good name earned by one's deeds is ranked above every inherited dignity.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural condemns those who prize hoarding over exactly this good name.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that misers do not go to heavenly realms and fools do not praise generosity, but the wise person rejoices in giving and is happy hereafter.
buddhism.explanation: The verse sets the stingy fool against the generous wise person whose giving brings joy and good standing.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's hoarders who care nothing for renown are the Dhammapada's misers who scorn generosity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who have, to the best of their ability, practised to any extent trifling acts of charity, will in another birth become great; while those who, when they have become wealthy, say, We will give alms some time or other, shall be punished and shall perish from all the sea-surrounded earth.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain poet contrasts small, real generosity with the wealthy man's endless postponement of giving.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees the wealthy non-giver as having no rightful place on the earth.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 2 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Earning a thousand, he runs after a hundred thousand. Satisfaction is not obtained by chasing after Maya.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan describes the restless accumulator who earns a thousand and at once runs after a hundred thousand, never satisfied.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural condemns people greedy only for piling up wealth; Guru Arjan pictures that endless piling up and shows that it never brings contentment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278-279, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: A fragment of the epic Cypria tells that Zeus, seeing the broad-bosomed Earth weighed down by the countless tribes of men, took pity on her and resolved to lighten her burden through the Trojan War.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth imagines humanity itself as a weight the Earth can groan under.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shares the Kural's image of people whose existence is a burden to the earth, though not its moral about hoarding.
greek_mythology.source: Cypria, fragment 1 (preserved in the scholia to Iliad 1.5)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that liberality and beneficence win people's goodwill and lasting glory, while wealth hoarded or spent only on oneself earns none.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, true and lasting renown is gained by using one's means to help others.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural blames exactly those who pursue accumulation and neglect the renown that giving would bring.

real_life_example.event_title: Verres plunders Sicily and is driven into exile
real_life_example.place: Sicily and Rome, Roman Republic (now Italy)
real_life_example.event: Gaius Verres governed the Roman province of Sicily from 73 to 71 BCE and used his office to extort money and seize works of art and other valuables from its people. In 70 BCE the Sicilians engaged Marcus Tullius Cicero to prosecute him for extortion; Cicero gathered evidence across the island in a few weeks and opened the case so forcefully that Verres's advocate, Hortensius, gave up the defence. Verres left Rome for exile before the trial ended, and Cicero's published speeches made his name a byword for official greed.
real_life_example.explanation: Verres pursued gain with no concern for his reputation, and what survives of him is a lasting record of disgrace.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that men greedy only for piling up wealth, with no care for an honourable name, are a burden to the earth, and Verres enriched himself at the expense of an entire province.

tamil:
எச்சமென்று என்எண்ணுங் கொல்லோ ஒருவரால்
நச்சப் படாஅ தவன்.
transliteration:
Echchamendru Enennung Kollo Oruvaraal
Nachchap Pataaa Thavan
meaning: What does a person whom no one loves think they will leave behind after they die?
elementary: When a kind teacher retires, the children remember her stories and her hugs for years. But if someone never helped anyone, what will people remember about him when he is gone? Valluvar asks: what is left of a person nobody loved?
university: The key word is echcham (எச்சம், 'remainder, what is left over'), which in the Kural can mean posterity or a lasting name; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss 'what remains after his death', Solomon Pappaiah 'what will stand to recall him after his time'. The man is described as oruvaraal nachchap padaaa-thavan, 'one not desired by even a single person'; nachchu (நச்சு, 'to desire, love') returns in Kural 1008, where the same unloved man's wealth is a poisonous tree, so the chapter plays on நச்சு 'love' and நச்சு 'poison'. Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the reason for his unpopularity, that he helped no one. Pope's explanation narrows echcham to what the miser can count as his own 'in the world to come', a reading that follows the classical tendency to interpret legacy in terms of merit for the next life. The rhetorical question (என் எண்ணும் கொல்லோ, 'what, pray, does he think?') turns the couplet into a mock of the miser's planning. The text is identical on both sources (ytamizh prints எண்ணுங் with the same ங்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu teaches that in the next world neither father nor mother, wife, sons nor kin remain as one's companions; leaving the body on the ground like a log, relatives turn away, and spiritual merit alone follows the dead.
hinduism.explanation: Only the good one has done survives a person; everything else is left behind.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's unloved hoarder has done no good, so nothing worthwhile remains of him.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells his hearers not to lay up treasures on earth, where moth and rust corrupt and thieves steal, but to lay up treasures in heaven, for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
christianity.explanation: Earthly hoards vanish; only what is invested in goodness endures.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural asks the same question of the miser: what lasting treasure has he laid up?

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an says that wealth and children are the adornment of worldly life, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord for reward and better for one's hope.
islam.explanation: Possessions are passing ornaments; only lasting good deeds (al-baqiyat al-salihat, 'the things that remain') endure.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's miser, having done no good, has none of these 'remaining' deeds to leave behind.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah teaches that when a person departs, neither silver nor gold nor precious stones and pearls accompany him, but only Torah and good deeds.
judaism.explanation: Wealth stays behind at death; only learning and good deeds go with a person.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural asks what the hoarder who has earned no one's love can possibly leave or take with him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says the fool frets, thinking, I have sons, I have wealth, yet he is not even his own master, so how can sons or wealth be his?
buddhism.explanation: Possessions and family give no lasting hold to someone who does not even possess himself.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's unloved miser likewise has nothing that will truly remain as his.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.”
jainism.explanation: The queen tells King Ishukâra that at death only dharma remains as a refuge, not property.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks what the man who has won no one's love by giving can hope to have left; the Jain answer is only the Law he practised.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The kings die, gathering and hoarding their money, burying great quantities of gold.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose hymns are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, points to kings who spent their lives hoarding and burying gold, and died with it still in the ground.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what legacy a man whom no one loves can leave; Kabir's buried gold is the hoarder's only legacy, of use to no one.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 654, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles, refusing Agamemnon's lavish gifts, says that cattle and treasure can be won by raiding but a man's life cannot be recovered, and that his mother foretold a choice between a long, obscure life and an early death with imperishable glory.
greek_mythology.explanation: In heroic thought, what outlasts a person is kleos, the remembered name, not possessions.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's unloved miser has no such remembered name to leave behind.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The aged Cephalus tells Socrates that the greatest benefit of wealth for a decent man is that, as death approaches, he need not depart owing sacrifices to the gods or money to anyone, having cheated no one.
philosophy.explanation: For Cephalus, wealth matters at the end only for the clean account it lets a man leave behind.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural presses the same end-of-life question on the miser: what will he have left that counts?

real_life_example.event_title: The miser John Camden Neild leaves his fortune to Queen Victoria
real_life_example.place: Chelsea, London, and North Marston, Buckinghamshire, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: John Camden Neild inherited a fortune of about 250,000 pounds from his father in 1814 and lived as a recluse and miser in his house in Cheyne Walk, Chelsea. When he died in August 1852 his will left almost his entire estate, then worth about 500,000 pounds, to Queen Victoria, whom he had never met, while making no provision for his longtime servants. The Queen increased the small bequests to his executors, provided for his servants, and later restored the chancel of North Marston church, where he was buried, inserting a window in his memory.
real_life_example.explanation: Neild left behind no circle of family or friends, and the only lasting memorial to him was raised by a stranger who had received his money.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what a man whom no one loves can expect to leave behind, and Neild's long, solitary hoarding left nothing of him but a bequest to someone he had never known.

tamil:
கொடுப்பதூஉம் துய்ப்பதூஉம் இல்லார்க்கு அடுக்கிய
கோடியுண் டாயினும் இல்.
transliteration:
Kotuppadhooum Thuyppadhooum Illaarkku Atukkiya
Kotiyun Taayinum Il
meaning: For people who neither give their money away nor enjoy it themselves, even crores upon crores (huge piles of money) are as good as nothing.
elementary: If you have a big box of crayons but never draw with them and never lend them to a friend, it is just like having no crayons at all. Valluvar says money works the same way: if you never use it and never share it, you are really poor.
university: The couplet names the two proper uses of wealth, koduppadhu (கொடுப்பது, 'giving') and thuyppadhu (துய்ப்பது, 'enjoying, consuming'), with the emphatic lengthening -ūum (கொடுப்பதூஉம், துய்ப்பதூஉம்) marking each as indispensable. Adukkiya kodi (அடுக்கிய கோடி) means 'crores stacked one upon another'; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'many crores ever increasing'. The verdict il (இல், 'there is not') says such people are effectively without wealth; Pope renders the sense as 'they are poor'. Solomon Pappaiah adds the qualifier that giving should be to those in need and enjoying should be as need requires, guarding against reading the couplet as licence for extravagance. The two-fold scheme parallels the Sanskrit gnomic triad of dāna, bhoga and nāśa (giving, enjoyment, destruction) found in Bhartrihari. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrihari's well-known stanza says that wealth has only three possible courses, giving, enjoyment and destruction; for the man who neither gives nor enjoys, the third course is what becomes of it.
hinduism.explanation: Wealth not given or used is bound simply to be lost.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's own scheme of giving and enjoying, with the same conclusion that otherwise the wealth amounts to nothing.
hinduism.source: Bhartrihari, Nītiśataka (dānaṃ bhogo nāśas tisro gatayo bhavanti vittasya; verse numbering varies by edition)

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul tells Timothy to charge the rich not to trust in uncertain riches but in God, who gives us richly all things to enjoy, and to be rich in good works, ready to distribute and willing to share.
christianity.explanation: Wealth is meant both to be enjoyed with gratitude and to be shared generously.
christianity.tie_back: It names the same two uses, enjoying and giving, that the Kural says give wealth its meaning.

islam.quote_or_event: “A servant says, My wealth. my wealth, but out of his wealth three things are only his: whatever he eats and makes use of or by means of which he dresses himself and it wears out or he gives as charity, and this is what he stored for himself (as a reward for the Hereafter), and what is beyond this (it is of no use to you) because you are to depart and leave it for other people.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that only what one consumes or gives away is truly one's own; the rest is merely left behind.
islam.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's teaching: wealth neither used nor given is as good as nothing to its owner.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs observes that one person gives freely and yet grows richer, while another withholds more than is right and only comes to want.
judaism.explanation: Withholding does not make one rich; generosity does.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the one who never gives is poor despite heaped-up crores.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that rightly earned wealth should be used to bring pleasure to oneself, to parents, family and workers, to friends, to protect against losses, and to make offerings to relatives, guests, the dead, kings, devas and contemplatives.
buddhism.explanation: Wealth's benefits lie in using it for one's own and others' good, not in storing it.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's pairing of enjoyment and giving as the purpose of riches.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who, though utterly poor, will not beg, are the truly rich. Even the rich are poor if they give not.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil quatrain redefines riches by conduct: the non-giver is poor whatever he owns.
jainism.tie_back: It restates the Kural's verdict that crores amount to nothing for one who does not give.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 27 ('Riches without goodness'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak names the right use of earnings: live on what you have earned by honest work and give part of it to others. This salok is the scriptural root of kirat karni (honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural names enjoying and giving as the two uses of wealth, without which crores are worth nothing; Guru Nanak names the same two, eating what one earns and giving some away.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop's fable a miser buries his gold and visits it daily; when a thief steals it and he laments, a neighbour advises him to bury a stone in its place, since it will serve him just as well as the gold he never used.
greek_mythology.explanation: Wealth that is never used has no more value than a stone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's point that unused, ungiven crores amount to nothing.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, 'The Miser and His Gold'

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle remarks that being rich consists in using things rather than in owning them, since it is the actual use of possessions that constitutes wealth.
philosophy.explanation: Wealth is defined by its use, not by mere ownership.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise denies that unused, ungiven riches are wealth at all.

real_life_example.event_title: Russell Sage dies with 70 million dollars after a lifetime of tight-fistedness
real_life_example.event: Russell Sage, a financier who helped organise American railroads and telegraphs and became a major Wall Street moneylender, died in 1906 with a fortune estimated at about 70 million dollars. He was known for his frugality, and over a marriage of 37 years he and his wife made only three major charitable gifts. His widow, Margaret Olivia Sage, then gave the fortune away, beginning with 10 million dollars in 1907 to establish the Russell Sage Foundation for the improvement of social and living conditions in the United States.
real_life_example.explanation: Sage's fortune did almost nothing for anyone in his own lifetime; it became a force for good only once it passed out of his hands.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those who neither give nor enjoy, wealth counts for nothing even if they own crores heaped upon crores, and Sage's millions achieved nothing until his widow gave them away.

tamil:
ஏதம் பெருஞ்செல்வம் தான்துவ்வான் தக்கார்க்கொன்று
ஈதல் இயல்பிலா தான்.
transliteration:
Edham Perunjelvam Thaandhuvvaan Thakkaarkkondru
Eedhal Iyalpilaa Thaan
meaning: A person who does not enjoy their great riches, and does not have it in their nature to give some to people who deserve it, is like a sickness to those riches.
elementary: Imagine a lovely garden where the owner never sits and never lets anyone else pick a flower. The garden is wasted, and the owner is like a sickness that keeps it from doing any good. Valluvar says a stingy rich person is like that sickness for his own money.
university: The opening word edham (ஏதம், 'harm, fault, affliction, disease') is the predicate, and its subject is the man described in the rest of the couplet: thaan thuvvaan (தான் துவ்வான், 'he himself does not enjoy') and thakkaarkku ondru eedhal iyalbu ilaan (தக்கார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈதல் இயல்பு இலான், 'one who has no disposition to give even one thing to the worthy'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar therefore read him as a disease (நோய்) to his own great wealth, as does Pope's explanation ('a disease to his wealth'); Solomon Pappaiah inverts it, making the wealth a disease in his keeping, and Sivayogi Sivakumar reads that he does harm to himself. The word iyalbu (இயல்பு, 'nature') stresses that the fault is temperamental, not circumstantial, and thakkaar (தக்கார், 'the deserving') narrows the duty of giving to worthy recipients, a classical criterion of proper gifts. Pope's verse rendering ('misery to men of churlish heart') follows the alternative sense. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna teaches that the righteous who eat what remains after offering are freed from sin, while those who prepare food only for their own enjoyment eat nothing but sin.
hinduism.explanation: Possessions kept wholly to oneself turn into a source of fault rather than blessing.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees self-enclosed wealth as a blight rather than a good.

christianity.quote_or_event: The Preacher calls it a grievous evil he has seen under the sun: riches kept by their owner to his own hurt, which are then lost in some misfortune so that nothing is left.
christianity.explanation: Hoarded riches can harm the very person who guards them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly makes the miser and his wealth a mutual affliction.

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those who [greedily] withhold what Allāh has given them of His bounty ever think that it is better for them. Rather, it is worse for them. Their necks will be encircled by what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches that withheld wealth becomes a burden and torment to the one who withholds it.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's claim that the non-giver's great wealth turns into an affliction.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah describes four kinds of givers, and calls wicked the one who neither wishes to give himself nor wants others to give.
judaism.explanation: Total unwillingness to give is classed as wickedness, not mere thrift.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's man with 'no nature for giving' fits this wicked type.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says that if beings knew, as he knows, the results of giving and sharing, they would not eat without having given, and the stain of selfishness would not overcome their minds.
buddhism.explanation: Stinginess is a mental stain; generosity, even of the last mouthful, is the remedy.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's man without a giving nature is overcome by exactly this stain.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The seeking to accumulate wealth is a cause of vexation. The guarding that collected shining wealth causes vexation. Again, if any of that wealth which is so guarded be diminished, there is vexation. If it be lost, how great the vexation! Truly this said wealth is the very abode of vexation.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain poet shows hoarded wealth as nothing but a source of trouble at every stage.
jainism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's description of great wealth unenjoyed and ungiven as an affliction (ஏதம்).
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He hoards gold and silver, but this wealth is false and poisonous, nothing more than ashes.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak says that gold and silver piled up for their own sake are false, poisonous and as worthless as ashes.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls the man who neither enjoys nor gives a disease to his own great wealth; Guru Nanak calls such hoarded wealth poison and ash.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 937, Raag Ramkali, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld Odysseus sees Tantalus standing in a pool beneath trees laden with fruit; whenever he stoops to drink the water vanishes, and whenever he reaches for the fruit the wind tosses it away.
greek_mythology.explanation: Tantalus suffers eternal want in the very midst of plenty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's miser, he is surrounded by goods that bring him only torment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Referring to a wealthy miser he said, He has not acquired a fortune; the fortune has acquired him.”
philosophy.explanation: Bion of Borysthenes jokes that the miser is possessed by his wealth rather than possessing it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise sees the non-enjoying, non-giving rich man as a bad relation to his own wealth.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 4.50 (Bion), tr. R. D. Hicks (Wikisource)

real_life_example.event_title: J. Paul Getty installs a pay telephone at Sutton Place
real_life_example.place: Sutton Place, Surrey, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: After the American oil billionaire J. Paul Getty, then counted among the richest men in the world, made the Tudor mansion Sutton Place in Surrey his base in 1959, Time reported that he had cut back the gardening staff and installed a pay telephone for visitors' use. Getty later explained in his autobiography that the coin-box phone was a response to soaring telephone bills run up by the many people passing through the house during renovations. The public nonetheless took the pay phone as a symbol of his tightness with money, and it became the best-known story of his frugality.
real_life_example.explanation: The story stuck to Getty because it seemed to sum up a vast fortune that its owner was reluctant to share even in small ways.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls a man who neither enjoys his wealth nor is disposed to give to others a blight upon that wealth, and the pay telephone became the public emblem of a fortune held back even from guests.

tamil:
அற்றார்க்கொன்று ஆற்றாதான் செல்வம் மிகநலம்
பெற்றாள் தமியள்மூத் தற்று.
transliteration:
Atraarkkondru Aatraadhaan Selvam Mikanalam
Petraal Thamiyalmooth Thatru
meaning: The riches of a person who gives nothing to the poor are like a very beautiful woman who grows old all alone.
elementary: Picture the most beautiful flower blooming inside a locked room where nobody ever sees it, until it slowly fades. Valluvar says money that never helps poor people is like that hidden flower: something lovely, wasted.
university: Atraar (அற்றார், 'those who have nothing, the destitute') are the intended recipients, and aatraadhaan (ஆற்றாதான்) is 'one who does not do (even one thing) for them'.
