The simile mika nalam petraaL thamiyaL mooththatru (மிக நலம் பெற்றாள் தமியள் மூத்தற்று) compares such wealth to 'a woman endowed with great beauty growing old alone'; Solomon Pappaiah and Pope's explanation specify 'without a husband', Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep 'alone'. The point of the comparison is waste: a good thing that exists to be shared lapses unused, the same logic as the chapter's poisonous-tree image in 1008 and its counterpart in Kural 216, where a generous man's wealth is a fruit tree in the middle of the village. The simile reflects the social world of classical Tamil literature, in which beauty fulfilled in married life is the norm; modern readers may note the period assumption while keeping the moral about unshared resources. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The man with food in store who, when the needy comes in miserable case begging for bread to eat, / Hardens his heart against him-even when of old he did him service-finds not one to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn on liberality condemns the man who refuses food to the needy and promises him a friendless end.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise condemns wealth that does nothing for the destitute.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.2 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith, sacred-texts.com)

christianity.quote_or_event: John asks how the love of God can dwell in anyone who has this world's goods, sees a brother in need, and shuts up his heart of compassion against him.
christianity.explanation: Possessions withheld from the needy are a sign that love is absent.
christianity.tie_back: It condemns exactly the Kural's wealthy man who gives nothing to the destitute.

islam.quote_or_event: Surat al-Ma'un describes the one who denies the Judgement as he who drives away the orphan and does not urge the feeding of the poor, and condemns those who withhold even small kindnesses.
islam.explanation: Refusing basic help to the destitute is presented as a mark of spiritual bankruptcy.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's man who does not give even one thing to the destitute is the Ma'un's withholder.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Torah commands that if there is a needy person among your brethren, you shall not harden your heart nor shut your hand, but open your hand wide and lend him enough for his need.
judaism.explanation: Withholding from the poor is forbidden; generosity to the needy is a commandment.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural blames the rich man who 'does not do one thing' for the destitute.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like water in a haunted place that, without being imbibed, dries up: such is the wealth acquired by a worthless person who neither enjoys it himself nor gives.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares unshared wealth to pure water in a place no one dares to drink from, which simply evaporates.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's beauty growing old alone, it pictures a good thing that withers unused because it is never shared.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 3.19, Aputtaka Sutta, closing verse (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The great wealth which the miserly-minded have attained, who neither know how to give it away nor to use it themselves, shall be like the beauteous damsels of a family, who when they have arrived at puberty are enjoyed by others; i.e. others than its owner shall enjoy it.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain poet uses the same image of a young woman's beauty to show that a miser's wealth benefits others, never its owner.
jainism.tie_back: Both texts compare unshared wealth to feminine beauty that its keeper does not rightly bring to fruition.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, the young Nanak was given money by his father Mehta Kalu to make a profitable bargain (sacha sauda), but on the way he met a group of hungry holy men and spent all of it on food for them, calling this the true bargain.
sikhism.explanation: The story is remembered as the first act of the Sikh duty to share with the needy, later embodied in the langar.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says wealth never given to the destitute is wasted like beauty that ages alone; the young Nanak's true bargain is the opposite, money spent at once on those who had nothing.
sikhism.source: Janamsakhi tradition, as retold in M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The beautiful youth Narcissus, sought by many, scorns every suitor, and in the end falls in love with his own reflection and wastes away beside the pool, his beauty consumed without ever being shared.
greek_mythology.explanation: Beauty turned wholly inward withers without bringing joy to anyone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It parallels the Kural's image of great beauty fading in solitude as a picture of wasted, unshared riches.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now the things that have a use may be used either well or badly; and riches is a useful thing; and everything is used best by the man who has the virtue concerned with it; riches, therefore, will be used best by the man who has the virtue concerned with wealth; and this is the liberal man.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that wealth exists to be used, and is used best by the generous person.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's simile makes the same claim negatively: wealth not used for the needy wastes its purpose.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross, MIT Internet Classics Archive)

real_life_example.event_title: Bokassa crowns himself emperor amid national poverty
real_life_example.place: Bangui, Central African Empire (now Central African Republic)
real_life_example.event: On 4 December 1977 Jean-Bedel Bokassa, ruler of the Central African Republic, which he had renamed the Central African Empire, crowned himself Emperor Bokassa I in a ceremony modelled on Napoleon's coronation, seated on a great gilded eagle throne. Britannica puts the cost at more than 20 million dollars, an enormous sum for one of the poorest countries in the world, and much of it was met by France. The spectacle drew international criticism, and Bokassa was overthrown in 1979.
real_life_example.explanation: Bokassa spent a fortune on his own glory in a country where most people lacked basic services, and the money vanished in a single ceremony.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the wealth of one who gives nothing to the destitute is wasted like great beauty growing old alone, and Bokassa poured national wealth into one day's display while his people remained poor.

tamil:
நச்சப் படாதவன் செல்வம் நடுவூருள்
நச்சு மரம்பழுத் தற்று.
transliteration:
Nachchap Pataadhavan Selvam Natuvoorul
Nachchu Marampazhuth Thatru
meaning: The riches of a person whom no one loves are like a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of town.
elementary: Imagine a tree in the middle of the playground covered in shiny fruit, but the fruit is poisonous, so nobody can eat it. Valluvar says a selfish rich person's money is like that tree: right there in front of everyone, but no use to anyone.
university: The couplet is built on a pun: nachchap padaadhavan (நச்சப் படாதவன், 'one not loved', from நச்சு- 'to desire') and nachchu maram (நச்சு மரம், 'poison tree'). Pope's explanation identifies it as the etty tree (எட்டி, the nux-vomica, Strychnos nux-vomica), and Sivayogi Sivakumar quotes the proverb எட்டி பழுத்தால் என்ன, ஈயாதான் வாழ்ந்தால் என்ன ('what if the etty ripens, what if the non-giver prospers'). The setting naduvooruL (நடுவூருள், 'in the middle of the town') heightens the irony: the fruit is in full view and within reach of all, yet useless. Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the reason the man is unloved, that he helps no one. The image is the exact inverse of Kural 216, where the wealth of the generous is a fruit-bearing tree in the midst of the village, so Valluvar deliberately pairs the two chapters on Oppuravu and Nandriyil Selvam. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “No friend is he who to his friend and comrade who comes imploring food, will offer nothing. / Let him depart-no home is that to rest in-, and rather seek a stranger to support him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic poet says the one who offers nothing to those who come to him is no friend, and his house is no refuge.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's unloved rich man is just such a 'house that is no home': present in the town but of no use to anyone.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.4 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith, sacred-texts.com)

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs says that the people curse the one who withholds grain, but blessing rests on the head of the one who sells it.
christianity.explanation: The hoarder of what others need earns the community's hatred.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's unloved man whose wealth benefits no one is the hoarder the people curse.

islam.quote_or_event: A hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi says the generous person is near to God, near to people and near to Paradise, while the miser is far from God, far from people and far from Paradise.
islam.explanation: Miserliness is pictured as distance from everyone, divine and human.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's miser whom no one loves and whose wealth no one can approach.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud says the people of Sodom grew arrogant through their abundance and resolved to stop travellers coming among them, since visitors would only diminish their wealth.
judaism.explanation: Sodom's riches, sealed off from strangers and the poor, became a byword for wickedness.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's poisonous tree in the town, Sodom's plenty stood in full view yet was deliberately made useless to others.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells General Siha that a giver, a master of giving, is dear and charming to people at large, and that good people associate with him.
buddhism.explanation: Generosity makes a person beloved; its absence leaves one unloved.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural describes the reverse case: the non-giver whom no one loves and whose wealth no one enjoys.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The bat will not go to the rough-stemmed wood-apple tree, though near and fruitful. So the riches of those who, though they be very near to one, have no greatness of soul, have not the excellence of being considered as profitable.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain poet compares the riches of small-souled men to a fruitful tree near at hand that no creature will approach.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's own tree image: wealth close by and laden with fruit, yet of no benefit to anyone.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 27 ('Riches without goodness'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Simmal tree is straight as an arrow; it is very tall, and very thick. But those birds which visit it hopefully, depart disappointed. Its fruits are tasteless, its flowers are nauseating, and its leaves are useless.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak uses the tall silk-cotton tree as an image of imposing greatness that offers nothing to those who come to it in hope.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares the unloved man's wealth to a poison tree fruiting in the middle of town; Guru Nanak's towering tree likewise stands in full view and sends everyone away empty.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aristophanes' comedy, Ploutos, the god of Wealth, is blind and so visits the wicked and the stingy instead of the good; when his sight is restored, he leaves the unworthy rich and enriches the deserving.
greek_mythology.explanation: The play mocks wealth that sits with the undeserving where it does no good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's unloved rich man is precisely the undeserving holder of wealth that benefits no one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Boethius has Lady Philosophy argue that money shows its worth in being spent rather than hoarded, and that avarice makes men hated while generosity makes them famous.
philosophy.explanation: Hoarding not only wastes money but makes its owner odious.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's unloved rich man is hated for the same avarice that makes his wealth useless.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy II, prose 5

real_life_example.event_title: Ceausescu clears a Bucharest district for the House of the People
real_life_example.event: From 1984 the Romanian leader Nicolae Ceausescu had an enormous palace built in the centre of Bucharest as a new political and administrative centre, on the site of the old Uranus district, a hillside neighbourhood of small cobbled streets and older houses that was demolished for the project. The construction required clearing large areas of the historic downtown. The building was still unfinished inside when Ceausescu fell in December 1989, and since 1991 it has housed Romania's Parliament.
real_life_example.explanation: The colossal palace stood in the heart of the capital as a monument to the ruler rather than a benefit to the people whose homes it replaced.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural likens the wealth of a man whom nobody loves to a poisonous tree bearing fruit in the middle of the town, and Ceausescu's vast palace rose in the centre of Bucharest offering nothing to the citizens around it.

tamil:
அன்பொரீஇத் தற்செற்று அறநோக்காது ஈட்டிய
ஒண்பொருள் கொள்வார் பிறர்.
transliteration:
Anporeeith Tharsetru Aranokkaadhu Eettiya
Onporul Kolvaar Pirar
meaning: Shining riches gathered by giving up love, making yourself go without, and ignoring what is right will be taken by others in the end.
elementary: A boy saves all his pocket money, never shares, never buys himself a treat, and even cheats a little to get more. One day he moves away and leaves the jar behind, and other kids spend it. Valluvar says money gathered in such a selfish, unhappy way ends up with someone else.
university: The couplet lists three things sacrificed in the getting: anbu oreei (அன்பு ஒரீஇ, 'having forsaken love', the -īi lengthening marking the verbal participle), thaR setRu (தற்செற்று, 'having afflicted oneself', i.e. denying oneself comfort), and aRam nokkaadhu (அறம் நோக்காது, 'without regard for virtue'). The resulting oNporuL (ஒண்பொருள், 'bright, glittering wealth') is taken by piRar (பிறர், 'others'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Sivayogi Sivakumar read 'others will enjoy it', Kalaignar sharpens it to 'others will plunder it', and Pope's explanation has 'strangers will inherit'; Pope glosses the three omissions as friendship, comfort and charity. Pappaiah reads anbu as love shown to others through giving, which ties the couplet to the chapter's theme rather than to domestic affection. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Isha Upanishad opens by saying that all this world is pervaded by the Lord; enjoy it through renunciation, and do not covet, for whose is wealth?
hinduism.explanation: Wealth never truly belongs to anyone, so grasping at it is futile.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's hoarder discovers this when the wealth he amassed passes to others.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is one alone, and there is not a second; yea, he hath neither child nor brother: yet is there no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches; neither saith he, For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good? This is also vanity, yea, it is a sore travail.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher portrays a solitary man who toils endlessly and denies himself, never asking who will benefit.
christianity.tie_back: It mirrors the Kural's three omissions, love, self-care and wisdom, and the question of who will finally have the wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who among you considers the wealth of his heirs dearer to him than his own wealth?” They replied, “O Allah's Messenger! There is none among us but loves his own wealth more.” The Prophet said, “So his wealth is whatever he spends (in Allah's Cause) during his life (on good deeds) while the wealth of his heirs is whatever he leaves after his death.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that what one does not spend on good belongs, in truth, to one's heirs.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's point that wealth amassed without virtue or generosity is really gathered for others.

judaism.quote_or_event: When King Monobaz gave away his treasures in a famine, his relatives protested; he replied that his fathers had stored treasures below and for others, while he was storing them above and for himself.
judaism.explanation: Giving converts wealth into a treasure one truly keeps; hoarding merely saves it for others.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise warns that wealth hoarded without virtue goes to others.

buddhism.quote_or_event: A deva tells the Buddha that when a house is on fire, the vessel carried out is of use, not what burns inside; so, since the world is ablaze with aging and death, one should take out wealth by giving, for what is given is well saved.
buddhism.explanation: Only wealth given away is truly rescued; what is kept is lost.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's hoarder, who never gave, loses all his amassed wealth to others.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Leaving behind bipeds and quadrupeds, his fields, his house, his wealth, his corn, and everything; against his will, and accompanied only by his Karman, he enters a new existence, either a good or a bad one. When they have burned with fire on the funeral pile his forlorn, helpless corpse, his wife and sons and kinsfolk will choose another man to provide for them.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra warns King Brahmadatta that at death all property is left behind and others carry on, while only one's karma goes with the soul.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows that wealth gathered without regard for dharma passes to others, leaving its gatherer only the karma of how he got it.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.24–25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
sikhism.explanation: Reflecting on the wealth of rulers ruined in Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak says that such riches are never amassed without wrongdoing and are left behind at death.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says wealth gathered by abandoning love and virtue will be taken by others; Guru Nanak says it is gathered through sin and stays behind when its owner dies.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Ashtpadi (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Cyrus's troops sack Sardis, the captured Croesus tells Cyrus that the soldiers are not plundering his city or his treasures, for nothing is his any longer, but are carrying off what now belongs to Cyrus.
greek_mythology.explanation: The richest king of his age sees his hoard pass in a single day to another.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus's fate illustrates the Kural's warning that amassed wealth is finally taken by others.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Horace reminds Postumus that the years slip away and death comes for all, and that a worthier heir will drink the Caecuban wine he guarded behind a hundred locks.
philosophy.explanation: What one jealously hoards will be enjoyed by an heir after one's death.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's verdict that the hoarder's shining wealth will be taken by others.

real_life_example.event_title: Louis XIV seizes Fouquet's wealth and takes his artists for Versailles
real_life_example.event: Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's superintendent of finances, amassed a vast fortune and built the magnificent chateau of Vaux-le-Vicomte, where he entertained the king at a lavish fete on 17 August 1661. Less than three weeks later, on 5 September 1661, he was arrested at Nantes and charged over his handling of state finances; his assets were seized, and many works of art from Vaux passed into the royal collections. The king took into his own service Fouquet's architect Louis Le Vau, painter Charles Le Brun and garden designer Andre Le Notre, with the team of craftsmen they had assembled, and set them to work on Versailles, while Fouquet spent the rest of his life in prison.
real_life_example.explanation: The splendour Fouquet had built up passed almost overnight to the king, who used it to create something even grander for himself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that shining wealth gathered without regard for virtue will in the end be taken by others, and Fouquet's fortune, artists and treasures were taken over by the king.

tamil:
சீருடைச் செல்வர் சிறுதுனி மாரி
வறங்கூர்ந் தனையது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Seerutaich Chelvar Sirudhuni Maari
Varangoorn Thanaiyadhu Utaiththu
meaning: When good rich people who are known for giving become poor for a short time, it is like a rain cloud that is empty for a while after giving its rain.
elementary: A rain cloud pours out all its water on the thirsty fields, and for a little while it looks thin and empty. But soon it fills up again. Valluvar says when kind, generous people run short for a while, it is just like that cloud: they gave a lot, and they will be full again.
university: After nine couplets on useless wealth, the chapter closes on its positive counterpart. Seerudaich chelvar (சீருடைச் செல்வர்) are 'rich men endowed with excellence', which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'famous' and Solomon Pappaiah 'famous for giving to others'. Their siRu thuni (சிறுதுனி) is 'a small distress', read by most commentators as a brief poverty; Pope renders 'brief poverty'. It is compared to maari vaRam koorndhanaiyadhu (மாரி வறங் கூர்ந்தனையது), 'like the rain cloud becoming impoverished', i.e. temporarily spent; Mu. Varadarasanar specifies 'the cloud that can protect the world'. The implication is that the generous man's want is temporary and itself a sign of his giving, as the cloud's emptiness follows its rain. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes a different line, reading the distress as the darkening that precedes rain and turns into good; Kalaignar reads the couplet as saying that even a shadow of poverty on such men is as grave as failed rain. The cloud image recalls Kural 211 on duty that expects no return, like the rain. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let the rich satisfy the poor implorer, and bend his eye upon a longer pathway. / Riches come now to one, now to another, and like the wheels of cars are ever rolling.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic poet urges the rich to give, knowing that fortune turns like a chariot wheel.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a giver's changes of fortune as passing turns of the wheel rather than lasting loss.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.5 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith, sacred-texts.com)

christianity.quote_or_event: “If the clouds be full of rain, they empty themselves upon the earth: and if the tree fall toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there it shall be.”
christianity.explanation: In a passage urging generous giving (casting bread on the waters, giving a portion to seven and eight), the Preacher points to clouds that pour out what they hold.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image: the generous rich empty themselves like rain clouds.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an assures believers that whatever they spend in charity, God will replace it, for He is the best of providers.
islam.explanation: Spending for good does not finally impoverish the giver; it is replenished.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's point that the generous man's want is temporary, like a spent cloud that will fill again.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person will never become impoverished from giving charity. No harm nor damage will ever be caused because of charity”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides rules that charity never truly impoverishes the giver.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats the generous rich man's poverty as brief and not real ruin.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:2 (tr. Eliyahu Touger, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In a verse spoken to the Buddha, devas say that those who share even from the little they have, like fellow travellers on the road, do not die among the dead.
buddhism.explanation: Generosity under scarcity is especially praised and never truly lost.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural honours the generous rich even in their short-lived poverty.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though they live near the mighty ocean whose waters overflow, men look on the spring of a small well whose water is almost dried up and live. The poverty of the great is better than the riches of those who know not of the next birth.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain poet says people still draw life from a nearly dry spring rather than the vast salt sea, and so the noble in poverty are worth more than the rich who give nothing.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's spent rain cloud, the noble man's depleted state is still a source of life for others.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 5 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Siblings of Destiny meet together, and eat and spend, but these resources do not diminish; they continue to increase.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan speaks of a treasure that grows the more it is shared and spent together. In context the treasure is the Lord's Name inherited from the Guru.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the brief poverty of generous men is like a cloud spent by its rain that soon fills again; Guru Arjan speaks of a store that never runs out however much is given away.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 186, Raag Gauri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor old couple Baucis and Philemon generously share their meagre food with disguised gods whom richer households had turned away; their wine jug refills itself, and the gods reward them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Generosity from scant means is miraculously replenished.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's cloud that will fill again, the generous couple's want is made good.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is not easy for the liberal man to be rich, since he is not apt either at taking or at keeping, but at giving away, and does not value wealth for its own sake but as a means to giving. Hence comes the charge that is brought against fortune, that those who deserve riches most get it least.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle observes that the generous often find themselves short of money precisely because they give.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains the Kural's 'brief poverty' of the generous rich: it is the natural cost of their giving.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross, MIT Internet Classics Archive)

real_life_example.event_title: Mark Twain recovers from bankruptcy and repays his creditors
real_life_example.place: United States and a world lecture tour
real_life_example.event: In 1894 Mark Twain's publishing firm, Charles L. Webster and Company, failed and, weakened further by heavy losses on the Paige typesetting machine, he was forced into personal bankruptcy. Though not legally required to repay his creditors in full, he resolved to do so, set out on a lecture tour around the world in 1895-96 and published an account of it, Following the Equator, in 1897. By 1898 the earnings from the tour and the book, with the help of his friend Henry H. Rogers's management of his money, had allowed him to pay his creditors in full.
real_life_example.explanation: Twain's reputation and talent remained intact through his financial collapse, and within a few years they had restored his fortune.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the brief poverty of an honoured rich man is like a rain cloud that has emptied itself for a while and will soon be full again, and Twain's honoured name refilled his empty purse within four years.

tamil:
கருமத்தால் நாணுதல் நாணுந் திருநுதல்
நல்லவர் நாணுப் பிற.
transliteration:
Karumaththaal naanudhal naanum thirunudhal
nallavar naanup pira.
meaning: True shame is pulling back from a bad deed. Other kinds of shyness are just the natural modesty of lovely young women with bright foreheads.
elementary: Some kids feel shy when they have to sing in front of the class; that is one kind of shy. But Valluvar says the shame that really matters is the feeling that stops your hand just before you do something mean or wrong. That feeling is like a good friend inside you.
university: The chapter opens by defining its subject: naanudhal (நாணுதல், 'shrinking, being abashed') that arises karumaththaal (கருமத்தால், 'on account of a deed'), i.e. recoiling from a base act, is the naan (நாண்) of the good. Puliyur Kesikan, following the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, glosses the second line as saying that the other shrinkings of mind, speech and body are the modesty proper to women of good family (thirunudhal nallavar, 'the good ones of beautiful brow'), so Valluvar separates a moral emotion open to everyone from a customary, gendered bashfulness. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, and Pope renders the moral sense as ‘generous shame’. Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Nanriyil Selvam (ch. 101) and before Kudiseyalvagai (ch. 103), the chapter treats naan as the inner guard of the well-born person. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh writes the same words; only spacing differs).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Hrī means that one should be very modest and must not perform some act which is abominable.”
hinduism.explanation: Commenting on the list of divine qualities in Gita 16.1-3, Prabhupada defines hrī, modesty, as the refusal to do anything abominable.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's own definition: real shame is recoiling from a base deed.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.1-3, purport (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
christianity.explanation: Joseph refuses the advances of Potiphar's wife, recoiling from the act itself rather than from the risk of being caught.
christianity.tie_back: Joseph's recoil is the ‘shame at a deed’ that the Kural calls true naan.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Prophet (ﷺ) was more shy than a virgin in her separate room. And if he saw a thing which he disliked, we would recognize that (feeling) in his face.”
islam.explanation: Abu Sa'id describes the Prophet's haya' as deeper than a secluded maiden's, and as showing on his face at anything objectionable.
islam.tie_back: The hadith brings together the two kinds of shame the Kural separates: a maiden's bashfulness and a good person's recoil from what is wrong.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is a good sign in a person that he is one who experiences shame. Others say: Any person who experiences shame will not quickly sin”
judaism.explanation: Reading Exodus 20:17 (‘that His fear may be upon your faces’) as shame, the baraita teaches that shame leads to fear of sin.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it values shame because it holds a person back from wrong deeds.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 20a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And what is the treasure of conscience? There is the case where a disciple of the noble ones feels shame at [the thought of engaging in] bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha counts hiri, shame at misconduct of body, speech and mind, among the seven noble treasures.
buddhism.tie_back: It defines shame exactly as the Kural does: shrinking from wrong action.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.6, Dhana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “By repenting of one's sins before the Guru the soul obtains humiliation; feeling humiliated, he will leave off all blameable occupations, and apply himself to praiseworthy occupations”
jainism.explanation: Among the exertions in righteousness, garhā, owning one's faults before the teacher, produces a humbling shame that turns a person away from blameworthy acts.
jainism.tie_back: For the Jain monk as for the Kural, the valuable shame is the one that makes a person drop blameworthy deeds.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make modesty your circumcision, and good conduct your fast. In this way, you shall be a true Muslim.”
sikhism.explanation: Speaking to Muslims in Majh ki Vaar, Guru Nanak turns outward religious marks into inner virtues, making saram (modesty, recoil from wrong) the real sign of faith.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural separates true shame, recoil from a wrong deed, from customary bashfulness; Guru Nanak likewise sets inward modesty above the outward form.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Raag Majh, Majh ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hector tells Andromache he cannot hang back from the fighting, because he would feel deep shame (aidos) before the Trojan men and long-robed women if he shrank from battle like a coward.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Iliad, aidos is the feeling that keeps a hero from a base act even when safety tempts him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hector's aidos, like the Kural's naan, is shame at a deed and not mere shyness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says shame (aidos) is a kind of fear of disrepute, more a feeling than a virtue. It suits the young, who still go wrong. A decent person should not need it, because he should not do disgraceful things in the first place.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle places shame in actions: it is felt for voluntary bad acts, and its value lies in steering us away from them.
philosophy.tie_back: He agrees with the Kural that real shame is about deeds, but he ranks it below virtue, where Valluvar treats it as an ornament of the noble.

real_life_example.event_title: General Ludwig Beck resigns rather than prepare an attack on Czechoslovakia
real_life_example.event: As chief of the German army general staff, Ludwig Beck sent Hitler memoranda in 1938 opposing the planned attack on Czechoslovakia. In the summer of 1938 he urged the senior generals to resign together to prevent a European war; when they would not, he stepped down from his post alone that August.
real_life_example.explanation: Beck recoiled from a deed he judged wrong even though going along with it was the safe and expected course, and he became a leading figure of the German resistance.
real_life_example.tie_back: Valluvar's first kural defines true shame as shrinking back from a wrongful deed, and Beck's resignation was exactly such a refusal to put his hand to a deed he found base.

tamil:
ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல
நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Oonudai echcham uyirkkellaam veralla
naanudaimai maandhar sirappu.
meaning: Food, clothing and the other needs of life are the same for every living being. What makes humans special is a sense of shame.
elementary: A puppy eats, a bird sleeps, and you eat and sleep too. So what makes a person special? Valluvar says it is the little voice that says “that would be wrong, I'd be ashamed to do it.” Animals don't have that voice. People do.
university: Oon (ஊண், 'food'), udai (உடை, 'clothing') and echcham (எச்சம், 'the remainder', i.e. the other bodily needs) are veralla (வேறல்ல, 'not different') for all uyir (உயிர், 'living beings'). By contrast naanudaimai (நாணுடைமை, 'the possession of shame') is maandhar sirappu (மாந்தர் சிறப்பு, 'the distinction of humans'). Kesikan and Varadarasanar take the first line to cover all beings and sets of people. Pappaiah narrows the contrast: food and clothing are common to all people, while shame distinguishes the good. Kalaignar explains naanudaimai as avoiding what others condemn. The kural thus makes shame the defining mark of the human, an idea that echoes widely in Indian (Hitopadesha) and Greek (Protagoras) ethics. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Hitopadesha says that eating, sleeping, fear and mating are common to humans and animals. Dharma is the one extra thing that marks out humans, and without it a person is the same as a beast.
hinduism.explanation: This well-known Sanskrit maxim sets the bodily needs shared by all creatures against the moral sense that only humans have.
hinduism.tie_back: Its structure matches the Kural's exactly: common bodily needs in the first line, and in the second the one quality that makes a person truly human, here dharma and in the Kural shame.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Introduction (Prastāvikā), verse beginning āhāra-nidrā-bhaya-maithunaṃ ca (verse numbering varies by edition)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.”
christianity.explanation: In Genesis the first humans, once their eyes are opened, feel a shame no animal feels and cover themselves.
christianity.tie_back: The verse treats shame as a uniquely human awareness, as the Kural does, though in Genesis it comes with the Fall.

islam.quote_or_event: “Every religion has its distinct characteristic, and the distinct characteristic of Islam is modesty.”
islam.explanation: The hadith names haya', modesty or shame, as the distinguishing character of Islam.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes shame the hallmark that sets a people apart.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are three distinguishing marks of this nation, the Jewish people. They are merciful, they are shamefaced, and they perform acts of kindness.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud attributes to David the teaching that being shamefaced is one of the three marks that identify the people of Israel.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a sense of shame is the distinctive quality of the people who have it.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 79a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, these two bright qualities guard the world. Which two? Conscience & concern. If these two bright qualities did not guard the world, there would be no recognition of ‘mother’ here... The world would be immersed in promiscuity, like rams with goats, roosters with pigs, or dogs with jackals.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that conscience (hiri) and concern (ottappa) are what separate human society from the indiscriminate life of animals.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point almost exactly: without shame, humans would be no different from other creatures.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.9, Lokapala Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Four things of paramount value are difficult to obtain here by a living being: human birth, instruction in the Law, belief in it, and energy in self-control.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's teaching holds that a human birth is valuable not for what it shares with other births but for the chance it gives for restraint and the Law.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it finds what is special about being human in moral restraint rather than in bodily life.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 3.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make virtue your bread, good conduct the ghee, and modesty the meat to eat.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Bihaagra ki Vaar headed Mardana 1 (traditionally Guru Nanak addressing his companion Bhai Mardana), the ordinary staples of life are turned into virtues, with modesty as the meat of the meal.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says food and clothing are common to all beings and that shame is what sets good people apart; the salok makes modesty itself the true food of a human life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 553, Raag Bihaagra, Bihaagra ki Vaar (salok headed Mardana 1) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Prometheus myth told in Plato's Protagoras, humans have fire and crafts but keep destroying one another, so Zeus sends Hermes to give every person aidos (shame) and dike (justice). Anyone who cannot share in them is to be put to death as a plague on the city.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the myth, shame is the gift that turns clever animals into people who can live together.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes shame, not the means of bodily survival, the defining human excellence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Life seems to be common even to plants, but we are seeking what is peculiar to man. Let us exclude, therefore, the life of nutrition and growth. Next there would be a life of perception, but it also seems to be common even to the horse, the ox, and every animal.”
philosophy.explanation: In his function argument, Aristotle sets aside the life of nourishment and of sensation, which humans share with plants and animals. He looks for what is proper to man alone and finds it in rational, virtuous activity.
philosophy.tie_back: The argument has the Kural's shape, setting aside the needs shared by all living things to find what marks out the good human. Valluvar finds that mark in shame where Aristotle finds it in reason.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7, 1097b-1098a (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Darwin calls blushing the most human of all expressions
real_life_example.event: In The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, published by John Murray in 1872, Charles Darwin gave a whole chapter to self-attention, shame, shyness, modesty and blushing. He opened it with the sentence "Blushing is the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions," and argued that no animal could be shown to blush.
real_life_example.explanation: A founder of modern biology concluded that the outward sign of shame is the one expression that sets humans apart from other animals.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says food and clothing are common to all living beings and that shame is what distinguishes humans; Darwin reached a strikingly similar conclusion from the study of expression.

tamil:
ஊனைக் குறித்த உயிரெல்லாம் நாண்என்னும்
நன்மை குறித்தது சால்பு.
transliteration:
Oonaik kuriththa uyirellaam naanennum
nanmai kuriththadhu saalpu.
meaning: Every living being lives in a body. In the same way, perfect character lives in the good quality called shame.
elementary: A snail lives in its shell and a turtle lives in its shell; they can't live without them. Valluvar says goodness lives inside shame the same way. If you take away a person's shame, their goodness has no home left.
university: The kural builds an exact parallel. Uyir ellaam oonaik kuriththa (உயிரெல்லாம் ஊனைக் குறித்த): all lives have the body of flesh (ஊன்) as their seat. Saalpu (சால்பு, 'fullness of noble character', the virtue treated in ch. 99, Saanraanmai) has as its seat the nanmai (நன்மை, 'goodness') called naan. The verb kuriththal ('to aim at, to take as one's place') is repeated in both lines. Kesikan presses the image further: as lives never willingly leave their body, saalpu never leaves shame. Kalaignar renders saalpu as maanbu ('dignity'). Pope's ‘perfect virtue ever dwells with shame’ keeps the doubled structure. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…gentleness; modesty; steady determination; vigor; forgiveness; fortitude; cleanliness; and freedom from envy and from the passion for honor – these transcendental qualities, O son of Bharata, belong to godly men endowed with divine nature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists hrīḥ, modesty, among the qualities that make up the ‘divine endowment’ (daivī sampad).
hinduism.tie_back: For the Gita as for the Kural, modesty is part of the seat of a perfected character.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.1-3 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?”
christianity.explanation: Paul pictures the body as the dwelling of the Spirit, and calls believers to purity because of who lives in them.
christianity.tie_back: The verse matches only the Kural's dwelling-place image (a body housing what is highest), not its claim about shame.

islam.quote_or_event: “Faith (Belief) consists of more than sixty branches (i.e. parts). And Haya … is a part of faith.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet counts haya', the sense of shame and modesty, as an inseparable branch of faith.
islam.tie_back: As the Kural seats saalpu in shame, the hadith makes shame part of the very body of faith.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When pride cometh, then cometh shame; But with the lowly is wisdom.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs holds that wisdom dwells with the tzenu'im, the modest or lowly, while pride ends in disgrace.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates the highest human excellence in modesty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Difficult is life for the modest one who always seeks purity, is detached and unassuming, clean in life, and discerning.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada lists modesty first among the traits of the one who pursues purity and discernment.
buddhism.tie_back: The verse ties modesty to the full set of noble qualities, much as the Kural seats saalpu in shame.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 245 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The body is the boat, life is the sailor, and the Circle of Births is the ocean which is crossed by the great sages.”
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue between Kesi and Gautama, the body is the vessel in which the jiva (life) dwells and travels across samsara.
jainism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's first-line image of life housed in flesh, though not the claim that nobility is housed in shame.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.73 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Modesty and righteousness both, O Nanak, are qualities of those who are blessed with true wealth.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak pairs saram (modesty) with dharam (righteousness), as two qualities that dwell together in those who are truly rich.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says noble character dwells in shame as life dwells in the body; Guru Nanak likewise treats modesty as the companion and seat of righteousness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1287, Raag Malaar, Malaar ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar calls Aidos (Shame or Reverence) the daughter of Prometheus (Forethought). She is a goddess who gives men excellence and joy, and when forgetfulness clouds the mind she slips away.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek religious imagination, Aidos is a divine power with whom excellence (arete) comes and goes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats shame as the place where excellence lives, so that losing it means losing excellence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza grants that shame is not a virtue, since it is a kind of pain, but says it is good insofar as it shows that the person feeling it wants to live honourably. In the same way, pain is good insofar as it shows the injured part is not yet putrefied.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, shame is a sign that the desire for an honourable life is still present.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he treats shame as evidence that goodness is still at home in a person.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics IV, Proposition 58, Scholium (tr. R.H.M. Elwes)

real_life_example.event_title: JAL's president takes responsibility after the Flight 123 crash
real_life_example.event: On 12 August 1985 a Japan Air Lines Boeing 747 crashed into a mountain in Gunma Prefecture, the worst single-aircraft accident in history up to that time. JAL president Yasumoto Takagi apologised in person to the victims' relatives, publicly accepted responsibility for the accident and told Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone that he would resign; a successor was named later that year.
real_life_example.explanation: Time noted that Japanese leaders considered it ethically required to leave office when something went disastrously wrong on their watch, even without direct personal fault.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural makes shame the very seat of nobility, as the body is the seat of life, and Takagi's response showed a leader's standing resting on his readiness to feel and answer for a disgrace.

tamil:
அணிஅன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு அஃதின்றேல்
பிணிஅன்றோ பீடு நடை.
transliteration:
Aniandro naanudaimai saandrorkku ahdhindrel
piniandro peedu nadai.
meaning: Isn't a sense of shame the jewel of good people? Without it, isn't their proud walk just like a sickness?
elementary: Imagine a champion who wins a race and then struts around boasting and laughing at everyone else. It spoils everything, like a sickness. But a champion who wins and stays kind and modest shines like someone wearing a beautiful necklace. Modesty is that necklace.
university: Two rhetorical questions with ‘andro’ (அன்றோ, ‘is it not?’) frame the kural. Naanudaimai is ani (அணி, 'ornament, jewel') to the saandror (சான்றோர், 'the noble, the perfected'). Without it (ahdhu indrel), their peedu nadai (பீடு நடை, 'gait of eminence, proud bearing') is pini (பிணி, 'disease'). Varadarasanar reads the disease as the proud walk itself. Pappaiah, more pointedly, says it is a disease to those who must watch it. Kalaignar glosses naan here as inward remorse for a wrong done. Pope: ‘without it step of stately pride is piteous thing to see.’ Thirukkural.net prints a final full stop that ytamizh.com omits; the words are otherwise identical, so the difference is only punctuation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Pride, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance – these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: Right after listing modesty among the divine qualities, the Gita lists pride and conceit among the demonic ones.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita sets modesty against pride the same way the Kural does, and treats pride as a corruption of nature, much like the Kural's ‘disease’.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.4 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells believers that their true jewellery is an inner, meek and quiet spirit, not gold or fine clothes.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's first line almost word for word: a humble spirit is the real ornament.

islam.quote_or_event: “O children of Adam, We have bestowed upon you clothing to conceal your private parts and as adornment. But the clothing of righteousness - that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an sets outward clothing and adornment beneath the garment of righteousness (libas al-taqwa).
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names an inner moral quality as a person's best adornment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “the arrogant is headed for Gehinnom and the blushing for the garden of Eden.”
judaism.explanation: Judah ben Tema contrasts the brazen-faced, who end in Gehinnom, with the shamefaced, who reach Eden.
judaism.tie_back: The same contrast as the Kural: the blushing are adorned, while the proud bearing leads to ruin.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:20 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To be proud of birth, of wealth or clan, and to despise one's own kinsmen — this is a cause of one's downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the causes of a person's decline, the Buddha names arrogance about birth, wealth and clan.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows that eminence carried without humility turns into a ruin.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 1.6, Parabhava Sutta (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: Bahubali stands so long in motionless meditation that vines climb his body, yet omniscience does not come. His sisters, the nuns Brahmi and Sundari, tell him to come down from the elephant of pride, since he still refuses to bow to younger brothers who became monks before him. When he lets go of that pride and takes his first step to go and honour them, kevala-jnana dawns.
jainism.explanation: In Jain narrative, even the greatest austerity is blocked by pride, and true greatness appears only when humility returns.
jainism.tie_back: Bahubali's lofty stance without humility is the Kural's ‘stately walk’ that becomes a sickness.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5 (tr. Helen M. Johnson); also in the Adipurana tradition

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Ego is a chronic disease, but it contains its own cure as well.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Asa di Vaar, Guru Angad calls haumai (ego), the root problem in Sikh teaching, a long-lasting disease that can still be cured through the Guru's grace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that without shame the proud, stately walk of the great is a sickness; Guru Angad names that pride, ego, as the disease itself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Niobe boasts that with her many children she is greater than the goddess Leto, who has only two. Apollo and Artemis kill all her children, and the grieving Niobe is turned to weeping stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Niobe's hubris, pride without restraint or reverence, brings ruin on her whole house.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Her boasting is the Kural's stately walk without modesty, and it ends in a fatal sickness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's chariot allegory the noble white horse is a lover of honour joined with temperance and modesty, and needs only a word of command. The dark horse is a companion of insolence and pride, and barely yields to whip and goad.
philosophy.explanation: Plato pictures the well-ordered soul as led by a modest, honour-loving nature, and the disordered soul as driven by arrogance.
philosophy.tie_back: The modest horse wears the Kural's jewel; the proud horse is the Kural's sickness of pride.

real_life_example.event_title: Turkmenistan's ruler raises a revolving gold statue of himself
real_life_example.event: In 1998 President Saparmurat Niyazov, who styled himself Turkmenbashi, 'Father of all Turkmen', built the Arch of Neutrality in Ashgabat, crowned with a gold-coloured statue of himself that rotated so as to face the sun throughout the day. He also renamed the months of the year after himself and members of his family. After his death his successor restored the old month names and removed the statue from the city centre in 2010.
real_life_example.explanation: The monument became a world-famous emblem of pomp without restraint, and it was quietly dismantled once its builder was gone.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that without shame the proud, stately bearing of the great becomes a sickness to behold, and Niyazov's self-glorifying statue was such a display.

tamil:
பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார் நாணுக்கு
உறைபதி என்னும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Pirarpazhiyum thampazhiyum naanuvaar naanukku
uraipadhi ennum ulagu.
meaning: People who feel ashamed of other people's wrongs as much as their own are the ones the world calls the true home of shame.
elementary: When your friend gets caught being unkind, do you just laugh? Or do you feel a little hot in the face, as if it were you? Valluvar says the people who feel ashamed even when someone else does wrong are the ones whose hearts are truly good.
university: Pirar pazhi (பிறர்பழி, 'the blame or disgrace of others') and tham pazhi (தம்பழி, 'one's own disgrace') are set side by side. The one who naanuvaar (நாணுவார், 'feels shame') at both is called by the world naanukku uraipadhi (நாணுக்கு உறைபதி, 'the dwelling-place of shame itself'). Kesikan stresses that such a person weighs the two kinds of blame equally. Pappaiah reads ‘not only one's own but also others' blame’. Pope's couplet, ‘Who feel ashamed for others' guilt as for their own’, follows the same line. The kural extends shame from a private brake to a shared moral sensitivity, which fits the Kudiyiyal's concern with the honour of family and community. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the dice-hall of the Mahabharata, while elders like Bhishma and Drona stay silent as Draupadi is humiliated, the young Kaurava prince Vikarna rises alone. He is stung by the shame the assembly is bringing on itself, and he protests that the wrong being done must be named.
hinduism.explanation: Vikarna feels the disgrace of his own kin and elders as if it were his own, and cannot keep silent.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural's naanukku uraipadhi: ashamed of others' wrongdoing as much as of his own.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta sub-parva), Vikarna's protest

christianity.quote_or_event: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that when any believer is made to stumble, he himself burns with distress.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's ideal, Paul feels another's moral fall as his own.

islam.quote_or_event: “You see the believers as regards their being merciful among themselves and showing love among themselves and being kind, resembling one body, so that, if any part of the body is not well then the whole body shares the sleeplessness (insomnia) and fever with it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the community as one body, so that one member's affliction is felt by all.
islam.tie_back: This solidarity underlies the Kural's ideal of feeling another's disgrace as one's own.

judaism.quote_or_event: “O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to Thee, my God; for our iniquities are increased over our head, and our guiltiness is grown up unto the heavens.”
judaism.explanation: Ezra, who had not himself transgressed, tears his garments and confesses the people's sin as ‘our iniquities’, blushing before God.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ideal exactly: an innocent man ashamed of others' guilt as if it were his own.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one's own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another's faults, but hides one's own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha criticises the habit of airing others' faults while hiding one's own.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's noble person does the opposite: he weighs others' blame and his own alike and feels both.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 252 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: Umasvati teaches four attitudes to cultivate: friendliness (maitri) toward all living beings, joy (pramoda) in the virtuous, compassion (karunya) for those in distress, and equanimity (madhyasthya) toward the ill-behaved.
jainism.explanation: These four reflections widen the Jain practitioner's moral feeling to include the condition of others.
jainism.tie_back: They share the Kural's outward-turned sensitivity, though Jainism asks for compassion and equanimity toward others' faults, not shame at them.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.6 (Svetambara numbering; 7.11 in Digambara numbering), tr. Nathmal Tatia

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the state reached in the company of the holy, in which no one is felt to be other than oneself.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises those who feel another's disgrace as keenly as their own; Guru Arjan's refusal to count anyone a stranger is the outlook from which such shared shame grows.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Paris shrinks back from facing Menelaus, his brother Hector rebukes him bitterly. Paris's cowardice is a disgrace to their father, their city and all their people, and Hector feels that disgrace keenly as his own family's.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector cannot treat his brother's shame as someone else's business; it stains the whole house.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's ideal, Hector feels his kinsman's disgrace as his own.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith observes that we blush for the impudence and rudeness of another person even when he himself seems to have no sense of how improperly he is behaving.
philosophy.explanation: Smith's account of sympathy explains how we come to feel a shame that properly belongs to someone else.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘ashamed of others' blame as of one's own’, explained through the psychology of sympathy.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments I.i.1.10 (1759)

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi calls off his campaign after the violence at Chauri Chaura
real_life_example.event: On 4 February 1922 a crowd of protesters in Chauri Chaura, in the United Provinces, set fire to a police station and 22 policemen died. Although Gandhi was far away and had not ordered it, he called the episode a sign that the country was not ready, suspended the mass civil disobedience he had planned to launch from Bardoli, and fasted as a penance; Britannica records that he described his own launch of the campaign as a "Himalayan blunder."
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi treated a wrong done by others in the name of his movement as his own fault, to the dismay of many colleagues who wanted the campaign to continue.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises those who feel ashamed of others' wrongs as of their own, and Gandhi's penance for the deed of a distant crowd is a near-literal example.

tamil:
நாண்வேலி கொள்ளாது மன்னோ வியன்ஞாலம்
பேணலர் மேலா யவர்.
transliteration:
Naanveli kollaadhu manno viyangnaalam
paenalar melaa yavar.
meaning: Great people would not want even the whole wide world if it meant losing shame, the fence that guards them.
elementary: A garden has a fence so goats can't come in and eat the flowers. Valluvar says good people keep a fence of shame around their hearts. Even if someone offered them the whole world, they wouldn't trade away that fence.
university: Naan veli (நாண்வேலி, 'the hedge or fence that is shame') is the central image. The melaayavar (மேலாயவர், 'the superior ones') will not paenal (பேணல், 'cherish, desire') the viyan gnaalam (வியன்ஞாலம், 'vast world') without taking (kollaadhu) that hedge; manno (மன்னோ) is an emphatic particle. Kesikan and Pappaiah, in the line of Parimelazhagar, take it to mean that the great choose shame rather than the wide world as their protection. Varadarasanar reads it as saying the great would not want to live in the wide world without the protecting hedge of shame. Pope gives a more poetic turn: ‘For men of lofty soul the earth's vast realms no charms retain’ unless the hedge stays intact. Sivayogi Sivakumar's modern reading, that one cannot rise to greatness without the hedge, is a minority interpretation. The text is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Yama offers the boy Nachiketas long life, cattle, horses, gold, wide lands and every pleasure if only he will stop asking about what lies beyond death. Nachiketas refuses: let Yama keep the horses, the dance and the song; he will hold to the one boon he asked for.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad praises the one who turns down the whole pleasant world for the sake of what is truly good (śreyas).
hinduism.tie_back: Nachiketas, like the Kural's great ones, would not take the vast world at the price of what guards his soul.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that winning the whole world is worthless if it costs a person his soul.
christianity.tie_back: The same trade the Kural rejects: the vast world is not worth losing the inner safeguard.

islam.quote_or_event: “Once Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) passed by an Ansari (man) who was admonishing his brother regarding Haya'. On that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said, ‘Leave him as Haya' is a part of faith.’”
islam.explanation: A man scolds his brother for being too bashful, presumably because it cost him worldly advantage, and the Prophet defends the bashfulness as part of faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's great ones, the Prophet would rather keep haya' than gain worldly advantage by giving it up.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Tradition is a fence to the Torah; Tithes a fence to wealth, Vows a fence to abstinence; A fence to wisdom is silence.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Akiva describes protective practices as fences (seyag) that guard a deeper good.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's image of shame as a fence guarding the good person.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:13 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who in the world is a man constrained by conscience, who awakens to censure like a fine stallion to the whip? Those restrained by conscience are rare”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures hiri (conscience, shame) as the restraint that keeps a person on the path, like a thoroughbred that answers to a mere touch of the whip.
buddhism.tie_back: Shame here is the guard of the noble person, as in the Kural's hedge.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 1.18, Hiri Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “…by hearing and understanding which the monks will reach a high degree of self-discipline, of Samvara, and of contemplation, will be well protected (by the three Guptis), will guard their senses, guard their chastity, and will thus never be remiss”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana sets out ten protective conditions around celibacy. Later Jain tradition calls these the nava vāḍa, literally ‘nine fences’, of brahmacarya.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's naan veli, these are deliberate fences that guard a monk's purity.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 16, prose introduction (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If I were to become an emperor and raise a huge army, and sit on a throne, issuing commands and collecting taxes-O Nanak, all of this could pass away like a puff of wind.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak imagines himself given an emperor's throne and power, and refuses to value it if it would make him forget the Name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the great would not want the whole wide world at the price of their hedge of shame; Guru Nanak would not want a whole empire at the price of forgetting God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 14, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Through twenty years and the pressure of many powerful suitors who could give her a new household and status, Penelope keeps her faith with absent Odysseus. She puts them off with the trick of weaving and unweaving Laertes' shroud.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope's guarded fidelity, which Homer praises as her renown, protects her and her house better than any worldly alliance could.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She is the Kural's noble one, who prefers the guard of honour to the gains the world offers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus tells someone urging him to get money for his friends that if it can be had while keeping his self-respect, fidelity and magnanimity, he will get it. But if he is asked to lose his own proper good so that others can gain what is not truly good, the request is foolish and unjust.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, a person's aidos (self-respect, modesty) and good faith are worth more than any external gain.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's great ones, Epictetus will not trade the guard of his own integrity for the goods of the world.

real_life_example.event_title: Nelson Mandela rejects a conditional release from prison
real_life_example.event: On 31 January 1985 State President P. W. Botha offered Nelson Mandela, in prison since the Rivonia Trial, his release on condition that he renounce violence as a means of political change. Mandela refused, and on 10 February 1985 his daughter Zindzi read his written reply to a rally at Jabulani Stadium in Soweto, where he said he could not accept freedom while his organisation remained banned and his people were not free.
real_life_example.explanation: Mandela chose to remain in prison, where he stayed for five more years, rather than accept personal freedom on terms he considered dishonourable to his cause.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the truly great would not take even the wide world without the hedge of shame, and Mandela declined freedom itself rather than accept it on dishonouring terms.

tamil:
நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால்
நாண்துறவார் நாணாள் பவர்.
transliteration:
Naanaal uyiraith thurappar uyirpporuttaal
naanthuravaar naanaal pavar.
meaning: People who live by shame will give up their life to keep it, but they will never give up shame to save their life.
elementary: Some heroes in stories are asked to do something really wrong, like betray a friend, or else they'll be hurt. And they say no, even though it's scary. Valluvar says people with real shame would rather lose everything than do something shameful.
university: The kural is built as a chiasmus. Naanaal uyiraith thurappar (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர், 'for shame's sake they renounce life') is mirrored by uyir poruttaal naan thuravaar (உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார், 'for life's sake they do not renounce shame'). Naan aalpavar (நாணாள்பவர், 'those who wield or rule by shame') are its subject. Kesikan frames it as a dilemma: when shame and life cannot both be kept, the noble let life go. Kalaignar substitutes maanam (honour), linking the kural to ch. 97 (Maanam), where similar sentiments appear (e.g. kural 969 on the yak that dies on losing its hair). Pope: ‘The men of modest soul for shame would life an offering make.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that for an honoured man, disgrace is worse than dying.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ranking exactly: losing one's shame or honour is worse than losing one's life.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.34 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples to value faithfulness above bodily survival.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks bodily life below the inner good one must never surrender.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘My Lord, prison is more to my liking than that to which they invite me. And if You do not avert from me their plan, I might incline toward them and [thus] be of the ignorant.’”
islam.explanation: Pressed to give in to seduction or face prison, Joseph (Yusuf) chooses the dungeon over a shameful act.
islam.tie_back: Yusuf would give up his freedom rather than his modesty, the Kural's choice made concrete.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud rules that for three sins, idol worship, forbidden sexual relations and bloodshed, a person must let himself be killed rather than transgress (yehareg ve'al ya'avor).
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic law sets certain boundaries that may not be crossed even to save one's life.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's principle as law: life is given up before the deepest integrity is.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells his monks that even if bandits were to saw them limb from limb with a two-handled saw, anyone who let his mind turn to hatred would not be following his teaching.
buddhism.explanation: The Saw Simile demands that a monk keep his inner discipline even at the cost of a terrible death.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks keeping one's moral self above keeping one's body alive.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (The Simile of the Saw)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Fie upon you, famous knight, who want to quaff the vomited drink for the sake of this life; it would be better for you to die.”
jainism.explanation: The nun Rajimati rebukes the monk Rathanemi when he tempts her to break their vows, telling him death would be better than such shamelessness. Shamed, he returns to the Law.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati states the Kural's principle outright: better to die than to give up shame for the sake of this life.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.42 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45); the same verse appears in Dasavaikalika Sutra 2

sikhism.quote_or_event: “those who merely live shall depart in dishonor; everything they eat is impure.”
sikhism.explanation: In Majh ki Vaar, Guru Nanak says that a life that goes on after its honour (pat) is lost is worthless, and everything it consumes is tainted.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who live by shame will give up life rather than shame; Guru Nanak says that life kept at the cost of honour is not worth living.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Majh, Majh ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Troy falls, the captive princess Polyxena is led to be sacrificed at Achilles' tomb. She refuses to be held and goes freely to her death rather than live as a slave, and even as she falls she takes care to fall modestly.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides presents Polyxena as choosing an honourable death over a shameful life and keeping her modesty to the end.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Polyxena is the Kural's naan-aalpavar: she gives up life for shame's sake and never gives up shame for life's sake.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At his trial Socrates says that a man worth anything should not weigh the chances of living or dying. He should ask only whether he is acting rightly or wrongly. Achilles chose death rather than disgrace.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates refuses to save his life by giving up philosophy or begging shamefully.
philosophy.tie_back: His stance is the Kural's: life may be given up, integrity may not.

real_life_example.event_title: Giordano Bruno refuses to recant
real_life_example.event: After years of imprisonment and trial by the Roman Inquisition, the philosopher Giordano Bruno declared that he had nothing to retract. Pope Clement VIII ordered him sentenced as an impenitent heretic; the sentence was read to him on 8 February 1600, and he was executed in the Campo de' Fiori on 17 February 1600.
real_life_example.explanation: Bruno is remembered as a person who gave up his life rather than disown the convictions he held, and a statue was raised to him at the place of his execution in 1889.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those who live by shame will give up life for its sake but never give it up to save life, and Bruno would not recant even to escape death.

tamil:
பிறர்நாணத் தக்கது தான்நாணா னாயின்
அறம்நாணத் தக்கது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Pirarnaanath thakkadhu thaannaanaa naayin
aramnaanath thakkadhu udaiththu.
meaning: If a person feels no shame at things that would make others ashamed, then goodness itself (what is right) will be ashamed of that person.
elementary: Imagine someone does something so rude that everyone watching feels embarrassed, but he just grins. Valluvar says that even Goodness itself would feel embarrassed to be his friend and would quietly walk away from him.
university: The kural personifies aram (அறம், 'virtue, dharma'). If one does not feel shame (thaan naanaan aayin) at what is pirar naanath thakkadhu (பிறர்நாணத் தக்கது, 'fit to make others ashamed'), then he udaiththu (உடைத்து, 'has in him') something aram naanath thakkadhu, at which virtue itself would blush. There are two lines of interpretation. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar say virtue, ashamed, abandons him. Pappaiah and Kesikan say he harbours a fault at which virtue is ashamed. Kesikan's gloss reads the first line as ‘what onlookers would blame’. Pope's ‘Virtue will shrink away ashamed of thee!’ follows the abandonment reading. The repeated naanath thakkadhu across both lines is characteristic Valluvar wordplay. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are demoniac do not know what is to be done and what is not to be done. Neither cleanliness nor proper behavior nor truth is found in them.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita describes the āsuric person as one from whom right conduct and truth have departed.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the shameless person of the Kural, from whom virtue has withdrawn.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.7 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes people who glory in what ought to shame them.
christianity.tie_back: They are the Kural's shameless ones, unashamed of what should shame anyone.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of the sayings of the early Prophets which the people have got is: If you don't feel ashamed … do whatever you like.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet quotes the ancient maxim that once shame is gone, nothing holds a person back from anything.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes shamelessness the moment moral restraint is lost.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They shall be put to shame because they have committed abomination; Yea, they are not at all ashamed, Neither know they how to blush; Therefore they shall fall among them that fall”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah condemns a people who commit abominations without the least blush.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's shameless man, who will not blush at what should shame him, and who falls.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easy is life for the shameless one who is impudent as a crow, is backbiting and forward, arrogant and corrupt.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the shameless, brazen as a crow, find life easy precisely because nothing restrains them.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's person who feels no shame where others would.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 244 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “By repenting of one's sins to oneself the soul obtains repentance, and becoming indifferent by repentance he prepares for himself an (ascending) scale of virtues, by which he destroys the Karman resulting from delusion.”
