jainism.explanation: Nindā, inwardly condemning one's own faults, is what keeps a soul climbing the scale of virtues.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point from the other side: without inner shame at wrongdoing, virtue has nowhere to stand.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Modesty and righteousness both have vanished, and falsehood struts around like a leader, O Lalo.”
sikhism.explanation: Describing the sack of Saidpur in his Babarvani hymns, Guru Nanak tells his disciple Lalo that saram (modesty) and dharam (righteousness) have both gone into hiding.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that when a person loses shame, virtue itself is ashamed and leaves; Guru Nanak shows modesty and righteousness leaving together.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 722, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And then Aidos and Nemesis … with their sweet forms wrapped in white robes, will go from the wide-pathed earth and forsake mankind to join the company of the deathless gods”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod foresees that when men grow utterly shameless, the goddesses Shame and Righteous Indignation will abandon the earth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's image exactly: a divine personified virtue, ashamed, departs from the shameless.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 197-200 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, Theoi Classical Texts Library)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Theophrastus sketches the Shameless Man (anaischyntos), who cheats the people he owes, borrows from the person he has just defrauded, and treats anything as acceptable as long as he gains by it, untroubled by what others think.
philosophy.explanation: Theophrastus' character sketch shows how one who feels no shame drifts from every decent norm.
philosophy.tie_back: It portrays the man the Kural warns of, who does unblushingly what would shame anyone else.

real_life_example.event_title: Joseph Welch asks Senator McCarthy whether he has any sense of decency
real_life_example.event: During the televised Army-McCarthy hearings, Senator Joseph McCarthy publicly accused Fred Fisher, a young lawyer in the firm of Army counsel Joseph Welch, of past links to a group he called a Communist front. Welch rebuked him before the cameras, ending with the question "Have you no sense of decency?", and the hearing room broke into applause. In December 1954 the Senate voted to condemn McCarthy's conduct.
real_life_example.explanation: The exchange is widely seen as the turning point at which public opinion turned against McCarthy.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that a man who feels no shame at what would shame others is abandoned by virtue itself, and McCarthy's standing collapsed soon after he was publicly shown to lack that shame.

tamil:
குலஞ்சுடும் கொள்கை பிழைப்பின் நலஞ்சுடும்
நாணின்மை நின்றக் கடை.
transliteration:
Kulanjudum kolgai pizhaippin nalanjudum
naaninmai nindrak kadai.
meaning: Slipping from good behaviour burns away the good name of your family. But once you become shameless, it burns away every good thing you have.
elementary: If you break a rule once, people might think less of your family for a while. But if you stop caring at all whether you do wrong, it's like a fire that keeps spreading and burns up everything good about you.
university: The kural ranks two fires with the same verb, sudum (சுடும், 'burns, destroys'). If kolgai (கொள்கை, 'one's settled conduct', glossed by the commentators as ozhukkam) pizhaippin (பிழைப்பின், 'should fail'), it burns the kulam (குலம், 'family, lineage'). But naaninmai (நாணின்மை, 'shamelessness') nindra kadai (நின்றக் கடை, 'once it becomes settled') burns all nalam (நலம், 'every good'). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the second fire as more total than the first; Kesikan says the first ruins only the family's standing while the second consumes everything. Kalaignar connects the lines: failing to feel shame at one's lapse lets ruin spread. Pope: ‘'Twill race consume if right observance fail; 'Twill every good consume if shamelessness prevail.’ The text (with the doubled consonant in நின்றக் கடை) is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “With the destruction of the dynasty, the eternal family tradition is vanquished, and thus the rest of the family becomes involved in irreligion.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna fears that once a family's dharma breaks down, adharma overtakes the whole line.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita shares the Kural's concern that a lapse in conduct ruins the kulam.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 1.39 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Speaking lies in hypocrisy; having their conscience seared with a hot iron”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes deceivers whose conscience has been cauterised until it no longer feels.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image of burning (sudum) for what happens when shame is lost.

islam.quote_or_event: “Haya' (pious shyness from committing religeous indiscretions) does not bring anything except good.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that haya' produces only good.
islam.tie_back: The positive counterpart of the Kural: where shame brings only good, shamelessness burns all good away.

judaism.quote_or_event: “one who does not have the capacity to be shamefaced, it is known that his forefathers did not stand at Mount Sinai.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud treats shamelessness as evidence that a person's lineage lacks the formative experience of Sinai.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links a person's shamelessness to the standing of his whole lineage.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 20a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who destroys life, utters lies, takes what is not given, goes to another man's wife, and is addicted to intoxicating drinks — such a man digs up his own root even in this world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that persistent wrongdoing uproots a person's own foundations, here and now.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's fire of shamelessness, settled misconduct destroys every good a person has.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 246-247 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The daughter of the best king, true to self-control and her vows, maintained the honour of her clan and family, and her virtue”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, refusing Rathanemi's advances, guards both her family's honour and her own virtue, and reminds him that those born into a noble family must not fall.
jainism.tie_back: The episode joins the Kural's two concerns: conduct guards the kulam, and shame guards one's whole good.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.40, with 22.43 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Modesty has left her home, and honor has gone away with her.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak pictures modesty walking out of the house and honour following her.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that once shamelessness settles in it burns away every good thing; Guru Nanak shows the same chain, with honour going the moment modesty leaves.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1243, Raag Sarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus' Oresteia the crimes of Atreus, including the feast he served his brother Thyestes, bring a curse on the house that passes from generation to generation: Agamemnon's sacrifice of Iphigenia, his murder by Clytemnestra, and Orestes' revenge.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek tragedy, one shameless outrage blights an entire family line.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's first line on a tragic scale: a breach of conduct burns the kulam.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And does not the legislator and every one who is good for anything, hold this fear in the greatest honour? This is what he terms reverence, and the confidence which is the reverse of this he terms insolence; and the latter he always deems to be a very great evil both to individuals and to states.”
philosophy.explanation: The Athenian Stranger defines shame as the fear of being thought evil for a dishonourable word or deed. Its opposite, a shameless boldness, he calls a very great evil for persons and cities alike.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato, like the Kural, treats the loss of shame as a ruin that goes deeper than any single lapse.

real_life_example.event_title: Boris Onishchenko's rigged epee gets the Soviet pentathlon team thrown out
real_life_example.event: During the fencing stage of the modern pentathlon at the 1976 Montreal Olympics, officials found that Soviet pentathlete Boris Onishchenko's epee had been modified with a hidden switch that could register a hit without any touch. He was disqualified from the Games and banned from the sport, and his disqualification also put the whole Soviet team out of the competition.
real_life_example.explanation: A single act of dishonesty ruined a decorated athlete's career and cost his teammates, who had done nothing wrong, their place in the event.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a lapse in conduct burns the name of one's 'family', and Onishchenko's cheating brought down his team along with himself.

tamil:
நாண்அகத் தில்லார் இயக்கம் மரப்பாவை
நாணால் உயிர்மருட்டி அற்று.
transliteration:
Naanagath thillaar iyakkam marappaavai
naanaal uyirmarutti atru.
meaning: The actions of people with no shame in their hearts are like a wooden puppet moved by strings, which only fools people into thinking it is alive.
elementary: Have you seen a puppet show? The puppet dances and waves, but it isn't really alive; someone is pulling strings. Valluvar says a person with no shame inside is like that: moving around, but with nothing real inside.
university: The chapter closes with a pun on naan (நாண்), which means both ‘shame’ and ‘cord, string’ (as in a bowstring). Those who lack naan agaththu (நாண் அகத்து, 'shame within') move like a marappaavai (மரப்பாவை, 'wooden doll, puppet') that, by naanaal (நாணால், 'by means of strings'), uyir maruttum (உயிர்மருட்டும், 'deceives people into thinking it has life'). Kesikan glosses the strings as the yantra cords of a mechanical doll, and Varadarasanar and Pappaiah describe a doll worked by rope to look alive. So the shameless are alive in appearance only, moved by outside pulls rather than by an inner moral life. The wordplay (shame in the first line, string in the second) is often singled out as one of Valluvar's finest. Pope: ‘'Tis as with strings a wooden puppet apes life's functions.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Lord is situated in everyone's heart, O Arjuna, and is directing the wanderings of all living entities, who are seated as on a machine, made of the material energy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes embodied beings as mounted on a mechanism (yantra), moved about by māyā.
hinduism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's image of a being moved like a mechanical figure, though the Gita applies it to all embodied life, not to the shameless.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.61 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.”
christianity.explanation: The risen Christ tells the church at Sardis that it looks alive but is spiritually dead.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's puppet: an appearance of life with no living core.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the hypocrites as impressive in appearance but hollow, like propped-up pieces of timber.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an and the Kural reach for the same image: wooden figures that only look alive, standing for people empty within.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Psalmist mocks idols of silver and gold: they have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, feet but do not walk. Those who make them, and trust in them, become like them.
judaism.explanation: Psalm 115 contrasts lifeless crafted figures with the living God, and warns that their devotees grow equally lifeless.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a person without a living inner core as no better than a crafted figure that only mimics life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Behold this body — a painted image, a mass of heaped up sores, infirm, full of hankering — of which nothing is lasting or stable!”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls the body a ‘painted image’ (cittakata bimba), a dressed-up figure without lasting substance.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's image of a decorated figure that only looks alive and lasting.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 147 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain doctrine sharply separates jiva, the conscious soul whose mark is awareness, from ajiva, non-sentient matter. The Uttaradhyayana's final lecture sets out this division, and karma is pictured as ajiva matter that binds the jiva and drives its movements through samsara.
jainism.explanation: For Jainism, movement driven by karmic matter rather than by the awakened soul is not true living.
jainism.tie_back: This loosely parallels the Kural's shameless puppet, whose motion comes from strings rather than an inner moral life.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45); Tattvartha Sutra 2.8 (consciousness as the mark of the soul)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “How does the puppet of clay dance?”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas, whose hymns are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, marvels at the human body, a puppet of clay, dancing about as if under its own power while it is pulled by worldly attachment.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares the shameless to a wooden puppet on strings that only seems alive; Ravidas uses the same image of a puppet that dances while having no life of its own.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 487, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hephaestus is attended by handmaidens made of gold that look like living young women. They move, speak and help him as if they had minds of their own, though they are his crafted works.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's golden automata are the classic Greek image of a made thing that imitates life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They are the Kural's marappaavai in myth: figures that fool the eye into seeing life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato's Athenian imagines each of us as a puppet of the gods, pulled by inner cords of pleasure, pain and fear. We should follow only the one soft golden cord of reason and law, and resist the hard iron ones.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, a person who is jerked about by appetites rather than guided by the golden cord lives a puppet's life.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's puppet image applied to ethics: without an inner guiding cord (for Valluvar, naan), a person is moved only by strings.

real_life_example.event_title: Puyi is installed as head of Japanese-controlled Manchukuo
real_life_example.event: After the Japanese army occupied Manchuria in 1931, Japan created the state of Manchukuo in March 1932 and brought Puyi, the last Qing emperor, from Tianjin to serve as its chief executive; he was enthroned as emperor in 1934. Although Manchukuo was proclaimed independent, its government was controlled and supervised by the Japanese, and the League of Nations refused to recognise it.
real_life_example.explanation: Manchukuo became the classic example of a puppet state, with a figurehead ruler moved by others.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural likens those without inner shame to a wooden puppet worked by strings to look alive, and Puyi in Manchukuo was a ruler in appearance only, moved by outside hands.

tamil:
கருமம் செயஒருவன் கைதூவேன் என்னும்
பெருமையின் பீடுடையது இல்.
transliteration:
Karumam seya oruvan kaithooven ennum
perumaiyin peedudaiyadhu il.
meaning: There is no greater honour than a person's promise, 'I will not stop working to help my family grow.'
elementary: Imagine a girl who promises, ‘I will keep helping my family every day, and I won’t give up when it gets boring.’ Valluvar says that promise, kept day after day, is the proudest thing a person can wear, prouder than any medal.
university: The chapter opens by naming its ideal: the person who says kai thooven (கைதூவேன், ‘I will not let my hand rest’) in karumam (கருமம், ‘the work’), understood by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan as the duty of raising one's kudi (குடி, ‘family, lineage, community’). Peedu (பீடு) means dignity or eminence, so the couplet ranks this self-imposed vow above every other form of perumai (பெருமை, ‘greatness’), the subject of chapter 98. Solomon Pappaiah widens kudi to ‘house and country’, a reading he keeps through the whole chapter, while Kesikan, in the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, keeps it to one's own family line. Pope renders it ‘Who says “I’ll do my work, nor slack my hand”, / His greatness, clothed with dignity supreme, shall stand.’ The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For if I ever failed to engage in carefully performing prescribed duties, O Pārtha, certainly all men would follow My path.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that although He needs nothing, He never stops working, because others take their cue from Him.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's ‘I will not rest my hand’, the greatest one refuses to slacken in his work.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.23 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher urges full-strength effort in whatever work lies at hand, since the chance to act does not last.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts honour the hand that does not hold back from its task.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one's own hands. The Prophet (ﷺ) of Allah, David used to eat from the earnings of his manual labor.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises food earned by one's own labour and holds up the prophet-king David as one who lived by his hands.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats tireless work with one's own hands as a mark of honour.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon teaches that no one person completes the great work, but no one may walk away from it either.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's vow ‘I will not slack my hand’ is the same refusal to neglect the work.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:16 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that renown keeps growing for the person who is energetic and disciplined.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say the highest honour belongs to the person of unflagging effort.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 24 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “You have crossed the great ocean; why do you halt so near the shore? make haste to get on the other side; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira urges his disciple Gautama not to slacken now that most of the journey is done, but to press on to the end.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain refrain shares the Kural's refusal to stop before the work is finished, though its goal is liberation, not a family's rise.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “With your hands and feet, do all your work, but let your consciousness remain with the Immaculate Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok among those of Bhagat Kabir, given as Namdev's reply to Trilochan, the devotee is told to keep doing all his work with his own hands and feet while his mind stays on God. It is a classic statement of the Sikh householder ideal of honest work joined to remembrance.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural honours the person who vows never to rest his hands from the work of raising his family; the salok likewise tells the devotee never to stop working with his hands.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1376, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 213, Namdev's reply to Trilochan) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Work is no disgrace: it is idleness which is a disgrace.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his brother Perses that honest toil is honourable and only idleness brings shame.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both poets place honour in the person who keeps working.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, passage at ll. 293-319 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, sacred-texts.com)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius tells himself, when he is reluctant to leave his bed at dawn, that he is rising to do the work of a human being and was not made merely to lie warm under the blankets.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic emperor treats unflagging effort at one's proper work as the very purpose of a human life.
philosophy.tie_back: His self-command matches the Kural's ‘I will not rest my hand.’

real_life_example.event_title: Mary McLeod Bethune opens her school with $1.50
real_life_example.event: Mary McLeod Bethune, the daughter of formerly enslaved parents, opened the Daytona Literary and Industrial Training School for Negro Girls in a rented house with $1.50, five girls and her own son. She raised money tirelessly to keep it going, and within a few years it had grown to some 250 students; it later merged with the Cookman Institute to become Bethune-Cookman.
real_life_example.explanation: Bethune built a lasting institution for her community from almost nothing through unceasing personal labour.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks above all other greatness the vow never to rest one's hands from raising one's people, and Bethune's school embodies that vow.

tamil:
ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும் எனஇரண்டின்
நீள்வினையால் நீளும் குடி.
transliteration:
Aalvinaiyum aandra arivum ena irandin
neelvinaiyaal neelum kudi.
meaning: A family grows and lasts through long, steady work that combines two things: hard effort and full knowledge.
elementary: Building a strong treehouse needs two things: strong arms to hammer and a smart plan so it doesn't fall. Valluvar says a family is the same: hard work plus good thinking, kept up for a long time, makes it grow tall.
university: The couplet names two instruments, aalvinai (ஆள்வினை, ‘manly exertion’, the theme of chapter 62) and aandra arivu (ஆன்ற அறிவு, ‘full, ripened knowledge’), and says that the neelvinai (நீள்வினை, ‘long, unbroken effort’) carried out with both makes the kudi neelum (நீளும், ‘lengthen, extend, flourish’). The play between neel- ‘long’ in the work and neel- ‘lengthen’ in the family is deliberate: duration in effort produces duration in the line. Pope captures this with ‘In deed prolonged, then lengthens out the race’s line.’ Kesikan and Varadarasanar both read the two as effort and knowledge joined in uninterrupted action; Karunanidhi adds ‘deep knowledge and perseverance.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore strive for yoga, which is the art of all work.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that yoga, the joining of right understanding to action, is the true skill in all work.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's pairing of effort with knowledge, the Gita asks for work guided by understanding.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.50 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: The book of Proverbs says that a house is built through wisdom and established by understanding, and that by knowledge its rooms are filled with precious and pleasant riches.
christianity.explanation: The sage teaches that a household rises and endures when skill and understanding work together.
christianity.tie_back: This is close to the Kural's claim that effort joined to knowledge makes a family grow.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Messenger of Allah! Shall I tie it and rely(upon Allah), or leave it loose and rely(upon Allah)?” He said: “Tie it and rely(upon Allah).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells a man to take sensible practical steps and trust God as well, not to trust while doing nothing.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's pairing of effort with prudent knowledge matches this joining of practical care to action.
islam.source: Jami` at-Tirmidhi 2517 (sunnah.com; graded Hasan by Darussalam)

judaism.quote_or_event: “excellent is the study of the Torah when combined with a worldly occupation, for toil in them both keeps sin out of one’s mind”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel praises a life that joins learning with practical work, warning that learning without labour comes to nothing.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says lasting good comes from two things worked at together: knowledge and labour.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:2 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “by whatsoever activity a householder earns his living ... at that he becomes skillful and is not lazy. He is endowed with the power of discernment as to the proper ways and means; he is able to carry out and allocate (duties). This is called the accomplishment of persistent effort.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells lay householders that their welfare rests first on diligent, skilful work guided by discernment.
buddhism.tie_back: It is almost the Kural's formula: effort plus knowledge, kept up, makes a household thrive.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 8.54, Dighajanu (Vyagghapajja) Sutta (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra opens by teaching that right faith, right knowledge and right conduct together make up the path to liberation; none of them is enough alone.
jainism.explanation: Jainism's three jewels insist that knowledge and conduct must be joined for any real progress.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's two-part recipe of knowledge plus effort echoes this Jain insistence on joining knowing and doing, though the goal is liberation, not a family's rise.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.1 (Umasvati, tr. Nathmal Tatia, ‘That Which Is’)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Wisdom leads us to serve our Lord and Master; through wisdom, honor is obtained.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak praises akal (practical wisdom) as what makes service fruitful and earns honour.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a family flourishes through sustained effort joined to full knowledge; Guru Nanak likewise makes wisdom the thing that turns service into lasting honour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus, given tools by Calypso, fells trees and builds his own raft with a craftsman's skill, then steers it home by the stars.
greek_mythology.explanation: His escape needs both hard labour and expert knowledge, working together over days.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hero's way home to his family is opened by effort and knowledge combined.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that virtue sets the right goal while practical wisdom (phronesis) finds the right means, and that a person needs both to act well.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, good character without practical intelligence, or cleverness without good aims, both fall short.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's pairing of effort and knowledge as joint causes of success.

real_life_example.event_title: Kongo Gumi, the temple builders who lasted fourteen centuries
real_life_example.event: Kongo Gumi, a temple-building firm traditionally founded in 578 by a craftsman brought from the Korean kingdom of Baekje to build the Shitennoji temple, was run by his descendants for some forty generations and is widely cited as the world's oldest continuously operating company. Temple construction still provided about 80 per cent of its revenue in 2004, but in 2006 heavy debts ended its independence as a family business.
real_life_example.explanation: The firm's long life rested on generations of skilled craft knowledge joined to steady, unbroken work.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a family lengthens through long, sustained effort combined with full knowledge, and Kongo Gumi's fourteen centuries are an extraordinary example.

tamil:
குடிசெய்வல் என்னும் ஒருவற்குத் தெய்வம்
மடிதற்றுத் தான்முந் துறும்.
transliteration:
Kudiseyval ennum oruvarkuth theyvam
madidhatruth thaanmun thurum.
meaning: When a person decides, 'I will lift up my family,' even the gods tuck in their clothes, ready for work, and hurry ahead to help.
elementary: Have you noticed that when you really decide to clean your room, things suddenly seem to fall into place? Valluvar says that when someone truly decides to lift up their family, it is as if heaven rolls up its sleeves and runs ahead to help.
university: The striking image is madi tharru (மடிதற்று, ‘having tucked up the fold of its garment’), the gesture of someone girding up to work or run, so that theyvam (தெய்வம்) mun urum (முந்துறும், ‘comes forward first’). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses theyvam as oozh (ஊழ், ‘destiny, fate’), keeping with the Kural's chapter 38; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a deity tightening its garment; Karunanidhi, rationalising, calls it the force of nature known as divine action. Pope gives ‘With vest succinct the goddess leads the way.’ The verb kudiseyval (‘I will make my family’) is a first-person vow, continuing 1021. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The demigods, being pleased by sacrifices, will also please you, and thus, by cooperation between men and demigods, prosperity will reign for all.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a partnership in which human effort offered rightly draws divine help, and prosperity follows.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the divine meets the person who first commits to the work.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.11 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: The Psalmist says that unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labour in vain.
christianity.explanation: The psalm teaches that human building succeeds only when God takes part in it.
christianity.tie_back: It shares the Kural's sense that unseen help joins the family-builder, but it puts God first where the Kural puts the human vow first.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ties God's change of a people's condition to the change they first make in themselves.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, divine help follows a human resolve.

judaism.quote_or_event: “do His will as though it were your will, so that He will do your will as though it were His.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel teaches that a person who makes God's purposes his own will find God taking up his purposes in turn.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly promises that heaven runs ahead to help the one who commits to a worthy task.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:4 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “You yourselves must strive; the Buddhas only point the way.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says no outside power does the work for you; teachers only show the road.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees that everything starts with personal resolve, but unlike the Kural it promises no deity running ahead to help.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 276 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anathi tells King Srenika that a person's own conduct, not any outside protector, makes happiness or misery.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism, which has no creator God, reads the Kural's ‘theyvam’ as the fruit of one's own action, much as Varadarasanar glosses it as destiny.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “A disciple who walks one step towards Guru to take his refuge and goes to him with devotion and humility, Guru advances to receive him (devotee) by taking million steps.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh scholar and scribe of the Adi Granth, says that the Guru comes a million steps forward to meet anyone who takes a single step toward him. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that when a person resolves to raise his family, fortune tucks up its garment and runs ahead to help; Bhai Gurdas says the Guru runs far ahead to meet the one who sets out.
sikhism.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye (the kabitt beginning ‘Charan saran gur ek painda jai chal’), English translation as given in the BaniDB database on SikhiToTheMax

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop's fable of Hercules and the Waggoner, a carter whose wagon is stuck prays to Hercules without lifting a finger; the god tells him to put his shoulder to the wheel and whip his horses, and only then to call on him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The god helps the one who is already working, not the one who waits.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural exactly: divine help comes running to the person who has started the work.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Terence's proverb that fortune helps the brave (fortes fortuna adiuvat), later repeated by Cicero and Seneca, holds that luck favours those who act boldly.
philosophy.explanation: Roman moralists turned the line into a maxim that bold, committed action draws good fortune to it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's fortune that hurries ahead of the committed family-builder is the same idea.

real_life_example.event_title: Mary Anning's family finds the first complete ichthyosaur
real_life_example.event: After cabinetmaker Richard Anning died in 1810 leaving his family poor and in debt, his children Mary and Joseph kept collecting and selling fossils from the cliffs to support the household. In 1811 Joseph found a large fossil skull, and Mary later uncovered the rest of the skeleton; the specimen, recognised as an ichthyosaur, sold for 23 pounds and helped the family out of debt.
real_life_example.explanation: The find launched Mary Anning's career as one of the most important fossil collectors in the history of palaeontology.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural promises that when someone resolves to raise the family, fortune itself girds up and runs ahead to help, and the Annings' striking find came while they were working to keep their family afloat.

tamil:
சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும் தம்குடியைத்
தாழாது உஞற்று பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Soozhaamal thaane mudiveydhum thamkudiyaith
thaazhaadhu unjatru bavarkku.
meaning: For people who work hard without delay to lift up their family, the work gets done by itself, even without careful planning.
elementary: When you practise piano every day without putting it off, one day a hard song just seems to play itself. Valluvar says that when people keep working for their family without delay, success often arrives before they even sit down to plan it.
university: Soozhaamal (சூழாமல், ‘without deliberating, without planning’) and thaane (தானே, ‘of itself’) frame the promise that the task mudiveydhum (முடிவெய்தும், ‘reaches completion’) for those who thaazhaadhu unjatrupavar (தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர், ‘strive without delay’). Kesikan, following the older commentary, attributes this to divine aid (தெய்வ உதவியால்), linking it to 1023; Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read it naturalistically, saying the capacity to finish comes to the prompt worker unsought. Karunanidhi has victories ‘pile up of themselves.’ Pope translates ‘Without a thought spontaneously, his end will gain.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, without being attached to the fruits of activities, one should act as a matter of duty, for by working without attachment one attains the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that steady action as duty, without fretting over results, itself brings the highest attainment.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the outcome comes of itself to the one who simply keeps working.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.19 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that the slack hand brings poverty but the hand of the diligent makes rich.
christianity.explanation: The sage links prosperity directly to diligent work.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say success comes almost naturally to the person who works without slackening.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says a person receives the good that matches his own striving.
islam.tie_back: It agrees with the Kural that the result follows from the effort itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “the day is short, and the work is plentiful, and the laborers are indolent, and the reward is great, and the master of the house is insistent.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon warns that the time is short and the work great, so delay is costly and the reward large.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it urges striving without delay and promises that great reward follows.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:15 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who acquires his wealth in harmless ways like to a bee that honey gathers, riches mount up for him like ant hill's rapid growth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the householder Sigala that steady, honest work makes wealth grow on its own, like an anthill.
buddhism.tie_back: Its image of riches mounting up by themselves matches the Kural's success that ‘comes of itself’ to the steady worker.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it?”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana warns that knowing and discussing the path achieves nothing without actually walking it.
jainism.tie_back: It agrees with the Kural that doing, not deliberating, brings results, though for liberation rather than family welfare.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 6.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
sikhism.explanation: In Gujri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan urges udam (active effort): those who exert themselves find life, and those who keep practising find peace. The salok goes on to say that through meditation one meets God and anxiety ends.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural promises that the work of those who strive without delay reaches its goal of itself; Guru Arjan likewise promises that effort, kept up, brings its own fulfilment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar (salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Through work men grow rich in flocks and substance, and working they are much better loved by the immortals”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod promises his brother that steady farm work brings both wealth and the favour of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says prosperity flows naturally to the one who keeps working.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, passage at ll. 293-319 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, sacred-texts.com)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts, so that repeated practice makes good action second nature.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, steady practice turns hard actions into habits that then come almost without effort.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains the Kural's claim that for the constant striver the work completes itself without deliberation.

real_life_example.event_title: Vinoba Bhave receives an unasked-for gift of land at Pochampalli
real_life_example.event: While walking through Telangana, Vinoba Bhave met landless Dalit families at Pochampalli who said they needed land to live. When he asked those present whether anything could be done, a landowner named Ramachandra Reddy rose and offered 100 acres, and from this unplanned beginning the Bhoodan (land-gift) movement grew, collecting millions of acres in later years.
real_life_example.explanation: A movement of national scale began not from a plan but from a single spontaneous response during Vinoba's tireless walking tour.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those who strive without delay to raise their people, the work reaches its goal of itself even before it is planned, as the first land gift came to Vinoba unasked.

tamil:
குற்றம் இலனாய்க் குடிசெய்து வாழ்வானைச்
சுற்றமாச் சுற்றும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kutram ilanaaik kudiseydhu vaazhvaanaich
sutramaach chutrum ulagu.
meaning: The world gathers around a person who lifts up their family without doing wrong, and treats them like one of its own family.
elementary: Think of a kind neighbour who works hard for her family and never cheats anyone. Soon the whole street treats her like family, bringing food and asking her advice. Valluvar says that is what happens to honest family-builders: everyone wants to be their relative.
university: Kutram ilanaai (குற்றம் இலனாய், ‘being without fault’) is the condition: the family must be raised by blameless means. The reward is a pun on sutram (சுற்றம், ‘kin, relatives’) and sutrum (சுற்றும், ‘surrounds, encircles’): the ulagu (உலகு, ‘world’) surrounds him as if it were his own relatives. Varadarasanar and Kesikan say people seek to become his kin; Pappaiah narrows ulagu to ‘the great’ (உயர்ந்தோர்), in keeping with the commentarial habit of reading ulagam as the worthy. Pope translates ‘The world shall circle him, and kindred claim.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Whatever action a great man performs, common men follow. And whatever standards he sets by exemplary acts, all the world pursues.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna notes that the world gathers behind and imitates the person of exemplary conduct.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's blameless family-builder whom the world surrounds, the exemplary person draws everyone to follow.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.21 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs tells the reader to keep mercy and truth close, and so to find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
christianity.explanation: The sage promises that a life of faithfulness wins goodwill from people as well as from God.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly says a blameless life makes the world want to be one's kin.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds - the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an promises that God will place love for the righteous in people's hearts.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the upright are surrounded by affection as if they were family.

judaism.quote_or_event: “which is the straight path that a man should choose for himself? One which is an honor to the person adopting it, and [on account of which] honor [accrues] to him from others.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince defines the right path as one that is honourable in itself and earns honour from others.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's blameless family-builder, embraced by the world, follows exactly this path.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:1 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who is full of faith and virtue, and possesses good repute and wealth — he is respected everywhere, in whatever land he travels.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the virtuous householder of good name and honest wealth is honoured wherever he goes.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the world embraces the blameless one who has raised his family.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 303 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: Hemachandra's Yogashastra lists, as the first quality of a householder fit for the Jain path, wealth acquired by just and honest means (nyaya-sampanna-vibhava).
jainism.explanation: Jain lay ethics makes honest earning the foundation of a good household life.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘without fault’ condition for raising one's family.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Yogashastra, Book 1 (the marganusari qualities of the householder)

sikhism.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, Guru Nanak stayed in Saidpur (Eminabad) with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter who lived by honest labour, and declined a feast offered by the rich official Malik Bhago, saying that Lalo's coarse bread was earned honestly while Bhago's food was wrung from the poor.
sikhism.explanation: The story is told to show that honest work, not wealth or rank, wins the Guru's company and honour.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the world gathers round and claims as kin the person who raises his family without doing wrong; in the story the Guru himself chooses to make his home with the blameless, honest-working Lalo.
sikhism.source: Janamsakhi tradition, as retold in M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plutarch tells how Theseus gathered the scattered villages of Attica into one city, Athens, and the people came together under him as one community.
greek_mythology.explanation: The hero's work for his people turned many separate households into a single family-like city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It loosely matches the Kural's picture of people drawn around a builder as his own kin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For nothing inspires love, nothing conciliates affection, like virtue. Why, in a certain sense we may be said to feel affection even for men we have never seen, owing to their honesty and virtue.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius argues that friendship springs from the natural pull of virtue: goodness draws affection so strongly that we love even good men we have never met.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's promise that people gather around the blameless man and treat him as their own kin.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia, ch. 8 (§§27-28) (tr. E. S. Shuckburgh)

real_life_example.event_title: Robert Owen's New Lanark becomes a place of pilgrimage
real_life_example.event: From 1800 Robert Owen managed the New Lanark cotton mills, where he shortened the working day, stopped children under ten from working in the mills, opened a nursery and infant school in 1816, and set up a village store selling good goods at fair prices. Paid for out of the mills' profits, these reforms drew visitors from many countries, and Britannica notes that the mills became a place of pilgrimage for political leaders, social reformers and royalty.
real_life_example.explanation: Owen showed that a working community could be raised without exploitation, and the world came to see and learn from it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the world gathers around the one who raises his people without fault, and New Lanark under Owen drew admirers from far and wide.

tamil:
நல்லாண்மை என்பது ஒருவற்குத் தான்பிறந்த
இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Nallaanmai enbadhu oruvarkuth thaanpirandha
illaanmai aakkik kolal.
meaning: True manliness means taking charge of and caring for the family you were born into.
elementary: Some people think being strong means winning fights. Valluvar says real strength is when you grow up and become the person your family can lean on, the one who takes care of things at home.
university: The couplet redefines nallaanmai (நல்லாண்மை, ‘good manliness, true valour’) by rhyming it with illaanmai (இல்லாண்மை, ‘mastery of the household’): real valour is aakkik kolal (ஆக்கிக் கொளல், ‘making one's own’) the governance of the home one was born in (thaan pirandha, தான் பிறந்த). Varadarasanar and Kesikan read it as taking on the ruling of one's birth-family; Pappaiah again extends it to house and country; Karunanidhi reverses the emphasis, saying the able ruler brings glory to the family of his birth. Pope gives ‘To him who gives his powers, the house from which he sprang to raise.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is far better to discharge one’s prescribed duties, even though faultily, than another’s duties perfectly.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that a person's own duty, the one that falls to him by his station, is the one he must take up.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly asks a person to take up the duty of the house he was born into.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.35 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes providing for one's own household a basic duty of faith.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats taking charge of one's own family as the measure of a person.

islam.quote_or_event: “All of you are guardians and responsible for your wards and the things under your care. The Imam (i.e. ruler) is the guardian of his subjects and is responsible for them and a man is the guardian of his family and is responsible for them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that every person is a shepherd responsible for those in his care, and a man for his family.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's ideal of ruling and caring for one's household is the same guardianship.

judaism.quote_or_event: After their father's death, Joseph reassures his frightened brothers that he will sustain them and their little ones, and he comforts them.
judaism.explanation: Joseph, now powerful, uses his position to provide for the whole family he was born into.
judaism.tie_back: He embodies the Kural's ideal of making oneself the head and support of one's birth-family.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Having supported me I shall support them, I shall do their duties, I shall keep the family tradition, I shall make myself worthy of my inheritance”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the duties a grown child takes on toward parents and the family line.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ideal of taking charge of the household one was born into.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Kalpa Sutra tells that Mahavira, out of regard for his parents, resolved not to renounce the world while they lived, and became a monk only after their death.
jainism.explanation: Even the future Tirthankara honoured his duty to the family he was born into before leaving it.
jainism.tie_back: It shows Jainism recognising the claim of one's birth-family that the Kural celebrates, though only as a stage before renunciation.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is a householder, who restrains his passions”
sikhism.explanation: In Ramkali ki Vaar, Guru Nanak defines the true grihasti (householder) not by property or family but by self-mastery. Sikhism prefers the householder path to renunciation.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural redefines true manliness as the mastery of one's own household; Guru Nanak redefines the true householder as one who first masters himself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 952, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus returns to Ithaca after twenty years, drives out the suitors who are wasting his estate, and takes his place again as head of his father's house.
greek_mythology.explanation: The hero's last and greatest labour is restoring order in his own household.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that true valour is mastery of one's own home.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Thus it is clear that household management attends more to men than to the acquisition of inanimate things, and to human excellence more than to the excellence of property which we call wealth, and to the virtue of freemen more than to the virtue of slaves.”
philosophy.explanation: After describing the head of the household as ruling his children like a king, by love and seniority (I.12), Aristotle concludes that running a household is chiefly about the excellence of its people, not about wealth.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle treats leading and caring for one's household as a test of a man's character.

real_life_example.event_title: Young Andrew Carnegie works to keep his family afloat
real_life_example.event: In 1848 the Carnegie family emigrated from Dunfermline, Scotland, to Allegheny, Pennsylvania, after mechanised looms ruined his father's handloom weaving. Young Andrew went straight to work as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill for $1.20 a week, then moved through better-paid jobs to the telegraph office; when his father died in 1855 he was the family's only breadwinner.
real_life_example.explanation: Carnegie took charge of the household he was born into while still a boy, the start of a career that later made him one of the world's richest men.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls true manliness making oneself the leader and support of the family one was born into, which is what young Carnegie did.

tamil:
அமரகத்து வன்கண்ணர் போலத் தமரகத்தும்
ஆற்றுவார் மேற்றே பொறை.
transliteration:
Amaragaththu vankannar polath thamaragaththum
aatruvaar metre porai.
meaning: In battle, the heavy load falls on the brave. In the same way, in a family, the load falls on those who are able to carry it.
elementary: In a soccer game, the toughest players stand in front when the other team attacks. Valluvar says families are the same: when trouble comes, the strongest, most capable person has to step forward and carry the load.
university: The couplet balances amaragaththu (அமரகத்து, ‘in the battlefield’) against thamaragaththum (தமரகத்தும், ‘among one's own people too’); the vankannar (வன்கண்ணர், ‘the hard-eyed, the fearless’) of war correspond to the aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், ‘those who are able’) in the family, and on them falls porai (பொறை, ‘burden, load’). Varadarasanar stresses that though many are born into a family, the burden lies on the capable. Text note: ytamizh.com reads தமரகத்தும் (with the inclusive -um) while thirukkural.net prints தமரகத்து ஆற்றுவார்; the meaning is the same and this edition follows the -um reading, which Pope's ‘Amid his kindred so’ also reflects.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Considering your specific duty as a kṣatriya, you should know that there is no better engagement for you than fighting on religious principles; and so there is no need for hesitation.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that the warrior's duty is to stand and fight, not to shrink back.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses exactly this warrior who does not shrink as its model for the family member who carries the load.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.31 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says those with strength must carry the burdens of the weaker members of the community.
christianity.tie_back: It is almost the Kural's rule: the burden belongs to those able to bear it.

islam.quote_or_event: “A strong believer is better and is more lovable to Allah than a weak believer, and there is good in everyone, (but) cherish that which gives you benefit (in the Hereafter) and seek help from Allah and do not lose heart”
islam.explanation: The Prophet prizes strength in the believer and tells him not to lose heart.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it honours the strong who stand firm, though it does not speak of carrying the family.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel teaches that when no one else steps up, you must be the one who takes responsibility.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the load falls on whoever has the strength to take it.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:5 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As an elephant in the battlefield withstands arrows shot from bows all around, even so shall I endure abuse.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares his patient endurance to a war elephant that stands firm under a hail of arrows.
buddhism.tie_back: Its battlefield image of steady endurance matches the Kural's fearless warrior who bears the brunt.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 320 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Do not get into an uneven road like a weak burden-bearer; for you will repent of it afterwards; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira warns his disciple not to stumble like a weak porter who leaves the smooth road under his load.
jainism.tie_back: The image of the strong and weak burden-bearer echoes the Kural's point that the load needs someone able to carry it, though the Jain load is the monastic path.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir describes the true soorma (hero) who stands his ground for the right even if cut to pieces. The verse is central to the Sikh ideal of the saint-soldier.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that as the burden of battle falls on the fearless, so the burden of a family falls on those able to bear it; Kabir's hero is the one who carries that burden and never leaves the field.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maru, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Trojans break through to the Greek ships, Ajax son of Telamon stands almost alone on the decks, fending off fire and spears to protect the whole army.
greek_mythology.explanation: With the other leaders wounded, the burden of defence falls on the one hero strong enough to bear it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's battlefield image in action: the load rests on the one who can carry it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Because in the army the most hazardous services are assigned to the bravest soldiers: a general sends his choicest troops to attack the enemy in a midnight ambuscade, to reconnoitre his line of march, or to drive the hostile garrisons from their strong places.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca explains why God sends hardship to the best of men: as a general gives the hardest tasks to his finest troops, they say not 'he has dealt hardly with me' but 'he has judged well of me'.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca uses the Kural's own battlefield image: the heaviest load falls on those strong enough to bear it.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Of Providence (De Providentia) 4.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)

real_life_example.event_title: The Widow Clicquot takes over her husband's wine firm
real_life_example.event: When Francois Clicquot died in 1805, his 27-year-old widow Barbe-Nicole Clicquot Ponsardin persuaded her father-in-law to back her and took control of the family's wine business. She ran it through difficult wartime years, and the house dates her invention of the riddling table, a method of clearing sediment from champagne still in use, to 1816.
real_life_example.explanation: A young widow with no business training carried the family firm and became one of the founders of the modern champagne industry.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that, as on the battlefield the load falls on the fearless, in a family it falls on those able to bear it, and the burden of the Clicquot house fell to Barbe-Nicole.

tamil:
குடிசெய்வார்க் கில்லை பருவம் மடிசெய்து
மானங் கருதக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kudiseyvaark killai paruvam madiseydhu
maanang karudhak kedum.
meaning: People who work for their family cannot wait for the right time. If they are lazy or worry too much about their pride, the family falls apart.
elementary: If you wait for the ‘perfect day’ to do your chores, it never comes, and the mess just grows. Valluvar says people who care for a family can't wait for a perfect time or think a job is beneath them; they just have to get going.
university: Paruvam (பருவம், ‘season, proper time’) is denied to the kudiseyvaar (குடிசெய்வார், ‘those who make the family’): any time is the time. The second line names two enemies, madi (மடி, ‘sloth’, the theme of chapter 61) and maanam karudhal (மானம் கருதல், ‘considering one's pride or honour’), either of which makes the family kedum (கெடும், ‘perish’). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read maanam as standing on one's dignity, refusing humble work; Karunanidhi reads it as being shaken by insults directed at oneself. Pope gives ‘Wait for no season, when you would your house uprear; / ’Twill perish, if you wait supine, or hold your honour dear.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Perform your prescribed duty, for doing so is better than not working. One cannot even maintain one’s physical body without work.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says work is always better than inaction and that even bodily survival needs it.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it rejects idleness, since nothing can be kept going without work.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.8 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher warns that the farmer who keeps waiting for perfect weather never plants or harvests.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘there is no season’: waiting for the ideal time means ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “There are two blessings that many people are deceived into losing: health and free time.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that people waste their health and spare time, thinking there will always be more.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns against letting time slip by in idleness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not: ‘when I shall have leisure I shall study;’ perhaps you will not have leisure.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel warns against putting off important work until a convenient time that may never come.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point that the family-builder has no ‘proper season’ to wait for.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:4 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who says it is too hot, too cold, too late, and leaves things undone, the opportunities for good go past such men. But he who does not regard cold or heat any more than a blade of grass and who does his duties manfully, does not fall away from happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns the householder that making excuses about weather and time loses every chance of prosperity.
buddhism.tie_back: It is almost the Kural itself: the one who raises a family has no season to wait for.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama that life falls like a dead leaf, so he must never be careless for a moment.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain call to constant heedfulness (apramada) matches the Kural's rejection of waiting and idling, though it aims at liberation rather than household welfare.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately! Later on, you will not be able to do anything, when death hangs over your head.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir warns against putting off what must be done, because the right moment does not wait.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says those who raise a family have no ‘right season’ to wait for, and that sloth will ruin the family; Kabir says the same of every duty, do it now, for later never comes.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 138) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Do not put your work off till to-morrow and the day after; for a sluggish worker does not fill his barn, nor one who puts off his work: industry makes work go well”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother that the farmer who delays his work ends with an empty barn.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a household is ruined by sloth and by waiting for a later time.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, passage at ll. 405-413 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, sacred-texts.com)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca opens his letters to Lucilius by urging him to seize each hour, because while we put things off, life runs past us.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic argues that postponement wastes the one thing we truly own, our time.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's warning that waiting for a right season ruins the work.

real_life_example.event_title: Maria Sklodowska works as a governess to put her sister through medical school
real_life_example.place: Poland (then part of the Russian Empire)
real_life_example.event: Young Maria Sklodowska, later Marie Curie, made an agreement with her elder sister Bronislawa that Maria would work first to pay for Bronya's medical studies in Paris, and Bronya would later help her in turn. Maria spent several years as a tutor and live-in governess, including a post with a family in the countryside north of Warsaw, before she was finally able to enrol at the Sorbonne in 1891.
real_life_example.explanation: She put her own ambitions on hold and took humble work at once so that the family could advance, and the plan succeeded for both sisters.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who raise a family cannot wait for the right season or stand on their dignity, and Maria took modest work immediately rather than wait for better times.

tamil:
இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம் கொல்லோ குடும்பத்தைக்
குற்ற மறைப்பான் உடம்பு.
transliteration:
Idumbaikke kolkalam kollo kudumbaththaik
kutra maraippaan udambu.
meaning: Is the body of a person who protects their family from harm made only to hold suffering?
elementary: Think of a parent who works late, carries heavy bags, and gets up at night when the baby cries. Their body is tired and sore. Valluvar asks: is that body only made for hardship? His answer is that their toil is also full of love and worth.
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: is the udambu (உடம்பு, ‘body’) of the one who kutram maraippaan (குற்றம் மறைப்பான், ‘wards off harm’ from his kudumbam, குடும்பம், ‘family’) merely an idumbaikke kolkalam (இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம், ‘a vessel for suffering alone’)? The particle kollo (கொல்லோ) marks wonder or doubt. Varadarasanar reads it plainly as ‘is his body only a home for suffering?’, conceding the hardship; Kesikan and Pappaiah draw the implied answer, that it is also a vessel of joy; Karunanidhi says such a person is honoured as one born to bear suffering. Pope gives ‘Is not his body vase that various sorrows fill, / Who would his household screen from every ill?’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, the nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons. They arise from sense perception, O scion of Bharata, and one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that bodily pain and pleasure come and go like seasons and must be borne with steadiness.
hinduism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's picture of a body that must bear hardship for the sake of duty.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus teaches that no one has greater love than the person who lays down his life for his friends.
christianity.explanation: Self-sacrifice for others is presented as the highest form of love.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's body given over to hardship to protect the family is this kind of love.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an commands believers to shield their families from ruin.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's family-protector, the believer is charged with guarding his household from harm.

judaism.quote_or_event: Nehemiah, rebuilding Jerusalem's walls under threat, tells the people not to fear but to remember the great and awesome Lord and fight for their brothers, sons, daughters, wives and homes.
judaism.explanation: The builders work with one hand and keep a weapon in the other, to protect their families while they build.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's picture of a body spent in shielding one's family.
judaism.source: Nehemiah 4:8 (Hebrew numbering; 4:14 in English Bibles), Tanakh via Sefaria

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahakapi Jataka the Bodhisatta, born as a monkey king, stretches his own body as a bridge across a river so his troop can escape the king's archers, and is fatally hurt doing so.
buddhism.explanation: The monkey king turns his own body into the means of his people's safety.
buddhism.tie_back: It vividly answers the Kural's question about the body of the one who shields his family.
buddhism.source: Mahakapi Jataka (Jataka No. 407, tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife, and sons will not be able to help me, when I suffer for my own deeds.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that no family member can share the suffering that one's own karma brings.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism sees bodily suffering as one's own karma and the family as no refuge, so it offers a contrast to the Kural's ideal of suffering for one's family.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 6.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: In 1675 the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, went to Delhi on behalf of Kashmiri Brahmins who were being forced to convert, refused to give up his faith himself, and was publicly executed on the emperor Aurangzeb's orders.
sikhism.explanation: Sikhs remember his martyrdom as giving his life to shield others' freedom of faith, people who were not even of his own religion.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether the body of one who shields his people from harm is only a vessel for suffering; Guru Tegh Bahadur took suffering and death on his own body to shield those who came to him for protection.
sikhism.source: M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 4, Life of Guru Tegh Bahadur

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus, chained to a rock as punishment for giving fire and the arts to humankind, endures endless bodily torment rather than betray those he protected.
greek_mythology.explanation: His body becomes a vessel of suffering because he chose to shield and raise up humanity.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He embodies the Kural's question about the body of the one who protects his own.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is true of the good man too that he does many acts for the sake of his friends and his country, and if necessary dies for them; for he will throw away both wealth and honours and in general the goods that are objects of competition, gaining for himself nobility …”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that the good man's sacrifices for others, even his life, are not losses, because he wins for himself the greater good of nobility.
philosophy.tie_back: This gives the answer the Kural's question implies: the protector's suffering body is not a mere vessel of pain, since his sacrifice is what makes him noble.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, 1169a (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Dostoevsky takes on his late brother's family and debts
real_life_example.event: When Fyodor Dostoevsky's brother and co-editor Mikhail died in 1864, Fyodor assumed financial responsibility for Mikhail's family and the debts of their journal Epoch, which collapsed in 1865. The years that followed were a time of acute financial hardship in which he wrote under heavy pressure and spent long periods abroad to escape creditors.
real_life_example.explanation: Dostoevsky shouldered burdens that were not strictly his own, and they shaped years of his life and work.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks whether the body of one who shields his family from harm is only a vessel for suffering, and Dostoevsky's hard years carrying his brother's family are a vivid case.

tamil:
இடுக்கண்கால் கொன்றிட வீழும் அடுத்தூன்றும்
நல்லாள் இலாத குடி.
transliteration:
Idukkankaal kondrida veezhum aduththoondrum
nallaal ilaadha kudi.
meaning: A family with no good person to hold it up will fall, like a tree, when trouble cuts at its roots.
elementary: A young tree needs a stick tied beside it so the wind doesn't knock it over. Valluvar says a family is like that tree: when hard times blow, it needs a strong, caring person standing beside it, or it will fall.
university: The image is of a tree: idukkan (இடுக்கண், ‘misfortune’) strikes at its kaal (கால், ‘foot, base’) and kondrida (கொன்றிட, ‘cutting, killing’) brings it down, unless there is a nallaal (நல்லாள், ‘good person’) who aduththu oondrum (அடுத்து ஊன்றும், ‘stands close and props it up’). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah make the axe explicit (துன்பமாகிய கோடாரி, ‘the axe of misfortune’), and Kesikan names the tree; Pappaiah reads nallaal as ‘good children’. The couplet closes the chapter by turning 1021's vow into a warning about its absence. Pope gives ‘When trouble the foundation saps the house must fall, / If no strong hand be nigh to prop the tottering wall.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “With the destruction of the dynasty, the eternal family tradition is vanquished, and thus the rest of the family becomes involved in irreligion.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna fears that once a family's leading men fall, the whole family collapses.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's warning: a family without its supporters falls.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 1.39 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus says that a house built on sand falls when the rains, floods and winds beat on it, and great is its fall.
christianity.explanation: A house without a solid foundation cannot survive the storm.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows a household with nothing to hold it up collapsing under misfortune.

islam.quote_or_event: “A faithful believer to a faithful believer is like the bricks of a wall, enforcing each other.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet, lacing his fingers together, describes believers as bricks that hold each other up.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a community stands only when its members prop one another up.

judaism.quote_or_event: Kohelet observes that two are better than one, for if one falls the other lifts him up, but woe to the one who falls alone with no one to raise him.
judaism.explanation: The sage warns that someone with no companion to help has nothing to save him when he falls.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's family with no one to prop it up suffers this same fall.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By effort and heedfulness, discipline and self-mastery, let the wise one make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges building, through effort, a refuge that disaster cannot sweep away.
buddhism.tie_back: It answers the Kural's warning from the other side: steady effort makes a refuge that misfortune cannot overturn.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 25 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)

jainism.quote_or_event: “My father would have spent all he possessed, for my sake; but he could not rid me of my pains, hence I say that I am without protection.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anathi explains that even a devoted family could not protect him from suffering, which led him to renounce the world.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism treats the family's support as finally unable to hold up the soul, so it gives an honest contrast to the Kural's faith in the family's prop.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When You stand over our heads, O Lord and Master, how can we suffer in pain?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that no pain can overwhelm those who have the Lord standing over them as protector.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a family with no good person to prop it up falls like a tree when misfortune strikes; Guru Arjan gives the other side, that those with a protector standing over them cannot be brought down by pain.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 749, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Achilles kills Hector, Troy's great defender, the city's lament is as though all Ilion were already burning, and with its prop gone Troy soon falls.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector was the one man holding up his city and family; his death leaves them defenceless.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's image exactly: a house with no one to prop it falls when misfortune strikes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Or how can prosperity be guarded and preserved without friends? The greater it is, the more exposed is it to risk. And in poverty and in other misfortunes men think friends are the only refuge.”
philosophy.explanation: Opening his account of friendship, Aristotle says that without others to stand by it no fortune can be kept safe, and that in misfortune they are the only support.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's family with no one to prop it up, Aristotle's prosperity left without friends is exposed to fall when misfortune strikes.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1, 1155a (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Medici are driven from Florence after Lorenzo's death
real_life_example.event: Lorenzo de' Medici, who had steered Florence and his family's fortunes for over two decades, died in April 1492.
