hinduism.quote_or_event: “He that is without wealth hath neither this world, nor the next, O best of men!”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna argues that without wealth a person can neither enjoy life nor perform the religious acts that secure the hereafter.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost word for word the Kural’s claim that poverty takes away both this world and the next.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs pictures poverty arriving like a traveller or an armed robber who overpowers the idle.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘wicked one’, poverty is personified as an intruder that comes and takes away.

islam.quote_or_event: “And He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient.”
islam.explanation: God reminds the Prophet that he too was once poor, and that his poverty did not cut him off from divine favour.
islam.tie_back: The verse quietly counters the Kural: in Islam poverty need not cost a person the next world.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Three classes of people do not see the face of Gehenna... Those suffering the depths of extreme poverty, those afflicted with intestinal disease, and those oppressed by creditors.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud teaches that the suffering of extreme poverty atones for sin, so the very poor are spared Gehenna.
judaism.tie_back: Where the Kural says poverty loses the next world, the rabbis hold that it can secure it, a pointed contrast on the same question.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Eruvin 41b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “But one with confidence, living at home, making gifts of his belongings, righteously-gained, wins both goals: advantage in the here-&-now, & happiness in the world beyond.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the householder who gives from rightly earned wealth as winning benefit both now and hereafter.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the mirror image of the Kural: wealth used for giving wins both worlds, so its absence forfeits both.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He will sink through anger; he will go down through pride; delusion will block up his path; through greed he will incur dangers in both worlds.”
jainism.explanation: Nami tells Indra that it is greed, not lack of wealth, that endangers a person in this world and the next.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain sage relocates the Kural’s threat to both worlds from poverty to the craving for possessions.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.54 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I am so hungry, I cannot perform devotional worship service. Here, Lord, take back Your mala.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir tells God bluntly that a starving man cannot pray, and goes on to ask only for simple flour, ghee, lentils and bedding so that he can worship with love. Gurbani here recognises that grinding want blocks both worldly life and spiritual life.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says poverty robs a person of the joys of this life and the good of the next; Kabir confesses that hunger has made even his devotion, his path to the next world, impossible.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 656, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aristophanes’ comedy Wealth (Plutus), Poverty (Penia) appears in person as a fearsome goddess, and Chremylus resolves to drive her out of Greece as the source of men’s miseries, while she argues that she is what keeps men industrious.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek imagination, like Valluvar’s, turned poverty into a personified being who stalks human households.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penia as a menacing figure parallels the Kural’s ‘poverty, a wicked one’ who comes and takes everything.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For it is better to die with hunger, exempt from grief and fear, than to live in affluence with perturbation.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus insists that peace of mind matters more than material security, even at the cost of hunger.
philosophy.tie_back: The Stoic denies the Kural’s premise that losing wealth means losing life’s good.

real_life_example.event_title: Germany's hyperinflation wipes out a lifetime of savings
real_life_example.event: During 1923 the German paper mark collapsed as the government printed ever more banknotes, and by November it took about 4.2 trillion marks to buy a single US dollar. Middle-class Germans who lived on savings, pensions, investments or rents saw the provision they had built up over a lifetime become almost worthless, and the crisis was ended only by the introduction of the Rentenmark late in 1923.
real_life_example.explanation: The hyperinflation reduced respectable, provident families to want almost overnight, and historians link the experience to a lasting loss of trust in money and in the Weimar Republic.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls poverty a wicked thing that robs a person of both this life and the next, and the hyperinflation took from savers at a stroke both their comfort in the present and the security they had stored up for the years ahead.

tamil:
தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும் தொகையாக
நல்குரவு என்னும் நசை.
transliteration:
Tholvaravum thoalum kedukkum thogaiyaaga
nalkuravu ennum nasai.
meaning: The hungry want called poverty destroys, all at once, a family's long history and its good name.
elementary: Imagine a family that has been known for generations as kind and honest. If someone in it becomes so desperate that wanting things takes over, they might do things that spoil the family’s good name all at once, like one spill ruining a whole painting.
university: The key word is nasai (நசை, ‘desire, craving’): Valluvar does not just say nalkuravu but ‘nalkuravu ennum nasai’, the craving that is called poverty, suggesting that destitution shows itself as a gnawing want. Tholvaravu (தொல்வரவு) is ‘what has come down from of old’, the dignity or heritage of one’s line, and thoal (தோல்) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan as pugazh (fame, honour); the English explanation carried on ytamizh.com renders it ‘the dignity of one’s speech’, reflecting an older reading that associates thoal with elevated, well-formed words. Thogaiyaaga (‘all together, at a stroke’) stresses the suddenness of the ruin. Kalaignar shifts the causation slightly, saying that poverty breeds greed which then ruins lineage and fame. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna identifies kama, craving, as the all-consuming enemy that degrades a person.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s nasai, the craving that comes with poverty, is the same all-devouring desire the Gita warns can destroy what a person has built.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.37 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that the craving to become rich drags people into ruinous desires.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see a desperate hunger for wealth as what wrecks a person’s standing.

islam.quote_or_event: “But when He tries him and restricts his provision, he says, ‘My Lord has humiliated me.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes how a person whose provision is narrowed feels himself disgraced, though the verse then corrects this view.
islam.tie_back: The felt loss of honour that comes with straitened means is exactly what the Kural describes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment, so the restless craving for more is itself a kind of poverty.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural calls poverty a nasai, a craving; the Mishnah answers that the cure lies in rejoicing in one’s portion.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, free from avarice amidst the avaricious. Amidst the avaricious men we dwell free from avarice.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises those who live free of craving even among the grasping.
buddhism.tie_back: Against the Kural’s ruinous nasai, the Buddhist ideal is freedom from that very craving.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means. Though two mâshas would do to supply your want, still you would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.”
jainism.explanation: Kapila, a poor Brahmin student, realised while deciding how much gold to ask a king for that his want kept swelling, and renounced the world on the spot.
jainism.tie_back: Kapila’s story shows exactly the ‘craving called poverty’ that, unchecked, ruins a man’s standing.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 8.17, with the Kapila legend in Jacobi’s note (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The fire of desire is deep within; unsatisfied, people remain hungry and thirsty.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad describes trishna (craving) as an inner fire that leaves people perpetually hungry and thirsty however much they have.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of the hungry craving called poverty that destroys a family's ancient standing and good name; Guru Angad likewise names an insatiable inner hunger as the fire that consumes a person.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 138, Raag Majh, Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon, cursed by Demeter with insatiable Hunger, devoured his whole family fortune and at last sold his own daughter Mestra to buy food.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s retelling, a hunger that could never be filled consumed an old and wealthy house and drove its head to shame his own child.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The myth dramatises the Kural’s ‘craving called poverty’ destroying a family’s heritage and honour in one sweep.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Don’t allow such considerations as these distress you. ‘I will live in dishonor, and be nobody anywhere.’”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the student not to fear the loss of public standing, since dishonour from outside cannot touch one’s character.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural laments the loss of name and heritage; the Stoic argues that such losses are not true evils.

real_life_example.event_title: Debt-ridden Benedict Arnold plots to hand West Point to the British
real_life_example.event: Benedict Arnold, born into a well-respected Connecticut family, had become one of the Continental Army's most celebrated generals, but he and his second wife lived lavishly in Philadelphia and ran deep into debt. After receiving command of the fort at West Point in 1780, he met the British officer Major John Andre on 21 September 1780 to arrange its surrender in return for a large sum of money and a British commission. Andre was captured with incriminating papers, the plot was exposed, and Arnold fled to the British side.
real_life_example.explanation: Historians count Arnold's debts, together with his resentment at being passed over for promotion, among the motives for his betrayal, and his name became a byword for traitor in the United States.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that the craving born of want destroys at a single stroke a family's old standing and good name, and Arnold's debt-driven treason erased a hero's reputation overnight.

tamil:
இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும் இன்மை இளிவந்த
சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு தரும்.
transliteration:
IRpiRandhaar kaNNaeyum inmai iLivandha
soRpiRakkum soarvu tharum.
meaning: Poverty makes even people from good families so tired and weak that low, shameful words come out of their mouths.
elementary: When you are very tired and hungry, you might snap at someone even though you are usually polite. Valluvar says being very poor can make even well-brought-up people so worn down that unkind or embarrassing words slip out.
university: IRpiRandhaar (இற்பிறந்தார்) are ‘those born in a (good) house’, i.e. of noble family, and the -um of kaNNaeyum (‘even in them’) concedes that breeding is no protection. Inmai gives soarvu (சோர்வு, ‘slackness, exhaustion, lapse of vigilance’) from which iLivandha sol (இளிவந்த சொல், ‘words that bring disgrace’) is born. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it this way: poverty causes the lapse, and the lapse produces demeaning speech. Puliyur Kesikan, notably, reverses the causation, saying that the slackness which leads to base acts is itself what brings poverty even to good families, a reading that turns the couplet into a warning rather than a lament. Pope’s ‘Oblivion that gives birth to words that bring disgrace’ takes soarvu as forgetfulness of one’s station. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “King Nahusha, having done many wicked acts in a state of poverty, cried fie on that state and said that poverty is for recluses.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna cites the royal Nahusha, who was driven to wicked acts when reduced to poverty.
hinduism.tie_back: Even a king of illustrious line fell into base conduct through want, just as the Kural says of those nobly born.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me: Lest I be full, and deny thee... or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.”
christianity.explanation: Agur prays to be spared poverty because it might push him to steal and to profane God’s name.
christianity.tie_back: The prayer names exactly the Kural’s danger: want driving a decent person to shameful deeds and words.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to immorality, while Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an pairs the fear of poverty with the pull toward shameful conduct, both ascribed to Satan’s whispering.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees poverty, or the dread of it, as the doorway to disgraceful behaviour.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Three matters cause a person to act against his own will and the will of his Maker, and they are: Gentiles, and an evil spirit, and the depths of extreme poverty.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud lists crushing poverty among forces that make a person act against both his own nature and God’s will, and therefore asks that we pray for such people.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point precisely: poverty can make even the well-born behave unlike themselves.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Eruvin 41b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta the Buddha relates how a king who failed to give wealth to the destitute let poverty spread, and from poverty came theft, then weapons, killing and lying, so that a whole people sank into degraded conduct.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta traces a causal chain in which poverty is the first step toward social and moral collapse.
buddhism.tie_back: It extends the Kural’s point from one family to a whole society: want breeds base acts and base words, including lying.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A houseless and poor monk who wanders from village to village may become tired of ascetic life: he should bear this trouble.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira names discontent (arati), the weariness of the poor wandering monk, as a trouble to be recognised and overcome.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism acknowledges the very soarvu (weariness) the Kural describes, but asks that it be mastered rather than allowed to degrade one.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The hungry person does not care about honor, dishonor or harsh words.”
sikhism.explanation: In Gauri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan observes that someone driven by hunger stops weighing honour and shame and will put up with insults or speak without restraint to get food; he uses this as a simile for the seeker's single-minded longing.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says poverty breeds, even in the well-born, a weariness from which mean and shameful words come; Guru Arjan likewise notes that hunger erases a person's sense of honour and dishonour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 317, Raag Gauri, Gauri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “An evil shame is the needy man’s companion, shame which both greatly harms and prospers men: shame is with poverty, but confidence with wealth.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod observes that need brings with it a crippling sense of shame, while wealth brings confidence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both poets see poverty as robbing a person of the dignity that normally governs speech and conduct.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 317-319 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Wealth, I said, and poverty; the one is the parent of luxury and indolence, and the other of meanness and viciousness, and both of discontent.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells Adeimantus that poverty breeds meanness and vice, which is why the guardians must keep both extremes out of the city.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s ‘poverty, the parent of meanness’ is the Kural’s claim that want gives birth to base conduct.

real_life_example.event_title: Mozart's letters to Michael Puchberg asking for loans
real_life_example.event: From June 1788, at a hard time for musicians in Vienna, Mozart began writing a series of letters to his friend and fellow Freemason, the merchant Michael Puchberg, asking for money. In one he admitted that he still owed Puchberg eight ducats and could not repay them, yet asked for a hundred gulden more; later letters asked for far larger sums. Puchberg lent smaller amounts again and again, and the appeals continued until a few months before Mozart's death in December 1791.
real_life_example.explanation: The letters show one of the most gifted and cultivated artists of his age reduced by money troubles to repeated, apologetic pleas.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that want breeds, even in the well-born, a weariness from which humbling words come out, and Mozart's pleading letters to Puchberg are a documented case of a refined man pressed into such speech.

tamil:
நல்குரவு என்னும் இடும்பையுள் பல்குரைத்
துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்.
transliteration:
Nalkuravu ennum idumbaiyuL palkuraith
thunbangaL sendru padum.
meaning: Inside the one trouble called poverty, many kinds of sorrows gather and settle.
elementary: Have you seen one leak in a roof let in rain that ruins the carpet, the books and the bed? Valluvar says poverty is like that one leak: many other troubles come pouring in through it.
university: Idumbai (இடும்பை, ‘affliction, distress’) names poverty as one trouble, and palkurai (பல்குரை, ‘of many kinds’) thunbangaL (‘sorrows’) are said to ‘go and settle’ (sendru padum) within it. Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah read this as all sorrows being contained in poverty, so that poverty is the sum of misfortunes; Mu. Varadarasanar says they ‘arise and grow’ inside it; Kalaignar reverses the image slightly, with many sorrows springing out of poverty. Either way poverty is the matrix of other ills, which prepares for the later couplets on lost respect (1046), estranged kin (1047) and sleepless dread (1048-1049). Pope’s ‘Attendant sorrows plenteous grow’ follows the ‘springing up’ reading. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The acts of a person who, possessed of little intelligence, suffers himself to be divested of wealth, are all dried up like shallow streams in the summer season.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna argues that once wealth is lost every undertaking withers, like streams in summer.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the loss of means is not one trouble but the drying-up of everything else.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs observes that for the afflicted every day brings trouble.
christianity.tie_back: The afflicted person’s days filled with evils echo the Kural’s many sorrows gathered in poverty.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits, but give good tidings to the patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an lists hunger and loss of wealth among a cluster of trials that come together.
islam.tie_back: Loss of wealth arrives alongside fear, hunger and other losses, as the Kural says many sorrows gather in poverty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Poverty in a person’s household is more difficult than fifty plagues.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Pinehas ben Hama, reading the friends’ words to Job, concludes that poverty at home outweighs fifty plagues.
judaism.tie_back: Fifty plagues gathered in one condition is the Kural’s ‘sorrows of every kind’ settling inside poverty.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Bava Batra 116a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Poverty is called suffering in the world; so, too, is getting into debt. A poor person, in debt, partaking of sensuality, suffers hardship. Then they hound him and put him into bondage.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces how poverty leads to debt, interest, notices, harassment and finally bondage, one suffering after another.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta lays out step by step how many sorrows flow into the one condition of poverty.

jainism.quote_or_event: “All men who are ignorant of the Truth are subject to pain; in the endless Samsâra they suffer in many ways.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that the root of manifold suffering is ignorance of the truth, which keeps beings bound in samsara.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural finds many sorrows gathered in poverty, Jainism locates their common root in spiritual ignorance.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 6.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So many endure distress, deprivation and constant abuse. Even these are Your Gifts, O Great Giver!”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak acknowledges that countless people live with suffering, hunger and continual blows, yet asks that even this be accepted as falling within God's hukam (divine order).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says every kind of sorrow gathers and settles within the single affliction of poverty; Guru Nanak names distress, hunger and abuse together as the lot of many, though he teaches acceptance rather than lament.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib (Pauri 25), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Disguised as a beggar, Odysseus says that nothing is more shameless than the hungry belly, which forces a man to remember it and drives men to endure many evils for its sake.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s hero, living as a poor wanderer, names hunger as the source of a whole train of hardships.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The beggar Odysseus shows the Kural’s point that want brings many sufferings with it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Of all the woes of luckless poverty none is harder to endure than this, that it exposes men to ridicule.”
philosophy.explanation: Juvenal’s Umbritius catalogues the many woes of the Roman poor: high rent, torn clothes, lost legacies, contempt and danger.
philosophy.tie_back: Juvenal’s ‘woes of luckless poverty’ is a satirist’s inventory of the Kural’s many sorrows gathered in want.

real_life_example.event_title: Victor Hugo publishes Les Miserables
real_life_example.place: Brussels and Paris (written at Hauteville House, Guernsey)
real_life_example.event: Victor Hugo, living in exile at Hauteville House on Guernsey, published Les Miserables in 1862, and it was an immediate popular success that was quickly translated into other languages. In its short preface Hugo named the degradation of men through poverty, the ruin of women through hunger and the stunting of children as the problems of the age, and the novel follows the ex-convict Jean Valjean and the impoverished single mother Fantine through a chain of misfortunes that grow out of want.
real_life_example.explanation: The novel made the many-sided suffering of the poor the centre of a work read across the world, and it remains one of the best-known portraits of social injustice in nineteenth-century France.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that within the single affliction of poverty sorrows of every kind gather, and Hugo's preface and story trace exactly that: hunger, prison, outcasting, illness and the ruin of children all rooted in want.

tamil:
நற்பொருள் நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும் நல்கூர்ந்தார்
சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்.
transliteration:
NaRporuL nangunarndhu sollinum nalkoorndhaar
soRporuL soarvu padum.
meaning: Even when poor people speak true and wise things that they fully understand, their words are ignored and come to nothing.
elementary: Imagine two children giving the same right answer in class, but everyone only listens to the one with the fancy new shoes. Valluvar noticed that people often ignore what poor people say, even when it is wise, and that this is unfair.
university: NaRporuL (நற்பொருள்) is ‘good matter’, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar specify as the sense of good books (nool), and nangunarndhu (‘having understood well’) stresses that the speaker is genuinely learned. Yet the soRporuL (சொற்பொருள், ‘the meaning of the words’) of nalkoorndhaar (நல்கூர்ந்தார், ‘those who have become poor’) suffers soarvu, here ‘failure, lapse’: it is not heard or heeded. The same word soarvu that meant inner weariness in 1044 here describes the social fate of the poor man’s speech, a deliberate echo. Solomon Pappaiah puts it simply: if the speaker is poor, his words are not honoured. Pope’s ‘Their sense from memory of mankind will fade away’ takes the lapse as being forgotten. The observation is descriptive and critical, not an endorsement of the bias. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He that has wealth is regarded as a learned man.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna bluntly notes that society credits the wealthy with learning, and adds that a poor man is accused falsely even when he stands near.
hinduism.tie_back: If wealth is taken for learning, then, as the Kural says, the poor man’s real learning goes unheard.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing... and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool.”
christianity.explanation: James rebukes a congregation that honours the rich visitor and pushes the poor one aside.
christianity.tie_back: The poor man is dismissed before he speaks, exactly the bias the Kural records, though James condemns it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they said, ‘Why was this Qur’an not sent down upon a great man from [one of] the two cities?’”
islam.explanation: The Meccan elite questioned the revelation because it came through a man without great wealth or rank.
islam.tie_back: They judged the message by the messenger’s means, the very prejudice the Kural observes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So I observed: Wisdom is better than valor; but The wisdom of the poor is scorned, And their words are not heeded.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet tells of a poor wise man who saved a city yet was forgotten, and concludes that the poor man’s wisdom is despised.
judaism.tie_back: This is a near-exact match: wise words from the poor go unheeded.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “...whoever has no conviction with regard to skillful mental qualities... no discernment with regard to skillful mental qualities is, in the discipline of a noble one, said to be poor, destitute, & penniless.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines real poverty as the lack of conviction, conscience, persistence and discernment.
buddhism.tie_back: Against the world’s habit of dismissing the materially poor, the Buddha says the truly poor are those without wisdom, a pointed counterpoint to the Kural’s observation.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
jainism.explanation: The mendicant, who owns nothing, must expect contempt and abuse from householders and bear it without resentment.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism assumes the poor will be slighted, as the Kural observes, and asks the voluntarily poor to meet it with equanimity.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “No one respects the poor man. He may make thousands of efforts, but no one pays any attention to him.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir describes with sharp realism how society ignores the destitute, however hard they try to be heard.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even when the poor speak sound truths, their words are disregarded; Kabir likewise says that whatever the poor man does, no one pays him any attention.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus, disguised as a beggar in his own hall, speaks wisely to the suitors, Antinous mocks him and hurls a footstool at him; his words carry no weight because he appears to be a destitute stranger.
greek_mythology.explanation: The rightful king is scorned because of his rags, even though his speech is shrewd.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer dramatises the Kural’s observation that a poor man’s well-understood words are brushed aside.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A man’s word is believed in exact proportion to the amount of cash which he keeps in his strong box.”
philosophy.explanation: Juvenal’s Umbritius complains that in Rome a witness is asked first about his wealth and last about his character.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point stated almost as a formula: credibility tracks money, not understanding.

real_life_example.event_title: The Jarrow March brings a petition of the unemployed to Parliament
real_life_example.place: Jarrow to London, England, United Kingdom
real_life_example.event: After the closure of Palmer's shipyard left most of Jarrow's workforce without jobs, about 200 unemployed men, each medically examined, marched nearly 300 miles to London carrying a petition signed by some 12,000 people asking for new industry. Their MP, Ellen Wilkinson, presented the petition to Parliament on 4 November 1936, but Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin did not meet the marchers, the petition was received without being debated, and the march produced few immediate results.
real_life_example.explanation: The marchers' orderly, well-reasoned plea won public sympathy along the route yet was largely passed over by the government, though the march later came to be seen as a defining event of the 1930s.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural observes that even sound and well-understood words lose their force when spoken by the poor, and the Jarrow men's carefully argued petition was received in Parliament and left undebated.

tamil:
அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு ஈன்றதா யானும்
பிறன்போல நோக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
ARanjaaraa nalkuravu eendradhaa yaanum
piRanpoala noakkap padum.
meaning: A person in poverty that has no goodness about it is looked at like a stranger, even by the mother who gave birth to them.
elementary: A mother’s love is the strongest love there is. Valluvar warns that if someone becomes poor because of bad choices and also turns away from doing right, people may turn away from him, and even his own family may feel hurt and distant.
university: The decisive qualifier is aRanjaaraa (அறஞ்சாரா, ‘not joined to aram, virtue’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as ‘poverty not in keeping with virtue’, i.e. destitution that is unrighteous in cause or accompaniment; Solomon Pappaiah glosses it as poverty without just reasons; Kalaignar makes it moral, the person who abandons virtue because of poverty. Eendra thaai (ஈன்ற தாய், ‘the mother who bore him’) is the strongest possible bond, and piRan poala (‘like another, a stranger’) marks its collapse. Read with the qualifier, the couplet does not say that every poor person is rejected, only that want combined with the loss of aram estranges even the closest kin. The ytamizh.com English explanation (‘reduced to absolute poverty’) passes over aRanjaaraa, a reminder that translations differ on how much moral weight to give it. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He that has wealth has friends. He that has wealth has kinsmen.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna says that friendship and kinship follow wealth.
hinduism.tie_back: The converse is the Kural’s picture: when wealth goes, even kin may look on a man as a stranger.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want... and no man gave unto him.”
christianity.explanation: The prodigal son, having squandered his inheritance, is left starving with no one to help, yet his father later runs to embrace him.
christianity.tie_back: The parable matches the Kural’s self-caused, unvirtuous poverty and its isolation, but reverses its ending: the parent does not treat the son as a stranger.

islam.quote_or_event: “On the Day a man will flee from his brother And his mother and his father”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an depicts the Day of Judgement as a time when even the closest kin flee from one another, each absorbed in his own fate.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s image of a mother’s bond giving way, though in an eschatological, not economic, setting.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The poor are despised even by their peers, But the rich have many friends.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that poverty brings contempt even from one’s own circle.
judaism.tie_back: Being despised by one’s own peers is the Kural’s being looked upon as a stranger by one’s own.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A trustworthy person is the best kinsman.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada locates true kinship in trustworthiness rather than in blood or wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s qualifier, poverty without virtue, finds an echo here: it is character, not birth, that makes and keeps kin.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife, and sons will not be able to help me, when I suffer for my own deeds.”
jainism.explanation: The monk reflects that no relative can share or lift the consequences of his own karma.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees family ties failing the person who has fallen through his own conduct, but draws from this a call to detachment.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 6.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When the poor man goes to the rich man, and sits right in front of him, the rich man turns his back on him.”
sikhism.explanation: In the same hymn, Kabir pictures the poor man sitting face to face with a wealthy acquaintance who simply turns away, treating him as a stranger.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says one sunk in poverty is looked upon as a stranger even by his own mother; Kabir shows the same estrangement, as the rich man turns his back on the poor man in front of him.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as poor travellers, were turned away from a thousand homes in Phrygia before the aged Baucis and Philemon took them in.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s tale shows how readily people treat the poor wayfarer as an unwelcome stranger.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The thousand closed doors illustrate the Kural’s observation that the destitute are looked upon as strangers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...though he is destitute and begging for a bite, no one will help him with a meal, no one offer him board or shelter.”
philosophy.explanation: Juvenal describes the poor scholar Codrus, whose few belongings burn and whom nobody will help.
philosophy.tie_back: Codrus, abandoned by all, embodies the Kural’s destitute man looked upon as a stranger.

real_life_example.event_title: Edgar Allan Poe's gambling debts estrange him from his foster father
real_life_example.place: Charlottesville and Richmond, Virginia, United States
real_life_example.event: Edgar Allan Poe, raised in Richmond as the foster son of the merchant John Allan, was sent to the University of Virginia in 1826 with too little money to cover his expenses. When Allan ignored his requests for help, Poe turned to gambling, ran up debts of about 2,000 dollars that Allan refused to pay, and left the university in December 1826. Estranged from Allan and facing his creditors, he left Richmond for Boston in 1827.
real_life_example.explanation: The quarrel over debts incurred through gambling began a lasting breach between Poe and the man who had brought him up.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that want unconnected with virtue makes a person a stranger even to the one who raised him, and Poe's gambling debts turned his foster father against him.

tamil:
இன்றும் வருவது கொல்லோ நெருநலும்
கொன்றது போலும் நிரப்பு.
transliteration:
Indrum varuvadhu kolloa nerunalum
kondradhu poalum nirappu.
meaning: A poor person asks in fear, 'Will the need that almost killed me yesterday come again today?'
elementary: Imagine having a very scary day, and waking up the next morning worried: “Will it happen again today?” Valluvar says a very poor person feels like that every single day, afraid that yesterday’s hunger and worry will come back.
university: The couplet is spoken in the voice of the poor man himself, an unusual dramatic touch in the Porutpaal. Nirappu (நிரப்பு, ‘want, need’) is a synonym of nalkuravu, and the particle kolloa (கொல்லோ) marks anxious questioning: ‘will it come today too?’. Nerunal (நெருநல், ‘yesterday’) and kondradhu poalum (‘as though it killed’) describe the daily ordeal as a near-death; Puliyur Kesikan adds the implied cry ‘if it comes, what shall I do?’, while Mu. Varadarasanar frames it as the poor man’s daily trembling. Kalaignar reads it as a longing that it may not return. The present-tense dread contrasts with the general statements of the earlier couplets and leads into the sleeplessness of 1049. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, the nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons. They arise from sense perception, O scion of Bharata, and one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that distress comes and goes like the seasons and must be endured without agitation.
hinduism.tie_back: Where the Kural voices dread of yesterday’s misery returning, the Gita counsels tolerating such recurring distress with equanimity.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his hearers not to be consumed by anxiety about tomorrow’s needs.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural records exactly the daily anxiety over provision that this teaching seeks to dissolve.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, with hardship [will be] ease.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an assures the believer that every hardship is accompanied by relief.
islam.tie_back: Against the poor man’s fear that yesterday’s hardship will return, the verse promises ease alongside it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Four are considered as if they were dead: A pauper, and a leper, and a blind person, and one who has no children.”
judaism.explanation: A baraita counts the pauper among those who are regarded as dead, deriving it from Exodus 4:19, where men who had lost their property are called dead.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural says poverty ‘as good as killed’ the poor man yesterday; the Talmud treats the pauper as one already counted among the dead.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Nedarim 64b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, we who possess nothing. Feeders on joy we shall be, like the Radiant Gods.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada celebrates monks who own nothing and yet live in joy.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s poor man fears each day’s want; the Buddhist renunciant, owning nothing, has nothing left to fear losing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “‘I get nothing to-day, perhaps I shall get something to-morrow;’ a monk who thinks thus, will not be grieved by his want of success.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches the alms-seeking monk to meet an empty bowl with calm hope instead of distress.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s day-by-day anxiety over want turned inside out: today’s lack is accepted and tomorrow is faced without dread.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Why, O mind, do you plot and plan, when the Dear Lord Himself provides for your care?”
sikhism.explanation: In the evening prayer So Dar (Rehras), Guru Arjan rebukes the anxious mind that keeps scheming about tomorrow's livelihood, reminding it that God has already taken on its care. Sikh commentators stress that this forbids worry, not honest effort.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural gives voice to the poor man's dread that yesterday's near-fatal want will return today; Guru Arjan addresses exactly that fearful planning and answers it with trust in God's provision.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Never dare to taunt a man with deadly poverty which eats out the heart; it is sent by the deathless gods.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod calls poverty ‘deadly’ and ‘heart-eating’, a slow killer that should never be mocked.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s ‘deadly poverty which eats out the heart’ is the Kural’s want that ‘as good as killed’ the poor man yesterday.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 717-718 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...my means are less to-day than they were yesterday, and to-morrow will rub off something from the little that is left...”
philosophy.explanation: Juvenal’s Umbritius explains why he is leaving Rome: each day his small means shrink further.
philosophy.tie_back: The yesterday-today-tomorrow arithmetic of want is the very rhythm of the Kural’s anxious question.

real_life_example.event_title: The Dutch Hunger Winter
real_life_example.event: In September 1944 the German occupiers imposed an embargo on food transport to the western Netherlands, and with an exceptionally harsh winter and poor harvests the region slid into famine. People lived on rations of roughly 400 to 800 calories a day and ate grass and tulip bulbs to survive, and about 20,000 people died before liberation in May 1945.
real_life_example.explanation: For months millions of people woke each day not knowing whether they would find enough to eat, and the famine left lasting effects on the health of survivors and their children.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural gives the voice of the poor man who asks each morning whether yesterday's crushing want will come again today, and the Hunger Winter was a whole population living that dread day after day.

tamil:
நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும் நிரப்பினுள்
யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது.
transliteration:
NeruppinuL thunjalum aagum nirappinuL
yaadhondrum kaNpaadu aridhu.
meaning: A person might somehow sleep in the middle of a fire, but in the middle of poverty, they cannot close their eyes at all.
elementary: Have you ever been so worried that you could not fall asleep? Valluvar says that worrying about having no food or money is so strong that it is even harder to sleep than if you were lying next to a fire.
university: The hyperbole sets two ‘insides’ side by side: neruppinuL (‘within fire’) and nirappinuL (‘within want’). Thunjal (துஞ்சல், ‘sleeping’) is said to be possible (aagum) in the first, while kaNpaadu (கண்பாடு, ‘the closing of the eyes, sleep’) is aridhu (‘rare, hard’) in the second, yaadhondrum (‘by any means at all’). Puliyur Kesikan explains how sleeping in fire might be possible, through the help of mantra and medicine, and Solomon Pappaiah through yogic power; Pappaiah also narrows nirappu to the torment of hunger. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep the image general. The couplet follows naturally from 1048: the dread of tomorrow’s want is what keeps the poor awake. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not disturbed in mind even amidst the threefold miseries or elated when there is happiness, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the sthita-prajna, whose mind remains calm in every kind of misery.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural observes that want makes rest impossible; the Gita holds up the sage whose peace no misery can disturb.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.56 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep.”
christianity.explanation: Kohelet says the labourer sleeps well whatever he eats, while the rich man’s wealth keeps him awake.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts tie sleep to one’s material state, but Ecclesiastes reverses the Kural, giving the sleepless nights to the rich.

islam.quote_or_event: “They were touched by poverty and hardship and were shaken until [even their] messenger and those who believed with him said, ‘When is the help of Allah?’ Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an recalls earlier believers so shaken by poverty and hardship that even their prophet cried out for help.
islam.tie_back: The deep agitation that poverty produces, the Kural’s sleeplessness, is acknowledged here before relief is promised.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Master of the universe, I accept upon myself all the suffering in the world, but not poverty, for when I go out to the marketplace and I do not have in my possession a peruta with which to purchase, what will I eat?”
judaism.explanation: In the Midrash, Job, offered a choice, prefers every other suffering to poverty because of the gnawing question of what he will eat.
judaism.tie_back: Job’s preference for any suffering over the anxiety of want parallels the Kural’s preference for sleeping in fire over lying awake in poverty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Yes, young man. I have slept in ease. Of those in the world who sleep in ease, I am one.”
buddhism.explanation: On a freezing winter night on a thin bed of leaves, the Buddha says he slept well, because passion, aversion and delusion, the real fevers that rob sleep, are gone.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says want makes sleep impossible; the Buddha shows that the one who has abandoned craving sleeps in ease even in extreme hardship.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
jainism.explanation: Told by Indra that his palace is burning, the renouncing king Nami replies that nothing of his can burn, since he owns nothing.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural sets fire against want; Nami shows that for one who has given up possession, neither fire nor want can disturb his peace.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, I thought that I was in trouble; the whole world is in trouble! When I climbed the hill and looked around, I saw this fire in each and every home.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid describes suffering as a fire that he first thought burned only in his own house, until a wider view showed it burning in every home.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a man might sleep in the middle of fire but never in the middle of want; Farid likewise pictures human distress as a fire burning inside each household.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 81) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, punished in the underworld, stands in water beneath laden fruit trees, yet the water recedes and the branches lift whenever he reaches for them, so he is never fed and never at rest.
greek_mythology.explanation: His torment is endless want in sight of plenty, a restlessness that never ends.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tantalus embodies the Kural’s claim that want allows no rest, more unbearable than physical torment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For what sleep is possible in a lodging? Who but the wealthy get sleep in Rome?”
philosophy.explanation: Juvenal complains that in Rome only the rich can afford quiet enough to sleep.
philosophy.tie_back: The satirist arrives at the Kural’s conclusion by a different road: poverty means no sleep.

real_life_example.event_title: George Orwell publishes Down and Out in Paris and London
real_life_example.event: George Orwell's first book, Down and Out in Paris and London, published in 1933, recounts in lightly fictionalised form his own time living among the poor. In Paris he lived in a slum and worked as a hotel dishwasher, and in London and on the roads of England he lived as a tramp, queuing for a bed in the casual wards and lodging houses where a mug of tea, a piece of bread and a blanket were all that was offered.
real_life_example.explanation: The book showed readers from the inside how destitution governs every hour of a poor person's day and night, and it helped change how homelessness was discussed in Britain.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a person may somehow sleep in fire but never in the midst of want, and Orwell's account shows the destitute spending their nights in anxious search of a place to lie down.

tamil:
துப்புர வில்லார் துவரத் துறவாமை
உப்பிற்கும் காடிக்கும் கூற்று.
transliteration:
Thuppura villaar thuvarath thuRavaamai
uppiRkum kaadikkum koottru.
meaning: If very poor people do not fully give up worldly life, they become like death to other people's salt and rice-water (thin rice soup), only eating up what others have.
elementary: Imagine someone who has nothing and keeps taking a little salt and soup from the neighbours, but does nothing else with his life. Valluvar says that person should either change his life completely or choose a simple life of giving things up, instead of just using up what others need.
university: Thuppuravu (துப்புரவு) means the things one enjoys or lives by, so thuppuravillaar are ‘those without any means’. Thuvara (‘completely’) thuRavaamai (‘not renouncing’) is the fault named: Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar say the only course left to such people is full renunciation, and failing it they are merely koottru (கூற்று, Yama, death) to uppu (salt) and kaadi (காடி, sour rice-water or gruel; Pope’s ‘vinegar’). Solomon Pappaiah sharpens the social point: by staying in household life they consume the salt and gruel in other people’s homes. Kalaignar reads thuppuravu as orderliness, so the subject becomes those impoverished by disorderly living. The chapter thus ends by pointing toward thuRavu (renunciation), linking the Porutpaal back to the Thuravaraviyal of the first book, and leads into Iravu (begging) in ch. 106. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “...said that poverty is for recluses. Making no provision for the morrow is a practice that suits Rishis.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna reports Nahusha’s verdict that a life without possessions suits only ascetics who have renounced the world.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s point: total want is fitting only for those who fully renounce.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Thessalonians that those who will not work should not live off others.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts object to the person who simply consumes others’ food, though Paul’s remedy is work, the Kural’s is renunciation.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the dignified poor who, through restraint, refrain from begging and burdening others.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that the destitute should not become a drain on others, commending restraint instead.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Skin a carcass in the market and take payment, but do not say: I am a priest, or: I am a great man, and this matter disgusts me.”
judaism.explanation: Rav tells Rav Kahana to take even the lowliest paid work rather than become dependent on others.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural condemns living off others’ salt and gruel; the Talmud insists on any honest labour to avoid dependence.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Pesachim 113a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that contentment with little is itself the highest form of wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the destitute to renounce fully; the Buddhist answer is that contentment turns having little into true riches.

jainism.quote_or_event: “An ascetic should not lay by any store, not even so little as the grease (sticking to his alms-bowl); but as a bird with its plumage, so he with his alms-bowl should wander about without desires.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk owns only his bowl, stores nothing, and lives on what is freely given for his bare survival.
jainism.tie_back: This is the complete renunciation (thuvarath thuRavu) the Kural says the destitute should embrace instead of lingering as a burden.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 6.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “But better than these is dry bread, if one sings the Glorious Praises of the Lord in the Society of the Saints.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir says that alms-bread eaten while praising God in holy company is better than royal wealth and pleasures. The Sikh Gurus, however, reject living by begging and ask even renunciants to earn by honest work.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the utterly destitute should renounce fully rather than live off other people's salt and gruel; Kabir likewise prefers a bare, devotional life to grasping, but Sikh teaching as a whole rejects the renunciant path the Kural recommends.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 150) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Both gods and men are angry with a man who lives idle, for in nature he is like the stingless drones...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod compares the idle man to drones who eat the honey that worker bees produce.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The drone that consumes others’ stores is the Kural’s destitute man who is death to his neighbours’ salt and gruel.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 303-304 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Provide things relating to the body no further than mere use; as meat, drink, clothing, house, family. But strike off and reject everything relating to show and delicacy.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus counsels limiting one’s bodily needs to bare use and rejecting everything beyond it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Stoic minimalism approaches the Kural’s call to renounce rather than to lean on others for more than one needs.

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi adopts the loincloth at Madurai
real_life_example.event: On his tour of South India in 1921, while urging people to boycott foreign cloth, Gandhi met many who said they were too poor to buy khadi to replace what they wore. In Madurai on 22 September 1921 he gave up his shirt and cap and adopted the simple loincloth (some accounts say dhoti and shawl), explaining that he hesitated to advise anything he was not prepared to follow himself and wanted to make the change easier for those who could not afford new clothes.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi chose to reduce his own needs to the level of the poorest rather than ask more of them, and the simple dress became his lasting symbol.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that those who have nothing should embrace full renunciation rather than linger as a burden on others, and Gandhi's decision at Madurai was a voluntary renunciation that identified him with India's poorest.

tamil:
இரக்க இரத்தக்கார்க் காணின் கரப்பின்
அவர்பழி தம்பழி அன்று.
transliteration:
Irakka iraththakkaark kaanin karappin
avarpazhi thampazhi andru.
meaning: If you meet people it is right to ask, you may ask them for help. If they hide what they have and say no, the blame is theirs, not yours.
elementary: Imagine you are really hungry and you politely ask a kind neighbour who has plenty of food for a little. If that neighbour pretends to have nothing, you did nothing wrong by asking. The person who hid the food is the one who acted badly.
university: The chapter on iravu (இரவு, 'asking, mendicancy') follows Nalkuravu (ch. 105, poverty) and is balanced by Iravachcham (ch. 107, dread of begging); together they permit asking only in real need and only of fitting givers. The key word irakka iraththakkaar (இரத்தக்கார், 'those of whom it is fit to ask') limits the permission: one may ask those able and willing to give. Karappin (கரப்பின், 'if they conceal') names the vice of hiding what one has, a word the chapter returns to again and again (karappu, karaththal); the commentarial line that follows Parimelazhagar, as reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, takes the blame (pazhi) as falling wholly on the one who conceals. Pope renders it 'Theirs is the sin, not yours, if they the gift deny.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The man with food in store who, when the needy comes in miserable case begging for bread to eat, / Hardens his heart against him-even when of old he did him service-finds not one to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn 'Liberality' condemns the well-stocked man who hardens his heart against a hungry beggar and warns that he will himself be left without comfort.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hymn puts the fault on the one who withholds, not on the one who asks.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.2 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it. Say not unto thy neighbour, Go, and come again, and to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs forbids putting off a neighbour in need when one actually has what he asks for.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's karappu, pretending to have nothing while having it, is exactly what Proverbs forbids.

islam.quote_or_event: “And withhold [simple] assistance.”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Ma'un ends its list of those it rebukes with people who refuse even small acts of help.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an, like the Kural, places the fault on those who hold back help from someone who asks.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Beware lest you harbor the base thought, ‘The seventh year, the year of remission, is approaching,’ so that you are mean and give nothing to your needy kindred—who will cry out to God against you, and you will incur guilt.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah warns that whoever refuses a needy kinsman out of meanness incurs guilt when the poor person cries out against him.
judaism.tie_back: Deuteronomy, like the Kural, says the guilt falls on the one who refuses, not on the one who asks.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 15:9 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak the truth; yield not to anger; when asked, give even if you only have a little. By these three means can one reach the presence of the gods.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists giving when asked, even from little, as one of three practices that lead to the heavens.
buddhism.tie_back: Dhammapada 224 holds the person who is asked responsible for answering the request, which is where the Kural puts the duty.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The hand (of the giver) is not always kindly stretched out to a monk when he is on his begging tour; but he should not think that it would be better to live as a householder.”
jainism.explanation: Among the twenty-two hardships a Jain monk must bear, Mahavira lists having to ask for everything and meeting givers whose hands are not always open.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain text admits what the Kural assumes, that some who could give will hold back, and it does not count asking as a fault in the one who asks.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Lentils, flour and ghee - these things, I beg of You.”
sikhism.explanation: In his aarti hymn in Dhanasri, Bhagat Dhanna, a farmer, asks God plainly for the simple food and goods he needs. In Gurbani the one fully fitting giver to ask is God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural permits asking when one meets someone it is fitting to ask; Dhanna asks without shame because he addresses the one Giver who is always fit to be asked.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 695, Raag Dhanasri, Bhagat Dhanna (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Your looks, my fine sir, are better than your breeding; if you were in your own house you would not spare a poor man so much as a pinch of salt, for though you are in another man's, and surrounded with abundance, you cannot find it in you to give him even a piece of bread.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Disguised as a beggar, Odysseus rebukes the suitor Antinous, who refuses him while sitting amid plenty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The epic, like the Kural, puts the disgrace on the man who hides behind excuses and refuses, not on the beggar.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you have already given to anyone else, give to me also; if not, begin with me.”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes the Cynic, who begged when he was poor, used this formula to ask for alms without apology.
philosophy.tie_back: Diogenes asked openly, as if asking a fitting person were no disgrace, which is the Kural's own position.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.49 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: Canada turns away the passengers of the Komagata Maru
real_life_example.event: The steamship Komagata Maru arrived in Vancouver harbour on 23 May 1914 carrying 376 South Asian passengers who hoped to settle in Canada. Under the immigration laws of the day the government refused almost all of them entry, and after two months aboard the ship was escorted out of the harbour by the Canadian military on 23 July and forced to return to India. In May 2016 Prime Minister Justin Trudeau formally apologised in the House of Commons, saying the Canadian government had been responsible for the laws that kept the passengers out.
real_life_example.explanation: More than a century later the Canadian state accepted that the fault lay with the laws and officials who refused the passengers, not with the people who had come asking to be admitted.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one may ask those whom it is fitting to ask, and if they withhold, the blame is theirs and not the asker's, and Canada's formal apology placed the blame squarely on those who refused.

tamil:
இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல் இரந்தவை
துன்பம் உறாஅ வரின்.
transliteration:
Inbam oruvarku iraththal irandhavai
thunbam uraaa varin.
meaning: Even asking for help can be a pleasure, if what you ask for comes to you without pain for either person.
elementary: If you ask a friend to share a crayon and they hand it over with a smile, asking feels nice, not embarrassing. Asking only hurts when the other person sighs or makes you feel small.
university: Valluvar makes the surprising claim that iraththal (இரத்தல், 'begging') can itself be inbam (இன்பம், 'pleasure'), on one condition: that what is begged comes thunbam uraaa (துன்பம் உறாஅ, 'without suffering'), where the lengthened uraaa is an alapedai (metrical lengthening). Commentators differ on whose suffering is meant: Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as the asker's (the gift comes without hardship), Solomon Pappaiah as the giver's reluctance, and Kalaignar as both minds, giver's and receiver's, being free of pain. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar stresses that the pleasure depends on the giver's goodwill (Puliyur Kesikan: ஈவாரது நல்லுணர்வால்). Pope: 'Even to ask an alms may pleasure give, / If what you ask without annoyance you receive.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhagavad Gita 17.21 classes as rajasic (passionate) the charity given grudgingly, or with an eye to some return, setting it below the sattvic gift given freely out of duty.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna grades gifts by the giver's state of mind, and a grudging gift falls to the lower, passionate grade.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's condition that the gift come 'without pain' matches the Gita's preference for gifts given without grudging.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.21 (paraphrase; cf. Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks the Corinthians to give willingly and without reluctance, because a cheerful gift is what pleases God.
christianity.tie_back: A cheerful gift is exactly what makes asking a pleasure in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “And as for the petitioner, do not repel [him].”
islam.explanation: God tells the Prophet not to drive away or rebuff someone who comes asking.
islam.tie_back: Not being repelled is what keeps asking free of pain, which is the Kural's condition for it being a pleasure.

judaism.quote_or_event: Maimonides ranks charity in eight ascending degrees, and the higher degrees are those that spare the poor person shame, for example when giver and receiver do not know each other, or when the poor person is helped to become self-supporting.
judaism.explanation: Maimonides judges a gift partly by how much it spares the recipient embarrassment.
judaism.tie_back: His concern that receiving should not hurt the poor matches the Kural's condition that the gift come without pain.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:7-14 (paraphrase; tr. Eliyahu Touger available on Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As a bee gathers honey from the flower without injuring its color or fragrance, even so the sage goes on his alms-round in the village.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the monk on his alms round to a bee that takes nectar without harming the flower.
buddhism.tie_back: Asking that harms no one is exactly the painless begging the Kural calls a pleasure.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra opens (ch. 1, 'Drumapushpika') with the image of the bee that drinks from flowers without harming them, and teaches that monks should take alms from householders in the same way, accepting only what is given freely and causing no distress.
jainism.explanation: The image underlies the Jain term madhukari (bee-like) for the mendicant's alms round, in which the monk takes a little from many houses so that no family is burdened.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain rule that alms must cost the giver no hardship is the Kural's 'without pain' made into monastic discipline.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra, ch. 1 (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When I am hungry, I ask for food; when I am full, I am totally at peace.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan speaks as a child to its parent: asking for food is natural and carries no shame, and being fed brings complete contentment.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says asking can itself be a pleasure if what is asked for comes without pain to either side; Guru Arjan pictures exactly such easy asking between a child and a loving parent.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1214, Raag Sarang, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Why should you want to see this stranger turned out of the house? Heaven forbid; take' something and give it him yourself; I do not grudge it; I bid you take it.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus tells Antinous to give the beggar something from the house's stores, saying he does not grudge it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A gift offered without grudging is what makes asking pleasant, which is the Kural's point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He was begging of a miserly man who was slow to respond; so he said, ‘My friend, it's for food that I'm asking, not for funeral expenses.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes mocks a miser whose slow, pained giving made a small request feel like a great burden.
philosophy.tie_back: The joke assumes the Kural's point: asking turns sour when the gift comes with pain.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.56 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: Beethoven's patrons grant him a lifelong annuity to stay in Vienna
real_life_example.event: When Beethoven was offered the post of music director at the court of Jerome Bonaparte in Kassel, he negotiated with three Viennese patrons, Archduke Rudolph, Prince Lobkowitz and Prince Kinsky, for support that would allow him to remain in Vienna. Their contract, signed on 1 March 1809, guaranteed him 4,000 florins a year, requiring only that he live in Vienna and compose. Archduke Rudolph, Beethoven's pupil, remained his most dependable patron, although the princes' payments were later disrupted by war, death and the devaluation of 1811.
real_life_example.explanation: Beethoven's request was met readily by admirers who considered it an honour to keep him in their city, and for years afterward he was provided for.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that asking itself can be a pleasure when what is asked comes without pain to either side, and Beethoven's patrons gave willingly to keep him as a composer in Vienna.

tamil:
கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சின் கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று
இரப்புமோ ரேஎர் உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Karappilaa nenjin kadanarivaar munnindru
irappumor eer udaiththu.
meaning: Asking can even have a kind of beauty, when you stand before people who hide nothing in their hearts and know what they should do.
elementary: Asking your grandmother, who loves to share, for a slice of cake doesn't feel bad at all. It can even feel nice, because she is happy you asked.
university: Karappilaa nenju (கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சு, 'a heart without concealment') and kadan arivaar (கடனறிவார், 'those who know their duty') describe the ideal giver. Kadan is read as duty (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah: 'this is my duty'), while Puliyur Kesikan glosses the givers as people who understand honour (மானம் அறிபவர்). The striking word is eer (ஏஎர், with alapedai lengthening, 'beauty, grace'): standing before such givers, even begging has beauty. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar reads the -um in irappum ('even begging') as conceding that begging is normally without grace. Pope: 'To stand as suppliants affords especial grace.' Texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, both printing the sandhi form இரப்புமோ ரேஎர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Charity given out of duty, without expectation of return, at the proper time and place, and to a worthy person is considered to be in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna calls sattvic, the highest kind, the gift given simply because it ought to be given (dātavyam iti), with no thought of return.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's kadan arivaar, givers who know their duty, are the Gita's sattvic givers.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.20 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.”
christianity.explanation: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his followers simply to give to whoever asks.
christianity.tie_back: Givers who never turn away a request are the open-hearted givers before whom the Kural says even asking has grace.

islam.quote_or_event: “And from their properties was [given] the right of the [needy] petitioner and the deprived.”
islam.explanation: Describing the righteous, the Qur'an says that the asker and the deprived had a right (haqq) in their wealth.
islam.tie_back: If the asker has a right to a share, then asking such people is not shameful, which is close to the Kural's 'grace'.

judaism.quote_or_event: “do not harden your heart and shut your hand against your needy kindred. Rather, you must open your hand and lend whatever is sufficient to meet the need.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands an open hand and an unhardened heart toward a needy kinsman, and lending enough to meet the need.
judaism.tie_back: The open hand and unhardened heart are the Kural's karappilaa nenju, the heart that hides nothing.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 15:7-8 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “I am a brahman, responsive to requests, open-handed, bearing my last body, an unsurpassed doctor & surgeon.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes himself as one who answers requests with an open hand, and then says that the gift of Dhamma is the highest gift.
buddhism.tie_back: 'Responsive to requests, open-handed' describes the kind of giver before whom, the Kural says, asking has grace.

jainism.quote_or_event: Atithi-samvibhaga, 'sharing with the guest', is one of the vows of the Jain householder: a duty to share pure food and requisites with mendicants who arrive unannounced.
jainism.explanation: Jain householders treat sharing with an arriving ascetic as a vow, part of their duty, rather than as an optional favour.
jainism.tie_back: A giver for whom sharing is a vow is the Kural's kadan arivaar, someone who knows giving as a duty.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7 (list of householder vows, incl. atithi-samvibhaga; verse numbering differs between Svetambara and Digambara recensions) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Balwand says that Khivi, the Guru's wife, is a noble woman, who gives soothing, leafy shade to all.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Ramkali ki Vaar of Satta and Balwand, Mata Khivi, wife of Guru Angad, is praised for running the Guru's langar and sheltering everyone who came. She is remembered as the model of open-hearted, dutiful giving.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says there is grace even in asking from those whose hearts hide nothing and who know their duty; Mata Khivi is the Sikh example of such a giver, whose shelter covered all who came.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar, Satta and Balwand (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Take this to the stranger, and tell him to go the round of the suitors, and beg from them; a beggar must not be shamefaced.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus sends the disguised Odysseus a whole loaf and tells him that a beggar need not be ashamed to ask.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In a house where the host gives freely, asking carries no shame, which is the Kural's point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says the liberal (generous) person gives for the sake of what is noble and gives rightly: to the right people, in the right amounts, at the right time, and with pleasure rather than pain.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, liberality is a settled disposition to give well, not an occasional act.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's ideal giver, open-hearted and knowing his duty, is close to Aristotle's liberal man.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.1 (tr. W. D. Ross) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Joseph Pulitzer's appeal pays for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal
real_life_example.event: When the American committee raising money for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal ran about 100,000 dollars short and construction stopped, the publisher Joseph Pulitzer used his newspaper, the New York World, to ask ordinary readers for small contributions and promised to print the name of every donor. By August 1885 the World had collected more than 100,000 dollars from some 120,000 people, most giving a dollar or less, and the pedestal was completed the following year.
real_life_example.explanation: The appeal turned a stalled project into a shared civic act, with ordinary people proud to see their names in print beside their gift.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that asking of people whose hearts hide nothing and who know their duty has a grace of its own, and Pulitzer's public appeal drew an open-handed response from a whole city.

tamil:
இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும் கரத்தல்
கனவிலும் தேற்றாதார் மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Iraththalum eedhale polum karaththal
kanavilum thetraadhaar maattu.
meaning: Asking people who would never hold back, not even in a dream, is as worthy of respect as giving.
elementary: Some people love sharing so much that when you ask them, it's like you're doing them a favour. With friends like that, asking feels almost as good as giving.
university: The line iraththalum eedhale polum (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும், 'begging too is just like giving') is one of the boldest claims in the Kural, and the emphatic ē in eedhale strengthens the equation. Its condition is that the giver karaththal kanavilum thetraadhaar (கரத்தல் கனவிலும் தேற்றாதார், 'does not know concealment even in a dream'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it as conferring the same dignity (சிறப்பு, பெருமை) on such asking as on giving. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar explains the equation by the giver's joy: asking such a person gives him the chance to give. Pope: 'To beg of such ... is in fact the same as giving.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.
