hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Vamana episode, Vishnu takes the form of a dwarf brahmin and asks King Bali for three paces of land. Bali gives without holding back, even after his preceptor warns him, and his giving earns him lasting glory and divine favour.
hinduism.explanation: When God himself becomes the asker, the request turns into an honour and a blessing for the one who gives.
hinduism.tie_back: The story makes the Kural's paradox literal: asking a giver who never withholds is a gift to that giver.

christianity.quote_or_event: The prophet Elijah asks a starving widow of Zarephath for water and a little bread, made from her last flour and oil. She gives, and her barrel of meal and cruse of oil do not run out for the rest of the famine.
christianity.explanation: The prophet's request, which looked like a burden on the widow, turned out to be a blessing for her.
christianity.tie_back: Asking a giver who does not hold back becomes, as the Kural says, like giving.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Saying], "We feed you only for the face [i.e., approval] of Allāh. We wish not from you reward or gratitude."”
islam.explanation: The righteous feed the needy, the orphan and the captive, and tell them that they want no reward or even thanks.
islam.tie_back: When a giver wants nothing back, the receiver owes nothing and is not lowered, so asking such a person costs no honour.

judaism.quote_or_event: “More than what the homeowner does for the poor person, the poor person does for the homeowner”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yehoshua reads Ruth's words about Boaz, 'for whom I acted today', as showing that by accepting his bread she did him a greater favour, giving him the merit of charity.
judaism.tie_back: The midrash says almost exactly what the Kural says: the one who receives also gives.
judaism.source: Vayikra Rabbah 34:8 (The Sefaria Midrash Rabbah, 2022, tr. Joshua Schreier)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, brahmans & householders are very helpful to you, as they provide you with the requisites of robes, alms food, lodgings, & medical requisites for the sick. And you, monks, are very helpful to brahmans & householders, as you teach them the Dhamma”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a two-way exchange: lay people give material support, and the monks who receive it give the Dhamma in return.
buddhism.tie_back: The almsman who asks is also a giver, which is the Kural's equation of asking with giving.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra defines dana (giving) as parting with one's own things for anugraha, the benefit of both oneself and the other, and teaches that its fruit depends on the manner, the thing given, the giver and the recipient.
jainism.explanation: In Jain doctrine a gift benefits the giver as much as the receiver, through the merit and the loosening of attachment it brings.
jainism.tie_back: If giving benefits both sides equally, then asking and giving share in the same good, which is the Kural's claim.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.38-39 (Svetambara numbering; paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Great Giver does not hold back anything.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak says God's gifts are beyond reckoning and the Giver keeps back not even a sesame seed's worth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says asking is as honourable as giving when the giver would never think of withholding, even in a dream; Guru Nanak describes the Great Giver as exactly such a one, who holds nothing back.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib (Pauri 25), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I too was a rich man once, and had a fine house of my own; in those days I gave to many a tramp such as I now am, no matter who he might be nor what he wanted.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The disguised Odysseus tells Antinous that he was once a rich giver to every tramp, and now stands asking himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Asker and giver are the same man at different times, which hints at the Kural's equation of the two.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Being asked why people give to beggars but not to philosophers, he said, ‘Because they think they may one day be lame or blind, but never expect that they will turn to philosophy.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes says that people give to beggars because they can picture themselves in the beggar's place.
philosophy.tie_back: His answer touches the Kural's insight that giver and asker are not so far apart.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.56 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: Abbe Pierre's winter appeal sets off an uprising of kindness
real_life_example.event: During an exceptionally harsh winter, after learning that a woman evicted from her home had died of cold in a Paris street, the priest Abbe Pierre wrote an appeal for the homeless that was broadcast on Paris-Inter and Radio Luxembourg on 1 February 1954, asking for blankets, tents and stoves. The public response was so great that the press called it an uprising of kindness; within days the government released funds for emergency housing, and the appeal led to the rapid growth of the Emmaus movement.
real_life_example.explanation: A single request on behalf of the destitute was answered so generously that the act of asking became the occasion for an entire nation's giving.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that asking of those who would never withhold, even in a dream, is as honourable as giving, and Abbe Pierre's appeal to a generous public was itself remembered as an act of great charity.

tamil:
கரப்பிலார் வையகத்து உண்மையால் கண்ணின்று
இரப்பவர் மேற்கொள் வது.
transliteration:
Karappilaar vaiyagaththu unmaiyaal kannindru
irappavar merkol vadhu.
meaning: Some people are willing to stand before others and ask for help only because the world has people who never hold back when asked.
elementary: People bring their empty buckets to a well because they know the well has water. In the same way, people in need ask because they know there are kind people who will share.
university: The kural explains why anyone begs at all: because karappilaar (கரப்பிலார், 'those without concealment') exist in the world (vaiyagaththu unmaiyaal). Kan nindru (கண்ணின்று, 'standing before the eyes') is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as standing in front of a giver, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as asking with the eyes rather than with words, the silent request of the proud poor. Puliyur Kesikan adds that such people beg only to preserve life. The sense of merkolvadhu (மேற்கொள்வது, 'taking up' a practice) suggests begging chosen reluctantly because generous givers are known to exist. The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree (மேற்கொள் வது with a space in both).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Bounteous is he who gives unto the beggar who comes to him in want of food and feeble.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn names as truly bountiful the man who gives to a feeble beggar who comes to him.
hinduism.tie_back: The beggar comes to him because such a giver exists, which is the logic of the Kural.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.3 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And a certain man lame from his mother's womb was carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask alms of them that entered into the temple”
christianity.explanation: A lame man is carried every day to the temple gate, where worshippers pass and might give.
christianity.tie_back: He is placed where givers are known to pass, which illustrates the Kural's point that asking exists because givers exist.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes poor people too dignified to ask, who must be recognised by their look rather than by any words.
islam.tie_back: This is Pappaiah's reading of kan nindru: the poor who ask with their eyes, trusting that a discerning giver will see.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let thy house be wide open, and let the poor be members of thy household.”
judaism.explanation: Yose ben Yochanan teaches that a home should stand open so that the poor come in as if they belonged.
judaism.tie_back: A house whose door is always open is why the needy come to it, which is the Kural's reasoning.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:5 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Alms food is next to nothing, both easy to gain & blameless.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha counts alms food among the requisites that are easy to get, so a monk can rely on it.
buddhism.tie_back: Alms are 'easy to gain' only because there are generous givers, which the Kural gives as the reason people take up asking.

jainism.quote_or_event: After Rishabhanatha renounced the world, people did not know how to give a mendicant proper alms. They offered jewels, horses and even daughters, and he went without food for about a year until Prince Shreyamsa recognised the right way and offered him sugarcane juice, the event remembered on Akshaya Tritiya.
jainism.explanation: The Jain tradition holds that the mendicant's alms round could only work once there were householders who knew how to give.
jainism.tie_back: The story dramatises the Kural's point: asking depends on the existence of givers who know how to give.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 1 (life of Rishabha) (tr. Helen M. Johnson) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “People beg and pray, "Give to us, give to us", and the Great Giver gives His Gifts.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak describes all creatures constantly asking and God constantly giving; asking makes sense because a Giver exists who answers it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says people take up asking only because there are those in the world who never hold back; Guru Nanak likewise grounds all asking in the existence of the Great Giver.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib (Pauri 4), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “a beggar can always do better in town than country, for any one who likes can give him something.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The disguised Odysseus says a beggar should go where there are many people able to give.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Beggars go where givers are, which is the Kural's explanation of why people take up asking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He was known as the ‘Door-opener’ – the caller to whom all doors fly open – from his habit of entering every house and admonishing those within.”
philosophy.explanation: The Cynic Crates lived without property and was welcome in every Athenian house.
philosophy.tie_back: He could live by asking only because doors opened to him, which is the Kural's point that asking exists because open-handed people exist.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.86 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr open Hull-House
real_life_example.event: Inspired by Toynbee Hall in London, Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr leased a large house built by Charles Hull in an immigrant district of Chicago in 1889 and moved in to live among their neighbours. They raised money, cared for children, nursed the sick and listened to people in trouble, and by its second year Hull-House was receiving some two thousand people a week, soon adding a public kitchen, kindergarten classes and evening courses.
real_life_example.explanation: Once it was known that Hull-House would not turn people away, the needy of the neighbourhood came to its door in great numbers.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says people take up asking only because there are those in the world who never hold back, and the stream of visitors to Hull-House grew precisely because its founders were known to give freely.

tamil:
கரப்பிடும்பை யில்லாரைக் காணின் நிரப்பிடும்பை
எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்.
transliteration:
Karappidumbai yillaaraik kaanin nirappidumbai
ellaam orungu kedum.
meaning: Just seeing people who never hide what they have is enough to make all the pains of being poor go away at once.
elementary: When a hungry child sees a kind lunch lady who always shares, the worry disappears right away. Just seeing someone generous makes the scary feeling go.
university: The kural plays on two compounds built on idumbai (இடும்பை, 'affliction'): karappidumbai, the affliction (or 'disease', in Pappaiah's gloss நோய்) of concealment that belongs to the miser, and nirappidumbai, the affliction of want that belongs to the poor. The miser's karappu is thus treated as a sickness of its own, the counterpart of the beggar's poverty. Kaanin (காணின், 'if one but sees') shows that the mere sight of such a giver ends ellaam orungu (எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு, 'all together') the beggar's distress. Puliyur Kesikan adds that this holds for one who begs without losing self-respect (மானம் விடாமல்), and Kalaignar calls concealment an இழிநிலை (base state). The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, both printing the sandhi form யில்லாரைக்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Rantideva, after fasting for forty-eight days, gives away his food and water in turn to a brahmin, a shudra, a man with dogs and finally an outcaste, praying only to take on the sufferings of all beings so that they may be free of pain.
hinduism.explanation: Rantideva's giving is so complete that every hungry person who comes to him leaves relieved.
hinduism.tie_back: A giver with no trace of withholding ends the misery of those who come to him, as the Kural says.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then Peter said, Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk.”
christianity.explanation: The lame beggar asks Peter for alms; Peter gives what he has, healing, and the man leaps up praising God.
christianity.tie_back: One meeting with an unstinting giver ends all of the beggar's affliction, the Kural's ellaam orungu kedum.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that whoever relieves a believer of one of the hardships of this world, God will relieve him of one of the hardships of the Day of Resurrection, and that God helps a servant as long as the servant helps his brother.
islam.explanation: The hadith treats removing another's distress as one of the most rewarded acts.
islam.tie_back: It stresses, as the Kural does, that a generous person can lift a needy person's affliction.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For I saved the pauper who cried out, / The orphan who had no helper. / I received the blessing of the lost; / I gladdened the heart of the widow.”
judaism.explanation: Job remembers his days of prosperity, when the poor who cried to him were rescued and the widow's heart was made glad.
judaism.tie_back: Job is the giver without the 'disease of withholding' whose presence ended the distress of those who turned to him.
judaism.source: Job 29:12-13 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The householder Sudatta was so constant in feeding the destitute that he became known as Anathapindika, 'feeder of the unprotected', and the tradition counts him the foremost lay donor among the Buddha's followers.
buddhism.explanation: His very name came to mean relief for the helpless who came to him.
buddhism.tie_back: A giver known never to hold back, whose name alone promises relief, fits the Kural's image well.
buddhism.source: Pali tradition on Anathapindika (e.g., SN 10.8; AN 1 'foremost' lists) (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain householder ethics lists four kinds of gift: ahara-dana (food), aushadha-dana (medicine), abhaya-dana (protection from fear) and jnana-dana (knowledge), which together aim to remove every kind of want.
jainism.explanation: Taken together, the four gifts address hunger, sickness, fear and ignorance, the whole range of a needy person's distress.
jainism.tie_back: The fourfold gift is a Jain picture of how a giver free of withholding can end all of a seeker's afflictions at once.
jainism.source: V. A. Sangave, Jaina ethics (jainworld.com), on the four kinds of dana (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Langar - the Kitchen of the Guru's Shabad has been opened, and its supplies never run short.”
sikhism.explanation: Satta and Balwand praise the langar of Guru Angad's court, a free kitchen open to all whose stores never run out, alongside the spiritual food of the Guru's word.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that at the mere sight of those free from withholding, the afflictions of want vanish; the Guru's langar, whose supplies never fail, is the Sikh institution where the hungry find their want relieved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar, Satta and Balwand (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the other suitors all gave him something, and filled his wallet with bread and meat”
greek_mythology.explanation: Most of the suitors give to the disguised Odysseus and fill his wallet.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Among those who did not withhold, the beggar's want was met at once, a partial picture of the Kural's claim.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca urges that a benefit be given promptly and without hesitation, since a gift that is long delayed and grudgingly given loses much of its value to the one who receives it.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, the giver's readiness is itself part of the benefit.
philosophy.tie_back: A giver with no impulse to hold back relieves need at once, which is the effect the Kural describes.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Benefits, Book II (tr. Aubrey Stewart) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Operation Manna drops food to the starving Dutch
real_life_example.event: With the occupied western Netherlands starving at the end of the Hunger Winter, the Allies negotiated with the German command so that their aircraft could fly unharmed along agreed corridors. From 29 April 1945 RAF Lancaster bombers flew very low over Dutch drop zones releasing food instead of bombs, and the American Operation Chowhound joined on 1 May; by the German surrender on 8 May the combined missions had dropped more than 10,000 tons of food. Dutch civilians waved at the low-flying aircraft and spelled out messages of thanks in tulips.
real_life_example.explanation: The sight of the bombers arriving with food became one of the most remembered moments of deliverance at the end of the war in Europe.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the mere sight of givers free from the vice of withholding ends at once all the afflictions of want, and for starving Dutch families the sight of the food planes overhead meant that their ordeal was ending.

tamil:
இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவாரைக் காணின் மகிழ்ந்துள்ளம்
உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Igazhndhellaadhu eevaaraik kaanin magizhndhullam
ullul uvappadhu udaiththu.
meaning: When someone who asks meets givers who give without looking down on them or mocking them, their heart is filled with deep joy.
elementary: If you ask for help and the person helps you with a kind smile instead of laughing at you, you feel warm and happy inside. How we give matters as much as what we give.
university: Igazhndhu ellaadhu (இகழ்ந்து எள்ளாது, 'without despising, without mocking') names the two insults a giver can add to a gift, contempt and derision; Pappaiah glosses them as அவமதிக்காமல், இழிவாகப் பேசாமல். The response is doubled for emphasis: magizhndhu (மகிழ்ந்து, 'rejoicing') and ullul uvappadhu (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது, 'delighting within the innermost heart'). The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar places the joy in the asker, and the next chapter, Iravachcham, will show the opposite case, where contempt makes asking unbearable. Pope: 'The minds of askers, through and through, will thrill with joy.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And charity performed at an impure place, at an improper time, to unworthy persons, or without proper attention and respect is said to be in the mode of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita places at the lowest grade the gift given without respect (asat-kṛtam) and with disdain (avajñātam).
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's avajñātam, contempt, is exactly the scorn (igazhchi, ellal) that the Kural says spoils a gift.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.22 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.”
christianity.explanation: James invites believers to ask God freely, because God gives generously and does not reproach the one who asks.
christianity.tie_back: 'Giveth liberally, and upbraideth not' is almost word for word the Kural's 'gives without scorn or ridicule'.

islam.quote_or_event: “Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allāh is Free of need and Forbearing.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ranks a kind word above a gift that is followed by hurt or humiliation.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's joy at a gift given without scorn is the other side of the Qur'an's warning against gifts that injure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whenever a person gives charity to a poor person with an unpleasant countenance and with his face buried in the earth, he loses and destroys his merit even if he gives him 1000 gold pieces. Instead, he should give him with a pleasant countenance and with happiness, commiserating with him about his troubles”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides rules that a gift given with a sour face loses all merit, while a gift given cheerfully and with sympathy is the proper way.
judaism.tie_back: This states the Kural's lesson as law: the manner of a gift decides whether the poor person's heart is gladdened.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:4 (tr. Eliyahu Touger, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sappurisadana Sutta the Buddha lists the gifts of a person of integrity: given with conviction, attentively and with respect, at the right time, with an empathetic heart, and without harming oneself or others, and each brings its own good result.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that a gift given respectfully and with empathy differs in kind from one carelessly thrown.
buddhism.tie_back: Giving with respect and empathy is what produces the asker's inner joy in the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Uttaradhyayana's twelfth lecture, the outcaste-born monk Harikesa comes begging to a Brahmin sacrifice and is mocked and beaten. A yaksha who serves him intervenes, and the Brahmins finally honour him and give him alms.
jainism.explanation: The story condemns those who insult a mendicant and shows that a gift offered with respect is what honours both sides.
jainism.tie_back: It is a negative example of the Kural's lesson: scorn spoils the giving, and respect brings joy.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 12 (Harikesa) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: In the Sikh langar, as Britannica describes it, everyone sits together in a straight line, neither ahead to claim higher status nor behind to mark inferiority; the institution began as a protest against caste, and under Guru Amar Das visitors ate in the casteless langar.
sikhism.explanation: The langar gives food freely and without any mark of contempt or rank: rich and poor, high and low caste sit side by side and are served the same meal as equals.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the asker's heart rejoices when givers give without scorn or ridicule; the langar is built precisely so that no one who receives food is looked down upon.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sikhism: Sikh practice' (sections on the rejection of caste and the worship service) and 'Guru Amar Das'

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “With these words he threw a footstool at him, and hit him on the right shoulder-blade near the top of his back.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Antinous answers the disguised Odysseus's request by throwing a footstool at him, and even the other suitors are shocked.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the opposite of the giver the Kural praises, and it shows why a gift without scorn gladdens the heart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca reports that Fabius Verrucosus called a favour granted harshly by an unfeeling man 'bread full of stones': welcome to a hungry man, but painful to swallow.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca holds that the manner of giving can spoil the benefit itself.
philosophy.tie_back: A gift given with scorn is the stony bread the Kural's asker cannot enjoy, while one given kindly makes the heart rejoice.

real_life_example.event_title: Mother Teresa opens Nirmal Hriday for the dying destitute
real_life_example.event: In 1952 Mother Teresa opened Nirmal Hriday, a hospice at Kalighat in Calcutta, for destitute people who were dying and whom many hospitals of the time would not admit. Residents were washed, fed and cared for so that they could die with dignity, and she required workers to respect each person's own religious beliefs; the Nobel Committee later described the dying destitute there as received with warm compassion devoid of condescension.
real_life_example.explanation: Nirmal Hriday became known worldwide for giving the poorest people care without contempt, and it was a central part of the work recognised by the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the heart of the one in need rejoices deep within when givers give without scorn or ridicule, and Nirmal Hriday was founded on giving the destitute care with respect rather than condescension.

tamil:
இரப்பாரை இல்லாயின் ஈர்ங்கண்மா ஞாலம்
மரப்பாவை சென்றுவந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Irappaarai illaayin eerngkanmaa nyaalam
marappaavai sendruvan thatru.
meaning: If there were no people who ask for help, all the coming and going in this cool, wide world would be like wooden puppets moving back and forth.
elementary: Imagine a toy theatre where wooden puppets bounce around on strings. They move, but they don't really care about anything. Valluvar says that if no one ever needed help, people would be like those puppets, busy but with no kindness to show.
university: Eerngkanmaa nyaalam (ஈர்ங்கண்மா ஞாலம், 'the cool, wide, great earth') and marappaavai (மரப்பாவை, 'wooden doll') give the image: Mu. Varadarasanar explains it as a wooden puppet moved by strings, so that human activity without askers would be mechanical motion without inner meaning. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar takes the point to be that giving is what gives life its moral content, and giving needs askers. Kalaignar reads the couplet differently, making those who keep the poor at a distance no different from operated puppets. Pope: 'The mighty earth ... Will be a stage where wooden puppets come and go.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree (சென்றுவந் தற்று in both).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He feeds no trusty friend, no man to love him. All guilt is he who eats with no partaker.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn says that someone who eats without sharing is 'all guilt', his life empty of bonds of love.
hinduism.tie_back: A life with no one to share with has lost its point, which comes close to the Kural's world of puppets.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.6 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.”
christianity.explanation: In the judgment scene, Christ says that what is done for the hungry, the stranger and the poor is done for him.
christianity.tie_back: Without the needy there would be no meeting with Christ through them, an echo of the Kural's claim that askers give the world its meaning.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allāh is like a seed [of grain] which grows seven spikes; in each spike is a hundred grains.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an compares charity to a seed that multiplies into hundreds of grains.
islam.tie_back: Giving is what makes wealth grow and bear fruit, and there is no giving without someone to receive.

judaism.quote_or_event: “the world stands upon three things: the Torah, the Temple service, and the practice of acts of piety.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon the Righteous names acts of kindness (gemilut chasadim) as one of the three pillars that hold up the world.
judaism.tie_back: If kindness is a pillar of the world, a world with no one to receive it would lose something essential, close to the Kural's image.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:2 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the recollection of the Sangha recited in the Dhajagga Sutta, the community of noble disciples is called worthy of gifts and of hospitality and 'an unsurpassed field of merit for the world'.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching treats the alms-receiving community as the 'field' in which the world's giving bears fruit.
buddhism.tie_back: Without such a field the world's generosity would have nowhere to take root, near the Kural's claim that askers give the world meaning.
buddhism.source: Dhajagga Sutta, SN 11.3 (recollection of the Sangha) (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain teaching on householder conduct (vaiyavrittya and gifts to ascetics) describes householders and mendicants as depending on each other: monks rely on pure alms freely given, and householders gain merit and spiritual progress by giving.
jainism.explanation: In Jain practice, lay giving finds its fullest meaning in supporting the mendicant order.
jainism.tie_back: A world with no one to give to would empty this exchange, roughly what the Kural pictures.
jainism.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaranda Shravakachara (section on vaiyavrittya / gifts) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, the young Nanak was given money by his father to make a profitable bargain, but spent it feeding a group of hungry holy men, calling this the true bargain (sacha sauda).
sikhism.explanation: The story presents giving to those in need as the only trade that gives worldly dealings real worth; it is hagiography rather than documented history.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that without askers the world's busy comings and goings would be mere puppet-motion; the Sacha Sauda story likewise implies that commerce gains meaning only when it meets the needs of those who ask.
sikhism.source: Janamsakhi tradition, as retold in Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1 (1909) (paraphrase)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “we know the gods go about disguised in all sorts of ways as people from foreign countries, and travel about the world to see who do amiss and who righteously.”
greek_mythology.explanation: A suitor warns Antinous that a beggar may be a god in disguise, testing who behaves rightly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In the Greek view the beggar at the door is how a person's character is shown, a sense close to the Kural's claim that askers give human life its meaning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca opens On Benefits by treating the giving and receiving of benefits as the practice that, more than any other, holds human society together.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, benefits are a social bond, not a private transaction.
philosophy.tie_back: Without people in need of benefits that bond would vanish, like the Kural's world of puppets.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Benefits, Book I (tr. Aubrey Stewart) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Marcel Mauss publishes The Gift
real_life_example.event: The French sociologist and anthropologist Marcel Mauss published Essai sur le don (The Gift) in 1925 in the journal L'Annee sociologique. Comparing forms of exchange in Melanesia, Polynesia and northwestern North America, he examined the religious, legal, economic and mythological sides of giving, receiving and repaying, and argued that such exchanges bind people together through mutual obligation.
real_life_example.explanation: The essay became one of the most influential works in the social sciences, showing that the giving and receiving of gifts is a basic thread of social life rather than a side matter.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that without people who ask, the busy world would be wooden puppets moving to and fro, and Mauss argued that the exchange of giving and receiving is what gives human society its living bonds.

tamil:
ஈவார்கண் என்னுண்டாம் தோற்றம் இரந்துகோள்
மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை.
transliteration:
Eevaarkan ennundaam thotram irandhukol
mevaar ilaaak kadai.
meaning: If no one wanted to ask and receive, what fame or honor could givers ever have?
elementary: A goalkeeper can only be a hero if someone kicks the ball. In the same way, a generous person can only shine if someone needs their help.
university: Thotram (தோற்றம், 'appearance, eminence') is glossed as pugazh (புகழ், 'fame') by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar. Irandhu kol mevaar (இரந்துகோள் மேவார், 'those who wish to take by asking') are the counterpart without whom the giver's eminence cannot exist; ilaaak kadai has the alapedai lengthening ilaaa. Read with 1058, the couplet pair makes askers necessary to the moral economy of giving, a theme going back to Ch. 23 (Eegai) and Ch. 24 (Pugazh), where fame is linked to giving. Pope: 'What glory will there be to men of generous soul, / When none are found to love the askers' role?' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Karna, famed as the great giver, never refused anyone who came asking. When Indra came disguised as a brahmin and asked for his natural armour and earrings, Karna cut them from his body and gave them, though it cost him his protection, and that gift sealed his fame.
hinduism.explanation: Karna's lasting glory as dana-vira, the hero of giving, rests on the askers he never turned away.
hinduism.tie_back: Without Indra's request there would be no story of Karna's supreme gift, as the Kural says: a giver's glory needs askers.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Kundala-harana sub-parva (tr. K. M. Ganguli) (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
christianity.explanation: Paul quotes a saying of Jesus that giving brings a greater blessing than receiving.
christianity.tie_back: If giving is the greater blessing, then receivers make that blessing possible, which is the Kural's point.

islam.quote_or_event: “O people! Give in charity as a time will come upon you when a person will wander about with his object of charity and will not find anybody to accept it”
islam.explanation: The Prophet urges people to give now, warning of a time when there will be no one left to accept charity.
islam.tie_back: He pictures exactly the world the Kural imagines, where givers can find no askers and lose their chance of merit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Akiva said to him: He commands us to sustain the poor, so that through them and the charity we give them we will be saved from the judgment of Gehenna.”
judaism.explanation: Answering why God does not feed the poor himself, Rabbi Akiva says the poor exist so that givers may earn merit through them.
judaism.tie_back: The poor are the means of the givers' merit, the Kural's point that askers make givers great.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 10a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: Prince Vessantara, in the Bodhisattva's last human birth before Gotama, gives away everything he is asked for, from the kingdom's white elephant to his own children, and his perfection of generosity (dana-parami) becomes legendary because of those who came asking.
buddhism.explanation: Vessantara's fame as the perfect giver rests on a series of supplicants.
buddhism.tie_back: Without askers, Vessantara's perfection of giving could not have been shown, which is the Kural's claim.

jainism.quote_or_event: Chandana (Chandanbala), a princess sold into servitude and kept in chains, offered boiled lentils to Mahavira at the end of his long fast, fulfilling the strict conditions of his abhigraha vow; her gift made her famous, and she later became head of his order of nuns.
jainism.explanation: In Jain memory Chandana's glory comes from having been the one able to give to the great ascetic.
jainism.tie_back: Her fame as a giver depended on the asker, Mahavira, which is the Kural's point.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 10 (life of Mahavira) (tr. Helen M. Johnson) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He continues to give, and His Provisions never run short.”
sikhism.explanation: In So Dar, Guru Nanak praises God as the endless Giver whose gifts to all creatures never run out; this giving is central to how Gurbani praises God's greatness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what glory givers could have if no one wished to receive; Gurbani likewise praises God above all as the Giver to countless receivers.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 9, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Asa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “you seem to be a chief, foremost among them all; therefore you should be the better giver, and I will tell far and wide of your bounty.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, offers Antinous fame in return for a gift: the beggar will spread the giver's name.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The beggar holds the key to the giver's renown, which is the Kural's idea in story form.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that liberal people are among the most loved of virtuous characters because they are useful to others, and that this depends on their giving.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, the honour of the liberal man rests on his giving to others.
philosophy.tie_back: Since that honour depends on giving, it depends on recipients, which matches the Kural's question.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.1 (tr. W. D. Ross) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Mansa Musa's lavish giving in Cairo spreads his fame
real_life_example.event: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with a vast caravan carrying great quantities of gold. In Cairo he met the Sultan of Egypt, and he and his caravan spent and gave away so much gold that its value in Egypt fell for about twelve years afterwards.
real_life_example.explanation: The pilgrimage made Mansa Musa and the wealth of Mali famous across North Africa, the Middle East and Europe.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what glory givers could have if there were no one to receive, and Mansa Musa's lasting renown as a giver was spread by the many in Cairo who received his gold.

tamil:
இரப்பான் வெகுளாமை வேண்டும் நிரப்பிடும்பை
தானேயும் சாலும் கரி.
transliteration:
Irappaan vegulaamai vendum nirappidumbai
thaaneyum saalum kari.
meaning: A person who asks should not get angry when refused. The pain of their own need is proof enough of how things stand.
elementary: If you ask a friend to share and they say no, don't get mad. You know how it feels not to have enough, so maybe they don't have enough either, or maybe it just wasn't the right time.
university: Vegulaamai (வெகுளாமை, 'not becoming angry') recalls Chapter 31 (Vegulaamai), here applied to the one who is refused. The second line is read in more than one way: nirappidumbai thaaneyum saalum kari (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி) can mean that the asker's own poverty is sufficient witness (kari, கரி) that things are not always available when wanted (Puliyur Kesikan, Pappaiah), that the asker's poverty teaches him (Mu. Varadarasanar), or that the refuser may be in the same plight as himself (Kalaignar). The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar takes the beggar's own want as reason enough for patience toward a refusal. Pope: 'Askers refused from wrath must stand aloof; / The plague of poverty itself is ample proof.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Riches come now to one, now to another, and like the wheels of cars are ever rolling.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn reminds the rich that wealth turns like a chariot wheel, moving from one person to another.
hinduism.tie_back: If fortune turns for everyone, the refused asker has no grounds for anger, since the giver too may be in want, which is Kalaignar's reading of the Kural.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.5 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.”
christianity.explanation: Thanking the Philippians for their gift, Paul says he has learned to be content whether he has plenty or is in want.
christianity.tie_back: Contentment in want is the inner freedom that lets an asker meet refusal without anger.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allāh] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allāh loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises those who restrain anger and pardon people, together with those who give in ease and hardship.
islam.tie_back: Holding back anger and forgiving is what the Kural asks of the refused asker.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma teaches that the rich person is the one who rejoices in his lot, and the mighty one is the one who conquers his own inclination.
judaism.explanation: Pirkei Avot locates wealth in contentment and strength in self-control.
judaism.tie_back: An asker who is content with his lot and masters his impulses will not rage at a refusal.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria) (paraphrase)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, we who possess nothing. Feeders on joy we shall be, like the Radiant Gods.”
buddhism.explanation: Tradition links this verse to the day the Buddha went for alms in a village and came back with an empty bowl, yet stayed joyful (cf. SN 4.18).
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha's calm in front of an empty bowl is the mendicant's freedom from anger at refusal that the Kural asks for.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should beg food from the householder when his dinner is ready; a wise man should not care whether he gets alms or not. ‘I get nothing to-day, perhaps I shall get something to-morrow;’ a monk who thinks thus, will not be grieved by his want of success.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira lists alabha, being refused, among the twenty-two hardships a monk must bear calmly, without grief or resentment.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's rule that the asker must not be angered by refusal, made into a monastic discipline.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.30-31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O mind, don't cry out that you are hungry, always hungry; stop complaining.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das tells the mind to stop its constant cry of hunger and its complaints, and to rest in trust instead of grievance.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the asker not to grow angry when refused, since his own want explains his situation; Guru Amar Das likewise counsels the needy mind to give up complaint and resentment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 27, Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For a moment he doubted whether or no to fly at Melanthius and kill him with his staff, or fling him to the ground and beat his brains out; he resolved, however, to endure it and keep himself in check”
greek_mythology.explanation: Kicked by the goatherd Melanthius while disguised as a beggar, Odysseus masters his anger and stays on the path.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The beggar who keeps himself in check is the Kural's asker who does not give way to anger.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He once begged alms of a statue, and, when asked why he did so, replied, ‘To get practice in being refused.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes trained himself to meet refusal calmly by begging from a statue that could never give.
philosophy.tie_back: Practising refusal until it no longer stings is the Kural's advice that the asker must not be angered.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.49 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: Marconi, rebuffed in Italy, takes his wireless to England
real_life_example.event: After his first wireless experiments at his family's estate near Bologna, the young Guglielmo Marconi offered his system to the Italian government, which showed little interest. In 1896 he took his apparatus to England, where William Preece, Engineer-in-Chief of the Post Office, supported his work and he was granted the world's first patent for a system of wireless telegraphy. In 1897 he returned to Italy to give a demonstration to the Italian government at La Spezia.
real_life_example.explanation: Marconi answered a refusal at home by seeking support elsewhere, and he later served Italy in war and diplomacy.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one who asks must not grow angry when refused, and Marconi, turned down by his own government, simply went where help could be had and later came back to demonstrate his invention to it.

tamil:
கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார் கண்ணும்
இரவாமை கோடி உறும்.
transliteration:
Karavaadhu uvandheeyum kannannaar kannum
iravaamai koadi urum.
meaning: Even when there are people as dear as your own eyes who would gladly give without hiding anything, never asking them at all is worth ten million times more.
elementary: Imagine your kindest aunt would happily give you anything you asked for. The Kural says it is still far better, and makes you stronger, to manage on your own and not ask, even from someone that kind.
university: The chapter Iravaccham (இரவச்சம், 'dread of begging') deliberately answers the preceding chapter Iravu (ch. 106), which permitted asking only of fitting, generous givers; here Valluvar raises the ideal higher, so that even such givers should not be asked. Karavaadhu (கரவாது, 'without concealing') and uvandhu eeyum (உவந்தீயும், 'who give with delight') describe the best possible donor, and kannannaar (கண்ணன்னார், 'those like one's eyes') marks them as most precious; the hyperbole koadi urum ('attains a crore', i.e. ten-million-fold good) is the commentators' measure of the superiority of not asking. In the line of interpretation that follows Parimelazhagar, as reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, the point is that dignity (maanam) lies in enduring want rather than in depending even on a willing friend. Pope renders it 'Ten million-fold 'tis greater gain, asking no alms to live, / Even from those, like eyes in worth, who nought concealing gladly give.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Laws of Manu teach that everything that depends on others brings pain, while everything that depends on oneself brings happiness, and call this the short definition of pain and pleasure.
hinduism.explanation: Manu's householder code makes self-reliance the very definition of happiness and dependence the definition of pain.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle so strictly that even a loving, willing giver should not be leaned on.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me.”
christianity.explanation: Paul reminds the Ephesian elders that, though the churches would gladly have supported him, he provided for himself with his own hands.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul declines to depend even on friends who were willing to give.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever abstains from asking others, Allah will make him contented, and whoever tries to make himself self-sufficient, Allah will make him self-sufficient.”
islam.explanation: After giving to the Ansar until nothing was left, the Prophet told them that refraining from asking brings contentment and self-sufficiency.
islam.tie_back: The hadith matches the Kural closely: the Prophet was himself a generous giver, yet he urged people not to ask even of him.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the Grace after Meals, the traditional text asks God not to make the worshipper dependent on the gifts or loans of flesh and blood, but only on God's own full and open hand, so that one may never be put to shame.
judaism.explanation: Jewish liturgy turns the wish never to depend on human gifts into a daily prayer.
judaism.tie_back: The prayer, like the Kural, treats dependence on even well-meaning human givers as something to be avoided.
judaism.source: Birkat HaMazon, third blessing (traditional siddur text) (paraphrase)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And what is the bliss of debtlessness? There is the case where the son of a good family owes no debt, great or small, to anyone at all.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that owing nothing to anyone is one of a householder's four kinds of bliss.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's ideal of asking no one, however kind, matches the Buddha's bliss of being beholden to no one.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Living without begging from friends, strong in affection and who are like the apple of our eyes, who withhold not their assistance from us, is life indeed.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil quatrains on the dread of mendicity call life without begging, even from loving and generous friends, the only true life.
jainism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural itself: friends 'like the apple of our eyes' who 'withhold not' are exactly the kannannaar who give without concealing.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 5 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Reliance on mortals is in vain - know this well. The Great Giver is the One Lord God.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan tells the seeker not to lean on any human being for support, because God alone is the real Giver.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says it is ten million times better not to ask even generous friends; Guru Arjan likewise turns the needy person away from human patrons and toward the one Giver.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 281, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “There is nothing worse than being always ways on the tramp; still, when men have once got low down in the world they will go through a great deal on behalf of their miserable bellies.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, thanks Eumaeus for sparing him from going about the town to beg.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Even the hero who must play the beggar calls a life of going about to ask the worst there is, which is the Kural's dread.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And he is the sort of man to confer benefits, but he is ashamed of receiving them; for the one is the mark of a superior, the other of an inferior.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle's great-souled man is happy to give but ashamed to receive, because receiving puts him in a lower position.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural shares the instinct that receiving, even from a willing benefactor, lowers one's standing.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Rochdale Pioneers open their own co-operative store
real_life_example.event: Twenty-eight working people of Rochdale, many of them weavers, pooled their own small savings to open a co-operative store at 31 Toad Lane on 21 December 1844, stocked with modest supplies of butter, sugar, flour, oatmeal and candles. At first it opened only two evenings a week, but within months it was open five days a week. The Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers set out principles such as open membership and democratic control that became the model for the modern co-operative movement.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than depend on others' help, a group of poor workers met their own needs by joining their resources, and their example spread around the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that not asking at all, even of the kindest givers, is worth ten million times more, and the Rochdale Pioneers chose to provide for themselves through their own pooled earnings.

tamil:
இரந்தும் உயிர்வாழ்தல் வேண்டின் பரந்து
கெடுக உலகியற்றி யான்.
transliteration:
Irandhum uyirvaazhdhal vendin parandhu
keduka ulagiyatri yaan.
meaning: If the maker of the world meant some people to live by begging, then let that maker also wander about like a beggar and die.
elementary: Imagine a game where the rules say some players must beg the others just to stay in. You would say the rules are unfair and the person who made them should try playing that way himself. That is how angry the Kural is that anyone should have to beg to live.
university: This is one of the boldest couplets in the Kural: Valluvar curses ulagiyatriyaan (உலகியற்றியான், 'he who fashioned the world') with the very fate of the beggar, parandhu keduga ('may he wander and perish'). Commentators in the tradition that follows Parimelazhagar read it as a conditional imprecation: if the creator had ordained begging as a means of life, he deserves to wander as beggars do; the force is ethical outrage that anyone should be reduced to irandhum ('even by begging') staying alive. Modern glosses differ in emphasis: Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the creator literal, while Kalaignar Karunanidhi's gloss pointedly says 'the one said to have created this world', distancing the verse from theism, and scholars have debated whether ulagiyatriyaan means a god, fate (ul), or the human order that permits destitution. Pope renders it 'If he that shaped the world desires that men should begging go, / Through life's long course, let him a wanderer be and perish so.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Beholding superior and well-behaved and modest persons persecuted, while the sinful are happy, I am sorely troubled. Beholding this thy distress and the prosperity of Suyodhana, I do not speak highly of the Great Ordainer who suffereth such inequality!”
hinduism.explanation: In exile, Draupadi openly reproaches the Ordainer for letting the virtuous suffer while the wicked prosper.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Draupadi dares to blame the world's maker for an unjust distribution of fortune.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section XXX (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Men groan from out of the city, and the soul of the wounded crieth out: yet God layeth not folly to them.”
christianity.explanation: Job complains that God seems to ignore the cries of the poor and oppressed.
christianity.tie_back: Job, like the Kural, questions a creator who lets people be reduced to misery.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when it is said to them, ‘Spend from that which Allāh has provided for you,’ those who disbelieve say to those who believe, ‘Should we feed one whom, if Allāh had willed, He would have fed? You are not but in clear error.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an rebukes those who blame God's will for others' hunger as an excuse not to feed them.
islam.tie_back: Islam rejects blaming God for poverty, so this is a contrast: where the Kural curses the maker, the Qur'an places the duty on those who could feed the poor.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Far be it from You to do such a thing, to bring death upon the innocent as well as the guilty, so that innocent and guilty fare alike. Far be it from You! Shall not the Judge of all the earth deal justly?”
judaism.explanation: Abraham challenges God directly, holding the Judge of all the earth to his own standard of justice.
judaism.tie_back: Abraham, like Valluvar, holds the maker of the world to account for unjust suffering.
judaism.source: Genesis 18:25 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bhuridatta Jataka, the Bodhisatta argues that if Brahma were truly lord and maker of the whole world, he would not have ordered it so full of misery and injustice, so the creator is either powerless or unjust.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka uses the suffering of beings as an argument against a just, all-powerful creator.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's 'if the maker willed begging' runs on the same logic: a world that forces people to beg indicts whoever made it.
buddhism.source: Bhuridatta Jataka (Jataka No. 543, tr. E. B. Cowell et al.) (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though Lakshmî withdraw from them and God be angry, the excellent will not stand with bended neck before the ignorant who bury their money in the earth.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil quatrains say that the noble will not bow to beg from hoarders even if fortune leaves them and heaven turns hostile.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it defies whatever higher power might force a person to beg, though it defies by endurance rather than by cursing.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Dadda: Do not blame anyone else; blame instead your own actions.”
sikhism.explanation: In his acrostic Patti, Guru Nanak teaches that suffering should not be blamed on anyone else, since it comes from one's own actions. This sits within the wider Sikh acceptance of hukam, the divine order.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural boldly curses the world's maker if he meant some people to live by begging; Guru Nanak takes the opposite course and tells people not to blame others for their condition but to look at their own deeds.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Asa, Patti, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For the gods keep hidden from men the means of life. Else you would easily do work enough in a day to supply you for a full year even without working.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says that Zeus in anger hid the easy means of life from mortals, so that people must struggle for their bread.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod, like the Kural, traces human want back to the will of the powers who ordered the world.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 42-44 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lactantius reports the argument attributed to Epicurus: God either wishes to take away evils and cannot, or can and does not wish to, or neither wishes nor is able; if he both wishes and is able, where do evils come from and why does he not remove them?
philosophy.explanation: The classical problem of evil asks how a good and powerful maker could allow suffering.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural puts the same dilemma as a curse: a maker who wills that people beg cannot be both just and worthy.
philosophy.source: Lactantius, On the Anger of God 13 (argument attributed to Epicurus) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: New Zealand passes the Old-age Pensions Act
real_life_example.event: Richard Seddon's Liberal government passed the Old-age Pensions Act in 1898, the first such scheme in the British Empire and paid for from general taxation. It gave a small, means-tested pension of up to 18 pounds a year to people aged 65 or over who had lived long in New Zealand and were judged to be of good character, though it shamefully excluded Chinese and other Asian residents.
real_life_example.explanation: The act treated support for the elderly poor as a public responsibility rather than leaving them to beg or to rely on charity, and it is regarded as the birth of social security in New Zealand.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural angrily rejects any order of the world in which people must beg to live, and New Zealand's pension law was an early attempt to change that order so that the old and poor need not beg.

tamil:
இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்துதீர் வாமென்னும்
வன்மையின் வன்பாட்ட தில்.
transliteration:
Inmai idumbai irandhudheer vaamennum
vanmaiyin vanpaatta thil.
meaning: Nothing is harsher than the idea that you can end the pain of being poor by begging instead of working.
elementary: If your bike breaks, you could keep asking friends to lend you theirs, or you could learn to fix your own. The Kural says choosing to ask forever instead of fixing things yourself is the worst choice of all.
university: The couplet plays on vanmai (வன்மை), 'hardness, toughness, boldness': the 'toughness' of deciding inmai idumbai (இன்மை இடும்பை, 'the affliction of want') will be ended by asking (irandhu theervaam) is called harder than any hardness (vanmaiyin vanpaattadhu il). Following Parimelazhagar's line, Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar supply the implied contrast with effort (muyarchi): the fault is abandoning work and choosing to live by others' gifts. Solomon Pappaiah adds the parenthesis '(without working it off)', and Pope's explanation speaks of remedying poverty 'by begging (rather than by working)'. Pope renders it 'Nothing is harder than the hardness that will say, / 'The plague of penury by asking alms we'll drive away'.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to perform his prescribed work, because action is better than inaction and even the maintenance of the body cannot be achieved without work.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita holds that no one can live, even physically, without doing one's own work.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle: the remedy for want is one's own work, not living off others.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.8 (cf. Bhagavad-gītā As It Is) (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you:”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he and his companions worked night and day so as not to live off anyone's bread.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul treats working, not relying on others' bread, as the answer to need.

islam.quote_or_event: “It is better for anyone of you to take a rope (and cut) and bring a bundle of wood (from the forest) over his back and sell it and Allah will save his face (from the Hell-Fire) because of that, rather than to ask the people who may give him or not.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says that even hauling firewood to sell is better than asking people for help.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact contrast: remove poverty by honest labour, however humble, not by begging.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And anyone who does not need to take [charity] and yet takes, will not depart from this world before he actually needs [charity] from others.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah warns that whoever takes charity without real need will end up truly needing it.
judaism.tie_back: The Mishnah, like the Kural, condemns choosing to live by others' gifts instead of one's own means.
judaism.source: Mishnah Peah 8:9 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta, the Buddha lists the dangers of idleness, such as refusing to work because it is too cold, too hot, too early or too late, so that new wealth is not earned and existing wealth runs out.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns lay people that excuses for not working lead to poverty.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's target is the same: the person who gives up effort and expects poverty to be solved some other way.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Since it is a means of removing the affliction of poverty for one to beg for himself, then let affliction be my portion, and let precious wealth depart from me.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet would rather keep his poverty than remove it by begging.
jainism.tie_back: This answers the Kural's very phrase inmai idumbai irandhu theervaam: the noble refuse to cure the affliction of want by asking.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 6 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself a guru or a spiritual teacher, while he goes around begging - don't ever touch his feet. One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Sarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak refuses respect to the holy man who lives by begging and praises the one who earns his food by work and shares part of it. This is the basis of kirat karni (honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls it the hardest folly to think poverty can be cured by begging instead of effort; Guru Nanak likewise rejects living by begging and points to honest labour as the true path.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Work the work which the gods ordained for men, lest in bitter anguish of spirit you with your wife and children seek your livelihood amongst your neighbours, and they do not heed you.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his idle brother Perses to work, or he will end up begging from neighbours who will stop listening.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod, like the Kural, rejects begging as a remedy for want and insists on work.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 397-400 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Xenophon's Memorabilia, Socrates advises Aristarchus, whose house is full of destitute kinswomen, to set them to useful work such as making clothes, and the household is soon both fed and happier.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates' answer to a household's poverty is productive work, not dependence or borrowing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise insists that want should be met by effort, not by asking.

real_life_example.event_title: South Korea launches the Saemaul Undong self-help movement
real_life_example.event: In 1970 South Korea launched Saemaul Undong, the New Village Movement, a rural development campaign built on the principles of diligence, self-help and cooperation, in which villagers worked together to improve their own communities. In 2013 UNESCO inscribed the movement's archives on its Memory of the World Register, noting that the campaign helped Korea move from being one of the world's poorest countries toward becoming a major economy.
real_life_example.explanation: The movement is widely studied as an example of a poor country reducing want through organised local effort, and its methods have been shared with other developing nations.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says there is no greater folly than thinking the misery of want can be cured by begging instead of effort, and Saemaul Undong was founded on curing rural poverty through villagers' own work.

tamil:
இடமெல்லாம் கொள்ளாத் தகைத்தே இடமில்லாக்
காலும் இரவொல்லாச் சால்பு.
transliteration:
Idamellaam kollaath thakaiththe idamillaak
kaalum iravollaach chaalbu.
meaning: A person who refuses to beg, even when they have nothing to live on, has a greatness so big that the whole world cannot hold it.
elementary: Think of someone who has almost nothing but still won't ask for handouts, because they want to stand on their own feet. The Kural says that kind of courage is so big that even the whole world isn't big enough to hold it.
university: The couplet turns on a pun on idam (இடம்): idamillaak kaalum means 'even when there is no means (of life)', while idamellaam kollaa means 'which all the room (of the world) cannot hold'. The quality praised is saalbu (சால்பு, 'nobility, fullness of character', the same root as saanraanmai, ch. 99), here specified as iravu ollaa, 'not consenting to beg'. In the line of commentary that follows Parimelazhagar, Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah take the second half as 'even when one is destitute' and the first as 'a greatness not equalled by all the worlds together'. Pope renders it 'Who ne'er consent to beg in utmost need, their worth / Has excellence of greatness that transcends the earth.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, the poor Brahmin Sudama visits his childhood friend Krishna, now a king, but out of self-respect does not ask him for anything; Krishna honours him and grants him prosperity unasked.
hinduism.explanation: Sudama's refusal to beg even from a willing, divine friend is celebrated as true greatness.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the story praises a destitute man who will not ask even when he has nothing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “That ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to work with their own hands so that they live honourably and depend on no one.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's dignity of not depending on others is the same aim Paul sets for the Thessalonians.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises poor people whose restraint is so great that others mistake them for well off.
islam.tie_back: These are exactly the Kural's people: destitute, yet unwilling to beg.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And anyone who needs to take and does not take, will not die of old age until he supports others with his own money. Concerning him the verse says: ‘Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord and whose hope is the Lord’ (Jeremiah 17:7).”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah blesses the needy person who refrains from taking charity and promises that he will one day support others.
judaism.tie_back: The Mishnah, like the Kural, honours the person who will not ask even in real need.
judaism.source: Mishnah Peah 8:9 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A monk who does not despise what he has received, even though it be little, who is pure in livelihood and unremitting in effort — him even the gods praise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises the monk who is content with little and pure in how he lives.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it gives cosmic praise to someone who keeps his dignity with very little.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Is it, therefore, a reproach to a man if he starve and keep his integrity inviolate, rather than fill his stomach by the disgraceful practice of mendicity?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet asks whether there is any shame in starving with one's integrity whole rather than eating by begging.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's idamillaak kaalum iravollaa saalbu: refusing to beg even when there is nothing to eat.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 2 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed begs, O Lord, do not make me sit at another's door. If this is the way you are going to keep me, then go ahead and take the life out of my body.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sufi Sheikh Farid prays never to be made dependent on another person's door, and says he would rather die.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the nobility that will not beg even when it has nothing to live on; Farid's salok shows the same spirit, preferring death to sitting at another's door.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1380, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 42) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Work is no disgrace: it is idleness which is a disgrace.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells Perses that no work is shameful; only idleness, which leads to want and begging, is.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's nobility likewise counts poverty without begging as honourable.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days l. 311 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant teaches that a person has a duty of self-respect and should not become anyone's lackey or let others trample on his rights with impunity, because servility betrays one's own dignity as a rational being.
philosophy.explanation: For Kant, abasing oneself before others violates a duty owed to the humanity in oneself.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's saalbu, refusing to beg even in want, is a form of the self-respect Kant calls a duty.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, The Metaphysics of Morals, Doctrine of Virtue, on servility (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Garibaldi refuses all rewards and returns to his farm on Caprera
real_life_example.event: After his Expedition of the Thousand conquered Sicily and Naples in 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi handed his dictatorship over southern Italy to King Victor Emmanuel II. He turned down all the rewards offered to him and went back at once to his small farm on the rocky island of Caprera, where he had settled to farm some years before.
real_life_example.explanation: Having won half a kingdom, Garibaldi accepted nothing for himself, and his refusal became a celebrated example of selflessness in the Italian Risorgimento.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the nobility that will not consent to take from others even when one has little, a greatness the whole world cannot contain, and Garibaldi chose a modest farm over every reward a grateful king could give.

tamil:
தெண்ணீர் அடுபுற்கை ஆயினும் தாள்தந்தது
உண்ணலின் ஊங்கினிய தில்.
transliteration:
Thenneer adupurkai aayinum thaaldhandhadhu
unnalin oonginiya thil.
meaning: Even if it is only porridge as thin as clear water, nothing is sweeter than food you have earned with your own hard work.
elementary: A sandwich you made yourself, even a plain one, can taste better than a fancy one someone handed you. The Kural says food you earned with your own work is the sweetest food of all.
university: Thenneer (தெண்ணீர், 'clear water') describes the gruel: adupurkai (அடுபுற்கை, 'cooked porridge', taken by Puliyur Kesikan as gruel of coarse grass-grain, pullarisi) so watery it looks like clear water. Thaal thandhadhu (தாள்தந்தது, literally 'what the foot/effort gave') is glossed by commentators following Parimelazhagar as what is brought by lawful effort (muyarchi); Puliyur Kesikan adds 'by effort joined with right conduct'. Oonginiyadhu il means 'there is nothing sweeter beyond it'. Pope renders it 'Nothing is sweeter than to taste the toil-won cheer, / Though mess of pottage as tasteless as the water clear.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man who cooketh in his own house, on the fifth or the sixth part of the day, with scanty vegetables, but who is not in debt and who stirreth not from home, is truly happy.”
hinduism.explanation: Asked by the Yaksha who is truly happy, Yudhishthira names the man who eats poor food at home but owes nothing to anyone.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it finds the greatest happiness in a meagre meal that is one's own.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section CCCXI (Yaksha's questions) (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm promises happiness to the one who eats the fruit of his own labour.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise finds sweetness in food earned by one's own effort.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one's own hands. The Prophet (ﷺ) of Allah, David used to eat from the earnings of his manual labor.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says no food is better than food earned by one's own hands.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim nearly word for word: nothing is sweeter than eating what one's effort has earned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One who benefits from his hard labor is greater than a God-fearing person … while with regard to one who benefits from his hard work, it is written: ‘By the labor of your hands you will live; you are happy and it is good for you’ (Psalms 128:2).”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud ranks a person who lives from his own labour above one who is merely God-fearing.
judaism.tie_back: The Talmud, like the Kural, puts the joy of living from one's own effort at the top.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 8a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where the son of a good family has wealth earned through his efforts & enterprise, amassed through the strength of his arm, and piled up through the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained. When he thinks, ‘I have wealth earned through my efforts & enterprise ...’ he experiences bliss, he experiences joy.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls the joy of having honestly earned wealth one of the householder's kinds of bliss.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the sutta finds a special sweetness in what one's own effort has gained.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga's account of Mahavira's ascetic years describes him living on rough food such as rice, pounded jujube and beans, accepting whatever plain fare came to him without craving for better.
jainism.explanation: Jain scripture holds up Mahavira's contentment with coarse food as a model of freedom from desire.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also finds even the thinnest gruel sweet; the Jain stress is on non-attachment rather than on earning it.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.8.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, Guru Nanak stayed at Saidpur (Eminabad) with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter, and ate his plain bread rather than attend the feast of the rich official Malik Bhago. He explained that Lalo's food came from honest labour, while Bhago's wealth was squeezed from the poor.
sikhism.explanation: The story is the best-known Sikh lesson on honestly earned food. In the popular retelling, Guru Nanak squeezed Lalo's bread and milk came out, and squeezed Bhago's and blood came out.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says even watery gruel earned by one's own effort is the sweetest food; in the Lalo story, the carpenter's coarse bread, earned by his own work, is preferred to a rich man's feast.
sikhism.source: Janamsakhi tradition, as summarised in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entries 'Bhago, Malik' and 'Lalo, Bhai'

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon serve disguised gods a humble meal of garden herbs, a little bacon, olives, cheese and eggs in plain earthenware, offered gladly from their own small store.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their meagre but honest meal, shared freely, is the most praised feast in the Metamorphoses.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's thin gruel, their humble food is made precious by being their own.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus says that plain fare gives as much pleasure as a costly diet once the pain of want is removed, and that bread and water give the highest pleasure when brought to hungry lips.
