philosophy.explanation: Epicurus argues that simple food fully satisfies and that self-sufficiency is a great good.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural shares the claim that the plainest food can be the sweetest, though it ties the sweetness to effort.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus (in Diogenes Laertius X, tr. R. D. Hicks) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Millet exhibits The Gleaners
real_life_example.event: Jean-Francois Millet showed The Gleaners at the Paris Salon of 1857. The painting depicts three peasant women bent over a harvested field gathering the stray ears of wheat left by the harvesters, which the rural poor were customarily allowed to collect, while the abundant harvest is gathered in the distance. The Musee d'Orsay, which holds the painting, notes that Millet gave the women an emblematic dignity, and some critics of the time read the picture as a political statement.
real_life_example.explanation: Millet presented the poor winning their meagre bread by their own labour as worthy of the grandeur usually reserved for history painting.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even gruel thin as water is sweetest when it is earned by one's own effort, and The Gleaners honours poor women gathering a scanty harvest with their own hands rather than asking for it.

tamil:
ஆவிற்கு நீரென்று இரப்பினும் நாவிற்கு
இரவின் இளிவந்த தில்.
transliteration:
Aavirku neerendru irappinum naavirku
iravin ilivandha thil.
meaning: Even if you beg only for water for a thirsty cow, nothing is more shameful for your tongue than begging.
elementary: Imagine you need to ask a stranger for water, not even for yourself but for a thirsty animal. The Kural says that even then, asking feels hard and lowering, which shows how heavy begging is.
university: The couplet chooses the most innocent possible request: aavirku neer (ஆவிற்கு நீர், 'water for a cow'), a deed of dharma, since caring for cattle was held highly meritorious. Puliyur Kesikan, following the Parimelazhagar line, adds that the cow is dying of thirst and the request is made out of compassion; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'asking out of regard for dharma'. Even so, naavirku iravin ilivandhadhu il, 'for the tongue there is nothing more debasing than begging'. The figure is an a fortiori argument: if even this is lowering, begging for oneself is far worse. Pope renders it 'E'en if a draught of water for a cow you ask, / Nought's so distasteful to the tongue as beggar's task.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Indian tradition often recalls that when Vishnu went to King Bali to beg for land, he had to take the form of Vamana, a dwarf, and the story is commonly read as showing that even God is made small by asking.
hinduism.explanation: The Vamana avatara is popularly cited to show how asking diminishes even the highest being.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's point is the same: asking lowers the asker even when the cause is good.
hinduism.source: Vamana and Bali (Bhagavata Purana 8.18-22) with the traditional reading of it (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then the steward said within himself, What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus' parable, the dismissed steward says he is too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg.
christianity.tie_back: The steward's shame at begging shows the same sense of degradation the Kural describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “A man keeps on asking others for something till he comes on the Day of Resurrection without any piece of flesh on his face.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that habitual begging strips away a person's face, that is, his honour.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hadith says asking disgraces the one who asks.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud records the counsel to make one's Sabbath like a weekday rather than become dependent on other people.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic teaching says it is better to give up even the honour due to the Sabbath than to ask others for help.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, avoiding the need to ask is placed above even a religious good.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kasibharadvaja Sutta, the Buddha refuses food offered to him after he has recited verses, saying that what is gained by reciting verses is not fit for him to eat.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha will not accept food that has been earned by what looks like asking or performing for it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows sensitivity to how a request, even a dignified one, can taint what is received.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Is the gently walking in the way of asceticism more grievous than the saying to others, Give me at least something, thus debasing one's dignity of the custom of doing homage to others, to whom he has attached himself by making their acquaintance?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet says even the hard ascetic path is easier than debasing oneself by saying 'give me something'.
jainism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that nothing degrades the tongue more than the words of asking.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 9 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Cursed is the life, and cursed are the clothes, of one who wanders around, begging from door to door.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Bihagre ki Vaar, Guru Amar Das condemns the life of someone who wears the clothes of a holy man yet lives by begging from house to house.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says nothing degrades the tongue more than asking, even for water for a cow; Guru Amar Das likewise calls a life of begging from door to door a cursed life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 550, Raag Bihagra, Bihagre ki Vaar (salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Odysseus, disguised as a beggar in his own hall, has to go round the suitors asking each for a scrap and endures their mockery and blows to carry out his plan.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even the hero, begging for a just purpose, is shown suffering the humiliation that begging brings.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, a good cause does not remove the indignity of asking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca writes that nothing costs so dear as what is bought with prayers, and that the words 'I ask' are heavy and painful to say, so a good benefactor should spare people the need to ask.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca treats the act of asking as itself painful and humiliating to the one who asks.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same: nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking.

real_life_example.event_title: Booker T. Washington describes the burden of raising money for Tuskegee
real_life_example.place: Tuskegee, Alabama, and the northern United States
real_life_example.event: In the chapter Raising Money in his autobiography Up From Slavery (1901), Booker T. Washington described years of travelling to ask northern donors for the funds that kept Tuskegee Institute running beyond its small state grant. He recalled walking through a cold storm in Stamford, Connecticut, to call on a possible donor who heard him out and gave nothing, and he explained that he kept to the rule of doing his duty whether or not money came.
real_life_example.explanation: Washington's account shows that even asking for a worthy cause on behalf of others was hard, wearing and often fruitless work.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even asking water for a thirsty cow is lowering to the tongue, and Washington's honest account of soliciting money for his students shows how heavy asking remains even for the noblest purpose.

tamil:
இரப்பன் இரப்பாரை எல்லாம் இரப்பின்
கரப்பார் இரவன்மின் என்று.
transliteration:
Irappan irappaarai ellaam irappin
karappaar iravanmin endru.
meaning: I beg everyone who begs: if you must beg, never beg from people who hide what they have.
elementary: If you ever really need help, ask someone with a kind and open heart, not someone who pretends to have nothing. The poet even says 'please' to everyone who has to ask for help, because he cares about them.
university: The couplet is a striking play on one verb, irattal ('to beg'): irappan ('I beg') irappaarai ellaam ('all beggars') irappin ('if you beg') karappaar iravanmin ('do not beg of concealers'). Valluvar thus makes himself a petitioner on behalf of petitioners, a rhetorical humility the commentators note. Karappaar (கரப்பார், 'those who conceal') recalls karappu in ch. 106 and 1061's karavaadhu; the advice, in the line following Parimelazhagar as given by Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar, is that a person forced to ask should at least avoid those who hide what they have. Pope renders it 'One thing I beg of beggars all, 'If beg ye may, / Of those who hide their wealth, beg not, I pray'.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Taittiriya Upanishad's parting instruction to students says that gifts should be given with faith and not without faith, with generosity, with modesty, with awe and with understanding.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad treats a grudging or faithless gift as defective giving.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's 'concealers' are exactly the grudging givers the Upanishad rejects, and it warns askers away from them.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye, neither desire thou his dainty meats: For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he: Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart is not with thee.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns against taking food from a stingy host whose heart is not in the giving.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's advice: do not seek from those who give with a hidden, unwilling heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who are stingy and enjoin upon [other] people stinginess and conceal what Allāh has given them of His bounty - and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment -”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an condemns those who conceal the bounty God has given them.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an's 'concealers' match the Kural's karappaar, the very people askers are told to avoid.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He who desires that he himself should not give and that others too should not give: he is a wicked man.”
judaism.explanation: Pirkei Avot sorts givers into four types and calls the one who neither gives nor wants others to give wicked.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's karappaar belong to this worst type, so the asker should not turn to them.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:13 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada sets the miser against the wise man who delights in giving.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural tells askers to go only to the open-handed, never to the miser the Dhammapada condemns.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Will the excellent then go for alms to any others but to those who will embrace them and say, Come to my house and eat?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet says that the noble, if they must ask, go only to those who welcome them warmly.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's advice in positive form: ask only of the open-hearted, never of concealers.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 3 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Great Giver keeps on giving, while those who receive grow weary of receiving.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak describes God as a Giver whose giving never stops, so that it is the receivers who tire first.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural begs every beggar never to ask from people who hide what they have; Guru Nanak points to the one Giver who never holds anything back.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib (pauri 3), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Give to one who gives, but do not give to one who does not give. A man gives to the free-handed, but no one gives to the close-fisted.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod contrasts the free-handed and the close-fisted and advises dealing with the generous.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hesiod separates open givers from tight-fisted ones and steers people towards the former.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 354-355 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca observes that a benefit given slowly and grudgingly, after the asker has been kept waiting, loses its value, since the giver who hesitates has long been unwilling.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca treats reluctant, hidden unwillingness as spoiling a gift.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's karappaar give, if at all, in just this spirit, so askers should avoid them.

real_life_example.event_title: Alexandre Petion equips Simon Bolivar for a new campaign
real_life_example.event: After defeats on the mainland and a period of exile in Jamaica, Simon Bolivar went to Haiti at the end of 1815. President Alexandre Petion supplied him with arms, munitions, provisions and men for a new expedition against Spanish rule, asking in return only that Bolivar abolish slavery in the lands he freed. Bolivar sailed for Venezuela in 1816 proclaiming the abolition of slavery as one of his aims.
real_life_example.explanation: Historians regard Petion's open-handed help as decisive for the revival of the independence struggle in northern South America.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural begs those who must ask to ask only of people who do not hide what they have, and Bolivar found in Petion a giver who gave freely, asking nothing for himself.

tamil:
இரவென்னும் ஏமாப்பில் தோணி கரவென்னும்
பார்தாக்கப் பக்கு விடும்.
transliteration:
Iravennum emaappil thoni karavennum
paardhaakkap pakku vidum.
meaning: Begging is like an unsafe little boat. When it hits the rock of someone who hides what they have, it breaks apart.
elementary: Picture a small paper boat floating on a stream. It looks fine until it bumps into a hard rock and breaks. Asking for help is like that boat, and someone's cold 'no' is the rock that breaks it.
university: The couplet is an extended metaphor (uruvakam): iravu ('begging') is a thoni (தோணி, 'small boat, raft') that is emaappil (ஏமாப்பில், 'without protection, unsafe'), and karavu (கரவு, 'concealment, refusal') is a paar (பார், 'submerged rock, reef'); when it strikes, it pakku vidum ('splits open'). Commentators in the Parimelazhagar line, as in Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah, supply the implied sea: the boat is taken to cross the ocean of poverty. Kalaignar Karunanidhi reads the rock as 'the stone heart that hides what it has and says no'. Pope renders it 'The fragile bark of beggary / Wrecked on denial's rock will lie.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Rig Veda hymn on liberality says that the riches of the generous never waste away, while the one who will not give finds no one to comfort him.
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn contrasts the lasting wealth of the giver with the friendlessness of the refuser.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural shows the other side of that refusal: the asker's fragile hope breaks on it.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.1 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith) (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?”
christianity.explanation: James condemns those who send the needy away with words instead of help.
christianity.tie_back: Such a refusal is the 'rock' on which the Kural's small boat of asking breaks.

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those who [greedily] withhold what Allāh has given them of His bounty ever think that it is better for them. Rather, it is worse for them. Their necks will be encircled by what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an warns that those who withhold God's bounty will be burdened with it on the Last Day.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's karavu, withholding, is the same fault, here seen from the side of the one who is refused.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The pauper speaks in terms of mercy; / The rich person’s answer is harsh.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that the poor plead gently while the rich answer them harshly.
judaism.tie_back: The poor man's plea and the rich man's hard reply are the Kural's frail boat and its rock.
judaism.source: Proverbs 18:23 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Parabhava Sutta lists among the causes of a person's downfall having much wealth, gold and food and yet enjoying it alone, and failing to support those who depend on one.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names solitary, ungenerous enjoyment of wealth as a road to ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: The rich man who hides his wealth is the 'rock' of the Kural, and the Buddha says he wrecks himself as well.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Will those who possess clear understanding follow after such men as constantly revile them, saying, These poor men will become rich through our means; they cannot acquire wealth of themselves?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet asks whether the wise will run after patrons who mock and despise those who depend on them.
jainism.tie_back: Such scornful patrons are the hard rock on which the Kural's frail boat of asking breaks, so the wise do not set out on it.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Guru is the Ladder, the Guru is the Boat, and the Guru is the Raft to take me to the Lord's Name.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak pictures the Guru as the safe boat and raft that carries the soul across the world's ocean.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls begging an unprotected little boat that splits apart on the rock of refusal; Gurbani uses the same image of a boat but offers the Guru as the vessel that does not fail.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 17, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, asks the suitor Antinous for food; Antinous refuses, insults him, and strikes him with a footstool, while the other suitors had at least given him something.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antinous' violent refusal of a beggar is the Odyssey's emblem of a hard heart.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The beggar's request breaks on Antinous' refusal just as the Kural's boat breaks on the rock.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He once begged alms of a statue, and, when asked why he did so, replied, ‘To get practice in being refused.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes the Cynic trained himself to bear refusal by begging from a statue.
philosophy.tie_back: Diogenes knew what the Kural knows: begging is fragile and refusal is the rock that breaks it, so he hardened himself against it.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.49 (tr. R. D. Hicks, via Wikisource)

real_life_example.event_title: Japan's racial equality proposal is blocked at the Paris Peace Conference
real_life_example.event: At the Paris Peace Conference Japan proposed adding to the Covenant of the League of Nations a clause affirming the equality of nations and the fair treatment of their nationals. On 11 April 1919 a majority of the League of Nations Commission voted in favour, but the chairman, US President Woodrow Wilson, ruled that it required unanimous support, and with Britain and Australia opposed, the clause was dropped.
real_life_example.explanation: The rejection was deeply resented in Japan and is often cited as a turning point in Japan's relations with the Western powers.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares asking to a frail little boat that splits apart when it strikes the rock of refusal, and Japan's appeal, though supported by a majority, broke on a single ruling.

tamil:
இரவுள்ள உள்ளம் உருகும் கரவுள்ள
உள்ளதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Iravulla ullam urugum karavulla
ulladhooum indrik kedum.
meaning: Just thinking about begging makes the heart melt with sadness. Thinking of people who hide what they have and refuse breaks it completely.
elementary: When you see someone who has to ask for help, your heart feels soft and sad. But when you think of someone who has plenty and still says 'I have nothing', your heart feels crushed. The Kural describes both feelings.
university: The couplet sets two thoughts side by side: iravu ulla (இரவுள்ள, 'when one thinks of begging') the ullam urugum ('heart melts'); karavu ulla ('when one thinks of concealment/refusal') ulladhooum ('even what there is', i.e. the melting heart itself) indrik kedum ('perishes, ceasing to exist'). The pun on ulla ('to think') and ullam ('heart') and ulladhu ('what exists') is characteristic. In the Parimelazhagar line, as given by Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah, the speaker's compassion for beggars is overwhelmed by horror at those who refuse while having plenty. Pope renders it 'The heart will melt away at thought of beggary, / With thought of stern repulse 'twill perish utterly.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita, Krishna says that those who cook food only for their own enjoyment, without first offering and sharing it, eat nothing but sin.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita condemns keeping one's food for oneself as sinful.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's horror at those who hide what they have reflects the same judgment on selfish keeping.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.13 (cf. Bhagavad-gītā As It Is) (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?”
christianity.explanation: John asks how anyone who closes his heart to a needy brother can have the love of God in him.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's melting heart and the heart 'shut up' against the needy are the two sides John sets against each other.

islam.quote_or_event: “Here you are - those invited to spend in the cause of Allāh - but among you are those who withhold [out of greed]. And whoever withholds only withholds [benefit] from himself.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says that those who withhold out of greed only harm themselves.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's karavu, greedy withholding, is condemned here as self-destructive.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If, however, there is a needy person among you, one of your kindred in any of your settlements in the land that the ETERNAL your God is giving you, do not harden your heart and shut your hand against your needy kindred.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids hardening one's heart and closing one's hand against a needy person.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's melting heart is what the Torah demands, and the hard, concealing heart is what it forbids.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 15:7 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the miser is to be overcome by generosity.
buddhism.tie_back: Where the Kural's heart is crushed by the concealer, the Dhammapada offers generosity as the answer to him.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Since one's mind melts with angnish when one reflects on a life of mendicity, what must their feelings be who receive alms!”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet says even the thought of begging melts the mind with anguish, so the actual experience must be far worse.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first line almost word for word: the heart melts at the very thought of begging.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 5 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir links greed with death and forgiveness with God's own presence.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the heart that melts at the thought of begging is destroyed at the thought of the misers who refuse; Kabir likewise ties the grasping, refusing spirit to death.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 155) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, Erysichthon cuts down Ceres' sacred oak and refuses all pity; he is punished with a hunger that consumes his wealth, makes him sell his own daughter, and finally drives him to devour himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: The pitiless, grasping man is destroyed from within by his own insatiable greed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's concealer, Erysichthon's hardness ends in his own utter ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith opens The Theory of Moral Sentiments by arguing that however selfish people may be, there are principles in human nature that make them care about the fortune of others, so that we feel sorrow at the sight of misery.
philosophy.explanation: Smith grounds morality in the natural sympathy we feel for those in distress.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's heart that melts at begging is Smith's sympathy, and the concealer is the one in whom it has died.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments I.i.1 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Dickens publishes A Christmas Carol
real_life_example.event: Troubled by a parliamentary report on child labour, Charles Dickens first planned a factual pamphlet but instead wrote A Christmas Carol in about six weeks, publishing it on 19 December 1843; the first printing of 6,000 copies sold out by Christmas Eve. In the story the miser Ebenezer Scrooge coldly turns away gentlemen collecting for the poor, before being shown the suffering his hardness causes and the joy of generosity.
real_life_example.explanation: The book became one of the best-loved stories in English and fixed Scrooge's name as the type of the person who refuses help to those in need.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the heart melts at the thought of those who must beg but is crushed at the thought of those who refuse them, and Dickens wrote his story out of pity for the poor and made the refuser its central figure.

tamil:
கரப்பவர்க்கு யாங்கொளிக்கும் கொல்லோ இரப்பவர்
சொல்லாடப் போஒம் உயிர்.
transliteration:
Karappavarkku yaangolikkum kollo irappavar
sollaadap pooom uyir.
meaning: The life of a beggar leaves them the moment they hear 'no.' So where does the life of the person who says 'no' hide itself?
elementary: When someone asks for help and hears a cold 'no', it can feel like all their hope has gone. The Kural wonders how the person who said 'no' while having plenty can keep living so easily, as if their heart has gone into hiding.
university: The chapter ends with a bitter rhetorical question built on a pun: karappavarkku yaangu olikkum kollo ('where does it hide for the concealers?'), the 'it' being uyir ('life'), which in the second line pooom ('goes away', with lengthening for metre) from the irappavar ('askers') as soon as the word of refusal is spoken (sollaada, 'when the word is uttered'). Commentators in the Parimelazhagar line, as given by Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar, read it as amazement: since the refusal kills the asker, the refuser's own life ought to depart too, so where does it hide? Pope renders it 'E'en as he asks, the shamefaced asker dies; / Where shall his spirit hide who help denies?' and paraphrases that the very word that kills the beggar should also kill the refuser. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A widely quoted verse of the Mahabharata and Puranas says that when a guest leaves a house with his hope broken, he leaves his sins to the householder and takes away the householder's merit.
hinduism.explanation: Hindu householder ethics hold that turning away a hopeful guest robs the householder of his own spiritual life.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the refusal that crushes the asker should rebound on the one who refuses.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, and Vishnu Purana 3.9, verse on the disappointed guest (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that whoever shuts his ears to the poor will one day cry out and not be heard.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Proverbs expects the refuser's own life to pay for the refusal.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who withholds and considers himself free of need / And denies the best [reward], / We will ease him toward difficulty. / And what will his wealth avail him when he falls?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says the one who withholds and thinks himself self-sufficient will be eased towards hardship, and his wealth will not save him.
islam.tie_back: The Kural asks where the refuser's life can hide; the Qur'an answers that his wealth will not shelter him.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that anyone who averts his eyes from giving charity is regarded as though he were worshipping idols.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic teaching treats refusing charity as one of the gravest sins.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's amazement that the refuser's life does not depart fits this view of refusal as near-idolatry.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Vasala Sutta says that whoever, when a brahmin or ascetic comes at mealtime, does not offer food but scolds him instead, is to be known as a true outcast.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines the outcast as someone who refuses and insults a person asking for food.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's refuser, whose 'no' kills the asker, is the Buddha's true outcast.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a person being tormented with poverty, rejecting true wisdom and allowing ignorance to abide in his mind, goes to a person and says, Give me alms, and if the person so asked refuse to give, will he not die from very shame at that moment?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet says that a poor man who asks and is refused dies of shame on the spot.
jainism.tie_back: This is the second line of the Kural: the asker's life departs at the word of refusal.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 8 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Asa, Guru Nanak says that hoarded wealth cannot be gathered without wrongdoing and cannot be carried past death.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural bitterly asks where the life of the refuser will hide when the asker's life leaves him at the word 'no'; Guru Nanak answers that the hoarded wealth the refuser clings to will not go with him either.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Asa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as weary travellers, are turned away from a thousand homes; only the poor couple Baucis and Philemon take them in, and the gods then drown the whole neighbourhood that refused them.
greek_mythology.explanation: The households that shut their doors on needy strangers are destroyed, while the generous poor are saved.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ovid answers the Kural's question: the refusers' lives cannot hide forever.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes meanness (illiberality) as falling short in giving and exceeding in taking, says it is incurable and more natural to people than prodigality, and counts it a greater evil.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the illiberal person, who will not give, has one of the most deep-rooted vices.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's refuser shows the vice Aristotle condemns.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: George III refuses to receive the Olive Branch Petition
real_life_example.event: In July 1775 the Second Continental Congress adopted the Olive Branch Petition, written chiefly by John Dickinson, professing loyalty to King George III and asking him to help end the conflict with the colonies. Richard Penn and Arthur Lee delivered it in London, but the king would not receive it, having already proclaimed on 23 August 1775 that the colonies were in open rebellion. Congress made no further attempt at reconciliation and declared independence the following July.
real_life_example.explanation: The refusal closed the last door to reconciliation, and within a few years Britain lost the thirteen colonies.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks where the life of the refuser can hide when a refusal crushes the one who asks, and the king's refusal of the colonists' petition led to the loss of Britain's own empire in America.

tamil:
மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர் அவரன்ன
ஒப்பாரி யாங்கண்ட தில்.
transliteration:
Makkale polvar kayavar avaranna
oppaari yaangkanda thil.
meaning: Low, mean people look exactly like human beings. I have never seen any two other things look so much alike.
elementary: Imagine a shiny plastic apple in a fruit bowl. It looks just like a real apple, but you cannot eat it. Some people are like that: they look like everyone else on the outside, but inside they lack the kindness and goodness that make a real person.
university: Kayamai (கயமை, 'baseness') closes the Porutpal and its Kudiyiyal section, as a dark mirror to the preceding chapters on nobility of birth, honour, greatness, perfect goodness and courtesy (chs. 96-100). The first couplet is a famous piece of irony: kayavar (கயவர், 'the base') are makkale polvar (மக்களே போல்வர், 'just like humans'), and oppaari (ஒப்பாரி, 'resemblance') so exact is found nowhere else. Parimelazhagar and the commentators who follow him (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan) read it as saying the base share only the outward form of humanity, so that the likeness is complete in shape and absent in substance; Solomon Pappaiah adds that no animal or bird species shows such a perfect double. Pope renders it 'The base resemble men in outward form, I ween; / But counterpart exact to them I've never seen.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Arrogance, pride, anger, conceit, harshness and ignorance—these qualities belong to those of demonic nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names the traits that mark the asuric (demonic) nature in people who are outwardly human.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita locates what is base not in a person's form but in qualities that hollow out their humanity.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.4 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus compares hypocrites to painted tombs that look fine outside and are full of decay inside.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's base person is likewise perfect on the outside and empty within.

islam.quote_or_event: “They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes people who have every human faculty but do not use them, and so fall below the animals.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says such people have the human frame but not what makes it human.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel teaches that being truly human is a moral achievement, especially where others fail at it.
judaism.tie_back: Hillel's saying assumes the Kural's point, that many who look like men are not men in the full sense.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:5 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by mere eloquence nor by beauty of form does a man become accomplished, if he is jealous, selfish and deceitful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says outward gifts like fine speech or good looks count for nothing in a person who is envious, selfish and deceitful.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, outward appearance cannot make up for a base character.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The base in prosperity will not do these things which those who are of high birth will do even in adversity. Though one place rings (of gold) upon the tusks of a hog, O thou who hast eyes like a lance! it will never become a warlike elephant.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Naladiyar says that dressing up a hog's tusks in gold rings does not turn it into a war elephant, and outward finery does not change the nature of the base.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the stanza says the base may look like the real thing but stay what they are underneath.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 36.8, chapter 'Baseness or Envy' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They belong to the human species, but they act like animals.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan describes people who are human by birth but whose conduct is that of beasts.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ironically says the base look exactly like human beings; Guru Arjan makes the same point, that a human form can hide conduct that is not human at all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 267, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Diogenes the Cynic is said to have lit a lamp in broad daylight and walked about saying he was looking for a man.
greek_mythology.explanation: The joke was that the streets were full of people but he could not find a real human being among them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Diogenes makes the Kural's ironic point: many look like men, but few are.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.41 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle writes that man, when perfected, is the best of animals, but when separated from law and justice he is the worst of all.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, being human is fulfilled only through virtue and justice; without them a human being sinks below the beasts.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like the Kural, separates the human form from the human excellence that should fill it.

real_life_example.event_title: Anna Anderson claims to be Grand Duchess Anastasia
real_life_example.place: Berlin, Germany, and Charlottesville, Virginia, United States
real_life_example.event: In 1922 a young woman who later became known as Anna Anderson appeared in Berlin claiming to be Anastasia, the youngest daughter of the murdered Russian tsar Nicholas II. For decades she persuaded many people, and she later lived in Charlottesville, Virginia, where she died in 1984. In 1994 separate British and American scientific teams tested her DNA and concluded that she was not a Romanov.
real_life_example.explanation: Her case shows how closely a person can match an outward likeness, even convincing people who had known the royal family, while the inner truth is quite different.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's irony is that the base look exactly like true human beings; Anderson's near-perfect outward resemblance to a princess, exposed only by DNA, shows how convincing a mere likeness can be.

tamil:
நன்றறி வாரிற் கயவர் திருவுடையர்
நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர்.
transliteration:
Nandrari vaarir kayavar thiruvudaiyar
nenjaththu avalam ilar.
meaning: Mean people are luckier than those who know what is good, because no worry ever troubles their hearts.
elementary: Think of two children who broke a vase. One feels bad, says sorry, and worries about it all day. The other just shrugs and goes on playing. The second one looks happier, but only because he does not care about doing right. The Kural is joking: being carefree like that is nothing to envy.
university: The couplet is sarcastic praise. Nandru arivaar (நன்றறிவார், 'those who know the good') are contrasted with kayavar, who are thiru udaiyar (திருவுடையர், 'possessed of fortune, blessed'), because they have no avalam (அவலம், 'anxiety, grief') in the nenjam (heart). Parimelazhagar explains that the wise are anxious about what is right and its consequences in this world and the next, while the base feel no such care; Puliyur Kesikan glosses nandru as 'what is truly beneficial to oneself'. Kalaignar keeps the irony explicit ('in one way they are fortunate'). Pope: 'Than those of grateful heart the base must luckier be, / Their minds from every anxious thought are free!' Pope's 'grateful' reflects a reading of nandri as 'gratitude'; most Tamil commentators take nandru as 'the good'. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And that happiness which is blind to self-realization, which is delusion from beginning to end and which arises from sleep, laziness and illusion is said to be of the nature of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita names a kind of happiness that comes from dullness and delusion and calls it tamasic, the lowest of the three kinds.
hinduism.tie_back: The carefree ease the Kural mocks in the base is just this blind, tamasic happiness.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.39 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. For there are no bands in their death: but their strength is firm. They are not in trouble as other men; neither are they plagued like other men.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist admits he envied the wicked because they seemed free of the troubles that weigh on good people.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's ironic observation that the base seem luckier because nothing troubles them.

islam.quote_or_event: “Let them eat and enjoy themselves and be diverted by [false] hope, for they are going to know.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an lets the heedless enjoy their carefree life for now, warning that they will learn the truth later.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows the base enjoying an untroubled life that is not really fortunate.

judaism.quote_or_event: “it is not in our hands [to explain the reason] either of the security of the wicked, or even of the afflictions of the righteous.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yannai admits that we cannot explain why the wicked live at ease while the righteous suffer.
judaism.tie_back: The Mishnah faces the same puzzle the Kural turns into sarcasm: the base seem secure while the good are troubled.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:15 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easy is life for the shameless one who is impudent as a crow, is backbiting and forward, arrogant and corrupt.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that life is easy for the shameless, while the next verse says it is hard for the modest who seek purity.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's ironic claim that the base, free of conscience, have the easier life.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A man attached to pleasures and amusements will be caught in the trap (of deceit). (He thinks): 'I never saw the next world, but I have seen with my own eyes the pleasures of this life.'”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira describes the fool who lives carelessly for present pleasure, untroubled by thoughts of karma or the next life, and the lecture goes on to show his dread at death.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is free of worry for the same reason: he does not care about what is good or what follows from his deeds.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 5.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The world is asleep in Maya, the house of Shakti; it dances, jumps and sings in duality. The self-willed manmukh has no devotion.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das pictures the world as carefree and dancing while it is really asleep in Maya (worldly illusion), and says the self-willed person (manmukh) has no devotion.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural sarcastically calls the base luckier than the wise because nothing troubles them; Guru Amar Das shows that this carefree dancing is really the sleep of people lost in illusion.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 506, Raag Gujri, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato's Gorgias, Polus argues that the unjust tyrant Archelaus, who seized power by murder, is happy, and Socrates insists that the wicked man is the most miserable of all.
greek_mythology.explanation: Polus judges by appearances: the wrongdoer seems to prosper without care, while Socrates holds that injustice ruins the soul.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's sarcasm makes Socrates' point: the base only seem fortunate.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.”
philosophy.explanation: Mill argues that the restless discontent of a thoughtful person is worth more than the easy contentment of someone who does not know what he is missing.
philosophy.tie_back: Mill states plainly what the Kural says through irony: the untroubled base are not the truly fortunate.

real_life_example.event_title: Charles Ponzi's investment scheme
real_life_example.event: Charles Ponzi promised investors a 50 percent return within 45 days, and in about seven months some 30,000 people gave him more than ten million dollars. He paid early investors with money from later ones. After the Boston Post questioned his finances in July 1920, state auditors found him insolvent by August, and he was later convicted and imprisoned.
real_life_example.explanation: Ponzi's scheme became the standard name for this kind of fraud, and the Boston Post won a Pulitzer Prize for exposing it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural sarcastically calls the base fortunate because no worry troubles them; Ponzi reportedly stayed confident to the end while thousands of ordinary savers bore the real risk.

tamil:
தேவர் அனையர் கயவர் அவருந்தாம்
மேவன செய்தொழுக லான்.
transliteration:
Thevar anaiyar kayavar avarundhaam
mevana seydhozhuga laan.
meaning: Mean people are like the gods, because they too do whatever they please.
elementary: Gods in stories can do anything they like, and nobody can tell them off. A spoiled bully acts the same way, doing whatever he wants without thinking of anyone else. The Kural jokes that this makes him 'like a god', but it really means he has no self-control at all.
university: Another ironic comparison: kayavar are thevar anaiyar (தேவர் அனையர், 'like the gods') because they too live mevana seydhu (மேவன செய்து, 'doing what they desire'). Puliyur Kesikan spells out the logic: like the gods, they have no one to restrain them (தம்மை நியமிப்பவர் இல்லாமல்), and Solomon Pappaiah glosses it the same way. Parimelazhagar's reading is that the gods are free because they stand above rules, while the base are 'free' because they ignore them, so the likeness is pure mockery. Kalaignar points to the gods 'of the Puranas' who act on every wish. Pope: 'The base are as the Gods; they too / Do ever what they list to do!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But he who discards scriptural injunctions and acts according to his own whims attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme destination.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a person who throws off all guidance and lives by whim reaches no good end.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's base man who 'does as he pleases' is exactly the whim-driven man the Gita condemns.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.23 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.”
christianity.explanation: The serpent tempts Eve with the promise that by grasping what is forbidden she will become like the gods.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural mocks the same delusion: acting without restraint makes one 'like the gods' only in a false and ruinous sense.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you seen he who has taken as his god his [own] desire”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the person who makes his own desires his god and so loses guidance.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's base man treats his wishes as law, as if he were a god; the Qur'an says he has made his wishes his god.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did that which was right in his own eyes.”
judaism.explanation: The book of Judges ends by describing a time of chaos when everyone did whatever he wanted.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats doing whatever one pleases, with no restraint, as a sign of moral collapse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Formerly this mind wandered about as it liked, where it wished and according to its pleasure, but now I shall thoroughly master it with wisdom as a mahout controls with his ankus an elephant in rut.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts a mind that roams wherever it likes with a mind tamed by wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the untamed mind of this verse, going 'where it wished and according to its pleasure'.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The worthy, though they have attained the wealth of the world, will at no time indulge in haughty speech, but if the mean have acquired the wealth of one cani (1/80 part) added to one muntheri (1/320) they will regard themselves as great as Indra king of heaven.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Naladiyar mocks the mean man who, with a tiny bit of wealth, thinks himself equal to Indra, king of the gods.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Naladiyar sarcastically likens the base to a god, a comparison that exposes their smallness.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 35.6, chapter 'Meanness' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, it is written that you shall obey the Hukam of His Command, and walk in the Way of His Will.”
sikhism.explanation: The first pauri of Japji Sahib teaches that the true person lives within hukam, the divine order, rather than by his own will.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural mocks the base as godlike because they too do whatever they please; Guru Nanak sets the opposite ideal, a life that walks in God's will instead of one's own wishes.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib (pauri 1), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Salmoneus, a mortal king, set himself up as Zeus, driving a chariot that dragged bronze kettles to imitate thunder and hurling torches as lightning, until Zeus struck him down.
greek_mythology.explanation: Salmoneus believed that doing whatever he liked made him the equal of the king of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Salmoneus is the Kural's base man who is 'like the gods' only in his unrestrained self-will.
greek_mythology.source: Apollodorus, The Library 1.9.7 (tr. J. G. Frazer)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Locke distinguishes liberty from licence: the state of nature is a state of liberty, but not one in which a person may do whatever he pleases, because reason and the law of nature still bind him.
philosophy.explanation: For Locke, true freedom is bounded by moral law; doing anything one likes is licence, not liberty.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's base man mistakes licence for the freedom of the gods.
philosophy.source: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, ch. 2 §6 (1690)

real_life_example.event_title: The Tweed Ring plunders New York City
real_life_example.event: William M. Tweed and his allies in the Tammany Hall political machine controlled New York City government and defrauded it of an estimated 30 to 200 million dollars. In 1871 reporting in The New York Times and the cartoons of Thomas Nast exposed the ring. Tweed was convicted in 1873, escaped to Spain in 1875, was recognised from a Nast cartoon and returned, and died in a New York jail in 1878.
real_life_example.explanation: The Tweed Ring became a lasting example of what happens when people in power face no checks until the press and the courts finally act.
real_life_example.tie_back: Like the 'gods' of the kural, the Tweed Ring did whatever it pleased because for years no one could restrain it.

tamil:
அகப்பட்டி ஆவாரைக் காணின் அவரின்
மிகப்பட்டுச் செம்மாக்கும் கீழ்.
transliteration:
Agappatti aavaaraik kaanin avarin
migappattuch chemmaakkum keezh.
meaning: When mean people meet others who behave even worse than they do, they puff up with pride at being better.
elementary: Imagine a child who got a bad mark on a test. Instead of trying to do better, he finds someone who did even worse and says, 'Ha, at least I'm better than you!' That is what the Kural means: base people feel big by looking down on someone lower.
university: Keezh (கீழ், 'the low, the base') is the chapter's second word for its subject. The difficult word agappatti (அகப்பட்டி) has divided commentators: Parimelazhagar and Puliyur Kesikan take aavaar as those who behave even more basely, so that the base man sees them and becomes migappattu (மிகப்பட்டு, 'superior, exalted') and semmaakkum (செம்மாக்கும், 'struts, exults'); Solomon Pappaiah glosses it as 'those who live like dogs, as they please'; Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as 'those beneath them'. The common sense is that baseness takes its self-esteem from someone lower. Pope's 'When base men those behold of conduct vile, / They straight surpass them, and exulting smile' follows the 'conduct vile' reading. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I am the richest man, surrounded by aristocratic relatives. There is none so powerful and happy as I am.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita gives the inner voice of the demonic person, who measures himself against others and swells with pride.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's base man also struts by comparing himself to others he thinks lower.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.13-15 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus' parable, the Pharisee builds himself up by pointing to a man he considers lower than himself.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's base man exactly: he feels superior by looking down on someone else.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people; perhaps they may be better than them”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an forbids mocking others, since those looked down on may be better in God's sight.
islam.tie_back: It forbids exactly the contemptuous comparison that the Kural says is how the base feel superior.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is he that is honored? He who honors his fellow human beings”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma teaches that real honour comes from honouring others, not from rising above them.
judaism.tie_back: This is the opposite of the Kural's base man, who seeks honour by despising those beneath him.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whosoever debased by his pride, exalts himself and belittles other — know him as an outcast.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Discourse on Outcasts, the Buddha says one becomes truly low by deeds, including exalting oneself and belittling others.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha's 'outcast' and the Kural's keezh are the same figure: the man who rises in his own eyes by putting others down.
buddhism.source: Vasala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.7, v. 17 (tr. Piyadassi Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “the base man is mighty in speaking harsh words. He regards no one, laughs at the misery of others, grows more and more enraged and will continually reproach others.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Naladiyar describes the base man who respects no one and laughs at others' misfortunes.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's keezh, he gains his sense of superiority from looking down on those worse off.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 35.8, chapter 'Meanness' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself good - goodness shall not draw near him.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan warns that self-praise is a sign of haumai (ego), and that goodness keeps away from the person who declares himself good.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural shows the base swelling with pride when they meet people worse than themselves; Guru Arjan says that whoever rates himself as good is thereby cut off from goodness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theophrastus' sketch of the arrogant man shows someone who looks down on everyone, makes others wait on him and treats those he thinks beneath him with contempt.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Greek character sketch catalogues the small habits of a man who builds himself up by belittling others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the same comparative pride as the Kural's base man, though less sharply focused on those even lower.
greek_mythology.source: Theophrastus, Characters, 'The Arrogant Man' (tr. R. C. Jebb)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hobbes defines 'sudden glory' as the passion behind laughter, caused either by something one does oneself or by seeing some defect in another, by comparison with which one suddenly applauds oneself; he adds that it is most common in those who know they have few abilities.
philosophy.explanation: Hobbes explains contemptuous laughter as a way the weak feel strong by noticing the weakness of others.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's psychology exactly: the base exult on finding someone lower than themselves.

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Commodus renames Rome after himself
real_life_example.event: The Roman emperor Commodus, son of Marcus Aurelius, presented himself as the god Hercules, posed with the lion skin and club, and appeared in the arena as a fighter. According to the historian Cassius Dio, he ordered that Rome itself be called Commodiana, and the months of the year were renamed after his own titles. His misrule ended with his murder at the end of 192 CE.
real_life_example.explanation: Commodus became a classic example of a ruler puffed up with self-glory rather than real achievement.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes the base swelling with pride and strutting; Commodus renaming the city and the calendar after himself is that strutting on an imperial scale.

tamil:
அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம் எச்சம்
அவாவுண்டேல் உண்டாம் சிறிது.
transliteration:
Achchame keezhgaladhu aasaaram echcham
avaavundel undaam siridhu.
meaning: Fear is the only thing that makes mean people behave well. Beyond that, they behave a little better only when they want something.
elementary: Some children only behave when the teacher is watching, or when they hope to get a sweet. When nobody is looking and there is no prize, they misbehave. The Kural says base people are like that: they are good only out of fear or for a reward.
university: Aasaaram (ஆசாரம், from Sanskrit ācāra, 'right conduct, propriety') in the base has two sources only: achcham (அச்சம், 'fear') and, as echcham (எச்சம், 'remainder'), avaa (அவா, 'desire, greed'). Parimelazhagar specifies the fear as fear of the king's punishment, and Puliyur Kesikan follows ('அரசரால் துன்பம் வரும் என்னும் அச்சம்'); Solomon Pappaiah likewise reads it as fear of the government. The second line says that if desire for some gain is present, a little more good conduct appears. The couplet thus defines the base by motive: they have no inner love of virtue. Pope: 'Fear is the base man's virtue; if that fail, / Intense desire some little may avail.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The whole world is kept in order by punishment, for a guiltless man is hard to find; through fear of punishment the whole world yields the enjoyments (which it owes).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches that fear of the king's rod (danda) is what keeps most people in line.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim about the base: fear of punishment, not virtue, produces their good behaviour.
hinduism.source: Laws of Manu 7.22 (tr. G. Bühler, SBE 25)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same:”
christianity.explanation: Paul says the authorities are something to fear only for wrongdoers, and that doing good earns praise.
christianity.tie_back: The verse names the two motives the Kural assigns to the base, fear of rulers and hope of reward.

islam.quote_or_event: “You [believers] are more fearful within their breasts than Allāh. That is because they are a people who do not understand.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says the hypocrites fear people more than God, so their conduct is governed by fear of others, not by faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's base, their behaviour comes from fear of an outside power rather than inner conviction.

judaism.quote_or_event: “pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear it inspires, every man would swallow his neighbor alive.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina teaches that fear of the ruling power is what keeps people from devouring one another.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first line: fear of authority is what keeps the base in order.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:2 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who appropriates be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he appropriates his friend's wealth, (ii) he gives little and asks much, (iii) he does his duty out of fear, (iv) he associates for his own advantage.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a false friend who does what he should only out of fear and for his own gain.
buddhism.tie_back: These are exactly the two motives the Kural gives the base: fear first, and a little more good conduct when there is something to gain.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (tr. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Better it is that I should subdue my Self by self-control and penance, than be subdued by others with fetters and corporal punishment.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's teaching sets self-restraint chosen from within against restraint forced from outside by chains and punishment.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the one who must be 'subdued by others' through fear, because he will not restrain himself.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the truly wise person as one who neither frightens others nor is ruled by fear of them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the base behave well mainly out of fear of punishment; Guru Tegh Bahadur's ideal person acts rightly without being driven by fear at all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato's Republic, Glaucon tells the story of Gyges, a shepherd who found a ring that made him invisible and then used it to seduce the queen, kill the king and seize the throne, arguing that anyone would act unjustly if he could do so without fear of being caught.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story suggests that for many people, justice is only fear of consequences.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Glaucon's Gyges is the Kural's base man: remove the fear and his good conduct disappears.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For these do not by nature obey the sense of shame, but only fear, and do not abstain from bad acts because of their baseness but through fear of punishment”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that most people are kept from wrongdoing not by shame or love of the noble but by fear of punishment, which is why laws are needed.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle states the Kural's point almost word for word, even naming 'baseness'.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10.9 (1179b) (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Shang Yang's laws of rewards and punishments in Qin
real_life_example.event: The statesman Shang Yang reorganised the state of Qin with strict, uniform laws, harsh penalties even for minor offences, and a system in which neighbours and relatives were held responsible for each other's crimes. He also created ranks of merit as rewards. He taught that people like rank and rewards and dislike punishments, so a ruler can steer them with both; Sima Qian credited him with making Qin's people law-abiding.
real_life_example.explanation: His Legalist approach helped Qin become the state that later unified China, and it remains the classic case of government built on fear of punishment and hope of gain.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says fear is the main reason the base behave, with a little good conduct when they want something; Shang Yang built a whole state on exactly those two motives.

tamil:
அறைபறை அன்னர் கயவர்தாம் கேட்ட
மறைபிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்க லான்.
transliteration:
Araiparai annar kayavardhaam ketta
maraipirarkku uyththuraikka laan.
meaning: Mean people are like a drum beaten to announce news, because they carry every secret they hear straight to others.
elementary: Long ago, a town crier would beat a big drum and shout the news to the whole village. Some people are like that drum: tell them a secret, and they run off and tell everyone. A good friend keeps a secret safe.
university: The simile is the araiparai (அறைபறை), the drum beaten in the streets to proclaim royal announcements; Kalaignar names it the thamukku. The base hear a marai (மறை, 'secret, confidential matter') and uyththu uraikkum (உய்த்துரைக்கும், 'carry it to others and tell it'), going out of their way to spread it, as Mu. Varadarasanar stresses (வலிய கொண்டுபோய்). Parimelazhagar's point is that the drum and the base both broadcast what they receive, with no judgement about whether it should be told. Sivayogi Sivakumar adds that the base repeat what they do not themselves understand. Pope: 'The base are like the beaten drum; for, when they hear / The sound the secret out in every neighbour's ear.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That king whose secret plans other people, (though) assembled (for the purpose), do not discover, (will) enjoy the whole earth, though he be poor in treasure.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu stresses that secret counsel must be guarded, and the following verses warn the king to keep it from those likely to betray it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the kind of person Manu warns against: one who cannot be trusted with a secret.
hinduism.source: Laws of Manu 7.148 (tr. G. Bühler, SBE 25)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the gossip who spreads secrets with the trustworthy person who keeps them.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's drum-like base man set beside the faithful friend.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when there comes to them something [i.e., information] about [public] security or fear, they spread it around.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an rebukes people who broadcast sensitive news instead of taking it to those who can judge it.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's base, they pass on whatever they hear without restraint.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Do not deal basely with members of your people.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah's command, which the translators note refers to slander and is often rendered 'do not go about as a talebearer', forbids spreading harmful talk.
judaism.tie_back: The Torah calls talebearing 'dealing basely', the very vice the Kural assigns to the base.
judaism.source: Leviticus 19:16 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he reveals his secrets, (ii) he conceals one's own secrets, (iii) in misfortune he does not forsake one”
buddhism.explanation: Among the marks of a true friend, the Buddha lists keeping one's friend's secrets hidden.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the opposite: whatever is told to him in confidence he broadcasts.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (tr. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra lists five transgressions of the layperson's vow of truthfulness, including rahobhyakhyana (divulging what was said or done in private) and sakaramantrabheda (revealing another's confidential intentions).
jainism.explanation: In Jain ethics, spreading secrets is not just bad manners but a breach of the vow of truth (satya-anuvrata).
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's base man commits exactly these faults by carrying every secret to others.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.26 (numbering of the Digambara recension; via wisdomlib.org glossary of satyanuvrata)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The impurity of the ears is to listen to the slander of others.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak lists the real impurities of each sense, and says that of the ears is listening to tale-bearing and slander about others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares the base to a town crier's drum that spreads every secret it hears; Guru Nanak names the eager ear for gossip and tale-bearing as a real impurity.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 472, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas's barber, who alone knew the king had ass's ears, could not bear to keep the secret, so he dug a hole and whispered it into the ground; reeds grew there and whispered the secret to everyone when the wind blew.
greek_mythology.explanation: The barber's need to tell what he knew ended with the secret broadcast to the whole world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The barber, and the reeds that spread his whisper, are like the Kural's drum that carries what it hears to everyone.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch's essay On Talkativeness describes the chatterer who cannot hold anything he hears, comparing his speech to leaking vessels and his secrets to things that slip out at once, and praises silence as the mark of a trustworthy person.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch treats the inability to keep a confidence as a serious defect of character.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's base man is Plutarch's chatterer, who passes on every secret he hears.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia: De garrulitate (On Talkativeness) (tr. W. C. Helmbold)

real_life_example.event_title: Klaus Fuchs passes atomic secrets to the Soviet Union
real_life_example.place: Los Alamos, United States, and Harwell, England
real_life_example.event: Klaus Fuchs, a German-born physicist who worked on the British atomic project, at Los Alamos, and later at Harwell, passed secret information on atomic bomb research to the Soviet Union. Confronted by British security officers in December 1949, he confessed in early 1950 that he had been spying since 1942. He pleaded guilty and received the maximum sentence of fourteen years in prison.
real_life_example.explanation: His case showed how much damage one person entrusted with secrets could do, and it shaped Cold War security for years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the base to a drum that carries every secret to others; Fuchs took the most closely guarded secrets he was trusted with and passed them on.

tamil:
ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார் கயவர் கொடிறுடைக்கும்
கூன்கையர் அல்லா தவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Eerngai vidhiraar kayavar kodirudaikkum
koonkaiyar allaa thavarkku.
meaning: After eating, mean people will not even shake the leftover grains off their wet hand for anyone, except for those who would break their jaw with a fist.
elementary: After lunch, a few crumbs stick to your hand. Shaking them off for the birds costs you nothing. The Kural says base people will not give even that much to someone gentle who asks, but they will hand over anything to a bully who threatens them.
university: The image is precise: eerngai (ஈர்ங்கை, 'the wet hand') just washed after a meal, which the base will not even vidhir (விதிர், 'shake') so that a few grains fall to others. They give only to the kodiru udaikkum koonkaiyar (கொடிறுடைக்கும் கூன்கையர், 'those with bent, clenched hands that break the jaw'). Parimelazhagar and Puliyur Kesikan read koonkai as the fist curled to strike; Kalaignar makes the contrast explicit between the poor, who get nothing, and the thugs, who get what they demand. The couplet joins the chapter's themes of meanness and fear (cf. 1075). Pope: 'From off their moistened hands no clinging grain they shake, / Unless to those with clenched fist their jaws who break.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But charity performed with the expectation of some return, or with a desire for fruitive results, or in a grudging mood, is said to be charity in the mode of passion.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita ranks grudging giving, or giving for some return, as a lower, rajasic kind of charity.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's base man gives only grudgingly, and only when forced, which the Gita would place well below true giving.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.21 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to give freely and cheerfully, not reluctantly or because they are compelled.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's base man gives only 'of necessity', the very opposite of Paul's cheerful giver.

islam.quote_or_event: “they come not to prayer except while they are lazy and that they do not spend except while they are unwilling.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes hypocrites who give only reluctantly, against their will.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's base, they part with nothing willingly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A lower level than that is giving him with sadness.”
judaism.explanation: In Maimonides' ladder of charity, the lowest rung is giving to the poor grudgingly, with a sad face.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's base man does not reach even this lowest rung unless he is forced.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:14 (tr. Eliyahu Touger, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts the miser, who does not even value generosity, with the wise person who delights in giving.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is this miser, who will not part with crumbs unless compelled.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those mean persons are of the nature of the chisel, which without being struck will not even penetrate a tender leaf, though resting upon it; they will give nothing to the kind-hearted, but will give anything to those who employ force, if they meet them.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Naladiyar compares the mean to a chisel that cuts nothing unless it is hammered: they give nothing to gentle people but everything to those who use force.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's couplet in another image: the base give only to those who strike them.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 36.5, chapter 'Baseness or Envy' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: The Sikh langar, the free communal kitchen attached to every gurdwara, serves food to all who come. Britannica notes that everyone sits in a line with no place of higher or lower rank, and that Guru Amar Das required visitors to eat in this casteless langar.
sikhism.explanation: The langar puts vand chhakna (sharing what one has) into practice: food is given freely and equally, without asking who the guest is.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the base will not even shake crumbs from their wet hand except for those who would break their jaw; the langar stands for the opposite, food shared freely with everyone without any pressure.
sikhism.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'langar' and 'Sikhism: Sikh practice'

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, asks the suitors in his own hall for scraps, the arrogant Antinous refuses him anything and hurls a footstool at him, though the food he withholds is not even his own.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antinous gives nothing to the weak man who asks humbly, and is later destroyed by the very man he despised.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's base man, Antinous will not spare a crumb for someone who cannot force him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes meanness (aneleutheria) as a vice of deficiency in giving and excess in taking, and calls it incurable and more natural to people than prodigality, noting that some mean people refuse to give even from fear that they will be asked for more.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the mean man's refusal to give is a settled vice, the opposite of the liberal person who gives gladly to the right people.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's base man shows Aristotle's meanness in its sharpest form, giving nothing unless compelled.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: King John seals Magna Carta
real_life_example.event: Faced with a rebellion by his barons and the threat of civil war, King John of England added his seal to Magna Carta on 15 June 1215, granting rights and limits on royal power. Soon afterwards he persuaded the Pope to condemn the charter.
real_life_example.explanation: Magna Carta became one of the founding documents of the rule of law, even though the king who granted it did so only under force.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the base give nothing except to those who would strike them; King John granted his barons their rights only when they took up arms, and tried to take them back at once.

tamil:
சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர் கரும்புபோல்
கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ்.
transliteration:
