Sollap payanpaduvar saandror karumbupol
kollap payanpadum keezh.
meaning: Good people help you as soon as you tell them your need. Mean people are like sugarcane: they give their juice only when they are crushed.
elementary: To get juice from sugarcane, you have to squeeze and crush it hard. A good person helps you as soon as you ask nicely. A mean person is like the sugarcane: he gives nothing until he is squeezed.
university: The couplet sets the saandror (சான்றோர், 'the noble, the perfect in virtue', the subject of ch. 99) against the keezh. The noble are solla (சொல்ல, 'on being told') useful: as Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss it, they give as soon as the needy describe their want. The base, karumbu pol (கரும்புபோல், 'like sugarcane'), yield only kolla (கொல்ல, 'on being crushed, killed'). Parimelazhagar takes kolla as being pressed to the point of torment, as cane is crushed in a mill; Pope's prose gloss follows ('only when they are tortured to death'). The image recurs in Tamil didactic poetry, though there the sweetness of crushed cane is sometimes used for the noble who stay sweet under pressure. Pope's verse: 'The good to those will profit yield fair words who use; / The base, like sugar-cane, will profit those who bruise.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That gift which is given out of duty, at the proper time and place, to a worthy person, and without expectation of return, is considered to be charity in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita describes the highest, sattvic giving: given freely, out of duty, with no thought of return.
hinduism.tie_back: This is how the Kural's saandror give, as soon as they are asked, in contrast to the base who must be crushed.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.20 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus' parable, an unjust judge finally grants a widow's plea only because her constant pressure wears him down.
christianity.tie_back: The unjust judge is the Kural's sugarcane: he gives only when squeezed.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Saying], "We feed you only for the face [i.e., approval] of Allāh. We wish not from you reward or gratitude."”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises the righteous who feed the needy freely, seeking nothing in return.
islam.tie_back: These are the Kural's saandror, who give at a word, unlike the base who must be crushed like cane.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He who desires that he himself should give, and that others should give: he is a pious man; He who desires that he himself should not give and that others too should not give: he is a wicked man.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah sorts givers by their willingness, calling the willing giver pious and the one who wants no giving at all wicked.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it judges people by whether they give freely or have to be forced.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:13 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A person of integrity gives a gift with a sense of conviction. A person of integrity gives a gift attentively. A person of integrity gives a gift in season. A person of integrity gives a gift with an empathetic heart.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes how a good person gives: with conviction, care, good timing and sympathy.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's saandror give in this way, promptly and with empathy, as soon as they hear of a need.
buddhism.source: Sappurisadana Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 5.148 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The high-born, even when they have not anything, will approach those who are in want, and be a prop when they totter.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Naladiyar says that the truly noble seek out the needy and support them even when they themselves have little.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's saandror, who give as soon as they learn of need, the opposite of the cane that yields only when crushed.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 15.10, chapter 'High Birth' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who performs selfless service, without thought of reward, shall attain his Lord and Master.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan praises seva done freely, without any wish for return.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the noble help as soon as they are told of a need, while the base give only when crushed like sugarcane; Guru Arjan praises service given freely, with no need to be forced or rewarded.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop's fable of the walnut tree, a tree by the roadside bears a rich crop, and passers-by beat its branches with sticks and stones to get the nuts.
greek_mythology.explanation: The tree complains that it is beaten by the very people who enjoy its fruit.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The fable shares the Kural's image of a giver from whom goods come only by beating, though Aesop's sympathy lies with the tree.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, 'The Walnut-Tree' (tr. George Fyler Townsend)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca teaches that a benefit should be given readily and without delay, since a gift that has to be dragged out of the giver, or that clings long to his hands, loses most of its value and earns little gratitude.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, promptness is part of what makes a gift a real benefit.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's ideal giver is the Kural's saandror; the gift wrung out under pressure is the base man's.

real_life_example.event_title: Tsar Nicholas II issues the October Manifesto
real_life_example.event: During the Revolution of 1905 a general political strike spread across Russia, shutting factories, transport and newspapers. Under that pressure Tsar Nicholas II issued the October Manifesto, promising civil liberties and an elected Duma. When the Fundamental Laws were issued in April 1906, the rights actually granted were narrower than the manifesto had promised.
real_life_example.explanation: The manifesto ended unlimited autocracy in Russia on paper, but it was a concession forced out of the government rather than freely given.
real_life_example.tie_back: Like sugarcane that gives juice only when crushed, the tsar granted reforms only when a nationwide strike pressed hard, and then gave less than he had promised.

tamil:
உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் காணின் பிறர்மேல்
வடுக்காண வற்றாகும் கீழ்.
transliteration:
Uduppadhoovum unbadhoovum kaanin pirarmel
vadukkaana vatraagum keezh.
meaning: When mean people see others wearing nice clothes and eating good food, they become experts at finding faults in them.
elementary: Imagine a classmate gets new shoes and a nice lunch. A jealous child might say, 'Those shoes are ugly' or 'Your lunch smells funny,' just because they feel envious. The Kural says base people do this: they invent faults in others because they cannot stand to see them happy.
university: The couplet describes envy (azhukkaaru, the subject of ch. 17) turned into fault-finding. Uduppadhum unbadhum (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம், with alapedai lengthening: 'what they wear and what they eat') are the most ordinary signs of others' well-being; on seeing them, the keezh become vatru (வற்று, 'strong, capable') at vadu kaana (வடுக்காண, 'finding a blemish'). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read envy as the cause and deliberate fault-finding as the result; Puliyur Kesikan adds that the base may even try to create a blemish (வடு உண்டாக்கவும் முயல்வான்). Pope: 'If neighbours clothed and fed he see, the base / Is mighty man some hidden fault to trace.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Duryodhana returns from the Pandavas' splendid assembly hall at Indraprastha burning with envy at their prosperity, tells his father he cannot bear to see their wealth, and plots the dice game to ruin them.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana's envy at the Pandavas' good fortune turns into scheming against them.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural's keezh: the sight of others' well-being drives him to find a way to harm them.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta sub-parva (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then the presidents and princes sought to find occasion against Daniel concerning the kingdom; but they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him.”
christianity.explanation: Envious officials, jealous of Daniel's high position, search his life for a fault to accuse him of.
christianity.tie_back: They are the Kural's base men, roused by another's success to hunt for blemishes.

islam.quote_or_event: “Or do they envy people for what Allāh has given them of His bounty?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an rebukes those who resent the blessings God has given to others.
islam.tie_back: This is the envy at others' well-being that, in the Kural, drives the base to look for faults.

judaism.quote_or_event: “envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ha-Kappar names envy as one of three passions that destroy a person.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural shows envy at work in the base, poisoning their view of anyone who prospers.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:21 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one's own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another's faults, but hides one's own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes how readily people sift out others' faults while hiding their own.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is this eager winnower of others' faults, set in motion by envy.

jainism.quote_or_event: “what are those wretches' tongues made of, who, standing in the presence of those persons, declare their faults, for the purpose of destroying their reputation?”
jainism.explanation: In its chapter 'Baseness or Envy', the Jain Naladiyar condemns those who announce others' faults in order to ruin their good name.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's keezh, skilled at finding blemishes in others out of envy.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 36.3, chapter 'Baseness or Envy' (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the clever person to stop listing other people's faults and to examine his own.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the base become experts at finding fault when they see others well clothed and fed; Farid's salok tells the fault-finder to look at himself instead.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 6) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid describes Envy (Invidia) as a figure who wastes away at the sight of others' success and is tormented by others' happiness; sent by Minerva, she poisons Aglauros with jealousy of her sister's good fortune.
greek_mythology.explanation: Envy in the myth cannot bear to see others thrive and turns that pain into malice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ovid's Envy is the Kural's base man made into a goddess: others' well-being is what torments her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines envy as hatred that makes a person sad at another's good fortune and glad at another's misfortune.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, envy is a form of hatred, and it naturally leads one to belittle the person envied.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural shows the same passion in action: the base, pained by others' comforts, look for faults to bring them down.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part III, Definitions of the Affects 23

real_life_example.event_title: Artists publish a protest against the Eiffel Tower
real_life_example.event: Soon after construction of Gustave Eiffel's tower began, a group of about forty well-known artists and writers, including Charles Gounod, Charles Garnier and Guy de Maupassant, published a protest on the front page of Le Temps. They called the tower useless and monstrous and said it would dishonour Paris. The authorities backed Eiffel, building continued, and the finished tower proved hugely popular.
real_life_example.explanation: The protest is remembered as a famous example of prominent critics finding fault with a bold new achievement that later became loved.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes people who become experts at finding faults when they see others' good fortune; the protesters poured out fault-finding at another man's conspicuous success.

tamil:
எற்றிற் குரியர் கயவரொன்று உற்றக்கால்
விற்றற்கு உரியர் விரைந்து.
transliteration:
Etrir kuriyar kayavarondru utrakkaal
vitrarku uriyar viraindhu.
meaning: What are mean people good for? When trouble comes, they rush to sell themselves, and that is all they are fit for.
elementary: Imagine a team captain who, the moment the game gets hard, switches to the other team because they promise him a prize. He cannot be trusted. The Kural says base people are like that: at the first sign of trouble, they will sell out anyone, even themselves.
university: The chapter, and the whole Porutpal, ends with a rhetorical question: etrirku uriyar (எற்றிற்கு உரியர், 'for what are they fit?'). The answer: ondru utrakkaal (ஒன்று உற்றக்கால், 'when some calamity comes') they are fit vitrarku (விற்றற்கு, 'for selling', i.e. selling themselves) viraindhu (விரைந்து, 'quickly'). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read it as the base hastening to sell themselves to others to escape a misfortune; Puliyur Kesikan adds that they are fit for no other work; Solomon Pappaiah extends it to profit or loss, saying they make themselves others' slaves. The final sarcasm returns to the first couplet: the base have the human form but none of the steadfastness that gives a person worth. Pope: 'For what is base man fit, if griefs assail? / Himself to offer, there and then, for sale!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, to keep his promised word to the sage Vishvamitra, sold his wife, his son and finally himself into servitude, enduring every hardship rather than break faith.
hinduism.explanation: Harishchandra's self-sale is the noble opposite of the Kural's: he sells himself to keep his truth, not to escape trouble.
hinduism.tie_back: The contrast sharpens the Kural's point: the base sell themselves to save their skins, while the noble suffer anything to keep faith.
hinduism.source: Markandeya Purana, Harishchandra episode (tr. F. E. Pargiter)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.”
christianity.explanation: Judas goes to the chief priests and offers to betray Jesus for money.
christianity.tie_back: Judas is the Kural's base man, ready to sell himself and his loyalty for a price.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, those who exchange the covenant of Allāh and their [own] oaths for a small price will have no share in the Hereafter”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an condemns those who sell their solemn word for a little worldly gain.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's base, they are quick to sell what should never be for sale.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Esau said: ‘Behold, I am at the point to die; and what profit shall the birthright do to me?’ And Jacob said: ‘Swear to me first’; and he swore unto him; and he sold his birthright unto Jacob.”
judaism.explanation: Faint with hunger, Esau sells his birthright on the spot for a bowl of lentils.
judaism.tie_back: Esau is the Kural's base man exactly: at the first hardship he hastens to sell what is most precious.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The good renounce (attachment for) everything. The virtuous do not prattle with a yearning for pleasures. The wise show no elation or depression when touched by happiness or sorrow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the wise stay steady whether fortune or misfortune comes.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the opposite: the first trouble knocks him off balance and he sells himself.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If any misfortune happens and he suffers pain, he should cheerfully steady his mind, and bear the ills that attack him.”
jainism.explanation: In the lecture on the twenty-two hardships (parishaha), Mahavira teaches the monk to meet misfortune with a steady mind and not be defeated by it.
jainism.tie_back: This is the opposite of the Kural's base man, who gives himself away the moment trouble comes.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok, Guru Nanak says the path of love for God is open only to someone ready to give his life. Sikhs read this as the root of the Gurus' readiness for martyrdom.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the base are good only for selling themselves the moment trouble comes; Guru Nanak's ideal is the opposite, a person who comes with head in hand and will not sell out at any price.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Thermopylae, the Malian Ephialtes went to Xerxes hoping for a large reward and showed the Persians the mountain path around the pass, betraying the Greeks who held it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ephialtes sold out his own side for gain at the decisive moment, and his name became a byword for traitor.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ephialtes is the Kural's base man, ready to sell himself and others when the crisis comes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is you who know yourself, how much you are worth to yourself, and at what price you sell yourself; for men sell themselves at various prices.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus says each person decides how cheaply he will sell his integrity, and the Stoic refuses to sell it at all.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's base man is the one whose price is lowest: he sells himself at the first trouble.

real_life_example.event_title: Alcibiades flees to Sparta
real_life_example.event: The Athenian general Alcibiades, a commander of the expedition against Syracuse, was recalled to face charges of sacrilege that carried the death penalty. Instead of returning, he escaped and went over to Athens' enemy Sparta. There he advised the Spartans to send help to Syracuse and to fortify Decelea in Athenian territory, which did serious harm to Athens.
real_life_example.explanation: His switch of sides became one of the most famous betrayals in ancient history and contributed to Athens' defeat in the Peloponnesian War.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when trouble comes, the base hurry to sell themselves; facing a death sentence, Alcibiades quickly offered his skills to his city's enemy.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

tamil:
அணங்குகொல் ஆய்மயில் கொல்லோ கனங்குழை
மாதர்கொல் மாலும்என் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Anangukol aaimayil kollo kananguzhai
maatharkol maalumen nenju.
meaning: Is she a goddess, a lovely peacock, or a human girl wearing heavy earrings? My heart is confused and cannot tell.
elementary: Imagine seeing a sunset so beautiful that you stop and wonder whether it is real or a painting. The young man in this verse sees a girl for the first time and is so amazed that he cannot decide whether she is a goddess, a lovely peacock, or an ordinary girl.
university: This kural opens the Kamattuppal and its Kalaviyal (the section on premarital, 'secret' love), voicing the hero's (talaivan's) first sight of the heroine. The chapter title combines takai (தகை, 'beauty, grace'), anangu (அணங்கு, a goddess or spirit that afflicts those who approach it) and uruttal (உறுத்தல், 'causing'), so it means the distress her beauty inflicts. The three-way doubt, anangu-kol, aaimayil-kollo, maathar-kol (goddess? choice peahen? woman?), is a classical Tamil figure of bewilderment (aiyam), and maalum (மாலும், 'is confused, infatuated') names the state. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses kananguzhai as 'a woman wearing heavy ear-ornaments', the detail that hints she is human after all; Pope renders 'Goddess? or peafowl rare?... All wildered is my mind!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And neither among celestials, nor among Yakshas, nor among men was anybody possessed of such beauty, seen or heard of before.”
hinduism.explanation: The Nala episode of the Mahabharata describes Damayanti as a beauty that no god, spirit or human could match.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's hero, the narrator can place her beauty neither among gods nor among humans.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 53 (Nalopakhyana; tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?”
christianity.explanation: In the Song of Songs onlookers ask who this woman can be, comparing her to dawn, moon and sun.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts react to beauty with a startled question about who, or what, she really is.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when they saw him, they greatly admired him and cut their hands and said, ‘Perfect is Allāh! This is not a man; this is none but a noble angel.’”
islam.explanation: When the women of Egypt first see Joseph, they are so struck that they cut their hands and declare he cannot be human.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, a first sight of beauty makes the viewers doubt whether the person is human or heavenly.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud lists four women of the Bible who were of outstanding beauty: Sarah, Rahab, Abigail and Esther, and records rabbinic remarks on how powerfully their beauty affected those who saw or even named them.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis treat extraordinary beauty as a real force that can unsettle the mind of an onlooker.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's bewildered hero is an example of exactly that unsettling force.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What do you think, Nanda? Which is lovelier, better looking, more charming: the Sakyan girl, the envy of the countryside, or these 500 dove-footed nymphs?”
buddhism.explanation: To cure Nanda's longing for a beautiful girl, the Buddha takes him to heaven and asks him to compare her with celestial nymphs.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's hero cannot tell a girl from a goddess; the Buddha deliberately sets a girl beside goddesses to loosen that spell.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though those who possess the three Guptis, cannot be disturbed even by well-adorned goddesses, still it is recommended to monks to live by themselves, as this is wholesome in every way.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana says that a monk whose mind, speech and body are fully guarded (the three guptis) cannot be shaken even by adorned goddesses, but still advises seclusion.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural shows the opposite case: an unguarded heart is thrown into confusion by a beauty that seems divine.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Wonderful is the sound current of the Naad, wonderful is the knowledge of the Vedas.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak begins a long salok of vismad (wonder), listing one thing after another in creation that leaves him astonished.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's hero is so bewildered by beauty that he cannot tell whether he sees a goddess, a peacock or a girl; Guru Nanak's vismad is the Sikh name for being overwhelmed and wonder-struck before the beauty of creation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I implore your aid- but tell me, are you a goddess or are you a mortal woman?”
greek_mythology.explanation: Shipwrecked Odysseus, meeting the princess Nausicaa on the shore, cannot tell whether she is the goddess Artemis or a human girl.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact question, goddess or human maiden, asked at a first meeting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...is amazed when he sees any one having a godlike face or form, which is the expression of divine beauty; and at first a shudder runs through him, and again the old awe steals over him.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates describes the soul that sees earthly beauty and is reminded of divine beauty, so that it shudders and feels awe before the beloved as before a god.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato explains philosophically why the Kural's hero confuses a girl with a goddess.

real_life_example.event_title: Dante first sees Beatrice Portinari
real_life_example.event: In 1274 the young Dante Alighieri, about nine years old, first saw Beatrice Portinari, a girl of about the same age, at her father's house in Florence. In his book La Vita Nuova he later described how she appeared dressed in modest red and how the sight overwhelmed him, so that from then on love ruled his soul. Beatrice married another man and died in 1290, and she became the guiding figure of his Divine Comedy.
real_life_example.explanation: Dante's account of this first sight became one of the most famous descriptions of love at first sight in world literature.
real_life_example.tie_back: Like the hero of the kural who cannot tell whether he has seen a goddess or a human girl, Dante wrote of Beatrice as a heavenly presence from the moment he first saw her.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

tamil:
நோக்கினாள் நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல் தாக்கணங்கு
தானைக்கொண் டன்ன துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Nokkinaal nokkethir nokkuthal thaakkanangu
thaanaikkon tanna thudaiththu.
meaning: When she looks back at me, it is as if a goddess who attacks had come with a whole army.
elementary: Have you ever been looked at so seriously that you suddenly felt shy and could not look back? Here the young man looks at the girl, and when she looks back at him he feels as if an entire army has charged at him.
university: The kural turns on the repeated root nokku (நோக்கு, 'look'): nokkinaal ('she who looked'), nokkethir ('against my look') and nokkuthal ('the looking back'). Thaakkanangu (தாக்கணங்கு) is an anangu that strikes or attacks on its own, and thaanai (தானை) is an army; Mu. Varadarasanar explains that her return glance is like such a self-attacking deity arriving with a whole army. Commentators in the Parimelazhagar line take the point to be that one glance already wounds, so a returned glance doubles the assault. Pope renders: 'As if the matchless goddess' hand / Led forth an armed band.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava, Kama, the god of love, waits with his flower-bow as Parvati approaches the meditating Shiva, and shoots at the moment her glance meets his, so that even the great ascetic is shaken.
hinduism.explanation: Love in Indian poetry is pictured as an archer-god whose arrows fly with a beloved's glance.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise turns a returned glance into an armed attack by a deity.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song of Songs finds the beloved both beautiful and overwhelming, like an army with banners.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same military image: her look arrives like an army.

islam.quote_or_event: “And women in the city said, ‘The wife of al-ʿAzeez is seeking to seduce her slave boy; he has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her [to be] in clear error.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the wife of al-Aziz as having been overpowered by love for Joseph through his beauty.
islam.tie_back: Both texts show beauty overpowering the one who looks at it, though the Qur'an judges the passion as error.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You have captured my heart, / My own, my bride, / You have captured my heart / With one [glance] of your eyes, / With one coil of your necklace.”
judaism.explanation: The lover says that a single glance of the beloved's eyes has taken his heart captive.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, says one returned look is enough to overcome him.
judaism.source: Song of Songs 4:9 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Sensual passions are your first army.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Padhana Sutta the Buddha-to-be names the forces Mara sends against him as armies, and sensual passion leads them.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's image of a glance arriving like an army matches the Buddhist picture of desire as an attacking army.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 3.2, Padhana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Śramaṇa, engaged in penance, should not allow himself to watch the shape, beauty, coquetry, laughter, prattle, gestures, and glances of women, nor retain a recollection of them in his mind.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's discipline lists glances among the things a monk must not dwell on, because they disturb the mind.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural shows why: a single returned glance overwhelms the one who meets it.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, the True Guru, the Spiritual Warrior, has shot me with His Arrow. As soon as it struck me, I fell to the ground, with a hole in my heart.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir describes the Guru's word as an arrow that strikes the devotee to the ground and pierces his heart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the woman's answering glance strikes like a goddess leading an army; Kabir uses the same image of being struck down by a warrior's single shot, here the Guru's word.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 194) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid's tale, Cupid shoots Apollo with a golden arrow so that the god falls in love the instant he sees the nymph Daphne, and even the mighty archer-god is helpless.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek and Roman myth make love an armed god whose arrows strike through the eyes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's 'attacking goddess with an army' is the Tamil form of love as a weapon-bearing deity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...as he receives the effluence of beauty through the eyes, the wing moistens and he warms.”
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes beauty as a stream that enters the lover through the eyes and overpowers him.
philosophy.tie_back: For the Kural, too, the eyes are the gate through which the attack comes.

real_life_example.event_title: Petrarch first sees Laura
real_life_example.event: The Italian poet Petrarch recorded in a note in his copy of Virgil that he first saw the woman he called Laura on 6 April 1327 in Avignon, in the church of Sainte-Claire. He wrote hundreds of love poems to her, collected in his Canzoniere. In the same note he recorded that she died in Avignon on 6 April 1348.
real_life_example.explanation: Petrarch's poems to Laura shaped the love sonnet for centuries across Europe.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes the overwhelming force of the beloved's returning glance; a single sight of Laura in church captured Petrarch for the rest of his life.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

tamil:
பண்டறியேன் கூற்றென் பதனை இனியறிந்தேன்
பெண்டகையால் பேரமர்க் கட்டு.
transliteration:
Pandariyen kootren pathanai iniyarinthen
pendakaiyaal peramark kattu.
meaning: I never knew before what people call Death. Now I know it: it has a lovely woman's form and big eyes that fight.
elementary: People sometimes say a scary film 'nearly killed' them, even though they were safe. The young man jokes in the same way: he had only heard of Death in stories, but now he has met it, in the shape of a girl with big, powerful eyes.
university: Kootru (கூற்று) is Death personified, Yama, the 'one who divides' body from life. Pandariyen ('I did not know before') and iniyarinthen ('now I have learned') frame a mock discovery. The second line packs pen-takai (பெண்டகை, 'womanly grace') with per-amar-kan (பேரமர்க்கண், 'large eyes that do battle'); Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as 'it has a woman's nature and large eyes that make war', while Kalaignar speaks of eye-arrows. The commentarial tradition treats the hyperbole as the lover's helplessness, not a moral judgment on the woman. Pope: 'Death's form I formerly / Knew not; but now 'tis plain to me; / He comes in lovely maiden's guise.' Identical on both web sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material modes of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring, sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna calls kama, desire, the all-devouring enemy of the world.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural playfully treats the beloved's eyes as Death; the Gita seriously treats desire itself as a devouring enemy.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.37 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, 1972)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that a woman's eyes can capture a man and lead him to ruin.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes the eyes the weapon that takes a man's life.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘My Lord, prison is more to my liking than that to which they invite me. And if You do not avert from me their plan, I might incline toward them and [thus] be of the ignorant.’”
islam.explanation: Joseph asks God to protect him, knowing how strongly beauty and attraction can pull even a righteous man.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat the pull of beauty as a danger strong enough to overcome a person.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For love is fierce as death, / Passion is mighty as Sheol; / Its darts are darts of fire, / A blazing flame.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs compares love to death and the grave and speaks of its fiery darts.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, puts love and Death side by side and gives love weapons.
judaism.source: Song of Songs 8:6 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Realizing that this body is like froth, penetrating its mirage-like nature, and plucking out Mara's flower-tipped arrows of sensuality, go beyond sight of the King of Death!”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada links Mara's flower-arrows of desire with the realm of the King of Death.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural discovers that the eyes of desire are Death itself; the Dhammapada makes the same link and urges escape.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares pleasures to a lovely fruit that turns out to be deadly poison.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural finds that something beautiful can be Death in disguise, which is the same idea.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, the world is afraid of death - that death fills my mind with bliss.”
sikhism.explanation: In another salok, Kabir says the dying that the world fears, which Sikh commentators read as dying to the ego, fills him with joy.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover says he has only now met Death, in the form of a woman's large eyes; Kabir also speaks of meeting a death that love makes welcome.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1365, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Small wonder that Trojans and Achaeans should endure so much and so long, for the sake of a woman so marvellously and divinely lovely.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The Trojan elders, watching Helen, admit that her beauty explains a war that has brought death to so many.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the elders tie a woman's beauty directly to death and battle.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plotinus says that the sight of true beauty brings wonder and a delicious trouble, longing and love, and a trembling that is all delight.
philosophy.explanation: For Plotinus, beauty strikes the soul with an overwhelming and pleasurable shock.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural expresses the same overwhelming shock in the playful language of meeting Death.
philosophy.source: Plotinus, Enneads I.6.4 (tr. Stephen MacKenna; paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: John Keats and Fanny Brawne
real_life_example.event: The poet John Keats met Fanny Brawne in late 1818, and in April 1819 she moved into the other half of Wentworth Place in Hampstead, next door to him. They became secretly engaged, and he wrote her passionate letters. In February 1820 a lung haemorrhage convinced Keats he was dying of tuberculosis, and he died in Rome in February 1821, aged 25, without being able to marry her.
real_life_example.explanation: Their love letters are among the most famous in English and show love and mortal illness bound together.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's lover says he has now learned what Death is, for it has a woman's grace; for Keats, love for Fanny and the approach of death arrived together.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

tamil:
கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றத்தால் பெண்டகைப்
பேதைக்கு அமர்த்தன கண்.
transliteration:
Kandaar uyirunnum thottraththaal pendakaip
pethaikku amarththana kan.
meaning: This gentle, innocent girl has eyes that seem to drink the life of anyone who sees them. Her eyes do not match her soft nature.
elementary: Think of a kitten with huge, shining eyes: it is small and gentle, yet one look can make everyone in the room stop what they are doing. The young man sees that the girl is shy and gentle, but her eyes are so powerful that they seem to belong to someone much fiercer.
university: Uyir-unnum (உயிருண்ணும்) means 'devouring life', and kandaar (கண்டார்) 'those who see', so her eyes have a look that eats the life of every viewer. Pethai (பேதை) here means an innocent young girl, not a 'fool', and pen-takai (பெண்டகை) is womanly grace. The key verb amarththana (அமர்த்தன) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as 'were at variance with one another', i.e. the eyes contradict her gentle nature; Solomon Pappaiah adds that they 'war against' her character and understanding. Pope renders: 'In sweet simplicity, / A woman's gracious form hath she; / But yet those eyes, that drink my life, / Are with the form at strife!' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And as he gazed on that lady of sweet smiles. Nala's love increased, but desirous of keeping his truth, he suppressed his passion.”
hinduism.explanation: When Nala sees Damayanti, her sweet beauty stirs a powerful love that he must struggle to master.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a gentle, smiling beauty has an overwhelming effect on the one who looks.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 55 (Nalopakhyana; tr. K. M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck.”
christianity.explanation: The lover says one look from the beloved's eyes has carried his heart away.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same claim: her eyes take the viewer's very life.

islam.quote_or_event: “Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells believers to lower their gaze, recognising how much power the eyes have over the heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural describes the force of a look; the Qur'an answers that force with restraint of the gaze.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Turn your eyes away from me, / For they overwhelm me!”
judaism.explanation: The lover begs the beloved to look away because her eyes overpower him.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's eyes that 'drink life' are the same overwhelming eyes.
judaism.source: Song of Songs 6:5 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The Destroyer brings under his sway the person of distracted mind who, insatiate in sense desires, only plucks the flowers (of pleasure).”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that the Destroyer (death) takes control of the person carried away by sense desire.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's 'life-devouring' eyes describe that same capture from inside the lover's experience.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of 'colours,' will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's teaching says that passion for what the eye sees destroys a person the way a flame draws a moth to its death.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's eyes that 'drink the life' of the viewer are the flame, and the lover is the moth.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Bani of the Lord's Love is the pointed arrow, which has pierced my mind, O Lord King.”
sikhism.explanation: In a chhant in Raag Asa, Guru Ram Das describes the Guru's word of divine love as a sharp-pointed arrow that has wounded his mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural marvels that a gentle, innocent girl has eyes that seem to drink the life of anyone who sees them; Guru Ram Das likewise finds that something sweet, the word of love, wounds like a sharp arrow.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 449, Raag Asa, Chhant, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid's version, Medusa was once a beautiful maiden; after her transformation her gaze turned everyone who looked at her to stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes a woman's eyes literally deadly to anyone who meets them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's 'life-devouring' eyes are a playful version of the deadly gaze, set against the girl's gentleness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's Symposium, Diotima describes Eros as a paradox: poor and soft in one way, yet a bold and mighty hunter who is always weaving snares.
philosophy.explanation: Plato sees love as made of opposites, gentle and fierce at once.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural finds the same opposition in the girl, whose gentle nature contrasts with her conquering eyes.

real_life_example.event_title: Vermeer paints Girl with a Pearl Earring
real_life_example.event: Around 1665 Johannes Vermeer painted a young woman in a turban and a large pearl earring, turning to look out at the viewer with her lips softly parted. The Mauritshuis in The Hague explains that it is a tronie, a study of an imaginary figure rather than a portrait of a named person. Its simple setting, light and direct gaze have made it one of the most recognised paintings in the world.
real_life_example.explanation: The painting shows how a gentle, quiet figure can hold every viewer through the power of a look.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of a gentle, innocent girl whose eyes seem to seize all who see them; Vermeer's quiet young woman draws in viewers above all through her gaze.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

tamil:
கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ மடவரல்
நோக்கமிம் மூன்றும் உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Kootramo kanno pinaiyo madavaral
nokkamim moondrum udaiththu.
meaning: Is it Death, is it an eye, or is it a shy female deer? This young girl's look has all three in it at once.
elementary: Some things can be several things at once: a rainbow is pretty, a bit mysterious and gone in a moment. The young man finds the girl's look like that. It is powerful enough to knock him over, warm like a friendly eye, and shy like a little deer.
university: The question again uses the doubting particle -o: kootramo (கூற்றமோ, 'Death?'), kanno (கண்ணோ, 'an eye?'), pinaiyo (பிணையோ, 'a hind/doe?'). Madavaral (மடவரல்) is a young, innocent woman, and nokkam (நோக்கம்) her look. Commentators explain the three qualities differently: Mu. Varadarasanar simply lists Death, eye and doe; Solomon Pappaiah reads the eye as a glance that spreads all over the viewer's body and the doe as a timid, fearful look; Puliyur Kesikan has 'the afflicting Death, the darting eye, the startled doe'. The point is that one look combines danger, warmth and shyness. Pope: 'Is it death's dart? or eye's bright beams? / Or fawn's shy glance? All three appear.' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa's Shakuntala begins with King Dushyanta chasing a frightened deer into a hermitage, where he meets Shakuntala, a girl raised among fawns, whose shy, darting glances the play repeatedly compares to a deer's.
hinduism.explanation: Sanskrit love poetry often likens a young woman's timid glance to a fawn's.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's pinai (doe) uses the same image of a shy, deer-like look that overwhelms the hero.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs repeatedly ties love to gentle deer, roes and hinds.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's look has the shyness of a doe, the same animal the Song uses for love.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [for them are] fair women with large, [beautiful] eyes,”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the companions of Paradise by their large, beautiful eyes, which commentators often compare to the eyes of a gazelle.
islam.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes a woman's large, deer-like eyes the centre of her beauty.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs urges a man to delight in the wife of his youth and likens her to a loving doe and a graceful mountain goat.
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew Bible, like Tamil poetry, uses the doe as an image of a beloved woman's grace.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's pinai, the shy doe in the girl's look, is the same figure.
judaism.source: Proverbs 5:18-19 (paraphrase; cf. JPS Tanakh on Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Mara fails to break the newly awakened Buddha, his three daughters, Craving, Discontent and Passion, try in many forms to tempt him, and fail.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist texts picture desire as several alluring forms working together.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's look holds three natures at once; Mara sends three daughters, each a face of desire.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As an impassioned deer allured (by a song) rushes into death, without being satisfied with the sound.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana uses the deer, drawn helplessly by music, as an example of how passion for a sense object leads to death.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural brings together a deer and Death in one look; Jain teaching joins the same two images.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, as given in his summary of vv. 35-47)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You have thousands of eyes, and yet You have no eyes. You have thousands of forms, and yet You do not have even one.”
sikhism.explanation: In the evening prayer Sohila, Guru Nanak marvels at a God who has countless eyes and forms yet is beyond all form.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover cannot decide whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a shy doe, since it seems to hold all three natures; Guru Nanak is likewise baffled by a Beloved whose eyes and forms are many and none.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 13, Sohila, Raag Dhanasari, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The hunter Actaeon happens to see the goddess Artemis bathing; she turns him into a stag, and he is killed by his own hounds.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this myth a single sight of divine beauty brings a deer's form and death together.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's look combines Death and a deer in the same way, though gently and playfully.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Edmund Burke separated the beautiful (small, smooth, delicate, inspiring love) from the sublime (vast, powerful, inspiring a kind of terror), while noting that strong experiences can mix the two.
philosophy.explanation: Burke's aesthetics explains how one sight can feel both gentle and terrifying.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's look is both a gentle doe (the beautiful) and Death (the terrible) at once.
philosophy.source: Edmund Burke, A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757), Parts 2-3 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Leonardo da Vinci paints the Mona Lisa
real_life_example.place: Florence, Italy (now in the Louvre, Paris)
real_life_example.event: Leonardo da Vinci began the portrait known as the Mona Lisa in Florence around 1503 and continued working on it for years; it is now in the Louvre. The sitter is traditionally identified as Lisa Gherardini, wife of the Florentine merchant Francesco del Giocondo. Her enigmatic smile and expression, painted with Leonardo's soft sfumato shading, have been studied and debated for centuries.
real_life_example.explanation: It is probably the most famous painting in the world, largely because viewers cannot settle on what her expression means.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's lover sees several natures in one young woman's look at once; the Mona Lisa's expression is famous for seeming to hold more than one meaning at the same time.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

tamil:
கொடும்புருவம் கோடா மறைப்பின் நடுங்கஞர்
செய்யல மன்இவள் கண்.
transliteration:
Kodumpuruvam kodaa maraippin nadungagnar
seyyala manival kan.
meaning: If her curved eyebrows would only stay straight and shade her eyes, her eyes would not make me tremble and suffer like this.
elementary: When the sun is too bright, a cap with a peak shades your eyes so you are not dazzled. The young man wishes her eyebrows would act like that cap and shade her eyes, so her look would not make him so nervous.
university: Kodum-puruvam (கொடும்புருவம்) means the 'curved' or 'cruel' brows; kodum carries both senses, so the curve itself is accused. Kodaa (கோடா, 'without bending') and maraippin (மறைப்பின், 'if they hid') give the wish: if the brows stayed straight and screened the eyes. Nadung-agnar (நடுங்கஞர்) is 'trembling distress', and man (மன்) adds regret, 'surely they would not...'. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both read it as 'if the bent brows stood straight and hid them, her eyes would not cause me trembling sorrow'. The image draws on the Indian convention of brows as a drawn bow from which the eyes shoot. Pope: 'If cruel eye-brow's bow, / Unbent, would veil those glances now.' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Katha Upanishad compares the body to a chariot, the senses to horses and the mind to the reins: only a person who keeps the reins firm stops the senses from running wild.
hinduism.explanation: Hindu teaching treats control over what reaches us through the senses as the key to a steady mind.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural wishes for a 'rein' on the eyes, the brows acting as a screen that would spare him distress.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me: thy hair is as a flock of goats that appear from Gilead.”
christianity.explanation: The lover asks the beloved to turn her eyes away because they overpower him.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same wish: if only her eyes were screened, he would stop trembling.

islam.quote_or_event: “And she certainly determined [to seduce] him, and he would have inclined to her had he not seen the proof [i.e., sign] of his Lord.”
islam.explanation: Joseph is kept from yielding only because a sign from God came between him and temptation.
islam.tie_back: The Kural wishes for a screen between him and her eyes; Joseph is saved by a divine screen.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Your eyes are like doves / Behind your veil.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs praises the beloved's eyes as they appear softened behind a veil.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural wishes her eyes were veiled by her brows, so their power would be softened.
judaism.source: Song of Songs 4:1 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Visuddhimagga tells of the elder Mahatissa, who passed a woman laughing on the road and, guarding his senses, noticed only her teeth, which became for him an object of meditation on the body.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist sense restraint means not letting the eye seize on beauty, so it cannot disturb the mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural wishes for a screen over her eyes; the monk builds that screen inside his own mind.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Not to look at, nor to long for, not to think of, nor to praise, womankind: this is becoming the meditation of the noble ones, and it is always wholesome to those who delight in chastity.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana makes not looking the first step of a monk's chastity.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's lover wishes the sight could be screened off; Jain discipline screens it by choice.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The soul-bride and the Husband Lord live together as one, but the hard wall of egotism has come between them.”
sikhism.explanation: Using the bride-soul image, Guru Ram Das says the soul and God already live together, but ego stands between them like a hard wall.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover wishes the curved brows would screen the girl's eyes; Gurbani also speaks of a screen between lover and Beloved, but there the screen is ego, and the devotee longs for it to be removed.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1263, Raag Malar, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...from whose eyes as they glanced flowed love that unnerves the limbs: and beautiful is their glance beneath their brows.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says that love flows from the Graces' eyes and singles out their glance beneath their brows.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural, too, places the danger in the eyes beneath curved brows.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal remarked that if Cleopatra's nose had been shorter, the whole face of the earth would have changed.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal's point is that a tiny feature of a face can decide enormous outcomes.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes everything depend on one small feature, the curve of her eyebrows.

real_life_example.event_title: Frida Kahlo paints Diego on My Mind
real_life_example.event: In 1943, a few years after she and Diego Rivera remarried in 1940, Frida Kahlo painted Diego on My Mind (Self-Portrait as Tehuana). She shows herself in a Tehuana headdress of starched lace framing her face, with a small portrait of Rivera placed on her forehead just above her dark, joined eyebrows. The painting is now in the Jacques and Natasha Gelman Collection.
real_life_example.explanation: The work is a famous image of a love so consuming that the beloved occupies the painter's very brow and thoughts.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural dwells on the beloved's brow and eyes as the source of the lover's trouble; Kahlo set her husband's image on her own forehead, between her brows, to show how he filled her mind.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

tamil:
கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேற் கட்படாம் மாதர்
படாஅ முலைமேல் துகில்.
transliteration:
Kadaaak kalitrinmer katpadaam maathar
padaaa mulaimel thukil.
meaning: The cloth over the young woman's chest is like the cloth placed over the eyes of a wild, angry elephant. It holds back a dangerous power.
elementary: At festivals, big temple elephants sometimes wear a decorated cloth over their faces. It looks beautiful, but it also helps keep the elephant calm. The young man thinks the scarf the girl wears works the same way, both lovely and protective.
university: Kadaaak kalitru (கடாஅக் களிறு) is a bull elephant in must (mada), and katpadaam (கட்படாம்) the cloth hung over its face and eyes to keep it from charging. Thukil (துகில்) is fine cloth worn by the maathar (மாதர், young woman). The lengthened forms kadaaa and padaaa are alapedai, vowel extension for metre. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read the comparison as protective: the covering stops her beauty from 'killing' the onlooker, just as the face-cloth restrains the elephant. Pope: 'As veil o'er angry eyes / Of raging elephant that lies, / The silken cincture's folds invest / This maiden's panting breast.' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Bhagavad Gita says that a person of steady wisdom draws the senses back from their objects as a tortoise draws its limbs into its shell.
hinduism.explanation: Restraint is pictured as a protective covering that keeps the senses from being dragged away.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's cloth is also a protective covering that keeps a dangerous force in check.

christianity.quote_or_event: “In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;”
christianity.explanation: Paul's letter recommends modest clothing over showy adornment.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, sees the covering garment as a modest restraint on beauty's power.

islam.quote_or_event: “...and to wrap [a portion of] their headcovers over their chests and not expose their adornment...”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an asks believing women to draw their head-coverings over their chests as a sign of modesty.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's image is of exactly such a covering cloth, which it treats as a restraint on beauty's force.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Rebekah first sees Isaac coming toward her across the field, she takes her veil and covers herself.
judaism.explanation: In Genesis, covering oneself at a first meeting is a sign of modesty and dignity.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's covering cloth likewise marks modesty and calms the power of first sight.
judaism.source: Genesis 24:64-65 (paraphrase; cf. JPS Tanakh on Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Formerly this mind wandered about as it liked, where it wished and according to its pleasure, but now I shall thoroughly master it with wisdom as a mahout controls with his ankus an elephant in rut.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures the untrained mind as an elephant in rut that must be kept in check.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same raging elephant and the means of restraining it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard these well-spoken words of the virtuous lady, he returned to the Law like an elephant driven by the hook.”
jainism.explanation: After Rajimati rebukes him, the monk Rathanemi is brought back under control like an elephant guided by the goad.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural, too, pictures the restraint of a dangerous elephant-like power, which here is the stirred heart.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.46 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The mind is the elephant, the Guru is the elephant-driver, and knowledge is the whip. Wherever the Guru drives the mind, it goes.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Gujri ki Vaar, Guru Amar Das compares the unruly mind to an elephant that obeys only when the Guru, as its driver, controls it with knowledge.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares the cloth on a maiden's bosom to the face-cloth that restrains a raging elephant; Guru Amar Das also uses the restrained elephant, here the mind held in check by the Guru.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 516, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar (salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Aphrodite lends Hera her embroidered band, in which love, desire and persuasive charm are woven, and its power overcomes even Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth imagines a garment that holds the full power of attraction.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's garment holds back the same power that Aphrodite's band releases.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you see an attractive person, you will find that self-restraint is the ability you have against your desire.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that every situation calls out a matching inner power, and attraction calls out self-restraint.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural describes an outward covering that restrains; Epictetus points to the inner one.
philosophy.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 10 (tr. Elizabeth Carter, as revised on classics.mit.edu)

real_life_example.event_title: Draperies are painted over Michelangelo's Last Judgment
real_life_example.event: In 1564, after the Council of Trent, church authorities decided that some figures in Michelangelo's Last Judgment fresco in the Sistine Chapel were improper and should be covered. The work of painting draperies over them was given to Michelangelo's follower Daniele da Volterra, who was nicknamed Il Braghettone, the breeches-maker. Encyclopaedia Britannica dates his commission to 1559 under Pope Paul IV.
real_life_example.explanation: The episode is a well-known example of cloth being added to cover a powerful image whose effect authorities feared.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares a garment over the beloved to the cloth over a raging elephant's face, a covering meant to hold a dangerous power in check; the draperies were added for the same kind of reason.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

tamil:
ஒண்ணுதற் கோஒ உடைந்ததே ஞாட்பினுள்
நண்ணாரும் உட்குமென் பீடு.
transliteration:
Onnuthar koo udainthathe gnaatpinul
nannaarum utkumen peedu.
meaning: Oh no! My strength, which made even my enemies shake on the battlefield, has broken in front of her shining forehead alone.
elementary: Imagine a champion wrestler who has never lost, but who becomes shy and tongue-tied when he meets someone he really admires. The young man is a brave warrior, yet one look at the girl's shining face makes all his toughness melt away.
university: On-nuthal (ஒண்ணுதல்) is a 'bright forehead', a standard metonymy for the heroine. Koo (கோஒ) is an exclamation of dismay lengthened by alapedai. Gnaatpu (ஞாட்பு) is the battlefield, nannaar (நண்ணார்) foes (literally 'those who do not draw near', i.e. are not friends), utkum (உட்கும்) 'fear', and peedu (பீடு) 'valour, prowess'. Mu. Varadarasanar reads: 'my strength, which made even foes fear in battle, has been defeated by her bright forehead'; Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah take nannaar as including those who only heard of his fame. The hero (talaivan) of Tamil akam poetry is ideally a warrior, so the defeat is sharpened. Pope: 'my might, / That awed my foemen in the fight, / By lustre of that beaming brow / Borne down, lies broken now!' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a boat on the water is swept away by a strong wind, even one of the senses on which the mind focuses can carry away a man's intelligence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a single sense the mind fixes on can overpower even a strong person.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's warrior is carried away in exactly this way by a single sight.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.67 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, 1972)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And she made him sleep upon her knees; and she called for a man, and she caused him to shave off the seven locks of his head; and she began to afflict him, and his strength went from him.”
christianity.explanation: Samson, the mightiest warrior of Israel, loses his strength through his love for Delilah.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's hero, a famous warrior's strength is broken through love.

islam.quote_or_event: “She said, ‘That is the one about whom you blamed me. And I certainly sought to seduce him, but he firmly refused...’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents Joseph as the one whose strength of will did not break before attraction.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows a strong man's will breaking; Joseph is the Qur'an's contrasting model of firmness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city.’”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah defines real strength as mastering one's own desires, not defeating enemies.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's warrior beats his foes but cannot master his heart, which is exactly Ben Zoma's point.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a storm throws down a weak tree, so does Mara overpower the man who lives for the pursuit of pleasures, who is uncontrolled in his senses...”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the person whose senses are uncontrolled is knocked down by Mara like a tree in a storm.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's warrior, strong in battle but unguarded in sense, is knocked down in the same way.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When Râgîmatî perceived that Rathanêmi's strength of will was broken, and temptation had got the better of him, she did not lose her presence of mind and defended her Self on that occasion.”
jainism.explanation: The prince and monk Rathanemi sees Rajimati unexpectedly and his strength of will breaks, until she brings him back to his vows.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's 'my might is broken' is told from the inside; the Uttaradhyayana describes the same collapse from outside.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Give up your selfhood, and so obtain your Husband Lord; what other clever tricks are of any use?”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak tells the soul-bride that only giving up her ego wins the Husband Lord, and that no cleverness can take its place.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's warrior, whose strength made enemies tremble, finds his might broken before one girl's bright forehead; Guru Nanak also teaches that pride and strength must give way in love.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 722, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...Eros (Love), fairest among the deathless gods, who unnerves the limbs and overcomes the mind and wise counsels of all gods and all men within them.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod makes Eros the power that defeats the strength and judgment of gods and men alike.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's warrior, whose valour breaks at one sight, is one of Eros's victims.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius opens his poem with Mars, the lord of war, lying in the lap of Venus, defeated by the eternal wound of love and gazing up at her.
philosophy.explanation: The Epicurean philosopher pictures the god of battle conquered by love.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's image on a cosmic scale: martial might surrendering to beauty.

real_life_example.event_title: Napoleon's love letters to Josephine from Italy
real_life_example.event: Napoleon Bonaparte married Josephine de Beauharnais in March 1796 and days later left to command the French army in Italy. While winning battles there, he wrote her frequent, passionate letters begging her to join him and complaining that she rarely wrote back. Josephine preferred to stay in Paris for several months.
real_life_example.explanation: The letters show the general who was conquering Italy as helpless and pleading in love.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's warrior laments that strength which made enemies tremble has broken before one woman's brow; Napoleon, victorious in the field, wrote to Josephine as a man at her mercy.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

tamil:
பிணையேர் மடநோக்கும் நாணும் உடையாட்கு
அணியெவனோ ஏதில தந்து.
transliteration:
Pinaiyer madanokkum naanum udaiyaatku
aniyevano ethila thanthu.
meaning: She already has the gentle look of a deer and a natural shyness. What use are other jewels, which are not part of her, on a girl like her?
elementary: A flower in a garden is already beautiful; you do not need to paint it or stick glitter on it. The young man feels the same about the girl: her kind eyes and shyness are her real jewels, so ordinary jewellery adds nothing.
university: Pinai-er (பிணையேர்) means 'like a doe', mada-nokku (மடநோக்கு) 'an innocent, gentle look', and naanum (நாணும்) 'and modesty'. Naanam (நாணம்) is one of the classical feminine virtues in Tamil poetics, alongside madam (innocence), accham (fear) and payirppu (delicacy). Ethila (ஏதில) is 'alien, unrelated', so other ornaments are foreign to her true beauty. Mu. Varadarasanar asks why one should put unrelated jewels on her; Kalaignar contrasts natural (iyarkai) and artificial (seyarkai) ornaments. Pope: 'Like tender fawn's her eye; / Clothed on is she with modesty; / What added beauty can be lent / By alien ornament?' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Act I of Kalidasa's Shakuntala, King Dushyanta notices that Shakuntala's rough bark garment does not dim her beauty, and reflects that a lovely form is adorned by anything, as a lotus stays lovely though covered with moss.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa makes the point that true beauty needs no costly ornament.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural asks the same question: what can outside ornaments add to natural grace?

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.”
christianity.explanation: Peter teaches that a gentle, quiet spirit is the true ornament, worth more than gold or fine clothes.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, names gentleness and modesty as her real ornaments.

islam.quote_or_event: “O children of Adam, We have bestowed upon you clothing to conceal your private parts and as adornment. But the clothing of righteousness - that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ranks the inner 'clothing' of righteousness above every outward garment and adornment.
islam.tie_back: The Kural ranks inner modesty above outward jewels in the same way.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Grace is deceptive, / Beauty is illusory; / It is for her fear of GOD / That a woman is to be praised.”
judaism.explanation: The poem of the 'woman of valour' places a woman's worth in her character rather than in outward charm.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, values her inner qualities over anything added from outside.
judaism.source: Proverbs 31:30 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Of all the fragrances — sandal, tagara, blue lotus and jasmine — the fragrance of virtue is the sweetest.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ranks virtue above every costly perfume.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks modesty above costly ornaments in the same spirit.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The daughter of the best king, true to self-control and her vows, maintained the honour of her clan and family, and her virtue...”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, praised earlier as beautiful, is finally honoured for her self-control and virtue.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes modesty and virtue a woman's chief adornment.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; excerpt)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Humility is the word, forgiveness is the virtue, and sweet speech is the magic mantra. Wear these three robes, O sister, and you will captivate your Husband Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the soul-bride that humility, forgiveness and sweet speech are the only dress she needs to win her Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use other ornaments are to a girl who already has a doe-like look and natural modesty; Farid likewise says inner virtues, not outward finery, are the bride's true adornment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 127) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod, the gods adorn the first woman, Pandora, with golden necklaces, a crown of flowers and fine clothing, yet her outward splendour hides the trouble she brings.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth sets dazzling outward adornment against what lies within.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural reverses Pandora: her inner qualities are the real beauty and outward ornaments add nothing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We should, therefore, fix our attention on making them sensible that they are valued for the appearance of decent, modest and discreet behavior.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus objects that young women are taught to rely on adornment, and says they should know they are valued for modesty and good conduct.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural, too, says modesty is worth more than any jewel.
philosophy.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 40 (tr. Elizabeth Carter, as revised on classics.mit.edu)

real_life_example.event_title: Marie Curie's plain wedding dress
real_life_example.event: When Marie Sklodowska married Pierre Curie in July 1895, they held a simple civil ceremony with no religious service, and they did not exchange rings. Instead of a white bridal gown she wore a dark blue outfit, chosen so that she could wear it afterwards in the laboratory.
real_life_example.explanation: The wedding is remembered as a sign of the Curies' simplicity and their devotion to each other and to their work.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use ornaments are to one who already has natural grace and modesty; Marie Curie married without a gown or rings and needed neither.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

tamil:
உண்டார்கண் அல்லது அடுநறாக் காமம்போல்
கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல் இன்று.
transliteration:
Undaarkan allathu adunaraak kaamampol
kandaar makizhseydhal indru.
meaning: Strong drink brings joy only to those who drink it. Love is different, because it brings joy even to those who only look.
elementary: A treat only makes you happy once you eat it. But seeing someone you love, like a parent coming home, makes you happy just by looking. The young man says love is special in this way: just seeing her fills him with joy.
university: Undaar (உண்டார்) is 'those who have drunk' and kandaar (கண்டார்) 'those who have seen'; the pairing undaar / kandaar carries the whole comparison. Adu-nara (அடுநறா) is literally 'cooked (boiled, distilled) toddy', i.e. strong drink, and makizh-seythal (மகிழ்செய்தல்) is 'causing delight or intoxication'. Mu. Varadarasanar: toddy intoxicates only those who drink it, not, like kaamam, those who merely see it. The verse closes the chapter by turning the hero's distress into joy, and its praise of love over drink sits easily with the Kural's earlier chapter against intoxicants (Kallunnaamai, ch. 93). Pope: 'The palm-tree's fragrant wine, / To those who taste yields joys divine; / But love hath rare felicity / For those that only see!' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita traces how merely dwelling on what the senses present gives rise to attachment and desire.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural celebrates the fact that mere seeing intoxicates; the Gita analyses the same process as a danger.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.62 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, 1972)

christianity.quote_or_event: “How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices!”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs declares love far more delightful than wine.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same comparison: love outdoes strong drink.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquility in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents love between spouses as a divine sign that brings peace and joy.
islam.tie_back: The Kural praises the joy of love; the Qur'an grounds that joy in God's design.

judaism.quote_or_event: Genesis says that Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him only a few days because of his love for her.
judaism.explanation: Love lets Jacob find delight simply in being near Rachel, even before marriage.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, says love gives joy just by seeing, before anything is 'tasted'.
judaism.source: Genesis 29:20 (paraphrase; cf. JPS Tanakh on Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “...a Sakyan girl — the envy of the countryside — glanced up at me, with her hair half-combed, and said, 'Hurry back, master.' Recollecting that, I don't enjoy leading the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: For Nanda, the memory of one glance is enough to unsettle his whole life as a monk.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says love intoxicates by sight alone; Nanda is intoxicated by the mere memory of a sight.
buddhism.source: Udana 3.2, Nanda Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu; excerpt)

jainism.quote_or_event: “...thus she was seen by Rathanêmi, whose (peace of) mind became (thereby) disturbed...”
jainism.explanation: In the Uttaradhyayana, the monk Rathanemi happens to see Rajimati sheltering from the rain in a cave, and the sight alone throws his mind into turmoil.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says love acts through sight alone; this Jain story shows the same, as a warning.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; excerpt)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Baba, the mind is intoxicated with the Naam, drinking in its Nectar. It remains absorbed in the Lord's Love.”
sikhism.explanation: Speaking to yogis who used intoxicants, Guru Nanak says the true intoxication is the mind drinking in the Naam (divine Name) and staying absorbed in God's love.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says strong drink delights only those who drink it, while love delights even those who merely look; Guru Nanak also sets love above wine, calling love of the Name the truer intoxication.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 360, Raag Asa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Narcissus falls in love simply by looking at a beautiful face in a pool, and cannot tear himself away from the sight.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's myth shows love born and fed entirely through the eyes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural, too, says love can intoxicate by sight alone.
