philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant argued that a judgment of beauty is a 'disinterested' delight: we take pleasure in the beautiful simply in contemplating it, without needing to possess or consume it.
philosophy.explanation: For Kant, beauty pleases in the act of looking, unlike the merely agreeable, which pleases through consumption.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's contrast exactly: drink must be consumed, but beauty delights the one who only sees.

real_life_example.event_title: Shah Jahan builds the Taj Mahal for Mumtaz Mahal
real_life_example.event: After his wife Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan ordered a great white marble mausoleum built in her memory at Agra. Construction ran from 1631 to 1648, and both of them are buried there. UNESCO, which listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1983, calls it one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage.
real_life_example.explanation: The Taj Mahal is the world's best-known monument to love, admired by people who never knew the couple.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says love, unlike strong drink, delights even those who only look; the love behind the Taj Mahal still moves the countless visitors who simply look at it.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

tamil:
இருநோக்கு இவளுண்கண் உள்ளது ஒருநோக்கு
நோய்நோக்கொன் றந்நோய் மருந்து.
transliteration:
Irunokku ivalunkan ulladhu orunokku
noinokkon randhnoi marundhu.
meaning: Her dark-lined eyes have two kinds of look. One look gives me the ache of love, and the other is the cure for that ache.
elementary: Think of a new classmate who is very shy. When she looks at you, you feel all fluttery and nervous inside. But when she looks again and gives a small friendly smile, the nervous feeling goes away. The same eyes made the worry and then made it better.
university: Chapter 110 opens the second stage of the kalaviyal (the section on secret, premarital love): after the first sight of ch. 109 (Takaiyananguruttal), the hero now reads the heroine’s kurippu (குறிப்பு, ‘sign, inward intention’) for proof that his love is returned. The chapter shares its title with ch. 71 of Porutpal, where kurippu arithal means reading a king’s mind, so the same art of reading the face is moved from the court to love. Unkan (உண்கண்) means eyes that have ‘eaten’ collyrium (mai), that is, kohl-darkened eyes, and every gloss on both source sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) reads the two looks as a nōy nōkku (நோய் நோக்கு, the look that causes love-sickness) and a remedy-look; in the line of Parimelazhagar the second look is her answering sign of consent, which ends his uncertainty. Pope renders: ‘A double witchery have glances of her liquid eye; / One glance is glance that brings me pain; the other heals again.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A remedy is being applied and it will soon be better. It is plain, sir, that you and she love each other.”
hinduism.explanation: When King Dushyanta asks whether Shakuntala’s illness is dangerous, her friend Priyamvada smiles and tells him the cure is already at hand, because the sickness is love for him.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the one who caused the love-sickness is also its medicine.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song of Songs begs the beloved to look away because her gaze overwhelms him.
christianity.tie_back: The beloved’s eyes have the same power to wound the lover that the Kural’s first look has.

islam.quote_or_event: “He has impassioned her with love.”
islam.explanation: The women of the city say that the sight of Joseph has filled the wife of al-Aziz with a love she cannot master.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an too knows that the mere sight of a person can strike the heart with love like an illness, though it judges this love as error.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Stay ye me with dainties, refresh me with apples; For I am love-sick.”
judaism.explanation: The maiden in the Song of Songs says she is sick with love and asks to be revived.
judaism.tie_back: Love as a sickness that longs for its own remedy is the image at the heart of the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that affection itself breeds sorrow and fear, and that freedom from it ends both.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees that love brings an ache, but it finds the cure in letting go of attachment rather than in the beloved’s second look.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mind of those who always live in unfrequented lodgings, who eat low food, and who subdue their senses, will not be attacked by the foe, Love, who is vanquished as disease is by medicine.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira’s teaching calls love an enemy that can be beaten the way medicine beats a disease, by self-restraint.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism also speaks of love as a sickness with a medicine, but its medicine is restraint of the senses, not the beloved’s answering look.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Suffering is the medicine, and pleasure the disease, because where there is pleasure, there is no desire for God.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak turns the usual order around: the pain that makes the soul long for God is its cure, while comfort that makes it forget Him is the real sickness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's beloved has one look that wounds and another that heals; Guru Nanak likewise sees the ache of longing and its cure as bound together, with the pain itself leading to the remedy.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “From whose eyes as they glanced flowed love that unnerves the limbs: and beautiful is their glance beneath their brows.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says that love pours from the glances of the Graces and weakens whoever receives it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hesiod places the source of love’s power in a glance of the eyes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus Socrates describes the lover’s soul as aching and stinging when apart from the beloved, and finding relief from its pangs as soon as it looks on the beloved’s beauty again.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the sight of the beloved both causes the soul’s agony of longing and soothes it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s double look: the same beauty gives the pain and the cure.

real_life_example.event_title: Ernest Hemingway and the nurse Agnes von Kurowsky
real_life_example.place: Milan, Italy, and Oak Park, Illinois, United States
real_life_example.event: After the young Ernest Hemingway was wounded on the Italian front in July 1918, he was treated at the American Red Cross hospital in Milan, where he fell in love with the nurse Agnes von Kurowsky. They exchanged daily notes and became engaged. In March 1919, after he had returned home to Oak Park, she ended the engagement by letter, and the rejection hurt him deeply.
real_life_example.explanation: The romance stayed with Hemingway and fed into his later fiction, including A Very Short Story and A Farewell to Arms.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says one look of the beloved brings the ache of love and another is its medicine; for Hemingway the same woman was the nurse who cared for him and the source of his heartache.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

tamil:
கண்களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம் காமத்தில்
செம்பாகம் அன்று பெரிது.
transliteration:
Kankalavu kollum sirunokkam kaamaththil
sempaakam andru peridhu.
meaning: The quick look she steals at me when I am not looking is not just half of love's joy. It is more than half.
elementary: Have you ever caught a friend secretly peeking at the drawing you were making, and then looking away? That tiny peek tells you they really like it, maybe even more than if they had said so out loud. A small secret look can say a lot.
university: Kan kalavu kollum (கண் களவு கொள்ளும்) is literally ‘the eye that steals’: a look taken by stealth (kalavu, the same word that names the whole kalavu, or secret-love, phase). Ciru nōkkam (சிறுநோக்கம்) is the brief, narrowed glance, which Puliyur Kesikan glosses as arukiya nōkkam, a sparing look cast without his knowledge. Sempākam (செம்பாகம்) means ‘exact half’; the commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar: nērpāti anru, atai vida periya pakuti) agree the stolen glance is greater than half of kāmam, the joy of union, because it reveals that his love is returned. Pope: ‘The furtive glance, that gleams one instant bright, / Is more than half of love’s supreme delight.’ No textual variants appear on the two source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “(She casts a lingering glance at the king, and goes out with her two friends.)”
hinduism.explanation: As Shakuntala leaves her first meeting with King Dushyanta, she makes an excuse to linger and looks back at him.
hinduism.tie_back: Her lingering backward look is exactly the kind of small, stolen sign the Kural says is worth more than half of love.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I, stage direction (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes.”
christianity.explanation: The lover says a single glance from the beloved has captured his heart.
christianity.tie_back: One look accomplishes almost everything, which is the Kural’s claim about the brief stolen glance.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not give a second look, Ali, (because) while you are not to blame for the first, you have no right to the second.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Ali that an unplanned first glance carries no blame, but he must not follow it with a deliberate second look.
islam.tie_back: Islam, like the Kural, treats a single glance as weighty, but it counsels restraint where the Kural celebrates the glance between future spouses.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 2149 (graded hasan by al-Albani)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Young man, please lift up your eyes and see what you choose for yourself for a wife.”
judaism.explanation: On the joyous fifteenth of Av, the daughters of Jerusalem danced in the vineyards and invited young men to look and choose a bride.
judaism.tie_back: The Mishnah gives the glance a real place at the start of courtship, as the Kural does.
judaism.source: Mishnah Ta’anit 4:8 (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Lord, as I was leaving home, a Sakyan girl–the envy of the countryside–glanced up at me, with her hair half-combed, and said, ‘Hurry back, master.’”
buddhism.explanation: Nanda tells the Buddha he cannot keep up the monk’s life because he keeps remembering the glance of the girl he left behind.
buddhism.tie_back: One brief glance outweighed everything else for Nanda, just as the Kural says the small stolen look is more than half of love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira warns that being captured by what the eye sees leads to ruin, like a moth drawn into a flame.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism agrees with the Kural that what the eye catches can seize the whole heart, but it sees this as danger rather than delight.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He is so beautiful to my eyes; beholding Him, I have been bewitched.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Asa, Guru Arjan speaks as the bride-soul who has only to see her Lord to be completely captivated.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says even a stolen glance is more than half of love's joy; Guru Arjan likewise makes a single sight of the Beloved enough to captivate the soul.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 397, Raag Asa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And the maiden looked at him with stealthy glance, holding her bright veil aside, her heart smouldering with pain.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Medea, struck by love for Jason, watches him leave her father’s hall with a secret look from behind her veil.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s kan kalavu, the eye that steals a look, almost word for word.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.444-446 (tr. R. C. Seaton, 1912)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says that goodwill is the beginning of friendship in the way that the pleasure of the eye is the beginning of love, since no one falls in love without first being delighted by the beloved’s appearance.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, love begins with the pleasure of seeing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural goes further, saying that one glance is already more than half of love.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.5, 1167a (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Clara Wieck and Robert Schumann's secret engagement
real_life_example.event: The pianist Clara Wieck and the composer Robert Schumann fell in love, but her father, Friedrich Wieck, forbade contact when she was sixteen and refused Robert's formal request to marry her. The couple kept their engagement secret and finally took the matter to court, which granted permission in 1840. They married on 12 September 1840.
real_life_example.explanation: Their love, carried on in secret against fierce opposition, became one of the best-known partnerships in the history of music.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural prizes the glance a lover steals when no one is looking; for years Clara and Robert's love could live only in such hidden moments and secret contact.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

tamil:
நோக்கினாள் நோக்கி இறைஞ்சினாள் அஃதவள்
யாப்பினுள் அட்டிய நீர்.
transliteration:
Nokkinaal nokki irainjinaal aqdhaval
yaappinul attiya neer.
meaning: She looked at me, and after looking, she lowered her head. That was like water poured on the growing plant of our love.
elementary: Imagine planting a seed with a friend. Every time you water it, it grows a little. When someone shyly looks at you and then looks down with a little smile, it is like giving water to the seed of a new friendship.
university: Iraiñcināḷ (இறைஞ்சினாள்) means ‘she bowed, lowered her head’, the classic sign of nāṇam (நாணம், maidenly modesty) that the hero reads as consent. The key image is yāppu (யாப்பு), which the commentators take as the bond or bed of love: Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as the love she is nurturing, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as the ‘crop’ (payir) of love, and Puliyur Kesikan as the anpup-payir watered by her sign. Aṭṭiya nīr (அட்டிய நீர்) is water poured into a channel or plot, an agricultural metaphor in keeping with the marutam landscape of settled love. Pope: ‘She looked, and looking drooped her head: / On springing shoot of love ’tis water shed!’ The text is the same on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “(SHAKUNTALA darts a glance at him, then looks down.)”
hinduism.explanation: In Act III, when the king speaks tenderly to her, Shakuntala glances at him and then lowers her eyes.
hinduism.tie_back: The glance followed by the lowered head is exactly the sequence the Kural describes as watering love.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III, stage direction (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.”
christianity.explanation: The lover calls the shy beloved, hidden like a dove, to show her face.
christianity.tie_back: The beloved’s shy hiding, which only deepens the lover’s longing, is close to the Kural’s modest bowed head.

islam.quote_or_event: “Then one of the two women came to him walking with shyness.”
islam.explanation: The daughter of the old man of Midian approaches Moses with modesty, and the meeting leads to their marriage.
islam.tie_back: Her shyness on meeting Moses is the same nāṇam that the Kural reads as a hopeful sign of love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Raising her eyes, Rebekah saw Isaac. She alighted from the camel and said to the servant, ‘Who is that man walking in the field toward us?’ And the servant said, ‘That is my master.’ So she took her veil and covered herself.”
judaism.explanation: Rebekah lifts her eyes, sees her future husband, and then modestly covers herself with her veil.
judaism.tie_back: She looks, then veils herself: the same pairing of a glance and modest withdrawal that the Kural describes.
judaism.source: Genesis 24:64-65 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Buddhist story of the past life of Gotama, the young ascetic Sumedha meets the maiden Sumitta, who gives him lotuses for the Buddha Dipankara on condition that she may be his companion in future lives.
buddhism.explanation: Their bond begins in one small exchange at a meeting and grows across lifetimes.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s watered shoot, a single modest gesture becomes the seed of a lasting love.
buddhism.source: Jataka Nidanakatha (story of Sumedha and Dipankara)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the crane is produced from an egg, and the egg is produced from a crane, so they call desire the origin of delusion, and delusion the origin of desire.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain scripture says that desire and delusion keep feeding each other in a cycle.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism sees the same self-feeding growth the Kural praises in watered love, but it judges it as a cycle to be broken.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make your mind the farmer, good deeds the farm, modesty the water, and your body the field.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak describes the spiritual life as a farm, with saram (modesty, or by another reading, effort) as the water that makes the crop of Naam grow.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the girl's modest bowing of the head is water poured on the young plant of love; Guru Nanak too names modesty as the water that makes a crop grow.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And ever she kept darting bright glances straight up at Aeson’s son, and within her breast her heart panted fast through anguish, all remembrance left her, and her soul melted with the sweet pain.”
greek_mythology.explanation: After Eros’ arrow strikes her, Medea keeps glancing at Jason as love takes root in her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Her repeated glances show love taking hold and growing, as the Kural’s watered shoot does.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.286-289 (tr. R. C. Seaton, 1912)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal compares the growth of love to a bare branch left in a Salzburg salt mine, which comes out covered in sparkling crystals; each small sign from the beloved adds new crystals to the lover’s idea of her.
philosophy.explanation: His theory of ‘crystallization’ explains how love grows from small signs and impressions.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s image of a look as water on a young plant describes the same growth of love from a small sign.
philosophy.source: Stendhal, On Love (De l’amour, 1822), Book I, ch. 2

real_life_example.event_title: Queen Victoria proposes to Prince Albert
real_life_example.event: Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha arrived at Windsor in October 1839, and five days later, on 15 October, Queen Victoria proposed to him. As the reigning monarch she could not traditionally be proposed to, so she had to take the first step. They married at the Chapel Royal, St James's Palace, on 10 February 1840.
real_life_example.explanation: Their marriage became one of the most famous royal love matches, and Victoria's journal records her joy at being loved.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes the moment the beloved shows her consent, which waters the growing plant of love; Victoria herself gave that sign, and the courtship at once became a marriage.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

tamil:
யான்நோக்கும் காலை நிலன்நோக்கும் நோக்காக்கால்
தான்நோக்கி மெல்ல நகும்.
transliteration:
Yaannokkum kaalai nilannokkum nokkaakkaal
thaannokki mella nagum.
meaning: When I look at her, she looks at the ground. When I do not look, she looks at me and smiles softly to herself.
elementary: Picture a shy kid in class. Whenever you turn to look, they quickly stare at their desk. But when you turn back to your book, you can feel them peeking at you with a small smile. That little game means they want to be your friend.
university: The couplet builds on a chiastic play of nōkku (நோக்கு, ‘look’): yān nōkkum kālai (when I look) she looks at nilan (நிலன், the ground); nōkkākkāl (when I do not look) she looks and mella nakum (மெல்ல நகும், smiles gently). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take nakum as smiling or rejoicing to herself, and Kalaignar adds that this is a sign announcing her love. Commentators in the Parimelazhagar tradition treat the lowered gaze as nāṇam and the secret smile as the kurippu of consent. Pope: ‘I look on her: her eyes are on the ground the while: / I look away: she looks on me with timid smile.’ The two source sites agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When I was near, she could not look at me; / She smiled–but not to me–and half denied it.”
hinduism.explanation: King Dushyanta tells his friend how the shy Shakuntala avoided his eyes yet smiled in a way that half gave her away.
hinduism.tie_back: Avoiding his gaze while smiling is precisely the Kural’s picture of the beloved who looks down when watched and smiles when unwatched.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act II (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved peers through the window lattice, watching while only half seen.
christianity.tie_back: Looking at the other from hiding is the game the Kural describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “And with them will be women limiting [their] glances, with large, [beautiful] eyes.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the modest companions of paradise for restraining their gaze.
islam.tie_back: Lowered and restrained eyes as a mark of modesty is the same virtue the Kural sees in the beloved who looks at the ground.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then she fell on her face, and bowed down to the ground, and said unto him: ‘Why have I found favour in thy sight, that thou shouldest take cognizance of me, seeing I am a foreigner?’”
judaism.explanation: Ruth bows to the ground before Boaz, wondering why he has noticed her kindly.
judaism.tie_back: Ruth lowers her eyes to the ground when Boaz notices her, and their story too ends in marriage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that two bright qualities protect the world: hiri (a sense of shame) and ottappa (moral dread), without which people would not know any restraint.
buddhism.explanation: Modesty is honored in Buddhism as one of the guardians of the moral life.
buddhism.tie_back: The beloved’s lowered eyes show the same hiri the Buddha praises, even if the Kural’s setting is romantic.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Not to look at, nor to long for, not to think of, nor to praise, womankind: this is becoming the meditation of the noble ones.”
jainism.explanation: For the Jain monk, keeping the eyes from looking at women is part of the discipline of chastity.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism also values the downcast eye, but as a monk’s renunciation, not as a shy sign of love.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He watches over all, but none see Him. How wonderful this is!”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak marvels that God looks on every creature while remaining unseen by them.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the girl looks at the lover only when he is not looking; Guru Nanak's wonder is a Lord who always looks on us while we fail to see Him.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7, Japji Sahib (pauri 30), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And now both were fixing their eyes on the ground abashed, and again were throwing glances at each other, smiling with the light of love beneath their radiant brows.”
greek_mythology.explanation: At their secret meeting Medea and Jason look down in shyness, then steal smiling looks at each other.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Eyes on the ground, then a smiling glance: this is the Kural’s scene almost exactly.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.1022-1024 (tr. R. C. Seaton, 1912)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle, discussing shame, cites the proverb that shame dwells in the eyes, which is why people feel it most before those who look at them.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, shame shows itself in how we meet or avoid another’s gaze.
philosophy.tie_back: The beloved who drops her eyes when looked at shows exactly this shame-in-the-eyes.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric II.6, 1384a (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)

real_life_example.event_title: Alexander Graham Bell and Mabel Hubbard
real_life_example.place: Boston and Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States
real_life_example.event: Mabel Hubbard, who had been left deaf by scarlet fever at the age of five and had learned to lip-read, met Alexander Graham Bell in 1873 when she came to him to improve her speech. Her journal records that at first she both did and did not like him. Her feelings grew into admiration and love; they became engaged in 1875 and married on 11 July 1877 in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
real_life_example.explanation: Their long marriage, carried on through speech, lip-reading and letters, was a lifelong partnership.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural pictures a young woman whose love shows only in shy, hidden ways at first; Mabel's early mixed feelings slowly gave way to open love.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

tamil:
குறிக்கொண்டு நோக்காமை அல்லால் ஒருகண்
சிறக்கணித்தாள் போல நகும்.
transliteration:
Kurikkondu nokkaamai allaal orukan
sirakkaniththaal poala nagum.
meaning: She does not look straight at me. Yet she glances sideways, as if narrowing one eye, and smiles to herself.
elementary: Sometimes a friend pretends not to watch you, but you catch them looking out of the corner of their eye with a little grin. They are not really ignoring you; they are just being shy and playful.
university: Kuṟikkoṇṭu nōkkāmai (குறிக்கொண்டு நோக்காமை) is ‘not looking with a fixed aim’, that is, avoiding a direct gaze. The difficult word ciṟakkaṇittāḷ (சிறக்கணித்தாள்) is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as ‘narrowing one eye’ (oru kaṇṇaic curukki), while Puliyur Kesikan takes it as tilting one eye to one side; Pope’s ‘smiling side-long glance’ follows the second sense, and the explanatory gloss on ytamizh renders it as looking ‘with a half-closed eye’. Either way the commentators read the sidelong smile as a kurippu that she returns his love while seeming not to. The Tamil is the same on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Her glance was loving–but ’twas not for me; / Her step was slow–’twas grace, not coquetry.”
hinduism.explanation: The king tries to talk himself out of reading Shakuntala’s side glances as love, then admits that a lover reads every sign in his own favor.
hinduism.tie_back: The puzzle of whether an indirect glance means love is exactly the puzzle the Kural answers.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act II (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not: The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid.”
christianity.explanation: The sage confesses that the hidden ways of love between a man and a woman are beyond his understanding.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s half-closed-eye smile is one of those mysterious ‘ways’ that only lovers can read.

islam.quote_or_event: “In them are women limiting [their] glances.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the companions of paradise as women who keep their gaze restrained.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved likewise does not look straight at her lover, though her restraint hides a smile.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; Thine eyes are as doves behind thy veil.”
judaism.explanation: The lover praises the beloved’s eyes glimpsed half-hidden behind her veil.
judaism.tie_back: Eyes that look out half-hidden recall the Kural’s narrowed, sidelong glance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Zen tradition’s Flower Sermon, the Buddha silently holds up a flower; only Mahakashyapa understands and answers with a smile, and the Buddha says the true teaching has passed to him.
buddhism.explanation: A wordless smile is shown as the sign of perfect understanding between two people.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a quiet smile carries a meaning that words do not.
buddhism.source: Wumenguan (The Gateless Gate), case 6, ‘The Buddha Holds Up a Flower’

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Sramana, engaged in penance, should not allow himself to watch the shape, beauty, coquetry, laughter, prattle, gestures, and glances of women, nor retain a recollection of them in his mind.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk is told not to dwell on the playful glances and laughter that the Kural celebrates.
jainism.tie_back: Jain scripture names the same playful glance and laughter as the Kural, but as things a renunciant must not watch.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Truth does not remain hidden, even though one may try to hide it.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Gauri, Guru Amar Das says that the divine light within a person shows itself even when he tries to keep it concealed.
sikhism.tie_back: The girl in the Kural will not look straight at her lover, yet her sidelong smile gives her away; Guru Amar Das says what is truly within cannot stay hidden.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 232, Raag Gauri, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “This honour she has from the beginning, and this is the portion allotted to her amongst men and undying gods, – the whisperings of maidens and smiles and deceits with sweet delight and love and graciousness.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod assigns to Aphrodite the realm of maidens’ whispers, smiles and playful deceits.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s sly half-smile, pretending not to look, belongs to exactly this province of Aphrodite.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Diotima describes Eros as bold and resourceful, a clever hunter always weaving some scheme to win what is beautiful.
philosophy.explanation: Love, for Diotima, works by stratagem and indirection.
philosophy.tie_back: The beloved’s pretended indifference with a sidelong smile is one of love’s small stratagems.

real_life_example.event_title: Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa and her famous smile
real_life_example.place: Florence, Italy (now in the Louvre, Paris)
real_life_example.event: Leonardo da Vinci began the portrait known as the Mona Lisa in Florence around 1503 and worked on it for years. The sitter is traditionally identified as Lisa Gherardini, wife of the merchant Francesco del Giocondo. Her slight, enigmatic smile, painted with soft sfumato shading, has fascinated viewers for centuries.
real_life_example.explanation: The quiet, half-hidden smile has made it probably the most famous painting in the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes a girl who does not look straight at her lover yet smiles quietly to herself; the Mona Lisa's restrained, private smile is the best-known image of such a look.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

tamil:
உறாஅ தவர்போல் சொலினும் செறாஅர்சொல்
ஒல்லை உணரப் படும்.
transliteration:
Uraaa thavarpol solinum seraaarsol
ollai unarap padum.
meaning: Even when people who feel no anger speak as if they were strangers, the true meaning of their words is quickly understood.
elementary: Sometimes a friend says, ‘I don’t care, go away!’ but they are smiling and not really cross. You can tell right away they are only pretending. Kind people cannot hide their kindness for long.
university: Uṟāatavar (உறாஅதவர்) and ceṟāar (செறாஅர்) both carry the long-vowel extension (alapeṭai) used for metre: ‘those who are not intimate’ and ‘those who are not angry’. Ollai (ஒல்லை) means ‘quickly’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses: though they speak outwardly like strangers without affection, the words of those with no enmity within are soon recognised; Solomon Pappaiah sets the scene with her reply ‘who are you?’ to his approach, and Kalaignar says the love she hides behind harsh words soon shows through. Puliyur Kesikan reads that the result (payan) of such words is soon felt. Pope: ‘Though with their lips affection they disown, / Yet, when they hate us not, ’tis quickly known.’ No variants on the two source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “She would not show her love for modesty, / Yet did not try so very hard to hide it.”
hinduism.explanation: King Dushyanta notes that Shakuntala hid her love out of modesty, but not so well that he could not see it.
hinduism.tie_back: Love that is outwardly hidden but quickly recognised is the Kural’s exact claim.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act II (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you.”
christianity.explanation: Paul explains that his severe letter came from love, not from a wish to hurt.
christianity.tie_back: Words that sound hard but carry no enmity, and whose love is soon understood, are what the Kural describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “I know when you are pleased with me or angry with me.” I said, “Whence do you know that?” He said, “When you are pleased with me, you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Muhammad,’ but when you are angry with me, then you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Abraham.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Aisha he can read her mood from the small way she words her oath, and she answers that even when cross she leaves only his name, not her love.
islam.tie_back: A spouse’s affection is read through the very words of a mock quarrel, as the Kural says it soon is.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; But the kisses of an enemy are importunate.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that hard treatment from a friend is trustworthy, while an enemy’s show of affection is false.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that harsh-sounding words from one who bears no anger are recognised for what they are.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It’s through living together that a person’s virtue may be known, and then only after a long period, not a short period; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a person’s true character is known only through long, attentive acquaintance.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees that the inner heart can be read beneath appearances, though it says this takes long attention where the Kural says love is read quickly.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.192, Thana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard these well-spoken words of the virtuous lady, he returned to the Law like an elephant driven by the hook.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati rebukes Rathanemi sharply, and he at once understands that her stern words were meant for his good.
jainism.tie_back: Severe words spoken without hatred are quickly understood, as the Kural says, though here they turn a man back to his vows rather than toward love.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.46 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without being spoken, without being told, You know all, O Searcher of hearts.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Saarang, Guru Arjan says God, the Antarjami or knower of hearts, understands what is within a person without any words being needed.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even when the beloved speaks like a stranger, the true feeling behind the words is quickly understood; Guru Arjan's Lord reads the heart directly, whatever the words.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1228, Raag Saarang, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Nausicaa asks her father for a wagon to wash clothes, too shy to speak of marriage, but Alcinous understands everything she has left unsaid and grants her request.
greek_mythology.explanation: A father reads his daughter’s unspoken wish beneath her ordinary words.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the scene shows a hidden heart being understood at once through plain-sounding words.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There is no disguise which can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.”
philosophy.explanation: La Rochefoucauld observes that real love always shows through any attempt to hide it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s point: love behind stranger-like words is soon found out.
philosophy.source: La Rochefoucauld, Maxims 70 (tr. J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell)

real_life_example.event_title: Robert Browning's first letter to Elizabeth Barrett
real_life_example.event: Elizabeth Barrett, an admired poet who was very ill and mostly confined to her room at 50 Wimpole Street, had praised Robert Browning's work. On 10 January 1845 Browning, who had never met her, wrote to tell her that he loved her verses with all his heart. They first met on 20 May 1845, and on 12 September 1846 they married at St Marylebone Church.
real_life_example.explanation: Their correspondence, begun between strangers, became one of the great love stories of English literature.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even when people speak as if they were strangers, their real meaning is quickly understood; a letter from one stranger to another carried a meaning both soon recognised as love.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

tamil:
செறாஅச் சிறுசொல்லும் செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும்
உறாஅர்போன்று உற்றார் குறிப்பு.
transliteration:
Seraaach chirusollum setraarpol nokkum
uraaarpondru utraar kurippu.
meaning: Little harsh words that hold no anger, and looks like an enemy's, are signs of people who love each other while acting like strangers.
elementary: Have you ever seen two best friends tease each other, saying ‘You’re so annoying!’ while grinning? Their pretend-grumpy faces are really a sign of how close they are. Sometimes people who like each other act as if they don’t.
university: The couplet balances ceṟāac ciṟucol (செறாஅச் சிறுசொல், ‘little words that are not angry’) against ceṟṟār pōl nōkku (செற்றார்போல் நோக்கு, ‘a look like that of enemies’), and names both the kuṟippu of uṟṟār (உற்றார், intimates, lovers) who behave uṟāar pōnṟu (like those not intimate). Mu. Varadarasanar reads ciṟucol as kaṭuñcol, harsh words that hold no hostility; Kalaignar speaks of lovers ‘acting’ like strangers outwardly while loving within; Solomon Pappaiah frames it as the hero now understanding her earlier coldness. The couplet completes the thought of 1096 by naming the signs. Pope: ‘The slighting words that anger feign, while eyes their love reveal, / Are signs of those that love, but would their love conceal.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Shakuntala (to herself): “I would never leave him if I could help myself.” … Shakuntala (aloud): “I am not your servant any longer. I will go when I like.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala speaks sharply and threatens to leave, while privately admitting she cannot bear to go from the king’s presence.
hinduism.tie_back: Her cross words that hide affection are the Kural’s ‘little words without anger’ of a lover acting aloof.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews teaches that God’s correction, though painful, is a sign of his love.
christianity.tie_back: Sternness that is really a sign of love is the Kural’s point, transposed from lovers to God and his children.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if We willed, We could show them to you, and you would know them by their mark; but you will surely know them by the tone of [their] speech.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says the Prophet would recognise people’s true inner state from the tone of their speech, whatever they say outwardly.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too says the inner heart is read from tone and look rather than from the literal words.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Joseph saw his brethren, and he knew them, but made himself strange unto them, and spoke roughly with them.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph recognises his brothers but treats them like strangers and speaks harshly, though he loves them and later weeps over them.
judaism.tie_back: Acting like a stranger and speaking roughly while loving within is exactly the Kural’s ‘intimates who seem like strangers’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Abhayarajakumara Sutta the Buddha says he will speak even unwelcome and disagreeable words if they are true and beneficial, comparing himself to a nurse who pulls a dangerous object from a baby’s throat even if it draws blood, out of compassion.
buddhism.explanation: Harsh-sounding speech can come from compassion rather than ill will.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s angerless sharp words, the Buddha’s hard words carry no hostility.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I am the daughter of the Bhoga-king, and you are an Andhakavrishni; being born in a noble family let us not become like Gandhana-snakes; firmly practise self-control!”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati speaks sternly to Rathanemi, not from hatred but to recall him to his vows.
jainism.tie_back: Her severe words without enmity resemble the Kural’s angerless sharp words, though their purpose is renunciation, not love.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.43 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “his father teaches him, and scolds him so many times, but still, he hugs him close in his embrace.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan compares God to a father whose child keeps making mistakes: he scolds the child many times, yet his scolding hides no anger, and he takes the child back into his arms.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural reads sharp words that hold no anger as a sign of hidden love; Guru Arjan's father likewise speaks harshly while his heart stays loving.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 624, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus at last stands before Penelope, she treats him coolly as if he were a stranger, and Telemachus rebukes her hard heart; she answers that if he is truly Odysseus they will know each other by secret signs known only to the two of them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope’s apparent coldness hides a deep love that is waiting for its sign.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A beloved who acts like a stranger while loving within is the Kural’s exact picture.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch argues that a true friend’s frankness may sting like medicine while a flatterer’s sweetness harms, so the harshness of a friend should be read by its intent, not its surface.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch teaches how to tell real affection behind sharp words from false affection behind sweet ones.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly says that sharp words without anger are a sign of real closeness.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend

real_life_example.event_title: John Adams lists Abigail Smith's faults
real_life_example.place: Braintree and Weymouth, Massachusetts, British America
real_life_example.event: During their courtship, John Adams, signing himself Lysander, wrote to Abigail Smith listing her supposed faults in a mock-serious voice: she did not play cards, had never learned to sing, sat with her legs crossed, and walked with her toes turned in. Abigail, signing herself Diana, replied two days later in the same teasing spirit, accepting some faults and rejecting others. They married in October 1764.
real_life_example.explanation: The exchange shows the playful affection that ran through one of the most famous marriages in American history.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says small sharp words with no anger in them are a sign of hidden love; John's list of faults and Abigail's witty reply were exactly that.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

tamil:
அசையியற்கு உண்டாண்டோர் ஏஎர்யான் நோக்கப்
பசையினள் பைய நகும்.
transliteration:
Asaiyiyarku undaandor eeryaan nokkap
pasaiyinal paiya nagum.
meaning: When I look at her, pleading, she softens and smiles gently. At that moment this delicate girl looks especially lovely.
elementary: When you look at someone with a hopeful, friendly face, and their serious look melts into a soft smile, it feels wonderful. That smile is a sign they are happy to be your friend.
university: Asaiyiyal (அசையியல்) is ‘she whose nature sways’, a soft, delicate girl; ēer (ஏஎர், ēr with alapeṭai) means beauty or grace, and āṇṭu (ஆண்டு) ‘then, there’. Pasaiyinaḷ (பசையினள்) is ‘she who has softened, become tender’. The commentators differ on ēer: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as a new beauty she has at that moment; Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan read the line as saying there is a sign (kuṟippu) or token of goodness in her smile; Kesikan also understands yān nōkka as ‘when I looked as if begging’. The ytamizh Sivayogi gloss reads differently again, showing real interpretive variety in this couplet. Pope: ‘I gaze, the tender maid relents the while; / And, oh the matchless grace of that soft smile!’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Shakuntala (to herself): “Oh, why do I have such feelings when I see this man? They seem wrong in a hermitage.”
hinduism.explanation: At her first sight of the king, Shakuntala feels her heart soften toward him and wonders at it.
hinduism.tie_back: Her heart softening at his look is the inner side of the Kural’s gentle, relenting smile.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then was I in his eyes as one that found favour.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved in the Song says that in her lover’s eyes she has found favour.
christianity.tie_back: Finding favour in the other’s eyes is the moment of mutual grace the Kural captures in the softened smile.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquility in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names the affection and tenderness placed between spouses as one of God’s signs.
islam.tie_back: The softening tenderness (pasai) of the Kural’s beloved is the ‘affection and mercy’ the verse praises.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it was so, when the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, that she obtained favour in his sight; and the king held out to Esther the golden sceptre that was in his hand.”
judaism.explanation: When Esther appears before the king, his look softens and he extends his sceptre to her.
judaism.tie_back: A look that brings about a relenting, gracious response is the turn the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha says a husband should honour his wife by courtesy and by not despising her, and that a wife who is so treated cares for him with love in return.
buddhism.explanation: Kindness offered is answered by kindness returned between partners.
buddhism.tie_back: The beloved’s softening in answer to his tender look is a small instance of this mutual courtesy.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching says it is our own attachment, not the object, that stirs our emotions.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism would trace the delight the lover finds in her smile to his own attachment, offering a sober counterpoint to the Kural.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.101 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Renouncing selfishness and conceit, I seek His Sanctuary, and speak sweet words to Him.”
sikhism.explanation: In Barah Maha in Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan describes the soul-bride humbly pleading with her Husband Lord in the hope that He will turn to her with kindness.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the lover looks at the girl imploringly and she softens and smiles; Guru Arjan's bride also pleads humbly and hopes the Beloved will soften toward her.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 136, Raag Maajh, Barah Maha, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Thus he spake, honouring her; and she cast her eyes down with a smile divinely sweet; and her soul melted within her, uplifted by his praise.”
greek_mythology.explanation: After Jason pleads with Medea as a suppliant, she looks down, smiles sweetly and melts toward him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A pleading look answered by a softened, gentle smile is the Kural’s scene exactly.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.1008-1010 (tr. R. C. Seaton, 1912)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates says the beloved, receiving the lover’s devoted gaze, comes to feel a returning love (anteros), an image of love reflected back, though he hardly knows what it is.
philosophy.explanation: Love given through the eyes calls forth love in return.
philosophy.tie_back: The beloved’s softening smile under the lover’s gaze is this returning love made visible.

real_life_example.event_title: Mark Twain courts Olivia Langdon
real_life_example.event: Samuel Clemens (Mark Twain) proposed to Olivia Langdon in 1868, soon after meeting her, and she refused. He kept writing to her for about seventeen months, sending more than 180 letters, and kept visiting Elmira. They became engaged in February 1869 and married at the Langdon home in Elmira on 2 February 1870.
real_life_example.explanation: Their marriage lasted until Olivia's death and was central to Twain's life and work.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's lover looks at his beloved imploringly until she softens; Twain's long, pleading courtship slowly turned Olivia's refusal into acceptance.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

tamil:
ஏதிலார் போலப் பொதுநோக்கு நோக்குதல்
காதலார் கண்ணே உள.
transliteration:
Edhilaar polap podhunokku nokkudhal
kaadhalaar kanne ula.
meaning: Looking at each other with a plain, ordinary look, as if they were strangers, is a habit found only among people in love.
elementary: Two good friends might act normal in front of everyone, as if they hardly know each other, but they still understand each other perfectly. Only close friends can play that ‘we’re just strangers’ game.
university: Ētilār (ஏதிலார்) means ‘strangers, people with no connection’, and potu nōkku (பொதுநோக்கு) is a ‘common’ or neutral look, the kind one gives anyone in a crowd. Kātalār kaṇṇē uḷa (காதலார் கண்ணே உள) asserts, with the emphatic -ē, that this is found only among lovers. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as lovers outwardly looking like strangers while loving within; Kalaignar specifies that they do this in public places; Puliyur Kesikan applies it to both lovers looking at each other. The couplet draws a general rule from the hero’s experience in 1096-1098. Pope: ‘The look indifferent, that would its love disguise, / Is only read aright by lovers’ eyes.’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Although she does not speak to me, / She listens while I speak; / Her eyes turn not to see my face, / But nothing else they seek.”
hinduism.explanation: The king observes that Shakuntala seems not to look at him or speak to him, yet her whole attention is on him.
hinduism.tie_back: An outwardly indifferent look that hides full attention is the Kural’s lovers’ ‘stranger’s look’.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “O that thou wert as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother! when I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, I should not be despised.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved wishes she could show her affection openly in public without reproach, as one may with a brother.
christianity.tie_back: Because lovers must look like mere acquaintances in public, the Kural says their neutral looks are a sign of love.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says that the dignified poor hide their need, but the perceptive recognise them by their sign.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the outward look misleads others, while the one who knows reads the hidden sign.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Esther had not made known her people nor her kindred; for Mordecai had charged her that she should not tell it. And Mordecai walked every day before the court of the women’s house, to know how Esther did.”
judaism.explanation: Esther and Mordecai hide their close bond in public, yet he watches over her every day.
judaism.tie_back: Two people who behave like strangers in public while staying deeply bound is the pattern the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dhammapada commentary, Patacara, a rich man’s daughter, falls in love with a household servant and hides the bond from her family until the two secretly leave together.
buddhism.explanation: A hidden love, kept from others’ eyes, is part of the background of the nun Patacara’s story.
buddhism.tie_back: Lovers concealing their bond in front of others reflects the Kural’s ‘stranger’s look’, though the Buddhist story leads to grief and renunciation.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 113 (story of Patacara)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though those who possess the three Guptis, cannot be disturbed even by well-adorned goddesses, still it is recommended to monks to live by themselves, as this is wholesome in every way.”
jainism.explanation: The disciplined monk remains outwardly and inwardly unmoved even before great beauty.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain monk’s unmoved look is genuine composure, while the Kural’s lovers only pretend to be unmoved, a telling contrast.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Only those who taste it know its sweet taste, like the mute, who eats the candy, and only smiles.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak says the sweetness of the Lord's Name is known only to those who have tasted it, and they cannot explain it to anyone else.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the cool look that lovers give each other in public is understood only by lovers; Guru Nanak too says only those who have known the love can read it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 635, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “No relatives had guessed their secret love, / for all their converse was by nods and signs.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Pyramus and Thisbe keep their love hidden from their families by speaking only through nods and signs.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Outsiders see nothing, but the lovers understand each other perfectly, which is the Kural’s point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: For Pascal, the heart perceives and acts on things that detached reasoning cannot see.
philosophy.tie_back: Lovers’ seemingly neutral looks carry a meaning that only the heart, not an observer’s reasoning, can read.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées 277 (Brunschvicg numbering; tr. W. F. Trotter)

real_life_example.event_title: Tchaikovsky and Nadezhda von Meck agree never to meet
real_life_example.event: The wealthy widow Nadezhda von Meck became the patron of the composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky after first writing to him in December 1876, and she later paid him an allowance that let him leave teaching and compose full time. For about fourteen years they exchanged more than 1,200 letters, yet by her wish they agreed never to meet in person. She ended the relationship and the allowance in 1890.
real_life_example.explanation: Their friendship is one of the most famous relationships in music history, intimate on paper yet kept at a distance in person.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that keeping up the appearance of strangers is something only those who are close do; Tchaikovsky and von Meck kept apart as strangers in person while sharing deep intimacy in letters.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

tamil:
கண்ணொடு கண்இணை நோக்கொக்கின் வாய்ச்சொற்கள்
என்ன பயனும் இல.
transliteration:
Kannodu kaninai nokkokkin vaaichchorkal
enna payanum ila.
meaning: When eyes meet eyes and the looks agree, the words of the mouth are no use at all.
elementary: Sometimes you and your best friend just look at each other and both burst out laughing, because you are thinking the same thing. You didn’t need to say a single word. Your eyes did all the talking.
university: Kaṇṇoṭu kaṇ iṇai nōkku okkin (கண்ணொடு கண்இணை நோக்கொக்கின்): ‘if the pair of eyes agree in look with the other pair’. Okkin (‘if they match’) is the key word: mutual, matching love, not one-sided longing. Vāyccoṟkaḷ (வாய்ச்சொற்கள்) are words of the mouth, which then have enna payanum ila, ‘no use whatever’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss: when eyes join in equal love, spoken words become unnecessary; Puliyur Kesikan specifies the two who are united in kāmam. The couplet closes the chapter by stating its principle: in love, the eyes are the true language, which is why the whole chapter has been about reading looks. Pope: ‘When eye to answering eye reveals the tale of love, / All words that lips can say must useless prove.’ The ytamizh transliteration writes kaN-inai, matching the Tamil கண்இணை; the text is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Why, the good king shows his love for her in his tender glances, and he has been wasting away, as if he were losing sleep.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala’s friend says the king’s love is already plain from his glances, before he has said anything.
hinduism.tie_back: Love declared through the eyes, making words unnecessary, is the Kural’s point.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.”
christianity.explanation: John teaches that real love is shown in what is done rather than in what is said.
christianity.tie_back: Both the epistle and the Kural place true love beyond mere words of the mouth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Souls are like recruited troops: Those who are like qualities are inclined to each other, but those who have dissimilar qualities, differ.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that kindred souls recognise and are drawn to each other.
islam.tie_back: Two hearts that ‘agree’ at a glance, needing no words, is the instant recognition the hadith describes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.”
judaism.explanation: At their first meeting Jonathan’s soul becomes bound to David’s.
judaism.tie_back: An instant union of souls that needs no long speeches matches the Kural’s agreement of the eyes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If both husband & wife want to see one another not only in the present life but also in the life to come, they should be in tune [with each other] in conviction, in tune in virtue, in tune in generosity, and in tune in discernment.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells a devoted couple that being in tune with each other in deeper qualities is what keeps them together.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s matching looks are a sign of the same deep agreement between two people.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: Rajimati was betrothed to Arishtanemi, who renounced the world on the way to their wedding; without any further exchange of words between them, she cut her hair and followed him into the ascetic life, and both reached perfection.
jainism.explanation: Rajimati’s devotion to Arishtanemi is shown by following his path, not by speeches.
jainism.tie_back: Jain narrative gives a love so in tune that words are unnecessary, though it ends in shared renunciation rather than union.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.27-30, 48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45); cf. the Nemidutakavya noted by Jacobi

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Says Nanak, the Saints savor this sublime essence, like the mute, who tastes the sweet candy, but only smiles.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Kaanra, Guru Arjan compares the joy of union with God to a mute person tasting sweets: the delight is complete, but it can only be shown by a smile, never put into words.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ends by saying that when two pairs of eyes agree, words are of no use; Guru Arjan likewise says the deepest joy of love is beyond speech.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1302, Raag Kaanra, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “So they two stood face to face without a word, without a sound, like oaks or lofty pines, which stand quietly side by side on the mountains when the wind is still.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Medea and Jason meet in secret, they stand facing each other in silence, already joined in love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Face to face with no words needed is the Kural’s final image.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.967-970 (tr. R. C. Seaton, 1912)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There is no less eloquence in the voice, in the eyes and in the air of a speaker than in his choice of words.”
philosophy.explanation: La Rochefoucauld notes that the eyes and manner speak as eloquently as words.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural goes further, saying that when the eyes agree, words are not needed at all.
philosophy.source: La Rochefoucauld, Maxims 249 (tr. J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell)

real_life_example.event_title: The golden throne of Tutankhamun
real_life_example.place: Thebes (Valley of the Kings), Egypt; now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo
real_life_example.event: Among the treasures found in the antechamber of Tutankhamun's tomb was a throne covered in gold and inlaid with silver, semi-precious stones and glass paste. Its back panel shows the young king seated and his queen, Ankhesenamun, facing him and reaching out to touch his shoulder, beneath the spreading rays of the sun. Howard Carter called it the most beautiful thing yet found in Egypt.
real_life_example.explanation: The scene is one of the most famous images of tenderness between a husband and wife to survive from the ancient world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when two lovers' looks meet, words are useless; the throne shows king and queen facing each other in a wordless moment of affection.

tamil:
கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும் ஐம்புலனும்
ஒண்தொடி கண்ணே உள.
transliteration:
Kandukettu unduyirththu utrariyum aimpulanum
ondhodi kanne ula.
meaning: All the joys of the five senses, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching, are found together in this one woman with bright bangles.
elementary: Think of the best day of a holiday: you see the lights, hear the music, taste the sweets, smell the flowers and feel a warm hug. Usually each good thing comes from a different place. The lover in this verse says that, for him, every one of those good feelings comes from one single person he loves.
university: Chapter 111 belongs to the kalaviyal (the section on premarital, secret love) and follows the exchange of glances in ch. 110; in the commentary tradition that runs through Parimelazhagar it voices the hero’s (talaivan’s) joy after the lovers’ first union, and nearly every couplet is his speech. The five verbs kaṇṭu (seeing), kēṭṭu (hearing), uṇṭu (eating, tasting), uyirttu (breathing in, smelling) and uṟṟu (touching) name the aimpulaṉ (ஐம்புலன், the five senses or sense-pleasures) in their classical order, and kaṇṇē uḷa means ‘are located in her’ (kaṇ as a locative). Oṇtoṭi (ஒண்தொடி, ‘she of the bright bangle’) is a standard metonymy for a young woman; the commentators on both source sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesikan) gloss the line as all five sense-joys being present in her alone. Pope renders: ‘All joys that senses five- sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch- can give, / In this resplendent armlets-bearing damsel live!’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the sung version printed on thirukkural.net writes ஒண்டொடி, an ordinary sandhi spelling of the same word.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “She seems a flower whose fragrance none has tasted, / A gem uncut by workman’s tool, / A branch no desecrating hands have wasted, / Fresh honey, beautifully cool.”
hinduism.explanation: King Dushyanta describes Shakuntala by piling up images for smell, sight, touch and taste, as if every kind of sweetness were gathered in her.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the lover finds the delights of all the senses summed up in one woman.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act II (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices! Thy lips, O my spouse, drop as the honeycomb: honey and milk are under thy tongue; and the smell of thy garments is like the smell of Lebanon.”
christianity.explanation: The bridegroom of the Song of Songs praises his bride through sight, taste and smell at once.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved alone satisfies several senses together.

islam.quote_or_event: “In this world, women and perfume have been made dear to me, and my comfort has been provided in prayer.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet names the love of women and of fragrance as good things of this world that God made dear to him, while placing his deepest comfort in prayer.
islam.tie_back: Islam affirms, as the Kural does, that the beloved is a rightful source of delight, but it ranks prayer above all sense-joys.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; For sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.”
judaism.explanation: The lover asks to see the beloved’s face and hear her voice, because both are sweet to him.
judaism.tie_back: Sight and hearing, two of the Kural’s five senses, both find their joy in the one beloved.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the opening suttas of the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha says he knows of no other single sight, sound, smell, taste or touch that so overpowers a man’s mind as those of a woman, and the same of a man’s for a woman.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the same five senses as the Kural and says that the beloved’s form, voice, scent, taste and touch are the strongest pull on the mind.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees with the Kural that all five sense-delights can meet in one person, but treats this as a danger to be understood, not a joy to be celebrated.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 1.1-10, Rupadi Vagga (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira’s lecture takes the five senses one by one (colour, sound, smell, taste, touch) and warns that passion for the objects of each sense ruins the soul.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism shares the Kural’s map of the five senses but sees their gathering in one beloved as a snare, the opposite of the lover’s delight.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.24, with 32.22-99 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O my eyes, the Lord has infused His Light into you; do not look upon any other than the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In Anand Sahib, Guru Amar Das speaks in turn to the body, the eyes and the ears, telling each sense that its true fulfilment lies in the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural finds the joys of all five senses in one woman; Anand Sahib directs the senses one by one to the one Beloved, God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 922, Raag Ramkali, Anand Sahib (pauri 36), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Aphrodite lends Hera an embroidered girdle in which every charm is woven: love, desire and the sweet persuasion that steals the wits even of the wise.
greek_mythology.explanation: The girdle gathers every power of attraction into one object, and whoever wears it becomes irresistible.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise imagines every delight of love gathered into one woman.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I know not how I can conceive the good, if I withdraw the pleasures of taste and withdraw the pleasures of love and those of hearing and sight.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus says he cannot even imagine the good without the pleasures of taste, love, hearing and sight.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural’s lover, Epicurus counts the pleasures of all the senses, including love, as part of the good.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, quoted in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers X.6 (tr. R. D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: The Lady and the Unicorn tapestries show the five senses
real_life_example.place: Woven probably in Flanders; now in the Musée de Cluny, Paris, France
real_life_example.event: Around 1500 a set of six large tapestries known as The Lady and the Unicorn was woven, probably in Flanders, for a patron whom historians identify from its coats of arms as a member of the Le Viste family. Five of the tapestries are understood to show the five senses, sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch, each with a lady accompanied by a lion and a unicorn. The sixth carries the inscription À mon seul désir, meaning to my only desire, and its meaning is still debated; the set now hangs in the Musée de Cluny in Paris.
real_life_example.explanation: The set is one of the best-known works of medieval art, and it gathers all five senses around a single figure before naming one only desire beyond them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that all the joys of the five senses are found together in one beloved woman, and the tapestries likewise gather sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch around one lady and crown them with a panel addressed to an only desire.

tamil:
பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிறமன் அணியிழை
தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து.
transliteration:
Pinikku marundhu piraman aniyizhai
thannoikkuth thaane marundhu.
meaning: For other illnesses, the medicine is something different from the illness. But for the love-sickness this jeweled girl causes, she herself is the only medicine.
elementary: When you miss your best friend who has moved away, no toy or sweet makes the sad feeling go. The only thing that fixes it is seeing that friend again. The person you miss is both the reason you feel sad and the cure.
university: The couplet sets ordinary medicine against love: for a piṇi (பிணி, disease) the marundu (மருந்து, remedy) is piṟa (‘something other’), while the nōy (நோய், sickness) caused by the aṇiyiḻai (அணியிழை, ‘she of fine jewels’) is cured only by her. Man in piṟaman is an expletive particle (asai) with no meaning of its own, as the commentators note. Solomon Pappaiah sharpens the logic: remedies usually have a nature opposite to the disease, yet here the cause and the cure are the same. The idea continues ch. 110’s opening kural (1091), where one glance wounds and another heals, and moves it from the look to union itself. Pope: ‘Disease and medicine antagonists we surely see; / This maid, to pain she gives, herself is remedy.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Dear Kṛṣṇa, please pour the nectar of Your lips upon the fire within our hearts — a fire You ignited with Your smiling glances and the sweet song of Your flute.”
hinduism.explanation: The gopis tell Krishna that the burning love he lit in them by his glances and his flute can be soothed only by his own nectar.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the one who causes the love-sickness is the only one who can cure it.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.29.35 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Come, and let us return unto the LORD: for he hath torn, and he will heal us; he hath smitten, and he will bind us up.”
christianity.explanation: The prophet tells Israel that the God who wounded them is the same God who will heal them.
christianity.tie_back: The pattern of the Kural, where the one who wounds is the one who heals, appears here in divine rather than human love.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is nothing like marriage, for two who love one another.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that for two people who love each other, marriage is the best answer to that love.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s cure for love-sickness is the beloved herself; this hadith names lawful union with the beloved as the cure.
islam.source: Sunan Ibn Majah 1847 (graded hasan by Darussalam)

judaism.quote_or_event: “I kill, and I make alive; I have wounded, and I heal; And there is none that can deliver out of My hand.”
judaism.explanation: In the Song of Moses, God declares that wounding and healing both come from Him alone.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural applies to the beloved what this verse says of God: the same hand gives the wound and the healing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fire like lust and no crime like hatred. There is no ill like the aggregates (of existence) and no bliss higher than the peace (of Nibbana).”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names lust as the worst fire and the peace of Nibbana as the true bliss that ends every ill.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees that love is a sickness, but it places the cure in Nibbana, not in the beloved who caused it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Misery ceases on the absence of delusion, delusion ceases on the absence of desire, desire ceases on the absence of greed, greed ceases on the absence of property.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira traces suffering back through delusion and desire, and teaches that it ends only when desire itself ends.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism also asks what cures the pain of desire, but its answer is the end of desire, not the beloved who stirred it.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The physician was called in; he touched my arm and felt my pulse. The foolish physician did not know that the pain was in the mind.”
sikhism.explanation: In a salok of Malar ki Vaar, Guru Nanak pictures a doctor taking the pulse of someone whose sickness is really the pain of separation from the Beloved, which no ordinary medicine can reach.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says ordinary illnesses have ordinary cures but love-sickness can be cured only by the beloved; Guru Nanak's foolish physician fails for the same reason, because the pain is love-longing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1279, Raag Malar, Malar ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Telephus was wounded by Achilles’ spear, an oracle told him that only the one who had wounded him could heal him, and he was cured by rust scraped from that same spear.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this story the weapon that caused the wound is the only thing that can close it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved is like Achilles’ spear: the source of the wound is also its only cure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus Socrates says that the soul of the lover, stung and aching when apart, forgets mother, brothers and friends and holds that the beloved is the only physician of its greatest pains.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the beloved is both what wounds the lover’s soul with longing and what alone can heal it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim almost word for word: she who causes the sickness is its only medicine.

real_life_example.event_title: Berlioz writes the Symphonie fantastique for Harriet Smithson
real_life_example.event: In 1827 the young composer Hector Berlioz saw the Irish actress Harriet Smithson play Ophelia in Hamlet in Paris and became infatuated with her, but she did not answer his letters. He poured his feelings into the Symphonie fantastique, first performed on 5 December 1830, in which a recurring melody called the idée fixe represents the beloved. Smithson attended a later performance in 1832, and the two married in October 1833, though they later separated.
real_life_example.explanation: One of the most famous symphonies of the Romantic era grew directly out of a lovesick obsession, and the woman who caused it went on to become the composer's wife.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that ordinary illnesses have cures different from their causes, but love-sickness is healed only by the woman who caused it; Berlioz's long fever of love was answered only when Smithson herself accepted him.

tamil:
தாம்வீழ்வார் மென்றோள் துயிலின் இனிதுகொல்
தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு.
transliteration:
Thaamveezhvaar mendrol thuyilin inidhukol
thaamaraik kannaan ulagu.
meaning: Is the heaven of the god with lotus-flower eyes any sweeter than sleeping on the soft shoulders of the one you love?
elementary: Imagine falling asleep safe and warm after a long trip, with someone who loves you right beside you. Grown-ups sometimes say heaven is the happiest place there is. This verse asks, with a smile, whether even heaven could feel better than that peaceful, loved feeling.
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: is tāmaraik kaṇṇāṉ ulagu (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு), ‘the world of the lotus-eyed one’, sweeter than sleep on the soft shoulders (meṉṟōḷ) of those one loves (tām vīḻvār)?
