Commentators in Parimelazhagar’s line identify the lotus-eyed one with Tirumal (Vishnu) and his world with his heaven (Vaikuntha), and Solomon Pappaiah glosses it this way; Kalaignar frames it as a sceptical question about what people call ‘the lotus-eyed one’s world’. The particle kol (கொல்) marks doubt, so the answer implied is ‘no’. The verse is one of the few places where the Kural names a deity by an epithet, and it ranks the joy of love above the reward of heaven only playfully, inside the love-poetry convention. Pope: ‘Than rest in her soft arms to whom the soul is giv’n, / Is any sweeter joy in his, the Lotus-eyed-one’s heaven?’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Ah, my eyes have found their heaven. Here is the darling of my thoughts, lying upon a flower-strewn bench of stone, and attended by her two friends.”
hinduism.explanation: Hidden among the branches, King Dushyanta catches sight of Shakuntala resting and says his eyes have reached heaven.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the lover calls the presence of his resting beloved a heaven in itself.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song of Songs describes resting in her beloved’s embrace.
christianity.tie_back: This is the restful embrace that the Kural says no heaven could surpass.

islam.quote_or_event: “It is He who created you from one soul and created from it its mate that he might dwell in security with her.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says God made the spouse so that each might find rest and security in the other.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s sweet rest on the beloved’s shoulder echoes this rest in the spouse, though Islam would never rank it above Paradise.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Enjoy life with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which He hath given thee under the sun.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet tells the reader to take joy in life with a beloved wife as one’s portion under the sun.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, this verse finds the sweetest portion of life in the company of the one you love, here and now.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Udana, the Buddha’s half-brother Nanda longs to leave the monks for his bride, until the Buddha shows him the nymphs of the heaven of the Thirty-three, beside whom Nanda says his bride looks plain; he then stays in the order.
buddhism.explanation: The story ranks heavenly delights far above earthly love, and then teaches Nanda to give up both.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural playfully ranks love above heaven; the Nanda story reverses the ranking, and Buddhism finally sets both aside.

jainism.quote_or_event: “From desire of pleasure arises the misery of the whole world, the gods included; whatever misery of body and mind there is, the dispassionate will put an end to it.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that even the gods in their heavens suffer from the desire for pleasure, and only the dispassionate are free.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural weighs love against heaven and prefers love; Jainism finds both heavenly and earthly pleasure bound up with misery.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.19 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I do not seek power, and I do not seek liberation. My mind is in love with Your Lotus Feet.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Devgandhari, Guru Arjan says he wants neither kingship nor even mukti (liberation), only to stay in love with the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether even the heaven of the Lotus-eyed god is sweeter than resting with one's beloved; Guru Arjan likewise puts loving closeness above every heavenly reward.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 534, Raag Devgandhari, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The goddess Calypso offers Odysseus immortality and ageless life if he stays with her, but he answers that though Penelope is mortal and less beautiful than a goddess, he still longs every day to go home to her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus chooses life with his mortal wife over the deathless existence of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Odysseus judges the company of his own beloved sweeter than the heaven of the immortals.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I have sought it, finally, because in the union of love I have seen, in a mystic miniature, the prefiguring vision of the heaven that saints and poets have imagined.”
philosophy.explanation: In the prologue to his autobiography, Bertrand Russell says the union of love gave him a glimpse of the heaven imagined by saints and poets.
philosophy.tie_back: Russell makes the Kural’s comparison directly: the joy of union rivals heaven itself.
philosophy.source: Bertrand Russell, ‘What I Have Lived For’, Prologue to The Autobiography of Bertrand Russell (1967)

real_life_example.event_title: Edward FitzGerald publishes the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám
real_life_example.event: In 1859 the English scholar Edward FitzGerald published, anonymously, a small pamphlet of verses freely translated from the Persian quatrains of Omar Khayyám. It attracted almost no notice until Dante Gabriel Rossetti came across it in 1860, after which it became one of the most quoted poems in English. In one quatrain of the first edition the speaker pictures bread, wine, a book of verse and the beloved singing beside him, and says that with these the wilderness is paradise enough; the next quatrain mocks those who long for the paradise to come.
real_life_example.explanation: The poem made a medieval Persian voice famous across the English-speaking world, and its picture of simple happiness beside a loved one became proverbial.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural playfully asks whether even the heaven of the lotus-eyed god could be sweeter than rest beside one's beloved, and the Rubáiyát likewise says the beloved's company makes a wilderness paradise enough, with no need of a paradise to come.

tamil:
நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும்
தீயாண்டுப் பெற்றாள் இவள்.
transliteration:
Neengin theruum kurugungaal thannennum
theeyaandup petraal ival.
meaning: If I move away it burns me, and if I come near it cools me. Where did she get such a strange fire?
elementary: Have you ever felt grumpy and hot inside when you had to leave someone you love, and calm again as soon as you were back together? The lover says she must own a magic fire: it burns when you go away and feels cool and gentle when you come close. Real fire does the opposite!
university: The conceit rests on reversing the nature of fire: ordinary fire burns those who come near and leaves those who move away, but this fire teṟūum (தெறூஉம், ‘burns’, with the vowel lengthening called uyiraḷapeṭai for metre) when he leaves (nīṅkiṉ) and taṇ eṉṉum (‘turns cool’) when he draws near (kuṟukuṅkāl). The question tī yāṇṭup peṟṟāḷ (‘from where did she get the fire?’) is wonder rather than inquiry, and every gloss on both source sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Kalaignar) calls it a putumaiyāṉa tī, a ‘new, unheard-of fire’; Solomon Pappaiah adds that she has lit it in his heart. The couplet anticipates the separation chapters of the kaṟpiyal, where absence is described as burning. Pope: ‘Withdraw, it burns; approach, it soothes the pain; / Whence did the maid this wondrous fire obtain?’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “’Twas love that caused the burning pain; / ’Tis love that eases it again; / As when, upon a sultry day, / Rain breaks, and washes grief away.”
hinduism.explanation: Overhearing that Shakuntala’s fever comes from love for him, the king says the love that burns is the same love that brings relief like rain.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s strange fire: love burns and love cools, depending on whether the lovers are apart or together.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn.”
christianity.explanation: Paul advises those who burn with desire to marry, so that union quiets the burning.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, love burns when lovers are apart and is cooled by union.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi opens the Masnavi with the reed flute that wails because it was cut from its reed-bed, and says that its cry is the fire of love, not mere wind.
islam.explanation: The reed’s burning lament comes from separation from its source, and only reunion would quiet it.
islam.tie_back: Rumi’s fire of separation is the Kural’s fire that burns when the lover moves away.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, opening verses (tr. R. A. Nicholson)

judaism.quote_or_event: “For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD. Many waters cannot quench love.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs calls love a fire so fierce that no flood can put it out.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too calls love a fire, though its fire has the strange gift of turning cool at the beloved’s side.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The eye is aflame. Forms are aflame... Aflame with what? Aflame with the fire of passion, the fire of aversion, the fire of delusion.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Fire Sermon the Buddha teaches that every sense burns with passion, and that only disenchantment puts the fire out.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees that passion is fire, but it cools that fire by letting go, not by drawing near to the beloved.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 35.28, Adittapariyaya Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As in a forest, full of fuel, a fire fanned by the wind cannot be extinguished, so the fire (as it were) of the senses of him who eats as he lists; it does not benefit any chaste man.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira likens the senses of an unrestrained person to a forest fire that cannot be put out.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism also calls desire a fire, but holds that indulgence only feeds it, while the Kural’s lover finds it cooled by nearness.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The month of Aasaarh seems burning hot, to those who are not close to their Husband Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Barah Maha (song of the twelve months), Guru Arjan says the scorching summer month burns those who are far from their Husband Lord, while those near Him find peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's fire burns when the lover moves away and cools when he comes near; Guru Arjan likewise says separation from the Beloved burns and nearness to Him cools.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 134, Raag Maajh, Barah Maha, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros glukupikron, ‘sweet-bitter’, the loosener of limbs, an irresistible creature that both delights and pains the lover.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Sappho love is a single power that gives sweetness and bitterness at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s fire that both scorches and cools is the same double nature of love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus Socrates describes the lover’s soul as throbbing and burning with pain when apart from the beloved, and finding relief from its pangs and a sweet release as soon as it sees the beloved again.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the lover’s soul suffers when the beloved is absent and is soothed in the beloved’s presence.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s fire that burns at a distance and cools close by.

real_life_example.event_title: June Carter co-writes Ring of Fire
real_life_example.event: June Carter, of the Carter Family of country musicians, co-wrote the song Ring of Fire with Merle Kilgore, picturing love as a burning ring of fire; she wrote it out of her feelings for Johnny Cash and her worries about his troubled life. Her sister Anita Carter recorded it first, and Cash's own version, recorded in March 1963 with Mexican-style horns, reached number one on the country chart and stayed there for seven weeks. June Carter and Johnny Cash married in 1968.
real_life_example.explanation: The song became one of the best-known love songs in American popular music, and its writer later married the man it was about.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural marvels at a strange fire that burns when the lover moves away and grows cool when he comes near; June Carter's song likewise pictures love itself as a fire, one that burned through the years before she and Cash were finally together.

tamil:
வேட்ட பொழுதின் அவையவை போலுமே
தோட்டார் கதுப்பினாள் தோள்.
transliteration:
Vetta pozhudhin avaiyavai polume
thottaar kadhuppinaal thol.
meaning: The shoulders of the girl with flowers in her hair give me joy, just like each thing I long for gives joy at the moment I want it.
elementary: Imagine a magic lunchbox that always holds exactly what you are hungry for: soup when you are cold, ice cream when you are hot. The lover says that being close to the one he loves is like that box: it always gives the right happiness at the right time.
university: Vēṭṭa poḻutiṉ avaiyavai pōlumē says that her shoulders (tōḷ, standing for her embrace) are ‘like each of those things at the time they are desired’: the comparison is with any object of desire enjoyed exactly when wished for. Tōṭṭār katuppiṉāḷ (தோட்டார் கதுப்பினாள்) is ‘she whose tresses (katuppu) are full of petals or flowers (tōṭu)’, an epithet of the adorned beloved. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both read it as ‘whenever one unites with her, she gives the delight of whatever one desires’, and Kalaignar compares it to a wished-for thing arriving whenever wished; the image recalls the wish-granting tree and cow of Indian lore, though the Kural does not name them. Pope: ‘In her embrace, whose locks with flowery wreaths are bound, / Each varied form of joy the soul can wish is found.’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Chandogya Upanishad teaches that one who has come to know the Self moves freely in all worlds: if he desires the world of the fathers, or of mothers, or of song, or of fragrance and garlands, by his mere wish it rises up for him.
hinduism.explanation: For the knower of the Self, every desired joy appears the moment it is wished for.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural gives the beloved this same power to supply each wished-for joy at the moment of wishing.
hinduism.source: Chandogya Upanishad 8.2.1-10 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 1)

christianity.quote_or_event: “How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love, for delights!”
christianity.explanation: The lover exclaims that the beloved is beautiful and pleasant, made for delights.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Song finds every kind of delight in the beloved.

islam.quote_or_event: “Circulated among them will be plates and vessels of gold. And therein is whatever the souls desire and [what] delights the eyes, and you will abide therein eternally.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes Paradise as a place where every soul finds whatever it desires.
islam.tie_back: The Kural gives the beloved’s embrace this Paradise-like quality of answering every desire.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the manna in the wilderness was a single food in which the Israelites could taste whatever flavour they wished, as an infant finds every taste in its mother’s milk.
judaism.explanation: One gift from heaven held every desired taste for each person who ate it.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved is like this manna: one source that gives each longed-for sweetness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no satisfying sensual desires, even with the rain of gold coins. For sensual pleasures give little satisfaction and much pain.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that no amount of pleasure can ever fill sensual desire.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural claims the beloved satisfies each desire as it arises; Buddhism denies that any pleasure can truly satisfy desire.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira compares pleasures to a fruit that tastes delicious but turns to poison.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises a delight that answers every wish; Jainism warns that every such delight is sweet only at first.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Guru is the Sacred Shrine of Pilgrimage, the Guru is the Wish-fulfilling Elysian Tree.”
sikhism.explanation: In Sri Raag, Guru Arjan calls the Guru the parjat, the wish-granting tree of Indian legend, which gives whatever one desires.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the beloved's embrace gives each desired joy exactly when it is wished for, an image the commentators link to the wish-granting tree; Guru Arjan uses that same tree for the Guru.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 52, Sri Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The horn of the goat Amalthea, which nursed the infant Zeus, was said to supply meat or drink in abundance, whatever one might wish.
greek_mythology.explanation: The horn of plenty gives each person exactly what they wish for.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved is like this horn, giving each desired joy at the moment it is wished.
greek_mythology.source: Apollodorus, Library 2.7.5, citing Pherecydes (tr. J. G. Frazer)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle teaches that friendships based on pleasure last only while the pleasure lasts, because such friends love one another not for their character but because each finds the other pleasant.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, love that rests only on pleasure is the least stable kind of friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural celebrates the pleasure of the beloved; Aristotle would add that lasting love needs more than pleasure.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3, 1156a (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Marc Chagall paints Birthday after Bella's visit
real_life_example.event: On Marc Chagall's birthday, 7 July 1915, Bella Rosenfeld, the young woman he was about to marry, came to his room in Vitebsk bringing flowers and food as birthday gifts. Chagall painted the scene as Birthday, in which he floats up from the floor and bends backwards through the air to kiss her while she holds the bouquet. The couple married later that same month, and the painting is now in the Museum of Modern Art, New York.
real_life_example.explanation: The painting became one of the best-known images of joyful love in modern art, showing a happiness so complete that it lifts the lover off the ground.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the beloved's embrace gives delight just as each longed-for thing does at the very moment it is wanted, and Bella arrived on Chagall's birthday with exactly the gifts of the day, filling his room with a joy he could only paint as flight.

tamil:
உறுதோறு உயிர்தளிர்ப்பத் தீண்டலால் பேதைக்கு
அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள்.
transliteration:
Urudhoru uyirthalirppath theendalaal pedhaikku
amizhdhin iyandrana thol.
meaning: Every time I hold her, my drooping life grows fresh shoots again. This innocent girl's shoulders must be made of amrita (the drink that makes gods live forever).
elementary: Think of a droopy plant that perks up the moment you give it water. When someone you love gives you a hug after a hard day, you can feel the same way. The lover says her hugs work like magic drink that makes him feel alive and fresh again every single time.
university: Uyir taḷirppa (உயிர் தளிர்ப்ப, ‘so that life puts forth tender shoots’) is a plant image: the lover’s withered life sprouts again, as Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah gloss it (vāṭiya uyir taḷirkka, ‘the wilted life sprouting’). Uṟutōṟu means ‘every time I come close’, and from this repeated reviving effect the lover infers that her shoulders are amiḻtiṉ iyaṉṟaṉa (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன), ‘fashioned of amizhtu’, the nectar of immortality (Sanskrit amṛta). Pētai (பேதை) here means a simple, innocent young woman; it is also the name of the youngest of the seven traditional stages of womanhood, but the commentators read it in the general sense. Pope: ‘Ambrosia are the simple maiden’s arms; when I attain / Their touch, my withered life puts forth its buds again!’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In a famous Rig Vedic hymn the singers declare that they have drunk the Soma and become immortal, have come to the light and found the gods.
hinduism.explanation: The sacred drink Soma, identified with amrita, is praised as giving fresh life and immortality to those who taste it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural borrows exactly this idea of a life-giving nectar to describe the beloved’s touch.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 8.48.3 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.”
christianity.explanation: The bride finds rest and sweetness in her beloved, like shade and fruit from a tree.
christianity.tie_back: As the Kural’s lover is refreshed by the beloved’s nectar, the bride is refreshed by her beloved’s sweetness.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Prophet came home trembling after the first revelation, he asked Khadijah to cover him; she wrapped him, comforted him and reassured him until his fear left him.
islam.explanation: The loving presence of his wife restored the Prophet’s calm and strength at the hardest moment of his life.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, this story shows the beloved spouse’s nearness reviving a shaken spirit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah’s tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her. And Isaac was comforted for his mother.”
judaism.explanation: Isaac, still grieving his mother, finds his grief eased by his love for Rebekah.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, love for the beloved brings a drooping spirit back to life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Having savored the taste of solitude and peace (of Nibbana), pain-free and stainless he becomes, drinking deep the taste of the bliss of the Truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the peace of Nibbana as a taste one drinks deeply, leaving one free of pain.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism also speaks of a drink that renews life, but it finds that nectar in Nibbana, not in the beloved’s touch.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He will get rid of all misery which always afflicts mankind; recovered from the long illness, as it were, and glorious, he becomes infinitely happy, and obtains the (final) aim.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira describes the liberated soul as one who has recovered from a long illness and become infinitely happy.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism also speaks of life restored, but it finds that revival in liberation from desire, not in the beloved’s embrace.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.110 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The dried branches are made green again in an instant.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Gauri, Guru Arjan describes the Guru's grace bringing spiritually withered people back to life at once, like dry wood putting out green shoots.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural each touch of the beloved makes the lover's wilting life sprout again; Guru Arjan uses the same picture of the withered made green.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 191, Raag Gauri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, when Zeus and Hera lie together on Mount Ida, the earth beneath them sends up fresh grass, dewy lotus, crocus and hyacinth, and a golden cloud covers them.
greek_mythology.explanation: The union of the gods makes the very ground burst into new growth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s lover feels his life sprout new shoots in the embrace, as the earth blooms beneath the divine lovers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus Socrates says that when the lover gazes on beauty, warmth flows into his soul, the stiffened roots of its wings soften, and the wings begin to swell and grow again.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the sight of the beloved makes the soul’s withered wings sprout anew.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s image of life putting forth fresh shoots in the beloved’s presence.

real_life_example.event_title: Fanny Osbourne nurses Robert Louis Stevenson back from illness
real_life_example.place: Monterey and San Francisco, California, United States
real_life_example.event: In August 1879 the Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson crossed the Atlantic and the American continent in cheap emigrant conditions to join Fanny Van de Grift Osbourne, the American woman he loved, arriving in Monterey thin and unwell. In early 1880 he fell gravely ill, and Fanny, who had divorced her first husband in December 1879, took him into her home and nursed him. They married in San Francisco on 19 May 1880, and she cared for his fragile health for the rest of his life.
real_life_example.explanation: The journey nearly ruined Stevenson's health, yet it gave him the wife who became his lifelong nurse and companion.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that every time the lover is close to his beloved, his wilting life puts out fresh shoots; Stevenson, worn down to skin and bone, was nursed back to life by the woman he had crossed the world to reach.

tamil:
தம்மில் இருந்து தமதுபாத்து உண்டற்றால்
அம்மா அரிவை முயக்கு.
transliteration:
Thammil irundhu thamadhupaaththu undatraal
ammaa arivai muyakku.
meaning: Holding this lovely young woman feels like living in your own home and eating food you earned yourself, after sharing it with others.
elementary: Remember how good it feels to eat a meal you helped cook, at your own table, after giving some to your friends? It feels honest and happy and safe. The lover says being close to the one he loves gives that same warm, at-home happiness.
university: The simile draws on the householder ideal of the Arattuppal: tammil iruntu (‘dwelling in one’s own home’), tamatu (‘one’s own’, i.e. what one has earned) pāttu uṇṭaṟṟāl (‘like eating after dividing and sharing it’). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses pāttu as distributing one’s earnings to others before eating, Solomon Pappaiah as sharing with one’s own people, and Puliyur Kesikan more narrowly as eating one’s own portion; all agree that the pleasure is one of independence, rightful ownership and generosity. Ammā is read as am (‘beautiful’) plus māmai (‘the dark-gold complexion praised in Tamil poetry’), and arivai (அரிவை) is a young woman, also the name of one of the seven traditional stages of womanhood. Muyakku (முயக்கு) is ‘embrace’. Pope: ‘As when one eats from household store, with kindly grace / Sharing his meal: such is this golden maid’s embrace.’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The devotees of the Lord are released from all kinds of sins because they eat food which is offered first for sacrifice. Others, who prepare food for personal sense enjoyment, verily eat only sin.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita praises eating only after first offering the food, and condemns cooking only for oneself.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ideal of eating one’s own food only after sharing it, which it uses as the measure of love’s joy, rests on this same ethic.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.13 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee. Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm joins the happiness of eating one’s own earnings with the blessing of a wife at home.
christianity.tie_back: Both halves of the Kural’s simile, one’s own earned food and the beloved wife, appear together in this verse.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one’s own hands.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises food earned by one’s own work as the best food of all, citing David who lived by his own labour.
islam.tie_back: The Kural measures love’s joy by the sweetness of one’s own earned food, which this hadith calls the best meal.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Drink waters out of thine own cistern, And running waters out of thine own well... Let thy fountain be blessed; And have joy of the wife of thy youth.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares faithful joy in one’s own wife to drinking from one’s own well.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Proverbs likens love for one’s own spouse to the satisfaction of using what is rightfully one’s own.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where the son of a good family, using the wealth earned through his efforts & enterprise... righteous wealth righteously gained, partakes of his wealth and makes merit... he experiences bliss, he experiences joy.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that a householder knows real bliss in enjoying and giving from wealth he has honestly earned.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the very pleasure the Kural uses as its measure for the joy of the beloved’s embrace.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: Among the vows of the Jain householder is atithi-samvibhaga, sharing one’s food and goods with a worthy guest or mendicant before eating oneself.
jainism.explanation: The Jain layperson is taught to divide what is his own and give a share away as a religious duty.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s picture of eating one’s own food only after sharing it reflects this same household ethic, which Jainism made a formal vow.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra, chapter 7, list of lay vows (tr. Nathmal Tatia, That Which Is)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has”
sikhism.explanation: In Sarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak says the person who lives on honest earnings and shares part of them with others is the one who knows the true path (kirat karni and vand chhakna).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares the beloved's embrace to eating one's own earned food in one's own home after sharing it; this is the Sikh ideal of honest work and sharing almost word for word.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how the old couple Baucis and Philemon, poor but devoted to each other, share their humble meal in their own cottage with two strangers, who turn out to be Jupiter and Mercury.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their happiness lies in a loving marriage, a small home of their own and a generous table.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s simile, the joy of sharing one’s own food at home, is lived out by this loving pair.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle writes that friendship between husband and wife seems to exist by nature, includes both utility and pleasure, and that the two help each other by putting their own gifts into the common stock.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle a good marriage is a partnership in which each shares what is their own.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s joy of sharing what is one’s own is, for Aristotle, built into the friendship of husband and wife.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.12, 1162a (tr. W. D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Carl Larsson publishes Ett hem (A Home)
real_life_example.event: In 1889 the painter Carl Larsson and his wife Karin, also an artist, were given a small cottage at Sundborn, which they enlarged and transformed into their family home, with Karin designing and weaving many of its textiles. From 1894 Carl painted everyday life there in a series of watercolours, published in 1899 as the book Ett hem (A Home). The pictures of the family's self-made home became a model for Swedish interior decoration, and the house is now a museum.
real_life_example.explanation: The book turned a modest, hand-made family home into a national ideal of comfort and warmth.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares the beloved's embrace to the contentment of living in one's own home and eating what one has earned after sharing it, and the Larssons' Sundborn home, built and furnished by their own hands and shared with the world through Carl's pictures, shows that contentment in real life.

tamil:
வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே வளியிடை
போழப் படாஅ முயக்கு.
transliteration:
Veezhum iruvarkku inidhe valiyidai
pozhap padaaa muyakku.
meaning: Sweet to two people in love is a hug so close that not even a breath of wind can pass between them.
elementary: Have you ever hugged someone so tightly that you felt like one person? The verse says that for two people who love each other, the sweetest hug is one so close that not even a tiny puff of air could slip in between.
university: Vīḻum iruvar (வீழும் இருவர், ‘two who desire each other’) stresses that the love is mutual, and the embrace (muyakku) is one that vaḷi iṭai pōḻap paṭāa (‘is not split apart in the middle by the wind’). Paṭāa carries the metrical lengthening (aḷapeṭai) also seen in teṟūum of kural 1104. Every gloss on both sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) reads it as an embrace so close that even air cannot enter. Pope, characteristically, turns the image moral: ‘Sweet is the strict embrace of those whom fond affection binds, / Where no dissevering breath of discord entrance finds’, treating the wind as discord, a reading the Tamil commentators do not share. Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Now as a man, when embraced by a beloved wife, knows nothing that is without, nothing that is within, thus this person, when embraced by the intelligent (prâgña) Self, knows nothing that is without, nothing that is within.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad uses the embrace of loving spouses, in which nothing outside or inside is felt, as an image of union with the Self.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s embrace that lets nothing come between is the same image of complete union.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.21 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 15)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
christianity.explanation: Genesis says that husband and wife cling together and become one flesh.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s embrace with no gap between the two is a picture of becoming one.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are a clothing for you and you are a clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes husband and wife as garments for each other, as close as clothing to the skin.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s embrace that admits no wind, the garment image leaves nothing between the spouses.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When our love was strong, we could have slept on a bed that was the width of a sword. Now that our love is not strong, a bed of sixty cubits is not sufficient for us.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud quotes a popular saying: loving spouses need almost no room between them, but estranged ones cannot be far enough apart.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: true lovers leave no space at all between them.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 7a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bhallatiya Jataka a pair of kinnaras (forest spirits) still weep for the one night, seven hundred years earlier, when a flooded stream kept them apart.
buddhism.explanation: The couple’s love is so close that a single night’s separation is mourned for centuries, and the story leads the king to value his own wife.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the tale shows lovers for whom even the smallest gap is unbearable.
buddhism.source: Jataka 504, Bhallatiya Jataka (tr. ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. IV)

jainism.quote_or_event: “But a man who is indifferent to ‘colours,’ is free from sorrows; though still in the Samsâra, he is not affected by that long succession of pains, just as the leaf of the Lotus (is not moistened) by water.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira holds up the lotus leaf, which stays untouched by the water around it, as the model of a detached soul.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises an embrace where nothing comes between; Jainism praises the opposite, a soul that nothing clings to.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They alone are called husband and wife, who have one light in two bodies.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Suhi, Guru Amar Das says that true marriage is not just living side by side, but two people sharing one inner light.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises an embrace so close that not even a breath of air can come between the two lovers; Guru Amar Das describes a union so close that two bodies share a single light.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Suhi, Suhi ki Vaar (salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how Alcyone, grieving her drowned husband Ceyx, is changed into a bird together with him, and the two stay faithful mates even as birds.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even transformation and death do not separate the loving pair.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s lovers allow not even a breath of wind between them; Ceyx and Alcyone remain together beyond death.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium Aristophanes imagines Hephaestus asking two lovers lying side by side whether they wish to be wholly one, day and night in each other’s company, and offering to melt them into one and let them grow together.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristophanes, love is the longing of two halves to become one whole.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s embrace that leaves no room even for air is the same wish to be wholly one.

real_life_example.event_title: Gustav Klimt paints The Kiss
real_life_example.event: The Austrian painter Gustav Klimt painted The Kiss, an image of a couple locked in an embrace, in oil on canvas with gold leaf. It was first shown at the Kunstschau exhibition in Vienna in 1908, and the Austrian state bought it there for 25,000 kronen. It is regarded as the high point of Klimt's Golden Period and hangs in the Belvedere museum in Vienna.
real_life_example.explanation: The painting became one of the best-known images of love in Western art.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises an embrace so close that not even a breath of wind can pass between the two lovers, and Klimt's couple are painted so tightly enfolded that they seem to become a single shape.

tamil:
ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல் இவைகாமம்
கூடியார் பெற்ற பயன்.
transliteration:
Oodal unardhal punardhal ivaikaamam
koodiyaar petra payan.
meaning: A small lovers' quarrel, making up, and coming close again: these are the rewards enjoyed by people whose love has come true.
elementary: Best friends sometimes have a small grumpy fight, then say sorry, and then feel even closer than before. The verse says that this little circle of a pretend sulk, making up and being together again is one of the sweet parts of love.
university: The couplet names the three-part movement that structures the closing chapters of the Kamattuppal: ūṭal (ஊடல், the lover’s feigned or playful sulking), uṇartal (உணர்தல், its resolution, the partner understanding and appeasing it) and puṇartal (புணர்தல், reunion). Kāmam kūṭiyār (‘those in whom love has come together’, i.e. lovers whose love is fulfilled) obtain these as payaṉ, ‘fruit’. Solomon Pappaiah places it explicitly in married life (a small tiff, reconciliation, then reunion), Puliyur Kesikan adds that the sulk should be kept within measure (aḷavōṭu), and Kalaignar gives a slightly different reading of uṇartal. The triad anticipates chapters 131-133 (Pulavi, Pulavi Nuṇukkam, Ūṭaluvakai), where the delight of the lovers’ quarrel becomes the main theme. Pope: ‘The jealous variance, the healing of the strife, reunion gained: / These are the fruits from wedded love obtained.’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana Krishna teases his wife Rukmini by suggesting she would have done better to marry another king; she is so distressed that she faints, and he lifts her up, comforts her and assures her of his love, after which they are happier than before.
hinduism.explanation: A playful provocation leads to hurt, then to tender reconciliation and renewed closeness.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s sequence of quarrel, making up and reunion between married lovers.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.60 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath.”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows that anger will come but insists that it be resolved before the day ends.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul expects quarrels to be followed quickly by reconciliation.

islam.quote_or_event: Ali and Fatima had a quarrel and Ali went off to sleep in the mosque; the Prophet found him lying covered in dust, brushed it off him and playfully called him ‘Abu Turab’ (father of dust), and the matter was smoothed over.
islam.explanation: A small marital quarrel is gently eased by the Prophet’s humour and affection.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ūṭal and uṇartal, this is a tiff between loving spouses that ends in reconciliation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; But my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him.”
judaism.explanation: In the Song of Songs the bride delays opening to her beloved, he turns away, and she searches for him until they are reunited and she says ‘I am my beloved’s’.
judaism.tie_back: The Song traces the Kural’s arc of estrangement, seeking and reunion between lovers.
judaism.source: Song of Songs 5:6, with 6:3 (JPS 1917, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that hatred is never ended by hatred in this world, but only by non-hatred; this, he says, is an eternal law.
buddhism.explanation: Quarrels end not by answering anger with anger but by letting it go.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s uṇartal, the healing of the quarrel, works by the same giving-up of resentment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Love and hatred are caused by Karman, and they say that Karman has its origin in delusion; Karman is the root of birth and death, and birth and death they call misery.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that attachment and aversion alike come from karma and lead to further suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural delights in love’s swing between sulking and union; Jainism sees that very swing of attraction and aversion as binding karma.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O foolish and ignorant soul-bride, why are you so proud?”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak gently scolds the bride-soul for her maan (sulky pride), which keeps her from her Husband Lord, and teaches that humility brings reunion.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural names the lovers' quarrel, its making up and their coming together again as love's reward; Gurbani knows the same pattern of the bride's pride, reconciliation and reunion.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 722, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus returns, Penelope tests him by ordering their bed moved; he angrily protests that he built it around a living olive trunk, and this proof melts her doubt, so that they embrace in tears and go together to their old bed.
greek_mythology.explanation: A moment of testing and anger between the spouses turns into recognition and joyful reunion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The scene follows the Kural’s order exactly: a quarrel, its resolution, and coming together.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Amantium irae amoris integratio est” (The quarrels of lovers are the renewal of love).
philosophy.explanation: In Terence’s comedy a father consoles himself that the lovers’ quarrel he hears of will only renew their love.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim in one line: the lovers’ sulk leads to a stronger reunion.

real_life_example.event_title: Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton remarry
real_life_example.event: The film stars Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton first married in Montreal in 1964 and divorced in 1974. About sixteen months later, on 10 October 1975, they quietly remarried beside the Chobe River in Botswana while on holiday there, and the news came out a few days afterwards. The second marriage lasted less than a year.
real_life_example.explanation: Their partings and reunions made them one of the most talked-about couples of the twentieth century.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural names quarrel, reconciliation and reunion as the fruits of love, and Taylor and Burton's return to each other after their divorce is a famous real-life case of falling out and coming back together.

tamil:
அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்றால் காமம்
செறிதோறும் சேயிழை மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Aridhoru ariyaamai kandatraal kaamam
seridhorum seyizhai maattu.
meaning: The more you learn, the more you see how much you do not know. In the same way, each time I come close to my jeweled love, my love for her feels new again.
elementary: When you read one good book about space, you find out there are a hundred more things about space you never knew. The more you learn, the more there is to learn! The lover says love is like that: the more time he spends with the one he loves, the more new things he finds to love.
university: The chapter ends with a celebrated simile from learning: aṟitōṟu aṟiyāmai kaṇṭaṟṟāl (‘like discovering one’s ignorance each time one learns’), so is kāmam (love) each time he draws close (ceṟitōṟum) to the cēyiḻai (சேயிழை, ‘she of red, i.e. gold, jewels’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah specify learning from books (nūl), and Solomon Pappaiah reads the second half as love’s savour appearing ever new; Kalaignar likewise has ‘knowing new things again and again’. The verse links the Kamattuppal to the Porutpal chapters on learning (ch. 40-43), and turns the humility of the scholar into a picture of inexhaustible love. Pope’s second line slightly shifts the sense: ‘The more men learn, the more their lack of learning they detect; / ’Tis so when I approach the maid with gleaming jewels decked.’ The ytamizh.com ‘Couplet Explanation’ reads it as repeated union only creating desire for more, a narrower gloss than the Tamil commentators give. Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Kena Upanishad says that Brahman is truly known by the one who thinks he does not know it, and is not known by the one who thinks he knows it; it is unknown to those who know and known to those who do not.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that the highest reality always exceeds what one thinks one has grasped.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it finds that deeper knowing reveals how much remains unknown.
hinduism.source: Kena Upanishad 2.3 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 1)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that whoever thinks he knows has not yet begun to know as he should.
christianity.tie_back: This is the first half of the Kural’s simile: true knowing reveals how much is still unknown.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘If the sea were ink for [writing] the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it in [continual] supplement.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says that God’s words are inexhaustible, so that all the oceans as ink could never write them all.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s endless discovery, the Qur’an points to a depth that can never be reached by learning.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ben Bag Bag said: Turn it over, and [again] turn it over, for all is therein. And look into it; And become gray and old therein.”
judaism.explanation: The sage teaches that the Torah can be studied again and again for a lifetime and still yield new meaning.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s love, which finds something new at every meeting, is like the Torah that is never exhausted by study.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:22 (tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that knowing the extent of one’s ignorance is the beginning of wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the learning half of the Kural’s simile: wisdom grows as one sees what one does not know.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a man who passionately desires ‘colours,’ be happy while he gets, keeps, uses, loses, and misses (those things). Even when he enjoys them, he is never satisfied.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that sense-desire is never satisfied, however much it enjoys.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural finds joy in a love that is always new and never used up; Jainism sees the same endlessness as the misery of a desire that can never be filled.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The more you say about them, the more there still remains to be said.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak says the greatness and virtues of God can never be fully described: every attempt only shows how much more there is.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that, as with learning, every meeting with the beloved shows how much more there is to discover; Guru Nanak says the same about the endless Beloved, God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib (pauri 24), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus and Penelope are reunited, Athena holds back the Dawn at the edge of the Ocean and lengthens the night, so that the couple can share their joy and tell each other all that has happened.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess stretches the night because the lovers’ delight in each other has no natural end.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s love, which finds something new at every meeting, is matched by a reunion so rich that the night itself must be lengthened.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Well, although I do not suppose that either of us knows anything really beautiful and good, I am better off than he is,—for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates concludes that his only wisdom is knowing that he does not know.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the classic statement of the first half of the Kural’s simile, the learner who sees his own ignorance.

real_life_example.event_title: Will and Ariel Durant write The Story of Civilization together
real_life_example.event: Will Durant met Ariel when he was her teacher at the Ferrer Modern School, and they married in 1913. She began as his research aide on The Story of Civilization, a many-volume history of the world, became his collaborator, and from the seventh volume onward was credited as co-author. In 1968 they won the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction for Rousseau and Revolution; Ariel died on 25 October 1981 and Will less than two weeks later.
real_life_example.explanation: The Durants' history became one of the most widely read popular histories of the twentieth century, and it was the work of a marriage as much as of one author.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says love keeps revealing something new, just as each new piece of learning shows how much more there is to know; the Durants joined their marriage to a lifetime of learning, volume after volume, until both lives ended within days of each other.

tamil:
நன்னீரை வாழி அனிச்சமே நின்னினும்
மென்னீரள் யாம்வீழ் பவள்.
transliteration:
Nanneerai vaazhi anichchamae ninninum
menneeral yaamveezh paval.
meaning: Anicham flower (a flower so delicate it wilts if you just smell it), long may you live! You are truly soft, but the one I love is even softer than you.
elementary: Imagine you hold the softest feather you have ever found and say, 'You are so soft!' Then you remember your baby sister's cheek and smile: 'But she is even softer.' The poet does the same with the softest flower he knows.
university: Chapter 112 belongs to the kalaviyal (the section on secret, premarital love) and follows ch. 111 (Punarchi Magizhthal, the joy of union): the hero now 'adorns in words' (punainthu uraiththal) the nalam (நலம், 'goodness, loveliness') of the heroine, a stock situation of Tamil akam poetry. The anicham (அனிச்சம்) is the proverbial most delicate flower in Tamil, said to wilt merely when smelled (cf. Kural 90, மோப்பக் குழையும் அனிச்சம்), and nanneerai (நன்னீரை, 'you are of fine nature') with the blessing vaazhi ('may you flourish') makes the flower a polite rival before it is surpassed by the beloved's men-neer (மென்னீர், 'softer nature'). In the line of Parimelazhagar the hero speaks this aside after union, praising what he has just experienced; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss it as 'my beloved is softer than you'. Pope renders: 'O flower of the sensitive plant! than thee / More tender's the maiden beloved by me.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Your body, soft as siris-flowers, / Engages passion’s utmost powers; / How comes it that your heart is hard / As stalks that siris-blossoms guard?”
hinduism.explanation: King Dushyanta teases Shakuntala that her body is as soft as the shirisha blossom, the flower Sanskrit poets treat as the most delicate of all.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s anicham, the siris flower is the poet’s yardstick for softness, and the beloved is measured against it.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.”
christianity.explanation: The lover sets his beloved beside a lily and says she stands out among other women as a lily among thorns.
christianity.tie_back: Both poems praise the beloved through a delicate flower and declare her finer than everything around her.

islam.quote_or_event: “I have never touched silk or Dibaj (i.e. thick silk) softer than the palm of the Prophet (ﷺ) nor have I smelt a perfume nicer than the sweat of the Prophet.”
islam.explanation: Anas, who served the Prophet for years, describes him by saying even the finest silk was not as soft as his hand.
islam.tie_back: The same rhetorical move as the Kural: take the softest thing known and declare the person softer still.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I am a rose of Sharon, A lily of the valleys.”
judaism.explanation: The maiden of the Song of Songs describes herself in the language of wild flowers.
judaism.tie_back: Jewish love poetry, like the Kural, reaches first for flowers when it speaks of the beloved’s loveliness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada asks the reader to look closely at the body that is adorned and admired, calling it a painted image that is in truth frail and subject to decay.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism treats physical beauty as fragile and impermanent, and teaches that seeing this clearly loosens attachment.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural delights in the beloved’s delicacy; Buddhism notes the same delicacy but reads it as a sign of how quickly beauty passes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Do they look on a perishable body, i.e. the wise? and are they loud in praise of woman 's beauty?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poem Naladiyar opens its chapter on the impure body by asking whether the wise would ever loudly praise a woman’s beauty.
jainism.tie_back: This is the exact act the Kural’s lover performs, and the Jain poet rejects it as a mistake born of attachment.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 5.1 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You are the Emperor, and I call You a chief - how does this add to Your greatness?”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Bilaval, Guru Nanak says that any praise he can give the Lord falls short, like calling an emperor a mere chief.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the anicham flower as soft, then says the beloved is softer still; Guru Nanak likewise says every comparison falls short of the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 795, Raag Bilaval, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I never yet saw any one so beautiful, neither man nor woman, and am lost in admiration as I behold you.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Shipwrecked Odysseus, meeting the princess Nausicaa, addresses her with this superlative praise.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s lover, Odysseus declares a young woman beyond comparison with anything he has known.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Edmund Burke argues that smoothness and softness are among the qualities that most constantly produce the feeling of beauty, in touch as well as in sight.
philosophy.explanation: For Burke, beauty is tied to qualities that please gently, such as smooth and soft surfaces, rather than to the rough or massive.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural ranks the beloved’s beauty by its softness, exactly the quality Burke places near the heart of the beautiful.
philosophy.source: Edmund Burke, A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757), Part III, sect. 14 'Smoothness' (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Robert Burns writes A Red, Red Rose
real_life_example.event: In 1794 the Scottish poet Robert Burns produced the song now known as A Red, Red Rose. It compares the speaker's love to a red rose newly sprung in June and to a sweetly played melody, and goes on to promise that his love will last until the seas run dry. It became one of the best-known love lyrics in English and Scots.
real_life_example.explanation: The song shows how naturally poets in very different cultures reach for the freshest flower they know as the measure of the person they love.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the delicate anicham flower and then says the beloved is more delicate still; Burns likewise reaches for the finest flower he knows, a rose just opened in June, as the measure of his love.

tamil:
மலர்காணின் மையாத்தி நெஞ்சே இவள்கண்
பலர்காணும் பூவொக்கும் என்று.
transliteration:
Malarkaanin maiyaaththi nenjae ivalkan
palarkaanum poovokkum endru.
meaning: My heart, whenever you see flowers you get confused and think her eyes are like them. But flowers can be seen by anyone, and her eyes are not like that.
elementary: Suppose your best friend has a special smile. Whenever you see a smiley sticker, you think, 'That looks like my friend!' and get excited. Then you laugh at yourself: a sticker anyone can buy is nothing like the real smile.
university: The hero addresses his own nenju (நெஞ்சு, 'heart'), a common device in Tamil love poetry, and scolds it for its confusion (மையாத்தல், maiyaaththal, 'to be bewildered'). The flowers in question are taken by the commentators as kuvalai (குவளை, blue water-lily), the standard comparison for dark eyes; Puliyur Kesikan names the kuvalai explicitly. The sting is in palar kaanum (பலர் காணும், 'seen by many'): common flowers that every passer-by may look at cannot resemble eyes that he alone beholds, which Solomon Pappaiah brings out ('the eyes of my wife whom I alone see'); Kalaignar instead reads it as 'her eyes are a flower that many marvel at', a minority interpretation. Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes the verse as the hero rejecting the conventional comparison as unworthy. Pope: 'You deemed, as you saw the flowers, her eyes were as flowers, my soul, / That many may see.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The lotus over your ear is so near your eye, and so like it, that I was confused.”
hinduism.explanation: Dushyanta, asked to blow pollen from Shakuntala’s eye, excuses his slowness by saying the lotus she wears is so like her eye that he could not tell them apart.
hinduism.tie_back: Both lovers are bewildered by flowers that resemble the beloved’s eyes, though Kalidasa lets the likeness stand while the Kural denies it.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “The flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our land;”
christianity.explanation: The beloved calls his love to come out into a spring world full of flowers.
christianity.tie_back: For the lover in both poems the flowering world keeps turning his thoughts to the beloved.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an tells believing men to lower their gaze and guard their modesty, saying this is purer for them.
islam.explanation: Islamic ethics asks the eye not to wander after beauty, because the look itself can mislead the heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s lover finds his heart misled by every flower that reminds him of her eyes; Islam would counsel restraint of the gaze itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My beloved is mine, and I am his, That feedeth among the lilies.”
judaism.explanation: The maiden of the Song pictures her beloved among the lilies, so that the flowers and the lover belong to one picture.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved and the flowers are bound together in the lover’s mind.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that perception can be distorted (vipallasa): the untrained mind sees the permanent in the impermanent and the beautiful in what is not, and so is led astray.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism treats the mind’s quick leap from a sight to a pleasant fantasy as a distortion to be recognised.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover catches his own heart making a false likeness between common flowers and her eyes, a small case of the distortion the Buddha describes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you fall in love with every woman you see, you will be without hold like the Hatha-plant, driven before the wind.”
jainism.explanation: The nun Rajimati warns the monk Rathanemi that a heart that runs after every attractive sight has no anchor.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover also finds his heart swept away by every flower that reminds him of her eyes; Jainism sees that unsteadiness as the danger.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I can see no other as great as You; O Lord of Wisdom, You are pleasing to my mind.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Gauri, Guru Ram Das tells the Lord that nothing else he sees can stand beside Him, and that He alone delights his mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover tells his heart that common flowers, which anyone may look at, are no match for his beloved's eyes; Guru Ram Das also refuses to set anything beside the One he loves.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 305, Raag Gauri, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Apollo’s beloved Hyacinthus is killed by a discus, the god makes a flower spring from his blood and marks its petals with his grief, so that the flower forever recalls the youth.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s telling the flower becomes a living reminder of the one Apollo loved.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In both poems a flower calls up the beloved in the lover’s mind, though the Kural’s lover insists no flower is truly like her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: David Hume argues that beauty is not a quality in things themselves but exists in the mind that contemplates them, so that each mind may perceive a different beauty.
philosophy.explanation: For Hume, judgments of beauty depend on the sentiment of the observer.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s lover shows this at work: the flowers others admire seem to him nothing beside the eyes his own mind treasures.
philosophy.source: David Hume, 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Shakespeare's Sonnet 130 rejects the usual comparisons
real_life_example.event: Shakespeare's sonnets were first printed in 1609 in a quarto published by Thomas Thorpe. Sonnet 130 begins by saying that the poet's mistress's eyes are nothing like the sun, and goes on to deny that her lips are coral red or her cheeks like roses. In its closing couplet the poet says his love is as rare as any woman who has been praised with false comparisons.
real_life_example.explanation: The sonnet is famous for poking fun at the stock flattery of love poetry while still declaring real love.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural scolds the lover's heart for imagining that common flowers anyone can see resemble his beloved's eyes, and Sonnet 130 likewise refuses the stock comparisons for a mistress's eyes, insisting that she is beyond such ordinary likenesses.

tamil:
முறிமேனி முத்தம் முறுவல் வெறிநாற்றம்
வேலுண்கண் வேய்த்தோ ளவட்கு.
transliteration:
Murimaeni muththam muruval verinaatram
vaelunkan vaeyththo lavatku.
meaning: Her shoulders are like bamboo. Her skin is the color of young leaves, her smile is like pearls, she smells sweet, and her dark-lined eyes are as sharp as spears.
elementary: This is like drawing a picture of someone you love using things from nature: new green leaves for skin, shiny pearls for teeth, a flower-garden smell, and smooth bamboo for shoulders. Every part gets its own beautiful match.
university: This kural is a compact catalogue of the heroine’s features, each paired with its classical Tamil upamaanam (standard of comparison): muri (முறி, tender sprout, esp. of mango) for her complexion, muththam (முத்தம், pearl) for her smiling teeth (muruval), veri naatram (வெறி நாற்றம், natural fragrance, not applied scent) for her body’s scent, vel (வேல், lance) for her un-kan (உண்கண், kohl-'eaten' eyes) and vey (வேய், bamboo) for her rounded shoulders. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan all parse it as 'for her of bamboo shoulders: tender shoot is the body, pearl the teeth, fragrance the scent, lance the eyes', which is the Parimelazhagar construction; Sivayogi Sivakumar alone reads muththam as 'kiss', an outlier. The printed division 'வேய்த்தோ ளவட்கு' (ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net) is a metrical split of வேய்த்தோள் அவட்கு and not a variant. Pope: 'As tender shoot her frame; teeth, pearls; around her odours blend; / Darts are the eyes of her whose shoulders like the bambu bend.'

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Her arms are tender shoots; her lips / Are blossoms red and warm; / Bewitching youth begins to flower / In beauty on her form.”
hinduism.explanation: Watching Shakuntala among the hermitage trees, the king describes her body part by part in images from the garden.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s 'tender shoot' (muri) and Kalidasa’s 'tender shoots' belong to the same pan-Indian catalogue of beauty.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “thou hast doves' eyes within thy locks: thy hair is as a flock of goats, that appear from mount Gilead. Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep that are even shorn, which came up from the washing;”
christianity.explanation: The lover of the Song praises his beloved feature by feature, each with its own image from the land.
christianity.tie_back: Both poems use the catalogue form, matching eyes, teeth and more to images from nature.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [for them are] fair women with large, [beautiful] eyes, The likenesses of pearls well-protected,”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the companions of Paradise with beautiful eyes and likens them to guarded pearls.
islam.tie_back: Eyes and pearls, two of the Kural’s images of beauty, appear together here too.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thy teeth are like a flock of ewes, Which are come up from the washing; Whereof all are paired, And none faileth among them. Thy temples are like a pomegranate split open Behind thy veil.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs continues its feature-by-feature praise of the beloved with images from flock and orchard.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it praises the beloved’s teeth and face through careful natural comparisons.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like plaintain buds in their color, my teeth were once splendid. With age, they’re broken & yellowed. The truth of the Truth-speaker’s words doesn’t change.”
buddhism.explanation: The former courtesan Ambapali lists her once-famous features with their classic comparisons and then shows what age has done to each.
buddhism.tie_back: Ambapali uses the very catalogue the Kural uses for praise, but turns it into a lesson on impermanence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Shall I forsake asceticism because the senseless crowd would excite me, saying, Woman's eye is like the lotus in clear water, the Gyal fish, and the battle-spear?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet hears the very comparisons of love poetry and refuses to be moved, choosing to see the eye as it physically is.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s lance-like eye (vel-un-kan) is exactly the battle-spear the Naladiyar names and then rejects.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 5.4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Your eyes are so beautiful, and Your teeth are delightful. Your nose is so graceful, and Your hair is so long. Your body is so precious, cast in gold.”
sikhism.explanation: In a Vadhans chhant, Guru Nanak describes the beauty of the Lord feature by feature (eyes, teeth, nose, hair and a body like gold), while the Sikh commentators note that all beauty in creation is His.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural lists the beloved's body, smile, fragrance, eyes and shoulders, each with its classic comparison; Guru Nanak gives the same kind of feature-by-feature praise of the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 567, Raag Vadhans, Chhant, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I can only compare you to a young palm tree which I saw when I was at Delos growing near the altar of Apollo”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus compares the princess Nausicaa to a young palm he once saw springing up at Delos.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s 'tender shoot', the Greek hero finds the image for a young woman’s beauty in fresh young growth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Diotima teaches that the lover begins by loving one beautiful body, then sees that the beauty of every body is akin, and rises from there to beauty of soul, of laws and of knowledge.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats admiration of bodily features as only the first step on a ladder toward beauty itself.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural lingers lovingly on the first rung, the beloved’s body; Plato honours that step but urges the lover to climb beyond it.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 210a-d (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Kalidasa's Meghaduta describes the yaksha's beloved
real_life_example.event: The Sanskrit poet Kalidasa, writing in about the fifth century CE, composed the Meghaduta (The Cloud Messenger), a lyric love poem of some 115 verses. In it an exiled yaksha, a nature spirit, asks a monsoon cloud to carry a message to his beloved in the Himalayan city of Alaka, and much of the poem describes the landscapes along the cloud's route. In its second part the yaksha describes his very beautiful wife and her lonely state at home.
real_life_example.explanation: The Meghaduta is one of the most admired poems of classical India, and it shaped how later Indian poets wrote about longing and beauty.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural paints the beloved's beauty through images taken from nature, and the Meghaduta likewise carries its reader through the natural world before arriving at a lover's description of his wife's beauty.

tamil:
காணின் குவளை கவிழ்ந்து நிலன்நோக்கும்
மாணிழை கண்ணொவ்வேம் என்று.
transliteration:
Kaanin kuvalai kavizhndhu nilannoakkum
maanizhai kannovvaem endru.
meaning: If the blue water lilies could see her, they would hang their heads and stare at the ground, saying, 'We cannot match the eyes of this girl with fine jewels.'
elementary: Picture the prettiest flowers in a garden suddenly able to see. They look at a girl’s lovely eyes, feel shy, and droop their heads, as if saying, 'We can’t compete with that!'
university: The conceit (a form of what later poetics calls tharkurippetram, attributing a feeling to something that has none) gives the kuvalai (குவளை, blue water-lily, the stock comparison for eyes) the power of sight and shame: it would kavizhndhu nilan nokkum (கவிழ்ந்து நிலன் நோக்கும், 'bend down and look at the ground'), the gesture of a defeated or abashed person. The botanical observation behind it is that the kuvalai flower droops on its stalk. Maanizhai (மாணிழை, 'she of excellent jewels') is a standard epithet for the heroine. Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah agree on the sense; Pappaiah adds 'out of shame' (நாணத்தால்). In the Parimelazhagar tradition this kural follows 1112 as its answer: the flower itself knows it cannot match her eyes. Pope (who translates kuvalai as 'lotus'): 'The lotus, seeing her, with head demiss, the ground would eye.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The meanest vesture glows / On beauty that enchants: / The lotus lovelier shows / Amid dull water-plants;”
hinduism.explanation: The king, seeing Shakuntala in her plain bark dress, says her beauty outshines its setting as a lotus outshines the dull water-plants around it.
hinduism.tie_back: Both poets measure the beloved against the water-flowers, and in both the flowers come off second.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices!”
christianity.explanation: The lover says his beloved surpasses the finest wine and every spice.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Song sets the beloved above the best things of nature, which lose by the comparison.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when they saw him, they greatly admired him and cut their hands and said, ‘Perfect is Allāh! This is not a man; this is none but a noble angel.’”
islam.explanation: The women of the city, seeing Joseph, are so overcome by his beauty that they cut their hands and declare him beyond any human standard.
islam.tie_back: As the Kural’s flowers admit defeat before her eyes, the onlookers here admit no human comparison can hold.

judaism.quote_or_event: “all people compared to Sarah are like a monkey compared to a human, as Sarah was exceedingly beautiful”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud expresses Sarah’s beauty by saying that everyone else, set beside her, looks like a monkey beside a person.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts praise beauty by showing how badly anything else fares in the comparison.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 58a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Radiant, brilliant like jewels, my eyes: With age, they’re no longer splendid. The truth of the Truth-speaker’s words doesn’t change.”
buddhism.explanation: Ambapali remembers that her eyes once shone like jewels and notes that age has dimmed them.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes outshine the water-lilies; Ambapali’s jewel-bright eyes remind the reader that such splendour too will fade.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you owned the beauty of Vaisramana, the pleasing manners of Nalakubara, if you were like Purandara himself, I should have no desire for you.”
jainism.explanation: The nun Rajimati tells the tempted monk that even the beauty of the gods would not move her from her vows.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural sets beauty above every rival; the Jain heroine sets her vow above every beauty.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.41 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the Fear of God, the sun shines, and in the Fear of God, the moon reflects.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak describes the whole of nature, sun, moon, wind and water, as moving in awe of God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural imagines the water-lilies bowing their heads in shame before the beloved's eyes; Guru Nanak pictures all of nature humbled in awe before God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 464, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “then is Leto proud at seeing her daughter stand a full head taller than the others, and eclipse the loveliest amid a whole bevy of beauties), even so did the girl outshine her handmaids.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer compares Nausicaa among her maids to Artemis among the nymphs, outshining even the loveliest.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s flowers that bow their heads, the other beauties here are eclipsed by the one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Hippias Major Socrates cites Heraclitus: the most beautiful ape is ugly compared with the human race, and the most beautiful girl would look plain beside a god.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the example to show that beauty judged by comparison always depends on what it is compared with.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural plays the same comparative game in reverse: the lovely kuvalai becomes plain beside her eyes.

real_life_example.event_title: The bust of Nefertiti is found at Amarna
real_life_example.place: Amarna, Egypt; now in the Neues Museum, Berlin, Germany
real_life_example.event: On 6 December 1912 a German excavation led by the archaeologist Ludwig Borchardt found a painted limestone bust of Queen Nefertiti in the ruins of the workshop of the court sculptor Thutmose at Amarna, Egypt. The bust is about 3,300 years old, and Nefertiti's name is usually translated as the beautiful one has come. Borchardt wrote in his diary of the find's liveliness, and the bust is now displayed in the Neues Museum in Berlin.
real_life_example.explanation: The bust became one of the most famous images of beauty from the ancient world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural imagines that the blue water-lilies, if they could see the beloved's eyes, would hang their heads in defeat; Nefertiti's face is a real-world case of beauty that, more than three thousand years later, still makes admirers feel that nothing else compares.

tamil:
அனிச்சப்பூக் கால்களையாள் பெய்தாள் நுகப்பிற்கு
நல்ல படாஅ பறை.
transliteration:
Anichchappook kaalkalaiyaal peydhaal nukappirku
nalla pataaa parai.
meaning: She has put anicham flowers (very light, delicate flowers) in her hair without taking off their stems. Their weight will break her slender waist, and no happy drums will play now.
elementary: This is a funny exaggeration, like saying, 'She is so light that one extra feather in her hair might tip her over!' The poet pretends her waist is so delicate that even tiny flower stems are too heavy for it.
