university: A deliberate hyperbole (உயர்வு நவிற்சி): the heroine has put anicham flowers in her hair kaal kalaiyaal (கால் களையாள், 'without plucking off the stalks'), and the poet pretends that the weight of those tiny stalks will break her nukappu (நுகப்பு, waist). Nalla padaa parai (நல்ல படாஅ பறை, with the metrical lengthening படாஅ) means 'drums that are good will not sound', i.e. only the drums of mourning, not festive drums; this is the reading of Parimelazhagar’s tradition followed by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, while Solomon Pappaiah glosses parai as 'auspicious sounds'. Kalaignar narrates it as already happened ('her waist has broken'), a dramatised variant of the same sense. Pope’s version alters the scene to a girdle of flowers: 'The flowers of the sensitive plant as a girdle around her she placed; / The stems she forgot to nip off; they’ll weigh down the delicate waist.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You are delicate as a jasmine blossom, yet he tells you to fill the trenches about the trees.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala’s friend teases that the hermit-father loads so delicate a girl with the work of watering the trees.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts imagine the beloved as too delicate for even a slight burden.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes.”
christianity.explanation: The Song asks for the little foxes to be caught because the young vines are tender and easily harmed.
christianity.tie_back: Both poems dwell on something so tender that the smallest thing can damage it.

islam.quote_or_event: “May Allah be merciful to you, O Anjasha! Drive the camels slowly, as they are carrying glass vessels!”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells the camel-driver to slow down because the women riding are delicate as glass.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it pictures women as so delicate that even small strain must be avoided.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For thou shalt no more be called Tender and delicate.”
judaism.explanation: The prophet addresses Babylon as a pampered young woman who will lose her tender, delicate life.
judaism.tie_back: 'Tender and delicate' is the Kural’s praise of the heroine, but Isaiah uses it of a city about to fall.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada warns that death carries off the person who goes about only gathering the flowers of pleasure, as a flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
buddhism.explanation: The image of plucking flowers stands for absorption in sense pleasures.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wearing anicham flowers is a playful image of fragile beauty; the Buddhist verse turns flower-gathering into a warning about fragile life.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Firm and decided she cut off her tresses which were black like bees and dressed with a brush and comb.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, abandoned on her wedding day by the future Jina Neminatha, renounces the world and cuts off her carefully dressed hair.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural lingers on flowers set in a lover’s hair; the Jain heroine’s hair, just as beautiful, is given up for the path of renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Your eyes are so beautiful, and Your teeth are delightful.”
sikhism.explanation: No passage in Gurbani matches this kural's playful hyperbole about a waist too delicate to bear flower stalks; the nearest Sikh parallel is Guru Nanak's Vadhans chhant, which praises the Beloved's beauty in loving detail.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural exaggerates the beloved's delicacy for comic effect; Gurbani shares only the loving attention to the Beloved's beauty, not the joke.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 567, Raag Vadhans, Chhant, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Aphrodite enters the battle at Troy to rescue her son, Diomedes wounds her delicate hand, and she flees to Olympus in pain, mocked as a goddess unfit for war.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer portrays the goddess of beauty as too tender for the harsh world of battle.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is too delicate even for flower stalks; Homer’s Aphrodite is too delicate for a spear-graze.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Burke holds that an air of robustness and strength is very prejudicial to beauty, while an appearance of delicacy, and even of fragility, is almost essential to it.
philosophy.explanation: In his account of the beautiful, Burke links beauty with smallness and delicacy rather than strength.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s joke about a waist too fragile for flower stalks is an extreme case of the delicacy Burke calls almost essential to beauty.
philosophy.source: Edmund Burke, A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757), Part III, sect. 16 'Delicacy' (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Anna Pavlova first dances The Dying Swan
real_life_example.event: The choreographer Michel Fokine created the short solo The Dying Swan for the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova, set to Le Cygne from Camille Saint-Saëns's Carnival of the Animals. The dance portrays the last moments of a fragile, wounded swan. It became the role for which Pavlova is best remembered, and she performed it throughout her career.
real_life_example.explanation: The solo became one of the most famous images in ballet of beauty so delicate that it seems about to break.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural jokes that the beloved's waist is so slender that the weight of a few flower stalks could break it and bring out the mourning drums; Pavlova's swan made that idea of breakable delicacy into a famous work of art.

tamil:
மதியும் மடந்தை முகனும் அறியா
பதியின் கலங்கிய மீன்.
transliteration:
Madhiyum madandhai mukanum ariyaa
padhiyin kalangiya meen.
meaning: The stars cannot tell the moon apart from this young woman's face, so they are confused and wander from their places.
elementary: Imagine the stars as a class of children who always stand near their teacher, the moon. One night a girl with a face as bright as the moon walks by, and the stars get mixed up: 'Which one is our moon?' They start running about in a muddle.
university: A cosmic hyperbole: the meen (மீன், stars; literally 'fish', the common Tamil word for stars) cannot tell madhi (மதி, moon) from the madandhai’s (மடந்தை, young woman’s) mukan (முகன், face) and are kalangiya (கலங்கிய, 'agitated, confused') in their pathi (பதி, 'fixed station'). In the Parimelazhagar tradition the stars, which in Indian astronomy move in fixed relation to the moon through the lunar mansions (naksatra), are thrown out of their courses by seeing two moons. All the modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesikan) agree on 'the stars are troubled and leave their places'. This kural opens a run of four (1116-1119) built on the moon-and-face comparison. Pope: 'The stars perplexed are rushing wildly from their spheres; / For like another moon this maiden’s face appears.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the moon and thou inspire confidence, only to deceive the host of lovers.”
hinduism.explanation: The love-sick king complains to the god of Love that both Love and the moon promise comfort but only torment lovers.
hinduism.tie_back: In both texts the moon’s light unsettles those who look on it, though Kalidasa blames the moon and the Kural blames the beloved’s rival brightness.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “My dove, my undefiled is but one; she is the only one of her mother, she is the choice one of her that bare her. The daughters saw her, and blessed her;”
christianity.explanation: The lover says his beloved is unique, and all who see her are moved to praise her.
christianity.tie_back: As the Kural’s stars are thrown into confusion by her face, everyone who sees the Song’s beloved is overwhelmed.

islam.quote_or_event: “I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) on a clear night, so I looked at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and at the moon, and he was wearing a red Hullah, and he looked better than the moon to me.”
islam.explanation: Jabir ibn Samurah recalls looking back and forth between the Prophet and the moon on a bright night and finding the Prophet the more beautiful.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s stars, Jabir compares a face with the moon on the same night, and the face wins.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Esther obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her.”
judaism.explanation: When Esther’s turn came to go before the king, everyone who saw her was won over.
judaism.tie_back: As the stars are unsettled by the Kural’s heroine, all who look on Esther are moved by her.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that one who takes up the good path after heedlessness lights up the world like the moon freed from clouds.
buddhism.explanation: The moon emerging from cloud is a Buddhist image for the radiance of a transformed life.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s face shines like the moon; Buddhism keeps the image of moonlight but gives it to the light of a purified mind.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The kingfisher, mistaking my wife's eyes for a gyal-fish, will fly after her, but when it sees her beautiful eyebrow it will forbear to strike, afraid and supposing it a bow.”
jainism.explanation: In the Naladiyar’s love chapter a kingfisher is fooled by the wife’s fish-like eyes and then frightened off by her bow-like brow.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s stars, a creature of nature mistakes the beloved’s features for the real thing and is thrown into confusion.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 40.5 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the bowl of the sky, the sun and moon are the lamps; the stars in the constellations are the pearls.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Aarti, Guru Nanak pictures the whole sky as a worship tray, with the sun, moon and stars arranged in praise of the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the stars are thrown into confusion because the beloved's face looks like a second moon; Guru Nanak too puts the moon and stars in the service of the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 663, Raag Dhanasari, Aarti, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The stars about the full moon lose their bright beauty when she, almost full, illumines all earth with silver.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho observes that the stars seem to hide their brightness when the full moon rises, a figure she uses for one woman outshining others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s stars are confused by a face like the moon; Sappho’s stars fade beside the moon itself, the same celestial picture of overwhelming radiance.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho, fragment 34 (Lobel-Page), as rendered in Poems of Sappho, no. 4 (sacred-texts.com)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato’s Socrates says that of all the Forms, beauty alone shines through the clearest of our senses, sight, so that it is the most visible and most loved.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, beauty is the one ideal whose radiance can be seen directly in the world.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s face is so radiant that even the stars mistake it for the moon, a playful picture of beauty that shines out beyond everything else.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 250b-d (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Chinese astronomers record the guest star of 1054
real_life_example.event: On 4 July 1054 astronomers of the Song dynasty in China recorded the sudden appearance of a new star, which they called a guest star, near the star now known as Zeta Tauri. It was bright enough to be seen in daylight for about 23 days and remained visible at night for nearly two years. Modern astronomers identify it as the supernova whose remains form the Crab Nebula.
real_life_example.explanation: The Chinese records are among the most important observations in the history of astronomy, linking an ancient sighting to an object still studied today.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural imagines the stars thrown into confusion because a second moon, the beloved's face, has appeared among them; the guest star of 1054 is a real occasion when a strange new brilliance appeared and disturbed the familiar order of the sky.

tamil:
அறுவாய் நிறைந்த அவிர்மதிக்குப் போல
மறுவுண்டோ மாதர் முகத்து.
transliteration:
Aruvaai niraindha avirmadhikkup poala
maruvundoa maadhar mukaththu.
meaning: The bright moon grows full again after shrinking, yet it has a dark spot. Is there any such mark on this woman's face?
elementary: The moon is lovely, but if you look closely you can see dark patches on it. The poet looks at his beloved’s face and says, 'The moon has spots, but her face has none at all.'
university: This kural answers the confusion of 1116: why should the stars be confused, when the face differs from the moon? Aruvaai niraindha (அறுவாய் நிறைந்த, 'whose cut-away parts have filled up') describes the moon that waxes after waning, and avir madhi (அவிர் மதி, 'shining moon') its full splendour; yet the moon has a maru (மறு, 'blemish, spot', the dark marks traditionally seen as a hare), which the woman’s face lacks. Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan make the link with 1116 explicit ('why should the stars be troubled?'); Sivayogi Sivakumar reads maru as 'change', an outlier gloss. The rhetorical question (வினா) carries the force of denial, as in Parimelazhagar’s construal. Pope: 'In moon, that waxing waning shines, as spots appear, / Are any spots discerned in face of maiden here?' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The moon in added splendour / Shines for its spot of dark; / Yet more the maiden slender / Charms in her dress of bark.”
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s king says that just as the moon’s dark spot only adds to its splendour, Shakuntala’s plain bark dress only adds to her charm.
hinduism.tie_back: Both poets set the beloved beside the moon’s spot: Kalidasa makes the flaw an ornament, the Kural says her face has no flaw at all.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.”
christianity.explanation: The lover of the Song declares his beloved wholly beautiful and without blemish.
christianity.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own claim: the beloved, unlike the moon, has no spot.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the moon - We have determined for it phases, until it returns [appearing] like the old date stalk.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an points to the moon’s waxing and waning as a sign of God’s ordering of creation.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too notes the moon’s waning and filling out; Islam reads the phases as a sign, the Kural as a mark of the moon’s imperfection beside her face.

judaism.quote_or_event: “the maiden was of beautiful form and fair to look on”
judaism.explanation: The Book of Esther introduces its heroine with a simple statement of her beauty.
judaism.tie_back: Esther is presented as beautiful without qualification, as the Kural’s heroine is praised as having no blemish.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He, who, like the moon, is spotless and pure, serene and clear, who has destroyed the delight in existence — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the perfected person to a spotless, clear moon.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural denies the moon is spotless in order to praise a face; the Dhammapada calls the moon spotless in order to praise a purified mind.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Even the hare in the wide, beauteous, and sublime heavens, since it is seen in the moon with refulgent beams, will be adored (by men).”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar notes that the dark hare-mark in the moon is admired only because it sits in the bright moon, and applies this to people raised by good company.
jainism.tie_back: The same hare-mark is the 'spot' the Kural says the beloved’s face is free of.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 18.6 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He has no stain, so I have no pollution.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Asa, Guru Arjan says the Lord is untouched by any stain of Maya, and the devotee who belongs to Him becomes stainless too.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the moon carries a spot but the beloved's face has none; Guru Arjan calls the Beloved Lord wholly without stain.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 391, Raag Asa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Homeric Hymn to Selene praises the Moon goddess, whose radiance spreads over the earth when she bathes and puts on shining garments, and is brightest when her orb is full.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek hymns treat the full moon as a figure of supreme radiance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural concedes the full moon’s brilliance before claiming that her face surpasses it by having no blemish.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Diotima describes beauty itself as everlasting, neither coming to be nor passing away, neither waxing nor waning, and not beautiful in one part and ugly in another.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, true beauty is free of the changes and flaws found in beautiful things.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s moon waxes, wanes and bears a spot; the beloved’s face, like Plato’s ideal, is praised as without blemish.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 211a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Galileo shows that the Moon is not flawless
real_life_example.event: From late November to mid-December 1609 Galileo Galilei observed and sketched the Moon through his telescope. In Sidereus Nuncius (The Starry Messenger), printed in Venice in March 1610, he reported that the Moon's surface was not smooth and perfect, as followers of Aristotle had taught, but rough and uneven, with dark markings, mountains and hollows.
real_life_example.explanation: Galileo's observation helped overturn the old belief that the heavens were perfect and unchanging.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks whether the beloved's face carries any blemish like the dark spots on the bright moon; Galileo's telescope showed that the moon really is marked and uneven, the very flaw the poet says her face does not share.

tamil:
மாதர் முகம்போல் ஒளிவிட வல்லையேல்
காதலை வாழி மதி.
transliteration:
Maadhar mukampoal olivida vallaiyael
kaadhalai vaazhi madhi.
meaning: Long live the moon! If you could shine like this woman's face, you would win my love too.
elementary: It is like telling the moon, 'You’re nice, Moon, but if you could glow as brightly as my best friend’s happy face, then I’d love you too!'
university: The hero now speaks to the moon directly (an apostrophe, as to the anicham in 1111), blessing it with vaazhi (வாழி, 'may you flourish') and offering a conditional: vallaiyel (வல்லையேல், 'if you are able') to shine (oli vida) like her face, kaadhalai (காதலை, 'you would be one beloved', the verbal noun as predicate) by him. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan: 'you too would earn my love as she does'; Solomon Pappaiah: 'if you shine so that I rejoice, you would win my love'; Kalaignar reads it rather differently, as advice to the moon to shine like her face if it wants to be loved. The playful implication, as Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes it, is that the moon cannot meet the condition. Pope: 'Farewell, O moon! If that thine orb could shine / Bright as her face, thou shouldst be love of mine.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And is it selfish longing then, / That draws our souls on high / Through eyes that have forgot to wink, / As the new moon climbs the sky?”
hinduism.explanation: The king defends his love for Shakuntala by comparing his rapt gaze at her to the way all eyes are drawn to the rising new moon.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts set the beloved and the moon side by side as objects of rapt, loving gaze.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act II (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?”
christianity.explanation: The Song praises the beloved as beautiful as the moon and bright as the sun.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Song sets the beloved’s radiance on a level with the moon’s.

islam.quote_or_event: Al-Bara' was asked, “Was the face of the Prophet (as bright) as a sword?” He said, “No, but (as bright) as a moon.”
islam.explanation: Asked to describe the Prophet’s face, a companion chooses the moon rather than a sword as the right image of its brightness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too measures a face against the moon’s brightness, though it claims the face shines brighter.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and favour in his sight more than all the virgins”
judaism.explanation: Esther wins the king’s love above every other candidate.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural says the moon could win the lover’s heart only by matching her; in Esther, no rival could match the one the king loved.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The sun shines by day, the moon shines by night. The warrior shines in armor, the holy man shines in meditation. But the Buddha shines resplendent all day and all night.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ranks the Buddha’s radiance above that of the sun and moon, which shine only in their own time.
buddhism.tie_back: As the Kural claims a face brighter than the moon, the Dhammapada claims a radiance that outshines it, but the radiance is spiritual.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Now this daughter of an excellent king was virtuous and well looking; she possessed all lucky marks of the body, and shone forth like the lightning Saudamani.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana describes the princess Rajimati, betrothed to Neminatha, as radiant like lightning.
jainism.tie_back: Jain scripture too reaches for a light in the sky to describe a woman’s radiance, as the Kural does with the moon.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Millions of moons twinkle in the sky.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir lists the vast powers that serve the Lord, among them millions of moons that give light at His door, as the Punjabi commentators explain.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the moon it would be loved only if it could shine like the beloved's face; Kabir's Lord is so radiant that millions of moons are merely His lamps.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1162, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Selene, the Moon, falls in love with the beautiful shepherd Endymion and visits him as he sleeps in eternal youth on Mount Latmos.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth the moon herself is a lover, drawn by mortal beauty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural offers the moon a chance to be loved; Greek myth makes the moon the one who loves a mortal’s beauty.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Thomas Aquinas names three conditions of beauty: integrity or perfection, due proportion or harmony, and clarity or brightness.
philosophy.explanation: For Aquinas, radiance is one of the marks by which a thing is beautiful.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes brightness the test the moon must pass to be loved, treating clarity as the heart of beauty as Aquinas does.
philosophy.source: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 39, a. 8 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Beethoven dedicates the Moonlight Sonata to Giulietta Guicciardi
real_life_example.event: In 1801 Ludwig van Beethoven completed his Piano Sonata in C-sharp minor, Op. 27 No. 2, which was published in Vienna in 1802 with a dedication to the young Countess Giulietta Guicciardi, who had studied with him. Beethoven was deeply drawn to her and described her to friends as a lovely, enchanting girl. The name Moonlight Sonata was given only in the 1830s, when the poet Ludwig Rellstab compared its first movement to a boat on Lake Lucerne in moonlight.
real_life_example.explanation: The sonata became one of the most famous piano pieces ever written, and its best-known name joins the moon to a work first offered to a young woman Beethoven admired.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural blesses the moon and tells it that it could win the poet's love only by shining like the beloved's face; in Beethoven's sonata the moon arrived only later as a nickname, while the music itself was given to the woman he admired.

tamil:
மலரன்ன கண்ணாள் முகமொத்தி யாயின்
பலர்காணத் தோன்றல் மதி.
transliteration:
Malaranna kannaal mukamoththi yaayin
palarkaanath thoandral madhi.
meaning: Moon, if you want to be like the face of the girl whose eyes are like flowers, do not show yourself where everyone can see you.
elementary: Think of a special treasure you keep in a box just for yourself. The poet tells the moon: 'If you want to be as special as her face, don’t show yourself to everyone. Her face is like a treasure only I get to see.'
university: The moon sequence closes with a second condition: if the moon is to resemble (oththi, ஒத்தி, 'you resemble') the face of malaranna kannaal (மலரன்ன கண்ணாள், 'she whose eyes are like flowers'), it must not appear palar kaana (பலர் காண, 'for many to see'), since her face is seen by him alone. The idea picks up palar kaanum ('seen by many') from 1112, and Solomon Pappaiah draws the link: 'appear for me alone, not for all to see'. Kalaignar reads it as advice to the moon to stay hidden so as not to lose the comparison; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan give the plain prohibition. The exclusivity reflects the kalavu (secret love) setting, in which the heroine is unseen by others. Pope: 'If as her face, whose eyes are flowers, thou wouldst have charms for me, / Shine for my eyes alone, O moon, shine not for all to see!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “She seems a flower whose fragrance none has tasted, / A gem uncut by workman’s tool, / A branch no desecrating hands have wasted, / Fresh honey, beautifully cool.”
hinduism.explanation: The king describes Shakuntala, raised in a forest hermitage, as a beauty no one else has yet known.
hinduism.tie_back: Both lovers treasure a beauty that is not on show to the world.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act II (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed.”
christianity.explanation: The lover pictures his beloved as an enclosed garden and a sealed fountain, kept for him alone.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s wish for exclusivity: a beauty not open to every passer-by.

islam.quote_or_event: “Fair ones reserved in pavilions -”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the companions of Paradise as beauties kept secluded in pavilions.
islam.tie_back: Like the face the Kural would keep from 'many eyes', this beauty is reserved and hidden.

judaism.quote_or_event: “O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the covert of the cliff, Let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; For sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.”
judaism.explanation: The lover calls to the beloved hidden like a dove in the rocks, asking that her face be shown to him.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved’s face is hidden from the world and longed for by one lover.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says he knows of no other single sight that so overpowers a man’s mind as the form of a woman.
buddhism.explanation: Early Buddhism recognises the overwhelming effect of visible beauty on the mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural wants such a beauty kept from many eyes; Buddhism explains why it unsettles every beholder.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though women be high in reputation and equal to the goddess Ayrani in conjugal fidelity, they must carefully avoid those who love them, and follow them in hopes of gratification, for such caution is the safeguard of the virtue of matrons with perfumed foreheads.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar counsels virtuous women to keep away from admirers who pursue them.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural wants the beloved’s beauty kept from many eyes; the Jain poet makes that reserve a safeguard of virtue.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 39.1 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Gurmukh sees Him with intuitive ease.”
sikhism.explanation: In Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak says the Lord, hidden from most people, is seen naturally by the Gurmukh, the one who follows the Guru.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks the moon not to shine for all to see, since the beloved's face is seen by the lover alone; in Gurbani the Beloved also stays hidden from the many and is seen by the one who loves Him through the Guru.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 222, Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Candaules of Lydia, proud of his wife’s beauty, insists that his bodyguard Gyges secretly see her; the queen discovers it, and the episode costs Candaules his throne and his life.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus tells the story as a warning about a man who would not keep his wife’s beauty private.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s lover wants the beloved’s face seen by no one else; Candaules’s ruin shows the opposite impulse punished.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that if a lover imagines the beloved joined to another as closely as to himself, he will feel hatred toward the beloved and envy toward the rival; this is jealousy.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza analyses the wish to possess the beloved’s attention exclusively.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s demand that the moon not appear for all to see is a gentle, poetic form of the possessive love Spinoza dissects.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Proposition 35 and Scholium (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Elizabeth Barrett Browning's private Sonnets from the Portuguese
real_life_example.event: During her courtship with the poet Robert Browning, around 1845 and 1846, Elizabeth Barrett wrote a sequence of 44 love sonnets that she had not intended to publish. Robert later persuaded her of their worth, and they appeared in her Poems of 1850. She called them Sonnets from the Portuguese, suggesting they were translations, to protect the privacy of such personal poems; the title probably came from Robert's pet name for her.
real_life_example.explanation: The sequence became one of the best-loved collections of love poetry in English, yet it began as words meant for one reader only.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural tells the moon that to resemble the beloved's face it must not show itself for everyone to see, because her face is for one viewer alone; Barrett's sonnets were likewise written for one reader, and even when published they were disguised as translations.

tamil:
அனிச்சமும் அன்னத்தின் தூவியும் மாதர்
அடிக்கு நெருஞ்சிப் பழம்.
transliteration:
Anichchamum annaththin thooviyum maadhar
atikku nerunjip pazham.
meaning: Even the anicham flower (a flower so soft it wilts at a touch) and a swan's soft feathers feel like prickly thorn burrs to this woman's feet.
elementary: Imagine feet so tender that walking on a fluffy cotton ball feels like stepping on a prickly burr. That is how gently the poet imagines his beloved, as a playful, loving exaggeration.
university: The chapter ends as it began, with the anicham (1111), now joined by the annaththin thuvi (அன்னத்தின் தூவி, the swan’s down), the two classical standards of softness; both are said to be nerunjip pazham (நெருஞ்சிப் பழம், the spiny fruit of the caltrop, Tribulus terrestris) to her adi (அடி, feet). The figure is a hyperbole of delicacy in which the softest things become sharp; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'like nerunji thorns', Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan 'they cause pain as the nerunji fruit does'. Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes pazham here as the ripe, hardened fruit with its spines. Some commentators take maadhar as women in general, others (Pappaiah, Kalaignar) as the speaker’s own beloved; the context of the chapter supports the latter. Pope: 'The flower of the sensitive plant, and the down on the swan’s white breast, / As the thorn are harsh, by the delicate feet of this maiden pressed.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Anusuya, my foot is cut on a sharp blade of grass, and my dress is caught on an amaranth twig. Wait for me while I loosen it.”
hinduism.explanation: As she leaves, Shakuntala claims a blade of grass has cut her foot, a pretext to linger and glance back at the king.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts imagine the heroine’s feet hurt by the gentlest of things, though in Kalidasa it is a coy excuse.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)

christianity.quote_or_event: “How beautiful are thy feet with shoes, O prince's daughter!”
christianity.explanation: The Song begins its praise of the beloved with her feet.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Song lingers on the beauty of the beloved’s feet.

islam.quote_or_event: “As if they were [delicate] eggs, well-protected.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an likens the companions of Paradise to delicate, carefully sheltered eggs.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes a beauty so delicate it must be shielded from any roughness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The tender and delicate woman among you, who would not adventure to set the sole of her foot upon the ground for delicateness and tenderness”
judaism.explanation: Deuteronomy describes a woman so pampered and delicate that she would not set her foot on the ground.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s image almost exactly: feet too delicate to touch even the softest surface.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As if they were stuffed with soft cotton, both my feet were once splendid. With age, they’re shriveled & cracked. The truth of the Truth-speaker’s words doesn’t change.”
buddhism.explanation: Ambapali remembers her once soft and lovely feet and shows how age has changed them.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural praises feet softer than swan’s down; Ambapali’s cotton-soft feet remind us that such softness does not last.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the henna-dyed cotton was applied to the foot of my daughter of beauteous form, and whose mouth is perfumed like the red lotus, she would say, Gently, gently, and withdraw her foot lest it should be hurt by the cotton. How then will that foot be able to travel the gravelly paths of the forest?”
jainism.explanation: A mother in the Naladiyar remembers that her daughter’s feet were so tender she flinched even at soft cotton, and fears for her on the rough forest road.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s own hyperbole of feet hurt by the softest things, in a Tamil Jain poem.
jainism.source: Naladiyar 40.6 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, the path is muddy, and the house of my Beloved is so far away.”
sikhism.explanation: In his saloks, Sheikh Farid describes the lover hesitating at a muddy lane on the way to the Beloved's house; the following lines (paraphrased) weigh a soaked blanket against a broken heart, and he chooses to go.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures feet so delicate that even swan's down feels like thorns; Farid also dwells on the hardships of the lover's path, though for him love makes the rough road worth walking.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells that when Aphrodite first stepped ashore on Cyprus, grass grew up beneath her shapely feet.
greek_mythology.explanation: The earth itself softens and blooms under the goddess of beauty’s tread.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural imagines the softest things too rough for her feet; Hesiod imagines the ground turning green to receive them.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Theogony 194-195 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Agathon says Love is tender: as Homer says the goddess Ate has tender feet because she walks not on the ground but on the heads of men, so Love walks and dwells in the softest of all things, the hearts and souls of gods and men.
philosophy.explanation: In Plato’s dialogue, tenderness of foot becomes a sign of delicacy so great that only the softest things can bear it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s conceit in philosophical form: feet so tender that only the softest of things will do.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 195d-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Hans Christian Andersen publishes The Princess and the Pea
real_life_example.event: On 8 May 1835 the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen published The Princess and the Pea in his first collection of Fairy Tales Told for Children. In the tale an old queen tests a young woman who claims to be a real princess by placing a single pea under twenty mattresses and twenty eiderdown feather beds. In the morning the woman says she slept badly because something hard bruised her, and this extreme sensitivity proves she is a true princess.
real_life_example.explanation: The tale became one of the best-known fairy tales in the world and a byword for extraordinary delicacy.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even the soft anicham flower and swan's down feel like thorny burrs to the beloved's tender feet, and Andersen's princess, bruised by a single pea through forty layers of bedding, is the most famous storybook version of the same playful exaggeration.

tamil:
பாலொடு தேன்கலந் தற்றே பணிமொழி
வாலெயிறு ஊறிய நீர்.
transliteration:
Paalodu thaenkalandh thatrae panimozhi
vaaleyiru ooriya neer.
meaning: The wetness on the white teeth of this softly speaking girl is like milk and honey mixed together.
elementary: Think of the sweetest drink you can imagine, warm milk with a spoon of honey stirred in. The poet says that being close to the person he loves feels that sweet. It is his way of saying that love makes everything about the beloved seem delightful.
university: Chapter 113 belongs to the kalaviyal (the section on secret, premarital love) and opens with the hero speaking after union, declaring the special excellence (sirappu) of the love itself rather than of the beloved's looks, which was the topic of ch. 112. Pani-mozhi (பணிமொழி, 'gentle, deferential speech') names the heroine by her soft voice, and vaal-eyiru (வாலெயிறு, 'white teeth') is a stock feature of the akam heroine; ooriya neer ('the water that wells up') is a decorous image for the sweetness of a kiss. Milk-and-honey (paalodu thaen) is the classical Tamil figure for perfect sweetness; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss the line this way, Pope renders 'The dew on her white teeth, whose voice is soft and low, / Is as when milk and honey mingled flow', and the commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar reads the chapter's first five couplets as the hero's words. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In an Atharvaveda love charm the speaker declares that honey is on the tip and at the root of his tongue, asking that his speech and presence become as sweet as honey to the one he loves.
hinduism.explanation: The hymn uses honey (madhu) as the measure of sweetness that love should carry between two people.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it reaches for honey on the tongue to express the sweetness of lovers' closeness.
hinduism.source: Atharvaveda 1.34 (charm with licorice to secure a woman's love; cf. tr. Maurice Bloomfield, SBE 42) (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs opens with the beloved longing for a kiss and ranking love above the best drink she knows.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise ranks the sweetness of the beloved's mouth above the finest drink, milk mixed with honey.

islam.quote_or_event: “rivers of milk the taste of which never changes, rivers of wine delicious to those who drink, and rivers of purified honey”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes Paradise with rivers of unspoiled milk and purified honey as images of perfect, lasting delight.
islam.tie_back: Milk and honey stand for supreme sweetness in both texts, though the Qur'an applies it to Paradise, not to a lover.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thy lips, O my bride, drop honey— Honey and milk are under thy tongue”
judaism.explanation: The lover of the Song of Songs says that honey and milk lie under his bride's tongue.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own image: the beloved's mouth holds milk and honey.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the opening suttas of the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha says he knows of no other taste that so overpowers a man's mind as the taste of a woman, and likewise for a woman and the taste of a man.
buddhism.explanation: The point is a warning: the sweetness lovers find in each other is the strongest of sensual bonds.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural celebrates exactly this overpowering sweetness; Buddhism names it in order to loosen its grip.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain sermon on carelessness compares sensual pleasure to a fruit that tastes sweet but proves poisonous.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural savours a sweetness like milk and honey, the Jain text warns that such sweetness is the bait of karmic bondage.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My Dear Lord and Master, my Friend, speaks so sweetly.”
sikhism.explanation: In a hymn of the bride-soul, Guru Arjan calls the Lord a friend (sajan) whose every word is sweet, using the Punjabi diminutive 'mith bolarha', the sweet-speaking one.
sikhism.tie_back: As the Kural's lover tastes milk and honey in the mouth of his soft-spoken beloved, the Guru delights in the sweetness of the Beloved's speech.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 784, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Homer introduces old Nestor, the clear-voiced speaker of Pylos, as a man from whose tongue speech flowed sweeter than honey.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek epic, like Tamil poetry, uses honey as the measure of sweet and gentle speech.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's heroine is pani-mozhi, 'soft of speech', and her mouth is likened to honey in the same way.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 1.247-249 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that self-indulgence and temperance concern the pleasures of touch and taste, the pleasures humans share with other animals, and that the self-indulgent delight above all in touch.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle these are the pleasures most in need of moderation because they are the most immediate.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural lingers over exactly such a pleasure of taste and touch, treating it as the high point of love rather than as a test of temperance.

real_life_example.event_title: Auguste Rodin's The Kiss
real_life_example.event: Around 1882 the French sculptor Auguste Rodin designed a pair of embracing lovers for his great bronze doorway The Gates of Hell, based on Paolo and Francesca from Dante's Divine Comedy. In 1886 he removed the group from the door because its mood of happiness did not suit the project, exhibited it on its own in 1887, and the public named it The Kiss. The French state commissioned a large marble version in 1888, which Rodin carved over nearly ten years and exhibited in 1898; it is now in the Musée Rodin in Paris.
real_life_example.explanation: The Kiss became one of the most famous sculptures in the world and a lasting symbol of tender love.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the sweetness of the beloved's kiss is like milk mixed with honey, and Rodin's The Kiss is the best-known work of art devoted to that very moment of sweetness.

tamil:
உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை என்னமற் றன்ன
மடந்தையொடு எம்மிடை நட்பு.
transliteration:
Udambodu uyiridai ennamat ranna
madandhaiyodu emmidai natpu.
meaning: Whatever the bond is between the body and the life inside it, that is the bond between this young woman and me.
elementary: Your body and the life inside it always go together; you can't send one to school and leave the other at home. The poet says he and the person he loves belong together in that same way.
university: The hero now states the inseparability of the lovers through the classic Indian pairing of udambu (உடம்பு, body) and uyir (உயிர், life or soul). The word chosen for the relationship is natpu (நட்பு, 'friendship, intimacy'), the same term that heads the Porutpaal chapters on friendship (ch. 79 onward), so the love is presented as a perfect friendship. Madandhai (மடந்தை) denotes a young woman, conventionally of marriageable age. Modern commentators agree on the sense: Mu. Varadarasanar ('as the ties between body and life'), Solomon Pappaiah ('the relation between body and life'), Kalaignar ('life and body never live apart; such is our relationship'); Pope translates 'Between this maid and me the friendship kind / Is as the bonds that soul and body bind.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Rigvedic wedding hymn the couple pray that the gods and the waters join their two hearts together into one.
hinduism.explanation: The verse is still recited at Hindu weddings as the moment the two lives are declared united.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes the bond of lovers as a union so close that two become one.
hinduism.source: Rigveda 10.85.47 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Ralph T.H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. He that loveth his wife loveth himself.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells husbands that a wife is as much a part of a man as his own body.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes the beloved as inseparable from the lover as life is from the body.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes husband and wife as garments for each other: closest to the body, protecting and covering one another.
islam.tie_back: Both texts pick the thing nearest the self, clothing or the body itself, to show how close the lovers are.

judaism.quote_or_event: “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh … and they shall be one flesh.”
judaism.explanation: On first seeing the woman, Adam recognises her as part of his own body, and the Torah adds that husband and wife become one flesh.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover too finds the beloved to be part of his very being.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If both husband & wife want to see one another not only in the present life but also in the life to come, they should be in tune [with each other] in conviction, in tune in virtue, in tune in generosity, and in tune in discernment.”
buddhism.explanation: When the devoted couple Nakula's father and mother ask to be together in future lives, the Buddha tells them how.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's bond as close as body and life finds its Buddhist counterpart in a couple joined across lives by shared virtue.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Sutrakritanga refutes the materialists who hold that the soul is the same as the body, insisting that soul and body are distinct, like a sword that can be drawn from its scabbard.
jainism.explanation: For Jainism the soul (jiva) is only temporarily bound to a body by karma, and liberation means separating them for good.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's ideal of a bond like body and life is, for a Jain, the very bond to be loosened, so the parallel is one of sharp contrast.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 2.1 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O mind, love the Lord, as the lotus loves the water.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak asks for a love so bound to the Lord that, like the lotus that cannot live apart from water, the soul draws its very life from Him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's bond of body and life (udambu and uyir) finds its Sikh counterpart in the lotus and the water, a pairing in which one cannot survive without the other.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 59, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “human nature was originally one and we were a whole, and the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aristophanes' myth, humans were once double beings that Zeus split in two, and love is each half seeking its other half.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's lovers belong together as body and life do; Aristophanes says lovers are literally two halves of one being.
greek_mythology.source: Plato, Symposium 192e-193a, speech of Aristophanes (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Asked what a friend is, Aristotle is reported to have answered: a single soul dwelling in two bodies.
philosophy.explanation: The saying sums up Aristotle's view that perfect friendship makes two people share one life.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural even calls the love natpu, friendship, and makes it as close as soul and body.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 5.20 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.D. Hicks)

real_life_example.event_title: The pair statue of King Menkaure and his queen
real_life_example.place: Giza, Egypt; now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, United States
real_life_example.event: During Egypt's Fourth Dynasty, sculptors carved a nearly life-size statue in greywacke showing King Menkaure standing beside a queen, probably his principal wife. The queen stands with one arm around his waist and her other hand on his arm, and the two figures share one base and back pillar. Excavators led by George Reisner found the statue in Menkaure's valley temple at Giza in January 1910, and it is now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
real_life_example.explanation: The statue is a masterpiece of Old Kingdom art and one of the earliest images of a couple shown as an affectionate pair.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the bond between the lovers is like the bond between body and life, and this statue, carved more than 4,000 years ago, presents king and queen as one joined form, standing together for eternity.

tamil:
கருமணியிற் பாவாய்நீ போதாயாம் வீழும்
திருநுதற்கு இல்லை இடம்.
transliteration:
Karumaniyir paavaainee poadhaayaam veezhum
thirunudharku illai idam.
meaning: Little image in the pupil (the dark center) of my eye, go away! There is no room in there for the girl with the lovely forehead whom I love.
elementary: When you look closely into someone's eye you can see a tiny picture of yourself in it. The poet tells that tiny picture to move out, because he wants his eye to hold only the person he loves.
university: The conceit rests on paavai (பாவை, 'doll, image'), the tiny reflected figure visible in the karumani (கருமணி, the dark pupil); the lover orders it to leave (poadhaai) because there is no idam (இடம், 'room') for thiru-nudhal (திருநுதல், 'she of the lovely brow'), a standard epithet for the heroine. The idea is that he wants to hold her image permanently in his sight. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree; Pope: 'For her with beauteous brow, the maid I love, there place is none; / To give her image room, O pupil of mine eye, begone!' Pulavar Kesikan's gloss adds 'there is no other place for her to stay', heightening the hyperbole. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Chandogya Upanishad, Prajapati first teaches that the person seen in the eye is the Self, a lesson Indra later finds incomplete.
hinduism.explanation: The figure reflected in the pupil was an old Indian puzzle, and the Upanishad uses it as a first step toward knowing the true Self.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural plays with the same figure in the eye but wants to replace it with the beloved, turning a metaphysical image into a lover's one.
hinduism.source: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7.4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 1)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist asks God to guard him as carefully as one guards the pupil of the eye.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat the pupil as the most cherished place, the place where the dearest one is kept.

islam.quote_or_event: “Our Lord, grant us from among our wives and offspring comfort to our eyes”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises those who pray that their spouses and children be qurrat a'yun, a delight or coolness to their eyes.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's lover wants his eyes filled with his beloved; the Qur'an calls a spouse the comfort of one's eyes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When our love was strong, we could have slept on a bed that was the width of a sword. Now that our love is not strong, a bed of sixty cubits is not sufficient for us.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud records a popular saying about marriage: love makes the smallest space enough, and its lack makes any space too small.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover finds no room in his eye except for her; the Talmudic saying likewise measures love by how much space it needs.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 7a (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Therigatha a man becomes infatuated with the nun Subha's eyes; she answers that the eye is only a ball of tissue and fluid and, to cure his obsession, plucks one out and gives it to him.
buddhism.explanation: The story uses the eye, the seat of attraction, to teach how infatuation fixes on a part of the body.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover fills his eye with his beloved; Subha's story treats such fixation as the illusion to be cut through.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of 'colours,' will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain sermon warns that the eye, captured by what it loves to see, leads the soul into ruin.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's lover wants his eye wholly taken up by the beloved's form; the Jain text calls that capture the moth's error.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The crows have searched my skeleton, and eaten all my flesh. But please do not touch these eyes; I hope to see my Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, wasted by longing, gives up his whole body to the crows but keeps his two eyes back, because they are reserved for the sight of the Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's lover who orders even the little image in his pupil to leave so that the eye holds only his beloved, Farid keeps his eyes for the Beloved alone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 91) (BaniDB English translation)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Narcissus falls in love with the image he sees in a pool and cannot bear to leave it.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth turns on an image seen with the eyes that captures the viewer completely.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's lover banishes the image of himself from his pupil to make room for his beloved, exactly the reverse of Narcissus's fixation on himself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates points out that when a person looks into another's eye, his face is reflected in the pupil as in a mirror, which the Greeks call the 'kore', the girl or doll.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses this to argue that the soul comes to know itself by looking into another soul.
philosophy.tie_back: The Greek kore and the Tamil paavai are the same 'little doll' in the eye that the Kural's lover tells to leave.

real_life_example.event_title: The Prince of Wales sends Maria Fitzherbert a portrait of his eye
real_life_example.event: George, Prince of Wales (later King George IV), fell in love with Maria Fitzherbert, a twice-widowed Catholic, in 1784, but the law and his father barred him from marrying her, and she left for the Continent. In November 1785 he sent her a proposal accompanied not by a ring but by a miniature painting of his own eye, made by the miniaturist Richard Cosway. She returned, and in December 1785 they married in a secret ceremony that was not legally valid because it lacked royal consent.
real_life_example.explanation: The gift helped start a fashion for lover's eye miniatures, small portraits of a single eye worn as private love tokens.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's lover tells the little image in his pupil to leave so that only his beloved may dwell in his eye; the prince built his love token on the same idea of the eye as love's dwelling place, sending his own eye so that his gaze would always be with her.

tamil:
வாழ்தல் உயிர்க்கன்னள் ஆயிழை சாதல்
அதற்கன்னள் நீங்கும் இடத்து.
transliteration:
Vaazhdhal uyirkkannal aayizhai saadhal
adharkannal neengum idaththu.
meaning: When my jeweled love is with me, she is like life to my soul. When she leaves, she is like death to it.
elementary: When your best friend is with you the whole day feels bright, and when they go home it can feel empty and dark. The poet says the person he loves feels like life itself when near, and leaving feels like losing life.
university: The couplet balances vaazhdhal (வாழ்தல், living) against saadhal (சாதல், dying), with annal (அன்னள், 'she is like') repeated in each half and neengum idaththu ('at the time she departs') as the hinge. Aayizhai (ஆயிழை) is an epithet, 'she of chosen jewels'; Kalaignar extends it to 'she who wears chosen virtues as her ornaments'. Mu. Varadarasanar: 'when she joins me she is like life to my soul, when she parts she is like death to it'; Solomon Pappaiah reads the first half as 'like the body to the soul', a slightly different construal of the same syntax. Pope: 'Life is she to my very soul when she draws nigh; / Dissevered from the maid with jewels rare, I die!' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama tries to leave her behind for his forest exile, Sita answers that being with him is heaven and being without him is hell, and insists on going with him.
hinduism.explanation: In Valmiki's Ramayana Sita treats separation from her husband as worse than any hardship of the forest.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, she makes the beloved's presence life and his absence a kind of death.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda, Sita's plea to accompany Rama (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that his whole life is bound up with Christ, so that even death is welcome because it brings him closer.
christianity.tie_back: As the Kural's beloved is life to the lover, Christ is life itself to Paul, though Paul reverses the Kural's fear of death.

islam.quote_or_event: “He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents spouses as a source of rest and of a God-given affection between two people.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's beloved is the life of the lover's soul; the Qur'an speaks of a spouse as the one in whom the soul finds rest.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Either friendship or death”
judaism.explanation: After Honi awakes from seventy years of sleep and finds no one who recognises him, he prays for death, and Rava cites this folk saying.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover feels that losing his companion is like dying; the Talmud's saying says the same of losing all companionship.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the pain of parting comes from holding someone dear in the first place.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover feels parting as death; the Buddha recognises the same pain and points to non-attachment as the way out.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra names, as one form of 'sorrowful' (arta) meditation, the anguished brooding over separation from what one holds dear and the longing to be reunited with it.
jainism.explanation: Jainism classes this grief among the unwholesome states of mind that bind fresh karma to the soul.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's 'like death when she leaves' is exactly the state of mind the Jain text diagnoses as a karmic danger.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.30-34, on arta-dhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. Nathmal Tatia)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Chanting it, I live; forgetting it, I die.”
sikhism.explanation: In the evening prayer So Dar (Rehras), Guru Nanak says that remembering the Name is life itself and that forgetting it is a kind of death.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's beloved is life when present and death when she leaves, exactly the two poles Guru Nanak sets between remembering and forgetting the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 9, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Eurydice dies, Orpheus descends to the underworld to bring her back; when he loses her a second time he grieves until his own death and refuses all other love.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes the loss of the beloved the end of the lover's life in all but name.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's lover says the beloved's departure is death to him; Orpheus lives that out.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Love will make men dare to die for their beloved-love alone; andwomen as well as men. Of this, Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, is a monument to all Hellas; for she was willing to lay down her life on behalf of her husband”
philosophy.explanation: In Plato's Symposium, Phaedrus praises love as the force that makes lovers value each other above their own lives.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's beloved is the lover's life; Phaedrus's example shows a lover giving up her life for the beloved.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 179b, speech of Phaedrus (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: The wife of Yi Eung-tae writes a farewell letter
real_life_example.event: In 1586 Yi Eung-tae, a member of the Goseong Yi clan in Andong, Korea, died young, and his pregnant wife wrote him a letter in the Korean script, addressing him as the father of their son Won. In it she wrote that she could not live without him and wanted to go to him, asked how their unborn child should know its father, and begged him to come and speak to her in her dreams. The letter was laid in his grave, where archaeologists found it centuries later, and it helped them identify him.
real_life_example.explanation: The letter is one of the most moving personal documents to survive from Joseon Korea, and it shows a deep marriage of love at a time when such feelings were rarely written down.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the beloved is like life to the soul when near and like death when parted, and this young widow's letter says almost exactly that: without her husband she felt she could not go on living.

tamil:
உள்ளுவன் மன்யான் மறப்பின் மறப்பறியேன்
ஒள்ளமர்க் கண்ணாள் குணம்.
transliteration:
Ulluvan manyaan marappin marappariyaen
ollamark kannaal gunam.
meaning: If I ever forgot the good qualities of the girl with bright, fighting eyes, I could remember them. But I never forget them at all.
elementary: You only need to remember something if you have forgotten it. The poet says he never needs to remember the girl he loves, because she is never out of his mind for a moment.
university: The paradox turns on ulluvan (உள்ளுவன், 'I would recall') against marappu ariyaen (மறப்பறியேன், 'I do not know forgetting'): recollection presupposes forgetting, and since he never forgets her, he never has to 'remember' her. The particle man (மன்) marks the conditional as unrealised. Ol-amar-kannaal (ஒள்ளமர்க் கண்ணாள்) is read two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Pope take amar as 'battle', hence 'bright, warring eyes' (Pope: 'whose eyes gleam like the warrior's dart'), while Pulavar Kesikan reads ollivaai amarndha, 'bright and calmly set'. Pope's note, following the commentators, says the hero speaks to the heroine's maid (tozhi), who had asked whether he still remembered her. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Under the sage Durvasa's curse, King Dushyanta forgets Shakuntala entirely, until he sees the ring he gave her and his memory and love flood back.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa's drama turns on forgetting and remembering a beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's lover insists he can never forget; Kalidasa shows the anguish when a lover does forget and must remember again.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Acts IV-VI (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.”
christianity.explanation: God assures his people that his love is more unforgetting than even a mother's.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts define deepest love as the impossibility of forgetting the one loved.

islam.quote_or_event: “I did not feel jealous of any of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) as much as I did of Khadija though I did not see her, but the Prophet (ﷺ) used to mention her very often”
islam.explanation: Aisha recalls that years after Khadija's death the Prophet kept speaking of her and honouring her friends.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's lover, the Prophet never forgot his beloved's qualities; she was always on his lips.

judaism.quote_or_event: The exiles by the rivers of Babylon swear that if they ever forget Jerusalem, their right hand should lose its skill and their tongue cleave to the roof of the mouth.
judaism.explanation: The psalm makes forgetting the beloved city unthinkable, something they would rather be maimed than do.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover too declares forgetting impossible; the psalm's beloved is a city instead of a person.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The aged brahmin Pingiya tells his teacher that he is never apart from the Buddha even for a moment: he sees him with his mind as with his eye, day and night, and spends the nights paying him homage.
buddhism.explanation: His devotion is so constant that the Buddha is always present in his recollection.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover never has to remember his beloved because he never forgets; Pingiya describes the same unbroken recollection, directed to his teacher.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 5.18, Pingiya's verses at the close of the Parayana Vagga (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Sramana, engaged in penance, should not allow himself to watch the shape, beauty, coquetry, laughter, prattle, gestures, and glances of women, nor retain a recollection of them in his mind.”
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic discipline forbids even keeping the memory of a woman's charms.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's lover cannot stop recalling the qualities of his beloved; the Jain ascetic is told to let precisely such recollection go.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They do not forget, even for an instant, the Support of the breath of life. They live by constantly meditating on Him, O Nanak.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes devotees who never let the Beloved slip from mind, so that unbroken remembrance (simran) becomes the very thing they live by.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover never forgets his beloved's qualities and so never needs to recall them; Gurbani's devotees likewise never forget, even for an instant.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 80, Sri Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Kept for years on Calypso's island and offered immortality, Odysseus still sits on the shore longing for Penelope and home, and tells the goddess that he wants to go back to her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus's longing for his wife does not fade over long separation or in the face of a goddess's love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's lover, Odysseus cannot forget the qualities of the one he loves.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Montaigne writes that after the death of his friend Étienne de La Boétie he had grown so used to being one of two that he now felt only half himself, and that he had never stopped missing him.
philosophy.explanation: The essay on friendship describes a union of two souls so complete that the friend's absence is felt constantly.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover never forgets his beloved; Montaigne describes a friend who is never out of his mind years after his death.
philosophy.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays I.28, 'Of Friendship' (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Su Shi dreams of his late wife Wang Fu
real_life_example.event: In 1075 the Song dynasty poet and official Su Shi wrote a lyric to the tune Jiang Chengzi after dreaming of his first wife, Wang Fu, who had died ten years earlier at about twenty-seven. The poem says that for ten years the living and the dead have known nothing of each other, and that although he does not try to think of her, he cannot forget her. In the dream he returns home and sees her, and he wakes in grief.
real_life_example.explanation: The poem is one of the most famous elegies in Chinese literature, admired for expressing lasting love in very plain words.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's lover says he would remember his beloved's qualities if he ever forgot them, but he never forgets; Su Shi's poem turns on the same paradox, saying he does not set out to remember his wife because he has never been able to forget her.

tamil:
கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார் இமைப்பின் பருகுவரா
நுண்ணியர்எம் காத லவர்.
transliteration:
Kannullin poakaar imaippin paruguvaraa
nunniyarem kaadha lavar.
meaning: My lover never leaves my eyes. Even when I blink, he is not hurt, because he is so fine and delicate.
elementary: Imagine keeping a picture of someone you love in your mind so clearly that it stays even when you blink. Blinking can't hurt that picture because it is not made of anything solid. The girl in this poem says her love lives in her eyes like that.
university: With this couplet the voice passes to the heroine (talaivi), who answers her companion's worry that the hero is far away: he is always in her eyes. Kannullin poagaar (கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார், 'he does not leave from within my eyes') is followed by imaippin paruguvaraa (இமைப்பின் பருகுவரா, 'he does not suffer if I blink'), and nunniyar (நுண்ணியர், 'subtle, fine') explains why: he is too fine to be crushed by the eyelids. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pulavar Kesikan and Kalaignar all read paruguvaraa as 'will not be pained'; Solomon Pappaiah adds that 'others cannot perceive his subtle nature'. Pope takes it differently, 'I wink them not, lest I should pain him where he lies', which anticipates the not-blinking motif of 1129. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In a well-known bhajan, Mirabai asks Krishna, the son of Nanda, to come and dwell in her eyes.
hinduism.explanation: The bhakti poet speaks of her divine beloved as living within her sight at every moment.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her lover never leaves her eyes; Mira makes the same request of Krishna.
hinduism.source: Mirabai, bhajan 'Baso more nainan mein Nandalal' (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go”
christianity.explanation: The woman in the Song of Songs finds her beloved after searching for him through the night and refuses to let him leave.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's heroine, she keeps her beloved close and will not let him go.

islam.quote_or_event: “To worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you cannot achieve this state of devotion then you must consider that He is looking at you.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet defines ihsan, the highest level of faith, as living as if the unseen Beloved were before one's eyes.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's heroine keeps her absent lover always before her eyes; ihsan asks the believer to keep God there.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have set the LORD always before me; Surely He is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist keeps God continually before his eyes; the verse is often displayed in synagogues as a shiviti.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine keeps her beloved always within her eyes; the psalmist does the same with God.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada traces anxiety for others to the affection we feel for them.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine worries that even her blinking might hurt her beloved; the Buddha would see that tender fear as born of endearment.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain philosophy classes the soul, like space and the principles of motion and rest, among the formless (arupa) substances; only matter has form, so the soul itself cannot be struck or crushed.
jainism.explanation: Because the soul has no material form, physical contact cannot injure it, even though the body it inhabits can be hurt.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine says her lover is too subtle to be harmed by her eyelids, which a Jain would say is literally true of the soul.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.4-5 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Nathmal Tatia)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer: with my eyes, I see You, Lord; with my ears, I hear Your Name.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir asks that his eyes behold only the Lord, so that the Beloved fills his sight wherever he looks.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her lover never leaves her eyes; Kabir likewise keeps the Beloved always before his eyes.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1370, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that from the eyes of the three Graces, as they glanced, flowed love that loosens the limbs, and that their glance from beneath their brows was beautiful.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth love itself is thought to pass through and dwell in the eyes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's heroine keeps her lover in her eyes; Hesiod makes the eyes the very fountain of love.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Theogony 907-911 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hugh G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius argues that the mind and soul are made of extremely small, smooth, round particles, so fine that when they leave the body at death its shape and weight seem unchanged.
philosophy.explanation: The Epicurean poet explains the subtlety of the soul by the fineness of its matter.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover is nunniyar, so subtle that blinking cannot hurt him; Lucretius gives a physical account of such subtlety.

real_life_example.event_title: Calpurnia keeps Pliny's writings in his place
real_life_example.event: The Roman senator and author Pliny the Younger wrote letters to his young wife Calpurnia while they were apart, and some were included in his published collection of letters. In one of them (Letters 6.7) he replies to her complaint that she misses him terribly and comforts herself by embracing his writings instead of him and putting them in the place where he usually sits. He answers that he rereads her letters again and again, and asks her to write as often as she can.
real_life_example.explanation: Pliny's letters to Calpurnia are among the rare surviving glimpses of affection inside a Roman marriage.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says her lover never leaves her eyes, so fine that even blinking cannot harm him; Calpurnia, too, kept her absent husband constantly before her by placing his words where he used to be.

tamil:
கண்ணுள்ளார் காத லவராகக் கண்ணும்
எழுதேம் கரப்பாக்கு அறிந்து.
transliteration:
Kannullaar kaadha lavaraagak kannum
ezhudhaem karappaakku arindhu.
meaning: Because my lover lives in my eyes, I do not even put kohl (dark eyeliner) on them, knowing it would hide him.
elementary: If you were keeping a tiny friend inside a glass jar, you wouldn't paint the jar, because then you couldn't see them. The girl in this poem doesn't put on eye makeup because she imagines her love is inside her eyes and the makeup would cover him.
university: The heroine continues the eye conceit: since her lover dwells in her eyes (kannullaar), she will not even 'write' her eyes (kannum ezhudhaem), ezhudhu (எழுது) being the Tamil verb for applying mai (மை, kohl or collyrium), for fear of karappu (கரப்பு, concealment) of him. Applying kohl was a basic daily adornment of the akam heroine, so giving it up shows how completely her life is ordered around him. The umm in kannum ('even the eyes') implies she forgoes other adornment too. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree on 'lest he be hidden'; Pope: 'My love doth ever in my eyes reside; / I stain them not, fearing his form to hide.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa's Cloud Messenger, the exiled yaksha imagines his wife at home giving up her ornaments, her hair bound in a single plain braid, as she waits for him.
hinduism.explanation: In Sanskrit poetry, a devoted woman lays aside adornment while her beloved is absent, because there is no one she wishes to adorn herself for.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also gives up adornment for her lover's sake, though for the playful reason that he lives in her eyes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart”
christianity.explanation: Peter advises that true beauty is the inner person, not outward adornment.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's heroine sets aside outward adornment for the sake of the one she carries within, a 'hidden man' of her own.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an directs believing women not to display their adornment except to their husbands and close family.
islam.explanation: Adornment is treated as something that belongs within the bond of marriage.
