islam.tie_back: The Kural's heroine arranges her adornment entirely around her beloved; Islam likewise orients a wife's adornment toward her husband.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jeremiah warns faithless Judah that though she paints her eyes and puts on finery to attract lovers, she beautifies herself in vain.
judaism.explanation: The prophet uses eye-paint as the image of adornment that seeks the wrong love.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine refuses eye-paint out of faithfulness to her one lover, the reverse of the prophet's image of faithless adornment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: On the Uposatha observance days, lay followers take extra precepts, including abstaining from garlands, perfumes and cosmetics.
buddhism.explanation: Setting aside adornment is a Buddhist practice of restraint, done for one's own spiritual progress.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also lays aside cosmetics, but out of love for the one in her eyes rather than for restraint.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra lists the use of collyrium on the eyes among the practices forbidden to a Jain monk.
jainism.explanation: Even eye-cosmetics count as self-adornment that feeds attachment to the body.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine gives up kohl out of love; the Jain monk gives it up out of detachment.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra, ch. 3 (Kshullakacara) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I have applied the healing ointment of spiritual wisdom to my eyes; the Naam, the Name of the Lord, is my food. These are all my decorations.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan's bride-soul replaces the usual kohl (anjan) and adornments with the Guru's wisdom and the Name, so that her eyes are made ready only for the Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine refuses kohl so as not to hide the lover dwelling in her eyes; the Sikh bride-soul sets aside ordinary kohl for the 'ointment of wisdom' that reveals the Lord.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 542, Raag Bihaagraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When her maid urges Penelope to wash and anoint her face before appearing to the suitors, she refuses, saying the gods destroyed her beauty on the day Odysseus sailed for Troy.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope's refusal to beautify herself is a sign of loyalty to her absent husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's heroine, Penelope lays aside adornment for the one she loves.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Socrates calls cosmetics a flattering imitation of gymnastics, giving a false appearance of beauty instead of real health.
philosophy.explanation: Plato distrusts adornment as a counterfeit of genuine good.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also sets cosmetics aside, though from love, not from Plato's suspicion of appearances.

real_life_example.event_title: Juliette Drouet gives up the stage for Victor Hugo
real_life_example.event: The French actress Juliette Drouet began her relationship with the writer Victor Hugo in 1833, and in the mid-1830s she gave up her stage career to devote herself to him. For about fifty years, until her death in 1883, she remained his companion, travelled with him and copied out his works for his publishers. She wrote him at least one letter a day, about 22,000 in all.
real_life_example.explanation: Her letters to Hugo form one of the largest bodies of correspondence in the history of literature.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine gives up even the daily adornment of kohl on her eyes so that nothing hides the lover who lives there; Drouet gave up the public life of the stage and ordered her whole life around Hugo.

tamil:
நெஞ்சத்தார் காத லவராக வெய்துண்டல்
அஞ்சுதும் வேபாக் கறிந்து.
transliteration:
Nenjaththaar kaadha lavaraaga veydhundal
anjudhum vaepaak karindhu.
meaning: Because my lover lives in my heart, I am afraid to eat anything hot, knowing it would burn him.
elementary: Have you ever carried a baby bird very carefully so it wouldn't get hurt? The girl in this poem feels her love is living right inside her chest, so she won't even drink something hot in case it burns him.
university: The conceit moves from the eyes to the heart: nenjaththaar (நெஞ்சத்தார், 'he who is in my heart') is so literally present that veydhu undal (வெய்துண்டல், eating hot food) is feared (anjudhum, அஞ்சுதும்) because of vaepaakku (வேபாக்கு, his being scorched). The first person plural is the heroine's dignified 'we'. All four commentators on thirukkural.net and ytamizh.com agree on the sense; Kalaignar generalises it into a definition: true lovers are those so blended heart with heart that they fear hot food might burn the other. Pope: 'Within my heart my lover dwells; from food I turn / That smacks of heat, lest he should feel it burn.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O dearly beloved! Your lotus feet are so soft that we place them gently on our breasts, fearing that Your feet will be hurt.”
hinduism.explanation: In their song of separation the gopis tell Krishna they fear even their own bodies might hurt his tender feet, and worry about him on the stony forest paths.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly as the Kural's heroine fears her own hot food might burn the lover within her, the gopis fear their own bodies might hurt their beloved.
hinduism.source: Srimad Bhagavatam 10.31.19 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, vedabase.io)

christianity.quote_or_event: “That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love,”
christianity.explanation: Paul prays that Christ will make his home in the believers' hearts.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's beloved also lives in the heroine's heart; Paul uses the same image of a dear one dwelling within.

islam.quote_or_event: “We are closer to him than [his] jugular vein”
islam.explanation: God declares that He is nearer to a person than the vein in his own neck.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's beloved is so near he is inside the heart; the Qur'an expresses a closeness even nearer than the body's own veins.

judaism.quote_or_event: The bride of the Song of Songs asks her beloved to set her as a seal upon his heart and upon his arm, for love is strong as death.
judaism.explanation: The seal on the heart is the image of a beloved permanently imprinted within.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine likewise carries her beloved inside her heart and guards him there.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even as a mother protects with her life / Her child, her only child, / So with a boundless heart / Should one cherish all living beings”
buddhism.explanation: The Metta Sutta takes a mother's protective love as the model for boundless kindness.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine guards the beloved within her as anxiously as a mother guards her only child.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 1.8, Karaniya Metta Sutta (tr. The Amaravati Sangha)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga Sutra teaches that fire-bodies, water-bodies and other tiny, unseen beings are alive, and that a careful person avoids harming them even in ordinary acts like cooking and eating.
jainism.explanation: Jain ahimsa extends care to beings too small to be seen, shaping how one eats and drinks.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine changes how she eats to avoid harming an unseen beloved; Jain practice changes how one eats to avoid harming unseen life.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.1 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Baba, the pleasures of other foods are false. Eating them, the body is ruined, and wickedness and corruption enter into the mind.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak warns against foods eaten for pleasure that harm the body and disturb the mind, setting restraint in eating within a life centred on the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine avoids hot food so as not to scorch the lover in her heart; Guru Nanak likewise guards what he eats for the sake of what dwells within the mind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Psyche secretly lights a lamp to look at her sleeping husband Cupid, a drop of hot oil falls on his shoulder and burns him, and he flies away.
greek_mythology.explanation: Psyche's moment of curiosity hurts the beloved she had never seen and costs her his presence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's heroine fears exactly this: that something hot from her might burn the lover she carries.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for he walks not upon the earth, nor yet upon skulls of men, which are not so very soft, but in the hearts and souls of both god, and men, which are of all things the softest: in them he walks and dwells and makes his home.”
philosophy.explanation: In Plato's Symposium, Agathon praises Love as the tenderest of gods, who lives only in soft and gentle hearts.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover also makes his home in the heart, and the heroine guards that tender place from anything that could burn him.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 195e, speech of Agathon (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Lady Dervorguilla keeps her husband's heart and founds Sweetheart Abbey
real_life_example.place: New Abbey, Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland
real_life_example.event: When John Balliol died in 1268, his widow, Lady Dervorguilla of Galloway, had his heart embalmed and placed in a casket of ivory (one account says silver and ivory), which she kept with her. In 1273 she founded a Cistercian abbey in his memory, which the monks named Dulce Cor, Latin for sweet heart. When she died in 1289 she was buried before the abbey's high altar with her husband's heart.
real_life_example.explanation: The ruined abbey, still known as Sweetheart Abbey, remains one of Scotland's best-known monuments to married love.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine keeps her lover so truly within her heart that she fears hot food might burn him, and Dervorguilla kept her husband's heart close to her for more than twenty years and was buried holding it.

tamil:
இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல் அனைத்திற்கே
ஏதிலர் என்னும்இவ் வூர்.
transliteration:
Imaippin karappaakku arival anaiththirkae
aedhilar ennumiv voor.
meaning: I know that if I blink he will be hidden, so I keep my eyes open. For that reason alone, this town says he does not love me.
elementary: Suppose you stayed up late because you were thinking about someone you love, and the next day people said, 'That person must be unkind to keep you awake!' The girl in this poem says the town blames her lover, though really it is just her love that keeps her eyes open.
university: The heroine explains her sleeplessness: she will not close her eyes because she knows that on blinking (imaippin) he would be hidden (karappaakku). Seeing her wakeful and pale, the ur (ஊர், 'town') concludes that he is aedhilar (ஏதிலர், 'a stranger, one without love') who has abandoned her, and she protests the injustice. Anaiththirkae ('for just that much') marks the town's verdict as unfair. This introduces alar (அலர், gossip), the theme of ch. 115. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pulavar Kesikan agree; Kalaignar adds that the town blames him for the 'pain of sleeplessness'. Pope: 'I fear his form to hide, nor close my eyes: / "Her love estranged is gone!" the village cries.' The second line is shared verbatim with 1130, a deliberate refrain. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “even when we can eagerly look upon Your beautiful face, so lovely with its adornment of curly locks, our pleasure is hindered by our eyelids, which were fashioned by the foolish creator.”
hinduism.explanation: The gopis complain to Krishna that even blinking costs them a glimpse of him, and blame the creator for making eyelids at all.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also refuses to blink for fear of losing sight of her lover; the gopis wish their eyelids had never been made.
hinduism.source: Srimad Bhagavatam 10.31.15 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, vedabase.io)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh”
christianity.explanation: The woman in the Song of Songs lies down to rest but her heart stays awake, alert for her beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's heroine likewise stays awake for her lover, even if in her case it is her eyes that will not close.

islam.quote_or_event: “My eyes sleep, but my heart does not sleep.”
islam.explanation: Asked whether he sleeps before the night prayer, the Prophet answers that only his eyes rest while his heart stays awake.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's heroine keeps her eyes open for the sake of the one in her heart; the Prophet's heart stays awake while his eyes sleep.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I will not give sleep to mine eyes, Nor slumber to mine eyelids;”
judaism.explanation: The psalm recalls David's vow not to rest until he had found a dwelling place for God.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also refuses to let her eyelids close for the sake of the one she loves.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are ever vigilant, who discipline themselves day and night, and are ever intent upon Nibbana — their defilements fade away.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises wakefulness and vigilance, day and night, as the path to liberation.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine is wakeful for love; Buddhism prizes the same unsleeping vigilance for the opposite goal of freedom from attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The Venerable One, exerting himself, did not seek sleep for the sake of pleasure; he waked up himself, and slept only a little, free from desires.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga describes Mahavira staying almost sleepless during his years of austerity, out of vigilance rather than desire.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also barely sleeps, but out of love; Mahavira's wakefulness is the ascetic counterpart.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.8.2.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Night and day, I utter, "Pri-a, Pri-a - Beloved, Beloved" with my mouth. I cannot sleep, even for an instant; I remain awake and aware.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan voices the bride-soul who stays wakeful through the night, calling out to the Beloved and refusing the sleep that would take Him from her.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine will not close her eyes lest her lover be hidden; the Sikh bride-soul likewise stays awake without blinking into sleep, held by her Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1203, Raag Saarang, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hera sets the hundred-eyed Argus to guard Io; he never closes all his eyes at once, so that some are always watching.
greek_mythology.explanation: Argus is the Greek image of a watcher who never fully sleeps.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also refuses to close her eyes, though she watches for love, not on a goddess's orders.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal observes that the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: For Pascal, love follows a logic that outsiders reasoning coolly cannot see.
philosophy.tie_back: The town judges the heroine's sleeplessness by outward signs and blames her lover; it cannot see the heart's real reason.

real_life_example.event_title: Chopin and George Sand's winter in Majorca
real_life_example.event: In November 1838 the composer Frédéric Chopin and the novelist George Sand travelled to Majorca, and from mid-December they lived in rented cells in the former Carthusian monastery at Valldemossa. Chopin fell seriously ill with a cough, and local people, fearing his illness was contagious, turned against the couple: one landlord made them leave, and villagers refused to sell them supplies. Sand cared for him while he completed his 24 Preludes, and they left in February 1839; she later described the stay in A Winter in Majorca (1842).
real_life_example.explanation: The winter produced some of Chopin's greatest music, even while the local community judged the couple harshly from the outside.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine protests that the town wrongly judges her lover from what it sees on the surface; the Majorcans likewise judged Chopin and Sand only by appearances, while the couple's devotion went on unseen inside the monastery.

tamil:
உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும் இகந்துறைவர்
ஏதிலர் என்னும்இவ் வூர்.
transliteration:
Uvandhuraivar ullaththul endrum igandhuraivar
aedhilar ennumiv voor.
meaning: He always lives happily in my heart, yet this town says he lives far away and does not love me.
elementary: Sometimes people only see what is on the outside. Someone might think two friends have drifted apart because they live in different places, but the friends know they still care about each other every day. The girl in this poem says her love is always in her heart, even if the town thinks he is gone.
university: The chapter closes by contrasting uvandhu uraivar (உவந்துறைவர், 'he dwells rejoicing') ullaththul endrum ('in my heart always') with the town's verdict that he igandhu uraivar (இகந்துறைவர், 'lives having gone away') and is aedhilar, unloving. The repetition of uraivar and the refrain line shared with 1129 sharpen the irony: physical distance is visible to the town, but inner presence is visible only to her. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pulavar Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree; Pope: 'Rejoicing in my very soul he ever lies; / "Her love estranged is gone far off!" the village cries.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You are never actually separated from Me, for I am the Soul of all creation.”
hinduism.explanation: Through his messenger Uddhava, Krishna tells the grieving gopis of Vraja that although he has gone to Mathura he is never truly apart from them.
hinduism.tie_back: Just as the Kural's heroine insists that her absent lover still dwells within her, Krishna assures the gopis that he dwells within them though others see only his absence.
hinduism.source: Srimad Bhagavatam 10.47.29 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, vedabase.io)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns his critics not to judge by what things look like on the surface.
christianity.tie_back: The town in the Kural judges the absent lover by appearances; the heroine knows the truth within.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an forbids jumping to suspicious conclusions about others and backbiting.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's town assumes the worst of an absent lover; the Qur'an names such assumption a sin.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Samuel is impressed by the appearance of Jesse's eldest son, God tells him that people look on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.
judaism.explanation: The story teaches that the truth of a person lies in the heart, not in what is outwardly visible.
judaism.tie_back: The town sees only the lover's absence; the heroine, like God in the story, sees what is in the heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “O Atula! Indeed, this is an ancient practice, not one only of today: they blame those who remain silent, they blame those who speak much, they blame those who speak in moderation. There is none in the world who is not blamed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada observes that people will find fault with anyone, whatever they do.
buddhism.tie_back: The town finds fault with the heroine's lover no matter what; the Buddha says such blame is as old as the world.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the resting-places there once, in a night, the single wanderers asked him (who he was, and why he was there); as he did not answer, they treated him badly; but he persevered in his meditations, free from resentment.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga records how people who did not understand Mahavira's silent practice misjudged and mistreated him.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's town also misreads what it cannot see, judging the lover by outward signs.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.8.2.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Why do you go looking for Him in the forest? Although he is unattached, he dwells everywhere. He is always with you as your companion.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur tells seekers who think the Lord is far away and must be sought in the wilderness that He already dwells with them, within.
sikhism.tie_back: The town in the Kural says the lover lives far away, while the heroine knows he dwells rejoicing in her heart; Gurbani answers those who think the Beloved distant with the same certainty that He is always near.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 684, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After her husband Protesilaus dies at Troy, Laodamia keeps a likeness of him in her room; a servant who sees her embracing it assumes she has a secret lover and reports her to her father.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her family misreads her devotion to her absent husband as betrayal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's town, onlookers misjudge a love they cannot see from outside.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the allegory of the cave, prisoners who see only shadows on a wall take them for the whole of reality.
philosophy.explanation: Plato's image shows how people who see only surfaces mistake them for the truth.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's town sees only the lover's absence and takes it for lack of love, while the heroine knows the reality within.

real_life_example.event_title: George IV is buried wearing Maria Fitzherbert's portrait
real_life_example.event: George IV and Maria Fitzherbert, whom he had secretly and invalidly married in 1785, finally parted in 1811, after which she lived privately on an allowance. Yet when George IV died in 1830 he was wearing a locket with her miniature portrait around his neck, and at his own request he was buried with it at his breast.
real_life_example.explanation: The burial revealed that a bond the public had long thought finished had stayed with the king to the end.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says the town calls her lover distant and unloving though he dwells joyfully in her heart; the world believed George IV had long left Maria behind, but her portrait stayed over his heart until his death.

tamil:
காமம் உழந்து வருந்தினார்க்கு ஏமம்
மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி.
transliteration:
Kaamam uzhandhu varundhinaarkku Emam
madalalladhu illai vali.
meaning: For those who suffer and are hurt by love, there is no protection and no strength except the madal. That is a horse of palm stems that a refused lover rides in public.
elementary: Imagine a boy who has asked and asked for something important and been told no every time. At last he decides to make a big, brave sign and carry it through the whole village so everyone knows how much it matters to him. In old Tamil stories, a young man who was kept away from the girl he loved could do something like this: ride a pretend horse made of palm leaves down the street.
university: Chapter 114 opens with the custom of madal ūrtal (மடல் ஊர்தல்): a lover refused access to his beloved would ride a hobby-horse made of palmyra stems (madal) through the streets, garlanded with erukkam flowers and carrying her likeness, to shame her family publicly into consenting; Kalittokai and Tolkāppiyam know the practice, and the grammatical tradition classes it as an extreme of love (peruntiṇai). Ēmam (ஏமம்) means 'safeguard, refuge' and vali (வலி) 'strength, support'; uḻantu (உழந்து) is 'having laboured/suffered in'. In the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar the opening couplets are the hero's words to the heroine's confidante (tōḻi) when she puts him off, and the threat of the madal is itself a way of abandoning nāṇ (நாண், 'shame, reserve'), which gives the chapter its name. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss the line as 'no strength but the madal'; Pope renders 'Except the helpful horse of palm, no other strength remains.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sanskrit dramatic theory lists the stages through which love in separation passes, from longing and anxious thought, through sleeplessness, raving and wasting, to the brink of death.
hinduism.explanation: The Natyashastra treats love denied (vipralambha) as a progressive illness with named stages that actors must be able to portray.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's lover speaks from deep inside that sickness, where ordinary remedies have failed and only a desperate public act seems left.
hinduism.source: Bharata, Natyashastra, section on the stages of love (kama-avasthas) (paraphrase; tr. Manomohan Ghosh)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved in the Song of Songs calls herself love-sick and begs for something to sustain her.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's sufferer, she treats love as an affliction that leaves her looking for any support at all.

islam.quote_or_event: In the Arabic and Persian tale of Layla and Majnun, the young Qays is kept from Layla by her family and is so consumed by love that he is called majnun, 'madman', and goes out into the wilderness reciting verses about her.
islam.explanation: The story, retold by Nizami Ganjavi in 1188, became the classic Islamicate picture of love that has no remedy and no shame left.
islam.tie_back: Majnun, like the Kural's lover, is refused by the beloved's family and lets his suffering become a public spectacle because nothing else is left to him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs describes love as a force as unstoppable as death itself.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover has found love just that strong: it has overpowered every defence but one.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From lust springs grief, from lust springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief back to desire and teaches that the only lasting cure is freedom from craving.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's sufferer seeks a remedy in the madal; Buddhism diagnoses the same pain but locates the cure in letting the desire go.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Gina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction.”
jainism.explanation: Princess Rajimati, betrothed to Arishtanemi, is left grief-stricken when he abandons the wedding to become a monk.
jainism.tie_back: She suffers the same pain of love denied as the Kural's lover, but in the Jain story the way out is renunciation, not a public protest.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. ... give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says the path of love demands total self-surrender, holding nothing back and caring nothing for what people will say.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover, refused his beloved, has no strength left but the public, shameless act of riding the madal; Guru Nanak likewise makes love a matter of laying one's head down and ignoring public opinion.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek (salok 20), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, the nymph Echo is rejected by Narcissus, hides herself in the woods in shame, and wastes away with grief until only her voice is left.
greek_mythology.explanation: Echo's unreturned love leaves her with no remedy at all, and it consumes her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She shows the danger the Kural's lover feels: love refused, with no ordinary way to relieve it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: For Pascal, love moves by a logic of its own that rational calculation cannot govern.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover has passed beyond calculation; his heart's 'reason' tells him only the madal is left.

real_life_example.event_title: W. B. Yeats proposes to Maud Gonne and is refused
real_life_example.event: The Irish poet W. B. Yeats met Maud Gonne in 1889 and fell in love with her; she admired and liked him but did not return his love, and he courted her for nearly three decades. He dedicated his play The Countess Kathleen (1892) to her and wrote Cathleen ni Houlihan (1902) with her in the title role. In 1899 he asked her to marry him and she declined, and in 1903 she married Major John MacBride.
real_life_example.explanation: Turned down in private, Yeats kept declaring his love in public through plays and poems that all Ireland could see.
real_life_example.tie_back: Like the refused lover in this kural who has no shelter left except to ride the palm-stem horse in the street, Yeats, denied in private, made his hopeless love a public matter.

tamil:
நோனா உடம்பும் உயிரும் மடலேறும்
நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து.
transliteration:
Nonaa udambum uyirum madalaerum
naaninai neekki niruththu.
meaning: My body and my life cannot bear this any longer. They have put shame aside and are ready to ride the madal (the palm-stem horse of a refused lover).
elementary: Have you ever been so upset that you cried in front of everyone, even though you usually would feel shy? The speaker here says his whole body and heart are hurting so much that his shyness has simply been set aside.
university: Nōṉā (நோனா) is the negative participle of nōl, 'to endure': the body and the life-breath (uyir) that 'cannot bear' the separation are made the subjects of the verb, as if they act on their own. Nāṇiṉai nīkki niṟuttu (நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து), 'having removed and set aside shame', is the key phrase of the chapter: nāṇ, the sense of reserve that Tamil ethics praises (cf. chapter 102, Nāṇuṭaimai), is not destroyed but deliberately put to one side. Commentators in Parimelazhagar's line take this as the hero telling the confidante that his resolve is already made; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'my body and life have resolved to ride the madal, having set shame aside', while Pappaiah softens it to 'are thinking of riding'. Pope: 'My body and my soul, that can no more endure, / Will lay reserve aside, and mount the horse of palm.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna plays his flute on the autumn night, the cowherd women of Vraja drop whatever they are doing, leave husbands and households, and run to him in the forest, heedless of what anyone will say.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana presents the gopis' abandonment of social propriety as the highest form of devotion.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's lover, the gopis set aside shame and reserve because love has become unbearable.

christianity.quote_or_event: A woman known in the town as a sinner enters a Pharisee's house where Jesus is dining, weeps over his feet, wipes them with her hair, and anoints them, ignoring the disapproval of everyone present.
christianity.explanation: Jesus defends her, saying her many sins are forgiven because she loved much.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, she lets love overrule every rule of decorum in front of onlookers.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi opens his Masnavi by saying that only one whose garment has been torn by a mighty love is cleansed of greed and every fault.
islam.explanation: For Rumi, being 'torn' by love is a purifying loss of self-protection.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's lover is similarly 'torn open': his reserve has been stripped away by love too strong to bear.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi I.22 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells that Rachel, daughter of the wealthy Ben Kalba Savua, chose the poor shepherd Akiva against her father's wishes, and her father vowed she would receive nothing from his property.
judaism.explanation: Rachel gave up wealth, status and family approval for the man she loved and believed in.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, she set aside what society expected of her because her love would not let her do otherwise.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 62b-63a (paraphrase; William Davidson Edition, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother, ordained on the day of his wedding, tells the monks he is discontented and wants to return to lay life because he keeps remembering his beautiful fiancée's parting words.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha then leads him to a higher understanding, and Nanda eventually becomes an arahant.
buddhism.tie_back: Nanda's longing, like the Kural lover's, is strong enough to make him ready to throw off the role he is expected to keep.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When Râgîmatî perceived that Rathanêmi's strength of will was broken, and temptation had got the better of him, she did not lose her presence of mind and defended her Self on that occasion.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Rathanemi, seeing Rajimati in a cave, loses his composure and proposes to her; she keeps hers.
jainism.tie_back: Rathanemi is in the Kural lover's state, with restraint overpowered, and the Jain text sets beside him a figure who refuses to let go of hers.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The three qualities are shattered, doubt and fear run away, and the clay pot of public opinion is broken.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das describes the devotee absorbed in the Lord's praise, for whom fear and the fragile 'pot' of worry about what people think are smashed.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's body and soul set shame aside to mount the madal; in Gurbani the lover of God likewise breaks the clay pot of public opinion (lok-laaj).
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 986, Raag Maalee Gauraa, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho describes how, at the sight of the beloved, her tongue breaks, a thin fire runs under her skin, her eyes see nothing, her ears roar, and she trembles until she seems close to death.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her famous poem lists the physical collapse that love brings about in the body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise says it is the body and the life-breath that can no longer bear love and so throw off restraint.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume argues that reason alone can never oppose a passion in directing the will, and that reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions.
philosophy.explanation: For Hume, feeling, not reason, ultimately moves us to act.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover is a living example: his considered sense of shame has been simply overruled by passion.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.3 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Longfellow persists after Fanny Appleton refuses him
real_life_example.place: Boston and Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States
real_life_example.event: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, a young widower, fell in love with Frances (Fanny) Appleton after travelling with her family in Switzerland. He was crushed when she rejected his marriage proposal in 1837, but he did not give up. She accepted him in the spring of 1843, and they married in July 1843; her father gave the couple Craigie House as a wedding gift.
real_life_example.explanation: A respected professor and poet kept up a suit that had already been refused, accepting the embarrassment of pressing on for six years.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's lover says that body and life can no longer bear the pain and so shame must be set aside; Longfellow likewise set aside the pride of a rejected suitor and kept pursuing the woman he loved.

tamil:
நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன் இன்றுடையேன்
காமுற்றார் ஏறும் மடல்.
transliteration:
Naanodu nallaanmai pandudaiyaen indrudaiyaen
kaamutraar aerum madal.
meaning: Once I had modesty and a man's honor. Today all I have is the palm-stem horse that lovesick men ride.
elementary: Think of a proud, well-behaved prince who always acted with dignity. Then he falls so deeply in love that he will do anything, even something silly in front of everyone, to be heard. He says, 'I used to be so proper; now look at me!'
university: The couplet sets paṇṭu (பண்டு, 'formerly') against iṉṟu (இன்று, 'today'), and nāṇ (நாண், 'modesty, sense of shame') together with nal-āṇmai (நல்லாண்மை, 'good manliness, honourable valour') against the single possession now left, the madal. Parimelazhagar's tradition reads this as the hero's lament that love has stripped him of the two qualities that defined him socially. Kāmuṟṟār (காமுற்றார்) is 'those seized by love'; the madal is thus marked as the emblem of a class of sufferers rather than a personal eccentricity. Pope: 'I once retained reserve and seemly manliness; / To-day I nought possess but lovers' horse of palm.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa's play, King Pururavas, maddened by the loss of the nymph Urvashi, wanders the forest asking a peacock, a cuckoo, a swan, a bee and even a mountain whether they have seen her.
hinduism.explanation: The great king forgets his royal dignity entirely in his grief and longing.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Pururavas once had kingly honour and self-command, and now has only the open madness of love.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul writes that whatever he once counted as gain, his status, lineage and reputation, he now counts as loss for the sake of Christ.
christianity.explanation: Paul describes giving up everything that once defined his honour for the one he loves above all.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's lover makes the same before-and-after reckoning: his old honour is gone, exchanged for love.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi was a respected jurist and preacher in Konya until his meeting with the wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz; afterwards he gave himself to ecstatic poetry and whirling, to the scandal of many of his followers.
islam.explanation: The hagiographic tradition tells how love for Shams overturned Rumi's dignified public role.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Rumi once had standing and reserve, and love left him with nothing but its open display.
islam.source: Shams al-Din Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin (paraphrase of the traditional account)

judaism.quote_or_event: Samson, the mighty judge of Israel, reveals the secret of his strength to Delilah because of her persistent pleading; his hair is cut and his strength leaves him.
judaism.explanation: The strongest man in Israel loses the very quality that defined him through his attachment to a woman.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover likewise laments that the 'good manliness' he once had has been taken from him by love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kusa Jataka, Prince Kusa, rejected by his bride Pabhavati, follows her to her father's kingdom and takes work as a potter, a basket-maker, a gardener and a cook, all to be near her.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta in this birth story lays aside royal dignity entirely for love.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Kusa once had a prince's honour and now has only the humble tasks love has driven him to.
buddhism.source: Kusa Jataka (Jataka 531) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard these well-spoken words of the virtuous lady, he returned to the Law like an elephant driven by the hook.”
jainism.explanation: Rathanemi, rebuked by Rajimati, recovers the self-control his passion had made him lose.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's lover says he once had reserve and now has only the madal; the Jain story shows the reverse path, from passion back to restraint.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.46 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I am dishonored; I have lost my honor.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir accepts that in the world's eyes he has lost all standing because of his devotion, and treats this loss as no loss at all.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover laments that the modesty and good name he once had are gone, leaving only the madal; Kabir likewise confesses that his love has cost him his worldly honour.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 324, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Deianira reproaches Heracles that the hero who conquered monsters now sits among serving-women spinning wool for the Lydian queen Omphale, wearing her clothes while she carries his club and lion-skin.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest of heroes lays aside his manly identity for love of Omphale.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's lament: 'nallāṇmai' (honourable manliness) once possessed, now given up for love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A man should allow himself to behave as lovers commonly do to their favorites—pressing their suit with supplications and entreaties, binding themselves with vows, sleeping on doorsteps, and submitting to such slavery as no slave would ever endure.”
philosophy.explanation: Pausanias notes that conduct which would bring sharp reproach in any other cause is tolerated in a lover.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover, like Plato's, is reduced to acts that would shame him in any other cause.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 183a (tr. W.R.M. Lamb, via Perseus)

real_life_example.event_title: John Donne's secret marriage costs him his career
real_life_example.event: In December 1601 the poet John Donne, then secretary to the powerful Sir Thomas Egerton, secretly married the seventeen-year-old Ann More. When Donne told her father months later, Sir George More demanded his dismissal; Donne lost his post in 1602 and was briefly imprisoned. The marriage was upheld, but Donne found no regular employment for more than twelve years and lived on the help of friends, relatives and patrons.
real_life_example.explanation: A rising young man of standing exchanged his position and reputation for the woman he loved.
real_life_example.tie_back: As the kural's lover says that he once had good name and honourable manhood and now has only his love, Donne's love left him with his wife but without the career and standing he had once enjoyed.

tamil:
காமக் கடும்புனல் உய்க்கும் நாணொடு
நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை.
transliteration:
Kaamak kadumpunal uykkum naanodu
nallaanmai ennum punai.
meaning: The wild flood of love sweeps away the raft made of modesty and a man's honor.
elementary: Imagine you are floating safely on a little raft. Then a huge flood rushes in and carries the raft away. The poet says love is like that flood, and being careful and well-behaved is the raft it sweeps off.
university: The image is a rūpakam (extended metaphor): kāmak kaṭum-puṉal (காமக் கடும்புனல்), 'the fierce torrent of love', against puṇai (புணை), a raft or float, which here is made of two things, nāṇ (modesty) and nal-āṇmai (honourable manliness), both named in the previous couplet. Uykkum (உய்க்கும்) means 'carries off, drives along'. Commentators (Parimelazhagar's line, Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah) all take it as the hero's explanation of why the qualities he once had could not save him; Puliyur Kesikan adds an exclamation, 'what shall I do!'. Pope: 'Love's rushing tide will sweep away the raft / Of seemly manliness and shame combined.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just as a strong wind sweeps a boat off its chartered course on the water, even one of the senses on which the mind focuses can lead the intellect astray.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a single sense, once the mind follows it, can carry away even a wise person's judgment.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts use the image of a small vessel carried off by a force on the water to describe desire overpowering self-control.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs says no flood can put out love.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural turns the image around: love is itself the flood, and it is reserve that drowns.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet is reported to have said that the Fire is surrounded by desires and passions, while Paradise is surrounded by things the self dislikes.
islam.explanation: The hadith teaches that unchecked desire draws a person easily toward harm, while restraint is hard.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's torrent of love sweeping off the raft of restraint shows how easily desire can overpower a person.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the evil inclination is at first like a spider's thread and in the end like a cart rope.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic teaching describes desire as something that starts slight and grows until it holds a person fast.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's 'fierce torrent' is love at the end of that process, when it has grown strong enough to sweep restraint away.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fire like lust; there is no grip like hatred; there is no net like delusion; there is no river like craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names craving as the strongest of rivers, one that carries beings along.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's 'torrent of love' is just such a river, sweeping off the raft of restraint.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you fall in love with every woman you see, you will be without hold like the Haṭha-plant, driven before the wind.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati warns Rathanemi that a person carried by desire has no anchor and drifts like a floating water-plant.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's image of restraint swept away by a flood matches this picture of a self driven helplessly by passion.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You were not able to make yourself a raft when you should have. When the ocean is churning and over-flowing, then it is very difficult to cross over it.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid warns that once the waters rise and churn it is too late to build the raft that would carry one across.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures the fierce flood of love sweeping away the raft made of modesty and manliness; Farid uses the same raft-and-flood image for a torrent too strong to cross.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 794, Raag Soohee, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Leander swims the Hellespont every night to reach Hero, guided by her lamp, until one stormy night the waves overwhelm him and he drowns.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid's Heroides and Musaeus' poem, Leander's love drives him into waters that finally carry him off.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's 'fierce flood' takes literal form in the strait that sweeps the lover away.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle compares the person overcome by passion to someone asleep, mad or drunk, who has knowledge but cannot use it at that moment.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, akrasia (weakness of will) is not ignorance but knowledge swept aside by feeling.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover still knows the worth of modesty, but the torrent of love has carried it away.

real_life_example.event_title: Emperor Xuanzong's devotion to Yang Guifei and the An Lushan Rebellion
real_life_example.event: Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, whose early reign brought reforms and the start of a golden age, came under the influence of his consorts in later life, above all Yang Guifei, and withdrew more and more from government while her relatives gained high posts. In 755 the general An Lushan rebelled, and Xuanzong fled the capital Chang'an with Yang Guifei and her family. During the flight his own troops demanded her death, the emperor consented, and he soon gave up the throne to his son.
real_life_example.explanation: A ruler once known for wise government let attachment carry away his judgement and his sense of duty, with grave results for his empire.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the fierce flood of love sweeps away the raft of restraint and honour; Xuanzong's passion swept away the careful rule that had once made his reign famous.

tamil:
தொடலைக் குறுந்தொடி தந்தாள் மடலொடு
மாலை உழக்கும் துயர்.
transliteration:
Thodalaik kurundhodi thandhaal madalodu
maalai uzhakkum thuyar.
meaning: The girl who wears small bangles strung like a garland has given me both the palm-stem horse and the sadness that hurts me every evening.
elementary: Sometimes a person we like very much can make us feel happy and sad at the same time. The speaker says the girl with the pretty little bangles has given him two things: a heavy heart every evening, and the idea of riding the palm horse.
university: Toṭalaik kuṟun-toṭi (தொடலைக் குறுந்தொடி) is an epithet standing for the heroine: 'she of the small bangles (kuṟun-toṭi) that are like a garland or string (toṭalai)'. Commentators differ on toṭalai: Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as 'garland-like, continuous', Kesikan as 'a linked set', while Kalaignar reads in a girdle (mēkalai) as well; Pappaiah's text appears to read 'like a mountain' (malai pōla), probably a misprint for mālai. Mālai uḻakkum tuyar (மாலை உழக்கும் துயர்), 'the sorrow that harrows in the evening', invokes the akam convention that evening is the hardest hour for separated lovers. Pope: 'The maid that slender armlets wears, like flowers entwined, / Has brought me horse of palm, and pangs of eventide!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa's play, King Dushyanta, after first meeting Shakuntala in the hermitage, grows pale and thin with longing and cannot rest, all because of the girl he has seen.
hinduism.explanation: The love-sickness of the hero is portrayed as caused by a single glimpse of the heroine.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Dushyanta can point to one girl as the source of all his torment.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck.”
christianity.explanation: The lover says that a single glance and a single necklace of the beloved have overpowered his heart.
christianity.tie_back: As the Kural names the beloved by her bangles, the Song names an ornament, a neck-chain, as part of what has undone him.

islam.quote_or_event: “When they saw him, they were so stunned ˹by his beauty˺ that they cut their hands.”
islam.explanation: The women of the city, invited to see Joseph, are so overwhelmed by his beauty that they cut their own hands with their knives.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, they suffer pain caused by nothing more than the sight of the beloved's beauty.
islam.source: Qur'an 12:31 (tr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Turn away thine eyes from me, For they have overcome me.”
judaism.explanation: The lover begs the beloved to look away because her eyes overwhelm him.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, he admits that the beloved herself is the source of the power that undoes him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Ummadanti Jataka, King Sivi sees the beautiful Ummadanti only once, from a distance, and falls so deeply in love that he grows ill and cannot attend to his duties, though in the end he masters himself.
buddhism.explanation: A single sight of the woman brings the king a sickness of longing that he must overcome.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's speaker also traces his torment to one girl, though in the Jataka the virtue lies in conquering it.
buddhism.source: Ummadanti Jataka (Jataka 527) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)

jainism.quote_or_event: On the way to his own wedding, Arishtanemi sees animals penned for the feast, gives his ornaments to his charioteer, and renounces the world, leaving his bride Rajimati in sorrow.
jainism.explanation: In the Jain account, one person's decision brings both release for himself and grief for the one who loved him.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's speaker says the beloved 'gave' him sorrow; Rajimati received hers from Arishtanemi in the same way.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.14-28 (paraphrase; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Enticing Lord, I cannot sleep; I sigh. I am adorned with necklaces, gowns, ornaments and make-up.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan's bride-soul, dressed in all her jewellery, still lies sighing and sleepless because her Beloved is away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural blames the girl of the garlanded bangles for the lover's evening torment; here the adorned bride herself bears the same sorrow of separation as night falls.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 830, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Struck by Cupid's golden arrow, Apollo burns with love for the nymph Daphne, who flees him; the god suffers while she remains untouched until she is changed into a laurel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows love as a wound inflicted on a lover by forces beyond his control, with the beloved as its focus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Apollo receives his torment through one maiden who does not share it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal describes 'crystallization': the lover's mind keeps covering the beloved with new perfections, so that every small detail about her deepens his attachment and his suffering.
philosophy.explanation: In On Love, the lover's imagination turns ordinary traits into sources of both delight and pain.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover identifies his beloved by a small detail, her little bangles, and blames her for all his sorrow.

real_life_example.event_title: Ivan Turgenev follows the singer Pauline Viardot abroad
real_life_example.place: St Petersburg, Russia; Paris, France; Baden-Baden, Germany
real_life_example.event: The Russian writer Ivan Turgenev fell in love with the singer Pauline Viardot when she first performed in Russia in 1843. In 1847 he left Russia for Paris with the Viardot circle and stayed there until 1850, and he later moved to Baden-Baden in Germany to be near her again. He wrote the libretto for her operetta Le dernier sorcier (1869) and spent his last years at Bougival near Paris.
real_life_example.explanation: One meeting with a singer reshaped the whole course of a great writer's life and kept him far from home for decades.
real_life_example.tie_back: In the kural the lover says that the girl with the small bangles has given him both the palm-stem horse and the sorrow of every evening; Turgenev's love for one woman likewise gave him a lifetime of devotion and longing.

tamil:
மடலூர்தல் யாமத்தும் உள்ளுவேன் மன்ற
படல்ஒல்லா பேதைக்கென் கண்.
transliteration:
Madaloordhal yaamaththum ulluvaen mandra
padalollaa paedhaikken kan.
meaning: Even at midnight I think about riding the palm-stem horse, since that innocent girl keeps my eyes from closing in sleep.
elementary: Have you ever been so worried or excited that you couldn't fall asleep? The speaker lies awake in the middle of the night, thinking about the girl he loves and about his big plan to tell the whole village.
university: Yāmam (யாமம்) is the deep watch of the night, midnight; uḷḷuvēṉ (உள்ளுவேன்) 'I shall think, brood on', with maṉṟa (மன்ற) 'certainly' as an intensifier. Paṭal ollā (படல் ஒல்லா), 'not consenting to close', describes eyes that will not shut, and pētai (பேதை), literally 'innocent, simple one', is a conventional endearment for the heroine (also a technical term for the youngest of the seven stages of womanhood). Commentators in Parimelazhagar's line take it as the hero assuring the confidante that his resolve is not a passing mood but something he dwells on even at midnight. The ytamizh.com text prints படல்ஒல்லா without a space, thirukkural.net the same; editions vary only in spacing. Pope: 'Of climbing horse of palm in midnight hour, I think; / My eyes know no repose for that same simple maid.'

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Damayanti, having heard of King Nala's virtues, falls in love with him before they meet; she grows pale and thin, sighs, and loses her rest, so that her companions notice her changed state.
hinduism.explanation: The Nala episode is the classic Sanskrit account of a lover kept awake and wasting through longing.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's lover, Damayanti cannot rest because of the one she loves.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved lies awake at night longing for the one she loves.
christianity.tie_back: Both lovers are awake in the night, their thoughts fixed on the beloved.

islam.quote_or_event: Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya is remembered as praying through the night, saying that while lovers are alone with their beloveds, she is alone with her Lord.
islam.explanation: The great woman saint of Basra turned the lover's sleepless night into an act of devotion.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's lover is also awake at midnight because of the one he loves; Rabi'a gives that wakefulness a mystical meaning.
islam.source: Farid al-Din 'Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, life of Rabi'a (paraphrase)

judaism.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved says that even when her body rests, her heart stays awake for the one she loves.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover is in the same state: his eyes will not close because his heart is with her.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the sleepless person's endless night as an image for the long round of existence of those without wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover is that sleepless one, and the Buddhist verse sees his long night as a symptom of attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jacobi notes that Rajimati's lament after Arishtanemi's renunciation is the subject of a later Jain Sanskrit poem, the Nemiduta of Vikrama, which borrows the last line of each stanza from Kalidasa's poem of a separated lover, the Meghaduta.
jainism.explanation: Jain poets themselves took up the longing of the abandoned bride as a theme of separation poetry.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's sleepless lover, Rajimati in this tradition is shown dwelling on the beloved who is gone.
jainism.source: Hermann Jacobi, note to Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.28 (SBE 45), on Vikrama's Nemiduta

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Separation from my Lord keeps my body awake, O my dear beloved; I cannot sleep at all.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das gives the bride-soul's cry that the pain of separation (birha) will not let her body rest, so the night passes without sleep.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover broods even at midnight because his eyes will not close; the Sikh bride-soul likewise lies awake through the night, kept up by longing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 452, Raag Aasaa, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Argonautica, Medea lies awake through the night, torn between shame, which holds her back, and love for Jason, which urges her on to help him against her own father.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius shows a young woman's night-long struggle between modesty and desire.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the heart of the chapter: a lover awake at night, weighing reserve against love.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And in her madness can neither sleep by night nor abide in her place by day.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates describes the soul of a lover separated from the beautiful one as unable to rest by night or day.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover is in exactly this state: his eyes will not close at midnight.

real_life_example.event_title: Kafka's hundreds of letters to Felice Bauer
real_life_example.place: Prague (now Czech Republic) and Berlin, Germany
real_life_example.event: Franz Kafka met Felice Bauer on 13 August 1912 at the home of his friend Max Brod in Prague and wrote her his first letter on 20 September 1912. Over the next five years he sent her more than five hundred letters and postcards, a romance carried on mostly on paper because they met in person only rarely. They were engaged twice, first in 1914, and both engagements were broken off; the final break came in 1917.
real_life_example.explanation: Kafka's restless letter-writing shows how a love that cannot be settled keeps the mind turning over the same longing again and again.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's lover cannot close his eyes even at midnight for thinking of the girl; Kafka's flood of letters shows the same sleepless, unending preoccupation with a beloved he could neither win nor give up.

tamil:
கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும் மடலேறாப்
பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்க தில்.
transliteration:
Kadalanna kaamam uzhandhum madalaeraap
pennin perundhakka thil.
meaning: There is nothing as great as a woman who suffers a love as big as the sea and still never rides the palm-stem horse.
elementary: Imagine two friends who both miss someone very much. One shouts about it all over town; the other keeps going quietly and patiently. The poet says the quiet, patient strength the woman shows is one of the greatest things in the world.
university: The couplet turns the chapter: kaṭal aṉṉa kāmam (கடலன்ன காமம்), 'love like the sea', is borne (uḻantum, 'even while suffering') by the woman who nonetheless does not ride the madal (maṭal ēṟā). This echoes the Tolkāppiyam rule that the madal is never proper for women, and the commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read it as praise of the endurance of women; Kesikan sharpens it into a comparison: no man has such worth. The speaker is disputed: some commentators give it to the hero, conceding the heroine's greater restraint, while others read it as the heroine's own words, and many hear the remaining couplets of the chapter in her voice. Perun-takkatu il (பெருந்தக்கது இல்) is 'there is nothing of greater worth'. Pope: 'There's nought of greater worth than woman's long-enduring soul, / Who, vexed by love like ocean waves, climbs not the horse of palm.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Held captive in Ravana's Ashoka grove, Sita endures long separation from Rama, refuses every threat and temptation, and keeps her dignity and faith until Hanuman finds her.
hinduism.explanation: The Sundara Kanda makes Sita's quiet endurance in separation the very picture of a noble woman's strength.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita's vast grief borne in dignified restraint is the kind of nobility the Kural praises.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes true love as patient endurance that does not give way.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural praises exactly this love that endures all things without breaking out in a public display.

islam.quote_or_event: When Jacob hears that Joseph has been lost, he answers that 'beautiful patience' (sabrun jamil) is his course, and he endures his grief with dignity.
islam.explanation: The Qur'an holds up patient, uncomplaining endurance of heartbreak as a mark of nobility.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's woman shows the same 'beautiful patience' in bearing a sea-wide love without display.

judaism.quote_or_event: “She said to him: If he would listen to me, he would sit and study for another twelve years.”
judaism.explanation: Rachel, wife of Rabbi Akiva, endures twelve years of separation and, when mocked as a 'widow of a living man', declares she would bear twelve more for his sake.
judaism.tie_back: Her long, uncomplaining endurance of separation is the kind of nobility the Kural assigns to women.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 63a (William Davidson Edition, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: Buddhist tradition tells that after Prince Siddhartha left home, Yasodhara chose to live as he did, wearing simple robes and eating once a day, enduring her loss with dignity and later becoming a nun.
buddhism.explanation: Yasodhara is remembered for bearing abandonment without bitterness or display.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's woman, Yasodhara bore a great love and loss with restraint.
buddhism.source: Jataka Nidanakatha and later Pali commentarial tradition (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Firm and decided she cut off her tresses which were black like bees and dressed with a brush and comb.”
jainism.explanation: Forsaken by Arishtanemi, Rajimati does not complain or make a display; she calmly takes up the life of a nun.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's woman, Rajimati carries a great love with steadiness instead of public protest, though she turns it toward renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Let patience be your purpose in life; implant this within your being. In this way, you will grow into a great river; you will not break off into a tiny stream.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid praises patience (sabar) firmly held within, which makes a person as deep and broad as a great river instead of a broken trickle.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural honours the woman who carries a love as vast as the sea yet never rides the madal; Farid likewise honours the patient endurance that holds a river-like fullness without breaking out.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 117) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope waits twenty years for Odysseus, putting off the suitors with the trick of the shroud she weaves by day and unravels by night, weeping in private but never giving way.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer makes her patient, controlled fidelity the model of a noble wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope bears a sea of longing without display, as the Kural's woman does.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle distinguishes endurance (karteria), the ability to hold out against pains and pressures most people give way to, from softness, which yields.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, enduring what most would not is a mark of strength of character.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural ranks the woman who endures love's sea without yielding to the madal above all others, the same esteem for endurance.

real_life_example.event_title: Princess Margaret announces she will not marry Peter Townsend
real_life_example.event: Princess Margaret, sister of Queen Elizabeth II, wished to marry Group Captain Peter Townsend, a former equerry who was divorced, at a time when the Church of England did not accept remarriage after divorce. Townsend was posted abroad as an air attaché, and after they met again in October 1955 she issued a public statement that she had decided not to marry him. In it she cited the Church's teaching that Christian marriage is indissoluble and her duty to the Commonwealth.
real_life_example.explanation: A young woman bore a deep and long-standing love but chose restraint over defiance, and made the choice herself in public.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises the woman who suffers a love as vast as the sea yet never rides the palm-stem horse; Margaret kept her love within the limits she felt bound by rather than breaking them openly.

tamil:
நிறையரியர் மன்அளியர் என்னாது காமம்
மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்.
transliteration:
Niraiyariyar manaliyar ennaadhu kaamam
maraiyirandhu mandru padum.
meaning: Love does not stop to think whether someone is self-controlled or deserves pity. It breaks out of hiding and shows itself in the open street.
elementary: Have you ever tried to keep a happy secret, but your big smile gave it away? Love can be like that. Even when someone tries very hard to hide it, it shows on their face and everyone in town finds out.
university: The key words are niṟai (நிறை), 'firmness of mind, the power to keep one's feelings in', aḷiyar (அளியர்), 'those deserving pity', maṟai (மறை), 'secrecy', and maṉṟu (மன்று), the village common or public assembly ground where talk spreads. The opening phrase niṟai-ariyar is read in two opposite ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take it as 'lacking restraint', while Solomon Pappaiah reads 'very restrained' (ariyar as 'hard to overcome'), and Pope follows the second ('In virtue hard to move, yet very tender, too, are we'). Pope's 'we' reflects the common view that from here the heroine is speaking, lamenting that her love is about to become public gossip (alar), which leads into chapter 115. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Rukmini, though a modest princess promised by her brother to another, sends a brahmin messenger with a letter to Krishna declaring her love and asking him to carry her away before the wedding.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana praises Rukmini's love for breaking through the reserve expected of her.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, love refuses to stay hidden in a well-guarded heart and makes itself known.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved openly asks the women of the city to carry word of her love-sickness.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, she finds that her love has passed beyond private feeling into public knowledge.

islam.quote_or_event: “Some women of the city gossiped, ‘The Chief Minister’s wife is trying to seduce her slave-boy. Love for him has plagued her heart.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells how the Egyptian noblewoman's passion for Joseph became the talk of the city.
islam.tie_back: The verse is a vivid case of the Kural's warning: love breaks out of secrecy and becomes public gossip.
islam.source: Qur'an 12:30 (tr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: “When I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; Yea, and none would despise me.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved wishes her love could be shown openly in the street without bringing scorn.
judaism.tie_back: She feels the same tension as the Kural: love pressing to be seen in public while society watches and judges.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha names three things that are carried on in secret rather than in the open, among them affairs with women, and contrasts them with things that shine openly, like the sun, the moon and the Dhamma.
buddhism.explanation: The discourse treats secrecy as a mark of what cannot bear the light.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural observes that love does not stay secret; the Buddhist saying explains why lovers try to keep it so.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The daughter of the best king, true to self-control and her vows, maintained the honour of her clan and family, and her virtue, and spoke to him.”
jainism.explanation: Faced with Rathanemi's sudden passion, Rajimati keeps her composure and her family's honour.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says love ignores a person's restraint and breaks into the open; the Jain text praises a woman whose restraint held firm.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “By various efforts, I have enshrined it within my heart; this jewel cannot be hidden by hiding it.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Bheekhan says the jewel of the Lord's Name, though carefully kept within the heart, cannot be hidden however one tries.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says love does not respect restraint but breaks its secrecy and shows itself in the public square; Bheekhan's jewel of love likewise will not stay concealed.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 659, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Bheekhan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides' Hippolytus, Queen Phaedra resolves to hide her love for her stepson in silence and even to starve herself, but her nurse draws the secret from her and it spreads, with tragic results.
greek_mythology.explanation: The play is built around a love that its bearer tries desperately to conceal and cannot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Phaedra's story is a tragic form of the Kural's point: love will not stay behind the screen of restraint.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There is no disguise which can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.”
philosophy.explanation: La Rochefoucauld observes that real love always shows itself in the end.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own statement: love breaks through every attempt to keep it hidden.
philosophy.source: François de La Rochefoucauld, Maxims, no. 70 (Project Gutenberg English edition)

real_life_example.event_title: Crown Prince Harald's secret romance with Sonja Haraldsen becomes public
real_life_example.event: Crown Prince Harald of Norway and Sonja Haraldsen, who was not of royal descent, were a couple for several years before the relationship became public; rumours of a girlfriend he wished to marry spread in 1967 and 1968. The press and public then debated whether a commoner could become queen, and Harald made clear that if he could not marry Sonja he would consider staying unmarried for life. After about nine years together King Olav V consented, and they married in Oslo Cathedral on 29 August 1968.
real_life_example.explanation: A love kept quiet for years could not stay hidden forever, and once it came out it was argued over by the whole nation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says love does not stop to weigh restraint but breaks out of its secrecy into the public square; Harald and Sonja's long-hidden love ended up debated across all of Norway.

tamil:
அறிகிலார் எல்லாரும் என்றேஎன் காமம்
மறுகின் மறுகும் மருண்டு.
transliteration:
Arikilaar ellaarum endrae-en kaamam
marukin marukum marundu.
meaning: As if it thinks not everyone knows about it yet, my love wanders confused through the streets.
elementary: Imagine a puppy that has escaped from its yard and runs up and down the street, bumping into everyone. The speaker says her love is like that: it has got out and is wandering around town where everyone can see it.
university: Love itself is personified: thinking 'not everyone knows' (aṟikilār ellārum), it maṟukiṉ maṟukum (மறுகின் மறுகும்), 'roams about in the street', maruṇṭu (மருண்டு), 'in confusion, bewildered'. The pun on maṟuku (street) and maṟukum (wanders, whirls) is characteristic of Valluvar's sound-play. Commentators note the irony: because the speaker had kept quiet (Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar: 'because I endured in silence'), love itself seems to have decided to announce itself; Pappaiah says it goes about the streets as gossip (ampal and alar), anticipating chapter 115. The ytamizh.com text prints என்றேஎன் as one unit and thirukkural.net the same; Pope reads 'There's no one knows my heart, so says my love'.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna vanishes from the circle dance, the gopis wander through the forest of Vrindavan as if mad, asking the trees, the creepers and the earth whether they have seen him.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana describes their bewildered search as a sign of love that has taken over their whole being.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's love that roams the streets bewildered, the gopis' love sends them wandering openly in search of the beloved.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved leaves her bed and searches the streets of the city for her lover.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's love wandering the streets in confusion is pictured here almost literally.

islam.quote_or_event: “Barira's husband was a slave called Mughith, as if I am seeing him now, going behind Barira and weeping with his tears flowing down his beard.”
islam.explanation: Ibn 'Abbas recalls how Mughith followed Barira through Medina in tears after she left him, and the Prophet remarked on the strength of his love.
islam.tie_back: Mughith's love, like the Kural's, wandered openly through the streets for all to see.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved goes out at night calling for her lover and cannot find him.
judaism.tie_back: Her calling and searching through the city is the same restless, public wandering the Kural gives to love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Kisa Gotami, grief-stricken at her child's death, carries him from house to house through the town asking for medicine, while people think she has lost her mind, until the Buddha gently leads her to understanding.
buddhism.explanation: The commentarial story shows how attachment can send a person wandering bewildered in public.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's love, her attachment drives her through the streets in confusion for all to see.
buddhism.source: Therigatha commentary, story of Kisa Gotami (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Sutrakritanga warns monks that one who gives way to infatuation with a woman loses the respect he had and ends up mocked and ordered about, his weakness known to all.
jainism.explanation: The chapter on women in this early Jain text describes how desire, once yielded to, becomes a public humiliation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural describes love becoming public; the Jain text treats that exposure as a warning.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4 (paraphrase; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Some call him a ghost; some say that he is a demon. ... Crazy Nanak has gone insane, after his Lord, the King.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak reports what people say about him as he goes about absorbed in the Lord, and accepts the name of madman (baurana) for his love.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's love roams the streets bewildered, as if wanting everyone to know; Guru Nanak's love likewise makes him a public spectacle, talked about by all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 991, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After losing Eurydice a second time, Orpheus wanders grieving through the wild lands of Thrace, refusing all other love and singing of his loss.
greek_mythology.explanation: Virgil and Ovid show love that has lost its object and roams openly in its sorrow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's bewildered love wandering the streets, Orpheus' love wanders openly with nowhere to rest.
