philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza remarks that people who are inflamed with love and dream night and day of nothing but their beloved are, like the greedy and the ambitious, in a kind of madness, though people do not usually call it so.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, an emotion that fixes the mind on one object takes away its freedom.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's love, wandering bewildered through the streets, is that kind of mind-possessing passion made visible.

real_life_example.event_title: Chagall paints himself floating to kiss Bella in Birthday
real_life_example.event: In July 1915, on the occasion of Marc Chagall's birthday, Bella Rosenfeld came to his room in Vitebsk with food and flowers wrapped in embroidered shawls. Chagall painted the scene as Birthday, showing himself floating in the air to kiss her; the oil-on-cardboard painting is now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. The two married on 25 July 1915, though her family still had doubts about the match.
real_life_example.explanation: Chagall turned his private joy into an image so open and exuberant that it has been shown to the world ever since.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural pictures love as if it were wandering bewildered through the streets so that everyone will know of it; Chagall's floating lovers show the same giddy love that cannot stay hidden.

tamil:
யாம்கண்ணின் காண நகுப அறிவில்லார்
யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா ஆறு.
transliteration:
Yaamkannin kaana nagupa arivillaar
yaampatta thaampadaa aaru.
meaning: People with no understanding laugh at me right in front of my eyes, only because they have never suffered what I suffer.
elementary: Have you ever seen someone laugh at a friend who was crying, just because they didn't understand how sad the friend felt? The speaker says people who laugh at lovers only do it because they have never felt that pain themselves.
university: The couplet is built on a balanced contrast: yām paṭṭa (யாம் பட்ட), 'what I have suffered', against tām paṭā (தாம் படா), 'what they have not suffered', with āṟu (ஆறு), 'the manner, the reason', at the end. Aṟivillār (அறிவில்லார்), 'those without understanding', laugh kaṇṇiṉ kāṇa (கண்ணின் காண), 'so that I see it with my eyes', that is, openly to the speaker's face. Commentators take it as the closing lament of the chapter, spoken in the tradition as the heroine's words once her love is known, and Kalaignar turns it into a general maxim: only those who have never known love's pain mock its sufferers. Pope: 'Before my eyes the foolish make a mock of me, / Because they ne'er endured the pangs I now must drie.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In her songs, the princess-poet Mirabai says that people call her mad and that she has thrown away family honour and public shame (lok-laj) for love of Krishna, and she accepts their mockery.
hinduism.explanation: The bhakti tradition preserves Mira's defiant answer to the scorn of her in-laws and her town.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Mira is laughed at by those who have never felt the love that has seized her.
hinduism.source: Mirabai, padas (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Alston, The Devotional Poems of Mirabai, 1980)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Others mocking said, These men are full of new wine.”
christianity.explanation: At Pentecost, onlookers who did not understand what had seized the apostles mocked them as drunk.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, people who have not shared an overwhelming experience laugh at those who have.

islam.quote_or_event: “This is the one for whose love you criticized me!”
islam.explanation: After the women of the city have seen Joseph for themselves and been overwhelmed, the noblewoman answers their earlier gossip.
islam.tie_back: Her retort makes the Kural's point: those who mock a lover change their tune once they have felt the same thing.
islam.source: Qur'an 12:32 (tr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

judaism.quote_or_event: When David dances with all his might before the Ark, Michal mocks him for shamelessly uncovering himself, and he answers: “And I will be yet more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight.”
judaism.explanation: David refuses to be shamed out of his joyous, undignified devotion by someone who does not share it.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, David is mocked for abandoning reserve by one who has not felt what moves him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Atula that people have always blamed others: they blame the one who sits silent, the one who speaks much, and the one who speaks little; there is no one in the world who is not blamed.
buddhism.explanation: The verse teaches that ridicule from others says more about the world than about the one ridiculed.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover is laughed at too; the Dhammapada advises not to measure oneself by such mockery.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga recounts that during Mahavira's wanderings in the rough Ladha country people struck him, set dogs on him and abused him, and he bore it all without anger.
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's calm under the scorn and violence of those who did not understand him is a model of Jain forbearance.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's lover is mocked by those who have not shared his experience; Mahavira shows a Jain answer to such ridicule, patient endurance.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra 1.8.3 (paraphrase; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “People say that Kabeer has gone insane. Only the Lord realizes the secret of Kabeer.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir answers those who mock him as mad by saying that only the Lord, who shares his love, understands what he feels.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover says thoughtless people laugh at him only because they have never suffered as he has; Kabir likewise says the mockers cannot know what only the Beloved knows.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1158, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Hephaestus traps Ares and Aphrodite in his net, he calls the gods to see, and they break into unquenchable laughter at the lovers.
greek_mythology.explanation: The bard Demodocus' song in the Odyssey shows lovers exposed to the laughter of onlookers.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, the lovers are laughed at openly once their love is known, though in Homer the laughter has more justification.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “As he forgets earthly interests and is rapt in the divine, the vulgar deem him mad, and rebuke him; they do not see that he is inspired.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says the person seized by the divine madness of love is mocked by ordinary people who do not understand it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's complaint exactly: those without understanding laugh at a lover because they have not felt what he feels.

real_life_example.event_title: Richard and Mildred Loving are convicted for their marriage
real_life_example.event: Richard Loving, who was white, and Mildred Jeter, who was of African American and Native American descent, married in Washington, D.C., on 2 June 1958 and returned home to Caroline County, Virginia, where interracial marriage was illegal. Weeks later the sheriff arrested them at home in the early morning, and in January 1959 they pleaded guilty and were sentenced to a year in prison, suspended on condition that they leave Virginia. In 1967 the United States Supreme Court unanimously struck the law down in Loving v. Virginia.
real_life_example.explanation: Officials who had no understanding of the couple's love treated it as a crime, and only years later did the nation's highest court see it differently.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's lover says thoughtless people mock him because they have never suffered as he has; the Lovings were judged and punished by people who did not understand what their love meant to them.

tamil:
அலரெழ ஆருயிர் நிற்கும் அதனைப்
பலரறியார் பாக்கியத் தால்.
transliteration:
alarezha aaruyir niRkum adhanaip
palaraRiyaar paakkiyath thaal
meaning: Now that the town gossips about our love, my precious life, which was slipping away, holds on. Luckily, the gossips do not know their talk is what keeps me alive.
elementary: Imagine you have a secret friend you are not allowed to play with, and you feel very sad. Then the other children start teasing, ‘You two are best friends!’ Strangely, the teasing makes you feel better, because now everyone treats you as a pair. The young man in this verse feels just like that, and he is glad the teasers have not worked out that they are helping him.
university: Chapter 115, alar aṟivuṟuttal (அலர் அறிவுறுத்தல்), concerns alar (அலர்) and its synonym kauvai (கௌவை), the village gossip that breaks out once a secret courtship (kaḷavu) becomes known; Parimelazhagar’s preface says the chapter has the hero telling the confidante (tōḻi) how the rumour serves him, and the heroine and tōḻi telling the hero of it to press him toward marriage (varaivu) or elopement (uṭanpōkku), and that it follows the chapter on abandoning reserve because it arises once nāṇ is given up. Parimelazhagar sets this couplet as the hero’s reply when the tōḻi, after a failed tryst, uses the rumour to urge marriage: the rumour makes the hard-to-win girl seem attainable, so his ‘precious life’ (ār uyir) has a support (paṟṟukkōṭu); pākkiyam (பாக்கியம்) is glossed teyvam, ‘fate, providence’, which keeps the gossips from realising this, for if they knew they would fall silent and his life would go. Manakkudavar instead reads ār uyir as the heroine’s life. The text is identical on ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com; Pope renders ‘By this same rumour’s rise, my precious life stands fast.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Gita Govinda opens with Nanda telling Radha to take Krishna home through the darkening forest, and the poem then follows the two lovers’ meeting by the Yamuna, away from the eyes of the village.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s poem treats Radha and Krishna’s love as something lived on the edge of village knowledge, half hidden and half known.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover lives in that same space, where a secret love becomes the talk of the village and the talk turns out to sustain it.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, canto 1, opening verse (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: When Joseph learns that Mary, to whom he is betrothed, is with child, he resolves to put her away privately rather than make her a public example.
christianity.explanation: Matthew shows a betrothed man weighing what public talk would do to the woman he is bound to.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s lover faces public talk about his beloved too, though for him the talk is welcome and keeps him alive.

islam.quote_or_event: “And women in the city said, ‘The wife of al-ʿAzeez is seeking to seduce her slave boy; he has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her [to be] in clear error.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an records the gossip of the city’s women about Zulaikha’s love for Joseph.
islam.tie_back: This is the same alar, a love that has become the talk of the town, though here the gossip is pure censure and does nothing to sustain the lover.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And she lay at his feet until the morning; and she rose up before one could discern another. For he said: ‘Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing-floor.’”
judaism.explanation: Boaz takes care that his night meeting with Ruth does not become the talk of the town before he can marry her properly.
judaism.tie_back: Boaz fears exactly the alar the Kural’s lover welcomes, which shows how unusual the Tamil hero’s attitude is.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When rival wanderers spread a slanderous rumour about the Buddha after the murder of the wanderer Sundari, the monks are reviled in the town, and the Buddha tells them the noise will not last long and will vanish after seven days.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats public talk as a passing noise that a calm mind can wait out.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover clings to the town’s talk as his lifeline; the Buddha teaches that such talk has no lasting power to give life or take it away.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jacobi’s note on the Kapila lecture retells the commentary story: the student Kapila fell in love with the servant girl who waited on him and, to buy her ornaments for a festival, set out at night to beg two pieces of gold, was arrested, and was brought before the king.
jainism.explanation: The Jain commentary uses a young man’s love affair, which ends in public exposure before the king, as the starting point of his conversion.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s hero, Kapila’s love is exposed to public view; the Jain tale, however, turns that exposure toward renunciation rather than marriage.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 8, Jacobi’s introductory note (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Slander me, slander me - go ahead, people, and slander me. ... The slanderer wishes me long life.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir welcomes the talk people spread about him, saying that the slanderer, without meaning to, actually wants him to live.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover says the town's gossip keeps his ebbing life from slipping away, though the gossips do not know it; Kabir likewise finds that the slander aimed at him only gives him life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod warns that Talk (Pheme) is light and easily raised but hard to be rid of, and that talk voiced by many people never wholly dies away, for she too is in some way a goddess.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Hesiod, rumour is almost a divine power with a life of its own once many mouths carry it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s lover experiences that self-sustaining life of rumour, but finds in it a power that keeps him alive rather than one to fear.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 760-764 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal observes that a very small degree of hope is enough to give birth to love, and that love can then survive for a while on almost nothing.
philosophy.explanation: In De l’amour, love lives on hope, and even slight evidence can keep it alive.
philosophy.tie_back: The town’s rumour gives the Kural’s lover exactly that small hope, and it is enough to keep his life from slipping away.
philosophy.source: Stendhal, On Love (De l’amour, 1822), early chapters on the birth of love (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: The 'Mitchy boom' greets Crown Prince Akihito's engagement to Michiko Shoda
real_life_example.event: Crown Prince Akihito met Michiko Shoda, the daughter of a flour-milling businessman, at a tennis match in Karuizawa in the summer of 1957, and the Imperial Household Agency announced their engagement in November 1958. Some conservatives objected to a commoner becoming crown princess, but the public took her to heart: a 'Mitchy boom' swept the country, women's magazines covered her closely, and television sales doubled as people prepared to watch the wedding. They married on 10 April 1959 before crowds of more than half a million along the parade route.
real_life_example.explanation: The public's warm talk and enthusiasm surrounded a match that broke with tradition and gave it strong popular support.
real_life_example.tie_back: In the kural the lover says that the town's gossip about the romance is what keeps him alive; for Akihito and Michiko, the nation's eager talk was a source of strength rather than shame.

tamil:
மலரன்ன கண்ணாள் அருமை அறியாது
அலரெமக்கு ஈந்ததிவ் வூர்.
transliteration:
malaranna kaNNaaL arumai aRiyaadhu
alaremakku eendhadhiv voor
meaning: This town does not know how rare and hard to win the girl with flower-like eyes is. By spreading a rumor about us, it has done me a favor.
elementary: Suppose there is a very special girl in your class whom everyone thinks is out of reach. One day people start saying, ‘Oh, she likes you!’ They are only gossiping, but the gossip makes her seem a little closer. The young man in this verse thanks the town for gossiping, because the town has no idea how precious she really is.
university: Parimelazhagar marks this as ‘itu um atu’, the same situation as 1141, the hero speaking to the tōḻi. Arumai (அருமை) here means ‘difficulty of attainment’, which he explains as caused by failed trysts (alla kuṟi) and obstacles (iṭaiyīṭu); the town, unaware of it, has made her seem ‘easy’ (eḷiyaḷ) and so has ‘given’ (īntatu) him the rumour, a word chosen because the rumour is his support. Malar aṉṉa kaṇṇāḷ, ‘she whose eyes are like flowers’ (Puliyur Kesikan specifies the kuvaḷai or blue water-lily), is a conventional epithet. Manakkudavar reads arumai as the nobility of her birth (iṟpiṟappu), so that the gossips speak of her as of a common girl. The text agrees on ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Uttara Kanda, Rama asks his companion Bhadra what the citizens are saying, and learns that the townspeople are gossiping about Sita, questioning how he could take her back after she lived in Ravana’s house.
hinduism.explanation: The people of Ayodhya talk about Sita without understanding her proven purity and worth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s town, Ayodhya talks without knowing the true rarity of the woman it discusses, though in the Ramayana the gossip brings sorrow, not help.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My dove, my undefiled is but one; she is the only one of her mother, she is the choice one of her that bare her. The daughters saw her, and blessed her; yea, the queens and the concubines, and they praised her.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song insists his beloved is unique, and pictures everyone who sees her recognising it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s lover also knows his beloved is beyond compare; his complaint and his comfort is that the gossiping town has not seen it.

islam.quote_or_event: “So when she heard of their scheming, she sent for them and prepared for them a banquet and gave each one of them a knife and said [to Joseph], ‘Come out before them.’ And when they saw him, they greatly admired him and cut their hands and said, ‘Perfect is Allāh! This is not a man; this is none but a noble angel.’”
islam.explanation: The women who gossiped about Zulaikha’s love change their tune the moment they see how extraordinary Joseph is.
islam.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s point: gossips talk about a love without knowing the rare worth of the beloved.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs asks who can find a woman of valour, and answers that her price is far above rubies.
judaism.explanation: The closing poem of Proverbs celebrates a woman whose worth is rare and hard to find.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero prizes his beloved for the same rarity (arumai) that the gossiping town fails to see.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that there never was, never will be and is not now anyone who is wholly blamed or wholly praised.
buddhism.explanation: The verse warns that public opinion is fickle and never a true measure of a person.
buddhism.tie_back: The town in the Kural misjudges the heroine’s worth, which illustrates exactly how unreliable public talk is.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Arishtanemi’s brother Rathanemi sees Rajimati alone and invites her to enjoy pleasures with him, she firmly rebukes him and recalls him to his monastic vows.
jainism.explanation: Rathanemi treats Rajimati as easily approachable and discovers her steadfastness and worth.
jainism.tie_back: Parimelazhagar says the gossips make the heroine seem ‘easy’ (eḷiyaḷ) without knowing her rarity; Rathanemi makes the same mistake about Rajimati.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “One who slanders me is my friend; the slanderer is in my thoughts.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir turns the slanderer into a friend, because the talk against him serves his spiritual good.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the town, not knowing how hard the girl is to win, hands the lover a rumour and so does him a favour; Kabir likewise counts the one who spreads talk about him a friend.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Helen walks to the wall of Troy, the old men of the city murmur that it is no cause for blame that Trojans and Achaeans should suffer so long for such a woman, so like is she to the immortal goddesses, though they wish she would go home.
greek_mythology.explanation: The elders of Troy gossip about Helen, and in the same breath admit her extraordinary worth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s town gossips without seeing the heroine’s rarity; Homer’s elders gossip and do see it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Montaigne argues that the judgment of the common crowd is too uncertain and ill-informed to be a measure of anyone’s true worth, and that a person should not live by it.
philosophy.explanation: In his essay on glory, Montaigne doubts that public reputation ever tracks real merit.
philosophy.tie_back: The gossiping town in the Kural proves his point by talking about a woman whose real value it has not grasped.

real_life_example.event_title: Tennyson and Emily Sellwood part, and a story spreads to explain it
real_life_example.event: Alfred Tennyson became engaged to Emily Sellwood in the late 1830s, but in 1840 the engagement was broken off. Accounts differ on why: one says her family ended it after he lost money in a bad investment, while another says Tennyson himself broke it off over money and fears about his family's health, and that a story was put about that her father had forbidden the match in order to spare Emily embarrassment. They were reunited and married quietly in 1850, shortly after In Memoriam was published.
real_life_example.explanation: Talk about a broken engagement could shape how a couple was seen, yet their bond survived ten years apart.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's lover is grateful that the town's rumour has linked him with the girl it does not know is so hard to win; Tennyson and Emily's story shows how what people said about a courtship could serve a purpose of its own.

tamil:
உறாஅதோ ஊரறிந்த கௌவை அதனைப்
பெறாஅது பெற்றன்ன நீர்த்து.
transliteration:
uRaaadhoa ooraRindha keLavai adhanaip
peRaaadhu petranna neerththu
meaning: Isn't the rumor the whole town knows a gain for me? Hearing it, my heart feels as if we are already together, though we are not yet.
elementary: Have you ever wanted a puppy so much that, when your friends started saying, ‘You’re getting a puppy!’, you felt almost as happy as if it were already sitting in your lap? The young man in this verse feels that way. The town’s talk about him and his beloved makes him feel as if they were already together.
university: Again ‘itu um atu’ in Parimelazhagar: the hero speaks. Uṟāatō (உறாஅதோ, with the alapeṭai lengthening) is a rhetorical question, ‘does it not come to me?’, and kauvai (கௌவை) is a synonym of alar; peṟāatu peṟṟaṉṉa nīrttu means ‘it has the nature of having got what was not got’. Parimelazhagar supplies maṉam, ‘my mind’, as the subject of nīrttu and glosses the phrase as having a joy like that of actual union. Manakkudavar reads it as the hero telling the tōḻi that the rumour should be welcomed, since through it the family will come to consent. The sources print கெளவை, which is a common encoding of கௌவை (kau) with separate vowel signs; this edition normalises it to கௌவை, as thirukkural.com’s Parimelazhagar text has it.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Meghaduta, the exiled Yaksha, separated from his wife, consoles himself by picturing her in detail and sending a cloud as his messenger, as though contact could be had through imagination alone.
hinduism.explanation: The poem shows a lover living on an imagined closeness when the real one is denied.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero, too, enjoys through the town’s rumour a union he has not yet obtained.

christianity.quote_or_event: The Letter to the Hebrews defines faith as the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
christianity.explanation: Faith, for the writer, makes what is hoped for present already in a real way.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s hero feels something similar: the rumour makes the union he hopes for feel already possessed.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn Hazm devotes a chapter of The Ring of the Dove to the lover’s contentment, describing how a lover separated from the beloved can be satisfied with very little, such as a glance, a token, or news of her.
islam.explanation: The Andalusian scholar sees that lovers make a feast out of the smallest share of the beloved.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s hero is content in just this way: the mere rumour gives him the feeling of having what he does not have.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapter on contentment (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)

judaism.quote_or_event: Jacob serves seven years for Rachel, and they seem to him but a few days, because of the love he has for her.
judaism.explanation: Love for Rachel makes the long wait feel short, as if the goal were already near.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero likewise feels the union he lacks as if it were already his, though for him it is rumour, not love alone, that does this.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares sensual pleasures to a dream: a man dreams of lovely parks and lakes, but on waking sees nothing of them.
buddhism.explanation: Pleasures enjoyed in the mind feel real but have no substance.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero enjoys a union that exists only in the town’s talk; Buddhism would call that pleasure dreamlike.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A miracle! O king, you give up those wonderful pleasures, in search of imaginary objects; your very hope will cause your ruin.”
jainism.explanation: Indra, testing King Nami, accuses him of giving up real pleasures for imaginary ones; Nami answers that it is worldly pleasure that is the illusion.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero takes delight in a union that so far exists only in talk; the Jain dialogue asks which pleasures are real and which are imagined.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.51 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If I am slandered, I go to heaven; the wealth of the Naam, the Name of the Lord, abides within my mind.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir says that being slandered is pure gain for him, since it brings him nearer to the Lord and settles the Name in his mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover asks whether the rumour the whole town knows is not a gain to him, making him feel he has the union he has not yet won; Kabir likewise counts the town's talk as a gain that brings him to the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pygmalion falls in love with the ivory statue he has carved, treats it as if it were his living bride, and at last Venus brings it to life.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s sculptor lives as though he already had a beloved he does not yet truly have, until the wish is granted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s hero, too, lives as if he already possessed the union that the rumour only promises.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal’s theory of crystallisation describes how the lover’s mind keeps adorning the beloved and imagining happiness with her, finding new perfections in every small piece of news.
philosophy.explanation: For Stendhal, imagination lets the lover enjoy a happiness that has not yet happened.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s hero crystallises around the town’s rumour, enjoying the union as if it were already his.

real_life_example.event_title: Longfellow keeps hoping for six years after Fanny Appleton's refusal
real_life_example.place: Boston and Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States
real_life_example.event: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow fell in love with Frances (Fanny) Appleton after travelling with her family in Switzerland, and was crushed when she rejected his marriage proposal in 1837. He resumed his friendship with her in Cambridge and Boston, and she finally accepted him in the spring of 1843. They married in July 1843, and her father gave them Craigie House as a wedding present.
real_life_example.explanation: For years Longfellow lived on the hope of a union he had not yet won, before it finally came true.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's lover says that hearing the town's talk makes his heart feel as though it already has the union it has not yet gained; Longfellow's long hope shows a heart living on a union still to come.

tamil:
கவ்வையால் கவ்விது காமம் அதுவின்றேல்
தவ்வென்னும் தன்மை இழந்து.
transliteration:
kavvaiyaal kavvidhu kaamam adhuvindrael
thavvennum thanmai izhandhu
meaning: My love grows and blooms because of the town's gossip. Without that gossip, it would lose its strength and shrink away.
elementary: Think of a small campfire. If nobody adds sticks, it gets smaller and goes out. The town’s chatter is like sticks thrown on this young man’s love: every time people talk, his love burns brighter. Without the talk, he says, it would shrink like a fire nobody feeds.
university: Parimelazhagar again treats this as the hero’s speech. He explains the pun kavvaiyāl kavvitu: just as one says cevvitu of what has cevvai, the poet coins kavvitu, ‘full of kavvai’, and he glosses it as ‘has blossomed’ (alartal), with a play on alar, ‘rumour’, and alar, ‘to blossom’; the line means love ‘blossoms more and more’ on the rumour. Tavveṉṉum is an onomatopoeic expression (kuṟippu moḻi) for shrinking, which he supports with Neṭunalvāṭai 184-85. Its ‘nature’ (iyalpu) he defines as giving joy. Kavvai here is a variant form of kauvai, used for the pun; all three sources print the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna traces how desire grows: by dwelling on sense objects a person becomes attached to them, from attachment desire is born, and from desire anger arises.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita describes desire as something that feeds on attention and grows step by step.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero describes his love growing in just this way, fed by the constant attention of the town’s talk.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.62 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Swami Mukundananda)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!”
christianity.explanation: James warns that a little talk can set a great blaze going.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s hero describes just this: the town’s small talk has kindled his love into something far larger.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn Hazm gives separate chapters of The Ring of the Dove to the figures who surround lovers, among them the reproacher who blames the lover and the slanderer who spreads talk, and he describes how lovers are affected by them.
islam.explanation: The Andalusian treatise treats gossip and reproach as forces that shape the course of a love affair.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s hero says the same: the town’s talk does not stay outside his love but makes it grow.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapters on the reproacher and the slanderer (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Where no wood is, the fire goeth out; And where there is no whisperer, contention ceaseth.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that whispering keeps a quarrel alive, just as wood keeps a fire burning.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same logic to love: without the town’s whispering, the hero says, his love would die down.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The craving of one given to heedless living grows like a creeper.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares craving to a creeper that keeps spreading as long as it is fed.
buddhism.tie_back: Kalaignar glosses this kural with the image of a love-creeper (kātalkoṭi) that withers without the town’s talk; the Buddha uses the same image for craving that keeps growing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If there were numberless mountains of gold and silver, as big as Kailâsa, they would not satisfy a greedy man; for his avidity is boundless like space.”
jainism.explanation: Nami teaches that craving has no natural limit and grows without end.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero describes a love that keeps growing as long as it is fed; Jainism sees that endless growth as the mark of craving.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “His love increases day by day, and when it is weighed, it does not decrease.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the devotee whose love for the Lord keeps growing and never shrinks when tested.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's love grows and blooms on the town's gossip and would shrink without it; Gurbani speaks of a love that grows day by day and never shrinks.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1074, Raag Maaroo, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In a myth retold by the orator Themistius, the child Eros would not grow until Aphrodite gave birth to his brother Anteros, ‘returned love’; with Anteros beside him Eros grew, and without him he shrank again.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth says love needs something outside itself to feed it, or it stays small.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s hero says his love likewise needs the town’s talk to grow, and without it would shrink.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that if we imagine others love, desire or hate the same thing we love, desire or hate, we will love, desire or hate it more steadily.
philosophy.explanation: Our feelings, for Spinoza, are strengthened when we see them reflected in others.
philosophy.tie_back: The town’s talk reflects the hero’s love back to him, and by Spinoza’s logic this makes it stronger.

real_life_example.event_title: Rumours of Crown Prince Harald's chosen bride spark a national debate
real_life_example.event: Crown Prince Harald and Sonja Haraldsen, a commoner, had been a couple for many years before rumours spread in 1967 and 1968 of a girlfriend he wished to marry. Newspapers and the public debated whether a commoner could become queen, while Harald made clear that if he could not marry Sonja he would consider staying single for life. King Olav V sought political advice and finally consented, and the couple married on 29 August 1968.
real_life_example.explanation: Once the romance became the subject of public talk, it moved from a private hope toward an open, accepted marriage.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says love blossoms on the town's gossip and would wither without it; Harald and Sonja's love, once talked about by the whole country, grew into a public marriage rather than fading.

tamil:
களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால் காமம்
வெளிப்படுந் தோறும் இனிது.
transliteration:
kaLiththoRum kaLLuNdal vaettatraal kaamam
veLippatunh thoaRum inidhu
meaning: Just as a drinker wants more toddy (palm wine) each time it makes him happy, my love grows sweeter each time the rumor makes it known.
elementary: Some sweets are so tasty that each one makes you want another. The young man says his love is like that. Each time people talk about it, it feels sweeter, and he wants it talked about even more.
university: Parimelazhagar again gives this to the hero and explains vēṭṭaṟṟāl as a shortened form of vēṭkappaṭṭaṟṟāl, ‘as it is desired’: for drinkers, drinking toddy (kaḷ) grows sweeter each time they become merry (kaḷittoṟum), and so the hero’s love grows sweeter each time it is made known (veḷippaṭuntoṟum) by rumour. His point is that the very strength of desire makes even scandal pleasant. Manakkudavar assigns the couplet differently, to the tōḻi answering a hero who asked whether the rumour distressed them. The simile is striking given that chapter 93, kaḷḷuṇṇāmai, condemns drink; here the image describes the lover’s state without endorsing drinking. The text agrees in all three sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Yayati, after a thousand years of enjoyment regained through his son’s youth, declares that desire is never satisfied by enjoying its objects but only blazes higher, like fire fed with clarified butter, and returns his son’s youth.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata uses Yayati to show that every indulgence of desire makes it want more.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s drinker wants more with each cup, and its lover finds love sweeter each time it is talked about; Yayati is the classic Indian picture of that endless appetite.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva, story of Yayati (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “They have stricken me, shalt thou say, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I felt it not: when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs portrays a drunkard who, in spite of every harm, only wants another drink.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same picture of the drinker who wants more, applying it to a lover who wants his love talked about more and more.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn al-Farid’s Wine Ode opens with the lovers drinking, in remembrance of the Beloved, a wine with which they were drunk before the vine was created.
islam.explanation: The Sufi poet makes intoxication the image of a love that is endlessly sweet and never sated.
islam.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes drinking the image of love that becomes sweeter the more it is tasted and revealed.
islam.source: Ibn al-Farid, al-Khamriyya (The Wine Ode), opening verse (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)

judaism.quote_or_event: The Song of Songs opens with the beloved saying that her lover’s love is better than wine.
judaism.explanation: The Song compares love and wine and finds love the sweeter.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, sets love beside drink and finds that love, made public, grows ever sweeter.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes a leper who scratches his sores and burns them over a pit of coals; the more he does it, the worse his wounds become, yet he finds a kind of pleasure in it.
buddhism.explanation: Sensual desire, says the Buddha, feeds on what makes it worse and is mistaken for pleasure.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s drinker and lover both find sweetness in what only increases their craving; the Buddha calls that the leper’s pleasure.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasures are the thorn that rankles, pleasures are poison, pleasures are like a venomous snake; he who is desirous of pleasures will not get them, and will come to a bad end at last.”
jainism.explanation: Nami teaches that the sweetness of pleasure is a trap that leads to more craving and suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover finds love sweeter each time it is revealed, just as the drinker finds drink sweeter; Jainism warns that this growing sweetness is the poison itself.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.53 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Do not drink the false wine at all, if it is in your power. O Nanak, the True Guru comes and meets the mortal; by His Grace, one obtains the True Wine.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das forbids ordinary intoxicating drink and offers instead the 'True Wine' of the Name, received through the Guru by grace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares love made public to toddy that grows sweeter each time the drinker is merry; Gurbani takes the same image of intoxication but redirects it to the true, sober intoxication of the Name.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 554, Raag Bihaagraa (Bihaagre ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus’ men who taste the lotus lose all wish to return home and want only to stay among the Lotus-eaters, eating more of it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s lotus is sweet in a way that makes people want nothing but more of it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s drinker and lover are caught by the same sweetness, which grows the more it is tasted.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius says that love is the one thing of which the more we have, the more fiercely the heart burns with desire.
philosophy.explanation: For Lucretius, love is unlike hunger or thirst, which are satisfied; possessing more of it only makes the craving stronger.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the logic of the Kural’s drinker: each taste makes the next one more wanted, and love revealed grows sweeter.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 4.1088-1090 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.H.D. Rouse)

real_life_example.event_title: John Lennon and Yoko Ono turn their honeymoon into a Bed-In
real_life_example.event: John Lennon and Yoko Ono married in Gibraltar on 20 March 1969 and, knowing the wedding would draw press attention, spent their honeymoon in bed at the Amsterdam Hilton from 25 to 31 March. Every day from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. they invited reporters into the room, where they sat in pyjamas talking about peace. A second week-long Bed-In followed in Montreal, where the song Give Peace a Chance was recorded.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than hide their new marriage from the press, the couple invited the world in, again and again.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares love made public to drink that grows sweeter each time; Lennon and Ono made their love public twice over and welcomed the attention rather than shrinking from it.

tamil:
கண்டது மன்னும் ஒருநாள் அலர்மன்னும்
திங்களைப் பாம்புகொண் டற்று.
transliteration:
kaNdadhu mannum orunhaaL alarmannum
thingaLaip paampukoN tatru
meaning: I saw my love only once, yet the rumor has spread everywhere, like the news when the snake swallows the moon (an old way of describing an eclipse).
elementary: When there is an eclipse and the moon goes dark, everybody in the whole town talks about it at once. The girl in this verse says she met her sweetheart just one single time, and now the whole town is talking about them, as if it were an eclipse!
university: Here the speaker changes. Parimelazhagar says the heroine, kept from the hero by obstacles and failed trysts, speaks to the tōḻi while the hero is within earshot (ciṟaippuṟam), announcing the rumour to press him to marry. Kaṇṭatu ‘what I saw’ took place ‘on one day’ (orunāḷ), but the alar is ‘like the serpent seizing the moon’ (tiṅkaḷaip pāmpu koṇṭaṟṟu), the eclipse caused by Rāhu that everyone sees and talks about; Parimelazhagar notes that the effect (the universal talk) is described by naming the cause, and that both maṉṉum and the um are expletives (acai nilai). His moral is that a love that draws rumour even without meetings cannot go on, and must end in marriage. Kalaignar glosses the image explicitly as the eclipse (kirakaṇam).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And from that time there is a long-standing quarrel between Rahu’s head and Surya and Soma. And to this day it swalloweth Surya and Soma (during solar and lunar eclipses).”
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata tells how the demon Rahu was beheaded for tasting the nectar of immortality and ever since swallows the sun and moon at eclipses.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the myth behind the Kural’s image of the serpent seizing the moon, an event the whole world sees at once, just as the whole town hears of the lovers’ single meeting.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 19 (Astika Parva) (tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: After Jesus heals a leper and tells him to say nothing, the man goes out and begins to spread the story everywhere, so that Jesus can no longer openly enter a city.
christianity.explanation: A single private event becomes, through one man’s telling, the talk of the whole region.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences the same thing: one private meeting becomes the talk of the whole town.

islam.quote_or_event: “When you received it with your tongues and said with your mouths that of which you had no knowledge and thought it was insignificant while it was, in the sight of Allāh, tremendous.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes, in the setting of the slander against Aisha, how a rumour passes from tongue to tongue among people who know nothing of the truth.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees the same mechanism: a rumour about one meeting passes from mouth to mouth until it is everywhere.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that an eclipse of the moon is a bad omen, a sign seen and feared by all the world.
judaism.explanation: For the rabbis an eclipse is a public event that everybody notices and interprets.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural also uses the eclipse as the image of something everyone sees and talks about at once.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Now at that time the Moon God had been seized by Rāhu, lord of titans.”
buddhism.explanation: The Moon God, seized by Rahu, calls on the Buddha for refuge, and Rahu releases him.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the same eclipse image the Kural uses for a rumour that spreads everywhere at once.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the royal Seer Nami retired from the world, at the occasion of his Pravragyâ there was an uproar in Mithilâ.”
jainism.explanation: Nami’s single act of renunciation sets the whole city of Mithila talking and crying out.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s single meeting, one event in one life becomes, in a moment, the noise of an entire city.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The news spread throughout the world, and the beings of the three worlds came.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das describes how word of the Guru's coming spread far and wide, drawing countless people.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine saw her beloved only once, yet the news spread everywhere like word of an eclipse; Gurbani likewise pictures one event whose news travels through the whole world.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1116, Raag Tukhaari, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Dido and Aeneas shelter together in a cave during a storm, Rumour (Fama), the swiftest of all evils, races through the great cities of Libya spreading the story of their love.
greek_mythology.explanation: Virgil personifies Rumour as a monster that grows as it travels, with as many tongues as feathers.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural: one meeting, and at once the rumour of it is everywhere.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon, in his unfinished essay ‘Of Fame’, takes up the poets’ picture of Fame as a monster with many feathers, eyes and tongues, and asks how rumours arise and spread.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon treats rumour as a force worth studying, with its own ways of growing and travelling.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has seen how fast such a monster runs: one meeting, and the whole town knows.

real_life_example.event_title: Princess Margaret's romance with Peter Townsend becomes known to all
real_life_example.place: London, United Kingdom, and Brussels, Belgium
real_life_example.event: Princess Margaret wished to marry Group Captain Peter Townsend, a divorced royal equerry, but under the Royal Marriages Act she needed the queen's permission, and the Church of England did not accept remarriage after divorce. Townsend was posted overseas as an air attaché, and after the two met again in October 1955 she publicly announced that she would not marry him. Her decision was made known in a public statement setting out her reasons.
real_life_example.explanation: A private love quickly became a matter that everyone discussed and that touched Church and state.
real_life_example.tie_back: In the kural the heroine says she saw her lover only once, yet the rumour has spread like news of an eclipse; Margaret's romance likewise became known far beyond the people involved.

tamil:
ஊரவர் கௌவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல்
நீராக நீளும்இந் நோய்.
transliteration:
ooravar kavai eruvaaka annaisol
neeraaka neeLum-inh noai
meaning: This love-sickness grows like a crop. The town's gossip is its fertilizer, and my mother's angry words are its water.
elementary: A farmer puts manure on a plant and waters it, and the plant grows tall. The girl in this verse says the town’s gossip is like manure for her love, and her mother’s scolding is like water. Instead of stopping her love, they make it grow bigger and bigger.
university: Parimelazhagar sets this in a later situation: the marriage is delayed, the heroine is suffering, and the tōḻi, knowing the hero is within earshot, tells her to bear up in view of the town’s talk and her mother’s words; this is her reply. Nōy (நோய்), ‘illness’, is the love-sickness, imagined as a crop (payir) through a partial metaphor (ēkatēca uruvakam): ūravar kauvai, the talk of the town’s women (he notes ūravar here excludes men, by what they do), is eru (எரு), ‘manure’, and aṉṉai col, the mother’s angry words (veñcol), is nīr, ‘water’, so it nīḷum, ‘keeps growing’. His comment is that the very things that should have made it shrink make it spread, and the intended effect is that the hero will marry. The sources print கெளவை for kauvai and the sandhi-joined நீளும்இந்; the reading is otherwise unvaried.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the gopis hear Krishna’s flute at night, they leave at once, and though husbands, fathers and brothers try to stop them, they cannot be held back.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata shows family opposition doing nothing to check the gopis’ love for Krishna.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds the same: her family’s scolding only makes her love grow stronger.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the parable of the barren fig tree, the gardener begs for one more year so that he may dig about the tree and dung it, in the hope that it will bear fruit.
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the familiar work of manuring a plant to speak about growth given a last chance.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same farming image of manure making a plant grow, but the ‘plant’ is love and the ‘manure’ is gossip.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s Layla and Majnun, when talk of the two young lovers spreads, Layla’s family takes her out of school and keeps her shut up at home, and the separation only makes Qays’s love burn more fiercely until he is called Majnun.
islam.explanation: Family restriction and public talk, meant to end the love, only deepen it.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same: town talk and her mother’s words make her love grow, not die.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Look not upon me, that I am swarthy, That the sun hath tanned me; My mother’s sons were incensed against me, They made me keeper of the vineyards; But mine own vineyard have I not kept.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved in the Song complains that her own family was angry with her and set her to work, yet she did not keep her own ‘vineyard’, her own heart.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also faces anger at home, and like the Song’s beloved her love grows in spite of it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever is overcome by this wretched and sticky craving, his sorrows grow like grass after the rains.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures sorrow growing from craving like grass that has been watered.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures love-sickness growing like a watered crop; the Buddha uses the same farming image for craving and its sorrows.

jainism.quote_or_event: In Hemachandra’s account, the young Jambu’s parents arrange his marriage to eight brides to hold him back from renunciation, but their pleading on the wedding night only strengthens his resolve, and he converts them instead.
jainism.explanation: The family’s efforts to turn Jambu from his chosen path end up confirming it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also finds that her mother’s opposition only strengthens what it was meant to stop, though her path is love, not renunciation.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Parishishtaparvan, life of Jambu (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Make your mind the farmer, good deeds the farm, modesty the water, and your body the field.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak builds a farming metaphor in which the mind, deeds, modesty and body each play a part in raising the crop of the Name.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures love-sickness as a crop with gossip for manure and the mother's harsh words for water; Guru Nanak uses the same farmer's allegory, naming the water and the field that make the spiritual crop grow.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the tale of Cupid and Psyche, Venus, Cupid’s mother, is furious at her son’s love for a mortal girl, scolds him harshly and persecutes Psyche, yet their love endures and ends in marriage.
greek_mythology.explanation: A mother’s anger, meant to break a love, cannot destroy it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says her mother’s angry words water her love rather than kill it.
greek_mythology.source: Apuleius, Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass) 4-6 (Cupid and Psyche) (paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume observes that opposition and difficulty, instead of weakening a passion, often rouse the spirits and give the passion more force.
philosophy.explanation: For Hume, obstacles can intensify the feelings they seem to oppose.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine describes exactly this: the town’s talk and her mother’s words make her love stronger.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.4 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Sir George More's fury fails to undo John Donne's marriage
real_life_example.event: In December 1601 John Donne secretly married Ann More, the young niece of Lady Egerton. When Donne told her father, Sir George More, some months later, he reacted with fury, sought an annulment, refused a dowry and had Donne dismissed from his post as Sir Thomas Egerton's secretary and briefly imprisoned. The marriage was nevertheless upheld, More was eventually reconciled to his son-in-law, and the couple stayed together, raising a large family.
real_life_example.explanation: A parent's anger and the scandal around a secret match did not break the marriage; the couple held together through years of hardship.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the town's gossip is the manure and the mother's harsh words the water that make love-sickness grow; for Donne and Ann, a parent's fury and the scandal only bound them more firmly to the life they had chosen.

tamil:
நெய்யால் எரிநுதுப்பேம் என்றற்றால் கௌவையால்
காமம் நுதுப்பேம் எனல்.
transliteration:
neyyaal erinhudhuppaem endratraal kavvaiyaal
Kaamam nudhuppeam enal
meaning: Thinking that gossip can put out love is like thinking you can put out a fire by pouring ghee (melted butter) on it.
elementary: If you pour water on a fire, it goes out. But if you pour oil or butter on it, it flares up even higher! The girl in this verse says people who try to stop love by gossiping are making the same mistake: they are pouring butter on the fire.
university: Parimelazhagar marks this ‘itu um atu’, continuing the heroine’s speech of 1147. Nutuppēm (நுதுப்பேம்) means ‘we shall extinguish’; ney (நெய்), ‘ghee, clarified butter’, is the classic accelerant of the sacrificial fire. He notes that the third-case endings (-āl) are instrumental and sums up: love cannot be extinguished by rumour, which is the very cause of its flaring up. Manakkudavar assigns the couplet to the tōḻi, speaking when the hero still wants to continue the secret affair. The comparison of desire to fire fed with ghee is widespread in Indian literature, notably in Manu and in the story of Yayati, which gives this couplet unusually direct parallels. The text agrees in all three sources apart from the கெளவை spelling, normalised here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects; it only grows stronger like a fire (fed) with clarified butter.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu uses the image of ghee poured on fire to show that feeding desire only makes it burn hotter.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the very same image: trying to put out love with gossip is like trying to put out fire with ghee.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence. For without the law sin was dead.”
christianity.explanation: Paul observes that a prohibition, instead of killing desire, can stir it up.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural says the same of gossip: what was meant to stifle love only inflames it.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s Layla and Majnun, Majnun’s father takes him to the Kaaba to pray to be cured of his love, but Majnun instead prays that his love may grow ever stronger.
islam.explanation: The attempt to extinguish Majnun’s love only makes him ask for more of it.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point dramatised: efforts to put out love become fuel for it.
islam.source: Nizami Ganjavi, Layla and Majnun (1188), the pilgrimage to Mecca (paraphrase)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it; If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs insists that nothing outside love can put it out.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural says the same with a sharper image: not water but ghee, gossip that only feeds the flame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Fire Sermon the Buddha declares that the eye, its objects and everything experienced through the senses are burning, burning with the fire of passion, aversion and delusion.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures sensual life as a fire that keeps burning on what the senses feed it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural, too, sees love as a fire that the town’s gossip only feeds; the Buddha’s remedy is to stop feeding it altogether.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 35.28 (Adittapariyaya Sutta, the Fire Sermon) (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means. Though two mâshas would do to supply your want, still you would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.”
jainism.explanation: Kapila, who began by wanting two pieces of gold for the girl he loved, discovers that each satisfaction only enlarges desire.
jainism.tie_back: Like ghee poured on fire, what was meant to satisfy Kapila’s love-driven wish only made it blaze higher, which is the Kural’s point about love.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 8.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “as fire is not satisfied by fuel.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan compares the slanderer's restless envy to a fire that is never satisfied however much fuel is fed to it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says hoping to quench love with gossip is like pouring ghee on a fire; Gurbani uses the same image of fire that only grows when fed, here for the talk of the slanderer.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 280, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Pyramus and Thisbe are forbidden by their fathers to marry, but the prohibition cannot stop their love: the more it is covered up, the more the hidden fire burns.
greek_mythology.explanation: Parental prohibition and concealment only make the young lovers’ passion fiercer.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says the same of gossip: what is meant to put out love only makes it burn harder.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld writes that absence lessens moderate passions and increases great ones, as the wind blows out candles and fans a fire.
philosophy.explanation: The same obstacle can extinguish a small feeling and inflame a great one.
philosophy.tie_back: The town’s gossip is such a wind: on the Kural’s great love it acts like fuel on a fire, not like a breath on a candle.

real_life_example.event_title: The Lovings' marriage outlasts banishment and reaches the Supreme Court
real_life_example.place: Caroline County, Virginia, and Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: Richard and Mildred Loving married in Washington, D.C., on 2 June 1958, were arrested at home in Virginia under its ban on interracial marriage, and in January 1959 were sentenced to a year in prison, suspended on condition that they leave the state. They moved to Washington but kept fighting, and the American Civil Liberties Union took up their case. On 12 June 1967 the United States Supreme Court unanimously struck down Virginia's law.
real_life_example.explanation: Punishment and public condemnation did not end the marriage; instead the couple's struggle changed the law of the whole country.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that trying to put out love with gossip is like pouring ghee on a fire; every attempt to break the Lovings apart only made their marriage a larger cause.

tamil:
அலர்நாண ஒல்வதோ அஞ்சலோம்பு என்றார்
பலர்நாண நீத்தக் கடை.
transliteration:
alarnhaaNa olvadhoa anjaloambu endraar
palarnhaaNa neeththak kadai
meaning: He once told me, 'Do not be afraid,' and now he has left me, shaming me in front of many. How can I still feel ashamed of the town's gossip?
elementary: Imagine a friend promised, ‘Don’t worry, I’ll always stay with you,’ and then went away, so everyone could see you were left alone. You might think, ‘Everyone already knows I’ve been left. Why should I be embarrassed about what they say now?’ That is how the girl in this verse feels.
university: Parimelazhagar sets this when the hero has gone away, leaving the marriage still pending; the heroine, aware he has returned and is within earshot, answers the tōḻi who told her to endure for fear of the rumour. Añcal ōmpu (அஞ்சல் ஓம்பு), ‘guard against fear, do not fear’, recalls the hero’s promise at their first meeting, ‘I will not leave you’; now he has abandoned her ‘so that the many are ashamed’ (palar nāṇa), and she asks whether she can still feel nāṇ before alar. He paraphrases her meaning: ‘We, who are in a state that makes onlookers blush, where is our shame?’ Manakkudavar takes the ‘many’ as the tōḻi, the foster-mother (cevili) and the household. Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss reads the line differently, as the hero having said ‘fear not’ even as he departed; the text itself agrees in all three sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Mirabai sings that she has thrown away the shame of the world (lok-laj): her family scolds her and people call her mad, but she will not hide her love for Krishna.
hinduism.explanation: The bhakti poet makes indifference to public shame a sign of a love that has gone beyond caring what people say.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine reaches the same point: having been left before everyone, she can no longer be ashamed of their gossip.
hinduism.source: Mirabai, padas (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Alston, The Devotional Poems of Mirabai)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Peter said unto him, Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee. Likewise also said all the disciples.” Later that night: “Then all the disciples forsook him, and fled.”
christianity.explanation: Those who promised never to abandon Jesus leave him at the moment of public shame.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has suffered the same: the one who promised ‘fear not’ has left her exposed before everyone.

islam.quote_or_event: Al-Hujwiri describes the Malamatiyya, the ‘people of blame’, Sufis who deliberately accept people’s reproach so that public opinion has no hold on their love for God.
islam.explanation: For these Sufis, being freed from concern about blame is part of loving sincerely.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, abandoned in public, also reaches the point where the town’s blame can no longer shame her.
islam.source: Al-Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, chapter on blame (malama) (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)

judaism.quote_or_event: Lamentations pictures Jerusalem as a woman weeping in the night, who among all her lovers has none to comfort her, for all her friends have dealt treacherously with her.
judaism.explanation: The city is portrayed as a woman abandoned by those who had pledged themselves to her, exposed before the nations.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is likewise abandoned by the one who promised to stay, and left exposed before everyone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that the wise person stands firm whatever others say.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also stops being shaken by blame, though out of grief rather than wisdom.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
jainism.explanation: Nami, having let go of everything, is untouched by the uproar and fire in his city.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, having lost what mattered most, is likewise beyond being hurt by the town’s talk, though she has not chosen that loss as Nami did.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You are my honor; You are my decoration.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan places all his honour (pat) and adornment in the Lord alone, so that what the world says can neither give nor take it away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine, already shamed by her lover's leaving, asks why she should still fear the town's gossip; Gurbani answers that one whose honour rests in the Beloved need not fear what people say.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 181, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides, Ariadne, abandoned on the island of Naxos by Theseus after she saved him, writes reproaching him for the promises he made and for leaving her alone and disgraced.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ariadne is the classic figure of the woman abandoned by the man who swore to protect her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has suffered the same broken promise of ‘do not fear’, and the same public exposure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises that if someone tells you a person has spoken ill of you, you should not defend yourself, but answer that he must not have known your other faults, or he would have mentioned them too.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, other people’s talk is outside our control and should not disturb us.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also refuses to be ashamed of the town’s talk, though from grief rather than Stoic calm.

real_life_example.event_title: Kierkegaard breaks his engagement to Regine Olsen
real_life_example.event: Søren Kierkegaard became engaged to Regine Olsen on 10 September 1840, but soon decided that he could not marry her. Despite her strong opposition, he broke the engagement for good on 12 October 1841, causing her great despair and provoking widespread indignation in Copenhagen, and he left for Berlin for a time. Regine married Johan Frederik Schlegel in 1847, and Kierkegaard, who never married, left her his remaining possessions in his will.
real_life_example.explanation: A promise of marriage was withdrawn in a way that exposed the young woman to public talk, though she later built her own life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says that the man who once told her not to fear has left her shamed before many, so why should she still fear the town's gossip; Regine was left by her betrothed in a break that all Copenhagen discussed.

tamil:
தாம்வேண்டின் நல்குவர் காதலர் யாம்வேண்டும்
கௌவை எடுக்கும்இவ் வூர்.
transliteration:
thaamvaeNtin nalkuvar kaadhalar yaamvaendum
kavvai edukkum-iv voor
meaning: The town is now spreading the very rumor we wanted. So if we ask him, our lover will gladly agree to what we want.
elementary: Imagine you have been hoping your parents will let you go on a trip with your best friend. Then everybody starts saying, ‘Those two always go everywhere together!’ The talk makes the trip seem natural, and you feel sure your friend will say yes when you ask. That is how the girl’s friend feels in this verse.
university: In Parimelazhagar’s reading the speaker is now the tōḻi, addressing the heroine while the hero is within earshot, to make him favour elopement (uṭaṉpōkku). ‘The rumour we have long wanted’ (yām vēṇṭum kauvai), wanted because it gives a reason for leaving together, ‘the town itself is raising’ (eṭukkum); kātalar, ‘the lover’, chosen to suggest that because he loves her he will not refuse, ‘will grant it if we ask’ (tām vēṇṭiṉ nalkuvar). He closes his commentary by noting that the twenty couplets of chapters 114 and 115 are all puṇartal nimittam, occasions leading toward union. Manakkudavar reads the second clause differently, that the family will now themselves agree to give her to the lover; modern glosses (Pappaiah: he will marry me; Varadarasanar: he will grant it) vary between marriage and elopement.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Rukmini, whose brother has promised her to Shishupala, sends a brahmin with a letter asking Krishna to come and carry her away; Krishna agrees at once and takes her from the temple before the wedding.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata tells of a woman who asks her beloved to take her away against her family’s plans, and of the lover who readily consents.
hinduism.tie_back: The tōḻi in the Kural is sure the lover will agree to take the heroine away if asked, just as Krishna answers Rukmini.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My beloved spake, and said unto me, Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song invites the beloved to leave with him.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s tōḻi expects the lover to give just such an invitation now that the town’s talk has made the way clear.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn Ishaq relates that Khadija, admiring Muhammad’s character, sent word through an intermediary proposing marriage, and he accepted.
islam.explanation: In this account the woman takes the initiative, confident her proposal will be welcomed, and it is.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s tōḻi is likewise confident the lover will grant what the heroine asks, now that the town has made their bond known.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, marriage of Khadija (paraphrase; cf. tr. A. Guillaume)

judaism.quote_or_event: When Abraham’s servant asks to take Rebekah to Isaac, her family say they will call the girl and ask her, and when asked whether she will go with this man, she answers, I will go.
judaism.explanation: Rebekah consents to leave her home and go to the man she is to marry.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, turns on a question of consent to leave home, with the tōḻi sure the answer will be yes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Pali commentaries tell that Patacara, a rich man’s daughter, fell in love with a family servant, and when her parents arranged another marriage she ran away with him to live in a distant village.
buddhism.explanation: Patacara’s story is a Buddhist account of an elopement, which later ends in tragedy and her conversion.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s tōḻi is urging exactly such an elopement (uṭaṉpōkku), though the Buddhist story shows where its sorrows can lead.
buddhism.source: Therigatha commentary and Dhammapada commentary, story of Patacara (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: When Arishtanemi leaves his wedding to become a monk, Rajimati, his bride, resolves to follow him, takes the vows herself, and goes to the mountain where he is practising austerities.
jainism.explanation: In the Jain story the bride follows the man she loves, but into renunciation rather than married life.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is urged to follow her lover away from home; Rajimati also follows hers, though to a very different end.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever I ask for, I receive; I have total faith in my Master.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan expresses complete confidence that the Master will grant whatever His devotee asks.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's companion is sure that, with the town raising the very rumour they wanted, the lover will gladly grant what they ask; Gurbani shows the same confident trust that the Beloved will give what is asked.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 619, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Medea, having helped Jason win the Golden Fleece, flees her father’s house by night and sails away with him, after he swears to make her his wedded wife.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Argonautica tells one of the classic elopements of Greek myth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s tōḻi hopes for just such a flight with the lover, now that the rumour has made it seem natural.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus, the beloved, receiving the lover’s affection, comes to feel a returning love (anteros), an image of the lover’s own, and begins to desire his company in turn.
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes how love, once shown, awakens an answering love in the beloved.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s tōḻi trusts that the lover’s own love (he is kātalar, ‘the one who loves’) will make him agree to what the heroine asks.

real_life_example.event_title: Bertha Kinsky secretly marries Arthur von Suttner and leaves with him for the Caucasus
real_life_example.event: Bertha Kinsky became engaged to Baron Arthur von Suttner, seven years her junior, but his family strongly opposed the match, so in 1876 she took a post in Paris as secretary to Alfred Nobel. After only a week or so she returned to Vienna, secretly married Arthur, and the couple left at once for the Caucasus, where they lived for nine years by teaching and writing. In 1885 they returned to Austria, welcomed by his now relenting family; she later won the 1905 Nobel Peace Prize.
real_life_example.explanation: Faced with family opposition, the couple chose to marry and leave together, and in time the family accepted them.
real_life_example.tie_back: In the kural the confidante urges the couple to go away together, sure that the lover will agree; Bertha and Arthur did just that, marrying secretly and leaving together despite his family's opposition.

tamil:
செல்லாமை உண்டேல் எனக்குரை மற்றுநின்
வல்வரவு வாழ்வார்க் குரை.
transliteration:
Sellaamai undael enakkurai matrunin
valvaravu vaazhvaark kurai.
meaning: If you are not leaving, tell me so. But if your news is that you will go and hurry back, tell it to whoever is still alive when you return.
elementary: Imagine your best friend says, ‘I’m moving away, but don’t worry, I’ll visit soon!’ You might answer, ‘Only tell me the part where you’re staying. The coming-back-soon part is too far away for me to hold on to.’ The wife in this couplet feels the same: a promise to return quickly is no comfort if her heart cannot last that long.
university: Chapter 116 opens the karpiyal (the section on married love) with the heroine’s distress when her husband announces a journey, conventionally to earn wealth or serve the king; commentators assign the couplets to the heroine herself or to her confidante (tōḻi) speaking for her. Cellāmai (செல்லாமை) is ‘not going’, and valvaravu (வல்வரவு) is ‘swift return’; the sting is in vāḻvārkku urai, ‘tell it to those who will live’, implying that she will not survive the interval. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘tell it to those able to stay alive until then’, while Kalaignar turns it into ‘say your farewells now to whoever will still be alive when you come back’. Pope renders: ‘If you will say, “I leave thee not,” then tell me so; / Of quick return tell those that can survive this woe.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama tells Sita he must go into forest exile and that she should stay behind in Ayodhya, she refuses, insisting that a wife’s place is at her husband’s side and that the forest with him is better than a palace without him.
hinduism.explanation: In the Ayodhya Kanda, Sita answers Rama’s farewell by declaring she will go with him, since separation from him would be worse than any hardship of the forest.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Sita will not accept a parting softened by assurances; for her there are only two options, staying together or not surviving the absence.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda, Sita’s plea to accompany Rama (sargas c. 27-30) (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And they all wept sore, and fell on Paul’s neck, and kissed him, Sorrowing most of all for the words which he spake, that they should see his face no more.”
christianity.explanation: When Paul announces his departure from Miletus, the elders of Ephesus are grieved above all by his words that they will not see him again.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, it is the announcement of the parting, the words themselves, that wounds most deeply.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Abraham! Where are you going, leaving us in this valley where there is no person whose company we may enjoy, nor is there anything (to enjoy)?”
islam.explanation: Hagar follows Abraham as he leaves her and the infant Ishmael in the empty valley of Mecca, repeating her question until she learns that God has commanded it.
islam.tie_back: Hagar, like the Kural’s heroine, confronts a departing husband with the question of how she is to survive his absence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Entreat me not to leave thee, and to return from following after thee; for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge.”
judaism.explanation: Ruth refuses Naomi’s urging to turn back, binding herself to go wherever Naomi goes until death parts them.
judaism.tie_back: Ruth voices the Kural’s refusal of separation as a vow: the only acceptable answer to a parting is not to part.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Lord, as I was leaving home, a Sakyan girl — the envy of the countryside — glanced up at me, with her hair half-combed, and said, ‘Hurry back, master.’”
buddhism.explanation: Nanda, the Buddha’s half-brother, confesses that the parting words of his bride keep pulling him back from the monastic life.
buddhism.tie_back: The bride’s ‘Hurry back’ is the very plea for a swift return that the Kural’s heroine says she cannot live on.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Râgîmatî thought: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.’”
jainism.explanation: When her betrothed, Arishtanemi, leaves on the wedding day to become a monk, Princess Rajimati feels her life as she knew it has ended and resolves to renounce the world herself.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati, like the Kural’s heroine, treats her beloved’s departure as the end of the life she had; the Jain story turns that ending into renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without my Beloved, I cannot survive even for an instant; without meeting Him, I cannot sleep.”
