sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak speaks as the soul-bride who cannot live, or even rest, for a moment apart from her Beloved Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine tells her husband to give news of a swift return only to those who will still be alive, because she will not survive the gap; Guru Nanak's bride likewise says she cannot survive even an instant without the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1274, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides, Laodamia writes to her husband Protesilaus, who sailed for Troy almost at once after their wedding, that she fainted as his ship left and begs him to come home to her quickly and safely.
greek_mythology.explanation: Laodamia’s letter is a whole poem of a newly married wife unable to bear her husband’s departure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She, too, receives a hasty departure and a hoped-for return, and finds the gap between them almost unendurable.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that just as lovers find the sight of the beloved the most delightful thing, so friends find nothing more desirable than living together.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, shared presence is not an extra but the very activity in which love and friendship consist.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same: the only news she wants is that he will stay.

real_life_example.event_title: Mumtaz Mahal dies at Burhanpur while on campaign with Shah Jahan
real_life_example.event: Mumtaz Mahal, married to the future Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in 1612, regularly travelled with his entourage on military campaigns rather than staying behind. In 1631, though pregnant, she went with him on his campaign in the Deccan. She died at Burhanpur that June shortly after giving birth, and her body was later carried to Agra, where Shah Jahan raised the Taj Mahal over her tomb.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than wait at home for news of a safe return, Mumtaz chose to go wherever her husband went, and the separation she dreaded came instead through her own death on the journey.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says that news of a quick return should be told to whoever will still be alive by then; Mumtaz refused to be left behind, and her story shows how a long absence can outlast a life.

tamil:
இன்கண் உடைத்தவர் பார்வல் பிரிவஞ்சும்
புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு.
transliteration:
Inkan udaiththavar paarval pirivanjum
punkan udaiththaal punarvu.
meaning: Once, even his look was pure joy. Now even our hugs are full of pain, because I fear the parting that is coming.
elementary: Think of the last day of a wonderful holiday. You are still at the beach, the sun is shining, but you keep thinking, ‘Tomorrow we go home,’ and the fun feels a little sad. The wife in this couplet feels that way: her husband is still with her, but knowing he will leave makes even being close to him hurt.
university: The couplet contrasts the past and present of the same relationship: avar pārval (அவர் பார்வல், ‘his look’) once had iṉkaṇ (இன்கண், ‘sweetness, joy’), but now even puṇarvu (புணர்வு, ‘union, being together’) has puṉkaṇ (புன்கண், ‘distress’) because of pirivu añcum, ‘fearing separation’. The two rhyming nouns iṉkaṇ and puṉkaṇ carry the turn from joy to grief. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read pārval as his loving look, while Solomon Pappaiah contrasts his pleasing look with his conduct, which signals that he is about to leave; Kalaignar sharpens the contrast between gazing and embracing. Pope: ‘It once was perfect joy to look upon his face; / But now the fear of parting saddens each embrace.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gopi Gita, the cowherd women tell Krishna that when he goes off to the forest by day, a single moment without seeing him feels like an age to them.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana makes the gopis’ longing for the sight of Krishna the model of devotion, and their pain in his absence its measure.
hinduism.tie_back: The gopis share the Kural’s sense that the sight of the beloved is pure joy, and that the shadow of his going spoils it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother’s house.”
christianity.explanation: The bride in the Song of Songs, having found her beloved after searching for him, clings to him for fear of losing him again.
christianity.tie_back: Her clinging embrace is shaped by the same fear of loss that, in the Kural, turns being together into anxiety.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Jacob] said, ‘Indeed, it saddens me that you should take him, and I fear that a wolf would eat him while you are of him unaware.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob is grieved by the mere proposal that Joseph leave his side, even for a day.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Jacob is pained in advance; the loved one is still present, but the coming separation already hurts.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another.”
judaism.explanation: Laban and Jacob name the cairn Mizpah as they part, asking God to keep watch over the bond while they are apart.
judaism.tie_back: The Mizpah words show a meeting already shaped by the coming absence, which is the mood of the Kural’s embrace.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that the same affection that delights us is the root of the grief and fear of losing what we love.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural describes this exact process: the joy of his presence has become the fear of his absence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “All singing is but prattle, all dancing is but mocking, all ornaments are but a burden, all pleasures produce but pains.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra warns his former brother, King Brahmadatta, that every pleasure carries the seed of its own suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds out the same thing in her own life: the delight of union has already turned into pain.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Previously in my spiritual tranquility, I had the happiness and bliss of being near Him, but I am now crying with pangs of separation.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh scholar and scribe of the Adi Granth, contrasts the bliss the devotee once knew in the Beloved's presence with the weeping of separation now. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says that his look was once pure delight but that dread of parting now fills even their embrace with pain; Bhai Gurdas sets the same before-and-after of nearness turned to grief.
sikhism.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 670, English translation as given in the BaniDB database

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orpheus is allowed to lead Eurydice back from the underworld on condition he does not look at her until they reach the light; near the end, afraid of losing her, he turns to look, and she slips away from him a second time.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s telling, it is Orpheus’s anxious love and fear of losing her that make him look back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved’s presence and the lover’s look are spoiled by dread of separation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises that when you kiss your child or your wife, you should remind yourself that you are kissing a human being, so that if they are taken from you, you will not be disturbed.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic exercise deliberately brings the thought of separation into moments of affection, in order to free the mind from dread.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has the same thought of parting in the middle of an embrace, but in her it brings only pain, which is exactly the disturbance Epictetus hopes to remove.

real_life_example.event_title: Fridtjof Nansen leaves his wife and baby daughter for the Fram expedition
real_life_example.event: The explorer Fridtjof Nansen, married to the singer Eva Nansen since 1889, left his home at Lysaker in June 1893 to begin the Fram expedition into the Arctic Ocean. In his published journal he described looking back at his home, seeing his small daughter Liv at an upstairs window, wishing he could turn back, and calling that parting the darkest hour of the whole journey. The voyage took just over three years, and the Fram returned in 1896.
real_life_example.explanation: Nansen's own record shows that, for him, the hardest moment of a dangerous polar voyage was not the ice but the farewell at his own door.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the shadow of a coming parting turns even the joy of being together into pain, which is the feeling Nansen set down on the day he left his family.

tamil:
அரிதரோ தேற்றம் அறிவுடையார் கண்ணும்
பிரிவோ ரிடத்துண்மை யான்.
transliteration:
Aridharo thaetram arivudaiyaar kannum
pirivo ritaththunmai yaan.
meaning: Even a wise and understanding lover leaves at some time. So it is hard to feel sure of anyone's promise never to leave.
elementary: Suppose the kindest, smartest grown-up you know promises, ‘I’ll always be here.’ Then one day they have to go away for work. Next time someone promises you that, it is harder to believe, even if they mean it. The wife in this couplet feels the same: if even a wise, loving husband sometimes leaves, how can she trust any promise to stay?
university: Tēṟṟam (தேற்றம்) means ‘certainty, confidence’ and arito (அரிதரோ, with the emphatic particle aro) ‘is indeed hard’. Aṟivuṭaiyār kaṇṇum (அறிவுடையார் கண்ணும்), ‘even in those who have understanding’, refers to the husband, who knows how much his absence will hurt; pirivu ōr iṭattu uṇmaiyāṉ (பிரிவு ஓர் இடத்து உண்மையான்), ‘since separation exists at one time or another’, gives the reason. The printed form pirivō riṭattuṇmai is a sandhi run-together of pirivu ōr iṭattu uṇmai, and editions agree on the wording. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take tēṟṟam to be her confidence in his ‘I will not leave’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as her inability to be sure of his love. Pope: ‘To trust henceforth is hard, if ever he depart, / E’en he, who knows his promise and my breaking heart.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: Nala, a king famed for virtue who had won Damayanti and sworn devotion to her, abandons her while she sleeps in the forest after he loses his kingdom at dice.
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata’s Nala episode, even a good and wise husband, under the pressure of misfortune, leaves the wife who trusted him.
hinduism.tie_back: Nala is a clear example of the Kural’s fear: even an understanding husband may, at some point, part from his wife.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Peter said unto him, Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee. Likewise also said all the disciples.”
christianity.explanation: Peter and the other disciples sincerely swear never to forsake Jesus, and within hours they scatter and deny him.
christianity.tie_back: As the Kural warns, even sincere and understanding people break their ‘I will never leave’, which makes such promises hard to rely on.

islam.quote_or_event: “Everyone upon it [i.e., the earth] will perish, And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that every created being passes away and only God endures.
islam.tie_back: If everything on earth is subject to passing, then, as the Kural concludes, no human promise of permanent presence can be fully trusted.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah teaches that any love that depends on some particular thing ceases when that thing ceases, while love that does not depend on anything never ceases; it contrasts Amnon’s love for Tamar with the love of David and Jonathan.
judaism.explanation: Pirkei Avot distinguishes love that will not last from love that does, and suggests that it is hard to know from outside which is which.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces the same uncertainty: she cannot be sure whether her husband’s love will outlast the reasons that now call him away.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘I will grow different, separate from all that is dear and appealing to me.’”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists separation from all that is dear among five facts that every person, lay or ordained, should reflect on often.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s premise stated as doctrine: separation comes to everyone, the wise included, so no promise can rule it out.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.57, Upajjhatthana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Time elapses and quickly pass the days; the pleasures of men are not permanent; they come to a man and leave him just as a bird leaves a tree void of fruit.”
jainism.explanation: King Brahmadatta admits to the monk Citra that worldly joys come and go and cannot be held on to.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has learned the same thing about love: what comes to us also leaves, so no promise of permanence is certain.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Union with Him, and separation from Him, come by His Will. We come to receive what is written in our destiny.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Japji Guru Nanak teaches that meeting and parting alike come by the divine order (hukam).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine finds it hard to trust any promise because parting comes in time even with a wise lover; the Japji agrees that separation is built into life, though it asks the Sikh to accept it as hukam rather than lose trust.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib (pauri 29), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Abandoned by Theseus on the island of Naxos after he had sworn to marry her, Ariadne laments that from now on no woman should believe a man’s oath or trust that his words are faithful.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Catullus’s retelling, Ariadne draws a general lesson about trust from one desertion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She reaches the Kural’s conclusion: once even a trusted lover has left, confidence in any promise becomes hard.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that friendships based on pleasure or usefulness are easily dissolved, because when the pleasure or use ends, so does the bond.
philosophy.explanation: Only friendship of character, he argues, is lasting; others depend on changing circumstances.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has reason to doubt because circumstances, such as the need to earn, can pull even a loving partner away.

real_life_example.event_title: Douglas Mawson misses his ship and spends an extra year in Antarctica
real_life_example.place: Cape Denison (Main Base), Commonwealth Bay, Antarctica, and Adelaide, Australia
real_life_example.event: Douglas Mawson led the Australasian Antarctic Expedition, leaving his fiancée, Francisca (Paquita) Delprat, behind in Australia. Returning alone from a sledging journey on which his two companions had died, he reached Main Base only about five hours after the relief ship Aurora had sailed, and he was forced to remain in Antarctica for another year. Soon after finally returning, he married Paquita on 31 March 1914.
real_life_example.explanation: However careful the plan, Mawson's promised return slipped by a whole year because of events no one could control.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural observes that even with a wise and loving partner separation comes at some time, so a promise of no parting or of a fixed return is hard to trust, and Mawson's lost year shows exactly how such a promise can fail.

tamil:
அளித்தஞ்சல் என்றவர் நீப்பின் தெளித்தசொல்
தேறியார்க்கு உண்டோ தவறு.
transliteration:
Aliththanjal endravar neeppin theliththasol
thaeriyaarkku undo thavaru.
meaning: If the one who lovingly said 'Do not be afraid' goes away, is it the fault of the one who believed his comforting words?
elementary: Imagine a parent says, ‘Don’t worry, I’ll be right here,’ and then leaves the room. Would it be your fault for believing them? Of course not. The wife in this couplet asks the same question: her husband promised she need not fear, so how can she be blamed for trusting him?
university: Aḷittu (அளித்து) is ‘having shown grace, having loved’ and añcal (அஞ்சல்) is the prohibitive ‘do not fear’; together they recall the husband’s reassurance at the start of their life together, which Solomon Pappaiah places at the time of marriage. Nīppiṉ (நீப்பின்) is ‘if he leaves’, and teḷitta col tēṟiyārkku (தெளித்த சொல் தேறியார்க்கு) ‘to those who trusted the words that made them clear (free of doubt)’. The question uṇṭō tavaṟu (உண்டோ தவறு, ‘is there any fault?’) is rhetorical: the fault lies with the one who promised. Commentators agree on this reading; Pope: ‘If he depart, who fondly said, “Fear not,” what blame’s incurred / By those who trusted to his reassuring word?’

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Dushyanta marries Shakuntala in the hermitage, gives her his signet ring and promises to send for her, but when she later comes to his court he does not recognise her and rejects her.
hinduism.explanation: In Kalidasa’s play, Shakuntala is publicly shamed for having trusted the king’s word, though the fault lies with his forgetting (caused by a curse).
hinduism.tie_back: Shakuntala’s position is the Kural’s question acted out: is the one who trusted a lover’s promise to blame when he fails her?

christianity.quote_or_event: “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.”
christianity.explanation: On the night before he leaves them, Jesus tells his disciples not to be afraid, and he promises to come again to them.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus’ ‘neither let it be afraid’ answers to the Kural’s añcal (‘fear not’); where the Kural fears a reassurance broken, the Gospel presents one meant to be kept.

islam.quote_or_event: “So We restored him to his mother that she might be content and not grieve and that she would know that the promise of Allah is true.”
islam.explanation: Moses’ mother sets her baby adrift on God’s assurance that he will be returned to her, and the Qur’an stresses that the promise was kept.
islam.tie_back: The verse contrasts with the Kural: God’s ‘do not fear’ proves true, while the human lover’s reassurance is what the heroine fears will be broken.

judaism.quote_or_event: In Hosea, God promises to betroth Israel to Himself forever, in righteousness, justice, lovingkindness, compassion and faithfulness, so that the bride may trust that this time she will not be abandoned.
judaism.explanation: The prophet uses the language of marriage to describe a faithfulness that does not break its word.
judaism.tie_back: Hosea offers the kind of promise the Kural’s heroine longs to trust, and shows by contrast how much hurt a broken ‘fear not’ can do.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In Ashvaghosha’s life of the Buddha, Yashodhara, waking to find that Siddhartha has left the palace in the night, laments that he abandoned her while she slept and did not take her with him as ancient kings took their wives into the forest.
buddhism.explanation: Yashodhara’s grief is sharpened by the sense that she trusted a husband who then left without warning.
buddhism.tie_back: She asks, in effect, the Kural’s question: what fault was it of mine, who trusted him, that he should go?

jainism.quote_or_event: Princess Rajimati is promised in marriage to Arishtanemi, but on the wedding day, seeing animals penned for the feast, he gives away his ornaments and leaves to become a monk; she is left overwhelmed with grief.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana tells how a betrothal everyone trusted ended on the wedding day itself.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati, who trusted the match, is left in the Kural’s position, though the Jain text treats the groom’s departure as an act of compassion rather than a broken promise.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.6-28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In separation, He is not separated from us; He is pervading and permeating amongst all.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that the divine Beloved never truly leaves, because He pervades everything, even when the soul feels parted from Him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine asks whether she is at fault for trusting the one who said 'Do not fear' and then left; Gurbani answers that the divine Beloved who reassures the soul never actually departs, so trust in Him is never misplaced.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 46, Sri Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Dido learns that Aeneas is secretly preparing his fleet to leave Carthage, she confronts him, reproaching him for hoping to slip away in silence and appealing to the pledges and union they had shared.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Virgil, Dido treats Aeneas’s departure as a betrayal of everything she had believed from him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Dido’s anguish asks the Kural’s question: is the one who trusted to blame when the lover leaves?

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant argues that making a promise one does not intend to keep cannot be made a universal law, because if everyone did it, no one would believe a promise at all.
philosophy.explanation: For Kant, promising depends on trust, and breaking one’s word harms the very practice of promising.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows the cost on a small scale: a broken ‘fear not’ damages her ability to trust any promise.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, section II (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: John Donne writes A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning
real_life_example.event: John Donne's poem A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning, first published in 1633, is a farewell in which the speaker tells his beloved not to grieve at their parting because their love cannot be divided by distance. According to Donne's early biographer Izaak Walton, Donne gave the poem to his wife shortly before setting out on a journey to France in 1611 or 1612.
real_life_example.explanation: The poem is one of the most famous reassurances ever written by a departing lover, telling the one left behind that there is no cause for fear or tears.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks whether any blame falls on the one who trusted the lover who said do not be afraid and then went away, and Donne's poem is that very do-not-fear spoken on the eve of a departure.

tamil:
ஓம்பின் அமைந்தார் பிரிவோம்பல் மற்றவர்
நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு.
transliteration:
Ompin amaindhaar pirivompal matravar
neengin aridhaal punarvu.
meaning: If you want to save me, stop my husband from going. Once he has left, it will be hard for us to be together again.
elementary: Have you ever seen a balloon start to float away? It is much easier to hold the string tight before it leaves your hand than to catch the balloon once it is in the sky. The wife in this couplet says the same: stop him from leaving now, because once he is gone, getting him back will be very hard.
university: Ompiṉ (ஓம்பின்) is ‘if you would protect (me)’, and amaintār (அமைந்தார்) ‘the one who is fitted (to me)’, that is, her destined husband; pirivu ōmpal (பிரிவு ஓம்பல்) means ‘prevent the parting’. The warning follows: avar nīṅkiṉ arito puṇarvu (அவர் நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு), ‘if he leaves, union is hard’, with the commentarial suggestion that she may not live to see his return. Commentators take the couplet as the heroine’s words to her confidante, asking her to stop the departure; Solomon Pappaiah instead has the husband himself, as the one whose role is to protect her life, avoid leaving her. Pope: ‘If you would guard my life, from going him restrain / Who fills my life! If he depart, hardly we meet again.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Akrura arrives to take Krishna and Balarama to Mathura, the gopis of Vraja lament, blame the ‘cruel’ Akrura and fate, and cling around the chariot in an attempt to keep Krishna from going.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana describes the gopis’ desperate attempt to prevent the separation they fear will be permanent.
hinduism.tie_back: The gopis do what the Kural’s heroine asks of her friend: they try to stop the departure, sure that reunion afterwards will be hard.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them.”
christianity.explanation: On the road to Emmaus, the two disciples urge the stranger, who is the risen Jesus, not to go on but to stay with them.
christianity.tie_back: Their plea ‘Abide with us’ is the action the Kural asks for: keep the beloved from going before the chance is lost.

islam.quote_or_event: “The date-palm cried like a child! The Prophet (ﷺ) descended (the pulpit) and embraced it while it continued moaning like a child being quietened.”
islam.explanation: When the Prophet stopped preaching beside the palm trunk and moved to a new pulpit, the trunk wept until he came back and held it.
islam.tie_back: The weeping trunk shows the Kural’s grief at the loved one’s moving away, a grief that only his return could quiet.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 3584 (Book of Virtues and Merits)

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; But my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song of Songs hesitates for a moment, and when she opens the door her beloved has gone; she then searches for him in vain.
judaism.tie_back: Her search illustrates the Kural’s warning: once the beloved has left, finding him again is hard.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that because parting from the beloved is painful, one should not cling to anything as dear.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural tries to prevent the painful parting; the Dhammapada prevents the pain at its root by releasing the attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Now, as this sacred tree Manôrama is shaken by the storm, the birds, suffering, destitute of refuge, and miserable, scream aloud.”
jainism.explanation: When King Nami leaves Mithila to become a monk and the city is in uproar, he compares his people to birds crying when the tree that sheltered them is shaken.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine fears becoming one of those birds, left without shelter when the one she depends on goes.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When the Husband goes away, the bride suffers in the pain of separation”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the image of a bride left behind when her husband travels to a distant land to describe the soul cut off from the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine begs her confidante to stop her husband leaving, since once he has gone reunion will be hard; Guru Nanak names exactly that suffering of the bride whose husband has gone away.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 56, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Andromache meets Hector at the Scaean gate and begs him to stay on the walls and not go out to fight, warning that if he goes she will be left a widow and their son an orphan.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Iliad, Andromache tries to prevent a departure she fears will be final.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She makes the Kural’s plea directly: keep him from going, because once he is gone there may be no meeting again.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Aristophanes’ speech, Hephaestus offers two lovers the chance to be welded into one, so that they need never be parted in life or in death, and Aristophanes says no lover would refuse.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s Aristophanes explains love as the desire of two halves never to be separated again.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wants what Hephaestus offers: a union where the parting simply never happens.

real_life_example.event_title: Matthew Flinders sails without his new wife and is parted from her for nine years
real_life_example.event: The navigator Matthew Flinders married Ann Chappelle on 17 April 1801, and the couple hoped she could sail with him on HMS Investigator, but the Admiralty disapproved and she was left behind. Flinders departed about three months after the wedding to chart the coast of Australia, and on his way home he was detained on Mauritius. Ann did not see him again for nine years, until he returned to England in 1810, and she endured distress and ill health during his absence.
real_life_example.explanation: A parting that both had hoped to avoid, and that was meant to last for one voyage, stretched to nearly a decade once events took over.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural pleads that the husband be kept from going, because once he has left, being together again will be hard to come by, and the Flinders' nine years apart show how true that fear could be.

tamil:
பிரிவுரைக்கும் வன்கண்ணர் ஆயின் அரிதவர்
நல்குவர் என்னும் நசை.
transliteration:
Pirivuraikkum vankannar aayin aridhavar
nalkuvar ennum nasai.
meaning: If he is cruel enough to tell me to my face that he is leaving, it is hard to keep hoping he will come back and be kind to me.
elementary: Imagine a friend who can say ‘I’m going, bye!’ without looking sad at all. You might think, ‘If leaving me is that easy for them, will they really hurry back?’ The wife in this couplet thinks the same about her husband.
university: Pirivu uraikkum (பிரிவு உரைக்கும்) is ‘who speaks of parting’ and vaṉkaṇṇar (வன்கண்ணர்) ‘the hard-eyed, the cruel’: the very fact that he can announce the separation shows a hardness she did not expect. Nalkuvar (நல்குவர்) is ‘he will show grace or love’ and nacai (நசை) ‘longing hope’, which is arito, ‘hard to hold’ or, as most commentators read it, futile. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses vaṉkaṇ as ‘a heart of stone’ and Kalaignar calls the hope ‘vain’; Solomon Pappaiah adds that the parting is for work. Pope: ‘To cherish longing hope that he should ever gracious be, / Is hard, when he could stand, and of departure speak to me.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Uddhava brings Krishna’s message from Mathura, the gopis, addressing a bee as if it were Krishna’s messenger, complain that he who once loved them has left them and doubt that he will ever come back to them.
hinduism.explanation: In the ‘Bee Song’ the gopis voice hurt and bitterness at a beloved who was able to leave and stay away.
hinduism.tie_back: Their doubt is the Kural’s: one who could leave so easily is unlikely to return with tenderness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But because I have said these things unto you, sorrow hath filled your heart.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus notes that his disciples are filled with grief simply because he has told them he is going away.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, it is the spoken announcement of departure that wounds.

islam.quote_or_event: “O my sons, go and find out about Joseph and his brother and despair not of relief from Allah. Indeed, no one despairs of relief from Allah except the disbelieving people.”
islam.explanation: Even after years of separation from Joseph, Jacob refuses to give up hope of reunion.
islam.tie_back: The verse is a counterpoint: the Kural’s heroine concludes her hope is futile, while Jacob holds that hope must never be abandoned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick; But desire fulfilled is a tree of life.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that hope endlessly postponed wears down the heart, while longing fulfilled gives life.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees nothing ahead but hope deferred, and her heart is already sick with it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From craving springs grief, from craving springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief and fear to craving (tanha), the hungry wanting that will not let go.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s nacai, her longing hope, is just such craving, and as the verse says, it brings her grief.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you have no intention of abandoning pleasure, and still long for undertakings and property, my long talk has been to no purpose. I go, king, farewell.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra, having failed to persuade his former brother to renounce, announces his departure plainly and leaves.
jainism.tie_back: A plainly spoken farewell like Citra’s is what the Kural’s heroine dreads; one who can say ‘I go’ so firmly is unlikely to turn back.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He Himself unites us in His Union; there is no more separation.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that the Lord Himself brings the soul back into union, and once He does so the separation is over.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine thinks the hope that a husband who can coolly announce his departure will return in kindness is hard to keep; Gurbani holds out the opposite hope, that the divine Beloved Himself ends the separation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 37, Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phyllis, queen of Thrace, writes to Demophoon, who left promising to return by an agreed time; the time has long passed, and she slowly realises that he does not mean to come back.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s Heroides, Phyllis’s hope fades as each day without his ship shows how easily he could leave her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She lives out the Kural’s conclusion that the hope of a departed lover’s kindness is hard to keep.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines hope as an inconstant joy and fear as an inconstant sadness, both born of the image of a future thing whose outcome we doubt, and notes that there is no hope without fear and no fear without hope.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, hope and fear are two sides of the same uncertainty.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows this: her hope that he will be kind on his return is inseparable from her fear that he will not.
philosophy.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part III, Definitions of the Affects 12-13 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Paul Gauguin leaves his wife and children to paint in Tahiti
real_life_example.place: Copenhagen, Denmark, and Tahiti, French Polynesia
real_life_example.event: Paul Gauguin, married to Mette Sophie Gad since the early 1870s, had five children with her, and in 1884 the family moved to Copenhagen to live with her relatives, while Gauguin returned to Paris the next year. In 1891, after a successful sale of his work, he paid a final visit to his family in Copenhagen and then set sail for Tahiti. He and Mette remained apart for the rest of his life, never divorcing and corresponding until 1897.
real_life_example.explanation: Gauguin chose his art over family life, came in person to say goodbye, and then left, and the separation that followed was never repaired.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that a husband hard enough to announce his departure to his wife's face leaves her little reason to hope he will return and be kind, and the Gauguins' lasting separation bears that fear out.

tamil:
துறைவன் துறந்தமை தூற்றாகொல் முன்கை
இறைஇறவா நின்ற வளை.
transliteration:
Thuraivan thurandhamai thootraakol munkai
iraiiravaa nindra valai.
meaning: My bangles are slipping down my thin arm past the wrist. Surely they will tell the whole town that the lord of the seashore has left me.
elementary: When you are very sad, people can often tell even if you say nothing: your face looks different and you don’t feel like eating. In this couplet the wife has grown so thin with sadness that her bangles slide down her arm, and everyone who sees them knows her husband has gone away.
university: Tuṟaivaṉ (துறைவன்) is ‘lord of the shore’, the hero of the neytal (seashore) landscape, and tuṟantamai (துறந்தமை) ‘his having left’; tūṟṟākol (தூற்றாகொல்) asks ‘will they not proclaim (it abroad)?’, from tūṟṟu, ‘to spread gossip, publicise’. Muṉkai iṟai iṟavā niṉṟa vaḷai (முன்கை இறை இறவா நின்ற வளை) describes bangles ‘passing beyond the wrist-joint of the forearm’ because her arm has wasted, the standard Sangam sign of a woman pining in separation. Most commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Kalaignar) read the bangles as announcing his departure to the town; Solomon Pappaiah reads them as telling the heroine herself that he plans to leave, and Pope’s ‘announced before’ follows that anticipatory sense. Pope: ‘The bracelet slipping from my wrist announced before / Departure of the Prince that rules the ocean shore.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the opening of Kalidasa’s Meghaduta, the exiled yaksha, separated from his wife, has grown so thin that his golden bracelet has slipped from his forearm.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa uses the slipping bracelet as the visible mark of a lover wasting away in separation.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the same sign as the Kural’s slipping bangles, a body that publicly announces the absence of the beloved.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes a sorrow so great that it shows in the body, in exhaustion and endless tears.
christianity.tie_back: As with the Kural’s bangles, grief that is not spoken still becomes visible in the body.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob tries to hold his grief for Joseph inside, but it shows in his body as his eyes whiten with sorrow.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s bangles, Jacob’s eyes show to everyone a grief of separation he did not proclaim himself.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Michal is taken from her husband Paltiel to be returned to David, Paltiel follows her, weeping as he goes, all the way to Bahurim, until he is ordered to go back.
judaism.explanation: The book of Samuel records a husband’s grief so open that he weeps along the road in front of everyone.
judaism.tie_back: Paltiel’s public tears, like the Kural’s slipping bangles, announce a separation to everyone who sees.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Patacara, having lost her husband, children and parents in a single disaster, wanders in grief so deep that her garment slips from her body without her noticing, and people call her Patacara because of it, until she meets the Buddha.
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada commentary tells how her grief became visible to everyone before she found peace in the Dhamma.
buddhism.tie_back: As with the Kural’s bangles, her outward state announces a loss she cannot hide.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 113, story of Patacara (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Firm and decided she cut off her tresses which were black like bees and dressed with a brush and comb.”
jainism.explanation: Forsaken by Arishtanemi, Rajimati gives up her beauty and cuts off her carefully dressed hair as she enters the order.
jainism.tie_back: Her shorn hair, like the Kural’s slipping bangles, is an outward sign everyone can see that her bridegroom has gone.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O black bird, what qualities have made you black? "I have been burnt by separation from my Beloved."”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid asks the black koel why it is black, and the bird answers that separation from its Beloved has scorched it, a visible mark of inner longing.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the bangles slipping from the heroine's wasted wrist proclaim to the town that her husband has left her; in Farid's hymn the bird's blackened body likewise displays the separation it suffers.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 794, Raag Soohee, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hippolytus, the chorus and the nurse notice that Queen Phaedra has kept to her bed and refused food for days, wasting away, and they try to discover the hidden love that is the cause.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaedra’s body gives away a love she is determined to keep secret.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As with the Kural’s slipping bangles, a lover’s wasting body makes public what she has not said.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Robert Burton lists the bodily symptoms of love-melancholy, including leanness, paleness, loss of appetite and sleeplessness, by which, he says, lovers are easily recognised by others.
philosophy.explanation: The Anatomy of Melancholy treats unhappy love as a condition with visible signs.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s slipping bangles are one such sign: the lover’s thinness gives her away to the whole town.
philosophy.source: Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy, Part 3, Section 2 (symptoms of love-melancholy) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Queen Victoria wears mourning black for the rest of her life
real_life_example.event: After her husband, Prince Albert, died in 1861 at the age of 42, Queen Victoria sank into depression and wore black for the rest of her reign. She kept to mourning far longer than the customary two years for a widow, and until the late 1860s she rarely appeared in public. Her visible grief was so well known that she became famous as a woman in black, and she was criticised for her long seclusion.
real_life_example.explanation: Victoria's clothing and withdrawal announced her loss to the whole nation every day for forty years, whether she spoke of it or not.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the bangles slipping from a wasted arm will announce to the whole town that her lord has left her, and Victoria's unending black did the same for the loss of Albert.

tamil:
இன்னாது இனன்இல்ஊர் வாழ்தல் அதனினும்
இன்னாது இனியார்ப் பிரிவு.
transliteration:
Innaadhu inanil oor vaazhdhal adhaninum
innaadhu iniyaarp pirivu.
meaning: It is painful to live in a town where no one is close to you. It is even more painful to be apart from the one you love.
elementary: Being the new kid in a school where you don’t know anyone feels lonely. But being far away from the person you love most feels even lonelier, even if you are surrounded by people. That is what this couplet says.
university: The couplet is built on a graded comparison: iṉṉātu (இன்னாது, ‘painful’) is repeated, first for living in an iṉaṉ il ūr (இனன் இல் ஊர்), ‘a town without one’s own kind or kin’, and then, with ataṉiṉum (அதனினும், ‘more than that’), for iṉiyār pirivu (இனியார்ப் பிரிவு), ‘separation from the sweet one’. Iṉam can mean kin, friends of one’s own sort, or (for the heroine) companions such as the confidante, which Puliyur Kesikan specifies; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as ‘those who love us as our own’. The repetition of iṉṉātu echoes the device of the Iṉṉā Nāṟpatu, a didactic work among the Eighteen Minor Classics. Pope: ‘’Tis sad to sojourn in the town where no kind kinsmen dwell; / ’Tis sadder still to bid a friend beloved farewell.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: Separated from Sita, Rama wanders the shores of Lake Pampa in spring, and the beauty of the season, which would delight others, only deepens his grief for her.
hinduism.explanation: In the Kishkindha Kanda, even a beautiful place feels desolate to Rama without his wife.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama’s lament shows the Kural’s ranking: separation from the beloved makes any place more painful than mere loneliness would.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 1 (Rama’s lament at Pampa) (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But we, brethren, being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart, endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face with great desire.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Thessalonians that his separation from them, though brief and only in body, has made his longing to see them stronger.
christianity.tie_back: Paul, like the Kural, finds being parted from those dear to him one of the keenest pains, however short.

islam.quote_or_event: “Hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains, / Lamenting its banishment from its home.”
islam.explanation: Rumi opens the Masnavi with the reed cut from its reed-bed, whose music is a lament for its lost origin, a symbol of the soul separated from the Beloved.
islam.tie_back: The reed’s exile is the Kural’s ‘town without one’s own’, and its deeper grief is for the Beloved it was parted from.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, Prologue (tr. E.H. Whinfield)

judaism.quote_or_event: “How shall we sing the LORD’S song In a foreign land?”
judaism.explanation: The exiles in Babylon cannot bring themselves to sing, because they are cut off from Zion, the place they love.
judaism.tie_back: The psalm joins both pains the Kural compares: living in a foreign place, and being cut off from what one loves most.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names two pains: being with those we do not love, and being without those we do.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks the same two pains and finds the second, absence of the beloved, the worse.

jainism.quote_or_event: “And we were gods having great power, in the regions of the gods. This is our sixth birth, in which we are separated from each other.”
jainism.explanation: King Brahmadatta recalls five past lives spent together with his brother Citra and grieves that in this sixth life they have been parted.
jainism.tie_back: After every hardship they shared together, it is separation that Brahmadatta names as the sorrow of this life, as the Kural ranks it above all else.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Many talk of the pain and suffering of separation; O pain, you are the ruler of all. Fareed, that body, within which love of the Lord does not well up - look upon that body as a cremation ground.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid calls the pain of separation (birha) the sovereign over every other pain, and says a body that never feels it is no better than a cremation ground.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks pains, saying living among strangers is bitter but parting from the beloved is bitterer still; Farid likewise crowns the pain of separation as the ruler of all sorrows.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 36) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On Calypso’s island, where a goddess loves him and offers him immortality, Odysseus spends his days sitting on the shore weeping, longing for home and for Penelope.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows that no comfort can make up for being parted from one’s own.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus lives the Kural’s comparison: a strange place is hard, but being parted from the beloved is harder still.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero’s Laelius says that life without friendship is hardly worth living, and that nothing in nature is so opposed to solitude as human beings.
philosophy.explanation: On Friendship argues that human beings are made for companionship, and that being cut off from those we love takes the savour out of life.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero supports the Kural’s first claim about friendless places, and the Kural adds that losing the one dearest is worse still.

real_life_example.event_title: Ovid is banished to Tomis on the Black Sea
real_life_example.event: In 8 CE the Roman emperor Augustus banished the poet Ovid from Rome to Tomis, a town on the far shore of the Black Sea. In exile Ovid wrote the Tristia, or Sorrows, poems that include letters addressed to his wife, along with long letters and poems appealing to be allowed to return to Rome. He was never recalled and died in Tomis in 17 CE.
real_life_example.explanation: Ovid's exile poems became the classic record of a person cut off from home, friends and spouse and forced to live among strangers.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural ranks living in a town where no one is close to you as painful and parting from one's beloved as more painful still, and Ovid suffered both together in Tomis.

tamil:
தொடிற்சுடின் அல்லது காமநோய் போல
விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ.
transliteration:
Thotirsudin alladhu kaamanoi pola
vitirsudal aatrumo thee.
meaning: Fire burns only when you touch it. Can fire, like love-sickness, burn you even when you move away from it?
elementary: A campfire only hurts if you touch it; step back and you are safe. But missing someone you love is a strange kind of fire: it hurts more the farther away they are. This couplet points out how odd and how painful that is.
university: The couplet is a vētṟumai (contrast) built on fire: toṭiṉ cuṭiṉ allatu (தொடின் சுடின் அல்லது), ‘other than burning when touched’, set against viṭiṉ cuṭal (விடின் சுடல்), ‘burning when let go of, when apart’. Kāmanōy (காமநோய்), ‘love-sickness’, is the subject that has this power, and āṟṟumō (ஆற்றுமோ), ‘is it able?’, makes it a rhetorical question to which the answer is no. Commentators agree on the reading; Kalaignar expands it to the lovers neither seeing nor touching each other, and Solomon Pappaiah renders it simply. The image is one of the most quoted in the Kāmattuppāl. Pope: ‘Fire burns the hands that touch; but smart of love / Will burn in hearts that far away remove.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Radha, separated from Krishna, feels sandal paste, cool breezes and moonlight, normally soothing, as burning fire, and her friend reports to Krishna that she is wasting in the heat of separation.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita Govinda uses the classical viraha theme, in which everything cool burns the separated lover.
hinduism.tie_back: Radha experiences the paradox of the Kural: in separation, love burns from a distance, and even cooling things become fire.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, cantos on Radha’s viraha (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs describes love as a fire of the fiercest kind.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s love-sickness is just such a fire, so fierce that it burns even at a distance.

islam.quote_or_event: “This plaint of the flute is fire, not mere air. / Let him who lacks this fire be accounted dead!”
islam.explanation: Rumi says the reed’s lament for its lost home is made of the fire of love, a fire every true lover carries.
islam.tie_back: The reed burns because it is separated, which is exactly the Kural’s fire that burns at a distance.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, Prologue (tr. E.H. Whinfield)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs says love’s fire cannot be put out by any amount of water.
judaism.tie_back: If love cannot be quenched by floods, it certainly cannot be quenched by distance, which is why it burns the Kural’s heroine from afar.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fire like lust; there is no grip like hatred; there is no net like delusion; there is no river like craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha ranks passion as the greatest of fires.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural agrees that love’s fire surpasses real fire; the Dhammapada sees this as reason to put it out.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami, having renounced his kingdom, is untouched when told his city is burning, because he no longer claims anything as his own.
jainism.tie_back: Nami is the reverse of the Kural’s lover: through non-attachment, fire cannot burn him even up close, while love burns her even from afar.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The separation of my beloved is not only appearing in my body, like the fire of jungle, but all these dainty dishes and dresses instead of giving me comfort are acting like oil in raising the intensity of fire and consequently my sufferings.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas describes separation from the Beloved as a forest fire inside the body, which comforts only feed like oil. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says ordinary fire burns only when touched, but love-sickness burns when one is far away; Bhai Gurdas likewise describes separation itself as a fire that blazes all the more in the Beloved's absence.
sikhism.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 668, English translation as given in the BaniDB database

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho describes the symptoms of love at the sight of the beloved: her tongue breaks, a thin fire runs beneath her skin, her eyes see nothing, her ears hum, and she feels close to death.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho’s poem is the classical description of love as a fire felt through the whole body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Sappho’s fire burns at the sight of the beloved; the Kural adds that it burns even more in her absence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato’s Socrates describes the lover’s soul when separated from the beloved: the passages through which the wings grow dry up and close, and the soul is stung and goaded in agony until the sight of the beloved brings relief.
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedrus, the absence of the beloved is a painful, burning torment, and his presence is the only cure.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato gives the Kural’s paradox a full account: love wounds most when the beloved is away.

real_life_example.event_title: Nizami of Ganja writes Layla and Majnun
real_life_example.event: In 1188 the Persian poet Nizami of Ganja, working under a commission from the Shirvanshah court, completed Layla and Majnun as part of his Khamsa, or Quintet. The poem tells of two young lovers in the Arabian desert who are forcibly separated when Layla's father refuses the marriage. Qays, the hero, flees into the desert, where he wanders singing of his love and longing and becomes known as Majnun, the one driven mad by love.
real_life_example.explanation: Nizami's poem became one of the best-known love stories of the Persian and Islamic world, and its central image is a love that burns hotter the farther the lovers are kept apart.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that fire burns only those who touch it, while love burns even those who move away from it, and Majnun, consumed by love far off in the desert, is that idea told as a story.

tamil:
அரிதாற்றி அல்லல்நோய் நீக்கிப் பிரிவாற்றிப்
பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்.
transliteration:
Aridhaatri allalnoi neekkip pirivaatrip
pinirundhu vaazhvaar palar.
meaning: Many people, it seems, can bear the unbearable, push away the pain, live through being apart, and still go on living afterwards.
elementary: Sometimes a grown-up says, ‘Lots of people manage when someone they love goes away,’ and you think, ‘Maybe they do, but I don’t know how I would!’ The wife in this couplet says something like that: other people may be able to bear it, but she is not sure she can.
university: The couplet strings together four participles: aritu āṟṟi (அரிது ஆற்றி), ‘bearing what is hard’ or consenting to the impossible; allal nōy nīkki (அல்லல் நோய் நீக்கி), ‘driving off the sickness of sorrow’; pirivu āṟṟi (பிரிவு ஆற்றி), ‘enduring the separation’; and piṉ iruntu vāḻvār (பின் இருந்து வாழ்வார்), ‘those who live on afterwards’, before the predicate palar (பலர்), ‘are many’. Commentators differ on the tone: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as a straightforward observation that many women endure, Solomon Pappaiah as a statement about wives whose husbands go to earn, while Kalaignar and Pope’s prose gloss (‘As if there were many indeed…’) take it as irony, so that the heroine implies she is not one of them. The chapter title, Pirivāṟṟāmai, ‘not being able to bear separation’, supports the ironic reading. Pope’s verse: ‘Sorrow’s sadness meek sustaining, Driving sore distress away, / Separation uncomplaining Many bear the livelong day!’

hinduism.quote_or_event: Held captive in Ravana’s Ashoka grove for many months, Sita endures separation from Rama, refusing every pressure and keeping herself alive by her hope in him.
hinduism.explanation: The Sundara Kanda presents Sita as the model of a wife who bears an almost unbearable separation and survives it.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita is one of the ‘many’ the Kural speaks of, who endure the impossible and live on.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to endure hardship patiently, sustained by hope.
christianity.tie_back: Paul describes the patient endurance that the Kural says many manage, and that its heroine doubts she can.

islam.quote_or_event: “Rather, your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them to me all together.”
islam.explanation: Having now lost two sons, Jacob chooses beautiful patience and lives on in hope of reunion.
islam.tie_back: Jacob is one of the many who bear separation and keep living, the very thing the Kural’s heroine says others manage.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells how Rachel, daughter of Kalba Savua, married Akiva and then sent him away to study Torah, enduring twelve years and then another twelve of separation in poverty until he returned as a great sage.
judaism.explanation: Rachel is honoured in rabbinic tradition for bearing a long separation for the sake of her husband’s learning.
judaism.tie_back: Rachel is a clear example of the ‘many’ who agree to a hard parting and live through it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “This is the greater: the tears you have shed while transmigrating & wandering this long, long time — crying & weeping from being joined with what is displeasing, being separated from what is pleasing — not the water in the four great oceans.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his monks that, across countless lives, every being has wept over separations more than all the oceans hold.
buddhism.tie_back: In the Buddhist view everyone has endured separation from what is dear countless times, which gives the Kural’s ‘many’ a cosmic scale.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 15.3, Assu Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: Forsaken by Arishtanemi on her wedding day, Rajimati does not die of grief but enters the order, leads many relatives and servants to follow her, and eventually attains omniscience and final liberation.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana shows Rajimati enduring her abandonment and turning it into a spiritual life.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati is one of the ‘many’ who bear separation and live on, though the Jain path transforms the grief rather than simply enduring it.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.29-48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Die before the one whom you love; to live after he dies is to live a worthless life in this world.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad says that a true lover would rather die first than go on living once the beloved is gone.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says, with irony, that many seem able to bear separation and live on afterwards, implying she is not one of them; Guru Angad says outright that such a life after the beloved is worthless.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 83, Sri Raag ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope waits twenty years for Odysseus, putting off her suitors by weaving and unweaving Laertes’ shroud, grieving for him constantly yet keeping the household going until he returns.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents Penelope as the classic example of a wife who endures a long separation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope is one of the ‘many’ the Kural speaks of, who bear the pain of absence and live on.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Writing to Lucilius on the death of a friend, Seneca allows that tears may fall but urges that grief be moderate, noting that time eventually ends grief even for those who will not end it themselves.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca treats the endurance of loss as something reason and time make possible for most people.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca speaks for the ‘many’ who recover from separation; the Kural’s heroine doubts she will be among them.

real_life_example.event_title: Nelson Mandela's prison letters to Winnie Mandela
real_life_example.place: Robben Island and other prisons, South Africa
real_life_example.event: Nelson Mandela was held as a sentenced prisoner from 1962 to 1990, in Pretoria Local, Robben Island, Pollsmoor and Victor Verster prisons. At first he was allowed to write and receive only one 500-word letter every six months, and censors read everything he sent. Among the letters he wrote were letters to his wife, Winnie, in which he professed his love and supported her through her own struggles under apartheid; they were published in 2018 as The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela.
real_life_example.explanation: For nearly three decades a husband and wife kept their bond alive through a few strictly limited and censored letters.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of people who somehow bear what seems unbearable, push back their sorrow and live on through a long separation, and the Mandelas endured such a parting for twenty-seven years.

tamil:
மறைப்பேன்மன் யானிஃதோ நோயை இறைப்பவர்க்கு
ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்.
transliteration:
Maraippaenman yaaniqdhoa noayai iraippavarkku
ootruneer poala mikum.
meaning: I would hide this pain of love from others, but like water in a spring that rises more the more you draw from it, it only grows the more I hide it.
elementary: Think of a well in a garden: every bucket you pull out, the spring at the bottom fills it up again, even higher. The wife in this verse misses her husband, and she tries to keep her sadness a secret, but every time she pushes it down, it bubbles back up, bigger than before.
university: Chapter 117 belongs to the karpiyal (married love) and follows the husband’s departure in Chapter 116; its title joins padar (படர், the anguish of longing), melindhu (மெலிந்து, growing thin) and irangal (இரங்கல், lamenting), and commentators read most of its couplets as the heroine’s replies to her confidante (tōḻi), who urges her to bear the separation quietly. The image turns on iṟaippavarkku (இறைப்பவர்க்கு, ‘for those who bail or draw water’) and ūṟṟunīr (ஊற்றுநீர், spring water): concealment works like drawing from a spring, which only makes it flow faster. Man (மன்) is a particle of unrealised wish, ‘I would indeed hide it, but…’, and nōy (நோய், ‘sickness’) is the standard Kural word for love-pain. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss ‘the more I hide it, the more it grows’, and Pope renders: ‘I would my pain conceal, but see! it surging swells, / As streams to those that draw from ever-springing wells.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In one of her best-known songs Mirabai cries that she has gone mad with love and that no one knows her pain, which only the one who has suffered such a wound can understand.
hinduism.explanation: Mira’s longing for Krishna overflows every attempt to keep it private, and she lets it pour out in song.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Mira finds that love-pain cannot be kept hidden; it rises and spills into the open.
hinduism.source: Mirabai, pada ‘Hey ri main to prem diwani’ (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.”
christianity.explanation: Jeremiah resolves to keep silent, but what he holds inside burns until he can no longer contain it.
christianity.tie_back: The same failure of concealment as the Kural: the harder the speaker holds it in, the more it presses to come out.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob holds in his grief for his lost son, yet it breaks out in his words and even whitens his eyes.
islam.tie_back: Jacob is a ‘suppressor’ of sorrow whose sorrow still shows, just as the Kural’s heroine hides a pain that keeps welling up.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I was dumb with silence; I held my peace, had no comfort; and my pain was held in check. My heart waxed hot within me; while I was musing, the fire kindled; Then spoke I with my tongue.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist tries to keep silent about his pain, but the restraint only makes it burn hotter until he must speak.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s spring in another image: pain that is held in check grows until it breaks out.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever is overcome by this wretched and sticky craving, his sorrows grow like grass after the rains.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that sorrow fed by craving does not shrink on its own but keeps sprouting and spreading.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds her love-pain multiplying like spring water; the Dhammapada traces the same growth of sorrow to attachment itself.

jainism.quote_or_event: “O Gautama, in the innermost heart there grows a plant which brings forth poisonous fruit; how have you torn it out?”
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, the plant growing in the heart is ‘love of existence’, which Gautama has torn out by the roots.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has a love growing in her heart that only spreads when hidden; the Jain image is the same hidden growth, though its cure is uprooting.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.45 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “That which is within them, comes out; it cannot be concealed by concealment.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak observes that whatever truly fills a person inside will surface, however hard they try to hide it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine tries to hide her love-pain, but it wells up like spring water the more she draws on it; Guru Nanak likewise says what is within cannot be hidden by hiding.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1243, Raag Saarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hippolytus, Phaedra hides her love for her stepson until she is wasting away and refusing food, and her nurse finally draws the secret from her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaedra’s concealment does not quiet her passion; it consumes her body until it can no longer be kept in.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Phaedra lives out the Kural’s complaint: the love she hides grows stronger and shows itself despite her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld observes that there is no disguise that can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.
philosophy.explanation: For the moralist, love is one passion that resists every effort at concealment.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine discovers exactly this: her attempt to hide love only reveals it.

real_life_example.event_title: Emily Dickinson's unsent Master letters
real_life_example.event: Emily Dickinson drafted three intensely emotional letters addressed only to an unnamed Master between about 1858 and 1861. The drafts were found among her papers after her death, and there is no evidence that finished versions were ever sent. Scholars still disagree about who the Master was, and some read the documents as a writing experiment rather than as real letters.
real_life_example.explanation: Feelings that Dickinson apparently never sent to anyone poured out on paper anyway, kept hidden in her own drawers.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that love-pain the heroine tries to hide only wells up the more, like a spring that rises as it is drawn, and Dickinson's secret drafts show strong feeling overflowing even while it was kept concealed.

tamil:
கரத்தலும் ஆற்றேன்இந் நோயைநோய் செய்தார்க்கு
உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Karaththalum aatraeninh noayainoai seydhaarkku
uraiththalum naanuth tharum.
meaning: I cannot keep this love-pain hidden, and yet I feel too ashamed to tell it to the one who caused it.
elementary: Imagine you miss someone so much that everyone can see it on your face, but when you think of phoning them to say ‘I miss you’, you feel too shy. You are stuck in the middle: you cannot hide it and you cannot say it. That is exactly how the wife in this verse feels.
university: The couplet sets two failures side by side with the double -um (‘both… and’): karattal (கரத்தல், concealing) is beyond her strength (āṟṟēṉ, ஆற்றேன், ‘I am unable’), and uraittal (உரைத்தல், telling) brings nāṇ (நாண், modesty, shame). The phrase nōy ceytārkku (நோய் செய்தார்க்கு, ‘to the one who caused the sickness’) is pointed: the cure and the cause are the same person. Puliyur Kesikan reads the telling as sending a message (tūtu) to the absent husband, which modesty forbids, while Solomon Pappaiah modernises it to writing or telephoning. Nāṇ is one of the defining virtues of the Tamil heroine, and the Kamattuppal repeatedly stages its struggle with kāmam (desire), most fully in Chapter 114 and in the next couplet. Pope: ‘I cannot hide this pain of mine, yet shame restrains / When I would tell it out to him who caused my pains.’ The words are identical on both base sources, with only a spacing difference at ஆற்றேன்இந்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Wasting with love for King Dushyanta, Shakuntala is too shy to declare herself, until her friends persuade her to write him a love-letter, which she composes in deep embarrassment.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s heroine is caught between a longing everyone can see and the modesty that keeps her from speaking.
hinduism.tie_back: Shakuntala stands exactly where the Kural’s heroine stands: unable to hide her love and ashamed to tell it to its cause.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride cannot keep her love-sickness to herself, yet she sends others to tell her beloved rather than telling him herself.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she cannot hide the sickness and can only send word of it through others.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allāh, and I know from Allāh that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob will not lay out his grief before those around him; he brings his complaint only to God.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Jacob carries a pain he cannot hide but will not voice to people; unlike her, he has a listener to whom it is no shame to speak.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Oh that thou wert as my brother, That sucked the breasts of my mother! When I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; Yea, and none would despise me.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved in the Song wishes she could show her love openly without incurring the scorn that convention would bring.
judaism.tie_back: She shares the Kural’s bind: love she cannot hide, but cannot express openly without shame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Ummadanti Jataka, King Sivi falls in love with the beautiful Ummadanti and, too ashamed to speak of it, keeps it to himself until he grows sick with longing and his minister guesses the cause.
buddhism.explanation: The king’s concealed passion shows itself in his wasting body, while shame keeps him from naming it.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the love-sickness cannot be hidden, yet shame forbids saying it aloud.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A stupid, ignorant sinner who never fixes his thoughts on the soul’s benefit and eternal welfare, but sinks down through hatred and the temptation of lust, will be ensnared as a fly is caught on glue.”
jainism.explanation: Kapila’s verses compare the person gripped by passion to a fly stuck fast in glue, unable to move either way.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is stuck just so: she can neither hide her love nor speak it; the Jain verse names that stuckness as the bondage of passion.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 8.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Let's hug Him close in our embrace, and not feel shy; let's bathe our minds in the dust of His feet.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan urges the devotee to hold the Beloved close without any bashfulness and to humble the mind at His feet.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine cannot hide her pain yet is too ashamed to tell it to the one who caused it; Guru Arjan asks the soul to set exactly that shyness aside before the divine Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 846, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides, Phaedra writes to Hippolytus that what modesty forbade her to say aloud, Love has commanded her to write, and that three times her tongue failed her when she tried to speak.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaedra can neither keep silent nor speak face to face, so shame drives her to a letter.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s double bind almost exactly: the love will not stay hidden, and shame stops the telling.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal devotes a chapter of On Love to modesty (pudeur), arguing that it makes a woman suffer in silence rather than reveal her feelings, even to the man she loves.
philosophy.explanation: For Stendhal, modesty is a powerful inner restraint that holds back the expression of love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural names the same force: nāṇ, which makes telling her beloved a source of shame.
philosophy.source: Stendhal, On Love, chapter on modesty (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Charlotte Bronte's letters to Constantin Heger
real_life_example.event: After studying and teaching in Brussels under the professor Constantin Heger, Charlotte Bronte returned to Haworth in 1844 and wrote him a series of letters in French; four survive, the last dated 18 November 1845. As her letters grew more needy he withdrew, and by the end of 1845 he had stopped replying. According to Heger's wife, he threw the letters away and she retrieved and mended them; the family gave them to the British Library in 1913.
real_life_example.explanation: The letters show a reserved woman unable to keep her feelings in, yet writing them out to the one man who could neither return them nor be told them plainly.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the heroine can no longer hide her love-pain, yet is ashamed to tell it to the very one who caused it, which is the struggle that runs through Bronte's letters to Heger.

tamil:
காமமும் நாணும் உயிர்காவாத் தூங்கும்என்
நோனா உடம்பின் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Kaamamum naanum uyirkaavaath thoongumen
noanaa udampin akaththu.
meaning: In my body, which cannot bear it any longer, love and modesty hang from the two ends of a carrying pole. My very life is that pole.
elementary: Have you seen someone carry two heavy buckets on a stick across their shoulders? The wife says her heart is like that stick: on one side hangs her love for her husband, on the other her shyness, and both are so heavy she feels she might break.
university: The central image is the kāvu (காவு) or kāvaḍi, a shoulder pole with loads at each end: uyir (உயிர், life) is the pole, and kāmam (காமம், desire) and nāṇ (நாண், modesty) hang (tūṅgum, தூங்கும்) in balance from it. Nōṉā uṭampu (நோனா உடம்பு) is ‘the body that cannot endure’, already worn thin by separation, which carries the whole apparatus. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah spell out the two loads exactly as love-pain and the shame of not being able to tell it, linking this couplet to 1162; Kalaignar describes the suffering body itself as a kāvaḍi. The image is admired in the commentary tradition because the balance is the torment: neither load can be dropped without the other swinging. Pope: ‘My soul, like porter’s pole, within my wearied frame, / Sustains a two-fold burthen poised, of love and shame.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Meghaduta, the exiled yaksha imagines his wife grown thin with separation, lying on one side of her bed like the last thin sliver of the waning moon.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa pictures the body of a separated wife worn down until it can barely hold her grief.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine speaks of the same body that can no longer bear its load of love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of mine iniquity, and my bones are consumed.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes grief that has worn down his strength and consumed his very frame.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the speaker feels sorrow as a weight his body can no longer carry.

islam.quote_or_event: “Our Lord, and burden us not with that which we have no ability to bear.”
islam.explanation: The closing prayer of Surat al-Baqarah asks God not to lay on believers a load beyond their capacity.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine describes just such a load: a body that cannot bear the double weight of love and shame.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Stay ye me with dainties, refresh me with apples; For I am love-sick.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved in the Song asks to be held up and revived because love has made her faint.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she feels love as a physical weight her body can scarcely sustain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces both grief and fear to the root of affection for what is dear.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine carries two loads, desire and shame; the Dhammapada sees such twin burdens growing from a single root of attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Love, hatred, &c., are heavy fetters, attachment is a dangerous one; having regularly destroyed them, I live up to the rules of conduct.”
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, Gautama names love and its opposite as the heavy fetters that bind beings.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels love as a heavy load hung on her life; Jain teaching calls such love a heavy fetter to be cut.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.43 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
