sikhism.quote_or_event: “Each and every hair on my head, and my mind and body, suffer the pains of separation; without seeing my God, I cannot sleep.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das describes separation from God as a pain carried in every part of the body and mind.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures the heroine's worn body carrying love and shame like loads on a shoulder pole; Guru Ram Das likewise describes a body and mind wholly burdened by the pain of separation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 836, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In her most famous poem Sappho describes love overwhelming her body: her tongue breaks, a thin fire runs under her skin, her eyes see nothing, she trembles and turns paler than grass, and seems to herself little short of dying.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho makes love a bodily crisis that the frame can scarcely survive.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also speaks of a body that cannot endure what love lays on it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus the lover’s soul is a charioteer with two horses, one restrained by modesty and shame, the other driven wildly by desire, so that the soul is pulled painfully in two directions.
philosophy.explanation: Plato pictures the lover’s inner life as a strained balance between desire and shame.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s carrying pole is a Tamil version of the same picture: love on one side, shame on the other, and the self stretched between them.

real_life_example.event_title: Chopin's silent love for the singer Konstancja Gladkowska
real_life_example.event: In a letter of 3 October 1829 to his friend Tytus Woyciechowski, the young Frederic Chopin wrote that he had found his ideal, whom he served faithfully without having spoken to her for half a year and of whom he dreamed. He added that the slow movement of his new concerto was created in remembrance of her. The Chopin Institute identifies this ideal as the singer Konstancja Gladkowska, for whom his feelings were overwhelming; the concerto, now known as the Piano Concerto in F minor, was inspired by those feelings.
real_life_example.explanation: Chopin's love was strong enough to shape a concerto, yet his shyness kept him from saying a word to her for months.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural pictures love and modesty hanging from the two ends of a carrying pole, and Chopin's letter shows a young man carrying both at once, unable to drop his love and unable to declare it.

tamil:
காமக் கடல்மன்னும் உண்டே அதுநீந்தும்
ஏமப் புணைமன்னும் இல்.
transliteration:
Kaamak kadalmannum undae adhuneendhum
aemap punaimannum il.
meaning: There is a sea of love in front of me, but there is no safe raft to cross it.
elementary: Picture standing on a beach looking at a huge ocean you need to cross, but there is no boat, not even a little raft. That is how the wife feels about her love while her husband is away: it is as big as the sea, and the one who could carry her across is not here.
university: The couplet balances two clauses with the emphatic particle maṉṉum (மன்னும், ‘indeed’): there is (uṇṭē) a sea of kāmam, and there is no (il) ēmap puṇai (ஏமப் புணை), a ‘raft of safety’. Puṇai (புணை) is a float or raft, and ēmam (ஏமம்) means protection or security. Puliyur Kesikan identifies the missing raft as the husband himself, who alone could carry her across and is now absent, while Solomon Pappaiah reads the sea as love-pain that has outgrown the shame of the previous couplet. The sea image recurs at 1166 and 1167, and readers have long noted its echo of the Kural’s opening chapter (Kural 10), where the ‘great sea of births’ is crossed only by those who cling to the feet of God: here the ocean is love and no such crossing is available. Pope: ‘A sea of love, ’tis true, I see stretched out before, / But not the trusty bark that wafts to yonder shore.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that even the worst of sinners, once in the boat of knowledge, will cross over the whole ocean of wrongdoing and misery.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita offers knowledge as the boat that carries a person across an otherwise impassable sea.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces a sea of love and finds no such boat; the Gita supplies the boat she lacks, but for a different ocean.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me.”
christianity.explanation: Peter, trying to cross the water to Jesus, begins to sink and cries out for rescue.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Peter is in water too great for him and without anything to hold him up but the one he is trying to reach.

islam.quote_or_event: “[But] he said, ‘I will take refuge on a mountain to protect me from the water.’ [Noah] said, ‘There is no protector today from the decree of Allāh, except for whom He gives mercy.’ And the waves came between them, and he was among the drowned.”
islam.explanation: Noah’s son refuses the ark and looks for his own refuge, but there is none, and the waves separate him from his father.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also faces a flood with no means of safety, and waves of distance lie between her and the one she loves.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Save me, O God; For the waters are come in even unto the soul. I am sunk in deep mire, where there is no standing; I am come into deep waters, and the flood overwhelmeth me.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes distress as deep water with no footing and no escape.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s sea of love is just such water: deep, overwhelming, and with nothing to keep her afloat.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Simile of the Raft, the Buddha describes a man facing a great expanse of water with no ferry or bridge, who gathers grass and branches, binds them into a raft, and crosses safely to the far shore.
buddhism.explanation: The Dhamma is compared to a raft built for crossing a flood and then set down once the crossing is made.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees the same flood but has no raft; the Buddha’s simile supplies exactly the vessel she says is missing.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (Simile of the Raft) (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “The body is the boat, life is the sailor, and the Circle of Births is the ocean which is crossed by the great sages.”
jainism.explanation: Gautama explains to Kesi that only a boat that does not leak reaches the far shore, and names the boat, the sailor and the ocean.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine has a sea before her and no boat; the Jain answer is that the disciplined body itself must become the vessel, though for the ocean of births, not of love.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.73 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The terrifying world-ocean is difficult and dreadful; there is no shore on this side or the one beyond. There is no boat, no raft, no oars and no boatman.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the world as a fearful ocean with no visible shore and no boat or raft to cross it, a crossing made possible only by the Guru.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says a sea of love lies before her but there is no safe raft to cross it; Guru Nanak uses the same image of a vast sea with no raft.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 59, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Poseidon wrecks the raft Odysseus built to leave Calypso, and he is left swimming for days in the open sea until the sea-goddess Ino gives him her veil to keep him afloat.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, trying to get home to his wife, loses his only means of crossing and is left at the mercy of the sea.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is in the same plight from the other side: a sea separates the couple and the raft is gone.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza calls the human lack of power to govern the emotions ‘bondage’, explaining that a person under their sway is not his own master but lies at the mercy of fortune.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, someone swept by passion has no secure footing of his own.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s sea without a raft is a picture of exactly this helplessness before a passion.

real_life_example.event_title: Lord Byron swims the Hellespont in imitation of Leander
real_life_example.place: Dardanelles (Hellespont), between Sestos and Abydos, Ottoman Empire (now Turkiye)
real_life_example.event: While his ship lay at anchor in the Dardanelles in 1810, the poet Lord Byron swam across the strait from Sestos to Abydos. In a letter to his mother dated 18 May 1810 he described the swim as done in imitation of Leander. In Greek legend the Hellespont was the scene of the love of Hero and Leander, in which Leander swam the strait at night to reach Hero.
real_life_example.explanation: Byron's swim recreated, in real life, the most famous image of a lover who has no boat and must cross a sea of water by strength alone.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says there is a sea of love before the heroine but no safe raft to carry her across, the same picture of love as a strait to be crossed without a boat that Byron's swim brought to life.

tamil:
துப்பின் எவனாவர் மன்கொல் துயர்வரவு
நட்பினுள் ஆற்று பவர்.
transliteration:
Thuppin evanaavar mankol thuyarvaravu
natpinul aatru pavar.
meaning: If he can bring me such sadness while we are lovers, what would he do to me if he were my enemy?
elementary: Imagine your best friend forgets your birthday and it really hurts. You might say, ‘If this is how much my friend can hurt me, I would hate to see what an enemy could do!’ The wife is half-joking, half-hurt in the same way about her husband who has gone away.
university: The couplet is ironic reproach: the husband ‘accomplishes the coming of sorrow’ (tuyar varavu āṟṟupavar, துயர்வரவு ஆற்றுபவர்) even within naṭpu (நட்பு, friendship, intimacy), so what (evaṉ, எவன்) would he become in tuppu (துப்பு)? The commentators divide over tuppu: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take it as ‘strength’, the power needed against a foe, while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take it directly as ‘enmity’ (pakai), and the sense is the same either way. Maṉ kol (மன்கொல்) adds wondering doubt. The reproach is affectionate rather than bitter, in keeping with the karpu ideal in which the wife complains of, but does not renounce, the absent husband. Pope: ‘Who work us woe in friendship’s trustful hour, / What will they prove when angry tempests lower?’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Shakuntala comes to Dushyanta’s court, the king, his memory clouded by a curse, denies he ever married her, and she reproaches him for treating with such cruelty the woman he had won with tender words.
hinduism.explanation: The very man who loved her becomes the source of her deepest wound.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Shakuntala finds that the one bound to her by love can hurt her more than any enemy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist laments that the wound came not from a stranger but from his trusted companion.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same complaint: the hurt comes from the one bound to her in love.

islam.quote_or_event: “Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken that one as a friend.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment the wrongdoer laments the friendship that led him to ruin.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, more gently, also counts the sorrow that comes through a bond of friendship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it was not an enemy that taunted me, Then I could have borne it; Neither was it mine adversary that did magnify himself against me, Then I would have hid myself from him. But it was thou, a man mine equal, My companion, and my familiar friend.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says he could have endured an enemy’s hostility; it is the hurt from a close companion that is unbearable.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s comparison of friend and foe turned the same way: the wound from one who loves is the hardest to bear.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that the beloved can cause pain just as surely as the disliked, simply by being absent.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds the same thing: the beloved, by being away, causes as much pain as an enemy could.

jainism.quote_or_event: In Kapila’s verses a monk is told to quit his former connections and set his affection on nothing, for one who loves not even those who love him will be free from sin and hatred.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching sees affection itself as the channel through which suffering enters, and so advises withdrawing it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers that the bond of love is what lets her husband hurt her; the Jain text draws the renunciant’s conclusion from that same fact.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 8.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O my Husband Lord, You are angry with me in Your Mind. The fault is with me, and not with my Husband Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, speaking as the soul-bride, feels the Husband Lord's displeasure but lays the blame on her own failings, not on Him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine reproaches her husband, asking what he would do as an enemy if he brings such sorrow as a lover; Farid's bride feels the same estrangement but turns the reproach on herself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 794, Raag Soohee, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides, Ariadne, abandoned on the island of Naxos by Theseus, writes that she saved his life and was repaid with desertion, so that the man she helped has wounded her worse than any foe.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ariadne’s complaint is that her pain comes from the very person she loved and served.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She voices the Kural’s question: if love does this, what could enmity do?

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Cicero’s On Friendship, Laelius reflects that friendships which break down often turn into bitter enmities, and that the hurt is the sharper because of the intimacy that preceded it.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero notes that closeness gives a friend unusual power to wound.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s rueful question rests on the same insight: love gives the beloved the power to cause the deepest pain.

real_life_example.event_title: Heloise writes her first letter to Abelard
real_life_example.place: Abbey of the Paraclete, near Nogent-sur-Seine, France
real_life_example.event: Around 1130 the philosopher Peter Abelard wrote a long letter of consolation to a friend, known as the Historia calamitatum, describing his misfortunes. Heloise, by then abbess of the Paraclete, wrote to him after it came into her hands, complaining that he had written to comfort a friend but had neglected her, and asking him to write to her of his dangers and of the convent he had founded. This letter opened one of the most famous correspondences of the Middle Ages.
real_life_example.explanation: Heloise's letter is a loving reproach: she does not renounce Abelard but asks why the man she loves has left her without a word.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine asks, half in reproach and half in love, what her husband would do as an enemy if he brings such grief as a lover, and Heloise's complaint of neglect has that same tender anger.

tamil:
இன்பம் கடல்மற்றுக் காமம் அஃதடுங்கால்
துன்பம் அதனிற் பெரிது.
transliteration:
Inpam kadalmatruk kaamam aqdhadungaal
thunpam adhanir peridhu.
meaning: The joy of love is as big as the sea. But when love turns to pain, its sadness is even bigger than the sea.
elementary: When your best friend is with you, the fun feels as big as the ocean. But when they move far away, the missing-them feeling can seem even bigger than that ocean. The wife says love works like that: the happy part is huge, and the sad part is huger still.
university: The couplet sets inpam (இன்பம், joy) against tunpam (துன்பம், sorrow) with kaṭal (கடல், sea) as the unit of measure: love’s joy is a sea, and its pain, when it aṭuṅkāl (அடுங்கால், ‘when it torments’), is periṭu (பெரிது), greater than that. Maṟṟu (மற்று) marks the turn, ‘but then’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take the contrast as union versus separation, which fits the chapter’s setting. The sea of 1164 thus grows: there it was a sea without a raft, here the sorrow exceeds the sea. Pope: ‘A happy love’s sea of joy; but mightier sorrows roll / From unpropitious love athwart the troubled soul.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Radha, separated from Krishna after their joy together, is described as wasting with longing, feeling even moonlight and cool breezes as burning, while her friend pleads with Krishna to return.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s poem moves from the bliss of union to an anguish of separation that seems to fill the whole world.
hinduism.tie_back: Radha experiences the Kural’s arithmetic: love’s joy is great, but the pain of its loss feels greater still.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, songs of Radha’s separation (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that joy can end in a sorrow that outweighs it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has lived this: love’s mirth has ended in a heaviness greater than the joy.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s Layla and Majnun, the brief joy of the young lovers’ first meeting gives way, after they are separated, to Majnun’s lifelong grief, which drives him to wander the desert.
islam.explanation: Nizami’s romance, read in Sufi tradition as an allegory of longing for the divine, makes the sorrow of separation far exceed the joy of union.
islam.tie_back: Majnun’s story is the Kural’s claim told as a life: love’s sorrow outgrows love’s joy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD. Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it.”
judaism.explanation: The Song measures love against death, the grave and the floods, and finds love the stronger.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Song uses the largest measures it knows, death and the floods, to show how vast love’s power is, including its power to hurt.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If one, longing for sensual pleasure, achieves it, yes, he’s enraptured at heart. The mortal gets what he wants. But if for that person, longing, desiring, the pleasures diminish, he’s shattered, as if shot with an arrow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Kama Sutta sets the rapture of getting what one desires against the shattering pain of losing it.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s two-part comparison: love’s joy is great, but its loss strikes harder still.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 4.1, Kama Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasures bring only a moment’s happiness, but suffering for a very long time, intense suffering, but slight happiness; they are an obstacle to the liberation from existence, and are a very mine of evils.”
jainism.explanation: The two sons of the priest Bhrigu tell their father that the pain pleasures bring far outweighs the pleasure itself.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same reckoning from inside love: its sorrow is greater than its joy.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Emotional attachment to Maya is a treacherous ocean of pain and poison, which cannot be crossed.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das calls attachment (moh) an ocean of pain so vast it cannot be crossed by one's own effort.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says love's joy is as wide as the sea but its sorrow is wider still; Guru Amar Das likewise measures the sorrow born of attachment as an uncrossable ocean.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1417, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros the ‘limb-loosener’ and names him ‘bittersweet’, a creature against whom there is no defence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho’s coined word holds love’s sweetness and its bitterness in a single breath.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural measures the same two sides of love and finds the bitter part the larger.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Schopenhauer argues that pain is positive and felt directly, while pleasure is merely the absence of pain, so that in any honest reckoning the suffering in life outweighs its enjoyment.
philosophy.explanation: For Schopenhauer, sorrow is always the heavier side of the scale.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine reaches the same verdict about love: its joy is a sea, but its sorrow is greater.
philosophy.source: Schopenhauer, ‘On the Sufferings of the World’ (Studies in Pessimism) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: The 1586 letter of Won's mother to her dead husband
real_life_example.event: In 1998, when a grave in Andong, South Korea, was being moved, archaeologists found a letter laid on the body of Yi Eung-tae, a member of the Goseong Yi clan who died in 1586. His pregnant wife had written it, addressed to Won's father. In it she said she could not go on without him, asked how she should bear her grief while raising their child, and begged him to come to her in her dreams.
real_life_example.explanation: The letter preserves, in one woman's words, the moment when the joy of a shared life turned into grief too great to bear.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that love's joy is as vast as the sea but its sorrow, when love brings pain, is greater still, and the Andong letter shows that greater sorrow overwhelming a happy marriage.

tamil:
காமக் கடும்புனல் நீந்திக் கரைகாணேன்
யாமத்தும் யானே உளேன்.
transliteration:
Kaamak kadumpunal neendhik karaikaanaen
yaamaththum yaanae ulaen.
meaning: I swim the wild flood of love but see no shore. Even in the middle of the night, I am the only one awake.
elementary: Imagine swimming and swimming in a huge lake at night, looking for the edge, and never finding it, while everyone else is fast asleep in bed. That is how the wife feels: her missing-him feeling seems to have no end, and at midnight she is the only one still awake.
university: Kaṭum puṉal (கடும்புனல்) is a ‘fierce flood’ or torrent, extending the sea of 1164 and 1166 into a current she must swim; karai kāṇēṉ (கரைகாணேன்) is ‘I see no shore’. Yāmam (யாமம்) is the midnight watch, and yāṉē uḷēṉ (யானே உளேன்), ‘I alone am’, is read by all four modern glossators as ‘I alone remain awake’, while Pope’s commentary-based prose adds ‘still I live’, catching the other shade of uḷēṉ (‘I exist, I survive’). The couplet introduces the night theme that the next two couplets develop. Pope’s verse: ‘I swim the cruel tide of love, and can no shore descry, / In watches of the night, too, ’mid the waters, only I!’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Nala abandons Damayanti while she sleeps in the forest, she wakes alone in the night, searches for him in vain, and wanders through the wilderness crying out his name.
hinduism.explanation: Damayanti’s night of waking to find herself alone is one of the great scenes of separation in the Mahabharata.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Damayanti is the one left awake and alone in the night, with no end to her searching in sight.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist, longing for God, feels himself overwhelmed by wave after wave.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also feels herself under a flood of longing that has no end.

islam.quote_or_event: “Or [they are] like darknesses within an unfathomable sea which is covered by waves, upon which are waves, over which are clouds - darknesses, some of them upon others. When one puts out his hand [therein], he can hardly see it.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes a person without light as lost in a deep, dark sea, wave on wave, with nothing visible.
islam.tie_back: The heroine’s midnight flood with no shore in sight is the same picture of being lost in dark waters.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved in the Song lies awake at night searching for her absent lover without finding him.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s heroine at midnight: awake, searching, and unable to reach the end of her longing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The misguided man in whom the thirty-six currents of craving strongly rush toward pleasurable objects, is swept away by the flood of his passionate thoughts.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures craving as a set of currents that carry the mind away like a flood.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s ‘fierce flood of love’ is this same current, and she, too, finds no shore.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The flood is old age and death, which carry away living beings; Law is the island, the firm ground, the refuge, the most excellent shelter.”
jainism.explanation: Asked whether there is any firm ground for beings swept off by the great flood, Gautama names the Law as the island.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine swims a flood and sees no shore; the Jain text names a shore, but for the flood of birth and death rather than love.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.68 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I cannot endure the night, and sleep does not come, without the Sight of the Beloved Guru's Court.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan writes of nights that will not end and sleep that will not come while he is parted from his Beloved Guru; Sikh tradition holds that these verses were sent as letters to his father, Guru Ram Das, while he was kept away in Lahore.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine swims a flood of love that has no shore and lies alone awake through the midnight watch; Guru Arjan likewise describes the sleepless night of one parted from the beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 97, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Leander swims the Hellespont each night to reach Hero, guided by her lamp, until one stormy night the lamp is blown out and he drowns before reaching the shore.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story of Hero and Leander makes love literally a night swim through a dangerous sea.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine swims love’s flood at midnight and sees no shore, just as Leander fails to reach his.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In The Anatomy of Melancholy, Robert Burton lists among the symptoms of love-melancholy that lovers cannot sleep, but lie awake through the night sighing and thinking of the absent beloved.
philosophy.explanation: Burton’s encyclopaedic study treats sleeplessness as a classic sign of love-sickness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, alone and awake at midnight, shows exactly this symptom.
philosophy.source: Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy, Part 3, Section 2 (Love-Melancholy) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Pliny the Younger's letter to his absent wife Calpurnia
real_life_example.event: The Roman senator and author Pliny the Younger wrote a short letter to his wife Calpurnia while she was away from Rome. He told her that he missed her intensely, that he stayed awake through much of the night thinking of her, and that at the hours when he used to visit her his feet carried him to her room, only for him to turn away from the empty doorway. He added that his only relief was his work in the law courts.
real_life_example.explanation: Pliny's letter is one of the earliest surviving descriptions, in a husband's own words, of sleepless longing for an absent spouse.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine swims a flood of love with no shore in sight and is the only one awake in the middle of the night, which is the state Pliny described in his letter.

tamil:
மன்னுயிர் எல்லாம் துயிற்றி அளித்திரா
என்னல்லது இல்லை துணை.
transliteration:
Mannuyir ellaam thuyitri aliththiraa
ennalladhu illai thunai.
meaning: Poor night! It has put every living thing to sleep, and now it has no friend left but me.
elementary: Have you ever been the only one awake in the house at night? Everyone is asleep, it is very quiet, and you feel like it is just you and the dark. The wife feels so lonely that she starts feeling sorry for the night itself, because the only friend the night has left is her.
university: The couplet personifies irā (இரா, night): it has put to sleep (tuyiṟṟi, துயிற்றி) all ‘abiding lives’ (maṉṉuyir, மன்னுயிர்), and now has no tuṇai (துணை, companion) except (allatu) me. Aḷittu (அளித்து) is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as ‘pitiable’ (‘this night is to be pitied’), while Pope’s commentary-based prose takes it as ‘graciously’ (‘the night which graciously lulls to sleep all living creatures’). The irony is turned inward: by pitying the night’s solitude the heroine reveals her own. Kalaignar makes it an address, ‘O Night!’. Pope’s verse: ‘All living souls in slumber soft she steeps; / But me alone kind night for her companing keeps!’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Searching Lanka by night while the city sleeps, Hanuman at last finds Sita in the Ashoka grove, worn with grief, keeping a lonely watch among sleeping guards.
hinduism.explanation: Sita, separated from Rama, is the one wakeful figure in a slumbering city.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she keeps company with the night while all others sleep.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.”
christianity.explanation: The afflicted psalmist lies awake, solitary as a lone bird on a roof.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also watches through the night with no companion but the dark.

islam.quote_or_event: “And made your sleep [a means for] rest.”
islam.explanation: Among the signs of God’s care, the Qur’an names sleep, given to all creatures for their rest.
islam.tie_back: The night gives this rest to every living being except the Kural’s heroine, who is left awake.

judaism.quote_or_event: “She weepeth sore in the night, And her tears are on her cheeks; She hath none to comfort her Among all her lovers.”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations pictures Jerusalem as a woman weeping alone through the night with no one to comfort her.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s heroine at night: weeping, wakeful, and without any companion.

buddhism.quote_or_event: On the night of his renunciation, Prince Siddhartha wakes in the palace to find everyone around him asleep, and leaves while Yasodhara and their newborn son sleep on, so that she wakes to find herself without him.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist narrative of the Great Departure is set in a sleeping palace with one figure awake.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s scene is the same night seen from Yasodhara’s side: all others sleep, and the one left behind keeps watch alone.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, a frightful fire is said to be blazing up and burning embodied beings, and Gautama explains that the fire is the passions, quenched only by knowledge, virtue and penance.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching describes the passions as a fire that keeps burning those who have not mastered them.
jainism.tie_back: While the night quiets every other being, the heroine alone is kept awake by the burning of her longing.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.50-53 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Like a patient nearing his death, whom should I tell this state that has resulted due to the fire of separation? All these things (moon, stars, dresses etc.) are becoming uncomfortable and painful for me, whereas all these are highly peace-giving and source of comfort for the whole world.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas has the separated lover say that the moon, stars and other things that comfort everyone else only torment her. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine pities the night, which has lulled every creature to sleep and is left with her alone for company; Bhai Gurdas's lover likewise finds that what soothes the whole world leaves her alone in her pain.
sikhism.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 668, English translation as given in the BaniDB database

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: A short poem traditionally attributed to Sappho says that the moon has set and the Pleiades, it is midnight, the hour goes by, and the speaker lies alone.
greek_mythology.explanation: The lines catch the precise moment of midnight solitude in a few words.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the speaker is awake at midnight with no companion but the night.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho (attributed), fragment 168B Voigt, ‘The moon has set’ (paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus distinguishes being alone from being forlorn: a forlorn person is one who has lost those he depended on and feels himself abandoned even in a crowd.
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus analyses loneliness as the feeling of being bereft of a needed companion.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s loneliness is of this kind, so complete that she imagines the night itself as her only companion.

real_life_example.event_title: Pablo Neruda publishes Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair
real_life_example.event: In 1924 the young Chilean poet Pablo Neruda, then about twenty, published Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair. Its Poem 20, often called Tonight I Can Write, is spoken on a starry night by a lover who remembers holding a woman he once loved on nights like this one and grieves that she is no longer with him.
real_life_example.explanation: The letters record years of wartime separation borne largely through writing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural pictures the night, after it has put every creature to sleep, keeping company only with the heroine, and Neruda's speaker likewise sits alone with the night, remembering the one who is gone.

tamil:
கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய இந்நாள்
நெடிய கழியும் இரா.
transliteration:
Kotiyaar kodumaiyin thaamkotiya innaal
netiya kazhiyum iraa.
meaning: These long, slow nights are even crueler than the cruel man who left me.
elementary: When you are waiting for something you really want, like a birthday, the days feel super long. The wife waiting for her husband says the long nights are even meaner to her than her husband was for going away.
university: The couplet plays on koṭu (கொடு, cruel): koṭiyār (கொடியார், ‘the cruel one’, the departed husband), koṭumai (கொடுமை, cruelty) and koṭiya (கொடிய, cruel) are stacked so that the nights, iṉṉāḷ neṭiya kaḻiyum irā (‘the nights which in these days pass so long’), outdo the husband in cruelty. The comparison lets the heroine blame the nights rather than the husband, softening the reproach of 1165. There is a sandhi variant in the first line: ytamizh.com prints தாம்கொடிய இந்நாள், while thirukkural.net prints தாம்கொடிய விந்நாள், with the glide v of koṭiya + iṉṉāḷ written out; the reading is the same. Pope: ‘More cruel than the cruelty of him, the cruel one, / In these sad times are lengthening hours of night I watch alone.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Meghaduta, the separated yaksha wishes that the night with its long watches could somehow be shortened to a moment, and that his days apart might pass more quickly.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s lover feels the night of separation stretch out unbearably.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same: the long nights of separation are her worst tormentors.

christianity.quote_or_event: “So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me. When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise, and the night be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day.”
christianity.explanation: Job describes nights that will not end, spent tossing and waiting for dawn.
christianity.tie_back: Job’s wearisome nights are the Kural’s nights that ‘pass so long’, felt as a torment in themselves.

islam.quote_or_event: “…to the point that the earth closed in on them in spite of its vastness and their souls confined them…”
islam.explanation: The three companions who were shunned after staying behind felt the wide earth itself shrink around them in their anguish.
islam.tie_back: As anguish made the vast earth feel narrow to them, longing makes the heroine’s nights feel endlessly long.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In the morning thou shalt say, Would God it were even! and at even thou shalt say, Would God it were morning!”
judaism.explanation: Among the curses of Deuteronomy is a dread so constant that every hour seems too long and the next one is wished for.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine lives this restlessness at night, when every hour drags and she longs for it to pass.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary. Long is worldly existence to fools who know not the Sublime Truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada begins its chapter on the fool by noting how the night stretches out for one who cannot sleep.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine knows exactly this: for the sleepless, the night is long and cruel.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse without profit to him who acts contrary to the Law.”
jainism.explanation: Bhrigu’s sons warn that time spent without the Law is lost; Jacobi notes that the original literally says ‘the nights’, the old way of counting time.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine counts her separation in nights that pass painfully; the Jain verse also counts life in nights, but urges using them for the Law rather than in longing.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When I could not be with You for just one moment, the Dark Age of Kali Yuga dawned for me.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that even a moment apart from his Beloved Guru stretched into a whole dark age; Sikh tradition places this verse among his letters from Lahore.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine finds the long nights of separation crueller even than the husband who left; Guru Arjan likewise describes how time apart from the beloved swells into an age of darkness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Penelope tells the disguised Odysseus that by day she can find relief in weeping and in her household tasks, but when night comes and all others are asleep, she lies awake with sharp cares crowding her heart.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope finds the nights of her husband’s long absence harder than the days.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Penelope finds the long nights the cruellest part of separation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Augustine argues that time is measured in the mind itself, so that a ‘long future’ is really a long expectation of the future, stretched out in the soul that waits.
philosophy.explanation: For Augustine, how long time seems depends on the stretching of the waiting mind.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s nights are long because her mind is stretched out in waiting for her husband’s return.

real_life_example.event_title: The Mother of Michitsuna's poem on a night spent alone
real_life_example.event: The Heian court poet known as the Mother of Michitsuna recorded about twenty years of her marriage to the courtier Fujiwara no Kaneie, from 954 to 974, in the Kagero Diary, a marriage that ended in separation. One of her poems, later chosen as poem 53 of the Hyakunin Isshu anthology, asks whether he can possibly know how long a night is for someone who lies alone grieving until dawn.
real_life_example.explanation: Her poem became one of the classic Japanese expressions of the endless night of a wife waiting for a husband who does not come.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the long nights are crueller even than the cruel husband who left, and this poem is built on exactly that complaint about the length of a night spent alone.

tamil:
உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின் வெள்ளநீர்
நீந்தல மன்னோஎன் கண்.
transliteration:
Ullampoandru ulvazhich chelkirpin vellaneer
neendhala mannoaen kan.
meaning: If my eyes could travel to where he is, the way my heart does, they would not have to swim in this flood of tears.
elementary: Your thoughts can fly anywhere: you can imagine being with your grandma far away in a second. But your eyes cannot go there to see her. The wife says her heart is already with her husband, but her eyes are stuck at home, so they just cry and cry.
university: The closing couplet contrasts uḷḷam (உள்ளம், heart or mind), which goes freely to uḷvaḻi (உள்வழி, ‘the place where he is’), with kaṇ (கண், the eyes), which cannot follow and so must ‘swim’ (nīntu, நீந்து) in veḷḷa nīr (வெள்ளநீர், a flood of water), that is, tears. Celkiṟpiṉ (செல்கிற்பின்) is ‘if they were able to go’, and maṉṉō (மன்னோ) adds regretful emphasis. Puliyur Kesikan extends the wish to her whole body going where her heart is, while the other glossators keep to the eyes. The flood of this couplet answers the floods of 1164 and 1167: the sea of love has become the water of her own tears, and the next chapter (118, kaṇ vitumpu aḻital) turns entirely to the eyes. Pope: ‘When eye of mine would as my soul go forth to him, / It knows not how through floods of its own tears to swim.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Uddhava brings Krishna’s message from Mathura, the gopis of Vraja tell him that their minds are always with Krishna, even though they themselves must remain behind, weeping, in the village.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis’ hearts have gone where Krishna is, but their bodies and eyes are left in Vraja.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s contrast exactly: the heart travels to the beloved, while the eyes stay behind in tears.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist, in great distress, weeps so much that he says his bed swims in tears.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine uses the same hyperbole: her eyes swim in a flood of tears.

islam.quote_or_event: “Ever since they tore me from my osier bed, My plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears. I burst my breast, striving to give vent to sighs, And to express the pangs of my yearning for my home.”
islam.explanation: Rumi’s reed-flute, cut from its reed bed, cries out with longing to return to where it belongs.
islam.tie_back: The reed’s heart is with its home and its body cannot go there, which is the heroine’s situation, and its lament moves others to tears as hers floods her eyes.
islam.source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book 1, Prologue (tr. E.H. Whinfield)

judaism.quote_or_event: “For these things I weep; Mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water; Because the comforter is far from me, Even he that should refresh my soul.”
judaism.explanation: The voice of Lamentations weeps endlessly because the one who should bring comfort is far away.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes are flooded for the same reason: the one who would comfort her is far off and cannot be reached.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Which is greater, the tears you have shed while transmigrating & wandering this long, long time — crying & weeping from being joined with what is displeasing, being separated from what is pleasing — or the water in the four great oceans?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha asks his monks to compare all the tears they have shed over separation with the oceans, and they answer that the tears are greater.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘flood of tears’ shed in separation becomes, in the Buddha’s reckoning, a flood greater than the seas.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 15.3, Assu Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: When her betrothed Arishtanemi leaves on their wedding day to become a monk, Princess Rajimati does not stay behind in grief but herself renounces the world and follows him to Mount Raivataka, where he practises austerities.
jainism.explanation: In the Jain story, Rajimati turns her longing into action and goes where her heart has already gone.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wishes she could go where her heart is; Rajimati actually does, though by way of renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22 (Rathanemi) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Ascending to His Mansion, I gaze upon His path, and my eyes are filled with tears.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan pictures the waiting bride climbing to the roof to watch the road for her Husband, her eyes filling with tears.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine wishes her eyes could go to her husband as her heart does, instead of swimming in a flood of tears; Guru Arjan's bride can only watch the road with tear-filled eyes while her heart goes out to the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 624, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Penelope opens her letter to the long-absent Odysseus by begging him not to write back but to come himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope wants not messages but presence; words and thoughts cannot cross the distance for her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also knows that thoughts can travel but she cannot, and longs for real presence instead.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Lucilius that he never receives a letter from him without at once feeling in his company, because the mind can be with an absent friend even when the body cannot.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca treats the mind as able to cross distance and make an absent friend present.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural agrees that the heart travels freely, but laments that the eyes cannot follow, which is why they fill with tears.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 40 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Kalidasa composes the Meghaduta, the Cloud Messenger
real_life_example.event: The Sanskrit poet Kalidasa composed the Meghaduta, a lyric love poem of about 115 verses. In it an exiled yaksha, a nature spirit, pines for his beloved while alone on a mountain peak. At the start of the monsoon he asks a passing cloud to carry a message to her in the Himalayan city of Alaka, and much of the poem describes the cities and landscapes the cloud will pass on its way.
real_life_example.explanation: The poem became one of the masterpieces of Sanskrit literature and the model for a whole genre of messenger poems in India.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural wishes that the eyes could travel to the beloved as freely as the heart does, and Kalidasa's exile, unable to go himself, sends his heart's message on a cloud instead.

tamil:
கண்தாம் கலுழ்வ தெவன்கொலோ தண்டாநோய்
தாம்காட்ட யாம்கண் டது.
transliteration:
Kandhaam kaluzhva thevan-koloa thandaanoi
thaamkaatta yaamkan dadhu.
meaning: This endless love-sickness came only because my eyes showed him to me. So why do those same eyes now cry and beg to see him?
elementary: Imagine you begged your friend to let you hold their puppy, and then you cried when it was time to give it back. Your friend might say, ‘But you were the one who wanted to hold it!’ The lady in this couplet scolds her own eyes the same way: they were the ones who looked at him first, so why are they crying now?
university: Chapter 118 continues the karpiyal (married love) sequence on separation, and its whole conceit is that the heroine turns on her own eyes: kaṇ (eye) plus vituppu (eager longing, impatience) plus aḻital (wasting away), i.e. the eyes are worn out by their own craving to see the absent husband. In the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar she speaks to her confidante (tōḻi), half-blaming, half-pitying the eyes as if they were separate persons. Kaluḻvatu (கலுழ்வது) is ‘weeping’, taṇṭā nōy (தண்டாநோய்) ‘the disease that does not abate’, and tām kāṭṭa yām kaṇṭatu ‘we saw it because they showed it’: the eyes are both cause and complainant. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar sharpen the irony by making the eyes weep to be shown him again, while Pope renders: ‘They showed me him, and then my endless pain / I saw: why then should weeping eyes complain?’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a strong wind sweeps away a boat on the water, even one of the roaming senses on which the mind focuses can carry away a man’s intelligence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a single sense, once the mind follows it, can drag the whole person off course.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine’s complaint is exactly this: one sense, her eyes, carried her into a love-sickness she cannot now steer out of.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.67 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus speaks of the eye as a member that can lead the whole person into ruin, and so may be treated as an offender.
christianity.tie_back: Like Jesus’ saying, the Kural treats the eye as a culprit separate from the self, the one that ‘caused’ the trouble.

islam.quote_or_event: “The adultery of the eyes is the sight (to gaze at a forbidden thing), the adultery of the tongue is the talk, and the inner self wishes and desires…”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes how desire begins with the eyes’ looking, which the inner self then turns into longing.
islam.tie_back: The Kural makes the same chain of cause: the eyes looked first, and the heart’s unending longing followed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The heart and the eyes are the ‘spies’ of the body — they act as its agents for sinning: the eye sees, the heart covets and the body commits the sin.”
judaism.explanation: Rashi, citing the Midrash, explains that the eyes are the body’s scouts: they go first, and the heart’s desire follows what they report.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine likewise names her eyes as the scouts that went ahead and led her heart into its present suffering.
judaism.source: Rashi on Numbers 15:39 (tr. M. Rosenbaum and A.M. Silbermann, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The eye is aflame. Forms are aflame. Consciousness at the eye is aflame. Contact at the eye is aflame.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Fire Sermon the Buddha teaches that seeing, and everything that arises from the eye’s contact with forms, burns with passion and brings sorrow and lamentation.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers the same thing in her own life: what began with the eye’s contact has become a fire of grief.
buddhism.source: Adittapariyaya Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.28 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who passionately hates (a colour), will at the same moment suffer pain. It is the fault of an undisciplined man that he is annoyed (by a colour); it is not the ‘colour’ itself that annoys him.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that suffering from what the eye perceives comes from one’s own undisciplined attachment or aversion, not from the object seen.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine likewise refuses to blame anyone outside herself: the fault lies with her own eyes, which looked and clung.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “These are the very eyes which used to see the extremely beautiful form of the beloved Lord and satisfying their desire would absorb themselves in the spiritual bliss. ... These are the eyes that used to suffer the most at the time of separation of the Lord, the Master of my life.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas devotes a whole kabitt to the eyes: the same eyes that once feasted on the Beloved's form are the ones that suffer most when He is gone. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her eyes showed her the beloved and so brought on her endless sickness, yet now they weep to see him; Bhai Gurdas likewise singles out the eyes as both the first to delight and the worst to suffer.
sikhism.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 669, English translation as given in the BaniDB database

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orpheus wins Eurydice back from the underworld on condition that he not look at her until they reach the upper air, but at the last moment, longing to see her, he turns his eyes and loses her for ever, and then weeps for her.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s telling, it is Orpheus’s own longing look that costs him the beloved he then mourns.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the eyes that looked out of love become the cause of the grief they then weep over.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that the pleasure of the eye is the beginning of love: no one falls in love who has not first been delighted by the beloved’s appearance, though delight in looks alone is not yet love.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, sight is the starting point of erotic love, which then grows into longing for the beloved’s presence.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine traces her ‘unending disease’ to that same beginning: her eyes’ first delighted look.

real_life_example.event_title: Mozart weeps after Aloysia Weber turns away from him
real_life_example.event: On his way to Paris in 1777 the young Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart met the Weber family in Mannheim and fell in love with the gifted singer Aloysia Weber, who was his pupil. When he reached Munich on his way home in late 1778, she had turned away from him, though she had once returned some of his affection. In a letter to his father dated 29 December 1778, Mozart wrote that today he could only weep and that his heart was too full of tears; four years later he married her sister Constanze.
real_life_example.explanation: Mozart's own letter records how a love that began with delight in seeing and hearing Aloysia ended, for the moment, in tears.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks why the eyes that first showed the heroine her beloved now weep for him, and Mozart's tears in Munich came from the same love his eyes had first welcomed in Mannheim.

tamil:
தெரிந்துணரா நோக்கிய உண்கண் பரிந்துணராப்
பைதல் உழப்பது எவன்.
transliteration:
Therindhunaraa noakkiya un-kan parindhunaraap
paidhal uzhappadhu evan.
meaning: My dark-lined eyes looked at him back then without thinking about what would follow. Why do they suffer now, not seeing that they caused this sadness themselves?
elementary: Think of someone who eats a whole bag of sweets without thinking, and then complains of a tummy ache as if it came from nowhere. The lady says her eyes did the same: they gazed at him without thinking ahead, and now they cry as if they don’t know why it hurts.
university: The couplet balances two negated verbs of knowing: terintu uṇarā nōkkiya, ‘looked without discerning and understanding’ (then), and parintu uṇarā, ‘not perceiving with sympathy’ or ‘not grasping’ (now). Uṇkaṇ (உண்கண்) is the conventional ‘eye fit to be eaten’, i.e. kohl-lined and lovely, and paital (பைதல்) is grief or affliction; uḻappatu evaṉ asks ‘why do they toil in it?’ Mu. Varadarasanar reads the second clause as the eyes failing to feel affection now; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as the eyes failing to recognise that they brought this on themselves and should bear it. Pope gives: ‘How glancing eyes, that rash unweeting looked that day, / With sorrow measureless are wasting now away!’ No textual variants were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna traces a chain that begins with merely dwelling on sense objects: from that contemplation arises attachment, from attachment desire, from desire anger, and so on down to the loss of discernment and ruin.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita teaches that unreflective attention to an object is the first link in a chain that ends in suffering.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes ‘looked without discerning’, and the whole chain of longing and pain followed from that first unweighed glance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat…”
christianity.explanation: In Eden, what is ‘pleasant to the eyes’ is taken without weighing the consequence, and sorrow follows.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise acted on delight without foresight, and are now left with the grief that followed.

islam.quote_or_event: “Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asks believers to restrain their gaze, recognising that unguarded looking leads the heart where it should not go.
islam.tie_back: The heroine wishes, in effect, that her eyes had been more guarded and discerning when they first looked.

judaism.quote_or_event: “…that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them; and that ye go not about after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go astray.”
judaism.explanation: The fringes (tzitzit) are given so that Israel will not follow wherever the heart and eyes wander.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes did just that, going ‘after’ what they saw without considering where it led.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seeing your eyes, my sensual delight grows all the more.” — to which the nun Subha replies: “you run blind after what is unreal.”
buddhism.explanation: A libertine stops the nun Subha and confesses he is captivated by her eyes; she answers that his vision is distorted and he chases a mirage.
buddhism.tie_back: The libertine’s undiscerning gaze is the Kural’s ‘looking without understanding’; the Kural’s heroine is now living with what such looking leads to.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares the person ruled by what the eye sees to a moth that flies into the flame it is drawn to.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes flew toward their beloved like the moth, without discernment, and are now burnt by the absence that followed.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In a dream, He came, and went away again; I cried so many tears.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak's soul-bride glimpses the Husband Lord only in a dream, and when He is gone again she weeps.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her eyes once looked at her lover without a thought for what would follow, and now they suffer; Guru Nanak's bride likewise has a fleeting sight of the Beloved and is left in tears.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 558, Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Narcissus falls in love with a reflection in a pool without understanding what he is seeing; Ovid’s narrator tells him that what he seeks is nowhere and that he is deceived by his own eyes.
greek_mythology.explanation: Narcissus’s eyes fasten on an image before his mind grasps what it is, and he wastes away from that undiscerning gaze.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Narcissus, the Kural’s eyes ‘looked without understanding’ and brought on a pining they cannot escape.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume argues that reason alone can never oppose a passion in directing the will, and that reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions.
philosophy.explanation: On Hume’s view, desires are not first weighed by reason; they move us, and reason only follows.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes illustrate Hume’s point: they acted on delight, not on reflection, and reason arrives only afterwards to complain.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.3 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Robert Burns writes Ae Fond Kiss on parting from Agnes McLehose
real_life_example.event: Robert Burns and Agnes McLehose of Glasgow carried on a passionate but platonic correspondence under the pen names Sylvander and Clarinda, since she was married. In December 1791, as she prepared to sail to Jamaica to try to reconcile with her husband, the two met for the last time, and Burns wrote the song Ae Fond Kiss for her on their parting. Decades later Agnes wrote in her journal that she had parted with Burns in 1791, never to meet again in this world.
real_life_example.explanation: The song's famous lament is that the lovers would never have been broken-hearted if they had never met, a reflection on how a love so gladly begun can lead to grief.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural blames the eyes that once gazed at the beloved without weighing what would follow and now suffer for it, which is the same thought Burns put into his farewell song.

tamil:
கதுமெனத் தாநோக்கித் தாமே கலுழும்
இதுநகத் தக்க துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Kadhumenath thaanoakkith thaamae kaluzhum
ithunakath thakka thudaiththu.
meaning: These eyes rushed on their own to look at him, and now they cry on their own. Surely that is something to laugh at.
elementary: Picture a child who runs to jump in a puddle, then cries because their socks are wet. It’s sad, but also a little funny, because they did it to themselves! The lady laughs at her eyes the same way: they hurried to look, and now they are the ones crying.
university: Katumeṉa (கதுமென) is an adverb of sudden speed, ‘in a flash’, and the parallel tām (themselves) / tāmē (they themselves) puts the whole action, the eager looking and the weeping, on the eyes alone. Naka-t-takkatu uṭaittu, ‘it has the quality of something to be laughed at’, gives the chapter its bitter humour: the heroine mocks her own organs. Puliyur Kesikan glosses the laughter as at the eyes’ ignorance; Solomon Pappaiah renders it colloquially, ‘when I see these eyes crying alone today, I can only laugh’. Pope: ‘The eyes that threw such eager glances round erewhile / Are weeping now. Such folly surely claims a smile!’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That happiness which is derived from contact of the senses with their objects and which appears like nectar at first but poison at the end is said to be of the nature of passion.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna classifies pleasure that rushes from the senses to their objects as passionate: sweet at the start, bitter at the end.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes enjoyed the nectar of the first eager look and now taste the poison of weeping, which she finds almost laughable.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.38 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs observes that laughter and sorrow sit close together, and that merriment can end in grief.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural joins the two in the same way: the heroine laughs at eyes whose eager joy has ended in tears.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that it is He who makes [one] laugh and weep.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names laughter and weeping together as conditions that come over human beings in turn.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds both in a single moment: she laughs at the eyes that are weeping.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All things toil to weariness; Man cannot utter it, The eye is not satisfied with seeing, Nor the ear filled with hearing.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth notes that the eye is never sated by looking; it keeps reaching out, and the reaching leads only to weariness.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes, which flew to look and now weep, show the same restless, never-satisfied seeing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “So long as an evil deed has not ripened, the fool thinks it as sweet as honey. But when the evil deed ripens, the fool comes to grief.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that what tastes sweet at first can ripen into grief, catching the unwary by surprise.
buddhism.tie_back: The eyes’ eager look was honey at first; now it has ripened into weeping, which the heroine finds fit for laughter.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares pleasures to the kimpaka fruit, lovely to look at and to taste but deadly afterwards.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s eager look was the lovely fruit; the weeping that followed is its bitter after-effect.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I used to see my beloved Lord without a blink of the eye as a ruddy sheldrake looks at moon. There used to be no break. But now I don't even see Him in a dream.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas recalls how the lover's eyes once gazed at the Beloved without blinking, like the chakor bird at the moon, and now cannot glimpse Him even in dreams. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine laughs bitterly at eyes that rushed of their own accord to look at the beloved and now weep of their own accord; Bhai Gurdas sets the same contrast between the eyes' eager gazing then and their deprivation now.
sikhism.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 670, English translation as given in the BaniDB database

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Psyche, unable to resist, lights a lamp to look at her sleeping husband, Eros; a drop of oil wakes him, he flies away, and she is left weeping for the husband her own eager look has driven off.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Apuleius’s tale, Psyche’s longing to see is the very thing that costs her the beloved and leaves her in tears.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the eyes that rushed to look are the same eyes that must now weep.
greek_mythology.source: Apuleius, Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass) 5.22-24, Cupid and Psyche (paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hobbes defines laughter as ‘sudden glory’, a passion that arises when we suddenly see some defect or absurdity and feel ourselves above it.
philosophy.explanation: On Hobbes’s account we laugh at folly when we catch it plainly in view.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s laughter at her eyes fits Hobbes’s description: she stands back and sees their folly, even though it is her own.

real_life_example.event_title: Berlioz's obsession with the actress Harriet Smithson
real_life_example.event: In 1827 the composer Hector Berlioz saw the Irish actress Harriet Smithson play Ophelia in an English-language Hamlet in Paris and became fixated on her. He waited at the stage door, bombarded her with love letters that she ignored, and rented rooms near her theatre, though neither spoke the other's language. He poured the unrequited passion into his Symphonie fantastique, premiered in December 1830; the two married in October 1833, but the marriage was unhappy and they later agreed to live apart.
real_life_example.explanation: Berlioz's headlong pursuit, set off by a single look at an actress on stage, became one of music history's most famous examples of love at first sight turning into torment.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural laughs at eyes that rushed of their own accord to look and now of their own accord weep, and Berlioz's eager gaze at the stage and the years of anguish that followed fit that rueful humour.

tamil:
பெயலாற்றா நீருலந்த உண்கண் உயலாற்றா
உய்வில்நோய் என்கண் நிறுத்து.
transliteration:
Peyalaatraa neerulandha un-kan uyalaatraa
uyvilnoi en-kan niruththu.
meaning: My lovely eyes planted in me a sickness I cannot escape or survive. Now they have cried so much that their tears have dried up.
elementary: Imagine crying so hard and so long that, in the end, no more tears come out. That is how the lady’s eyes feel: they cried and cried, and now they are dry, but the sadness is still there.
university: Peyal (பெயல்) is literally ‘rain’, so peyal āṟṟā nīr ulanta is ‘the water dried up, no longer able to rain’: the tears themselves are exhausted. Uyal āṟṟā uyvil nōy is a doubled image of fatality, ‘a disease with no escape, which one cannot survive’, and eṉkaṇ niṟuttu ‘having fixed it in me’ (with a pun on kaṇ as both ‘eye’ and ‘in’). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree that the eyes, having caused the incurable love-sickness, are now too dry even to weep. Pope: ‘Those eyes have wept till all the fount of tears is dry, / That brought upon me pain that knows no remedy.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Cloud Messenger, the exiled Yaksha imagines his wife far away, wasted by separation, her eyes swollen and reddened from incessant weeping, lying awake and counting the days until his return.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s poem pictures the separated wife as worn out by tears and sleeplessness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is the same figure, her eyes exhausted by weeping over an absent husband.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta (Uttaramegha), description of the Yaksha’s wife (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears. Mine eye is consumed because of grief.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes nights of weeping until his eye is worn out with sorrow.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Mine eye is consumed because of grief’ could serve as a title for the Kural’s chapter, whose eyes have wept themselves dry.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob grieves so long for his lost son that his eyes are worn white with sorrow.
islam.tie_back: As with the Kural’s heroine, the eyes themselves bear the damage of grief for an absent beloved.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mine eyes do fail with tears, Mine inwards burn, My liver is poured upon the earth…”
judaism.explanation: The poet of Lamentations weeps until his eyes give out and his whole body is undone by grief.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise ‘fail with tears’ until there are no more to shed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada traces grief to its root in endearment: to hold someone dear is to be exposed to sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s ‘incurable disease’ is the grief that springs from endearment, and her dried-up eyes are its sign.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mind of those who always live in unfrequented lodgings, who eat low food, and who subdue their senses, will not be attacked by the foe, Love, who is vanquished as disease is by medicine.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana speaks of love as a disease that can be cured by the medicine of discipline and sense restraint.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural shares the image of love as a disease but denies the cure: for the heroine it is uyvil nōy, a sickness with no escape.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I cannot survive without seeing my Beloved. My eyes are welling up with tears.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that without the sight of the Beloved he cannot live, and his eyes overflow with tears.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her eyes, having planted in her a sickness she cannot survive, have wept until no tears are left; Guru Ram Das likewise joins a longing he cannot survive to eyes running with tears.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 94, Raag Maajh, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Spurned by Narcissus, the nymph Echo hides in the woods and wastes away with grief until her body is gone and only her voice and bones remain.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Echo is consumed by an unreturned love until nothing of her is left but a voice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Echo is worn away by a love-sickness she cannot escape, until even its outward signs are spent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius describes love as a sore that, if fed, grows inflamed and becomes chronic, a madness that worsens day by day unless it is broken off early.
philosophy.explanation: For Lucretius, erotic love is a wound that festers rather than heals when one keeps nourishing it.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine calls her love ‘a disease with no escape’; Lucretius explains why it has become so.

real_life_example.event_title: Theodore Roosevelt's diary on the day his wife died
real_life_example.event: On 14 February 1884 Theodore Roosevelt's mother died of typhoid fever early in the morning, and his wife, Alice Hathaway Lee Roosevelt, died that afternoon in the same house, two days after giving birth to their daughter. In his pocket diary Roosevelt marked a large X on the page and wrote, The light has gone out of my life. He chose never to speak Alice's name again and did not mention her in his autobiography.
real_life_example.explanation: Roosevelt's single line and his lifelong silence show a grief so deep that it could not be cured and was never again put into words.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of eyes that have wept until no tears remain, leaving behind a sickness with no remedy, and Roosevelt's eight-word entry and later silence suggest that kind of exhausted, incurable sorrow.

tamil:
படலாற்றா பைதல் உழக்கும் கடலாற்றாக்
காமநோய் செய்தஎன் கண்.
transliteration:
Padalaatraa paidhal uzhakkum kadalaatraak
kaamanoi seydha-en kan.
meaning: My eyes brought on a love-sickness bigger than the sea. Now they suffer the pain of not being able to sleep.
elementary: Have you ever been so worried about something that you couldn’t fall asleep, even though you were tired? The lady’s eyes feel that way every night. Her missing-him feeling is so big, bigger than the ocean, that her eyes just can’t close.
university: The couplet sets two ‘cannot’ compounds against each other: paṭal āṟṟā, ‘unable to lie down (sleep)’, and kaṭal āṟṟā, ‘which the sea cannot hold’, so that the eyes are punished by sleeplessness for a love-sickness larger than the ocean. Paital uḻakkum is ‘are tormented by affliction’. Puliyur Kesikan adds that the eyes suffer ‘through this evil deed’, at night, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar stress that the sickness was caused by the eyes and they now cannot sleep. Pope: ‘The eye that wrought me more than sea could hold of woes, / Is suffering pangs that banish all repose.’ No variant readings were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: During the monsoon at Kishkindha, Rama, parted from Sita, cannot rest; the clouds, the rain and the night only sharpen his longing, and he passes the season in sleepless grief.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki depicts Rama’s separation from Sita as a sorrow that keeps him awake through the rainy nights.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama, like the Kural’s heroine, suffers a separation so vast that his eyes find no sleep.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, Rama’s lament in the rainy season (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes a distress so deep that his eyes are held open through the night.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes are held waking in the same way, troubled beyond rest.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob, rebuked for endlessly remembering Joseph, answers that he lays his unbearable grief before God alone.
islam.tie_back: His grief, like the heroine’s, is too large to be contained or put to rest; it can only be poured out.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mine eye is poured out, and ceaseth not, Without any intermission,”
judaism.explanation: The poet of Lamentations describes eyes that weep without pause, day and night.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise know no intermission: they cannot even lie down to sleep.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Which is greater, the tears you have shed while transmigrating & wandering this long, long time — crying & weeping from being joined with what is displeasing, being separated from what is pleasing — or the water in the four great oceans?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his monks that the tears shed over separation from the beloved across countless lives exceed all the oceans.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s love-sickness is likewise more than the sea can hold; the Buddha measures the grief of separation by the same ocean.
buddhism.source: Assu Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 15.3 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Desiring happiness and being submerged in the ocean of delusion, he forms many plans for warding off misery; and for their sake an impassioned man exerts himself.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana pictures the passionate person as sunk in an ocean of delusion, restlessly scheming to escape misery.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is likewise sunk in a sea-sized love-sickness, too restless to sleep.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.105 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My eyes long for the Blessed Vision of Your Darshan; the night passes, but I cannot sleep.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes eyes that thirst for the sight of the Lord and so stay open through the whole night.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the eyes that brought on a love-sickness greater than the sea are now tormented by being unable to sleep; Guru Arjan's eyes likewise long for the Beloved and cannot close all night.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 542, Raag Bihaagraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Eros’s arrow strikes her, Medea lies awake through the night, torn by love for Jason and fear for him, while all the city sleeps around her.
