greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius shows Medea’s new love as a torment that will not let her sleep.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s eyes, Medea’s are kept open by a love too great for her to contain.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza calls human weakness in moderating and restraining the emotions ‘bondage’: a person subject to the emotions is not his own master but is at the mercy of fortune.
philosophy.explanation: On Spinoza’s view, strong passions overpower the mind and leave it unable to rest in its own power.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes are in exactly this bondage: a passion larger than the sea keeps them from sleep.

real_life_example.event_title: Juliette Drouet's fifty years of daily letters to Victor Hugo
real_life_example.place: Paris, France, and the Channel Islands
real_life_example.event: From 1833 until her death in 1883, the actress Juliette Drouet wrote to the writer Victor Hugo every day, producing about 22,000 letters over fifty years. Around 17,000 of them are now held by the Bibliotheque nationale de France and others by institutions such as the University of Leeds. Scholars describe her as Hugo's soulmate, collaborator, first reader and copyist, and her letters as a kind of journal of their relationship.
real_life_example.explanation: Her letters are a record of a love so large that it filled a page or more every day for half a century.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of a love-sickness too great even for the sea to hold, and Drouet's ocean of letters, written day after day for fifty years, gives that size a measurable form.

tamil:
ஓஒ இனிதே எமக்கிந்நோய் செய்தகண்
தாஅம் இதற்பட் டது.
transliteration:
Ohoh inidhae emakkinnoi seydhakan
thaa-am itharpat tadhu.
meaning: Oh, how sweet this is! The eyes that gave me this sickness have now fallen into the same suffering themselves.
elementary: Imagine a friend talked you into jumping into a cold pool, and then they slipped and fell in too. You might shiver and giggle, ‘Ha! Now you know how it feels!’ The lady says that to her eyes: they got her into this sadness, and now they are stuck in it too.
university: The couplet opens with the long exclamation ōo (ஓஒ), an alapeṭai (prosodic lengthening) expressing intense feeling, and closes with the lengthened tāam (தாஅம், ‘they themselves’), both stretched for metre and emphasis. Iṉitē, ‘it is sweet’, is ironic satisfaction: the eyes that ‘made this sickness for us’ (emakku innōy ceyta kaṇ) have ‘fallen into it’ (itaṟpaṭṭatu). Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah specify that the eyes now cannot sleep and weep, while Kalaignar renders the tone as ‘this is a joy to me’. Pope: ‘Oho! how sweet a thing to see! the eye / That wrought this pain, in the same gulf doth lie.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One must deliver himself with the help of his mind, and not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that one’s own faculties can act as one’s friend or as one’s enemy, depending on how they are governed.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine has discovered her eyes to be her enemy, and takes grim pleasure that the enemy now suffers along with her.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.5 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that every action returns upon the one who did it.
christianity.tie_back: The eyes sowed this sickness and now reap it, which is why the heroine calls their suffering ‘sweet’.

islam.quote_or_event: “So let them laugh a little and [then] weep much as recompense for what they used to earn.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says that those who delighted briefly will weep at length as the fitting return for their deeds.
islam.tie_back: The Kural sees the same justice in the eyes: they delighted once, and now they weep as their due.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein; And he that rolleth a stone, it shall return upon him.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that harm one causes tends to come back upon oneself.
judaism.tie_back: The eyes dug the pit of love-sickness and have fallen into it themselves, which the heroine finds fitting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Fools of little wit are enemies unto themselves as they move about doing evil deeds, the fruits of which are bitter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that people who act heedlessly become their own enemies, reaping bitter fruit from their own actions.
buddhism.tie_back: The eyes acted as the heroine’s enemy and now taste the bitter fruit themselves.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Thus the objects of the senses and of the mind cause pain to passionate men, but they never in the least cause any pain to the dispassionate.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that the senses, once passionately attached, bring pain back on the one who indulges them.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes, having been passionate, now feel the pain that passion brings, just as the sutra says.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.100 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, that human body, in which there is no pain of separation from the Lord-take that body and burn it.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad says the pain of separation from the Lord is so precious that a body without it is worth only burning.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine calls it sweet that the eyes which gave her this sickness have fallen into the same suffering; Guru Angad likewise treats the pain of separation as something to be welcomed rather than escaped.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 89, Sri Raag ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Oedipus learns the truth, he blinds himself, saying that his eyes shall no longer see the evils he has suffered and done.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Sophocles’ play, Oedipus turns on his own eyes as the guilty organs and punishes them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The heroine likewise treats her eyes as culprits deserving to suffer, though only in a lover’s hyperbole.
greek_mythology.source: Sophocles, Oedipus the King, lines c. 1268-1274 (messenger’s report) (paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Socrates argues that it is better for a wrongdoer to pay the penalty than to escape it, because just punishment is a cure for the soul.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato’s Socrates, suffering that answers to one’s own wrongdoing is fitting, even good.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s ‘How sweet!’ treats the eyes’ suffering as a just and fitting penalty in exactly this spirit, if with more humour.

real_life_example.event_title: Cleopatra meets Mark Antony at Tarsus
real_life_example.event: In 41 BCE the Roman general Mark Antony summoned Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, to Tarsus to answer charges that she had helped his enemies. According to Plutarch, she sailed up the river Cydnus in a gilded barge with purple sails, and Antony was so taken with her that he returned with her to Alexandria. Their alliance ended in defeat at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE, and both died in Egypt the following year.
real_life_example.explanation: Cleopatra came to Tarsus to win over Antony, and the attachment she created drew her, as well as him, into the same disaster.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural takes grim satisfaction that the eyes which caused the heroine's love-sickness have fallen into the same suffering, much as Cleopatra, who captivated Antony, was caught in the ruin that their love brought on them both.

tamil:
உழந்துழந் துள்நீர் அறுக விழைந்திழைந்து
வேண்டி அவர்க்கண்ட கண்.
transliteration:
Uzhandhuzhan thulneer aruka vizhaindhizhaindhu
vaenti avarkkanda kan.
meaning: My eyes once looked at him with melting, eager longing. Now let them ache and ache until every tear in them is gone.
elementary: Sometimes when we feel very sad, we get a little cross with ourselves too. The lady is so sad that she tells her own eyes, ‘You wanted to look at him so much, so now you can cry until you have no tears left!’ It is her way of showing how much she misses him.
university: The couplet is built on two reduplicated verbs: uḻantu uḻantu, ‘suffering, suffering’, and viḻaintu iḻaintu, ‘desiring, melting with tenderness’, so that the present agony mirrors the past yearning sound for sound. Uḷ nīr aṟuka is an optative, ‘may the water within be cut off’, a mock-curse on the eyes that ‘longed and saw him’ (vēṇṭi avark kaṇṭa kaṇ). Commentators differ on whether the curse is sleeplessness plus tears (Mu. Varadarasanar) or an address directly to the eyes (Kalaignar: ‘O eyes… suffer!’); Puliyur Kesikan reads viḻaintu as part of the past delight. Pope: ‘Aching, aching, let those exhaust their stream, / That melting, melting, that day gazed on him.’ No variants were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Held captive in Ravana’s Ashoka grove, Sita, separated from Rama, weeps continually, grows thin and pale, and longs only to see him again.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki’s Sundara Kanda shows Sita wasted by tears and longing for her absent husband.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita’s endless weeping is what the Kural’s heroine wishes on her eyes: tears until they are spent.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, Hanuman finds Sita in the Ashoka grove (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!”
christianity.explanation: Jeremiah wishes his eyes could become an unending fountain so that he could weep enough for his grief.
christianity.tie_back: Jeremiah and the Kural both speak to the eyes as wells of tears, though Jeremiah longs for more and the heroine for them to run dry.

islam.quote_or_event: “The eyes are shedding tears and the heart is grieved, and we will not say except what pleases our Lord, O Ibrahim! Indeed we are grieved by your separation.”
islam.explanation: At the death of his infant son, the Prophet weeps openly and names the tears of the eyes as the honest sign of the heart’s grief.
islam.tie_back: In both texts the eyes carry the whole weight of grief at separation from a beloved.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For these things I weep; Mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water; Because the comforter is far from me…”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations repeats ‘mine eye, mine eye’ as it pours out tears because the one who could comfort is far away.
judaism.tie_back: The doubled ‘mine eye, mine eye’ echoes the Kural’s doubled uḻantu uḻantu, both for eyes weeping because the beloved comforter is absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ill done is that action of doing which one repents later, and the fruit of which one, weeping, reaps with tears.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada describes an action whose fruit is harvested in tears and regret.
buddhism.tie_back: The eyes’ eager gaze was such an action; the heroine now bids them reap its fruit in tears until none remain.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a man who passionately desires ‘colours,’ be happy while he gets, keeps, uses, loses, and misses (those things). Even when he enjoys them, he is never satisfied.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that the eye’s passion brings misery at every stage, including when the thing desired is lost and missed.
jainism.tie_back: The eyes that once ‘longed and melted’ at the sight of him are now in the ‘missing’ stage the sutra describes, and the heroine says they must bear it.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I cherish and remember that Friend; the eyes of this soul-bride are filled with tears.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak's soul-bride keeps remembering her divine Friend, and her eyes fill with tears as she does.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural wishes that the eyes which once melted with longing as they gazed on him may ache until their tears run dry; Guru Nanak's bride remembers her Beloved with eyes that are full of tears.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1111, Raag Tukhaari, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After the loss of all her children, Niobe weeps until she is turned to stone, and even as a rock on a mountain she goes on shedding tears.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Niobe is the image of grief that drains a person of everything but tears.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wishes such unending weeping on her eyes, though she imagines the tears finally running dry.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato tells of Leontius, who wanted to look at corpses lying by the wall, struggled against the desire, and finally ran to them with his eyes wide open, crying to his eyes, ‘Look, you wretches, take your fill of the fine sight!’
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the story to show that a part of the soul can be angry with its own desires, even speaking to the eyes as separate culprits.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine curses her eyes in the same way, telling them to suffer their fill for the looking they insisted on.

real_life_example.event_title: Rembrandt draws Saskia days after their betrothal
real_life_example.place: Dutch Republic (now the Netherlands); drawing now in Berlin, Germany
real_life_example.event: On 6 June 1633 Rembrandt became engaged to Saskia van Uylenburgh, the cousin of his business partner Hendrick Uylenburgh. On 8 June he made a silverpoint drawing of her, inscribed in Dutch that it was drawn of his wife when she was 21 years old, on the third day after their betrothal; it is now in the Kupferstichkabinett in Berlin. After three children who did not survive infancy, Saskia gave birth to their son Titus, and Rembrandt's later decline in productivity followed her death.
real_life_example.explanation: The tender drawing preserves the moment when Rembrandt gazed on his bride-to-be with delight, before the losses that later came to the marriage.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of eyes that once gazed on the beloved with melting, eager longing and must now ache, and Rembrandt's betrothal drawing is a record of such a loving gaze that later turned to grief.

tamil:
பேணாது பெட்டார் உளர்மன்னோ மற்றவர்க்
காணாது அமைவில கண்.
transliteration:
Paenaadhu pettaar ularmanno matravark
kaanaadhu amaivila kan.
meaning: There is someone who wanted me but did not truly care for me. And yet my eyes cannot rest without seeing him.
elementary: Have you ever had a friend who said they liked you but didn’t really act like it, and still you kept looking for them on the playground? The lady feels like that. She knows he isn’t caring for her the way he should, but her eyes still keep searching for him.
university: Pēṇātu peṭṭār, ‘one who desired (me) without cherishing (me)’, sets peṭṭal (to desire, to love) against pēṇutal (to care for, to tend); uḷar maṉṉō, ‘there is indeed such a one’, carries a sigh of reproach. Avark kāṇātu amaivila kaṇ: ‘without seeing him, the eyes do not settle’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss the first line as ‘loved in word only, not in heart’, and Pope’s prose follows this: ‘He is indeed here who loved me with his lips but not with his heart but mine eyes suffer from not seeing him’, while his verse reads ‘Who loved me once, unloving now doth here remain’. Commentators thus differ on whether the husband is physically near but emotionally absent or simply away; the eyes’ restlessness is the same either way. No variants were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Radha, hurt that Krishna has gone off to sport with other cowherd women, still cannot stop longing for him and sends her friend to find him.
hinduism.explanation: Radha is wounded by Krishna’s neglect, yet her longing to see him only grows.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Radha knows her beloved has not cared for her as he should, but she cannot rest without seeing him.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, early cantos (Radha’s jealousy and longing) (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song of Songs searches through the night for her beloved and cannot find him.
christianity.tie_back: Her restless seeking is exactly the Kural’s eyes that ‘cannot rest without seeing him’.

islam.quote_or_event: “So We restored him to his mother that she might be content and not grieve and that she would know that the promise of Allah is true.”
islam.explanation: Moses is returned to his mother; the Arabic phrase rendered ‘be content’ is literally that ‘her eye might be cooled’, i.e. at rest, by seeing him.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes have no such rest: only seeing the beloved could ‘cool’ them.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; But my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved withdraws without explanation, and the woman goes out searching and calling though he does not answer.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved seems not to care, yet she cannot stop seeking to see him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada names ‘not seeing the beloved’ as one of the two great sources of pain.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine lives exactly this pain: her eyes cannot rest because they do not see the one they love.

jainism.quote_or_event: Arishtanemi (Neminatha) abandons his bride Rajimati on their wedding day to become a monk; she, though forsaken, sets her heart on following him, and later renounces the world herself.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana tells how Rajimati, left by the groom she loved, still turns her whole life toward him.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Rajimati is loved and yet left uncared for, and still cannot turn her eyes from him.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (Rathanemi) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My mind longs for the Blessed Vision of the Guru's Darshan. It cries out like the thirsty song-bird. My thirst is not quenched, and I can find no peace, without the Blessed Vision of the Beloved Saint.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan compares himself to the rain-bird (chatrik) crying for water: without the sight of his Beloved Guru, his thirst is never quenched and he has no peace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her eyes cannot rest without seeing him even though he does not truly care for her; Guru Arjan likewise says he finds no peace at all without the sight of the beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Clytie, abandoned by the Sun god Helios for another, sits on the bare ground for days without food, gazing only at him as he crosses the sky, until she turns into a flower that always faces the sun.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Clytie loves a god who no longer cares for her, yet her eyes never leave him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She is the Kural’s heroine exactly: loved and then neglected, with eyes that cannot rest unless they see him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that friendships based on pleasure or usefulness are easily dissolved, since when one party no longer finds the other pleasant or useful, he ceases to love.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, love that is not grounded in care for the other person for their own sake does not last.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s husband ‘loved without caring’, the kind of love Aristotle says fades, while her own eyes go on loving.

real_life_example.event_title: Izumi Shikibu asks for one last meeting
real_life_example.event: Izumi Shikibu, one of the leading women poets of the Heian court, wrote a poem addressed to her beloved when she believed her life was drawing to a close. In it she asks for just one more meeting with him, so that she may carry its memory with her beyond this world. The poem was later chosen as number 56 of the Hyakunin Isshu anthology.
real_life_example.explanation: Her poem became one of Japan's best-known expressions of the simple, overwhelming need to see the beloved once more.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the heroine's eyes cannot rest without seeing him, and Izumi Shikibu's plea for a single last meeting shows that same longing to see the beloved again.

tamil:
வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின்துஞ்சா ஆயிடை
ஆரஞர் உற்றன கண்.
transliteration:
Vaaraakkaal thunjaa varindhunjaa aayidai
aaranjar utrana kan.
meaning: When he does not come, my eyes cannot sleep, and when he comes, they still cannot sleep. Either way, they suffer terrible pain.
elementary: Imagine waiting up for someone you love to come home: you can’t sleep because you’re waiting. Then they come, and you still can’t sleep because you’re so happy, and maybe worried they’ll leave again. The lady’s eyes get no rest either way.
university: The couplet is a neat antithesis: vārākkāl tuñcā, ‘when he does not come, they do not sleep’, and varin tuñcā, ‘if he comes, they do not sleep’; āyiṭai, ‘between these two’, the eyes uṟṟaṉa ār añar, ‘have met with grievous pain’. Commentators supply the reasons: in absence the eyes watch for his coming, and in presence they fear his departure (Solomon Pappaiah, Puliyur Kesikan: pirivu añci, ‘dreading separation’). Kalaignar generalises it to ‘such suffering can only belong to lovers’ eyes’. Pope: ‘When he comes not, all slumber flies; no sleep when he is there; / Thus every way my eyes have troubles hard to bear.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gopi Gita, the cowherd women tell Krishna that when he goes to the forest by day, even a moment without seeing him feels like an age, and when they do see his face, they curse the creator who made eyelids that blink and interrupt their gaze.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis find no rest either in Krishna’s absence or in his presence: absence is an age, and presence is spoiled by the blink of an eye.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s double bind exactly: the eyes suffer when he does not come and are restless even when he does.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh…”
christianity.explanation: The bride lies down but cannot truly rest, because her heart is always listening for the beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes know the same half-sleep: they cannot let go of watchfulness for him, whether he is absent or near.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s romance, Majnun, separated from Layla, wanders the desert sleepless with longing, and even when he is allowed near her he cannot be at peace, so consuming is his love.
islam.explanation: Majnun’s love leaves him no rest, whether apart from Layla or close to her.
islam.tie_back: His restlessness on both sides of meeting mirrors the Kural’s eyes that sleep neither when the beloved stays away nor when he comes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thus I was: in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep fled from mine eyes.”
judaism.explanation: Jacob reminds Laban of his years of service, during which he gave up sleep; he had first served seven years out of love for Rachel.
judaism.tie_back: Jacob’s eyes, like the Kural’s, lost their sleep in a life shaped by love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary. Long is worldly existence to fools who know not the Sublime Truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada begins its chapter on the fool with the image of the sleepless night that never seems to end.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes know that long night, whether her husband is away or present.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How, then, can a man who is devoted to ‘colours,’ ever derive any happiness from anything? He suffers pain at the time of their enjoyment to procure which he had suffered misery.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana says that the one attached to what the eye loves suffers both while seeking it and while enjoying it.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s double bind in Jain terms: pain when he is absent, and pain still when he is present.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The pain of separation has grown shy, for I have obtained the Blessed Vision of His Darshan; His Ambrosial Glance of Grace has filled me with bliss.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that once the soul-bride has seen her Lord, the pain of separation slinks away and His glance fills her with bliss.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's eyes find no sleep either when he is away or when he comes, because even his presence brings fear of parting; in Gurbani, by contrast, the Beloved's arrival ends the pain of separation and brings rest.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 460, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Throughout the Odyssey, Penelope weeps for her absent husband night after night until Athena sheds sleep on her eyelids; and even after Odysseus returns, the couple stay awake through the night of their reunion talking.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s Penelope cannot sleep for grief in Odysseus’s absence, and the night of his return is also a night without sleep.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Her sleepless nights in both absence and presence give the Kural’s double bind a gentler, happier mirror.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates describes the lover’s soul, parted from the beloved, as maddened and in pain, unable to sleep by night or stay still by day, and running to wherever it hopes to see the beautiful one.
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedrus, the absence of the beloved leaves the soul sleepless and restless, relieved only by seeing him.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes suffer the same sleeplessness when he is away.

real_life_example.event_title: Franz Kafka's engagements to Felice Bauer
real_life_example.place: Prague (now Czech Republic) and Berlin, Germany
real_life_example.event: Franz Kafka met Felice Bauer at the home of his friend Max Brod in Prague on 13 August 1912. Over the next five years he sent her more than five hundred letters and postcards, and the two became engaged twice, but each engagement was broken off, the second and last time in December 1917. Felice later married another man and, years afterwards, gave Kafka's letters to Schocken publishers, who published them in the 1960s.
real_life_example.explanation: Kafka's letters show a man who longed for Felice when they were apart and drew back when marriage came close, so that neither distance nor nearness gave him peace.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the eyes cannot sleep when the beloved is away, nor when he comes, and suffer in between, which describes the restless back-and-forth of Kafka's two engagements.

tamil:
மறைபெறல் ஊரார்க்கு அரிதன்றால் எம்போல்
அறைபறை கண்ணார் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Maraiperal ooraarkku aridhandraal empoal
araiparai kannaar agaththu.
meaning: Townspeople easily learn the secret in the hearts of women like me, because our eyes announce it like a beaten drum.
elementary: Have you ever tried to keep a secret, but your face gave it away? Maybe you were trying not to smile about a surprise, and everyone could tell! The lady says her red, teary eyes are like a loud drum telling the whole town, ‘She misses him!’
university: Maṟai (மறை) is ‘secret’ and aṟai paṟai (அறைபறை) ‘a drum that is beaten’, the town crier’s drum used for public proclamations; kaṇṇār akattu, ‘in the hearts of those whose eyes (are such drums)’. The couplet closes the chapter by turning from the eyes’ private suffering to their public betrayal: whatever the heroine hides, her tear-stained eyes broadcast it. It also links back to chapter 115 (alar, village gossip). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read the drum as the weeping that reveals the inner state; Pope: ‘It is not hard for all the town the knowledge to obtain, / When eyes, as mine, like beaten tambours, make the mystery plain.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s play, Shakuntala tries to hide her love for King Dushyanta, but her friends Anasuya and Priyamvada read her pallor, sighs and fevered looks and gently draw the secret out of her.
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala’s body and eyes betray the love she is too modest to speak.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she cannot keep her love secret, because her eyes and face announce it to those around her.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known and come abroad.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says that what is hidden will in time come into the open.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine’s secret is ‘made manifest’ by her own eyes, as surely as if it were proclaimed.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they have recognized of the truth.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an notes that the tears in people’s eyes openly show what has moved their hearts.
islam.tie_back: In both texts the eyes make the inner state visible to everyone who looks.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance; But by sorrow of heart the spirit is broken.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that the state of the heart shows plainly in the face.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle to the eyes: the heart’s sorrow drums itself out through them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Ummadanti Jataka, a king catches one glimpse of the beautiful Ummadanti and is so overcome with longing that he can no longer hide it; his minister sees his condition and learns its cause.
buddhism.explanation: The king’s love-sickness shows itself so plainly that those around him discover what he would keep hidden.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the lover’s secret is broadcast by the state of his body and eyes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anger, pride, deceit, greed; disgust, aversion to self-control and delight in sensual things; mirth, fear, sorrow, carnal desire for women, men, or both; all these manifold passions arise in him who is attached to pleasures…”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana lists the many emotions, sorrow among them, that well up in one who is attached through the senses.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s sorrow is such an emotion, and it wells up so strongly that it shows in her eyes for all to see.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.102-103 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Just as the beat of the drum is heard on all four sides (its sound cannot be hidden) ... Similarly, the Guru-oriented Sikh whose heart is enlightened by the love of the Lord and His meditation, cannot remain hidden. His silence gives him away.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas says that love for the Lord cannot be hidden any more than a beaten drum can, and that even the lover's silence reveals it. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the town easily learns the secret of women whose eyes proclaim it like a beaten drum; Bhai Gurdas uses the same image of a drum heard on every side for love that cannot be concealed.
sikhism.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 411, English translation as given in the BaniDB database

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hippolytus, Phaedra wastes away, refusing food and hiding her love for her stepson, but the chorus and her nurse can see that she is sick at heart, and the nurse finally draws the secret out of her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaedra’s concealed love is betrayed by her visible decline.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As the Kural says, a secret love cannot stay hidden when the body and eyes announce it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld observes that no disguise can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.
philosophy.explanation: The moralist holds that real love inevitably shows itself, whatever one does to conceal it.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s drum-like eyes prove his maxim: her love cannot be hidden from the town.
philosophy.source: François de La Rochefoucauld, Maxims, no. 70 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Princess Margaret's gesture at the coronation reveals her romance
real_life_example.event: At the coronation of her sister, Queen Elizabeth II, on 2 June 1953, Princess Margaret was seen brushing a piece of lint from the uniform jacket of Group Captain Peter Townsend, her late father's former equerry. A journalist noticed the moment, and it set off public speculation about their relationship. Because Townsend was divorced, the match was opposed, and in 1955 Margaret issued a statement that she would not marry him.
real_life_example.explanation: One small, unguarded gesture in front of the world's cameras revealed a private love that the palace had kept quiet.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the secret in a lover's heart is no secret to the town when her own eyes beat it out like a drum, and Margaret's single gesture at the coronation announced her hidden love to everyone watching.

tamil:
நயந்தவர்க்கு நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன் பசந்தவென்
பண்பியார்க்கு உரைக்கோ பிற.
transliteration:
nayandhavarkku nalkaamai naerndhaen pasandhaven
panpiyaarkku uraikko pira
meaning: I myself agreed to let my loving husband go away. Now that my body has turned pale with longing, who else can I complain to?
elementary: Imagine you told your best friend, ‘It’s okay, go on the trip without me,’ and then you missed them so much you felt sick. You can’t really complain to anyone, because you said yes! The wife in this couplet feels exactly that way.
university: Chapter 119 of the karpiyal (married love) section turns on pasalai or pasappu (பசலை / பசப்பு), the sallow, pallid tint that classical Tamil poetics treats as the visible sign of a wife’s grief in separation; both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net title the chapter பசப்புறு பருவரல் (pasappuṟu paruvaral, ‘the distress of having become pallid’), while this edition’s chapter list spells it பசப்பறு. In this opening couplet the heroine admits that she nērntēn (நேர்ந்தேன், ‘consented’) to nalkāmai (நல்காமை, literally ‘not showing grace’, which the modern commentators Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss as the husband’s separation); having agreed, she has forfeited the right to complain, hence yārkku uraikkō piṟa, ‘to whom else shall I tell it?’. In the traditional commentary associated with Parimelazhagar the chapter is voiced by the heroine to her confidante (tōḻi), and the irony of complaining while saying one cannot complain is the point. Pope renders: ‘I willed my lover absent should remain; / Of pining’s sickly hue to whom shall I complain?’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Dushyanta leaves the hermitage to return to his capital, Shakuntala, who has accepted his going, sits so lost in thoughts of him that she fails even to notice the sage Durvasas at the door, and her friends must keep her sorrow to themselves.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa shows a young wife who agreed to her husband’s departure and is then consumed by an absence she cannot openly lament.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Shakuntala has consented to the parting and is left with a private grief she has no one to tell.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride, separated from her beloved, has no way to reach him and must ask others to carry word of her love-sickness.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine asks the same question in reverse: she is sick with love and has no one she can rightly tell.

islam.quote_or_event: “I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allāh, and I know from Allāh that which you do not know.”
islam.explanation: Jacob, grieving for the absent Joseph and rebuked by his sons for his endless sorrow, says he will bring his complaint to God alone.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also has no human listener for her grief; Jacob’s answer is that the only fitting hearer is God.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The heart knoweth its own bitterness; And with its joy no stranger can intermeddle.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that the deepest sorrows of the heart are its own and cannot really be shared with another.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s pallor is exactly such a bitterness known only to her own heart, with no one to whom she can hand it over.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “So don’t make anything dear, for it’s dreadful to be far from what’s dear.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that holding someone dear makes distance from them a source of dread and pain.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine has discovered just this: being far from the one she loves has turned her body pale with grief.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Gina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, betrothed to Arishtanemi, learns that he has turned away from the wedding to become a monk, and her joy vanishes.
jainism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a woman is left to bear the sorrow of a beloved’s departure, though Rajimati soon turns it into her own renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “By the actions we have committed, we are separated from You. Please show Your Mercy, and unite us with Yourself, Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Barah Maha (the song of the twelve months), Guru Arjan has the separated soul-bride admit that her separation comes from her own deeds, so she can only ask the Lord for mercy and reunion.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife admits she herself agreed to her husband's going and so has no one to complain to; the soul-bride in Gurbani likewise owns that the separation is her own doing and turns only to the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 133, Raag Maajh, Barah Maha, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope recalls that when Odysseus set out for Troy he took her by the wrist, entrusted the household to her care and told her what to do if he did not return; she accepted, and for twenty years she weeps for him in private while the suitors crowd her hall.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope agreed to her husband’s going and is left to grieve with no one in the house she can trust with her sorrow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife, Penelope consented to the parting and now pines with no proper listener.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that people in grief are comforted when friends share their sorrow, as if the burden were lightened by being divided.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, the presence of a sympathetic friend is one of the main reliefs of sorrow.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine lacks exactly that relief: she has no one to share her grief with, because she agreed to its cause.

real_life_example.event_title: Eva Nansen at home while the Fram drifts through the Arctic
real_life_example.event: The singer Eva Sars married the polar explorer Fridtjof Nansen on 6 September 1889, and he was often away on expeditions. In June 1893 Nansen sailed north on the Fram, which was frozen into the Arctic ice and drifted for about three years before returning to Christiania in September 1896. During his absences Eva continued to sing at concerts and kept a warm home for the family.
real_life_example.explanation: Eva Nansen's life shows the long, quiet side of a famous expedition: the spouse who stays behind for years while the journey goes on.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife says she herself let her husband go and so has no one else to blame for her pining, and Eva Nansen lived through three years of a separation that came with marrying an explorer.

tamil:
அவர்தந்தார் என்னும் தகையால் இவர்தந்தென்
மேனிமேல் ஊரும் பசப்பு.
transliteration:
avardhandhaar ennum thakaiyaal ivardhandhaen
maenimael oorum pasappu
meaning: Proud that he gave it to me, this paleness climbs all over my body and spreads as if it owned it.
elementary: Think of a sticker your favourite person gave you: you might put it everywhere, proud of it because of who gave it. The wife says the pale colour on her skin acts like that sticker. It spreads all over her, proud because her husband ‘gave’ it to her by going away.
university: The heroine personifies pasappu (பசப்பு) as a proud guest: avar tantār ennum takaiyāl, ‘with the dignity of “he gave it”’, it ivarntu (இவர்ந்து, ‘mounting, climbing’) and ūrum (ஊரும், ‘creeps, spreads, rides’) over her mēni (மேனி, body, complexion). Takai here is ‘worth, pride’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both render the pallor as spreading ‘with pride’ (பெருமிதம்) because the lover caused it. Pope’s rendering takes ūrum in the sense of riding: ‘“He gave”: this sickly hue thus proudly speaks, / Then climbs, and all my frame its chariot makes.’ The conceit, that even the affliction is precious because it comes from him, is characteristic of the karpiyal chapters and of the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar, in which the wife cannot fully resent what her husband’s absence has given her. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Meghaduta the exiled yaksha pictures his wife at home, wasted and pale with separation, lying on one side of her bed like the last thin crescent of the moon, her beauty itself changed by her grief for him.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa makes the wife’s altered, pallid body the very sign and record of her husband’s absence.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same: the pallor spreading over her is his gift, the mark his absence has left on her.

christianity.quote_or_event: “From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Paul treats the scars he has suffered for Christ as marks of belonging that he carries with pride.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine’s pallor is likewise a bodily mark she wears proudly because it comes from the one she loves.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s long grief for his absent son visibly changes his body, whitening his eyes.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, separation from a beloved writes itself on the body as a change of colour.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Set me as a seal upon thy heart, As a seal upon thine arm; For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved asks to be pressed onto the lover’s heart and arm like a seal, a mark that shows whose they are.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s pallor is that kind of seal: a mark on her body that proclaims whose love caused it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From what’s dear is born grief, from what’s dear is born fear. For one freed from what’s dear there’s no grief — so how fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief back to its source in holding someone dear.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine says her pallor was ‘given by him’; the Dhammapada agrees that the grief is born from the dear one, though it draws the opposite lesson.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that inner and outer changes come not from objects or other people but from one’s own attachment to them.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine credits her lover with ‘giving’ her pallor; the Jain view would locate the cause in her own attachment, an honest contrast to the Kural’s conceit.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.101 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Your actions seem so sweet to me.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that whatever the Lord does, including what brings pain, tastes sweet to the devotee, because it comes from Him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's pallor spreads proudly over her body because it was given by her husband; Gurbani likewise finds even hardship sweet because the Beloved sent it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho describes what happens to her when she sees the beloved: her tongue breaks, a thin fire runs under her skin, her eyes see nothing, sweat pours down, trembling seizes her, and she becomes greener than grass, seeming to herself little short of dying.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this famous poem love shows itself as a physical change of colour, a pallor or greenness that takes over the whole body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s pasappu that ‘climbs over my body’ is the same idea: love’s pallor spreading across the lover’s frame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius warns that lovers waste their strength and are worn out with toil, their bodies and fortunes spent while they live at another’s beck and call.
philosophy.explanation: The Epicurean poet treats love’s physical toll on the lover as a reason for caution.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s pallor is that physical toll, but where Lucretius sees only harm, the heroine sees a gift from her husband.

real_life_example.event_title: Ramesses II honours Queen Nefertari in temple and tomb
real_life_example.place: Abu Simbel and the Valley of the Queens, Egypt
real_life_example.event: Nefertari was the first wife and favourite queen of the pharaoh Ramesses II. Ramesses had her likeness carved on temple walls and statues long after he had taken other wives, and at Abu Simbel a temple was dedicated to the goddess Hathor and to Nefertari. Her tomb in the Valley of the Queens was decorated with paintings regarded as masterpieces of the age.
real_life_example.explanation: Nefertari's monuments show a queen whose standing came from the honour her husband publicly gave her.
real_life_example.tie_back: In the kural the pallor spreads proudly over the wife's body because 'he gave it', and Nefertari's image was spread across Egypt's monuments with the pride of something her husband had bestowed.

tamil:
சாயலும் நாணும் அவர்கொண்டார் கைம்மாறா
நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து.
transliteration:
saayalum naanum avarkondaar kaimmaaraa
noayum pasalaiyum thandhu
meaning: He took away my beauty and my modesty. In return, he gave me love-sickness and this paleness.
elementary: Imagine trading your shiny new toy for a broken one and a bad cold. Not a fair swap! The wife jokes sadly that her husband made a swap like that: he took her bright looks and her shyness, and left her with sadness and a pale face.
university: The couplet is built on the language of exchange: kaimmāṟā (கைம்மாறா, ‘as a return, in exchange’) the husband took (koṇṭār) her sāyal (சாயல், grace, soft beauty) and nāṇ (நாண், modesty, the sense of shame proper to a woman in Sangam poetics) and gave (tantu) nōy (நோய், the disease of love) and pasalai (பசலை). The loss of nāṇ ties back to chapter 114 (நாணுத் துறவுரைத்தல், ‘declaring the abandonment of modesty’). Solomon Pappaiah reads the exchange as happening at the very moment of parting; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep the bare trade. Pope renders: ‘Of comeliness and shame he me bereft, / While pain and sickly hue, in recompense, he left.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda Radha’s companion tells Krishna how Radha, pining for him, has wasted away: her ornaments feel like burdens, her beauty fades and she languishes in the bower thinking only of him.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva describes separation stripping the beloved of her loveliness and leaving only longing.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine names the same exchange: her beauty taken, love-sickness left in its place.

christianity.quote_or_event: “To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness …”
christianity.explanation: The prophet promises a divine exchange in which mourners receive beauty in place of ashes.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine describes the exact reverse trade: her beauty taken, sorrow and pallor given back.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s Layla and Majnun, Layla, kept apart from Majnun, slowly loses her bloom; the poet describes her as fading and wasting in secret, hiding her grief from those around her until it consumes her.
islam.explanation: Separation in the great Persian romance takes the beloved’s beauty and leaves only hidden suffering.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, love’s parting has traded away beauty for illness and pallor.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Call me not Naomi, call me Marah; for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me. I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me back home empty.”
judaism.explanation: Naomi (‘pleasant’) says her very name no longer fits: her life has exchanged sweetness for bitterness.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also describes an exchange that has left her changed: grace and modesty gone, pallor and sorrow in their place.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The former courtesan Ambapali, now a nun, describes how her once-celebrated beauty has changed with time: her black hair has turned like hemp bark, her eyes and skin have lost their lustre, and she concludes that the words of the Truth-speaker hold true.
buddhism.explanation: Ambapali’s verses watch beauty being taken away and replaced by its opposite.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also inventories lost beauty, though she blames her husband’s absence, while Ambapali sees the impermanence of all forms.

jainism.quote_or_event: The emperor Sanatkumara, famous for his beauty, invited two gods who had praised it to see him in full splendour at court; they told him that in that short time his body had already been taken over by disease, and on seeing it was so he renounced the world.
jainism.explanation: Jain narrative uses Sanatkumara to show how quickly beauty can be taken and illness given in its place.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences the same swift exchange, her beauty for sickness, though she blames her husband’s absence rather than impermanence.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 4 (life of Sanatkumara) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So many endure distress, deprivation and constant abuse. Even these are Your Gifts, O Great Giver!”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib Guru Nanak counts even suffering and want among the gifts of the Giver, since they too come from His hand and can teach the soul.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her husband took her beauty and modesty and gave her love-sickness and pallor in exchange; Guru Nanak likewise calls pain and loss gifts of the Beloved Giver.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib (pauri 25), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo, spurned by Narcissus, hides in the woods; her love clings to her and grows with grief, sleepless care wastes her body, her skin shrinks and the bloom of her body vanishes into the air until only her voice and bones remain.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows unrequited, separated love literally consuming a lover’s beauty and body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echo’s fate dramatises the Kural’s complaint: love has taken her beauty and left only sickness and wasting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Diotima’s account, Eros, the child of Poverty and Resource, is not delicate and beautiful as people think but always poor, hard and squalid, barefoot and homeless, sharing his mother’s neediness.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s Symposium portrays love itself as a state of lack rather than of beauty.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds the same: love has left her poorer, stripped of beauty and modesty.

real_life_example.event_title: Sappho describes the bodily symptoms of love
real_life_example.event: The Greek lyric poet Sappho of Lesbos (c. 620-570 BCE) wrote a famous poem, often numbered fragment 31, in which the speaker watches the person she loves sitting with someone else. The poem lists what love does to her body: her voice fails, a thin fire runs under her skin, her ears roar, she sweats and trembles, and she turns the colour of dried grass. Only about 650 lines of Sappho's poetry survive.
real_life_example.explanation: The poem is the oldest well-known description in Western literature of love as a bodily illness that changes the lover's colour.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says love took her beauty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange, and Sappho, centuries earlier and far away, recorded the same pale, fevered body that love leaves behind.

tamil:
உள்ளுவன் மன்யான் உரைப்பது அவர்திறமால்
கள்ளம் பிறவோ பசப்பு.
transliteration:
ulluvan manyaan uraippadhu avardhiramaal
kallam piravo pasappu
meaning: I think only of him and speak only of his goodness, yet the paleness has come anyway. Isn't that a trick?
elementary: Imagine you did all your homework and studied hard, and still got a bad mark. You’d say, ‘That’s not fair, I did everything right!’ The wife says the same: she thinks about her husband all day and only says good things about him, yet the sad pale colour still came. It feels like a trick.
university: The heroine protests that she has kept faith in thought and speech: uḷḷuvan maṉ yāṉ (உள்ளுவன் மன் யான், ‘I do indeed think of him’), uraippatu avar tiṟam (உரைப்பது அவர் திறம், ‘what I speak is his worth’), so the pallor must be kaḷḷam (கள்ளம், ‘deceit, theft’) or come by some other way (piṟavō). The implied logic, made explicit by the commentators, is that constant remembrance should keep the absent one ‘present’, so the pallor of separation has no right to appear. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah render kaḷḷam as vañcaṉai/vañcakam (treachery); Kalaignar instead asks how the pallor came ‘without my knowing or by some other path’. Pope: ‘I meditate his words, his worth is theme of all I say, / This sickly hue is false that would my trust betray.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Uddhava brings Krishna’s message to Vraja, the gopis can speak of nothing but Krishna’s deeds and qualities, remembering every pastime with him, and yet their constant remembrance only deepens the grief of his absence.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata’s gopis show a love that lives on unceasing remembrance and praise of the absent beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also thinks and speaks only of her husband’s virtues, and is still overtaken by the pallor of separation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I remembered God, and was troubled: I complained, and my spirit was overwhelmed. Selah.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist finds that remembering the one he longs for brings not comfort but trouble.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine likewise remembers her beloved constantly and is surprised that remembrance does not keep sorrow away.

islam.quote_or_event: “They said, ‘By Allāh, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s sons warn him that his unceasing remembrance of the absent Joseph is wasting his body.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also never stops remembering her beloved, and that very remembrance has not spared her body from wasting pallor.

judaism.quote_or_event: “His mouth is most sweet; Yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.”
judaism.explanation: Separated from him and asked what makes him special, the bride answers with a long praise of her beloved’s every quality.
judaism.tie_back: Like the bride, the Kural’s heroine says that all she speaks of is her absent husband’s excellence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever a monk keeps pursuing with his thinking & pondering, that becomes the inclination of his awareness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that whatever the mind dwells on repeatedly shapes the whole bent of a person.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine dwells on her husband all day, and the Buddhist view would say that this very dwelling bends her toward the grief she complains of.
buddhism.source: Dvedhavitakka Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 19 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: Among the forms of arta-dhyana (sorrowful, afflicted meditation) the Tattvartha Sutra lists the mind’s repeated dwelling on how to regain something agreeable from which one has been separated.
jainism.explanation: Jain psychology names constant longing for a lost beloved object as a kind of painful concentration that binds karma.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s ceaseless thinking about her absent husband is exactly this ‘afflicted meditation’, and the Jain view would see her pallor as its fruit rather than a trick.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.31 (on arta-dhyana) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I sing His Glories, I describe His Glories, I speak of His Glories, O my mother.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das gives the voice of a soul-bride who fills her speech with the virtues of her Beloved, talking of nothing else.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife protests that she thinks only of him and speaks only of his goodness, yet the pallor came anyway; the Sikh soul-bride likewise speaks only of the Beloved's virtues, though in Gurbani this praise is the way to union rather than something the pallor cheats.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 40, Sri Raag, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: While her husband Ceyx is away at sea, Alcyone counts the nights, prays daily to Juno for his safe return and thinks of nothing but him, unaware that he has already drowned.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Alcyone keeps faith through constant thought and prayer for an absent husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Alcyone, the Kural’s heroine thinks only of her absent husband, and still sorrow finds its way to her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines longing (desiderium) as the desire to possess something that is kept alive by remembering it, while the remembrance of other things excludes its existence.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, remembering an absent beloved breeds not satisfaction but a sorrowful longing.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains the heroine’s puzzle: her constant remembrance of him is precisely what feeds the longing that turns her pale.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Definitions of the Affects 32 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Queen Artemisia builds the Mausoleum for King Mausolus
real_life_example.event: Artemisia II was the sister and wife of King Mausolus of Caria, and after his death around 353 BCE she ruled alone for about three years. She built for him at Halicarnassus the great tomb called the Mausoleum, which was counted among the Seven Wonders of the World. Artemisia died before it was completed and was buried there with her husband; later the Romans called any grand tomb a mausoleum after it.
real_life_example.explanation: Artemisia devoted her short reign to a monument that kept her husband's name before the world, which it still does in the word mausoleum.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife says she thinks only of her husband and speaks only of his worth, and Artemisia turned her whole reign into a monument to her husband's name.

tamil:
உவக்காண்எம் காதலர் செல்வார் இவக்காண்என்
மேனி பசப்பூர் வது.
transliteration:
uvakkaan-em kaadhalar selvaar ivakkaan-en
maeni pasappoor vadhu
meaning: Look there, my lover is walking away. And look here, the paleness is already spreading over my body.
elementary: Picture an ice cream on a hot day: the moment you take it out of the freezer, it starts to melt. The wife says that the moment her husband started walking away, before he was even out of sight, her face started going pale.
university: The couplet’s force lies in two deictic phrases: uvakkāṇ (உவக்காண், ‘see, over there’, using the mid-distance demonstrative u-) and ivakkāṇ (இவக்காண், ‘see, right here’), setting the departing husband and the arriving pallor side by side as simultaneous events; pasappu ūrvatu (பசப்பு ஊர்வது) is ‘the creeping of pallor’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan keep the present tense (‘there he goes; here it spreads’), whereas Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a memory of how, even in earlier partings, the pallor came the instant he left, so that the present absence must be worse. Pope’s version, ‘My lover there went forth to roam; / This pallor of my frame usurps his place at home’, adds the idea of the pallor taking his place. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Akrura takes Krishna away to Mathura, the gopis of Vraja stand watching his chariot as it goes, gazing after it until the banner and even the dust it raised can no longer be seen, and are left stricken and lamenting.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata dwells on the exact moment of the beloved’s departure and the grief that begins as he recedes from sight.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural catches the same instant: ‘there he goes’ and, at once, ‘here comes the pallor’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.”
christianity.explanation: The disciples watch their beloved master depart before their eyes until he is hidden from them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘look there, he goes’ freezes the same moment of watching the loved one leave.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi opens the Masnavi with the reed-flute, which complains of separation and says that ever since it was cut from the reed-bed its lament has made men and women weep.
islam.explanation: For the Sufi poet, the moment of being cut off from the beloved source is where all longing and lament begins.
islam.tie_back: The Kural places the onset of the pallor at that same moment of severance, as the beloved walks away.
islam.source: Rumi, Masnavi I.1-2 (paraphrase of R.A. Nicholson’s translation)

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; But my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The bride finds her beloved gone and at once her soul fails within her.
judaism.tie_back: In both texts the beloved’s going and the lover’s collapse happen in the same breath.

buddhism.quote_or_event: On his wedding day the Buddha’s half-brother Nanda follows the Buddha to the monastery carrying his bowl, while his bride Janapada Kalyani calls after him to come back quickly; he is ordained and afterwards pines for her.
buddhism.explanation: The canonical story of Nanda captures a bride watching her groom walk away on the very day of their union.
buddhism.tie_back: The scene is the Kural’s ‘there he goes’ seen from the bride’s doorway, though the Buddhist story follows the monk rather than her grief.
buddhism.source: Nanda Sutta, Udana 3.2, and Dhammapada commentary on verses 13-14 (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: Riding in his wedding procession to marry Rajimati, Arishtanemi hears the cries of animals penned for the wedding feast, gives his ornaments to his charioteer and turns away to renounce the world, leaving the bride whose wedding was about to begin.
jainism.explanation: In the Jain account the groom turns back at the very threshold of marriage out of compassion for living beings.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati’s sorrow begins the moment her bridegroom turns away, the same instant the Kural captures.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.13-23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If her Husband Lord does not return home, how can the soul-bride find peace? Her body is wasting away with the sorrow of separation.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Barah Maha in Raag Tukhaari, Guru Nanak describes the soul-bride whose body visibly wastes away while her Husband Lord stays away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife watches her husband walk off and sees the pallor creep over her body at once; Guru Nanak likewise shows the body of the separated bride giving way the moment the Beloved is absent.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1108, Raag Tukhaari, Barah Maha, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides Laodamia writes to Protesilaus that as his ship sailed out of Aulis she watched it while she could, and when it vanished she fell senseless and turned pale, lifeless as the dead.
greek_mythology.explanation: Laodamia describes her body failing and paling at the very moment her husband’s ship disappeared.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Her letter is almost the Kural verbatim in narrative form: there goes the husband, here comes the pallor.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato describes the lover’s soul as warmed and growing its wings while the beloved is present, but when they are parted the passages dry up and close, and the soul is stung all over and in anguish until it sees the beloved again.
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedrus the lover’s pain begins as soon as the beloved is absent, as an almost physical change.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural records the same immediacy: absence begins and the bodily change, the pallor, begins with it.

real_life_example.event_title: Ovid's last night in Rome before exile
real_life_example.event: In 8 CE the emperor Augustus banished the poet Ovid to Tomis on the Black Sea (modern Constanta, Romania). In his Tristia, poems largely addressed to his wife, Ovid describes his last night in Rome: his wife weeping in his arms and praying at the household shrine, his own repeated delays at the threshold, and his wife clinging to him and asking to follow him into exile. When he refused and left, she collapsed in grief.
real_life_example.explanation: Ovid's account is one of the most vivid surviving descriptions from the ancient world of the moment of parting between husband and wife.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural sets side by side the husband walking away and the pallor already spreading over the wife, and Ovid records his wife falling in grief at the very moment he went out of the door.

tamil:
விளக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும் இருளேபோல் கொண்கன்
முயக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும் பசப்பு.
transliteration:
vilakkatram paarkkum irulepoal kon-kan
muyakkatram paarkkum pasappu
meaning: Just as darkness waits for a lamp to go out, the paleness waits for the moment my husband's hug loosens.
elementary: When you blow out a candle, the dark rushes in right away, as if it had been waiting just outside the light. The wife says the sad pale colour is like that dark: it waits, and as soon as her husband’s hug ends, it rushes in.
university: A celebrated simile: viḷakku aṟṟam pārkkum iruḷ (விளக்கு அற்றம் பார்க்கும் இருள், ‘darkness that watches for the lamp’s lapse’) is set against koṇkaṉ muyakku aṟṟam pārkkum pasappu (‘pallor that watches for the lapse of my husband’s embrace’). Aṟṟam (அற்றம்) means a gap, failing or unguarded moment; pārkkum is ‘watches for, lies in wait’. Koṇkaṉ (கொண்கன்) is a classical word for husband, traditionally associated with the seashore (neytal) landscape. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the embrace’s aṟṟam as its slackening, Solomon Pappaiah as its loosening, and Kalaignar as the moment the tight hold relaxes. Pope: ‘As darkness waits till lamp expires, to fill the place, / This pallor waits till I enjoy no more my lord’s embrace.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the transliteration kon-kan follows ytamizh.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Hanuman first finds Sita in Ravana’s Ashoka grove, Valmiki likens the grieving, pale, emaciated wife separated from Rama to a flame veiled in smoke and to the moon’s crescent dimmed by clouds.
hinduism.explanation: The Ramayana pictures the separated wife as a light obscured, her radiance darkened by the absence of her husband.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same light-and-darkness image: without the husband’s presence the wife’s brightness is overtaken by pallor.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then Jesus said unto them, Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you: for he that walketh in darkness knoweth not whither he goeth.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that darkness is waiting to come in as soon as the light he brings is withdrawn.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s darkness ‘waiting for the lamp to fail’ is the same picture applied to a wife’s pallor in the beloved’s absence.

islam.quote_or_event: “And from the evil of darkness when it settles”
islam.explanation: The short sura of refuge treats the settling darkness of night as a power from which one seeks protection.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s darkness and pallor are similarly forces poised to settle over the unprotected moment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Until the day breathe, and the shadows flee away, Turn, my beloved, and be thou like a gazelle or a young hart Upon the mountains of spices.”
judaism.explanation: The Song pairs the beloved’s presence with light and the fleeing of shadows.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural uses the reverse of this image: when the beloved’s embrace lapses, the shadow of pallor returns.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When this world is ever ablaze, why this laughter, why this jubilation? Shrouded in darkness, will you not see the light?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures ordinary life as shrouded in darkness and urges people to seek the light.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s darkness waiting to cover the lamp is a similar image, though for the Buddha the darkness is ignorance rather than a lover’s grief.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana uses the moth and the lamp to show how attachment to what the senses love leads to suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also turns on a lamp image; the Jain lesson would be that dependence on the beloved’s ‘light’ is what lets the darkness of pallor in.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Like a lamp lit in the darkness, the spiritual wisdom of the Guru dispels ignorance.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das uses the lamp and darkness to show how the Guru's wisdom drives out the darkness of ignorance.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures darkness waiting for the lamp to fail, as pallor waits for the embrace to loosen; Gurbani uses the same lamp and darkness, but turned the other way: while the light burns, darkness cannot stay.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 39, Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Every night Hero set a lamp in her tower so that Leander could swim the Hellespont to her; on a stormy night the wind blew the lamp out, darkness took the strait, and Leander drowned.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the legend the lovers’ union depends on the lamp, and when it fails the darkness brings the lovers’ ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural makes the same link between a failing lamp and the onset of a lover’s grief.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld observes that absence lessens small passions and increases great ones, just as the wind puts out candles but fans a fire.
philosophy.explanation: The moralist uses the image of a flame exposed to the wind to describe what absence does to love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural pairs love and a failing lamp in the same way; the heroine’s love is the great kind that absence inflames into pallor.

real_life_example.event_title: Martha Washington joins George at his winter camps
real_life_example.place: Valley Forge, Morristown and other encampments, United States
real_life_example.event: During the eight years of the American Revolutionary War, Martha Washington travelled each winter, when fighting largely paused, to join her husband at his headquarters, including Valley Forge and Morristown. Her stays often lasted several months in cramped quarters shared with his officers, and she is estimated to have spent about half the war at his side.
real_life_example.explanation: Martha Washington chose hardship in camp rather than long separation at home whenever the war allowed it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says pallor lies in wait for the moment the husband's embrace loosens, as darkness waits for a lamp to fail, and Martha Washington went to her husband whenever she could so as not to leave that gap open longer than necessary.

tamil:
புல்லிக் கிடந்தேன் புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில்
அள்ளிக்கொள் வற்றே பசப்பு.
transliteration:
pullik kidandhen pudaipeyarndhaen avvalavil
allikkol vatre pasappu
meaning: I lay held close in his arms. I turned away just a little, and in that instant the paleness rushed over me as if scooping me up.
elementary: You know how a snowman starts melting the second the sun comes out? The wife says she was cuddled up safe and happy, turned over for just a moment, and in that tiny moment the sad pale colour grabbed her, like a big scoop.
university: The couplet heightens the previous one by shrinking the interval to almost nothing: pullik kiṭantēṉ (புல்லிக் கிடந்தேன், ‘I lay embracing’), puṭai peyarntēṉ (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன், ‘I shifted to one side’), avvaḷavil (‘in just that much’), the pallor aḷḷik koḷvaṟṟē (அள்ளிக்கொள்வற்றே, ‘was like something scooped up in handfuls’, i.e. it came in a rush). Solomon Pappaiah frames it as a recollection of an earlier occasion, making the point a fortiori for the present long absence, while Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesikan keep it as a vivid present. Pope: ‘I lay in his embrace, I turned unwittingly; / Forthwith this hue, as you might grasp it, came on me.’ The treatment is tasteful and hyperbolic, the conventional rhetoric of the heroine’s extreme sensitivity. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata’s story of Nala and Damayanti, Nala, ruined and wandering in the forest with his wife, leaves her while she sleeps; Damayanti wakes to find him gone and searches the forest crying out for him, wasting with grief.
hinduism.explanation: The Nalopakhyana gives the classic Indian scene of a wife who was beside her husband one moment and abandoned the next.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Damayanti passes from closeness to desolation in the space of a single turning in sleep.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast in those days.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says the joy of the bridegroom’s presence gives way to fasting and mourning as soon as he is taken away.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural shows the same switch in miniature: closeness, a moment’s parting, and grief at once.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are a clothing for you and you are a clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes husband and wife as each other’s garment, giving closeness, covering and protection.
islam.tie_back: In the Kural, the instant that ‘garment’ of closeness slips away, the wife is left exposed to pallor.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: The bride reaches for her beloved in the night and finds he is not there.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also turns in the night and finds the closeness gone, with grief rushing in.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Don’t ever — regardless — be conjoined with what’s dear or undear. It’s painful not to see what’s dear or to see what’s not.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that being bound to a dear one makes even a moment of not seeing them painful.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows how sharp that pain can be: a moment of not holding her husband is enough.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasures bring only a moment’s happiness, but suffering for a very long time, intense suffering, but slight happiness; they are an obstacle to the liberation from existence, and are a very mine of evils.”
jainism.explanation: The sons of Bhrigu tell their father that the happiness of pleasure is brief while the suffering it brings is long.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural shows that imbalance in a single night: a moment’s closeness, and at the slightest parting a flood of pallor.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “This night, I did not sleep with my Husband Lord, and now my body is suffering in pain.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that being apart from the Husband Lord for just one night leaves the body aching.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that she merely turned aside in his arms and the pallor swept over her at once; Farid likewise feels a single night without the Beloved at once in the body.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 30) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Psyche, forbidden to look on her unseen husband, raises a lamp over him as he sleeps; a drop of hot oil wakes Cupid, who at once flies away, leaving her alone and grieving.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Apuleius’s tale a single small movement in the bridal chamber ends the lovers’ closeness in an instant.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also turns for a moment and finds closeness gone and grief already upon her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Aristophanes’ speech, humans are halves of an original whole who, once divided, long for each other, throw their arms around each other, and pine away when apart, wishing never to be separated even for a moment.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s Aristophanes explains love as the desire of two halves to be whole, so that any separation is felt as a wound.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels exactly that: the slightest parting from her other half brings immediate suffering.

real_life_example.event_title: Ida Straus stays with her husband on the Titanic
real_life_example.event: Isidor Straus, co-owner of Macy's department store, and his wife Ida, aged 63, were passengers on the RMS Titanic.
