Isidor declined a place in a lifeboat under the rule of women and children first, and Ida, who had nearly entered a lifeboat, turned back to stay with him despite friends urging her to go. Both were lost in the sinking.
real_life_example.explanation: Ida Straus's choice became one of the most remembered acts of devotion of the disaster.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife says that even turning aside a little from her husband's embrace let the pallor rush over her, and Ida Straus refused to be parted from her husband even for the safety of a lifeboat.

tamil:
பசந்தாள் இவள்என்பது அல்லால் இவளைத்
துறந்தார் அவர்என்பார் இல்.
transliteration:
pasandhaal ival-enpadhu allaal ivalaith
thurandhaar avar-enpaar il
meaning: People only say, 'She has turned pale.' No one says, 'He has left her.'
elementary: Imagine your friend broke your toy, and everyone said, ‘Why is that toy broken? You must be careless!’ but nobody said, ‘Your friend broke it.’ That feels unfair. The wife feels the same: everybody notices her pale face, but nobody says it’s because her husband went away.
university: A couplet about public opinion (alar, the village gossip that runs through the Kamattuppal): people say pasantāḷ ivaḷ (பசந்தாள் இவள், ‘she has grown pale’), but none says tuṟantār avar (துறந்தார் அவர், ‘he has abandoned her’). Tuṟa- is the same root as tuṟavu, ‘renunciation, forsaking’, giving the complaint a sharp edge. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the first clause as blame (பழி) directed at the woman for showing her grief, while the man’s departure, the real cause, escapes comment. Pope: ‘On me, because I pine, they cast a slur; / But no one says, “He first deserted her.”’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Shakuntala arrives at Dushyanta’s court, the king, under Durvasas’s curse, does not remember her; it is she whose honesty and conduct are questioned before the assembly, while the husband who forgot her is not blamed.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa stages a scene in which public suspicion falls on the wife rather than on the husband who failed her.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine complains of the same imbalance: people remark on her, not on the man who left.

christianity.quote_or_event: The scribes and Pharisees bring to Jesus a woman taken in adultery and set her in the midst for judgment; the man is not brought, and Jesus answers that whoever is without sin should cast the first stone.
christianity.explanation: The episode exposes a public judgment that singles out the woman while the man escapes notice.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s complaint has the same shape: the woman’s condition is talked about, the man’s part is ignored.

islam.quote_or_event: “Why, when you heard it, did not the believing men and believing women think good of themselves [i.e., one another] and say, ‘This is an obvious falsehood’?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an rebukes the community for repeating talk that wrongly blamed a woman instead of assuming the best.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also suffers from talk that blames her while ignoring the true cause.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Look not upon me, that I am swarthy, That the sun hath tanned me; My mother’s sons were incensed against me, They made me keeper of the vineyards; But mine own vineyard have I not kept.”
judaism.explanation: The bride asks onlookers not to stare at her darkened skin, explaining that it was caused by others who sent her out under the sun.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she knows people will judge her changed colour without seeing who caused it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “O Atula! Indeed, this is an ancient practice, not one only of today: they blame those who remain silent, they blame those who speak much, they blame those who speak in moderation. There is none in the world who is not blamed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that public blame is universal and arbitrary.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine discovers the same arbitrariness: the village blames her pallor, never his absence.

jainism.quote_or_event: Anjana Sundari, neglected for years by her husband Pavananjaya, is visited by him secretly before he leaves for war; when she is found to be with child, her mother-in-law accuses her of misconduct and drives her out, and even her own family refuses to take her in, while no one questions the absent husband.
jainism.explanation: In this Jain narrative, the mother of Hanuman bears all the blame for a situation her absent husband created.
jainism.tie_back: Her story is the Kural’s complaint writ large: everyone speaks of what has happened to her, and no one speaks of him.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 7 (story of Anjana) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Dadda: Do not blame anyone else; blame instead your own actions.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Patti (acrostic) in Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak teaches that one should not blame others for one's suffering but look at one's own deeds.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife complains that people blame her for turning pale while no one blames the husband who left; Gurbani turns this around, telling the sufferer never to blame the other but to look at her own actions.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Aasaa, Patti, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Virgil’s Rumour (Fama) spreads through the cities of Libya the tale of Dido’s love for Aeneas and her neglect of her kingdom; when Aeneas sails away, it is Dido who is left disgraced and talked about.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Aeneid public talk fastens on the abandoned woman while the departing hero sails on.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine complains of the same: the talk is all about her, never about the man who left.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle holds that praise and blame are properly given only for voluntary actions, while what is involuntary, done under compulsion or in ignorance, deserves pardon and sometimes pity.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, blame should follow responsibility.
philosophy.tie_back: By that standard the village has it backward: her pallor is involuntary, while his departure was his choice.

real_life_example.event_title: Catherine of Aragon refuses to accept the annulment of her marriage
real_life_example.event: Henry VIII sought to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon mainly because she had not given him a male heir. Archbishop Thomas Cranmer annulled the marriage on 23 May 1533, but Catherine refused to accept it and kept calling herself queen, until the 1534 Act of Succession required her to use the title Princess Dowager. She was separated from her daughter Mary, confined to residences including Kimbolton, and died there in January 1536.
real_life_example.explanation: The official reasons for ending the marriage centred on Catherine, while it was Henry who set her aside.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural complains that people say 'she has grown pale' but no one says 'he has left her', and Catherine bore the official blame for a marriage that her husband chose to end.

tamil:
பசக்கமன் பட்டாங்கென் மேனி நயப்பித்தார்
நன்னிலையர் ஆவர் எனின்.
transliteration:
pasakkaman pattaangen maeni nayappiththaar
nannilaiyar aavar enin
meaning: If the man who sweetly talked me into letting him go is doing well, then let my body turn as pale as it wants.
elementary: Imagine your big brother goes away to camp and you miss him so much you feel sad. But then you think, ‘As long as he’s having fun and is safe, I don’t mind being a bit sad.’ That is what the wife says: if her husband is doing well, she doesn’t mind the pale colour.
university: Here the heroine turns from complaint to self-sacrifice: pasakka maṉ (பசக்க மன், ‘let it grow pale indeed’), paṭṭāṅku (பட்டாங்கு, ‘as it actually is, to its full measure’) eṉ mēṉi, if nayappittār (நயப்பித்தார், ‘he who made me consent by sweet persuasion’, from nayam, pleasantness) is nannilaiyar (நன்னிலையர், ‘of good standing’). Commentators divide on nannilaiyar: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as ‘good, blameless’, so the verse is half ironic, while Kalaignar reads ‘is well, prospers’, making it a wish for his welfare; the Pope translation (‘in good estate remain’) supports the latter, and the alternative rendering on ytamizh, ‘if he is clear of guilt’, supports the former. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Narada Bhakti Sutra, taking the gopis of Vraja as its model, describes the highest love as finding one’s happiness in the beloved’s happiness, and says that a love lacking this is not true love.
hinduism.explanation: The bhakti tradition treats tat-sukha-sukhitvam, being happy in the beloved’s happiness, as the mark of pure love.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows exactly this: if he is well, her own suffering does not matter.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up …”
christianity.explanation: Paul defines love as patient endurance that does not put itself first.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine’s willingness to suffer the pallor so long as her husband prospers is love that ‘suffereth long’.

islam.quote_or_event: “… but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul — it is those who will be the successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who put others’ good before their own even when they themselves are in need.
islam.tie_back: The heroine likewise prefers her husband’s well-being to her own, accepting her pallor as the price.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jonathan, heir to Saul’s throne, loves David as his own soul; he strengthens David in hiding and tells him that David will be king over Israel and he himself will be second to him, gladly giving up his own claim for his friend’s good.
judaism.explanation: The Bible’s great story of devoted friendship shows a love that wishes the beloved well at one’s own cost.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows the same spirit: let her suffer, provided the one she loves fares well.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Karaniya Metta Sutta teaches wishing that all beings be happy and at ease, and cherishing them with a boundless heart, as a mother would protect her only child with her own life.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist loving-kindness wishes others’ welfare without condition, even at the cost of oneself.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s wish that her husband fare well, whatever it costs her own body, is a personal form of that goodwill.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.”
jainism.explanation: Rather than resent Arishtanemi for leaving, Rajimati resolves to follow the same path of renunciation he has chosen, and later attains perfection.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she does not curse the one who left; she accepts her own loss and honours his choice.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If You will bless me with happiness, then I will worship and adore You. Even in pain, I will meditate on You.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says the devotee's love does not depend on comfort: in happiness and in pain alike the mind stays on the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her body may grow as pale as it likes so long as her husband is well; Gurbani likewise accepts pain without letting it lessen love for the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Admetus is fated to die unless someone takes his place, his wife Alcestis alone agrees to die in his stead so that he may live.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Euripides’ play Alcestis is the model of a wife who accepts her own suffering for her husband’s welfare.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows the same spirit on a smaller scale: let her body suffer so long as he fares well.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that friendship consists more in loving than in being loved, and points to mothers who delight in loving their children and wish them well even when they receive no love in return.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, the deepest affection wishes the other’s good for its own sake, regardless of return.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s wish that her husband prosper, whatever it costs her, is love of exactly this kind.

real_life_example.event_title: George Washington writes to Martha on taking command of the army
real_life_example.event: On 18 June 1775 George Washington wrote to his wife Martha from Philadelphia that Congress had placed the army under his command and that he must go to Boston. He told her he had tried to avoid the post, partly because he did not want to leave his family, that his chief unhappiness would be knowing she was uneasy at being left alone, and he asked her to summon her fortitude and spend the time as agreeably as she could. In the months that followed Martha remained at home amid fears for her safety, and later joined him at his winter camps.
real_life_example.explanation: The letter shows a husband persuading his wife to accept a separation for the sake of his duty and standing.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife says that if the man who sweetly persuaded her to let him go is well and in good standing, her own pallor does not matter, and Washington's letter is exactly such a gentle persuasion to bear his absence for the sake of his public duty.

tamil:
பசப்பெனப் பேர்பெறுதல் நன்றே நயப்பித்தார்
நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்.
transliteration:
pasappenap paerperudhal nandre nayappiththaar
nalkaamai thootraar enin
meaning: I don't mind being called 'the pale one,' as long as people do not blame the man who talked me into letting him go for being unkind.
elementary: Imagine your friend forgot your birthday, and you felt sad. If people started saying mean things about your friend, you might say, ‘It’s okay, just call me the sad one, but please don’t be mean to my friend.’ That’s what the wife says: call me pale, but don’t blame him.
university: The chapter closes on the heroine’s protectiveness: pasappu eṉap pēr peṟutal naṉṟē (பசப்பெனப் பேர்பெறுதல் நன்றே, ‘it is good to get the name of pallor’), if people tūṟṟār (தூற்றார், ‘do not slander, broadcast in blame’) the nalkāmai (நல்காமை, ‘lack of grace, unkindness’) of nayappittār (‘him who won my consent’). The verse answers 1188: there she resented that people blamed her and not him; here she would rather keep the blame herself than have his name spoiled, a turn the commentators read as the ideal of the karpu (chaste, loyal) wife. Solomon Pappaiah takes the people as those who would otherwise abuse him for not returning; Kalaignar as those who would call him loveless. Pope: ‘’Tis well, though men deride me for my sickly hue of pain; / If they from calling him unkind, who won my love, refrain.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the opening verb nalkāmai echoes Kural 1181, framing the chapter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Lakshmana leaves the pregnant Sita at Valmiki’s hermitage on Rama’s orders because of the people’s talk, Sita sends word that she grieves not for herself but wishes Rama to protect his good name and treat his subjects as he would his own kin.
hinduism.explanation: In the Uttara Kanda Sita, though abandoned, chooses to guard her husband’s reputation rather than accuse him.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same choice: let her bear the name of pallor, so long as no one blames him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.”
christianity.explanation: Peter teaches that love covers over the faults of the one loved rather than exposing them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine covers her husband’s unkindness the same way, keeping the reproach on herself.

islam.quote_or_event: “… and whoever screened a Muslim, Allah will screen him on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises those who cover the faults of others rather than exposing them.
islam.tie_back: The heroine would screen her husband’s unkindness from public blame, accepting the talk about her own pallor instead.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hatred stirreth up strifes; but love covereth all transgressions.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts hatred, which exposes and inflames, with love, which covers another’s wrongs.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s love covers her husband’s unkindness; she will take the name of pallor rather than let him be blamed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one’s own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha counsels against dwelling on others’ faults and failures.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine refuses to dwell on her husband’s neglect and would have no one else dwell on it either.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Silappatikaram, Kannagi, whose husband Kovalan has left her for years for the dancer Madhavi, lays aside her ornaments and lives quietly in grief; when he returns ruined, she speaks no reproach and gives him her anklets to rebuild their life.
jainism.explanation: The Tamil epic portrays a wife who bears long neglect without exposing her husband’s fault.
jainism.tie_back: Kannagi lives out the Kural’s choice: she endures the marks of grief herself rather than speak against her husband.
jainism.source: Ilango Adigal, Silappatikaram, Puhar Kandam (cantos 4 and 9) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I am not good; no one is bad.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak gives the humble prayer of one who takes no credit for himself and puts blame on no one else.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife would rather be known as 'the pale one' than have people call her husband unkind; Gurbani likewise keeps the fault for oneself and will not speak ill of anyone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 728, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Of the fifty daughters of Danaus ordered to kill their husbands on the wedding night, Hypermnestra alone spared hers, Lynceus, helping him escape and accepting her father’s anger and imprisonment rather than harm him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hypermnestra chooses to bear punishment herself rather than let harm come to her husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes a gentler version of the same choice: let the reproach fall on her, not on him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Works of Love Kierkegaard devotes a deliberation to the theme ‘Love hides a multitude of sins’, arguing that the loving person does not discover or publicise the faults of the beloved but mitigates and hides them.
philosophy.explanation: Kierkegaard treats concealing the beloved’s fault as an act of love, not of deception.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine practises exactly that: she would rather be known as ‘the pale one’ than have his unkindness exposed.
philosophy.source: Søren Kierkegaard, Works of Love (1847), Second Series, V (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Eliza Hamilton spends fifty years defending her husband's memory
real_life_example.event: In 1797 Alexander Hamilton's affair with Maria Reynolds became public, humiliating his wife Eliza. After Hamilton's death in 1804 she lived another fifty years, hired assistants to organize his papers, recruited biographers, and in 1846 petitioned Congress to fund publication of his writings, after which Congress passed legislation to publish and preserve them. She also helped found New York's first private orphanage in 1806 and died in 1854, aged 97.
real_life_example.explanation: Despite the public humiliation his conduct had caused her, Eliza devoted the rest of her life to making sure her husband's name was remembered with honour.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife would rather carry the name of 'the pale one' herself than have people slander the husband who was unkind to her, and Eliza Hamilton bore her own humiliation while spending decades protecting her husband's reputation.

tamil:
தாம்வீழ்வார் தம்வீழப் பெற்றவர் பெற்றாரே
காமத்துக் காழில் கனி.
transliteration:
Thaamveezhvaar thamveezhap petravar petraare
kaamaththuk kaazhil kani.
meaning: Those who are loved back by the very one they love have won love's best prize. It is like a fruit with no hard seed inside, all sweetness.
elementary: Imagine you save half your sandwich for your best friend, and your best friend has saved half of theirs for you. That happy feeling of sharing both ways is like biting into a fruit with no pit at all: nothing hard to spoil it.
university: Chapter 120, tanippaṭar mikuti (‘the excess of solitary suffering’), belongs to the karpiyal (married love) sequence on separation; in the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar the heroine, left alone, fears that her longing is not matched by her absent husband’s and speaks to her confidante (tōḻi). The chapter opens by defining what she lacks: tām vīḻvār tam vīḻap peṟṟavar, those whom the ones they desire (vīḻ, ‘to desire, fall for’) desire in turn. Kāḻ il kaṉi is ‘a fruit without a stone (kāḻ)’, i.e. pleasure without any hard residue of pain; Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both gloss it as the seedless fruit that is the yield (payaṉ) of married love. Pope renders: ‘The bliss to be beloved by those they love who gains, / Of love the stoneless, luscious fruit obtains.’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In that family, where the husband is pleased with his wife and the wife with her husband, happiness will assuredly be lasting.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu’s household code makes lasting happiness depend on the delight being mutual, the husband pleased with the wife and the wife with the husband.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘stoneless fruit’ is exactly this two-way pleasure, which Manu calls the secure root of a happy home.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.”
christianity.explanation: The bride in the Song of Solomon sums up her joy in a single line of perfect reciprocity.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Mine, and I am his’ is the Kural’s condition for the seedless fruit: the one I love loves me.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is nothing like marriage, for two who love one another.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says that for two people who already love each other, nothing compares with marriage.
islam.tie_back: Both texts single out love that runs both ways as the best thing married life can give.
islam.source: Sunan Ibn Majah 1847 (graded hasan by Darussalam)

judaism.quote_or_event: “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine, That feedeth among the lilies.”
judaism.explanation: The Shulammite states the reciprocity of love as a balanced formula, her belonging to him matched by his to her.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s happy lovers are those for whom this formula is true in both directions.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The householders Nakula’s father and Nakula’s mother tell the Buddha that since their youthful marriage neither has been unfaithful even in thought, and that they wish to see each other in this life and the next; the Buddha teaches that a couple matched in faith, virtue, generosity and discernment will meet again.
buddhism.explanation: The Samajivina discourse treats a wholly mutual marriage as a real good worth wishing to prolong.
buddhism.tie_back: Nakula’s parents are the Buddhist picture of the Kural’s fortunate pair whose love is returned in full.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: Among the lay vows, the vow of chastity for a householder is framed as svadāra-santoṣa, contentment with one’s own spouse, which channels desire into a single faithful marriage.
jainism.explanation: Jain householder ethics do not praise love’s sweetness, but they do honour a marriage in which each partner’s desire rests contentedly on the other alone.
jainism.tie_back: The closest Jain counterpart to the Kural’s fortunate lovers is the householder couple content in each other, though Jainism ranks even this below renunciation.
jainism.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara, on the vow of brahmacarya-anuvrata (paraphrase; cf. tr. Champat Rai Jain)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “She alone is the happy soul-bride, who is pleasing to God.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that the true sohagan, the fortunate wedded soul-bride, is the one her Lord loves in return.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that those loved back by the one they love have won love's stoneless fruit; Gurbani likewise names the soul-bride who pleases her Beloved as the truly blessed one.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 391, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus wishes the young princess Nausicaa a husband and a home of one mind, saying there is nothing better or nobler than when husband and wife keep house together in harmony, a grief to their enemies and a joy to their friends.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer has his hero name like-mindedness between husband and wife as the greatest blessing of life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s seedless fruit and Homer’s best of all gifts are the same thing: two hearts that agree.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.180-185 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that the friendship of husband and wife is natural and can include usefulness, pleasure and, where both are good, virtue, each delighting in the other’s goodness.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the best marriage is a friendship in which the good and the pleasure flow both ways.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s happiest lovers are Aristotle’s married friends, whose delight is returned in kind.

real_life_example.event_title: Robert Schumann and Clara Wieck win the right to marry
real_life_example.event: Clara Wieck's father, Friedrich Wieck, opposed her marriage to the composer Robert Schumann, rejected his written proposal and kept the couple apart. Robert and Clara took Wieck to court, and in 1840 the court ruled in their favour. They married on 12 September 1840 in the parish church at Schönefeld, near Leipzig.
real_life_example.explanation: Because the love ran equally in both directions, the couple were willing to go to law together to win it, and their marriage became one of the great partnerships in music.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls love that is returned by the very one you love a seedless, all-sweet fruit, and the Schumanns fought for exactly that kind of matched love.

tamil:
வாழ்வார்க்கு வானம் பயந்தற்றால் வீழ்வார்க்கு
வீழ்வார் அளிக்கும் அளி.
transliteration:
Vaazhvaarkku vaanam payandhatraal veezhvaarkku
veezhvaar alikkum ali.
meaning: The kindness a lover shows to the one who loves him is like rain from the sky to those whose lives depend on it.
elementary: Think of a thirsty garden in summer. When the rain finally comes, every leaf perks up. When someone you love is kind to you, your heart perks up the same way.
university: The couplet sets the beloved’s aḷi (grace, tender kindness) beside the rain that the sky (vāṉam) yields (payanta) to living beings (vāḻvār), echoing the Kural’s own chapter on rain (vāṉ ciṟappu, ch. 2). Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators take vāḻvār as ‘those who live by it’ and insist on timeliness: Pappaiah stresses rain at the proper season, and Kalaignar reads it as lovers meeting at the right time. The point in this chapter is implicit contrast: the heroine is the parched field to whom no such rain is coming. Pope: ‘As heaven on living men showers blessings from above, / Is tender grace by lovers shown to those they love.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna teaches that living beings are sustained by food, food is produced from rain, and rain comes from sacrifice, so that the whole order of life hangs on the rain that falls in due season.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita presents rain as the link on which all living beings depend.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural borrows exactly this dependence of life on rain to describe how a loving spouse’s kindness keeps the beloved alive.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.14 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth.”
christianity.explanation: Hosea pictures the coming of the beloved Lord to his people as seasonal rain on dry ground.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hosea likens the arrival of love to rain that revives those who wait for it.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an names as one of God’s signs that He created spouses for people so that they may find tranquillity in them, placing affection and mercy between them; a few verses later it names as another sign the rain He sends down to give life to the earth after its death.
islam.explanation: Surah ar-Rum sets marital affection and life-giving rain side by side among the signs of divine care.
islam.tie_back: The Kural joins the same two signs into one simile: a spouse’s kindness is rain to the one who lives by it.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that any man who has no wife lives without joy, without blessing and without goodness.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis treat the love of a spouse as the source from which joy and blessing reach a person’s life.
judaism.tie_back: As the Kural says love is rain to the one who lives by it, the Talmud says a life without that love is dry of joy and blessing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dhaniya Sutta a contented cowherd, his roof thatched and his fire lit, tells the sky it may rain if it likes, praising his wife as faithful, long his companion and pleasing to him; the Buddha answers each verse with his own freedom from all such supports.
buddhism.explanation: The herdsman’s security rests on a loving wife and on rain that can do him no harm, while the Buddha points beyond both.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s rain-and-love pairing appears here too, though the Buddhist sutta finally sets both aside in favour of non-attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Tamil Jain epic Jivaka Chintamani, the hero Jivaka wins and marries a series of brides, and the poet dwells on the mutual delight of each newly united couple before Jivaka finally renounces the world.
jainism.explanation: The Jain epic describes reciprocal married love with real warmth, while framing it as a stage to be outgrown.
jainism.tie_back: Its scenes of shared delight answer the Kural’s picture of a lover’s kindness falling like rain, though the Jain poem ends in renunciation.
jainism.source: Tiruttakkatevar, Jivaka Chintamani (paraphrase of the epic’s marriage episodes)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Just as the earth looks beautiful when the rain falls, so does the Sikh blossom forth meeting the Guru.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das compares the Sikh's joy on meeting the Guru to the dry earth turning green and beautiful under rain.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a lover's kindness to the one who loves him is like rain to those whose life depends on it; Gurbani uses the same rain image for the Guru's grace to the longing Sikh.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 758, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In a fragment of Aeschylus’ lost Danaids, Aphrodite says the holy sky longs to wed the earth and the earth longs for union; rain falls from the bridegroom sky and the earth conceives pasture for flocks and grain for mortals.
greek_mythology.explanation: Aphrodite herself presents rain as the act of love by which heaven gives life to the earth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s simile run in reverse: rain is love, as for the Kural love is rain.
greek_mythology.source: Aeschylus, Danaids, fragment 44 (Radt), preserved in Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 13.600b (paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Boethius’ Lady Philosophy sings that it is love which holds earth and sea together and rules the heavens, keeping the seasons in their order; if love slackened its reins, everything now bound in concord would fall into war.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius makes love the force that keeps the whole cosmos, seasons included, alive and in order.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s comparison of love to life-sustaining rain fits Boethius’ claim that love is what keeps the world going.
philosophy.source: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2, metre 8 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Robert Browning's letters reach the invalid Elizabeth Barrett
real_life_example.event: For years the poet Elizabeth Barrett lived as a chronic invalid, mostly confined to her room at 50 Wimpole Street. In January 1845 Robert Browning wrote to tell her he loved her verses with all his heart, and over the next twenty months the two exchanged 574 letters. They married secretly at St Marylebone Parish Church on 12 September 1846 and left for Italy, where her health improved and their son was born in 1849.
real_life_example.explanation: Browning's love came into a shut-in, sickly life and helped open it up into marriage, travel, motherhood and her best-known love poetry.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural likens a lover's tenderness to rain for those whose life depends on it, and Browning's devotion arrived like that rain in Elizabeth Barrett's confined life.

tamil:
வீழுநர் வீழப் படுவார்க்கு அமையுமே
வாழுநம் என்னும் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Veezhunar veezhap paduvaarkku amaiyume
vaazhunam ennum serukku.
meaning: Only a woman truly loved by the one she loves can proudly say, 'We will live happily again,' even while he is away.
elementary: If your mom goes on a trip and you know she loves you and will come back, you can wait bravely and even smile. Knowing you are loved makes waiting easier.
university: Vīḻunar vīḻappaṭuvār is ‘those who are desired by the ones who desire them’; for such women alone amaiyumē (it is fitting) to hold the ceruukku (pride, proud confidence) of saying vāḻunam, ‘we shall live (in joy).’ In the separation context Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar read the pride as forward-looking: despite present parting, the loved wife can be sure that reunion and happiness will come; Pappaiah adds ‘by the certainty that he will soon return.’ The heroine’s unspoken complaint is that she cannot claim this pride. Pope: ‘Who love and are beloved to them alone / Belongs the boast, “We’ve made life’s very joys our own.”’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Yama comes for her husband Satyavan, the devoted Savitri follows the god of death, and her steadfast love and wisdom win back Satyavan’s life so that the two can return home together.
hinduism.explanation: Savitri’s certainty in a love that is mutual gives her the courage to argue with Death himself.
hinduism.tie_back: Savitri embodies the Kural’s ‘we shall live’ confidence that belongs to the wife who knows her love is shared.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva (Savitri episode) (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Solomon declares love able to survive every flood that might overwhelm it.
christianity.tie_back: This is the ground of the loved wife’s confidence in the Kural: real, returned love will outlast the present separation.

islam.quote_or_event: In the hadith of Umm Zar‘, Aisha relates eleven women describing their husbands; Umm Zar‘ proudly recalls a husband who treated her with lavish kindness, and the Prophet tells Aisha that he is to her as Abu Zar‘ was to Umm Zar‘.
islam.explanation: A wife’s happy boast about a loving husband is affirmed by the Prophet as true of his own marriage.
islam.tie_back: Umm Zar‘’s pride is the ‘boast’ the Kural says belongs only to a wife whose love is returned.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage, hadith of Umm Zar‘ (paraphrase)

judaism.quote_or_event: “for love is strong as death, jealousy is cruel as the grave; the flashes thereof are flashes of fire, a very flame of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Song’s climax claims for love a strength equal to death itself.
judaism.tie_back: The loved wife of the Kural can say ‘we shall live’ because she trusts a love as strong as this.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Describing seven kinds of wives, the Buddha praises the wife who is like a friend: she rejoices on seeing her husband as one rejoices at seeing a long-absent companion.
buddhism.explanation: The ‘friend-wife’ of this sutta is marked by glad, confident affection toward her husband.
buddhism.tie_back: Her joy at reunion is the Kural’s ‘we shall live’, available only where affection runs both ways.
buddhism.source: Bhariya Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya, Book of Sevens (paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain story of Shripal and Mayanasundari, the princess is married off in anger to a man suffering from leprosy; trusting in her husband and in her faith, she remains devoted and confident, and through their shared worship of the Siddhachakra he is healed and the couple prosper.
jainism.explanation: Mayanasundari’s calm certainty that she and her husband will flourish together is a celebrated Jain model of faithful love.
jainism.tie_back: Her confidence echoes the Kural’s ‘we shall live’, though the Jain story credits faith and merit rather than love alone.
jainism.source: Shripal Ras (Vinayavijaya and Yashovijaya, 17th c.), story of Shripal and Mayanasundari (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, the soul-bride is forever the Lord's favorite wife; her Husband Lord does not die, and He shall never leave.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das says the soul-bride who is truly loved by the Lord is sure of her happiness, because her Husband never dies and never leaves her.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says only a woman loved by the one she loves can say with proud confidence, 'We shall live happily yet'; Gurbani gives the loved soul-bride the same sure confidence, since her Beloved will never leave.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 245, Raag Gauree, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After twenty years apart, Penelope tests Odysseus with the secret of their marriage bed, carved from a living olive tree; when he describes it, she knows him, and the two are reunited in the home he built.
greek_mythology.explanation: The bed rooted in a living tree is the sign that their love was fixed on both sides throughout the long separation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope’s long patience could hold because, as the Kural says, the one she loved also loved her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that most people, out of ambition, wish to be loved rather than to love, since being loved is close to being honoured, and that people enjoy being loved for its own sake.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle recognises the special satisfaction and standing that comes from being loved.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘pride’ of the loved wife is the same satisfaction Aristotle describes in being loved.

real_life_example.event_title: Sullivan Ballou's last letter to his wife Sarah
real_life_example.place: Camp Clark, Washington, D.C., United States
real_life_example.event: A week before the First Battle of Bull Run (First Manassas), Union Major Sullivan Ballou wrote a long letter to his wife Sarah, telling her of his love and of the possibility that he might not return. He was killed in the battle. The letter was never mailed; it was found among his belongings when Rhode Island's governor went to Virginia to recover the remains of the state's soldiers.
real_life_example.explanation: The letter became one of the most famous love letters in American history because it speaks of a love so secure that even separation and death could not shake it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says only a woman truly loved can say with proud confidence that they will yet live happily even while he is away, and Ballou's letter is the kind of assurance that gives a wife that confidence.

tamil:
வீழப் படுவார் கெழீஇயிலர் தாம்வீழ்வார்
வீழப் படாஅர் எனின்.
transliteration:
Veezhap paduvaar kezhee-iyilar thaamveezhvaar
veezhap pataa-ar enin.
meaning: Even a woman loved by many is truly unlucky if the one she loves does not love her back.
elementary: Imagine everyone at school likes your drawing, but the one person you made it for doesn’t care about it. All the other praise wouldn’t feel like enough. The Kural says love works like that.
university: The couplet turns on a contrast within the same verb: vīḻappaṭuvār, ‘those who are desired’ (by others, or by the world), are kezhīiyilar, ‘not endowed (with good fortune)’, if they are vīḻappaṭār, ‘not desired’, by tām vīḻvār, ‘those whom they themselves desire.’ Parimelazhagar’s line, followed by Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, glosses kezhīiyilar as lacking nalviṉai (the fruit of past merit); Pappaiah sharpens it to being under tīviṉai, while Kalaignar instead reads the lover as lacking the friendly feeling. Pope: ‘Those well-beloved will luckless prove, / Unless beloved by those they love.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, both with the alapeṭai spelling படாஅர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Shakuntala, married in secret to King Dushyanta, comes to his court with her child, but under a curse he fails to recognise her and sends her away; a woman honoured by sages and loved by her forest home is left desolate because the one she loves does not know her.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s heroine is cherished by everyone except the one person whose love she needs.
hinduism.tie_back: Shakuntala’s rejection is the Kural’s point exactly: being loved by many is no fortune without the beloved’s love.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Abhijnanashakuntalam, Act 5 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)

christianity.quote_or_event: “and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that every gift and achievement counts for nothing without love.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly says every other kind of admiration counts for little without the love that matters most.

islam.quote_or_event: “And you will never be able to be equal [in feeling] between wives, even if you should strive [to do so]. So do not incline completely [toward one] and leave another hanging.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns husbands not to leave a wife ‘hanging’, neither truly married nor free, because his heart has turned away.
islam.tie_back: The neglected wife of this verse, honoured in name but unloved in fact, is the woman the Kural calls unfortunate.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Michal Saul’s daughter loved David”
judaism.explanation: Michal, a king’s daughter, is one of the few women in the Bible explicitly said to love a man, yet the text never says David loved her in return, and her story ends in estrangement.
judaism.tie_back: A princess with every advantage who is not loved by the man she loves is the Kural’s ‘unfortunate’ in biblical form.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sambula Jataka, Princess Sambula faithfully nurses her husband through a loathsome illness in the forest, but once he is healed and becomes king he neglects her; though she is his chief queen in name, she wastes away until her father intervenes.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka tells of a virtuous queen honoured by all yet left without her husband’s love.
buddhism.tie_back: Sambula is the very woman of this couplet: honoured in every way, yet unfortunate because her husband does not love her.
buddhism.source: Sambula Jataka (Jataka 519) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain Ramayana tradition, the princess Anjana is married to Pavananjaya, who, over a misunderstanding, refuses to speak to or look at her for many years; honoured as a queen, she lives in grief until he finally realises his error and returns to her, and she becomes the mother of Hanuman.
jainism.explanation: Anjana’s story is the classic Jain tale of a noble, admired wife who is ignored by the one husband whose love she wants.
jainism.tie_back: Anjana is the Kural’s unfortunate woman exactly: esteemed by all, yet bereft because her beloved does not love her.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 7 (Jain Ramayana), story of Anjana and Pavananjaya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson); also in Vimalasuri’s Paumacariya

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without the Name of the Lord, the beautiful are just like the noseless ones.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that beauty and the admiration it wins mean nothing without love for the Lord's Name; such a person is as disgraced as one whose nose has been cut off.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that even a woman everyone admires is unfortunate if the one she loves does not love her back; Gurbani likewise says the admired and beautiful are without real worth if they lack the love that matters.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 528, Raag Dayv Gandhaaree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ariadne, the Cretan princess who saved Theseus from the Labyrinth, wakes on the shore of Naxos to find him sailing away, and pours out her grief at being abandoned by the man for whom she gave up everything.
greek_mythology.explanation: A royal heroine with every claim to honour is left wretched because the man she loves has not loved her as she loved him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ariadne illustrates the Kural’s claim that no rank or regard makes up for unreturned love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that the fortunate man still needs friends, since no one would choose to have every good thing on condition of being alone.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, all other goods together cannot make a life happy without the bond of love with others.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural applies the same insight to lovers: all other blessings leave one unfortunate without the beloved’s love.

real_life_example.event_title: Catherine of Aragon is set aside by Henry VIII
real_life_example.event: In 1527 Henry VIII asked the pope to annul his long marriage to Catherine of Aragon, arguing that it broke a biblical rule. Catherine appealed to Rome and insisted she was his lawful wife; Britannica notes that she had always been loved by the English people. Henry separated from her in 1531, Archbishop Thomas Cranmer declared the marriage void on 23 May 1533, and she died at Kimbolton in January 1536, still signing herself queen.
real_life_example.explanation: Catherine kept the affection and respect of the country, yet none of it could make up for the husband who had turned away from her.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a woman admired by everyone is still unfortunate if the one she loves does not love her back, which is the shape of Catherine's last years.

tamil:
நாம்காதல் கொண்டார் நமக்கெவன் செய்பவோ
தாம்காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Naamkaadhal kondaar namakkevan seypavo
thaamkaadhal kollaak kadai.
meaning: If the one I love does not love me back, what good can he possibly do for me?
elementary: If you keep waving at someone across the playground and they never wave back, the waving can’t make you happy. Love needs someone answering from the other side.
university: The question form nam(a)kku evaṉ ceypavō, ‘what will they do for us?’, is rhetorical: the heroine admits that her own love (nām kātal koṇṭār, ‘the one we have taken love for’) can bring her nothing if tām kātal koḷḷā kaṭai, ‘when he does not take love (for us).’ Parimelazhagar’s reading, followed by Varadarasanar, makes the implied answer ‘no good at all’; Pappaiah and Kalaignar render ‘what joy will he give?’ The polite plural (koṇṭār, ceypa) keeps the husband at a distance even as she complains. Pope: ‘From him I love to me what gain can be, / Unless, as I love him, he loveth me?’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhramara Gita, a gopi who has been left behind by Krishna sees a bee and addresses it as his messenger, bitterly asking what use his sweet words are when he has forgotten them, and comparing him to a bee that leaves each flower once it has drunk its nectar.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis voice the bitterness of a love that is not answered with presence or care.
hinduism.tie_back: The gopi’s question ‘what good is he to us now?’ is the heroine’s question in the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that love which only answers love is nothing special, and calls for love that expects no return.
christianity.tie_back: Here Christianity pushes against the Kural’s complaint: the Gospel asks for love that does not depend on being loved back.

islam.quote_or_event: “O `Abbas ! are you not astonished at the love of Mughith for Barira and the hatred of Barira for Mughith?” … She said, “I am not in need of him.”
islam.explanation: Ibn Abbas recalls Mughith following his freed wife Barira through Medina, weeping, while she refused even the Prophet’s intercession for him.
islam.tie_back: Mughith’s tears show the Kural’s truth: love given to one who does not return it brings nothing but grief.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Because the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; for now my husband will love me.”
judaism.explanation: Leah, married to Jacob who loves her sister Rachel, names her firstborn in the hope that this at last will win her husband’s love.
judaism.tie_back: Leah’s repeated longing for a husband who does not love her is the heroine’s question in the Kural lived out across a family history.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sakkapanha Sutta the heavenly musician Pancasikha sings to his lute a love song for Bhadda, who does not return his love, mixing his longing with praise of the Buddha and the arahants; the Buddha remarks on how well the song and the strings agree.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta preserves a song of one-sided longing, set within a discourse that leads toward freedom from desire.
buddhism.tie_back: Pancasikha’s unanswered song is the Kural’s situation: love offered to one who gives nothing back.

jainism.quote_or_event: Princess Rajimati is betrothed to Arishtanemi, but on the way to the wedding he hears the cries of animals penned for the feast, turns back and renounces the world; Rajimati, grieving, resolves that a love he will not return as a husband can only be followed into renunciation, and becomes a nun.
jainism.explanation: The twenty-second Tirthankara’s story makes the bride’s unreturned love the turning point of her own spiritual life.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati faces the Kural’s question, what can he do for me if he does not love me, and answers it the Jain way, by renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (Rathanemi) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “But one who feels good only when good is done for him, and feels bad when things go badly - do not call him a lover. He trades only for his own account.”
sikhism.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Angad says that love which asks what it will get, and sours when it gets nothing, is not love but trading.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife asks what good her beloved can do her if he does not love her back; Guru Angad answers that real love does not ask what it gains, so the verse is a gentle Sikh counterpoint to her complaint.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar, Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In her hymn to Aphrodite, Sappho begs the goddess to come again, and recalls Aphrodite smilingly asking whom she must now persuade to love her, promising that one who now flees will soon pursue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho’s prayer arises because the one she loves does not love her back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine and Sappho share the same ache: love that is not returned brings only pain.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that when we love something like ourselves, we strive as far as we can to bring it about that it loves us in return.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, the desire to be loved back is built into the very nature of love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s question rests on this same law: love naturally seeks its return, and suffers when it fails.

real_life_example.event_title: Ivan Turgenev's lifelong devotion to Pauline Viardot
real_life_example.place: St Petersburg, Russia; Paris, France; Baden-Baden, Germany
real_life_example.event: The Russian writer Ivan Turgenev fell in love with the singer Pauline Viardot when she first performed in Russia in 1843. In 1847 he left Russia for Paris to be near her, and after the Crimean War he moved to Baden-Baden, again to be with her; he wrote the libretto for her operetta Le dernier sorcier (1869). He later settled at Bougival, near Paris, where he died in 1883.
real_life_example.explanation: Turgenev organised his whole adult life around a woman who gave him friendship and artistic partnership but never married him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what good the beloved can do if he does not love in return, and Turgenev's decades of following Viardot show both how much such love asks and how little it can be sure of receiving.

tamil:
ஒருதலையான் இன்னாது காமம்காப் போல
இருதலை யானும் இனிது.
transliteration:
Orudhalaiyaan innaadhu kaamamkaap pola
irudhalai yaanum inidhu.
meaning: Love on one side only is painful. Like the load on a carrying pole, it is sweet only when it is balanced at both ends.
elementary: Have you tried carrying two buckets on a stick across your shoulders? With one bucket it tips and hurts, but with one on each side it’s easy. Love is the same: it feels good only when both people carry it.
university: This is the Kural’s most famous image for mutual love. Kā is the kāvaṭi or shoulder-pole carried with a load at each end; orutalai (‘one end’) and irutalai (‘two ends’) give Tamil the still-current phrase orutalaik kātal for one-sided love. Kāmam orutalaiyāṉ iṉṉātu, ‘love on one end is painful’, irutalaiyāṉum iṉitu, ‘on both ends it is sweet.’ Parimelazhagar takes the kā simile as governing both halves; Kalaignar spells out that the pole’s two sides must be equally weighted, as love must bloom in both man and woman. Pope: ‘Love on one side is bad; like balanced load / By porter borne, love on both sides is good.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The closing hymn of the Rigveda prays for concord: that those gathered may have a common purpose, hearts in accord and minds alike, so that all may live together in harmony.
hinduism.explanation: The Samjnana hymn makes agreement of hearts the basis of a good shared life.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s balanced carrying pole is the domestic form of this Vedic ideal of hearts in accord.
hinduism.source: Rigveda 10.191.4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Ralph T.H. Griffith)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers”
christianity.explanation: Paul uses the image of an unevenly matched yoke to warn against a partnership in which the two sides are not one.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s carrying pole, Paul’s yoke works only when both sides bear equally.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi teaches that no lover ever seeks union unless the beloved is also seeking him; the thirst in the lover is matched by a drawing from the other side, as the thirsty seek water and water seeks the thirsty.
islam.explanation: For Rumi true love is never one-sided: longing on one side always implies a pull from the other.
islam.tie_back: Rumi’s mutual seeking is the Kural’s two-ended pole, love sweet because it is carried from both sides.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book III (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him that is alone when he falleth”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth praises the shared load of two who support each other, and pities the one left to carry life alone.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s carrying pole in words: two sides make the burden light, one side makes it painful.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kusa Jataka, the wise but ugly King Kusa loves Princess Pabhavati, who flees from him; he follows her to her father’s city and toils as a potter, basket-maker and cook to be near her, suffering greatly until she finally returns his love.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka dramatises the long misery of a love carried by one side only, and the happiness when it is shared.
buddhism.tie_back: Kusa’s story is the Kural’s carrying pole: unbearable at one end, sweet once both ends bear the weight.
buddhism.source: Kusa Jataka (Jataka 531) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)

jainism.quote_or_event: “But all kinds of objects of the senses, sounds, &c., will cause to the indifferent neither a pleasant nor an unpleasant feeling.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that pain and pleasure come from one’s own attachment, and that the dispassionate are untouched by either.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural seeks balance by making love mutual, Jainism seeks it by laying the burden of attachment down altogether.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.106 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Lord, if You will not break with me, then I will not break with You.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas describes his love for God as a two-way bond, kept whole because neither side breaks it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says love is painful when it rests on one end only and sweet, like a balanced carrying-pole, when it rests on both; Ravidas likewise sees true love as a bond held up from both sides.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 658, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Themistius tells how Aphrodite’s child Eros would not grow until Themis advised her to give him a brother, Anteros (‘love returned’); with Anteros beside him Eros flourished, but whenever they were parted Eros dwindled again.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes requited love the condition for love to grow at all.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Eros and Anteros are the two ends of the Kural’s pole: love thrives only when it is returned.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says goodwill is not yet friendship unless it is returned and each party knows of the other’s goodwill; friendship is goodwill that is reciprocated.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle love on one side only is not yet the real thing; reciprocity is part of its definition.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the philosophical form of the Kural’s claim that love is sweet only when it runs both ways.

real_life_example.event_title: Goethe falls in love with the engaged Charlotte Buff
real_life_example.event: In May 1772 the young Goethe went to Wetzlar as a trainee at the Imperial Chamber Court. At a dance on 9 June he met Charlotte Buff, the fiancée of his friend Johann Christian Kestner, and fell in love with her; on 11 September he left the town. Within two years he turned the experience into his first novel, The Sorrows of Young Werther, in which the hero loves a Lotte who is engaged to another man, and the book became an immense success.
real_life_example.explanation: Goethe's one-sided love was painful enough to drive him away, while Charlotte and her fiancé, whose love ran both ways, stayed together and became the models for Lotte and Albert.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares love to a carrying pole that is painful when loaded at one end and sweet when balanced at both, and Wetzlar showed both ends: Goethe's lopsided love and the engaged couple's balanced one.

tamil:
பருவரலும் பைதலும் காணான்கொல் காமன்
ஒருவர்கண் நின்றொழுகு வான்.
transliteration:
Paruvaralum paidhalum kaanaankol kaaman
oruvar-kan nindrozhuku vaan.
meaning: Kaman, the god of love, works on only one side. Does he not see the pain and sadness he leaves in me?
elementary: It’s like a game where only one team is allowed to play and the other just has to watch. It doesn’t seem fair. Here the girl feels that love has been fair to her husband but very unfair to her.
university: Kāmaṉ is the god of love (Sanskrit Kāma, Manmatha), whose flower-arrows awaken desire. The heroine complains that he oruvarkaṇ niṉṟu oḻukuvāṉ, ‘stays and works upon one person only’, i.e. on her, not on her absent husband, and asks whether he does not see her paruvaral (distress) and paital (sorrow). Parimelazhagar’s reading, followed by Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, takes the complaint as against Kāma’s partiality; Pappaiah and Kalaignar connect paital with the pallor (pacalai) of the previous chapter. Pope: ‘While Kaman rushes straight at me alone, / Is all my pain and wasting grief unknown?’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sent by the gods, Kama aims his flower-arrow at the meditating Shiva so that he will love Parvati; Shiva, disturbed, opens his third eye and burns Kama to ashes, leaving Parvati’s love unanswered until she wins him through austerity.
hinduism.explanation: In Kalidasa’s telling, Kama’s arrow stirs longing in one lover while the other remains untouched.
hinduism.tie_back: Parvati, yearning while Shiva is unmoved, is the Kural’s heroine on whom Kama works from one side alone.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride confesses herself weakened and ill with love.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is likewise laid low by a love that overpowers her body and spirit.

islam.quote_or_event: The women of the city gossip that the governor’s wife has been seeking to seduce her young servant Joseph, saying he has struck her heart with love, while Joseph himself remains unmoved.
islam.explanation: Surah Yusuf portrays a passion that seizes one person entirely while the other stays untouched.
islam.tie_back: As the Kural’s Kama acts on one side only, here love has overpowered one heart and left the other free.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles, and by the hinds of the field, that ye awaken not, nor stir up love, until it please.”
judaism.explanation: The Song warns that love is a power that should not be roused before its time, because once awakened it cannot be controlled.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has felt love roused in her alone, the danger the Song warns against.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Padhana Sutta, Mara approaches the striving Bodhisatta and is answered that Mara’s first army is sensual desire, followed by discontent, hunger and craving; the Bodhisatta resolves not to be overcome by them.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism personifies desire as Mara, also called Kama, whose forces attack the mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s Kama who torments one person is, in Buddhist terms, Mara’s first army, to be resisted rather than appealed to.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that suffering comes not from objects or outside powers but from one’s own attachment.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural’s heroine blames Kama for her pain, the Jain text locates its source in her own love itself.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.101 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O sexual desire, you lead the mortals to hell; you make them wander in reincarnation through countless species.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Saloks Sehskritee, Guru Arjan addresses kaam (lust), one of the five thieves, as a force that drags people into suffering and rebirth.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife complains that Kama, the god of love, works only on her and ignores her pain; Gurbani also speaks to desire directly, but treats it as a thief to be overcome, not a god to be pleaded with.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Saloks Sehskritee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stung by Apollo’s mockery, Cupid fires two arrows: a golden one that sets Apollo burning with love for the nymph Daphne, and a leaden one that makes Daphne flee from love; Apollo pursues while she escapes, until she is turned into a laurel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Cupid deliberately makes love one-sided, wounding one heart with desire and the other with aversion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s complaint exactly: the love-god has struck one side only and left the lover to suffer.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius describes the lover as wounded by the darts of Venus, so that the wound festers and the craving grows, and he advises against feeding a passion that brings such pain.
philosophy.explanation: Lucretius treats love as a wound inflicted by Venus that torments the one who receives it.
philosophy.tie_back: His wounded lover is the Kural’s heroine struck by Kama, though Lucretius answers with Epicurean detachment.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things 4.1048-1072 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: W. B. Yeats and his unreturned love for Maud Gonne
real_life_example.event: The Irish poet W. B. Yeats met Maud Gonne in 1889 and later wrote that the troubling of his life began then. About two years later he proposed and she refused; he asked again in 1899 and she declined, admiring him but not returning his love, since her passion was for Ireland's cause. In 1903 she married Major John MacBride, and Yeats's unreturned love fed many of his greatest poems over some forty years.
real_life_example.explanation: Yeats's case is a classic of love that took hold of one person completely while leaving the other untouched in the same way.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural complains that the god of love works on one side only, and in Yeats's story love struck the poet again and again while Maud Gonne stayed free of it.

tamil:
வீழ்வாரின் இன்சொல் பெறாஅது உலகத்து
வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்.
transliteration:
Veezhvaarin insol peraaadhu ulakaththu
vaazhvaarin vankanaar il.
meaning: No one in the world is as hard-hearted, or as brave, as a woman who keeps on living without even one kind word from the one she loves.
elementary: Imagine waiting every day for a letter from someone you love, and none ever comes, yet you keep getting up and going to school. That takes a very strong heart. The Kural says it is almost too strong.
university: Vaṉkaṇār means both ‘the hard-hearted, cruel’ and ‘the brave, enduring’, and the couplet exploits the ambiguity with self-irony: the heroine says that those who go on living in the world (ulakattu vāḻvār) without receiving (peṟāatu) even a sweet word (iṉcol) from their beloved (vīḻvār) are the most vaṉkaṇ of all. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar read vaṉkaṇmai as the stony endurance of separation; Pappaiah’s ‘no one is more cruel’ and Kalaignar’s ‘no one has so stony a heart’ stress self-reproach, while Pope chooses the heroic sense: ‘Who hear from lover’s lips no pleasant word from day to day, / Yet in the world live out their life,- no braver souls than they!’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Abandoned by her husband Nala in the forest while she sleeps, Damayanti wanders alone through wild country and strange cities for years, without word from him, yet keeps herself alive and devises a way to find him again.
hinduism.explanation: The Nala episode is the great Indian tale of a wife who endures long separation without any message from her husband.
hinduism.tie_back: Damayanti is the Kural’s ‘brave, hard heart’ who goes on living without a single kind word from her beloved.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs observes how long-delayed hope wears down the heart, while its fulfilment restores life.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine lives in this ‘hope deferred’, waiting for a sweet word that never comes.

islam.quote_or_event: “so patience is most fitting. And Allāh is the one sought for help against that which you describe.”
islam.explanation: Jacob, told that his beloved son Joseph is dead and given no true word of him, chooses beautiful patience.
islam.tie_back: Jacob’s years of patient endurance without news of Joseph parallel the heroine’s enduring life without a word from her beloved.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that a person’s spirit can sustain him through sickness, but a broken spirit is something no one can bear.
judaism.explanation: The proverb distinguishes bodily suffering, which the spirit can endure, from the wound of the spirit itself.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural marvels that the heroine goes on living with exactly such a broken spirit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The nun Isidasi recounts how, though she served each husband with complete devotion, she was rejected again and again without cause, until she renounced household life and, as a nun, came to understand the past deeds behind her suffering.
buddhism.explanation: Isidasi’s verses tell of a faithful wife who received no love in return, yet endured and found release.
buddhism.tie_back: Isidasi endured, as the Kural’s heroine does, a life without kind words from those she loved.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain Ramayana, Sita is sent away into the forest by Rama on account of public rumour, though she is pregnant and innocent; she survives, raises her sons, and when at last recalled to prove her purity she passes the ordeal and chooses to become a nun.
jainism.explanation: The Jain telling shows Sita enduring long abandonment by her husband with dignity and then turning to renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: Sita’s survival without word from Rama mirrors the Kural’s heroine, though the Jain story ends in renunciation rather than longing.
jainism.source: Vimalasuri, Paumacariya (Jain Ramayana), Sita’s banishment and renunciation (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Many talk of the pain and suffering of separation; O pain, you are the ruler of all. Fareed, that body, within which love of the Lord does not well up - look upon that body as a cremation ground.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid calls the pain of separation the ruler of all and says that a body which can live untouched by longing for the Beloved is no better than a cremation ground.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that anyone who goes on living without even one kind word from the beloved must be the hardest of hearts; Farid likewise sees a life untouched by longing for the Beloved as already dead.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 36) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: For twenty years Penelope receives no word from Odysseus; she weeps nightly for him, weaving and unweaving the shroud to hold off her suitors, and tells the disguised stranger that she wastes her heart away in longing.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope’s endurance without any message from her husband is the Greek model of faithful waiting.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope is the Kural’s ‘brave soul’ who lives on without a single sweet word from her beloved.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that distance does not dissolve friendship outright but interrupts its activity, and quotes the saying that lack of conversation has broken many a friendship.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, love lives through shared words and company, and withers when communication stops.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine endures exactly what Aristotle says love can hardly survive: no conversation, not even a kind word.

real_life_example.event_title: Beethoven's letter to the Immortal Beloved
real_life_example.event: In July 1812, at the spa town of Teplitz, Beethoven wrote a passionate ten-page letter in pencil to a woman he addressed only as his Immortal Beloved. The letter was apparently never sent; it was found among his belongings after his death on 26 March 1827, and scholars still do not know for certain who it was meant for. Beethoven never married.
real_life_example.explanation: The letter shows a great love that, as far as the record shows, never became a shared life, and Beethoven went on working for fifteen more years without it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls those who go on living without a sweet word from their beloved the hardest, or bravest, of all, and Beethoven's unsent letter points to that kind of endurance.

tamil:
நசைஇயார் நல்கார் எனினும் அவர்மாட்டு
இசையும் இனிய செவிக்கு.
transliteration:
Nasai-iyaar nalkaar eninum avarmaattu
isaiyum iniya sevikku.
meaning: Even if the one I long for shows me no kindness, anything I hear about him is still sweet to my ears.
elementary: Sometimes when you miss someone, just hearing their name makes you smile, even if they haven’t called you. The girl in this couplet feels that way: anything about him sounds like music.
university: Nacaiiyār (with alapeṭai) is ‘the one longed for’; nalkār eṉiṉum, ‘even though he grants no grace’; avar māṭṭu icaiyum, ‘even what is heard of / from him’, is iṉiya cevikku, ‘sweet to the ear.’ The word icai is read two ways: as ‘fame, praise’ (Parimelazhagar’s line, followed by Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan and Kalaignar: hearing others praise him is honey to her), or as ‘word, sound’ (Pappaiah: any word from him is sweet). Pope follows the second: ‘Though he my heart desires no grace accords to me, / Yet every accent of his voice is melody.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Venu Gita, the gopis, apart from Krishna as he grazes the cattle in the forest, describe to one another how the sound of his flute enchants them, the deer, the cows and even the rivers.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis find even the distant sound of Krishna’s flute overwhelmingly sweet while they cannot be with him.
hinduism.tie_back: As the heroine finds any word of her beloved sweet, the gopis delight in the far-off music that tells them of Krishna.

christianity.quote_or_event: “let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.”
christianity.explanation: In the Song of Solomon the lover asks only to hear the beloved’s voice, because it is sweet.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that the beloved’s voice and words are sweet to the ear whatever else he gives.

islam.quote_or_event: A verse attributed to Majnun says that he passes by the walls of Layla’s dwelling and kisses this wall and that, not for love of the houses, but for love of the one who lives within them.
islam.explanation: Majnun, kept from Layla, finds sweetness in anything connected with her.
islam.tie_back: Majnun’s love for her very walls matches the heroine’s delight in anything heard of her beloved, though he gives her nothing.
islam.source: Attributed to Qays ibn al-Mulawwah (Majnun Layla), Diwan (paraphrase)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hark! my beloved! behold, he cometh, leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills.”
judaism.explanation: The maiden’s heart leaps at the mere sound of her beloved before she even sees him.
judaism.tie_back: The sound of the beloved delights her just as, in the Kural, every word of him is sweet to the heroine’s ears.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Nanda, the Buddha’s half-brother, is led into the order on his wedding day, but he cannot stop thinking of his bride, the Beauty of the Land, who called after him to come back soon; he tells the monks he is discontent because her parting words stay with him.
buddhism.explanation: The Udana tells how a single remembered word from the beloved kept Nanda’s heart bound to her.
buddhism.tie_back: Nanda’s memory of his bride’s words mirrors the heroine’s sense that every word of her beloved is sweet, though the Buddha leads Nanda beyond it.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain tradition holds that when a Tirthankara preaches in the samavasarana, his divine sound (divya-dhvani) is understood by every listener in its own language and delights gods, humans and even animals.
jainism.explanation: For Jains the voice of the Jina is the sweetest of all sounds, attracting every being.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine finds her beloved’s words sweet even without his grace; Jainism directs that delight in a voice toward the Jina instead.
jainism.source: Jain doctrine of the samavasarana and divya-dhvani (paraphrase; cf. Tattvartha tradition and the Kalpa Sutra’s account of Mahavira’s preaching)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Continually listening to Your Glory, I live.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that hearing about the Lord's glory is what keeps him alive.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that even if her beloved shows her no kindness, every word about him is sweet to her ears; Guru Arjan likewise lives on simply hearing the Beloved's praise.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 388, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo, able only to repeat the last words she hears, falls in love with Narcissus, who rejects her; she follows him, cherishing and repeating his words, and wastes away until only her voice remains.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Echo lives on the words of a beloved who gives her no love in return.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echo is the Kural’s heroine taken to its extreme: his words are all she has, and they are still sweet to her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal recognises that love follows its own logic, which argument cannot overturn.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s delight in the words of one who shows her no kindness is just such a reason of the heart.

real_life_example.event_title: Dante writes La Vita Nuova in praise of Beatrice
real_life_example.event: Dante first saw Beatrice, usually identified as Beatrice Portinari, when he was nine, and he saw her only rarely after that. She married Simone de' Bardi and died in 1290 at about twenty-four. Around 1293 Dante wrote La Vita Nuova, prose and poems tracing his devotion to her, and ended it with a vow to write of her as no woman had been written of before, a vow he fulfilled in the Divine Comedy.
real_life_example.explanation: Dante received almost nothing from Beatrice in life, yet speaking and writing of her became the centre of his poetry.
