sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das, speaking as the longing soul-bride, says she would give herself away to whoever brings her Beloved to meet her.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife wonders what feast could repay the dream that brought word of her husband; the Guru's bride likewise has nothing smaller to offer such a go-between than her whole self.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: While Penelope sleeps in grief, Athena sends a phantom in the likeness of her sister Iphthime, who stands over her head and comforts her with the message that her absent son Telemachus will return safely.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer gives the anxious wife a dream-messenger sent from outside to carry word of an absent loved one.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope’s dream-envoy is the Greek twin of the Kural’s dream ‘that came with my beloved’s messenger’.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 4.795-841 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In prison Socrates tells Crito he has dreamed of a fair woman in white who called him and spoke a line from Homer, telling him that on the third day he would come to fertile Phthia.
philosophy.explanation: Plato presents a dream as a gracious visitor delivering a message that Socrates trusts and acts upon.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates’ dream-woman, like the Kural’s dream, arrives as a courier from beyond and is welcomed rather than dismissed.
philosophy.source: Plato, Crito 44a-b (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Thutmose IV sets up the Dream Stela at the Sphinx
real_life_example.event: A granite stela set up in front of the Great Sphinx at Giza records that Prince Thutmose fell asleep in the Sphinx's shade and dreamed that the Sphinx, speaking as the sun god, promised him the throne if he would clear away the sand that buried it. After becoming king, Thutmose IV restored the Sphinx and erected the stela to record the dream. Scholars often read the inscription as royal propaganda supporting the legitimacy of his reign.
real_life_example.explanation: The stela is one of the oldest surviving records of a dream treated as a message worth honouring with action and a monument.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine wonders what feast she could give to the dream that brought her a message, and Thutmose IV repaid his dream-messenger with a restoration and a monument.

tamil:
கயலுண்கண் யானிரப்பத் துஞ்சிற் கலந்தார்க்கு
உயலுண்மை சாற்றுவேன் மன்.
transliteration:
Kayalunkan yaanirappath thunjir kalandhaarkku
uyalunmai saatruvaen man.
meaning: If my fish-shaped eyes would only fall asleep when I beg them, I could tell my love, when he comes in my dream, how hard it has been to stay alive.
elementary: Have you ever had so much to tell someone that you lay awake and couldn’t sleep? This girl wants to fall asleep so she can meet her faraway husband in a dream and tell him how hard it has been, but the worry keeps her eyes wide open.
university: Kayal uṇ kaṇ, ‘carp-like eyes lined with collyrium’, is a stock Sangam image of feminine beauty, here made pathetic: the eyes that once drew the lover now refuse the sleep (tuñcil, ‘if they sleep’) that would let her meet him. Yāṉ irappa means ‘as I beg’, casting the heroine as a supplicant to her own eyes. Kalantārkku, ‘to him who united with me’, names the husband by their past union; uyal uṇmai is ‘the truth of my survival’, i.e. how she has scraped through the separation, and cāṟṟuvēṉ ‘I would declare’. The closing particle maṉ marks a wish that cannot be fulfilled, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan render as ‘I would tell him, if only’. Pope: ‘If my dark, carp-like eye will close in sleep, as I implore, / The tale of my long-suffering life I’ll tell my loved one o’er.’ Both base sources print the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Captive in Lanka, Sita entrusts Hanuman with a message for Rama telling him how she has endured, and warns that she can hold on to life only a little longer unless he comes.
hinduism.explanation: The Sundara Kanda turns a separated wife’s account of her own survival into the message she most needs her husband to hear.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita’s message is what the Kural’s heroine longs to deliver, the ‘truth of how I have survived’, if only sleep would let her meet her husband.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, Sita’s message to Rama through Hanuman (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song of Solomon lies awake at night seeking the beloved who is absent.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s sleepless heroine, she spends the night on her bed searching for a meeting that will not come.

islam.quote_or_event: “I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.”
islam.explanation: Jacob, long separated from Joseph, will pour out his grief only before God.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also has a tale of suffering she longs to pour out; she seeks a hearing from her beloved in sleep, where Jacob seeks it from God.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou holdest fast the lids of mine eyes; I am troubled, and cannot speak.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist lies awake in distress, his eyelids held open, unable to put his trouble into words.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s predicament exactly reversed into lament: sleeplessness that keeps one from speaking one’s sorrow.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Asked whether he slept well on a cold night on leaves, the Buddha says he did, and explains that a householder in a fine bed may still lie awake, burned by fevers born of passion, while one who has let passion go sleeps at ease.
buddhism.explanation: The Hatthaka discourse ties sleeplessness directly to desire.
buddhism.tie_back: From a Buddhist angle, the Kural’s heroine cannot sleep for exactly this reason: her longing is the fever that keeps her eyes open.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 3.35, Hatthaka Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that one who becomes attached to beautiful forms through the eye brings misery on himself, never finding satisfaction and suffering when the object is absent.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching traces suffering to the senses’ attachment to what they love to see.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine suffers precisely because her eyes are bound to a beloved they cannot see; Jainism would counsel loosening that attachment rather than seeking it in sleep.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 32 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “This night, I did not sleep with my Husband Lord, and now my body is suffering in pain. Go and ask the deserted bride, how she passes her night.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid speaks as a bride kept from her Husband Lord for a single night, and says only a deserted wife knows how such nights are survived.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife begs her eyes to sleep so that she can tell her beloved in a dream how barely she has lived through his absence; Farid's bride likewise wants someone to hear how the night of separation is endured.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 30) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: A short lyric fragment traditionally attributed to Sappho says that the moon and the Pleiades have set, it is midnight, the hours pass, and the speaker lies alone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek lyric captures the lover lying awake through the hours of night without the beloved.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shares that midnight vigil, with the added ache that sleep itself would bring her love to her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle explains sleep as a natural seizing of the primary sense-faculty that renders it unable to function, arising from bodily processes rather than from choice.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, sleep is not something the will can summon; it comes by nature.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine begs her eyes to sleep, and Aristotle explains why begging does not work: sleep is not under the will’s command.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, On Sleep and Waking (De Somno), Parva Naturalia (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Mary Shelley's waking dream gives her Frankenstein
real_life_example.event: In June 1816 Mary Godwin, later Mary Shelley, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Lord Byron and their companions were kept indoors by bleak weather near Lake Geneva, and Byron proposed that each of them write a ghost story. Mary struggled to think of one until a waking dream showed her a pale student kneeling beside the figure he had put together and seeing it stir to life. That image grew into Frankenstein, published anonymously in 1818.
real_life_example.explanation: What she could not find by trying while awake came to her only in a dream-like state at night.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine pleads with her eyes to sleep so that a dream can give her what waking will not; Mary Shelley likewise found in a waking dream what days of effort had failed to give her.

tamil:
நனவினால் நல்கா தவரைக் கனவினால்
காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்.
transliteration:
Nanavinaal nalkaa thavaraik kanavinaal
kaantalin unten uyir.
meaning: He is not kind to me while I am awake. But I see him in my dreams, and that is what keeps me alive.
elementary: Think of a plant on a windowsill that only gets a little sunlight each morning. It is just enough to keep it alive. For this woman, seeing her husband in dreams is that little bit of sunlight that keeps her going until he comes home.
university: The couplet sets up the chapter’s governing antithesis of naṉavu (waking) and kaṉavu (dream), each in the instrumental (naṉaviṉāl, kaṉaviṉāl, ‘by waking’, ‘by dream’). Nalkātavar, ‘he who does not grant grace’, from nalku (to show favour, bestow love), names the absent husband by his failure to come; the word recurs through the chapter (1214, 1217, 1219) and functions almost as an epithet. Kāṇṭaliṉ, ‘because of seeing’, gives the cause, and uṇṭu eṉ uyir, ‘my life exists’, makes the dream the slender thread on which her life hangs. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss it as ‘my life has not yet left me only because I see him in dreams’. Pope: ‘Him, who in waking hour no kindness shows, / In dreams I see; and so my lifetime goes!’ The text is identical in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Bhasa’s play, King Udayana, believing his queen Vasavadatta dead, murmurs to her in his sleep; she, actually alive and in disguise nearby, gently touches him and slips away, and on waking he cannot tell whether he has dreamed her or truly seen her.
hinduism.explanation: The ‘Vision of Vasavadatta’ makes a dream the only place where a grieving husband can still meet his wife.
hinduism.tie_back: Udayana, like the Kural’s heroine, is kept going by seeing in dreams the spouse whom waking life denies him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It was but a little that I passed from them, but I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go.”
christianity.explanation: After a night of fruitless searching, the bride in the Song of Solomon at last finds her beloved and clings to him; many interpreters read the scene as a night-vision.
christianity.tie_back: Her finding the beloved after vain searching is the Kural’s dream-meeting, the encounter that keeps the seeker alive.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever sees me in a dream will see me in his wakefulness, and Satan cannot imitate me in shape.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet assures believers who long for him that seeing him in a dream is a true sight, a promise of meeting him in waking.
islam.tie_back: For the Kural’s heroine too, the dream-sight of the absent beloved is real enough to sustain her until waking union returns.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh; Hark! my beloved knocketh: ‘Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled.’”
judaism.explanation: The Shulammite, asleep, hears her beloved come to her door in what reads as a dream-visit.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved comes to the sleeper when he cannot be had by day, and that visit keeps the heart awake and alive.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that from what is dear springs grief and from what is dear springs fear; for one wholly free from endearment there is no grief.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism sees the heart’s dependence on a loved one as the very source of sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine stakes her life on dream-glimpses of the beloved; the Buddhist verse explains why such dependence brings both her sustenance and her pain.

jainism.quote_or_event: In Jain retellings of the Ramayana, Sita in Ravana’s captivity is sustained by unbroken fidelity to Rama and by the news of him that Hanuman brings.
jainism.explanation: Jain narrative presents a separated wife whose constancy to an absent husband keeps her alive through captivity.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise survives on the image of the husband who is not with her, though she finds it in dreams rather than in vows.
jainism.source: Vimalasuri, Paumacariya, Sita’s captivity (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In a dream, I was lifted up; why didn't I grasp the hem of His Robe?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan's soul-bride recalls rising to meet her Lord in a dream, the only place she glimpsed Him, and reproaches herself for not holding on.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that he who shows no grace while she is awake is still seen in her dreams, and that this keeps her alive; the Guru's bride too has her Lord only in a dream.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1362, Phunhay, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Often you will gladden me, appearing in my dreams; for sweet it is to look on those we love in dreams, however brief the night.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Admetus, about to lose his wife Alcestis, consoles himself that she will still come to him in dreams.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s comfort almost word for word: when waking life withholds the beloved, dream-sight keeps the lover going.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Alcestis 354-356 (tr. Richard Aldington, via the Internet Classics Archive)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that dream-images are residual movements left in the sense-organs by earlier perceptions, which persist after the perceived object has gone and present themselves in sleep.
philosophy.explanation: On Aristotle’s account, the sight of an absent person survives within us after the person departs.
philosophy.tie_back: The beloved who no longer comes by day still reaches the Kural’s heroine at night because, as Aristotle explains, his image lingers in her.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, On Dreams (De Insomniis) 460b-461a, Parva Naturalia (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Ono no Komachi's dream poems enter the Kokinshu
real_life_example.event: Ono no Komachi was a ninth-century poet of the Heian court, and eighteen of her poems were included in the imperial anthology Kokinshu, compiled in 905. Several are dream poems: in one, having seen the man dear to her while she napped, she says she has begun to trust the things called dreams; in another she says that had she known it was a dream, she would never have woken.
real_life_example.explanation: Komachi's poems are among the most famous in Japanese literature on meeting a lover only in dreams.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says that though her husband shows no kindness while she is awake, seeing him in dreams keeps her alive, which is the very theme of Komachi's dream poems.

tamil:
கனவினான் உண்டாகும் காமம் நனவினான்
நல்காரை நாடித் தரற்கு.
transliteration:
Kanavinaan undaakum kaamam nanavinaan
nalkaarai naatith thararku.
meaning: Love's joy comes to me in my dreams, because the dream goes looking for the one who is not kind to me when I am awake, and brings him to me.
elementary: Imagine a friendly dog that runs off every night and comes back pulling your best friend by the sleeve so you can play together. Here the dream is like that helpful dog: it goes and finds the husband who is far away and brings him home, just for the night.
university: Here the dream is not merely a place but an agent: nāṭi, ‘having searched out’, and taraṟku, ‘in order to give, bring’, make it a go-between who fetches the reluctant lover. The forms kaṉaviṉāṉ and naṉaviṉāṉ use the older instrumental ending -āṉ for -āl, a metrical variant noted in Tamil grammatical tradition. Kāmam here is the pleasure of love, not mere desire; nalkārai repeats the epithet ‘him who grants no grace’ from 1213. Varadarasanar reads the couplet as ‘love-incidents arise in dreams in order to seek out and bring the lover’, while Pappaiah and Kalaignar shift the stress to the joy the dream gives by bringing him. Pope: ‘Some pleasure I enjoy when him who loves not me / In waking hours, the vision searches out and makes me see.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Princess Usha sees in a dream a handsome youth she has never met and falls in love; her friend Chitralekha paints portraits until Usha recognises him as Aniruddha, Krishna’s grandson, and then by her yogic power fetches him from Dvaraka to Usha’s chamber.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana tells of a dream that first reveals the beloved and then leads to his being searched out and brought to the dreamer.
hinduism.tie_back: Usha’s dream, which ends with the beloved literally fetched to her side, is the Kural’s ‘dream that seeks him out and brings him’ made into narrative.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: In the night-scene of the Song of Solomon, the bride rises from her bed to go searching the city for her beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The night-search the bride undertakes is what the Kural’s dream does on the heroine’s behalf: it goes looking for the lover who does not come.

islam.quote_or_event: “O my father, this is the explanation of my vision of before. My Lord has made it reality.”
islam.explanation: Joseph, reunited at last with the father from whom he was torn, recognises in the reunion the fulfilment of his boyhood dream.
islam.tie_back: Joseph’s dream finally brought the separated family together, as the Kural’s dream brings the absent husband to his wife.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person is shown in his dream only the thoughts of his heart.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani, citing Rabbi Yonatan, teaches that dreams draw their images from the dreamer’s waking thoughts.
judaism.tie_back: This explains the Kural’s dream: the heart that dwells on the absent husband all day sends the dream to find him by night.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 55b (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: Nagasena tells King Milinda that dreams arise in six ways, among them from what the dreamer has been habitually occupied with, and from portents of what is to come.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist analysis recognises that the mind’s habitual preoccupations generate dream-images.
buddhism.tie_back: On Nagasena’s account, the Kural’s dream is fetched by the heroine’s own constant preoccupation with her husband.
buddhism.source: Milindapanha, the dilemma on dreams (paraphrase; cf. tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, SBE 36)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Bhagavati Sutra’s discussion of dreams distinguishes several kinds, including a dream that arises from what one has been thinking about while awake (cinta-svapna).
jainism.explanation: Jain canonical teaching recognises dreams produced by the waking mind’s preoccupations.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s love-dream that ‘seeks out’ the husband is, in Jain terms, a cinta-svapna born of her constant thought of him.
jainism.source: Bhagavati Sutra (Vyakhyaprajnapti), Shataka 16, on dreams (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “... the friendly True Guru has come into my dream beautifully attired and adored.”
sikhism.explanation: In one of his Kabits Bhai Gurdas describes the True Guru coming to him in a dream, dressed in beauty, so that the meeting denied in waking life happens in sleep.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says love's joy comes in dreams because the dream seeks out and brings the one who will not come by day; Bhai Gurdas likewise receives his Beloved through a dream.
sikhism.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabit Savaiye, Kabit 205 (English translation as given on BaniDB)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Juno sends Iris to the house of Sleep, who dispatches his son Morpheus to take the form of the drowned king Ceyx and stand by the bed of his longing wife Alcyone, so that she may see him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid has the god of dreams go out and fetch the absent husband’s likeness to his waiting wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Morpheus does exactly what the Kural’s dream does: he goes and brings the husband who cannot come in waking life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Freud argues that, when the work of interpretation is completed, a dream proves to be the fulfilment of a wish.
philosophy.explanation: For Freud the dream stages the very satisfaction waking life withholds.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s dream, which supplies the love denied by day, is a textbook instance of Freud’s wish-fulfilling dream, stated two thousand years earlier.
philosophy.source: Sigmund Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams, ch. 3 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.A. Brill)

real_life_example.event_title: Otto Loewi's dream leads to the frog-heart experiment
real_life_example.event: The pharmacologist Otto Loewi, professor at Graz, said that one night in 1921 he woke from a dream about an experiment, scribbled notes and in the morning could not read them. The next night the idea returned around 3 a.m. and he went straight to his laboratory. By transferring fluid from a frog heart slowed through its vagus nerve to a second heart, which then also slowed, he showed that nerves pass signals by chemicals, work for which he shared the 1936 Nobel Prize with Henry Dale.
real_life_example.explanation: Loewi's own account credits a dream with bringing back an answer that his waking mind had lost.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says love's joy comes in dreams because the dream goes out, finds the one who will not come in waking life, and brings him back; Loewi's dream likewise fetched what waking could not hold.

tamil:
நனவினால் கண்டதூஉம் ஆங்கே கனவுந்தான்
கண்ட பொழுதே இனிது.
transliteration:
Nanavinaal kandadhooum aange kanavundhaan
kanda pozhudhae inidhu.
meaning: Seeing him while I was awake was sweet only while it lasted. Seeing him in a dream is just the same, sweet for the moment I see him.
elementary: An ice-cream cone is lovely while you are eating it, and then it’s gone. A dream about someone you love is the same: it is just as lovely while it lasts. This woman says both kinds of seeing, awake and dreaming, are sweet, but only in the moment.
university: Kaṇṭatūum is kaṇṭatu, ‘what was seen’, with uyir-aḷapeṭai, the metrical prolongation of the vowel (-ūum) that Tamil prosody uses to fill out a foot. Āṅkē, ‘just then, at that time’, and kaṇṭa poḻutē, ‘at the very moment of seeing’, set the two experiences on a level: both sweetnesses are bounded by the moment. Varadarasanar stresses the limitation (‘only at that time… only at the time it is seen’), whereas Pappaiah and Kalaignar stress the equality (‘both were pleasures to me’); the couplet can carry both, a consolation tinged with the knowledge that waking joy too was fleeting. Pope: ‘As what I then beheld in waking hour was sweet, / So pleasant dreams in hour of sleep my spirit greet.’ Both base sources print the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Mandukya Upanishad describes the dream state (taijasa) as a condition of consciousness turned inward that enjoys its own subtle objects, as the waking state enjoys gross ones.
hinduism.explanation: Vedantic analysis treats dreaming and waking as parallel states of experience, each with its own real enjoyment.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine reaches the same parity from the side of feeling: the dream-sight of her husband is enjoyed as fully as the waking one was.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song of Solomon savours the sweetness of being near her beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural measures dream-sight against exactly this remembered sweetness of being with the beloved, and finds it equal.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that nothing of prophethood remains after him except glad tidings, and explained these as good, true dreams.
islam.explanation: In the Sunni tradition, a good dream is a real portion of blessing granted to the believer.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise refuses to discount the dream: its sweetness is as real as waking joy.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Interpretation of Dreams, on al-mubashshirat (paraphrase)

judaism.quote_or_event: “When the LORD brought back those that returned to Zion, We were like unto them that dream. Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist likens the joy of a longed-for homecoming to the joy of dreaming.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts set dream-joy and real joy side by side as equally sweet, the psalm by simile, the Kural by experience.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The closing verse of the Diamond Sutra bids the disciple regard all conditioned things as a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, as dew or a flash of lightning.
buddhism.explanation: Mahayana teaching places waking experience and dreams on the same fleeting footing.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine arrives at the same parity, waking sweetness and dream sweetness both lasting only ‘while seen’, but she treasures what the sutra counsels letting go.

jainism.quote_or_event: “These my excellent and pre-eminent dreams shall not be counteracted by other bad dreams.” Accordingly she remained awake to save her dreams by means of (hearing) good, auspicious, pious, agreeable stories about gods and religious men.
jainism.explanation: Queen Trisala treasures her auspicious dreams so much that she stays awake to keep their sweetness intact.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Trisala holds that a good dream is a real treasure whose sweetness belongs to the time it is seen and must be guarded.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §§54-55 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The world is a drama, staged in a dream. In a moment, the play is played out.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that worldly life is as passing as a dream, a show that ends in a moment.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife finds that seeing her husband awake was sweet only while it lasted, just like seeing him in a dream; Gurbani goes further and calls waking life itself a dream that is over in a moment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 18, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “This very night methought there was one lying by my side who was like Ulysses as he was when he went away with his host, and I rejoiced, for I believed that it was no dream, but the very truth itself.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope tells how, in a dream, her long-absent husband seemed beside her as he was when he left, and her joy was as full as if it were real.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim lived out: the dream-sight of the absent husband was, while it lasted, as sweet as waking union.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 20 (tr. Samuel Butler, via the Internet Classics Archive)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates asks Theaetetus how anyone could prove whether we are now asleep or awake, noting that in dreams we believe what we see just as firmly as in waking life.
philosophy.explanation: Plato observes that, at the time it is had, a dream experience carries the same conviction as waking experience.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the emotional version of Plato’s point: in the moment of seeing, dream and waking are equally sweet.
philosophy.source: Plato, Theaetetus 158b-d (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Kekulé describes the dream behind the benzene ring
real_life_example.place: Berlin, Germany, recalling his time at Ghent, Belgium
real_life_example.event: In 1865, while a professor at Ghent, August Kekulé published his proposal that the six carbon atoms of benzene form a ring. At a celebration in Berlin in 1890 marking the 25th anniversary of the theory, he told his audience that the idea had come to him while dozing by the fire, when he saw a snake seize its own tail. Most historians accept the account, though some suspect he was strengthening his claim to priority.
real_life_example.explanation: A fleeting dream image, gone the moment he woke, became one of the foundations of organic chemistry.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that a dream meeting is sweet for exactly the moment it is seen, just as a waking one was; Kekulé's brief dream image mattered only in the moment of seeing it, and he had to seize it before it vanished.

tamil:
நனவென ஒன்றில்லை ஆயின் கனவினால்
காதலர் நீங்கலர் மன்.
transliteration:
Nanavena ondrillai aayin kanavinaal
kaadhalar neengalar man.
meaning: If there were no such thing as being awake, my love, who comes to me in dreams, would never leave me.
elementary: Have you ever had a really happy dream and felt sad when the alarm clock rang? This woman wishes there were no alarm clock at all, no waking up, so that the husband she sees in her dreams could stay with her forever.
university: Naṉavu eṉa oṉṟu illai āyiṉ, ‘if there were no one thing called waking’, is a bold counterfactual that makes waking itself the villain; Pappaiah even calls it ‘a cruel sinner’ (koṭiya pāvi), and Kalaignar has it ‘suddenly coming to spoil’ the meeting. Nīṅkalar, ‘he would not depart’, describes the lover in the dream, and the final particle maṉ again marks an impossible wish, as in 1212. The couplet inverts the common wisdom that dreams are unreal and waking true: for the heroine, waking is what takes the beloved away. Pope: ‘And if there were no waking hour, my love / In dreams would never from my side remove.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says that in dreams there are no chariots, horses or roads, yet the self creates chariots, horses and roads, joys and delights, for itself, being their maker.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad describes the dream-world as one the self fashions and fully inhabits while it lasts.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wishes she could live wholly in that self-made world where her beloved never departs.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.”
christianity.explanation: The bride in the Song of Solomon repeatedly asks that love not be roused before its time, guarding a blissful repose.
christianity.tie_back: Her plea not to wake echoes the Kural’s wish that waking would never come to break the lovers’ union.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die [He takes] during their sleep. Then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others for a specified term.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes sleep as a temporary taking of the soul, released again at waking.
islam.tie_back: For the Kural’s heroine the soul’s nightly absence is where she meets her beloved; its release into waking is the parting she laments.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it shall be as when a hungry man dreameth, and, behold, he eateth, But he awaketh, and his soul is empty.”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah’s image captures the dreamer who is satisfied in sleep and left empty on waking.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s complaint exactly: in the dream the beloved is present, and waking leaves her empty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a man doesn’t see, on awakening, what he met in a dream, even so he doesn’t see, when they are dead, their time done, those he held dear.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the vanishing of dream-companions at waking as the image of how loved ones are lost.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural states the same experience from inside: waking is what makes the beloved met in the dream disappear.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 4.6, Jara Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga Sutra contrasts the unwise, who sleep, with the sages, who are always awake, making wakefulness the mark of spiritual life.
jainism.explanation: Jain scripture prizes vigilance and treats ‘sleep’ as delusion.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wishes waking away; Jainism, by contrast, would call her dream-bound love the true sleep from which one must awake.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.3.1 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Enjoying the bliss of divine dream, I was woken up by the voice of rain-bird and that broke my celestial dream. The awe and marvel of love-filled state disappeared reawakening the pangs of separation. I was restless like a fish out of water.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas describes a dream of union with the Guru broken by the call of the rain-bird, so that waking brings back the pain of separation.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that if there were no such thing as waking, her beloved would never leave her; in Bhai Gurdas it is exactly the moment of waking that ends the meeting and leaves the lover like a fish out of water.
sikhism.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabit Savaiye, Kabit 205 (English translation as given on BaniDB)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The ghost of Patroclus comes to Achilles in his sleep and asks for burial; Achilles stretches out his arms to embrace his friend, but the spirit vanishes like smoke beneath the earth, and Achilles springs up awake in amazement.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows the beloved met in sleep slipping away at the very moment the dreamer reaches for him and wakes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ lost embrace is what the Kural’s heroine fears every dawn: waking is what makes the beloved leave.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 23.65-107 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal remarks that if we dreamed the same thing every night, it would affect us as much as the objects we see every day; it is chiefly the continuity of waking life that makes us call it real.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal suggests that what separates dream from waking is only waking’s steady continuity.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural imagines removing that very continuity, abolishing waking, so that the dream-beloved would become her whole reality.

real_life_example.event_title: Coleridge's Kubla Khan and the person from Porlock
real_life_example.event: Samuel Taylor Coleridge said that several hundred lines of a poem came to him in a dream while he was under the influence of laudanum. On waking he began writing them down but, by his account, was interrupted by a person on business from Porlock, after which the rest of the vision was gone. The surviving 54-line fragment, Kubla Khan, was published in 1816, and some scholars think the interruption story was an excuse.
real_life_example.explanation: The 'person from Porlock' has become a byword for the waking world breaking into, and ending, a precious vision.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says that if there were no such thing as waking, the beloved who comes to her in dreams would never leave; Coleridge's lost poem is the classic case of waking chasing a dream away.

tamil:
நனவினால் நல்காக் கொடியார் கனவனால்
என்எம்மைப் பீழிப் பது.
transliteration:
Nanavinaal nalkaak kotiyaar kanavanaal
en-emmaip peezhip padhu.
meaning: He is cruel and not kind to me when I am awake. So why does he come into my dreams only to hurt me?
elementary: Imagine a friend who never answers your calls in the daytime but keeps popping up in your dreams. You might grumble, ‘If you won’t come and play when I’m awake, why do you keep visiting me at night and making me miss you even more?’
university: The mood turns from gratitude to reproach. Koṭiyār, ‘the cruel one’ (honorific plural), is a lover’s accusation, and pīḻippatu, ‘tormenting’, from pīḻ (to afflict, squeeze), names the pain of a dream that teases without fulfilling. Eṉ is the interrogative ‘why’, and emmai the plural ‘us’, the heroine speaking of herself with the inclusive dignity common in akam speech. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print kaṉavaṉāl in the first line, where many editions have the regular instrumental kaṉaviṉāl; the sense is unaffected. Kalaignar glosses the torment as the dream ‘enlarging the grief of separation’. Pope: ‘The cruel one, in waking hour, who all ungracious seems, / Why should he thus torment my soul in nightly dreams?’

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa’s exiled yaksha tells his wife, through the cloud, that when at last he finds her in a dream and stretches his arms into empty air to embrace her, even the forest deities shed tears like pearls at his plight.
hinduism.explanation: The ‘Cloud Messenger’ dwells on the cruelty of a dream-meeting that ends in arms closing on nothing.
hinduism.tie_back: The yaksha’s empty embrace is the torment the Kural’s heroine complains of: a lover who comes in dreams only to leave her more bereft.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta, Uttaramegha (paraphrase; verse number varies by recension)

christianity.quote_or_event: “When I say, My bed shall comfort me, my couch shall ease my complaint; Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions.”
christianity.explanation: Job finds that even the refuge of sleep becomes a place of torment through dreams.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same complaint: the night that should console her brings dreams that afflict.

islam.quote_or_event: “[It is but] a mixture of false dreams, and we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams.”
islam.explanation: Pharaoh’s courtiers dismiss his troubling dream as a jumble of confused visions.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine might wish to dismiss her teasing dreams the same way, but they torment her precisely because they feel real.

judaism.quote_or_event: Shmuel, when he saw a bad dream, would say “And the dreams speak falsely” (Zechariah 10:2); when he saw a good dream, he would ask whether dreams speak falsely, citing “I speak with him in a dream” (Numbers 12:6).
judaism.explanation: The Talmud records a sage who answered distressing dreams by declaring them empty and welcomed good ones as true.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is caught between those two attitudes: the dream-lover delights her, yet torments her because he will not come in truth.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 55b (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Potaliya discourse the Buddha compares sensual pleasures to a dream: a man dreams of delightful parks, groves and lakes, but on waking sees none of them.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism uses the dream to show how pleasures promise satisfaction and leave nothing behind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels exactly this cheat: the dream gives her the beloved and then leaves her with nothing, which is why she calls it torment.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 54, Potaliya Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Nanamoli and Bodhi)

jainism.quote_or_event: In the dialogue of Citta and Sambhuta, the monk Citta warns his brother, now a pleasure-loving king, that all pleasures in the end bring pain and that delight in them is empty.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that pleasures, however sweet, carry their own suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers this at night: the pleasure of the dream-lover is itself what pains her.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 13, Citta and Sambhuta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In a dream, He came, and went away again; I cried so many tears.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak's soul-bride says her Lord visited her in a dream and left again, and she was left weeping.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife asks why the hard-hearted one who will not come while she is awake visits her dreams only to torment her; Guru Nanak's bride feels the same pain of a dream-visit that ends in tears.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 558, Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope tells the disguised Odysseus that dreams pass through two gates: those that come through the gate of ivory deceive and bring words that are never fulfilled, while those through the gate of horn come true.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer gives the separated wife a theory of deceiving dreams that promise what waking does not deliver.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘cruel one’ who comes only in dreams is just such an ivory-gate dream, sweet in sleep and false by day.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 19.560-567 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius compares lovers to a thirsty man who in sleep seeks to drink and is given only images of water, so that he thirsts still while drinking; so Venus mocks lovers with images that never satisfy.
philosophy.explanation: For Lucretius, love fed on images, above all in dreams, inflames longing instead of quenching it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine suffers exactly this: the dream-image of her husband torments because it cannot satisfy.

real_life_example.event_title: Goya publishes The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters
real_life_example.event: In February 1799 Francisco Goya advertised Los Caprichos, a series of 80 aquatint etchings, in the Diario de Madrid. Plate 43, The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters, shows an artist asleep at his drawing table while owls and bats close in and a lynx watches. Goya's caption explains that imagination abandoned by reason produces impossible monsters, but united with reason it is the mother of the arts.
real_life_example.explanation: The print became one of the most famous images in Western art of sleep bringing torment instead of rest.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine asks why the cruel one who will not come while she is awake visits her dreams only to torment her; Goya's sleeper is likewise beset in sleep by what he cannot escape.

tamil:
துஞ்சுங்கால் தோள்மேலர் ஆகி விழிக்குங்கால்
நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் விரைந்து.
transliteration:
Thunjungaal thoalmelar aaki vizhikkungaal
nenjaththar aavar viraindhu.
meaning: When I sleep, he rests on my shoulders. The moment I wake up, he quickly slips back into my heart.
elementary: Think of a kitten that naps on your shoulder, and when you sit up it darts inside your jacket to stay warm. The husband in this poem is like that: in sleep he is right beside her, and when she wakes up he hurries to hide in her heart, so he is never really gone.
university: This is the chapter’s most celebrated couplet for its grace. Tuñcuṅkāl / viḻikkuṅkāl (‘when I sleep’ / ‘when I wake’) frame a perfect parallel, and tōḷmēlar (‘he who is on my shoulders’) answers neñcattar (‘he who is in my heart’), so that the beloved merely changes residence and is never absent. Viraintu, ‘swiftly’, gives the image a playful quickness, as if he darts inward at the first stir of waking. Pappaiah reads it as ‘my lord, who always lives in my heart, lies on my shoulder when I sleep’, while Kalaignar stresses that on waking ‘he went nowhere, but leapt into my heart and settled there’. The couplet softens the reproach of 1217 into consolation. Pope: ‘And when I sleep he holds my form embraced; / And when I wake to fill my heart makes haste!’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna sends word to the gopis of Vraja through Uddhava that he is never really separated from them, and that he stays far away so that their minds may dwell on him all the more constantly.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana teaches that the absent beloved is held all the closer within the heart of the one who longs.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband who ‘hastens into the heart’ on waking is Krishna’s message in miniature: absence becomes indwelling.

christianity.quote_or_event: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song of Solomon pictures her beloved holding her as she rests.
christianity.tie_back: This is the first half of the Kural’s picture, the beloved resting close as she sleeps; the Kural adds that on waking he moves into her heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We have already created man and know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than [his] jugular vein.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that God, though unseen, is nearer to a person than his own life-vein.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved, unseen by day yet lodged within the heart, is near in this same intimate, invisible way.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Set me as a seal upon thy heart, As a seal upon thine arm; For love is strong as death.”
judaism.explanation: The Shulammite asks to be impressed on her beloved’s heart and arm, so that she is never separate from him.
judaism.tie_back: Heart and arm in the Song match heart and shoulder in the Kural: the beloved is borne on the body and sealed within.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dvedhavitakka discourse the Buddha teaches that whatever one frequently thinks and ponders becomes the inclination of one’s mind.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism observes that sustained attention shapes what the mind turns to of its own accord.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved leaps into the heart the moment she wakes because, as the Buddha notes, the mind turns by habit to what it dwells on.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 19, Dvedhavitakka Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: When Neminatha abandons his wedding procession to renounce the world, his bride Rajimati, keeping him in her heart, refuses another match and herself takes vows, following him on the path.
jainism.explanation: Jain narrative tells of a bride whose devotion to an absent bridegroom becomes the guiding presence of her life.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati, like the Kural’s heroine, carries the departed beloved within; Jainism turns that inner presence toward renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22, Rathanemi (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When I look within my being, I find that my Beloved is with me.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan's bride-soul discovers that the Beloved she longs for is not far off but present inside her.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her husband rests on her shoulders while she sleeps and slips into her heart the moment she wakes; Guru Arjan likewise finds the Beloved dwelling within, never truly absent.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1095, Raag Maaroo, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato’s myth of the winged soul, the lover parted from the beloved is in anguish, but the memory of the beloved’s beauty, held within, gives him joy, and he longs to return to his side.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Phaedrus makes the beloved’s image, kept in the soul, the lover’s consolation in absence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved who moves from shoulder to heart is the same inward image that sustains Plato’s lover between meetings.
greek_mythology.source: Plato, Phaedrus 251d-252a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle compares memory to the impression a signet-ring leaves in wax, a lasting imprint of what was once perceived.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, those we have known leave a stamp in the soul that remains after they are gone.
philosophy.tie_back: The beloved who ‘hastens into the heart’ the moment she wakes is such an imprint, always present to recall.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, On Memory (De Memoria) 450a, Parva Naturalia (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Henri Rousseau paints The Dream for his long-lost Yadwigha
real_life_example.event: Henri Rousseau's last painting, The Dream, was shown at the Salon des Indépendants in Paris in 1910, a few months before his death. It shows a woman reclining on a red sofa in a dense jungle among animals and a flute-playing snake charmer. Rousseau explained that the sleeping woman dreams she has been carried into the forest, and he attached a poem addressed to Yadwigha, a Polish woman he had loved many years before; the painting is now in the Museum of Modern Art, New York.
real_life_example.explanation: At the end of his life Rousseau placed a love from his past inside a dream, where she still lived for him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the beloved rests on the shoulders in sleep and slips into the heart on waking, never truly absent; Rousseau kept his Yadwigha present in a dream picture decades after she was gone from his life.

tamil:
நனவினால் நல்காரை நோவர் கனவினால்
காதலர்க் காணா தவர்.
transliteration:
Nanavinaal nalkaarai noavar kanavinaal
kaadhalark kaanaa thavar.
meaning: Only women who never see their loved ones in dreams will complain about men who are not kind to them while they are awake.
elementary: Suppose your friend moved away, but you write letters every week. Someone who has never had a pen pal might say, ‘Your friend forgot you!’ But you know better, because you hear from them all the time. This woman says the same about her dreams: people who don’t have such dreams just don’t understand.
university: The heroine turns outward to defend her husband against criticism. Nōvar, ‘they grieve over / reproach’, has as subject kaṉaviṉāl kātalark kāṇātavar, ‘those who do not see their lovers through dreams’; nalkārai repeats the chapter’s epithet for the man who ‘shows no grace’. The implication is that her own dreams vindicate him, since he visits her every night. Commentators differ on whom she means: Varadarasanar and Kalaignar make it general (‘women who do not see their lovers in dreams’), while Pappaiah specifies the young women of the town who are unmarried or have never known separation and so blame her husband as loveless. Pope: ‘In dreams who ne’er their lover’s form perceive, / For those in waking hours who show no love will grieve.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Uddhava, sent by Krishna to console the gopis with philosophy, is humbled by the depth of their love for the absent Krishna and comes to wish he could be even a creeper in Vrindavan touched by the dust of their feet.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana shows an outsider, learned but untouched by such love, misjudging the gopis until he sees their devotion from within.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the critics in the Kural, Uddhava first speaks without knowing the inner experience of the lovers; once he sees it, his view reverses.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm describes sleep itself as a gift given to those who are beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees her dream-visits as such a gift; those who lack it are left with ‘the bread of sorrows’ and complaint.

islam.quote_or_event: “They said, ‘By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s sons, who do not share his bond with Joseph, chide him for his unceasing longing.
islam.tie_back: Like the critics in the Kural, Jacob’s sons judge a love they do not share and cannot see from inside.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Zeira says that anyone who sleeps seven days without a dream is called evil, since it suggests that God does not wish to appear to him even in that indirect way.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud treats an absence of dreams as a sign of estrangement from the divine.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly marks those who do not dream of their beloved as the ones who lack the bond, and who therefore misjudge.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 55b (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: Kisa Gotami, mad with grief, carries her dead child from house to house seeking medicine; told to fetch mustard seed from a house where no one has died, she finds none and comes to understand loss from within.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist story shows that understanding of another’s sorrow comes only from shared experience.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s critics blame her husband because they have no share in her dream-experience; Kisa Gotami learns compassion only when she sees her grief is common to all.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 114 / Therigatha commentary, Kisa Gotami (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.W. Burlingame)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Seeing that these fourteen illustrious, beautiful, lucky, blest, auspicious, fortunate, great dreams were taken from her by the Kshatriyani Trisala, she awoke.”
jainism.explanation: The Brahmani Devananda, from whose womb the embryo of Mahavira is transferred, wakes to find her auspicious dreams have passed to another woman.
jainism.tie_back: Devananda is the Jain picture of one who has lost her blessed dreams; the Kural notes that it is those without such dreams who grieve and complain.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Even in her dreams, she does not meet her Husband Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the self-willed soul-bride who is so far from God that she does not meet Him even in her dreams.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says only women who never see their lovers in dreams blame men who stay away; Guru Amar Das likewise singles out the bride who does not meet her Husband even in dreams as the truly forsaken one.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 127, Raag Maajh, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The suitor Agelaus tells Telemachus that while there was hope of Odysseus returning, Penelope’s waiting was understandable, but that it is now clear he will never come home, and she should marry the best of the suitors.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer gives voice to outsiders who, not sharing Penelope’s hope, declare the absent husband gone for good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agelaus is the Kural’s critic in action, judging the absent husband lost because he cannot see what keeps the wife’s faith alive.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 20 (paraphrase of the Samuel Butler translation)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith argues that we have no immediate experience of what others feel and can form an idea of it only by imagining ourselves in their situation.
philosophy.explanation: For Smith, sympathy depends on imaginatively entering another’s circumstances.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s critics, never having been visited by a lover in dreams, cannot enter the heroine’s situation, and so they misjudge her husband.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments I.i.1 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Tchaikovsky and Nadezhda von Meck: a bond without meeting
real_life_example.event: Nadezhda von Meck, the widow of a railway magnate, contacted Tchaikovsky in 1876 and from 1877 paid him an allowance of 6,000 rubles a year, which let him leave teaching at the Moscow Conservatory and compose full time. They exchanged more than 1,200 letters, but she insisted they never meet, and apart from two accidental encounters they never did. In 1890 she abruptly ended the allowance and the correspondence.
real_life_example.explanation: For thirteen years an intense, trusting relationship existed entirely at a distance, without the two ever sitting together.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says only those who never see their lovers in dreams blame them for not coming in waking life; von Meck sustained a deep bond with someone she chose never to meet, finding presence without meeting.

tamil:
நனவினால் நம்நீத்தார் என்பர் கனவினால்
காணார்கொல் இவ்வூ ரவர்.
transliteration:
Nanavinaal namneeththaar enpar kanavinaal
kaanaarkol ivvoo ravar.
meaning: The people of this town say he left me in waking life. Do they not see him coming to me in my dreams?
elementary: Imagine the neighbours saying, ‘Poor girl, her friend never visits.’ But every night her friend calls her on a secret walkie-talkie. She thinks, ‘They just can’t hear what I hear!’ That is how this woman feels about the town’s gossip.
university: The chapter closes by setting the heroine’s private knowledge against public opinion (alar, the town’s gossip that runs through the Kāmattuppāl). Nam nīttār eṉpar, ‘they say he has forsaken us’, reports the townsfolk’s verdict; ivvūravar, ‘the people of this town’, are the critics already glimpsed in 1219. The particle kol makes kāṇārkol a wondering question, ‘do they not see?’, which can be read two ways: Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take it as ‘do they not know that he visits me in dreams?’, whereas Kalaignar turns it back on the townsfolk, ‘do they never see their own departed lovers in dreams?’ Either way the dream, invisible to others, is her proof of his faithfulness. Pope: ‘They say, that he in waking hours has left me lone; / In dreams they surely see him not,- these people of the town.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Sita’s return to Ayodhya, the townspeople whisper doubts about her, unaware of the fidelity she kept through captivity, and Rama, hearing of the talk, bows to public opinion.
hinduism.explanation: The Ramayana’s final book dramatises the cruelty of town gossip that cannot see a wife’s inner truth.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s townsfolk likewise pronounce judgement on a marriage whose real life, here the nightly dream-visits, they cannot see.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, the townspeople’s gossip about Sita (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women? what is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us?”
christianity.explanation: The daughters of Jerusalem, not sharing the bride’s love, question why she prizes an absent beloved so highly.
christianity.tie_back: They are the Kural’s ‘people of this town’: outsiders puzzled by a devotion whose grounds they cannot see.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, I find the smell of Joseph [and would say that he was alive] if you did not think me weakened in mind.” They said, “By Allah, indeed you are in your [same] old error.”
islam.explanation: Jacob senses his long-lost son is near, and those around him dismiss his inner certainty as an old delusion.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces the same scepticism: she knows her beloved has not truly left her, while the town sees only his absence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And they said one to another: ‘Behold, this dreamer cometh.’”
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s brothers mock him as ‘the master of dreams’, scorning visions they do not share.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s townsfolk, likewise dismissing what is seen only in dreams, are blind to the truth the dreamer holds.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells of blind men who each touch one part of an elephant and then quarrel, each sure the whole elephant is like the part he felt.
buddhism.explanation: The parable warns against confident judgements formed from a partial view.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s townsfolk see only the waking half of the marriage and confidently declare the husband gone, missing the nightly half.
buddhism.source: Udana 6.4, Tittha Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain epistemology teaches that reality is known through valid knowledge and partial standpoints (nayas), and that any single standpoint, taken as the whole truth, misleads.
jainism.explanation: Anekantavada warns that judgements formed from one angle grasp only part of a many-sided reality.
jainism.tie_back: The townsfolk judge the marriage from the single standpoint of waking life; the Kural’s heroine knows a second standpoint that changes the verdict.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.6 and 1.33 on pramana and naya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Nathmal Tatia)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The miracle of a dream is known to the one who has seen it. No one else can see it. Then how can anyone else know about it?”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas uses the dream as an image for the Sikh's private meeting with the Guru, which outsiders cannot see or judge.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife answers the town's gossip that her husband has abandoned her by asking whether they cannot see him coming to her in dreams; Bhai Gurdas agrees that what happens in a dream is known only to the one who sees it.
sikhism.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabit Savaiye, Kabit 305 (English translation as given on BaniDB)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Laodamia, whose husband Protesilaus fell at Troy, keeps a likeness of him in her chamber and embraces it; a servant who glimpses this reports that she has a lover, and her father, misunderstanding, has the image burned.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows outsiders misreading a wife’s private communion with her absent husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Laodamia’s household, the Kural’s townsfolk see only the outside and misjudge a love whose real life is hidden from them.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heraclitus is reported as saying that the waking share one common world, whereas each sleeper turns aside into a private world of his own.
philosophy.explanation: The fragment marks the dream as a world others cannot enter or verify.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s townsfolk live only in the common waking world; the heroine’s husband visits her in the private world Heraclitus describes, which they cannot see.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, fragment B89 Diels-Kranz, reported by Plutarch (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Lady Jane Franklin refuses to give up on her husband
real_life_example.place: London, England, and the Canadian Arctic
real_life_example.event: Sir John Franklin's Arctic expedition, which sailed in 1845, was never heard from again. His wife Jane supported the searches from 1848, offered rewards and paid for ships of her own; after the government ended its searches, she bought and equipped the yacht Fox under Leopold McClintock. In 1859 the Fox expedition found a written record near Point Victory on King William Island confirming that the ships had been abandoned and Franklin had died.
real_life_example.explanation: While official opinion gave the expedition up, Jane Franklin kept faith with her husband's memory and finally brought home the truth of his fate.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says the townsfolk claim her husband has abandoned her, but they do not see him with her in her dreams; Jane Franklin likewise held to her own conviction about her husband while the authorities gave him up.

tamil:
மாலையோ அல்லை மணந்தார் உயிருண்ணும்
வேலைநீ வாழி பொழுது.
transliteration:
Maalaiyo allai manandhaar uyirunnum
vaelainee vaazhi pozhudhu.
meaning: Long live you, evening! But you are not really evening at all. You are a deadly time that eats up the lives of wives whose husbands are far away.
elementary: Think of the time of day you used to love most, like when a parent came home and played with you. If that parent had to go far away for a long time, the same hour might suddenly feel sad and heavy instead of happy. The wife in this verse feels that way about evening.
university: Chapter 123, poḻutu kaṇṭu iraṅkal (‘lamenting on seeing the hour’), belongs to the kaṟpiyal (wedded love) section: the wife, separated from her husband, finds that dusk (mālai), once the hour of reunion, now sharpens her grief. The opening couplet is an ironic apostrophe: vāḻi (‘may you live long!’) is a blessing turned to reproach, and maṇantār (‘those who were united/wedded’) is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan as women who knew union and now live apart. The key word vēlai is read two ways: Varadarasanar and Kesikan take it as ‘time, end-time’ (muṭivu kālam), while Mu. Karunanidhi reads vēl, ‘spear’, which is also Pope’s choice (‘a spear that doth devour / The souls of brides’). The couplet text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (the latter spells the chapter title as two words, poḻutukaṇṭu iraṅkal).

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the lake Pampa in springtime, Rama, separated from Sita, finds that the blossoming trees, the bird-calls and the fragrant breeze, which should delight him, only inflame his grief, and he tells Lakshmana that the season itself is tormenting him.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki shows a lover for whom the loveliest scenes of nature become instruments of pain because the beloved is absent.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s evening, Rama’s springtime is a beautiful hour that has turned into an assailant of the separated heart.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs, read in Christian tradition as an image of love between Christ and the soul, gives the bride’s ache when night comes and the beloved is absent.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s wife suffers in exactly that hour when she reaches for her husband and finds him gone.

islam.quote_or_event: “And from the evil of darkness when it settles”
islam.explanation: In Surat al-Falaq the believer seeks refuge in God from the harm that comes as darkness falls.
islam.tie_back: The Kural also treats the coming of dusk as a menace that preys on the vulnerable, though Islam answers it with refuge in God rather than lament.

judaism.quote_or_event: “She weepeth sore in the night, And her tears are on her cheeks; She hath none to comfort her Among all her lovers”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations pictures Jerusalem as a forsaken woman whose grief is sharpest at night, when no one comforts her.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife is likewise a woman whose sorrow peaks as darkness comes and her beloved is not there.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names separation from what is dear as a direct cause of pain and advises loosening the bond.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows that pain at its sharpest; Buddhism diagnoses its root in attachment, so the fit is real but the response differs.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira’s teaching warns that pleasures which are sweet at first turn deadly in the end.
jainism.tie_back: The evening that once brought the wife sweetness now ‘devours lives’, which is the very reversal the Kimpaka simile describes.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “This dream like happening did not let me meet my beloved. Now the death-like night of separation neither ends nor terminates.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhai Gurdas laments that the meeting with his Beloved slipped away, leaving a night of separation that feels like death and will not end.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife tells the evening it is no gentle dusk but a killing time for wives whose husbands are away; Bhai Gurdas likewise feels the night of separation as death itself.
sikhism.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabit Savaiye, Kabit 219 (English translation as given on BaniDB)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope tells the disguised Odysseus that by day she can distract herself with her work and household, but when night comes and everyone sleeps she lies awake and sharp cares crowd her grieving heart.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s faithful wife finds that the coming of night, not the day, is when the absence of her husband becomes unbearable.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s complaint exactly: the day is endurable, but the closing hour turns on the waiting wife.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 19.509-517 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes tells how the original double humans were cut in two, and each half so longed for its other that the halves clung together and began to die of hunger and idleness, unwilling to do anything apart.
philosophy.explanation: The myth makes the longing of separated lovers literally life-threatening.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s claim that the evening ‘eats the lives’ of separated wives speaks the same idea of love-longing as something that can consume life itself.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 191a-b (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Hürrem Sultan's letters to Suleiman on campaign
real_life_example.event: Hürrem, a captive Slavic woman who became the favourite and later the legal wife of the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, wrote him long letters whenever he was away on military campaigns. Historians describe these letters as filled with her love and longing for him, her distress at his absence and her prayers for his safety in battle.
real_life_example.explanation: Her letters are one of the best-documented records from the early modern world of a wife's grief at a husband's long absence, written by the wife herself.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls the evening a killing time for wives whose husbands are away, and Hürrem's letters show exactly that kind of wife, consumed by grief while her husband was far off on campaign.

tamil:
புன்கண்ணை வாழி மருள்மாலை எம்கேள்போல்
வன்கண்ண தோநின் துணை.
transliteration:
Punkannai vaazhi marulmaalai emkaelpoal
vankanna dhoanin thunai.
meaning: Long live you, confused evening! Your eyes look dim and sad like mine. Is your partner as hard-hearted as my husband?
elementary: Sometimes when we are sad, the whole world seems sad with us: a grey sky looks like it is crying too. The wife looks at the fading evening light and asks it, kindly, ‘Did someone leave you too?’
university: Here the wife turns from accusing the evening to commiserating with it: mālai is marul (‘bewildered, dim’, the twilight in which day and night mingle, as Solomon Pappaiah explains) and puṉkaṇṇai (‘you have afflicted, dull eyes’), a picture of fading light as tear-dimmed sight. Kēḷ means a kinsman or intimate, here the husband, and vaṉkaṇṇatu (‘hard-eyed, pitiless’) mirrors puṉkaṇ: her eyes are sad because his are hard. Varadarasanar and Kesikan read the question as ‘is your companion too as merciless as my lover?’, while Pappaiah explicitly asks whether the evening’s husband is cruel like hers. Pope: ‘Thine eye is sad; Hail, doubtful hour of eventide! / Of cruel eye, as is my spouse, is too thy bride?’ The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the close of the Meghaduta, the exiled Yaksha, who has spoken to a passing cloud as a friend and asked it to carry his message to his wife, blesses the cloud that it may never be parted, even for a moment, from its own beloved, the lightning.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s separated lover treats a piece of the sky as a fellow being with a spouse of its own.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife does the same with the evening, imagining that it too has a partner and may share her suffering.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to share one another’s joys and sorrows.
christianity.tie_back: The wife imagines the dusk ‘weeping with her’, the fellow-feeling Paul commends, though here it is projected onto nature.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes Jacob’s eyes clouded by long grief for his absent son.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s dim-eyed dusk (puṉkaṇ) is the same image: eyes dulled by sorrow for someone far away.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For these things I weep; Mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water; Because the comforter is far from me”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations voices grief through the eye, flowing with tears because the one who should comfort is far away.
judaism.tie_back: The wife sees in the evening’s ‘sad eye’ her own tear-dimmed eye, both caused by a comforter who has gone far off.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that not seeing the one we love is itself a form of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife and the evening she pities are both caught in that pain of not seeing the beloved.

jainism.quote_or_event: Prince Arishtanemi (Neminatha), riding to his wedding with Rajimati, hears the cries of animals penned for the wedding feast, has them released and renounces the world; Rajimati is left grieving her bridegroom before she too takes the vows.
jainism.explanation: The Jain canon tells of a bride whose betrothed left her for a higher calling, a departure that seemed hard to her though it was born of compassion.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati could have asked the Kural’s question, ‘is your partner as hard-hearted as mine?’, though Jain tradition frames Neminatha’s leaving as the opposite of cruelty.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The chakvi bird does not long for sleepy eyes; without her beloved, she does not sleep.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak points to the chakvi, the bird said to be parted from her mate every night, as an image of the soul that cannot rest without its Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife sees the dim dusk as a fellow sufferer and asks whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Guru Nanak too finds in nature, in the chakvi parted from her mate at nightfall, a companion in the pain of separation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1273, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Spurned by Narcissus, the nymph Echo hides in lonely caves and wastes away with sleepless grief until her body is gone and only her voice remains among the hills.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid turns a rejected lover’s sorrow into a feature of the landscape itself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife sees a fellow sufferer in the dimming evening, much as Greek myth sees one in the lonely echo.

philosophy.quote_or_event: John Ruskin coined the term ‘pathetic fallacy’ for the way strong emotion leads a poet to credit nature with human feelings, as when a grieving speaker sees cruelty or sorrow in the sea, the crocus or the sky.
philosophy.explanation: Ruskin analyses the habit of the passionate mind to lend its own mood to the outside world.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s question to the ‘sad-eyed’ dusk is a textbook case of the pathetic fallacy, used deliberately by the poet to show how grief colours perception.
philosophy.source: John Ruskin, Modern Painters, vol. 3, part 4, ch. 12 ‘Of the Pathetic Fallacy’ (1856) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Héloïse writes to Abelard of feeling neglected and forgotten
real_life_example.event: After their love affair ended in separation, Héloïse entered the convent of Argenteuil and Peter Abelard became a monk; around 1126 Abelard handed over his foundation, the Paraclete, to Héloïse and her nuns. In the famous letters the two later exchanged, Héloïse called herself the most wretched and unhappy of women and told Abelard that she had been neglected and forgotten by him.
real_life_example.explanation: The letters are among the most celebrated documents of medieval love, showing a woman who kept loving a partner she felt had grown distant.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife asks whether the evening's partner is as hard-hearted as her own, and Héloïse likewise accused her beloved of neglecting her while she went on grieving for him.

tamil:
பனிஅரும்பிப் பைதல்கொள் மாலை துனிஅரும்பித்
துன்பம் வளர வரும்.
transliteration:
Paniarumpip paidhalkol maalai thuniarumpith
thunpam valara varum.
meaning: The pale evening comes as drops of dew begin to form. With it, my distress begins to grow, and my sorrow keeps getting bigger.
elementary: Picture tiny dewdrops forming on leaves as the sun goes down. The wife says her sadness grows the same way, drop by drop, every evening, until it feels much bigger than it did in the morning.
university: The couplet is built on a parallel of two ‘buddings’: paṉi arumpi (dew forms like buds) and tuṉi arumpi (aversion or distress begins to sprout), so that the evening’s dew and the wife’s grief swell together. Paital koḷ describes the evening taking on a sallow, faded hue, recalling the wife’s own pasalai (love-pallor) of chapter 119. Commentators divide on time: Varadarasanar and Kesikan read the whole as the present evening, while Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Karunanidhi contrast an earlier evening that came ‘trembling and pale’ while the husband was near with the present one that brings mounting sorrow; Pope’s couplet explanation follows the latter (‘once came in with trembling and dimness’). Pope: ‘With buds of chilly dew wan evening’s shade enclose; / My anguish buds space and all my sorrow grows.’ Both web texts agree on the wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Radha’s friend tells Krishna that in his absence the cool things of evening, sandal paste, moonlight and the soft breeze, feel to Radha like fire and poison, and her suffering grows night by night.
hinduism.explanation: The great Sanskrit poem of viraha (love in separation) makes the soothing features of dusk into torments for the waiting beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s dewy evening, which should cool, instead makes the wife’s sorrow grow, exactly the reversal Jayadeva paints for Radha.

christianity.quote_or_event: “When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise, and the night be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day.”
christianity.explanation: Job, in his suffering, dreads the coming of night because it stretches his misery until dawn (the KJV margin notes the Hebrew as ‘the evening be measured’).
christianity.tie_back: Like Job, the Kural’s wife finds that the evening does not bring rest but lengthens and deepens her distress.
