islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob, still separated from Joseph, voices a grief that has kept growing, and turns it toward God.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s sorrow likewise keeps ‘growing’; Islam’s model is to pour that mounting grief out before God rather than before the evening.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I am weary with my groaning; Every night make I my bed to swim; I melt away my couch with my tears.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist describes sorrow that returns and swells each night.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife also finds that each nightfall brings a fresh and larger flood of grief.
judaism.source: Psalms 6:7 (JPS 1917, via Sefaria; 6:6 in KJV numbering)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief back to the affection from which it grows.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows grief ‘budding’ and growing each evening; the Dhammapada names the root it grows from.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the same way he who hates ‘colours,’ incurs a long succession of pains; when his mind is filled with hatred, he accumulates Karman which in the end again produces misery.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that aversion to what we perceive is as binding as desire and lengthens our suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The wife now loathes the very sight of evening, and Jain teaching would say that this aversion is itself what makes her sorrow keep growing.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “In the month of Poh, the cold does not touch those, whom the Husband Lord hugs close in His Embrace.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Barah Maha (song of the twelve months), Guru Arjan says the frost of the winter month cannot touch the bride whom her Lord holds close.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's pale evening arrives beaded with dew, and the wife's sorrow buds with it; Guru Arjan implies the converse, that cold and frost wound only the bride whose Husband is away.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 135, Raag Maajh, Barah Maha, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After her son Memnon is killed at Troy, Aurora (Eos), goddess of the dawn, never stops mourning him, and Ovid says her tears still fall over the whole world as the morning dew.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth explains dew as a goddess’s tears of grief for one she has lost.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘dew budding’ at dusk, rising alongside the wife’s sorrow, links dew and grief in the same way.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines longing (desiderium) as the desire to possess a thing that is fed by remembering it and, at the same time, checked by remembering other things that exclude its presence.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, longing is a painful tension between memory of the beloved and awareness that the beloved is absent.
philosophy.tie_back: Each evening reminds the wife both of her husband and of his absence, so by Spinoza’s account her longing must grow, as the Kural says.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part III, Definitions of the Affects 32 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.H.M. Elwes)

real_life_example.event_title: Dante writes La Vita Nuova after the death of Beatrice
real_life_example.event: As a boy of nine, Dante Alighieri glimpsed Beatrice Portinari and fell in love with her, and he remained in love with her until her death in 1290. Stricken with grief, he wrote La Vita Nuova (The New Life) around 1293, a book of sonnets and other poems linked by prose that traces his love from their first meeting through her death and his mourning.
real_life_example.explanation: The book is a founding work of Italian literature and a lasting record of how grief for a lost beloved can grow and take over a life.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes sorrow budding and growing in the one left alone, and Dante's grief after Beatrice's death grew into a whole book of mourning.

tamil:
காதலர் இல்வழி மாலை கொலைக்களத்து
ஏதிலர் போல வரும்.
transliteration:
Kaadhalar ilvazhi maalai kolaikkalaththu
aedhilar poala varum.
meaning: When my love is not here, evening comes at me like enemies marching onto a killing field.
elementary: Imagine a game where a scary character slowly walks toward you and you cannot run. When the wife is alone, the evening feels like that: it creeps closer and closer, and she dreads it.
university: The simile is military and stark: kolaikkaḷam is a ‘field of slaughter’ or execution ground, and ētilar are strangers or foes, so evening approaches the lonely wife like men coming to kill. Kesikan glosses ētilar as highway robbers (āṟalaippār) at a place of murder, Varadarasanar as enemies, and Karunanidhi shifts the image to an enemy’s raised sword; Solomon Pappaiah adds the contrast implicit in the chapter, that the same evening once made her life flourish when her husband was home. Pope’s couplet runs: ‘When absent is my love, the evening hour descends, / As when an alien host to field of battle wends.’ Both web sources give ētilar; a song setting by P. A. Muthukrishnan quoted on thirukkural.net sings it as ētilār, a lyrical lengthening rather than a textual variant.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ashoka grove of Lanka, Sita, separated from Rama, is surrounded by fierce rakshasi guards who threaten to kill and devour her if she will not yield to Ravana, and in her despair she longs for death.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki places the separated wife literally among would-be killers, her grief for Rama sharpened by their menace.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife only feels the evening as such killers; Sita lives the image, alone and threatened while her husband is far away.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, the rakshasis’ threats to Sita (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Prepare ye war against her; arise, and let us go up at noon. Woe unto us! for the day goeth away, for the shadows of the evening are stretched out.”
christianity.explanation: In Jeremiah, invaders preparing to attack cry out as the evening shadows lengthen, linking the fall of evening with the onset of assault.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s evening also arrives with the lengthening shadows of an attacking enemy.

islam.quote_or_event: “When night falls (or it is evening), keep your children close to you for the devils spread out at that time.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet treats nightfall as a dangerous hour when harmful forces spread abroad.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise feels the coming of evening as the arrival of hostile powers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not be afraid of the terror by night, Nor of the arrow that flieth by day; Of the pestilence that walketh in darkness, Nor of the destruction that wasteth at noonday.”
judaism.explanation: Psalm 91 names the terror that walks in the dark and promises that one sheltered by God need not fear it.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife experiences just such a ‘terror by night’ approaching her; the Psalm answers it with trust in divine protection.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada compares death to a great flood that sweeps away a sleeping village, carrying off the person whose mind clings to children and cattle.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism pictures death advancing suddenly on those absorbed in their attachments.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s evening comes like killers to a heart wholly bound up in an absent love, the clinging mind the Dhammapada warns about.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mind of those who always live in unfrequented lodgings, who eat low food, and who subdue their senses, will not be attacked by the foe, Love, who is vanquished as disease is by medicine.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana calls Love a foe that attacks the undisciplined mind.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife feels herself attacked at evening as if by enemies; Jain teaching names the real attacker as love itself.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, that body, within which love of the Lord does not well up - look upon that body as a cremation ground.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid uses the grim image of the cremation ground for a body untouched by the longing of separation from God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife feels the evening come at her like enemies onto a field of slaughter; Farid also reaches for a place of the dead, though he applies it to the heart that feels no longing at all.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 36) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod’s Theogony, Night (Nyx) gives birth to hateful Doom, black Fate and Death, and to Sleep and the tribe of Dreams.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth makes Night the mother of the powers that destroy human life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s evening, coming like killers, is the same dark power that Hesiod sees as the mother of Death.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Theogony 211-212 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius says that as children tremble and fear everything in the blind darkness, so we adults in daylight sometimes fear things no more real than what children dread in the dark.
philosophy.explanation: The Epicurean poet treats dread of the dark as a product of the mind, to be dispelled by understanding.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife dreads the evening as if it were an assassin; Lucretius would say the terror comes from within, not from the hour.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 2.55-58 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.H.D. Rouse)

real_life_example.event_title: The Blitz begins with an evening of bombing over London
real_life_example.event: On Saturday 7 September 1940, starting around 4 pm, hundreds of German planes attacked the docks of east London, beginning the Blitz. London was then bombed for 57 nights in a row; blackout rules dimmed the city's lights, and within weeks about 120,000 people a night were sheltering in Underground stations.
real_life_example.explanation: For Londoners in 1940 nightfall became the hour when the enemy arrived, so the coming of evening itself was something to dread.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that, without her beloved, evening approaches the wife like enemies advancing on a killing ground, and in the Blitz the coming of evening literally meant the coming of an enemy.

tamil:
காலைக்குச் செய்தநன்று என்கொல் எவன்கொல்யான்
மாலைக்குச் செய்த பகை.
transliteration:
Kaalaikkuch cheydhanandru enkol evankolyaan
maalaikkuch cheydha pakai.
meaning: What good did I ever do for the morning, that it is gentle with me? And what wrong did I do to the evening, that it hurts me so much?
elementary: Have you ever felt that one part of the day is friendly and another part is mean to you? The wife feels mornings are kind and evenings are cruel, and she asks, puzzled, what she did to deserve it.
university: The couplet is a pair of rhetorical questions built on the parallel kālaikku / mālaikku (‘to the morning / to the evening’) and naṉṟu / pakai (‘a good turn / enmity’): the wife treats the two times of day as persons who repay her for imagined past conduct. Varadarasanar glosses pakai as ‘a hostile evil’ done to the evening, and Kalaignar adds the implied reason: love-pain grows sharpest when evening comes. The playful logic of reciprocity echoes the Kural’s ethical chapters on returning good for good, now applied absurdly to the hours. Pope: ‘O morn, how have I won thy grace? thou bring’st relief / O eve, why art thou foe! thou dost renew my grief.’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, the nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons. They arise from sense perception, O scion of Bharata, and one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that pleasure and pain come and go with the turning of times and must be borne with equanimity.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife feels the morning as friend and the evening as foe; the Gita answers that such alternations arise from perception and pass in their season.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami, As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is of the LORD’S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.”
christianity.explanation: In the midst of lament, the poet finds that mercy returns fresh with each morning.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise feels the morning as a kindly presence set against a cruel evening.

islam.quote_or_event: “By the morning brightness, And [by] the night when it covers with darkness, Your Lord has not taken leave of you, [O Muhammad], nor has He detested [you].”
islam.explanation: Revealed when the Prophet feared he had been abandoned, Surat ad-Duha sets morning against night and reassures him he has not been forsaken.
islam.tie_back: The wife sets morning against evening and feels herself abandoned; the Qur’an uses the same pair of times to deny abandonment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For His anger is but for a moment, His favour is for a life-time; weeping may tarry for the night, but joy cometh in the morning.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist sets the weeping of the night against the joy of the morning.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s very contrast: night brings tears and the morning brings relief.
judaism.source: Psalms 30:6 (JPS 1917, via Sefaria; 30:5 in KJV numbering)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The opening verses of the Dhammapada teach that the mind goes before all mental states: if one acts or speaks with a corrupted mind, suffering follows as the wheel follows the ox’s foot, and with a pure mind, happiness follows like a shadow.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism locates the source of pain and joy in the mind, not in outside conditions.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife asks what she did to the evening; the Dhammapada would answer that the hour is neutral and the suffering is shaped within.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who passionately hates (a colour), will at the same moment suffer pain. It is the fault of an undisciplined man that he is annoyed (by a colour); it is not the ‘colour’ itself that annoys him.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that the objects of the senses do not themselves cause pain; our passion toward them does.
jainism.tie_back: The wife asks what she did to make the evening her enemy; Jain teaching answers that the evening has done nothing, the pain lies in the mind’s attachment and aversion.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When the sun rises, she sees her beloved with her eyes; she bows and touches his feet.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak completes the image of the chakvi: parted from her mate all night, she is reunited with him when the sun comes up.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife asks what kindness she did the morning that it treats her gently, and what wrong she did the evening that it torments her; the chakvi's lot shows the same pattern, with nightfall bringing separation and sunrise bringing reunion.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1273, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus is favoured throughout his wanderings by Athena yet pursued by the unrelenting anger of Poseidon, so that one god helps and another harms him, and he endures years of suffering for a grudge he only half understands.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s hero lives between a friendly power and a hostile one.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife feels the same split, with a kindly morning and a hostile evening, and asks what she has done to earn each.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 1.19-21, 1.68-79 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus teaches that people are disturbed not by things themselves but by their judgements about things, so that one should blame neither others nor circumstances for one’s distress.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic locates the source of suffering in our opinions rather than in events.
philosophy.tie_back: The evening is not truly the wife’s enemy; on Epictetus’s view it is her judgement of the evening, coloured by absence, that wounds her.
philosophy.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5 (paraphrase; cf. tr. George Long)

real_life_example.event_title: Michitsuna's Mother records lonely nights in the Kagerō Diary
real_life_example.event: The Heian noblewoman known as Michitsuna's Mother recorded twenty years of her life, from 954 to 974, in the Kagerō Diary, centred on her marriage to the powerful courtier Fujiwara no Kaneie, which ended in divorce. One of her poems, later chosen as poem 53 of the anthology Hyakunin Isshu, describes lying alone through the hours of the night until daylight comes and asks whether anyone can understand how empty such a night is.
real_life_example.explanation: The diary is one of the earliest autobiographies by a woman and gives a frank picture of a wife's long waits for a husband who seldom came.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife finds the morning kind and the evening cruel, and this poet's most famous poem dwells on a night of lonely waiting that ends only when daylight comes.

tamil:
மாலைநோய் செய்தல் மணந்தார் அகலாத
காலை அறிந்த திலேன்.
transliteration:
Maalainoi seydhal manandhaar akalaadha
kaalai arindha thilaen.
meaning: While my husband had not yet left my side, I never knew how much pain evening could bring.
elementary: When your best friend is next to you, you do not notice how quiet the house is. Only when they go away do you notice the silence. The wife says she never knew evenings could hurt until her husband left.
university: The couplet turns on the contrast between maṇantār akalāta kālai (‘the time when he who wed me had not departed’) and the present, in which mālai nōy, ‘the evening sickness’, has made itself known. Kālai here is a pun: in the previous couplet it meant ‘morning’, but here it is the old Tamil word for ‘time, season’, a play the commentators make explicit by glossing it as kālam. Solomon Pappaiah stresses that the same evening once gave her joy; Varadarasanar and Kesikan read aṟintatilēṉ as ‘I did not know at all’. Pope: ‘The pangs that evening brings I never knew, / Till he, my wedded spouse, from me withdrew.’ Both web sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Nala, ruined at dice, slips away at night while Damayanti sleeps in the forest; she wakes alone, searches for him, and laments that she never imagined he would leave her.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata’s tale shows a devoted wife who discovers the full pain of the night only after her husband has gone.
hinduism.tie_back: Like Damayanti, the Kural’s wife learned what night-time grief was only after her husband left her side.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus explains that there is no mourning while the bridegroom is present, but sorrow will come when he is taken away.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural states the same truth from the wife’s side: while her bridegroom was with her she knew no evening sorrow, and it came only when he left.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the heart of Moses’ mother became empty [of all else]. She was about to disclose [the matter concerning] him had We not bound fast her heart that she would be of the believers.”
islam.explanation: After setting her infant afloat, Moses’ mother feels the full emptiness of separation, and God steadies her heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise discovers an emptiness she had never known once her beloved is gone.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; But my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved in the Song of Songs discovers his absence only after the moment of nearness has passed.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife also learns the depth of her love’s pain only when he has gone and she cannot find him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In Ashvaghosha’s Buddhacarita, when the charioteer Chandaka returns without Prince Siddhartha, his wife Yashodhara falls to the ground and laments bitterly that her husband has gone and left her alone.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist epic gives voice to the wife whose life changed in an instant when her husband departed.
buddhism.tie_back: Yashodhara, like the Kural’s wife, learns the full weight of grief only when her husband has gone away.
buddhism.source: Ashvaghosha, Buddhacarita, canto 8 (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell, SBE 49)

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a man who passionately desires ‘colours,’ be happy while he gets, keeps, uses, loses, and misses (those things). Even when he enjoys them, he is never satisfied.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that whatever we cling to will bring pain at the stages of losing and missing it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife has reached the ‘losing and missing’ stage, and finds a pain she never suspected while she still possessed his company.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If my Husband Lord comes to my home, then I obtain everything.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan's bride-soul says that the Lord's presence in her home is all she needs; everything else follows from it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife never knew evening could hurt until her husband left; the Guru's bride likewise finds that with the Husband at home nothing is lacking, so pain enters only with his absence.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1361, Phunhay, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Laodamia, newly married to Protesilaus, writes to him after he sails for Troy, describing how his departure has turned her days and nights into anxious grief she never knew while he was home.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s heroine is a young wife who learns the meaning of separation only when her husband goes away.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife and Laodamia make the same discovery: the pain of absence was unknown until the husband left.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy reminds Boethius that in every adversity of fortune, the most wretched kind of misfortune is to have once been happy.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius observes that past happiness sharpens present loss.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s evenings hurt because they were once happy with her husband, exactly the bitterness Boethius describes.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2, prose 4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.R. James)

real_life_example.event_title: Maria Theresa goes into lifelong mourning for Francis Stephen
real_life_example.event: In 1765 Emperor Francis Stephen died suddenly at Innsbruck, where the imperial family had gathered for the wedding of their son Leopold. His widow, Empress Maria Theresa, cut her hair short, wore widow's black for the rest of her life, largely withdrew from public life and gave up most of her jewellery. She lived about fifteen more years and was buried beside him in a double sarcophagus in the Capuchin crypt in Vienna.
real_life_example.explanation: Her mourning is a well-documented example of a ruler whose life was visibly changed by the loss of her husband.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife says she never knew such suffering while her husband was still at her side, and Maria Theresa's life after 1765 was marked by a grief she had not known while Francis Stephen lived.

tamil:
காலை அரும்பிப் பகலெல்லாம் போதாகி
மாலை மலரும்இந் நோய்.
transliteration:
Kaalai arumpip pakalellaam poadhaaki
maalai malarumin noai.
meaning: This love-sickness starts as a tiny bud in the morning, grows bigger all day, and bursts into full flower in the evening.
elementary: Watch a flower: first a tiny bud, then a bigger bud, then it opens wide. The wife says her missing-him feeling grows the same way each day: small in the morning, bigger at noon, and wide open by evening.
university: One of the most admired images in the Kāmattuppāl, the couplet maps the growth of nōy (the love-sickness) onto the three stages of a flower: arumpu (bud) in the morning, pōtu (the full bud on the point of opening; Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss it as pērarumpu, ‘large bud’) through the day, and malar (open bloom) at evening. The irony is pointed: the flower, symbol of love’s beauty, becomes the shape of love’s pain, and its daily cycle explains why the evening is worst. Solomon Pappaiah calls the disease ‘this flower of love-suffering’, and Karunanidhi generalises it to love itself. Pope: ‘My grief at morn a bud, all day an opening flower, / Full-blown expands in evening hour.’ The text is identical on both web sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When You go off to the forest during the day, a tiny fraction of a second becomes like a millennium for us because we cannot see You.”
hinduism.explanation: In their song of separation, the gopis tell Krishna that every moment of the day without him swells into an age.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s love-sickness that grows through the day toward evening, the gopis’ longing expands hour by hour while Krishna is away.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.31.15 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami, via vedabase.io)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride in the Song of Songs names her longing as a sickness.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural too calls love-longing a nōy, a disease, and traces its growth through the day.

islam.quote_or_event: “They said, ‘By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s sons warn that his unending remembrance of his lost son will grow into a fatal illness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise describes longing for an absent loved one as a sickness that keeps growing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick; But desire fulfilled is a tree of life.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that longing which is put off becomes a sickness of the heart, while its fulfilment is like a living, flowering tree.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife suffers the first half of the proverb, and pictures her deferred longing as a plant that buds and blooms into sickness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever is overcome by this wretched and sticky craving, his sorrows grow like grass after the rains.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the sorrow that comes from craving to vegetation springing up after rain.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also pictures love-sorrow as a growing plant, though as a flower that opens by evening.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When he is not satisfied with those ‘colours,’ and his craving for them grows stronger and stronger, he will become discontented, and unhappy by dint of his discontent”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana describes how craving, once unsatisfied, grows stronger and brings ever-deeper unhappiness.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s love-sickness grows from bud to bloom in exactly this way, stronger and stronger through the day.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Many talk of the pain and suffering of separation; O pain, you are the ruler of all.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid crowns the pain of separation (birha) as a sovereign whose rule nothing escapes.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural traces love-sickness budding in the morning and blooming fully by evening; Farid too sees the pain of separation grow until it rules over everything.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 36) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros the limb-loosener who shakes her, a bittersweet creature against which there is no defence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek lyric presents love as a force that overpowers the body, both sweet and painful.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s love-sickness, which blooms into full pain by evening, is the same bittersweet power Sappho names.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates describes how the soul in love begins to grow its feathers again: the growth throbs and aches like teething, and when the beloved is absent the sprouting points are pinched shut and the soul is stung with pain.
philosophy.explanation: Plato pictures love as an organic growth within the soul, painful when the beloved is away.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s love-sickness also grows like a living thing, budding and opening, and hurts most in absence.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 251b-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Nizami completes the romance of Layla and Majnun
real_life_example.event: The Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi completed his verse romance Layla and Majnun around 1188 as part of his Khamsa (Quintet), at the request of the Shirvanshah ruler. In the story Qays loves Layla so completely that he becomes known as Majnun, meaning madman; when her father refuses the match he flees into the desert, the thought of Layla keeps him awake at night, and after she dies of heartbreak he dies at her grave.
real_life_example.explanation: The poem became the most influential love story of the Persian and wider Islamic world, the classic picture of love as a sickness that grows until it consumes the lover.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural shows love-sickness growing from bud to full flower as the day goes on, and Nizami's poem traces Majnun's love growing in the same way until it overwhelms him.

tamil:
அழல்போலும் மாலைக்குத் தூதாகி ஆயன்
குழல்போலும் கொல்லும் படை.
transliteration:
Azhalpoalum maalaikkuth thoodhaaki aayan
kuzhalpoalum kollum padai.
meaning: Evening burns like fire, and the cowherd's flute is its messenger. Even that flute has become a weapon that kills me.
elementary: Sometimes a song you used to love can make you sad if it reminds you of someone who is far away. The herdsman plays his flute every evening; it used to sound sweet to the wife, but now it tells her that the lonely evening is coming, so it hurts to hear.
university: At dusk the herdsman (āyaṉ) plays his flute (kuḻal) as he brings the cattle home, and in classical Tamil poetics this belongs to the mullai landscape, whose mood is patient waiting (iruttal) and whose hour is evening. The flute becomes the tūtu (herald, envoy) of a mālai that burns like aḻal (fire), and so a paṭai (weapon) that kills; the repeated pōlum is read by the commentators as a particle of emphasis (‘the flute too’), not as ‘like’. Solomon Pappaiah notes that the flute once sounded sweet, and Karunanidhi likens its notes to the clang of a weapon. Pope: ‘The shepherd’s pipe is like a murderous weapon, to my ear, / For it proclaims the hour of ev’ning’s fiery anguish near.’ Both web sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Venu-gita, the gopis of Vraja, hearing the flute that the cowherd Krishna plays as he wanders with the cows, are so overwhelmed by longing that they can only describe to one another, in agitation, the power of its music.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata makes the cowherd’s flute the very sound of love’s longing for those separated from him.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s āyaṉ kuḻal is exactly a cowherd’s flute; for the gopis as for the wife, its music stirs unbearable longing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep.”
christianity.explanation: Job laments that the instruments which once gave him joy now sound only grief.
christianity.tie_back: The herdsman’s flute, once sweet to the Kural’s wife, has likewise turned into a voice of mourning, even a weapon.

islam.quote_or_event: “HEARKEN to the reed-flute, how it complains, Lamenting its banishment from its home: ‘Ever since they tore me from my osier bed, My plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears.’”
islam.explanation: Rumi opens the Masnavi with the reed flute whose music is a lament of separation, read in Sufi tradition as the soul’s longing for God.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s flute and Rumi’s reed both sing of separation and wound those who hear it.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book 1, Prologue (tr. E.H. Whinfield, 1898)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Upon the willows in the midst thereof We hanged up our harps. For there they that led us captive asked of us words of song, And our tormentors asked of us mirth: ‘Sing us one of the songs of Zion.’ How shall we sing the LORD’S song In a foreign land?”
judaism.explanation: The exiles by the rivers of Babylon find that music, once joyful, has become unbearable in separation from home.
judaism.tie_back: For the separated wife too, music that once delighted now only deepens her pain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha’s half-brother Nanda, ordained as a monk, grows discontented and wants to return to lay life because he keeps remembering the parting words of his beautiful Sakyan bride, who asked him to hurry back.
buddhism.explanation: The Udana shows how a single remembered sound of the beloved can keep longing alive and painful.
buddhism.tie_back: The flute’s notes act on the Kural’s wife as the bride’s parting words act on Nanda, reviving longing each time they are recalled.
buddhism.source: Udana 3.2 (Nanda Sutta) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “As an impassioned deer allured (by a song) rushes into death, without being satisfied with the sound.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares one enslaved by the sense of hearing to a deer drawn to its death by music.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife finds the herdsman’s music literally a ‘killing weapon’; the Jain verse uses the same image of a song that leads to death.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; given in Jacobi’s summary note to verses 35-47)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Blessed, blessed is that flute which the Lord plays.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Namdev celebrates the flute of the Lord, the pastoral image of Krishna, as the sound of divine sweetness.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the herdsman's flute at dusk heralds the burning evening and wounds the lonely wife; in Namdev the cowherd's flute is a blessing, so the two use the same instrument with opposite feeling.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 988, Raag Maalee Gauraa, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Syrinx flees the god Pan and is turned into marsh reeds; as Pan sighs over them, the wind in the reeds makes a soft, mournful sound, and he binds reeds of different lengths into the pipe that bears her name.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells how the shepherd’s pipe was born from a love that ended in loss.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The herdsman’s pipe in the Kural also carries the sound of love’s loss, which is why it wounds the waiting wife.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates proposes to banish the dirge-like musical modes, such as the Mixolydian, because music of lament makes the listener’s soul sorrowful and soft.
philosophy.explanation: Plato holds that musical modes have direct power over the emotions of those who hear them.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural shows that power at its extreme: the flute’s evening music can wound the grieving wife like a weapon.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic 398d-399a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Taps is first sounded at Harrison's Landing
real_life_example.event: In July 1862, after the Seven Days battles, Union Brigadier General Daniel Butterfield had his brigade bugler Oliver W. Norton sound a new call in place of the usual Lights Out at the end of the day. The call, now known as Taps, spread through the Army of the Potomac and was soon being played at military funerals, and Army regulations made it mandatory at funerals in 1891. Some scholars think Butterfield revised an older call rather than composing it from scratch.
real_life_example.explanation: A simple tune that marked the close of each day became, almost at once, the sound of mourning and loss.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's herdsman's flute, which announces the evening, becomes a weapon that wounds the lonely wife, just as Taps, the bugle call of nightfall, became the call that announces grief.

tamil:
பதிமருண்டு பைதல் உழக்கும் மதிமருண்டு
மாலை படர்தரும் போழ்து.
transliteration:
Padhimarundu paidhal uzhakkum madhimarundu
maalai padardharum poazhdhu.
meaning: When evening spreads over everything and confuses my mind, the whole town seems confused too, and suffers in sorrow just like me.
elementary: When you are very sad, it can feel as if the whole world is sad with you, even the street and the houses. As evening darkness spreads over the town, the wife feels that everyone there must be as unhappy as she is.
university: The couplet balances two phrases with maruṇṭu (‘bewildered, confused’): pati maruṇṭu, ‘the town bewildered’, and mati maruṇṭu, ‘the mind bewildered’, as evening ‘spreads’ (paṭartarum) over all. Varadarasanar, Kesikan and Karunanidhi take mati as ‘understanding’, so that the dusk confuses the mind and the whole town seems to share the wife’s grief; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a prediction that from now on the whole town will suffer as she has. Sivayogi Sivakumar alone takes mati as ‘moon’ (the moon itself bewildered), an alternative reading worth noting. Pope: ‘If evening’s shades, that darken all my soul, extend; / From this afflicted town will would of grief ascend.’ The text is identical on both web sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama leaves Ayodhya for exile, the whole city falls into mourning: the citizens weep, households neglect their fires and food, and Ayodhya seems lifeless in its grief for him.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki shows one departure plunging an entire city into shared sorrow.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife imagines the whole town grieving with her at dusk; Ayodhya actually does so at Rama’s parting.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda, the city’s grief at Rama’s exile (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.”
christianity.explanation: Matthew uses Jeremiah’s image of a whole town filled with a woman’s inconsolable lament.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise feels her grief spreading until the whole town seems to share it.

islam.quote_or_event: “You see the believers as regards their being merciful among themselves and showing love among themselves and being kind, resembling one body, so that, if any part of the body is not well then the whole body shares the sleeplessness (insomnia) and fever with it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes a community bound so closely that one member’s pain is felt by all.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife imagines exactly this: her evening sleeplessness and sorrow spreading to the whole town.

judaism.quote_or_event: “How doth the city sit solitary, That was full of people! How is she become as a widow!”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations opens by picturing the whole city as a woman bereft of her husband.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural blends the woman and the town in the same way: as dusk falls, the whole town seems to share her bereaved grief.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Kisa Gotami, mad with grief for her dead child, is told by the Buddha to bring a mustard seed from a house where no one has died; going from door to door through the whole town, she finds that every household has known loss, and her grief is transformed.
buddhism.explanation: The story shows a mourner discovering that sorrow is shared by the whole community.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife imagines the whole town sharing her sorrow; Kisa Gotami finds the whole town really does, and is freed by that knowledge.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 114 (Kisa Gotami) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.W. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends)

jainism.quote_or_event: “From desire of pleasure arises the misery of the whole world, the gods included; whatever misery of body and mind there is, the dispassionate will put an end to it.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana sees the misery of the whole world, not just one person, as springing from desire.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife imagines her sorrow spread over the whole town; Jain teaching agrees that such misery is universal, and traces it to desire.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.19 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, I thought that I was in trouble; the whole world is in trouble!”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid discovers that the suffering he thought was his alone is shared by everyone around him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife feels that as evening spreads, the whole town is bewildered and grieving just as she is; Farid likewise looks out and finds his own pain mirrored in all the world.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Persephone is carried off, her mother Demeter grieves so deeply that she withholds growth from the earth, and the whole world suffers famine until her daughter is returned.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Homeric Hymn, one goddess’s grief at separation spreads until all of humanity shares in it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife feels her separation-grief spreading over the whole town; Demeter’s spreads over the whole earth.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn to Demeter (Hymn 2) (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith argues that we come to feel others’ sorrows by imagining ourselves in their place, and that this sympathy is the root of shared moral feeling.
philosophy.explanation: Smith explains how one person’s grief can be reproduced, through imagination, in the hearts of others.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife runs the process in reverse: she imagines the whole town feeling what she feels at dusk.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I, section i, ch. 1 ‘Of Sympathy’ (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Nehru tells India the light has gone out after Gandhi's death
real_life_example.event: At 5.17 pm on 30 January 1948, Mahatma Gandhi was shot and killed as he walked to his evening prayer meeting in the garden of Birla House, New Delhi. Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, who had wept at the scene, spoke to the nation on All India Radio and told listeners that the light had gone out of their lives and there was darkness everywhere. The killing caused widespread shock and mourning across India and around the world.
real_life_example.explanation: It is one of the clearest documented cases of a whole nation sharing one sudden grief as night fell.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife feels that when evening spreads, the whole town is bewildered and grieving as she is, and on that evening in 1948 an entire country was plunged into shared grief and darkness.

tamil:
பொருள்மாலை யாளரை உள்ளி மருள்மாலை
மாயும்என் மாயா உயிர்.
transliteration:
Porulmaalai yaalarai ulli marulmaalai
maayumen maayaa uyir.
meaning: I think of him, whose mind is set on earning money. In this confusing evening, my life, which has lasted until now, is dying away.
elementary: Imagine a parent who works far away to earn money for the family. Even if it is for a good reason, the child at home can feel very lonely at night. The wife feels this way: her husband went to earn wealth, and in the evening she misses him so much it feels unbearable.
university: The closing couplet names the cause of the separation: the husband is poruḷ-mālaiyāḷar, ‘one whose nature (mālai) is wealth’, who has gone away to earn; Solomon Pappaiah sharpens this to ‘one for whom the delusion of wealth is everything’. The poet plays on mālai three ways, ‘nature, disposition’ in poruḷmālai, ‘evening’ in maruḷ mālai (‘bewildering dusk’), and by sound with māyum (‘dies’) and māyā (‘undying’): the life that did not perish (māyā uyir) through the separation so far now perishes (māyum) at this dusk. Varadarasanar glosses māyā uyir as a life that ‘stood as if by magic’ despite grief. Pope: ‘This darkening eve, my darkling soul must perish utterly; / Remembering him who seeks for wealth, but seeks not me.’ Both web sources give identical text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Offered wealth, long life and every pleasure by Yama, the boy Nachiketas refuses them all, saying that no man can be made happy by wealth and that he wants only the knowledge of what lies beyond death.
hinduism.explanation: The Katha Upanishad sets the pursuit of wealth below the pursuit of what truly matters.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife suffers because her husband has chosen wealth over her presence, the very trade-off Nachiketas refuses.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that the pursuit of wealth leads people astray and brings many sorrows.
christianity.tie_back: In the Kural, it is the wife who is ‘pierced with sorrows’ because her husband has gone after wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Competition in [worldly] increase diverts you Until you visit the graveyards.”
islam.explanation: Surat at-Takathur warns that the race for more distracts people from what matters until death overtakes them.
islam.tie_back: The wife sees her husband diverted by the pursuit of wealth while her own life ebbs away in the evening.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The more property, the more anxiety”
judaism.explanation: Hillel, in Pirkei Avot, observes that increasing possessions brings increasing worry.
judaism.tie_back: In the Kural the anxiety falls on the wife left at home while her husband pursues property abroad.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:7 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “That is not a strong fetter, the wise say, which is made of iron, wood or hemp. But the infatuation and longing for jewels and ornaments, children and wives — that, they say, is a far stronger fetter”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names longing for both wealth and family as the strongest of bonds.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s couple are held by both fetters at once: he by wealth, she by love for him, and the strain kills her at evening.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Misery ceases on the absence of delusion, delusion ceases on the absence of desire, desire ceases on the absence of greed, greed ceases on the absence of property.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana traces misery back through a chain of causes that ends in property.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s whole chapter of misery begins with a husband who has gone after property, the first link in the Jain chain.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, the snake of separation from the Lord abides within my mind; it does not respond to any mantra. One who is separated from the Lord does not live; if he does live, he goes insane.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir describes separation from God as a snakebite no charm can cure, one that either kills or drives the sufferer mad.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says the life that has held on until now is dying this evening as she thinks of her husband gone after wealth; Kabir likewise says that one parted from the beloved cannot go on living.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1368, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 76) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Disguised as a beggar, Odysseus tells Penelope that her husband is alive and could have been home long ago, but chose to travel from land to land gathering wealth before returning.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer has the faithful wife hear that her husband’s long absence was stretched out by the pursuit of riches.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Penelope, the Kural’s wife waits, night after night, for a husband whose return is delayed by wealth-seeking.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 19.282-286 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The life of money-making is one undertaken under compulsion, and wealth is evidently not the good we are seeking; for it is merely useful and for the sake of something else.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle ranks wealth as a mere means, never the final good of a human life.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife suffers because her husband is ‘a man of wealth’ by nature; Aristotle reminds us that wealth is only ever for the sake of something else, such as the shared life she is losing.

real_life_example.event_title: Gold Mountain wives wait in China for husbands working in America
real_life_example.place: Southern China and the United States
real_life_example.event: Many Chinese men went to work in the United States, which they called Gold Mountain, to earn money for their families, and laws such as the Page Law of 1875 and the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 kept most of them from bringing their wives. The wives who stayed behind, sometimes called grass widows or living widows, lived apart from their husbands for years or even decades, relying on letters and the money sent home.
real_life_example.explanation: Their long separations show the human cost borne by families when husbands went abroad to earn a living.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife pines at evening for a husband whose heart is set on earning wealth far away, which was the daily life of the Gold Mountain wives.

tamil:
சிறுமை நமக்கொழியச் சேட்சென்றார் உள்ளி
நறுமலர் நாணின கண்.
transliteration:
Sirumai namakkozhiyach chaetchendraar ulli
narumalar naanina kan.
meaning: Thinking of him who went far away and left you this sorrow, your eyes have cried away their beauty. Now they feel ashamed in front of the sweet-smelling flowers they once outshone.
elementary: Imagine a girl whose eyes were once as bright as the flowers in her garden. Her dearest person goes on a long trip, and she cries so much that her eyes become red and tired. Now when she looks at the fresh flowers, she feels shy, because the flowers look brighter than her eyes do.
university: Chapter 124, uṟuppu nalaṉ aḻital (‘the wasting of the beauty of the limbs’), continues the kaṟpiyal sequence on separation (pirivu): the wife, parted from her husband, loses her nalam (bodily loveliness) limb by limb, eyes, shoulders, bangles, forehead. Pope’s prose gloss (‘your eyes weep for him who is gone afar’) follows the traditional reading, associated with Parimelazhagar, in which the confidante (tōḻi) speaks to the heroine. The key words are ciṟumai (here ‘distress, grief’, glossed துன்பம் by Mu. Varadarasanar), cēṭ ceṉṟār (‘he who has gone far’), and naṟumalar nāṇiṉa kaṇ (‘the eyes were ashamed before fragrant flowers’): Sangam convention compares a woman’s eyes to blue water-lilies (kuvaḷai), so eyes that once shamed the flowers now hang back before them. Solomon Pappaiah reads ciṟumai as the ‘weakness of not bearing separation’ left with her while he bore it and went. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; ytamizh writes the chapter title as one word (உறுப்புநலனழிதல்), thirukkural.net as two (உறுப்புநலன் அழிதல்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Hanuman finally finds Sita in Ravana’s Ashoka grove, she is thin from fasting and grief, her face wet with tears, sighing again and again, a woman whose beauty is dimmed like a moon behind cloud as she thinks only of the far-off Rama.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki shows separation from the beloved literally wearing away the heroine’s radiance.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Sita’s eyes and looks are spent by weeping for a husband who is far away.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Mine eye also is dim by reason of sorrow, and all my members are as a shadow.”
christianity.explanation: Job describes grief so heavy that it dims his eyes and leaves his whole body a shadow of itself.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes the eye the first part of the body to lose its brightness under sorrow.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells how Jacob’s long grief for his lost son Joseph physically ruined his eyes.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, longing for one who is far away is written on the eyes, which lose their former lustre.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mine eye is dimmed because of vexation; It waxeth old because of all mine adversaries.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist, worn out with weeping through the night, says his eye has aged and dimmed from distress.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise ‘grow old’ before their time, losing the beauty that once outshone the flowers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the story told when the Buddha first visited Rahula’s mother (Yasodhara), King Suddhodana relates that after the prince left home she lived as he did: on hearing he wore yellow robes she wore yellow, she ate one meal a day as he did, and she gave up garlands and perfumes.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka commentary portrays the deserted wife setting aside flowers and adornment out of loyalty to her absent husband.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also turns away from fragrant flowers, her beauty given up to grief for the one who went far away.
buddhism.source: Canda-Kinnara Jataka (Jataka 485), introductory story (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Gina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction.”
jainism.explanation: When Arishtanemi (Neminatha) left his own wedding procession to renounce the world, his bride Rajimati lost all her joy.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati’s brightness, like the heroine’s eyes in the Kural, is extinguished at once by the departure of the one she was to marry.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, those eyes which have enticed the world - I have seen those eyes. Once, they could not endure even a bit of mascara; now, the birds hatch their young in them!”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid looks at eyes once so lovely and delicate that they bewitched the world, and sees what has become of them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's confidante tells the wife that her eyes, which once outshone the flowers, have wept away their beauty; Farid too sets the former loveliness of eyes against their ruin.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 14) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Clytie, abandoned by the Sun-god she loved, sits on the bare ground for nine days without food, living only on dew and her own tears, gazing at him as he crosses the sky, until her wasted body turns into a flower that still follows the sun.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid turns a woman’s wasting for an absent lover into a metamorphosis: her body becomes a flower.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine weeps until her eyes are outdone by flowers; Clytie weeps until she becomes one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates describes the lover’s soul when parted from the beautiful one: the openings through which its wings grew dry up and close, and the soul, stung all over, writhes in pain, until the sight of the beloved again refreshes it.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats separation from the beloved as a bodily-feeling drought that withers the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural shows the same drying and withering, but on the outside, in eyes that lose their bloom.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 251d-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Ono no Komachi's poem of the faded flowers
real_life_example.event: Ono no Komachi, a poet at the Japanese court in the mid-9th century, wrote a famous poem, preserved in the Kokinshū anthology compiled in 905 and later chosen for the Hyakunin Isshu, in which the colour of the flowers has faded while she has let her days slip away, lost in brooding as the long rains fell. Her poems often use fading blossoms as a sign of passing time and fading beauty.
real_life_example.explanation: The poem is one of the best-known expressions in Japanese literature of beauty withering while the heart is absorbed in sorrow.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the wife's eyes have wept away their beauty and now shrink before the flowers they once outshone, and Komachi's poem likewise sets her own fading against faded flowers during days of brooding.

tamil:
நயந்தவர் நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும்
பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண்.
transliteration:
Nayandhavar nalkaamai solluva poalum
pasandhu panivaarum kan.
meaning: My eyes have turned pale and keep filling with tears. They seem to tell everyone that the one I love is no longer kind to me.
elementary: When you are sad, you might try to hide it, but your red, teary eyes give you away, and people can guess something is wrong. The girl in this verse feels her pale, wet eyes are telling the whole town that the person she loves is far away and not caring for her right now.
university: The heroine imagines her eyes as informers: pasantu (‘having turned sallow’, from pacappu/pacalai, the greenish-yellow pallor of love-sickness that Chapter 119 treats at length) and paṉi vārum (‘streaming with dew’, i.e. tears) they ‘seem to speak’ (colluva pōlum) of nayantavar nalkāmai, the ‘unkindness’ or ‘failure to bestow grace’ of the one she desired. Nalkāmai is the negative of nalku, ‘to show favour, to be gracious’, a word used of kings and gods as well as lovers. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan add that the eyes tell this ‘to others’ (piṟarkku), which makes the poem about exposure as much as grief: the body betrays what modesty (nāṇ) would conceal. Pope renders: ‘The eye, with sorrow wan, all wet with dew of tears, / As witness of the lover’s lack of love appears.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Radha’s friend goes to Krishna and describes Radha’s state in his absence: she finds sandal paste and moonlight painful, she is wasted and tearful, and her whole condition testifies to his neglect.
hinduism.explanation: The friend’s report makes Radha’s suffering body the evidence of Krishna’s absence.
hinduism.tie_back: In the Kural the heroine’s pale, tearful eyes play the friend’s part, announcing the lover’s unkindness to everyone.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Canto 4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Barbara Stoler Miller)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Have mercy upon me, O LORD, for I am in trouble: mine eye is consumed with grief, yea, my soul and my belly.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist points to his worn-out eye as visible proof of his distress.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise display inner grief openly, as if testifying to it.

islam.quote_or_event: In The Ring of the Dove, Ibn Hazm lists the outward signs by which love betrays itself, such as the lover’s fixed gaze, sleeplessness, sighing, and, when the beloved is absent or unkind, wasting and pallor that others can read.
islam.explanation: The Andalusian scholar treats the lover’s body as a text that onlookers can read even when the lover keeps silent.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine fears exactly this: her pale, wet eyes are telling others what she would not say.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapter on the signs of love (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mine eyes do fail with tears, mine inwards burn, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the breach of the daughter of my people.”
judaism.explanation: The poet of Lamentations describes eyes exhausted by tears as the outward face of a heartbreak.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s tear-streaming eyes are likewise the visible sign of an inner wound.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha asks which is greater, the water of the four oceans or the tears his monks have shed over the long round of births while weeping at union with what is displeasing and separation from what is pleasing; the tears, he says, are greater.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta makes separation from the dear the source of an ocean of tears.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s streaming eyes are one small instance of the tears the Buddha says separation always brings.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 15.3, Assu Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Uttaradhyayana’s lecture on carelessness teaches that the eye’s attachment to pleasing colour and form leads to suffering: one who is passionately fond of colours comes to grief and is never satisfied.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching traces the misery of the senses to raga, attachment, beginning with the eye.
jainism.tie_back: In the Kural the eye that once delighted in the beloved is now the very organ that suffers and shows the loss, which Jain doctrine would read as the fruit of attachment.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 32, verses on the eye and colour (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The eyes of the soul-bride are filled with tears; I dwell upon Your Glorious Virtues. How can I meet my Beloved Lord God?”
sikhism.explanation: In his Barah Maha in Raag Tukhari, Guru Nanak's soul-bride weeps as she remembers her Lord's virtues and asks how she can meet Him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her pale, streaming eyes tell everyone that her beloved has stopped being kind to her; Guru Nanak's bride also shows her separation through eyes filled with tears.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1111, Raag Tukhari, Barah Maha, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Penelope listens to the disguised Odysseus tell of her husband, her tears flow down her cheeks like snow melting on the mountain-tops, so that her fair cheeks seem to dissolve as she weeps for the man who is sitting beside her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer pictures a faithful wife’s face visibly wasting with tears for a long-absent husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope’s melting cheeks, like the Kural’s streaming eyes, publish her grief for an absent husband before others.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 19.204-209 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch tells how the physician Erasistratus discovered that Prince Antiochus was wasting away from a hidden love for his stepmother Stratonice: whenever she entered, the prince showed Sappho’s symptoms, faltering speech, burning flushes, pallor and sudden faintness.
philosophy.explanation: A Greek physician reads a secret love straight off a patient’s body.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine fears the same thing: her pallid, wet eyes tell onlookers what she has not said.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Demetrius 38 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Bernadotte Perrin)

real_life_example.event_title: Sappho describes the symptoms of longing in fragment 31
real_life_example.event: In the poem now known as fragment 31, the Greek poet Sappho describes watching the person she loves talking with a man and lists what longing does to her body: her tongue breaks, a thin fire runs under her skin, sweat pours down, trembling seizes her and she is greener than grass. The ancient critic Longinus quoted the poem in his treatise On the Sublime as a model description of the symptoms of passion.
real_life_example.explanation: It is the most famous ancient description of love's effect on the body, and it survives because a later critic thought it a perfect example.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's eyes, gone sallow and tearful, tell everyone what the heart would hide, and Sappho's poem shows the same thing: a body whose pallor and trembling announce the speaker's longing.

tamil:
தணந்தமை சால அறிவிப்ப போலும்
மணந்தநாள் வீங்கிய தோள்.
transliteration:
Thanandhamai saala arivippa poalum
manandha-naal veengiya thoal.
meaning: On our wedding day my shoulders were full and happy. Now they have grown thin, and they seem to tell everyone loudly that we are apart.
elementary: Think of a balloon at a birthday party, round and full, and then the same balloon a week later, small and wrinkled. The girl’s arms were full and strong when she was happy with the person she loves; now that he is away they have become thin, and anyone can see that she misses him.
university: The contrast is temporal and physical: maṇanta nāḷ (‘the day of union’, which may mean the wedding day or any day of togetherness) set against taṇantamai (‘the having-parted’, from taṇa, ‘to separate’). Vīṅkiya tōḷ (‘shoulders that swelled’) uses the Sangam convention that a woman’s tōḷ, shoulders or upper arms, grow plump (pūrittal) in happiness and thin in grief, so they become public evidence; cāla aṟivippa pōlum means ‘they seem to proclaim it fully’. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all add that the thinning announces the separation ‘to others’, continuing the motif of 1232 in which the body exposes private grief. Pope: ‘These withered arms, desertion’s pangs abundantly display, / That swelled with joy on that glad nuptial day.’ Pope transliterates the compound as ‘manandha-naal’; ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the Tamil text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Nala story, Damayanti, longing for Nala after the swan’s message, grows pale and thin and loses interest in everything, until her companions report to King Bhima that his daughter is unwell, and he resolves to hold her svayamvara.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata shows a young woman’s love-sick wasting being noticed by others and reported to her father.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved’s absence is announced to the world by a body visibly growing thin.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “By reason of the voice of my groaning my bones cleave to my skin.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist’s sorrow has wasted him until his body shows nothing but skin and bone.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s shoulders, once full, similarly shrink and make grief visible.

islam.quote_or_event: “They said, ‘By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s sons warn him that his unending remembrance of Joseph is wasting him away.
islam.tie_back: Like Jacob, the Kural’s heroine is being worn down by constant remembrance of the absent one, and onlookers can see it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Her princes were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk… Their visage is blacker than coal; they are not known in the streets; their skin is shrivelled upon their bones; it is withered, it is become like a stick.”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations sets the former radiance of Jerusalem’s nobles against their present shrunken, unrecognisable bodies.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural makes the same ‘then and now’ contrast between shoulders that swelled on the day of union and shoulders now wasted.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada observes that even splendid royal chariots wear out, and the body too grows old, while only the Dhamma of the good does not decay.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching treats the fading of bodily beauty as an instance of universal impermanence (anicca).
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s shoulders, full on the day of union and thin today, show that same impermanence, hastened by grief.

jainism.quote_or_event: In Hemachandra’s account of the emperor Sanatkumara, gods come to see his famed beauty; when he proudly receives them again in royal dress, they tell him that disease has already entered his body and his beauty has faded, and he renounces the world.
jainism.explanation: The Jain story makes the sudden loss of bodily beauty a lesson in the impermanence of the body.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural, too, contrasts a body glowing on one day with the same body visibly diminished later.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 4, life of Sanatkumara (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, my withered body has become a skeleton; the crows are pecking at my palms. Even now, God has not come to help me; behold, this is the fate of all mortal beings.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid describes a body wasted to bone while the Beloved he longs for has still not come.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her shoulders, once full on the day of union, have grown thin and loudly announce the separation; Farid's withered body tells the same story of waiting in vain.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 90) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Spurned by Narcissus, the nymph Echo hides in the woods; her love clings to her and grows with grief, her body wastes with wakeful care, her skin shrivels, her moisture dries into the air, until only her voice and bones remain, and the bones turn to stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells of a lover literally wasting away from unreturned love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s shrunken shoulders are an early stage of what Ovid carries to its end in Echo.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius warns that lovers waste their strength and are worn out by their labour, their life spent at another’s beck, their wealth slipping away and their good name sickening.
philosophy.explanation: The Epicurean poet counts physical wasting among the costs of romantic passion.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural records the same toll on the body, though it treats the heroine with sympathy rather than as a warning.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 4.1121-1124 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.H.D. Rouse)

real_life_example.event_title: Shah Jahan lives as a mourner after the death of Mumtaz Mahal
real_life_example.event: Mumtaz Mahal, the wife of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, died in 1631. For about two years afterwards the emperor lived as a mourner, going without music, fine clothing and the lavish display of his court.
real_life_example.explanation: The change in the emperor's dress and court life made his private grief visible to everyone around him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's shoulders, once full with the joy of union, grow thin and proclaim the separation to all, and Shah Jahan's plain dress and silent court likewise announced his loss to the whole empire.

tamil:
பணைநீங்கிப் பைந்தொடி சோரும் துணைநீங்கித்
தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்.
transliteration:
Panai-neengip paindhoti soarum thunaineengith
tholkavin vaadiya thoal.
meaning: With your partner gone, your gold bangles slip off, and your shoulders have lost their old beauty and fullness.
elementary: Have you ever worn a ring or bracelet that fit perfectly, and then it got loose after you were sick for a while? In this verse, a girl is so sad that her loved one has gone away that she grows thin, and her bangles keep sliding off her arms.
university: The couplet builds a double loss with two parallel absolutives: paṇai nīṅki (‘the plumpness having gone’) and tuṇai nīṅki (‘the companion having gone’), so the departure of the tuṇai, the spouse, causes the departure of the paṇai, the fullness of the arm. Tolkaviṉ vāṭiya tōḷ means ‘shoulders whose former (tol) beauty (kaviṉ) has withered’, and pain̮toṭi cōrum, ‘the fresh-gold bangles slip down’, introduces the image of the loose bangle (toṭi, vaḷai) that dominates 1234-1236. The slipping bangle is a stock sign of separation in Sangam akam poetry and in Sanskrit kāvya alike. Pope’s gloss (‘In the absence of your consort, your shoulders… your bracelets… have become loose’) makes the confidante the speaker. Mu. Varadarasanar reads the shoulders as causing the bangles to slip; Kalaignar glosses paintoṭi as பசும்பொன் வளையல்கள். Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the very opening of the Meghaduta, the exiled Yaksha, separated from his wife, has grown so thin that the golden bracelet has slipped from his forearm, leaving the wrist bare.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa uses the slipped bracelet as the first, defining image of a lover wasted by separation.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s loose bangles are exactly this sign, here worn by the abandoned wife rather than the exiled husband.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta, Purvamegha 2 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can a maid forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? yet my people have forgotten me days without number.”
christianity.explanation: Jeremiah uses a bride’s ornaments as the image of what a loving partner would never forget.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has lost the bloom her ornaments once graced because the partner seems to have forgotten her.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s romance, Layla, married against her will and separated from Majnun, pines in secret; her beauty wanes, she grows thin and pale, and she finally sickens and dies of her longing.
islam.explanation: The Persian poem makes the beloved’s slow physical wasting the measure of her hidden love.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Layla loses her former beauty because the one she loves is out of reach.
islam.source: Nizami Ganjavi, Layla and Majnun (paraphrase; cf. tr. R. Gelpke)

judaism.quote_or_event: “And gone is from the daughter of Zion all her splendour.”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations personifies Jerusalem as a woman whose former glory has departed with her losses.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, too, has seen her ‘old beauty’ (tolkaviṉ) depart along with her companion.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like rounded door-bars — both of them — my arms were once splendid. With age, they’re like dried up patali trees.” Ambapali adds that her hands, once adorned with gold and delicate rings, are now like onions and tubers.
buddhism.explanation: The former courtesan, now a nun, describes how her once-lovely arms and jewelled hands have withered.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees the same withering of arms that once filled their ornaments, though grief, not age, has done it.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Jain didactic anthology Naladiyar repeatedly warns that youth and bodily beauty wither like a flower, so that the body once admired soon becomes something no one wishes to look at.
jainism.explanation: Tamil Jain ethics uses the fading of beauty to turn the mind from the body to dharma.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural shows that fading happening in a single season of grief; the Jain poets would draw from it a lesson about the body’s impermanence.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, chapters on the instability of youth and the body (paraphrase; cf. tr. G.U. Pope, 1893)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Lord! Without my Husband, all these adornments are useless.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan's bride-soul has put on every ornament, but says none of it means anything while her Husband is away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife, her partner gone, has lost the fullness of her shoulders, and her gold bangles slip from her arms; the Guru's bride likewise finds her ornaments worthless without the Husband.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1361, Phunhay, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Writing to her husband Protesilaus at Troy, Laodamia says that while he is at war she will not dress her hair or wear gold and fine robes; she lives like a widow in mourning until he comes home.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s heroine sets aside her ornaments as a sign of her husband’s absence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine does not remove her bangles; grief makes them fall away on their own.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Robert Burton lists the symptoms of love-melancholy: lovers grow lean, pale and hollow-eyed, lose their appetite and sleep, and pine away, so that the disease can be read in their bodies.
philosophy.explanation: Burton’s encyclopedia of melancholy treats love-sickness as a real wasting illness with visible signs.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s thin shoulders and loose bangles are just such symptoms, recorded from the patient’s side.
philosophy.source: Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy, Part 3, Section 2, Member 3 (Symptoms of Love-Melancholy) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Li Qingzhao grows thinner than the yellow flowers
real_life_example.event: Li Qingzhao, the Song dynasty poet, married the official and antiquarian Zhao Mingcheng in 1101, and during his frequent absences she wrote poems of longing for his return. In her song lyric to the tune Drunk under the Shadow of Flowers, set on the Double Ninth festival, the speaker drinks alone by the eastern hedge after dusk and says she has grown thinner than the yellow flowers.
real_life_example.explanation: She is China's most celebrated woman poet, and her lyrics are the classic Chinese picture of a wife wasting away while her husband is gone.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that with her partner gone the wife's shoulders have lost their fullness and her bangles slip, and Li Qingzhao's speaker, alone at dusk, has grown thinner than the flowers.

tamil:
கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும் தொடியொடு
தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்.
transliteration:
Kotiyaar kodumai uraikkum thotiyodu
tholkavin vaadiya thoal.
meaning: My thin shoulders, their old beauty gone and their bangles slipping off, tell everyone how cruel the hard-hearted one was to me.
elementary: Sometimes our bodies tell a story we don’t say out loud, like a droopy face when we’re upset. Here the girl’s thin arms and falling bangles seem to tell the whole town, “Look how much he has hurt her by staying away so long.”
university: Koṭiyār koṭumai uraikkum (‘they speak the cruelty of the cruel one’) is an emphatic figura etymologica: koṭiyār (‘the cruel/crooked one’, honorific plural used of the husband) and koṭumai (‘cruelty’) share the root koṭu, ‘bent, harsh’. The second line repeats 1234’s tolkaviṉ vāṭiya tōḷ verbatim, a deliberate echo, while toṭiyoṭu (‘together with the bangles’) makes the slipping bracelets co-witnesses. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses koṭiyār as ‘the cruel one who does not feel my suffering’; Puliyur Kesikan adds that the shoulders say it ‘for the town to know’ (ūraṟiya).
