The accusation is ventured here only to be withdrawn in 1236, where the heroine is pained to hear him so called. Pope: ‘These wasted arms, the bracelet with their wonted beauty gone, / The cruelty declare of that most cruel one.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, when Krishna finally comes to Radha at dawn bearing the marks of a night spent with another, she sends him away in reproach, calling him faithless and telling him to go back to the one he chose.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva gives the wronged heroine a sharp, public voice of reproach against her lover.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine lets her wasted shoulders make the same charge of cruelty on her behalf.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Canto 8 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Barbara Stoler Miller)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me: my mother’s children were angry with me; they made me the keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song explains her changed looks as the visible result of others’ harshness.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise points to her altered body as proof of the harsh treatment she has suffered.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if a woman fears from her husband contempt or evasion, there is no sin upon them if they make terms of settlement between them - and settlement is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names a husband’s neglect or turning away as a real wrong to a wife and urges reconciliation.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine suffers exactly such ‘evasion’, and her body bears witness to it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the LORD hath called thee as a wife forsaken and grieved in spirit; and a wife of youth, can she be rejected? saith thy God.”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah uses the figure of a young wife left grieving to describe Israel, and protests that such a wife cannot rightly be cast off.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is just such a ‘wife forsaken and grieved in spirit’, whose body cries out against the one who left.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha lists a husband’s duties to his wife: to honour her, not to disparage her, to be faithful, to give her authority in the home and to provide her with adornments.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist lay ethics treats a husband’s neglect of his wife as a failure of duty.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s bare, wasted arms indict a husband who has not fulfilled these duties, including the gift of ornaments that now fall away.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Narada Thera)

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain Ramayana, Prince Pavananjaya, offended on his wedding day, refuses even to look at his bride Anjana and neglects her for many years; she wastes away in grief, while those around her see the injustice of her lot.
jainism.explanation: The story is the Jain tradition’s classic portrait of a faithful wife wasting under a husband’s cruelty.
jainism.tie_back: Anjana’s wasted body makes the same silent accusation as the Kural’s shoulders and slipping bangles.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 7, story of Anjana and Pavananjaya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If her Husband Lord does not return home, how can the soul-bride find peace? Her body is wasting away with the sorrow of separation.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the soul-bride whose Husband has not come home, her body wasting away from the grief of separation.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the wife's faded shoulders and slipping bangles proclaim to everyone the cruelty of the one who left; Guru Nanak too makes the bride's wasting body the visible sign of the Husband's absence.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1108, Raag Tukhari, Barah Maha, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Catullus’ telling, Ariadne, waking on Naxos to see Theseus’ ship sailing away, calls him faithless and forgetful, and cries out against the cruelty of the man for whom she gave up her home.
greek_mythology.explanation: The deserted Ariadne is the Roman poets’ model of a woman denouncing a cruel lover.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also names her lover ‘the cruel one’ (koṭiyār), though she lets her body speak the charge.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Pausanias says the common, bodily lover is not constant, because he loves what is itself inconstant; when the bloom of youth he desired has faded, he takes wing and flies away, breaking all his promises.
philosophy.explanation: Pausanias explains a lover’s desertion as the natural result of loving only the body’s bloom.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine fears this cruelty, her bloom gone, her lover away; Pausanias offers the philosophical diagnosis of such a lover.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 183d-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Octavia's loyalty turns Rome against Mark Antony
real_life_example.event: Octavia, sister of Octavian, the future Emperor Augustus, married Mark Antony in 40 BCE to seal the alliance between the two men. After Antony returned to Cleopatra in the East and sent Octavia back to Rome, she went on living in his house as if he were at home, raising her own children and his children by his earlier marriage. Plutarch records that her loyal conduct, without her intending it, damaged Antony, because people hated him for wronging such a woman; he divorced her in 32 BCE.
real_life_example.explanation: Octavia's faithful conduct did more to expose Antony's treatment of her than any accusation could have done.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wasted shoulders and slipping bangles proclaim the cruelty of the one who left, and Octavia's visible, faithful waiting proclaimed Antony's cruelty to all of Rome.

tamil:
தொடியொடு தோள்நெகிழ நோவல் அவரைக்
கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து.
transliteration:
Thotiyodu thoalnekizha noval avaraik
kotiyar enakkooral nondhu.
meaning: Because my bangles slip and my shoulders are thin, people call him cruel. Hearing him blamed hurts me more than my own pain.
elementary: Imagine your best friend moves away for a while, and you are sad. If someone says, “Your friend is mean for leaving you,” you might feel even worse, because you still love your friend and don’t want anyone to speak badly of them. That is how the girl in this verse feels.
university: Here the tone turns: after 1235’s accusation, the heroine is pained (nōval, ‘I grieve’) when others, or the confidante, call him koṭiyar (‘cruel’) because of her loosened bangles and thinned shoulders (toṭiyoṭu tōḷ nekiḻa). The final word nontu (‘in sorrow, being hurt’) can be taken with the speakers or with the heroine, and the commentators divide: Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar have the onlookers (kāṇpavar) say it, while Solomon Pappaiah makes the shoulders and bangles themselves the speakers. Pope’s gloss (‘I am greatly pained to hear you call him a cruel man’) addresses the confidante, which accords with the reading associated with Parimelazhagar that the heroine answers her tōḻi. The ethic is the wife’s loyalty (kaṟpu), which forbids hearing the husband reproached even when she is the one who suffers. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama, bowing to public gossip, has Sita left in the forest, she sends him a message through Lakshmana that blames no one but her own fate, asks him to care for his people as he would his brothers, and says she grieves less for herself than for the slander against his name.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki’s Sita refuses to accuse the husband who has caused her suffering and worries instead about his reputation.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Sita is pained by his blame rather than by her own wasting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul’s portrait of love describes a charity that keeps trusting and enduring instead of accusing.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows that love: she bears the wasting but will not hear her husband condemned.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that a believing man should not hate a believing woman: if he dislikes one of her traits, he will be pleased with another.
islam.explanation: The hadith asks a spouse not to define the other by a single fault.
islam.tie_back: The heroine applies this generosity in reverse: she will not let her husband be judged by the one hurt his absence causes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joshua ben Perahiah used to say: appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah asks that others, especially companions, be judged favourably rather than condemned.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine judges her absent husband exactly so, refusing the verdict ‘cruel’ that others pass on him.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:6 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada observes that the faults of others are easily seen while one’s own are hard to see, and that people winnow others’ faults like chaff.
buddhism.explanation: The verse warns against the quick, public fault-finding that comes so easily to onlookers.
buddhism.tie_back: The onlookers in the Kural do just this, pronouncing the husband cruel, and the heroine is hurt by their easy verdict.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Râgîmatî thought: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.’”
jainism.explanation: Abandoned at her wedding when Arishtanemi renounced the world, Rajimati blames her own life, not him, and resolves to follow him into the ascetic path.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Rajimati suffers the loss but will not call the one who left her cruel.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Your actions seem so sweet to me.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan accepts whatever God does as sweet, the Sikh attitude of living in His will (bhana) without complaint.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife is hurt more by hearing others call her husband cruel than by her own wasting; the Sikh devotee likewise refuses to call the Beloved's doings harsh and finds even hardship from Him sweet.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld, Agamemnon’s shade praises Penelope above all wives because she kept faith with her absent husband through twenty years, so that the gods would make her fame a song for all mankind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer holds up Penelope as the model of a wife who stays loyal to a husband who has been away for a very long time.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows the same steadfast loyalty, defending a husband whom others are ready to condemn.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 24.192-198 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero says a true friend must not only refrain from bringing charges against his friend but must not even believe charges that others bring.
philosophy.explanation: On Friendship makes loyalty against outside accusation a mark of genuine love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine practises this loyalty, refusing to accept the charge of cruelty that others make against her husband.

real_life_example.event_title: Libbie Custer defends her husband's name for 57 years
real_life_example.event: After George Armstrong Custer died at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876, his widow Elizabeth (Libbie) Bacon Custer learned that President Ulysses S. Grant and senior officers blamed him for the defeat. Widowed at 34 and never remarrying, she spent the rest of her long life protecting his reputation, writing the memoirs Boots and Saddles (1885), Tenting on the Plains (1887) and Following the Guidon (1890). She was buried beside him at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point.
real_life_example.explanation: Her devotion shaped how Americans remembered Custer for half a century, and critics largely held back while she lived.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife is pained more by hearing her husband called cruel than by her own suffering, and Libbie Custer could not bear to hear her husband blamed and spent decades answering his critics.

tamil:
பாடு பெறுதியோ நெஞ்சே கொடியார்க்கென்
வாடுதோட் பூசல் உரைத்து.
transliteration:
Paadu perudhiyo nenje kotiyaarkken
vaatudhot poosal uraiththu.
meaning: My heart, why not go to that hard-hearted man and tell him how loudly my thin shoulders cry out? Wouldn't that bring you praise?
elementary: Sometimes when we miss someone, we talk to ourselves, like “Come on, brave heart, go tell them how we feel!” The girl in this verse talks to her own heart and asks it to go to the person she loves and tell him how sad and thin she has become.
university: The heroine now addresses her own nenjam (heart, mind) as a possible messenger, a device developed at length in the next chapter, 125 (neñcoṭu kiḷattal, ‘speaking to the heart’). Pāṭu peṟutiyō means ‘will you gain greatness/glory?’; the question can be read as an exhortation (Kalaignar: ‘will you not gain glory?’) or as a rueful challenge (Solomon Pappaiah: ‘will you gain glory by telling him these empty rumours?’). Vāṭu tōḷ pūcal is ‘the clamour of my withering shoulders’, pūcal being a noisy outcry or public uproar, so the wasting body is imagined as shouting. Koṭiyārkku (‘to the cruel one’) resumes the word the heroine resisted in 1236, which Mu. Varadarasanar softens to ‘the one who is called cruel’. Pope: ‘My heart! say ought of glory wilt thou gain, / If to that cruel one thou of thy wasted arms complain?’ Ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text, including the sandhi form வாடுதோட் பூசல்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Meghaduta, the exiled Yaksha, unable to reach his wife, asks a passing rain-cloud to carry his message to her across India and tell her of his suffering and enduring love.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s poem makes an improvised messenger carry a separated lover’s complaint to the beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also searches for a go-between and settles on her own heart to carry her complaint.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song begs others to carry word of her love-sickness to her absent beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sends her own heart on the same errand: to tell him how she wastes away.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob refuses to air his grief before people and takes his complaint only to God.
islam.tie_back: The heroine’s complaint likewise has one proper recipient: she would carry it only to the one who can end it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I pour out my complaint before Him, I declare before Him my trouble.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist, alone in a cave, sets out his distress before the one who can help.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wants her heart to pour out the ‘clamour’ of her wasting body before her husband in the same way.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In his long verses in the Theragatha, the monk Talaputa speaks directly to his own mind, reasoning with it, pleading with it and reproaching it, asking when it will at last do what he wishes.
buddhism.explanation: The Theragatha preserves a monk’s dramatic dialogue with his own heart.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also turns and addresses her heart as a separate person who could act for her.
buddhism.source: Theragatha 19, Talaputa (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra defines one form of arta-dhyana, ‘sorrowful brooding’, as the mind’s repeated dwelling on regaining a pleasing object from which one has been separated.
jainism.explanation: Jain psychology names exactly the anxious, circling thought that separation from the beloved produces, and classes it as karmically binding.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s urging of her heart to run to the absent one is such brooding, which Jain teaching would counsel her to still.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.31 (arta-dhyana on separation from the desired) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My mind longs for the Blessed Vision of the Guru's Darshan.”
sikhism.explanation: These are the opening words of the Shabad Hazare, which Sikh tradition says the young Guru Arjan sent as verse-letters to his father, Guru Ram Das, while he was kept away in Lahore.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife urges her heart to go to the hard-hearted one and tell him how her shoulders cry out; Guru Arjan's longing mind likewise speaks across the distance to the one he is parted from.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Penelope opens her letter to Ulysses by telling him not to write back but to come himself, and then pours out the sleepless nights and fears she has endured while Troy has fallen and he still has not returned.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Heroides are letters in which waiting women send their complaints to absent men.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has no letter, so she would send her heart to carry the complaint of her wasting body.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius repeatedly speaks to his own soul as to another person, chiding it that it is doing itself wrong and that time to honour itself is running short.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic emperor’s private notebook uses self-address to argue with his own mind.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also speaks to her heart as a separate agent, though to spur it toward love, not toward Stoic self-command.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 2.6 (paraphrase; cf. tr. George Long)

real_life_example.event_title: Kalidasa writes the Meghaduta, the Cloud Messenger
real_life_example.event: Around the 5th century CE the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa wrote the Meghaduta (Cloud Messenger), a lyric love poem of about 115 verses. In it an exiled yaksha, a nature spirit grieving for his beloved on a remote mountain, asks a passing cloud at the start of the monsoon to carry his message to her in the Himalayan city of Alaka, and much of the poem describes the landscapes the cloud will cross.
real_life_example.explanation: The poem became the model for a whole genre of messenger poems in Indian literature.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife asks her own heart to go to her husband and tell him of her suffering, just as Kalidasa's grieving lover sends a cloud to carry his message to his distant beloved.

tamil:
முயங்கிய கைகளை ஊக்கப் பசந்தது
பைந்தொடிப் பேதை நுதல்.
transliteration:
Muyangiya kaikalai ookkap pasandhadhu
paindhotip paedhai nudhal.
meaning: Once, when I only loosened my arms from our hug, the forehead of my innocent wife with her gold bangles turned pale at once.
elementary: Imagine a little child holding a parent’s hand at a busy fair. If the parent lets go for just a second, the child’s face might look worried right away. The husband in this verse remembers that his wife looked worried and pale even when he let go of a hug for just a moment, so he knows how much she must be missing him now that he is far away.
university: With 1238 the voice changes: Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar gloss in the husband’s first person (‘when I loosened my arms’), and the traditional reading has the talaivaṉ, away from home, recalling his wife’s fragility to explain why he must hurry back. Muyaṅkiya kaikaḷai ūkka is ‘when [I] loosened (ūkka, ‘to slacken, withdraw’) the arms that embraced’; pacantatu… nutal, ‘the forehead turned sallow’, applies pacappu, the pallor of love-longing, to her brow, the classic site of a woman’s brightness (oḷ nutal, 1240). Paintoṭip pētai, ‘the innocent one with fresh-gold bangles’, uses pētai, ‘young, guileless woman’, a tender term. The logic is a fortiori: if a moment’s slackening paled her, what must long absence do? Solomon Pappaiah adds that he loosened his grip fearing his tight hold would hurt her. Pope: ‘One day the fervent pressure of embracing arms I checked, / Grew wan the forehead of the maid with golden armlet decked.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Bhavabhuti’s Uttararamacharita, Rama, looking at paintings of their forest exile, recalls how Sita used to fall asleep with her head on his arm, and his tenderness for her is mixed with the pain of knowing he must soon part from her.
hinduism.explanation: Bhavabhuti dwells on a husband’s memory of his wife’s closeness in his arms.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband likewise remembers the embrace and how fragile she was within it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song describes the beloved’s embrace as her rest and security.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural shows the reverse side of the same embrace: when it is loosened even slightly, the beloved’s brightness falters.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes spouses as each other’s garment, close, protecting and covering.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows how a wife feels when that ‘garment’ is drawn back even for a moment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother’s house.”
judaism.explanation: Having found her beloved after a night of searching, the woman of the Song will not loosen her hold.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, cannot bear even a slackened embrace; she pales the moment it loosens.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From affection springs grief, from affection springs fear. For one who is wholly free from affection there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada traces grief and fear to affection itself.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s instant pallor at a loosened embrace is the fear that affection brings, exactly as the verse diagnoses.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Uttaradhyayana’s lecture on carelessness teaches that one passionately attached to pleasant touch suffers as soon as it is withdrawn, and never finds satisfaction in it.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching treats attachment to touch as one of the senses’ bonds that produce pain at every loss.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s pallor at a slackened embrace is the pain of withdrawn touch; Jain doctrine would read it as the fruit of attachment.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 32, verses on touch (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without water, she cannot live, even for an instant. God knows the suffering of her mind.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak compares the soul's love to a fish that cannot live a moment out of water, and says God knows her inner pain.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the husband remembers that the moment he loosened his embrace, his wife's forehead turned pale; Guru Nanak too speaks of a love that cannot bear a moment's separation, and of a Beloved who knows that pain.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 60, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho describes what happens to her in the beloved’s presence: her tongue breaks, a fine fire runs under her skin, her ears hum, a sweat comes over her, and she is ‘greener than grass’, seeming to herself little short of dying.
greek_mythology.explanation: The most famous Greek poem of love-sickness names a greenish pallor as love’s mark on the body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s pacappu, the sallow-green pallor that spreads over the wife’s forehead, is the same colour of love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes tells how humans were split in two, so that each half longs for its other; when they find each other they embrace and do not want to be parted even for a moment.
philosophy.explanation: Aristophanes’ myth explains lovers’ desire never to loosen their embrace as a longing to be whole again.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife pales at a slackened embrace because, in Aristophanes’ terms, she feels herself made half again.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 191a-192e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Nelson Mandela's prison letters to Winnie
real_life_example.place: Robben Island and other prisons, South Africa
real_life_example.event: Nelson Mandela was a sentenced political prisoner from 1962 to 1990, held in four prisons. At first he could write and receive only one 500-word letter every six months, and on Robben Island he was allowed one visitor a year for 30 minutes. In his letters to his wife Winnie he professed his love and gave her moral support in her own struggle.
real_life_example.explanation: The letters show how a separated husband kept his marriage alive through rare, censored words over decades.
real_life_example.tie_back: In this kural the absent husband remembers his wife's tenderness and worries about her, and Mandela, separated from Winnie for decades, poured the same remembering love into his few permitted letters.

tamil:
முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழப் பசப்புற்ற
பேதை பெருமழைக் கண்.
transliteration:
Muyakkidaith thanvali poazhap pasapputra
paedhai perumazhaik kan.
meaning: When even a little breeze slipped in between us as we hugged, the big, cool eyes of my innocent wife turned pale.
elementary: Think of two friends sitting so close on a cold night that not even the wind can get between them. If a tiny gust slips in, one of them shivers. The husband here remembers that even a little breeze between them made his wife look sad, so he knows a long trip away must be very hard for her.
university: The husband’s recollection continues and intensifies 1238: now not his arms but a cool breeze (taṇ vaḷi) ‘split’ (pōḻa, ‘to cleave, pierce’) their embrace (muyakku iṭai, ‘in the midst of the embrace’), and at that hair’s-breadth separation her eyes, not her forehead, were touched with pacappu. Perumaḻaik kaṇ, ‘large rain-eyes’, is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘large eyes like rain’ (cool and moist) and by Kalaignar as ‘wide, long eyes’; the image may suggest both their coolness and their readiness for tears. Solomon Pappaiah ends his gloss with the husband’s worried question, ‘how must they be now?’, which captures the a fortiori logic of 1238-1240. Pope: ‘As we embraced a breath of wind found entrance there; / The maid’s large liquid eyes were dimmed with care.’ Ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, when Krishna suddenly vanishes from the circle of dancing gopis at night, they are overwhelmed at once, searching for him from tree to tree and asking the creepers and deer where he has gone.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata shows a moment’s disappearance of the beloved producing instant, overwhelming distress.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, is stricken by the smallest break in closeness, a breeze slipping between them.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Again, if two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone?”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher observes plainly that two together keep each other warm, and one alone cannot.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s cold breeze slipping between the lovers is exactly the chill the verse describes.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an presents spouses as a source of tranquillity for each other, bound by affection and mercy.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows how fragile that tranquillity feels to a loving wife, broken even by a breath of air between them.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When our love was strong, we could have slept on a bed that was the width of a sword. Now that our love is not strong, a bed of sixty cubits is not sufficient for us.”
judaism.explanation: A Talmudic proverb measures love by how little space a couple needs between them.
judaism.tie_back: In the Kural the lovers’ closeness is so complete that even a breeze in the gap is felt as a wound.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 7a (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Canda-Kinnara Jataka, a pair of kinnaras are separated for a single night when a sudden flood fills the stream between them; they spend the night calling to each other, and for the rest of their long lives they grieve over that one lost night.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka makes a single night’s separation the cause of lifelong lament between devoted mates.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife reacts the same way to the slightest gap, a breeze in the embrace.
buddhism.source: Canda-Kinnara Jataka (Jataka 485) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain Ramayana, Pavananjaya, encamped on a campaign, sees a female chakravaka bird crying all night for her mate, from whom she is parted till dawn; realising that his neglected wife Anjana must suffer far more, he secretly flies back to her that very night.
jainism.explanation: The Jain narrative makes a bird’s single night of separation open a husband’s eyes to his wife’s pain.
jainism.tie_back: Like Pavananjaya, the Kural’s husband reasons from a small separation, a breeze in an embrace, to how much his wife must suffer in a long absence.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 7, story of Anjana and Pavananjaya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “When I could not be with You for just one moment, the Dark Age of Kali Yuga dawned for me.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Shabad Hazare, Guru Arjan says that even a moment away from the beloved Guru felt like the darkest age of the world.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural even a cool breeze slipping between the embracing couple was enough to make the wife's eyes turn pale; Guru Arjan likewise finds a single moment's separation unbearable.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Ceyx resolves to sail to consult an oracle, his wife Alcyone turns pale, weeps and begs him not to go, or at least to take her with him, since even a short parting by sea terrifies her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s devoted wife cannot bear the thought of even a brief separation from her husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife pales at a breath of wind between them; Alcyone pales at the mere mention of a voyage.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius says lovers clasp and press each other close, mouth to mouth, yet can take nothing from each other, since body cannot pass into body, and so even the tightest embrace leaves a gap that desire cannot close.
philosophy.explanation: The Epicurean poet sees in lovers’ embraces a longing for a total union that bodies cannot achieve.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s breeze slipping into the embrace is the gap Lucretius points to, felt by the wife as a wound.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 4.1105-1111 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.H.D. Rouse)

real_life_example.event_title: Captain Scott's last letter to his wife Kathleen
real_life_example.event: During the fatal return journey from the South Pole in 1912, Captain Robert Falcon Scott wrote last letters from his tent, including one to his wife Kathleen addressed To my widow. He wrote of the cold, 70 degrees below zero, and asked her to make their son Peter, then about three, interested in natural history if she could. The letter was given to the Scott Polar Research Institute at Cambridge and put on public display in 2007.
real_life_example.explanation: Written as he faced death, the letter shows a husband's last thoughts turning to his wife and child far away.
real_life_example.tie_back: In this kural the husband, far from home, remembers his wife's delicacy and worries how she will bear the separation, and Scott's last letter turns from his own plight to her and their son's future.

tamil:
கண்ணின் பசப்போ பருவரல் எய்தின்றே
ஒண்ணுதல் செய்தது கண்டு.
transliteration:
Kannin pasappoa paruvaral eydhindrae
onnudhal seydhadhu kandu.
meaning: Her bright forehead turned pale first. Did the paleness in her eyes see this and become even sadder?
elementary: When one person in a family is sad, the others often feel sad too, just from seeing them. In this verse the husband imagines his wife’s face as a little family: when her forehead turned pale, her eyes saw it and became even sadder.
university: The closing couplet is a conceit (taṟkuṟippēṟṟa aṇi, poetic fancy) in which parts of the wife’s face react to one another. Kaṇṇiṉ pacappō paruvaral eytiṉṟē, ‘did the pallor of the eyes fall into distress?’, uses the particle ō for wondering doubt, and oṇ nutal ceytatu kaṇṭu, ‘having seen what the bright forehead did’, refers back to 1238, where the forehead paled first. Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar read: seeing the forehead turn sallow, the pallor of her eyes grew into greater suffering. Solomon Pappaiah offers a different reading, in which the eye, once ashamed before the forehead’s delicacy, now shares its distress. The chapter thus ends where it began, with the eyes (1231), now joined by the forehead, so that the ‘wasting of the limbs’ is complete from head to arm. Pope: ‘The dimness of her eye felt sorrow now, / Beholding what was done by that bright brow.’ Text identical on both sites; ytamizh’s transliteration renders the archaic eytiṉṟē as ‘eydhindrae’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Chandogya Upanishad, the senses and breath quarrel over which is greatest; each departs for a year and the body carries on, but when breath begins to leave, all the others are torn loose with it and beg it to stay.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad pictures the body’s faculties as a community that rises or falls together.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s eye grieving at the forehead’s pallor is a small, tender version of the same solidarity of the body’s parts.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes the community as a body whose parts feel each other’s pain.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural pictures this literally: when the forehead suffers, the eyes suffer with it.

islam.quote_or_event: “You see the believers as regards their being merciful among themselves and showing love among themselves and being kind, resembling one body, so that, if any part of the body is not well then the whole body shares the sleeplessness (insomnia) and fever with it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a loving community to a body whose parts share each other’s illness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes share the forehead’s ‘illness’ of pallor in just this way.

judaism.quote_or_event: Isaiah pictures a people so afflicted that the whole head is sick and the whole heart faint, with no soundness from the sole of the foot to the head.
judaism.explanation: The prophet describes suffering that spreads through every part of the body.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wasting likewise spreads from part to part, until even the eyes grieve at the forehead’s pallor.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha summarises dependent arising: when this is, that is; from the arising of this comes the arising of that.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching sees every state as conditioned by others, arising together.
buddhism.tie_back: The eyes’ grief arising from the forehead’s pallor is a poetic picture of one condition giving rise to another.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 79, Culasakuludayi Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra states that the function of souls is to render service to one another (parasparopagraho jivanam).
jainism.explanation: This aphorism, now the motto of the Jain community, teaches that living beings exist in mutual support.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes grieving with the forehead are a tender picture of mutual support between parts that share one life.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.21 (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I cannot survive without seeing my Beloved. My eyes are welling up with tears.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says he cannot live without the sight of his Beloved, and his eyes fill with tears.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural imagines the wife's eyes falling into distress on seeing what pallor has done to her forehead; in Guru Ram Das too it is the eyes that carry the grief of separation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 94, Raag Maajh, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Narcissus wastes away at the pool, Echo, though still hurt by his rejection, grieves to see him; each time he cries ‘alas’, she echoes ‘alas’, and when he says ‘farewell’ she says ‘farewell’ too.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Echo shares in the wasting of the one she loves, repeating his grief back to him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise mirror and deepen the grief they see in the forehead.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that the best-ordered city is most like a single person: when a finger is hurt, the whole community of body and soul feels it and suffers together with the injured part.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the body’s shared feeling of pain as the model for social unity.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural pictures the same shared feeling within one face: the eyes suffer with the pale forehead.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic 462c-d (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Rembrandt draws his bride Saskia three days after their betrothal
real_life_example.event: In 1633 Rembrandt van Rijn made a silverpoint drawing on parchment of Saskia and wrote beneath it, in Dutch, that it was a likeness of his wife made when she was 21 years old, on the third day after their betrothal. The drawing is now in the Kupferstichkabinett of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin.
real_life_example.explanation: It is a rare record of an artist studying the face of the woman he loved at the very start of their life together.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's husband remembers every small change in his wife's face, her brow and her eyes, and Rembrandt's drawing shows a lover attending closely to his bride's face.

tamil:
நினைத்தொன்று சொல்லாயோ நெஞ்சே எனைத்தொன்றும்
எவ்வநோய் தீர்க்கும் மருந்து.
transliteration:
Ninaiththondru sollaayo nenje enaiththondrum
evvanoai theerkkum marundhu.
meaning: My heart, won't you think hard and tell me some medicine, any kind at all, that can cure this sickness of sorrow?
elementary: Imagine you miss someone so much that it feels like a tummy ache that no medicine can fix. So you talk to yourself: “Come on, heart, you are clever, think of something that will make me feel better!”
university: Chapter 125, neñcoṭu kiḷattal (‘speaking with one’s heart’), belongs to the kaṟpiyal (wedded-love) section: the wife, alone in separation (pirivu), turns her own neñcu (heart/mind) into a confidant and argues with it, a device Pope renders ‘Soliloquy’. The key compound evvanōy joins evvam (‘distress, sorrow’) with nōy (‘disease’), and enaittonṟum (‘whatever it may be, of any kind’) stresses that she will accept any remedy at all; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the sickness as grown out of love (காதலால் வளர்ந்த), and Kalaignar as kātal nōy ‘incurable by any medicine’. The commentary tradition reads the opening ninaittu onṟu collāyō as a plea to the heart, the one faculty still ‘with’ her, to think on her behalf. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the chapter title is printed as one word (நெஞ்சொடுகிளத்தல்) on ytamizh and as நெஞ்சோடு கிளத்தல் (long ō) on thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I can find no means to drive away this grief which is drying up my senses.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna, overwhelmed by sorrow, confesses that nothing he can think of will remove the grief that is withering him, and turns to Krishna for a remedy.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise admits her grief is beyond ordinary cures and begs her own heart to find the medicine.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.8 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuseth to be healed?”
christianity.explanation: Jeremiah cries out that his inner wound will not heal no matter what is tried.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘sickness no medicine cures’, Jeremiah’s pain is described as incurable, prompting a desperate question.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when I am ill, it is He who cures me”
islam.explanation: Abraham names God as the one true healer of every illness.
islam.tie_back: Where the Kural’s heroine searches her own heart for a cure, the Qur’an points the sufferer to God as the source of healing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah asks, in grief, why no remedy or healer seems able to cure his people’s wound.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s plea for ‘any medicine at all’ echoes this famous lament asking whether any balm exists for an aching heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha diagnoses grief as springing from attachment to the dear, and names freedom from attachment as its only real cure.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural asks for a medicine for love-grief; the Dhammapada answers that the cure lies in loosening the endearment itself.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mind of those who always live in unfrequented lodgings, who eat low food, and who subdue their senses, will not be attacked by the foe, Love, who is vanquished as disease is by medicine.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira’s teaching treats Love as an enemy-sickness and prescribes the discipline of the senses as its medicine.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks what medicine can cure love-sickness; the Uttaradhyayana names one, though it is the monk’s cure of renunciation, not the lover’s cure of reunion.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O mind, there is only the One medicine, mantra and healing herb - center your consciousness firmly on the One Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak speaks directly to his own mind and tells it that there is a single remedy for its sickness: steady remembrance of the One Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife begs her heart to think of some medicine, any medicine, for a grief nothing else can cure; Guru Nanak, also addressing the mind, names the one medicine that heals the longing soul.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 156, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poet Theocritus tells of the Cyclops Polyphemus, hopelessly in love with the sea-nymph Galatea, and opens by saying there is no other remedy for love, neither ointment nor salve, except the Muses; Polyphemus eased his love by sitting on a rock and singing to her.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Idyll treats love as an illness with almost no cure, and finds relief only in song, a kind of talking to oneself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise looks for a medicine for love and, finding none, pours her heart out in words to herself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero, discussing the passions, sets out the ‘cure’ for love: show the lover how trivial the object of desire is, turn his mind to other cares and interests, and sometimes treat it like other illnesses by change of place.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero treats erotic love as a disturbance of the mind that philosophy can treat like a disease.
philosophy.tie_back: Where the Kural’s heroine begs for any medicine for love-sickness, Cicero offers a philosopher’s prescription.

real_life_example.event_title: Ancient Egyptian love songs on lovesickness no physician can cure
real_life_example.event: Love songs from Egypt's Ramesside period, linked with the craftsmen's village of Deir el-Medina, survive on papyri including Papyrus Chester Beatty I, now in Dublin. In one stanza the young man says that his sickness cannot be relieved by the remedies of physicians and that only his beloved's presence can cure him; the songs also describe the beloved herself as a medicine whose sight brings health.
real_life_example.explanation: These are among the oldest surviving love poems in the world, and they already treat love-longing as an illness beyond ordinary medicine.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife begs her heart to name any medicine at all for a sickness nothing else can cure, and the Egyptian lover, more than three thousand years ago, found that no physician's remedy could touch his.

tamil:
காதல் அவரிலர் ஆகநீ நோவது
பேதைமை வாழியென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Kaadhal avarilar aakanee noavadhu
paedhaimai vaazhiyen nenju.
meaning: Long live you, my heart! He has no love for us, so your suffering over him is just foolish.
elementary: Imagine you keep waiting by the door for a friend who has forgotten all about you. You might say to yourself, “Silly heart, why are you sad about someone who isn’t even thinking about you?”
university: The heroine now scolds her heart: kātal avar ilar āka (‘he being without love’), nī nōvatu (‘your aching’) is pētaimai (‘folly, simple-mindedness’, from pētai ‘simpleton’). The interjection vāḻi eṉ neñcu (‘long may you live, my heart!’) is a conventional blessing that here carries gentle irony, as Solomon Pappaiah’s rendering ‘நீ வாழ்ந்து போ’ makes explicit. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both gloss pētaimai as aṟiyāmai (ignorance), and Pope translates ‘thy smart is folly, fare thee well my heart’. The traditional reading, which modern commentators follow, takes the accusation of lovelessness as the wife’s overstatement in grief rather than a settled judgment of her husband. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For him who has conquered the mind, the mind is the best of friends; but for one who has failed to do so, his very mind will be the greatest enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the mind can be either one’s closest ally or one’s worst foe, depending on whether it is mastered.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers this double nature: her heart is both her only confidant and the foolish source of her pain.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.6 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs urges a person to guard the heart carefully, since everything in life flows from it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, seeing her heart ache foolishly, is in effect trying to keep watch over it.

islam.quote_or_event: “But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah Knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that what the heart loves is not always good for it, since human knowledge is limited.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine tells her heart that loving one who does not love back is folly, a love that is ‘bad for you’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? And why moanest thou within me? Hope thou in God; for I shall yet praise Him for the salvation of His countenance.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist questions his own downcast soul as if it were another person, challenging its sorrow.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same inner dialogue the Kural stages: the speaker addresses her heart and asks why it aches.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that recognising one’s own foolishness is already the beginning of wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: By calling her own heart foolish (pētai), the Kural’s heroine shows exactly this first glimmer of self-knowledge.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you owned the beauty of Vaiśramaṇa, the pleasing manners of Nalakūbara, if you were like Purandara himself, I should have no desire for you.”
jainism.explanation: Rājīmatī, now a nun, tells Rathanemi, who has fallen for her, that his longing is hopeless and recalls him to his vows.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine tells her heart the same hard truth: aching for someone who does not return your love is folly.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.41 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I am ungraceful and ill-mannered, full of endless faults. How can I go to enjoy my Husband Lord?”
sikhism.explanation: In the hymn known as Kuchajji, Guru Nanak speaks as a soul-bride who blames her own faults, not her Husband, for the distance between them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife tells her heart that its pain is folly because he has no love for them; Gurbani turns the charge around, teaching that the divine Husband never lacks love and the gap lies in the bride's own failings.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 762, Raag Soohee (Kuchajji), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Back in his own palace, Odysseus lies awake seething, strikes his breast and rebukes his own heart, telling it to endure, since it once endured something worse, the day the Cyclops devoured his companions.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows a hero talking sternly to his own heart (kradiē) to master an overwhelming emotion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Odysseus speaks to his heart as to a separate person, reproaching it for what it feels.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal observes that the heart has its own reasons, which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal sees the heart as a faculty that loves and judges by its own logic, often against what reason advises.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces exactly this: her reason calls the heart’s ache folly, yet the heart goes on aching.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, no. 277 (Brunschvicg numbering; 423 in Lafuma) (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Charlotte Brontë's unanswered letters to Constantin Héger
real_life_example.event: After studying and teaching in Brussels, Charlotte Brontë kept writing to her former teacher Constantin Héger, a married man, making her feelings plain in January 1845. Héger barely replied and by the end of 1845 had stopped replying altogether; in one letter she wrote that a friend had brought her neither letter nor message from him. Four of her letters survive because Héger's wife retrieved the torn letters from the wastebasket and mended them, and his family gave them to the British Library in 1913.
real_life_example.explanation: The letters reveal the private heartbreak behind one of England's greatest novelists and show how long she went on hoping for an answer that never came.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine tells her heart that since he has no love for them, its suffering is mere foolishness, and Brontë kept pouring out her feelings to a man who would not reply.

tamil:
இருந்துள்ளி என்பரிதல் நெஞ்சே பரிந்துள்ளல்
பைதல்நோய் செய்தார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Irundhulli enparidhal nenje parindhullal
paidhalnoai seydhaarkan il.
meaning: My heart, why stay here thinking of him and suffering? The one who gave us this sickness of sorrow has no kind thoughts for us.
elementary: Think of sitting by the window all day thinking about a friend who moved away, while that friend is busy and not thinking about you. You might ask yourself, “Why am I sitting here feeling sad when they aren’t even missing me?”
university: The heart is questioned for sitting idle: iruntu uḷḷi (‘remaining here and thinking’) eṉ paritaltal (‘why grieve?’), while parintu uḷḷal (‘thinking with tender pity’) is absent in the one who caused paital nōy (‘the sickness of sorrow’; paital = distress). Solomon Pappaiah unpacks iruntu as ‘neither going to where he is, nor dying here’, a reading that sharpens the reproach of passive pining. Pope’s explanation on ytamizh.com prints ‘there are no lewd thoughts (of you) in him’, which looks like a transcription slip for ‘loving thoughts’; all four Tamil glosses render parintu uḷḷal as anpu or irakkam (love, pity). The commentary tradition treats the line as the heroine voicing a suspicion she does not finally believe. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While speaking learned words, you are mourning for what is not worthy of grief.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna gently rebukes Arjuna for indulging a grief that true understanding would not sustain.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine rebukes her heart in the same way: why sit here grieving over one who is not grieving for you?
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.11 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs observes that waiting endlessly for what one longs for makes the heart literally ill.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sits pining for a husband who does not come, and names her state a ‘sickness of sorrow’.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those who have believed and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allah. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are assured.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that the heart finds true rest in remembering God.
islam.tie_back: In contrast to the Kural’s heart, which finds only sickness in dwelling on an absent man, the Qur’an names a remembrance that brings peace.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Return, O my soul, unto Thy rest; For the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist tells his own soul to stop its restless distress and come back to rest.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise tells her heart to stop sitting and pining in vain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha notes that being apart from a loved one is itself a form of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is living exactly this pain of ‘not seeing the beloved’.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra lists ārta-dhyāna, ‘sorrowful brooding’, as an inauspicious form of meditation, one kind being the constant thought of regaining a cherished person or thing from which one has been separated.
jainism.explanation: Jain psychology classes repeated grieving over a lost beloved as a harmful mental state that binds karma.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, ‘sitting and thinking’ of the husband who has gone, is caught in exactly this kind of brooding, which her own heart questions.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra ch. 9, sutras on ārta-dhyāna (tr. Nathmal Tatia, paraphrase; sutra numbers differ between Svetambara and Digambara recensions)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My body is cooking like an oven; my bones are burning like firewood. If my feet become tired, I will walk on my head, if I can meet my Beloved.”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid describes a longing so fierce that he would go to his Beloved even on his head once his feet gave out.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife asks her heart why it sits here pining for one who has no tender thought for them; Farid shows the opposite of idle pining, a lover ready to go to the Beloved at any cost.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 119) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ariadne, waking on the island of Naxos to find Theseus has sailed away, writes to him from the shore, lamenting that she still thinks of him while he has no thought or pity for her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid gives voice to an abandoned heroine whose love is met only by the beloved’s indifference.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, too, sits grieving for one who ‘has no tender thought’ for her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus begins his handbook by dividing things into those within our power, such as our judgments and desires, and those not within our power, which we must not let disturb us.
philosophy.explanation: Stoic practice trains the mind to stop agonising over what lies in another’s control.
philosophy.tie_back: Whether the absent husband thinks of her is not in the heroine’s power, which is why her reason questions her heart’s pining.

real_life_example.event_title: Petrarch first sees Laura in Avignon
real_life_example.event: In 1327, at Avignon, the Italian poet Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch) first saw the woman he called Laura. She became the idealised subject of his chaste love and the main subject of his poetry for the rest of his life, and he gathered his lyrics into the Canzoniere, which eventually held 366 poems.
real_life_example.explanation: Petrarch's lifelong poetry for a love he could never have shaped the European love sonnet for centuries.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine asks her heart why it sits thinking and suffering over someone who gives no tender thought in return, and Petrarch spent decades pining in verse for a woman his love could never possess.

tamil:
கண்ணும் கொளச்சேறி நெஞ்சே இவையென்னைத்
தின்னும் அவர்க்காணல் உற்று.
transliteration:
Kannum kolachchaeri nenje ivaiyennaith
thinnum avarkkaanal utru.
meaning: My heart, when you go to him, take my eyes with you too. They want so badly to see him that they are eating me alive.
elementary: Imagine your heart can fly to visit someone you miss, but your eyes are stuck at home and keep crying because they want to see that person too. So you say, “Heart, please take my eyes with you, they won’t stop bothering me!”
university: This couplet presupposes that the heart has already gone to the absent husband (a convention developed in neighbouring couplets), so the heroine asks it to take the eyes too: kaṇṇum koḷa (‘taking the eyes also’) cēṟi (‘you will go’). The eyes, left behind, ivai eṉṉait tiṉṉum (‘these devour me’) avar kāṇal uṟṟu (‘set on seeing him’); Mu. Varadarasanar glosses tiṉṉum as பிடுங்கித் தின்கின்றன (‘pluck and eat’), and Pappaiah softens it to ‘grieve as though eating me’. The image of a body divided against itself, heart travelling while eyes torment the one who stays, extends the Kāmattuppāl motif of personified eyes (compare chapter 118, kaṇ vitumpu aḻital). Pope renders the line ‘O rid me of these eyes, my heart’. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When You go off to the forest during the day, a tiny fraction of a second becomes like a millennium for us because we cannot see You.”
hinduism.explanation: The gopis tell Krishna that every moment their eyes cannot see him is unbearable.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise suffers through her eyes, which torment her with their craving to see the absent beloved.
hinduism.source: Srimad Bhagavatam 10.31.15 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Mine eyes fail for thy word, saying, When wilt thou comfort me?”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes his eyes wearing out with longing as he waits for a comfort that does not come.
christianity.tie_back: In the Kural the eyes, too, are consumed by longing for one who stays away.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an distinguishes the eyes from the heart and locates true seeing in the heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural also separates eyes and heart, imagining the heart going off while the eyes stay behind and suffer.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I am weary of my crying; my throat is dried; Mine eyes fail while I wait for my God.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes his eyes worn out with waiting and weeping for one who has not yet come.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes are similarly ‘eaten up’ by waiting to see the absent beloved.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The monk Vakkali loved simply to gaze at the Buddha’s body; when he was ill and longed to see him, the Buddha came and told him that there was no point in looking at this body, for whoever sees the Dhamma sees the Buddha.
buddhism.explanation: The story treats the eyes’ craving to see a beloved form as something to be redirected inward.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes are consumed by the same craving to see the beloved, which the Buddha gently tells Vakkali to look beyond.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: In Jain teaching each sense, beginning with the eye, can destroy a person through its passionate attachment to its object.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes, ‘eating’ the heroine with their craving to see her husband, are just such a sense consuming its owner.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My eyes long for You; when will I see Your Vision?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan voices the soul's eyes as aching for a single sight of the Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her eyes, set on seeing him, are eating her alive and asks her heart to take them along; Guru Arjan likewise gives the eyes their own longing for the Beloved's vision.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1094, Raag Maaroo, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Clytie, abandoned by the sun-god Helios, sat on the bare ground for nine days without food, turning her face and eyes to follow him across the sky, until she was changed into a flower that still turns toward the sun.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s story makes the abandoned lover’s gaze itself the thing that consumes her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s eyes, which ‘eat’ the heroine in their longing to see her husband, Clytie’s eyes follow her beloved until she wastes away.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates describes how the lover’s soul, when parted from the beloved, becomes parched and frantic, unable to sleep or rest, and runs wherever it hopes to catch sight of the beautiful one, finding relief only in seeing him.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats the sight of the beloved as what nourishes the lover’s soul, and its absence as torment.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes, tormenting the heroine in their need to see her husband, express the same dependence on sight.

real_life_example.event_title: Abigail Adams crosses the Atlantic to rejoin John Adams
real_life_example.place: Boston, Massachusetts, to England and Auteuil, France
real_life_example.event: John Adams's long absences on public service, including diplomatic posts in Europe, left his wife Abigail to raise their children and run the farm and household in Massachusetts. In the summer of 1784, after nearly five years apart, she made a month-long voyage from Boston to England with their daughter and joined John in Europe, settling with him at Auteuil, near Paris.
real_life_example.explanation: Her journey ended one of the longest separations of any founding American couple, and her record of the voyage survives in the Adams Papers.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine, longing to see her husband, wants her eyes carried to him, and Abigail Adams, after years of longing, went herself to see the husband her heart had followed.

tamil:
செற்றார் எனக்கை விடல்உண்டோ நெஞ்சேயாம்
உற்றால் உறாஅ தவர்.
transliteration:
Setraar enakkai vidtalundo nenjaeyaam
utraal uraaa thavar.
meaning: My heart, he does not come to us even when we long for him. But can we really give him up, saying, "He hates us"?
elementary: Imagine a friend who hasn’t called you back in a long time. You could decide, “They don’t like me anymore, I’ll forget them,” but deep down you know you can’t stop caring about them.
university: The heroine tests the idea of abandoning her husband and rejects it: ceṟṟār eṉa (‘saying he is one who hates us’, from ceṟu ‘to hate, be hostile’) kaiviṭal uṇṭō (‘is there such a thing as letting go?’). The second line contrasts yām uṟṟāl (‘though we draw close, long for him’) with uṟāatavar (‘he who does not draw close’), the lengthened uṟāa being an alapeṭai (prosodic lengthening) for metre. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the question as rhetorical (‘can we give him up?’), whereas Pappaiah turns it toward her own will (‘do I have the firmness of heart to give him up?’). The couplet thus marks the chapter’s turn from reproaching the heart to confessing its constancy. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “So let us give up all friendship with this dark-complexioned boy, even if we can’t give up talking about Him.”
hinduism.explanation: In the ‘Song of the Bee’, the gopis, feeling abandoned by Krishna, list his apparent cruelties and resolve to give him up, yet admit they cannot stop speaking of him.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine reaches the same impasse: she can call him unloving, but she cannot let him go.
hinduism.source: Srimad Bhagavatam 10.47.17 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes true love as something that does not give up, however much it must endure.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds her love for her absent husband cannot be abandoned, even when he seems not to return it.

islam.quote_or_event: “…he has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her [to be] in clear error.”
islam.explanation: The women of the city say that the governor’s wife is so consumed with love for Joseph, who does not return it, that she has lost all judgment.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she loves one who does not draw near to her and cannot give that love up.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it; If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs declares that love, once kindled, cannot be put out by any force.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds that even the thought ‘he hates us’ cannot quench her love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that holding someone dear creates a bond that makes separation painful.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers just such a bond: she cannot let go of the one she holds dear, even though it hurts.

jainism.quote_or_event: The courtesan Kośā loved Sthūlabhadra, who left her to become a monk; when he returned years later to spend a rainy season in her house, he did not return her love, yet her devotion did not die, and in the end she was won over to the Jain path herself.
jainism.explanation: This famous Jain story shows a woman whose love outlasts the beloved’s withdrawal, until it is transformed rather than abandoned.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Kośā cannot simply give up the one who no longer draws near to her.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Pariśiṣṭaparvan, story of Sthūlabhadra and Kośā (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “What sort of love is this, which clings to duality? O Nanak, he alone is called a lover, who remains forever immersed in absorption.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Angad teaches that true love does not drift elsewhere when the Beloved seems distant; a real lover stays absorbed in the one Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife decides she cannot give up a husband who does not come, calling him hostile; Guru Angad likewise holds that a true lover never turns away from the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo, rejected by Narcissus, hides in the woods in shame, yet her love clings to her and even grows with the pain of being refused.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid portrays a love that survives open rejection and cannot be torn out.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds the same: even if he does not come to her, she cannot cast her love aside.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle asks whether a friendship should be broken off when the other person changes, and answers that one should not break it off hastily, but keep some regard for the friend for the sake of the past.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that a bond once formed should not be lightly abandoned even when the other has changed.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine reaches a similar conclusion about her husband: she cannot write him off as one who hates her.

real_life_example.event_title: Juliette Drouet's fifty years of devotion to Victor Hugo
real_life_example.event: Juliette Drouet was Victor Hugo's companion for about fifty years and wrote him some 22,000 letters, at least one a day. After the coup of 1851 she helped Hugo escape France with false papers and joined him in Brussels within days of his arrival. Through his long exile she never lived with him, staying with friends, in hotels or in rented rooms, and from 1864 in a house he bought for her, yet she did not leave his side for a single day.
real_life_example.explanation: Her letters are one of the largest records of a single love in literary history.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine asks whether she can ever give up a man who does not come to her when she longs for him, and Drouet, never sharing Hugo's home, still could not give him up in fifty years.

tamil:
கலந்துணர்த்தும் காதலர்க் கண்டாற் புலந்துணராய்
பொய்க்காய்வு காய்திஎன் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Kalandhunarththum kaadhalark kandaar pulandhunaraai
poikkaaivu kaaidhi-en nenju.
meaning: My heart, when you see the one you love, who ends our sulking by holding us close, you cannot even stay upset. So the anger you show him now is fake.
elementary: Imagine pretending to be cross with your best friend, but the moment they come and give you a hug, you start smiling. So you tell yourself, “I’m not really angry, I’m just pretending!”
university: The couplet turns on the Tamil love-poetry concept of ūṭal / pulavi (a lover’s feigned sulking that is meant to be dissolved): the husband is one who kalantu uṇarttum (‘removes the sulk by union’), and when the heart sees him it does not pulantu uṇar (‘sulk and then make up’) at all. Hence its present anger is poykkāyvu (‘false heat, sham anger’, from kāy ‘to burn, be angry’) that it kāyti (‘burns with’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan follow this reading closely, while Solomon Pappaiah expands it into an exhortation: ‘give up this pretended hatred and go to him’. The couplet anticipates the later chapters on pulavi (131-133). Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (both read kaṇṭāṟ with the sandhi ṟ).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Radha, hurt by Krishna’s wandering, holds herself aloof in proud anger (mana), and her friend urges her not to be harsh with Krishna, since her resentment hurts only herself, and to go to him.
hinduism.explanation: The poem portrays a lover’s anger as a pose that melts away when faced with the beloved’s return.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine admits the same: the anger her heart shows her husband is false and would vanish at the sight of him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows that anger arises but insists it must not be held on to.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees that her anger toward her husband cannot and should not last, for it is not real.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allah] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who hold back their anger and forgive.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine recognises that her anger toward her husband is hollow and gives way at once to love.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the Song of Songs, the woman at first makes excuses not to open the door to her beloved, but her heart is moved for him and she rises to open, only to find he has gone.
judaism.explanation: Her show of reluctance gives way immediately to longing once she senses him near.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise knows her reluctance and anger are a pose that her heart cannot keep up when the beloved is near.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who checks rising anger as a charioteer checks a rolling chariot, him I call a true charioteer. Others only hold the reins.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises the person who can stop anger the moment it arises.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees that her anger toward her husband is not even worth reining in, for it is false and gives way at the sight of him.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching traces both love and anger to the same root of delusion, so that one easily turns into the other.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees that her anger at her husband is only the other face of her love, and so is not real anger at all.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.101 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The happy soul-bride knows the worth of her Husband Lord. Renouncing pride, she enjoys peace and pleasure.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas says the bride who truly values her Husband lets go of her pride, and so enjoys union with Him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife tells her heart its anger is false, since it melts the moment the beloved embraces them; Ravidas likewise teaches that the bride who knows her Husband's worth drops her pride and enjoys His company.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 793, Raag Soohee, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Troy fell, Menelaus came upon Helen intending to kill her for her betrayal, but at the sight of her beauty he let his sword fall and took her back.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this well-known tradition, the husband’s anger cannot survive the sight of the woman he loves.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine knows her anger is equally hollow and would collapse the moment she saw her husband.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Andromache c. 627-631; cf. Aristophanes, Lysistrata 155-156 (paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues that anger is not a natural necessity but a choice of the mind, which can be checked at its first stirring by reason.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, anger exists only because the mind assents to it, and so it can be dissolved.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees through her own anger in just this way: it is a pose her heart has adopted, not something real.

real_life_example.event_title: Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton remarry in Botswana
real_life_example.place: Kasane, near Chobe Game Park, Botswana
real_life_example.event: Actors Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton married in Montreal in 1964 and divorced in 1974 after stormy years together. About sixteen months later, on 10 October 1975, they secretly remarried in a ceremony performed by a district commissioner at Kasane, near Chobe Game Park in Botswana. The second marriage lasted about nine months.
real_life_example.explanation: Their remarriage became the best-known modern example of a couple whose quarrels could not keep them apart.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the heart cannot even keep up a sulk when it sees the beloved, so its anger is false, and Taylor and Burton's divorce gave way to remarriage as soon as they were together again.

tamil:
காமம் விடுஒன்றோ நாண்விடு நன்னெஞ்சே
யானோ பொறேன்இவ் விரண்டு.
transliteration:
Kaamam viduondroa naanvidu nannenjae
yaanoa poraen-iv virandu.
meaning: My good heart, either let go of your love or let go of your modesty. I cannot carry both of them at once.
elementary: Imagine wanting very badly to tell someone how much you miss them, but feeling too shy to say it. Holding both feelings at once is hard, so you tell yourself, “Either stop missing them, or stop being shy and just tell them!”
university: This is the chapter’s best-known dilemma: kāmam viṭu oṉṟō (‘either let go of desire’) nāṇ viṭu (‘or let go of modesty’), for yāṉō poṟēṉ iv iraṇṭu (‘I cannot bear these two together’). Nāṇ (modesty, shame) is a defining virtue of the Tamil heroine, which normally forbids her from going to the man or declaring her longing; kāmam here means love-desire, not merely physical lust. The heart is called naṉṉeñcu (‘good heart’), a coaxing address. Kalaignar makes the conflict explicit (desire drives her to speak, modesty stops her), and Pappaiah stresses that the two pull in opposite directions; Pope renders it ‘Or bid thy love, or bid thy shame depart’. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the gopis of Vraja hear Krishna’s flute at night, they abandon their household duties and the restraints of family and propriety, and hurry to meet him in the forest.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata’s account, love for Krishna overpowers the gopis’ sense of social shame.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces the same choice between love and modesty; the gopis resolve it by letting modesty go.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes a self torn between two opposing pulls that he cannot reconcile.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is likewise torn between two forces, desire and modesty, and finds she cannot bear both.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet, passing a man who was admonishing his brother for being too modest, told him to leave him, for modesty (haya’) is part of faith.
islam.explanation: Islamic teaching holds modesty to be an essential virtue, not a weakness to be overcome.
