islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels modesty as a real value even while love presses her to abandon it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Oh that thou wert as my brother, That sucked the breasts of my mother! When I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; Yea, and none would despise me.”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song wishes she could show her love openly without incurring public shame.
judaism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s dilemma: love wants to show itself, but modesty and fear of reproach hold it back.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that two bright qualities, hiri (moral shame) and ottappa (fear of wrongdoing), protect the world; without them, people would lose all restraint.
buddhism.explanation: In Buddhism, a sense of shame is a guardian virtue that keeps desire in check.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels the pull of this guardian, modesty, against her desire, and cannot bear both.

jainism.quote_or_event: “…all these manifold passions arise in him who is attached to pleasures; and so do other emotions produced by those (before mentioned) arise in him who is to be pitied, who (ought to be) ashamed of himself, and who is hateful.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain text lists the many passions, including fear and sorrow, that spring up in one attached to pleasures, leaving him a figure of shame.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels desire and shame at war within her; the Jain answer would be to let go of desire, not modesty.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.102-103 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, when you are in love with the One Lord, duality and alienation depart.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir says that a heart wholly given to the One Lord is no longer torn between rival pulls.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife tells her heart to give up either desire or modesty, because she cannot bear both at once; Kabir offers the Sikh answer to a divided heart, single-minded love that ends the inner tug-of-war.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1365, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Medea, falling in love with Jason, spends a sleepless night torn between shame (aidōs) and love: her modesty and loyalty to her father hold her back, while love drives her to help the stranger.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius gives a famous portrait of a young woman divided between modesty and passion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural’s dilemma: the heroine cannot carry both love and modesty and begs her heart to drop one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s image of the soul as a chariot, one horse is restrained by modesty and shame, while the other is driven by desire toward the beloved, and the charioteer is pulled painfully between them.
philosophy.explanation: Plato pictures the lover’s soul as divided between a horse of shame and a horse of desire.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences exactly this divided pull between modesty and desire, and finds it unbearable.

real_life_example.event_title: Clara Wieck goes to court against her father to marry Robert Schumann
real_life_example.event: The pianist Clara Wieck and the composer Robert Schumann became secretly engaged in 1837, but her father Friedrich Wieck rejected Robert's written request for her hand and did everything he could to keep them apart. Rather than give Robert up, Clara joined him in taking her father to court for permission to marry; her father disowned her, the court gave them permission in 1840, and they married on 12 September 1840 at Schönefeld near Leipzig.
real_life_example.explanation: For a young woman of her time, suing her own father was a startling break with the duty of obedience expected of a daughter.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says she cannot bear both her desire and her modesty and must give up one, and Clara Wieck, caught between a daughter's duty and her love, finally chose love.

tamil:
பரிந்தவர் நல்காரென்று ஏங்கிப் பிரிந்தவர்
பின்செல்வாய் பேதைஎன் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Parindhavar nalkaarendru aengip pirindhavar
pinselvaai paedhaien nenju.
meaning: My foolish heart, you are sad that he will not feel sorry for us and be kind. Yet you still run after the one who left us.
elementary: Imagine saying, “My friend doesn’t care about me!” and then running after that same friend anyway. You might laugh at yourself: “Silly heart, you complain about them and then follow them everywhere!”
university: The heart is again called pētai (‘simpleton’), now for a contradiction: it laments (ēṅki) that the husband, out of pity (parintu), nalkār (‘will not show favour’), yet it goes piṉ cel (‘following behind’) the one who has pirintavar (‘parted’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the line as exposing the heart’s inconsistency; Solomon Pappaiah gives the more sympathetic reading that the heart follows him to tell him of her suffering, which he simply does not know. The verb nalku (‘to bestow grace, be kind’) is a key word of Tamil love poetry, often used of the hero’s favour to the heroine. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna suddenly vanishes from the rasa dance, the gopis wander through the forest searching for him, asking the trees and creepers whether they have seen him pass.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata portrays lovers who, though left behind, cannot stop following the one who has gone.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart likewise runs after the husband who has left, even while complaining that he shows no kindness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
christianity.explanation: The bride seeks and calls after a beloved who has withdrawn and does not answer.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heart, too, goes after one who has left and gives no response to its longing.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s romance, Majnun, separated from Layla, leaves everything behind and wanders the desert in pursuit of her, though she cannot come to him.
islam.explanation: The poem portrays a lover whose heart follows the beloved wherever she has gone, regardless of reason.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heart, called foolish, likewise follows the one who has parted from it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not. ’I will rise now, and go about the city, In the streets and in the broad ways, I will seek him whom my soul loveth.’ I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song rises at night and goes out through the city in search of her absent beloved.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart, too, cannot stay still but goes after the one who has gone away.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Wonderful, indeed, it is to subdue the mind, so difficult to subdue, ever swift, and seizing whatever it desires. A tamed mind brings happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the untamed mind as swift and always rushing after what it wants.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart behaves exactly so, rushing after the departed husband against the heroine’s own judgment.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Prince Ariṣṭanemi (Neminatha) renounced the world on his wedding day and went up Mount Raivataka, his bride Rājīmatī, overwhelmed with grief, cut off her hair, became a nun, and herself set out for Mount Raivataka.
jainism.explanation: The Jain story shows a forsaken bride following the one who left her, though along the path of renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart likewise follows the one who has parted from it, though Rājīmatī’s following is spiritual, not romantic.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.22-33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Thirsty with desire, I wander around; when will I behold the Lord of the World?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan pictures the longing soul roaming about in search of the Beloved she cannot yet see.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife chides her foolish heart for running after the one who left even as it complains he will not come back in kindness; Guru Arjan's bride likewise wanders in thirsting search of the absent Lord.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 928, Raag Raamkalee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After losing Eurydice, Orpheus follows her down into the underworld itself, unable to accept being parted from her.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows a lover who will follow the beloved even beyond the limits of the living world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heart, too, follows the one who has left, even though doing so is called foolish.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes tells how humans were split in two, and how each half now searches for and runs after its other half, longing to be reunited.
philosophy.explanation: The myth explains love as the restless pursuit of the missing part of oneself.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heart, following the one who has parted from it, enacts just this pursuit of the missing half.

real_life_example.event_title: Decembrist wives follow their husbands into Siberian exile
real_life_example.place: From European Russia to Nerchinsk, Siberia
real_life_example.event: After the failed Decembrist revolt of 14 December 1825, its leaders were sent into exile in Siberia. Princess Katherine Trubetskaya left to join her husband about a week behind the prisoner convoy in July 1826, and Princess Maria Volkonskaya, married to Prince Sergei Volkonsky only in January 1825, petitioned Tsar Nicholas I for permission to follow him. To go, Maria had to leave her son with her husband's family and accept that she could never return to European Russia, even if her husband died.
real_life_example.explanation: Their decision became a lasting symbol in Russia of a wife's loyalty at any cost.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine chides her heart for running after the one who has gone away, and the Decembrist wives did just that, following their husbands to the far end of the empire.

tamil:
உள்ளத்தார் காத லவரால் உள்ளிநீ
யாருழைச் சேறியென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Ullaththaar kaadha lavaraal ulli-nee
yaaruzhaich cheriyaen nenju.
meaning: My heart, the one we love lives right here inside you. So when you think of him, where are you going to look for him?
elementary: Imagine searching the whole house for your favourite toy while holding it in your hand the whole time. The Kural says the same to the heart: “The person you miss is already inside you, why go looking for them outside?”
university: The heroine catches her heart in a paradox: kātalavar uḷḷattār āl (‘the beloved is in the heart’, with āl as an emphatic particle), so when nī uḷḷi (‘you, thinking of him’) set off, yār uḻai cēṟi (‘to whom will you go?’; uḻai = ‘to the side of, to the place of’). Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it as ‘to whom do you go searching, when he is within?’; Pope gives ‘Roaming, whom dost thou think to find?’. The line is a rare moment of consolation in the chapter, and has often been read devotionally, the beloved dwelling in the heart being a common image in Tamil bhakti. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh prints a spaced kāta lavarāl).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Lord is situated in everyone’s heart, O Arjuna, and is directing the wanderings of all living entities, who are seated as on a machine, made of the material energy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the One whom beings seek already dwells within their own hearts.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine realises the same of her beloved: he lives inside her heart, so there is nowhere outside to search.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.61 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his hearers not to look for the kingdom here or there, for it is already within them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly tells the heart not to go searching outside for the one who already lives inside it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We have already created man and know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than [his] jugular vein”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says God is nearer to a person than their own life-vein, so there is no need to seek Him far away.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers that her beloved, too, is nearer than anywhere her heart might wander to find him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Set me as a seal upon thy heart, As a seal upon thine arm; For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved asks to be pressed into the heart like a seal, a permanent mark within.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved already is such a seal: he dwells in the heroine’s heart, so the heart need not seek him elsewhere.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Dwelling in the cave (of the heart), the mind, without form, wanders far and alone. Those who subdue this mind are liberated from the bonds of Mara.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the mind as dwelling in the heart yet constantly wandering far away.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart behaves just so: its beloved lives inside it, yet it wanders off to search for him.

jainism.quote_or_event: Kundakunda teaches that the pure soul is to be found and known within oneself, by turning inward, and that seeking it among outward things is a delusion.
jainism.explanation: Digambara mysticism insists that what one truly seeks is found within, not in external objects.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural tells the heart a similar truth about its beloved, who already dwells within, though Jainism would point to the self rather than a lover.
jainism.source: Kundakunda, Samayasara (general teaching; paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, why do you wander from jungle to jungle, crashing through the thorny trees? The Lord abides in the heart; why are you looking for Him in the jungle?”
sikhism.explanation: Sheikh Farid tells the seeker that the Beloved already lives in the heart, so roaming outside to find Him is pointless.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife asks her heart where it is going to look for the beloved who already dwells inside it; Farid asks the very same question of the soul searching the jungles for a Lord who abides within.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 19) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Laodamia, whose husband Protesilaus was killed at Troy, kept a likeness of him in her chamber and devoted herself to it as if he were still present.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows a wife keeping her absent husband present to herself through an image she holds close.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine keeps her husband present in her heart, which makes any outward search unnecessary.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Too late did I love You, O Fairness, so ancient, and yet so new! Too late did I love You! For behold, You were within, and I without, and there did I seek You”
philosophy.explanation: Augustine confesses that he searched outside himself for the One he loved, who was all the while within him.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine catches her heart making the same mistake: running outside to seek a beloved who lives within.

real_life_example.event_title: Rumi's Divan-e Shams after Shams of Tabriz disappears
real_life_example.event: In Konya in the 1240s the scholar and preacher Jalal al-Din Rumi met the wandering dervish Shams al-Din of Tabriz, and the two became close companions who were rarely apart. Shams later disappeared and was never seen again; Rumi turned to poetry, music and dance, and his great collection of lyric poems, the Divan-e Shams, is named after his lost companion and expresses his love and longing for him.
real_life_example.explanation: Rumi's grief for a vanished companion produced some of the most widely read poetry in the world.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural reminds the heart that the beloved lives within it, so there is no one outside to search for, and Rumi, having lost Shams, came to speak in his name in poems that carried Shams within them.

tamil:
துன்னாத் துறந்தாரை நெஞ்சத்து உடையேமா
இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்.
transliteration:
Thunnaath thurandhaarai nenjaththu udaiyaemaa
innum izhaththum kavin.
meaning: If we keep in our heart the one who left us and does not come near, we will lose even more of the beauty we have left.
elementary: Imagine thinking all day about a friend who went away and never visits. The more you think about it, the more tired and sad you look. So you tell yourself, “If I keep holding on like this, I’ll lose even more of my sparkle.”
university: The closing couplet weighs the cost of constancy: tuṉṉāt tuṟantārai (‘him who, not drawing near, has left us’; tuṉṉu ‘to approach, be joined’, tuṟa ‘to leave, renounce’) neñcattu uṭaiyēmā (‘if we hold in the heart’), iṉṉum iḻattum kaviṉ (‘we shall lose still more of our beauty’). Kaviṉ is beauty or comeliness, linking back to chapter 124 on the wasting of the limbs. Solomon Pappaiah draws out the force of iṉṉum (‘still more’): having already lost her outer beauty, she will now lose her inner beauty too, a reading echoed in Pope’s ‘further loss of dignity’. The line ends the soliloquy on the heroine’s awareness that her loyalty is consuming her, without any resolve to give it up. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces how continually dwelling on an object in the mind deepens attachment and leads to ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees the same pattern in herself: by keeping the absent man in her heart, she is wearing herself away further.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.62 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “My heart is smitten, and withered like grass; so that I forget to eat my bread.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes grief so deep that his heart withers and he neglects even to eat.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, holding on to the man who left, is likewise withering and losing what beauty she has left.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an counsels believers not to be consumed by grief over what has passed out of their reach.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees that clinging to one who has left her is consuming her, the very despair this verse warns against.

judaism.quote_or_event: “’Stay ye me with dainties, refresh me with apples; For I am love-sick.’”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song says her love has made her literally faint and ill.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, too, is being worn down in body by the love she keeps in her heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From craving springs grief, from craving springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that holding on to what one craves is the source of grief.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine recognises that holding the departed man in her heart is what keeps her grieving and wasting.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Jina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction. Rājīmatī thought: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.’”
jainism.explanation: Rājīmatī, abandoned on her wedding day when Neminatha renounced the world, loses all her joy, then turns her grief into renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she is forsaken by the one who ‘renounced’ (tuṟantār), and her gaiety drains away.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.28-29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So smash your bracelets along with your bed, O soul-bride, and break your arms, along with the arms of your couch.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak tells the adorned bride whose Husband does not love her that all her ornaments are worthless and might as well be broken.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife fears that holding in her heart one who has left her will cost her still more of her beauty; Guru Nanak likewise says that adornment and beauty are wasted when the Husband's love is absent.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 557, Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Spurned by Narcissus, Echo wastes away with sleepless care: her body grows thin, her beauty dries up, and at last only her voice and bones remain.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows a lover literally consumed by holding on to one who will not return her love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine foresees the same fate: keeping the departed man in her heart will strip away what beauty she has left.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius warns that love is a wound that festers and grows worse the more it is fed, and advises the lover to stop feeding it with images of the absent beloved before it becomes incurable.
philosophy.explanation: Lucretius sees dwelling on the beloved’s image as the very thing that makes love’s sickness worse.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine comes to the same realisation: holding him in her heart only deepens her loss.

real_life_example.event_title: Queen Victoria's long seclusion after Prince Albert's death
real_life_example.event: Prince Albert died of typhoid fever in 1861 at the age of 42, and Queen Victoria sank into deep mourning. She wore black for the rest of her life and for years rarely appeared in public, spending more than a decade largely in seclusion. She was widely criticised for her withdrawal, her popularity sank, and a strong republican movement developed in Britain.
real_life_example.explanation: Her case shows how holding on to grief for a lost husband cost even a queen her standing with her people.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural warns that keeping in the heart the one who has gone will cost still more of one's beauty and standing, and Victoria's devotion to the absent Albert cost her much of her public esteem.

tamil:
காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும்
நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு.
transliteration:
Kaamak kanichchi utaikkum niraiyennum
naanuththaazh veezhththa kadhavu.
meaning: My self-control was like a door locked tight with the bolt of modesty. But the axe of love smashes that door down.
elementary: Imagine a girl who keeps her feelings locked behind a strong door, with shyness as the bolt. But her love for someone is like a big axe, and one swing breaks the whole door open. Feelings that strong cannot stay locked away.
university: Chapter 126, niṟai aḻital (‘the breaking of reserve’), opens with the heroine (talaivi), parted from her husband, admitting that the self-command she prized has given way. The image is architectural: niṟai (reserve, the firmness that keeps inner feeling from showing) is the door (katavu), nāṇ (modesty, shame) is the bolt (tāḻ) that holds it, and kāmam (love-longing) is the kaṇicci, a heavy axe or pick, which breaks it; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss kaṇicci as an axe (கோடாலி/கோடரி). In the reading associated with Parimelazhagar, niṟai is the faculty that guards what should be kept within and nāṇ is its fastening, so the couplet states the chapter’s claim that love overpowers both together. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. Textual note: ytamizh.com’s English ‘Couplet Explanation’ for 1251 (‘My precious life is saved by the raise of rumour…’) does not fit this couplet and appears to be misplaced from another kural; its Pope couplet (‘The axe of lust can break the door of chastity…’) is the relevant rendering.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The senses are so strong and impetuous, O Arjuna, that they forcibly carry away the mind even of a man of discrimination who is endeavoring to control them.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that even a wise person who is trying to stay in control can have his mind seized by the force of the senses.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine had the same careful control, and love carries it off by force like an axe through a bolted door.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.60 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my bowels were moved for him. I rose up to open to my beloved; and my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with sweet smelling myrrh, upon the handles of the lock.”
christianity.explanation: The bride, already settled for the night, is so moved by her beloved’s hand at the door that she rises to unbolt it.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts use a bolted door to picture a woman’s reserve, and in both love gets through it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him. She closed the doors and said, ‘Come, you.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells how the wife of al-Aziz, overcome by longing for Joseph, set aside her position and modesty.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows love breaking down a woman’s reserve; here the same passion overrides a noblewoman’s dignity, though the Qur’an condemns her intent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “…for love is strong as death, jealousy is cruel as the grave; the flashes thereof are flashes of fire, a very flame of the LORD. Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it…”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs declares love a force as unstoppable as death that nothing can put out.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s axe expresses the same conviction: no bolt of modesty can hold love back.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, so passion penetrates an undeveloped mind.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares an untrained mind to a badly roofed house that passion gets into as easily as rain.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts picture the self as a house that passion breaks into; the Buddha’s answer is to train the mind, while the Kural’s heroine simply admits the house has been breached.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When Râgîmatî perceived that Rathanêmi’s strength of will was broken, and temptation had got the better of him, she did not lose her presence of mind and defended her Self on that occasion.”
jainism.explanation: In a cave on Mount Raivataka, the monk Rathanemi’s resolve gives way on seeing Rajimati, while she keeps hers.
jainism.tie_back: Rathanemi is the Kural’s broken door in a monk’s robe: his will is broken by passion, exactly the collapse of niṟai the heroine describes.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Behold, O Siblings of Destiny, the storm of spiritual wisdom has come. It has totally blown away the thatched huts of doubt, and torn apart the bonds of Maya.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir describes an overwhelming inner force that sweeps away the flimsy shelter the mind had built around itself.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures love as an axe smashing the door of reserve bolted with modesty; Kabir likewise pictures a force too strong for the mind's defences, which simply tears the old structure down.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 331, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho says that Eros the limb-loosener shakes her once again, a bittersweet creature against which there is no defence.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek lyric, Eros is a force that seizes the lover from outside and undoes her body and composure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Sappho and the Kural’s heroine both describe love as an attacker that breaks through a self-possession they cannot defend.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume argues that reason alone can never oppose a passion in directing the will, and that reason is, and ought only to be, the servant of the passions.
philosophy.explanation: Hume denies that calm reasoning can stand guard against a strong passion on its own.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the same point in a lover’s terms: the reasoned restraint of niṟai cannot hold against love.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.3 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Rumi meets Shams of Tabriz in Konya
real_life_example.event: Jalal al-Din Rumi, a scholar and teacher who had taken over his father's post in Konya, met the wandering Sufi Shams of Tabriz around 1244, and the two became close companions. The friendship strained Rumi's relations with his students, family and associates, and Shams later left the city and was never seen again, around 1248. After this Rumi turned to mystical poetry, music and dance, and his major works, including the collection of lyrics named after Shams, date from this period.
real_life_example.explanation: A respected and self-contained scholar was so overcome by a single bond of love that his settled life and reputation gave way, and the feeling poured out in poetry.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the axe of love smashes the door of reserve; Rumi's scholarly composure was broken open by his love for Shams in just this way.

tamil:
காமம் எனவொன்றோ கண்ணின்றென் நெஞ்சத்தை
யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Kaamam enavondroa kannindren nenjaththai
yaamaththum aalum thozhil.
meaning: This thing called love has no pity. Even at midnight, it keeps giving orders to my heart.
elementary: Think of a strict boss who makes you work even in the middle of the night while everyone else is asleep. The heroine says love is like that boss: it never lets her heart rest, not even at midnight.
university: The heroine personifies kāmam as a harsh ruler: kaṇ iṉṟu means ‘without kaṇṇōṭṭam’ (without kindly regard, pitiless), as Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாதது), and yāmattum āḷum toḻil is ‘the work of ruling even at yāmam’, the dead of night. Solomon Pappaiah draws out the image of a master who makes a servant toil at midnight while all others sleep, which sharpens the chapter’s theme: niṟai cannot survive a power that never rests. The phrase eṉa oṉṟō (‘this one thing called…’) carries a note of exasperated contempt in the traditional commentary associated with Parimelazhagar. Sivayogi Sivakumar alone reads kaṇ iṉṟu as ‘standing in the eye’ (கண்ணில் நின்று), a minority interpretation. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On a bright autumn night the gopis of Vraja hear Krishna’s flute and, leaving whatever they were doing, run to him through the dark, unable to stay at home.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata shows love for Krishna taking command of the gopis precisely at night, overriding every household duty.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the gopis find that love rules their hearts at the hour when all others rest.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.29 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh.”
christianity.explanation: The bride is asleep, yet her heart stays awake, listening for her beloved at night.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also finds that her heart cannot rest at night; love keeps it at work.

islam.quote_or_event: Nizami tells how Qays, separated from Layla, roams the desert by night and day, so mastered by his love that he loses his name and is called Majnun, the madman.
islam.explanation: In the Persian romance, love becomes a ruler that leaves the lover no rest and no command over himself.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says love rules her heart even at midnight; Majnun’s love rules him so completely that it costs him his reason.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: In the night the woman of the Song cannot sleep; her longing sends her searching for the one she loves.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise finds love at work in her heart in the middle of the night.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Lord, as I was leaving home, a Sakyan girl — the envy of the countryside — glanced up at me, with her hair half-combed, and said, ‘Hurry back, master.’ Recollecting that, I don’t enjoy leading the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: Nanda, the Buddha’s half-brother, tells the Buddha that the memory of his betrothed has such a hold on him that he cannot keep up his monastic life.
buddhism.tie_back: Nanda’s heart, like the heroine’s, is governed by love even when everything around him calls for calm.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you fall in love with every woman you see, you will be without hold like the Haṭha-plant, driven before the wind.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati warns the monk Rathanemi that a mind ruled by desire has no anchor and is pushed wherever passion blows it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine describes exactly such a mind: love rules it at every hour, and she has lost her hold.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I am thirsty, thirsty for the Lord; the soul-bride gazes upon Him all through the night.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes a bride so possessed by longing that she keeps watch the whole night instead of sleeping.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife complains that love is a pitiless master that rules her heart even at midnight when everyone else rests; Guru Nanak's bride is likewise kept awake all night by her thirst for the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1232, Raag Saarang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After first seeing Jason, Medea lies awake through the night: sleep will not come to her, her heart throbs like sunlight flickering on water in a pail, and she turns her choices over and over until dawn.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius gives one of ancient literature’s fullest portraits of a young woman whose love keeps her awake and torments her at night.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Medea’s sleepless heart is the Kural’s heart ruled by love even at midnight.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.744-801 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates says the lover, parted from the beautiful one, is in such distress that he can neither sleep by night nor stay quietly in one place by day, but runs wherever he hopes to see the beloved.
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes love as a restlessness that takes away the lover’s sleep and composure.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels the same: love will not let her heart rest even at midnight.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 251d-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Pliny the Younger writes to Calpurnia of his sleepless nights
real_life_example.event: In a short letter to his wife Calpurnia, who was away from him, the Roman senator and author Pliny the Younger wrote that he missed her badly, partly from love and partly because they were not used to being apart. He told her that he lay awake much of the night thinking of her, and that at the hours when he used to visit her, his feet carried him to her room, where he turned away sad from the empty doorway. He said he found relief only in the hard work of pleading cases in court.
real_life_example.explanation: The letter is one of the best-known personal records from ancient Rome of a husband's longing during a separation, and scholars note how it borrows the language of Latin love poetry.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says pitiless love keeps working on the heart even at midnight while others rest; Pliny describes exactly this, lying awake at night and drawn by longing to an empty room.

tamil:
மறைப்பேன்மன் காமத்தை யானோ குறிப்பின்றித்
தும்மல்போல் தோன்றி விடும்.
transliteration:
Maraippaenman kaamaththai yaanoa kurippindrith
thummalpoal thoandri vidum.
meaning: I try to hide my love, but it gives no warning. Like a sneeze, it just bursts out.
elementary: Have you ever tried to stop a sneeze in a quiet room? You hold your nose, but out it comes anyway. The heroine says her love is like that: she tries to keep it secret, but it pops out all by itself.
university: The homely simile of the sneeze (tummal) is one of the most memorable images in the Kāmattuppāl: the heroine would conceal (maṟaippēṉ) her kāmam, but it appears kuṟippiṉṟi, ‘without regard to my intention’ or ‘without warning’. The particle maṉ in maṟaippēṉmaṉ marks an intention that fails (‘I would indeed hide it, but…’), a construction repeated in 1254 (eṉpēṉmaṉ). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses kuṟippiṉṟi as ‘not staying as I intend’ (என் குறிப்பின்படி நிற்காமல்), while Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘without my even knowing’, stressing involuntariness. Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘like a sneeze / It shows itself, and gives no warning sign’) keeps the image. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Act 3 of Kalidasa’s play, Shakuntala, wasting with love for King Dushyanta, tries to keep her feelings to herself, but her friends Anasuya and Priyamvada read the signs on her body and draw the confession from her.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa shows a young woman’s love becoming visible to those around her despite her silence.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s sneeze, Shakuntala’s love shows itself before she chooses to reveal it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind, and the ointment of his right hand, which bewrayeth itself.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says some things simply cannot be hidden: trying is like hiding the wind, or perfume on your hand that gives itself away.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s sneeze is the same kind of image: something that reveals itself however you try to hide it.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn Hazm devotes chapters to the signs of love and to the keeping of the lover’s secret, observing that lovers try to hide their passion but are betrayed by their glances, their confusion and their changing colour.
islam.explanation: The Andalusian treatise on love treats concealment as a duty the lover attempts and often fails.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine attempts the same concealment, and her love likewise breaks through without warning.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapters on the signs of love and on concealing the secret (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)

judaism.quote_or_event: “And if I say: ‘I will not make mention of Him, nor speak any more in His name’, then there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I weary myself to hold it in, but cannot.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah resolves to stay silent, but what is in his heart forces its way out.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine resolves to hide her love and likewise cannot hold it in.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Ummadanti Jataka, King Sivi glimpses the beautiful Ummadanti and is so struck that he cannot hide his condition: he becomes lovesick and absent-minded, and his longing becomes plain to those around him.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka shows a king’s concealed passion making itself known despite his position and self-command.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the king finds that love shows itself without his consent.
buddhism.source: Ummadanti Jataka (Jataka 527) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)

jainism.quote_or_event: When the monk Rathanemi sees Rajimati sheltering in a cave from the rain, his peace of mind is disturbed and he at once speaks his desire aloud to her, unable to keep it to himself.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana shows a disciplined monk whose sudden passion breaks out in words the moment it arises.
jainism.tie_back: Rathanemi’s passion, like the heroine’s love, bursts out before restraint can contain it.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.33-38 (paraphrase of tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Now the moon emerged in the sky of heart cannot remain hidden in spite of efforts to cover its light with flour kneading basin.”
sikhism.explanation: In a stanza describing the delight of those drenched in love, Bhai Gurdas says such love shows itself however hard one tries to cover it, like moonlight under an upturned bowl.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says she tries to hide her love but it bursts out without warning like a sneeze; Bhai Gurdas likewise says love that has risen in the heart cannot be kept covered.
sikhism.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 13, Pauri 6 (English translation as given on BaniDB)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hippolytus, Phaedra explains that she first tried to bear her love in silence and hide it, then to master it by self-control, and only when both failed resolved to die rather than be shamed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides dramatizes a woman’s doomed effort to conceal a love that keeps showing itself in her wasting body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Phaedra’s first strategy is the Kural heroine’s ‘I would hide it’, and both find that love will not stay hidden.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Hippolytus, Phaedra’s speech to the women of Troezen (c. lines 373-430; paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld observes that there is no disguise that can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.
philosophy.explanation: The French moralist states as a general maxim that real love cannot be kept hidden.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s sneeze turned into a maxim: love reveals itself whatever the lover intends.

real_life_example.event_title: Elizabeth Barrett's Sonnets from the Portuguese
real_life_example.event: Elizabeth Barrett wrote a sequence of 44 love sonnets during her courtship with the poet Robert Browning, whom she met in 1845. She kept them as a private record and gave them to him only after their secret marriage and move to Italy in 1846. When they were published in her Poems of 1850, she titled them Sonnets from the Portuguese, a disguise that made them look like translations and hid how personal they were.
real_life_example.explanation: Barrett tried to keep her love private and then to veil it with a misleading title, yet the feeling in the poems made them some of the most famous love poems in English.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine would hide her love but it bursts out like a sneeze; Barrett's love, written in secret and then disguised, still came out for all to read.

tamil:
நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன் யானோஎன் காமம்
மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்.
transliteration:
Niraiyutaiyaen enpaenman yaanoa-en kaamam
maraiyirandhu mandru patum.
meaning: I used to say I had strong self-control. But my love has come out of hiding and now shows itself for everyone to see.
elementary: Imagine being sure you could keep a big secret, and then finding the whole town talking about it. The heroine thought she was strong enough to keep her love quiet, but now everyone can see it.
university: The heroine contrasts what she used to say (niṟaiyuṭaiyēṉ eṉpēṉmaṉ, ‘I would say I have reserve’, the maṉ again marking a claim now undone) with what happens: her kāmam, passing beyond concealment (maṟai iṟantu), appears in the maṉṟu, the village common or assembly place. The word maṉṟu makes the exposure social: her longing is now matter for public talk, recalling the alar (gossip) of chapter 115. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss maṉṟam as the public assembly; Solomon Pappaiah renders the result as ‘known to the townspeople’ (ஊரவர் அறிய). Pope’s English on ytamizh.com (‘In womanly reserve I deemed myself beyond assail; / But love will come abroad, and casts away the veil’) brings out the gendered sense of niṟai in the commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar. The couplet is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In her letter to Krishna, Princess Rukmini writes that, having heard of his qualities, her heart has set aside shame and entered into him, and she asks him to carry her off before her unwanted wedding.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata presents a high-born maiden openly declaring a love that propriety would have kept hidden.
hinduism.tie_back: Rukmini’s love, like the heroine’s, passes beyond concealment and declares itself.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.52.37-43 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him… And he wept aloud: and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard.”
christianity.explanation: Joseph has long hidden who he is from his brothers, but his feeling finally bursts out so loudly that all Egypt hears it.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, a restraint the person relied on gives way, and the feeling becomes public.

islam.quote_or_event: “And women in the city said, ‘The wife of al-’Azeez is seeking to seduce her slave boy; he has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her [to be] in clear error.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an records how a noblewoman’s hidden passion for Joseph became the talk of the city’s women.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds exactly this: her love has left its hiding place and become public talk.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, what will ye tell him? that I am love-sick.”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song no longer hides her state; she tells the women of the city outright that she is sick with love.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also finds her love has gone beyond concealment and become known to others.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Venerable Nanda, they say, has been hired. Venerable Nanda, they say, has been bought.”
buddhism.explanation: When it became known that Nanda was keeping the holy life only for the sake of the promised nymphs, his fellow monks went around saying this, and he was humiliated and ashamed.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the heroine, Nanda finds that the longing he kept inside has become the common talk of his whole community.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Sutrakritanga warns that when relations and friends see a monk becoming intimate with a woman, they grow angry and openly tell him that, being a man, he should protect and support her.
jainism.explanation: The Jain text shows a monk’s concealed attachment exposed to public judgement.
jainism.tie_back: Like the heroine, the monk who thought himself restrained finds his attachment has become known to all.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.14 (paraphrase of tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My shyness and hesitation have died and gone, and I walk with my face unveiled.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak speaks as a soul-bride whose fear of what people will say has vanished, so that she now goes about openly, without her veil.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife admits that the reserve she once claimed is gone and her love now shows in the public square; Guru Nanak's bride likewise has shed her shyness and walks unveiled before everyone.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 931, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, the minstrel Demodocus sings how Hephaestus caught Ares and Aphrodite together in an invisible net and then called the gods to come and see, so that their secret love was exposed before the company of Olympus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s comic tale shows a hidden love dragged into public view.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences the same thing in gentler form: her love has left its hiding place and stands in the public square.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 8.266-366 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says the person who lacks self-control knows what is right, but under passion holds that knowledge only as a drunk or sleeping man holds it, like someone reciting verses of Empedocles without understanding them.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle explains how a person who believes himself self-controlled can still be overrun by passion.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s ‘I used to say I had reserve’ is a lover’s version of Aristotle’s akrasia: her restraint existed, but passion overrode it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VII.3, 1147a (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: The Bamangwato kgotla debates Seretse Khama's marriage
real_life_example.event: Seretse Khama, heir to the chieftaincy of the Bamangwato people, married Ruth Williams, an Englishwoman, in a London registry office in September 1948, against the wishes of his uncle and regent Tshekedi Khama. The marriage was then debated at three meetings of the kgotla, the people's public assembly; at the December 1948 meeting most of those present opposed it. At the third kgotla, in June 1949, the assembly changed its position and accepted Seretse as chief and Ruth as his wife.
real_life_example.explanation: A private marriage became a matter for open debate in the community's assembly and later for the British government, showing how personal love can become public business.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says her love has left concealment and now shows itself in the maṉṟu, the public assembly; Seretse's love was literally argued over in the kgotla.

tamil:
செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை காமநோய்
உற்றார் அறிவதொன்று அன்று.
transliteration:
Setraarpin sellaap perundhakaimai kaamanoai
utraar aRivadhondru andru.
meaning: People sick with love do not know the self-respect that refuses to run after someone who has turned away from them.
elementary: When a friend walks away from you, pride might say, ‘Fine, I won’t chase after them.’ But the heroine says that when you love someone very much, that kind of pride disappears, and you want to follow them anyway.
university: Ceṟṟār, literally ‘those who hate’ or ‘enemies’, is here the husband who has gone away, seen through the heroine’s hurt as one who has spurned her; peruntakaimai is the noble self-respect (Mu. Varadarasanar: மானத்தோடு நிற்கும் பெருந்தகைமை) of not following such a person. Kāmanōy uṟṟār, ‘those who have caught the sickness of love’, do not know that dignity, so the couplet extends the chapter’s theme from concealment to pride. Commentators divide on the logic: Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take it as a direct statement that the lovesick lack such dignity, Solomon Pappaiah turns it around (only those who have not known love can manage it), and Kalaignar stresses that the lovesick cannot treat the departed lover as an enemy. In the reading associated with Parimelazhagar, the heroine is explaining to her confidante why she cannot simply hold her ground. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Mirabai sings that for the sake of her Giridhar (Krishna) she has thrown off family honour and the shame the world expects of a noblewoman, and goes after him whatever people say.
hinduism.explanation: The bhakti poet makes a virtue of the loss of decorum that the Kural’s heroine confesses.
hinduism.tie_back: Both women find that love leaves no room for the dignified reserve society expects.
hinduism.source: Mirabai, padas on abandoning lok-lāj (family honour) (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Alston)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, a father who has every reason to stand on his dignity runs to the son who left him.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s lover, the father cannot keep the dignified stance of not going after one who went away.

islam.quote_or_event: “She said, ‘That is the one about whom you blamed me. And I certainly sought to seduce him, but he firmly refused…’”
islam.explanation: Before the women of the city, the wife of al-Aziz openly admits that she pursued Joseph even though he refused her.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says the lovesick lack the dignity of not following one who turns away; here a noblewoman confesses to exactly that loss.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I will rise now, and go about the city, In the streets and in the broad ways, I will seek him whom my soul loveth.”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song gives up all reserve and goes out through the city streets at night to look for her beloved.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise cannot keep the dignity of staying put; love sends her after the one who has gone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha advises against binding oneself to anyone, because separation from the beloved is itself suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows the pain this verse foresees: the one who loves cannot stand apart from the beloved, even with dignity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Fie upon you, famous knight, who want to quaff the vomited drink for the sake of this life; it would be better for you to die.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, herself forsaken by Arishtanemi, rebukes his brother Rathanemi for pursuing her, keeping her dignity and her vows.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati shows the dignity the Kural says the lovesick cannot have; her strength comes from having turned her grief toward renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.42 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Cutting off my head, I give it to Him to sit upon; without my head, I shall still serve Him.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak's soul-bride is ready to give up even her head, the seat of pride, to serve the one who brings her news of the Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that those sick with love do not know the dignity of refusing to follow one who has turned away; Guru Nanak's bride likewise sets all self-regard aside for the sake of her Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 558, Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo falls in love with Narcissus and secretly follows his footsteps through the woods; when she shows herself he recoils and spurns her, yet she keeps loving him, wasting away until only her voice remains.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells the classic story of a lover who cannot stop following the one who rejects her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echo is the Kural’s lovesick heroine in mythic form: she does not know the dignity of not following one who turns away.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates says the lover forgets mother, brothers and friends, cares nothing if his property is wasted, and despises all the rules and proprieties of life on which he once prided himself, ready to sleep wherever he is allowed, as near as he can to his beloved.
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes love as a madness that strips the lover of the dignity and decorum he once valued.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same admission: the lovesick do not know the dignity of holding back.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 252a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Berlioz pursues Harriet Smithson, who does not answer
real_life_example.event: In 1827 the young composer Hector Berlioz fell in love with the Irish-born actress Harriet Smithson after seeing her play Ophelia with an English theatre company in Paris. They had not met, and she left his many passionate letters unanswered for a long time. His obsession inspired the Symphonie fantastique, first performed on 5 December 1830; Smithson heard a revised version in 1832, the two were introduced soon after, and they married in October 1833.
real_life_example.explanation: Berlioz kept pursuing a woman who showed no interest in him, turning his unreturned feeling into one of the most famous symphonies of the Romantic era.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says those sick with love do not know the dignity of refusing to follow someone who has turned away; Berlioz, unanswered, kept writing and kept pursuing.

tamil:
செற்றவர் பின்சேறல் வேண்டி அளித்தரோ
எற்றென்னை உற்ற துயர்.
transliteration:
Setravar pinsaeral vaendi aliththaroa
etrennai utra thuyar.
meaning: How strange is this sorrow that has taken hold of me! It makes me want to follow the very one who turned away from me.
elementary: Sometimes when a friend goes away, we feel so sad that we want to run after them, even if they did not say a kind goodbye. The heroine wonders at this sadness: it is so strong that it makes her want to follow him anyway.
university: The heroine marvels at her own grief: eṟṟu (‘of what kind?’) and the exclamatory aḷittarō, which can be heard ironically as ‘how gracious!’, frame a sorrow (tuyar) that makes her wish to go after (piṉ cēṟal) ceṟṟavar, the one who has scorned or left her. Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘My grief how full of grace, I pray you see! / It seeks to follow him that hateth me’) captures this irony. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan treat tuyar as the kāmanōy (love-sickness) itself, and Solomon Pappaiah calls it exceedingly cruel because it drives her to follow. The couplet continues 1255: having denied that she has the dignity not to follow, the heroine now wonders at the grief that compels her. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna suddenly disappears from the rasa dance, the gopis, stricken with grief, search the forest for him, asking the trees and creepers whether they have seen him pass.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata shows women whose grief at their beloved’s withdrawal sends them looking for him everywhere.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the gopis are driven by grief to follow the one who has left them.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.30 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
christianity.explanation: When the bride finally opens the door, her beloved has gone, and she goes searching and calling for him.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also longs to follow the one who has turned away, and wonders at the grief that drives her.

islam.quote_or_event: “Barira’s husband was a slave called Mughith, as if I am seeing him now, going behind Barira and weeping with his tears flowing down his beard. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to ’Abbas, ‘O ’Abbas! are you not astonished at the love of Mughith for Barira and the hatred of Barira for Mughith?’”
islam.explanation: After Barira, newly freed, chose to leave her marriage, her husband Mughith followed her through the streets of Medina in tears.
islam.tie_back: Mughith is the Kural’s lover exactly: grief makes him follow the one who has turned away, and the Prophet himself remarks on the wonder of it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The watchmen that go about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my mantle from me.”
judaism.explanation: Searching through the city for the beloved who has gone, the woman of the Song is beaten and stripped of her mantle, yet keeps searching.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also marvels at a grief that makes her follow the one who left, whatever it costs her.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From lust springs grief, from lust springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief back to desire and attachment.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences what this verse names: her grief comes from a longing that drives her after the one who has gone.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Râgîmatî thought: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.’”
jainism.explanation: Forsaken by Arishtanemi on their wedding day, Rajimati follows him into renunciation and later sets out for Mount Raivataka, where he had gone.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati’s grief, like the heroine’s, makes her follow the one who left her, though she follows him on the path of renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My mind and body are so thirsty for the Blessed Vision of His Darshan. Won't someone please come and lead me to him, O my mother.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Barah Maha, Guru Arjan describes a longing so strong that the bride begs anyone at all to take her to her Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife marvels at the grief that makes her long to follow the very one who left her; Guru Arjan's bride is likewise driven by her ache to seek out the absent Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 135, Raag Maajh, Barah Maha, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Medea, falling in love with Jason against her duty to her father, argues with herself and confesses that she sees the better course and approves it, yet follows the worse.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid captures a lover driven by a force she recognizes as harmful to herself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also wonders at a grief that drives her where her dignity tells her not to go.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pausanias says that a lover may beg and pray, swear oaths, sleep on the beloved’s doorstep and submit to a slavery no slave would accept, and yet gods and men excuse him because he is in love.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s speaker describes how lovers do humiliating things that would disgrace anyone not in love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wonders at the same humbling power: her grief makes her want to follow one who has turned away.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 183a-b (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.R.M. Lamb)

real_life_example.event_title: Charlotte Bronte's letters to Constantin Heger
real_life_example.event: After returning home from Brussels in 1844, Charlotte Bronte wrote a series of letters to Constantin Heger, her former teacher there. He replied rarely and, by the end of 1845, had stopped answering, while her letters grew more desperate; four survive, the last dated 18 November 1845. The letters were torn up at some point and later mended, and Heger's children gave them to the British Museum in 1913; they are now in the British Library.
real_life_example.explanation: The letters show a proud and private writer unable to stop reaching out to someone who had withdrawn from her.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine marvels at a strange grief that makes her long to follow the one who has turned away; Bronte's letters to a silent Heger are a documented case of just such longing.

tamil:
நாணென ஒன்றோ அறியலம் காமத்தால்
பேணியார் பெட்ப செயின்.
transliteration:
Naanena ondroa ariyalam kaamaththaal
paeniyaar petpa seyin.
meaning: When the one I love, out of love, does the things I long for, I no longer know anything called modesty.
elementary: When someone you love is kind to you and does just what you hoped, you forget to be shy around them. You just feel happy and close. The heroine says that is how she feels when her husband shows his love.
university: Here nāṇ (shyness, modesty) is not broken by force but forgotten: when pēṇiyār (the one I cherish) does peṭpa (what I desire) out of kāmam, ‘we do not know anything called shame’ (nāṇ eṉa oṉṟō aṟiyalam). The plural aṟiyalam can be inclusive (‘we women’) or the heroine’s own, and commentators differ on tense: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it conditionally (‘if he does…, we shall not know’), Solomon Pappaiah as past experience (‘when he did… I did not know shame’). Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘No sense of shame my gladdened mind shall prove, / When he returns my longing heart to bless with love’) takes it as a hope for his return. Read within the chapter, the couplet explains why reserve fails: in the presence of a loving husband, nāṇ has no place. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the last canto of the Gita Govinda, after Radha and Krishna are reunited, Radha playfully asks Krishna to paint her forehead mark, set her ornaments and arrange her hair, and he gladly does as she asks.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva ends his poem with a beloved who, with a loving partner, sets shyness aside entirely.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same: when her beloved does what she desires, she knows no shyness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
christianity.explanation: In the garden before the fall, the first husband and wife stand before each other with no shame at all.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine describes the same freedom: in love returned, shame has no place.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes husband and wife as each other’s garment: closeness, comfort and covering.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s couple share the same closeness: in mutual love, the wife no longer needs the cover of shyness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Oh that thou wert as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother! When I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, and none would despise me.”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song wishes she could show her love openly, without anyone thinking it shameful.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says that when her love is returned, she does not even feel shyness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Nakula’s father and Nakula’s mother tell the Buddha that since they were married young they have never been unfaithful to each other even in thought, and that they wish to see each other in this life and in lives to come.
buddhism.explanation: The Anguttara Nikaya praises a lay couple whose love is open, mutual and wholehearted.
buddhism.tie_back: Their unguarded devotion parallels the Kural’s picture of love so mutual that shyness falls away.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Come, let us enjoy pleasures, for it is a rare chance to be born a human being; after we have enjoyed pleasures, we shall enter on the path of the Ginas.”
jainism.explanation: Overcome by passion, the monk Rathanemi forgets his vows and the shame they should bring, and urges Rajimati to enjoy pleasures with him.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Rathanemi forgets shame in desire; but the Jain text treats this forgetting as a fall, whereas the Kural sees it within a loving marriage.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “She surrenders her body and mind to Him, and does not remain separate from Him.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas describes the beloved bride who holds nothing back from her Husband and keeps no distance from Him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that when her beloved lovingly does what she desires she no longer knows anything called shyness; Ravidas's bride likewise keeps no reserve at all before the Husband she loves.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 793, Raag Soohee, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho says the most beautiful thing is whatever one loves, and gives Helen as proof: she left behind her husband, her child and her parents and sailed to Troy, led astray by love.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho uses Helen to show that love can make a person forget every claim of propriety and family.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also forgets shyness in love, though within her own marriage.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal argues that the heart follows a logic of its own that calm reason cannot fully grasp.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds this in her own heart: when love is returned, the reasoned reserve of shyness simply disappears.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, no. 277 (Brunschvicg numbering; paraphrase; cf. tr. W.F. Trotter)

real_life_example.event_title: Queen Victoria's journal on her wedding day
real_life_example.event: Queen Victoria married Prince Albert on 10 February 1840. That night she wrote in her journal about Albert's great love and affection, calling him her precious Angel and saying his love gave her a happiness she had never hoped to feel. She ended the entry by calling it the happiest day of her life.
real_life_example.explanation: A reigning monarch, trained to be reserved in public, wrote with complete openness once her husband showed her love.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when the beloved, out of love, does what one longs for, shyness is forgotten; Victoria's unguarded wedding-night journal shows reserve melting in the warmth of returned love.

tamil:
பன்மாயக் கள்வன் பணிமொழி அன்றோநம்
பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை.
transliteration:
Panmaayak kalvan panimozhi androa-nam
penmai udaikkum padai.
meaning: My love is a clever thief with many tricks. Aren't his soft, sweet words the army that breaks down my firmness as a woman?
elementary: Imagine building a strong sandcastle wall, and then a friend says something so sweet and kind that you happily knock the wall down yourself. The heroine says her husband’s gentle words are like that: they break down her strong ‘I won’t give in’ feeling.
university: The heroine calls her beloved pal-māyak kaḷvaṉ, ‘a thief of many wiles’, an affectionate reproach familiar from Tamil love poetry, and names his paṇimoḻi (humble, coaxing words) as the paṭai (army, weapon) that breaks her peṇmai (womanliness, here the firmness that resists). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses peṇmai as a fortress (அரண்) and Solomon Pappaiah as the fort of self-restraint (மன அடக்கமாகிய கோட்டை), sustaining the military image of breaking. Puliyur Kesikan reads the couplet as past (‘were they not, on that day…’), referring to their courtship, while others read it as a present truth. Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘The words of that deceiver, versed in every wily art, / Are instruments that break through every guard of woman’s heart!’) pushes kaḷvaṉ toward ‘deceiver’, though the Tamil glosses keep the tone fond and playful. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the tenth canto of the Gita Govinda, Krishna comes to Radha while she is still angry and pleads with her in the sweetest words, begging her to give up her anger and set her foot upon his head.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva shows a lover’s gentle, humble pleading overcoming a woman’s proud resistance.
hinduism.tie_back: Krishna’s words are the Kural’s paṇimoḻi: coaxing speech that breaks down a woman’s firmness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb describes how smooth, flattering words can overcome a person’s resolve.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same idea: sweet, coaxing speech is the weapon that breaks down firmness.

islam.quote_or_event: “Some eloquent speech has the influence of magic.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet observed that well-chosen words can move people to do what they had refused to do.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same of her husband’s coaxing words, which work on her firmness like a spell.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My beloved spoke, and said unto me: ‘Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away.’”
judaism.explanation: The Song’s beloved wins the woman over with tender, coaxing words.
judaism.tie_back: In the Kural too, the beloved’s gentle words are what overcome the woman’s reserve.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After the Buddha’s awakening, Mara’s three daughters, Craving, Discontent and Passion, approach him with flattering words and alluring forms to break his resolve, but he is unmoved.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta shows coaxing words used as a weapon against a person’s firmness, and the firmness holding.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces the same weapon of coaxing speech, but, unlike the Buddha, she gives way.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Meekly and politely they approach him with their manifold arts to win his heart; and talking sweetly in confidential conversation they make him do (what they like).”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns monks that gentle, sweet speech is the means by which their resolve is overcome.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural names the same weapon, humble and sweet words used with many arts, as what breaks the heroine’s firmness.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “So listen, O my sisters - the Enticer has enticed my mind. My body and mind are drenched with Nectar.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak's bride tells her companions that the Beloved, the Enticer, has won her mind completely.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife calls her beloved a thief of many wiles whose coaxing words broke down her womanly firmness; Guru Nanak's bride likewise confesses to her friends that the Enticer has captured her mind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 764, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Hera borrows Aphrodite’s embroidered band, Homer says it holds love, desire, and the persuasive whispering that steals the wits even of the wise.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, lovers’ persuasive speech is literally a divine weapon that can overcome even Zeus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine names her beloved’s sweet words as the weapon that breaks her firmness, the same power Aphrodite’s band contains.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 14.214-217 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Gorgias argues that Helen cannot be blamed if she was persuaded by speech, because speech is a mighty lord that, with the smallest and least visible body, achieves the most divine works.
philosophy.explanation: Gorgias makes the power of persuasive words a defence of the one who yielded to them.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine offers a similar plea: it was her beloved’s coaxing words, a whole army, that broke her firmness.

real_life_example.event_title: Pierre Curie's letters persuade Marie Sklodowska to return to Paris
real_life_example.event: Marie Sklodowska met the physicist Pierre Curie in Paris in the spring of 1894. Her plan had always been to return to Poland and teach, and in the summer of 1894 she went home unsure whether she would come back; she later wrote that marriage would have meant abandoning her country and family. Pierre's heartfelt letters helped persuade her to return to Paris and work alongside him, and they married in a simple civil ceremony at Sceaux on 25 July 1895.
real_life_example.explanation: Marie's firm plan to return home gave way before Pierre's patient, persuasive words, beginning one of the most famous partnerships in science.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says her beloved's gentle, coaxing words were the army that broke down her firmness; Pierre's letters did the same to Marie's resolve to leave France.

tamil:
புலப்பல் எனச்சென்றேன் புல்லினேன் நெஞ்சம்
கலத்தல் உறுவது கண்டு.
transliteration:
Pulappal enachchendraen pullinaen nenjam
kalaththal uruvadhu kandu.
meaning: I went to him meaning to sulk and hold back. But when I saw my heart already rushing to join him, I hugged him.
elementary: Imagine planning to stay grumpy with a friend who came back late. But when you see them, your heart feels so happy that you forget to be grumpy and give them a big hug instead. That is what happened to the heroine.
university: The couplet turns on the Tamil love convention of ūṭal (lovers’ sulking or feigned pique): pulappal, ‘I will sulk’, was her plan, but pulliṉēṉ, ‘I embraced’, was the result, because she saw her neñcam (heart) already beginning kalattal (union, mingling) with him. The heart acting independently of the self continues the preceding chapter, neñcoṭu kiḷattal (‘speaking to one’s heart’). Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘my heart leaving me and joining him’, and Solomon Pappaiah elaborates that she stepped away to sulk but, seeing her heart go to him without restraint, gave up and embraced him. Sivayogi Sivakumar’s gloss gives an allegorical (yogic) reading, a minority view. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; Pope’s rendering there (‘I’ll shun his greeting’; saying thus with pride away I went: / I held him in my arms, for straight I felt my heart relent) follows the standard reading.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Radha, who had held out against Krishna in wounded pride, is urged by her friend to go to him; she finally enters his bower, and her anger dissolves in the joy of seeing him.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s poem turns on Radha’s māna (proud sulking) giving way when she sees her beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s situation: she meant to sulk, but on seeing him her resolve melted into embrace.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go.”
christianity.explanation: After searching anxiously, the bride finds her beloved and holds him fast.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also ends up embracing the one she meant to hold off, because her heart has already gone to him.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an sees affection and mercy between spouses as a sign of God, a force that brings them back to calm together.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences that affection overriding her plan to sulk.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him; and they wept.”
judaism.explanation: Esau, who had long held a grievance against Jacob, runs to him and embraces him the moment they meet.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a resolve to hold back gives way at the meeting, and an embrace takes its place.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that resentment ends only when it is met with its opposite.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds her small resentment dissolved not by argument but by her own heart’s affection.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard these well-spoken words of the virtuous lady, he returned to the Law like an elephant driven by the hook.”
