jainism.explanation: The monk Rathanemi had set out to win Rajimati, but on hearing her words his intention reverses and he returns to his vows.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Rathanemi meets the other person intending one thing and does the opposite, though his reversal runs from passion to restraint, not from sulking to embrace.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.46 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The bride may be hunch-backed and short, but if she is loved by her Lord Master, she becomes beautiful, and she melts in the Lord's embrace.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that whatever the bride's flaws, once her Lord loves her she melts into His embrace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife went meaning to sulk but, seeing her heart already rushing to him, embraced him instead; Guru Ram Das's bride likewise melts into her Lord's embrace.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 527, Raag Dayv Gandhaaree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus describes the secret of their bed, Penelope, who had held back from him in doubt, feels her knees and heart give way, bursts into tears, runs to him and throws her arms around his neck.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows a wife’s long-guarded reserve dissolving in a single moment into an embrace.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s scene: she came holding back, but when her heart went to him she embraced him.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 23.205-208 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristophanes describes how the separated halves of the original human beings, longing for each other, run together and throw their arms about each other, wanting to grow into one.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s speaker presents love as an irresistible drive toward union with one’s other half.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s heart going to ‘mingle’ (kalattal) with her husband is this same drive toward union, which overrides her plan to sulk.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 191a-b (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Abraham Lincoln and Mary Todd reconcile and marry
real_life_example.event: Abraham Lincoln and Mary Todd, engaged in Springfield, broke off their courtship on 1 January 1841, a day Lincoln later called the fatal first of January; Mary's sister and brother-in-law disapproved of the match. After more than a year apart, friends brought them together again and they resumed their courtship in secret. They married on 4 November 1842 at her sister's house, and Mary told her sister they were courting again only on the wedding day.
real_life_example.explanation: A couple who had separated in hurt found, when brought together again, that their attachment was stronger than their resolve to stay apart.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine set out to sulk but embraced her husband when she saw her heart already running to him; Lincoln and Mary Todd likewise gave up their separation once they met again.

tamil:
நிணந்தீயில் இட்டன்ன நெஞ்சினார்க்கு உண்டோ
புணர்ந்தூடி நிற்பேம் எனல்.
transliteration:
Ninandheeyil ittanna nenjinaarkku undoa
punarndhoodi niRpaem enal.
meaning: Can those whose hearts melt like fat thrown into a fire ever say, "We will be close to him and still keep up our sulking"?
elementary: Put a pat of butter in a hot pan and it melts almost at once. The heroine says her heart is like that butter: the moment her husband is near, she cannot stay cross with him.
university: The chapter closes with a vivid simile: niṇam tīyil iṭṭaṉṉa neñciṉār, ‘those whose hearts are like fat (niṇam) put into fire’, cannot say puṇarntu ūṭi niṟpēm, ‘we will unite and yet stand firm in ūṭal (sulking)’. Commentators differ over the construction: Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘can those like me, with melting hearts, keep up a sulk once they have agreed to it’, Kalaignar takes it as ‘can they hold firm in sulking after having been together’, and Solomon Pappaiah expands it into a general statement about women whose hearts melt at the sight of their lovers. The couplet answers 1259 in general form and closes the chapter’s argument: with a heart like this, no niṟai can last. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the musical setting by P.A. Muthukrishnan reproduced on thirukkural.net paraphrases the image as butter in the flame (தழலிடை வெண்ணெய்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A devotee whose speech is sometimes choked up, whose heart melts, who cries continually and sometimes laughs, who feels ashamed and cries out loudly and then dances — a devotee thus fixed in loving service to Me purifies the entire universe.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a love so strong that the devotee’s heart melts and outward composure disappears.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has the same melting heart (dravate cittam), which leaves no room for holding back.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 11.14.24 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Srimad-Bhagavatam)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint: my heart is like wax; it is melted in the midst of my bowels.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes a heart that has melted like wax, all strength gone.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses almost the same image, fat melting in fire, for a heart that cannot hold firm.

islam.quote_or_event: “The skins shiver therefrom of those who fear their Lord; then their skins and their hearts relax at the remembrance of Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes hearts that soften and yield at the remembrance of God.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has a heart that softens and yields the moment her beloved is near.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Joseph made haste; for his heart yearned toward his brother; and he sought where to weep; and he entered into his chamber, and wept there. And he washed his face, and came out; and he refrained himself…”
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s heart melts at the sight of Benjamin, and he has to hurry away to weep before he can compose himself again.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether a melting heart can hold firm; Joseph barely manages it, and only by leaving the room.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fire like lust; there is no grip like hatred; there is no net like delusion; there is no river like craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls passion the fiercest of fires.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows that fire at work: her heart melts in it like fat, unable to keep any resolve.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A pot filled with lac thrown into the fire melts quickly and is destroyed; so monks are lost through intercourse with women.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga uses the image of lac melting in fire for a monk whose resolve dissolves in the presence of desire.
jainism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s simile, fat melting in fire, applied to the same dissolving of firmness.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “As metal melts into metal again, so does love melt into love.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the image of molten metal flowing into metal to show how love naturally merges with the one it loves.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether those whose hearts melt like fat in the fire could ever hold firm in a sulk once they are together; Guru Nanak likewise pictures love as something that melts and merges on contact.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 725, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid says Narcissus, consumed by love, wastes away as yellow wax melts before a gentle flame or as morning frost melts in the sun.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid uses a melting image for a lover dissolved by passion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heart like fat in the fire is the same picture of a lover who cannot hold firm.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza holds that an emotion can be restrained or removed only by an opposite and stronger emotion, not by knowledge or resolution alone.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza argues that a resolution cannot hold against a strong feeling unless a stronger feeling opposes it.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s plan to sulk is too weak against her melting love, just as Spinoza would predict.

real_life_example.event_title: Charles Darwin weighs marriage on paper, then proposes
real_life_example.event: In 1838 Charles Darwin wrote two notes weighing the case for and against marriage, listing companionship, a home and children against lost time, money and freedom. The second note, probably written in July 1838, came down on the side of marrying. On 11 November 1838 he proposed to his cousin Emma Wedgwood, who accepted, and they married on 29 January 1839; the notes are kept at Cambridge University Library.
real_life_example.explanation: Even one of history's most methodical minds could not keep his feelings in the cool columns of a list; the case for love won.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks whether hearts that melt like fat in fire can ever hold firm; Darwin's careful balance sheet tipped toward marriage, showing calculation giving way to feeling.

tamil:
வாளற்றுப் புற்கென்ற கண்ணும் அவர்சென்ற
நாளொற்றித் தேய்ந்த விரல்.
transliteration:
Vaalatrup purkendra kannum avarsendra
naalotrith thaeyndha viral.
meaning: My eyes have lost their shine from watching the road for him. My fingers are worn out from touching the marks I made to count the days since he left.
elementary: Imagine someone you love goes on a long trip. Every day you stand at the window looking down the road, and every night you make a mark on the wall and count them all again. After many days your eyes are tired from looking and your finger is sore from counting. That is how much the lady in this verse misses her husband.
university: Chapter 127, avarvayiṉ vitumpal (‘eager longing for him’; vitumpal = impatient yearning), continues the kaṟpu (wedded love) section: the time the husband (talaivaṉ) fixed for his return is passing, and the wife (talaivi) speaks her impatience; in two couplets (1268, 1270) the husband’s own eagerness is voiced, which is why Pope titles the chapter ‘Mutual Desire’. Here the heroine offers two physical proofs: her eyes are vāḷ aṟṟu (stripped of their lustre, vāḷ = brightness) and puṟkeṉṟa (dimmed, unable to see fine things, as Solomon Pappaiah glosses), and her finger is worn from nāḷ oṟṟi, pressing the day-marks she has drawn on the wall; Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all supply the wall (சுவர்) on which the days are scored. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as the heroine telling her friend (tōḻi) that she can no longer bear the delay. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Cloud Messenger, the exiled yaksha pictures his wife at home counting the months still left of their separation by laying flowers on the threshold, one for each, and wasting with longing.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Sanskrit love poetry gives the separated wife a counting ritual very like the Kural’s day-marks on the wall.
hinduism.tie_back: Both wives keep a tally of the days apart, and both are worn down by the counting itself.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta (Uttaramegha), the yaksha’s description of his wife (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am weary of my crying: my throat is dried: mine eyes fail while I wait for my God.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes waiting so long and so hard that his eyes give out.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same of her eyes: they have lost their light from watching for the one she waits for.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s long grief for his absent son Joseph costs him his sight.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, years of longing for an absent loved one are written in the eyes, which lose their brightness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mine eyes fail for Thy word, saying: ‘When wilt Thou comfort me?’”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist’s eyes wear out as he keeps asking when the promised comfort will come.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s dimmed eyes carry the same unspoken question: when will he come back?

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names not seeing the one you love as one of the basic forms of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s worn eyes and fingers are exactly the pain of not seeing the beloved, though the Buddha’s answer is to loosen the attachment rather than keep counting.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Gina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, betrothed to Arishtanemi, is left grieving when he turns away from their wedding to become a monk.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati’s lost gaiety is the Jain counterpart of the heroine’s lost brightness of eye: both are women worn down by a beloved’s absence.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Looking for Him, my eyes have become blood-shot.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir describes the seeker who has searched for the Lord so long and so hard that the eyes themselves are worn and reddened.
sikhism.tie_back: The wife in the Kural says her eyes have grown dim from watching the road for her husband; Kabir's eyes are likewise worn out by looking for the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 341, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Penelope weeps for Odysseus as she listens to the disguised stranger, her cheeks melting with tears like snow thawing on the mountains, though her husband sits beside her unrecognised.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s faithful wife has spent nearly twenty years waiting, and her grief shows in her face.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope’s tear-worn face and the heroine’s dimmed eyes are the same mark of long waiting for a husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Roland Barthes, describing the lover’s experience of waiting, suggests that the lover is defined as the one who waits, and that waiting itself is a kind of enchantment that fixes the lover in place.
philosophy.explanation: Barthes treats waiting not as empty time but as the very shape that love takes in absence.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s whole existence has become waiting: eyes on the road, finger on the calendar.
philosophy.source: Roland Barthes, A Lover’s Discourse: Fragments, ‘Waiting’ (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Hachiko waits at Shibuya Station for his master
real_life_example.event: Hachiko was an Akita dog owned by Hidesaburo Ueno, a professor of agricultural engineering at the University of Tokyo, and he used to wait at Shibuya Station for Ueno to come home. Ueno died suddenly at work on 21 May 1925, but Hachiko kept going to the station to wait for him for about ten more years. A statue of Hachiko now stands at Shibuya Station.
real_life_example.explanation: Hachiko's daily vigil became a national symbol of faithful waiting for someone who has gone away.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine has worn out her eyes watching the road for her husband's return; Hachiko watched the station day after day for a master who never came back.

tamil:
இலங்கிழாய் இன்று மறப்பின்என் தோள்மேல்
கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து.
transliteration:
Ilangizhaai indru marappin-en thoalmael
kalangazhiyum kaarikai neeththu.
meaning: My friend in shining jewels, if I forgot him even now, my arms would lose their beauty and my bangles would slip off.
elementary: A girl tells her best friend: “Even though missing him hurts, I won’t stop thinking about him. If I tried to forget him, I would only become sadder and thinner, so thin that my bracelets would fall off.” Remembering him, even when it is hard, is what keeps her going.
university: The heroine addresses her friend as ilaṅkiḻāy, ‘you of shining ornaments’ (Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take the addressee as the tōḻi; Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss ஒளிரும் நகை அணிந்தவனே uses a masculine ending, apparently a slip). Kalam aḻiyum (‘the ornaments come off’) is the stock Tamil sign of a wasting body: the arms (tōḷ) grow thin and the bangles slide off, and kārikai (beauty, grace) departs. The logic is a reversal: one might expect forgetting to ease her pain, but she says that even to try to forget him today would ruin her further, so she chooses to keep remembering. The Drew/Lazarus explanation printed on ytamizh.com reads ‘even in the other life’, reflecting a reading of iṉṟu that some commentators extend; the main modern glosses take iṉṟu simply as ‘today, while I suffer’. The Tamil text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ashoka grove, Hanuman finds Sita pale and thin, wearing a single braid and no ornaments, her thoughts fixed on Rama alone.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki pictures the separated Sita as a wife whose body is wasting while her mind never leaves her husband.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita and the Kural’s heroine both lose their outward beauty in separation yet refuse to let the beloved slip from memory.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.”
christianity.explanation: God answers the fear of being forgotten with a promise stronger than a mother’s memory.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine makes the same vow toward her husband: whatever it costs her, she will not forget him.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi opens the Masnavi with the reed flute, cut from its reed-bed, whose every note is a lament of separation and a longing to return to the source it remembers.
islam.explanation: For Rumi the soul’s song comes from remembering where it belongs; the remembering is both its pain and its life.
islam.tie_back: Like the reed, the heroine keeps the absent one alive in memory, and that remembering is what sustains her.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi I.1-18, ‘Song of the Reed’ (tr. R.A. Nicholson; paraphrase)

judaism.quote_or_event: “If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning. Let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth, if I remember thee not; if I set not Jerusalem above my chiefest joy.”
judaism.explanation: The exiles in Babylon bind their own bodies to their memory of Zion.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural uses the very same structure: if I forget, let my body suffer for it, with arms that lose their beauty and bangles that fall.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Nakula’s father and Nakula’s mother tell the Buddha that they have never been unfaithful even in thought and wish to see each other in this life and in lives to come; the Buddha says that a couple matched in faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom will meet again.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats a devoted couple’s wish to remain together as something that shared virtue can sustain.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s refusal to forget her husband is the same steadfast devotion that the Buddha praises in this model couple.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu; paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Firm and decided she cut off her tresses which were black like bees and dressed with a brush and comb.”
jainism.explanation: Abandoned by Arishtanemi, Rajimati gives up her beauty deliberately and becomes a nun.
jainism.tie_back: Both women lose their adornment in separation, but Rajimati lays it down by choice to follow the path, while the Kural’s heroine fears losing it and clings to memory instead.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “How could I forget Him from my mind, even for an instant? He is the Most Worthy; He is my very life!”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that forgetting the Lord is unthinkable, because the Lord is the very life of the devotee.
sikhism.tie_back: The wife says that if she forgot her husband even now, her arms would lose their beauty; Guru Arjan likewise cannot imagine forgetting the Beloved who is his life.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 80, Sri Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s letter of Laodamia to Protesilaus at Troy, she says she has no care to comb her hair or wear gold-woven clothes while her husband is at war, and that she lives on thoughts of him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The mythic wife lets her beauty go untended because her whole mind is with the absent husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Laodamia and the Kural’s heroine both let outward grace fall away while holding their husband constantly in mind.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that distance does not break friendship outright but interrupts its activity, and that a long absence seems to make people forget it, citing the saying that lack of converse has broken many a friendship.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle sees forgetting as the natural danger of long absence.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine sees the same danger and refuses it: she will not let absence turn into forgetting.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.5 (tr. W.D. Ross; paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Edward I raises the Eleanor Crosses
real_life_example.event: Eleanor of Castile, wife of King Edward I of England, died at Harby in Nottinghamshire on 28 November 1290. Her funeral procession travelled from Lincoln to Westminster in December, and Edward had a memorial cross built at each place where her body rested overnight, twelve in all. Three of the original crosses survive, at Geddington, Hardingstone and Waltham Cross.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than let his grief fade, the king set his love for his wife in stone along the road from Lincoln to London.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine refuses to forget her husband even though remembering costs her; Edward chose lasting remembrance of Eleanor over forgetting.

tamil:
உரன்நசைஇ உள்ளம் துணையாகச் சென்றார்
வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்.
transliteration:
Urannasaii ullam thunaiyaakach chendraar
varalnasaii innum ulen.
meaning: He went away to win success, with only his own courage for company. I am still alive only because I long to see him come back.
elementary: A brave soldier leaves home to win a great contest, taking only his courage with him. His wife at home is very sad, but one thing keeps her going: the hope of seeing him walk back through the door. That hope is like a lamp that keeps her heart from going dark.
university: The couplet balances two desires with the same verb, nacai (‘longing’, here in the old verbal form nacaii): he left out of uraṉ nacai, desire for strength or victory, with uḷḷam tuṇaiyāka, his own spirit as his only companion; she lives on out of varal nacai, desire for his return. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss uraṉ as victory (வெற்றி) and uḷḷam as zeal (ஊக்கம்); Solomon Pappaiah adds a note of reproach, reading that he spurned her companionship to make his resolve his companion. Iṉṉum uḷēṉ, ‘I still exist’, implies that only this hope keeps her alive, a recurring motif in the kaṟpu section. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sita tells Hanuman that she will keep herself alive for one more month in the hope that Rama will come for her, and that she cannot live beyond that.
hinduism.explanation: Sita’s life in captivity is sustained only by the expectation of her husband’s coming.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Sita says plainly that she lives on only for the day of his return.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, Sita’s message to Rama through Hanuman (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes hope as the patient waiting for what is not yet seen.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine lives in exactly that hope: she cannot see him, but waiting for him keeps her alive.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Jacob] said, ‘Rather, your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them to me all together. Indeed it is He who is the Knowing, the Wise.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob, having lost two sons, holds on through patience and the hope that they will be returned to him.
islam.tie_back: The heroine’s will to live rests on the same hope that the absent one will be brought back.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Israel said: ‘It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive; I will go and see him before I die.’”
judaism.explanation: Jacob’s spirit revives at the news that Joseph lives, and seeing him becomes the one thing left to live for.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine too is kept alive by one wish: to see him again.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sambula Jataka, the princess Sambula follows her husband into the forest when he falls gravely ill and tends him faithfully, refusing to abandon him.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka holds up Sambula as a model of a wife whose devotion carries her through hardship.
buddhism.tie_back: Sambula’s steadfastness and the heroine’s will to live for her husband’s return are the same devotion under strain.
buddhism.source: Sambula Jataka (Jataka No. 519, tr. E.B. Cowell et al.; paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: Jacobi notes that Rajimati’s lament for Arishtanemi became the subject of a Jain Sanskrit poem, the Nemidutakavya of Vikrama, in which each stanza ends with a line borrowed from Kalidasa’s Meghaduta, turning her into a separated lover sending a message to her beloved.
jainism.explanation: Jain poets themselves took up the viraha (separation) form to voice Rajimati’s longing for the Jina.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Rajimati in this poem lives in longing for one who has gone away on a lofty purpose of his own.
jainism.source: Nemidutakavya of Vikrama, as described in Hermann Jacobi’s note to Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.28 (SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without Him, I cannot live, even for a moment. Without His Name, I die.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says the soul's life depends entirely on the Lord; without Him there is only death.
sikhism.tie_back: The wife in the Kural lives on only because she longs for her husband's return; Guru Nanak too says life itself hangs on the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 58, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: While Ceyx is at sea, his wife Alcyone burns incense to the gods every day, weaves garments for his homecoming and prays for his safe return, not knowing he has already drowned.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s myth shows a wife whose every day is organised around her husband’s expected return.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Alcyone and the Kural’s heroine both live for the moment the absent husband comes home.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Nietzsche writes that if we have our own why of life, we can put up with almost any how.
philosophy.explanation: A clear reason to live makes even hard conditions bearable.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s ‘why’ is his return, and it is what lets her endure the ‘how’ of separation.
philosophy.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols, ‘Maxims and Arrows’ 12 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Douglas Mawson's extra year in Antarctica and Paquita Delprat's wait
real_life_example.place: Commonwealth Bay, Antarctica, and Adelaide, Australia
real_life_example.event: The geologist Douglas Mawson, engaged to Paquita Delprat, led the Australasian Antarctic Expedition from 1911. On a sledging journey in 1912 his companions Belgrave Ninnis and Xavier Mertz died, and Mawson struggled back alone to his base only to find that the relief ship Aurora had just left. He and six volunteers spent another winter there, he returned in 1914, and he and Paquita married on 31 March 1914 in Melbourne.
real_life_example.explanation: Mawson went south in pursuit of discovery, and his fiancee had to wait more than two years, including an unplanned extra year, for his return.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says her husband left in pursuit of achievement with only his resolve for company, and she lives on only in the hope of his return; Paquita Delprat waited through Mawson's long absence in just this situation.

tamil:
கூடிய காமம் பிரிந்தார் வரவுள்ளிக்
கோடுகொ டேறுமென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Kootiya kaamam pirindhaar varavullik
koaduko daerumen nenju.
meaning: Thinking of the return of the one who left, with all the love we shared, my heart climbs from branch to branch to look out for him.
elementary: Have you ever climbed a tree to see far away? The lady in this verse feels so excited thinking her husband might be coming home that it is as if her heart climbs up into the treetops, branch after branch, trying to spot him on the road.
university: The striking image is kōṭu koṭu ēṟum eṉ neñcu, ‘my heart climbs branch upon branch’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take it literally as the heart climbing to the treetop to watch the road; Sivayogi Sivakumar compares it to a creeper that outgrows the pole it climbs; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as the heart, freed of sorrow, spreading branches and growing upward in joy, which is close to Pope’s ‘my heart with rapture swells’. Kūṭiya kāmam pirintār, ‘he who parted from the love we had joined in’, recalls their earlier union. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar takes the couplet as the heroine’s eager anticipation at news or thought of his coming. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Radha’s companion describes her waiting for Krishna in the forest bower, starting at every rustle and decking the bower in expectation of his coming.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s Radha lives in a state of eager, restless anticipation of her beloved’s arrival.
hinduism.tie_back: Radha’s restless watching is the same leap of the heart the Kural pictures as climbing branch after branch.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Radha’s waiting in the bower (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb sets the sickness of delayed hope against the life that floods back when the desire is fulfilled.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine’s heart, at the very thought of his return, rises like a tree; the proverb uses the same image for fulfilled desire.

islam.quote_or_event: As the caravan carrying Joseph’s shirt leaves Egypt, Jacob tells those around him that he perceives the scent of Joseph, even though they think him weak in mind.
islam.explanation: Before any news arrives, the longing father’s heart already senses that his son is on the way back to him.
islam.tie_back: The heroine’s heart likewise runs ahead to meet the returning beloved before he has arrived.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hark! my beloved! behold, he cometh, leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills. My beloved is like a gazelle or a young hart; behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh in through the windows, he peereth through the lattice.”
judaism.explanation: The bride hears and imagines her beloved’s approach before he has even reached her.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s heart climbing to look out for him is the same eager picture of a lover’s coming.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The craving of one given to heedless living grows like a creeper. Like the monkey seeking fruits in the forest, he leaps from life to life (tasting the fruit of his kamma).”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures craving as a creeper and a monkey, always climbing and leaping toward the next thing it wants.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart climbing branch to branch is almost the same image, though the Kural celebrates the climbing while the Dhammapada warns against it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Cast aside from you all attachments, as the (leaves of) a lotus let drop off the autumnal water, exempt from every attachment, Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama to let attachments fall away as water runs off a lotus leaf.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart reaches up and out toward the beloved; Jain teaching counsels the opposite movement, letting attachment drop away.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, the soul-bride is gazing upon Your Path; please listen, O Supreme Soul.”
sikhism.explanation: In the opening of his Barah Maha (song of the twelve months), Guru Nanak pictures the soul-bride watching the road for her Husband Lord and begging Him to hear her.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heart climbs from branch to branch to look out for the returning husband; Guru Nanak's soul-bride likewise keeps watch on the road for the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1107, Raag Tukhaari, Barah Maha, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Night after night, Hero climbs her tower at Sestos and lights a lamp, watching across the Hellespont for Leander to swim to her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hero’s tower and lamp make her whole being a watch for the beloved’s coming.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hero climbs her tower to watch for him; the Kural’s heroine sends her heart up the branches to do the same.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines hope as an inconstant pleasure arising from the idea of something future or past whose outcome we still doubt.
philosophy.explanation: Hope, for Spinoza, is a real joy, but an unsteady one, because it depends on something not yet certain.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s heart leaps with exactly this inconstant joy at the mere thought of his return.
philosophy.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics III, Definitions of the Affects 12 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Alexander Selkirk is rescued after four years marooned
real_life_example.place: Mas a Tierra, Juan Fernandez Islands (now Chile)
real_life_example.event: After a quarrel with his captain in September 1704, the Scottish sailor Alexander Selkirk asked to be put ashore on the uninhabited island of Mas a Tierra, and he regretted the decision as soon as the ship sailed. During more than four years alone, two ships landed, but they were Spanish and he had to hide from their crews. In February 1709 he was picked up by an English ship commanded by Woodes Rogers.
real_life_example.explanation: Selkirk's long wait for a friendly sail later helped inspire the story of Robinson Crusoe.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine sends her heart climbing from branch to branch to look out for her beloved's return; Selkirk's years of hope for a rescuing ship are a documented case of such watching.

tamil:
காண்கமன் கொண்கனைக் கண்ணாரக் கண்டபின்
நீங்கும்என் மென்தோள் பசப்பு.
transliteration:
Kaankaman konkanaik kannaarak kandapin
neengum-en men-dhoal pasappu.
meaning: Let me just see my husband until my eyes are full. Once I have seen him, the paleness on my soft arms will go away by itself.
elementary: When you are missing someone, you can feel pale and tired. But the moment you see them, you feel better right away. The lady in this verse says: “I just need to see him properly, and all my paleness will disappear like magic.”
university: Kāṇka maṉ is an optative: ‘may I see’, with maṉ marking an intense wish. Koṇkaṉ, ‘husband’ (originally ‘lord of the seashore’ in the neytal landscape), is to be seen kaṇṇāra, ‘to the eyes’ full’. Pacappu is pacalai, the sallow pallor that in Tamil love convention spreads over a woman’s body in separation; chapter 119 is devoted to it. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar say it will vanish ‘of itself’ (தானே) once she sees him, so the cure is sight alone. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar treats this as her answer to the friend who urges patience. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna reappears among the gopis after vanishing from the rasa dance, they rise up all at once, their eyes wide with love, as if life had returned to their bodies.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata, the mere sight of the returning beloved revives those who were wasting in separation.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine expects exactly this: one full look at him and her pallor will vanish.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.32.2-3 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada; paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And ye now therefore have sorrow: but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises his grieving disciples that seeing him again will turn their sorrow into lasting joy.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same promise to herself: seeing him will cure her sorrow.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when the bearer of good tidings arrived, he cast it over his face, and he returned [once again] seeing. He said, ‘Did I not tell you that I know from Allah that which you do not know?’”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s sight, lost through grief for Joseph, returns when Joseph’s shirt is laid on his face.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the bodily mark of separation is healed by contact with the beloved’s return.

judaism.quote_or_event: “O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the covert of the cliff, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.”
judaism.explanation: The lover asks only to see the beloved’s face and hear her voice.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s whole wish is the same: let me see him, and that will be enough.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The introduction to the Canda-Kinnara Jataka tells how, when the Buddha first returned to Kapilavatthu, Yasodhara stayed in her chamber, saying he would come to her if she had any worth; he came, and she held his feet and wept.
buddhism.explanation: The commentarial story gives Yasodhara a long, faithful waiting rewarded by the sight of her former husband.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Yasodhara’s long sorrow finds release the moment she sees him again.
buddhism.source: Canda-Kinnara Jataka (Jataka No. 485), introductory story (tr. E.B. Cowell et al.; paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “After practising severe austerities both of them became Kêvalins, and having completely annihilated their Karman, they reached the highest perfection.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati and Rathanemi end not in reunion with a beloved but in liberation, each through their own discipline.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine expects healing from seeing her husband; the Jain story places final healing in liberation rather than in any human reunion.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Gazing upon my Beloved with my eyes, I have obtained all treasures;”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that simply seeing the Beloved Lord with one's own eyes gives everything a person could want.
sikhism.tie_back: The wife says that once she sees her husband to her eyes' content, her paleness will vanish of itself; Guru Arjan likewise finds that the sight of the Beloved fulfils every lack.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 372, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles brings a veiled woman back from the dead to Admetus, who at first refuses her; when the veil is lifted he sees his wife Alcestis and his grief turns to joy.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides stages a reunion in which the mere sight of the lost wife ends the mourning.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Admetus’ grief, like the heroine’s pallor, vanishes the moment he sees the one he lost.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates says that when the soul is parted from the beloved it is stung and in pain, but when it looks on the beloved again it is refreshed and its pangs cease.
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes the lover’s suffering in absence and the relief that comes from sight of the beloved.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point in philosophical form: separation makes the lover ill, and seeing the beloved heals.

real_life_example.event_title: Natan and Avital Sharansky are reunited after twelve years
real_life_example.event: Natan (Anatoly) Sharansky married Natalya Stiglitz in 1974, and she was allowed to emigrate to Israel the day after the wedding, expecting him to follow. He was arrested in March 1977 and sentenced to 13 years in prison and labour camps, while she, taking the name Avital, campaigned for his release from Jerusalem and abroad. He was freed in an East-West prisoner exchange on 11 February 1986 and arrived in Israel that day, where the couple were together again.
real_life_example.explanation: Avital's long campaign was driven by a single wish: to see her husband again, after a marriage that had lasted only one day before their separation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine asks only to see her husband until her eyes are full, sure that her pallor will then fade; Avital spent twelve years working toward exactly that sight.

tamil:
வருகமன் கொண்கன் ஒருநாள் பருகுவன்
பைதல்நோய் எல்லாம் கெட.
transliteration:
Varukaman kon-kan oru-naal parukuvan
paidhalnhoi ellaam keda.
meaning: Let my husband come back, even for one day. I will drink in his love until all this sickness of sorrow is gone.
elementary: When you are very thirsty, a cool drink makes you feel better all over. The lady says being with her husband again would be like that: after missing him for so long, being with him would wash away all her sadness.
university: Again an optative: varuka maṉ, ‘may he come’, with oru nāḷ, ‘even one day’, suggesting that a single day would suffice. Parukuvaṉ, ‘I shall drink’, is the chapter’s boldest metaphor: she will take in his presence as one drinks to slake thirst (Pope: ‘I’ll drink that nectar’), so that paital nōy, the anguished sickness of separation, is wholly destroyed (ellām keṭa). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss parukuvaṉ as ‘enjoy fully’ (நுகர்வேன்), and Puliyur Kesikan as ‘drink in delight’ (இன்பத்தை பருகுவேன்). The image belongs to the conventions of akam poetry and should be read as the delight of reunion. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the gopis meet Krishna again at Kurukshetra after long separation, they drink him in with their eyes, cursing the creator of eyelids for interrupting their gaze, and embrace him within their hearts.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata pictures reunion as a thirsty drinking-in of the beloved through the eyes.
hinduism.tie_back: The gopis and the Kural’s heroine use the same metaphor: the long-absent beloved is drunk in until the pain of separation is gone.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.82 (Krishna meets the gopis at Kurukshetra) (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “It was but a little that I passed from them, but I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me.”
christianity.explanation: After searching the city at night, the bride finds her beloved and holds him fast.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine longs for exactly this: to have him back and not let go until all the ache of absence is gone.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names a spouse as a source of tranquillity, bound by affection and mercy.
islam.tie_back: The heroine seeks just that: in her husband’s return she will find rest from her anguish.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Stay ye me with dainties, refresh me with apples; for I am love-sick.”
judaism.explanation: The bride calls herself love-sick and asks to be revived with sweet things.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also names her longing a sickness and expects to drink her cure in the beloved’s presence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Canda-Kinnara Jataka, a king shoots the kinnara Canda; his wife Canda laments over him until Sakka restores him to life, and the two rejoice together again.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka tells of a wife’s grief over her lost husband turned to joy when he is restored to her.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the kinnari’s sorrow ends only with her husband given back to her.
buddhism.source: Canda-Kinnara Jataka (Jataka No. 485, tr. E.B. Cowell et al.; paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: Citta and Sambhuta, brothers through five successive births, are born apart in the sixth; when they meet again, Citta the monk urges King Brahmadatta to renounce, but Brahmadatta, bound by pleasures, cannot.
jainism.explanation: The Jain story of a long-separated pair reunited turns the reunion into a test of whether one can let go of worldly delight.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine longs to drink in the delight of reunion; the Jain reunion story warns that such delight is what binds the soul.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13, Citta and Sambhuta (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Dear Lord is the fruit-bearing tree; drinking in the Ambrosial Nectar, thirst is quenched.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das pictures the Lord as a tree that gives nourishing fruit; drinking in His nectar ends the soul's thirst.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife wants to drink in her husband's presence until her sickness of longing is gone; Guru Amar Das likewise speaks of drinking in the Beloved's nectar until thirst is satisfied.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 114, Raag Maajh, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Penelope at last recognises Odysseus, Homer compares her joy to that of shipwrecked sailors who reach the shore, and she cannot take her arms from around his neck.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Odyssey’s great reunion turns twenty years of grief into overwhelming relief.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the reunion the Kural’s heroine longs for, when all her anguish will drain away at once.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Symposium, Aristophanes says that love is the desire and pursuit of the whole, the healer who seeks to make one of two and so cure the wound of human nature.
philosophy.explanation: Aristophanes’ myth treats love as the cure for the pain of having been divided from one’s other half.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine likewise sees reunion with her husband as the cure for the sickness of separation.

real_life_example.event_title: Operation Homecoming brings American prisoners of war home
real_life_example.place: Hanoi, Vietnam; Clark Air Base, Philippines; Travis Air Force Base, California
real_life_example.event: Under the Paris Peace Accords, the first flight of Operation Homecoming carried 40 American prisoners of war out of Hanoi on 12 February 1973 to Clark Air Base in the Philippines. Flights continued into late March, and 591 prisoners returned to the United States, some after more than seven years in captivity. The first group of 20 reached Travis Air Force Base in California on 14 February 1973.
real_life_example.explanation: After years of uncertainty for their families, the return flights ended long separations in a matter of days.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine says that if her husband comes back even for one day, all her grief will be gone; for the families of these prisoners, the day of return ended years of anxious waiting.

tamil:
புலப்பேன்கொல் புல்லுவேன் கொல்லோ கலப்பேன்கொல்
கண்அன்ன கேளிர் விரன்.
transliteration:
Pulappaen-kol pulluvaen kolloa kalappaenkol
kan-anna kaelir viran.
meaning: When he comes back, he who is as dear to me as my own eyes, should I sulk, or hug him, or do both? I cannot decide.
elementary: Imagine your best friend went away for a long time without visiting. When they finally come back, part of you wants to say “Hmph, where were you?” and part of you wants to give them a big hug. The lady in this verse feels both at once, and she just can’t decide which to do first.
university: Three rhetorical questions, each with the doubt particle kol: pulappēṉ (shall I show pulavi, the lover’s feigned sulk), pulluvēṉ (shall I embrace), kalappēṉ (shall I mingle the two, or simply unite). Kaṇ aṉṉa kēḷir, ‘the beloved who is like my eyes’, and viraṉ (‘should he come’) set the scene. Solomon Pappaiah reads kalappēṉ as ‘doing both together’ and Kalaignar adds that she is too overwhelmed even to know; the couplet anticipates the later chapters on ūṭal (lovers’ quarrel, chapters 131-133). Textual note: ytamizh.com’s ‘English Couplet’ slot for 1267 contains a prose explanation, and its ‘Couplet Explanation’ (‘This malady (of lust) is manured by the talk of women…’) belongs to Kural 1147, not this couplet. The Tamil text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, when Krishna comes to Radha at dawn after a night away, she rebukes him in wounded pride, and only later, after his pleading, does her anger melt into reconciliation.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva gives Radha the full sequence of māna (proud sulk) followed by reunion.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees both moves ahead of her, the sulk and the embrace, and cannot choose between them.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Radha’s rebuke and reconciliation (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me… I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?”
christianity.explanation: The bride’s heart wakes for her beloved, yet she hesitates and makes excuses before rising.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she is caught between eager love and a reluctance that holds her back.

islam.quote_or_event: “I know when you are pleased with me or angry with me… When you are pleased with me, you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Muhammad,’ but when you are angry with me, then you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Abraham.’” Aisha replies that even then she leaves nothing but his name.
islam.explanation: The Prophet gently notices Aisha’s small sulks, and she answers that even in anger her love for him remains.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s mix of pulavi and embrace: the sulk is only on the surface, and the love beneath it never leaves.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him; and they wept.”
judaism.explanation: After twenty years of estrangement and grievance, Esau meets Jacob not with reproach but with an embrace.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wonders whether her grievance or her embrace will win; in Esau’s case the embrace wins.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From affection springs grief, from affection springs fear. For one who is wholly free from affection there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces both grief and fear to the root of affection.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s sulk and her embrace both spring from one root, her love, which is just what the verse names as the source of turmoil.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard the Buddha’s well-delivered sermon, adorned by illustrations, Gautama cut off love and hatred and reached perfection.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching names love (raga) and hatred (dvesha) as the twin bonds to be cut for liberation (‘Buddha’ here is a title for Mahavira).
jainism.tie_back: The heroine is caught between those very two, the pull to sulk and the pull to embrace, which Jainism counsels cutting away together.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “whether your Lord and Master is angry with you or in love with you.”
sikhism.explanation: In this hymn Kabir speaks of the devotee's relationship with the Master as one that holds both displeasure and love.
sikhism.tie_back: The wife wonders whether, when her husband returns, she will sulk, embrace him, or both; Kabir's line likewise holds anger and love together in one bond.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 338, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus stands before her at last, Penelope sits silent, pondering whether to question her husband from a distance or to go to him and kiss his head and hands, and Telemachus scolds her for her hardness of heart.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer gives Penelope a long moment of doubt between reserve and embrace before she yields.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s dilemma almost exactly: hold back or embrace, or somehow both.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza calls it vacillation of mind when the same thing is at once the cause of both joy and sorrow, so that we love and hate it at once.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza explains how one object can stir opposite feelings at the same moment.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s undecided ‘shall I sulk or embrace?’ is exactly such a vacillation toward one beloved person.
philosophy.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics III, Proposition 17 and Scholium (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Heloise writes to Abelard with reproach and love
real_life_example.event: After Peter Abelard, then abbot of Saint-Gildas in Brittany, wrote an account of his misfortunes, Heloise, by then head of the convent of the Paraclete, wrote to him. In her letter she reproached him for not comforting her, either in person or by letter, since they had both entered religious life. In the same letter she declared that she had always loved him and that her heart still belonged to him.
real_life_example.explanation: Heloise's letter is famous for holding complaint and devotion together in the same breath.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine cannot decide whether to sulk at her returning beloved, embrace him, or do both; Heloise's letter does both at once.

tamil:
வினைகலந்து வென்றீக வேந்தன் மனைகலந்து
மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து.
transliteration:
Vinaikalandhu vendreeka vaendhan manaikalandhu
maalai ayarkam virundhu.
meaning: Let the king fight on and win the war. Then I will join my wife at home, and we will have a feast together this evening.
elementary: Now the husband speaks. He is far away helping the king in a big contest. He thinks: “Let us finish this job and win, and then I can rush home and have a happy dinner with my wife tonight.” He misses her just as much as she misses him.
university: Here the speaker changes: it is the husband, serving with the king (vēntaṉ) on campaign, who voices his own vitumpal, which is why the chapter is ‘mutual’. Viṉai kalantu veṉṟīka, ‘may [the king] engage in the task and win’, is followed by maṉai kalantu, ‘joining my home (wife)’, and mālai ayarkam viruntu, ‘we shall hold a feast in the evening’. The parallel kalantu…kalantu sets the king’s battle beside the husband’s reunion. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read the hero’s eagerness for victory as eagerness to be home; Puliyur Kesikan specifies ‘with her in the evening’. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: During the monsoon at Kishkindha, Rama, separated from Sita, laments that the rains delay the campaign to recover her, and longs for the season to end so that he can march and win her back.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki shows a hero whose impatience for the campaign is really impatience to be reunited with his wife.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s husband, Rama wants the fighting done because his heart is with his wife.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, Rama’s lament in the rains (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which he hath given thee under the sun… for that is thy portion in this life, and in thy labour which thou takest under the sun.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher names joy with one’s beloved wife as the true portion of life amid all labour.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s husband feels the same: the campaign is labour, and the evening with his wife is his real reward.

islam.quote_or_event: When Abdullah ibn Amr fasted every day and prayed all night, the Prophet told him not to, saying that his body, his eyes and his wife each have a right over him.
islam.explanation: The Prophet restrains even devout effort that crowds out a man’s duty of companionship to his wife.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s husband feels the same claim: his wife’s right draws him home once the task is done.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When a man taketh a new wife, he shall not go out in the host, neither shall he be charged with any business; he shall be free for his house one year, and shall cheer his wife whom he hath taken.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah exempts a newly married man from war so that he can make his wife happy.
judaism.tie_back: Torah law gives priority to exactly what the Kural’s husband longs for: leaving the campaign to be with his wife.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When, after a long absence, a man safely returns from afar, his relatives, friends and well-wishers welcome him home on arrival.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses a traveller’s homecoming as a picture of joyful welcome.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the homecoming the Kural’s husband is already imagining: the work done, a welcome and a feast at home.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Give up your wealth and your wife; you have entered the state of the houseless; do not, as it were, return to your vomit; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira tells a monk not to look back toward the household and wife he has left.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband longs to hurry home to his wife; Jain teaching for the renouncer points the other way, though it does not forbid this to the householder.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My sought-after Husband Lord has come home, and now, congratulations are pouring in.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the joy of the soul-bride when the Husband Lord she longed for finally comes home, and everyone celebrates.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the husband longs to finish the campaign and come home to feast with his wife; Guru Arjan pictures the happy homecoming itself and its celebration.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 704, Raag Jaithsree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On Calypso’s island, Odysseus sits on the shore day after day weeping, longing for his homecoming and his wife, though a goddess offers him immortality to stay.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s hero values the return to his home and wife above everything else on offer.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s husband shares this pull: whatever the task, his heart is set on the evening at home with his wife.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle writes that we are busy in order to have leisure, and make war in order to live in peace.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, work and war are not ends in themselves but are for the sake of the life lived afterward.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s husband sees the king’s war the same way: it is for the sake of the evening feast at home.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10.7 (tr. W.D. Ross; paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: George Washington writes to Martha on taking command
real_life_example.event: Days after the Continental Congress made him commander of the new army, George Washington wrote to his wife Martha from Philadelphia. He told her he had not sought the command, partly because he did not want to be parted from her and the family, and that he would find more real happiness in one month with her at home than in the most distant prospect abroad, even if his stay lasted seven times seven years. The letter is one of the very few between them to survive, because Martha is believed to have destroyed most of their correspondence.
real_life_example.explanation: At the start of a long war, the new commander's private letter shows that his heart was at home with his wife.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural gives the husband's voice: let the king's campaign be won, and he will go home to feast with his wife; Washington, taking up command of a war, wrote that a month at home with Martha outweighed any glory abroad.

tamil:
ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல் செல்லும்சேண் சென்றார்
வருநாள்வைத்து ஏங்கு பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Orunaal ezhunaalpoal sellumsaen sendraar
varunaal-vaiththu aengu pavarkku.
meaning: For those who long for the day their faraway love will come back, one day drags by as slowly as seven days.
elementary: Do you remember waiting for your birthday or a holiday? The last few days feel sooo long! The verse says that when you are waiting for someone you love to come home, one day can feel as long as a whole week.
university: A general maxim (note the plural ēṅkupavarkku, ‘for those who pine’) caps the chapter’s experience: oru nāḷ eḻu nāḷ pōl cellum, ‘one day passes like seven’, for those who have fixed in mind (vaittu) the day (varu nāḷ) of return of one who has gone far (cēṇ ceṉṟār). Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the seven; Solomon Pappaiah generalises to ‘many days’; Kalaignar heightens it to ‘each day like an age (yugam)’. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar takes it as spoken by the heroine of herself, generalised into a truth. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When You go off to the forest during the day, a tiny fraction of a second becomes like a millennium for us because we cannot see You.”
hinduism.explanation: The gopis tell Krishna that every moment without the sight of him stretches into an age.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim, magnified: for the one who waits, a day is seven days, or a moment a millennium.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.31.15 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist compares his waiting to night watchmen longing for the dawn, when every hour drags.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s waiter, the watchman knows how slowly time passes when you are waiting for an arrival.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they urge you to hasten the punishment. But Allah will never fail in His promise. And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of those which you count.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an reminds the impatient that time is measured differently with God than by human counting.
islam.tie_back: The Kural also says that a day is not always a day: for the yearning heart, it stretches far beyond its count.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.”
judaism.explanation: Jacob’s love for Rachel makes seven years of labour feel like a few days.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say love bends time by the number seven; for Jacob, with his goal in sight, years shrink, while for the Kural’s waiting lover a day swells into seven.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary. Long is worldly existence to fools who know not the Sublime Truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that time and distance stretch for those who are suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s waiting lover lives the first line: her nights and days are long because she is restless with longing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira reminds Gautama that human life is short and urges him not to waste a single moment.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover feels each day as long; Jain teaching asks one to feel each moment as precious, a contrasting lesson about the weight of time.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “With each and every breath, I think of You, day and night; I do not forget You, for an instant, even for a moment.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes a mind fixed on the Beloved through every breath, day and night.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that for those whose minds are fixed on the day of the beloved's return, one day drags like seven; Guru Arjan likewise speaks of a mind that holds the Beloved in thought through every moment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 247, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theocritus opens an idyll of welcome to a returning beloved by saying that those who long grow old in a single day.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek pastoral poetry states that longing makes one day as heavy as years.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s own maxim: for the one who waits, a day is far longer than a day.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Bergson observes that if he wants a glass of sugar-water he must wait until the sugar melts, and that this time of waiting is not a mathematical quantity but coincides with his impatience, a portion of his own lived duration.
philosophy.explanation: Bergson distinguishes clock time from lived time, which stretches with impatience.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same: by the clock it is one day, but in the waiting heart it is seven.

real_life_example.event_title: Anne Bradstreet's poems to her absent husband
real_life_example.place: Massachusetts Bay Colony (now Massachusetts, United States)
real_life_example.event: The Puritan poet Anne Bradstreet was married to Simon Bradstreet, whose duties as a colonial magistrate frequently took him away from home. She wrote love poems to him, including A Letter to her Husband, absent upon Publick employment, in which she pictures him as the sun and herself as chilled and numb while he stays away, begging him to return. The poems appeared in the Boston edition of her Several Poems in 1678.
real_life_example.explanation: Bradstreet's poems are among the earliest records in American literature of a wife's longing during her husband's absences on public duty.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that for those waiting for a faraway beloved's return, one day passes like seven; Bradstreet describes the time of her husband's absence as a long cold season waiting for the sun to come back.

tamil:
பெறின்என்னாம் பெற்றக்கால் என்னாம் உறினென்னாம்
உள்ளம் உடைந்துக்கக் கால்.
transliteration:
Perin-ennaam petrakkaal ennaam urinennaam
ullam udaindhukkak kaal.
meaning: If her heart breaks with sorrow and she dies, what good will it be that she gets me back, or has me, or even holds me close?
elementary: The husband worries: “If I stay away too long, she might become so sad that her heart breaks. Then what good would it be to come home? I must hurry back while there is still time.” It is like a promise that is only worth something if you keep it in time.
university: Most commentators, following the tradition associated with Parimelazhagar, give this closing couplet to the husband, who fears for his wife: Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘if her heart breaks… what use is it that she gets me?’, and Pope translates ‘If she heart-broken lie, with all her life poured forth’. The triple question peṟiṉ eṉ ām / peṟṟakkāl eṉ ām / uṟiṉ eṉ ām moves from ‘should she obtain [me]’ to ‘having obtained’ to ‘having embraced’, and uḷḷam uṭaintu ukkakkāl means ‘when the heart has broken and spilled away’, a euphemism for dying of grief. Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the first person plural (நம்மை) and Kalaignar a neutral ‘each other’, so the speaker is not unanimous, but the sense of urgency is shared. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Queen Indumati dies suddenly, King Aja laments that without her his kingdom, his pleasures and his very life have lost their meaning, and he lives on only for his son’s sake.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa shows that every good a husband possesses becomes empty once the beloved wife is gone.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the fear behind the Kural: if she dies of grief, no reunion, victory or embrace will be worth anything.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Raghuvamsha, canto 8, Aja’s lament for Indumati (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus asks what any gain is worth if the one thing that matters is lost.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s husband asks the same kind of question: what use is any homecoming if she is lost?

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s romance, Majnun, kept apart from Layla all his life, learns of her death and goes to her grave, where he dies; their union comes only in death.
islam.explanation: The great Persian love story shows separation lasting until it is too late for any earthly reunion.
islam.tie_back: This is the outcome the Kural’s husband dreads: a heart broken by separation, after which meeting means nothing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a broken spirit who can bear?”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says the spirit can carry bodily illness, but nothing can carry a broken spirit.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband fears precisely a broken spirit (uḷḷam uṭaintu) that nothing afterward could mend.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that separation from loved ones is inherently painful and counsels non-attachment.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s couple know that pain of separation all too well; the husband’s answer is to hurry home, the Buddha’s is to loosen the bond.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.”
jainism.explanation: Forsaken by Arishtanemi, Rajimati feels that her life as it was has lost its worth, and turns to renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati is the heart-broken wife the Kural’s husband fears to leave behind, though in Jainism her grief opens onto a new path.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My Beloved has not come home, and I am dying of the sorrow of separation. The lightning flashes, and I am scared.”
sikhism.explanation: In his Barah Maha Guru Nanak's soul-bride says that while her Beloved stays away she is dying of the grief of separation.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's husband fears his wife will die of the grief of waiting, so that his return will come too late; Guru Nanak's soul-bride voices that very danger of dying while the Beloved is away.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1108, Raag Tukhaari, Barah Maha, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theseus, sailing home victorious from Crete, forgets to raise the white sail; his father Aegeus, watching from the cliff and seeing the black sail, throws himself into the sea, so that Theseus’ triumphant return comes too late.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows a victory made empty because the one waiting at home did not survive the wait.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s warning in story form: if the one at home is lost to grief, the return and the victory are worth nothing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca urges his friend to hold every hour fast, since everything else belongs to others and time alone is truly ours, and once lost it cannot be recovered.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca treats time as the one irreplaceable possession, which delay squanders.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s husband sees the same danger: delay could cost what no later return can restore.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 1 (tr. R.M. Gummere; paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Mumtaz Mahal dies on Shah Jahan's Deccan campaign
real_life_example.event: In 1631 Mumtaz Mahal, wife of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, accompanied him while pregnant on a military campaign in the Deccan. She died at Burhanpur after giving birth to the couple's fourteenth child. Her body was moved to Agra in January 1632, and work began there on the Taj Mahal as her tomb.
real_life_example.explanation: The emperor's campaign went on, but the loss of his wife turned his energies to building one of the world's most famous monuments of grief.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's husband, away on campaign, asks what use any reunion would be if his wife's heart broke and she died; Shah Jahan's campaign ended with exactly such a loss.

tamil:
கரப்பினுங் கையிகந் தொல்லாநின் உண்கண்
உரைக்கல் உறுவதொன் றுண்டு.
transliteration:
Karappinung kaiyikan thollaanin unkan
uraikkal uruvadhon rundu.
meaning: Even though you try to hide it, your eyes, darkened with eye makeup, will not stay quiet. They have something to tell me.
elementary: Imagine a friend who says ‘I’m fine’ but whose eyes look sad. You can tell something is wrong, because eyes often say what words keep hidden. The poet says love works the same way: the eyes give away the secret.
university: The chapter title kuṟippaṟivuṟuttal means ‘making known by signs’ (kuṟippu, a hint or covert sign; aṟivuṟuttal, causing to be known), and it belongs to the kaṟpu (wedded love) section, where partners communicate feelings about separation without open speech. Here the husband addresses his wife: karappiṉum (‘though you hide it’), her uṇkaṇ (eyes darkened with collyrium) kai ikantu ollā (‘will not stay within bounds’) and are about to utter (uraikkal uṟuvatu) one thing. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as a message the eyes force past her concealment; Solomon Pappaiah stresses the painted eyes; Kalaignar names the hidden message as a love that does not want separation, which fits the chapter’s setting of an impending departure. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh prints the sandhi as கையிகந் தொல்லாநின்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s play, King Dushyanta notes that Shakuntala does not join her words to his, yet she listens when he speaks, and though she does not turn her face to him, her eyes rest on nothing else for long.
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala is too modest to speak her love, but her eyes betray it, and the king reads them.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts describe a woman whose speech hides her heart while her eyes give it away to the one who loves her.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that what people keep hidden will in the end come to light.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle to a lover’s heart: what she hides, her eyes reveal.

islam.quote_or_event: “He knows that which deceives the eyes and what the breasts conceal.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says God knows both the stolen glance and the secret held in the heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural links the same two things, hidden feeling in the heart and its leak through the eyes, though here it is the husband, not God, who reads them.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my bride; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one bead of thy necklace.”
judaism.explanation: The lover in the Song says a single glance from his bride is enough to capture him.
judaism.tie_back: In both poems the beloved’s eyes speak with a force that needs no words.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists three things that are carried on in secret and three that shine openly, the sun, the moon and the Dhamma, which need no concealment.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta contrasts what must hide from view with what is naturally open and shining.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows a secret that cannot stay hidden; the sutta’s contrast between the concealed and the openly shining is the nearest Buddhist parallel, though its concern is truth, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the assembly he pronounces holy (words), yet secretly he commits sins; but the wise know him to be a deceiver and great rogue.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga observes that a monk who hides his lapses behind pious words is still seen through by the discerning.
jainism.tie_back: As in the Kural, concealment fails before someone who knows how to read the signs, though the Jain text is exposing hypocrisy, not tender feeling.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O my Lord and Master, You alone know the state of my inner being.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that the Lord sees what is hidden inside the devotee, whatever is shown outwardly.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the husband sees through his wife's attempt to hide her feelings, because her eyes speak; Guru Ram Das likewise says the inner state cannot be hidden from the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 735, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Medea first sees Jason in the palace of Aeetes, she keeps stealing glances at him, and her eyes and blushing cheeks betray the love she is struggling to hide from her family.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius shows a young woman’s secret passion leaking out through her gaze despite her efforts to keep it silent.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Medea’s eyes, like the wife’s in the Kural, refuse to keep the heart’s secret.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Emerson writes that the eyes of men converse at least as much as their tongues, and that this ocular dialect needs no dictionary but is understood all the world over.
philosophy.explanation: Emerson treats the eye as a language of its own that communicates even when speech is guarded.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s whole point is that the eyes speak a message the tongue holds back.
philosophy.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, The Conduct of Life, ‘Behavior’ (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Jeremiah Denton blinks a hidden message in Morse code
real_life_example.event: U.S. Navy pilot Jeremiah Denton was shot down and captured on 18 July 1965 during the Vietnam War. In 1966 he was made to give an interview to a Japanese television crew for a North Vietnamese propaganda film, and while answering the questions he blinked the letters T-O-R-T-U-R-E in Morse code.
