The film reached the United States, where the hidden message was read, and Denton was released in February 1973 after more than seven years as a prisoner.
real_life_example.explanation: Though he was forced to speak words chosen by his captors, Denton's eyes carried the true message past them.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that however much one hides a feeling, the eyes will not stay within bounds and are trying to say something; Denton's eyes said what his spoken words were not allowed to.

tamil:
கண்ணிறைந்த காரிகைக் காம்பேர்தோட் பேதைக்குப்
பெண்நிறைந்த நீர்மை பெரிது.
transliteration:
Kanniraindha kaarikaik kaamperdhot pedhaikkup
penniraindha neermai peridhu.
meaning: My innocent love, whose beauty fills my eyes and whose shoulders are smooth like bamboo, is full of a deep womanly modesty.
elementary: Some people are beautiful to look at, but what makes them special is how gentle and kind they are. The poet says his beloved is lovely, but her quiet, modest nature is even bigger than her beauty.
university: The speaker praises the heroine’s kārikai (beauty) that fills the eye (kaṇ niṟainta) and her shoulders like the bamboo (kāmpu ēr tōḷ), a stock Tamil image of smooth, rounded grace; pētai here means an artless, innocent young woman. Her peṇ niṟainta nīrmai (‘a nature full of womanliness’) is said to be peritu, very great. Commentators gloss peṇmai variously: Mu. Varadarasanar as the quality of womanhood, Solomon Pappaiah as an excellence surpassing that found in all women, and Kalaignar as womanliness that is itself her greatest beauty. In the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar, the speaker is the husband telling the confidante (tōḻi) that his wife’s modesty is so great that she cannot voice her own feelings, which is why they must be read through signs. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Parvati comes before Shiva and his composure stirs, she betrays her own feeling only through her trembling limbs and stands with her lovely face turned aside, too shy to speak.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa portrays Parvati’s love as visible in her bashful bearing rather than in any words.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Parvati is beautiful but her modesty is what governs how her love can be expressed.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.”
christianity.explanation: The apostle ranks a gentle, quiet spirit above outward beauty and adornment.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the beloved’s modest nature is greater than the beauty that fills the eye.

islam.quote_or_event: “Then one of the two women came to him walking with shyness.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an notes the modest bearing of the daughter of Madyan who came to invite Moses to her father’s house.
islam.tie_back: The Kural, too, singles out a young woman’s shyness as her most notable quality.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain; but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.”
judaism.explanation: The poem of the woman of valour ends by placing character above charm and beauty.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker reaches the same verdict: her womanly nature is greater than her looks.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Queen Mallika asks the Buddha why some women are beautiful and others plain, and he explains that outward appearance follows from inner qualities such as freedom from anger.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta ties a woman’s beauty to her character rather than treating it as independent of it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also looks past beauty to the womanly nature beneath it, though without any teaching on karma.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Now this daughter of an excellent king was virtuous and well looking; she possessed all lucky marks of the body, and shone forth like the lightning Saudâmanî.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana introduces Rajimati, betrothed to Arishtanemi, by naming her virtue before her beauty.
jainism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the bride is beautiful, but her virtue comes first.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They are also known as 'satee', who abide in modesty and contentment.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das redefines the 'satee' (the virtuous wife): she is honoured for her modesty and contentment, not, as in the custom he rejected, for dying on her husband's pyre.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises a woman whose modesty is greater even than her beauty; Guru Amar Das likewise says a woman's true honour lies in her modesty.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 787, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar (salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus, meeting Nausicaa on the shore, compares her to a young palm shoot he once saw springing up beside Apollo’s altar on Delos, and speaks to her with awe.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer pictures a modest young woman’s grace through a slender growing plant.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s bamboo shoulders and Odysseus’s palm sapling are parallel plant images for a modest girl’s beauty.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.160-169 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Diotima teaches that the lover should come to value beauty of soul above beauty of the body.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s ladder of love moves from bodily beauty toward the higher beauty of character.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker makes the same move, praising her nature as greater than her looks.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 210b-c (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Emily Dickinson's poems are found after her death
real_life_example.event: Emily Dickinson lived a quiet, secluded life in Amherst and published only a handful of poems during her lifetime. After her death in 1886, her family found hand-sewn booklets of her poems among her belongings. A first selection was published in 1890, and she is now regarded as one of the two leading American poets of the nineteenth century.
real_life_example.explanation: Dickinson's reserve was so great that the depth of her inner life became known only after she was gone.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's husband says his wife's modesty is even greater than her beauty, so great that her feelings must be read through signs; Dickinson's retiring nature kept her greatest gift hidden in the same way.

tamil:
மணியில் திகழ்தரு நூல்போல் மடந்தை
அணியில் திகழ்வதொன்று உண்டு.
transliteration:
Maniyil thikazhdharu noolpol madandhai
aniyil thikazhvadhondru undu.
meaning: Just as the thread shows through the clear beads strung on it, something shines through this young woman's beauty.
elementary: If you thread clear glass beads on a string, you can see the string running through them. The poet says his beloved’s beauty is like those beads: you can see a hidden feeling running through it, if you look closely.
university: The image is of a string of maṇi (gems or crystal beads) through which the nūl (thread) can be seen; the maṭantai (young woman) has something that likewise tikaḻvatu, shines through her aṇi (beauty or adornment). Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss that ‘something’ as a kuṟippu, a hidden intent visible within her beauty; Solomon Pappaiah takes the gems as clear crystal (paḷiṅku) through which the thread is seen, and Kalaignar as a sign that enchants the speaker. In the traditional arrangement the husband speaks to the confidante, saying the wife’s hidden feeling is legible through her looks. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the thread-and-gem simile is also famous from Bhagavad Gita 7.7, though there it describes the divine as the string on which the world is threaded.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O conqueror of wealth, there is no truth superior to Me. Everything rests upon Me, as pearls are strung on a thread.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says he is the hidden thread holding all things together, as a string holds a necklace of pearls.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same thread-through-gems image for a hidden meaning running through visible beauty.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 7.7 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that what is inside a person shows itself on the outside.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural sees the same movement from inside to outside, an inner feeling showing through her beauty.

islam.quote_or_event: “Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says the inner devotion of the faithful leaves a visible sign on their faces.
islam.tie_back: As the thread shows through the beads, an inner state shows through the face in both texts.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A man’s wisdom maketh his face to shine, and the boldness of his face is changed.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes says inner wisdom becomes visible as a light in the face.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural also sees something inward shining through outward beauty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares the meditator’s insight to a man of good eyesight holding a clear, well-polished beryl gem through which a coloured thread runs, and seeing both the gem and the thread inside it.
buddhism.explanation: The simile describes seeing clearly how consciousness is bound up with the body, as a thread is seen through a gem.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural uses the identical picture of a thread visible within a gem, but for a feeling seen within beauty.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “A young woman, putting on fine ornaments and clothes, will say to a Sramana: ‘I shall give up (my former way of life) and practise the rough (viz. control). Reverend sir, teach me the Law!’”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns monks that a woman’s ornaments and pious words may carry a hidden intention.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also sees an intention running beneath a woman’s adornment, but reads it tenderly where the Jain text reads it with suspicion.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The universe is strung on His Thread.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says that all creation is held together by the Lord, like beads on a string that is hidden but runs through them all.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural sees the thread showing through crystal beads as a picture of the hidden feeling shining through the young woman's beauty; Guru Arjan uses the same thread-and-beads image for the hidden Lord running through all things.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1150, Raag Bhairao, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells how the gods adorned Pandora with a golden band, garlands and every grace, while Hermes placed within her a hidden nature of his own devising.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod the first woman’s adornment conceals something set inside her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural also sees something within a woman’s beauty, though for Valluvar it is a tender feeling, while for Hesiod it is guile.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 60-82 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Alcibiades compares Socrates to the statues of Silenus sold in workshops, which open up to reveal images of the gods inside.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the image to say that something precious lies inside an outward form and can be seen by those who look within.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural also speaks of something within a visible form that shines out to the attentive eye.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 215a-b (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Dorothy Hodgkin reveals the structures hidden inside crystals
real_life_example.event: Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin became a leading practitioner of X-ray crystallography, which uses the way X-rays pass through a crystal to work out the arrangement of the atoms within it. Using this method she determined the structures of penicillin in the 1940s, vitamin B12 in 1956, and later insulin. She received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964.
real_life_example.explanation: Her work showed that the inner pattern of a substance can be read by looking through the crystal that contains it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural compares a hidden feeling showing through a woman's beauty to the thread visible through crystal beads; Hodgkin's science literally read the hidden structure through the crystal.

tamil:
முகைமொக்குள் உள்ளது நாற்றம்போல் பேதை
நகைமொக்குள் உள்ளதொன் றுண்டு.
transliteration:
Mukaimokkul ulladhu naatrampol pedhai
nakaimokkul ulladhon rundu.
meaning: Just as a sweet smell is hidden inside a flower bud that has not opened, something is hidden inside this innocent girl's small, shy smile.
elementary: A flower bud doesn’t smell much yet, but the sweet smell is already inside, waiting. The poet says his beloved’s small smile is like that bud: it holds a feeling she hasn’t said out loud yet.
university: The couplet pairs two ‘buds’: mukai-mokkuḷ, the closed bud of a flower that holds its nāṟṟam (fragrance), and nakai-mokkuḷ, the bud of a smile, the half-formed smile of the pētai (innocent young woman), which holds ‘something’. Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss that something as a kuṟippu, a hidden intent; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar make it explicit as her thoughts of her lover filling the smile. As in 1272-1273, the speaker is traditionally the husband addressing the confidante about signs he can read in the heroine. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; Pope’s rendering on ytamizh (‘budding smile of this dear damsel’s eyes’) adds the eyes, which are not in the Tamil.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Seeing Shakuntala, Dushyanta describes her lower lip as having the colour of a young leaf, her arms as tender shoots, and youth, alluring as a flower, as bound up in her limbs.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa describes a young woman’s beauty as a flower that has not yet fully opened.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same budding-flower image for a girl whose feeling is still folded within her smile.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our land; The fig tree putteth forth her green figs, and the vines with the tender grape give a good smell. Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away.”
christianity.explanation: The Song pictures love as a spring of budding vines already giving off their fragrance.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, fragrance from unopened growth stands for love that is about to blossom.

islam.quote_or_event: A hadith teaches that smiling in the face of one’s brother is an act of charity.
islam.explanation: The Prophet treats a smile as something that carries real meaning and value to the one who receives it.
islam.tie_back: The Kural also treats a smile as carrying a message, though a lover’s rather than a charitable one.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out. Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his precious fruits.”
judaism.explanation: The bride asks the winds to release the fragrance held within her garden for her beloved.
judaism.tie_back: In both poems a fragrance held within waits to be released to the beloved.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of color and also fragrant, even so, fruitful are the fair words of one who practices them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada distinguishes a flower that only looks beautiful from one that also carries fragrance.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also prizes the fragrance inside the flower, the hidden meaning behind the visible smile.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Meekly and politely they approach him with their manifold arts to win his heart; and talking sweetly in confidential conversation they make him do (what they like).”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns monks that sweet manners and pleasant talk may carry a hidden purpose.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also reads a hidden meaning in a gentle outward sign, but with delight rather than the Jain monk’s caution.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Like the fragrance which remains in the flower, and like the reflection in the mirror,”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur goes on to say that, like fragrance in a flower, the Lord dwells deep within, so one should search for Him in one's own heart.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says something lies hidden in the young woman's budding smile as fragrance lies hidden in an unopened bud; Guru Tegh Bahadur uses the same image of hidden fragrance for the Lord hidden in the heart.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 684, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that Aphrodite’s portion among gods and men includes the whispers of maidens and their smiles, along with sweet delight, love and gentleness.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod a maiden’s smile belongs to Aphrodite’s domain and carries love’s meaning.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise finds love folded inside a girl’s smile.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Theogony 203-206 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle distinguishes what exists only potentially from what exists actually, as the oak is present in the acorn before it grows.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, things can contain what they will become before it is visible.
philosophy.tie_back: The bud that already holds its scent, and the smile that already holds a feeling, are poetic cases of the potential within the actual.

real_life_example.event_title: Paul Laurence Dunbar writes We Wear the Mask
real_life_example.event: The African American poet Paul Laurence Dunbar, whose early collections Majors and Minors (1895) and Lyrics of Lowly Life (1896) won the praise of the critic William Dean Howells, wrote the poem We Wear the Mask. The poem describes people who smile and sing in public while hiding pain and grief behind that cheerful face. It asks the world not to look too closely, while the speaker cries out privately to God.
real_life_example.explanation: The poem became one of the best-known statements in American literature of feeling hidden behind a smile.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says something lies hidden inside a young woman's budding smile, as fragrance lies inside a closed bud; Dunbar's poem is about what lies concealed behind a smile.

tamil:
செறிதொடி செய்திறந்த கள்ளம் உறுதுயர்
தீர்க்கும் மருந்தொன்று உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Seridhodi seydhirandha kallam urudhuyar
theerkkum marundhondru udaiththu.
meaning: As she left, my love with the tight bangles gave me a secret sign. That sign holds a medicine that cures my deep sorrow.
elementary: Sometimes a friend gives you a small wink or a smile that only you understand, and it makes you feel better right away. The poet says the secret look his beloved gave him was like medicine for his sadness.
university: The heroine is named by her ceṟi toṭi (closely set bangles), and what she did and left behind (ceytu iṟanta) is a kaḷḷam, a stealthy or covert sign. That sign holds one maruntu (medicine) that cures uṟu tuyar, great sorrow. Varadarasanar and Kesikan read kaḷḷam as a covert sign; Solomon Pappaiah stresses that it was shown so that only he would understand it; Kalaignar makes it her mischievous glance. The traditional reading has the husband, anxious about her reaction to his journey, comforted by a hidden sign of her consent or reassurance. Both sites give the same text; ytamizh’s English explanation (‘The well-meant departure of her whose bangles are tight-fitting...’) is a loose rendering of ceytu iṟanta, while Pope’s couplet calls the sign ‘secret wiles’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the tenth canto, Krishna pleads with the offended Radha and begs her to place her tender foot on his head, calling that gesture the antidote that destroys the poison of love.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva makes a single gesture from the beloved the cure for the lover’s suffering.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural, too, finds the cure for great sorrow in one small sign from the beloved.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride calls herself lovesick and asks for remedies to restore her.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat love’s sorrow as an illness needing a cure; in the Kural the cure is the beloved’s secret sign.

islam.quote_or_event: “Take this, my shirt, and cast it over the face of my father; he will become seeing.”
islam.explanation: Joseph sends his shirt as a token whose touch will heal his father’s grief-blinded eyes.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, a token from the one longed for becomes the medicine for long sorrow.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick; but desire fulfilled is a tree of life.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says waiting sickens the heart, while a hope fulfilled restores life.
judaism.tie_back: The beloved’s sign in the Kural works the same way, turning sickening worry into healing reassurance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Nanda pines for the beautiful Janapada Kalyani he left behind, the Buddha cures his longing by showing him the nymphs of the heavens, so that Nanda turns to the holy life.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats lovesickness as a malady and applies a skilful remedy to cure it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also speaks of a cure for love’s distress, but for Valluvar the cure is the beloved’s sign, while the Buddha’s cure leads away from her.
buddhism.source: Udana 3.2, Nanda Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Afterwards he will feel remorse like one who has drunk milk mixed with poison; considering the consequences, a worthy monk should have no intercourse with women.”
jainism.explanation: For the Jain monk, what seems sweet in a woman’s company is a poison disguised as milk.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls the beloved’s secret sign a medicine; the Jain text inverts the image, warning that such sweetness is poison for one seeking liberation.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Holy Saint has given me the Medicine of the Naam.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan says the Saint gave him the Name of the Lord as a medicine that cures the soul's suffering.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says the secret sign the beloved gave as she left holds a medicine for deep sorrow; Guru Arjan likewise speaks of a gift from another that heals sorrow.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 101, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Helen puts into the wine a drug from Egypt that banishes grief and anger, so that whoever drinks it sheds no tear that day even for the dearest loss.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer imagines a medicine that dissolves sorrow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s secret sign does what Helen’s drug does: it cures sorrow at once.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 4.219-226 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates describes the lover who finds in the beautiful beloved the only physician for his greatest pains.
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedrus the beloved’s presence alone eases the anguish love produces.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the beloved’s sign the medicine for the lover’s sorrow, just as Plato makes the beloved the physician.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 252a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: American prisoners of war adopt the tap code
real_life_example.place: Hoa Lo Prison, Hanoi, North Vietnam
real_life_example.event: In June 1965 four American prisoners sharing a cell in Hoa Lo Prison, including Air Force Captain Carlyle Harris, who had learned the method from an instructor, began using a tap code in which letters were set in a five-by-five grid and sent as two groups of taps. When the guards separated them, they taught the code to others, and by August 1965 most of the prisoners knew it. The code spread through the camps and helped the prisoners keep up morale and their chain of command.
real_life_example.explanation: A secret sign that only the prisoners understood became their main source of comfort and companionship in isolation.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's husband finds that the covert sign his beloved left him holds a medicine for his deep sorrow; for isolated prisoners, the secret taps on the wall were just such a medicine.

tamil:
பெரிதாற்றிப் பெட்பக் கலத்தல் அரிதாற்றி
அன்பின்மை சூழ்வ துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Peridhaatrip petpak kalaththal aridhaatri
anpinmai soozhva thudaiththu.
meaning: He hugs me with great love and joy. But this hints that he is about to do the hard thing again and leave me, without caring how I feel.
elementary: Imagine a parent who gives you an extra-long hug at the door, and you suddenly realise they are about to go on a trip. The heroine notices her husband’s extra-loving embrace and guesses that he is getting ready to leave her again.
university: The wife, speaking to her confidante, reads her husband’s unusually tender union (peritu āṟṟi, ‘showing great love’; peṭpak kalattal, ‘uniting so as to delight’) as a kuṟippu of something else: aritu āṟṟi, doing the hard thing, separation, and anpiṉmai cūḻvatu, contemplating lovelessness. Varadarasanar and Kesikan take it this way, as does Kalaignar, who says the embrace seems to signal another parting. Solomon Pappaiah reads the first half differently, as her having endured the past separation, so that his present embrace makes her think of his lack of love. Pope’s couplet on ytamizh (‘While lovingly embracing me, his heart is only grieved’) follows the separation reading. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Rasa dance, when the gopis grow proud of Krishna’s attention after he has delighted them, he suddenly vanishes from among them, leaving them searching the forest for him.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata shows an intense union with the beloved followed at once by his disappearance.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife fears exactly this pattern: closeness that signals an imminent departure.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.29-30 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;”
christianity.explanation: Ecclesiastes says that embracing and parting each have their season.
christianity.tie_back: The wife in the Kural senses that a time of embracing is about to give way to a time apart.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if a woman fears from her husband contempt or evasion, there is no sin upon them if they make terms of settlement between them - and settlement is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an addresses a wife who senses her husband drawing away and urges reconciliation.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise detects signs of his withdrawal, though in her case through his very tenderness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “How canst thou say: I love thee, when thy heart is not with me?”
judaism.explanation: Delilah confronts Samson because his words of love do not match what she senses in his heart.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife also senses a gap between loving gestures and an intention to leave.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that attachment to the dear brings with it the fear of losing them.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s fear in the Kural, that even his embrace foretells parting, is the fear the Dhammapada says endearment produces.

jainism.quote_or_event: On his wedding procession Arishtanemi turns back, renounces the world and leaves his bride Rajimati, who exclaims: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him!’
jainism.explanation: The Jain story centres on a bridegroom who leaves his bride at the very moment of union.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati suffers the departure that the Kural’s wife fears behind her husband’s embrace, though Arishtanemi leaves for renunciation, not for another journey.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.14-29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; Rajimati’s words at 22.29)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Beholding His wondrous beauty, the milk-maid was entranced, and said, "Please don't leave me; please don't come and go!"”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir pictures a milk-maid so captivated by the Lord's beauty that, even while with Him, she begs Him not to leave.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the wife reads her husband's unusually loving embrace as a hint that he means to leave again; Kabir's milk-maid, too, feels the fear of parting in the very moment of closeness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 338, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Ariadne helps Theseus escape the Labyrinth and sails with him, he abandons her asleep on the island of Naxos.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth tells of a lover who leaves just after a time of closeness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife fears that her husband’s tender embrace is a prelude to such a leaving.
greek_mythology.source: Ariadne on Naxos, as told in Ovid, Heroides 10 and Catullus 64 (paraphrase)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pausanias says the common lover, who loves the body rather than the soul, is not constant, and when the bloom fades he takes wing and flies away.
philosophy.explanation: Plato contrasts unstable love, which ends in departure, with lasting love of character.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife in the Kural fears that intensity of embrace may signal a love that is about to fly away.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 183e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Lincoln's Farewell Address at Springfield
real_life_example.event: On 11 February 1861, the day before his 52nd birthday, President-elect Abraham Lincoln spoke to friends and neighbours gathered at the Great Western Railroad depot in Springfield before boarding a train for Washington. He spoke of his sadness at leaving the town where he had lived for 25 years, said he did not know when or whether he would return, and compared the task ahead to the one George Washington had faced. He asked the crowd to pray for him.
real_life_example.explanation: The unusual tenderness of Lincoln's brief speech reflected the long and uncertain separation that lay ahead.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife reads her husband's unusually tender embrace as a sign that a hard parting is coming; the warmth of Lincoln's farewell carried the same sign of a long separation.

tamil:
தண்ணந் துறைவன் தணந்தமை நம்மினும்
முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை.
transliteration:
Thannan thuraivan thanandhamai namminum
munnam unarndha valai.
meaning: My bangles knew before I did that my husband, the lord of the cool seashore, had left me.
elementary: Sometimes your body knows you are sad before your mind does, like when you lose your appetite. The heroine says her arms grew so thin from missing her husband that her bangles slipped off, even before she understood he had left her in his heart.
university: The husband is called taṇṇam tuṟaivaṉ, ‘lord of the cool shore’, the conventional epithet of the hero of the neytal (seashore) landscape, whose mood in classical Tamil poetics is anxious waiting. His taṇantamai (having parted) was sensed by her vaḷai (bangles) even before (muṉṉam) by herself. The image rests on a classical convention: grief at separation makes the wife’s arms grow thin, so her bangles slip. Varadarasanar and Kesikan read it as the bangles loosening at his departure; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar sharpen it, saying he had parted in mind while still with her in body, and her bangles knew it first. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa’s exiled Yaksha, pining for his wife, has grown so thin that his golden bracelet has slipped from his wasted forearm.
hinduism.explanation: The slipping bracelet is a classical Indian sign of a body wasted by separation from the beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same sign, bangles loosened by grief, to show separation felt in the body.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh”
christianity.explanation: The bride’s heart registers her beloved’s presence even while she sleeps.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly has something other than the conscious mind, her bangles, register the beloved’s absence first.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when the caravan departed [from Egypt], their father said, ‘Indeed, I find the smell of Joseph [and would say that he was alive] if you did not think me weakened in mind.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob senses Joseph before any news of him arrives.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s bangles, Jacob perceives the truth about his beloved before anyone tells him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke.”
judaism.explanation: The bride discovers too late that her beloved has already withdrawn.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, realises only after the fact that her beloved had already turned away.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When a deva is about to pass away from the company of devas, five omens appear: his garlands wither, his clothes get soiled, sweat comes out of his armpits, a dullness descends on his body, he no longer delights in his own deva-seat.”
buddhism.explanation: The Itivuttaka lists bodily omens that announce a coming departure before it happens.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s slipping bangles are such an omen: the body’s adornments signal a parting before the mind admits it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Then the famous man presented the charioteer with his pair of earrings, his neck-chain, and all his ornaments.”
jainism.explanation: Arishtanemi’s giving away his ornaments is the first outward sign that he is about to leave his bride for the ascetic life.
jainism.tie_back: In the Kural the slipping bangles mark a separation; in the Jain story the removed ornaments mark a groom’s departure from his bride.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The soul-bride has grown weak, in the pain of separation from her Husband Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the soul-bride's body wasting with the pain of being apart from the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the wife's bangles slip from her thinned wrists, showing the parting before she admits it; Guru Nanak likewise shows separation written on the body of the soul-bride.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 242, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Dido senses Aeneas’s secret preparations to sail before he tells her, for, as Virgil asks, who can deceive a lover?
greek_mythology.explanation: Virgil shows a lover perceiving her beloved’s intent to leave before any word is spoken.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, like Dido, knows of the parting before being told, through her bangles.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal holds that the heart perceives some truths before and apart from reasoning.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural gives the same priority to a non-rational knowing, voiced through her bangles before her mind.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, no. 277 (Brunschvicg numbering; paraphrase; cf. tr. W.F. Trotter)

real_life_example.event_title: Doctors in Japan describe broken heart syndrome
real_life_example.event: In 1990 doctors in Japan first identified takotsubo cardiomyopathy, now also called broken heart syndrome. It is a temporary weakening of the heart's main pumping chamber, usually triggered by intense emotional or physical stress such as the death of a loved one, and its symptoms can resemble a heart attack. Most patients recover fully within weeks to a few months.
real_life_example.explanation: The discovery showed that grief and loss can register in the body itself, sometimes before a person has fully taken them in.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife says her bangles, slipping from her thinning arms, knew of her husband's parting before she did; broken heart syndrome is medical evidence that the body can react to loss on its own.

tamil:
நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார்எம் காதலர் யாமும்
எழுநாளேம் மேனி பசந்து.
transliteration:
Nerunatruch chendraarem kaadhalar yaamum
ezhunaalem meni pasandhu.
meaning: My love left only yesterday, yet my body has turned pale as if seven days had passed.
elementary: When someone you love goes away, even one day can feel like a whole week. The heroine says her husband left just yesterday, but she already looks as tired and pale as if he had been gone seven days.
university: The wife tells her confidante that her kātalar (beloved) left only neṟunaṟṟu (yesterday), yet she is like one parted for eḻu nāḷ (seven days), her mēṉi (body, complexion) pacantu, turned pale with pacalai, the sallow pallor that classical Tamil love poetry treats as the visible sign of separation. All four commentators on both sites agree on the sense; Kalaignar loosens ‘seven days’ to ‘many days’. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. The pallor here is itself one of the chapter’s ‘signs’, read on the body rather than in speech.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gopi Gita the cowherd women tell Krishna that when they cannot see him even a fraction of a second becomes like an age.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis describe how separation from the beloved stretches time beyond measure.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife feels one day as seven for the same reason.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.31.15 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.”
christianity.explanation: Love made seven years of waiting feel like a few days to Jacob.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural shows the reverse distortion of time by love: one day apart feels like seven.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s grief at separation from Joseph shows itself physically in his eyes.
islam.tie_back: In the Kural, too, separation from a loved one is written on the body, as pallor.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My heart is smitten like grass, and withered; for I forget to eat my bread.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes affliction so deep that the body withers and forgets food.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife shows the same bodily withering, as pallor brought on by separation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary. Long is worldly existence to fools who know not the Sublime Truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada observes that suffering stretches time and distance.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife experiences exactly that stretching: one day of separation is long as seven.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Gina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati’s grief at Arishtanemi’s departure shows at once in her lost cheer.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural’s wife turns pale a day after her husband leaves, Rajimati’s brightness leaves her the moment she hears of his going.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The soul-bride is wasting away, in the pain of separation from her Husband; how can she see Him with her eyes?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak pictures the soul-bride worn down by separation and longing to see her Husband Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife has grown pale in a single day as if a week had passed since he left; Guru Nanak's soul-bride is likewise visibly wasting from the pain of separation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 242, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho describes the symptoms that overcome her at the sight of the beloved: her tongue breaks, fire runs under her skin, her eyes see nothing, and she becomes paler than grass.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho treats love’s turmoil as a set of visible bodily symptoms, including pallor.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s pasalai is the same pallor, read by all as a sign of love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Augustine concludes that time is measured in the mind, as the stretching of the soul through memory, attention and expectation.
philosophy.explanation: For Augustine, how long time is depends on the mind that experiences it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife lives this out: her mind stretches one day of absence into seven.

real_life_example.event_title: Sappho describes the bodily signs of love
real_life_example.event: The Greek poet Sappho, who lived on the island of Lesbos around 600 BCE, wrote a poem, known today as fragment 31, that lists the physical symptoms of love-longing she feels while watching her beloved talk with a man. The list of symptoms is long and is set out one after another. The ancient critic Longinus quoted the poem in his treatise On the Sublime, which is how it survives.
real_life_example.explanation: The poem is one of the oldest surviving descriptions of love showing itself in the body, and it has been imitated by poets ever since.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife says that one day after her beloved left, her body had already turned pale as if seven days had passed; Sappho's poem likewise records how love-longing changes the body at once.

tamil:
தொடிநோக்கி மென்தோளும் நோக்கி அடிநோக்கி
அஃதாண் டவள்செய் தது.
transliteration:
Thodinokki mendholum nokki adinokki
ahdhaandaval seydhadhu.
meaning: She looked at her bangles, looked at her soft shoulders, and looked at her feet. That is what she did there.
elementary: Without saying a word, the girl looks at her bangles, then her arms, then her feet. Her friend explains what she means: ‘If you leave, I will grow thin and my bangles will slip off, so I’d rather walk with you.’ Her looks said it all.
university: This couplet is a pure kuṟippu: three looks, at her toṭi (bangles), her meṉ tōḷ (soft shoulders) and her aṭi (feet), with the comment ‘that is what she did there’ (aḵtu āṇṭu avaḷ ceytatu). It is traditionally spoken by the confidante to the hero, explaining the heroine’s silent gestures. Varadarasanar and Kesikan identify the sign as uṭaṉpōkku, her resolve to go with him on his journey; Solomon Pappaiah spells out the logic: the bangles will slip and the shoulders waste if he leaves her, and her looking at her feet means she will walk with him. Kalaignar reads it the same way. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, which print the āytam form அஃதாண் டவள்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama is exiled to the forest, Sita refuses to be left behind and insists that a wife’s place is beside her husband, saying she will walk ahead of him through the wilderness.
hinduism.explanation: Sita chooses to share Rama’s hard journey rather than be separated from him.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine’s look at her feet in the Kural signals the same resolve: she will go with him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:”
christianity.explanation: Ruth refuses to be parted from Naomi and vows to go wherever she goes.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine’s silent glance at her feet carries Ruth’s spoken vow: where you go, I go.

islam.quote_or_event: When Abraham leaves Hagar and her infant in the barren valley of Mecca, she follows him asking to whom he is leaving them, until he indicates that God commanded it, and she accepts.
islam.explanation: Hagar follows her departing husband and seeks his meaning when he gives no words.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Hagar confronts a husband’s departure; but where she stays by God’s command, the heroine signals she will go.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I remember for thee the affection of thy youth, the love of thine espousals; how thou wentest after Me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown.”
judaism.explanation: God recalls Israel’s early love as a bride who followed her beloved into the wilderness.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s look at her feet promises the same bridal devotion: to follow her husband even into a hard land.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Prince Vessantara is banished to the mountains, his wife Maddi refuses to stay behind in comfort and goes with him into the forest with their children.
buddhism.explanation: Maddi chooses hardship beside her husband over safety apart from him.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine of the Kural signals the same choice with a glance at her feet.
buddhism.source: Vessantara Jataka (Jataka 547) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell and W.H.D. Rouse)

jainism.quote_or_event: After Arishtanemi renounces the world, Rajimati cuts off her hair, takes vows herself, and sets out for Mount Raivataka, where he had gone.
jainism.explanation: Rajimati follows her betrothed, but along the path of renunciation rather than of married life.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine resolves to go where her husband goes; Rajimati does too, though her journey is toward liberation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.29-33 (paraphrase of tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “I tell them the state of my soul, and pray that I may be united with the Sovereign Lord King, my Friend.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the seeker who tells the holy ones the state of her soul and asks them to help her meet the Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the confidante explains the heroine's silent gestures to the husband; Guru Arjan likewise has the inner state made known through a go-between so that union may come.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 958, Raag Raamkalee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Medea leaves her father’s house at night and flees with Jason aboard the Argo rather than be parted from him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius tells of a young woman who chooses to leave home and go with her beloved.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Udanpokku, the heroine’s resolve to go with her lover, is exactly what Medea does.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Augustine recalls that as an infant he learned what adults meant from their gestures, the movements of the face and eyes and limbs that he calls the natural language of all peoples.
philosophy.explanation: Augustine treats gesture and glance as a language understood before and beneath words.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s three glances are such a natural language, and the confidante reads them perfectly.
philosophy.source: Augustine, Confessions I.8 (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Pusey)

real_life_example.event_title: Florence Baker travels with Samuel Baker to find the Nile's sources
real_life_example.place: Upper Nile region of East Africa (now South Sudan and Uganda)
real_life_example.event: In 1861 the English explorer Samuel Baker went to Africa with Florence von Sass, who later became his second wife, and they spent about a year exploring Nile tributaries near the border of Sudan and Ethiopia. Florence went on with him into the interior in search of the sources of the Nile, as his confidante and fellow explorer. Their discoveries included Lake Albert and Murchison Falls, which earned Samuel the Royal Geographical Society's gold medal and a knighthood.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than wait at home, Florence chose to share every step of a dangerous journey.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's heroine silently looks at her bangles, her shoulders and her feet to show she will go with her husband rather than be left behind; Florence Baker did exactly that.

tamil:
பெண்ணினால் பெண்மை உடைத்தென்ப கண்ணினால்
காமநோய் சொல்லி இரவு.
transliteration:
Penninaal penmai udaiththenpa kanninaal
kaamanoi solli iravu.
meaning: People say that to show the pain of love with your eyes, and so to plead with the one you love, is the most womanly thing a woman can do.
elementary: Sometimes the bravest thing a shy person can do is to show with their eyes how much they need someone, without saying it out loud. The poet says that this gentle, silent asking is the finest kind of grace.
university: The couplet generalises the chapter: kaṇṇiṉāl kāma nōy colli iravu, ‘telling the sickness of love with the eyes and entreating’, is said (eṉpa, ‘they say’) to be peṇmai, womanliness, added to womanliness (peṇṇiṉāl peṇmai uṭaittu). Varadarasanar and Kesikan specify the entreaty as asking the husband not to leave; Kalaignar makes it a plea to be taken along, linking it to 1279’s udanpokku; Solomon Pappaiah frames it as asking that the love-sickness be cured. Pope renders the sense as ‘womanhood’s most womanly device’. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; its framing assumes the classical ideal that a woman should not declare love in words, which modern readers may note as a convention of its time.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the fourth canto, Radha’s friend goes to Krishna and describes how Radha, wasting with longing, can only show her love-sickness in her sighs and looks, pleading for him to come.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s Radha conveys her love-sickness through signs that her friend interprets to Krishna.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural praises exactly this: love-sickness told without words, as a silent plea.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride wants her beloved to know of her love-sickness and sends word through others.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same plea, telling her love-sickness, but with her eyes alone.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those in need who, out of dignity, do not ask aloud but whose need can be read in their bearing.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise honours an entreaty made through signs rather than open asking.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it was so, when the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, that she obtained favour in his sight; and the king held out to Esther the golden sceptre that was in his hand.”
judaism.explanation: Esther’s first plea to the king is made simply by standing before him, and he grants her favour before she speaks.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, honours a plea made by presence and look rather than by words.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As a bee gathers honey from the flower without injuring its color or fragrance, even so the sage goes on his alms-round in the village.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist monk asks for alms only by his quiet presence, taking without burdening the giver.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly honours an asking done gently and wordlessly.

jainism.quote_or_event: “It will always cause difficulties to a houseless monk to get everything by begging, and nothing without begging.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana counts the need to ask (yacana) among the troubles a monk must bear with dignity.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also concerns the dignity of asking, honouring a woman who pleads through her eyes rather than in words.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Listen, O my Friend, to my message of love; my eyes are fixed upon You.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das pleads with the Beloved, with his eyes fixed on Him, to hear his message of love.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural praises the woman who tells her love-sickness with her eyes and so pleads with her beloved; Guru Ram Das likewise pleads with eyes fixed on the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 302, Raag Gauree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Nausicaa asks her father for a wagon to wash clothes, too shy to mention her hopes of marriage, but he understands everything she leaves unsaid.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows a young woman’s unspoken wish read perfectly by someone who loves her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural praises the same modest, unspoken asking that is nonetheless understood.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.66-67 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Montaigne lists the many things we do with our hands, head, eyes and brows, asking, promising, entreating, refusing, and says they form a language anyone can understand.
philosophy.explanation: Montaigne argues that gestures and looks make up a full, universal language.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s entreaty made with the eyes is a case of this silent language at its most delicate.
philosophy.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays II.12, ‘Apology for Raymond Sebond’ (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Dorothea Lange photographs Migrant Mother
real_life_example.event: In March 1936, while photographing migrant farm workers for the federal Resettlement Administration, Dorothea Lange came upon Florence Owens Thompson and her children in a camp of pea pickers whose crop had failed. She made five exposures, moving closer each time. The photograph known as Migrant Mother was widely circulated in magazines and newspapers and became a symbol of the hardship of the Great Depression, though Thompson later disputed parts of Lange's account of their meeting.
real_life_example.explanation: Without a word of appeal, the mother's face and gaze moved the public to feel the plight of migrant families.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural praises pleading with the eyes rather than with words; the silent, worried look in Migrant Mother made a plea that words could not.

tamil:
உள்ளக் களித்தலும் காண மகிழ்தலும்
கள்ளுக்கில் காமத்திற் குண்டு.
transliteration:
Ullak kaliththalum kaana makizhdhalum
kallukkil kaamaththir kundu.
meaning: To feel joy just by thinking of someone, and to be happy just by seeing them: strong drink cannot do this, but love can.
elementary: A treat only makes you happy once you eat it. But when you miss someone you love, just thinking of them makes you smile, and seeing them makes you jump for joy. The poet says love is stronger than any treat, because it works even before it arrives.
university: The chapter title puṇarcci vitumpal combines puṇarcci (union, coming together) and vitumpal (eager longing, impatient haste); it belongs to the kaṟpu (wedded love) section and follows kuṟippaṟivuṟuttal, describing the eagerness of husband and wife to be reunited, an eagerness strong enough to override the playful sulking (ūṭal) that convention expects. The couplet contrasts kaḷ (toddy, palm wine) with kāmam (love): uḷḷak kaḷittal is intoxication from mere thought (uḷḷal, to think) and kāṇa makiḻtal is joy from mere sight, and neither belongs to wine, which must actually be drunk. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss it as two states (nilai) that wine lacks but love possesses; Solomon Pappaiah adds that thought excites without overwhelming the senses while sight overwhelms them; Kalaignar sums it up as ‘wine gives pleasure only when drunk, love gives it at a thought or a glance.’ The comparison with wine recurs in kural 1288 of this chapter and echoes the earlier chapter on abstaining from toddy (kaḷḷuṇṇāmai, ch. 93). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the gopis of Vraja hear Krishna’s flute on the autumn night, they drop whatever they are doing, milking, cooking, serving their families, and hurry toward the sound, already overwhelmed before they have even reached him.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata presents the gopis as so absorbed in Krishna that the mere sound and thought of him carries them away.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s lover, the gopis are intoxicated by love at a hint of the beloved, before any meeting.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.29.4-8 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices!”
christianity.explanation: The bridegroom of the Song declares the delight of his beloved’s love to surpass wine itself.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same comparison: love outdoes wine in the joy it gives.

islam.quote_or_event: “Hail to thee, then, O LOVE, sweet madness! Thou who healest all our infirmities!”
islam.explanation: In the prologue to his Masnavi, the Sufi poet Rumi praises love as a sweet madness that cures every ill.
islam.tie_back: The Kural calls love an intoxication greater than wine; Rumi likewise names love a ‘sweet madness’, a delight beyond reason.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, Prologue (tr. E.H. Whinfield)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth— For thy love is better than wine.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs opens with the beloved’s longing and her declaration that love surpasses wine.
judaism.tie_back: This is the closest scriptural twin to the Kural’s claim that love gives a joy wine cannot.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From lust springs grief, from lust springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that passionate desire, however sweet, is the root of grief and fear.
buddhism.tie_back: Where the Kural celebrates love as a delight greater than wine, the Buddhist view treats such intoxication as a source of suffering, so the parallel is one of contrast.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana warns that sensual pleasures are like a fruit that is delicious at first and poisonous afterwards.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural ranks love above wine as a delight; Jain teaching treats both alike as sweet poisons, so the parallel is a sharp contrast.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “All the rest of the world is deluded by doubt, while my mind is intoxicated with the Sublime Essence of the Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir says his mind is drunk not on any worldly drink but on the sweet essence of the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says love, not wine, can delight a person merely by thinking of or seeing the beloved; Kabir likewise speaks of an intoxication that comes from love of the Lord rather than from drink.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 92, Sri Raag, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes Eros as the fairest of the deathless gods, who loosens the limbs and overcomes the mind and wise counsel of all gods and men.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Theogony, Eros is a primal power whose effect on the mind is overwhelming, like a drug.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise presents love as a force that intoxicates the mind more surely than wine.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Theogony 120-122 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that the greatest blessings come through a divine madness, and that the madness of love is the best of these, sent by the gods for the lover’s happiness.
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedrus, Plato reverses the usual view that love’s intoxication is merely harmful and calls it a god-given madness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s praise of love as an elation that comes at a thought or a glance is close to Plato’s idea of love as a blessed madness.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 244a-245c (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Crown Prince Akihito meets Shōda Michiko on a Karuizawa tennis court
real_life_example.event: In August 1957 Japan’s Crown Prince Akihito met Shōda Michiko, the daughter of a flour-milling company president, on a tennis court in the mountain resort of Karuizawa. The two kept meeting over games of tennis, and in April 1959 they married, breaking a long tradition: she was the first commoner to marry a Japanese crown prince. The romance set off a wave of public enthusiasm in Japan, including a national craze for tennis.
real_life_example.explanation: A courtship that began simply with seeing each other across a tennis net became one of the most celebrated royal marriages of the twentieth century.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says love, unlike wine, brings joy just by seeing and thinking of the beloved, and this romance grew out of nothing more than repeated meetings on a tennis court.

tamil:
தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை வேண்டும் பனைத்துணையும்
காமம் நிறைய வரின்.
transliteration:
Thinaiththunaiyum oodaamai vaendum panaiththunaiyum
kaamam niraiya varin.
meaning: When love comes in full, as tall as a palm tree, you should not sulk even as much as a tiny grain of millet.
elementary: If you have a mountain of love for someone, it makes no sense to stay grumpy with them over a crumb-sized thing. The poet compares the love to a tall palm tree and the grumpiness to a tiny seed.
university: The couplet sets two proverbial Tamil measures against each other: tiṉai (Italian millet, the smallest grain) and paṉai (the palmyra palm, the tallest tree), each with tuṇai (‘measure, extent’). When kāmam comes niṟaiya (‘in fullness’) to the measure of a palmyra, one should not engage in ūṭal (lovers’ feigned sulking) even to the measure of a millet seed. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as general advice, while Solomon Pappaiah applies it specifically to the wife and her husband; in the traditional reading the heroine says this when her companion suggests she show displeasure at her husband’s long absence. Ūṭal is otherwise a valued convention of akam poetry (the final chapters 130-133 are devoted to it), so the couplet’s point is that eagerness for reunion overrides it here. Pope’s translation (‘Distrust can find no place small as the millet grain’) renders ūṭal loosely as distrust. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna, coming to Radha after she has withdrawn in wounded pride, pleads with her to give up her anger, telling her that her displeasure torments him and asking her to let love win over pique.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s Radha nurses mana (proud sulking) against Krishna, and Krishna begs her to set it aside.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same: where love is great, even a little sulking has no place.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as patient and slow to take offence.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s advice not to sulk even a little when love is great is a lover’s version of love that ‘is not easily provoked’.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes marriage as a bond of tranquillity, affection and mercy.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ideal of spouses whose love leaves no room for petty sulking fits this picture of affection and mercy between mates.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hatred stirreth up strifes; but love covereth all transgressions.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that love passes over offences while hatred feeds quarrels.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, great love leaves no room for nursing a grievance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that resentment is ended only by letting it go.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural asks the lover to drop even the smallest resentment; the Buddhist verse gives the general principle, though in a far graver register.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra lists anger as the destroyer of love (priti), pride as the destroyer of humility, deceit as the destroyer of friendship, and greed as the destroyer of everything.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching names anger (krodha), one of the four passions (kashayas), as the specific enemy of affection.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns against even a millet-grain of sulking because it cuts against great love; the Jain verse explains why: anger destroys love.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 8.38 (verse numbering varies by edition; paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Don't be angry - drink in the Ambrosial Nectar; you shall not remain in this world forever.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak tells the listener to give up anger and drink in the nectar of the Name, because life is short.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that when love is as tall as a palm tree one should not sulk even a millet-grain's worth; Guru Nanak likewise counsels dropping anger in favour of the sweetness of love while there is time.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 931, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, the poor old couple who welcomed the disguised gods, had lived together in perfect accord since youth, and asked only that neither should outlive the other.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s tale portrays a marriage so united that no discord ever came between the pair.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They are the picture of the Kural’s ideal: love so full that no sulking finds room.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch advises newly married couples to guard against small quarrels and petty grievances, since harmony (homonoia) between husband and wife is the foundation of their shared life.
philosophy.explanation: His Conjugal Precepts repeatedly counsel spouses to let minor offences go quickly.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s advice to sulk not even a millet-grain’s worth is the same counsel, given in a lover’s voice.

real_life_example.event_title: Young Gandhi’s jealous quarrels with Kasturba
real_life_example.date: 1880s (early years of their marriage, which began in 1882)
real_life_example.event: Mohandas Gandhi and Kasturba were married in 1882, when both were about thirteen. In his autobiography, in the chapter Playing the Husband, Gandhi wrote that he soon became a jealous husband without any reason to suspect her, and insisted that she could not go anywhere without his permission. Kasturba did not accept these restrictions, and Gandhi recalled that the two child-spouses often ended up refusing to speak to each other; he later called her innocent in taking liberties with his rules and admitted his strictness had been misguided.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi himself presented these quarrels as the foolishness of a young husband whose petty suspicions were out of all proportion to the bond between them, a bond that lasted the rest of their lives.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when love is as tall as a palmyra palm one should not sulk even as much as a millet seed, and Gandhi looked back on his small-minded jealous sulks as exactly that kind of mistake.

tamil:
பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும் கொண்கனைக்
காணா தமையல கண்.
transliteration:
Paenaadhu petpavae seyyinum konkanaik
kaanaa thamaiyala kan.
meaning: Even if my husband ignores me and does only what he likes, my eyes cannot rest without seeing him.
elementary: Sometimes a friend ignores you, and you feel hurt, but you still keep looking out for them at the window. The wife in this poem feels the same: even when her husband seems careless, her eyes keep searching for him.
university: Pēṇātu means ‘without caring for (me)’, ‘neglecting’, and peṭpavē ceyyiṉum ‘even if he does only what he desires’; koṇkaṉ (‘husband, the one who took me’) is the object of kāṇātu (‘without seeing’), and amaiyala kaṇ ‘the eyes do not rest/settle’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘my eyes do not settle without seeing my lover’, Puliyur Kesikan ‘my eyes find no peace’, and Kalaignar ‘though he does not embrace me and does what pleases him, my eyes are not at peace without seeing him’. The couplet shows the heroine’s will to resent overruled by her eyes’ longing, a motif that links to chapter 118 (kaṇvitumpaḻital, the eyes’ eager suffering). Pope’s prose explanation (‘Though my eyes disregard me and do what is pleasing to my husband’) takes the eyes as the subject of the first clause, a construal not followed by the modern commentators cited here. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the ‘song to the bumblebee’, a gopi rebukes Krishna’s messenger, calling Krishna fickle and ungrateful for leaving them, yet confesses that the women of Vraja cannot stop speaking and thinking of him.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis feel slighted by Krishna’s departure to Mathura but are unable to turn their minds away from him.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the wife in the Kural, they are neglected by the beloved yet cannot rest without him.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.47 (Bhramara Gita) (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song cannot rest at night for longing to find her absent beloved.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the lover’s restlessness ends only when the beloved is seen.

islam.quote_or_event: “And women in the city said, ‘The wife of al-'Azeez is seeking to seduce her slave boy; he has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her [to be] in clear error.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the wife of al-Aziz consumed by love for Joseph even though he refuses her.
islam.tie_back: Her love persists despite being spurned, as the Kural’s wife longs for a husband who slights her, though the Qur’anic context is an unlawful passion it criticises.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And if I say: ‘I will not make mention of Him, nor speak any more in His name’, then there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I weary myself to hold it in, but cannot.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah, mistreated for his calling, resolves to give it up but finds the fire in his heart too strong to contain.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise cannot hold back her longing for one who has slighted her.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada names not seeing the beloved as a specific form of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes that cannot rest without seeing the husband are exactly this pain, though the Buddha’s remedy is detachment rather than reunion.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a man who passionately desires ‘colours,’ be happy while he gets, keeps, uses, loses, and misses (those things). Even when he enjoys them, he is never satisfied.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana describes the eye’s attachment to what it sees as a craving that is never satisfied.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes that cannot rest without seeing the husband show the same restless craving of sight, though the Jain text diagnoses it as bondage.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Even if You cut my body apart, I shall not pull my limbs away from You.”
sikhism.explanation: Kabir declares that whatever the Lord does to him, even cutting his body apart, he will not turn away.
sikhism.tie_back: The wife in the Kural says that even if her husband neglects her and does as he pleases, her eyes cannot rest without seeing him; Kabir likewise vows a love that does not turn away whatever the beloved does.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 484, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo, spurned by Narcissus, still follows him and pines for him, wasting away until only her voice remains.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Echo keeps loving a youth who scorns her and cannot tear herself away from him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife, Echo is slighted by the one she loves yet cannot rest away from him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristophanes, in Plato’s Symposium, tells how lovers are halves of a once-whole being; when they find each other they do not wish to be parted even for a moment, and cannot say what they want except to be together.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s myth explains love as an irresistible longing for one’s missing half.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes that will not rest until they see the husband reflect that longing for the missing half.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 192b-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Sofya Tolstaya at the window of the stationmaster’s house at Astapovo
real_life_example.place: Astapovo railway station, Ryazan province, Russia
real_life_example.event: In late October 1910 the 82-year-old Leo Tolstoy secretly left his estate at Yasnaya Polyana, leaving behind his wife Sofya, to whom he had been married for 48 years. He fell ill with pneumonia on the journey and lay dying in the stationmaster’s house at the small railway station of Astapovo. Sofya rushed there, but in keeping with his wishes his followers kept her out; she paced the platform and tried to look in through the windows, watched by photographers and film crews, and was allowed to his side only at the very end.
real_life_example.explanation: Though her husband had walked out on her without a word of farewell, Sofya could not stay away and could not stop trying to see him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural’s wife says that even if her husband slights her and does as he pleases, her eyes cannot rest without seeing him, which is almost exactly what the world watched Sofya Tolstaya do at Astapovo.

tamil:
ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன்மன் தோழி அதுமறந்து
கூடற்கண் சென்றதுஎன் னெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Ootarkan sendraenman thoazhi adhumarandhu
koodarkan sendradhuen nenju.
meaning: My friend, I went to him meaning to sulk. But my heart forgot all that and went straight to making up with him.
elementary: Imagine planning to stay cross with a friend who came back late from a trip, but the moment you see them you forget and run to hug them. That is what happens to the wife in this poem: her plan to be cross melts away.
university: The heroine addresses her companion (tōḻi): ūṭaṟkaṇ ceṉṟēṉ maṉ, ‘I did go toward sulking’, where the particle maṉ marks a past intention that came to nothing; but atu maṟantu, ‘forgetting it’, eṉ neñcu (‘my heart’) went kūṭaṟkaṇ, ‘toward union’. The neat opposition of ūṭal (lovers’ sulking) and kūṭal (coming together) carries the chapter’s theme: eagerness for reunion overruling the convention of feigned displeasure. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it this way; Solomon Pappaiah specifies that she planned to sulk over his fault before seeing him and forgot it once she saw him; Kalaignar generalises it as the special nature of love. The heart acting apart from the speaker’s will anticipates the next chapter, neñcoṭu pulattal (‘quarrelling with one’s heart’). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After nursing her anger through the night, Radha is persuaded by her friend that Krishna waits for her, and she goes to him, her pride dissolving as she enters the bower.
hinduism.explanation: In Jayadeva’s poem Radha’s resolve to stay offended gives way to her eagerness to meet Krishna.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise sets out to sulk and finds her heart has gone to reunion instead.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes the experience of intending one thing and finding oneself doing another.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine intends to sulk but her heart carries her to embrace; the divided will is the same, though Paul speaks of moral struggle.

islam.quote_or_event: “Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that answering hostility with goodness can turn estrangement into close friendship.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows estrangement turning to closeness in a moment; the Qur’an names the same turn, though as a moral strategy rather than a lover’s impulse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him; and they wept.”
judaism.explanation: Esau, who had set out with four hundred men against his brother, embraces Jacob the moment they meet.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, an intended hostility vanishes at the meeting and the heart runs to embrace.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada compares the mind to an arrow shaft that the wise must straighten, describing it as fickle, unsteady and hard to guard.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching recognises that the mind runs where it will unless it is trained.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart that forgets the plan and runs to reunion is an example of this unruly mind, though the Buddhist aim is to restrain it.
