jainism.quote_or_event: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, Gautama explains that the mind is an unruly, dreadful horse that runs about, and that he keeps it in check by the discipline of the Law.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana pictures the mind as a wild horse that bolts unless reined in.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart bolts toward reunion against the heroine’s plan; the Jain image captures that runaway mind, though it calls for restraint.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 23 (Kesi and Gautama) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The bumble bee becomes enticed by the lotus, intoxicated by its fragrance, and does not leave it, even for a moment.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan pictures the devotee drawn to the Lord as a bee is drawn to the lotus, unable to leave it.
sikhism.tie_back: In the Kural the wife set out to sulk, but her heart forgot and went straight to union; Guru Arjan's bee likewise cannot hold back from the lotus that draws it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 454, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Procris flees in anger and shame over a test of fidelity, Cephalus seeks her out, and the two are reconciled and live for years in harmony.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s couple quarrel and part, but their love draws them back together.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, displeasure gives way to the stronger pull of reunion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, the charioteer of the soul tries to hold back the unruly horse, but at the sight of the beloved that horse drags the whole team forward toward him despite the charioteer’s resolve.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s image shows desire overpowering the reasoned intention of the soul when the beloved appears.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine intends to sulk, but her heart, like Plato’s horse, carries her straight to the beloved.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 253c-254e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Napoleon locks his door on Joséphine, then forgives her
real_life_example.place: Rue de la Victoire, Paris, France
real_life_example.event: After seventeen months away on the Egyptian expedition, Napoleon Bonaparte returned secretly to France in the autumn of 1799, angry at reports about his wife Joséphine’s conduct in his absence. Joséphine had driven south to meet him and missed him on the road, and when she reached their house in Paris he kept his bedroom door locked against her despite hours of pleading and tears, joined by her children Hortense and Eugène. In the end he let her in and they were fully reconciled, to the annoyance of his family.
real_life_example.explanation: Napoleon had come home determined to stay cold, but his resolve gave way almost at once.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural describes a heart that set out to sulk but forgot it and went straight toward reunion; Napoleon’s locked door, opened within a day or two, shows the same collapse of a planned sulk.

tamil:
எழுதுங்கால் கோல்காணாக் கண்ணேபோல் கொண்கன்
பழிகாணேன் கண்ட இடத்து.
transliteration:
Ezhudhungaal koalkaanaak kannaepoal konkan
pazhikaanaen kanda idaththu.
meaning: Just as the eye cannot see the brush that puts dark eye makeup on it, I cannot see my husband's faults at the moment I see him.
elementary: Your eye can see everything around it, but it cannot see the little brush that touches it when someone puts on eyeliner, because it is too close. The wife says her husband’s faults are like that brush: when he is right in front of her, she cannot see them.
university: The simile draws on the practice of applying mai (collyrium, kohl) with a slender rod (kōl): eḻutuṅkāl, ‘while painting/applying’, the eye does not see the kōl, though it saw it a moment earlier. So too, kaṇṭa iṭattu (‘at the place/time of seeing him’), she does not see the paḻi (fault, blame) of her koṇkaṉ (husband). Solomon Pappaiah makes the comparison exact: the eye saw the rod before but not while it paints; she brooded on his fault in his absence but cannot see it in his presence. Kalaignar names the fault as his having left her. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan follow the same line. The domestic, almost tactile image is characteristic of the Kural’s Inbam section, and the couplet pairs closely with the next (1286). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Nala, who had abandoned Damayanti in the forest, is at last recognised and restored to her, she receives him without reproach, and the couple are reunited in joy.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata’s story of Nala and Damayanti ends with a wife whose grievance over desertion gives way entirely to reunion.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife, Damayanti cannot hold her husband’s fault against him once he stands before her.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.”
christianity.explanation: Peter teaches that fervent love covers over many faults.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s wife experiences this directly: in her husband’s presence, love hides his faults from her sight.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘No blame will there be upon you today. Allah will forgive you; and He is the most merciful of the merciful.’”
islam.explanation: Joseph, meeting the brothers who wronged him, declares at once that he holds no blame against them.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the moment of meeting erases the fault that had been borne in absence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that harpeth on a matter estrangeth a familiar friend.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that love chooses to cover an offence, while dwelling on it drives people apart.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife does not ‘harp on the matter’ once she sees her husband; love covers his fault.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada observes that the faults of others are easily seen, while one’s own are hard to see, and that people winnow others’ faults like chaff.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching notes how perception of faults is distorted by one’s position and attachments.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows the reverse distortion: love so close that it cannot see the beloved’s fault, like the eye and the brush.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the crane is produced from an egg, and the egg is produced from a crane, so they call desire the origin of delusion, and delusion the origin of desire.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that desire and delusion feed each other, clouding clear perception.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife cannot see her husband’s faults in his presence; in Jain terms her desire produces exactly this blindness (moha).
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He covers the faults of His servant.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan says the Lord hides and overlooks the faults of His devotee.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife cannot see her husband's faults when she sees him, as the eye cannot see the kohl brush; Guru Arjan's line, in reverse, has the Beloved overlooking the devotee's faults.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 285, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Troy fell, Menelaus went to kill his faithless wife Helen, but at the sight of her he threw down his sword and took her back.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the tradition recorded by Euripides and others, Helen’s presence alone undoes Menelaus’s resolve to punish her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise finds the fault she meant to punish invisible once she sees her husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates remarks that a lover finds every feature of his beloved charming: a snub nose he calls winsome, a hooked nose royal, a dark skin manly, a pale one divine, so that no blemish is ever seen.
philosophy.explanation: Plato observes that love transforms perception so that the beloved’s defects disappear or become virtues.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s insight exactly: in the beloved’s presence the lover cannot see faults.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic V, 474d-475a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Ulysses S. Grant tells Julia to keep the eyes he fell in love with
real_life_example.event: Julia Dent Grant had strabismus (crossed eyes) all her life and was self-conscious about it, especially once her husband became famous during the Civil War. In late 1863 she asked the St. Louis surgeon Charles Pope about an operation to straighten her eyes and was told it was too late. In her memoirs she recorded that when she told her husband, Ulysses S. Grant told her he had fallen in love with her with those same eyes, liked them as they were, and did not want her to change them.
real_life_example.explanation: Grant simply did not see as a flaw what Julia feared made her a plain wife for a great man.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that just as the eye cannot see the kohl brush touching it, the lover cannot see the beloved’s faults when close to them, and Grant could not see his wife’s squint as a fault at all.

tamil:
காணுங்கால் காணேன் தவறாய காணாக்கால்
காணேன் தவறல் லவை.
transliteration:
Kaanungaal kaanaen thavaraaya kaanaakkaal
kaanaen thavaral lavai.
meaning: When I see him, I see none of his faults. When I do not see him, I see nothing but his faults.
elementary: When your best friend is with you, you only remember how fun they are. When they are away and forgot to call, you can only think of what they did wrong. The wife in this poem notices she does exactly this with her husband.
university: The couplet is built on a chiasmus of kāṇ- (‘see’): kāṇuṅkāl kāṇēṉ tavaṟāya (‘when I see [him], I do not see what is wrong’), kāṇākkāl kāṇēṉ tavaṟu allavai (‘when I do not see [him], I do not see what is not wrong’). The wordplay turns on two senses of seeing, physical sight of the husband and mental perception of faults. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the second half as ‘I do not see the good things that are not faults’; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as ‘I see nothing but faults’. The couplet extends the previous one (1285) by adding the opposite case and so explains why the heroine plans to sulk in absence yet forgets it in presence (1284). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh prints the sandhi as தவறல் லவை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna vanishes from the rasa dance, the gopis in their song of longing call him a deceiver who abandons women who came to him, while in his presence they had seen only his beauty and kindness.
hinduism.explanation: The Gopi Gita shows the gopis’ view of Krishna shifting to reproach in his absence.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise sees only faults in her husband’s absence and none in his presence.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.31 (Gopi Gita) (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that our perception of others’ faults is distorted by our own condition.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural observes how the wife’s perception of faults swings with presence and absence; both texts expose the bias in fault-finding.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns believers against suspicion and imagining the worst of others.
islam.tie_back: In absence the Kural’s wife imagines only faults; the Qur’an names this habit of negative assumption and warns against it.

judaism.quote_or_event: Joshua ben Perachiah teaches in Pirkei Avot that one should judge every person favourably, giving them the benefit of the doubt.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah urges a charitable reading of others’ actions.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife judges favourably in her husband’s presence and harshly in his absence; the rabbinic maxim asks for the favourable judgment always.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one’s own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada counsels against dwelling on others’ faults.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows how fault-finding in absence is driven by longing; the Buddhist verse warns against such fault-finding itself.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that attraction and aversion come from the mind’s attachment, not from the object itself.
jainism.tie_back: The husband is the same person whether present or absent; the Jain verse explains that it is the wife’s love and resentment that change how she sees him.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.101 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “They complain about other peoples' faults, while their own self-conceit only increases.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das warns that those who keep finding fault in others only feed their own ego.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife sees nothing but her husband's faults when he is away, and none when he is present; Guru Ram Das likewise shows that fault-finding grows when the heart is cut off from love and ego takes over.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 366, Raag Aasaa, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros, the loosener of limbs, a bittersweet creature against whom there is no defence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho’s coinage glukupikron (‘sweet-bitter’) captures love’s double nature.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s lover feels both sides in turn: sweet in the beloved’s presence, bitter with fault-finding in absence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza describes a ‘vacillation of mind’ in which the same thing is at once the cause of pleasure and of pain, so that we both love and hate it.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza analyses how one object can arouse contrary emotions depending on how we imagine it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife experiences this vacillation as her husband appears or disappears from view.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Proposition 17 and Scholium (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Einstein and Mileva Marić: love letters, then bitterness at a distance
real_life_example.event: Albert Einstein and Mileva Marić met as students at the Federal Polytechnic in Zürich, and 54 surviving letters from 1897 to shortly after their marriage in 1903 show a warm romance carried on while they were often apart. Einstein married her in 1903 despite his parents’ strong objections. The couple separated in 1914, when Mileva lived in Zürich and Einstein in Berlin, divorced in 1919, and their communication afterwards was often bitter.
real_life_example.explanation: The same couple whose early letters overflowed with affection came, once living apart for good, to see mainly each other’s faults.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural speaks of seeing no faults in the beloved when together and nothing but faults when apart, and the Einstein letters trace a love that turned toward grievance once distance became permanent.

tamil:
உய்த்தல் அறிந்து புனல்பாய் பவரேபோல்
பொய்த்தல் அறிந்தென் புலந்து.
transliteration:
Uyththal arindhu punalpaai pavaraepoal
poiththal arindhen pulandhu.
meaning: I am like people who jump into a flood knowing it will sweep them away. What is the use of sulking when I know it will not work?
elementary: If you know the river is too strong and will carry you off, it is silly to jump in. The wife says staying cross with her husband is like that: she knows her anger will be swept away the moment she sees him, so why even try?
university: Uyttal means ‘carrying off, sweeping away’ (of a current), and puṉal pāyvar are ‘those who leap into the flood’; poyttal is ‘failing, proving false’, and pulantu ‘having sulked’. The last word eṉ is taken by Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as the interrogative ‘what (use)?’, giving ‘what is gained by sulking, knowing it will fail?’, with Pappaiah specifying that her anger cannot succeed. The Sivayogi Sivakumar gloss on ytamizh instead reads eṉ as ‘I’ (‘knowing it will come to nothing, I sulk’), and Pope’s couplet likewise renders it as a confession (‘So did I anger feign’), so the line can be read as a rhetorical question or as a rueful admission. The flood simile expresses the overwhelming force of the desire for reunion that the chapter describes. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a strong wind sweeps away a boat on the water, even one of the roaming senses on which the mind focuses can carry away a man’s intelligence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a sense on which the mind dwells can sweep away one’s judgment like wind carrying off a boat.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife knows her resolve will be swept away by love as surely as a swimmer by the flood; the Gita uses the same image of being carried off on water.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.67 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.”
christianity.explanation: The Song declares love stronger than any flood.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural pictures sulking swept away by a flood of love; the Song names love as the force no flood can overcome.

islam.quote_or_event: “And spend in the way of Allah and do not throw [yourselves] with your [own] hands into destruction [by refraining].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids knowingly casting oneself into ruin.
islam.tie_back: The Kural compares futile sulking to knowingly leaping into a flood; the Qur’an names the folly of throwing oneself into destruction, though its context is spending in God’s cause.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water; therefore leave off contention, before the quarrel break out.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares starting a quarrel to releasing water that cannot be controlled, and advises stopping before it begins.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, uses the image of water to argue that sulking is futile and better abandoned.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells of a man carried along by a pleasant, alluring river, warned by someone on the bank that downstream lie whirlpools and monsters; the river stands for craving and the pleasant current for the senses.
buddhism.explanation: The Itivuttaka uses the image of a river current to show how desire carries a person off.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s flood that sweeps the swimmer away is the same image of desire’s current, though the Buddhist parable urges escape.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Just as an impassioned buffalo who dives in cold water, is taken hold of by a crocodile and dies.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares one enslaved by the pleasures of touch to a buffalo that plunges into water and is seized.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural, too, pictures plunging into water and being carried off, though for the Jain text the plunge is into ruinous passion.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.76 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; Jacobi gives this line in his summary of verses 74-86)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The storm rages and the rain floods the land; thousands of waves rise and surge.”
sikhism.explanation: In these extra saloks Guru Nanak pictures a world of storm and flood, in which the seeker must hold on to the Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural compares useless sulking to leaping into a flood one knows will sweep one away; Guru Nanak's line shares the image of an overwhelming flood.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1410, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Leander swam the Hellespont each night to reach Hero, and on a stormy night plunged in again despite the danger and was drowned.
greek_mythology.explanation: The legend of Hero and Leander shows a lover throwing himself into dangerous waters for love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural compares love’s pull to leaping into a flood; Leander literally does so.
greek_mythology.source: Musaeus, Hero and Leander (paraphrase; cf. Ovid, Heroides 18-19)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza quotes Ovid’s Medea: I see and approve the better, yet I follow the worse, as an example of how knowledge of the good does not by itself restrain a strong emotion.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza explains that true knowledge can be overpowered by emotion, so people act against what they know.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife knows her sulking will fail yet sulks anyway, like the swimmer who knows the flood will take him.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics IV, Proposition 17, Scholium (paraphrase; quoting Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.20-21)

real_life_example.event_title: Edward VIII abdicates to marry Wallis Simpson
real_life_example.event: King Edward VIII had fallen in love with the American Wallis Simpson, and in 1936 it became clear he was determined to marry her once her divorce was final. The government, the Church of England, the opposition parties and the Dominions would not accept a twice-divorced woman as queen, and Edward came to see that he had to choose between the crown and her. On 10 December 1936 he signed an Instrument of Abdication, which took legal effect the next day, and he married Wallis Simpson in France on 3 June 1937.
real_life_example.explanation: Edward chose the woman he loved over the throne, knowing in advance that the marriage could not be reconciled with remaining king.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use it is to resist when one already knows the current will sweep one away, like those who leap into a flood knowing it will carry them off; Edward’s love carried him over the edge of the throne with his eyes open.

tamil:
இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும் களித்தார்க்குக்
கள்ளற்றே கள்வநின் மார்பு.
transliteration:
Iliththakka innaa seyinum kaliththaarkkuk
kallatrae kalvanin maarbu.
meaning: You thief! Even though you do hurtful, shameful things to me, your chest draws me the way strong drink draws someone who craves it.
elementary: Some people keep going back to something even when it is bad for them, because they just can’t resist it. The wife playfully calls her husband a ‘thief’ who stole her heart: even when he hurts her by being away, she can’t stop wanting to be close to him.
university: The wife addresses her husband as kaḷva (‘thief’, a term of endearment for one who has stolen her heart, with a hint of reproach). Iḷittakka iṉṉā ceyiṉum means ‘though it does painful things fit to bring disgrace’; kaḷittārkku kaḷ aṟṟē, ‘like toddy to those who have revelled in it’; niṉ mārpu, ‘your breast’, i.e. his embrace. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss it as toddy that, despite the shame it brings, makes drinkers crave it more and more; Kalaignar renders kaḷva as ‘thief who stole my heart’; Solomon Pappaiah uses ‘deceiver’ and adds that the husband reads her thoughts in her glance and comforts her, a bridge to 1290. The wine comparison returns from 1281 but now stresses compulsive attraction despite harm, recalling the ruinous drinker of chapter 93. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna comes to Radha at dawn bearing the marks of a night spent elsewhere, she rebukes him bitterly as a deceiver, yet her love for him remains undiminished.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s Radha is wounded by Krishna but cannot stop loving him.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise calls her husband a ‘thief’ yet craves his embrace like a drinker his wine.

christianity.quote_or_event: “They have stricken me, shalt thou say, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I felt it not: when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs describes the drunkard who, though harmed by wine, resolves to seek it again as soon as he wakes.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s simile is the same: the drinker returns to wine despite the shame and pain, as the wife to her husband’s embrace.

islam.quote_or_event: “They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, ‘In them is great sin and [yet, some] benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an acknowledges that wine has some appeal but declares its harm the greater.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s comparison rests on wine’s pull despite its harm, which the Qur’an names directly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend and an adulteress, even as the LORD loveth the children of Israel, though they turn unto other gods, and love cakes of raisins.”
judaism.explanation: Hosea is told to keep loving a wife who has wronged him, as God keeps loving Israel.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife keeps loving a husband who causes her pain; Hosea models love that persists despite injury.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares a man given to sensual pleasure to a leper who scratches his sores and cauterises them over a fire, finding relief in the very thing that worsens his wounds.
buddhism.explanation: In the Magandiya Sutta, sensual craving is pictured as finding pleasure in what actually harms.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s drinker who craves wine despite its shame is the same pattern the Buddha describes.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 75, Magandiya Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares one enslaved by attraction to a moth drawn into the flame.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife is drawn to the embrace that pains her as a drinker to wine; the Jain moth image captures the same fatal attraction.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Even if You give me hunger, I will still feel satisfied; I am joyful, even in the midst of sorrow.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that whatever the Beloved gives, even hunger and sorrow, he accepts with joy.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her husband's embrace still draws her like drink draws the drinker, even though it brings her pain; Guru Ram Das likewise clings to the Beloved even when it brings hardship.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Helen scorns Paris after his defeat by Menelaus, but when Aphrodite insists, she goes to him nonetheless, unable to resist the goddess of desire.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Iliad, Helen despises Paris’s weakness yet is drawn back to him by Aphrodite’s power.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise reproaches the ‘thief’ yet cannot keep from his embrace.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 3.383-447 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato tells of Leontius, who, angry at himself, still ran to gaze at corpses by the city wall, crying to his eyes to take their fill of the sight.
philosophy.explanation: The Republic uses the story to show desire overpowering the part of the soul that disapproves.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, like Leontius, is drawn irresistibly to what she half-reproaches.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic IV, 439e-440a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera remarry in San Francisco
real_life_example.event: The Mexican painters Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera married in 1929, but their marriage was strained by a series of extramarital affairs, notably Rivera’s with Kahlo’s younger sister, and they divorced in 1939. In late 1940 Kahlo travelled to San Francisco, where Rivera was working for the Golden Gate International Exposition, and the two reconciled. They remarried there on 8 December 1940, barely a year after their divorce.
real_life_example.explanation: Despite the real and public hurt Rivera had caused her, Kahlo could not stay away from him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural’s wife calls her husband a thief and says that though he brings her shameful pain, his embrace is to her what wine is to the drinker who keeps craving more, which fits Kahlo’s return to Rivera after all he had done.

tamil:
மலரினும் மெல்லிது காமம் சிலர்அதன்
செவ்வி தலைப்படு வார்.
transliteration:
Malarinum mellidhu kaamam silaradhan
sevvi thalaippadu vaar.
meaning: Love is softer than a flower. Only a few people know how to enjoy it at its very best.
elementary: A flower petal is so soft that if you squeeze it, it gets crushed. The poet says love is even softer than that, so you must be gentle and patient with it. Not many people learn how to care for it properly.
university: Malariṉum melliti kāmam: ‘love (kāmam) is softer/more delicate than a flower’. Puliyur Kesikan specifies the flower as aṉiccam, the proverbially delicate flower that withers even at a breath (cf. kural 90 and 1111). Cevvi means ‘ripeness, right moment, perfection’ and talaippaṭuvār ‘those who attain/grasp’; so few attain love’s cevvi. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘few know this truth and obtain its good fruit’; Solomon Pappaiah stresses having the right place, time and circumstances; Kalaignar ‘few enjoy it with the same delicacy’. The couplet is often quoted independently as the Kural’s most celebrated statement on love, and here it explains why both partners must set aside sulking: a love so delicate is easily bruised. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh joins சிலர்அதன்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kama, the god of love, carries a bow of sugarcane strung with bees and five arrows tipped with flowers; in the Kumarasambhava he aims his flower-arrow at Shiva to awaken love for Parvati.
hinduism.explanation: Indian tradition imagines love’s weapons as flowers, signalling its delicacy and sweetness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural calls love softer than a flower; the image of Kama’s flower-arrows makes the same association.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song compares his beloved to a lily, delicate and rare among thorns.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, joins love with the delicacy of a flower and its rarity among the many.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that God is gentle and loves gentleness, and grants for gentleness what He does not grant for harshness.
islam.explanation: The hadith praises gentleness (rifq) as a quality God loves and rewards.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says love must be handled with more gentleness than a flower; the hadith sets gentleness as a divine ideal.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem: Why should ye awaken, or stir up love, until it please?”
judaism.explanation: The Song’s refrain warns against rousing love before its proper time.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s cevvi, love’s right moment, is exactly what the Song guards: love is delicate and must not be forced.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Upon a heap of rubbish in the road-side ditch blooms a lotus, fragrant and pleasing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada uses the rare lotus blooming in a ditch as an image of the few who rise to wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural, too, joins a delicate flower with the rarity of the few who attain its essence, though the Buddhist lotus stands for wisdom, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra lists among the ten supreme virtues mardava, literally ‘softness’, the humility and gentleness that dissolves pride.
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics names softness of heart as one of the ten dharmas practised to stop the influx of karma.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls love softer than a flower; Jainism prizes softness of heart, though as a renunciant virtue rather than a quality of love.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.6 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Nathmal Tatia)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The path they take is sharper than a two-edged sword, and finer than a hair.”
sikhism.explanation: In the Anand Sahib Guru Amar Das says the way of the devotees is so fine and demanding that few can walk it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says love is more delicate than a flower and few grasp its finest moment; Guru Amar Das likewise says the path of love for God is finer than a hair and walked by few.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 918, Raag Raamkalee, Anand Sahib (pauri 14), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho compares a maiden to a sweet apple reddening on the topmost bough, which the apple-pickers missed, or rather could not reach.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho’s image presents beauty and love as rare, ripe and out of reach for most.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural, too, speaks of love’s ripeness (cevvi) that only a few manage to attain.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Agathon, in Plato’s Symposium, praises Love as the most tender of the gods, who walks not on the earth but in the softest of places, the hearts and souls of gods and men, and who dwells among flowers.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s Agathon describes Love as supremely soft and delicate, living only where there is gentleness.
philosophy.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that love is softer than a flower.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 195c-196b (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)

real_life_example.event_title: Wagner wakes Cosima with the Siegfried Idyll
real_life_example.event: Richard Wagner secretly composed a gentle piece for small orchestra as a birthday present for his new wife, Cosima. On Christmas morning 1870, when they were to celebrate her birthday, a small group of musicians directed by Wagner played it on the stairs outside her bedroom to wake her. The piece, first named after their home at Tribschen, became known as the Siegfried Idyll, after their young son.
real_life_example.explanation: Wagner, known for vast and stormy operas, chose an intimate, quiet gesture for the right moment.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says love is more delicate than a flower and few grasp its perfect moment; the Siegfried Idyll is a rare documented case of a lover choosing exactly the right, tender moment to express love.

tamil:
கண்ணின் துனித்தே கலங்கினாள் புல்லுதல்
என்னினும் தான்விதுப் புற்று.
transliteration:
Kannin thuniththae kalanginaal pulludhal
enninum thaanvidhup putru.
meaning: She showed she was upset only with her eyes. Then, wanting the hug even more than I did, she melted into my arms.
elementary: Have you ever tried to look cross at someone you missed, only to break into a smile and give them a hug first? The husband in this poem says his wife did just that: her eyes looked upset, but she was quicker than him to hug.
university: Here the husband speaks, recalling a meeting: kaṇṇiṉ tuṉittē, ‘sulking (tuṉi, displeasure) only by/with the eyes’; kalaṅkiṉāḷ, ‘she was stirred, melted’; pullutal eṉṉiṉum tāṉ vituppuṟṟu, ‘she being more eager (vitumpu, the root of the chapter title) than I to embrace’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss that she sulked only as far as a glance, and then, wanting the embrace more eagerly than he did, forgot her displeasure and came into his arms; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read the same. The Sivayogi Sivakumar gloss on ytamizh takes kalaṅkiṉāḷ more literally as her eyes clouding with tears. By ending with the husband’s voice, the chapter confirms that the eagerness for reunion was mutual and that it overcame the convention of ūṭal on both sides. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna reappears to the gopis after vanishing, one clasps his hand, another places his arm on her shoulder, while another, biting her lip with knitted brows, glares at him as if wounded by his absence, before all rejoice in his presence.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata depicts the gopis’ mingled reproach and eager welcome when Krishna returns.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise shows displeasure only with her eyes before rushing into her husband’s embrace.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.32.4-8 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, the father runs to embrace his returning son before any word of apology.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, outruns her partner in eagerness to embrace, any grievance forgotten.

islam.quote_or_event: In a hadith qudsi, God says that if His servant draws near Him by a hand’s span He draws near by an arm’s length, and if the servant comes walking He comes running.
islam.explanation: The hadith pictures divine love outpacing human approach in eagerness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife is more eager than her husband to embrace; the hadith uses the same image of one party running ahead in love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Scarce had I passed from them, when I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go.”
judaism.explanation: The bride of the Song, finding her beloved after searching, clings to him.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, seizes the moment of reunion with an eagerness greater than her beloved’s.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the Buddha first returned to Kapilavastu, Yasodhara stayed in her chamber, saying that if she had any worth he would come to her himself; when he came, she fell at his feet, clasped his ankles and laid her head upon them.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka introduction tells of Yasodhara’s reserve giving way to an overwhelming welcome.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a show of reserve dissolves into eager reunion, though Yasodhara’s greeting is reverential rather than marital.
buddhism.source: Jataka Nidanakatha (paraphrase; cf. tr. T.W. Rhys Davids)

jainism.quote_or_event: After Prince Aristanemi (Neminatha) turned back from his wedding to renounce the world, his bride Rajimati, instead of resenting him, chose to follow him by taking vows herself.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana tells how Rajimati’s love for Neminatha led her to follow him into the ascetic life.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife overcomes her displeasure in eagerness to join her husband; Rajimati also follows her beloved, though into renunciation rather than embrace.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The Gurmukhs are honored in the Court of the Lord. The Lord Himself takes them in His Loving Embrace.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says the Lord Himself draws those who follow the Guru into His loving embrace.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's husband recalls how his wife, after a brief sulk with her eyes, melted into his arms more eagerly than he; Guru Ram Das likewise ends in the Beloved's loving embrace.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 42, Sri Raag, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope holds back from Odysseus, testing him coldly, until he describes their bed; then her knees and heart give way, and she runs to him, throws her arms around his neck and kisses him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows Penelope’s reserve dissolving all at once into an eager embrace.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s scene: displeasure shown first, then an embrace more eager than the husband’s.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 23.205-208 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Terence’s line that the quarrels of lovers are the renewal of love became a classic maxim of European moral writing.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman playwright observes that lovers’ quarrels end by strengthening their love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural ends the chapter the same way: a brief glance of displeasure leads straight to a fuller reunion.

real_life_example.event_title: Eleanor of Castile goes on crusade with Edward
real_life_example.place: Acre, Kingdom of Jerusalem (now in Israel)
real_life_example.event: In August 1270 the future Edward I of England set out on crusade to the Holy Land, and his wife Eleanor of Castile went with him instead of staying behind. They reached Acre in 1271, and their daughter Joan, known as Joan of Acre, was born there about a year later. Eleanor travelled with Edward until 1273; the popular story that she saved his life by sucking poison from a dagger wound is regarded as legend.
real_life_example.explanation: Rather than wait years at home, Eleanor chose to share a long and dangerous journey so as not to be parted from her husband.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural’s husband says his wife was even more eager than he for their embrace, and Eleanor’s choice to follow Edward across the world shows a wife whose eagerness for togetherness outran convention.

tamil:
அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல் கண்டும் எவன்நெஞ்சே
நீஎமக்கு ஆகா தது.
transliteration:
Avarnenju avarkkaadhal kandum evannenjae
nee-emakku aakaa thadhu.
meaning: My heart, you have seen how his heart stays on his side alone. So why do you not stay on my side?
elementary: Imagine two friends on a team. One friend’s helper always sticks by him, but your own helper keeps running over to the other side. You would ask, ‘Why aren’t you on my side?’ The wife in this poem asks her own heart that same question.
university: The chapter title neñcoṭu pulattal means ‘sulking with (one’s own) heart’: in the kaṟpu (wedded love) section, the husband has returned, the wife wishes to stage a lovers’ quarrel (ūṭal/pulavi) over his long absence, but her heart refuses to cooperate and rushes toward him, so she turns her reproach on the heart itself. Here she observes that avar neñcu avarkku ātal (‘his heart being his own’, i.e. siding with him and not thinking of her) is plain to see, yet her heart (neñcē) will not be emakku (‘ours’, on her side). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read ātal as ‘becoming a companion/ally (tuṇai)’, and Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar add that her heart keeps melting toward him instead; Pope renders it ‘You see his heart is his alone; O heart, why not be all my own?’ The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the chapter title is printed நெஞ்சொடுபுலத்தல் on ytamizh and நெஞ்சோடு புலத்தல் on thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Katha Upanishad pictures the self as the rider in a chariot, the body as the chariot, intelligence as the charioteer and the mind as the reins, with the senses as horses; for one without understanding, the senses run wild like vicious horses that will not obey their driver.
hinduism.explanation: The image shows the mind as something meant to serve the self but able to pull away from it.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife’s heart behaves like reins slipping from the driver’s hand, running toward the husband instead of obeying her.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes a self divided against itself, wanting one thing while doing another.
christianity.tie_back: The wife meets the same split: she wills to hold back from her husband, yet her heart goes the other way.

islam.quote_or_event: “And I do not acquit myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: In the story of Yusuf, this confession admits that one’s own soul (nafs) pushes toward what the person knows she should resist.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s speaker, the confessor admits that her own inner self has not been on her side.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why moanest thou within me? Hope thou in God; for I shall yet praise Him for the salvation of His countenance.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist speaks to his own soul as if it were a second person, questioning and rebuking it.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same form, a person addressing her own heart and asking why it acts as it does.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever harm an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater, an ill-directed mind inflicts on oneself a greater harm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that one’s own badly aimed mind can hurt a person more than any outside enemy.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife finds that her own heart, not her husband, is the one working against her.

jainism.quote_or_event: “My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anathi teaches King Srenika that a person’s own self can be either friend or enemy.
jainism.tie_back: The wife complains that her heart, which ought to be her friend, has gone over to the other side.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “My mind longs for the Blessed Vision of the Guru's Darshan.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan describes a mind that runs of its own accord toward the one it loves, longing only to see him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heart has already gone over to the beloved and will not stay with the speaker; Guru Arjan's mind likewise belongs wholly to the one it longs for.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In a short fragment Sappho says that she does not know what to do, because her mind is split in two.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet describes love leaving her inner self divided and unable to settle.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife feels the same split: one part of her wants to sulk while her heart wants to run to him.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho, fragment 51 (paraphrase; cf. tr. D.A. Campbell, Greek Lyric I)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal holds that the heart moves by a logic of its own that the reasoning mind cannot overrule.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s reason says to hold back; her heart, following its own reasons, goes to him anyway.

real_life_example.event_title: Nietzsche’s marriage proposal to Lou Salomé is refused
real_life_example.event: In 1882, at the writer Malwida von Meysenbug’s salon in Rome, the philosophers Friedrich Nietzsche and Paul Rée met Lou Salomé, a brilliant young Russian student. Both men fell in love with her, but she turned down their proposals of marriage and suggested instead that the three live and study together; apart from three weeks sharing an apartment in Leipzig, the plan came to nothing. After Nietzsche’s unsuccessful proposal, Salomé and Rée left together for Berlin, and the friendship ended painfully for him.
real_life_example.explanation: Nietzsche gave his heart completely while Salomé kept hers firmly her own.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural’s speaker complains that the beloved’s heart stays loyal to him alone while her own heart runs off to him; Nietzsche’s heart went to Salomé while hers remained entirely her own.

tamil:
உறாஅ தவர்க்கண்ட கண்ணும் அவரைச்
செறாஅரெனச் சேறியென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Uraaa thavarkkanda kannum avaraich
cheraa-arenach chaeriyen nenju.
meaning: My heart, even after seeing that he does not care for me, you still go to him, thinking he will not be angry.
elementary: Think of a puppy that keeps running to someone who ignores it, wagging its tail and hoping for a pat. The puppy does not stop to think. The wife says her heart is like that puppy: it runs to her husband even when he has not shown much love.
university: Uṟāatavar is ‘one who does not draw near’, i.e. who shows no love (uṟu, to approach, be attached); ceṟāar is ‘he will not be angry’, and cēṟi ‘you go’. Both uṟāa and ceṟāa show the long-vowel extension (aḷapeṭai) used for metre, also seen in 1295. The commentators agree on the sense: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan have the heart go to the beloved ‘thinking he will not hate us’, and Solomon Pappaiah adds ‘thinking he will not be angry if we go’; Pope renders ‘Why go to him as though he were not enemy?’ The point within the chapter is that the heart’s eagerness undercuts the wife’s plan to sulk. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Radha learns that Krishna is dancing with other cowherd women, yet in her loneliness her heart keeps recalling him and longing for him rather than turning away.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva shows Radha unable to stop loving Krishna even when he seems indifferent to her.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heart, Radha’s heart goes on seeking a beloved who, for now, does not seem to seek her.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as endlessly patient and willing to hope for the best.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s heart ‘believes all things’: it hopes he will not be angry even after seeing his coldness.

islam.quote_or_event: “But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah Knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that what the heart loves is not always what is good for it.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s heart loves one who does not love it back, against what she can plainly see.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song keeps seeking her beloved even after he has withdrawn and does not answer.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, love goes on reaching toward a beloved who seems to hold himself back.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Wonderful, indeed, it is to subdue the mind, so difficult to subdue, ever swift, and seizing whatever it desires. A tamed mind brings happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the untrained mind as quick to grab at whatever it wants.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s heart rushes after what it desires without weighing what it has already seen.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana warns that passionate attachment drives a being toward what will hurt it, like a moth to a flame.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s heart flies toward him just as blindly, though she has seen that he does not care.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If You seat me near You, then I worship and adore You. Even if You beat me and drive me out, I will still meditate on You.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das says the devotee's love does not depend on how the Lord treats him; welcomed or driven away, he keeps turning to God.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's heart that goes to the beloved even when he shows no care, the devotee's heart keeps going to God whatever the treatment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo falls in love with Narcissus and follows him through the woods even after he coldly rejects her, wasting away until only her voice remains.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells of a love that keeps pursuing a beloved who gives nothing back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echo’s heart, like the wife’s, goes after one who has shown no love, unable to stop itself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume argues that reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions, and can never by itself oppose a passion in directing the will.
philosophy.explanation: For Hume, knowing a fact does not by itself stop desire; feeling drives action.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart knows he is cold, yet that knowledge cannot hold it back from going to him.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.3 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Mary Wollstonecraft travels to Scandinavia on Gilbert Imlay’s business
real_life_example.event: In Paris during the French Revolution, Mary Wollstonecraft lived with the American adventurer Gilbert Imlay and in 1794 gave birth to their daughter, Fanny, but he soon drifted away from her. In 1795, after a Norwegian captain had made off with a valuable silver cargo from one of Imlay’s ships, Imlay asked her to go to Scandinavia to recover it, and she set out in June with her baby and a maid, spending more than three months negotiating with officials and travelling. She wrote letters to Imlay throughout, and on returning to London found that he had taken up with another woman; the letters became her book Letters Written During a Short Residence in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark (1796).
real_life_example.explanation: Even after Imlay had made clear how little he valued her, Wollstonecraft went far out of her way for him and kept writing to him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural’s wife tells her heart that even after seeing he does not care, it still goes to him, assuming he will not be angry; Wollstonecraft’s journey and letters show a heart that kept going toward a man who had stopped caring.

tamil:
கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார்இல் என்பதோ நெஞ்சேநீ
பெட்டாங்கு அவர்பின் செலல்.
transliteration:
Kettaarkku nattaar-il enpadho nenjaenee
pettaangu avarpin selal.
meaning: My heart, is it because "people who are ruined have no friends" that you leave me and follow him as you please?
elementary: There is an old saying that when someone is in trouble, their friends disappear. The wife feels sad and alone, and even her own heart has left her to go after her husband. So she asks her heart, ‘Did you leave me because I am having a hard time?’
university: The first line quotes a proverb: keṭṭārkku naṭṭār il, ‘the ruined have no friends’; the wife bitterly applies it to herself, worn down by separation. Peṭṭāṅku means ‘as you please, at your own desire’ and avar piṉ celal ‘going after him’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read keṭṭār as ‘those ruined by suffering’, and Kalaignar puts it as ‘those destroyed by sorrow have no friends to stand by them’; Pope renders ‘The ruined have no friends, they say; and so, my heart, / To follow him, at thy desire, from me thou dost depart.’ The rhetorical question (eṉpatō, ‘is it that…?’) carries the chapter’s tone of affectionate reproach. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a boat on the water is swept away by a strong wind, even one of the senses on which the mind focuses can carry away a man’s intelligence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that the mind, once fixed on one object, can sweep a person’s judgement away with it.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife’s heart, fixed on her husband, is carried off after him, leaving her judgement behind.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.67 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that the heart follows whatever a person values most.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s treasure is her husband, so her heart goes where he is, whatever she tells it.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you seen the one who takes as his god his own desire? Then would you be responsible for him?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes a person who simply follows wherever desire leads.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s heart goes peṭṭāṅku, ‘as it pleases’, following its desire rather than her will.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song rises and goes out through the city in search of her beloved.
judaism.tie_back: Her soul goes after the one it loves, just as the wife’s heart follows her husband.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Dwelling in the cave (of the heart), the mind, without form, wanders far and alone. Those who subdue this mind are liberated from the bonds of Mara.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the mind as roaming far from its owner on its own.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s heart has wandered far off after her husband and left her behind.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Prince Neminatha turned back from his own wedding procession and renounced the world, his bride Rajimati was left grief-stricken; yet her heart stayed fixed on him, and in time she too renounced and followed the path he had taken.
jainism.explanation: Jain tradition tells of a bride whose love for Nemi led her to follow him even after he left her.
jainism.tie_back: Like the wife’s heart in the Kural, Rajimati’s heart goes after the one who has gone away from her.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (Rathanemi) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Emotional attachment to children and spouse is poison; in the end, no one will go along with you as your helper.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das warns that worldly ties do not stay with us when we most need them.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural quotes the proverb that the ruined have no friends and feels even her heart has left her; Gurbani makes the same point that no worldly companion stays to the end.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 41, Siree Raag, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Clytie, abandoned by the sun god Helios, sits on the bare ground day after day, turning her face to follow his course across the sky until she becomes the heliotrope, the flower that always faces the sun.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells of a rejected lover whose whole being keeps turning after the one who left her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Clytie’s gaze follows Helios just as the wife’s heart follows her husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes tells how humans were once double beings who were split in two, so that each half now longs for and pursues its missing other half.
philosophy.explanation: The myth explains love as the pull of a part toward the whole it belongs to.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart behaves as if it belongs with him, and so it leaves her to go after its other half.

real_life_example.event_title: Emma Hamilton dies in debt and exile at Calais
real_life_example.event: On the morning of the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805, Admiral Lord Nelson added a codicil to his will asking the British government to provide for Emma Hamilton, but the government, which gave money and honours to Nelson’s family, ignored her. Deep in debt, she had to sell Nelson’s house at Merton and her mementoes of him, and in 1813 she was arrested for debt and lived within the bounds of the King’s Bench debtors’ prison, cut off by many people she had once entertained lavishly. She fled abroad to escape her creditors and died at Calais on 15 January 1815.
real_life_example.explanation: Once Nelson was gone and her fortunes collapsed, the society and state that had celebrated her abandoned her.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural quotes the saying that the ruined have no friends, and Emma Hamilton’s last years are a textbook case of friends vanishing once misfortune struck.

tamil:
இனிஅன்ன நின்னொடு சூழ்வார்யார் நெஞ்சே
துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்காண் மற்று.
transliteration:
Ini-anna ninnodu soozhvaaryaar nenjae
thuniseydhu thuvvaaikaan matru.
meaning: My heart, you will not sulk first and then enjoy making up. So who will ever plan such things with you again?
elementary: Imagine you and a friend plan to act a little upset with someone to show your feelings, and then make up. But the moment that person walks in, your friend runs and hugs him. You might say, ‘I’m never planning anything with you again!’ That is what the wife says to her heart.
university: Tuṉi is a strong form of ūṭal (lovers’ sulking), and tuvvāy means ‘you will not enjoy’; the commentators read the line as ‘you will not first sulk and then enjoy (the reunion that follows)’. In Tamil love poetics the reconciliation after ūṭal is itself a pleasure, which is why the wife complains that her eager heart skips it. Iṉi aṉṉa niṉṉoṭu cūḻvār yār, ‘hereafter who will consult with you about such things?’, is her mock threat to stop taking the heart into her counsels; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar add ‘I will not’. Pope renders ‘See, thou first show offended pride, and then submit, I bade; / Henceforth such council who will share with thee my heart?’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, when Krishna comes back to Radha, she at first holds on to her wounded pride (mana), and her friend urges her to give up the sulk and go to him while the moment lasts.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva stages the lovers’ quarrel and its reconciliation as a set stage of love.
hinduism.tie_back: Radha can sustain the sulk that the Kural’s heart cannot; both poems treat quarrel-then-reunion as part of love’s pleasure.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows anger but tells believers to let it go quickly.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s heart lets its anger go even faster than Paul asks, before it has served its purpose.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allah] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who hold back anger and forgive.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s heart forgives at once, but she wishes it had held its displeasure a little longer.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my heart was moved for him.”
judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song first makes excuses not to open to her beloved, then her heart is stirred and she rises.
judaism.tie_back: Her show of reluctance melts the moment he appears, much as the wife’s heart gives up its sulk at once.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a fletcher straightens an arrow shaft, even so the discerning man straightens his mind — so fickle and unsteady, so difficult to guard.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls the mind fickle and hard to keep on a chosen course.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s heart could not keep to the plan they had made; it wavered the moment he came home.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that it is one’s own love or aversion, not the object, that throws the mind from one state to another.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s heart swings from planned anger to eager love the moment it sees him, just the kind of change the sutra describes.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.101 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The fickle mind continuously runs after fleeting things.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes a mind that will not stay put or follow sound counsel but chases whatever draws it.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's speaker complains that her heart will not keep to her plan of sulking first; Gurbani likewise names the restless mind that cannot be held to any plan.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 222, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus finally returns, Penelope does not rush to embrace him; though her son calls her heart harder than stone, she holds back and tests him with the secret of their bed before she yields and runs to him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows a wife who keeps her composure before the joyful reunion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope manages the reserve before reunion that the Kural’s wife wanted, and her heart would not allow.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 23.85-240 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Terence’s comedy The Girl from Andros, a character remarks that lovers’ quarrels are the renewal of love (amantium irae amoris integratio est).
philosophy.explanation: The line, which became proverbial, holds that a quarrel between lovers ends by making their love fresh again.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the pleasure the wife says her heart throws away by refusing to quarrel first.

real_life_example.event_title: Gustav Mahler walks with Sigmund Freud in Leiden
real_life_example.event: In July 1910 the composer Gustav Mahler, then fifty and at the height of his fame, discovered that his wife Alma had become romantically involved with the young architect Walter Gropius. In August he travelled to Leiden in the Netherlands to consult Sigmund Freud, who came by tram from his holiday at Noordwijk aan Zee. The two men talked for about four hours while walking through the city; Mahler died nine months later.
real_life_example.explanation: Faced with the threat of losing Alma, Mahler did not break with her but sought to understand his own feelings and keep the marriage.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural’s wife complains that her heart will not first sulk and then enjoy the making-up; Mahler, instead of turning his hurt into a quarrel, put his effort into holding on to the one he loved.

tamil:
பெறாஅமை அஞ்சும் பெறின்பிரிவு அஞ்சும்
அறாஅ இடும்பைத்தென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Peraaamai anjum perinpirivu anjum
araaa idumpaiththen nenju.
meaning: When he is away, my heart fears it will not have him. When he is here, it fears he will leave. So my heart is never free from pain.
elementary: Think of a child waiting for a favourite toy: before getting it, she worries she never will, and after getting it, she worries she will lose it. The wife’s heart is like that with her husband: worried when he is gone, and worried when he is home that he will go again.
university: The couplet is built on parallel clauses: peṟāamai añcum (‘it fears not having him’) and peṟiṉ pirivu añcum (‘having him, it fears separation’), leading to aṟāa iṭumpaittu eṉ neñcu, ‘my heart is (a thing) of unceasing distress’. Peṟāamai and aṟāa again show metrical vowel lengthening (aḷapeṭai). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan agree on the reading; Solomon Pappaiah makes the setting explicit, ‘when my husband was away… when he has come’. Pope renders ‘I fear I shall not gain, I fear to lose him when I gain; / And thus my heart endures unceasing pain.’ Within the chapter this explains why the heart cannot afford to sulk: even in his presence it already fears his next departure. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrihari observes that every worldly good comes with its own fear: in enjoyment there is fear of disease, in family pride fear of a fall, in wealth fear of kings, and so on, so that only detachment is free of fear.
hinduism.explanation: The verse lists how each thing we hold brings the dread of losing it.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife’s heart lives this exactly: having her husband brings only the fear of losing him.
hinduism.source: Bhartrihari, Vairagya Shataka, verse beginning bhoge roga-bhayam (paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.”
christianity.explanation: John teaches that perfect love leaves no room for fear, because fear itself is a torment.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s heart is the opposite case: its love is full of fear, and so it lives in torment.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you. And Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful -”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches calm both over what one lacks and over what one has.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s heart has neither calm: it frets over what it lacks and over what it might lose.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick; but desire fulfilled is a tree of life.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that waiting for what one longs for wears the heart down.
judaism.tie_back: The first half of the Kural, the heart afraid while he is away, is this heartsickness; the Kural adds that even fulfilment brings fear.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful. Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that loving someone brings pain both in absence and in the threat of separation.
buddhism.tie_back: This names both halves of the wife’s distress: pain at not seeing him and dread of parting from him.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a man who passionately desires ‘colours,’ be happy while he gets, keeps, uses, loses, and misses (those things). Even when he enjoys them, he is never satisfied.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that attachment brings unhappiness at every stage, in getting, keeping and losing.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s heart suffers at every stage of her love, whether he is absent or present.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without Him, I cannot survive even for an instant, and my life-night passes in anguish.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das voices the soul-bride's constant pain while she is apart from her Lord.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heart is never free of fear, dreading his absence and then dreading his leaving; Guru Amar Das likewise describes a soul in unbroken anguish over separation.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 35, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros the loosener of limbs, a bittersweet creature against whom there is no defence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho coined the idea of love as sweet and bitter at the same time.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The wife’s love is bittersweet in just this way: even its sweetness carries pain.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho, fragment 130 (paraphrase; cf. tr. D.A. Campbell, Greek Lyric I)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines hope and fear as unsteady pleasure and pain arising from an uncertain outcome, and adds that there is no hope unmingled with fear, and no fear unmingled with hope.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, hope and fear always come together because both rest on uncertainty.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart never escapes fear because its joy in her husband is always shadowed by uncertainty about losing him.
philosophy.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part III, Definitions of the Emotions XII-XIII (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Mary Livingstone rejoins David Livingstone on the Zambezi
real_life_example.place: Shupanga (Chupanga), on the Zambezi River, Mozambique
real_life_example.event: Mary Moffat married the missionary-explorer David Livingstone in 1845 and travelled with him on many journeys in southern Africa, until in 1852 he sent her and their four children back to Britain for their health and safety. She lived there in near poverty during his long years of exploration. Determined to return to Africa with him, she joined his Zambezi expedition in 1862 but caught malaria and died at Shupanga in April 1862.
real_life_example.explanation: Mary Livingstone suffered first from long separation and then, when reunited, lost her husband again within months through her own death.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural’s heart fears not having the beloved when he is away and fears parting when he is near, and Mary Livingstone’s story moved from years of separation to a reunion that was itself cut short.

tamil:
தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால் என்னைத்
தினிய இருந்ததென் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Thaniye irundhu ninaiththakkaal ennaith
thiniya irundhadhen nenju.
meaning: Whenever I sat alone and thought of him, my own heart seemed ready to eat me alive.
elementary: Have you ever been alone and kept thinking about something sad until you felt worse and worse? Your thoughts can feel like they are gnawing at you. The wife says that when she was alone, her own heart chewed at her like that.
university: Taṉiyē iruntu niṉaittakkāl means ‘when I sat alone and thought’, and tiṉiya iruntatu ‘it was there to eat (me)’: the heart, instead of comforting her, devoured her. Commentators differ on what she was thinking of: Mu. Varadarasanar says ‘his faults’ (avaruṭaiya tavaṟukaḷ), which fits the chapter’s quarrel; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar say ‘the separation from her lover’; Puliyur Kesikan adds that the heart, ‘not being a companion to me’, tormented her. Pope renders ‘My heart consumes me when I ponder lone, / And all my lover’s cruelty bemoan.’ The past tense (iruntatu) recalls the time of separation now that he is back. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For the mind is restless, turbulent, obstinate and very strong, O Krsna, and to subdue it is, it seems to me, more difficult than controlling the wind.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna admits that his mind is turbulent and nearly impossible to calm.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife finds her own heart just as turbulent, turning against her when she is alone.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.34 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death: tarry ye here, and watch.”
christianity.explanation: In Gethsemane Jesus speaks of a sorrow so heavy it seems to crush him.
christianity.tie_back: The wife too feels an inner sorrow strong enough to consume her when she is alone.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Yaqub, grieving alone for his lost son Yusuf, keeps his sorrow to himself and to God.
islam.tie_back: Like Yaqub, the wife carries a grief that works on her in solitude, though she has only her own heart to speak to.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh;”
judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song says that even when she lies down, her heart stays awake, listening for her beloved.
judaism.tie_back: Like the wife alone at night, her body rests but her heart will not let her be.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares painful feeling to being struck by an arrow; the untaught person, by brooding and lamenting over it, is struck by a second arrow of mental pain, while the wise person feels the first and not the second.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta shows how the mind adds its own suffering on top of what has happened.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s solitary brooding is that second arrow: her own heart adds to the pain of separation.

jainism.quote_or_event: Asked how he manages the wild horse that runs about, Gautama tells Kesi that the horse is the mind, unruly and dreadful, and that he keeps it in check by the discipline of the Law.
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue between Kesi and Gautama, the untrained mind is a wild horse that runs where it will.
jainism.tie_back: Left alone, the wife’s heart runs wild like that horse and turns on its rider.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 23 (Kesi and Gautama) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The beautiful song-bird sings, perched on the mango tree; but how can I endure the pain in the depths of my being?”
sikhism.explanation: In his Barah Maha (song of the twelve months), Guru Nanak's soul-bride sits alone in spring and finds the beauty around her only deepens her inner pain.
sikhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker whose own heart seems to devour her when she sits alone thinking of her husband, Guru Nanak's bride is consumed from within by longing.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1108, Raag Tukhaari (Barah Maha), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ariadne, waking alone on the shore of Naxos after Theseus has sailed away, wanders the empty beach recalling him and is consumed by grief and memory.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Ariadne shows a woman tormented by her own thoughts once she is left by herself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Ariadne, the wife alone finds her own memories devouring her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Boethius begins the Consolation of Philosophy alone in prison, writing laments with the Muses of poetry, who only feed his grief until Lady Philosophy drives them away.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius shows how a mind left to itself in sorrow can nourish its own pain.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart, like Boethius’s Muses, fed her grief when she sat alone.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book I, prose 1 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Mary Shelley begins her Journal of Sorrow
real_life_example.event: In the summer of 1822 the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley and his friend Edward Williams drowned when their boat sank in a storm while sailing to Lerici in Italy. Left a widow at twenty-four, Mary Shelley began a new journal on 2 October 1822, later known as her Journal of Sorrow, addressing the blank page as the confidant to whom she could pour out her innermost thoughts. Her only regular companions at this time were her young son, Percy Florence, and the journal itself.
real_life_example.explanation: Alone with her memories, Mary Shelley turned her grief inward onto the page, where it could be expressed but not escaped.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural’s wife says that whenever she sat alone and thought of her husband, her own heart seemed ready to devour her, which matches Mary Shelley’s solitary, grieving journal.

tamil:
நாணும் மறந்தேன் அவர்மறக் கல்லாஎன்
மாணா மடநெஞ்சிற் பட்டு.
transliteration:
Naanum marandhaen avarmarak kallaaen
maanaa madanenjir pattu.
meaning: My silly heart has no dignity and cannot forget him. Stuck with such a heart, I have even forgotten my modesty.
