elementary: Sometimes when we miss someone very much, we do things we would normally feel shy about, like crying in front of others or running to hug them in public. The wife says her heart missed her husband so much that she forgot to be shy.
university: Nāṇ is the feminine modesty or sense of shame that classical Tamil poetics treats as a woman’s guarding virtue; avar maṟakkallā is ‘unable to forget him’, and māṇā maṭa neñcu ‘my undignified, foolish heart’ (māṇā, lacking excellence; maṭam, simplicity/folly). Paṭṭu, ‘having fallen in with’, makes the heart the bad company that led her astray. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan add that nāṇ is ‘something that should not be forgotten’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads the heart as ‘unsteady’ and the husband as one ‘who has forgotten me’. Pope renders ‘Fall’n ’neath the sway of this ignoble foolish heart, / Which will not him forget, I have forgotten shame.’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the cowherd women of Vraja hear Krishna’s flute on the autumn night, they leave their work and families and rush to him in the forest, setting aside the propriety expected of them.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana shows love for Krishna so strong that the gopis forget ordinary restraint.
hinduism.tie_back: As with the gopis, the wife’s longing has overridden the modesty she would normally keep.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment.”
christianity.explanation: A woman at a Pharisee’s dinner, ignoring what the guests think, pours out her love at Jesus’ feet.
christianity.tie_back: Like the wife, she is carried past ordinary decorum by the depth of her feeling.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that faith has many branches and that haya, modesty or a sense of shame, is one branch of faith.
islam.explanation: Islam treats modesty as part of faith itself, not merely good manners.
islam.tie_back: The Kural assumes the same high value for modesty, which is why the wife is dismayed to have lost it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Oh that thou wert as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother! When I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, and none would despise me.”
judaism.explanation: The woman in the Song wishes she could show her love openly without being scorned.
judaism.tie_back: Both poems feel the tension between love’s urge to show itself and the modesty society expects.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that two bright qualities protect the world, a sense of shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa); without them, people would not respect even the bonds of family.
buddhism.explanation: Shame and conscience are treated as the guardians that keep people within bounds.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife laments that love has made her lose nāṇ, a guardian Buddhism also prizes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Sramana, engaged in penance, should not allow himself to watch the shape, beauty, coquetry, laughter, prattle, gestures, and glances of women, nor retain a recollection of them in his mind.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana tells monks not even to keep the memory of attraction in their minds.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart does the opposite, unable to stop remembering the beloved, and so loses its restraint.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. ... give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that true love for God means giving up concern for what people say, even giving one's head.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's speaker has lost her modesty to a heart that cannot forget her beloved; Guru Nanak says the path of love requires leaving behind the shame of public opinion.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Medea, falling in love with Jason, struggles through a sleepless night between shame (aidos) before her father and her passion; in the end love overcomes her shame and she goes to help him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius shows a young woman whose modesty gives way before love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Medea, the wife finds that her heart’s love has overpowered her sense of shame.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates pictures the soul as a charioteer with two horses; when the beloved comes into view, the unruly horse, deaf to shame, drags the charioteer and the modest horse toward the beloved.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows passion pulling the soul past its own sense of shame.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart is the unruly horse that has dragged her past her modesty.

real_life_example.event_title: Lady Caroline Lamb’s open pursuit of Lord Byron
real_life_example.event: Early in 1812 Lady Caroline Lamb, wife of William Lamb (a future prime minister), read Lord Byron’s new poem Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage and wrote him an anonymous admiring letter. Their relationship that year became a public scandal: Byron’s friend John Cam Hobhouse said all London agreed she had set her heart on him, and Hobhouse barely prevented the two from eloping. In 1816 she published the novel Glenarvon, a thinly veiled account of the affair.
real_life_example.explanation: Caroline Lamb’s feelings for Byron overrode every rule of reserve expected of a married woman of her class, and she paid for it with lasting notoriety.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural’s speaker says that, caught up with a heart that cannot forget her beloved, she has forgotten even her modesty, which is how London saw Caroline Lamb’s conduct in 1812.

tamil:
எள்ளின் இளிவாம்என்று எண்ணி அவர்திறம்
உள்ளும் உயிர்க்காதல் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Ellin ilivaam-endru enni avarthiram
ullum uyirkkaadhal nenju.
meaning: My heart loves him as much as life itself. It thinks that looking down on him would only shame itself, so it keeps thinking of his good points.
elementary: When someone you love lets you down, you might want to say mean things about them. But a loving heart thinks, ‘If I say bad things about him, it makes me look bad too,’ and remembers his good side instead. The wife’s heart does exactly that.
university: Eḷḷiṉ iḷivām means ‘if (I) scorn (him), it will be a disgrace (to me)’; avar tiṟam uḷḷum, ‘it thinks of his qualities (or ways)’. Uyirkkātal neñcu is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as ‘the heart that loves life’ (fearing disgrace as worse than death), while Puliyur Kesikan and Kalaignar take it as ‘the heart that loves him as its own life’. Commentators also differ on avar tiṟam: ‘his noble qualities’ (Varadarasanar, Kesikan, Kalaignar) versus ‘his coming and our union’ (Pappaiah). Pope renders ‘If I contemn him, then disgrace awaits me evermore; / My soul that seeks to live his virtues numbers o’er.’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Held captive in Ravana’s grove in Lanka, Sita refuses every attempt to turn her against Rama and keeps her mind on his virtues, declaring that she belongs to him as light belongs to the sun.
hinduism.explanation: The Ramayana shows Sita’s devotion holding firm and dwelling on Rama’s goodness even in long separation.
hinduism.tie_back: Like Sita, the wife’s heart will not think ill of her absent husband but keeps recalling his good qualities.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as refusing to think the worst of the beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s heart ‘thinketh no evil’ of her husband and turns to his good qualities instead.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells believers to avoid thinking the worst of others.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s heart refuses to think ill of her husband and chooses to dwell on his merits.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joshua ben Perahiah used to say: appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The sage teaches that one should always give others the benefit of the doubt.
judaism.tie_back: The wife’s heart judges her husband favourably, dwelling on his good qualities rather than his neglect.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:6 (tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada advises not to look for the faults of others or at what they have done or left undone, but only at what one has done or left undone oneself.
buddhism.explanation: The verse turns attention away from another’s failings.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s heart refuses to dwell on her husband’s faults, though for love rather than self-examination.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra lists four attitudes to cultivate: friendliness toward all beings, delight (pramoda) in those with greater virtues, compassion for the afflicted, and equanimity toward the ill-behaved.
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics trains the mind to rejoice in others’ good qualities rather than dwell on their faults.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s heart does something like pramoda, fixing on her husband’s good qualities instead of scorning him.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.11 (Digambara numbering; 7.6 in Svetambara) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Vijay K. Jain)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Some sing of His Glorious Virtues, Greatness and Beauty.”
sikhism.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak describes devotees who dwell on God's qualities and beauty in praise.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's loving heart refuses to scorn the beloved and dwells on his good qualities instead; Japji describes the devotee's heart dwelling on the Lord's virtues.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Alcyone, while her husband Ceyx is away at sea, prays daily to Juno for his safe return and thinks only of his welfare, never of blame.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid portrays a wife whose thoughts of her absent husband are wholly loving.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Alcyone, the wife’s heart dwells on her husband with love rather than complaint.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises that when someone treats you badly or speaks ill of you, you should remember that he acted as he thought right, and so you will be gentle with him.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic refuses to let another’s fault provoke him into contempt.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s heart, too, declines to answer neglect with scorn.

real_life_example.event_title: Nadezhda Mandelstam memorises her husband’s poems
real_life_example.event: The Russian poet Osip Mandelstam was arrested by Stalin’s police in 1934 and again in May 1938, and died later that year in a transit prison camp near Vladivostok. His wife, Nadezhda, committed his poems to memory in the hope that one day she could publish them, and she eventually did. She later wrote the memoir Hope Against Hope, which records their life together and preserves his memory.
real_life_example.explanation: Through years of danger and loss, Nadezhda Mandelstam chose to carry her husband’s best qualities, his poetry, in her own mind.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says the loving heart, rather than scorning the beloved, dwells on his good qualities, and Nadezhda Mandelstam devoted her life to holding on to her husband’s finest work.

tamil:
துன்பத்திற்கு யாரே துணையாவார் தாமுடைய
நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி.
transliteration:
Thunpaththirku yaarae thunaiyaavaar thaamudaiya
nenjan thunaiyal vazhi.
meaning: When you are in trouble, who will help you, if even your own heart does not?
elementary: When you feel sad, the first one who can comfort you is you: you can tell yourself, ‘It will be okay.’ But if even your own feelings turn against you, who else can help? The wife asks this when her heart will not stand by her.
university: Tuṉpattiṟku yārē tuṇaiyāvār, ‘who indeed will be a companion in sorrow?’, with the emphatic -ē, and tām uṭaiya neñcam tuṇai al vaḻi, ‘when the heart that one owns is not a companion’. Here the wife generalises her complaint into a maxim (the plural tām gives it the force of ‘anyone’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah stress tām urimaiyākap peṟṟa, ‘that one possesses by right’; Kalaignar reads tuṇai as ‘support to bear’ the sorrow. Pope renders ‘And who will aid me in my hour of grief, / If my own heart comes not to my relief?’ With 1300 this forms the chapter’s closing pair of general sayings. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (thirukkural.net prints நெஞ்சந் with the same sandhi).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man must elevate himself by his own mind, not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that a person’s own mind is meant to be the helper that lifts him up.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural assumes the same: one’s own heart should be the first companion in trouble.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.5 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says a person’s own spirit carries him through suffering, but nothing can help when that spirit itself is broken.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point almost exactly: if one’s own heart fails, who else can bear the sorrow?

islam.quote_or_event: “Those who have believed and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allah. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are assured.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that a heart at peace is the source of steadiness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shares the sense that the heart must be settled to sustain a person, though it sees no other source of help if the heart fails.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If I am not for myself, who is for me? But if I am for my own self [only], what am I? And if not now, when?”
judaism.explanation: Hillel teaches that a person must first be his own support before he can look to others.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural asks the same question: if one’s own heart will not stand by one, who will?
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:14 (tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One truly is the protector of oneself; who else could the protector be? With oneself fully controlled, one gains a mastery that is hard to gain.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that no one else can be one’s refuge if one is not one’s own.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same ‘who else?’ question about one’s own heart as one’s companion.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Thus I became the protector of myself and of others besides, of all living beings, whether they move or not.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anathi tells how father, mother, brothers, sisters and loving wife all failed to relieve his pain, so that he learned to become his own protector.
jainism.tie_back: As in the Kural, when trouble comes, no outside companion can take the place of one’s own self.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.35, with 20.23-30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “He alone is called your companion, who will not be separated from you, here or hereafter.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan defines a true companion as the one who never leaves, which in Gurbani is God (and His Name).
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks who will stand by us in sorrow if our own heart does not; Gurbani answers that the only sure companion is the One who never departs.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 677, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Lying awake in his own palace among the suitors, Odysseus strikes his breast and speaks to his heart, telling it to endure, since it had endured worse on the day the Cyclops devoured his companions.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows a hero turning to his own heart as companion and support in a hard hour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus’s heart stands by him as the Kural says one’s heart should; the wife’s, sadly, does not.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 20.17-21 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that the good person is of one mind with himself and is his own best friend, while the bad are at variance with themselves and cannot even be friends to themselves.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, being a friend to oneself is the root of every other friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s plight is the divided self Aristotle describes: her own heart is not her friend.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.4 and IX.8 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Viktor Frankl holds on to the image of his wife in the camps
real_life_example.event: The Viennese psychiatrist Viktor Frankl was deported with his family in 1942 to Theresienstadt and in 1944 to Auschwitz; his wife later died at Bergen-Belsen. In his book Man’s Search for Meaning (1946) he described marching to a work site in the dark when a fellow prisoner whispered about their wives, and how his own mind then clung to his wife’s image with great vividness. He wrote that this inner image sustained him and taught him that love is the highest goal a person can aspire to.
real_life_example.explanation: Stripped of everything else, Frankl found that what he carried in his own heart could still keep him company in suffering.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks who will stand by one in sorrow if one’s own heart will not; Frankl’s experience shows the other side of the same truth, a heart that did stand by him when nothing else could.

tamil:
தஞ்சம் தமரல்லர் ஏதிலார் தாமுடைய
நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி.
transliteration:
Thanjam thamarallar aedhilaar thaamudaiya
nenjam thamaral vazhi.
meaning: When your own heart does not act like your family, it is no surprise that strangers do not either.
elementary: If even your own feelings won’t be kind to you, you can’t be surprised when people you hardly know aren’t kind either. The wife says that since her heart has left her, she can hardly blame others for not standing by her.
university: Tañcam here is glossed by the commentators as ‘easy, a slight matter’ (eḷitu): Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read ‘it is easy (natural) for strangers (ētilār) not to be kin (tamar allar) when one’s own heart (tām uṭaiya neñcam) is not kin’. Puliyur Kesikan agrees, calling it ‘natural’ (iyalpāṉatē). Sivayogi Sivakumar instead takes tañcam in its other sense, ‘refuge’: ‘there is no kin to give refuge if one’s own heart is not one’s own’, a variant reading of the same text. Pope renders ‘A trifle is unfriendliness by aliens shown, / When our own heart itself is not our own!’ The couplet closes the chapter by turning the wife’s quarrel into a general truth about the self; it is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For him who has conquered the mind, the mind is the best of friends; but for one who has failed to do so, his very mind will be the greatest enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that one’s own mind can be the closest friend or the worst enemy.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same: when one’s own heart is not kin, it is a greater blow than any stranger’s coldness.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.6 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that a person divided within cannot stand firm in anything.
christianity.tie_back: The wife, at odds with her own heart, finds she can expect little steadiness from anyone else.

islam.quote_or_event: “And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart and that to Him you will be gathered.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that a person does not fully command even his own heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker has found exactly this: her heart is not wholly her own.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The heart knoweth its own bitterness; and with its joy no stranger can intermeddle.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that each heart lives its own inner life that outsiders cannot share.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural draws on the same contrast between one’s own heart and strangers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither mother, father, nor any other relative can do one greater good than one’s own well-directed mind.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha ranks one’s own well-directed mind above any kinsman as a source of good.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural makes the same comparison: one’s heart should be closer kin than any relative or stranger.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that no outside enemy harms a person as much as his own misdirected self.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural likewise finds one’s own heart a worse betrayer than any stranger.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that mastering one's own mind is the key that sets right one's relation to the whole world.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says that when one's own heart is not kin, strangers will not be either; Japji likewise makes the mind the starting point for everything outside it.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib (Pauri 28), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Euripides’ Medea, before her terrible act, says that she understands the evil she is about to do, but her passion (thumos) is stronger than her reasoning.
greek_mythology.explanation: Medea’s own heart overrules her and becomes her worst enemy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, when one’s own heart is not on one’s side, nothing outside can make up for it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Augustine marvels that the mind commands the body and is obeyed at once, but when the mind commands itself it is resisted.
philosophy.explanation: Augustine finds the strangest disobedience not in others but within his own will.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife discovers the same: the one who will not obey her is her own heart, so strangers’ coldness is no surprise.

real_life_example.event_title: Beethoven writes the Heiligenstadt Testament
real_life_example.event: On 6 October 1802, in the village of Heiligenstadt outside Vienna, Ludwig van Beethoven wrote a long letter to his brothers Carl and Johann that has become known as the Heiligenstadt Testament. In it he explained that people who thought him unfriendly, stubborn or misanthropic misjudged him, because they did not know the secret cause of his behaviour, his growing deafness. He wrote that such experiences had brought him to the edge of despair.
real_life_example.explanation: Beethoven’s own failing hearing cut him off from people, and the people around him, not knowing why, turned against him in their judgements.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that when even one’s own heart will not act like kin, it is no wonder strangers do not, and Beethoven found that when his own body failed him, outsiders also failed to understand him.

tamil:
புல்லா திராஅப் புலத்தை அவர்உறும்
அல்லல்நோய் காண்கம் சிறிது.
transliteration:
Pullaa thiraaap pulaththai avar-urum
allalnoai kaankam siridhu.
meaning: Hold back your hug and sulk a little. Then we can watch, for a short while, the pain of love that he goes through.
elementary: Imagine a friend comes home very late after promising to be early. Your sister whispers, ‘Pretend to be a tiny bit upset for a minute, so he sees how much he was missed.’ It is a small, gentle game, not real anger, and it only lasts a moment.
university: The chapter on pulavi (a lovers’ sulk within married love, kaṟpu) opens with the speaker, read as the confidante (tōḻi), urging the wife: pullātu irā (‘remain without embracing’) and pulattai (‘sulk’), so that ‘we’ may see (kāṇkam) for a little (ciṟitu) the allal nōy (‘anguished love-sickness’) he will feel. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesikan all gloss it this way, the first-person plural binding the confidante to the wife’s side, and Pope’s verse likewise asks her to stay reserved and decline his proffered love so as to prove his distress a little while. The limiting word ciṟitu anticipates the next couplet’s warning that the sulk must not be prolonged. ytamizh.com prints அவர்உறும் where thirukkural.net prints the joined form அவருறும், a difference of word division only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna, wishing to see his queen Rukmini’s face in loving pique, teases her by suggesting she would have done better to marry a king of her own rank; she is so stricken that she faints, and he at once lifts her up and consoles her.
hinduism.explanation: The god himself plays a brief game of provocation to see how deeply his beloved feels, then ends it quickly with tenderness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s confidante proposes the same short test from the other side: hold back a little and see how much he cares.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
christianity.explanation: The bride is slow to open the door to her beloved, and by the time she does he has gone, leaving her searching in distress.
christianity.tie_back: The Song shows how a moment of holding back makes the lover’s absence felt sharply, which is the effect the Kural’s confidante wants to produce in the husband.

islam.quote_or_event: In his treatise on love, Ibn Hazm describes a kind of ‘breaking off’ (hajr) that lovers adopt playfully, out of coquetry, and says that such feigned avoidance can be sweeter than many a meeting.
islam.explanation: The Andalusian scholar treats mock coldness between lovers as part of love’s pleasure rather than a real rupture.
islam.tie_back: The confidante’s advice is exactly this kind of playful, temporary coldness meant to be enjoyed rather than to wound.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapter on Breaking Off (paraphrase; tr. A.J. Arberry)

judaism.quote_or_event: When his brothers come to Egypt, Joseph hides who he is, speaks roughly to them and tests them, turning aside to weep in private before he finally reveals himself.
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s concealment lets him see how his brothers really feel, though it costs him tears of his own.
judaism.tie_back: Like the sulking wife, Joseph holds back his embrace for a little while to see the other side’s heart, then ends the test in reunion.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada warns that those who keep thinking ‘he abused me, he wronged me’ never quiet their resentment, while those who let such thoughts go find peace.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism treats dwelling on a grievance, even a small one, as something that feeds suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural enjoys a little staged grievance; the Dhammapada would gently caution that even play-resentment should be dropped quickly.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga Sutra teaches that all beings are fond of life, like pleasure and hate pain, so a mendicant should cause pain to none.
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics extends non-harm (ahimsa) even to the small pains we cause others in thought and word.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural takes playful pleasure in a lover’s brief distress, which Jain teaching on non-harm would treat with caution rather than delight.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra 1.2.3 (paraphrase; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “It is so long since this rainbird has had even a glimpse of water.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan compares the soul's long longing for the Guru to the rainbird thirsting for rain.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's confidante wants the husband to feel the ache of love for a while; Gurbani gives the same ache of longing, though felt by the devotee rather than inflicted on another.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus finally returns, Penelope will not run to embrace him; she holds back and tests him by ordering their bed moved, and only when he protests that it cannot be moved does she weep and embrace him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope’s cool reserve draws out a burst of feeling from her husband that proves who he is.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife, Penelope withholds her embrace for a little while and watches his distress before yielding.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld observes that absence lessens moderate passions and increases great ones, as the wind puts out candles but fans a fire.
philosophy.explanation: A little distance, he suggests, reveals how strong a love really is.
philosophy.tie_back: The confidante’s plan rests on the same insight: a brief coldness will show, and even heighten, how much he loves.

real_life_example.event_title: Martin Luther teases Katharina about her worrying
real_life_example.event: In early 1546 Martin Luther was away from home at Eisleben, the town of his birth, while his wife Katharina von Bora stayed in Wittenberg and worried about him. On 10 February he wrote to her with mock solemnity, addressing her as an anxious lady and doctor, and joked that ever since she had started worrying, a fire had nearly broken out at their inn and that her holy worries might make the very earth swallow him up. He told her to pray and leave the worrying to God. Luther died at Eisleben eight days later, on 18 February 1546.
real_life_example.explanation: Luther’s teasing turned his wife’s anxious fussing into a shared joke, a playful exchange that only works between two people secure in each other’s love.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural advises a small, gentle show of displeasure so that the loved one’s longing can be seen for a moment; Luther’s playful mock-complaint about Katharina’s worrying is the same kind of light, loving game.

tamil:
உப்பமைந் தற்றால் புலவி அதுசிறிது
மிக்கற்றால் நீள விடல்.
transliteration:
Uppamain thatraal pulavi adhusiridhu
mikkatraal neela vidal.
meaning: A little sulking is like the right amount of salt in food. Letting it go on too long is like putting in too much salt.
elementary: A pinch of salt makes soup taste wonderful, but too much salt spoils it. A small, short sulk between people who love each other is like that pinch; a long one ruins everything.
university: The famous image here is culinary: pulavi is uppu amaintaṟṟu (‘like salt properly set’ in food), but to let it lengthen (nīḷa viṭal) is like salt that has become a little excessive (atu ciṟitu mikkaṟṟu). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read ciṟitu with mikku (‘even slightly too much’), stressing how quickly the right measure is lost, while Kalaignar reads the measure as the interval between quarrel (ūṭal) and reunion (kūṭal), and Solomon Pappaiah relates it to the joy of union it is meant to season. The couplet is generally taken as the confidante’s counsel to the wife, balancing the previous verse’s encouragement. Pope renders ‘A cool reserve is like the salt that seasons well the mess, / Too long maintained, ’tis like the salt’s excess.’ ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Radha’s friend urges her not to keep up her proud anger (mana) against Krishna, who has come to her humbly, warning her that by being harsh to one so gentle she only hurts herself.
hinduism.explanation: The sakhi plays exactly the Kural confidante’s role, telling the heroine that her pique has gone on long enough.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the salt warning in Sanskrit lyric form: a little pique adds savour, but prolonged pride spoils the love it was meant to season.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Sarga 9 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Barbara Stoler Miller)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows that anger may arise but insists it must not be carried past the end of the day.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural accepts a little sulking but, like Paul, sets a firm limit on how long it may last.

islam.quote_or_event: “It is not lawful for a man to desert his brother Muslim for more than three nights. (It is unlawful for them that) when they meet, one of them turns his face away from the other, and the other turns his face from the former, and the better of the two will be the one who greets the other first.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet sets a strict time limit on estrangement and praises whoever ends it first.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s salt image makes the same point: a short coolness is tolerable, a prolonged one corrupts the relationship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For His anger is but for a moment, His favour is for a life-time; weeping may tarry for the night, but joy cometh in the morning.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes divine anger as brief and divine favour as lasting.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural wants love’s anger in the same proportion: a moment of sulk inside a lifetime of affection.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the monk Sona strains too hard in his practice, the Buddha reminds him that a lute is neither in tune nor playable when its strings are too tight or too slack, but only when they are evenly tuned.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches balance: too much or too little effort both spoil the practice.
buddhism.tie_back: The lute string and the Kural’s salt teach the same lesson of right measure, applied here to a lovers’ sulk.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra teaches that anger destroys affection, pride destroys humility, deceit destroys friendship and greed destroys everything.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching names anger (krodha) and pride (mana) as passions that eat away at relationships.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a sulk kept up too long, like over-salting, destroys the affection it was meant to spice.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 8.38 (some editions 8.37; paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak names gentle sweetness and humility as the heart of good conduct.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says a lovers' sulk is good only in small measure, like salt; Gurbani points to the same balance, keeping sweetness rather than letting pride or sourness take over.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Asa di Vaar, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Angered over the loss of Briseis, Achilles withdraws to his tent and refuses even the generous amends Agamemnon’s envoys bring, prolonging his wrath until it costs the life of his dearest friend Patroclus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles’ wrath, held too long, turns from a just grievance into a disaster.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s too-much-salt in epic form: a grievance nursed beyond its measure ruins what it was meant to defend.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle places good temper at the mean in anger and describes ‘sulky’ people as hard to appease, holding their anger a long time.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the virtuous person feels anger at the right things, toward the right people, and for the right length of time.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s salt is Aristotle’s mean in the kitchen: the right amount of sulk at the right moment, and not a moment longer.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.5 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Chopin and George Sand’s rift is never mended
real_life_example.event: The composer Frédéric Chopin and the novelist George Sand were together for nearly a decade, spending their summers at her country house at Nohant. A family dispute arising from the marriage of Sand’s daughter, Solange, strained their relationship, and in 1847 it ended bitterly. By 1848 the rift was complete, and, as Britannica puts it, pride prevented either of them from making the reconciliation both actually wanted; Chopin, already in poor health, died in 1849.
real_life_example.explanation: A quarrel that might have passed was allowed to harden until it could no longer be undone, ending one of the best-known partnerships of the Romantic era.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says a lovers’ sulk is like salt, good in the right measure but ruinous when it runs on too long, and Chopin and Sand let their quarrel run on until it spoiled everything.

tamil:
அலந்தாரை அல்லல்நோய் செய்தற்றால் தம்மைப்
புலந்தாரைப் புல்லா விடல்.
transliteration:
Alandhaarai allalnoai seydhatraal thammaip
pulandhaaraip pullaa vidal.
meaning: Not hugging and making up with the one who is sulking is like adding fresh pain to someone who is already suffering.
elementary: If your little sister is sad and pretending not to talk to you, and you just walk away, she feels even worse than before. A hug at the right moment is what she was secretly waiting for.
university: The address now turns to the husband: to leave unembraced (pullā viṭal) those who have sulked with him (tammaip pulantār) is like inflicting allal nōy (‘anguish, sickness’) on alantār, ‘those already distressed.’ Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss ‘not dispelling the sulk and embracing’ (ūṭal uṇarttit taḻuvāmal), Solomon Pappaiah names the wife explicitly, and Puliyur Kesikan calls such neglect a cruelty; the point is that the sulk is itself a symptom of the pain of separation, so ignoring it compounds that pain. Pope’s explanation reads ‘For men not to embrace those who have feigned dislike is like torturing those already in agony.’ The two web texts agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Krishna comes to Radha in her anger and pleads with her at length, begging her to give up her pique, offering himself to any punishment she chooses, and asking her to place her foot on his head as a sign of forgiveness.
hinduism.explanation: The divine lover does not leave his beloved to her sulk; he humbles himself to end it.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the response the Kural asks of the husband: go to the one who sulks and reconcile, rather than adding to her pain.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Sarga 10 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Barbara Stoler Miller)

christianity.quote_or_event: “As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb lists actions that make a bad situation worse for someone already hurting.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural also uses a comparison to show that ignoring a hurting partner adds pain to pain.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if a woman fears from her husband contempt or evasion, there is no sin upon them if they make terms of settlement between them - and settlement is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an urges spouses who drift apart to seek reconciliation, declaring that settlement is best.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise tells the husband that the right response to his wife’s withdrawal is to make peace, not to leave her alone.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rav says: A person must always be careful about mistreatment of his wife. Since her tear is easily elicited, punishment for her mistreatment is immediate.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud warns husbands that a wife’s hurt is close to the surface and wronging her carries quick consequences.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural gives the husband the same warning: his sulking wife is already in pain, and neglect only deepens it.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59a (William Davidson Edition, Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: Finding a monk lying sick and neglected in his own filth, the Buddha and Ananda wash and tend him, and the Buddha tells the monks that whoever would tend him should tend the sick.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha makes caring for the suffering a duty and rebukes those who leave a sufferer alone.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly condemns leaving someone already in distress without the comfort they need.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra names four attitudes to cultivate: friendliness toward all beings, joy at the virtuous, compassion (karunya) toward the afflicted, and equanimity toward the ill-behaved.
jainism.explanation: Compassion toward those already suffering is a core Jain disposition.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband is asked for exactly this compassion toward a partner whose sulk is itself a form of suffering.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.11 (Digambara numbering; 7.6 in the Svetambara recension) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Humility is the word, forgiveness is the virtue, and sweet speech is the magic mantra.”
sikhism.explanation: Shaikh Farid teaches that humility, forgiveness and gentle words are what win the Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says it is cruel not to embrace and reconcile with one who is sulking; Farid's verse gives the forgiving, gentle way that ends such a rift.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Farid, Bhagat Shaikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Once Penelope has tested and recognized Odysseus, she runs to him in tears and embraces him, and he holds her weeping, the reunion as welcome as land to shipwrecked swimmers.
greek_mythology.explanation: The long estrangement and testing end in an embrace that heals both.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural insists that a sulk must end in such an embrace, since withholding it would only prolong pain.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch praises the Pythagoreans who, whenever anger led them to harsh words, would join right hands and embrace before the sun went down and be reconciled.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch holds up quick, physical reconciliation as the mark of people bound by real affection.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural asks the husband for the same prompt embrace that ends a quarrel before it hardens.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, On Brotherly Love (De fraterno amore), Moralia (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Gandhi nearly turns Kasturba out of the house, then shuts the gate
real_life_example.event: In early 1898, at the Gandhis’ home in Durban, a Christian Indian guest of so-called untouchable parentage left his chamber pot to be emptied, and Gandhi expected Kasturba to help clean it. She carried it out but was in tears and angry, and Gandhi, furious that she did not do it cheerfully, took her by the hand and dragged her to the gate meaning to push her out. Weeping, she asked whether he had no sense of shame and where she could possibly go; ashamed, he shut the gate, and he later wrote that their many quarrels always ended in peace.
real_life_example.explanation: Gandhi later presented the incident as one of the most shameful of his life, a moment when he added to his wife’s distress instead of easing it.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that refusing to embrace and reconcile a hurt and sulking partner is like heaping fresh pain on someone already suffering, which is what Gandhi came to see he had done before he shut the gate.

tamil:
ஊடி யவரை உணராமை வாடிய
வள்ளி முதலரிந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Ooti yavarai unaraamai vaatiya
valli mudhalarin thatru.
meaning: Not making up with the one who is sulking is like cutting the root of a vine that is already drooping.
elementary: A thirsty plant droops when it needs water. If, instead of watering it, someone cut its root, it would never recover. Someone who is sulking is like that drooping plant: they need care, not to be ignored.
university: Ūṭiyavarai uṇarāmai, ‘not making those who sulk understand (and so ending the sulk),’ is likened to cutting at the root (mutal arital) a valli creeper that is already wilted (vāṭiya). Uṇartal here is the technical term for appeasing a lover’s sulk by explanation and tenderness; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss ‘without showing love,’ while Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah add that the creeper had already withered for want of water, so the cutting destroys any chance of recovery. The image completes the previous couplet: the sulk is a sign of a love already parched by separation, and neglect kills it outright. Pope renders the explanation ‘Not to reconcile those who have feigned dislike is like cutting a faded creeper at its root.’ The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Where the female relations live in grief, the family soon wholly perishes; but that family where they are not unhappy ever prospers.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu tie the survival of a household to the contentment of its women.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s withering creeper is the same warning in a single image: a grieving partner left uncomforted means the family’s love dies at the root.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.”
christianity.explanation: Matthew applies Isaiah’s prophecy to Jesus, who does not crush what is already weak and fading.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s plant image says the same: what is already drooping should be restored, not cut down.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes marriage as a bond meant to be sustained by affection and mercy.
islam.tie_back: Neglecting a sulking partner withholds the very mercy that keeps this bond alive, as the Kural’s cut creeper shows.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, behold, I will allure her, And bring her into the wilderness, And speak tenderly unto her.”
judaism.explanation: Hosea pictures God, the estranged husband of Israel, winning back his alienated bride with tender words rather than abandoning her.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural asks the husband to do the same: woo back the one who has withdrawn instead of letting the bond wither.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the monks of Kosambi quarrel bitterly, the Buddha urges them to reconcile and teaches that hatred is never appeased by hatred, but only by non-hatred.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats lingering estrangement as something that destroys community unless met with goodwill.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns that a quarrel left unhealed destroys the relationship at its root.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain Ramayana, Prince Pavananjaya, stung by a slight on his wedding day, neglects his wife Anjana for years while she pines; on campaign he sees a chakravaka bird crying for its lost mate, realizes his cruelty, and hurries back to her.
jainism.explanation: The story shows a husband who nearly destroys his marriage through stubborn neglect and is brought back by an image of grieving love.
jainism.tie_back: Pavananjaya’s neglect of the pining Anjana is the Kural’s withered creeper cut at the root, narrowly averted.
jainism.source: Vimalasuri, Paumacariya (Anjana-Pavananjaya episode; paraphrase; also in Hemacandra’s Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra, book 7)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger.”
sikhism.explanation: Shaikh Farid tells the seeker to meet hurt with kindness rather than anger.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural warns that failing to soothe a sulking partner is like cutting a wilting creeper at the root; Farid likewise asks us to heal a wounded bond with kindness instead of harshness.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Farid, Bhagat Shaikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Echo, rejected by Narcissus, wastes away in grief until only her voice remains.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows love that is spurned withering until nothing of the lover is left.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wilting creeper cut at the root is the same fate: love ignored does not survive.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle quotes the saying that lack of conversation has broken many a friendship, noting that friends who do not meet and share their lives let affection fade.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, even good friendships need active upkeep or they die away.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same about love: if the sulking partner is not drawn back, the bond withers at its root.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.5 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.D. Ross)

real_life_example.event_title: Charles Dickens separates from his wife Catherine
real_life_example.event: Charles Dickens married Catherine Hogarth in 1836, and they had nine children who survived infancy. After years of growing unhappiness he separated from her in May 1858, and from then on she lived apart from him. A painful public scandal followed, during which, according to Britannica, Dickens did not act with tact, patience or consideration; he even printed a public statement about the separation in his magazine Household Words on 12 June 1858, while Catherine kept a dignified silence.
real_life_example.explanation: Instead of seeking to soothe a wife who was already hurt, Dickens cut her off completely and publicly.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that failing to soothe and win back the one who is hurt is like cutting at the root a creeper that is already wilting, and Dickens’s handling of the separation cut the marriage off at its root.

tamil:
நலத்தகை நல்லவர்க்கு ஏஎர் புலத்தகை
பூஅன்ன கண்ணார் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Nalaththakai nallavarkku aeer pulaththakai
pooanna kannaar akaththu.
meaning: Even for good men with fine qualities, the real beauty is the sulking that rises in the hearts of their wives with flower-like eyes.
elementary: A kind, good person is like a fine house. What makes the house feel truly loved is that someone inside cares enough to be a little upset when you are late. That small fuss is a sign of how much you matter.
university: Nalattakai nallavar are ‘good men of excellent quality’; their ēr (‘beauty, ornament’) is the pulattakai (‘the excellence of sulking’) that arises akattu (‘within,’ in the heart) of pū aṉṉa kaṇṇār, ‘those with flower-like eyes.’ The paradox is that the husband’s virtues are crowned not by praise but by his beloved’s pique, which proves her attachment; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it this way, Solomon Pappaiah speaks of the abundance of sulking in the wife’s mind, and Kalaignar says such pique ‘adds beauty’ to noble lovers. Pope translates ‘Even to men of good and worthy mind, the petulance / Of wives with flowery eyes lacks not a lovely grace.’ ytamizh.com divides நல்லவர்க்கு ஏஎர் and பூஅன்ன, while thirukkural.net prints the sandhi forms நல்லவர்க் கேஎர் and பூவன்ன.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Harivamsa, Satyabhama, roused to jealousy when Krishna gives a celestial flower to Rukmini, retires in sulking anger, and Krishna, the ideal husband, appeases her by promising to bring her the whole Parijata tree from heaven.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna’s greatness is displayed precisely in how he honours and answers his queen’s pique.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural says, a good man’s glory is shown in the loving pique of his wife and in his response to it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.”
christianity.explanation: The epistle tells husbands to live with understanding and to honour their wives as co-heirs.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise measures a good husband by how he receives his wife’s feelings, including her pique.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet is reported to have said that the best of people are those who are best to their families, and that he was the best of them to his own family.
islam.explanation: A man’s true excellence is measured inside his home, by how he treats his wife.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly locates a good man’s real beauty in his relationship with his wife and her feelings toward him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my bride; Thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, With one bead of thy necklace.”
judaism.explanation: The lover is overcome by a single glance of his bride’s eyes.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too gives the power to the beloved’s eyes, likened to flowers, whose moods shape her husband’s happiness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta, the Buddha teaches that a husband should minister to his wife by honouring her, not disparaging her, being faithful, handing over authority in the home and providing her with adornments.
buddhism.explanation: A good layman’s virtue is shown in how respectfully he treats his wife.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural locates a good man’s ornament in his wife’s feelings; the sutta shows the respect that makes such loving pique safe to express.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tamil Jain epic Jivaka Chintamani follows its hero through a series of courtships and marriages, portraying each bride’s feelings with care before Jivaka finally renounces the world.
jainism.explanation: Jain literature can depict married love vividly, though it treats it as a stage on the way to renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural celebrates a wife’s pique as a husband’s ornament, a valuation Jain narrative would admire as poetry but not as a final goal.
jainism.source: Tiruttakkatevar, Jivaka Chintamani (general paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Wear these three robes, O sister, and you will captivate your Husband Lord.”
sikhism.explanation: Following his lines on humility, forgiveness and sweet speech, Farid says these virtues are the soul-bride's true garments.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural calls a wife's loving pique the ornament of a good husband; Farid names the soul-bride's true ornaments as the virtues that win the Beloved.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Farid, Bhagat Shaikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the walls of Troy, Andromache reproaches Hector for his recklessness in battle and pleads with him to stay; he answers her tenderly, holding their son and comforting her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector’s nobility shines most clearly in the scene where his wife scolds him out of love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the hero’s best ornament is the loving reproach of his wife and his gentle reply.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Terence has a character remark that the quarrels of lovers are the renewal of love.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman playwright turns lovers’ anger into a sign of love’s vitality.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats a wife’s pique as something that adorns, rather than diminishes, a good man’s love.
philosophy.source: Terence, Andria, Act III, sc. 3 (amantium irae amoris integratio est; paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Clementine Churchill warns Winston about his manner
real_life_example.event: In June 1940, with France defeated and a German invasion feared, Clementine Churchill wrote to her husband, Prime Minister Winston Churchill, that a devoted member of his staff had told her he risked being disliked by colleagues and subordinates because of his rough, sarcastic and overbearing manner. She told him she had noticed the change herself and that he was not as kind as he used to be. She urged him to combine his great power with courtesy, kindness and calm; it is the only known letter between them from 1940.
real_life_example.explanation: Clementine’s loving rebuke, written at the height of national crisis, came from someone who cared enough about her husband to tell him what no one else dared.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that the true ornament of good men is the loving pique of their wives, and Clementine’s reproachful letter is a famous case of a wife’s affectionate displeasure helping to make a great man better.

tamil:
துனியும் புலவியும் இல்லாயின் காமம்
கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று.
transliteration:
Thuniyum pulaviyum illaayin kaamam
kaniyum karukkaayum atru.
meaning: Love without its deep sulks and light sulks is like fruit that is either too ripe or still hard and green.
elementary: A mango that is too soft and mushy is no good, and one that is still hard and green is no good either. Love that never has a single little disagreement is a bit like that: it has lost its just-right sweetness.
university: Two grades of lovers’ anger are named: tuṉi, the grown or deep sulk, and pulavi, the young or light sulk, as Solomon Pappaiah glosses them (vaḷarnta ūṭal and iḷam ūṭal); without them kāmam is like kaṉi (fruit gone too ripe) and karukkāy (fruit not yet ripe). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read both fruits as useless, the over-ripe one past its best and the unripe one inedible, while Kalaignar adds ‘rotten’ to the over-ripe fruit; some readers pair the two terms with the two fruits, but the commentators quoted take the comparison as a whole. Pope’s couplet, ‘Love without hatred is ripened fruit; / Without some lesser strife, fruit immature,’ makes that pairing explicit. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A much-quoted verse of Sanskrit poetics holds that love in union does not reach its fullness without love in separation, just as a cloth first treated with astringent takes a deeper dye.
hinduism.explanation: Indian aesthetic theory treats separation and pique (vipralambha, including mana) as what gives union its depth of flavour.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ripe-fruit image makes the same claim: without its quarrels, love lacks its full savour.
hinduism.source: Verse on śṛṅgāra cited in alaṅkāra works such as Viśvanātha’s Sāhityadarpaṇa (paraphrase; attribution not verified)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews teaches that what is painful at the moment can ripen into good fruit.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise sees love’s small pains as part of how it ripens.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an twice declares that with hardship comes ease.
islam.explanation: Difficulty and relief are presented as bound together in the divine order of things.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats the friction of sulking as inseparable from love’s sweetness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; A time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes sees both embracing and holding back as part of life’s proper seasons.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too gives holding back a place within love, without which love would lose its right ripeness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that attachment to the beloved brings pain, and advises freedom from both liking and disliking.
buddhism.tie_back: Where the Kural welcomes love’s little pains as part of its sweetness, the Dhammapada sees them as a reason to loosen attachment altogether.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain karma theory grades each passion, such as anger (krodha) and pride (mana), by intensity and duration, from the most binding kind that can last a lifetime down to the mildest, flickering kind that passes in about a fortnight.
jainism.explanation: Jainism carefully distinguishes deep from light passions, but treats all of them as binding karma to be overcome.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also distinguishes a deep sulk (tuni) from a light one (pulavi), though it values both where Jainism would seek to remove them.
jainism.source: Jain doctrine of the four grades of kashaya (e.g. Karmagrantha; summarized in P.S. Jaini, The Jaina Path of Purification) (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The color of my Lord's Love, however, is permanent, like the dye of the madder plant. So says Ravi Daas, the tanner.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas contrasts passing worldly attachments with the deep, fast colour of love for God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says love without its quarrels is like fruit too ripe or too green; Ravidas also speaks of love in its mature, lasting state, like a dye that does not fade.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 346, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros glukupikron, ‘sweet-bitter,’ a creature that cannot be fought off.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Sappho love is by nature a mixture of sweetness and pain.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural agrees that love without its bitter edge is not fully ripe.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho, fragment 130 (paraphrase; cf. tr. D.A. Campbell, Greek Lyric I)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that hatred which is fully overcome by love passes into love, and that the love is then greater than if hatred had not come before it.
philosophy.explanation: On Spinoza’s account, a conflict overcome can leave affection stronger than before.
philosophy.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that love’s quarrels, once resolved, make it richer, like fruit brought to the right ripeness.

real_life_example.event_title: Pablo Neruda publishes The Captain’s Verses anonymously
real_life_example.event: While in exile in Italy, the Chilean poet Pablo Neruda finished writing The Captain’s Verses on the island of Capri in 1952, addressing the poems to Matilde Urrutia. The collection contains poems of love, ecstasy and devotion, but also of fury, including lovers’ anger and quarrels. Later that year he published it anonymously in an edition of fifty copies, fourteen years before he and Matilde legally married.
real_life_example.explanation: Neruda’s book treated anger and quarrelling as part of the full experience of love rather than its opposite.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says love without its deeper quarrels and small sulks is like fruit that is over-ripe or still green, and Neruda’s love poems deliberately include fury alongside tenderness.

tamil:
ஊடலின் உண்டாங்கோர் துன்பம் புணர்வது
நீடுவ தன்றுகொல் என்று.
transliteration:
Oodalin untaangoar thunpam punarvadhu
needuva thandrukol endru.
meaning: Even in a lovers' sulk there is a kind of pain: the worry, "Will our time together last long enough?"
elementary: When you pretend to be cross with a friend during a sleepover, part of you worries, ‘What if this wastes our fun time together?’ The game is nice, but it also has a little worry inside it.
university: Ūṭalin uṇṭu āṅku ōr tuṉpam, ‘in sulking too there is a certain sorrow,’ namely the fear, puṇarvatu nīṭuvatu aṉṟu kol, ‘whether union will not last long.’ Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read nīṭuvatu as ‘prolonging, lasting’: the lovers fear that time lost to sulking shortens their time together. Pope’s verse instead asks ‘Will reunion sweet be long delayed?’, reading the worry as delay of reconciliation rather than brevity of union, and his prose explanation follows the same line; both readings keep the paradox that the sulk, meant to heighten love, carries its own anxiety. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Cloud Messenger, an exiled yaksha, separated from his wife for a year, frets over whether she is surviving the separation and sends a cloud to reassure her that their reunion will come.
hinduism.explanation: The poem is a long meditation on the anxiety that separation may cut love short.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s lovers feel a small version of the same fear: that their time apart, even in a sulk, might cost them their union.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb names the sickness of waiting for what one longs for and the joy of finally receiving it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s sulking lover feels exactly this ache of deferred union inside the game of pique.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi opens his Masnavi with the reed flute, which tells its tale by complaining of separation from the reed-bed it was cut from.
islam.explanation: The reed’s lament is Sufism’s classic image of longing for reunion with the beloved.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s lover, even while sulking, feels the reed’s pang: the fear of being kept from the beloved.
islam.source: Rumi, Masnavi I.1 ff. (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved lies awake searching for the one she loves and cannot find him.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover shares this anxious search for union, even when the separation is self-imposed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that loving attachment inevitably brings the fear of losing what one loves.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural observes this very fear inside love’s quarrel, though it accepts it as part of love rather than a reason to let go.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Uttaradhyayana Sutra teaches that one who is attached to pleasing objects is never free from anxiety, suffering in getting them, in keeping them and in losing them.
jainism.explanation: For Jainism, attachment (raga) carries its own built-in worry about loss.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover experiences exactly this worry, fearing the loss of union even in the middle of a playful sulk.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32 (paraphrase; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “If I forget my Beloved, even for an instant, suffering overtakes me and peace departs.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says even a moment away from the Beloved's remembrance brings pain.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's lovers feel a pain even inside a quarrel, fearing their time together will be cut short; Guru Nanak likewise treats any moment lost from the Beloved as loss.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 59, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Leading Eurydice up from the underworld, Orpheus, afraid she might be failing and eager to see her, looks back too soon and loses her forever.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s telling, the lover’s anxious fear of losing his beloved is what costs him their reunion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s lover carries a gentler form of the same fear, that union may slip away.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal describes a ‘second crystallization’ in love, born when doubt arises about whether one is loved, and says this anxious phase makes love far stronger.
philosophy.explanation: Stendhal treats the lover’s fear of losing the beloved as both painful and intensifying.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly finds a sorrow in the lovers’ quarrel that comes from fear for the union itself.
philosophy.source: Stendhal, On Love (De l’amour), Book I (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Shen Fu writes Six Records of a Floating Life
real_life_example.event: In 1809 Shen Fu, a man educated as a scholar who earned his living as a civil servant and art dealer, wrote Six Records of a Floating Life, a blend of autobiography and love story. Its first record, The Joys of the Wedding Chamber, describes his marriage to Yun, the artistic girl he had loved since childhood, and their shared pleasures. The third record, The Sorrows of Misfortune, tells of their money troubles and of Yun’s death.
real_life_example.explanation: Shen Fu’s memoir is one of the most famous portraits of married love in Chinese literature, and its happiness is shadowed throughout by how short their time together turned out to be.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that even in lovers’ small quarrels there is a hidden pain, the fear that their time together will not last long enough, and Shen Fu’s record of a loving marriage cut short gives that fear a real-life ending.

tamil:
நோதல் எவன்மற்று நொந்தாரென்று அஃதறியும்
காதலர் இல்லா வழி.
transliteration:
Noadhal evanmatru nondhaarendru aqdhariyum
kaadhalar illaa vazhi.
meaning: What use is it to feel sad when there is no loved one who will understand, "They are hurting because of me"?
elementary: If you sulk in your room, it only helps if someone who loves you notices and comes to ask what is wrong. If nobody notices at all, the sulking just makes you lonely.
university: Nōtal evaṉ maṟṟu, ‘what then is the use of grieving,’ when there are no kātalar, ‘lovers,’ who know it (aḵtu aṟiyum) as nontār eṉṟu, ‘she has grieved (because of us).’ Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take the lover’s grief as worthwhile only when the beloved recognizes himself as its cause; Kesikan adds that such a lover would then try to remove it. The verse states the precondition of the whole pulavi convention: a sulk is a message, and it needs a receiver. Pope’s prose explanation, ‘What avails sorrow when I am without a wife who can understand the cause of my sorrow?’, puts the words in the husband’s mouth, whereas the Tamil commentators leave the speaker general. ytamizh.com prints நொந்தாரென்று அஃதறியும் and thirukkural.net the sandhi form நொந்தாரென் றஃதறியும்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, the gopis of Vraja pour out their grief at Krishna’s absence to his messenger Uddhava, addressing a passing bee and asking what use their longing is when the one who caused it has gone away to the city.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis feel their grief is wasted unless the beloved knows and answers it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural states the same complaint: sorrow means little when the beloved does not recognize that it is for him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to share in one another’s feelings, so no one grieves alone.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural assumes the same need: grief has meaning only when someone who loves us shares and understands it.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob, grieving for Joseph, directs his complaint only to the One who truly knows and cares.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise holds that grief should be addressed to one who will understand it; without such a listener, it is wasted.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Look on my right hand, and see, For there is no man that knoweth me; I have no way to flee; No man careth for my soul.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist laments that no one recognizes him or cares about his distress.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s situation exactly: sorrow with no one who knows it is for them, and so no one to answer it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that one does not gain peace by weeping and lamenting; grieving only increases one’s pain and harms the body, and does nothing for the one mourned.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism sees lamentation as useless suffering that should be pulled out like an arrow.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also asks what grief accomplishes, though it answers that it helps only when a loving partner recognizes it.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Prince Neminatha turns back from his own wedding and renounces the world, his bride Rajimati grieves for the one who has left her, then follows him into the ascetic life.
jainism.explanation: Rajimati’s grief has no one to answer it, so she transforms it into renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks what grief is for when the beloved will not acknowledge it; Rajimati’s answer is to let it lead beyond worldly love.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22 (paraphrase; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Without water, she cannot live, even for an instant. God knows the suffering of her mind.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak compares the soul to a fish that cannot live without water, and says God knows its inner suffering.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural asks what use grieving is when no lover knows it is for him; Gurbani answers that the soul's grief is never unseen, because God knows the pain of the mind.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 60, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Abandoned by Theseus on the shore of Naxos, Ariadne pours out her lament to the empty sea and the winds, with no one to hear her complaint.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her grief is all the more bitter because the one who caused it is gone and cannot hear it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s grief without a knowing lover is exactly Ariadne’s situation on the deserted shore.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon writes that friendship doubles joys and cuts griefs in half, since no one shares a sorrow with a friend without grieving the less.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon sees grief as lightened only when another person receives it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s question rests on the same insight: sorrow has its use only when someone who loves us understands it.

real_life_example.event_title: Eleanor Roosevelt discovers the Lucy Mercer letters
real_life_example.event: In 1918 Eleanor Roosevelt discovered that her husband, Franklin D. Roosevelt, was romantically involved with her social secretary, Lucy Mercer. She offered him a divorce, but he refused, for reasons that included his political career and his mother’s financial support, and he agreed to stop seeing Mercer. He later resumed contact with Mercer, who was with him when he died at Warm Springs, Georgia, in 1945.
real_life_example.explanation: Eleanor’s grief produced a promise, but whether her husband truly understood the hurt he had caused is doubtful, since political reasons weighed heavily and the promise was not kept.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural asks what use grieving is when the beloved does not truly understand that the sorrow is his doing; Eleanor Roosevelt’s experience shows how hollow a reconciliation can be when that understanding is missing.

tamil:
நீரும் நிழலது இனிதே புலவியும்
வீழுநர் கண்ணே இனிது.
transliteration:
Neerum nizhaladhu inidhae pulaviyum
veezhunar kannae inidhu.
meaning: Water is sweet only when it is in the shade. In the same way, sulking is sweet only with those who truly love you.
elementary: Water in a sunny puddle gets hot and yucky, but water in a cool shady pond tastes lovely. A little sulk is only nice between people who love each other; with someone who does not care, it is just unpleasant.
university: Nīrum niḻalatu iṉitē, ‘even water is sweet only when in the shade,’ and pulaviyum vīḻunar kaṇṇē iṉitu, ‘sulking too is sweet only with (vīḻunar) those who desire/love.’ The emphatic -ē particles stress exclusivity: pique has its charm only inside a secure, mutual love. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss vīḻunar as those who show love; Solomon Pappaiah contrasts water under the sun with water under the shade; Kalaignar notes that water by the shade is cool. Pope renders ‘Water is pleasant in the cooling shade; / So coolness for a time with those we love.’ ytamizh.com divides நிழலது இனிதே, while thirukkural.net prints the metrical division நிழல தினிதே, the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Please tolerate the wrongs that I may have done to You and bear with me as a father with his son, or a friend with his friend, or a lover with his beloved.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna appeals to the special forbearance that exists within loving relationships.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that friction is sweet only within such relationships, where love bears it gladly.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 11.44 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb holds that hurt from someone who truly loves you is trustworthy, while sweetness from an enemy is not.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly says that a sulk is sweet only from those who love; its value depends on the love behind it.

islam.quote_or_event: “I know when you are pleased with me or angry with me.” … “When you are pleased with me, you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Muhammad,’ but when you are angry with me, then you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Abraham.’” Thereupon I said, “Yes (you are right), but by Allah, O Allah’s Messenger, I leave nothing but your name.”
islam.explanation: Aisha’s sulks with the Prophet are gentle and affectionate: even when cross she leaves out only his name, never him.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s sweet pique between those who love, where the anger is only skin deep and the love remains whole.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For whom the LORD loveth He correcteth, Even as a father the son in whom he delighteth.”
judaism.explanation: Correction is presented as a sign of love, not of rejection.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats a sulk as sweet because it comes from love; between strangers it would be only bitter.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: Reproof from the right person, a wise friend, is welcomed as treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural too says a reproach is sweet when it comes from the right person, one who loves.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Quitting your former connections place your affection on nothing; a monk who loves not even those who love him, will be freed from sin and hatred.”
jainism.explanation: Kapila’s verses tell the monk to give up affection even for those who love him.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural finds sweetness in pique only among those who love; Jain monastic teaching would set aside even that loving bond.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 8.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Those brides who enjoy their Husband Lord are very blessed, resting in the shade of the mango tree.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak pictures the soul-brides united with the Lord as resting at ease in cool shade.
