sikhism.tie_back: The Kural says water is sweet only in the shade, as sulking is sweet only with one who truly loves; Guru Nanak likewise pictures the shade of a secure, mutual love as where sweetness lives.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 762, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls on Aphrodite, who comes down smiling and gently asks what troubles her this time and whom she should persuade to love her.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess meets Sappho’s complaint with amused tenderness rather than annoyance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Complaint received with such loving indulgence is the Kural’s sweet pique: it is pleasant only where love already exists.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch argues that the true friend is known by his frank speech, which stings but heals, while the flatterer only pleases.
philosophy.explanation: For Plutarch, sharpness is welcome when it comes from genuine goodwill.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly says a lover’s sharpness is sweet only because it comes from real love.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend, Moralia (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Abigail Adams tells John to Remember the Ladies
real_life_example.place: Braintree, Massachusetts, and Philadelphia, United States
real_life_example.event: On 31 March 1776, while John Adams was at the Continental Congress in Philadelphia, Abigail Adams wrote to him from Braintree asking that in the new code of laws he would "Remember the Ladies" and be more generous to women than earlier lawmakers, warning playfully that women might start a rebellion of their own. John replied on 14 April that he could not help laughing at her extraordinary code of laws and teasingly called her saucy. Abigail answered on 7 May that she did not think him very generous to the ladies, since men proclaiming liberty for all still insisted on keeping absolute power over their wives.
real_life_example.explanation: The exchange mixes a serious argument for women’s rights with the affectionate teasing of a couple who were completely secure in each other.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural says that just as water is sweet only in the shade, a sulk is sweet only between those who truly love each other, and the Adamses’ spirited, mock-indignant letters show pique that delights because the love beneath it is never in doubt.

tamil:
ஊடல் உணங்க விடுவாரோடு என்நெஞ்சம்
கூடுவேம் என்பது அவா.
transliteration:
Oodal unanga viduvaaroadu en-nenjam
kooduvaem enpadhu avaa.
meaning: He leaves my sulk to dry up without comforting me, yet my heart still says, "Let us be with him." That is nothing but pure desire.
elementary: Sometimes a friend does not even notice you are upset, and yet you still want to play with them. Your heart just wants to be with them anyway. That is how strong caring can be.
university: Ūṭal uṇaṅka viṭuvār, ‘one who leaves (my) sulk to dry up and wither’ (uṇaṅku, ‘to wither, dry’), without soothing it; that my heart (eṉ neñcam) still says kūṭuvēm, ‘we shall unite,’ with such a person is avā, ‘longing, desire.’ Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read the wife as speaker, explaining her heart’s persistence as untameable desire, which links the chapter to the preceding one on quarrelling with one’s own heart. Pope’s verse, ‘Of her who leaves me thus in variance languishing,’ and his prose explanation take the husband as speaker; the Tamil itself leaves the gender open. ytamizh.com prints விடுவாரோடு என்நெஞ்சம் … என்பது அவா, and thirukkural.net the sandhi forms விடுவாரோ டென்னெஞ்சம் … என்ப தவா.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Blessed Lord said: It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material modes of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring, sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Asked what drives a person against their own will, Krishna names desire (kama) as the force behind it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker reaches the same diagnosis: what drives her heart toward one who neglects her is nothing but desire.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.37 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as enduring every slight and still hoping.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heart shows this endurance, still seeking union with one who has left its sulk unsoothed.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s romance, Majnun goes on longing for Layla through every obstacle and rejection, unable to turn his heart away even when union is impossible.
islam.explanation: Majnun’s love has become a desire beyond reason or reward.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker recognizes the same helpless longing in her own heart, which seeks union despite being neglected.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it; If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned.”
judaism.explanation: The Song declares that love cannot be put out by any obstacle.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart proves the point: not even the beloved’s neglect can quench its longing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From craving springs grief, from craving springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha identifies craving (tanha) as the root of the grief that comes with love.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker names her heart’s pull as avā, desire, the very craving the Dhammapada says breeds sorrow.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means.”
jainism.explanation: Kapila’s verses describe desire as something that only grows as it is fed.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker sees the same restless desire in her heart, which keeps seeking union even with one who neglects her.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 8.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Even if You cut my body apart, I shall not pull my limbs away from You.”
sikhism.explanation: Bhagat Kabir declares that no harshness from the Lord will make him draw away.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's heart still wants union with one who lets her sulk wither unsoothed; Kabir's devotion likewise clings to the Beloved whatever the treatment.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 484, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides, Dido writes to Aeneas as he prepares to abandon her, reproaching him yet still unable to stop loving him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Dido’s letter mixes complaint with a desire she cannot master.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker also still longs for one who leaves her hurt unsoothed, and calls it simply desire.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume argues that reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions, and can never by itself oppose a passion in directing the will.
philosophy.explanation: For Hume, desire, not reason, ultimately moves us.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker discovers the same thing: her judgment says the neglectful one deserves no union, but desire alone drives her heart.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.3 (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Heinrich Heine's hopeless love for his cousin Amalie
real_life_example.event: As a young man working in Hamburg in the business of his rich uncle Salomon Heine, the German poet Heinrich Heine fell in love with his cousin Amalie, a love that German reference works describe as quiet but hopeless. She did not return it, and when she became engaged to another man in 1821 his old love grew stronger than ever. That disappointed love fed some of the most tender poems in his Buch der Lieder (Book of Songs), published in 1827, which made him widely known.
real_life_example.explanation: Heine's longing outlived a plain refusal and turned into some of the best-known love poetry in German.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural calls it sheer desire when the heart still wants to be with one who leaves its sorrow unsoothed; Heine's heart kept turning to a cousin who gave it no comfort.

tamil:
பெண்ணியலார் எல்லாரும் கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்
நண்ணேன் பரத்தநின் மார்பு.
transliteration:
Penniyalaar ellaarum kannin podhu-unpar
nannen paraththa-nin maarpu
meaning: You unfaithful man! All women feast their eyes on your broad chest as if it belongs to everyone. So I will not come near it.
elementary: Imagine your favourite teddy bear being passed around the whole class until it no longer feels like yours. A wife in this poem playfully tells her husband that since everyone admires him, she will pretend she does not want to sit close to him.
university: The chapter title pulavi nuṇukkam means ‘the fine points (nuṇukkam) of love-sulking (pulavi)’: in the kaṟpu (wedded love) section, Valluvar sketches how a loving wife turns the smallest innocent word or act of her husband into a pretext for a mock quarrel, and Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes this first couplet as the wife’s own speech. She addresses him as paratta (‘man of wandering ways’) and says that all of feminine nature (peṇ-iyalār) ‘eat’ his chest with their eyes as a common possession (potu uṇpar), so she will not approach (naṇṇēn) it. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read the eye-feasting literally as other women’s admiring glances, while Solomon Pappaiah sharpens it into a charge that he is ‘shared’ with women of the street; Pope renders it ‘From thy regard all womankind enjoys an equal grace; O thou of wandering fickle mind, I shrink from thine embrace.’ The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the eighth canto of Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Krishna comes to Radha at dawn still showing the signs of a night spent with another cowherd girl, and Radha, cast as the wounded heroine (khandita), sends him away with bitter teasing: go to the one you were with.
hinduism.explanation: Radha’s anger is the classic Sanskrit picture of a beloved who refuses an embrace because her lover has been shared with others.
hinduism.tie_back: Like Radha, the Kural’s wife declares she will not come near a chest that, in her playful accusation, belongs to every woman.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that in marriage each spouse belongs to the other, so neither is a common possession.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s complaint rests on the same idea: her husband should be hers, not shared by every admiring eye.

islam.quote_or_event: “Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asks believers, with a parallel command for women in the next verse, to lower their gaze rather than feast their eyes on others.
islam.tie_back: The wife objects to exactly the kind of looking the verse forbids: other women feasting their eyes on her husband.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously, though she is thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.”
judaism.explanation: Malachi rebukes husbands who betray the wife of their youth and reminds them that she is their covenant partner.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife voices, in play, the same claim Malachi makes in earnest: a husband owes himself to his own wife.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha lists the ways a husband should care for his wife, including by honouring her, not despising her, and not being unfaithful to her.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist lay ethics make faithfulness one of a husband’s plain duties to his wife.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s teasing charge of ‘wandering’ presumes this same duty of faithfulness.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (tr. Narada Thera; paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you fall in love with every woman you see, you will be without hold like the Haṭha-plant, driven before the wind.”
jainism.explanation: The nun Rajimati rebukes Rathanemi, warning that a heart which goes after every woman it sees has no anchor.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife teases her husband as a ‘wanderer’ whose chest belongs to everyone, the same rootless love Rajimati condemns.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “The One God is our father; we are the children of the One God. You are our Guru.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that God belongs equally to all people, who are all His children.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife will not come near a chest she says all women gaze on as common property; Gurbani, by contrast, rejoices that the Lord is shared by all, with no room for jealousy.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 611, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, the goddess Calypso offers Odysseus immortality if he stays with her, but he tells her that, though Penelope cannot match her beauty, he still longs every day to go home.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus keeps his heart for his own wife even when another, more dazzling partner wants him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife wants exactly this: a husband who belongs to her, not to every woman who admires him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Pausanias distinguishes a ‘common’ (Pandemos) love, which attaches to anyone and loves the body more than the soul, from a ‘heavenly’ love that is faithful and lasting.
philosophy.explanation: Pausanias contrasts love that belongs to everyone and no one with love that is constant to one person.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s word potu (‘common’) makes the same contrast: she refuses a chest she pretends has become common property.

real_life_example.event_title: The Beatles appear on The Ed Sullivan Show
real_life_example.event: On the evening of 9 February 1964 the Beatles made their debut on the CBS programme The Ed Sullivan Show. About 73 million people tuned in, and the band played to a studio audience filled with screaming teenage fans. The appearance helped spread the craze that British newspapers had already named Beatlemania across the United States.
real_life_example.explanation: It is one of the best-documented moments when millions of admirers fixed their eyes on the same few performers at once, a kind of shared adoration that television made possible.
real_life_example.tie_back: The wife in this kural refuses to come near a man whom every woman already gazes at as if he belonged to all, and the screaming crowds of 1964 show what that kind of shared, public admiration looks like.

tamil:
ஊடி இருந்தேமாத் தும்மினார் யாம்தம்மை
நீடுவாழ் கென்பாக் கறிந்து.
transliteration:
Ooti irundhaemaath thumminaar yaamdhammai
neetuvaazh kenpaak karindhu
meaning: While I sat sulking, he sneezed. He knew I would have to break my silence and wish him a long life.
elementary: Imagine you are not talking to your brother after a squabble, and he pretends to sneeze so that you will say ‘Bless you!’ without thinking. Now you have spoken, and the game is over. That is the clever trick the husband plays here.
university: This couplet is the wife’s speech (talaivi kūṟṟu): ūṭi iruntēmā means ‘as we were sulking’, and she reports that he sneezed (tummiṉār) knowing (aṟintu) that we would say nīṭu vāḻka (‘live long’) to him. It rests on the old Tamil custom of blessing a person who sneezes, which forces the sulking wife to speak and so end her silence. Solomon Pappaiah adds that he sneezed deliberately and that she, despite herself, did bless him; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it the same way. Pope renders it ‘One day we silent sulked; he sneezed: the reason well I knew; he thought that I, to speak well pleased, would say, “Long life to you!”’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the ninth canto of the Gita Govinda, Radha’s friend urges her to drop her proud sulk (mana) toward Krishna, who is eager to make up, telling her not to be proud with Madhava.
hinduism.explanation: Sanskrit love poetry treats the beloved’s sulk as something that must eventually be coaxed into giving way.
hinduism.tie_back: The husband’s sneeze is his own trick for making the sulking wife give way and speak.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then he returned, and walked in the house to and fro; and went up, and stretched himself upon him: and the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.”
christianity.explanation: When Elisha revives the Shunammite’s son, the child’s sneezing is the first sign that life has returned.
christianity.tie_back: The sneeze in the Kural also signals life, which is why custom answers it with a wish for long life.

islam.quote_or_event: “If anyone of you sneezes, he should say ‘Al-Hamduli l-lah’ (Praise be to Allah), and his (Muslim) brother or companion should say to him, ‘Yar-hamuka-l-lah’ (May Allah bestow his Mercy on you).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes answering a sneeze with a blessing a duty of companionship.
islam.tie_back: The husband counts on just such a duty: a sneeze obliges the person beside you to bless you, even mid-quarrel.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The members of the house of Rabban Gamliel would not say good health when someone sneezed in the study hall, due to the fact that it would lead to suspension of study in the study hall.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud takes for granted that people wish ‘good health’ (marpe) to someone who sneezes, noting only one setting where it was skipped.
judaism.tie_back: The husband relies on the same reflex: a sneeze draws out a wish for health, here the Tamil ‘Live long!’.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 53a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Vinaya, when the Buddha sneezed while teaching, the monks called out ‘Long life to you, Lord!’; he asked whether such a wish could make anyone live or die and forbade monks to say it, but later allowed them to answer laypeople who wished them long life.
buddhism.explanation: The story records the same custom of answering a sneeze with ‘long life’, and the Buddha’s cool view of it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s whole joke depends on this very custom of wishing long life to someone who sneezes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As an impassioned deer allured (by a song) rushes into death, without being satisfied with the sound.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira’s teaching warns that the ear, like the eye, can be used to lure a being toward what it longs for.
jainism.tie_back: The husband’s sneeze is a sound used as a lure, drawing his wife out of her silence before she can stop herself.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Good omens and bad omens affect those who do not keep the Lord in the mind.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that one who remembers God is not ruled by signs and omens.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's husband sneezes to force his sulking wife to speak the customary blessing; Gurbani sets aside such customs around signs, saying they bind only those who forget God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 401, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, as Penelope speaks of the hoped-for return of Odysseus, Telemachus sneezes loudly so that the hall rings, and Penelope laughs and takes the sneeze as a good omen for her words.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Homer’s Greeks, a sneeze at a meaningful moment was a sign worth answering.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In the Kural too, a well-timed sneeze carries meaning and demands a response from the woman who hears it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The Aristotelian Problems asks why people regard a sneeze as sacred or divine while they do not treat a cough that way, and tries to explain the custom.
philosophy.explanation: Greek natural philosophy noticed that sneezes, unlike other bodily noises, were greeted with reverence and good wishes.
philosophy.tie_back: The husband exploits exactly this special status of the sneeze, which compels a blessing.

real_life_example.event_title: Fred Ott sneezes for Edison's camera
real_life_example.event: When a journalist from Harper's Weekly asked Thomas Edison's laboratory for someone to perform a sneeze for the Kinetograph camera, the mechanic Fred Ott agreed. W. K. L. Dickson and William Heise filmed his sneeze in the first week of January 1894, and the record was deposited for copyright at the Library of Congress on 9 January 1894 as Edison Kinetoscopic Record of a Sneeze. It became one of the most famous early motion pictures.
real_life_example.explanation: The sneeze was performed on purpose, at a request, so that it would be seen and noticed, which made an ordinary bodily act into a famous piece of film history.
real_life_example.tie_back: In the kural the husband sneezes on purpose, knowing it will force his sulking wife to speak, and Fred Ott's sneeze is a documented case of a sneeze made deliberately to get a reaction.

tamil:
கோட்டுப்பூச் சூடினும் காயும் ஒருத்தியைக்
காட்டிய சூடினீர் என்று.
transliteration:
Koattup-pooch chootinum kaayum oruththiyaik
kaattiya sootineer endru
meaning: Even if I wear flowers picked from a tree, she gets angry and says I put them on to show off to some other woman.
elementary: Suppose you wear a new cap to school and your best friend frowns, ‘Who are you trying to impress?’ You only wanted to look nice! The husband here wears flowers and his wife pretends he must be dressing up for someone else.
university: From here the speaker is generally taken to be the husband, reporting the ‘fine points’ of his wife’s sulking. Kōṭṭuppū means flowers that bloom on tree branches (kōṭu), as opposed to creeper or water flowers; even if he wears (cūṭiṉum) such a garland, she grows hot with anger (kāyum), saying ‘you wore them to show (kāṭṭiya) to some woman (oruttiyai)’. Puliyur Kesikan reads the line as the husband putting the flowers on her, while Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take him to be wearing them himself; Pope follows the latter: ‘She cries, “Pray, for what woman now do you put on your flowers?”’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Harivamsa and later retellings, Krishna gives a blossom of the heavenly Parijata tree to Rukmini, and Satyabhama, hurt that the flower went to another wife, sulks until Krishna promises to bring her the whole tree.
hinduism.explanation: The story makes a single flower the trigger for a queen’s jealous, sulking anger.
hinduism.tie_back: In the Kural, too, a garland of flowers is enough to make the wife suspect another woman.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs admits that love brings jealousy with it, burning as fiercely as love itself.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s quick flare of jealousy over a garland is a small spark of the fire this verse describes.

islam.quote_or_event: When one of the Prophet’s wives sent a dish of food to the house where he was staying, the wife of that house struck the servant’s hand so the dish broke; the Prophet gathered the pieces and said, “Your mother (my wife) felt jealous,” and replaced the dish.
islam.explanation: The Prophet met a wife’s sudden jealousy with gentle understanding instead of anger.
islam.tie_back: Like that broken dish, the garland in the Kural is an innocent object that jealousy turns into a grievance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wrath is cruel, and anger is overwhelming; but who is able to stand before jealousy?”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs ranks jealousy as harder to withstand than plain anger.
judaism.tie_back: The husband finds that no innocent explanation of his flowers can stand before his wife’s jealousy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that fondness for someone breeds fear of losing them.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s fear that the flowers are meant for another woman grows out of her very fondness for her husband.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you owned the beauty of Vaiśramaṇa, the pleasing manners of Nalakūbara, if you were like Purandara himself, I should have no desire for you.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati tells the would-be lover Rathanemi that no amount of beauty or charm will win her.
jainism.tie_back: The husband’s adornment likewise fails to soften his wife, who reads his flowers as a fault rather than a charm.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.41 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O soul-bride, without your Husband Lord, what good are your decorations?”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that the soul's adornments mean nothing unless they are for the Beloved.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife accuses her husband of wearing a garland to show some other woman; Gurbani also asks whom one's adornment is for, saying only the Beloved gives it meaning.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 18, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Women of Trachis, Deianira, afraid that Heracles has come to love the captive Iole, sends him a robe to win back his love, not knowing it is poisoned.
greek_mythology.explanation: The tragedy shows how a wife’s jealous fear, centred on clothing and adornment, can spiral out of control.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s scene is the gentle, comic version: an adornment provokes a wife’s suspicion of another woman.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines jealousy as hatred toward a loved object joined with envy of a rival, arising when we imagine the one we love being bound to another as closely as to us.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, jealousy begins in imagination: we picture the beloved united with someone else.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife imagines her husband dressing up for another woman, exactly the imagined rival Spinoza describes.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Prop. 35 and Scholium (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Othello, the play of the misread handkerchief, is staged at court
real_life_example.event: William Shakespeare wrote Othello in about 1603 to 1604. The Revels accounts for 1604 to 1605 record a performance of the Moor of Venis by the King's Men at the court of King James I, one of the earliest records of the play. In the story the villain Iago uses a handkerchief that Desdemona has innocently lost to persuade her husband Othello that she has given it to another man as a love token.
real_life_example.explanation: The play became one of the most famous studies of jealousy in world literature because it shows how an innocent object can be twisted into false proof of love for someone else.
real_life_example.tie_back: Like the wife in this kural who decides that a simple garland must have been worn to impress another woman, Othello reads an innocent handkerchief as a sign meant for a rival.

tamil:
யாரினும் காதலம் என்றேனா ஊடினாள்
யாரினும் யாரினும் என்று.
transliteration:
Yaarinum kaadhalam endraenaa ootinaal
yaarinum yaarinum endru
meaning: When I said, "We love each other more than anyone," she sulked and asked, "More than whom? More than whom?"
elementary: If you tell your friend, ‘You are my best friend, better than all the others,’ a cheeky friend might reply, ‘Which others? Who else is on your list?’ The wife turns her husband’s compliment into a question to tease him.
university: Yāriṉum kātalam means ‘we are lovers beyond anyone’; the husband meant it as the highest praise, but she seizes on yāriṉum (‘than anyone’) as if it implied a list of other women he loves less, and repeats yāriṉum yāriṉum (‘than whom? than whom?’). Solomon Pappaiah spells out her reading: she took him to mean that he loves many and her the most. The humour depends on the comparative form, which presupposes rivals; Kalaignar notes that she ‘misread a natural remark’. Pope renders it ‘“I love you more than all beside,” ’t was thus I gently spoke; “What all, what all?” she instant cried; and all her anger woke.’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Narada visits Krishna’s palaces in Dvaraka and finds him in each queen’s house at the same moment, wholly present with every one of them.
hinduism.explanation: The story imagines a love so complete that no wife is loved ‘more’ or ‘less’ than another.
hinduism.tie_back: It answers the wife’s teasing ‘more than whom?’ by picturing a love that needs no comparison at all.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as slow to take offence and unwilling to read bad meaning into what it hears.
christianity.tie_back: The wife does the opposite in play: she reads a hidden rival into her husband’s loving words.

islam.quote_or_event: “And you will never be able to be equal [in feeling] between wives, even if you should strive [to do so]. So do not incline completely [toward one] and leave another hanging.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an admits frankly that love cannot be measured out equally between people.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s ‘more than whom?’ seizes on this very idea that love can be ranked between rivals.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And he went in also unto Rachel, and he loved Rachel more than Leah.”
judaism.explanation: Genesis records Jacob’s love in comparative terms, and the rivalry between the two sisters follows directly from it.
judaism.tie_back: The husband’s ‘more than anyone’ sounds to his wife like Jacob’s ‘more than Leah’, a love that implies a rival.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who seeks another’s faults, who is ever censorious — his cankers grow. He is far from destruction of the cankers.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that a mind bent on finding fault keeps feeding its own unrest.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife hunts for a fault in a compliment, though here the fault-finding is a loving game.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is very fond of a lovely ‘colour,’ hates all others; hence a fool will suffer misery, but a dispassionate sage is not affected by it.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching observes that strong attachment to one thing breeds aversion to everything compared with it.
jainism.tie_back: The wife hears ‘more than anyone’ as a ranking that sets her against unseen others, the comparing mind this verse describes.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “You are the Primal Being, the Most Wonderful Creator. There is no other as Great as You.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Ram Das declares that God has no equal and cannot be compared with anyone.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife bristles at 'more than anyone', as if her husband were ranking her against others; Gurbani's praise of the Beloved avoids ranking because no one can stand beside Him.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 11, So Purakh (Raag Aasaa), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Zeus tells Hera that desire has never overcome him as it does now, not even for the wife of Ixion, nor Danae, nor Europa, nor Semele, nor Alcmene, nor Demeter, nor Leto, nor Hera herself before.
greek_mythology.explanation: Zeus tries to flatter Hera by comparing his love for her with a long list of other loves, comically naming the very rivals she resents.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s joke made explicit: loving someone ‘more than anyone’ invites the question ‘which others?’

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus teaches that people are disturbed not by things themselves but by their judgements about things.
philosophy.explanation: A word or event becomes upsetting only through the meaning we give it.
philosophy.tie_back: The husband’s compliment upsets the wife only because of the meaning she chooses to read into it.

real_life_example.event_title: One clause of the Treaty of Wichale is read two different ways
real_life_example.event: On 2 May 1889 Emperor Menilek II of Ethiopia signed a treaty of friendship and commerce with Italy at Wichale. The Italian text of Article XVII made Rome the channel for all of Ethiopia's foreign relations, while the Amharic text was only permissive, saying Ethiopia could use Italy's help if it wished. Italy used the Italian wording to claim a protectorate over Ethiopia, Menilek rejected that reading, and the treaty was finally cancelled by the Treaty of Addis Ababa in October 1896.
real_life_example.explanation: The episode is a classic example of how a small difference in wording can be read as implying something the other side never meant, with very large consequences.
real_life_example.tie_back: In this kural the wife seizes on the word than anyone and reads into it a list of rivals the husband never had in mind, just as one side at Wichale read a much bigger meaning into a single clause.

tamil:
இம்மைப் பிறப்பில் பிரியலம் என்றேனாக்
கண்நிறை நீர்கொண் டனள்.
transliteration:
Immaip pirappil piriyalam endraenaak
kannirai neerkon danal
meaning: When I said, "We will never be apart in this life," her eyes filled with tears, as if I meant we would part in the next life.
elementary: Imagine telling your grandmother, ‘I will visit you every day this summer!’ and she asks, sadly, ‘Only this summer?’ The wife hears ‘in this life’ and worries it means ‘not in the next one’.
university: Immaip piṟappil means ‘in this present birth’ and piriyalam ‘we shall not part’; the wife takes the limiting phrase to imply that in a later birth (maṟumai) they will part, and her eyes fill (kaṇ niṟai nīr koṇṭaṉaḷ). The couplet assumes the belief in rebirth shared by the Tamil tradition and depends on the idea that true lovers should remain together across births. Puliyur Kesikan, Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah all read it this way, while Kalaignar has her ask, more sceptically, whether there is a next birth at all. Pope: ‘“While here I live, I leave you not,” I said to calm her fears. She cried, “There, then, I read your thought”; and straight dissolved in tears.’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, when Yama comes to take the soul of Satyavan, his wife Savitri follows the god of death and, through her steadfast devotion and wisdom, wins her husband back from him.
hinduism.explanation: Savitri refuses to let even death part her from her husband.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife in the Kural weeps because she wants exactly what Savitri won: a union that does not end with this life.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya (Savitri story) (tr. K.M. Ganguli; paraphrase)

christianity.quote_or_event: “For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that marriage as we know it belongs to this age and does not continue in the same form after the resurrection.
christianity.tie_back: This is the very thought that makes the Kural’s wife weep: that the bond of this life might not carry into the next.

islam.quote_or_event: “Gardens of perpetual residence; they will enter them with whoever were righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their descendants.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an promises that righteous spouses will be reunited in Paradise.
islam.tie_back: It offers the hope the Kural’s wife longs for: that husband and wife will not be parted after this life.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Concerning anyone who divorces his first wife, even the altar sheds tears about him.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer teaches that the parting of husband and wife is so grievous that even the altar weeps.
judaism.tie_back: The wife’s tears at the mere thought of a future parting echo this rabbinic sense that separation of spouses calls for weeping.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 22a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “We want to see one another not only in the present life but also in the life to come.”
buddhism.explanation: Nakula’s parents tell the Buddha they wish to be together in future lives, and he explains that spouses matched in faith, virtue, generosity and discernment will meet again.
buddhism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural wife’s wish: not only this life together, but the next one too.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

jainism.quote_or_event: “Râgîmatî thought: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.’”
jainism.explanation: When Neminatha renounced the world on his wedding day, his bride Rajimati was overwhelmed with grief at being parted from him, and then followed him into the ascetic life.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife weeps at the mere thought of a parting; Rajimati lived that parting and met it by following her beloved on the same path.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.28-29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that this present human life is the precious opportunity for union with God.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's husband promises they will not part in this birth and his wife weeps at the limit; Gurbani also treats this present life as the decisive time for union.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, the old couple Baucis and Philemon ask the gods that they may die at the same hour so neither must see the other’s grave, and they are turned together into an oak and a linden.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their one wish is never to be parted, not even by death.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife weeps because she wants the same thing: a love that no life or death divides.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes imagines Hephaestus offering two lovers to weld them into one, so that they live as one and, when they die, remain one even in Hades.
philosophy.explanation: Aristophanes’ myth says lovers long to be united not only in life but beyond it.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s tears express the same longing: she will not settle for a union that ends with this life.

real_life_example.event_title: Etruscan artists make the Sarcophagus of the Spouses
real_life_example.event: In the Etruscan city of Cerveteri, artists modelled a nearly life-size terracotta sarcophagus showing a husband and wife reclining side by side on a banqueting couch, close and affectionate, as if sharing a meal. The work, now in the Louvre, has a nearly identical companion in the Villa Giulia museum in Rome, which was discovered near Cerveteri on 9 April 1881. Scholars note that the figures may once have held objects for the journey from this life to the next.
real_life_example.explanation: The sarcophagus is one of the best-known ancient images of a married couple who expected to stay together beyond death.
real_life_example.tie_back: The wife in this kural weeps because she hears in never part in this life a hint that they might part in the next, and the Etruscan couple show the opposite hope, of being together after this life too.

tamil:
உள்ளினேன் என்றேன்மற் றென்மறந்தீர் என்றென்னைப்
புல்லாள் புலத்தக் கனள்.
transliteration:
Ullinaen endraen-mat ren-marandheer endrennaip
pullaal pulaththak kanal
meaning: When I said, "I thought of you," she asked, "So you had forgotten me?" Then, instead of hugging me, she began to sulk.
elementary: If you tell your friend, ‘I remembered you today!’ a teasing friend might say, ‘Only today? So you forgot me yesterday?’ The wife plays the same word game with her husband.
university: Uḷḷiṉēṉ means ‘I recalled (you)’; the wife argues, as Mu. Varadarasanar puts it, that recalling presupposes forgetting (niṉaippukku muṉ maṟappu uṇṭu), so she asks eṉ maṟantīr (‘why did you forget?’), and, though about to embrace him (pullāḷ, ‘she did not embrace’), turns to sulking (pulattakkaṉaḷ). The logic is the same as in 1314: a loving word is pressed for an implication it never had. Solomon Pappaiah notes that she had begun to embrace him and stopped; Pope: ‘“Each day I called to mind your charms,” “O, then, you had forgot,” she cried, and then her opened arms, forthwith embraced me not.’ The line division reads மற் றென்மறந்தீர் on both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Shakuntala, King Dushyanta, under a curse, forgets his wife Shakuntala, and only the sight of the ring he gave her brings his memory and grief back.
hinduism.explanation: The drama turns on the anguish of a beloved who has been forgotten and the joy of being remembered again.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife treats even a passing lapse of memory as a small version of Shakuntala’s wound.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.”
christianity.explanation: God promises a love that never forgets, even more constant than a mother’s.
christianity.tie_back: The wife demands this kind of never-forgetting love, so that ‘I remembered you’ already sounds like a confession of forgetting.

islam.quote_or_event: “I know when you are pleased with me or angry with me… When you are pleased with me, you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Muhammad,’ but when you are angry with me, then you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Abraham.’” Aisha replied, “by Allah, O Allah’s Messenger, I leave nothing but your name.”
islam.explanation: Aisha’s anger at the Prophet only went as far as leaving out his name, while her love stayed whole.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise withholds only her embrace for a moment, while her love remains underneath the sulk.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: In the Song of Songs, the beloved hesitates to open the door, and by the time she does, her lover has gone.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Song, a moment of holding back between lovers, here the wife’s withheld embrace, interrupts their meeting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who harbor such thoughts do not still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that dwelling on supposed slights keeps resentment alive.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife holds onto an imagined slight, ‘you forgot me’, and so keeps the sulk going, though only in play.

jainism.quote_or_event: Mahavira’s teaching tells the ascetic not to watch the beauty, laughter and glances of women nor to keep a recollection of them in his mind.
jainism.explanation: For the Jain monk, deliberately not remembering the beloved is part of the discipline of chastity.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s scene runs the other way: for the loving wife, any gap in remembering is itself an offence.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Chanting it, I live; forgetting it, I die.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says remembering the Name is life and forgetting it is death.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife hears 'I thought of you' and asks, 'So you had forgotten me?'; Gurbani makes the same link between remembrance and forgetting central to love for God.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 9, So Dar (Raag Aasaa), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus finally returns, Penelope holds back from embracing him until he proves himself by the secret of their bed built around an olive tree; only then does she run to him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope deliberately withholds her embrace, testing her husband before she yields.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise stops short of embracing her husband, holding back to test him with her question.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle lists among the things that make people angry being slighted by those who forget us, even forgetting our names, because forgetting seems a sign that we do not matter to them.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle sees forgetting as a form of slight that naturally provokes anger.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s mock anger works on the same logic: if he had to ‘remember’ her, he must once have forgotten.

real_life_example.event_title: William Jones publishes Sacontala, or The Fatal Ring
real_life_example.event: In 1789 Sir William Jones published in Calcutta an English translation of Kalidasa's Sanskrit and Prakrit drama Shakuntala under the title Sacontala; or, The Fatal Ring. The play's Sanskrit title means Shakuntala recalled through recognition, and it turns on a king who must be brought to remember his wife with the help of a ring. Jones's translation was soon reprinted in London and Edinburgh and became widely influential in Europe.
real_life_example.explanation: The translation introduced Europe to one of the great love dramas of India, a story built around forgetting and remembering a beloved.
real_life_example.tie_back: The wife in this kural turns I remembered you into So you had forgotten me, and Shakuntala is the classic Indian drama of a lover who forgets and must be made to remember.

tamil:
வழுத்தினாள் தும்மினேன் ஆக அழித்தழுதாள்
யாருள்ளித் தும்மினீர் என்று.
transliteration:
Vazhuththinaal thumminen aaka azhiththazhudhaal
yaarullith thummineer endru
meaning: When I sneezed, she first wished me a long life. Then she took it back and cried, asking, "Who was thinking of you, that you sneezed?"
elementary: Some people say that when you sneeze, someone somewhere is thinking about you. Here the wife first says ‘Bless you!’, then suddenly cries, ‘Wait, who was thinking about you?’
university: The couplet turns on a second Tamil belief about sneezing: that one sneezes when someone is thinking of (uḷḷi) one. She first blesses him (vaḻuttiṉāḷ), as custom requires, then cancels it (aḻittu) and weeps (aḻutāḷ), asking yār uḷḷit tummiṉīr (‘thinking of whom did you sneeze?’, or ‘at whose thought’). Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss the blessing as the wish of ‘a hundred years’ (nūṟāṇṭu). Pope: ‘She hailed me when I sneezed one day; but straight with anger seized, she cried; “Who was the woman, pray, thinking of whom you sneezed?”’ The text matches on ytamizh.com (which omits the closing full stop) and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Bhagavad Gita traces how dwelling on something breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, thwarted desire breeds anger, and anger clouds judgement and memory.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita describes how quickly a loving mind can slide into anger and confusion.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife’s swift slide from blessing to suspicious tears is a small, comic instance of that chain.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.”
christianity.explanation: James notes how the same mouth can bless and then turn to reproach.
christianity.tie_back: The wife does just that: her mouth blesses her husband and, a moment later, accuses him.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns against building suspicion on mere guesses about others.
islam.tie_back: The wife builds a whole rival out of one sneeze, the kind of guesswork the verse warns against, though in playful form.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joshua ben Perahiah used to say: appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches giving others the benefit of the doubt.
judaism.tie_back: The wife does the reverse in jest, weighting the scale against her husband over a simple sneeze.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that what we experience is shaped first by the mind that meets it.
buddhism.tie_back: A sneeze is just a sneeze; it is the wife’s loving, anxious mind that turns it into a sign of a rival.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching holds that our passions come not from things themselves but from the love or aversion we bring to them.
jainism.tie_back: The sneeze itself is neutral; the wife’s love turns it, in an instant, from a cause for blessing into a cause for tears.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.101 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Only idiots and fools worry about these omens and days.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Amar Das dismisses worry over omens and auspicious days as foolishness.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife reads a sneeze as a sign that another woman is thinking of her husband; Gurbani rejects reading meaning into such signs.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 843, Raag Bilaaval (Vaar Sat), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, Procris hears that her husband Cephalus, resting after the hunt, keeps calling to ‘Aura’; she takes the word for a woman’s name, though he is only calling to the cooling breeze, and her jealous mistake ends in tragedy.
greek_mythology.explanation: A harmless word, misheard as the name of a rival, sets off a wife’s jealous grief.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife does the same with a harmless sneeze, hearing in it the thoughts of another woman.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza describes ‘vacillation of mind’ as the state in which we are moved by contrary feelings, such as love and hatred, toward the same object at once.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, the mind can be pulled by opposite emotions toward one person in the same moment.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s blessing and her tears, toward the same husband in the same breath, are a lively picture of such vacillation.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Prop. 17 and Scholium (paraphrase)

real_life_example.event_title: Murasaki Shikibu writes The Tale of Genji
real_life_example.event: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady serving at the Japanese imperial court, wrote The Tale of Genji in the early eleventh century; her own diary shows she was writing it in 1008, and she probably completed it about 1010. Most of its 54 chapters concern the loves of the handsome courtier Genji, and each of the women in his life is drawn with great sensitivity. It is often called the world's first novel.
real_life_example.explanation: The work is a landmark of world literature and a detailed record of the emotional lives, including the hurt feelings and suspicions, of lovers at the Heian court.
real_life_example.tie_back: The kural's wife first blesses her husband and then weeps, wondering which other woman is thinking of him, and Murasaki's novel is the classic early portrait of women who must share the attention of one admired man.

tamil:
தும்முச் செறுப்ப அழுதாள் நுமர்உள்ளல்
எம்மை மறைத்திரோ என்று.
transliteration:
Thummuch cheruppa azhudhaal numar-ullal
emmai maraiththiroa endru
meaning: So I held back my sneeze. Then she cried and said, "Are you hiding from me that your people are thinking of you?"
elementary: Imagine you are told off for sneezing, so next time you hold it in, and then you get told off for hiding it! The poor husband cannot win: sneeze or no sneeze, his wife finds something to pretend-cry about.
university: This couplet is the sequel to 1317: afraid of another quarrel, he suppresses (ceṟuppa) his sneeze (tummu), and she weeps, asking whether he is hiding from us (emmai maṟaittirō) the thought of him held by ‘your people’ (numar uḷḷal). Numar (‘your own ones’) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘those dear to you’ and by Solomon Pappaiah as ‘someone you care for’, a veiled hint at another woman. The two couplets together show the ‘subtlety’ of pulavi: every possible response becomes an occasion for sulking. Pope: ‘And so next time I checked my sneeze; she forthwith wept and cried, (that woman difficult to please), “Your thoughts from me you hide.”’ The wording is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, during the rasa dance, Krishna vanishes from the cowherd girls, and they search the forest in anguish, suspecting he has gone off with one favoured companion.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis’ grief springs from a beloved who has hidden himself and from their guess about whom he is with.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife weeps because she thinks her husband is hiding something, and imagines who might be behind it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that what is hidden will come to light.
christianity.tie_back: The wife assumes the same: whatever her husband hides, even a sneeze, must conceal something waiting to come out.

islam.quote_or_event: Aisha said that she was never as jealous of any of the Prophet’s wives as she was of Khadija, because the Prophet used to remember and praise her so often.
islam.explanation: Aisha’s jealousy was stirred not by any rival present, but by someone held in her husband’s memory.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife is jealous in the same way, of whoever might be holding her husband in their thoughts.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is open rebuke than love that is hidden.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs prizes openness, even when it stings, over feelings that are kept concealed.
judaism.tie_back: The wife’s complaint is exactly that her husband is hiding something; she would rather have it out in the open.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one’s own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another’s faults, but hides one’s own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes how quickly we suspect hidden faults in others while overlooking our own.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife imagines her husband hiding behind his held-back sneeze like the fowler behind his branches.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra teaches that anger destroys love, pride destroys humility, deceit destroys friendship, and greed destroys everything.
jainism.explanation: Among the four passions (kashayas), deceit (maya) is singled out as what ruins friendship and trust.
jainism.tie_back: The wife treats her husband’s held-back sneeze as a small deceit, the very thing Jain teaching says erodes intimacy.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 8.38 (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Even without our speaking, He knows everything.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak says the Lord knows our inner state without our telling Him.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife accuses her husband of hiding who is thinking of him; Gurbani reminds that nothing can be hidden from the One who knows every heart.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 661, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, after seeing Thetis plead with Zeus, Hera reproaches him: it is always his pleasure, she says, to plan and decide things in secret, apart from her, and never to tell her his mind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hera’s complaint is not about what Zeus did but about what he kept from her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife makes the same charge over a stifled sneeze: you are hiding your thoughts from me.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld writes that jealousy feeds on doubt, turning into fury or ending as soon as doubt gives way to certainty.
philosophy.explanation: Jealousy, he notes, lives on what is uncertain or hidden.
philosophy.tie_back: The husband’s hidden sneeze gives his wife exactly the doubt on which her playful jealousy feeds.

real_life_example.event_title: The Affair of the Diamond Necklace
real_life_example.event: In 1784 and 1785 the confidence trickster Jeanne de La Motte persuaded Cardinal de Rohan that Queen Marie Antoinette secretly wanted a famous diamond necklace, arranging a night meeting with a woman who impersonated the queen. Rohan obtained the necklace on 1 February 1785 and handed it to La Motte, who disappeared with it. When the jewellers asked for payment the plot came to light, Rohan was arrested at Versailles on 15 August 1785 and acquitted by the Parlement de Paris on 31 May 1786, yet the innocent queen's reputation was badly damaged.
real_life_example.explanation: The affair shows how a secret kept or a story hidden can make an innocent person look guilty in the eyes of others.
real_life_example.tie_back: In this kural the husband holds back even a sneeze to avoid suspicion, only to be accused of hiding something, and Marie Antoinette, who had done nothing, was blamed all the more because the affair seemed to involve secrets.

tamil:
தன்னை உணர்த்தினும் காயும் பிறர்க்கும்நீர்
இந்நீரர் ஆகுதிர் என்று.
transliteration:
Thannai unarththinum kaayum pirarkkum-neer
inneerar aakudhir endru
meaning: Even when I comfort her out of her sulk, she gets angry again and says, "So this is how you sweet-talk other women too!"
elementary: Imagine you finally cheer up a grumpy friend with a funny joke, and she says, ‘Hmph, I bet you tell that joke to everyone!’ Even making up becomes a new reason to tease.
university: Taṉṉai uṇarttiṉum means ‘even if I appease her (end her sulk)’; uṇarttal is the technical term for coaxing a lover out of ūṭal. Yet she grows angry (kāyum), saying piṟarkkum nīr innīrar ākutir (‘you must be like this with others too’). Puliyur Kesikan, Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah agree on this reading, and Kalaignar adds that the husband had humbled himself to win her back. The couplet shows pulavi feeding on its own remedy, the reconciliation itself becoming fresh evidence; Pope: ‘I then began to soothe and coax, to calm her jealous mind; “I see,” quoth she, “to other folks how you are wondrous kind.”’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the tenth canto of the Gita Govinda, Krishna pleads with the angry Radha with tender flattery, begging her to set her foot upon his head as a sign of forgiveness.
hinduism.explanation: Indian love poetry made the lover’s coaxing of a sulking beloved into an art of its own.
hinduism.tie_back: The husband here is doing the same coaxing, but his wife turns even his skill at it into a new charge.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as willing to believe and bear with the other.
christianity.tie_back: The wife plays at refusing to believe even her husband’s reconciliation, the opposite of love that ‘believeth all things’.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if a woman fears from her husband contempt or evasion, there is no sin upon them if they make terms of settlement between them - and settlement is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an counsels husband and wife to settle their differences, declaring reconciliation the better way.
islam.tie_back: The husband offers just such a settlement, and the wife’s refusal to accept it is the comic heart of the couplet.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A soft answer turneth away wrath; but a grievous word stirreth up anger.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that gentle words usually calm anger.
judaism.tie_back: The joke of the Kural is that the husband’s soft answer does not turn away his wife’s wrath, but stirs up a new sulk.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one’s own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges people to stop examining others for faults and look at themselves instead.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife keeps finding fault even in her husband’s kindness, the habit the verse asks us to drop.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the crane is produced from an egg, and the egg is produced from a crane, so they call desire the origin of delusion, and delusion the origin of desire.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching pictures desire and delusion as an endless loop, each producing the other.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s sulking works like that loop: each reconciliation gives birth to a new sulk.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, the Husband Lord enjoys His bride when she is pleasing to His Mind.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that union comes to the soul-bride who pleases the Lord, not to one who frets about others.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife grows angry that her husband must soothe other women the same way; Gurbani turns the bride's attention from rivals to being pleasing herself.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 243, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, when Jupiter hides his love Io by turning her into a heifer, Juno is not soothed by his explanations but asks for the heifer as a gift and sets hundred-eyed Argus to guard her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Juno’s suspicion survives every attempt by her husband to smooth things over.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, will not let her husband’s soothing words put her suspicion to rest.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Terence’s comedy The Girl from Andros, an old man says that the quarrels of lovers are the renewal of love (amantium irae amoris integratio est).
philosophy.explanation: The line, from Roman comic drama rather than philosophy proper, became a proverb for the idea that lovers’ quarrels refresh love.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the spirit of the whole chapter: the wife’s endless mock quarrels keep love lively.
philosophy.source: Terence, Andria 555 (paraphrase of a proverbial line)

real_life_example.event_title: Franz Liszt's years of adulation end his life with Marie d'Agoult
real_life_example.place: Europe (Paris and the Rhine island of Nonnenwerth)
real_life_example.event: Franz Liszt and the Countess Marie d'Agoult lived together in Switzerland and Italy and had three children, but late in 1839 their relationship became strained and she returned to Paris. Liszt then spent about eight years touring Europe, where his concerts caused a sensation and he was received everywhere with great adulation. The couple still spent summers together on the Rhine island of Nonnenwerth until 1844, when their stormy relationship ended in a bitter parting.
real_life_example.explanation: Liszt was the first great celebrity performer, and his story shows how a lover's charm for the whole world can unsettle the person closest to him.
real_life_example.tie_back: The wife in this kural cannot enjoy her husband's coaxing because she thinks he must charm other women the same way, and Marie d'Agoult watched Liszt's charm win over audiences across Europe before their relationship broke apart.

tamil:
நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும் காயும் அனைத்துநீர்
யாருள்ளி நோக்கினீர் என்று.
transliteration:
Ninaiththirundhu noakkinum kaayum anaiththu-neer
yaarulli noakkineer endru
meaning: Even when I just sit and look at her, thinking of her, she gets angry and asks, "Who are you thinking of as you look at me like that?"
elementary: Imagine staring happily at your favourite painting, and your sister asks, ‘Are you comparing it to some other painting?’ The husband just wants to admire his wife, but she pretends he must be comparing her to someone else.
university: Niṉaittiruntu nōkkiṉum means ‘even if I look, having (silently) contemplated’, i.e. gazing at her while dwelling on her beauty; she grows hot (kāyum) and asks yār uḷḷi nōkkiṉīr (‘with whom in mind did you look?’). Aṉaittum is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘all (her features) by comparison’ (ollumaiyāka ellām) and by Solomon Pappaiah as gazing at each of her features, which she takes as matching them against another woman’s. As the chapter’s last couplet it caps the series: speech (1314-1316), sneezing (1317-1318), coaxing (1319), and finally even silent admiration all provoke pulavi. Pope: ‘I silent sat, but thought the more, and gazed on her. Then she cried out, “While thus you eye me o’er, tell me whose form you see.”’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna teases his devoted wife Rukmini by asking why she chose him over more suitable kings; she takes his playful words seriously and is overcome, and he must comfort her.
hinduism.explanation: The scene shows a loving wife reading hurt into her husband’s light-hearted attention.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise reads a slight into her husband’s loving gaze, though here he meant no teasing at all.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song of Songs gazes on his beloved and finds her wholly beautiful, with no comparison to anyone.
christianity.tie_back: This is what the husband is thinking as he gazes, even while his wife pretends he is comparing her to another.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an presents spouses as a source of peace and affection for each other.
islam.tie_back: The husband’s quiet gaze is that tranquil affection; the wife’s mock anger is only a playful ripple on it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My dove, my undefiled, is but one; she is the only one of her mother; she is the choice one of her that bore her.”
judaism.explanation: Surrounded by queens and maidens without number, the lover insists that his beloved is the only one.
judaism.tie_back: The husband’s gaze means just this: there is no one else he is measuring her against.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bhariya Sutta, the Buddha describes seven kinds of wives, among them the ‘friend-wife’, who rejoices on seeing her husband as one friend rejoices at seeing another after a long time.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha holds up a marriage where seeing each other brings simple gladness.
buddhism.tie_back: The husband’s loving gaze invites that gladness, though his wife, in play, answers with suspicion instead.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who passionately hates (a colour), will at the same moment suffer pain. It is the fault of an undisciplined man that he is annoyed (by a colour); it is not the ‘colour’ itself that annoys him.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching places the source of annoyance in the mind of the one annoyed, not in the thing seen.
jainism.tie_back: Nothing in the husband’s gaze is wrong; any annoyance is created by the wife’s own playful mind.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Wherever I look, I see only You. The True Guru has inspired me to see You.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak describes a gaze so filled with the Beloved that he sees Him everywhere.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife asks whom her husband is thinking of as he gazes; in Gurbani the devotee's gaze holds only the Beloved, the very single-mindedness she wants.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 55, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho’s famous poem describes watching the man who sits close to her beloved and listens to her sweet voice, and the overwhelming tumult the sight stirs in the watcher.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poem is antiquity’s classic portrait of gazing, love and jealous turmoil all at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural joins the same elements: a loving gaze and an imagined third person stirring jealousy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates describes the lover who, gazing on the beauty of the beloved, is filled with awe and warmth and wants only to keep looking.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats the lover’s gaze as a wholehearted response to the beauty in front of him.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the husband’s silent gaze in the Kural, wholly fixed on his wife, though she teasingly suspects otherwise.

real_life_example.event_title: Rossetti paints his wife as Dante's Beatrice in Beata Beatrix
real_life_example.event: Dante Gabriel Rossetti married his model Elizabeth Siddal in 1860, and she died in 1862. In the following years he painted Beata Beatrix, now in Tate Britain, in which a figure based on his late wife represents Beatrice, the beloved of the poet Dante, in a dreamlike trance. Britannica notes that the painting shows he saw his love for his wife as like Dante's idealised love for Beatrice.
real_life_example.explanation: The painting is a famous example of an artist gazing at his own wife's features while thinking of a woman from literature.
real_life_example.tie_back: The wife in this kural asks whom her husband is thinking of while he gazes at her, and in Beata Beatrix Rossetti literally looked at his wife's face and painted another woman, Dante's Beatrice.

tamil:
இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு ஆயினும் ஊடுதல்
வல்லது அவர்அளிக்கு மாறு.
transliteration:
Illai thavaravarkku aayinum ootudhal
Valladhu avaralikku maaru.
meaning: Even when he has done nothing wrong, a little sulking can make him show me even more love.
elementary: Sometimes two best friends pretend to be cross for a minute, just so the other one will come and make a fuss over them. Nobody did anything wrong; the little pout simply makes the kindness show. The wife in this poem says a small, pretend quarrel does the same for her husband’s love.
university: The final chapter of the Kural, ūṭal uvakai (‘the joy of lovers’ pique’), turns ūṭal, the feigned or playful sulking of a beloved, from a source of pain in the preceding chapters (pulavi, pulavi nuṇukkam) into a source of delight. Here the wife concedes illai tavaṟu avarkku (‘there is no fault in him’), yet ūṭutal (sulking) is vallatu (‘has the power’) to bring about avar aḷi (his tender grace, aḷi meaning lavish affection). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss the line as ūṭal making him shower greater love on her, and Kalaignar generalises it to lovers on both sides; Pope’s ‘fretful jealousy’ reads the pique more darkly than the Tamil commentators do. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; commentators traditionally assign the opening couplets of the chapter to the wife.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna playfully teases his devoted queen Rukmini by suggesting she would have done better to marry a worthier king; she is so stricken that she faints, and he at once lifts and consoles her, after which their affection is described as all the sweeter.
hinduism.explanation: The episode is the tradition’s classic lovers’ quarrel (praṇaya-kalaha) in which no real wrong has been done, yet the brief hurt brings out an outpouring of tenderness.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife, the quarrel has no fault behind it, and its only result is a greater show of love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs, read in Christian tradition as a love poem and an allegory of divine love, joins love’s strength to the burning intensity of jealousy.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, treats a flare of pique as part of love’s strength rather than a sign that love has failed.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet told Aisha that he could tell when she was pleased with him and when she was cross: when pleased she swore by the Lord of Muhammad, and when cross by the Lord of Abraham. Aisha answered that even then she left out only his name, not her love for him.
islam.explanation: The hadith shows a loving marriage in which small displeasures are noticed, gently teased, and understood as love in disguise.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the wife’s little pique is affectionate rather than hostile, and her husband meets it with fond attention.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah teaches that any love which depends on some particular thing ends when that thing is gone, but love which depends on nothing never ends, giving David and Jonathan as its example.
judaism.explanation: Pirkei Avot distinguishes conditional love from love that needs no cause and therefore cannot be undone.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s couple has such a love: because nothing is wrong, the sulk cannot threaten it and only makes it show.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells a householder that a husband should honour his wife by courtesy, by not despising her, by faithfulness, by handing over authority to her and by giving her adornments, and that she in turn shows him love in her own ways.
buddhism.explanation: The Sigalovada Sutta describes marriage as mutual, attentive regard on both sides.
buddhism.tie_back: The tenderness the Kural’s wife draws out by sulking is the kind of attentive regard the Buddha asks husbands to show.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (tr. Narada Thera; paraphrase)

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra teaches that anger destroys affection, pride destroys humility, deceit destroys friendship, and greed destroys everything.
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics treats anger (krodha) as one of the four passions (kaṣāya) and warns that it ruins love between people.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural claims the opposite for a playful, faultless sulk, which the Jain text would still count as a small stirring of passion.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 8.38 (paraphrase)

sikhism.quote_or_event: “Everyone makes mistakes; only the Guru and the Creator are infallible.”
sikhism.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that every person errs, but the Guru and the Creator are without fault.
sikhism.tie_back: The Kural's wife admits there is no fault in her beloved and sulks anyway; Gurbani's soul-bride likewise knows the faults are all on her side and that the Beloved is faultless.
sikhism.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 61, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pausanias tells how Hera, angry with Zeus, withdrew from him to Euboea; Zeus, unable to win her back, dressed a wooden image as a bride and pretended to be marrying it. Hera rushed to the procession, tore off the veil, found the statue, laughed, and was reconciled to him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Boeotian Daedala festival remembered a divine lovers’ quarrel that ended in laughter and reunion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hera’s withdrawal, like the Kural’s sulk, serves to draw out a wooing that ends in renewed affection.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Terence’s comedy Andria, an old man remarks that the quarrels of lovers are the renewal of love (Latin: amantium irae amoris integratio est).
philosophy.explanation: The line became proverbial in Europe for the idea that a lovers’ quarrel freshens rather than ends their love.
philosophy.tie_back: It is almost a Latin restatement of this couplet’s claim that a faultless sulk draws out greater love.

real_life_example.event_title: Nizami tells how Khosrow pleads at the gate of Shirin's castle
real_life_example.event: The Persian poet Nizami of Ganja wrote the romance Khosrow and Shirin, later counted among the five poems of his Khamsa, about the Sasanian king Khosrow Parviz and the Armenian princess Shirin. In one of its most famous episodes Shirin, displeased with Khosrow's behaviour and his marriage to another woman, withdraws to her castle. After his queen's death Khosrow comes again and again to see her, standing at her gate at dawn in the depth of winter, until Shirin finally yields and the lovers are reconciled.
real_life_example.explanation: The scene became one of the most painted subjects in Persian art, a classic image of a beloved's withdrawal drawing out a lover's humble and devoted pleading.
real_life_example.tie_back: This kural says a little sulking has the power to draw out more of a lover's tenderness, and Shirin's retreat to her castle draws from King Khosrow the most devoted pleading of the whole romance.

tamil:
ஊடலின் தோன்றும் சிறுதுனி நல்லளி
வாடினும் பாடு பெறும்.
transliteration:
Oodalin thoandrum sirudhuni nallali
Vaatinum paadu perum.
meaning: The small pain that a lovers' sulk brings may make his kindness droop for a while, but it will come back even stronger.
elementary: A plant that is not watered for one day droops a little, and when you water it again it seems to stand up even taller. A short, small quarrel is like that: love looks a little wilted for a moment, then bounces back stronger.
university: The couplet sets ciṟu tuṉi (‘a small distress’, tuṉi meaning grief or estrangement) arising from ūṭal against nal aḷi (‘good tender love’), which may vāṭiṉum (‘even if it should wither’, a plant metaphor) yet pāṭu peṟum (‘will gain greatness’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take aḷi as the husband’s love that seems to fade during the sulk and then grows in worth; Puliyur Kesikan adds pinnar (‘afterwards’), making the gain explicitly temporal, and Pope renders the sense as feigned anger making drooping affection ‘bloom again’. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the same text; the botanical verb vāṭu (to wilt) is characteristic of the Kural’s Inbam imagery.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Rasa-lila of the Bhagavata Purana, when the gopis grow proud of Krishna’s attention he suddenly vanishes; they search the forest for him in anguish, and when he reappears their joy and his tenderness are greater than before.
hinduism.explanation: The tradition presents a brief separation within love as a way of deepening it.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a short spell in which love seems to wilt ends with that love shining more brightly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows anger but sets it a short limit, so that it ends before it can harden.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s sulk is a short, harmless anger of exactly this kind, ending before it does damage.
